subjects.title: License Law and Regulations
subjects.blurb: Who needs a license, how you get and keep one, and the DOS rules that end careers when broken. Expect a steady stream of exam items on escrow, ads, net listings, penalties, and who can be paid.

lessons.title: Who Needs a License, and How You Keep It
lessons.tagline: A license is permission from the State to handle other people's real estate deals. Lose track of the rules and you lose the permission.
objectives: Explain why New York licenses brokers and salespersons and who runs the system
Compare broker, associate broker, and salesperson duties and education requirements
Identify acts that require a license and the people exempt from licensing
Describe how a license is held, changed, transferred, renewed, and kept current with CE

blocks.title: Jackson Heights, a favor between friends
blocks.html: Before Jordan's license came through, a neighbor asked Jordan to find a tenant for her basement apartment on 84th Street. "I'll give you half a month's rent, cash, for your trouble." Jordan found a nurse from Elmhurst Hospital in two days. The neighbor is happy. Is Jordan?
blocks.casual: So Jordan's license hasn't come through yet. A neighbor on 84th Street says, "Find me a tenant for the basement and I'll give you half a month's rent, cash." Two days later Jordan has a nurse from Elmhurst Hospital signed up. Neighbor's thrilled. Jordan's got cash in hand. Feels like a win, right? Hold that thought.

deeper.plain: Doing a real estate job for someone else and getting paid for it is exactly what the license is for. Being friendly about it doesn't change that.
deeper.picture: It's like cutting your cousin's hair for twenty bucks in your kitchen. Once money changes hands for a licensed service, the State cares whether you're licensed.
deeper.street: Say the basement rents for $1,800. Jordan pockets $900. A month later the tenant and landlord fight over a leak, the landlord gets annoyed, and she remembers that Jordan wasn't licensed. Now she can demand the fee back and then some.
deeper.stakes: Jordan's real career hasn't even started and there's already a misdemeanor exposure and a fee that can be clawed back. DOS also asks about past conduct on applications, so a sloppy favor can follow you.
deeper.exam: Stems that mention a "favor", "friend", or "neighbor" plus any payment are testing whether you spot unlicensed activity. If there's a fee and it's for another person, the answer is a license was required.

blocks.text: Why New York licenses real estate agents

blocks.html: Real estate deals move huge sums through people who are not the owners. The licensing law exists to protect the public: it screens who may act for others, sets minimum education, and gives the State a way to discipline people who cheat. It does not exist to protect licensees from competition.
blocks.casual: Here's the thing about real estate: huge money moves through people who don't own the property. So the licensing law is there to protect the public. It decides who's allowed to act for others, makes sure they've had at least some training, and gives the State a stick to discipline people who cheat. What it's not there for is keeping out competition so licensees make more money.

deeper.plain: The license exists so regular people handing over deposits and signing deals are dealing with someone screened and accountable.
deeper.picture: Think of the health grade in a restaurant window. It's not there to help the restaurant beat the food truck. It's there so you don't get sick.
deeper.street: The Okafors are selling a Bed-Stuy brownstone they've owned 28 years. They'll trust an agent with a $150,000 deposit conversation and their biggest asset. The license means that agent passed a course and an exam, and that DOS can yank the license if the agent lies to them.
deeper.stakes: Forget the purpose and you'll misread the rules. Every license rule, from escrow to disclosure, makes sense once you ask "how does this protect the consumer?"
deeper.exam: If a question asks the purpose of license law, pick "protect the public." The distractor is "protect licensees" or "limit competition," and both are wrong.

blocks.html: The law is Article 12-A of the Real Property Law (RPL sections 440 to 442-k). The Department of State (DOS), Division of Licensing Services, administers it and writes the regulations in 19 NYCRR Part 175 (conduct) and Part 176 (education).
blocks.casual: The rulebook is Article 12-A of the Real Property Law, sections 440 to 442-k. The Department of State (DOS), through its Division of Licensing Services, runs it. DOS also writes the detailed regs: 19 NYCRR Part 175 covers how you behave, Part 176 covers your education.

deeper.plain: The legislature wrote the main law, and DOS fills in the details with regulations and enforces both.
deeper.picture: The law is the rules of baseball. The regulations are the umpire's handbook. DOS is the umpire who can throw you out of the game.
deeper.street: When Marcus gets a complaint for a sloppy escrow deposit, the letter comes from DOS citing Part 175, not from the legislature. Part 176 is what told Jordan's school how many hours to teach and how to proctor the final.
deeper.stakes: If you quote the wrong source to a client or a broker, you look green. Knowing that conduct rules live in Part 175 helps you look up the actual rule before you act.
deeper.exam: Cue words: "Article 12-A," "RPL 440," "administers." The answer is the Department of State. Part 175 is conduct, Part 176 is education. Don't flip them.

blocks.title: Who is in charge
blocks.html: Licensing, exams, complaints, and discipline: NYS Department of State. Not HCR, not the Attorney General (the AG prosecutes crimes), not the local Board of Realtors. A Realtor association is a private trade group with no power to license anyone.
blocks.casual: Who runs the show? Licensing, exams, complaints and discipline all sit with the NYS Department of State. Not HCR. Not the Attorney General (the AG goes after crimes). Not your local Board of Realtors. A Realtor association is a private trade group. It can kick you out of its club, but it can't license or unlicense anybody.

deeper.plain: Only DOS can give you a license or take it away.
deeper.picture: Your gym can cancel your membership, but only the DMV can take your driver's license. The Realtor board is the gym. DOS is the DMV.
deeper.street: A buyer in Park Slope is furious that Marcus hid a leak. She files with the Brooklyn Board of Realtors and DOS. The board can expel Marcus from membership. Only DOS can suspend his license or fine him, and if there's fraud, a prosecutor or the AG might get involved separately.
deeper.stakes: Tell a client to complain to the wrong agency and nothing happens to the bad actor. And don't assume a trade group's rules are the law; they're private ethics codes.
deeper.exam: Distractors love HCR (rent regulation), the Attorney General, and the "local Board of Realtors." For anything about licensing or discipline of licensees, the answer is DOS.

head: Salesperson
Associate broker
Broker
rows: 2 years licensed salesperson (3,500 points) or 3 years general real estate (5,250 points), or a mix
No. Must be sponsored by a broker
No. Chooses to work under a sponsoring broker
blocks.caption: Exam: $15 per attempt, 75 questions, 90 minutes, 70% to pass, results good for 2 years.

deeper.plain: Salesperson is the entry license and always works under a broker. A broker runs the business. An associate broker is broker-qualified but chooses to work under someone else.
deeper.picture: Think of a restaurant. The salesperson is a line cook, the associate broker is a sous chef who could open a place but doesn't, and the broker is the owner whose name is on the permit.
deeper.street: Jordan, 23, took the 77 hours and passed the exam. In two years with 3,500 points, Jordan can take the 75-hour broker course. Diane, the principal broker, holds the $185 license and every paycheck at Hudson & Hart flows through her.
deeper.stakes: A salesperson who takes a check directly from a client, or works without a sponsoring broker, is breaking the law even with a valid license. The money path matters as much as the license.
deeper.exam: Watch the numbers: 18 vs 20, 77 vs 152, $65 vs $185. The exam itself is $15 per try, 75 questions, 90 minutes, 70% to pass, and results last 2 years.

blocks.html: A real estate broker is responsible to the public (honesty, escrow, disclosures) and to every licensee they sponsor (training and supervision). An associate real estate broker has a broker's qualifications but works under another broker, often as an office manager. A real estate salesperson owes duties to the sponsoring broker (follow office policy, turn over all money and documents) and to the public (honesty, disclosures, fair housing).
blocks.casual: Who owes what to whom? A real estate broker answers to the public (honesty, escrow, disclosures) and to every licensee they sponsor (training and supervision). An associate real estate broker has everything a broker needs but works under another broker, often as the office manager. A real estate salesperson owes the sponsoring broker (follow office policy, hand over all money and documents) and the public (honesty, disclosures, fair housing).

deeper.plain: Everyone owes honesty to the public. The broker also owes supervision downward, and the salesperson owes obedience upward.
deeper.picture: It's a chain of custody. Anything that comes into a salesperson's hands, money or paper, passes up to the broker, and responsibility for the salesperson passes down from the broker.
deeper.street: A buyer hands Jordan a $20,000 deposit check at a showing in Crown Heights. Jordan doesn't hold onto it or deposit it personally. It goes to Diane's office the same day, because the broker is the one accountable for escrow.
deeper.stakes: Hang onto client money or paperwork and you've broken your duty to the broker and possibly committed conversion. The broker can also get disciplined for failing to supervise you.
deeper.exam: Questions ask who is responsible for supervising, or to whom a salesperson must turn over funds. Answer: the sponsoring broker. An associate broker works under a broker even though they could be one.

blocks.caption: Follow the salesperson path: 77 hours, school final, state exam, sponsoring broker, application, then 22.5 hours of CE every 2 years.

blocks.title: 75 or 77?
blocks.html: The qualifying course has been 77 hours since December 21, 2022 (it was 75). Old practice tests still say 75. Answer 77 for the salesperson course. The broker course is 75 hours, which is how you get 152.
blocks.casual: Heads up on a number trap. The salesperson qualifying course is 77 hours, and has been since December 21, 2022. It used to be 75. Old practice tests still say 75. For the salesperson course, answer 77. The broker course is the one that's 75 hours, which is how 77 plus 75 gets you to 152.

deeper.plain: Salesperson course: 77. Broker course: 75. Together: 152.
deeper.picture: It's like a phone number that changed area code. Old business cards still show the old one, but calling it gets you nowhere.
deeper.street: Leo's cousin passed in 2021 and swears the course is 75 hours. He's remembering the old rule. Jordan, who started in 2025, sat for 77, including the extra hours on topics like implicit bias and fair housing.
deeper.stakes: Get this wrong while advising someone thinking about the career and you look out of date. On the exam it's a free point you'd be throwing away.
deeper.exam: If answer choices include both 75 and 77 for the salesperson course, pick 77. If the question asks for the broker course alone, 75 is right. Total broker education is 152.

blocks.q: Dana is a fully broker-qualified licensee who wants to manage a branch office for someone else's firm rather than open her own. Which license fits?
c: Salesperson
Associate broker
Broker of record
Apartment information vendor
blocks.x: An associate broker meets broker requirements but chooses to work under a sponsoring broker. A broker license is for someone who runs their own brokerage.

blocks.html: Under RPL 440 you need a license if, for another person and for a fee (or the expectation of one), you do any of these with real estate or co-op shares:
blocks.casual: RPL 440 is the trigger. You need a license if you do any of the following with real estate or co-op shares for another person and for a fee (or even the expectation of one):

deeper.plain: Two things together trigger the license: you're acting for someone else, and you expect to get paid.
deeper.picture: Picture two light switches. Flip only one and nothing turns on. Flip "for another" and "for a fee" together and the license requirement lights up.
deeper.street: Sal sells his own Astoria six-family himself: no license needed, it's his. Sal's nephew helps for free as a favor: no fee, no license. The nephew says, "Give me 2% if it closes": now he needs one.
deeper.stakes: A promise of payment later counts. People get burned thinking they're fine because they hadn't been paid yet. The expectation of a fee is enough.
deeper.exam: Cue words "for another" and "for a fee or valuable consideration." Remember co-op shares count as real estate here even though legally they're personal property.

items: List, sell, buy, or exchange
Lease or rent, or offer to
Negotiate any of the above
Collect rents (that is property management)
Negotiate a loan secured by real estate (mortgage brokering is now separately licensed by DFS)
Sell or rent information about apartments (that needs an apartment information vendor license)
blocks.casual: The licensed activities: listing, selling, buying or exchanging; leasing or renting, or even offering to; negotiating any of that; collecting rents (that's property management); negotiating a loan secured by real estate (though mortgage brokering is now separately licensed by DFS); and selling or renting information about apartments, which needs its own apartment information vendor license.

deeper.plain: Most hands-on deal work for others is covered, including just negotiating or collecting rent.
deeper.picture: Anything where you stand between an owner and a stranger and help money and keys change hands is in the license zone.
deeper.street: Tasha arranges mortgages, so she's licensed by DFS, not DOS, for that work. Sal hires someone to collect rent from his six units for a percentage: that person needs a real estate license. A website charging renters for listings in Washington Heights needs an apartment information vendor license.
deeper.stakes: Property managers who collect rents without a broker license are a classic violation. So are "rental finders" who sell lists without the vendor license.
deeper.exam: Collecting rents for others is on the list; people forget it. Offering to rent counts too, even if no deal happens. Mortgage brokering points to DFS, not DOS.

blocks.html: Back to the scenario. Jordan, unlicensed, found a tenant for another person for half a month's rent. That is unlicensed brokerage: a misdemeanor, and the neighbor could sue to recover up to four times the fee. The fix: never take money for a deal until licensed and sponsored, and then only through the broker.
blocks.casual: Back to Jordan. Unlicensed, Jordan found a tenant for someone else and took half a month's rent. That's unlicensed brokerage, a misdemeanor, and the neighbor could sue to get back up to four times the fee. The fix is simple: don't take money for a deal until you're licensed and sponsored, and then only through your broker.

deeper.plain: Jordan broke the law, and the person who paid can sue to get back much more than the fee.
deeper.picture: It's like being paid for a delivery in a car with no registration. The job got done, but you're on the hook for how you did it.
deeper.street: Rent is $2,000, so Jordan took $1,000. Under RPL 442-e the neighbor could sue for up to four times that, $4,000. Even once licensed, Jordan has to route any fee through Diane at Hudson & Hart.
deeper.stakes: Criminal exposure, a civil penalty, and a mark DOS may weigh when deciding on the license application. All for a favor fee.
deeper.exam: Penalty facts: unlicensed activity is a misdemeanor, and the payer may recover up to 4 times the fee. Distractors offer "felony" or "double the fee."

blocks.html: An exemption means the person can do the act without a license. Know these cold:
blocks.casual: An exemption just means that person can do the thing without a license. Learn these cold:

deeper.plain: Some people can do real estate acts without a license because they're the owner, a lawyer, a public official, or acting under a court's authority.
deeper.picture: It's like the rule that you need a permit to fish, except on your own pond. The exemption covers a specific person in a specific role, not everyone nearby.
deeper.street: Priya, a NY attorney, negotiates a sale for a client in Downtown Brooklyn. No broker license needed. If she hires two people to show apartments for her firm, she now needs a broker license.
deeper.stakes: People stretch exemptions past their edges. A building super who rents units for the owner's other buildings for a cut isn't the owner, so he isn't exempt.
deeper.exam: The trap is always the catch in each row. Attorney yes, attorney with salespersons no. Owner yes, owner's employee doing it as a business for others no.

head: Exempt person
The catch
rows: Owners dealing with their own property
An owner's employee doing it as a business for others is not covered
An attorney who hires salespersons needs a broker license
People acting under a court order: receivers, referees, executors, administrators, guardians
The authority comes from the court
Tenants associations and nonprofits acting for members

deeper.plain: Each exemption is narrow. It covers the person in that role and nothing more.
deeper.picture: An exemption is a backstage pass for one show. Wander into another venue and security stops you.
deeper.street: An executor sells her late uncle's Flatbush house under authority from the Surrogate's Court: exempt. A tenants association on the Grand Concourse helps members find a sublet without charging the public: exempt. A town assessor showing land as part of an official auction: exempt, but only on the job.
deeper.stakes: Overreading an exemption leads to unlicensed activity, the misdemeanor, and fee clawbacks. When in doubt, the person isn't exempt.
deeper.exam: Common exempt list: owners, NY attorneys, public officers, court-appointed people (receivers, referees, executors, administrators, guardians). Not exempt: an unlicensed assistant, a building super working for a fee, an out-of-state lawyer.

blocks.title: Related licenses are separate
blocks.html: A real estate appraiser (Executive Law Article 6-E) and a home inspector (RPL Article 12-B) are also licensed by DOS, but under different laws. Your salesperson license does not let you appraise or inspect, and you may never call a CMA an appraisal.
blocks.casual: Don't mix these up. A real estate appraiser (Executive Law Article 6-E) and a home inspector (RPL Article 12-B) are licensed by DOS too, but under separate laws. Your salesperson license doesn't let you appraise or inspect anything. And never, ever call a CMA an appraisal.

deeper.plain: Same agency, different licenses. Being a salesperson doesn't make you an appraiser or an inspector.
deeper.picture: Same hospital, different badges. A nurse can't perform surgery just because she works down the hall from the OR.
deeper.street: Leo asks Jordan to "appraise" a Sunnyside condo. Jordan can run a CMA showing recent sales, but has to call it a CMA. Ray, the licensed inspector, is the one who checks the boiler and points at the beams.
deeper.stakes: Calling a CMA an appraisal is misrepresentation. A buyer who relied on it can complain to DOS, and a lender won't accept it anyway.
deeper.exam: Watch for answers saying a salesperson may perform an appraisal "for a fee" or "if supervised." Wrong. Appraisers fall under Executive Law 6-E, inspectors under RPL 12-B.

blocks.html: Two niche DOS licenses show up on the exam. An apartment information vendor sells lists of available rentals for a fee. It holds a one-year license, keeps a trust account (at least $5,000), may not charge more than one month's rent, and must refund the advance fee (less up to $15) if the customer does not rent through its information. An apartment sharing agent matches people who want to share housing (trust account at least $2,500). Neither license lets anyone negotiate leases.
blocks.casual: Two oddball DOS licenses show up on the exam. An apartment information vendor sells lists of available rentals for a fee. It gets a one-year license, keeps a trust account of at least $5,000, can't charge more than one month's rent, and has to refund the advance fee (less up to $15) if the customer doesn't rent through its info. An apartment sharing agent matches people who want to share housing, with a trust account of at least $2,500. Neither one can negotiate leases.

deeper.plain: These licenses cover selling rental info or roommate matching. They don't let you act as a broker.
deeper.picture: A vendor is like a paid tip sheet at the racetrack. It tells you which horses are running; it can't place your bet.
deeper.street: A renter pays a Washington Heights listing service $200 up front. She ends up renting through a friend instead. The vendor must refund her fee, keeping at most $15.
deeper.stakes: A vendor that starts negotiating lease terms is doing unlicensed brokerage. One that won't refund is violating its license and draining a trust account meant to protect renters.
deeper.exam: Numbers to separate: vendor trust account $5,000, sharing agent $2,500, refund less up to $15, one-year license. Neither may negotiate.

blocks.q: Which person needs a real estate license?
c: A NY attorney closing a sale for a client
An executor selling a house under a court's letters testamentary
A property manager collecting rent for three different owners for a percentage fee
A homeowner selling her own Staten Island colonial
blocks.x: Collecting rent for others for a fee is licensed activity. The attorney, the court-appointed executor, and the owner selling her own home are all exempt.

blocks.title: Life of a license

items.title: Issued
items.html: DOS issues the license; the sponsoring broker keeps salesperson and associate broker licenses on file at the office. The broker's own license is displayed conspicuously in the office.

items.title: Carried
items.html: You carry a pocket card and must show it on request. It proves you are licensed and with which broker.

items.title: Changed
items.html: Changes of name, address, or status (for example salesperson to associate broker) are filed with DOS, mostly through eAccessNY. A broker who moves the office notifies DOS and updates every associated licensee.

items.title: Branched
items.html: Each branch office needs its own DOS branch license ($185) and must be supervised by the broker or an associate broker acting as manager. The branch license is displayed at the branch.

items.title: Renewed
items.html: Every 2 years: renewal fee, CE completed, and (for brokers) affirmation of the standardized operating procedures.

blocks.casual:
Here's a license's life. Issued: DOS issues it, and your sponsoring broker keeps salesperson and associate broker licenses on file at the office. The broker's own license hangs conspicuously on the wall.
Carried: you carry a pocket card and show it when asked. It proves you're licensed and who your broker is.
Changed: name, address or status changes (like salesperson to associate broker) get filed with DOS, mostly in eAccessNY. If the broker moves offices, the broker tells DOS and updates everyone attached.
Branched: every branch office needs its own DOS branch license ($185), supervised by the broker or an associate broker acting as manager, and displayed at the branch.
Renewed: every 2 years: fee, CE done, and for brokers, affirming the standardized operating procedures.

deeper.plain: A license gets issued, carried, updated, extended to branches, and renewed every two years.
deeper.picture: It's like a car: you get the title, keep the registration card in the glovebox, update the DMV when you move, and renew on schedule.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart opens a second office in Bay Ridge. Diane pays $185 for a branch license, posts it there, and names an associate broker as manager. Jordan, now at Bay Ridge, still carries the pocket card naming Hudson & Hart.
deeper.stakes: An unlicensed branch, or a branch with no qualified manager, is a violation for the broker. Forgetting to update an address can mean missing DOS notices.
deeper.exam: Who displays what: broker's license displayed in the office; salesperson's license kept by the broker; pocket card carried by the licensee. Branch license fee $185.

blocks.html: When a salesperson leaves, the old broker files a termination of association with DOS and the salesperson cannot act as an agent while unattached. The new broker files a change of association. Only after the new association is on file may the salesperson work. Listings belong to the broker, not the salesperson, so they stay behind.
blocks.casual: When a salesperson leaves, the old broker files a termination of association with DOS, and you can't act as an agent while you're unattached. Then the new broker files a change of association. Only once that's on file can you work again. And the listings? They belong to the broker, not you, so they stay put.

deeper.plain: Between brokers, you can't work. And your listings don't come with you.
deeper.picture: Switching teams mid-season: you can't play until the league records the trade, and the jersey stays with the old team.
deeper.street: Marcus storms out of Hudson & Hart on Friday and wants to take his three Clinton Hill listings to a new firm Monday. Those listings belong to Diane. Until the new broker's change of association is filed, Marcus can't show a single apartment.
deeper.stakes: Working while unattached is unlicensed activity. Walking off with listings invites a lawsuit from the old broker and complaints from confused sellers.
deeper.exam: "Who owns the listing?" The broker. "Can a salesperson work while the change is pending?" No.

blocks.html: Dual licensure: New York allows a licensee to be associated with more than one broker, or to hold a broker license while also associated with another broker, as long as each broker knows and agrees in writing. Commission still flows only through the broker on each deal.
blocks.casual: Dual licensure is allowed in New York. You can be associated with more than one broker, or hold a broker license while also associated with another broker, as long as each broker knows and agrees in writing. The money still only flows through the broker on each deal.

deeper.plain: You can hang your license with two brokers if both agree in writing.
deeper.picture: It's like working two restaurant jobs with both managers' blessing. Each one pays you for the shifts you work there.
deeper.street: Priya's paralegal friend is licensed with a Manhattan rental firm and a Queens sales firm. Both brokers sign off. When she closes a rental in Murray Hill, the commission goes through the Manhattan broker only.
deeper.stakes: Doing it without written consent, or getting paid by the wrong broker, can lead to discipline and commission fights.
deeper.exam: Key condition: written knowledge and consent of each broker. Payment always comes from the broker on that transaction, never directly from a client.

blocks.html: Nonresident licensees must file an irrevocable consent with DOS, agreeing that lawsuits arising from NY business can be served on the Secretary of State on their behalf. It makes out-of-state licensees answerable in New York courts.
blocks.casual: If you're licensed but live out of state, you file an irrevocable consent with DOS. You're agreeing that lawsuits from your New York business can be served on the Secretary of State for you. Bottom line: out-of-state licensees can be dragged into New York courts.

deeper.plain: Nonresidents agree in advance that New York can sue them through the Secretary of State.
deeper.picture: It's like leaving a spare key with the building super so you can't dodge a package delivery by being out of town.
deeper.street: A New Jersey broker lists a Staten Island two-family. The buyer later sues over a hidden defect. Because of the irrevocable consent, the papers go to the Secretary of State in Albany and the NJ broker can't argue NY courts have no reach.
deeper.stakes: Nonresidents can't hide across the river. Consumers get a way to hold them accountable here.
deeper.exam: Cue: "nonresident" or "out-of-state licensee." Answer: irrevocable consent, service on the Secretary of State.

blocks.q: Marcus quits Hudson & Hart on Friday and joins a Manhattan firm on Monday. When may he start showing apartments for the new firm?
c: Immediately, his license is still valid
When the new broker files the change of association with DOS
After 30 days
After he retakes the state exam
blocks.x: A salesperson must be associated with a sponsoring broker on DOS records to act. The license stays valid, but he cannot work until the change of association is filed.

blocks.html: Continuing education: 22.5 hours every 2-year term, for salespersons and brokers alike. Inside those hours:
blocks.casual: Continuing education: 22.5 hours every 2-year term, same for salespersons and brokers. Here's what has to be inside those hours:

deeper.plain: To renew, you need 22.5 hours of classes every two years, with some required topics.
deeper.picture: It's like a gym membership with mandatory classes: you choose most of your workouts, but some sessions are on the schedule no matter what.
deeper.street: Jordan's license runs two years. Around month 20, Jordan books 22.5 hours online, making sure fair housing, implicit bias, cultural competency, ethics, legal updates and agency are all in there.
deeper.stakes: Missing CE means you can't renew. Work after expiration and you're acting unlicensed, and your broker shares the violation.
deeper.exam: 22.5 hours, every 2 years, salespersons and brokers alike. Distractors: 22 hours, every year, or brokers exempt.

deeper.plain: Of the 22.5 hours, 11.5 are assigned topics (12.5 on your first renewal), and you pick the rest.
deeper.picture: Like a prix fixe dinner: a few courses are set, then you fill the rest from the menu.
deeper.street: Jordan's first renewal: 3 fair housing, 2 implicit bias, 2 cultural competency, 2.5 ethics, 1 recent legal matters, 2 agency. That's 12.5, so 10 elective hours. Diane's later renewals need only 1 agency hour, leaving 11 electives.
deeper.stakes: Take 22.5 hours of electives and skip a required topic and DOS won't accept the renewal. That's a renewal you have to redo.
deeper.exam: The odd one: agency is 2 hours the first renewal, 1 after. Ethics is 2.5. Implicit bias and cultural competency are 2 each.

blocks.title: Old exemptions are gone
blocks.html: Older books say brokers licensed 15 years were exempt from CE. That exemption ended in 2021. Today only NY attorneys are exempt. The 2 hours each of implicit bias and cultural competency apply to terms expiring on or after September 21, 2022.
blocks.casual: Old books say brokers licensed 15 years didn't need CE. That's gone, it ended in 2021. Now only NY attorneys are exempt. And the 2 hours each of implicit bias and cultural competency apply to terms expiring on or after September 21, 2022.

deeper.plain: No more veteran exemption. Only New York attorneys skip CE.
deeper.picture: Like a frequent-flier perk that got cancelled. Some people still talk about it, but it doesn't work at the counter.
deeper.street: Diane has been a broker for 30 years. Under the old rule she'd have been exempt. Now she sits through the same 22.5 hours as Jordan. Priya, a NY attorney, doesn't have to.
deeper.stakes: A veteran broker who skips CE thinking they're grandfathered ends up with an expired license and every deal they touch at risk.
deeper.exam: If the answer choices include "brokers with 15 years" as exempt, that's the old rule. Pick NY attorneys.

blocks.html: The sponsoring broker is responsible for the salesperson's conduct, supervision, and record keeping. A broker who lets a salesperson keep working with a lapsed license shares the violation.
blocks.casual: Your sponsoring broker is on the hook for your conduct, supervision and record keeping. If a broker lets a salesperson keep working on a lapsed license, the broker shares the violation.

deeper.plain: Your mistakes can become your broker's mistakes.
deeper.picture: A driving instructor in the passenger seat with their own brake. If the student crashes, the instructor answers for it too.
deeper.street: Marcus's license lapsed in March and he kept showing apartments in April. Diane knew and let it slide. DOS can discipline both of them.
deeper.stakes: Brokers face fines or suspension for weak supervision. That's why good brokers track every salesperson's expiration date.
deeper.exam: Supervision questions point to the sponsoring broker. A broker who "knew or should have known" shares liability.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: 18 / 77 / 22.5 / 2. Age 18, 77 hours, 22.5 CE hours, every 2 years. Broker: 20 / 152 / 2 years.
blocks.casual: Memorize this: 18 / 77 / 22.5 / 2. Age 18, 77 hours, 22.5 CE hours, every 2 years. For broker: 20 / 152 / 2 years.

deeper.plain: Four numbers for a salesperson, three for a broker.
deeper.picture: Say it like a combination lock: 18, 77, 22.5, 2. Then a second lock for broker: 20, 152, 2.
deeper.street: Jordan wrote "18/77/22.5/2" on a sticky note on the laptop and "20/152/2" underneath for later. By exam day it was automatic.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up these numbers costs easy points and makes you sound unprepared when friends ask how to get licensed.
deeper.exam: Expect several questions asking just one of these numbers. The distractors are usually the neighboring number: 75 for 77, 18 for 20, 22 for 22.5.

story.title: Half a Month's Rent
story.setting: Hudson & Hart Realty, Brooklyn, Jordan's first Monday

beats.text: Jordan arrives early, coffee in hand, ready to confess something.
So, before I was licensed, I found my neighbor a tenant. She gave me $800.
Did she. For another person, for a fee, renting real estate. Tell me which of those three wasn't true.
beats.tag: For another + for a fee = license needed

beats.text: All three were true.
Then it was unlicensed activity. A misdemeanor, and she could sue you for up to four times that $800. Give it back and don't do it again.
beats.tag: Unlicensed fee: up to 4x civil penalty

check.q: What is the most Jordan's neighbor could recover in a civil suit over the $800?
check.x: RPL 442-e lets an aggrieved person recover between the amount received and four times it. Four times $800 is $3,200.

beats.text: Relax, kid. Lawyers sell houses without licenses all the time.
Lawyers admitted in New York are exempt. You are not a lawyer, Marcus. And a lawyer who hires salespeople needs a broker license.
Where's my license? Do I frame it?
I keep your license on file here. You carry the pocket card and show it when anyone asks. Mine hangs on the wall.
beats.tag: Broker holds salesperson license; you carry the pocket card

beats.text: And if you ever leave, you can take your listings with you.
Listings belong to the broker. And you can't work a single day until your new broker files the change of association.
Got it. Renew every two years?
With 22.5 hours of CE. Three of fair housing, two implicit bias, two cultural competency, two and a half ethics, one recent legal matters, and two of agency on your first renewal.

check.q: How many agency hours does Jordan need for the first renewal?
c: None
check.x: The law of agency requirement is 2 hours on the first renewal and 1 hour after that.

beats.text: The license exists to protect the public, Jordan. Every rule in this office traces back to that sentence.

board.prompt: Draw the path from 'curious about real estate' to 'first renewal'. Put the number (age, hours, fees, years) on each step.

facts.text: The license law exists to protect the public, not to shield licensees from competition.
The license law is RPL Article 12-A (sections 440 to 442-k); DOS rules are 19 NYCRR Part 175 (conduct) and Part 176 (education).
The Department of State licenses and disciplines licensees; not HCR, the Attorney General, or a Realtor association.
A salesperson must be at least 18 and complete the 77-hour course (75 before December 21, 2022), and must be sponsored by a broker.
A broker must be at least 20, complete 152 hours (77 + 75), and have 2 years as a salesperson (3,500 points) or 3 years in general real estate (5,250 points).
An associate broker is broker-qualified but chooses to work under a sponsoring broker, often as an office manager.
The state exam costs $15, has 75 questions in 90 minutes, needs 70% to pass, and results are good for 2 years.
A 2-year license costs $65 for a salesperson and $185 for a broker or associate broker.
A license is needed to list, sell, buy, exchange, lease, negotiate or collect rents for another for a fee; doing it unlicensed is a misdemeanor.
Exempt: owners with their own property, NY attorneys, public officers on duty, people acting under court order, and tenants associations or nonprofits for members.
An attorney who hires salespersons needs a broker license.
Appraisers (Executive Law 6-E) and home inspectors (RPL 12-B) are licensed separately; a salesperson may not call a CMA an appraisal.
An apartment information vendor holds a one-year license, keeps a $5,000 trust account, and refunds the fee less up to $15 if the customer does not rent through it.
An apartment sharing agent matches people who want to share housing (trust account $2,500); neither niche license allows negotiating leases.
The sponsoring broker keeps salesperson and associate broker licenses at the office; the broker's own license is displayed.
Licensees carry a DOS pocket card and must show it on request.
Each branch office needs its own license and a broker or associate broker as manager.
Name, address and status changes are filed with DOS, mostly through eAccessNY; renewal is every 2 years, and brokers affirm their SOPs at renewal.

When a salesperson changes brokers, the old broker files a termination and the new broker a change of association; the salesperson may not act until it is filed, and listings stay with the old broker.
A licensee may be associated with more than one broker if each broker knows and agrees in writing.
Nonresident licensees file an irrevocable consent letting NY lawsuits be served on the Secretary of State.
Continuing education is 22.5 hours every 2-year term for salespersons and brokers.
CE includes 3 hours fair housing, 2 implicit bias, 2 cultural competency, 2.5 ethics, 1 recent legal matters, and 1 agency (2 on the first renewal).
Only NY attorneys are exempt from CE; the old 15-year broker exemption is gone.
The sponsoring broker is responsible for its salespersons and shares the violation if one works with a lapsed license.

lessons.title: DOS Rules, Ads, Disclosures, and Discipline
lessons.tagline: Most licensees who lose their license do it over money, ads, or paperwork. Here is the short list of how not to.
objectives: Apply the key Part 175 rules: escrow, commingling, net listings, records, supervision, kickbacks, and compensation
Spot an advertising violation, including blind ads and illegal team names
Describe what unlicensed assistants may and may not do
Explain the PCDS (post-March 2024), uncapped gas well disclosure, stigmatized property, and standardized operating procedures
Match violations to penalties, from reprimand to misdemeanor, and know how to appeal

blocks.title: Park Slope, deposit day
blocks.html: A buyer hands Marcus a $25,000 good-faith deposit check on a Thursday night. The firm's escrow account is at a bank across town, so Marcus deposits it into his personal checking "just until Monday." He also posts an Instagram ad that says "Gorgeous 3BR, call Marcus" with his cell number and nothing else. How many rules did Marcus break before the weekend?
blocks.casual: Thursday night in Park Slope. A buyer hands Marcus a $25,000 good-faith deposit check. The firm's escrow account is at a bank across town, so Marcus drops it in his personal checking "just till Monday." Same night he posts an Instagram ad: "Gorgeous 3BR, call Marcus," his cell number, and nothing else. So how many rules did Marcus break before the weekend even started?

deeper.plain: Marcus mixed client money with his own and ran an ad that hides his broker. Both are violations, even if nothing bad happens later.
deeper.picture: It's like a coat check attendant wearing your coat home overnight and promising to bring it back. Even if it comes back clean, that's not the deal.
deeper.street: Over the weekend Marcus's account gets hit by a $3,000 auto payment and a garnishment he forgot about. Monday the buyer's attorney asks for proof the deposit is in escrow. Marcus can't show it.
deeper.stakes: Commingling is a revocation-level offense, and the blind ad is a separate fine. Diane can get hit too for failing to supervise. The buyer could lose trust and walk.
deeper.exam: Scenario questions with "just until Monday" or "for convenience" are testing that intent doesn't matter. Commingling is commingling the moment the money hits the wrong account.

blocks.html: Money a broker holds for others (deposits, rents, security) goes into a separate escrow or special account. Mixing it with the broker's own money is commingling, and spending it is conversion. Both are grounds for revocation (19 NYCRR 175.1).
blocks.casual: Any money a broker holds for other people (deposits, rents, security) goes in a separate escrow or special account. Mix it with the broker's own money and that's commingling. Spend it and that's conversion. Either one can cost you your license (19 NYCRR 175.1).

deeper.plain: Other people's money gets its own account. Mixing it is bad; spending it is worse.
deeper.picture: Think of the money as a borrowed umbrella. Commingling is tossing it in your closet with your own umbrellas. Conversion is taking it out in the rain like it's yours.
deeper.street: Sal's managing broker collects $14,000 in rents from his Astoria building. That money lands in the broker's escrow account, not the operating account that pays the firm's rent. If the broker uses it to cover payroll, that's conversion.
deeper.stakes: Both are grounds for revocation. Conversion can also be criminal larceny. Owners and tenants lose money; you lose your career.
deeper.exam: Know the pair: commingling = mixing, conversion = using. The reg is 175.1. If a stem says the broker "temporarily used" escrow funds, that's conversion.

blocks.html: Salespersons never hold client funds personally. They hand everything to the broker promptly. Marcus's personal account deposit is commingling even if every dollar comes back Monday.
blocks.casual: Salespersons never hold client money personally. Everything goes to the broker, promptly. So Marcus putting that check in his own account is commingling, even if every single dollar is back on Monday.

deeper.plain: If you're a salesperson, client money passes straight through your hands to the broker.
deeper.picture: You're the mail carrier, not the mailbox. Deliver it; don't store it.
deeper.street: Jordan gets a $3,600 first month's rent check from a tenant in Sunset Park. Jordan walks it into the Hudson & Hart office that afternoon and Diane deposits it into escrow. No detours.
deeper.stakes: Even a well-meaning salesperson who holds a check for a few days is exposed to discipline and makes the broker look like a weak supervisor.
deeper.exam: "May a salesperson deposit funds in their own account if they intend to transfer them?" No. Correct answer: turn funds over to the broker promptly.

blocks.title: Downstate practice
blocks.html: In NYC and most of downstate, the seller's attorney usually holds the contract deposit in an attorney escrow account. Brokers more often hold rental deposits and first month's rent. Whoever holds it, the no-commingling rule is the same.
blocks.casual: How it actually works downstate: in NYC and most of downstate, the seller's attorney usually holds the contract deposit in an attorney escrow account. Brokers more often end up holding rental deposits and first month's rent. Doesn't matter who's holding it, though. The no-commingling rule is identical.

deeper.plain: Downstate, lawyers usually hold the purchase deposit. Brokers usually handle rental money.
deeper.picture: Two different safes in the same building: the attorney's safe for sales deposits, the broker's safe for rental money. Same lock rules on both.
deeper.street: The Okafors accept an offer on their Bed-Stuy brownstone. The buyer's 10% deposit goes to Priya's escrow account as the seller's attorney. Meanwhile Jordan's rental client in Bushwick hands over a security deposit that goes into Diane's escrow account.
deeper.stakes: A broker who assumes sales deposits always go to the attorney might fumble an upstate deal where the broker is the escrow agent. Know who's holding the money on every deal.
deeper.exam: If a question asks who usually holds the contract deposit in NYC, the answer is the seller's attorney. The commingling rule applies to whoever holds funds.

head: Rule
What it says
Why
rows: Prohibited. A net listing lets the broker keep everything above a price the seller names.
Invites the broker to hide the true value
Give each party a copy of any document they sign, promptly
So consumers know what they agreed to
Keep transaction records for 3 years: listings, contracts, closing statements, agency disclosures, and the like
Broker must regularly and closely supervise associated licensees
The broker is accountable for their acts
No fee from more than one party without full disclosure and consent of all parties
No undisclosed payments for referrals; never share commission with unlicensed people
Steers consumers for secret profit (also RESPA Section 8)
Exclusive listing agreements must state expiration; give the seller the required explanation of exclusive right to sell vs exclusive agency

deeper.plain: Part 175 is a list of behavior rules that keep brokers from secretly profiting at clients' expense.
deeper.picture: Each rule closes a door a dishonest broker might sneak through: hidden profits, missing paperwork, double dipping, secret referrals.
deeper.street: A seller in Bay Ridge says, "Get me $900,000 and keep anything over that." That's a net listing and Diane refuses. She writes a regular percentage listing with a clear expiration date and hands the seller a copy right after signing.
deeper.stakes: Net listings, hidden dual payments and secret referral fees all end in discipline. Missing records make it impossible to defend yourself in a DOS audit.
deeper.exam: Numbers and cites to know: net listings prohibited (175.19), records 3 years (175.23), compensation from more than one party only with consent of all (175.7). Kickbacks also violate RESPA Section 8.

blocks.html: A salesperson may be paid only by the sponsoring broker. A broker may pay another licensed broker (a co-broke through the multiple listing service or directly) but never an unlicensed person for doing licensed work. A "finder's fee" to your cousin who sent you a buyer is a kickback to an unlicensed person.
blocks.casual: A salesperson gets paid only by the sponsoring broker. Period. A broker can pay another licensed broker (a co-broke through the multiple listing service or directly) but never an unlicensed person for licensed work. That "finder's fee" to your cousin who sent you a buyer? It's a kickback to an unlicensed person.

deeper.plain: Commission money only flows between licensed brokers and from a broker to their own agents.
deeper.picture: It's a closed pipe. Money can move from broker to broker or broker to salesperson, but it can't leak out to anyone outside the pipe.
deeper.street: Leo's coworker sends Jordan a buyer who closes on a $1.1M Fort Greene condo. Jordan wants to send the coworker $1,000 as thanks. Diane says no: that's paying an unlicensed person for a referral.
deeper.stakes: Paying unlicensed people gets brokers fined and suspended. It also gives the unlicensed person a reason to steer buyers for cash.
deeper.exam: A salesperson can't pay or be paid by anyone but their broker. Co-broking between licensed brokers is fine. Finder's fees to unlicensed people are kickbacks.

blocks.q: A seller tells Jordan, "Get me $900,000 net and keep anything over that." What should Jordan do?
c: Accept, since it is in writing
Accept only if the broker approves
Decline and offer a percentage or flat-fee listing; net listings are prohibited in New York
Accept but disclose it to buyers
blocks.x: 19 NYCRR 175.19 prohibits net listings. Broker approval or written form does not fix it.

blocks.html: Only the broker places ads, or approves ads placed by its salespersons and teams. Every ad must identify the broker: the broker's name plus the broker's address or phone number. An ad that hides the fact that a broker is behind it is a blind ad, and it is illegal.
blocks.casual: Only the broker places ads, or signs off on ads from its salespersons and teams. Every ad has to name the broker: the broker's name plus the broker's address or phone. An ad that hides that a broker is behind it is a blind ad, and it's illegal.

deeper.plain: Every ad needs the broker's name and a way to reach the broker.
deeper.picture: Every ad is a letter from the brokerage. It needs a return address, and it's the broker's address, not yours.
deeper.street: Marcus's "Gorgeous 3BR, call Marcus" post has no Hudson & Hart and no broker phone or address. It's a blind ad. The fixed version: "Marcus Webb, Licensed Real Estate Salesperson, Hudson & Hart Realty, (718) office number."
deeper.stakes: Blind ads get fined and pulled. They also make it look like a private seller is advertising, which misleads consumers.
deeper.exam: Required: broker's name plus address or phone. "Agent's cell only" is a blind ad. The broker controls advertising.

items: State your license type accurately. "Licensed real estate salesperson" or "associate broker" is fine. "Sales associate," "licensed sales agent," or simply "broker" for a salesperson is prohibited.
Use your licensed name. A nickname is fine only if the full licensed name also appears.
Other phone numbers (cell, desk) are fine if labeled.
Websites and social media: every page that promotes licensed activity needs the required broker information; an agent or team site needs broker approval and a link to the broker's site.
First email to a new client carries the required information; later emails may omit it.
Never advertise another broker's exclusive without permission, and then credit them ("Listing courtesy of...").
No guaranteed profits. Neighborhood names must be accurate.
blocks.casual:
The ad rules:
Say your license type right. "Licensed real estate salesperson" or "associate broker" works. "Sales associate," "licensed sales agent," or calling a salesperson a "broker" doesn't.
Use your licensed name. A nickname is fine only if your full licensed name is there too.
Extra phone numbers (cell, desk) are fine if labeled.
Websites and social: every page promoting licensed activity needs the broker info, and an agent or team site needs broker approval and a link to the broker's site.
Your first email to a new client carries the required info; later ones can skip it.
Never advertise another broker's exclusive without permission, and then credit them ("Listing courtesy of...").
No guaranteed profits. Neighborhood names have to be accurate.

deeper.plain: Tell the truth about who you are, who your broker is, and what you're selling.
deeper.picture: An ad is a name tag at a conference. It has to show your real name, your real title, and the company that sent you.
deeper.street: Jordan's Instagram bio reads "JR, Brooklyn's top sales agent." Diane makes Jordan change it to "Jordan Reyes, Licensed Real Estate Salesperson, Hudson & Hart Realty." Jordan also stops calling a Crown Heights listing "Prospect Heights adjacent" when it's half a mile away.
deeper.stakes: Wrong titles, nicknames without legal names and rebranded neighborhoods all draw DOS complaints. Advertising someone else's listing without permission can start a fight with that broker.
deeper.exam: Watch the forbidden titles: "sales associate" and "licensed sales agent." Correct: "licensed real estate salesperson." First email needs the info; later ones don't.

blocks.html: A team is two or more people at the same brokerage who hold themselves out as a team. The name must use the word "team" and either include the members' full licensed names or be followed by "at" or "of" plus the broker's full name. Words like "realty," "group," or "associates" are prohibited because they imply a separate brokerage. An unlicensed person's name may not be in a team name.
blocks.casual: A team is two or more people at the same brokerage who present themselves as a team. The name has to include the word "team", and either list the members' full licensed names or be followed by "at" or "of" plus the broker's full name. Words like "realty," "group" or "associates" are out, because they sound like a separate brokerage. And no unlicensed person's name in the team name.

deeper.plain: A team name can't make it look like the team is its own company.
deeper.picture: A team is a band inside a record label. You can name the band, but the album has to say which label put it out.
deeper.street: Jordan and Marcus want to call themselves "Brooklyn Brownstone Associates." Diane kills it: "associates" implies a brokerage. They go with "The Brownstone Team at Hudson & Hart Realty."
deeper.stakes: A misleading team name can mean fines, rebranding costs and consumers who think they hired an independent firm.
deeper.exam: Must include "team." Banned words: realty, group, associates. Broker named with "at" or "of," or full licensed names of members.

blocks.title: Spot the bad team name
blocks.html: "Slope Luxury Group": illegal (group, no broker). "The Reyes Team at Hudson & Hart Realty": legal. "Reyes Realty Team": illegal (realty).
blocks.casual: Quick quiz on team names. "Slope Luxury Group": illegal ("group," no broker). "The Reyes Team at Hudson & Hart Realty": legal. "Reyes Realty Team": illegal ("realty").

deeper.plain: Look for the word team, the broker's name, and no fake-brokerage words.
deeper.picture: Run each name through a three-item checklist like a bouncer checking IDs: "team" present, broker named, no realty or group.
deeper.street: A Park Slope duo prints 5,000 postcards as "Slope Luxury Group." A DOS complaint comes in. They pay a fine and reprint everything as "The Slope Team at Hudson & Hart Realty."
deeper.stakes: Printing, signs and websites under an illegal name cost real money to redo, on top of the fine.
deeper.exam: Expect three or four names and one legal answer. The legal one has "team" plus "at" or "of" the full broker name.

blocks.q: Which ad complies with NY advertising rules?
c: "Bushwick loft, call Marcus 917-555-0101"
"Marcus Webb, Licensed Sales Agent, Hudson & Hart"
"Marcus Webb, Licensed Real Estate Salesperson, Hudson & Hart Realty, 718-555-0100"
"Brooklyn Brownstone Group, call us"
blocks.x: It names the broker, gives the broker's phone, and states the license type correctly. The first is a blind ad; the second uses a prohibited title; the fourth is a blind ad with an illegal group name.

blocks.title: What an unlicensed assistant can and cannot do

left.title: May
items: Answer phones and take messages
Schedule appointments for licensees
Type, file, assemble documents
Place broker-approved ads
Order keys, signs, inspections
Track closings and compute commissions

right.title: May not
items: Show property or host open houses
Answer questions about listings, price, or terms
Negotiate or discuss offers
Give opinions of value
Sign contracts or agency forms
Be paid by commission on deals

deeper.plain: An unlicensed assistant can run the office but can't touch the deal itself.
deeper.picture: A stage manager can schedule rehearsals and order props, but can't step on stage and say the actor's lines.
deeper.street: Diane's office assistant books Jordan's 2 pm showing in Greenpoint and orders the lockbox. When the buyer calls asking if the seller would take $40,000 less, the assistant says, "Let me have Jordan call you right back."
deeper.stakes: If the assistant shows the apartment or chats about price, that's unlicensed activity and Diane is on the hook for supervision.
deeper.exam: Can: phones, scheduling, paperwork, broker-approved ads, computing commissions. Cannot: show, host open houses, discuss price or terms, negotiate, give value opinions, sign forms.

blocks.html: An unlicensed assistant is paid by salary or hourly wage, never per transaction. Paying a share of commission is paying an unlicensed person for licensed work.
blocks.casual: An unlicensed assistant gets a salary or hourly wage, never paid per deal. Hand them a cut of a commission and you're paying an unlicensed person for licensed work.

deeper.plain: Pay your assistant like an employee, not like an agent.
deeper.picture: A receptionist at a dental office gets a paycheck, not a cut of every filling.
deeper.street: Marcus promises his assistant $250 for every lease she "helps close." Even if she only typed paperwork, a per-deal bonus looks like commission. Diane switches her to a flat hourly rate.
deeper.stakes: Per-transaction pay is the paper trail DOS uses to prove an assistant was doing licensed work. Fines follow for the broker and the agent.
deeper.exam: "How may an unlicensed assistant be compensated?" Salary or hourly. Never a share of commission or per-deal pay.

blocks.html: After the 2019 Newsday investigation into steering on Long Island, New York required every broker to adopt written standardized operating procedures for prospective homebuyers. They must say whether the broker requires: (1) photo ID, (2) an exclusive buyer agreement, (3) mortgage pre-approval. The SOP is date-stamped, notarized, posted on the broker's website and apps, available at every office, and updated within 30 days of any change. Brokers affirm compliance at renewal. The point: treat every buyer the same.
blocks.casual: After Newsday's 2019 investigation found steering on Long Island, New York made every broker adopt written standardized operating procedures for prospective homebuyers. The SOP has to say whether the broker requires (1) photo ID, (2) an exclusive buyer agreement, (3) mortgage pre-approval. It's date-stamped, notarized, posted on the broker's website and apps, available at every office, and updated within 30 days of any change. Brokers affirm compliance when they renew. The whole point: treat every buyer the same way.

deeper.plain: Brokers must publish the same entry rules for every homebuyer and then actually follow them.
deeper.picture: It's a posted dress code at a club door. If the sign says "ID required," the bouncer checks everyone's ID, not just some people's.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart's SOP says: photo ID and pre-approval before showings, no exclusive buyer agreement. When a buyer from Canarsie and a buyer from Cobble Hill both call, Jordan asks both for the same two things.
deeper.stakes: Asking only some buyers for pre-approval is how steering hides. Uneven treatment can mean fair housing complaints and DOS discipline.
deeper.exam: Three items: ID, exclusive buyer agreement, pre-approval. Posted, notarized, date-stamped, updated within 30 days. Statute: RPL 442-h.

blocks.q: Hudson & Hart's SOP says buyers must show pre-approval before showings. Jordan skips it for a buyer who "seems wealthy." What is the problem?
c: None, the SOP is only a guideline
Applying the SOP unequally invites fair housing claims and violates RPL 442-h
Only the broker can waive it, so it is fine if Diane agrees
Pre-approval rules apply only to rentals
blocks.x: The SOP exists so every buyer gets the same treatment. Selective waiver is exactly the steering pattern the law targets.

blocks.html: Property Condition Disclosure Act (RPL Article 14). Sellers of 1 to 4 family residential property must deliver the property condition disclosure statement (PCDS) before the buyer signs the contract. Since March 20, 2024, the old option to skip it by giving a $500 credit is gone, and the form adds flood questions: floodplain location, flood insurance, past flood damage and claims, and FEMA assistance. A seller is liable for actual damages for a willful failure. The agent's role: tell the seller about the duty, and never fill out the form for them.
blocks.casual: Property Condition Disclosure Act (RPL Article 14). If you're selling a 1 to 4 family home, you have to hand the buyer the property condition disclosure statement (PCDS) before they sign the contract. Since March 20, 2024, you can't skip it by giving a $500 credit anymore, and the form now asks about floods: floodplain location, flood insurance, past flood damage and claims, and FEMA assistance. A seller who willfully fails to deliver it is liable for actual damages. Your job as the agent: tell the seller about the duty, and never fill out the form for them.

deeper.plain: Sellers of 1 to 4 family homes must fill out and deliver a condition form before the buyer signs.
deeper.picture: It's the seller's medical history for the house, filled out by the patient, not by the nurse.
deeper.street: The Okafors fill out the PCDS for their Bed-Stuy brownstone and check that the basement took water during Hurricane Ida and they got FEMA help. Jordan reminds them it must reach the buyer before contract, but doesn't write a single answer.
deeper.stakes: A seller who willfully skips it can owe actual damages. An agent who fills it in takes on the risk of every wrong answer.
deeper.exam: Delivered before the contract is signed. No $500 credit since March 20, 2024. Flood questions now required. Seller fills it out, not the agent.

head: PCDS not required
Examples
rows: Foreclosure sales, sheriff's sales, partition, bankruptcy
To a spouse or children, between co-owners, divorce transfers
Transfers to or from government; new homes never lived in
Condos, co-ops, commercial, vacant land are outside the act

deeper.plain: Some transfers skip the PCDS, mostly where the seller wouldn't know the house or the property isn't a 1 to 4 family home.
deeper.picture: Exemptions are for sellers who never lived in the house or are handing it over under a court order. You can't give a health history for someone you never met.
deeper.street: An executor sells her late aunt's Flatbush house: no PCDS. A bank sells a foreclosed Staten Island home: no PCDS. Kim's Upper West Side co-op unit: outside the act entirely.
deeper.stakes: Claiming an exemption that doesn't apply means the seller skipped a required form. Requiring one for a co-op just confuses everyone.
deeper.exam: Exempt: foreclosure and court transfers, fiduciaries, transfers between family or co-owners, government transfers, new never-occupied homes, and condos, co-ops, commercial, vacant land.

blocks.title: The $500 credit
blocks.html: The 2022 syllabus and older books teach the $500 credit opt-out. It was repealed effective March 20, 2024. If an item asks what a seller does instead of the PCDS today, the answer is that 1 to 4 family sellers must give it (unless exempt).
blocks.casual: Big trap. The 2022 syllabus and older books still teach the $500 credit opt-out. It was repealed effective March 20, 2024. If a question asks what a seller does instead of the PCDS today, the answer is: 1 to 4 family sellers have to give it (unless they're exempt).

deeper.plain: Sellers can no longer pay $500 to skip the form.
deeper.picture: It's like an old parking loophole the city closed. People still swear by it, and they still get ticketed.
deeper.street: Sal tells his nephew, selling a Ridgewood two-family, "Just give the buyer 500 bucks off and skip the paperwork." Jordan explains that ended March 20, 2024. The nephew fills out the form.
deeper.stakes: A seller who relies on the old credit hasn't complied and can face liability. Agents who repeat old advice look careless.
deeper.exam: Older items may offer "$500 credit" as a correct choice. Under current law, the seller must deliver the PCDS unless exempt.

blocks.html: Uncapped natural gas wells (RPL 242). A seller who knows of an uncapped natural gas well on the property must inform the buyer before the contract is signed (the statute does not say how; writing is the way to prove it). It is a real issue in parts of western and central New York.
blocks.casual: Uncapped natural gas wells (RPL 242). If the seller knows about an uncapped natural gas well on the property, they have to tell the buyer before the contract's signed. The law doesn't say how, so smart sellers put it in writing. This is a real thing in parts of western and central New York.

deeper.plain: Sellers must tell buyers, before contract, about any uncapped gas well they know about. Writing is the safe way to prove it.
deeper.picture: An open, unsealed pipe in the backyard leading to gas underground. You'd want to know before you buy.
deeper.street: A buyer is looking at farmland near Jamestown. The sellers know an old gas well near the barn was never capped. They put it in a written disclosure before contract.
deeper.stakes: Gas leaks are a safety risk and capping a well costs serious money. Hiding one invites lawsuits.
deeper.exam: Cue: "uncapped gas well." Answer: disclose before contract, RPL 242, only if the seller has knowledge (writing is best practice, not the statute's wording).

blocks.html: Stigmatized property (RPL 443-a). A stigmatized property is one with a psychological, not physical, defect. Sellers and agents have no duty to disclose that an occupant had HIV/AIDS or another condition not transmitted by living there, or that the property was the site of a homicide, suicide, or other death. A buyer may ask in writing; the agent may answer only with the seller's permission and must never lie.
blocks.casual: Stigmatized property (RPL 443-a). A stigmatized property has a psychological defect, not a physical one. Sellers and agents don't have to disclose that someone who lived there had HIV/AIDS or another condition you can't catch by living there, or that there was a homicide, suicide or other death there. A buyer can ask in writing, and the agent can answer only with the seller's permission. And you never lie.

deeper.plain: Bad history isn't a physical defect, so you don't have to bring it up. But if asked in writing, you can't lie.
deeper.picture: It's the house's gossip, not its plumbing. The law cares about the plumbing.
deeper.street: A Harlem townhouse was the site of a suicide years ago. A buyer sends a written question about deaths in the house. Jordan checks with the seller. The seller says Jordan may answer, and Jordan answers truthfully.
deeper.stakes: Volunteering a prior occupant's illness can violate fair housing law. Lying when asked is misrepresentation.
deeper.exam: No duty to disclose: HIV/AIDS or non-transmissible conditions, homicide, suicide, other death. Buyer asks in writing; agent answers with seller permission; never lie.

blocks.title: Fair housing tie-in
blocks.html: Disclosing a prior occupant's HIV status could violate fair housing law (disability). That is why 443-a protects silence.
blocks.casual: Here's why the law protects silence: telling a buyer a former occupant had HIV could itself violate fair housing law, because that's a disability. So 443-a lets you stay quiet.

deeper.plain: Talking about a past occupant's illness can be discrimination, so the law takes away any duty to mention it.
deeper.picture: It's like HR not being allowed to share a coworker's medical file. Silence protects the person, not just the deal.
deeper.street: A buyer in Chelsea asks Marcus if "anyone sick lived there." Marcus starts to say the last owner had AIDS. Diane stops him: that's protected health information tied to a disability.
deeper.stakes: Disclosing it could draw a fair housing complaint against the agent and broker, on top of a privacy mess.
deeper.exam: Link: HIV/AIDS status is a disability under fair housing law. That's the reason 443-a exists.

blocks.html: The most common DOS complaints: commingling or failing to return deposits, unlicensed activity, blind or misleading ads, missing agency or fair housing disclosures, misrepresentation, failure to supervise, paying unlicensed people, and untrustworthiness (RPL 441-c).
blocks.casual: What DOS hears about most: commingling or not returning deposits, unlicensed activity, blind or misleading ads, missing agency or fair housing disclosures, misrepresentation, failure to supervise, paying unlicensed people, and untrustworthiness (RPL 441-c).

deeper.plain: Most complaints come from money mistakes, bad ads, skipped forms and lying.
deeper.picture: Like the top reasons people fail a driving test: they're common, predictable and avoidable.
deeper.street: A renter in Astoria never gets her $2,500 deposit back after the deal falls through. She files with DOS. That one complaint pulls in the agent's ads, disclosures and the broker's supervision too.
deeper.stakes: One complaint opens your whole file. A small sloppy habit can turn into a pile of charges.
deeper.exam: RPL 441-c is the discipline section. "Untrustworthiness" and "incompetency" are catch-all grounds.

head: Penalty
Who imposes
Notes
rows: Administrative discipline: reprimand, fine up to $2,000 per violation, suspension, revocation
DOS, after a hearing before an administrative law judge
After revocation, generally no new license for 1 year
Any violation of Article 12-A, including unlicensed activity
Court, sued by the person harmed
Between the fee received and 4 times it, against anyone paid in violation
An unlicensed person cannot sue to collect a commission

deeper.plain: Bad conduct can be punished by DOS, by a criminal court, and by a civil lawsuit, all from one act.
deeper.picture: Three separate referees: DOS can bench you, a criminal court can charge you, and the person you hurt can sue you.
deeper.street: An unlicensed "rental finder" in Washington Heights collects $3,000 from a tenant. The AG can prosecute the misdemeanor, the tenant can sue for between $3,000 and $12,000, and the finder can't sue the landlord for any unpaid fee.
deeper.stakes: Losing your license, a criminal record, and owing up to four times your fee can all come from one deal.
deeper.exam: DOS fines up to $2,000 per violation (old materials say $1,000); 1 year wait after revocation; civil penalty between the fee and 4 times it; unlicensed people can't sue for a commission.

blocks.html: A licensee who disagrees with a DOS decision does not appeal within DOS forever. The route is an Article 78 proceeding in NY Supreme Court, which reviews whether the agency acted arbitrarily or outside the law.
blocks.casual: If you disagree with a DOS decision, you don't just keep appealing inside DOS. You go to court with an Article 78 proceeding in NY Supreme Court, which looks at whether the agency acted arbitrarily or outside the law.

deeper.plain: To fight a DOS ruling, you sue in state court under Article 78.
deeper.picture: It's like asking a referee's boss to review the tape. The court checks whether the call followed the rules, not whether it would have made the same call.
deeper.street: Marcus's license gets suspended for 90 days. He thinks the judge ignored evidence. His lawyer files an Article 78 petition in Supreme Court, Kings County.
deeper.stakes: Pick the wrong route or miss the deadline and the DOS decision stands.
deeper.exam: Cue: "appeal a DOS decision." Answer: Article 78 proceeding. Not the Court of Claims, not the Board of Realtors.

blocks.title: Case studies from DOS hearings (composites)
blocks.html:
1. The rent deposit. A Queens salesperson took a $4,800 rental deposit in cash, never gave it to the broker, and stopped answering calls. Result: revocation, restitution ordered, and the broker fined for failure to supervise.

2. The "group." A Manhattan team advertised as "Uptown Elite Group" with no broker named. Result: fine, ads pulled, team renamed "The Elite Team at [broker]."

3. The finder's fee. A broker paid a doorman $500 per referred tenant. Result: fine for paying an unlicensed person, plus a suspension when repeated.
blocks.casual:
Three real-style cases (composites from DOS hearings).
1. The rent deposit. A Queens salesperson took a $4,800 rental deposit in cash, never gave it to the broker, and went silent. Result: revocation, restitution ordered, and the broker fined for failure to supervise.
2. The "group." A Manhattan team advertised as "Uptown Elite Group" with no broker named. Result: fine, ads pulled, team renamed "The Elite Team at [broker]."
3. The finder's fee. A broker paid a doorman $500 per referred tenant. Result: fine for paying an unlicensed person, plus a suspension when it kept happening.

deeper.plain: Pocketing deposits, illegal team names and paying unlicensed referrers each lead to real penalties.
deeper.picture: Three different holes in the same boat: money, advertising, and payments to outsiders.
deeper.street: That doorman on the Upper East Side sent 12 tenants in a year and got $6,000. Each payment is a separate violation, which is why repeat conduct turned a fine into a suspension.
deeper.stakes: The salesperson lost the license for good on one cash deposit. The broker paid too, just for not watching closely.
deeper.exam: Pattern: keeping client funds leads to revocation; misleading team names lead to fines; paying unlicensed people leads to fines and, if repeated, suspension.

blocks.q: DOS revokes Marcus's license after a hearing. He believes the judge ignored evidence. What is his legal route?
c: Appeal to the local Realtor board
Reapply the next day
File an Article 78 proceeding in State Supreme Court
Ask the Attorney General to reverse it
blocks.x: Article 78 is how NY courts review state agency decisions. Realtor boards have no licensing power, and he generally must wait a year to reapply.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Money, Ads, Paper. Keep money separate, put the broker in every ad, and keep the paper 3 years. Most DOS cases are one of the three.
blocks.casual: Remember three words: Money, Ads, Paper. Keep money separate, put the broker in every ad, and hang on to the paper for 3 years. Most DOS cases come down to one of those.

deeper.plain: Separate the money, name the broker, keep records.
deeper.picture: Three pockets: one for client money, one for your broker's name card, and one for files you'll keep for 3 years.
deeper.street: Before every deal, Jordan runs a quick check: Is the deposit going to escrow? Does the listing ad name Hudson & Hart? Are the signed disclosures in the file?
deeper.stakes: Miss one and you're exposed to the most common DOS complaints. Hit all three and most trouble never starts.
deeper.exam: Records: 3 years. Escrow: no commingling. Ads: broker's name plus address or phone.

story.title: Marcus Has a Weekend
story.setting: Hudson & Hart Realty, Monday 9 am

beats.text: Diane is holding two printouts: a bank deposit slip and an Instagram screenshot.
Marcus. Twenty-five thousand dollars of a buyer's money went into your personal checking.
For three days! The escrow bank was closed.
Commingling doesn't come with a grace period. That's revocation territory, and I'm on the hook for not supervising you.
What's wrong with the Instagram post? It's a nice photo.
"Gorgeous 3BR, call Marcus." No broker name, no broker phone. That's a blind ad.

check.q: What is missing from Marcus's post?
c: The price
The broker's name and address or phone
The square footage
The seller's consent signature
check.x: Under 175.25 every ad must identify the broker with name plus address or phone. Without it, it is a blind ad.

beats.text: Fine. I'll call my page "Slope Luxury Group."
Group is banned. Use "team," and put my firm's full name after it. "The Webb Team at Hudson & Hart Realty."
Also, my cousin sent me the buyer. I promised him ten percent.
Is your cousin licensed? No? Then he gets a thank-you card. Paying him is a kickback to an unlicensed person.
beats.tag: No fee sharing with unlicensed people

beats.text: And the sellers want to skip the disclosure form and just give a $500 credit.
Not since March 2024. One to four family sellers give the PCDS before the contract, flood questions and all.

check.q: What changed for the PCDS on March 20, 2024?
c: It became optional
The $500 credit opt-out ended and flood questions were added
It now applies to co-ops
Agents must complete it for sellers
check.x: The 2023 amendment, effective March 20, 2024, eliminated the $500 credit and added flood disclosures.

beats.text: And if DOS comes after me?
Hearing, then reprimand, fine up to a thousand per violation, suspension, or revocation. If you don't like it, Article 78. Better plan: deposit the money in escrow today.
Money, ads, paper. Got it.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: left side 'Unlicensed assistant may', right side 'May not'. Then add three ad mistakes you've seen online.

facts.text: Money held for others goes in a separate escrow account; mixing it with the broker's own is commingling, spending it is conversion, and both can cost the license (175.1).
Salespersons never hold client funds; they hand them to the broker promptly, and a personal deposit is commingling even if repaid.
Downstate, the seller's attorney usually holds the contract deposit, and brokers more often hold rental deposits.
Net listings are prohibited by DOS regulation (175.19).
Each party must promptly get a copy of any document they sign (175.12).
Brokers keep transaction records for 3 years (175.23).
No undisclosed referral payments or kickbacks, and no fee from more than one party without everyone's consent (175.7, RESPA Section 8).
A listing agreement is the owner's employment contract with a broker; exclusive listings must state an expiration and include the required explanation of listing types.
A salesperson is paid only by the sponsoring broker; brokers may pay other brokers (such as through an MLS) but never an unlicensed person, so a finder's fee to a non-licensee is illegal.
Every ad is placed or approved by the broker and shows the broker's name plus address or phone; an ad hiding the broker is a blind ad.
Salespersons must state their license type accurately; titles like "sales associate" or "licensed sales agent" are prohibited.
A nickname needs the full licensed name too; agent sites need broker approval and a link; another firm's exclusive needs permission and credit; no guaranteed profits.
Team names use the word "team" and either members' licensed names or "at/of" the broker; "realty," "group" or "associates" are prohibited.
Unlicensed assistants do clerical work only: no showing, discussing price or terms, negotiating, or giving opinions of value.
Unlicensed assistants are paid salary or hourly, never per transaction or by commission.
RPL 442-h SOPs state whether the broker requires photo ID, an exclusive buyer agreement, and mortgage pre-approval.
