SOPs are date-stamped, notarized, posted on the broker's website and apps and at every office, and updated within 30 days of a change.
Since March 20, 2024, non-exempt 1 to 4 family sellers must give the PCDS before contract signing; the $500 credit opt-out is gone.
The agent tells the seller of the PCDS duty but never fills it out; a willful failure makes the seller liable for actual damages.
PCDS exemptions include court-ordered and foreclosure sales, fiduciaries, family transfers, new homes never lived in, and condos, co-ops and land.
RPL 242: a seller must disclose a known uncapped natural gas well before the contract is signed.
RPL 443-a: a death, homicide, suicide or an occupant's HIV/AIDS need not be disclosed; a written question may be answered only with the seller's permission, never with a lie.
After a hearing DOS can reprimand, fine up to $2,000 per violation, suspend or revoke; after revocation a new license generally waits 1 year.
Any violation of Article 12-A, including unlicensed activity, is a misdemeanor.
Anyone paid in violation can be sued for up to 4 times the fee, and an unlicensed person cannot sue for a commission.
A DOS decision is challenged in NY Supreme Court through an Article 78 proceeding.

lessons.title: Case file: The Branch on Austin Street
lessons.tagline: Diane opens a Queens office in a month. The lease was the easy part.
objectives: Decide what DOS must approve before a branch office, a transferring salesperson, or a renewed license can do business
Apply the duties a broker, an associate broker, and a salesperson owe to each other and to the public
Sort walk-in requests into licensed work, exempt work, and work that needs a different license
Apply the rules on paying unlicensed people and the penalties that follow

blocks.title: Hudson & Hart goes to Queens
blocks.html: Diane Hart has signed a lease on a storefront on Austin Street in Forest Hills, two blocks from the LIRR station. It will be the firm's first office outside Brooklyn. She has hired Noor Haddad, an associate broker who spent twelve years selling co-ops in Rego Park and Kew Gardens, to run it. Two salespersons are coming over from a rival firm, a receptionist starts Monday, and Jordan has been lent to the branch for its first month. The keys arrive on a Thursday. The branch office application went to the Department of State the day before. Noor has a two-bedroom co-op on Queens Boulevard to show and wants to run a walk-in open house out of the new storefront on Saturday, with flyers in the window. Can Austin Street open for business this weekend?

Diane's rule for the month is simple: the license law exists to protect the public, so every place and every person the public deals with has to be on file with DOS before the public deals with it. A branch is a place where consumers walk in, hand over deposits, and sign agreements. DOS licenses it separately ($185, two-year term), wants it displayed on the wall there, and wants a broker or associate broker supervising it.

She gave Jordan the same speech she gives every new hire. New York licenses real estate brokers because they hold other people's money and other people's biggest decisions, usually for people who are not real estate experts. The license law (Article 12-A) screens who may act for others, sets minimum education, and gives DOS a way to discipline people who cheat. Nothing in it exists to protect brokers from each other. Hold on to that, she said, because by the end of the month somebody will forget it.

blocks.q: The branch application was filed Wednesday and DOS has issued nothing yet. What should Noor do about Saturday?
c: Run the event from the storefront, since Diane's main office license covers every office the firm operates
Open the storefront now and confirm the branch with DOS once the first deal there is signed
Show the co-op at the apartment and keep the storefront closed until the branch license issues
Open the storefront if a copy of Diane's main office license is posted where the public can see it
blocks.x: Each branch needs its own DOS branch license before it operates as an office, and that license is displayed at the branch. Nothing stops Noor from showing the co-op at the apartment, because a listed unit is not an office. The tempting answer is the main office license: it covers one address in Brooklyn, and posting a copy in Queens would misstate which office is licensed.

blocks.html: Noor moved the open house to the apartment. The branch license arrived the next Wednesday, and Diane had it framed beside Noor's own license and the fair housing notice. The salesperson licenses are kept on file by Diane, not on the wall. What each person carries is a pocket card, which shows who the licensee is and which broker they work for, and which they show on request.

Noor is qualified to be a broker. She chose to work under Diane instead, which is exactly what an associate broker is. That choice has consequences she explained to Jordan over coffee: she cannot take a listing in her own name, cannot collect a fee from a client, and is paid only by Diane. In return, she runs the branch day to day.

head: Person
Owes the firm
Owes the public
rows: Training and close supervision of every licensee she sponsors, at both offices
Escrow handled correctly, records kept 3 years, lawful ads, posted SOPs, fair dealing
Noor Haddad, associate broker and branch manager
Follows Diane's policies, supervises the branch daily, reports problems up
The same honesty, disclosure, and fair housing duties as any licensee
Follows office policy, turns over every deposit and document at once
Honesty, required disclosures, fair housing, no misrepresentation
blocks.caption: The Austin Street org chart, by duty

blocks.q: In the branch's second month, a buyer complains to DOS that a branch salesperson misstated a co-op's monthly maintenance. Noor manages the branch. Who can DOS hold responsible for supervision?
c: Diane as the sponsoring broker, and Noor as well for the way she managed the branch
Noor alone, since a branch license that names a manager moves supervision duty to that manager
The salesperson alone, because supervision duties end once a licensee passes the state exam
The co-op's managing agent, because the maintenance figure came from the building
blocks.x: Naming a manager delegates the daily work, not the legal responsibility. The sponsoring broker must supervise every associated licensee, and DOS can discipline a broker for failing to do so. An associate broker who manages a branch is also a licensee who can answer for her own conduct. The trap is thinking the manager absorbs all of it: Diane cannot hand off her license obligations by hiring someone.

blocks.title: Where DOS sees all of this
blocks.html: Branch licenses, associations, terminations, and renewals all run through eAccessNY, the DOS online licensing system. A licensee's record there shows the license type, expiration date, and the broker they are associated with. Noor checks it before anyone at Austin Street touches a client.

blocks.text: The salespersons who wanted to bring their listings

blocks.html: Tomasz Bielski and Renata Flores are leaving Queensboro Homes for Austin Street. Tomasz is the bigger producer. He sent Noor this on Sunday night:

blocks.title: Text from Tomasz, 11:48 pm
blocks.html: "My six listings come with me. I already told the sellers to sign new agreements with H&H on Monday. Queensboro hasn't terminated me in eAccessNY yet but that's on them, so I'll start showing Monday anyway. I still have my pocket card."

blocks.q: How should Noor answer Tomasz's text?
c: His six listings may follow him if each seller signs a release, and he may show them Monday with his pocket card
He may start Monday, because filing the termination is Queensboro's job and its delay cannot be held against him
He may bring the listings he personally sourced, but has to wait 30 days before showing any property for the firm
Listings stay with Queensboro; he may act for Hudson & Hart once his association with Diane is filed
blocks.x: A listing agreement is a contract between the seller and the broker, so Tomasz's listings belong to Queensboro. He may work for Hudson & Hart only after DOS has his change of association to Diane on file; until then he is not authorized to act for her. The tempting choice blames Queensboro's delay, but a filing problem never authorizes unlicensed work, and his old pocket card names the wrong broker.

blocks.html: Noor also told him to stop calling the sellers. Urging a seller to break an exclusive listing with another firm can expose Tomasz and Hudson & Hart to a lawsuit, and DOS treats it as untrustworthy conduct. If a seller independently wants out, that is a conversation between the seller and Queensboro. Tomasz's change of association posted on Wednesday. He showed his first Hudson & Hart listing on Thursday, with a new pocket card.

Renata's problem surfaced when Noor ran her license in eAccessNY. It had expired on August 31. Renata had been licensed two years earlier, so this was her first renewal, and she thought she had finished her continuing education. Her certificates showed 22.5 hours:

head: Course
Hours
blocks.caption: Renata's CE certificates

blocks.q: Renata's certificates total 22.5 hours. What still stands between her and a renewal?
c: Nothing. The total is correct and each mandatory topic is covered
Two hours of implicit bias training, which no elective can replace
One more hour of law of agency, since first renewals need three
A third elective, because electives have to make up half of the total
blocks.x: For terms expiring on or after September 21, 2022, the 22.5 hours must include 2 hours of implicit bias, alongside fair housing, cultural competency, ethics, recent legal matters, and agency. Renata's electives cannot substitute, so she must take implicit bias before renewing. The agency choice is the trap: first renewals need 2 hours of agency, not 3, and she has 2.

blocks.html: The harder question was September. On September 14, while expired, Renata had shown a one-bedroom in Kew Gardens to a couple who signed a lease, and Queensboro had collected a one-month fee from the landlord. Renata wanted to know if she could still get her split once she renewed.

blocks.q: What is the right way to look at Renata's September rental?
c: A license renewed within 60 days covers work done during the gap, so her split is payable
It was unlicensed activity, so no split is owed for it and she should have stopped work at once
The work is fine because she was still on file with Queensboro, which held a valid broker license
Queensboro alone is exposed, since an expired salesperson license is a broker's problem, not hers
blocks.x: New York has no grace period. From September 1 Renata was unlicensed, so showing and negotiating that lease was unlicensed activity, and a broker may not pay a commission split to an unlicensed person for it. Her broker's valid license does not cover her, because each person acting must hold an active license. The idea of a short renewal window covering past work is the trap: renewal restores the license going forward only.

blocks.title: Renewing late is not renewing backward
blocks.html: A late renewal fixes the future. It does not license what you did while expired. Brokers who let an expired salesperson keep working share the violation, which is why Noor now checks every expiration date on the first of the month.

Bella Ortiz is a college student hired as receptionist. She is good with people, and on her second Saturday Noor was double-booked. So Bella took the keys to a Kew Gardens one-bedroom, unlocked it for a waiting buyer, and walked him through. The buyer asked, "Would the owner take $410,000?" Bella said, "Probably, they've been sitting a while." Noor was pleased with how the buyer liked her and proposed paying Bella $250 for every deal she helps close.

blocks.q: Which of Bella's Saturday activities was within the rules for an unlicensed assistant?
c: Walking the buyer through the unit, since showing is clerical when no contract is signed
Answering the price question, since she merely passed along her own general impression
Unlocking the apartment and staying with the buyer while he decided on an offer
Picking up the keys from the building's front desk and returning them after the visit
blocks.x: An unlicensed assistant can do clerical and logistical work: answer phones, schedule, collect and return keys, prepare documents for a licensee. Showing a property and offering any opinion on price or terms are licensed acts. The trap is the 'just an impression' answer: telling a buyer the owner would probably accept a lower price is negotiating, and it also leaks the seller's position.

blocks.html: Then the money. Noor's $250 per closed deal sounded like a bonus. It is not. An unlicensed assistant is paid by salary or hourly wage. Paying her per transaction is paying an unlicensed person for licensed work, and it is a violation for Diane even if Bella never shows another apartment. Diane raised Bella's hourly rate instead and wrote a one-page list of what the front desk may and may not do.

blocks.q: Diane wants to reward Bella for a busy month. Which payment is allowed?
c: A higher hourly rate from next pay period
$250 for each lease she helped close that month
1% of each commission the branch earns in the month
A share of Noor's split on the Kew Gardens sale
blocks.x: Unlicensed staff may be paid salary or hourly wages, and a raise in the wage rate is fine. Any payment tied to a closed transaction or a commission is compensation for licensed activity, which an unlicensed person cannot receive. The per-deal bonus is the trap because it feels like a reward for effort; the law looks at what triggers the payment, and here it is a closed deal.

blocks.html: By week three the branch was busy, and not every walk-in was a client. Noor kept a list of the people who asked for a business relationship. Jordan was told to sort them.

head: Walk-in
What they do
What they want
rows: Mr. Okonjo, attorney admitted in NY
To refer executors who need to sell homes
Dmitri, superintendent of a 40-unit rental on 108th Street
Finds tenants for vacancies, "tips" from landlords
$500 from Hudson & Hart for each tenant he sends
Patrice, executor of her late father's estate
Selling his Forest Hills Gardens house herself
Advice on whether she needs a broker at all
Sells a list of available rentals for a $200 fee
To sell "quick appraisals" to the branch's sellers
blocks.caption: Noor's walk-in list

blocks.q: Which walk-in is doing work that needs a real estate license he or she does not have?
c: Mr. Okonjo, who handles probate and wants to refer executors
Patrice, who is selling her father's house as the executor
Dmitri, who finds tenants for landlords in return for tips
Leon, the inspector who reviews a house's physical condition
blocks.x: Finding tenants for other people's apartments for money, even money called a tip, is leasing activity under RPL 440 and needs a license. NY attorneys are exempt, and an executor acting under court authority is exempt when selling estate property. Leon's inspection work needs his home inspector license, not a real estate license. The trap is the executor: she is selling property she does not own personally, but the court appointment is her authority.

blocks.html: Patrice turned out to be the easiest walk-in and the best client. She is the court-appointed executor of her father's estate, so she may sell his house without a license, the same way an owner may sell her own. But she lives in Philadelphia, works full time, and the house on Puritan Avenue needs a buyer who understands Forest Hills Gardens and its private-community rules. She listed with Noor the following week. That raised a paperwork question Jordan got wrong at first.

blocks.q: Patrice, as executor, signs an exclusive listing with Hudson & Hart for her late father's one-family house. Before a buyer signs a contract, what does the Property Condition Disclosure Act require?
c: A completed PCDS, because listing with a broker brings any sale under the act
A PCDS marked "unknown" throughout, since an executor did not live in the house
A $500 credit to the buyer at closing in place of the statement
Nothing from Patrice, because a sale by a fiduciary administering an estate is exempt
blocks.x: RPL 463 exempts transfers by a fiduciary in the course of administering a decedent's estate, so Patrice owes no PCDS. Using a broker does not change that. The $500 credit is the old opt-out, repealed in 2024. Hudson & Hart still must disclose material defects it actually knows about, because the agent's own duty of honesty does not depend on the PCDS.

blocks.html: Jordan's first instinct had been to hand Patrice a blank PCDS, on the theory that every 1 to 4 family sale needs one. Noor walked him through the exemption list in RPL 463 and then made the more useful point: an exemption from the form is not an exemption from honesty. Patrice had mentioned that her father fought water in the basement every spring. That fact goes to buyers, form or no form, and Noor put it in the listing's disclosure notes that afternoon.

Dmitri's offer is the one Noor nearly took. Forty-unit buildings turn over constantly, and $500 per tenant is cheap. But a broker may never pay an unlicensed person for referring business. That is a kickback in the license law sense, and DOS has fined brokers for paying doormen and supers exactly this way. Dmitri himself is exposed too: anyone collecting a fee for licensed work without a license commits a misdemeanor and can be sued for up to four times what he collected. He also cannot sue the landlords to collect a promised "tip," because an unlicensed person cannot enforce a commission.

blocks.q: Noor tells Dmitri the firm cannot pay him per tenant. Which arrangement would let Hudson & Hart work with the building legally?
c: Pay Dmitri a flat $500 monthly retainer instead of a per-tenant fee
Pay the $500 to Dmitri's wife, who is not employed by the building
Sign an exclusive leasing agreement with the building's owner
Let Dmitri keep the fee if the tenant signs a waiver acknowledging it
blocks.x: The legal route is to go to the owner: an exclusive leasing agreement makes Hudson & Hart the owner's agent, and the owner pays the broker. A flat retainer is the tempting choice, but it is still money paid to an unlicensed person because he sends tenants, which is the same violation in a different wrapper. Routing it through a relative or a tenant waiver changes nothing.

blocks.html: QueensRentList was a different animal. Selling lists of available rentals for a fee is the business of an apartment information vendor, which needs its own DOS license, a trust account, and refunds when the customer does not rent through the list. Noor could not share Hudson & Hart's exclusives with them without each landlord's consent, and the vendor's license would never let its staff negotiate a lease. She passed.

blocks.q: Leon offers sellers a $150 "quick appraisal" he will write after his inspection. What is the problem?
c: Nothing, as long as the report is labeled an estimate and the seller pays Leon directly
Appraisals require a state appraiser license or certification, which his inspector license is not
He needs a real estate salesperson license, because a value opinion is a brokerage service
Appraisals for mortgage lenders are regulated, but a seller's appraisal is not
blocks.x: A real estate appraiser is licensed or certified by DOS under a separate law, and a home inspector license does not include valuation. Leon may report on condition, not value. The salesperson-license answer is the trap: a licensee can prepare a CMA to price a listing, but a CMA is not an appraisal and may never be called one, and the license still would not let Leon sell appraisals.

blocks.html: Leon took it well. He kept doing inspections, which buyers at the branch needed anyway, and Noor added him to the list of inspectors the office gives buyers, with a line on the list saying the firm receives nothing from any of them. Pricing stayed where it belongs: Noor's salespersons prepare comparative market analyses for sellers, label them as CMAs, and tell sellers that a lender will order its own appraisal from a licensed or certified appraiser.

Late in the month a Connecticut broker, Graham Pell, called. He had clients relocating from Stamford to Forest Hills and wanted to get a New York nonresident broker license so he could work the deals himself. Noor told him what DOS would ask for, including an irrevocable consent form.

blocks.q: What does Graham's irrevocable consent accomplish?
c: It names the Secretary of State to accept lawsuits served on him
It lets him practice in NY for one year before taking any exam
It commits him to having each NY deal supervised by a NY broker
It waives his right to challenge DOS discipline in a court
blocks.x: A nonresident licensee files an irrevocable consent so that a lawsuit arising from New York business can be served on the Secretary of State on his behalf. It keeps out-of-state licensees answerable in New York courts. The supervision answer is tempting because NY salespersons need a sponsoring broker, but Graham would hold a broker license and the consent is about service of process, not supervision.

blocks.html: Graham filed. Until DOS issued his nonresident license, he did what out-of-state brokers commonly do: he referred his Stamford clients to Hudson & Hart and was paid a referral fee by Diane, broker to broker, under a written agreement. Diane checked his Connecticut license on that state's lookup before signing it. RPL 442 lets a broker share a fee with another licensed broker or with someone regularly in the brokerage business in another state. The same check written to Dmitri the super would have been a violation, and the only difference is the license.

Six weeks in, Queensboro's owner filed a complaint with DOS. It said Hudson & Hart had "poached two agents" and was "undercutting" Queensboro by charging sellers 5% instead of 6%. Noor was furious. Diane was calm.

blocks.q: How is DOS likely to treat Queensboro's complaint?
c: As no violation, since the law protects the public, not rivals
As a valid claim, because DOS sets standard commission rates by region
As a valid claim, because recruiting another firm's agents breaks Part 175
As a fair housing matter, because the lower rate targets one neighborhood
blocks.x: The licensing law protects consumers. Hiring licensees away from another broker and charging a lower commission are ordinary competition. Commissions are negotiable, and an agreement among brokers to fix them would itself violate antitrust law. The trap is assuming DOS polices fairness between firms. It polices conduct toward the public, such as escrow, ads, disclosures, and honesty.

blocks.html: DOS closed the complaint. Tomasz's old sellers stayed with Queensboro, two of them relisted with Hudson & Hart when their agreements expired, and Renata renewed after a Saturday implicit bias class. Bella still works the front desk, at a higher hourly rate, with Diane's one-page list taped beside the phone.

items: A branch office needs its own DOS license, displayed there, and a broker or associate broker supervising it before it operates.
Supervision can be delegated to a manager, but the sponsoring broker stays responsible for every licensee it sponsors.
Listings belong to the broker. A transferring salesperson works for the new firm only after the change of association is on file.
There is no grace period on an expired license, and CE must include the mandatory topics, including 2 hours of implicit bias.
Unlicensed people, including assistants, supers, and doormen, may never be paid per deal or per referral for licensed work.
Exemptions (attorneys, court-appointed fiduciaries, owners) and separate licenses (appraiser, inspector, apartment information vendor) each have their own limits.

lessons.title: Case file: The Team That Called Itself a Group
lessons.tagline: Fourteen thousand followers, one DOS investigator, and a broker who never saw the posts.
objectives: Find the advertising violations in a real social media account and rewrite it to comply with 19 NYCRR 175.25
Apply the team, title, and other-broker listing rules to ads placed by salespersons
Trace a DOS complaint from investigation to hearing and decide who is exposed to which penalty
Decide when the broker's standardized operating procedures and supervision duties are breached by an agent's conduct

blocks.title: The call from Albany
blocks.html: On a Tuesday morning a DOS investigator called Diane Hart about a consumer complaint. A buyer said she drove to a "Prospect Heights" open house she found on Instagram and ended up on Sterling Place in Crown Heights, where the agent told her the block "will be up 20% in three years, guaranteed." The account was called Brownstone Collective Group. Diane had never heard of it. It turned out to belong to Marcus Webb and two other Hudson & Hart salespersons, Kayla Brooks and Andre Simmons, plus Marcus's cousin Teddy, an unlicensed photographer who shoots their listings. It had 14,000 followers and two years of posts. The investigator asked Diane to send copies of the account's ads and her approval records within two weeks. Diane opened the account on her phone and handed it to Jordan. "Count," she said.

blocks.title: Instagram bio, @brownstonecollectivegroup
blocks.html:
Brownstone Collective Group
Brooklyn's luxury brownstone specialists
Marcus Webb, Licensed Sales Agent | Kayla | Andre | Teddy
DM us or call 917-555-0142
Link: brownstonecollective.nyc

Jordan started with the top line. Under 19 NYCRR 175.25, a team is a group of licensees at one brokerage who advertise together. Its name must use the word "team," may not use words that suggest a separate company (realty, group, associates), and must either include the members' full licensed names or be followed by "at" or "of" and the broker's name. An unlicensed person's name may never be part of it.

blocks.q: Which name could the account lawfully use?
c: Brownstone Collective Group at Hudson & Hart Realty
Brownstone Collective Realty Team, Brooklyn's specialists
The Brownstone Collective Team at Hudson & Hart Realty
The Marcus, Kayla, Andre and Teddy Team
blocks.x: A team name must contain "team," avoid words that imply a separate firm such as "group" or "realty," and either list the members' full licensed names or say "at" or "of" the broker. The first choice adds the broker but keeps "Group." The four-name choice is the trap: listing names is allowed only with full licensed names, and Teddy is not licensed, so his name cannot be in a team name at all.

blocks.html: The second line of trouble was Marcus's title. The rule wants the license type stated accurately. A salesperson is a "licensed real estate salesperson" (abbreviations are fine if they do not mislead). Three titles are specifically banned for salespersons: "sales associate," "licensed sales agent," and plain "broker." Marcus picked one of the three.

blocks.q: How should Marcus describe himself in the bio?
c: Marcus Webb, Licensed Real Estate Salesperson
Marcus Webb, Licensed Sales Agent and Brownstone Advisor
Marcus Webb, Licensed Brooklyn Sales Associate
Marcus Webb, Brownstone Broker
blocks.x: The license type has to be accurate, and "licensed real estate salesperson" is the plain correct form. "Sales associate" and "licensed sales agent" are expressly prohibited even though they sound professional, and "broker" misstates the license. Adding a title such as "advisor" does not cure a prohibited one; extra titles are allowed only on top of an accurate license type.

blocks.html: Then the biggest gap. Nowhere in the bio, the posts, or the linked website did the name Hudson & Hart Realty appear. The phone number was Marcus's cell. An ad for real estate that does not identify the broker is a blind ad, and it is the single most common advertising violation DOS sees. The rule is that the broker's name plus the broker's full address or phone number appears in the ad. Agent cell numbers can appear too, labeled as cell numbers.

blocks.q: Which version of the bio's contact line complies?
c: Call Marcus 917-555-0142 (cell), or DM us for the broker's details
Brownstone Collective, a Brooklyn firm, 917-555-0142 (office line)
Licensed agents of a Brooklyn brokerage, 917-555-0142
Hudson & Hart Realty, 718-555-0100. Marcus (cell): 917-555-0142
blocks.x: Every ad must name the broker and give the broker's address or phone. Additional numbers are fine if labeled, so Marcus's cell can stay as long as it says cell. Offering the broker's details by DM is the tempting fix, but the information must be in the ad itself, and "a Brooklyn brokerage" without a name is still a blind ad.

head: Post
Caption
Facts Jordan found
rows: JUST LISTED: Stunning 4BR brownstone in Prospect Heights. This block will appreciate 20% by 2028, guaranteed.
The house is on Sterling Place east of Washington Avenue, in Crown Heights. Hudson & Hart exclusive.
COMING SOON: Classic six in prime Park Slope. DM for early access!
An exclusive of Slope Partners Realty. Marcus heard about it from a friend there. No permission asked.
Meet the crew! Teddy behind the lens, Kayla and Andre on the deals.
Photo of all four. No indication of who is licensed.
blocks.caption: Three posts from the account, with Jordan's notes

blocks.q: What is wrong with the March 3 post?
c: The guarantee alone; neighborhood names are marketing judgment calls
It misplaces the house in a nearby area and guarantees future profit
The neighborhood alone; projections are fine if the agent believes them
Nothing, since the house really is a Hudson & Hart exclusive
blocks.x: Property descriptions must be accurate, and an ad that places a home near a desirable area must name the area where it actually sits. Ads also may not guarantee future profits. Both rules apply here. The trap is treating neighborhood names as puffery: in New York the regulation specifically targets misleading area names because they move prices.

blocks.html: The March 10 post was worse in a different way. Marcus had advertised another broker's exclusive without permission. The rule is that you may advertise another broker's exclusive only with that broker's authorization, and then the ad must disclose the listing broker right after a phrase such as "Listing courtesy of." Advertising a "coming soon" you have no right to sell also misleads buyers who think Marcus can get them in.

blocks.q: Slope Partners agrees to let Hudson & Hart advertise the classic six. What must the revised post include?
c: Nothing extra, since permission was already granted by Slope Partners
The listing broker's name after a phrase like "Listing courtesy of"
A statement that Marcus will split his fee with the listing agent
Slope Partners' written permission letter, posted as an image
blocks.x: Authorization from the exclusive listing broker is the first requirement, and the ad must then clearly disclose that broker right after a phrase such as "Listing courtesy of" or "Listing provided by." The trap is thinking permission alone is enough. The disclosure tells buyers who actually holds the listing. Commission terms and permission letters do not go in the ad.

blocks.html: The March 17 post was the subtle one. Teams may mention unlicensed staff in their ads, but the ad must make clear who is licensed and who is not. A photo of four smiling people under a team name tells a buyer that all four can help them buy a house. Teddy cannot.

blocks.q: Which caption fixes the March 17 post?
c: "Meet the crew!" with the team name changed so that Teddy is no longer in it
"Meet the crew!" with a pinned comment underneath naming the brokerage
"Meet the crew of licensed pros at the Brownstone Collective Team!"
"Kayla, Andre: licensed salespersons. Teddy: photographer, not licensed"
blocks.x: When an ad names unlicensed people, it must say clearly which people are licensees and which are not. The second caption does that and uses the correct license titles. Calling everyone "licensed pros" is the trap: it is worse than silence, because it affirmatively misstates Teddy's status. Removing him from the team name helps but leaves the post unclear about who can act.

blocks.title: Neighborhood names are a Brooklyn sport
blocks.html: Brokers in NYC have stretched neighborhood names for decades: "East Williamsburg" for Bushwick, "Prospect Heights" for Crown Heights, "ProCro" for both. DOS's rule cuts through it: if you say a property is near a well-known area, name the area it is actually in. "Crown Heights, near Prospect Heights" is fine. "Prospect Heights" for a Crown Heights house is not.

blocks.text: Exhibit C: the website and the DMs

blocks.html: The bio linked to brownstonecollective.nyc, a site Andre built. Its home page had the team logo and an IDX search of the whole Brooklyn market. Hudson & Hart appeared nowhere, Diane had never been told the site existed, and the search results pages carried no broker information at all.

blocks.q: What does the regulation require for Andre's site?
c: Diane's approval, broker info on every page, and a link to her site
Nothing, since a personal website is not an advertisement under the rule
Broker information on the home page, since search pages are automated
A disclaimer that the team, not Hudson & Hart, is responsible for the content
blocks.x: A salesperson or team site may exist only with the supervising broker's authorization, stays under the broker's supervision, must show the required broker information on every page including search results pages, and must link from the home page to the broker's site. The home-page-only answer is the trap because it sounds practical; the rule names search results pages specifically.

blocks.html: Andre had built the site on a weekend because buyers kept asking for "your website." He was not trying to hide anything; it simply never occurred to him that a site needs the broker's permission. That is the pattern Diane saw in the whole account. None of the violations made the team more money. Each one was a shortcut that made the team look like its own company, and that impression is exactly what the advertising rule exists to prevent, because a buyer who thinks she is dealing with "Brownstone Collective" does not know which broker is responsible for her deposit.

Kayla had her own version. To push the Crown Heights brownstone, she bought a $300 sponsored Instagram ad on her personal credit card, aimed at renters in Prospect Heights. The listing really was Hudson & Hart's exclusive, and Kayla assumed that was enough.

blocks.q: Was Kayla allowed to buy the sponsored ad for a Hudson & Hart exclusive on her own card?
c: Yes, because a salesperson may advertise any listing her firm holds
Yes, once she adds the broker's name, even without Diane's approval
Only with Diane's approval, since only the broker places or approves ads
No, because paid ads must be bought by the seller and approved by DOS
blocks.x: Only a broker may place ads, and salespersons and teams may advertise only property listed with their own broker and only with that broker's approval. Kayla's listing was the firm's, which is necessary but not enough. Adding the broker's name is the trap: correct content does not replace approval, because the broker supervises everything published in the firm's name. DOS does not pre-approve ads.

blocks.html: The direct messages had a second issue. When a buyer who saw a post asked for details, Andre often moved the conversation to email. Under the rule, the first email to a client or prospect must carry the same broker information an ad does. Later emails in the same thread may omit it. Andre's emails had no signature at all.

blocks.q: Andre sends a new Instagram lead three emails over a week. Which emails need the required broker information?
c: Each of the three, because any email to a consumer is an ad
No email, since email is private correspondence
The one that attaches a listing sheet or a price
The first one, since later emails to the same person may omit it
blocks.x: The regulation requires the broker information in the initial email to a client or prospect, and lets later emails to the same recipient leave it out. Putting a signature block on every email is good practice, but the rule does not demand it. The 'private correspondence' answer is the trap: email is covered by the advertising rule because it is used to solicit business.

blocks.html: Then Jordan read the direct messages. For the Crown Heights brownstone, Marcus had answered some inquiries with "Send me your pre-approval first and I'll set up a time" and others with "Come by Saturday!" Hudson & Hart's standardized operating procedures, posted on the firm's website and notarized as RPL 442-h requires, say pre-approval is not required before a showing.

blocks.q: Why is Marcus's uneven pre-approval demand a problem even if he never meant to discriminate?
c: The SOP is a suggestion, so it matters just when a buyer complains about it
Pre-approval can be required at any time, as long as the agent applies it to some buyers
The posted SOP binds every agent, and uneven use is what the law targets
It becomes a problem if the buyers asked to show pre-approval were in a protected class
blocks.x: Brokers must adopt written procedures saying whether they require ID, an exclusive buyer agreement, or pre-approval, and must apply them to every prospective homebuyer. The law came out of steering findings on Long Island, so unequal treatment is the harm even without proof of intent. The protected-class answer is the trap: the SOP rule does not wait for a fair housing case to be proven.

blocks.title: "I didn't place the ad, the team did"
blocks.html: Only a broker may place ads. Salespersons and teams may advertise only property listed with their own broker, and only with the broker's approval. When an ad breaks the rules, the salesperson who wrote it and the broker who failed to supervise it both answer to DOS. Diane's "I never saw it" is not a defense; it is the violation.

Diane asked one more question: how was Teddy paid? Marcus said Teddy got $400 per shoot, which was fine, and also "a little thank-you" of 10% of Marcus's share whenever a listing Teddy photographed closed. Marcus paid it from his own account, after Hudson & Hart paid him.

blocks.q: Is the 10% "thank-you" a problem if Marcus pays it from his own money after receiving his split?
c: No, because once the split is paid it is Marcus's personal money to spend
Yes, because it shares commissions with an unlicensed person
No, because a photographer is a vendor and vendor bonuses are unregulated
Yes, once the payments total more than $1,000 in one year
blocks.x: A payment that rises with closed deals is a share of commission, and licensees may not share commissions with unlicensed people. A flat fee per photo shoot is a vendor payment and is fine. The trap is the 'my money now' argument: routing the cut through Marcus's personal account changes the path, not the nature of the payment, which DOS treats as a kickback.

blocks.html: Diane stopped the payments that day and paid Teddy a flat day rate going forward. She also wrote down what the case had shown her about her own office: four licensees had run a public brand for two years, and no one at Hudson & Hart had asked where their buyers were coming from. Supervision under Part 175 means regular, frequent, consistent oversight, not a policy binder. A broker who learns about an agent's advertising from a DOS investigator has a supervision problem by definition.

Diane sent the investigator everything, with a cover letter listing what the firm had already done: account renamed "The Brownstone Collective Team at Hudson & Hart Realty," titles fixed, broker information added to every page, the Slope Partners post deleted, Teddy marked as unlicensed, the 10% payments stopped, and a written ad-approval procedure adopted. Many DOS matters end with a settlement in which the licensee pays a fine and agrees to fix the conduct. Marcus's did not, because the complaining buyer had also reported the "guaranteed" appreciation pitch in person, and DOS treated that as misrepresentation.

blocks.title: How a DOS disciplinary case moves

items.title: Complaint
items.html: A consumer, another licensee, or DOS itself raises the issue. Anyone can file.

items.title: Investigation
items.html: An investigator gathers ads, records, and statements. Licensees must cooperate, and brokers must produce the records they are required to keep.

items.title: Notice of hearing
items.html: Under RPL 441-e, written charges go to the licensee at least 10 days before the hearing. If the licensee is a salesperson, the broker is also notified by certified mail.

items.title: Hearing
items.html: An administrative law judge hears evidence. The licensee may appear in person or with a lawyer, and witnesses can be subpoenaed.

items.title: Decision
items.html: Reprimand, fine, suspension, or revocation. A licensee who thinks the decision was arbitrary can bring an Article 78 proceeding in State Supreme Court.

blocks.q: Marcus receives a notice of hearing. He tells Jordan he will skip it, because "salespersons can't be disciplined, the broker's license is the one on the line." What is true?
c: His own license is at risk, and he may appear with a lawyer to defend it
He is right that discipline falls on the broker, but he should attend to support Diane
He may skip it, because DOS needs a criminal conviction first to act against him
He may skip it, because a salesperson's case is decided on written submissions alone
blocks.x: Every licensee, salesperson included, can be reprimanded, fined, suspended, or revoked after a hearing, and RPL 441-e lets him be heard in person or through counsel. Discipline is administrative, so no criminal conviction is needed. The trap is the broker-only belief: Diane can also be charged for failing to supervise, but that adds a respondent; it does not shield Marcus.

blocks.html: The hearing took a morning. The administrative law judge found the blind ads, the misleading area name, the profit guarantee, the unauthorized ad of Slope Partners' listing, and the commission sharing with Teddy. Diane was charged too, for failure to supervise, and settled with a fine and a written supervision plan. Marcus asked Jordan afterward what the worst case could have been.

blocks.q: Which consequence could DOS impose on Marcus by itself, without going to a court?
c: A suspension of his license for a set period
A jail sentence for the misleading advertising
An order that he pay the buyer four times his fee
A conviction for the misdemeanor of misrepresentation
blocks.x: DOS's administrative discipline is reprimand, fine, suspension, or revocation. A misdemeanor charge and any jail time come only through criminal court, prosecuted outside DOS. The four-times penalty is the trap: it is a civil remedy a court awards against someone paid without a license, which DOS cannot impose and which does not fit a licensed salesperson anyway.

blocks.html: Marcus got a fine and a 60-day suspension. During those 60 days he could not show, list, negotiate, or advertise, and Hudson & Hart could not pay him for anything he did in that period. Kayla and Andre took over his active deals under Diane's supervision. Had DOS revoked his license instead, he could not have applied for a new one for a year.

The complaining buyer got something too, though not from DOS. Administrative discipline punishes the licensee; it does not award the consumer damages. Her remedy for the misrepresentation, if she had one, was a civil claim in court, and she had none worth bringing because she never bought the house. What she wanted was for it to stop, and it did. Jordan wrote that distinction in the margin of his notes: DOS protects the public by policing licensees, the courts compensate people who were actually harmed, and criminal prosecutors handle unlicensed activity and other crimes. Three systems, three different questions.

blocks.title: Where the money from fines goes
blocks.html: Under RPL 441-c, half of what DOS collects in license-law fines goes to an anti-discrimination in housing fund. Advertising violations and steering complaints end up paying for fair housing enforcement, which is one reason DOS pursues blind ads and uneven buyer treatment as hard as it does.

items: Every ad, post, website, and team page goes through a written approval log before it goes live.
Agents list every social account they use for business, and Diane follows each one.
The firm's SOP is printed on the back of every showing sheet, so agents see it before they answer a buyer.
Unlicensed staff are paid hourly or per job, never per closed deal.

blocks.html: The Brownstone Collective Team at Hudson & Hart Realty still has 14,000 followers. Jordan noticed that engagement did not drop when the bio got longer.

items: Every ad needs the broker's name plus the broker's address or phone; anything less is a blind ad.

Team names use "team," avoid "group," "realty," and "associates," and either list full licensed names or add "at" or "of" the broker. Unlicensed people stay out of the name and must be labeled in ads.
Salespersons are "licensed real estate salespersons," never "licensed sales agents" or "sales associates."
Another broker's exclusive needs that broker's permission and a "Listing courtesy of" credit; area names must be accurate and profits never guaranteed.
The posted SOP binds every agent, and uneven treatment of buyers is the harm the law targets.
DOS discipline (reprimand, fine, suspension, revocation) follows notice and a hearing and reaches salespersons and the supervising broker alike.

lessons.title: Case file: The Well Behind the Barn
lessons.tagline: A Brooklyn couple, a farmhouse in Chautauqua County, and three things the seller would rather not say.
objectives: Apply the Property Condition Disclosure Act to a real sale: who fills out the form, when it is due, when it must be revised, and what a willful failure costs
Decide what a seller must say about an uncapped gas well under RPL 242 and what the agent does with that information
Apply RPL 443-a to a stigma question asked in writing, without lying and without breaching confidentiality
Apply the listing, escrow, referral, and record rules a broker must follow on an upstate sale

blocks.title: From Crown Heights to Chautauqua
blocks.html: Sam and Ruth Adler have rented in Crown Heights for eleven years. Ruth now works remotely, and they want land: a farmhouse, a barn, room for goats. They asked Jordan to help, and Jordan explained that Hudson & Hart does not work in western New York. He did know someone who does. Hannah Lisowski took the salesperson course with him and now works for Lakeshore Realty in Jamestown, under broker Gil Moreno. Hannah has a new listing that fits: a 1910 farmhouse on 38 acres in the town of Ellery, owned by Walt Dziedzic, 74, whose family farmed it for three generations. Before Jordan sends the Adlers' contact information, Hannah says Lakeshore will pay "a referral fee, 25% of my side." Jordan wonders who should get that check.

Referrals between brokers are ordinary. What matters is the path the money takes. Under RPL 442 a broker may share a fee with another licensed broker, and a salesperson may be paid for real estate work only by his own sponsoring broker. Jordan is a salesperson. Hannah is a salesperson. Neither of them can write or receive this check personally.

blocks.q: How must the referral fee be paid?
c: Hannah pays Jordan directly, since both hold NY salesperson licenses
Lakeshore pays Jordan directly, since he did the referring
Lakeshore pays Hudson & Hart, and Diane pays Jordan his share
Hannah pays Jordan through Venmo, reported as a gift
blocks.x: A salesperson can receive compensation for real estate work only from the sponsoring broker, and brokers share fees broker to broker. So Lakeshore pays Hudson & Hart under a written referral agreement, and Diane pays Jordan under his agreement with the firm. Salesperson-to-salesperson payment is the trap: two licenses do not make it lawful, because neither of them is the other's broker.

blocks.html: Gil sent Diane a one-page referral agreement. Jordan's role ended there, though he stayed on the email chain as a courtesy to the Adlers. Everything that follows is Hannah's deal, with Jordan watching and asking questions.

Hannah's listing appointment with Walt was at his kitchen table. Walt had two requests. First, he wanted $310,000 "in my pocket" and told Hannah to keep anything she got above that. Second, he handed her the blank Property Condition Disclosure Statement and said, "You know what they want to hear. Fill it out and I'll sign it." Hannah's listing agreement form also had a blank she had forgotten to complete: the expiration date.

blocks.q: Which response to Walt keeps Hannah within the rules?
c: Set a percentage fee, have Walt complete the PCDS himself, and fill in an end date
Accept the $310,000 net terms, complete the PCDS with Walt, and leave the end date open
Accept net terms if Walt signs a waiver, and complete the PCDS from the town's records
Set a percentage commission, complete the PCDS herself, and have Walt initial each page
blocks.x: Net listings are prohibited in New York, so Hannah needs a commission she can disclose. The PCDS is the seller's statement, made from his own knowledge; the form itself says it is not the agent's representation, so Hannah may explain it but not fill it in. Exclusive listings must state when they expire. The initialing choice is the trap: Walt's initials do not turn Hannah's answers into his knowledge.

blocks.html: Walt signed a six-month exclusive right to sell at 6%, with the expiration date filled in. Hannah gave him the required explanation of what an exclusive right to sell means compared with an exclusive agency, and left him the PCDS to complete. She told him the form is due to a buyer before the buyer signs a binding contract, and that he could check "UNKN" (unknown) for anything he truly did not know.
Walt returned the PCDS three days later. Hannah read it at her desk with the listing photos open beside it.

head: Question (paraphrased)
Walt's answer
What Hannah knows
rows: Any flooding, water seepage, or dampness in the basement?
Walt showed her the sump pump he runs every April and the water line on the fieldstone wall
Is any of the property in a FEMA designated floodplain?
A creek runs along the south edge of the property; the FEMA map shows the lower pasture in a flood zone
Have you received FEMA or other federal assistance for flood damage?
Walt mentioned a federal grant after a creek flood took out the barn floor in 2019
Any known material defects not listed above?
Walt said the property has "an old gas well that's been there forever"
Age of the structure, heating, water source
blocks.caption: Walt's PCDS, and Hannah's notes

blocks.q: Walt checked "UNKN" for basement water even though he runs a sump pump every April. What is the legal significance?
c: It has no significance, since "unknown" is an accepted answer on the PCDS
It shifts responsibility to Hannah, who saw the pump during the listing
It is harmless, because the PCDS is not a warranty and the buyer can inspect
A willful misstatement that exposes him to the buyer's actual damages
blocks.x: "UNKN" is for facts the seller truly does not know. Using it to hide a known condition is a false answer, and RPL 465 makes a seller liable for the buyer's actual losses for a willful failure to comply. The not-a-warranty answer is the trap: the form is not a guarantee of condition, but it is a statement of the seller's actual knowledge, and lying on it is still lying.

blocks.html: Hannah called Walt and walked him through each line. She did not change his form. She told him what she had seen, what he had told her, and that she, as his agent, could not stay silent with buyers about known material defects no matter what the form said. Walt revised the basement answer to YES and described the spring water. Then they got to the flood questions.

blocks.q: Since March 20, 2024, which flood item must Walt answer on the PCDS?
c: The flood insurance premium he expects the buyer to pay over the next year
Whether he ever got FEMA or other federal aid for flood damage
The dollar amount of any flood loss that he chose not to insure
Whether he will provide a $500 credit in place of the flood section
blocks.x: The 2024 form added flood questions: whether the property is in a FEMA floodplain or special flood hazard area, whether federal law requires flood insurance, whether there is flood insurance, whether there are past flood claims, and whether the seller received federal assistance such as FEMA aid for flood damage. The $500 credit is the trap: it was the old opt-out, repealed when the flood questions arrived.

blocks.html: Walt corrected the floodplain answer after Hannah showed him the FEMA map, and answered YES to the 2019 assistance. He was annoyed but not surprised. "Everybody up here knows that creek," he said. That is exactly the point: everybody up here knows, and a couple from Crown Heights does not.

blocks.title: "The buyer can inspect" does not cure a false answer
blocks.html: Sellers and some agents argue that an inspection makes the PCDS irrelevant. It does not. The seller's statement covers what the seller actually knows, including things an inspector cannot see in April sunshine: spring flooding, a well, a past claim. A false answer remains a willful failure even if a sharp inspector might have caught it.

The last line on Walt's form was blank. When Hannah asked about the "old gas well," Walt took her out past the barn. In a stand of sumac sat a rusted pipe about eight inches across, sticking a foot out of the ground with no cap on it. Walt said his father drilled it in the 1950s to heat the house and abandoned it decades ago. On cold mornings you could sometimes smell gas near it. Chautauqua County sits over old gas fields, and wells like this one are scattered across western New York.

Walt's first reaction was the one Hannah had been warned about in class. "Leave that line blank," he said. "Nobody's going to walk back here, and I don't want city people spooked." Hannah owed Walt loyalty and confidentiality as his agent. She also owed every buyer honesty about known material facts, and a licensee who helps hide a defect is acting with the kind of untrustworthiness RPL 441-c lets DOS punish.

blocks.q: Walt tells Hannah not to mention the well to anyone. What is her best course?
c: Keep quiet, since confidentiality to the seller outranks duties to buyers
Explain she cannot hide it, and withdraw if Walt insists
Mention it to buyers who ask directly whether there are gas wells
Keep quiet but note the well in her private file to protect herself later
blocks.x: Confidentiality covers things like the seller's bottom line, not known material defects. A licensee may not take part in hiding a physical hazard, so Hannah explains the rule and, if Walt still refuses, ends the listing. The 'only if asked' answer is the trap: it borrows the written-inquiry idea from stigma law, which applies to psychological stigma, not to a leaking well.

blocks.html: Walt grumbled, then gave in once Hannah pointed out that a buyer who found the pipe after closing would have his name on a lawsuit and hers on a DOS complaint. Then she explained what the statute itself requires.

blocks.q: What does RPL 242 require of Walt regarding the well?
c: Nothing, since the well was drilled before any disclosure laws existed
Cap the well at his own expense before he is allowed to list the farm
Disclose the well if the buyer's lender asks about gas wells
Inform the buyer about the uncapped well before the contract
blocks.x: RPL 242 requires a seller with actual knowledge of an uncapped natural gas well on the property to inform the purchaser before entering into the contract. The law requires disclosure, not repair, so the capping choice is the trap: capping may be wise and buyers may demand it, but it is a negotiation, not a condition of listing. When the well was drilled does not matter.

blocks.html: Walt put it in writing on the PCDS and Hannah added it to the listing's disclosure sheet, which is safer than the bare statutory duty to "inform." She also told Walt what buyers would likely do with the information: ask for an inspection by someone who knows wells, call the Department of Environmental Conservation about plugging, and negotiate the cost. Methane near an open pipe is a safety issue first and a price issue second. Walt's uncapped gas well was now a known, priced problem instead of a lawsuit waiting to happen.

The Adlers drove up on a Saturday in May and loved everything, including the creek. On the drive home Ruth read local news archives on her phone and found an article: in 1987, Walt's younger brother had died by suicide in the barn. The Adlers' buyer agent, Craig Mott of Southern Tier Homes, emailed Hannah on Monday: "My clients ask in writing whether anyone died on the property, and how."

blocks.q: How should Hannah handle Craig's written question?
c: Ask Walt if he wants to respond; relay any answer with his consent
Tell Craig that nothing of that kind happened, to protect the seller
Answer fully right away, since a written question overrides the seller's privacy
Refuse to pass the question to Walt, since the law bars any discussion of deaths
blocks.x: Under RPL 443-a a death, suicide, or homicide on the property is not a material defect and need not be disclosed. When a buyer asks in writing, the seller decides whether to answer, and the seller's agent may report the answer with the seller's consent. The trap is the protective lie: silence is allowed, but a false denial is misrepresentation, the one thing the statute never permits.

blocks.html: Walt answered, through Hannah, in one sentence: yes, his brother died in the barn in 1987, and the family would rather not discuss it further. The Adlers thanked him and did not ask again. Ruth said later that the honest answer made her trust the rest of the PCDS. That is the practical case for stigma disclosure handled the right way: the law protects the seller's silence, and the agent protects the seller from the lie.

The Adlers wanted to make an offer that Sunday night, from Brooklyn, before a couple from Erie who had also seen the farm could act. Craig had the purchase and sale form ready to e-sign. Walt's corrected PCDS, with the new flood answers and the well, had been typed up but never signed, and Walt was at his granddaughter's graduation until Monday afternoon. The only signed version in the file was his first one, with the wrong answers. The Adlers had seen the listing's disclosure sheet, but not the form itself.

blocks.q: The Adlers want to sign the purchase and sale form Sunday. Walt can sign the corrected PCDS Monday. What should happen?
c: The Adlers sign Sunday, and Walt delivers the corrected PCDS at closing
The Adlers sign Sunday after getting the first signed PCDS, since some form was delivered
Walt delivers the corrected PCDS before the Adlers sign a binding contract
Walt gives a $500 credit in the contract instead of the corrected PCDS
blocks.x: The PCDS must reach the buyer before the buyer signs a binding contract, and the version that counts is the one the seller knows to be accurate. Delivering a form Walt already knows is wrong does not satisfy the law. The 'some form was delivered' answer is the trap: an inaccurate statement knowingly left in place is the willful failure the statute punishes.

blocks.html: Hannah had Walt sign and scan the revised form from the graduation party on Monday at noon. Craig sent it to the Adlers, they read it on the subway, and they signed at 6 p.m. The Erie couple never made an offer.

That same Monday, Walt called Hannah with a new idea. His nephew, who is not licensed, had a friend from Buffalo who might pay $300,000 cash. "If I sell to him myself, I don't owe Lakeshore anything, right? You didn't find him." Walt's listing agreement was an exclusive right to sell, signed eleven days earlier.

blocks.q: If Walt sells to his nephew's friend during the listing term, what does he owe Lakeshore?
c: Nothing, since Lakeshore did not find the buyer
Half the commission, since the broker was not the cause
Nothing, if he pays the nephew a finder's fee instead
The full commission under the exclusive right to sell
blocks.x: Under an exclusive right to sell, the broker earns the commission if the property sells during the term, no matter who finds the buyer. That is the difference from an exclusive agency listing, where an owner who finds his own buyer owes nothing. The finder's fee choice is doubly wrong: it does not cancel the listing, and paying an unlicensed person for procuring a buyer creates its own problem.

blocks.html: Walt laughed and said he had read that paragraph and forgotten it. The nephew's friend never called anyway.

Upstate, the offer is usually the contract. Craig filled in the regional purchase and sale form for $296,000, subject to attorney approval, a well and septic inspection, a gas well inspection, and financing. The Adlers signed it on a Thursday evening, and Craig handed Hannah a $5,000 deposit check payable to Lakeshore Realty. Hannah's next stop was her daughter's soccer game. The bank was closed. The firm's escrow account is at a bank in Jamestown; Hannah's personal account is at a credit union two blocks from the field with a night drop.

blocks.q: What should Hannah do with the $5,000 check?
c: Put it in her personal account overnight and transfer it on Friday
Endorse it to Walt so the seller holds his own buyer's deposit
Hold the check safely and turn it over to Gil for the escrow account
Deposit it into Lakeshore's operating account, which is in the same bank
blocks.x: Client money goes to the broker for deposit into a special escrow account, never mixed with a licensee's own funds or the firm's operating money. A salesperson's job is to deliver it to the broker promptly. The overnight deposit is the trap because the money comes back intact; it is still commingling, and DOS treats the intent to return it as no defense.

blocks.html: Hannah kept the check in a sealed envelope and gave it to Gil at 8 a.m. Friday. He deposited it into Lakeshore's escrow account that morning, logged it, and gave the Adlers a receipt. Gil keeps the deposit there until closing or until the parties agree in writing (or a court orders) who gets it.

Two weeks after the attorneys approved the contract, a June storm sent the creek over its banks for the first time since 2019. Water reached the barn foundation and, Walt told Hannah, came within a foot of the house. The house stayed dry, but Walt's homeowner's insurer sent an adjuster for the barn, and Walt filed a claim.

blocks.q: The contract is signed and closing is set for August. Does Walt owe the Adlers anything under the PCDS law?
c: No, because the PCDS duty ends when the buyer signs the contract
Yes, a revised PCDS as soon as practicable, since his form is now wrong
No, because flood events after signing are covered by the risk of loss rule instead
Yes, if the buyers' lender requires flood insurance for the mortgage
blocks.x: If a seller learns something before title passes (or the buyer moves in) that makes the delivered statement materially inaccurate, RPL 462 requires a revised statement as soon as practicable. Walt's form says no flood claims; now there is one. The risk-of-loss answer is the trap: that rule decides who bears damage before closing, but it does not erase the separate duty to update the disclosure.

blocks.html: Walt delivered a revised PCDS that week. The Adlers' attorney asked for a credit toward drainage work, Walt agreed to $4,000, and the deal closed in August. The well was plugged in September, at the Adlers' expense, with the cost already priced into the deal.

Gil's last task was the file. Lakeshore keeps everything: the listing agreement with its expiration date, the agency and fair housing disclosure forms, the original and revised PCDS, the gas well notice, the purchase and sale contract, the escrow receipt and disbursement record, the referral agreement with Hudson & Hart, and the closing statement. Diane does the same on her side for the referral.

blocks.q: How long must Lakeshore keep the transaction file under DOS rules?
c: Three years, the record retention period in 19 NYCRR 175.23
One year from closing, the same period as a revoked licensee's waiting period
Six years, the statute of limitations for a breach of contract suit
Until the listing agreement expires, since that ends the broker's duties
blocks.x: Brokers must keep transaction records, including listings, contracts, disclosures, and closing statements, for at least 3 years. The 6-year choice is the trap: it is the contract statute of limitations, and many brokers keep files that long by choice, but the DOS rule is 3 years. One year is the relicensing wait after revocation, a different rule.

blocks.title: Disclosure rules that are New York's own
blocks.html: Three of this case's rules exist only in New York statutes: the PCDS under RPL Article 14 (with flood questions since 2024), the uncapped gas well disclosure in RPL 242, and the stigma rule in RPL 443-a. Gas wells come up most in western and southern-tier counties. Stigma questions come up everywhere.
Jordan got his referral share from Diane in his next commission check. The Adlers sent a photo in October: two goats, a capped pipe behind the barn, and a creek well inside its banks.

items: Referral fees move broker to broker; salespersons are paid only by their own sponsoring broker.

The PCDS is the seller's statement of actual knowledge, delivered before the buyer signs a binding contract. Agents explain it but never fill it in, and "unknown" is only for what the seller truly does not know.
A willful failure exposes the seller to the buyer's actual damages, and new information before closing requires a revised PCDS as soon as practicable.
RPL 242 requires a seller who knows of an uncapped gas well to inform the buyer before the contract; disclosure, not repair, is the legal duty.
Under RPL 443-a deaths and similar stigmas need not be disclosed; a written question is answered only with the seller's consent, and never with a lie.
Deposits go to the broker's escrow account without stopping in anyone's personal account, and the file is kept at least 3 years.

lessons.title: Case file: The Last Month on New Dorp Lane
lessons.tagline: A Staten Island broker retires after 38 years. His license ends with him. His listings, his escrow account, his files, and six salespersons do not.
objectives: Decide what happens to listings, pending deals, and associated licensees when a broker winds down a brokerage and a successor firm opens
Apply the licensing rules for an LLC brokerage, an associate broker who also holds a broker license, and changes of name, address, and association, including the fees
Apply the escrow, record-keeping, and compensation rules (including 175.7 and the bar on paying unlicensed people) to money left over when a firm closes
Decide who may collect, pay, or sue for a commission after a licensee changes firms or leaves the business

blocks.title: Coffee and an announcement
blocks.html: Frank Castellano has run Castellano Realty from a storefront on New Dorp Lane in Staten Island since 1988. He is 72, his knees are done with walk-up showings, and his wife has already bought the condo in Sarasota. On the first Friday in October he brings in coffee and tells his office the news: he stops taking new business on October 31, and his broker license, which expires December 31, will not be renewed. His associate broker of eleven years, Gina Morales, will open her own firm in the same neighborhood. Frank has 41 active listings, 7 deals under contract, $31,400 in his escrow account, three filing cabinets, and six salespersons who want to know where they will be working in November. Diane Hart has known Frank for twenty years, and two of his salespersons have called her about joining Hudson & Hart. She sends Jordan to New Dorp Lane on Monday to help with the paperwork and, she says, "to watch how a brokerage ends, because nobody teaches that." Frank's first idea is simple: "Gina takes over everything. Listings, deals, the account. We just change the sign."

Jordan pulled the listing file first. Every agreement had the same parties: the seller and Castellano Realty, Frank Castellano, broker. The salesperson's name appeared only on the signature line as the person who took the listing "on behalf of" the broker. Most were exclusive right to sell agreements running six months, and eleven ran past the end of the year.

blocks.q: Frank wants all 41 listings to move to Gina's new firm on November 1. How do they get there?
c: They move automatically, because Gina supervised most of them as associate broker
They move with the salesperson who took each listing, if that salesperson joins Gina
Each seller decides; a seller who wants Gina signs a new agreement with her
Frank may sell the listings to Gina as an asset of his business, without seller consent
blocks.x: A listing agreement is an agency contract between the seller and the broker. It does not follow a supervisor or a salesperson, and an agency relationship cannot be handed to a new principal without the client agreeing. Frank should tell each seller he is closing, offer a release, and let the seller choose. The 'sell the book' choice is the trap: a seller's trust is not inventory, and a new firm needs its own agreement and its own agency disclosure.

blocks.html: Frank wrote a short letter to all 41 sellers. It said he was retiring, that their agreements with Castellano Realty would be released effective October 31 if they wished, and that they were free to list with any broker, including Gina's new firm, Hudson & Hart, or anyone else. Thirty-two sellers signed new agreements with Gina. Five went to other firms. Four took their homes off the market for the winter. Jordan noticed that the letter did not tell anyone where to go. Diane had told him why: steering a client to a friend's firm in exchange for anything of value is a kickback, and the seller's choice has to be the seller's.

blocks.title: Why the State cares when a brokerage closes
blocks.html: The license law exists to protect the public, not licensees. A closing brokerage is exactly when the public gets hurt: deposits sit in an account nobody watches, sellers are bound to a firm that no longer answers the phone, and files disappear. DOS licenses the broker personally, holds the broker accountable for every associated licensee and every dollar in escrow, and expects the broker to wind down as carefully as the broker ran the business.

Gina had been an associate broker since 2014: broker-qualified, but working under Frank's name and supervision. She wanted a limited liability company, Morales Realty LLC, with herself as the sole member. Her accountant filed the articles of organization with the Department of State's Division of Corporations in early October. Gina assumed that filing made her a brokerage.

blocks.q: Morales Realty LLC has been formed. What else must happen before the company can take listings?
c: Nothing more, since Gina already holds a license that qualifies her as a broker
The LLC must be licensed as a broker, with Gina licensed as its representative broker
Gina must pass the broker exam again, because her qualifying exam was taken as an individual
The LLC must register with the county clerk, which issues licenses for business entities
blocks.x: RPL Article 12-A requires a license for any person, partnership, LLC, or corporation in the brokerage business. Forming the company is corporate paperwork; the company itself needs a DOS broker license, issued through a member or manager who is licensed as its broker. The 'already licensed' choice is the trap: Gina's associate broker license lets her work under someone else's brokerage, not run her own.

blocks.html: Gina filed the LLC's broker application in eAccessNY with the $185 fee. Then she asked a question that Jordan did not expect. Frank still had seven pending deals and two months on his license, and he wanted her help closing them. Could she stay Frank's associate broker through December while also being the broker of Morales Realty?

blocks.q: Can Gina remain Frank's associate broker through December while she holds the broker license for Morales Realty LLC?
c: Yes, the law lets an associate broker also keep a separate broker's license
No, a licensee holds one license at a time, with one sponsoring broker
Yes, provided Frank and Gina merge their firms into a single licensed company
No, she has to surrender the associate broker license when her LLC applies
blocks.x: RPL 440 says an associate broker may also retain a separate broker's license under an individual name, trade name, partnership, LLC, or corporation. This is the dual licensure the syllabus mentions. Both firms should know and agree, and each deal's commission flows through the broker on that deal. The one-license choice is the trap: it describes the general one-sponsor expectation for salespersons, not the statutory exception for associate brokers.

blocks.html: That settled Gina. Then Tony Bianchi, a salesperson with nine years at Castellano and the office's best rental agent, asked Gina if he could put in $20,000 and become a 20% member of the LLC. "I'd keep selling, same as now, just as an owner." Tony had never taken the broker course.

blocks.q: Tony wants to become a member of Morales Realty LLC while staying a licensed salesperson for the firm. What does the license law say?
c: He may, as long as his share is 49% or less and Gina keeps control of the company
He may, if Gina signs a written consent and files it with DOS as a dual license
He may not become a member until he has been a salesperson for at least ten years
He may not; an LLC member cannot also hold a salesperson license
blocks.x: RPL 441-b bars DOS from issuing a salesperson license to an officer of a corporation, a manager or member of an LLC, or a member of a partnership licensed as a broker. Owners of a brokerage who act in it must be broker-qualified. The percentage choice is the trap: the bar applies to any membership, not just controlling ones. Tony could invest only by first qualifying as a broker, or stay a salesperson paid a larger split.

blocks.html: Tony stayed a salesperson and enrolled in the 75-hour broker course. Gina gave him a better split instead of a share of the company.

DOS issued the LLC's license on October 24. Gina's first office was a sublet room in the back of an insurance agency on New Dorp Lane, two doors from Frank's. She framed the broker license and hung it beside the fair housing notice, because a broker's license must be conspicuously displayed at the principal place of business. Her four salespersons, including Tony and two others from Castellano, were associated with Morales Realty in eAccessNY, at $20 per record of association, after Frank filed their terminations. Each received a new pocket card showing Morales Realty as sponsoring broker.

One of the four had a different problem. Lisa Chen had married in September and now used the name Lisa Chen Walsh. Her new business cards, email signature, and Instagram all said Lisa Walsh. Her license still said Lisa Chen.

blocks.q: What should Lisa do about her new name?
c: Nothing until renewal, since DOS updates names on the renewal application for free
Have Gina note the new name in the office file, since the broker keeps the license
File a name change with DOS and advertise under the name her license shows
Use either name freely, since a marriage certificate proves she is the same licensee
blocks.x: Ads must use the licensee's licensed name, so the name on the cards and posts has to match DOS records. A salesperson's name change is filed with DOS (the fee is $50 outside of renewal, under RPL 441-a). The renewal choice is the trap: Lisa's license runs another year, and she cannot advertise under an unlicensed name until then. A broker's name change or change of license status costs $150.

blocks.html: In January, Gina's lease for a real storefront on Hylan Boulevard started. She moved the computers on a Saturday and planned to deal with DOS "when things calm down." Jordan, by then helping Diane with Hudson & Hart's own records, mentioned it to Diane, who called Gina that night.

blocks.q: Gina moves Morales Realty's principal office. What does the license law require, and what is the risk of waiting?
c: Notice for each licensee at $10 apiece; moving without it suspends licenses
Notice to DOS within 90 days at no charge, after which a late fee of $50 applies
Notice on the LLC's next renewal application, since addresses update at renewal
Notice to the Division of Corporations, which forwards address changes to DOS
blocks.x: RPL 441-a requires the broker to notify DOS of a change in the principal business address for the broker and each associated licensee, with a $10 fee per licensee named. A change made without notice operates to suspend the licenses until DOS lifts the suspension. Gina and her four salespersons cost $50. The corporations choice is the trap: the LLC's corporate filing address and its license record are separate systems.

blocks.html: Gina filed the change of address Monday morning, before anyone showed a property. Five licenses, $50, and no suspension. She hung the license on the Hylan Boulevard wall the same day.

Back in October, Frank's bookkeeper printed the escrow ledger. On Staten Island, as in the rest of downstate, the seller's attorney usually holds the contract down payment, so Frank's account held smaller money.

head: Item
Amount
Status
rows: Good faith deposits on 3 accepted offers (no contracts yet)
Security deposits and first month's rent, 5 leases starting Nov. 1
Owed to landlords at lease start, per agreements
Security deposit, Richmond Road apartment Frank manages
Tenant in place; Frank's management agreement ends Dec. 31
blocks.caption: Castellano Realty special escrow account, October 6

blocks.html: Frank's plan for the account was practical, by his standards. He had a final payroll, a final rent check, and a printer lease to buy out. "I'll move it into operating, pay the bills, and pay everybody back from the November commissions. Every dollar is accounted for."

blocks.q: What should Frank do with the $31,400 in his escrow account?
c: Borrow it for closing costs if each dollar is repaid within 30 days and documented
Move it to his operating account, since he is personally liable for it either way
Keep the whole balance in escrow until his license expires, then mail out refunds
Pay each item out under its agreement or move it with written consent
blocks.x: Escrow money belongs to the people who deposited it, not to the broker. Moving it into operating funds is commingling, and spending it is conversion, both grounds for revocation even if every dollar comes back. Frank should disburse each item as its agreement provides and get written consent before transferring any balance to a successor broker. The 'repay in 30 days' choice is the trap: a documented loan from escrow is still conversion.
