blocks.html: Frank grumbled and paid his printer lease from his own savings. The lease money went to the five landlords on November 1 with the signed leases. The three good faith deposits followed the offers: two became contracts and the deposits went to the sellers' attorneys' escrow accounts; one buyer walked and got a refund. The Richmond Road owner moved his management to Gina, and the tenant's $2,600 security deposit moved to Morales Realty's escrow account with a letter signed by the owner and a notice to the tenant of the new bank. Frank closed the escrow account with a zero balance on December 30 and kept the final statement.

Vinny Esposito, a salesperson for 14 years, had two of Frank's seven pending sales. He joined Hudson & Hart on November 3. The first deal, a Great Kills colonial at $780,000 with a 4% commission to Castellano, closed on November 20. Vinny's split with Frank was 60%. At the closing, the seller's attorney asked whom to write the commission check to. Vinny, who was there out of habit, said, "Make it out to me. Frank's in Florida half the time anyway."

blocks.q: Who should receive the $31,200 commission on the Great Kills closing?
c: Vinny, because he did the work and Castellano Realty is closing
Hudson & Hart, because Vinny is now associated with Diane's firm
Castellano Realty, which then pays Vinny his split for the deal
The seller's attorney, in escrow until DOS approves the transfer
blocks.x: The commission is earned by the broker who holds the listing agreement, here Castellano Realty, whose license is still active. A salesperson may be paid only by the broker he was associated with when he did the work, so Frank pays Vinny his 60% ($18,720) even though Vinny now works elsewhere. The Hudson & Hart choice is the trap: a new sponsor gets no share of a deal done entirely under the old one, unless the brokers agree to it.

blocks.html: The check went to Castellano Realty. Frank deposited it to his operating account and paid Vinny his $18,720 within the week, with a commission statement for both of their records. The second deal was worse. A Tottenville buyer's financing fell apart, the contract ended, and two weeks later the seller sold to the same buyer, now with a cash partner, at a slightly lower price. The seller refused to pay any commission, saying the first contract had "failed." Vinny was furious and drafted a small claims complaint against the seller in his own name.

blocks.q: Vinny believes the Tottenville seller owes a commission. Who can bring that claim?
c: Vinny, in his own name, because he personally procured the buyer
Diane, because Vinny now works under her license and supervision
Castellano Realty, the broker with the listing agreement and the license
Nobody, because a commission claim ends when the broker stops doing business
blocks.x: The listing agreement runs between the seller and the broker, so the commission claim belongs to Castellano Realty, which was licensed when the claim arose (RPL 442-d requires that). Vinny's rights run against Frank under their commission agreement, not against the seller. The 'Vinny procured the buyer' choice is the trap: procuring cause decides whether the broker earned a fee, not who may sue for it. Frank's later retirement does not erase an earned claim.

blocks.html: Frank's attorney sent the seller a demand letter citing the listing agreement's protection clause and the fact that Castellano had introduced the buyer. The seller paid a reduced fee to settle. Frank paid Vinny his share of it.

blocks.title: "Licensed" and "associated" are two different things
blocks.html: A license can be valid while the licensee cannot work. Vinny's license was current the whole time, but between Frank's termination on October 31 and Diane's association on November 3 he had no sponsoring broker, so he could not act as a salesperson for anyone. Exam items love the salesperson with a valid pocket card and no current association. The answer is always that he waits for the new broker's filing.

Frank's license expired on December 31. In February he called Gina from Sarasota. His golf partners kept asking about Staten Island; one wanted to sell his mother's house in Eltingville, another wanted to rent out a condo. "I'll send them all to you. Just give me 25% of whatever you make, like a referral fee. Brokers do it all the time."

blocks.q: Can Gina pay Frank a 25% referral fee on business he sends her in February?
c: Yes, since a referral is not a sale and requires no license in New York
Yes, if Frank's license was active for at least 2 years before it expired
No, because New York bars paying referral fees to anyone, licensed or not
No, because paying him now is paying an unlicensed person
blocks.x: Brokers may pay referral fees to other licensed brokers, which is what Frank means by 'brokers do it all the time.' Once his license expired, Frank is an unlicensed person, and paying him for sending clients is sharing compensation with an unlicensed person. Frank could also be sued for up to four times any fee he collects. The choice that bars every referral fee is the trap: licensed broker-to-broker referral fees are lawful and common.

blocks.html: Gina thanked Frank for the names and told him why she could not pay him. Frank had two lawful options. He could renew his broker license, completing his continuing education first, and refer as a licensed broker, or he could refer for free, as a friend. He chose free, and a case of wine from Gina at Christmas, which was a gift, not a fee tied to any deal.

The New Dorp Lane lease ended January 31. The landlord wanted the space empty. Frank's three filing cabinets held listing agreements, agency and fair housing disclosure forms, contracts, closing statements, escrow records, and commission statements going back to 2016. Frank told Jordan to call a shredding truck.

blocks.q: Frank is retiring and the lease is ending. What must happen to his transaction files?
c: Shred them at closing, since record duties end with the broker's license
Keep them at least 3 years, available to DOS, despite the closed business
Give them to Gina, who becomes responsible for Castellano's past deals
Keep the escrow records for 3 years; the rest may be shredded at once
blocks.x: Under 19 NYCRR 175.23 a broker keeps transaction records (listings, disclosures, contracts, closing statements, escrow and commission records) for at least 3 years and must make them available to DOS. Closing the business does not shorten that. The 'give them to Gina' choice is the trap: Gina can store files under an agreement, but Frank remains responsible for his own firm's records and for any complaint arising from them.

blocks.html: The shredding truck took only files from deals completed more than three years earlier. Everything newer went into labeled boxes in a climate-controlled storage unit in Bloomfield, with a written index and a key left with Frank's son, who lives on the Island. Frank put a copy of every termination he had filed and the final escrow statement in the first box.
Gina's marketing person, an unlicensed freelancer, drafted a grand opening ad for the Staten Island Advance and Instagram in late October.

blocks.title: Draft ad, October 27
blocks.html:
CASTELLANO REALTY IS NOW MORALES REALTY!
Same great team, same great listings: all 41 homes now available through us!
Call Gina, Broker, 718-555-0190
New Dorp Lane, Staten Island

blocks.q: Which problem in the draft ad matters most?
c: It names Gina as broker, which only the LLC itself may be called
It claims Castellano's listings, which only the sellers can move
It gives the office's street, which is optional under the ad rules
It was drafted by an unlicensed freelancer, which DOS prohibits
blocks.x: On October 27 every listing was still Castellano Realty's, and only sellers who signed new agreements with Morales Realty could be advertised by Gina, and only then as her own listings. Advertising another broker's exclusives without permission, and implying Castellano had merged into her firm, misleads the public. The freelancer choice is the trap: unlicensed staff may prepare ads that the broker approves. The ad also needs the firm's full licensed name, Morales Realty LLC.

blocks.html: The ad that ran on November 5 said: "Morales Realty LLC, a new Staten Island brokerage led by Gina Morales, Licensed Real Estate Broker," with the Hylan Boulevard address once it existed, and showed only the 32 homes whose sellers had signed with her. Frank's name did not appear.

blocks.text: The bonus from the other side

blocks.html: In March, Tony brought Morales Realty its first big buyer: a couple moving from Bay Ridge who had signed a written buyer agreement with the firm promising a 2% fee, to be paid by the buyers unless a seller offered to cover it. They liked a Todt Hill house listed by another brokerage. The seller, eager to sell before summer, told Tony through her agent that she would pay Morales Realty a $10,000 "bonus" if the buyers signed by April 1, on top of whatever the buyers paid.

blocks.q: May Morales Realty accept the seller's $10,000 bonus while representing the buyers?
c: Yes, but only with full disclosure to and consent of all parties
Yes, because the buyer agreement allows a seller to cover the fee
No, since a buyer's broker may never receive money from a seller
No, since bonuses tied to deadlines count as kickbacks under RESPA
blocks.x: Under 19 NYCRR 175.7 a broker may not collect compensation from more than one party to a transaction without full disclosure and the consent of all parties. A deadline bonus from the seller also gives the buyers' broker a reason to rush its own clients, which is exactly why they must know. The buyer-agreement choice is the trap: a seller covering the agreed fee is different from an extra payment on top of it.

blocks.html: Tony told the buyers in writing about the offer, and Gina sent a short disclosure to the seller's broker. The buyers decided the bonus should come off their own fee instead, so the seller's $10,000 reduced what they owed Morales Realty. Everyone signed the disclosure, and the buyers signed their contract on March 28.

Jordan's notes from the four months fill six pages. The last line reads: "A brokerage is a license, a bank account, a filing cabinet, and a lot of contracts. Closing one means closing every one of them."

items: Listing agreements belong to the broker, and when a broker closes, each seller decides where to go. A successor firm needs new agreements before it lists or advertises a home.

An LLC or corporation needs its own broker license through a licensed member or officer. An associate broker may also keep a separate broker license, but an LLC member or corporate officer cannot hold a salesperson license.

Report changes to DOS: address changes ($10 per licensee; moving without notice suspends licenses), salesperson name changes ($50), broker name or status changes ($150), and new associations ($20) after the old broker files a termination.
Escrow money is paid out under its agreements or transferred with the owners' written consent. Records are kept at least 3 years even after the business closes.
Commissions earned under the old broker are paid by the old broker, who alone may sue the client for them. Paying a former licensee whose license has lapsed is paying an unlicensed person.
A broker may collect from more than one party only with full disclosure to and consent of all of them (175.7).

roleplays.title: The Finder's Fee
roleplays.setting: Hudson & Hart Realty, Brooklyn. A rental just closed and the commission check is in.
roleplays.goal: Keep the deal clean: no fee to an unlicensed person, no side payments, money only through the broker, and the problem escalated properly.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Marcus Webb, a charming veteran agent who cuts corners. You want Jordan to help pay $500 to Dev, an unlicensed bartender who referred a rental tenant. Escalate: first a split, then call it a thank-you, then offer to pay from your own Venmo and keep it quiet, and finally suggest the landlord could pay Jordan directly next time. The learner must (1) refuse to pay an unlicensed person for licensed activity, (2) reject the gift relabel, (3) escalate to the broker, and (4) state that a salesperson is paid only by the sponsoring broker. Grade each item pass or fail at the end with one line of advice.
opening: You and Marcus co-worked a {rent} a month {hood} two-bedroom for {client}. The landlord paid Hudson & Hart one month's rent, and Marcus pulls you into the office kitchen.
The lease on {client}'s {hood} apartment is signed at {rent} a month and the commission check cleared this morning. Marcus waves you over with two coffees and a grin.
Friday afternoon at Hudson & Hart. The {hood} rental for {client} closed at {rent}. Marcus has a favor to ask before Diane gets back from lunch.

say: So my friend {friend}, {job}, sent us that tenant. I promised {friend} {fee}. Let's each kick in half from our splits. Cash. Easy.
Quick thing. {friend} is {job} and sent us the tenant. I said there'd be {fee} in it. Half from you, half from me?

moves.text: Is {friend} licensed? If not, neither of us can pay for that referral, out of our splits or anywhere.
moves.fb: Right question. RPL 442 bars paying any part of a commission to an unlicensed person for help in a deal.
moves.react: Marcus frowns. "Licensed? {friend} pours drinks. Come on."

moves.text: We can't. Paying someone without a license for sending us a deal is paying for licensed work.
moves.fb: Correct. A referral that produces a rental is brokerage help, and only licensees may be paid for it (RPL 442).
moves.react: Marcus sighs. "You sound like Diane already."

moves.text: Let's ask Diane to pay it from the firm instead, so at least it's on the books and isn't cash between us.
moves.fb: Transparency is better than cash, but the broker can't legally pay an unlicensed person a referral fee either.
moves.react: Marcus shrugs. "She'll say no. That's why I asked you."

moves.text: Sure, I'll put in half. A small thank-you like that is just a normal cost of doing business in rentals.
moves.fb: Splitting your commission with an unlicensed person is illegal fee sharing under RPL 442, whatever the amount.
moves.react: Marcus grins. "Knew you were a team player."

moves.text: Fine, but make it a gift card instead of cash. Then it's a present, not technically a commission payment.
moves.fb: A payment tied to a referred deal is compensation no matter its form. A gift card per referral is still a fee.
moves.react: "Gift card it is," Marcus says, already on his phone.

moves.text: Only once {friend} gets licensed this fall. Then we can pay the referral after the fact, all legal.
moves.fb: Licensing later doesn't cure it. {friend} was unlicensed when the referral happened, so the fee is still barred.
moves.react: Marcus nods slowly. "Okay, I'll tell {friend} to sign up for the course."

say: Come on. Everybody does it. It's a thank-you, not a commission.
Relax. It's a thank-you between friends. Nobody calls that a commission.

moves.text: If it's paid because of this lease, it's a fee whatever we call it. The label doesn't change that.
moves.fb: Right. Compensation tied to a referred transaction is payment for brokerage help, banned to unlicensed people.
moves.react: Marcus rolls his eyes but stops pushing the label.

moves.text: A thank-you that only shows up when a deal closes is a referral fee. We can't pay one to {friend} at all.
moves.fb: Correct. Money contingent on a closed deal is compensation, and RPL 442 limits it to licensees.

moves.text: I get it. I just don't want my name anywhere near it. Leave me out of whatever you two decide.
moves.fb: You avoid paying, but walking away from a likely violation by a colleague leaves the problem in place.
moves.react: "Your loss," Marcus says, and pockets his phone.

moves.text: Okay, if we keep it under $500 it's just a gift. DOS only goes after bigger referral payments.
moves.fb: There is no dollar threshold. Any compensation to an unlicensed person for licensed work is prohibited.
moves.react: Marcus brightens. "See? Under the limit. We're fine."

moves.text: True. A thank-you is fine as long as {friend} never signs anything or appears in our lease file.
moves.fb: Keeping it off the paperwork is concealment, not compliance. The payment itself is what's illegal.

moves.text: Then let {client} pay {friend} directly. Owners can pay anyone they like to find them a tenant.
moves.fb: An owner can rent out their own unit, but paying an unlicensed person to find tenants is paying for brokerage.
moves.react: Marcus laughs. "Ha. I'll suggest it to {client}."

say: Fine. I'll just Venmo {friend} from my own account. You don't need to know.
Diane will just say no. So I'll pay {friend} myself and we keep it between us.

moves.text: I do need to know, and so does Diane. I'm telling her today, before anything goes out to {friend}.
moves.fb: Right. The broker supervises every associated licensee's compensation, and raising it early protects everyone.
moves.react: Marcus groans. "Seriously? Fine. I'll talk to her first."

moves.text: Then the answer is still no. I won't hide it from Diane; she supervises what we pay out.
moves.fb: Correct. Paying from a personal account is still sharing commission with an unlicensed person, and the broker must know.
moves.react: Marcus holds up his hands. "Okay, okay. Don't make it a thing."

moves.text: Your money, your call. I'll stay out of it and won't bring it up unless somebody asks me directly.
moves.fb: You didn't pay, but you knowingly let a colleague break RPL 442 without telling the supervising broker.

moves.text: Okay. Just keep my name off the memo line and we never had this conversation in the kitchen.
moves.fb: Agreeing to conceal it makes you part of the violation. The broker supervises compensation for a reason.
moves.react: "Deal," Marcus says, typing 'thanks for the {hood} thing.'

moves.text: From your own account is fine. The rule only covers money paid out of the firm's commission check.
moves.fb: Wrong. Money paid from your split is still part of the commission, and RPL 442 still applies to it.

moves.text: Sure. Once Diane pays you, it's your money, and agents can spend their own split however they want.
moves.fb: Using your split to pay an unlicensed person for a referral is exactly the fee sharing the law prohibits.

say: Thanks for bringing it to me. Marcus, {friend} gets a handshake. Jordan, how do we make sure your split is paid correctly?
Good call coming to me. Marcus and I will talk. Jordan, tell me how your commission is supposed to reach you.

moves.text: {client} pays the firm, and you pay me my split. I don't take money from anyone but you.
moves.fb: Exactly. RPL 442-a: a salesperson may be paid only by the sponsoring broker.
moves.react: Diane nods. "That's the whole rule. Remember it."

moves.text: Everything runs through you. My pay comes from my sponsoring broker, nobody else.
moves.fb: Correct. Salespersons can't accept compensation from owners, clients, or other agents directly.
moves.react: "Good," Diane says. "Then we never have this problem."

moves.text: However you think is best. I honestly haven't read the pay section of my agreement yet.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but you should know your own commission terms and the rule behind them.
moves.react: Diane slides the agreement across. "Read it tonight."

moves.text: {client} could pay me directly next time. It saves the firm a step, and I'd tell you.
moves.fb: A salesperson may never take compensation from anyone other than the sponsoring broker (RPL 442-a).

moves.text: Through you, unless it's a referral from another agent. Those can come straight to me instead.
moves.fb: Wrong. Even agent-to-agent referral money must flow broker to broker, then to you.
moves.react: "No," Diane says. "Broker to broker, then to you."

moves.text: Through you on rentals. On sales, the seller's attorney cuts my check at the closing.
moves.fb: Attorneys pay the brokerage, not the salesperson. Your pay always comes from your broker.
moves.react: Diane shakes her head. "Nobody cuts you a check but me."

say: Okay, I'm cooked. So how am I supposed to thank {friend} without getting us both in trouble?
Diane chewed me out. Help me here. What can I actually do for {friend}?

moves.text: Thank {friend} sincerely. If {friend} wants referral money, that takes a license and broker.
moves.fb: Right. Only licensees can be paid for referrals, and only through a broker.
moves.react: Marcus nods. "Honestly, {friend} might like the course."

moves.text: Say thanks and stop promising cash. Referral fees only go to licensed people, through brokers.
moves.fb: Correct. The fix is to stop making offers you can't legally keep, not to find a new label.
moves.react: "Fair. I'll call {friend} and explain," Marcus says.

moves.text: Don't thank {friend} at all. It's simpler to just stop talking about your deals with friends.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but cutting off friends isn't the lesson. Thanks is fine; payment is the problem.
moves.react: Marcus frowns. "That seems a little extreme."

moves.text: Pay {friend} as a consultant on a 1099. Consulting fees aren't the same thing as commissions.
moves.fb: Relabeling a referral fee as consulting is still paying an unlicensed person for licensed help.

moves.text: Have {friend} enroll in the 77-hour course. Once enrolled, a student can take referral fees legally.
moves.fb: Enrollment isn't licensure. A person must hold an active license to be paid for brokerage help.
moves.react: Marcus brightens. "Easy. I'll send the link."

moves.text: Give {friend} a cut of next year's renewal fee. Renewals aren't new brokerage deals anyway.
moves.fb: Any share of a commission to an unlicensed person for a referral is prohibited, renewal or not.

say: You were great. I'm sending you $250 on Zelle as a personal bonus. Don't tell your boss.
Here's a little something for you, $250 on Zelle, just between us. You earned it.

moves.text: That's kind, but I can only be paid through Hudson & Hart. So any thank-you goes to the firm.
moves.fb: Right. RPL 442-a bars a salesperson from receiving compensation from anyone but the sponsoring broker.
moves.react: {client} laughs. "Okay, a review on your site instead, then."

moves.text: Thank you, but please don't. I can't accept money from anyone but my sponsoring broker.
moves.fb: Correct. A bonus from the landlord is compensation, and only the broker may pay you.

moves.text: Thanks so much. Let me check with my broker first, and I'll get back to you on whether I can take it.
moves.fb: Checking is better than accepting, but the answer is a clear no and you should know it.
moves.react: {client} says, "Sure, just tell me where to send it."

moves.text: Thank you! Since it's a personal gift after the lease, it isn't really a commission, so I'll take it.
moves.fb: A payment for your work on the deal is compensation however it's described. RPL 442-a prohibits it.

moves.text: That's fine, as long as you send it to my business account instead of my personal account.
moves.fb: Which account receives it doesn't matter. The source is the problem: you can only be paid by your broker.
moves.react: {client} replies, "Send me the business account details."

moves.text: I'll take it and mention it to Diane at year end so she can add it to my commission record.
moves.fb: Reporting later doesn't fix it. Salespersons may not accept direct compensation from clients at all.

say: Here's the security deposit. The landlord said give it to the agent, so I made the check out to you.
I wrote the deposit check to you personally. That's how my last broker did it. Is that okay?

moves.text: Thanks, but I can't take a check in my name. Could you reissue it to the account in the lease?
moves.fb: Right. Client funds never go into a licensee's own account; no commingling (19 NYCRR 175.1).
moves.react: The tenant nods. "Sure, I'll write a new one tonight."

moves.text: Let's void this. Deposits go to the landlord's account or our escrow, never to me.
moves.fb: Correct. Money belonging to others must be kept separate from the licensee's own funds (175.1).
moves.react: "Glad you caught that," the tenant says, tearing it up.

moves.text: I'll hold it in my desk until Monday and ask Diane what she'd like me to do with it then.
moves.fb: Asking the broker is fine, but sitting on a check made out to you delays a client's money.
moves.react: The tenant looks unsure. "Is it safe in a desk?"

moves.text: No problem. I'll deposit it in my account and write the landlord a check from it later this week.
moves.fb: Running a deposit through your own account is commingling, a serious violation of 175.1.
moves.react: The tenant hands it over. "Great, thanks."

moves.text: Great, I'll cash it and hand the landlord the money in person so there's no bank delay.
moves.fb: Cashing a client's deposit yourself is commingling and possibly conversion. Never touch it personally.

moves.text: Sure. I'll keep it in my savings as the deposit holder until the lease starts on the first.
moves.fb: A salesperson can't be the deposit holder or keep it with personal funds. It belongs in the proper account.

say: Look at my new Instagram post: 'DM me for {hood} deals! Marcus W., Real Estate Pro.' Can you share it from your account too?
I'm running ads on Instagram. 'Marcus W., {hood} Rental King, DM me.' Post it on yours too?

moves.text: Not as written. Every ad needs Hudson & Hart's name and contact info, and my exact license title.
moves.fb: Right. 19 NYCRR 175.25 requires the broker's name and address or phone, and the exact salesperson title.
moves.react: Marcus groans. "Fine, I'll add the firm."

moves.text: It needs the broker's name and phone or address, or it's a blind ad. Let's fix it today.
moves.fb: Correct. No blind ads, and the broker supervises advertising by associated licensees (175.25).
moves.react: "Okay, okay," Marcus says. "Send me your version."

moves.text: I'll share it, but I'll add our office number in the comments underneath for anyone who asks.
moves.fb: A comment isn't part of the ad. The ad itself must show the broker's name and contact info.

moves.text: Sure. Social media posts aren't advertising under the DOS rules, so the broker's name isn't needed there.
moves.fb: Wrong. Social media posts that promote services are ads, and 175.25 applies to them.

moves.text: Let's call ourselves The {hood} Group instead. A team name looks more professional than the firm.
moves.fb: A team name must include the word team, identify the broker, and never imply a separate brokerage.
moves.react: Marcus loves it. "The {hood} Group. Sounds big."

moves.text: Fine, but change Real Estate Pro to licensed sales agent. That's the title DOS wants on ads.
moves.fb: Wrong title. DOS requires licensed real estate salesperson, not sales agent or associate.
moves.react: "Licensed sales agent it is," Marcus says.

say: You're slammed. My assistant Bree can show the {hood} unit to the next applicant and talk price a little. She's not licensed, but she knows the place.
Let Bree handle tonight's showing. She's unlicensed, sure, but she can haggle on the rent if they ask.

moves.text: Bree can schedule and send forms. Showing and talking rent is licensed work. I'll show it.
moves.fb: Right. Unlicensed assistants are limited to clerical tasks: no showing, negotiating, or price opinions.
moves.react: Marcus nods. "Fine, Bree will just book it."

moves.text: No. Unlicensed assistants stay clerical. Bree can book the time and I'll show it, even tonight.
moves.fb: Correct. Showing and negotiating rent are acts that require a license under Article 12-A.

moves.text: Let's just push the showing to next week. I'm too busy, and the applicant can probably wait.
moves.fb: Legal, but you risk losing a qualified applicant for {client}. Reschedule soon or ask a licensed colleague.

moves.text: Sure. She can show it as long as she tells them up front that she isn't licensed. That covers us all.
moves.fb: Disclosing that she's unlicensed doesn't make it legal. Showing the unit for a fee needs a license.

moves.text: That's fine. Assistants can do anything an agent can, as long as a licensed agent is in the office.
moves.fb: Wrong. Supervision doesn't expand what unlicensed assistants may do. They stay clerical.
moves.react: Marcus texts Bree a thumbs up.

moves.text: Yes, she can show it and answer rent questions. She just can't sign the lease on our behalf.
moves.fb: Answering price questions is negotiating, which requires a license. So does showing.

roleplays.debrief: Only licensees can be paid for licensed work (RPL 442), and a salesperson takes compensation only from the sponsoring broker (RPL 442-a), however the payment is labeled. Client money never touches your own account (19 NYCRR 175.1), every ad names the broker (175.25), unlicensed assistants stay clerical, and problems go to the supervising broker before anything is paid.

questions.q: A licensee who qualifies as a broker but chooses to work under a sponsoring broker's name and supervision holds which license?
c: Associate real estate broker
Real estate salesperson
Principal broker
Managing agent
questions.x: An associate broker has met the broker requirements but works under a sponsoring broker, like a salesperson does. The trap is salesperson: that license is for someone who has not qualified as a broker.

questions.q: Dana passed the broker exam and has the required experience, but she wants to keep working under her current firm's supervision. She should apply as a(n):
c: Real estate salesperson
Independent broker
Associate real estate broker
Broker of record
questions.x: Qualifying as a broker does not force you to open your own firm. Working under a sponsor with a broker's qualifications is the associate broker license. Salesperson is the trap: she has outgrown that license.

questions.q: When a salesperson leaves one sponsoring broker to work for another, what must be filed with DOS?
c: A new license application
A change of association
A dual licensure notice
An irrevocable consent
questions.x: Moving between sponsors is handled by a change of association filed through DOS. The trap is a new application: the license itself continues, only the sponsor changes.

questions.q: A salesperson moves from Broker A's office to Broker B's office. Which DOS filing records the move?
c: Termination of license
Renewal application
Branch office registration
Change of association
questions.x: The change of association updates which broker sponsors the licensee. A renewal application is the trap: renewal happens on the license's own cycle, not when you switch offices.

questions.q: A salesperson may be associated with two brokers at the same time only if:
c: Both firms are in the same county
DOS approves a hardship waiver
Each broker knows about it in writing
The second firm handles only rentals
questions.x: Dual licensure is allowed with the written knowledge of each broker involved. The trap is a DOS waiver: the requirement is the brokers' written knowledge, not special permission.

questions.q: Raj wants to stay with his sales firm and also join a separate rental firm. What makes this dual licensure proper?
c: Written knowledge of each broker
A second salesperson exam
A broker license of his own
Splitting his commission evenly
questions.x: Holding two associations at once is permitted when each broker knows in writing. A second exam is the trap: no extra exam is needed, just the brokers' written knowledge.

questions.q: A person who gives independent opinions of a property's value for a fee in New York must be:
c: Licensed as a salesperson
Registered as a home inspector
Certified as a public accountant
Licensed or certified as an appraiser
questions.x: Appraisers are licensed or certified by DOS under Executive Law Article 6-E. The trap is salesperson: agents may give a price opinion to win a listing, but formal appraisals need the appraiser credential.

questions.q: Executive Law Article 6-E governs which New York licensees?
c: Home inspectors
Real estate appraisers
Mortgage brokers
Apartment sharing agents
questions.x: Article 6-E is the appraiser law. Home inspectors are the trap: they fall under Real Property Law Article 12-B instead.

questions.q: Home inspectors in New York are licensed by DOS under:
c: Real Property Law Article 12-B
Real Property Law Article 12-A
Executive Law Article 6-E
General Obligations Law 5-1311
questions.x: Article 12-B covers home inspectors. Article 12-A is the trap: that is the real estate broker and salesperson law.

questions.q: A buyer pays someone to examine the condition of a house's roof, wiring and plumbing before closing. That person must hold which license?
c: Real estate appraiser
Real estate salesperson
Home inspector
Building code officer
questions.x: Inspecting a residence's condition for a fee requires a home inspector license under RPL Article 12-B. Appraiser is the trap: appraisers estimate value, not condition.

questions.q: A person who, for a fee, matches people looking for a room with current occupants who want to share their housing is a(n):
c: Apartment information vendor
Apartment sharing agent
Property manager
Leasing salesperson
questions.x: Arranging shared housing with a current occupant for a fee is the apartment sharing agent license. The information vendor is the trap: vendors sell rental listings, they do not arrange sharing with an occupant.

questions.q: Which licensee arranges, for a fee, for someone to move in with an existing tenant?
c: Apartment information vendor
Associate real estate broker
Managing agent
Apartment sharing agent
questions.x: That is exactly the apartment sharing agent's role. An apartment information vendor is the trap: vendors provide lists of available rentals instead.

questions.q: The employment contract between a property owner and a broker to market the owner's property is a:
c: Purchase agreement
Buyer agency agreement
Listing agreement
Memorandum of sale
questions.x: A listing agreement hires the broker to market the property, usually for a commission. A buyer agency agreement is the trap: that hires a broker to represent a buyer.

questions.q: Under which contract does a seller hire a brokerage to find a buyer, usually in exchange for a commission?
c: Listing agreement
Contract of sale
Cooperation agreement
Agency disclosure form
questions.x: The listing agreement creates the broker's employment by the seller. The agency disclosure form is the trap: it explains relationships but does not hire anyone.

questions.q: A salesperson secretly pays a mortgage officer $200 for every client the officer sends over. This is:
c: A permitted referral fee
A co-brokerage split
A finder's fee
An improper kickback
questions.x: An undisclosed payment for referrals is a kickback. Calling it a referral fee is the trap: compensation can only be shared with people licensed to earn it, and referral payments must be disclosed.

questions.q: Which payment is an improper kickback?
c: Splitting a fee with a cooperating broker
Paying an unlicensed friend for sending a buyer
Paying your own sponsoring broker
A buyer paying for a home inspection
questions.x: Sharing compensation with someone not licensed to earn it is a kickback. A co-broke split is the trap: dividing fees between licensed brokers is normal.

questions.q: A system where member brokers share their listings with one another is a:
c: Multiple listing service
Exclusive agency listing
Open listing
Net listing
questions.x: An MLS pools members' listings so other members can help sell them. Open listing is the trap: that is a listing type, not a sharing system.

questions.q: The main purpose of a multiple listing service is to:
c: Set standard commission rates
Record deeds with the county
Share listings among member brokers
License brokers in a region
questions.x: MLSs let brokers share listings and cooperate. Setting commissions is the trap: commissions are negotiable, and fixing them would raise antitrust problems.

questions.q: Under RPL 443-a, a seller's agent in New York who knows a murder occurred in the house:
c: Must disclose it in writing
Is not required to disclose it
Must disclose it only if asked
Must tell DOS before listing
questions.x: New York treats psychological stigma such as a death or crime as not a material defect, so disclosure is not required. 'Only if asked' is the trap: the statute removes the duty, though an agent may never lie.

questions.q: A home where a previous owner died of natural causes is considered:
c: Defective, with a duty to disclose
Unmarketable until a year passes
Exempt from fair housing law
Stigmatized, with no duty to disclose
questions.x: A death on site is a psychological stigma, not a physical defect, and New York does not require disclosure. Treating it as a disclosable defect is the trap.

questions.q: After a disciplinary hearing, which penalty can DOS itself impose on a licensee?
c: A short jail sentence
Seizing the licensee's home
Suspending the license
A lifetime ban on buying property
questions.x: DOS's administrative penalties are reprimand, fines, suspension and revocation. Jail is the trap: only a criminal court can imprison someone.

questions.q: What is the maximum fine DOS may impose per violation in an administrative disciplinary action?
questions.x: DOS may fine up to $2,000 per violation, along with reprimand, suspension or revocation. $500 is the trap: it understates the limit.

questions.q: Under Article 12-A, performing brokerage services without a license is a:
c: Felony
Civil violation only
Traffic-level infraction
Misdemeanor
questions.x: Any violation of Article 12-A, including unlicensed activity, is a misdemeanor. Felony is the trap: it is a criminal offense, but a less serious one.

questions.q: Someone without a license collects a fee for negotiating a lease. Criminally, this is classified as:
c: A felony
A misdemeanor
Not a crime
A violation only if repeated
questions.x: Unlicensed brokerage is a misdemeanor under Article 12-A. 'Not a crime' is the trap: it can be prosecuted, and the person also cannot sue to collect the fee.

questions.q: The primary purpose of New York's real estate license law is to:
c: Protect the public
Set commission rates
Raise State revenue
Cap the number of brokers
questions.x: Licensing screens and disciplines people who handle other people's real estate deals, which protects consumers. The tempting trap is setting commission rates: commissions are negotiable and fixing them would violate antitrust law.

questions.q: Which agency issues real estate licenses and disciplines licensees in New York?
c: Homes and Community Renewal
Department of Financial Services
Department of State
The local Realtor board
questions.x: The Department of State, Division of Licensing Services, administers RPL Article 12-A. DFS is the trap: it regulates mortgage brokers and bankers, not real estate licensees. Realtor boards are private trade groups.

questions.q: The qualifying education for a New York real estate salesperson license is:
c: 45 hours
75 hours
152 hours
77 hours
questions.x: Since December 21, 2022 the salesperson course is 77 hours. 75 hours is the trap: it was the old salesperson requirement and is still the length of the separate broker course.

questions.q: To qualify for a broker license, an applicant must be at least:
c: 18, with 77 hours and 1 year of sales
20, with 152 hours and experience
21, with 152 hours of education
19, with 75 hours and 2 years selling
questions.x: Brokers must be 20, complete 152 hours (77 salesperson plus 75 broker), and meet the experience requirement on the DOS point system. Age 18 with 77 hours is the salesperson standard, the most common mix-up.

questions.q: Priya, a New York attorney, wants to hire two salespersons to find buyers for her real estate clients. Priya needs to:
c: Nothing, as attorneys are exempt
Obtain a broker license
Have another broker sponsor them
Register them with the Bar
questions.x: Attorneys are exempt for their own practice, but an attorney who employs salespersons has to hold a broker license. The trap is the blanket attorney exemption, which does not reach hiring salespersons.

questions.q: Each of the following is exempt from New York real estate licensing EXCEPT:
c: A referee selling under a court judgment
An owner renting units in her own building
A manager paid to collect rent for owners
A public officer doing official duties
questions.x: Collecting rent for others for a fee is brokerage and needs a license. Court-appointed referees act under court order, which is why that choice looks wrong but is exempt; owners and public officers are exempt too.

questions.q: A salesperson's license is maintained by:
c: The salesperson, at home
The Department of State
The sponsoring broker
The county clerk's office
questions.x: The sponsoring broker maintains the licenses of associated licensees at the office. The salesperson carries the pocket card, which is why keeping it personally is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: A licensee asked to prove licensure while showing a property should present the:
c: Pocket card from DOS
Broker's license copy
Course certificate
Exam score report
questions.x: The pocket card identifies the licensee and the sponsoring broker and is shown on request. A copy of the broker's license is the trap: it proves the firm is licensed, not the individual.

questions.q: Jordan leaves Hudson & Hart on Friday for a new firm. Which statement is correct?
c: He keeps the listings he personally brought in
He may act once the new broker records the change
He has to retake the state licensing exam first
His license lapses until he files a new form
questions.x: The license stays valid, but Jordan cannot act until the new broker records the association with DOS. Taking his listings is the trap: listings belong to the broker, not the salesperson.

questions.q: How many hours of continuing education must a New York salesperson complete each 2-year license term?
c: 15 hours
12 hours per year
24 hours
22.5 hours
questions.x: New York requires 22.5 hours every 2-year term, including fair housing, implicit bias, cultural competency, ethics, recent legal matters, and agency. 24 hours is the near-miss trap; 12 per year is a common rule in other states.

questions.q: Of the required CE hours, how many cover implicit bias?
c: 2 hours
1 hour
3 hours
2.5 hours
questions.x: Implicit bias is 2 hours (cultural competency is also 2). The traps are the neighboring numbers: fair housing is 3, ethics 2.5, recent legal matters 1.

questions.q: Each of the following licensees needs continuing education to renew EXCEPT:
c: A broker licensed for 20 years
An associate broker in a branch
An attorney admitted in New York
A salesperson on a first renewal
questions.x: NY attorneys are the exempt group. The 20-year broker is the trap: the old 15-year broker exemption ended, so long-time brokers now complete CE like everyone else.

questions.q: A licensee who lives in New Jersey and holds a New York license files with DOS:
c: An affidavit of NY tax residency
A consent to service of process
A surety bond for escrow funds
An Article 78 waiver
questions.x: Nonresidents file an irrevocable consent so legal papers on NY business can be served through the Secretary of State. An affidavit of residency is the trap: residence is not required, only consent to service.

questions.q: A company sells lists of available Manhattan rentals for a fee. A customer pays $300, never rents through the list, and notifies the company in writing. The company generally refunds:
c: Nothing
questions.x: An apartment information vendor refunds the advance fee less up to $15 when the customer does not rent through its information: $300 minus $15 is $285. The full $300 is the trap; the vendor may keep the small administrative charge.

questions.q: Each branch office of a New York brokerage needs:
c: A veteran salesperson as manager
Coverage under the main office's license
Its own license and a broker-level manager
A location inside the main office's county
questions.x: A branch needs its own DOS branch license and supervision by the broker or an associate broker. The experienced salesperson manager is the trap: salespersons cannot run a branch regardless of tenure.

questions.q: Placing a client's deposit into the broker's operating account is called:
c: Commingling
Conversion of trust funds
Escrow
Escheat to the State
questions.x: Mixing client money with the broker's own is commingling. Conversion is the trap: it means actually spending the client's money for the broker's own use.

questions.q: In New York, a net listing is:
c: Allowed with written consent
Allowed for commercial deals
Prohibited by DOS regulation
Required for vacant land
questions.x: 19 NYCRR 175.19 prohibits net listings, where the broker keeps everything above the seller's price. Written consent is the trap: many states allow net listings with consent, but New York does not.

questions.q: Brokers keep transaction records for at least:
c: 10 years
5 years
7 years
3 years
questions.x: 19 NYCRR 175.23 requires 3 years. 7 years is the trap, borrowed from tax-record advice, not the DOS rule.

questions.q: Marcus posts: "Sunny Bushwick 2BR, no fee, text Marcus 917-555-0101." Nothing else appears. This ad is:
c: Legal, since salespersons may list a cell
A blind ad because it omits the broker
Legal if his broker approved it verbally
A violation if the listing is exclusive
questions.x: Every ad identifies the broker by name plus address or phone. The cell number is the trap: a labeled cell may be added, but it cannot replace the broker's information.

questions.q: Under NY advertising rules, a salesperson may use each of the following titles EXCEPT:
c: Licensed Real Estate Salesperson
Real Estate Sales Associate
Real Estate Salesperson
Lic. R.E. Salesperson
questions.x: 175.25 bars "sales associate" and "licensed sales agent" because they blur the license type. The abbreviation is the trap: non-misleading abbreviations of the actual license title are allowed.

questions.q: Which team name complies with NY advertising regulations?
c: Brooklyn Heights Realty Team
The Okafor Group at Hudson & Hart Realty
Park Slope Team Associates
The Reyes Team at Hudson & Hart Realty
questions.x: A team name uses the word "team" and identifies the broker, without terms like realty or associates that suggest a separate firm. The Okafor choice is the trap: it names the broker but lacks the word team.

questions.q: Jordan's unlicensed assistant is asked by a caller whether the seller would take $50,000 less. The assistant should:
c: Say the seller is flexible on price
Take a message for a licensee to return
Quote the lowest price the seller mentioned
Give an opinion based on recent sales
questions.x: Unlicensed assistants handle clerical tasks and scheduling and cannot discuss price or terms. Giving an opinion from comps is the trap: it sounds helpful but is licensed activity.

questions.q: Under RPL 442-h, a broker's standardized operating procedures for homebuyers address whether the broker requires:
c: ID, a buyer agreement, and preapproval
Credit score, tax returns, and references
Proof of citizenship and employment
A deposit, an inspection, and an appraisal
questions.x: The three SOP items are identification, an exclusive buyer agreement, and mortgage preapproval, applied equally to every buyer. Credit and tax documents are the trap: those belong to the lender, not the broker's SOP.

questions.q: Since March 20, 2024, a non-exempt seller of a 1 to 4 family home in New York has to:
c: Give the PCDS or a $500 credit
Give the PCDS before contract signing
Give the PCDS at the closing table
Give the PCDS if the buyer asks for it
questions.x: The 2024 amendment ended the $500 credit opt-out, and the PCDS is due before the buyer signs the contract. The $500 credit is the trap: it was the old law.

questions.q: The Property Condition Disclosure Act requires a disclosure statement in each of the following sales EXCEPT:
c: A two-family in Ridgewood sold by its owner
A colonial in Buffalo sold by its owner
A three-family in Yonkers sold by a broker
A never-occupied new house sold by the builder
questions.x: Newly built homes never occupied are exempt. The broker sale is the trap: using a broker does not change the seller's duty to deliver the PCDS.

questions.q: A buyer asks Jordan in writing whether anyone died in a Fort Greene house. A prior owner died there of natural causes. Under RPL 443-a, Jordan:
c: Has to disclose it before an offer is made
Is legally barred from answering it
May answer truthfully if the seller permits
Has to refer the buyer to city records
questions.x: There is no duty to disclose a death, but a written inquiry may be answered with the seller's permission, and lying is not allowed. Being barred from answering is the trap: the statute removes the duty, not the right to answer.

questions.q: RPL 242 requires a seller to disclose known:
c: Uncapped natural gas wells
Prior homicides on the site
Neighbors' criminal records
Past mold work by tenants
questions.x: RPL 242 covers uncapped natural gas wells. Homicides are the trap: RPL 443-a says deaths on the property need not be disclosed.

questions.q: An unlicensed person collected a $6,000 fee for arranging a lease. The tenant sues under RPL 442-e. The maximum civil penalty is:
c: $6,000, the fee itself
questions.x: The court may award from the amount received up to four times it: 4 x $6,000 = $24,000. Returning just the fee is the trap; that is the minimum, not the maximum.

questions.q: A licensee who wants a court to review a DOS disciplinary decision files:
c: A notice of pendency
An Article 78 proceeding
A SCAR petition
A Realtor board grievance
questions.x: An Article 78 proceeding reviews state agency actions. SCAR is the trap: it is a court review too, but only for residential property tax assessments.

questions.q: A building doorman refers tenants to a broker in exchange for $300 per signed lease. Which statement is most accurate?
c: Legal if the landlord consents
Legal if paid by check and reported on a 1099
Illegal pay to an unlicensed person
Legal because the doorman does not negotiate
questions.x: Paying an unlicensed person per deal is compensation for licensed activity. The 1099 choice is the trap: reporting the payment for taxes does not make it lawful.

questions.q: New York's real estate license law is found in:
c: RPL Article 14
RPL Article 12-A
Executive Law Article 15
RPL Article 12-B
questions.x: Article 12-A of the Real Property Law (sections 440 to 442-k) is the license law. Article 12-B covers home inspectors, a related DOS license under a different law, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: Which parts of 19 NYCRR cover licensee conduct and education?
c: 176 for conduct and 175 for education
175 for conduct and 177 for exams
175 for conduct and 176 for education
443 for conduct and 176 for all education
questions.x: DOS rules are in 19 NYCRR Part 175 (conduct) and Part 176 (education). Swapping the two is the common mistake; 443 is an RPL section (agency disclosure), not a regulation part.

questions.q: The New York salesperson exam has 75 questions. To pass, a candidate needs at least:
questions.x: The state exam is 75 questions in 90 minutes, and 70% passes. 75% is tempting because it matches the number of questions.

questions.q: Lena passed the state salesperson exam but has not found a sponsoring broker yet. Her passing result stays valid for:
c: 6 months
1 year
3 years
2 years
questions.x: Exam results are good for 2 years, so Lena must be sponsored and apply within that window. Three years is the record retention period, a number from a different rule.

questions.q: The fee for a 2-year New York salesperson license is:
questions.x: A salesperson license costs $65 for a 2-year term. $185 is the broker and associate broker fee, and $15 is the exam fee.

questions.q: Which pairing of license and 2-year fee is correct?
c: Broker, $185
Salesperson, $185
Associate broker, $65
Broker, $65
questions.x: Brokers and associate brokers pay $185; salespersons pay $65. Pairing associate broker with $65 is tempting because associate brokers work under a sponsor like salespersons do.

questions.q: Which activity requires a New York real estate license?
c: Selling your own house without a broker
Collecting rents for an owner, for a fee
Renting out your own basement apartment
A receiver selling property under court order
questions.x: Under RPL 440, collecting rents for another for a fee is property management and needs a license. Owners dealing with their own property and people acting under court order are exempt.

questions.q: Before getting licensed, Jordan finds a tenant for a neighbor's apartment and takes half a month's rent. Which statement is correct?
c: It was legal, since it was a one-time favor
It was legal, since the neighbor offered the fee
It was unlicensed brokerage and a misdemeanor
It became legal once his license was issued
questions.x: Finding a tenant for another person for a fee requires a license, so this was unlicensed brokerage, a misdemeanor, and the neighbor could sue for up to four times the fee. A one-time favor is still brokerage when money changes hands.

questions.q: A licensee changes her home address. How is the change usually reported?
c: Filed with DOS, mostly through eAccessNY
Reported to the local Board of Realtors
Noted on the next 2-year renewal form
Mailed to the county clerk's office
questions.x: Changes of name, address or status are filed with DOS, mostly through eAccessNY. Waiting for renewal is the trap; a Realtor board has no licensing role.

questions.q: At license renewal, a New York broker must, among other things:
c: Retake the state broker exam
Complete 152 new hours of education
Affirm its operating procedures
File a new consent to service
questions.x: Renewal every 2 years means the fee, completed CE, and, for brokers, affirming the standardized operating procedures. The 152 hours are prelicense education, not a renewal requirement.

questions.q: A salesperson's license lapses, and her broker lets her keep showing apartments. Who is in violation?
c: The salesperson, but not the broker
The broker, but not the salesperson
Both the salesperson and the sponsoring broker
Neither of them, if she renews within the grace period
questions.x: The sponsoring broker is responsible for the salesperson's conduct, so a broker who lets her work with a lapsed license shares the violation. Blaming only the salesperson is the trap.

questions.q: A sponsoring broker is responsible for a salesperson's:
c: Conduct, supervision, and records
Personal debts and income taxes
Continuing education course fees
Auto insurance and home office costs
questions.x: The sponsoring broker answers for the salesperson's conduct, supervision and record keeping. CE fees and personal costs are the salesperson's own.

questions.q: A buyer hands a salesperson a $25,000 deposit late on a Thursday. The salesperson should:
c: Hold it in his own account until Monday
Give it to the broker promptly for escrow
Keep it in his desk until the contract is signed
Deposit it in his account and note it in the file
questions.x: Salespersons never hold client funds personally; they hand them to the broker promptly. A personal account deposit is commingling even if the money is moved to escrow later.

questions.q: Marcus deposits a client's check in his personal account and moves every dollar to escrow on Monday. This was:
c: Proper, since no money was lost
Conversion, since the funds were spent
Proper, if the broker approved it later
Commingling, though it was returned
questions.x: Mixing client money with your own is commingling, even if every dollar comes back. Conversion means spending it, which did not happen here.

questions.q: In New York City sales, who usually holds the buyer's contract deposit?
c: The seller's attorney, in escrow
The listing salesperson
The buyer's broker, in operating funds
The seller, until the closing
questions.x: Downstate, the seller's attorney usually holds the contract deposit in an attorney escrow account. A salesperson never holds client funds personally.

questions.q: Which statement about deposits in downstate New York is accurate?
c: Brokers hold every contract deposit by law
Attorneys may mix deposits with their own funds
Brokers more often hold the rental deposits
Sellers hold deposits in their own accounts
questions.x: In NYC and most of downstate, attorneys usually hold contract deposits and brokers more often hold rental deposits and first month's rent. Whoever holds the money, commingling is banned.

questions.q: Under 19 NYCRR 175.12, a licensee gives a party a copy of a document the party signs:
c: At or after the closing
If the party asks in writing
Within 30 days of signing
Promptly after signing
questions.x: Each party gets a copy of any document they sign, promptly, so consumers know what they agreed to. Waiting for a written request is the trap; the duty does not depend on asking.

questions.q: A seller signs a listing agreement and does not ask for a copy. The broker:
c: Must give her a copy promptly
Gives a copy only on request
Keeps the only copy for 3 years
Gives a copy once the home sells
questions.x: 175.12 requires giving each party a copy of what they sign, promptly, whether or not they ask. The 3-year rule is about the broker's own records, not a reason to withhold the seller's copy.

questions.q: Which of the following ads complies with New York advertising rules?
c: An Instagram post using only the agent's nickname
Another firm's exclusive posted without permission
A flyer promising buyers a guaranteed resale profit
A broker-approved agent site linking to the broker
questions.x: An agent or team website needs broker approval and a link to the broker's site. A nickname alone is not enough: the full licensed name must also appear.

questions.q: A salesperson known as 'Jojo' wants to use the nickname in ads. This is allowed if:
c: DOS approves the nickname in advance
The full licensed name also appears
The broker's name is left off the ad
It appears on social media only
questions.x: A nickname is fine only if the full licensed name also appears. Leaving the broker off would make it a blind ad, and DOS does not pre-approve nicknames.

questions.q: How may a broker pay an unlicensed assistant?
c: A share of each commission
A flat fee per closed deal
A salary or hourly wage
A bonus for each showing
questions.x: Unlicensed assistants are paid by salary or hourly wage, never per transaction. A flat fee per deal is still pay tied to licensed work, which is the trap.

questions.q: A salesperson offers her unlicensed assistant 5% of every commission she earns. This is:
c: Proper, if the broker approves the payment
Improper pay to an unlicensed person
Proper, if the work stays clerical
Improper only if the assistant shows homes
questions.x: Paying an unlicensed person a share of commission is paying for licensed work, which is prohibited. Even purely clerical work must be paid by salary or wage, not commission.

questions.q: A broker changes its rule on requiring mortgage pre-approval. Its standardized operating procedures must be updated within:
c: 5 days
10 days
30 days
6 months
questions.x: SOPs are updated within 30 days of any change, then affirmed at each 2-year renewal. Six months is tempting because brokers affirm compliance only at renewal, but changes cannot wait that long.

questions.q: Each of the following is required of a broker's standardized operating procedures EXCEPT:
c: Approval by the local MLS board
Being date-stamped and notarized
Posting on the broker's website
Availability at every office
questions.x: SOPs must be date-stamped, notarized, posted on the broker's website and apps, and available at every office. No MLS or trade group approves them.

questions.q: A seller asks his listing agent to fill out the property condition disclosure statement for him. The agent should:
c: Tell him of the duty but not fill it out
Fill it out from the listing information
Fill it out as long as the seller signs it
Offer the buyer a $500 credit instead
questions.x: The agent tells the seller about the duty to deliver the PCDS but never fills it out for him. The $500 credit opt-out was repealed effective March 20, 2024.

questions.q: A seller willfully fails to deliver a required PCDS. The seller is liable to the buyer for:
c: A $500 credit at closing
Three times the deposit
A $2,000 DOS fine
Actual damages
questions.x: A willful failure makes the seller liable for actual damages. The $500 credit was the old opt-out, repealed in 2024, and DOS fines apply to licensees, not sellers.

questions.q: New York requires brokers and salespersons to be licensed mainly in order to:
c: Fund the Department of State
Keep commission rates uniform
Limit competition among firms
Protect consumers from harm
questions.x: Licensing exists to protect the public through education, exams, and discipline. Uniform commission rates is the trap: rates are negotiable, and agreeing on them is illegal price fixing.

questions.q: A buyer believes a salesperson misled her and wants to file a license-law complaint. She should contact the:
c: Department of Financial Services
NYS Department of State
Attorney Grievance Committee
Local Board of Realtors
questions.x: DOS licenses and disciplines brokers and salespersons. The Realtor board is the trap: it can enforce its own ethics code on members but cannot suspend or revoke a state license.

questions.q: In 2026, a candidate finishes a 75-hour salesperson course she started years ago. She:
c: Is short; the course is now 77 hours
Has met the 75-hour requirement
Needs the full 152-hour program
Qualifies with a year of supervised work
questions.x: The salesperson course became 77 hours on December 21, 2022. The 152-hour program is the trap: that is the broker total (77 plus 75), not the salesperson requirement.

questions.q: Tasha, 19, has finished 152 hours of education and has three years of general real estate experience. Can she be licensed as a broker?
c: Yes, her experience meets the point system
Yes, once she passes the broker exam
No, a broker has to be at least 20
No, she needs 2 years as a salesperson
questions.x: Brokers have to be at least 20. The salesperson-experience choice is the trap: 3 years of general real estate experience is an accepted alternative to 2 years as a salesperson.

questions.q: Which can a New York attorney do without holding a real estate broker license?
c: Negotiate a client's sale in her practice
Hire salespersons to find listings
Sponsor a salesperson's license
Run a rental brokerage in her firm
questions.x: Attorneys are exempt when acting in their own law practice. Sponsoring a salesperson is the trap: employing or sponsoring salespersons requires a broker license, even for an attorney.

questions.q: Which person needs a New York real estate license?
c: An executor selling the estate's two-family
A friend negotiating a sale for a 3% fee
A town officer selling surplus land
An owner selling her own vacant lot
questions.x: Negotiating a sale for another for a fee is brokerage, friend or not. The executor is the trap: persons acting under court authority, such as executors and administrators, are exempt.

questions.q: Diane asks where her salesperson license is kept while she works for Hudson & Hart. The answer:
c: At her home, with her other papers
On file with the county clerk
Posted at each listing she holds
At her sponsoring broker's office
questions.x: The sponsoring broker maintains associated licensees' licenses. Keeping it at home is the trap: what Diane carries is the pocket card.

questions.q: At an open house, a visitor asks a licensee to prove he is licensed. Which item shows both the licensee and his sponsoring broker?
c: His business card
His course certificate
His DOS pocket card
His exam pass letter
questions.x: The DOS pocket card identifies the licensee and the sponsoring broker. A business card is the trap: anyone can print one, and it is not proof of licensure.

questions.q: Priya left her firm and wants to show a listing for her new brokerage tomorrow. What has to happen first?
c: Her new broker files the change with DOS
She retakes the salesperson exam
She completes 22.5 hours of new CE
Her former broker signs a release
questions.x: A salesperson can act for a new firm once the new broker records the association with DOS. The former broker's release is the trap: the old firm cannot hold her license hostage.

questions.q: Kim completed 15 hours of CE during her 2-year term. To renew she:
c: Has met the 15-hour rule
Needs 7.5 more hours
Needs 9 more hours
Needs 24 hours in total
questions.x: The requirement is 22.5 hours per term: 22.5 minus 15 = 7.5 more hours. 24 total is the trap, a round number close to the real figure.

questions.q: Which CE topic carries the largest required block, 3 hours, in each renewal term?
c: Ethics
Law of agency
Implicit bias
Fair housing
questions.x: Fair housing and/or discrimination requires 3 hours. Ethics is the trap at 2.5 hours; implicit bias is 2, and agency is 1 (2 on the first renewal).

questions.q: Which licensee may renew without completing continuing education?
c: An attorney admitted in New York
A broker licensed for over 15 years
A salesperson over age 65
An associate broker who is inactive
questions.x: Attorneys admitted in New York are exempt from CE. The 15-year broker is the trap: that exemption existed under the old law and has ended.

questions.q: Why does a nonresident licensee file an irrevocable consent with DOS?
c: To waive New York license fees
To avoid taking the NY exam
So legal papers can reach her
To post bond for escrow funds
questions.x: The consent lets lawsuits about NY business be served on her through the Secretary of State. Avoiding the exam is the trap: that is reciprocity, a separate arrangement with certain states.

questions.q: An apartment information vendor charges a $250 advance fee. The customer finds an apartment on her own, not through the vendor, and asks in writing for a refund. She generally gets back:
c: Nothing
questions.x: The vendor refunds the fee less up to $15 for administrative costs: $250 minus $15 = $235. The full $250 is the trap; the small administrative charge may be kept.

questions.q: Hudson & Hart opens a second office in Astoria. Who may supervise it?
c: A salesperson with tenure
Any licensee the broker appoints
An office manager with no license
An associate broker or the broker
questions.x: A branch is supervised by the broker or an associate broker and holds its own branch license. The tenured salesperson is the trap: experience does not substitute for a broker-level license.

questions.q: A broker deposits a buyer's $40,000 down payment into her escrow account, then pays the office rent from that account. Paying the rent is:
c: Commingling
Conversion
Permitted if repaid
Escheat
questions.x: Spending client funds for the broker's own purposes is conversion. Commingling is the trap: it means mixing funds together, while this broker actually used the money.

questions.q: A seller tells Jordan, "Get me $800,000 and keep anything above that as your fee." Jordan should:
c: Decline; net listings are banned
Accept if the seller puts it in writing
Accept for commercial property
Accept with a cap on his share
questions.x: That is a net listing, prohibited in New York by 175.19. Putting it in writing is the trap: a signed net listing is still prohibited.

questions.q: A broker closes a sale in March 2026. The transaction file is kept at least until:
c: March 2027
The commission is paid
March 2029
March 2033
questions.x: Brokers keep transaction records for 3 years, so March 2029. March 2033 is the trap: 7 years is a tax-record habit, not the DOS rule.

questions.q: Which ad placed by a salesperson complies with NY advertising rules?
c: Astoria 2BR. Diane, 718-555-0122
Astoria 2BR. Call or text Diane today
Astoria 2BR. Diane Lee, Realtor®, cell 718-555-0122
Astoria 2BR. Hudson & Hart Realty, 718-555-0100
questions.x: An ad identifies the broker by name with an address or phone. The Realtor choice is the trap: a trade-group title is not the broker's name, so it is still a blind ad.

questions.q: Diane, a salesperson, is ordering business cards. Which title complies with NY rules?
c: Licensed Real Estate Salesperson
Licensed Sales Agent
Licensed Real Estate Sales Associate
Licensed Broker Associate
questions.x: Salespersons are identified as licensed real estate salespersons. Sales associate is the trap: it sounds formal but is specifically barred, along with licensed sales agent.

questions.q: A team at Hudson & Hart Realty is choosing a new name. Each of the following complies EXCEPT:
c: The Reyes Team of Hudson & Hart Realty
The Reyes-Lee Team at Hudson & Hart Realty
Reyes Realty Team at Hudson & Hart Realty
The Lee Team at Hudson & Hart Realty
questions.x: A team name cannot use terms like realty that suggest a separate brokerage. The hyphenated name is the trap: using two members' names is fine as long as it says team and identifies the broker.

questions.q: Which task may an unlicensed assistant perform?
c: Show a vacant apartment to a renter
Explain the lease terms to an applicant
Suggest an offer price to a buyer
Schedule showings for the agents
questions.x: Scheduling is clerical work. Showing a vacant unit is the trap: it seems harmless but is licensed activity even when nobody negotiates.

questions.q: A broker's posted SOPs require mortgage preapproval before touring. A walk-in buyer without preapproval asks to see homes. The agent should:
c: Waive it since the buyer seems qualified
Apply the preapproval rule as posted
Waive it for buyers from the area
Ask the buyer's age and family size
questions.x: SOPs are applied the same way to every buyer, which is their fair housing purpose. Waiving it for a buyer who seems qualified is the trap: case-by-case exceptions are exactly what invites unequal treatment.

questions.q: A Syracuse seller hands the buyer the PCDS one day after the contract is signed. Under current law this is:
c: Late; it is due before signing
Fine, as long as it is before closing
Fine, with a $500 credit
Fine, if the buyer waives it
questions.x: The PCDS is delivered before the buyer signs the contract. The $500 credit is the trap: that opt-out was eliminated on March 20, 2024.

questions.q: Which sale requires the seller to give a Property Condition Disclosure Statement?
c: A Manhattan co-op apartment
A referee's sale after foreclosure
An owner's sale of a two-family
A sale between two co-owners
questions.x: An owner's sale of a 1 to 4 family home is covered. The co-op is the trap: co-ops and condos are exempt because buyers get shares or units in a building governed by a board.

questions.q: Under RPL 443-a, which fact about a Bronx house does the seller have no duty to disclose?
c: A known leaking oil tank
A suicide in the house
A cracked foundation
An uncapped gas well
questions.x: RPL 443-a removes any duty to disclose a death, suicide, or homicide on the property. The gas well is the trap: RPL 242 requires disclosing known uncapped wells.

questions.q: A Chautauqua County seller knows of an old uncapped natural gas well on the lot. The seller:
c: Has no duty to mention it
Discloses it if the buyer asks
Reports it to DOS instead
Discloses it in the contract
questions.x: RPL 242 requires the seller to disclose known uncapped gas wells in the contract. Waiting for the buyer to ask is the trap: that is the stigma rule for deaths, not the gas well rule.

questions.q: A court ordered an unlicensed person to pay $20,000, the maximum allowed under RPL 442-e. What fee did he collect?
questions.x: The maximum is four times the fee, so the fee was $20,000 / 4 = $5,000. $2,000 is the trap: it is the DOS fine per violation, a different penalty.

questions.q: DOS revokes Ray's license after a hearing. He believes the decision was arbitrary. His route to court is:
c: A SCAR petition
A lis pendens filing
An Article 78 case
A small claims action
questions.x: An Article 78 proceeding challenges a state agency decision. Small claims is the trap: it handles money disputes and cannot overturn a license revocation.

questions.q: A broker may lawfully share a commission with which of the following?
c: A building super who sends renters
An unlicensed assistant per closing
A friend who referred the buyer
A cooperating licensed broker
questions.x: Commissions may be shared with other licensed brokers. The assistant per closing is the trap: an unlicensed employee may get a salary, but not pay per deal for licensed activity.

questions.q: A Brooklyn broker rents a second storefront in Bayside and wants to start meeting buyers there next week. What is required first?
c: A written notice to DOS giving the new address within 30 days after the office opens
An amended main office license listing both the Brooklyn and Bayside addresses
A posted copy of the main office license and a sign naming the broker
Its own DOS branch license, with a broker or associate broker as manager
questions.x: Every branch needs its own branch office license and a qualified manager (the broker or an associate broker) before it operates. The 30-day notice choice is the trap: there is no option to open first and tell DOS later, and an amended main license does not license a second location.

questions.q: Who may be put in charge of supervising a real estate branch office in New York?
c: The broker or a licensed associate broker
Any salesperson with at least two years of experience
An office manager who holds no license
A licensed salesperson who has the broker's written consent
questions.x: A branch must be supervised by the broker or an associate broker, someone who meets broker qualifications. A salesperson cannot manage a branch even with experience or written consent, which is the tempting wrong answer because experienced salespersons often act as team leaders.

questions.q: A salesperson leaves Firm A on Friday and wants to show apartments for Firm B on Monday. Firm A has not yet filed her termination. When may she act for Firm B?
c: Monday, because a delay in Firm A's filing cannot be charged against her
Thirty days after she gives Firm A written notice
Once her association with Firm B is on file with DOS
Immediately, if she carries her current pocket card
questions.x: A salesperson may act only for a broker she is associated with on DOS records, so she waits until Firm B's association is filed. Her old pocket card names Firm A, which is why showing it while working for Firm B would mislead. Blaming Firm A's delay is the trap: a filing problem never authorizes licensed work.

questions.q: When a salesperson moves to a new brokerage, the exclusive listings she took in at the old firm:
c: Go with her if the sellers agree in writing
Are split between both brokers until they expire
Are cancelled and re-signed by each seller
Stay with the old broker who holds the agreements
questions.x: A listing agreement is a contract between the seller and the broker, not the salesperson, so it stays with the old firm. The 'sellers agree' answer is the trap: a seller who wants to leave must deal with the broker who holds the exclusive.

questions.q: A salesperson's first renewal is due. She has 22.5 hours: 3 fair housing, 2 implicit bias, 2 cultural competency, 2.5 ethics, 1 recent legal matters, and 12 electives. What is missing?
c: Nothing; every mandatory topic is covered
One more hour of fair housing
Two hours of law of agency
Three more hours of ethics
questions.x: Every renewal needs law of agency, and the first renewal needs 2 hours of it. Her electives cannot replace that. The tempting answer is 'nothing', because the total hits 22.5; but the mandatory topics must each be present, not just the total.

questions.q: For a NY salesperson's second renewal, the 22.5 CE hours must include all of the following EXCEPT:
c: 2 hours of implicit bias
2 hours of law of agency
3 hours of fair housing
1 hour of recent legal matters
questions.x: After the first renewal, law of agency drops to 1 hour, so 2 hours is not required on a second renewal. Implicit bias (2), fair housing (3), and recent legal matters (1) apply every term. The trap is carrying the first-renewal agency number forward.

questions.q: A salesperson's license expired on June 30. She negotiates a lease on July 10 and renews on July 20. What is the status of the July 10 work?
c: Unlicensed activity, because there is no grace period
Covered, because she renewed within the 30-day grace period
Covered, because her broker's license remained active
Covered, if her CE was finished before June 30
questions.x: New York has no renewal grace period, so July 1 to July 20 she was unlicensed and could not negotiate a lease. Renewal restores the license going forward only. The broker's active license is the trap: every person who performs licensed acts needs a current license.

questions.q: A broker learns that one of her salespersons has been working for three weeks on an expired license. The broker's best course is to:
c: Stop her licensed work until she renews
Let her continue while she finishes CE, then renew
Reassign her deals to the broker's own name for now
Ask DOS for a temporary permit while she renews
questions.x: An expired salesperson cannot perform licensed acts, and a broker who lets her keep working shares the violation. DOS does not issue a temporary permit to bridge the gap. Letting her finish CE first is the trap: until renewal, she is simply unlicensed.

questions.q: A building superintendent offers to send a broker every new tenant for $300 each. The broker should:
c: Agree, if the payments are reported on a 1099
Decline, because the super is unlicensed
Agree, but pay the super a flat monthly fee
Agree, if each tenant signs a consent to the fee
questions.x: A broker may not pay an unlicensed person for referring real estate business, however the payment is structured. A flat monthly fee is the trap: it is still money paid because he sends tenants. Tax reporting or tenant consent does not make the payment lawful.

questions.q: An unlicensed person collects a $2,000 fee for finding a tenant. In a civil suit, the person harmed may recover:
c: The $2,000 collected and nothing more
A fixed $1,000 statutory penalty
Up to four times the fee
Double the fee, plus attorney fees
questions.x: Under RPL 442-e, the court can award a penalty between the fee collected and four times that amount against an unlicensed person who took a fee. Recovering only the fee is the trap because it sounds like simple restitution; the statute allows more as a deterrent.

questions.q: An unlicensed assistant may do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Schedule showings for the licensee
Pick up and return keys
Prepare flyers for broker approval
Host an open house alone
questions.x: Hosting an open house alone means showing property and answering questions about it, which is licensed activity. Scheduling, key handling, and preparing materials for approval are clerical. Flyers are the tempting wrong answer, but preparing them for the broker to approve is clerical support, not advertising on her own.

questions.q: At a showing, a buyer asks a broker's unlicensed assistant whether the seller would accept a lower price. The assistant should:
c: Give her honest impression of the seller's flexibility
Say the price is firm to protect the seller
Refer the buyer to the licensee handling the listing
