Write down the buyer's number and suggest a counter
questions.x: Discussing price or terms is negotiation, a licensed act. The assistant passes the question to a licensee. Saying the price is firm is the trap: it feels protective, but it is still a statement about negotiating terms, and the assistant has no authority to make it.

questions.q: Three salespersons at Bay Ridge Realty want to advertise as a team. Which name is permitted?
c: Narrows Group at Bay Ridge Realty
Narrows Associates Team of Bay Ridge Realty
Narrows Realty Team, Brooklyn's best
The Narrows Team of Bay Ridge Realty
questions.x: A team name must include "team" and either list the members' full licensed names or be followed by "at" or "of" plus the broker's name. "Group," "associates," and "realty" are banned because they suggest a separate brokerage. The first choice is the trap: it names the broker but keeps "Group."

questions.q: Under New York advertising rules, a team name may include all of the following EXCEPT:
c: An unlicensed assistant's name
The word "team" in the name
The broker's full name after "at"
Full licensed names of members
questions.x: An unlicensed person's name may not appear in a team name. The word "team," the members' full licensed names, and "at" or "of" plus the broker's name are all ways to build a compliant name. Members' names are the tempting wrong pick, but they are allowed when they are the full licensed names.

questions.q: In an ad, a New York salesperson may describe herself as a:
c: Licensed sales agent and advisor
Real estate sales associate
Licensed real estate salesperson
Real estate broker-salesperson
questions.x: The license type must be stated accurately, and "licensed real estate salesperson" does that. "Licensed sales agent" and "sales associate" are specifically prohibited, which makes them the traps because they are common in other states. "Broker" misstates the license.

questions.q: A salesperson's business card reads "Dana Cole, Sales Associate, Certified Luxury Specialist." What must change?
c: Nothing, if her broker approved the card
Remove the luxury designation
Add her license number below her name
Replace the "Sales Associate" title
questions.x: "Sales associate" is a prohibited title, so the license type must be stated accurately. Additional designations such as a luxury certification are permitted on top of the correct title, which is why removing it is the trap. Broker approval does not cure a prohibited title.

questions.q: A blind ad is one that:
c: Omits the property's price
Omits the property's address
Omits the broker's identity
Omits the agent's cell phone
questions.x: An ad that does not identify the broker (name plus address or phone) is a blind ad, which the regulation prohibits. Ads may leave out a price or exact address. The agent's cell is the trap: a salesperson's own number is optional, but the broker's information is required.

questions.q: A salesperson posts "Sunny 2BR, Astoria, $3,100. Text me: 347-555-0188" on a neighborhood Facebook group. To comply, the post must add:
c: The salesperson's license number and expiration
The broker's name and the broker's address or phone
The landlord's name and the building's address
A fair housing logo and the words "equal opportunity"
questions.x: Every ad must show the broker's name plus the broker's address or phone number, and a social post advertising a listing is an ad. The fair housing logo is the tempting choice because offices and websites must post fair housing notices, but the missing element that makes this a blind ad is the broker.

questions.q: A salesperson wants to post another firm's exclusive listing on her team page. She may do so:
c: With the listing broker's consent and credit
Freely, once the listing appears in the MLS
If the seller tells her it is fine by text
If she adds a note saying she does not hold it
questions.x: Advertising another broker's exclusive requires that broker's authorization, and the ad must name the listing broker right after a phrase like "Listing courtesy of." Seller permission is the trap: the seller has given the exclusive to the listing broker, whose consent the rule requires.

questions.q: Which ad statement is required when a broker, with permission, advertises another broker's exclusive listing?
c: "Listing courtesy of" plus the listing broker
"Commission available to cooperating brokers"
"Exclusive" followed by the advertising agent's name
"Shown by appointment with the seller"
questions.x: The ad must clearly disclose the listing broker immediately after a phrase such as "Listing courtesy of," "Listing provided by," or "Listing agent contact." The "Exclusive" choice is the trap because it suggests the advertiser holds the listing, which is exactly the confusion the rule prevents.

questions.q: Before DOS holds a hearing on charges against a salesperson, the law requires:
c: A criminal conviction of the licensee for the same conduct
Written charges 10 or more days before, copied to the broker
Written approval from the Attorney General to go forward
A vote by the professional standards committee of the local Board of Realtors
questions.x: RPL 441-e requires written charges at least 10 days before the hearing, and when the licensee is a salesperson the broker is notified by certified mail. The licensee may appear with counsel. The criminal-conviction choice is the trap: discipline is administrative and does not need a criminal case first.

questions.q: A salesperson charged by DOS wants a lawyer to speak for him at the hearing. Under RPL 441-e, he:
c: May not, since hearings are informal interviews
May submit written statements, not appear
May appear in person or through counsel
May use a lawyer once a suspension issues
questions.x: The statute gives the licensee the opportunity to be heard in person or through counsel. Hearings are run by a designated officer such as an administrative law judge, with subpoenas and testimony. The written-statement choice is the trap: written submissions are possible, but the right to appear is not limited to them.

questions.q: After a hearing, DOS may impose all of the following on a licensee EXCEPT:
c: A reprimand
A fine
A suspension
A jail term
questions.x: DOS's administrative penalties are reprimand, fine, suspension, and revocation. Jail is possible only for a criminal conviction, such as a misdemeanor under the license law, in criminal court. The fine is the tempting wrong pick for students who think fines need a court, but DOS imposes them directly.

questions.q: DOS revokes a salesperson's license after a hearing. Which statement about her future is correct?
c: She may reapply as a broker at once, since revocation was of a salesperson license
She may keep working under supervision while an Article 78 case is pending
She is generally barred from any real estate license for a year
She is barred from licensing for life after any revocation
questions.x: Under RPL 441-c, a revoked licensee is ineligible to be relicensed as a broker or salesperson until one year after the revocation. Switching license types does not get around it. The Article 78 choice is the trap: filing a court challenge does not by itself restore a revoked license.

questions.q: A seller asks her listing agent to fill out the Property Condition Disclosure Statement because "you know the house better than I do." The agent should:
c: Complete it for her and have the seller sign it
Complete the questions about flooding
Withhold the form from the seller
Explain it and let the seller complete it
questions.x: The PCDS states the seller's own knowledge, and the form says its answers are not the agent's representations. The agent may explain it and should remind the seller of the duty to deliver it, but the seller fills it in. Completing it for the seller is the trap: her signature would sit on answers that are really the agent's.

questions.q: The answers on a New York PCDS are representations of:
c: The seller
The seller's agent
The home inspector
The buyer's lender
questions.x: The PCDS is the seller's statement of actual knowledge. The form states that its representations are not those of the seller's agent and that it is not a warranty. The agent is the tempting answer because agents often hand the form over, but delivering it does not make the answers the agent's.

questions.q: A seller who knows his roof leaks checks "UNKN" for roof leaks on the PCDS. After closing, the buyer spends $9,000 on repairs. The seller is most likely:
c: Protected, because unknown is a permitted answer
Protected, because the buyer could have inspected the roof
Liable for actual damages for a willful failure
Liable for a flat $500 statutory penalty
questions.x: "UNKN" is for facts the seller does not know. Using it to hide a known leak is a willful failure, and RPL 465 makes the seller liable for the buyer's actual losses. The $500 figure is the trap: it echoes the old credit opt-out, which was repealed in 2024 and was never a penalty.

questions.q: Under the Property Condition Disclosure Act, a seller is liable to the buyer for:
c: Any defect found after closing
Defects the seller should have found by investigating
Twice the cost of repairing undisclosed defects
A willful failure to comply, for actual damages
questions.x: RPL 465 limits the seller's liability under the act to a willful failure, and the buyer recovers actual losses. The act does not require the seller to investigate or check public records, which is why the 'should have found' answer is the trap. It also does not make the seller warrant everything.

questions.q: After the contract is signed but before closing, a seller discovers termites the PCDS said were absent. The seller must:
c: Do nothing, since the PCDS duty ended at contract signing
Cancel the contract and return the deposit
Deliver a revised PCDS as soon as practicable
Disclose it at the closing table
questions.x: RPL 462 requires a revised statement as soon as practicable when the seller learns something before title transfer or occupancy that makes the delivered form materially inaccurate. The trap is thinking the duty ends at signing; it continues until closing or occupancy, whichever is first.

questions.q: A seller's duty to revise a delivered PCDS ends at the earlier of:
c: Contract signing or the buyer's inspection
Title transfer or the buyer's occupancy
The mortgage commitment or the appraisal
Attorney approval or the final walk-through
questions.x: No revised statement is required after the earlier of title transfer or the buyer taking occupancy. Contract signing is the trap: delivery of the original form is due before signing, but the duty to revise runs past it.

questions.q: A seller in Cattaraugus County knows of an uncapped natural gas well in his woodlot. Under RPL 242 he must:
c: Tell the buyer before the contract is signed
Cap the well before he lists the property
Report the well to the county clerk at closing
Disclose it if the buyer asks in writing
questions.x: RPL 242 requires a seller with actual knowledge of an uncapped natural gas well to inform the buyer before entering into a contract. It requires disclosure, not repair. The ask-in-writing choice is the trap: that procedure belongs to stigmatized property under RPL 443-a, not gas wells.

questions.q: The seller's duty to disclose an uncapped natural gas well applies when the seller:
c: Has actual knowledge of the well
Drilled the well personally
Has a well permit on file with DEC
Sells to a buyer from out of state
questions.x: The disclosure duty in RPL 242 turns on the seller's actual knowledge of the uncapped well, regardless of who drilled it or when. The permit choice is the trap: abandoned wells often have no permit on file, and the duty does not depend on paperwork.

questions.q: A buyer's agent asks in writing whether a homicide occurred in a listed house. One did. The listing agent should:
c: Deny it, since the law does not require disclosure
Ask the seller; answer only with consent
Answer at once, since a written question compels a reply
Report the question to DOS as a fair housing issue
questions.x: Under RPL 443-a, a homicide is not a material defect and need not be volunteered. When a buyer asks in writing, the seller decides whether to respond, and the seller's agent reports the answer with the seller's consent. The denial is the trap: the law allows silence, never a false statement.

questions.q: Under RPL 443-a, a seller need not disclose all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A suicide in the house
A prior owner's HIV status
A cracked foundation wall
A natural death in the home
questions.x: RPL 443-a covers psychological stigma: deaths of any kind, felony crimes, and an occupant's HIV or other condition not spread by living there. A cracked foundation is a physical defect, which belongs on the PCDS and which an agent who knows of it must disclose. The natural death is the trap; the statute now covers accidental and natural deaths too.

questions.q: A Brooklyn salesperson refers a buyer to a Buffalo brokerage. The referral fee may lawfully be paid:
c: By the Buffalo agent to the Brooklyn salesperson directly
By the buyer to the Brooklyn salesperson at closing
By the seller to the Brooklyn salesperson as a gift
By the Buffalo broker to the Brooklyn broker
questions.x: Brokers share fees with other brokers, and a salesperson is paid only by his own sponsoring broker, who then pays him his share. The direct agent-to-salesperson payment is the trap: both may be licensed, but neither is the other's broker.

questions.q: Under RPL 442, a New York broker may share a commission with each of the following EXCEPT:
c: A broker licensed in New York
A salesperson associated with that broker
A salesperson associated with a different broker
A person regularly in the brokerage business in another state
questions.x: RPL 442 lets a broker pay its own associated salespersons, other NY licensed brokers, and people regularly in the brokerage business in another state. A salesperson at another firm must be paid through her own broker. The out-of-state choice is the trap, because many expect only NY licensees to qualify.

questions.q: A Queens broker is closing her firm. Her top salesperson is joining another brokerage and says his 12 listings will come with him. The listings:
c: Move with him, since he took each one and knows the sellers
Move with him once his new broker files the change of association
Stay with the closing broker unless each seller relists elsewhere
Pass to the new broker automatically when the old firm stops operating
questions.x: A listing agreement is a contract between the seller and the broker, not the salesperson. The salesperson cannot carry it to a new firm, and it does not pass automatically to anyone. Each seller decides whether to be released and relist. The change of association choice is the trap: that filing lets him work for the new broker, but it transfers no clients.

questions.q: In an exclusive right to sell listing taken by a salesperson, the seller's contract is with:
c: The salesperson who signed it
The salesperson's broker
The multiple listing service
Both the broker and salesperson
questions.x: The salesperson signs on behalf of the sponsoring broker, so the listing agreement is between the seller and the broker. That is why listings stay with the firm when a salesperson leaves. The 'both' choice is the trap: the salesperson acts for the broker but is not a party to the agency contract.

questions.q: Two licensed brokers form a corporation to run a new brokerage in Yonkers. Their office manager, a licensed salesperson, wants to become an officer of the corporation. Which is true?
c: She may be an officer if she owns no shares in the corporation
She may be an officer once the brokers sign a dual licensure consent
She cannot be an officer and keep her license as a salesperson
She cannot be an officer until the corporation has been licensed 2 years
questions.x: RPL 441-b bars DOS from issuing a salesperson license to an officer of a corporation, a manager or member of an LLC, or a partner in a partnership licensed as a broker. To be an officer who acts in the brokerage, she would need to qualify as a broker. The dual licensure choice is the trap: dual licensure lets an associate broker also hold a broker license, not a salesperson become an officer.

questions.q: A licensed associate broker forms an LLC to open her own firm. Before the LLC may list property for others:
c: The LLC needs a broker license, issued through her as a licensed member
She would give up her associate broker license and retake the broker exam
The LLC files its articles of organization, which serve as its license
Her sponsoring broker has to consent in writing to the LLC's formation
questions.x: Article 12-A requires a license for any LLC or corporation in the brokerage business, so the entity applies to DOS for a broker license through a licensed member or officer. Forming the LLC is only corporate paperwork, which is the trap in the articles choice. She may keep her associate broker license too, because RPL 440 allows an associate broker to retain a separate broker license.

questions.q: A Bronx broker moves her principal office. She and three associated salespersons are licensed there. What filing fee must accompany the change of address notice to DOS?
questions.x: RPL 441-a requires a $10 fee for each licensee named in the change of address notice: four licensees times $10 is $40. The $10 choice is the trap for anyone who thinks the fee is per office. The $150 figure is the fee for changing a broker's name or license status, a different filing.

questions.q: A Suffolk County broker moves his office to a new address in March and plans to report it on his renewal in December. Meanwhile, his licenses and those of his salespersons are:
c: Valid, because address changes may be reported at the next renewal
Valid, but he owes a late fee for each month the notice is overdue
Revoked, because operating from an unlicensed address is unlicensed activity
Suspended, because a move without notice to DOS suspends them
questions.x: Under RPL 441-a a change of business address made without notice to DOS operates to suspend the licenses until DOS lifts the suspension. The broker must file the change, with $10 per licensee, when he moves. The renewal choice is the trap: a renewal application can update an address, but waiting nine months leaves everyone working on suspended licenses.

questions.q: A salesperson leaves Broker A for Broker B in May. A sale she brought in while with Broker A closes in June. Her commission split on that sale is paid by:
c: Broker B, because she is associated with Broker B when the deal closes
Broker A, the broker she worked for when she did the work
The seller, directly, since her association with Broker A has ended
Broker A and Broker B equally, unless the brokers agree otherwise
questions.x: A salesperson may be paid only by a broker she was associated with, and the commission on this deal is earned by Broker A, who holds the listing or buyer agreement. Broker A pays her split even though she has moved. The Broker B choice is the trap: her current sponsor did nothing on the deal and is not entitled to the fee unless the brokers agree.

questions.q: A salesperson brought a buyer to a Rochester house while working for her former broker. All of the following are true EXCEPT:
c: Her former broker may still collect the commission on the sale
Her former broker may pay her the split agreed for that sale
She may sue the seller in her own name for the unpaid commission
Her claim for her split runs against her former broker
questions.x: The commission claim against the seller belongs to the broker who holds the agreement and was licensed when the claim arose (RPL 442-d). The salesperson's rights run against her own broker under their agreement. The former-broker choices are true: a broker may collect a fee earned while she worked there and pay her for that work after she leaves.

questions.q: An associate broker manages a branch office for a Manhattan firm. She also wants to hold a broker license for her own small property management company. Under RPL 440 she:
c: May do both, since an associate broker may keep a broker license
May do both, but not until she gives up the associate broker license
May not, because a licensee may hold one real estate license at a time
May not, because office managers are required to work for one broker
questions.x: RPL 440 says an associate broker, including one who works as an office manager, may also retain a separate real estate broker license under an individual, trade name, partnership, LLC, or corporation. Both brokers should know and agree, and each deal's fee flows through the broker on that deal. The one-license choice is the trap: it ignores the statutory exception for associate brokers.

questions.q: A licensed salesperson who wants to be associated with two different brokers at the same time must:
c: Upgrade to an associate broker license, the one license allowed two sponsors
Ask DOS for a hardship waiver, since two associations are an exception
Choose one broker as primary and list the other on her pocket card as a secondary sponsor
File a separate application and fee for each association, with every broker's consent
questions.x: DOS's salesperson application instructions say a licensee who intends to be associated with more than one broker files separate applications and fees for each association, with the consent of all sponsoring brokers obtained first. The associate broker choice is the trap: RPL 440 lets an associate broker keep a separate broker license, but it does not stop a salesperson from having two consenting sponsors.

questions.concept: Compensation from more than one party
questions.q: A buyer's broker in Westchester is paid by her buyer client. The seller offers the buyer's broker an extra $5,000 if the buyer signs this week. The buyer's broker may accept:
c: Only if the seller's broker agrees to the payment in writing
Only with full disclosure to and consent of all the parties
Only if the payment goes to her broker's escrow account
Only if the buyer's fee is reduced by the same amount
questions.x: Under 19 NYCRR 175.7 a broker may not receive compensation from more than one party to a transaction without full disclosure and the consent of all parties. The buyer must know her own broker has a financial reason to close fast. Reducing the buyer's fee is one way to resolve it, which makes it the trap: the rule requires disclosure and consent, not a particular fee arrangement.

questions.concept: Compensation from more than one party
questions.q: Under New York's DOS rules, a broker who wants to be paid by both the buyer and the seller in the same deal needs:
c: Full disclosure to and consent of all parties
Approval from the multiple listing service
A dual agency consent signed by the seller only
A fee no larger than the customary commission
questions.x: 19 NYCRR 175.7 allows compensation from more than one party only with full disclosure to and consent of all parties. The seller-only dual agency consent is the trap: dual agency itself requires informed written consent of both buyer and seller, and payment from both sides must also be disclosed to everyone. An MLS has no say over who pays a broker.

cram.html: Licensing law: RPL Article 12-A, run by the Department of State. Purpose: protect the public.
Salesperson: age 18, 77 hours, $65 for 2 years. Broker: age 20, 152 hours, 2 years (3,500 points) as salesperson or 3 years general (5,250 points), $185.
State exam: $15, 75 questions, 90 minutes, 70% to pass, results valid 2 years.
CE: 22.5 hours every 2 years: 3 fair housing, 2 implicit bias, 2 cultural competency, 2.5 ethics, 1 legal matters, 1 agency (2 on first renewal). Only NY attorneys exempt.
Broker keeps the salesperson's license at the office. Salesperson carries the pocket card.
Changing firms: cannot work until the new broker files the change of association. Listings stay with the broker.
Each branch office: own license ($185), supervised by broker or associate broker.
Exempt: owners, NY attorneys (not if they hire salespersons), public officers, court appointees (referees, receivers, executors).
Salespersons are paid only by their sponsoring broker. Never pay an unlicensed person for licensed work.
Commingling = mixing client money with your own. Conversion = spending it. Both can cost the license.
Net listings: prohibited (175.19). Records: keep 3 years (175.23).
Every ad names the broker plus address or phone. No broker = blind ad.
Banned titles: "sales associate," "licensed sales agent," "broker" for a non-broker. Team names need "team"; no "group," "realty," "associates".
Unlicensed assistants: clerical only. No showing, no price talk, no commission pay.
SOPs (RPL 442-h): ID? exclusive buyer agreement? pre-approval? Posted, notarized, applied equally.
PCDS: 1 to 4 family, before contract. $500 credit opt-out ended March 20, 2024; flood questions added.
Stigmatized property (443-a): no duty to disclose death, crime, or HIV/AIDS on site. Never lie if asked in writing.
Uncapped natural gas wells: seller discloses known wells (RPL 242).
DOS penalties: reprimand, fine up to $2,000 per violation, suspension, revocation (wait 1 year to reapply).
Unlicensed activity: misdemeanor, plus civil suit for up to 4 times the fee.
Challenge a DOS decision in court: Article 78 proceeding.
Apartment information vendor: refund advance fee minus up to $15 if no rental; fee capped at one month's rent.
Nonresident licensee files an irrevocable consent to service of process.

subjects.title: Law of Agency
subjects.blurb: The single biggest block of the DOS exam. Who you represent, what you owe them, what you owe everyone else, and the NY forms that prove you said so out loud.

lessons.title: The Agent as Fiduciary
lessons.tagline: Your client gets your loyalty. Everyone else gets your honesty. Never mix those up.
objectives: Tell a client from a customer and say what each is owed
Name the six fiduciary duties (OLD CAR) and spot a breach of each
Classify an agent as universal, general, or special and state what a listing broker may not do
Explain misrepresentation, puffing, and vicarious liability, and their consequences

blocks.title: Two secrets in one afternoon, Sheepshead Bay
blocks.html: Jordan lists a semi-attached house on East 19th Street for $1,100,000. At the open house a buyer lingers and says, "I'd go to $1.15M for this block. My lease is up in 60 days." That evening the seller calls: "Between us, I'd take $1.05M if it closes fast." Jordan is now holding both secrets. Which one must Jordan pass along, and which one must Jordan never repeat?
blocks.casual: Picture this. Jordan's got a semi-attached on East 19th Street in Sheepshead Bay listed at $1,100,000. At the open house a buyer hangs back and says, 'I'd go to $1.15M for this block. My lease is up in 60 days.' That night the seller calls: 'Between us, I'd take $1.05M if it closes fast.' So now Jordan's sitting on two secrets. One of them has to go to somebody. The other one can never leave Jordan's mouth. Which is which?

deeper.plain: An agent hears things from both sides. What you do with each piece depends entirely on who you work for.
deeper.picture: Think of a lawyer in a hallway. If the other side's lawyer blurts out their client's bottom line, your lawyer runs it straight back to you. Your bottom line never leaves the room.
deeper.street: Jordan texts the sellers that night: 'Open house buyer said $1.15M, lease ends in 60 days.' The next morning that same buyer calls and asks, 'Would they take less?' Jordan says, 'I can't discuss my sellers' position, but I'll present any offer you want to make.'
deeper.stakes: Swap the secrets and Jordan just cost the sellers $50,000 to $100,000 of negotiating room. That is a loyalty and confidentiality breach: the sellers can sue for the difference, refuse the commission, and file a DOS complaint.
deeper.exam: Scenario questions hand you two pieces of information and ask what the agent must do. First find the client (who signed the listing). Information from the customer goes to the client; the client's information stays put.

blocks.html: Agency is a relationship of trust in which one person, the agent, is authorized to act on behalf of another, the principal. In real estate the principal is the seller, buyer, landlord, or tenant who hired the brokerage. The agent is the broker (the firm). Salespersons work under that broker and carry out the broker's agency.
blocks.casual: Agency is a trust relationship: you, the agent, get authority to act for somebody else, the principal. In real estate the principal is whoever hired the brokerage: a seller, buyer, landlord, or tenant. And here's the part people miss: the agent is the broker, meaning the firm. If you're a salesperson, you work under that broker and you're carrying out the broker's agency, not your own.

deeper.plain: The client hires the firm, not you personally. You are the firm's hands on that deal.
deeper.picture: It is like hiring a moving company. The contract is with the company; the crew that shows up carries out the company's promise.
deeper.street: The Okafors sign a listing with Diane's brokerage in Bed-Stuy. Jordan, a salesperson Diane sponsors, runs the listing day to day. If Jordan leaves the firm next month, the listing stays with Diane, and the Okafors are still Diane's clients.
deeper.stakes: New salespeople think the listing is theirs and try to take it when they switch firms. It isn't. Walking off with a client or their file can mean a lawsuit from the broker and trouble with DOS.
deeper.exam: Watch for 'the listing belongs to the salesperson' or 'the salesperson is the seller's agent.' The correct answer names the broker as the agent; the salesperson acts on the broker's behalf.

blocks.html: Licensure comes first. In New York only a licensed broker or a salesperson sponsored by one may list, sell, rent, negotiate, or collect a fee for someone else's real estate (RPL Article 12-A). A license lets you act as an agent. The agreement with a client makes you one.
blocks.casual: Before any of this, you need the license. In New York only a licensed broker, or a salesperson sponsored by one, can list, sell, rent, negotiate, or collect a fee for someone else's real estate (RPL Article 12-A). Think of it this way: the license lets you be an agent. Signing the agreement with a client is what actually makes you one.

deeper.plain: A license is permission to do the work. A client agreement is the actual job.
deeper.picture: A driver's license lets you drive, but you are not anybody's chauffeur until someone hires you.
deeper.street: Leo passes the exam in March but hasn't found a sponsoring broker yet. His cousin asks him to help rent out her Astoria two-family for a fee. Leo can't: without sponsorship his license isn't active, so he can't take the fee.
deeper.stakes: Collecting a fee without an active license is a misdemeanor, and the person who paid can sue for up to 4 times the amount collected (RPL 442-e). No license, no enforceable commission.
deeper.exam: Questions test the two steps: licensure to act, agreement to create agency. If a stem says a licensee 'automatically' represents anyone they talk to, that's wrong.

blocks.text: Client or customer: the line everything hangs on

left.title: Client (principal)
items: Hired you, by agreement or by conduct
Owed all six fiduciary duties
Gets your advice on price, strategy, and terms
Their secrets are protected, even after closing

right.title: Customer (third party)
items: The other side, or someone you have not agreed to represent
Owed honesty, fair dealing, good faith
Owed disclosure of known material defects
Not owed loyalty, advice, or confidentiality

deeper.plain: Your client gets your full team effort. Everyone else gets honesty, but not your advice or your secrets.
deeper.picture: Think of a sports agent at a negotiation. He's polite and truthful with the team's general manager, but he's playing for his athlete.
deeper.street: Priya represents the seller of a Ridgewood condo. She tells the buyer, Marcus, about the known roof leak because that's a material defect. She does not tell Marcus the sellers already bought in Florida and need to close by June.
deeper.stakes: Treat a customer like a client and you might give advice that hurts your real client, which is a loyalty breach. Treat a client like a customer and you shortchange them on advice and protection, which invites a lawsuit or lost fee.
deeper.exam: Cue words: 'the agent owes the buyer' when the agent represents the seller. Answer: honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material defects. Not loyalty, not confidentiality, not advice.

blocks.html: A client is the person you represent. A customer is a party you deal with but do not represent. In the scenario the seller signed the listing, so the seller is the client. The charming buyer is a customer.
blocks.casual: Your client is the person you represent. A customer is somebody you're dealing with but not representing. Back in Sheepshead Bay the seller signed the listing, so the seller's the client. That charming buyer at the open house? Customer.

deeper.plain: Ask one question: who did I agree to work for? That person is the client. Everyone else is a customer.
deeper.picture: It is like a waiter. The table that's seated is his; the people waiting by the door are polite company, not his tables.
deeper.street: Tasha is the seller's agent on a Harlem brownstone. A friendly buyer brings coffee to every showing and starts calling her 'my agent.' Tasha says plainly, 'I represent the sellers. I'm happy to show you the house, but you may want your own agent.'
deeper.stakes: When a buyer starts thinking you are their agent, you can create an agency by accident, and suddenly you owe duties to both sides without anyone's consent. That's undisclosed dual agency.
deeper.exam: Friendliness, chatting, or bringing coffee doesn't make someone a client. Watch for answers that say a buyer becomes a client by touring with the listing agent.

blocks.title: Who pays is not who you represent
blocks.html: Payment does not create agency. A buyer's agent can be paid out of the seller's proceeds and still owe every duty to the buyer. If a question says "the seller pays the commission, so the agent represents the seller," reject it.
blocks.casual: Here's a trap that catches people: who pays you doesn't decide who you work for. A buyer's agent can get paid out of the seller's proceeds and still owe every single duty to the buyer. If a question says 'the seller pays the commission, so the agent represents the seller,' throw it out.

deeper.plain: The money's source and the loyalty's direction are two separate things.
deeper.picture: Your boss's company pays for your health plan, but your doctor still works for you, not your boss.
deeper.street: Marcus hires Ray as his buyer's agent for a Bay Ridge co-op. At closing the seller agrees to cover Ray's 2.5% fee out of the sale price. Ray still negotiates hard against the seller, because Marcus is his client.
deeper.stakes: An agent who thinks 'the seller pays me' and goes soft in negotiation has breached loyalty to the buyer. The buyer can recover damages and the agent can face DOS discipline.
deeper.exam: This is a classic distractor. Any answer that ties representation to the source of payment is wrong. Agency comes from agreement or conduct.

blocks.q: In the scenario, the buyer tells Jordan she would pay $1.15M. What must Jordan do with that information?
c: Keep it confidential, since the buyer shared it in trust
Tell the seller, because Jordan owes the seller full disclosure
Ignore it until the buyer makes a written offer
Share it only if the buyer agrees
blocks.x: The buyer is a customer, so Jordan owes her no confidentiality. Jordan owes the seller disclosure of everything material, and a buyer's ceiling is very material.

blocks.text: The six fiduciary duties: OLD CAR

blocks.html: A fiduciary is someone in a position of trust who must put the principal's interests ahead of everyone else's, including their own. NY's agency disclosure form lists the fiduciary duties as reasonable care, undivided loyalty, confidentiality, full disclosure, obedience, and duty to account.
blocks.casual: A fiduciary is someone in a position of trust who has to put the principal's interests ahead of everyone else's, including their own. New York's agency disclosure form spells out the fiduciary duties: reasonable care, undivided loyalty, confidentiality, full disclosure, obedience, and duty to account.

deeper.plain: You are the guardian of the client's interests in the deal. Your own wants come last.
deeper.picture: A babysitter holds the house keys and the kids. She doesn't throw a party there, and she doesn't let strangers in.
deeper.street: Sal is listing Evelyn's Forest Hills Tudor. A buyer offers $10,000 more if Sal agrees to list the buyer's own house later. Sal must tell Evelyn about that side deal, because it puts Sal's interest in the mix.
deeper.stakes: Fiduciary breaches are the most common source of broker lawsuits. The remedy can be loss of the entire commission plus damages, even if the client still got a fair price.
deeper.exam: Expect a list of six duties with one fake one, like 'duty to guarantee price' or 'duty of performance bond.' Match against the six on the NY disclosure form.

blocks.caption: Flip each card. The back shows a one-line violation. On the exam you will get the violation and have to name the duty.

head: Duty
What it requires
Classic breach
rows: Holding back an offer because you think it is too low
Client's interest above all others, including yours
Steering the client to the deal that pays you more
Tell the client every material fact you learn
Not telling the seller the buyer is a relative of yours
Protect the client's private information, forever
Telling a buyer the seller is getting divorced
Account for all money and documents; no commingling
Depositing a client's deposit into your operating account
Pricing a two-family off a single-family comp without checking

deeper.plain: Six promises. Each one has a classic way to break it, and the exam loves the breaks.
deeper.picture: Think of a valet. Park where told (obedience), don't joyride (loyalty), report the dent (disclosure), don't tell anyone what's in the glovebox (confidentiality), hand back the keys and ticket (accounting), drive carefully (reasonable care).
deeper.street: Kim takes a $25,000 deposit on a Jackson Heights condo and drops it in her firm's operating account 'for a day.' Even if every dollar comes back, that's an accounting breach: escrow money goes into a separate escrow account.
deeper.stakes: Each breach has its own victim. Holding back a low offer can cost a seller the only real buyer. Commingling a deposit can lead to revocation. Pricing off the wrong comp can cost a client tens of thousands.
deeper.exam: The test describes a breach and asks which duty was violated. Hiding an offer is obedience and disclosure; mixing funds is accounting; sharing secrets is confidentiality; carelessness is reasonable care.

blocks.html: Obedience is limited to lawful instructions. "Don't show to families with kids" or "don't mention the leak" are not instructions you may follow. Refuse, and withdraw if the client insists.
blocks.casual: Obedience only covers lawful instructions. 'Don't show it to families with kids' or 'don't mention the leak'? You can't follow those. Say no, and if the client won't back off, walk away from the listing.

deeper.plain: Do what the client asks, unless what they ask is illegal or unethical.
deeper.picture: A personal assistant books your flights and picks up your dry cleaning. He doesn't forge your signature because you asked nicely.
deeper.street: The seller of a Flatbush two-family tells Diane, 'No Section 8 applicants for the upstairs unit.' Source of income is protected in New York. Diane refuses, explains the law, and says she'll withdraw if the seller insists.
deeper.stakes: Following an illegal instruction doesn't protect you. You take the fair housing complaint or fraud lawsuit right alongside the client, and you can lose your license.
deeper.exam: The phrase 'the agent followed the principal's instructions' is not a defense if the instruction was illegal. The correct move is to refuse and, if needed, withdraw.

blocks.html: Loyalty forbids self-dealing: buying the listing yourself, or through a relative or a company you own, without full disclosure to the client. If you want to buy your client's property, tell them in writing that you are the buyer. Undivided loyalty is the version a single agent gives. A dual agent cannot give it.
blocks.casual: Loyalty means no self-dealing. You don't buy the listing yourself, or through a relative, or through a company you own, without telling the client everything. Want to buy your client's place? Tell them in writing that you're the buyer. Undivided loyalty is what a single agent gives. A dual agent can't give it.

deeper.plain: You can't quietly be on the other side of your own client's deal.
deeper.picture: It's like a referee secretly betting on the game. Even a fair call looks crooked once the bet comes out.
deeper.street: Ray lists a Staten Island ranch at $650,000 and his brother-in-law's LLC offers $620,000. Ray must tell the seller, in writing, that the buyer is family. If he hides it and the LLC flips the house for $720,000, the seller has a strong case.
deeper.stakes: Hidden self-dealing can wipe out the commission, make Ray pay back the flip profit, and bring a DOS charge of untrustworthiness.
deeper.exam: Look for buyers who are 'a corporation the agent controls' or 'the agent's spouse.' The answer: allowed only with full written disclosure to the principal.

blocks.html: Confidentiality survives the end of the agency. Gossiping after closing that the seller "would have taken $1.05M" is still a breach. Confidentiality does not cover facts you are legally required to disclose, like a known material defect.
blocks.casual: Confidentiality doesn't end when the deal does. Saying after closing that the seller 'would have taken $1.05M' is still a breach. But confidentiality never covers what the law makes you disclose, like a known material defect.

deeper.plain: Client secrets stay secret forever. Known defects are not secrets you can keep.
deeper.picture: Like a therapist: the session ends, the secrets don't walk out with you.
deeper.street: A year after closing, at a Park Slope dinner party, Jordan jokes that his old sellers 'were desperate and would've taken way less.' The buyers are at the table. That's a breach, even though the agency ended.
deeper.stakes: Former clients can sue for breach of confidentiality after closing, and DOS can discipline the licensee. It also kills referrals in a neighborhood market that runs on word of mouth.
deeper.exam: The trap: 'duties end at closing.' Confidentiality survives. Also watch for answers that let an agent hide a defect 'because the seller asked for confidentiality.' Defects must be disclosed.

blocks.title: OLD CAR
blocks.html: Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care. Picture the client's old car: you drive it carefully, you do not sell its parts, and you return every receipt.
blocks.casual: Here's the memory trick: OLD CAR. Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care. Picture your client's old car: you drive it carefully, you don't sell off its parts, and you bring back every receipt.

deeper.plain: One acronym, six duties. If you can say it, you can spot the fake answer.
deeper.picture: Your client lends you their beat-up old car for a week. You follow their rules, you don't use it for Uber, you tell them about the noise, you don't post their stuff online, you return the gas receipts, and you don't crash it.
deeper.street: On exam day Leo sees 'Which is NOT a fiduciary duty: obedience, accounting, advertising, confidentiality.' He runs OLD CAR in his head. Advertising isn't in it, so that's the answer.
deeper.stakes: If you can't recall all six under pressure, you can't spot when you're breaching one in the field, either. Memorize it once and it pays off for both.
deeper.exam: Some books use 'COALD' or 'OLD CAR'; same six. The NY form words them as reasonable care, undivided loyalty, confidentiality, full disclosure, obedience, and duty to account.

blocks.q: Three weeks after closing, Jordan tells another agent the seller "was desperate, going through a divorce." Which duty did Jordan breach?
c: None, because the agency ended at closing
Accounting
Confidentiality, which survives the agency
Obedience
blocks.x: Agency ends at closing, but the duty to keep the client's confidences does not. Most duties end with the agency; confidentiality continues.

blocks.title: Jordan's two secrets, resolved
blocks.html:
Start by naming the client. The sellers signed the listing, so they are the client; the open house buyer is a customer.
1. The buyer's "I'd go to $1.15M, my lease ends in 60 days" is material to the sellers and the buyer is owed no confidentiality. Disclosure requires Jordan to pass it on to the sellers.
2. The sellers' "I'd take $1.05M" is the client's bargaining position. Confidentiality and loyalty forbid Jordan from sharing it with any buyer, now or after closing.
Flip the facts so Jordan is the buyer's agent, and both answers flip. Identify the client first; every duty question follows from that.
blocks.casual:
Start by naming the client. The sellers signed the listing, so they're the client. The open house buyer is a customer.
1. The buyer's 'I'd go to $1.15M, my lease ends in 60 days' matters to the sellers, and the buyer isn't owed any confidentiality. Disclosure says Jordan passes it to the sellers.
2. The sellers' 'I'd take $1.05M' is the client's bargaining position. Confidentiality and loyalty mean Jordan never shares it with any buyer, now or after closing.
Now flip it so Jordan's the buyer's agent, and both answers flip too. Find the client first. Every duty question falls out of that.

deeper.plain: Information flows toward your client and never away from them.
deeper.picture: Think of a one-way valve. Anything useful from the other side flows in to your client; nothing about your client flows out.
deeper.street: Same house, new facts: Marcus hired Jordan as his buyer's agent and the seller's agent lets slip, 'They'd take $1.05M.' Now Jordan tells Marcus immediately, and keeps Marcus's $1.15M ceiling locked up.
deeper.stakes: Get the direction wrong and you hand the other side your client's leverage. On a $1.1M house that can be a $100,000 swing, and the fee you earned on it becomes a lawsuit.
deeper.exam: Many questions are this exact flip. Underline who signed the agreement before you read the answer choices.

blocks.html: When do the duties start and stop? Fiduciary duties attach when the agency is created, usually at the signing of a listing or buyer agreement, though conduct can create it earlier. They end when the agency ends: at closing, expiration, or termination. Two things outlast it: the duty of confidentiality, and the duty to account for any money still in your hands.
blocks.casual: So when do the duties kick in and when do they stop? They attach when the agency is created, usually when the listing or buyer agreement gets signed, though your conduct can create it earlier. They end when the agency ends: closing, expiration, or termination. Two things outlast it: confidentiality, and your duty to account for any money still in your hands.

deeper.plain: Duties start when the relationship starts and end when it ends, with two leftovers.
deeper.picture: Like a house-sitting gig. Your job ends when the owners get home, but you still return the spare key and you still don't tell people what's in their closets.
deeper.street: Kim's listing on a Long Island City condo expires with a $5,000 deposit from a failed deal still in her firm's escrow. The agency is over, but Kim must still account for that money and return it as the contract requires.
deeper.stakes: Agents who treat expiration as a clean break sometimes sit on deposits or start talking. Both can lead to DOS discipline, and an unreturned deposit can lead to a lawsuit.
deeper.exam: Look for 'all duties end at closing.' False. Confidentiality and accounting survive. Also, duties can start before signing if your conduct created the agency.

blocks.title: Put it in writing
blocks.html: When a client gives an unusual instruction ("don't present offers below $900K," "no showings on Saturdays"), confirm it by email. If a dispute comes later, the email proves you obeyed, and it gives you a moment to spot an instruction that is not lawful.
blocks.casual: Quick pro move: when a client gives you an unusual instruction ('don't present offers under $900K,' 'no showings on Saturdays'), confirm it by email. If there's a fight later, that email proves you obeyed. And writing it down gives you a beat to notice if the instruction isn't legal.

deeper.plain: Odd instructions belong in writing so nobody can rewrite history later.
deeper.picture: It's like getting a receipt. You don't need it until you really need it.
deeper.street: Evelyn tells Sal, 'Don't bring me anything under $900K.' Sal emails, 'Confirming: you've instructed me not to present offers below $900,000.' Three months later the house is still unsold and Evelyn says Sal hid a good offer. Sal forwards the email.
deeper.stakes: Without the email it's your word against your client's, and the default rule is that you present all offers. A written instruction is the difference between a dismissed complaint and a refunded commission.
deeper.exam: The default rule tested on the exam is that all offers get presented, unless the client has said otherwise. A documented instruction is the exception.

head: Type
Authority
Real estate example
rows: Everything the principal could legally do
Holder of a broad power of attorney
A range of ongoing matters in one business
Property manager; a broker relative to its salespersons
blocks.caption: Most brokers are special agents to their clients.

deeper.plain: How much power an agent has depends on how much the principal handed over. Brokers usually get the smallest slice.
deeper.picture: Universal agent: you hand someone your whole wallet. General agent: you give them your work credit card. Special agent: you hand them $20 to buy one thing.
deeper.street: Evelyn signs a listing with Sal (special agent: sell one house). She also hires a property manager for her Sunnyside rental building (general agent: handle rents, repairs, tenants, ongoing). Her daughter holds a broad power of attorney (universal agent).
deeper.stakes: Overstep your authority and the principal isn't bound, but you may be personally liable for what you promised. That can leave a buyer with no deal and you facing a claim.
deeper.exam: The exam answer for a listing or buyer's broker is almost always 'special agent.' Property manager is the go-to example of a general agent.

blocks.html: A listing broker is a special agent. The broker markets, shows, and negotiates. The broker cannot sign a contract of sale, accept an offer, or sign a deed for the seller unless the seller grants that power separately in writing. The principal decides; the agent brings offers.
blocks.casual: A listing broker is a special agent. You market, you show, you negotiate. What you can't do is sign the contract of sale, accept an offer, or sign the deed for the seller, unless the seller separately gives you that power in writing. The principal decides. The agent brings the offers.

deeper.plain: You carry offers to the seller; the seller says yes or no and signs.
deeper.picture: You're the messenger between two kings. You can carry letters, but you can't sign the treaty.
deeper.street: A buyer offers $780,000 on a Kensington co-op and wants an answer in an hour. Priya calls the seller, who says yes on the phone. Priya tells the buyer's agent it's accepted in principle, and the seller signs through her attorney's contract later.
deeper.stakes: If an agent 'accepts' and the seller later backs out, the buyer has no enforceable deal and may go after the agent for the costs they incurred relying on it.
deeper.exam: Ask whether the broker had a separate written power of attorney. No POA, no authority to accept or sign. 'Special agent' and 'cannot bind the principal' go together.

blocks.title: The listing agent cannot accept
blocks.html: "The seller is in Florida, so the listing broker accepted the offer for her." Without a separate written power of attorney, that acceptance does not bind the seller.
blocks.casual: Watch for this one: 'The seller's in Florida, so the listing broker accepted the offer for her.' Without a separate written power of attorney, that acceptance doesn't bind the seller.

deeper.plain: Distance doesn't give the broker extra power. Only a written grant does.
deeper.picture: Your roommate can't sign your new lease just because you're on vacation.
deeper.street: The seller of a Fort Greene condo is wintering in Boca. Diane emails her the contract; she signs electronically from Florida. That is how distance gets handled, not by Diane signing for her.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who thinks they have a deal may cancel their lease or lock a rate. When the seller backs out, the buyer's losses can land on the broker who 'accepted.'
deeper.exam: Cue words: 'out of state,' 'unreachable,' 'urgent.' None of these expand a special agent's authority. Only a power of attorney does.

blocks.html: Inside the firm, salespersons are general agents of the broker: they act for the broker across its whole business, not just one deal. The broker, in turn, answers for everything they do. That is why a seller's complaint about Jordan lands on Diane's desk too, and why DOS can discipline a broker for failing to supervise.
blocks.casual: Inside the firm, salespersons are general agents of the broker. They act for the broker across the whole business, not just one deal. And the broker answers for everything they do. That's why a seller's complaint about Jordan lands on Diane's desk too, and why DOS can discipline a broker for failing to supervise.

deeper.plain: To the client you're working a single deal. To your own broker you're an all-purpose representative.
deeper.picture: Think of a bank teller. To you she's handling one deposit, but to the bank she's representing them all day long on everything.
deeper.street: Jordan misstates the taxes on a listing and the buyer sues. The complaint names Jordan and Diane, his broker, because Diane is responsible for supervising him.
deeper.stakes: Brokers who don't supervise get fined or suspended along with the salesperson. That's why firms run transaction reviews and require agents to copy the broker on key emails.
deeper.exam: Two relationships, two answers: broker to client is special agency; salesperson to broker is general agency.

blocks.text: What you owe the other side

blocks.html: Even though the customer gets no loyalty, NY requires every agent to deal with all parties honestly, fairly, and in good faith, and to disclose known facts that materially affect the value or desirability of the property, unless the law says otherwise. You may decline to advise the customer. You may never deceive them.
blocks.casual: The customer doesn't get your loyalty, but New York still makes every agent deal with all parties honestly, fairly, and in good faith. You also have to disclose known facts that materially affect the value or desirability of the property, unless the law says otherwise. You can decline to advise a customer. You can never deceive one.

deeper.plain: You don't work for the other side, but you can't lie to them either.
deeper.picture: Think of a poker game. You don't show your cards, but you also don't mark the deck.
deeper.street: A buyer asks Tasha, the seller's agent, 'Is $1.2M a good price?' Tasha says, 'I represent the seller, so I can't advise you there.' When the buyer asks about the boiler, she says it was replaced in 2022, which is true.
deeper.stakes: Lying to a customer is fraud, and the customer can sue. Even if your seller is happy, DOS can discipline you for dishonest dealing.
deeper.exam: The answer choice for 'what does a seller's agent owe a buyer?' is honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material defects. 'Nothing' is wrong. 'Loyalty' is wrong.

items: OK: "I represent the seller, so I can't advise you on price. Here are the recent sales."
OK: "The roof was replaced in 2019; here's the invoice."
Not OK: "The basement is bone dry" when you know it flooded last spring.
Not OK: staying silent about a known cracked foundation because the buyer did not ask.
blocks.casual:
Fine: 'I represent the seller, so I can't advise you on price. Here are the recent sales.'
Fine: 'The roof was replaced in 2019. Here's the invoice.'
Not fine: 'The basement's bone dry' when you know it flooded last spring.
Not fine: keeping quiet about a cracked foundation you know about just because the buyer didn't ask.

deeper.plain: Facts are fine, refusing to advise is fine. Lies and hidden defects are not.
deeper.picture: You're a tour guide for someone else's house. You can skip giving opinions, but you can't paint over the hole in the floor.
deeper.street: At a Canarsie showing Marcus asks Ray, 'Any water problems?' Ray knows the basement flooded during Ida. He says, 'Yes, it took on water in 2021. The seller installed a sump pump; here's the receipt.' The deal survives.
deeper.stakes: Silence about a known defect is still deception. After closing, the buyer can sue for the repair cost, and a jury will not like that the agent knew.
deeper.exam: Two tested points: you can refuse to give advice to a customer, and staying silent about a known material defect is not acceptable just because nobody asked.

blocks.html: Where does the customer's protection come from? Partly from common law fraud rules, partly from the agency disclosure form itself (which tells buyers what a seller's agent owes them), and partly from DOS's power to discipline any licensee who is dishonest or untrustworthy. A licensee who deceives a customer can lose the license even if the client was thrilled with the result.
blocks.casual: So where does the customer's protection actually come from? Partly from common law fraud rules, partly from the agency disclosure form itself (it tells buyers what a seller's agent owes them), and partly from DOS's power to discipline any licensee who's dishonest or untrustworthy. Deceive a customer and you can lose your license, even if your client loved the result.

deeper.plain: Three safety nets protect the other side: fraud law, the disclosure form, and DOS.
deeper.picture: Like a store with a security camera, a posted return policy, and a manager on call. Any one of them can catch you.
deeper.street: A buyer in Bensonhurst discovers the 'legal two-family' was never legal. The buyer sues the seller's agent for fraud and files a DOS complaint. Both proceed even though the seller praised the agent.
deeper.stakes: A happy client doesn't shield you. Customers can take your money through the courts and your license through DOS.
deeper.exam: If a stem says 'the seller was satisfied, so no violation occurred,' reject it. DOS judges the licensee's honesty, not the client's mood.

blocks.html: Misrepresentation is a false statement or concealment of a material fact that someone relies on. It comes in degrees: innocent (you believed it was true), negligent (you should have known), and intentional (fraud: you knew it was false). Concealing a defect, sometimes called negative fraud, counts too.
blocks.casual: Misrepresentation is a false statement, or hiding a material fact, that someone relies on. There are levels. Innocent: you honestly thought it was true. Negligent: you should have known better. Intentional: that's fraud, you knew it was false. Hiding a defect, sometimes called negative fraud, counts too.

deeper.plain: Saying something false, or hiding something true, that leads someone into a bad decision.
deeper.picture: Spilled coffee: an accident (innocent), you set it on the edge of the table (negligent), or you poured it on purpose (intentional).
deeper.street: Sal tells a buyer the Astoria house has 'a 2,400 square foot lot' because the old listing said so. It's really 1,800. If Sal never checked the records, that's negligent misrepresentation.
deeper.stakes: Even innocent misrepresentation can unwind a deal. Negligent can cost damages. Intentional can bring punitive damages and license revocation.
deeper.exam: Know the three levels and know that concealment (silence about a known defect) is treated like a false statement.

blocks.html: Puffing is exaggerated opinion ("the best light in Park Slope") and is generally not misrepresentation because no reasonable buyer treats it as fact. "The building has a new boiler" is a fact and had better be true.
blocks.casual: Puffing is over-the-top opinion ('the best light in Park Slope'). It's generally not misrepresentation, because no reasonable buyer takes it as fact. 'The building has a new boiler' is a fact, though, and it better be true.

deeper.plain: Opinions and hype are allowed. Checkable facts must be accurate.
deeper.picture: A pizza place that says 'best slice in Brooklyn' is puffing. Saying 'open until 2 a.m.' when it closes at 10 is a lie.
deeper.street: Priya's listing says 'charming, sun-drenched prewar gem.' Fine. It also says 'new roof 2023.' She double-checks the permit before posting, because that one is a fact a buyer can rely on.
deeper.stakes: Agents get in trouble when puffing slides into specific claims: 'quiet block,' 'no flooding,' 'legal basement apartment.' Those are facts, and buyers sue over them.
deeper.exam: Choose 'puffing' for vague opinion words (best, stunning, amazing). Measurable statements (new, legal, square footage) are facts.

head: Consequence
Who brings it
rows: Money damages, possibly punitive for fraud

deeper.plain: Lies cost you in four ways: the deal, the money, the fee, and the license.
deeper.picture: Like a bad restaurant review, a refund, a fine from the health department, and losing your permit all at once.
deeper.street: Leo tells a buyer the Ridgewood two-family has a legal CO for two units; it doesn't. The buyer rescinds the contract, sues for her costs, the seller refuses to pay Leo's firm, and DOS opens a file for untrustworthiness under RPL 441-c.
deeper.stakes: These stack. One misstatement can trigger all four at once, and DOS can act even if the civil case settles.
deeper.exam: Match remedy to party: rescission and damages come from the injured party in court; fine, suspension, or revocation come from the Department of State.

blocks.html: Vicarious liability means one person is liable for another's acts. A principal can be liable for misstatements its agent makes within the scope of the agency, and a broker answers for the salespersons it supervises. This is why who appoints whom matters so much in the next lessons.
blocks.casual: Vicarious liability means you can be on the hook for someone else's acts. A principal can be liable for misstatements its agent makes within the scope of the agency, and a broker answers for the salespersons it supervises. That's why who appoints whom matters so much in the next lessons.

deeper.plain: If your agent messes up while working for you, you can pay for it.
deeper.picture: A pizza shop is responsible when its delivery guy dents your car on the delivery run.
deeper.street: Jordan tells a buyer the taxes on a Gravesend house are $6,000; they're $11,000. The buyer sues the sellers too, because Jordan was speaking as their agent.
deeper.stakes: This is why sellers care which agents get authority to speak for them, and why NY sellers often refuse subagency: every subagent's mistake can become theirs.
deeper.exam: Cue words: 'liable for the acts of.' Vicarious liability runs upward: client for its agents, broker for its salespersons.

blocks.title: Imputed knowledge
blocks.html: What the agent knows, the principal is legally treated as knowing. If Jordan learns the buyer's mortgage commitment was withdrawn, the sellers are charged with that knowledge even if Jordan never passes it on. That is why prompt disclosure to the client is a fiduciary duty: silence does not protect the principal, it only leaves them exposed.
blocks.casual: Here's the law: whatever the agent knows, the principal is legally treated as knowing. If Jordan learns the buyer's mortgage commitment got pulled, the sellers are charged with knowing that, even if Jordan never tells them. That's why fast disclosure to the client is a fiduciary duty. Staying quiet doesn't protect your client. It just leaves them exposed.

deeper.plain: In the eyes of the law, if you know it, your client knows it.
deeper.picture: Your phone gets a text. Whether or not you read it, the sender can say 'I told you.'
deeper.street: Jordan hears from the buyer's loan officer that the commitment fell through, but forgets to tell the sellers. Thinking the deal is solid, they turn away a backup buyer at $1.08M. When the deal dies two weeks later, that lost backup traces straight to Jordan's silence.
deeper.stakes: Imputed knowledge can cost the client rights they'd have kept if they had actually known. That loss usually comes back on the agent who sat on it.
deeper.exam: 'Notice to the agent is notice to the principal.' Look for that phrase; it's the correct statement of the rule.

blocks.q: A seller's agent tells a buyer, "This is the most charming block in Ditmas Park." Legally this is:
c: Fraud, because it cannot be proven
Negligent misrepresentation
Puffing, a statement of opinion
A breach of loyalty to the seller
blocks.x: Opinion and sales talk is puffing. Misrepresentation requires a false statement of material fact that the buyer reasonably relies on.

blocks.title: Stigma is not a defect
blocks.html: Under RPL 443-a a seller and agent need not disclose that a death, murder, or suicide happened in the home, or that an occupant had HIV/AIDS. That is not misrepresentation, because it is not a material physical fact. Never lie if asked; you may answer truthfully with the seller's permission.
blocks.casual: Under RPL 443-a, neither the seller nor the agent has to disclose that a death, murder, or suicide happened in the home, or that an occupant had HIV/AIDS. That's not misrepresentation, because it isn't a material physical fact. But never lie if you're asked. With the seller's permission, you can answer truthfully.

deeper.plain: Bad history isn't a physical defect, so you don't have to bring it up. You still can't lie about it.
deeper.picture: A used car that once belonged to someone who died isn't a broken car. Its brakes are what you have to tell people about.
deeper.street: A buyer asks Diane in writing whether anyone died in the Bay Ridge house. The owner passed away there last year. Diane checks with the estate's executor, who says she may answer, and she answers truthfully.
deeper.stakes: Lying about stigma turns a protected silence into fraud. Volunteering it without the seller's permission can breach confidentiality.
deeper.exam: Stigma (death, crime, HIV/AIDS) is not a material defect and need not be disclosed. A physical defect like a cracked foundation always must be.

story.title: Two Secrets
story.setting: Sheepshead Bay, a windy Sunday in April

beats.text: Jordan's second open house. A semi-attached on East 19th, listed at $1.1M, and a buyer who will not leave.
Honestly? I'd go to $1.15 for this block. My lease ends in 60 days. Don't tell anyone.
I should say up front: I work for the sellers. Anything you tell me, I'm obligated to pass on to them.
Huh. Okay, then... I'd go to $1.12.
That night the seller calls.
Jordan, off the record, I'd take $1.05M if it closes before June.
That stays with me. Nobody hears that number.
Monday morning. Marcus leans on Jordan's desk with coffee.
Rookie move, telling the buyer who you work for. I let them talk. Then I tell them what the seller would 'probably' take. Everybody's happy.
Everybody except the seller whose bottom line you just sold for a quicker commission. That's loyalty and confidentiality in one breach, Marcus.
beats.tag: Loyalty: client first, even over your fee

beats.text: And the buyer asked if the basement floods. It did, in 2023. I told her.

check.q: Jordan represents the seller. Why did Jordan have to tell the buyer about the 2023 flooding?
c: Because the buyer is a client too
Because agents must disclose known material defects to all parties
Because the buyer asked politely
Because the seller told Jordan to
check.x: Customers are owed honesty and disclosure of known material facts about the property. That is not loyalty; it is the minimum every party gets.

beats.text: Right. You don't advise her. You don't lie to her. Those are different things.
So what, I can't even say it's the best block in Brooklyn?
Say it all day. That's puffing. Say the boiler is new when it's from 1987, and that's misrepresentation, and the seller may be on the hook for what you said.
Client gets your loyalty. Everyone gets your honesty. Write that on your hand if you have to.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: left side, what Jordan owes the sellers; right side, what Jordan owes the buyer. Put the two secrets on the correct side.

facts.text: The agent is the brokerage; salespersons carry out the broker's agency for the principal.
Only a licensed broker, or a salesperson sponsored by one, may act for others for a fee; the client agreement is what creates the agency.
A client (principal) is represented and owed fiduciary duties; a customer is dealt with but not represented.
Who pays the commission does not decide whom the agent represents.
A fiduciary puts the principal first; the six duties are obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, reasonable care (OLD CAR).
Obedience covers only lawful instructions; refuse unlawful ones and withdraw if the client insists.
Loyalty forbids self-dealing, such as buying the listing yourself or through a relative without full written disclosure.
Only a single agent can give undivided loyalty; a dual agent cannot.
Disclosure: tell the client every material fact you learn, including what the other side would pay and any conflict of interest.
Confidentiality protects the client's private information and survives the end of the agency, but never covers facts the law requires you to disclose.
Accounting: safeguard and account for all money and documents; never commingle a deposit with operating funds.
Reasonable care means competence, skill and diligence, such as using proper comparables.
Fiduciary duties begin when the agency is created and end at closing, expiration or termination; confidentiality and accounting for money held outlast it.
Universal agent: everything (broad power of attorney); general agent: ongoing matters in one business (property manager); special agent: one transaction (listing broker).
A listing broker is a special agent: it markets and presents offers but cannot accept an offer or sign for the seller without a separate written power of attorney.
Salespersons are general agents of their broker, and the broker answers for their acts and can be disciplined for failing to supervise.
Customers are owed honesty, fair dealing and disclosure of known material defects, but not loyalty or advice.
Misrepresentation can be innocent, negligent or intentional (fraud); concealing a defect counts.
Puffing is exaggerated opinion and is generally not misrepresentation; statements of fact are.
Misrepresentation can bring rescission, damages, loss of commission, and DOS discipline.
Vicarious liability: one party is liable for another's acts, such as a principal for its agent or a broker for its salespersons.
Imputed knowledge: what the agent knows, the principal is treated as knowing.
Under RPL 443-a, a death, murder, suicide or an occupant's HIV/AIDS is not a material defect and need not be disclosed; never lie if asked.

lessons.title: Creating Agency, Getting Paid, Staying Legal
lessons.tagline: Agency can start with a signature, a handshake, or just the way you act. Your fee is always negotiable and never coordinated.
objectives: Name the four ways agency is created: express, implied, ratification, estoppel
Explain how a commission is set and when it is earned
Identify price fixing, group boycotts, market allocation, and tie-in arrangements
Decide whom you represent before the conversation turns substantive

blocks.title: The brokers' breakfast, Bay Ridge
blocks.html: Five Bay Ridge brokers meet for bagels on Third Avenue. One sighs that discount firms are "ruining the neighborhood" and suggests everyone hold the line at 6% and stop showing listings from the new flat-fee company. Another adds, "And let's quit stepping on each other: you take south of 86th, I'll take north." Jordan, there with Diane, keeps eating. How many federal crimes were just proposed over one bagel?
blocks.casual: Five Bay Ridge brokers grab bagels on Third Avenue. One complains that discount firms are 'ruining the neighborhood' and floats a plan: everybody holds at 6%, and nobody shows listings from the new flat-fee company. Another chimes in, 'And let's stop stepping on each other. You take south of 86th, I'll take north.' Jordan's there with Diane, quietly eating. Count them: how many federal crimes just got pitched over one bagel?

deeper.plain: Competitors who agree on prices, who to shut out, or who gets which turf are breaking federal law, even over breakfast.
deeper.picture: Picture the gas stations on one corner agreeing to all charge $5 a gallon. Drivers lose, and that's exactly what antitrust law exists to stop.
deeper.street: Three proposals hit the table: hold at 6% (price fixing), freeze out the flat-fee firm (group boycott), and split the neighborhood at 86th Street (market allocation). Jordan and Diane say they won't discuss it and leave before the check comes.
deeper.stakes: Each of those is a per se Sherman Act violation. Individuals face up to 10 years and $1 million in fines, plus civil suits for triple damages and DOS discipline.
deeper.exam: Count the violations in a story. The test expects you to name each: price fixing, group boycott, market allocation, and sometimes a tie-in.

head: Method
How it happens
Example
rows: Spoken or written agreement stating the relationship
Exclusive right to sell listing; buyer agency agreement
Conduct of the parties shows an agency exists
An agent who advises a buyer on what to offer, without any agreement
Principal approves an unauthorized act after the fact
Seller accepts the deal an agent negotiated without authority and keeps the deposit
Principal let a third party reasonably believe someone was its agent, so it cannot deny it
Owner lets a cousin hand out keys and quote rents for months

deeper.plain: Agency happens four ways: you agree to it, you act like it, the principal approves it afterward, or the principal lets people believe it.
deeper.picture: A friend becomes your house-sitter because you asked (express), because they started watering your plants and you let them (implied), because you thanked them after the fact (ratification), or because you let the neighbors think they were in charge (estoppel).
deeper.street: Sal's landlord client in Sunnyside lets his cousin hand out keys and quote rents for six months. A tenant pays the cousin a deposit. The landlord can't later say 'he never worked for me'; that's estoppel.
deeper.stakes: Every way except express can sneak up on you. Implied and estoppel agencies are how agents end up with duties to people they never meant to represent.
deeper.exam: Match the cue: 'by words or in writing' is express; 'by actions' is implied; 'after the fact' is ratification; 'the principal led others to believe' is estoppel.

blocks.html: Express agency is the safe way. Listing agreements and buyer agreements are express agency in writing. Exclusive agreements should always be written, and the NAR settlement now requires a written buyer agreement before an MLS participant tours a home with a buyer.
blocks.casual: Express agency is the safe route. Listing agreements and buyer agreements are express agency, in writing. Exclusive agreements should always be in writing, and under the NAR settlement an MLS participant now needs a written buyer agreement before touring a home with a buyer.

deeper.plain: Put the relationship in writing up front and nobody argues later about who you worked for.
deeper.picture: It's a signed work order at the auto shop. Without it, you're arguing about what you agreed to with grease on your hands.
deeper.street: Kim meets a buyer at an open house in Astoria who wants to tour three more condos on Saturday. Before the first showing, Kim has her sign a written buyer agreement that states the compensation and the term.
deeper.stakes: Tour first and paper later, and an MLS broker is breaking the post-settlement rule. A fee dispute without a written agreement is also very hard to win.
deeper.exam: Since Aug 17, 2024 the correct answer is: written buyer agreement before touring, for MLS participants. Watch for answers that say 'before the offer' or 'before closing.'

blocks.html: Implied agency is the danger zone. If a seller's agent tells a buyer "offer $40K under, they're desperate," a court could find the agent was acting as the buyer's agent too. That is accidental, undisclosed dual agency. Say who you represent early, and act like it.
blocks.casual: Implied agency is where people get burned. Say a seller's agent tells a buyer, 'Offer $40K under, they're desperate.' A court could decide that agent was also acting as the buyer's agent. That's accidental, undisclosed dual agency. Tell people early who you represent, and then act like it.

deeper.plain: If you act like someone's agent, the law may treat you as one, whether you meant it or not.
deeper.picture: Like a store clerk who starts giving you advice about suing the store. At some point he's not really working for the store anymore.
deeper.street: Tasha, the seller's agent on a Harlem condo, tells an unrepresented buyer what to offer and which inspector to use. When the deal goes sideways, the buyer's attorney argues Tasha was the buyer's agent too.
deeper.stakes: Undisclosed dual agency can cost the firm its whole commission, expose it to damages from both sides, and get the agent disciplined.
deeper.exam: Advice on price or strategy given to the other side is the trigger. 'Implied agency' and 'undisclosed dual agency' are often the paired correct answers.

blocks.title: Estoppel vs ratification
blocks.html: Ratification looks back: the principal approves after the act. Estoppel is about appearances: the principal created the impression of authority and a third party relied on it. Estoppel is also called ostensible or apparent agency.
blocks.casual: Don't mix these two up. Ratification looks backward: the principal approves something after it already happened. Estoppel is about appearances: the principal made it look like someone had authority, and somebody else relied on it. Estoppel also goes by ostensible or apparent agency.

deeper.plain: Ratification is 'yes, I approve that' after the fact. Estoppel is 'you let them believe it, so you're stuck.'
