deeper.picture: Ratification is keeping the birthday gift your friend bought with your card. Estoppel is letting your friend use your card all year and then telling the store it was unauthorized.
deeper.street: Ray negotiates a lease for a Staten Island storefront without authority. The owner signs the lease and cashes the first check: ratification. Separately, the owner lets his nephew collect rents for a year, so tenants can rely on the nephew: estoppel.
deeper.stakes: Confuse them and you misjudge whether the principal is bound. That decides whether a deposit, lease, or deal holds up.
deeper.exam: Cue words: 'later approved' or 'accepted the benefits' mean ratification. 'Led third parties to believe' or 'apparent authority' mean estoppel.

blocks.q: An agent with no listing negotiates a lease for a Bushwick loft. The owner, learning of it, signs the lease and accepts the first month's rent. Agency was created by:
c: Estoppel
Ratification
Express agreement
Implied agency
blocks.x: Approving an unauthorized act after the fact is ratification. Estoppel would require the owner to have created the appearance of authority beforehand.

blocks.title: Implied agency at the kitchen island
blocks.html:
Marcus lists a Kensington co-op. A buyer without an agent asks, "What would you offer if you were me?" Marcus answers, "Go $40K under. They've already bought in Jersey." Then he helps her draft her inspection requests.
1. Marcus is the seller's agent by express agreement.
2. His advice and help look like representation of the buyer, so a court could find implied agency with her.
3. Representing both without written consent is undisclosed dual agency, and revealing the sellers' situation is a separate breach of confidentiality.
Result: the firm risks its commission and Marcus risks his license.
blocks.casual:
Marcus lists a Kensington co-op. A buyer with no agent asks him, 'What would you offer if you were me?' He answers, 'Go $40K under. They've already bought in Jersey.' Then he helps her draft inspection requests.
1. By express agreement, Marcus is the seller's agent.
2. His advice and help look like he's representing the buyer, so a court could find implied agency with her.
3. Representing both without written consent is undisclosed dual agency. Spilling the sellers' situation is a separate confidentiality breach.
Bottom line: the firm's commission is at risk and so is Marcus's license.

deeper.plain: One friendly conversation created two problems: an accidental second client and a leaked secret.
deeper.picture: Like a referee who, mid-game, starts coaching the other team and then tells them his own team's playbook.
deeper.street: The sellers learn from the buyer's lawyer that Marcus said they 'already bought in Jersey.' They refuse to pay Diane's firm and file a DOS complaint. The buyer, now feeling represented, also blames Marcus when the inspection misses a problem.
deeper.stakes: Both clients can turn on the agent. The seller withholds the fee; the buyer sues for advice she relied on. One kitchen-island chat can cost tens of thousands.
deeper.exam: When a seller's agent gives advice to an unrepresented buyer, look for implied agency and undisclosed dual agency. Disclosing the seller's motivation is a confidentiality breach.

blocks.text: How agents decide whom they represent

blocks.html: Before money or motivation comes up, you must know your role. Your answer comes from (1) your firm's written agency policy, (2) any agreement already signed, and (3) the facts: are you the listing side, or is this person asking you to help them buy? Then say it out loud and hand over the disclosure form. Lesson 6 covers the form.
blocks.casual: Before anyone talks money or motivation, you need to know your role. You figure it out from (1) your firm's written agency policy, (2) any agreement already signed, and (3) the facts: are you on the listing side, or is this person asking you to help them buy? Then say it out loud and hand over the disclosure form. Lesson 6 covers the form.

deeper.plain: Know your role before anyone tells you anything, then tell them your role.
deeper.picture: Like a doctor saying 'I'm the hospital's doctor, not yours' before you start explaining your symptoms.
deeper.street: A buyer walks into Diane's Bay Ridge office about a listing Diane's firm has. Firm policy says agents on in-house listings are seller's agents unless dual agency is consented. The agent says so and hands over the RPL 443 form before the buyer shares anything.
deeper.stakes: Figure out your role after hearing the buyer's budget and you may already owe duties you can't honor. That's where accidental dual agency starts.
deeper.exam: Timing is tested: decide your role and disclose it at the first substantive contact, before confidential information is exchanged.

items: By agreement. The commission is whatever the broker and the principal negotiate: a percentage, a flat fee, or hourly. No law, board, or MLS sets it.
Paid to the broker. Salespersons are paid only by their sponsoring broker, never directly by a client or another broker.
Only a licensed broker can sue for a commission, and must have been licensed when the services were performed (RPL 442-d).
Never to the unlicensed. Sharing a commission with an unlicensed person (a finder, a doorman, a friend) is prohibited.
No net listings. A net listing, where the broker keeps everything above the seller's number, is banned in NY (19 NYCRR 175.19).
blocks.casual:
How the money works:
By agreement. The commission is whatever the broker and principal negotiate: percentage, flat fee, or hourly. No law, board, or MLS sets it.
Paid to the broker. Salespersons get paid only by their sponsoring broker, never straight from a client or another broker.
Only a licensed broker can sue for a commission, and they had to be licensed when they did the work (RPL 442-d).
Never to the unlicensed. You can't split a commission with an unlicensed person: no finder, no doorman, no buddy.
No net listings. A net listing, where the broker keeps everything over the seller's number, is banned in NY (19 NYCRR 175.19).

deeper.plain: The fee is negotiated, goes to the broker, and stays inside the licensed world.
deeper.picture: Think of a restaurant tip pool. Tips go to the house first, then get split among staff. You don't hand cash to the guy who held the door.
deeper.street: A doorman on the Upper West Side tips Leo off to an owner who wants to sell, and asks for $2,000 when it closes. Leo has to say no. He can thank him, but he can't share the commission with someone unlicensed.
deeper.stakes: Paying an unlicensed person, or taking a fee directly from a client, can cost you your license. A broker who wasn't licensed when the work was done can't sue to collect.
deeper.exam: Classic stems: 'the salesperson accepted a bonus directly from the seller' (wrong, broker only) and 'the broker agreed to keep anything above $500,000' (net listing, illegal in NY).

blocks.html: When is the fee earned? Traditionally, when the broker produces a buyer who is ready, willing, and able to buy on the seller's terms, or when the parties reach a meeting of the minds on the essential terms. If the seller then backs out, the broker may still be owed. Most NY listings say the fee is payable at closing, and courts enforce that language, so read the agreement. Under an open listing, the broker who was the procuring cause, the one whose efforts started the unbroken chain that led to the sale, gets paid.
blocks.casual: So when is the fee actually earned? The traditional rule: when the broker brings a buyer who's ready, willing, and able to buy on the seller's terms, or when the parties reach a meeting of the minds on the key terms. If the seller then backs out, the broker may still be owed. Most NY listings say the fee is payable at closing, and courts enforce that, so read the agreement. Under an open listing, the broker who was the procuring cause gets paid: that's the one whose efforts started the unbroken chain that led to the sale.

deeper.plain: Earned means you did the job. Payable means when the check is due. The contract decides which matters.
deeper.picture: A contractor finishes your kitchen (earned) but the contract says you pay after the inspection passes (payable).
deeper.street: Two brokers show the same Flushing house under open listings. Priya shows the buyer first, sends the disclosures, and negotiates the price. Another broker just writes up the final paperwork. Priya was the procuring cause and gets the fee.
deeper.stakes: Agents who skim the listing language can lose a fee they earned or chase one that was never due. Procuring-cause fights between brokers often end up in arbitration or court.
deeper.exam: 'Ready, willing, and able' is the classic earning trigger. 'Procuring cause' is the answer for who gets paid under an open listing.

blocks.title: Earned vs payable
blocks.html:
Grace and Emmanuel Okafor list with an exclusive right to sell at 5%. Jordan brings a buyer at full price, all cash, no contingencies. The Okafors change their minds and refuse to sign.

If the listing says the commission is earned on producing a ready, willing, and able buyer at the listed terms: the commission is likely owed even with no sale. If it says the fee is due "only if and when title closes": nothing is owed, though the broker may have other claims. The agreement controls.
blocks.casual:
Grace and Emmanuel Okafor sign an exclusive right to sell at 5%. Jordan brings a buyer at full price: all cash, no contingencies. Then the Okafors change their minds and won't sign.

If the listing says the commission is earned when Jordan produces a ready, willing, and able buyer at the listed terms: the commission is probably owed even though nothing sold. If it says the fee is due 'only if and when title closes': nothing's owed, though the broker may have other claims. The agreement controls.

deeper.plain: The same seller cold feet can cost them a full commission or nothing, depending on one sentence in the listing.
deeper.picture: Like hiring a caterer for a party you cancel. Whether you still pay depends on the cancellation clause.
deeper.street: The Okafors' house was listed at $1,200,000. At 5%, that's a $60,000 question. Diane pulls the listing and reads the compensation clause before deciding whether to send a demand letter.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who back out can owe a full fee for a sale that never happened. Brokers who promise clients 'you only pay if it closes' had better write that into the agreement.
deeper.exam: Default exam rule: produce a ready, willing, and able buyer on the seller's terms and the fee is earned. If the stem quotes 'only upon closing,' the contract language wins.

blocks.html: Two compensation myths to clear up. First, a salesperson never has a separate fee agreement with the client; the client's contract is with the broker, and the salesperson's share comes from the broker under their own agreement. Second, "cooperating commission" offers between brokers are just that, offers. After the 2024 NAR settlement they cannot appear on the MLS, but brokers may still negotiate them off the MLS, and buyers may negotiate their own broker's fee directly.
blocks.casual: Two money myths to kill. First: a salesperson never has a separate fee deal with the client. The client's contract is with the broker, and the salesperson's share comes from the broker under their own agreement. Second: 'cooperating commission' offers between brokers are just that, offers. After the 2024 NAR settlement they can't go on the MLS, but brokers can still negotiate them off the MLS, and buyers can negotiate their own broker's fee directly.

deeper.plain: You get paid through your broker, and co-broke offers are negotiable side deals, not MLS fields anymore.
deeper.picture: A waiter doesn't send you his own bill. Your check goes to the restaurant, and the restaurant pays him.
deeper.street: Marcus is buying in Bay Ridge with Ray as his agent. The listing broker offers, by email, to pay Ray's firm 2%. Marcus's buyer agreement says 2.5%, so Marcus and Ray work out how the gap gets handled before the offer goes in.
deeper.stakes: A salesperson who cuts a private fee deal with a client is outside the law. And a broker who posts compensation on the MLS now is violating MLS rules.
deeper.exam: Look for 'the salesperson's contract with the seller' (no such thing) and 'compensation offers on the MLS' (no longer allowed after Aug 17, 2024).

blocks.text: Antitrust: the four you must never do

blocks.html: The federal Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) and New York's Donnelly Act outlaw agreements among competitors that restrain trade. Brokers are competitors. The four classic violations are per se illegal: no excuse, no "but it was good for consumers" defense.
blocks.casual: The federal Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) and New York's Donnelly Act outlaw deals between competitors that restrain trade. Brokers are competitors. The four classic violations are per se illegal. No excuses, no 'but it was good for consumers' defense.

deeper.plain: Competing brokers can't team up on prices or customers. Doing it is automatically illegal.
deeper.picture: Rival coffee shops can each set their own prices. If they meet in back and all agree on $6 lattes, that's a crime.
deeper.street: A Long Island brokers' Facebook group starts a thread: 'Nobody should go under 5%.' Three agents like it. Kim reads it, posts 'I set my own fees and won't discuss this,' and leaves the group.
deeper.stakes: 'Per se' means a prosecutor doesn't have to show harm. The agreement itself is the crime, and good intentions don't help.
deeper.exam: Per se means no defense based on reasonableness. Sherman is federal, Donnelly is New York's version (GBL 340).

head: Violation
What it looks like
rows: Competing brokers agree on commission rates or splits, or publish a "standard" rate
Brokers agree not to work with, or show listings of, a competitor (often a discount firm)
Competitors divide territory, customers, or price ranges: "you take south of 86th"
Selling one service on the condition the buyer also buys another: "I'll sell you this lot only if you list your current house with me"

deeper.plain: Four things competitors can't agree on: price, who to shut out, who gets which turf, and forced bundling.
deeper.picture: Four ways to rig the game: fix the score, keep a team out of the league, split up the stadium seats, and make you buy a hot dog to get a ticket.
deeper.street: A developer tells Evelyn she can buy his Bayside lot only if she lists her current house with his brokerage. That's a tie-in. Down the block, two brokers agree one handles co-ops and the other condos: that's market allocation by product.
deeper.stakes: These look like ordinary business habits ('our zone,' 'our rate'), which is why agents fall into them. Each one carries the same federal penalties.
deeper.exam: Map the facts. Agreeing on a rate or split: price fixing. Refusing to deal with a firm: boycott. Dividing territory, customers, or price ranges: allocation. Conditioning one sale on another: tie-in.

blocks.html: Penalties are serious. Under the Sherman Act, individuals face up to 10 years in prison and $1 million in fines, corporations up to $100 million, plus civil suits for triple damages. DOS can also discipline the license.
blocks.casual: The penalties are no joke. Under the Sherman Act, individuals face up to 10 years in prison and $1 million in fines. Corporations face up to $100 million. Add civil suits for triple damages, and DOS can discipline your license on top of it.

deeper.plain: Antitrust can mean prison, giant fines, triple damages, and losing your license.
deeper.picture: It's like a parking ticket that turns into a felony, a lawsuit, and the loss of your driver's license.
deeper.street: If a group of brokers overcharged sellers by $300,000 through a price-fixing pact, the sellers could sue for triple: $900,000, before any criminal fines.
deeper.stakes: Triple damages make these suits attractive to plaintiffs' lawyers. Even a small brokerage can be wiped out by one class action.
deeper.exam: Memorize the numbers: 10 years, $1 million individual, $100 million corporation, triple (treble) damages.

blocks.html: New York adds its own antitrust statute, the Donnelly Act (General Business Law 340), which mirrors the Sherman Act and lets the Attorney General prosecute in state court. You do not need a written agreement to be guilty: a wink, a nod, and everyone raising rates the next week can be enough evidence of a conspiracy. Even a casual "let's all keep it at 6%" in an online agent group is dangerous.
blocks.casual: New York has its own antitrust law, the Donnelly Act (General Business Law 340). It mirrors the Sherman Act and lets the Attorney General prosecute in state court. You don't need a written agreement to be guilty. A wink, a nod, and everybody raising rates the next week can be enough to show a conspiracy. Even a casual 'let's all keep it at 6%' in an online agent group is dangerous.

deeper.plain: New York can prosecute too, and an unspoken agreement still counts.
deeper.picture: Like kids who all 'happen' to skip class the same day after one whispered conversation. The teacher can figure it out.
deeper.street: After a Tuesday dinner, four Westchester brokers all raise their listing rates to 6% the following week. No contract exists, but emails and timing are evidence the Attorney General can use.
deeper.stakes: Prosecutors build cases from circumstantial evidence. Group chats, texts, and meeting notes all become exhibits.
deeper.exam: Trap: 'no violation without a written agreement.' Wrong. Conspiracy can be proven from conduct.

blocks.title: How to answer at a breakfast
blocks.html: If competitors start talking rates or boycotts, say clearly that you won't discuss it, and leave. Silence while everyone else agrees can be read as joining. Set your fees alone, in your own office.
blocks.casual: If competitors start talking rates or boycotts, say clearly that you won't discuss it, and leave. Sitting there silently while everyone else agrees can look like you're in on it. Set your fees on your own, in your own office.

deeper.plain: Object out loud and walk away. Silence can look like agreement.
deeper.picture: If your friends start planning a shoplift, staying in the store and saying nothing doesn't make you look innocent.
deeper.street: At a Queens board mixer, an agent says 'we should all stop showing that discount firm's listings.' Sal says, 'I'm not discussing that,' and moves to the bar. He also tells his broker what happened the next morning.
deeper.stakes: Being present and silent can be used as evidence you joined. A clear refusal, ideally documented, is your best defense.
deeper.exam: The correct response is always to refuse to participate and leave, not to 'stay quiet' or 'report it later only if asked.'

blocks.q: Two Astoria brokerages agree that one will handle only rentals and the other only sales, so they "stop competing." This is:
c: Price fixing
A tie-in arrangement
Market allocation
Lawful specialization
blocks.x: Dividing a market by type of service, territory, or customer is market allocation. One firm choosing on its own to do only rentals is fine; the agreement between competitors is what makes it illegal.

blocks.title: "Standard commission"
blocks.html: There is no standard commission in New York. A listing that says rates are "set by the local board" or an agent who tells a seller "everyone charges 6%" is a red flag. On the exam, rates are always negotiable between broker and principal.
blocks.casual: There's no such thing as a standard commission in New York. If a listing says rates are 'set by the local board,' or an agent tells a seller 'everyone charges 6%,' that's a red flag. On the exam, rates are always negotiable between the broker and the principal.

deeper.plain: Every fee is a negotiation. 'Standard' is a warning sign.
deeper.picture: There's no 'standard' price for a haircut in Brooklyn. Every barber sets their own.
deeper.street: A seller asks Priya, 'What's the usual commission?' Priya says, 'There's no usual. My fee is 5%, and here's what you get for it.' She never says 'everyone charges.'
deeper.stakes: Telling sellers that a rate is standard or required can be evidence of price fixing and is misleading to the consumer.
deeper.exam: Any answer suggesting commissions are set by law, a board, or the MLS is wrong. The right answer: negotiated between broker and principal.

blocks.q: A developer tells buyers they may purchase a lot only if they also list their current home with the developer's brokerage. This is:
c: A tie-in arrangement
A group boycott
Market allocation
Legal bundling
blocks.x: Conditioning one product on the purchase of another is a tie-in. A group boycott requires competitors agreeing to shut someone out.

blocks.title: The four antitrust sins
blocks.html: Price, Boycott, Map, Tie. Fix the price, freeze out a rival, split the map, tie the deals. All four need competitors (or a seller) agreeing, and all four are illegal per se.
blocks.casual: Remember it as Price, Boycott, Map, Tie. Fix the price, freeze out a rival, split the map, tie the deals. All four need competitors (or a seller) agreeing, and all four are illegal per se.

deeper.plain: Four words, four crimes. Any time two businesses agree on one of them, stop.
deeper.picture: Picture a map of Brooklyn with a price tag stapled to it, a door slammed on a rival, and a rope tying two houses together.
deeper.street: On the exam Leo reads: 'Two brokers agree that one will handle all listings over $2 million.' He runs Price, Boycott, Map, Tie. Dividing by price range is splitting the map: market allocation.
deeper.stakes: Remembering four labels helps you notice them in real conversations, which is where agents actually get in trouble.
deeper.exam: Allocation can be by geography, customer type, or price range. Students often miss price-range splits and call them price fixing.

story.title: Bagels and Felonies
story.setting: A diner on Third Avenue, Bay Ridge, 8 a.m.

beats.text: Diane brings Jordan to the monthly brokers' breakfast. Jordan expected networking. Jordan got a crime seminar.
Here's my idea. We all hold 6%. Nobody shows the flat-fee guys' listings. They'll be gone by summer.
Marcus, I'm going to stop you before the FBI needs a bagel order. That's price fixing and a group boycott.
Okay, okay. What if we just split the neighborhood? You take south of 86th, I take north.
Market allocation. Same Sherman Act. Up to ten years for individuals.
Is it legal for us to just decide on our own fee?
Completely. Inside our office, alone, with our client. The second it's an agreement between competitors, it's a crime.
Diane stands up, drops a twenty on the table, and nods toward the door. Jordan follows.
Do we have to leave? Can't we just not say anything?
Sitting quietly while everyone agrees can look like agreeing. Speak up, then walk out.

check.q: Why did Diane leave instead of staying silent?
c: It was rude to stay
Silence while competitors agree on prices can be treated as joining the agreement
Brokers may never meet socially
She owed Marcus a lesson
check.x: Antitrust conspiracies can be inferred from conduct. Objecting clearly and leaving is the safe response.

beats.text: On the sidewalk, Jordan's phone buzzes. The Okafors: a full-price, all-cash offer came in and they want to back out of selling.
If they refuse a ready, willing, and able buyer, do we still get paid?
Depends on the listing language. Earned at ready, willing, and able, or payable only at closing. Contracts matter more than vibes.
And by the way, the buyer's cousin who 'found' them doesn't get a dime. Unlicensed people never share a fee.

board.prompt: Draw four boxes: price fixing, group boycott, market allocation, tie-in. In each, write one sentence a broker might say that would cross the line.

facts.text: Agency is created four ways: express agreement, implied by conduct, ratification after the fact, or estoppel.
Estoppel (apparent or ostensible agency) rests on appearances the principal created; ratification is approval after the act.
Express written agreements are the safe way; since the NAR settlement, a written buyer agreement is required before touring a home with a buyer.
Advising the other side can create implied agency and accidental, undisclosed dual agency.
Decide whom you represent from the firm's agency policy, any signed agreement and the facts, then say it and give the disclosure form.
Commissions are set only by negotiation between broker and principal; there is no standard rate.
Salespersons are paid only by their sponsoring broker; the client's contract is with the broker, and the payer is not necessarily the client.
Only a broker licensed when the services were performed can sue for a commission (RPL 442-d).
A commission may never be shared with an unlicensed person.
Net listings are prohibited in New York (19 NYCRR 175.19).
A commission is traditionally earned on producing a ready, willing and able buyer, but the listing's terms (such as payable at closing) control.
Under an open listing, the procuring cause of the sale earns the commission.
After the 2024 NAR settlement, cooperating commission offers cannot appear on the MLS but may be negotiated off it.
The Sherman Antitrust Act bars agreements among competitors; the classic violations are illegal per se, with no defense.
The four antitrust violations: price fixing, group boycott, market allocation, tie-in arrangement.
Sherman Act penalties: up to 10 years and $1 million for individuals, $100 million for corporations, plus triple damages.
NY's Donnelly Act mirrors the Sherman Act; a conspiracy can be shown without a written agreement, but a broker setting fees alone is legal.
If competitors discuss rates or boycotts, object and leave; silence can look like joining.

lessons.title: Who Represents Whom: Seller, Buyer, Subagent, Broker's Agent
lessons.tagline: Every person in a deal is either your client, your client's helper, or a customer. Draw the lines before you talk.
objectives: Explain why agency and brokerage are not the same thing
Describe the salesperson's place inside the broker's agency
Compare a subagent, a buyer's agent, and a broker's agent, including who carries vicarious liability
Describe seller, buyer, landlord, and tenant agency and how each gets paid

blocks.title: Co-broke on Halsey Street
blocks.html: The Okafors list their Bed-Stuy brownstone with Hudson & Hart. An agent from a Manhattan firm calls Jordan: "I've got a buyer. Am I working for your sellers or for my buyer?" A second firm offers to "help market it" by holding open houses. If either of them misstates the square footage, are the Okafors on the hook?
blocks.casual: The Okafors list their Bed-Stuy brownstone with Hudson & Hart. An agent from a Manhattan firm calls Jordan: 'I've got a buyer. Am I working for your sellers or my buyer?' Then a second firm offers to 'help market it' by running open houses. Here's the question: if either one of them gets the square footage wrong, are the Okafors on the hook?

deeper.plain: Outside agents can help with a sale in different roles, and the role decides whose mistakes land on the seller.
deeper.picture: When a plumber brings a helper, it matters whether the helper works for you, for the plumber, or for nobody in particular when something floods.
deeper.street: The Manhattan agent decides to work as the buyer's agent. The second firm signs on as a broker's agent to Hudson & Hart. Jordan puts both roles in writing before anyone talks price.
deeper.stakes: If an outside agent is the Okafors' subagent and overstates the square footage, the buyer can come after the Okafors. If the role is never pinned down, everyone's exposed.
deeper.exam: These questions ask who is vicariously liable. Subagent: the seller. Broker's agent: the engaging broker. Buyer's agent: neither the seller nor the listing broker.

blocks.text: Agency and brokerage are not synonyms

blocks.html: Brokerage is the business: bringing buyers and sellers (or landlords and tenants) together for a fee. Agency is a legal relationship of trust. Most NY brokerage is done as agency, but not all of it. RPL 443 recognizes a licensee who works with a party "in a capacity other than as an agent" by agreement, owing honesty but no fiduciary duties.
blocks.casual: Brokerage is the business: bringing buyers and sellers (or landlords and tenants) together for a fee. Agency is a legal trust relationship. Most NY brokerage runs as agency, but not all of it. RPL 443 recognizes a licensee who works with a party 'in a capacity other than as an agent' by agreement. That licensee owes honesty, but no fiduciary duties.

deeper.plain: Brokerage is what you do. Agency is whom you're loyal to. You can do the first without the second.
deeper.picture: A matchmaker introduces people (brokerage). A wingman is on your side (agency).
deeper.street: A sophisticated investor buying a Bushwick warehouse tells Ray, 'I don't want you representing me. Just find me deals.' They sign an agreement saying Ray acts as a non-agent. Ray still has to be honest, but owes no loyalty or advice.
deeper.stakes: If you never agreed to non-agency in writing and you start advising, you may slip into an agency anyway, with all its duties.
deeper.exam: Know that brokerage and agency are different words. RPL 443 allows a non-agency role, but only by agreement, and honesty is still required.

blocks.html: Who is the agent? The broker. The listing agreement is between the client and the brokerage. A salesperson who takes the listing is acting for the broker, as the broker's agent, and the broker supervises and answers for that salesperson. If Jordan leaves Hudson & Hart, the Okafors' listing stays with the firm.
blocks.casual: So who's the agent? The broker. The listing agreement is between the client and the brokerage. The salesperson who takes the listing acts for the broker, as the broker's agent, and the broker supervises and answers for that salesperson. If Jordan quits Hudson & Hart, the Okafors' listing stays put with the firm.

deeper.plain: The firm holds the client. The salesperson runs the deal for the firm.
deeper.picture: A gym membership is with the gym, not your favorite trainer. If he leaves, your membership doesn't follow him out the door.
deeper.street: Jordan moves from Hudson & Hart to a Park Slope firm. He calls the Okafors to say he'd love to keep working with them. Their listing stays with Hudson & Hart unless the firm releases it.
deeper.stakes: Salespeople who take files or redirect clients on the way out face lawsuits from the old broker. The broker also stays on the hook for anything Jordan did while there.
deeper.exam: The listing belongs to the broker. Wrong answers say 'the salesperson owns the listing' or 'the listing transfers with the salesperson.'

blocks.title: Every agent in the firm
blocks.html: When a brokerage represents the seller, every salesperson in that firm owes the seller fiduciary duties, not just the one who took the listing. That is why an in-house buyer creates dual agency (Lesson 4).
blocks.casual: When a brokerage represents the seller, every salesperson in that firm owes the seller fiduciary duties, not just the one who took the listing. That's why an in-house buyer creates dual agency (Lesson 4).

deeper.plain: The whole firm is the seller's agent, so every agent there is on the seller's team.
deeper.picture: If a law firm represents you, the associate down the hall can't take your opponent as a client.
deeper.street: Kim's colleague at the same Astoria office has a buyer who loves Kim's listing. Because the firm already represents the seller, that colleague can't just act as the buyer's agent. It's dual agency and needs both sides' written consent.
deeper.stakes: Firms that ignore this end up in undisclosed dual agency. Both clients can sue, and the commission is at risk.
deeper.exam: Trap: 'Only the listing salesperson represents the seller.' Wrong. The firm does, and every licensee there carries the duties.

blocks.caption: Toggle seller agency, buyer agency, and broker's agent. Solid lines are fiduciary duties. Notice that a broker's agent has no line to the client at all.

head: Role
Represents
Owes the other side
rows: Honesty, fair dealing, known material defects
Honesty, fair dealing, known material facts
Helps the listing or buyer's broker; no direct client

deeper.plain: Each role answers one question: whose side are you on? The other side always gets honesty.
deeper.picture: Think of a pickup basketball game. You know which team you're on, and nobody, on either team, gets to cheat.
deeper.street: In a Sunnyside rental, Sal represents the landlord and owes the tenant honesty about the radiator problem. Across town, Priya represents a tenant looking for a two-bedroom and owes landlords honesty about her tenant's income documents.
deeper.stakes: Not knowing your role means not knowing your duties. That's how agents breach loyalty or confidentiality without noticing.
deeper.exam: Expect a role and a question about what is owed to the other party. The answer is almost always honesty and disclosure of known material facts; never loyalty.

blocks.html: Single agency means the firm represents one side only, never both. A single agent can give full advice to the client: what to offer, what to counter, which inspection items matter. It owes the other side only honesty and fair dealing.
blocks.casual: Single agency means the firm represents one side only, never both. A single agent can give the client full advice: what to offer, what to counter, which inspection items matter. The other side gets only honesty and fair dealing.

deeper.plain: One side, full help. That's the cleanest setup there is.
deeper.picture: A personal trainer who trains only you. Nobody else's goals compete with yours.
deeper.street: Marcus hires Leo to buy in Ditmas Park, and Leo's firm has a single-agency policy: it never takes listings. Leo can tell Marcus to offer $60,000 under on a stale listing without any conflict.
deeper.stakes: Single agency is why buyers and sellers hire agents. Lose it through careless in-house deals and you lose the right to give real advice.
deeper.exam: Single agency equals undivided loyalty. Dual agency cannot provide it.

blocks.text: Subagency: helping the listing broker, the old way

blocks.html: A cooperating agent is any licensee from another firm who helps produce the deal. The question is in what capacity. Historically, MLS listings carried a blanket unilateral offer of subagency: any member who brought a buyer automatically became the seller's subagent. Buyers thought "their" agent worked for them. Legally, that agent was working for the seller.
blocks.casual: A cooperating agent is any licensee from another firm who helps make the deal. The real question is: in what role? Back in the day, MLS listings came with a blanket unilateral offer of subagency. Any member who brought a buyer automatically became the seller's subagent. Buyers figured 'their' agent worked for them. Legally, that agent was working for the seller.

deeper.plain: Under the old system, the agent driving a buyer around was often legally working for the seller.
deeper.picture: Like a car salesman you thought was your advocate, who was actually on the dealership's payroll.
deeper.street: In 1985 Evelyn's parents bought in Bayside with an agent they adored. Under the MLS rules then, that agent was the seller's subagent and had to tell the seller everything they shared about their budget.
deeper.stakes: That confusion caused real harm and lawsuits, and it's a big reason buyer agency and NY's disclosure form exist today.
deeper.exam: Know the term 'blanket unilateral offer of subagency' and that it made cooperating brokers the seller's subagents.

items: Who creates subagency? The listing broker, but only with the seller's authorization in the listing agreement.
Principal to subagent: the seller is the principal and is vicariously liable for the subagent's misstatements, even though the seller never met them.
Subagent to seller: full fiduciary duties: loyalty, confidentiality, disclosure, and the rest.
Subagent to buyer: honesty and disclosure of known material facts. No advice, no loyalty.
Does the blanket offer still exist? MLSs made it optional decades ago and it is rarely used today. Sellers dislike the liability.
Rejecting subagency: a cooperating broker may decline the offer and work as a buyer's agent or a broker's agent instead.
blocks.casual:
Subagency in a nutshell:
Who creates it? The listing broker, but only if the seller authorizes it in the listing agreement.
Seller to subagent: the seller is the principal and is vicariously liable for the subagent's misstatements, even if they never met.
Subagent to seller: full fiduciary duties: loyalty, confidentiality, disclosure, all of it.
Subagent to buyer: honesty and disclosure of known material facts. No advice, no loyalty.
Is the blanket offer still around? MLSs made it optional decades ago, and it's rarely used now. Sellers don't like the liability.
Saying no: a cooperating broker can turn down subagency and work as a buyer's agent or a broker's agent instead.

deeper.plain: A subagent is the seller's agent once removed, and the seller carries the risk for what they say.
deeper.picture: Like a subcontractor on your renovation. You never hired him directly, but if he floods your neighbor's apartment, you get the call.
deeper.street: A seller in Bay Ridge allows subagency. A subagent from another firm tells a buyer the boiler is two years old; it's twelve. The buyer sues the seller, who never even met the subagent.
deeper.stakes: That's why most NY sellers and listing brokers avoid subagency. One stranger's mistake can become the seller's lawsuit.
deeper.exam: Subagency requires the seller's authorization. The seller is vicariously liable. The buyer is a customer of the subagent.

blocks.q: A subagent working through the listing broker exaggerates the lot size to a buyer. Who may be liable to the buyer besides the subagent?
c: Only the buyer's attorney
The seller, through vicarious liability
No one, since the seller never met the subagent
The MLS
blocks.x: A subagent is the seller's agent once removed, so the seller can be vicariously liable. A broker's agent is different: the seller is not vicariously liable for a broker's agent.

blocks.text: Broker's agent: help without the liability

blocks.html: A broker's agent is engaged by the listing broker (or a buyer's broker) from a different firm to help. The broker's agent has no direct relationship with the seller or buyer. The client cannot instruct it directly and is not vicariously liable for its acts. The broker who engaged it directs it and bears that liability. It still owes fiduciary duties to the client through that broker.
blocks.casual: A broker's agent is brought in by the listing broker (or a buyer's broker) from a different firm to help out. The broker's agent has no direct relationship with the seller or buyer. The client can't give it instructions directly and is not vicariously liable for what it does. The broker who brought it in directs it and carries that liability. It still owes fiduciary duties to the client through that broker.

deeper.plain: A broker's agent helps your broker. Your broker, not you, is on the hook if it messes up.
deeper.picture: Your contractor hires a tile guy. You don't boss the tile guy around, and the contractor answers for his work.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart engages a Clinton Hill firm as broker's agent to run Sunday open houses for the Okafors. When that firm's agent misquotes the taxes, the buyer's claim goes to Hudson & Hart, not the Okafors.
deeper.stakes: Sellers prefer this setup because it shields them. Brokers accept it knowing they're taking on the risk, so they choose broker's agents carefully.
deeper.exam: Key line: client is NOT vicariously liable for a broker's agent. The engaging broker is. The client can't direct the broker's agent.

left.title: Subagent
items: Agent of the seller via the listing broker
Seller vicariously liable
Created by blanket or specific offer
Old MLS model

right.title: Broker's agent
items: Agent of the listing (or buyer's) broker
Client not vicariously liable; engaging broker is
Client cannot direct it
Defined in RPL 443

deeper.plain: Both help the listing side. The difference is who pays the price when they slip up.
deeper.picture: A subagent is like a babysitter your nanny hired with your permission: you're responsible. A broker's agent is like the nanny agency's backup sitter: the agency is responsible.
deeper.street: Diane can let a Fort Greene firm help sell the Okafors' house as a subagent (Okafors liable) or as a broker's agent (Hudson & Hart liable). Diane picks broker's agent and explains why to the Okafors.
deeper.stakes: Pick the wrong structure and your sellers could be sued over words they never heard. That's a client relationship you won't get back.
deeper.exam: Subagent: client vicariously liable, old MLS model. Broker's agent: engaging broker liable, client can't direct it, defined in RPL 443.

blocks.html: Can brokerage be done without subagency? Yes, and in NY it mostly is. Cooperating brokers usually act as buyer's agents, or occasionally as broker's agents.
blocks.casual: Can you do brokerage without subagency? Yes, and in NY that's mostly how it works. Cooperating brokers usually act as buyer's agents, and sometimes as broker's agents.

deeper.plain: Today the agent on the other side of your listing is almost always the buyer's agent.
deeper.picture: Like two lawyers in a settlement meeting, each with their own client, instead of one side's lawyer pretending to help both.
deeper.street: Priya lists a Ridgewood condo. Four agents bring buyers. All four are buyer's agents, each negotiating against Priya. Nobody is a subagent.
deeper.stakes: Assuming the agent across the table works for your seller is a costly mistake. Anything you tell them about your client goes straight to the buyer.
deeper.exam: If a question asks how cooperating brokers usually work in NY today, the answer is as buyer's agents.

blocks.title: The Okafors' deal, three ways
blocks.html:
Same buyer, same brownstone, three arrangements for the outside agent from Chelsea:
1. Buyer's agent: she represents the buyer. The Okafors owe her nothing and are not liable for what she says. Hudson & Hart deals with her at arm's length.
2. Subagent: she represents the Okafors through Hudson & Hart. The buyer is her customer, and the Okafors are vicariously liable for her misstatements.
3. Broker's agent: she assists Hudson & Hart, takes direction only from it, and Hudson & Hart, not the Okafors, answers for her.
The role must be settled before she discusses price with anyone.
blocks.casual:
Same buyer, same brownstone, three different setups for the outside agent from Chelsea:
1. Buyer's agent: she represents the buyer. The Okafors owe her nothing and aren't liable for what she says. Hudson & Hart deals with her at arm's length.
2. Subagent: she represents the Okafors through Hudson & Hart. The buyer is her customer, and the Okafors are vicariously liable for her misstatements.
3. Broker's agent: she helps Hudson & Hart, takes direction only from it, and Hudson & Hart, not the Okafors, answers for her.
Her role has to be locked in before she talks price with anybody.

deeper.plain: Same person, three possible jobs, three different answers about loyalty and liability.
deeper.picture: One actor can play the hero, the villain, or the narrator. Before filming starts, everyone needs to know which.
deeper.street: The Chelsea agent's buyer says, 'I'd go to $2.1M.' As a buyer's agent she keeps that quiet. As a subagent she must tell the Okafors. Same sentence, opposite duty.
deeper.stakes: If the role is fuzzy when that sentence is spoken, someone's confidences get breached no matter what she does.
deeper.exam: Be ready to name who is liable and what's owed under each of the three setups for the same facts.

blocks.html: Seller agency is usually express, by the listing agreement, but it can be implied by conduct. Within it, the salesperson acts for the broker. Two common setups:
blocks.casual: Seller agency usually comes from the listing agreement, but it can also be implied by how you act. Inside it, the salesperson acts for the broker. There are two common setups:

deeper.plain: You usually become a seller's agent by signing a listing, but behavior can do it too.
deeper.picture: A friend becomes your wedding planner by contract, or by just taking over and you letting them.
deeper.street: An owner in Woodside asks Kim to 'see what you can get' for her house, and Kim starts marketing it without a signed listing. That conduct may create a seller agency, with all the duties and none of the protection of a written fee clause.
deeper.stakes: Implied seller agency leaves you owing duties with no clear right to a commission. Get it signed.
deeper.exam: Express agency comes from the listing agreement. Implied agency can arise from conduct even without one.

items: Cooperative sale: a buyer's agent from another firm brings the buyer. Each side has its own representation. Clean.

In-house sale: a buyer comes through your own firm. If the firm represents that buyer too, it is a dual agent and needs written consent. If the buyer stays an unrepresented customer, the firm stays the seller's agent and must make that clear.
blocks.casual:
Cooperative sale: a buyer's agent from another firm brings the buyer. Each side has its own representation. Clean.
In-house sale: the buyer comes through your own firm. If the firm represents that buyer too, it's a dual agent and needs written consent. If the buyer stays an unrepresented customer, the firm stays the seller's agent and has to make that clear.

deeper.plain: Two firms, two sides is easy. One firm with both sides is where you need extra care.
deeper.picture: Two families at a yard sale, each with their own haggler, versus one haggler working both families.
deeper.street: A buyer walks into Diane's office asking about a listing Diane holds. Diane can treat him as a customer (no advice), or, with written consent from both, act as a dual agent. She can't quietly help him.
deeper.stakes: In-house deals are where most undisclosed dual agency complaints come from. Getting the paperwork right protects the fee.
deeper.exam: In-house sale plus representing the buyer equals dual agency, which requires informed written consent of both parties.

blocks.title: NYC FARE Act (June 11, 2025)
blocks.html: In NYC, a broker hired by the landlord to list an apartment is paid by the landlord, not the tenant. Any fee a tenant must pay has to be disclosed in the listing and the lease. A tenant who hires their own tenant's agent can agree to pay that agent.
blocks.casual: In NYC, if a landlord hires a broker to list an apartment, the landlord pays that broker, not the tenant. Any fee a tenant has to pay must be disclosed in the listing and in the lease. If a tenant hires their own tenant's agent, the tenant can agree to pay that agent.

deeper.plain: Whoever hires the broker pays the broker. Tenants no longer foot the bill for the landlord's agent in NYC.
deeper.picture: If a restaurant hires a host to seat people, the restaurant pays the host, not the diners.
deeper.street: A Crown Heights landlord lists a one-bedroom at $2,900 with Tasha's firm. Before the FARE Act, the tenant might have paid a 15% fee. Since June 11, 2025, the landlord pays Tasha's firm.
deeper.stakes: Charging a tenant for a landlord-hired broker violates the FARE Act and can bring city enforcement and civil penalties.
deeper.exam: Know the date (June 11, 2025), the rule (landlord's broker is paid by the landlord), and the exception (a tenant can hire and pay their own agent).

blocks.html: Handling an in-house sale as a seller's agent: if the firm's policy is seller agency only, the buyer is a customer. Tell the buyer plainly, give the disclosure form, and do not advise. Handling a cooperative sale: confirm the other agent's role in writing, send the agency disclosure to the buyer's agent at first substantive contact, and route all offers to your client. Never discuss your client's motivation with the cooperating agent.
blocks.casual: Running an in-house sale as the seller's agent: if your firm's policy is seller agency only, the buyer's a customer. Tell the buyer straight up, give the disclosure form, and don't advise. Running a cooperative sale: confirm the other agent's role in writing, send the agency disclosure to the buyer's agent at first substantive contact, and send every offer to your client. Never discuss your client's motivation with the cooperating agent.

deeper.plain: Say your role, hand over the form, and keep your client's reasons to yourself.
deeper.picture: You're the bouncer at your client's door. Friendly to everyone, but nobody gets past you to the private room.
deeper.street: A buyer's agent asks Jordan, 'Why are the Okafors selling?' Jordan answers, 'They're ready to move on. Send me your best offer.' He doesn't mention the job transfer to Atlanta.
deeper.stakes: One slip about motivation ('they need to close by August') can cost your seller thousands in negotiating power and you your fee.
deeper.exam: The seller's agent may not reveal the seller's motivation or bottom line to the other side. Disclosure goes to the buyer's agent at first substantive contact.

items: Why buyer brokerage? Someone advises the buyer on price, terms, inspection, and negotiation, and keeps the buyer's budget confidential.
Does everyone need an agent? No. A buyer can proceed as a customer, receiving honesty but no advice. Many sophisticated buyers do.
Who pays? Whatever the agreement says: the buyer directly, the listing broker by an offer of cooperation, or the seller as a negotiated term. Payment does not change loyalty.
Buyers as clients: signed buyer agreement, full fiduciary duties.
Buyers as customers: working with a seller's agent; disclosure of known material facts, no advice, no confidentiality.
blocks.casual:
Why have a buyer's agent? Someone advises the buyer on price, terms, inspection, and negotiation, and keeps the buyer's budget confidential.
Does everyone need one? No. A buyer can go it alone as a customer and get honesty but no advice. Plenty of sophisticated buyers do.
Who pays? Whatever the agreement says: the buyer directly, the listing broker through an offer of cooperation, or the seller as a negotiated term. Payment doesn't change loyalty.
Buyer as client: signed buyer agreement, full fiduciary duties.
Buyer as customer: working with the seller's agent; gets disclosure of known material facts, but no advice and no confidentiality.

deeper.plain: A buyer's agent is the buyer's advocate. Without one, a buyer gets honesty and nothing more.
deeper.picture: Going to court with a lawyer versus representing yourself. You're allowed to do either; one gets you advice.
deeper.street: Marcus is an investor who's bought five Queens buildings and goes without an agent. His cousin Leo, a first-time buyer in Inwood, signs a buyer agreement with Priya so someone has his back on price and inspection.
deeper.stakes: An unrepresented buyer who tells the listing agent their max has handed that number straight to the seller. Passing it on isn't sneaky; it's the listing agent's duty.
deeper.exam: Buyer customers get no advice and no confidentiality. Who pays the buyer's agent does not determine loyalty.

blocks.q: Leo hires Jordan as buyer's agent. The listing broker pays Jordan's firm out of the seller's commission. Jordan owes fiduciary duties to:
c: The seller, who funds the commission
Both, since both benefit
Leo, the buyer
The listing broker
blocks.x: The agreement, not the source of the money, decides whom you represent. Jordan is Leo's agent.

blocks.html: Practicing single agency in a firm that also lists property takes discipline. The buyer's agent and the listing agent in the same office must not swap information about their clients, and the firm's written policy must say what happens when a buyer client wants an in-house listing: decline, refer out, or seek dual agency consent. Whatever the policy, the consumer must hear it before money is discussed.
blocks.casual: Running single agency in a firm that also takes listings takes discipline. The buyer's agent and the listing agent in the same office can't swap information about their clients. The firm's written policy has to say what happens when a buyer client wants an in-house listing: decline, refer out, or get dual agency consent. Whatever the policy is, the consumer hears it before anyone talks money.

deeper.plain: If you work both sides of the market in one office, you need walls and a plan.
deeper.picture: Like a newspaper keeping the advertising team out of the newsroom.
deeper.street: Kim represents a buyer who falls for her colleague Sal's listing. The firm's policy says: get dual agency consent or refer the buyer out. Kim tells her buyer about both options before they discuss an offer amount.
deeper.stakes: Hallway talk between colleagues is the classic way firms breach confidentiality. One overheard 'my seller's desperate' can sink a client.
deeper.exam: A firm must have a written agency policy and tell consumers how it handles in-house conflicts before confidential information is exchanged.

blocks.title: Liability rhymes
blocks.html: Sub binds the seller; broker's agent binds the broker.
blocks.casual: Here's the rhyme: Sub binds the seller; broker's agent binds the broker.

deeper.plain: Liability flows to whoever the helper is legally working for.
deeper.picture: A subagent is on the seller's leash. A broker's agent is on the broker's leash. Whoever holds the leash pays for the bite.
deeper.street: A subagent misquotes the HOA fee on a Long Island City condo: the seller gets sued. A broker's agent misquotes the same fee: the listing broker gets sued.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who understand this rhyme will ask which setup you're using, and you should have a good answer.
deeper.exam: Use the rhyme to eliminate answers fast whenever a question asks who is vicariously liable for a cooperating licensee.

blocks.q: Which statement about a broker's agent is TRUE?
c: It works for the same firm as the listing agent
The seller can direct it directly
The seller is not vicariously liable for its acts
It owes no duties to the seller
blocks.x: A broker's agent is from another firm, takes direction from the broker who engaged it, and the client is not vicariously liable for it. It still owes the seller fiduciary duties through the listing broker.

story.title: The Helper Problem
story.setting: Hudson & Hart office, Fulton Street, a rainy Thursday

beats.text: The Okafors' brownstone is live. The phone will not stop.
Agent from Chelsea here. I've got a buyer. Am I your subagent, or do I work for my buyer?
We don't offer subagency. You'd be the buyer's agent. Our sellers aren't on the hook for what you say.
Emmanuel: Wait. If someone from another company lies about our house, we could be sued?
Only if they're your subagent. That's why we don't use subagency. Vicarious liability is a nasty houseguest.
An hour later, a second firm offers to run weekend open houses.
That one we'll hire as a broker's agent. They help us. They answer to us. If they mess up, it's our liability, not yours.
Grace: So can I call them and tell them what to say?
You'd tell us, and we'd tell them. You don't have a direct relationship with a broker's agent.

check.q: Why can't Grace instruct the broker's agent directly?
c: Because broker's agents only work for buyers
Because the broker's agent has no direct relationship with the seller; the listing broker directs it
Because instructions must be in writing
Because the broker's agent is unlicensed
check.x: Under RPL 443, the client cannot give instructions directly to a broker's agent; the engaging broker directs it and bears its liability.

beats.text: Meanwhile, I've got a buyer for it. In-house. Easy money.
Not easy. Our firm represents the Okafors. Every one of us does, including you. If you start advising that buyer, we're dual agents.
So I just don't advise them?
Either they're a customer and you tell them plainly you work for the sellers, or we get written consent from both sides. Pick one before lunch.
Got it. Who pays doesn't decide who we work for. The paperwork and the way we act does.

board.prompt: Draw the seller, the listing broker, Jordan, a subagent, a broker's agent, and a buyer's agent. Draw solid lines for fiduciary duty and dashed lines for vicarious liability.

facts.text: Brokerage is the business; agency is the fiduciary relationship. A licensee may work in a non-agent capacity by agreement, owing honesty only.
The listing belongs to the brokerage; the salesperson acts as the broker's agent, so the listing stays if the salesperson leaves.
When a firm represents the seller, every licensee in the firm owes the seller fiduciary duties.
Seller's, buyer's, landlord's and tenant's agents each represent their own party and owe the other side honesty.
Single agency: the firm represents one side only and can fully advise that client.
A cooperating agent is any licensee from another firm who helps make the deal; the old MLS blanket offer of subagency made them seller's subagents.
Subagency is created by the listing broker with the seller's authorization; a subagent owes the seller fiduciary duties and the buyer honesty, and a cooperating broker may reject it.
The seller is vicariously liable for a subagent's misstatements.
A broker's agent is engaged by and answers to the broker; the client cannot direct it and is not vicariously liable for it.
In NY, cooperating brokers usually act as buyer's agents or broker's agents rather than subagents, which limits the seller's liability.
In an in-house sale, if the firm also represents the buyer it is a dual agent and needs written consent; otherwise the buyer stays an unrepresented customer.
Under the NYC FARE Act (2025), the landlord pays the broker it hires to list an apartment; any tenant fee must be disclosed.
In a cooperative sale, confirm the other agent's role, give the disclosure at first substantive contact, route offers to your client, and never discuss your client's motivation.
A buyer client gets advice and confidentiality; a buyer customer gets honesty only; who pays does not change loyalty.
Single agency inside a firm that also lists requires no information swapping between agents and a written policy for in-house listings.

lessons.title: Dual Agency and Designated Sales Agents
lessons.tagline: Representing both sides is legal in New York only when both sides agree in writing, knowing exactly what they give up.
objectives: Define dual agency and explain why it limits the duties each side receives
Obtain informed written consent, including advance consent on the disclosure form
Explain designated sales agents and why the broker remains a dual agent
Apply Reg 175.7 to compensation from more than one party, including mortgage referral fees
Compare the company agency policies a NY firm may adopt

blocks.title: Leo loves the Okafors' house
blocks.html: Leo Brandt, Jordan's buyer client, walks through the Okafors' Bed-Stuy brownstone and texts Jordan a spreadsheet titled "MAX OFFER." The Okafors are also Hudson & Hart clients. Jordan's firm now represents a seller who wants the highest price and a buyer who wants the lowest. Can Jordan keep both clients? What does each of them lose?
blocks.casual: Leo Brandt, Jordan's buyer client, walks through the Okafors' Bed-Stuy brownstone and texts Jordan a spreadsheet called 'MAX OFFER.' Problem: the Okafors are Hudson & Hart clients too. So now Jordan's firm represents a seller who wants the highest price and a buyer who wants the lowest. Can Jordan keep both? And what does each one give up?

deeper.plain: When your firm represents both buyer and seller on one deal, somebody's going to get less than full loyalty.
deeper.picture: Picture one coach training both boxers before the same fight. He can tape both their hands, but he can't tell either one how to beat the other.
deeper.street: Leo's spreadsheet says his max is $1.45M. The Okafors told Marcus at Hudson & Hart they'd take $1.35M. If the firm stays on both sides, nobody at the firm can use either number against the other.
deeper.stakes: Handle it right and the firm keeps both clients with written consent. Handle it wrong and it's undisclosed dual agency: lost commission, possible rescission, and DOS discipline.
deeper.exam: The first question in any in-house scenario: has each party given informed written consent? If not, the firm can't act for both.

blocks.html: Dual agency exists when one brokerage represents both buyer and seller (or landlord and tenant) in the same transaction. It is legal in New York only with the informed consent of both parties, in writing. Most dual agency arises from in-house sales: the firm has the listing and a buyer client wants it.
blocks.casual: Dual agency is when one brokerage represents both the buyer and seller (or landlord and tenant) in the same deal. In New York it's legal only with both parties' informed consent, in writing. Most dual agency comes from in-house sales: the firm has the listing, and one of its buyer clients wants it.

deeper.plain: One firm, both sides, and it's only OK if both people knowingly sign off.
deeper.picture: Like one wedding planner hired by two families who disagree on the budget. It can work, but only if both families know and agree up front.
deeper.street: Kim's firm lists a Jackson Heights co-op, and Kim's coworker has a buyer client who wants it. Before anyone talks numbers, both the seller and buyer get the dual agency explanation and sign.
deeper.stakes: Skip the written consent and the arrangement is illegal, no matter how fair the deal turned out.
deeper.exam: The exam answer requires both: informed and written. 'Verbal consent' or 'consent of the seller only' are wrong.

head: Form of dual agency
What it looks like
rows: The same salesperson works with both seller and buyer
Two salespersons in one firm, one with the seller, one with the buyer. The firm is still a dual agent
Dual agency with designated sales agents
Broker dual agency plus formal appointments, with consent, of one agent for each side

deeper.plain: Dual agency comes in three flavors, but the firm is a dual agent in all of them.
deeper.picture: One chef cooking for two rival tables; two chefs from the same kitchen each cooking for one table; same thing, but with the head chef formally assigning each.
deeper.street: At Diane's firm: Sal alone handling both a Forest Hills seller and buyer is single licensee dual agency. Sal for the seller and Priya for the buyer is broker dual agency. If Diane formally appoints them with written consent, it's dual agency with designated sales agents.
deeper.stakes: Agents who think 'different salespeople means no dual agency' skip the consent and land in undisclosed dual agency.
deeper.exam: Two salespersons in the same firm still create dual agency. Designation doesn't change that the broker is dual.

blocks.html: The cost: a dual agent cannot provide undivided loyalty to either party and cannot give the full range of fiduciary duties. A dual agent cannot advise the seller to hold out for more or the buyer to offer less, and must keep each side's bargaining position confidential from the other.
blocks.casual: Here's the price: a dual agent can't give undivided loyalty to either side and can't deliver the full set of fiduciary duties. A dual agent can't tell the seller to hold out for more or the buyer to offer less, and has to keep each side's bargaining position secret from the other.

deeper.plain: In dual agency, nobody gets a coach in the negotiation. Both get a careful referee.
deeper.picture: Think of a mediator in a divorce. Helpful, fair, but not in your corner.
deeper.street: Leo asks Jordan, 'Should I come in at $1.3M?' Under dual agency, Jordan can share recent comps on Halsey Street but can't say, 'They'll take it, go low.'
deeper.stakes: Clients who don't understand what they're giving up later claim they were shortchanged. That's why the explanation, not just the signature, matters.
deeper.exam: What's lost in dual agency: undivided loyalty and full advocacy. What remains: confidentiality of each side's position, honesty, reasonable care.

blocks.caption: Switch to "dual" and then "dual with designated agents." Watch the broker's line to both clients stay in place even after the designated agents appear.

blocks.title: How consent is obtained in NY

items.title: Explain
items.html: Tell both parties the firm would represent both, what that means, and what they give up (undivided loyalty, full advocacy).

items.title: Use the form
items.html: Both sign the dual agency consent on the NY agency disclosure form. Consent must be written.

items.title: Advance consent (optional)
items.html: A seller or buyer may check advance consent to dual agency when first signing the form, agreeing ahead of time that in-house deals may happen.

items.title: Confirm when it happens
items.html: When an in-house deal actually arises, disclose it to both parties right away and confirm consent. Advance consent is not permission to stay silent.

blocks.casual:
Explain. Tell both parties the firm would represent both, what that means, and what they give up (undivided loyalty, full advocacy).
Use the form. Both sign the dual agency consent on the NY agency disclosure form. Consent has to be written.
Advance consent (optional). When first signing the form, a seller or buyer can check advance consent to dual agency, agreeing ahead of time that in-house deals might happen.
Confirm when it happens. When an in-house deal actually comes up, tell both parties right away and confirm consent. Advance consent isn't permission to stay quiet.

deeper.plain: Explain it, get it in writing, and when it actually happens, tell them again.
deeper.picture: Like signing a waiver at a climbing gym, then the instructor still checks your harness before you climb.
deeper.street: When Evelyn listed in Bayside she checked advance consent. Six weeks later Sal's colleague brings an in-house buyer. Sal calls Evelyn that day: 'A buyer from our firm wants to make an offer; here's what that means.' He confirms by email.
deeper.stakes: Relying on a checkbox from months ago without telling the client is how firms end up in disputes. The client can say they never really knew.
deeper.exam: Advance consent is allowed, but the firm must still disclose the actual dual agency when it arises.

blocks.title: One signature is not enough
blocks.html: Seller consents, buyer is never told: the firm is an undisclosed dual agent as to the buyer. Consent must come from both. Verbal consent is not enough either.
blocks.casual: If the seller consents and the buyer is never told, the firm is an undisclosed dual agent as to the buyer. Consent has to come from both. And saying yes out loud doesn't cut it.

deeper.plain: Half the consent is no consent. Both people sign, or it doesn't count.
deeper.picture: Like a group trip where only one roommate agrees to share a bed. The other one still gets a vote.
deeper.street: A Harlem seller signed advance consent. Tasha's colleague shows a buyer client the listing and writes an offer without ever mentioning dual agency to him. The buyer finds out at the closing table and refuses to close.
deeper.stakes: The firm can lose its commission, and the buyer may be able to undo the deal. DOS can discipline both the agent and the broker.
deeper.exam: Look for 'the seller agreed' or 'the buyer verbally agreed.' Both are wrong. It must be both parties, in writing.

blocks.q: Hudson & Hart lists a Crown Heights condo. Another Hudson & Hart salesperson represents a buyer who wants it. Which is TRUE?
c: It is not dual agency because two different salespersons are involved
The firm is a dual agent and needs written informed consent from both parties
Only the buyer must consent
The firm must refuse the buyer
blocks.x: The agency belongs to the broker. Two salespersons in one firm still make the firm a dual agent. Both parties must consent in writing; refusal is an option but not required.

blocks.html: With written consent of both parties, the broker can appoint a designated sales agent for each: one salesperson represents the seller, a different one represents the buyer. Each designated agent can advocate and negotiate for their own client. The broker remains a dual agent and supervises both.
blocks.casual: With both parties' written consent, the broker can appoint a designated sales agent for each: one salesperson represents the seller, a different one represents the buyer. Each designated agent can advocate and negotiate for their own client. But the broker is still a dual agent and supervises both.

deeper.plain: Each side gets its own agent who can fight for them, inside a firm that's still on both sides.
deeper.picture: Two lawyers from the same big firm on opposite sides of a case, with an ethical wall between them and the senior partner overseeing both.
deeper.street: Diane designates Priya for a Flushing seller and Ray for an in-house buyer. Priya can tell her seller to counter at $980,000. Ray can tell his buyer that $940,000 is reasonable based on comps.
deeper.stakes: Designated agents restore real advocacy, which clients value. But if one agent leaks what they knew, the whole structure fails and the firm is exposed.
deeper.exam: Designated sales agents can advocate for their own client. The broker remains a dual agent. Written consent of both parties is required.

items: Must be two different licensees (a salesperson or associate broker for each side), not the same person.
The broker cannot be one of the designated agents, because the broker supervises both sides.
Designated agents still cannot provide undivided loyalty, because the firm represents both. They also may not share what they learned earlier from the other side.
Consent can be given in advance: advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents, naming who will be the client's designated agent.
blocks.casual:
The rules on designated agents:
It has to be two different licensees (a salesperson or associate broker for each side), not the same person.
The broker can't be one of the designated agents, because the broker supervises both sides.
Designated agents still can't give undivided loyalty, because the firm represents both. And they can't share anything they learned earlier from the other side.
Consent can be given in advance: advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents, naming who'll be the client's designated agent.

deeper.plain: Two different people, never the broker, and no carrying secrets across the wall.
deeper.picture: Two goalies from the same club playing for opposing teams in a scrimmage. The coach watches both, and neither one gets to share the other's playbook.
deeper.street: Sal had been helping a buyer, then switched to helping the seller on the same Woodside house. He can't be the seller's designated agent now, because he already knows the buyer's budget.
deeper.stakes: Using the broker as a designated agent, or a licensee who already knows the other side's secrets, defeats the purpose and invites a breach claim.
deeper.exam: Trap answers: 'the broker may be one designated agent' (no) and 'one salesperson can be designated for both' (no).

blocks.title: Designated does not mean single
blocks.html: "Once designated agents are appointed, the broker is no longer a dual agent." False. The broker is still a dual agent. Designation lets each salesperson advocate; it does not erase the firm's dual role.
blocks.casual: Here's the false statement they love: 'Once designated agents are appointed, the broker isn't a dual agent anymore.' Wrong. The broker is still a dual agent. Designation lets each salesperson advocate. It doesn't erase the firm's dual role.

deeper.plain: Designation changes what the salespeople can do, not what the firm is.
deeper.picture: Putting a divider in a fridge doesn't make it two fridges.
deeper.street: A seller asks Diane, 'Now that Marcus is my designated agent, you're just mine too, right?' Diane says, 'No. The firm still represents both of you. Marcus is your advocate inside that arrangement.'
deeper.stakes: Overselling designated agency to a client is a misrepresentation about your own role, which can come back in a complaint.
deeper.exam: Any answer claiming designation ends the broker's dual agency is wrong.

blocks.q: Under dual agency with designated sales agents, the broker:
c: Represents only the seller
Remains a dual agent and supervises both designated agents
Must act as the buyer's designated agent
Is released from all fiduciary duties
blocks.x: Designation assigns one salesperson to each party, but the brokerage still represents both, so the broker remains a dual agent.

blocks.html: Dual agency is risky even when legal: each side may later claim the agent favored the other. Undisclosed dual agency is far worse. It is a breach of loyalty to both sides.
blocks.casual: Dual agency is risky even when it's legal: either side can later claim the agent played favorites. Undisclosed dual agency is way worse. It's a loyalty breach to both sides at once.

deeper.plain: Legal dual agency is a tightrope. Secret dual agency is falling off it.
deeper.picture: Dating two people who both know about it is complicated. Dating two people who don't is a disaster waiting to happen.
deeper.street: After closing on a Bay Ridge co-op, the seller learns the buyer was also a client of the same firm. He claims he'd have held out for $30,000 more with a real advocate, and sues.
deeper.stakes: Even with consent, documentation is your defense. Without consent, you have no defense.
deeper.exam: Undisclosed dual agency is a breach of loyalty to both principals.

items: Forfeiture of the entire commission, often to both sides
Rescission: either party may be able to void the deal
Damages in a civil suit
DOS discipline: fine, suspension, or revocation for untrustworthiness
blocks.casual:
What undisclosed dual agency can cost you:
Forfeiture of the whole commission, often to both sides.
Rescission: either party may be able to void the deal.
Damages in a civil suit.
DOS discipline: a fine, suspension, or revocation for untrustworthiness.

deeper.plain: You can lose the fee, the deal, money in court, and your license, all at once.
deeper.picture: It's like getting caught cheating on a test: the grade, the class, and the scholarship all go.
deeper.street: A Staten Island firm earns $42,000 on an in-house sale it never disclosed as dual. The buyer sues, a court orders the fee returned, and DOS suspends the salesperson.
deeper.stakes: The firm, the broker, and the salesperson can all be hit. Clients lose trust and the firm's reputation in the neighborhood takes years to rebuild.
deeper.exam: Know the four consequences: forfeiture, rescission, damages, and DOS discipline. Rescission means the deal can be undone.

blocks.html: Undisclosed dual agency often happens by accident through implied agency: a seller's agent starts advising a buyer customer ("offer $50K less, they'll take it"). The conduct creates a second agency nobody consented to.
blocks.casual: Undisclosed dual agency usually happens by accident, through implied agency. A seller's agent starts advising a buyer customer ('offer $50K less, they'll take it'). That behavior creates a second agency nobody agreed to.

deeper.plain: One piece of advice to the wrong person can turn you into their agent.
deeper.picture: Like a shopkeeper telling a customer which competitor sells it cheaper. Helpful, but now whose side is he on?
deeper.street: At a Flatbush open house, the listing agent tells an unrepresented buyer, 'They've had no offers in 60 days. Come in at $50K under.' The buyer does. Now the seller has a claim and the buyer thinks she has an agent.
deeper.stakes: Accidental dual agency still carries every penalty of the intentional kind. 'I was just being nice' is not a defense.
deeper.exam: When a stem describes a seller's agent advising a buyer customer, answer implied agency leading to undisclosed dual agency.

blocks.title: Leo and the Okafors, step by step
blocks.html:
1. Leo, a buyer client, asks to see the Okafors' listing, also held by Hudson & Hart.
2. Jordan stops and explains: the firm represents both; neither will get undivided loyalty; the Okafors' bottom line and Leo's maximum stay confidential.
3. Leo signs dual agency consent. The Okafors checked advance consent at listing, and Diane now tells them about Leo and confirms in writing.
4. With both parties' written consent, Diane designates Jordan for Leo and Marcus for the Okafors.
5. Now each designated agent can give full advice and negotiate for their own client: Jordan for Leo (including what to offer), Marcus for the Okafors (including whether to accept). Neither passes along what the other side said in confidence, and Diane, as broker, stays neutral.
Result: a lawful dual agency with designated sales agents, and the broker is still the dual agent.
blocks.casual:
1. Leo, a buyer client, asks to see the Okafors' listing, which Hudson & Hart also holds.
2. Jordan hits pause and explains: the firm represents both, neither will get undivided loyalty, and the Okafors' bottom line and Leo's max both stay confidential.
3. Leo signs dual agency consent. The Okafors checked advance consent when they listed, and Diane now tells them about Leo and confirms in writing.
4. With both parties' written consent, Diane designates Jordan for Leo and Marcus for the Okafors.
5. Now each one gets to be a real advocate: Jordan tells Leo what to offer, Marcus tells the Okafors whether to take it. What each side said in confidence stays on that side, and Diane stays neutral.
Result: a lawful dual agency with designated sales agents, and the broker is still the dual agent.

deeper.plain: Pause, explain, get both signatures, assign two agents, keep the wall up.
deeper.picture: Like a hospital running two surgeries in neighboring rooms: separate teams, one chief of surgery, and nobody wanders between rooms.
deeper.street: Leo offers $1.38M. Marcus advises the Okafors to counter at $1.42M based on two recent Halsey Street sales. Jordan tells Leo $1.40M is supported by the same comps. They meet at $1.40M, and nobody's MAX OFFER spreadsheet left the building.
deeper.stakes: Skipping step 3 for either party turns this into undisclosed dual agency. Skipping step 4 leaves both clients with a neutral referee instead of advocates.
deeper.exam: Order matters: disclose and get written consent from both before designation and before any negotiation advice.

blocks.html: Single licensee dual agency is the hardest version to do well. One person holds both clients' secrets and must advise neither against the other. Many NY firms ban it and require designated agents or a referral. If you ever find yourself the only agent on both sides, slow down: confirm written consent, stop giving advice on price, and stick to facts and paperwork.
blocks.casual: Single licensee dual agency is the hardest version to pull off. One person holds both clients' secrets and can't advise either one against the other. Plenty of NY firms ban it and require designated agents or a referral instead.
