If you ever end up as the only agent on both sides, slow down: confirm written consent, stop giving price advice, and stick to facts and paperwork.

deeper.plain: When you alone have both clients, you become a careful note-taker, not an advisor.
deeper.picture: You're the only waiter for two tables having a fight. You serve both, take orders, and keep your opinions to yourself.
deeper.street: Ray, a solo licensee in a tiny Bayside firm, ends up with both buyer and seller on a ranch house. He gets written consent from both, then answers price questions with 'Here are the last six sales; the decision is yours.'
deeper.stakes: One slip, like a hint that the seller is flexible, breaches a confidence and gives the other side a lawsuit.
deeper.exam: Single licensee dual agency is legal with informed written consent, but the agent cannot advise either party on price or strategy against the other.

blocks.text: Getting paid by more than one party: Reg 175.7

blocks.title: 19 NYCRR 175.7
blocks.html: A broker must make clear which party it is acting for, and may not receive compensation from more than one party except with the full knowledge and consent of all parties. RPL 443 implements this for residential deals: the form tells consumers whom you represent; 175.7 governs who may pay you.
blocks.casual: Under 19 NYCRR 175.7, a broker has to make clear which party it's acting for, and can't get paid by more than one party unless all parties fully know and consent. RPL 443 carries this out for residential deals: the form tells consumers who you represent, and 175.7 controls who's allowed to pay you.

deeper.plain: Getting paid by both sides is allowed only if everyone knows and agrees.
deeper.picture: A wedding DJ who's secretly also paid by the venue to push their bar package. Fine if the couple knows; shady if they don't.
deeper.street: A landlord pays Sal's firm to fill a Sunnyside unit, and the tenant also agreed to pay Sal a fee. Sal must disclose both payments to both parties and get their consent.
deeper.stakes: Hidden double pay is a classic DOS charge. The firm can lose both fees and face fines.
deeper.exam: Reg 175.7: compensation from more than one party requires full disclosure to and consent of all parties.

blocks.html: Mortgage brokerage referral fees. A real estate licensee who simply refers a buyer to a lender or mortgage broker may not take a referral fee: that is a kickback under RESPA Section 8. A licensee who is also properly licensed by DFS and actually performs mortgage brokerage services may be paid for that work, but only with full disclosure to, and consent of, all parties under 175.7.
blocks.casual: Mortgage referral fees. If you're a real estate licensee who just refers a buyer to a lender or mortgage broker, you can't take a referral fee. That's a kickback under RESPA Section 8. If you're also properly licensed by DFS and actually do mortgage brokerage work, you can get paid for that work, but only with full disclosure to, and consent from, all parties under 175.7.

deeper.plain: Pointing a buyer to a lender earns you nothing. Doing licensed mortgage work can, if everyone knows.
deeper.picture: A doctor can't take cash for sending you to a certain pharmacy, but a doctor who also runs a licensed clinic can bill for real treatment.
deeper.street: A Long Island lender offers Kim $500 per buyer she sends over. Kim says no. Her colleague, who holds a DFS mortgage broker license and processes a buyer's loan, gets paid for that service with written disclosure to buyer and seller.
deeper.stakes: RESPA kickbacks are a federal violation with fines and possible jail, plus DOS discipline. 'It was just a thank-you' doesn't help.
deeper.exam: Referral fee for simply sending business to a lender: illegal kickback under RESPA Section 8. Payment for actual licensed services: allowed with disclosure and consent.

blocks.q: A mortgage broker offers Jordan $500 for every buyer Jordan refers. Jordan performs no loan services. Taking the money would be:
c: Legal if Jordan tells the buyer
Legal if under $600 per year
A prohibited kickback under RESPA
Legal because Jordan is licensed
blocks.x: A fee for a mere referral, with no services performed, is a RESPA Section 8 kickback. Disclosure does not cure a fee that is illegal in itself.

blocks.html: Every NY brokerage should decide its agency policy in writing and train every licensee on it, because the policy determines what an agent says at first substantive contact. A buyer who walks into an exclusive seller-agency firm must hear, right away, that nobody there can represent them. A firm that allows consensual dual agency must have a consent process ready before the first in-house deal, not after.
blocks.casual: Every NY brokerage should put its agency policy in writing and train every licensee on it, because that policy decides what an agent says at first substantive contact. A buyer who walks into a seller-agency-only firm has to hear right away that nobody there can represent them. A firm that allows consensual dual agency needs its consent process ready before the first in-house deal, not after.

deeper.plain: Decide your firm's rules before a client walks in, and make sure every agent can explain them.
deeper.picture: Like a restaurant deciding its allergy policy before the first customer orders, not while the ambulance is on the way.
deeper.street: A buyer walks into a Fort Greene firm that only represents sellers. The agent says on the spot, 'We only represent sellers. I can show you our listings, but I can't advise you. You might want your own buyer's agent.'
deeper.stakes: A firm without a clear policy improvises, and improvisation is how undisclosed dual agency and confidentiality breaches happen.
deeper.exam: Agency policy should be written, known to all agents, and communicated to consumers at first substantive contact.

head: Policy
How it works
Trade-off
rows: Firm represents only sellers; buyers are customers
No dual agency, but buyers get no advice
Firm represents only buyers; never lists
No dual agency, but no listing income
Consensual dual agency, seller agency as the norm
Represents sellers; in-house buyers become clients only with dual consent
Consensual dual agency, buyer agency for all other deals
Buyer agency on outside listings; dual agency with consent on in-house sales
Common in NYC; needs strong procedures
In-house deals handled with designated sales agents
Most advocacy within a dual arrangement

deeper.plain: Firms choose how they handle both sides of the market. Each choice trades flexibility against risk.
deeper.picture: Like a restaurant choosing between dine-in only, takeout only, or both with a system to keep orders straight.
deeper.street: A Manhattan firm that does both listings and buyer work picks consensual dual agency with designated agents. A tiny Bayside office that only does listings picks seller agency exclusively, so buyers are always customers.
deeper.stakes: The policy you pick shapes your income and your risk. Exclusive policies avoid dual agency but leave money or clients on the table.
deeper.exam: Match the policy to the result: exclusive seller agency means buyers are customers; exclusive buyer agency means the firm never lists; designated agents give the most advocacy within dual agency.

blocks.title: Two signatures, two agents, one broker
blocks.html: Dual agency: both consent in writing. Designated agents: two different salespersons, and the broker is still dual.
blocks.casual: Lock it in: two signatures, two agents, one broker. Dual agency means both consent in writing. Designated agents means two different salespersons, and the broker is still dual.

deeper.plain: Both parties sign, two different agents get designated, and the broker never stops being dual.
deeper.picture: Picture a referee standing between two coaches. Two coaches, one ref, and the ref never switches jerseys.
deeper.street: On the exam Kim reads: 'Under designated agency, which is true?' She recites the line and picks 'the broker remains a dual agent.'
deeper.stakes: Mix up any one of the three pieces and you either skip consent, use the wrong person, or misdescribe the firm's role.
deeper.exam: Expect at least one question on each piece: written consent from both, two different licensees, broker still dual.

story.title: Both Sides of the Stoop
story.setting: Hudson & Hart conference room, a Wednesday in May

beats.text: I made a spreadsheet. Column F is my max offer. Can you tell me what the Okafors will actually take?
Leo, the Okafors are also our clients. Before we go any further, I need to explain dual agency.
Is that like a dual-core processor? Twice as good?
beats.tag: Dual agency: one firm, both sides

beats.text: More like half. If you both consent, our firm represents both of you, but nobody gets undivided loyalty. I can't tell you their bottom line, and I can't tell them column F.
beats.tag: Dual agent cannot give undivided loyalty

beats.text: Diane slides two copies of the disclosure form across the table.
Both sides sign, in writing. The Okafors already checked advance consent when they listed. We still tell them today, because now it's real.
beats.tag: Advance consent still needs disclosure when it happens

beats.text: What if I want someone who's actually on my side?
Designated sales agents. Jordan stays yours, Marcus is assigned to the Okafors. Each of them negotiates for their own client.
And Diane's out of it?
I'm the broker. I supervise both of you, so the firm is still a dual agent. Designation doesn't change that.

check.q: After designated agents are appointed, what is Diane's status?
c: Seller's agent only
Buyer's agent only
Still a dual agent
No longer an agent
check.x: The brokerage still represents both parties. Designation lets each salesperson advocate, but the broker remains a dual agent.

beats.text: Later, Marcus's phone lights up. A mortgage broker: "Send me Leo, I'll send you five hundred."
Easy money.
Kickback. RESPA. And under 175.7 you can't take money from more than one party without everyone's knowledge and consent anyway.
So dual agency is legal, but only with both signatures. And designated agents still leave the broker in the middle.
Consent in writing, secrets kept on both sides, and nobody gets paid behind anybody's back.

board.prompt: Draw the firm in the middle with the Okafors on one side and Leo on the other. Add Jordan and Marcus as designated agents. Mark which lines still run through the broker.

facts.text: Dual agency is one brokerage representing both buyer and seller (or landlord and tenant) in the same deal; in NY it is legal only with the informed written consent of both.
Most dual agency comes from in-house sales; two salespersons of one firm on opposite sides still makes the broker a dual agent.
A dual agent cannot give undivided loyalty or advise either side on price, but may give both sides factual information and must keep each side's bargaining position confidential.
Consent is written, on the NY agency disclosure form; advance consent may be checked at signing, but when an in-house deal arises both parties must be told and consent confirmed.
If only one party consents (or consent is only verbal), the firm is an undisclosed dual agent as to the other.
With written consent of both, the broker may appoint a designated sales agent for each side, who can advocate for that client; the broker remains a dual agent.
Designated agents must be two different licensees, the broker cannot be one, and they may not share what they learned earlier from the other side.
Advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents can be given on the form, naming the client's designated agent.
Undisclosed dual agency can bring forfeiture of the commission, rescission, civil damages, and DOS discipline.
A seller's agent who advises a buyer customer on price creates an implied agency and an undisclosed dual agency.
Single licensee dual agency is the hardest form; many firms ban it, and an agent on both sides should stop price advice and stick to facts and paperwork.
Under 19 NYCRR 175.7 a broker must make clear whom it acts for and may not be paid by more than one party without the full knowledge and consent of all.
RPL 443 tells residential consumers whom the licensee represents; 175.7 governs whom the broker acts for and who may pay it.
Taking a fee just for referring a buyer to a lender is a RESPA Section 8 kickback; a DFS-licensed licensee who actually brokers the loan may be paid with disclosure and consent of all.
Each brokerage should adopt a written agency policy and train on it, because it decides what agents say at first substantive contact.
Firm policies include exclusive seller agency, exclusive buyer agency (never lists), consensual dual agency, and designated agents, each with its trade-off.

lessons.title: Listing and Buyer Agreements, and How Agency Ends
lessons.tagline: The agreement decides who gets paid when the house sells. The calendar, the parties, and the property decide when it ends.
objectives: Compare exclusive right to sell, exclusive agency, and open listings, and say who gets paid in each
Describe the exclusive right to rent and the exclusive right to represent (buyer agency) agreements
Apply 19 NYCRR 175.24 and the 2024 NAR settlement rules
List the ways an agency terminates, including by operation of law
Work a commission split from sale price to salesperson

blocks.title: "My neighbor might buy it"
blocks.html: Rosa owns a Park Slope brownstone and is ready to list with Jordan at 5%. She hesitates: "My downstairs neighbor said he might buy it. If he does, do I still owe you $87,500? And what if another broker brings someone?" The answer depends entirely on one phrase at the top of the agreement.
blocks.casual: Rosa owns a Park Slope brownstone and she's ready to list with Jordan at 5%. Then she hesitates: 'My downstairs neighbor said he might buy it. If he does, do I still owe you $87,500? And what if some other broker brings a buyer?' The whole answer comes down to one phrase at the top of the agreement.

deeper.plain: The type of listing decides who gets paid when the buyer comes from somewhere unexpected.
deeper.picture: It's like a gym contract: some charge you even if you work out at home, some don't. Read the first line before you sign.
deeper.street: Jordan shows Rosa two forms. Under an exclusive right to sell, the neighbor deal still pays Hudson & Hart. Under exclusive agency, Rosa could sell to the neighbor and owe nothing. Rosa picks exclusive agency and Jordan adjusts his marketing plan.
deeper.stakes: A seller who doesn't understand the listing type can owe a $87,500 fee they didn't expect, or a broker can spend months marketing a house and get nothing.
deeper.exam: Any 'owner finds the buyer' question is really asking which listing type was signed.

blocks.html: A listing agreement is the employment contract between an owner and a broker. It creates express agency, usually special agency. Three kinds:
blocks.casual: A listing agreement is the employment contract between an owner and a broker. It creates express agency, usually special agency. There are three kinds:

deeper.plain: The listing is the seller hiring the broker for one job: sell this property.
deeper.picture: It's a job offer letter for a single project, not a full-time job.
deeper.street: The Okafors sign a listing with Hudson & Hart for their Bed-Stuy brownstone. That one document makes the firm their special agent: market, show, negotiate, but not sign for them.
deeper.stakes: No signed listing means no express agency and a hard time collecting a fee. Sloppy terms mean fights later about who's owed what.
deeper.exam: Listing agreement equals express agency, usually special agency. It's an employment contract, not a contract of sale.

head: Listing type
Listing broker finds buyer
Another broker finds buyer
Owner finds buyer
rows: Listing broker paid (shares per its agreements)
Listing broker paid; owner may owe the other broker too
Only the broker who was procuring cause
blocks.caption: Exclusive right to sell is the most protective for the broker and the most common.

deeper.plain: The more exclusive the listing, the more ways the broker gets paid.
deeper.picture: Exclusive right to sell is a lifeguard paid for the whole summer no matter who saves the swimmer. Exclusive agency pays the lifeguard unless the swimmer's own mom pulls him out. Open listing pays whichever lifeguard actually got there first.
deeper.street: Evelyn gives open listings on her Forest Hills Tudor to three firms. Sal shows it first and negotiates the deal. Sal's firm is procuring cause and collects; the other two get nothing for their open houses.
deeper.stakes: Open listings make brokers spend less on marketing, because they may get nothing. Sellers trade a lower risk of paying for a weaker effort.
deeper.exam: Classic table question: owner finds buyer. Exclusive right to sell: broker paid. Exclusive agency: no commission. Open: no commission.

blocks.caption: Pick who found the buyer: the listing broker, a cooperating broker, or the owner. Watch which column pays out under each agreement.

blocks.title: 19 NYCRR 175.24
blocks.html: Every exclusive listing of NY residential property (1 to 4 family, condos, co-ops) must include a printed explanation, at least 6-point type, of exclusive right to sell vs exclusive agency, signed or initialed by the owner. If the broker belongs to an MLS, the owner must be given the choice of having offers submitted through the listing broker or directly by the selling broker.
blocks.casual: Under 19 NYCRR 175.24, every exclusive listing of NY residential property (1 to 4 family, condos, co-ops) has to include a printed explanation, in at least 6-point type, of exclusive right to sell versus exclusive agency, signed or initialed by the owner. If the broker's in an MLS, the owner has to get a choice: have offers come in through the listing broker, or directly from the selling broker.

deeper.plain: Before signing an exclusive, the owner has to see the difference in writing and initial it.
deeper.picture: Like the 'I understand the risks' box at the bottom of a medical consent form.
deeper.street: Kim's listing paperwork for a Woodside two-family includes the 175.24 explanation page. The seller initials it. Kim keeps the signed copy in the file.
deeper.stakes: Leave out the explanation and the broker may face DOS discipline, and the seller has an argument against paying the fee.
deeper.exam: Know three things: residential 1 to 4 family, condos, co-ops; owner signs or initials the explanation; MLS brokers give the owner a choice on how offers are submitted.

blocks.q: Rosa signs an exclusive agency listing. Her neighbor buys directly from her with no broker. Rosa owes Jordan's firm:
c: The full commission
Half the commission
Nothing
Advertising costs only
blocks.x: Exclusive agency lets the owner sell on her own commission-free. Only exclusive right to sell pays the broker when the owner finds the buyer.

blocks.html: Every exclusive listing should have a definite expiration date. Automatic renewal clauses invite trouble and DOS complaints. A net listing ("I want $1.75M, you keep the rest") is prohibited in NY no matter who proposes it.
blocks.casual: Every exclusive listing should have a real expiration date. Automatic renewal clauses invite trouble and DOS complaints. And a net listing ('I want $1.75M, you keep the rest') is banned in NY no matter who suggests it.

deeper.plain: Put an end date on it, don't make it renew by itself, and never take 'everything above my number.'
deeper.picture: A lease with no end date or one that renews itself forever: nobody likes being trapped.
deeper.street: A Riverdale seller offers Ray a deal: 'Get me $900,000 and keep whatever's over.' Ray declines and proposes a 5% listing with a six-month term instead.
deeper.stakes: Net listings tempt a broker to underprice for the owner and pocket the gap, which is why they're banned (19 NYCRR 175.19). An auto-renewal can trap a seller and land the broker in a DOS complaint.
deeper.exam: Net listings are illegal in NY even if the seller proposes it. Exclusive listings need a definite expiration.

blocks.title: Who gets paid on Rosa's house
blocks.html:
Rosa lists at 5% and the house sells for $1,750,000. Fee = $1,750,000 x 0.05 = $87,500.
1. Exclusive right to sell, neighbor buys directly: Hudson & Hart is owed $87,500.
2. Exclusive agency, neighbor buys directly: $0.
3. Exclusive agency, a Cobble Hill broker brings the buyer: Hudson & Hart is still owed its fee, and Rosa may owe the other broker too if she agreed to pay it.
4. Open listing with three firms: only the procuring cause is paid.
blocks.casual:
Rosa lists at 5% and the house sells for $1,750,000. Fee = $1,750,000 x 0.05 = $87,500.
1. Exclusive right to sell, neighbor buys directly: Hudson & Hart is owed $87,500.
2. Exclusive agency, neighbor buys directly: $0.
3. Exclusive agency, a Cobble Hill broker brings the buyer: Hudson & Hart still gets its fee, and Rosa may owe the other broker too if she agreed to pay them.
4. Open listing with three firms: only the procuring cause gets paid.

deeper.plain: Same sale, same price, four different paychecks depending on the paperwork.
deeper.picture: Like four different insurance policies covering the same fender bender: the payout depends on the fine print.
deeper.street: In case 3, Rosa signed an agreement with the Cobble Hill broker's buyer promising a fee too. She now owes Hudson & Hart $87,500 and the Cobble Hill firm whatever she agreed. That's the double-commission risk.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who sign side agreements during an exclusive can pay twice. Brokers who don't explain this can face angry clients and complaints.
deeper.exam: Do the math first ($1,750,000 x 5%), then apply the listing type. Exclusive agency protects the owner only when the owner personally finds the buyer.

items: Exclusive right to rent: the landlord's version of exclusive right to sell. The broker is paid if the unit rents during the term, whoever finds the tenant. In NYC, under the FARE Act, that broker is paid by the landlord.

Exclusive right to represent (exclusive buyer agency): the buyer agrees to work with one buyer's broker for a period. The broker is paid per the agreement if the buyer buys during the term, often even if the buyer finds the home alone.
Non-exclusive buyer agreement: the buyer may use several brokers; pay usually goes to the procuring broker.
blocks.casual:
Exclusive right to rent is the landlord's version of exclusive right to sell. The broker gets paid if the unit rents during the term, no matter who finds the tenant. In NYC, under the FARE Act, the landlord pays that broker.
Exclusive right to represent (exclusive buyer agency): the buyer agrees to work with one buyer's broker for a set time. The broker gets paid per the agreement if the buyer buys during the term, often even if the buyer finds the home alone.
Non-exclusive buyer agreement: the buyer can use several brokers, and pay usually goes to the procuring broker.

deeper.plain: Landlords and buyers sign their own versions of exclusive and non-exclusive deals.
deeper.picture: Exclusive buyer agency is like hiring one personal shopper for the season. If you buy a coat on your own, you might still owe them.
deeper.street: Priya signs a 90-day exclusive right to represent with a buyer looking in Sunset Park. In week six the buyer finds a condo on Zillow and buys it without telling her. Under her agreement, Priya's firm is still owed its fee.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who sign exclusives casually can owe a fee on a home they found themselves. Brokers who don't explain this get complaints.
deeper.exam: Exclusive right to rent mirrors exclusive right to sell. Exclusive right to represent is the buyer's exclusive. Non-exclusive pays the procuring cause.

blocks.title: NAR settlement, effective August 17, 2024
blocks.html: MLS participants working with a buyer must have a written buyer agreement before touring a home, in person or virtually. The agreement must state the compensation in a specific, objective amount (not open-ended) and the broker cannot receive more than that from any source. Offers of compensation to buyer brokers can no longer be published on the MLS. Compensation remains negotiable.
blocks.casual: Since August 17, 2024, MLS participants working with a buyer need a written buyer agreement before touring a home, in person or virtually. The agreement has to state compensation as a specific, objective amount (not open-ended), and the broker can't collect more than that from any source. Offers of compensation to buyer brokers can't be published on the MLS anymore. Compensation is still negotiable.

deeper.plain: Sign first, tour second, and the fee in the agreement is the ceiling.
deeper.picture: Like a contractor who gives you a written quote before stepping in the door, and can't bill you more later.
deeper.street: A buyer wants a FaceTime tour of an Astoria condo with Leo tonight. Leo emails a buyer agreement first stating 2% of the purchase price. Later the seller offers 2.5%; Leo's firm can only take 2%.
deeper.stakes: Touring without the agreement violates MLS rules. Taking more than the stated amount violates the agreement and exposes the firm to claims.
deeper.exam: Virtual tours count. The amount must be specific and objective. No compensation offers on the MLS. Fees remain negotiable.

blocks.title: Standardized operating procedures (RPL 442-h)
blocks.html: NY brokers must adopt written procedures for prospective buyers (for example, whether ID, pre-approval, or an exclusive buyer agreement is required), file them with DOS, and apply them to everyone equally. A firm that requires a buyer agreement must require it of all buyers.
blocks.casual: NY brokers have to adopt written procedures for prospective buyers (say, whether ID, pre-approval, or an exclusive buyer agreement is required), file them with DOS, and apply them to everyone equally. If a firm requires a buyer agreement, it requires it from every buyer.

deeper.plain: Whatever you ask one buyer for, you ask every buyer for.
deeper.picture: Like a club that checks every ID at the door, not just some people's.
deeper.street: Diane's firm's posted SOPs require pre-approval before showings. When a well-dressed buyer asks to skip it, Jordan says no, the same way he did for the young couple last week.
deeper.stakes: Asking only some buyers for pre-approval or ID is a fair housing red flag. Inconsistent treatment is what Newsday's 2019 Long Island investigation exposed, and it led to this law.
deeper.exam: RPL 442-h: written SOPs, filed with DOS, applied equally. The point is fair housing.

blocks.q: Under the 2024 NAR settlement, when must an MLS participant have a written agreement with a buyer?
c: Before the buyer signs a contract of sale
Before touring a home with the buyer
Before the first phone call
Only if the buyer is paying the fee
blocks.x: The trigger is touring, in person or live virtual. Waiting until contract is too late.

blocks.html: Read a buyer agreement as carefully as a listing. It should state the term, the geographic area or property types covered, the fee in a specific amount or percentage, who pays it (the buyer, or the buyer's broker by agreement with the listing side or seller), and what happens if the buyer purchases on their own during the term. A buyer can always negotiate the fee, the term, and whether the agreement is exclusive.
blocks.casual: Read a buyer agreement as carefully as a listing. It should spell out the term, the area or property types it covers, the fee as a specific amount or percentage, who pays it (the buyer, or the buyer's broker by agreement with the listing side or seller), and what happens if the buyer buys on their own during the term. A buyer can always negotiate the fee, the term, and whether it's exclusive.

deeper.plain: A buyer agreement is a contract. Know exactly what you're signing and what you owe.
deeper.picture: Like a phone plan: the term, the coverage map, the price, and the cancellation fee.
deeper.street: Marcus signs with Ray for 'condos in Brooklyn, 60 days, 2% paid by the seller if offered, otherwise by Marcus.' When Marcus buys a co-op in Queens, it's outside the agreement and he owes Ray nothing.
deeper.stakes: Vague agreements lead to fee fights. A buyer can end up owing money out of pocket if no one else agrees to pay.
deeper.exam: Everything in a buyer agreement is negotiable: fee, term, area, exclusivity.

blocks.caption: Slide the sale price and the split percentages. Follow one dollar from the seller to the listing firm, the buyer's firm, and each salesperson.

blocks.title: From sale price to Jordan's check
blocks.html:
Sale price $1,250,000. Listing agreement: 5% to Hudson & Hart, which has agreed to pay a cooperating buyer's broker 2.5%.
Total commission: $1,250,000 x 0.05 = $62,500.
Buyer's firm: $1,250,000 x 0.025 = $31,250. Hudson & Hart keeps $62,500 minus $31,250 = $31,250.
Jordan's split with Diane is 60/40 in Jordan's favor: $31,250 x 0.60 = $18,750 to Jordan, paid by Hudson & Hart, never by the seller directly.
blocks.casual:
Sale price $1,250,000. Listing agreement: 5% to Hudson & Hart, which agreed to pay a cooperating buyer's broker 2.5%.
Total commission: $1,250,000 x 0.05 = $62,500.
Buyer's firm: $1,250,000 x 0.025 = $31,250. Hudson & Hart keeps $62,500 minus $31,250 = $31,250.
Jordan's split with Diane is 60/40 in Jordan's favor: $31,250 x 0.60 = $18,750 to Jordan, paid by Hudson & Hart, never by the seller directly.

deeper.plain: Commission math is a waterfall: total, then the co-broke, then the agent's split.
deeper.picture: Picture a pizza: the seller pays for the whole pie, the buyer's firm takes half, and Jordan gets 60% of the half left in his firm's box.
deeper.street: Jordan's 1099 for the year shows $18,750 from this sale. Diane's firm keeps $12,500 to cover the office, insurance, and marketing for the brownstone.
deeper.stakes: Get the order wrong and you'll quote a client or yourself the wrong number. A math mistake on a listing presentation can kill trust fast.
deeper.exam: Work it step by step: price x rate, minus co-op share, then x the agent's split. Watch whether the split is applied to the total or the firm's side.

blocks.html: Splits are a private matter between the broker and the salesperson and are set by their independent contractor agreement: 50/50, 60/40, 70/30, or a cap model. The client never sees them and never pays the salesperson directly. Cooperating fees between firms are set by agreement between those firms, not by any board or MLS.
blocks.casual: Splits are private, between the broker and the salesperson, set by their independent contractor agreement: 50/50, 60/40, 70/30, or a cap model. The client never sees them and never pays the salesperson directly. Fees between firms come from agreements between those firms, not from any board or MLS.

deeper.plain: How a broker and agent divide the fee is their business, not the client's.
deeper.picture: Like a hair salon and its stylist splitting what you paid. You pay the salon at the front desk.
deeper.street: Kim moves to a cap-model firm in Long Island City: 80/20 until she's paid the firm $20,000 in a year, then 100%. Her sellers never know or care.
deeper.stakes: Letting a client pay you directly violates the rule that salespersons are paid only by their broker. That's a disciplinary issue.
deeper.exam: Splits are set by the broker and salesperson agreement. Cooperating fees are set between firms, never by a board or MLS.

head: By acts of the parties
By operation of law
rows: Revocation by the principal (may owe damages)
Destruction or condemnation of the property
Renunciation by the agent (may owe damages)
Loss of the broker's license; change in law making it illegal

deeper.plain: Agency ends either because the parties ended it or because something made it impossible.
deeper.picture: A band breaks up because the members chose to (acts of the parties) or because the venue burned down and the singer lost his voice (operation of law).
deeper.street: Evelyn's listing on her Bayside home ends early when she dies in March. The agency ends by operation of law; her estate's executor would have to sign a new listing with Sal.
deeper.stakes: Agents who keep marketing after agency ended may have no right to a fee and no authority to act. Revocation or renunciation can also bring damages.
deeper.exam: Sort them: performance, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation, renunciation are acts of the parties. Death, incapacity, bankruptcy, destruction or condemnation, loss of license are operation of law.

blocks.html: A principal can always revoke the agent's authority, but may still owe the broker damages or expenses for breaking an exclusive agreement. An agency coupled with an interest (the agent has its own stake in the property, such as a lender-broker who financed it) cannot be revoked by the principal and does not end at the principal's death.
blocks.casual: A principal can always revoke the agent's authority, but may still owe the broker damages or expenses for breaking an exclusive agreement. An agency coupled with an interest is different: if the agent has its own stake in the property, like a lender-broker who financed it, the principal can't revoke it, and it doesn't end when the principal dies.

deeper.plain: You can fire your agent anytime, but it may cost you. If the agent has its own stake, you can't.
deeper.picture: You can cancel a gym membership but owe the fee. You can't kick out a co-owner of your car.
deeper.street: A Staten Island seller fires Ray three weeks into a six-month exclusive to list with a friend. Ray's firm sends a bill for marketing costs and damages under the agreement.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who revoke casually can end up paying two brokers. Agents with an interest keep their authority even through the owner's death.
deeper.exam: Revocation is always possible but may cost damages. Agency coupled with an interest is irrevocable and survives the principal's death.

blocks.title: Death of the salesperson
blocks.html: The listing is with the broker. If the salesperson dies or leaves the firm, the listing continues. If the broker (a sole proprietor) dies, the agency ends.
blocks.casual: Remember, the listing is with the broker. If the salesperson dies or leaves the firm, the listing keeps going. If the broker (a sole proprietor) dies, the agency ends.

deeper.plain: Lose the salesperson, keep the listing. Lose the broker, lose the listing.
deeper.picture: If a store clerk quits, the store stays open. If the store owner dies and it's a one-person business, it closes.
deeper.street: Jordan leaves Hudson & Hart in June. Diane reassigns the Okafors' listing to Marcus that afternoon. The Okafors' agreement is untouched.
deeper.stakes: A salesperson who thinks the listing follows them may try to take it and face a lawsuit. A seller whose sole proprietor broker dies needs a new listing.
deeper.exam: Trap: 'the listing ends when the salesperson dies.' False. Only the broker's death (as sole proprietor) ends it.

blocks.q: Which of these does NOT terminate a listing agreement?
c: The seller's death
The house burning down
The listing salesperson moving to another firm
Expiration of the listing period
blocks.x: The listing belongs to the broker, so a salesperson leaving does not end it. Death, destruction, and expiration all do.

blocks.title: Who pays when the owner finds the buyer
blocks.html: Exclusive RIGHT to sell: the RIGHT is the broker's, so the broker always gets paid. Exclusive agency: the owner kept the right to sell alone.
blocks.casual: Here's the trick: Exclusive RIGHT to sell means the RIGHT belongs to the broker, so the broker always gets paid. Exclusive agency means the owner kept the right to sell on their own.

deeper.plain: Whoever holds the 'right to sell' gets paid when the house sells.
deeper.picture: Think of a ticket: whoever's holding it gets in. Under exclusive right to sell, the broker is holding it.
deeper.street: Rosa's neighbor buys directly. Rosa asks Jordan which form she signed. It says 'Exclusive Right to Sell.' Jordan's firm gets paid.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who mix these up end up surprised at closing, and surprised sellers file complaints.
deeper.exam: Use the word RIGHT as your cue every time an owner finds the buyer.

story.title: The Downstairs Neighbor
story.setting: Rosa's parlor floor, Park Slope, Saturday morning

beats.text: Rosa: Before I sign, my downstairs neighbor might buy. Do I still owe you?
Depends which agreement. Exclusive right to sell, yes. Exclusive agency, no, if you find him yourself.
Rosa: Then why would anyone sign exclusive right to sell?
Because brokers spend more on marketing when we know we won't be cut out. And it's the norm here, which is why New York makes you initial this explanation.
Rosa: Okay, new idea. I want $1.75M in my pocket. Anything over, keep it.
That's a net listing. Illegal in New York. Our fee has to be a stated amount or percentage you agree to.
Rosa signs exclusive agency, 5%, expiring in 6 months. Then her phone rings.
Rosa: My cousin wants to tour this afternoon with his own agent. Can they just come by?
Sure. His agent will need a written buyer agreement with him before the tour. That's the NAR settlement rule since August 2024.

check.q: What must the cousin's agent have before the tour?
c: A pre-approval letter
A written buyer agreement with the cousin
Rosa's written permission
A signed contract of sale
check.x: Under the 2024 NAR settlement, MLS participants need a written agreement with a buyer before touring a home.

beats.text: Three weeks later, Rosa calls, shaken. A pipe burst and the parlor floor is gutted.
Rosa: Does our listing even exist anymore?
If the property is destroyed, the agency ends by operation of law. If it's damaged and repairable, we talk and probably pause.
And if I quit tomorrow, the listing stays with Hudson & Hart. It was never mine. It's the broker's.
Right. Read the top of the agreement before you read anything else. It tells you who gets paid.

board.prompt: Make a grid: rows are the three listing types, columns are who found the buyer. Fill in who gets paid in each cell.

facts.text: A listing agreement is the owner's employment contract with a broker and creates express, usually special, agency.
Exclusive right to sell: the listing broker is paid whoever sells during the term, even the owner.
Exclusive agency: no commission if the owner sells alone, but the listing broker is paid if any broker sells.
Open listing: several brokers may list, and only the procuring cause is paid.
19 NYCRR 175.24: every exclusive listing of NY residential property must include an explanation of exclusive right to sell vs exclusive agency, signed or initialed by the owner.
If the listing broker is in an MLS, the owner must be offered the choice of having offers submitted through the listing broker or directly by the selling broker.
Every exclusive listing should have a definite expiration date; automatic renewals invite DOS complaints.
Net listings are prohibited in NY no matter who proposes them.
Exclusive right to rent pays the broker if the unit rents during the term, whoever finds the tenant; in NYC under the FARE Act the landlord pays that broker.
An exclusive right to represent is exclusive buyer agency; under a non-exclusive buyer agreement the procuring broker is usually paid.
Since August 17, 2024, an MLS participant working with a buyer needs a written buyer agreement before touring a home, in person or virtually.
Buyer agreements state compensation in a specific, objective amount the broker cannot exceed; buyer-broker compensation offers are not published on the MLS; fees stay negotiable.
RPL 442-h: brokers adopt written standardized procedures for prospective buyers, file them with DOS, and apply them to everyone equally.
A buyer agreement should state the term, area, fee, who pays, and what happens if the buyer buys alone; the buyer can negotiate fee, term and exclusivity.
Commission = sale price x rate; a seller's net divided by (1 - rate) gives the sale price.
Commission splits flow from the total to the cooperating firm, then from the listing firm to its salesperson by their split percentage.
Broker-salesperson splits are private and set by their contract; the client never pays the salesperson directly, and co-op fees are set between firms, not by any board or MLS.

Agency ends by acts of the parties (performance, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation, renunciation) or by operation of law (death, incapacity, bankruptcy, destruction of the property, loss of license).
A principal can always revoke an agency but may owe the broker damages for breaking an exclusive.
An agency coupled with an interest cannot be revoked by the principal and survives the principal's death.
The listing is with the broker: a salesperson's death or departure does not end it, but a sole-proprietor broker's death does.

lessons.title: The RPL 443 Disclosure Form
lessons.tagline: One form, four moments, three years in the file. Money talk means paper walk.
objectives: State which transactions RPL 443 covers and which it does not
Give the disclosure at the right moment for each role
Handle a consumer who refuses to sign
Explain the 2011 changes and whether an agent can change roles

blocks.title: Sunday, 2:15 pm, Jackson Heights
blocks.html: Marcus hosts an open house for a two-bedroom co-op on 35th Avenue listed at $625,000. A visitor loves the kitchen, then asks: "I'm pre-approved to $650K. Would they take $610? What are the maintenance charges?" Marcus starts negotiating. Fifteen minutes later she has shared her budget, timeline, and bottom line. He has handed her a flyer. What did he owe her the moment she said "$650K"?
blocks.casual: Sunday, 2:15. Marcus is hosting an open house for a two-bedroom co-op on 35th Avenue in Jackson Heights, listed at $625,000. A visitor loves the kitchen and asks, 'I'm pre-approved to $650K. Would they take $610? What are the maintenance charges?' Marcus starts negotiating. Fifteen minutes later she's told him her budget, her timeline, and her bottom line. He's handed her a flyer. So what did he owe her the second she said '$650K'?

deeper.plain: The moment a visitor starts talking money, she needs to know who you work for.
deeper.picture: It's like a stranger at a party who turns out to be the other side's lawyer. You'd want to know before you told him your strategy.
deeper.street: The visitor later learns Marcus represents the seller and that her $650K approval reached the seller that night. The seller counters at $645,000. She files a DOS complaint saying nobody told her.
deeper.stakes: Skipping the form doesn't change who Marcus represents, but it costs the buyer her leverage and exposes Marcus to discipline.
deeper.exam: Answer: the agency disclosure form (and the fair housing form) at first substantive contact, which began when she mentioned her budget.

blocks.html: RPL 443 requires the agency disclosure form in transactions involving residential real property: 1 to 4 family dwellings, condominiums, and co-ops, for sales and for rentals. There are two versions: one for buyers and sellers, one for landlords and tenants. Vacant land and commercial property are not covered.
blocks.casual: RPL 443 requires the agency disclosure form in deals involving residential real property: 1 to 4 family homes, condos, and co-ops, for both sales and rentals. There are two versions: one for buyers and sellers, one for landlords and tenants. Vacant land and commercial property aren't covered.

deeper.plain: If someone's buying, selling, or renting a home, they get this form. Land and commercial don't.
deeper.picture: It's like a nutrition label: required on packaged food, not on raw lumber.
deeper.street: Sal handles a rental for a Sunnyside two-family (landlord and tenant form required) and a sale of a vacant lot in Staten Island (no agency form required, but the fair housing form still applies).
deeper.stakes: Forgetting the form on a co-op or rental is a common DOS violation. Agents wrongly think it's only for house sales.
deeper.exam: Covered: 1 to 4 family, condos, co-ops, sales and rentals. Not covered: commercial, vacant land, 5+ unit buildings sold as a whole.

blocks.html: The form is headed "THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT." It creates no agency and obligates no one to pay. It explains the roles (seller's agent, buyer's agent, broker's agent, dual agent, dual agent with designated sales agents), lists the fiduciary duties, and records which role this licensee is playing.
blocks.casual: The top of the form says it in capital letters: 'THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT.' It doesn't create agency and doesn't obligate anyone to pay. It explains the roles (seller's agent, buyer's agent, broker's agent, dual agent, dual agent with designated sales agents), lists the fiduciary duties, and records which role this licensee is playing.

deeper.plain: The form tells you who's who. It doesn't sign you up for anything.
deeper.picture: It's a name tag with a job description, not an employment contract.
deeper.street: A cautious buyer in Ditmas Park refuses to sign, worried she'll owe Kim money. Kim points to the heading: 'This is not a contract. It just shows you got the information.'
deeper.stakes: Agents who treat the form as a buyer agreement end up with no real agreement and no enforceable fee.
deeper.exam: Trap: 'signing the disclosure form creates agency' or 'obligates the buyer to pay.' Both false.

blocks.title: Two forms, same moment
blocks.html: At first substantive contact you also give the NYS Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (19 NYCRR 175.28). That one covers all property types, including commercial and vacant land. Agency disclosure covers only residential 1 to 4 family, condos, and co-ops.
blocks.casual: At first substantive contact you also hand over the NYS Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (19 NYCRR 175.28). That one covers all property types, including commercial and vacant land. Agency disclosure covers only residential 1 to 4 family, condos, and co-ops.

deeper.plain: Two forms at the same moment, but the fair housing one applies to everything.
deeper.picture: Like showing both your ID and your boarding pass. The ID is needed for every flight, the pass only for this one.
deeper.street: Ray meets a buyer for a Bushwick warehouse. No agency form needed for commercial, but Ray hands over the fair housing form at first substantive contact.
deeper.stakes: Missing the fair housing form is its own violation, even on commercial deals where agents assume no forms apply.
deeper.exam: Scope question: fair housing form covers all property types; agency form only residential 1 to 4 family, condos, co-ops.

blocks.caption: Walk a deal from first call to closing. The agency disclosure markers sit at the listing appointment and at first substantive contact with the other side.

head: Who gives it
To whom
When
rows: Before entering the buyer or tenant agency agreement

deeper.plain: Your own client gets the form before signing up. The other side gets it at first real conversation.
deeper.picture: Like a waiter introducing himself before taking your order, and to the kitchen manager before starting his shift.
deeper.street: Priya signs up a buyer for a Ridgewood search: form before the buyer agreement. When she calls the listing agent to discuss a condo, she sends the listing agent her disclosure for the sellers at that first substantive contact.
deeper.stakes: Giving the form after the listing is signed, or after the buyer has shared their budget, defeats its purpose and is a violation.
deeper.exam: Key words: 'before entering' for your own client, 'first substantive contact' for the other party.

blocks.html: First substantive contact is the first time the conversation goes beyond small talk and property facts into the consumer's needs, motivation, or finances. "Where's the subway?" is not it. "We're approved to $650K, would they take $610?" is.
blocks.casual: First substantive contact is the first time the conversation moves past small talk and property facts into the consumer's needs, motivation, or finances. 'Where's the subway?' isn't it. 'We're approved to $650K, would they take $610?' definitely is.

deeper.plain: When the talk turns to their money or reasons, the clock has started.
deeper.picture: Small talk is the weather. Substantive contact is when they open their wallet and show you what's inside.
deeper.street: At a Bay Ridge open house a visitor asks about the boiler age (property fact, not yet). Then she says, 'We need three bedrooms by September and can't go over $900K.' That's the moment Diane hands over both forms.
deeper.stakes: Wait too long and the consumer has already revealed what the form was meant to protect.
deeper.exam: Cue words: budget, pre-approval, timeline, motivation, needs. Questions about the property's features are not yet substantive.

blocks.q: In the scenario, when did Marcus owe the visitor the agency disclosure form?
c: When she walked in the door
When she mentioned her pre-approval and asked about $610
Only if she made a written offer
At contract signing
blocks.x: Talk of her finances and price was first substantive contact. Walking into an open house alone does not trigger the form; waiting for an offer is too late.

blocks.title: One deal, every disclosure moment
blocks.html:
1. Monday: Jordan meets the Okafors to list. Agency disclosure (and fair housing form) given and signed before the listing agreement.
2. Sunday: a visitor at the open house says she must move by June and is approved to $1.6M. First substantive contact: both forms now, Jordan checks "seller's agent."
3. Tuesday: a buyer's agent from another firm calls to discuss price. Jordan sends the disclosure to that buyer's agent at first substantive contact; the buyer's agent sends hers to Jordan for the sellers.
4. Later: Leo, a firm buyer client, wants the house. New dual agency disclosure and consent from both sides.
Every acknowledgment or declaration goes in the file for 3 years.
blocks.casual:
1. Monday: Jordan meets the Okafors to list. Agency disclosure (and the fair housing form) gets given and signed before the listing agreement.
2. Sunday: a visitor at the open house says she has to move by June and is approved to $1.6M. First substantive contact: both forms now, and Jordan checks 'seller's agent.'
3. Tuesday: a buyer's agent from another firm calls to talk price. Jordan sends the disclosure to that buyer's agent at first substantive contact, and the buyer's agent sends hers to Jordan for the sellers.
4. Later: Leo, a firm buyer client, wants the house. New dual agency disclosure and consent from both sides.
Every acknowledgment or declaration goes in the file for 3 years.

deeper.plain: One sale can trigger the form four separate times, for four different people.
deeper.picture: Like showing your badge at every door in a secure building, not just the front entrance.
deeper.street: Diane audits Jordan's Okafor file: four signed forms, dated Monday, Sunday, Tuesday, and the day Leo consented. Each one matches a moment when a new party started talking money.
deeper.stakes: DOS audits files. A missing form at any one of these moments is a violation, even if all the others are perfect.
deeper.exam: Expect a timeline question asking when a form is due. Map each new party and each role change to a new disclosure.

blocks.title: The 60-second explanation

items.title: Your role
items.html: "I represent the seller." (Or the buyer, or both with consent.) Point to the box you are checking.

items.title: What that means for them
items.html: "I'll be honest with you and tell you known material defects, but I can't advise you on price, and what you tell me goes to my client."

items.title: Their options
items.html: "You can hire your own buyer's agent." Explain dual agency and advance consent if your firm might represent both.

items.title: Sign or declare
items.html: Ask for the signed acknowledgment. Give them a copy. Keep yours 3 years.

blocks.casual:
Your role. 'I represent the seller.' (Or the buyer, or both with consent.) Point to the box you're checking.
What that means for them. 'I'll be honest with you and tell you about known material defects, but I can't advise you on price, and what you tell me goes to my client.'
Their options. 'You can hire your own buyer's agent.' Explain dual agency and advance consent if your firm might represent both.
Sign or declare. Ask for the signed acknowledgment. Give them a copy. Keep yours 3 years.

deeper.plain: Say who you work for, what that means, what else they can do, and get it signed.
deeper.picture: Like a flight attendant's safety talk: short, same every time, and it actually matters.
deeper.street: At a Harlem open house Tasha greets a couple: 'Hi, I represent the sellers. I'll tell you about any known issues, but anything you share about price goes to them. You're welcome to bring your own agent.' Then she hands them the form.
deeper.stakes: A rushed or skipped explanation leaves a buyer who later says, 'Nobody told me she worked for the seller.' That's a complaint you'll lose.
deeper.exam: The licensee must explain the form, not just hand it over. The consumer's signature is an acknowledgment of receipt.

blocks.html: Substantive contact does not need to be in person. A phone call where a caller explains a job relocation, an email listing a budget, or a text asking "would they take 50 under?" all count. Send the form electronically right away and get the acknowledgment back the same way. Many firms attach the agency and fair housing forms to their first reply to every inquiry, so there is never a gap.
blocks.casual: Substantive contact doesn't have to happen in person. A phone call where someone explains a job relocation, an email with a budget, a text asking 'would they take 50 under?' all count. Send the form electronically right away and get the acknowledgment back the same way. Plenty of firms attach the agency and fair housing forms to their first reply to every inquiry, so there's never a gap.

deeper.plain: If they talk money by text or email, the form goes out by text or email.
deeper.picture: Like an automatic reply that includes the store's return policy before you even ask.
deeper.street: A buyer emails Kim at 11 p.m.: 'Relocating from Chicago, budget $800K, need to close by August.' Kim's reply the next morning attaches both forms and an e-signature link before she answers a single question.
deeper.stakes: Agents who wait for an in-person meeting have often already received the information the form was meant to protect.
deeper.exam: Phone, email, and text conversations can be first substantive contact. The form can be delivered and acknowledged electronically.

blocks.title: Say it before they share it
blocks.html: The point of the form is to warn the consumer before they reveal something that could hurt them. If you represent the seller, say so in your first sentence, before the buyer volunteers a budget.
blocks.casual: The whole point of the form is to warn the consumer before they spill something that could hurt them. If you represent the seller, say it in your first sentence, before the buyer volunteers a budget.

deeper.plain: Lead with who you work for, so people can choose what to tell you.
deeper.picture: Like a reporter saying 'this is on the record' before you start talking.
deeper.street: At a Long Island City condo showing, Leo opens with 'I'm the sellers' agent' before the buyer says a word. The buyer smiles and says, 'Then I'll keep my number to myself.' Exactly right.
deeper.stakes: An agent who lets a buyer share first, then discloses, has technically received information that must go to the seller. The buyer feels tricked.
deeper.exam: Timing beats paperwork. The disclosure's purpose is to inform before confidential information is shared.

blocks.html: The consumer signs an acknowledgment that they received the form, not an agreement to anything. The licensee checks their role and signs. If the consumer gave advance consent to dual agency or to designated agents, it is marked here. The licensee gives the consumer a copy and keeps one for at least 3 years.
blocks.casual: The consumer signs an acknowledgment that they got the form, not an agreement to anything. The licensee checks their role and signs. If the consumer gave advance consent to dual agency or to designated agents, that gets marked here. The licensee gives the consumer a copy and keeps one for at least 3 years.

deeper.plain: They sign to say 'I got it.' You sign to say 'this is my role.' Both keep copies.
deeper.picture: It's a delivery receipt, not a purchase order.
deeper.street: Jordan's seller clients check the advance consent box when they list. Jordan saves the signed page to the firm's system, where it will sit for at least 3 years.
deeper.stakes: No signed acknowledgment and no declaration in the file means no proof you complied. DOS assumes you didn't.
deeper.exam: Retention: at least 3 years. Signature: acknowledgment of receipt, not consent to agency (except where advance consent boxes are checked).

blocks.html: If they refuse to sign: keep going. The licensee completes a declaration of refusal, a written statement under oath or affirmation of the facts of the refusal, and keeps it at least 3 years.
blocks.casual: If they won't sign: keep going. The licensee fills out a declaration of refusal, a written statement under oath or affirmation of the facts of the refusal, and keeps it at least 3 years.

deeper.plain: A refusal doesn't stop you. You just document it under oath.
deeper.picture: Like a process server writing down 'served, refused to take the papers.'
deeper.street: A Bensonhurst buyer won't sign anything 'without my lawyer.' Ray gives her the form anyway, then completes the declaration of refusal noting the date, time, and her words, and files it.
deeper.stakes: Without the declaration, a refusal looks exactly like a form you never gave. That's a violation on paper.
deeper.exam: Declaration of refusal: written, under oath or affirmation, kept 3 years.

blocks.title: Refusal is not fatal
blocks.html: "The buyer refused to sign, so the agent must stop working with her." False. And "refusal waives the requirement" is also false. The agent still had to present it, and documents the refusal under oath.
blocks.casual: Two false statements to watch for: 'The buyer refused to sign, so the agent has to stop working with her.' Nope. 'Refusing waives the requirement.' Also nope. The agent still had to present it, and documents the refusal under oath.

deeper.plain: Refusal neither ends the relationship nor excuses the form.
deeper.picture: If a patient won't sign the privacy notice, the doctor still treats them and notes the refusal.
deeper.street: A Flushing seller refuses to sign the disclosure. Priya keeps the listing, completes the declaration, and moves forward with marketing.
deeper.stakes: Agents who stop working lose business for no reason. Agents who skip documentation are exposed to discipline.
deeper.exam: Both extremes are traps. The right answer is: present the form, and if refused, complete a declaration of refusal.

blocks.q: A tenant refuses to sign the landlord-tenant disclosure acknowledgment. The landlord's agent should:
c: Stop showing the apartment to the tenant
Ask the landlord to sign for the tenant
Execute a sworn declaration of the refusal and keep it 3 years
Mail the form to DOS
blocks.x: RPL 443 requires a written declaration of the facts of the refusal under oath or affirmation, kept at least 3 years. The deal continues.

blocks.text: The form before and after January 1, 2011

left.title: Before 2011
items: Covered 1 to 4 family homes
Condos and co-ops were exempt from the definition
No advance consent to dual agency on the form

right.title: Since January 1, 2011
items: Condos and co-ops covered
Separate landlord and tenant form for rentals
Advance consent to dual agency and to designated sales agents
Written form required in every residential deal

deeper.plain: Since 2011 the form covers condos, co-ops, and rentals, and lets people consent to dual agency in advance.
deeper.picture: Like a phone software update that suddenly covers apps it used to ignore.
deeper.street: In 2009, a buyer touring Upper West Side co-ops might never see a form. Today Tasha hands one over at the first co-op showing where the buyer talks budget.
deeper.stakes: Following outdated rules from an old textbook could mean skipping the form on a co-op sale, which is a violation today.
deeper.exam: Know the changes on January 1, 2011: condos and co-ops covered, a separate landlord and tenant form, advance consent options.

blocks.html: Why did the law change? Before 2011, a buyer touring Manhattan co-ops, the bulk of the city's sales, might never see a disclosure form, because co-ops and condos fell outside the definition. The 2011 amendments closed that gap, extended written disclosure to residential rentals, and let consumers give advance consent to dual agency so firms would not need a fresh form before every in-house showing. Older textbooks and some exam items may still describe the pre-2011 rules, so know both.
blocks.casual: Why'd the law change? Before 2011, a buyer touring Manhattan co-ops, which are most of the city's sales, might never see a disclosure form, because co-ops and condos fell outside the definition. The 2011 amendments closed that gap, extended written disclosure to residential rentals, and let consumers give advance consent to dual agency so firms wouldn't need a fresh form before every in-house showing. Older textbooks and some exam questions may still describe the pre-2011 rules, so know both.

deeper.plain: The old law skipped most NYC apartments. The 2011 fix covered them.
deeper.picture: Like a seatbelt law that originally exempted taxis, the vehicles most people actually ride in.
deeper.street: An Upper East Side co-op buyer in 2008 thought the friendly listing agent was helping her. In 2012 her daughter got a form at the first showing that said exactly whom that agent represented.
deeper.stakes: An agent relying on pre-2011 rules would skip forms on co-ops, condos, and rentals, which is now most of the city's work.
deeper.exam: If an answer says condos and co-ops are exempt from agency disclosure, it's describing the old law. Current law covers them.

blocks.html: Yes, with care and new paperwork. A buyer who was your customer at an open house can become your client for other properties under a buyer agreement. But in the same transaction, a seller's agent cannot simply switch to the buyer's side: the firm would become a dual agent, which needs written informed consent from both. Any time your role changes, give a new disclosure, explain the change, and get it acknowledged. Never switch roles quietly.
blocks.casual: Yes, you can switch roles, but carefully and with new paperwork. A buyer who was your customer at an open house can become your client for other properties under a buyer agreement. But in the same deal, a seller's agent can't just hop to the buyer's side: the firm would become a dual agent, which needs written informed consent from both. Any time your role changes, give a new disclosure, explain the change, and get it acknowledged. Never switch roles quietly.

deeper.plain: New role, new form. Same deal, both sides have to consent.
deeper.picture: Like a referee who wants to coach one of the teams. Fine for next season, not mid-game without everyone's agreement.
deeper.street: A buyer meets Sal at his Astoria listing, doesn't buy it, and asks Sal to help her find something else. Sal signs a buyer agreement for other properties and gives a new disclosure checking 'buyer's agent.'
deeper.stakes: Quiet role changes are how undisclosed dual agency happens. Each switch needs a paper trail.
deeper.exam: Role change requires a new disclosure. Switching sides in the same transaction requires dual agency consent from both.

blocks.q: Which transaction does NOT require the RPL 443 agency disclosure form?
c: Rental of a Bronx two-family unit
Sale of an Upper West Side co-op
Sale of a vacant lot in Staten Island
Sale of a Flushing condo
blocks.x: RPL 443 covers residential 1 to 4 family, condos, and co-ops, for sales and rentals. Vacant land is excluded, though the anti-discrimination form still applies.

blocks.title: Money talk means paper walk
blocks.html: The moment a consumer talks budget, motivation, or needs: stop, hand over both forms, sign or declare, keep 3 years.
blocks.casual: Remember it like this: money talk means paper walk. The second a consumer talks budget, motivation, or needs: stop, hand over both forms, sign or declare, keep 3 years.

deeper.plain: When the talk turns to money, the forms come out.
deeper.picture: Like a bell that rings in your head the instant someone says 'pre-approved.'
deeper.street: At a Bed-Stuy showing a buyer starts, 'Okay, so our budget is...' and Jordan gently holds up a hand: 'Before you go on, let me give you two forms.'
deeper.stakes: That habit protects both the consumer and your license. Agents who build it rarely see a disclosure complaint.
deeper.exam: Four steps in order: stop, both forms, signature or declaration, 3-year retention.

story.title: The Flyer Is Not a Form
story.setting: Jackson Heights, Monday after the open house

beats.text: Diane is reading Marcus's open house sign-in sheet. Her eyebrows climb.
She told you her pre-approval amount. Where's her disclosure?
I gave her a flyer.
A flyer is not a form. First substantive contact was the second she said $650K.
I did a co-op open house last week. Does 443 even cover co-ops?
Since 2011, yes. Condos and co-ops, plus rentals on the landlord and tenant version.
My visitor wouldn't sign anything. I panicked and left the form on the counter.
Next time, you fill out a declaration of the facts of her refusal, under oath, and keep it three years. Then you keep talking.

check.q: What should Jordan have done when the visitor refused to sign?
c: Ended the conversation
Completed a sworn declaration of the refusal and kept it 3 years
Signed the form for her
Asked the seller what to do
check.x: RPL 443 requires a written declaration under oath or affirmation of the refusal, kept at least 3 years. The conversation may continue.

beats.text: Anyway, she wants me to represent her now. On this same co-op.
Then we're dual agents on it, and that needs written consent from the seller and from her. Or she gets her own agent. You don't just switch teams at halftime.
beats.tag: Changing roles needs new disclosure and consent

beats.text: And the fair housing form goes out at the same moment, right?
Same moment, every property type. Agency disclosure is residential only. Both are kept three years.
beats.tag: Two forms at first substantive contact

beats.text: Fine. I'll print a stack.
Print two stacks. Money talk means paper walk.

board.prompt: Draw a timeline from listing appointment to closing. Mark every point where an agency disclosure form changes hands, and who gives it to whom.

facts.text: The RPL 443 form is required for residential 1 to 4 family homes, condos and co-ops, for sales and rentals (two versions), but not for vacant land or commercial property.
The form says "THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT":  it creates no agency and obligates no one to pay.
The form explains the agency roles and fiduciary duties and records which role this licensee is playing.
At first substantive contact the licensee also gives the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (175.28), which covers every property type.
A listing agent gives the form to the seller before the listing agreement; a buyer's agent gives it to the buyer before the buyer agency agreement.
Each agent gives the form to the other side (or its agent) at first substantive contact.
First substantive contact is when talk moves past small talk and property facts into the consumer's needs, motivation or finances.
Substantive contact can be by phone, email or text; disclose your role and send the form before the consumer shares more.
Explain the form in seconds: whom you represent, what that means for them, their options (such as their own agent), then ask for the acknowledgment.
The consumer signs only an acknowledgment of receipt; the licensee checks its role, and any advance consent to dual or designated agency is marked there.
The licensee gives the consumer a copy and keeps the acknowledgment for at least 3 years.
If the consumer refuses to sign, the licensee keeps working and completes a sworn declaration of refusal, kept 3 years; refusal neither stops the deal nor waives the form.
Since January 1, 2011 the form covers condos and co-ops, has a landlord-tenant version, and allows advance consent to dual and designated agency.
A seller's agent cannot switch to the buyer's side in the same deal without becoming a dual agent, which needs both parties' written consent and a new disclosure.
A buyer customer can become a client for other properties under a buyer agreement; any role change needs a new, acknowledged disclosure.

lessons.title: Independent Contractor or Employee?
lessons.tagline: Your broker must supervise you but may not boss you. That line decides who pays your taxes.
objectives: State the conditions of NY's 1986 independent contractor law and IRC Section 3508
Tell supervision (required) from direction and control (fatal)
List the consequences to broker and salesperson when status fails
Apply Reg 175.21 (supervision) and Reg 175.23 (records)

blocks.title: First day, Williamsburg
blocks.html: A newly licensed salesperson signs onboarding papers at a Williamsburg firm. The big one says Independent Contractor Agreement: commission only, no taxes withheld, set your own hours. Then the office manager adds: "Desk hours are 9 to 5, Monday to Friday, mandatory. Miss one and we dock your split." Can both of those be true?
blocks.casual: Day one at a Williamsburg firm. A newly licensed salesperson is signing onboarding papers, and the big one says Independent Contractor Agreement: commission only, no taxes withheld, set your own hours. Then the office manager adds, 'Desk hours are 9 to 5, Monday to Friday, mandatory. Miss one and we dock your split.' Can both of those actually be true?

deeper.plain: The paper says contractor, but the rules sound like a job. The law looks at the rules.
deeper.picture: Calling a cat a dog on its adoption papers doesn't make it bark.
deeper.street: Leo signs at the Williamsburg firm, then gets docked $500 off a split for missing a Tuesday desk shift. Six months later he leaves and files for unemployment. The state asks how the office really ran.
deeper.stakes: If the state decides Leo was an employee, the broker owes back unemployment premiums, workers' comp, and withholding for every salesperson treated the same way.
deeper.exam: When a stem mixes a contractor agreement with mandatory hours or time-based penalties, the answer is that the relationship looks like employment.

blocks.text: Two ways to work for a broker

left.title: Independent contractor
items: Paid by results (commission), not hours
No tax withholding; files Schedule C and pays self-employment tax
Sets own hours and methods
Pays own expenses: car, marketing, MLS dues
No unemployment insurance or workers' comp through broker

right.title: Employee
items: May be paid salary or hourly
Broker withholds income and Social Security taxes
Broker directs when, where, and how work is done
Broker usually pays business expenses
Broker pays unemployment, workers' comp, disability

deeper.plain: Contractors run their own business inside the broker's. Employees work the broker's way on the broker's dime.
deeper.picture: A contractor is a food truck parked in a lot; an employee is the cook inside the restaurant.
deeper.street: Kim, a contractor in Long Island City, pays her own $1,200 a year in MLS dues and her car costs, and deducts them on Schedule C. Her friend at a salaried NYC rental firm has taxes withheld and gets workers' comp through the company.
deeper.stakes: Each side carries different costs. A contractor who doesn't save for self-employment tax gets a painful April. A broker who misclassifies gets a painful audit.
deeper.exam: Contractor: no withholding, Schedule C, own expenses, own hours. Employee: withholding, broker pays unemployment, workers' comp, and disability.

blocks.html: Most NY salespersons are independent contractors. Some firms hire salespersons as employees, which is legal too. What is not legal is calling someone a contractor while treating them like an employee.
blocks.casual: Most NY salespersons are independent contractors. Some firms hire salespersons as employees, which is legal too. What's not legal is calling someone a contractor while treating them like an employee.

deeper.plain: Both setups are fine. Mislabeling one as the other is not.
deeper.picture: You can rent a car or own one. You can't drive someone else's car and claim it's yours.
deeper.street: One Manhattan rental firm pays new agents a salary plus a small bonus and withholds taxes: employees, done right. A Bay Ridge firm pays commission only and leaves hours alone: contractors, done right.
deeper.stakes: Misclassification can trigger back taxes, penalties, and claims from every agent in the office, not just the one who complained.
deeper.exam: Either status is legal. The violation is the mismatch between label and reality.

blocks.text: How the law decides: common law, IRS, New York

blocks.html: Courts traditionally ask about direction and control: does the hiring party control not just the result but how, when, and where the work is done? The IRS applies a similar multi-factor test. Because real estate sales was a gray area, both Washington and Albany wrote specific rules for licensees.
blocks.casual: Courts have always asked about direction and control: does the hiring party control not just the result, but how, when, and where the work gets done? The IRS uses a similar multi-factor test. Because real estate sales was a gray area, both Washington and Albany wrote specific rules for licensees.

deeper.plain: If they tell you how, when, and where to work, you're probably an employee.
deeper.picture: Hiring a plumber to fix a leak (you care about the result) versus hiring one to work your shifts your way (you're the boss).
deeper.street: A Queens broker tells agents which neighborhoods to farm, which hours to call, and what script to use. That level of control is the classic sign of employment.
deeper.stakes: Real estate firms that drift into control without noticing get caught when an agent files for benefits.
deeper.exam: Direction and control is the common law test. Real estate has its own special statutes layered on top.

blocks.title: IRC Section 3508 and NY's 1986 law
blocks.html: Federal law (IRC 3508) treats a licensed real estate agent as a non-employee for federal tax purposes if (1) substantially all pay is directly related to sales or other output, not hours, and (2) there is a written contract saying the agent will not be treated as an employee for tax purposes. In 1986 New York added matching rules to its Labor Law (unemployment insurance) and Workers' Compensation Law. NY also requires that the contract was not signed under duress. New York adds its own test for state unemployment insurance and workers' compensation (Labor Law §511(19)): the salesperson is licensed, substantially all pay comes from commissions, and the work is done under a written contract that says they are an independent contractor, was executed within the past 12 to 15 months (so brokers renew it every year), and was not signed under duress. A broker who lets the agreement lapse can owe unemployment and comp coverage for that agent.
blocks.casual: Federal law (IRC 3508) treats a licensed real estate agent as a non-employee for federal tax purposes if (1) substantially all pay is directly tied to sales or other output, not hours, and (2) there's a written contract saying the agent won't be treated as an employee for tax purposes. In 1986 New York added matching rules to its Labor Law (unemployment insurance) and Workers' Compensation Law. NY also requires that the contract wasn't signed under duress. New York stacks its own test on top for unemployment and comp (Labor Law §511(19)): licensed, paid by commission, and a written independent contractor agreement signed in the last 12 to 15 months. Translation: the broker re-signs it with every agent each year.

deeper.plain: Licensed, paid for results, and a signed contract: that's the safe harbor.
deeper.picture: Three locks on one door. Open all three and you're in contractor territory.
deeper.street: Priya's firm renews every agent's contractor agreement each January. NY's unemployment rule looks for a contract signed within the past 12 to 15 months, so an annual renewal keeps everyone covered.
deeper.stakes: A missing signature or a contract signed under pressure ('sign now or no desk') can knock out the safe harbor for that agent.
deeper.exam: IRC 3508 is the federal statutory non-employee rule. NY's 1986 law mirrors it for unemployment and workers' comp, plus the no-duress requirement. NY twist: the written agreement must have been signed within the past 12 to 15 months.

blocks.title: The three legs of the stool

items.title: Licensed
items.html: A licensed real estate salesperson or associate broker.

items.title: Paid by output
items.html: Substantially all compensation is commission tied to sales, not hours worked.

items.title: Written contract
items.html: Signed agreement, not under duress, stating the licensee is not an employee for federal and state tax purposes. Both federal and state law require it in writing.

blocks.casual:
Licensed. A licensed real estate salesperson or associate broker.
Paid by output. Substantially all pay is commission tied to sales, not hours worked.
Written contract. Signed, not under duress, saying the licensee isn't an employee for federal and state tax purposes. Both federal and state law require it in writing.

deeper.plain: Kick out any one leg and the stool falls over.
deeper.picture: A three-legged stool. It stands on any floor, but only with all three legs.
deeper.street: A Staten Island firm hires an unlicensed assistant on commission with a contractor agreement. Leg one is missing, so the safe harbor doesn't apply to her at all.
deeper.stakes: Unlicensed staff, hourly pay, or an unsigned contract each sink the classification on their own.
deeper.exam: The three legs: licensed, paid by output, written contract. An exam answer missing any of these is wrong.

blocks.html: Notice what is not on the list: the salesperson's license being held by the broker, the broker's name on all advertising, and the broker's review of contracts. Those come from license law and are required no matter how the salesperson is classified. They do not turn a contractor into an employee.
blocks.casual: Notice what's not on the list: the broker holding the salesperson's license, the broker's name on all ads, and the broker reviewing contracts. Those come from license law and apply no matter how the salesperson is classified. They don't turn a contractor into an employee.

deeper.plain: Following license law doesn't count as controlling the agent.
deeper.picture: A building inspector checking your wiring doesn't make you his employee.
