deeper.street: A new agent in Bensonhurst complains, 'Diane reviews my contracts and puts the firm name on my ads, so I'm basically an employee.' Not so. Those are legal requirements for every broker.
deeper.stakes: Brokers sometimes avoid required supervision out of fear it creates employment. That's backward and gets them in trouble with DOS.
deeper.exam: Trap: listing license-law requirements (ad name, contract review, license held at the office) as evidence of employment. They aren't.

blocks.text: What a real contractor relationship looks like

items: Commissions paid without deductions for taxes, directly related to output
No pay for hours worked; no salary, no draw tied to time
Salesperson chooses their own hours
Works from home or from the broker's office
Broker may provide desks and supplies, but the salesperson pays their own business expenses
Broker supervises but does not direct and control
Either party may end the relationship at any time
blocks.casual: Here's what a real contractor setup looks like: commissions paid with no tax deductions, tied directly to output. No pay for hours: no salary, no draw tied to time. The salesperson picks their own hours and works from home or from the broker's office. The broker can supply desks and supplies, but the salesperson pays their own business expenses. The broker supervises but doesn't direct and control. And either side can end it any time.

deeper.plain: You get paid when deals close, you set your schedule, and you can walk away any time.
deeper.picture: Like a freelance photographer renting studio space: the studio gives you a room, you run your own shoots.
deeper.street: Sal works mostly from his Forest Hills apartment, drops into the office twice a week, pays for his own Instagram ads, and gets a check only after closings. That's a textbook contractor.
deeper.stakes: Each item on this list is something an auditor checks. One hourly draw or one mandatory schedule can tip the result.
deeper.exam: Look for these features in a correct answer. 'Paid an hourly draw' or 'required to attend daily' point to employment.

blocks.q: Which arrangement is INCONSISTENT with independent contractor status?
c: Broker provides a desk and printer
Commission split paid with no tax withholding
Mandatory desk hours 9 to 5, five days a week, with penalties
Written contract stating the salesperson is not an employee for tax purposes
blocks.x: Required fixed hours with penalties is direction and control, the mark of employment. Office space, commission pay, and the written clause are normal contractor features.

blocks.title: The Williamsburg contract, examined
blocks.html:
1. Licensed? Yes. 2. Paid by output? Yes, commission only. 3. Written contract? Yes, with the tax clause, and signed voluntarily.
4. But "mandatory desk hours, docked splits for absences" is direction and control and pay penalties tied to time.
If those rules are enforced, an auditor can treat every salesperson in the office as an employee. If the firm reframes them as optional floor time sign-ups for lead access, the arrangement survives.
Offered is fine. Required is employment.
blocks.casual:
1. Licensed? Yes. 2. Paid by output? Yes, commission only. 3. Written contract? Yes, with the tax clause, signed voluntarily.
4. But 'mandatory desk hours, docked splits for absences' is direction and control, plus pay penalties tied to time.
If those rules get enforced, an auditor can treat every salesperson in the office as an employee. If the firm turns them into optional floor time sign-ups for lead access, the arrangement holds up.
Offered is fine. Required is employment.

deeper.plain: Three legs passed, but the hour rules break the deal. Make them optional and it's fixed.
deeper.picture: A gym that offers free classes versus a gym that fines you for skipping them.
deeper.street: The Williamsburg firm rewrites its policy: agents who sign up for floor shifts get walk-in leads; nobody is required or penalized. Leo picks two shifts a week because he wants the leads.
deeper.stakes: One sentence in an office policy can decide whether a firm owes years of back premiums for its whole roster.
deeper.exam: The cue word is 'mandatory.' Optional benefits are fine; required time with pay penalties signals employment.

blocks.html: A signed contract does not save a relationship that, in fact, looks like employment. If the broker sets mandatory hours, pays by the hour, assigns territories, or docks pay for absences, regulators can treat the salespersons as employees whatever the paper says.
blocks.casual: A signed contract won't save a relationship that actually looks like employment. If the broker sets mandatory hours, pays by the hour, assigns territories, or docks pay for absences, regulators can treat the salespersons as employees no matter what the paper says.

deeper.plain: What you do matters more than what you signed.
deeper.picture: Calling a lunch a 'business meeting' on the receipt doesn't make it one if you spent the hour talking football.
deeper.street: A Flatbush firm's contracts are perfect, but managers assign each agent a zip code and require 40 cold calls a day. When an agent files for unemployment, the state looks past the contract to those daily rules.
deeper.stakes: Brokers relying only on paperwork get the worst surprise: the contract they trusted doesn't protect them.
deeper.exam: Substance over form. Assigned territories, hourly pay, mandatory hours, or time-based penalties defeat the contract.

head: If status fails, the broker owes
The salesperson loses
rows: State unemployment insurance premiums and federal unemployment tax
The ability to file Schedule C and deduct business expenses
Workers' compensation and disability insurance coverage
Control of their own schedule and methods
Federal and state income tax withholding, Social Security and Medicare
All pay becomes subject to withholding

deeper.plain: If the contractor label fails, the broker picks up a stack of bills and the agent loses the freedoms and deductions.
deeper.picture: Like a roommate who suddenly gets classified as a tenant: now there's a lease, deposits, and rules for both of you.
deeper.street: An auditor reclassifies 20 agents at a Queens firm. The broker owes back unemployment premiums, workers' comp coverage, and withholding. The agents lose their Schedule C deductions for car and marketing costs.
deeper.stakes: For a mid-size office, back premiums and penalties can run into six figures, enough to close a firm.
deeper.exam: Broker owes: unemployment insurance, workers' comp, disability, withholding. Salesperson loses: Schedule C deductions and control of schedule.

blocks.html: Why it matters in practice: unemployment insurance audits often start when one departing salesperson files for benefits. The state then looks at the whole office. Brokers protect themselves with a signed agreement for every licensee, policies that offer rather than require, commission records that show pay tied to closings, and no hourly or salaried arrangements for licensees treated as contractors.
blocks.casual: Why it matters in real life: unemployment insurance audits often start when one departing salesperson files for benefits. Then the state looks at the whole office. Brokers protect themselves with a signed agreement for every licensee, policies that offer rather than require, commission records showing pay tied to closings, and no hourly or salaried arrangements for licensees treated as contractors.

deeper.plain: One unhappy ex-agent can trigger a review of everyone.
deeper.picture: Like one complaint to the health department bringing an inspector who checks the whole kitchen.
deeper.street: Tasha leaves a Harlem firm on bad terms and files for unemployment. The Labor Department requests contracts and pay records for all 15 agents. The firm's clean files end it in a week.
deeper.stakes: Missing agreements or a single hourly arrangement can turn one claim into an office-wide finding.
deeper.exam: Protective practices: signed agreements for everyone, optional policies, commission-only records, no hourly pay.

blocks.html: Here is the tension. NY requires brokers to supervise. 19 NYCRR 175.21 calls for supervision that is regular, frequent, and consistent personal guidance, instruction, oversight, and superintendence of the salesperson's real estate work. The broker is responsible for the salesperson's conduct.
blocks.casual: Here's the tension. NY requires brokers to supervise. Under 19 NYCRR 175.21, supervision means regular, frequent, and consistent personal guidance, instruction, oversight, and superintendence of the salesperson's real estate work. And the broker is responsible for the salesperson's conduct.

deeper.plain: The broker must watch over your work without bossing how you do it.
deeper.picture: Like a driving instructor in the passenger seat: there to catch mistakes, not to steer for you.
deeper.street: Diane meets weekly with each agent to review open deals, checks every contract and escrow deposit, and runs monthly fair housing refreshers. She never tells Jordan which hours to work.
deeper.stakes: Too little supervision brings DOS discipline. Too much control risks employment status. Brokers have to hit the middle.
deeper.exam: Supervision is required by 175.21: regular, frequent, consistent. It does not by itself create employment.

left.title: Supervision (required)
items: Training on fair housing and disclosure
Reviewing contracts, ads, and escrow handling
Office policies on legal compliance
Optional floor time sign-ups

right.title: Direction and control (risky)
items: Mandatory schedules and quotas
Hourly pay or salary
Telling the salesperson which leads to call and when
Penalties for missing office hours

deeper.plain: Train, review, and set legal rules: yes. Set schedules, quotas, and pay by the hour: no.
deeper.picture: A coach can teach technique and enforce the rulebook. He doesn't decide when you eat dinner.
deeper.street: Ray's Staten Island office offers optional Saturday floor time and requires every ad to pass compliance review. That's supervision. His competitor requires 10 open houses a month or a split cut. That's control.
deeper.stakes: Brokers who blur the two face both risks: DOS complaints for poor supervision and audits for misclassification.
deeper.exam: Sort the item: compliance training, contract review, escrow oversight are supervision. Quotas, mandatory hours, hourly pay are control.

blocks.title: 19 NYCRR 175.23: records
blocks.html: Brokers must keep records of each transaction (parties, property, price, commission, and related documents) for at least 3 years, and make them available to DOS. Agency disclosures and the independent contractor agreements belong in the file too.
blocks.casual: Under 19 NYCRR 175.23, brokers have to keep records of each transaction (parties, property, price, commission, and related documents) for at least 3 years, and make them available to DOS. Agency disclosures and the independent contractor agreements belong in the file too.

deeper.plain: Keep every deal's paperwork for at least 3 years, ready for DOS.
deeper.picture: Like keeping tax receipts in a shoebox, except DOS can ask to see the shoebox.
deeper.street: DOS requests Diane's files for a 2024 Bed-Stuy sale. She pulls the contract, commission statement, agency disclosure, fair housing form, and Jordan's signed contractor agreement in ten minutes.
deeper.stakes: Missing records are their own violation, and they leave the broker unable to prove compliance on anything else.
deeper.exam: Retention under 175.23: 3 years. The number 3 shows up for disclosure forms too.

blocks.q: A brokerage is reclassified after an audit and its salespersons are treated as employees. Who bears the main financial consequences?
c: The salespersons must repay commissions
The broker owes unemployment insurance, workers' comp, disability, and withholding
The clients owe the taxes
DOS revokes every salesperson's license
blocks.x: Reclassification puts payroll obligations on the broker. Salespersons lose contractor tax treatment but do not forfeit commissions or licenses.

blocks.html: Will licensees become employees? Pressure exists: misclassification enforcement, team structures, and firms that pay salaries to new agents. For now, the 3508 safe harbor keeps most NY salespersons as contractors, provided brokers supervise without controlling.
blocks.casual: Will licensees end up as employees? There's pressure: misclassification enforcement, team structures, and firms that pay new agents salaries. For now, the 3508 safe harbor keeps most NY salespersons as contractors, as long as brokers supervise without controlling.

deeper.plain: Contractor status is the norm today, but it depends on brokers staying on the right side of control.
deeper.picture: Like a beach that's open as long as the tide stays out. Push too far and the water comes in.
deeper.street: A big Manhattan team pays two junior agents a salary to handle leads. Those two are employees, correctly classified. The rest of the team stays commission-only contractors.
deeper.stakes: Teams and salaried juniors create mixed offices where mistakes happen. Each person's status has to match how they're actually paid and managed.
deeper.exam: Current rule: most NY salespersons are independent contractors under the safe harbor, if supervision stays short of direction and control.

blocks.title: LOW-C
blocks.html: Licensed, Output pay, Written contract, no Control. Miss any one and the contractor label falls off.
blocks.casual: Remember LOW-C: Licensed, Output pay, Written contract, no Control. Miss any one and the contractor label falls off.

deeper.plain: Four checks. Fail one and you're looking at an employee.
deeper.picture: Picture a low ceiling: hit any of the four beams and you're knocked back into employee status.
deeper.street: On the exam Kim reads: 'A licensed agent paid commission only, with a written agreement, but required to work set hours.' LOW-C fails at C, so she picks 'likely an employee.'
deeper.stakes: Running LOW-C on your own firm's onboarding papers before you sign can save you a messy tax surprise later.
deeper.exam: Use LOW-C to eliminate answers quickly. Control is the item the exam most often hides in the stem.

story.title: Desk Duty
story.setting: Hudson & Hart office, Monday 9:05 a.m.

beats.text: Marcus has been put in charge of onboarding two new salespersons. Diane is at a closing. This is going well.
Rules: you're here nine to five, Monday through Friday. Late is a fifty-dollar fine off your split.
Marcus, they signed independent contractor agreements.
So? Paper says contractor. They're contractors.
Paper doesn't win. If we control their hours and dock them, the state can call them employees anyway.
Diane walks in, reads the whiteboard, and caps Marcus's marker.
Erase 'mandatory.' Write 'sign up for floor time if you want the leads.' Offered is fine. Required is employment.
New agent: So do you supervise us at all?
Constantly. 175.21 requires regular, frequent, consistent supervision. I review your contracts, your ads, your escrow handling. I just don't set your hours.

check.q: Which of Diane's practices is consistent with contractor status?
c: Fining agents for arriving late
Reviewing contracts and ads for legal compliance
Paying agents by the hour
Assigning mandatory weekly call quotas
check.x: Compliance supervision is required and does not create employment. Fines, hourly pay, and quotas are direction and control.

beats.text: And if we got it wrong?
Then I owe unemployment insurance, workers' comp, disability, and withholding on everyone, and they lose their Schedule C deductions.
Licensed, paid by output, written contract, no control.
And keep every deal file three years. That's 175.23. Now go sell something, on your own schedule.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: supervision the broker must provide vs direction and control that would make a salesperson an employee. Add three items to each side.

facts.text: Contractors are paid by results, pay their own taxes and expenses, and set their own hours; employees may get salary, have taxes withheld, and are directed by the broker.
Most NY salespersons are independent contractors; hiring them as employees is legal, but labeling an employee a contractor is not.
The common law test asks whether the hiring party directs and controls how, when and where the work is done.
IRC 3508 treats a licensed agent as a non-employee if substantially all pay is tied to output and a written contract says so for tax purposes.
NY's 1986 law adds matching rules for unemployment and workers' comp: licensed, paid by commission, written contract not signed under duress.
For NY unemployment insurance the contract must have been executed within the past 12 to 15 months, so brokers renew it each year.
Holding the license, putting the broker's name on ads and reviewing contracts are license law duties and do not make a contractor an employee.
In a true contractor relationship there is no hourly pay, the salesperson picks their hours and pays their expenses, and either party may end it at any time.
Substance beats form: mandatory hours, hourly pay or docked splits can make salespersons employees whatever the contract says.
If status fails, the broker owes unemployment insurance, workers' comp, disability and tax withholding.
Reclassified salespersons lose Schedule C business deductions and have all pay subject to withholding.
19 NYCRR 175.21 requires regular, frequent and consistent supervision, and the broker is responsible for the salesperson's conduct.
Brokers supervise (training, reviewing contracts and ads, compliance policies) but must not control schedules, quotas or methods.
19 NYCRR 175.23: brokers keep transaction records for at least 3 years and make them available to DOS.

lessons.title: Case file: The Seller in Sarasota
lessons.tagline: The owner is 1,200 miles away, her son has the keys, and everyone wants to sign something. Who is the client, and who can say yes?
objectives: Decide who the principal is when a family member, not the owner, contacts the broker
Apply the limits of a listing broker's authority to offers, price changes, and contract signing
Evaluate whether a power of attorney is effective and what authority it gives
Apply licensing rules to finder's fees, unlicensed assistants, and a departing salesperson

blocks.title: A call from Great Kills
blocks.html: Vincent Castellano calls Hudson & Hart on a Monday in April. His mother, Ruth, is 81 and moved to Sarasota last fall to live near his sister. Her house, a detached three-bedroom ranch on a quiet street in Great Kills, Staten Island, has been empty since. "I'm handling everything," Vincent tells Jordan. "Mom said whatever I decide is fine. Can you come by Thursday, sign me up, and get it on the market at $749,000?" The deed, Jordan finds on ACRIS that afternoon, is in Ruth's name alone. Vincent has keys, opinions, and a deadline. What he does not obviously have is the right to hire a broker.

Every agency question starts with the same move: name the principal. In New York the agent is a licensed broker acting in a fiduciary capacity for someone (RPL 443 defines "agent" that way). The someone is whoever owns the thing being sold or has the legal power to act for the owner. Enthusiasm does not count. Neither does being the child who mows the lawn.

Jordan pulls the deed: Ruth Castellano, as sole owner, since 1979. No co-owner, no trust, no LLC. Vincent has no ownership interest. He mentions that his mother "gave him a paper" two years ago when she had surgery, but he cannot find it and thinks it was "a medical thing.

blocks.q: Vincent wants to sign an exclusive right to sell listing with Hudson & Hart on Thursday. What should Jordan do?
c: Let Vincent sign, since a family member with keys has implied authority to list
Have Ruth sign it, or someone holding a valid power of attorney from her
Let Vincent sign now and have Ruth ratify it later by email
Take the listing from Vincent as an open listing, which needs no owner signature
blocks.x: Ruth owns the house, so Ruth is the principal and only she, or an agent she has validly authorized, can create the listing agency. Being her son and holding keys gives Vincent no authority to bind her. The tempting choice is planning on ratification: it can rescue an unauthorized act after the fact, but a careful broker does not build a listing on the hope that an absent owner will approve it later.

blocks.html: Diane agrees and adds a practical point. A health care proxy, which is what the "medical thing" probably was, gives authority over medical decisions only. It says nothing about real estate. Jordan emails Ruth the listing agreement and the agency disclosure form, then calls her. Ruth is sharp, funny, and clear: she wants to sell, she wants $739,000 not $749,000 ("Vincent always rounds up"), and she wants Vincent to let people in, because he lives ten minutes away.

blocks.title: The listing, as signed
blocks.html:
Exclusive Right to Sell Agreement
Owner: Ruth Castellano. Broker: Hudson & Hart Realty, Inc.
Property: 1 to 4 family residence, Great Kills, Staten Island, NY.
List price: $739,000. Term: April 18 to July 31.
Commission: 5% of the sale price, earned and payable at closing.
Special instructions (owner's handwriting): "My son Vincent may give access for showings and inspections. All decisions on price and offers are mine. Call me first."
Signed: Ruth Castellano (by e-signature). For the broker: Diane Hart.

Read the special instructions twice, because they define two different relationships. Hudson & Hart is now Ruth's agent for one job, finding a buyer for this house. That makes the firm a special agent. Vincent has been given a narrow task too: open the door. Neither of them can decide price or accept an offer. Ruth kept those powers.

blocks.q: Two weeks in, Vincent texts Jordan: "No bites. Drop it to $699K today, Mom won't care." What should Jordan do?
c: Lower the price, because Vincent manages access and speaks for the family
Lower the price on the MLS but tell Ruth about it at the next weekly update
Ignore the text, since Vincent is a customer and is owed no response
Call Ruth with the feedback and change the price only on her written OK
blocks.x: Ruth's written instruction reserves price decisions to her, and obedience to lawful instructions is owed to the principal, not to whoever is loudest. Jordan should bring Ruth the facts (feedback, showings, comps) so she can decide, and get her change in writing. The trap is treating Vincent's access role as general authority. Ignoring him is also wrong: he is not a customer, he is the person Ruth chose to handle access.

blocks.html: Jordan calls Ruth with the numbers: 22 showings, three second visits, every buyer asking about the 1979 kitchen. Ruth approves $719,000 by email that night. The email goes into the transaction file, because it is the proof that Jordan obeyed the principal and not the son.

On the same call Ruth adds something private. "Between us, I'd go to $700,000 if I had to. Don't tell Vincent. He talks at the bar, and the whole South Shore will know by Sunday." Two days later Vincent asks Jordan, casually, "So what's Mom's real bottom number? I'm the one showing the place."

blocks.q: How should Jordan answer Vincent's question about Ruth's bottom number?
c: Decline politely and suggest he ask his mother directly
Tell him, since he is family and Ruth chose him to handle the showings
Tell him, but ask him in writing to keep the figure confidential
Give him a slightly higher number so the real floor stays protected
blocks.x: Confidentiality runs to the client, and Ruth told Jordan in so many words that the floor stays away from Vincent. Vincent's access role does not make him a principal entitled to her bargaining position. The tempting answer is sharing with a confidentiality request, but the duty is to follow Ruth's instruction, not to manage the risk of breaking it. Inventing a number is a lie, and agents do not lie to protect secrets.

blocks.text: Who is allowed to work this listing

blocks.html: With the price change, traffic picks up, and so do helpers. Three of them raise licensing questions that land on Diane's desk in the same week.

The first is Bree, Hudson & Hart's unlicensed office assistant. Jordan is double booked on Saturday and asks whether Bree can run the open house "just to hand out flyers and let people walk through." Bree is great at flyers. She has never taken the salesperson course.

blocks.q: Can Bree host the Saturday open house for the Castellano listing?
c: Yes, if she wears a badge saying she is an assistant and answers no questions
Yes, as long as Diane, the broker, is reachable by phone during the open house
No, because showing property and talking with buyers about it needs a license
No, unless Ruth signs a consent allowing an unlicensed person to show the house
blocks.x: In New York, showing property and dealing with prospective buyers about it are brokerage activities that need a license. Unlicensed assistants are limited to clerical work: flyers, scheduling, data entry. The tempting answer is the badge plus silence, but an open house is showing by definition, and buyers will ask questions. Ruth's consent cannot license anyone; only the Department of State can.

blocks.html: The second helper is Tony, Vincent's friend, who tends bar on Hylan Boulevard. Tony tells a regular about the house, the regular comes to the next open house, and Tony calls Jordan: "When this closes I want five grand out of the commission. I found your buyer." The regular, a nurse named Denise Alvarado, does seem serious.

blocks.q: If Denise buys, may Hudson & Hart pay Tony a $5,000 referral fee out of its commission?
c: No, a broker may share fees only with licensees or out-of-state brokers
Yes, a one-time finder's fee is allowed if the amount is stated in writing
Yes, if Ruth approves the payment, since the money comes from her proceeds
No, unless Tony registers as an unlicensed referral agent with the firm first
blocks.x: RPL 442 bars a broker from paying any part of its fee to a person who is not licensed, with narrow exceptions such as licensed salespersons and brokers or brokers engaged in business in another state. A bartender who sends a customer over is not on that list. The trap is seller approval: Ruth cannot waive a licensing statute. There is also no such thing as a registered unlicensed referral agent in New York.

blocks.title: Who can be paid, in one breath
blocks.html: RPL 442 lets a broker share a fee with its own licensed salespersons and associate brokers, with other licensed brokers, and with brokers regularly engaged in business in another state. It also lets a broker offer part of its compensation to a party to the deal (a buyer or seller), but not as payment for doing licensed work. Anyone else who expects a cut is asking you to break the law. And a person who collects a fee without a license can be sued for up to four times the amount (RPL 442-e).

The third is closer to home. Marcus, who covers Staten Island with Jordan, gives notice: he is moving to a Tottenville firm at the end of the month. On his way out he calls Vincent. "When I go, the Castellano house comes with me. Tell your mom." Vincent, confused, calls Jordan.

blocks.q: Does the Castellano listing move with Marcus to his new firm?
c: Yes, because the salesperson who works the listing is the seller's agent
Yes, if Ruth agrees, since a listing follows the salesperson she prefers
No, but Marcus may keep his share of any commission paid after he leaves
No, the listing is a contract between Ruth and Hudson & Hart
blocks.x: The agent is the broker. A listing agreement is between the owner and the brokerage; salespersons carry out the broker's agency as the broker's general agents. When a salesperson leaves, the listing stays. Ruth could choose to end her agreement with Hudson & Hart according to its terms and hire Marcus's new firm, but the listing does not travel by itself. Any money Marcus receives later depends on his own agreement with Diane, not on the listing.

blocks.html: Diane calls Ruth that afternoon, confirms the listing remains with Hudson & Hart, and documents the call. She also reminds Marcus in writing that soliciting a firm client on his way out the door is a conversation he will not enjoy having with the Department of State.

blocks.text: The buyer at the kitchen island

blocks.html: Denise comes back twice. She has no agent of her own, which is fine. On the second visit she sits at the kitchen island with Jordan and asks three questions in a row: "What's the lowest she'll take? Why is she selling? And is there an oil tank in the yard?"

Jordan gave Denise the agency disclosure form at her first visit, which showed Jordan and Hudson & Hart as the seller's agent. Denise signed the acknowledgment. So Ruth is the client. Denise is a customer.

blocks.q: Which response handles all three of Denise's questions correctly?
c: Share Ruth's bottom line to keep Denise interested, explain the move, and say the tank is gone
Decline the bottom line, keep Ruth's personal reasons private, and find out the tank's status
Decline every question, since a customer is owed no information by the seller's agent
Give Ruth's bottom line if Denise agrees in writing to make an offer that same day
blocks.x: Ruth's price floor and her personal reasons belong to the client and stay confidential. But a seller's agent still owes a customer honesty and disclosure of known material facts, so the oil tank question gets a real answer, not a guess and not a dodge. The trap is the blanket refusal: customers are not owed advice or loyalty, but they are owed truthful answers about the property.

blocks.html: Jordan says, "I represent the seller, so I can't discuss her price or her plans. On the tank, I don't know and I'm not going to guess. I'll find out." Ruth remembers a contractor "taking out the tank" in the 1990s but has no paperwork. Jordan tells Denise exactly that, in writing, and suggests her inspector or attorney look into it. A guess like "it's gone" would have been a misstatement of fact made to a customer, the kind of statement that costs commissions and licenses.

blocks.text: The offer, and who can accept it

blocks.html: Denise offers $705,000 with a mortgage contingency. It arrives on a Friday at 6 p.m. Ruth is on a cruise until Wednesday with spotty email. Vincent is at the house when Jordan calls. "Just accept it," he says. "I'll sign for Mom. Or you sign it. You're her agent, right?"

blocks.q: Can Jordan or Hudson & Hart accept Denise's offer on Ruth's behalf?
c: Yes, because the listing broker is Ruth's agent for the sale of the house
Yes, if the price is within the range Ruth approved in her last email
No, a listing is a special agency to find a buyer, not to accept offers
No, unless Vincent also signs the acceptance as a witness for the family
blocks.x: A listing broker is a special agent: it markets, shows, and negotiates, and it presents offers to the principal. It has no power to accept an offer or sign a contract for the seller unless the seller separately grants that authority in writing. The tempting answer is the price range, but approving a list price is not authorizing anyone to bind Ruth to a deal. Vincent's signature adds nothing; he has no authority either.

blocks.html: Jordan presents the offer to Ruth by email and text, tells Denise's side it is with the seller, and keeps negotiating terms on paper. When Ruth surfaces on Wednesday she counters at $712,000, Denise accepts, and the attorneys start on the contract. Ruth then makes a decision for the months ahead: "I'm not flying up for a closing. Let Vincent sign." Her Sarasota lawyer prepares a New York statutory short form power of attorney.

blocks.title: Making a NY power of attorney work (GOL 5-1501B)
blocks.html: A New York power of attorney must be signed and dated by the principal, with her signature acknowledged the way a deed is acknowledged, and signed in front of two witnesses (the notary may be one of them). The agent must also sign it, with that signature acknowledged too. The power takes effect when the agent's signature is acknowledged. Since 2021, the form needs to substantially conform to the statutory form, not match it word for word.

blocks.title: The POA packet that arrives from Florida
blocks.html:
Principal: Ruth Castellano. Agent: Vincent Castellano.
Authority: Ruth initials every category of authority on the form, including real estate transactions.
Signed and dated by Ruth: yes. Two witnesses: yes (a neighbor and the notary).
Ruth's signature acknowledged before a Florida notary: yes.
Agent's signature section: blank. Vincent has not signed yet.

blocks.q: Vincent wants to sign the contract of sale under the POA tomorrow morning. Looking at the packet, can he?
c: Yes, because Ruth's signature is witnessed twice and acknowledged before a notary
Yes, but just for documents that Ruth has already reviewed and initialed herself
Not yet, because a POA signed out of state needs approval from a New York court
Not yet: the power takes effect when Vincent signs with an acknowledgment
blocks.x: Under GOL 5-1501B the agent must sign and date the power with the signature acknowledged, and the power takes effect on that acknowledgment. Ruth did her part; Vincent has not done his. The tempting answer looks at Ruth's side only. No court approval is needed for an out-of-state execution; Florida notaries can take acknowledgments for New York use, and title companies review the form when they insure the deal.

blocks.html: Vincent signs at a Staten Island notary the next morning. Now the cast has three kinds of agents, and it helps to line them up.

head: Who
Authority
Type of agent
rows: Vincent, under the POA with every category initialed
Nearly anything Ruth could legally do in her affairs
The full range of the firm's brokerage business
General agent of the broker
Find a buyer for one house; present offers
blocks.caption: Same deal, three scopes of authority

blocks.q: With the POA effective, Vincent asks Jordan to have Hudson & Hart sign the contract "for the family" since Jordan knows the deal best. What is the right answer?
c: Vincent signs as Ruth's attorney in fact; the broker still has no authority to sign
Hudson & Hart may sign, because Vincent can delegate his POA authority to the broker
Hudson & Hart may sign, if Ruth's attorney approves the contract terms by email
Jordan may sign as a salesperson, since the listing names her as the seller's contact
blocks.x: The POA made Vincent Ruth's agent for signing. It did not expand Hudson & Hart's special agency, and nothing in the packet lets Vincent pass his authority on to the broker. He signs the contract as "Ruth Castellano by Vincent Castellano, attorney in fact." The tempting answer is attorney approval, but a lawyer approving terms is not the principal granting signing authority to the broker.

blocks.title: "Mom said it's fine" is not authority
blocks.html: Exam stems love the relative who "handles everything." A spouse, child, or friend has no power to list, price, accept, or sign for an owner just by being close to her. Authority comes from the principal: in the listing, in a written instruction, or in a valid power of attorney. A health care proxy is not a power of attorney for property. When the stem says the deed is in one person's name, that person is the principal.

The contract signs. Denise's lender appraises at value. A week before closing Denise's attorney sends Jordan a short email: "Buyer wants a $4,000 credit for the old kitchen faucet and the cracked tile. Can you just say yes so we keep this moving?" Vincent, copied, replies first: "Fine by me."

blocks.q: Who can agree to the $4,000 credit, and what should Jordan do with the request?
c: Jordan can agree, since a broker may negotiate minor credits under the listing
Ruth's attorney alone can agree, because the deal is now under a signed contract
Vincent can agree under the POA; Jordan tells Ruth and confirms in writing
Denise's attorney can treat Vincent's reply as final, since he is copied as family
blocks.x: Vincent now holds a broad power of attorney, so he can agree to the credit for Ruth. Jordan's job is disclosure and documentation: tell Ruth, confirm Vincent's approval in writing, and loop in Ruth's attorney, who papers changes to the signed contract. The tempting answer is the attorney, but lawyers document and advise; they do not replace the principal's consent. Jordan never had authority to agree.

blocks.html: Ruth, reached by phone from Sarasota, says, "Fine, but tell Vincent he owes me a faucet." The deal closes in July at $712,000 less the $4,000 credit. Vincent signs the deed as attorney in fact, and the title company records the power of attorney along with the deed so the chain of title shows who signed and why.

head: Moment
Who decided
Paper that proves it
rows: Exclusive right to sell, e-signed by Ruth
Ruth's email approval in the file
blocks.caption: The decision trail Diane wants in every file

blocks.q: Looking back, which fact made Ruth, not Vincent, the principal from the first phone call?
c: Ruth was over 75, so the law treats her as the default decision maker
Ruth held title alone, so only she could grant authority over the house
Ruth answered her phone, so Jordan could reach her before signing anything
Ruth lived out of state, so Vincent had no standing to sign in New York
blocks.x: The principal is the party with the legal power to act over the property, and Ruth held title as sole owner. Her age and location are irrelevant to who the principal is; they only affected how the deal got done. The tempting answer is reachability: being able to call Ruth made things easier, but even an unreachable owner is still the principal, and someone else needs her valid authority to act.

blocks.title: Diane's opening questions for any family seller
blocks.html: Whose name is on the deed? Is any owner deceased, and if so, who is the executor? Is there a trust, an LLC, or a power of attorney, and can I see it? Who will sign the listing and the contract? Ask on the first call, before you price anything. The answers tell you who your client is.

items: Name the principal first. The owner of record, or a person she has validly authorized, creates the agency. Relatives and helpers do not.
A listing broker is a special agent: it finds buyers, presents offers, and negotiates. Price changes, acceptances, and signatures belong to the principal.
A New York power of attorney needs the principal's acknowledged signature, two witnesses, and the agent's acknowledged signature; it takes effect when the agent's signature is acknowledged.
The broker is the agent. Salespersons act as the broker's general agents, and listings stay with the firm when a salesperson leaves.
Only licensees may show property or share a commission. Finder's fees to unlicensed people and open houses run by unlicensed assistants violate Article 12-A.
Customers get honesty and known material facts. Clients also get confidentiality, so the price floor stays private while the oil tank question gets a truthful answer.

lessons.title: Case file: The Offer in the Drawer
lessons.tagline: A Kew Gardens listing, an offer held over a weekend, and a buyer's LLC with a familiar name inside it.
objectives: Decide which seller instructions an agent must obey, which to advise against, and which to refuse
Apply the duty of loyalty to an agent's hidden interest in a buyer and to the timing of offers
Evaluate what full disclosure of self-dealing requires under 19 NYCRR 175.4
Apply obedience and loyalty after an offer is accepted but before a NY contract is signed

blocks.title: Friday night on Austin Street
blocks.html: Lena and Arthur Kaplan are selling the attached brick Tudor in Kew Gardens, Queens, where they raised three kids. Marcus took the listing for Hudson & Hart at $1,250,000, with Jordan as co-listing agent. At the listing appointment Lena said, "Don't bring us anything under $1.2 million. We're not giving it away." Nobody wrote it down. At 7 p.m. on a Friday, a buyer's agent from Forest Hills emails an offer: $1,190,000, all cash, 30-day closing, no contingencies besides the attorney review. Marcus forwards it to Jordan with one word: "Drawer." Then he adds, "They said nothing under 1.2. We'll talk Monday."

Obedience means following the client's lawful instructions, even ones you would not have chosen. An instruction like "don't present offers below a number" is lawful. Sellers give it to save themselves from lowball noise. But obedience sits next to two other duties. Disclosure requires telling the client material facts. Loyalty requires that the agent's own interests never drive the timing of what the client hears. When an instruction is oral, vague, and suddenly tested by an offer that is close and unusually clean, the agent's job is to make sure the client actually decides.

blocks.q: What should happen with the $1,190,000 all-cash offer on Friday night?
c: Hold it until Monday, since the sellers told Marcus they want nothing below $1.2M
Tell the Kaplans an offer under their floor came in; ask if they want it
Reject it on the sellers' behalf and invite the buyer to come back at $1.2M or more
Present the offer in full with a recommendation to accept, since cash is worth more
blocks.x: The floor instruction is lawful, so Jordan should not override it by pushing the offer on the sellers. But the instruction was oral and loose, and a cash offer $10,000 under it is a material fact. Telling the sellers it exists and letting them decide respects both obedience and disclosure. The drawer is the trap: holding an offer over a weekend by the agent's choice is not obedience, it is the agent deciding for the client.

blocks.html: Jordan calls the Kaplans at 8 p.m. Lena's answer takes four seconds: "All cash? Send it." The next morning Jordan emails a confirmation that both Kaplans sign: Present all offers of $1,150,000 or more. Tell us about anything lower, and we will decide whether to see it. An instruction in writing protects everyone, including the agent who has to follow it.

blocks.title: How Diane papers an instruction
blocks.html: Restate it in plain words in an email the same day: what the client wants, any number or condition attached, and when it starts. Ask the client to reply "confirmed" or sign. When a later instruction changes it, send a fresh confirmation rather than editing the old one. If an offer ever tests the instruction, the file shows exactly what the client said and when, and nobody has to rely on memory of a kitchen-table conversation.

blocks.text: Instructions you advise against, and one you refuse

blocks.html: While the Kaplans think about the cash offer, Saturday showings continue, and Lena sends a list of house rules by text. Jordan reads them in the car outside the house on 82nd Avenue.

blocks.title: Lena's Saturday text
blocks.html:
1. No lockbox. Arthur will be home for every showing.
2. No open houses on weekends. We have the grandkids.
3. No showings to families with little kids. Those front stairs are a lawsuit waiting to happen.
4. If anyone asks, tell them we have another offer at $1.25M. It'll light a fire.

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle rules 1 and 2, no lockbox and no weekend open houses?
c: Refuse them, since restricting access breaches the duty to market the home
Follow them, but hold one open house anyway to protect the sellers' interests
Refuse them unless the sellers sign a release of the firm's liability
Follow them, after telling the sellers how they may slow the sale
blocks.x: Both rules are lawful choices about the sellers' own home, so obedience applies. Reasonable care means Jordan explains the cost (fewer showings, slower feedback) so the choice is informed, then follows it. The tempting answer is holding an open house anyway "for their benefit": an agent who substitutes judgment for a lawful instruction breaches obedience even when trying to help. A release is unnecessary for lawful instructions.

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle rule 3, no showings to families with small children?
c: Follow it, because a seller may choose buyers who fit the home's safety needs
Follow it quietly, but warn families about the stairs if they ask to see the house
Refuse it, explain fair housing law, and tell Diane if the sellers insist
Refuse it in writing, but keep showing just to families the sellers would approve
blocks.x: Familial status is protected by the federal Fair Housing Act and the New York State Human Rights Law. An instruction to exclude families with children is unlawful, and obedience covers lawful instructions only. Jordan refuses, explains why, and involves the broker; if the sellers insist, the firm withdraws. The tempting answer frames exclusion as safety, but describing the stairs to everyone is fine, while screening out families is discrimination.

blocks.title: New York widens the list
blocks.html: The NYS Human Rights Law protects every class the federal act covers, including familial status, and adds more, such as age, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, military status, and lawful source of income. A seller's instruction that touches any protected class is outside the duty of obedience. A licensee who follows it risks DOS discipline under RPL 441-c, which lists violations of the Human Rights Law (Executive Law Article 15) as a ground.

blocks.q: Rule 4 asks Jordan to tell buyers there is another offer at $1.25M. There is none. What should Jordan do?
c: Refuse, since a false statement of fact to a buyer is a misrepresentation
Say it, because sellers' agents may use negotiating tactics for the client
Say it, but phrase it as a possibility so it is puffing rather than a fact
Refuse, unless the buyer's agent asks directly whether other offers exist
blocks.x: A seller's agent may keep the client's position confidential, but may not invent facts. A fake competing offer is a false statement of a material fact that buyers rely on when deciding how much to pay. Following that instruction would be misrepresentation, and obedience does not reach unlawful acts. The tempting answer is dressing it up as puffing: puffing is opinion about quality, not a made-up offer with a number attached.

blocks.html: Jordan calls the Kaplans and walks through all four rules. Arthur laughs at rule 2 ("fine, Sundays are for the grandkids"), says nothing about rule 1, and goes quiet on rules 3 and 4. Lena pushes back on rule 4: "Everybody does it." Jordan asks Diane to join the call.

blocks.q: Lena repeats on the call that the firm must mention a "competing offer." What is Diane's correct position?
c: Comply this once, since the sellers have now put the instruction in writing
Comply, but have the sellers sign a statement taking responsibility for it
Refuse, and report the sellers to the Department of State for the request
Refuse, and the firm may withdraw if the sellers insist on it
blocks.x: Writing does not make an unlawful instruction lawful, and a client cannot take responsibility for a licensee's own misrepresentation. When a principal insists on conduct that breaks the law, the agent refuses and may end the relationship. The tempting choice is the signed statement, but DOS disciplines the licensee who makes the false statement, regardless of who asked. Reporting the sellers is not required; DOS licenses brokers, not homeowners.

blocks.html: Lena relents. Rule 3 disappears too, and Diane notes both conversations in the file. The house is shown to everyone who asks, and the stairs get a new handrail the following week, which is the lawful answer to Lena's real worry.

On Monday morning Marcus arrives with a second offer: $1,200,000 from Austin Street Holdings LLC, 20% down, mortgage contingency, 60-day closing. "Clean buyer, investor, I know them," he says. "This is the one." Jordan, entering the offer into the file, looks up the LLC in the Department of State's corporation database. The organizer is Peter Webb. Marcus's brother-in-law is named Pete.

Jordan asks Marcus directly. Marcus admits Pete is his brother-in-law and, after a pause, that he has put in $60,000 for a quarter share of the LLC. "It's an investment," he says. "It doesn't change anything. The Kaplans get their number."

blocks.title: 19 NYCRR 175.4: buying your own listing
blocks.html: A broker may not, directly or indirectly, buy property listed with the broker, or acquire any interest in it, without first making the broker's true position clearly known to the listing owner. The rule reaches purchases through relatives, partners, and companies. Because the listing belongs to the firm and Marcus works it, his quarter interest in the buying LLC puts this rule squarely in play.

blocks.q: What must happen before the Kaplans consider the Austin Street Holdings offer?
c: Nothing more, since Peter Webb, not Marcus, is the named buyer on the offer
Marcus discloses the family tie and his LLC stake in writing
Marcus sells his LLC interest back to Pete before the offer is presented
Diane approves the offer as fair market value, which cures any conflict
blocks.x: Self-dealing is allowed only with full disclosure: the client must know the agent's true position before deciding. That means the relationship and the financial interest, in writing, before the offer is weighed. The trap is the named buyer: 175.4 covers indirect purchases through relatives and companies. Selling the interest at the last minute would not erase the conflict that already shaped Marcus's handling of the offers, and a broker's approval is not the client's informed consent.

blocks.q: Looking back at Friday, what was wrong with Marcus putting the cash offer in the drawer?
c: He breached loyalty: he delayed a rival offer to help his own deal
Nothing, since he was following the sellers' oral floor of $1.2 million
He breached accounting, because offers are documents that need to be logged
He breached confidentiality by telling Jordan about the offer by email
blocks.x: Loyalty puts the client's interest ahead of the agent's own. Marcus delayed a cash offer that competed with an LLC he partly owned, so his interest shaped what the clients heard and when. The floor instruction is the trap: it gave cover for the delay, but the motive was the conflict, and the instruction never authorized him to sit on offers for his own benefit. Telling a co-listing agent inside the firm is not a breach of confidentiality.

blocks.html: One more thing nags at Jordan. She pulls the pricing file Marcus prepared for the listing appointment. His comparative market analysis used four sales. Jordan's own search turns up six. The two Marcus left out were the highest: a Tudor two blocks away that sold for $1,340,000 in March and a similar attached house on Abingdon Road at $1,310,000. With them, the range runs well above the $1,250,000 list price Marcus recommended. A low list price draws more offers, which can be good for a seller. It also makes a $1,200,000 offer from your brother-in-law's LLC look generous.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do about the missing comparables?
c: Nothing, since the Kaplans approved the list price and a CMA is just an opinion
Tell the cash buyer's agent about the higher sales so the buyer raises the offer
Give the Kaplans an updated analysis with all six sales before they choose
Ask Marcus to add the sales quietly so the file looks complete if DOS reviews it
blocks.x: The higher sales are material to the Kaplans' decision, and Jordan, as co-listing agent, owes them disclosure and reasonable care. An updated analysis lets them judge both offers against the real market. The trap is treating their earlier approval as final: they approved a price based on an incomplete picture shaped by an agent with a hidden interest. Sharing the comps with a buyer helps the customer, not the client, and fixing the file quietly is concealment.

blocks.html: Diane acts the same afternoon. Marcus is taken off the listing. Diane writes to the Kaplans herself, disclosing Marcus's relationship to the LLC, his quarter interest, and the weekend delay, and offers to keep marketing with Jordan as sole listing agent. She also keeps a copy of everything for the file. She knows the rule in RPL 442-c: a salesperson's violation does not put the broker's own license at risk unless the broker knew about it or keeps the benefits after learning of it.

blocks.q: Why does it matter that Diane acted the day she learned of Marcus's interest?
c: A broker is liable for a salesperson's violation once a court finds fraud
A broker's license is at risk for any violation by any salesperson, regardless
A broker who keeps benefits after learning of it can be disciplined
A broker has to report a salesperson's conflict to DOS within 10 business days
blocks.x: Under RPL 442-c, a salesperson's violation is not by itself grounds to discipline the broker, unless the broker had actual knowledge of it or retains the benefits of the deal after being notified of the misconduct. Diane's quick disclosure and removal of Marcus keep the firm on the right side of that line. The trap is strict liability for every salesperson's act: the broker still must supervise, but discipline turns on knowledge and benefit.

head: Lena's rule
Lawful?
What the firm did
rows: Advised on the cost, then obeyed
Advised on the cost, then obeyed
Refused and explained fair housing law
Refused; ready to withdraw if pressed
Confirmed in writing, signed by both sellers
blocks.caption: Every instruction in the file, sorted

blocks.html: Jordan sends the Kaplans the updated analysis with all six sales. Arthur reads it twice and says, "So we priced it low." Jordan answers honestly: maybe a little, and the strong offers show the market agrees. The Kaplans decide to keep the price where it is and negotiate from the offers in hand, which is their call to make.

The Kaplans now have two offers and full information. Lena asks Jordan the question every seller asks: "What would you do?" A seller's agent may answer. Advice is part of what the client is paying for. The trick is giving advice that serves the client, not the firm.

head: Term
Forest Hills buyer (cash)
Austin Street Holdings LLC
rows: All cash, proof of funds attached
Loan denial could unwind the deal
blocks.caption: The two offers, side by side

blocks.q: Which response to Lena's "What would you do?" best reflects undivided loyalty?
c: Favor the LLC, since the firm earns more with no cooperating broker to pay
Compare net, risk, and timing, give an honest view, let them choose
Decline to give an opinion, since advice would favor one buyer over the other
Favor the cash buyer, to make up for the harm Marcus caused over the weekend
blocks.x: Undivided loyalty means advice aimed at the client's goals: net proceeds, certainty, and timing, with the agent's honest opinion. A seller's agent owes the buyers no neutrality, so refusing to advise shortchanges the client. The trap is the firm's commission, which is exactly the self-interest loyalty excludes. Favoring a buyer to repair the firm's image is also a firm-centered reason, even if it happens to point the right way.

blocks.html: The Kaplans counter the cash buyer at $1,205,000. The buyer accepts by email on Wednesday. The attorneys exchange the contract draft on Thursday. Then, on Friday, a fourth buyer's agent calls: her client saw the house Sunday and wants to offer $1,260,000, cash.

blocks.title: An accepted offer is not a contract downstate
blocks.html: In New York City and most of downstate, an "accepted offer" is a handshake. The binding moment is when both parties sign the contract of sale prepared by the attorneys and the buyer delivers the down payment, usually 10%, to the seller's attorney in escrow. Until then either side can walk away. That gap is where loyalty and obedience get tested.

blocks.q: Marcus, now off the listing, tells Jordan the new $1,260,000 offer is irrelevant because "the deal is done." What should Jordan do?
c: Tell the new agent the house is under contract and decline the offer
Hold the offer until the cash buyer's attorney signs the contract
Present it to the cash buyer's agent so the buyer can match it
Present it to the Kaplans now, since no contract has been signed
blocks.x: No contract exists yet, so the new offer is a material fact for the clients, and loyalty runs to the Kaplans, not to keeping a deal tidy. Jordan presents it promptly and lets them decide. The trap is calling the house "under contract": that misstates the facts and decides for the client. Sending it to the cash buyer's side first would hand a customer leverage the sellers never authorized.

blocks.html: The Kaplans talk it over for an hour. Then Arthur calls. "We shook on it. We're not that kind of people. Tell the new agent thank you, and go to contract with the cash buyer." Jordan, who had already mentally spent part of the bigger commission, swallows hard.

blocks.q: Arthur instructs Jordan to decline the higher offer and proceed with the accepted one. What does Jordan owe now?
c: Obey, once sure they understand the $55,000 they leave behind
Push back until they agree, since loyalty requires getting the highest price
Obey, but forward the higher offer to the cash buyer to speed up the contract
Refuse, because accepting a lower price harms the clients' financial interest
blocks.x: Honoring a handshake is a lawful choice, and the decision belongs to the principal. Jordan's duties are to make sure the choice is informed (the $55,000 difference, the fact that nothing is binding yet) and then follow it. The trap is reading loyalty as "maximize the price no matter what": loyalty means serving the client's goals, and the Kaplans' goals include keeping their word. Leaking the offer to the buyer would breach confidentiality.

blocks.html: Contracts are signed the next Tuesday with a $120,500 down payment to the Kaplans' attorney. The deal closes in 30 days. Marcus keeps his license, after a long meeting with Diane, a written reprimand in his file, and a firm policy memo that now requires every agent to disclose any personal or family interest in a buyer on the day it arises. The Kaplans, for their part, send Jordan a card from Rhinebeck. It says the stairs are someone else's problem now, and thanks Jordan for telling them the truth on the Friday night it mattered.

blocks.title: "I was just following instructions"
blocks.html: Exam stems test obedience at its edges. Following a lawful instruction you dislike (no lockbox, no open houses, a price floor) is correct. Following an unlawful instruction (exclude a protected class, invent an offer, hide a defect) is a violation, and the client's insistence is no defense. The other edge: using a client's instruction as cover for your own interest, as Marcus did with the drawer, is a loyalty breach, even if the words of the instruction seem to fit.

blocks.q: Which of Marcus's acts would have been acceptable if he had handled it differently?
c: Holding the cash offer to give his LLC a head start, with a later apology
Describing the LLC as an unrelated investor, since it was a separate legal entity
Owning part of the buyer LLC, disclosed in writing up front
Keeping his interest private, as long as the price matched the sellers' floor
blocks.x: An agent may have an interest in a buyer, even one buying the agent's own listing, if the agent makes the true position clearly known to the client before the client decides (175.4). Disclosure turns a conflict into an informed choice. The trap is the separate entity: an LLC is a separate legal person, but the rule expressly covers indirect purchases. Delaying a rival offer has no cure; it was a breach the moment it happened.

items: Obedience covers lawful instructions: follow them, advise on their costs, and get them in writing.
Unlawful instructions (excluding a protected class, inventing an offer) are refused, even if the client insists or signs something; the firm may withdraw.
Loyalty bars the agent's own interest from shaping advice or the timing of offers. A held offer that helps the agent's deal is a breach.
Under 19 NYCRR 175.4 an agent who buys, directly or indirectly, must make the true position clearly known to the owner before the owner decides.
Downstate, an accepted offer is not a contract. New offers keep coming to the client until the contract is signed, and the client decides what to do with them.
A broker who learns of a salesperson's violation must act; under RPL 442-c, knowledge or keeping the benefits puts the broker's own license at risk.

lessons.title: Case file: What the Super Said in Riverdale
lessons.tagline: Leo's first condo, a scaffold nobody mentioned, and a listing agent who talks too much. Who has to tell whom what?
objectives: Decide which facts a buyer's agent must pass to the client and which client facts stay confidential
Apply the duty of honesty owed to the other side when your own client has a secret
Classify a misstatement as innocent, negligent, or intentional and connect it to its consequences
Apply RPL 443-a to a stigma question raised during negotiation

blocks.title: Twelve floors above the Hudson
blocks.html: Leo Brandt has a spreadsheet with 41 rows, one for every apartment he has toured. Row 41 is a two-bedroom condo on the eighth floor of a 12-story building in Riverdale, the Bronx, listed at $615,000 by Carla Ruiz of a Manhattan firm. Leo hired Jordan as his buyer's agent under a written exclusive buyer agreement, so Hudson & Hart represents him. He is pre-approved to $650,000 and wants to stay under $600,000. As Jordan and Leo leave the second showing, the building's superintendent holds the elevator and says, "You know they're putting up a sidewalk shed next month, right? Facade report came back bad. Board's talking about an assessment." Then the doors close. Leo looks at Jordan. Carla, upstairs, has said nothing about any of it.

A buyer's agent sits in the middle of a lot of information flowing two ways. Facts that come in, from the building, the seller's side, the records, or the street, go to the client if they are material. That is the duty of disclosure. Facts about the client that could go out, such as budget, deadlines, and personal pressures, stay inside the relationship. That is confidentiality. And whatever Jordan does say to the seller's side has to be true, because every agent owes honesty to the other parties in a deal. In this case all three duties get tested in the same week, sometimes in the same phone call, and the hard part is keeping them separate when they collide.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do with the super's remark about the facade and a possible assessment?
c: Wait until it is confirmed in writing, since a super's comment is just hearsay
Tell Leo now and have his attorney get the minutes and facade report
Ask Carla privately and tell Leo if she confirms the assessment is real
Mention it to Leo after he has an accepted offer, to avoid scaring him off
blocks.x: A possible assessment and a failed facade report bear directly on what the apartment costs to own, so they are material. Disclosure means telling the client what you learn, including unconfirmed information, labeled as such, along with how to verify it. Waiting for confirmation is the trap: an agent who sits on a material lead is choosing for the client. Timing it after acceptance would cost Leo his best moment to negotiate.

blocks.title: Why the super's words matter: FISP
blocks.html: New York City's Facade Inspection Safety Program (FISP, still often called Local Law 11) requires owners of buildings taller than six stories to have the exterior walls examined by a licensed engineer or architect every five years and to file a report with the Department of Buildings. A facade classified as unsafe must be protected right away, usually with a sidewalk shed, and repaired. In a condo, that repair is paid by the owners through common charges or a special assessment.

Leo's attorney asks the seller's attorney for the last two years of board minutes, the building's financials, and the most recent facade report. That takes a week. Meanwhile, Leo is impatient and has a secret.

blocks.title: Passing along what you cannot yet prove
blocks.html: Say where it came from, say it is unconfirmed, and say how you will check it. "The super mentioned a facade problem and a possible assessment. I can't confirm it yet. Your attorney should request the board minutes and the FISP report before you sign." Then put the same three sentences in an email. The client gets the fact in time to use it, nobody treats gossip as gospel, and the file shows the disclosure happened on the day you learned it.

Over coffee, Leo tells Jordan something he has not told anyone outside his family. "My company announced a reorganization. I'll know in six weeks if my team survives. If I'm laid off, I lose the mortgage approval, right? Don't tell anyone." He wants to make an offer anyway.

blocks.q: What does Jordan owe Leo after hearing about the possible layoff?
c: Keep it from the seller's side, and explain how a job loss can end his loan approval
Tell Carla, since a seller is entitled to know about any risk to the buyer's financing
Keep it private and say nothing more, since financing is the lender's concern
Advise Leo to delay telling his lender until after the contract is signed
blocks.x: Leo's job situation is his confidential information, so it stays away from the seller's side. Reasonable care means Jordan explains the practical risk: lenders typically reverify employment before closing, and a lost job can collapse the commitment, so his contract's mortgage contingency matters. Silence is the trap: confidentiality is not a reason to withhold useful advice. Coaching Leo to hide a change from his lender would invite loan fraud.

blocks.html: Leo decides to offer anyway, with a full mortgage contingency, and Jordan makes sure his attorney knows to protect it. Then Carla calls Jordan to talk numbers.

blocks.q: Carla asks, "What's your buyer approved for? Is he flexible on price?" What is Jordan's best answer?
c: "He's approved to $650,000, but he'd like to stay under $600,000."
"He's approved for well over your list price, so he can go higher if needed."
"He's paying cash, so approval isn't an issue for this deal."
"I can't share that. He'll send a pre-approval letter for his offer amount."
blocks.x: Leo's approval ceiling and his flexibility are his bargaining position, and confidentiality protects them. Many buyer's agents, with the client's OK, provide a pre-approval letter written to the offer amount so the seller sees the deal is fundable without seeing the ceiling. The tempting answer hints that he can go higher, which is a confidentiality breach dressed as salesmanship. Claiming cash would be a plain misrepresentation.

blocks.text: What Carla said, and what she knew

blocks.html: Leo goes to Carla's Sunday open house on his own to measure the bedroom. Carla tells him, while he holds one end of the tape, "The building's in great shape. Roof was done in 2022, and there's no assessment planned. The board is very conservative." Leo texts Jordan from the lobby: "She says no assessment. Super must be wrong?"

blocks.q: Jordan has a direct conflict between the super's remark and Carla's statement. What should Jordan do?
c: Tell Leo that Carla's statement settles it, since a listing agent knows the building
Tell Leo the two accounts conflict and keep the document request moving before signing
Confront Carla publicly at the open house so other buyers hear the truth
Drop the issue, since a condo seller's agent is not liable for statements about the building
blocks.x: Two conflicting accounts of a material fact is exactly when a buyer's agent earns the fee: report both to the client and get the documents that resolve it. The trap is deferring to the listing agent, who represents the seller and may be wrong or worse. Every agent remains liable for false statements of fact, condo or not. Confronting Carla in front of other buyers does nothing for Leo and is not Jordan's job.

blocks.html: The documents arrive the following Wednesday. Jordan reads them with Leo and his attorney.

blocks.title: From the board minutes, March and May
blocks.html:
March 14: Engineer presented the FISP report. Facade classified UNSAFE at the 10th and 11th floor parapets. Board directed the managing agent to install a sidewalk shed and seek repair bids.
May 9: Low bid $1.1 million. Reserve fund covers $300,000. Board voted to levy a special assessment of $800,000, allocated by common interest, payable over 24 months starting September 1. Notice to unit owners to follow. Unit 8C's share: $27,600.
Listing packet distributed by the seller's broker in April (from Carla's file): includes the March minutes.

blocks.q: Carla had the March minutes in her own listing packet when she told Leo "no assessment planned." How is her statement best classified?
c: Puffing, since "great shape" and "conservative board" are matters of opinion
Innocent misrepresentation, since the vote had not happened when she spoke
At least negligent, and intentional if she read the minutes and spoke anyway
No misrepresentation, since Leo had a buyer's agent and could check for himself
blocks.x: The assessment claim is a statement of fact, not opinion, and the document in her own file pointed the other way. If she knew, it was intentional misrepresentation (fraud); if she should have known, it was negligent. Puffing is the trap: "great shape" may be puffing, but "no assessment planned" is a checkable fact. A buyer having an agent does not license the other side to state false facts.

head: Kind of misrepresentation
Agent's state of mind
Typical consequences
rows: Honestly believed it, had no reason to doubt
Rescission of the contract possible; damages less likely
Should have known (the facts were in reach)
Rescission, money damages, DOS discipline for incompetency
Knew it was false, or spoke recklessly
Rescission, damages (punitive possible), loss of commission, license revocation
blocks.caption: Same false sentence, three levels of trouble

blocks.html: Because the statement came before any contract, Leo has not been harmed yet. He has simply learned the truth in time, which is the point of the document request. Jordan reports Carla's statement to Diane, who decides whether a complaint to the Department of State is warranted. Leo's attorney uses the minutes to reprice the deal.
Leo, rattled, asks a fair question. "When I looked at houses in Yonkers, the sellers had to give me a form listing problems. Why didn't this seller give me anything?"

blocks.q: What is the accurate answer to Leo's question about a disclosure form?
c: Condos are exempt from the PCDS; his protection is document review
The seller broke the law by skipping the Property Condition Disclosure Statement
The seller can skip the PCDS form by giving the buyer a $500 credit at closing
The listing agent should have filled out the PCDS for the seller as part of the listing
blocks.x: New York's Property Condition Disclosure Act applies to 1 to 4 family residential sales and excludes condominium units and co-op apartments. A condo buyer's protection is the attorney's review of the offering plan, financials, and minutes, plus the rule that no agent may misstate facts. The $500 credit is the trap: that opt-out was eliminated for contracts after March 20, 2024. And agents never complete the seller's disclosure form.

blocks.html: There is one more physical fact to run down. Leo's inspector, hired even though the seller owes no condition form, notices fresh paint on a 3-foot patch of the second bedroom ceiling, directly under the 9th floor unit's bathroom. A moisture meter reads normal today. Jordan emails Carla and asks whether there has been any leak into 8C. Carla calls back instead of writing. "Off the record, there was a leak from 9C last winter. Monica had it patched and painted. She asked me not to bring it up. It's fixed, so it doesn't matter, right?"

blocks.q: What are Carla's obligations regarding the leak from 9C?
c: Nothing, since condo sellers owe no disclosure and the leak was repaired
To keep it confidential, since Monica gave a lawful instruction about it
To disclose it once Leo submits a written inquiry under RPL 443-a
To disclose it, since a seller's agent owes buyers known material defects
blocks.x: The PCDS exemption for condos does not excuse agents from honesty. A seller's agent must disclose known material defects to buyers, and a recent leak from the unit above, painted over, is material: it can recur, and it raises questions about the building's plumbing and who paid. Monica's instruction to stay quiet is not lawful, so obedience does not cover it. The 443-a inquiry process is for psychological stigma, not physical defects.

blocks.html: Jordan tells Carla that Leo will need the details in writing, and Carla, realizing what she had been asked to do, gets Monica's permission and sends the plumber's invoice and the managing agent's incident report. The leak was a failed wax ring on 9C's toilet, repaired by 9C's owner, with no further claims. Leo's attorney adds a representation to the contract that the seller knows of no other water infiltration. Painting over a known defect and staying silent is concealment, sometimes called negative fraud, and it can unwind a deal after closing just as surely as a spoken lie.

Leo offers $570,000, citing the $27,600 assessment. Carla calls Jordan back the same evening and, sounding tired, overshares. "Look, between us, the seller's in the middle of a divorce. She needs this closed by June or her lawyer's going to kill her. Can your guy come up?"

blocks.q: What should Jordan do with Carla's remark about the seller's divorce and June deadline?
c: Keep it to herself, since Carla said it in confidence between agents
Pass it on to Leo, because it is material to his negotiating position
Report it to the seller, so she knows her agent revealed private facts
Ignore it, since a seller's personal life is not a fact about the property
blocks.x: Jordan owes Carla and the seller honesty, not confidentiality. Leo is the client, and the seller's deadline is material to how hard he can push, so disclosure requires passing it on. The trap is "between us": a promise one agent asks of another cannot override a duty to the agent's own client. Carla is the one who breached a fiduciary duty, to her client; it is not Jordan's role to manage that relationship.

blocks.html: Leo holds at $575,000 with a June 15 closing. The seller accepts, with the assessment to be paid by the buyer going forward, priced into the deal. Before the contract goes out, the seller, reaching out directly because Carla is out sick, emails Jordan.

blocks.title: The seller's email to Jordan
blocks.html: "Hi Jordan, Carla's out this week. I need to know this is real before I turn away other buyers. Is your client's job secure? Is the money definitely there? I can't afford another deal falling apart. Thanks, Monica"

blocks.q: How should Jordan answer Monica's questions about Leo's job and money?
c: "His job is secure and the money is there, so you can turn the others away."
"He's reorganizing at work, but I expect he'll keep his job and close."
"He has a pre-approval for this deal. I can't discuss his finances."
"I'd rather not answer, but you should keep other buyers on hold for now."
blocks.x: Jordan cannot breach Leo's confidence by revealing the reorganization, and cannot lie to Monica by calling the job secure. The honest middle path is to state what is true and shareable (the pre-approval) and decline the rest. The trap is reassurance: an agent who tells a customer something false to save a deal commits misrepresentation. Monica, who is represented, should route questions through Carla, and Jordan can say so too.

blocks.title: Confidential does not mean you can lie
blocks.html: Exam items pair these two duties to catch people. Confidentiality lets you say "I can't discuss that." It never lets you say something false. A buyer's agent who tells a seller "he has plenty of cash" to protect a client's secret has traded a confidentiality problem for a misrepresentation problem, and the second one costs licenses. When the truthful answer would hurt the client, decline to answer.

A week before contract signing, a neighbor in the elevator tells Leo, kindly, that the previous owner of 8C, Monica's late father, from whom she inherited it, died in the apartment two years ago. Leo is not superstitious, but his mother is. He asks Jordan to find out whether it is true and how it happened.

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle Leo's question about a death in the unit?
c: Tell Leo the seller is required to disclose any death in the home on request
Tell Leo the topic is off limits, since the law forbids questions about deaths
Ask the neighbor for details, since the seller's side has no duty to respond
Send a written inquiry to Carla; the seller decides whether to answer it
blocks.x: Under RPL 443-a a death, natural or otherwise, is not a material fact that must be disclosed. If it matters to the buyer, the buyer or buyer's agent may submit a written inquiry to the seller's agent, and the seller decides whether to answer; the agent reports the answer only with the seller's consent. The trap is assuming a duty to disclose on request. The law limits disclosure duties, not questions.

blocks.title: RPL 443-a in practice
blocks.html: The statute covers homicide, suicide, other deaths, felonies on the property, and an occupant's HIV/AIDS or other illness highly unlikely to be transmitted through occupancy. No lawsuit lies against the seller, the seller's agent, or the buyer's agent for not disclosing these facts, and not disclosing them is not grounds for license discipline. The buyer's tool is the written inquiry during negotiation. The seller may decline. Nobody may lie.

Monica answers through Carla, in writing: her father died peacefully of natural causes in 2023. Leo's mother is satisfied. The contract is signed with a $57,500 down payment, the 10% customary in New York City, held in escrow by Monica's attorney.

blocks.text: How Jordan is paid, and after the closing

blocks.html: At contract signing Leo asks a question Jordan should have welcomed earlier: "How exactly do you get paid on this? Do you make more if I pay more?" Under Leo's buyer agreement, Hudson & Hart's fee is 2.5% of the price, paid at closing out of the seller's proceeds as negotiated in the contract, with Leo responsible for any shortfall.

blocks.q: How should Jordan answer Leo's question about compensation?
c: Explain the 2.5% fee, who pays it, and how price affects it
Say the seller pays, so the fee does not affect Leo's interests
Decline, since compensation terms are between the brokers
Say the fee is flat, which is how most buyer agreements work
blocks.x: How the agent is paid is a material fact to the client, because a percentage fee creates a built-in pull toward a higher price. Disclosure means saying so plainly. The trap is "the seller pays": payment source does not determine agency, and Leo's agreement makes him responsible for any shortfall anyway. Leo is a party to his own buyer agreement, so its terms are not a private matter between brokers.

blocks.html: The deal closes June 12. The sidewalk shed is up, the first assessment bill arrives in September, and Leo has already put it in a new spreadsheet tab.
