His team survived the reorganization, which means the secret he worried about never mattered to the deal. It still mattered to the duty: Jordan protected it for six weeks without once saying anything false to Monica or Carla, and that is the whole skill. The client's secret stays in; the truth about the property comes out; and nothing untrue gets said to anyone. In August, at a Hudson & Hart barbecue, Marcus asks Jordan how the Riverdale deal went. "Fine," Jordan says. "Buyer almost walked. Something about his job." Marcus raises an eyebrow. Diane, standing behind them, raises two.

blocks.q: Did Jordan's comment at the barbecue breach a duty to Leo, now that the deal has closed?
c: No, since the agency ended at closing and Marcus is a colleague in the firm
No, because Jordan gave no names, so nothing identifying was revealed
Yes, since confidentiality outlasts the agency and covers casual remarks
Yes, if Marcus then repeats it to someone outside the brokerage
blocks.x: Most fiduciary duties end with the agency, but confidentiality survives it. Leo's job situation was shared in confidence, and it stays protected after closing, including in casual talk with colleagues who never worked the deal. Saying "the buyer" while telling the story of a deal everyone in the office knows is not anonymous. The trap is the end of the agency: closing ends most duties, not this one.

items: Disclosure runs to the client: pass along material facts you learn, even unconfirmed ones, labeled as such, with a way to verify them.
Confidentiality protects the client's budget, deadlines, and personal pressures, and it survives the end of the agency.
Honesty runs to everyone. When the truth would hurt your client, decline to answer; never say something false.
A false statement of fact is innocent, negligent, or intentional depending on what the agent knew or should have known, and the consequences scale from rescission to revocation.
Under RPL 443-a, deaths, felonies, and non-transmissible illness are not material facts; a buyer may ask in writing, and the seller decides whether to answer.
A client is entitled to know how the agent is paid, because the fee structure can pull against the client's interest.

lessons.title: Case file: The Check in the Glovebox
lessons.tagline: An upstate deposit, a broker short on rent, a two-family that might be one, and a plumber's generous offer. Accounting and reasonable care, in Saratoga Springs.
objectives: Apply 19 NYCRR 175.1 deposit rules to a buyer's check from receipt to release
Decide how a broker must handle escrow interest, a deposit dispute, and duplicate originals
Apply 175.3 and GOL 7-103 to a managing broker's rebates and tenant security deposits
Evaluate whether an agent's marketing claims and advice meet the duty of reasonable care

blocks.title: Friday, 4:40 p.m., East Side
blocks.html: Hannah Cole, two years licensed, works for Spa City Realty in Saratoga Springs under broker Tom Brennan. Her listing is a Victorian on the East Side, marketed as a "legal two-family, live in one, rent the other," at $585,000. On a Friday afternoon, buyers Ellen and Raj Mehta sit at the seller's dining table and sign a purchase offer Hannah prepared on the regional association's form, with an attorney approval contingency. They hand her a $10,000 check payable to Spa City Realty's escrow account. Hannah drops the envelope in her glovebox, drives to her daughter's soccer game, and figures she will get to the bank sometime next week. The seller, Gary Duquette, signs the acceptance that evening. Upstate, unlike in New York City, it is common for the broker, not an attorney, to hold that first deposit. Which means the duty to account for it is Hannah's firm's.

The duty to account (accounting) is the least glamorous of the six fiduciary duties and the one DOS enforces most mechanically. It means safeguarding money and documents that belong to others, keeping them separate, and delivering them to whoever is entitled. In New York the rules are written down in 19 NYCRR Part 175, and they apply whether or not a client complains. DOS auditors do not ask whether anyone lost money. They ask where the money was on each day, who could touch it, and whether the paper matches the bank statement. A broker whose escrow ledger is a shoebox has violated the rule even if every dollar eventually reached the right person.

blocks.q: Hannah received the check on Friday. Under 19 NYCRR 175.1, what is her deadline, and what about the weekend?
c: Deposit it within three business days, keeping it secure until then
Deposit it within ten days, as long as the check is not lost before then
Hold it uncashed until the attorneys approve, since a deal may still collapse
Deposit it the same day, since any delay is commingling under the rule
blocks.x: Section 175.1 requires deposit in the broker's separate special account within three business days, and until then the money must be kept in a secure location to prevent loss or misappropriation. Receipt on Friday puts the deadline at the end of Wednesday. Holding it until attorney approval is the trap: the rule has no exception for contingent deals. An envelope in an unlocked glovebox at a soccer field is not a secure location.

blocks.html: Tom, hearing about the glovebox on Saturday, drives to Hannah's house, takes the check, and locks it in the office safe. On Monday morning he deposits it in the firm's escrow account at a federally insured bank, and logs it in the escrow ledger: date received, payer, amount, property, date deposited. Then Tom has a problem of his own.

Spa City Realty's office rent, $4,800, is due Wednesday. Two closings slipped to next month. The operating account holds $1,900. The escrow account holds $46,000 in buyer deposits on five pending deals, including the Mehtas' $10,000. Tom's bookkeeper suggests a short-term transfer. "You'll put it back in two weeks when the Henderson commission comes in. Nobody will even notice."

blocks.q: Can Tom move $3,000 from escrow to the operating account for two weeks?
c: Yes, if he signs a promissory note to the escrow account for the amount
Yes, because his expected commissions exceed the amount he would borrow
No, the deposits belong to others; using them is conversion
No, unless every depositor whose money is in the account agrees in writing
blocks.x: Escrow money is held in trust; it is not the broker's to lend, even to himself and even briefly. Mixing it with firm money is commingling, and spending it on firm expenses is conversion, a ground for revocation and potentially a crime. The trap is the written consent of depositors: buyers who give a deposit for a purchase have not agreed to finance the broker's rent, and a broker should not be asking. Tom borrows from his own savings instead.

blocks.title: 175.1 in one paragraph
blocks.html: A broker may not commingle a principal's money with the broker's own. Money held for others goes into a separate, special bank account, federally insured, within three business days of receipt, and stays secure until then. Interest earned on those funds may not be kept by the broker, except that it may be applied to an earned commission with the consent of all parties. Brokers keep transaction records, including escrow records, for at least three years (175.23).

blocks.q: The firm's escrow account earns a little interest. At year end, $380 has accrued. What may Tom do with it?
c: Keep it, since the account is in the brokerage's name and tax ID
Apply it to an earned commission with all parties' consent
Keep it as an administrative fee of 1% per year of the deposits
Donate it to charity, since no single depositor can claim it
blocks.x: Under 175.1, interest on funds held for others may not be kept by or for the broker, except that it may be applied to and deducted from an earned commission with the consent of all parties. The 1% administrative fee is the trap: that is a landlord's allowance on tenant security deposits under GOL 7-103, a different statute for a different kind of money.

blocks.html: On Monday, Raj Mehta emails Hannah. "Can you send us a copy of what we signed? We gave you the only one and our attorney wants it." Hannah had planned to wait until Gary signed and then send everyone the finished version, but that took until Friday night, and she has not sent it yet.

blocks.q: What does 19 NYCRR 175.12 require of Hannah regarding the signed purchase offer?
c: Send a copy when the attorneys finish their review and approve the deal
Send a copy to the buyers' attorney, who then distributes it to the buyers
Keep the original in the file and send copies to anyone who requests them
Promptly give a copy to each person who signed it
blocks.x: Section 175.12 requires a broker to deliver a copy of any instrument the broker prepared, or had prepared, to each person who signs it. Hannah prepared the offer on the association form, so the Mehtas and Gary each get one promptly. The trap is waiting for the attorney review: the duty runs from the signing, not from approval, and parties need their copies precisely so their attorneys can review.

blocks.html: Hannah sends the fully signed offer to the Mehtas, Gary, and both attorneys within the hour, and writes the delivery date in the file. Accounting covers documents as well as dollars.

The Mehtas' attorney, Joan Barrett, starts her review. Two days later she calls Hannah. "Your listing says legal two-family. The city assessment roll lists it as a single-family residence, and the building department has no certificate of occupancy or permit for a second unit. Where did 'legal' come from?" Hannah checks her listing file. The answer is Gary, who told her at the listing appointment that "it's always been a two-family." The second kitchen was put in by Gary's uncle in the 1980s.

blocks.q: Did Hannah meet the duty of reasonable care in advertising the house as a "legal two-family"?
c: Yes, because she repeated what the owner told her in good faith
No, she stated a checkable legal fact without checking it first
Yes, because verifying the legal use is the buyer's attorney's job
No, because agents may not describe a home's use in ads
blocks.x: Reasonable care means the competence and diligence expected of a licensee. "Legal two-family" is a factual claim about legal use that a licensee can verify through the assessment roll and the building department, and it drives the price of a house marketed for rental income. Good-faith reliance on the seller is the trap: repeating an owner's claim without checking, when checking is easy, is what turns an innocent mistake into negligent misrepresentation.

blocks.html: Joan's letter disapproves the contract within the attorney approval period, citing the unpermitted unit. The Mehtas would still buy as a single-family, at a lower price. Gary is angry, mostly at Hannah. Tom pulls the listing photos and ad copy that afternoon and replaces "legal two-family" with "single-family with a second kitchen; buyer to verify legal use," which is accurate, if less exciting. Then Gary calls with a demand.

blocks.q: Gary says the Mehtas "backed out" and demands that Spa City Realty release the $10,000 deposit to him. The escrow clause says the broker holds the deposit until both parties agree in writing or a court orders otherwise. What should Tom do?
c: Release it to Gary, since the seller is the firm's client
Return it to the Mehtas, since their attorney disapproved in time
Keep holding it under the escrow clause and tell both sides
Split it evenly, which is the fair result when both sides object
blocks.x: An escrow holder follows the escrow terms, not loyalty to the client and not its own view of who is right. Here those terms require joint written instructions or a court order. Tom tells both sides where the money is and what release requires. The trap is releasing to the client: Tom is Gary's agent, but as escrow holder he owes a duty to both depositor and payee. Returning it to the Mehtas is probably where it ends up, but only on the clause's terms.

blocks.html: Gary's attorney reads the approval clause, concedes it was exercised on time, and signs a joint release. Tom refunds the $10,000 to the Mehtas the same day and records the release and the outgoing check in the escrow ledger. The deposit is fully accounted for. The relationship with Gary is another matter.

blocks.title: Hannah's new listing checklist
blocks.html: Before any ad goes live: pull the deed and the assessment record (property class, number of units, square footage); ask the building department for the certificate of occupancy or permit history if the ad will mention units, a finished basement, or an addition; check the FEMA flood map; and save printouts of everything in the listing file. If the owner's story and the records disagree, the ad says what the records say, and the owner's story goes to his attorney. Twenty minutes of checking would have saved the Mehta deal from a three-week detour.

blocks.q: Gary asks Hannah, "Is there anything I can do to make the second unit legal? Should I just sell it as-is?" What is the best response?
c: Explain how to get a variance and draft the application for him
Tell him the unit is legal enough to rent, since it has been for decades
Refuse to discuss it, since anything about zoning is legal advice
Give her view of how each option affects price and marketing time
blocks.x: A licensee can and should advise a client on market consequences: what a single-family with a second kitchen sells for, how long legalization might take, and who to talk to (an attorney, an architect, the building department). Drafting land use applications and opining on legal rights is attorney work. Refusing to discuss it at all is the trap: reasonable care includes useful market advice. Calling an unpermitted unit "legal enough" would be a fresh misrepresentation.

blocks.title: Reasonable care is not perfection, and not lawyering
blocks.html: The exam tests both edges. An agent who repeats an owner's factual claim that could easily be checked (square footage from a floor plan, legal use from the assessment roll, flood zone from the FEMA map) has fallen below reasonable care. An agent who drafts contract clauses, interprets title exceptions, or tells a client how to hold title is practicing law, which a licensee may not do. The safe middle: verify facts you state, advise on the market, and send legal questions to a lawyer.

Three weeks later the Mehtas and Gary meet in the middle. Gary, after a talk with his own attorney about what legalizing the unit would cost, accepts $540,000 for the house as a single-family with a second kitchen. Hannah prepares a new purchase offer, delivers copies to everyone who signs it the same day, deposits the Mehtas' new $10,000 check on the next business day, and logs every step. The deal closes in July. Spa City Realty's commission, 5% under the listing, is $27,000, split with no one, since the Mehtas came to the open house without an agent.
In December, Tom decides to clear out a filing cabinet that has been jammed since 2019. The Duquette file is near the top, closed, paid, and done. He reaches for the shredder bag.

blocks.q: Under 19 NYCRR 175.23, how should Tom treat the Duquette file?
c: Shred it, since the deal closed and the commission has been paid
Keep it at least three years: listing, offer, deposit, and commission
Keep the closing statement for seven years and shred the rest of the file
Send it to the seller's attorney, who is the official record keeper
blocks.x: Section 175.23 requires brokers to keep records of each residential transaction for three years, on paper or electronically: names and addresses of the parties, the contract or binder if the broker prepared it, the deposit amount if the broker collected it, the commission received, the listing agreement, and any document Article 12-A requires, such as the agency disclosure acknowledgment. The trap is that a closed, paid file is finished. Seven years is a tax-records habit, not this rule.

blocks.text: Tom's other business: managing a building

blocks.html: Spa City Realty also manages a 12-unit apartment building on Lake Avenue for its owner, Margaret Ellis, who lives in Vermont. The management agreement makes the firm her general agent for the building's ongoing business: collect rents, hold security deposits, hire and pay contractors, and send her a monthly statement with the net. Hannah helps with leasing and maintenance calls. Compare the two jobs: on the Duquette sale the firm was a special agent for one transaction, holding one deposit for a few weeks. On Lake Avenue it handles Margaret's money every single month, which means every accounting rule gets tested twelve times a year.

In March, a plumbing contractor who does most of the building's repairs makes Tom an offer. "You send me all the Lake Avenue work, I'll send you back 10% of every invoice. Call it a referral fee. Your owner pays my normal rate either way."

blocks.q: May Spa City Realty accept the plumber's 10% rebate on work it orders for Margaret's building?
c: No, unless Margaret is told about it fully and agrees to it
Yes, because Margaret pays the same invoice price regardless
Yes, if the plumber reports the payment as a referral fee on a 1099
No, because managing brokers may not hire contractors themselves
blocks.x: Under 19 NYCRR 175.3, a broker managing property may not accept a commission, rebate, or profit on expenditures made for the client without the client's full knowledge and consent. The trap is "same price either way": a secret rebate gives the manager a reason to send work to one contractor rather than shop for the best price, which is exactly the loyalty and accounting problem the rule targets. With full disclosure, Margaret could choose to allow it or take the 10% herself.

blocks.html: Tom declines and tells Margaret about the offer anyway. She asks him to get competing bids on the next big job. Then Hannah, signing a new tenant to Unit 4, takes a $1,650 security deposit and asks Tom where it goes.

blocks.q: Where must the Unit 4 security deposit be held?
c: In Spa City Realty's operating account, since the firm manages the building
In Margaret's personal savings account, since she owns the building
In the sales escrow account, together with buyers' purchase deposits
In an interest-bearing NY bank account, with written notice to the tenant
blocks.x: GOL 7-103 makes a security deposit the tenant's money, held in trust and not commingled. Buildings with six or more units must place deposits in an interest-bearing account at a bank in New York, and the tenant gets written notice of the bank and amount. The landlord may keep 1% a year for administrative costs; the rest of the interest belongs to the tenant. Section 175.3 makes a managing broker follow the same rules. The trap is the sales escrow account: different money, different purposes.

blocks.title: Margaret's April statement
blocks.html:
Rents collected (12 units): $19,860
Less: plumbing repair, Unit 7 (bid of three): $1,240
Less: hallway lighting: $385
Less: management fee per agreement (6% of collections): $1,191.60
Less: "Leasing bonus, Unit 4": $1,650
Net to owner: $15,393.40

blocks.q: Margaret's management agreement provides a 6% fee and nothing else. What is wrong with the April statement?
c: The $1,650 leasing bonus is not in the agreement
The 6% fee should be computed on net rents, not on collections
The plumbing repair needs Margaret's approval before it is listed
The statement should not show expenses, just the net amount sent
blocks.x: Section 175.2 requires a broker to render an account to the client within a reasonable time and pay over money collected for the client that the broker has not spent on the client's behalf. A leasing bonus the agreement does not provide is the client's money taken without authority. The trap is the fee base: 6% of collections matches the agreement as stated. Showing every expense is what an accounting is; netting them out silently would be the problem.

blocks.html: The "bonus" turns out to be the bookkeeper's mistake: Hannah's commission on the new lease was supposed to come out of the firm's management fee, not Margaret's rents. Tom corrects the statement, sends Margaret the $1,650 with an explanation, and changes the firm's procedure so that he reviews every owner statement before it goes out. Accounting errors that are found and fixed promptly, with an honest explanation, are a management problem. The same errors hidden or repeated are a license problem.

In May, Margaret asks Hannah to sell a small strip of four storefronts she owns in Glens Falls. Hannah has never sold commercial property, never read a commercial lease abstract, and does not know how to value an income property beyond what she half remembers from her licensing course.

blocks.q: What does reasonable care require of Hannah when offered a listing outside her experience?
c: Take it alone, since a salesperson license covers every property type
Decline it, since salespersons are limited to residential sales
Take it with help from an experienced agent, or refer it out
Take it, and tell Margaret about her inexperience after it closes
blocks.x: Reasonable care means the competence the task requires. A license authorizes commercial work, but an agent who lacks the skill must get it, by working with an experienced colleague under the broker's supervision, or refer the client to someone who has it. The trap is that the license allows it: permission is not competence. Salespersons may handle commercial deals, and disclosing inexperience after the fact defeats the point.

head: Event
Duty
What fixed it
rows: Locked in safe, deposited within three business days
No escrow "loans"; broker used own funds
Copies to every signer the same day
Ad corrected; verify legal use before stating it
blocks.caption: Spa City Realty's spring, in one table

items: Money held for others goes into a separate, federally insured escrow account within three business days, kept secure until then, and is never borrowed or mixed with the broker's funds.
Escrow interest is not the broker's; it may be applied to an earned commission only with the consent of all parties.
A broker gives every signer a copy of any instrument the broker prepared, promptly (175.12), and renders an account and pays over client money within a reasonable time (175.2).
An escrow holder follows the escrow terms, not its client's demands, when a deposit is disputed.
A managing broker may not keep rebates or profits on client expenses without full disclosure and consent (175.3), and tenant security deposits follow GOL 7-103.
Reasonable care means verifying facts you state, giving market advice without practicing law, and getting help or referring work beyond your competence.

lessons.title: Case file: The Nephew with the Keys
lessons.tagline: A Ridgewood storefront, a coffee entrepreneur, and a landlord who swears her nephew never worked for her. How agency gets made, on purpose and by accident.
objectives: Decide how a licensee chooses whom to represent and how express agency is formed for a commercial lease
Distinguish implied agency, ratification, and estoppel on a set of mixed facts
Apply the difference between agency and brokerage, including a non-agency role under RPL 443
Determine who owes a commission and why payment does not decide representation

blocks.title: A sign on Myrtle Avenue
blocks.html: Rosa Delgado has run a coffee cart near the Forest Avenue M stop for six years. She is ready for a real store. On Myrtle Avenue in Ridgewood, Queens, she finds a vacant 900-square-foot storefront in a three-story mixed-use building with apartments above. The sign in the window reads FOR RENT, CALL DANNY, with a cell number. Before she calls, she calls Jordan, whom she met when Jordan was still pulling espresso shots in Jackson Heights. "Can you help me get this place? I don't know what I'm doing with commercial leases." The building is owned by Evelyn Park, an investor with retail and office property in three boroughs. Danny is her nephew. Jordan has no agreement with anyone yet. That is the first problem.

blocks.text: Before the first conversation about money

blocks.html: Agency is a relationship; brokerage is a business. A licensee can be in the business of bringing landlords and tenants together without yet being anyone's agent. The relationship starts when someone agrees, in words or by conduct, that the licensee will act on their behalf. So before Jordan says a word to Rosa about rent, Jordan has to answer the question the syllabus asks: whom do I represent here, and how do I decide?

blocks.q: Rosa wants Jordan's help. Hudson & Hart has no agreement with Evelyn. What is Jordan's best first step?
c: Call Danny and ask to list the space for Evelyn, then show it to Rosa
Check firm policy, then offer Rosa a written tenant representation agreement
Start advising Rosa on rent and sort out the paperwork after she signs a lease
Help Rosa without any role, since commercial leases have no agency rules
blocks.x: An agent decides whom to represent from the firm's written policy, any existing agreements, and the facts. Here Rosa asked for help, and the firm has no tie to Evelyn, so the clean path is express tenant agency in writing. Advising first and papering later is the trap: advice creates an agency by conduct with none of its terms settled. Commercial deals fall outside RPL 443's disclosure form, but agency law and fiduciary duties apply fully.

blocks.html: Rosa signs Hudson & Hart's exclusive tenant representation agreement that afternoon. It names Hudson & Hart as her agent to find and negotiate a retail lease in Ridgewood and Bushwick for six months. Jordan also hands her New York's Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form, which, unlike the agency disclosure form, applies to commercial property too.

blocks.q: Which New York disclosure forms belong in Rosa's file for this commercial lease?
c: The RPL 443 agency disclosure form alone, since Rosa is now a client
Both the RPL 443 agency form and the fair housing disclosure form
No forms, since commercial tenants are sophisticated parties
The fair housing disclosure form, but not the RPL 443 agency form
blocks.x: The RPL 443 agency disclosure form is required for residential 1 to 4 family sales and residential rentals, not commercial leases. The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (19 NYCRR 175.28) covers all property types, commercial included, at first substantive contact. The trap is giving both: harmless in practice, but the question is what the law requires. The fiduciary duties Hudson & Hart owes Rosa are the same either way; the forms only document them.

blocks.title: Compensation clause, Rosa's agreement
blocks.html: "Broker's fee: an amount equal to 10% of the first year's base rent under any lease Tenant signs during the term. Broker will first seek payment from the landlord. If the landlord does not agree in writing to pay the fee, Tenant shall pay it at lease signing."

blocks.q: Rosa asks, "Is 10% the standard fee for commercial leases?" What is the accurate answer?
c: Yes, the Real Estate Board sets 10% as the standard rate for retail leases
No, the state sets a 6% maximum on commercial lease commissions
No, fees are set by agreement between the broker and the client
Yes, the MLS publishes standard rates that every broker has to honor
blocks.x: No law, board, or listing service sets commission rates. Each broker sets its own fees and negotiates them with the client; Rosa could have asked for a different number. The trap is the "standard" rate: describing a fee as set by a board or as what everyone charges suggests price coordination among competitors, the antitrust problem the syllabus pairs with compensation. There is no state cap on commissions either.

blocks.html: Jordan calls the number on the sign. Danny Park, 26, meets them at the storefront with a ring of keys. He has been the face of the building for a year: he shows the vacant units, hands applications to prospective tenants, quotes rents, and texts Evelyn when something breaks. Evelyn has seen his sign in her window every time she visits. He says he does not get paid. "I'm just helping my aunt."

Danny walks them through the space and makes an offer on the spot. "Aunt Evelyn wants $6,500 a month. Sign a five-year lease and I can give you the first three months free while you build out. She's done that before." He puts it in a text to Jordan: $6,500/mo, 5 yrs, 3 months free rent, OK from Evelyn. Rosa, thrilled, says she is ordering a $14,000 espresso machine tonight so it arrives in time for a summer opening.

blocks.q: What should Jordan advise Rosa before she orders the machine on the strength of Danny's text?
c: Wait for Evelyn to confirm the terms and for a signed lease
Order it, since Danny's text is a binding offer from the owner
Order it, but ask Danny to sign the text so it counts as a lease
Order it, since an oral lease for five years is enforceable
blocks.x: Reasonable care for a tenant client includes flagging authority risk: nothing binds the owner until the owner, or someone with real authority, signs. Danny's role so far is opening doors and relaying numbers, and a text from a relative is not a lease. The trap is Danny's signature: a signature from someone without authority adds nothing. A five-year lease must be in writing under the statute of frauds, so an oral deal would not hold either.

blocks.html: Rosa thanks Jordan for the advice and orders it anyway. "If I wait, I lose the summer." That is her call to make. Jordan notes the advice in an email to her and moves on.

blocks.q: Danny is not licensed. Is his activity, by itself, a violation of the license law?
c: Yes, quoting rents and showing space for another requires a broker license
No, because the license law covers sales, not rentals or leases
Not as described, since a license is needed to act for another for a fee
Yes, unless he registers with DOS as an unlicensed leasing assistant
blocks.x: RPL 440 defines a broker as one who, for another and for a fee, commission, or other valuable consideration, lists, rents, negotiates, or collects rent. An unpaid relative helping a family owner falls outside the definition as long as he is truly unpaid. The trap is the first choice, which drops the fee element. Leasing is fully covered by the license law, and there is no DOS registration for unlicensed leasing assistants.

blocks.html: Jordan forwards Danny's text to Evelyn's office to confirm. Evelyn calls back the next day, cool and precise. "Danny opens doors. He doesn't negotiate. The rent is $7,500, and nobody gets free rent from me. I never authorized any of that." Rosa's espresso machine is already on a truck from Milan.

blocks.q: Can Rosa argue that Evelyn is bound by Danny's terms even though Evelyn never authorized them?
c: No, because authority to negotiate a lease needs a written agreement
Yes, by ratification, since Evelyn approved Danny's role after the fact
No, because an unpaid relative cannot be anyone's agent under New York law
Yes, by estoppel, if Evelyn made his authority look real and Rosa relied
blocks.x: Agency by estoppel arises when a principal lets a third party reasonably believe someone is her agent, and the third party relies on that appearance. Evelyn let Danny run showings and quote rents in her name for a year, with her own sign in the window. Ratification is the trap: Evelyn has done the opposite of approving Danny's terms. Whether a court enforces them depends on how reasonable Rosa's reliance was, which is a fact question.

blocks.title: Estoppel looks at appearances, ratification looks back
blocks.html: Ratification: the principal learns of an unauthorized act and approves it, by words or by accepting its benefits; the act is treated as authorized from the start. Estoppel (apparent or ostensible authority): the principal's own words or conduct made it reasonable for a third party to believe the person had authority, and the third party relied to its detriment; the principal cannot deny the agency. Ratification needs the principal's approval. Estoppel needs the principal's conduct and the third party's reliance.
Two days after Evelyn's call, Rosa's contractor offers her a deal on $8,000 of custom cabinetry if she commits this week. "Danny's text says three months free. I'm covered, right?"

blocks.q: Can Rosa rely on Danny's terms for the new $8,000 commitment?
c: No, once Evelyn denied his authority, new reliance is unreasonable
Yes, since estoppel binds Evelyn to Danny's terms going forward
Yes, because Evelyn has not yet put her denial of authority in writing
No, because estoppel requires a written agreement to be enforced
blocks.x: Estoppel protects reliance that was reasonable when it happened. After Evelyn told Jordan, Rosa's agent, that Danny had no authority to negotiate, Rosa knows the truth, and anything she spends on Danny's terms from now on is at her own risk. The trap is the missing writing: an oral denial is enough to end reasonable reliance. Estoppel needs no written agreement; that is the whole point of the doctrine.

blocks.html: Jordan does not want Rosa in a lawsuit over an espresso machine. The better play is negotiation. Jordan uses Danny's text, and the year of Evelyn's tolerance of his role, as leverage. Meanwhile, Danny's authority problem turns out to have a second chapter, upstairs.

While Jordan and Rosa wait in the storefront, a young couple arrives to see the vacant second-floor apartment. Danny shows it. Without telling Evelyn, he accepts their $2,400 deposit and first month's rent and hands them a lease he printed from the internet, signing it "for E. Park." When Evelyn learns of it a week later, she is furious, then pragmatic: she deposits the check, lets the couple move in on the first, and starts sending them her own rent invoices.

blocks.q: Evelyn never authorized Danny to sign that lease. Is she bound by it now?
c: No, because Danny signed without authority and the lease is void
Yes, she ratified it by keeping the money
Yes, by estoppel, since the couple believed Danny was the owner
No, unless Evelyn signs a new lease on the same terms herself
blocks.x: Ratification occurs when a principal, knowing of an unauthorized act, accepts its benefits or otherwise approves it. Depositing the money and treating the couple as tenants is approval by conduct, and it binds Evelyn as if Danny had been authorized from the start. Estoppel is the trap here: it rests on the appearance of authority before the act, while these facts show Evelyn's approval after it, which is the cleaner and stronger ground.

blocks.html: The couple, Mira and Tomás, now have a lease of uncertain quality and questions. Standing in the hallway, Tomás asks Jordan, since Jordan is "obviously a broker," whether the internet lease is any good, whether they should ask Evelyn for a rent reduction, and how much to ask for.

blocks.q: Jordan represents Rosa, not Mira and Tomás. How should Jordan respond to Tomás in the hallway?
c: Answer his questions, since helping people is good practice and costs nothing
Advise them to ask for a $200 reduction, since Evelyn wants to avoid a dispute
Tell them to call Danny, since he is the landlord's agent for the building
Say Jordan doesn't represent them and decline to advise them
blocks.x: Implied agency can arise from conduct: an agent who advises someone on what to offer and how to negotiate may be found to be their agent, with duties Jordan could not perform without conflicts. Jordan should say who Jordan represents and decline. The tempting answer is helping for free: free advice is still advice. Using what Jordan knows about Evelyn's mood to coach them is worse, and calling Danny the landlord's agent would misstate his status.

blocks.html: Jordan tells Tomás, kindly, "I represent the tenant downstairs, so I can't advise you. A lawyer can look at that lease in twenty minutes, or you can hire your own agent." Tomás is a little offended, then grateful when his cousin's attorney finds the internet lease missing the lead paint disclosure the building's 1920s age requires and a security deposit clause that conflicts with state law. Evelyn's attorney replaces it with a proper lease. Had Jordan coached Tomás instead, Jordan would have been negotiating against Evelyn for two parties in the same building at once, with confidential information from one possibly helping the other.

blocks.title: Four ways an agency comes into being

left.title: On purpose
items: Express: Rosa's signed tenant representation agreement
Express can be oral, but exclusive arrangements belong in writing
Ratification: Evelyn keeps the upstairs rent after learning of Danny's lease

right.title: By accident
items: Implied: an agent who coaches Tomás on his rent negotiation
Estoppel: a year of Danny quoting rents with Evelyn's knowledge
Both bind the principal without a signed agreement

blocks.text: Negotiating with an owner who negotiates herself

blocks.html: Evelyn agrees to meet. She owns a dozen buildings and has never paid a tenant's broker. She opens with a proposal Jordan has not heard before. "I don't want an agent. I want someone to run the paperwork: collect the documents, coordinate the attorneys, keep the timeline. I'll negotiate for myself. Can your firm do that for me on my other vacancies?"

blocks.q: Can a New York licensee assist Evelyn with paperwork and coordination without becoming her agent?
c: No, any licensed activity for another automatically makes the licensee her agent
Yes, by written agreement to act in a capacity other than agent, owing her honesty
Yes, but the licensee then owes her the six fiduciary duties regardless of the agreement
No, because New York law requires every licensee to be a single or dual agent
blocks.x: Agency and brokerage are not the same thing. RPL 443 itself recognizes a licensee who works with a party, under agreed terms, "in a capacity other than as an agent." Such a licensee owes honesty and fair dealing but not loyalty, confidentiality, or advice. The trap is the automatic-agency answer: agency comes from an agreement or from conduct, and a clear written non-agency arrangement, honored in practice, avoids it. Hudson & Hart cannot take that role while representing Rosa against Evelyn, though.

blocks.html: Jordan tells Evelyn the firm will consider that arrangement for her other buildings but not for this deal, because Hudson & Hart is Rosa's agent here and owes Rosa undivided loyalty. Evelyn shrugs. Then she negotiates hard. Watching her, Jordan sees why the non-agency role exists: Evelyn knows the market better than most brokers and wants no one speaking for her. What she lacks is time. A licensee in a non-agency role gives her the time without the fiduciary relationship, and both sides know exactly what they are getting.

head: Term
Danny's text
Evelyn's opening
Signed lease
blocks.caption: How Rosa's lease got made

blocks.html: Danny's text did its work as leverage. Evelyn's attorney told her that a year of letting Danny run her vacancies would make an estoppel argument expensive to litigate, and two months of free rent was cheaper than finding out. Rosa signs a seven-year lease, reviewed by her own attorney. Her espresso machine fits.

First-year base rent: $6,900 x 12 = $82,800. Under Rosa's agreement, the fee is 10% of that, $8,280. In retail leasing, landlords often do pay tenant brokers, because a filled storefront raises the value of the whole building, and many landlords budget for it. But nothing requires them to, and Evelyn has made a career of not paying. Jordan, as instructed by the agreement, first asks Evelyn to pay it. Evelyn refuses. "I never hired you." Diane gets a call from Rosa: "Wait, if I'm paying, does that change anything? Were you working for me the whole time?"

blocks.q: Evelyn refuses to pay the $8,280 fee. Who owes it, and does that change whom Hudson & Hart represented?
c: Evelyn owes it, because Hudson & Hart was the procuring cause of the lease
No one owes it, since the landlord refused and there was no listing agreement
Rosa owes it under her agreement, and Hudson & Hart represented her throughout
Rosa owes it, which makes Hudson & Hart her agent from the moment she pays
blocks.x: A commission is owed by the party who agreed to pay it. Evelyn never agreed, so procuring cause gives Hudson & Hart no claim against her; procuring cause decides which broker earned a fee someone agreed to pay, not who must pay. Rosa's agreement makes her responsible if the landlord declines. Who pays has no bearing on whom the firm represents: Rosa was the client from the day she signed.

blocks.title: Getting paid in New York: three rules that matter here
blocks.html: A broker must hold a license when the services are performed to sue for a commission (RPL 442-d). New York's statute of frauds generally requires a written agreement to pay a finder's or negotiation fee for real estate, but it expressly exempts licensed real estate brokers and salespersons (GOL 5-701(a)(10)), so a broker's oral fee agreement can be enforced. Still, a written agreement is what proves the terms, which is why Diane never starts work without one.

blocks.title: "The seller pays, so the agent works for the seller"
blocks.html: Exam writers love this one. Payment does not create agency, and it does not decide representation. A tenant's agent paid by the landlord still represents the tenant. A buyer's agent paid from the seller's proceeds still represents the buyer. The question is always: who agreed, by words or conduct, to have this licensee act for them?

blocks.q: Looking back, which event created Hudson & Hart's agency for Rosa?
c: Her signing the written tenant representation agreement
Her first phone call asking Jordan for help with the lease
Evelyn's refusal to pay, which left Rosa paying the fee
Jordan's first negotiation with Evelyn on Rosa's behalf
blocks.x: Express agency was created when Rosa signed the agreement naming Hudson & Hart as her agent. The phone call is the trap: asking for help can be the start of an implied agency if the licensee starts acting for the person, but here Jordan deliberately papered the relationship before advising. Who ends up paying does not create or change the agency, and negotiating for Rosa was performance of an agency already in place.

blocks.html: Rosa pays the fee at lease signing, without complaint once Diane walks her through it. She had read the clause when she signed; she had simply hoped Evelyn would pay. Diane's lesson for Jordan: explain the fee fallback at the first meeting, not the last one. Danny gets a new job, unrelated to real estate. Evelyn takes his sign out of the window and, two weeks later, calls Diane to ask about that non-agency paperwork arrangement for her Bushwick vacancies. Diane says yes, in writing, with a clause spelling out exactly what the firm will and will not do.

items: Decide whom you represent before discussing money: firm policy, existing agreements, and the facts, then put the relationship in writing.
Express agency is created by agreement; implied agency by conduct, such as advising someone on what to offer.
Ratification is the principal's later approval, often by keeping the benefits; estoppel binds a principal whose conduct made someone's authority look real to a third party who relied on it.
Agency and brokerage are different: by written agreement a NY licensee may assist a party in a capacity other than agent, owing honesty but not fiduciary duties.
Commissions are owed by whoever agreed to pay them and are set by negotiation, never by a board or a standard rate; who pays does not decide whom the broker represents.
The license law reaches people who act for another for a fee. An unpaid relative is outside it, but his conduct can still bind the owner through estoppel.

lessons.title: Case file: The Group Chat on the South Shore
lessons.tagline: A flat-fee competitor arrives in Nassau County, and a friendly agents' chat turns into a federal case in about forty messages.
objectives: Identify price fixing, group boycotts, market allocation, and tie-ins in informal agent conversations
Decide how a licensee should respond when competitors raise fees, territories, or a rival firm
Distinguish a single firm's lawful business decisions from unlawful agreements among competitors
Apply antitrust rules and fiduciary duties together to buyer-agent compensation after the NAR settlement

blocks.title: Massapequa, a Tuesday in February
blocks.html: Hudson & Hart has opened a small branch on Merrick Road in Massapequa, and Diane sends Jordan out two days a week to build a Long Island book. Within a week, a friendly broker named Bob Kessler adds Jordan to a group chat called "South Shore Agents," 38 members from a dozen firms between Bellmore and Amityville. It is mostly open house announcements, contractor recommendations, and photos of bagels. Then FlatList, a flat-fee brokerage that lists homes for $5,000 regardless of price, opens an office on Sunrise Highway. At 9:14 p.m. on a Tuesday, Bob posts: "FlatList is going to wreck this market. We need to talk about it." Forty messages follow before midnight. Jordan reads them all the next morning, coffee going cold, and realizes that a few of them could end careers.

blocks.text: Why brokers are an antitrust risk

blocks.html: Competing brokers in one town know each other, refer to each other, and cooperate on half their deals. That closeness is what makes real estate a classic antitrust setting. The federal Sherman Act and New York's Donnelly Act (General Business Law 340) outlaw agreements among competitors that restrain trade. An agreement does not need a contract or even a handshake. Courts infer it from communications followed by parallel conduct. And the people at risk are individuals as well as firms: the salesperson who types "agreed" can be named in a lawsuit or an indictment personally, not just the company whose name is on the door. In United States v. Foley (4th Cir. 1979), Maryland brokers were convicted of conspiring to fix commissions after one announced at a dinner that he was raising his rate to 7%, and the others followed within months.

blocks.title: From the South Shore Agents chat (excerpts)
blocks.html:
Bob Kessler (Kessler Homes): FlatList is going to wreck this market. We need to talk about it.
Theresa Nolan (Nolan Realty): If we all hold at 6 they can't undercut everybody. Nobody go below 6. Agreed?
Marcus Webb (Hudson & Hart): 👍 6 is the number.
Bob Kessler: And nobody show their listings. Let their sellers sit.
Vikram Shah (Shah Properties): Honestly we should stop stepping on each other too. Kessler takes Massapequa Park, I'll take Bellmore and Wantagh, Theresa takes Seaford.
Theresa Nolan: Works for me. Jordan, you in?

blocks.q: Theresa asks Jordan directly, "You in?" What is Jordan's best response?
c: Stay silent, since Jordan did not agree to anything and silence is not consent
Say Jordan won't discuss fees or other firms, leave, and tell Diane
Reply with a thumbs up to stay friendly, then set fees independently anyway
Reply that Hudson & Hart already charges 6%, so the agreement changes nothing
blocks.x: Price fixing, boycotts, and market allocation are agreements, and staying in the conversation while others agree can be read as joining. The safe response is a clear, written refusal, an exit, and a report to the broker so the firm can document its independence. The trap is silence: a member who stays quiet in a chat where everyone else agrees, and then charges the agreed rate, looks like a participant. A thumbs up is worse.

blocks.html: Jordan posts: "I'm not going to discuss commissions or other firms' listings here. Leaving the group." Then Jordan forwards the screenshots to Diane. Diane reads them in silence, then calls Marcus into her office and closes the door.

blocks.q: Theresa's "Nobody go below 6. Agreed?" and Marcus's thumbs up are best described as:
c: Price fixing: competitors agreeing on commission rates
Lawful information sharing, since 6% was already the common rate
A group boycott, since it targets a single discount competitor
Market allocation, since it divides the market by price level
blocks.x: Price fixing is any agreement among competitors about the price of their services, including a floor on commissions. It does not matter that 6% was common before: agreeing to hold it is the violation. The boycott answer is the trap because FlatList is the target, but this message is about the rate competitors will charge. The next message, refusing to show FlatList listings, is the boycott.

blocks.q: Bob's "nobody show their listings" message proposes:
c: A tie-in, since showings are tied to commission levels
A lawful choice, since each broker decides which homes to show
A group boycott of a competing brokerage
Market allocation, since it divides listings by firm
blocks.x: A group boycott is an agreement among competitors to refuse to deal with another competitor, often a discounter, to drive it out. Each broker choosing alone is one thing; brokers agreeing together to freeze out FlatList is the violation. The lawful choice answer is the trap: the word "nobody" turns individual decisions into a collective one, and for buyer's agents it also collides with their duty to show clients suitable homes.

blocks.q: Vikram's "Kessler takes Massapequa Park, I'll take Bellmore and Wantagh, Theresa takes Seaford" is:
c: Lawful specialization, since each firm focuses on what it knows
Price fixing, since it reduces competition on commission rates
A group boycott of firms outside the three named towns
Market allocation, dividing territory among competitors
blocks.x: Market allocation is competitors agreeing to divide territories, customers, or product lines so they stop competing. A firm may choose on its own to focus on Seaford; three firms agreeing to stay out of each other's towns is the violation. Lawful specialization is the trap: the difference is the agreement, not the focus. It also raises prices indirectly, but the label for dividing territory is allocation.

head: Violation
In the chat
What makes it illegal
rows: Competitors agreeing on the price of their services
Competitors agreeing to shut out a rival
Selling one thing only on the condition that the buyer takes another
blocks.caption: Three of the four, in one evening

blocks.title: New York's own antitrust law
blocks.html: The Donnelly Act (General Business Law 340) mirrors the Sherman Act and lets the New York Attorney General and private parties sue in state court. A broker who joins a price-fixing or boycott agreement also risks Department of State discipline for untrustworthiness under RPL 441-c. Federal penalties for individuals under the Sherman Act reach 10 years in prison and $1 million in fines, with triple damages in civil suits.

Marcus is not contrite. "It was a group chat. Nobody signed anything. And Hudson & Hart charges 6% anyway, so what's the harm?" Two weeks later, Jordan notices that every firm in the chat has dropped its listings' advertised "negotiable" language and is quoting 6% to every seller who asks.

blocks.q: If prosecutors looked at the chat and the firms' later conduct, could they prove an agreement without any signed document?
c: No, because antitrust conspiracy requires a written or signed agreement
Yes, communications plus later parallel conduct can prove it
No, because each firm can show it set its rate before the chat took place
Yes, but just against Theresa, who proposed the rate in the first message
blocks.x: Conspiracies are rarely written down. Courts infer agreement from communications followed by matching conduct, as in Foley, where an announcement at a dinner and later identical rate changes were enough. The trap is the signed document: no paperwork is needed. A firm's earlier 6% rate is some evidence of independence, but it does not erase a later agreement to hold that rate. Everyone who joined, including Marcus with his thumbs up, is exposed.

blocks.q: Marcus is still in the chat, and his thumbs up is still there. What is the most protective step for him and the firm?
c: Post a clear withdrawal, leave, and document independent pricing
Delete the thumbs up, so no record of agreement remains
Stay in the chat quietly to monitor what the other firms are planning
Change the firm's rate to 5.5% so its pricing looks independent
blocks.x: Someone who has signaled agreement needs an affirmative, communicated withdrawal, not a quiet exit. Marcus should say plainly in the chat that he and the firm do not agree to any rate or boycott, then leave, and Diane should document how the firm actually sets its fees. Deleting the message is the trap: it looks like concealment, and screenshots already exist. Staying to monitor competitors' plans keeps the firm in the conversation.

blocks.html: Diane's response is a written firm policy, delivered to every licensee at both offices, and a note in Marcus's file. Then a Hudson & Hart agent asks a fair question at the next sales meeting: "If we can't agree on fees, how can Diane tell us what our fee is?"

blocks.q: Diane sets a firm-wide policy that Hudson & Hart's listing fee starts at 5%, with any reduction approved by her. Is that price fixing?
c: Yes, because it sets a minimum commission across many separate licensees
Yes, unless every agent at the firm votes to approve the new policy
No, one firm setting its own prices is not a competitor agreement
No, because rates at or below 6% fall outside the antitrust laws
blocks.x: Price fixing requires an agreement between separate competitors. A brokerage and its own salespersons are a single business, and a broker deciding the firm's fee schedule is ordinary pricing, as long as the firm sets it alone and the client can still negotiate. The trap is counting licensees: many agents at one firm are not many competitors. No rate level is exempt from antitrust law; the problem is the agreement, not the number.

blocks.title: Diane's policy, in four lines
blocks.html:
1. We set our fees alone, in this office, and every fee is negotiable with the client.
2. We do not discuss our fees or any competitor's fees with other firms, in person, by phone, or in any chat.
3. We show every property that fits a client's needs, whatever firm lists it and whatever it pays.
4. If a conversation with competitors turns to fees, territories, or a rival firm: object, leave, and tell Diane in writing.

In March, Jordan takes a buyer client, Maya Collins, to a new subdivision of 24 lots in Riverhead. The builder's sales manager explains the deal. "Lots start at $210,000. One condition: if you own a home now, you list it with our affiliated brokerage. No exceptions." Maya owns a condo in Bay Shore she plans to sell.

blocks.q: The builder sells lots only to buyers who list their current homes with its affiliated brokerage. This is:
c: Market allocation, since the builder controls the subdivision
A tie-in: one sale conditioned on buying another service
A lawful package deal, since buyers can choose another subdivision
A group boycott, since outside brokers are excluded from listings
blocks.x: A tie-in arrangement conditions the sale of one product (the lot) on the purchase of another (listing services from the builder's brokerage). The lawful package answer is the trap: a buyer may voluntarily choose both, but making the second a condition of the first is what the law forbids. A boycott needs competitors agreeing among themselves, not one seller's condition imposed on buyers.

blocks.html: Jordan tells Maya, as her agent, that the condition is a red flag and that she should talk to her attorney before agreeing to it. Maya's attorney writes to the builder. The condition quietly disappears from the sales sheet the following week, and Maya buys lot 17. She lists her Bay Shore condo with a broker she chooses on her own.

Why does the law care? The builder controls something buyers want and cannot get elsewhere: these particular lots in this particular subdivision. Using that leverage to force buyers into a separate market, listing services, shuts out every competing brokerage on Long Island from those listings without any of them losing on price or service. The same logic applies to a landlord who rents a storefront only to tenants who buy insurance from his agency, or a manager who takes a building only if the owner also lists it for sale with him. Offering a discount for bundling is different; forcing the bundle is the problem.

The industry learned how expensive this area of law can be. In October 2023 a federal jury in Missouri, in Burnett v. National Association of REALTORS, found NAR and several large brokerages liable for conspiring to inflate commissions through rules that required listing brokers to offer buyer-broker compensation, and awarded about $1.78 billion in damages, which antitrust law can triple. NAR settled the national claims in March 2024 for $418 million and agreed to change its rules. Several big brokerages settled separately. None of it involved a group chat, which is a reminder that rules, not just conversations, can be agreements.

Since August 17, 2024, under the National Association of REALTORS settlement, MLS participants working with a buyer must have a written agreement with that buyer before touring a home, and offers of compensation to buyer's brokers may not appear on the MLS. Sellers can still offer to pay a buyer's broker, negotiated off the MLS, and buyers can pay their own broker directly. Jordan has a signed buyer agreement with Maya.

blocks.title: Compensation clause, Hudson & Hart exclusive buyer agreement
blocks.html: "Broker's compensation: 2.5% of the purchase price, earned at closing. Buyer may ask the seller, in the offer or otherwise, to pay all or part of this amount. Any amount the seller or listing broker agrees in writing to pay will be credited against it. Buyer pays any balance at closing. Broker will not accept compensation from any source greater than this amount. This fee was set by Hudson & Hart and is negotiable."

Read the last two sentences closely. The cap stops the buyer's agent from being paid more by a seller than the client agreed to, which keeps the agent's incentives lined up with the buyer. And the fee is the firm's own, set alone and open to negotiation: exactly what Diane's policy requires, and exactly what the South Shore chat tried to replace with a group number.

Dev Malhotra, a nurse at Good Samaritan in West Islip, calls Jordan from a listing website on a Saturday morning. "There's an open house in Seaford at noon. Can you just meet me there? We can sign paperwork later."

blocks.q: Hudson & Hart is an MLS participant. Can Jordan tour the Seaford house with Dev today before any agreement is signed?
c: Yes, as long as the agreement is signed before Dev makes an offer
Yes, because an open house is public and needs no agreement
No, unless the listing agent first agrees in writing to pay Jordan
No, Jordan needs a signed agreement with Dev before touring
blocks.x: Under the NAR settlement practice changes, an MLS participant working with a buyer must have a written agreement with that buyer before touring a home, and the agreement must state the agent's compensation in a specific, objectively ascertainable amount or rate. Jordan can send Dev a buyer agreement to sign before noon. The open house answer is the trap: Dev may walk into a public open house alone, but Jordan touring it as his agent triggers the requirement.

blocks.html: Dev signs the agreement on his phone at 11:30. Back on the South Shore, a new rumor: some buyer's agents are telling each other they will not show homes listed by FlatList, because FlatList sellers often decline to pay buyer's brokers. One of those homes is the Seaford cape Dev just toured, at $649,000, and it fits his search almost exactly.

blocks.q: Dev's agreement says he pays his agent's fee if the seller won't. The Seaford cape fits his search. FlatList's seller offers nothing to buyer's agents. What should Jordan do?
c: Skip it, since the seller offers no compensation to buyer's brokers
Show it, but tell Dev it is overpriced so he loses interest in it
Skip it, since the other agents in the area have agreed not to show it
Show it to Dev, explain how the fee works, and let him decide
blocks.x: Loyalty requires showing a buyer client the homes that fit the client's needs, not the homes that pay the agent best. Jordan shows the cape and explains that under Dev's agreement he would owe the fee if the seller won't pay, or could ask for a seller concession. Skipping it because of compensation is steering against the client. Skipping it because other agents agreed to is joining a group boycott.

blocks.html: Dev likes the cape. His offer asks the seller to pay a 2% concession toward his costs; the seller agrees to 1.5%. Dev covers the rest of the fee himself, without complaint, because he knew from the start how it worked.

blocks.q: A listing agent in the old chat proposes that all buyer's agents ask sellers for the same 2.5% so "sellers can't play us off each other." What is that?
c: Price fixing, even though it concerns buyer-side fees
Lawful, because buyer's agent fees are paid by sellers
Lawful after the NAR settlement, which set 2.5% as the norm
A tie-in, since the fee is tied to the listing agreement
blocks.x: Any agreement among competing brokers on what they will charge is price fixing, whichever side of the deal pays it. The NAR settlement did not set any rate; it changed where compensation offers may be communicated and required written buyer agreements. The trap is the settlement answer, because many agents misread it as setting a new standard. Who ends up writing the check does not change the analysis of an agreement among competitors.

blocks.title: "Everybody charges 6%"
blocks.html: There is no standard commission. A licensee who tells a seller "the standard is 6%" or "all the brokers around here charge the same" invites two problems: the seller is misled about whether fees are negotiable, and the statement sounds like evidence of an agreement. Say instead: "Our fee is 5%. Fees are negotiable, and other firms set their own." On the exam, the answer that rates are set by the board, the MLS, or custom is always the wrong one.

blocks.q: A seller asks Jordan, "Why is your fee 5% when FlatList charges $5,000 flat?" What answer fits antitrust rules and loyalty to a prospective client?
c: "Everyone in Nassau charges about the same; FlatList is the outlier."
"FlatList will be gone soon, since the local firms won't show its listings."
"Here's what our fee covers. It's negotiable; FlatList may suit some."
"The board sets a suggested range, and our fee sits near the middle of it."
blocks.x: Competing on service is exactly what antitrust law protects: explain what your fee buys, say it is negotiable, and be honest that a flat-fee model may suit some sellers. The trap is the "everyone charges the same" answer, which misleads the seller and hints at coordination. Predicting that local firms won't show FlatList listings describes a boycott out loud, and no board sets suggested commission ranges.

blocks.html: By June, FlatList has eleven listings in the South Shore and several have sold through buyer's agents from other firms, Hudson & Hart included. The chat still exists. Jordan is not in it. Marcus has left it, on Diane's instruction, and sits through a compliance session with the firm's attorney, who walks the whole Massapequa office through the four violations using the chat's own screenshots. Nobody has been charged with anything, which Diane tells Jordan is the best possible outcome of a bad Tuesday night.

items: Price fixing, group boycotts, market allocation, and tie-ins are agreements; courts infer them from communications plus parallel conduct, with no signed document needed.
When competitors raise fees, territories, or a rival firm, object clearly, leave, and report to your broker in writing. Silence can look like agreement.
One firm setting its own fees, or one broker choosing its own focus, is lawful; the violation is competitors agreeing.
Conditioning the sale of one thing on buying another, such as a lot on listing your home with the builder's firm, is a tie-in.
After the NAR settlement, buyer's agents need a written agreement before touring, and compensation is negotiated off the MLS; no rate was set.
A buyer's agent shows clients every suitable home regardless of what the listing pays. Skipping homes for compensation breaches loyalty; skipping them by agreement is a boycott.

lessons.title: Case file: Four Agents and a Colonial in New Rochelle
lessons.tagline: One house, one listing broker, a buyer's agent from Brooklyn, a broker's agent at the open house, and a seller who thinks they all work for her.
objectives: Decide who may create subagency and when a cooperating broker should reject it
Compare the seller's liability for a subagent with the liability for a broker's agent
Apply the duties a subagent or broker's agent owes the seller and the buyer to specific statements
Distinguish landlord's agents and tenant's agents and explain why payment does not decide representation

blocks.title: Pinebrook Boulevard, Westchester
blocks.html: June and Walter Haskins are selling the center-hall colonial in New Rochelle where they lived for 31 years. They list with Paula Fenn of Sound Shore Realty at $1,095,000 under an exclusive right to sell. Within a week three other licensees are circling the house. Jordan, from Hudson & Hart in Brooklyn, represents buyers Ben and Carla Ito, who are leaving Park Slope for the schools. Greg Lund, from a Larchmont firm, has been hired by Paula to run Saturday open houses while she is at her daughter's wedding in Ohio. And Rena Ortiz, from a White Plains firm, has a buyer of her own and asks Paula, "Can I come in as a subagent?" Walter's view of all this is simple: "They're all working for us, right? We're paying everybody." He is wrong about most of it, and the differences decide who is liable when something goes sideways.

A subagent is an agent of the listing broker's principal, appointed through the listing broker. A cooperating agent is any licensee from another firm who works on the deal, in whatever capacity. A broker's agent is engaged by a listing broker or buyer's broker from a different firm and has no direct relationship with the client (RPL 443). New York's definition of a seller's agent includes all three on the seller's side: the listing agent, a subagent, and a broker's agent. They differ in one crucial way: whose agent they are, and who answers for their mistakes.

blocks.title: Haskins listing agreement, cooperation section
blocks.html:
"Seller authorizes Broker to cooperate with other licensed brokers as follows (check all that apply):
[ ] Subagents of Seller, who will represent Seller through Broker.
[X] Buyer's agents, who represent the buyer and not Seller.
[X] Broker's agents engaged by Broker, who represent Seller through Broker and take direction only from Broker.
Seller understands that Seller may be liable for the acts of subagents and is not liable for the acts of buyer's agents or broker's agents."
Initials: J.H., W.H.

blocks.q: Rena asks Paula to work as a subagent. Looking at the listing agreement, can Paula appoint her?
c: Yes, a listing broker may appoint any cooperating licensee as a subagent
Yes, if Rena's buyer signs a statement agreeing to deal with a subagent
No, the Haskinses did not authorize subagency in their listing agreement
No, because subagency was abolished in New York after the 2011 form change
blocks.x: Subagency is created by the listing broker, but only with the seller's authorization, because it makes the seller a principal of someone the seller never hired and exposes the seller to that person's mistakes. The Haskinses left the subagent box empty. The trap is the first answer, which treats the listing broker as free to delegate. Subagency still exists in New York; it is simply rare, and here unauthorized.

blocks.html: Paula tells Rena she can cooperate as a buyer's agent instead. Rena, whose buyer has not signed any agreement with her, considers her options. Her firm is an MLS participant.

blocks.q: Rena's buyer wants to see the Haskins house Saturday. Which path keeps Rena on solid ground?
c: Sign a written buyer agreement before touring, then cooperate as buyer's agent
Tour first as an informal subagent, then decide her role once there is an offer
Bring the buyer as a customer and advise him on price without an agreement
Present herself as the sellers' agent, since Paula's firm controls the listing
blocks.x: With subagency off the table, Rena's clean role is buyer's agent, and as an MLS participant she needs a written agreement with the buyer before touring under the NAR settlement practice changes. The trap is touring first and sorting out roles later: duties attach with conduct, and advising an unsigned buyer creates an implied agency anyway. Claiming to be the sellers' agent without their authorization would misstate her role to everyone.

blocks.html: Rena's buyer signs her agreement Friday night. That leaves Jordan's call.

Jordan calls Paula to book a showing. Paula, old school and in a hurry, says, "Fine, you're my subagent for the showing, right? Everybody's on the seller's side here." Jordan has a signed exclusive buyer agreement with the Itos and a pre-approval letter in the file. Jordan also gave the Itos the agency disclosure form at their first meeting, marked as buyer's agent.

blocks.q: How should Jordan answer Paula's "you're my subagent" assumption?
c: Accept it for the showing, then switch back to buyer's agent for the offer
Reject it and state in writing that Jordan represents the buyers only
Accept it, since the seller pays the commission and so controls the agency
Stay vague, since roles only matter once an offer is presented
blocks.x: A cooperating broker may reject an offer of subagency, and Jordan must: the Itos are Jordan's clients, and becoming the sellers' subagent would make Jordan an undisclosed dual agent. The role should be stated clearly and early, in writing, before price or motivation comes up. The trap is switching roles mid-deal: duties attach as soon as the agency does. Who pays does not determine whose agent Jordan is.

blocks.html: Jordan emails Paula: "Confirming that Hudson & Hart represents the buyers, Ben and Carla Ito, as buyer's agent. We are not a subagent of the sellers." Paula replies with a thumbs up and the lockbox code.

blocks.title: Settle the role before the first showing
blocks.html: Every cooperating licensee should answer three questions in writing before discussing price with anyone: whom do I represent, who engaged me, and who pays me. Jordan's one-line email to Paula answers the first. Greg's written agreement with Sound Shore answers all three for him. When a listing agent assumes a role for you, as Paula did, correct it the same day. A role left vague becomes whatever a court later decides your conduct implied.

Greg runs the Saturday open house under a written broker's agent agreement between Sound Shore and his Larchmont firm. Paula pays his firm a flat $1,500 per weekend from her own commission. The Itos come by with Jordan. Carla Ito, who has a weakness for honesty, asks Greg about the finished basement. Greg, who has not read the property file, says, "Oh, it's bone dry. Never had water." The Haskinses' own disclosure statement, in Paula's file, notes water in the basement during Hurricane Ida in 2021 and a sump pump installed afterward.

blocks.q: If the Itos buy in reliance on Greg's statement and later sue, who may be liable to them?
c: Greg, his firm, and Sound Shore as the broker that engaged him
The Haskinses, who are vicariously liable for any seller's agent
Greg alone, since a broker's agent acts entirely on his own account
No one, since the disclosure statement already revealed the water
blocks.x: A broker's agent takes direction only from the broker who engaged it, and that broker, not the client, bears the vicarious liability. Greg is liable for his own misstatement, and his firm and Sound Shore can be reached too, but the Haskinses are not vicariously liable for a broker's agent. The trap is the sellers: that is the rule for subagents. A written disclosure does not license a contradictory oral statement either.

blocks.html: Jordan, standing next to Carla, hands her a copy of the property condition disclosure statement from the listing packet. "Page two. Hurricane Ida. There's a sump pump." Greg turns red and corrects himself. It is a cheap fix because it happened before anyone relied on the statement.

blocks.q: Change one fact: suppose the Haskinses had checked the subagent box and Greg were their subagent. Who could the Itos then reach for Greg's statement?
c: Greg and his firm, but no one on the sellers' side
The Haskinses alone, since a subagent acts in their name
Sound Shore alone, since it made the subagency offer
Greg, and the Haskinses through vicarious liability
blocks.x: A subagent is the seller's agent through the listing broker, so the seller is a principal and can be vicariously liable for the subagent's misstatements within the scope of the agency, even though the seller never met him. Greg remains liable for his own statement too. This is the exposure the listing agreement warned about, and the main reason sellers stopped authorizing subagency. The trap is placing liability on Sound Shore alone.

head: Subagent
Broker's agent
Buyer's agent
blocks.caption: Three cooperating roles on the Haskins listing

blocks.html: Notice what the table says about the relationship between a principal and a subagent. The Haskinses would be principals of someone they never interviewed, never signed with, and might never meet, yet that person would owe them loyalty, confidentiality, and obedience, and they would answer for his statements. That is a lot to accept for a little more foot traffic. It is also why brokerage in New York now runs mostly without subagency: buyer's agents bring buyers, broker's agents fill gaps for the listing firm, and each seller's exposure stays limited to people its own broker chose and supervises.

Later that Saturday, after Jordan and the Itos leave, Carla calls Greg back with one more question about the boiler, and in passing says, "We'd honestly go to $1.1 million for this place. Ben loves the yard." Greg writes it down.

blocks.q: What does Greg, as Sound Shore's broker's agent, do with Carla's remark about $1.1 million?
c: Keep it confidential, since Carla shared it with him directly
Tell Jordan, since Carla's own agent should know she said it
Report it to Paula; he owes the sellers' side disclosure
Ignore it, since a broker's agent owes the sellers no duties
blocks.x: A broker's agent owes fiduciary duties to the seller through the broker that engaged it, including disclosure of material facts. A buyer's willingness to pay $1.1 million is material, so Greg passes it to Paula, who decides how to use it for the Haskinses. The trap is confidentiality: Carla is a customer to Greg, owed honesty, not secrecy. The "no duties" answer confuses "no direct relationship" with "no duties."

blocks.title: No direct relationship does not mean no duties
blocks.html: A broker's agent has no direct relationship with the seller: the seller cannot instruct it and is not liable for it. But it still works for the seller's side, through the listing broker, and owes the seller loyalty, confidentiality, and disclosure through that broker. Exam items flip this both ways. The correct answers: the broker's agent owes the seller fiduciary duties; the seller cannot direct it; the seller is not vicariously liable for it.
Jordan, separately, has told the Itos never to share their ceiling with anyone on the sellers' side, including people at open houses. Carla apologizes; Jordan sighs and adjusts the negotiating plan.

On Sunday night June Haskins, anxious, finds Greg's number on the open house sign-in sheet and calls him directly. "Paula's in Ohio. You're working for us. Drop the price to $1,049,000 tomorrow and tell the buyers we're flexible."

blocks.q: How should Greg respond to June's instruction?
c: Lower the price, since he represents the sellers through Sound Shore
Lower the price, but not until June signs a written price change form
Ignore June, since a broker's agent owes the sellers no duty to respond
Explain he takes direction from Sound Shore; relay it to Paula
blocks.x: A broker's agent has no direct relationship with the client and takes direction only from the broker that engaged it. Greg should explain that politely and pass June's request to Paula immediately, who will advise June and act on her decision. The trap is the first choice: representing the sellers' side does not give the sellers control over Sound Shore's helper. Saying the sellers are "flexible" would also reveal their position, which only they and Paula should decide to do.

blocks.html: Paula, reached at the wedding reception, talks June down: the price stays, and an offer is likely this week. It arrives Wednesday.

Walter, impressed by the Saturday crowd, has an idea. "More agents is more buyers. Why not let Rena and anyone else who wants it be our subagents? Check the box." Paula pulls out the listing agreement again.

blocks.q: What should Paula advise the Haskinses about authorizing subagency now?
c: Check the box, since subagents bring more buyers at no added risk
Explain the liability for subagents' statements; the choice is theirs
Check the box, since a broker's agent is the same thing as a subagent
Leave it blank, since New York sellers cannot authorize subagency today
blocks.x: Paula owes the Haskinses reasonable care in advising them, and the key fact is vicarious liability: subagents make the sellers principals of agents they never chose. Buyer's agents and broker's agents already bring buyers through the door without that exposure. The decision is the sellers', made with that information. The trap is "no added risk." Subagency is lawful in New York; it is just rarely worth it.

blocks.html: Walter thinks about Greg's "bone dry" and leaves the box empty.

blocks.text: The old system, and why it faded

blocks.html: While waiting, Walter asks Paula a question from his last sale, in 1994. "Back then, every agent in the multiple listing service worked for the seller. Doesn't that still happen?" He means the blanket unilateral offer of subagency: a listing posted to the MLS automatically offered subagency to every member, so any agent who brought a buyer became the seller's subagent. Buyers thought their agent was theirs. Legally, it was the seller's.

blocks.q: What is the accurate answer to Walter's question about blanket subagency?
c: It still applies to every MLS listing unless the seller opts out in writing
It's optional and rare now; most cooperating agents represent buyers
It was replaced by automatic dual agency for every MLS transaction
It applies today to listings above $1 million in Westchester
blocks.x: Multiple listing services made offers of subagency optional decades ago, and sellers rarely authorize them because of vicarious liability. Today most cooperating brokers in New York work as buyer's agents, occasionally as broker's agents, so brokerage is routinely done without subagency. The trap is the opt-out answer, which describes the old default. Dual agency is never automatic: it requires informed written consent.

blocks.title: Seller's agent, as RPL 443 defines it
