blocks.html: New York's definition of a seller's agent covers a listing agent acting alone or an agent cooperating with a listing agent who acts as the seller's subagent or as a broker's agent to find or obtain a buyer. So on the agency disclosure form, Greg checks "seller's agent" and can indicate that he is acting as a broker's agent. The landlord's agent definition parallels it for rentals.

blocks.text: The offer, the fee, and Walter's assumption

blocks.html: The Itos offer $1,060,000. Their offer, drafted with Jordan, asks the sellers to pay 2% of the price toward the Itos' buyer's broker fee, which under their buyer agreement with Hudson & Hart is 2.5%. After two rounds, the Haskinses accept $1,080,000, with a seller contribution of 2% ($21,600) toward the buyer's broker fee. The Itos will pay the remaining 0.5% ($5,400) at closing.

blocks.q: Walter says, "We're paying Jordan's firm $21,600. So Jordan works for us now too, right?" What is correct?
c: Yes, paying part of the fee makes Hudson & Hart a dual agent
Yes, but just for the portion of the fee the sellers are paying
No, because sellers may not pay any part of a buyer's broker fee
No, Jordan represents the Itos; payment doesn't change that
blocks.x: Agency is created by agreement, and Hudson & Hart's agreement is with the Itos. A seller's contribution toward the buyer's broker fee is a negotiated term of the sale; it buys nothing in the way of loyalty. The trap is the first answer: dual agency requires both parties' informed written consent, not a payment. Sellers are allowed to pay a buyer's broker; after the NAR settlement it is simply negotiated off the MLS.

blocks.html: Who pays Greg? Not the Haskinses directly, and not by MLS offer. Sound Shore pays Greg's firm the agreed $1,500 a weekend from its own commission, and Greg's firm pays Greg under his agreement with his own broker. A salesperson is paid only through his sponsoring broker.

The Itos' Park Slope lease ends six weeks before the closing. They need a short furnished rental in New Rochelle. They ask Jordan to find one and sign Hudson & Hart's tenant representation agreement. Jordan finds a two-bedroom near the train listed by Harborview Rentals, which has an exclusive right to rent from the owner. The Harborview agent, Dana, tells Jordan on the phone, "Owner's had it empty three months, he's dying to fill it."

blocks.q: In the rental, how do the roles line up, and what may Jordan do with Dana's remark?
c: Dana is the landlord's agent and Jordan the tenant's; Jordan tells the Itos
Dana is the tenant's agent and Jordan the landlord's; Jordan keeps the remark private
Both are landlord's agents, since the landlord's broker controls the listing
Both are dual agents, since two firms are involved in one rental
blocks.x: Harborview holds the listing, so Dana is the landlord's agent. The Itos hired Hudson & Hart, so Jordan is their tenant's agent. The owner's three-month vacancy is material to the Itos' negotiation, and Jordan owes them disclosure, not confidentiality to Dana. Dana, not Jordan, breached a duty by revealing it. The trap is lumping everyone onto the side of whoever controls the listing: each agent represents the party who hired it.

blocks.html: The Itos negotiate a lower rent for a two-month term and move in. Six weeks later they close on Pinebrook Boulevard. Walter, at the closing table, finally sorts it out out loud. "So Paula was ours, Greg was Paula's, Jordan was theirs, and Rena never came back." Paula says that is exactly right, and that if he had checked the subagent box, Greg's "bone dry" could have been his problem. June asks the last question: "And Rena?" Rena's buyer, Paula explains, toured on Saturday under a signed buyer agreement, liked the house, and lost interest when he saw the sump pump. Rena represented him properly the whole way, which is all anyone can ask of a cooperating agent who never closes the deal. Jordan drives back to Brooklyn with the Itos' file closed and one more lesson filed away: in a four-agent deal, the first thing to sort out is never the price.

blocks.q: Which statement best summarizes why sellers like the Haskinses usually leave the subagent box unchecked?
c: Subagents cost more because they split the listing commission
Subagents cannot show property without a buyer agreement in place
They'd be liable for statements by agents they never chose
Subagents owe the buyer full fiduciary duties, which weakens the seller
blocks.x: Authorizing subagency makes every subagent the seller's agent, so the seller can be liable for statements by agents the seller never met or supervised. Broker's agents give the listing broker help without that exposure, and buyer's agents represent the other side. The trap is the last choice: a subagent owes the seller full duties and the buyer only honesty. Compensation for cooperating brokers is negotiated either way.

items: Subagency is created by the listing broker only with the seller's authorization, usually in the listing agreement, and a cooperating broker may reject it.
A buyer's agent who accepts subagency becomes an undisclosed dual agent; state your role in writing before any discussion of price.
The seller is vicariously liable for a subagent's misstatements, but not for a broker's agent's; the engaging broker answers for its broker's agent.
Subagents and broker's agents owe the seller fiduciary duties and owe buyers honesty and known material facts. A broker's agent takes direction only from the broker that engaged it.
The blanket unilateral offer of subagency is a relic; most New York cooperation today is buyer agency.
Landlord's agents and tenant's agents represent whoever hired them, and a fee paid by the other side does not change representation.

lessons.title: Case file: The Second Offer on Argyle Road
lessons.tagline: Marcus has the listing and the buyer. Both clients trust him. Only one paper stands between him and a forfeited commission.
objectives: Decide when an in-house sale turns a firm into a dual agent and what consent is needed before it acts for both sides
Apply the limits on a dual agent's advice to real questions from a buyer client and a seller client
Analyze how implied agency creates undisclosed dual agency and what it costs the firm
Apply Reg 175.7 and RESPA to bonuses, double fees, and mortgage referral payments

blocks.title: A Victorian, two clients, one agent
blocks.html: Helen and Victor Castellano list their detached Victorian on Argyle Road in Ditmas Park with Hudson & Hart Realty at $1,895,000. Marcus Webb is the listing agent. Three weeks earlier Marcus signed Dev Malhotra, a nurse anesthetist relocating from Albany, to an exclusive buyer agreement with the same firm. Dev has toured eleven houses with Marcus and passed on all of them. On Saturday he walks through Argyle Road with his partner, stands in the wraparound porch for ten minutes, and texts Marcus that night: "This is the one. What will they really take?" Marcus is the Castellanos' agent and Dev's agent at the same time. Before he types a single word back, what has changed?

blocks.text: Saturday night: the firm changes roles

blocks.html: Nothing about Marcus's paperwork changed on Saturday. What changed is the transaction. Hudson & Hart holds a listing agreement with the Castellanos and an exclusive buyer agreement with Dev. The moment Dev pursues the firm's own listing, the firm is on track to represent both sides of one deal. That is dual agency, and in New York it is lawful only with the informed consent of both clients, in writing. Because Marcus personally holds both relationships, this is the hardest version: single licensee dual agency.

blocks.q: Dev's text arrives. What is Hudson & Hart's status, and what must happen before Marcus acts for Dev on Argyle Road?
c: Still a seller's agent only, because Dev has not made a written offer yet
A dual agent in waiting; both clients must give informed written consent first
A buyer's agent for Dev alone, because his buyer agreement predates this showing
A broker's agent for both sides until the attorneys sign a contract
blocks.x: The firm already represents both people, and Dev now wants the firm's listing. Acting for him on this house makes the firm a dual agent, which needs written informed consent from the Castellanos and from Dev before Marcus advises either side about this deal. Waiting for a written offer is the trap: by then Marcus would already have acted for both without consent, which is undisclosed dual agency.

blocks.html: Marcus pulls both files on Sunday morning. The Castellanos' agency disclosure, signed at the listing appointment, shows a check in the box for advance consent to dual agency. Dev's form, signed when he hired the firm, shows his role box checked as buyer's agent and the advance consent box blank. Marcus figures he is half done.

blocks.title: The two signature pages in Marcus's files
blocks.html:
Castellano listing file (March 4): Licensee: Marcus Webb, Hudson & Hart Realty. Role: seller's agent. Advance consent to dual agency: checked, initialed H.C. and V.C. Advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents: blank.
Malhotra buyer file (February 11): Licensee: Marcus Webb. Role: buyer's agent. Advance consent to dual agency: blank. Signed D. Malhotra.
Note in Marcus's handwriting: "Sellers OK with dual. Dev?"

blocks.q: Given those two files, what does the Castellanos' advance consent let the firm do?
c: Act as dual agent once Dev consents in writing and the sellers are told
Proceed as dual agent now, since one side's written consent covers the deal
Skip any further disclosure to the sellers, because advance consent is final
Nothing, because advance consent is void in a single licensee deal
blocks.x: Advance consent is one party agreeing ahead of time that in-house deals may happen. It covers only the party who gave it. Dev never consented, so the firm needs his informed written consent, and the Castellanos must be told the specific buyer is a firm client when it actually happens. The trap is treating one checked box as covering both sides. Consent must come from every client the firm represents in the deal.

blocks.title: Advance consent is not silence
blocks.html: Advance consent saves a fresh signature at the moment of the in-house deal. It does not save a phone call. When the deal arises, the firm still tells each client that it now represents the other side and confirms consent. A firm that relies on a box checked months ago and says nothing has a disclosure problem, not a consent.

Marcus drafts an email to Dev: "Quick formality, please sign the attached so we can move on Argyle." He shows it to Diane Hart before sending. Diane deletes it. A signature on a form the client does not understand is a signature, not informed consent. If the deal goes bad, a court will ask what Dev was told about what he was giving up, and "quick formality" is the worst possible answer.

blocks.q: Which explanation to Dev comes closest to what makes his consent informed?
c: Dual agency is common in Brooklyn, everyone uses it, and in practice it rarely changes what a buyer pays
The sellers have already agreed, so his signature simply keeps the firm from losing a valuable listing
The firm would serve both sides, so Marcus cannot advise on price or reveal either side's position
Signing turns Marcus into a neutral facilitator who owes Dev no duties of any kind on this one deal
blocks.x: Informed consent means Dev understands what he gives up: undivided loyalty and advice on what to offer, plus the fact that his own bargaining position stays private and the sellers' does too. The neutral facilitator choice is the trap. A dual agent is still an agent with duties of honesty, care, confidentiality, and accounting to both sides; it just cannot advocate for one against the other.

blocks.html: Diane and Marcus meet Dev on a video call Monday night. Marcus explains the firm's two clients, what a dual agent can and cannot do, and Dev's alternatives: decline consent and bring in a buyer's broker from another firm for this house, or proceed as a customer with no representation. Dev asks good questions and signs the dual agency consent on a new agency disclosure form with the dual agent box checked. Diane calls the Castellanos the same night, tells them the buyer is Marcus's own client, and gets their written confirmation by email. Both forms go into both files.

head: Step
Who
Paper
rows: Explain the dual role and its costs
Dev, on video, with Diane present
New agency disclosure, dual agent box checked
Notice that the buyer is a firm client
blocks.caption: How Hudson & Hart papered the switch to dual agency

blocks.html: Consent changes the job. On Tuesday morning Dev calls: "Okay, you're dual now. But off the record, what will Victor take? You've been in that kitchen ten times." At noon Victor Castellano calls too: "Dev is your guy. How high can he go?" Both clients think they are asking a friend. Both are asking a dual agent.

blocks.q: How should Marcus answer Dev's question about the sellers' bottom line?
c: Give a range rather than an exact number, since a range is not confidential
Tell him, because Dev became a client first and those earlier duties prevail
Say the sellers are flexible, which is general enough to avoid a breach
Decline, and give him the comparable sales so he can decide his own offer
blocks.x: A dual agent must keep each client's bargaining position confidential from the other, so the sellers' bottom line stays private. What Marcus can give Dev is facts: recent sales on Argyle and nearby blocks, days on market, the property's condition. The trap is the range or the hint that sellers are flexible. Either one leaks the sellers' position as surely as a number does, and "Dev was first" does not rank loyalty in a dual agency.

blocks.html: Marcus gives Victor the mirror answer: he cannot share Dev's ceiling, but he can walk the Castellanos through every offer's terms and the market data. That is the trade single licensee dual agency forces. Marcus holds both clients' secrets in one head, and the only safe way to work is to stick to facts and paperwork. Many New York firms forbid it outright for exactly this reason.

Then a second buyer surfaces. At the Sunday open house two weeks earlier, a visitor named Sung-min Cho told Marcus she was paying cash from a co-op sale in Park Slope. Marcus gave her his seller's agent disclosure, and she signed it. Then he got chatty. In the hallway he told her, "Offer around $1,840,000. They've already bought in Maplewood, so they'll want speed. And skip the inspection contingency, I know this house." On Wednesday her attorney sends an all-cash offer at $1,870,000 with a ten-day closing. Her cover letter says, "Per Marcus's advice."

blocks.q: What did Marcus's hallway advice to Sung-min most likely create?
c: Nothing, because she signed a form saying that Marcus was the seller's agent
Implied agency with her, a second dual role that nobody consented to
A broker's agent relationship that runs through the listing broker
Subagency, which the sellers are deemed to have authorized at listing
blocks.x: Agency can be created by conduct. Telling a buyer what to offer, revealing the sellers' motivation, and advising her on contingencies is acting as her agent. That is implied agency, and because no one consented to Marcus representing both, it is undisclosed dual agency. The signed form is the trap. A disclosure that says "I represent the seller" does not protect an agent whose conduct says otherwise.

blocks.html: Worse, Marcus breached his duty to the Castellanos twice in one sentence: he disclosed that they had already bought a second home, which weakens their bargaining position, and he told a buyer what price they would accept. He also exposed Sung-min to a risk without any real basis, by telling her to skip an inspection. A buyer customer is owed honesty and care in what the agent says, and she relied on him.

head: Consequence
Who can pursue it
What it looks like here
rows: The firm's fee on Argyle Road could be lost entirely
Either could try to unwind a contract tainted by the breach
The sellers could claim the price they lost; the buyer, inspection costs and repairs
Fine, suspension, or revocation for Marcus; supervision questions for Diane
blocks.caption: What undisclosed dual agency can cost

blocks.q: Suppose the Castellanos accept Sung-min's offer, close, and then learn about the hallway conversation. Which remedy are they LEAST likely to have?
c: Forfeiture of the firm's entire commission on the Argyle Road sale
A civil claim against the firm for the price they may have lost
A complaint to the Department of State seeking discipline of Marcus
A criminal charge against Sung-min for relying on the advice
blocks.x: Undisclosed dual agency is the agent's breach, so the remedies run against the agent and the firm: commission forfeiture, damages, possible rescission, and license discipline. Sung-min did nothing wrong by listening to advice an agent volunteered. Forfeiture is the tempting wrong pick because it sounds extreme, but courts routinely deny a disloyal agent the fee, sometimes even when the client suffered no measurable loss.

blocks.q: Diane learns about the hallway conversation on Wednesday afternoon. What should she do first?
c: Tell the sellers in writing what Marcus said, and correct the record with the buyer
Say nothing, since Sung-min's offer is strong and the sellers come out ahead
Reject Sung-min's offer on the sellers' behalf so the firm is not exposed
Ask Sung-min to withdraw and resubmit the offer without the cover letter
blocks.x: The sellers are the firm's clients and are owed full disclosure of facts that affect them, including an agent's breach that weakened their position. The buyer is owed honesty, so the firm must make clear that Marcus never represented her. Silence is the trap: a good offer does not erase the breach, and hiding it compounds the disloyalty. Rejecting the offer is the sellers' decision, not the firm's.

blocks.html: Diane does what a supervising broker should. She tells the Castellanos, in writing, exactly what Marcus said, including that he revealed their Maplewood purchase. She tells Sung-min's attorney that Marcus represents the sellers only and that his comments about contingencies were not advice she should rely on. She documents both calls. Then she pulls Marcus off the Argyle file and handles the rest of the deal herself, with both offers still on the table.

Thursday brings three money conversations. First, Tasha Monroe, the mortgage broker Marcus refers most of his buyers to, emails: "Send Dev my way. Same as always, $750 for you when it funds." Second, Victor Castellano offers Marcus a private $5,000 bonus if the house closes over $1,900,000. Third, the firm's commission. The listing agreement pays Hudson & Hart 5% of the sale price. Dev's buyer agreement says the buyer's broker fee is 2.5%, payable by the buyer if the seller does not pay it.

blocks.q: Marcus performs no loan work for Dev. Accepting Tasha's $750 would be:
c: Legal if Marcus discloses it to Dev in writing before the loan funds
A referral fee barred by RESPA, disclosure or not
Legal because Tasha is licensed by DFS and Marcus is licensed by DOS
A Reg 175.7 issue, solved by the sellers' written consent
blocks.x: RESPA Section 8 prohibits fees for referring settlement service business on federally related loans. A fee for a referral, with no services performed, is a kickback, and disclosure does not cure it. The disclosure choice is the trap: disclosure and consent under Reg 175.7 matter when a licensee actually performs and is properly licensed for mortgage brokerage services, not when the licensee just sends a name.

blocks.title: 19 NYCRR 175.7
blocks.html: A broker must make clear for which party it is acting and may not receive compensation from more than one party except with the full knowledge and consent of all parties. RPL 443 tells the consumer whom you represent; Reg 175.7 controls who may pay you. In a dual agency, both rules apply at once.

blocks.q: What is the right way to handle Victor's offer of a private $5,000 bonus to Marcus?
c: Accept it in cash, since bonuses are gifts and not commissions
Accept it quietly, because Dev pays nothing extra
Route it through Hudson & Hart, with Dev's full knowledge and consent
Accept it as a referral fee, since Marcus brought the buyer to the deal
blocks.x: A salesperson may be paid only through the sponsoring broker, so any bonus goes to Hudson & Hart and then to Marcus under his split. And because the firm is a dual agent, a seller incentive tied to a higher price works directly against the buyer client. Under Reg 175.7 and basic loyalty, Dev must know about it and consent. Keeping it quiet is the trap: a secret payment from one side of a dual agency is self-dealing.

blocks.title: The commission, if Dev buys at $1,880,000
blocks.html:
Listing fee: $1,880,000 x 0.05 = $94,000, payable by the Castellanos to Hudson & Hart.
Dev's buyer agreement: 2.5% = $47,000, payable by Dev unless the seller pays it.
The listing agreement covers the whole 5% for an in-house sale, so the firm earns $94,000 total from the sellers and nothing from Dev, and Dev's agreement is satisfied because the seller paid.
If the firm tried to collect $94,000 from the sellers and $47,000 from Dev, that is compensation from both parties. Reg 175.7 requires the full knowledge and consent of all parties, and the clients would rightly ask why one firm doing one job is paid 7.5%.

blocks.q: Diane wants to be clean on fees. Which arrangement best satisfies Reg 175.7 for this in-house deal?
c: Collect both fees and disclose them in the closing statement
Collect just the buyer fee, since Dev was the firm's client first
Collect both fees, because each client signed a separate agreement
Spell out in writing to both clients who pays the firm and how much
blocks.x: Reg 175.7 requires full knowledge and consent of all parties before a broker takes compensation from more than one. The cleanest practice is a written fee acknowledgment that both clients see before the contract: who pays, how much, and that the firm will not collect twice for the same work. Separate agreements are the trap. Each client signing their own agreement is not the same as each client knowing what the other is paying.

blocks.text: Friday: two offers and a change of heart

blocks.html: By Friday the Castellanos hold two offers: Dev at $1,880,000 with a 60-day mortgage contingency and a home inspection, and Sung-min at $1,870,000, all cash, ten-day close, now with an inspection after her attorney talked to her. Helen asks Diane the obvious question: "Which one should we take?" Diane is supervising a dual agency, and one of the bidders is the firm's own client.

blocks.q: Helen asks Diane which offer to accept. What should Diane do?
c: Recommend Dev's offer, since it is higher and Dev is the firm's client
Lay out both offers' terms and risks side by side without steering
Recommend Sung-min's offer to prove the firm is not favoring its buyer
Refuse to discuss the offers until Dev withdraws his consent to dual agency
blocks.x: A dual agent presents every offer and helps the seller understand the terms: price, financing risk, timing, contingencies. It cannot advocate for or against its own buyer client. Recommending Sung-min to look neutral is the trap; it is still steering, just in the other direction, and it hurts a client the firm represents. Diane can also suggest the Castellanos ask their attorney, Priya Nair, to weigh the financing risk.

blocks.html: Saturday, Dev calls Diane. He read about dual agency online and changed his mind: "I want someone who's only on my side." Consent to dual agency is a client's choice, and a client who gave it can take it back for a deal that has not been signed.

blocks.q: Dev revokes his consent to dual agency before any contract is signed. What is Hudson & Hart's best course?
c: Release Dev for this house so he can hire an outside buyer's broker, and keep representing the sellers
Keep acting for both, since his earlier signature stays binding once given
Drop the Castellanos and represent Dev alone, since his agreement came first
Treat Dev as a customer from now on without telling him his status changed
blocks.x: Without Dev's consent the firm cannot be a dual agent, so it must pick a lane it already has: the listing. Dev gets a written release for Argyle Road so an outside buyer's broker can represent him there. The firm stays the Castellanos' agent. The trap is treating the first signature as irrevocable. Consent can be revoked for a deal not yet made, and acting for both after revocation is undisclosed dual agency.

blocks.html: Dev hires a buyer's broker from a Prospect Lefferts Gardens firm, who negotiates against Diane. The Castellanos accept Dev's offer at $1,895,000 after his new agent drops the mortgage contingency to 45 days. Hudson & Hart earns its listing fee and pays the buyer's broker under a written cooperation agreement the Castellanos approved. Marcus gets a written warning in his file and a month of supervised deals.

Diane also writes a note to her own file. Under 19 NYCRR 175.21 she must give her salespersons regular, frequent, and consistent supervision, and DOS will ask where she was when one of them advised both sides of the same house. Her note lists what she changed: every in-house deal now comes to her desk the day a firm buyer asks about a firm listing, single licensee dual agency needs her approval in advance, and open house hosts get a one-page script that starts with "I represent the sellers."

blocks.q: Next month Jordan, not Marcus, represents a buyer who wants another Hudson & Hart listing that Marcus holds. Which statement is accurate?
c: No dual agency exists, because two different salespersons are each representing one side
Dual agency exists if Jordan and Marcus split the commission
The firm is a dual agent and needs both clients' informed written consent
Dual agency exists, but consent is needed from the buyer alone
blocks.x: Agency belongs to the broker, not the salesperson. If the firm represents the seller through Marcus and the buyer through Jordan, the firm represents both: broker dual agency. It needs informed written consent from both clients, and with that consent the broker may designate Jordan and Marcus as designated sales agents. The trap is thinking two salespersons make two firms. They do not.

blocks.title: New York's dual agency scheme in one breath
blocks.html: RPL 443 requires the written agency disclosure in 1 to 4 family, condo, and co-op deals and lets clients give advance consent to dual agency on the form. Common law agency still applies: undisclosed dual agency is disloyalty. Reg 175.7 adds that a broker paid by more than one party needs everyone's full knowledge and consent. The three rules stack; meeting one does not excuse the others.

items: An in-house sale makes the firm a dual agent; it needs written informed consent from every client it represents in the deal before acting for both.
Advance consent covers only the party who gave it, and the firm still tells that party when an in-house deal arises.
A dual agent gives facts, not strategy: no bottom lines, no ceilings, no recommendation for or against its own client.
Advice to an unrepresented buyer can create implied agency, and implied agency on top of a listing is undisclosed dual agency, with forfeiture, rescission, damages, and DOS discipline on the table.
Bonuses run through the broker, payments from more than one party need everyone's knowledge and consent under Reg 175.7, and a fee for a bare referral is a RESPA kickback.
A client can revoke dual agency consent before a deal is made; the firm then keeps one client and releases the other.

lessons.title: Case file: The Tudor on Puritan Avenue
lessons.tagline: A new Forest Hills branch, an inherited listing, and a buyer client from Brooklyn. Diane has to pick a policy and then live with it.
objectives: Choose a written company agency policy that fits a brokerage's business and explain what each policy tells consumers
Apply the rules for dual agency with designated sales agents: who may be designated, what consent is needed, and what the broker may do
Decide how confidential information learned before designation limits a designated sales agent
Analyze whether consensual dual agency with designated agents actually works for each client

blocks.title: A branch with a history
blocks.html: Hudson & Hart is opening its first Queens office, on Austin Street in Forest Hills, by absorbing a retiring broker's three-person shop. The deal brings fourteen active listings, six salespersons, and an associate broker, Renata Silva, who will manage the branch. The retiring broker never did in-house deals; he represented sellers only, and every buyer who walked in was a customer. Diane Hart's Brooklyn office does the opposite: most of its income comes from buyer clients. The week the sign goes up, Jordan's buyer clients from Park Slope, Mei and Daniel Lau, ask to see a Tudor on Puritan Avenue in Forest Hills Gardens. It is one of the inherited listings. Before anyone books a showing, Diane has to answer a question the old firm never faced: what is Hudson & Hart's agency policy in Queens?

Every New York brokerage should have its agency policy in writing, and every licensee should be able to recite it, because the policy decides what an agent says at first substantive contact. Diane writes the options on the whiteboard in the empty branch office, with Renata and Jordan watching.

head: Policy
What the firm does
Who loses something
rows: Represents sellers only; buyers are customers
Buyers get no advice; buyer clients like the Laus cannot stay
Represents buyers only; never takes listings
The fourteen inherited listings would have to go
Consensual dual agency, seller agency as the norm
Represents sellers; in-house buyers become clients only with dual consent
Consensual dual agency, buyer agency on all other deals
Buyer agency on outside listings; dual agency with consent in-house
Consensual dual agency, with a designated sales agent for each side
The broker stays neutral and dual
blocks.caption: Diane's whiteboard, Austin Street

blocks.q: Diane wants to keep the inherited listings, keep representing buyers like the Laus, and give each side an advocate when they meet in-house. Which policy fits best?
c: Seller agency exclusively, exactly as the retiring broker practiced for decades
Buyer agency exclusively, with the inherited listings referred out
Consensual dual agency, using designated sales agents in-house
Single agency, with each in-house buyer converted to a customer
blocks.x: Designated agents let the firm keep both businesses and still give each client someone who can advise and negotiate for them, with written consent from both. Seller agency exclusively is the trap because it is what the branch already does. It would force Jordan to drop the Laus as clients for any in-house house, and the Laus would get no advice on price at all.

blocks.html: Diane adopts the policy in writing that afternoon: buyer agency on outside listings, seller agency on the firm's listings, and consensual dual agency with designated sales agents whenever the two meet. Single licensee dual agency needs her advance approval, and she does not expect to give it. Renata will train the six inherited salespersons, who have never once said the words "I represent you" to a buyer.

The Puritan Avenue listing belongs to sellers Paul and Ruth Weissman, who are moving to be near grandchildren in Westchester. Their listing agent is Ahmed Rahman, one of the inherited salespersons. The Laus want to offer. Ahmed is nervous about working against a Brooklyn agent from his own new firm, and Diane offers a solution: "I'll be the Weissmans' designated agent myself. I know Forest Hills." Renata stops her.

blocks.q: Why can't Diane designate herself as the Weissmans' designated sales agent?
c: Designated agents need a broker license, and Diane's is a sole proprietorship
The broker remains the dual agent supervising both sides, so she cannot advocate for one
The Weissmans' listing came from another firm, so Ahmed alone can represent them
Designated agents have to work in the same office where the listed property is located
blocks.x: Under RPL 443 a designated sales agent is a salesperson or associate broker working under the broker's supervision, assigned to one client when the broker represents a different client in the same deal. The broker herself stays the dual agent and supervises both designated agents, so she must stay neutral. The office location choice is the trap; nothing ties designation to a branch.

blocks.title: What RPL 443 says a designated sales agent is
blocks.html: A licensed real estate salesperson or associate broker, working under the supervision of a broker, assigned to represent one client when a different client is also represented by that broker in the same transaction. The form tells consumers that a designated sales agent cannot provide the full range of fiduciary duties, and that the broker remains a dual agent.

Renata raises a point first. The fourteen listings were signed with the retiring broker's firm, not with Hudson & Hart. A listing agreement is a personal service contract between an owner and a particular broker. The salespersons who worked those listings are moving over, but the contracts do not simply follow them, and the retiring broker cannot hand his clients to a new firm the way he can sell his desks and his phone number.

blocks.q: How does Hudson & Hart properly take over the retiring broker's fourteen listings?
c: Each owner signs a new listing agreement and agency disclosure with Hudson & Hart
Automatically, because the listing salespersons are joining Hudson & Hart
By a written assignment from the retiring broker, with no owner involvement
By filing a change of association for each salesperson with the Department of State
blocks.x: A listing is the broker's contract with the owner, and agency is a consensual relationship the owner chooses. Each owner must agree to hire Hudson & Hart, which means a new listing agreement and a new agency disclosure. The salespersons' move is the trap: listings stay with the broker who holds them, and a salesperson's change of association moves the license, not the clients.

blocks.html: So the designations will be Ahmed for the Weissmans and Jordan for the Laus. Renata checks the paperwork. The Weissmans signed an agency disclosure at listing with the old firm, then a new one with Hudson & Hart when the listings transferred. On the new form they checked advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents and wrote Ahmed's name in the space for their designated agent. The Laus signed their form in Brooklyn in January. They checked advance consent to dual agency. The designated agent line is blank.

blocks.title: The two consent lines
blocks.html:
Weissman form (Hudson & Hart, April 2): Advance consent to dual agency: checked. Advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents: checked. Designated sales agent for seller: Ahmed Rahman.
Lau form (Hudson & Hart Brooklyn, January 14): Advance consent to dual agency: checked. Advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents: blank. Designated sales agent for buyer: blank.

blocks.q: What does the firm still need before Jordan and Ahmed act as designated agents on Puritan Avenue?
c: Nothing, since both clients gave advance consent to some form of dual agency
A new listing agreement from the Weissmans naming Jordan as a cooperating broker
The Laus' written consent to designated agency, naming Jordan as their agent
A written waiver from the Laus of every fiduciary duty owed by Hudson & Hart
blocks.x: Advance consent to plain dual agency is not consent to designated agency. The form treats them as separate choices, and advance consent to designated agents requires naming the agent. The Laus must consent in writing to dual agency with designated sales agents, with Jordan named. The trap is reading one checked box as covering the other. Each client consents to the specific arrangement.

blocks.html: Then Jordan remembers something uncomfortable. Two Sundays ago, before the Laus ever mentioned Forest Hills, Jordan covered an open house at Puritan Avenue as a favor to Ahmed. Ruth Weissman stayed for the first hour. Over coffee in the kitchen she told Jordan, as the firm's representative, that they had already signed on a condo in White Plains and would take $1,600,000 if they could close before September. The house is listed at $1,749,000.

blocks.q: Jordan holds the Weissmans' bottom line from the open house. What is the best course for the firm?
c: Designate Jordan anyway, since designation starts the duties fresh
Designate a different salesperson for the Laus and keep Jordan out of it
Let Jordan use the number, since the sellers spoke at a public open house
Tell the Laus the number now, before designation, while it is still allowed
blocks.x: Information a seller gave the firm in confidence stays confidential. A designated agent may not use what was learned earlier from the other side, and Jordan cannot unlearn a number. The cleanest fix is to designate a salesperson with no history on the listing. The trap is that designation wipes the slate; it does not. Duties of confidentiality to the Weissmans began when Ruth confided in the firm.

blocks.q: Daniel Lau asks Jordan why a colleague is suddenly taking over on Puritan Avenue. What can Jordan say?
c: That the sellers already bought in White Plains, which explains the conflict
That Jordan helped the listing side earlier and must keep those confidences
That Jordan learned what the sellers would accept and must stay out of it
Nothing at all, since any explanation would breach a duty to the sellers
blocks.x: Jordan can disclose the fact of the conflict without disclosing its content. Saying Jordan worked the listing side and owes the sellers confidentiality is honest and complete enough. The second choice is the trap: announcing that Jordan knows what the sellers would accept tells the Laus there is a number to be had, which leaks the sellers' position by implication.

blocks.html: Diane agrees. She asks Kofi Mensah, a Brooklyn salesperson who has never touched the Puritan file, to serve as the Laus' designated agent. Jordan explains to the Laus, without saying why in any detail, that a colleague will represent them on this one house because Jordan helped the listing side earlier. Jordan stays their agent for every other property. The Laus sign the consent to dual agency with designated sales agents with Kofi's name on it, and the Weissmans are told who the buyer's designated agent is.

blocks.title: Designated does not mean single
blocks.html: Once designated agents are appointed, each can advocate for their own client. But the firm still represents both sides. The broker is still a dual agent, nobody gets undivided loyalty, and nothing either side told the firm before designation becomes fair game.

blocks.text: Thursday: what designated agents can do

blocks.html: Kofi meets the Laus at the house. Daniel has a spreadsheet. Mei has questions about the slate roof. Kofi pulls five Forest Hills Gardens sales from the last nine months, adjusts for the roof's age and the unfinished basement, and they talk numbers. The Laus ask Kofi to say, plainly, what he would offer.

blocks.q: May Kofi recommend a specific offer price to the Laus?
c: Yes, a designated agent may advise and negotiate for the client he was assigned
No, because the firm is a dual agent and nobody in the firm may give advice on price
With the Weissmans' written approval first, since the firm represents them
If Diane reviews the recommendation first and confirms that it is neutral
blocks.x: That is the whole point of designation: each designated agent can give advice and negotiate for the client assigned to them, including what to offer or whether to counter. The trap is applying the plain dual agency rule, where no one may advise on price. Designation changes that for the two salespersons, though the broker herself stays neutral.

blocks.html: The Laus offer $1,620,000 with a mortgage contingency. Ahmed advises the Weissmans to counter at $1,710,000 and to ask for a 75-day closing. On Friday morning Daniel Lau calls Diane directly. "You're the boss. Between us, is $1,680,000 too much for that house?"

blocks.q: How should Diane respond to Daniel's call?
c: Give her honest view, because the Laus are clients of the firm she owns
Say $1,680,000 is fair, since that number is public once he offers it
Tell him the sellers' counter is firm so the deal does not drag on
Stay neutral and send him back to Kofi for advice on price
blocks.x: The broker remains a dual agent under designated agency and supervises both sides, so she cannot advise either client on price or strategy. Daniel's question belongs to Kofi. The trap is the first choice: the Laus are indeed clients of the firm, but so are the Weissmans, and the broker is the one person in the deal who represents both.

blocks.html: Renata spots a problem nobody planned for. Hudson & Hart's client management system is shared across both offices. Ahmed's notes on the Weissman file, including "sellers must close by 9/1, will go to 1.6," are visible to every salesperson in the firm, including Kofi. Kofi says he has not opened the file. Renata wants to be sure he never does.

blocks.q: What is the best way for the firm to protect each side's confidences in this deal?
c: Rely on Kofi's word, since designated agents promise not to look
Delete Ahmed's notes so that nothing confidential stays in the file
Restrict each file to its designated agent and the supervising broker
Move the Weissman file to paper and keep it in Renata's office drawer
blocks.x: Designated agency works only if each side's confidences stay with that side's agent and the supervising broker. Limiting file access in the shared system is the practical safeguard. Deleting notes is the trap. Brokers must keep transaction records, and destroying file notes mid-deal creates a record-keeping problem without solving the access problem.

blocks.html: Renata locks both files to their designated agents and Diane, and adds a line to the branch policy manual: in every in-house deal, the two files are walled off on the day of designation. Then she holds a short training for the six inherited salespersons, who will now meet buyers as Hudson & Hart agents for the first time.

The wall has a cost Diane accepts. Ahmed and Kofi cannot compare notes in the kitchen, cannot share a lunch table conversation about the deal, and cannot be copied on each other's emails. Diane can see both files because she supervises both agents under 19 NYCRR 175.21, but she uses what she sees only to supervise, never to coach one side against the other. If she ever slipped, both clients could claim the firm's neutrality was a fiction, and the consent they signed would be worth very little.

One of the inherited salespersons, Gloria Ferrante, asks the question everyone is thinking: "For twenty years I told every buyer, 'I work for the seller.' Now what do I tell them?" Renata walks through the scripts. A buyer who walks into an open house of a firm listing hears that the agent represents the seller, gets the agency disclosure, and is told she may hire her own buyer's agent, including one from Hudson & Hart under the designated agent policy.

blocks.q: A competitor on Queens Boulevard practices seller agency exclusively. A buyer there asks, "Can you be my agent?" The licensee should say:
c: Yes, but only for homes listed with other firms in the area
Yes, once the buyer signs an advance consent to dual agency
No, and the firm cannot help, so the buyer should leave
No, the firm represents only sellers, but it can show homes
blocks.x: Under a seller-agency-only policy, buyers are customers. The firm can show homes, answer factual questions, and deal honestly, but it represents no buyers. The licensee should say so at first substantive contact and mention the buyer may hire a buyer's agent elsewhere. The first choice is the trap: representing buyers on outside listings is a different policy, not this one.

blocks.html: Gloria asks about the other extreme. A buyer brokerage in Bayside represents buyers only. A homeowner calls it wanting to list a Cape Cod. The firm cannot take the listing without abandoning its own model, so it refers the seller to a listing firm, perhaps for a referral fee between brokers if both agree. A buyer-only firm never faces in-house dual agency, which is why some brokers choose it. The cost is giving up listing income.

blocks.q: Which policy description matches Hudson & Hart's new rule: buyer agency on outside listings, dual agency with consent for in-house sales?
c: Consensual dual agency for in-house sales, buyer agency for all other deals
Consensual dual agency for in-house sales, seller agency as the norm
Buyer agency exclusively, with listings referred to cooperating firms
Seller agency exclusively, with designated sales agents assigned on every sale
blocks.x: The syllabus names this policy directly: consensual dual agency for in-house sales with buyer agency for all other transactions. With seller agency as the norm, by contrast, buyers on outside listings would be customers, not clients. That near match is the trap, because both policies use consensual dual agency in-house. What differs is how the firm treats buyers on everyone else's listings.

blocks.html: The parties agree at $1,675,000 with a 75-day closing, and attorneys draft the contract. Then Ahmed has emergency surgery and will be out for a month. The Weissmans still need someone to handle the buyer's inspection requests, the appraisal, and the co-ordination with their White Plains closing. Diane gets a call from Ruth: "Can't you just take over?"

blocks.q: Ahmed cannot continue. What should the firm do for the Weissmans?
c: Have Diane step in as their advocate until Ahmed returns from leave
Leave the Weissmans unrepresented, since the price is already agreed
Have Kofi handle both sides, since paperwork is what is left to do
Designate another salesperson for them, with their written consent
blocks.x: The broker cannot become one side's advocate while remaining the dual agent over both. Another salesperson with no ties to the Lau side can be designated, with the Weissmans' consent documented. Kofi taking both sides is the trap: it turns designated agency into single licensee dual agency, and inspection requests are still a negotiation, not mere paperwork.

blocks.html: Renata is an associate broker working under Diane's supervision, and she has not worked the Lau side. Diane designates her for the Weissmans, Ruth and Paul sign an updated consent naming her, and the Laus are told. Renata negotiates a $9,000 credit for a cracked sewer line instead of the $22,000 the Laus' inspector priced. The deal closes on schedule.

blocks.title: The designated agent consent conversation
blocks.html: Before a client signs, say three things out loud. First: our firm represents both you and the other side, and our broker supervises both of us and stays neutral. Second: I can advise you on price and terms, and your information stays with me and the broker. Third: you will not get undivided loyalty from the firm, and you may decline and hire an outside agent for this property. Then hand over the form and let them read it.

Afterward Mei Lau asks Kofi the honest question: "Were we really represented?" Kofi's answer is the honest one too. Each side had an advocate who could advise them on price and terms, and their confidences were walled off. What neither side had was a firm with undivided loyalty. If the deal had gone sideways, both clients would have been dealing with one broker who could not take either side. That is why some buyers insist on a firm with no listings, and why the agency disclosure form exists to make the choice visible.

blocks.q: Which statement about the Puritan Avenue deal is accurate?
c: Each designated agent gave undivided loyalty once the files were walled off
Hudson & Hart stopped being a dual agent once two agents were designated
The firm stayed a dual agent; each client gave up undivided loyalty
The Laus became customers of the firm once Kofi was designated as their agent
blocks.x: Designation gives each client an advocate, but the broker remains a dual agent and neither client receives undivided loyalty from the firm. That is the trade both sides consented to in writing. The walled-off files choice is the trap. Good confidentiality practice protects secrets, but it cannot turn a firm that represents both sides into a single agent for either.

items: A brokerage needs a written agency policy, because the policy determines what every licensee tells consumers at first substantive contact.
Designated sales agents are salespersons or associate brokers under the broker's supervision; the broker stays the dual agent and cannot designate herself.
Consent to dual agency and consent to designated agency are separate choices, and advance consent to designated agents names the agent.
Confidences learned before designation stay confidential; when an agent already holds the other side's secrets, designate someone else.
Designated agents may advise and negotiate for their own client; the broker stays neutral and walls off each side's file.
Consensual dual agency gives each side an advocate but never undivided loyalty, and the clients must understand that trade before they sign.

lessons.title: Case file: One Week, Four Doors in Queens
lessons.tagline: A condo rental, a co-op sale, a bakery lease, and Sal's six-family. Same agent, same week, four different answers to "who is my client?"
objectives: Apply landlord and tenant agency rules, including the NYC FARE Act, to a residential rental
Decide whom a listing agent represents in a co-op sale and what the agent owes the board and the buyer
Decide when the RPL 443 form applies to rentals, co-ops, commercial leases, and buildings of five or more units, and what still applies when it does not
Analyze dual agency and duties to customers in a commercial lease

blocks.title: Monday morning, Astoria
blocks.html: Diane Hart sends Jordan to cover the firm's Queens desk for a week while Renata is on vacation. Four files sit on the desk. A condo owner in Long Island City wants a tenant for his one-bedroom. A shareholder in a Jackson Heights garden co-op is selling her two-bedroom. Evelyn Park, the commercial investor, wants a tenant for an empty storefront on Steinway Street. And Sal Russo, owner of a six-unit building on 31st Avenue, has finally decided to sell. At 9:15 the first call comes in: a nurse named Aisha Rahimi saw the condo listing on a rental site and wants to see it at lunch. She opens with: "Is there a broker fee, and can you get the owner to come down on rent?"

The owner, Rafael Ortiz, signed an exclusive right to rent with Hudson & Hart: one month's rent as the fee, $3,150, payable when a lease is signed. That makes the firm a landlord's agent. Rafael asked on the phone whether he could "just add the fee to the tenant's move-in costs, like everyone used to."

blocks.q: Under the NYC FARE Act, who pays Hudson & Hart's $3,150 fee on Rafael's listing?
c: Aisha, if she signs a lease, since she benefits from the apartment
Rafael, because the firm was hired by and works for the landlord
Aisha and Rafael equally, if the split is disclosed in the listing
Whichever party the lease names, since lease terms are negotiable
blocks.x: Since June 11, 2025, a broker hired by the landlord in NYC is paid by the landlord, not the tenant. Rafael cannot pass Hudson & Hart's fee to Aisha, in the lease or in move-in costs. The disclosed split is the trap: the law requires that any fees a tenant must pay be disclosed, but disclosure does not make a landlord's agent's fee chargeable to the tenant.

blocks.title: FARE Act, in practice
blocks.html: The Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses Act took effect June 11, 2025. A landlord's agent, including an agent who publishes a listing with the landlord's permission, cannot charge the tenant a fee. An agent who publishes a rental listing is presumed to have the landlord's permission. Any fee a tenant must pay has to be disclosed in the listing and the lease. A tenant who hires their own agent may agree to pay that agent.

Jordan answers Aisha's first question easily: no broker fee for her on this apartment. The second question is harder. "Can you get him to come down?" is a request for representation, and Jordan already has a client in this deal.

blocks.q: How should Jordan answer Aisha's request to negotiate the rent down for her?
c: Agree to help, since she pays nothing and so is owed nothing in return
Agree, and keep it quiet, since rental deals are too small for dual agency
Say the firm represents the owner, and she may hire her own agent
Refuse to speak with her further until she signs a tenant agency agreement
blocks.x: Jordan is the landlord's agent and owes Rafael loyalty, including getting him the best rent. Jordan can be honest and helpful to Aisha as a customer, but cannot advocate against Rafael. Telling her she may hire a tenant's agent is the honest answer. The trap is thinking rentals are too small for agency rules; dual agency in a rental needs the same informed written consent.

blocks.html: Aisha tours at lunch. Before she gets to her budget, Jordan hands her two forms: the New York State Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form, and the agency disclosure form in its landlord and tenant version, with the landlord's agent box checked. A condo unit is residential real property under RPL 443, and rentals have their own version of the form.

blocks.q: When was Jordan required to give Aisha the landlord-tenant agency disclosure?
c: Before Rafael signed his exclusive right to rent agreement
At first substantive contact with her as a prospective tenant
At lease signing, together with the lease and its riders
When she asked whether Jordan represented the owner
blocks.x: RPL 443 requires a landlord's agent to give the disclosure to a prospective tenant at first substantive contact. The form is due to Rafael, the landlord, before he signs the listing agreement; that timing is the trap, because it applies to the agent's own client, not to the tenant. Waiting for lease signing defeats the point, which is to warn her before she reveals anything.

blocks.html: While Aisha is still in the lobby, Rafael texts Jordan: "Also, I had a bad experience last time. No vouchers, no Section 8, okay? Just screen them out quietly." Rafael is the client, and an agent owes the client obedience. But the duty of obedience covers lawful instructions only.

blocks.q: How should Jordan respond to Rafael's instruction to screen out applicants who use housing vouchers?
c: Follow it quietly, since obedience to the client's instructions comes first
Follow it, but just for applicants who have not yet submitted paperwork
Refuse, explain that source of income is protected, and document it
Follow it, since the condo is owned by an individual and not a company
blocks.x: Lawful source of income, including housing vouchers, is a protected class under the New York State Human Rights Law and the NYC Human Rights Law. An agent's duty of obedience extends only to lawful instructions, so Jordan must refuse, explain why, and note it in the file. The individual-owner choice is the trap: an individual owner renting a condo through a broker is not exempt from source of income rules.

blocks.html: Rafael grumbles but agrees after Jordan sends him a one-paragraph summary of the law and Diane's office policy. If he had insisted, the firm's next step would have been to end the listing. A landlord's agent who carries out an unlawful instruction is liable alongside the landlord, and the license is the agent's, not the owner's.

That evening Aisha hires her own tenant's agent, Kwame Asante, from a Sunnyside firm, under a written agreement that she will pay him $1,500 if she rents through him. Kwame calls Jordan and offers $2,850 a month on a two-year lease. He also asks Jordan to have Rafael pay half of Kwame's fee "to make it fair."

blocks.q: Who is responsible for Kwame's $1,500 fee?
c: Aisha, under her agreement, unless Rafael agrees to pay it
Rafael, because the FARE Act bans every fee paid by tenants
Hudson & Hart, out of its $3,150 fee as a cooperating split
Nobody, since a tenant's agent may not charge in NYC rentals
blocks.x: The FARE Act stops a landlord's agent from charging the tenant. It does not stop a tenant from hiring and paying her own agent. Aisha owes Kwame under her agreement, and Rafael may choose to pay some of it as a negotiated point. The trap is reading the FARE Act as banning every tenant-paid fee. It targets the fee of the agent who works for the landlord.

blocks.html: Jordan takes the offer to Rafael and recommends a counter at $3,000 for two years, because the building's last three rentals closed between $2,975 and $3,100. Rafael counters, Kwame pushes back, and they land at $2,975. Each agent advocated for one client. That is single agency on both sides, and nobody needed a consent form.

blocks.text: Door two: the Jackson Heights co-op

blocks.html: Beatriz Almeida owns 400 shares allocated to a two-bedroom in a 1920s garden co-op on 80th Street. She listed with Hudson & Hart at $489,000. Her buyer, Tomasz Nowak, has his own buyer's agent, Lena Brooks. Contract is signed. Now comes the board package: financial statements, tax returns, bank letters, reference letters, and a purchase application, due to the managing agent in two weeks.

blocks.q: In Beatriz's sale, who is Hudson & Hart's client?
c: The co-op corporation, because it has to approve the transfer
The board, because the firm has to deliver the purchase package to it
Beatriz, the shareholder who signed the listing agreement
Tomasz, because a buyer is needed to complete the sale
blocks.x: The listing agent represents the selling shareholder. The co-op corporation and its board are a third party that must approve the transfer of shares and the proprietary lease, but they are not the agent's principal. The board choice is the trap: delivering papers to someone does not make them your client, and the board has its own counsel and managing agent.

blocks.title: Co-ops are covered
blocks.html: Since the 2011 amendments to RPL 443, co-op and condo sales and rentals require the agency disclosure form. Before 2011 they fell outside the definition, which meant many Manhattan buyers never saw a form. Jordan gave Beatriz her form at the listing appointment, and Lena gave hers to Tomasz before he signed her buyer agreement and to Jordan, for Beatriz, at first substantive contact.

Lena calls Jordan with a problem. Tomasz's income on his tax return is $96,000. The co-op's informal rule is that maintenance and debt service should not exceed about 30 percent of gross income, and on his numbers he is right at the edge. Tomasz expects a raise in January. Lena asks: "Can we list his income at $110,000? That's what he'll make next year, it's basically true."

blocks.q: What should Jordan, the seller's agent, do about Lena's proposal?
c: Go along, since helping the deal close serves Beatriz
Refuse to submit a package that misstates his income
Go along, if Tomasz signs a note saying the raise is likely
Stay silent, since the package is the buyer side's paperwork
blocks.x: Agents owe honesty to everyone in the deal, including a board that relies on the package. Stating an income that does not exist is a misrepresentation, and an agent who knowingly passes it along shares the liability. The trap is that it serves the seller. Loyalty to a client never extends to helping deceive a third party, and a deal built on a false package can unravel later.

blocks.html: Lena drops the idea. Instead the package shows the $96,000 income, an offer letter for the January raise, and fourteen months of maintenance in post-closing liquid assets, which the board weighs as a cushion. The board interviews Tomasz on a Wednesday evening. Afterward the treasurer catches Jordan in the lobby: "Off the record, would you rent to this guy if it were your building?"

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle the treasurer's question?
c: Give a strong endorsement, since Beatriz wants the sale approved
Share anything the buyer's agent has mentioned about his finances
Say the buyer seems risky, so the board trusts Jordan in future
Stay factual: the package speaks for itself and the board decides
blocks.x: Jordan represents Beatriz and wants approval, but must not overstate facts to the board or pass along anything the buyer side shared in confidence. A factual answer that points to the package is honest and protects everyone. The strong endorsement is the trap: puffing about a buyer's reliability to a board that relies on it can become a misrepresentation.

blocks.html: The board approves Tomasz two weeks later. Jordan's job does not end at approval. Jordan confirms the closing date with the managing agent, makes sure Beatriz has ordered her stock certificate and proprietary lease for transfer, and reminds her that the co-op charges a flip tax of 2 percent of the price, paid by the seller under the building's rules. Every one of those tasks is service to Beatriz, and every conversation with the buyer side stays limited to what Beatriz would want shared.

blocks.text: Door three: the Steinway Street storefront

blocks.html: Evelyn Park owns a 1,500 square foot storefront near 30th Avenue. She hires Hudson & Hart under an exclusive right to lease at a commission of 6 percent of the first year's base rent. Asking rent is $7,500 a month. The best prospect is Yiannis Petrakis, who runs a bakery in Bay Ridge and wants a second location. He has no broker. He tells Jordan he will pay up to $8,200 a month if he can get a ten-year term, then asks Jordan to "help me get it cheaper, I'll make it worth your while."

blocks.title: The commission on a $7,500 a month lease
blocks.html:
First-year base rent: $7,500 x 12 = $90,000.
Commission: $90,000 x 0.06 = $5,400, payable by Evelyn to Hudson & Hart.
If Yiannis signs at $8,000: $8,000 x 12 x 0.06 = $5,760. The firm's fee rises with the rent, which is one more reason the firm cannot also quietly represent the tenant.

blocks.q: Which disclosure forms must Jordan give Yiannis for this commercial lease?
c: The RPL 443 agency form plus the fair housing disclosure form
The RPL 443 form alone, because Yiannis is unrepresented
The fair housing disclosure form, but not the RPL 443 form
Neither form, because commercial deals are exempt from both of them
blocks.x: RPL 443 applies only to residential real property: 1 to 4 family dwellings, condos, and co-ops. A retail lease is outside it. The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form under 19 NYCRR 175.28 covers all property types, commercial included, at first substantive contact. The exempt-from-both choice is the trap; only the agency form drops out.

blocks.html: No agency form does not mean no agency law. Common law agency applies in full to commercial deals: Jordan owes Evelyn loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, and reasonable care, and owes Yiannis honesty and fair dealing. Diane reminds Jordan that a clear oral and written statement of whom the firm represents is still the professional standard, and that Reg 175.7 requires a broker to make clear for which party it is acting in every transaction. Commercial tenants are often small business owners like Yiannis, with no broker and no lawyer yet. They are exactly the people who mistake a friendly landlord's agent for their own, so Jordan says it early and puts it in an email: "I represent the owner, Evelyn Park."

blocks.q: Yiannis asks Jordan to represent him too, for a side fee. Without an RPL 443 form in this deal, what does the firm need to act for both?
c: Nothing, since RPL 443 governs dual agency and does not reach commercial deals
Yiannis's consent alone, since he would be the one paying the side fee
Evelyn's consent alone, since the listing makes her the firm's principal
Informed consent from both, plus everyone's knowledge and consent of fees
blocks.x: Dual agency without consent is disloyalty under common law, whatever the property type. Both principals must give informed consent, and under Reg 175.7 the broker may not take pay from more than one party without everyone's full knowledge and consent. The trap is assuming that because the 443 form does not apply, nothing does. Written consent is still the only safe practice.

blocks.html: Jordan declines Yiannis's offer and tells him plainly that the firm represents Evelyn. Then Jordan faces a quieter question. Yiannis said he would pay up to $8,200 for a ten-year term. Evelyn's asking rent is $7,500.

blocks.q: Must Jordan tell Evelyn that Yiannis said he would pay up to $8,200?
c: Yes, a landlord's agent must disclose material facts to the client
No, because an unrepresented tenant's statements are confidential to him
No, because sharing it would be unfair to an unrepresented party
Only if Yiannis first signs a written offer at that rent before the call
blocks.x: Jordan's fiduciary duty of disclosure runs to Evelyn, the client. Information a customer volunteers to the other side's agent is not confidential, and a tenant's ceiling is about as material as facts get. The fairness choice is the trap: Jordan owes Yiannis honesty, not secrecy. This is exactly why the agent should state the firm's role before a customer starts talking money.

blocks.html: Evelyn holds at $7,900 for ten years with 3 percent annual increases, and Yiannis signs after his own attorney reviews the lease. Jordan notes in the file that Yiannis was told on day one that the firm represents the landlord, and that he received the fair housing form.

On Friday Sal Russo comes in to list his 31st Avenue building: six rent-stabilized and market units, rent roll potential of $12,850 a month. He is in a good mood. "Six families, so you don't need any of that agency paperwork, right? My cousin sold his four-family in Ridgewood and they made him sign a whole pile."

blocks.q: Does RPL 443 require the agency disclosure form for the sale of Sal's six-unit building?
c: Yes, because any building with apartments is residential property
No, so Hudson & Hart owes Sal no fiduciary duties in this deal
Yes, but just toward buyers who plan to live in the building
No, but fiduciary duties and the fair housing form still apply
blocks.x: RPL 443 covers 1 to 4 family dwellings, condos, and co-ops. A six-unit rental building is outside that definition, so the statutory form is not required, although nothing stops the firm from explaining its role in writing anyway. The trap is the second choice. Agency law, Sal's fiduciary rights, and the fair housing disclosure form under 175.28 apply regardless.

blocks.html: Sal's cousin was right about Ridgewood: a four-family is inside RPL 443, so his cousin's agent needed the form. Sal's six-family is not. Diane's policy, though, is to give a written statement of the firm's role in every deal, form or no form, because the dispute that matters later is always "you never told me whom you represented."

Sal has one more request before he signs. "When buyers call, tell them the units are all free market. Two of them are stabilized, but the new owner can figure that out. It'll get me a better price." A buyer of a six-family prices the building on its rent roll, and stabilized rents cap what two of those units can earn.

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle Sal's request to describe all six units as free market?
c: Agree, since a seller's agent is bound to follow the client's lawful wishes on marketing
Refuse; misstating the units' status to buyers is a misrepresentation
Agree, but tell buyers to verify the regulatory status with their own lawyers
Agree, since buyers of investment property are presumed to do their own checks
blocks.x: A seller's agent owes buyers honesty and may not misrepresent material facts. Whether units are rent stabilized goes straight to the building's value, and stating otherwise is misrepresentation that exposes the firm and Sal. The verify-with-a-lawyer choice is the trap. A disclaimer does not cure a false statement, and obedience never covers a client's instruction to deceive.

blocks.html: Sal backs down when Jordan points out that any buyer's attorney will pull the building's rent registration history from HCR, and that a buyer who was lied to can sue both of them. The listing goes out with an accurate rent roll: four free market units, two stabilized, and the total potential rent shown as it really is.

blocks.title: No form is not no duty
blocks.html: Students often reason backward: no RPL 443 form, so no agency. Wrong. The form is a disclosure tool for consumers in residential deals. Agency itself comes from the relationship, and every client, residential or commercial, gets the full set of fiduciary duties. Every party in every property type gets the fair housing disclosure.

blocks.q: Looking back at the week, in which deal was Hudson & Hart required to use the RPL 443 form?
c: The condo rental and the co-op sale, not the storefront or six-family
The co-op sale alone, since co-ops are the reason the form was expanded
Every deal of the week, since each involved property in New York City
The condo rental, the co-op sale, and the six-family, but not the storefront
blocks.x: RPL 443 reaches residential real property: 1 to 4 family dwellings, condos, and co-ops, for sales and rentals. The condo rental and the co-op sale qualify. A retail lease does not, and a six-unit building is beyond the 1 to 4 family limit. The last choice is the trap, because the six-family is residential in everyday speech but not under the statute's definition.

items: A landlord's agent in NYC is paid by the landlord under the FARE Act; a tenant may still hire and pay her own tenant's agent.
The landlord-tenant version of the agency form goes to a prospective tenant at first substantive contact, and to the landlord before the listing is signed.
In a co-op sale the listing agent represents the selling shareholder, not the board, and owes the board honesty: no inflated board packages, no puffed endorsements.
Commercial deals and buildings of five or more units fall outside RPL 443, but common law agency, Reg 175.7, and the fair housing disclosure form still apply.
Dual agency in any property type needs informed consent from both principals.
Facts a customer volunteers to the other side's agent are not confidential and must be passed to that agent's client.

lessons.title: Case file: The Listing That Outlived Its Owner
lessons.tagline: A Great Kills listing with a renewal clause nobody should have signed, a seller who dies in June, and a summer of agencies ending in every way the law allows.
objectives: Choose between exclusive right to sell, exclusive agency, open listing, exclusive right to rent, and exclusive buyer agreements for a client's actual goals
Apply 19 NYCRR 175.15 to automatic renewal clauses and distinguish a lawful protection period
Decide whether an agency has ended by act of the parties or by operation of law, and what duties survive
Analyze who can hire the broker after a seller dies and what the firm may do in the meantime

blocks.title: Great Kills, the first of March
blocks.html: Harold Bennett, 81, has lived in his center hall colonial in Great Kills, Staten Island, since 1974. His wife died two years ago, the stairs are getting hard, and he wants to move to a senior community near his daughter in New Jersey. He owns the house alone. Jordan meets him at his kitchen table with Hudson & Hart's listing packet. The price is set at $899,000 and the commission at 5 percent. Harold has one condition: "My nephew Kevin keeps saying he might buy it. If he does, I'm not paying anybody." Jordan slides the firm's standard exclusive right to sell across the table and notices, on page two, a clause Marcus added to the template last year.

blocks.text: March: the paper on the kitchen table

blocks.title: Hudson & Hart template, paragraph 4 (Marcus's version)
blocks.html: "Term. This agreement begins March 1 and ends August 31. Unless Owner gives Broker written notice of cancellation at least 30 days before the end of any term, this agreement shall renew automatically for successive 90-day periods. Protection period. If within 90 days after this agreement ends Owner sells to anyone Broker showed the property to during the term, and whose name Broker delivered to Owner in writing within 10 days after the term ends, Owner shall pay the commission, unless Owner has then listed exclusively with another broker."

blocks.q: Jordan flags paragraph 4. Which part is the problem under New York rules?
c: The protection period for buyers shown during the term
The automatic 90-day renewal without fresh agreement
The six-month term, which is longer than DOS allows
The written list of buyer names due after the term
blocks.x: 19 NYCRR 175.15 bars a broker from being party to an exclusive listing that automatically continues beyond its fixed termination date. A protection period is different: it does not extend the listing, it protects the fee for buyers the broker actually produced during the term. That makes the protection clause the trap. Nothing in the rules caps a listing at six months.

blocks.title: 19 NYCRR 175.15
blocks.html: No real estate broker may be a party to an exclusive listing contract that contains an automatic continuation of the listing period beyond the fixed termination date in the contract. Every exclusive listing needs a definite end. If the owner and broker want more time, they sign an extension.

Jordan strikes the renewal sentence, Harold initials the change, and Diane later pulls the clause out of the template for good. Then they deal with Kevin. Harold wants a listing, a sign, and the MLS, but he wants to keep the right to sell to Kevin for nothing.

blocks.q: Which listing form gives Harold full MLS marketing while leaving him free to sell to a buyer he finds himself, commission free?
c: Exclusive right to sell, since the broker controls the marketing
Exclusive agency, since the owner keeps the right to sell
Open listing, since that form lets the owner sell to anyone alone
Net listing, since Harold sets his number and Kevin pays the rest
blocks.x: In an exclusive agency listing, Hudson & Hart is the only broker, but Harold keeps the right to sell on his own with no commission. An open listing also lets the owner sell alone, which makes it the trap, but it is non-exclusive and many firms will not market it heavily. Another option is an exclusive right to sell that names Kevin as an excluded buyer. Net listings are prohibited in New York.

blocks.html: Harold chooses the exclusive right to sell with a written exclusion: if Kevin Bennett buys during the term, no commission is due. Jordan explains why that is better for both sides than exclusive agency. Harold gets the protection he wants for Kevin, and the firm is not exposed to Harold finding some other buyer through a neighbor and paying nothing after the firm spent money on photos and ads. Harold initials the printed explanation of exclusive right to sell and exclusive agency that 19 NYCRR 175.24 requires on residential exclusive listings, and signs the agency disclosure form first.

blocks.q: Which document does 19 NYCRR 175.24 require Harold to sign or initial with this residential exclusive listing?
c: A sworn statement that he has no other broker for the house
A printed explanation of exclusive right to sell and exclusive agency
A waiver of his right to receive offers from cooperating brokers
An acknowledgment that the listing renews unless he cancels it
blocks.x: For exclusive listings of 1 to 4 family homes, condos, and co-ops, 175.24 requires a printed explanation, in at least 6-point type, of the difference between exclusive right to sell and exclusive agency, signed or initialed by the owner. The renewal acknowledgment is the trap: an automatic renewal is prohibited by 175.15 whether or not the owner acknowledges it.

blocks.text: June: the listing ends without anyone signing anything

blocks.html: The house shows well. In May the Morales family, buyers with a Hudson & Hart buyer's agent, tour twice. On June 9 they send an offer of $870,000. Jordan calls Harold to present it and gets his daughter, Claire, who is crying. Harold died in his sleep the night before.

blocks.q: What is the status of Hudson & Hart's listing after Harold's death?
c: It continues, binding Harold's heirs until August 31
It continues, but Claire signs the next counteroffer
It is suspended until his will is admitted to probate
It ended by operation of law on Harold's death in June
blocks.x: Death of either the principal or the broker ends an agency by operation of law. The listing does not pass to heirs like a piece of property, and no one can accept the Morales offer on Harold's behalf. Continuing until August 31 is the trap. A listing is a personal service contract, and the authority behind it died with Harold. The firm must wait for someone with legal authority over the estate.

blocks.html: The Morales family's agent, a colleague in the Brooklyn office, is already texting: "Any response yet? My buyers have an inspection booked for Thursday." Jordan has to say something. Claire has asked Jordan to keep the death quiet until the family can tell relatives, and she suggests telling the buyers the seller "is considering it."

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell the Morales family's agent about the offer?
c: That the seller is considering the offer, as Claire suggested
Nothing, until the estate has been through the Surrogate's Court
That the listing has ended and no one can act on the offer now
That the seller accepted, so the buyers keep their inspection date
blocks.x: Jordan owes honesty to buyers and their agent, and Claire is not Jordan's principal, so her request cannot authorize a misleading answer. The truthful answer is that the listing has ended and no one can respond until someone has authority over the estate. Saying the seller is considering it is the trap: it is a false statement about a seller who cannot consider anything, and it could cost the buyers money on an inspection.

blocks.html: Jordan tells the Morales family's agent the truth: the seller has died, the listing has ended, and there is no one who can accept their offer right now. Their deposit check never left their attorney's office. A week later Claire calls with a plan. "I'm his only child. I'll inherit it anyway. Put it back on the market, take the Morales offer, and I'll sign whatever you need."

blocks.q: Who can hire Hudson & Hart to sell the Bennett house now?
c: The executor, once the Surrogate's Court issues letters
Claire, today, because she is Harold's sole child and heir
Jordan, as the agent who was already marketing the house
The Morales family, since their offer predates his death
blocks.x: A dead person's property is managed by a court-appointed fiduciary. Once the Surrogate's Court issues letters testamentary to the executor named in the will (or letters of administration if there is no will), that person can act for the estate, including signing a listing. The trap is Claire as heir. She may well end up as executor, but expecting to inherit is not authority to sell before appointment.
