blocks.html: Claire is named executor in the will. Priya Nair, who handles the estate's real estate work, gets letters testamentary issued in August. Claire, as executor, signs a new exclusive right to sell with Hudson & Hart, with a new agency disclosure. The Morales family has bought elsewhere by then. The new listing price is $879,000 and the deed, when it comes, will be an executor's deed. Persons acting under court authority, such as executors, do not need a real estate license to sell the estate's property, but this one wants a broker. Jordan writes a short note for the file: dates of the old listing, its end on June 8 by Harold's death, the date letters issued, and the new listing's start. If anyone later questions whether marketing in the gap was authorized, the file answers it.

blocks.title: Whose death ends the listing?
blocks.html: The principal's death ends the agency. So does the death of the broker when the broker is a sole proprietor. The death or departure of the salesperson does not: the listing belongs to the broker, and another salesperson steps in. Exam items love to swap these.

Meanwhile Nadia Haddad, a first-time buyer and hospital pharmacist, signed a four-month exclusive right to represent with Hudson & Hart in May. Her agreement says the firm is owed a fee of 2 percent of the price if she buys any one to four family home or condo in Brooklyn during the term, whoever finds it. In July, after an argument about whether to waive an appraisal contingency, Nadia emails Diane: "I'm terminating. I'll find my own place."

blocks.q: Can Nadia end the agency before the term runs out?
c: No, because an exclusive buyer agreement is irrevocable during its term
Yes, and she owes nothing, because a buyer pays no commission in New York
Yes, she can revoke, but she may owe damages under the contract
No, unless Hudson & Hart first breaches one of its fiduciary duties to her
blocks.x: A principal always has the power to revoke an agent's authority, even if doing so breaks the contract. The broker's remedy is damages or the fee the agreement provides, not forcing the relationship to continue. The irrevocable choice is the trap. Only an agency coupled with an interest is irrevocable, and nothing in Nadia's buyer agreement gives the firm an interest in any property.

blocks.html: Diane does not argue. She sends Nadia a written release ending the agreement as of the date of her email, waives any fee on homes she finds on her own afterward, and keeps the fee language for the two homes Hudson & Hart showed her in June, in case she buys one of them within the term. Then Nadia asks a pointed question: "So you can tell the next buyer what my budget was?"

blocks.q: After the agency with Nadia ends, what does Hudson & Hart still owe her?
c: Nothing, because every duty of an agent ends with the agency
Continued confidentiality about her finances and her strategy
Loyalty for the rest of the original four-month term
Ongoing advice on any home she buys this year
blocks.x: Most fiduciary duties end with the agency, but confidentiality survives it. Nadia's budget, her pre-approval, and her negotiating limits stay private even after she leaves and even if she later bids against a firm client. The first choice is the trap because it is mostly true. Loyalty and advice end with the relationship, which is why the confidentiality exception is what exams test.

blocks.html: Marcus has his own problem. His sellers in Tottenville, the Kowalczyks, have rejected four offers within 3 percent of asking, screamed at two buyers' agents, and told him to stop showing to "people with car seats." Marcus wants to drop them. The listing still has three months to run.

blocks.q: The Kowalczyks tell Marcus not to show the house to families with children. Which is the correct response?
c: Follow the instruction, since a seller may choose a buyer for any reason
Follow it for showings, since offers from families still go in
Refuse and explain; the firm may end the listing if they insist
Follow it until the term ends, then decline to renew the listing agreement
blocks.x: Familial status is protected under federal and New York fair housing law, and an agent's duty of obedience covers lawful instructions only. Marcus must refuse and explain. If the sellers insist, the firm can renounce the agency rather than carry out discrimination. The first choice is the trap: sellers can choose among buyers for many reasons, but not for a protected one.

blocks.html: The sellers back off on the car seats but keep rejecting offers. Diane lets Marcus renounce the listing in writing, effective in 30 days, and offers to have another salesperson take over. A renunciation by the agent ends the agency by act of the parties. If it breaches the listing contract, the firm can owe the sellers damages, which is why Diane gives notice and offers a transition instead of walking out the door.

On August 3, a kitchen fire guts a Hudson & Hart listing in Midland Beach, a bungalow listed at $615,000 under an exclusive right to sell. The owners are safe and the lot is untouched, but the house is uninhabitable. The same week, a separate listing in New Dorp reaches its August 31 end date with no sale. In September, the New Dorp owners sell to a couple Diane's salesperson showed the house to on August 20, whose names Diane delivered in writing on September 4. The owners had not relisted with anyone.

blocks.q: What happened to the Midland Beach listing when the fire destroyed the house?
c: It ended by operation of law when the property was destroyed
Nothing, because a listing continues until its stated end date
It ended when the owners later gave written notice of cancellation
It became an open listing until the house could be rebuilt
blocks.x: Destruction of the property ends the agency by operation of law, along with death, incapacity, and bankruptcy of a party and a change in law making the deal illegal. The written notice choice is the trap; notice is how the parties end an agency by their own acts. If the owners want to sell the lot or the damaged house, they sign a new listing for what they now own.

blocks.q: The New Dorp listing expired August 31. Is Hudson & Hart owed a commission on the September sale?
c: No, because every listing duty and right ended on August 31
No, because 175.15 voids any clause that reaches past the term
Yes, provided the buyers' own agent agrees to share the fee
Yes, under the protection clause, which is not a renewal
blocks.x: The protection period applies to buyers the firm showed during the term and named in writing on time, and the owners had not relisted exclusively elsewhere. Courts have held that such a clause does not violate 175.15, because it does not extend the listing itself. That rule is the trap. It bans automatic continuation of the listing, not protection for buyers the broker actually produced.

blocks.text: September: the estate rents, and a different kind of agency

blocks.html: The Bennett house does not sell over Labor Day weekend. Claire, as executor, wants to rent it for a year while the market cools, and asks Jordan to handle it. Jordan sets her up with an exclusive right to rent: the firm earns a fee if the house rents during the 90-day term, whoever finds the tenant. Because Great Kills is in New York City, the FARE Act applies. The firm is the landlord's agent, and the estate pays its fee, not the tenant.

blocks.q: A walk-in tenant finds the Bennett house on her own and rents it directly from Claire during the term. Under the exclusive right to rent, Hudson & Hart is:
c: Owed its fee by the estate, whoever found the tenant
Owed its fee by the tenant, because she found the home
Owed nothing, since the tenant came in without a broker
Owed half its fee, because it did not procure the tenant
blocks.x: An exclusive right to rent works like an exclusive right to sell: the broker earns its fee if the property rents during the term, no matter who finds the tenant. In NYC the landlord pays the landlord's agent. The no-broker choice is the trap; that result belongs to an exclusive agency, where the owner keeps the right to deal directly without paying.

blocks.html: The last file of the summer is the strangest. Years ago Diane lent a longtime client, Mr. Ferraro, $60,000 to finish a basement apartment in his Eltingville two-family, secured by a recorded mortgage, and in the same document he gave her firm the exclusive authority to sell the house and repay the loan from the proceeds. In August Mr. Ferraro, angry about the slow market, tells Diane he is revoking the listing.

blocks.q: Can Mr. Ferraro revoke Diane's authority to sell?
c: Yes, because a principal can revoke an agent's authority at will
Yes, by giving the 30 days of notice in the listing
No, because the agency is coupled with an interest in the house
No, because a listing on a two-family house cannot be revoked
blocks.x: When the agent has its own interest in the property, here a secured loan to be repaid from the sale, the agency is coupled with an interest. The principal cannot revoke it, and it does not end at the principal's death. The always-revoke choice is the trap. It is the general rule, and an agency coupled with an interest is the classic exception.

blocks.html: Diane does not force the point. She tells Mr. Ferraro that the firm's authority continues until the loan is repaid, that she will keep marketing at a price he approves, and that he can end the arrangement at any time by paying off the $60,000. He calms down and agrees to a price cut. The lesson for Jordan is narrower than it sounds: an ordinary commission, however large, is not an interest in the property. Only a real stake, like a secured loan or part ownership, makes an agency irrevocable.

head: How the agency ended
File
Type
rows: Nadia emailed that she was terminating
Not ended: coupled with an interest
blocks.caption: Hudson & Hart's summer, sorted

blocks.title: New York paperwork that keeps endings clean
blocks.html: Every exclusive listing has a fixed end date and no automatic renewal (175.15). Residential exclusive listings include the printed explanation of exclusive right to sell versus exclusive agency, initialed by the owner (175.24). A new principal, such as an executor, signs a new listing and receives a new agency disclosure. Releases, renunciations, and buyer name lists are put in writing and kept with the transaction records for at least 3 years.

blocks.q: Which of these events ends an agency by operation of law rather than by act of the parties?
c: The listing reaches its stated termination date unsold
The seller and broker agree in writing to cancel early
The buyer emails the broker that he is terminating
The seller is adjudged bankrupt by a federal court
blocks.x: Death, incapacity, bankruptcy, destruction of the property, and a change in law end an agency by operation of law, without anyone choosing it. Expiration, mutual cancellation, revocation, and renunciation are acts of the parties. Expiration is the trap because it happens automatically, but the parties chose that date when they signed.

items: Match the agreement to the client's goal: exclusive right to sell with a named exclusion, exclusive agency, open listing, exclusive right to rent, or an exclusive buyer agreement.
Under 175.15 no exclusive listing may renew automatically; a protection period for buyers produced during the term is a different, lawful clause.
Death, incapacity, bankruptcy, destruction of the property, and a change in law end an agency by operation of law; after a seller dies, only a court-appointed fiduciary can sign a new listing.
A principal can revoke and an agent can renounce, though either may owe damages; an agency coupled with an interest cannot be revoked.
Confidentiality survives the end of the agency, and obedience never covers an unlawful instruction.

lessons.title: Case file: The Complaint Letter from Albany
lessons.tagline: A buyer tells the Department of State nobody ever said whom Marcus represented. Diane pulls every file from the quarter and finds out what the paper actually proves.
objectives: Decide when first substantive contact occurs in emails, texts, calls, and open houses, and who owes the agency disclosure to whom
Complete and audit the RPL 443 signature page, finding the defects that matter
Apply the refusal procedure: a written declaration of the facts under oath or affirmation, kept 3 years
Decide when a licensee may change roles and what new disclosure the change requires

blocks.title: A letter on Diane's desk
blocks.html: On a Monday in October, Diane Hart opens a letter from the Department of State, Division of Licensing Services. A buyer named Farah Siddiqui has filed a complaint against Marcus Webb and Hudson & Hart. She says she shared her budget, her pre-approval, and her deadline with Marcus over three weeks of emails about a Bay Ridge two-family, believing he was helping her, and learned only at contract signing that he represented the sellers. She paid $1,285,000. She believes she overpaid. DOS asks the firm to respond in writing by a stated deadline and to provide the agency disclosure records for the transaction. Diane decides not to stop at one file. She pulls every residential file from the quarter and calls Jordan into the conference room.

blocks.title: Farah's emails to Marcus, as printed from the file
blocks.html:
Aug 2, 9:14 pm: "Hi, is the 82nd Street two-family still available? What are the taxes?"
Aug 2, 10:02 pm (Marcus): "Yes! Taxes about $9,800. Showing Saturday?"
Aug 4, 7:40 am: "Saturday works. FYI I'm pre-approved to $1.35M and my lease ends Oct 31, so I need to close fast. Do you think they'd take $1.25M?"
Aug 4, 8:15 am (Marcus): "Let's talk Saturday, I think we can make something work."
Aug 24: Agency disclosure form signed by Farah at the contract meeting, seller's agent box checked.

blocks.q: When did Marcus's first substantive contact with Farah occur?
c: Aug 2, when she first asked whether the house was available
Aug 4, when she shared her budget and asked about price
The Saturday showing, because contact has to be in person
Aug 24, when the parties met to sign the contract
blocks.x: First substantive contact is when the conversation moves past property facts into the consumer's finances, motivation, or negotiating position. A question about availability and taxes is not it. A pre-approval amount, a deadline, and "would they take $1.25M" plainly are. The in-person choice is the trap: substantive contact can happen by email, text, or phone, and the form can be sent electronically.

blocks.html: Marcus's reply makes it worse. "I think we can make something work" sounds like an agent working for her. He should have answered the August 4 email with the disclosure form attached and one sentence on top: "Before we go further, I represent the sellers, please read this." Instead Farah had three more weeks of emails in which she told him her lease situation and her parents' gift amount. The form she finally signed on August 24 was accurate. It was also 20 days late.

blocks.q: Marcus tells Diane the late form does not matter because Farah signed one before the contract. What is the best answer?
c: He is right, since the statute requires a form before contract
He is right, because Farah had an attorney who could have warned her
He is wrong, since the form was due at first substantive contact
He is wrong, but mainly because the form should have been notarized
blocks.x: RPL 443 requires a seller's agent to give the disclosure to a buyer at first substantive contact, precisely so the buyer is warned before revealing anything. A signature at contract time cannot undo three weeks of disclosures. The attorney choice is the trap: a buyer's lawyer handles the contract, but the licensee's disclosure duty is the licensee's and arises long before an attorney is involved.

blocks.q: Farah never met Marcus in person before the Saturday showing. How could he have met the disclosure duty on August 4?
c: He could not, so waiting for the Saturday showing was proper
Read the form aloud to her on the phone, since email is not enough
Mail a paper copy, since an electronic signature is not accepted
Email the form and get an electronic acknowledgment
blocks.x: Substantive contact by email calls for a disclosure by email. Licensees routinely attach the agency and fair housing forms to a reply and collect the acknowledgment by electronic signature. Waiting for an in-person meeting is the trap: it lets the consumer keep talking with no warning, which is the harm the statute is aimed at.

blocks.title: RPL 443, subdivision 3: who gives it, to whom, when
blocks.html: A listing agent gives the form to the seller or landlord before entering into the listing agreement. A seller's or landlord's agent gives it to the buyer or tenant at the first substantive contact. A buyer's or tenant's agent gives it to the buyer or tenant before entering into the agency agreement, and to the seller or landlord (or that party's agent) at first substantive contact. Each time, the licensee gets a signed acknowledgment, gives the consumer a copy, and keeps one for at least 3 years.

blocks.title: The first reply, written once and reused
blocks.html: Diane's new template for every inquiry that mentions money, timing, or motivation: "Thanks for reaching out. Before we go further, please know that I represent the sellers of this property, not buyers. The attached New York agency disclosure explains what that means for you, and the fair housing disclosure is attached too. Please sign and return the acknowledgment. If you would like your own buyer's agent, you are free to hire one."

Jordan's file for a Sunday open house at a Windsor Terrace condo has a sign-in sheet with fourteen names and two signed agency disclosures. Diane asks about the other twelve. Jordan's notes show that most visitors asked about the HOA charges, the boiler, and whether the roof deck was common or private. Two visitors stayed to talk about their budgets and timing, and those two got forms.

blocks.q: Did Jordan violate RPL 443 by not giving forms to the twelve visitors who asked only about the building?
c: No, the duty is triggered by substantive contact, not by attendance
Yes, every open house visitor needs to sign before entering the unit
Yes, because condo open houses are held to a stricter written standard
No, because open houses are exempt from RPL 443 entirely
blocks.x: The form is due at first substantive contact, not at the door. Questions about charges, the boiler, and the roof deck are property facts. DOS guidance dating to the 1990s says a seller's agent need not give the form to every open house visitor when no substantive contact occurs. The exempt choice is the trap: open houses are not exempt, and the moment a visitor talks budget or motivation, the form is due.

blocks.html: Diane still tightens practice. Every open house now has a stack of agency and fair housing forms on the counter, a fair housing notice displayed, and a host who says "I represent the sellers" to every visitor who lingers. Jordan's file is fine. Marcus's is next.

blocks.text: File 3: the seller who would not sign

blocks.html: In Marcus's Dyker Heights listing file, the agency disclosure has the seller's agent box checked, Marcus's signature, and, across the consumer signature line, the word "REFUSED" in Marcus's handwriting. The seller, Mr. Gallo, told Marcus he "doesn't sign anything his lawyer hasn't read." Marcus took the listing anyway, and Mr. Gallo signed the listing agreement two days later after his lawyer reviewed it.

blocks.q: What should Marcus have done when Mr. Gallo refused to sign the acknowledgment?
c: Stop work, because no listing may be taken without the signed form
Write "refused" on the form, which serves as the declaration
Prepare a written declaration of the facts under oath or affirmation
Ask the seller's attorney to sign the acknowledgment on his behalf
blocks.x: When a consumer refuses to sign, RPL 443 requires the licensee to set forth under oath or affirmation a written declaration of the facts of the refusal and keep it at least 3 years. One word on a signature line is not a declaration. Stopping work is the trap: refusal does not bar the listing, and the duty to present the form was met when Marcus presented and explained it.

blocks.title: The declaration Marcus should have made
blocks.html: "I, Marcus Webb, a licensed real estate salesperson with Hudson & Hart Realty, affirm that on June 3, at the owner's home in Dyker Heights, I presented the New York State agency disclosure form to the owner, Anthony Gallo, before entering into a listing agreement. I explained that I would act as the seller's agent. Mr. Gallo read the form and declined to sign the acknowledgment, stating that he does not sign documents his attorney has not reviewed. I left a copy with him." Signed, dated, and sworn or affirmed in the form the firm's attorney approves, then kept for at least 3 years.

Diane has Marcus prepare the declaration now, dated today and stating truthfully when the events occurred, rather than backdating anything. A late declaration that tells the truth is a cure. A backdated one is a new violation, and an untrustworthy one.

blocks.q: Marcus offers to write the declaration and date it June 3, so the file looks complete. What should Diane say?
c: Fine, since the facts in it are true and just the date is adjusted
Fine, because DOS reviews just whether a declaration exists
No; date it today and describe June 3 truthfully
No, a declaration cannot be made after the listing is signed
blocks.x: A sworn declaration has to be true in every part, including when it was made. Backdating a document submitted in a DOS inquiry is a false statement and a fresh ground for discipline. A late but honest declaration is the right fix. The first choice is the trap: the date on a sworn document is itself a fact being sworn to.

blocks.html: File 4 is a buyer client of Marcus's, signed in July for a Sunset Park search. The form has been signed. Diane reads the signature page line by line, and Jordan writes down what is wrong.

head: Line on the form
What the file shows
rows: Advance consent with designated sales agents
blocks.caption: Signature page, buyer file, July 9

blocks.q: Which defect on File 4's signature page defeats the form's main purpose?
c: No role box is checked, so it never says whom Marcus represents
The consumer's signature lacks a printed name below it
The advance consent boxes were initialed but not fully signed
The date is written in numbers instead of being spelled out
blocks.x: The form exists to tell the consumer, in writing, what role this licensee is playing. With no role checked, the acknowledgment proves the buyer received a form but not what Marcus told her about his role. The advance consent choice is the trap: initials are how those boxes are completed. The designated agent line, though, should name an agent, and that blank is a real but secondary defect.

blocks.html: The rest is housekeeping that still matters. The licensee signs and dates the form too. The consumer gets a copy, and the file should show how and when it was delivered. If the buyer gave advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents, the designated agent line should carry a name. Marcus meets the buyer the next week, explains the form again, and they complete a new one together. The old one stays in the file next to it, because records are kept, not replaced.

blocks.text: File 5: Jordan on the buyer side

blocks.html: File 5 is Jordan's. Jordan represents buyers, the Adeyemi family, under an exclusive buyer agreement. In September they liked a for-sale-by-owner house in Marine Park. Jordan called the owner, Mrs. Healy, introduced the family, and asked whether she would consider $40,000 under asking with a quick close.

blocks.q: What did RPL 443 require of Jordan toward Mrs. Healy, the FSBO seller?
c: Nothing, since Mrs. Healy has no broker and is not Jordan's client
A buyer's agent disclosure at first substantive contact with her
A listing agreement before discussing any price with the seller
A dual agency consent, since Jordan was speaking to both parties
blocks.x: A buyer's agent must give the disclosure to the seller at first substantive contact, so the seller knows the person on the phone works for the buyer. An unrepresented FSBO seller needs that warning most. The first choice is the trap. The form is not limited to the licensee's own clients; it goes to the other side too, and Jordan's price question was plainly substantive.

blocks.html: Jordan's file shows an email to Mrs. Healy the same afternoon with the form attached and a signed copy returned by e-signature the next day. The timing is a few hours after the call rather than at the start of it, and Diane notes that Jordan should lead with the role next time. But the file is honest and nearly on time, and that is what a regulator looks for.

The same file has the flip side. A week after the Healy call, a buyer's agent from a Gerritsen Beach firm, Owen Price, emailed Jordan about a Hudson & Hart listing on Avenue U: his buyers wanted to know whether the sellers would cover closing costs. Attached to Owen's email was his own agency disclosure, buyer's agent box checked, addressed to Jordan's sellers. Jordan forwarded it to the sellers, got their signed acknowledgment, and sent it back.

blocks.q: Why did Owen send his disclosure to Jordan instead of to the sellers directly?
c: Because RPL 443 lets the buyer's agent give it to the seller's agent
Because a buyer's agent may not speak to a represented seller
Because the seller's agent signs the acknowledgment for the sellers
Because a buyer's agent owes no disclosure when sellers have an agent
blocks.x: RPL 443 lets a buyer's agent give the disclosure to the seller or to the seller's agent at first substantive contact. Sending it through Jordan respects the sellers' representation and still gets the form to them. The third choice is the trap: Jordan delivers it, but the acknowledgment belongs to the sellers, not to their agent.

blocks.html: Diane likes this exchange because it shows the system working in both directions. Each side's agent told the other side, in writing and before negotiating, whom they represented. Neither consumer had to guess.

blocks.text: File 6: the customer who became a client

blocks.html: File 6 shows a role change. At a Kensington open house in August, a visitor named Tobias Lindqvist received Jordan's seller's agent disclosure as a customer. He did not buy that house. Two weeks later he asked Jordan to represent him in his search. Jordan had him sign an exclusive buyer agreement and a new agency disclosure with the buyer's agent box checked.

blocks.q: Tobias now wants to make an offer on the Kensington house, still listed by Hudson & Hart. What must happen?
c: Nothing new, because Tobias already signed a disclosure at the open house
Jordan simply switches sides and represents Tobias against the seller
Tobias signs a new buyer agreement for this house, and nothing more
The firm becomes a dual agent and needs both clients' written consent
blocks.x: Tobias is now a firm client, and the seller is too. On this house the firm would represent both, so it needs informed written dual agency consent from both before proceeding, and a new disclosure reflecting the dual role. Switching sides quietly is the trap. A licensee can change roles, but never silently, and never by dropping a client in the middle of a deal.

blocks.title: Changing roles is allowed. Changing them quietly is not.
blocks.html: A customer at an open house can become a client next month. A seller's agent can become a buyer's agent for other properties. What cannot happen is a role change without a new disclosure, or a role change inside a single deal that turns the firm into a dual agent without both parties' written consent.

blocks.text: File 7: the form in Marcus's car

blocks.html: One more problem turns up in Marcus's rental file for a Bushwick condo unit. The disclosure he used is a photocopy of an old form from his glove compartment. It has no landlord and tenant version, no advance consent boxes, and a definitions section that leaves out condos and co-ops.

blocks.q: What is wrong with using that old form for a condo rental today?
c: Nothing, as long as the consumer signs and the licensee keeps a copy
It omits the commission rate, which agency forms are required to state
It predates 2011, when the law added condos, co-ops, and rentals
It should have been notarized, which makes the old version acceptable
blocks.x: The form changed effective January 1, 2011: condos and co-ops came within the definition, rentals got a landlord and tenant version, and consumers could give advance consent to dual agency and to designated agents. An outdated form misdescribes the law to the consumer. The commission choice is the trap; the form is expressly not a contract and states no fee.

blocks.title: Before and after January 1, 2011
blocks.html: Before 2011, buyers of Manhattan co-ops, most of the city's sales, might never see a disclosure, because co-ops and condos fell outside the definition, and rentals had no form. The 2011 amendments added condos and co-ops, created the landlord-tenant version, and put advance consent to dual agency and designated sales agents on the form. Some exam items still describe the older rules, so know both.

Farah's complaint also says she thought signing the form in August committed her to paying Marcus a fee. Diane wants the response to address that misunderstanding, because the firm's training should prevent it from happening again.

blocks.q: How should a licensee explain what signing the acknowledgment means?
c: It hires the firm and sets its commission at the listed rate
It is a contract that binds the consumer to work with the firm
It waives the consumer's right to hire a different agent later
It confirms receipt of the form and is not a contract
blocks.x: The form is headed "This is not a contract." The signature acknowledges receipt of the disclosure; it creates no agency, obligates no one to pay, and waives nothing. Agency and fees come from separate agreements. The second choice is the trap, because consumers often hesitate to sign for exactly that reason, which is why the explanation matters.

blocks.html: Diane's written response to DOS does not argue. It admits the form in File 1 was given late, includes the full email chain, describes the firm's new procedures (a form attached to the first reply to every inquiry, open house scripts, quarterly file audits), and notes that Marcus completed additional agency training. The firm keeps all of it with the transaction records.

blocks.q: How long must Hudson & Hart keep the signed acknowledgments and Marcus's refusal declaration?
c: At least 3 years
At least 1 year
Until the deal closes
At least 6 years
blocks.x: RPL 443 requires the licensee to keep a copy of each signed acknowledgment, and each declaration of refusal, for not less than 3 years, which matches the broker's 3-year transaction record rule in 19 NYCRR 175.23. Six years is the trap; it sounds like a statute of limitations, but it is not the retention rule for these records.

blocks.html: DOS later resolves the complaint with a fine against Marcus and a letter to Diane about supervision. Farah's separate claim that she overpaid goes nowhere, because Marcus never revealed anything about the sellers and her attorney negotiated the final price. But the real damage was avoidable. One form, attached to one email on August 4, would have made the whole file a non-event.

items: First substantive contact happens when the talk turns to finances, motivation, or negotiating position, whether by email, text, phone, or in person; open house small talk about the property does not trigger it.
The listing agent gives the form to the seller before the listing agreement; the other side's agent gives it at first substantive contact, including a buyer's agent calling a FSBO seller.
A complete signature page shows the licensee's role, any advance consent with named designated agents, both signatures and dates, and a copy delivered.
A refusal is documented by a written declaration of the facts under oath or affirmation, made truthfully and never backdated, and kept 3 years.
Roles may change with a new disclosure, but a change inside one deal that makes the firm a dual agent needs both clients' written consent.
Use the current form: since January 1, 2011 it covers condos, co-ops, and rentals and includes advance consent options.

lessons.title: Case file: The Unemployment Claim in Massapequa
lessons.tagline: One salesperson leaves, files for benefits, and a Long Island broker learns that her contractor agreement expired a year ago.
objectives: Apply New York's 1986 independent contractor rules and IRC 3508 to a real brokerage's contracts, pay plans, and policies
Distinguish required broker supervision under 19 NYCRR 175.21 from direction and control that makes a salesperson an employee
Calculate what is at stake for the broker and the salesperson when contractor status fails
Build a compliance plan using written contracts, pay records, and the records rule in 19 NYCRR 175.23

blocks.title: A letter from the Department of Labor
blocks.html: Linda Marchetti owns Harborview Realty, a twelve-agent brokerage on Merrick Road in Massapequa. In March, one of her salespersons, Priscilla Ortega, left the business after a slow winter and filed a claim for unemployment insurance benefits. Six weeks later Linda receives a questionnaire from the New York State Department of Labor asking whether Priscilla was an employee, with a request for her contract, pay records, and office policies. Linda is not worried. "Everyone here signs an independent contractor agreement. It's in the file." She calls Priya Nair, who handles brokerage compliance for several Long Island firms, and asks her to look at the file before Linda answers. Priya opens it and finds Priscilla's agreement. It is dated January 2023.

blocks.text: Before the paper: how the law used to decide

blocks.html: Priya starts with history, because it explains the rules. Under the common law, courts decide whether a worker is an employee by asking who controls the work: not just the result, but the manner and means of getting there. Who sets the hours? Who decides where the work happens? Who pays the expenses? Can the worker quit, or work for others? The IRS developed its own multi-factor version of the same idea, and New York agencies applied theirs. Real estate sales never fit neatly. Salespersons work on commission and set their own schedules, but brokers must supervise them under the license law. For years brokers could not predict how an audit would come out.

blocks.q: Under the common law test, which question matters most in deciding whether a salesperson is an employee?
c: Whether the salesperson holds a real estate license from the state
Whether the broker controls the manner and means of the work
Whether the salesperson earns more than half of the office's income
Whether the salesperson has signed the brokerage's policy manual
blocks.x: The common law test turns on direction and control: whether the hiring party controls how, when, and where the work is done, not just the result. A license is the trap. Every salesperson has one and must be supervised by a broker, so licensure alone says nothing about status. That uncertainty is what the 1986 New York rules and IRC 3508 were written to resolve.

blocks.html: Congress answered the uncertainty for federal employment taxes in 1982 with IRC Section 3508, and New York followed in 1986 with matching rules for state unemployment insurance and workers' compensation. Both replace the open-ended control test with a checklist. Meet the checklist and the licensee is a contractor for those purposes. Miss it and the broker is back in the gray area, where the facts in the policy manual decide the case.

blocks.text: The three-part test Priya starts with

blocks.html: Priya explains the frame before she reads anything else. New York's 1986 amendments to the Labor Law (unemployment insurance) and the Workers' Compensation Law carve licensed real estate salespersons and associate brokers out of "employment" if three things are true. Federal law, IRC Section 3508, does the same for federal employment taxes with a similar but shorter list. If the conditions are met, the salesperson is an independent contractor. If not, the default rules apply, and the default in a direction-and-control world often looks like an employee.

head: Condition
New York (Labor Law 511 and WCL)
Federal (IRC 3508)
rows: Substantially all pay from sales or other output, not hours
Required, with listed provisions on hours, location, expenses, other work, and termination
Required, stating the agent is not an employee for federal tax purposes
Executed within the past 12 to 15 months
blocks.caption: The safe harbors side by side

blocks.q: Priscilla's agreement is dated January 2023 and was never renewed. She left in March 2025. What does that do to New York's unemployment insurance exclusion?
c: Nothing, because a signed agreement stays valid until either party ends it
Nothing, because the federal rule under IRC 3508 sets no time limit
It fails: the contract was not signed in the past 12 to 15 months
It fails if Priscilla can show she signed the agreement under duress
blocks.x: New York's exclusion requires a written contract executed within the past 12 to 15 months, which is why compliant brokers re-sign every licensee every year. A contract more than two years old does not meet the condition, so the state exclusion fails on that ground alone. The federal choice is the trap: IRC 3508 has no freshness rule, but it governs federal taxes, not New York unemployment insurance.

blocks.html: Linda is stunned. "Nobody told me it expired." It did not expire as a contract; it simply stopped satisfying the statute. Priya checks the rest of the office. Of Harborview's twelve agreements, five are more than 15 months old. Then she turns to how Priscilla was actually paid. Five agents, any one of whom could file the next claim, are working today under agreements that no longer meet the statute. Priya puts their renewal at the top of the list.

blocks.title: Priscilla's compensation, 2024
blocks.html:
Commission splits on 6 closings: $41,300 (paid through Harborview, no taxes withheld).
"Starter draw," January to March: $600 a week for 13 weeks = $7,800, not repayable from commissions.
Floor-time stipend: $25 an hour for 140 hours of desk duty = $3,500.
Total: $41,300 + $7,800 + $3,500 = $52,600. Pay tied to time rather than output: $7,800 + $3,500 = $11,300, about 21 percent of the total.

blocks.q: Which part of Priscilla's pay plan most undermines the output-based pay condition?
c: The commission splits, since splits are set by the broker alone
The lack of tax withholding on her commission checks
The six closings, since that is too few for a full-time agent
The weekly draw and the hourly stipend, which pay for time
blocks.x: The statutes require that substantially all of the salesperson's pay be directly related to sales or other output rather than hours worked. A non-repayable weekly draw and an hourly stipend are pay for time, here about 21 percent of the total. No withholding is the trap: it is what contractor status permits, not evidence for or against it. Commission splits are output-based by definition.

blocks.html: Priya notes the fix for the future. A draw that is a true advance, repaid from later commissions, is still pay for output. A floor-time program can stay if agents choose to sign up for it in exchange for leads, not hours, and nobody is paid by the clock. What cannot continue is a salary by another name.
Harborview's policy manual runs 22 pages. Most of it is what a broker should be doing. Some of it is not. Priya marks four items.

head: Policy
Text in the manual
rows: All licensees complete the firm's fair housing and agency disclosure training each year.
Desk duty is mandatory, 9 to 5, two weekdays a week. Missed shifts reduce the agent's split by 5 points for the month.
The broker reviews every contract, every ad, and every escrow deposit before it goes out.
Licensees may not hold any other job while affiliated with Harborview.
blocks.caption: Four excerpts from the Harborview policy manual

blocks.q: Which pair of policies is direction and control rather than required supervision?
c: A and C, because training and contract review both control the work
A and D, because both apply to every licensee in the office
B and D, because they set hours and bar the agent's other work
C and D, because both require the broker's approval in advance
blocks.x: Training and reviewing contracts, ads, and escrow are the regular, frequent, and consistent supervision that 19 NYCRR 175.21 requires. Mandatory hours enforced by pay penalties, and a ban on other employment, are control over when and whether the person works. New York's statute requires the contract to let the salesperson take outside work. The A and C choice is the trap: supervision is required, not a sign of employment.

blocks.title: What the New York contract must say
blocks.html: Labor Law 511 lists the provisions: the licensee is engaged as an independent contractor for all purposes; pay is commission tied to output, without tax deductions and not tied to hours; the licensee may work any hours; may work from home or the broker's office; may take outside employment; the broker may provide office space and supplies, but the licensee pays their own expenses such as car, travel, and entertainment; both follow the license law; and either party may end the relationship at any time on notice.

Priya reads Harborview's contract against that list. It says the agent pays their own car and marketing costs, which is right. But clause 9 says "Licensee agrees to give 60 days' written notice of termination and forfeits all pending commissions if notice is not given."

blocks.q: What is the problem with clause 9?
c: Nothing, because a long notice period protects the firm's listings
It is fine, as long as the broker has the same 60-day notice obligation
Nothing, because pending commissions belong to the firm in any case
It conflicts with the rule that either party may end it on notice
blocks.x: The New York statute expects the contract to let either party terminate at any time, with notice to the other. A 60-day lock-in backed by forfeiting earned commissions pushes the relationship toward employment control. Making it mutual is the trap: a symmetrical restriction is still a restriction. Listings belong to the broker regardless, so the firm does not need the clause to protect them.

blocks.html: Priya also finds a line item in the firm's books: Harborview reimbursed Priscilla's mileage at 70 cents a mile for showings, $2,240 in 2024, and paid her MLS dues. Linda calls it a perk that helped recruit agents.

blocks.q: How do the mileage reimbursements and dues payments fit the New York contract provisions?
c: They fit, since a broker may cover any expense it chooses to
They cut against it; the agent should bear her own expenses
They fit, so long as each payment shows up on her 1099
They cut against it if the agent asked to be repaid
blocks.x: The New York statute lets the broker provide office space, supplies, and facilities, but expects the licensee to pay her own business expenses such as car, travel, and entertainment. Reimbursing mileage and dues looks like an employer covering an employee's costs. The 1099 choice is the trap: reporting a payment correctly does not change what the payment is.

blocks.html: Linda pushes back. "Every agent signed a contract saying they're independent. Doesn't that settle it?" Priya's answer is the core idea of this whole area. Regulators look at how the relationship actually works. A contract that says independent contractor, sitting next to a manual that sets mandatory hours, docks pay for absences, and bans other jobs, describes an employee with a misleading label.

blocks.q: An agreement says "independent contractor," but the broker sets mandatory hours and pays by the hour. How will a regulator most likely treat the salesperson?
c: As a contractor, because the signed agreement controls the label
As an employee, because the actual conduct outweighs the label
As a contractor, as long as the commission split is above 50 percent
As a contractor, because the license law requires broker supervision
blocks.x: Substance wins over form. Written documentation does not overcome a broker's actual direction and control, especially hours set and enforced by the broker and pay by the hour. The supervision choice is the trap: the license law requires supervision, but supervision of legal compliance is different from controlling when, where, and how the salesperson works.

blocks.html: Priya walks Linda through the downside. If Priscilla is found to be an employee for unemployment insurance, Linda's firm owes unemployment contributions on her wages and Priscilla can collect benefits. And the DOL rarely stops at one person: an audit triggered by a single claim commonly looks at everyone in the same arrangement. If the IRS later takes the same view, the federal exposure follows.

head: If status fails, the broker faces
If status fails, the salesperson faces
rows: State unemployment insurance contributions and federal unemployment tax
Loss of Schedule C, where business expenses are deducted
Workers' compensation and New York disability coverage
Withholding of federal and state income tax, plus Social Security and Medicare
Less control over hours, methods, and outside work
Penalties and interest on all of the above, across every agent in the same arrangement
Benefits such as unemployment become available
blocks.caption: Consequences of noncompliance

blocks.q: If Harborview's agents are reclassified as employees, which obligation falls on Linda rather than on the agents?
c: Paying unemployment insurance contributions on their pay
Filing Schedule C for each agent's business expenses
Paying self-employment tax on each agent's commissions
Buying each agent's car insurance and paying MLS dues
blocks.x: An employer pays unemployment insurance contributions and carries workers' compensation and disability coverage, and withholds income and payroll taxes. Schedule C and self-employment tax belong to people who are self-employed, so reclassification takes those away rather than shifting them to the broker. Self-employment tax is the trap: as employees, the agents would owe the employee share of Social Security and Medicare through withholding instead.

blocks.html: Priscilla's side has costs too, which is why many salespersons want contractor status. Her 2024 Schedule C deducted $9,400 in car, phone, marketing, and MLS expenses. As an employee, all of her pay would have been subject to withholding, and those business deductions would have been largely unavailable to her.

blocks.q: From the salesperson's side, what is the main tax consequence of being treated as an employee?
c: Tax is withheld from her pay, and she loses Schedule C deductions
She owes both halves of Social Security and Medicare on her own commissions
She may no longer receive any commission, since employees are paid hourly
She has to give up her license and reapply for it under the broker as employer
blocks.x: Employees have taxes withheld from all compensation and cannot use Schedule C to deduct business expenses the way a self-employed contractor can. Paying both halves of Social Security and Medicare is the trap: that describes the self-employment tax a contractor pays, which an employee does not. Employees can still be paid by commission, and the license is unaffected.

blocks.html: One more item turns up. Harborview's top producer, Dominic Ferri, runs a three-person team inside the firm. He pays his two licensed team members a percentage of team closings out of his own account, by Venmo, and Linda never sees those payments. Dominic considers it his business.

blocks.q: What is wrong with Dominic paying his licensed team members directly?
c: Nothing, because a team is a separate business from the brokerage
Nothing, as long as Dominic issues each of them a Form 1099
Only the sponsoring broker may pay a salesperson
Team members must be employees, so the payments need payroll
blocks.x: In New York, a salesperson may receive compensation for real estate work only through the sponsoring broker. Commission money must flow through Harborview, appear in its records, and then go to each licensee. The 1099 choice is the trap: proper tax reporting does not fix a payment that should never have bypassed the broker. Teams also may not present themselves as separate brokerages.

blocks.title: Supervision and records do not make an employee
blocks.html: 19 NYCRR 175.21 requires a broker to supervise salespersons with regular, frequent, and consistent guidance, instruction, oversight, and superintendence. 19 NYCRR 175.23 requires records of each transaction, including the parties, price, and commission, kept at least 3 years. A broker who does both well is meeting the license law. Neither is the kind of control that defeats contractor status.

blocks.title: The contract that quietly stops working
blocks.html: Students learn "written contract" and stop there. New York's version has a clock: the contract must have been executed within the past 12 to 15 months. A firm that signed everyone up in 2022 and never looked again may have no valid exclusion for anyone today. The federal rule has no clock, which is exactly why the two get confused on exams.

Linda answers the DOL questionnaire truthfully with Priya's help. Priscilla's claim is likely to be allowed: the contract was stale, part of her pay was for time, and the desk duty rule was enforced with pay cuts. Priya's goal now is the other eleven agents and the firm's future.

blocks.q: Which plan best protects Harborview's contractor relationships going forward?
c: Add a stronger independent contractor clause and keep the current manual
Stop supervising agents entirely, so that there is no evidence of control
Move every agent to a salary, since employees are simpler to manage
Re-sign yearly, pay only for output, make floor time optional
blocks.x: The fix aligns substance with the paper: annually executed contracts with the required provisions, signed freely; pay tied to closings; optional floor time; no ban on outside work; and supervision limited to compliance, training, and review. Ending supervision is the trap. It would violate 175.21 and solve nothing, because supervision was never the problem. Salaried employment is legal but a different business model.

blocks.html: By June every Harborview licensee has a fresh agreement, signed at a meeting where Linda tells them they may take it home to read first, which helps show it was not signed under duress. The draw becomes a true advance against commissions. Desk duty becomes "lead desk," open to anyone who signs up, with no pay and no penalties. Linda calendars the next renewal date, 12 months out, in red. She also files each signed agreement with the agent's commission records, so a future auditor sees in one folder the contract, the date it was signed, and pay that rises and falls only with closings. Under 175.23 those records stay at least 3 years, and Priya suggests keeping the agreements longer, since an unemployment audit can reach back further than a single renewal cycle.

blocks.q: Why does Linda let agents take the new agreement home before signing?
c: Because the license law requires a 3-day review period for any contract
Because the agreement has to be notarized, which cannot happen at the office
Because IRC 3508 requires the agent to have legal advice before signing
Because New York requires that the contract not be signed under duress
blocks.x: New York's exclusion requires a written contract not executed under duress. Giving agents time to read the agreement, ask questions, and sign freely is good evidence on that point. IRC 3508 is the trap: the federal safe harbor requires output-based pay and a written contract, but it has no duress element and no legal advice requirement.

blocks.html: A month later a newly licensed applicant asks Linda for a guaranteed salary for her first year. Linda asks Priya whether that is even allowed. It is. Nothing in the license law requires salespersons to be contractors, and some firms hire licensees as employees. The question every broker must answer is which model the firm is running, and then follow its rules completely.

blocks.q: Linda wants to pay one new licensee a salary of $45,000 a year. What must she do?
c: Treat her as an employee, with withholding, unemployment insurance, and comp coverage
Call her an independent contractor, since she still holds a salesperson license
Pay the salary through the sponsoring broker and treat it as commission income
Refuse, because New York prohibits paying any real estate salesperson a salary
blocks.x: A broker may employ a salesperson, but then the full employer obligations follow: withholding, unemployment insurance, workers' compensation, and disability coverage. A salary is pay for time, so the contractor safe harbors cannot apply. The prohibition choice is the trap. Salaried licensees are legal; mislabeling them as contractors is what gets brokers in trouble.

items: New York's 1986 rules treat licensees as contractors only if they are licensed, paid substantially by output, and working under a written contract executed within the past 12 to 15 months, not under duress, with the provisions the statute lists.
IRC 3508 sets the federal test: licensed, paid by output, and a written contract saying the agent is not an employee for federal tax purposes.
Substance beats form: mandatory hours, pay by the hour, pay penalties for absences, and bans on outside work can make a contractor an employee whatever the contract says.
If status fails, the broker owes unemployment insurance, workers' compensation, disability coverage, and withholding; the salesperson loses Schedule C deductions and has pay withheld.
Supervision under 175.21 and records under 175.23 are required and do not create employment; all commission money flows through the sponsoring broker.

lessons.title: Case file: The Transferee and the Sales Gallery
lessons.tagline: A relocation company sends a name, a sponsor offers a bonus, and an amendment opens a 15-day door. Everyone has an interest in Samira's condo. Only one of them is the client.
objectives: Decide who the principal is when a relocation company refers a buyer, and which client information the referring company may receive
Apply RPL 442 and RESPA to referral fees, sponsor bonuses, and credits to the buyer, and decide what must be disclosed
Apply agency roles to a new development sponsor sale, from gallery registration to the Attorney General's offering plan rules
Decide what a buyer's agent does, and does not do, when an offering plan amendment creates a rescission right

blocks.title: A transferee from Chicago
blocks.html: Samira Haddad lands at LaGuardia on a Thursday in February with a new job, a corporate relocation package, and six weeks of temporary housing in a Long Island City extended-stay hotel. She is the incoming director of pharmacy for a hospital network in Queens, transferring from Chicago. Her employer outsources the move to Keystone Relocation Partners, a relocation management company that holds broker licenses in New York and Illinois. On Monday Keystone emailed Diane Hart: "We have a transferee for you. Our broker network agreement is attached. Referral fee 35% of gross commission received. Please have your agent contact her within 24 hours and copy us weekly." Samira wants a new two-bedroom condo near the 7 train for under $1.2 million. Before Jordan picks up the phone to offer a buyer agreement, Diane asks what sounds like an easy question: when this deal works, who is Jordan's client?

blocks.title: Keystone broker network agreement, key clauses
blocks.html:
1. Referral fee. Broker pays Keystone 35% of the gross commission Broker receives on the transferee's purchase, at closing.
2. Reporting. Broker sends weekly status reports: properties shown, offers made, and the transferee's price range.
3. Standard of service. Broker will act in the best interests of Keystone's corporate client and the transferee.
4. Protection. The referral is protected for 12 months from the date of this agreement.

blocks.q: Once Samira signs Hudson & Hart's exclusive buyer agreement, who is the firm's client in the purchase?
c: Samira, the transferee who signs the agency agreement
Keystone, because it sent the referral and earns a fee
Samira's employer, since its package pays for the move
Keystone and Samira jointly, as clause 3 names both
blocks.x: Samira signs the buyer agreement and receives the agency disclosure; she is the principal. Keystone is another brokerage that earned a referral fee, and the employer is funding benefits, but neither is buying anything. Clause 3 is the trap: a contract between two brokers cannot make a corporation a second principal and split a fiduciary's loyalty between the buyer and the company paying her moving bills.

blocks.html: Diane strikes "Keystone's corporate client and" from clause 3, initials the change, and sends it back with one line: "We represent the transferee." Keystone accepts it. Relocation companies see that edit often. Then Jordan asks about the money. The sponsor of whatever building Samira picks will pay the buyer's broker, and Keystone will take 35% of that check. Keystone will never show an apartment, read a contract, or attend a closing. Is it legal to pay a company for sending a name?

blocks.q: May Hudson & Hart pay Keystone the 35% referral fee?
c: Yes, since Keystone is a licensed broker and broker referrals are exempt
No, since RESPA Section 8 bans fees paid for referring settlement business
Yes, but Samira has to pay the referral fee herself at the closing
No, since a New York broker may split fees with New York brokers alone
blocks.x: RPL 442 lets a New York broker share compensation with licensed brokers and with a person regularly in the brokerage business in another state. RESPA Section 8 bans kickbacks for referring settlement business, but it expressly exempts cooperative brokerage and referral arrangements between real estate brokers. The RESPA choice is the trap: the ban is real and catches referral payments to and from lenders, title agents, and other providers, not a fee split between two brokerages.

blocks.title: Referral fees: who may be paid
blocks.html: Under RPL 442 a broker may share a commission with another licensed broker, with its own sponsored salespersons, and with a broker regularly engaged in the business in another state. It may not pay an unlicensed person for a referral: not a doorman, not a friend, not a relocation "coordinator" without a license. The same section allows one exception for parties: a broker may give part of its compensation to the buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant in the deal, as long as it is not payment for licensed work.

Paying the fee is legal. Telling Samira about it is Diane's rule. The fee does not raise Samira's cost, since it comes out of the firm's side. It does change the firm's incentives. Keystone controls the next fifty transferees, and an agent who wants them may be tempted to keep Keystone happy. A fiduciary discloses facts that could color the advice. Jordan's first email to Samira attaches the agency disclosure form, the buyer agreement, and a paragraph explaining the referral fee in dollars.

blocks.q: Clause 2 asks for weekly reports that include Samira's price range. What should Jordan do?
c: Send the reports exactly as written, since the firm signed the agreement
Ask Samira in writing what Keystone may see, and report only that
Refuse to send anything, since a client's whole file is confidential
Send full reports but leave out offers, since only offers are secret
blocks.x: Confidential information belongs to the client, and only she can release it. Samira may want Keystone to know her dates so her hotel and moving benefits line up. She may not want her ceiling price traveling through a vendor that reports to her employer. Refusing everything is the trap: confidentiality is Samira's to waive, and ignoring what she wants shared would fail the duty of obedience. Her written instructions decide.

blocks.html: Samira's answer comes the same night: Keystone may see the addresses she tours, her target move date, and the closing date. Nothing about price, offers, her loan, or her savings. Jordan forwards it to Diane, saves it to the file, and sets up the weekly report as two lines of dates.

Samira has already found her favorite online: The Lumen, a 31-story new condominium on Jackson Avenue with 212 units. The sponsor is a single-purpose company, Jackson Lumen Owner LLC. Sales are run by Meridian Development Marketing, the sponsor's exclusive sales agent, from a ground-floor gallery with a model kitchen and a scale model of the tower. On Friday night Samira texts: "I'll just pop into the Lumen tomorrow on my own, I'm walking by anyway." Jordan opens the building's broker page. In bold: Cooperating brokers must accompany the purchaser on the first visit or register the purchaser in writing before it. No exceptions.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do before Samira walks in?
c: Nothing; a sponsor's policy has no effect on who represents her
Ask Samira to skip the gallery until a resale showing is booked
Tell Samira to hand Meridian Jordan's card at the front desk
Register Samira with Meridian in writing tonight, as her agent
blocks.x: Registration rules are business terms, not law, but they decide whether the sponsor pays a buyer's broker. If Samira walks in unregistered, Meridian may treat her as an unrepresented customer and refuse the co-broke, and her buyer agreement may then make her responsible for the fee. The business card is the trap: many sponsors treat it as too late. Registering does not create the agency; it protects the client's pocket.

blocks.html: Jordan emails the registration form at 9:40 p.m. and gets a confirmation at 10:05 the next morning, ten minutes before meeting Samira on the sidewalk. Inside, a Meridian salesperson named Bianca Lowe offers coffee, hands Samira an agency disclosure form, and asks her to sign it. The box checked is "seller's agent." While Bianca walks them past the model kitchen, Samira mentions that her employer covers closing costs up to $25,000 and that she has to be out of the hotel by June 15.

blocks.q: What does the form Bianca handed over tell Samira about Bianca's role?
c: Bianca works for the sponsor and owes Samira honesty, not loyalty
Bianca is a dual agent, since the sponsor pays both brokerages
Bianca represents Samira on this visit, since she is the host
Bianca is acting as a broker's agent for Hudson & Hart today
blocks.x: A sponsor's sales team represents the sponsor as seller's agent. RPL 443 covers condominium units, new ones included, so Meridian gives the seller's agent disclosure at first substantive contact. Bianca owes Samira honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material facts; her loyalty belongs to the sponsor. The dual agency choice is the trap: who pays a broker never decides whom the broker represents. Here the sponsor pays both firms, and each still has one client.

blocks.html: Samira's chatter about the $25,000 and June 15 is now Meridian's information, and it will reach the sponsor's pricing desk by Monday. Jordan cannot unsay it. Outside, Jordan explains the rule in a sentence: everything said in the gallery is said to the seller. Samira laughs and says it felt like a hotel lobby. That is the point of a hotel lobby.
Back inside, Bianca closes her pitch: "And the offering plan is AG-approved, so you're fully protected." Samira looks at Jordan.

blocks.title: "AG-approved" is not a thing
blocks.html: Under the Martin Act (GBL 352-e), a sponsor must file an offering plan with the Attorney General's office before offering condo units in New York, and it may not sign purchase agreements until the plan is accepted for filing. The AG reviews the plan for required disclosure. It does not approve the price, the construction, the projected budget, or the wisdom of buying. Learners, and buyers, confuse "accepted for filing" with "approved."

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle Bianca's "AG-approved" comment?
c: Agree with it, since the AG reviews the pricing and the budget
Let it pass, since a sponsor's agent cannot bind the sponsor
Correct it for Samira and send the plan to her attorney
Ask Bianca to put the AG approval in the purchase agreement
blocks.x: Acceptance for filing means the plan made the disclosures the law requires; it is not a seal on price, quality, or the budget. Reasonable care means correcting a misimpression the client heard and making sure her attorney, not a salesperson, reviews the plan, its budget, and its amendments. Letting it pass is the trap: a buyer's agent who hears a misleading statement made to the client should address it, no matter who said it or whether it binds anyone.

blocks.text: The bonus on the low floors

blocks.html: Samira narrows it to two units with the same layout. Unit 14C, $1,150,000, faces east with a slice of the river. Unit 5F, $1,085,000, faces the courtyard. That evening Jordan reads Meridian's broker bulletin.

blocks.title: Meridian broker bulletin, March
blocks.html:
Co-broke: 3% of purchase price on contracts fully executed.
March incentive: an additional $7,500 to the cooperating broker on any unit on floors 3 through 6, contract signed by March 31.
Purchaser must be registered per building policy.

blocks.q: What does Jordan owe Samira about the $7,500 incentive?
c: Disclosure in writing before she chooses between the two units
Nothing, since sponsors pay buyers' brokers in every new building
A refusal of it, since buyers' agents may not take sponsor money
Disclosure if she picks 5F, the unit that actually triggers it
blocks.x: Loyalty requires disclosing any interest that could color the advice. The bonus pays the firm more if Samira chooses 5F, so she has to know before she weighs 5F against 14C, not after. Disclosing only if she picks 5F is the trap: the conflict exists while the advice is being given. Taking a sponsor-paid co-broke is normal and lawful; hiding a unit-specific bonus is not.

blocks.html: Samira reads Jordan's email and replies with a question: "If the sponsor is handing out money, can some of it come to me?" Diane likes the idea for a different reason. If the firm passes the full $7,500 to Samira when she picks a bonus unit, the firm has no reason to prefer 5F, and the conflict disappears.

blocks.q: May Hudson & Hart credit Samira the $7,500 at closing?
c: No, because a broker may not share any fee with unlicensed people
No, because a credit to a buyer counts as a kickback under RESPA
Yes, but Keystone has to waive its share of the commission first
Yes, a broker may share its fee with a buyer if the lender allows it
blocks.x: RPL 442 generally bars paying unlicensed people, but it expressly lets a broker give part of its compensation to a buyer or seller in the deal, as long as it is not payment for licensed work. The credit must appear on the closing documents, and Samira's lender must allow it. The unlicensed-person choice is the trap: the rule is real, and the party exception is written into the same section.

blocks.html: In the end Samira picks 14C. She wants the river. The bonus never triggers, and Jordan never has to explain why the courtyard is "really quieter."

Samira's attorney, Priya Nair, receives the sponsor's purchase agreement and the offering plan. Jordan builds Samira a cost sheet from the agreement so she can see what her employer's $25,000 will and will not cover.

head: Item
Who pays under the sponsor's form
Amount
rows: Deposit, held in escrow by the sponsor's escrow agent
Working capital contribution, 2 months of common charges
Mortgage recording tax on an $800,000 loan, 1.925%
blocks.caption: Transfer taxes fall on the seller by law. In NYC sponsor sales, the sponsor's form usually shifts them to the buyer.

blocks.q: What is Jordan's role with the shifted transfer taxes?
c: Rewrite the transfer tax clause, since the sponsor's form is negotiable
Flag the shifted costs for Samira's budget and her attorney's review
Tell Samira that buyers pay these taxes by law in every NYC new sale
Say nothing, since the contract terms are entirely the lawyers' job
blocks.x: Downstate, attorneys draft and negotiate the contract; a salesperson who rewrites clauses is practicing law. But reasonable care means a client should not discover at closing that she is paying about $21,000 of the seller's taxes. Jordan flags it, puts it in her budget, and leaves the negotiating to Priya. The "by law" choice is the trap: these taxes are imposed on the grantor and moved only by contract, which is why they can be negotiated.

blocks.html: Priya gets the sponsor to pay the NYC RPTT in exchange for a faster closing once the temporary certificate of occupancy issues. Samira signs. The day before the deposit is due, she forwards Jordan an email "from the sponsor's attorney" with new wire instructions and a note: "Our escrow bank changed, please use the account below."

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell Samira about the new wire instructions?
c: Use them, since the email came from the law firm's own domain
Wire the deposit to Hudson & Hart's escrow account instead
Ask Bianca to confirm them, since she is the sponsor's agent
Call the escrow agent at a number taken from the offering plan
blocks.x: Reasonable care includes protecting the client from the most common way deposits disappear: spoofed wire instructions. Verify by phone using a number from a trusted source, here the offering plan, which names the escrow agent. Bianca is the trap: she is not the escrow agent, and her email could be compromised too. Redirecting the deposit to the firm is wrong because the offering plan fixes who holds purchaser deposits in trust.

blocks.html: The "new account" is fraudulent. The escrow agent's paralegal, reached at the plan's number, has never heard of a bank change. Samira wires $172,500 to the right account, where the Martin Act requires it to be held in trust and not commingled with the sponsor's money.
In May the sponsor files an amendment to the offering plan, and every purchaser gets a copy by mail and email.

blocks.title: Amendment No. 4, summary page
blocks.html:
1. The rooftop pool is eliminated and replaced with a landscaped terrace.
2. The first-year budget is revised; common charges for Unit 14C rise from $1,040 to $1,227 a month (18%).
3. The anticipated first closing date moves from July to November.
4. Because this amendment contains material changes adverse to purchasers, purchasers may rescind their purchase agreements by written notice within 15 days of the date of this amendment and receive a refund of their deposits.

blocks.q: Samira calls Jordan on day 9. What should Jordan tell her?
c: Her deposit is at risk if she backs out of a signed contract now
She has a short rescission window and should call Priya today
She can decide any time before closing, since the date moved
Jordan can send the rescission to Meridian on her behalf now
blocks.x: Under the Attorney General's regulations for new condo offering plans, an amendment that materially and adversely affects purchasers must give them a right to rescind and at least 15 days to use it. Whether to rescind is Samira's legal and financial decision, made with her attorney. Jordan's job is to make sure she does not miss the window. Sending the notice is the trap: a buyer's agent is a special agent with no authority to terminate the client's contract.

blocks.html: Keystone calls the next morning. The account manager is friendly and blunt. "Our corporate client needs her out of temporary housing by July. Extending her costs them $9,000 a month. Encourage her to stay in the deal. And let us know if she's thinking about rescinding, we'd need to plan for that."

blocks.q: How should Jordan respond to Keystone?
c: Agree to encourage her, since the firm's referral fee rides on closing
Tell Keystone she may rescind, since her timing is reportable to them
Decline to steer her, and share only the dates she has authorized
Ask Samira to sign a release letting Keystone guide the negotiation
blocks.x: Obedience and loyalty run to Samira. Whether she rescinds is not a date; it is her decision and her leverage, because a sponsor facing rescissions may offer concessions to keep buyers. The firm's interest in its referral relationship and the employer's housing budget cannot shape the advice. The "timing" choice is the trap: Samira authorized dates, not her thinking. Her hesitation is exactly the information she withheld from Keystone.

blocks.html: Samira does not rescind, and she does not have to decide for free. With nine days left, Priya tells the sponsor's counsel her client is "evaluating her options." The sponsor, facing a building full of buyers with the same option, offers every purchaser who stays a credit equal to twelve months of the common charge increase. Samira's credit is $2,244. Keystone learns about it from the closing statement in November.

In September Keystone refers another transferee from the same hospital network, Dr. Tomasz Wrona, and he asks for Jordan. He wants a studio at The Lumen as a pied-a-terre near the hospital. Only one studio is left, 6B. The same week, Samira asks Jordan to help her buy a studio for her mother, who is moving from Chicago in the spring. She wants 6B too.

blocks.q: Samira and Tomasz both want studio 6B. What should Hudson & Hart do?
c: Represent both quietly, since two buyers are on the same side of the deal
Treat it as dual agency and get the sponsor's written consent to it
Represent Tomasz alone, since Samira is already in contract for 14C
Disclose the conflict to both and get consent, or refer one of them out
blocks.x: Two buyer clients competing for one unit is not dual agency, because the firm represents no seller. But the firm cannot push both buyers at once without divided loyalty: what it learns from one helps it against the other. It discloses the conflict to both, gets informed consent with separate agents and screened files, or refers one buyer to another firm. The dual agency choice is the trap: the sponsor's consent is irrelevant when the sponsor is not the firm's client.

blocks.html: Diane calls both. Tomasz chooses a referral to a Manhattan firm that handles new development all day, and Hudson & Hart takes a 25% referral fee on his purchase, disclosed to him in writing. Samira's mother gets 6B.

Samira closes on 14C in November. The sponsor pays the 3% co-broke, $34,500, to Hudson & Hart. Hudson & Hart pays Keystone its 35%, $12,075, and Jordan is paid a share of the remaining $22,425 under the firm's commission plan. Two days later a package arrives at the office addressed to Jordan: a $500 gift card from Keystone with a card reading "Top producer: closed in under 120 days!"

blocks.q: May Jordan keep Keystone's $500 gift card?
c: Yes, since a gift card is a thank-you rather than a commission
Yes, as long as Jordan reports it as income on the tax return
No, since a salesperson is paid only through the sponsoring broker
No, since Keystone may reward the transferee but not her agent
blocks.x: A salesperson receives compensation for brokerage work only from the sponsoring broker. A gift card tied to closing speed is compensation in another wrapper; it goes to Diane, who decides whether the firm accepts it and accounts for it. The "thank-you" choice is the trap: a label does not change what a payment is for. Here it also rewards speed, the one thing Jordan was right to ignore in May.

blocks.html: Diane accepts the card for the firm's holiday party fund and writes Keystone a short note: future rewards go to the brokerage, not to individual agents. Then she adds a page to the firm's relocation file: the edited clause 3, Samira's written instructions on what Keystone could see, and the bonus disclosure. "Next transferee," she tells Jordan, "starts with these three documents."

items: A relocation referral does not change agency: the transferee who signs the buyer agreement is the client, not the relocation company or the employer.
Broker-to-broker referral fees are lawful under RPL 442 and exempt from RESPA Section 8; paying an unlicensed person is not, and a fee that could color advice should be disclosed to the client.
In a sponsor sale the sponsor's sales team represents the sponsor; register a buyer client before the first visit, and treat everything said in the gallery as said to the seller.

An offering plan is accepted for filing by the AG, not approved; amendments that materially and adversely affect buyers carry a rescission right of at least 15 days, and the decision belongs to the buyer and her attorney.
Sponsor bonuses must be disclosed before the client chooses; a broker may credit part of its fee to the buyer, and a salesperson is paid only through the sponsoring broker.

lessons.title: Case file: The Short Sale on East 92nd Street
lessons.tagline: A new team, a Canarsie short sale, three offers, and one of them from Marcus's brother-in-law. Then a teammate lists her late aunt's house and finds out she is the principal.
objectives: Apply New York's team rules to decide who the client is, when a team creates in-house dual agency, and how a team may advertise
Decide whose instructions control in a short sale and how confidentiality and honesty apply to the lienholder
Apply 19 NYCRR 175.4 and 175.6 to licensees and relatives who buy or sell property in a deal they work on
Decide what an executor-licensee needs, discloses, and clears with other beneficiaries when selling an estate property

blocks.title: Marcus becomes a brand
blocks.html: In January Marcus Webb decides he is a brand. He forms a team inside Hudson & Hart with two salespersons, Kiara Dawson and Theo Grant, prints 2,000 postcards, and mails one to every owner in Canarsie. The first call comes from Andre and Nicole Baptiste, who own a two-family on East 92nd Street. Andre's trucking hours were cut in half last year. They are seven payments behind on an $812,000 first mortgage, they owe another $41,000 on a home equity line, and the servicer started a foreclosure action in March. Comparable two-families are selling around $745,000. "We can't sell for what we owe," Nicole says. "Can you still sell it?" Before Diane signs off on the listing, she asks to see the postcard.

blocks.title: The postcard
blocks.html:
WEBB HOME GROUP
Canarsie's Short Sale Specialists
Behind on your mortgage? We stop foreclosures!
Call Marcus, Kiara or Theo: 718-555-0192
[team logo, gold house on a black square]

blocks.q: What is wrong with the postcard under New York's advertising rules?
c: Nothing, as long as the three people named on it hold licenses
It uses "group" instead of "team" and leaves out Hudson & Hart
It names three salespersons, but a team ad may name the leader alone
It needed approval from the Department of State before mailing
blocks.x: Under 19 NYCRR 175.25 a team name must use the word "team"; "group," "realty," and "associate" are prohibited, and any ad with a team name must also show the broker's name.
