The broker, not DOS, approves team advertising, which is the trap in the last choice. "We stop foreclosures" is a separate problem: no licensee can promise that, and distressed owners are exactly the audience most likely to believe it.

blocks.html: The reprint reads "The Webb Team at Hudson & Hart Realty," and the foreclosure promise is gone. Diane uses the moment to say what a team is and is not. It is a marketing label and a way to divide work among licensees who share listings and leads. It is not a brokerage. Every listing a team member takes is Hudson & Hart's listing, every buyer who signs is Hudson & Hart's client, and every commission is paid to the firm and then to the salespersons under the firm's plan.

blocks.title: Teams in the New York rules
blocks.html: 19 NYCRR 175.25 defines a team as two or more persons, at least one an associate broker or salesperson, associated with the same brokerage, who hold themselves out or operate as a team. The team name must use "team," may not use an unlicensed person's name, and must appear with the broker's name. The team may advertise only property listed with or represented by its own broker, and only with that broker's approval.

blocks.text: A listing that needs a third party's blessing

blocks.title: Short sale addendum to the exclusive right to sell
blocks.html:
1. Sellers owe more than the expected sale price. Any sale is subject to written approval by every lienholder.
2. Commission: 6% of the sale price, or any lesser amount a lienholder approves in writing as a condition of its approval.
3. Sellers acknowledge that Broker does not give legal or tax advice and that they have been advised to consult an attorney and a tax adviser.
4. Sellers authorize Broker to communicate with lienholders and to deliver documents that Sellers provide.

The servicer's letter says the loan is owned by Fannie Mae. A negotiator, Brenda Cole, orders a broker price opinion. Two weeks later she emails Marcus: "Investor will not consider a list price under $799,000. Please relist accordingly. Do not accept any offer below $760,000." The Baptistes want $749,000. They are trying to sell before a referee's sale, and they think a sharp price brings a fast buyer.

blocks.q: Whose instructions control the list price?
c: The servicer's, since no sale closes without its written approval
Fannie Mae's, because it owns the loan secured by the house
Marcus's, since the listing agent sets price from market data
The Baptistes', once Marcus explains what the servicer has said
blocks.x: The sellers are the principal, and obedience runs to them. The lienholder is a third party whose consent is a condition of closing, not a client. Marcus must tell the Baptistes exactly what the servicer said and what a low list price risks, recommend, and then follow their lawful instructions. The servicer choice is the trap: its approval matters in practice, but practical power does not make it the principal.

blocks.html: The Baptistes split the difference at $769,000. Then comes the hardship package: tax returns, bank statements, a hardship letter, and a financial statement the sellers sign. At the kitchen table Nicole tells Marcus she has about $30,000 in a 401(k) and that her mother "could probably help." A week later Brenda calls Marcus. "Off the record, do they have money somewhere? The investor will want a contribution."

blocks.q: How should Marcus answer Brenda's question?
c: Mention the 401(k), since hiding assets from a lender is fraud
Say they have nothing left, since a seller's agent protects them
Decline to discuss it and point her to the sellers' own package
Mention the mother's help but not the 401(k) the sellers own
blocks.x: Confidentiality bars Marcus from volunteering his clients' finances without consent, and honesty bars him from lying. The sellers report their own assets on the financial statement they sign, prepared with their attorney, and Marcus tells Nicole what the lender asked. The first choice is the trap for honest agents: the fraud risk is real, but the cure is an accurate package from the sellers, not an agent disclosing confidences on an "off the record" call.

blocks.html: Nicole lists the 401(k) on the statement, accurately, because she is signing it. The investor later asks for a $5,000 contribution at closing, and the Baptistes' attorney negotiates it down to $2,500. Nobody had to lie.

head: Offer
Buyer
Price
Terms
rows: All cash, as is; side letter: sellers stay as tenants 2 years at $2,400 a month, option to buy back at $790,000
blocks.caption: The offers on East 92nd Street, received the second week of May.

blocks.html: Gary Pruitt is married to Marcus's sister. Marcus forwards offer C to the Baptistes with a note: "This one keeps you in the house." He does not forward A or B. Theo, meanwhile, tells Diane that his client Yvonne's offer is no problem for the firm. "Marcus and I are different team members with different clients. It's not dual agency."

blocks.q: Is Theo right about offer A?
c: Yes, since team members are separate agents with separate clients
Yes, as long as Theo and Marcus keep each client's file to themselves
No, the firm represents both sides and needs both clients' consent
No, a team is barred from selling its listings to its own buyers
blocks.x: Clients belong to the broker. A team is a group of the same broker's agents, so a team buyer on a team listing makes Hudson & Hart a dual agent, which requires informed written consent from the Baptistes and Yvonne. Designated agents are possible with advance consent. Silence between teammates is the trap: it may protect confidences, but it does not change the firm's status, and here the teammates share a leader, a group chat, and a lead inbox.

blocks.html: Diane pulls up the team's group chat before deciding anything. Three days before the offers came in, Marcus posted: "Baptistes are desperate. Between us, they'd take anything over 740 if the bank goes along." Theo reacted with a thumbs up. So did Kiara.

blocks.q: Yvonne asks Theo how low the sellers will really go. May Theo tell her about Marcus's post?
c: Yes, since a buyer's agent owes his client every material fact he knows
Yes, since the post was shared in a chat and is no longer confidential
No, unless Yvonne signs a consent to dual agency before he tells her
No, he learned it as the sellers' agent and must flag it to Diane
blocks.x: Theo learned the sellers' bottom line because his firm represents them. Passing it to the buyer would breach the firm's duty of confidentiality to the Baptistes, and a dual agency consent does not license it; it is the reason such consent limits what each side hears. The first choice is the trap: disclosure to one's own client never reaches confidences the firm holds for the other side. The right move is to tell Diane, so she can manage who works which side.

blocks.html: Theo tells Diane, and Diane makes a decision the team will not like. Anyone who saw the post is out of position to negotiate against the Baptistes. Yvonne agrees, in writing, to be represented going forward by Nina Brooks, a Hudson & Hart salesperson outside the team who never had access to the chat. Theo stays on Yvonne's file for scheduling only. Diane also shuts the team's shared chat for client matters: "Teams share leads. They do not share confidences across the table."

blocks.q: Marcus forwarded only Gary's offer. What did his duties require?
c: Present all three offers promptly and disclose that Gary is family
Present Gary's first, since it is the offer that saves their home
Present only offers at or above the servicer's $760,000 floor
Present all three and leave the family tie for Gary to mention
blocks.x: A listing agent presents every offer to the sellers, who decide what goes to the servicer; a buyer at $750,000 may be approved even below a negotiator's stated floor. Before the Baptistes weigh offer C, loyalty requires Marcus to tell them Gary is his brother-in-law. Leaving the tie for Gary to mention is the trap: the duty to disclose a conflict is the agent's, and it belongs before the decision, in writing.

blocks.html: Diane hears about the forwarding from Theo and calls Marcus in. Marcus says Gary is "just trying to help family friends," and then adds a detail he has not told anyone: he is putting up half of Gary's cash. They planned to hold title in Gary's name and split the profit when the Baptistes buy back or when they sell.

blocks.q: Under 19 NYCRR 175.4, what did Marcus's plan to fund half of Gary's purchase require?
c: Nothing, since the deed would name Gary and not Marcus
Making his true position clearly known to the Baptistes first
Disclosure to the servicer, since the sellers already trust him
Giving up the listing, since an agent may not buy a listing
blocks.x: 175.4 says a broker shall not directly or indirectly buy listed property or acquire any interest in it without first making his true position clearly known to the listing owner. Money behind a relative's name is the definition of indirectly. The nominee-title choice is the trap. The last choice overstates the rule: New York requires full disclosure before self-dealing, not a flat ban, though few clients consent once they hear the whole story.

blocks.html: Diane takes Marcus off the file that afternoon and assigns Kiara to the Baptistes. Kiara sends the sellers all three offers, a written disclosure of the Gary relationship and Marcus's planned stake, and a recommendation that their attorney read offer C's side letter before anyone signs anything.

Offer C has a second problem that full disclosure cannot fix. For a short sale of a Fannie Mae loan, the servicer requires a short sale affidavit signed at closing by the sellers, the buyer, and the agents, under penalty of perjury. It certifies an arm's-length sale with no family, marriage, or business tie between the parties, no hidden agreement letting the sellers stay beyond a short, customary period or take title back, and, for the listing broker, that every offer was presented.

blocks.q: What happens to offer C under the short sale affidavit?
c: It works if the leaseback moves into a separate private side letter
It works if the negotiator approves the leaseback on a phone call
It works, because Gary is related to Marcus and not to the Baptistes
It cannot close as written, since the buyback is what the affidavit bars
blocks.x: The lender takes a loss because it believes the sellers are walking away. A two-year tenancy with an option to buy back at a profit is the arrangement the affidavit certifies does not exist. Moving it into a private letter is the trap: that turns a rejected offer into a false sworn statement, and the agents who sign the affidavit share the exposure. Gary's family tie to the listing agent is a further problem, not a cure.

blocks.title: "Rescue" deals have their own statute
blocks.html: New York's Home Equity Theft Prevention Act, RPL 265-a, covers investors who buy owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes in foreclosure or default. A deal where the seller keeps an option to repurchase is presumed to be a loan secured by a mortgage, the contract must meet strict content and cancellation rules, and the purchaser must verify that the seller can realistically afford the buyback. Agents who wrap a lease-and-buy-back in "we're saving your home" language are describing the transaction the statute was written to stop.

The Baptistes accept offer A, Yvonne Clarke at $758,000, after signing the firm's dual agency consent. Diane designates Nina for Yvonne and Kiara for the sellers, with consent from both sides. In July the approval letter arrives.

blocks.title: Short sale approval letter, excerpts
blocks.html:
Approved sale price: $758,000. Minimum net proceeds to servicer: $689,500.
Real estate commission approved: 5% ($37,900). (Requested: 6%.)
Payment to second lienholder for release of home equity line: $6,000.
Seller contribution at closing: $2,500.
Closing must occur by August 29 or this approval is void.
This approval does not waive any deficiency balance. The investor reserves all rights to collect amounts remaining due.

blocks.q: Which term should Kiara make sure the Baptistes' attorney reviews before they sign the approval?
c: The cut in commission from 6% down to 5% of the price
The $6,000 payment to release the home equity line
The reservation of the right to collect a deficiency
The August 29 deadline to close the short sale
blocks.x: Without a waiver, the Baptistes could still owe the gap between the debt and what the servicer receives, which here exceeds $100,000. Whether to negotiate a waiver, and what forgiven debt means for their taxes, are legal and tax questions, which is why the addendum sends them to an attorney and a tax adviser. The commission cut is the trap: under the addendum the firm already agreed to accept the lesser amount, so it is the firm's cost, not the sellers' risk.

blocks.html: The Baptistes' attorney negotiates a deficiency waiver into a revised approval. Yvonne closes August 22. The firm's 5% is paid at closing and split under the firm's plan, with Theo's share for the work he did before the chat surfaced settled by Diane. Marcus, off the file, receives nothing from it, and Diane files a note on his supervision record.

In September Kiara's aunt, Bernice Dawson, dies at 84. Her will leaves her one-family house in East Flatbush to Kiara and Kiara's cousin Dwayne in equal shares and names Kiara executor. The roof has leaked over the back bedroom for two winters; Kiara has put out the buckets herself. She wants to list the house with the team at $689,000 and a 5% commission. Theo already has a buyer client, Kwame Osei, who loves the block.

blocks.q: What does Kiara need before she signs a listing agreement for the estate?
c: Letters testamentary issued to her by the Surrogate's Court
The will and death certificate in the listing file at the firm
Dwayne's signature, because both heirs have to sign a listing
The power of attorney Bernice signed for her three years ago
blocks.x: A will names an executor, but the authority to act for the estate comes from letters testamentary issued by the Surrogate's Court. Until they issue, nobody can hire a broker for the estate. The power of attorney is the trap: an agency ends by operation of law when the principal dies, and a power of attorney is an agency. Dwayne's signature is not what gives the executor authority, though his consent will matter for another reason.

blocks.q: Once Kiara signs the listing as executor, who is Hudson & Hart's principal?
c: The estate, acting through Kiara in her role as its executor
Kiara personally, since she is an heir and also a firm salesperson
Kiara and Dwayne as the two heirs, each one for a half share
The estate's attorney, who supervises the sale for the court
blocks.x: The client is the estate, and Kiara signs for it as executor, a fiduciary role she holds for both beneficiaries. That is why her personal wishes and the estate's interests have to be kept apart. Choosing Kiara personally is the trap: she wears three hats here, heir, executor, and salesperson, and the listing is signed under only one of them.

blocks.q: What must Kiara disclose to Kwame and any other buyer?
c: Nothing more, since she sells as an executor and not as an owner
Her ownership interest as an heir, under the rule for selling it
Her license alone, since estate sales are outside agency rules
Her interest, but just if a buyer asks whether the agent is related
blocks.x: 19 NYCRR 175.6 requires a licensee who sells property in which she owns an interest to make that interest known to the purchaser. As a half beneficiary, Kiara has one, whatever capacity she signs in. The first choice is the trap: the executor role does not erase the beneficial interest. Waiting for a buyer to ask turns a required disclosure into a guessing game.

blocks.html: Kiara rewrites the listing remarks the same day: "Listing salesperson is a beneficiary of the estate and its executor." It costs her nothing with serious buyers, and it protects the estate from the claim she is most exposed to: that a buyer paid more because the agent across the table hid a personal stake. Kwame reads it, shrugs, and says the house is still the house. His agent, Theo, now knows exactly whom he is negotiating against, which is the point of the rule.

blocks.q: Kiara wants the firm to earn the full 5%, with her usual share. Dwayne inherits half. What is the safest course?
c: Sign the listing as executor, since a fair market fee needs no consent
Waive her share, since the firm's share raises no conflict of its own
Rely on the will, since naming her executor approves any listing
Disclose her share of the fee to Dwayne and get his written consent
blocks.x: As executor, Kiara owes loyalty to both beneficiaries. Hiring her own firm and taking part of the commission benefits her personally at the estate's expense, which is self-dealing on the estate side. Full written disclosure to Dwayne, his informed consent, and the estate attorney's advice are the safe route. The "fair fee" choice is the trap: fairness of the number does not cure an undisclosed conflict, in an estate or in a brokerage.

blocks.q: Does the estate have to give Kwame a Property Condition Disclosure Statement?
c: No, but Kiara still has to disclose the roof leak she knows about
Yes, since every 1 to 4 family seller has had to give one since 2024
No, and an estate also has no duty to mention any defect it knows
Yes, unless Kwame waives it in exchange for a $500 closing credit
blocks.x: RPL 463 exempts a transfer by a fiduciary in the course of administering a decedent's estate, so no PCDS form is required. The exemption covers the form, not honesty: Kiara is a licensee who has personally emptied buckets under that leak, and a known material defect cannot be concealed. The $500 choice is the trap: the credit opt-out was repealed in March 2024, and here no form is required anyway.

blocks.html: Dwayne signs a one-page consent after reading Kiara's disclosure and calling the estate's attorney. Diane designates Theo for Kwame and Diane's associate broker, Renata Silva, for the estate, so that Kiara, a principal on the sell side, never handles the negotiation for the estate. Kwame's offer comes in at $672,000 with a roof credit of $9,000, and the estate accepts.

items: A team is a marketing and work-sharing label inside one brokerage: team names must use "team" and show the broker, and every team listing and team buyer is the firm's client, so a team buyer on a team listing is dual agency.
In a short sale the sellers are the principal; the lienholder's approval is a condition, not a source of instructions, and confidences stay confidential without any license to lie.
Present every offer, and disclose any family or financial tie to a buyer before the sellers decide; 175.4 reaches indirect interests held through relatives or nominees.
Short sale affidavits and RPL 265-a make lease-and-buy-back "rescue" deals a fraud and statute problem, not a negotiating tactic.

A licensee who is an heir and executor needs letters testamentary, must disclose her interest under 175.6, and must clear her commission with the other beneficiaries; the estate is PCDS-exempt but known defects are still disclosed.

roleplays.title: Column F
roleplays.setting: Hudson & Hart conference room, Bed-Stuy. Your buyer client wants your firm's own listing.
roleplays.you: Jordan, the buyer's agent at Hudson & Hart
roleplays.goal: Turn an in-house sale into a properly consented dual agency (ideally with designated agents) without leaking either client's confidential information.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play a buyer client (an anxious first-time buyer) and briefly Marcus, a corner-cutting agent, and Grace Okafor, a seller. The buyer wants a brownstone listed by the learner's own firm and repeatedly asks what the sellers will take. Marcus later offers the sellers' bottom line in the hallway. Grace Okafor fishes for the buyer's budget. The learner is the buyer's agent and must (1) recognize the in-house sale as dual agency and get informed written consent, explaining what the buyer gives up, (2) offer designated sales agents and note the broker remains a dual agent, (3) insist the sellers be told when it actually happens despite advance consent, (4) refuse and report Marcus's leak, (5) protect the buyer's confidences from the sellers, (6) advise the buyer using market data only and avoid neighborhood demographics. Grade each item and give one sentence of advice.
opening: Hudson & Hart conference room, Bed-Stuy. Your buyer client {client} has fallen for the Okafors' brownstone on {block}, listed at {price}. Your own firm holds the listing.
{client} texts you at 7 a.m.: 'The {block} brownstone. That's the one.' It's the Okafors' house, asking {price}, and Hudson & Hart is the listing broker.
You've shown {client} eleven houses. Number twelve, the Okafors' {price} brownstone on {block}, is the one. Marcus, at your own firm, is the listing agent. {client} arrives {mood}.

say: This is perfect. My spreadsheet max is in column F. Your firm has the listing, so you probably know what they'll take, right?
Your office listed it, so you must know their real number. What will the Okafors actually accept?

moves.text: First thing: our firm represents the Okafors too. That's dual agency, and it needs your written consent.
moves.fb: Right first move. An in-house sale makes the firm a dual agent, which needs informed written consent from both sides (RPL 443).
moves.react: {client} blinks. "Wait, you work for them too? Okay, explain."

moves.text: Can't share that. We list this house, so let me explain dual agency first, or you can go outside.
moves.fb: Correct. You protect the sellers' confidences and offer the options before acting for both sides.
moves.react: "Huh. I didn't know that was a thing," {client} says. "Go on."

moves.text: Let's write the offer first, and we'll sort out the consent paperwork before the contract is signed.
moves.fb: Not a breach yet, but consent must come before you act for both sides. Raise dual agency now.

moves.text: I'll ask Marcus quietly what they would take and get back to you before we write anything up at all.
moves.fb: Fishing for your seller clients' bottom line to help another client breaches loyalty and confidentiality to the Okafors.
moves.react: "You're the best," {client} says. "Text me the number."

moves.text: Probably near the asking. And don't worry about dual agency here, that rule is really for condos and rentals.
moves.fb: Wrong. The RPL 443 disclosure covers 1 to 4 family homes, condos, and co-ops, and dual agency applies to all of them.

moves.text: No new forms needed. You already signed our buyer agreement, so that covers an in-house sale automatically.
moves.fb: A buyer agreement is not informed consent to dual agency. That consent must be specific and in writing.

say: Okay, what does dual agency actually cost me?
So if I sign this consent, what am I giving up?

moves.text: Nobody gets undivided loyalty. I can't share their bottom line or yours or push you to beat them down.
moves.fb: Informed consent means explaining what each side gives up. That's what makes the consent valid.
moves.react: {client} nods slowly. "That's fair. What are my options?"

moves.text: You'd lose full advocacy. With designated agents, I advise you, and Marcus advises them. Diane remains dual.
moves.fb: Correct. Designated sales agents each represent one side while the broker remains a dual agent.

moves.text: It's a trade-off. Read the form tonight and tell me tomorrow whether you're comfortable signing it.
moves.fb: Giving time is fine, but consent isn't informed unless you explain the trade-offs yourself.
moves.react: {client} sighs. "I was hoping you'd just tell me."

moves.text: Nothing, really. It's a formality we do on every in-house deal, so just sign wherever I flagged it.
moves.fb: Consent that isn't informed isn't valid. Each side loses undivided loyalty and full advocacy.

moves.text: It means I represent you both equally, so I can tell each side what the other is really thinking.
moves.fb: Backwards. A dual agent may not pass either side's confidences to the other.
moves.react: {client} grins. "Even better. So what's their number?"

moves.text: You'd pay more in commission, since our firm earns both sides. Honestly, that's the only real difference.
moves.fb: Wrong about cost and silent on what matters: the loss of undivided loyalty and full advocacy.
moves.react: {client} frowns. "I have to pay more? That's annoying."

say: Grace Okafor: We checked that advance consent box months ago. Do you even need to tell us about this buyer?
Grace Okafor: Marcus says a buyer from your own office is interested. We already consented in the listing, didn't we?

moves.text: Yes. Your advance consent covers the setup, but you get told now that it's real, and confirm in writing.
moves.fb: Right. Advance consent is not permission to stay silent. Disclose and confirm when the dual situation actually arises.
moves.react: Grace smiles. "Thank you for being straight with us."

moves.text: Marcus will go through it, but yes: you get told now that our firm is on both sides, in writing.
moves.fb: Correct. You point her to her own designated agent and confirm disclosure when the dual role becomes real.
moves.react: "Good," Grace says. "We'll talk to Marcus tonight."

moves.text: I'll have Diane email you about it later. It's mostly a formality since you already checked the box.
moves.fb: Getting it to the broker is fine, but calling it a formality undercuts informed consent.
moves.react: Grace frowns. "A formality? That's not how it sounds."

moves.text: No, the box covers it. Advance consent means we don't need to mention each new buyer to you at all.
moves.fb: The firm must disclose the actual dual agency when it arises. Silence risks an undisclosed dual agency claim.
moves.react: Grace nods, unsure. "If you say so."

moves.text: Not really. I'm the buyer's designated agent and Marcus is yours, so it isn't dual agency anymore.
moves.fb: Wrong. With designated agents the broker is still a dual agent, and both sides must know it.
moves.react: "Oh, so nothing to worry about," Grace says.

moves.text: Only if the buyer offers over asking. Below that price, the advance consent handles the disclosure for you.
moves.fb: There's no price trigger. Disclosure turns on the firm representing both sides, not on the offer.
moves.react: Grace looks puzzled. "That seems like an odd rule."

say: (in the hallway) Off the record, the Okafors already bought in Atlanta. They'll take way less than {price}. Tell your buyer to come in low.
(quietly) Between us, the Okafors need this closed by summer. Tell {client} to lowball. They'll fold.

moves.text: Don't tell me that. You're their agent, and I can't use it. I'm letting Diane know it happened.
moves.fb: Correct. Each designated agent must protect their own client's confidences, and the broker must know of a breach.
moves.react: Marcus winces. "Relax, I was just helping."

moves.text: Stop. I won't use their confidences for {client}, and Diane needs to hear about it today.
moves.fb: Right. Using the sellers' confidential motivation would be a fiduciary breach by the firm, which represents both.
moves.react: "Fine, forget I said anything," Marcus mutters.

moves.text: I'll pretend I didn't hear that. Let's both just get back to work and drop it for now, okay?
moves.fb: You didn't use it, which matters, but the supervising broker needs to know a breach happened.

moves.text: Thanks, that helps {client} a lot. I'll suggest we open well under asking and see what happens.
moves.fb: Using the seller's confidential information against them breaches loyalty and confidentiality.

moves.text: I'll only hint at it to {client}. If I never give an exact number, it isn't really a breach.
moves.fb: A hint is still a disclosure of a client's confidence. There is no partial version that's allowed.

moves.text: Since we're designated agents, info shared between us is fine. It all belongs to the firm, anyway.
moves.fb: Wrong. Designated agents must keep their own client's confidences from each other.

say: So what should I offer? Just give me a number. You're MY designated agent now.
Okay, consent's signed. Now advocate for me. What's the offer?

moves.text: These are the last six sales near {block}, and my read on value. I'd open a little under asking.
moves.fb: As a designated agent you may advise and advocate for your client using market data.
moves.react: {client} studies the comps. "Okay. That feels defensible."

moves.text: Here is a range I can defend from recent comps. I won't use what I may know about the sellers.
moves.fb: Correct. You advocate with market evidence while respecting the firm's dual role.
moves.react: "I like that you showed your work," {client} says.

moves.text: I can't advise you at all since our firm is a dual agent. You'll have to pick the number yourself.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but you were appointed a designated agent so you could advocate for {client}.
moves.react: {client} looks lost. "Then what am I paying you for?"

moves.text: Offer well under asking. Trust me, I have a feeling they're motivated, I just can't tell you why.
moves.fb: Signaling that you know the sellers' motivation leaks their confidence, even without details.

moves.text: Offer full asking. As a dual agent I have to protect the sellers too, so no lowball offers from you.
moves.fb: A designated agent advocates for one client. You don't argue the sellers' side to your own buyer.

moves.text: Go to your max in column F. If it's in your spreadsheet, you can afford it, so we'll win the house.
moves.fb: Advice should come from value evidence, not the client's ceiling. This puts closing ahead of the client.

say: Real question: what's the neighborhood like these days? Who's moving in? Is it, you know, changing?
Be honest with me. What kind of people live on {block}? Is it a good area for someone like me?

moves.text: I can share facts: sales, transit, school data sources. I don't describe who lives where.
moves.fb: Right. Describing a neighborhood by who lives there is steering under the Fair Housing Act and NYS Human Rights Law.

moves.text: Fair housing rules keep me off demographics. Here are public sources, so you can judge yourself.
moves.fb: Correct. You point to objective sources and let the buyer decide where to live.

moves.text: Hard to say. Walk around on a Saturday morning and you'll get a feel for the area yourself.
moves.fb: Not steering, but you could have offered objective data sources instead of a shrug.

moves.text: It's changing fast. Lots of young professionals like you moving in, so prices should keep climbing.
moves.fb: Describing who is moving in, and implying it's good, is steering by demographics.
moves.react: {client} perks up. "People like me? Good to know."

moves.text: I'd rather not say in writing, but I'll tell you off the record over coffee what I noticed.
moves.fb: Steering off the record is still steering. Fair housing duties don't depend on the channel.

moves.text: It's a great family block, mostly long-time owners. Someone like you would fit right in here.
moves.fb: 'Fit right in' plus a description of residents is the kind of comment that steers buyers.
moves.react: {client} smiles. "That's what I wanted to hear."

say: Do I really have to sign this disclosure form? My lawyer friend says it's a contract and I shouldn't sign.
I don't sign things I haven't had a lawyer read. Is this form a contract?

moves.text: It isn't a contract. It confirms I explained who represents whom. You can decline to sign.
moves.fb: Right. The RPL 443 form says on its face that it is not a contract. It's an acknowledgment.
moves.react: {client} reads it. "Oh. It literally says that."

moves.text: The form says right on it that it's not a contract. If you'd rather not sign, I'll note that and we go on.
moves.fb: Correct. If the consumer won't sign, the licensee completes a sworn declaration of the refusal.

moves.text: Have your friend read it first. We can hold off on seeing more houses until you've signed it.
moves.fb: Letting a lawyer review is fine, but refusal doesn't stop the relationship. It's documented, not fatal.

moves.text: It's a contract that binds you to our firm, so yes, you need to sign it before we do anything else.
moves.fb: Wrong. The disclosure is not a contract, and a refusal is handled with a sworn declaration.
moves.react: {client} hesitates. "Then I really want my lawyer to see it."

moves.text: You don't need it. These forms are only required on the seller side, not when I work with buyers.
moves.fb: Wrong. RPL 443 applies to buyers and sellers of 1 to 4 family homes at first substantive contact.

moves.text: Skip it. Once you've signed the dual agency consent, the disclosure form really doesn't matter.
moves.fb: Both are required. The disclosure comes first, and consent doesn't replace it.

say: Grace Okafor calls you: Between us, is your buyer approved? What's their real budget?
Grace Okafor, at the open house: You work at the same firm, so tell me. How high can your buyer go?

moves.text: I represent {client}, so I can't share that. Marcus will get you the offer and proof of funds.
moves.fb: Right. As the buyer's designated agent, you keep the buyer's finances confidential.
moves.react: Grace laughs. "Worth a try. I'll ask Marcus."

moves.text: That's {client}'s confidential information. Marcus is your agent; he'll get you what a seller sees.
moves.fb: Correct. You protect your client's confidences and route the seller to her own agent.

moves.text: You would have to ask Marcus. I'm honestly not sure what I'm allowed to say to you right now, Grace.
moves.fb: No leak, but sounding unsure invites more questions. Say clearly that it's confidential.

moves.text: They're preapproved well over asking, so hold firm on your price. Just don't tell anyone I said that.
moves.fb: Disclosing your buyer's financial capacity to the seller is a breach of loyalty and confidentiality.
moves.react: Grace thanks you warmly and hangs up.

moves.text: Since our firm represents you too, I can share it. Their max is a bit over your asking price.
moves.fb: Dual agency means neither side's confidences cross over. The firm's dual role makes this worse, not okay.
moves.react: "I knew it," Grace says. "We'll hold firm."

moves.text: I can share the budget, just not the down payment. Budgets aren't covered by confidentiality.
moves.fb: A buyer's budget is classic confidential information. Sharing it hurts your client's negotiating position.

say: My buyer agreement says I'd pay your firm 2%. If the sellers are paying your firm too, do I still pay?
Wait. Is your firm getting paid by me and by the Okafors on the same house?

moves.text: Good question. Our firm can't be paid by both sides unless everyone knows and agrees, in writing.
moves.fb: Right. 19 NYCRR 175.7 bars compensation from more than one party without full disclosure and consent.
moves.react: {client} relaxes. "Okay, so it all gets spelled out."

moves.text: Let's lay out exactly who pays what. Fees from more than one party need full disclosure and consent.
moves.fb: Correct. Transparency about compensation is required, and terms are negotiated, not assumed.

moves.text: Probably not. Let me ask Diane how she usually handles commission on these in-house deals.
moves.fb: Checking with the broker is fine, but you should know the disclosure and consent rule yourself.

moves.text: Yes, you'll both pay. That's standard for dual agency, so there's no need to tell the sellers about it.
moves.fb: Collecting from both parties without telling each one violates 175.7.
moves.react: {client} frowns. "That doesn't sound standard to me."

moves.text: Fees aren't up for discussion. Commissions are set by the board, so it's the same everywhere.
moves.fb: No board sets commissions. Fees are negotiable, and claiming otherwise suggests price fixing.

moves.text: Don't worry, the sellers' fee is confidential, so we can take yours too without telling them.
moves.fb: Hiding a second fee from either client is exactly what 175.7 forbids.

roleplays.debrief: An in-house sale makes the firm a dual agent, which needs informed written consent from buyer and seller (RPL 443), ideally with designated sales agents while the broker stays the dual agent. Disclose when it actually arises, keep each client's confidences, advise from market data only, keep neighborhood talk free of demographics (Fair Housing Act, NYS Human Rights Law), and collect from more than one party only with everyone's informed consent (19 NYCRR 175.7).

roleplays.title: Sal's Vacancy
roleplays.setting: Sal Russo's six-unit building in Astoria. A 2BR just opened up and Sal wants it rented fast.
roleplays.you: Jordan, pitching to be Sal's landlord's agent
roleplays.goal: Sign a lawful exclusive right to rent with a negotiated fee, stay clear of antitrust and net listing traps, and treat prospective tenants correctly.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Sal Russo, an old-school Astoria landlord, then a chatty prospective tenant. Sal claims all brokers charge the same fee, proposes a net deal (keep anything over $3,100), and instructs the agent to refuse vouchers and make tenants pay the broker fee. The tenant volunteers budget and urgency and refuses to sign forms. The learner is the landlord's agent and must (1) state fees are negotiable and set independently, (2) refuse the net listing, (3) refuse unlawful instructions citing source of income protection and the FARE Act, (4) disclose the landlord-agent role at first substantive contact, (5) handle refusal with a sworn declaration. Grade each and give one tip.
opening: Sal Russo's six-unit building in Astoria. Apartment {unit} just opened up at {rent} a month, and Sal wants it rented by the first.
Sal meets you on the stoop of his Astoria six-family with a coffee and a key ring. Unit {unit} is empty, asking {rent}.
Your first landlord pitch: Sal Russo, six units in Astoria, apartment {unit} vacant at {rent}. He's already talked to two other brokers.

say: I want it rented by the first. What's your fee? Everybody in Astoria charges the same thing anyway, right? You brokers all agree on it.
So what do you charge? Same as everyone else, I figure. You all set the number together.

moves.text: Fees are negotiable, and every firm sets its own. Ours is one month's rent, paid by you as landlord.
moves.fb: Right. No standard rate exists, and in NYC the FARE Act makes the landlord's broker the landlord's expense.
moves.react: Sal grunts. "One month. The last guy said fifteen percent."

moves.text: There's no standard rate. Each firm sets its own. Here's ours, and here's what the agreement covers.
moves.fb: Correct. Fees are set independently by each firm. Implying otherwise suggests price fixing.
moves.react: "Okay, show me," Sal says, taking the agreement.

moves.text: Honestly I'm not sure what we charge. Let me check with Diane and text you our number tomorrow.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but walking into a listing pitch without knowing your firm's fee costs you credibility.
moves.react: Sal raises an eyebrow. "You don't know your own price?"

moves.text: Yeah, we all keep it at fifteen percent of the annual rent. That keeps things fair and nobody undercuts.
moves.fb: Saying competitors agree on a rate describes price fixing, a Sherman Act violation.

moves.text: We follow the board's suggested fee schedule, so it's the same everywhere in Queens anyway.
moves.fb: No board sets or suggests fees. Commissions are negotiable between each firm and its client.

moves.text: Fifteen percent, and since you're the landlord the tenant pays it at lease signing, like always.
moves.fb: Under the FARE Act, the broker the landlord hires is paid by the landlord, not the tenant.
moves.react: Sal smiles. "Even better. Costs me nothing."

say: Tell you what. I want {rent} a month. Rent it for more, and you keep everything over {rent} for the year.
Here's my deal. I net {rent}. Whatever you get above that, it's all yours.

moves.text: That's a net listing, and New York doesn't allow it. Let's agree on a stated fee instead.
moves.fb: Right. Net listings are prohibited by 19 NYCRR 175.19. The fee must be a stated amount or percentage.
moves.react: Sal shrugs. "Worth a shot. Stated fee, then."

moves.text: I can't take a deal where my pay is whatever's left over. It must be a set amount or percent.
moves.fb: Correct. A net arrangement sets your profit against your client's interest in true market rent.

moves.text: Let me think about it. It might work if we write it up carefully and you sign off on the rent.
moves.fb: Hesitating is better than agreeing, but there's nothing to think about. Net listings are banned.
moves.react: Sal leans in. "So that's a maybe?"

moves.text: Deal. I'll list it a few hundred higher and we both come out ahead. Easy money for everybody.
moves.fb: A net arrangement is banned in NY, and pricing to pad your own fee betrays the client.

moves.text: That works if we put it in writing. Net deals are fine in New York once both sides have signed.
moves.fb: Wrong. Putting a net listing in writing doesn't make it legal under 175.19.

moves.text: Okay, but only on rentals. Net listings are banned on sales, but leases are a different story.
moves.fb: The prohibition covers rentals too. There's no lease exception.

say: And just so you know: no vouchers, and tell the tenants they pay your fee. That's how we always did it.
Two rules. No Section 8, and the tenant covers your commission. That's how it works in my building.

moves.text: I can't do either. Refusing vouchers is income discrimination, and you pay the broker you hire.
moves.fb: Right. Lawful source of income is protected under the NYS Human Rights Law, and the FARE Act puts our fee on you.
moves.react: Sal scowls. "Since when?" Then: "Fine. Put it in writing for me."

moves.text: Both are off the table. Source of income is protected, and the FARE Act puts our fee on you.
moves.fb: Correct. Obedience covers lawful instructions only, and these two aren't lawful.

moves.text: I'll check with Diane on both of those and get back to you before the listing goes live, okay?
moves.fb: Checking is better than complying, but you should know both rules and say so now.
moves.react: Sal waves a hand. "Just make it happen."

moves.text: Okay, I'll quietly screen out voucher holders. We just won't say it anywhere in the listing.
moves.fb: Following an unlawful instruction is discrimination, not obedience, and it threatens your license.

moves.text: Vouchers I'll handle, but the fee is fine. Tenants always pay in Queens. Only Manhattan changed.
moves.fb: The FARE Act applies across all five boroughs, Queens included.

moves.text: Fee's on you, but vouchers are only protected for tenants with a disability. I'll screen the rest.
moves.fb: Wrong. Lawful source of income is protected for everyone under the NYS Human Rights Law.

say: Hi! I'm {applicant}, moving from {from}. My budget's tight and I need something by the first. Can you get me a deal?
I'm {applicant}. I start a job here in two weeks and I can't go over {rent}. Can you work on the landlord for me?

moves.text: Happy to show you. First, I represent the landlord, so I can't negotiate for you. Here's the form.
moves.fb: Budget and timing make this first substantive contact. Disclose your landlord-agent role and present the form now (RPL 443).
moves.react: {applicant} reads it. "Oh, okay. Good to know."

moves.text: Quick note before we talk numbers: I work for the landlord. This form explains what that means.
moves.fb: Correct. The landlord-tenant agency disclosure comes before substantive talk about terms.

moves.text: I work for the landlord, so keep your budget to yourself. Want to see the bedroom first?
moves.fb: Disclosing the role is right, but the written form should be presented now too.

moves.text: Sure, I'll get you the best price I can. Leave the negotiating with Sal to me, I know him well.
moves.fb: Promising to negotiate for the tenant while representing the landlord risks undisclosed dual agency.

moves.text: Let's skip the paperwork. Agency forms are only for sales, and rentals don't need a disclosure.
moves.fb: Wrong. RPL 443 has a landlord and tenant version for residential rentals.

moves.text: I can represent you both. You don't need a form since you're not paying me anything here.
moves.fb: Who pays doesn't decide agency. Dual agency would need informed written consent of both.

say: I don't sign forms at showings. Is that a problem?
I'd rather not sign anything today. Can we still look?

moves.text: Not at all. I'll note your refusal in a sworn declaration, and we'll keep going.
moves.fb: Right. RPL 443 requires a sworn declaration of the refusal, kept at least 3 years. The showing continues.

moves.text: That's okay. I'll record, under oath, that you declined to sign, and keep it on file.
moves.fb: Correct. Refusal is documented by the licensee, not a reason to stop.

moves.text: Then I can't show you the apartment today. Come back once you're ready to sign.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but unnecessary. A refusal is documented, and you just lost Sal an applicant.

moves.text: No problem, I'll sign your name on the acknowledgment line so the file is complete.
moves.fb: Signing for a consumer is falsifying a record. The licensee signs a declaration of refusal instead.

moves.text: Fine. If you won't sign, the disclosure doesn't count, so we can skip it altogether.
moves.fb: Wrong. The disclosure still must be given, and the refusal must be documented under oath.

moves.text: Then you can't apply. The law says no tenant can rent without signing the agency form.
moves.fb: No such rule. A refusal is recorded in a sworn declaration and the process goes on.

say: That {applicant} seems great, but there's a toddler. The floors are thin. Find me someone without kids.
No little kids, okay? The tenant downstairs complains about noise. Pick someone single.

moves.text: I can't screen out families with kids. Familial status is protected by federal and state law.
moves.fb: Right. The Fair Housing Act and NYS Human Rights Law protect familial status.

moves.text: That's familial status discrimination. We pick the most qualified applicant, kids or no kids.
moves.fb: Correct. You refuse an unlawful instruction and explain the standard you'll apply.

moves.text: Let me check how Diane wants us to handle that, and I'll call you back this afternoon.
moves.fb: Checking isn't complying, but this is a clear rule you should state right away.
moves.react: Sal says, "Call me back with a yes."

moves.text: Okay, I'll just tell her the unit's been rented. That way there's no record of the reason.
moves.fb: Falsely saying a unit is unavailable because of a protected class is discrimination.

moves.text: Small buildings are exempt, so you can pass on families if the floors are really a problem.
moves.fb: A six-unit building isn't exempt, and using a broker removes the owner exemptions anyway.

moves.text: Fine, as long as we offer her a ground-floor unit instead. Steering is allowed to nicer units.
moves.fb: Steering by familial status is illegal even toward a unit you think is better.

say: Brokers from three firms are refusing to show listings from that new flat-fee brokerage. They want us in too. You in?
Group chat says nobody co-brokes with the discount firm anymore. We're joining, right?

moves.text: No. Agreeing with competitors to shut out a firm is a group boycott under the Sherman Act.
moves.fb: Right. Concerted refusals to deal are illegal group boycotts under antitrust law.
moves.react: Marcus shrugs. "Your loss. I'll tell them."

moves.text: We decide on our own whether to co-broke, deal by deal. Deciding together is antitrust trouble.
moves.fb: Correct. Each firm decides independently. A joint decision is the violation.
moves.react: "Fine, I'll leave the chat," Marcus says.

moves.text: I'd rather stay out of it. Let's just not reply to the group chat at all and see what happens.
moves.fb: Staying out is better than joining, but you should object and tell your broker.
moves.react: Marcus shrugs. "Silent is a yes to them."

moves.text: Sure, it protects our fees. If we never put it in writing anywhere, it isn't an antitrust thing.
moves.fb: An unwritten agreement is still an agreement. Group boycotts are illegal either way.

moves.text: Fine for rentals. Antitrust law only covers sales commissions, not the fees on lease deals.
moves.fb: Wrong. The Sherman Act applies to rental brokerage too.

moves.text: Let's just slow-walk their showings instead of refusing them outright. That part is legal.
moves.fb: A coordinated slow-walk is still a concerted refusal to deal.
moves.react: Marcus grins. "Even better. Nobody can prove it."

say: Is this apartment rent stabilized? My friend said old buildings with six units usually are.
Quick question. Is {unit} rent stabilized? I'd like to know before I apply.

moves.text: It might be. I'll check the HCR rent registration history and get you an answer, not a guess.
moves.fb: Right. Buildings with 6+ units built before 1974 are often stabilized under the ETPA; HCR records confirm.

moves.text: I don't want to guess. Older six-unit buildings often are, so let's confirm with HCR records.
moves.fb: Correct. You give an accurate frame and verify instead of guessing about a legal status.

moves.text: I think it's market rate, but I'm not certain. You could look it up yourself online tonight.
moves.fb: Not a lie, but as the agent you should verify rather than guess and pass the job off.

moves.text: No. Stabilization ended back in 2019 when the state passed that big new tenant protection law.
moves.fb: Backwards. The 2019 HSTPA made rent stabilization permanent and strengthened it.
moves.react: {applicant} looks confused. "Oh. I thought it was the opposite."

moves.text: No, Sal owns the building outright, so it's market rate. Only the big complexes get stabilized.
moves.fb: Ownership doesn't decide it. Stabilization can apply to buildings with as few as 6 units.

moves.text: Yes, but Sal can deregulate it once the rent passes the luxury threshold, so it won't matter.
moves.fb: High-rent luxury decontrol was repealed in 2019.

say: I have an emotional support dog. The listing says no pets. Can I still apply?
My therapist wrote a letter for my support animal. Does the no-pets rule apply to me?

moves.text: Yes, please apply. You can request a reasonable accommodation, and I'll bring it to Sal.
moves.fb: Right. Fair housing law requires reasonable accommodations for people with disabilities, including support animals.

moves.text: You can. A disability accommodation request is handled apart from the no-pets rule.
moves.fb: Correct. A no-pets policy can't block a reasonable accommodation for a disability.

moves.text: Probably, but I'm not sure how that works. Apply, and we'll sort it out with Sal later.
moves.fb: Not unlawful, but you should know the accommodation rule and explain it.

moves.text: No pets means no pets. Support animals only count in buildings that have an elevator.
moves.fb: Wrong. There's no elevator rule. Reasonable accommodations apply regardless.

moves.text: Sure, but there's an extra pet deposit of one more month's rent for support animals.
moves.fb: Charging extra for an accommodation is improper, and deposits are capped at one month.

moves.text: Only with a letter from a New York psychiatrist. Out-of-state letters don't count here.
moves.fb: No such rule. Reliable documentation of the disability-related need is enough.
moves.react: "I just moved," {applicant} says. "I don't have one."

roleplays.debrief: Each firm sets its own fee (Sherman Act), and joint boycotts are illegal. Net listings are banned (19 NYCRR 175.19). Obedience never covers illegal orders: lawful source of income, familial status, and disability are protected, and in NYC the FARE Act puts the landlord's broker fee on the landlord. Give the landlord-tenant agency disclosure at first substantive contact (RPL 443) and document a refusal with a sworn declaration.

questions.q: Which kind of agent can give a client undivided loyalty?
c: A single agent
A dual agent
A designated sales agent
A transaction broker
questions.x: Undivided loyalty means one client and no competing client on the other side, which only a single agent offers. Designated agent is the trap: designated agents work within a dual agency, so the firm's loyalty is divided.

questions.q: Once a broker becomes a dual agent with the informed consent of both sides, what does each client give up?
c: The right to a written contract
Confidentiality of everything
The broker's undivided loyalty
The right to negotiate price
questions.x: Dual agents represent both sides, so neither gets undivided loyalty. Confidentiality is the trap: the dual agent must still keep each side's confidences.

questions.q: An agent's duty to safeguard and account for all money and documents belonging to the client or others is:
c: Obedience
Accountability
Disclosure
Reasonable care
questions.x: Accountability covers holding and accounting for other people's money and papers. Reasonable care is the trap: it is about competence, not handling funds.

questions.q: A broker deposits a buyer's earnest money in a proper escrow account and keeps records of it. Which fiduciary duty is this?
c: Loyalty
Obedience
Confidentiality
Accountability
questions.x: Safeguarding and accounting for funds is the duty of accountability. Loyalty is the trap: it is about putting the client's interests first, not about handling money.

questions.concept: Advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents
questions.q: A seller signs, at the listing, written consent to dual agency with designated sales agents and the form names her agent. This is:
c: An exclusive agency listing
A waiver of agency disclosure
Advance informed consent
Undisclosed dual agency
questions.x: New York's disclosure form lets a party consent in advance to dual agency with designated sales agents, naming the agent appointed to them. Waiver is the trap: consent does not waive disclosure; it is part of it.

questions.concept: Advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents
questions.q: For a designated sales agent arrangement to be valid in New York, each party must:
c: Give informed written consent
Use separate brokerage firms
Pay the agents directly
Waive all fiduciary duties
questions.x: Designated agency requires written informed consent, which can be given in advance on the state form. Separate firms is the trap: designated agents work within the same firm.

questions.q: Under an exclusive right to rent agreement, the broker is paid if the unit is leased during the term:
c: Only if the broker finds the tenant
Only if another broker finds the tenant
Only after the lease ends
No matter who finds the tenant
questions.x: Exclusive right to rent pays the broker whoever finds the tenant. 'Only if the broker finds the tenant' is the trap: that describes an exclusive agency arrangement.

questions.q: A landlord signs an exclusive right to rent with Broker A, then rents the apartment to his own cousin. Broker A:
c: Is owed nothing
Is still owed the commission
Is owed half the commission
Must refund the deposit
questions.x: Exclusive right to rent earns the fee even if the owner finds the tenant. 'Owed nothing' is the trap: that is how an exclusive agency or open listing would work.

questions.q: In an agency relationship, the party who hires the broker and is represented by the broker is the:
c: Principal
Customer
Subagent
Third party
questions.x: The principal (client) authorizes the agent to act for them and is owed fiduciary duties. The trap is customer: a customer deals with the agent but is not represented.

questions.q: Which duty requires an agent to keep a client's bargaining position private, even after the transaction closes?
c: Reasonable skill and care
Accounting
Confidentiality
Full disclosure
questions.x: Confidentiality protects the client's private information and survives the end of the agency. Disclosure is the tempting pick, but it runs the other way: the agent tells the client facts, not the reverse.

questions.q: A seller's agent owes a buyer customer:
c: Loyalty and advice on how much to offer
Honesty and disclosure of known defects
Confidentiality about the buyer's finances
Obedience to the buyer's lawful instructions
questions.x: Customers get honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material defects. Confidentiality, loyalty, and obedience are fiduciary duties owed to the client, which is the trap in the confidentiality choice.

questions.q: A seller tells her listing agent to present every offer. The agent withholds a low offer because he expects better ones. Which duty did the agent most directly breach?
c: Accounting
Confidentiality
Reasonable care
Obedience
questions.x: Ignoring a client's lawful instruction to present all offers breaches obedience. Reasonable care is tempting, but the core wrong here is disregarding a direct, lawful instruction, not careless work.

questions.q: A listing agent deposits a buyer's $25,000 good faith deposit into the brokerage's operating account to cover rent until month-end. Which duty is most directly violated?
c: Obedience
Disclosure
Loyalty to the seller
Accounting
questions.x: Accounting requires safeguarding other people's money in a proper escrow account and forbids commingling it with the firm's funds. Loyalty is tempting, but the specific wrong is mishandling money.

questions.q: A listing agent quietly has his brother-in-law buy the listing below market, planning to resell it later. This is:
c: Self-dealing
Agency by estoppel
Ratification
Estoppel
questions.x: Buying a client's property directly or through a relative without full written disclosure is self-dealing, a breach of loyalty. Ratification is the trap: it describes a principal approving an act after the fact, not an agent's conflict.

questions.q: A property manager who handles leasing, rent collection, and repairs for an owner's building under an ongoing agreement is usually a:
c: Special agent
Universal agent
General agent
Subagent
questions.x: A general agent handles a range of matters in one line of business on an ongoing basis. Special agent is the trap: a listing broker hired for one sale is a special agent.

questions.q: A listing broker, as a special agent, ordinarily has authority to:
c: Sign the contract of sale for the seller
Market the property and present offers
Accept an offer at the full asking price
Sign the deed for the seller at closing
questions.x: A special agent's authority is limited to the task, here finding a buyer. Accepting a full-price offer is tempting, but binding the seller to a contract requires separate written authority such as a power of attorney.

questions.q: A person granted a broad power of attorney to handle every aspect of another's affairs is a:
c: General agent
Universal agent
Special agent
Designated agent
questions.x: A universal agent may do anything the principal could legally delegate. General agent is the trap: its authority covers one line of business, such as managing a building.

questions.q: An agent tells buyers, "This is the best view in Brooklyn Heights." The buyers later find a building on the next block with a better view. The statement was:
c: Negligent misrepresentation
Fraud
Breach of disclosure
Puffing
questions.x: Opinion and exaggerated sales talk is puffing and is not actionable. Negligent misrepresentation is the trap: it requires a false statement of checkable material fact, not an opinion about a view.

questions.q: An agent tells a buyer the boiler is two years old, relying on the seller's word without checking. It is actually 25 years old. This is best described as:
c: Negligent misrepresentation
Puffing
Lawful nondisclosure
Fraudulent misrepresentation
questions.x: A false statement of fact the agent should have verified is negligent misrepresentation. Fraudulent misrepresentation is the trap: fraud requires knowing the statement is false, and this agent was careless, not knowing.

questions.q: A buyer purchases after a salesperson knowingly says the basement does not flood. It floods every spring. Which remedy is LEAST likely to be available to the buyer?
c: Rescission of the contract
DOS discipline of the salesperson
Prosecution of the buyer's attorney
Money damages paid by the salesperson personally
questions.x: Fraud can support rescission, damages, and license discipline. The buyer's attorney did nothing wrong. DOS discipline may look unlikely because the buyer is not the client, but licensees answer to DOS for dishonesty toward anyone.

questions.q: Vicarious liability means:
c: One party is liable for another's acts
An agent is liable for its own fraud or negligence
A broker's liability ends at closing
Liability requires a written contract
questions.x: Vicarious liability makes one person answer for another's acts, such as a principal for its agent acting within the scope of the agency. The trap is liability for one's own fraud: that is direct liability, not vicarious.

questions.q: All of the following are fiduciary duties an agent owes a client EXCEPT:
c: Obedience to lawful instructions
Loyalty
Guaranteeing the sale price
Reasonable care
questions.x: OLD CAR: obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, reasonable care. No agent guarantees a price. Reasonable care can sound like a mere courtesy, but it is one of the six duties.

questions.q: A seller asks his listing agent to do each of the following. The agent may lawfully follow each instruction EXCEPT:
c: Limit showings to weekend afternoons
Avoid showing to families with children
Keep his reason for selling confidential
Require pre-approval letters with offers
questions.x: Obedience covers lawful instructions. Excluding families with children is familial status discrimination. Requiring pre-approval may feel exclusionary, but it is a lawful condition if applied to every buyer.

questions.q: A buyer asks a seller's agent whether anyone died in the house. A prior owner died there of natural causes. Under NY law, the agent:
c: Has a duty to disclose it in writing before contract
Should deny it to protect the seller
Has to stop showing the property
May answer truthfully if the seller permits
questions.x: RPL 443-a says a death on the property is not a material defect requiring disclosure, but the agent may not lie, and may answer with the seller's permission. The trap is a written disclosure duty, which the statute removes.

questions.q: The duty of disclosure requires a listing agent to tell the seller:
c: Facts that support the seller's asking price
Whatever information the buyer authorizes it to share
Facts about the property but not the buyer
Any material fact, including a buyer's top price
questions.x: A client is owed every material fact the agent learns, and a buyer's willingness to pay more is material to the seller. Limiting disclosure to what the buyer authorizes is the trap: the agent's duty runs to the seller, not the buyer.

questions.q: A listing agent learns the buyer customer is the agent's cousin and does not tell the seller. The seller accepts the cousin's low offer. The agent most likely breached:
c: Disclosure and loyalty
Accounting and obedience
Obedience and reasonable care
No duty, since the cousin is a customer
questions.x: A relationship with the buyer is a material fact the client needed to know; hiding it creates a conflict that breaches disclosure and loyalty. The customer defense fails because the duty runs to the seller.

questions.q: Who is the agent in a listing agreement?
c: The salesperson, personally
The seller's attorney
The brokerage
The listing service
questions.x: The agency runs to the broker; salespersons act for the broker, which is why the listing stays with the firm if the salesperson leaves. The salesperson is the trap because that is the person the seller meets.

questions.q: The term "fiduciary" best describes:
c: Any person who holds or handles another person's money
A person in a position of trust who puts the client first
Any party who signs a contract to buy or sell real property
A licensee who has passed the state exam and holds a license
questions.x: A fiduciary relationship is one of special trust and confidence. Handling money is the trap: it is one part of the relationship (accounting), not its definition.

questions.q: Agency created by a written listing agreement is:
c: Implied agency
Express agency
Agency by estoppel
Agency by ratification
questions.x: A written or spoken agreement that states the relationship creates express agency. Implied agency is the trap: it arises from conduct, not from words of agreement.

questions.q: A salesperson never signs anything with a buyer but repeatedly advises her on what to offer and how to negotiate the seller down. A court could find:
c: Agency by ratification
Agency coupled with an interest
Express agency with the buyer
Implied agency with the buyer
questions.x: Conduct that looks like representation can create implied agency. Express agency is the trap: it requires a stated agreement, which never happened. If the salesperson also represents the seller, this is undisclosed dual agency.

questions.q: An agent without authority negotiates a sale. The owner learns of it and signs the contract, accepting the benefit. The agency was created by:
c: Ratification
Estoppel
Express agreement
Implied conduct
questions.x: Approving an unauthorized act after the fact is ratification. Estoppel is the trap: it requires the principal's earlier conduct to have created the appearance of authority.

questions.q: For months an owner lets his nephew show his Ridgewood apartments, quote rents, and collect applications. A tenant relies on the nephew's promises. The owner cannot now deny the nephew's authority because of:
c: Ratification
Express agency
Estoppel
Necessity
questions.x: When a principal's conduct leads a third party to reasonably believe someone is its agent, the principal is estopped from denying it. Ratification is the trap: it means approving a specific act after it happens.

questions.q: In New York, the amount of a real estate commission is set by:
c: Negotiation between broker and client
The Department of State, by regulation
The local REALTOR board's rate schedule
State law, at 6% of the sale price
questions.x: Commissions are negotiable between the broker and the client. A board schedule is the trap: any rate set by a board or by agreement among competitors would be price fixing.

questions.q: Which listing arrangement is prohibited in New York?
c: Open listing
Exclusive agency
Net listing
Exclusive right to sell
questions.x: 19 NYCRR 175.19 bans net listings, where the broker keeps everything above the seller's figure. Open listings may seem too loose to be legal, but they are lawful.

questions.q: Five brokers agree to charge no less than 5% on every sale. This is:
c: Market allocation
Price fixing
A tie-in arrangement
Lawful if disclosed to sellers
questions.x: Competitors agreeing on rates is price fixing, illegal per se under the Sherman Act. Disclosure to sellers is the trap: it does not cure an illegal agreement.

questions.q: Several Queens brokerages agree not to show listings of a new discount brokerage. This is:
c: Price fixing
Market allocation
Lawful competition
A group boycott
questions.x: Competitors agreeing to shut out another competitor is a group boycott. Lawful competition is the trap: each firm may decide alone whom to work with, but not by agreement with rivals.

questions.q: Two brokers agree that one will serve buyers above $2 million and the other buyers below. This is:
c: Group boycott
Tie-in arrangement
Price fixing
Market allocation
questions.x: Dividing customers by price range, like dividing territory, is market allocation. Price fixing is the trap because a dollar figure appears, but no rate or fee is being agreed.

questions.q: A broker tells an owner, "I'll handle your sale if you also hire my firm to manage your other building." This is:
c: A tie-in arrangement
Price fixing on management fees
Market allocation
A group boycott
questions.x: Conditioning one service on the purchase of another is a tie-in arrangement. Market allocation is the trap, but no competitors are dividing customers here.

questions.q: A licensed salesperson meets a homeowner at a barbecue and chats about the market. No agreement is signed. Which statement is correct?
c: The salesperson is the homeowner's agent because a license creates agency
The homeowner becomes a client once any pricing advice is given
No agency exists yet; the license permits agency, the agreement creates it
The salesperson's sponsoring broker becomes the homeowner's agent automatically
questions.x: A license lets you act as an agent; an agreement with a client (or conduct showing one) makes you one. The trap is thinking the license itself creates agency with anyone you talk to.

questions.q: Under RPL Article 12-A, who may negotiate the sale of someone else's house for a fee in New York?
c: Any adult holding the owner's written permission
A licensed broker or a salesperson it sponsors
Only an attorney admitted to practice in New York
A salesperson with a license, whether sponsored or not
questions.x: Only a licensed broker, or a salesperson sponsored by a broker, may list, sell, rent or negotiate for others for a fee. An unsponsored salesperson license is inactive, so it does not qualify.

questions.q: A buyer's agent will be paid from the seller's sale proceeds at closing. Whom does the buyer's agent represent?
c: The seller, since the seller pays the commission
Both parties equally, since money flows to each
Neither party until the commission is actually paid
The buyer, who owed nothing toward the commission
questions.x: Agency follows the agreement, not the money. A buyer's agent paid from the seller's proceeds still owes every fiduciary duty to the buyer. The trap is 'whoever pays is the client.'

questions.q: Which factor decides whom a real estate agent represents?
c: The agency agreement, or conduct creating one
Which party pays the brokerage commission at closing
Which party first called the brokerage
Which party's name appears on the purchase contract
questions.x: Representation comes from the agency agreement (or conduct that creates one). Payment of the commission does not decide it, which is the most common wrong answer on this topic.

questions.q: An agent prices a two-family house using only single-family sales and the house sits unsold for months. Which duty did the agent most likely breach?
c: Obedience
Confidentiality and loyalty
Reasonable care
Accounting
questions.x: Reasonable care requires competence, skill and diligence, such as choosing proper comparables. Obedience is tempting, but the client gave no instruction that was ignored.

questions.q: The fiduciary duty of reasonable care requires an agent to:
c: Follow every instruction the client gives
Act with competence, skill and diligence
Keep the client's motives fully private
Hold client money in a separate account
questions.x: Reasonable care is about competence and diligence. Following instructions is obedience, privacy is confidentiality, and separate accounts are accounting.

questions.q: After a sale closes, which fiduciary duties does the listing agent still owe the former client?
c: Loyalty and obedience, for one year after closing
All six duties, until the deed has been recorded
No duties at all, since the agency has ended
Confidentiality, and accounting for funds held
questions.x: Agency duties end with the agency, but confidentiality lasts forever and the duty to account continues for any money still in the agent's hands. 'No duties at all' is the trap.

questions.q: Fiduciary duties to a seller usually begin when:
c: The listing or buyer agreement is signed
The first buyer makes a written offer on the property
The contract of sale is signed by both parties
The seller pays the commission at the closing
questions.x: Duties attach when the agency is created, usually at the signing of the listing or buyer agreement, though conduct can create it earlier. The offer, contract and payment all come later.

questions.q: A salesperson misleads a buyer about a leak. The seller complains to DOS. Why can the sponsoring broker also be disciplined?
c: Because the broker signed the purchase contract too
Because the salesperson acted as the buyer's agent
Because the broker must supervise its salespersons
Because the seller paid the broker the commission
questions.x: Salespersons are general agents of their broker, and the broker answers for what they do; DOS can discipline a broker for failing to supervise. The commission answer is tempting but irrelevant.

questions.q: In relation to their sponsoring broker, salespersons are best described as:
c: Special agents, separately for each listing
General agents of the broker's business
Universal agents with power of attorney
Independent principals of their own clients
questions.x: Salespersons act for the broker across its whole business, which makes them general agents of the broker. Special agent describes the broker's relationship to a single client.

questions.q: A listing agent learns the buyer's mortgage commitment was withdrawn but forgets to tell the sellers. Legally, the sellers are:
c: Treated as knowing whatever the agent knew
Not responsible until they are told in writing
Free to cancel the listing without giving notice
Owed the commission back by the brokerage
questions.x: Under imputed knowledge, what the agent knows the principal is treated as knowing. That is why prompt disclosure to the client matters: silence leaves the principal exposed.

questions.q: The rule that a principal is legally charged with what its agent knows is called:
c: Vicarious liability
Imputed knowledge
Constructive notice
Undivided loyalty
questions.x: Imputed knowledge charges the principal with the agent's knowledge. Vicarious liability is the neighbor concept: liability for another's acts, not their knowledge.

questions.q: Under the 2024 NAR settlement rules, before an MLS participant tours a home with a buyer, the agent must have:
c: A preapproval letter from the buyer's lender
A written agreement signed with the buyer
A signed agency disclosure from seller
A cooperating fee offer posted on the MLS
questions.x: The settlement requires a written buyer agreement before touring. The disclosure form is still required in NY, but it is not the agreement; and fee offers can no longer appear on the MLS.

questions.q: Which way of creating agency is the safest for a broker to rely on?
c: Implied agency shown by the parties' conduct
Ratification of the broker's acts afterward
An express agreement put in writing
Estoppel based on the principal's conduct
questions.x: Express written agreements are the safe way, and exclusive agreements should always be written. Implied agency is the danger zone, and ratification and estoppel come only after a problem.

questions.q: A walk-in asks a salesperson for help buying. What should the salesperson do before discussing price or the buyer's motivation?
c: Ask how much the buyer can spend in total
Show the firm's own listings to the buyer before others
Explain the commission the seller will pay
Say whom the firm represents, with the form
questions.x: Know your role and say it first, using the firm's agency policy, any signed agreement and the facts, then hand over the disclosure form. Asking about money first invites confidential information you may not be able to protect.

questions.q: Which source does NOT help an agent decide whom they represent in a new contact?
c: Which party has the higher budget
The firm's written agency policy
Any agreement already signed
Whether the agent holds the listing
questions.x: Representation comes from the firm's policy, signed agreements and the facts of the role. A party's budget has nothing to do with whom you represent.

questions.q: After the 2024 NAR settlement, an offer of compensation to a buyer's broker:
c: Must be posted on the MLS for every listing
Is now banned in any form nationwide
Negotiable, but not shown on the MLS
Is set by the local board for all members
questions.x: Cooperating commission offers can no longer appear on the MLS, but brokers may still negotiate them off the MLS, and buyers may negotiate their own broker's fee. They were not banned outright.

questions.q: A seller asks whether the listing broker's offer to pay a buyer's broker is a fixed requirement. The best answer is that it is:
c: Required by law at half the commission
Fixed by the MLS for each price range
An offer, negotiated off the MLS now
Owed only when the buyer has no agent at all
questions.x: Cooperating commissions are offers, not requirements, and since 2024 they are negotiated off the MLS. Nothing in law or the MLS fixes the amount.

questions.q: Under the Sherman Antitrust Act, an individual broker convicted of price fixing faces up to:
c: 1 year in prison and a $10,000 fine, at most
3 years in prison and a $100,000 fine
5 years in prison and a $500,000 fine
10 years in prison and a $1 million fine
questions.x: Individuals face up to 10 years and $1 million; corporations up to $100 million, plus civil suits for triple damages. The smaller numbers mix up older or state-level penalties.

questions.q: Besides criminal penalties, victims of a brokers' price-fixing conspiracy may sue for:
c: Triple their actual damages
Only their actual damages
Double damages, capped at $1 million
Return of the commission only
questions.x: Antitrust civil suits allow triple (treble) damages, on top of criminal fines and prison. Limiting recovery to actual damages or the commission understates the exposure.

questions.q: A buyer who has signed a buyer agreement with Hudson & Hart wants to see a Hudson & Hart listing. Before going further the firm needs:
c: Nothing, since both sides are firm clients
A cooperating fee offer from the seller
A new listing agreement with the seller
Written informed consent to dual agency
questions.x: Representing both the buyer and the seller in one deal makes the firm a dual agent, which requires written informed consent from both. Having both as clients is the problem, not the solution.

questions.q: An unrepresented buyer calls about a firm's listing, and the firm practices seller agency only. The buyer is:
c: A customer, owed honesty, not advice
A client, owed every fiduciary duty
A dual agency principal after consent
A subagency client of the listing firm
questions.x: If the firm stays the seller's agent, the in-house buyer is a customer: honesty and disclosure of known defects, but no advice. Treating the buyer as a client would create dual agency.

questions.q: A buyer's agent from another firm calls the listing agent about a listing. Which step is the listing agent's job?
c: Share why the sellers are moving
Advise the buyer's agent on a winning price
Confirm the agent's role, then disclose it
Wait for a written offer before giving any disclosure
questions.x: Confirm the other agent's role in writing and give the agency disclosure at first substantive contact. Sharing the sellers' motivation breaches confidentiality, and the disclosure cannot wait for an offer.

questions.q: In a cooperative sale, the listing agent receives an offer through the buyer's agent. The listing agent should:
c: Hold it until a better offer comes in
Route it to the seller client promptly
Counter it based on the buyer's budget
