Return it if it is below the asking price
questions.x: All offers go to the client. Holding or returning one breaches obedience and disclosure, and the listing agent does not decide which offers the seller sees.

questions.concept: Single agency inside a listing firm
questions.q: A firm lists homes and also represents buyers, but avoids dual agency. Which practice does that require?
c: Agents may share client notes at weekly meetings
The firm may show buyer clients its own listings freely
Buyer and listing agents never swap client information
Only the broker may speak with buyer clients
questions.x: Single agency inside a listing firm takes discipline: agents must not swap client information, and a written policy must say what happens when a buyer client wants an in-house listing.

questions.concept: Single agency inside a listing firm
questions.q: A firm's policy must address what happens when a buyer client wants one of the firm's own listings. Acceptable options include:
c: Decline, refer out, or seek dual consent
Charging the buyer a second, larger fee
Quietly treating the buyer as a customer instead
Having the listing agent advise the buyer
questions.x: The firm can decline, refer the buyer out, or seek informed dual agency consent, and the consumer must hear the policy before money is discussed. Quietly switching roles is undisclosed dual agency.

questions.q: Priya signs an exclusive agreement with a broker to find her a condo. In that relationship, Priya is the broker's:
c: Customer
Principal
Subagent
Third party
questions.x: Signing the agreement makes Priya the principal (client) who is owed fiduciary duties. Customer is the trap: that term describes someone the agent deals with but does not represent.

questions.q: Two years after closing, a former seller client's neighbor asks the listing agent what the lowest price was that the seller would have accepted. The agent should:
c: Share it, since the agency has ended
Decline to share the seller's price
Share it if the price is a public record
Share it if the neighbor is a client
questions.x: Confidentiality survives the end of the agency, so the seller's bottom line stays private. The trap is thinking duties end at closing: accounting and loyalty wind down, but confidentiality does not.

questions.q: A seller's agent owes a buyer customer each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Honest answers to questions
Disclosure of known defects
Fair dealing in the transaction
Advice on negotiating strategy
questions.x: Customers get honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material defects. Negotiating advice is a client service; giving it to the buyer could create implied agency. Fair dealing may sound like a fiduciary duty, but it is owed to everyone.

questions.q: A listing agent may refuse a seller client's instruction in each of these cases EXCEPT when the seller asks the agent to:
c: Hold showings on weekdays only
Conceal a known leak in the roof
Reject buyers who use Section 8
Misstate the home's square footage
questions.x: Obedience covers every lawful instruction, and limiting showings to weekdays is lawful. The Section 8 choice is the trap: lawful source of income is protected in NY, so that instruction is unlawful and may be refused.

questions.q: The duty of accounting requires an agent to:
c: Keep the client's motives confidential
Follow the client's lawful instructions
Safeguard and account for others' money
Present every offer to the client promptly
questions.x: Accounting covers money and documents: escrow deposits, no commingling, and reporting on funds. Presenting offers is the trap: that falls under obedience and disclosure.

questions.q: A listing agent may lawfully buy the seller client's property if the agent:
c: Fully discloses the interest in writing
Pays the full listed price for the property
Buys it through a relative or an LLC
Waives the commission on the purchase
questions.x: An agent may buy a client's property only after full written disclosure of the agent's interest. Paying full price is the trap: it does not cure undisclosed self-dealing, and buying through a relative is the same conflict in disguise.

questions.q: Which relationship best illustrates a general agent?
c: A broker hired to sell one condo
A buyer's agent for one purchase
A manager running an owner's building
An agent holding a full power of attorney
questions.x: A general agent handles a range of matters in one line of business over time, like managing a building. A full power of attorney is the trap: that broader authority makes a universal agent.

questions.q: A seller is traveling. The listing agent receives a full-price offer with no contingencies. Without a power of attorney, the agent may:
c: Accept it for the seller
Present it to the seller
Sign the contract of sale
Countersign as the seller
questions.x: A special agent finds buyers and presents offers; binding the seller to a contract needs separate written authority. Accepting a full-price offer is the trap: matching the asking price does not give the agent power to bind the seller.

questions.q: Which agent has the broadest scope of authority?
c: A general agent
A special agent
A designated agent
A universal agent
questions.x: A universal agent may do anything the principal could legally delegate, typically under a broad power of attorney. A general agent is the trap: it acts in one line of business only.

questions.q: Each of the following statements is puffing EXCEPT:
c: "This kitchen is simply stunning."
"It's the best block in Astoria."
"You'll love the morning light."
"The roof was replaced in 2022."
questions.x: Puffing is opinion or sales talk. A roof replacement date is a checkable fact, so a false one is misrepresentation. "Best block" sounds factual but is still an opinion.

questions.q: A listing agent repeats a seller's claim that the house has a new septic system without checking records. The system is 30 years old. The agent's best defense would have been to:
c: Verify the claim before repeating it
Call the claim an opinion when sued
Say it orally rather than in writing
Rely on the buyer's own home inspection
questions.x: Repeating an unverified factual claim the agent could have checked is negligent misrepresentation. Calling it opinion is the trap: a system's age is a fact, not puffing.

questions.q: A salesperson knowingly lies about a material defect and the buyer relies on it. Which set of consequences can follow?
c: License discipline by DOS, but no civil remedies
Damages, but from the seller client alone
Rescission, damages, and license discipline
Rescission, but no license consequences
questions.x: Fraud can support rescission, money damages against the licensee, and DOS discipline. The seller-only choice is the trap: the licensee is personally liable for their own fraud.

questions.q: A salesperson makes a false statement to a buyer while handling a firm listing. Besides the salesperson, who is most exposed to liability for it?
c: The buyer's lender
The sponsoring broker
The home inspector
The buyer's title insurer
questions.x: Vicarious liability makes the broker answer for a salesperson acting within the scope of the agency, and the seller may be exposed too. The lender is the trap: it had no role in the statement.

questions.q: Which list matches the OLD CAR fiduciary duties?
c: Obedience, loyalty, diligence, candor, appraisal, and compliance
Obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, care
Openness, loyalty, disclosure, consent, accounting, courtesy
Obedience, legality, disclosure, contract, advocacy, recordkeeping
questions.x: OLD CAR is obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, and reasonable care. The openness list is the trap: it swaps in words that sound similar but are not the six duties.

questions.q: A seller tells his agent not to accept offers from buyers using housing vouchers. The agent should:
c: Follow it, since obedience applies
Follow it, if the seller puts it in writing
Follow it, for this listing alone
Explain it is unlawful and decline
questions.x: Obedience covers lawful instructions. Refusing voucher holders is source-of-income discrimination under NY law, so the agent must decline. A signed instruction is the trap: putting it in writing does not make it lawful.

questions.q: Under RPL 443-a, a seller has no duty to disclose each of the following EXCEPT:
c: A cracked foundation
A suicide in the home
A prior owner's HIV status
A homicide on the property
questions.x: RPL 443-a covers psychological stigma: deaths, homicides, suicides, and an occupant's HIV/AIDS or other non-transmittable condition. A cracked foundation is a physical defect, which is the real material fact here.

questions.q: A buyer customer tells the listing agent, "I'd go to $900,000 if I have to," after offering $850,000. The listing agent should:
c: Keep it from the seller
Share it if the buyer agrees
Share it with the seller
Share it after the closing
questions.x: A listing agent owes the seller disclosure of every material fact, including a buyer's willingness to pay more. Asking the buyer's permission is the trap: the buyer is a customer, and confidentiality runs to the seller, not the buyer.

questions.q: A listing agent's spouse wants to make an offer on the agent's listing. The agent should first:
c: Disclose the relationship to the seller
Withdraw from the listing at once
Refer the spouse to an agent at another firm
Reduce the commission charged on the sale
questions.x: A personal relationship with the buyer is a material fact the client must know, so disclosure comes first. Referring the spouse elsewhere is the trap: it does not remove the agent's conflict or the duty to tell the seller.

questions.q: A seller's listing salesperson goes on leave for three months. The seller's agency relationship:
c: Ends until the salesperson returns
Shifts to the seller's attorney
Continues with the brokerage
Converts to an open listing
questions.x: The agency belongs to the broker, so another licensee in the firm can serve the seller. Ending it is the trap: the salesperson was never the principal party to the listing.

questions.q: Each of the following describes a fiduciary relationship EXCEPT:
c: A broker acting for a listing client
A seller dealing with a buyer customer
A trustee managing a family trust's assets
A buyer's agent acting for its client
questions.x: A fiduciary relationship is one of special trust in which one party acts for another. A seller and a buyer customer deal at arm's length. The trustee choice is the trap: trustees are classic fiduciaries outside real estate too.

questions.q: A buyer and a broker shake hands after the buyer says, "I want you to represent me in finding a co-op." The agency created is:
c: Implied agency
Agency by estoppel
No agency yet
Express agency
questions.x: Express agency may be created by spoken words that state the relationship. No agency yet is the trap: a writing helps prove it, but an oral agreement still creates express agency.

questions.q: Each of the following could create implied agency with a buyer EXCEPT:
c: Advising the buyer on what to offer
Coaching the buyer on negotiation tactics
Revealing the seller's bottom price
Answering questions about the lot size
questions.x: Implied agency arises from conduct that looks like representation, such as advising or coaching. Answering factual questions is ordinary customer service. Revealing the seller's price is the trap: it is also a breach of confidentiality.

questions.q: Ratification creates agency when a principal:
c: Approves an unauthorized act afterward
Signs a listing agreement beforehand
Lets someone appear to be its agent
Lets the agent act for it over a long period
questions.x: Ratification is after-the-fact approval of an act done without authority. Letting someone appear to be the agent is the trap: that describes estoppel.

questions.q: Which fact pattern best shows agency by estoppel?
c: An owner signs a listing with a broker
An owner later approves a deal by a friend
An owner lets a friend act as agent
A broker advises a buyer on an offer
questions.x: Estoppel arises when the principal's conduct leads a third party to reasonably believe someone is its agent. Later approval of a deal is the trap: that is ratification.

questions.q: A seller says, "I heard the law sets commissions at 6% in New York." The agent should explain that:
c: The rate is set by DOS
The rate is negotiable
The rate is set by the MLS
The rate is set by statute
questions.x: No law, regulator, or MLS sets commission rates; they are negotiated between broker and client. DOS is the trap: it licenses and disciplines brokers but does not set fees.

questions.q: A seller says, "Get me $700,000 and keep anything above that as your fee." In New York, the broker should:
c: Accept it if put in writing
Decline the net arrangement
Accept it if the MLS allows
Accept it with the fee capped at 6%
questions.x: 19 NYCRR 175.19 bans net listings because they put the broker's interest against the seller's. Getting it in writing is the trap: a written net listing is still prohibited.

questions.q: Each of the following could support a price fixing claim EXCEPT:
c: Rivals agreeing on a minimum fee
Rivals sharing a common fee schedule
Rivals agreeing to raise fees together
A firm setting its rates on its own
questions.x: Price fixing requires an agreement among competitors. A firm setting its own rates independently is lawful. A shared fee schedule is the trap: circulating rates among rivals is evidence of an agreement.

questions.q: A group boycott occurs when competitors:
c: Agree to refuse to deal with another firm
Agree to charge the same commission rate
Agree to divide up customers by territory
Agree to tie one service to the purchase of another
questions.x: A group boycott is an agreement to shut out a competitor or supplier. Agreeing on the same rate is the trap: that is price fixing, a different violation.

questions.q: Three Westchester brokers agree that each will take listings in only one town. This is:
c: A group boycott
Price fixing
Market allocation
A tie-in arrangement
questions.x: Dividing territory among competitors is market allocation. Group boycott is the trap: no firm is being shut out, the competitors are splitting the market.

questions.q: A tie-in arrangement is an agreement to:
c: Condition one service on buying another
Divide customers among competing firms
Refuse, with rivals, to cooperate with a firm
Set commission rates with competitors
questions.x: A tie-in conditions one product or service on the purchase of another. Dividing customers is the trap: that is market allocation.

questions.q: The federal law most directly prohibiting price fixing among real estate brokers is the:
c: Fair Housing Act
Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
Sherman Antitrust Act
Truth in Lending Act
questions.x: The Sherman Act of 1890 outlaws agreements in restraint of trade, including price fixing. RESPA is the trap: it targets kickbacks in settlement services, not rate agreements.

questions.q: All of the following are antitrust violations EXCEPT:
c: Brokers agreeing to split Brooklyn by area
A broker deciding alone to charge 4%
Brokers agreeing to shun a flat-fee firm
Brokers agreeing on a minimum commission
questions.x: A single firm setting its own price independently is lawful; antitrust violations require an agreement among competitors. Dividing neighborhoods may sound harmless, but it is market allocation.

questions.q: To sue for a commission in New York, a person needs to:
c: Hold a salesperson license and have found the buyer personally
Have been a licensed broker when the services were performed
Hold a seller's oral promise to pay and a licensed associate
Hold active membership in the multiple listing service
questions.x: RPL 442-d lets a licensed broker sue for a commission if licensed when the services were rendered. The salesperson choice is the trap: salespersons collect from their own sponsoring broker, not from the client.

questions.q: A commission is traditionally earned when the broker:
c: Enters the property in the listing service
Receives the buyer's good faith deposit
Holds the first open house for the property
Produces a ready, willing, and able buyer
questions.x: Producing a ready, willing, and able buyer on the seller's terms is the traditional trigger, though the listing may make payment depend on closing. Receiving the deposit is the trap: it is a step in the deal, not the legal trigger.

questions.q: Under an open listing, two brokers showed the same buyer the property. The buyer bought after the second broker's showing and negotiation. Who is entitled to the commission?
c: The procuring cause of the sale
The first broker to show it
Both brokers, split equally
Neither broker, on an open listing
questions.x: Under an open listing, the broker whose efforts started the unbroken chain leading to the sale gets paid. Showing first is the trap: it is not decisive by itself.

questions.q: A building superintendent introduces a buyer to a listing broker. The buyer purchases. The broker wants to thank the super with $1,000 from the commission. The broker:
c: May pay it if the seller consents in writing
May pay it as a gift rather than a fee
May not pay the super from the fee
May pay it if the amount is under $1,500
questions.x: Paying any part of a commission to an unlicensed person for bringing a buyer is prohibited in NY. Seller consent is the trap: no consent makes the payment lawful.

questions.q: Which statement about who pays the commission is correct?
c: The payer is not necessarily the client
The party who pays the fee is the client
A buyer's agent is paid by the buyer
A seller's agent is paid by the seller
questions.x: Agency is created by agreement and conduct, not by the source of payment. The trap is that the payer is the client: a buyer's agent is often paid from the seller's proceeds.

questions.q: Antitrust violations such as price fixing are called per se illegal, which means:
c: They are legal if prices are reasonable
Proof of harm to a consumer is required
No justification is a defense
They are governed by state law alone
questions.x: Per se illegal conduct is unlawful in itself; courts do not weigh reasons or benefits. The reasonable-price defense is the trap: it is exactly what per se treatment refuses to consider.

questions.q: At a networking event, competitors begin discussing a plan to raise commissions together. The best action for a licensee is to:
c: Stay quiet and listen without commenting on it
Object, refuse to take part, and leave
Agree, then quietly not follow through
Agree, then report it to the local MLS
questions.x: Silent presence while competitors agree can be treated as participation. Staying quiet is the trap: it can look like assent. Objecting and leaving is the safe course.

questions.q: Apparent or ostensible agency is another name for agency by:
c: Ratification
Express agreement
Necessity
Estoppel
questions.x: Estoppel arises when a principal's conduct creates the appearance of authority that a third party relies on. Ratification is the trap: it is approval after the act, not an appearance created beforehand.

questions.q: When a brokerage takes a listing, which licensees in the firm owe fiduciary duties to the seller?
c: The listing salesperson and no one else
The broker, but not the salespersons
No one, until a contract of sale is signed
The broker and every affiliated licensee
questions.x: The agency belongs to the brokerage, so every licensee in the firm owes duties to the client. That is why an in-house buyer client creates dual agency. The listing salesperson choice is the trap.

questions.q: A subagent in a sales transaction owes fiduciary duties to:
c: The seller, through the listing broker
The buyer the subagent is working with
Both the buyer and the seller equally
The cooperating broker's own firm alone
questions.x: A subagent is the agent of the listing broker and therefore of the seller. The buyer is the trap: the subagent works with the buyer, but the buyer is a customer.

questions.q: Under RPL 443, a broker's agent:
c: Works for the same firm as the listing agent and takes instructions from the seller directly
Has a direct relationship with the seller, who may give it instructions
Is engaged by another firm's agent, and the client is not vicariously liable for it
Represents the buyer and seller together with their informed written consent
questions.x: A broker's agent comes from a different firm, takes direction from the agent who engaged it, and the client is not vicariously liable for its acts. The direct-relationship choice is the trap: the client cannot instruct a broker's agent.

questions.q: A subagent misrepresents the age of a roof to a buyer. Which party is most likely to face vicarious liability along with the listing broker?
c: The buyer's lender
The seller
The buyer's agent
The home inspector
questions.x: Because a subagent is the seller's agent through the listing broker, the seller can be vicariously liable. That risk is why sellers avoid subagency. The buyer's agent is the trap: it did not make the statement and represents the other side.

questions.q: Subagency is created by:
c: The cooperating broker acting on its own initiative
The listing broker, with the seller's authorization
The buyer, by signing a buyer agency agreement
The Department of State, through the RPL 443 form
questions.x: The listing broker extends subagency, but only if the seller authorized it in the listing agreement. The cooperating broker is the trap: it can accept or reject an offer of subagency, but cannot create one alone.

questions.q: The "blanket unilateral offer of subagency" refers to:
c: A buyer agency agreement that covers any listed property
A standing offer of dual agency made to every party in the deal
A broker's agent agreement filed with the listing service
An old MLS practice that made cooperating brokers subagents
questions.x: Under the old MLS model, listings carried an automatic offer of subagency to any member who brought a buyer. It is now optional and rarely used. The dual agency choice is the trap: the offer concerned the seller's side only.

questions.q: A cooperating broker does not want to be the seller's subagent. The broker may:
c: Reject subagency and act as the buyer's agent
Stay out of the sale, since cooperation means subagency
Accept subagency anyway, since it attaches automatically
Represent both sides without seeking anyone's consent
questions.x: A cooperating broker may reject subagency and work as a buyer's agent or a broker's agent. The automatic-subagency choice is the trap: that reflects the old MLS model, not current practice.

questions.q: An agent who represents one side of a transaction, either the seller or the buyer but not both, is practicing:
c: Dual agency
Subagency
Single agency
Designated agency
questions.x: Single agency means representing one side, allowing full advice and undivided loyalty. Designated agency is the trap: it arises when the firm represents both sides and assigns separate agents.

questions.q: Leo hires a buyer's agent. The listing broker pays the buyer's agent out of the seller's commission. The buyer's agent owes loyalty to:
c: Leo, the buyer
The seller client
The listing broker
Leo and the seller
questions.x: The buyer agreement creates the agency, and the payment source does not shift loyalty. The seller is the trap because the money comes from the seller's proceeds.

questions.q: A buyer's agent may do each of the following for a buyer client EXCEPT:
c: Keep the buyer's top budget confidential
Advise the buyer on what price to offer
Hide a known defect from the seller's side
Recommend asking the seller for repairs
questions.x: Agents owe honesty to everyone. Advising and keeping confidences are proper for a client, but deceiving the other side is not. Keeping the budget secret may seem like concealment, but it is the duty of confidentiality.

questions.q: An agent hired by an owner to find tenants for an apartment is a:
c: Tenant's agent
Landlord's agent
Broker's agent
Buyer's agent
questions.x: An agent representing the owner in leasing is the landlord's agent. Broker's agent is the trap: that is an outside firm engaged by another agent, not the owner's direct agent.

questions.q: Under the NYC FARE Act, a landlord lists an apartment with a broker. Who pays that broker's fee?
c: The tenant
Split evenly
Whoever signs first
The landlord
questions.x: Since June 11, 2025, a broker hired by the landlord is paid by the landlord in NYC. A tenant pays a broker only if the tenant hires that broker. The tenant choice is the trap because it was the old NYC custom.

questions.q: A buyer working with a seller's agent, without a buyer agreement, is the agent's:
c: Principal
Client
Subagent
Customer
questions.x: Someone the agent deals with but does not represent is a customer, owed honesty but not loyalty. Client is the trap: the client is the seller who signed the listing.

questions.q: A listing salesperson leaves her brokerage for a competitor. The seller's exclusive listing:
c: Stays with the original brokerage
Moves with the salesperson
Ends when the salesperson leaves the firm
Becomes an open listing
questions.x: The listing contract is with the broker, not the salesperson, so the firm keeps it unless the seller and broker agree otherwise. Moving with the salesperson is the trap because the seller knows the salesperson personally.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the difference between brokerage and agency?
c: Brokerage covers sales; agency covers leasing and rental transactions
Brokerage is the relationship; agency is the licensed business
Brokerage is the business; agency is the fiduciary relationship
Brokerage needs a license; agency needs a written contract
questions.x: Brokerage is bringing parties together for a fee; agency is the legal relationship of trust. The reversed choice is the trap: it swaps the two definitions.

questions.q: A seller's listing broker engages a broker's agent from another firm. Each of the following is true EXCEPT:
c: The broker's agent assists the listing broker
The seller can instruct the broker's agent directly
The listing broker is liable for the broker's agent
The broker's agent owes duties to the seller
questions.x: Under RPL 443, the seller has no direct relationship with the broker's agent and cannot instruct it; the listing broker directs it. Liability is the trap: the listing broker, not the seller, answers for the broker's agent.

questions.q: A licensee from another firm who helps bring about a sale, in whatever capacity, is generally called a:
c: Designated sales agent
Cooperating agent
Universal agent
Escrow agent
questions.x: A cooperating agent (co-broker) is any outside licensee helping produce the deal, whether as buyer's agent, subagent, or broker's agent. Designated agent is the trap: designated agents work within the same firm.

questions.q: An agent working with tenants in Astoria has them sign a tenant agency agreement. The agent's fiduciary duties run to:
c: The landlord
Each party equally
No one, for rentals
The tenants
questions.x: A tenant's agent represents the tenant and owes the tenant full fiduciary duties. The landlord is the trap: owning the property does not make the landlord this agent's client.

questions.q: A seller wants wide exposure but no liability for what other firms' agents tell buyers. The listing broker should:
c: Work with buyer's agents and broker's agents, not subagents
Offer blanket subagency to every member of the MLS
Make each cooperating agent a dual agent with written consent
Refuse cooperation and market the listing in-house
questions.x: Subagency exposes the seller to vicarious liability. Buyer's agents represent buyers, and broker's agents leave liability with the listing broker. Blanket subagency is the trap: it maximizes exposure but also the seller's liability.

questions.q: A salesperson's relationship to the sponsoring broker is best described as:
c: A partner sharing equally in the firm
A principal who directs the broker's work
An agent of the broker, under supervision
An independent firm with no supervision
questions.x: The salesperson works under and on behalf of the broker, carrying out the broker's agency with clients. Independent contractor tax status is the trap behind the last choice: it does not remove the broker's duty to supervise.

questions.q: Jordan alone is working with both the seller and the buyer on an in-house sale, and both have signed dual agency consent. What should Jordan do?
c: Advise each side on price, since both consented in writing
Stop advising on price and stick to facts and paperwork
Name himself the buyer's designated agent going forward
Tell the seller the buyer's maximum, since the firm is dual
questions.x: One licensee holding both clients' secrets must stop giving price advice and stick to facts and paperwork. Consent makes the dual agency lawful but does not restore full advocacy, which is the trap in 'advise each side on price.'

questions.q: Why do many New York firms ban single licensee dual agency and use designated agents or a referral instead?
c: One agent would hold both sides' secrets and advise neither
The law forbids one salesperson working with two parties
DOS requires a separate license for each side of a deal
Designated agents let the broker drop its dual agent role
questions.x: Single licensee dual agency is legal with written consent, but one person holds both clients' secrets and can advise neither against the other, so many firms ban it. It is not forbidden by law, and designated agents never end the broker's dual role.

questions.q: Why should a New York brokerage put its agency policy in writing and train every licensee on it?
c: DOS must approve each firm's policy before it may list property
It lets the firm skip the disclosure form for its own buyers
It shapes what agents say at first substantive contact
It sets the commission splits agents may offer cooperating firms
questions.x: The written policy determines what an agent says at first substantive contact, such as telling a buyer at a seller-only firm that nobody there can represent them. No firm policy excuses the disclosure form, which is the tempting wrong answer for in-house buyers.

questions.q: A buyer walks into a firm whose policy is exclusive seller agency and asks for help making an offer. An agent should tell the buyer right away that:
c: The firm will represent her once dual consent is signed
A designated agent will be assigned to represent her
She becomes a client as soon as the form is signed
Nobody at the firm can represent her as a client
questions.x: An exclusive seller agency firm represents only sellers, so buyers are customers and must hear that at once. Dual consent and designated agents belong to firms that allow consensual dual agency, which this firm does not.

questions.q: A listing agreement between an owner and a broker usually creates which kind of agency?
c: Express special agency
Implied general agency
Express universal agency
Implied special agency
questions.x: A listing is a written employment contract, so the agency is express, and the broker is hired for one transaction, so it is special. 'Implied special agency' is tempting, but agency created by a signed agreement is express, not implied.

questions.q: Which statement about a listing agreement is correct?
c: It is the buyer's contract to purchase the property
It is the owner's employment contract with a broker
It makes the broker the owner's general agent
It binds the parties only once an offer is accepted
questions.x: A listing agreement is the employment contract between an owner and a broker, and it usually creates special agency for one sale. The 'general agent' choice confuses it with a property manager's ongoing role.

questions.q: A seller tells a broker, "Get me $1,750,000 and keep anything above that as your fee." The broker should:
c: Accept, since the seller proposed the terms
Accept, as long as the terms are in writing
Decline, as net listings are banned in NY
Accept if the fee stays under 6 percent
questions.x: This is a net listing, which New York prohibits no matter who proposes it. The trap is thinking it becomes acceptable because the seller suggested it or because it is written down.

questions.q: A seller asks for a listing where the firm keeps everything above $900,000. In New York this arrangement is:
c: Allowed if the seller signs it in writing
Allowed only for commercial property
Allowed once it is disclosed on the MLS
A net listing, which NY prohibits
questions.x: Keeping everything above the seller's number is a net listing, banned in New York by 19 NYCRR 175.19. A written signature or MLS disclosure does not make it legal.

questions.q: Which item should a well-drafted buyer agreement state?
c: The seller's lowest acceptable price
What happens if the buyer finds a home alone
The compensation offer published on the MLS
The salesperson's private split with the broker
questions.x: A buyer agreement should state the term, area, fee, who pays, and what happens if the buyer buys on their own during the term. MLS compensation offers can no longer be published, and splits are private to the broker and salesperson.

questions.q: Which terms of a buyer agreement can the buyer negotiate?
c: The term, but not the fee
The fee, but not exclusivity
None of them since the 2024 settlement
The fee, the term, and exclusivity
questions.x: A buyer can always negotiate the fee, the term, and whether the agreement is exclusive. The settlement made compensation explicit, not fixed, so 'none of them' is the trap.

questions.q: Who sets the commission split between a broker and its salesperson?
c: The seller, in the listing agreement
The local MLS or board of Realtors
The broker and salesperson, by contract
DOS, by regulation for each license type
questions.x: Splits are a private matter set by the broker and salesperson's independent contractor agreement. Neither the client nor any MLS or board sets them; the MLS choice is tempting because cooperating fees come up there, but those too are set by the firms.

questions.q: A seller asks to pay her listing salesperson's share directly to the salesperson at closing. The correct response is that:
c: Direct payment is fine if the broker agrees to it
The salesperson is paid only through the broker
Direct payment is fine once title has passed
Either may be paid, since both are her agents
questions.x: The client pays the broker, and the broker pays the salesperson under their split; the client never pays the salesperson directly. Broker approval does not change who may pay a salesperson, which is the most tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: Rosa's listing salesperson dies two months into a six-month exclusive with Hudson & Hart. The listing:
c: Continues, because it belongs to the broker
Ends, because agency ends at a death
Ends unless Rosa signs a new listing
Continues only if the estate agrees
questions.x: The listing is with the broker, not the salesperson, so it continues and the firm assigns another agent. Death ends agency only when the principal or the agent (the broker) dies, which is the trap in 'agency ends at a death.'

questions.q: A sole-proprietor broker dies during an exclusive listing that one of the firm's salespersons was handling. The agency:
c: Continues under the salesperson
Continues until the stated expiration
Ends, because the broker was the agent
Passes to the broker's estate for the term
questions.x: The broker is the agent, so its death ends the agency by operation of law. The salesperson only carried out the broker's agency and cannot keep it going alone.

questions.q: Which of the following does the NY agency disclosure form do?
c: Creates the agency relationship once signed
Obligates the consumer to pay a broker fee
Explains roles and records the licensee's role
Serves as consent to dual agency in every deal
questions.x: The form explains the agency roles, lists the fiduciary duties, and records which role this licensee is playing. It is not a contract: it creates no agency and obligates no one to pay, which is the trap in the first choice.

questions.q: The RPL 443 disclosure form explains each of the following roles EXCEPT:
c: Broker's agent
Dual agent with designated sales agents
Seller's agent
Transaction broker
questions.x: The form describes seller's agent, buyer's agent, broker's agent, dual agent, and dual agent with designated sales agents. Transaction brokerage, a non-agency role used in some other states, is not one of the roles on the NY form.

questions.q: A seller's agent explains the disclosure form to a buyer customer at an open house. Which statement belongs in that explanation?
c: I can help you decide how much to offer
Signing this form makes you my client too
You must buy through me if you buy this home
What you tell me goes to my client, the seller
questions.x: A seller's agent warns the buyer that information shared goes to the seller and that the agent can't advise on price. Offering price help is the trap: that is advocacy owed only to a client.

questions.q: When explaining the disclosure form, a seller's agent tells a buyer customer that the buyer's options include:
c: Hiring a separate buyer's agent
Having the seller's agent advise on price
Waiving the disclosure requirement
Making the seller's agent her subagent
questions.x: The buyer can hire her own buyer's agent to get advice and confidentiality. The seller's agent cannot advise her on price, and the disclosure requirement cannot be waived by the consumer.

questions.q: A buyer customer Marcus met at his listing's open house asks him to represent her in finding other homes. Marcus may:
c: Become her buyer's agent under a buyer agreement
Not represent her, since they met as agent and customer
Represent her only after his open house listing sells
Represent her without new forms, as she already has one
questions.x: A customer can become a client for other properties under a buyer agreement, with a new disclosure. The no-new-forms choice is the trap: any role change needs a fresh disclosure and acknowledgment.

questions.q: When a licensee's agency role with a consumer changes, the licensee should:
c: Keep the original form, which covers all roles
Notify DOS of the change within 10 days
Get the other side's agent to approve the change
Give a new disclosure and get it acknowledged
questions.x: Any time your role changes, give a new disclosure, explain the change, and get it acknowledged. The original form records only the role checked at the time, so keeping it is the trap; DOS is not notified.

questions.q: Which feature fits an independent contractor salesperson rather than an employee?
c: Has income and Social Security tax withheld
Pays her own car, marketing and MLS costs
Is covered by the broker's workers' comp
Works hours the broker sets each week
questions.x: Contractors pay their own business expenses, are paid by results, and set their own hours. Withholding, workers' comp through the broker, and broker-set hours all point to employment.

questions.q: A brokerage pays a salesperson a salary and withholds income tax from each check. The salesperson is most likely:
c: An independent contractor
An employee of the broker
A statutory nonemployee under IRC 3508
A contractor under NY's 1986 law
questions.x: Salary and tax withholding are hallmarks of employment. IRC 3508 nonemployee status requires pay tied to output, not salary, so that choice is the trap.

questions.q: Under the traditional common law test, a worker is most likely an employee when the hiring party controls:
c: The end result, but not the methods
How, when, and where the work is done
Whether the worker holds a license
The firm name shown in the worker's ads
questions.x: Courts ask whether the hiring party controls not just the result but how, when, and where the work is done. Controlling only the end result is consistent with contractor status, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: Courts deciding whether a worker is an employee traditionally focus on:
c: The title on the worker's business card
Whether the broker holds the license
The size of the commission split
Direction and control of the work
questions.x: The common law test is direction and control. Holding the license is a license law requirement for every salesperson and does not decide employment status.

questions.q: Under New York's test for unemployment insurance, a broker's independent contractor agreement must have been executed within the past:
c: 12 to 15 months
24 to 36 months
6 months
3 years
questions.x: Labor Law 511 requires a written contract executed within the past 12 to 15 months, so brokers renew it every year. Three years is the record retention period, a number from a different rule.

questions.q: A broker had salespersons sign contractor agreements in 2021 and never renewed them. One leaves in 2026 and files for unemployment benefits. The broker's main risk is that:
c: Her license was kept at the broker's office
The broker's name appeared in all her ads
The agreement lapsed, so coverage may be owed
She sometimes worked from home on weekdays
questions.x: NY requires a contract executed within the past 12 to 15 months; a lapsed agreement can leave the broker owing unemployment and comp coverage. Holding the license and naming the broker in ads are license law duties and do not create employment.

questions.q: Which broker practice, required by license law, does NOT turn an independent contractor into an employee?
c: Paying the salesperson by the hour
Holding the salesperson's license on file
Requiring set desk hours every weekday
Docking splits for missed office days
questions.x: Holding the license, naming the broker in ads, and reviewing contracts come from license law and apply however the salesperson is classified. Hourly pay, mandatory hours and docked splits are direction and control.

questions.q: Each of the following comes from license law and applies whether a salesperson is a contractor or an employee EXCEPT:
c: Broker review of contracts
The broker's name in all ads
The broker holding the license
Mandatory 9 to 5 desk hours
questions.x: Mandatory desk hours are direction and control, not a license law requirement, and they threaten contractor status. The other three are license law duties that do not make anyone an employee.

questions.concept: Contractor or employee is a choice
questions.q: Which statement about how New York salespersons work for brokers is correct?
c: Most are contractors, though employment is legal
Firms may not hire salespersons as employees
Supervision rules require them to be employees
Most are employees, and contractor status is rare
questions.x: Most NY salespersons are independent contractors, but hiring them as employees is legal too. What is illegal is calling someone a contractor while treating them as an employee; 'firms may not hire employees' is the trap.

questions.concept: Contractor or employee is a choice
questions.q: A broker hires new salespersons as salaried employees with full tax withholding. This arrangement is:
c: Illegal, since salespersons must be contractors
Legal only for associate brokers
Legal, if they are treated as employees
Illegal under IRC Section 3508
questions.x: Brokers may hire salespersons as employees, with withholding and benefits. IRC 3508 is a safe harbor that lets licensees be treated as contractors; it does not forbid employment.

questions.q: Each of the following is enforced under the Sherman Antitrust Act EXCEPT:
c: A ban on price fixing
A ban on group boycotts of rivals
A ban on referral kickbacks
A ban on market allocation
questions.x: The Sherman Act targets agreements in restraint of trade: price fixing, boycotts, allocation, and tie-ins. Referral kickbacks fall under RESPA Section 8, which is the trap.

questions.q: A broker independently decides to raise her firm's rate to 6%, then mentions it at a dinner where two rival brokers agree to match it. Which conduct raises an antitrust problem?
c: The broker's decision to raise
The rivals' agreement to match
The broker's mention of her rate
Neither the decision nor the deal
questions.x: A firm may set its own price alone; the violation is an agreement among competitors. Raising the rate is the trap: unilateral pricing is lawful. Discussing rates with rivals is risky, but the agreement is the violation.

questions.q: A salesperson who found the buyer is owed a share of the commission, but the seller refuses to pay the firm. The salesperson's claim is against:
c: The seller, directly
The buyer, directly
The multiple listing service
The sponsoring broker
questions.x: Only the broker may sue the client for a commission; a salesperson looks to their sponsoring broker. Suing the seller directly is the trap: the salesperson has no contract with the seller.

questions.q: A broker brings a buyer who meets every term in the listing. The seller changes his mind and refuses to sell. Under the traditional rule, the commission is:
c: Not yet earned
Due at closing
Owed by buyer
Earned anyway
questions.x: Under the traditional rule, the commission is earned once the broker produces a ready, willing, and able buyer on the seller's terms. The listing could tie payment to closing, but that is the trap here, since no such term is stated.

questions.q: Procuring cause refers to the broker who:
c: Started the unbroken chain leading to the sale
Showed the property to the buyer before anyone else
Had the listing in the MLS the longest
Wrote and submitted the buyer's purchase offer
questions.x: Procuring cause is the broker whose efforts started an unbroken chain of events ending in the sale. Showing first is the trap: a first showing that went nowhere is not decisive.

questions.q: A NY broker may share a commission with each of the following EXCEPT:
c: A cooperating broker from another firm
A salesperson the broker sponsors
An unlicensed neighbor who sent the buyer
An associate broker working under the broker's sponsorship
questions.x: Commissions may be shared with licensees, not with unlicensed people who brought a buyer. The associate broker is the trap: although broker-qualified, they work under a sponsor and are paid through that broker.

questions.q: A buyer's agent is paid from the seller's proceeds at closing. Whom does the buyer's agent represent?
c: The seller
The buyer
Both parties
Neither party
questions.x: Agency comes from the agreement and conduct, not the source of payment. The seller is the trap: paying the fee does not make the seller the client.

questions.q: Brokers accused of agreeing on commission rates argue the rates were fair and consumers benefited. Under per se analysis, this argument:
c: Defeats the claim
Is not a defense
Reduces the fine
Shifts the burden
questions.x: Per se illegal conduct is unlawful in itself; courts do not weigh fairness or consumer benefit. Reducing the fine is the trap: the defense does not excuse the conduct at all.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects safe antitrust practice for a licensee?
c: Discuss common rates with rivals if prices fall
Discuss rates with rivals at trade associations
Discuss rates with rivals as long as no deal is signed
Discuss your own rates with clients, not rivals
questions.x: Rate talk among competitors can be evidence of price fixing, even without a signed deal. The trade association choice is the trap: those settings are where many antitrust cases begin.

questions.q: A buyer reasonably relies on a man who, with the owner's knowledge, has been showing the house and quoting price. The owner later denies he was an agent. The buyer argues:
c: Apparent agency
Ratification
Express agency
Agency by necessity
questions.x: Apparent (ostensible) agency, also called agency by estoppel, arises from the principal's conduct that led a third party to rely. Ratification is the trap: the owner did not approve a specific act afterward.

questions.q: A seller lists with Kim at a 40-agent firm. Another agent at the same firm, who never met the seller, learns the seller's bottom line. That agent:
c: Owes no duty to the seller
Can share it with a buyer client
Owes the seller confidentiality
Owes duties after a sale contract
questions.x: The agency belongs to the brokerage, so every licensee in the firm owes the seller fiduciary duties. The owes-nothing choice is the trap: never having met the seller does not matter.

questions.q: Tasha, from another firm, accepts the listing broker's offer of subagency and shows the home to a buyer. The buyer asks Tasha what the seller would accept. Tasha should:
c: Keep the seller's position confidential
Share it, since she works with the buyer
Share it, since she is from another firm
Ask the listing broker if she may share it
questions.x: A subagent owes the seller fiduciary duties through the listing broker, including confidentiality. Being from another firm is the trap: accepting subagency makes her the seller's agent anyway.

questions.q: A buyer's agent engages an agent from another firm to help find properties for the buyer. Under RPL 443, that helper is a:
c: Subagent
Dual agent
Broker's agent
Designated agent
questions.x: A broker's agent is engaged by a listing or buyer's agent from a different firm and takes direction from that agent. Subagent is the trap: subagency runs through the listing broker to the seller.

questions.q: Why do many sellers decline to authorize subagency?
c: Subagents cannot show their listed property
Exposure to liability for subagents' acts
Subagency is prohibited by New York law
Subagents are not allowed to be paid
questions.x: A subagent is the seller's agent, so the seller can be vicariously liable for what it says. The prohibition choice is the trap: subagency is lawful in NY, just rarely used.

questions.q: A listing agreement says nothing about subagency. A cooperating broker shows the property and claims to be the seller's subagent. The claim is weak because:
c: Subagency needs a separate DOS filing
Subagents have to be from the same firm
Cooperating brokers cannot be subagents
The seller never authorized subagency
questions.x: Subagency is extended by the listing broker with the seller's authorization. Without that authorization, there is no subagency. The same-firm choice is the trap: subagents come from other firms.

questions.q: Under current practice, an MLS offer of subagency to cooperating brokers is:
c: Automatic for each listing
Required by RPL 443
Banned in New York
Optional and rarely used
questions.x: The old blanket unilateral offer of subagency made cooperating brokers automatic subagents; it is now optional and uncommon. Banned in NY is the trap: subagency is allowed, just disfavored.

questions.q: A cooperating broker from another firm may work on a sale in each of these roles EXCEPT:
c: An undisclosed agent for both sides
A buyer's agent for its buyer client
A subagent of the listing broker
A broker's agent engaged by the lister
questions.x: A cooperating broker may act as buyer's agent, subagent (if offered), or broker's agent. Acting for both sides without consent is undisclosed dual agency. The broker's agent role is the trap: it is a lawful RPL 443 role.

questions.q: Which is the main advantage of single agency for the client?
c: The client pays a lower commission
Liability shifts to the other side
Full advice and undivided loyalty
No disclosure form is required
questions.x: Single agency lets the agent advocate fully for one client. The disclosure choice is the trap: single agents still give the RPL 443 form.

questions.q: Each of the following can create an agency relationship EXCEPT:
c: Signing a buyer agency agreement
Paying the agent's commission
Conduct that implies representation
Approving an agent's act afterward
questions.x: Agency arises from agreement, conduct, ratification, or estoppel, not from who pays. Approving an act afterward is the trap: that is ratification, a recognized way to create agency.

questions.q: A buyer's agent knows the buyer plans to tear down the house. The seller asks the agent directly whether the buyer plans to keep it. The agent should:
c: Say the buyer plans to keep the house
Decline to discuss the buyer's plans
Share the plans to keep the deal fair
Say the buyer has no plans either way
questions.x: The buyer's plans are confidential, but the agent may not lie to the seller. Declining to answer is proper. Saying the buyer has no plans is the trap: it sounds neutral but is a false statement.

questions.q: A renter signs an agreement with a broker to find her an apartment in Harlem. The broker is a:
c: Landlord's agent
Broker's agent
Seller's agent
Tenant's agent
questions.x: An agent representing the renter is a tenant's agent. Landlord's agent is the trap: the broker shows landlords' apartments but represents the renter.

questions.q: The NYC FARE Act, effective June 11, 2025, requires that:
c: The party that hires the broker pays it
Tenants pay one month's rent to the broker
Landlords and tenants split broker fees
Broker fees are capped at one month's rent
questions.x: A broker hired by the landlord is paid by the landlord; any fees a tenant must pay must be disclosed in the listing and lease. The cap is the trap: the law shifts who pays rather than setting a fee cap.

questions.q: A listing agent takes buyer Marcus to see the listing. Marcus has signed nothing with anyone. What duty does the agent owe Marcus?
c: Loyalty
Obedience
Honesty
Confidentiality
questions.x: Marcus is a customer, owed honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material defects. Confidentiality is the trap: it belongs to the seller client.

questions.q: A buyer's agent leaves her firm. The buyer client wants to keep working with her at the new firm. The buyer agency agreement is:
c: With the original firm
With the agent, personally
Void when she leaves the firm
Moved to her new firm
questions.x: Buyer agreements, like listings, are contracts with the broker. Moving it requires the client and the original firm to agree. The personal choice is the trap: salespersons cannot hold agency contracts in their own name.

questions.q: A licensee helps two parties complete a deal while both agree in writing that the licensee represents neither of them. This shows that:
c: Agency exists whenever a fee is paid
Agency requires a buyer agreement
Brokerage can exist without agency
A license is not needed for brokerage
questions.x: Brokerage is the business of bringing parties together for a fee, and the parties can agree it involves no agency. The fee choice is the trap: payment does not create agency.

questions.q: Under RPL 443, who directs the work of a broker's agent engaged by a listing agent?
c: The seller, as principal
The listing agent
The buyer customer
The seller's attorney
questions.x: The broker's agent takes direction from the agent who engaged it, and the seller has no direct relationship with it. The seller is the trap: the seller is the ultimate client but cannot instruct the broker's agent.

questions.q: A cooperating agent may be each of the following EXCEPT:
c: A buyer's agent at another firm
A subagent from another firm
A broker's agent from another firm
A salesperson at the listing firm
questions.x: A cooperating agent is an outside licensee helping produce the deal. A salesperson at the listing firm is in-house, not cooperating. The broker's agent is the trap: it is one of the cooperating roles.

questions.q: A tenant's agent may do which of the following for the tenant?
c: Tell the landlord the tenant's top rent
Collect a fee from both without consent
Hide known defects from the landlord
Negotiate lease terms for the tenant
questions.x: A tenant's agent owes the tenant full fiduciary duties, including advocacy in negotiation. Revealing the top rent is the trap: it breaches the tenant's confidentiality.

questions.q: Compared with subagency, using a broker's agent changes who is liable for the helper's acts by placing liability on:
c: The listing broker
The seller client
The buyer customer
The Department of State
questions.x: Under RPL 443, the listing broker answers for its broker's agent, and the seller is not vicariously liable. The seller is the trap because sellers bear that risk under subagency.

questions.q: A salesperson signs a listing with a seller. In law, the salesperson acted as:
c: The seller's principal
The broker's principal
The broker's agent
An independent broker
questions.x: A salesperson acts on behalf of the sponsoring broker, who holds the listing. Independent broker is the trap: a salesperson cannot act as a broker or hold listings alone.

questions.q: In New York, dual agency is lawful if:
c: Buyer and seller both give informed written consent
The broker discloses it orally to the seller
The broker reduces its commission on the deal
The seller's attorney approves the arrangement in writing
questions.x: Both parties must give informed consent in writing. Oral notice to one side is the trap: it is neither written nor from both parties.

questions.q: What does each party give up when consenting to dual agency?
c: Honesty
An attorney
Undivided loyalty
Disclosure of defects
questions.x: A dual agent cannot give undivided loyalty or advocate for either side against the other. Honesty is the trap: it is still owed to both parties.

questions.q: Two salespersons from the same firm work on one deal: one with the seller client, one with the buyer client. This is:
c: Single agency on each side
Dual agency by the broker
Subagency for the seller
No agency for the buyer
questions.x: The agency belongs to the broker. Two salespersons in one firm representing opposite sides make the firm a dual agent. Single agency is the trap because two different people are involved.

questions.q: A designated sales agent is:
c: A subagent from another firm who assists the listing broker on a sale
An unlicensed assistant assigned by the broker to handle the transaction paperwork
The broker who personally supervises a consensual dual agency deal
A licensee assigned, with consent, to one party when the firm represents both
questions.x: RPL 443 defines designated sales agents as licensees under the broker's supervision assigned to one client when the broker represents both sides. The supervising broker is the trap: the broker remains a dual agent, not a designated agent.

questions.q: When designated sales agents are appointed in an in-house sale, the broker:
c: Becomes the seller's single agent
Becomes the buyer's single agent
Steps out of the transaction
Remains a dual agent
questions.x: Designation lets each salesperson advocate for one side, but the firm still represents both, so the broker stays a dual agent. Stepping out is the trap: the broker continues to supervise both designated agents.

questions.q: Advance consent to dual agency is given:
c: On the NY agency disclosure form
Orally, at the closing table, by both parties
In writing, after an offer is accepted
By DOS, on behalf of both parties
questions.x: The disclosure form lets a client consent ahead of time, usually when the listing or buyer agreement is signed. Consent after acceptance is the trap: the point of advance consent is to settle it before an in-house deal arises.

questions.q: A firm gets the seller's written consent to dual agency but never tells its buyer client. The firm is:
c: A consensual dual agent
A subagent of the seller
An undisclosed dual agent
A seller's designated sales agent
questions.x: Consent from one side is not enough; the buyer did not consent, so the firm is an undisclosed dual agent. Consensual dual agent is the trap because the seller's consent is in writing.

questions.q: Consequences of undisclosed dual agency may include each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Forfeiture of the commission
Transfer of title to the broker
License suspension or revocation
Rescission of the contract
questions.x: Undisclosed dual agency can cost the commission, unwind the deal, and lead to discipline. It does not transfer title to anyone. Rescission may sound extreme, but a court can unwind the contract.

questions.q: 19 NYCRR 175.7 provides that a broker:
c: May be paid by both parties if the total is under 6%
Needs everyone's consent to be paid by more than one party
Has to be paid by the seller in every residential sale
May be paid by the buyer as well, as long as the seller consents
questions.x: 175.7 bars compensation from more than one party without the full knowledge and consent of all parties. The seller-consent choice is the trap: every party must consent, not one.
questions.concept: Compensation from more than one party

questions.q: A lender offers a salesperson $300 per buyer referred. The salesperson performs no loan services. Accepting is:
c: Legal with written disclosure
Legal for cash buyers
Legal if paid to the broker
A RESPA kickback
questions.x: RESPA Section 8 bars fees for mere referrals of settlement business. Written disclosure is the trap: disclosing a kickback, or routing it through the broker, does not make it legal.

questions.q: A licensee who is also licensed as a mortgage broker arranges a buyer's loan and will be paid for that work. Under NY rules, the licensee should:
c: Disclose the arrangement and get every party's consent
Keep the mortgage fee confidential from the seller
Decline, since licensees cannot be mortgage brokers
Let the lender disclose the fee in closing documents
questions.x: Being paid by more than one party for services in the same deal requires full disclosure and consent of all parties under 175.7. Letting the lender disclose it is the trap: the licensee owes the disclosure, and it must come before consent, not at closing.
questions.concept: Compensation from more than one party

questions.q: A brokerage that represents buyers and never takes listings has adopted which policy?
c: Consensual dual agency
Designated sales agency
Exclusive buyer agency
Seller subagency
questions.x: An exclusive buyer agency firm avoids in-house dual agency by never representing sellers. Designated agency is the trap: it is a way to manage dual agency, not avoid it.

questions.q: Under a designated sales agent arrangement, each of the following is true EXCEPT:
c: One salesperson may be designated for both sides
Both parties consent to the arrangement in writing
Each designated agent advocates for its own client
The broker supervises both of the designated agents
questions.x: Designated agents are two different licensees, one per party; one person on both sides is plain dual agency. The supervision choice is the trap: the broker does supervise both, which is why the broker remains a dual agent.

questions.q: A seller's agent tells a buyer customer, "Offer $60K under; my sellers are desperate." Besides breaching duties to the sellers, the agent risks:
c: Nothing more, because the buyer is a customer, not a client
Becoming a broker's agent for the buyer's side of the deal
Implied agency with the buyer and undisclosed dual agency
Ratifying the buyer's offer on behalf of the selling owners
questions.x: Advising a customer can create implied agency, and representing both sides without consent is undisclosed dual agency. The customer defense is the trap: conduct, not labels, decides whether agency exists.

questions.q: Dual agency most commonly arises from:
c: Open listings
In-house sales
Commercial leases
For-sale-by-owner deals
questions.x: When a firm's buyer client wants a firm listing, both sides are firm clients. Open listings are the trap: several brokers may be involved, but each still represents one side.

questions.q: A dual agent may do which of the following?
c: Tell the seller the buyer's top price
Advise the buyer to offer much less
Tell the buyer the seller's lowest price
Give both sides factual market data
questions.x: A dual agent can facilitate and share objective information but cannot reveal either side's confidential positions or advocate against either party. Advising the buyer on price is the trap: that is advocacy against the seller.

questions.q: How do RPL 443 and 19 NYCRR 175.7 relate?
c: 443 governs commercial agency disclosure; 175.7 governs residential agency disclosure and dual agency consent forms
443 and 175.7 conflict on dual agency consent, and 175.7 controls because it is the more recent rule
175.7 replaced 443 in 2011, so the agency disclosure form and its timing are now governed entirely by the regulation
443 covers residential agency disclosure; 175.7 covers whom the broker acts for and consent to fees from more than one party
questions.x: Both rest on disclosure: 443 sets the residential form, and 175.7 is the broader rule on whom you act for and who may pay you. The commercial/residential split is the trap: 443 is the residential statute.

questions.q: Under an exclusive right to sell listing, the broker earns a commission if:
c: Anyone sells the property during the term
The listing broker personally finds the buyer
The owner sells without a broker's help
Another broker's buyer goes to contract
questions.x: The exclusive right to sell pays the broker no matter who procures the buyer during the term, the owner included. The owner-sells choice is the trap: that is the one case exclusive agency would not pay.

questions.q: Which listing lets the owner sell personally without owing a commission, while giving one broker exclusivity against other brokers?
c: Exclusive right to sell
Open listing
Exclusive agency
Net listing
questions.x: Exclusive agency names one broker but reserves the owner's right to sell commission-free. Open listing is the trap: it also lets the owner sell free, but gives no broker exclusivity.

questions.q: An owner gives listings to three brokers and promises a commission to whichever one produces the buyer. This is:
c: An exclusive agency
An open listing
A multiple dual agency
A net listing
questions.x: An open listing is non-exclusive and pays the procuring broker. Exclusive agency is the trap: it names one broker, not three.

questions.q: Under 19 NYCRR 175.24, an exclusive listing of NY residential property has to include:
c: A guaranteed minimum sale price, signed by the broker
An explanation of listing types, initialed by the owner
The buyer's mortgage pre-approval, once it is received
An agency disclosure form signed by the listing broker
questions.x: 175.24 requires a printed explanation of exclusive right to sell versus exclusive agency, signed or initialed by the owner. The agency disclosure form is the trap: it is a separate RPL 443 requirement, signed by the consumer, not this explanation.

questions.q: If a NY listing broker belongs to an MLS, 175.24 requires that the owner be given the option to:
c: Set the cooperating broker's commission at zero
Cancel the listing at any time without any notice
Choose the buyer's attorney for the whole transaction
Route offers via the lister or the selling broker
questions.x: The regulation gives MLS sellers the choice of having offers submitted through the listing broker or directly by the selling broker. Cancelling at will is the trap: nothing in 175.24 gives that right.

questions.q: A buyer signs an agreement to work with one buyer's broker for 90 days. This is commonly called an:
c: Exclusive right to represent
Exclusive agency listing
Exclusive right to sell
Open (nonexclusive) buyer agreement
questions.x: An exclusive right to represent (exclusive buyer agency agreement) commits the buyer to one broker for the term. Exclusive right to sell is the trap: it is the seller-side equivalent.

questions.q: Under the NAR settlement effective August 17, 2024, an MLS participant working with a buyer needs a written agreement:
c: Before the closing
Before an offer is made
Before touring a home
Within 10 days of an offer
questions.x: The rule requires a written buyer agreement before touring, in person or virtually. Before an offer is the trap: it was a common pre-settlement practice, but the deadline is the first tour.

questions.q: Under the 2024 NAR settlement rules, each of the following is true EXCEPT:
c: Commissions are set at 2.5% per side
Buyer-broker pay offers are off the MLS
Buyer agreements state pay objectively
Buyer brokers cannot exceed agreed pay
questions.x: Commissions remain fully negotiable; fixing them would be price fixing. The objective-amount rule is the trap: buyer agreements do have to state compensation in a specific, objective amount.

questions.q: A Queens home sells for $850,000 with a 5% commission. What is the total commission?
questions.x: $850,000 x 0.05 = $42,500. $51,000 is the trap: it applies the familiar 6% figure instead of the stated 5%.

questions.q: A $1,200,000 sale carries a 5% commission. The listing firm pays the buyer's firm half. The listing salesperson receives 60% of the listing firm's share. What does the salesperson receive?
questions.x: $1,200,000 x 0.05 = $60,000. Half to the buyer's firm leaves $30,000; 60% of $30,000 = $18,000. $36,000 is the trap: it applies 60% to the whole commission and skips the co-broke split.

questions.q: A salesperson received $9,600, which was 40% of the listing firm's side. The listing firm's side was half of a 6% total commission. What was the sale price?
questions.x: Firm side = $9,600 / 0.40 = $24,000. Total commission = $48,000. Price = $48,000 / 0.06 = $800,000. $400,000 is the trap: it treats the firm's $24,000 side as the whole commission. $160,000 divides the salesperson's share straight by 6%.

questions.q: A landlord pays a broker one month's rent plus 5% of the first year's rent for a $4,000 per month apartment. What is the fee?
questions.x: One month = $4,000. Annual rent = $48,000; 5% = $2,400. Total = $6,400. $4,200 is the trap: it takes 5% of one month's rent instead of the year's.

questions.q: A broker charges a 4.5% commission and the seller nets $955,000 after paying the commission and nothing else. What was the sale price, to the nearest dollar?
questions.x: Net = price x (1 - 0.045), so $955,000 / 0.955 = $1,000,000. $997,975 is the trap: it adds 4.5% to the net instead of dividing.

questions.q: Each of the following is required for lawful dual agency in New York EXCEPT:
c: Consent from the seller
A reduced commission
Consent from the buyer
Consent made in writing
questions.x: Dual agency requires the informed written consent of both buyer and seller. No commission reduction is required. Consent in writing is the trap: it is required, not optional.

questions.q: A buyer consents to dual agency and later asks the agent, "Should I offer less? Is the seller desperate?" The agent may:
c: Advise the buyer to make a low offer
Share facts but not advise or reveal
Reveal the seller's reason for selling
Refuse to discuss the deal with the buyer
questions.x: A dual agent gives up advocacy and cannot reveal confidences, but can share facts and facilitate. Refusing to speak is the trap: a dual agent still serves both parties.

questions.q: A firm becomes a dual agent when:
c: Two firms cooperate on a single listing
A subagent shows a buyer the listing
A buyer's agent is paid by the seller
Its seller client and buyer client deal
questions.x: Agency belongs to the broker, so any deal between two clients of the same firm makes the firm a dual agent. Payment by the seller is the trap: the payment source does not create agency.

questions.q: Kim lists the Okafors' condo; Ray, in the same firm, has a buyer client who wants it. With prior consent, the broker assigns Kim to the Okafors and Ray to the buyer. Kim and Ray are:
c: Designated sales agents
Subagents of the seller
Broker's agents for each side
Cooperating agents
questions.x: With consent, a broker may designate separate licensees to represent each side of an in-house deal. Cooperating agents is the trap: that describes licensees from outside firms.

questions.q: When designated sales agents are appointed, each of the following is true EXCEPT:
c: Each agent advocates for one client
Both parties have consented in writing
The broker is no longer a dual agent
The broker supervises both agents
questions.x: Designation lets each salesperson advocate for one side, but the firm still represents both, so the broker stays a dual agent. Supervision is the trap: the broker does supervise both.

questions.q: A seller checks advance consent to dual agency when listing. Months later, a firm buyer client wants the home. The firm should:
c: Tell both parties of the dual agency
Proceed without telling the seller
Get a new listing agreement signed first
Refer the buyer to another firm
questions.x: Advance consent authorizes the dual agency ahead of time, but the firm still informs both parties when it arises. Proceeding silently is the trap: advance consent is not consent to be kept in the dark.

questions.q: Undisclosed dual agency occurs in each of these cases EXCEPT when:
c: The buyer is not told
The seller is not told
Both sides consent in writing
Agency arises from conduct alone
questions.x: Written informed consent from both sides is lawful dual agency. Conduct-created agency is the trap: implied agency with the other side, without consent, is a classic form of undisclosed dual agency.

questions.q: Which party can seek to rescind a contract because of undisclosed dual agency?
c: The broker who acted dually
A party who did not consent
The DOS licensing division
The listing service operator
questions.x: A principal who did not consent to the dual agency may seek to unwind the deal and deny the commission. DOS is the trap: it disciplines licenses but does not rescind private contracts.

questions.q: A broker wants a $2,000 fee from the buyer on top of the seller-paid commission. Under 175.7, the broker:
c: Needs consent from neither
Needs consent from the buyer
Needs consent from DOS
Needs consent from both
questions.x: Compensation from more than one party requires full disclosure and consent of all parties. Buyer consent is the trap: the seller must also know and agree.
questions.concept: Compensation from more than one party

questions.q: Under RESPA Section 8, each of the following is prohibited EXCEPT:
c: A flat fee for each referral made
A gift per referred loan
A kickback via the broker
Payment for actual services
questions.x: RESPA bars fees and things of value given for mere referrals; payment for services actually performed is allowed. A kickback routed through the broker is the trap: rerouting does not cure it.

questions.q: A licensee earns a fee from the seller for the sale and a fee from the buyer for loan work. What separates this from a kickback?
c: Real services, disclosed, with consent
Payment made through the sponsoring broker
A fee below the RESPA limit
Advance approval by the buyer's lender
questions.x: Payment for actual services, with full disclosure and consent of all parties under 175.7, distinguishes it from a referral kickback. Routing through the broker is the trap: it does not change the nature of the payment.
questions.concept: Compensation from more than one party

questions.q: Leo wants a firm that will not face dual agency if he likes one of its listings. He should look for a firm that:
c: Uses designated agents
Offers subagency
Takes no listings
Lowers commissions
questions.x: An exclusive buyer agency firm never represents sellers, so in-house dual agency cannot arise. Designated agents is the trap: it manages dual agency, but the firm is still a dual agent.

questions.q: A firm's sole licensee in a small office lists a home and then has a buyer client who wants it. With consent, the arrangement is:
c: Designated agency, one agent
Dual agency, not designated
Single agency for each side
Subagency for the seller side
questions.x: Designated agency requires two different licensees, one per party. With one licensee on both sides, it is dual agency. Designated agency with one agent is the trap.

questions.q: A seller's agent who gives a buyer customer negotiating advice risks:
c: Ratifying the buyer's offer
Creating implied buyer agency
Forming a group boycott
Creating express agency by contract
questions.x: Advising a customer can create implied agency, which with the seller agency becomes undisclosed dual agency. Express agency is the trap: no agreement was stated, so any agency is implied.

questions.q: Which situation creates in-house dual agency?
c: A firm's buyer wants another listing
A subagent brings a buyer to a seller
Two firms co-broke on one sale deal
A firm's buyer wants a firm listing
questions.x: In-house dual agency arises when both the buyer and the seller are clients of the same firm. Co-broking is the trap: two firms each represent one side.

questions.q: A dual agent may do each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Tell the buyer the seller's floor
Present offers to the seller
Share comparable sales data
Arrange showings for the buyer client
questions.x: A dual agent facilitates and shares objective information but cannot reveal either side's confidential positions. Sharing comparables is the trap: factual market data is allowed.

questions.q: A broker in a commercial office sale will be paid by both the buyer and the seller. Which rule requires the broker to disclose and obtain consent?
c: RPL 443 (agency form)
RPL 443-a (stigma)
19 NYCRR 175.7
RPL 442-h (SOPs)
questions.x: 175.7 applies broadly, including commercial deals, and bars compensation from more than one party without everyone's consent. RPL 443 is the trap: its disclosure form covers residential property only.

questions.q: During an exclusive right to sell listing, the owner's sister finds a buyer on her own and the owner sells to that buyer. The broker:
c: Earns the commission
Earns half the fee
Earns no commission
Earns expenses alone
questions.x: Under an exclusive right to sell, the broker is paid if anyone sells during the term. Earning nothing is the trap: that would be the result under exclusive agency if the owner sold personally.

questions.q: Under an exclusive agency listing, the owner finds a buyer through a neighbor and sells without the broker's help. The broker:
c: Earns the full fee
Earns half the fee
Earns no commission
Earns a referral fee
questions.x: Exclusive agency reserves the owner's right to sell personally without owing a commission. Full fee is the trap: that is the exclusive right to sell result.

questions.q: Which is a feature of an open listing?
c: The owner owes each listing broker a fee
Several brokers may each list the property
One broker is exclusive against others
The broker keeps the excess over a net price
questions.x: An open listing is non-exclusive, and only the procuring broker is paid. Owing every broker is the trap: unsuccessful brokers on an open listing earn nothing.

questions.q: A broker takes an exclusive listing on a Staten Island two-family but skips the printed explanation of listing types. Under 175.24, the listing is missing:
c: A DOS filing and approval stamp
The seller's property condition form
The broker's guaranteed sale price
The owner's initialed explanation
questions.x: 175.24 requires a printed explanation of exclusive right to sell versus exclusive agency, signed or initialed by the owner. The property condition form is the trap: it is a separate seller duty under RPL Article 14.

questions.q: A listing broker in an MLS asks a seller how offers from other brokers should reach her. This follows 175.24, which lets the seller choose:
c: Whether offers are oral or are put in writing
Which of the MLS brokers may submit offers
Whether to see offers below asking price
Via the lister or direct from selling broker
