questions.x: 175.24 requires that MLS sellers be given the choice of offers through the listing broker or directly from the selling broker. Choosing which brokers may submit is the trap: that could be an exclusion problem, not this option.

questions.q: Leo signs a 90-day exclusive right to represent with a buyer's broker, then buys a house he found with another broker's help. Leo most likely:
c: Owes his own broker under the agreement
Owes nothing, since the other broker helped
Owes the seller a share of the commission
Owes the other broker but not his own broker
questions.x: An exclusive right to represent commits the buyer to one broker for the term, much like an exclusive right to sell. Owing nothing is the trap: the exclusive was meant to cover that situation.

questions.q: A buyer calls an MLS agent and wants to see a Park Slope condo that afternoon. Under the 2024 NAR settlement rules, before the tour the agent needs:
c: A mortgage pre-approval
A signed purchase offer
A written buyer agreement
A seller's written consent
questions.x: MLS participants working with a buyer need a written agreement before touring, in person or virtually. Pre-approval is the trap: a firm may require it under its SOPs, but the settlement rule concerns the buyer agreement.

questions.q: Under the 2024 NAR settlement rules, offers of buyer-broker compensation:
c: Are set at 3% in every deal
Cannot be posted on the MLS
Are paid by the buyer alone
Need DOS approval in advance
questions.x: Offers of buyer-broker compensation can no longer be published on the MLS; they may still be negotiated off-MLS. The buyer-alone choice is the trap: sellers may still agree to pay buyer brokers.

questions.q: A Bronx two-family sells for $735,000 with a 6% commission. What is the total commission?
questions.x: $735,000 x 0.06 = $44,100. $36,750 is the trap: it uses 5% instead of 6%.

questions.q: A $950,000 sale carries a 6% commission split equally between the listing and buyer's firms. The buyer's agent receives 70% of the buyer's firm's share. What does the buyer's agent receive?
questions.x: $950,000 x 0.06 = $57,000. Half to the buyer's firm = $28,500. 70% of $28,500 = $19,950. $39,900 is the trap: it applies 70% to the whole commission.

questions.q: A salesperson received $11,250, which was 50% of the listing firm's side. The listing firm's side was 60% of a 5% total commission. What was the sale price?
A landlord agrees to pay a broker 12% of the first year's rent on a $3,500 per month lease. What is the fee?
questions.x: $3,500 x 12 = $42,000 a year; 12% of $42,000 = $5,040. $3,500 is the trap: it equals one month's rent, a common fee but not this agreement.

questions.q: A seller wants to net $570,000 after a 5% commission and $12,000 in other closing costs. What is the lowest sale price that does it, to the nearest dollar?
questions.x: Price x 0.95 = $570,000 + $12,000, so price = $582,000 / 0.95 = $612,632. $611,100 is the trap: it adds 5% to $582,000 instead of dividing by 0.95.

questions.q: An agency relationship is terminated by operation of law by each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Death of the principal
Destruction of the property
A drop in market prices
Bankruptcy of the principal
questions.x: Death, incapacity, bankruptcy, and destruction of the property end agency by operation of law. A market downturn does not. Bankruptcy is the trap: it does end the agency, even though the property still exists.

questions.q: Halfway through a 6-month exclusive, the seller fires the broker for no reason. The seller:
c: Has no power to end the agency
Can end it but may owe damages
Owes a double commission
Turns it into an open listing
questions.x: A principal has the power to revoke but not always the right; breaking an exclusive can create liability for damages or expenses. No power to end it is the trap: the agency itself ends, even if wrongfully.

questions.q: An agency coupled with an interest:
c: Ends at the principal's death, like other agencies
Arises whenever a broker earns a commission
Is another name for an open listing agreement
Survives the principal's death and cannot be revoked
questions.x: When the agent holds its own interest in the property, the principal cannot revoke the agency and death does not end it. Earning a commission is the trap: a commission alone is not such an interest.

questions.q: Which is the best practice for every exclusive listing agreement?
c: No end date, to protect the broker
An automatic renewal clause
A net price clause for the seller
A definite expiration date
questions.x: A definite term protects the owner and avoids disputes. Automatic renewal is the trap: it can trap the seller in an agency they never chose to extend. Net clauses are illegal in NY.

questions.q: A NY brokerage's written standardized operating procedures for prospective homebuyers (RPL 442-h) require the firm to:
c: Apply its buyer requirements equally
Charge every buyer the same commission
Refuse buyers who are not pre-approved
Publish its commissions on the MLS
questions.x: The SOP law targets fair treatment: whatever the firm requires of one buyer, such as ID or pre-approval, it requires of all. The pre-approval choice is the trap: a firm may require it, but the law does not mandate it.

questions.q: The NY agency disclosure form required by RPL 443 applies to:
c: Every property type, commercial included
Vacant land and new construction alone
1 to 4 family homes, condos, and co-ops
Residential sales, but not any rentals
questions.x: RPL 443 covers residential property: 1 to 4 family dwellings plus condos and co-ops, with a landlord-tenant version for rentals. Every property type is the trap: that describes the anti-discrimination form, not the agency form.

questions.q: A listing agent presents the agency disclosure form to the seller:
c: At the first showing of the home
Before the listing agreement
At the closing
After an offer comes in
questions.x: RPL 443 requires the listing agent to give it to the seller before entering into the listing agreement. First showing is the trap: by then the listing is already signed.

questions.q: A seller's agent gives a buyer the agency disclosure form:
c: Before the listing agreement
At first substantive contact
When the buyer signs a contract
If the buyer has no agent
questions.x: The seller's agent gives the form to the buyer (or the buyer's agent) at first substantive contact. Before the listing agreement is the trap: that is when the seller gets it.

questions.q: A buyer's agent gives the disclosure form to the buyer client:
c: At the closing table, with the deed
After the buyer's first written offer
At the first showing of a property
Before the buyer agency agreement
questions.x: RPL 443 requires it before entering into the agreement to act as buyer's agent. The first showing is the trap: by then the buyer may already have committed to the agent.

questions.q: At an open house a visitor asks only about the age of the windows and the school zone. Has first substantive contact occurred?
c: No, needs and finances were not discussed
Yes, any question about the home triggers it
Yes, entering a listed property triggers it
Yes, if the visitor signs the sign-in sheet
questions.x: Property facts and small talk do not trigger it; discussion of the consumer's needs, motivation, or finances does. Any question is the trap: questions about the property itself are not substantive.

questions.q: A buyer refuses to sign the agency disclosure acknowledgment. The seller's agent should:
c: Stop working with the buyer until the form is signed
Have the seller sign the form on the buyer's behalf
Sign a sworn declaration of the refusal and keep it
Mail the unsigned form to DOS within ten days
questions.x: RPL 443 requires a written declaration of the refusal under oath or affirmation, kept at least 3 years, and the deal can continue. Stopping work is the trap: refusal does not end the relationship.

questions.q: How long must a licensee keep signed agency disclosure acknowledgments?
c: 3 years
1 year
2 years
7 years
questions.x: At least 3 years, the same as declarations of refusal and transaction records. 2 years is the trap: that is the license term, not the retention period.

questions.q: The NY agency disclosure form states that it:
c: Is a listing contract
Binds the buyer to pay
Is not a contract
Creates dual agency
questions.x: The form is headed "This is not a contract." It explains roles and documents that the consumer was informed. Creating dual agency is the trap: the form can record consent, but it does not itself create any agency.
questions.concept: Disclosure form is not a contract

questions.q: The RPL 443 agency disclosure form is required in each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Sale of a Harlem condo unit
Lease of a Midtown office suite
Rental in a Bronx three-family
Sale of a Bay Ridge co-op unit
questions.x: Office space is commercial and outside RPL 443; the anti-discrimination form still applies to it. The co-op is the trap: co-ops were exempt before 2011 but are covered now.

questions.q: Which change took effect with the January 1, 2011 version of the NY agency disclosure law?
c: Commercial property was brought under it
The form became optional for rentals
Dual agency was banned in residential sales
Condos and co-ops were brought under it
questions.x: Before 2011, condos and co-ops were exempt; the amendments covered them, extended disclosure to rentals, and added advance consent to dual agency. Commercial property is the trap: it remains outside RPL 443.

questions.q: A seller's agent's buyer customer asks the agent to represent her in buying the same listing. The agent should:
c: Switch sides at once, since customers become clients freely
Drop the seller and sign a buyer agency agreement instead
Represent the buyer informally without telling the seller
Get informed written consent of both, with new disclosure
questions.x: Changing roles in the same deal makes the firm a dual agent, which requires new disclosure and the written consent of both parties. Dropping the seller is the trap: abandoning a client mid-listing raises its own duties and does not erase what the agent knows.

questions.q: Which form is given at first substantive contact for every property type, including commercial and vacant land?
c: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination form
The RPL 443 agency disclosure form
The federal lead-based paint disclosure
The property condition disclosure statement
questions.x: The NYS Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (175.28) covers every property type. The agency form is the trap: it shares the same timing but applies to residential property only.

questions.q: On a call about a Forest Hills condo listing, a caller says he has to move within 30 days for a new job and asks what the seller would accept. The listing agent should:
c: Answer the price question and send the form after the deal
Decline to speak with callers who have no buyer's agent
Disclose the agent's role and send the form before going on
Tell him the seller's lowest price to keep the deal moving
questions.x: Motivation and price talk is first substantive contact, by phone as much as in person, so the agent discloses its role and provides the form. Sending it after the deal is the trap: the timing is first substantive contact.

questions.q: On the disclosure form, a seller who checks advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents is agreeing that:
c: The firm may not represent any buyer on the sale
The firm may act as dual agent with designated agents
The seller waives the agent's fiduciary duties
The seller will pay the buyer's agent's commission
questions.x: Advance consent authorizes dual agency with designated agents ahead of time; the firm still informs the seller when it happens. Waiving duties is the trap: consent limits advocacy but does not waive honesty or confidentiality.

questions.q: Under IRC Section 3508, a licensed real estate agent is treated as a non-employee if substantially all pay is tied to output and:
c: The agent works at least 40 hours a week
A written contract says so for tax purposes
The agent receives a modest base salary
The broker withholds the agent's taxes
questions.x: IRC 3508 requires output-based pay and a written contract stating the agent will not be treated as an employee for tax purposes. A base salary is the trap: time-based pay points toward employment.

questions.q: To comply with NY's 1986 independent contractor law, each of the following is required EXCEPT:
c: A licensed salesperson
Pay based on sales output
A contract signed freely
A guaranteed weekly salary
questions.x: A salary based on time would defeat contractor status. Licensing, output-based pay, and a written contract not signed under duress are the requirements. The free-signing choice is the trap: the no-duress rule is real.

questions.q: A broker requires salespersons to work set office hours and docks their splits for absences, though each signed an independent contractor agreement. Most likely:
c: They may be treated as employees
The written contract controls
The broker did nothing wrong
They will lose their licenses
questions.x: Substance controls over form: a contract will not overcome actual direction and control of hours. The contract-controls choice is the trap: the label is not decisive.

questions.q: If salespersons are deemed employees, the broker becomes responsible for:
c: Their MLS dues and license fees
Their continuing education costs
Payroll taxes and employee insurance
Their personal auto and phone bills
questions.x: Reclassification puts payroll obligations on the broker: withholding, Social Security, unemployment insurance, workers' compensation, and disability insurance. License fees are the trap: they are not an employer mandate.

questions.q: A consequence to salespersons who are reclassified as employees is that they:
c: Lose Schedule C business deductions
Repay commissions earned that year
Lose their licenses until renewal
Have to apply for broker licenses
questions.x: Employees cannot deduct business expenses on Schedule C, and their pay becomes subject to withholding. Losing their licenses is the trap: tax status does not affect licensure.

questions.q: 19 NYCRR 175.21 requires brokers to provide salespersons with:
c: A salary or draw against commission
Assigned territories and set floor hours
Regular, frequent, consistent supervision
Health insurance and paid office space
questions.x: 175.21 requires real supervision of salespersons' real estate activities. Territories and hours are the trap: they would point toward employment and are not required.

questions.q: Under 19 NYCRR 175.23, brokers keep records of transactions for at least:
c: 1 year
3 years
2 years
5 years
questions.x: Transaction records must be kept at least 3 years and made available to DOS. 2 years is the trap: it is the license term.

questions.q: A broker can do each of the following without undermining independent contractor status EXCEPT:
c: Review ads for compliance
Provide desks and phones
Offer optional floor time
Pay hourly for open houses
questions.x: Hourly pay is pay for time, not output, and is inconsistent with contractor status. Compliance review is the trap: it is supervision the broker is required to provide.

questions.q: Under a compliant independent contractor relationship, who may end the relationship?
c: The broker, with 30 days notice
The salesperson, with cause
The DOS, on the broker's request
Either party, at any time
questions.x: Either the broker or the salesperson may terminate the relationship at any time. The broker-notice choice is the trap: a one-sided termination right looks like employment control.

questions.q: A broker tells new salespersons to sign independent contractor agreements immediately or lose their desks that day, with no chance to read them. The arrangement is vulnerable because:
c: The contract cannot be signed under duress
Contractor agreements need a notary's seal
Contractor agreements need DOS approval
Contractor agreements need an attorney
questions.x: New York's 1986 law requires that the written contract not be signed under duress. Notarization and DOS approval are the traps: neither is required.

questions.q: Which statement about supervision and independent contractor status is correct?
c: Any supervision converts a salesperson to an employee
Experienced salespersons need no broker supervision
Brokers supervise but do not control methods and hours
Supervision is optional under an independent contract
questions.x: NY requires supervision under 175.21; what creates employment is direction and control of how, when, and where the work is done. The any-supervision choice is the trap.

questions.q: Which event ends a listing by operation of law rather than by an act of the parties?
c: Mutual agreement to cancel
Death of the principal
The broker's renunciation
The seller's revocation
questions.x: Death, incapacity, bankruptcy, and destruction of the property end agency by operation of law. The seller's revocation is the trap: it ends the agency, but by an act of a party.

questions.q: A broker quits an exclusive listing two months early to take a better job. The broker:
c: Has no power to end the agency
Keeps a right to the commission
Converts the listing to an open listing
Can renounce but may owe damages
questions.x: Either party has the power to end an agency, but ending it in breach of contract can create liability. Keeping a right to the commission is the trap: abandoning the listing forfeits it.

questions.q: Which is an agency coupled with an interest?
c: A broker who co-owns the listed home
A broker owed a 5% commission
A broker under an exclusive listing
A broker who has a signed buyer
questions.x: An agency coupled with an interest exists when the agent holds its own interest in the property, such as part ownership. The commission choice is the trap: expecting a commission is not an interest in the property.

questions.q: Why should every exclusive listing state a definite expiration date?
c: It lets the broker renew the listing alone
It allows a net price clause to apply
It sets when the seller's duty ends
It replaces the agency disclosure form
questions.x: A definite term tells the seller when the exclusive obligation ends and prevents disputes. Letting the broker renew alone is the trap: renewal needs the seller's agreement.

questions.q: A brokerage's SOP requires buyers to show photo ID before touring. An agent skips the ID check for a friend. Under RPL 442-h, this is a problem because:
c: SOPs apply equally to all buyers
Photo ID is barred by fair housing
SOPs need DOS approval for waivers
Friends need a separate agreement
questions.x: The SOP law requires the firm to apply its requirements, like ID or pre-approval, equally to every prospective buyer. The fair housing choice is the trap: ID is a permitted requirement if applied uniformly.

questions.q: Which transaction calls for the RPL 443 agency disclosure form?
c: Lease of a Queens warehouse
Sale of a Midtown office tower
Sale of a Brooklyn condo unit
Sale of a vacant commercial lot
questions.x: RPL 443 covers residential property: 1 to 4 family homes, condos, and co-ops, plus residential rentals. Vacant land is the trap: it falls under the anti-discrimination form, not the agency form.

questions.q: A listing agent sits down with a seller to sign an exclusive right to sell. When should the agency disclosure form be presented?
c: Right after the listing is signed
Before the listing is signed
At the first open house
When an offer comes in
questions.x: RPL 443 requires the listing agent to give the form before entering into the listing agreement. Right after signing is the trap: disclosure is supposed to inform the seller's decision to sign.

questions.q: A seller's agent may give the agency disclosure form to a buyer at each of these moments EXCEPT:
c: When the buyer first discusses needs
During a call about the buyer's budget
Before discussing the buyer's motives
After the buyer signs a contract
questions.x: The form goes to the buyer at first substantive contact, which is when needs, motivation, or finances come up, or before. After the contract is the trap: that is far too late.

questions.q: A buyer's agent meets a new buyer, discusses her budget, and plans to sign a buyer agency agreement. The disclosure form should be given:
c: After the agreement is signed
When she makes her first offer
At her first showing of a home
Before the agreement is signed
questions.x: RPL 443 requires a buyer's agent to give the form before entering into the buyer agency agreement. After signing is the trap: disclosure has to precede the commitment.

questions.q: First substantive contact occurs when a consumer discusses each of the following EXCEPT:
c: The age of the roof
Her moving deadline
Her maximum budget
Her mortgage status
questions.x: First substantive contact is triggered by discussing the consumer's needs, motivation, or finances. The roof's age is a property fact. The moving deadline is the trap: it reveals motivation.

questions.q: A declaration of refusal under RPL 443 is:
c: A form the consumer signs at once
A DOS notice sent to the consumer
A sworn statement by the licensee
An addendum to the listing contract
questions.x: When a consumer refuses to sign, the licensee signs a written declaration under oath or affirmation of the facts of the refusal and keeps it at least 3 years. A consumer-signed form is the trap: the consumer just refused to sign.

questions.q: A licensee obtained a signed agency disclosure acknowledgment in March 2026. Until at least when does the licensee keep it?
c: March 2027
March 2029
March 2028
March 2033
questions.x: Agency disclosure acknowledgments are kept at least 3 years. March 2028 is the trap: it reflects the 2-year license term rather than the 3-year rule.

questions.q: A buyer hesitates to sign the agency disclosure form, worried it commits her to the agent. The agent can truthfully say:
c: The form binds both of us
The form is not a contract
The form is optional now
The form sets the fee due
questions.x: The form states "This is not a contract"; signing acknowledges receipt of the information. Optional is the trap: giving the form is required, though the consumer may refuse to sign.
questions.concept: Disclosure form is not a contract

questions.q: Which property type falls outside the RPL 443 agency disclosure requirement?
c: A Manhattan co-op
A Queens condo unit
A two-family home
A retail storefront
questions.x: RPL 443 covers residential 1 to 4 family, condos, and co-ops; commercial property is outside it. The co-op is the trap: co-ops were brought under the law in 2011.

questions.q: The 2011 amendments to the NY agency disclosure law did each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Add commercial property
Add condos and co-ops
Add residential rentals
Add advance dual consent
questions.x: The 2011 amendments covered condos and co-ops, extended disclosure to residential rentals, and added advance consent to dual agency. Commercial property stayed outside, which is the answer. Advance consent is the trap because it sounds procedural.

questions.q: Can a licensee switch from customer service to representing that customer in the same transaction?
c: No, roles are fixed once the deal starts
Yes, with the customer's consent alone
Yes, with new disclosure and both consents
Yes, by giving written notice to the DOS
questions.x: Changing roles in the same deal makes the firm a dual agent, so it needs new disclosure and informed written consent of both parties. The customer-consent choice is the trap: the existing client has to consent too.

questions.q: A licensee meets a buyer interested in a vacant commercial lot in Albany. Which disclosure form is required at first substantive contact?
c: The anti-discrimination form
The RPL 443 agency form
The lead paint disclosure
The property condition form
questions.x: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form applies to every property type, including vacant land. The agency form is the trap: it covers residential property only.

questions.q: First substantive contact can occur in each of these settings EXCEPT:
c: A phone call about budget
An email about motivation
A chat about the weather
A text about a job move
questions.x: First substantive contact is about the substance of the conversation, not the medium: phone, email, and text all count once needs, motivation, or finances come up. Small talk does not trigger it.

questions.q: A buyer checked advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents. Her agent's firm now has a listing she wants. The firm:
c: May proceed without telling her about it
May proceed, and informs her it is happening
Needs DOS approval before proceeding
Has to refer her to a different brokerage
questions.x: Advance consent authorizes dual agency with designated agents ahead of time, but the firm still informs her when it arises. Proceeding silently is the trap: consent does not mean secrecy.

questions.q: Each of the following supports statutory nonemployee status under IRC 3508 EXCEPT:
c: Being a licensed real estate agent
Pay tied to sales or other output
A written non-employee contract
An hourly wage from the broker
questions.x: IRC 3508 requires a licensed agent, substantially all pay tied to output, and a written contract. Hourly wages are time-based and point toward employment. Licensing is the trap: it is part of the test.

questions.q: A broker pays a new salesperson a weekly $500 draw that never has to be repaid, regardless of sales. Under NY's 1986 law, this threatens contractor status because:
c: The draw needs DOS approval
The draw needs a CPA review
Draws are barred for new licensees
Pay has to depend on output
questions.x: NY's independent contractor law requires compensation directly related to sales or other output. A guaranteed weekly payment is time-based. The DOS approval choice is the trap: no agency approves draws.

questions.q: Each of the following suggests a broker exercises employee-like direction and control EXCEPT:
c: Reviewing contracts for legal compliance
Requiring fixed hours at the office desk
Docking splits when agents miss meetings
Dictating which days agents may prospect
questions.x: Fixed hours, penalties, and dictating schedules are direction and control. Reviewing contracts is supervision the broker is required to provide. The meeting-penalty choice is the trap: it punishes absence like an employer would.

questions.q: DOL auditors reclassify a firm's salespersons as employees. Which new cost falls on the broker?
c: The agents' continuing education
The agents' license renewal fees
Workers' compensation coverage
The agents' MLS membership dues
questions.x: Employers owe workers' compensation, unemployment and disability insurance, and tax withholding. License fees are the trap: they are an individual licensee cost in either status.

questions.q: A salesperson who deducts car and marketing costs on Schedule C is reclassified as an employee. The main tax effect on the salesperson is that:
c: Past commissions are repaid
Schedule C deductions go away
Income tax is no longer due
The license is suspended
questions.x: Employees cannot deduct business expenses on Schedule C, and their pay becomes subject to withholding. License suspension is the trap: tax status has nothing to do with licensing.

questions.q: Which broker practice best satisfies 19 NYCRR 175.21?
c: A fixed salary for each agent
Regular review of agents' deals
Assigned territories by street
Set daily hours in the office
questions.x: 175.21 requires regular, frequent, and consistent supervision of salespersons' real estate activities. Set hours is the trap: it is control that points toward employment, not supervision.

questions.q: A broker closes a deal in June 2026. Under 175.23, the transaction file is kept until at least:
c: June 2027
June 2028
June 2031
June 2029
questions.x: Brokers keep transaction records at least 3 years. June 2028 is the trap: it reflects the 2-year license term.

questions.q: Which broker policy is most likely to undermine independent contractor status?
c: A $20 hourly rate for floor time
Ad review for legal compliance
Use of a shared conference room
Optional training classes offered
questions.x: Hourly pay rewards time rather than output, which is inconsistent with contractor status. Ad review is the trap: it is required supervision.

questions.q: Under NY's independent contractor rules, each of the following is consistent with contractor status EXCEPT:
c: Pay that depends on closed sales
A written contract signed freely
Termination by the broker alone
The agent may leave at any time
questions.x: Either party may end a compliant relationship at any time; a one-sided termination right is employer-like control. Leaving at any time is the trap: it is a feature of contractor status.

questions.q: Under NY's 1986 independent contractor law, the written contract between broker and salesperson is valid only if it:
c: Was not signed under duress
Was approved by DOS first
Was signed before a notary
Was drafted by an attorney
questions.x: The 1986 law requires that the written contract not be executed under duress. DOS approval is the trap: DOS does not review contractor agreements.

questions.q: A broker reviews every listing agreement and holds monthly compliance meetings, but lets agents set their own hours and methods. This broker is:
c: Turning agents into employees
Violating the supervision rule
Supervising without controlling
Acting as a dual agent for each
questions.x: 175.21 requires supervision; employment comes from direction and control of hours and methods. Turning agents into employees is the trap: compliance oversight is not control.

questions.q: A homeowner's adult daughter asks a broker to list her father's house. The deed is in the father's name alone, and he is alive and competent. Who must authorize the listing?
c: The daughter, because she manages her father's affairs informally
The father, or someone holding a valid power of attorney from him
Either of them, since family members share implied authority to sell
The broker, once the daughter confirms the price in writing
questions.x: The owner of record is the principal, so the father (or an agent he validly appointed) must create the agency. Informal family management is the trap: helping with bills or keys gives no legal authority to hire a broker or bind the owner.

questions.q: In a listing for a house owned by one person, the principal is the:
c: Salesperson who takes the listing
Listing broker named in the agreement
Owner who signs the listing agreement
Buyer who eventually signs the contract
questions.x: The principal is the party who hires the agent and is represented, here the owner. The listing broker is the agent, not the principal, which is the most common mix-up: the broker acts for the principal and owes the principal fiduciary duties.

questions.q: A seller's listing broker receives a full-price offer while the seller is traveling and unreachable. Without any other authorization, the broker may:
c: Present the offer when the seller can be reached and keep the buyer informed
Accept the offer, since it matches the seller's list price exactly
Sign the contract for the seller and send it to the seller for initials later
Accept the offer if the listing is an exclusive right to sell agreement
questions.x: A listing broker is a special agent with authority to find buyers and present offers, not to accept them or sign contracts. Matching the list price is the trap: a list price is an invitation to make offers, and acceptance still belongs to the seller unless the seller grants written signing authority.

questions.q: A listing broker, acting under an ordinary exclusive right to sell agreement, may do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Advertise the property and hold open houses
Present every offer to the seller promptly
Negotiate price and terms with buyers
Accept an offer for the seller
questions.x: Marketing, presenting offers, and negotiating are all within a listing broker's special agency. Accepting an offer binds the seller to a contract, and that power stays with the seller unless separately granted in writing, such as through a power of attorney.

questions.q: Under New York's General Obligations Law, a power of attorney signed in 2025 becomes effective when:
c: The principal signs it in front of two witnesses
The agent signs it and the agent's signature is acknowledged
The principal's signature is acknowledged by a notary
The power of attorney is recorded with the county clerk's office
questions.x: GOL 5-1501B requires the principal's acknowledged signature, two witnesses, and the agent's acknowledged signature, and the power takes effect on the acknowledgment of the agent's signature. The principal's acknowledgment is the trap: it is required, but it does not by itself make the power effective.

questions.q: An owner signs a NY power of attorney before a notary and two witnesses, naming her nephew to sell her condo. The nephew has not signed the form. Before closing, what is missing?
c: Nothing, because the owner's acknowledged signature completes it
A court order approving the power for a real estate sale
Recording the power before the contract can be signed
The nephew's own signature, acknowledged like a deed
questions.x: A New York power of attorney is not effective until the agent signs and that signature is acknowledged. The owner's side is complete, which is why the first choice tempts. No court order is needed, and recording happens with the deed when the power is used to convey, not as a condition of signing.

questions.q: A buyer's neighbor, who holds no license, tells a broker about a listing and later asks for $2,000 when the sale closes. The broker may:
c: Pay it, if the seller signs a written consent to the payment
Pay it, because one referral does not make the neighbor a broker
Decline, because NY bars sharing a fee with unlicensed people
Pay it, if the amount is shown on the closing statement
questions.x: RPL 442 forbids a broker from paying any part of its compensation to an unlicensed person, outside narrow exceptions such as out-of-state brokers and parties to the transaction. The one-time referral is the trap: the statute has no occasional-referral exception, and seller consent or disclosure cannot cure it.

questions.q: A New York broker may share part of a commission with each of the following EXCEPT:
c: A salesperson licensed with that broker
A broker regularly doing business in another state
A doorman who sent the buyer to the open house
A licensed broker at a cooperating firm
questions.x: RPL 442 permits fee sharing with the broker's own licensees, other licensed brokers, and out-of-state brokers. A doorman who refers a buyer is an unlicensed person, so paying him violates the law no matter how small the amount or how helpful the tip.

questions.q: A salesperson who took a listing leaves for another brokerage. The listing:
c: Stays with the original broker, who is the agent
Moves with the salesperson, who is the seller's agent
Ends automatically when the salesperson resigns
Becomes an open listing shared by both firms
questions.x: The listing contract is between the seller and the brokerage, and the salesperson acts for the broker. When the salesperson leaves, the listing stays. The trap is thinking the salesperson is personally the seller's agent: the salesperson carries out the broker's agency and has no separate contract with the seller.

questions.q: Within a brokerage, a salesperson who works on the firm's listings and buyer clients is best described as the broker's:
c: Special agent
Universal agent
Subagent of each seller
General agent
questions.x: A salesperson acts for the broker across a range of ongoing matters in the broker's business, which makes the salesperson a general agent of the broker. Special agent is the trap: that describes the broker's relationship to a single seller or buyer for one transaction.

questions.q: An owner signs a power of attorney giving her son authority over every category of her financial affairs, including real estate. Relative to the owner, the son is a:
c: Universal agent
Special agent
General agent
Subagent of the owner
questions.x: A broad power of attorney covering everything the principal could legally do in her affairs creates a universal agent. General agent is the closest wrong answer: a general agent handles a range of matters in one business, like a property manager, not all of the principal's affairs.

questions.q: A broker hired under a listing to find a buyer for one particular house is acting as a:
c: General agent
Special agent
Universal agent
Dual agent
questions.x: A listing is authority for one specific transaction, so the listing broker is a special agent. General agent is the trap: a property manager running a building's ongoing business is a general agent, but a broker selling one house is not.

questions.q: A seller tells her listing agent in writing not to hold open houses. The agent believes open houses would bring a higher price. The agent should:
c: Hold one open house, since loyalty requires seeking the best price
Explain the likely cost of the choice, then follow the instruction
Refuse the instruction, since it limits the agent's ability to market
Ask the broker to override the seller's instruction for her benefit
questions.x: Skipping open houses is a lawful choice, so obedience applies; the agent advises and then follows it. The trap is using loyalty to justify overriding the client. Loyalty serves the client's goals, and an agent who substitutes judgment for a lawful instruction breaches obedience.

questions.q: A listing agent must follow each of the following seller instructions EXCEPT:
c: Show the home by appointment with the owner present
Do not install a lockbox on the front door
Do not show the home to buyers who use wheelchairs
Present offers above a stated minimum price, and no others
questions.x: Obedience covers lawful instructions only. Refusing to show to buyers with disabilities violates fair housing law, so the agent must refuse it. The other three are lawful choices about the seller's own property, including a minimum price threshold for offers, which many sellers set in writing.

questions.q: A seller asks his agent to tell buyers there is a competing offer when there is none. If the agent complies, the agent has committed:
c: Puffing, which is lawful negotiating opinion
A breach of obedience to the seller
Misrepresentation to the buyers
No violation, since the seller instructed it
questions.x: A made-up competing offer is a false statement of material fact that buyers rely on, so it is misrepresentation. Puffing is the trap: puffing is exaggerated opinion about quality, like "the best block in Astoria," not an invented fact. A client's instruction is no defense.

questions.q: When a seller insists that the listing broker carry out an unlawful instruction, the broker's best course is to:
c: Comply after getting the instruction signed by the seller
Comply, since the seller bears the legal risk of the act
Refuse and keep marketing while ignoring the dispute
Refuse and, if the seller persists, withdraw
questions.x: Obedience does not extend to unlawful acts, so the broker refuses, and if the client insists, ends the relationship. The signed instruction is the trap: DOS disciplines the licensee who commits the violation, and a client's signature does not shift that responsibility.

questions.q: A salesperson owns 30% of an LLC that wants to buy a house listed with her brokerage. Under NY rules, she must:
c: Make her interest clearly known to the seller first
Sell her LLC interest before the offer is presented to the seller
Get the broker's written approval, which replaces seller consent
Do nothing, since the LLC is a separate legal entity
questions.x: 19 NYCRR 175.4 bars a broker from buying a listing, directly or indirectly, without first making the true position clearly known to the owner. The separate-entity argument is the trap: buying through a company is an indirect purchase that the rule covers.

questions.q: A listing agent's sister makes an offer on the agent's listing. The agent mentions nothing. The seller accepts and later learns the truth. The main breach is:
c: Obedience, since the seller did not tell the agent to disclose
Accounting, since no deposit records named the sister
Confidentiality, since the sister learned about the listing
Loyalty and disclosure, by hiding her personal interest
questions.x: An agent with a family tie to the buyer has a personal interest the client must know about before deciding. Hiding it breaches loyalty and disclosure. Obedience is the trap: the duty to disclose a conflict exists whether or not the client asks for it.

questions.q: In Brooklyn, a seller accepted an offer by email last week. Contracts are not yet signed. A higher offer arrives. The listing agent should:
c: Decline it, since an accepted offer binds the seller
Present it to the seller, who decides what to do
Forward it to the first buyer so he can match it
Hold it until the first buyer's attorney responds
questions.x: Downstate, an accepted offer is not a binding contract; the deal binds when the attorney-drafted contract is signed and the deposit delivered. Until then the seller is entitled to hear new offers. Declining it is the trap: the agent would be deciding for the client and misstating that the home is under contract.

questions.q: After a higher offer arrives before contract signing, a Queens seller tells his agent he will honor the first accepted offer. The agent should:
c: Keep urging the higher offer, since loyalty requires the top price
Refuse, because the instruction lowers the seller's proceeds
Tell the second buyer the first deal is binding under NY law
Confirm the seller understands the difference, then follow it
questions.x: Honoring a handshake is a lawful choice for the principal. The agent makes sure it is informed and then obeys. The trap is reading loyalty as maximizing price at all costs. Telling the second buyer the first deal is legally binding would also be false, since no contract has been signed.

questions.q: Under RPL 442-c, a salesperson's violation of the license law can lead to discipline of the supervising broker when the broker:
c: Employed the salesperson at the time of the violation
Had actual knowledge of it or kept the benefits after notice
Failed to report it to DOS within 30 days of the closing
Signed the listing agreement under which the violation occurred
questions.x: RPL 442-c says a salesperson's violation is not by itself cause to discipline the broker, unless the broker had actual knowledge or retains the benefits of the transaction after notice. Mere employment is the trap: brokers must supervise, but discipline under this section turns on knowledge or benefit.

questions.q: A broker learns that a salesperson hid a conflict from a seller client. The deal has not closed. To protect the firm's license, the broker should:
c: Act promptly: disclose to the client and remove the salesperson
Let the deal close, then refund the salesperson's share of the fee
Wait for a complaint, since the broker did not commit the act
Have the salesperson sign a statement accepting full blame
questions.x: Once the broker has actual knowledge, keeping the benefits of the tainted deal without acting exposes the broker under RPL 442-c. Prompt disclosure and removal are the answer. Waiting for a complaint is the trap: knowledge, not a complaint, is what changes the broker's position.

questions.q: A seller asks her agent which of two offers to take. One buyer is in-house, so the firm would keep the full fee. The agent's advice should rest on:
c: The seller's net proceeds, risk, and timing
Which offer earns the brokerage the larger fee
Which buyer the agent personally likes better
Staying neutral, since advice favors one buyer
questions.x: Loyalty means advice aimed at the client's interests: price, certainty, and timing. The firm's fee is the self-interest loyalty excludes. Neutrality is the trap: a seller's agent owes the buyers no neutrality, and refusing to advise shortchanges the client.

questions.q: All of the following are breaches of the duty of loyalty EXCEPT:
c: Steering a client to the offer that pays the agent more
Delaying an offer to help a buyer the agent favors
Advising the client to take a safer cash offer
Buying the client's property secretly through a relative
questions.x: Candid advice that serves the client's goals, such as favoring certainty of closing, is what loyalty requires. Steering for a bigger fee, delaying offers for a favored buyer, and secret purchases through relatives all place the agent's interest ahead of the client's.

questions.q: During a showing, a building superintendent tells a buyer's agent that the board is about to vote on a large assessment. The agent should:
c: Wait for written confirmation before mentioning it
Tell the buyer client and suggest how to verify it
Ask the seller's agent first, then decide whether to tell
Keep it quiet, since the source was not the seller
questions.concept: Disclosure of material facts to client
questions.x: A pending assessment is material to the buyer, so disclosure requires passing it on, labeled as unconfirmed, with a plan to check it. Waiting for written confirmation is the trap: holding back a material lead lets the agent, not the client, decide what matters.

questions.q: The fiduciary duty that requires an agent to tell the client every material fact the agent learns is:
c: Accounting
Obedience
Confidentiality
Disclosure
questions.concept: Disclosure of material facts to client
questions.x: Disclosure obligates the agent to pass material information to the principal. Confidentiality is the trap because it is the mirror image: it governs what the agent keeps about the client, not what the agent must tell the client.

questions.q: A seller asks a buyer's agent whether the buyer's job is stable. The agent knows the buyer may be laid off. The agent should:
c: Say the job is secure, to protect the client's deal
Reveal the layoff risk, since honesty is owed to sellers
Decline to discuss the buyer's finances further
Say the buyer is paying cash, so employment is not relevant
questions.x: The layoff risk is the client's confidential information, so the agent declines to discuss it; the agent also may not lie. The trap is the false reassurance: protecting a secret with a false statement turns a confidentiality issue into misrepresentation.

questions.q: A seller's agent is asked by a buyer why the sellers are moving. The sellers are divorcing. Each of these answers is acceptable EXCEPT:
c: "I can't discuss my clients' personal situation."
"They're relocating for a new job in Albany."
"You'd have to ask your attorney to raise it."
"I'm not able to share that, sorry."
questions.x: Confidentiality allows the agent to decline, but inventing a reason is a false statement to a customer. The tempting choice sounds harmless, yet it is a fabricated fact, and honesty to the other side has no exception for small lies.

questions.q: A listing agent says "no assessments are planned" while the board minutes in her own file show an assessment vote scheduled. Her statement is best described as:
c: Puffing about the building's condition
At least negligent misrepresentation
Innocent misrepresentation by the agent
A breach of confidentiality to the seller
questions.x: A specific claim about assessments is a fact, and the contrary information was in her own file, so she knew or should have known: negligent at minimum, intentional if she knew. Innocent misrepresentation is the trap: it requires an honest belief with no reason to doubt.

questions.q: An agent repeats the seller's claim that the boiler is two years old. The agent had no reason to doubt it, but it is actually twelve years old. This is:
c: Intentional misrepresentation
Negligent misrepresentation
Puffing
Innocent misrepresentation
questions.x: An honest belief with no reason to doubt makes it innocent misrepresentation, which can still support rescission. Negligent misrepresentation is the trap: it applies when the agent should have known, for example if the boiler's date plate was in plain view.

questions.q: A listing agent tells a buyer's agent, "Between us, my seller has to close by June." The buyer's agent should:
c: Tell the buyer client; it bears on negotiation
Keep it private, honoring the other agent's request
Report the listing agent to the seller right away
Ignore it, since it is not a fact about the property
questions.x: The buyer's agent owes disclosure to the buyer, and a seller's deadline is material to the buyer's negotiating position. Keeping it private is the trap: the buyer's agent owes the seller's side honesty, not confidentiality. The listing agent is the one who breached a duty.

questions.q: A seller's agent hears a buyer say, "I'd pay $40,000 more if I had to." The buyer has no agent. The seller's agent should:
c: Keep it private, since the buyer spoke freely
Tell the seller after the buyer signs a contract
Tell the seller, who is the agent's client
Advise the buyer to retract the statement first
questions.x: The buyer is a customer and is owed honesty, not confidentiality. The seller is the client and is owed disclosure of material facts, including what a buyer would pay. Advising the buyer is the trap: that would be acting as the buyer's agent and risks implied dual agency.

questions.q: Under RPL 443-a, if a buyer wants to know whether a death occurred in a home, the buyer may:
c: Submit a written inquiry that the seller may answer
Demand a sworn statement from the seller's agent
Require the seller to answer, since asking makes it material
Ask the Department of State to search its records
questions.x: RPL 443-a provides a written inquiry route through the seller's agent; the seller chooses whether to respond, and the agent reports the answer only with the seller's consent. The trap is thinking that asking creates a duty to disclose. It does not.

questions.q: Under RPL 443-a, each of the following is NOT a material fact a seller's agent must disclose EXCEPT:
c: A suicide in the home three years ago
An occupant's HIV diagnosis
A natural death in the bedroom
A known crack in a foundation wall
questions.x: RPL 443-a removes psychological stigma, such as deaths, felonies, and non-transmissible illness, from the list of material facts. A known structural defect is a physical material fact that must be disclosed. The other three are exactly what the statute covers.

questions.q: Which fiduciary duty continues after the agency relationship has ended at closing?
c: Obedience
Loyalty
Confidentiality
Reasonable care and skill
questions.x: Confidentiality survives the end of the agency, so a former client's private information stays protected. Loyalty is the tempting choice, but the duty to act for the client ends when the agency ends; the duty to keep the client's secrets does not.

questions.q: A year after closing, an agent tells a dinner guest that a former seller client "took a lowball because of debts." The agent has:
c: Breached confidentiality, which outlasts the agency
Done nothing wrong, since the agency ended at closing
Breached loyalty, which lasts one year after closing
Breached disclosure, owed to the dinner guest
questions.x: The client's finances were confidential and remain so after closing. The trap is believing all duties end with the agency: most do, but confidentiality continues. There is no one-year loyalty tail, and no duty of disclosure runs to a stranger at dinner.

questions.q: A broker receives a buyer's deposit check on a Thursday. Under 19 NYCRR 175.1, the check must be deposited in the escrow account by the end of:
c: Friday, the next business day
The following Tuesday
The following Thursday, one week later
The day the contract is fully signed
questions.concept: Escrow deposit within three business days
questions.x: 175.1 allows three business days: Friday, Monday, and Tuesday. The contract signing date is the trap: the deadline runs from receipt of the money, not from when the deal becomes binding, and the check must be kept secure until it is deposited.

questions.q: Under 19 NYCRR 175.1, each of the following is required for money a broker holds for others EXCEPT:
c: A separate, special bank account
A federally insured depository
Deposit within three business days
A separate account for each deal
questions.concept: Escrow deposit within three business days
questions.x: The rule requires a separate special account, federally insured, with deposit within three business days, but one escrow account may hold deposits from many transactions if the broker's records track each one. A separate account per deal is the trap: it sounds careful, but the rule does not require it.

questions.q: A broker short on cash moves $2,000 from the escrow account to pay office rent, intending to repay it next week. This is:
c: Allowed, if repaid before any closing needs the funds
Commingling and conversion of others' money
Allowed, if the broker's commissions cover it
A bookkeeping error, if recorded in the ledger
questions.x: Escrow funds belong to others and may not be mixed with or used for the broker's business. Using them for rent is conversion, grounds for revocation and possibly criminal. Repaying before closing is the trap: the violation happens when the money is taken, not when someone notices.

questions.q: Depositing a client's earnest money into the broker's own operating account is called:
c: Commingling
Puffing
Self-dealing
Ratification
questions.x: Commingling is mixing client funds with the broker's own. Self-dealing is the trap: it describes an agent's undisclosed personal interest in the transaction, such as buying the listing, not mixing money.

questions.q: Under 19 NYCRR 175.1, interest earned on money a broker holds in escrow may be:
c: Kept by the broker as a custodial fee
Kept at 1% per year, with the balance paid to the buyer
Split evenly between the buyer and the seller
Applied to the earned commission, with consent of all
questions.x: The broker may not keep the interest, except that it may be applied to and deducted from an earned commission with the consent of all parties. The 1% figure is the trap: that is the landlord's allowance on tenant security deposits under GOL 7-103.

questions.q: A buyer's $20,000 deposit earned $150 while in a broker's escrow account. The seller, buyer, and broker all agree in writing that it may reduce the commission. The broker:
c: Still has to remit it to the buyer by law
Has to remit it to the seller at closing
May apply it to the earned commission
May keep it in addition to the commission
questions.x: With the consent of all parties, escrow interest may be applied to and deducted from the earned commission. Keeping it on top of the commission is the trap: the broker may never pocket escrow interest as extra income.

questions.q: A managing agent is offered a 10% rebate by a roofer on all work ordered for the owner's building. Under 19 NYCRR 175.3, the agent:
c: May accept it with the owner's informed consent
May accept it, since the owner's price does not change
May accept it if the rebate is under 15% of each invoice
May accept it, if it is reported to the IRS as income
questions.x: 175.3 bars a managing broker from taking a commission, rebate, or profit on expenditures for the client without the client's full knowledge and consent. The unchanged price is the trap: a secret rebate still distorts the manager's choice of contractor.

questions.q: A broker managing an owner's building may do each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Collect rents and deposit them for the owner
Hire contractors and pay them from owner funds
Keep a secret discount from a supplier
Charge the management fee the owner agreed to
questions.x: A secret discount or rebate on purchases made for the owner is a profit on client expenditures without consent, barred by 175.3. Collecting rents, hiring contractors, and charging the agreed fee are ordinary parts of a management agency.

questions.q: A landlord of a 9-unit building in Buffalo collects security deposits. Under GOL 7-103, the deposits must be:
c: Kept in the landlord's operating account
Placed in an interest-bearing account at a NY bank
Invested in any fund that earns a market return
Paid to the tenants at the start of each lease year
questions.x: In buildings with six or more units, deposits must go into an interest-bearing account at a New York bank, held in trust and not commingled, with the tenant notified of the bank and amount. Any market fund is the trap: the statute requires a bank account, not investments.

questions.q: Under GOL 7-103, a landlord holding a tenant's security deposit in an interest-bearing account may keep:
c: The entire interest as a custodial fee
Half of the interest earned each year
1% per year of the deposit for administration
Nothing, since the interest goes to the tenant
questions.x: GOL 7-103 lets the landlord retain 1% per year of the deposit as an administrative fee, in place of all other charges; the remaining interest belongs to the tenant. "Nothing" is the trap: the tenant's share is the interest after that 1% allowance.

questions.q: A listing agent advertises a house as having a "legal finished basement apartment" based on the seller's word. Records show no permit. The agent's main failure is:
c: Reasonable care
Obedience to the seller
Confidentiality
Accounting
questions.x: Stating a checkable fact about legal use without checking it falls below the competence expected of a licensee. Obedience is the trap: following the seller's description is not an instruction-following issue, and lawful obedience never covers spreading an unverified claim.

questions.q: Each of the following reflects the duty of reasonable care EXCEPT:
c: Checking the assessment roll before stating legal use
Getting help on a deal type the agent has not handled before
Pulling recent sales before recommending a price
Drafting a land use application for the client
questions.x: Drafting legal applications and giving legal opinions is attorney work, so a licensee who does it is overstepping, not exercising care. Verifying facts, getting help when inexperienced, and basing price advice on sales data are all what reasonable care looks like.

questions.q: A building owner lets her brother quote rents and show vacancies for a year. A tenant, reasonably relying on the brother's offer, signs and moves in. The owner may be bound by:
c: Ratification
Express agency
Estoppel
Implied agency with the tenant
questions.x: Estoppel (apparent authority) binds a principal whose conduct made someone's authority look real to a third party who relied on it. Ratification is the trap: it requires the principal's approval after the act, and nothing in these facts shows approval.

questions.q: Without authority, a broker signs a lease for an owner's apartment. The owner learns of it, cashes the tenant's rent checks, and sends her own invoices. Agency was created by:
c: Estoppel
Ratification
Express agreement
Implied agency
questions.x: Ratification is the principal's approval, after the fact and with knowledge, of an unauthorized act, often shown by accepting its benefits. Estoppel is the trap: it rests on the principal creating an appearance of authority before the act, not on approval afterward.

questions.q: A seller's agent tells a buyer with no agent, "Offer $30,000 under; I'll help you write the inspection demands." The agent risks:
c: Estoppel with the seller
Implied buyer agency
Ratification by the seller
A net listing violation
questions.x: Advising a party on price and helping them negotiate is conduct that can create an implied agency with that party, producing an undisclosed dual agency. Estoppel is the trap: it concerns a principal's conduct toward third parties, not an agent's conduct toward a customer.

questions.q: An agency relationship created by the words and actions of the parties, without any express agreement, is:
c: Implied agency
Universal agency
Ratified agency
Express agency
questions.x: Implied agency arises from conduct showing that one person is acting for another. Ratified agency is the trap: ratification requires a principal approving an unauthorized act after the fact, which is a different route to agency.

questions.q: Under RPL 443, a licensee may work with a buyer or seller in a capacity other than as an agent when:
c: The property is worth less than $1 million
The parties agree to those terms
The licensee works for a dual agent firm
The buyer has signed no disclosure form
questions.x: RPL 443 recognizes licensees who work with a party, under agreed terms, in a capacity other than as an agent; such a licensee owes honesty but not fiduciary duties. The missing disclosure form is the trap: failing to give the form does not create a non-agency role, it is just a violation.

questions.q: A licensee agrees in writing to coordinate paperwork for an owner without acting as the owner's agent. The licensee owes the owner each of these EXCEPT:
c: Honesty
Fair dealing
Undivided loyalty
Truthful statements
questions.x: A licensee acting in a non-agency capacity owes honesty and fair dealing, but not fiduciary duties such as undivided loyalty. Brokerage can be performed without agency when the parties agree to it; the licensee still may not deceive anyone.

questions.q: A tenant signs a representation agreement with a broker. The landlord, not the tenant, ends up paying the broker's fee. The broker represents:
c: The landlord, who paid the fee
Both parties, as a dual agent
The tenant, under her agreement
Neither, since the fee was shifted
questions.x: Agency comes from the agreement, not from who pays. The tenant signed the representation agreement, so she is the client. The landlord-pays answer is the trap: a fee paid by the other side does not move the broker's loyalty.

questions.q: A broker introduces a tenant to a landlord who never agreed to pay any fee. The lease is signed. Can the broker collect from the landlord as procuring cause?
c: Yes, procuring cause entitles any broker to a fee
Yes, if the broker was licensed during the deal
No, procuring cause applies only to sales
No, the landlord never agreed to pay a fee
questions.x: A commission is owed by the party who agreed to pay it. Procuring cause decides which broker earned a fee that someone agreed to pay; it does not create an obligation from a party who never agreed. A license is required to sue, but it is not enough by itself.

questions.q: Under RPL 440, a person who rents property for another needs a broker's license when the person:
c: Is paid for the work
Is related to the owner
Shows the space more than twice
Signs a lease for the owner
questions.x: The definition of a broker covers one who, for another and for a fee, commission, or other valuable consideration, rents or negotiates. Signing a lease is the trap: authority to sign is an agency question, while the licensing question turns on acting for another for compensation.

questions.q: An owner's unpaid niece shows his vacant apartments and hands out applications. Under the license law, the niece:
c: Needs a salesperson license to show units
Needs to register with DOS as an assistant
Needs a license once she quotes any rent
Does not need a license while unpaid
questions.x: RPL 440 reaches people who act for another for a fee, commission, or other valuable consideration. An unpaid relative is outside that definition. Quoting rent is the trap: it is brokerage activity, but without compensation the license requirement is not triggered.

questions.q: Real estate commission rates in New York are determined by:
c: Agreement between broker and client
The local board of REALTORS
The Department of State fee schedule
The multiple listing service rules
questions.x: Commissions are negotiated between each broker and its client. A board, MLS, or state schedule setting rates would be price fixing or does not exist. The board answer is the trap because agents sometimes describe a common rate as "standard."

questions.q: A licensed broker and a seller agree orally on a 5% fee. Under New York's statute of frauds (GOL 5-701), the oral agreement is:
c: Void, since fee agreements for real estate need a writing
Valid if it covers a lease under one year
Enforceable if the fee is under $10,000
Enforceable, since licensed brokers are exempt
questions.x: GOL 5-701(a)(10) requires a writing for agreements to pay compensation for negotiating real estate deals, but it expressly exempts licensed real estate brokers and salespersons. The trap is the general rule: finders and other unlicensed parties need a writing; licensed brokers do not, though a writing is still the best proof.

questions.q: In a group chat, three brokers from different firms agree not to accept listings below a 5% commission. This is:
c: Market allocation
Price fixing
A tie-in arrangement
Lawful if 5% is the market rate
questions.x: An agreement among competitors on the price of their services, including a commission floor, is price fixing. The market-rate answer is the trap: the violation is the agreement itself, whatever the number.

questions.q: A broker sets a 6% minimum fee for all salespersons at her own firm. A competitor says this is price fixing. The broker's policy is:
c: Lawful, since one firm may set its own prices
Price fixing, since it binds many licensees
Price fixing, unless filed with the Department of State
Lawful, since 6% is below the legal maximum
questions.x: Price fixing requires an agreement between separate competitors. A single firm setting its own fee schedule for its own licensees is ordinary pricing. The legal maximum answer is the trap: there is no legal maximum commission; fees are set by each firm and negotiated with clients.

questions.q: Several brokerages agree that their agents will not show homes listed by a new discount firm. This is:
c: Market allocation
A tie-in arrangement
Lawful independent conduct
A group boycott
questions.x: Competitors agreeing to refuse to deal with a rival is a group boycott. Independent conduct is the trap: one firm's own business choice can be lawful, but several firms agreeing together is a violation.

questions.q: Each of the following could be evidence of a group boycott of a discount broker EXCEPT:
c: A chat where brokers agree not to show its listings
Several firms refusing to co-broke after a meeting
One broker deciding alone not to advertise with it
An association rule barring its members from the MLS
questions.x: A boycott requires concerted action among competitors. One broker deciding alone how to advertise is a unilateral business choice. The chat agreement, the coordinated refusal after a meeting, and an association rule excluding a rival all involve competitors acting together.

questions.q: Two competing firms agree that one will handle listings north of a highway and the other south of it. This is:
c: Price fixing
Group boycotting
Market allocation
A tie-in arrangement
questions.x: Competitors dividing territory so they stop competing is market allocation. Price fixing is the trap because allocation often raises prices, but the label for dividing territories, customers, or price ranges is market allocation.

questions.q: Two firms agree that one will take sellers whose homes are priced over $1 million and the other will take everyone below. This is:
c: Market allocation by customer type
Lawful specialization
Price fixing on luxury fees
A group boycott of sellers
questions.x: Market allocation includes dividing customers or price ranges, not just geography. A firm may choose on its own to specialize in luxury homes; two competitors agreeing to split the market is the violation, which is why specialization is the trap.

questions.q: A developer will sell its condo units only to buyers who use the developer's affiliated brokerage to sell their current homes. This is:
c: A tie-in arrangement
Market allocation by project
A lawful package deal
A group boycott of brokers
questions.x: Conditioning the sale of one product on the purchase of another is a tie-in. The lawful package is the trap: buyers may choose both voluntarily, but making one a condition of the other is the problem.

questions.q: Each of the following describes a tie-in arrangement EXCEPT:
c: Lots sold on condition that buyers list their homes with the seller's firm
Management offered on condition that owners list sales with the firm
A lease offered on condition that the tenant buys the landlord's insurance
A builder offering a discount to buyers who choose its lender
questions.x: A tie-in conditions one sale on buying another product. An optional discount for choosing an affiliate leaves the buyer free to decline, so it is not a condition. The other three make the second purchase mandatory.

questions.q: A buyer's agent skips showing a home that fits the client because the seller offers no buyer-broker compensation. The agent has primarily breached:
c: Confidentiality
Loyalty
Accounting
Obedience
questions.x: Loyalty puts the client's interests ahead of the agent's. Filtering out suitable homes because of the agent's pay favors the agent. Obedience is the trap: the client did not instruct the agent to skip the home, so the issue is loyalty, not following instructions.

questions.q: Under the NAR settlement effective August 17, 2024, which statement is accurate?
c: Buyer-broker fees were capped at 2.5% across the nation
Sellers may no longer pay any buyer's broker
Offers of buyer-broker pay may not appear on the MLS
Buyer agreements are required once an offer is made
questions.x: The settlement barred offers of buyer-broker compensation on the MLS and required written buyer agreements before touring. It set no rate and did not stop sellers from paying buyer's brokers through off-MLS negotiation, which is why the 2.5% cap is the trap.

questions.q: At a networking event, competitors start discussing raising commissions together. A licensee who stays and says nothing:
c: Is protected, since silence is not agreement
Has violated the law if later paid more
Is liable once a contract is signed
May be seen as joining any agreement
questions.x: Agreement can be inferred from participation plus later parallel conduct, so a silent attendee who then charges the discussed rate looks like a participant. The safe course is to object clearly and leave. The silence answer is the trap.

questions.q: New York's state antitrust statute that mirrors the Sherman Act is the:
c: Martin Act
Donnelly Act
Human Rights Law
Real Property Law 443
questions.x: The Donnelly Act, General Business Law 340, is New York's antitrust law and lets the Attorney General and private parties sue in state court. The Martin Act is the trap: it is New York's securities fraud statute, which also governs co-op and condo offering plans.

questions.q: Subagency in a residential sale is created by:
c: The buyer's agent, by accepting a showing
The MLS, automatically for every listing
The listing broker, with seller authorization
The buyer, by signing the agency disclosure form
questions.x: The listing broker appoints subagents, and only with the seller's authorization, because the seller becomes their principal and takes on liability for them. The MLS answer is the trap: blanket subagency through the MLS was made optional decades ago and is rare today.

questions.q: A buyer's agent with a signed buyer agreement is told by the listing agent, "You'll be my subagent." The buyer's agent should:
c: Accept for showings and keep the buyer as a client
Reject subagency; confirm buyer agency in writing
Accept, since the seller is paying the commission
Accept, then disclose dual agency at the closing
questions.x: A cooperating broker may reject an offer of subagency and must do so when representing the buyer; accepting would create undisclosed dual agency. The commission answer is the trap: who pays does not determine whom the agent represents.

questions.q: A subagent tells a buyer that a house has central air when it does not. Besides the subagent, who may be liable to the buyer?
c: The seller, through vicarious liability
The buyer's attorney, for not checking
No one, since the seller did not meet the subagent
The MLS that carried the listing
questions.concept: Liability for subagents vs broker's agents
questions.x: A subagent is the seller's agent through the listing broker, so the seller can be vicariously liable for the subagent's misstatements. Never meeting the subagent is the trap: the seller authorized subagency and became the principal.

questions.q: A listing broker engages another firm's agent as a broker's agent to hold open houses. The broker's agent misstates the roof's age. Who bears vicarious liability for it?
c: The seller, as principal
The buyer's agent
The listing broker
No one besides the agent
questions.concept: Liability for subagents vs broker's agents
questions.x: A broker's agent works for the engaging broker and has no direct relationship with the seller, so the engaging broker, not the seller, answers for its acts. The seller is the trap, since that is the rule for subagents.

questions.q: A seller calls a broker's agent engaged by her listing broker and tells him to cut the price. The broker's agent should:
c: Refer the instruction to the listing broker
Cut the price, since he represents the seller
Refuse, since he owes the seller no duties
Cut it after the seller confirms by email
questions.concept: Broker's agent takes direction from broker
questions.x: A broker's agent has no direct relationship with the seller and takes direction only from the broker that engaged it. He passes the request to that broker. The "no duties" answer is the trap: he still owes the seller fiduciary duties through the listing broker; the seller just cannot direct him.

questions.q: Each of the following is true of a broker's agent working for a listing broker EXCEPT:
c: It works for a different firm than the listing broker
It owes the seller duties through the listing broker
The seller is not vicariously liable for its acts
The seller may give it instructions directly
questions.concept: Broker's agent takes direction from broker
questions.x: Under RPL 443 a broker's agent cooperates with or is engaged by the listing agent, is at a different firm, and has no direct relationship with the seller, so the seller cannot direct it. It still owes the seller duties through the listing broker, and the seller is not vicariously liable for it.

questions.q: At an open house, a buyer with no agent tells the listing broker's broker's agent, "We'd pay $40,000 over asking." The broker's agent should:
c: Keep it confidential for the buyer
Report it to the listing broker
Tell the buyer to retract it
Ignore it, since it was casual
questions.x: A broker's agent on the seller's side owes the seller disclosure through the listing broker, and a buyer's stated willingness to pay more is material. The buyer is a customer, owed honesty, not confidentiality, which is why keeping it secret is the trap.

questions.q: A subagent of the seller owes a buyer-customer each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Honest answers to questions
Disclosure of known material defects
Advice on how much to offer
Fair dealing in negotiations
questions.x: A subagent represents the seller, so it owes the buyer honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material defects, but not advice or loyalty. Giving the buyer offer advice could create an implied agency with the buyer.

questions.q: The blanket unilateral offer of subagency referred to:
c: A seller's written consent to dual agency
An automatic MLS offer of seller subagency
A buyer agreement covering every listing in an MLS
A broker's offer to share fees with unlicensed finders
questions.x: Under the old MLS model, listing a property automatically offered subagency to every member, so agents bringing buyers were legally the seller's subagents. Dual agency consent is the trap: blanket subagency made cooperating agents work for the seller, not for both sides.

questions.q: Today, most cooperating brokers who bring buyers to New York listings act as:
c: Subagents of the seller's broker
Dual agents for both sides
Agents of the MLS itself
Buyer's agents for the buyer
questions.x: Blanket subagency was made optional decades ago and sellers rarely authorize subagency because of vicarious liability, so brokerage is routinely done without it; cooperating brokers usually represent buyers. Subagent is the trap, since it describes the old model.

questions.q: A tenant hires a broker to find an apartment. The landlord agrees to pay that broker's fee. The broker represents:
c: The tenant who hired it
The landlord, who pays the fee
Both parties, as a dual agent
Neither party, as a facilitator
questions.x: A tenant's agent represents the tenant who hired it, whoever ends up paying. The landlord-pays answer is the trap: payment does not create agency, and dual agency requires informed written consent from both sides.

questions.q: A broker holds an exclusive right to rent from an owner. A tenant calls about the apartment. Toward the tenant, the broker is acting as:
c: The tenant's agent
A dual agent
A broker's agent for the owner
The landlord's agent
questions.x: A broker with an exclusive right to rent represents the owner, so it is the landlord's agent and owes the tenant honesty but not loyalty. Tenant's agent is the trap: a tenant who calls about a listing is a customer unless the tenant separately hires a broker.

questions.q: A Bayside seller checked advance consent to dual agency when she listed. Months later a buyer client of the same firm wants the house. The buyer never gave any consent. The firm may act as dual agent:
c: Right away, because the seller's advance consent covers the transaction
After the buyer gives informed written consent and the seller is told
After the buyer gives oral consent, since the seller's is already written
If the seller first signs a brand new listing agreement for the deal
questions.x: Advance consent binds only the party who gave it. The buyer must give informed written consent, and the seller must be told when the in-house deal actually arises. Proceeding on the seller's box alone is the trap: the buyer would be in an undisclosed dual agency.
questions.concept: Scope of advance consent to dual agency

questions.q: Advance consent to dual agency on the New York agency disclosure form means that the consenting party:
c: Waives the right to be told when an in-house deal later arises
Has agreed for both sides of any later in-house transaction
Agrees ahead of time that the firm may represent both sides
Gives up every fiduciary duty the firm owes going forward
questions.x: Advance consent lets a client agree, when first signing the form, that the firm may later act as dual agent in an in-house deal. It does not bind the other party, and it does not excuse the firm from telling the client when the deal arises. The waiver choice is the trap.
questions.concept: Scope of advance consent to dual agency

questions.q: With both clients' written consent, a firm is a dual agent on a Yonkers colonial. The buyer asks the agent, "Off the record, would they take $20,000 less?" The agent should:
c: Hint that the seller is motivated, since a hint is not a number
Answer honestly, since a dual agent owes the buyer full disclosure
Ask the seller for permission and then answer the buyer's question
Decline to share it and offer the buyer comparable sales data
