questions.x: A dual agent keeps each side's bargaining position confidential from the other. It can give facts such as comparable sales, but not the seller's floor or motivation. A hint leaks the position just as a number does. Disclosure is the trap: the duty of disclosure covers material facts, not the other client's confidences.

questions.q: A consensual dual agent may do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Present every offer to the seller promptly
Give both parties data on recent nearby sales
Tell the seller the buyer's maximum price
Explain each offer's financing and timing terms
questions.x: Each client's bargaining position stays confidential, so the buyer's maximum price cannot go to the seller. Presenting offers, sharing market data, and explaining terms are all facts and services a dual agent still provides. Explaining financing risk may look like advocacy, but it is a factual service to the seller.

questions.q: A listing agent gives an unrepresented open house visitor a signed seller's agent disclosure, then tells her what to offer and to waive the inspection. The most serious problem is that the agent:
c: Probably created implied agency, an undisclosed dual agency
Should have handed the visitor the disclosure form after the conversation
Failed to get the visitor's written buyer agreement before advising her
Became a subagent of the visitor's lender by advising her on contingencies
questions.x: Conduct can create agency. Advising a buyer on price and contingencies is acting for her, so the listing agent may now represent both sides with no consent. The signed form does not help, because conduct contradicted it. The buyer agreement choice is the trap: the problem is the advice itself, not a missing contract.

questions.q: A seller's agent who coaches a buyer customer on negotiating strategy risks creating:
c: An agency coupled with an interest
Implied agency with the buyer
A broker's agent relationship
An open listing with the seller
questions.x: Agency can arise from conduct. Coaching a buyer customer looks like representing her, which can create implied agency on top of the listing, making the agent an undisclosed dual agent. A broker's agent is the trap: that is a licensee engaged by another agent, with no direct relationship to the buyer.

questions.q: A seller learns after closing that the firm secretly represented the buyer too. The seller may pursue all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Forfeiture of the firm's commission
A complaint to the Department of State
A civil claim for damages against the firm
Automatic revocation of the buyer's deed
questions.x: Undisclosed dual agency is the agent's breach, so remedies run against the agent: commission forfeiture, damages, possible rescission, and DOS discipline. A deed is not automatically revoked; rescission takes a court. Forfeiture is the tempting wrong pick because it seems harsh, but courts routinely deny a disloyal agent its fee.

questions.q: A broker who acted as an undisclosed dual agent sues for its commission. The seller's strongest defense is that:
c: The listing broker was not the procuring cause of the sale
The listing agreement expired before the parties signed the contract
A disloyal agent may forfeit its fee even without proof of loss
Dual agency is illegal in New York under every set of circumstances
questions.x: Courts treat undisclosed dual agency as a breach of loyalty and may deny the agent any commission, even if the client cannot show a dollar of harm. The trap is that dual agency is always illegal; it is lawful with informed written consent of both parties. Here the lack of consent is what defeats the fee.

questions.q: A mortgage broker offers a Rochester salesperson $400 for each buyer referred. The salesperson does no loan work. Taking the money is:
c: Allowed if every buyer is told in writing
Allowed if the sponsoring broker approves
A kickback prohibited by RESPA Section 8
Allowed if the fee is paid at the closing
questions.x: RESPA Section 8 bans fees for referring settlement service business on federally related mortgage loans. With no services performed, the payment is a kickback, and disclosure does not cure it. Written notice is the trap: disclosure matters only when the licensee actually performs licensed mortgage brokerage work.

questions.q: A real estate licensee may be paid by a lender in the same deal when the licensee:
c: Refers the buyer and the buyer signs a disclosure about the fee
Is properly licensed, performs loan services, and all parties consent
Refers the buyer and splits the fee evenly with the sponsoring broker
Refers at least three buyers to that lender in the same calendar year
questions.x: Pay for actual mortgage brokerage services by a properly licensed person is not a kickback, and Reg 175.7 then requires full knowledge and consent of all parties. A referral alone, even disclosed, remains a RESPA Section 8 violation. The signed disclosure is the trap.

questions.q: Under 19 NYCRR 175.7, a broker may accept compensation from both the buyer and the seller in one transaction:
c: With the full knowledge and consent of all parties
When each party signed a separate fee agreement
When the total fee stays under the local average
When the closing statement lists both payments
questions.x: Reg 175.7 requires the broker to make clear whom it acts for and bars compensation from more than one party without the full knowledge and consent of all parties. Separate agreements are the trap: each party signing its own agreement does not mean each knows what the other is paying.
questions.concept: Reg 175.7 compensation from more than one party

questions.q: In a consented dual agency in Forest Hills, the seller privately offers the salesperson a $3,000 bonus if the price tops $1.2 million. The best handling is to:
c: Accept it directly, since bonuses are gifts rather than commissions
Accept it, since the buyer pays nothing extra under the offer
Pay it through the broker, with the buyer informed and consenting
Pay it to the salesperson at closing through the seller's attorney
questions.x: Salespersons are paid only through their sponsoring broker, and a seller incentive tied to price works against the buyer client in a dual agency. Reg 175.7 and the duty of loyalty require the buyer's knowledge and consent. Keeping it quiet because the buyer pays nothing is the trap: the harm is the conflict, not the cost.
questions.concept: Reg 175.7 compensation from more than one party

questions.q: A Staten Island firm represents buyers on other firms' listings and, with consent, both sides when its own buyer wants its own listing. This company policy is:
c: Consensual dual agency in-house, buyer agency on other deals
Consensual dual agency in-house, with seller agency as the norm
Buyer agency exclusively, with cooperating fees from listing firms
Seller agency exclusively, with subagency offered to every buyer
questions.x: The firm acts as a buyer's agent on outside listings and as a consensual dual agent in-house, which is the policy of consensual dual agency with buyer agency for all other transactions. Seller agency as the norm is the trap: under that policy, buyers looking at outside listings would be customers, not clients.

questions.q: Which company policy eliminates in-house dual agency but leaves the firm with no listing income?
c: Seller agency exclusively
Buyer agency exclusively
Designated agent policy
Consensual dual agency
questions.x: A buyer-only firm never lists property, so its buyers can never want its own listing, and in-house dual agency cannot arise. The cost is giving up listing income. Seller agency exclusively also avoids dual agency, which makes it the trap, but that firm keeps its listings and gives up buyer clients instead.

questions.q: Under RPL 443, a designated sales agent is:
c: The principal broker, assigned to whichever client signed first
A cooperating agent from another firm engaged by the listing broker
A salesperson or associate broker assigned by the supervising broker
Any licensee the seller chooses, whether or not from the same firm
questions.x: RPL 443 defines a designated sales agent as a licensed salesperson or associate broker working under a broker's supervision, assigned to one client when the broker also represents a different client in the same deal. The principal broker is the trap: the broker stays the dual agent supervising both designated agents.
questions.concept: Who may be a designated sales agent

questions.q: In an in-house sale handled with designated sales agents, each of the following could serve as a designated agent EXCEPT:
c: A salesperson in the branch where the house is listed
An associate broker supervised by the principal broker
A salesperson from the firm's office in another borough
The principal broker who supervises both of the agents
questions.x: Designated sales agents are salespersons or associate brokers under the broker's supervision. The supervising broker remains the dual agent and cannot be one side's designated agent. Office location is the trap: nothing requires designated agents to work in the same branch as the listing.
questions.concept: Who may be a designated sales agent

questions.q: During an in-house deal handled by designated agents, the buyer calls the principal broker and asks whether her offer is too high. The broker should:
c: Answer, because the buyer is a client of the broker's firm
Ask the seller's designated agent before giving any answer
Answer, provided the seller's agent is copied on the reply
Stay neutral and refer the buyer to her designated agent
questions.x: Under designated agency the broker remains a dual agent supervising both sides, so the broker cannot advise either client on price. The buyer's designated agent can. The first choice is the trap: the buyer is a client of the firm, but so is the seller, and the broker is the one person who represents both.

questions.q: When a broker appoints designated sales agents with both clients' consent, the broker:
c: Remains a dual agent and supervises both agents
Becomes a single agent for the seller who listed
Becomes a broker's agent with no direct duties
Is released from its duties for that transaction
questions.x: Designation lets each salesperson advocate for one client, but the firm still represents both, so the broker remains a dual agent and supervises the designated agents. The single agent choice is the trap: listing first does not give the seller the broker's undivided loyalty.

questions.q: A buyer checked advance consent to dual agency on her form but left the designated agent section blank. Her firm now wants to use designated agents on its own listing. The firm needs:
c: Nothing more, because dual agency consent includes designated agents
Her written consent to designated agency, naming her designated agent
A sworn declaration of her refusal, since that section was left blank
The seller's consent, because the seller's agent picks the agents
questions.x: The form treats advance consent to dual agency and advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents as separate choices, and designation names the agent. She must consent to the specific arrangement. Reading the dual agency box as covering designation is the trap. A blank section is not a refusal to sign.

questions.q: Advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents on the New York form requires the consenting party to:
c: Waive the duty of confidentiality owed by the broker
Agree to pay both sides' commissions in the transaction
Name the person who will be their designated agent
Sign again in front of a notary public at the closing
questions.x: The advance consent section for designated agents asks the client to name the agent who will represent them if an in-house deal arises. Nothing in it waives confidentiality; designated agents must keep each side's confidences. The notary choice is the trap: notarization belongs to the declaration of refusal, not to consent.

questions.q: At an open house, a seller told salesperson Ana her rock-bottom price. Two weeks later Ana's buyer client wants the house and the firm plans designated agents. The firm should:
c: Designate Ana, since designation lets her start with fresh duties
Designate Ana, and let her share the price because it was said in public
Designate a different salesperson with no history on the listing
Cancel the listing so that no dual agency can arise in the deal
questions.x: Confidences the seller gave the firm stay confidential, and a designated agent cannot use what was learned earlier from the other side. Ana cannot unlearn the number, so the firm should designate someone else for the buyer. The fresh-duties choice is the trap; designation does not wipe out earlier confidences.

questions.q: A designated sales agent representing a buyer may use which of the following in advising the buyer?
c: Recent comparable sales and the property's condition
Notes the seller's agent left in the shared office file
The seller's deadline, overheard in the office kitchen
What the seller said to the agent before designation
questions.x: A designated agent may advise freely using facts and market data. Anything that came from the other client's confidences, whether learned before designation, read in a shared file, or overheard, stays off limits. The pre-designation choice is the trap: a confidence does not expire because the agent's role changed.

questions.q: A Mineola salesperson moves to a new firm and wants to bring her six listings. How do the listings legally move?
c: They follow her automatically, since she generated each one
Each owner must sign a new listing with the new firm's broker
Her new broker files a change of association covering them
The old broker must assign them to the new broker in writing
questions.x: A listing is a contract between the owner and the broker, not the salesperson. The listings stay with the old broker unless released, and an owner who wants to move must sign a new agreement with the new broker. The change of association choice is the trap: it moves the salesperson's license, not any client.

questions.q: When a listing salesperson leaves the brokerage, the listing agreement generally:
c: Ends, because agency is personal to the salesperson
Moves with the salesperson to the new brokerage
Stays with the broker who signed it with the owner
Converts into an open listing for the remaining term
questions.x: The broker is the agent and the party to the listing; the salesperson acts under the broker. The listing continues with the broker when a salesperson leaves. Ending the agency is the trap: that happens when the broker, not the salesperson, can no longer act, as on a sole proprietor broker's death.

questions.q: A Washington Heights landlord hires a broker under an exclusive right to rent and asks the broker to collect the fee from the incoming tenant. Under the NYC FARE Act:
c: The tenant may be charged if the fee appears in the lease
The landlord pays, because the broker works for the landlord
The tenant may be charged if the fee is under one month's rent
The landlord and tenant split it unless the lease says otherwise
questions.x: Since June 11, 2025, a broker hired by the landlord in NYC is paid by the landlord, not the tenant. Disclosure in the listing and lease is required for any fees a tenant must pay, but disclosure does not make the landlord's agent's fee chargeable to the tenant. That disclosure idea is the trap.
questions.concept: FARE Act fee for landlord's agent

questions.q: Under the NYC FARE Act, which fee may a tenant lawfully agree to pay?
c: The fee of the listing agent who advertised the unit
A fee to the agent the landlord hired to fill the unit
The fee of a tenant's agent the tenant hired herself
A fee to the landlord's agent, if stated in the lease
questions.x: The FARE Act bars charging tenants for the landlord's agent, including an agent who lists the unit with the landlord's permission. A tenant who hires her own agent may agree to pay that agent. The lease-disclosure choice is the trap: the law requires disclosure of tenant fees, but disclosure does not permit charging the landlord's agent's fee.
questions.concept: FARE Act fee for landlord's agent

questions.q: The RPL 443 agency disclosure form is required in each of these transactions EXCEPT:
c: The sale of a six-unit building in Astoria
The rental of a condo unit in Long Island City
The sale of a co-op apartment in Jackson Heights
The sale of a two-family house in Canarsie
questions.x: RPL 443 covers residential real property improved by a 1 to 4 family dwelling or by condo or co-op apartments, for sales and rentals. A six-unit building is beyond the 1 to 4 family limit. The co-op is the trap for anyone relying on the pre-2011 rules, when co-ops and condos were outside the definition.
questions.concept: Agency disclosure scope by property type

questions.q: A Buffalo broker lists a retail building for lease. At first substantive contact with a prospective tenant, the broker must provide:
c: Both the RPL 443 form and the fair housing disclosure
The fair housing disclosure, but not the RPL 443 form
The RPL 443 form, but not the fair housing disclosure
Neither, because commercial leasing is exempt from both
questions.x: The agency disclosure form applies only to residential 1 to 4 family, condo, and co-op transactions, so a retail lease is outside it. The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form under 19 NYCRR 175.28 covers all property types. Exempt from both is the trap; only the agency form drops out.
questions.concept: Agency disclosure scope by property type

questions.q: In the sale of a co-op apartment, the listing broker's principal is the:
c: Selling shareholder
Co-op corporation
Board of directors
Building's managing agent
questions.x: The listing broker represents the shareholder who signed the listing. The co-op corporation, acting through its board and managing agent, must approve the transfer but is a third party to the agency. The board is the trap: the agent deals with the board and owes it honesty, not loyalty.

questions.q: A co-op board member asks the seller's agent for an off-the-record opinion of the buyer after the interview. The agent's best response is to:
c: Endorse the buyer strongly, since the seller wants approval
Pass along the buyer agent's remarks about the buyer's job
Decline to speak to the board, since it is not a client
Stay factual and point to the board package
questions.x: The seller's agent wants approval for the client but owes the board honesty and owes no one a leak of the buyer side's confidences. A factual answer is honest and protects the seller. Strong endorsement is the trap: puffing about a buyer to a board relying on it can become misrepresentation. Refusing to speak at all is needlessly unhelpful.

questions.q: A broker listing an office building for lease is asked by a prospective tenant to represent him too. The RPL 443 form does not apply. To act for both, the broker needs:
c: Nothing, because dual agency rules come from RPL 443
The tenant's consent, because he would pay the extra fee
The owner's consent, because the owner hired the broker
Informed consent from both principals
questions.x: Common law forbids representing both sides without the informed consent of both principals, whatever the property type, and Reg 175.7 requires everyone's knowledge and consent before a broker takes pay from more than one party. The trap is assuming no RPL 443 means no dual agency rules.

questions.q: Which statement about agency in New York commercial transactions is accurate?
c: Fiduciary duties depend on whether the RPL 443 form is required
Common law agency duties apply to commercial deals in full
Commercial brokers owe their clients loyalty but not disclosure
Dual agency is allowed in commercial deals without any consent
questions.x: RPL 443 is a disclosure statute for residential deals; it does not create or limit agency. Commercial clients receive the full fiduciary duties under common law, and dual agency still needs informed consent. Tying duties to the form is the trap; the statute itself says it does not limit the common law of agency.

questions.q: An unrepresented tenant tells the landlord's agent he would pay $500 a month more than the asking rent for a longer term. The agent should:
c: Keep it private, because the tenant spoke in confidence
Tell the landlord; it is material to the client
Tell the landlord, but wait until the lease is signed
Keep it private, unless the tenant puts it in writing
questions.x: The landlord's agent owes the landlord full disclosure of material facts, and a tenant's willingness to pay more is highly material. A customer's statements to the other side's agent are not confidential. The confidence choice is the trap: the agent owes the tenant honesty, not secrecy, which is why the agent should state its role before the tenant talks money.

questions.q: A landlord's agent owes an unrepresented prospective tenant:
c: Confidentiality about the tenant's budget
Advice on what rent the tenant should offer
Honesty and fair dealing in what it says
Loyalty equal to what it owes the landlord
questions.x: A customer gets honesty and fair dealing, including no misrepresentations. Confidentiality, advice, and loyalty are fiduciary duties owed only to the client, here the landlord. The confidentiality choice is the trap: what the tenant tells the landlord's agent can and usually must go to the landlord.

questions.q: A Queens landlord tells his rental agent to quietly reject applicants who pay with housing vouchers. The agent should:
c: Refuse, because the instruction is unlawful
Follow it, since an agent owes the client obedience
Follow it for apartments in two-family houses
Follow it if the listing omits any mention of it
questions.x: Lawful source of income, including vouchers, is protected under the NYS and NYC Human Rights Laws, and the duty of obedience covers lawful instructions only. The agent must refuse and should document it. The two-family choice is the trap: nothing in the facts creates an exemption, and an agent may not carry out discrimination on a client's behalf.

questions.q: A seller tells his listing agent to tell buyers that two rent-stabilized units are free market. The agent's duty of obedience:
c: Requires compliance, since the seller is the principal
Requires compliance if buyers can verify it elsewhere
Ends only when the listing agreement is cancelled
Covers lawful instructions only
questions.x: Obedience means following the client's lawful instructions. Misstating units' regulatory status is a misrepresentation of a material fact, so the agent must refuse. The verify-elsewhere choice is the trap: a buyer's chance to check does not excuse the agent's false statement.

questions.q: A Syracuse exclusive listing ends June 30 but says it renews for 60-day periods unless the owner cancels in writing. Under 19 NYCRR 175.15, this clause is:
c: Valid, as long as the owner initialed it at signing
Valid, as long as each renewal is under six months
Prohibited as an automatic continuation of the term
Valid, because the owner keeps a right to cancel
questions.x: 175.15 bars a broker from being party to an exclusive listing that automatically continues past its fixed termination date. Initials, short renewal periods, and a cancellation right do not cure it. The initials choice is the trap: owner consent at signing is exactly what the rule overrides.

questions.q: Which listing clause is consistent with New York's rule against automatic continuation of exclusive listings?
c: A fee is owed on sales to buyers shown during the term
The term rolls over monthly until either party cancels
The term extends 90 days if no contract is signed by then
The term extends while the property is under contract
questions.x: A protection period does not extend the listing; it protects the fee for buyers the broker produced during the term, and courts have held such clauses do not violate 175.15. Every other choice continues the listing itself past its fixed date. The under-contract extension is the trap because it sounds reasonable, but it is still automatic continuation.

questions.q: A Hempstead owner wants one broker marketing her house but wants to owe nothing if she sells to a buyer she finds herself. The best fit is:
c: An exclusive right to sell
An exclusive agency listing
A net listing at her price
An exclusive right to rent
questions.x: In an exclusive agency listing one broker is the owner's agent, but the owner keeps the right to sell on her own without paying a commission. Under an exclusive right to sell, the broker is paid no matter who finds the buyer, which makes it the trap. Net listings are prohibited in New York.
questions.concept: Exclusive agency vs exclusive right to sell

questions.q: During an exclusive right to sell, the owner's coworker buys the house directly with no broker involved. The listing broker is owed:
c: Nothing, because the broker was not the procuring cause
Half the commission, as a reasonable compromise
The full commission under the listing agreement
Nothing, unless the broker had shown the coworker
questions.x: Under an exclusive right to sell the broker earns the commission if the property sells during the term, whoever finds the buyer, unless the agreement names an exclusion. Procuring cause is the trap: it decides who is paid under an open listing, not under an exclusive right to sell.
questions.concept: Exclusive agency vs exclusive right to sell

questions.q: A Bronx seller dies two weeks into a six-month exclusive listing. His son, the only heir, tells the broker to keep marketing. The listing:
c: Continues for its term, binding the son as heir to the property
Continues if the son signs a letter ratifying the listing today
Is suspended until probate ends, then resumes for its remaining term
Ended at the seller's death, so the executor must sign a new one
questions.x: Death of the principal ends the agency by operation of law. A new listing must come from someone with authority over the estate, the executor or administrator appointed by the Surrogate's Court. The ratification choice is the trap: an heir who has not been appointed has no authority to ratify or to list.

questions.q: All of the following end a listing by operation of law EXCEPT:
c: Death of the owner
Death of the listing salesperson
Destruction of the house by fire
Bankruptcy of the owner
questions.x: The listing is the broker's contract, so a salesperson's death or departure does not end it; another salesperson takes over. Death, bankruptcy, or incapacity of a party and destruction of the property end it by operation of law. Bankruptcy is the trap for students who remember only death and destruction.

questions.q: Two months into a four-month exclusive buyer agreement, the buyer emails her broker that she is ending it. Legally, the buyer:
c: Cannot end it, since an exclusive agreement is irrevocable
Can end it and owes nothing for doing so
Can end it by first proving a breach of fiduciary duty
Can revoke, though she may owe damages under the contract
questions.x: A principal always has the power to revoke an agent's authority, but may have no right to do so under the contract, so damages or a contractual fee can follow. The irrevocable choice is the trap: only an agency coupled with an interest is irrevocable by the principal.

questions.q: A broker lent a seller $50,000 secured by the house, and the seller gave the broker authority to sell and repay the loan from the proceeds. This agency:
c: Is coupled with an interest and not revocable
Ends if the seller revokes it in writing
Ends at the seller's death, like any listing
Becomes an open listing if the seller objects
questions.x: When the agent holds its own interest in the property, the agency is coupled with an interest: the principal cannot revoke it, and it does not end at the principal's death. The death choice is the trap, because death ends ordinary agencies. A large commission alone is not such an interest.

questions.q: After a buyer agency ends, which duty does the former buyer's agent still owe the buyer?
c: Loyalty
Obedience
Confidentiality
Reasonable care
questions.x: Confidentiality survives the end of the agency. The former client's budget, motivation, and negotiating limits stay private even if the agent later works with someone negotiating against them. Loyalty is the trap: it ends with the relationship, which is exactly why confidentiality's survival is tested.

questions.q: A year after closing, a former seller client's neighbor lists with the same agent and asks what the old client's lowest acceptable price had been. The agent should:
c: Share it, since the agency ended at the closing
Share it, since the sale price is now public
Share it, since the neighbor is now a client
Keep it private; that duty survives
questions.x: Most duties end with the agency, but confidentiality continues. The former client's bottom line stays private even though the sale price is public. The public-price choice is the trap: the recorded price is public, but what the client privately would have accepted is not.

questions.q: Which event ends an agency by act of the parties rather than by operation of law?
c: Expiration of the listing's term
Incapacity of the property owner
Condemnation of the listed property
Death of a sole proprietor broker
questions.x: Expiration, performance, mutual agreement, revocation, and renunciation are acts of the parties; the parties chose the end date when they signed. Incapacity, death, bankruptcy, and destruction or condemnation of the property end an agency by operation of law. Condemnation is the trap because the owner may seem to have chosen nothing either way.

questions.q: An agency relationship ends by operation of law in all of these cases EXCEPT:
c: The principal is declared incompetent
The broker renounces the agency in writing
A fire destroys the listed house
The principal files for bankruptcy
questions.x: Renunciation is an act of the agent, so it ends the agency by act of the parties, and it may expose the broker to damages. Incapacity, destruction, and bankruptcy end the agency by operation of law. The incompetence choice is the trap for students who treat only death as automatic.

questions.q: A Flushing listing agent gets three texts from a buyer: one asking about parking, one asking about the HOA fee, and one saying "we're approved to $900K, would they take $860K?" The disclosure is due:
c: After the first text, since any contact triggers the form
After the third text, when finances and price came up
At the first in-person showing of the condo unit
When the buyer submits a written offer on the unit
questions.x: First substantive contact is when talk moves from property facts to the buyer's finances, motivation, or negotiating position. Parking and HOA fees are property facts; a pre-approval amount and a proposed price are substantive. The in-person choice is the trap: texts and emails count, and the form can be sent electronically.

questions.q: Each of the following would most likely be first substantive contact with a buyer EXCEPT:
c: The buyer emails her budget and asks if the seller is flexible
The buyer phones to explain a job transfer and a closing deadline
The buyer asks at an open house when the roof was last replaced
The buyer texts asking what offer the seller would likely accept
questions.x: A question about the roof's age is a property fact, so no form is triggered yet. Budgets, deadlines, motivation, and price strategy are substantive whether they arrive by email, phone, or text. The phone call is the trap for anyone who thinks substantive contact must be about money; motivation and timing count too.

questions.q: Under RPL 443, a buyer's agent must give the agency disclosure to the seller:
c: Before entering into the buyer agency agreement
When the seller has no agent of its own
At contract signing, through the seller's attorney
At first substantive contact with the seller
questions.x: A buyer's agent gives the form to the buyer before the buyer agency agreement, and to the seller, or the seller's agent, at first substantive contact. The first choice is the trap: that is the timing for the buyer's agent's own client, not for the other side.

questions.q: A listing agent must present the agency disclosure form to the seller:
c: Before entering into the listing agreement
At the first showing of the listed property
When the first written offer comes in
At first substantive contact with a buyer
questions.x: The listing agent gives the form to the seller before the listing agreement is signed. First substantive contact is the trigger for the other side, the buyer, which is why that choice is the trap.

questions.q: A Rye seller reads the agency disclosure but refuses to sign the acknowledgment. The listing agent should:
c: Stop working with the seller until the acknowledgment is signed
Write "refused" on the signature line and keep going
Ask the seller's attorney to sign the form on the seller's behalf
Make a sworn or affirmed written declaration
questions.x: RPL 443 requires the licensee to set forth under oath or affirmation a written declaration of the facts of the refusal and keep it at least 3 years. A one-word notation is not that declaration. Stopping work is the trap: a refusal does not bar the listing once the form was presented.

questions.q: How long must a licensee keep a declaration of a consumer's refusal to sign the agency disclosure?
c: Until the transaction closes
At least 1 year
At least 3 years
At least 7 years
questions.x: RPL 443 requires the licensee to keep each signed acknowledgment and each declaration of refusal for not less than 3 years. Until closing is the trap; disputes and DOS complaints often surface after closing, which is why the record outlives the deal.

questions.q: An audit finds an agency disclosure with the consumer's signature but no role box checked. The main problem is that the form:
c: Lacks a notary stamp for the consumer's signature
Does not show whom the licensee represented
Was signed by the consumer before the licensee
Should have stated the commission rate
questions.x: The point of the signature page is to record, in writing, which role the licensee is playing. With no role checked, the acknowledgment proves receipt of a form but not what the consumer was told. The commission choice is the trap: the form is not a contract and states no fee.

questions.q: The consumer's signature on the New York agency disclosure form means the consumer:
c: Received the disclosure, not a contract
Hired the licensee and agreed to pay a fee
Agreed to work with no other licensee
Gave advance consent to dual agency
questions.x: The form is headed "This is not a contract." The signature acknowledges receipt; it creates no agency and obligates no payment. Advance consent is the trap: it is a separate box the consumer may check or leave blank, not something every signature implies.

questions.q: A buyer who was a customer at a firm's open house later signs a buyer agreement with that firm, then wants the open house listing. The firm must:
c: Do nothing new, since he signed a disclosure at the open house
Switch the firm to buyer's agent and release the seller as a client
Have the buyer re-sign his buyer agreement for this property
Get both clients' informed written consent to dual agency
questions.x: The firm now represents both the seller and the buyer on one property, so it is a dual agent and needs informed written consent from both, with a new disclosure showing the dual role. Switching sides is the trap: roles may change, but never by dropping a client mid-deal or without new paperwork.

questions.q: When a licensee who acted as a seller's agent toward a buyer becomes that buyer's agent for other properties, the licensee should:
c: Rely on the first form, since it already explained every role
Give a new disclosure showing the new role
Tell the buyer orally, since role changes need no paperwork
Wait until the buyer makes an offer before changing anything
questions.x: Any change in role calls for a new disclosure that records the new relationship and a new acknowledgment, plus the buyer agency agreement itself. Relying on the old form is the trap: it says the licensee represented the seller, which is no longer the relationship.

questions.q: Which change took effect with the agency disclosure amendments of January 1, 2011?
c: Condos, co-ops, and rentals were brought under the form
Commercial leases were added to the form's coverage
Vacant land sales were added to the form's coverage
The refusal declaration was replaced by a signature
questions.x: The 2011 amendments added condos and co-ops to the definition, created a landlord and tenant version for rentals, and added advance consent to dual agency and to designated sales agents. Commercial property and vacant land remain outside RPL 443. The commercial choice is the trap: the fair housing form covers commercial deals, but the agency form does not.

questions.q: The current New York agency disclosure form, in use since 2011, includes all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A landlord and tenant version
Advance consent to dual agency
A box to state the commission
Advance consent to designated agents
questions.x: The form is not a contract and states no fee. Since 2011 it has a landlord and tenant version and lets consumers give advance consent to dual agency and to dual agency with designated sales agents. The designated agents choice is the trap for anyone working from the pre-2011 form, which had no advance consent options.

questions.q: A White Plains broker had every salesperson sign an independent contractor agreement in 2022 and never renewed them. For New York unemployment insurance purposes, the agreements:
c: Still qualify, since a signed contract lasts until terminated
Still qualify, as long as the pay remains commission-based
No longer qualify under New York's 12 to 15 month rule
No longer qualify, since IRC 3508 requires an annual contract
questions.x: New York's exclusion requires a written contract executed within the past 12 to 15 months, so brokers re-sign every year. An older agreement may still bind the parties as a contract but no longer satisfies the statute. The IRC 3508 choice is the trap: the federal rule has no freshness requirement; the clock is New York's.

questions.q: To keep New York's independent contractor exclusion for a salesperson, how often should a broker have the written agreement executed?
c: About every year, within 12 to 15 months
Once, when the salesperson first affiliates
Every 2 years, at each license renewal
Every 5 years, or whenever splits change
questions.x: New York requires that the written contract have been executed within the past 12 to 15 months, so compliant brokers renew it annually. Tying it to the 2-year license renewal is the trap: it sounds administratively neat, but a 2-year-old contract fails the statute.

questions.q: All of the following are consistent with pay that is directly related to sales or output EXCEPT:
c: A 70/30 commission split on each closing
An advance repaid from later commissions
A $500 bonus for each listing that closes
A $20 hourly stipend for desk duty
questions.x: Contractor status requires substantially all pay to be tied to sales or other output, not hours. An hourly stipend pays for time. An advance repaid from future commissions is still output-based, which makes it the trap: it looks like a salary, but the agent ultimately earns it only by closing deals.

questions.q: A Utica broker pays new salespersons $500 a week for their first three months, never repaid, plus commissions. This arrangement:
c: Is fine, since most of a successful agent's pay is commission
Pays for time, which undermines contractor status
Is fine, since new agents need support to get started
Is required by the license law for new licensees
questions.x: A guaranteed weekly payment that is not repaid from commissions is pay for time, not output, and cuts against the requirement that substantially all pay be output-based. The first choice is the trap: for a new agent with few closings, the stipend may be most of the pay, and even a smaller share erodes the safe harbor.

questions.q: Which broker practice is required supervision under 19 NYCRR 175.21 rather than direction and control?
c: Setting mandatory office hours for every salesperson
Reviewing salespersons' contracts and advertising
Docking a split when a salesperson misses a shift
Barring salespersons from holding any outside job
questions.x: 175.21 requires regular, frequent, and consistent supervision, including review of contracts, ads, and escrow handling. Mandatory hours, pay penalties, and bans on outside work control when and whether the person works. The outside job ban is the trap: it may sound like a loyalty policy, but New York's statute expects the contract to allow outside employment.

questions.q: A broker's agreements say "independent contractor," but the broker assigns hours, pays hourly for floor time, and fines agents for absences. An auditor will most likely:
c: Follow the agreement, since the parties chose the label
Accept contractor status, since brokers are required to supervise
Accept contractor status if splits exceed 50 percent
Treat the agents as employees, looking past the label
questions.x: Substance beats form: written documentation does not overcome a broker's actual direction and control. Assigned hours, hourly pay, and fines are hallmarks of employment. The supervision choice is the trap. Brokers must supervise compliance, but that duty does not authorize controlling when and how agents work.

questions.q: If a New York broker's salespersons are reclassified as employees, the broker becomes responsible for all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Unemployment insurance contributions
Workers' compensation coverage
The salespersons' Schedule C filings
Income tax and Social Security withholding
questions.x: Employers pay unemployment insurance, carry workers' compensation and disability coverage, and withhold income and payroll taxes. Schedule C is a self-employed person's form, so reclassification takes it away from the salesperson rather than shifting it to the broker. Withholding is the trap for anyone who thinks the agent keeps handling her own taxes.

questions.q: A salesperson who is treated as an employee rather than an independent contractor will typically:
c: Lose Schedule C expense deductions and have pay withheld
Pay both halves of Social Security on her commissions
Lose the right to be paid any commission on closings
Need to transfer her license to a new sponsoring broker
questions.x: Employees have tax withheld from all compensation and cannot deduct business expenses on Schedule C the way contractors can. Paying both halves of Social Security is the trap: that is the self-employment tax contractors pay. Employees can still earn commissions, and the license stays where it is.

questions.q: Which requirement appears in New York's 1986 independent contractor rules but NOT in IRC Section 3508?
c: The contract was not signed under duress
The worker holds a real estate license
Pay is tied to sales or other output
There is a written contract in place
questions.x: IRC 3508 requires a license, output-based pay, and a written contract stating the agent is not an employee for federal tax purposes. New York adds that the contract was not executed under duress and was executed within the past 12 to 15 months. The written contract is the trap: both laws require one.

questions.q: Under IRC Section 3508, a licensed real estate agent is not treated as an employee for federal tax purposes if:
c: The agent works fewer than 40 hours a week for the broker
Pay is mostly output-based, under a written non-employee contract
The broker does not supervise or review the agent's transactions
The agent pays at least half of the office's operating expenses
questions.x: The federal safe harbor has two conditions beyond the license: substantially all pay directly related to sales or other output, and a written contract stating the agent will not be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes. The no-supervision choice is the trap; brokers must supervise under state license law, and the safe harbor does not require them to stop.

questions.q: A team leader at a Huntington brokerage pays his two licensed team members a share of team closings from his personal account. This is:
c: Allowed, since the team is the leader's own business
Allowed, if the leader issues each member a Form 1099
Improper; only the sponsoring broker may pay them
Allowed, if the broker approves the split in writing
questions.x: A salesperson may receive compensation for real estate work only through the sponsoring broker, so commission money must flow through the brokerage and its records. Broker approval is the trap: approving a split is fine, but the payment itself still has to come from the broker, not from a fellow licensee.

questions.q: In New York, a licensed salesperson may lawfully receive a commission from:
c: The seller, directly at the closing table
The buyer, as a thank-you after closing
A team leader in the same brokerage
The salesperson's sponsoring broker
questions.x: Salespersons are paid only by their sponsoring broker. A client, a party, or a fellow licensee such as a team leader may not pay them directly, even with good intentions. The team leader is the trap because the team is inside the same firm, but the money must still go through the broker.

questions.q: A relocation company refers a transferring executive to a Rochester brokerage for a 30% referral fee. The executive signs the brokerage's buyer agency agreement. Whom does the brokerage represent in the purchase?
c: The relocation company, since it originated the referral
The executive's employer, since it pays relocation benefits
The executive, who signed the buyer agency agreement
The relocation company and the executive together
questions.x: Agency runs to the person who hires the broker for the transaction, here the executive. The relocation company earned a referral fee from another broker and the employer funds benefits, but neither is the principal. The joint choice is the trap: a referral agreement between brokers cannot add a corporate co-principal and split the agent's loyalty.

questions.q: A buyer's agent works with a transferee referred by a relocation company. All of the following are consistent with the agent's duties EXCEPT:
c: Telling the relocation company her top price without her consent
Sending the relocation company dates the buyer has approved in writing
Disclosing to the buyer that the firm pays the relocation company a fee
Following the buyer's instructions even when they slow down the closing
questions.x: The transferee is the client, so her price ceiling is her confidence to release, not the relocation company's to request. Sharing approved dates, disclosing the referral fee, and obeying her lawful instructions are all consistent with the agency. The disclosure choice may look odd, but telling a client about a fee that could color the firm's incentives is what a fiduciary does.

questions.q: A New York broker may pay a share of a commission as a referral fee to:
c: A friend who sent the buyer, if the buyer agrees in writing
A broker regularly in the business in another state
The building's doorman, if the fee is under $500
A mortgage loan officer who referred the buyer
questions.x: RPL 442 allows commission sharing with licensed brokers and salespersons and with a person regularly engaged in the brokerage business in another state. Unlicensed people cannot be paid for referrals, whatever the amount or consent. The loan officer is the trap: besides lacking a broker license, a payment for referring settlement business to or from a lender is the kickback RESPA Section 8 targets.

questions.q: A Westchester brokerage pays a national relocation company, licensed as a broker, 35% of its commission for referring a buyer. Under RESPA, the payment is:
c: Prohibited, since every referral fee in a mortgage deal is a kickback
Allowed, since cooperative referral deals between brokers are exempt
Allowed, provided the buyer pays it as a separate closing charge
Prohibited, unless the lender approves it on the Closing Disclosure
questions.x: RESPA Section 8 bans kickbacks and unearned fees for referring settlement business, but it expressly exempts cooperative brokerage and referral arrangements between real estate brokers. The first choice is the trap: it states the general ban and ignores the broker-to-broker exemption. The fee comes out of the brokerage's commission, so the buyer does not pay it separately.

questions.q: A buyer with no broker visits a new condo's sales office in Long Island City. The sponsor's exclusive sales agent gives her an agency disclosure form. Which box should be checked?
c: Seller's agent, since the sales agent represents the sponsor
Buyer's agent, since the buyer has no broker of her own
Dual agent, since the sponsor pays the commission either way
No box, since RPL 443 does not cover new construction units
questions.x: The sponsor's sales team represents the sponsor, and RPL 443 covers condominium units, new ones included, so the seller's agent disclosure is due at first substantive contact. The buyer is a customer owed honesty and fair dealing. The new construction choice is the trap: the statute excludes unimproved land, not newly built condos.

questions.q: In a New York new development sale, the sponsor's in-house sales agent owes an unrepresented buyer:
c: Loyalty and confidentiality, as with any client
Honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known defects
Nothing beyond what the offering plan already states
The duties of a buyer's agent until a contract is signed
questions.x: A seller's agent owes customers honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material facts, while loyalty and confidentiality go to the sponsor. The offering plan choice is the trap: a plan's disclosures do not license a salesperson to misrepresent or conceal what the salesperson knows.

questions.q: A sponsor's ad calls a new Brooklyn condo's offering plan "approved by the Attorney General." The statement is:
c: Accurate, since the AG approves the price and budget of every plan
Accurate, once the AG has also issued the certificate of occupancy
Misleading, since the AG accepts plans for filing without approving them
Misleading, since offering plans are filed with the Department of State
questions.x: Under the Martin Act, GBL 352-e, the sponsor files the offering plan with the Attorney General's office, which accepts it for filing after reviewing required disclosures. The AG does not approve the merits, price, construction, or budget. The Department of State choice is the trap: DOS licenses brokers, but condo and co-op offering plans go to the AG.

questions.q: All of the following are true of a New York condominium offering plan EXCEPT:
c: The sponsor files it with the Attorney General's office
Contracts may not be signed before it is accepted for filing
Buyers' deposits are held in trust under the Martin Act
The AG's acceptance confirms the projected budget is sound
questions.x: Acceptance for filing means the plan contains the disclosures the law requires; the AG does not vouch for the budget, price, or quality. The other statements are true: the plan is filed with the AG under GBL 352-e, the sponsor cannot sign purchase agreements before acceptance, and deposits are held in trust. The trust choice can look too protective to be true, but it is the rule.

questions.q: A sponsor amends a new condo's offering plan to drop the gym and raise common charges 15%, a material adverse change. A contract vendee who wants out should know that:
c: Her deposit is forfeited, because she already signed a contract
Her buyer's agent may rescind for her without her signature
She may rescind at any time before the first closing date
She may rescind within the period stated, at least 15 days
questions.x: The Attorney General's regulations for new condo plans require that an amendment materially and adversely affecting purchasers give them a right to rescind, with no fewer than 15 days to exercise it. The window is short, so the buyer should involve her attorney at once. The agent choice is the trap: a buyer's agent is a special agent with no authority to terminate the client's contract.

questions.q: On day 10 of a 15-day rescission period created by a sponsor's amendment, a buyer asks her agent whether to rescind. The agent's best course is to:
c: Tell her to rescind, since amendments usually lead to more cuts
Tell her to stay, since a second sponsor credit is likely coming
Send the notice for her now, since just five days are left to act
Flag the deadline and have her decide with her attorney promptly
questions.x: Rescinding is a legal and financial decision for the buyer and her attorney. The agent's job is to make sure she understands the deadline and does not lose the right by delay. Sending the notice is the trap: urgency does not give a buyer's agent authority to terminate the client's contract, and only the purchaser can exercise the right.

questions.q: A sponsor offers buyers' brokers a $10,000 bonus on units on floors 2 through 5. A buyer's agent's client is choosing between a 4th-floor unit and a 12th-floor unit. The agent should:
c: Disclose the bonus to her before she picks a unit
Disclose the bonus if and when the client picks the 4th floor
Keep quiet, since the sponsor, not the client, pays it
Turn down the bonus, since a buyer's agent may not take it
questions.x: The bonus gives the agent a financial reason to favor one unit, and loyalty requires disclosing that interest while the advice is being given. Disclosing after the choice is the trap: by then the conflict has already shaped the recommendation. Accepting sponsor-paid compensation is lawful when the client knows about it.

questions.q: A buyer's agent learns the sponsor pays an extra bonus on certain units. All of the following help manage the conflict EXCEPT:
c: Telling the client in writing which units carry the bonus
Offering to credit the bonus to the client at the closing
Recommending bonus units without mentioning the payment
Comparing the units on price, layout, and resale data alone
questions.x: Steering a client toward bonus units without disclosure is exactly the divided loyalty the duty forbids. Written disclosure, a credit to the client (a broker may share compensation with a party under RPL 442), and advice based on the units' merits all reduce the conflict. The credit choice is the trap for anyone who thinks every commission share with an unlicensed person is illegal.

questions.q: Which team name complies with New York's advertising rule for teams?
c: The Ortiz Group at Bay Ridge Realty
Ortiz Realty Associates of Bay Ridge
The Ortiz Team at Bay Ridge Realty
Ortiz and Partners Home Sales
questions.x: 19 NYCRR 175.25 requires a team name to use the word "team" and bars "group," "realty," and "associate," and any ad using a team name must also show the broker's name. The "Realty Associates" choice is the trap: it uses two prohibited terms and implies a separate brokerage.

questions.q: Under New York's team advertising rules, all of the following are required or permitted EXCEPT:
c: Showing the broker's name in an ad that uses the team name
Including an unlicensed assistant's name in the team name
Using the team's own logo along with the broker's name
Advertising listings that are held by the team's own broker
questions.x: A team name may not include the name of an unlicensed person. Ads with a team name must show the broker's name, a team may use its own logo if the broker's name or logo also appears, and a team advertises only property listed with or represented by its broker. The logo choice is the trap: separate team branding is allowed as long as the broker stays visible.

questions.q: On a Staten Island team, one member lists a house and another member's buyer client wants to make an offer. Both work under the same broker. The firm is:
c: A dual agent, needing both clients' informed written consent
A single agent, since each team member has a separate client
A subagent of the seller, since the buyer came through the team
Barred from the sale, since a team may not sell its own listings
questions.x: Clients belong to the broker, and a team is a group of the same broker's licensees, so the firm represents both sides and needs informed written consent from each. Designated agents are possible with advance consent. The single agent choice is the trap: splitting work between teammates does not split the brokerage into two agencies.
questions.concept: Team buyer on a team listing

questions.q: A team leader posts a seller client's bottom price in the team's chat. A teammate who represents a buyer for that listing saw it. The teammate should:
c: Share it with the buyer, since a buyer's agent discloses material facts
Share it once the buyer signs the firm's dual agency consent form
Keep it confidential and report the conflict to the supervising broker
Keep it until the seller rejects an offer, then share it with the buyer
questions.x: The firm represents the seller, so the seller's bottom line is a confidence the whole firm must keep, even when a teammate also represents the buyer. Dual agency consent limits what each side hears; it does not authorize passing confidences. The disclosure choice is the trap: a buyer's agent's duty of disclosure never reaches information held in confidence for the other client.
questions.concept: Team buyer on a team listing

questions.q: In a short sale, the servicer's negotiator emails the listing agent: "Do not accept any offer under $500,000." The sellers want to submit a $485,000 offer. The agent should:
c: Reject the offer, since the servicer's approval is required
Submit it with the sellers' authority after telling them the risk
Hold the offer until the servicer lowers its stated floor price
Ask the buyer to raise the price before the sellers can see it
questions.x: The sellers are the principal; the lienholder's approval is a condition of closing, not a source of instructions. The agent tells the sellers what the servicer said, advises them, and follows their lawful decision. The rejection choice is the trap: the servicer may decline, but the decision to submit belongs to the clients.

questions.q: In a short sale listing, the lender that must approve the sale is best described as:
c: The listing broker's principal for pricing decisions
A co-principal along with the sellers in the listing
A subagent of the listing broker during approval
A third party whose consent the sale depends on
questions.x: The listing broker's principal is the seller. The lender is a third party whose written approval is a condition of the sale, and the agent deals with it honestly but without owing it loyalty or obedience. The co-principal choice is the trap: practical power over closing does not create an agency relationship.

questions.q: A listing agent plans to fund half of her cousin's all-cash purchase of the agent's own listing, with title in the cousin's name. Under 19 NYCRR 175.4, she must:
c: Make her true position clearly known to the seller first
Do nothing extra, since the deed will name her cousin alone
Tell the buyer's attorney, since the cousin is the buyer
Give up the listing, since a licensee may not buy one
questions.x: 175.4 bars a broker from directly or indirectly buying listed property, or acquiring any interest in it, without first making the broker's true position clearly known to the listing owner. Money behind a relative's name is an indirect interest. The deed choice is the trap, and the last choice overstates the rule: New York requires disclosure, not a flat ban.

questions.q: A listing agent's brother-in-law makes an offer on the agent's listing. All of the following are proper EXCEPT:
c: Disclosing the family tie to the sellers in writing
Presenting every other offer to the sellers as well, promptly
Disclosing any money the agent is putting into it
Forwarding just the relative's offer to the sellers
questions.x: A listing agent presents all offers, and loyalty requires disclosing a family or financial tie to a buyer before the sellers decide; 175.4 makes disclosure mandatory for any direct or indirect interest. Forwarding only the relative's offer is self-dealing. In a short sale, the affidavit the agents sign also certifies that every offer was presented.

questions.q: An executor named in a will wants to list the decedent's Queens home. Her authority to sign for the estate comes from:
c: The will itself, once it is located and read
A power of attorney the decedent signed earlier
Letters testamentary from the Surrogate's Court
A death certificate filed with the county clerk's office
questions.x: A will names an executor, but authority to act for the estate comes from letters testamentary issued by the Surrogate's Court. The power of attorney is the trap: a power of attorney creates an agency, and agency ends by operation of law when the principal dies.

questions.q: A daughter holds her late father's power of attorney and asks a broker to list his Albany house the week after the funeral. The broker should:
c: Take the listing under the power of attorney she holds
Wait for an executor holding letters from the Surrogate's Court
Take the listing if every heir signs it along with the daughter
Take the listing as an open listing, which needs no authority
questions.x: The power of attorney ended when her father died, because death of the principal ends an agency. Only a court-appointed fiduciary, an executor with letters testamentary or an administrator with letters of administration, can hire a broker for the estate. The heirs' signature choice is the trap: heirs do not hold title free of the estate during administration.

questions.q: A salesperson is one of three heirs to a Buffalo house and lists it through her own firm. Under 19 NYCRR 175.6, she must:
c: Make her ownership interest known to the purchaser
Tell buyers about her interest if they happen to ask about it
Disclose nothing, since she is not the sole owner of record
Get DOS approval before she lists the property
questions.x: 175.6 requires a licensee who sells property in which she owns an interest to make that interest known to the purchaser, whether she owns all of it or a share. Waiting for a buyer to ask is the trap: the duty is affirmative. No DOS approval is involved.

questions.q: A licensee who is executor and an heir of an estate lists its house through her firm. All of the following are sound EXCEPT:
c: Stating her interest as an heir in the listing remarks
Getting the other heirs' written consent to her commission
Disclosing a roof leak she knows about to every buyer
Omitting her interest, since she signs as executor only
questions.x: Signing as executor does not erase her beneficial interest, so 175.6 still requires telling purchasers. Clearing her commission with the other heirs addresses her conflict as a fiduciary, and known material defects must be disclosed even though an estate sale is exempt from the PCDS form. The consent choice is the trap for anyone who thinks a fair fee needs no consent.

cram.html: Fiduciary duties: OLD CAR: Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care.
Client gets loyalty, advice, confidentiality. Customer gets honesty, fair dealing, and known material defects.
Confidentiality survives the end of the agency.
Who pays the commission does not decide whom the agent represents.
Listing broker = special agent. Property manager = general agent. Power of attorney over everything = universal agent.
Agency is created by express agreement, implied conduct, ratification (approval after), or estoppel (appearance before).
Antitrust four: price fixing, group boycott, market allocation, tie-in. Sherman Act, per se illegal. Commissions are always negotiable.
Net listings are illegal in NY (175.19).
Only a licensed broker sues for a commission, and must have been licensed when the work was done (RPL 442-d). Never pay the unlicensed.
Subagent: seller is vicariously liable. Broker's agent: client is not; the engaging broker is.
Dual agency: informed written consent of both parties. Nobody gets undivided loyalty.
Designated sales agents: two different licensees, written consent, broker stays a dual agent.
Reg 175.7: no compensation from more than one party without full knowledge and consent of all.
Referral fee from a lender for a mere referral = RESPA kickback.
Exclusive right to sell: broker paid even if owner finds buyer. Exclusive agency: owner finds buyer, no fee. Open: only procuring cause.
175.24: exclusive residential listings need a printed ERTS vs EA explanation, min 6-point type, initialed by owner.
NAR settlement, Aug 17, 2024: written buyer agreement before touring; no buyer-broker comp offers on the MLS.
Agency ends by performance, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation, renunciation, death, incapacity, bankruptcy, destruction. Salesperson leaving does not end it.
RPL 443 form: residential 1 to 4 family, condos, co-ops, sales and rentals. Not commercial, not vacant land. "This is not a contract."
Listing agent gives the form before the listing agreement; the other side gets it at first substantive contact.
Refusal to sign: sworn declaration of the refusal. Keep forms and declarations 3 years.
Since Jan 1, 2011: condos and co-ops covered, landlord-tenant form, advance consent to dual agency.
NYC FARE Act (June 11, 2025): the landlord pays the broker the landlord hired.
Independent contractor: licensed, paid by output, written contract not under duress, no direction and control (IRC 3508, NY 1986 law).
Misclassified? Broker owes unemployment insurance, workers' comp, disability, withholding. Salesperson loses Schedule C.
175.21 supervision is required; 175.23 transaction records kept 3 years.

subjects.title: Legal Issues
subjects.blurb: Estates, co-ownership, liens, easements, deeds, and the closing table are the legal skeleton of every deal, and they supply a big slice of DOS exam items, including the transfer tax and proration math.

lessons.title: What You Actually Own
lessons.tagline: Land, real estate, real property, and the stuff that leaves with the seller: the line decides what is in the deal.
objectives: Tell land, real estate, real property, and personal property apart
Name the five rights in the bundle and what takes a stick away
Apply the fixture tests (MARIA) and spot a trade fixture
Explain air, subsurface, riparian, and littoral rights in NY terms
List the uses and the physical and economic characteristics of real property

blocks.title: The chandelier standoff, Bed-Stuy
blocks.html: The Okafors are selling their brownstone on Macon Street. At the final walk-through the buyer finds bare wires where a crystal chandelier hung, a missing window AC unit, and the backyard tomato plants pulled out. Grace says the chandelier was her grandmother's and "obviously ours." The contract is silent. Who is right about each item?
blocks.casual: Picture the final walk-through on Macon Street. The Okafors are selling their brownstone, and the buyer walks in to find bare wires hanging where a crystal chandelier used to be. The window AC unit is gone. The tomato plants out back got yanked. Grace says the chandelier was her grandmother's, so obviously it's theirs. The contract doesn't say a word about any of it. So who wins each fight?

deeper.plain: When a house sells, some things go with it and some things leave with the seller. This lesson gives you the rules for sorting them.
deeper.picture: Think of moving out of a rental. Your lamps and couch come with you, but you don't unscrew the kitchen faucet. Everyone senses the line; the law draws it precisely.
deeper.street: The buyer's attorney emails Priya, the Okafors' attorney, the night before closing demanding a $4,000 credit for the chandelier. Priya has to tell Grace that a hard-wired light is almost certainly a fixture, and that she should have excluded it in writing months ago.
deeper.stakes: Fights over what stays can delay a closing, cost the seller a credit, or sour a deal at the last minute. An agent who flags these items at the listing appointment saves everyone the headache.
deeper.exam: Scenario questions describe an item and ask whether it is real or personal property. Look for cue words like bolted, wired, plumbed, or custom-fitted, and check whether the contract says anything, because a written agreement beats every other test.

blocks.html: Three words that sound the same mean three different layers. Land is the earth's surface, everything below it to the center of the earth, and the air above it, plus things attached by nature (trees, water, minerals). Add things attached by people (buildings, fences, sidewalks) and you have real estate. Add the legal rights of ownership and you have real property.
blocks.casual: These three words sound like twins, but each one stacks on the last. Land is the dirt plus everything below it down to the center of the earth and the air above it, along with stuff nature attached (trees, water, minerals). Add what people attached (buildings, fences, sidewalks) and now it's real estate. Add the legal rights that come with owning it and you've got real property.

deeper.plain: Land is the ground. Real estate is the ground plus buildings. Real property is all that plus your legal rights to it.
deeper.picture: Think of a phone. The bare hardware is land, the phone with apps installed is real estate, and the phone plus your account, warranty, and right to sell it is real property.
deeper.street: Evelyn buys a vacant lot in Hunts Point (land), puts up a warehouse (now real estate), and then leases it to a distributor. That lease is a right she holds as owner, which is what makes it real property.
deeper.stakes: In daily deals nobody gets sued over this vocabulary, but sloppy use confuses clients when you later explain air rights or easements, which are rights, not dirt.
deeper.exam: The test asks which term includes the rights of ownership. The answer is real property. If the stem stresses man-made attachments only, it wants real estate; if it mentions the center of the earth and airspace, it wants land.

blocks.html: Everything else is personal property, also called personalty or a chattel: movable things not attached to the land. A couch, a car, a co-op apartment's shares of stock. Real property moves by deed. Personal property moves by a bill of sale.
blocks.casual: Anything else is personal property, a.k.a. personalty or a chattel. It's the stuff you can move that isn't attached to the land: a couch, a car, and yes, the shares of stock you own in a co-op. Real property changes hands by deed. Personal property changes hands by a bill of sale.

deeper.plain: If it's movable and not attached, it's personal property, and you sell it with a bill of sale instead of a deed.
deeper.picture: A deed is like the title to the parking spot; a bill of sale is the receipt for the car you park in it.
deeper.street: Leo buys a two-bedroom co-op in Jackson Heights. At closing he gets a stock certificate and a proprietary lease, not a deed, because co-op shares are personal property. The sellers also hand him a bill of sale for the washer-dryer they agreed to leave.
deeper.stakes: Treating a co-op like real estate leads to wrong advice on taxes and paperwork. For example, a co-op share loan is not a mortgage, so no mortgage recording tax applies.
deeper.exam: Expect a question asking what a co-op owner holds: shares of stock and a proprietary lease, which are personal property. Another classic: personal property is transferred by a bill of sale, not a deed.

head: Term
Formula
Example
rows: A vacant lot in Hunts Point with its soil and trees
That lot with a warehouse on it
Real estate + the bundle of legal rights
Owning the warehouse lot and the right to lease, sell, mortgage it
blocks.caption: Each layer adds something to the one above it

deeper.plain: Each row adds one thing to the row above it, and personal property sits off to the side as anything movable.
deeper.picture: Think of a sandwich: bread is land, the fillings are buildings, and the wrapper with your name on it is the bundle of rights.
deeper.street: Evelyn's Hunts Point deal shows every row: the bare lot, the warehouse on it, her right to lease and mortgage it, and the forklifts and racks inside, which she sells to the tenant separately with a bill of sale.
deeper.stakes: When you write up a commercial deal, the equipment inside is personal property and must be listed and transferred separately, or the buyer may end up without the inventory they thought they bought.
deeper.exam: Memorize the formula order: land, then real estate (plus improvements), then real property (plus rights). Distractors swap real estate and real property, so read the stem for the word rights.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: Many questions use "real estate" and "real property" as synonyms, and in daily practice they are. If a question asks which term includes the rights of ownership, the answer is real property.
blocks.casual: Lots of questions treat "real estate" and "real property" like they mean the same thing, and honestly, in day to day work they do. But if a question asks which term includes the rights of ownership, pick real property.

deeper.plain: Most of the time the two words are interchangeable, except when the question is about rights.
deeper.picture: It's like Coke and soda: in conversation they swap, but on an ingredient label only one is exact.
deeper.street: Jordan writes "real estate" in a listing description and nobody cares. On the practice exam, though, a question asks what adds the bundle of rights, and Jordan picks real estate and loses the point.
deeper.stakes: On the job, nothing. On the exam, this one word costs points every year because the choices look so close.
deeper.exam: Scan the stem for rights, interests, or benefits of ownership. Those cue words point to real property. If the stem only describes physical things, real estate is fine.

blocks.html: Owning real property means holding a bundle of rights, like a bundle of sticks. You can hand individual sticks to other people without giving up the whole bundle. The five classic sticks:
blocks.casual: Owning real property means you hold a bundle of rights. Think of it like a bundle of sticks. You can hand a stick or two to someone else and still keep the bundle. Here are the five classic sticks:

deeper.plain: Ownership is a set of separate rights, and you can give some away while keeping the rest.
deeper.picture: Think of a key ring. You can give a copy of one key to a dog walker without handing over the house.
deeper.street: Sal owns his 6-unit Astoria building. He leases five apartments (giving away possession), gives Con Ed an easement for a gas line, and mortgages the building to a bank. He still owns it and can still sell it.
deeper.stakes: Every lease, easement, and mortgage is a stick someone else holds. Buyers inherit those deals, so you need to know which sticks are already out before you promise a buyer anything.
deeper.exam: The exam asks which action transfers only part of the bundle. A lease transfers possession, a mortgage pledges the property as security, and a deed transfers the whole bundle.

items: Possession: the right to occupy
Control: the right to use and alter it within the law
Enjoyment: the right to use it free from interference
Exclusion: the right to keep others out
Disposition: the right to sell, lease, mortgage, give away, or leave it by will
blocks.casual:
Possession means you get to live there or occupy it.
Control means you can use it and change it, as long as you stay within the law.
Enjoyment means you get to use it without anyone interfering.
Exclusion means you can keep people out.
Disposition means you can sell it, lease it, mortgage it, give it away, or leave it in your will.

deeper.plain: The five sticks are: live there, change it, use it in peace, keep people out, and get rid of it however you like.
deeper.picture: Think of your own phone: you hold it, set it up how you like, use it without people grabbing it, lock it, and can sell or gift it.
deeper.street: The Okafors lease their garden unit to a tenant, which hands over possession and part of the exclusion stick. During the lease, Grace can't just walk in, because the tenant now holds those rights. She still keeps disposition and can sell the building subject to the lease.
deeper.stakes: Owners who forget what they've handed out get into trouble, like a landlord who enters without notice and violates the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.
deeper.exam: Expect a question that names one right and asks which stick it is. Selling, leasing, mortgaging, and willing it all fall under disposition. Keeping trespassers out is exclusion.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: PC-EED: Possession, Control, Enjoyment, Exclusion, Disposition. Or picture a key ring: you can lend a key (lease) without selling the house.
blocks.casual: Remember PC-EED: Possession, Control, Enjoyment, Exclusion, Disposition. Or picture a key ring. You can lend somebody a key (that's a lease) and still own the house.

deeper.plain: PC-EED is just a shortcut for the five rights of ownership.
deeper.picture: Imagine a PC that needs EEDs to run: one possession chip, one control chip, two E chips, and a D drive you can sell.
deeper.street: When Leo asks what he's really buying, Jordan pulls out keys: one for living there, one for renovating, one for peace and quiet, one for locking the door, and the last one for selling someday.
deeper.stakes: Getting one of the five wrong on the exam is a cheap lost point. The hook works because the exam lists them in different orders to throw you off.
deeper.exam: A distractor will slip in something that isn't a bundle right, like taxation or escheat (those are government powers). If it's something the state holds, it's not one of the owner's sticks.

blocks.caption: Click each stick. A lease hands away possession and exclusion for a term; a mortgage pledges disposition; zoning trims control; an easement cuts into exclusion.

blocks.html: The government holds four powers over every owner's bundle (taught in Land Use): police power (zoning, codes), eminent domain (taking with just compensation), taxation, and escheat (the state takes property when an owner dies with no will and no heirs). Remember them as PETE.
blocks.casual: The government also holds four powers over every owner's bundle (you'll get the full rundown in Land Use). Police power (zoning and codes), eminent domain (taking property but paying just compensation), taxation, and escheat (the state takes the property when the owner dies with no will and no heirs). Remember them as PETE.

deeper.plain: No matter how much you own, the government can regulate it, take it with payment, tax it, or claim it if no one inherits.
deeper.picture: Think of an apartment you own in a building with house rules. You own the unit, but the building can still set rules and collect fees. The government plays that role for everyone.
deeper.street: The city rezones a block in Gowanus (police power), condemns a corner lot for a school with fair payment (eminent domain), sends Sal his quarterly tax bill (taxation), and takes a house in Ozone Park whose owner died with no will and no relatives (escheat).
