deeper.stakes: Buyers who ignore zoning or pending condemnation can pay for a plan they can't build. Unpaid taxes also become a lien that comes first, ahead of the buyer's lender.
deeper.exam: PETE shows up as "which is NOT a government power." Escheat means no will and no heirs; if there is any heir, there's no escheat. Eminent domain always comes with just compensation.

blocks.q: Sal leases a ground-floor store in his Astoria building to a bakery for 10 years. Which sticks has he mainly transferred for the term?
c: Possession and exclusion
Disposition and control
Enjoyment and disposition
All five rights
blocks.x: A tenant gets the right to occupy and to keep others (including, mostly, the landlord) out. Sal keeps disposition: he can still sell or mortgage the building subject to the lease.

blocks.text: Fixtures: when personal property becomes real

blocks.html: A fixture is an item that started as personal property and became real property by being attached to or adapted for the building. Fixtures transfer with the deed unless the contract says otherwise. Courts and the exam use five tests:
blocks.casual: A fixture starts out as personal property and turns into real property once it's attached to the building or adapted to fit it. Fixtures go with the deed unless the contract says otherwise. Courts and the exam use five tests to decide:

deeper.plain: A fixture is something that used to be movable but got attached, so now it's part of the house and goes with the sale.
deeper.picture: A bookshelf from the store is just furniture. Bolt it into the wall, cut to fit an alcove, and it's now part of the room.
deeper.street: The Okafors' built-in window seat and the radiator covers Emmanuel custom-built in 2004 are fixtures. Buyers expect them to be there on closing day, and Priya warns that removing them would breach the deal.
deeper.stakes: If a seller strips fixtures, the buyer can demand a credit, delay the closing, or sue. Agents who promise buyers that something stays without checking the contract invite a complaint.
deeper.exam: Know the default: fixtures transfer with the property unless excluded in writing. The question may describe an item that was personal property before installation, and the right answer is that it became real property.

head: Test
Question
Leans fixture when
rows: Bolted, wired, plumbed, cemented; removal causes damage
Was it made or fitted for this property?
Custom-cut shelving, storm windows sized for these frames
Owner installed it (presumed to improve the property)
Meant to stay permanently; this is the most important test
A written agreement overrides everything else
blocks.caption: MARIA. Intention is the key test; a written agreement beats all of them

deeper.plain: To decide if something is a fixture, ask how it's attached, if it was fitted for this place, who put it in, what they meant, and what the contract says.
deeper.picture: Think of MARIA as a judge with five questions on her clipboard, but the last line (agreement) is written in red ink and overrides the rest.
deeper.street: Diane walks Jordan through a Park Slope listing: built-in bookcases (adapted, fixture), a freestanding wine fridge (personal), a mounted TV bracket (attached, fixture) but the TV itself (personal). Then she says, "And none of that matters if the contract lists it."
deeper.stakes: When the contract is silent, the fight goes to MARIA, and both sides can argue. Writing it into the contract avoids the whole argument.
deeper.exam: Intention is the most important test when there's no agreement. A written agreement beats everything. Watch for a stem that describes heavy attachment but says the contract excludes the item: the contract wins.

blocks.html: Apply it to the Okafors. The chandelier was hard-wired into the ceiling: a fixture, so it goes with the house unless the contract excluded it. The window AC unit sits in the window on brackets: usually personal property. The tomatoes are emblements, annual crops planted by labor, which are personal property. Trees, shrubs, and perennials growing naturally are real property.
blocks.casual: Let's run the Okafors through it. The chandelier was hard-wired into the ceiling, so it's a fixture and it goes with the house unless the contract carved it out. The window AC unit just sits in the window on brackets, so it's usually personal property. The tomatoes are emblements: annual crops you plant with your own work, which count as personal property. Trees, shrubs, and perennials that grow on their own are real property.

deeper.plain: The chandelier stays, the AC unit can go, and the tomatoes belong to the person who planted them.
deeper.picture: Emblements are like a pot of soup you cooked in someone else's kitchen: the stove stays, but the soup is yours.
deeper.street: Grace keeps the AC and the tomatoes with no problem. The chandelier is the issue. Priya negotiates: Grace can keep her grandmother's chandelier if she installs a comparable fixture and gives a $500 credit, and the buyer agrees.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who act on what feels fair rather than the rule end up paying credits or replacing items at the last minute.
deeper.exam: Emblements are annual crops planted by labor and are personal property, even if still in the ground. Natural trees and perennials are real property. A stem about a tenant farmer harvesting after the lease ends is testing emblements.

blocks.title: Field tip
blocks.html: Sellers who want to keep a chandelier should swap it out before listing photos, or exclude it in writing in the contract. In NY the attorneys draft that inclusion/exclusion list, but you can flag it at the listing appointment and save a closing-day fight.
blocks.casual: If your sellers want to keep a chandelier, tell them to swap it out before the listing photos, or exclude it in writing in the contract. In NY the attorneys draft the list of what's included and excluded, but you can raise it at the listing appointment and spare everyone a closing-day fight.

deeper.plain: If a seller wants to keep something attached, remove it before marketing or put the exclusion in writing.
deeper.picture: It's like taking a photo of a car with custom rims and then trying to sell it without them. The buyer fell for what was in the picture.
deeper.street: Diane's listing checklist has a line: "What are you taking?" When a seller in Ditmas Park says the antique sconces, Jordan swaps them for basic fixtures before the photographer comes, and the attorney adds the exclusion.
deeper.stakes: If the item shows in photos and the contract is silent, the buyer can argue it was part of the deal. That can mean a credit, a delayed closing, or a DOS complaint if the agent promised it stays.
deeper.exam: This tests the rule that an agreement controls. If an item is excluded in writing, it doesn't transfer, even if it's a fixture.

blocks.html: A trade fixture is equipment a commercial tenant installs to run its business: pizza ovens, salon chairs, bar coolers, display racks. Trade fixtures remain the tenant's personal property even if bolted down. The tenant may remove them before the lease ends but must repair damage caused by removal. Trade fixtures left behind after the lease ends can become the landlord's property by accession.
blocks.casual: A trade fixture is equipment a commercial tenant puts in to run the business: pizza ovens, salon chairs, bar coolers, display racks. Even if it's bolted down, it stays the tenant's personal property. The tenant can take it out before the lease ends but has to fix any damage from pulling it. If the tenant leaves it behind after the lease is over, it can become the landlord's property by accession.

deeper.plain: Business equipment a tenant installs belongs to the tenant, as long as they take it out on time and patch up the damage.
deeper.picture: It's like bringing your own espresso machine to a shared office. It's plugged into their wall, but it's yours, unless you forget it when you move out.
deeper.street: A pizzeria in Evelyn's Bay Ridge retail strip bolts a $30,000 deck oven to the floor. When the lease ends, the owner removes it, patches the floor, and takes it to the new spot. A bakery that walked away from its racks last year lost them to Evelyn by accession.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who miss the move-out deadline can lose expensive equipment. Landlords who block removal of a trade fixture invite a lawsuit.
deeper.exam: Cue words: commercial tenant, business equipment, installed for the trade. The answer is trade fixture, which is personal property, even when bolted down. Left behind after lease end, it goes to the landlord by accession.

left.title: Fixture
items: Installed by an owner (usually)
Becomes real property
Passes with the deed
Mortgage lender's collateral too

right.title: Trade fixture
items: Installed by a commercial tenant for business
Stays the tenant's personal property
Removable before lease ends; tenant repairs damage
Left behind: landlord may keep it by accession

deeper.plain: A regular fixture becomes part of the building; a trade fixture stays the tenant's stuff.
deeper.picture: A fixture is like a tattoo: it's part of you now. A trade fixture is a temporary tattoo the tenant can wash off before leaving.
deeper.street: When Evelyn refinances her retail building, the lender's appraisal counts the owner-installed HVAC (fixture, real property) but not the salon chairs and dryers of the tenant on the ground floor (trade fixtures).
deeper.stakes: Lenders, buyers, and appraisers need to know which equipment is real property. Counting a tenant's trade fixtures as part of the building overstates value and collateral.
deeper.exam: The exam pairs these side by side: who installed it (owner vs commercial tenant) and why (improve the property vs run a business). The repair duty on removal and accession for leftovers are both fair game.

blocks.q: A tenant who ran a Williamsburg cafe bolted an espresso bar to the floor. The lease expired last month and the tenant left it. Who owns it now?
c: The tenant, because trade fixtures are always personal property
The landlord, by accession, because it was not removed before the lease ended
The city, by escheat
Whoever paid for the floor
blocks.x: Trade fixtures are removable only during the lease term. Abandoned ones can become the landlord's property through accession. Escheat applies only when an owner dies with no will and no heirs.

blocks.text: Above, below, and beside the water

blocks.html: Air rights are the right to use the space above the land. They can be sold or leased separately. In NYC this is big business: unused development rights (floor area the zoning allows but the building does not use) are transferred to neighbors through zoning lot mergers or landmark transfers, which is how slim Midtown towers rise next to low churches and theaters.
blocks.casual: Air rights are your right to use the space above your land, and you can sell or lease them separately. In NYC this is serious money. Unused development rights (floor area zoning allows but your building doesn't use) get transferred to neighbors through zoning lot mergers or landmark transfers. That's how those skinny Midtown towers go up right next to low-slung churches and theaters.

deeper.plain: You own some of the sky above your land, and you can sell that space to someone who wants to build taller.
deeper.picture: Imagine a group data plan. If you're not using all your gigabytes, you can hand them to someone who is, and they can stream more.
deeper.street: A small church in Midtown sells its unused development rights to a developer next door for millions. The church stays three stories, and the tower next door rises extra floors using the church's air rights.
deeper.stakes: A seller who has already sold air rights can't market the property as having expansion potential. Buyers who assume they can build up may overpay.
deeper.exam: The exam tests that air rights can be separated from the land and sold or leased independently. A question about building above railroad tracks or transferring development rights points to air rights.

blocks.html: Subsurface rights (mineral rights) cover what lies below: minerals, oil, gas. An owner can sell them separately and keep the surface. Upstate, gas leases on farms in the Southern Tier are the classic example.
blocks.casual: Subsurface rights, also called mineral rights, cover what's underneath: minerals, oil, gas. An owner can sell those off and keep the surface. The classic NY example is gas leases on farms in the Southern Tier.

deeper.plain: You can own the top of the land while someone else owns what's buried below it.
deeper.picture: It's like a house where you rent out the basement storage. You live upstairs, but someone else has rights below.
deeper.street: A farmer near Binghamton leases the gas rights under his 200 acres to an energy company for signing money and royalties. He keeps farming the surface. Years later, a buyer finds the lease in the title search and has to decide whether to proceed.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't check for a severed mineral estate may find they don't control what happens under their land, which can affect use, value, and financing.
deeper.exam: The exam tests that subsurface rights can be sold separately from surface rights. If the stem says someone owns the land but another party owns the oil or gas, the answer is severed subsurface or mineral rights.

blocks.html: Water rights come in two flavors. Riparian rights belong to owners along flowing water (rivers, streams). Owners on a non-navigable stream usually own to the center line; on navigable water, the state owns the bed and the owner holds to the water's edge. Littoral rights belong to owners along still or tidal water (lakes, ponds, the ocean); they usually own to the mean high water mark. Both give reasonable use of the water and access to it, not ownership of the water itself.
blocks.casual: Water rights come in two flavors. Riparian rights go to owners along flowing water like rivers and streams. On a non-navigable stream, you usually own to the center line. On navigable water, the state owns the bed and you own to the water's edge. Littoral rights go to owners along still or tidal water like lakes, ponds, and the ocean, and you usually own to the mean high water mark. Either way, you get reasonable use of the water and access to it, but you don't own the water itself.

deeper.plain: If your land touches a river, you have riparian rights; if it touches a lake or the ocean, you have littoral rights. Neither means you own the water.
deeper.picture: Think of a shared office kitchen. You can use the water cooler, but you can't take the whole jug home.
deeper.street: A family with a cabin on a creek in the Catskills owns to the center of the creek and can draw water for the garden. Their cousins with a house on Lake George own to the mean high water mark and have access to the lake, but the state owns the lake bed beyond.
deeper.stakes: Buyers of waterfront property assume they own more than they do. Damming or diverting water can lead to lawsuits from downstream owners.
deeper.exam: Flowing equals riparian. Still or tidal equals littoral. For navigable water, the owner goes to the water's edge; for non-navigable, the center line. Neither right means owning the water itself.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Riparian = River. Littoral = Lake (and Long Island's Littoral coast). Both start with the letter of the water they touch.
blocks.casual: Riparian = River. Littoral = Lake (and the Long Island coast, if it helps). Each one starts with the same letter as the water it touches.

deeper.plain: Match the first letter: R for river, L for lake.
deeper.picture: Picture a road sign with an R pointing to a river and an L pointing to a lake.
deeper.street: Jordan, prepping for the exam on the Q train, writes R-River and L-Lake on a sticky note. On test day, a question about a house on Seneca Lake takes four seconds.
deeper.stakes: These two words look alike under time pressure, and a quick hook saves you a guess.
deeper.exam: Remember that ocean and tidal water also count as littoral, even though they don't start with L. A stem mentioning the shoreline of Long Island Sound is littoral.

blocks.title: New York uses riparian doctrine
blocks.html: New York is an eastern, water-rich state that follows the riparian rule (reasonable use by adjoining owners). The western prior appropriation doctrine (first to use, first in right, by permit) is not New York law.
blocks.casual: New York is in the water-rich East, so it uses the riparian rule: owners next to the water get reasonable use. The western prior appropriation idea (first to use it, first in right, by permit) is not New York law.

deeper.plain: In New York, everyone along the water shares it reasonably. It's not first come, first served.
deeper.picture: Think of a pizza shared at a table: everyone gets a fair slice. Prior appropriation is more like whoever grabbed it first gets the whole pie.
deeper.street: An orchard owner in the Hudson Valley wants to pump heavily from a stream for irrigation. Downstream neighbors can object under the reasonable use rule, and he can't claim priority just because he started first.
deeper.stakes: Agents who repeat western rules to NY clients give bad advice about water use, which can lead to disputes or lawsuits among neighbors.
deeper.exam: If an answer choice mentions prior appropriation or a state permit system for water rights, it's the western rule and the wrong choice for New York.

head: Use
Examples in NY
rows: One to four family homes, co-ops, condos, rental buildings
Retail on Fordham Road, Midtown office, hotels, parking garages
Warehouses in Sunset Park, factories, distribution centers
Dairy farms in the North Country, orchards in the Hudson Valley, vineyards in the Finger Lakes
Churches, schools, hospitals, cemeteries, government buildings

deeper.plain: Real estate gets grouped by what it's used for: homes, business, industry, farming, or a single special purpose.
deeper.picture: Think of a department store directory: each floor holds a different kind of stuff, and shoppers go to different floors.
deeper.street: In one week, Hudson & Hart handles a two-family in Bushwick (residential), a storefront on Fordham Road (commercial), a warehouse lease in Sunset Park (industrial), and a church sale in Harlem (special purpose).
deeper.stakes: Each category has its own rules, financing, and buyers. Using residential comps for a warehouse produces a useless price.
deeper.exam: The exam may ask you to classify a property. Hotels and parking garages are commercial, and churches, schools, and hospitals are special purpose.

blocks.html: Special purpose real estate is designed for one use and is hard to convert, so it has a thin buyer pool. Appraisers often value it by the cost approach because comparable sales are rare.
blocks.casual: Special purpose real estate is built for one job and is hard to convert to anything else, so few buyers want it. Appraisers often value it with the cost approach, since comparable sales are rare.

deeper.plain: A building made for one use is hard to sell, so appraisers figure its value by what it would cost to build.
deeper.picture: It's like a custom wedding dress: great for one purpose, but there aren't many people looking to buy it secondhand.
deeper.street: When a parish in the Bronx sells a church building, there are maybe two other church sales in the borough in five years. The appraiser estimates what it would cost to rebuild, minus depreciation, plus land value.
deeper.stakes: Pricing special purpose property like a typical building leads to a listing that sits for years, or a buyer who overpays.
deeper.exam: Cue words: church, school, hospital, cemetery, few comparables. The answer is the cost approach.

left.title: Physical
items: Immobility: land cannot move; this is why real estate is local
Indestructibility: land is permanent (buildings are not)
Nonhomogeneity (uniqueness): no two parcels are identical, so courts can order specific performance

right.title: Economic
items: Scarcity: limited supply in a given area
Improvements: building on one parcel changes nearby values
Permanence of investment: long payback, slow to change
Situs / area preference: people's preference for a location; the most important economic factor

deeper.plain: Physical traits are about the land itself; economic traits are about how people value it.
deeper.picture: Think of a concert ticket: the seat location is fixed (physical), but its price depends on the band and demand (economic).
deeper.street: A brownstone in Fort Greene can't move (immobility), will always have land under it (indestructibility), and has no twin (nonhomogeneity). It sells for more than a similar house in the Bronx because buyers want the neighborhood (situs).
deeper.stakes: Uniqueness lets a buyer sue for specific performance if a seller backs out, since money can't buy an identical house. Situs explains why price per square foot swings so much by block.
deeper.exam: Know which list each trait belongs to. Situs (area preference) is the most important economic factor. Nonhomogeneity is why courts order specific performance.

blocks.html: Immobility, indestructibility, and nonhomogeneity are physical. Situs is why a two-family on a quiet block of Park Slope sells for triple the same house in another borough. Real estate also has illiquidity: it cannot be turned into cash quickly without a price cut. Selling a brownstone takes months; selling a stock takes seconds.
blocks.casual: Immobility, indestructibility, and nonhomogeneity are the physical ones. Situs is why a two-family on a quiet Park Slope block goes for triple what the same house fetches in another borough. Real estate also has illiquidity: you can't turn it into cash fast without cutting the price. A brownstone takes months to sell; a stock takes seconds.

deeper.plain: Location drives price, and real estate is slow to turn into cash.
deeper.picture: Selling a house is like selling a vintage guitar: the right buyer pays top dollar, but finding them takes time unless you cut the price.
deeper.street: The Okafors need cash fast for a move. Jordan explains that listing at market will take 60 to 90 days; pricing 10% under might get a deal in two weeks. That gap is illiquidity in action.
deeper.stakes: Clients who need money quickly may take a lower price. Agents who promise a quick sale at full price set up disappointment.
deeper.exam: Illiquidity means you can't convert to cash quickly without losing value. Situs means people prefer a location. Don't mix up immobility (land can't move) with illiquidity (can't sell fast).

blocks.html: A parcel is one separately owned and described piece of land, the unit that a deed conveys and a tax map numbers.
blocks.casual: A parcel is one separately owned and described piece of land. It's the unit a deed conveys and the thing a tax map gives a number to.

deeper.plain: A parcel is one piece of land with its own owner and description.
deeper.picture: Think of an apartment number in a big building: each one is a separate unit with its own address.
deeper.street: When Evelyn buys two side-by-side lots in Long Island City, they show as two parcels with two block and lot numbers until she merges them with the city.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up parcels can lead to a deed that conveys the wrong land or misses part of it, which means title trouble down the road.
deeper.exam: A parcel is the basic unit for deeds and tax maps. If a stem asks what a deed or tax map identifies, the answer is a parcel.

blocks.q: Why can a buyer sue a seller for specific performance of a real estate contract but usually not for a contract to buy a mass-produced TV?
c: Immobility
Nonhomogeneity
Indestructibility
Illiquidity
blocks.x: Because every parcel is unique (nonhomogeneity), money damages cannot buy an identical substitute, so courts order the sale itself. Immobility explains why real estate markets are local.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Physical is I-I-N (Immobile, Indestructible, Nonhomogeneous). Economic is SIPA (Scarcity, Improvements, Permanence, Area preference).
blocks.casual: Physical traits are I-I-N: Immobile, Indestructible, Nonhomogeneous. Economic traits are SIPA: Scarcity, Improvements, Permanence, Area preference.

deeper.plain: Two shortcuts: I-I-N for physical, SIPA for economic.
deeper.picture: Picture the land saying "I-I-N" (I'm in) because it's stuck in place, then sipping (SIPA) a coffee while its value changes around it.
deeper.street: Jordan quizzes Leo on the walk to an open house. Leo gets I-I-N right but forgets permanence of investment, so Jordan makes him say SIPA twice.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up the two lists is a common way to lose a point, since distractors swap physical and economic traits.
deeper.exam: The question usually asks which is an economic characteristic. If you see scarcity, improvements, permanence, or area preference, it's economic; anything about the land itself is physical.

story.title: Grandma's Chandelier
story.setting: Bed-Stuy, a rainy Thursday walk-through

beats.text: Final walk-through on Macon Street. Leo the buyer has a printed checklist. Grace Okafor has a ladder and a cardboard box.
Why is there a box with a chandelier in it? It's in the listing photos. Row three of my spreadsheet.
That was my grandmother's. We always planned to take it.
Did the contract exclude it? Because it's wired into the ceiling. That makes it a fixture, and fixtures go with the house unless the contract says otherwise.
I checked. Contract is silent. Written agreement would have won. Without one, intention and attachment point to the buyer.

check.q: Which fixture test would have settled the chandelier fight before it started?
c: Method of attachment
Adaptation
Relationship of the parties
Agreement
check.x: A written agreement in the contract overrides the other tests. Without it, the hard wiring and the owner installing it point to fixture.

beats.text: And the window AC?
Sits on brackets, unplugs, walks out the door. Personal property. A chattel. It leaves with them.
The tomatoes?
Emmanuel planted those in April. He is not leaving them to a man who uses spreadsheets for tomatoes.
Annual crops are emblements. Personal property. The fig tree out back, though, stays.
Grace hands the box to Leo with a long sigh. Leo promises to send her a photo of it every Christmas.
Back at the office, Marcus overhears.
I'd have told the seller to just take it. Who checks?
The buyer's attorney checks, Marcus. Right before they refuse to close.
Jordan, next listing: ask about anything sentimental that's attached. Swap it before photos or exclude it in writing. MARIA settles the fight. Agreement prevents it.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: Real property on the left, Personal property on the right. Sort 12 things from a brownstone sale (built-in bookcase, area rug, boiler, fridge, window AC, chandelier, fig tree, tomatoes, ceiling fan, mirror hung on a nail, storm windows, washing machine).

facts.text: Land is the surface, below and above plus natural attachments; real estate adds man-made permanent attachments; real property adds the bundle of legal rights.
Personal property (personalty, a chattel) is movable and not attached, such as co-op shares; real property transfers by deed, personal property by bill of sale.
The owner's bundle of rights is possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion and disposition (PC-EED), and single sticks can be given to others.
Government holds four powers over every owner: police power, eminent domain, taxation and escheat (PETE); escheat takes property when an owner dies with no will and no heirs.
A fixture is personal property that became real property by attachment or adaptation and passes with the deed; courts test it by MARIA (method, adaptation, relationship, intention, agreement).
Intention is the most important fixture test, and a written agreement overrides all the tests.
A hard-wired chandelier is a fixture that goes with the house unless excluded in writing; a window AC unit on brackets is usually personal property.
Emblements (annual crops planted by labor) are personal property; trees, shrubs and perennials growing naturally are real property.
Trade fixtures stay the commercial tenant's personal property even if bolted down; the tenant removes them before the lease ends and repairs the damage, or the landlord may keep them by accession.
Air rights can be sold or leased apart from the land; in NYC unused development rights are transferred to neighbors to build taller.
Subsurface (mineral) rights to minerals, oil and gas can be sold or leased while the owner keeps the surface.

Riparian rights belong to owners along flowing water; littoral rights to owners along lakes, ponds and the ocean, usually to the mean high water mark; both give reasonable use, not ownership of the water.
New York follows the riparian doctrine of reasonable use, not the western prior appropriation rule.
Special purpose property (churches, schools, hospitals) is built for one use, has few buyers, and is often appraised by the cost approach.
The physical characteristics are immobility, indestructibility and nonhomogeneity (uniqueness), which is why courts can order specific performance.
The economic characteristics are scarcity, improvements, permanence of investment and situs (area preference), and situs is the most important.
Real estate is illiquid: it cannot be turned into cash quickly without a price cut.
A parcel is one separately owned and described piece of land, the unit a deed conveys and a tax map numbers.

lessons.title: Estates: How Long and How Much You Own
lessons.tagline: An estate is the size of your ownership measured in time. Forever, for a life, or for a lease.
objectives: Distinguish freehold from leasehold estates
Explain fee simple absolute and the two defeasible fees, with their future interests
Work through life estates, remainders, reversions, and waste
Classify the four leasehold estates and how each ends in New York
State what replaced dower and curtesy in New York

blocks.title: The will on Albemarle Road
blocks.html: Mr. Haddad's will leaves his Flatbush Victorian "to my wife Noor for her life, then to my nephew Sami." Noor, 71, wants to list it with Jordan and move to Florida. Sami lives in Ohio and hasn't been asked. Can Noor sell the house? What exactly does she own?
blocks.casual: Mr. Haddad's will leaves his Flatbush Victorian "to my wife Noor for her life, then to my nephew Sami." Noor is 71, wants Jordan to list the place, and plans to move to Florida. Sami lives in Ohio and nobody's asked him anything. So can Noor sell the house? And what does she actually own?

deeper.plain: Noor owns the right to use the house while she's alive, and Sami owns what's left after. Neither one owns the whole thing alone.
deeper.picture: It's like a season pass that one person holds until they die, after which a different person gets the house keys for good.
deeper.street: Jordan is thrilled about a $1.4 million listing on Albemarle Road until Priya reads the will. She explains that a buyer's title company will insist on Sami's signature, so Jordan's first call isn't to a photographer; it's to Ohio.
deeper.stakes: An agent who lists the house on Noor's word alone wastes months of marketing and could have a deal collapse at title, with the buyer's deposit and everyone's time on the line.
deeper.exam: Cue words "for her life, then to" create a life estate with a remainder. Expect the question to ask what the life tenant can convey: only her life estate, not the fee.

blocks.text: Estate means the degree of ownership

blocks.html: An estate in land is the degree, quantity, nature, and extent of an interest in real property. The first split is by time. A freehold estate lasts an indeterminable time (forever, or for someone's life). It is ownership. A leasehold estate lasts a determinable time set by a lease. It is tenancy, and it is treated as personal property.
blocks.casual: An estate in land just describes how much of an interest you have in real property: the degree, quantity, nature, and extent. The first big split is about time. A freehold estate lasts an open-ended time (forever, or for someone's life), and that's ownership. A leasehold estate lasts a set time spelled out in a lease. That's being a tenant, and the law treats it as personal property.

deeper.plain: Freehold means you own it with no fixed end date. Leasehold means you're renting it for a set time.
deeper.picture: Owning a car outright versus leasing one for 36 months: you drive both, but only one is yours with no clock running.
deeper.street: Sal owns his Astoria building in fee, a freehold. Each tenant on a two-year lease holds a leasehold. If Sal dies, the building passes to his heirs; the tenants' leases keep running but don't make them owners.
deeper.stakes: Mixing these up leads to bad advice, like telling a tenant a long lease gives them ownership rights, or forgetting that a lease is personal property for estate and tax purposes.
deeper.exam: Know that a leasehold is personal property, even a 99-year ground lease. Freehold estates are life estates and fee estates. Indeterminable duration means freehold.

blocks.caption: Follow the two trunks: freehold (fee simple absolute, defeasible fees, life estates) and leasehold (years, periodic, at will, sufferance). Notice which ones carry a future interest for someone else.

blocks.html: The fee simple estate (also fee, fee simple, fee simple absolute, fee absolute) is the most complete ownership the law allows. It is unlimited in time, inheritable, and freely transferable. Almost every house and condo sale in New York conveys fee simple absolute. It is still subject to government powers and to private encumbrances like mortgages and easements.
blocks.casual: The fee simple estate (you'll also hear fee, fee simple, fee simple absolute, fee absolute) is the most complete ownership the law gives you. It never runs out, your heirs can inherit it, and you can sell or give it to anyone. Nearly every house and condo sale in New York passes fee simple absolute. But it's still subject to government powers and to private stuff like mortgages and easements.

deeper.plain: Fee simple is full ownership with no time limit, and it's what almost every NY buyer gets.
deeper.picture: It's like owning a song outright, not just a license to play it. You can sell it, gift it, or leave it to your kids.
deeper.street: When Leo buys a condo in Long Island City, his deed conveys fee simple absolute. He still pays property taxes, his bank holds a mortgage lien, and the building has a utility easement. None of that cuts his fee simple; those are just strings attached.
deeper.stakes: Clients sometimes believe fee simple means nobody can tell them what to do. Then a zoning violation or an easement surprises them. Setting expectations early prevents angry calls later.
deeper.exam: Fee simple absolute is the highest form of ownership: unlimited duration, inheritable, freely transferable. A trap answer says fee simple is free of all limits; it's still subject to government powers and encumbrances.

blocks.html: A qualified fee (fee simple defeasible) is a fee that can be lost if a condition is broken. Two kinds:
blocks.casual: A qualified fee (fee simple defeasible) is ownership you can lose if you break a condition. It comes in two kinds:

deeper.plain: It's ownership with a string attached: break the rule and you could lose it.
deeper.picture: Think of a scholarship that lasts as long as you keep a B average. Drop below and the money's gone.
deeper.street: A family gave land in the Bronx to a church decades ago "so long as used for worship." When the parish shut down and the church wanted to sell to a developer, the family's heirs showed up claiming the land.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't catch a condition in the chain of title can lose the property or face a costly lawsuit. Title insurance companies flag these restrictions.
deeper.exam: Defeasible means it can be defeated. The exam tests the two types and their wording, covered in the next table.

head: Fee simple determinable
Fee on condition (subject to condition subsequent)
rows: Grantor must act (go to court) to take it back
"To the church so long as used for worship"
"To the town, but if alcohol is ever sold, grantor may re-enter"

deeper.plain: "So long as" ends things automatically; "but if" means the original owner has to step in and take it back.
deeper.picture: A determinable fee is a parking meter that shuts off by itself. A fee on condition is a parking ticket: nothing happens until someone comes and tows you.
deeper.street: The town in Westchester got land "but if alcohol is ever sold, grantor may re-enter." When the town leased the pavilion to a beer garden, the grantor's heirs had to go to court to take it back. Until they sued, the town kept title.
deeper.stakes: With a determinable fee, the owner may have lost title years ago without knowing. A buyer gets nothing. With a condition subsequent, the owner keeps title until the grantor acts.
deeper.exam: Match the magic words to the future interest: so long as, while, during go with possibility of reverter (automatic). But if, provided that, on condition that go with right of re-entry (must act).

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: "So long as" = so automatic. "But if" = but you have to sue. Fee on condition gives a right of re-entry; determinable gives a possibility of reverter.
blocks.casual: "So long as" means so automatic. "But if" means but you have to sue. A fee on condition gives the grantor a right of re-entry; a determinable fee gives a possibility of reverter.

deeper.plain: Two phrases, two outcomes: automatic loss or loss only after a lawsuit.
deeper.picture: So long as is a timer that pops by itself; but if is an alarm that someone has to answer.
deeper.street: Jordan reads an old deed for a lot in Riverhead and spots "so long as used for farming." Diane nods: "If they stopped farming in 1995, title reverted automatically. Call the title company before you list it."
deeper.stakes: Missing the difference can mean marketing a property the seller doesn't own anymore.
deeper.exam: A question gives you the deed language and asks for the grantor's interest. So long as = possibility of reverter. But if = right of re-entry.

blocks.q: A Westchester family deeds land to a village "so long as it is used as a public park." Twenty years later the village paves it for a parking lot. What happens?
c: Nothing until the family sues and wins
The land escheats to the state
The village owes damages but keeps title
Title automatically reverts to the family or its heirs
blocks.x: "So long as" creates a fee simple determinable. Breaking the condition ends the estate automatically and title reverts. A suit would be needed only for a fee on condition subsequent ("but if").

blocks.html: A life estate is a freehold limited to the lifetime of a person. The holder is the life tenant. When the measuring life ends, the property goes to the holder of the future interest:
blocks.casual: A life estate is ownership that lasts only as long as a particular person lives. The person who holds it is the life tenant. Once that measuring life ends, the property moves on to whoever holds the future interest:

deeper.plain: A life estate is ownership that lasts while someone is alive, then passes to someone else.
deeper.picture: It's like a library book you can keep as long as you live, after which it goes to the next name on the hold list.
deeper.street: Noor gets to live in the Flatbush house, collect rent from the top floor if she wants, and stay as long as she lives. The day she dies, Sami owns it outright without needing a court or a new deed.
deeper.stakes: Families use life estates to keep a parent in the house while guaranteeing it goes to the kids. Agents who don't spot one can list a house the seller can't fully convey.
deeper.exam: The life tenant holds a freehold estate, not a leasehold. The measuring life is usually the life tenant's own. Watch for wording that names a different person's life.

items: Remainder interest: goes to a third party named by the grantor, the remainderman (Sami in our scenario).
Reversionary interest: goes back to the grantor or the grantor's heirs because no remainderman was named.
A life estate pur autre vie is measured by someone else's life: "to Noor for the life of her brother." If Noor dies first, her heirs keep it until the brother dies.
blocks.casual:
With a remainder interest, the property goes to a third person the grantor named, called the remainderman. That's Sami here.
With a reversionary interest, the property goes back to the grantor or the grantor's heirs because nobody was named to take it next.
A life estate pur autre vie is measured by somebody else's life, like "to Noor for the life of her brother." If Noor dies first, her heirs hold on to it until the brother dies.

deeper.plain: After the life estate ends, the property goes either to a named person (remainder) or back to the original owner's side (reversion).
deeper.picture: A remainder is like a relay race baton handed to the next runner. A reversion is the baton going back to the coach.
deeper.street: Had Mr. Haddad's will said only "to Noor for her life" with no next name, the house would revert to his estate when Noor dies, passing under the rest of his will or to his heirs.
deeper.stakes: If the wrong person signs or the right person is missed, the buyer gets a cloud on title and the deal stalls.
deeper.exam: Named third party = remainder and remainderman. Back to grantor = reversion. Pur autre vie means another person's life measures it, and the estate passes to the life tenant's heirs if the life tenant dies first.

blocks.html: The life tenant can live there, rent it out, mortgage it, or sell it, but can only convey what she has: an interest that ends at her death (or the measuring person's death). That is why Noor alone cannot sell a fee simple. A buyer would get a life estate that evaporates when she dies. To sell the whole fee, Noor and Sami must both sign the deed.
blocks.casual: The life tenant can live there, rent it out, mortgage it, or sell it. But she can only hand over what she has: an interest that ends when she dies (or when the measuring person does). That's why Noor can't sell a fee simple on her own. A buyer would get a life estate that disappears the day she dies. To sell the whole fee, Noor and Sami both have to sign the deed.

deeper.plain: Noor can only sell what she owns, which ends when she dies, so Sami has to sign too.
deeper.picture: It's like trying to sell the rest of your gym membership when it expires at your death. Nobody wants to pay full price for that.
deeper.street: Jordan calls Sami in Ohio, who agrees to sell and split the proceeds with Noor based on an actuarial value of her life estate. Priya drafts the deed with both signatures, and the buyer closes on fee simple.
deeper.stakes: If Jordan lists without Sami, the buyer's title search catches it, the contract stalls, and Jordan may face a complaint for misrepresenting what was for sale.
deeper.exam: A life tenant can sell, lease, or mortgage only the life estate. To convey fee simple, both the life tenant and remainderman must sign. A lease by a life tenant ends when the life tenant dies.

blocks.html: The life tenant must not commit an act of waste: damaging, neglecting, or materially changing the property in a way that hurts the future owner. Letting the roof cave in, tearing out the stained glass to sell it, or stripping timber are waste. The remainderman can sue to stop it. The life tenant pays ordinary taxes and upkeep.
blocks.casual: The life tenant can't commit an act of waste, meaning damage, neglect, or a major change that hurts the future owner. Letting the roof cave in, ripping out the stained glass to sell it, or cutting down the timber all count. The remainderman can sue to stop it. The life tenant also pays the ordinary taxes and upkeep.

deeper.plain: The life tenant has to take reasonable care of the property for whoever gets it next.
deeper.picture: It's like borrowing your friend's car for a year: drive it, gas it up, but don't strip the stereo or let the engine die.
deeper.street: Noor stops paying for repairs and a roof leak starts rotting the top floor. Sami, worried about his future house, has his lawyer send a letter and then files suit to force repairs.
deeper.stakes: If the life tenant lets the property decline, the remainderman can sue for damages or an injunction, and taxes in default can lead to a lien.
deeper.exam: The remainderman's remedy for waste is a lawsuit. The life tenant, not the remainderman, pays ordinary taxes and maintenance.

blocks.q: Noor holds a life estate; Sami holds the remainder. Noor deeds "all her interest" to a buyer and then dies. Who owns the house?
c: The buyer, in fee simple
The buyer and Sami as tenants in common
Noor's heirs
Sami, the remainderman
blocks.x: Noor could convey only her life estate. It ended at her death and the remainder vested in Sami. The buyer's interest died with Noor.

blocks.text: Legal life estates: dower, curtesy, homestead

blocks.html: Some life estates are created by law, not by deed. Historically a widow had dower (a life estate in one third of her husband's land) and a widower had curtesy.
blocks.casual: Some life estates come from the law instead of a deed. Back in the day, a widow got dower (a life estate in one third of her husband's land) and a widower got curtesy.

deeper.plain: Old laws gave a surviving spouse automatic rights in the other spouse's land.
deeper.picture: It's like an old rule in a family game that's been replaced with a new house rule.
deeper.street: A title examiner on an old Brooklyn chain of title spots a 1920s transfer where a widow's dower rights were never released, and checks whether it still matters for current title.
deeper.stakes: In modern New York, dower and curtesy don't apply to recent marriages, but agents who mention them as current law confuse clients.
deeper.exam: Know the definitions: dower for widows, curtesy for widowers, both legal life estates. Then remember New York abolished them.

blocks.title: New York abolished dower and curtesy
blocks.html: New York abolished dower and curtesy (for marriages and property after 1930). A surviving spouse is protected instead by the elective share: the right to take the greater of $50,000 or one third of the net estate, even if the will leaves the spouse less. NY is also not a community property state.
blocks.casual: New York got rid of dower and curtesy (for marriages and property after 1930). Now a surviving spouse is protected by the elective share: the right to take the larger of $50,000 or one third of the net estate, even if the will leaves the spouse less. NY is also not a community property state.

deeper.plain: In New York, a surviving spouse can claim a minimum share of the estate no matter what the will says.
deeper.picture: It's like a guaranteed minimum on a contract: even if the deal changes, you get at least this much.
deeper.street: A husband in Staten Island leaves his whole estate to his brother. His widow elects to take one third of the $900,000 net estate, $300,000, instead of the nothing the will gave her.
deeper.stakes: Selling estate property without understanding a spouse's elective share can lead to disputes that hold up closings and cloud title.
deeper.exam: A trap answer lists dower as current NY law. The right answer is that NY abolished dower and curtesy and uses the elective share. Also, NY is not community property.

blocks.html: A homestead exemption protects a set dollar amount of equity in a primary residence from unsecured creditors who win a judgment. In New York the amount depends on the county (highest downstate) and is adjusted every few years. It does not protect against a mortgage foreclosure or tax liens.
blocks.casual: A homestead exemption shields a set dollar amount of equity in your primary home from unsecured creditors who win a judgment against you. In New York the amount depends on the county (it's highest downstate) and gets adjusted every few years. It won't protect you from a mortgage foreclosure or tax liens.

deeper.plain: Some of the equity in your home is protected from creditors who sue you for unpaid debts like credit cards.
deeper.picture: It's like a lockbox inside your house that certain debt collectors can't open.
deeper.street: A Queens homeowner loses a lawsuit over a car accident. The judgment creditor wants to force a sale, but the homestead exemption protects a chunk of equity first, and the creditor gets only what's above it.
deeper.stakes: Homeowners often think they're fully protected. The exemption doesn't stop the bank from foreclosing or the city from collecting taxes.
deeper.exam: Homestead protects against unsecured judgment creditors only. Mortgages and tax liens are not affected. Amount varies by county in NY.

blocks.html: The lessor (landlord) keeps the fee and a reversion; the lessee (tenant) gets possession. Four types:
blocks.casual: With a lease, the lessor (landlord) keeps the fee plus a reversion, and the lessee (tenant) gets possession. There are four types:

deeper.plain: A landlord still owns the building, and the tenant just gets to live there for a time.
deeper.picture: Think of lending your bike: your friend rides it, but it comes back to you when they're done.
deeper.street: Sal leases 3R in his Astoria building to Tasha's cousin for two years. Sal still owns the building and can sell it. The tenant has possession and, when the lease ends, the apartment reverts to Sal.
deeper.stakes: A buyer of a rented building takes it subject to existing leases. Sellers who promise vacant delivery while a lease is running set up a breach.
deeper.exam: The landlord's retained interest is called a reversion. The lessor is the landlord; the lessee is the tenant. Many students flip these two.

head: Estate
Defining feature
How it ends
rows: Definite start and end date, any length (even 6 months)
Automatically at the end date; no notice needed
Renews automatically period to period (month to month)
Indefinite, with the landlord's consent; no fixed term
Notice by either party, or death of either party
Tenant holds over after the lease ends, without consent
Landlord evicts, or accepts rent and creates a new tenancy
blocks.caption: Years, periodic, will, sufferance: from most to least secure

deeper.plain: The four leaseholds run from a fixed-term lease, to a rolling lease, to an open-ended arrangement, to a tenant staying without permission.
deeper.picture: A gym membership: a 12-month contract (years), monthly auto-renew (periodic), a friend letting you use their pass until they say stop (will), or sneaking in after your card expired (sufferance).
deeper.street: One of Sal's tenants signs a one-year lease (estate for years). When it ends, Sal keeps taking her rent without a new lease (periodic, month to month). A tenant down the hall stays after his lease expires and Sal refuses his rent (sufferance).
deeper.stakes: Knowing which type you're in decides how much notice is needed. Getting it wrong can void an eviction and send the landlord back to start.
deeper.exam: Estate for years ends automatically, no notice needed. Periodic needs notice. At will ends by notice or death. Sufferance is a holdover without consent.

blocks.title: New York notice rules
blocks.html: Since the 2019 HSTPA, a residential landlord who will not renew or will raise rent 5% or more must give 30, 60, or 90 days' written notice depending on how long the tenant has been there (under 1 year, 1 to 2 years, 2+ years). Tenancies at will or by sufferance can be ended by a written 30-day notice. A landlord who accepts rent from a holdover generally creates a month-to-month tenancy.
blocks.casual: Since the 2019 HSTPA, a residential landlord who won't renew, or who's raising rent 5% or more, has to give written notice of 30, 60, or 90 days, depending on how long the tenant has been there (under 1 year, 1 to 2 years, 2+ years). Tenancies at will or by sufferance can be ended with a written 30-day notice. And if a landlord accepts rent from a holdover, that usually creates a month-to-month tenancy.

deeper.plain: Longer tenancy, longer notice; and taking rent from someone who stayed over usually starts a month to month.
deeper.picture: It's like breaking up with a roommate: if they've been there years, you owe them more warning than someone who moved in last spring.
deeper.street: Sal wants to raise a 3-year tenant's rent by 8%. He has to send written notice at least 90 days before the lease ends. He sends it 45 days out, so the increase can't take effect on schedule.
deeper.stakes: Short notice means the increase or nonrenewal can't take effect when the landlord wants, which delays rent or eviction and can lead to court losses.
deeper.exam: Memorize 30/60/90 tied to under 1 year, 1 to 2 years, 2+ years. The trigger is nonrenewal or a rent increase of 5% or more. Accepting rent from a holdover usually creates month to month.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: "Estate for years" does not mean years. A 9-month lease with fixed dates is an estate for years. The test is a definite end date, not the length.
blocks.casual: Don't let "estate for years" fool you. It doesn't have to be years. A 9-month lease with fixed dates is still an estate for years. What matters is that there's a definite end date, not how long it runs.

deeper.plain: Any lease with a set start and end date is an estate for years, even if it's short.
deeper.picture: It's like a concert ticket for a specific date: the show could be 2 hours or 3 days, but the date is fixed.
deeper.street: A grad student signs a lease in Morningside Heights from September 1 to May 31. That 9-month lease is an estate for years, and it ends on May 31 with no notice needed.
deeper.stakes: Treating a fixed-term lease like a periodic one leads landlords to send pointless notices or tenants to think they can stay longer.
deeper.exam: If a stem says a short lease has specific dates and asks what estate it creates, answer estate for years. The word years is a deliberate trap.

blocks.q: Leo's one-year lease in Astoria ended May 31. On June 3 he is still there, the landlord has not accepted any rent, and has not agreed to anything. Leo holds:
c: An estate for years
A periodic estate
An estate at will
An estate at sufferance
blocks.x: Holding over without the landlord's consent is a tenancy at sufferance. If the landlord had accepted June rent, it would typically become a month-to-month periodic tenancy.

blocks.title: Classify any estate in three questions

items.title: Is there a lease?
items.html: Yes: leasehold. Go to step 3. No: freehold.

items.title: Freehold: does it end?
items.html: Never: fee simple absolute. On a condition: qualified fee (determinable or on condition). At a death: life estate.

items.title: Leasehold: is there an end date?
items.html: Fixed date: estate for years. Rolls over: periodic. Consent but no term: at will. No consent: sufferance.

blocks.casual:
Step one: is there a lease? If yes, it's a leasehold, so skip to step three. If no, it's a freehold.
Step two, freehold: does it end? If never, it's fee simple absolute. If it ends on a condition, it's a qualified fee (determinable or on condition). If it ends at someone's death, it's a life estate.
Step three, leasehold: is there an end date? A fixed date means estate for years. Rolls over means periodic. Consent but no term means at will. No consent means sufferance.

deeper.plain: Ask three yes or no questions and you can name any estate.
deeper.picture: It's a flowchart like the ones at a coffee shop: hot or iced, milk or not, size. Answer in order and you land on the drink.
deeper.street: Jordan runs a quiz for Leo. "Deed says to the museum so long as it stays open to the public." No lease, freehold, ends on a condition, automatic: fee simple determinable. Leo gets it in ten seconds.
deeper.stakes: Agents who can sort estates quickly spot problems in listings before they reach the closing table.
deeper.exam: Most estate questions can be solved in this order. Start with lease or no lease, then follow the branches, and watch for the magic words.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Leaseholds from strongest to weakest: Years, Periods, Will, Suffer. "Your Pal Will Suffers."
blocks.casual: Leaseholds from strongest to weakest: Years, Periods, Will, Suffer. Just remember "Your Pal Will Suffers."

deeper.plain: The four leaseholds in order, with a silly sentence to keep them straight.
deeper.picture: Picture your pal Will moving from a signed lease, to month to month, to a handshake, to sleeping on your couch uninvited.
deeper.street: On the train to the exam site in Brooklyn, Jordan mutters "Your Pal Will Suffers" twice and nails a question that ranks tenancies by security.
deeper.stakes: Ranking questions are easy points if you have the order down, and frustrating if you don't.
deeper.exam: Expect a question asking which tenancy gives the tenant the most or least security. Years is strongest; sufferance is weakest.

story.title: For Her Life, Then Sami
story.setting: Flatbush, Noor Haddad's kitchen, late morning

beats.text: Jordan arrives with a listing agreement and a CMA. Noor arrives with a 2014 will in a plastic sleeve.
The house is mine. Read it. My husband left it to me.
It says to you "for your life, then to my nephew Sami." Can I call Priya before we sign anything?
That's a life estate. Noor owns the house for her lifetime. Sami holds the remainder. He's the remainderman.
So I can't sell?
You can sell what you have. Which is a house that disappears when you do. Nobody pays $1.3 million for that.
beats.tag: Life tenant conveys only a life estate

check.q: What must happen for a buyer to get fee simple title to Noor's house?
c: Noor signs the deed alone
Sami signs the deed alone
The Surrogate's Court approves a sale by Noor
Noor and Sami both sign the deed
check.x: The fee is split between the life estate and the remainder. Both holders must convey to put the whole fee in the buyer.

beats.text: So we call Sami in Ohio, and the proceeds get split by an actuarial formula based on Noor's age?
Exactly. Usually by IRS life-expectancy tables. The attorneys work out the split.
And if I just rent it out and move to Boca?
You can. You pay the taxes and keep it up. If you let the roof go, Sami can sue you for waste.
beats.tag: Life tenant must not commit waste

beats.text: In my day the widow got her dower.
New York abolished dower. A surviving spouse gets the elective share now, at least $50,000 or a third of the estate. But your husband gave you more than that already.
Sami answers on the second ring. He would very much like a share of $1.3 million.
Always read the deed or the will before you price anything. Ownership is a question of how much and how long, not just who.

board.prompt: Draw the estates tree: freehold on one branch, leasehold on the other. Under each freehold estate, write who holds the future interest (if anyone).

facts.text: A freehold estate lasts an indeterminable time and is ownership; a leasehold lasts a set time under a lease and is personal property.
Fee simple absolute is the most complete ownership: unlimited in time, inheritable and freely transferable, yet still subject to government powers and private encumbrances.
A qualified fee (fee simple defeasible) is a fee that can be lost if a stated condition is broken.
Fee simple determinable uses 'so long as' or 'while', ends automatically when the condition breaks, and leaves the grantor a possibility of reverter.
A fee on condition subsequent uses 'but if' or 'provided that'; the grantor must act to take title back under a right of re-entry.
A life estate lasts for a person's lifetime; when it ends, a remainder goes to the named third party, the remainderman.
If no remainderman is named, the property reverts to the grantor or the grantor's heirs (a reversionary interest).
A life estate pur autre vie is measured by someone else's life; if the life tenant dies first, her heirs hold until the measuring life ends.
A life tenant may live in, rent, mortgage or sell her interest, but can convey only what she has; selling the fee needs the remainderman's signature too.
A life tenant must not commit waste (damaging, neglecting or materially changing the property); the remainderman can sue, and the life tenant pays ordinary taxes and upkeep.
New York abolished dower and curtesy, the old legal life estates for a widow or widower, and is not a community property state.
A NY surviving spouse has an elective share: the greater of $50,000 or one third of the net estate, even if the will leaves less.
The NY homestead exemption shields a county-based amount of home equity from unsecured judgment creditors, but not from a mortgage foreclosure or tax liens.
The landlord keeps the fee and a reversion; leaseholds rank from most to least secure: years, periodic, at will, sufferance.
An estate for years has a definite start and end date of any length, even 9 months, and ends automatically without notice.
A periodic estate renews period to period until proper notice; an estate at will has no fixed term and ends by notice or the death of either party.
A holdover without consent is a tenancy at sufferance; a landlord who accepts rent from a holdover generally creates a month-to-month tenancy.

Under the 2019 HSTPA, a landlord who will not renew or will raise rent 5% or more must give 30, 60 or 90 days' written notice (under 1 year, 1 to 2 years, 2+ years); at will and sufferance tenancies end on 30 days' written notice.

lessons.title: Who Owns It: Severalty, Co-ownership, Trusts, and Entities
lessons.tagline: Two names on a deed can mean four different things when one of them dies.
objectives: Compare severalty, tenancy in common, joint tenancy, and tenancy by the entirety
Apply New York's default rules for co-owners who are and are not married
Explain how co-ownership ends: severance, divorce, and partition
Identify trustor, trustee, and beneficiary, and how partnerships, corporations, LLCs, syndicates, and joint ventures hold title
State what a buyer actually receives in a co-op versus a condo

blocks.title: Three roommates, one Ridgewood two-family
blocks.html: Leo and two college friends, Ana and Dev, buy a two-family in Ridgewood together. Ana put in 50% of the cash, Leo and Dev 25% each. Their deed just says "to Leo Brandt, Ana Ruiz, and Dev Shah." Two years later Dev dies, leaving everything to his sister. Does Dev's sister own part of the house, or do Leo and Ana now own it all?
blocks.casual: Leo and two college buddies, Ana and Dev, go in together on a two-family in Ridgewood. Ana put up half the cash; Leo and Dev each put in 25%. The deed just says "to Leo Brandt, Ana Ruiz, and Dev Shah." Two years later Dev dies and leaves everything to his sister. So does his sister now own a piece of the house, or do Leo and Ana own the whole thing?

deeper.plain: How friends word the deed decides whether a dead owner's share goes to his family or to the other owners.
deeper.picture: It's like a group chat with a shared Netflix account: if one person leaves, does their login go to their sibling, or do the rest just split the plan?
deeper.street: Dev's sister calls Leo from Philadelphia asking when she can see "her" apartment. Leo, who assumed he and Ana now owned it all, calls Priya in a panic.
deeper.stakes: Co-buyers who don't think about how they take title can end up co-owning with a stranger, which makes selling, refinancing, or even renting a nightmare.
deeper.exam: The exam gives a deed with no survivorship language and unequal shares, then asks what happens on death. In New York, unmarried co-owners default to tenancy in common, so the share passes by will.

blocks.html: Severalty means ownership by one person or one legal entity alone. The word comes from "severed": cut off from others. A corporation or an LLC that owns a building owns it in severalty even though it has many shareholders or members. When a severalty owner dies, the property passes by will or by intestate succession.
blocks.casual: Severalty means one person or one legal entity owns it alone. Think "severed," as in cut off from everyone else. If a corporation or an LLC owns a building, that's severalty, even if the company has a hundred shareholders or members. When a severalty owner dies, the property passes by will or by intestate succession.

deeper.plain: Severalty is solo ownership, whether by a person or a single company.
deeper.picture: A company is like a person in a costume: lots of people may be inside, but the law sees one owner.
deeper.street: Evelyn owns three buildings through Park Holdings LLC. Even though she and two partners are members, the LLC holds title in severalty, and the deed names only the LLC.
deeper.stakes: Buyers and lenders need to know who actually signs. If an LLC owns, its authorized member signs, not every investor.
deeper.exam: If a question says a corporation owns property and asks the form of ownership, answer severalty. On death of a sole owner, property goes by will or intestacy, not survivorship.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: Severalty sounds like "several" owners. It means the opposite: one owner.
blocks.casual: Severalty sounds like "several" owners, right? Nope. It means the exact opposite: one owner.

deeper.plain: Severalty means one owner, not many.
deeper.picture: Think of severing a rope: you cut one piece away to stand alone.
deeper.street: Jordan almost writes "held in severalty by the three buyers" in a listing note. Diane crosses it out: "Severalty is one. Three is co-ownership."
deeper.stakes: Using the term wrong on paperwork confuses attorneys and makes you look green in front of clients.
deeper.exam: Distractors pair severalty with phrases like several owners or multiple parties. If more than one person holds title directly, it's not severalty.

blocks.html: Co-owners each hold an undivided interest: every owner has the right to possess the whole property. Ana cannot claim the top floor as "her 50%." Shares can be unequal in value, but possession is shared. New York recognizes three forms of co-ownership.
blocks.casual: Co-owners each hold an undivided interest, which means every owner gets to possess the whole place. Ana can't claim the top floor as "her 50%." Shares can be unequal in value, but possession is shared. New York recognizes three forms of co-ownership.

deeper.plain: Everyone owns a share of the whole property, not a specific room or floor.
deeper.picture: It's like co-owning a pizza before it's sliced: you each own a percentage, but nobody owns a specific slice yet.
deeper.street: Ana wants to rent out the top-floor unit and keep all the rent since she paid more. Leo and Dev point out they each have the right to possess the whole building, so rent from it is shared by ownership share.
deeper.stakes: Co-owners who try to wall off "their" part start fights that end in partition suits, where a court can force a sale.
deeper.exam: Undivided interest means each owner has the right to possess the entire property. Unequal shares are allowed in a tenancy in common, but possession is never divided.

head: Tenancy in common
Joint tenancy
Tenancy by the entirety
rows: Share passes to the owner's heirs or devisees
Share passes to surviving joint tenants (survivorship)
Yes, but it breaks the joint tenancy for that share
No, neither spouse can convey alone

deeper.plain: Tenancy in common is the flexible one, joint tenancy adds survivorship, and tenancy by the entirety is the married-couple version that neither spouse can break alone.
deeper.picture: TIC is a group of roommates who each own their own furniture. Joint tenancy is a pact where the last one standing gets everything. TBE is a couple's joint bank account that needs both signatures.
deeper.street: Priya explains options to three sets of clients in one day: two friends buying a Bushwick condo (TIC unless they ask for survivorship), siblings who want the survivor to keep the house (joint tenancy, spelled out), and a married couple in Bay Ridge (TBE by default).
deeper.stakes: Picking the wrong form, or not choosing at all, can send a share to an heir nobody expected or let a creditor of one spouse reach the house.
deeper.exam: Know each row. TBE can't be partitioned, and neither spouse can convey alone. Joint tenancy requires TTIP and equal shares. TIC needs only possession.

blocks.caption: Toggle each form and run the "one owner dies" animation. Watch where the dead owner's share goes and which unities are checked.

blocks.html: Tenancy in common (TIC) needs only unity of possession. Each owner's share is inheritable and can be sold or mortgaged without the others' consent. A buyer of that share becomes a new tenant in common.
blocks.casual: Tenancy in common (TIC) only needs unity of possession. Each owner's share can be inherited, and you can sell or mortgage yours without asking the others. Whoever buys your share just becomes a new tenant in common.

deeper.plain: Tenants in common can sell or leave their share to anyone, and the buyer steps right in.
deeper.picture: It's like owning a share of a food truck: you can sell your share, and the new owner joins the others behind the counter.
deeper.street: Ana gets a job in Austin and sells her 50% to an investor named Marco. Leo and Dev don't get a vote. Marco is now a tenant in common with them.
deeper.stakes: You can end up co-owning with a stranger. Smart co-buyers sign a separate co-ownership agreement with buy-out rights and a right of first refusal.
deeper.exam: TIC is the only form where shares can be unequal and pass by will. A buyer of a share becomes a tenant in common, even if the other owners were joint tenants among themselves.

blocks.html: Joint tenancy carries the right of survivorship: when a joint tenant dies, the share does not go through the will. It is absorbed by the surviving joint tenants. The last survivor owns in severalty. Joint tenancy requires the four unities:
blocks.casual: Joint tenancy comes with the right of survivorship. When a joint tenant dies, their share doesn't go through the will. It gets absorbed by the surviving joint tenants. The last one standing owns it in severalty. Joint tenancy needs the four unities:

deeper.plain: In a joint tenancy, when one owner dies, the others automatically take their share, no matter what the will says.
deeper.picture: It's like a tontine or last-one-standing pool: whoever outlives the others ends up with the whole pot.
deeper.street: Two sisters in Bensonhurst hold their mother's house as joint tenants with right of survivorship. When one dies, her will leaves everything to her son, but the house goes to the surviving sister automatically. The son gets nothing from the house.
deeper.stakes: Families who don't understand survivorship can disinherit children by accident. The will can't override it.
deeper.exam: A will cannot pass a joint tenant's share; survivorship beats the will. The last survivor owns in severalty.

items: Time: all acquired at the same moment
Title: by the same deed or will
Interest: equal shares
Possession: equal right to possess the whole
blocks.casual:
Time: everyone got it at the same moment.
Title: everyone got it from the same deed or will.
Interest: everyone has equal shares.
Possession: everyone has the same right to possess the whole thing.

deeper.plain: To be joint tenants, owners need to start together, on the same document, with equal shares, and equal rights to use it.
deeper.picture: Think of four friends who all buy concert tickets in the same transaction, for the same show, at the same price, with access to the whole venue.
deeper.street: Leo, Ana, and Dev put in 50/25/25. Even if their deed said joint tenancy, the unequal shares would break unity of interest, and a court would likely treat them as tenants in common.
deeper.stakes: If any unity is missing, survivorship can fail, and the share goes to heirs nobody planned for.
deeper.exam: The exam asks which unity is missing in a fact pattern. Different deed dates break time; unequal shares break interest.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: TTIP: Time, Title, Interest, Possession. Add Marriage and you get TTIP-M for tenancy by the entirety. Joint tenants "TTIP" the share over to the survivors.
blocks.casual: TTIP: Time, Title, Interest, Possession. Add Marriage and it's TTIP-M, which gets you tenancy by the entirety. Joint tenants "TTIP" the share over to the survivors.

deeper.plain: TTIP is a shortcut for the four unities, and adding an M covers married couples.
deeper.picture: Imagine a tipping jar where the departing owner tips their share into the survivors' jar.
deeper.street: Diane grills Jordan before an exam review: "What does TBE need that joint tenancy doesn't?" Jordan: "TTIP plus M." Diane: "Good. Coffee's on you."
deeper.stakes: It's an easy hook for a question that shows up on almost every exam.
deeper.exam: Know that TBE requires all four unities plus marriage. A question asking for the fifth unity is fishing for marriage.

blocks.title: New York default rules (EPTL 6-2.2)
blocks.html: A deed to two or more unmarried people creates a tenancy in common unless it expressly says joint tenancy ("as joint tenants with right of survivorship"). A deed to two people who are married to each other creates a tenancy by the entirety unless it expressly says otherwise. Since 1996, spouses can also hold co-op shares as tenants by the entirety.
blocks.casual: Here's the NY default (EPTL 6-2.2). If a deed goes to two or more unmarried people, they're tenants in common unless the deed spells out joint tenancy ("as joint tenants with right of survivorship"). If a deed goes to two people married to each other, they're tenants by the entirety unless the deed says otherwise. And since 1996, spouses can hold co-op shares as tenants by the entirety too.

deeper.plain: Unmarried co-owners get tenancy in common by default; married couples get tenancy by the entirety by default.
deeper.picture: It's like a phone's default settings: you get the standard choice unless you go in and change it on purpose.
deeper.street: A married couple buying a co-op on the Upper West Side don't have to say anything special to hold their shares as tenants by the entirety. Two friends buying the apartment next door would be tenants in common unless their documents say joint tenancy.
deeper.stakes: If co-buyers want survivorship and their attorney doesn't write it in, the default can send a share to someone's estate instead of the co-owner.
deeper.exam: Memorize the defaults. Unmarried, silent deed: TIC. Married, silent deed: TBE. Joint tenancy must be expressly stated.

blocks.html: Back to Ridgewood. The deed did not say joint tenancy, and the shares were unequal anyway, so Leo, Ana, and Dev are tenants in common. Dev's 25% passes under his will to his sister, who is now a tenant in common with Leo and Ana.
blocks.casual: Back to Ridgewood. The deed didn't say joint tenancy, and the shares weren't equal anyway, so Leo, Ana, and Dev are tenants in common. Dev's 25% goes under his will to his sister, and now she's a tenant in common with Leo and Ana.

deeper.plain: Dev's sister now owns his quarter of the house.
deeper.picture: It's like a seat at a poker table: when Dev leaves, his chips go to whoever he named, and she sits down at the table.
deeper.street: Dev's sister wants cash, not a building in Queens. She offers to sell her 25% to Leo and Ana for $210,000 based on an appraisal. If they can't agree, she can sue for partition.
deeper.stakes: Leo and Ana now have to deal with a co-owner they didn't pick, and her leverage includes forcing a sale of the whole house.
deeper.exam: Silent deed plus unmarried owners equals TIC, so the share passes by will. If the stem had said with right of survivorship and equal shares, the answer flips.

blocks.q: A deed reads "to Kim Alvarez and Rosa Alvarez, as joint tenants with right of survivorship." Kim and Rosa are sisters. Kim later sells her half to Evelyn. What is the result?
c: Evelyn and Rosa are joint tenants
Evelyn and Rosa are tenants in common
The sale is void without Rosa's consent
Rosa owns 100% by survivorship
blocks.x: A joint tenant can convey her share, but the buyer did not take at the same time and by the same deed, so the unities of time and title break. Evelyn and Rosa become tenants in common.

blocks.html: Tenancy by the entirety treats a married couple as one owner. Neither spouse can sell, mortgage, or force a sale of the property without the other. On death, the survivor owns everything automatically, no probate. Divorce turns it into a tenancy in common. It cannot be partitioned while the marriage lasts.
blocks.casual: Tenancy by the entirety treats a married couple as one owner. Neither spouse can sell it, mortgage it, or force a sale without the other. When one dies, the survivor owns everything automatically, no probate. A divorce turns it into a tenancy in common. And it can't be partitioned while the marriage lasts.

deeper.plain: Married couples own as a single unit, and neither can act alone.
deeper.picture: It's like a bank safe deposit box that needs both keys turned at the same time.
deeper.street: The Okafors own their Bed-Stuy brownstone as tenants by the entirety. Emmanuel wants to take out a home equity loan for his business, but the bank needs Grace's signature too. When they sell, both sign the deed.
deeper.stakes: Agents who take a listing from just one spouse can waste months marketing a house that can't be sold without the other signature.
deeper.exam: TBE can't be partitioned and neither spouse can convey alone. Divorce converts it to a tenancy in common. The survivor takes all, without probate.

blocks.html: When tenants in common or joint tenants cannot agree, any one of them can bring a partition action in State Supreme Court. The court divides the land physically (partition in kind) if that is fair, or, far more often in NYC, orders it sold by a referee and splits the proceeds by ownership share. Joint tenancy also ends by conveyance of a share (severance), by agreement, or when only one survivor remains.
blocks.casual: When tenants in common or joint tenants can't agree, any one of them can file a partition action in State Supreme Court. The court will split the land physically (partition in kind) if that's fair. But much more often in NYC, it orders a referee to sell the property and splits the money by ownership share. A joint tenancy also ends when someone conveys their share (severance), when everyone agrees, or when there's only one survivor left.

deeper.plain: If co-owners can't get along, a court can split the property or sell it and divide the money.
deeper.picture: It's like a band breaking up: either you divide the gear, or you sell it all and split the cash.
deeper.street: Dev's sister sues for partition of the Ridgewood two-family. You can't fairly slice a house into thirds, so the court appoints a referee, the house sells for $1.2 million, and the proceeds split 50/25/25 after costs.
deeper.stakes: Forced sales usually bring less than a normal listing, plus legal fees. Co-owners who could have negotiated a buyout end up with less.
deeper.exam: Partition is available to TICs and joint tenants, never to tenants by the entirety. Conveying a joint tenant's share severs the joint tenancy for that share.
