blocks.title: Community property: an understanding
blocks.html: Nine states (such as California, Texas, and Arizona) treat most property acquired during marriage as community property owned 50/50. New York is not a community property state. In a NY divorce, marital property is divided by equitable distribution, which means fairly, not necessarily equally.
blocks.casual: Nine states (like California, Texas, and Arizona) treat most property bought during a marriage as community property, owned 50/50. New York is not one of them. In a NY divorce, marital property is split by equitable distribution, which means fairly, not necessarily equally.

deeper.plain: New York doesn't automatically split marital property in half; a court splits it fairly.
deeper.picture: Community property is cutting a cake exactly in half. Equitable distribution is a judge deciding who gets which slices based on what each person put in and needs.
deeper.street: A couple divorcing in Westchester owns a house worth $900,000. The judge awards the wife 60% of the equity because she gave up her career to raise their kids, which a community property state wouldn't consider in the same way.
deeper.stakes: Clients who moved from California sometimes assume a 50/50 split. Agents shouldn't give legal advice here; refer them to a matrimonial attorney.
deeper.exam: If a question asks whether NY is a community property state, the answer is no. NY uses equitable distribution.

blocks.q: Emmanuel and Grace Okafor bought their brownstone as a married couple in 1997 with a deed naming both. Emmanuel dies. Who owns the house?
c: Grace and Emmanuel's heirs as tenants in common
Emmanuel's estate until probate is complete
Grace alone, by survivorship
Grace owns a life estate
blocks.x: Spouses in NY are presumed tenants by the entirety. On one spouse's death the survivor owns 100% automatically, outside of probate.

blocks.html: A trust is an arrangement where one person holds legal title for the benefit of another. The trustor (settlor, grantor) creates the trust and transfers the property. The trustee holds legal title and manages it as a fiduciary. The beneficiary receives the benefits. A living (inter vivos) trust is created during life; a testamentary trust is created by will. Many NY families put homes in revocable living trusts to avoid probate.
blocks.casual: A trust is a setup where one person holds legal title for someone else's benefit. The trustor (also called settlor or grantor) creates the trust and puts the property in. The trustee holds legal title and manages it as a fiduciary. The beneficiary gets the benefits. A living (inter vivos) trust is set up while you're alive; a testamentary trust is created by a will. Lots of NY families put their homes in revocable living trusts to skip probate.

deeper.plain: A trust lets one person manage property for someone else's benefit.
deeper.picture: It's like a parent managing a teenager's savings account: the money is for the kid, but the parent controls it.
deeper.street: Evelyn's aunt in Forest Hills puts her house in a revocable living trust, naming herself trustee and her nieces as beneficiaries. When she dies, a successor trustee sells the house without going through Surrogate's Court.
deeper.stakes: Families who skip trusts may wait many months for probate before selling. Agents who know the structure can explain why a trust listing moves faster.
deeper.exam: Trustor creates, trustee holds legal title and manages, beneficiary benefits. Inter vivos is during life; testamentary is by will.

blocks.title: Field tip
blocks.html: When a trust sells, the trustee signs the listing agreement and the deed, not the beneficiaries. Ask for the trust agreement (or a certification of trust) early so the attorneys can confirm the trustee's power to sell.
blocks.casual: When a trust sells, the trustee signs the listing agreement and the deed, not the beneficiaries. Ask early for the trust agreement (or a certification of trust) so the attorneys can confirm the trustee actually has the power to sell.

deeper.plain: Get the trustee's signature and proof they can sell.
deeper.picture: It's like checking that the person signing for a company has the authority to sign.
deeper.street: A beneficiary in Bay Ridge calls Jordan to list her late father's house, held in a trust. Jordan asks who the trustee is. It's her brother in Albany, so Jordan gets him to sign and sends the certification of trust to Priya.
deeper.stakes: A listing signed by the wrong person may be unenforceable, meaning no commission and possibly a claim against you if the deal falls through.
deeper.exam: Questions ask who has authority to sell trust property. The answer is the trustee, not the beneficiaries or trustor (unless the trustor is also the trustee).

head: Form
How it holds title
Liability and tax
rows: Partnership name (NY Partnership Law, based on the Uniform Partnership Act); partners hold as tenants in partnership
Every partner manages and is personally liable for all debts; income passes through
Partnership name; at least one general and one limited partner
General partner runs it with unlimited liability; limited partners are passive, liable only up to their investment
Owns in severalty as a legal person; shareholders own stock, not real estate
Shareholders' liability is limited; C corporations face double taxation (corporate level, then dividends)
Owns in severalty; members own membership interests
Limited liability plus pass-through taxation; the most common NYC investment vehicle
Not its own legal form: a group of investors pooling money, usually organized as an LP or LLC
Two or more parties for one specific project, for a limited time
Treated like a partnership for that project

deeper.plain: Businesses hold real estate in several forms, each with different control, liability, and taxes.
deeper.picture: Pick a vehicle for a road trip: a partnership is a carpool where everyone drives and shares the ticket, an LP has a driver and silent passengers, and an LLC is a car with airbags for every seat.
deeper.street: Evelyn forms an LLC for each building she buys, so a lawsuit at one property can't reach the others. For a bigger tower deal, she joins a syndicate organized as an LP, and partners with a developer as a joint venture for a single Long Island City project.
deeper.stakes: General partners have unlimited personal liability, so investors who pick the wrong entity can lose personal assets. C corporations face double taxation.
deeper.exam: LLCs offer limited liability and pass-through taxation. Limited partners are passive and liable only up to their investment. A syndicate isn't its own legal form.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: A joint venture is a one-night stand for one project. A partnership is a relationship for ongoing business. A syndicate is the money pool, dressed up as an LP or LLC.
blocks.casual: A joint venture is a one-night stand for one project. A partnership is a relationship for ongoing business. A syndicate is the money pool, dressed up as an LP or LLC.

deeper.plain: Joint venture is one project, partnership is ongoing, and syndicate is a group pooling money.
deeper.picture: A joint venture is a pop-up shop, a partnership is a restaurant, and a syndicate is the investor group funding a new chain.
deeper.street: Evelyn and a builder form a joint venture just to develop one lot in Long Island City. When it's sold, the venture ends. Her ongoing property management business with her brother is a partnership.
deeper.stakes: Mixing these up can mean the wrong liability or tax treatment, which costs real money.
deeper.exam: Cue words: one project or limited time equals joint venture. Ongoing business equals partnership. Pooled investors equals syndicate.

blocks.q: Evelyn invests $400,000 as a limited partner in a partnership that buys a Bronx apartment building. The building's lender sues after a default for $3 million more than the property sells for. What is Evelyn's maximum loss?
c: $3 million plus costs
One third of the deficiency
Her $400,000 investment
Nothing, limited partners never lose money
blocks.x: A limited partner's liability is capped at her investment, as long as she stays passive. The general partner has unlimited liability.

blocks.text: Co-ops vs condos: what you actually buy

left.title: Cooperative
items: Buyer gets shares of stock in the corporation that owns the building plus a proprietary lease for one unit
Personal property (shares), transferred by assignment and stock certificate, not a deed
Board approval required; board may reject for any non-discriminatory reason
Financed with a share loan, not a mortgage: no mortgage recording tax
One underlying building mortgage and tax bill shared through maintenance

right.title: Condominium
items: Buyer gets a deed to the unit in fee simple plus an undivided percentage interest in the common elements
Real property, governed by NY Condominium Act (RPL Article 9-B)
Board usually has only a right of first refusal
Financed with a regular mortgage; mortgage recording tax applies
Each unit separately taxed; owner pays common charges

deeper.plain: Co-op buyers get shares and a lease; condo buyers get a deed.
deeper.picture: A co-op is like joining a club and getting a membership card for one room. A condo is like buying one apartment in a building and owning it outright.
deeper.street: Leo compares two units in Jackson Heights. The co-op is $50,000 cheaper but needs board approval and he'll pay maintenance. The condo needs no board interview but carries a mortgage recording tax and higher closing costs.
deeper.stakes: Agents who don't know the difference misquote closing costs and approval timelines, and buyers walk into surprises.
deeper.exam: Co-op is personal property (shares and a proprietary lease), no deed, no mortgage recording tax. Condo is real property with a deed. Condo boards usually have only a right of first refusal.

blocks.html: In a cooperative, the corporation owns the whole building in severalty. Shareholders are tenants under a proprietary lease. In a condominium, each owner owns real property: a unit plus a share of hallways, roof, lobby, and land as tenants in common with the other owners. Subject 15 covers the boards, documents, and offering plans.
blocks.casual: In a cooperative, the corporation owns the whole building in severalty, and the shareholders are tenants under a proprietary lease. In a condominium, each owner owns real property: the unit itself plus a share of the hallways, roof, lobby, and land as tenants in common with the other owners. Subject 15 gets into boards, documents, and offering plans.

deeper.plain: Co-op owners own shares and lease their unit; condo owners own their unit plus a slice of the common areas.
deeper.picture: A co-op is like a company that owns the building and lets shareholders live in assigned units. A condo is like a set of individually owned apartments that share a lobby.
deeper.street: Kim, the co-op board president on the Upper West Side, reminds a seller that the corporation owns the building. When the seller wants to replace windows, the board has the final say because the building isn't his.
deeper.stakes: Co-op buyers who think they own real estate get surprised by board rules on renovations, sublets, and sales.
deeper.exam: In a co-op the corporation owns in severalty. In a condo, common elements are owned as tenants in common by the unit owners.

blocks.caption: Compare what sits in the buyer's hands at closing: a deed and title policy (condo) versus a stock certificate and proprietary lease (co-op).

blocks.q: Which item does a co-op buyer on the Upper West Side receive at closing?
c: A bargain and sale deed to the apartment
A stock certificate and a proprietary lease
A fee simple title to the unit and its common elements
A certificate of title from the City Register
blocks.x: Co-op buyers get shares and a proprietary lease, which are personal property. A deed and fee simple title to the unit describe a condo.

story.title: Three Names on a Deed
story.setting: Ridgewood, a two-family on Woodbine Street

beats.text: Leo, Ana, and Dev are at Priya's office the week before closing. Leo has a spreadsheet titled "OWNERSHIP v4 FINAL FINAL."
Ana's putting in half. Dev and I are 25 each. How does the deed show that?
Tenancy in common lets shares be unequal. We write "Ana Ruiz as to a 50% interest, Leo Brandt and Dev Shah each as to a 25% interest, as tenants in common."
(Dev) What if one of us dies? I want my sister to get my share.
Under tenancy in common, she would. Your share passes by your will. No survivorship.
And if we wanted survivorship?
Joint tenancy. But you'd all need equal shares, the same deed, the same moment. Time, title, interest, possession.

check.q: Why can't Leo, Ana, and Dev be joint tenants under their current plan?
c: Their interests are unequal
They are not married
They live in Queens
Joint tenancy is abolished in NY
check.x: Joint tenancy requires unity of interest, meaning equal shares. Their 50/25/25 split rules it out. Marriage is required only for tenancy by the entirety.

beats.text: And if nobody writes anything, unmarried buyers default to tenants in common in New York, right?
Right. Married couples default to tenancy by the entirety.
What if Ana and I fight about the house in five years?
Either of you can sue for partition. In a two-family in Queens, that usually means a court-ordered sale and a split of the money. Write a co-ownership agreement now and you'll never need it.
Leo creates a new tab: "Exit Plan."
Two names on a deed can mean four different things when someone dies. Ask how they want to hold title, then send them to the attorney to say it on paper.

board.prompt: Draw a Venn diagram: joint tenancy vs tenancy by the entirety. Put the four unities, marriage, survivorship, partition, and "one owner can sell alone" in the right zones.

facts.text: Severalty is ownership by one person or one entity alone, including a corporation or LLC; it does not mean several owners.
Co-owners hold undivided interests: each may possess the whole property, even when shares are unequal in value.
Tenancy in common needs only unity of possession; shares may be unequal and each share can be sold, mortgaged or inherited without the others.
Joint tenancy carries the right of survivorship: a deceased joint tenant's share goes to the survivors, not through the will, and the last survivor owns in severalty.
Joint tenancy requires the four unities of time, title, interest and possession (TTIP); tenancy by the entirety adds marriage.
Under EPTL 6-2.2 a deed to unmarried co-owners creates a tenancy in common unless it expressly says joint tenancy; a deed to spouses creates a tenancy by the entirety.
Tenancy by the entirety is for spouses only: neither can sell, mortgage or partition alone, the survivor takes all without probate, and divorce turns it into a tenancy in common.
Since 1996, New York spouses can also hold co-op shares as tenants by the entirety.
A co-owner can bring a partition action in State Supreme Court, which divides the land in kind or, more often in NYC, orders a sale and splits the proceeds.
A joint tenancy ends by conveyance of a share (severance), by agreement, or when one survivor remains; a buyer of a joint tenant's share holds as a tenant in common.
New York is not a community property state; marital property in a divorce is divided by equitable distribution, fairly but not necessarily equally.
In a trust the trustor creates it, the trustee holds legal title as a fiduciary, and the beneficiary receives the benefits; living trusts are made during life, testamentary trusts by will.
When a trust sells, the trustee signs the listing and the deed; ask early for the trust agreement or a certification of trust.
In a general partnership every partner manages and is personally liable for all the partnership's debts.
A limited partnership has at least one general partner with unlimited liability who runs it and passive limited partners liable only up to their investment.
A corporation owns in severalty as a legal person; shareholders own stock with limited liability, and C corporations face double taxation.
An LLC gives limited liability plus pass-through taxation and is the most common NYC investment vehicle.
A joint venture joins parties for one specific project for a limited time; a syndicate is a pool of investors, usually organized as an LP or LLC.
A co-op buyer gets shares in the corporation that owns the building plus a proprietary lease: personal property, board approval, a share loan and no mortgage recording tax.
A condo buyer gets a deed to the unit in fee simple plus an undivided share of the common elements: real property, a regular mortgage, separate taxes and usually only a board right of first refusal.

lessons.title: Liens, Priority, and Other Encumbrances
lessons.tagline: Every claim on the property gets in line. Taxes cut to the front. Everyone else waits by recording date.
objectives: Classify liens as voluntary or involuntary and general or specific
Explain judgments, lis pendens, tax liens, mortgage liens, and mechanic's liens under NY rules and deadlines
Rank liens in priority and show how a subordination agreement changes the order
Explain how liens affect title and how they are cleared at closing
Identify deed restrictions and encroachments as non-money encumbrances

blocks.title: The title report on Sal's building
blocks.html: Sal Russo is refinancing his 6-unit in Astoria. The title report comes back with five items: a 2019 first mortgage, a $38,000 mechanic's lien from a roofer he refused to pay, a 2021 judgment from a car accident lawsuit, unpaid water charges, and a notice of pendency from a neighbor's lawsuit over the property line. Sal says, "It's all junk, the bank will figure it out." Will it?
blocks.casual: Sal Russo is refinancing his 6-unit in Astoria, and the title report comes back with five items: a 2019 first mortgage, a $38,000 mechanic's lien from a roofer he stiffed, a 2021 judgment from a car accident lawsuit, unpaid water charges, and a notice of pendency from a neighbor suing over the property line. Sal waves it off: "It's all junk, the bank will figure it out." Will it?

deeper.plain: Every item on that report is a real claim against Sal's building, and the bank won't lend until they're dealt with.
deeper.picture: It's like trying to sell a car with three parking tickets, a repair shop's claim, and a court case attached. The buyer wants it clean first.
deeper.street: The new lender's title company refuses to insure until the roofer's lien is paid or bonded, the water charges are paid, and the neighbor's lawsuit is resolved. Sal's refi slides from 30 days to four months.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring liens delays or kills deals. A seller who hides them from an agent sets up a failed closing and wasted fees on all sides.
deeper.exam: Expect a list of title report items and a question about which is not a lien (the notice of pendency) or which gets paid first (the taxes and water charges).

blocks.html: An encumbrance is any claim, charge, or limit on property that may lower its value or restrict its use, without preventing the owner from transferring it. Two families:
blocks.casual: An encumbrance is any claim, charge, or limit on property that can drag down its value or restrict how it's used, but that doesn't stop the owner from transferring it. They come in two families:

deeper.plain: An encumbrance is a string attached to a property that a buyer inherits.
deeper.picture: Think of a used phone with a carrier lock or a payment plan still running. You can still sell it, but the buyer takes on the hassle.
deeper.street: The Okafors' brownstone has a mortgage (money claim) and a shared-driveway easement with the neighbor (use limit). Both show up on the buyer's title report, and both have to be dealt with or accepted.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't understand encumbrances may close on a property they can't use the way they planned, or find a lien they didn't price in.
deeper.exam: Know that all liens are encumbrances, but not all encumbrances are liens. An easement is an encumbrance, not a lien.

left.title: Money claims (liens)
items: Mortgages
Tax liens and special assessments
Judgments
Mechanic's liens
Federal and state tax liens

right.title: Physical or use limits
items: Easements
Deed restrictions (restrictive covenants)
Encroachments
Licenses (technically not an interest in land)
Leases

deeper.plain: Some encumbrances are about money owed, and others limit what you can physically do with the property.
deeper.picture: A money claim is a bill stapled to the deed. A use limit is a rule taped to the front door.
deeper.street: A Park Slope buyer's title report shows a mortgage to be paid at closing (money) and a 1920s covenant banning commercial signs (use). The mortgage disappears at closing; the covenant stays forever.
deeper.stakes: Money claims usually get paid off at closing. Use limits stay with the property, so buyers need to know about them before signing.
deeper.exam: Sort the list: mortgages, taxes, judgments, and mechanic's liens are liens. Easements, deed restrictions, encroachments, and leases are non-money encumbrances.

blocks.html: A lien is a claim against property as security for a debt. If the debt is not paid, the lienholder can force a sale (foreclose) and get paid from the proceeds. Liens run with the land: a buyer takes the property subject to them unless they are paid off.
blocks.casual: A lien is a claim against property that secures a debt. If the debt doesn't get paid, the lienholder can force a sale (foreclose) and get paid out of the proceeds. Liens run with the land, so a buyer takes the property subject to them unless they're paid off.

deeper.plain: A lien is a debt tied to a property, and it follows the property even if it's sold.
deeper.picture: It's like a pawn ticket: the shop holds a claim on your guitar until you pay up.
deeper.street: A buyer in Flushing closes on a house without a proper title search. Six months later a contractor's lien surfaces, and the buyer has to pay it off to avoid a foreclosure, even though the seller ran up the debt.
deeper.stakes: That's why buyers get title insurance and attorneys insist on payoff letters. Liens that aren't cleared become the buyer's problem.
deeper.exam: Liens run with the land. A new owner takes subject to existing liens unless they're satisfied at or before closing.

head: Voluntary (owner agrees)
Involuntary (created by law)
rows: Real property tax lien, special assessment, mechanic's lien, attachment
Judgment, IRS tax lien, NY estate tax, debts of a deceased person, corporation franchise tax

deeper.plain: Liens are sorted two ways: did the owner agree, and does it hit one property or all of them.
deeper.picture: A specific lien is a sticker on one item; a general lien is a sticker on your whole house of stuff.
deeper.street: Sal's mortgage is voluntary and specific. The roofer's mechanic's lien is involuntary and specific to the building. His car accident judgment is involuntary and general, hitting his Astoria building and the condo he owns in Florida if docketed there.
deeper.stakes: A general lien can reach every property a debtor owns, so one bad lawsuit can freeze several deals.
deeper.exam: Mortgage: voluntary specific. Property tax and mechanic's lien: involuntary specific. Judgment and IRS lien: involuntary general.

blocks.html: A voluntary lien is one the owner chooses, almost always a mortgage. An involuntary lien is imposed by law without the owner's consent. A specific lien attaches to one identified property. A general lien attaches to everything the debtor owns in the area (real and personal property).
blocks.casual: A voluntary lien is one the owner picks, which almost always means a mortgage. An involuntary lien gets slapped on by law without the owner's okay. A specific lien hits one particular property. A general lien hits everything the debtor owns in the area, real and personal property both.

deeper.plain: Voluntary means you agreed to it; involuntary means the law imposed it. Specific hits one property; general hits everything.
deeper.picture: A voluntary lien is a loan you signed for; an involuntary lien is a tow truck that showed up uninvited.
deeper.street: Leo signs a mortgage on his condo: voluntary and specific. A year later, the IRS files a lien for unpaid taxes from his side gig: involuntary and general, covering his condo and his car.
deeper.stakes: Clients often don't realize a lawsuit or tax debt in their personal life can block a property sale.
deeper.exam: If the stem says the owner signed it, it's voluntary. If it covers all property, it's general. Mortgages are the classic voluntary specific lien.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: General = Government and Gavels (IRS, estate tax, franchise tax, judgments). Specific = the building itself (taxes on it, the mortgage on it, the roofer who worked on it).
blocks.casual: General = Government and Gavels (IRS, estate tax, franchise tax, judgments). Specific = the building itself (taxes on it, the mortgage on it, the roofer who worked on it).

deeper.plain: General liens come from tax agencies and courts; specific liens come from the property itself.
deeper.picture: Picture a judge's gavel smacking everything you own, while a roofer's ladder leans against one building.
deeper.street: Jordan, running through flashcards, sees "judgment lien" and thinks gavel, so general. Then "special assessment for new sidewalk" and thinks the building, so specific.
deeper.stakes: It's an easy way to avoid losing points on a type of question that shows up almost every exam.
deeper.exam: One trap: property tax is from the government but is specific, because it's tied to one parcel. Only the government's general taxes (IRS, estate, franchise) are general.

blocks.q: Which lien is both voluntary and specific?
c: A judgment lien
A federal tax lien
A mechanic's lien
A mortgage
blocks.x: The owner signs a mortgage (voluntary) on one property (specific). A mechanic's lien is specific but involuntary. Judgments and IRS liens are general and involuntary.

items: Judgment: a court's decision that one party owes another money. Once docketed with the county clerk, it is a lien on the debtor's real property in that county for 10 years in NY. The creditor can enforce it with a writ of execution (sheriff's sale).

Lis pendens (NY calls it a notice of pendency): a recorded notice that a lawsuit affecting title or possession is pending. It is not a lien itself, but anyone who buys or lends afterward is bound by the outcome. Good for 3 years in NY, extendable by court order. Every NY foreclosure starts with one.
Estate and inheritance tax liens: federal and NY estate taxes are a lien on a deceased person's property until paid.
Debts of a deceased person: creditors can be paid from estate assets, including real property, through the Surrogate's Court.
Corporation franchise tax lien: a state lien on a corporation's property for unpaid franchise (business) taxes.
IRS (federal) tax lien: unpaid federal taxes create a general lien on all of the taxpayer's property, effective against buyers and lenders once a notice is filed.
blocks.casual:
A judgment is a court ruling that one party owes another money. Once it's docketed with the county clerk, it's a lien on the debtor's real property in that county for 10 years in NY, and the creditor can enforce it with a writ of execution (a sheriff's sale).
Lis pendens (NY calls it a notice of pendency) is a recorded notice that a lawsuit about title or possession is pending. It's not a lien itself, but anyone who buys or lends after it's filed is bound by how the case comes out. It's good for 3 years in NY, and a court can extend it. Every NY foreclosure starts with one.
Estate and inheritance tax liens: federal and NY estate taxes are a lien on a deceased person's property until they're paid.
Debts of a deceased person: creditors can get paid from estate assets, including real property, through the Surrogate's Court.
A corporation franchise tax lien is a state lien on a corporation's property for unpaid franchise (business) taxes.
An IRS (federal) tax lien comes from unpaid federal taxes. It's a general lien on everything the taxpayer owns, and it's effective against buyers and lenders once a notice is filed.

deeper.plain: Courts, the IRS, the state, and estate creditors can all put claims on a person's property, and a pending lawsuit can freeze a deal even before anyone wins.
deeper.picture: A lis pendens is like a "case pending" sign hung on the front door: you can still walk in, but you're bound by whatever the judge decides.
deeper.street: Sal's neighbor files a notice of pendency in a fight over a 2-foot strip. Sal's refinance lender won't close because it would be bound by the outcome. Sal settles with the neighbor in three weeks just to clear it.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who ignores a lis pendens can lose the property to the plaintiff. A judgment creditor can force a sheriff's sale of the debtor's real estate.
deeper.exam: A lis pendens is not a lien. NY judgment liens last 10 years; notices of pendency last 3 years. The IRS lien is general and effective once notice is filed.

blocks.html: A real property tax lien arises automatically for unpaid property taxes. A special assessment is a charge on properties that benefit from a local improvement (new sidewalk, sewer line) and is also a tax lien. In NYC, unpaid water and sewer charges are liens too and can end up in the city's tax lien sale.
blocks.casual: A real property tax lien kicks in automatically when property taxes go unpaid. A special assessment is a charge on properties that benefit from a local improvement (a new sidewalk, a sewer line), and it's a tax lien too. In NYC, unpaid water and sewer charges also become liens and can get swept into the city's tax lien sale.

deeper.plain: Unpaid taxes, improvement charges, and NYC water bills all become liens on the property.
deeper.picture: It's like a utility bill that, if ignored, gets sold to a collection agency that can come after the house.
deeper.street: Sal's $6,400 in unpaid water charges ends up in the city's tax lien sale. A private lien servicer buys the debt, adds interest and fees, and can eventually foreclose if he doesn't pay.
deeper.stakes: Small unpaid bills can turn into big ones fast, and tax liens jump ahead of the mortgage in priority.
deeper.exam: Special assessments are specific involuntary liens tied to improvements that benefit the property. They share first priority with property taxes.

blocks.html: A mechanic's lien protects contractors, subcontractors, laborers, and suppliers who improved the property and were not paid. In NY it is filed in the county clerk's office (Lien Law Article 2).
blocks.casual: A mechanic's lien protects contractors, subcontractors, laborers, and suppliers who improved the property and didn't get paid. In NY you file it in the county clerk's office (Lien Law Article 2).

deeper.plain: If you work on a property and don't get paid, you can put a claim on that property.
deeper.picture: It's like a mechanic keeping your car until you pay for the repair, except here the claim sits on the deed.
deeper.street: The roofer who redid Sal's roof for $38,000 files a mechanic's lien with the Queens County Clerk after Sal stops answering his calls. Now Sal can't refinance until it's paid or bonded.
deeper.stakes: Owners who withhold payment to contractors can find their sale or refinance blocked. Sellers need to settle any open bills before listing.
deeper.exam: Mechanic's liens are specific and involuntary. They protect contractors, subcontractors, laborers, and suppliers, and are filed in the county clerk's office in NY.

blocks.title: NY mechanic's lien deadlines
blocks.html: File within 8 months after the last work or materials, or 4 months for a single-family dwelling. The lien lasts 1 year from filing. Within that year the lienor must start a foreclosure action or file a notice of extension with the county clerk, which adds one more year; a lien on a single-family dwelling can be extended only by court order, and so can any further extension (Lien Law §17). Work done for a tenant without the owner's consent does not support a lien against the owner.
blocks.casual: You've got 8 months after the last work or materials to file, or 4 months for a single-family home. The lien lasts 1 year from filing. Before that year is up, the contractor has to sue to foreclose or file a notice of extension, which buys one more year. Single-family homes are different: only a court can extend those, and any extension past that second year also takes a court order. And if the work was done for a tenant without the owner's consent, it doesn't support a lien against the owner.

deeper.plain: Contractors have a short window to file, and a limited time to act on it after filing.
deeper.picture: It's like a return window at a store: miss it, and you're out of luck.
deeper.street: A plumber finishes a job in a single-family house in Massapequa in January and waits until June to file. That's past 4 months, so the lien is invalid. On Sal's 6-unit, the roofer had 8 months.
deeper.stakes: Contractors who file late lose their lien rights. Owners who don't track deadlines may pay off a lien that couldn't have been enforced.
deeper.exam: Memorize 8 months general, 4 months single-family, and 1 year duration. One extension by notice adds a year (court order only for single-family, and for anything beyond). Tenant work without owner consent can't support a lien against the owner.

blocks.q: A contractor finished a kitchen in a single-family home in Bayside on February 1 and was never paid. What is the last month to file a mechanic's lien?
c: March
June
October
February of the next year
blocks.x: Single-family dwellings get the short 4-month window, so early June. For other property the window is 8 months (early October).

blocks.html: Lien priority decides the order of payment when foreclosure sale proceeds do not cover everyone. The rule:
blocks.casual: Lien priority decides who gets paid first when a foreclosure sale doesn't bring in enough money to cover everybody. Here's the rule:

deeper.plain: When there isn't enough money to go around, priority decides who gets paid and who gets stiffed.
deeper.picture: It's like a line at a bakery that's running out of bread: the people up front get loaves, the people in back go home hungry.
deeper.street: When a mixed-use building in Bushwick sells at a foreclosure auction for less than the debts, the city's tax bill gets paid first, then the bank, then the judgment creditor. The contractor at the back gets nothing.
deeper.stakes: Lenders care about priority above everything, which is why they insist on being first and run title searches before funding.
deeper.exam: The exam asks who gets paid first. Taxes and special assessments, then everyone else by date of recording or filing.

blocks.title: The payment line

items.title: 1. Real property taxes and special assessments
items.html: Always first, no matter when they arose. The government cuts the line.

items.title: 2. Everyone else by recording date
items.html: First in time, first in right. The earlier recorded (or docketed, or filed) lien is paid first. NY mechanic's liens rank from their filing date.

items.title: 3. Junior lienholders get leftovers
items.html: If the money runs out, later liens may get nothing and keep only a claim against the debtor personally.

items.title: 4. Owner gets any surplus
items.html: After all liens are paid, any remaining money goes to the former owner.

blocks.casual:
First in line: real property taxes and special assessments. They always go first, no matter when they came up. The government cuts the line.
Next: everyone else, by recording date. First in time, first in right, so the lien recorded (or docketed, or filed) earliest gets paid first. In NY, mechanic's liens rank from their filing date.
Then: junior lienholders get whatever's left. If the money runs out, later liens may get zero and be stuck with just a personal claim against the debtor.
Last: the owner gets any surplus once every lien is paid.

deeper.plain: Taxes first, then everyone else by date, then the owner gets whatever's left.
deeper.picture: Picture a champagne tower: the top glass (taxes) fills first, then each glass below in order. If the bottle runs dry, the bottom glasses stay empty.
deeper.street: A judgment against a Bronx homeowner was docketed in 2020, and a home equity loan was recorded in 2022. At a foreclosure sale, the judgment gets paid before the home equity lender, because it got on the record first.
deeper.stakes: Junior lienholders can be wiped out completely. That's why second-mortgage lenders charge more and why everyone races to record.
deeper.exam: Know that property taxes beat even an earlier-recorded first mortgage. Among others, it's first in time, first in right, based on recording, docketing, or filing date.

blocks.caption: Slide the sale price down and watch who goes unpaid. Then flip the subordination toggle and see the first mortgage step behind the new loan.

blocks.title: Worked example: a foreclosure sale in Astoria
blocks.html:
Sale price at referee's auction: $1,150,000. Liens: unpaid property taxes $22,000; first mortgage (recorded 2019) $900,000; judgment (docketed 2021) $150,000; mechanic's lien (filed 2023) $38,000.
1. Taxes: $22,000. Left: $1,128,000.
2. First mortgage: $900,000. Left: $228,000.
3. Judgment: $150,000. Left: $78,000.
4. Mechanic's lien: $38,000. Left: $40,000.
5. Surplus to Sal (before costs of sale): $40,000.
Drop the price to $1,050,000 and the judgment gets only $128,000 of its $150,000, while the roofer and Sal get nothing.
blocks.casual:
The referee's auction brings in $1,150,000. The liens: $22,000 in unpaid property taxes, a $900,000 first mortgage (recorded 2019), a $150,000 judgment (docketed 2021), and a $38,000 mechanic's lien (filed 2023).
Taxes get paid first: $22,000, leaving $1,128,000.
The first mortgage takes $900,000, leaving $228,000.
The judgment takes $150,000, leaving $78,000.
The mechanic's lien takes $38,000, leaving $40,000.
Sal gets the surplus (before costs of sale): $40,000.
Now drop the price to $1,050,000. The judgment gets only $128,000 of its $150,000, and the roofer and Sal get nothing.

deeper.plain: Pay each lien in order until the money runs out; whatever's left goes to the owner.
deeper.picture: It's like splitting a dinner bill where the people who ordered first get covered first, and late arrivals may be stuck paying their own.
deeper.street: The roofer who filed in 2023 learns that a $100,000 drop in the sale price meant he got nothing. Now he's left suing Sal personally, which is slower and may never pay.
deeper.stakes: Junior creditors get wiped out when values fall. Owners lose their equity entirely if the sale comes in low.
deeper.exam: Expect a math question like this one. Subtract taxes first, then each lien by date, and see what's left for the owner or the last lienholder.

blocks.html: A subordination agreement is a written agreement in which a lienholder voluntarily accepts a lower priority. Typical case: a ground lessor or a seller holding a purchase-money second mortgage agrees to stand behind a new construction or refinance loan, because the new lender insists on being first.
blocks.casual: A subordination agreement is a written deal where a lienholder voluntarily agrees to take a back seat. The usual case: a ground lessor, or a seller holding a purchase-money second mortgage, agrees to stand behind a new construction or refinance loan because the new lender insists on being first.

deeper.plain: A lender agrees in writing to step back in line so another lender can go first.
deeper.picture: It's like letting someone with one item cut ahead at the grocery line because they won't shop there otherwise.
deeper.street: The Okafors sell to a buyer and hold a $100,000 second mortgage to help with financing. Two years later the buyer refinances the first mortgage, and the new bank requires the Okafors to sign a subordination agreement so the new loan stays first.
deeper.stakes: Without the subordination agreement, the refinance doesn't happen. A lienholder who refuses can block the deal.
deeper.exam: A subordination agreement changes priority voluntarily. Cue words: agrees to a lower priority, new lender insists on first position.

blocks.q: A home equity line was recorded in 2020; the first mortgage is refinanced in 2025. Without any agreement, how would the refinanced first mortgage rank?
c: First, because it is called a first mortgage
Ahead of property taxes
Equal with the home equity line
Behind the 2020 home equity line, unless the HELOC lender signs a subordination agreement
blocks.x: Priority follows recording date. The new loan was recorded in 2025, after the HELOC. That is why refinance lenders demand a subordination agreement from the HELOC lender. Nothing outranks property taxes.

blocks.caption: New York uses judicial foreclosure: default, acceleration, lis pendens, judgment, referee's sale. Note where junior liens are wiped out.

blocks.title: Lien theory and judicial foreclosure
blocks.html: New York is a lien theory state: the borrower keeps title and the mortgage is only a lien. Foreclosure goes through the courts and the property is sold by a court-appointed referee who gives a referee's deed. A foreclosure wipes out liens junior to the foreclosing mortgage, but not senior ones.
blocks.casual: New York is a lien theory state, which means the borrower keeps title and the mortgage is just a lien. Foreclosure goes through the courts, and a court-appointed referee sells the property and hands over a referee's deed. A foreclosure wipes out liens that are junior to the foreclosing mortgage, but not the senior ones.

deeper.plain: In New York the borrower holds title, and the bank has to go to court to foreclose.
deeper.picture: It's like a lender holding an IOU on your car rather than the car itself. To take it, they need a judge's okay.
deeper.street: A second mortgage lender forecloses on a house in Canarsie. The buyer at the auction takes it free of that second lien and any judgments recorded after it, but still subject to the first mortgage, which was senior.
deeper.stakes: Buyers at foreclosure auctions who don't check senior liens can end up owning a house with a big first mortgage still attached.
deeper.exam: NY is lien theory with judicial foreclosure. Foreclosure wipes out junior liens, not senior ones. The deed at sale is a referee's deed.

blocks.html: Liens do not stop an owner from selling, but they cloud the title and make it unmarketable until cleared. At closing the seller's attorney pays them from the proceeds: a payoff letter goes to each lender, and a satisfaction of mortgage (or release, or discharge) is recorded afterward. A disputed mechanic's lien can be bonded or discharged by a deposit so the closing proceeds.
blocks.casual: Liens don't stop an owner from selling, but they cloud the title and make it unmarketable until they're cleared. At closing, the seller's attorney pays them off from the proceeds: a payoff letter goes to each lender, and a satisfaction of mortgage (or release, or discharge) gets recorded afterward. If a mechanic's lien is disputed, it can be bonded or discharged with a deposit so the closing can go forward.

deeper.plain: The seller can still sell, but the liens get paid from the sale money at closing.
deeper.picture: It's like paying off the remaining balance on a phone before trading it in. The money comes out of the trade-in value.
deeper.street: The Okafors sell for $1.6 million. Priya orders a payoff letter from their lender showing $212,000 due. At closing, the bank's payoff is wired, and a satisfaction of mortgage gets recorded a few weeks later.
deeper.stakes: If a lien isn't caught and paid, the buyer's title insurer may have to pay it, and the seller could face a lawsuit. A disputed lien left unbonded can freeze the closing.
deeper.exam: Liens make title unmarketable but don't prevent transfer. The document that removes a mortgage lien is a satisfaction of mortgage.

blocks.html: A deed restriction (restrictive covenant) is a private limit on use written into a deed or a subdivision's declaration: no fences over 4 feet, single-family only, no commercial signs. Restrictions run with the land and are enforced by injunction. When a public zoning law and a private restriction conflict, the more restrictive one controls. Discriminatory restrictions (for example, race) are void and unenforceable.
blocks.casual: A deed restriction (restrictive covenant) is a private limit on how you can use the property, written into a deed or a subdivision's declaration: no fences over 4 feet, single-family only, no commercial signs. These restrictions run with the land and get enforced by injunction. When a zoning law and a private restriction clash, the stricter one wins. Discriminatory restrictions (based on race, for example) are void and can't be enforced.

deeper.plain: A deed restriction is a private rule about what you can do with your property, and it follows the property forever.
deeper.picture: It's like an HOA rule baked into the house itself: every future owner has to follow it.
deeper.street: A buyer in Forest Hills Gardens wants to put up a 6-foot fence. The community's 1910s covenants ban fences over 4 feet, even though zoning would allow it. The stricter covenant wins, and a neighbor can get an injunction.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who plan renovations without checking covenants can be forced to tear down what they built.
deeper.exam: The stricter rule controls between zoning and a deed restriction. Discriminatory covenants are void. Restrictions are enforced by injunction.

blocks.html: An encroachment is an improvement that illegally extends onto a neighbor's land or a street: a garage 1 foot over the line, a fence, roof eaves. A survey reveals it. Encroachments make title unmarketable and can ripen into adverse possession or a prescriptive easement if left alone for 10 years in NY. The exception: under RPAPL 543 (2008), minor non-structural encroachments such as fences, hedges, shrubbery, plantings and sheds are deemed permissive, so they alone do not create an adverse possession claim. A garage over the line is structural and still can.
blocks.casual: An encroachment is an improvement that illegally pokes onto a neighbor's land or a street: a garage 1 foot over the line, a fence, roof eaves. A survey is what reveals it. Encroachments make title unmarketable, and if nobody does anything for 10 years in NY, they can ripen into adverse possession or a prescriptive easement. One catch: since 2008, NY treats minor non-structural encroachments like fences, hedges, plantings, and sheds as permissive (RPAPL 543), so those alone don't ripen into adverse possession. A garage is structural, so it still can.

deeper.plain: An encroachment is a structure that crosses onto someone else's land, and a survey is how you find it.
deeper.picture: It's like your neighbor's car parked half in your driveway every day for years.
deeper.street: Ray inspects a house in Bayside and notices the garage looks close to the line. The buyer orders a survey, which shows the garage sits 14 inches onto the neighbor's lot. Priya negotiates a boundary-line agreement before closing.
deeper.stakes: An encroachment can mean tearing down part of a structure, a lawsuit, or losing land to a neighbor's claim. Lenders often won't fund until it's resolved.
deeper.exam: Surveys find encroachments; title searches find recorded documents. In NY, de minimis non-structural items like fences and hedges are deemed permissive under the 2008 rules.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: "A title search will reveal encroachments." False. Encroachments are physical, so you find them with a survey or inspection. A title search finds recorded documents.
blocks.casual: "A title search will reveal encroachments." False. Encroachments are physical things, so you find them with a survey or an inspection. A title search only turns up recorded documents.

deeper.plain: Title searches check paperwork; surveys check what's on the ground.
deeper.picture: A title search reads the house's diary; a survey measures where it actually stands.
deeper.street: Marcus tells a buyer they can skip the survey because the title search came back clean. After closing, the buyer finds the deck sits 3 feet onto the neighbor's land, and the title policy excludes survey matters.
deeper.stakes: Skipping a survey can leave a buyer with an expensive boundary fight and no title insurance coverage for it.
deeper.exam: If a question asks how to discover an encroachment, the answer is survey. Title searches find liens, deeds, easements of record, and judgments.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Priority line: Taxes first, then Time. A subordination agreement is a lien saying "after you."
blocks.casual: Priority line: Taxes first, then Time. And a subordination agreement is just a lien saying "after you."

deeper.plain: Taxes go first, then it's by date, unless a lienholder agrees to step back.
deeper.picture: Picture a polite lienholder holding the door open for a newer lender.
deeper.street: Jordan studies with Leo on the 7 train: "Taxes first, then time." Leo adds, "Unless someone subordinates." Jordan nods; Leo is learning.
deeper.stakes: Knowing the order cold lets you answer priority math questions quickly and explain to clients why taxes matter more than they think.
deeper.exam: Expect priority to show up as math or a ranking question. Taxes and special assessments always lead, regardless of date.

story.title: Junk on the Title
story.setting: Astoria, Sal's kitchen table, a hot July afternoon

beats.text: Sal waves the title report like a parking ticket. Jordan is there because Sal wants to list after the refinance.
Five items. All junk. The roofer did a lousy job, he gets nothing.
The roofer filed a mechanic's lien. It's a specific, involuntary lien on this building. It stays until it's paid, bonded, or expires.
Expires when?
One year from filing unless he sues to foreclose. He filed in May. If he sues by next May, it stays.
And the judgment from the car accident?
General lien. Docketed in Queens, so it hits everything Sal owns in Queens for ten years.

check.q: Why does the car accident judgment affect Sal's building even though the accident had nothing to do with it?
c: It is a specific lien on the building
It is a general lien on all his real property in the county
Because the building was the accident site
It doesn't, judgments never attach to real estate
check.x: A docketed money judgment is a general lien on all of the debtor's real property in that county, regardless of what the lawsuit was about.

beats.text: Water bill? That's the city's problem.
It's a lien. And taxes and water charges jump to the front of the line, ahead of your bank.
beats.tag: Taxes first, then by recording date

beats.text: What about the notice of pendency?
That's the neighbor's lawsuit over the property line. Any new lender or buyer is bound by however it ends. No bank will touch this refinance until it's resolved.
So the bank won't figure it out.
The bank will figure out how to say no.
Sal calls the roofer. It is a short, loud call. Then a calmer one with his checkbook out.
Pull title before you list. A seller who learns about his liens at the closing table is a seller who doesn't close.

board.prompt: Draw the payment line for a foreclosure sale: taxes at the front, then each lien by date. Mark where a subordination agreement would move one lien.

facts.text: An encumbrance is any claim, charge or limit that may lower a property's value or restrict its use without preventing transfer; liens are money claims, easements and restrictions are use limits.
A lien is a claim against property as security for a debt; the lienholder can foreclose, and liens run with the land to a buyer unless paid off.
A voluntary lien is one the owner agrees to, almost always a mortgage; an involuntary lien is imposed by law. A mortgage is a specific, voluntary lien.
A specific lien attaches to one property (taxes, assessments, mortgage, mechanic's lien); a general lien attaches to all the debtor's property (judgments, IRS liens, estate taxes, franchise taxes).
A docketed NY judgment is a lien on the debtor's real property in that county for 10 years, enforced by a writ of execution.
A lis pendens (NY notice of pendency) is not a lien but binds later buyers and lenders to the lawsuit's outcome; it lasts 3 years and is extendable by court order.
Estate taxes, debts of a deceased person, corporation franchise taxes and IRS taxes all create general liens.
Unpaid property taxes and special assessments for local improvements are automatic tax liens; in NYC, unpaid water and sewer charges are liens too.

A mechanic's lien protects unpaid contractors, subcontractors, laborers and suppliers and is filed with the county clerk; work for a tenant without the owner's consent supports no lien against the owner.
A NY mechanic's lien must be filed within 8 months after the last work or materials, or 4 months for a single-family dwelling.
A mechanic's lien lasts 1 year from filing; the lienor must foreclose or file a notice of extension, and a single-family lien can be extended only by court order.
Real property taxes and special assessments are paid first from a foreclosure sale, no matter when they arose.
After taxes, liens rank first in time by recording, docketing or filing date (NY mechanic's liens from filing); juniors get leftovers and the owner gets any surplus.
To distribute sale proceeds, subtract taxes first, then each lien in priority order until the money runs out.
A subordination agreement is a lienholder's written agreement to accept a lower priority, typically to let a new lender go first.
New York is a lien theory state with judicial foreclosure: the borrower keeps title, and a court-appointed referee sells and gives a referee's deed.
Foreclosure wipes out liens junior to the foreclosing mortgage but not senior ones such as property taxes.
Liens cloud title until cleared; they are paid from closing proceeds and a satisfaction of mortgage is recorded, and a disputed mechanic's lien can be bonded or discharged by deposit.
Deed restrictions run with the land and are enforced by injunction; when they conflict with zoning the more restrictive rule controls, and discriminatory ones are void.
An encroachment is an improvement extending onto a neighbor's land or a street; it makes title unmarketable and can ripen into adverse possession or a prescriptive easement after 10 years.
Under RPAPL 543, minor non-structural encroachments such as fences, hedges and sheds are deemed permissive and cannot alone create adverse possession; a garage still can.
Encroachments are found by a survey or inspection, not by a title search, which finds only recorded documents.

lessons.title: Easements, Party Walls, and Licenses
lessons.tagline: The right to use someone else's land without owning it, and the many ways it starts and stops.
objectives: Distinguish easements appurtenant from easements in gross, and name the dominant and servient tenements
Explain each way an easement is created: grant, reservation, implication, necessity, prescription, condemnation, dedication
List the ways an easement terminates
Explain party walls and easements for light and air in NY
Tell an easement from a license and a possessory from a non-possessory interest

blocks.title: The shared driveway in Bay Ridge
blocks.html: Two detached houses on 82nd Street share a 9-foot driveway that sits entirely on the Morales lot. The Chens, next door, have driven over it to reach their back garage since a 1962 deed gave them the right. The Moraleses now want to sell, and their buyer wants to put a gate across the driveway. Can he lock the Chens out?
blocks.casual: Two detached houses on 82nd Street in Bay Ridge share a 9-foot driveway, and it sits entirely on the Morales lot. The Chens next door have been driving over it to their back garage ever since a 1962 deed gave them the right. Now the Moraleses are selling, and their buyer wants to put a gate across the driveway. Can he lock the Chens out?

deeper.plain: The Chens have a written right to use the driveway, and that right doesn't go away when the Moraleses sell.
deeper.picture: It's like buying a house that comes with a neighbor's key to the side gate. The key came with the house, and you can't change the lock.
deeper.street: The buyer's attorney spots the 1962 easement in the title report and tells him a gate is fine only if the Chens get a key or a remote. Otherwise, the Chens can go to court and have it removed.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who blocks a recorded easement faces an injunction and legal fees. An agent who tells him the gate is fine invites a complaint.
deeper.exam: Cue words: shared driveway, deed giving a neighbor the right. That's an easement appurtenant, and it runs with the land.

blocks.html: An easement is a right to use another person's land for a specific purpose without owning or possessing it. It is a non-possessory interest in land: the holder can cross, run pipes under, or keep a view over the land, but cannot occupy it the way an owner or tenant does.
blocks.casual: An easement is a right to use somebody else's land for a specific purpose without owning it or living on it. It's a non-possessory interest in land. The holder can drive across, run pipes underneath, or keep a view over the land, but can't move in and occupy it the way an owner or tenant would.

deeper.plain: An easement lets you use someone else's land for one purpose without owning it.
deeper.picture: It's like having a hallway pass: you can walk through, but you can't set up a desk in the hall.
deeper.street: The Chens drive over the Morales driveway every morning. They can't park a boat there or plant tomatoes, because their right is only to pass through to their garage.
deeper.stakes: Easement holders who go beyond their purpose can be sued, and owners who block a valid easement can be forced to remove the obstruction.
deeper.exam: Easements are non-possessory interests in land. Holders can use, not occupy. Watch for distractors that call an easement a type of lease.

left.title: Possessory interests
items: Fee simple, life estate, leasehold
Right to occupy and exclude
Tenant can keep the landlord out

right.title: Non-possessory interests
items: Easements, liens, deed restrictions
Right to use or to a claim, not to occupy
Utility can enter only for its purpose

deeper.plain: Possessory means you get to occupy it; non-possessory means you only get a right to use it or a claim on it.
deeper.picture: A possessory interest is the hotel room key. A non-possessory interest is permission to use the hotel pool.
deeper.street: Sal's tenants can keep Sal out of their apartments (possessory). Con Ed can come onto Sal's lot to service a gas line, but only for that purpose (non-possessory).
deeper.stakes: Mixing these up leads to bad advice, like telling a utility it can't enter for repairs or telling a tenant the landlord can walk in anytime.
deeper.exam: Easements, liens, and deed restrictions are non-possessory. Fee simple, life estates, and leaseholds are possessory.

blocks.html: Possessory vs non-possessory is the cleanest way to sort an interest on the exam: does the holder get to occupy it? If not, it is non-possessory.
blocks.casual: Possessory vs non-possessory is the cleanest way to sort an interest on the exam. Just ask: does the holder get to occupy it? If not, it's non-possessory.

deeper.plain: Ask one question: can they move in? If not, it's non-possessory.
deeper.picture: Can you sleep there? Then it's possessory. Can you only walk through? Then it's not.
deeper.street: Jordan uses this test on a quiz: a cable company's right to run a wire across a backyard. Can the company occupy the yard? No, so it's non-possessory.
deeper.stakes: It's a quick sort that saves time on the exam and in conversations with buyers.
deeper.exam: A tenant has a possessory interest even though the tenant doesn't own the property. Don't confuse ownership with possession.

blocks.html: An easement appurtenant benefits a neighboring parcel. It always involves two parcels. The dominant tenement is the land that benefits (the Chens'). The servient tenement is the land that carries the burden (the Moraleses'). An appurtenant easement runs with the land: when either parcel is sold, the easement transfers automatically, even if the deed does not mention it.
blocks.casual: An easement appurtenant benefits a neighboring parcel, so there are always two parcels involved. The dominant tenement is the land getting the benefit (the Chens'). The servient tenement is the land carrying the burden (the Moraleses'). An appurtenant easement runs with the land: if either parcel sells, the easement goes right along with it, even if the deed never mentions it.

deeper.plain: This easement is attached to the land, so it goes with the property when either side sells.
deeper.picture: Think of a parking spot that comes with an apartment. If the apartment is sold, the new owner gets the spot.
deeper.street: When the Chens sell their house in five years, the new owners automatically get the driveway right. When the Moraleses sell, their buyer must keep letting the Chens' successors through.
deeper.stakes: Buyers on both sides need to know about appurtenant easements. A seller who hides one can be sued; a buyer who ignores one can be enjoined.
deeper.exam: Dominant benefits; servient is burdened. Appurtenant easements run with the land and transfer automatically on sale of either parcel.

blocks.html: Appurtenances are all the rights and privileges that belong to a parcel and pass with it: easements appurtenant, improvements, water rights, air rights. The deed's phrase "together with all appurtenances" carries them.
blocks.casual: Appurtenances are all the rights and privileges that belong to a parcel and go with it: easements appurtenant, improvements, water rights, air rights. When a deed says "together with all appurtenances," that's what carries them over.

deeper.plain: Appurtenances are the extras that come with the land when it's sold.
deeper.picture: Like a phone that comes with its charger, case, and warranty included.
deeper.street: When the Chens sell, their deed includes "together with all appurtenances," so the driveway easement, their garage, and their water rights pass to the buyer.
deeper.stakes: Leaving appurtenances out of a deed can cause title confusion, though appurtenant easements generally pass anyway.
deeper.exam: Appurtenances include easements appurtenant, improvements, water rights, and air rights. The deed phrase "together with all appurtenances" carries them.

blocks.html: An easement in gross benefits a person or company, not a parcel. There is a servient tenement but no dominant tenement. Commercial easements in gross (Con Edison's power lines, a gas pipeline, a cable company, a railroad) are assignable and long-lasting. Personal easements in gross ("my friend may fish in my pond") usually end when the holder dies.
blocks.casual: An easement in gross benefits a person or a company, not a piece of land. There's a servient tenement but no dominant tenement. Commercial easements in gross (Con Edison's power lines, a gas pipeline, a cable company, a railroad) can be assigned and last a long time. Personal ones ("my friend can fish in my pond") usually end when the holder dies.

deeper.plain: An easement in gross belongs to a person or company, not to a neighboring lot.
deeper.picture: It's like a subscription tied to a person's account, not to a house.
deeper.street: Verizon holds an easement in gross to run fiber along the back of lots in Bayside. When a homeowner sells, the new owner takes subject to it. Verizon can assign it if it sells its network.
deeper.stakes: Buyers often don't know a utility can enter for repairs. Personal easements in gross usually die with the holder, which matters for estate planning.
deeper.exam: In gross means no dominant tenement. Utilities and railroads are the classic commercial easement in gross.

blocks.caption: Click each scenario: the shared driveway (appurtenant, dominant and servient), the utility line (in gross, servient only), the landlocked lot (necessity), and the shortcut path used for years (prescription).

head: Appurtenant
In gross
rows: On sale of the servient land
On sale of the dominant land
Shared driveway, right of way to a beach
Con Edison, Verizon, LIPA, a pipeline

deeper.plain: Appurtenant easements help a neighbor's land; easements in gross help a person or company.
deeper.picture: Appurtenant is a key that belongs to the house next door. In gross is a key that belongs to the utility worker.
deeper.street: The Bay Ridge driveway is appurtenant. The Con Ed line under the same block is in gross. Both stay when the Moraleses sell.
deeper.stakes: Agents who misidentify the type may give buyers wrong expectations about who can use the property and for how long.
deeper.exam: Count the parcels: two means appurtenant; one means in gross. Both stay with the servient land when it sells.

blocks.html: A right of way is the most common easement: the right to pass over land, on foot or by vehicle. Bay Ridge's shared driveway is a right of way appurtenant. So the buyer cannot lock the Chens out. He takes subject to the easement.
blocks.casual: A right of way is the most common kind of easement: the right to pass over land, on foot or by car. The Bay Ridge shared driveway is a right of way appurtenant. So no, the buyer can't lock the Chens out. He takes the property subject to the easement.

deeper.plain: A right of way lets someone pass over your land, and the buyer has to honor it.
deeper.picture: It's like a public path through a park that you can't fence off just because you bought land next to it.
deeper.street: The Morales buyer installs a gate anyway. The Chens call their attorney, who sends a letter. Within a week the buyer gives them a remote, avoiding a lawsuit he would lose.
deeper.stakes: Blocking a right of way leads to an injunction, legal fees, and a bad relationship with neighbors.
deeper.exam: A right of way is an easement to pass over. The buyer of a servient parcel takes subject to it.

blocks.q: The Chens sell their house to a new family. The deed does not mention the driveway. Can the new family use it?
c: No, the easement had to be listed in the new deed
Only with the Moraleses' new written permission
Yes, an easement appurtenant runs with the dominant land
Only for 10 years
blocks.x: An easement appurtenant is an appurtenance of the dominant tenement and transfers automatically with it, mentioned or not.

head: Method
How it works
NY example
rows: Owner of the servient land grants it in writing (deed or separate agreement), recorded
Seller keeps an easement over the land being sold
Farmer sells a back field but reserves a lane to the barn
Implied from a prior, apparent, continuous use when one owner splits a parcel
A sewer line that crosses a lot when the owner sells half
A parcel is landlocked after a split; law implies access over the land it came from
Back lot in the Catskills with no road frontage
Open, notorious, hostile (without permission), continuous use for the statutory period: 10 years in NY
Neighbors cut across a lot to the beach for 15 years
Government takes an easement by eminent domain and pays just compensation
State takes a strip for a highway drainage line
Owner gives a right to the public, accepted by the government
Developer dedicates sidewalks and roads in a subdivision

deeper.plain: Easements are created by writing, by implication from past use, by necessity, by long unpermitted use, or by government action.
deeper.picture: Think of the different ways to get into a club: a ticket (grant), being grandfathered in (implication), the only way out (necessity), sneaking in for years until it's allowed (prescription), or a government pass (condemnation).
deeper.street: A Catskills landowner sells the back half of his land, leaving it with no road. The law gives the buyer an easement by necessity over the front parcel. Nearby, hikers who cut across a farm for 15 years openly and without permission may have a prescriptive easement.
deeper.stakes: Owners who allow long, open use without giving permission risk losing rights. Buyers of landlocked lots need to confirm access before closing.
deeper.exam: Know the 10-year NY prescription period and that necessity applies to landlocked parcels created by a split.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: Prescriptive easements and adverse possession use similar elements and the same 10-year NY period, but the result differs: prescription gives a right to use; adverse possession gives title. Prescription does not require exclusive use; adverse possession does.
blocks.casual: Prescriptive easements and adverse possession use similar elements and the same 10-year NY period, but you end up with different things. Prescription gets you a right to use the land. Adverse possession gets you title. And prescription doesn't need exclusive use, while adverse possession does.

deeper.plain: Same 10 years, but one gets you a path, the other gets you the land.
deeper.picture: Prescription is earning the right to cut through a neighbor's yard. Adverse possession is earning the yard itself.
deeper.street: Beachgoers in Montauk who crossed a private lot openly for 12 years may have a prescriptive easement to keep walking. A neighbor who fenced in part of the lot and used it alone for 12 years could claim title.
deeper.stakes: Owners who don't object to long-term use can lose rights or land. Posting signs or giving written permission defeats hostility.
deeper.exam: Prescription equals use; adverse possession equals ownership. Exclusive use is required only for adverse possession.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: How easements are born: "Grandma Rarely Imagines Needing Proper Cops": Grant, Reservation, Implication, Necessity, Prescription, Condemnation.
blocks.casual: How easements are born: "Grandma Rarely Imagines Needing Proper Cops": Grant, Reservation, Implication, Necessity, Prescription, Condemnation.

deeper.plain: Six ways to create an easement, in one silly sentence.
deeper.picture: Picture Grandma calling the police over a neighbor's path through her garden.
deeper.street: Jordan recites the sentence to Leo over coffee. Leo laughs but remembers it on his own practice quiz.
deeper.stakes: It's a handy hook for a list the exam likes to test.
deeper.exam: A distractor may slip in a lease or license as a way to create an easement. Neither creates one.

blocks.q: Ray's client bought a wooded lot in Ulster County that was carved out of a larger farm. The only road access is across the farm. No easement was written. What does the client most likely have?
c: An easement by necessity
An easement in gross
A license
Nothing, he must buy access
blocks.x: When a parcel is landlocked by a split from a common owner, the law implies an easement by necessity over the remaining land. It ends when the necessity ends (for example, a new road is built).

blocks.text: Party walls and light and air

blocks.html: A party wall is a single wall on the boundary line shared by two buildings. Each owner owns the half on his side and holds a cross-easement in the other half for support. Neither can remove it or weaken it. Brooklyn and Manhattan rowhouses are built on party walls, which is why a renovation next door can trigger access and support disputes.
blocks.casual: A party wall is a single wall on the property line that two buildings share. Each owner owns the half on their side and holds a cross-easement in the other half for support. Neither one can remove it or weaken it. Brooklyn and Manhattan rowhouses sit on party walls, which is why a gut renovation next door can set off fights over access and support.

deeper.plain: A party wall is shared by two buildings, and neither owner can mess with it.
deeper.picture: It's like a shared bookshelf between two roommates: each owns one side, but neither can yank it out.
deeper.street: The Okafors' neighbors on Macon Street gut-renovate and want to cut into the party wall for new beams. The Okafors' engineer reviews the plans, and their attorney negotiates protections before work begins.
deeper.stakes: Damage to a party wall can cause cracks, leaks, or worse. Owners who cut into one without care face lawsuits.
deeper.exam: Each owner owns half and has a cross-easement in the other half for support. Neither can remove or weaken it.

blocks.title: Construction next door
blocks.html: When an NYC owner needs to enter a neighbor's property to make repairs or build (scaffolding, roof protection), and the neighbor refuses, the owner can ask the court for a license under RPAPL 881. Courts often require the builder to pay license fees and insurance.
blocks.casual: When an NYC owner needs to get onto a neighbor's property to make repairs or build (scaffolding, roof protection), and the neighbor says no, the owner can ask a court for a license under RPAPL 881. Courts often make the builder pay license fees and carry insurance.

deeper.plain: If your neighbor won't let you access their property to do work, you can ask a court to order it.
deeper.picture: It's like needing to borrow a neighbor's ladder to fix your own gutter, and a judge says yes if you pay rent for it.
deeper.street: A developer in Williamsburg needs to put roof protection on a neighboring brownstone. The owner refuses. A court grants access under RPAPL 881 but orders the developer to pay $3,000 a month and cover the neighbor's insurance.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring RPAPL 881 and going onto a neighbor's property anyway is trespass. Neighbors who refuse often end up getting paid.
deeper.exam: RPAPL 881 lets a court grant a license to enter a neighbor's property for repairs or construction when access is refused.

blocks.html: An easement for light and air keeps a neighbor from building something that blocks your windows or view. New York does not create light and air easements by prescription or long use. You get one only by express grant, usually bought and recorded. Apartment developers in NYC sometimes pay neighbors for "light and air" easements so a lot line window stays legal.
blocks.casual: An easement for light and air stops a neighbor from building something that blocks your windows or view. New York does not create light and air easements just from long use or prescription. The only way to get one is an express grant, usually bought and recorded. NYC apartment developers sometimes pay neighbors for these so a lot line window can stay legal.

deeper.plain: In New York, you only have a right to keep your view if you paid for it in writing.
deeper.picture: It's like a seat at a show with a clear view: you only get it if your ticket says so.
deeper.street: A buyer loves a Hell's Kitchen condo with big west windows. Next door is a parking lot. Without a recorded light and air easement, a tower can go up there and block everything.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who assume a view is permanent can lose value overnight. Agents should never promise a view will stay.
deeper.exam: NY doesn't recognize light and air easements by prescription. They must be expressly granted.

items: Merger: one owner acquires both the dominant and servient parcels
Release: the holder signs a written release (usually a quitclaim deed) to the servient owner
Abandonment: the holder shows intent to give it up plus an act (in NY, mere nonuse of a granted easement is not enough)
Purpose or necessity ends: a new public road ends an easement by necessity
Expiration of a stated term or condition
Condemnation of the servient land
Adverse use by the servient owner blocking it for 10 years
Destruction of a structure the easement depended on (a party wall in a building that burns down)
blocks.casual:
Here's how an easement ends.
Merger: one owner ends up with both the dominant and servient parcels.
Release: the holder signs a written release (usually a quitclaim deed) to the servient owner.
Abandonment: the holder shows intent to give it up and does something about it. In NY, just not using a granted easement isn't enough.
Purpose or necessity ends: a new public road ends an easement by necessity.
Expiration of a stated term or condition.
Condemnation of the servient land.
Adverse use by the servient owner blocking it for 10 years.
Destruction of a structure the easement depended on (like a party wall in a building that burns down).

deeper.plain: Easements end when one person owns both sides, the holder gives it up, the need disappears, a term runs out, or the government takes the land.
deeper.picture: Like a subscription: it ends when you cancel, when it expires, or when the service shuts down.
deeper.street: The Chens buy the Morales house. Now one family owns both lots, and the driveway easement ends by merger. Years later, if they sell one lot, they need to grant a new easement.
deeper.stakes: Owners who assume an easement ended just because no one used it may get a surprise. In NY, nonuse alone isn't abandonment.
deeper.exam: Merger, release, abandonment with intent, end of necessity, expiration, condemnation, adverse use, destruction. Mere nonuse doesn't end a granted easement in NY.

blocks.q: Evelyn owns an office building with an easement appurtenant over the parking lot next door. She buys the parking lot. What happens to the easement?
c: It continues, now held in gross
It ends only if recorded as released
It ends by merger
It becomes a license
blocks.x: You cannot hold an easement over your own land. When one owner holds both the dominant and servient parcels, the easement ends by merger.

blocks.html: A license is personal permission to do something on another's land: park in a neighbor's driveway for the weekend, attend a Mets game, set up a hot dog cart in a lobby. A license is not an interest in land, is usually revocable at any time, can be oral, and ends when the owner dies or sells.
blocks.casual: A license is personal permission to do something on someone else's land: park in a neighbor's driveway for the weekend, go to a Mets game, set up a hot dog cart in a lobby. A license is not an interest in land. It's usually revocable anytime, it can be oral, and it ends when the owner dies or sells.

deeper.plain: A license is just permission that can be taken back.
deeper.picture: It's like a friend letting you crash on their couch: they can change their mind anytime.
deeper.street: Sal lets a neighbor park in his driveway on weekends. When Sal sells the building, the buyer tells the neighbor to stop. There was no easement, just a license that ended with the sale.
deeper.stakes: People who rely on informal permission can lose access suddenly. If they need lasting access, they need a written easement.
deeper.exam: A license is not an interest in land, can be oral, and is revocable. It ends on death or sale. A ticket to a game is a license.

left.title: Easement
items: Interest in land
Usually written and recorded
Generally irrevocable
Appurtenant runs with land

right.title: License
items: Personal privilege, not an interest
Can be oral
Revocable at will
Ends on sale or death of the licensor

deeper.plain: An easement is a lasting right in land; a license is temporary permission.
