deeper.picture: An easement is owning a season pass; a license is a one-time guest pass that can be pulled.
deeper.street: The Chens' driveway right is an easement (written, recorded, runs with the land). Sal's weekend parking arrangement was a license (oral, revocable, gone at sale).
deeper.stakes: Buyers relying on a license think they have a permanent right. They don't, and it can end without notice.
deeper.exam: Easement: interest in land, usually written, generally irrevocable. License: personal privilege, can be oral, revocable at will, ends on sale or death.

blocks.q: A Long Island homeowner tells a neighbor, "Sure, park your boat trailer on my side lot this winter." This creates:
c: An easement appurtenant
A license
An easement by prescription
A lease
blocks.x: Informal, personal permission that can be withdrawn is a license. It is not an interest in land and does not run with the land.

story.title: The Gate
story.setting: Bay Ridge, 82nd Street, Saturday morning

beats.text: Jordan is showing the Morales house to a buyer who loves the garage and hates sharing anything.
First thing I'm doing is putting a gate across this driveway. Neighbors can park on the street.
Hold on. The Chens have a deeded right of way over this driveway from 1962. Their lot is the dominant tenement. This one is servient.
That was 60 years ago and a different owner.
An easement appurtenant runs with the land. It survived every sale since 1962. It'll survive yours.

check.q: If the buyer locks a gate across the driveway, what can the Chens do?
c: Nothing, their easement ended with the sale
Only ask nicely, it's a license
Sue to enforce the easement and remove the gate
Claim title to the driveway
check.x: An express easement appurtenant binds every later owner of the servient land. The Chens can get an injunction. They get a right of use, not title.

beats.text: What if they never use it?
In New York, just not using a granted easement doesn't end it. They'd have to release it in writing or clearly abandon it.
And the wires over the backyard?
Con Edison. That's an easement in gross. No dominant land, just a company with the right to run lines.
Mr. Chen waves from his garage. The buyer waves back, unconvinced.
Could I just buy the Chens' house too?
Then the easement ends by merger. You'd own both sides. Very expensive gate, though.
Monday, Diane reads Jordan's showing notes.
Good catch on the deed. Buyers who plan to change something should hear about easements before the offer, not after the survey.

board.prompt: Sketch two side-by-side lots with a shared driveway, a power line, and a footpath to the beach. Label dominant, servient, in gross, and how each was created.

facts.text: An easement is a non-possessory right to use another's land for a purpose; easements, liens and deed restrictions are non-possessory, while fee, life and leasehold estates are possessory.
An easement appurtenant involves two parcels: the dominant tenement benefits and the servient tenement carries the burden.
An appurtenant easement runs with the land: it passes with either parcel even if the deed is silent, and a buyer of the servient lot takes subject to it.
Appurtenances are the rights that belong to a parcel and pass with it, such as easements appurtenant, improvements, water and air rights.
An easement in gross benefits a person or company with no dominant parcel; commercial ones (utilities, pipelines) are assignable, personal ones usually end at the holder's death.
A right of way, the right to pass over land, is the most common easement.
An express easement is created by a written grant from the servient owner or by a seller's reservation over the land sold.
An easement by implication arises from a prior, apparent, continuous use when one owner splits a parcel.
An easement by necessity gives a landlocked parcel access over the land it was split from.
A prescriptive easement needs open, notorious, hostile and continuous use for 10 years in New York.
Prescription gives a right to use and does not need exclusive use; adverse possession gives title and does.
Government can take an easement by condemnation with just compensation, and an owner can dedicate a right to the public.
A party wall sits on the boundary; each owner owns the half on his side with a cross-easement for support in the other half.
Under RPAPL 881 an owner refused access to a neighbor's property for repairs can get a court license, often paying license fees and insurance.
New York does not create light and air easements by long use; one exists only by express grant.
Easements end by merger, release, abandonment, end of necessity, expiration, condemnation, 10 years of adverse blocking, or destruction; sale of the servient parcel does not end one.
In New York, abandonment needs intent plus an act; mere nonuse of a granted easement is not enough.
A license is personal permission, not an interest in land: it can be oral, is revocable at will, and ends when the licensor dies or sells.

lessons.title: Deeds: Elements, Descriptions, and Types
lessons.tagline: A deed is a short document with a long memory. Every clause has a job.
objectives: List the essential elements of a valid deed and which ones are needed only for recording
Read a metes and bounds description and a lot and block reference
Rank NY deeds by the warranties they give, and name the five full covenants
Match executor's, referee's, and quitclaim deeds to the situations that call for them

blocks.title: The deed in the drawer
blocks.html: Grace Okafor's late mother signed a deed in 2019 giving her Crown Heights condo to Grace's nephew, then put it in her dresser drawer. Nobody recorded it, and the nephew never knew it existed. Grace found it while cleaning out the apartment. Does the nephew own the condo?
blocks.casual: Back in 2019, Grace Okafor's late mother signed a deed giving her Crown Heights condo to Grace's nephew. Then she stuck it in her dresser drawer. Nobody recorded it, and the nephew had no idea it existed. Grace found it while cleaning out the apartment. So does the nephew own the condo?

deeper.plain: A signed deed nobody handed over usually doesn't transfer anything.
deeper.picture: It's like writing someone a birthday check and leaving it in your own desk. Until you give it to them, it's just paper.
deeper.street: Grace brings the deed to Priya, who explains that because her mother never delivered it, the condo is part of the estate. The nephew may still get it, but only if the will or intestacy says so.
deeper.stakes: Families fight over found deeds all the time. An agent who lists the condo for the nephew based on this paper could be marketing property he doesn't own.
deeper.exam: Cue words: signed but kept by the grantor, never handed over, found after death. The answer is no transfer for lack of delivery.

blocks.text: What a deed is and does

blocks.html: A deed is a written instrument by which an owner transfers title to real property. The transfer itself is a conveyance. The owner who gives title is the grantor; the one who receives it is the grantee. The deed is the evidence of title; title is the ownership itself.
blocks.casual: A deed is the written document an owner uses to transfer title to real property. The transfer itself is called a conveyance. The owner handing over title is the grantor, and the person getting it is the grantee. The deed is the proof of title; title is the ownership itself.

deeper.plain: The deed is the paper; title is the ownership the paper proves.
deeper.picture: A deed is like a car's pink slip: the slip isn't the car, but it proves who owns it.
deeper.street: When the Okafors sell, they're the grantors and their buyer is the grantee. Priya drafts the deed, the Okafors sign it, and title passes when it's delivered at closing.
deeper.stakes: Losing a deed doesn't mean losing title. Clients panic about a missing original, but recorded copies and title insurance protect them.
deeper.exam: Title is ownership; the deed is the evidence. The grantor transfers; the grantee receives.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Grantor gives, grantee gets. The -OR gives (lessor, mortgagor, grantor, offeror). The -EE receives.
blocks.casual: Grantor gives, grantee gets. Anything ending in -OR is the one giving (lessor, mortgagor, grantor, offeror). Anything ending in -EE is the one receiving.

deeper.plain: -OR gives, -EE gets.
deeper.picture: Picture a giver with a big OR on their shirt handing a gift to someone with EE on theirs.
deeper.street: Jordan almost writes that the bank is the mortgagor. Diane points out the borrower gives the mortgage to the bank, so the borrower is the mortgagor and the bank is the mortgagee.
deeper.stakes: Mortgagor and mortgagee trip up nearly everyone, because people think the lender gives the money so it must be the giver.
deeper.exam: The borrower gives the mortgage (a lien), so the borrower is the mortgagor. The lessor is the landlord, and the offeror makes the offer.

head: Element
What it means
NY note
rows: Of legal age and sound mind; entity signs through an authorized officer
Living person or existing entity, named clearly
Grantee need not be competent (a child can receive)
NY deeds often recite "ten dollars and other valuable consideration"; a gift deed recites love and affection
Words of transfer: "grants and releases" or "conveys"
Shows intent to pass title now
Street address alone is not enough
"To have and to hold": defines the estate granted
Fee simple, life estate, and so on
Exceptions and reservations: easements, restrictions, mortgages the buyer takes subject to
Grantor signs; grantee does not need to
All grantors (both spouses in TBE) must sign
Grantor intends to pass title now and hands it over; grantee accepts
Grantor declares before a notary that signing was voluntary
Needed to record, not for validity between the parties
Filed with the county clerk (in NYC, the City Register)
Protects the grantee against later buyers; not needed for validity

deeper.plain: A valid deed needs writing, a competent grantor, a clear grantee, a description, words of transfer, a signature, and delivery; acknowledgment and recording protect it against outsiders.
deeper.picture: Think of a recipe: some ingredients are required to make the cake (writing, signature, delivery), and some are frosting that protects it from the outside world (acknowledgment, recording).
deeper.street: A deed for a Bensonhurst two-family describes the property only as "123 Main Street." The title company kicks it back: the street address isn't a legal description. Priya fixes it with a full metes and bounds before recording.
deeper.stakes: A defective deed can void the transfer or leave the buyer unable to record, which means no title insurance and trouble with any future sale or refinance.
deeper.exam: Know which elements are required for validity and which protect against third parties. Grantee signature, acknowledgment, and recording are not required for validity.

blocks.html: The drawer deed fails on delivery. A signed deed the grantor keeps in her own drawer shows no intent to transfer title during her life. Title never passed, so the condo belongs to her estate. (A deed meant to take effect only at death is really an attempted will and fails without will formalities.)
blocks.casual: The drawer deed fails on delivery. If the grantor signs a deed and keeps it in her own drawer, that shows no intent to hand over title while she's alive. Title never passed, so the condo belongs to her estate. (And a deed that's only supposed to kick in at death is really an attempted will, which fails without the formalities a will needs.)

deeper.plain: If the grantor keeps the deed, it never transferred anything.
deeper.picture: It's like signing a car title over to your kid but locking it in your glove box. The kid doesn't own the car.
deeper.street: The nephew hires a lawyer and argues his grandmother clearly meant for him to have it. The Surrogate's Court looks at intent to deliver during life and finds none, so the condo goes through the estate.
deeper.stakes: Families can lose years and thousands in legal fees fighting over undelivered deeds. Owners who want to pass property should either deliver a deed or put it in a will.
deeper.exam: Delivery requires intent to pass title now. A deed meant to take effect at death is an attempted will and fails without will formalities.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: Three things are not needed for a deed to be valid between grantor and grantee: the grantee's signature, acknowledgment, and recording. Acknowledgment and recording protect against third parties. Title passes on delivery and acceptance.
blocks.casual: Three things are not needed for a deed to be valid between the grantor and grantee: the grantee's signature, acknowledgment, and recording. Acknowledgment and recording protect against third parties. Title passes on delivery and acceptance.

deeper.plain: A deed works between the two parties once it's delivered and accepted, even if it's never recorded.
deeper.picture: It's like handing someone a signed check: it's valid between you two, even if the bank hasn't seen it yet.
deeper.street: A buyer in Sunnyside closes but his attorney forgets to record the deed for six months. He still owns the house. But if the seller had sold it again to someone who recorded first, he'd have a fight.
deeper.stakes: Unrecorded deeds leave buyers exposed to later buyers and lenders. Recording right after closing is the whole point.
deeper.exam: If an answer says recording or acknowledgment is required for a deed to be valid, it's wrong. They're needed to protect against third parties.

blocks.q: Which is required for a deed to be valid between the parties?
c: Recording with the county clerk
Acknowledgment before a notary
The grantor's signature
The grantee's signature
blocks.x: The grantor must sign. Acknowledgment is required only to record, and recording only protects against third parties. The grantee usually does not sign.

blocks.html: A legal description identifies land so precisely that a surveyor could find it with no other help. New York uses two systems (the federal rectangular survey system is not used in NY, an original colony).
blocks.casual: A legal description pins down the land so precisely that a surveyor could find it with nothing else to go on. New York uses two systems. (The federal rectangular survey system doesn't apply here, because NY was one of the original colonies.)

deeper.plain: A legal description is a precise way to identify the land that a surveyor could follow.
deeper.picture: It's like GPS coordinates instead of saying "the house with the red door."
deeper.street: When a buyer in Saratoga Springs asks about townships and sections, Jordan explains those don't exist in NY. Deeds here use metes and bounds or a reference to a filed map.
deeper.stakes: Using the wrong system or a vague description can make a deed defective, leading to title problems later.
deeper.exam: New York uses metes and bounds and lot and block. The rectangular (government) survey system isn't used in NY.

blocks.html: Metes and bounds describes the boundary as a walk. Metes are measurements (distances and directions); bounds are boundaries and monuments (iron pins, stone walls, trees, street lines). The walk starts at a point of beginning, follows each course ("North 45 degrees East, 120 feet"), and must return to the point of beginning to close.
blocks.casual: Metes and bounds describes the boundary as a walk. Metes are measurements (distances and directions); bounds are boundaries and monuments (iron pins, stone walls, trees, street lines). The walk starts at a point of beginning, follows each course ("North 45 degrees East, 120 feet"), and has to end up back at the point of beginning to close.

deeper.plain: Metes and bounds walks the edges of the property and comes back to where it started.
deeper.picture: It's like giving walking directions around a block: start here, go north 120 feet, turn east, and come back to start.
deeper.street: A surveyor in Woodstock follows a 1910 deed: start at the iron pin by the old oak, go north 200 feet to the stone wall, then east along the wall. The oak is gone, so he uses other monuments to reconstruct the line.
deeper.stakes: A description that doesn't close leaves a gap or overlap, which can spark boundary disputes and title issues.
deeper.exam: Metes are measurements; bounds are boundaries and monuments. The description must return to the point of beginning.

blocks.caption: Walk the metes and bounds course from the point of beginning and watch the shape close. Then switch to the tax map to find the same land by lot and block.

blocks.title: Reading a metes and bounds call
blocks.html:
"BEGINNING at a point on the southerly side of Macon Street, distant 100 feet westerly from the corner formed by Macon Street and Tompkins Avenue; running thence southerly parallel with Tompkins Avenue 100 feet; thence westerly parallel with Macon Street 20 feet; thence northerly 100 feet to Macon Street; thence easterly along Macon Street 20 feet to the point or place of BEGINNING."
Shape: a 20 by 100 foot lot (2,000 square feet), the classic Brooklyn brownstone lot. The description closes because the last course returns to the beginning.
blocks.casual:
Here's the call: "BEGINNING at a point on the southerly side of Macon Street, distant 100 feet westerly from the corner formed by Macon Street and Tompkins Avenue; running thence southerly parallel with Tompkins Avenue 100 feet; thence westerly parallel with Macon Street 20 feet; thence northerly 100 feet to Macon Street; thence easterly along Macon Street 20 feet to the point or place of BEGINNING."
Walk it and you get a 20 by 100 foot lot (2,000 square feet), the classic Brooklyn brownstone lot. It closes because the last leg lands right back at the start.

deeper.plain: Follow the directions and you get a rectangle 20 feet wide and 100 feet deep.
deeper.picture: Draw it on graph paper: down 100, left 20, up 100, right 20. You've made a long thin box.
deeper.street: Ray, inspecting the Okafors' brownstone, jokes that he's measured a hundred of these 20 by 100 lots. The buyer's attorney checks the survey against this call to confirm the house sits within the lines.
deeper.stakes: If the deed description is off by even a few feet, the buyer may not own the whole house, or the neighbor's wall may sit on their lot.
deeper.exam: Expect a question asking for the area: multiply width by depth (20 x 100 = 2,000 sq ft). The description must close.

blocks.title: When measurements and monuments disagree
blocks.html: Monuments control over distances. If the deed says "120 feet to the stone wall" and the wall is actually 118 feet away, the boundary is the wall. Courts trust the physical marker over the measurement.
blocks.casual: When measurements and monuments don't match, monuments win. If the deed says "120 feet to the stone wall" and the wall is really 118 feet away, the boundary is the wall. Courts trust the physical marker over the number.

deeper.plain: The physical marker beats the measured distance.
deeper.picture: If directions say walk 100 steps to the big oak but the oak is at 95, you stop at the oak.
deeper.street: A Hudson Valley survey shows a farm's line at the stone wall, 2 feet short of the deed's measurement. The neighbor wants the extra 2 feet. Under the rule, the wall controls.
deeper.stakes: Owners who rely on measurements alone may think they own more than they do and build on the neighbor's land.
deeper.exam: Monuments control over distances. A question showing a conflict between them wants you to pick the monument.

blocks.html: Lot and block refers to a numbered lot on a recorded subdivision plat (filed map) or tax map. The deed makes a reference to a plat: "Lot 14 in Block 3 on the Map of Sunnyside Estates filed in the Nassau County Clerk's Office as Map No. 4512." The filed map incorporates all its measurements.
blocks.casual: Lot and block means a numbered lot on a recorded subdivision plat (a filed map) or tax map. The deed makes a reference to a plat, like "Lot 14 in Block 3 on the Map of Sunnyside Estates filed in the Nassau County Clerk's Office as Map No. 4512." That filed map brings in all its measurements.

deeper.plain: Lot and block points to a lot on an official map filed with the county.
deeper.picture: It's like a seat number on a stadium map: Lot 14, Block 3, and the map shows exactly where.
deeper.street: A buyer in Levittown gets a deed describing Lot 14 in Block 3 on the developer's 1950s filed map. The map shows the lot's dimensions and the easements along the back.
deeper.stakes: If the plat is wrong or was never filed, the description fails. Title companies always check the map.
deeper.exam: Lot and block references a recorded plat, which incorporates the plat's measurements.

blocks.title: Borough, block, and lot
blocks.html: Every NYC parcel has a BBL: borough (1 to 5), block, and lot, used on the tax map and in ACRIS. A condo unit gets its own lot number. NYC deeds still carry a full metes and bounds description, plus the block and lot.
blocks.casual: Every NYC parcel has a BBL: borough (1 to 5), block, and lot. It shows up on the tax map and in ACRIS. Each condo unit gets its own lot number. And NYC deeds still carry a full metes and bounds description along with the block and lot.

deeper.plain: Every NYC property has a borough, block, and lot number.
deeper.picture: It's like a phone number with an area code: borough first, then block, then lot.
deeper.street: Jordan looks up the Okafors' brownstone in ACRIS by BBL 3 (Brooklyn), block 1680, lot 22, and pulls every deed and mortgage recorded on it since 1966.
deeper.stakes: Using the wrong BBL can pull the wrong documents or tax info and lead to a mistake in a listing or closing.
deeper.exam: Borough codes: 1 Manhattan, 2 Bronx, 3 Brooklyn, 4 Queens, 5 Staten Island. Condo units have their own lot numbers.

blocks.html: A survey is a licensed land surveyor's drawing of the boundaries, improvements, easements, and any encroachments. Buyers' attorneys and title companies use it to confirm the land matches the description.
blocks.casual: A survey is a licensed land surveyor's drawing of the boundaries, improvements, easements, and any encroachments. Buyers' attorneys and title companies use it to make sure the land actually matches the description.

deeper.plain: A survey shows what's really on the ground and where the lines are.
deeper.picture: It's like an X-ray of the lot: it shows what's inside the lines and anything poking over.
deeper.street: The buyer of a Bayside house orders a survey, which shows the neighbor's shed sits 2 feet onto the lot. Priya gets the neighbor to sign an agreement before closing.
deeper.stakes: Without a survey, the buyer and title company can't spot encroachments, and title insurance often excludes survey issues.
deeper.exam: A survey finds encroachments and confirms the legal description. A title search finds recorded documents.

blocks.q: A deed describes a boundary as "200 feet to an iron pipe." The pipe is found 197 feet from the prior point. Which controls?
c: The 200-foot distance
An average of the two
The iron pipe
Whichever favors the grantee
blocks.x: Monuments control over distances and directions. The boundary runs to the pipe.

blocks.html: Deeds differ in what the grantor promises about the title. The more covenants, the more protection for the grantee.
blocks.casual: What separates one deed from another is what the grantor promises about the title. More promises (covenants) means more protection for the grantee.

deeper.plain: Some deeds come with strong guarantees, and some come with none.
deeper.picture: It's like buying a used car: one comes with a full warranty, one with a 30-day guarantee, and one sold as is.
deeper.street: Leo buys a condo with a bargain and sale deed and a title insurance policy. His friend buys a foreclosure with a referee's deed. Both rely on title insurance, because neither seller promised much.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't know what the deed promises may assume the seller will cover title problems that the seller never promised to cover.
deeper.exam: Rank deeds by protection. The more covenants, the higher the protection for the grantee.

blocks.caption: Climb from the quitclaim (no promises) up to the full covenant and warranty deed. Note which rung most NY home sales use.

blocks.html: The full covenant and warranty deed gives the most protection. The grantor makes five promises covering the title's whole history, not just the grantor's time:
blocks.casual: The full covenant and warranty deed gives you the most protection. The grantor makes five promises that cover the title's entire history, not just the time the grantor owned it:

deeper.plain: This deed guarantees the title all the way back, not just during the seller's time.
deeper.picture: It's like a lifetime warranty that covers the car's history before you even owned it.
deeper.street: An upstate buyer in Ithaca gets a full covenant and warranty deed. Years later, a forgotten 1950s claim surfaces, and the seller is on the hook to defend the title.
deeper.stakes: Sellers rarely want to give this deed because it exposes them to claims from before they owned it.
deeper.exam: The full covenant and warranty deed gives the most protection and covers the entire chain of title.

head: Covenant
Promise
rows: I own this estate and have the right to convey it
No one with better title will disturb your possession
No liens or encumbrances except those stated in the deed
I will sign any document needed to perfect your title
I will defend your title against all lawful claims, forever
blocks.caption: "Some Quiet Elephants Fear Warriors": Seizin, Quiet enjoyment, Encumbrances, Further assurance, Warranty

deeper.plain: The five promises are: I own it, nobody will kick you out, there are no hidden claims, I'll fix paperwork, and I'll defend you forever.
deeper.picture: Think of five bodyguards: one proves ownership, one keeps the peace, one checks for debts, one handles paperwork, and one fights off claims forever.
deeper.street: A buyer in Cooperstown later learns of an old unpaid lien from the 1980s. Because he got a full covenant and warranty deed, the seller's covenant against encumbrances lets him go after the seller for the cost.
deeper.stakes: A seller who gives these promises takes on real legal risk, which is why NY sellers usually rely on title insurance instead.
deeper.exam: Know the five covenants. Seizin is ownership; quiet enjoyment means no one with better title disturbs you; warranty forever means defending title against all lawful claims.

head: Deed
What the grantor promises
Typical NY use
rows: All five covenants, whole chain of title
Rare in NY; more common in other states
Bargain and sale with covenant against grantor's acts
Grantor owns it and has done nothing to encumber it
Implies the grantor holds title; no promises
Some estate, bank-owned, and investor sales
Executor has not encumbered the property
Sale from a decedent's estate under a will (administrator's deed if no will)
No personal covenants; conveys what the court sale conveys
Foreclosure or partition sales by a court-appointed referee
None. Releases whatever interest the grantor may have, if any
Clearing a cloud on title, divorce transfers, releasing an easement

deeper.plain: The deeds run from the most promises (full covenant) to none (quitclaim), with court and estate deeds offering very little.
deeper.picture: Think of a ladder: full warranty on top, quitclaim at the bottom, with estate and court deeds on low rungs.
deeper.street: The Okafors give their buyer a bargain and sale deed with covenant. A Queens estate sale uses an executor's deed. A foreclosure in Jamaica uses a referee's deed. A divorce transfer in Staten Island uses a quitclaim.
deeper.stakes: Picking the wrong deed can leave a buyer with no recourse against the seller if a title issue turns up.
deeper.exam: Bargain and sale with covenant is the standard NY deed. Referee's deed is for court sales. Quitclaim conveys whatever interest the grantor has, with no promises.

blocks.title: Special warranty deed
blocks.html: National exam prep loves the special warranty deed: the grantor warrants title only against defects created during the grantor's own ownership. New York rarely uses that name. Its local equivalent is the bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts, which makes the same limited promise. If a question asks which deed protects only against the seller's own acts, either name is the answer; if it asks which deed protects against the entire chain of title, the answer is the full covenant and warranty deed.
blocks.casual: National exam prep loves the special warranty deed: the grantor only warrants against defects that happened while the grantor owned the property. New York rarely uses that name. Here, the local version is the bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts, which makes the same limited promise. If a question asks which deed protects only against the seller's own acts, either name works. If it asks which deed protects against the whole chain of title, the answer is the full covenant and warranty deed.

deeper.plain: Special warranty and NY's bargain and sale with covenant both only cover the seller's own time.
deeper.picture: It's like a car seller saying, "I'll vouch for it since I bought it, but not what happened before."
deeper.street: A buyer from Texas asks Jordan for a special warranty deed. Jordan explains that in NY, the bargain and sale with covenant is essentially the same thing, backed by title insurance.
deeper.stakes: Agents who don't know the local term can confuse out-of-state clients.
deeper.exam: Protects only against the seller's acts: special warranty or bargain and sale with covenant. Protects against the whole chain: full covenant and warranty.

blocks.title: The NY standard deed and the Lien Law covenant
blocks.html: Most NY home sales use a bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts, since the buyer is protected by title insurance rather than the seller's promises. NY deeds also include the Lien Law Section 13 covenant: the grantor will hold the sale money as a trust fund to pay for any recent improvements before using it for anything else.
blocks.casual: Most NY home sales use a bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts, because the buyer's real protection comes from title insurance, not from the seller's promises. NY deeds also include the Lien Law Section 13 covenant: the grantor will hold the sale money as a trust fund to pay for any recent improvements before spending it on anything else.

deeper.plain: NY homes usually sell with a limited-promise deed, and title insurance does the heavy lifting.
deeper.picture: It's like buying something with a basic store guarantee and an extended warranty you paid for separately.
deeper.street: The Okafors redid their kitchen last year. Under the Lien Law covenant in their deed, they must use sale proceeds to pay any unpaid contractors first.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who pocket proceeds without paying for recent improvements can face claims under the trust fund covenant.
deeper.exam: The standard NY residential deed is a bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts. The Lien Law covenant makes sale proceeds a trust fund for improvement costs.

blocks.q: A divorcing husband gives up any claim to the marital co-owned home in Yonkers so his ex-wife can refinance. Which deed is most appropriate?
c: Full covenant and warranty deed
Quitclaim deed
Referee's deed
Executor's deed
blocks.x: A quitclaim releases whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties. It is the tool for clearing claims, not for selling with promises.

blocks.q: Which deed gives the grantee the greatest protection?
c: Bargain and sale with covenant against grantor's acts
Full covenant and warranty deed
Referee's deed
Bargain and sale without covenant
blocks.x: Full covenant and warranty covers the entire history of title with five covenants. The bargain and sale with covenant covers only the grantor's own acts.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: The deed ladder from top to bottom: Full, Bargain With, Bargain Without, Quit. Court and estate deeds (referee, executor) sit low because the seller never lived there and promises little.
blocks.casual: The deed ladder, top to bottom: Full, Bargain With, Bargain Without, Quit. Court and estate deeds (referee, executor) sit near the bottom because the seller never lived there and promises very little.

deeper.plain: Four rungs from most to least protection, with court and estate deeds low on the ladder.
deeper.picture: Picture climbing a ladder that gets shakier as you go down, until you're on the quitclaim rung with nothing to hold.
deeper.street: Jordan walks Leo through it: "Full is the gold standard, bargain with is what you'll get here, bargain without is common with estates and banks, quitclaim is what divorcing couples use."
deeper.stakes: Knowing the ladder lets you explain to buyers why title insurance matters so much in NY.
deeper.exam: Ranking questions are common. Full covenant is the most protective; quitclaim is the least.

story.title: The Drawer
story.setting: Crown Heights, an empty condo on Eastern Parkway

beats.text: Grace Okafor is clearing out her late mother's condo. Jordan came to talk about listing it. Grace holds up a yellowed deed.
Mama signed this in 2019. It gives the condo to my nephew Tunde. Signed, notarized. So it's his?
It was in her drawer? Did Tunde ever get it?
He doesn't even know about it.
Then it was never delivered. A deed passes title only when the grantor delivers it intending to transfer ownership now, and the grantee accepts.

check.q: Why didn't the 2019 deed transfer title to Tunde?
c: It was not recorded
Tunde didn't sign it
It was never delivered
It lacked a habendum clause
check.x: Delivery with present intent is essential. Recording and the grantee's signature are not required for validity.

beats.text: But it was notarized.
The acknowledgment lets it be recorded. It doesn't replace delivery. The condo is in your mother's estate, and the will controls.
So when the estate sells, what kind of deed does the buyer get?
An executor's deed, signed by Grace as executrix. She promises only that she didn't encumber it herself. The buyer relies on title insurance.
What did we get when we bought Macon Street in 1997?
Probably what most New Yorkers get. Bargain and sale with covenant against grantor's acts.
beats.tag: NY standard: bargain and sale with covenant

beats.text: Grace calls Tunde anyway. He is relieved: he did not want to pay the common charges.
Signed is not delivered, and notarized is not recorded. When a seller hands you a deed, ask who held it and when.

board.prompt: Draw a deed as a stack of labeled boxes, top to bottom: grantor, grantee, consideration, granting clause, legal description, habendum, subject to, signature, acknowledgment. Star the elements needed for validity and circle the ones needed only to record.

facts.text: The grantor gives title by deed and the grantee receives it; the deed is the evidence of title, the transfer is the conveyance.
A valid deed needs a writing, a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, recited consideration, a granting clause, a legal description, the grantor's signature, and delivery and acceptance.
The grantee need not be competent or sign (a child can receive), but every grantor must sign, both spouses in a tenancy by the entirety; a minor's deed is voidable.
The granting clause holds the words of conveyance; the habendum clause ("to have and to hold") defines the estate granted.
Title passes when the deed is delivered and accepted; a signed deed the grantor keeps in a drawer was never delivered, and a deed meant to work only at death fails as an attempted will.
The grantee's signature, acknowledgment and recording are not needed for a deed to be valid between the parties; acknowledgment and recording protect against third parties.
Acknowledgment is the grantor's declaration before a notary that signing was voluntary; it is needed to record the deed.
NY deeds usually recite "ten dollars and other valuable consideration"; a gift deed recites love and affection.
A legal description must let a surveyor find the land with no other help; a street address is not enough, and NY does not use the rectangular survey system.
Metes and bounds walks the boundary from a point of beginning by courses and distances and must return to the point of beginning to close.
When monuments and measured distances disagree, the monument controls.
Lot and block describes land by reference to a numbered lot on a recorded plat (filed map) or tax map.
Every NYC parcel has a borough, block and lot (BBL); a condo unit gets its own lot, and NYC deeds still carry a full metes and bounds description.
A survey is a licensed land surveyor's drawing of boundaries, improvements, easements and encroachments.
The full covenant and warranty deed gives the most protection: five covenants (seizin, quiet enjoyment, against encumbrances, further assurance, warranty forever) covering the whole chain of title.
Seizin promises the grantor owns the estate and may convey it; quiet enjoyment promises no one with better title will disturb the grantee's possession.
The covenant against encumbrances promises no liens or encumbrances except those stated in the deed.
The covenant of further assurance promises the grantor will sign any document needed to perfect the grantee's title.
The covenant of warranty forever promises to defend the title against all lawful claims.
The standard NY residential deed is the bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts, since the buyer relies on title insurance.
The special warranty deed of national exam prep protects only against the grantor's own acts; NY's equivalent is the bargain and sale deed with covenant.
A bargain and sale deed without covenant implies title but promises nothing; an executor's deed promises only that the executor has not encumbered the property (administrator's deed if no will).
A referee's deed conveys property sold by court order (foreclosure or partition) with no personal covenants.
A quitclaim deed has no warranties and releases whatever interest the grantor may have; it is used to clear clouds, in divorces, and to release easements.
Every NY deed includes the Lien Law Section 13 covenant: the grantor holds the sale money in trust to pay for recent improvements first.

lessons.title: Transfers Without a Sale: Death, Possession, and Nature
lessons.tagline: Title also moves by will, by intestacy, by ten years of open use, and by a river that changes its mind.
objectives: Separate voluntary from involuntary alienation
Explain testate transfers: will, testator, probate, executor, devise, devisee
Explain intestate transfers under NY law: administrator, distributees, descent, escheat
State NY's adverse possession elements, the 10-year period, and the 2008 limits
Distinguish accession, accretion, alluvion, reliction, and avulsion, and define public grant, land patent, and dedication

blocks.title: The fence on Staten Island
blocks.html: In 2012 the Russos' neighbor in Great Kills built a 6-foot fence that, a 2025 survey shows, sits 14 feet onto the Russo lot. Behind the fence the neighbor built a paved patio and a hot tub and has used the strip ever since. The Russos never objected. Now they want to sell, and the neighbor says the strip is hers. Is it?
blocks.casual: Back in 2012, the Russos' neighbor in Great Kills put up a 6-foot fence. A 2025 survey shows it sits 14 feet onto the Russo lot. Behind that fence, the neighbor built a paved patio and a hot tub, and she's used the strip ever since. The Russos never said a word. Now they want to sell, and the neighbor says that strip is hers. Is it?

deeper.plain: If someone uses your land openly as their own for long enough, they might end up owning it.
deeper.picture: It's like a roommate who takes over your closet for years while you never say anything. Eventually it starts to feel like theirs, and the law might agree.
deeper.street: The Russos' buyer's attorney sees the survey and refuses to close until the strip dispute is settled. The neighbor's lawyer files a quiet title action, and the sale stalls for a year.
deeper.stakes: Owners who ignore an encroachment can lose land, and buyers can't get clean title until it's resolved. Deals die in the meantime.
deeper.exam: Cue words: open use, built improvements, years without objection. Count the years against NY's 10-year period and check whether the use is more than a de minimis encroachment.

blocks.html: Alienation means transfer of title. Voluntary alienation is a transfer the owner chooses: a deed during life (sale or gift) or a will at death. Involuntary alienation happens without the owner's consent: intestate descent, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure, tax sales, partition, adverse possession, and natural forces like erosion.
blocks.casual: Alienation just means transferring title. Voluntary alienation is when the owner chooses to transfer, by deed while alive (a sale or gift) or by will at death. Involuntary alienation happens without the owner's consent: intestate descent, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure, tax sales, partition, adverse possession, and natural forces like erosion.

deeper.plain: You can give property away on purpose, or lose it without choosing to.
deeper.picture: Voluntary is selling your bike; involuntary is having it towed, washed away in a flood, or claimed by someone who used it for years.
deeper.street: In one month, Hudson & Hart sees a regular sale in Park Slope (voluntary), a foreclosure auction in East New York (involuntary), and a family taking over a house after a parent died without a will (involuntary, by descent).
deeper.stakes: Involuntary transfers often come with title problems that need extra work from attorneys and title companies before anyone can sell.
deeper.exam: Deeds and wills are voluntary. Descent, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure, adverse possession, and erosion are involuntary.

head: Voluntary
Involuntary
rows: Dedication of land to the public

deeper.plain: The left column is the owner's choice; the right column happens to the owner.
deeper.picture: One side is handing over your keys; the other side is the locksmith changing the locks without asking.
deeper.street: A developer in Long Island dedicates new roads to the town (voluntary). Down the street, the state takes a strip of a homeowner's yard to widen a highway (eminent domain, involuntary).
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't know how a property was last transferred may miss issues, like a tax sale that might be challenged.
deeper.exam: Dedication is voluntary even though the government receives it. Intestate descent is involuntary because the owner didn't choose who gets it.

blocks.html: Title can also start with the government. A public grant is a transfer of land from the government to a private party. The original document is a land patent. In NY, many chains of title trace back to colonial Dutch or English patents (the Van Rensselaer patent near Albany) or state grants. Going the other way, dedication is a private owner giving land to public use: a developer dedicates streets and parks on a filed subdivision map (dedication by plat) or deeds a strip to the town (dedication by deed). It needs acceptance by the government.
blocks.casual: Title can also start with the government. A public grant is when the government transfers land to a private party, and the original document is a land patent. In NY, plenty of chains of title trace back to colonial Dutch or English patents (like the Van Rensselaer patent near Albany) or state grants. Going the other direction, dedication is a private owner giving land for public use. A developer dedicates streets and parks on a filed subdivision map (dedication by plat) or deeds a strip to the town (dedication by deed). The government has to accept it.

deeper.plain: Land can start with the government and go private, or go from private hands to public use.
deeper.picture: It's like a library giving away an old book to a reader, or a reader donating a book to the library.
deeper.street: A title search on an Albany County farm traces back to the 1600s Van Rensselaer patent. Meanwhile, a Suffolk developer dedicates new roads to the town, which accepts them and takes over plowing.
deeper.stakes: If a dedication was never accepted, the developer or homeowners may still own and maintain the road, which affects taxes and liability.
deeper.exam: A land patent is the original government grant. Dedication requires acceptance by the government.

blocks.q: Which is an example of involuntary alienation?
c: A county sells a house at a tax foreclosure sale
A testator leaves her farm to a niece by will
A father deeds his house to his daughter as a gift
A developer dedicates a street to the town
blocks.x: A tax foreclosure takes title without the owner's consent. Gifts, wills, and dedications are all the owner's choice.

blocks.html: A person who dies with a valid will dies testate. The maker is the testator (traditionally testatrix for a woman). A gift of real property by will is a devise, and the recipient is the devisee. A gift of personal property is a bequest or legacy.
blocks.casual: If someone dies with a valid will, they die testate. The person who made the will is the testator (traditionally testatrix for a woman). A gift of real property in a will is a devise, and the person getting it is the devisee. A gift of personal property is a bequest or legacy.

deeper.plain: A will that leaves real estate is a devise; personal stuff is a bequest.
deeper.picture: Think of a will as a gift list: houses are devises, jewelry and cash are bequests.
deeper.street: A grandmother in Astoria leaves her house to her granddaughter (a devise) and her china set to her nephew (a bequest). The granddaughter is the devisee.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up these terms makes you look unprepared in front of estate attorneys and clients.
deeper.exam: Devise and devisee go with real property; bequest and legacy go with personal property. Testate means with a will.

blocks.html: Probate is the court process that proves the will is valid and supervises the estate. In NY it takes place in the Surrogate's Court of the county where the decedent lived. The court issues letters testamentary to the executor (executrix) named in the will, who gathers assets, pays debts and taxes, and conveys real property to devisees or sells it by executor's deed.
blocks.casual: Probate is the court process that proves a will is valid and oversees the estate. In NY it happens in the Surrogate's Court of the county where the person lived. The court issues letters testamentary to the executor (executrix) named in the will. That person gathers the assets, pays the debts and taxes, and either conveys real property to the devisees or sells it with an executor's deed.

deeper.plain: Probate is the court process to confirm a will and put someone in charge of the estate.
deeper.picture: It's like a referee confirming the rules of a game before anyone gets to play.
deeper.street: After Mrs. Haddad dies, her executor files the will in Kings County Surrogate's Court. Once letters testamentary are issued, the executor can sign a listing with Jordan and later an executor's deed.
deeper.stakes: Agents who list an estate property before letters are issued may have no one with legal authority to sign. Deals stall or fall apart.
deeper.exam: Probate is in Surrogate's Court in NY. The executor gets letters testamentary and sells with an executor's deed.

blocks.title: NY will basics
blocks.html: A NY will must be in writing, signed at the end by the testator (18 or older, of sound mind), and witnessed by at least two witnesses. Handwritten unwitnessed (holographic) and oral (nuncupative) wills are valid only for members of the armed forces in wartime and mariners at sea. A change to a will is a codicil, with the same formalities.
blocks.casual: In NY, a will has to be in writing, signed at the end by the testator (18 or older, of sound mind), and witnessed by at least two people. Handwritten unwitnessed (holographic) wills and oral (nuncupative) wills only count for members of the armed forces in wartime and mariners at sea. A change to a will is a codicil, and it needs the same formalities.

deeper.plain: A New York will needs to be written, signed at the end, and witnessed by two people.
deeper.picture: It's like a contract that needs two witnesses to be official.
deeper.street: A Bronx man writes a will by hand and signs it but has no witnesses. When he dies, the Surrogate's Court rejects it, and his estate passes by intestacy instead.
deeper.stakes: A defective will can send property to people the deceased never intended, and families end up in court.
deeper.exam: Two witnesses, signed at the end, testator 18 or older. Holographic and oral wills are valid only for military in wartime or mariners at sea. A codicil amends a will.

blocks.html: A person who dies without a valid will dies intestate. The Surrogate's Court appoints an administrator (administratrix), usually a close relative, through letters of administration. Property passes by intestate succession to the heirs (NY law calls them distributees). Receiving real property this way is title by descent.
blocks.casual: If someone dies without a valid will, they die intestate. The Surrogate's Court appoints an administrator (administratrix), usually a close relative, by issuing letters of administration. The property passes by intestate succession to the heirs (NY law calls them distributees). Getting real property this way is called title by descent.

deeper.plain: No will means the state decides who inherits, and a court picks someone to run the estate.
deeper.picture: It's like dying without a playlist: the state queues up your songs in a default order.
deeper.street: A man in Corona dies without a will. His son petitions the Queens Surrogate's Court and becomes administrator. Before the house can be sold, the son needs letters of administration.
deeper.stakes: Without a will, property can go to relatives the deceased wouldn't have chosen, and probate can take longer.
deeper.exam: Intestate means no will. Administrator is appointed; title passes by descent to heirs, also called distributees in NY.

head: Survivors
Who takes under NY law (EPTL 4-1.1)
rows: Spouse gets $50,000 plus half of the rest; children share the balance
Children take everything (equally; a deceased child's share goes to that child's children)
Grandparents, aunts, uncles, first cousins in a set order
Escheat: the property goes to the State of New York

deeper.plain: New York has a fixed order for who inherits when there's no will, starting with the spouse and kids.
deeper.picture: It's like a family seating chart at a wedding: closest relatives first, and if no one shows up, the state takes the seat.
deeper.street: A widow in Bayside dies without a will, leaving no children but a sister. Her parents are dead, so the sister takes everything under EPTL 4-1.1.
deeper.stakes: Families are often surprised by who inherits under the default rules, especially in blended families.
deeper.exam: Spouse plus children: $50,000 plus half to the spouse, the rest to the kids. Spouse only: all. No relatives: escheat to the state.

blocks.title: Worked example: intestate estate in Queens
blocks.html:
Arturo dies without a will, leaving a wife and two adult children. His solely owned two-family in Corona is worth $950,000 and is his only asset (no debts).
1. Spouse first takes $50,000. Remaining: $900,000.
2. Spouse takes half of the rest: $450,000. Spouse total: $500,000.
3. Children split the other $450,000: $225,000 each.
If the house had been held as tenants by the entirety, none of this would apply: the wife would own it all by survivorship.
blocks.casual:
Arturo dies without a will, leaving a wife and two adult children. His solely owned two-family in Corona is worth $950,000, and it's his only asset (no debts).
First, his wife takes $50,000. That leaves $900,000.
Then she takes half of what's left: $450,000. Her total is $500,000.
The kids split the other $450,000: $225,000 each.
If the house had been held as tenants by the entirety, none of this would matter. The wife would own the whole thing by survivorship.

deeper.plain: The spouse gets $50,000 first, then half of what's left; the kids split the other half.
deeper.picture: It's like splitting a pizza: Mom gets her own slice first, then half of the rest; the kids share the other half.
deeper.street: Arturo's wife wants to keep the house, but she only has a $500,000 share. She has to buy out the children's $450,000 or the family may have to sell.
deeper.stakes: A surviving spouse can be forced to sell or buy out kids, all because the deed wasn't set up as tenants by the entirety and there was no will.
deeper.exam: Do the math step by step. Start with $50,000 to the spouse, then split the remainder in half. Tenancy by the entirety bypasses all of this.

left.title: Testate (will)
items: Testator / testatrix
Executor / executrix named in the will
Letters testamentary
Devise to a devisee
Probate proves the will

right.title: Intestate (no will)
items: Decedent
Administrator / administratrix appointed by court
Letters of administration
Title by descent to heirs (distributees)
No heirs: escheat to the state

deeper.plain: With a will, an executor carries it out; without one, a court-appointed administrator follows state rules.
deeper.picture: Testate is following a recipe the cook wrote; intestate is the state handing you its standard recipe.
deeper.street: Two estates in Queens: one with a will (executor, letters testamentary, executor's deed) and one without (administrator, letters of administration, distributees). Both use Surrogate's Court, but the paperwork differs.
deeper.stakes: Agents need to know who has authority to sign a listing and deed, which depends on whether there was a will.
deeper.exam: Executor goes with a will; administrator goes with no will. Devisee takes by will; heir takes by descent.

blocks.q: A Buffalo widow dies with no will, no children, no parents, but one brother. Who inherits her house?
c: Her brother
The State of New York by escheat
Her late husband's relatives
The administrator personally
blocks.x: With no spouse, descendants, or parents, siblings take under NY intestate succession. Escheat happens only when there are no distributees at all.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: Executor = will. Administrator = no will. A "devisee" receives real property by will; an heir receives by descent. And escheat is a government power, not a lien.
blocks.casual: Executor means there's a will. Administrator means there isn't. A "devisee" gets real property by will; an heir gets it by descent. And escheat is a government power, not a lien.

deeper.plain: Match executor to will, administrator to no will, devisee to will, and heir to descent.
deeper.picture: Think of two doors: the will door leads to executor and devisee, and the no-will door leads to administrator and heir.
deeper.street: Jordan, prepping a listing for an estate in Bushwick, asks the client whether he's an executor or administrator. The answer tells Jordan which court papers to ask for.
deeper.stakes: Using the wrong term in a listing agreement or contract can raise questions about authority to sell.
deeper.exam: Swapped pairs are classic distractors. Escheat is a government power, not a lien.

blocks.html: Adverse possession lets a person who occupies someone else's land long enough, in the right way, acquire title. It rewards use and punishes owners who sleep on their rights. In New York (RPAPL Article 5) the possession must be:
blocks.casual: Adverse possession lets someone who occupies another person's land long enough, and in the right way, end up with title. It rewards people who use land and punishes owners who sleep on their rights. In New York (RPAPL Article 5), the possession has to be:

deeper.plain: If you use someone else's land as your own for long enough, openly and without permission, you can become the owner.
deeper.picture: It's like squatting in an abandoned garden plot for a decade while the owner never shows up, until the law says it's yours.
deeper.street: A Bronx man fenced and farmed a vacant city lot for 12 years. He sued for title, but the city owned it, and adverse possession can't run against government land held for public use.
deeper.stakes: Owners who don't watch their land can lose part of it. Buyers can't get clean title until the claim is resolved.
deeper.exam: Adverse possession transfers title. In NY it's governed by RPAPL Article 5, with a 10-year period.

items: Hostile under a claim of right: without permission, and (since 2008) with a reasonable basis to believe the land is the possessor's
Actual: really using it as an owner would
Open and notorious: visible, not hidden
Exclusive: not shared with the owner or the public
Continuous for 10 years
blocks.casual:
Hostile under a claim of right: no permission, and (since 2008) the person has a reasonable basis to believe the land is theirs.
Actual: they really use it the way an owner would.
Open and notorious: it's visible, not hidden.
Exclusive: they don't share it with the owner or the public.
Continuous for 10 years.

deeper.plain: No permission, real use, out in the open, not shared, and nonstop for 10 years.
deeper.picture: Picture a neighbor who moves in, puts up their own sign, and acts like the owner every day for 10 years while you watch.
deeper.street: A Yonkers man uses a strip of his neighbor's yard as a driveway for 11 years, but the neighbor parks there too on weekends. Because the use wasn't exclusive, his adverse possession claim fails.
deeper.stakes: Missing just one element sinks the claim. Owners who give written permission destroy the hostility element.
deeper.exam: Remember the elements and the 10-year NY period. Since 2008, claim of right requires a reasonable basis for believing the land is the possessor's.

blocks.title: The 2008 amendments
blocks.html: Since 2008, de minimis non-structural encroachments (fences, hedges, shrubs, plantings, sheds, non-structural walls) are treated as permissive and cannot by themselves support adverse possession. Mowing or maintaining a strip across the line is also treated as permissive. Successive possessors can add their time together (tacking) if one passed possession to the next. The claimant gets clear record title through a quiet title action.
blocks.casual: Since 2008, minor non-structural encroachments (fences, hedges, shrubs, plantings, sheds, non-structural walls) count as permissive and can't support adverse possession on their own. Mowing or maintaining a strip across the line is treated as permissive too. People can add their time together (tacking) if one handed possession to the next. And the claimant gets clean record title through a quiet title action.

deeper.plain: Small stuff like fences and hedges doesn't count, but owners can add their time together.
deeper.picture: It's like the law saying a neighbor's flowerpot on your step isn't a takeover, but a whole new deck is.
deeper.street: A homeowner in Bayside mows a strip of his neighbor's lawn for 15 years. Under the 2008 law, that's permissive, and he can't claim it. His other neighbor, who built a garage over the line, is in a different situation.
deeper.stakes: Owners who assume a fence settles the issue may be wrong, and claimants who rely on mowing may lose.
deeper.exam: De minimis non-structural encroachments are deemed permissive. Tacking lets successive possessors combine time. Quiet title action clears record title.

blocks.html: Back to Great Kills. The fence alone would not do it after 2008. But a paved patio and hot tub inside a fence for 13 years is actual, open, exclusive, continuous use well beyond a de minimis encroachment. The neighbor has a strong claim if she can also show a reasonable belief the strip was hers. The Russos' sale is stuck until a court or a settlement resolves it.
blocks.casual: Back to Great Kills. The fence alone wouldn't do it after 2008. But a paved patio and a hot tub behind a fence for 13 years is actual, open, exclusive, continuous use, way past a minor encroachment. The neighbor has a strong claim if she can also show she reasonably believed the strip was hers. Until a court or a settlement sorts it out, the Russos' sale is stuck.

deeper.plain: The patio and hot tub go beyond a small encroachment, so the neighbor might really win.
deeper.picture: A fence is a doodle on your notebook; a patio and hot tub is redecorating your whole room.
deeper.street: The Russos settle: the neighbor pays them $45,000 for the strip and they sign a deed. Their sale to a buyer goes through with a new survey.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring encroachments for years can cost an owner land and money. A quick letter or written permission early on would have prevented it.
deeper.exam: Check each element and the 10-year clock. Substantial improvements like a patio support the claim even after 2008.

blocks.q: Which fact would most likely defeat an adverse possession claim in New York?
c: The use lasted 11 years
The owner gave written permission to use the land
The claimant built a garage on the strip
The claimant was not the original possessor but bought from one
blocks.x: Permission destroys hostility. Eleven years beats the 10-year period, a garage is open use, and tacking lets successive possessors combine time.

head: Term
What happens
Effect on title
rows: Gradual build-up of land along a shore or riverbank
The soil itself deposited by accretion
Belongs to the riparian or littoral owner
Gradual wearing away of land by water or wind
Sudden loss or shift of land by a storm, flood, or river changing course
Boundary stays where it was; owner keeps title to the moved land if it can be identified

deeper.plain: Water and weather can add or take land, slowly or suddenly, and the law treats each differently.
deeper.picture: Accretion is sand piling up grain by grain; avulsion is a chunk of beach washed away in one storm.
deeper.street: A beach house owner in Montauk gains 20 feet of sand over a decade (accretion, she owns it). In Breezy Point, a Sandy storm surge rips a chunk off a lot (avulsion, the boundary stays put).
deeper.stakes: Buyers of waterfront land need to know whether the property lines on the survey still match the shoreline, or they may overpay.
deeper.exam: Gradual equals accretion, reliction, or erosion. Sudden equals avulsion, and the boundary stays where it was.

blocks.html: Accession is the broad term for acquiring title to additions to your property: natural ones like accretion and alluvion, and man-made ones like a trade fixture a tenant abandons, which becomes the landlord's.
blocks.casual: Accession is the big umbrella term for gaining title to stuff added to your property. That includes natural additions like accretion and alluvion, and man-made ones like a trade fixture a tenant walks away from, which becomes the landlord's.

deeper.plain: Accession means you own what gets added to your property.
deeper.picture: It's like a snowball rolling downhill and picking up more snow: what sticks becomes part of it.
deeper.street: A bakery in Evelyn's building leaves its ovens behind after the lease. By accession, Evelyn now owns them. On her lakefront property in the Finger Lakes, new sand piling up also becomes hers.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who leave equipment behind lose it, and owners may gain land without realizing it.
deeper.exam: Accession is the broad term that covers natural accretion and abandoned trade fixtures.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Accretion Adds slowly. Avulsion is Abrupt. Hurricane Sandy ripping away a chunk of a Breezy Point lot was avulsion; sand slowly building up on a Montauk beach is accretion.
blocks.casual: Accretion Adds slowly. Avulsion is Abrupt. Hurricane Sandy tearing a chunk off a Breezy Point lot was avulsion. Sand slowly piling up on a Montauk beach is accretion.

deeper.plain: Slow buildup is accretion; sudden loss is avulsion.
deeper.picture: Think of a slow drip filling a glass versus a glass suddenly knocked over.
deeper.street: Jordan uses Sandy as the anchor: nobody in Breezy Point forgets how fast the land disappeared, so avulsion means abrupt.
deeper.stakes: It's a quick hook for a question that often trips people up.
deeper.exam: If the stem says suddenly or storm, pick avulsion. If it says gradually, pick accretion (or erosion if land is lost).

blocks.q: Over 30 years, sand slowly builds up along a Fire Island lot, adding 40 feet of beach. Who owns the new land?
c: The State of New York
Whoever uses it first for 10 years
The lot owner, by accretion
The town, by dedication
blocks.x: Gradual build-up is accretion, and the deposited soil (alluvion) belongs to the adjoining owner. Sudden changes are avulsion.

story.title: Fourteen Feet
story.setting: Great Kills, Staten Island, a windy October afternoon

beats.text: Jordan is measuring for a listing. Ray the inspector is pointing at a fence, which is his second favorite thing after beams.
Survey says that fence is 14 feet on your sellers' side. Patio, hot tub, string lights. Very nice. On your sellers' land.
Since 2012? That's more than ten years.
Ten years of open, notorious, exclusive, continuous, hostile possession can ripen into title. The neighbor may own that strip now.
I thought fences didn't count anymore.
A fence or a hedge alone is treated as permissive since 2008. A paved patio and a hot tub are not de minimis. That's acting like an owner.

check.q: Under NY's 2008 amendments, which use by itself is treated as permissive, not adverse?
c: Building a garage
Fencing and building a shed and patio together
Paving a patio and installing a hot tub
Planting a hedge
check.x: De minimis non-structural encroachments like hedges, fences, and plantings, plus lawn mowing, are deemed permissive. Substantial structures and exclusive use are different.

beats.text: What if the sellers had given her permission back in 2012?
Then it was never hostile and the clock never started.
Meanwhile, out back, the bay's eaten 6 feet of their lawn since Sandy.
If it went in one storm, that's avulsion and the boundary doesn't move. If it wore away slowly, that's erosion and they lost it.
beats.tag: Avulsion is sudden; erosion is gradual

beats.text: Mr. Russo calls his cousin Sal for advice. Sal tells him to fight. Priya tells him to settle.
Order the survey before you list, not after the buyer's attorney does. Fourteen feet is a price conversation and maybe a lawsuit.

board.prompt: Draw a family tree for someone who dies intestate in NY with a spouse and two children, and show who gets what from a $650,000 estate. Then redo it with no spouse.

facts.text: Voluntary alienation is a deed or will (or dedication); involuntary alienation includes descent, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure, tax sales, partition, adverse possession and erosion.
A public grant is a government transfer of land to a private owner, evidenced by a land patent.
Dedication gives private land to public use by plat or deed and requires the government's acceptance.
A person who dies with a valid will dies testate; without one, intestate.
A devise is a gift of real property by will to a devisee; a bequest or legacy is a gift of personal property.
NY wills are probated in the Surrogate's Court of the county where the decedent lived, which issues letters testamentary to the executor.
A NY will must be written, signed at the end by a testator 18 or older of sound mind, and witnessed by two; holographic and oral wills are valid only for armed forces in wartime and mariners at sea.
Executor means a will; an administrator is appointed by the court through letters of administration when there is no will.
Without a will, property passes by intestate succession to heirs (distributees), and taking real property that way is title by descent.
Under EPTL 4-1.1 a spouse with children takes $50,000 plus half the rest, and the children share the balance.
A spouse with no children takes everything; children with no spouse take everything; then parents, then siblings, then more distant relatives.
With no distributees at all, property escheats to the State of New York; escheat is a government power, not a lien.
Property held as tenants by the entirety passes to the surviving spouse by survivorship, outside intestacy.
The NY adverse possession period is 10 years.
Adverse possession must be hostile under a claim of right (with a reasonable belief since 2008), actual, open and notorious, exclusive and continuous.
Since 2008, de minimis non-structural encroachments (fences, hedges, sheds) and mowing across the line are permissive and cannot alone support adverse possession.
Successive possessors may add their time together (tacking), and the claimant gets record title through a quiet title action.
Accretion is gradual build-up and the owner gains the land; avulsion is sudden and the boundary stays where it was.
Reliction (water receding) adds land to the owner; erosion (gradual wearing away) takes it.
Alluvion is the soil a river deposits by accretion; it belongs to the riparian or littoral owner.
Accession is acquiring title to additions to your property, natural (accretion) or man-made (an abandoned trade fixture).

lessons.title: Title and the Closing Table
lessons.tagline: The closing is where the money, the deed, and the liens all change hands in one room. Recording makes it stick.
objectives: Explain recording acts, race-notice, constructive and actual notice
Define title, marketable title, chain of title, abstract of title, and title search
Explain what owner's and lender's title insurance cover and who pays in NY
Name who attends a NY closing and what each person does, including the licensee's role before closing
Apply RESPA and TRID timing rules

blocks.title: Sold twice
blocks.html: On March 3 a Rochester owner sells a duplex to Buyer A, who takes the deed but forgets to record it. On March 10 the same owner sells it again to Buyer B, who pays full price, knows nothing about Buyer A, and records the deed March 11. Buyer A finally records March 20. Who owns the duplex?
blocks.casual: On March 3, a Rochester owner sells a duplex to Buyer A, who gets the deed but forgets to record it. On March 10, the same owner sells it again to Buyer B, who pays full price, has no clue about Buyer A, and records the deed on March 11. Buyer A finally records on March 20. So who owns the duplex?

deeper.plain: When one property gets sold twice, the law looks at who recorded first and who knew what.
deeper.picture: It's like two people buying the same concert seat; the one who registered the ticket first, without knowing about the other sale, gets the seat.
deeper.street: Buyer A shows up to move in and finds Buyer B's moving truck already there. Buyer A's attorney checks the county clerk's records and realizes B recorded first and had no notice. Buyer A sues the seller for fraud.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who doesn't record promptly can lose the property entirely and be stuck chasing a dishonest seller for money.
deeper.exam: Cue words: sold twice, forgot to record, second buyer had no knowledge. In NY (race-notice), the good faith buyer who records first wins.

blocks.html: Title is ownership itself, the right to possess and use property, and the evidence of it. A deed is the document that transfers title. A title closing (settlement) is the meeting where the transaction is consummated: the buyer pays the balance of the price (usually with a new mortgage plus the buyer's own funds), the seller delivers the deed, existing liens are paid off, and documents are signed for recording.
blocks.casual: Title is ownership itself, meaning the right to possess and use property, plus the proof of it. A deed is the document that moves title from one person to another. A title closing (also called settlement) is the meeting where the deal gets done: the buyer pays the rest of the price (usually a new mortgage plus their own money), the seller hands over the deed, existing liens get paid off, and everyone signs the documents that'll be recorded.

deeper.plain: Closing is when money changes hands and the seller gives the buyer the deed.
deeper.picture: It's like the handshake at the end of a used car deal, except with a room full of lawyers and a stack of papers.
deeper.street: At the Okafors' closing in Downtown Brooklyn, Leo's lender wires $1.2 million, Leo brings his down payment balance, Priya hands over the signed deed, and the old mortgage gets paid off on the spot.
deeper.stakes: If anything is missing at closing (a payoff letter, a signature, funds), the closing gets adjourned, which can cost rate locks and moving dates.
deeper.exam: Title is ownership; the deed is the document. Closing (settlement) is when title transfers and liens are paid.

blocks.html: Buyers want marketable title: title free from reasonable doubt, which a reasonable, informed buyer would accept and could resell. Unpaid liens, a missing heir, an unreleased old mortgage, or an encroachment make title unmarketable. Standard NY contracts require the seller to deliver title that a reputable title company will insure.
blocks.casual: Buyers want marketable title: title free from reasonable doubt, something a reasonable, informed buyer would accept and could turn around and resell. Unpaid liens, a missing heir, an old mortgage that was never released, or an encroachment all make title unmarketable. Standard NY contracts require the seller to deliver title that a reputable title company will insure.

deeper.plain: Marketable title means a buyer could resell it without anyone questioning ownership.
deeper.picture: It's like a used phone that's fully paid off and unlocked: anyone can buy it with no strings.
deeper.street: The title report on a Crown Heights brownstone shows a 1998 mortgage that was paid but never released. Priya tracks down the old bank's successor, gets a satisfaction recorded, and the title becomes marketable.
deeper.stakes: If the seller can't deliver insurable title, the buyer can walk away and get the deposit back, and the agent's commission may disappear.
deeper.exam: Marketable title is free from reasonable doubt. NY contracts typically require title a reputable title company will insure.

blocks.html: Recording acts decide who wins when two people claim the same land. Recording a deed in the public records gives constructive notice to the whole world: everyone is legally presumed to know about it, whether or not they looked. Actual notice is what a person really knows or has been told or has seen.
blocks.casual: Recording acts decide who wins when two people claim the same land. When a deed gets recorded in the public records, that gives constructive notice to the whole world. Everyone is legally presumed to know about it, whether they checked or not. Actual notice is what someone really knows, was told, or saw.

deeper.plain: Once a deed is recorded, the law treats everyone as knowing about it.
deeper.picture: It's like posting something on a public bulletin board: you can't say you didn't know, because it was there for anyone to read.
deeper.street: A buyer in Utica skips the title search and later claims he didn't know about a recorded easement. The court says he had constructive notice because it was in the county records.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who skip title searches are still bound by what's on record, which is why attorneys never skip them.
deeper.exam: Recording creates constructive notice. Actual notice is real knowledge. Both can defeat a later buyer's claim.

blocks.title: New York is a race-notice state (RPL 291)
blocks.html: An unrecorded conveyance is void against a later buyer who pays value, takes without notice of the earlier deed, and records first. In the scenario, Buyer B wins: paid value, had no notice, recorded first. Buyer A's remedy is against the seller.
blocks.casual: Under RPL 291, an unrecorded deed is void against a later buyer who pays value, takes without notice of the earlier deed, and records first. In our scenario, Buyer B wins: paid value, didn't know, recorded first. Buyer A's only move is to go after the seller.

deeper.plain: In New York, you win if you paid, didn't know about an earlier sale, and recorded first.
deeper.picture: It's a race with a rule: you have to cross the finish line first and not have peeked at the other runner's head start.
deeper.street: Buyer A's attorney files a fraud claim against the Rochester seller. Buyer B keeps the duplex. The seller faces possible criminal charges for selling the same property twice.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who delays recording takes a real risk. That's why title companies record right after closing.
deeper.exam: NY is race-notice: good faith (no notice) plus value plus recording first. Pure race and pure notice states are different; don't confuse them.

left.title: Constructive notice
items: Presumed by law
Created by recording
Also by visible possession: you must ask who is living there (inquiry notice)
Applies whether or not you searched

right.title: Actual notice
items: What you actually know
You read the deed, were told, or saw it
A buyer with actual notice of an earlier unrecorded deed loses in NY even if he records first

deeper.plain: Constructive notice is what the law says you should know; actual notice is what you really know.
deeper.picture: Constructive notice is the speed limit sign you drove past without reading. Actual notice is the cop telling you the limit.
deeper.street: A buyer in Jamaica sees a family living in a house but never asks who they are. They hold an unrecorded lease. The buyer is on inquiry notice and takes subject to their rights.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who ignore people living in a property can inherit their claims. Always ask who is in possession.
deeper.exam: Visible possession creates inquiry notice. A buyer with actual notice of an earlier deed loses in NY even if they record first.

blocks.title: Where documents are recorded
blocks.html: Outside NYC, deeds and mortgages are recorded with the county clerk. In Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens they are recorded with the Office of the City Register (NYC Department of Finance) through ACRIS. Staten Island records with the Richmond County Clerk.
blocks.casual: Outside NYC, deeds and mortgages get recorded with the county clerk. In Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens, they're recorded with the Office of the City Register (part of the NYC Department of Finance) through ACRIS. Staten Island records with the Richmond County Clerk.

deeper.plain: NYC uses the City Register for four boroughs; everywhere else uses the county clerk.
deeper.picture: It's like two post offices: one for four boroughs, another for Staten Island and the rest of the state.
deeper.street: Jordan pulls up the Okafors' deed in ACRIS. A week later, for a listing in St. George, Jordan has to search the Richmond County Clerk's records instead.
deeper.stakes: Searching the wrong office can miss documents and lead to a bad title report.
deeper.exam: Know that Staten Island is the exception within NYC. ACRIS covers Manhattan, Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens.
