blocks.q: A tenant has lived in a Bronx two-family for years. The buyer never asked about her and later learns she holds a recorded option to buy. Is the buyer bound?
c: No, the buyer had no actual notice
Only if the broker told him
Yes, recording and the tenant's visible possession gave constructive notice
Only if the option was in the contract
blocks.x: Recording gives constructive notice to everyone. Visible possession also puts a buyer on inquiry notice. Lack of actual knowledge does not help.

items: A title search examines the public records (deeds, mortgages, liens, judgments, lis pendens, taxes, bankruptcies) for the property and its owners.
The chain of title is the unbroken succession of owners from the original grant (often a land patent) to today. A missing link is a gap and clouds the title.

An abstract of title is a condensed written history summarizing every recorded document in the chain. An attorney reads it and gives an opinion of title. In NY practice the title company's title report (certificate of title) does the same job and lists exceptions the buyer must clear.
blocks.casual:
A title search digs through the public records (deeds, mortgages, liens, judgments, lis pendens, taxes, bankruptcies) on the property and its owners.
The chain of title is the unbroken line of owners from the original grant (often a land patent) to today. A missing link is a gap, and it clouds the title.
An abstract of title is a condensed written history that sums up every recorded document in the chain. An attorney reads it and gives an opinion of title. In NY practice, the title company's title report (certificate of title) does the same job and lists the exceptions the buyer has to clear.

deeper.plain: A title search checks the property's history to make sure ownership passed cleanly.
deeper.picture: It's like a family tree for the property: every owner must link to the next with no missing generations.
deeper.street: The title search on a Harlem brownstone finds a 1950s transfer from an estate with no recorded probate. That's a gap. The title company asks for proof of heirship before insuring.
deeper.stakes: Gaps or unresolved liens can block a closing or lead to future lawsuits if missed.
deeper.exam: Chain of title is the history of ownership. An abstract summarizes recorded documents; a title report lists exceptions to clear.

blocks.html: A cloud on title that cannot be cleared by a release or quitclaim may need a quiet title action in court. Common NY fixes at closing: payoff letters for open mortgages, a satisfaction of an old mortgage that was paid but never released, an affidavit that the seller is not the same "John Smith" with a judgment.
blocks.casual: If a cloud on title can't be cleared with a release or quitclaim, it might take a quiet title action in court. Common NY fixes at closing: payoff letters for open mortgages, a satisfaction for an old mortgage that was paid but never released, or an affidavit that the seller isn't the same "John Smith" who has a judgment against him.

deeper.plain: Most title problems get fixed with paperwork at closing; the rest go to court.
deeper.picture: It's like clearing your credit report: most errors get fixed with a letter, but some need a formal dispute.
deeper.street: The title report for a seller named Maria Rodriguez in Washington Heights shows three judgments against people with the same name. She signs a name affidavit confirming she's not those people, and the title company omits them.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring a cloud can stall closings or leave the buyer with an uninsurable title.
deeper.exam: A quiet title action clears a cloud that can't be fixed with a release or quitclaim.

blocks.html: Title insurance protects against loss from title defects that existed before the policy date but were missed or hidden: forged deeds, unknown heirs, errors in the public records, undisclosed spouses, incorrect legal descriptions. It does not cover defects that arise after closing, and it excludes items listed as exceptions in the policy (often survey matters unless a survey was provided).
blocks.casual: Title insurance protects you from losses caused by title defects that already existed before the policy date but got missed or were hidden: forged deeds, unknown heirs, mistakes in the public records, undisclosed spouses, wrong legal descriptions. It doesn't cover problems that pop up after closing, and it excludes anything listed as an exception in the policy (survey matters, often, unless you provided a survey).

deeper.plain: Title insurance covers hidden problems from the past, not new ones after you buy.
deeper.picture: It's like insurance on a used car that covers a hidden accident from before you bought it, not a fender bender you get next week.
deeper.street: Two years after Leo closes, a man claims he's an heir of a prior owner who never signed off. Leo's owner's title policy pays for the lawyer and settles the claim.
deeper.stakes: Without title insurance, a buyer could lose the property or pay huge legal fees to defend it.
deeper.exam: Title insurance covers past defects, not future ones. Exceptions in the policy aren't covered.

head: Owner's policy
Lender's (loan) policy
rows: Loan amount; shrinks as the loan is paid
As long as the owner or heirs hold title
Until the loan is paid off

deeper.plain: The owner's policy protects the buyer; the lender's policy protects the bank.
deeper.picture: Two umbrellas: one for you, one for the bank, both bought at closing.
deeper.street: Leo pays for both policies at closing. When he pays off the mortgage 15 years later, the lender's policy ends, but his owner's policy keeps protecting him and his heirs.
deeper.stakes: Skipping the owner's policy saves money but leaves the buyer exposed.
deeper.exam: Owner's policy covers the purchase price and lasts as long as the owner or heirs hold title. Lender's policy covers the loan amount and ends at payoff.

blocks.title: NY title insurance is rate-regulated
blocks.html: Title premiums in NY are set by filed rate manuals approved by the Department of Financial Services, so every title company charges the same premium for the same coverage. Co-op purchases usually do not get title insurance; the buyer's attorney orders a lien search on the seller and the shares instead.
blocks.casual: In NY, title premiums are set by filed rate manuals that the Department of Financial Services approves, so every title company charges the same premium for the same coverage. Co-op purchases usually don't get title insurance. Instead, the buyer's attorney orders a lien search on the seller and the shares.

deeper.plain: Title insurance prices are fixed by the state, and co-ops use a lien search instead.
deeper.picture: It's like taxi fares set by the city: every cab charges the same meter.
deeper.street: Leo asks if he should shop around for title insurance on his condo. Priya explains that premiums are the same across companies, so he should focus on service. His friend's co-op only needs a lien search.
deeper.stakes: Agents who tell clients to shop for a lower premium give bad advice. Co-op buyers who expect title insurance are confused.
deeper.exam: Title premiums in NY are rate-regulated. Co-ops typically get a lien search, not title insurance.

blocks.q: Two years after closing, a long-lost heir proves a 1990s deed in the chain was forged. Who protects the owner?
c: The owner's title insurance policy
The homeowner's insurance policy
The listing broker's E&O insurance
The lender's title policy
blocks.x: Owner's title insurance covers pre-existing hidden defects like forgery for as long as the owner holds title. The lender's policy protects only the lender. Homeowner's insurance covers physical loss.

blocks.text: Who is at a NY closing

head: Person
Role
rows: Prepares the deed and transfer tax forms, collects payoffs, receives the balance, holds the down payment until closing
Reviews title report and survey, the closing statement, and the loan documents; delivers the funds
Runs the loan side, has the buyer sign the note and mortgage, disburses loan funds
Representative of the title company: collects recording fees and taxes, checks that title exceptions are cleared, records the deed and mortgage
Sign documents; seller signs the deed (may sign in advance or by power of attorney)

deeper.plain: A closing has a cast: two or three attorneys, a title closer, the buyer and seller, and the agents.
deeper.picture: It's like a wedding: each person has a role, and the ceremony doesn't happen until everyone signs.
deeper.street: At Leo's closing, Priya hands over the deed, the bank attorney gets Leo's signature on the note and mortgage, the title closer collects the transfer tax checks, and Jordan and Diane wait for the commission check.
deeper.stakes: If a role is missing, the closing gets pushed. Agents who know who does what can head off delays.
deeper.exam: Seller's attorney prepares the deed and transfer tax forms. Title closer records documents. Lender's attorney handles loan documents.

blocks.html: Downstate closings are usually held at the lender's attorney's office, a title company, or the seller's attorney's office; co-op closings often happen at the managing agent's or lender's attorney's office. Some upstate and many commercial deals close "in escrow" with documents and funds sent to an escrow agent instead of meeting in person.
blocks.casual: Downstate, closings usually happen at the lender's attorney's office, a title company, or the seller's attorney's office. Co-op closings often happen at the managing agent's or the lender's attorney's office. Some upstate deals and lots of commercial ones close "in escrow": documents and money go to an escrow agent instead of everyone meeting in person.

deeper.plain: Closings happen in a lawyer's or title company's office, or by mail through an escrow agent.
deeper.picture: It's like signing a lease in person versus signing everything online and mailing it in.
deeper.street: Leo's closing is at the lender's attorney's office in Midtown. Evelyn's warehouse purchase in Rochester closes in escrow while she's in Florida.
deeper.stakes: Agents who don't know the format can schedule the wrong people or miss deadlines.
deeper.exam: Know that escrow closings don't require the parties to meet. Downstate in-person closings are common.

blocks.text: Your job before and at closing

blocks.title: The licensee's checklist

items.title: Keep the file moving
items.html: Track the mortgage commitment, appraisal, co-op board package, and inspections. Communicate between attorneys and the lender.

items.title: Final walk-through
items.html: Accompany the buyer on the walk-through, usually within 24 hours before closing: confirm the property is vacant (if promised), in the same condition as at contract, and that included fixtures and appliances are there and working.

items.title: Homeowner's insurance
items.html: The lender requires proof of hazard insurance (a binder or paid first-year premium naming the lender) before closing, plus flood insurance if the property is in a FEMA special flood hazard area.

items.title: Commission
items.html: The commission is paid at closing as the listing agreement provides, usually by a check from the seller's proceeds to the broker, never directly to a salesperson. The broker then pays the salesperson.

blocks.casual:
Keep the file moving. Track the mortgage commitment, the appraisal, the co-op board package, and the inspections, and keep the attorneys and lender talking.
Final walk-through. Go with the buyer on the walk-through, usually within 24 hours before closing. Make sure the place is vacant (if that was promised), in the same condition as at contract, and that the included fixtures and appliances are there and working.
Homeowner's insurance. The lender needs proof of hazard insurance (a binder or paid first-year premium naming the lender) before closing, plus flood insurance if the property is in a FEMA special flood hazard area.
Commission. It's paid at closing the way the listing agreement says, usually by a check from the seller's proceeds to the broker, never straight to a salesperson. The broker then pays the salesperson.

deeper.plain: The agent keeps everyone on track, checks the property, makes sure insurance is ready, and gets the commission paid to the broker.
deeper.picture: It's like being a stage manager: you don't perform, but nothing happens without you.
deeper.street: At the Okafors' walk-through, Jordan finds the dishwasher was removed. He calls Priya, who negotiates a $700 credit at closing. Then the commission check goes to Hudson & Hart, and Diane pays Jordan.
deeper.stakes: Missed walk-through issues mean post-closing fights. Accepting a commission check made out to you directly breaks the rules.
deeper.exam: Commission is paid to the broker, never directly to a salesperson. The lender requires proof of hazard insurance, plus flood insurance in a special flood hazard area.

blocks.html: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) applies to federally related mortgage loans on 1 to 4 family residential property (nearly every residential mortgage). It does not cover all-cash deals or commercial loans. Its core rules:
blocks.casual: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) covers federally related mortgage loans on 1 to 4 family residential property, which is pretty much every residential mortgage. It doesn't apply to all-cash deals or commercial loans. Here are its core rules:

deeper.plain: RESPA is a federal law that makes residential mortgage closings transparent and fair.
deeper.picture: It's like a referee at the closing table making sure nobody's slipping money under the table.
deeper.street: Leo's condo loan is covered by RESPA. Evelyn's all-cash purchase of a warehouse isn't, and neither is her commercial loan on a retail strip.
deeper.stakes: Violating RESPA can bring fines, lawsuits, and license trouble for agents who take kickbacks.
deeper.exam: RESPA applies to federally related loans on 1 to 4 family residential property. All-cash and commercial deals are not covered.

items: No kickbacks or referral fees (Section 8) for settlement service business: a broker cannot take money from a title company, lender, or inspector for referrals. Affiliated businesses must be disclosed in writing, and the consumer cannot be required to use them.
Lenders give a Loan Estimate within 3 business days of the loan application.

Borrowers receive the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing (consummation). A change in the APR beyond tolerance, the loan product, or an added prepayment penalty restarts the 3-day clock.
Limits on escrow account cushions and required notices when loan servicing is transferred.
The seller cannot require the buyer to use a particular title insurer.
blocks.casual:
No kickbacks or referral fees (Section 8) for settlement service business. A broker can't take money from a title company, lender, or inspector for sending them clients. Affiliated businesses have to be disclosed in writing, and the consumer can't be forced to use them.
Lenders have to give a Loan Estimate within 3 business days of the loan application.
Borrowers get the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing (consummation). If the APR changes beyond tolerance, the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty gets added, the 3-day clock starts over.
There are limits on escrow account cushions, and required notices when loan servicing gets transferred.
The seller can't require the buyer to use a particular title insurer.

deeper.plain: No kickbacks, early cost estimates, a final cost review 3 days before closing, and the buyer picks the title insurer.
deeper.picture: It's like a restaurant that must show the menu prices up front, can't pay the concierge for sending you in, and can't force you to order the house wine.
deeper.street: Marcus gets offered $250 per referral by a title agency. Diane shuts it down: that's a Section 8 kickback. Meanwhile, Leo's lender changes his loan product two days before closing, so the 3-day clock resets.
deeper.stakes: Kickbacks can bring federal penalties and DOS discipline. Missing the Closing Disclosure timeline delays the closing.
deeper.exam: Loan Estimate within 3 business days of application; Closing Disclosure 3 business days before closing. Section 8 bans kickbacks. Sellers can't require a particular title insurer.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: The HUD-1 settlement statement was replaced for most consumer mortgages in 2015 by the Closing Disclosure (the TRID rule: TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosures). Older questions may still say HUD-1. Same purpose: a line-by-line account of every charge.
blocks.casual: Back in 2015, the HUD-1 settlement statement got replaced for most consumer mortgages by the Closing Disclosure (the TRID rule: TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosures). Older questions may still say HUD-1. Same purpose either way: a line-by-line account of every charge.

deeper.plain: The Closing Disclosure replaced the HUD-1 for most home loans in 2015.
deeper.picture: It's like an old app version being replaced by a new one that does the same job with a cleaner layout.
deeper.street: Diane still has a stack of old HUD-1s from the 2000s. Jordan's closings all use the Closing Disclosure, but an exam question mentions HUD-1, and Jordan knows it's the same idea.
deeper.stakes: Confusing forms can lead to missed deadlines or bad advice to buyers.
deeper.exam: If you see HUD-1, think Closing Disclosure. TRID combines TILA and RESPA disclosures.

blocks.q: Tasha's lender client offers Jordan $250 for every buyer Jordan sends who closes a loan. Under RESPA this is:
c: An illegal kickback for a referral
Legal if under $500
Legal if disclosed to the buyer
Legal because Jordan is not the lender
blocks.x: RESPA Section 8 prohibits any fee or thing of value for referring settlement service business. Disclosure does not cure a referral fee.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: 3 and 3: Loan Estimate within 3 business days after applying, Closing Disclosure 3 business days before closing. Recording = Race won with No notice in NY.
blocks.casual: 3 and 3: Loan Estimate within 3 business days after applying, Closing Disclosure 3 business days before closing. And in NY, recording comes down to this: the Race is won with No notice.

deeper.plain: Two 3-day rules for disclosures, and NY rewards whoever records first without knowing about an earlier sale.
deeper.picture: Picture two stopwatches at 3 days each, and a race where runners have to wear blindfolds.
deeper.street: Jordan writes "3 and 3" on a sticky note on his monitor. Leo, closing on his condo, asks why the bank keeps mentioning 3 days, and Jordan explains it in ten seconds.
deeper.stakes: These numbers come up on nearly every exam and in real closings.
deeper.exam: Race-notice: record first, no notice, pay value. 3 and 3: Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure timelines.

story.title: The Room With All the Pens
story.setting: Downtown Brooklyn, the lender's attorney's conference room

beats.text: Leo's closing on a Prospect Lefferts Gardens condo. Eleven people, one table, forty pens. Leo brought his own pen.
Who are all these people?
Seller's attorney, your attorney Priya, the bank's attorney, the title closer, the seller, the listing agent, and me.
And the title closer does what?
Makes sure every exception on the title report is cleared, collects the taxes and recording fees, and records your deed and mortgage with the City Register.
Why record? I have the deed right here.
New York is race-notice. If the seller sold it twice, whoever records first without notice wins. Recording gives the world constructive notice that it's yours.

check.q: What does recording Leo's deed accomplish?
c: It makes the deed valid between Leo and the seller
It transfers title
It replaces the need for title insurance
It gives constructive notice and protects Leo against later buyers
check.x: Title passed at delivery. Recording protects Leo against later claimants by giving constructive notice under NY's race-notice statute.

beats.text: I'm paying for two title policies?
Lender's policy protects the bank, and they require it. The owner's policy protects you. One premium, covers you as long as you own it.
I got the Closing Disclosure Monday. Today's Friday.
Three business days, as required. You're welcome.
(whispering to Jordan) The title company always sends me a gift card for referrals. You want in?
That's a RESPA kickback, Marcus. No.
Good. The walk-through this morning, the insurance binder, the commission check made out to the firm. That's the job. And never take a gift card from a title company.

board.prompt: Draw the closing table. Put each person in a seat and write one sentence for what they hand over or receive.

facts.text: A title closing is the meeting where the buyer pays the balance, the seller delivers the deed, liens are paid off and documents are signed for recording.
Marketable title is free from reasonable doubt, one a reasonable buyer would accept; NY contracts require title a reputable title company will insure.
Recording acts decide priority between competing claims to the same land.
Recording gives constructive notice to the whole world; actual notice is what a person really knows.
NY is a race-notice state (RPL 291): a later buyer who pays value, has no notice of the earlier deed, and records first wins.
A buyer with actual notice of an earlier unrecorded deed loses even if he records first, and visible possession puts a buyer on inquiry notice.
In Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens, deeds are recorded with the Office of the City Register (ACRIS); Staten Island and the rest of the state use the county clerk.
A title search examines the public records for the property and its owners.
The chain of title is the unbroken succession of owners from the original grant; a missing link clouds the title.
An abstract of title is a condensed history of every recorded document; in NY the title company's title report lists exceptions the buyer must clear.
A cloud not cleared by a release or quitclaim may need a quiet title action; common closing fixes are payoff letters, satisfactions of old mortgages and same-name affidavits.
Title insurance covers defects that existed before the policy date (forgery, unknown heirs, record errors), not defects arising after closing or listed exceptions.
An owner's policy protects the buyer for the price as long as they own; a lender's policy protects the lender for the loan amount until it is paid; the NY buyer pays for both.
NY title premiums are set by filed rate manuals approved by DFS, and co-op purchases usually get a lien search instead of title insurance.
At a NY closing the seller's attorney prepares the deed and transfer tax forms, the lender's attorney runs the loan, and the title closer collects fees and records the documents.
Before closing the licensee keeps the file moving and accompanies the buyer on the final walk-through, usually within 24 hours of closing.
The lender requires proof of hazard insurance before closing, plus flood insurance in a FEMA special flood hazard area.
The commission is paid to the broker at closing, never directly to a salesperson; the broker pays the salesperson.
RESPA applies to federally related mortgage loans on 1 to 4 family homes, not to all-cash deals or commercial loans.
RESPA Section 8 bans kickbacks and referral fees for settlement services; affiliated businesses must be disclosed, and the seller cannot require a particular title insurer.
The Loan Estimate comes within 3 business days of application and the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing; certain changes restart the clock.
Since 2015 the Closing Disclosure (TRID) has replaced the HUD-1 for most consumer mortgages.

lessons.title: Closing Costs, Transfer Taxes, and Prorations
lessons.tagline: Who pays what, how much, and the day-count math that splits the bills.
objectives: Sort seller and buyer closing costs in NY, including co-op and condo extras
Calculate NYS transfer tax, NYC RPTT, the mansion tax, and mortgage recording tax
Read a closing statement as debits and credits and reconcile cash due
Prorate taxes, rent, fuel, and water using 365-day and 360-day methods, and transfer security deposits

blocks.title: The Okafors' net sheet
blocks.html: The Okafors accept $2,150,000 for their Bed-Stuy two-family. The buyer is borrowing $1,500,000. Grace asks Jordan, "After all the taxes and fees, what do we actually walk away with? And why does the buyer pay a tax with the word mansion in it? It's a brownstone."
blocks.casual: The Okafors take an offer of $2,150,000 for their Bed-Stuy two-family. The buyer's borrowing $1,500,000. Grace asks Jordan, "After all the taxes and fees, what do we actually walk away with? And why is the buyer paying a tax called mansion? It's a brownstone."

deeper.plain: Sellers and buyers each pay their own set of taxes and fees at closing, and the names can be misleading.
deeper.picture: It's like a restaurant bill with tax, tip, and service charges split between two people, each with their own line items.
deeper.street: Jordan sits down at the Okafors' kitchen table with a calculator. By the end, Grace understands why about $39,000 of transfer taxes come out of her side, and why the buyer pays over $55,000 in mansion and mortgage recording taxes.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who aren't warned about closing costs feel blindsided and blame the agent. Buyers who underestimate costs can come up short at closing.
deeper.exam: Expect a question asking who pays which tax: transfer taxes are the seller's; mansion tax and mortgage recording tax are the buyer's.

head: Seller usually pays
Buyer usually pays
rows: NYC RPTT (in NYC) or local transfer tax (a few localities)
Payoff of existing mortgages and liens
Bank fees: application, origination, points, appraisal, credit report
Recording fees for satisfactions and documents to clear title
Recording fees for the deed and mortgage
Co-op: flip tax (if the building has one), managing agent fees, stock transfer fees
Condo: managing agent and right of first refusal waiver fees
Mortgage insurance (PMI) and prepaid escrow for taxes and insurance
Co-op: lien search, recognition agreement fee, move-in deposit. Condo: prepaid common charges, sometimes a working capital contribution

deeper.plain: Sellers pay transfer taxes, the commission, and payoffs. Buyers pay the mansion tax, mortgage recording tax, title insurance, and loan fees.
deeper.picture: Think of a moving day: the person leaving pays to clear out and settle old bills; the person arriving pays to move in and set up new accounts.
deeper.street: Leo buys a condo in Long Island City. His closing costs include the mortgage recording tax, title insurance, bank fees, and a working capital contribution. The seller pays the NYS transfer tax, NYC RPTT, and the commission.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up who pays what in a net sheet can blow up a negotiation or leave a client short at closing.
deeper.exam: Know the default split. Seller: transfer taxes, commission, payoffs. Buyer: mansion tax, mortgage recording tax, title insurance, loan costs.

blocks.html: A flip tax is a transfer fee some co-ops (and a few condos) charge on a sale, usually paid by the seller: often 1% to 3% of the price or a dollar amount per share. It is a building rule in the bylaws or proprietary lease, not a government tax.
blocks.casual: A flip tax is a transfer fee some co-ops (and a few condos) charge when a unit sells, usually paid by the seller. It's often 1% to 3% of the price, or a dollar amount per share. It's a building rule in the bylaws or proprietary lease, not a government tax.

deeper.plain: A flip tax is a fee the building charges when you sell, and it's usually on the seller.
deeper.picture: It's like a club exit fee: you pay the club when you leave so it can keep the lights on.
deeper.street: A seller in a Park Slope co-op sells for $900,000 and owes a 2% flip tax to the building: $18,000. Jordan included it in the net sheet, so there are no surprises.
deeper.stakes: Agents who forget the flip tax misstate the seller's net and can lose the client's trust.
deeper.exam: A flip tax is a building fee, not a government tax, and usually paid by the seller.

blocks.title: New construction twist
blocks.html: In NYC sponsor (new development) sales, the contract often shifts the seller's transfer taxes to the buyer. Because the buyer is paying a tax that is legally the seller's, the payment counts as extra consideration and is grossed up. Always read who pays in the offering plan and contract.
blocks.casual: In NYC sponsor sales (new development), the contract often shifts the seller's transfer taxes onto the buyer. Since the buyer is paying a tax that legally belongs to the seller, that payment counts as extra consideration and gets grossed up. Always check the offering plan and contract to see who's paying.

deeper.plain: In new construction, buyers often pay the seller's transfer taxes, and that payment gets taxed too.
deeper.picture: It's like covering a friend's tip and having the restaurant charge tax on the tip too.
deeper.street: Leo looks at a new development in Greenpoint. The contract says he pays the NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT. Because those payments count as extra price, the taxes are computed on a higher number.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who miss this clause can owe tens of thousands more at closing than they budgeted.
deeper.exam: In sponsor sales, the buyer often pays the seller's transfer taxes. That payment is treated as additional consideration and grossed up.

head: Tax
Who pays
Rate
rows: NYS real estate transfer tax
$2 per $500 of consideration (0.4%), each fraction of $500 counts as a full $500. In NYC: 0.65% for residential $3M+ and other property $2M+
NYC Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT)
1 to 3 family, condo, co-op: 1% if $500,000 or less; 1.425% if over $500,000. Other property: 1.425% if $500,000 or less; 2.625% above
Residential $1M or more. Outside NYC: 1%. In NYC: graduated from 1% ($1M to under $2M) up to 3.9% ($25M+)
Borrower (lender pays 0.25% on 1 to 6 family homes)

NYC 1 to 3 family/condo: borrower 1.8% under $500,000 loan, 1.925% at $500,000+. MCTD suburbs (Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester, and others): 1.05% total. Most upstate counties: about 1% total. Co-op share loans: none
blocks.caption: Rates apply to the full amount, not just the part above a threshold

deeper.plain: Four taxes: two for the seller (state transfer tax, NYC RPTT) and two for the buyer (mansion tax, mortgage recording tax).
deeper.picture: It's like a toll road where each car pays a different toll depending on which way it's going.
deeper.street: A Brooklyn condo sells for $800,000 with a $600,000 loan. Seller: $3,200 NYS tax and $11,400 RPTT. Buyer: no mansion tax (under $1M) and $11,550 mortgage recording tax at 1.925%.
deeper.stakes: Getting the rate wrong in a net sheet throws off a seller's expectations or a buyer's cash to close.
deeper.exam: Rates apply to the full price, not just the amount over a threshold. Co-op share loans have no mortgage recording tax.

blocks.title: NYC mansion tax brackets
blocks.html: $1M to under $2M: 1%. $2M to under $3M: 1.25%. $3M to under $5M: 1.5%. $5M to under $10M: 2.25%. $10M to under $15M: 3.25%. $15M to under $20M: 3.5%. $20M to under $25M: 3.75%. $25M and up: 3.9%. The rate applies to the whole price.
blocks.casual: Here are the NYC mansion tax brackets. $1M to under $2M: 1%. $2M to under $3M: 1.25%. $3M to under $5M: 1.5%. $5M to under $10M: 2.25%. $10M to under $15M: 3.25%. $15M to under $20M: 3.5%. $20M to under $25M: 3.75%. $25M and up: 3.9%. And the rate hits the whole price.

deeper.plain: In NYC, the mansion tax gets bigger as the price goes up, and the rate applies to the whole price.
deeper.picture: It's like a gym where the monthly fee jumps at certain tiers, and once you're in a tier, the whole fee is at that rate.
deeper.street: A buyer pays $3,050,000 for a Tribeca loft. That's in the 1.5% bracket, so the mansion tax is $45,750 on the whole price, not just the amount over $3M.
deeper.stakes: Buyers near a bracket line sometimes negotiate the price down to save thousands in mansion tax.
deeper.exam: Mansion tax is a cliff, not a marginal rate. Know the first two NYC brackets: 1% under $2M, 1.25% from $2M to under $3M.

blocks.caption: Enter a price, location, property type, and loan amount. Watch which taxes land on the seller's side and which on the buyer's, and how crossing $500,000, $1M, or $3M changes the rate.

blocks.title: Worked example: the Okafors' sale ($2,150,000, Brooklyn two-family, $1,500,000 loan)
blocks.html:
Seller
NYS transfer tax: under $3M, so 0.4%. $2,150,000 x 0.004 = $8,600 (check: 4,300 units of $500 x $2).
NYC RPTT: over $500,000, so 1.425% of the whole price. $2,150,000 x 0.01425 = $30,637.50.
Seller's transfer taxes: $39,237.50.
Buyer
Mansion tax: $2M to under $3M bracket, 1.25%. $2,150,000 x 0.0125 = $26,875.
Mortgage recording tax: loan $500,000+, borrower rate 1.925%. $1,500,000 x 0.01925 = $28,875.
blocks.casual:
Seller side
NYS transfer tax: under $3M, so 0.4%. $2,150,000 x 0.004 = $8,600 (check: 4,300 units of $500 x $2).
NYC RPTT: over $500,000, so 1.425% of the whole price. $2,150,000 x 0.01425 = $30,637.50.
Total seller transfer taxes: $39,237.50.
Buyer side
Mansion tax: the $2M to under $3M bracket, so 1.25%. $2,150,000 x 0.0125 = $26,875.
Mortgage recording tax: the loan is $500,000+, so the borrower rate is 1.925%. $1,500,000 x 0.01925 = $28,875.

deeper.plain: The Okafors owe about $39,000 in transfer taxes; their buyer owes about $55,750 in mansion and mortgage recording taxes.
deeper.picture: Think of two receipts printed at closing: one for the sellers, one for the buyer, each with its own tax lines.
deeper.street: Grace sees the $39,237.50 and sighs. Jordan reminds her it's 1.825% of the price, and that her buyer is paying even more in taxes. She relaxes a bit.
deeper.stakes: Wrong math on a net sheet means a seller expects more cash than they'll get, which can sour the deal.
deeper.exam: Expect a calculation using these rates. Apply each rate to the full amount. Mortgage recording tax uses the loan amount, not the price.

blocks.title: Worked example: fractions of $500 (upstate)
blocks.html:
A house in Schenectady sells for $412,300.
1. $412,300 / $500 = 824.6 units.
2. Any fraction counts as a full unit: 825 units.
3. 825 x $2 = $1,650 NYS transfer tax, paid by the seller. No mansion tax (under $1M).
blocks.casual:
A house in Schenectady sells for $412,300.
First, divide by $500: $412,300 / $500 = 824.6 units.
Any fraction counts as a full unit, so that's 825 units.
825 x $2 = $1,650 in NYS transfer tax, paid by the seller. No mansion tax, since it's under $1M.

deeper.plain: Divide the price by $500, round up, and multiply by $2.
deeper.picture: It's like paying for parking by the hour: 10 minutes into the next hour still costs a full hour.
deeper.street: A seller in Schenectady expects to pay $1,649.20 using 0.4%. The attorney explains that the fraction rounds up to a full unit, so it's $1,650.
deeper.stakes: The difference is small, but getting it wrong on a tax return or exam shows you don't know the rule.
deeper.exam: Expect a stem where the price doesn't divide evenly by $500. Round up to the next whole unit.

blocks.title: Exam traps
blocks.html: Mansion tax is the buyer's; transfer tax is the seller's. A $999,999 purchase owes no mansion tax; $1,000,000 owes $10,000 (a cliff, not a marginal rate). Co-op share loans are not mortgages, so they owe no mortgage recording tax, but co-op sales still owe transfer taxes and the mansion tax.
blocks.casual: Mansion tax is on the buyer; transfer tax is on the seller. Buy at $999,999 and you owe no mansion tax. Buy at $1,000,000 and you owe $10,000. It's a cliff, not a marginal rate. Co-op share loans aren't mortgages, so they don't owe mortgage recording tax. But co-op sales still owe transfer taxes and the mansion tax.

deeper.plain: Buyer pays mansion tax, seller pays transfer tax, and co-ops still get hit with transfer and mansion taxes.
deeper.picture: The mansion tax is a cliff edge: step one dollar over and you fall the whole way.
deeper.street: A buyer in Riverdale negotiates a co-op down from $1,010,000 to $995,000. By dropping under $1M, she saves $10,100 in mansion tax.
deeper.stakes: Buyers near $1M often negotiate to stay under the line. Agents who don't flag it leave money on the table.
deeper.exam: Watch for co-op questions: no mortgage recording tax, but transfer taxes and mansion tax still apply.

blocks.q: A buyer pays $1,250,000 for a single-family home in Westchester. How much mansion tax is due and who pays it?
c: $12,500, paid by the buyer
$12,500, paid by the seller
$2,500, paid by the buyer on the amount over $1M
$5,000, paid by the buyer
blocks.x: Outside NYC the mansion tax is a flat 1% of the entire price for residential purchases of $1M or more, paid by the grantee. 1% x $1,250,000 = $12,500.

blocks.html: A closing statement lists every amount each party pays or receives. Each party has two columns. A debit is a charge: money that party owes. A credit is money that party receives or is credited with. Reconciliation balances it: the buyer's debits minus credits equals the cash the buyer brings; the seller's credits minus debits equals the seller's net proceeds.
blocks.casual: A closing statement lists every dollar each party pays or receives. Each party gets two columns. A debit is a charge, money that party owes. A credit is money that party gets or is credited with. Reconciliation balances it all out: the buyer's debits minus credits equals the cash the buyer brings to closing, and the seller's credits minus debits equals what the seller walks away with.

deeper.plain: Debits are what you owe; credits are what you get. Subtract to find what each side brings or takes home.
deeper.picture: It's like splitting a group trip: track who owes what and who paid what, then settle up at the end.
deeper.street: On the Okafors' closing statement, the price is a credit to them and a debit to the buyer. Their mortgage payoff and transfer taxes are debits. Subtract and you get their net proceeds.
deeper.stakes: Agents who can't read a closing statement can't catch mistakes like a missing credit or double charge.
deeper.exam: The purchase price is a buyer debit and a seller credit. Debits are charges; credits are amounts received.

blocks.caption: Drag each item onto the buyer and seller columns. Watch which items hit both parties (prorations, price) and which hit only one (down payment, commission, loan).

head: Item
Buyer
Seller
rows: No entry (already part of the price)
Rent collected in advance by seller (buyer's share)
Mansion tax, mortgage recording tax, title insurance

deeper.plain: Each line on a closing statement hits one side, the other, or both, and you need to know which.
deeper.picture: It's like a seesaw: when one side gets a credit, the other often takes a debit of the same amount.
deeper.street: When Sal sells his 6-unit, the tenant security deposits show as a debit to Sal and a credit to the buyer. The buyer now holds those deposits for the tenants.
deeper.stakes: Getting an entry backward flips the money and can cost thousands for one party at closing.
deeper.exam: Prorations hit both sides. Items like commissions and transfer taxes hit only the seller; mansion tax and title insurance hit only the buyer.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Prorations are always a double entry: debit one party, credit the other, same amount. If the seller prepaid, the buyer pays the seller back (credit seller). If the seller owes (arrears) or collected in advance, the seller pays the buyer (credit buyer).
blocks.casual: Prorations are always a double entry: debit one side, credit the other, same amount. If the seller prepaid, the buyer pays the seller back (credit the seller). If the seller owes (arrears) or collected in advance, the seller pays the buyer (credit the buyer).

deeper.plain: Every proration moves the same amount from one side to the other.
deeper.picture: It's like Venmo: one person sends, the other receives, and the amount matches.
deeper.street: The Okafors prepaid their property taxes through December. The buyer reimburses them for the days after closing: credit seller, debit buyer.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up the direction reverses the money and can cause a closing statement to be wrong by thousands.
deeper.exam: Prepaid by seller: credit seller. Unpaid or collected in advance by seller: credit buyer.

blocks.html: Proration (in NY usually called adjustments or apportionments) divides expenses and income between buyer and seller by the days each owns the property. Commonly prorated: real estate taxes and assessments, water and sewer charges, fuel oil, rents, co-op maintenance or condo common charges, and sometimes insurance if the buyer takes over the policy.
blocks.casual: Proration (in NY you'll mostly hear adjustments or apportionments) splits expenses and income between buyer and seller based on how many days each one owns the property. Things that usually get prorated: real estate taxes and assessments, water and sewer charges, fuel oil, rents, co-op maintenance or condo common charges, and sometimes insurance if the buyer takes over the policy.

deeper.plain: Each side pays for the days they own the property, and the closing statement evens it out.
deeper.picture: It's like splitting a monthly phone bill when a roommate moves out halfway through the month.
deeper.street: Leo closes on a condo on the 15th. The seller already paid the month's common charges, so Leo reimburses the seller for the days from the 15th on.
deeper.stakes: Missed or miscalculated adjustments shift real money from one party to the other, and someone ends up chasing it after closing.
deeper.exam: NY calls prorations adjustments. Common items: taxes, water, fuel oil, rents, maintenance, and common charges.

blocks.title: Prorate anything in five steps

items.title: 1. Find the period
items.html: What period does the bill cover? (NYC property taxes: July 1 to June 30. Many upstate town and county taxes: the calendar year. School taxes: July 1 to June 30.)

items.title: 2. Paid or unpaid?
items.html: Prepaid by seller: buyer reimburses seller for buyer's days. Unpaid (in arrears): seller credits buyer for seller's days.

items.title: 3. Who owns closing day?
items.html: NY standard contracts apportion as of midnight before closing, so the buyer owns the closing day. On the exam, follow whatever the question says.

items.title: 4. Daily rate
items.html: Actual-day method: annual / 365 (or monthly / days in that month). Statutory method: annual / 360, every month 30 days.

items.title: 5. Multiply and enter
items.html: Daily rate x the days owed. Debit the paying party, credit the other.

blocks.casual:
Step 1, find the period. What stretch does the bill cover? NYC property taxes run July 1 to June 30. Lots of upstate town and county taxes run on the calendar year. School taxes run July 1 to June 30.
Step 2, paid or unpaid? If the seller prepaid, the buyer reimburses the seller for the buyer's days. If it's unpaid (in arrears), the seller credits the buyer for the seller's days.
Step 3, who owns closing day? NY standard contracts apportion as of midnight before closing, so the buyer owns closing day. On the exam, go with whatever the question says.
Step 4, daily rate. Actual-day method: annual / 365 (or monthly / days in that month). Statutory method: annual / 360, with every month counted as 30 days.
Step 5, multiply and enter. Daily rate x the days owed. Debit the side that pays, credit the other.

deeper.plain: Figure out the period, who paid, who owns closing day, the daily rate, then multiply and enter.
deeper.picture: It's like a recipe with five steps. Skip one and the cake falls.
deeper.street: Jordan prorates the Okafors' water bill: quarterly, unpaid, closing on the 20th, buyer owns closing day. Daily rate times the seller's days, then debit seller, credit buyer.
deeper.stakes: A wrong step, like using 365 when the question says 360, gives the wrong answer and costs exam points.
deeper.exam: Read the stem for who owns the closing day and which day count to use. Default NY practice: buyer owns closing day.

blocks.caption: Slide the closing date and switch between 365-day and 360-day methods. Notice who gets the credit when taxes are paid in advance versus in arrears.

blocks.title: Taxes paid in advance, 365-day method (NYC)
blocks.html:
Annual tax $6,480; NYC fiscal year July 1 to June 30. The seller paid the first half ($3,240) covering July 1 to December 31. Closing is October 15; buyer owns closing day.
1. Buyer's days in the paid period: October 15 to 31 (17) + November (30) + December (31) = 78 days.
2. Daily rate: $6,480 / 365 = $17.7534.
3. 78 x $17.7534 = $1,384.77.
Entry: credit seller, debit buyer $1,384.77. (Check: seller's 106 days + buyer's 78 days = 184 days in the half year.)
blocks.casual:
Annual tax is $6,480, and NYC's fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30. The seller paid the first half ($3,240), covering July 1 to December 31. Closing is October 15, and the buyer owns closing day.
First, count the buyer's days in the paid period: October 15 to 31 (17) + November (30) + December (31) = 78 days.
Daily rate: $6,480 / 365 = $17.7534.
Then 78 x $17.7534 = $1,384.77.
Entry: credit seller, debit buyer $1,384.77. (Double-check: seller's 106 days + buyer's 78 days = 184 days in the half year.)

deeper.plain: The seller prepaid through December, so the buyer pays back the seller for 78 days.
deeper.picture: It's like a friend who prepaid a six-month gym membership and you take it over in October: you pay them back for the remaining months.
deeper.street: On the Okafors' closing statement, Priya lists $1,384.77 as a credit to the Okafors. The buyer's attorney checks the math and agrees.
deeper.stakes: A wrong day count can cost one side a few hundred dollars and trigger a dispute at the closing table.
deeper.exam: Count days carefully, including the closing day if the buyer owns it. Use 365 if the question says actual days.

blocks.title: Taxes unpaid, 360-day method (exam style)
blocks.html:
Annual taxes of $4,320 for the calendar year are unpaid. Closing is April 20, and the seller owns the day of closing.
1. Seller's days: January, February, March (3 x 30 = 90) + 20 days of April = 110 days.
2. Daily rate: $4,320 / 360 = $12.
3. 110 x $12 = $1,320.
Entry: debit seller, credit buyer $1,320, because the buyer will pay the whole year's bill later.
blocks.casual:
Annual taxes of $4,320 for the calendar year haven't been paid. Closing is April 20, and this time the seller owns the day of closing.
Seller's days: January, February, March (3 x 30 = 90) + 20 days of April = 110 days.
Daily rate: $4,320 / 360 = $12.
Then 110 x $12 = $1,320.
Entry: debit seller, credit buyer $1,320, since the buyer is going to pay the whole year's bill later.

deeper.plain: The seller hasn't paid, so the seller credits the buyer for the days the seller owned it.
deeper.picture: It's like leaving an apartment without paying your share of the utility bill: you hand your roommate cash for your days.
deeper.street: A seller in Buffalo hasn't paid the year's county taxes by an April closing. The buyer will get the bill, so the seller credits the buyer $1,320 at the table.
deeper.stakes: If the credit is missed, the buyer ends up paying the seller's share of taxes.
deeper.exam: Arrears equals debit seller, credit buyer. Statutory method: 30-day months, 360-day year. Check who owns closing day in the stem.

blocks.title: Rent, deposits, and fuel (Sal's 6-unit in Astoria)
blocks.html:
Closing November 10, buyer owns closing day. Sal collected November rents of $10,250 (five occupied units; 1B is vacant) on November 1.
1. Buyer's days: November 10 to 30 = 21 days. Daily rent: $10,250 / 30 = $341.67.
2. $10,250 x 21 / 30 = $7,175: debit seller, credit buyer.
3. Security deposits of $8,750 are transferred: debit seller, credit buyer $8,750 (NY requires the seller to turn deposits over to the buyer and notify tenants).
4. Oil in the tank: 210 gallons at $3.80 = $798: credit seller, debit buyer.
5. Water and sewer: read the meter on or just before closing; the seller pays (debit seller) for usage up to the reading.
blocks.casual:
Closing is November 10, and the buyer owns closing day. Sal collected $10,250 in November rents from the five occupied units on November 1.
Buyer's days: November 10 to 30 = 21 days. Daily rent: $10,250 / 30 = $341.67.
$10,250 x 21 / 30 = $7,175: debit seller, credit buyer.
Security deposits of $8,750 get handed over: debit seller, credit buyer $8,750 (NY requires the seller to turn deposits over to the buyer and notify the tenants).
Oil in the tank: 210 gallons at $3.80 = $798: credit seller, debit buyer.
Water and sewer: read the meter on or right before closing, and the seller pays (debit seller) for usage up to that reading.

deeper.plain: Sal gives back rent and deposits for the buyer's days and tenants, and the buyer pays Sal for the oil he left.
deeper.picture: It's like selling a car with a full tank and prepaid parking: the buyer pays you for the gas, and you hand over the parking refund.
deeper.street: At Sal's closing, the buyer's attorney insists on a rent roll and deposit list. Sal tries to keep the deposits, but Priya explains he must turn them over and notify tenants by registered or certified mail.
deeper.stakes: A seller who keeps tenant deposits remains liable to tenants, and the buyer faces angry tenants at move-out.
deeper.exam: Rent collected in advance: credit buyer. Security deposits: credit buyer. Fuel oil left: credit seller.

blocks.q: The seller prepaid a $2,400 annual water and sewer charge for the calendar year. Closing is July 1, and the buyer owns closing day. Using a 360-day year, what is the proration entry?
c: Credit seller, debit buyer $1,200
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,200
Credit seller, debit buyer $1,000
No entry, water is not prorated
blocks.x: The seller paid for the full year, so the buyer reimburses the seller for July 1 to December 31: 6 months x $200 = $1,200. Credit seller, debit buyer.

blocks.q: On a closing statement, the buyer's new $600,000 mortgage loan appears as:
c: A debit to the buyer
A credit to the seller
A debit to the seller
A credit to the buyer
blocks.x: The loan is a source of the buyer's funds, so it is credited to the buyer. It does not appear on the seller's side at all.

blocks.title: Field tip
blocks.html: Give sellers a net sheet at the listing appointment: price minus commission, transfer taxes, attorney fees, payoffs, and expected adjustments. In NYC, a seller of a $1.2M condo pays about 1.825% in transfer taxes alone (0.4% + 1.425%). Surprises at the closing table kill trust.
blocks.casual: Hand sellers a net sheet at the listing appointment: price minus commission, transfer taxes, attorney fees, payoffs, and expected adjustments. In NYC, a seller of a $1.2M condo pays about 1.825% in transfer taxes alone (0.4% + 1.425%). Surprises at the closing table kill trust.

deeper.plain: Show sellers what they'll actually net before they list.
deeper.picture: It's like showing someone the full price with tax and fees before they order, not after.
deeper.street: Jordan shows a Long Island City condo seller a net sheet: $1,200,000 price, $21,900 in transfer taxes, commission, attorney fees, and a $640,000 payoff. The seller adjusts the asking price with eyes open.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who are surprised at closing blame the agent, may refuse to close, or leave bad reviews.
deeper.exam: The exam may ask what a net sheet shows or which costs reduce the seller's proceeds. Transfer taxes and commission are seller costs.

story.title: The Mansion Tax on a Brownstone
story.setting: Bed-Stuy, the Okafors' parlor floor, the night after contracts were signed

beats.text: Jordan brings a printed net sheet. Emmanuel brings reading glasses and a calculator from 1991.
Two million one fifty. What comes off the top?
Two transfer taxes, both yours as sellers. New York State at 0.4% is $8,600. New York City RPTT at 1.425% is $30,637.50.
beats.tag: Seller pays NYS and NYC transfer taxes

beats.text: One point four two five. On the whole price?
On the whole price. It's not a bracket that only hits the part over $500,000.
And the mansion tax Grace keeps asking about?
That's the buyer's. Any residential purchase of a million or more. At $2.15 million in the city it's 1.25%, so $26,875 for them.

check.q: Who pays the mansion tax on the Okafors' sale and how much?
c: The buyer, $26,875
The Okafors, $21,500
The buyer, $21,500
Split evenly, $13,437.50 each
check.x: The mansion tax is the grantee's. NYC's $2M to under $3M bracket is 1.25%: $2,150,000 x 0.0125 = $26,875.

beats.text: We paid the first half of this year's property taxes in July. Do we lose that?
(on speaker) No. You get credited for the days after closing. The buyer reimburses you. It's an adjustment.
And the tenant upstairs paid October rent on the first.
Then you credit the buyer for the days after closing, and hand over her security deposit too.
beats.tag: Prepaid rent and deposits: credit buyer

beats.text: Emmanuel taps the calculator, frowns, taps again, and finally smiles.
Still more than we paid in 1997. By a little.
Net sheets at the first meeting, not the last. Sellers forgive a big number they saw coming. They never forgive a small one they didn't.

board.prompt: Build a two-column closing ledger for a $900,000 Queens sale closing September 15. Enter price, $180,000 down payment, $720,000 loan, a prepaid tax adjustment, commission, and transfer taxes. Reconcile cash due from the buyer.

facts.text: The seller pays the NYS transfer tax (and NYC RPTT); the buyer pays the mansion tax and the mortgage recording tax.
Buyers usually pay title insurance, lender fees, inspections and deed and mortgage recording fees; sellers pay the commission, payoffs and their attorney.
A flip tax is a co-op building's transfer fee set by its bylaws or proprietary lease, usually paid by the seller, not a government tax.
In NYC sponsor sales the contract often shifts the seller's transfer taxes to the buyer, and that payment is grossed up as extra consideration.
The NYS transfer tax is $2 per $500 of consideration (0.4%), and any fraction of $500 counts as a full $500.
In NYC the NYS transfer tax rises to 0.65% for residential sales of $3M or more (other property $2M or more).
NYC RPTT on 1 to 3 family homes, condos and co-ops is 1% at $500,000 or less and 1.425% above, applied to the whole price.
The mansion tax is the buyer's 1% (outside NYC) on residential purchases of $1M or more, on the whole price: $999,999 owes nothing, $1,000,000 owes $10,000.
The NYC mansion tax is graduated from 1% ($1M to under $2M) up to 3.9% ($25M and up), and the bracket rate applies to the whole price.
Mortgage recording tax in NYC on 1 to 3 family homes and condos is 1.8% for the borrower on loans under $500,000 and 1.925% at $500,000 or more.
Co-op share loans are not mortgages and owe no mortgage recording tax, but co-op sales still owe transfer taxes and the mansion tax.
A NYC seller of a home priced over $500,000 and under $3M pays 1.825% in transfer taxes (0.4% state plus 1.425% city).
On a closing statement a debit is a charge to that party and a credit is money received; the price is a debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller.
Buyer's debits minus credits equals the cash the buyer brings; seller's credits minus debits equals the seller's net proceeds.
Single-entry items: the down payment and new loan credit only the buyer; a paid-off mortgage, commission and transfer taxes debit only the seller.
Taxes the seller prepaid are prorated as a credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer for the buyer's days.
Unpaid taxes in arrears are prorated as a debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer for the seller's days.
Proration (NY adjustments or apportionments) divides taxes, assessments, water, fuel, rents and maintenance by the days each party owns.
NY standard contracts apportion as of midnight before closing, so the buyer owns the closing day unless a question says otherwise.
The actual-day method divides by 365 (or the month's days); the statutory method divides by 360 with 30-day months.
Rent the seller collected in advance is a debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer for the buyer's days.
Tenant security deposits are a debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer, and NY requires them turned over with notice to tenants.
Fuel oil left in the tank is a credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer.
Water and sewer charges are settled by a meter reading at or just before closing, with the seller paying for usage up to the reading.
NYC property and school taxes run July 1 to June 30; many upstate town and county taxes run on the calendar year.

lessons.title: Case file: The House Rosa Kept for Life
lessons.tagline: Rosa Bianchi wants to sell "her" Staten Island two-family. Her 2012 deed says she owns far less than she thinks.
objectives: Decide who must sign a listing and a deed when one person holds a life estate and others hold the remainder.
Apply the rules on waste, leases, and merger to a life tenant who wants to sell, rent, or give up her interest.
Calculate how sale proceeds split between a life tenant and remaindermen from an actuarial factor.
Classify the leasehold and freehold interests in a family property, including a fee on condition that may have expired.

blocks.title: A call from Westerleigh
blocks.html: Rosa Bianchi is 84 and has lived in her detached two-family on a quiet block in Westerleigh, Staten Island, since 1971. She calls Hudson & Hart because her friend's grandson sold a house with Jordan. "I want to list my house and move near my daughter's family," she says. "It's mine, it's paid off, and I'd like it on the market by spring." Before the listing appointment, Jordan pulls the last deed from ACRIS. It is dated March 2012 and runs from Rosa Bianchi to her two children, Paul Bianchi and Gina Ferraro, "reserving unto the grantor a life estate in the premises." Rosa's upstairs tenant, a nurse named Kwame Osei, has rented there since 2019. Jordan now has to decide who the client actually is.

Rosa's estate planning attorney did what many New York families do: Rosa deeded the house to her children years ago but kept the right to live there for the rest of her life. That split the ownership into two pieces. Rosa holds a life estate, a freehold estate measured by her own life. Paul and Gina hold the remainder: the fee simple that becomes theirs in possession the moment Rosa dies. Nobody in this family owns the whole fee simple alone. Rosa feels like the owner because she pays the taxes, lives downstairs, and collects Kwame's rent. Legally, the deed she signed in 2012 is the one that controls.

blocks.title: Deed abstract, Richmond County (from ACRIS)
blocks.html:
Document type: Deed (bargain and sale with covenant)
Recorded: March 2012
Grantor: Rosa Bianchi
Grantees: Paul Bianchi and Gina Ferraro
Consideration: $10.00 and love and affection
Habendum excerpt: "...to have and to hold unto the parties of the second part, their heirs and assigns forever, reserving unto the grantor, ROSA BIANCHI, a life estate in the premises for and during the term of her natural life."
Notes: Deed silent on the form of co-ownership between the grantees.

blocks.q: Rosa wants to sign an exclusive right to sell listing for the whole house in fee simple. Whose signatures should Jordan get on the listing agreement?
c: Rosa alone, because she possesses the house
Paul and Gina only, because they hold the fee
Rosa, Paul, and Gina together
Rosa, plus a court order allowing the sale
blocks.x: Selling the full fee simple requires everyone who holds a piece of it: the life tenant and both remaindermen. The trap is Rosa alone. Possession and paying the taxes do not make her the fee owner; she can list and sell only her life estate. Paul and Gina alone fail too, because a buyer would have to wait for Rosa's death to move in. No court order is needed when all three sign voluntarily.

blocks.html: Jordan explains this gently at the kitchen table. Rosa is annoyed, then relieved: she always meant the house to go to the kids, and both of them want her settled near Gina in Tottenville anyway. Paul lives in Scottsdale and agrees by phone. Gina hesitates. She has heard that her mother could "just sell her part" and keep everything simple. A local investor who buys estate properties has already called Rosa with that idea.

blocks.q: Suppose Rosa alone deeds "all her right, title and interest" to the investor. What does the investor own?
c: A life estate that ends when Rosa dies
A fee simple subject to Paul and Gina's lien
A life estate measured by the investor's own life
A tenancy at will that Paul and Gina can end
blocks.x: A life tenant can convey only what she has. The investor gets a life estate pur autre vie: it lasts for Rosa's life, not his own. The tempting wrong answer is a life estate measured by the investor's life, which would let a life tenant stretch the estate by selling to someone younger. When Rosa dies, Paul and Gina take possession and the investor's interest simply ends.

blocks.html: The investor's offer reflects that risk. He would pay a deep discount for an interest that could vanish next month, and no bank will lend against it. Gina sees the point. A life estate pur autre vie is a hard thing to sell, and the full fee simple, sold by all three, is worth far more than the sum of the pieces sold separately.

blocks.text: How the children hold the remainder

blocks.html: Priya Nair, the attorney the family hires, reads the deed's last line again: it is silent on how Paul and Gina hold. That matters, because one of them might die before Rosa does. Paul is 58 and had heart surgery last year.

blocks.q: Under New York's default rule, how do Paul and Gina, a brother and sister, hold their remainder?
c: As joint tenants, since they both took by the same deed
As tenants by the entirety, since they are family
In severalty, each owning one specific apartment
As tenants in common with equal undivided shares
blocks.x: A conveyance to two or more people who are not married to each other creates a tenancy in common unless the deed expressly says joint tenancy. Joint tenancy is the trap: the four unities happen to be present here, but New York still requires express language for survivorship. Entirety is only for spouses, and co-owners hold undivided interests, not separate floors.

blocks.html: Because they are tenants in common, each sibling's half of the remainder is inheritable. Priya walks through the risk out loud. If Paul died before closing, the people who would need to sign in his place would come from his will, not from Gina.

blocks.q: Paul dies in February while Rosa is still alive. His will leaves everything to his wife, Lorraine. What happens to Paul's half of the remainder?
c: It passes to Gina by survivorship
It passes to Lorraine under Paul's will
It reverts to Rosa as the original grantor
It is extinguished because Paul never took possession
blocks.x: A remainder held as a tenancy in common is a present, transferable property interest even before it becomes possessory, so it passes under Paul's will to Lorraine. Survivorship to Gina is the trap: it would apply only if the deed had created a joint tenancy. Nothing reverts to Rosa, because she gave the remainder away in 2012 and kept only her life estate.

blocks.html: Paul is fine, but the question shapes the paperwork. Priya asks both children for current photo ID and has Paul sign a power of attorney naming Gina, so a closing does not depend on a flight from Arizona. She also notes that if a remainderman dies before closing, the estate's executor signs for that share and a New York estate tax release may be needed before title will insure.

Kwame Osei has been upstairs since 2019. His current lease, signed by Rosa alone, runs from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2027 at $2,450 a month. A buyer who wants to live in the whole house will ask what happens to that lease. Jordan also wonders about a different risk: what if Rosa dies before any sale closes?

blocks.caption: Rent roll, upstairs unit
head: Tenant
Lease signed by
Term
Rent
In occupancy since

blocks.q: If Rosa dies in December 2026, what is the status of Kwame's lease that runs to June 2027?
c: It binds Paul and Gina until June 30, 2027
It converts to a lease for Kwame's lifetime
It ends, since Rosa could lease only her life estate
It continues, because a lease runs with the land to the new owners
blocks.x: A life tenant may lease, but the lease can last no longer than the life estate. When Rosa dies, her interest ends and the lease falls with it. The trap is that leases run with the land: they do survive a sale by a fee owner, but a lease carved out of a life estate cannot outlast the estate it came from. Paul and Gina were never parties to it.

blocks.html: That does not mean Kwame would be on the sidewalk the next morning. In practice, remaindermen who want rent usually keep the tenant, and what they do next decides what kind of leasehold he holds.

blocks.q: After Rosa's death, Paul and Gina sign nothing new but accept Kwame's $2,450 each month. What estate does Kwame most likely hold?
c: A periodic estate, month to month
An estate for years ending June 30, 2027
An estate at sufferance with no rights
A life estate pur autre vie for Rosa's life
blocks.x: Accepting regular monthly rent with no fixed term creates a month-to-month periodic tenancy. The estate for years is the trap: the old end date came from Rosa's lease, which ended at her death, and nobody agreed to a new fixed term. Sufferance describes a holdover the owner has not accepted, and here the owners are taking his money.

blocks.title: Notice still matters
blocks.html: Even a month-to-month tenant in New York gets statutory notice before the owner ends the tenancy or raises the rent 5% or more. Kwame has occupied the unit since 2019, more than two years, so he is owed 90 days' written notice under the 2019 HSTPA rules. A buyer who wants the house delivered vacant needs that timeline in the contract, or a negotiated move-out agreement.

blocks.text: The roof, the window, and the word waste

blocks.html: Ray Kowalski does a pre-listing inspection. The rear slope of the roof has leaked for at least two winters. Rosa put buckets in the attic and called it handled. Ray finds soft sheathing and staining on the upstairs ceiling. In the front hall, Jordan notices a bare frame where an original leaded-glass panel used to be. Rosa gave it to her church's rummage sale in 2023. Gina is upset about both.

blocks.q: Who is responsible for the roof damage, and what could Paul and Gina do about it if there were no sale?
c: Paul and Gina, since they will own the house in the future
Nobody, since a life tenant may use the house any way she likes
The city, since an owner over 65 may defer all repairs
Rosa, whose neglect is waste the remaindermen can sue to stop
blocks.x: A life tenant must keep the property in reasonable repair, pay ordinary taxes, and avoid harming the future interest. Letting a known leak rot the roof is permissive waste, and removing a fixture like the leaded glass is affirmative waste. Paul and Gina could seek an injunction or damages. The trap is that remaindermen carry upkeep: they hold a future interest, not the duty to maintain it.

blocks.title: "She owns it for life, so she can do what she wants"
blocks.html: Learners treat a life estate like a fee simple with an expiration date. It is narrower than that. The life tenant gets possession and income, but she holds the property in a sense for the people next in line: no stripping fixtures, no letting it fall apart, no tearing it down. The same limits apply to a buyer of the life estate, and to anyone the life tenant leases to.

In this family nobody sues. The siblings agree the roof is a sale problem now. Ray estimates $18,000 for a tear-off and new sheathing on the rear slope. The family decides to sell as is and price for it, and the stained glass becomes a footnote in a family argument rather than a lawsuit.

blocks.text: An offer, and how the money splits

blocks.html: Jordan lists the house with all three signatures. After three weekends of showings, a buyer couple who want to live downstairs and rent the top floor offer $960,000, and all three owners accept. Now Rosa asks the question Jordan was waiting for: "How much of that is mine?" She pays her own way and wants an apartment near Gina in Tottenville.

When a life tenant and remaindermen sell together and do not agree to some other split, the usual approach is to value the life estate with actuarial tables based on the life tenant's age and a current interest rate (the IRS Section 7520 tables are the common reference). An older life tenant has fewer expected years left, so her share is smaller. The family can also agree to any other division in writing; this is a negotiation, not a formula they are forced to use.

blocks.title: Priya's allocation worksheet (before closing costs)
blocks.html:
Contract price: $960,000
Life estate factor for a life tenant age 84 at this month's table rate: 0.26
Rosa's life estate: $960,000 x 0.26 = $249,600
Remainder (1 minus 0.26 = 0.74): $960,000 x 0.74 = $710,400
Paul and Gina are tenants in common in equal shares: $710,400 / 2 = ?

blocks.q: Using Priya's worksheet, what is each child's share of the $960,000 before closing costs?
blocks.x: The remainder is 74% of $960,000, or $710,400, split equally between two tenants in common: $355,200 each. $480,000 is the trap, an even half of the whole price that ignores Rosa's life estate. $320,000 is an equal three-way split, which treats the life tenant as a co-owner of the fee. $249,600 is Rosa's share.

blocks.html: Rosa looks at $249,600 and frowns. She thought she would get most of it. Gina, embarrassed, offers to give her mother more. Priya points out that the children can agree to any split they like, but anything beyond Rosa's actuarial share may be a gift for tax purposes, so the family's accountant should weigh in. The family settles on the table split, with Gina covering part of Rosa's first year of rent.

blocks.text: A detour: what if Rosa simply gave it up?

blocks.html: Before signing the contract, Paul asks whether there is a simpler structure: Rosa could deed her life estate to him and Gina now, and the two of them could sell. It would mean one fewer seller at the table and no actuarial split on the contract.

blocks.q: If Rosa deeds her life estate to Paul and Gina, what do Paul and Gina then hold?
c: A life estate pur autre vie, measured by Rosa's life
A remainder that still waits for Rosa's death
Fee simple absolute as tenants in common
A leasehold for the rest of Rosa's life
blocks.x: When the life estate and the remainder land in the same hands, they merge into a fee simple absolute. Paul and Gina would own it outright as tenants in common. The trap is the pur autre vie answer: that would be right if Rosa sold her life estate to a stranger. Here the people receiving it already own everything that comes after, so nothing is left to wait for.

blocks.html: Merger works, but Priya talks them out of it. A gratuitous transfer of the life estate could be a gift by Rosa, and it would leave her with no ownership stake and no voice in the sale. The family keeps all three names on the contract.

During the title review, Priya flags an old family connection. The lot behind Rosa's yard belongs to a small neighborhood church. In 1961, Rosa's father-in-law, Carmine Bianchi, deeded it to the church. The church stopped using it for anything religious in 2020 and now rents it to a landscaping company for equipment storage. Rosa wants to know if the lot "came back" to the family.

blocks.title: 1961 deed, Carmine Bianchi to the church (excerpt)
blocks.html: "...on condition that the said premises shall be used for church and parish purposes only, and if the said premises shall at any time cease to be so used, the grantor or his heirs may re-enter and repossess the same."

blocks.q: Read only the 1961 language. In 2021, a year after the church stopped using the lot for parish purposes, who held title?
c: The church, until Carmine's heirs took action to re-enter
Carmine's heirs, because title reverted automatically in 2020
The City of New York, because the charitable use ended
Rosa alone, as the surviving spouse of Carmine's son
blocks.x: "On condition that" plus a power to re-enter creates a fee on condition subsequent. Breach does not end the church's estate by itself; the grantor's heirs must exercise the right of re-entry, usually through a lawsuit. Automatic reversion is the trap: that is the rule for a fee simple determinable ("so long as"). The city has no claim, and heirship is not decided by a spouse's status alone.

blocks.html: Priya then checks something Carmine never knew about. New York does not let these old conditions linger forever. Under RPL 345, a condition subsequent restricting land use, and the right of re-entry that goes with it, is extinguished unless the holder records a "Declaration of Intention to Preserve Restrictions on the Use of Land" between 27 and 30 years after the condition was created, and then renews it on a 10-year cycle. For a 1961 deed, the first declaration was due between 1988 and 1991. Priya searches the county records. Nobody in the Bianchi family ever recorded one.

blocks.q: Given that no declaration was ever recorded, what is the best description of the family's rights in the church lot today?
c: The heirs may still re-enter, but only within 10 years of the 2020 breach
The heirs hold the lot as tenants in common with the church
Rosa may re-enter, because the condition was created by her family
The right was extinguished; the church holds the lot free of it
blocks.x: RPL 345 extinguishes a use condition and its right of re-entry when no preservation declaration is recorded in the statutory window. The church now holds the lot free of Carmine's condition. The trap is the 10-year window after breach, which borrows the adverse possession period; but the statute had already cut off the right decades before the breach. Family history alone creates no right.

blocks.title: Read old deeds for magic words
blocks.html: Qualified fees still turn up in Staten Island, Westchester, and upstate deeds to churches, schools, fire companies, and villages. When you see "so long as," "while," "on condition that," or "provided that," flag it for the attorney. Whether the restriction still has teeth can depend on recording rules most families never heard of.

The buyer's attorney sends Priya a checklist. One item asks for Lorraine Bianchi, Paul's wife, to sign the deed "to release any marital interest." Lorraine is not on title. Paul calls Jordan, confused.

blocks.q: Must Lorraine sign the deed for the buyers to get good title to Paul's share?
c: Yes, to release her dower interest in Paul's share
No, New York abolished dower, and she holds no title
Yes, a spouse must sign any deed under the elective share
No, but only because Paul lives in Arizona, not New York
blocks.x: New York abolished dower and curtesy, so a non-owner spouse has no lien-like interest in a deeded share that must be released. The trap is the elective share: it protects a surviving spouse against the estate at death, not against a living owner's sale. Where Paul lives is irrelevant; New York law governs title to New York land.

blocks.html: The second loose end is Rosa's grandson, Nico, 22, who has lived in the finished basement for a year while he works at the ferry terminal. He pays nothing, has no lease, and is there because his grandmother said he could stay as long as he liked.

blocks.q: If the sale did not happen and Rosa died next year, what would happen to Nico's right to stay in the basement?
c: It would continue until the remaindermen gave 90 days' notice
It would ripen into ownership after 10 years of residence
It would end, since an estate at will ends on Rosa's death
It would convert into a periodic estate, month to month
blocks.x: Nico has an estate at will (some would call it a mere license, since he pays nothing): open-ended, by permission, and terminable by either side or by the death of either party. It ends when Rosa dies. The 90-day notice answer is the trap: those HSTPA notice periods apply to a tenant's non-renewal or rent increase, and Nico has no lease or rent. Permission defeats any adverse possession theory.

blocks.html: For the sale, Nico's arrangement simply ends when Rosa moves. He finds a share in St. George. Kwame negotiates a lease with the buyers, who are glad to keep a reliable tenant at $2,450.

blocks.q: Consider the alternate ending. Rosa dies before any sale and the deed is unchanged. How do Paul and Gina get possession of the house?
c: Automatically at her death, as the holders of the remainder
Through probate, because the house is part of Rosa's estate
Only after recording a new deed from Rosa's executor
Only after a court partitions the life estate between them
blocks.x: The remainder was conveyed in 2012, so the house is not part of Rosa's probate estate. At her death the life estate ends and Paul and Gina hold the fee simple in possession. The probate answer is the trap, and it is why families use this structure. In practice the family records a death certificate and an affidavit so the record shows the life estate ended.

blocks.html: The real ending is calmer. The sale closes in May. Rosa signs as life tenant, Gina signs for herself and for Paul under the power of attorney, and the buyers take fee simple absolute. Rosa moves into a garden apartment ten minutes from Gina's house and calls Jordan the next month to ask whether her friend's grandson is single.

items: A reserved life estate splits a house into a life estate and a remainder. Selling the full fee simple needs the life tenant and every remainderman.
A life tenant can sell, lease, or mortgage only what she holds. A buyer gets a life estate pur autre vie, and a lease ends when the life estate does.
Remaindermen who take by a deed silent on survivorship are tenants in common, so a remainderman's share passes under his will.
The life tenant must repair and must not commit waste. When the life estate and remainder end up in the same hands, they merge into a fee simple.
Sale proceeds are commonly split by actuarial value: the life estate factor times the price, with the rest to the remaindermen.

"On condition that" needs action by the grantor's heirs; "so long as" reverts automatically. In New York, RPL 345 can extinguish an old use condition that was never preserved by a recorded declaration.

lessons.title: Case file: Four Heirs on East 92nd Street
lessons.tagline: A mother dies without a will, an investor buys one sibling's quarter, and the family home lands in partition court.
objectives: Decide how heirs, buyers, and devisees hold title when a home passes without a will and shares are later sold.
Apply New York's heirs property partition rules, including the co-tenant buyout, and calculate a buyout price.
Determine when a joint tenancy is severed and when survivorship still controls.
Apply tenancy by the entirety rules to a creditor of one spouse and to a divorce.

blocks.title: Papers on the stoop
