blocks.html: Denise Clarke has lived on the ground floor of her late mother's two-family on East 92nd Street in Canarsie her whole adult life. Her mother, Hortense, a retired transit worker and a widow, died in 2019 without a will. Last week a process server handed Denise a summons. A company called Bridgeview Equity LLC says it owns a quarter of the house and wants the court to order the whole property sold. Denise calls Jordan, whose firm sold her neighbor's house, and asks two things: "How can a stranger own part of my mother's house?" and "Can they really make me leave?" Jordan is not her lawyer, and says so. But Jordan can help Denise understand what is happening while Priya takes the case.

blocks.text: How four children came to own one house

blocks.html: Hortense owned the house in severalty after her husband died in 2004. With no will, her property passed by intestate succession. She left no spouse and four children: Denise, Marlon, Keisha, and Andre. Under New York's intestacy statute, children with no surviving spouse take equal shares. Nobody ever signed a new deed. The family assumed the house was "Mom's" and that Denise, who lived there and paid the bills, was in charge.

blocks.q: When Hortense died intestate, how did her four children hold title to the house?
c: As joint tenants with right of survivorship
As tenants in common, 25% each
In severalty through Denise as the occupant
As tenants in common in shares set by contributions
blocks.x: Heirs who inherit together take as tenants in common, here in equal 25% shares under the intestacy statute. Joint tenancy is the trap: survivorship has to be created expressly, and heirs do not acquire by one deed at one moment. Occupancy does not give Denise sole title, and shares follow the statute, not who paid the bills.

blocks.html: Each child holds an undivided interest. That means none of them owns "the top floor" or "the yard." Each has the right to possess the whole house. Denise lives downstairs. Upstairs, a tenant pays $2,200 a month, and Denise has been collecting it since 2019, using it for insurance, a boiler repair, and the water bill. She has paid the property taxes out of her own pocket.

blocks.caption: What Denise has handled since 2019
head: Item
Amount
Paid from

blocks.q: Marlon once told Denise she "owes rent" to her siblings for living downstairs. Absent any agreement, what does Denise owe her co-owners?
c: Each sibling's 25% share of the market rent for her own apartment
Nothing at all, including any share of the upstairs rent she collects
Market rent for her apartment, but only from her mother's death
No rent for her own use, but an accounting of the net upstairs rent
blocks.x: Each tenant in common may occupy the whole, so a co-tenant living there owes the others nothing for her own use unless she ousted them or agreed to pay. Rent from a third party is different: she must account for the net upstairs rent. The trap is "nothing at all," which ignores that third-party rent belongs to all four owners in proportion to their shares.

blocks.text: Two shares leave the family circle

blocks.html: Andre, the youngest, died in 2023. His will left "everything I own" to his son Tyrell, who is 24 and lives in East Flatbush. Then, in 2025, Marlon, who lives in Atlanta and needed money for a business, answered a mailer that said "We buy inherited homes, any condition." He agreed to sell his 25% to Bridgeview Equity LLC for $60,000. Because the house is heirs property, Bridgeview's lawyer served Denise, Keisha, and Tyrell with a formal notice of the pending offer. Denise thought it was one more investor flyer and put it in the drawer with the others. Keisha never opened hers. Six months later, Marlon signed the deed.

blocks.q: Who owns Andre's 25% after his death in 2023?
c: Tyrell, under Andre's will
Denise, Marlon, and Keisha by survivorship
Andre's estate until the house is sold
Hortense's estate, since it was never probated
blocks.x: A tenant in common's share is inheritable and passes under the owner's will, so Tyrell steps into Andre's 25%. Survivorship among the siblings is the trap: it exists only in a joint tenancy or a tenancy by the entirety. The share does pass through Andre's estate administration, but it belongs to Tyrell as the devisee, not to the remaining siblings.

blocks.html: Tyrell's share is the easy one. The family never thought of Andre's quarter as anything but "Andre's," and now it is his son's. Marlon's share is harder. He had not set foot in the house in ten years, he resented that Denise lived there rent free, and he wanted cash, not a quarter of a house he could not use. A tenant in common in that position has exactly two exits: sell the share, or ask a court to divide or sell the whole. Investors know this, and they mail heirs constantly.

blocks.q: Marlon conveyed his 25% to Bridgeview without asking his sisters. What is the legal effect of that deed?
c: It is void, since co-owners have a right of first refusal
It is voidable within one year by any co-owner
It is valid, and Bridgeview is now a tenant in common
It is valid, and Bridgeview may occupy the upstairs unit
blocks.x: A tenant in common may sell or mortgage a share without the others' consent, and the buyer becomes a tenant in common for that share. The tempting wrong answer gives Bridgeview the upstairs unit: it gets an undivided interest in the whole, not a particular apartment. The heirs property statute adds a notice and matching right before such a sale, but once that window passes, the deed stands.

blocks.html: Priya pulls the notice from Denise's drawer. It is the document that mattered most in this whole story, and it looked like junk mail. Under subdivision 13 of RPAPL 993, when a co-tenant of heirs property gets a good-faith offer from an outsider for a share, the co-tenants who inherited (or are relatives of those who did) may buy that share on the same price and terms. The seller and the outside buyer must use due diligence to find and notify them.

blocks.q: What could Denise, Keisha, and Tyrell have done after they were served with notice of Bridgeview's $60,000 offer?
c: Sued to void the offer, since heirs property may not be sold to investors
Nothing, since Marlon may sell his share to anyone he likes
Demanded the court-appraised value instead of the offer price
Matched the $60,000 offer within 180 days and bought the share
blocks.x: The notified co-tenants had 180 days from notice to buy Marlon's share on the same price and terms as Bridgeview's offer. They let the window pass. The trap is "nothing": that was the rule for an ordinary tenancy in common, and still is outside heirs property. Heirs may sell to investors, and the appraised-value buyout belongs to the later partition action, not to this matching right.

blocks.html: Had Bridgeview skipped the notice, the statute gives the family a remedy after the fact: buy the share from the outsider for the price it paid plus 2% a year in interest, within 180 days after they learn of the sale. Bridgeview's lawyer did it by the book, so that door is closed. The family will pay for the drawer.

blocks.title: The "we buy inherited homes" play
blocks.html: Investors buy one heir's fractional share cheaply, then sue for partition and a court-ordered sale of the whole. Before 2019 that often meant a forced auction at a low price. Learners assume a co-owner can stop a partition by refusing to sell. Generally they cannot: any tenant in common or joint tenant has a right to partition. What New York changed is how heirs property is valued and sold.

Bridgeview's complaint asks Kings County Supreme Court to order a sale and split the proceeds. Priya's first move is to ask the court to treat the house as heirs property under RPAPL 993, New York's version of the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act, adopted in 2019. Heirs property is residential or agricultural land held by tenants in common with no written agreement about partition, where at least one co-tenant got its interest from a relative and the family connection is strong. One test: 20% or more of the interests are held by relatives, or by people who got their interests from relatives, or a co-tenant who inherited lives there.

blocks.caption: Ownership on the date Bridgeview filed
head: Co-tenant
Share
How acquired
Lives there?

blocks.q: The court finds the Clarke house is heirs property. Which protection does that give Denise that an ordinary partition would not?
c: A right to block any sale for as long as she lives there
A right to buy Bridgeview's share at the court-set value
A right to buy Bridgeview's share at the $60,000 it paid
A right to have the sale delayed until the market recovers
blocks.x: Under the heirs property rules, the court sets the property's value, usually through an independent licensed appraisal, and the co-tenants who did not ask for a sale may buy out the co-tenant who did, at that value. The $60,000 answer is the trap: Bridgeview is paid fair value for its share, not what it paid Marlon. There is no lifetime veto and no market-timing delay.

blocks.html: The court also holds a mandatory settlement conference, which the statute requires and at which both sides must negotiate in good faith. Bridgeview offers to drop the case if the family sells it the rest of the house for $700,000. The family declines. The court orders an appraisal by a disinterested New York licensed appraiser. The appraisal assumes the whole fee simple held by one owner and comes in at $1,040,000. Notice of the value goes out, and the co-tenants who did not request the sale have 45 days to elect to buy.

blocks.q: Denise, Keisha, and Tyrell elect to buy Bridgeview's interest. What is the buyout price?
blocks.x: The buyout price is the court's determination of value times the share being bought: $1,040,000 x 25% = $260,000. $346,667 is the trap, a third of the value, which treats the buyers as splitting the house three ways instead of buying one quarter. $60,000 is what Bridgeview paid Marlon, and $175,000 is a quarter of Bridgeview's lowball $700,000 offer.

blocks.html: Bridgeview paid $60,000 and walks away with $260,000, which is the business model. But the family keeps the house. Denise, Keisha, and Tyrell now hold it as tenants in common, each with one third. To raise the money, Tasha arranges a loan on Keisha's Rosedale house and Tyrell puts in savings. The court sets a payment date, at least 60 days after notice, and the family meets it.

blocks.title: Jordan's listing lesson
blocks.html: When the owner of record is dead, find out who holds title before you take a listing. Ask for the death certificate, letters of administration or testamentary from the Surrogate's Court, and a family tree. An executor or administrator may have power to sell, but heirs who inherited without administration each hold a share, and every one of them must sign. One heir in the kitchen saying "I'm handling it" is not a seller.

blocks.title: If the buyout had failed
blocks.html: Under RPAPL 993, if no one buys out the requesting co-tenant, the court must order partition in kind (a physical division) unless that would cause great manifest prejudice to the co-tenants as a group. A two-family on a 20-by-100 lot cannot sensibly be split into two separately owned parcels, so a sale would follow. Even then, the default is an open-market sale through a licensed broker at a price no lower than the court-determined value, not a courthouse auction.

With Bridgeview gone, the siblings and Tyrell want to clean up six years of money before they sign a co-ownership agreement. Denise paid $7,200 a year in property taxes from her own savings for six years, $43,200 in total. New York partition accounting lets a co-tenant who paid more than her share of taxes and necessary repairs recover the excess from the others.

blocks.q: The four 25% owners during those six years should have shared the taxes equally. How much of the $43,200 should Denise be reimbursed by the other shares combined?
blocks.x: Denise's own 25% share of the taxes is $10,800, so the other three quarters, $32,400, is the excess she carried for her co-owners. The trap is $43,200, which would have the others repay her own share too. $21,600 is half, and $10,800 is only her own share. Bridgeview's quarter is usually settled in the buyout accounting rather than chased separately.

blocks.html: Against that credit, Denise accounts for the net upstairs rent after insurance, water, and repairs. The family nets it out and puts the result in a written co-ownership agreement: who lives where, who pays what, and a right of first refusal if anyone wants to sell. That agreement also means the house would no longer meet the heirs property definition, which requires that no written partition agreement exist. The family decided the clarity was worth it.

While reviewing the family's paperwork, Priya finds a second deed. In 2015, Denise and Keisha bought a one-bedroom condo in Rockaway Park as a summer place. The deed reads "to Denise Clarke and Keisha Clarke-Boyd, as joint tenants with right of survivorship." After the partition fight, Keisha wants her half to go to her own two children, not to Denise. Denise is hurt but not opposed. The unities were all there in 2015: the sisters took at the same time, by the same deed, in equal halves, with equal rights to possess the whole. That is why the joint tenancy held. Keisha's question is how to break it without Denise's cooperation, and whether her two children would then inherit her half.

blocks.q: Keisha wants to end survivorship on her half without Denise's signature. Which method works in New York?
c: Sign and record a deed of her interest to herself
Write a will leaving her half of the condo to her children
Send Denise a certified letter stating her intent
Ask the condo board to note the change on its records
blocks.x: Under RPL 240-c, a joint tenant may sever without the others' consent by deeding her interest to a third person or by a written instrument showing intent to sever, including a deed to herself. The will is the trap: a joint tenant's share passes to the survivor at the instant of death, so there is nothing left for a will to carry. A letter or a board record does not convey anything.

blocks.html: Keisha signs the self-deed at Priya's office in March. Priya explains one more condition, and Jordan writes it down because it is exactly the kind of detail that ends up in court.

blocks.q: Keisha signs the severance deed but dies before anyone records it. Who owns the condo?
c: Denise and Keisha's children as tenants in common
Keisha's children alone, under her will
Denise alone, by survivorship
Denise and Keisha's estate until probate ends
blocks.x: RPL 240-c makes a unilateral severance effective against the other joint tenant's survivorship right only if the instrument is recorded in the county where the property sits before the severing tenant dies. Unrecorded, it fails, and Denise takes everything by survivorship. The trap is the tenancy in common with Keisha's children, which is exactly what would have happened had the deed been recorded in time.

blocks.html: In this case Priya records the deed in Queens County the same week. Denise and Keisha are now tenants in common, 50% each. The four unities of time, title, interest, and possession were broken the moment Keisha's recorded deed replaced her original title with a new one.

blocks.text: Keisha's own house, and Dwayne's problem

blocks.html: Keisha and her husband Dwayne Boyd own their Rosedale house under a 2010 deed "to Dwayne Boyd and Keisha Clarke-Boyd, his wife." That language, between spouses, creates a tenancy by the entirety. Dwayne's catering business failed in 2024, and a food supplier has an $85,000 money judgment against Dwayne alone, docketed in Queens County. The supplier's lawyer writes that the house "will be sold to satisfy the judgment."

blocks.q: What can Dwayne's creditor actually reach in the Rosedale house?
c: Half the house, which can be partitioned and sold off
The whole house, because Dwayne is a co-owner
Nothing, because a judgment can never attach to entirety property at all
Dwayne's interest only, subject to Keisha's survivorship right
blocks.x: A creditor of one spouse can reach that spouse's interest, but cannot partition entirety property or defeat the other spouse's survivorship right. If Dwayne dies first, Keisha owns the whole house and the lien is gone. The trap is "half the house," which treats entirety property like a tenancy in common. "Never attach" goes too far: the lien sits on Dwayne's interest and would bite if he survives Keisha.

blocks.html: The supplier backs off once Priya's letter lays this out, and eventually settles for a payment plan. But the stress takes a toll on the marriage. Dwayne, who grew up in Houston, tells Keisha he is entitled to half of everything she inherited from her mother "because that's how it works in Texas."

blocks.q: If Keisha and Dwayne divorce in New York, how is Keisha's inherited share of the Canarsie house most likely treated?
c: As community property, split 50/50 with Dwayne
As separate property, not divided as marital property
As marital property, because she inherited during marriage
As entirety property, since she is married to Dwayne
blocks.x: New York is not a community property state. In a divorce, marital property is divided by equitable distribution, and property acquired by inheritance is generally separate property, even if received during the marriage. Community property is the trap, and even community property states usually exclude inheritances. Keisha took her share from her mother alone, so it cannot be held by the entirety with Dwayne.

blocks.html: The couple separates, and in 2027 a judgment of divorce is entered. Nothing in the judgment addresses the Rosedale house yet; they agree to sell it in the spring and split the proceeds. Jordan is asked to list it.

blocks.q: After the divorce judgment, how do Keisha and Dwayne hold the Rosedale house if the decree is silent?
c: As tenants in common, with no survivorship
As joint tenants, keeping survivorship
As tenants by the entirety until the house sells
In severalty, by whoever keeps living there
blocks.x: Divorce destroys the unity of marriage, and New York treats former spouses as tenants in common unless the decree says otherwise. Survivorship ends, and either can now seek partition. The trap is joint tenancy: survivorship between ex-spouses would need an express new conveyance. Who stays in the house does not change title. The listing agreement needs both signatures.

blocks.html: Jordan takes the Rosedale listing with both signatures, an RPL 443 disclosure signed by each seller separately, and a note to send every update to both. Back in Canarsie, Denise still lives downstairs. The co-ownership agreement now sits in a folder labeled "Mom's house, for real this time."

items: Heirs take as tenants in common. Each share is undivided, can be sold without consent, and passes under the owner's will, not to the other co-owners.
A co-tenant in possession owes no rent for her own use absent an ouster or agreement, but must account for third-party rent, and can recover taxes she paid beyond her share.
Under RPAPL 993, heirs property gets a court-set value, a buyout right at that value, a preference for partition in kind, and an open-market sale by a broker instead of an auction.
A joint tenant can sever alone by a deed to herself, but under RPL 240-c it must be recorded before she dies or survivorship still controls.
Entirety property cannot be partitioned by one spouse's creditor, and the creditor cannot defeat the other spouse's survivorship right. Divorce converts it to a tenancy in common.
New York uses equitable distribution, not community property, and inherited property is generally separate property.

lessons.title: Case file: The Trustee's Two Apartments
lessons.tagline: A successor trustee must sell an Upper West Side co-op and a Long Island City condo owned through an LLC. They are not the same kind of property.
objectives: Decide who has authority to list and convey property held in a trust or an LLC, and what beneficiaries can and cannot do.
Compare what transfers in a co-op sale and a condo sale, including the documents, the lien search, and the lender's collateral.
Apply New York condominium rules on common elements and common charge liens to a unit sale.
Identify a trustee's conflict of interest and the steps that make a sale to the trustee proper.

blocks.title: Two sets of keys
blocks.html: Margaret Sato, a retired music teacher, died in February at 88. In 2018 she put her two homes into the Margaret Sato Revocable Trust: a two-bedroom co-op on West 104th Street, where she lived, and a one-bedroom condo in Long Island City that she bought in 2016 as an investment. Her nephew Ben Sato is the successor trustee. Ben and his sisters, Lena and Aiko, are the three equal beneficiaries. Ben calls Hudson & Hart because Diane once sold his parents' house. Lena calls Jordan the same afternoon, separately, to say she wants to keep the co-op and that "nothing gets signed without me." Jordan has two apartments, three family members, and one question: who is the client?

A trust splits ownership in two. The trustee holds legal title and manages the property as a fiduciary. The beneficiaries hold the equitable interest: the right to benefit under the trust's terms. Margaret was the trustor and her own first trustee. While she lived she could change or revoke the trust. At her death it became irrevocable, and Ben stepped in under the successor trustee clause.

blocks.title: Trust agreement, excerpts Priya flags
blocks.html:
Article 4 (Successor Trustee): "Upon the death or incapacity of the Grantor, BENJAMIN SATO shall serve as successor Trustee."
Article 7 (Powers): "The Trustee may sell, lease, or exchange any property of the trust, at public or private sale, for such price and on such terms as the Trustee deems advisable, without order of any court."
Article 9 (Distribution): "Upon the Grantor's death, the Trustee shall distribute the remaining trust property in equal shares to BENJAMIN, LENA, and AIKO SATO."
Schedule A: 410 shares of 104th Street Owners Corp. and the appurtenant proprietary lease for Apartment 6C; 100% of the membership interests in Sato Court Square LLC.

blocks.q: Who should sign the exclusive listing agreement for the West 104th Street co-op?
c: Ben, as successor trustee
Ben, Lena, and Aiko together, as the owners
Lena, since she holds a one-third interest
Margaret's executor, after probate is complete
blocks.x: The trustee holds legal title and Article 7 gives him the power to sell without court approval, so Ben signs as trustee. The trap is having all three beneficiaries sign: they hold equitable interests, not title, and their signatures are not what a buyer, a board, or a title reviewer needs. Probate is not involved because the trust, not Margaret's estate, owns the shares.

blocks.html: Jordan calls Lena back and explains, kindly, that Ben is the seller of record and that Jordan's firm will represent the trust. Lena is not happy. "I own a third of that apartment," she says. "Mom always said it would be ours."

blocks.q: What does Lena actually hold in the co-op right now?
c: One third of the shares, as a tenant in common
A life estate in Apartment 6C
An equitable interest in the trust, not title
Nothing, until the trust finishes its sale
blocks.x: Lena is a beneficiary with an equitable right to a third of what the trust distributes, and the trustee owes her fiduciary duties. She does not hold legal title. The trap is the one-third tenancy in common: that would be true only if Ben distributed the shares in kind to the three of them. "Nothing" goes too far; beneficiaries can demand accountings and sue a trustee who breaches his duties.

blocks.html: Lena could ask Ben to distribute the co-op to her and buy out her siblings, and Article 9 would let him distribute in kind if the three agree on values. But that requires board approval of Lena as a shareholder, financing she does not have, and a deal her siblings accept. After a week of family calls, Lena agrees to a sale.

blocks.text: The co-op: shares, a lease, and a board

blocks.html: Kim Alvarez is board president at 104th Street Owners Corp. She sends the managing agent's file. In it Jordan finds a 2018 board consent to Margaret's transfer of her shares to her revocable trust, conditioned on Margaret remaining the occupant. Many co-op boards require exactly that before shares move into a trust, because a transfer of shares is a transfer of the right to occupy.

Jordan reads the proprietary lease too, because it is the document that defines what a co-op buyer actually gets. It is a long-term lease from the corporation for Apartment 6C, tied to the 410 shares. It obligates the shareholder to pay maintenance, sets the house rules, limits subletting to board approval, and lets the corporation terminate the lease and cancel the shares for serious defaults. In a cooperative, the shareholder is legally a tenant of a corporation she partly owns. That is why the board, acting as landlord, gets to approve who moves in.

blocks.q: Why can Ben sell Apartment 6C without waiting for a Surrogate's Court probate proceeding?
c: Co-op shares are personal property, which never passes through probate
The shares were in the trust before death, so they are not probate assets
The board's 2018 consent acts as a court order allowing a sale
A trustee's power of sale overrides any probate court order
blocks.x: Property already titled in a living trust at death is owned by the trust, so it passes under the trust's terms, not through probate. The trap is the personal property answer: co-op shares are personal property, but personal property owned by a decedent in her own name absolutely goes through the estate. The board consent was permission to transfer, not a court order.

blocks.html: A buyer is found in five weeks: a couple from Park Slope, offering $1,195,000 with 20% down. The contract is the standard co-op form. Jordan notices the buyers' attorney's first question is not about the deed. In a co-op there is no deed.

blocks.q: At the co-op closing, what does the trust deliver to the buyers?
c: A bargain and sale deed to Apartment 6C from the trustee
A trustee's deed to the unit plus an undivided share of the common elements
A recorded condominium unit deed signed by Ben as trustee
The stock certificate and an assignment of the proprietary lease
blocks.x: A co-op apartment owner owns shares in the corporation that owns the building, plus a proprietary lease for the unit. Both are personal property. The seller endorses or assigns the stock certificate and assigns the proprietary lease, and the corporation issues new ones. The trap is any deed: the corporation owns the real property in severalty, and that title never changes hands.

blocks.html: Because there is no real property transfer by the shareholder, there is no title search of the apartment in the usual sense. Instead, the buyer's side orders a lien search: a check of UCC filings against the seller's shares (in New York City they are filed with the City Register and searchable in ACRIS), plus judgment, bankruptcy, and tax lien searches against the seller's name.

blocks.title: "The buyer gets a deed to the apartment"
blocks.html: Exam writers love this one. A co-op buyer never gets a deed, never gets title insurance on the apartment in the usual sense, and never gives a mortgage on it. She gets stock and a lease, a lien search instead of a title search, and a share loan secured by a UCC filing. If an answer choice mentions a deed, a recorded mortgage, or common elements, it is describing a condo.

blocks.title: Co-op lien search results, Apt. 6C
blocks.html:
1. UCC-1 financing statement, filed 2015. Debtor: Margaret Sato. Secured party: Riverside Savings Bank. Collateral: 410 shares of 104th Street Owners Corp. and proprietary lease, Apt. 6C. No UCC-3 termination of record.
2. Judgments: none.
3. Federal tax liens: none.
Managing agent's letter: maintenance paid through current month; no arrears; flip tax per house rules.

blocks.q: Margaret paid off the Riverside Savings share loan in 2020. What should the trust's attorney do about item 1 before closing?
c: Nothing, since a paid-off share loan disappears from the record automatically
Get the bank to file a UCC-3 termination and return the stock
Record a satisfaction of mortgage with the City Register
Ask the co-op board to remove the filing from its records
blocks.x: A co-op share loan is secured by a UCC-1 filing on the shares, not a mortgage, so it is cleared by a UCC-3 termination. The lender also returns the original stock certificate and lease it held as collateral. The trap is the satisfaction of mortgage, the correct document for a house or condo loan. Paid-off filings stay on the record until someone terminates them.

blocks.html: Riverside Savings finds the original certificate in a vault in Yonkers and files the UCC-3. The buyers' lender, meanwhile, will make a share loan. It will file its own UCC-1 on the shares and sign a recognition agreement with the co-op corporation, in which the corporation acknowledges the lender's interest and agrees to notify it of defaults in maintenance.

blocks.q: Which statement about the buyers' $956,000 co-op loan is accurate?
c: It is secured by the shares, so no mortgage recording tax is due
It is a mortgage on Apartment 6C recorded against the building
It needs the trust's consent, since the trust is still the lessee
It is a lien behind the building's underlying mortgage on the unit
blocks.x: A co-op loan is secured by personal property, the shares and proprietary lease, so it is not a mortgage and New York's mortgage recording tax does not apply. The trap is the underlying mortgage answer: the building's own mortgage is a lien on the corporation's land and building, and the shareholder's loan sits on a different asset entirely. After closing the trust has no role.

blocks.html: The board interview goes badly. One board member presses the buyers on their work schedules and why they need a second bedroom. A week later, the managing agent sends a one-line letter: the board declines to consent to the transfer. No reason is given.

blocks.q: The buyers ask Jordan whether the board can do that. What is the best answer?
c: No, a co-op board must state a reason for every rejection in writing
No, the trust can sell to anyone once the contract is signed
Yes, without a stated reason, as long as it is not discriminatory
Yes, but only if the buyers' finances fall below the house rules
blocks.x: Under the business judgment rule, a co-op board may reject a purchaser for any reason or no stated reason, as long as it is not an illegal reason such as discrimination based on a protected class. The trap is a required written reason: bills to require written reasons keep being introduced in Albany and the City Council, but in New York City the general rule still lets a board decline without explanation. Some counties differ: Westchester's co-op law sets approval deadlines and, since 2021, requires written reasons for a rejection. Questions about family plans deserve attention; familial status is protected.

blocks.title: When a rejection smells wrong
blocks.html: If buyers believe a rejection was based on a protected class, they can file a complaint with the NYC Commission on Human Rights or the NYS Division of Human Rights. Jordan documents what was asked at the interview and keeps those notes. Jordan does not tell the buyers what the board's motives were, and does not speculate. A second buyer, at $1,170,000, is approved six weeks later.

blocks.text: The condo, owned by an LLC

blocks.html: The Long Island City condo is different in every way that matters. The deed to Unit 2207 in a Court Square tower runs to Sato Court Square LLC, a single-member LLC whose only member is now the trust. Margaret formed the LLC for liability protection when she started renting the unit out. A tenant, a physical therapist, has a lease from June 1, 2026 to May 31, 2027 at $3,650 a month.

blocks.q: How does Sato Court Square LLC hold title to Unit 2207?
c: As tenants in common with the trust, its sole member
As trustee for Ben, Lena, and Aiko
In severalty, as a single legal owner
As a leasehold held from the condo board
blocks.x: An LLC is a separate legal person, so when it owns real property it owns in severalty, even if it has many members. The members own membership interests, not the unit. The trap is a co-ownership with the member: the trust owns the LLC, and the LLC owns the condo. Whoever the operating agreement names as manager or authorized signatory signs the deed for the LLC.

blocks.html: Priya reviews the LLC's operating agreement. It is member-managed, so the member (the trust, acting through Ben as trustee) authorizes the sale, and Ben signs the deed as authorized signatory. The title company will want the operating agreement, a member's consent resolution, and the trust documents showing Ben's authority. The condo board's managing agent sends its own surprise.

The LLC did its job for nine years. When a guest of the tenant slipped on the unit's balcony in 2021, the claim ran against the LLC and its insurance, not against Margaret personally. But the LLC adds paperwork to a sale. A buyer's title insurer wants proof that the entity exists and is in good standing, that the person signing has authority, and that the members approved the sale the way the operating agreement requires. With a single member, one written consent handles it.

blocks.caption: Title report and managing agent letter, Unit 2207 (summary)
head: Item
Holder
Amount
Recorded or filed

blocks.html: During the months after Margaret's death, nobody paid the condo's common charges. The board of managers filed a lien under RPL 339-z, the New York Condominium Act's provision for unpaid common charges. Ben asks how that lien compares with the bank's mortgage.

blocks.q: Under RPL 339-z, how does the board's $6,200 common charge lien rank on a residential unit?
c: Ahead of everything, because condo boards come first
Behind taxes and the first mortgage of record
Ahead of the mortgage but behind real property taxes
Equal with the first mortgage, shared pro rata
blocks.x: The statute makes the common charge lien subordinate to tax liens on the unit and to all sums unpaid on a first mortgage of record. The trap is ranking it just behind taxes: some states give condo associations a limited "super lien" ahead of the mortgage, but New York does not, outside a narrow exception for non-residential condos. At closing, the $6,200 is paid from the proceeds anyway.

blocks.html: A buyer appears quickly: an investor who already owns two units in the building. She makes an odd request. Unit 2207 comes with a deeded 0.42% interest in the common elements, and she would like the trust to keep the common element interest out of the sale and lower the price. She says she does not use the gym.

blocks.q: Can the trust sell Unit 2207 while keeping its 0.42% common element interest?
c: No, the common interest cannot be separated from the unit
Yes, if the board of managers approves the split in writing
Yes, since the trust could later partition the gym
No, unless the buyer agrees to keep paying the common charges anyway
blocks.x: The Condominium Act provides that the common interest shall not be separated from the unit it belongs to, and the common elements stay undivided with no right to partition them. Board approval is the trap: the board has no power to waive a statutory rule. A condo owner owns the unit in fee simple and an undivided percentage of everything else, as one package.

blocks.html: The investor withdraws the idea and signs a contract at $865,000. The condo board's by-laws give it a right of first refusal, which it waives in writing within the 30 days its by-laws allow. Unlike the co-op, no interview and no approval of the buyer are required.

Everything about this closing is real property practice. The trust's LLC signs a deed to the unit, the buyer gets a title search and title insurance on the unit and its common interest, Harborline Bank's mortgage is paid off and a satisfaction is recorded, and the buyer's lender takes a recorded mortgage, which carries mortgage recording tax. In a condominium the buyer owns the unit in fee simple and pays the city's tax bill for that unit directly, plus common charges to the board.

blocks.q: The tenant's lease runs to May 31, 2027. The sale closes in January. What happens to the lease?
c: It ends at closing, since a sale breaks a lease
It converts to a month-to-month tenancy at closing
It continues, and the buyer becomes the landlord
It continues only if the tenant consents in writing
blocks.x: The tenant holds an estate for years, a possessory interest the owner granted before the sale. A buyer of the fee takes subject to it and steps into the landlord's role, including the security deposit, which must be transferred. The trap is "a sale breaks a lease," a folk rule with no basis in New York law. Contrast a lease made by a life tenant, which ends with the life estate.

blocks.text: The trustee who wanted to buy

blocks.html: Before the condo contract is signed, Ben makes a confession to Diane. He has always liked the LIC unit and would happily buy it himself at the $865,000 the investor offered. He is the trustee, the market price is known, and "it keeps it in the family." Diane asks Priya to call him.

blocks.q: What does Ben need before he, as trustee, can properly buy trust property for himself?
c: Nothing more, since $865,000 is a real arm's length market offer
Only an independent appraisal showing that $865,000 is fair
Only the condo board's written waiver of its right of first refusal
Trust authority, every beneficiary's informed consent, or a court
blocks.x: A trustee who buys trust property is on both sides of the deal. That is self-dealing, and New York treats it as voidable by the beneficiaries unless the trust instrument authorizes it, the beneficiaries give informed consent, or a court approves. The trap is the appraisal answer: a fair price helps, but it does not cure the conflict by itself. The board's waiver addresses a different issue.

blocks.html: Lena and Aiko, after talking with their own lawyer, consent in writing. Ben buys at $865,000, the investor is gracious about it, and the tenant stays. Priya puts the consents, the appraisal, and the comparables in the trust file, because a trustee who deals with himself should assume someone will ask about it later.

Just before the co-op closes, Kim calls with news. A developer next door has offered the co-op corporation $2.4 million for the building's unused development rights, its air rights. The board will put it to a shareholder vote. Ben asks whether the trust, still the shareholder for a few more days, gets a piece of the check.

blocks.q: If the co-op sells its air rights, who receives the $2.4 million?
c: Each shareholder directly, in proportion to their shares
The top-floor shareholders, whose units are closest to the air
The City of New York, which controls all development rights
The co-op corporation, which owns the land and building
blocks.x: Air rights are part of the real property, and in a co-op the corporation owns the real property in severalty. The money goes to the corporation, which may reduce maintenance, fund repairs, or distribute it as the board and shareholders decide. The trap is a direct payout per share: shareholders benefit only through the corporation. In a condo, by contrast, the rights belong with the common elements owned by all unit owners.

blocks.html: The vote is scheduled for after the closing, so the benefit, if any, goes to the new owners through lower maintenance or a stronger reserve fund. Ben distributes the co-op proceeds in three equal shares under Article 9, files a final accounting, and sends Jordan a note: next time a relative asks him to be a trustee, he is going to read the trust first.

items: In a trust the trustee holds legal title and signs; beneficiaries hold equitable interests. Property already in a living trust at death avoids probate.
A co-op seller transfers shares and a proprietary lease, which are personal property. The lien search covers UCC filings, and a paid share loan is cleared with a UCC-3.
A co-op loan is secured by the shares and lease, not a mortgage. A board may reject a buyer without a stated reason, but never for a discriminatory one.
An LLC owns in severalty; its authorized signatory signs the deed. A condo is real property: fee simple in the unit plus an undivided common interest that cannot be separated from it.
A New York condo board's common charge lien ranks behind tax liens and the first mortgage of record. A sale does not end an existing lease.
A trustee who buys trust property is self-dealing unless the trust, the beneficiaries' informed consent, or a court allows it.

lessons.title: Case file: Nine Exceptions on a Levittown Cape
lessons.tagline: Gerald Pike thinks his house is free and clear except for the mortgage. His title report lists nine exceptions, and two of them are not even his.
objectives: Classify the liens on a title report as general or specific and voluntary or involuntary, and decide which must be cleared at closing.
Apply New York's time limits for mechanic's liens, money judgments, and notices of pendency to decide whether a recorded item is still a valid lien.
Calculate a mechanic's lien discharge bond and a seller's net proceeds after liens are paid.
Decide how priority, subordination, and foreclosure affect each lienholder.

blocks.title: "Just the mortgage"
blocks.html: Gerald Pike, a 61-year-old retired corrections officer, is selling the Cape in Levittown, Nassau County, that he inherited from his mother in 2019. Marcus, who lives in Wantagh, took the listing for Hudson & Hart and brought Jordan in to help. The house went into contract in September at $640,000 with a young couple from Hicksville. When Marcus asked about liens at the listing appointment, Gerald said, "Just the mortgage and a little home equity line." Three weeks later, the buyers' title company sends its report. Schedule B lists nine exceptions. The closing is set for mid-November, and Gerald needs the money for a condo in Florida.

A title report's Schedule B lists every encumbrance the title insurer will not insure over unless it is cleared. Some items are routine and stay (a utility easement, a survey reading). The money items, the liens, must be paid, released, bonded, or proven invalid before the buyers' lender will fund. Gerald's seller's attorney, Priya, reads the report with Marcus and Jordan on a call.

blocks.caption: Title report, Schedule B (money items and two others)
head: No.
Item
Amount
Recorded, filed, or docketed
rows: Home equity line mortgage to Harbor Federal Credit Union
Mechanic's lien, Blue Wave Pools Inc.
Judgment, Island Auto Credit v. Gerald Pike
Judgment, Atlantic Card Services v. Gerald R. Pike
Notice of Federal Tax Lien, IRS, v. Gerald Pike
Notice of pendency, Maloney v. Pike (fence dispute)
Possible NYS estate tax lien, Estate of Dolores Pike (died 2018)
No release of lien of record
Unpaid second half school tax and sewer district charge

blocks.q: How should Jordan classify item 6, the IRS notice of federal tax lien?
c: Specific and voluntary, like the mortgage he signed on the house
Specific and involuntary, like the mechanic's lien
General and voluntary, since Gerald filed the tax return
General and involuntary, reaching all of Gerald's property
blocks.x: A federal tax lien arises by law, without Gerald's consent, and attaches to everything he owns, so it is general and involuntary. The tempting wrong answer is specific and involuntary: it gets the involuntary half right but confuses the IRS lien with liens tied to one property, like the pool contractor's. Filing a return is not consent to a lien.

blocks.html: Gerald is stunned by most of the list. He knew about the IRS: an early pension withdrawal he did not pay tax on, and a payment plan he stopped making. He forgot the 2015 car loan judgment entirely. He has never heard of Atlantic Card Services. And he is furious about the pool company.

In early 2026 Gerald had an above-ground pool replaced with an in-ground one to help the house sell. Blue Wave Pools finished the installation on March 10. Gerald withheld the last $28,000 because the coping cracked within a month. Blue Wave sent a technician on July 1 to look at the cracks; he left without fixing anything. Blue Wave then filed a notice of mechanic's lien with the Nassau County Clerk on August 20, listing July 1 as the date of last work, and mailed Gerald a copy the same week.

blocks.q: If the pool work was in fact completed on March 10, was Blue Wave's August 20 filing timely?
c: Yes, a contractor has 8 months after the last work to file
No, the single-family deadline was 4 months, so July 10
Yes, the clock started when Gerald refused the final payment
No, a lien had to be filed within 30 days of finishing the work
blocks.x: Under Lien Law section 10, a lien on a single-family dwelling must be filed within 4 months after the last work or materials, so a March 10 completion meant a July 10 deadline. The trap is 8 months, which is the general rule for other property. Blue Wave's July 1 date matters because a later "last work" date restarts the clock, but an inspection visit that fixes nothing is usually not lienable work.

blocks.html: Priya thinks the lien is late and probably invalid, and she can ask a court to discharge it. But that takes time, and the closing is in six weeks. Blue Wave also served Gerald properly: Lien Law section 11 requires service on the owner within 5 days before or 30 days after filing, with proof of service filed within 35 days, or the lien lapses. Blue Wave did both. The fastest path is to take the lien off the property and fight about the money later.

blocks.title: Discharging a mechanic's lien by bond
blocks.html: Under Lien Law section 19, the owner can discharge a lien on private property by filing an undertaking (a surety bond) for 110% of the lien amount with the county clerk and serving it on the lienor. The lien moves off the land and onto the bond. The contractor can still sue, and if it wins, it collects from the bond. The closing goes forward with clear title.

blocks.q: What face amount of bond must Gerald's surety post to discharge Blue Wave's $28,000 lien?
blocks.x: The undertaking must equal 110% of the lien: $28,000 x 1.10 = $30,800. $28,000 is the trap, the lien itself with no cushion. $56,000 reflects the rule that individual sureties must together be worth double the undertaking, which is a different requirement. $33,600 is 120%, a number from no rule here.

blocks.html: Gerald pays a surety a premium of about $1,200, and the bond is filed and served in ten days. Blue Wave does not object. Item 3 comes off the list. Gerald still owes Blue Wave a lawsuit, or a settlement, but not at the closing table.

A money judgment becomes a lien on the debtor's real property in a county once it is docketed with that county's clerk. Island Auto Credit's judgment was docketed in Nassau in March 2015. Priya checks the docket for a renewal judgment and finds none. Island Auto Credit never asked.

blocks.q: What is the status of item 4, the March 2015 Island Auto Credit judgment, in October 2026?
c: It no longer liens the house, since 10 years passed with no renewal
It is a valid lien until the debt is paid in full, however long that takes
It liens the house for 20 years, the period for enforcing judgments
It is a valid lien because Gerald did not inherit the house until 2019
blocks.x: A docketed judgment is a lien on New York real property for 10 years from docketing. The creditor can extend it only by suing for a renewal judgment in the year before the 10 years run out. Island Auto Credit did not, so the lien ended in March 2025. The trap is the 20-year answer: the judgment itself may still be enforceable against Gerald, but the real property lien expired.

blocks.title: New York's lien clocks
blocks.html: Three New York time limits decide whether an old item on Schedule B still matters. A mechanic's lien must be filed within 8 months of the last work (4 months for a single-family dwelling) and lasts 1 year unless enforced or extended. A docketed money judgment liens real property in that county for 10 years unless renewed. A notice of pendency lasts 3 years unless a court extends it.

Priya still asks the title company to omit item 4 and gives it the docket printout. The debt may be collectible from Gerald in other ways, but that is now his problem, not the buyers'. Item 5 is a different puzzle. Gerald's middle name is Thomas. He has never had an Atlantic Card account. The judgment debtor is "Gerald R. Pike," with an address in Hempstead.

blocks.q: How is item 5, the judgment against "Gerald R. Pike," normally cleared for closing?
c: Gerald pays it from the proceeds and sues to get the money back
Gerald signs an affidavit that he is not that judgment debtor
The buyers take title subject to it and buy extra title coverage
The court vacates it after Gerald files a motion in Hempstead
blocks.x: Title searches run by name, so judgments against people with similar names show up all the time. The fix is a sworn statement from the seller, often with ID and address history, that he is not the debtor named, and the title company omits the item. The trap is paying it: that wastes Gerald's money on someone else's debt. No court proceeding is needed against a judgment that was never his.

blocks.text: The IRS, the old lawsuit, and Mom's estate

blocks.html: The IRS lien is real and Gerald owes it. A federal tax lien attaches to every property he owns, and the notice filed with the county clerk makes it good against buyers and later lenders. Gerald asks whether the IRS gets paid before his bank.

blocks.q: How does the 2024 IRS lien rank against First Meadow's 2016 mortgage, and what happens to it at closing?
c: Ahead of the mortgage, since federal taxes come before private debts
Behind it, but it must be paid or discharged at closing
Behind the mortgage, so it can stay and follow Gerald to Florida
Equal with the mortgage, with both paid pro rata from the price
blocks.x: Apart from local real property taxes and assessments, liens generally rank by when they were recorded or filed, and the IRS notice came eight years after the mortgage. But a lien attaches to the property, so a buyer would take subject to it. It is paid from proceeds, or the IRS issues a certificate of discharge. The trap is assuming federal taxes always jump the line; that is the property tax rule, not the IRS rule.

blocks.html: Item 7 is a notice of pendency, which New York uses for what other states call a lis pendens. In 2022 Gerald's neighbor, Mrs. Maloney, sued over a fence she claimed was on her side of the line. A survey proved it was not, and she discontinued the case in 2023. Nobody filed anything to cancel the notice.

blocks.q: What is the effect of the June 2022 notice of pendency today?
c: It still binds buyers until Mrs. Maloney signs a release
It turned into a judgment lien when the case was discontinued
It has lapsed, though title will want it canceled of record
It binds the house for 10 years, the same as a docketed judgment
blocks.x: A notice of pendency is good for 3 years unless a court extends it, so this one lapsed in June 2025, and the case was discontinued anyway. A discontinued action is grounds for the court to cancel the notice, and title companies prefer a cancellation on the record. The trap is the 10-year answer, which borrows the judgment lien period. A notice of pendency is not a lien and never becomes one.

blocks.html: Item 8 is the one that surprises Marcus most. Gerald's mother, Dolores, died in 2018. Her executor, Gerald's late brother, deeded the house to Gerald in 2019. New York estate tax is a lien on a decedent's New York real property until it is paid or released. The 2019 deed was recorded with no release of lien, so the title company will not insure until that is fixed, even though the estate was probably far below the filing threshold.

blocks.q: What document will the title company most likely require to clear item 8?
c: A new executor's deed from Dolores's estate to Gerald
An IRS certificate of discharge covering Dolores's estate
A satisfaction of judgment from the Surrogate's Court
A Form ET-117 release of lien from the NYS Tax Department
blocks.x: The New York State Tax Department releases the estate tax lien on a decedent's real property with Form ET-117, filed with an estate tax return or, for an estate that owed no tax, a certification. The trap is a new executor's deed: the 2019 deed transferred title fine; what is missing is the state's release of its lien. An IRS discharge covers federal liens, not New York estate tax.

blocks.html: The Tax Department says to allow three to four weeks to process a release, plus mailing, and not to schedule the closing until the stamped release arrives. Priya files that afternoon. The closing slides from mid-November to early December. The buyers' attorney agrees in writing.

Item 9 looks like housekeeping: the second half of the 2026 school tax and a sewer district charge, $6,800 together. Nassau County bills general and school taxes separately, in halves, and special districts for sewers, water, garbage, and lighting add their own charges to the bill. Gerald let the school tax slide when his pension check was garnished by the IRS. Unpaid real property taxes and special assessments are specific, involuntary liens on this parcel alone, and they carry interest and penalties until paid. Marcus wonders aloud whether the newest charge on the report could really matter more than a ten-year-old mortgage.

blocks.q: The 2026 school tax and sewer district charge were levied ten years after First Meadow recorded its mortgage. How do they rank?
c: Ahead of the mortgage, since taxes and assessments come first
Behind the mortgage, because liens rank by recording date
Behind the mortgage, unless the county records a subordination
Ahead of the mortgage, but only for the school tax portion
blocks.x: Real property taxes and special assessments take first priority regardless of when they arose. Every mortgage is made subject to them, which is why lenders often collect taxes in escrow. The trap is "first in time, first in right": that rule ranks the private liens against each other, after taxes are paid. A special district charge on the tax bill is treated like the tax itself, not split off.

blocks.html: Marcus takes a lesson of his own from item 9 and the rest of the list. At the listing appointment he asked Gerald a yes-or-no question about liens and accepted the answer. A better habit is to order a preliminary title or lien search early for any seller with an estate in the chain, a business that failed, or a tax problem, so the surprises come before the house is in contract. Diane makes it office policy for inherited properties.

While waiting, Gerald mentions he tried to refinance First Meadow's mortgage in 2024 to lower his rate. The new lender backed out at the last minute, saying something about "the credit union." Jordan now understands why.

blocks.q: Why would Gerald's 2024 refinance lender insist on something from Harbor Federal, the 2021 home equity lender?
c: To get a subordination agreement putting the new loan ahead of the HELOC
To get a payoff letter, since a refinance must pay off every loan
To get the HELOC lender's consent, which every New York refinance requires
To get the HELOC moved behind the property tax lien on the house
blocks.x: A refinance pays off the old first mortgage and records a new one. Without an agreement, the new mortgage is recorded after the 2021 HELOC and ranks behind it. A subordination agreement, in which Harbor Federal agrees to stand behind the new loan, keeps the refinance in first position. The trap is a mandatory payoff: a borrower can keep a HELOC if its lender subordinates. Taxes already come first.

blocks.html: One non-money item remains in Schedule B: "Covenants and restrictions recorded by the original developer in 1949." Jordan reads the copy. Most of it is ordinary: one single-family dwelling per lot, a front setback, no livestock. One clause, typed in the same font as the rest, restricts occupancy by race. The buyers, who are Black, see it in the title package before Jordan can call them.

blocks.q: What is the legal effect of the 1949 race restriction, and of the rest of the covenants?
c: The whole declaration is void because one clause is illegal
The race clause binds until a court strikes it on the buyers' petition
The race clause is void; lawful ones like the setback can still bind
Both still bind, but only buyers from the original subdivision
blocks.x: Racially restrictive covenants have been judicially unenforceable since 1948 and violate federal and New York fair housing law. The clause is void and the buyers need no lawsuit. Lawful private restrictions in the same declaration, like the setback and single-family use, can still run with the land. The trap is voiding everything: courts strike the illegal clause and leave the rest.

blocks.title: "It's in the deed, so it must count"
blocks.html: Recording a document does not make it lawful. A race or religion restriction in an old deed or declaration is unenforceable, and a licensee who points to it, or treats it as a reason to steer anyone, is violating fair housing law. Jordan calls the buyers, explains that the clause is void, and that it appears only because title reports list everything of record. Their attorney adds that they can never be bound by it.

The stamped ET-117 release arrives in late November. Priya builds the seller's side of the closing statement. To keep the math clean for Gerald, she ignores prorations and leaves the surety premium off, since he paid it in October.

blocks.title: Gerald's simplified seller's statement
blocks.html:
Contract price: $640,000
Less NYS transfer tax ($2 per $500, 0.4%): $2,560
Less brokerage commission per listing agreement: $32,000
Less seller's attorney fee: $2,000
Less First Meadow Bank payoff: $398,500
Less Harbor Federal HELOC payoff: $46,200
Less IRS federal tax lien payoff: $19,500
Less unpaid school tax and sewer charge: $6,800
Items 3, 4, 5, 7, and 8: cleared without payment at closing
Net to Gerald: ?

blocks.q: What are Gerald's net proceeds from the statement above?
blocks.x: $640,000 minus $2,560, $32,000, $2,000, $398,500, $46,200, $19,500, and $6,800 leaves $132,440. $120,040 is the trap: it also pays the expired 2015 judgment. $151,940 forgets the IRS lien, which must be paid because it attaches to the house. $104,440 pays Blue Wave's $28,000, although the bond already took that lien off the property.

blocks.html: Gerald grumbles about the IRS and the school tax, but $132,440 buys the Florida condo outright. After closing, Priya's office sends the payoff checks and tracks the satisfactions: First Meadow and Harbor Federal must deliver recordable satisfactions of their mortgages, and the IRS issues a certificate of release once it is paid.

Back in the office, Diane asks Jordan a what-if. Suppose Gerald had stopped paying First Meadow instead of selling, and the bank had foreclosed. New York foreclosures are judicial, and a referee's sale wipes out liens junior to the foreclosing mortgage, as long as those lienholders were named in the action.

blocks.q: If First Meadow foreclosed on its 2016 mortgage, which item would survive the referee's sale and bind the buyer at auction?
c: The 2021 Harbor Federal home equity line mortgage
The 2024 IRS notice of federal tax lien
The unpaid school tax and sewer district charge
The bonded Blue Wave Pools mechanic's lien
blocks.x: Real property taxes and assessments are senior to every private lien, so a mortgage foreclosure cannot cut them off; the auction buyer takes subject to them. The HELOC and the IRS lien are junior to the 2016 mortgage and are wiped out as liens if properly named, though the IRS has special notice and redemption rights. The trap is the bonded mechanic's lien: it is no longer on the land at all.

items: Sort every lien two ways: general or specific, voluntary or involuntary. The mortgage and HELOC are voluntary and specific; IRS liens and judgments are involuntary and general.
A mechanic's lien on a single-family home must be filed within 4 months of the last work (8 months for other property) and can be taken off the land with a bond for 110% of the lien.

A docketed judgment liens New York real property for 10 years unless renewed. A notice of pendency lasts 3 years unless extended and is never a lien itself. Similar-name judgments are cleared by affidavit.

Property taxes come first; other liens generally rank by recording or filing date. A subordination agreement lets a later loan move ahead, and a foreclosure wipes out junior liens but never the taxes.
An estate tax lien on inherited New York real property is cleared with a Form ET-117 release. Discriminatory deed restrictions are void, while lawful ones in the same document can still bind.

lessons.title: Case file: The Path to Keuka Lake
lessons.tagline: The listing promised "deeded lake rights." The survey found a porch over the line, a neighbor's shed, a hunter's shortcut, and a path nobody had used in fifteen years.
objectives: Decide what an appurtenant right of way carries, how far its scope reaches, and whether it has been abandoned or merged.
Distinguish an easement by necessity, a prescriptive claim, and a license on a set of upstate facts.
Apply New York's adverse possession rules, including the de minimis encroachment rule, to encroachments found on a survey.
Identify what a buyer's title insurer and lender will require before an encroachment or easement problem is cured.

blocks.title: A cottage with "deeded lake rights"
blocks.html: Ana and Rafael Delgado, Jordan's clients from Park Slope, want a summer place in the Finger Lakes. They fall for a shingled cottage on the west side of Keuka Lake, in Yates County, listed at $485,000 by a Penn Yan broker named Carol Whitcomb. Jordan refers them to Carol, who will work as their buyer's agent there, and stays on the phone as the family's sounding board. The cottage sits uphill on West Lake Road and does not touch the water. The listing says "deeded lake rights with dock." Below the cottage, a lakefront lot owned by the Hollis family separates it from the shore. The Delgados ask Jordan the obvious question before they make an offer: if the lake is on someone else's land, what exactly are they buying?

Carol emails the sellers' 1978 deed. The cottage parcel (Lot 2) came with an express grant over the lakefront parcel (Lot 1). In easement language, Lot 2 is the dominant tenement and the Hollis lot is the servient tenement.

blocks.title: 1978 deed to Lot 2, the appurtenance clause
blocks.html: "TOGETHER WITH a right of way ten (10) feet in width, for ingress and egress on foot, over and across the northerly ten feet of Lot 1 as shown on the map hereinafter referred to, from the westerly line of Lot 1 to the shore of Keuka Lake, and the right to construct, maintain and use one (1) seasonal dock at the shore at the end of said right of way, for the benefit of the owners from time to time of Lot 2."

blocks.q: The sellers' attorney drafts a new deed that describes Lot 2 but forgets to mention the right of way. Do the Delgados still get it?
c: No, an easement must be restated in every deed to survive
No, unless the Hollis family signs a new grant to the Delgados
Yes, an easement appurtenant passes with Lot 2 automatically
Yes, but only for the remaining years of the original grant
blocks.x: An easement appurtenant belongs to the dominant land and transfers with it, even if a later deed is silent; the standard "together with the appurtenances" language carries it anyway. The trap is the restatement answer. Good practice is still to describe the easement in the new deed so the record is clear, and Priya will ask for that. The 1978 grant states no term, so it is not limited in years.

blocks.html: The grant is a right of way on foot plus one seasonal dock. The Delgados like that. Rafael pictures a boathouse. Ana pictures a swim float. Before anyone pictures anything else, Jordan wants to know who owns the shoreline itself.

blocks.q: Who holds the littoral rights that come with owning land along this part of the Keuka Lake shore?
c: The Hollis family, subject to the dock easement
The Delgados, since their deed mentions the lake
Both lots equally, since both reach the water
The State of New York, which owns all shorelines
blocks.x: Littoral rights (the rights of an owner bordering a lake) belong to the owner of the land that touches the water, here Lot 1. The Delgados get only what the grant gives: passage on foot and one seasonal dock. The trap is assuming the lake mention makes them shore owners. Lot 2 does not touch the water, and the state's interest in navigable waters does not make it the owner of private upland.

blocks.html: That answers Rafael's boathouse question, too, at least in theory. An easement holder may use the servient land only for the purpose and in the manner the grant describes. A heavier, different, or permanent use needs the servient owner's agreement.

blocks.q: After closing, Rafael wants to build a boathouse and a second dock at the end of the right of way. What does the 1978 grant allow?
c: Both, because the easement includes reasonable lake access
The boathouse, since it replaces the dock at the same spot
Both, as long as the Delgados pay Lot 1's added property tax
One seasonal dock only, unless the Hollis family agrees to more
blocks.x: The scope of an express easement is set by its terms. This one grants foot passage and one seasonal dock, so a boathouse and a second dock would overburden the servient land. The trap is "reasonable lake access," which reads the grant more broadly than it was written. Paying a share of taxes does not enlarge an easement; only a new written grant from the Hollis family does.

blocks.html: Carol walks the property with the Delgados. The deeded ten-foot strip along the north edge of Lot 1 is a thicket of sumac and wild grape. Nobody has walked it in at least fifteen years. The sellers, Hal and Judy Ostrander, used a shorter mowed path through the middle of the Hollis lawn instead, and kept their dock at the bottom of that path. Glen Hollis, 70, stops by during the showing. Friendly but firm, he says the deeded strip "was abandoned years ago" and the mowed path "was always a favor from my dad."

blocks.q: Is the deeded right of way over the north strip extinguished because nobody used it for fifteen years?
c: Yes, nonuse for 10 years extinguishes any easement in New York
No, nonuse alone does not abandon an easement created by grant
Yes, because the Ostranders chose a different path instead
No, because a recorded easement can never be terminated
blocks.x: In New York, abandonment of an easement created by grant needs more than nonuse: there must be intent to abandon shown by some clear act, such as a written release or conduct that unmistakably gives it up. Using a more convenient path with the owner's blessing is not that. The trap is the 10-year nonuse rule, which borrows the prescription period. Recorded easements can end, by release or merger, for example.

blocks.html: Glen's second point is about the mowed path. The Ostranders and the owners before them crossed the middle of the lawn every summer since at least 1999, which is longer than New York's 10-year period for an easement by prescription. Glen produces a yellowed letter from his father, dated May 1999: "Hal, Judy: use the lawn path to your dock whenever you like. Happy to have you. Walt."

blocks.q: Do the Ostranders, and through them the Delgados, have a prescriptive easement over the mowed lawn path?
c: Yes, 27 years of open, continuous use is more than enough
Yes, because the Delgados can tack the sellers' years of use
No, the written permission means the use was never hostile
No, because a prescriptive easement requires exclusive use
blocks.x: Prescription requires use that is open, notorious, continuous for 10 years, and hostile, meaning without the owner's permission. Walt Hollis's 1999 letter made the use permissive, so the clock never ran. The trap is the 27 years: duration alone does not create an easement. Tacking is real but cannot cure permission, and exclusivity is an adverse possession element that prescription does not require.

blocks.html: So the Delgados will have a legal right to the overgrown strip and a friendly neighbor's permission for the lawn. Priya suggests a cleaner deal, and Glen likes it: a recorded relocation agreement moving the right of way from the north strip to the lawn path, signed by both owners. Until then, the Delgados can clear the deeded strip, since an easement holder may maintain the way to make it usable.

blocks.text: Parking, and a hunter in the side yard

blocks.html: The cottage has room for one car. On busy weekends the Ostranders parked a second car on the Hollis lawn by the road. Glen says the Delgados can do the same, "long as I'm here." Nothing is in writing.

blocks.q: What is the Delgados' right to park on the Hollis lawn?
c: A license Glen can revoke, ending if he sells
An easement by implication, from the Ostranders' long use
An easement appurtenant that passes with the cottage
A prescriptive easement, once 10 summers have passed
blocks.x: Oral permission to do something on another's land is a license: a personal privilege, not an interest in land, revocable at will and ended by the owner's sale or death. The trap is implication, which requires a use that existed when a single owner split one parcel into two, not a neighbor's later courtesy. Because the use is permitted, no number of summers turns it into a prescriptive easement.

blocks.html: Jordan points out that a license is fine for a weekend guest and fragile for anything the Delgados count on. If a second parking space matters to them, the fix is to buy it: a written, recorded parking easement from the Hollis family, appurtenant to Lot 2, so it survives a sale of either lot. Glen is open to it for a modest price once they close. For now, the Delgados decide one car plus a bicycle rack will do.

Then the survey arrives, and with it a dotted line Carol has never noticed: a worn track runs from West Lake Road along the south edge of Lot 2 and into the woods behind it. Hal Ostrander explains. Dale Morse, a retired mail carrier, owns the four wooded acres behind the cottage (Lot 5) and drives his truck through the Ostranders' side yard to reach them in deer season. Morse's land has no road frontage at all.

blocks.title: Chain of title notes, Lots 2 and 5 (from the abstract)
blocks.html:
Until 1990: Lots 2 and 5 were one 5-acre parcel owned by Edna Frey, with frontage only on West Lake Road.
1990: Frey conveys the rear 4 acres (now Lot 5) to Dale Morse. Deed silent on access.
1993: Frey's estate conveys the front parcel (now Lot 2) to the Ostranders. Deed silent on Morse's access.
Today: Lot 5 is bordered by Lot 2, a state forest, and two private parcels. No public road touches it.

blocks.q: Can the Delgados block Dale Morse from crossing Lot 2 after they buy it?
c: Yes, his deed was silent, so he has no right of access
Yes, unless Morse has crossed for 10 years without permission
No, he holds an easement in gross for hunting access
No, he likely holds an easement by necessity over Lot 2
blocks.x: When one owner splits a parcel and the piece sold off has no access except across the piece retained, the law implies an easement by necessity over the retained land. Frey's 1990 split left Lot 5 landlocked, so Lot 2 carries the burden. The trap is the silent deed: necessity easements arise precisely when the deed says nothing. An easement in gross would benefit Morse personally, not his land.

blocks.html: Priya adds a refinement that matters for the Delgados' future. An easement by necessity lasts only as long as the necessity. Morse's daughter has been negotiating to buy a strip of one of the private parcels that touches County Road 14.

blocks.q: If Morse's family buys a strip that gives Lot 5 its own road access, what happens to the easement across Lot 2?
c: It continues, since an easement once created is permanent
It ends, because the necessity has ended
It continues until the Delgados buy a written release
It converts into a license that the Delgados can revoke
blocks.x: An easement by necessity exists only because the land is landlocked. When the dominant parcel gains other access, the necessity ends and so does the easement. The trap is permanence: that describes most express easements, which end only by release, merger, or another recognized method. The Delgados need not buy a release, though a recorded acknowledgment from Morse would tidy the record.

blocks.html: The title report lists a 1971 easement to New York State Electric & Gas for an overhead distribution line across the rear of Lot 2. Rafael wants to build a two-car garage in that corner, and the line runs right over it.

blocks.q: What is the effect of the recorded utility easement on Rafael's garage plan?
c: None, since an easement in gross ends when the land is sold
None, since the utility must move its line at its own expense
He cannot build where it interferes with the line
He can build only after 10 years of the utility's nonuse
blocks.x: A commercial easement in gross, like a utility line, burdens the servient land no matter who owns it, and the servient owner may not interfere with its purpose. Building under the line would violate clearance requirements and the easement. The trap is that easements in gross end on sale: personal easements in gross may end with the holder, but commercial ones are assignable and run with the burdened land.

blocks.html: Rafael moves the garage to the north side of the lot. If he wanted the line moved, he would have to ask the utility and usually pay for the relocation himself. The easement itself will outlast everyone involved. A commercial easement in gross is freely assignable, so if the utility sells its distribution system or merges with another company, the right to keep the line there goes with it. A personal easement in gross, like Glen letting a friend fish from his dock, is the kind that usually ends with the person.

The survey shows two more problems, and they point in opposite directions. First, the cottage's screened porch, built in 1985, extends 1.8 feet over the north line onto Lot 3, owned by the Fennimore family. The Ostranders always believed a stake that marked the corner of their porch was the line. Second, the Fennimores' wire fence and a small garden shed sit 4 feet inside Lot 2, along the south line, and have for about fifteen years.

blocks.q: Can the Fennimores claim title to the 4-foot strip of Lot 2 under their fence and shed by adverse possession?
c: Yes, they have held it openly and continuously for 15 years
No, fences and sheds are treated as permissive in New York
Yes, but only the land under the shed, not under the fence
No, because adverse possession requires 20 years upstate
blocks.x: Since 2008, RPAPL 543 deems de minimis non-structural encroachments, including fences, hedges, plantings, sheds, and non-structural walls, to be permissive and non-adverse. Without hostility there is no adverse possession, no matter how long they stay. The trap is the 15-year answer, which counts years without testing the element. The New York period is 10 years everywhere in the state; the old 20-year figure is not current law.

blocks.html: The porch is different. It is a structure, part of the house, built in 1985 and occupied openly, exclusively, and continuously for over 40 years. The Ostranders had a reasonable basis to believe the land was theirs, the corner stake, which is what New York's claim of right element requires. They very likely acquired the 1.8-foot sliver by adverse possession decades ago. But the deed still describes the old line.

blocks.title: Adverse possession in New York after 2008
blocks.html: RPAPL 501 requires possession that is adverse, under claim of right, open and notorious, continuous, exclusive, and actual, for the 10-year statute of limitations. A claim of right means a reasonable basis for believing the property belongs to the possessor. Title vests when the 10 years run, but it is not record title until a court says so in a quiet title action (RPAPL Article 15) or the record owner signs a deed.

blocks.q: The Delgados' lender wants the porch issue resolved before closing. What will satisfy the title insurer most directly?
c: An affidavit from the Ostranders that they have used the porch since 1985
A new survey moving the line to match the porch, filed with the county
A note in the contract that the Delgados accept the encroachment
A recorded deed or boundary agreement from the Fennimores for the strip
blocks.x: A title insurer wants record title. The fastest way to get it is a deed or boundary line agreement from the record owner of the sliver, recorded; the alternative is a quiet title judgment. The trap is the Ostranders' affidavit: it supports an adverse possession claim but does not put title of record. A surveyor cannot move a legal boundary, and a buyer's acceptance leaves the lender's problem unsolved.

blocks.html: The Fennimores sign. In exchange, the Ostranders give them a matching deed for the 4-foot strip under the fence and shed, so the record lines finally match what everyone has used for years. Both deeds are recorded with the Yates County Clerk before closing. The Delgados close at $472,000, a $13,000 credit reflecting the legal costs and the overgrown right of way.

blocks.title: "A title search would have caught that"
blocks.html: None of the porch, the fence, the shed, the lawn path, the parking, or Morse's track appears in a title search, because none of them is a recorded document. They are physical facts. A survey and a walk of the land find them. Buyers who skip the survey to save money upstate, where lots are bigger and lines are fuzzier, buy these problems without knowing it.

Glen Hollis decides to move to his daughter's house in Rochester and offers the lakefront Lot 1 to the Delgados before listing it. Ana asks two questions. The first is about the view: Glen once mentioned that a buyer might put a two-story boathouse at the shore, right in front of their porch.

blocks.q: If someone else bought Lot 1 and built a tall boathouse, would the Delgados have a right to keep their lake view?
c: Yes, 40 years of an unobstructed view creates a light and air easement
Yes, the dock easement includes a right to see the dock from Lot 2
No, a view easement exists only by express grant, and they have none
No, because views are protected only inside New York City limits
blocks.x: New York does not create easements for light, air, or view by prescription or long enjoyment. A view is protected only by an express written grant or a restrictive covenant, typically bought and recorded. The trap is the 40-year answer, which treats a view like a path that can ripen by use. The dock easement gives passage and a dock, not an unobstructed sightline.
