blocks.html: The second question is the one Priya was waiting for: if the Delgados buy Lot 1, what happens to the right of way they now hold over it?

blocks.q: The Delgados buy Lot 1. Five years later they sell Lot 2 alone. Does the new owner of Lot 2 have the old right of way to the lake?
c: No, merger ended it unless the Delgados grant a new one
Yes, the 1978 easement revives automatically on the split
Yes, because it was recorded and is still in the chain
No, unless the new owner uses it for 10 more years
blocks.x: When one owner holds both the dominant and servient parcels, the easement ends by merger, since nobody needs an easement over their own land. It does not spring back when the parcels are later separated. The trap is automatic revival because the old grant is still of record. If the Delgados sell Lot 2 later, Priya will write a new right of way into that deed.

blocks.html: Priya also reminds them what merger does not affect. The utility easement over the back of Lot 2 and Dale Morse's old necessity route are separate interests held by other people, and owning both lake lots changes nothing about them. Merger only ends an easement when the same owner holds both the benefit and the burden of that particular easement.

They buy Lot 1 the next spring. The dock moves to the bottom of the lawn path, now on land they own, the sumac strip goes back to sumac, and Dale Morse, who finally bought his road strip, waves from his truck on County Road 14.

items: An easement appurtenant passes with the dominant land even if a later deed omits it, but its scope is limited to the terms of the grant. Littoral rights stay with the land that touches the water.
Nonuse alone does not abandon an easement created by grant. Written permission defeats a prescriptive claim, and oral permission creates only a revocable license.
Splitting a parcel that leaves one piece landlocked creates an easement by necessity, which ends when the necessity does. Commercial easements in gross, like utility lines, bind every later owner.

Under RPAPL 543, fences, sheds, hedges, and plantings over a line are permissive and cannot support adverse possession; a structural encroachment held 10 years under a claim of right can. Record title still needs a deed or a court judgment.
New York creates no view or light and air easements by long use. When one owner acquires both parcels, the easement ends by merger and does not revive on a later split.

lessons.title: Case file: The Driveway on Lot 38
lessons.tagline: A father deeds his Hollis house to his daughter with an online form. Three years later she tries to sell it, and the garage turns out to belong to someone else: him.
objectives: Decide whether a deed actually conveyed a parcel by reading its legal description against the tax map and a survey
Apply the rules on grantor signature, delivery, acknowledgment, and agency authority to a family transfer
Determine what a gift deed owes in transfer taxes and which returns are still filed
Identify who must sign the contract and the deeds when title to one house sits in two names

blocks.title: The listing that was bigger than the deed
blocks.html: Simone Clarke, a nurse in Hempstead, wants to sell the house she grew up in on 196th Street in Hollis, Queens. Her father, Desmond, is 81, sharp as ever, and now lives in an assisted living residence in Jamaica. In 2023 he signed a deed giving her the house, on a form a neighbor downloaded. Simone signs an exclusive listing with Jordan at Hudson & Hart. Jordan measures the yard, photographs the long private driveway and the detached garage in back, and drafts an MLS listing: “58 x 100 lot, private driveway, one-car garage.” Diane reads it and asks one question: “Have you seen the deed?”

Jordan pulls the 2023 deed from ACRIS, the City Register's online records. It is a bargain and sale deed from Desmond Clarke to “Simone Clark.” The consideration clause reads “Ten dollars and love and affection.” The legal description runs four courses, about 40 feet by 100 feet, and ends with “Being known as Block 10512, Lot 37 on the Tax Map of the City of New York, County of Queens.” There is no mention of Lot 38.

Priya, Simone's attorney, orders a title report. It explains the gap. Desmond and his late wife Marjorie bought Lot 37, with the house, in 1979. In 1991 Desmond alone bought an 18-foot strip next door, tax Lot 38, from the estate of a neighbor. The driveway and the garage sit on that strip. The 2023 deed copied the 1979 description and never touched Lot 38.

head: Tax lot
Size
What is on it
Owner of record
blocks.caption: What the title report shows

blocks.q: Simone wants the listing to stay live as written. What should Jordan do?
c: Keep the listing as is, because one family controls both lots and the buyer gets the same house either way
List Lot 37 and the house now, and add Lot 38 once Desmond deeds it or joins the sale as a seller
Keep the 58-foot listing but add a note that the driveway and garage are shared with an adjoining owner
Take the listing down entirely until Simone files a quiet title action to merge the two tax lots into one
blocks.x: Simone can only contract to sell what she owns, and today that is Lot 37. Advertising 58 feet with a garage she does not own misrepresents the property. The fix is simple: Desmond is alive and competent, so he can deed Lot 38 or sign the contract too. Calling the driveway “shared” is the trap: it is not shared, it is Desmond's, and the description would still be wrong.

blocks.html: Jordan pulls the listing back to “40 x 100, house only, see broker” for a week and calls Desmond. He laughs. “I thought the house was the house. The driveway came with it in my head.” He is happy to give Simone the strip. Before anyone signs anything, Priya wants a survey, because a deed is only as good as the description it carries.

blocks.title: Listing intake: four papers before the photos
blocks.html: Before you write a single line of a listing, pull four things: the vesting deed from ACRIS (or the county clerk), the tax map page showing every lot the seller uses, the most recent property tax bill (it names the tax lot being billed), and any survey the seller has from their own purchase. Then walk the property with the tax map in hand. A driveway, a side yard, or a garage that sits on a second lot shows up fast. Ten minutes here saves a dead deal at the title report.

blocks.text: Metes, bounds, and an iron pipe

blocks.title: The 1991 deed for Lot 38 (description, condensed)
blocks.html: BEGINNING at a point on the westerly side of 196th Street, distant 140 feet southerly from the corner formed by 196th Street and 104th Avenue; running thence westerly at right angles to 196th Street, 100 feet; thence southerly parallel with 196th Street, 18 feet to an iron pipe; thence easterly parallel with the first course, 100 feet to 196th Street; thence northerly along 196th Street, 18 feet to the point or place of BEGINNING. Said premises being Lot 112 on a certain map entitled “Map of Hollis Park Gardens,” filed in the Office of the Register of Queens County. Also known as Block 10512, Lot 38.

The surveyor finds the iron pipe 18.6 feet south of the line it should mark, not 18. The garage's south wall sits 18.4 feet from that line. Measured by the numbers, the garage pokes 0.4 feet onto the neighbor at Lot 39. Measured to the pipe, it fits.

blocks.q: The deed calls for “18 feet to an iron pipe,” and the pipe is found at 18.6 feet. Where is the boundary?
c: At 18 feet, because the stated distance is the more precise and reliable part of the call
Split the difference at 18.3 feet, since both parts of the call are in the deed
At the iron pipe, because a monument controls over a conflicting distance
Wherever the neighbor's own deed puts it, since the later deed governs
blocks.x: When a call names both a measurement and a physical monument, the monument wins. A surveyor in 1991 set that pipe on the ground, and courts trust what was marked over a number typed into the deed. Choosing the 18 feet is the trap: it feels more exact, but the distance is the part most likely to be an error. Here the rule saves the garage.

blocks.html: Priya's paralegal asks a sharper question: is a filed map reference even a real description? It is. A reference to a recorded plat pulls in every measurement on the filed map, so “Lot 112 on the Map of Hollis Park Gardens” would locate the strip on its own. The tax lot number is different. Block and lot on the NYC tax map is an assessment tool, which is why NYC deeds carry the full metes and bounds and then add the tax lot as an extra identifier.

blocks.q: A buyer's attorney asks which part of the 1991 deed is a legally sufficient description of the strip by itself. Which is the best answer?
c: The metes and bounds and the filed map lot, each of which would locate the land on its own
The tax lot by itself, because the City's tax map is the official record of parcel boundaries
The metes and bounds alone, because filed subdivision maps are not used in New York City
The street address and tax lot together, because New York abolished metes and bounds in 1991
blocks.x: A metes and bounds walk that closes is a full description, and so is a lot on a recorded subdivision map, because the map supplies the measurements. The tax lot is a useful cross-reference for the assessor and ACRIS, not a boundary source. The tax-lot-only choice is the trap: tax maps are redrawn and lots are merged or split for billing, which is exactly why deeds do not rely on them alone.

blocks.html: Now someone has to sign a deed for Lot 38. Simone tells Priya she can handle it herself. She holds her father's New York statutory short form power of attorney, signed in 2022, and she would rather not drag him to a notary. She proposes signing the deed for Lot 38 as “Desmond Clarke, by Simone Clarke, his attorney in fact,” conveying the strip to herself.

blocks.q: Can Simone use the power of attorney to deed Lot 38 to herself?
c: Yes, because an agent under a statutory short form may do any act the principal could do himself
Yes, but only after the power of attorney is recorded in ACRIS ahead of the deed
No, because a power of attorney stops working once the principal moves into a care facility
Only if the document expressly gives her authority to make gifts, including gifts to herself
blocks.x: Under New York's power of attorney law, an agent may not make gifts of the principal's property, and especially not to herself, unless the document expressly grants gift authority. Real estate powers let an agent sell for value, not give the house away. Recording matters for a deed signed by an agent, but it does not create authority that is missing. Moving to assisted living ends nothing; only death or revocation or incapacity under a nondurable form would.

blocks.html: Priya reads the form. No gift authority. Even if it had been there, she would want Desmond to sign: he is competent, he is the grantor, and a gift signed by the grantor himself is hard to attack later. (When an agent does sign a deed properly, on an arm's length sale, the power of attorney is recorded along with the deed so the chain of title shows where the agent's authority came from.) Who else has to sign? Simone wonders whether her mother's estate does, since her parents owned the house together.

blocks.q: Who must sign the new deed conveying Lot 38 to Simone?
c: Desmond and Simone, because the grantee signs to accept a gift of land
Desmond alone, because he took Lot 38 in his own name in 1991
Desmond and the executor of Marjorie's estate, because the couple owned the house as spouses
Desmond and his other children, because a gift to one child needs the others' consent
blocks.x: Only the grantor signs a deed, and the grantor here is the sole owner of record, Desmond. Marjorie never owned Lot 38. (She did own Lot 37 with Desmond as tenants by the entirety, so at her death in 2017 it passed to him by survivorship, with no estate involved.) The grantee's signature is the trap: the grantee accepts a deed by taking it, and New York presumes acceptance of a beneficial gift.

blocks.text: Delivery, and a notary who wasn't

blocks.html: Priya drafts a bargain and sale deed for Lot 38 and brings it to the residence on a Thursday. Desmond reads every word, signs, and then folds it into his jacket. “I'll put it in my lockbox at the bank,” he says. “When I'm gone, Simone gets it. No reason to make a fuss while I'm here.” Simone is sitting right there.

blocks.q: If Desmond keeps the signed deed in his lockbox to take effect at his death, what does Simone own?
c: Lot 38, because the deed was signed in her presence, which counts as delivery
Lot 38, but she cannot sell or mortgage it until the deed is recorded after his death
Nothing yet, because the deed was never delivered with intent to pass title now
A life estate in Lot 38, with Desmond keeping the remainder interest
blocks.x: Title passes on delivery and acceptance: the grantor must intend to give up control now. A deed held back to take effect at death shows the opposite intent. It is really an attempted will, and it fails because it lacks will formalities. Being present at the signing is the trap: watching someone sign is not delivery. The deed has to leave the grantor's control, to the grantee or to an escrow agent with no right to recall it.

blocks.html: Priya explains it gently, and Desmond hands the deed to Simone across the table. Delivered and accepted. But Priya catches a second problem before they leave. The residence's activities director signed at the bottom as a “witness.” She is not a notary. The deed has no acknowledgment.

blocks.q: What is the effect of the missing acknowledgment?
c: The deed is void, because an unacknowledged deed transfers nothing in New York
The deed is valid once the witness signs a sworn affidavit and files it with the City Register
The deed is valid for one year, after which it has to be acknowledged or re-signed
The deed works between Desmond and Simone, but it cannot be recorded until he acknowledges it
blocks.x: Acknowledgment is the grantor's sworn statement before a notary or other officer that the signature is his and voluntary. It is not needed for validity between the parties. It is needed to record, and recording is what protects Simone against the rest of the world. Calling the deed void is the trap. A fix is easy: Desmond acknowledges his signature before a notary, and the deed can then be recorded.

blocks.html: Priya has a mobile notary at the residence the next morning. Desmond acknowledges, the notary completes the certificate, and Priya prepares the recording package: the acknowledged deed, the NYS transfer tax return (Form TP-584-NYC), the NYC RPT return, and the RP-5217NYC real property transfer report, all prepared through ACRIS and submitted with the recording fees. Once the City Register accepts it, the deed gets a City Register File Number (CRFN) that every future title search on the strip will cite. That number, not the paper in Simone's drawer, is what tells the world she owns it.
Simone asks what the gift will cost. “Is there a tax on giving your kid a driveway?” The deed recites “Ten dollars and love and affection.” No money changes hands, and Lot 38 carries no mortgage.

blocks.q: What transfer tax filing is required for the gift deed of Lot 38?
c: No transfer tax is owed, but the NYS and NYC transfer tax returns are still filed with the deed
Transfer tax is owed on the strip's market value, since a gift is measured by fair value
No returns are needed, because a deed with no consideration is exempt from every filing
Simone pays the mansion tax as grantee, because the transfer completes a house worth more than $1 million
blocks.x: The NYS transfer tax and the NYC RPTT are measured by consideration. A true gift with no money and no mortgage has none, so no tax is due. The returns are still filed (New York City requires the RPT return even when the tax is zero), and the deed will not record without them. Market value is the trap: transfer taxes follow the price paid, not what the land is worth.

blocks.title: Where a Queens deed goes
blocks.html: In Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens, deeds are recorded with the Office of the City Register (NYC Department of Finance) through ACRIS, along with the NYS and NYC transfer tax returns and the real property transfer report (RP-5217NYC). Staten Island records with the Richmond County Clerk. Elsewhere in the state, it is the county clerk.

blocks.q: Priya's paralegal asks where to record the acknowledged deed for Lot 38. Where does it go?
c: The Queens County Clerk, because Queens is its own county with its own clerk
The Queens Surrogate's Court, because the deed is a gift within a family
The NYC Office of the City Register, through ACRIS
The NYS Department of State, Division of Licensing Services
blocks.x: In four of the five boroughs, the City Register records deeds and mortgages, and ACRIS is the filing and search system. The Queens County Clerk is the trap: county clerks record deeds everywhere upstate and on Long Island, and Richmond County (Staten Island) still does, but Queens land records moved to the City Register. Surrogate's Court handles wills and estates, not deeds.

blocks.html: The deed records. Now title work for the sale turns up a smaller wrinkle. Simone's 2023 deed names “Simone Clark.” Her driver's license, her bank account, and the new deed for Lot 38 say “Simone A. Clarke.” The buyer's title company wants to be sure the woman selling is the woman who took title.

blocks.q: What will the title company most likely require to clear the name variance?
c: A new deed from Desmond to Simone for Lot 37, re-signed and re-recorded under her correct name
A Surrogate's Court order confirming that Simone is Desmond's daughter
A quiet title action naming every person called “Simone Clark” in the county
An affidavit that she is one and the same person, recited in her deed to the buyer
blocks.x: A spelling variance between how someone took title and how they sign later is common and cheap to fix. Title companies take a same-name affidavit, and the deed out recites “Simone A. Clarke, who acquired title as Simone Clark.” That keeps the chain of title readable. A corrective deed from Desmond is the trap: it would work, but it is unnecessary when an affidavit does the job.

blocks.html: One more item sits on Schedule B of the title report: a 1958 agreement, recorded, giving the owner of Lot 39 a right to use the first 30 feet of the Lot 38 driveway to reach a side door. The online-form deed Simone's lawyer would draft for the sale has a short “subject to” clause that lists only zoning and the street lines.

blocks.q: If the sale deed's “subject to” clause leaves out the 1958 driveway agreement, what happens to the neighbor's right?
c: It ends, because a deed conveys everything not expressly excepted in it
It survives, because a recorded easement runs with the land and binds the buyer
It survives if the neighbor sends the buyer written notice of the easement within one year
It becomes a license that the buyer may revoke at any time after closing
blocks.x: A recorded easement gives constructive notice and stays with the land no matter what a later deed says. Leaving it out of the “subject to” clause does not erase it. It only sets up a fight, because the contract usually promises title free of encumbrances except those listed. The “deed conveys everything” answer is the trap: a seller cannot convey more than she owns, and a neighbor's easement is not hers to give away.

blocks.title: Copying last time's description
blocks.html: Most bad family deeds in New York are not fraud. They are copies. Someone pastes the description from the old deed, misses a second parcel bought later, or drops a strip that was merged on the tax map but never in a deed. Before you list, compare the deed, the tax map, and what the seller thinks they own. If the three disagree, the seller's attorney fixes it before the photos go up.

With the Lot 38 deed recorded, Jordan relists at the full 58 by 100 with driveway and garage, now accurate. Three weeks later Kwame Mensah, a transit engineer renting in Jamaica, offers $1,060,000, and Simone accepts. Kwame's attorney reads the title report, sees two deeds into Simone two years apart, and sends Priya an email: “Since the father owned the strip until recently, we want him to sign the contract and the deed too, belt and suspenders.”

blocks.q: How should the sale be papered now that Simone holds record title to both lots?
c: Simone and Desmond both sign the contract and deed, because he owned Lot 38 within the past three years
Simone signs the contract and one deed describing both parcels, and Desmond signs nothing
Simone signs for Lot 37, and Desmond signs a separate deed for Lot 38 to bring it back into the chain
Simone signs both, but not until Desmond records a quitclaim releasing any remaining interest in the lots
blocks.x: The seller is whoever holds title now. Simone owns both lots by delivered, acknowledged, recorded deeds, so she alone signs the contract and a single deed with two descriptions (Parcel I and Parcel II). Desmond has nothing left to convey. Having him sign anyway is the trap: it is harmless only in the sense that it does nothing, and it invites the question of why the buyer doubts the gift. If title is in doubt, the fix is title insurance, not extra signatures.

blocks.html: Priya answers with the recorded deeds and the title company's commitment to insure. Kwame's attorney drops the request. The sale deed describes Lot 37 as Parcel I and Lot 38 as Parcel II, each by metes and bounds, and recites the 1958 driveway agreement in the “subject to” clause. Simone pays NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT on the full $1,060,000. Kwame pays the mansion tax, 1% or $10,600, because the residential price crossed $1,000,000. Desmond comes to the closing anyway, by car service, to shake the hand of the man who now owns his garage.

blocks.q: At what moment does Kwame own the house and the strip?
c: When Simone signs the deed in front of the title closer
When the title closer records the deed with the City Register in ACRIS
When the City's tax map is updated to show Kwame as the owner
When Simone delivers the deed and Kwame accepts it at closing
blocks.x: Ownership passes when a signed deed is delivered and accepted. Signing alone does nothing until the grantor lets go of the deed with intent to transfer. Recording is the trap: it usually happens days later, and it protects Kwame against later buyers and creditors under the race-notice statute, but title had already passed at the table. The tax map just follows the recorded deed.

items: Check the deed against the tax map and the seller's story before you list. A house can sit on two tax lots with two owners.
A full description stands on its own: a closed metes and bounds walk, or a lot on a recorded plat. The tax lot is a cross-reference. When a distance and a monument disagree, the monument controls.
Only the grantor signs. An agent under a power of attorney cannot give the principal's land away, even to herself, without express gift authority.
No delivery, no transfer. A deed kept to take effect at death is a failed will. Acknowledgment is not needed for validity, but no acknowledgment means no recording.
A gift deed owes no transfer tax, but the returns are still filed. Recorded easements survive whatever the next deed leaves out.

lessons.title: Case file: Five Deeds in One Month
lessons.tagline: A condo in Park Slope, an estate in Yonkers, an auction in the Bronx, a divorce in Massapequa, and a farmhouse in Saratoga. Same month, five different deeds, and each one promises something different.
objectives: Decide which form of deed fits a sale by an owner, an executor, a court referee, a bank, or a departing spouse
Determine what each deed's covenants promise and which covenant a given title defect breaches
Choose the right remedy for a title defect: a covenant claim against the seller, a title insurance claim, or neither
Explain why foreclosure is involuntary alienation and what a referee's deed does not wipe out

blocks.title: Diane's whiteboard
blocks.html: It is the first Monday of March at Hudson & Hart. Diane writes five addresses on the whiteboard: a condo on Fifth Avenue in Park Slope, a colonial in Yonkers, a two-family in the Bronx going to auction, a ranch in Massapequa, and a farmhouse outside Saratoga Springs. “Every one of these closes or gets signed this month,” she says, “and every one uses a different deed. By April, Jordan, you'll be able to tell me why.” Jordan's first stop is the condo, where the buyer's attorney has just sent an email that starts with “My client wants a real deed.”

blocks.text: Park Slope: the standard New York deed

blocks.html: Rafael Ortiz, Jordan's buyer, is paying $1,180,000 for a two-bedroom condo on Fifth Avenue. The seller, Ingrid Holm, has owned it since 2014. Her attorney's draft deed is the New York standard: a bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts. Rafael's attorney, who trained in Texas, asks for a general warranty deed instead. Ingrid's attorney replies in one line: “Not in this city.”

blocks.title: The covenant in Ingrid's draft deed
blocks.html:
“AND the party of the first part covenants that the party of the first part has not done or suffered anything whereby the said premises have been encumbered in any way whatever, except as aforesaid.”

Translation: I have not encumbered this property during my ownership. Nothing about what happened before 2014.

blocks.q: What does Ingrid's covenant protect Rafael against?
c: Any defect in the title back to the original grant, because a bargain and sale deed warrants the full chain
Liens and encumbrances that Ingrid herself created or allowed while she owned the unit
Nothing, since a bargain and sale deed with covenant is the same as a quitclaim
Defects found within one year of closing, after which title insurance takes over
blocks.x: The covenant against grantor's acts is limited to Ingrid's own watch: a mortgage she signed, a judgment against her, a contractor she didn't pay. It says nothing about owners before 2014. The full-chain answer is the trap: that is the promise of a full covenant and warranty deed. And it is not a quitclaim either, because a quitclaim makes no promise of any kind.

blocks.html: Rafael's attorney pushes once more, then drops it. The reason is on the title bill. Rafael is buying an owner's title insurance policy for the full price. A New York seller who sells and moves to Lisbon is a poor source of money for a defect discovered in 2031. A title insurer with reserves is a better one.

blocks.q: Why do most New York residential buyers accept a bargain and sale deed with covenant instead of insisting on full warranties?
c: Because New York law forbids full covenant and warranty deeds in residential sales of 1 to 4 family homes
Because full warranties are implied in every New York deed by statute regardless of the form used
Because a seller's warranties end at closing, when the purchase price is paid out to the seller
Because the owner's title policy covers older defects, and an insurer can actually pay
blocks.x: In New York practice, protection comes from the title insurer, not from the seller's promises. A seller's warranty is only as good as the seller's ability to pay years later. The statutory-ban answer is the trap: full covenant and warranty deeds are perfectly legal here, and some upstate sellers still use them. They are simply rare downstate, where buyers rely on title insurance.

blocks.html: Eighteen months after closing, a stranger sues Rafael. The heir of a 2009 owner, two owners before Ingrid, claims the 2009 deed out of his father was forged by a relative, and he wants the unit back. Rafael calls Jordan in a panic.

blocks.q: Where does Rafael turn first?
c: To his owner's title insurer, since a pre-policy forgery is a covered risk
To Ingrid, on her covenant against grantor's acts, because she sold him the unit
To the city, because the City Register accepted and recorded the forged satisfaction
To Hudson & Hart, because Jordan represented him as the buyer's agent in the purchase
blocks.x: A forged document in the chain before the policy date is a classic covered risk. The insurer defends Rafael and pays any loss up to the policy amount. Ingrid is the trap: her covenant reached only what she did after 2014, and the forgery is from 2009. The recording office does not guarantee what it records; recording gives notice, not a warranty of genuineness.

blocks.html: The Yonkers colonial belonged to Vincent Antonelli, who died last spring. His will names his son Paul as executor, gives the house to his three children equally, and gives the executor power to sell real property. The Westchester County Surrogate's Court has admitted the will to probate and issued letters testamentary to Paul. The buyer's attorney asks who will sign the deed.

blocks.q: Who signs the deed conveying the Yonkers house to the buyer?
c: The three children, because they are the devisees who inherited it under the will
The Surrogate's Court clerk, because the estate is still open in probate
Paul, as executor, under his letters testamentary and the will's power of sale
Paul and his two siblings together, each signing as both devisee and heir
blocks.x: An executor's deed is signed by the executor in that capacity, and the letters testamentary are the proof of authority the title company will want. The will's power of sale lets Paul sell without asking the court. Having all three children sign is the trap: it can work when there is no power of sale, but here it is unnecessary, and the title company will insure off Paul's deed and letters.

blocks.html: The same logic ran through the listing. When Hudson & Hart took the Yonkers listing in the fall, Paul signed the exclusive listing agreement as executor, and the file held a copy of his letters testamentary. His siblings were kept informed, but they were not the sellers. Had Paul signed the listing before the court issued letters, the firm would have been taking instructions from someone with no legal power yet to sell, and its commission claim would have been shaky.

Paul's deed recites that he signs “as Executor of the Last Will and Testament of Vincent Antonelli.” The buyer's attorney notices the covenant clause is short. Paul covenants only that he, as executor, has not encumbered the property.

blocks.q: Why does an executor's deed promise so little?
c: Because executors are personally liable for every title defect, so the law limits the deed's wording
Because an executor's deed is a form of quitclaim, and quitclaims carry the same limited covenant
Because the executor never owned the property and can only speak to his own acts as fiduciary
Because the probate court has already guaranteed the estate's title when it issued letters testamentary
blocks.x: Paul is a fiduciary, not a long-time owner. He can honestly promise only that he did nothing as executor to encumber the house. The probate answer is the trap: letters testamentary prove Paul's authority to act, not that his father's title was clean. The buyer still needs a title search and title insurance.

blocks.title: Executor or administrator
blocks.html: With a will, the Surrogate's Court issues letters testamentary to the executor, who conveys by executor's deed. Without a will, it issues letters of administration to an administrator, who conveys by administrator's deed. Both deeds carry the same narrow fiduciary covenant. Licensees who list estate property should ask for a copy of the letters at the listing appointment: no letters, no one with authority to sign.

blocks.text: The Bronx: a referee and an auction

blocks.html: Marcus has an investor client, Delroy Grant, who wants to bid at a foreclosure auction for a two-family on Gun Hill Road. The auction happens on the courthouse steps under a judgment of foreclosure and sale. A court-appointed referee runs the sale and will sign the deed. Marcus tells Delroy, “Referee's deed, court-approved, clean as a whistle.”

blocks.q: What does a referee's deed promise the buyer about title?
c: No personal covenants; it conveys what the court-ordered sale can convey
Full warranties, because a court ordered the sale and stands behind its result
That the property is free of every lien, because the foreclosure judgment wipes the record
A covenant against grantor's acts covering the borrower's period of ownership
blocks.x: A referee's deed is signed by a court officer who never owned the property and makes no personal promises. It conveys the interest the judgment authorized the referee to sell. The “court stands behind it” answer is the trap, and it is exactly Marcus's mistake. Bidders buy subject to whatever the foreclosure did not cut off, so they search title before the auction, not after.

blocks.html: Jordan reads the notice of sale over Marcus's shoulder. The foreclosing lender holds a second mortgage, a $90,000 home equity line from 2021. A first mortgage of about $410,000 from 2017 is not being foreclosed.

blocks.q: If Delroy buys at this auction, what happens to the 2017 first mortgage?
c: It is paid in full from the auction proceeds before the second lender gets anything
It is wiped out, because a foreclosure sale extinguishes every mortgage on the property
It converts into a personal debt of the old borrower and leaves the property entirely
It survives, and Delroy takes title subject to the senior first mortgage
blocks.x: Foreclosing a junior lien cuts off the borrower's interest and liens junior to the one foreclosed. It does not touch a senior lien, which keeps its priority. Delroy would own a two-family that still secures a $410,000 loan. The wipe-out answer is the trap: it is true only for interests junior to the foreclosing lender. Bid amounts at a junior foreclosure must account for the senior debt.

blocks.html: Delroy lowers his bid ceiling by $410,000 and is outbid. Marcus is annoyed. Diane is not. “The only bad auction,” she says, “is the one you win without reading the notice.” Her checklist for any bidder: order a title search before the sale, read the judgment and the terms of sale, find out whether any senior mortgage survives, and ask who pays unpaid real estate taxes and water charges. Those municipal charges outrank even a first mortgage, and many terms of sale have the referee pay them from the proceeds, but a bidder confirms that in writing rather than assuming it. Occupants are the last question: a buyer at auction may inherit tenants with their own legal protections.

blocks.q: A foreclosure that ends with a referee's deed is an example of:
c: Voluntary alienation, because the owner signed the mortgage years earlier
Involuntary alienation, because title passes without the owner's consent
Escheat, because the court takes the property for the public
Dedication, because the sale is held on public courthouse steps
blocks.x: Involuntary alienation is a transfer the owner does not choose at the time: foreclosure, tax sale, eminent domain, partition, adverse possession. The voluntary answer is the trap. Signing the mortgage was voluntary, but the later transfer of title happens against the owner's will. Escheat is the state taking property when no heirs exist.

blocks.html: Lena and Tom Brady-Ruiz are divorcing. Their Massapequa ranch is held as tenants by the entirety, and the settlement gives the house to Lena. Tom will sign a quitclaim deed to her, which their attorneys will record with the Nassau County Clerk. Tom asks Jordan, who sold them the house in 2019, a practical question: “Once I sign this, I'm off the mortgage, right?”

blocks.q: What does Tom's quitclaim do to his obligation on the mortgage?
c: Nothing; he stays liable on the note until a release or a refinance
It releases him, because he no longer owns any interest in the house
It releases him once the deed is recorded and the lender is sent a copy
It shifts half of the remaining debt to Lena and leaves the other half on Tom
blocks.x: A deed moves title. The note is a separate personal promise to the lender, and the lender is not a party to the deed. Tom remains liable until Lena refinances in her own name or the lender signs a release. The “I no longer own it” answer is the trap, and it is the most common post-divorce surprise. Jordan should point Tom to his attorney and his lender, not answer the legal question himself.

blocks.html: Their attorneys add a refinance deadline to the settlement. Then a second issue: Tom's brother, who once lived in the basement, offers to sign a quitclaim too, “just in case he has rights.” He never had any interest of record.

blocks.q: If Tom's brother signs a quitclaim deed to Lena, what does she receive from him?
c: A one-third interest, because a quitclaim conveys a share of the title by default
A full warranty from him that the title is good
Whatever interest he had, which appears to be nothing
An easement to keep using the basement entrance
blocks.x: A quitclaim releases whatever interest the grantor has, if any, with no promise that there is any. If the brother owns nothing, nothing passes, and nothing is lost by taking it. That is why quitclaims are used to clear possible claims and clouds. The warranty answer is the trap: a quitclaim is the only deed with no covenants at all.

blocks.text: Saratoga Springs: the full set of promises

blocks.html: The last whiteboard address is a farmhouse in the town of Greenfield, outside Saratoga Springs. The seller, Martin Kessler, is a retired attorney who insists on giving a full covenant and warranty deed, because that is what his father gave. The buyers, Ji-woo and Dan Park, are cash buyers who decline an owner's title policy. Their attorney gets an abstract update and gives an opinion of title. (Upstate, many closings still run on an abstract of title: a bound, updated history of every recorded document affecting the land, which the buyer's attorney reads before writing an opinion on whether title is marketable.) Seven months after closing, a 1979 mortgage to a long-gone savings bank turns up, never satisfied, and the bank's successor sends a letter.

head: Covenant
What Martin promised
Breached by the 1979 mortgage?
rows: I own the estate I am conveying
No one with better title will disturb you
Only if the lender actually enforces it
No liens or encumbrances except those listed
Yes, the day the deed was delivered
I will sign whatever is needed to perfect your title
I will defend your title against all lawful claims
Triggered if the claim is pressed
blocks.caption: Martin's five promises, tested against one old mortgage

blocks.q: Which covenant was breached at the moment Martin delivered the deed?
c: The covenant of seizin, because Martin's ownership was subject to a lender
The covenant of quiet enjoyment, because the Parks received a letter
No covenant, because the mortgage was recorded years before Martin ever bought the property
The covenant against encumbrances, because the open mortgage existed at delivery
blocks.x: The covenant against encumbrances promises no liens except those listed, and the 1979 mortgage was on the record at delivery. It was breached the day of closing. Seizin is the trap: Martin did own the land, so his promise of ownership was true. A full covenant deed reaches back through the whole chain, so it does not matter that the mortgage predates Martin.

blocks.html: Martin pulls out his father's papers and finds a canceled 1994 check marked “final payment” to the old bank. The successor bank agrees the loan was paid, but it needs a document signed for the record, and Martin must provide an affidavit of payment and the canceled check.

blocks.q: Which covenant obligates Martin to sign the affidavit and help get the satisfaction recorded?
c: Quiet enjoyment
Further assurance
Seizin and right to convey
Warranty of title forever
blocks.x: The covenant of further assurance is the grantor's promise to sign whatever is reasonably needed to perfect the grantee's title. It fits exactly here. Warranty forever is the trap: it obligates Martin to defend the Parks if someone actually asserts the claim in court, while further assurance covers the paperwork that keeps it from getting there.

blocks.title: More covenants, more protection, more risk to collect
blocks.html: The full covenant and warranty deed is the best deed on paper. It is only as good as the grantor. Martin is solvent, nearby, and cooperative. If he had died, the Parks would be chasing his estate. That is why even upstate buyers who receive full warranties usually also buy owner's title insurance: the deed tells you who promised, the policy tells you who pays.

blocks.text: Canarsie: the bank that promises nothing

blocks.html: Back in Brooklyn, Jordan's last March closing is a bank-owned house in Canarsie. The bank took title at its own foreclosure sale and is now selling. Its deed form is a bargain and sale deed without covenants. Jordan's buyers, first-timers, ask whether that is a red flag. The bank's contract rider adds that the house is sold as is, with no representations about condition or occupancy, and that the bank will not cure title objections beyond a set dollar amount.

blocks.q: Why does the bank sell with a bargain and sale deed without covenants?
c: Because banks are barred by federal law from giving deed warranties on residential property
Because a deed without covenants removes the need for a title search before closing
Because the property is sold as is, and covenants apply only to the physical condition
Because the bank never lived there and won't warrant title it took by foreclosure
blocks.x: A bargain and sale deed without covenants implies the grantor holds title but makes no promises about it. Banks, investors, and some estates use it because they never lived in the property and will not stand behind its history. The “no title search” answer is the trap: less promised by the seller means more reliance on the buyer's own search and title insurance, not less.

blocks.title: One more promise in every New York deed
blocks.html: New York deeds carry the Lien Law Section 13 covenant: the grantor will receive the sale money as a trust fund to be applied first to paying the cost of any improvement, and will apply it to that before using any part of it for anything else. It protects contractors who improved the property shortly before the sale.
Diane spots it on Ingrid's Park Slope deal. Ingrid renovated the kitchen in January, and her contractor's final invoice of $18,500 is still open.

blocks.q: What does the Lien Law covenant in Ingrid's deed require her to do with the sale proceeds?
c: Pay the open improvement cost from the proceeds before any other use
Hold $18,500 in her attorney's escrow for one year in case the contractor sues
Give Rafael a credit of $18,500 at closing so he can pay the contractor himself
Nothing, because the covenant applies just to new construction sold by a sponsor
blocks.x: The covenant makes the sale money a trust fund for improvement costs, so the contractor gets paid first. Ingrid's attorney simply pays the invoice out of the proceeds at closing, which also keeps a mechanic's lien from appearing against Rafael's unit. The credit answer is the trap: the obligation is the seller's, and the buyer should not be left to settle the seller's construction bills.

head: Property
Grantor
Deed
What the grantor promised
Where the buyer's real protection came from
rows: Nothing done by me as executor
blocks.caption: Six deeds, ranked by promises, and who actually protected each buyer

blocks.q: Which of the March buyers received the most protection from the deed itself?
c: Rafael, because his bargain and sale deed carried a covenant against Ingrid's acts
Delroy's competitor, because a court-ordered sale carries the court's own warranty
The Parks, because a full covenant and warranty deed warrants the entire chain
Lena, because a quitclaim between spouses passes the entire marital interest
blocks.x: The full covenant and warranty deed sits at the top of the deed ladder: five covenants, reaching back through the whole chain of title. Rafael's covenant is the trap. It is the New York standard, but it covers only Ingrid's own acts. Notice the gap between “protection from the deed” and real protection: the Parks had the best deed and no insurance, and they were rescued by a cooperative seller.

blocks.caption: Place each March deal on a rung. Then notice how many buyers at the bottom rungs were still well protected by title insurance.

items: New York's standard residential deed is the bargain and sale with covenant against grantor's acts. It covers only the seller's own ownership period; title insurance covers the rest.
Fiduciaries sign in their capacity: an executor with letters testamentary, an administrator with letters of administration, a referee under a judgment. None of them warrants the chain.
A referee's deed conveys what the foreclosure cut off, which never includes liens senior to the one foreclosed. Foreclosure is involuntary alienation.
A quitclaim passes whatever the grantor has, possibly nothing, and does not release anyone from a mortgage note.
Match the defect to the covenant: an existing lien breaches the covenant against encumbrances at delivery; further assurance makes the grantor sign the fix; warranty makes him defend.
Every New York deed carries the Lien Law Section 13 trust fund covenant: recent improvement costs come out of the sale money first.

lessons.title: Case file: The House on Titus Avenue
lessons.tagline: A mother dies without a will, one son never leaves the house, the tax bills stop getting paid, and a lake lot arrives from an uncle's will addressed to someone who is already gone.
objectives: Apply New York's intestate succession rules to find each heir's share, including grandchildren who take by representation
Decide who has authority to sign a deed for a decedent's real property, with and without a will
Analyze an heir's adverse possession and partition threats against co-heirs, and the risk of a county tax foreclosure
Apply the will vocabulary (devise, devisee, probate, anti-lapse, escheat) to a real estate inheritance

blocks.title: A call from Carla
blocks.html: Carla Whitaker is Jordan's buyer client, hunting for a co-op in Flatbush. In April 2026 she calls with a different problem. Her mother, Delores, died in January 2025 in the house where Carla grew up, a three-bedroom on Titus Avenue in Irondequoit, just outside Rochester. Delores never made a will. Carla's brother Andre has lived with their mother since 2012 and still lives there. “Andre says the house is his now,” Carla says. “He also hasn't paid the taxes. Can you sell it for us? And whose is it?”

Jordan gets the family facts on paper. Delores was a widow; her husband died in 2008. She had three children: Andre, 52, Carla, 47, and Kevin, who died in 2019 and left two children, Tiana, 24, and Jalen, 16. The house is in Delores's name alone, mortgage-free, and worth about $190,000. She died intestate, so New York's intestate succession statute (EPTL 4-1.1) decides who takes.

blocks.q: What share of the house does each person take?
c: Andre and Carla one-half each, because Kevin died before his mother
Andre, Carla, Tiana, and Jalen one-quarter each, because each is a living descendant of Delores
Andre, Carla, and Kevin's line one-third each, with Tiana and Jalen splitting Kevin's third
Andre the whole house, because he is the oldest child and was living there
blocks.x: With no spouse, the children take, and a child who died first is represented by his own children. Each child's line gets one-third; Tiana and Jalen share Kevin's third, one-sixth each. The one-half answer is the trap: a predeceased child's share does not vanish when he leaves children. The equal-quarters answer misreads representation, which splits by family line first.

head: Heir
Relationship
Share
Can sign a deed today?
rows: Yes, as an adult, for his own share only
Yes, as an adult, for her own share only
Yes, as an adult, for her own share only
blocks.caption: The heirs of Delores Whitaker (New York calls them distributees)

blocks.html: Andre disagrees. He produces a sheet of notebook paper in his mother's handwriting, dated 2023, that says “The house goes to Andre, he took care of me.” It is signed “Mom.” Nobody witnessed it.

blocks.q: What is the effect of the handwritten note?
c: It is not a valid will, so the house still passes by intestacy
It is a valid will, because it is entirely in Delores's handwriting and signed by her
It gives Andre a life estate, with the remainder passing to the other heirs
It is valid if two family members swear in Surrogate's Court that it is genuine
blocks.x: A New York will must be signed at the end and witnessed by at least two witnesses. An unwitnessed handwritten (holographic) will counts only for members of the armed forces in wartime and mariners at sea. The handwriting answer is the trap: some states accept holographic wills, New York does not. The note may explain Delores's wishes, but it does not change who inherits.

blocks.html: So four people own the house, and they own it together. Jordan asks Diane how. Diane draws two columns: heirs who take by intestacy hold as tenants in common, each with an undivided share, no survivorship.

blocks.q: How do the four heirs hold title, and what happens if Carla dies next year?
c: As joint tenants, so Carla's share passes to the other three by survivorship
As tenants by the entirety, because they are members of one family
In severalty, with the house held in the name of the oldest heir until it is sold
As tenants in common, so Carla's one-third passes through her own estate
blocks.x: Title by descent creates a tenancy in common: separate undivided shares, each one inheritable and transferable. Joint tenancy is the trap. It requires the four unities plus express survivorship language in the deed, and New York presumes a tenancy in common for co-owners who are not spouses. Tenancy by the entirety is only for married couples.

blocks.html: Andre's next idea: he will sign a deed himself, since he lives there. Carla's idea: the three adults sign a deed together and “figure out Jalen's part later.” A title company in Rochester gives Jordan a one-line answer to both: “We need an administrator.”

blocks.q: Why does the title company insist on an administrator instead of a deed from the adult heirs?
c: Heirs can never convey inherited real property in New York without first going through probate
Jalen is a minor and cannot sign, so only a court-appointed fiduciary can convey it all
A deed from heirs is valid only after the estate has paid the state's estate tax in full
Andre lives in the house, so he must sign alone as the heir in possession of the property
blocks.x: The adults can each convey their own shares, but no buyer wants five-sixths of a house. Jalen cannot sign a deed, and nobody has authority to sign for him without the court. The Surrogate's Court appoints an administrator through letters of administration, who can sell the whole property by administrator's deed. The probate answer is the trap: probate is for wills. With no will, the process is administration.

blocks.html: Jordan asks the obvious follow-up: if the heirs already own the house, why do they need anyone's permission? Diane explains the two layers. Under New York law, Delores's real property passed to her distributees at the moment she died, which is why Andre, Carla, Tiana, and Jalen are already co-owners. But the estate also has debts, funeral bills, and now taxes, and the administrator is the person the law empowers to collect, pay, and, when needed, sell. A buyer's title insurer wants one signature it can rely on, backed by a court's letters, not three adult signatures and a promise about the minor's share.

blocks.title: Listing an estate property: what to ask for
blocks.html: Before you take an estate listing, ask for the death certificate, the letters (testamentary if there is a will, of administration if not), the name of the estate's attorney, and a list of everyone living in the property. The person who signs your listing agreement must be the fiduciary named in the letters, signing in that capacity. A relative with the keys is not a seller. If no letters have issued, you can advise the family to see an attorney, but you have no one with authority to list.

Carla files for letters of administration in Monroe County Surrogate's Court. Andre, Tiana, and Jalen's mother (as his guardian) are served. When there is no will, the court picks the administrator from the distributees in an order of priority set by statute, spouse first, then children, and any adult child is eligible. Andre objects, saying he should serve because he lives in the house, but living in the property gives no priority, and his unpaid tax bills do not help his case. The court appoints Carla as administrator in July. Andre is furious. Then the tax bills arrive.

The town and county bills for 2025 and 2026 were never paid. Neither was the 2025 school bill. The county treasurer has sent a notice. In most towns around Rochester the school tax runs on a July to June fiscal year and is billed in September, while the town and county tax runs on the calendar year and is billed in January, so a family that misses one bill tends to miss both. Interest and penalties start running right away, and they will come off the top of any sale. In New York, unpaid real property taxes are a lien with priority over almost everything, and counties enforce them by in rem tax foreclosure: a proceeding against the property itself, which ends with the county taking title and usually selling it at auction.

blocks.q: Andre says the county “can't take the house while the estate is open.” What should Carla understand about the tax foreclosure risk?
c: The county may foreclose and take title, leaving the owners only a claim to any sale surplus
The county must wait until the estate closes, because an estate is immune from tax enforcement
The county can add penalties but cannot foreclose on property owned by heirs who are still minors
The county can foreclose only after the property has been vacant for at least two full years
blocks.x: A tax foreclosure is involuntary alienation: title passes to the county without the owners' consent. Since the U.S. Supreme Court's 2023 decision in Tyler v. Hennepin County, New York counties must let former owners claim surplus auction proceeds, and a 2024 state law set up that process. But an auction price can be well below market value. Paying the taxes from estate funds or the sale is far better than collecting a surplus later.

blocks.html: Carla, as administrator, has no estate cash. She asks Jordan the faster question: how quickly can the house be sold so the taxes are paid at closing? First, she has to deal with Andre.

Andre's lawyer sends a letter with two arguments. First, Andre has lived in the house for 14 years, so he owns it by adverse possession. Second, if the others will not sign the house over to him, he will sue for partition and force a sale on his terms.

blocks.q: How strong is Andre's adverse possession claim against his co-heirs?
c: Strong, because he has lived there openly and continuously for more than 10 years
Strong, because he took care of his mother, which shows a claim of right to the house
Weak, because adverse possession cannot be claimed against a decedent's estate at all
Weak, because a co-tenant's possession is presumed to benefit all co-owners
blocks.x: Two problems sink it. His years with his mother were with her permission, so they were never hostile. And since her death he has been a co-tenant; RPAPL 541 presumes one co-tenant's occupancy is possession for all of them until 10 years of exclusive occupancy pass, after which the ordinary 10-year clock can start, about 20 years in all. The 14-year answer is the trap: it counts permissive time and ignores the co-tenant rule.

blocks.html: Jordan gets a call from Andre that evening. He does not want legal advice; he wants to know if he could just buy the house. He can. Nothing stops an heir from buying from the estate at a fair price with his own mortgage, and his one-third share could count toward the price by agreement. Jordan tells him that is a question for his lawyer and Carla's, and that a lender would want an appraisal and an administrator's deed like any other buyer would. Andre says he will think about it. He never applies. Partition is a real tool. Any co-tenant can ask a court to divide the property or, when it cannot be divided fairly (a single house cannot), to order a sale and split the proceeds. But New York gives inherited family property extra protection.

blocks.title: Heirs property and partition
blocks.html: New York adopted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (RPAPL 993) in 2019. When a partition action involves “heirs property,” such as a house held as tenants in common by relatives who inherited it, the court must determine the property's value, the other co-tenants get a chance to buy out the co-tenant who sued, and the court can require good faith settlement efforts before any sale. It exists because forced partition sales stripped many families, often Black families, of inherited land at bargain prices.

blocks.q: If Andre sues to partition, what happens first under New York's heirs property rules?
c: The court orders an immediate public auction, with the proceeds split by share
The court awards the house to Andre as the co-tenant who lives there
The court values it, and the other co-tenants may buy out Andre's share
The court dismisses the case, because heirs property cannot be partitioned
blocks.x: The heirs property law slows partition down: value first, then a buyout right for the co-tenants who did not sue, then a sale only if that fails. The auction answer is the trap: that was the old pattern the law was written to prevent. Partition is still available; it is just harder to use as a weapon. Andre's lawyer, reading the statute, recommends a negotiated sale instead.

blocks.html: In September the family agrees: Carla, as administrator, sells the house, the taxes come off the top, and each heir gets a share of the net, with Jalen's share protected under court supervision until he turns 18. Andre gets a moving allowance from the estate and a share of the furniture. Now Carla asks Jordan to list it.

blocks.q: Jordan is licensed in New York but has never sold a house in Monroe County. What is the best course?
c: Decline to help, because a Brooklyn salesperson's license is not valid upstate
Refer Carla to a Rochester-area broker, with a broker-to-broker referral fee
List it personally, because a New York license is statewide and competence is not required
Have Carla list it herself and pay Jordan a finder's fee directly at closing
blocks.x: A New York license is statewide, so Jordan could legally list it, but reasonable care includes knowing the local market. A referral to a Rochester broker serves Carla better, and brokers may pay each other referral fees. Any fee to Jordan must flow through Hudson & Hart, never directly from a client. The “license not valid upstate” answer is the trap: licenses are not regional.

blocks.html: The Rochester broker lists at $195,000. A buyer offers $189,500, and the Surrogate's Court-appointed administrator accepts. Carla signs the contract “as Administrator of the Estate of Delores Whitaker.” She will convey by administrator's deed, which, like an executor's deed, carries only a covenant that she has not encumbered the property while serving.

blocks.title: Seller's transfer tax at $189,500 (outside New York City)
blocks.html:
1. NYS real estate transfer tax: $2 per $500 of consideration.
2. $189,500 / $500 = 379 units exactly.
3. 379 x $2 = $758, paid by the estate as grantor.
4. No NYC RPTT (outside the city) and no mansion tax (under $1,000,000).
5. The deed is recorded with the Monroe County Clerk, with Form TP-584 and the RP-5217 real property transfer report ($125 filing fee for residential property).

blocks.q: At closing, what does the estate pay in New York State transfer tax?
blocks.x: At $2 per $500, $189,500 is 379 units, or $758. The estate pays it because the grantor pays the NYS tax. $1,895 is the trap: it is 1% of the price, the mansion tax rate, and the mansion tax does not apply below $1,000,000 (and it would be the buyer's). $379 is half the right figure, as if the rate were $1 per $500.

blocks.html: The closing happens in December at the buyer's attorney's office in Pittsford. The administrator's statement shows how the money moves. The estate's net is then split by the intestate shares, under the Surrogate's Court's supervision.

head: Item
Amount
rows: Less: broker's commission (6%, split with the referring broker by agreement)
Less: unpaid 2025 and 2026 town, county, and school taxes with interest
Less: estate attorney's fees and court costs
Less: moving allowance to Andre (family agreement)
Net to the estate for distribution
blocks.caption: Estate of Delores Whitaker: proceeds of the Titus Avenue sale

blocks.q: How much of the $160,032 net goes to Jalen, and how is it handled?
c: $40,008, paid to his mother at closing as his one-quarter share
$53,344, held under court supervision until he turns 18
$26,672, held under court supervision until he turns 18
$26,672, paid to Andre, who lived with the family longest
blocks.x: Jalen's share is one-sixth: half of his father Kevin's one-third. $160,032 / 6 = $26,672. Because he is a minor, the court controls how his money is held, usually in a restricted account or with a guardian of the property, until he turns 18. $53,344 is the trap: it is a full one-third share, which belongs to each of Andre and Carla, not to each of Kevin's children.

blocks.text: A lake lot from Uncle Harold

blocks.html: In November, a letter arrives from a Canandaigua law firm. Delores's brother, Harold, died in October with a will. It leaves his vacant lake lot near Canandaigua Lake “to my sister Delores Whitaker” and names his friend Pete Lindgren as executor. Harold's will has been offered for probate in Ontario County Surrogate's Court.

blocks.q: In Harold's will, what are the gift of the lake lot and Delores's role called?
c: A devise, with Delores as the devisee
A bequest, with Delores as the legatee
A descent, with Delores as an heir
A dedication, with Delores as the grantee
blocks.x: A gift of real property by will is a devise, and the person named to receive it is the devisee. A bequest or legacy is a gift of personal property by will, which is the trap: the vocabulary is the same idea, applied to the wrong kind of property. Descent and heirs describe intestacy, which does not apply because Harold left a will.

blocks.html: But Delores died first. Does the gift fail? Normally a gift to a beneficiary who dies before the testator lapses. New York's anti-lapse statute (EPTL 3-3.3) makes an exception when the beneficiary was the testator's child, descendant, brother, or sister and left issue of her own.

blocks.q: Who takes the lake lot?
c: Harold's residuary beneficiary, because the gift to Delores lapsed when she died first
Delores's issue by representation: Andre, Carla, and Kevin's children
Delores's estate, to be distributed by Carla as administrator along with the house
The State of New York, because the named devisee is no longer living
blocks.x: Delores was Harold's sister and left descendants, so the gift does not lapse. It vests in her issue by representation: one-third each to Andre and Carla, and one-sixth each to Tiana and Jalen. Her own estate is the trap: anti-lapse passes the gift directly to her issue, not through her estate. Pete, as executor, will convey to them by executor's deed once letters testamentary issue.

blocks.html: Pete obtains letters testamentary in Ontario County in January and conveys the lake lot by executor's deed to Andre, Carla, Tiana, and Jalen, recorded with the Ontario County Clerk. They hold it as tenants in common, in the same one-third, one-third, one-sixth, one-sixth shares. This time the family talks before anyone threatens anyone. They decide to keep the lot until Jalen turns 18 and then vote on selling it.

blocks.title: Escheat is the last resort, not the default
blocks.html: Escheat sends property to the State of New York only when a person dies without a valid will and without any distributees at all, down through first cousins in the statute's order. A lapsed gift does not escheat; it falls into the will's residuary clause, or into intestacy if there is no residuary clause. Exam writers love to offer escheat for any death where the named person is gone. Run the chain of relatives first.

blocks.q: Suppose Harold had died with no will, no spouse, no descendants, no parents, no siblings or their issue, and no grandparents, aunts, uncles, or cousins. What happens to the lake lot?
c: It escheats to the State of New York
It passes to Pete, his friend, as the person closest to him
It is sold at a county tax auction
It passes to Ontario County, where the land sits
blocks.x: With no will and no distributees anywhere in the statute's order, the property escheats to the State. Friends take nothing under intestacy, however close. The county answer is the trap: escheat runs to the state, and a county tax auction is a different process triggered by unpaid taxes, not by the lack of heirs.

items: Intestacy follows EPTL 4-1.1. With no spouse, children take by family line, and a predeceased child's children share that child's portion.
New York requires two witnesses for a will. An unwitnessed handwritten note does not change intestate succession.
Heirs take as tenants in common. To sell the whole, especially with a minor heir, you need an administrator (no will) or executor (will) with letters from the Surrogate's Court.

Co-heirs rarely win adverse possession against each other: RPAPL 541 presumes possession is for all co-tenants for 10 years. Partition of inherited family homes runs through the heirs property law's buyout steps.
Unpaid taxes can end in county tax foreclosure, involuntary alienation where the family may recover only a surplus. Pay them out of the sale.
A gift of land by will is a devise to a devisee. Anti-lapse saves gifts to a predeceased child, descendant, or sibling for that person's issue. Escheat happens only when there is no one.

lessons.title: Case file: Nine Exceptions on Schedule B
lessons.tagline: A Ditmas Park Victorian, a seller in Florida, a title report with nine exceptions, and a lender that changes the loan three days before closing. Every one of them has to be cleared at one table on Court Street.
objectives: Read a New York title report and decide how each exception is cleared before or at closing
Distinguish what an owner's policy, a lender's policy, and the seller's deed each protect against
Apply the Closing Disclosure timing rules and the walk-through to last-minute changes
Explain who records what after closing and why the title closer runs a final search on closing day

blocks.title: The report arrives
blocks.html: Farida and Daniel Haque, both teachers, are buying a 1905 Victorian on Rugby Road in Ditmas Park for $1,385,000, with a $1,108,000 loan. Jordan represents them. The seller, Harold Lindqvist, is 88, lives in Sarasota, and will sign through his niece, Karin, who holds his power of attorney. Contract was signed in August with a 10% deposit held in escrow by the seller's attorney. On September 22 the buyers' attorney, Priya, forwards the title report with a note: “Nine exceptions on Schedule B. Most are routine. Two are not. Closing is set for October 30.”

A New York title report (often called a title commitment or certificate of title) has two halves. Schedule A says who owns the property, describes it, and states the policy the company will issue. Schedule B lists every matter the company will not insure against unless it is cleared: mortgages, liens, judgments, violations, survey issues, and recorded rights of others. The title search behind it covers deeds, mortgages, liens, judgments, a lis pendens, bankruptcies, and municipal departmental searches. Priya's job is to get every removable item removed and to make sure the buyers can live with the rest.

head: Schedule B exception
Type
rows: Mortgage to The Dime Savings Bank of Williamsburgh, $210,000, recorded 2004
Mortgage to JPMorgan Chase Bank, $400,000, recorded 2019
Judgment, Kings County, $46,300, docketed 2022, against Harold Lindquist
Survey reading: stoop and areaway project beyond the street line; rear fence 0.7 feet onto Lot 52
Declaration of restrictions, 1899, limiting use to single family dwellings
Deed in chain, 1977, from Rose Klein as executrix; letters testamentary not of record
Power of attorney from Harold Lindqvist to Karin Lindqvist to be recorded; proof that principal is living at closing
Rights of tenants or persons in possession, if any
blocks.caption: Title report for Block 5167, Lot 48, Brooklyn (condensed)

blocks.html: Priya sorts the nine items into three piles before she calls anyone. Removable at closing with money: exceptions 2 and 4. Removable with paper: 1, 3, 7, and 8. Accept or walk: 5 and 6. Exception 9 is standard boilerplate; because the house will be delivered vacant, a seller's affidavit and Jordan's walk-through let the company drop it at closing.

Exception 2 is easy. Harold still owes about $212,000 on the 2019 Chase loan. His attorney orders a payoff letter good through the closing date, and at closing the seller's side hands the title closer a check for the payoff amount out of Harold's proceeds. The closer sends it to Chase, and Chase files a satisfaction afterward.
Exception 1 is the problem. Harold says he paid off the 2004 Dime loan when he refinanced in 2015. No satisfaction was ever recorded. The Dime was absorbed into a larger bank years ago.

blocks.q: What is the right way to clear the 2004 mortgage?
c: Ignore it, because a mortgage of record more than 20 years old expires automatically
Have the buyers take title subject to it and rely on their owner's policy if it is ever enforced
Have Harold sign an affidavit that it was paid, which then serves as the recorded satisfaction
Get a satisfaction from the successor bank, or proof of payoff the title company will accept
blocks.x: A paid mortgage stays on the record until a satisfaction is recorded. The seller's attorney asks the successor bank for one, using the 2015 payoff records. If that drags, title companies may omit the exception on proof of payment plus an indemnity. Taking title subject to it is the trap: the owner's policy would list it as an exception, so it would not cover that risk at all.

blocks.html: Exception 3 is a 2022 judgment against “Harold Lindquist,” with a u. The title company found it because name searches catch close spellings. Harold has never been sued, never lived anywhere but Rugby Road and Sarasota, and spells his name with a v.

blocks.q: How does the seller's attorney most likely clear the judgment?
c: Paying the $46,300 at closing and seeking reimbursement from the real debtor
A non-identity affidavit from Harold, with details showing he is not the debtor
A quitclaim deed from Harold to himself under the correct spelling of his name
Asking the court to vacate the judgment, since it was docketed against a stranger
blocks.x: Name hits are common. The usual cure is an affidavit stating the seller is not the judgment debtor, with identifying details such as date of birth, addresses, and the last four digits of a Social Security number, which the title company checks against the judgment record. Paying it is the trap: Harold would be paying a stranger's debt. A court motion is overkill for a debt that was never his.

blocks.html: Exception 4, the water and sewer charges, is simple: in New York City, unpaid water and sewer charges are a lien on the property. Harold's side orders a final meter reading, and the title closer collects the open balance plus usage through the reading from Harold's proceeds at closing.

blocks.q: Who pays the open water and sewer balance, and how?
c: Harold, through the title closer, who collects it from his proceeds at closing
The buyers, who take a credit for it and pay the City after closing
No one at closing, because water charges are Harold's personal debt and not a lien
Harold and the buyers equally, since both will have used water during the billing period
blocks.x: In New York City, unpaid water and sewer charges are a lien on the property, so they must be cleared for the title company to insure. The closer collects the balance and the usage through the final reading from the seller's proceeds and pays the Department of Environmental Protection. The personal-debt answer is the trap: unlike a credit card bill, this one follows the house.

blocks.html: Exception 5 is a survey reading. Brooklyn rowhouses and Victorians are full of stoops, areaways, and fences that are not exactly where the lot lines are. The stoop projecting into the sidewalk area is so common in the city that buyers routinely accept it. The fence at the back is 0.7 feet onto the neighbor's lot.

blocks.q: The buyers accept exception 5. If the rear neighbor later demands the fence be moved, will their owner's policy cover the cost?
c: Yes, because owner's policies cover any boundary dispute arising after closing
Yes, because the survey was paid for by the buyers and delivered before closing
No, because survey matters listed as exceptions are excluded from the coverage
No, because an owner's policy does not cover matters that involve a survey
blocks.x: Title insurance covers what it does not except. An item listed on Schedule B and accepted by the buyer is carved out of coverage. The fence is a small risk, which is why the buyers accept it, but they should accept it knowingly. The “never covers survey matters” answer is the trap: when a survey is provided and the company reads it, survey coverage is often given except for the specific items the survey shows.

blocks.html: Exception 6 is an 1899 declaration that limits the block to single family dwellings, part of how the Ditmas Park houses were developed. The Haques plan to live in the house as a one-family, so it does not bother them. If they had wanted to add a rental unit, Priya would have flagged it before contract, because a recorded restriction binds them even if zoning would allow it.

blocks.q: Suppose the Haques later wanted to add a legal second unit, and zoning allowed it. What role could the 1899 restriction play?
c: None, because zoning overrides private restrictions recorded before it
No role, because restrictions recorded more than 100 years ago expire on their own
It could still bar it, since a valid private restriction binds them too
It binds the original 1899 buyers, not anyone who bought later
blocks.x: Zoning and private deed restrictions are separate layers. An owner must satisfy both, so the stricter one controls. A restriction that is part of a recorded neighborhood plan generally runs with the land and binds later owners. The “zoning overrides” answer is the trap. Old restrictions can sometimes be challenged in court as obsolete, but no restriction simply vanishes because it is old.

blocks.html: Exception 7 is older. In 1977 Rose Klein, “as executrix” of her husband's estate, deeded the house to the Lindqvists. The deed is in the record, but nothing in the title file shows that Rose was ever appointed executrix. If she was not, the chain of title has a missing link: the estate's interest may never have passed.

blocks.q: What does the title company most likely do with exception 7?
c: Insure over it with no further work, since the deed is nearly 50 years old
Search the Surrogate's Court file for the Klein estate's letters
Require Harold to sue the Klein heirs in a quiet title action before closing
Require a new deed from Rose Klein's heirs, whoever and wherever they are
blocks.x: The missing proof is likely in the Surrogate's Court file, not missing in reality. A search there for Rose's letters testamentary closes the gap in the chain. A quiet title action is the trap: it is the remedy when a gap cannot be closed by records or releases, and it would delay the closing by months. Old defects are often low risk, but title companies confirm before they insure over them.

blocks.html: The clerk at the Kings County Surrogate's Court finds the 1976 file in two days. Rose's letters were issued in October 1976. The exception comes off. In a 1977 transaction, a buyer's attorney would have read an abstract of title and given an opinion on the gap. Today the title report does that work, and the policy backs it with money.

Exception 8 is about Harold himself. Karin will sign the deed as his attorney in fact. The title company wants the power of attorney recorded with the deed and wants proof that Harold is alive on the day of closing.

blocks.q: Why does the title company insist on proof that Harold is alive on closing day?
c: Because the mansion tax return is signed by the seller himself on the day of closing
Because a seller over 85 has to appear by video under New York's elder protection law
Because the seller's transfer tax is waived if the seller dies before the closing date
Because an agent's power ends at the principal's death, voiding a later deed
blocks.x: An agent's authority ends when the principal dies. If Harold died the night before and Karin signed anyway, the deed would convey nothing; his property would belong to his estate. The usual proof is a phone or video call with Harold before closing, documented in the file. The mansion tax answer is the trap: it is the buyer's tax and has nothing to do with the seller's signature.

blocks.title: Where it happens in Brooklyn
blocks.html: Downstate closings are usually in person, at the lender's attorney's office, the seller's attorney's office, or a title company. The title closer collects the transfer taxes, mortgage recording tax, and recording fees, then records the deed and mortgage through ACRIS with the City Register after closing. Many sellers do not attend; they sign the deed and transfer tax forms in advance or, like Harold, through a recorded power of attorney.

Meanwhile the lender's closing conditions arrive. Among them: proof of homeowner's insurance on the house, effective the day of closing, naming the lender as mortgagee. Ditmas Park is not in a FEMA special flood hazard area, so flood insurance is not required, though the agent can still quote it. Farida asks whether Harold's existing policy can simply be transferred to them.

blocks.q: What will the lender accept as proof of hazard insurance at closing?
c: A binder or paid first-year policy naming the lender
Harold's existing policy, assigned to the Haques at the closing table
The owner's title insurance policy, which also covers fire and storm damage
Nothing yet, since insurance can be bound within 30 days after closing
blocks.x: The buyers must buy their own policy, effective at closing, with the lender named as mortgagee, usually shown by a binder or a paid first-year premium. A seller's homeowner's policy covers the seller and ends when he no longer owns the house. Title insurance is the trap: it covers defects in ownership, not physical damage. A lender will not fund an uninsured house even for a day.
