blocks.html: Daniel builds a spreadsheet of closing costs and finds the title bill. The lender requires a loan policy for $1,108,000. The owner's policy for $1,385,000 is a separate premium. “The bank already makes us buy title insurance,” he writes. “Why pay twice?”

blocks.q: What should Jordan explain about skipping the owner's policy?
c: The loan policy protects both the lender and the buyers, so a second policy adds nothing
The loan policy protects only the lender; the owner's policy protects the Haques
The owner's policy is required by New York law on any purchase that uses a mortgage
The owner's policy lasts until the loan is paid off, then the Haques must buy a new one
blocks.x: The lender's policy runs to the lender and shrinks as the loan is paid down. The owner's policy protects the Haques (and their heirs) for the full price for as long as they own the house, with a one-time premium. The “protects both” answer is the trap, and it is the reason buyers skip coverage they need. Jordan explains the difference and leaves the choice to them and Priya; the Haques buy it.

blocks.html: On Monday, October 26, the loan officer calls Daniel. Rates moved, and the lender can offer a 7/1 adjustable rate mortgage at a lower starting rate than the 30-year fixed in their Closing Disclosure. Daniel likes the payment. He switches. The lender sends a revised Closing Disclosure Tuesday morning. Closing is Friday.

blocks.q: Can the Haques still close on Friday, October 30?
c: Yes, because they received the original Closing Disclosure more than 3 business days ago
Yes, if they sign a waiver of the waiting period at the lender's office on Friday
No, they wait a full 30 days, because the new loan needs a new Loan Estimate
No, a change in loan product starts a new 3-business-day waiting period
blocks.x: Under the TRID rules that implement RESPA and TILA, most changes just get a corrected disclosure at closing, but three restart the 3-business-day clock: an APR change beyond tolerance, a change in loan product, or an added prepayment penalty. Switching from fixed to adjustable is a product change. The original-disclosure answer is the trap. Delivered Tuesday, the new disclosure lets them close Saturday at the earliest, so the closing moves to Monday.

blocks.html: Priya moves the closing to Monday, November 2. The payoff letters, the tax proration, and the lender's per diem interest are all recalculated. The extra weekend turns out to matter.

Sunday at 10 a.m., Jordan meets the Haques at Rugby Road for the final walk-through. The house is empty and broom clean. The boiler runs. Then Farida looks up in the dining room. The 1905 gas-and-electric chandelier, listed in the contract as included, is gone; a bare ceiling box hangs in its place. Karin, reached by phone, says her uncle wanted it shipped to Florida.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do?
c: Tell the buyers to close anyway and take it up with Harold in small claims court later
Tell the buyers to refuse to close and demand their deposit back from the seller
Tell both attorneys now so they can agree on a return, credit, or escrow
Negotiate a price reduction directly with Karin and confirm it in a text to her
blocks.x: The walk-through exists to catch exactly this before money moves. Jordan reports it to both attorneys, who can agree that the fixture comes back, the buyers get a credit, or money is held in escrow from the seller's proceeds until it is returned. Refusing to close is the trap: a missing chandelier is not grounds to walk away from a $1,385,000 contract. Negotiating terms directly with the seller's side cuts out the lawyers who will write the deal.

blocks.html: The attorneys agree on a $4,500 escrow from Harold's proceeds, released when the chandelier is reinstalled. It arrives from Sarasota in nine days.

Monday at 11 a.m., the closing convenes at the lender's attorney's office on Court Street. Present: the Haques, Priya, the seller's attorney (holding Karin's signed deed and the recorded power of attorney), the lender's attorney, the title closer, Jordan, and the listing agent. Harold was on video with the title closer at 9:15.

blocks.q: Before funds are released, the title closer runs a final search of the records, called a continuation or rundown. Why?
c: To catch any lien, judgment, or deed recorded since the last search
To recalculate the mortgage recording tax using the final loan amount
To confirm that the seller has paid the broker's commission in full
To confirm that the buyers' homeowner's insurance policy has been issued
blocks.x: Weeks pass between the report and the closing. Under New York's race-notice recording act, anything recorded in that gap, such as a new judgment or a lis pendens, would bind the buyers. The rundown brings the search up to the moment of closing so the policy can be issued with no surprises. The insurance answer is the trap: proof of insurance is the lender's requirement, checked separately.

blocks.html: The rundown is clean. The Haques sign the note and mortgage. The lender's attorney releases the loan funds. The seller's attorney releases the 10% deposit from escrow. Payoff checks go to Chase, to the City for water, and to the title company for taxes and fees. Then the commission.

blocks.q: The listing broker's commission and the cooperating fee for Hudson & Hart are being paid. Jordan asks for his share as a separate check. How should it be paid?
c: By a check payable to Jordan, since he is the licensee who worked with the buyers
By a check payable to Jordan, as long as Diane initials the closing statement
By a credit to the buyers, who then pay Jordan directly after the closing
By a check payable to Hudson & Hart, which then pays Jordan under his agreement
blocks.x: A salesperson may be paid only by his own sponsoring broker. Commission checks are payable to the brokerage, which pays Jordan under their agreement. The “Jordan worked with the buyers” answer is the trap: who did the work does not change who may be paid by an outside party. Payment through the buyers would be worse still.

blocks.html: The deed is delivered and accepted. The Haques own the house. That afternoon the title closer submits the deed, the transfer tax returns, the mortgage, and the power of attorney through ACRIS. Recording gives constructive notice to everyone who comes later.

Two loose ends follow the closing, and Jordan puts both on his calendar. First, Chase has been paid, but its mortgage is still of record. New York's RPAPL 1921 gives a lender 30 days after payoff to present a satisfaction for recording, with penalties payable to the borrower at 30, 60, and 90 days if it does not. The title company tracks it because the Haques' policy depends on it. Second, the chandelier escrow: the seller's attorney holds $4,500 until Priya confirms the fixture is back on the dining room ceiling. Small items like these are where a closed deal turns into a bad review months later, so a good agent follows them to the end even though the commission has already been paid.

blocks.title: The title report is not the policy
blocks.html: Buyers often think the title report is their protection. It is not. The report is the company's offer to insure, subject to its exceptions. The policy is issued after closing, once every required item is cleared and the deed and mortgage are recorded. If an exception is accepted at closing instead of removed, it rides into the policy as a permanent carve-out. Read Schedule B of the final policy, not just the report.

items: Schedule B lists what the title company will not insure. Each item is cleared (satisfaction, payoff, affidavit, search), accepted knowingly, or the deal stops.
Paid mortgages stay of record until satisfied. Name hits are cleared by affidavit. Gaps in the chain are often closed by searching other public records before anyone sues.
A power of attorney ends at death; title companies want proof the principal is living on closing day and the power recorded with the deed.
The loan policy protects the lender; only the owner's policy protects the buyer. Accepted exceptions are excluded from coverage.
A change in loan product, an APR change beyond tolerance, or a new prepayment penalty restarts the 3-business-day Closing Disclosure wait.

The walk-through finds problems before money moves; the attorneys fix them with a return, credit, or escrow. The rundown on closing day closes the recording gap. Commissions go to the broker, never to the salesperson directly.

lessons.title: Case file: Two Columns on Seneca Avenue
lessons.tagline: A Ridgewood three-family with two tenants, oil in the tank, and a quarter's taxes already paid. Build the closing statement line by line and find out who brings what to the table.
objectives: Calculate rent, real estate tax, and fuel prorations for a New York closing and enter each as a debit or credit
Calculate the NYS transfer tax, NYC RPTT, mansion tax, and mortgage recording tax on a New York City sale and assign each to the right party
Prepare and reconcile a full buyer and seller closing statement, including deposits, loan proceeds, payoffs, and tenant security deposits
Explain how the statement would change for a co-op or an upstate sale

blocks.title: The net sheet that has to be right
blocks.html: Teresa and Luis Ocasio have owned a brick three-family on Seneca Avenue in Ridgewood, Queens, since 2003. They live on the top floor and rent the other two. They are selling for $1,725,000 to Yvonne Baptiste, a nurse practitioner who will live upstairs and keep the tenants. Yvonne put down a $172,500 deposit at contract, held in escrow by the Ocasios' attorney, and is borrowing $1,200,000. Closing is Thursday, November 19, 2026. Jordan represented the Ocasios. Diane hands Jordan the file: “Before the attorneys send theirs, build the closing statement yourself. Every line. If your numbers don't match theirs, one of you is wrong, and you need to know which.”

head: Item
Facts
rows: Unit 1: $2,450 a month. Unit 2: $2,600 a month. November rents ($5,050) collected by the Ocasios on November 1. Unit 2 still owes October rent of $2,600.
Unit 1: $2,450. Unit 2: $2,600. Total $5,050, held by the Ocasios
Class 1, billed quarterly. Annual tax $9,490. The Ocasios paid the October 1 to December 31 quarter on October 1.
Final meter reading November 17; unbilled usage since the last bill $386.40
180 gallons in the tank at $3.85 a gallon
5% of the price, paid by the sellers
Apportionments as of midnight of the day before closing (the buyer owns closing day); taxes prorated on a 365-day year; rents by the actual days in the month
blocks.caption: Closing file, 1867 Seneca Avenue (Block 3474, Lot 22)

blocks.html: Two rules run through every line. First, a proration is a double entry: the same amount is a debit to one party and a credit to the other. Second, items that involve only one party (a loan, a payoff, a commission, a buyer's tax) appear in only that party's columns. A debit is money that party owes into the closing; a credit is money that party receives or is credited with.

The Ocasios collected all of November's rent on November 1, but Yvonne will own the building from November 19 on. Under the contract, the buyer owns closing day, so Yvonne's days are November 19 through 30.

blocks.q: Which entry records the November rent proration?
c: Credit the sellers and debit the buyer, because the sellers collected it
Debit the sellers and credit the buyer, since the sellers hold her days' rent
No entry, because rent belongs to whoever owned the building on the 1st
Debit both parties, because rent is shared income during the month of the sale
blocks.x: The sellers collected rent covering days the buyer will own, so they owe it to her: debit sellers, credit buyer. The reverse is the trap, and it is the most common proration error: collecting the money does not make it theirs. The question is always whose days the money covers.

blocks.q: How much is the rent proration?
blocks.x: November has 30 days; the buyer has 12 of them (November 19 through 30, counting closing day). $5,050 / 30 = $168.33 a day; $5,050 x 12 / 30 = $2,020.00. $1,851.67 is the trap: it gives the buyer only 11 days, as if the seller owned closing day. $3,030 is the sellers' 18 days, the right math for the wrong party.

blocks.html: Then the October arrears. Unit 2 never paid October's $2,600. Luis asks whether Yvonne should credit him for it, since “the building is earning it.”

blocks.q: How is the unpaid October rent handled at closing?
c: No entry; the sellers keep their claim, on terms the contract sets
Credit the sellers $2,600, because the rent was earned while they owned the building
Credit the buyer $2,600, because she takes over the tenant along with the debt
Split it between the parties based on the days each owns the building in October
blocks.x: Arrears are not prorated, because no one has the money. The sellers keep their claim. Typical New York contracts say rent the buyer collects after closing goes first to current rent and then to the sellers' arrears, which the buyer passes along. Crediting the sellers is the trap: the buyer would be paying cash for a debt that may never be collected.

blocks.html: The tenants' $5,050 in deposits are not the Ocasios' money. They hold it in trust for the tenants. When the building changes hands, the obligation to return it moves to Yvonne, so the money has to move with it.

blocks.q: How are the $5,050 in security deposits handled?
c: Credit the sellers and debit the buyer, because the sellers originally collected them
No entry; the sellers return the deposits to the tenants before closing
Debit the sellers, credit the buyer, and notify the tenants of the transfer
Debit the buyer, since she will owe the deposits back when the leases end
blocks.x: The deposits go to the buyer by a credit to her and a debit to the sellers. Under General Obligations Law 7-105, the sellers must turn them over at closing or within 5 days and notify each tenant by registered or certified mail of the new holder's name and address; that is what releases the sellers from liability. Returning them to the tenants is the trap: the leases continue, so the deposits stay in place under the new owner.

blocks.html: New York City's tax year runs July 1 to June 30. Class 1 properties with an assessed value of $250,000 or less are billed quarterly. The Ocasios paid the October to December quarter, so they have prepaid taxes for days Yvonne will own.

blocks.q: What is the direction of the tax proration?
c: Debit the sellers and credit the buyer, since taxes are the sellers' expense
Credit the sellers and debit the buyer, since the sellers prepaid her days
No entry, since NYC taxes are paid by the owner of record on the due date
Debit the buyer and credit the City, since the next quarter is still unpaid
blocks.x: Prepaid by the seller means the buyer reimburses the seller for the buyer's days: credit sellers, debit buyer. The reverse is the trap: it is the right entry for taxes in arrears, when the seller has not paid and the buyer will pay the whole bill later. Always ask first whether the bill was paid.

blocks.title: Tax proration, 365-day method
blocks.html:
1. Daily rate: $9,490 / 365 = $26.00.
2. Buyer's days in the paid quarter: November 19 to 30 (12) + December (31) = 43 days.
3. 43 x $26.00 = $1,118.00: credit sellers, debit buyer.
4. Check: the sellers' days, October 1 to November 18, are 31 + 18 = 49. 49 + 43 = 92, the number of days in the quarter.

blocks.q: Under a 360-day year (every month 30 days), the buyer's days in the paid quarter would be 42 instead of 43. Why?
c: Because the buyer would no longer own the day of closing
Because November counts as 31 days under the statutory method
Because a quarterly bill is treated as exactly 89 days long
Because December counts as 30 days instead of 31
blocks.x: On a 360-day basis, November 19 to 30 is still 12 days (30 minus 18), but December counts as 30, for 42 days. Losing closing day is the trap: who owns closing day is a separate contract term, and it does not change with the day-count method. Exam questions say which method to use; New York contracts usually use actual days, and the method has to match what the contract says.

blocks.html: Water and sewer in the city is billed by the Department of Environmental Protection, and unpaid charges are a lien. The attorneys ordered a final reading on November 17. The $386.40 of usage since the last bill is the Ocasios' to pay. The title closer will collect it from their proceeds and pay DEP, so it appears only in their debit column. The usage between the reading and closing is a few dollars, and the attorneys agree to ignore it.

blocks.q: Why does the $386.40 water charge appear only in the sellers' debit column?
c: Because water charges are split, and the buyer's half is billed to her after closing
Because the buyer pays it outside closing and the sellers repay her at the next quarter
Because it is paid out of the sellers' proceeds to the City, so no money passes to the buyer
Because the City requires the buyer to pay a separate water deposit on any transfer
blocks.x: The usage belongs entirely to the sellers' period, and the money goes to a third party, the Department of Environmental Protection, not to the buyer. A payment to an outsider appears only on the paying party's side. The split answer is the trap: proration applies to a bill that covers both parties' days. A final reading lets the attorneys bill each side for its own usage instead.

blocks.html: The oil is different. The 180 gallons in the tank were bought by the Ocasios and will heat Yvonne's building.

blocks.q: How is the heating oil entered?
c: Credit the sellers $693 and debit the buyer $693
Debit the sellers $693, since they used most of the heat this season
No entry, because fixtures and fuel pass to the buyer with the building
Credit the buyer $693, since she will refill the tank this winter
blocks.x: The sellers paid for fuel the buyer will use, so the buyer pays them for it: 180 x $3.85 = $693, credit sellers, debit buyer. The “passes with the building” answer is the trap: oil is personal property consumed over time, and New York contracts adjust for it at closing unless they say otherwise.

blocks.text: Line 6: the transfer taxes and the mortgage tax

head: Tax
Who pays
Rate here and why
Amount
rows: 0.4% ($2 per $500): residential under $3,000,000, so the NYC additional rate does not apply
1.425%: 1 to 3 family over $500,000, applied to the whole price
1%: residential $1,000,000 to under $2,000,000 (the NYC supplemental rate starts at $2,000,000)
1.925%: 1 to 3 family, loan $500,000 or more; the lender separately pays 0.25%
blocks.caption: The four taxes on a $1,725,000 Ridgewood three-family with a $1,200,000 loan

blocks.q: What do the Ocasios pay in transfer taxes in total?
blocks.x: NYS $6,900 plus NYC RPTT $24,581.25 equals $31,481.25. $48,731.25 is the trap: it adds the $17,250 mansion tax, which is the buyer's. $24,581.25 is the RPTT alone, forgetting that city sellers pay the state tax too. $314,812.50 is a decimal slip, ten times the right answer.

blocks.q: What mansion tax does Yvonne pay?
blocks.x: The price is $1,725,000, residential, so the 1% mansion tax applies to the whole price: $17,250. $21,562.50 is the trap: it applies 1.25%, the NYC rate for $2,000,000 to under $3,000,000. The mansion tax is a cliff, not a marginal tax: crossing $1,000,000 puts 1% on every dollar, but the higher NYC tiers start at $2,000,000.

blocks.q: What mortgage recording tax does Yvonne pay on her $1,200,000 loan?
blocks.x: For 1 to 3 family homes and condos in NYC, the borrower pays 1.925% on loans of $500,000 or more: $1,200,000 x 0.01925 = $23,100. $26,100 is the trap: it is the combined 2.175% including the lender's 0.25% share. $21,600 uses the 1.8% rate for loans under $500,000, and $231,000 is a decimal slip.

blocks.html: Two details on the mortgage recording tax are worth a second look. The lender pays its own 0.25% (here $3,000) on loans secured by homes with up to six units, so it never appears on Yvonne's side of the statement. And New York deducts the first $10,000 of principal when computing part of the tax on one and two family homes, a $30 saving. Seneca Avenue is a three-family, so Yvonne gets no deduction. Exam questions rarely go that deep, but title bills do, and Jordan's number has to match the closer's to the dollar.

blocks.caption: Enter $1,725,000, Queens, three-family, and a $1,200,000 loan. Then raise the price to $2,000,000 and watch the mansion tax jump to 1.25% on the whole price.

blocks.html: Teresa reads the tax table and goes quiet. “Thirty-one thousand dollars in transfer taxes. Plus the commission.” Jordan walks her back to the net sheet he gave her at the listing appointment, which estimated transfer taxes at about 1.825% of the price. At $1,725,000 that is the same $31,481.25. Nothing on this line is a surprise to her, which is the whole point of doing the math before the listing is signed.

With the adjustments and taxes done, Jordan fills in the rest from the title bill, the payoff letter, and the lender's Closing Disclosure. The title company's bill shows the owner's and loan policy premiums together at $9,250 and recording fees for the deed and mortgage at $650, all the buyer's. The sellers' side pays $300 in payoff processing and satisfaction recording fees. The payoff letter from the Ocasios' lender gives a figure good through November 19 plus a per diem, the daily interest, in case the closing slips; the seller's attorney will use the exact figure for the actual closing date. The lender's Closing Disclosure shows its fees and a three-month initial deposit into Yvonne's tax escrow account ($9,490 / 12 x 3, rounded to $2,372), because the lender will pay her future tax bills out of her monthly payment.

head: Line
Buyer debit
Buyer credit
Seller debit
Seller credit
rows: Water and sewer through final reading
blocks.caption: Closing statement, 1867 Seneca Avenue, November 19, 2026

blocks.html: Look at the deposit line. Yvonne gets credit for the $172,500 she already paid. The Ocasios show no debit for it. It was always part of the price, and it is their money: the escrow agent releases it to them at closing.

The commission line deserves a word too. The listing agreement set 5%, which the Ocasios negotiated; commissions in New York are never set by law or by any board. The title closer does not pay it. The seller's attorney writes the commission check to Hudson & Hart from the sellers' proceeds, and the firm pays the cooperating broker its share and Jordan his split under their agreements.

blocks.q: Why does the $172,500 deposit appear as a buyer credit but not as a seller debit?
c: Because the buyer already paid it toward the price, and it is released to the sellers
Because the deposit belongs to the escrow agent until both attorneys sign a release
Because the deposit is returned to the buyer at closing and paid again as part of the price
Because deposits are treated as the broker's commission and leave the sellers' side entirely
blocks.x: The buyer paid it at contract as part of the price, so she gets credit for it against what she owes. The sellers already have a credit for the full price; the deposit is simply the first piece of that price, now released from escrow. Treating it as a seller debit is the trap: that would make the sellers pay $172,500 for money that was always theirs.

blocks.html: Reconciliation is the proof. The buyer's debits minus her credits is the money she wires in. The sellers' credits minus their debits is what they net, part of which they already hold in escrow.

blocks.q: How much does Yvonne bring to closing?
blocks.x: Buyer debits $1,785,133 minus buyer credits $1,379,570 = $405,563. $578,063 is the trap: it forgets to credit her for the deposit she already paid. $410,613 misses the $5,050 security deposit credit. $1,379,570 is just the credit column total. Always total both columns before subtracting.

blocks.q: What do the Ocasios net, and how much of it comes at the closing table?
c: $1,186,504.58 net, every dollar paid at the closing table
$1,014,004.58 net, after the deposit is deducted from the sellers' proceeds
$1,186,504.58 net; $172,500 from escrow and $1,014,004.58 at the table
$1,359,004.58 net, adding the deposit to their proceeds as extra money
blocks.x: Seller credits $1,726,811.00 minus debits $540,306.42 = $1,186,504.58. The escrow agent releases the $172,500 deposit, and the rest, $1,014,004.58, is paid at the table. $1,014,004.58 as the total net is the trap: it treats the deposit as gone, when it was always part of the sellers' price. Adding it on top would count it twice.

blocks.html: Jordan emails his statement to Diane on Tuesday. The seller's attorney's version arrives Wednesday morning, and the two match on every line but one: the attorney's tax adjustment is $1,092, not $1,118. The difference is exactly $26, one day. The attorney's paralegal had given the sellers closing day. Jordan points to the apportionment clause, the attorney corrects it, and the buyer's attorney, who had caught the same thing, signs off. That is the reason Diane wanted Jordan to build it himself.

blocks.title: Read the apportionment clause first
blocks.html: Before you prorate anything, find the contract's apportionment clause. It tells you the date and time adjustments are made as of (New York forms usually say midnight of the day before closing, so the buyer owns closing day), the day-count method, and which items are adjusted at all. Exam questions supply these facts in the stem. Real contracts bury them on page 6. Either way, the answer turns on them.

blocks.title: Prorations always balance; taxes and fees usually don't
blocks.html: Every proration line has the same number in a buyer column and a seller column, on opposite sides. Every one-party line does not. If your statement shows a buyer-only tax in the seller's column (mansion tax, mortgage recording tax) or a seller-only tax in the buyer's (transfer tax, RPTT), stop: either the contract shifted it, as sponsor contracts for new condos often do, or you made the error the exam is waiting for.

blocks.text: If this were a co-op, or upstate

left.title: Same price, but a Ridgewood co-op apartment
items: No mortgage recording tax: a share loan is not a mortgage
No title insurance; the buyer's attorney orders a lien search on the shares and the seller
NYS transfer tax, NYC RPTT, and mansion tax still apply
Maintenance is prorated instead of taxes and water; seller usually pays any flip tax
Lender recognition agreement and managing agent fees appear on the statement

right.title: Same price, but a three-family in Albany
items: No NYC RPTT; NYS transfer tax at 0.4% (no NYC additional rate)
Mansion tax 1% still applies at $1,000,000 and up
Mortgage recording tax at the county's rate (about 1% in most upstate counties), not 1.925%
Taxes prorated in two pieces: town and county (calendar year) and school (July 1 to June 30)
Deed recorded with the county clerk with Form TP-584 and the RP-5217

blocks.title: What the city adds
blocks.html: Inside the five boroughs, a residential seller pays two transfer taxes, not one: NYS at 0.4% (0.65% at $3,000,000 and up) plus NYC RPTT at 1% or 1.425%. A buyer pays the mansion tax, graduated in the city from 1% up to 3.9% at $25,000,000, and a mortgage recording tax that runs nearly twice the suburban rate. On this sale the four taxes together come to $71,831.25, more than 4% of the price.

items: Prorations are double entries. Prepaid by the seller: credit seller, debit buyer. Collected in advance or owed by the seller: debit seller, credit buyer. Arrears no one has collected are not prorated.
Count the buyer's days carefully. In New York the buyer usually owns closing day, and the contract sets the 365-day or 360-day method.
Security deposits move to the buyer as a credit, and the seller notifies the tenants by registered or certified mail (GOL 7-105).

Sellers pay NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT; buyers pay the mansion tax and mortgage recording tax. Know the brackets: $500,000 for RPTT and MRT rates, $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 for the mansion tax, $3,000,000 for the higher NYS rate.
One-party lines (loan, payoff, commission, each side's taxes and fees) appear only in that party's columns. The deposit is a buyer credit only.
Reconcile: buyer's debits minus credits is cash to close; seller's credits minus debits is net proceeds, including the deposit released from escrow.

lessons.title: Case file: The Notice Filed on Wednesday
lessons.tagline: An open permit, a time of the essence letter, a roofer's lien, and a stepdaughter's lawsuit filed the day before a Bay Ridge closing.
objectives: Decide whether a missed "on or about" closing date is a default, and apply the rules for making time of the essence by notice.
Distinguish open permits, violations, liens, and a notice of pendency, and choose the right way to clear each before a closing.
Apply the mechanic's lien filing, bonding, and duration rules and the CPLR cancellation grounds for a notice of pendency.
Explain the buyer's remedy when a seller cannot convey insurable title, when a conditional commission is earned, and how the recording gap is closed.

blocks.title: Bay Ridge, the week before the closing that did not happen
blocks.html: Margaret Doyle, 74, is selling the brick one-family on 79th Street in Bay Ridge where she raised three children. Her husband Tom died in 2023. Jordan listed the house at $1,295,000, and in April Ines Carvalho and Kwame Mensah, a pharmacist and a structural engineer, signed a contract at $1,240,000 with a $124,000 down payment held in escrow by Margaret's attorney, Howard Lutz. Priya represents the buyers. Their lender has committed to a $992,000 loan, and their rate lock runs out June 30. The contract says closing will take place "on or about June 12, 2026." On May 28 Priya emails Howard and Jordan: "Departmental searches are in. We have a problem in the basement."

Every New York closing runs on two clocks. One is the contract: what the seller must deliver, by when, and what happens if she cannot. The other is the public record, which keeps changing until the minute the deed is recorded. This case is about a closing where both clocks went wrong at once, and about who bore the risk each time.

blocks.title: The contract terms that will matter (excerpts)
blocks.html:
Closing date: on or about June 12, 2026, at the office of Purchaser's lender's attorney.
Title: Seller shall convey such title as a reputable title company licensed in New York will approve and insure at regular rates, subject only to the permitted exceptions listed in the rider.
Violations: Seller shall comply with notes or notices of violations of law noted or issued by any governmental department against the premises at or before closing.
Seller's inability to convey: If Seller is unable to convey title in accordance with this contract, Purchaser's sole remedy shall be to receive a refund of the down payment and reimbursement of the net cost of title examination and survey, unless Seller has willfully caused the defect.
Commission (listing agreement, separate document): earned and payable if, as, and when title closes.

Along with the title search, the title company orders municipal or departmental searches: Department of Buildings records, Environmental Control Board violations, Housing Preservation and Development, the Fire Department, a street report, and an emergency repair search. These are not searches of liens. They show what the City knows about the building.

head: Search
Result
What it means
rows: Alteration permit, 2011, "convert cellar to recreation room with half bath." Status: permit issued, never signed off
Work was permitted, but the City never confirmed it was finished to code
2019 violation, "work without a permit, rear deck," penalty $1,250 unpaid
An unpaid penalty the City can collect from the owner
blocks.caption: Departmental search results, 79th Street

blocks.q: Margaret says the 2011 permit is "paperwork, not a lien," so the buyers have no reason to complain. How should Jordan understand the open permit?
c: As a lien that the title closer will pay off from Margaret's proceeds at the closing
As a defect that voids the contract, since the buyers did not know about the permit
As no lien, but a record the title company will except and a lender may not accept
As irrelevant to the sale, because the 1931 certificate of occupancy controls the use
blocks.x: An open permit is not a lien and has no dollar amount to pay off. It is a public record that work started under a permit was never inspected and signed off. The title company reports it and may except it, and many lenders and buyers' attorneys insist it be closed out. The payoff answer is the trap: money clears liens, but closing out a permit takes inspections and an expediter.

blocks.html: Howard's first answer is the contract: the violations clause covers notes and notices of violations, and an unsigned permit is not a violation. Priya's answer is practical. The lender's attorney has already written that the bank will not fund over an open alteration permit for a habitable cellar room, and the buyers will not take a basement bathroom the City has never inspected. The ECB penalty is easier: it is a notice of violation, the clause covers it, and Howard agrees Margaret will pay it and get the violation dismissed.

blocks.q: Under the contract's violations clause, who deals with the 2019 ECB deck penalty, and when?
c: The buyers, after closing, because the deck was built before they signed the contract
Nobody, because ECB penalties expire once the person who built the deck has died
The buyers and Margaret equally, as an adjustment on the closing statement
Margaret, at or before closing, since it is a notice of violation the clause covers
blocks.x: The clause makes the seller comply with notes or notices of violation issued at or before closing, so the ECB penalty is Margaret's to pay and clear. Unpaid City penalties can follow the owner and complicate title, so attorneys clear them before the table. The proration answer is the trap: prorations split shared periodic charges like taxes and rent, not a penalty for one owner's past work.

blocks.html: Then Margaret mentions something to Jordan on the phone. Tom also put a full shower in that cellar bathroom around 2015, long after the permit was pulled. "He did it himself. It's beautiful. Nobody ever came to look at it."

blocks.q: Margaret asks Jordan to "leave the shower out of it" until the expediter is done. What should Jordan do?
c: Keep it confidential, since a seller's agent owes the seller confidentiality on every fact
Tell Margaret the work must be disclosed through the attorneys and the expediter
Tell the buyers directly by text, since a known defect must reach them the same day
Wait for the DOB inspector to find it, which will settle whether it needs to be disclosed
blocks.x: Confidentiality protects a client's bargaining position, not the concealment of a material fact. A licensee who keeps quiet about unpermitted work that will block the sign-off risks misrepresentation and license discipline. The right move is to tell Margaret it has to come out and route it through Howard and the expediter, who must include it anyway. Texting the buyers directly skips Margaret's attorney and does not fix the problem.

blocks.html: The expediter's estimate: amend the 2011 job to include the shower, a plumber's sign-off, a DOB inspection, and the final sign-off. Six to eight weeks if inspections go well. June 12 is two weeks away.

Priya writes to Howard on June 8 asking for an adjournment until the permit is closed out. Howard, under pressure from Margaret, who has already signed a lease on an apartment near her daughter in Pearl River, answers: "My client will be at the closing table on June 12. If your clients do not appear, they are in default."

blocks.q: The buyers do not appear on June 12. Can Margaret declare them in default and keep the $124,000?
c: Yes, because a closing date written in a signed contract binds both parties to that date
Yes, if Margaret appears at the table on June 12 with a deed ready to deliver
No, because a deposit can be kept by a seller once the lender has denied the loan
No. An "on or about" date is not of the essence, so either side gets a reasonable adjournment
blocks.x: In New York, a closing date in a residential contract is not of the essence unless the contract says so clearly. "On or about" is the opposite of that: either party is entitled to a reasonable adjournment, and missing the date is not a default. Appearing with a deed does not change the rule. The trap is treating the written date as a deadline; it becomes one only by agreement or by a proper time of the essence notice.

blocks.html: The adjournment costs real money. The buyers' rate lock expires June 30, and their lender charges $2,480 to extend it 30 days. The loan commitment itself expires July 10. Jordan cannot negotiate legal terms, but he can do arithmetic and keep both sides talking. He points out to Howard that the delay is coming from Margaret's side of the house, and Margaret agrees to credit the buyers $2,480 at closing. Both attorneys confirm it in writing.

blocks.text: June 19: the time of the essence letter

blocks.html: A week later, with the expediter promising a sign-off by early July, Howard tries to lock the buyers in so they cannot drift past their own commitment date and walk away.

blocks.title: Howard's letter, sent to the buyers and to Priya by overnight mail and email
blocks.html: "Seller hereby sets the closing for Thursday, July 9, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. at the offices of Purchaser's lender's attorney. TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE as to Purchaser's obligation to close on that date. Should Purchaser fail to close on that date and time, Purchaser will be deemed in default and Seller will retain the down payment as liquidated damages."

blocks.q: Is Howard's letter likely to make July 9 a binding date?
c: Yes. It is clear, gives a reasonable time, and warns that failing to close is a default
No, because New York requires at least 30 days between the letter and the new date
No, because time of the essence can be added only by a signed amendment to the contract
Yes, but only the buyers are bound, since the seller is the party that sent the notice
blocks.x: New York courts let a party make time of the essence after the fact with a notice that is clear and unequivocal, sets a reasonable date, and warns that failure to perform will be a default. Twenty days is generally reasonable, though it is a question of fact. There is no statutory 30-day minimum. The amendment answer is the trap: unilateral notice works once the original date has passed and the other side has had its reasonable adjournment.

blocks.html: What Margaret does not appreciate is the mirror image. Once July 9 is of the essence, it is of the essence for both sides. If the buyers are ready, willing, and able on July 9 and Margaret cannot deliver the title the contract promises, she is the party in default. Howard has just set a deadline for his own client.
The permit is signed off on July 2. The ECB penalty is paid and the violation dismissed. Priya clears both items with the title company. Everyone plans to close on July 9.
The afternoon before closing, the title closer runs the continuation search, bringing the title down from the last search date. Two new documents have been filed in Kings County in the past 48 hours.

head: Filed
Document
Detail
rows: Bay Ridge Roofing & Siding, $18,400, for a new roof. Last work March 20. Margaret withheld the final payment over leaks
Notice of pendency (lis pendens)
Corinne Doyle v. Margaret Doyle, Supreme Court, Kings County. Claims a one-half interest in the house
blocks.caption: New items on the continuation search

blocks.title: Was the roofer on time?
blocks.html: Lien Law section 10 gives a contractor 8 months after the last work to file, but only 4 months on a single-family dwelling. The last work was March 20, so the deadline was July 20. A July 7 filing is timely. Once filed, the lien lasts one year unless the lienor starts a foreclosure action or gets an extension.

blocks.q: Margaret disputes the roof bill and wants to close tomorrow anyway. Which route lets the closing go forward without first resolving the dispute?
c: Close subject to the lien, since a lien filed after the contract was signed binds only the seller
Bond or escrow it: a bond of 110% of the lien, or a title company escrow from her proceeds
Ask the county clerk to strike the lien because the roof leaks and the work was defective
Pay the roofer the full $18,400 at closing, which is the one way to remove a timely lien
blocks.x: Lien Law section 19 lets the owner discharge a mechanic's lien by filing a bond or undertaking for 110% of the lien. In practice title companies also insure over a lien if enough of the seller's proceeds are held in escrow. Either way the dispute moves off the house and onto the money. The trap is the clerk answer: a clerk records liens and does not decide whether work was defective.

blocks.html: The title company agrees to insure over the roofer's lien with an escrow of $27,600 from Margaret's proceeds, a cushion of 150% under its own underwriting rules. Margaret is furious but signs. The second item is harder.

Corinne is Tom's daughter from his first marriage. Her complaint says Tom promised her for years that she would get half of the house, and asks the court to impose a constructive trust. The 1988 deed ran to "Thomas Doyle and Margaret Doyle, his wife," which made them tenants by the entirety. When Tom died, Margaret became sole owner by right of survivorship, and nothing passed through his estate. Howard calls the claim meritless. He may be right. It does not matter tonight.

A notice of pendency does not say who will win. It tells the world that a lawsuit has been filed that could affect title to this property. Filed with the county clerk, it is constructive notice: anyone who takes title or a mortgage afterward is bound by the judgment as if they had been a party. It lasts three years and can be extended.

blocks.q: Kwame asks whether they can close on July 9 anyway and rely on their owner's title policy if Corinne wins. What is the realistic answer?
c: Yes, because a title policy protects the owner against any claim filed by a relative of the seller
Yes, because Margaret's survivorship rights make the lawsuit meritless as a matter of law
No. The company will except the pending action, and buyers who close take subject to its outcome
No, because a notice of pendency transfers title to the court until the lawsuit is decided
blocks.x: A title policy covers defects the company did not know about. A recorded notice of pendency is known, so it goes on Schedule B as an exception, and a buyer who closes over it is bound by whatever judgment Corinne gets. The lender will not fund either. The meritless answer is the trap: the claim may well lose, but no one at the table can decide that tonight, and the record controls until a court or Corinne clears it.

blocks.title: A lis pendens cannot be paid off
blocks.html: Sellers treat every item on the rundown as a bill. A notice of pendency is not a lien and has no payoff amount. It comes off the record only three ways: the plaintiff cancels it (usually as part of a settlement), the court orders it cancelled, or it expires. Writing a check to the title closer does nothing.

Howard pulls the CPLR. Section 6512 says a notice of pendency is effective only if the summons is served on the defendant within 30 days after filing. Section 6514 lists the grounds for cancellation, and section 6515 lets the court cancel the notice if the plaintiff can be protected by an undertaking (a bond) instead.

blocks.q: Which fact, if it happens, would require the court to cancel Corinne's notice of pendency on Margaret's motion?
c: Corinne fails to serve the summons on Margaret within 30 days after filing the notice
Margaret shows that the house was held by the entirety and passed to her when Tom died
The buyers show that they signed their contract months before Corinne filed her notice
The title company refuses to insure the buyers because the notice is on the record
blocks.x: Under CPLR 6514(a), cancellation is mandatory if service of the summons is not completed within the 30 days that section 6512 allows, or if the action is settled, discontinued, or ends in a final judgment against the plaintiff. A strong defense on the merits is not a ground for mandatory cancellation; it is argued in the lawsuit, and a bad-faith filing is only a discretionary ground. The contract date is the trap: the buyers have no recorded interest, so the notice binds them.

blocks.html: Everyone comes to the closing. Priya places on the record that the buyers are ready, willing, and able: the lender's attorney has the loan funds, the buyers have their certified balance, and the title company is ready to insure except for the Doyle action. Howard cannot deliver title that a reputable company will insure at regular rates. Under Howard's own letter, time is of the essence today.

blocks.q: If Ines and Kwame decide to cancel the contract, what does the contract give them?
c: Their down payment back plus the difference between the price and the house's appraised value
Their down payment back and nothing more, because the delay was caused by a third party
Their down payment, plus the cost of title and survey, unless the defect was willful
Nothing yet, because Margaret is entitled to one more reasonable adjournment to fix it
blocks.x: The seller's inability-to-convey clause, common in New York residential contracts, limits the buyer's remedy to a refund of the down payment and the net cost of title examination and survey, unless the seller willfully caused the defect. Corinne's filing was not Margaret's doing. The adjournment answer is the trap: Howard's letter made July 9 of the essence for both sides, so Margaret has no further adjournment as of right.

blocks.html: The buyers like the house and do not want to start over. Priya and Howard sign a written extension: closing on or before September 15, time of the essence for both parties, with the buyers free to cancel and recover their deposit and title costs if the notice is not cancelled by then. Margaret also credits the second rate lock extension. That afternoon Margaret calls Jordan and asks a pointed question: she has done everything, the buyers are still in, so is Hudson & Hart's commission due now?

blocks.q: Is the commission due to Hudson & Hart before the closing takes place?
c: Yes, because Jordan produced buyers who were ready, willing, and able on July 9
No, because a commission is never due unless the closing happens on the contract date
Yes, but just half, since the contract was signed and the deposit is in escrow
No. The listing agreement makes it payable if, as, and when title closes
blocks.x: Without special language, a New York broker generally earns a commission by producing a ready, willing, and able buyer on terms the seller accepts. Listing agreements often change that by making the fee payable "if, as, and when title closes," and Margaret's does. The ready-willing-able answer is the trap: it states the default rule, but the parties contracted around it. The "never" answer is wrong too: a closing on a later date still triggers the fee.

blocks.text: July 30: an email about the wire

blocks.html: Late one evening the buyers receive an email that appears to come from Howard's office, copying Jordan: because of "an audit of our IOLA account," the buyers should wire the balance due at closing to a new account, and here are the instructions. The address is one letter off from Howard's real domain.

blocks.q: Ines forwards the email to Jordan and asks if it is real. What should Jordan tell her?
c: Reply to the email and ask the sender to confirm the new account number in writing
Wire a small test amount first, then send the balance once the test arrives safely
Send nothing and call Priya, who will confirm with Howard at a number she already has
Follow it, since the email copies Jordan and uses the case name and the closing date
blocks.x: Wire instructions that change by email are the classic sign of closing fraud: criminals watch a hacked inbox, copy the details, and spoof a lookalike domain. Verify by phone at a number from the file, never one in the suspicious email, and through the buyers' own attorney. The test-wire answer is the trap: a small transfer to the thief's account arrives safely too and proves nothing. Funds lost this way are rarely recovered.

blocks.html: Corinne's lawyer files the complaint but never serves Margaret. On August 10, two days after the 30-day window closes, Howard moves to cancel the notice under CPLR 6514(a). On August 27 the court grants the motion and directs the county clerk to cancel it. Corinne can still pursue her lawsuit, but her notice is gone, and a buyer who takes title now is not bound by her case through it. The title company removes the exception. Closing is set for Thursday, September 3.

At the table, the title closer runs one last rundown that morning: clean. The buyers sign the loan papers, the down payment is released from Howard's escrow, the roofer's escrow of $27,600 is held back, and the deed is delivered and accepted. In Brooklyn the closer records through ACRIS, with the City Register, and submits the documents that afternoon.

blocks.q: Why does it matter that the title company, not the buyers, runs the final rundown and submits the deed for recording right away?
c: Because a New York deed has no legal effect until it appears in the public records
Because the company insures the gap between its last search and the recording
Because only a title company may lawfully record a deed in the City Register
Because recording on the day of closing exempts the deed from the mansion tax
blocks.x: Title passes on delivery and acceptance of the deed. Recording protects the buyers against later claimants under New York's race-notice recording act. Between the last rundown and recording there is a gap in which something new could be filed. When the title company handles the closing and the recording, it insures that gap. The first answer is the trap: an unrecorded deed is valid between the parties; it is vulnerable to later buyers and lienors, not void.

blocks.title: NYC specifics at this closing
blocks.html: In Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and the Bronx, deeds and mortgages are recorded through ACRIS with the City Register; Staten Island records with the Richmond County Clerk. Departmental searches (DOB, ECB, HPD, Fire, street report) are routine in NYC deals because so many issues live in City agency records rather than in the land records.
The roofer never sues. Margaret's attorney calendars the date.

blocks.q: Bay Ridge Roofing never starts a foreclosure action and never gets an extension. What happens to its lien and to the escrow?
c: The lien expires one year after filing, and the title company can release the escrow to Margaret
The lien lasts ten years like a money judgment, so the escrow stays until the decade is up
The lien attaches to the buyers, who must pay it at their own sale, so the escrow goes to them
The lien converts to a judgment lien on Margaret's other property and the escrow goes to the roofer
blocks.x: A mechanic's lien on private property lasts one year from filing unless the lienor starts an action to foreclose it or obtains an extension. If neither happens, the lien lapses and the escrow that secured the title company's coverage goes back to the seller. The judgment answer is the trap: ten years is the life of a docketed money judgment, which the roofer would have to win in court first.

blocks.html: On July 8, 2027, the lien lapses. The title company releases the $27,600 to Margaret, who by then has stopped answering the roofer's calls. Corinne's lawsuit is dismissed a month later.

items: Departmental searches show what City agencies know: open permits, ECB penalties, certificate of occupancy problems. An open permit is not a lien; it is cleared with an expediter and inspections, not money.

"On or about" closing dates are not of the essence. Either side gets a reasonable adjournment. A clear notice setting a reasonable date and warning of default makes time of the essence, and it binds the sender too.

The rundown can find new filings the day before closing. A mechanic's lien is bonded at 110% or insured over with an escrow; on a single-family house it must be filed within 4 months and lasts 1 year unless enforced.

A notice of pendency is constructive notice of a lawsuit, not a lien. It cannot be paid off. It is cancelled by the plaintiff, by court order (mandatory if the summons is not served within 30 days), or on an undertaking.

When the seller cannot convey insurable title, the typical New York contract limits the buyer to the deposit plus title and survey costs, unless the seller acted willfully. A commission payable "if, as, and when title closes" waits for the closing.
Verify any change in wire instructions by phone at a known number. The title company's rundown and prompt recording close the gap.

roleplays.title: Whose House Is It?
roleplays.setting: A widow's kitchen in Brooklyn. She wants to list today.
roleplays.goal: Find out who actually holds title before taking the listing, bring in the remainderman and an attorney, and never give legal advice you are not licensed to give.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play a 71-year-old Brooklyn widow who believes she owns her house outright. Her late husband's will leaves it to her for life, then to a relative (the remainderman) who lives out of state. Be warm but impatient: you want to list this weekend, you resent involving the relative, and you ask whether they get any money. Later ask whether you can remove and sell the stained glass windows, rent the house out, or ignore a tax bill. The learner must verify title before listing, identify the life estate and remainder, insist both must sign, refer legal questions to an attorney, and warn about waste, fixtures, and taxes. Grade on accuracy, refusal to give legal advice, and tact.
opening: A kitchen in {hood}. {client}, widowed last year, has the will on the table and wants her house on the market this weekend at {price}.
{client} called Hudson & Hart about listing her {hood} home. Over tea, she slides her late husband's will across the table.
Saturday morning in {hood}. {client} has lived in the house for 40 years and wants to sell at {price}, fast.

say: My husband left me the house. Here's his will. I want it listed this weekend at {price}. Where do I sign?
It's my house now. I'd like the sign on the lawn by Saturday. Bring the papers and let's get started.

moves.text: Before we sign anything, may I read the will and pull the deed? I want to list it correctly.
moves.fb: Right. Confirm ownership before taking a listing. Whoever signs must have authority to sell what you advertise.
moves.react: {client} pushes the will over. "Read away, dear."

moves.text: Let's confirm title first. I'll pull the recorded deed, so we know exactly who can sign.
moves.fb: Correct. Checking the record before listing prevents marketing a house the client can't convey.
moves.react: "If you must," {client} sighs. "It's all mine, you'll see."

moves.text: Let's sign today, and I'll check the deed on ACRIS before the photos go up on Monday.
moves.fb: Checking is good, but sign the listing after you know who has authority, not before.

moves.text: Right here. A will that names you means you own it, so the paperwork can wait until contract.
moves.fb: A will can create lesser interests. Listing without checking sets up a failed deal and possible misrepresentation.

moves.text: Sign here. Any widow inherits the house automatically in New York through her dower rights.
moves.fb: New York abolished dower. A surviving spouse's interest depends on the deed and the will.

moves.text: Right here. If the will left it to you, the estate is settled, so there's no need to see the deed.
moves.fb: A will doesn't settle title by itself, and the wording may give her less than full ownership.

say: See? It says 'to my wife for her life, then to my {heir}.' That's just how lawyers write. It's my house.
It says I get it for my life and then my {heir} gets it. But it's mine. My {heir} doesn't need to be bothered.

moves.text: This gives you a life estate and your {heir} the remainder. A buyer needs both of you to sign.
moves.fb: Right. A life tenant alone can convey only a life estate. The remainderman must join for a full sale.

moves.text: You hold the house for life; your {heir} holds what comes after. A full sale needs both signatures.
moves.fb: Correct reading, explained without legal conclusions about the estate itself.
moves.react: "I never thought of it that way," {client} says.

moves.text: Let's list it anyway and let the attorneys sort out the will language once we get to contract.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but you'd be marketing a property she can't convey alone. Get the remainderman on board first.

moves.text: You're the owner here. Your {heir} has no say in anything at all until after you've passed away.
moves.fb: Wrong on the law, and it's legal advice. The remainderman holds a present interest and must sign.

moves.text: It's a life estate, so you can sell the whole house alone as long as you live there until the closing.
moves.fb: A life tenant can't sell more than she owns. Living there until closing changes nothing.

moves.text: That wording makes you joint tenants with your {heir}, so either of you can sell the whole thing.
moves.fb: Wrong estate. 'For life, then to' creates a life estate and remainder, not a joint tenancy.
moves.react: {client} looks relieved. "So I can sell it myself."

say: Fine. But if my {heir} signs, do they get money? I'm the one who lived here 40 years.
So who gets the money? I've paid for this roof twice.

moves.text: The split is a legal question. Your attorney works it out with theirs, often using life tables.
moves.fb: Right. You explain the concept and refer specifics to counsel. Licensees may not practice law.
moves.react: {client} sighs. "Fine. Give me an attorney's number."

moves.text: Both of you own something real, so both get a share. The exact split is for your attorneys to set.
moves.fb: Correct. Both interests have value, and the allocation is a legal matter for attorneys.

moves.text: Probably, but I'd hate to guess. Let's not talk money until everyone has signed the listing.
moves.fb: Not wrong, but you could explain the concept and send her to an attorney now.

moves.text: They get nothing while you're alive. A remainder only turns into money once the life tenant has died.
moves.fb: False. A remainderman holds a present property interest that has value in a sale today.

moves.text: They get half, always. New York splits life estate sales fifty-fifty between the two owners.
moves.fb: No fixed split exists. It depends on the facts, often life expectancy tables, and attorneys decide.

moves.text: No, they just sign to be polite. All the proceeds legally go to whoever lives in the house.
moves.fb: Wrong and harmful legal advice. Both interests have value in the sale.
moves.react: {client} relaxes. "Good. A signature and that's it."

say: And while we wait, can I take out the stained glass windows and sell them? They're worth a fortune.
The stained glass in the stairwell is antique. A dealer offered me good money. I can sell those, can't I?

moves.text: I'd hold off. Removing them could be waste your {heir} could sue over, and buyers expect them.
moves.fb: Right. A life tenant may not commit waste, and stained glass is likely a fixture that passes with the house.
moves.react: {client} touches the glass. "I'd hate a lawsuit."

moves.text: Please don't. They're likely fixtures; stripping them could be waste. Ask your attorney.
moves.fb: Correct. Fixtures stay unless excluded in writing, and the remainderman can sue for waste.

moves.text: Let's ask your attorney first. My guess is it's okay, but I'd rather a lawyer say so.
moves.fb: Referring is right, but guessing 'okay' signals permission for possible waste.

moves.text: Sure, and we just won't show them in the listing photos, so no buyer knows they were there.
moves.fb: That invites a waste claim and hides a change in what the buyer is getting.

moves.text: Go ahead. Windows are personal property, so they're yours to sell no matter who owns the house.
moves.fb: Built-in windows are fixtures, part of the real property, not personal property.

moves.text: Yes, a life tenant can remove anything she paid for. Just keep the receipts to show it's yours.
moves.fb: Paying for a fixture doesn't make it removable. Stripping it can be waste against the remainderman.

say: Fine. My {heir} lives in {heirtown}. How do we even do this from that far away?
My {heir} is in {heirtown} and never visits. How would we get their signature?

moves.text: Their attorney can review it, and they can sign before a notary where they live. Call yours now.
moves.fb: Right. Documents can be acknowledged before a notary out of state, and each owner should have counsel.
moves.react: {client} nods. "I'll call my attorney this afternoon."

moves.text: We bring in an attorney for each of you. Signatures can be notarized wherever your {heir} lives.
moves.fb: Correct. You keep the legal work with attorneys and explain the practical path.

moves.text: I'll call your {heir} myself tonight and explain the will, and then we'll see what they think.
moves.fb: Reaching out is fine, but explaining a will's legal effect is the attorneys' job, not yours.

moves.text: Easy. You can sign their name for them, since you're family and they already agreed on the phone.
moves.fb: Signing another owner's name is forgery. Each owner signs, before a notary, for recording.

moves.text: They can just text us a yes. A written listing isn't needed when it's family property like this.
moves.fb: Listings and sale contracts need proper written signatures. A text from an owner isn't enough here.

moves.text: We'll list now with only your signature and add your {heir} later, once we actually have a buyer.
moves.fb: Marketing a full fee sale with only the life tenant's authority misleads buyers.

say: Buyer's attorney on the {hood} listing is asking about some {heir} in the will. Can you just tell them it's handled?
The buyer's lawyer keeps asking about a remainder thing. Just say it's fine so we can get to contract.

moves.text: No. I'll tell them the truth: there's a remainder interest the attorneys are handling.
moves.fb: Right. You disclose the known title issue and keep legal resolution with counsel.

moves.text: I can't call it handled when it isn't. Let's connect their attorney with {client}'s attorney.
moves.fb: Correct. Attorney to attorney is the right channel for a title question.
moves.react: "Okay, send me the number," Marcus says.

moves.text: Tell them I'm looking into it. I'll call back once I talk to {client} later this week.
moves.fb: Not false, but stalling a buyer's attorney on a known issue wastes time and trust.

moves.text: Sure. Tell them it's handled. The heir will sign eventually, and nobody needs details now.
moves.fb: Telling a buyer's attorney a title issue is handled when it isn't is misrepresentation.

moves.text: Tell them the remainder ended when the husband died, so it isn't an issue for the closing.
moves.fb: Wrong. The remainder takes effect when the life tenant dies, not the testator.
moves.react: "Great, I'll pass that on," Marcus says.

moves.text: Say the will is in probate, so they're not allowed to ask about it until probate is done.
moves.fb: A false reason to block a fair question is still misrepresentation.

say: My {heir} called. They want to list the house themselves, right now, with a different broker.
My {heir} found a broker in {heirtown} who says they can list it without me. Is that true?

moves.text: Both of you have to agree on any sale. Let's get both attorneys talking before anyone lists.
moves.fb: Right. Neither the life tenant nor the remainderman can sell the full fee alone.

moves.text: Neither of you can sell the whole house alone. It's time to bring both attorneys in together.
moves.fb: Correct. A full sale needs both interests, so the path is agreement through counsel.

moves.text: Then maybe just let them handle it, and I'll step back from the listing for the time being.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but you leave your client without guidance when she needs it.

moves.text: They can't. A remainderman has no rights at all until you pass, so you can just ignore them for now.
moves.fb: Wrong. The remainderman holds a present interest and must join any sale of the fee.

moves.text: Fine, whoever signs first gets the listing. In New York the first broker to list wins.
moves.fb: No such rule. A listing doesn't give authority to sell interests the signer doesn't own.

moves.text: Then we'd better list it today, before they do. A signed listing blocks the other broker.
moves.fb: Rushing to list without the remainderman markets a sale your client can't complete.

say: Can I just rent the house out instead and move in with my sister? The rent would help.
What if I lease it to a nice family and live with my daughter? Is that allowed?

moves.text: You may be able to lease your interest, but a lease ends at your death. Ask your attorney.
moves.fb: Right. A life tenant may lease her interest, but the lease can't outlast the life estate without the remainderman.

moves.text: Possibly, since the right to use the house is yours. The terms are for your attorney.
moves.fb: Correct. You flag the concept and leave the legal terms to counsel.

moves.text: I'm not sure that's allowed. Let's focus on the sale and skip the rental idea for now.
moves.fb: Not harmful, but she does have use rights. Refer her to her attorney instead.

moves.text: No. A life tenant has to live in the house personally, or the life estate ends right away for you.
moves.fb: Wrong. A life estate doesn't require personal occupancy.

moves.text: Sure, and you could even sign a 20-year lease. It binds your {heir} after you're gone too.
moves.fb: A lease from a life tenant generally ends when the life estate ends.

moves.text: Yes, and the rent goes half to your {heir} every month, since they own the property too.
moves.fb: The life tenant is generally entitled to the income during her life.

say: There's a letter here about unpaid property taxes. Isn't that my {heir}'s problem now?
The city says I owe property taxes. Shouldn't my {heir} pay, since they'll own it someday?

moves.text: Usually the life tenant pays ongoing taxes. Unpaid taxes become a lien, so call your attorney.
moves.fb: Right. A life tenant generally owes ordinary taxes, and tax liens take priority over other liens.
moves.react: {client} winces. "I'll bring the letter to the attorney."

moves.text: Taxes come first among liens, so this matters for the sale. Your attorney can sort it out.
moves.fb: Correct. Real property taxes are a first-priority lien and must be cleared to close.
moves.react: "I didn't know it was that serious," {client} says.

moves.text: I'm not sure who pays. Let's set it aside and deal with it when the title report comes in.
moves.fb: Not wrong to refer it, but waiting lets a priority lien grow. Get it to the attorney now.

moves.text: Yes. Remaindermen pay the taxes, since they'll own the house eventually. Send it to them.
moves.fb: Generally backwards. The life tenant in possession pays ordinary taxes.

moves.text: Don't worry about it. Property taxes are wiped out when a house sells, so the buyer never sees them.
moves.fb: Wrong. Unpaid taxes are a lien that must be paid off at closing.

moves.text: Just ignore it. A tax lien sits behind the mortgage, so it won't affect the sale much.
moves.fb: Wrong. Real property tax liens come first, ahead of mortgages.
moves.react: {client} drops the letter in a drawer.

roleplays.debrief: A life tenant can convey only a life estate, so selling the whole house needs the remainderman's signature too. Verify title before listing, send ownership and proceeds questions to attorneys (licensees may not practice law), and warn against waste: fixtures stay with the house, and the life tenant generally keeps up the property and pays the taxes, which are a first-priority lien.

roleplays.title: Closing Day Surprises
roleplays.setting: A Brooklyn condo: final walk-through at 9 a.m., closing at 11 a.m.
roleplays.goal: Protect your buyer at the walk-through, handle a title problem through the attorneys, and turn down an illegal referral fee.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play an anxious first-time condo buyer who wants to rush the final walk-through, and briefly Marcus, a corner-cutting colleague who texts about a $300-per-closing title company referral offer. Plant a walk-through defect and a missing contracted item, an attorney's report of an old paid but unsatisfied mortgage, an emailed change in wiring instructions, and a cash thank-you after closing. The learner must insist on a thorough walk-through, document problems, route remedies and title issues through the attorneys, verify wiring instructions by phone, answer transfer tax questions accurately, refuse the referral fee as a RESPA Section 8 violation, and decline direct payment from the client. Grade on buyer protection, staying within role, and compliance.

defect: the kitchen faucet won't stop dripping

opening: A {hood} condo, {price}. Final walk-through at 9 a.m., closing at 11 at the seller's attorney's office. Your buyer {client} hasn't slept.
Closing day for {client}'s {price} condo in {hood}. You meet in the lobby at 9 for the final walk-through.
{client} texts at 6 a.m.: 'Closing today!!' The {hood} condo is {price}. Walk-through first, then the attorneys.

say: Walk-through time. Everything looks fine. Can we skip the rest and grab coffee? I'm so nervous.
It looks the same as last time. Do we really need to check everything? I just want the keys.

moves.text: Ten more minutes. Run every faucet, test appliances, and confirm what the contract includes.
moves.fb: The walk-through confirms condition and included items before money moves. After closing, leverage disappears.
moves.react: {client} nods and turns on the kitchen tap.

moves.text: This is your last look before any money moves. Let's check the systems and the contract items first.
moves.fb: Correct. You protect the buyer by verifying condition and inclusions while there's still leverage.

moves.text: Sure, a quick lap is fine. If something's broken, you can call the seller's agent after closing.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but after closing the buyer's leverage is mostly gone. Check now.
moves.react: {client} looks relieved and heads for the door.

moves.text: Sure, the seller seems like a kind person. If anything breaks later, the condo board will fix it.
moves.fb: Condo boards maintain common elements, not unit appliances. Skipping leaves the buyer with no proof.

moves.text: We can skip it. The home inspection already covered all of this before you signed the contract.
moves.fb: The inspection was weeks ago. The walk-through checks what changed since, including contract items.

moves.text: Go grab coffee. I'll do the walk-through alone and sign off on it for you as your agent.
moves.fb: The buyer should see the property personally. Signing off for the buyer oversteps your role.

say: Wait, look: {defect}, and {item} from the contract is gone. What do we do?
Uh oh, {defect}. And where is {item}? That was in the contract.

moves.text: Let's photograph them both and call Priya now, so the attorneys can work out a credit or escrow.
moves.fb: Document, then route it through the attorneys. A holdback or credit is decided by counsel.

moves.text: Document it, then Priya handles the remedy, usually a credit or holdback at the table.
moves.fb: Correct. You protect the buyer and keep the legal remedy with the buyer's attorney.

moves.text: I'll tell the seller's agent we won't close unless it's fixed in an hour. Pressure works.
moves.fb: Pressure may work, but refusing to close is a legal position. Let the buyer's attorney decide.

moves.text: Small stuff. Close anyway, and I'll make sure the seller pays you back sometime next week.
moves.fb: You can't promise a post-closing payment. Once the deed passes, the buyer's leverage is gone.

moves.text: Let's take the seller's word they'll fix it. A spoken promise at closing is legally binding.
moves.fb: An oral promise is hard to enforce, and contract terms generally merge into the deed at closing.

moves.text: I'll work out a $500 credit with the seller's agent now so the attorneys don't slow us down.
moves.fb: Changing deal terms around the buyer's attorney oversteps your role, and the amount may be wrong.

say: One more thing. Title shows a 2016 mortgage that was paid off but never satisfied of record. The seller's attorney is on it.
Heads up: a 2016 loan was paid off, but the satisfaction was never recorded. We're getting a payoff letter and an affidavit.

moves.text: What do you need from me? I can ask the seller's agent to chase the old lender for paperwork.
moves.fb: Right. You help the attorneys clear the cloud without trying to resolve a title question yourself.
moves.react: Priya nods. "Have them send the payoff letter to me."

moves.text: Got it. I'll keep {client} calm and get you anything you need from the listing side today.
moves.fb: Correct. You support the attorney and stay in your role.
moves.react: "Perfect. That's all I need," Priya says.

moves.text: Should we push the closing to next week? I don't want {client} anywhere near a title problem.
moves.fb: Caution is understandable, but whether to delay is the attorney's call.
moves.react: Priya shakes her head. "Let's see if we can clear it today."

moves.text: It's paid off, so it doesn't matter. {client}, go ahead and sign, the old loan is gone.
moves.fb: An unsatisfied mortgage of record clouds title. Telling the buyer it doesn't matter is legal advice.
moves.react: Priya frowns. "Please let me handle the title advice."

moves.text: Title insurance covers that, so nobody needs to do anything about it before we close this morning.
moves.fb: The title company may except it. Clearing the record is how the cloud is removed.
moves.react: Priya sighs. "That's not how it works."

moves.text: Old mortgages expire after ten years in New York, so a 2016 loan can't cloud title anyway.
moves.fb: False. A mortgage lien of record stays until it's satisfied or released.
moves.react: Priya stares. "Where did you hear that?"

say: Do I owe the transfer tax? My friend said the buyer pays it at closing.
What about all these taxes? My coworker said buyers get hit with the transfer tax.

moves.text: In New York the seller usually pays transfer taxes. You pay mortgage recording tax if you finance.
moves.fb: Right. NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT are customarily paid by the seller; the borrower pays mortgage recording tax.

moves.text: Normally the seller pays those. Priya will walk you through your own costs on the statement.
moves.fb: Correct, and you send the line-by-line costs to the attorney.

moves.text: I think the seller pays, but I'm not sure. Ask Priya, she knows the exact numbers better.
moves.fb: Honest, but you should know the basic rule on who pays transfer taxes.

moves.text: Yes, the buyer always pays the transfer taxes. Plus there's a 1% mansion tax on each NYC condo.
moves.fb: Sellers usually pay transfer taxes, and the mansion tax applies only at $1 million or more.

moves.text: You'd pay half. New York splits the transfer taxes evenly between the buyer and the seller at closing.
moves.fb: There's no automatic split. The seller customarily pays NYS and NYC transfer taxes.

moves.text: No taxes at all on condos. Only houses pay transfer and recording taxes in New York City.
moves.fb: Condos pay transfer taxes and, if financed, mortgage recording tax.

say: We closed! I want to thank you. Can I give you $500 cash? You saved me so much today.
Keys in hand! Let me Venmo you something. You earned it.

moves.text: That's kind, but I'm paid only through my broker. A review or a referral means even more.
moves.fb: Right. RPL 442-a: a salesperson may receive compensation only from the sponsoring broker.

moves.text: Thank you, but I can't accept cash from you. Anything like that goes through Diane.
moves.fb: Correct. Payment from a client to a salesperson must run through the broker.

moves.text: Let me check with Diane first and I'll let you know. I don't want to get anything wrong here.
moves.fb: Asking is better than accepting, but the answer is a clear no.

moves.text: Thanks! A closing gift from a happy client isn't commission, so cash is totally fine.
moves.fb: A payment for your work is compensation, which may come only from your broker.

moves.text: Sure, Venmo's easier for me. Diane only cares about payments over a thousand dollars.
moves.fb: There's no threshold. Any direct compensation from a client violates RPL 442-a.

moves.text: Yes please. And if the title company sends something, have it go to my personal email.
moves.fb: Taking anything from a settlement provider for the deal raises RESPA and 442-a problems.

say: (texting) The title company's rep says they'll send us $300 a closing if we steer buyers their way. Want in?
(texting) Easy money: that title company pays $300 per buyer we send them. I'll add you to the list.

moves.text: No. That's a RESPA referral kickback. And tell Diane if they offer it to anyone else.
moves.fb: RESPA Section 8 prohibits fees for referrals of settlement services. Disclosure doesn't cure it.

moves.text: Pass. Fees for referring settlement services are banned under RESPA Section 8.
moves.fb: Correct. A per-closing referral payment is a kickback on a federally related loan.

moves.text: I'll think about it after this closing. Today is not the day to decide something like that.
moves.fb: You didn't accept, but there's nothing to think about. Say no.

moves.text: Only if we disclose it to the buyer. Once it's disclosed, a referral fee is fine under RESPA.
moves.fb: Disclosure doesn't make a referral fee legal under RESPA. It's still a kickback.

moves.text: Sure, as long as it goes to the firm, not us. Payments to a business are allowed.
moves.fb: RESPA bans the referral payment no matter who receives it.
moves.react: Marcus: "I'll tell them to pay the firm."

moves.text: Yes, if they call it a marketing fee. RESPA only covers fees labeled as referral payments.
moves.fb: Relabeling doesn't help. RESPA looks at what the payment is for.

say: I just got an email from Priya with new wiring instructions for the balance. Different bank. Should I send it?
Priya's email says the escrow bank changed and I should wire the balance to a new account today.

moves.text: Stop. Call Priya at the number you already have, not the one in the email, before sending a cent.
moves.fb: Right. Changed wiring instructions by email are a classic closing fraud. Verify by a known phone number.
moves.react: {client} calls. Priya never sent it. "Oh my god."

moves.text: Don't wire anything yet. Changed instructions by email are a known scam. Call to verify first.
moves.fb: Correct. Independent verification protects the buyer's funds.

moves.text: It's probably fine, but maybe hit reply on the email and ask Priya to confirm that it's really her.
