moves.fb: Replying may go straight to the scammer. Call a number you already know.
moves.react: {client} replies. A reply comes back: "Yes, it's me."

moves.text: If it came from Priya's address, it's safe. Send it now so we don't hold up the closing.
moves.fb: Email addresses are easily spoofed or hacked. Never act on changed instructions without calling.

moves.text: Send half now and half after closing. That way you're only risking part of the money.
moves.fb: Splitting doesn't make a fraudulent account safe. Verify first.

moves.text: Banks reverse wrong wires within a day, so send it, and we'll fix it later if it's wrong.
moves.fb: Wire transfers are very hard to recover once sent.

say: The seller's agent wants me to sign a paper saying I accept the condo 'as is' before we sit down. Should I?
They handed me a release to sign before closing. It says I accept everything as is.

moves.text: Not before Priya has read it. Signing a release now could waive the credits we just documented.
moves.fb: Right. Anything that affects the buyer's rights goes to the buyer's attorney first.

moves.text: Let's hand it to Priya first. Anything changing your rights goes through your attorney.
moves.fb: Correct. You protect the buyer without interpreting the document yourself.

moves.text: Let me read it over first, and I'll tell you whether it looks okay for you to sign it today.
moves.fb: Reading is fine, but judging a release's legal effect is the attorney's job.

moves.text: Sure, it's just a formality. Everybody signs an as-is paper like this one before closing on a condo.
moves.fb: It may waive the buyer's claims for the problems you just found.

moves.text: Sign it. As-is releases aren't enforceable in New York, so it doesn't matter anyway.
moves.fb: Wrong and legal advice. Releases can be enforceable.

moves.text: Yes, and I'll sign it as your agent too, so the seller's side knows that we're all on board.
moves.fb: You can't waive the buyer's rights for them, and you shouldn't encourage signing.

roleplays.debrief: Use the final walk-through to verify condition and contract items, document problems, and route remedies and title clouds through the attorneys. Fees for referring settlement services are kickbacks under RESPA Section 8, disclosed or not. Verify changed wiring instructions by phone, know that sellers customarily pay NYS and NYC transfer taxes while borrowers pay mortgage recording tax, and remember a salesperson is paid only by the sponsoring broker (RPL 442-a).

roleplays.title: Fourteen Feet Over the Line
roleplays.setting: Staten Island: a listing appointment after a survey surprise
roleplays.goal: Handle a boundary encroachment honestly: disclose it, keep out of legal advice, and set the sellers' expectations.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play a Staten Island seller who just learned from a survey that the neighbor's improvements sit several feet onto the lot, for more than ten years. You want to list fast with the old survey and say nothing, then ask whether the neighbor really owns the strip, what to put in the listing, and whether you can tear the fence out tonight. The learner must refuse to conceal the encroachment, explain NY's 10-year adverse possession concept (including the 2008 rule that de minimis non-structural encroachments like fences and hedges are permissive) without giving legal conclusions, bring in an attorney, disclose to buyers, price realistically, and keep records. Grade on honesty, accuracy, and staying out of legal advice.
opening: A listing appointment in {hood}, Staten Island. The new survey shows the neighbor's {things} sit {feet} onto {client}'s lot, there since about {year}.
{client} hands you a fresh survey at the kitchen table in {hood}. The neighbor's {things} run {feet} over the line. They've been there since {year}.
You came to take a {hood} listing. Instead {client} shows you a survey: the neighbor's {things}, {feet} onto the lot, in place since {year}.

say: Let's just list it with the old survey. Buyers won't notice a fence.
Forget the new survey. The old one looks fine. Nobody measures the backyard.

moves.text: We can't hide a known boundary issue. Any buyer's survey finds it. Let's call Priya.
moves.fb: Knowingly concealing a material defect is misrepresentation. Encroachments affect marketable title.

moves.text: A known encroachment is material. We disclose it, and an attorney helps us work out the fix.
moves.fb: Correct. You disclose the known material fact and bring in counsel.

moves.text: Let's hold off listing for a month and see whether the neighbor moves things back on their own.
moves.fb: Not illegal, but waiting rarely fixes an encroachment. An attorney should be involved now.

moves.text: Fine, but don't tell me anything else about it. What I don't know, I can't be blamed for.
moves.fb: You already know. Deliberately avoiding details of a known defect is still concealment.

moves.text: Sure. Encroachments under 20 feet don't count as material in New York, so we can skip it.
moves.fb: There's no footage threshold. A known encroachment is a material fact.

moves.text: We'll list it, and if a buyer's attorney asks, we'll say the old survey is all we have.
moves.fb: Saying the old survey is all you have, when you hold a new one, is a lie.

say: The neighbor says that strip is hers now. Is she right?
My neighbor told me the land under her {things} belongs to her after all this time. Can that be true?

moves.text: Ten years' open, exclusive, hostile use can support a claim. Priya can say if she'd win.
moves.fb: You explain NY's 10-year adverse possession concept and leave the conclusion to counsel.

moves.text: She might have a claim after ten years, depending on facts. That's a question for an attorney.
moves.fb: Correct. Concept yes, legal conclusion no.

moves.text: No idea, honestly. I'm not a lawyer, so I'd rather not say anything about it at all, sorry.
moves.fb: Safe, but you can explain the general concept without giving a legal conclusion.
moves.react: {client} looks frustrated. "Then who do I ask?"

moves.text: No way. She'd need 20 years of use before she could claim it, so she's nowhere close.
moves.fb: Wrong. New York's adverse possession period is 10 years.

moves.text: Yes, it's hers. Anything over the line for a decade automatically transfers to the neighbor's name.
moves.fb: Not automatic. All elements must be proven, and fences alone are deemed permissive since 2008.

moves.text: No. Fences and patios never count in New York since 2008, so she has no claim at all.
moves.fb: Partly wrong. RPAPL 543 treats de minimis non-structural items like fences as permissive, but structures can count.

say: Priya says a boundary line agreement, a sale of the strip, or court. All slow. So what do I put in the listing?
Okay, the lawyer's working on it. What do we tell buyers in the meantime?

moves.text: We price it for the issue and tell every buyer up front that it's being resolved.
moves.fb: Honest marketing and realistic pricing protect the seller and you.
moves.react: {client} nods. "Better than a deal dying at contract."

moves.text: We disclose the encroachment from day one and price with it in mind while Priya works on it.
moves.fb: Correct. Disclosure plus pricing keeps buyers from walking at the survey.

moves.text: We list at full price, disclose it, and hope buyers don't care much about a few feet.
moves.fb: Disclosure is right, but ignoring the issue in pricing invites failed deals.

moves.text: We list it as is and say nothing. 'As is' covers anything a buyer finds out later on.
moves.fb: 'As is' doesn't excuse concealing a known material fact.

moves.text: We call the lot 'approximately' its full size. That one word protects us from any claim.
moves.fb: A hedge word doesn't cure a known misstatement of the lot.

moves.text: We mention a 'friendly neighbor' and leave the details for the buyer's survey to find.
moves.fb: Leaving a known defect for the buyer to discover is concealment.

say: Okay, I'll just go rip out that fence tonight. It's my land.
I'm getting a crowbar. If it's on my side, it comes down this weekend.

moves.text: Please don't. Self-help could escalate or hurt your position. Let Priya handle her.
moves.fb: Right. Physical self-help invites conflict and legal risk. Route it through counsel.

moves.text: I'd hold off. Tearing it out could start a new dispute. Talk to Priya before you touch it.
moves.fb: Correct. You protect the client without giving legal conclusions.

moves.text: That's your call as the owner. Just maybe wait until after the listing photos are done.
moves.fb: Not illegal advice, but it ignores the risk of escalating a legal dispute.

moves.text: Good idea. Once it's gone, the encroachment disappears and we can use the old survey.
moves.fb: Removing it doesn't erase a possible claim or the duty to disclose what you know.

moves.text: Go for it. Removing it resets her ten-year clock back to zero, so her claim is gone for good.
moves.fb: If the period already ran, removal doesn't undo it. And this is legal advice.

moves.text: Sure, and anything else of hers on your side too. It's all legally your property now.
moves.fb: Destroying a neighbor's property during a dispute is risky and may be unlawful.

say: Good work so far. What goes in the file on this one?
Before you go, tell me what you're keeping on the {hood} listing.

moves.text: The survey, my written disclosure to buyers and notes on Priya's advice, kept three years.
moves.fb: Right. Brokers keep transaction records for 3 years (19 NYCRR 175.23).

moves.text: All of it: the survey, the disclosures, and emails. The firm keeps files for three years.
moves.fb: Correct. A complete file proves the disclosure happened.

moves.text: My notes are on my phone. I'll send them over if anyone ever asks about the listing.
moves.fb: Notes on a phone aren't a firm record. Put them in the file now.

moves.text: Nothing at all. If we don't put it in writing, there's nothing for anyone to subpoena later on.
moves.fb: Records are required for 3 years, and no record means no proof you disclosed.
moves.react: Diane stares. "That is the wrong answer."

moves.text: Just the listing agreement. Disclosures don't need keeping once the deal has closed.
moves.fb: Wrong. Transaction records, including disclosures, are kept 3 years.

moves.text: Only the old survey. Keeping the new one could be used against the seller in court.
moves.fb: Destroying the new survey hides a known defect and breaks recordkeeping rules.

say: A buyer at my open house asked straight out about boundary issues. I said 'not that I know of.' That okay?
Some buyer asked me if the survey's clean. I said yes. We're good, right?

moves.text: We know there's one. Let's call that buyer today and correct it in writing.
moves.fb: Right. A misstatement of a known material fact must be corrected promptly.

moves.text: That's a misstatement. We correct it with the buyer now and tell Diane what we did.
moves.fb: Correct. Fix it and escalate to the supervising broker.

moves.text: Let's just make sure the next buyer hears about it. That one may not even make an offer.
moves.fb: Better than nothing, but the buyer who heard the false answer must be corrected.

moves.text: It's fine. They asked you, not me, and you hadn't read the new survey yourself.
moves.fb: The firm knows. A co-listing agent can't hide behind not having read the file.

moves.text: Fine. Verbal answers at open houses don't count. Only the written disclosures matter.
moves.fb: Oral misrepresentations count too.

moves.text: Good answer. Admitting it before an offer just gives the buyer leverage on the price.
moves.fb: Concealing a material fact to protect price is misrepresentation.

say: The neighbor offered me $5,000 to just sign the strip over. Should I take it?
Neighbor says she'll pay me to deed her the strip and be done. Good deal?

moves.text: That's for you and Priya to weigh. I can show you how the strip affects the lot's value.
moves.fb: Right. You offer value data and leave the legal decision to the attorney.

moves.text: Before you sign, have Priya review it. I can pull data on what that land is worth.
moves.fb: Correct. Price data is your lane; the deed is the attorney's.

moves.text: Sounds fair to me, but I don't really know. Maybe ask a friend who has sold a house before.
moves.fb: A friend isn't counsel. Send it to the attorney and offer real value data.

moves.text: Take it. A quitclaim to the neighbor is just a formality and won't affect your sale at all.
moves.fb: Conveying part of the lot changes what you're selling, and it's legal advice.

moves.text: Don't take it. Hold out for more. She has to buy it, since she's legally trespassing.
moves.fb: That's a legal conclusion you can't make, and it may be wrong.

moves.text: Sign it, and I'll draw up the deed for the strip myself so you save the attorney fee.
moves.fb: Drafting a deed is practicing law. Licensees may not.

say: The title company will list it as an exception. Can we just tell buyers title insurance covers it?
Priya says title will insure 'subject to' the survey. That means it's covered, right?

moves.text: An exception means the policy excludes it, so no. Let's tell buyers what it means.
moves.fb: Right. An exception is carved out of coverage. Saying otherwise misleads buyers.

moves.text: We can't say that. An exception is the opposite of coverage. Priya can explain it to buyers.
moves.fb: Correct. You keep the description accurate and leave legal detail to the attorney.

moves.text: Let's not bring up the title policy at all. Buyers' attorneys can read it themselves.
moves.fb: Not false, but you already disclosed the issue. Be clear if asked.

moves.text: Yes. Title insurance covers anything that shows on a survey, so it's a selling point.
moves.fb: Wrong. Survey matters are often excepted from coverage.

moves.text: Sure. An exception just means the issue gets extra coverage at no cost to the buyer.
moves.fb: Backwards. An exception removes coverage for that item.

moves.text: Yes. Once it's insured, the encroachment legally no longer exists for the new owner.
moves.fb: Insurance doesn't erase a boundary problem.

roleplays.debrief: A known encroachment is a material fact: disclose it and never paper over it with an old survey. New York adverse possession takes 10 years of open, notorious, hostile, exclusive, continuous use, and since 2008 de minimis non-structural items like fences and hedges are deemed permissive (RPAPL 543), but whether a claim wins is for an attorney. A title exception removes coverage, and the firm keeps the file for 3 years (19 NYCRR 175.23).

questions.q: The characteristic that no two parcels of land are exactly alike is called:
c: Nonhomogeneity
Immobility
Indestructibility
Scarcity
questions.x: Nonhomogeneity, also called uniqueness, means every parcel differs. Immobility is the trap: it means land cannot be moved.

questions.q: Because every parcel is unique, a buyer can sue to force a seller to complete a sale. This rests on which characteristic?
c: Permanence of investment
Immobility
Nonhomogeneity
Situs
questions.x: Courts grant specific performance because no other parcel is the same: that is nonhomogeneity. Situs is the trap: it means area preference, an economic characteristic.

questions.q: The most complete form of ownership, unlimited in time and freely transferable, is:
c: Life estate
Fee simple absolute
Fee simple defeasible
Leasehold estate
questions.x: Fee simple absolute is the fullest ownership. Fee simple defeasible is the trap: it can be lost if a condition is broken.

questions.q: Which estate can be inherited, sold or given away without limit on its duration?
c: Life estate pur autre vie
Estate for years
Periodic tenancy
Fee simple
questions.x: A fee simple is inheritable and unlimited in time. An estate for years is the trap: it is a lease with a fixed end.

questions.q: Land is deeded 'so long as it is used as a park.' The buyer holds a:
c: Fee simple absolute
Life estate
Fee simple defeasible
Easement in gross
questions.x: Ownership that ends if a stated condition is broken is a qualified, or defeasible, fee. Fee simple absolute is the trap: that has no conditions.

questions.q: A qualified fee differs from a fee simple absolute because it:
c: Can be lost if a condition is broken
Ends when the owner dies
Cannot be sold to anyone
Gives only a right of way
questions.x: A defeasible fee lasts forever unless the stated condition or event occurs. 'Ends at death' is the trap: that describes a life estate.

questions.q: An owner grants a life estate to her brother and keeps the right to get the property back when he dies. She holds a:
c: Remainder interest
Leasehold interest
Easement appurtenant
Reversionary interest
questions.x: When property returns to the grantor or her heirs, the grantor holds a reversion. Remainder is the trap: a remainder goes to a third party, not back to the grantor.

questions.q: A landlord's right to get the apartment back when the lease ends is an example of a:
c: Remainder
Reversionary interest
Life estate
Right of first refusal
questions.x: The owner who gave a lesser estate and gets it back holds a reversion. Remainder is the trap: that names someone other than the grantor to receive it.

questions.q: A life tenant tears out the home's plumbing and lets the roof collapse. This is:
c: Waste
Accession
Adverse possession
Partition
questions.x: Damage or neglect by a life tenant that hurts the future owner's value is waste. Accession is the trap: it means acquiring additions to property.

questions.q: Who can sue a life tenant for committing waste?
c: The county assessor
Any neighbor
The remainderman or reversioner
The tenant's lender only
questions.x: Waste harms the person who will own the property next, so the remainderman or reversioner may sue. A neighbor is the trap: they have no future interest in the property.

questions.concept: Dower and curtesy in New York
questions.q: In New York today, dower and curtesy:
c: Give a surviving spouse one-third
Are abolished
Apply only to married women
Apply only to co-ops
questions.x: New York abolished dower and curtesy; surviving spouses are protected by the elective share instead. 'One-third' is the trap: that was the historic dower share.

questions.concept: Dower and curtesy in New York
questions.q: Historically, dower gave a widow an interest in her husband's real property. Its status in New York now is:
c: In force for homes only
Replaced by curtesy
Required in every deed
Abolished
questions.x: Both dower and curtesy are abolished in New York. 'Replaced by curtesy' is the trap: curtesy was the widower's version and is abolished too.

questions.q: In a general partnership, each partner is:
c: Liable only up to their investment
Shielded like a corporate shareholder
Personally liable for all partnership debts
Liable only for their own deals
questions.x: General partners share management and unlimited personal liability. 'Liable up to their investment' is the trap: that describes a limited partner.

questions.q: Three friends buy a building as general partners. The partnership defaults on a $300,000 loan. A creditor may collect from:
c: Any partner's personal assets
Only the partnership's assets
Only the managing partner
Only the partner who signed
questions.x: Every general partner is personally liable for all partnership debts. 'Only the partnership's assets' is the trap: that shield belongs to corporations and LLCs.

questions.q: In a limited partnership, the limited partners:
c: Manage daily operations
Have unlimited personal liability
Must hold real estate licenses
Invest passively and risk only their investment
questions.x: Limited partners are passive investors with liability capped at their investment. 'Manage operations' is the trap: that is the general partner's role.

questions.q: A limited partnership must have at least one:
c: Licensed broker as a partner
General partner with unlimited liability
Corporate shareholder
Limited partner who manages
questions.x: Every LP needs a general partner who manages and carries unlimited liability. 'A limited partner who manages' is the trap: managing can cost a limited partner their protection.

questions.q: Which business form gives owners limited liability while letting profits pass through to their personal tax returns?
c: Limited liability company
General partnership
Sole proprietorship
Joint tenancy
questions.x: An LLC combines limited liability with pass-through taxation. General partnership is the trap: it passes profits through but gives no liability protection.

questions.q: Investors who want protection from the business's debts and no separate corporate income tax would most likely form a(n):
c: General partnership
C corporation
LLC
Tenancy in common
questions.x: An LLC shields members' personal assets and passes profits through. C corporation is the trap: it shields owners but is taxed at the corporate level.

questions.q: A lien that attaches only to one identified property is a:
c: General lien
Specific lien
Judgment lien
Estate tax lien
questions.x: Specific liens, such as mortgages and property tax liens, attach to one parcel. Judgment lien is the trap: it is a general lien on all the debtor's property in the county.

questions.q: Which is an example of a specific lien?
c: A court judgment
A federal estate tax lien
A state income tax lien
A mortgage on one house
questions.x: A mortgage attaches only to the property pledged. A court judgment is the trap: it reaches all of the debtor's real property in the county.

questions.q: A New York State lien on a corporation's property for unpaid business taxes is a:
c: Mechanic's lien
Vendor's lien
Corporation franchise tax lien
Lis pendens
questions.x: Unpaid corporate franchise taxes create a state lien on the corporation's property. Mechanic's lien is the trap: it secures payment for work or materials.

questions.q: A buyer's title search shows that the corporate seller owes New York State back business taxes. The likely encumbrance is a:
c: Corporation franchise tax lien
Special assessment
Mortgage lien
Deed restriction
questions.x: Back corporate taxes owed to the state appear as a franchise tax lien. Special assessment is the trap: that is a local charge for an improvement.

questions.q: At a foreclosure sale, which liens are generally paid first?
c: The oldest recorded mortgage
Mechanic's liens
The newest recorded judgment
Real estate taxes and special assessments
questions.x: Property taxes and special assessments come first, then other liens generally in order of recording. The oldest mortgage is the trap: it is paid after taxes.

questions.q: Apart from taxes and special assessments, liens are generally paid in what order?
c: By size of the debt
By date of recording
By who filed suit first
Equally, at the same time
questions.x: Most liens rank by recording date: first in time, first in right. Size of the debt is the trap: a larger lien does not jump ahead.

questions.q: Rights that belong to a parcel and pass automatically with it when sold, such as an easement appurtenant, are:
c: Appurtenances
Encumbrances
Emblements
Chattels
questions.x: Appurtenances run with the land to the new owner. Encumbrances are the trap: they burden the property rather than benefit it.

questions.q: Unless excluded, a deed transfers the land together with its:
c: Personal property
Trade fixtures
Appurtenances
Emblements of the tenant
questions.x: Appurtenant rights go with the land automatically. Trade fixtures are the trap: they are the tenant's personal property.

questions.q: An owner signs a deed giving her neighbor the right to cross her driveway. This creates an easement by:
c: Necessity
Grant
Prescription
Condemnation
questions.x: An easement created expressly in writing by the servient owner is by grant. Prescription is the trap: that arises from long, hostile use, not a writing.

questions.q: An easement by grant is created:
c: By open use for ten years
When a parcel is landlocked
By government taking
Expressly, in a written deed or agreement
questions.x: A grant is an express written creation. 'Open use for ten years' is the trap: that describes prescription.

questions.q: The state takes a strip of a farm for a pipeline right of way and pays the owner. This creates an easement by:
c: Grant
Prescription
Condemnation
Implication
questions.x: An easement taken through eminent domain, with just compensation, is by condemnation. Grant is the trap: a grant is given voluntarily by the owner.

questions.q: When an easement is acquired by condemnation, the owner must receive:
c: Just compensation
Nothing, under police power
A tax exemption instead
A replacement parcel
questions.x: Eminent domain requires just compensation. Police power is the trap: regulation such as zoning requires no payment, but a taking does.

questions.q: Which is a non-possessory interest in real property?
c: A life estate
A lease
A fee simple
An easement
questions.x: An easement gives a right to use, not to occupy. Lease is the trap: a tenant has a possessory right to occupy.

questions.q: Which interest gives the holder the right to occupy the property?
c: A mortgage lien
A leasehold
A utility easement
A license to fish
questions.x: Leaseholds, life estates and fees are possessory. A mortgage lien is the trap: it is only a claim against the property.

questions.q: 'Lot 14, Block 3, on the map of Maple Grove filed in the county clerk's office' is a legal description by:
c: Reference to a recorded plat
Metes and bounds
Government survey
Monuments only
questions.x: Citing a lot on a recorded subdivision map is description by reference to a plat. Metes and bounds is the trap: that traces boundaries by distances and directions.

questions.q: Which legal description method relies on a recorded subdivision map?
c: Metes and bounds
Rectangular survey
Lot and block (plat)
Street address
questions.x: Lot and block descriptions refer to the recorded plat. Street address is the trap: it is not a legal description at all.

questions.q: In a deed, the grantor's promise that no one with a better title will disturb the grantee's possession is the covenant of:
c: Seisin
Quiet enjoyment
Further assurance
Against encumbrances
questions.x: Quiet enjoyment protects possession against superior claims. Seisin is the trap: that promises the grantor owns the property and can convey it.

questions.q: A grantee is evicted by someone holding superior title. Which deed covenant was broken?
c: Further assurance
Against encumbrances
Seisin only
Quiet enjoyment
questions.x: Being disturbed by someone with a better claim breaches quiet enjoyment. Against encumbrances is the trap: it is about undisclosed liens.

questions.q: The grantor's promise that there are no liens on the property other than those stated in the deed is the covenant:
c: Of seisin
Of quiet enjoyment
Against encumbrances
Of further assurance
questions.x: That promise is the covenant against encumbrances. Quiet enjoyment is the trap: it protects possession, not freedom from liens.

questions.q: After closing, the buyer discovers an unpaid mechanic's lien the deed did not mention. Which covenant was breached?
c: Against encumbrances
Of warranty forever
Of further assurance
Of quiet enjoyment
questions.x: An undisclosed lien breaches the covenant against encumbrances. Further assurance is the trap: that only promises to sign any documents needed to perfect title.

questions.q: The grantor's promise to sign any additional documents needed to perfect the grantee's title is the covenant of:
c: Warranty forever
Seisin
Quiet enjoyment
Further assurance
questions.x: Further assurance obliges the grantor to fix paperwork problems. Warranty forever is the trap: that promises to defend the title against claims.

questions.q: A deed has a misspelled legal description and the seller must sign a corrective deed. Which covenant requires this?
c: Against encumbrances
Further assurance
Quiet enjoyment
Warranty forever
questions.x: Signing corrective documents is what further assurance promises. Warranty forever is the trap: it is about defending title, not fixing paperwork.

questions.q: The grantor's promise to defend the title against all lawful claims and compensate the grantee for loss is the covenant of:
c: Warranty forever
Further assurance
Seisin
Against encumbrances
questions.x: Warranty forever is the grantor's guarantee to defend title. Further assurance is the trap: it only covers signing extra documents.

questions.q: Which deed covenant makes a full warranty deed the strongest protection for a buyer?
c: Quiet enjoyment only
Bargain and sale
Warranty forever
Quitclaim release
questions.x: The warranty forever covenant puts the grantor on the hook to defend title for good. Bargain and sale is the trap: that is a deed type with fewer or no covenants.

questions.q: When someone dies without a valid will, their property passes to relatives under:
c: Escheat
Intestate succession
Adverse possession
Devise
questions.x: The statutory order of heirs governs when there is no will. Escheat is the trap: property goes to the state only when there are no heirs at all.

questions.q: A New York owner dies without a will, survived by a spouse and children. Who decides who inherits?
c: The executor named in the will
The county assessor
The listing broker
The state's intestacy statute
questions.x: Without a will, New York's intestate succession law sets the heirs and shares. Executor is the trap: there is no will to name one.

questions.q: A son receives his father's house because his father died without a will. The son took title by:
c: Devise
Escheat
Descent
Accession
questions.x: Inheriting under intestacy is title by descent. Devise is the trap: that is receiving real property through a will.

questions.q: Title by descent and title by devise differ because descent:
c: Happens when there is no will
Requires a recorded deed
Applies only to personal property
Transfers to the state
questions.x: Descent is inheritance without a will; devise is by will. 'Transfers to the state' is the trap: that is escheat.

questions.q: Acquiring title to additions to your land, such as soil built up by a river, is called:
c: Avulsion
Escheat
Alienation
Accession
questions.x: Accession covers natural and man-made additions. Avulsion is the trap: it is the sudden loss of land to water.

questions.q: A tenant leaves trade fixtures behind after the lease ends and the landlord now owns them. The landlord acquired them by:
c: Descent
Accession
Devise
Prescription
questions.x: Abandoned trade fixtures become the owner's by accession. Prescription is the trap: it creates easements through long use.

questions.q: The soil and sediment a river gradually deposits on its bank is called:
c: Alluvion
Avulsion
Erosion
Reliction
questions.x: Alluvion is the deposit left by accretion. Reliction is the trap: it is land exposed when water recedes.

questions.q: Who owns alluvion deposited along a riverbank?
c: The state, as navigable land
The upstream owner
The owner of the bank where it builds up
Whoever fences it first
questions.x: Alluvion added by accretion belongs to the riparian owner whose land it builds up. The state is the trap: gradual additions go to the adjoining owner.

questions.q: The meeting where the price is paid, the deed is delivered and liens are paid off is the:
c: Contract signing
Title closing
Final walkthrough
Mortgage commitment
questions.x: The closing is where the sale is completed. Contract signing is the trap: that comes earlier and only creates obligations to close.

questions.q: Which event normally happens at the title closing?
c: The buyer first sees the home
The listing agreement is signed
The offer is accepted
The deed is delivered to the buyer
questions.x: Delivery of the deed at closing passes title. The accepted offer is the trap: that happens weeks before.

questions.q: State laws that make recorded documents give public notice and decide priority between competing claims are:
c: Statutes of frauds
Statutes of limitations
Recording acts
Usury laws
questions.x: Recording acts set priority and give constructive notice. Statute of frauds is the trap: it requires certain contracts to be in writing.

questions.q: A seller deeds the same house to two buyers. Under New York's recording act, the one who generally wins is the buyer who:
c: Records first in good faith for value
Signed the contract first
Paid the larger price
Moved in first
questions.x: New York is a race-notice state: a good-faith buyer for value who records first wins. 'Signed first' is the trap: recording, not signing, decides it.

questions.q: Examining public records for a property's ownership history and any liens is a:
c: Survey
Appraisal
Home inspection
Title search
questions.x: A title search reviews the records for ownership and encumbrances. Survey is the trap: it locates boundaries physically.

questions.q: A title search is mainly meant to find:
c: Structural problems in the house
Liens and defects in the chain of title
The property's market value
Zoning violations inside the unit
questions.x: Title searches look for recorded problems with ownership. Structural problems is the trap: that is a home inspection's job.

questions.q: On a closing statement, the buyer's total debits are $412,000 and total credits are $330,000. How much cash must the buyer bring?
questions.x: Cash due from the buyer is debits minus credits: $412,000 minus $330,000 = $82,000. $742,000 is the trap: adding the two instead of subtracting.

questions.q: The seller's credits total $500,000 and debits total $318,500. What are the seller's net proceeds?
questions.x: Seller's net is credits minus debits: $500,000 minus $318,500 = $181,500. $818,500 is the trap: adding instead of subtracting.

questions.q: A city charges the owners on one block for a new sidewalk that benefits their properties. This charge is a:
c: General property tax
Special assessment
Transfer tax
Mortgage recording tax
questions.x: A charge for a local improvement that benefits specific properties is a special assessment. General property tax is the trap: it funds general services for everyone.

questions.q: The value a municipality assigns to a property for computing property tax is its:
c: Market value
Appraised value
Insured value
Assessed value
questions.x: Taxes are computed on assessed value. Market value is the trap: assessed value may be a fraction of market value.

questions.q: Which term covers land, its permanent attachments, AND the legal rights of ownership?
c: Land
Personal property
Real estate
Real property
questions.x: Real property is real estate plus the bundle of legal rights. The trap is real estate, which means the physical land and improvements without the rights.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a stick in an owner's traditional bundle of rights?
c: Possession
Exclusion
Disposition
Taxation
questions.x: Taxation is a government power over property, not an owner's right. Disposition sounds technical but is the owner's right to sell, give, or will the property.

questions.q: Absent a written agreement, which fixture test do courts treat as the most important?
c: The intention of the annexor
The cost of attaching the item
How firmly the item is attached
How the item is adapted to the room
questions.x: The annexor's intention controls when the parties have no written agreement. Method of attachment is the tempting pick, but it is only evidence of that intent.

questions.q: A nail salon tenant in Jackson Heights bolted pedicure chairs to the floor and plumbed them in. The lease ends in two weeks. The chairs:
c: Became the landlord's real property once bolted down
Stay put, because removal would damage the plumbing
Are trade fixtures removable before the lease ends
Are emblements the tenant may take after the lease ends
questions.x: Equipment a commercial tenant installs for its business is a trade fixture: the tenant's personal property, removable before the lease ends with damage repaired. Bolting it down does not make it the landlord's.

questions.q: Annual crops such as corn or tomatoes, planted and cultivated by a tenant farmer, are called:
c: Emblements
Appurtenances
Fixtures
Fructus naturales
questions.x: Emblements are crops produced by annual labor and are personal property. Fructus naturales, the trap, are naturally growing trees and perennials, which are real property.

questions.q: The owner of a lot on a Finger Lakes lake shore holds:
c: Riparian rights
Prior appropriation rights
Littoral rights
Subsurface rights
questions.x: Littoral rights belong to owners along lakes, ponds, and oceans. Riparian rights, the trap, attach to flowing water such as rivers and streams. NY does not use prior appropriation.

questions.q: A Midtown church sells its unused development rights to the developer next door, who uses them to build a taller tower. What did the church sell?
c: Air rights
Subsurface rights
Riparian rights
An easement in gross
questions.x: Unused floor area above a parcel is an air right and can be sold apart from the land. Subsurface rights concern what lies below the surface.

questions.q: The economic characteristic most responsible for two identical houses selling at very different prices in different neighborhoods is:
c: Indestructibility
Permanence of investment
Immobility
Situs (area preference)
questions.x: Situs, people's preference for a location, is the most important economic characteristic. Immobility is physical and explains why markets are local, but the price gap comes from preference.

questions.q: Real estate is considered illiquid because:
c: It usually cannot be sold quickly at full value
Its land is physically indestructible
No two parcels anywhere are exactly alike
It is taxed annually by local governments
questions.x: Illiquidity means difficulty turning an asset into cash quickly without a loss. Uniqueness (no two parcels alike) is a separate physical characteristic.

questions.q: All of the following are examples of special purpose real estate EXCEPT:
c: A strip mall
A hospital
A house of worship
A cemetery
questions.x: A strip mall is ordinary commercial property with a broad market of buyers. Cemeteries, hospitals, and houses of worship are built for one use and are hard to convert.

questions.q: The most complete form of ownership recognized by law is:
c: Fee simple absolute
Fee simple determinable
Life estate
Estate for years
questions.x: Fee simple absolute is unlimited in time, inheritable, and freely transferable. Fee simple determinable is the trap: it can end automatically if a stated condition is broken.

questions.q: Land is deeded to a library "but if it is ever used for anything other than a library, the grantor may re-enter and reclaim it." The library becomes a cafe. What happens?
c: Title reverts to the grantor automatically
Nothing happens, because use conditions in deeds are void
The grantor or heirs may act to reclaim title
The land escheats to the State of New York
questions.x: "But if" creates a fee on condition subsequent with a right of re-entry, so the grantor must act to reclaim. Automatic reversion is the trap: that happens with a fee simple determinable ("so long as").

questions.q: A grantor deeds property "to Ana for life." No one else is named. When Ana dies, the property passes to:
c: Ana's heirs, by descent
Ana's estate, for one year
The State of New York, by escheat
The grantor or grantor's heirs
questions.x: With no remainderman named, the future interest is a reversion to the grantor or the grantor's heirs. Ana's heirs are the trap: her interest ended at her death, so nothing passes to them.

questions.q: A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant is called a life estate:
c: In remainder
In severalty
By the entirety
Pur autre vie
questions.x: Pur autre vie means "for the life of another." In remainder is the trap: a remainder is the future interest that follows a life estate, not a type of life estate.

questions.q: A life tenant in a Saratoga Springs Victorian cuts down every mature tree on the lot and sells the timber. The remainderman's best claim is for:
c: Partition
Adverse possession
Waste
Escheat
questions.x: A life tenant may not damage or materially reduce the property's value for the future owner. Stripping timber is classic waste. Partition is the trap: it divides co-owned property and does not apply between life tenant and remainderman.

questions.q: In New York, the surviving spouse's protection that replaced dower and curtesy is the:
c: Homestead exemption
Right of survivorship
Life estate pur autre vie
Elective share
questions.x: NY abolished dower and curtesy. A surviving spouse may elect the greater of $50,000 or one third of the net estate. Survivorship is the trap: it comes from how title is held, not from the marriage itself.

questions.q: A lease with a definite beginning and ending date creates:
c: An estate for years
A periodic estate
An estate at will
An estate at sufferance
questions.x: Any lease with a fixed end date is an estate for years, even if it lasts only months. A periodic estate, the trap, renews automatically until someone gives notice.

questions.q: A tenant's lease in Yonkers expired. The tenant stayed and the landlord accepted the next month's rent without signing anything new. The tenancy is most likely now:
c: A month-to-month tenancy
An estate for years
An estate at sufferance
A tenancy at will by statute
questions.x: Accepting rent from a holdover generally creates a month-to-month tenancy in NY. Sufferance is the trap: it describes a holdover whose rent the landlord has not accepted.

questions.q: Which estate is a freehold estate?
c: Estate for years
Estate at will
Periodic tenancy
Life estate
questions.x: Freehold estates are ownership of indeterminate length: fee simple and life estates. Estate for years is the trap because of the long-sounding name, but it is a leasehold.

questions.q: A life tenant may do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Lease the property to a tenant for income
Mortgage her interest in the life estate
Convey fee simple title by herself
Sell the life estate to a third party
questions.x: A life tenant can transfer only what she holds: an interest ending at her death. Mortgaging is the tempting wrong pick, but she can mortgage the life estate itself.

questions.q: The words "so long as" in a deed typically create a fee simple determinable, leaving the grantor with:
c: A right of re-entry
A remainder
A possibility of reverter
A vested remainder for heirs
questions.x: A fee simple determinable ends automatically, and the grantor holds a possibility of reverter. A right of re-entry is the trap: it goes with a fee on condition subsequent.

questions.q: Ownership of real property by one person or one entity alone is called:
c: Severalty
Tenancy in common
Joint tenancy
Partition
questions.x: Severalty means sole ownership, severed from others. The word is often confused with "several" owners, which would be co-ownership.

questions.q: In New York, a deed to two unmarried people that says nothing about the form of ownership creates:
c: A joint tenancy
A tenancy by the entirety
A tenancy in common
Ownership in severalty
questions.x: NY presumes a tenancy in common for unmarried co-owners unless the deed expressly creates a joint tenancy. Joint tenancy is the trap: survivorship must be stated, not assumed.

questions.q: All of the following are unities required for a joint tenancy EXCEPT:
c: Possession
Title
Interest
Marriage
questions.x: Joint tenancy needs time, title, interest, and possession. Marriage is the fifth unity, required only for tenancy by the entirety.

questions.q: Three friends own a Bushwick building as joint tenants. One dies with a will leaving everything to her son. Who owns the building?
c: The two surviving friends
The two friends and the son as tenants in common
The two friends and the son as joint tenants
The son and the estate's executor
questions.x: The right of survivorship passes a deceased joint tenant's interest to the surviving joint tenants, overriding the will. The tenants-in-common answer is the trap: it would be right only if she had severed the joint tenancy before death.

questions.q: Which form of co-ownership cannot be ended by a partition action while the owners remain married?
c: Tenancy in common
Joint tenancy
Joint tenancy with survivorship
Tenancy by the entirety
questions.x: Tenancy by the entirety cannot be partitioned, and neither spouse can convey alone. Joint tenancy is the trap: it also has survivorship, but any joint tenant may seek partition.

questions.q: A court action by a co-owner to divide the property or force a sale and split the proceeds is called:
c: Lis pendens
Escheat
Quiet title
Partition
questions.x: Partition ends co-ownership, either in kind or by a court-ordered sale. Quiet title is the trap: it resolves competing ownership claims, not disagreements between co-owners.

questions.q: In a trust, the party who holds legal title and manages the property for others is the:
c: Trustee
Beneficiary
Trustor
Remainderman
questions.x: The trustee holds legal title as a fiduciary. The trustor is the trap: the trustor creates the trust, and the beneficiary receives its benefits.

questions.q: A corporation that owns an office building holds title:
c: As tenants in common with its shareholders
In partnership
As joint tenants with its directors
In severalty
questions.x: A corporation is a single legal person, so it owns in severalty. Tenancy in common with shareholders is the trap: shareholders own stock, not the real estate.

questions.q: Two developers team up to build one specific townhouse project and plan to part ways once it sells out. Their arrangement is best described as a:
c: Syndicate
Real estate investment trust
Joint venture
Cooperative
questions.x: A joint venture is formed for a single project for a limited time. A syndicate is the trap: it pools many investors' money, usually through an LP or LLC, for an ongoing investment.

questions.q: Kim's neighbor on the Upper West Side buys a co-op apartment. What does she legally own?
c: Fee simple title to the apartment
A life estate in the unit
An undivided interest in the land as a tenant in common
Shares in the corporation plus a proprietary lease
questions.x: Co-op owners hold shares (personal property) and a proprietary lease. Fee simple title to a unit is the trap: that plus a share of common elements describes a condo.

questions.q: All of the following are true of a New York condominium unit EXCEPT:
c: The owner receives a deed at closing
The unit is separately assessed for taxes
The owner holds a share of the common elements
The purchase is financed with a share loan
questions.x: Share loans belong to co-ops. Condo buyers get deeds, separate tax lots, and a percentage of the common elements, and finance with ordinary mortgages. Separate assessment is the tempting pick, but each condo unit is its own tax lot.

questions.q: Which statement about community property is accurate for New York?
c: NY divides marital property by equitable distribution
Spouses own marital property 50/50 during the marriage
NY is a community property state like California
Community property replaced tenancy by the entirety
questions.x: NY does not use community property; marital property is divided fairly (equitable distribution) at divorce. The 50/50 answer is the trap: that is the community property rule of other states.

questions.q: A seller includes a freestanding washer and dryer in a house sale. Which document normally transfers them to the buyer?
c: The deed, since they are inside the house
A recorded memorandum of the contract
The title insurance policy issued at closing
A bill of sale for the personal property
questions.x: Movable items not attached to the land are personal property and pass by a bill of sale. The deed conveys only real property, so 'the deed' is the trap for items that merely sit inside the house.

questions.q: Shares of stock in a cooperative housing corporation are classified as:
c: Real property, because they relate to an apartment
Real estate, because the building sits on land
Personal property, also called personalty
A fixture, because the unit is permanent
questions.x: Co-op shares are personal property (personalty or a chattel), which is why a co-op is not transferred by deed. The trap is linking the shares to the building and calling them real property.

questions.q: A homeowner dies with no will and no heirs who can be found. Which government power lets the state take the property?
c: Eminent domain, with just compensation
Escheat, as the owner left no heirs
Police power under the zoning laws
Taxation through a tax lien sale
questions.x: Escheat passes property to the state when an owner dies with no will and no heirs. Eminent domain is the tempting wrong answer, but it is a taking for public use, paid for with just compensation.

questions.q: All of the following are powers the government holds over private property EXCEPT:
c: Police power
Escheat
Eminent domain
Exclusion
questions.x: The four government powers are police power, eminent domain, taxation and escheat (PETE). Exclusion is a stick in the owner's own bundle of rights, the right to keep others out.

questions.q: An item that began as personal property but became real property by being attached to or adapted for the building is a:
c: Fixture
Appurtenance
Emblement
Trade fixture
questions.x: A fixture started as personal property and became real property through attachment or adaptation, so it passes with the deed. A trade fixture is the trap: a commercial tenant installs it and it stays the tenant's personal property.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five tests courts use to decide whether an item is a fixture?
c: Method of attachment
Adaptation to the property
Price paid for the item
Relationship of the parties
questions.x: The tests are MARIA: Method of attachment, Adaptation, Relationship of the parties, Intention, Agreement. What the item cost is not a test; an expensive item can still be personal property.

questions.q: The contract is silent about two items: a chandelier hard-wired into the dining room ceiling and a window AC unit resting on brackets. Which goes to the buyer?
c: Both, because both are attached to the building
Neither, because the contract does not list them
The AC unit only, because it cools the house
The chandelier only, because it is a fixture
questions.x: The hard-wired chandelier is a fixture and passes with the deed unless excluded; a window unit on brackets is usually personal property the seller takes. 'Neither' is the trap: silence in the contract means fixtures go with the house.

questions.q: A seller wants to keep a dining room chandelier that is wired into the ceiling. What is the best advice at the listing appointment?
c: Swap it out before photos or exclude it in the contract
Remove it on closing day, since it was hers first
Nothing, since chandeliers are personal property by law
Tell buyers at showings; an oral statement is enough
questions.x: A wired-in chandelier is a fixture that passes with the deed, so the seller should replace it before listing or exclude it in writing. Removing it on closing day is the trap: that is exactly the fight a written exclusion prevents.

questions.q: A Southern Tier farmer leases the right to extract natural gas beneath her land but keeps farming the surface. What has she leased?
c: Development rights
Subsurface rights
Riparian rights
Appurtenant rights
questions.x: Subsurface (mineral) rights cover minerals, oil and gas below the surface and can be sold or leased apart from it. Development rights are the trap: they concern unused floor area above the land, not what lies beneath.

questions.q: Which statement about subsurface rights is correct?
c: They pass with the surface and cannot be sold apart
An owner may sell them and keep the surface land
They belong to the state wherever gas is found
They cover only water flowing beneath the land
questions.x: Subsurface rights are a separate stick: an owner can sell or lease them and keep the surface. The trap is assuming the surface and the minerals cannot be split.

questions.q: Which water rights doctrine does New York follow?
c: Prior appropriation: first to use, first in right
Public trust: all water use requires a state permit
Community use: water shared equally by the county
Riparian: reasonable use by owners along the water
questions.x: New York, a water-rich eastern state, follows the riparian rule: owners along the water get reasonable use. Prior appropriation is the trap; it is the western, permit-based rule.

questions.q: A buyer moving from Colorado asks whether she can claim a stream's water upstate by being the first to use it. Under New York law:
c: No, owners along the stream share reasonable use
Yes, first in time is first in right under a permit
Yes, if she files a water use claim within one year
No, the state owns all flowing water and leases it
questions.x: NY follows riparian doctrine: adjoining owners share reasonable use, and no one gains priority by using water first. 'First in time' is prior appropriation, the western rule Colorado uses.

questions.q: One separately owned and described piece of land, the unit a deed conveys and a tax map numbers, is a:
c: Subdivision
Tenement
Parcel
Lot line
questions.x: A parcel is one separately owned and described piece of land. A subdivision is the trap: it is a tract split into many parcels, not one.

questions.q: A tax map gives each separately owned piece of land its own number. Each numbered unit is a:
c: Subdivision
Tax block
Parcel
Easement
questions.x: Each numbered unit on a tax map is a parcel, the same unit a deed conveys. A tax block is the trap: in NYC a block holds many lots, not one.

questions.q: A deed reads 'to Noor for life, then to Sami.' What interest does Sami hold while Noor is alive?
c: A reversionary interest
A remainder interest
A life estate pur autre vie
A leasehold estate
questions.x: A third party named to take after the life estate is the remainderman and holds a remainder. Reversion is the trap: it applies only when the property goes back to the grantor because no one else was named.

questions.q: In a life estate, the person who holds possession during the measuring life is the:
c: Remainderman
Grantor
Trustee
Life tenant
questions.x: The life tenant holds and uses the property for the measuring life. The remainderman is the trap: that person waits for the future interest and has no right to possess yet.

questions.q: New York's homestead exemption protects a homeowner's equity in a primary residence from:
c: Unsecured creditors holding a judgment
A foreclosure by the mortgage lender
Unpaid real property tax liens
Any creditor, up to the home's full value
questions.x: The homestead exemption shields a set dollar amount of equity from unsecured judgment creditors. It does not stop a mortgage foreclosure or tax liens, which makes the foreclosure choice the trap.

questions.q: How is the amount of New York's homestead exemption set?
c: It varies by county and is highest downstate
One flat dollar amount set for the whole state
One third of the home's full assessed value
All of the owner's equity in a primary home
questions.x: The NY homestead amount depends on the county (highest downstate) and is adjusted every few years. A single statewide figure is the trap.

questions.q: Which leasehold estate gives the tenant the most security?
c: Periodic estate
Estate at will
Estate for years
Estate at sufferance
questions.x: An estate for years has a definite end date, so the tenant is secure for the whole term. A periodic estate is the trap: it renews but can be ended by proper notice at the end of any period.

questions.q: Which list ranks leasehold estates from most to least secure for the tenant?
c: Periodic, years, sufferance, will
Will, years, periodic, sufferance
Years, will, periodic, sufferance
Years, periodic, will, sufferance
questions.x: From strongest to weakest: years, periodic, will, sufferance ('Your Pal Will Suffers'). Sufferance is last because the tenant holds over without consent; putting will ahead of periodic is the trap.

questions.q: A tenant rents with no end date, and the tenancy renews each month until someone ends it with proper notice. This is a(n):
c: Estate for years
Periodic estate
Estate at sufferance
Estate at will
questions.x: A periodic estate renews automatically from period to period and ends by proper notice. Estate at will is the trap: it has no set period at all, just the landlord's consent, and also ends on either party's death.

questions.q: Which leasehold estate ends if either the landlord or the tenant dies?
c: Estate for years
Periodic estate
Estate at will
Estate at sufferance
questions.x: An estate at will has no fixed term and ends by notice or by the death of either party. A periodic estate is the trap: it rolls over until proper notice is given.

questions.q: A landlord will not renew the lease of a residential tenant who has lived in the unit for 18 months. Under the 2019 HSTPA, how much written notice is required?
c: 30 days
60 days
90 days
120 days
questions.x: HSTPA notice runs 30 days for under 1 year, 60 days for 1 to 2 years, and 90 days for 2 years or more. Thirty days is the trap: that tier is for tenants there less than a year.

questions.q: Under the 2019 HSTPA, a residential landlord must give 30, 60 or 90 days' written notice before which action?
c: Raising the rent by 5% or more
Raising the rent by any amount
Making a repair inside the unit
Showing the unit to a buyer
questions.x: The notice rule applies when the landlord will not renew or will raise the rent 5% or more. 'Any amount' is the trap: smaller increases do not trigger it.

questions.q: Ana owns 50% of a two-family as a tenant in common with two others. Which right does she have?
c: Exclusive use of one floor matching her share
The right to possess the whole property
Half the rooms, chosen before the others
Possession only after the others agree
questions.x: Co-owners hold undivided interests: each may possess the whole property, even when shares are unequal. Claiming a floor as 'her 50%' is the trap; the share is in value, not in space.

questions.q: Co-owners who hold undivided interests in a property:
c: Must hold exactly equal shares in the property
Each own a specific, marked-off portion
Cannot sell or mortgage their own shares
Share possession, even with unequal shares
questions.x: An undivided interest means each owner may possess the whole, and shares can differ in value. Equal shares are required only for joint tenancy, which is the trap.

questions.q: A tenant in common wants to sell her one-third share to an outside buyer. Which is true?
c: She may sell; the buyer becomes a tenant in common
She needs the other co-owners' written consent
The sale converts the property to a joint tenancy
She may sell only to one of the existing co-owners
questions.x: A tenant in common can sell or mortgage her share without consent, and the buyer steps in as a new tenant in common. Needing consent is the trap; that is closer to tenancy by the entirety.

questions.q: A tenant in common dies with a will leaving everything to her daughter. Her share passes to:
c: The surviving co-owners
The co-owners and daughter equally
The state, by escheat
Her daughter, under the will
questions.x: A tenancy in common has no survivorship, so the share passes by will or intestacy. The surviving co-owners are the trap; survivorship belongs to joint tenancy.

questions.q: A married couple buys a Manhattan co-op in 2024. Under New York law, they can hold the shares as:
c: Tenants by the entirety
Community property owners
Tenants in common only
Joint tenants only
questions.x: Since 1996, NY lets spouses hold co-op shares as tenants by the entirety, just like a house. 'Tenants in common only' is the trap: it reflects the old rule for shares, and NY has no community property.

questions.q: Which statement about tenancy by the entirety in New York is correct?
c: It applies to houses, but never to co-op shares
Since 1996 it can cover a couple's co-op shares
Unmarried partners may use it by deed
It is created only if the deed says so expressly
questions.x: Since 1996 spouses may hold co-op shares as tenants by the entirety. 'Only if the deed says so' is the trap: a deed to spouses creates it by default unless it says otherwise.

questions.q: Three joint tenants own a building. One sells her share to an outsider. What is the result?
c: The sale is void unless both others consent in writing
The buyer becomes a joint tenant with the other two
The buyer holds in common; the others stay joint tenants
The whole joint tenancy becomes a tenancy by the entirety
questions.x: Conveying a share severs the joint tenancy for that share: the buyer lacks the unities of time and title, so holds as a tenant in common, while the other two keep survivorship between them. 'Becomes a joint tenant' is the trap.

questions.q: A joint tenancy can end in all of the following ways EXCEPT:
c: Conveyance of one tenant's share
Agreement of all the joint tenants
Only one survivor remaining
A will leaving a share to a child
questions.x: A will cannot pass a joint tenant's share, because survivorship takes it at death. Conveyance (severance), agreement and a single survivor all end a joint tenancy.

questions.q: A house held in a revocable living trust is being sold. Who signs the listing agreement and the deed?
c: The beneficiaries
The trustee
The trustor's heirs
The probate court
questions.x: The trustee holds legal title, so the trustee signs. The beneficiaries are the trap: they receive the benefits but do not hold title.

questions.q: Before listing a property owned by a trust, what should the agent ask for early?
c: A court order approving the sale
Written consent from every beneficiary
The trust agreement or certification
The trustor's last will and testament
questions.x: The trust agreement (or a certification of trust) lets the attorneys confirm the trustee's power to sell. Beneficiary consent is the trap: the trustee, not the beneficiaries, has the authority.

questions.q: A C corporation owns a Queens warehouse. Which statement is correct?
c: It owns in severalty; profits are taxed twice
Shareholders own it as tenants in common
Shareholders are personally liable for its debts
Profits pass through with no corporate-level tax
questions.x: A corporation is a legal person that owns in severalty, and C corporation income is taxed at the corporate level and again as dividends. Pass-through taxation is the trap: that describes an LLC.

questions.q: Shareholders of a corporation that owns a building hold:
c: A deeded share of the building as joint tenants
An undivided interest as tenants in common
Stock, with limited liability
Unlimited personal liability for its debts
questions.x: Shareholders own stock, not real estate, and their liability is limited. Tenants in common is the trap: the corporation alone holds title, in severalty.

questions.q: A lien is best described as:
c: A right to use another's land for a purpose
A claim against property that secures a debt
A private limit on use written into a deed
An improvement extending onto a neighbor's lot
questions.x: A lien is a claim against property as security for a debt; if it is unpaid, the lienholder can foreclose. The right to use another's land is an easement, the closest trap.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a house without paying off a recorded judgment lien against the seller. What happens to the lien?
c: It ends automatically when the deed is recorded
It becomes the title company's debt by law
It moves to the seller's next home
It remains, since liens run with the land
questions.x: Liens run with the land: a buyer takes subject to them unless they are paid off. Ending automatically at transfer is the trap; that is why liens are paid from the seller's proceeds at closing.

questions.q: A town installs a new sewer line and charges the cost to the lots that benefit. The charge is a:
c: Special assessment, a specific tax lien
Mechanic's lien held by the contractor
Judgment lien on all the owners' property
Voluntary lien accepted by each owner
questions.x: A special assessment charges properties that benefit from a local improvement and is a specific tax lien. A mechanic's lien is the trap: the contractor is paid by the town, and the lien here is the government's.

questions.q: In New York City, unpaid water and sewer charges:
c: Are a personal debt of the owner alone
Are a lien and can go into the tax lien sale
Are wiped out when the property is sold
Become a lien only if the owner agrees in writing
questions.x: Unpaid NYC water and sewer charges are liens and can end up in the city's tax lien sale. A purely personal debt is the trap; these charges attach to the property.

questions.q: A tenant hires a contractor to renovate a store without the owner's consent and then fails to pay. Can the contractor file a mechanic's lien against the owner's interest?
c: Yes, any unpaid work supports a lien
Yes, but only within 4 months of the last work
No, the owner did not consent to the work
No, mechanic's liens cover only single-family homes
questions.x: Under the NY Lien Law, work ordered by a tenant without the owner's consent does not support a lien against the owner. The 4-month answer is the trap; that deadline applies to single-family dwellings.

questions.q: Under the NY Lien Law, a mechanic's lien protects all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A subcontractor who installed the wiring
A supplier who delivered the lumber
A laborer who worked on the job site
A broker who found the building's buyer
questions.x: Mechanic's liens protect contractors, subcontractors, laborers and suppliers who improved the property. A broker improved nothing, so a commission claim is not a mechanic's lien.

questions.q: A contractor files a mechanic's lien on a Bronx 6-unit building. Under the NY Lien Law, unless extended, how long does the lien last?
c: 4 months from filing
8 months from filing
1 year from filing
10 years from filing
questions.x: A NY mechanic's lien lasts 1 year from filing; the lienor must foreclose or file a notice of extension within that year. Eight months is the trap: that is the deadline to file the lien, not how long it lasts.

questions.q: A mechanic's lien on a single-family home is about to expire after one year. How can the lienor extend it?
c: By court order; a filed notice will not work
By filing a notice of extension with the county clerk
By re-filing a new lien with the county clerk
It extends itself until the debt is paid
questions.x: For a single-family dwelling, a mechanic's lien can be extended only by court order. Filing a notice of extension is the trap: that works once for other properties, not single-family homes.

questions.concept: First in time, first in right
questions.q: Apart from real property taxes and assessments, how are liens ranked when foreclosure sale proceeds are paid out?
c: By size, largest lien paid first
In order of recording or filing date
Voluntary liens before involuntary liens
Equally, pro rata by amount owed
questions.x: After taxes, it is first in time, first in right: the earliest recorded, docketed or filed lien is paid first. Voluntary before involuntary is the trap; a mortgage recorded after a judgment ranks behind it.

questions.concept: First in time, first in right
questions.q: A roofer did the work in 2022 but filed his NY mechanic's lien in 2023. A judgment was docketed in late 2022. Which ranks first?
c: The mechanic's lien, since the work came first
Both share equally as involuntary liens
The judgment, since it was docketed first
The mechanic's lien, as a specific lien
questions.x: NY mechanic's liens rank from their filing date, so the judgment docketed before the filing comes first. Ranking by when the work was done is the trap.

questions.q: At closing, the seller's mortgage is paid off from the proceeds. What is recorded afterward to clear it from the record?
c: A subordination agreement
A notice of pendency
A referee's deed
A mortgage satisfaction
questions.x: A satisfaction (release or discharge) of mortgage is recorded after payoff. A subordination agreement is the trap: it reorders priority but does not clear a lien.

questions.q: A disputed mechanic's lien threatens to delay a sale. How can the closing still proceed?
c: The lien can be bonded or discharged by deposit
Ignore it, since mechanic's liens are not recorded
Record a lis pendens against the contractor
Have the buyer take title subject to it by law
questions.x: A disputed mechanic's lien can be bonded or discharged by a deposit so the closing goes ahead. Ignoring it is the trap: liens cloud title and make it unmarketable until cleared.

questions.q: A neighbor's hedge and fence have stood two feet onto an owner's lot for 12 years. Under RPAPL 543, the neighbor:
c: Has gained title by adverse possession
Has a prescriptive easement for the fence
Gains nothing; they are deemed permissive
Owns the strip if taxes were paid on it
questions.x: RPAPL 543 deems minor non-structural encroachments, such as fences, hedges and sheds, permissive, so they alone cannot support adverse possession. Adverse possession is the trap: the 10-year period has run, but the use is not hostile.

questions.q: Which encroachment can still support an adverse possession claim in New York after 10 years?
c: A hedge planted over the line
A garage built over the line
A fence placed over the line
A shed placed over the line
questions.x: RPAPL 543 deems fences, hedges, plantings and sheds permissive, but a garage is a structural encroachment and can still ripen into adverse possession. The fence is the trap: it is the classic minor item the 2008 law covers.

questions.q: Which is most likely to reveal that a neighbor's garage extends onto the seller's lot?
c: A survey
An abstract of title
A title search
A title insurance commitment
questions.x: Encroachments are physical, so a survey or inspection finds them. A title search is the trap: it finds recorded documents, not a garage over the line.

questions.q: Why does a title search usually fail to reveal an encroachment?
c: Encroachments are kept secret under state law
The neighbor must report it to the county
Title searches cover only the last 10 years
It is physical, not a recorded document
questions.x: A title search finds recorded documents, but an encroachment is a physical fact found by survey or inspection. The 10-year answer is the trap: the length of the search is not the reason.

questions.q: The Moraleses sell their lot, which carries a recorded driveway easement benefiting the Chens' lot next door. The new deed does not mention it. The buyer:
c: Is bound by it, because it runs with the land
Takes free of it, since his own deed omits it
Can end it by putting up a locked gate
Must sign a new grant before it binds him
questions.x: An appurtenant easement runs with the land and binds a buyer of the servient lot even if the deed is silent. 'Takes free of it' is the trap: the recorded easement, not the new deed, controls.

questions.q: The Chens sell their lot, the dominant tenement benefiting from a driveway easement. What happens to the easement?
c: It ends, since the Chens no longer own the lot
It stays with the Chens personally
It passes to the buyer automatically
It reverts to the servient owner
questions.x: An easement appurtenant belongs to the dominant land, so it passes to the buyer of that land automatically. 'Stays with the Chens' is the trap: that describes a personal easement in gross.

questions.q: The most common type of easement, a right to pass over land on foot or by vehicle, is a:
c: Right of entry
Right of way
Party wall
Encroachment
questions.x: A right of way is the right to pass over another's land and is the most common easement. Right of entry is the trap: it is a grantor's power to retake a fee on condition, not a right to pass.

questions.q: A shared driveway that one neighbor may use to reach a back garage on the next lot is best described as a:
c: Encroachment by the neighbor
Personal easement in gross
Revocable license to park
Right of way appurtenant
questions.x: A shared driveway benefiting the next lot is a right of way appurtenant: it involves two parcels and runs with both. An easement in gross is the trap: it benefits a person or company, with no dominant parcel.

questions.q: Neighbors openly and without permission cut across a lot to the beach for 12 years, while the owner keeps using it too. What have they most likely acquired?
c: Title by adverse possession
An easement by prescription
A revocable license to cross
An easement by necessity
questions.x: Open, hostile, continuous use for 10 years gives a prescriptive easement, a right to use. Adverse possession is the trap: it gives title and needs exclusive use, and the owner kept using the lot too.

questions.q: Prescriptive easements and adverse possession in New York share all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Open and notorious use
Hostile use, without permission
A 10-year period
A requirement of exclusive use
questions.x: Both need open, notorious, hostile, continuous use for 10 years. Only adverse possession requires exclusive use; prescription gives a right to use and does not.

questions.q: A Brooklyn owner needs scaffolding on the neighbor's roof to repair his own building, and the neighbor refuses. Under RPAPL 881, the owner can:
c: Petition the court for a license to enter
Enter anyway, since party walls carry access
Claim an easement by necessity over the roof
File a mechanic's lien to force the neighbor
questions.x: RPAPL 881 lets an owner who is refused access ask the court for a license to enter for repairs, and courts often require fees and insurance. Entering anyway is the trap: a party wall's cross-easement is for support, not a right onto the neighbor's roof.

questions.q: When a court grants an owner a license under RPAPL 881 to enter a neighbor's property for construction, it often requires the owner to:
c: Purchase the neighbor's unused air rights
Record a permanent easement first
Pay license fees and carry insurance
Post a bond equal to the property value
questions.x: Courts granting an RPAPL 881 license often order license fees and insurance to protect the neighbor. A permanent easement is the trap: the license is temporary, for the work only.

questions.q: A granted right of way across a neighbor's lot has gone unused for 15 years, but the holder did nothing to show intent to give it up. In New York the easement:
c: Ended by abandonment after 10 years of nonuse
Ended by merger when the servient lot was sold
Survives, because nonuse alone is not enough
Became a license the owner can now revoke
questions.x: In NY, abandonment needs intent to give up the easement plus an act; mere nonuse of a granted easement is not enough. The 10-year nonuse answer is the trap: 10 years matters only when the servient owner adversely blocks the use.

questions.q: Which of these ends an easement?
c: Sale of the servient parcel
Death of the servient owner
Nonuse of a granted easement for years
The holder signing a written release
questions.x: A written release (usually a quitclaim deed) to the servient owner ends an easement. Nonuse is the trap: in NY, nonuse alone does not prove abandonment.

questions.q: The physical land and everything permanently attached to it, without regard to the rights of ownership, is called:
c: Real property
Chattel
Real estate
Appurtenance
questions.x: Real estate is the physical thing: land plus permanent improvements. Real property is the tempting pick, but it adds the bundle of legal rights.

questions.q: An owner sells part of her land, gives a lot to her son, and leaves the rest by will. She is exercising which right in the bundle?
c: Quiet enjoyment
Control
Disposition
Exclusion
questions.x: Disposition is the right to transfer the property by sale, gift, or will. Quiet enjoyment is a deed covenant about undisturbed possession, not the right to transfer.

questions.q: A sales contract lists a dining room chandelier as excluded from the sale, though it is wired into the ceiling. Who gets the chandelier?
c: The buyer, because wiring makes it a fixture
The buyer, unless the seller swaps in an equal fixture
The buyer, because the annexor intended permanence
The seller, because the written agreement controls
questions.x: A written agreement between the parties overrides every fixture test. The wiring argument is the trap: attachment matters only when the parties have not agreed in writing.

questions.q: A bakery tenant moves out at the end of its lease and leaves its bolted-in commercial ovens behind. The ovens most likely:
c: Stay the tenant's property for one more year
Pass to the landlord after a 10-year waiting period
Are sold at a public auction for the tenant
Become the landlord's property by accession
questions.x: Trade fixtures not removed by the end of the lease become the landlord's property by accession. There is no grace year; the tenant's right to remove ends with the lease.

questions.q: A tenant farmer's lease ends early through no fault of his own, after he planted soybeans. As to the crop, he generally:
c: Loses it, because growing crops are real property
Keeps it as a trade fixture until it is sold
May come back to harvest it as emblements
Is paid its value by the incoming tenant
questions.x: Emblements are personal property, and a tenant whose lease ends through no fault of his own may return to harvest them. Treating planted crops as real property is the trap.

questions.q: An owner whose land borders the Hudson River, a flowing body of water, holds:
c: Littoral rights
Air rights
Prior appropriation rights
Riparian rights
questions.x: Land along a river or stream carries riparian rights. Littoral rights are the trap: they attach to lakes, ponds, and oceans, not flowing water.

questions.q: In New York City, the transferable development rights an owner sells to a neighboring developer are a form of:
c: Mineral rights
A license
Littoral rights
Air rights
questions.x: Development rights are unused buildable space above a lot, which is an air right. Mineral rights are the mirror-image trap: they are subsurface rights.

questions.q: Buyers pay a premium to live near a top-rated school district in Scarsdale. This reflects which characteristic of real estate?
c: Immobility
Indestructibility
Scarcity of buildable land
Area preference (situs)
questions.x: Paying more for a preferred location is situs, or area preference. Scarcity is the trap: it explains high prices overall, not the premium for one neighborhood over another.

questions.q: An investor needs cash within a week and decides to sell a rental building. The risk she faces most directly comes from real estate's:
c: Indestructibility
Heterogeneity
Immobility
Illiquidity
questions.x: Illiquidity is why a quick sale usually means a lower price. Immobility is the trap: it explains why markets are local, not why a fast sale costs money.

questions.q: Which property is most likely to be classified as special purpose real estate?
c: A suburban office park
A neighborhood strip mall
A distribution warehouse
A private school
questions.x: A school is designed for one use and has few potential buyers, which makes it special purpose. Office parks, warehouses, and strip malls are commercial or industrial property with broad markets.

questions.q: Which estate is inheritable, unlimited in duration, and not subject to any condition that could end it?
c: Fee simple determinable
Life estate pur autre vie
