Fee simple absolute
Fee on condition subsequent
questions.x: Fee simple absolute has no conditions and no end date. Fee simple determinable and fee on condition subsequent are also inheritable, but each can be lost if a condition is broken.

questions.q: Which deed wording most likely creates a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent?
c: "to the town for as long as it remains a public park"
"to the town and its successors and assigns"
"to the town for the life of its current mayor"
"to the town, but if not a park, grantor may re-enter"
questions.x: "But if" plus a right of re-entry signals a fee on condition subsequent. "For as long as" is the trap: durational words like "so long as" create a fee simple determinable, which ends automatically.

questions.q: A deed reads "to Ben for life, then to Carla." When Ben dies, Carla takes title as the:
c: Reversioner
Grantee in severalty
Life tenant pur autre vie
Remainderman
questions.x: A third party named to take after a life estate holds a remainder. Reversioner is the trap: a reversion goes back to the grantor only when no remainderman is named.

questions.q: A deed grants "to Dev for the life of his mother, Rosa." Dev dies before Rosa. Who holds the estate until Rosa dies?
c: Rosa herself
The remainderman at once
The grantor, by reversion
Dev's heirs
questions.x: In a life estate pur autre vie, the measuring life is Rosa's, so the estate continues and passes to Dev's heirs until she dies. Reversion is the trap: it happens only when the measuring life ends.

questions.q: A life tenant may do which of the following without committing waste?
c: Demolish the garage to sell the lumber
Strip and sell the mature timber on the lot
Let the roof leak for years without repair
Rent the house to a tenant at market rent
questions.x: Leasing for income is a normal use of a life estate. Neglecting repairs is the subtle trap: letting the roof leak is permissive waste even though the tenant did nothing active.

questions.q: A New York husband's will leaves his wife nothing. His net estate is $300,000. Using her elective share, she may take:
c: Nothing, because the will controls
questions.x: The elective share is the greater of $50,000 or one third of the net estate: $300,000 / 3 = $100,000. $150,000 is the trap: half is the intestate split with children, not the elective share.

questions.q: A commercial lease runs from March 1 to August 31 of the same year. To end it on August 31, the landlord needs to give:
c: No notice; it ends by its terms
30 days' written notice
One month's written notice
Notice equal to one rent period
questions.x: A lease with a fixed end date is an estate for years and ends automatically, even if it is shorter than a year. Notice of one rent period is the trap: that rule applies to periodic tenancies.

questions.q: A Rochester tenant's lease expires. The tenant stays on, and the landlord neither consents nor accepts any rent. The tenant holds:
c: A month-to-month tenancy
An estate for years
A tenancy at sufferance
A periodic estate from year to year
questions.x: A holdover without the landlord's consent is a tenant at sufferance. Month-to-month is the trap: it arises only if the landlord accepts rent or otherwise consents.

questions.q: Which of these is a leasehold (non-freehold) estate?
c: Fee simple absolute
Life estate pur autre vie
Estate at will
Fee simple determinable
questions.x: An estate at will is a tenancy, which is a leasehold. A life estate pur autre vie is the trap: it is measured by another person's life but is still a freehold.

questions.q: A life tenant sells her interest to a buyer. The buyer receives:
c: A fee simple absolute
A remainder interest
A leasehold estate for years
A life estate pur autre vie
questions.x: The buyer gets a life estate measured by the seller's life, which is pur autre vie. Fee simple is the trap: a life tenant cannot convey more than she owns.

questions.q: A deed conveys land "to the church so long as it is used for worship." The church converts the building to condos. Title:
c: Reverts to the grantor automatically
Stays with the church until the grantor sues
Passes to the state by escheat
Is shared by the grantor and the church
questions.x: "So long as" creates a fee simple determinable, which ends automatically when the use stops. Waiting for the grantor to sue is the trap: that describes a fee on condition subsequent.

questions.q: Maria owns a Queens house in her own name; her husband is not on the deed. She owns it:
c: In severalty
By the entirety
As a tenant in common
As community property
questions.x: One owner on the deed is ownership in severalty. Tenancy by the entirety is the trap: it arises only when both spouses take title together.

questions.q: A deed conveys a Buffalo house to a married couple and says nothing about the form of ownership. In New York they hold title as:
c: Tenants in common
Owners in severalty
Joint tenants with survivorship
Tenants by the entirety
questions.x: Spouses who take title together are presumed tenants by the entirety in NY. Tenants in common is the trap: that presumption applies to unmarried co-owners.

questions.q: Three siblings take title to a building on different dates through separate deeds. They cannot be joint tenants because they lack the unities of:
c: Time and title
Possession and interest
Marriage and title
Interest and time
questions.x: Different dates break unity of time, and separate deeds break unity of title. Marriage is the trap: it matters for tenancy by the entirety, not joint tenancy.

questions.q: Which form of co-ownership lets a co-owner's share pass under her will rather than to the other co-owners?
c: Joint tenancy
Tenancy by the entirety
Tenancy in common
Joint tenancy with survivorship
questions.x: Tenants in common have no right of survivorship, so each share passes by will or intestacy. Joint tenancy and tenancy by the entirety both carry survivorship, which overrides a will.

questions.q: Spouses own their Staten Island home as tenants by the entirety and later divorce. Their ownership becomes:
c: A tenancy in common
Severalty in the higher earner
A joint tenancy
A life estate in each
questions.x: Divorce ends the unity of marriage and converts a tenancy by the entirety into a tenancy in common. Joint tenancy is the trap: survivorship does not carry over after divorce.

questions.q: Two siblings own a Catskills cabin as tenants in common and cannot agree whether to sell. Either may ask a court to:
c: Order partition in kind or a sale
Quiet title in the older sibling
File a lis pendens to force a sale
Escheat the cabin to the county
questions.x: A partition action lets any tenant in common end the co-ownership by division or sale. A lis pendens is the trap: it only gives notice of a pending suit and cannot itself force a sale.

questions.q: In a land trust, the person who creates the trust and transfers the property into it is the:
c: Remainderman
Trustee
Beneficiary
Trustor
questions.x: The trustor (grantor) creates the trust and conveys the property into it. The trustee is the trap: the trustee receives legal title and manages it.

questions.q: Which of these owners holds title to real estate in severalty?
c: A corporation buying a warehouse
Two friends named on one deed
Spouses who take title together
Three siblings who inherit a house
questions.x: A corporation is one legal person, so it owns in severalty no matter how many shareholders it has. The other three are co-ownership: tenancy in common or tenancy by the entirety.

questions.q: Dozens of passive investors pool money in an LLC run by a sponsor to buy and hold a portfolio of apartment buildings. This is best called a:
c: Joint venture
Land trust
Cooperative
Syndicate
questions.x: Pooling many investors' capital under a sponsor is a syndicate. Joint venture is the trap: it is a limited-time partnership for one specific project.

questions.q: A Park Slope co-op owner's interest is classified legally as:
c: Real property
A fee simple condominium
A freehold estate
Personal property
questions.x: Co-op shares and the proprietary lease are personal property. Real property is the trap: that classification fits a condo unit, which is conveyed by deed.

questions.q: Which feature is true of a New York co-op but NOT of a condominium?
c: Each unit is assessed as its own tax lot
The unit is financed with a recorded mortgage
The owner buys a title insurance policy
The buyer signs a proprietary lease
questions.x: Co-op buyers receive shares and a proprietary lease. Separate tax lots are the trap: that is a condo feature, since a co-op building is taxed as one lot.

questions.q: In a New York divorce, how is marital property divided?
c: Equally, 50/50, as community property
By whichever spouse holds title
Fairly, by equitable distribution
Under the rules of dower and curtesy
questions.x: NY courts divide marital property by equitable distribution, which is fair but not necessarily equal. The 50/50 answer is the trap: NY is not a community property state.

questions.q: Any claim, charge, or limit on property that may lower its value or restrict its use, but does not prevent transfer, is a(n):
c: Emblement
Escheat
Estate in land
Encumbrance
questions.x: Encumbrance is the umbrella term covering liens, easements, restrictions, and encroachments. Estate is the trap: it describes the degree of ownership itself, not a burden on it.

questions.q: A mortgage is best classified as a:
c: General, involuntary lien
Specific, involuntary lien
Specific, voluntary lien
General, voluntary lien
questions.x: The owner agrees to the mortgage (voluntary) and it attaches to one property (specific). Specific and involuntary is the trap: that describes a real property tax lien.

questions.q: All of the following are general liens EXCEPT:
c: A money judgment
An IRS tax lien
A mechanic's lien
A NY estate tax lien
questions.x: A mechanic's lien attaches only to the property that was improved, so it is specific. An IRS lien is the tempting pick, but federal tax liens reach all of the debtor's property.

questions.q: In New York, a docketed money judgment is a lien on the debtor's real property in that county for:
c: 1 year
3 years
10 years
20 years
questions.x: A NY judgment lien on real property lasts 10 years from docketing. Three years is the trap: that is the life of a notice of pendency.

questions.q: A recorded notice that a lawsuit affecting title to a property is pending is called a:
c: Lis pendens
Satisfaction of judgment
Writ of execution
Subordination agreement
questions.x: A lis pendens (notice of pendency) warns buyers and lenders that they will be bound by the lawsuit's outcome. A writ of execution is the trap: it enforces a judgment already won.

questions.q: A plumber finished work on an 8-unit apartment building in the Bronx on March 1 and was not paid. Under the NY Lien Law, the plumber must file a mechanic's lien by about:
c: April 1
July 1
March 1 of the next year
November 1
questions.x: For property other than a single-family dwelling, the deadline is 8 months after the last work, about November 1. July 1 is the trap: the 4-month deadline applies only to single-family dwellings.

questions.q: Which lien is generally paid first from foreclosure sale proceeds, regardless of when it arose?
c: Real property taxes
The first recorded mortgage
A mechanic's lien
A docketed judgment lien
questions.x: Real property taxes and special assessments take priority over other liens. The first recorded mortgage is the trap: it ranks first among the remaining liens, which go by date of recording.

questions.q: A foreclosure sale nets $610,000. Liens: unpaid property taxes $15,000; first mortgage (2018) $480,000; second mortgage (2021) $90,000; judgment (2023) $60,000. How much does the judgment creditor receive?
questions.x: $610,000 - $15,000 taxes = $595,000; - $480,000 = $115,000; - $90,000 = $25,000 left for the judgment. $40,000 is the trap: it forgets that taxes are paid first.

questions.q: A written agreement in which a lienholder voluntarily accepts a lower priority than another lien is a:
c: Satisfaction of mortgage
Release
Subordination agreement
Estoppel certificate
questions.x: A subordination agreement changes the normal first-in-time order. A satisfaction or release is the trap: those remove a lien entirely rather than reorder it.

questions.q: A survey shows the seller's detached garage extends 18 inches onto the neighbor's lot. This is:
c: An easement appurtenant
A deed restriction
A license
An encroachment
questions.x: An improvement that extends onto another's land is an encroachment. Easement is the trap: an easement is a right to use land, granted or acquired, not an intrusion onto it.

questions.q: A subdivision's recorded declaration bans fences over four feet; the town's zoning allows six-foot fences. A homeowner wants a five-foot fence. Which rule controls?
c: The declaration, as the stricter rule
Zoning, because public law beats private covenants
Neither, because the two rules conflict
Whichever rule was adopted first
questions.x: When a deed restriction and zoning conflict, the more restrictive one controls, so the owner must meet both. Zoning beating private covenants is the trap: zoning sets a floor, not a ceiling.

questions.q: New York is a lien theory state. This means:
c: The lender holds title until the loan is repaid
Liens cannot attach to an owner-occupied homestead
The borrower keeps title; the lender holds a lien
The lender may foreclose without going to court
questions.x: In lien theory states the borrower keeps title and the lender has a lien enforced by judicial foreclosure. The lender holding title is the trap: that is title theory.

questions.q: A foreclosure of a first mortgage will generally wipe out all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A second mortgage recorded later
A judgment docketed after the first mortgage
Unpaid real property taxes
A home equity line recorded later
questions.x: Foreclosure extinguishes liens junior to the foreclosing mortgage. Real property taxes are senior to the mortgage and survive. The later judgment is the tempting pick, but it is junior and is cut off.

questions.q: In an easement appurtenant, the parcel that benefits from the easement is the:
c: Servient tenement
Easement in gross
Remainder interest
Dominant tenement
questions.x: The dominant tenement benefits; the servient tenement is burdened. Mixing the two is the trap. An easement in gross has no dominant tenement at all.

questions.q: The right of a utility company to run power lines across private property is usually an:
c: Easement appurtenant
Easement by necessity
Easement in gross
Encroachment
questions.x: Utility easements benefit a company, not a neighboring parcel, so they are commercial easements in gross. Easement appurtenant is the trap: it requires a dominant parcel.

questions.q: To acquire an easement by prescription in New York, the use must be open, notorious, hostile, and continuous for:
c: 10 years
5 years
15 years
20 years
questions.x: NY's prescriptive period is 10 years, the same as adverse possession. Twenty years is the trap: it is the period in some other states.

questions.q: A farmer in Delaware County sells the back 20 acres of her farm. The parcel has no road frontage and the deed says nothing about access. The buyer most likely has:
c: A license
An easement by prescription
An easement by necessity
An easement for light and air
questions.x: A landlocked parcel created by splitting land in common ownership gets an implied easement by necessity over the seller's remaining land. Prescription is the trap: it needs 10 years of hostile use.

questions.q: A wall built on the boundary line between two Brooklyn rowhouses, used by both, is a:
c: License
Encroachment
Party wall
Monument
questions.x: A party wall straddles the line; each owner owns his half and holds a cross-easement for support in the other half. Encroachment is the trap: a party wall is shared by design, not an intrusion.

questions.q: An easement can be terminated by all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Sale of the servient parcel to a new owner
A written release by the easement holder
Merger of the dominant and servient parcels
The end of the need behind an easement by necessity
questions.x: An easement appurtenant runs with the land, so a sale of the servient parcel does not end it. End of necessity is the tempting pick, but it does terminate an easement by necessity.

questions.q: Which is NOT an interest in land and can generally be revoked at any time?
c: Easement appurtenant
Easement in gross
License
Life estate
questions.x: A license is personal permission, revocable, and ends on the licensor's death or sale. Easement in gross is the trap: it is personal to a holder but is still an interest in land.

questions.q: A Manhattan owner's windows have overlooked a vacant neighboring lot for 40 years. The neighbor now plans a building that will block them. Under NY law, the owner has:
c: A prescriptive easement for light after 10 years
Title to the lot by adverse possession of the view
No right to light and air without a written grant
An implied easement by necessity for window light
questions.x: New York does not recognize easements for light and air by prescription or long use; they exist only by express grant. The prescriptive answer is the trap: 10 years of use creates other easements, but not this one.

questions.q: The owner of a dominant parcel in Montauk buys the servient parcel next door. The easement between them:
c: Continues as an easement in gross
Converts to a license
Continues until released in writing
Ends by merger
questions.x: An owner cannot hold an easement over his own land, so common ownership of both parcels ends the easement by merger. A written release is the trap: merger ends it without one.

questions.q: An easement and a lien are both examples of:
c: Possessory interests
Leasehold estates
Freehold ownership estates
Non-possessory interests
questions.x: Neither gives the right to occupy the property. Leasehold estate is the trap: a tenant does have the right of possession.

questions.q: A seller splits his lot and sells the rear half. A buried sewer line from the rear house has always run under the front lot to the street, visibly marked by cleanouts. The deed is silent. The rear owner most likely has:
c: An easement by prescription
No right, because the deed is silent
An easement by implication
A license revocable by the front owner
questions.x: When an owner splits land, an apparent, continuous prior use that is reasonably necessary is implied as an easement. Prescription is the trap: it needs 10 years of hostile use by a separate owner.

questions.q: The party who conveys title by deed is the:
c: Grantor
Grantee
Vendee
Mortgagee
questions.x: The grantor gives title; the grantee receives it. Grantee is the trap: the -or gives, the -ee receives.

questions.q: Title to real property passes from grantor to grantee when the deed is:
c: Signed by the grantor
Acknowledged before a notary
Delivered and accepted
Recorded
questions.x: Delivery with intent to pass title, and acceptance, transfer title. Recording is the trap: it protects against third parties but does not itself pass title.

questions.q: All of the following are required for a deed to be valid between the parties EXCEPT:
c: A competent grantor
A legal description
Recording
Words of conveyance
questions.x: An unrecorded deed is still valid between grantor and grantee; recording protects the grantee against later purchasers and creditors. A legal description is the tempting pick, but a deed needs one to identify the land.

questions.q: The deed clause that begins "to have and to hold" and defines the estate being granted is the:
c: Granting clause
Acknowledgment
Subject to clause
Habendum clause
questions.x: The habendum clause defines the extent of ownership granted, such as fee simple or life estate. Granting clause is the trap: it contains the words of conveyance.

questions.q: A formal declaration before a notary public by the grantor that signing the deed was a voluntary act is a(n):
c: Affidavit of title
Attestation
Acknowledgment
Habendum
questions.x: An acknowledgment is required before a deed can be recorded in NY, though not for validity between the parties. Attestation is the trap: it is witnesses signing, not the grantor declaring before a notary.

questions.q: A legal description that starts at a point of beginning and follows courses and distances around the parcel back to that point is:
c: Lot and block
Metes and bounds
Rectangular survey
Street address
questions.x: Metes and bounds walks the boundary from a point of beginning and must return to it. Lot and block is the trap: it refers to a lot on a recorded map.

questions.q: A deed calls for a line "300 feet to the center of an old stone wall." The surveyor finds the wall 306 feet from the prior corner. The boundary is:
c: At 300 feet, as the deed states
At the stone wall
At the midpoint, 303 feet
At the grantee's choice of line
questions.x: Monuments control over distances and directions, so the boundary follows the stone wall. The stated distance is the trap: measurements yield to a fixed monument.

questions.q: The deed most commonly used in New York residential sales is the:
c: Full covenant and warranty deed
Referee's deed
Bargain and sale deed without covenants
Bargain and sale deed with covenant
questions.x: Most NY home sales use a bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts, with buyers relying on title insurance. Full covenant and warranty is the trap: it gives more protection but is less common in NY.

questions.q: A full covenant and warranty deed includes all of the following covenants EXCEPT:
c: Seizin
Quiet enjoyment
Habitability
Further assurance
questions.x: The five covenants are seizin, quiet enjoyment, against encumbrances, further assurance, and warranty forever. Habitability is a lease concept. Quiet enjoyment is the tempting pick because it also appears in leases.

questions.q: The covenant in which the grantor promises to sign any additional documents needed to perfect the grantee's title is the covenant of:
c: Seizin
Further assurance
Quiet enjoyment
Against encumbrances
questions.x: Further assurance is the promise to do whatever is reasonably needed to perfect title. Seizin is the trap: it is the promise that the grantor owns the estate.

questions.q: A house in Suffolk County is sold at a court-ordered foreclosure auction. The buyer receives a:
c: Referee's deed
Executor's deed
Full covenant and warranty deed
Bargain and sale deed with covenant
questions.x: In NY's judicial foreclosure, a court-appointed referee conducts the sale and signs a referee's deed. Executor's deed is the trap: it comes from a decedent's estate.

questions.q: Which deed contains no warranties and conveys only whatever interest the grantor may have?
c: Bargain and sale deed with covenant
Quitclaim deed
Full covenant and warranty deed
Executor's deed
questions.x: A quitclaim promises nothing and is used to clear clouds on title or release interests. Executor's deed is the trap: it at least covenants that the executor did not encumber the property.

questions.q: Every NY deed for consideration includes a Lien Law covenant in which the grantor promises to:
c: Defend the title against lawful claims forever
Pay recent improvement costs first from proceeds
Pay the state and city transfer taxes on the sale
Remove any encroachments found by the buyer's survey
questions.x: Lien Law Section 13 makes sale proceeds a trust fund to pay for recent improvements first, protecting contractors. Defending title forever is the trap: that is the warranty covenant.

questions.q: Which of these is an essential element of a valid deed in New York?
c: Recording at the county clerk
The grantee's notarized signature
A legal description of the land
A recital of the actual sale price
questions.x: A deed must identify the land with a legal description. The grantee does not sign, recording protects against third parties but is not needed for validity, and consideration may be nominal ("ten dollars and other valuable consideration"). The trap is recording, which feels essential but is not.

questions.q: A deed identifies the property only as "14 Elm Street, Utica." What is the problem?
c: No legal description, so the land is not identified
Nothing; a street address is a full description
It lacks the grantee's signature on the last page
It must also recite the actual price paid at closing
questions.x: A street address alone is not a legal description; the deed must let a surveyor find the exact land. The grantee's signature is not required, so that choice is the tempting wrong one.

questions.q: A grandmother deeds her house to her 8-year-old grandson. Which is true?
c: The deed is void because the grantee is a minor
The deed is voidable by the grandmother for 10 years
The deed is valid only if the grandson also signs it
It can be valid; a grantee need not be competent
questions.x: The grantor must be competent, but the grantee only has to be identifiable, so a child can receive title. The trap is applying the competence rule to the grantee; a minor GRANTOR's deed would be voidable.

questions.q: Spouses own a house as tenants by the entirety. Who must sign the deed when they sell?
c: Either spouse, acting alone for both
Both spouses, since all grantors must sign
The buyer and the spouse named first on title
Only the spouse who paid the mortgage
questions.x: Every grantor must sign, so both spouses in a tenancy by the entirety sign the deed. The trap is thinking one spouse can act for both; the grantee (buyer) does not need to sign at all.

questions.q: A New York deed recites "ten dollars and other valuable consideration." This recital:
c: Shows the buyer paid exactly ten dollars in cash
Meets the consideration element without the price
Makes the deed a gift deed with no warranties
Is needed only for deeds recorded in NYC
questions.x: The customary NY recital satisfies the consideration element without putting the real price in the deed. It does not mean ten dollars changed hands, which is the literal-reading trap.

questions.q: A parent deeds a house to a child as a gift. What consideration does the deed typically recite?
c: Fair market value as set by an appraiser
None, so the deed is void
The assessed value on the tax roll
Love and affection
questions.x: A gift deed recites love and affection as its consideration. The trap is 'none, so the deed is void': a gift deed is valid, it just recites good rather than valuable consideration.

questions.q: Which legal description system is NOT used in New York?
c: Rectangular (government) survey
Lot and block on a filed subdivision map
Metes and bounds
Reference to a tax map lot
questions.x: New York, an original colony, does not use the federal rectangular survey system. Metes and bounds and lot and block (filed map or tax map) are both used, so either is the trap if you mix up national and NY practice.

questions.q: A legal description is adequate when:
c: It gives the full street address and the ZIP code
The tax assessor has approved its wording
A surveyor could locate the land from it alone
It names the owners of every adjoining lot
questions.x: A legal description identifies land so precisely that a surveyor could find it with no other help. A street address, however complete, is not enough, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: In New York City, a parcel's BBL identifies its:
c: Block, building, and lien status
Building, boundary, and lien
Borough, block, and lot
Base, bulk, and land use
questions.x: BBL stands for borough (1 to 5), block, and lot, used on the tax map and in ACRIS. 'Block, building, and lien status' borrows one right word, which is the trap.

questions.q: A Manhattan condo unit is being sold. How is the unit identified on the NYC tax map?
c: It gets its own lot number within the block
It shares the building's single lot number
It is listed only by street address and unit
It has no tax lot; the co-op corporation pays
questions.x: Each NYC condo unit gets its own tax lot number. Sharing one lot is what happens with a co-op, where the corporation owns the building, so that is the trap.

questions.q: A buyer's attorney orders a survey mainly to:
c: Set the assessed value used for property taxes
Estimate the cost of needed repairs
Confirm the seller's mortgage is paid off
Show boundaries, easements, and encroachments
questions.x: A survey is a licensed surveyor's drawing of boundaries, improvements, easements and encroachments, used to confirm the land matches the description. Assessed value comes from the assessor, not a survey.

questions.q: A survey shows the neighbor's garage extends 2 feet onto the seller's lot. This is:
c: An easement appurtenant
An encroachment
A license to use
Adverse possession
questions.x: A structure that crosses onto another's land is an encroachment, exactly what a survey is ordered to reveal. Adverse possession is tempting, but it needs 10 years of qualifying use and a court ruling, not just a survey finding.

questions.q: A national exam question asks which deed protects the buyer only against defects created during the seller's ownership. In New York terms the answer is:
c: Full covenant and warranty deed
Bargain and sale with covenant
Quitclaim deed with release
Referee's deed from a court sale
questions.x: The special warranty deed covers only the grantor's own acts; NY's equivalent is the bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts. The full covenant deed is the trap: it covers the entire chain of title.

questions.q: Which deed protects the grantee against title defects from the entire chain of title, not just the grantor's time?
c: Special warranty deed
Bargain and sale deed with covenant
Executor's deed under a will
Full covenant and warranty deed
questions.x: Only the full covenant and warranty deed's five covenants reach the whole history of the title. The bargain and sale deed with covenant (special warranty) is the trap: it covers only the grantor's own acts.

questions.concept: Executor's and bargain and sale deeds
questions.q: An estate sells a house left under a will, and the executor signs an executor's deed. What does that deed promise?
c: The executor has not encumbered the property
The title is good against all claims forever
The decedent never mortgaged the property
Nothing at all; it is a quitclaim by law
questions.x: An executor's deed is a limited deed: the executor promises only that the executor has done nothing to encumber the property. A warranty against all claims forever belongs to the full covenant deed, the tempting overstatement.

questions.concept: Executor's and bargain and sale deeds
questions.q: If the decedent left no will, the court-appointed fiduciary conveys the house by a(n):
c: Executor's deed
Referee's deed in partition
Administrator's deed
Sheriff's quitclaim deed
questions.x: With no will, the Surrogate's Court appoints an administrator, who conveys by administrator's deed. Executor's deed is the trap: an executor is named in a will.

questions.q: Which will is valid for an ordinary New York civilian?
c: A handwritten will with no witnesses
An oral will spoken before two friends
A signed will with two witnesses
A typed will signed only at the top
questions.x: A NY will must be in writing, signed at the end by the testator, and witnessed by at least two people. Handwritten unwitnessed (holographic) and oral wills are valid only for the military in wartime and mariners at sea, which is the trap.

questions.q: A holographic (handwritten, unwitnessed) will is valid in New York only for:
c: Soldiers in wartime and mariners at sea
Testators over age 65
Wills leaving only personal property
Testators who own no real property in NY
questions.x: NY accepts holographic and oral wills only from members of the armed forces in wartime and mariners at sea. Limiting it to personal property sounds like a reasonable compromise, but no such rule exists.

questions.q: A widow dies without a will. She has no children but is survived by her parents and a brother. Under EPTL 4-1.1, who inherits?
c: The State of New York by escheat
Her parents and brother equally
Her brother only
Her parents
questions.x: With no spouse or descendants, parents take everything; siblings inherit only if there are no parents. Splitting with the brother is the trap.

questions.q: A married man with no children dies without a will. Under NY law, his spouse receives:
c: $50,000 plus half the rest
The entire estate
Half; his parents get the other half
A life estate in the home only
questions.x: A spouse with no children takes everything. The $50,000 plus half split applies only when there are children, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: A husband dies intestate. The couple's home was held as tenants by the entirety. Who owns the home?
c: The wife and children under the intestacy split
The wife alone, by right of survivorship
The children, since the husband had no will
The estate, until the Surrogate's Court rules
questions.x: Tenancy by the entirety carries survivorship, so the wife owns the whole home at once and intestacy never reaches it. Applying the $50,000 plus half split is the trap.

questions.q: Why does intestate succession not apply to a house held as tenants by the entirety?
c: Such property is exempt from estate taxes
The tenancy ends at divorce, not at death
The Surrogate's Court lacks power over homes
The survivor takes it outside of the estate
questions.x: Survivorship passes the house to the surviving spouse automatically, outside the probate estate. Tax exemption is unrelated; the trap mixes up estate tax with how title passes.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the elements of adverse possession in New York?
c: Payment of the property taxes
Exclusive possession
Open and notorious use
Hostile possession under a claim of right
questions.x: NY requires possession that is hostile under a claim of right, actual, open and notorious, exclusive and continuous for 10 years. Paying taxes is a requirement in some other states, which is why it tempts.

questions.q: A neighbor has used a strip of land for 12 years with the owner's written permission. Can she claim it by adverse possession?
c: Yes, because 10 years have passed
Yes, if she also paid the taxes
No, permissive use is not hostile
No, because 20 years are required
questions.x: Use with the owner's permission is not hostile, so the clock never runs no matter how long it lasts. The 10-year answer is the trap: time alone is not enough.

questions.q: Owner A openly occupied a strip for 6 years, then sold his house and passed possession of the strip to B, who held it 5 more years. Combining the two periods is called:
c: Novation
Accession
Tacking
Reliction
questions.x: Tacking lets successive possessors add their time together when one passes possession to the next. Accession is acquiring additions to land, a different idea that sounds similar.

questions.q: An adverse possessor who has met all the elements gets clear record title by:
c: Bringing an action to quiet title
Recording an affidavit of possession
Filing a lis pendens on the lot
Asking the assessor to change the roll
questions.x: A court judgment in a quiet title action turns adverse possession into clear record title. Recording a self-made affidavit is the trap: it proves nothing in the public record.

questions.q: A lake slowly recedes over decades, exposing dry land along a lakefront lot. The owner gains the land by:
c: Avulsion
Dedication
Escheat
Reliction
questions.x: Reliction is the gradual retreat of water, and the owner gains the exposed land. Avulsion is sudden, the trap for anyone who matches 'water moves' to the wrong speed.

questions.q: Wind and waves gradually wear away 20 feet of a Montauk bluff lot. Which is true?
c: The boundary stays put because of avulsion
The owner loses that land by erosion
The state must pay for the land taken
The owner gains land by reliction
questions.x: Erosion is gradual wearing away, and the owner loses the land. Avulsion keeps the boundary in place only for sudden events like a storm, which is the trap.

questions.q: Buyer 2 knew the owner had already sold to Buyer 1, who never recorded. Buyer 2 pays value and records first. In New York, who owns the property?
c: Buyer 2, because Buyer 2 was first to record
Buyer 1, because Buyer 2 had actual notice
Buyer 2, because Buyer 1's deed is void
Both buyers, as tenants in common by law
questions.x: NY is race-notice: a later buyer wins only by recording first AND taking without notice. Buyer 2 knew of the earlier sale, so Buyer 1 keeps title. 'First to record' is the pure-race trap.

questions.q: A buyer never visits the property. A tenant there holds an unrecorded 10-year lease. The buyer is charged with notice of the lease because:
c: The seller's attorney sends notice to all tenants
Leases over 1 year are recorded by the clerk
Tenants must register their leases with the state
Visible possession puts him on inquiry notice
questions.x: Someone visibly in possession puts a buyer on inquiry notice: you must ask who is living there. The trap is assuming the lease must be in the public record for the buyer to be bound.

questions.q: A condensed written history summarizing every recorded document affecting a property is a(n):
c: Abstract of title
Chain of title
Survey
Certificate of occupancy
questions.x: An abstract condenses every recorded document in the chain, and an attorney reads it to give an opinion of title. The chain of title is just the succession of owners, the close neighbor that tempts.

questions.q: In New York practice, which document lists the exceptions a buyer must clear before closing?
c: The seller's PCDS
The certificate of occupancy for the building
The title report from the title company
The broker's listing agreement
questions.x: The title company's title report (certificate of title) does the abstract's job in NY and lists exceptions to clear. The PCDS covers physical condition, not title, which makes it the tempting wrong pick.

questions.q: An old mortgage was paid off years ago but never released of record. The usual fix at closing is to obtain a:
c: New lender's title policy
Quiet title judgment
Satisfaction of mortgage
Mortgage recording tax waiver
questions.x: A satisfaction of the paid mortgage, recorded at closing, clears the record. A quiet title action is for clouds that cannot be cleared by a release, so it is overkill here and the trap.

questions.q: A cloud on title that cannot be cleared by a release or quitclaim deed may require:
c: A quiet title action
A new survey of the lot
A lis pendens by the buyer
A rider to the contract
questions.x: When no release or quitclaim will fix it, a court action to quiet title is the remedy. A new survey can reveal problems but cannot clear them, which is the trap.

questions.q: Two title companies quote premiums on the same NY home purchase. Which is most likely?
c: Each premium is negotiated freely
The cheaper company offers less coverage
The broker picks the insurer and splits the fee
The same premium, set by filed rates
questions.x: NY title premiums come from rate manuals approved by the Department of Financial Services, so the same coverage costs the same everywhere. Free negotiation is the trap; a broker taking a fee would also violate RESPA.

questions.q: A buyer is purchasing a Manhattan co-op. Instead of title insurance, the buyer's attorney usually orders:
c: An owner's title insurance policy
A lien search on the shares
A metes and bounds survey
A lender's title policy
questions.x: A co-op buyer gets shares and a proprietary lease, not real property, so the attorney orders a lien search on the seller and the shares. An owner's title policy is the trap: that is for houses and condos.

questions.q: At a downstate closing, who typically prepares the deed and the transfer tax forms?
c: The buyer's attorney
The seller's attorney
The title closer
The listing broker
questions.x: The seller's attorney prepares the deed and transfer tax forms and collects payoffs. The title closer records the documents but does not draft them, which is the tempting mix-up.

questions.q: At a NY closing, the person who collects recording fees and taxes and records the deed and mortgage is the:
c: Lender's attorney
Seller's attorney
Listing broker
Title closer
questions.x: The title closer represents the title company, collects fees and taxes, checks exceptions are cleared and records the documents. The lender's attorney runs the loan side, the likely wrong pick.

questions.concept: Hazard and flood insurance at closing
questions.q: Before closing, the buyer's lender will require proof of:
c: Hazard insurance naming the lender
A home warranty paid by the seller
Title insurance for the seller
A survey certified to the broker
questions.x: The lender needs a hazard insurance binder or paid first-year premium naming the lender. A home warranty is optional and not a lender requirement, which is the trap.

questions.concept: Hazard and flood insurance at closing
questions.q: A buyer with a mortgage is purchasing a house in a FEMA special flood hazard area. The lender will require:
c: A larger down payment of at least 20 percent
An elevation certificate filed with the DOS
Flood insurance as well as hazard insurance
No added coverage beyond homeowner's insurance
questions.x: In a special flood hazard area the lender requires flood insurance in addition to hazard insurance; standard homeowner's policies exclude flood. Assuming the homeowner's policy is enough is the trap.

questions.q: At closing, the seller wants to hand the salesperson a commission check directly. The check should be made payable to:
c: The salesperson
The seller's attorney
The sponsoring broker
The title closer
questions.x: Commission is paid to the broker, never directly to a salesperson; the broker then pays the salesperson. Paying the salesperson because they did the work is the trap.

questions.q: How does a salesperson receive commission earned on a sale?
c: From the sponsoring broker
From the buyer's attorney
From the seller's check at closing
From the title company
questions.x: Salespersons are paid only by their sponsoring broker. The seller's closing check goes to the broker, so 'from the seller' is the tempting shortcut.

questions.q: Since 2015, most consumer mortgage closings use which form in place of the HUD-1 settlement statement?
c: Loan Estimate
Truth in Lending statement
Good Faith Estimate
Closing Disclosure
questions.x: TRID replaced the HUD-1 with the Closing Disclosure, a line-by-line account of every charge. The Loan Estimate replaced the Good Faith Estimate at application, which is the trap.

questions.q: An older practice question refers to the HUD-1. Today the equivalent document for most residential mortgages comes from which rule?
c: RPL 443
TRID
HSTPA
ECOA rule
questions.x: The TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule (TRID) created the Closing Disclosure that replaced the HUD-1. RPL 443 is NY's agency disclosure law, an easy mix-up of acronyms.

questions.q: In an NYC new-development sponsor sale, the contract makes the buyer pay the seller's transfer taxes. Which is true?
c: Transfer taxes are waived for new construction
It counts as extra consideration (grossed up)
The buyer's payment also cancels the mansion tax
The sponsor must pay the taxes a second time
questions.x: A buyer paying a tax that is legally the seller's is extra consideration, so the taxes are grossed up. The trap is thinking new construction is exempt from transfer tax.

questions.q: Where should a buyer of an NYC sponsor unit look to learn who pays the transfer taxes?
c: The county clerk's tax lien file
The Rent Guidelines Board order
The building's certificate of occupancy
The offering plan and the contract
questions.x: Sponsor sales often shift the seller's transfer taxes to the buyer, and the offering plan and contract say so. The CO shows legal use, not who pays taxes, which is the tempting wrong document.

questions.q: The seller of a $1,200,000 Queens condo pays both state and city transfer taxes. What is the combined rate?
questions.x: NYS transfer tax is 0.4% (under $3M) and NYC RPTT is 1.425% above $500,000: 1.825% in all. 1.425% is the trap, the city tax alone.

questions.q: A Brooklyn one-family sells for $800,000. What do the NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT total?
questions.x: NYS: $800,000 x 0.4% = $3,200. NYC RPTT over $500,000: 1.425% x $800,000 = $11,400. Total $14,600. $11,400 is the trap: the city tax without the state tax.

questions.q: On a closing statement, the buyer's new mortgage loan appears as:
c: Debit buyer only
Debit buyer, credit seller
Credit buyer only
Credit seller, debit buyer
questions.x: The new loan is money provided for the buyer, so it is a credit to the buyer with no entry for the seller. Treating it as a double entry like a proration is the trap.

questions.q: The seller's existing mortgage, paid off at closing, appears as:
c: Debit seller only
Debit buyer, credit seller
Debit buyer only
Credit buyer, debit seller
questions.x: The payoff is a charge against the seller's proceeds and touches only the seller. 'Credit buyer, debit seller' is right only for a mortgage the buyer assumes.

questions.q: Under a standard NY contract that apportions as of midnight before closing, who is charged for the day of closing?
c: The seller
Whoever holds the deed at noon
Each pays half the day
The buyer
questions.x: Apportioning as of midnight before closing means the buyer owns the closing day. Many textbook problems give the day to the seller, so follow the question's facts; that habit is the trap.

questions.q: Taxes are prepaid and closing is October 15 under a NY standard contract. The buyer's share of the paid period starts on:
c: October 14
October 15
October 16
November 1
questions.x: With the buyer owning closing day, the buyer's days start October 15. October 16 is the trap from treating the closing day as the seller's.

questions.q: Under the statutory (360-day) method, the daily rate for annual taxes of $5,040 is:
questions.x: $5,040 / 360 = $14.00. $13.81 is the trap: that is $5,040 / 365, the actual-day method.

questions.q: Using the 360-day method, how many days does the seller own from January 1 through March 15, counting March 15?
questions.x: Each month counts as 30 days: January 30 + February 30 + 15 days of March = 75. 73 is the trap from using February's real 28 days.

questions.q: How are water and sewer charges usually handled at a NY closing?
c: Meter read at closing; seller pays to the reading
Buyer pays the whole billing period after closing
Split evenly between buyer and seller by custom
Prorated by the 360-day method from the tax bill
questions.x: The meter is read on or just before closing and the seller pays for usage up to that reading. Prorating by days is the trap: actual usage is measurable, so no estimate is needed.

questions.q: A final water meter reading is taken the day before closing. The charges for usage up to that reading are:
c: Credited to the seller
Debited to the buyer
Debited to the seller
Split between both parties
questions.x: The seller used that water, so the seller pays: a debit to the seller. Crediting the seller is the trap from confusing it with fuel oil, which the seller leaves behind for the buyer.

questions.q: The NYC property tax fiscal year runs:
c: January 1 to December 31
April 1 to March 31
July 1 through June 30
October 1 to September 30
questions.x: NYC property taxes (and school taxes) run July 1 to June 30. The calendar year is the trap: it fits many upstate town and county taxes.

questions.q: When prorating, which bill most often covers the calendar year in upstate NY?
c: Town and county taxes
School taxes
NYC property taxes
Co-op maintenance charges
questions.x: Many upstate town and county taxes follow the calendar year. School taxes run July 1 to June 30, which makes them the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: Which of these is an encumbrance on a property?
c: A recorded utility easement
A fee simple title
A certificate of occupancy for the house
A bargain and sale deed
questions.x: An easement burdens the land and limits its use, so it is an encumbrance. The certificate of occupancy is the trap: it is a building-code approval, not a claim against the property.

questions.q: A real property tax lien is best classified as a:
c: General, voluntary lien
Specific, involuntary lien
Specific, voluntary lien
General, involuntary lien
questions.x: A property tax lien attaches to one parcel (specific) and arises by law without the owner's consent (involuntary). General and involuntary is the trap: that describes a judgment or IRS lien.

questions.q: Which lien can attach to every parcel a debtor owns in the county where it is docketed?
c: A mortgage
A mechanic's lien
A money judgment
A property tax lien
questions.x: A docketed judgment is a general lien on all the debtor's real property in that county. The property tax lien is the trap: it is involuntary but specific to one parcel.

questions.q: A creditor docketed a money judgment against a Utica homeowner in 2020. Absent renewal, the lien on his house expires in:
questions.x: A judgment lien on NY real property lasts 10 years from docketing: 2020 + 10 = 2030. 2023 is the trap: three years is the notice of pendency period.

questions.q: In New York, a filed notice of pendency remains effective for:
c: 1 year
3 years
8 months
10 years
questions.x: A NY notice of pendency is good for 3 years and can be extended by court order. One year is the trap: that is the life of a filed mechanic's lien.

questions.q: A contractor finished a kitchen in a single-family home in Ithaca on May 1 and was not paid. The deadline to file a mechanic's lien is about:
c: July 1
September 1
January 1
May 1 of the next year
questions.x: For a single-family dwelling the filing deadline is 4 months after the last work: May 1 to September 1. January 1 is the trap: it applies the 8-month rule for other property.

questions.q: Ignoring taxes, a 2016 mortgage, a 2018 judgment, and a 2020 mortgage all encumber one house. Which is paid first at a foreclosure sale?
c: The 2018 judgment
The 2020 mortgage
The 2016 mortgage
The three share pro rata
questions.x: After taxes, liens generally rank by date of recording or docketing, so the 2016 mortgage comes first. A pro rata share is the trap: liens are paid in order, not split.

questions.q: A foreclosure sale nets $400,000. Liens: unpaid taxes $10,000; first mortgage $300,000; second mortgage $120,000. How much does the second mortgagee receive?
questions.x: $400,000 - $10,000 taxes = $390,000; - $300,000 first mortgage = $90,000 for the second mortgagee. $100,000 is the trap: it skips the tax lien that is paid first.

questions.q: A homeowner refinances her first mortgage and needs her home equity lender to stay in second position behind the new loan. The equity lender will sign a:
c: Satisfaction of mortgage
Subordination agreement
Release of lien
Estoppel certificate
questions.x: Without a subordination agreement, the older equity line would jump ahead of the new first mortgage. A release is the trap: it would wipe out the equity lender's lien.

questions.q: A neighbor's roof eaves overhang a Hempstead lot line by a foot. A buyer would most likely discover this through a(n):
c: Survey
Title search
Appraisal
Lis pendens
questions.x: Encroachments are physical and are found by survey. A title search is the trap: it reviews recorded documents and will not show an unrecorded overhang.

questions.q: Zoning permits a store on a lot, but a recorded restrictive covenant limits the lot to one-family homes. A buyer planning a store:
c: May build, because zoning overrides covenants
Is bound by the stricter private covenant
May build once the covenant is 10 years old
Needs a variance from the covenant holders
questions.x: The more restrictive rule controls, so the covenant blocks the store even though zoning allows it. A variance is the trap: variances come from the zoning board and cannot waive a private covenant.

questions.q: Because New York is a lien theory state, foreclosure of a defaulted home mortgage generally proceeds:
c: By a judicial action in court
By a power-of-sale clause, out of court
By the lender's automatic retaking of title
By recording a deed in lieu with the county
questions.x: The NY lender holds only a lien, so it must sue to foreclose. Power of sale is the trap: nonjudicial foreclosure is used in many other states, not for NY homes.

questions.q: The holder of a second mortgage forecloses on a house that also has an older first mortgage. The buyer at the sale takes title:
c: Free of both mortgages
Subject to the first mortgage
Subject to the second mortgage
Free of liens but subject to a lis pendens
questions.x: Foreclosure wipes out only liens junior to the foreclosing lien. The senior first mortgage survives. Free of both is the trap: a junior lienholder cannot cut off a senior lien.

questions.q: Lot A has a recorded right to cross Lot B's driveway to reach the road. Lot B is the:
c: Dominant tenement
Servient tenement
Easement in gross
Appurtenant estate
questions.x: Lot B carries the burden, so it is the servient tenement. Dominant is the trap: Lot A, which benefits, is the dominant tenement.

questions.q: Which easement has a servient tenement but NO dominant tenement?
c: Easement appurtenant
Easement in gross
Party wall easement
Easement by necessity
questions.x: An easement in gross benefits a person or company, not land, so there is no dominant tenement. Easement by necessity is the trap: it benefits a landlocked parcel, which is dominant.

questions.q: Unlike adverse possession, an easement by prescription in New York does NOT require use that is:
c: Hostile
Exclusive
Continuous
Open and notorious
questions.x: Prescription can be shared with the owner and others, so exclusivity is not required, and it gives a right of use, not title. Continuous is the trap: both doctrines need 10 continuous years.

questions.q: An easement by necessity over a seller's remaining land ends when:
c: The landlocked owner gains other road access
The servient parcel is sold to a new owner
Ten years pass without the easement being used
The dominant owner dies
questions.x: An easement by necessity lasts only as long as the necessity. Sale of the servient parcel is the trap: easements run with the land and survive a sale.

questions.q: Each owner of a party wall between two Park Slope rowhouses typically owns:
c: Half, plus a support easement in the other half
The whole wall jointly, as tenants in common
The full wall, if his house was built first
A revocable license to lean on the neighbor's half
questions.x: Each owner owns the half on his side, with a cross-easement for support. Tenants in common is the trap: party walls are divided ownership, not undivided co-ownership.

questions.q: An easement appurtenant is terminated when:
c: The dominant parcel is sold to a buyer
The servient parcel is sold to a buyer
The holder signs a written release
Ten years pass after the grant
questions.x: A written release by the easement holder ends the easement. Sale of either parcel is the trap: the benefit and burden run with the land to the new owners.

questions.q: A homeowner lets a neighbor park in his driveway during a block party. The neighbor has a:
c: License
Easement in gross
Prescriptive easement
Easement appurtenant
questions.x: Temporary permission to use land is a license, which is revocable. Easement in gross is the trap: it is a lasting interest in land, usually created by written grant.

questions.q: A Brooklyn developer wants to be sure the neighbor never builds against his new lot-line windows. In New York, the developer should:
c: Rely on a prescriptive easement after 10 years
Buy a light-and-air easement
Wait for an implied easement to arise over time
Record a notice of pendency against the lot
questions.x: NY recognizes light-and-air easements only by express grant, so the developer must buy one. Relying on prescription is the trap: long use never creates a light-and-air easement in NY.

questions.q: Two neighbors share a driveway easement. Which event ends the easement by merger?
c: One owner buys both lots
The servient owner sells to a stranger
The dominant owner rents his house out
The easement goes unused for a year
questions.x: Merger happens when one person owns both the dominant and servient parcels. Sale to a stranger is the trap: the easement runs with the land to the new owner.

questions.q: Which of these is a possessory interest in real estate?
c: An easement
A mortgage lien
A leasehold estate
A recorded deed restriction
questions.x: A leasehold gives the tenant the right to occupy, so it is possessory. Easements, liens, and deed restrictions burden the land without giving possession.

questions.q: Which fact pattern most likely creates an easement by implication?
c: A neighbor openly crosses a lot for 10 years
A visible prior use continues after a lot split
A utility company records a written right of way
A homeowner lets a friend swim in her pool each summer
questions.x: An implied easement arises from an apparent, continuous use that existed when a single owner split the land. The 10-year crossing is the trap: that pattern points to prescription.

questions.q: On a deed, the buyer who receives title is called the:
c: Grantor
Grantee
Mortgagor
Vendor
questions.x: The grantee receives title. Vendor is the trap: vendor means seller, the same side as the grantor.

questions.q: A father signs a deed to his son but locks it in his own desk, intending to keep control. When the father dies, title:
c: Passed to the son when signed
Did not pass; there was no delivery
Passes when the son records it
Passed when it was notarized
questions.x: Title passes only on delivery with intent to transfer, and keeping the deed under his control is not delivery. Passing at signing is the trap: a signed but undelivered deed transfers nothing.

questions.q: Which is required for a deed to be valid between grantor and grantee?
c: Recording with the county clerk
The grantor's signature
A title insurance policy
A survey of the property
questions.x: A deed must be signed by the grantor. Recording is the trap: it protects against third parties but is not needed between the parties.

questions.q: The deed clause containing words of conveyance, such as "grants and releases," is the:
c: Habendum clause
Granting clause
Testimonium clause
Reddendum clause
questions.x: The granting clause holds the words that actually convey the property. Habendum is the trap: it defines the estate granted ("to have and to hold").

questions.q: In New York, a deed that was signed and delivered but never acknowledged is:
c: Void between grantor and grantee
Valid, but cannot be recorded
Recordable but unenforceable
Void unless notarized within 1 year
questions.x: Acknowledgment is needed to record a deed, not to make it valid between the parties. Void between the parties is the trap: delivery and acceptance already passed title.

questions.q: In a metes and bounds description, "metes" refers to:
c: Distances and compass directions
Monuments such as walls and trees
Lot numbers on a recorded map
Township and range lines
questions.x: Metes are measurements of distance and direction; bounds are the boundaries and monuments. Monuments are the trap: they are the "bounds."

questions.q: When a deed's stated distance conflicts with a natural monument, surveyors generally follow:
c: The stated distance
The compass bearing
The tax map
The monument
questions.x: Monuments control over courses and distances. The compass bearing is the trap: directions also yield to a fixed monument.

questions.q: In the deed most often used in New York home sales, the grantor promises:
c: That the grantor did nothing to encumber title
That title is good against every claim forever
No promise of any kind about title
That the grantor will pay off future liens
questions.x: The bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts promises only that the grantor did nothing to encumber the title. Good against every claim is the trap: that is the full covenant and warranty deed.

questions.q: The warranty deed covenant promising that the grantor actually owns the estate being conveyed is the covenant of:
c: Seizin
Quiet enjoyment
Further assurance
Against encumbrances
questions.x: Seizin is the promise that the grantor owns what the deed conveys. Quiet enjoyment is the trap: it promises the grantee will not be disturbed by someone with better title.

questions.q: After closing, a defect turns up that the grantor could cure by signing a corrective deed. Which warranty deed covenant obligates her to sign it?
c: Seizin
Quiet enjoyment
Against encumbrances
Further assurance
questions.x: Further assurance requires the grantor to sign what is reasonably needed to perfect the grantee's title. Quiet enjoyment is the trap: it protects possession against superior claims but does not require new documents.

questions.q: Co-owners cannot agree, and a court orders their Albany house sold in a partition action. The buyer receives a(n):
c: Executor's deed
Referee's deed
Quitclaim deed
Administrator's deed
questions.x: Court-ordered sales, including partition and foreclosure, are conveyed by a referee's deed. Administrator's deed is the trap: it is used to sell property of someone who died without a will.

questions.q: A cousin who may hold a stray inherited interest in a lot is asked to sign a deed clearing that cloud on title. The usual instrument is a:
c: Quitclaim deed
Warranty deed
Referee's deed
Bargain and sale deed
questions.x: A quitclaim releases whatever interest the cousin may have without promising that any exists. Warranty deed is the trap: no one would warrant title to an interest they may not even hold.

questions.q: The Lien Law covenant included in New York deeds mainly protects:
c: Unpaid contractors
The buyer's mortgage lender
Tenants with security deposits
The seller's prior title insurer
questions.x: The covenant requires the seller to use sale proceeds first to pay for improvements, protecting contractors and suppliers. The buyer's lender is the trap: lenders are protected by title insurance and lien priority, not this covenant.

questions.q: A deed that describes a parcel as "Lot 22, Block 7, on the Map of Glen Oaks Estates filed in the Queens County Clerk's Office" uses which method?
c: Metes and bounds
Monuments and courses
Lot and block
Government survey system
questions.x: Lot and block identifies land by reference to a filed subdivision map. Government survey is the trap: the rectangular survey system is not used in New York.

questions.q: A person who dies without a valid will is said to die:
c: Testate
By devise
In severalty
Intestate
questions.x: Intestate means without a will, so property passes by statute to heirs. Testate is the trap: it means with a valid will.

questions.q: A gift of real property by will is a:
c: Devise
Bequest
Legacy
Descent
questions.x: A devise is a gift of real property by will, received by a devisee. Bequest is the trap: bequests and legacies are gifts of personal property.

questions.q: In New York, the court that probates wills and appoints administrators is the:
c: Supreme Court (trial level)
Court of Claims
Housing Court
Surrogate's Court
questions.x: Surrogate's Court handles probate and estates in each NY county. Supreme Court is the trap: despite its name it is NY's trial court, handling partition and foreclosure actions.

questions.q: The person appointed by the court to settle the estate of someone who died without a will is the:
c: Executor
Testamentary trustee
Administrator
Remainderman
questions.x: An administrator is court-appointed when there is no will or no executor. Executor is the trap: an executor is named in the will.

questions.q: When a person dies intestate with no heirs at all, the property passes to the state by:
c: Eminent domain
Dedication
Adverse possession
Escheat
questions.x: Escheat is the state's power to take property of an owner who dies without a will and without heirs. Eminent domain is the trap: it is a taking for public use with just compensation.

questions.q: A Long Island man dies without a will, leaving a wife, three children, and a $650,000 estate. Under NY intestacy law, how much does each child receive?
questions.x: The spouse takes $50,000 plus half the rest: $50,000 + $300,000 = $350,000. The children split the other $300,000: $100,000 each. $216,667 is the trap: it ignores the spouse's share.

questions.q: The statutory period for adverse possession in New York is:
c: 5 years
10 years
15 years
21 years
questions.x: NY requires 10 years of hostile, actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous possession. Twenty-one years is the trap: that is the rule in some other states.

questions.q: Under NY's 2008 adverse possession amendments, all of the following are treated as permissive and do not by themselves establish adverse possession EXCEPT:
c: Planting a hedge across the line
Building a permanent garage on the lot
Building a fence slightly over the line
Mowing and tending a strip of the neighbor's lawn
questions.x: De minimis non-structural encroachments (hedges, fences, plantings, sheds) and lawn care are deemed permissive. A permanent garage is substantial use as an owner. The fence is the tempting pick, but the 2008 law lists fences as de minimis.

questions.q: The gradual addition of land along a riverbank by deposits of soil is:
c: Accretion
Avulsion
Erosion
Reliction
questions.x: Accretion is gradual build-up, and the owner gains the new land. Avulsion is the trap: it is a sudden change, which does not move the boundary.

questions.q: A hurricane suddenly cuts a new channel and moves a creek 200 feet, putting part of Owner A's land on Owner B's side. Who owns the land that moved?
c: Owner B, by accretion to B's side
Owner A; avulsion does not move the line
The state, by escheat of submerged land
A and B, split evenly as tenants in common
questions.x: Avulsion is sudden, and the boundary stays where it was, so Owner A keeps title. Accretion is the trap: it is gradual and does shift ownership to the riparian owner.

questions.q: All of the following are forms of involuntary alienation EXCEPT:
c: Foreclosure sale
Condemnation by eminent domain
Adverse possession
Transfer by will
questions.x: A will reflects the owner's own choice, so it is voluntary alienation. Foreclosure, condemnation, and adverse possession transfer title without the owner's consent. Foreclosure is the tempting pick because the owner signed the mortgage, but the sale itself is forced.

questions.q: The original transfer of land from a government to a private owner is evidenced by a:
c: Lis pendens
Quitclaim deed
Referee's deed
Land patent
questions.x: A land patent is the instrument of a public grant from the government; many NY chains of title trace to colonial patents. Quitclaim is the trap: it is a private conveyance with no warranties.

questions.q: A developer files a subdivision map in Orange County showing new streets and a park, which the town accepts. The developer has made a:
c: Public grant
Reversion
Partition
Dedication
questions.x: Dedication is a private owner's gift of land to public use, which the government accepts. Public grant is the trap: it runs the other way, from government to a private party.

questions.q: An owner sells to Buyer 1, who does not record. A week later the owner sells to Buyer 2, who pays value, knows nothing of Buyer 1, and records first. Under NY's recording act, who owns the property?
c: Buyer 1, because the first deed delivered wins
Both buyers, as tenants in common by law
Buyer 2, who recorded first in good faith
The seller, since both deeds are void
questions.x: NY is a race-notice state: a later good-faith purchaser for value without notice who records first prevails. First in time is the trap: that is the common-law rule the recording act displaces. Buyer 1's remedy is against the seller.

questions.q: Recording a deed in the public records gives:
c: Actual notice
No notice until the next tax bill
Inquiry notice to neighbors
Constructive notice
questions.x: Recording gives constructive notice: the law presumes everyone knows. Actual notice is the trap: it is what a person really knows.

questions.q: The unbroken succession of owners of a property, traced from the original grant to the present, is the:
c: Chain of title
Abstract of title
Certificate of occupancy
Survey
questions.x: The chain of title is the sequence of ownership. Abstract of title is the trap: it is a written summary of the recorded documents in that chain.

questions.q: Title that is free from reasonable doubt and that a reasonable, informed buyer would accept is called:
c: Marketable title
Equitable title
Color of title
Constructive title
questions.x: Marketable title can be resold without fear of litigation. Equitable title is the trap: it is the buyer's interest between contract and closing.

questions.q: An owner's title insurance policy protects the owner against:
c: Defects existing before the policy date
Fire, wind, and storm damage to the house
Liens the owner creates after closing
Losses from rezoning after the closing
questions.x: Title insurance covers hidden defects that predate the policy, such as a forged deed. Fire and storm damage is the trap: that is homeowner's insurance.

questions.q: All of the following are true of a lender's title insurance policy EXCEPT:
c: It protects the lender
It protects the buyer's equity
It is usually required by the lender
Its coverage decreases as the loan is paid down
questions.x: Only an owner's policy protects the buyer's equity. Shrinking coverage is the tempting pick, but the lender's policy does track the loan balance as it is repaid.

questions.q: Under the TRID rule, the borrower must receive the Closing Disclosure at least how long before consummation?
c: 24 hours
7 calendar days
3 business days
10 days
questions.x: The Closing Disclosure must arrive at least 3 business days before closing. Twenty-four hours is the trap: that was the old HUD-1 review practice before TRID.

questions.q: A home inspector offers a salesperson $100 for each client referred. Under RESPA, accepting would be:
c: Legal, if disclosed to the client in writing
Legal, since inspectors are not lenders
An illegal referral fee under RESPA
Legal, if the supervising broker approves
questions.x: RESPA Section 8 bans fees for referrals of settlement services on federally related loans. Written disclosure is the trap: disclosure does not make a kickback legal.

questions.q: RESPA applies to:
c: Cash purchases of commercial buildings
FHA-insured home loans and nothing else
Federally related 1 to 4 family home loans
Residential leases with terms longer than one year
questions.x: RESPA covers federally related mortgage loans on 1 to 4 family residential property, which includes nearly all home mortgages. FHA loans alone is the trap: conventional loans from federally insured lenders are covered too.

questions.q: The broker or salesperson's main role in the days just before closing typically includes:
c: Preparing and drafting the deed for signing
Attending the buyer's final walk-through
Issuing the buyer's title insurance policy
Recording the new mortgage with the clerk
questions.x: Licensees accompany the buyer on the walk-through to confirm condition and included items. Drafting the deed is the trap: in NY the attorneys prepare it, and drafting it would be practicing law.

questions.q: In Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens, and the Bronx, deeds and mortgages are recorded with the:
c: County clerk of each borough
NYS Department of State
Office of the City Register
Surrogate's Court
questions.x: NYC's Office of the City Register (Department of Finance, via ACRIS) records documents for four boroughs. County clerk is the trap: Staten Island and the rest of the state record there.

questions.q: Who customarily pays the New York State real estate transfer tax?
c: The seller
The buyer (grantee)
The buyer's lender
The listing broker
questions.x: The NYS transfer tax is the grantor's obligation. The buyer is the trap: the buyer pays the mansion tax, not the transfer tax.

questions.q: A house in Albany sells for $735,000. What is the NYS real estate transfer tax?
questions.x: $2 per $500: $735,000 / $500 = 1,470 units x $2 = $2,940 (0.4%). $1,470 is the trap: it counts the units but forgets to multiply by $2.

questions.q: A buyer pays $3,400,000 for a Tribeca condo. What is the NYC mansion tax?
questions.x: The $3M to under $5M bracket is 1.5% of the whole price: $3,400,000 x 0.015 = $51,000. $34,000 is the trap: it uses the flat 1% that applies outside NYC.

questions.q: A Queens condo sells for $480,000. What NYC Real Property Transfer Tax does the seller pay?
questions.x: Residential sales of $500,000 or less pay 1%: $480,000 x 0.01 = $4,800. $6,840 is the trap: the 1.425% rate applies only above $500,000.

questions.q: The seller of a $3,400,000 Manhattan condo owes the NYS transfer tax at the higher NYC rate. How much is it?
questions.x: In NYC, residential conveyances of $3M or more pay 0.65%: $3,400,000 x 0.0065 = $22,100. $13,600 is the trap: it applies the ordinary 0.4% rate.

questions.q: A Bronx buyer takes a $420,000 mortgage on a two-family. At the borrower's rate of 1.8%, what mortgage recording tax does the borrower pay?
questions.x: Loans under $500,000 on 1 to 3 family homes in NYC: borrower pays 1.8%. $420,000 x 0.018 = $7,560. $8,085 is the trap: it uses the 1.925% rate for loans of $500,000 or more.

questions.q: Which purchase does NOT owe mortgage recording tax?
c: A Westchester house with a mortgage
A Brooklyn condo with a mortgage
A Buffalo two-family bought with a mortgage
A Manhattan co-op with a share loan
questions.x: A co-op share loan is secured by stock and a proprietary lease, not a recorded mortgage, so no mortgage recording tax applies. The condo is the trap: condos are real property financed with mortgages.

questions.q: Annual property taxes of $9,125 were paid in full by the seller for the calendar year. Closing is August 20 and the buyer owns the day of closing. Using a 365-day year, what is the proration?
c: Debit seller, credit buyer $3,350
Credit seller, debit buyer $3,350
Credit seller, debit buyer $3,325
Debit buyer, credit seller $5,775
questions.x: Daily rate $9,125 / 365 = $25. Buyer's days: Aug 20 to 31 (12) + 30 + 31 + 30 + 31 = 134. 134 x $25 = $3,350. The seller prepaid, so credit seller, debit buyer. $3,325 is the trap: it gives the closing day to the seller.

questions.q: Annual taxes of $5,400 for the calendar year are unpaid at a September 10 closing. The seller owns the day of closing. Using a 360-day year, the entry is:
c: Debit seller, credit buyer $3,600
Credit seller, debit buyer $3,750
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,650
Debit seller, credit buyer $3,750
questions.x: Seller's days: 8 months x 30 = 240 + 10 = 250. Daily rate $5,400 / 360 = $15. 250 x $15 = $3,750. Taxes are unpaid, so the seller owes the buyer: debit seller, credit buyer. $1,650 is the trap: it prorates the buyer's days.

questions.q: A seller collected June rent of $3,000 on June 1. Closing is June 16 and the seller owns the day of closing. Using a 30-day month, what is the rent proration?
c: Debit seller, credit buyer $1,500
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,400
Credit seller, debit buyer $1,400
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,600
questions.x: Buyer's days are June 17 to 30, 14 days. $3,000 / 30 = $100 x 14 = $1,400. The seller collected rent the buyer is entitled to, so debit seller, credit buyer. $1,500 is the trap: it gives the closing day to the buyer.

questions.q: Tenant security deposits held by the seller of a rental building are shown on the closing statement as:
c: Credit seller, debit buyer
A debit to both parties
Debit seller, credit buyer
Omitted; tenants are refunded at closing
questions.x: The buyer takes over the duty to return deposits, so the seller transfers them: debit seller, credit buyer. Credit seller is the trap: the deposits were never the seller's money to keep.

questions.q: At closing, 275 gallons of heating oil remain in the tank, priced at $3.60 per gallon. The entry is:
c: Credit seller, debit buyer $990
Debit seller, credit buyer $990
Credit seller, debit buyer $275
No entry; oil conveys with the house
questions.x: The seller paid for oil the buyer will use: 275 x $3.60 = $990. Credit seller, debit buyer. Debit seller is the trap: the buyer is receiving value, so the buyer pays.

questions.q: Price $800,000. Buyer's credits: $80,000 deposit, $640,000 new loan, $1,200 tax proration. Buyer's debits: price plus $14,500 in closing costs. How much cash must the buyer bring to closing?
questions.x: Debits $814,500 minus credits $721,200 = $93,300. $94,500 is the trap: it forgets the $1,200 tax credit.

questions.concept: NY buyer vs seller closing costs
questions.q: All of the following are customarily seller closing costs in a NY sale EXCEPT:
c: Lender's title insurance
NYS transfer tax
Payoff of the seller's mortgage
Broker's commission
questions.x: The lender's title policy protects the buyer's lender and is paid by the buyer in NY. The transfer tax is the tempting pick, but it is the seller's obligation.

questions.q: On a closing statement, the purchase price is entered as:
c: A credit to the buyer, a debit to the seller
A debit to buyer and credit to seller
A debit to both
A credit to both
questions.x: The buyer owes the price (debit) and the seller receives it (credit). The reversed entry is the trap: credits are what a party receives or has already paid.

questions.q: A buyer pays exactly $999,000 for a house in Nassau County. How much mansion tax is due?
questions.x: The mansion tax applies to residential purchases of $1,000,000 or more. At $999,000 nothing is owed. $9,990 is the trap: it applies 1% below the threshold.

questions.q: A co-op's fee charged on a sale, set by the building's bylaws or proprietary lease and usually paid by the seller, is a:
c: Mansion tax
Flip tax
Mortgage recording tax
Special assessment
questions.x: A flip tax is a private building transfer fee, not a government tax. Mansion tax is the trap: it is a state tax paid by buyers of $1M+ residences.

questions.q: Which legal description method is NOT used to describe land in New York?
c: Metes and bounds
Lot and block
Rectangular survey
Reference to a filed map
questions.x: The rectangular (government) survey system is used in many western and midwestern states but not New York. Reference to a filed map is the trap: it is simply lot and block, which NY uses.

questions.q: A person who dies leaving a valid will is said to die:
c: Intestate
Testate
By descent
In escheat
questions.x: Testate means with a valid will. By descent is the trap: descent is how heirs take when there is no will.

questions.q: A will leaves a car and a coin collection to a nephew. This gift of personal property is a:
c: Devise
Dedication
Descent
Bequest
questions.x: A gift of personal property by will is a bequest. Devise is the trap: it is a gift of real property by will.

questions.q: An executor named in a Westchester will needs the will probated and letters testamentary issued. She applies to the:
c: County Clerk
Surrogate's Court
Supreme Court
Department of State
questions.x: Surrogate's Court probates wills and issues letters testamentary. County Clerk is the trap: the clerk records deeds but does not probate wills.
