questions.q: The person named in a will to carry out its terms is the:
c: Administrator
Executor
Devisee
Grantee
questions.x: The testator names an executor in the will. Administrator is the trap: the court appoints one when there is no will.

questions.q: Escheat occurs when an owner:
c: Dies intestate with no heirs
Fails to pay real property taxes
Abandons a building for 10 years
Refuses to sell for a public project
questions.x: Escheat transfers property to the state when no will and no heirs exist. Unpaid taxes is the trap: that leads to a tax lien sale or tax foreclosure, not escheat.

questions.q: A Bronx woman dies intestate, survived by her husband and her parents but no children. Her $400,000 estate passes:
c: Entirely to her husband
$50,000 plus half to her husband
Half to her husband, half to her parents
One third to her husband
questions.x: With a spouse and no children, the spouse takes the entire estate under NY intestacy. $50,000 plus half is the trap: that split applies when there are children.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT required for adverse possession in New York?
c: Hostile use under a claim of right
Exclusive possession
Continuous use for 10 years
Payment of the property taxes
questions.x: NY does not require the claimant to pay the taxes. Exclusive possession is the trap: it is required for adverse possession, though not for a prescriptive easement.

questions.q: Under NY's 2008 amendments, a neighbor who has mowed and weeded a strip of your lawn for 12 years has:
c: Title to the strip by adverse possession
No claim; mowing is deemed permissive
A prescriptive easement over the strip
Title, if he also paid the taxes
questions.x: The 2008 amendments treat lawn mowing and similar maintenance as permissive, so it cannot ripen into title. The 12-year period is the trap: time alone does not help when the use is deemed permissive.

questions.q: Over decades, a creek slowly deposits silt that adds a quarter acre to Ruth's lot. The added land:
c: Belongs to the state by escheat
Belongs to Ruth by accretion
Belongs to the upstream owner
Stays unowned until surveyed
questions.x: Gradual deposits are accretion, and the new land belongs to the riparian owner. The upstream owner is the trap: soil carried downstream does not stay with the parcel it came from.

questions.q: Which event moves a property boundary along a river?
c: A flood suddenly carving a new channel
Gradual deposits of soil over many years
A hurricane shifting the riverbed overnight
Sudden erosion from an ice jam
questions.x: Gradual accretion shifts the boundary with the water. The sudden events are the trap: avulsion, however dramatic, leaves the boundary where it was.

questions.q: Which is an example of voluntary alienation?
c: A tax foreclosure sale
A gift deed to a daughter
Condemnation for a highway
Title by adverse possession
questions.x: A gift deed is the owner's own choice to transfer, so it is voluntary. Condemnation is the trap: the owner is paid, but the transfer is still forced.

questions.q: A land patent transfers title:
c: From the government to a private party
From a private owner to the town for a park
From a debtor to a foreclosing bank
From a decedent to his heirs
questions.x: A patent is the original grant from the sovereign to a private party. The town park is the trap: a private gift of land to the public is a dedication, the reverse direction.

questions.q: Which is required for a valid dedication of a private road to a town?
c: Acceptance by the town
Ten years of public use
Payment of just compensation
A referee's deed
questions.x: A dedication is complete when the government accepts it. Just compensation is the trap: that belongs to eminent domain, where the government takes land, not receives a gift.

questions.q: An owner sells to Buyer 1, who does not record. The owner then sells to Buyer 2, who knows of the first sale and records first. Who prevails in New York?
c: Buyer 2, because she won the race to record
Buyer 1, because Buyer 2 had notice
Both, as tenants in common
Neither; the seller keeps title
questions.x: Under race-notice, the later buyer must be without notice AND record first. Buyer 2 knew, so Buyer 1 keeps title. Winning the race is the trap: in a pure race state it would be enough, but not in NY.

questions.q: A buyer never checked the county records, but an earlier easement on the lot was properly recorded. The buyer:
c: Takes free of it, lacking actual notice
Is bound by it through constructive notice
Is bound if the seller disclosed it in writing
Can void it by recording her deed first
questions.x: A recorded document gives constructive notice to everyone, whether or not they searched. Lack of actual notice is the trap: the law presumes knowledge of the public record.

questions.q: A condensed written summary of every recorded document affecting a parcel is the:
c: Chain of title
Abstract of title
Title insurance policy
Certificate of title
questions.x: An abstract summarizes the recorded history. Chain of title is the trap: it is the sequence of owners, not the summary of documents.

questions.q: A buyer's contract requires marketable title. Which would most likely make the title unmarketable?
c: An unreleased old mortgage of record
A recorded utility easement the contract lists
A pending sale of the house next door
The seller's plan to buy another home
questions.x: An open mortgage of record is a cloud that a reasonable buyer would refuse until it is cleared. The easement is the trap: a known encumbrance the buyer agreed to in the contract does not defeat marketability.

questions.q: A forged signature in a deed from 20 years ago surfaces after closing. Which policy covers the new owner's loss?
c: Homeowner's (HO-3) policy
Lender's title insurance
Owner's title insurance
Seller's errors and omissions
questions.x: An owner's title policy covers pre-existing title defects like forgery. Lender's title insurance is the trap: it protects only the lender's loan, not the owner's equity.

questions.q: A buyer asks why she should buy an owner's policy when her lender already requires a lender's policy. The best answer is:
c: The lender's policy protects the loan alone
The lender's policy already covers her equity
An owner's policy is required by state law
An owner's policy also covers the home against fire
questions.x: A lender's policy covers the lender up to the loan balance and leaves the owner's equity uninsured. Covering her equity is the trap: that protection comes only from an owner's policy.

questions.q: Under TRID, the Loan Estimate must be delivered within how long after a loan application?
c: 24 hours
3 business days
7 business days
10 calendar days
questions.x: The Loan Estimate is due within 3 business days after application. Seven business days is the trap: that is the waiting period before consummation after the Loan Estimate is delivered.

questions.q: Which payment is permitted under RESPA Section 8?
c: A title agent's $200 gift card for each referral
A lender's fee to a broker for steering borrowers
Payment for services actually performed
A free trip from a lender for sending it clients
questions.x: RESPA allows payment for services actually performed; it bans things of value given for referrals. The gift card is the trap: a small non-cash reward is still a kickback.

questions.q: Which transaction is most likely outside RESPA?
c: A conventional loan on a Queens two-family
An FHA loan on a Syracuse single-family
A cash purchase of a Bronx warehouse
A refinance of a Brooklyn condo mortgage
questions.x: RESPA reaches federally related residential mortgage loans; an all-cash commercial purchase has neither. The refinance is the trap: RESPA covers refinances of 1 to 4 family loans, not just purchases.

questions.q: In a typical New York home sale, which pre-closing task belongs to the attorneys rather than the brokers?
c: Scheduling the final walk-through
Drafting the deed and reviewing title
Keeping the buyer updated on the timeline
Coordinating access for the appraiser
questions.x: NY attorneys draft the deed and review the title report. The walk-through is the trap: brokers commonly schedule and attend it.

questions.q: A deed for a house on Staten Island is recorded with the:
c: Office of the City Register
Richmond County Clerk
NYS Department of State
Surrogate's Court
questions.x: Staten Island (Richmond County) records with its county clerk. The City Register is the trap: it handles the other four boroughs.

questions.q: If the seller fails to pay the NYS real estate transfer tax, who becomes liable for it?
c: The listing broker
The county clerk
The buyer (grantee)
The title insurer
questions.x: The grantor owes the tax, but if the grantor fails to pay, the grantee becomes liable. The title insurer is the trap: it may collect the tax at closing but is not the backup obligor.

questions.q: A Syracuse house sells for $412,000. What is the NYS real estate transfer tax?
questions.x: $412,000 / $500 = 824 units x $2 = $1,648. $824 is the trap: it stops at the number of units.

questions.q: A Brooklyn buyer pays $2,500,000 for a brownstone. What NYC mansion tax is due?
questions.x: The $2M to under $3M bracket is 1.25% of the whole price: $2,500,000 x 0.0125 = $31,250. $25,000 is the trap: the flat 1% rate applies in NYC only from $1M to under $2M.

questions.q: A Bronx two-family sells for $750,000. What NYC Real Property Transfer Tax does the seller owe?
questions.x: Residential sales above $500,000 pay 1.425% on the whole price: $750,000 x 0.01425 = $10,687.50. $19,687.50 is the trap: 2.625% is the commercial rate.

questions.q: A Manhattan condo sells for $2,800,000. What NYS real estate transfer tax does the seller owe?
questions.x: The 0.65% NYC rate starts at $3M for residential property, so this sale pays the ordinary 0.4%: $2,800,000 x 0.004 = $11,200. $18,200 is the trap: it applies the higher rate below its threshold.

questions.q: A Queens condo buyer takes a $600,000 mortgage. How much NYC mortgage recording tax does the borrower pay?
questions.x: Loans of $500,000 or more on 1 to 3 family homes and condos: borrower pays 1.925%. $600,000 x 0.01925 = $11,550. $10,800 is the trap: 1.8% applies only to loans under $500,000.

questions.q: Why does a co-op buyer financing with a share loan pay no mortgage recording tax?
c: Shares are personal property, not real estate
Co-op buyers are exempt as first-time buyers
The co-op corporation pays the tax instead
Share loans are taxed through the mansion tax
questions.x: The share loan is secured by stock and a proprietary lease, which are personal property, so there is no mortgage to record. The co-op paying instead is the trap: the building's own mortgage is separate from the buyer's loan.

questions.q: Annual taxes of $7,300 were prepaid by the seller for the calendar year. Closing is October 1, and the buyer owns the day of closing. Using a 365-day year, the proration is:
c: Credit seller, debit buyer $1,840
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,840
Credit seller, debit buyer $1,820
Credit seller, debit buyer $5,460
questions.x: Daily rate $7,300 / 365 = $20. Buyer's days: October 31 + November 30 + December 31 = 92. 92 x $20 = $1,840, credited to the seller who prepaid. $5,460 is the trap: it prorates the seller's 273 days instead of the buyer's.

questions.q: Annual taxes of $4,320 are unpaid at a May 15 closing; the seller owns the day of closing. Using a 360-day year, the entry is:
c: Credit seller, debit buyer $1,620
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,620
Debit seller, credit buyer $2,700
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,608
questions.x: Seller's days: 4 months x 30 = 120 + 15 = 135. $4,320 / 360 = $12 x 135 = $1,620. Unpaid taxes mean the seller owes the buyer: debit seller, credit buyer. Crediting the seller is the trap: that direction applies only when taxes were prepaid.

questions.q: A seller collected $2,400 of June rent on June 1. Closing is June 21 and the buyer owns the day of closing. Using a 30-day month, the entry is:
c: Debit seller, credit buyer $720
Credit seller, debit buyer $800
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,600
Debit seller, credit buyer $800
questions.x: Buyer's days: June 21 to 30 = 10. $2,400 / 30 = $80 x 10 = $800, owed by the seller who collected it. Crediting the seller is the trap: prepaid rent goes to the buyer, the reverse of prepaid taxes.

questions.q: A buyer of a six-unit Ridgewood building asks what happens to the tenants' security deposits at closing. They are:
c: Refunded to tenants by the seller at closing
Kept by the seller as earned income
Credited to the buyer
Held by the broker until the leases expire
questions.x: The new owner must return deposits at lease end, so the seller turns them over as a credit to the buyer. Refunding the tenants is the trap: the leases continue, so the deposits stay in place under the new owner.

questions.q: At closing, 180 gallons of heating oil remain in the tank at $3.50 per gallon. The entry is:
c: Debit seller, credit buyer $630
Credit seller, debit buyer $630
Credit seller, debit buyer $180
No entry, since fuel conveys as a fixture
questions.x: 180 x $3.50 = $630, owed to the seller who paid for oil the buyer will burn: credit seller, debit buyer. Treating oil as a fixture is the trap: it is a prepaid item that is prorated.

questions.q: Price $500,000. Buyer's credits: $50,000 deposit, $400,000 loan, $900 tax credit. Buyer's debits: price plus $9,600 in closing costs. How much cash does the buyer bring to closing?
questions.x: Debits $509,600 minus credits $450,900 = $58,700. $59,600 is the trap: it forgets the $900 tax credit.

questions.concept: NY buyer vs seller closing costs
questions.q: Which closing cost is customarily paid by the BUYER in a New York sale?
c: NYS transfer tax
Mansion tax on a $1.2M home
Broker's commission
Satisfaction of the seller's mortgage
questions.x: The mansion tax on residential purchases of $1M or more is the buyer's. The NYS transfer tax is the trap: it is paid by the seller.

questions.q: The buyer's earnest money deposit appears on the closing statement as:
c: A credit to the buyer
A debit to the buyer
A credit to the seller
A debit to both parties
questions.x: The buyer already paid the deposit, so it is credited against what the buyer owes. Credit to the seller is the trap: the seller already gets credit for the full price.

questions.q: A Rockland County buyer pays exactly $1,000,000 for a house. How much mansion tax is due?
questions.x: At $1,000,000 the threshold is met, and the 1% tax applies to the whole price: $10,000. $0 is the trap: the threshold is $1M or more, not above $1M.

questions.q: A co-op flip tax is imposed by:
c: New York State's Tax Department
The City of New York
The co-op corporation
The county clerk
questions.x: The flip tax is a private fee set by the co-op's bylaws or proprietary lease. The City is the trap: NYC's transfer tax is a separate government tax.

questions.concept: Life tenant conveys only a life estate
questions.q: Walter, 79, holds a life estate in a Yonkers house; his niece holds the remainder. Walter sells "all his interest" to Dana, age 35. What does Dana own?
c: A life estate measured by Dana's own life
A life estate that ends when Walter dies
A fee simple subject to the niece's remainder
A tenancy at will the niece may end at any time
questions.x: A life tenant can transfer only what he holds, so Dana gets a life estate pur autre vie, measured by Walter's life. The trap is a life estate measured by Dana's life: if that were the rule, a life tenant could extend the estate decades by selling to a younger buyer. When Walter dies, the niece takes possession.

questions.concept: Life tenant conveys only a life estate
questions.q: A life tenant deeds her interest to a buyer and then dies two months later. What happens to the buyer's interest?
c: It ends, and the remainderman takes possession
It continues for the rest of the buyer's own lifetime
It passes to the life tenant's heirs by will
It ripens into a fee simple after probate
questions.x: The buyer received a life estate pur autre vie, which lasts only as long as the original life tenant lives. At her death it ends and the remainderman takes the property in possession. The trap is the buyer's lifetime: the measuring life never changed. Nothing passes to the life tenant's heirs because her estate ended with her.

questions.concept: Lease by life tenant ends at death
questions.q: A life tenant leases a Bronx apartment to a tenant for 3 years and dies after 1 year. The remaindermen did not sign the lease. What is the tenant's position?
c: The lease binds the remaindermen for the last 2 years
The lease converts to a lifetime lease for the tenant
The lease continues until the estate finishes probate
The lease ends when the life estate ends
questions.x: A life tenant may lease, but only out of the life estate, so the lease ends when the life estate does. The trap is that the lease binds the remaindermen: leases from a fee owner survive a sale, but the remaindermen never granted this one. They can choose to keep the tenant, and accepting rent would usually create a month-to-month tenancy.

questions.concept: Lease by life tenant ends at death
questions.q: A life tenant signs a 2-year lease with a tenant and dies during its first year. All of the following are true EXCEPT:
c: The remaindermen can accept rent and keep the tenant
The lease could last no longer than the life estate
The remaindermen are bound by the lease's end date
The life tenant had the right to lease the property
questions.x: The remaindermen are not bound by the lease's end date, because the lease was carved out of a life estate that ended at death. Everything else is true: a life tenant may lease, the lease cannot outlast her estate, and the remaindermen may keep the tenant by agreement or by accepting rent. The trap is treating the lease like one from a fee owner.

questions.q: A life tenant lets a known roof leak go unrepaired for three years, and the rafters rot. Who may sue, and on what theory?
c: The remainderman, for waste
The remainderman, for trespass
The town, for a code violation
No one, the life tenant may neglect it
questions.x: A life tenant must keep the property in reasonable repair and may not harm the future interest. Letting it deteriorate is permissive waste, and the remainderman can seek damages or an injunction. The trap is trespass: the life tenant is lawfully in possession, so the claim is waste, not trespass. A code violation may also exist but does not protect the remainderman's interest.

questions.q: A life tenant in a Saratoga Victorian removes and sells the original stained-glass windows. Which describes her conduct?
c: A permitted use, since the life tenant controls the fixtures
Affirmative waste the remainderman can sue to stop
A sale of personal property she owned outright
A partial conveyance of the remainder interest
questions.x: Stained-glass windows are fixtures, part of the real property, and removing them damages the remainder. That is affirmative (voluntary) waste. The trap is that the life tenant "controls the fixtures": she may use and enjoy them, but not strip them for cash. Fixtures are not her personal property, and she owns no part of the remainder to convey.

questions.concept: Splitting proceeds by life estate factor
questions.q: A life tenant and two remaindermen sell a house for $800,000. Using an actuarial life estate factor of 0.35, how much does each remainderman receive before costs?
questions.x: The remainder is 1 minus 0.35, or 0.65, of $800,000, which is $520,000, split between two remaindermen: $260,000 each. The trap is $400,000, an even half of the whole price that ignores the life estate. $266,667 is a three-way split, and $280,000 is the life tenant's share ($800,000 x 0.35).

questions.concept: Splitting proceeds by life estate factor
questions.q: A house sells for $650,000. The life tenant's actuarial factor is 0.22. How much goes to the life tenant before costs?
questions.x: The life tenant's share is the price times the life estate factor: $650,000 x 0.22 = $143,000. $507,000 is the trap, the remainder share (0.78 of the price), which goes to the remaindermen. $216,667 is a three-way split, and $325,000 is half, neither of which reflects the actuarial value of a life estate.

questions.concept: Merger of life estate and remainder
questions.q: A life tenant deeds her life estate to the sole remainderman. What does the remainderman now hold?
c: A life estate pur autre vie plus a remainder
A remainder that becomes possessory at her death
A fee simple absolute, by merger
A leasehold for the life tenant's life
questions.x: When the present life estate and the future remainder come together in one owner, they merge into a fee simple absolute. The trap is the pur autre vie answer: that describes the result when a stranger buys the life estate. Here nothing is left to wait for, because the person who would take next already holds the life estate too.

questions.concept: Merger of life estate and remainder
questions.q: Ines holds a life estate; her two sons hold the remainder as tenants in common. Ines deeds her life estate to both sons. How do the sons now hold?
c: As remaindermen waiting for Ines's death
As life tenants measured by Ines's life
As joint tenants with right of survivorship
As tenants in common in fee simple
questions.x: The life estate merges into the remainder, so the sons own the fee simple absolute, and they keep their existing form of co-ownership: tenancy in common. The trap is joint tenancy: merger does not add survivorship, which in New York must be stated expressly. They no longer wait for anything, because Ines gave up her estate.

questions.q: A 1990 deed gives land to a fire district "on condition that it be used as a firehouse, and if not, the grantor may re-enter." The district closes the firehouse. Who holds title the next day?
c: The fire district, until the grantor acts to re-enter
The grantor, because title reverted to him automatically
The state, by escheat of the abandoned land
The grantor and the district as tenants in common
questions.x: "On condition that" plus a power to re-enter creates a fee on condition subsequent. A breach gives the grantor a right of re-entry, but the district keeps title until the grantor acts, usually in court. The trap is automatic reversion, which is the rule for a fee simple determinable ("so long as"). Escheat applies when an owner dies without heirs.

questions.q: A 1960 deed gave land to a church on a use condition with a right of re-entry. The grantor's heirs never recorded a preservation declaration. Under New York's RPL 345, what is the likely result?
c: The heirs may re-enter whenever the use condition is broken
The heirs' right of re-entry was extinguished
The church has to buy out the heirs before any other use
The condition converts into a fee simple determinable
questions.x: RPL 345 extinguishes a use condition and its right of re-entry unless a declaration of intention to preserve it is recorded in the statutory window (27 to 30 years after creation) and renewed every 10 years. With no declaration, the heirs lost the right. The trap is the general rule that heirs may re-enter on breach, which is true only while the right survives.

questions.concept: Heirs take as tenants in common
questions.q: A widower in Utica dies without a will, owning his house alone. His three adult daughters inherit. How do they hold title?
c: As joint tenants, since they inherited at the same moment
As tenants in common, one third each
In severalty, through the eldest daughter
As tenants by the entirety, as close family
questions.x: Heirs who inherit together take as tenants in common, here in equal thirds under New York's intestacy statute. The trap is joint tenancy: inheriting at one moment does not create survivorship, which New York requires to be stated expressly. Severalty means one owner, and tenancy by the entirety exists only between spouses.

questions.concept: Heirs take as tenants in common
questions.q: Four siblings inherited a Queens house without a will. One sibling dies, leaving a will that gives everything to her husband. Who owns her share?
c: The other three siblings, by survivorship
Her estate, until the house is sold
The other siblings and her husband equally
Her husband, under her will
questions.x: Inheriting siblings are tenants in common, and a tenant in common's share passes under her will. Her husband takes her quarter. The trap is survivorship, which belongs only to joint tenancy and tenancy by the entirety. The share is administered through her estate, but it belongs to her devisee, not to the house's other owners.

questions.concept: Co-tenant in possession owes no rent
questions.q: Two brothers own a Buffalo house as tenants in common. One lives there; the other lives in Ohio and never asked to move in. Absent an agreement, what does the occupying brother owe for his own use?
c: Nothing, absent an ouster of his brother
Half the fair rental value, from the day he moved in
Half the fair rental value, starting after a written demand
The full rental value, held in trust for both
questions.x: Each tenant in common may possess the whole, so mere occupancy creates no liability for use and occupancy unless there is an agreement or an ouster. The trap is half the rental value: that sounds fair but is not New York's rule. If the occupant collected rent from a third party, he would have to account for the other brother's share.

questions.concept: Co-tenant in possession owes no rent
questions.q: One of three tenants in common lives in their two-family and rents out the other unit. In a later partition accounting, all of the following are likely EXCEPT:
c: She shares the net rent from the rented unit
She gets credit for taxes paid beyond her share
She is not charged for living in her own unit
She owes rent for her own unit at market value
questions.x: Without an ouster or agreement, a co-tenant owes nothing for her own occupancy, so market rent for her unit is the exception. She must share net rent collected from a third party and can recover taxes she paid beyond her share. The trap is treating her like a tenant of her co-owners, which she is not.

questions.concept: Heirs property buyout at court-set value
questions.q: In a partition of heirs property, the court sets the value at $900,000. An investor who bought a 20% share for $50,000 asked for a sale. What must the other co-tenants pay to buy the investor out?
questions.x: Under RPAPL 993 the buyout price is the court-determined value times the share bought: $900,000 x 20% = $180,000. $50,000 is the trap, what the investor paid, which is not the measure in the buyout. $225,000 is 25%, and $300,000 is a third, neither of which matches the investor's share.

questions.concept: Heirs property buyout at court-set value
questions.q: Under New York's heirs property partition rules, a co-tenant asks for a sale. How is the price set if the other co-tenants elect to buy that co-tenant's share?
c: At what the requesting co-tenant paid for the share
At the price a courthouse auction would bring
At the court-determined value times that share
At the assessed value on the town tax roll
questions.x: The court determines the property's value, usually by ordering an appraisal by a disinterested licensed appraiser, and the buyout price is that value times the share being purchased. The trap is the acquisition price, which would let co-tenants buy out an investor at a bargain. Auction prices and assessed values are not the statutory measure.

questions.q: Joint tenants Mia and Rose own a Hudson condo. Mia signs a deed of her interest to herself to end survivorship, but dies before it is recorded. Who owns the condo?
c: Rose alone, by survivorship
Rose and Mia's heirs, half each
Mia's estate until probate ends
Rose and Mia's devisees, as joint tenants
questions.x: Under RPL 240-c, a joint tenant may sever without consent by a deed to herself, but the severance does not defeat the others' survivorship rights unless it is recorded in the county before she dies. Unrecorded, it fails, so Rose owns everything. The trap is the half-and-half answer, which would be right had the deed been recorded in time.

questions.q: Which step lets one New York joint tenant end survivorship on her share without the other joint tenant's consent?
c: Leaving her share to her two children in a will
Mailing the other owner a notice of intent
Asking the assessor to split the tax bill
Recording a deed of her interest to herself
questions.x: RPL 240-c allows a joint tenant to sever unilaterally by a recorded deed to a third person or to herself, or by another written instrument of severance, recorded before death. The trap is the will: survivorship takes effect at the moment of death, so a will cannot carry a joint tenancy share. A notice or a tax bill change conveys nothing.

questions.concept: Creditor of one spouse in a tenancy by the entirety
questions.q: A creditor holds a judgment against Paul alone. Paul and his wife own their Albany home as tenants by the entirety. Paul dies first. What happens to the judgment lien on the house?
c: It continues as a lien against half of the house
It becomes a lien on his wife's whole interest
It has to be paid before his wife can sell the house
It ends, and his wife owns the house free of it
questions.x: A creditor of one spouse can reach only that spouse's interest, which is subject to the other spouse's survivorship right. When Paul dies first, his interest ends and his wife owns the whole house free of his creditor's lien. The trap is that the lien survives on half: entirety property is not divided into halves. His wife was never a judgment debtor.

questions.concept: Creditor of one spouse in a tenancy by the entirety
questions.q: A judgment creditor of only one spouse targets a home held by the entirety. All of the following are true EXCEPT:
c: The lien attaches to the debtor spouse's interest
The creditor cannot defeat the other's survivorship
The creditor can force a partition of the home
The lien is wiped out if the debtor spouse dies first
questions.x: Entirety property cannot be partitioned while the marriage lasts, and a creditor of one spouse cannot force that result either. The other statements are true: the lien attaches to the debtor's interest, survivorship is protected, and the lien ends if the debtor dies first. The trap is treating the home like a tenancy in common, where partition is available.

questions.concept: Divorce converts entirety to tenancy in common
questions.q: A couple owns a Rochester home as tenants by the entirety and divorces. The decree says nothing about the house. How do they now hold it?
c: As tenants in common
As joint tenants
As tenants by the entirety
In severalty by the occupant
questions.x: Divorce ends the unity of marriage, and the former spouses become tenants in common unless the decree provides otherwise. The trap is joint tenancy: survivorship would need an express new conveyance. Entirety cannot exist without a marriage, and staying in the house does not give one ex-spouse title in severalty.

questions.concept: Divorce converts entirety to tenancy in common
questions.q: Former spouses still own their Staten Island house together a year after a divorce that did not address it. The ex-husband dies. Who owns his share?
c: His former wife, by survivorship
His former wife, as the occupant
The court that granted the divorce
His heirs or devisees
questions.x: The divorce turned their tenancy by the entirety into a tenancy in common, so the ex-husband's half passes under his will or by intestacy. The trap is survivorship: it disappeared with the marriage. Occupancy gives no title, and the divorce court holds no ownership interest.

questions.q: A house is held in an irrevocable trust for three beneficiaries. Who signs the listing agreement and the deed?
c: The trustee
The three beneficiaries together
The trustor's executor
Any one beneficiary
questions.x: The trustee holds legal title and exercises the power of sale the trust gives, so the trustee signs. The trap is the beneficiaries: they hold equitable interests and are owed fiduciary duties, but they do not hold title. Property already in a trust is not part of the trustor's probate estate, so an executor has no role.

questions.q: A beneficiary of a family trust that owns a Westchester rental tells the listing agent, "I own a third of that building, so I want the price raised." What does she hold?
c: A one-third interest as a tenant in common
An equitable interest under the trust
Legal title shared with the trustee
A life estate in one third of the units
questions.x: A beneficiary holds an equitable interest: the right to benefit under the trust's terms and to hold the trustee to fiduciary duties. Legal title sits with the trustee, who decides the price. The trap is the tenancy in common, which would be right only after the trustee distributed the building to the beneficiaries in kind.

questions.concept: What transfers in a co-op sale
questions.q: At a Manhattan co-op closing, what does the seller transfer to the buyer?
c: A deed to the unit and its common elements
A deed from the corporation to the buyer
A recorded leasehold estate from the board
Shares and the proprietary lease
questions.x: A co-op owner holds shares in the corporation that owns the building plus a proprietary lease for the apartment, both personal property. The seller assigns them and the corporation issues new ones. The trap is the deed with common elements, which describes a condominium. The corporation's title to the building never changes.

questions.concept: What transfers in a co-op sale
questions.q: A buyer is purchasing a Brooklyn co-op apartment. All of the following describe the interest she acquires EXCEPT:
c: It is personal property, not real property
It includes a proprietary lease for the unit
It is conveyed by a deed recorded to her
It requires the board's consent to transfer
questions.x: Co-op shares and the proprietary lease pass by assignment and new certificates, not by a recorded deed to the shareholder. The other statements are true: the interest is personal property, it includes a proprietary lease, and boards typically must consent. The trap is assuming every apartment purchase involves a deed, as a condo does.

questions.q: A seller paid off his co-op share loan years ago, but a lien search shows the lender's UCC-1 is still of record. What clears it?
c: A satisfaction of mortgage from the lender
A release signed by the co-op board
A UCC-3 termination from the lender
A quitclaim deed back to the seller
questions.x: A co-op loan is secured by the shares and lease through a UCC-1 financing statement, so the lender terminates it with a UCC-3. The trap is a satisfaction of mortgage, the right document for a house or condo loan. The board cannot release a lender's security interest, and no deed is involved in a co-op.

questions.q: Why does a New York co-op purchase loan carry no mortgage recording tax?
c: Shares and a lease are not real property
Co-op buyers are exempt as first-time buyers
The tax is paid by the corporation's mortgage
The lender pays the whole tax at closing
questions.x: Mortgage recording tax applies to mortgages on real property. A co-op loan is secured by personal property (shares and a proprietary lease), filed as a UCC-1, so there is no mortgage to tax. The trap is the corporation's mortgage: the building's underlying mortgage is a separate loan on a separate asset. The tax applies statewide, NYC included.

questions.q: Under New York's Condominium Act, a residential condo board's lien for unpaid common charges ranks:
c: Behind tax liens and the first mortgage of record
Ahead of the first mortgage but behind tax liens
Ahead of every lien, including real property taxes
Equal with the first mortgage, paid pro rata
questions.x: RPL 339-z makes the common charge lien subordinate to tax liens on the unit and to sums unpaid on a first mortgage of record. The trap is "ahead of the first mortgage," which describes the limited super-lien some other states give condo associations. New York allows a superior lien only for exclusively non-residential condominiums whose declaration provides for it.

questions.q: A Long Island City condo unit is sold at foreclosure. Liens: unpaid city taxes, a first mortgage recorded 2019, and the board's common charge lien filed 2025. In what order are they paid?
c: Board lien, taxes, then first mortgage
Taxes, board lien, then first mortgage
First mortgage, taxes, then board lien
Taxes, first mortgage, then board lien
questions.x: Taxes come first, and under RPL 339-z the board's lien also yields to the first mortgage of record, so the board is paid last. The trap is putting the board ahead of the mortgage, the rule in some other states. A mortgage never outranks real property taxes.

questions.q: A condo owner wants to sell his unit but keep his 0.5% interest in the building's common elements, including the roof deck. Can he?
c: No, it stays attached to the unit
Yes, if the board of managers approves it
Yes, if he records a separate deed for it
No, unless the other owners buy it first
questions.x: Under RPL 339-i, the common interest cannot be separated from the unit it belongs to, and common elements stay undivided with no right to partition. The trap is board approval: a board cannot waive the statute. Owners buy a unit and its percentage of the common elements as one package.

questions.q: All of the following are true of a New York condominium unit owner's interest EXCEPT:
c: She owns her unit in fee simple
She owns an undivided share of the common elements
She may sue to partition the lobby and gym
She receives a deed when she buys the unit
questions.x: Common elements remain undivided, and the Condominium Act gives no right to partition them. The rest is true: the unit is owned in fee simple, with an undivided percentage of the common elements, conveyed by deed. The trap is treating the common elements like any tenancy in common, where partition is normally available.

questions.q: An LLC with four members owns a mixed-use building in Astoria. How does the LLC hold title?
c: In severalty
As tenants in common
As joint tenants
In trust for its members
questions.x: An LLC is a separate legal person, so it owns real property alone, in severalty, no matter how many members it has. The members own membership interests, not the building. The trap is tenancy in common, which counts the members as owners of the real estate. An LLC is not a trustee for its members.

questions.q: A corporation with 200 shareholders owns a Syracuse office building. A shareholder dies. What happens to title to the building?
c: Her share of the building passes under her will
Nothing; the corporation owns it in severalty
The other shareholders take her share by survivorship
Title is reconveyed to the remaining shareholders
questions.x: The corporation owns the building in severalty as one legal person. A shareholder owns stock, so her stock passes under her will, but title to the building is unaffected. The trap is that her "share of the building" passes: she never owned any part of the real estate directly. Survivorship and reconveyance do not apply.

questions.q: A roofer finished work on a single-family home in Babylon on April 15 and was not paid. What is the last day to file a mechanic's lien?
c: May 15
August 15
October 15
December 15
questions.x: Under Lien Law section 10, a lien on a single-family dwelling must be filed within 4 months after the last work or materials: April 15 plus 4 months is August 15. December 15 is the trap, the 8-month period for other property such as a multifamily or commercial building. There is no 1-month or 6-month filing rule.

questions.q: An electrician finished rewiring a 12-unit apartment building in the Bronx on January 31 and was not paid. By when must the lien be filed?
c: May 31
July 31
September 30
January 31 of the next year
questions.x: For property other than a single-family dwelling, the deadline is 8 months after the last work, which here is the end of September. May 31 is the trap: 4 months applies only to a single-family dwelling. One year is how long a filed lien lasts before it must be enforced or extended, not the filing deadline.

questions.q: A homeowner wants to close on a sale despite a disputed $45,000 mechanic's lien. What bond amount discharges the lien under New York's Lien Law?
questions.x: An undertaking to discharge a mechanic's lien must be 110% of the lien: $45,000 x 1.10 = $49,500. $45,000 is the trap, the lien with no cushion. $54,000 is 120%, and $90,000 is double, a figure that confuses the bond amount with the worth individual sureties must show.

questions.q: What happens when an owner files and serves a proper bond to discharge a mechanic's lien before closing?
c: The contractor loses its claim for payment
The buyer takes title subject to the lien
The lien shifts from the land to the bond
The closing waits for a court hearing on it
questions.x: A discharge bond substitutes security: the lien no longer burdens the property, and the contractor can still sue and collect from the bond if it wins. The trap is that the contractor loses its claim; the bond protects both sides. Because the land is clear, the buyer takes free of the lien and the closing can go ahead.

questions.q: A money judgment against a Suffolk homeowner was docketed in the county in 2014. It was never renewed or paid. In 2026 the owner sells. What is its effect on the sale?
c: It is still a lien, since judgment liens last 20 years
It is still a lien until the judgment is satisfied
It binds the buyer for 1 year after the closing
It is no longer a lien on the house after 10 years
questions.x: A docketed money judgment is a lien on the debtor's real property in that county for 10 years. Without a renewal judgment, obtained in the final year, the lien ends. The trap is the 20-year answer: the judgment itself may remain enforceable against the debtor personally, but the real property lien has expired. The title company can omit it.

questions.q: A creditor's judgment was docketed against real property 9 years and 6 months ago. What should the creditor do to keep its lien?
c: Nothing, since the lien lasts until the debt is paid
Record a new notice of pendency against the house
Sue for a renewal judgment before 10 years run
Ask the county clerk to re-docket it after 10 years
questions.x: Under CPLR 5014, a judgment creditor may sue for a renewal judgment during the year before the 10-year lien expires, keeping the lien alive. The trap is "nothing": the lien on real property ends at 10 years without renewal. A notice of pendency is not a lien, and simply re-docketing after expiration does not preserve priority.

questions.q: How long is a New York notice of pendency (lis pendens) effective unless a court extends it?
c: 1 year
3 years
10 years
Until the lawsuit ends
questions.x: A notice of pendency is good for 3 years from filing and can be extended by court order for good cause. The trap is "until the lawsuit ends": the notice can lapse while a slow case is still pending. 10 years is the money judgment lien period, and 1 year is how long a mechanic's lien lasts without enforcement.

questions.q: All of the following are true of a New York notice of pendency EXCEPT:
c: Buyers who take after filing are bound by the outcome
It is a lien that secures a money debt
It lasts 3 years unless a court extends it
Every foreclosure action begins with one
questions.x: A notice of pendency is not a lien and secures no debt; it warns that a lawsuit affecting title or possession is pending. The rest is true: later buyers and lenders are bound by the result, it lasts 3 years unless extended, and New York foreclosures start with one. The trap is that it appears on title reports alongside liens.

questions.concept: Property taxes come first in priority
questions.q: A house sells at a foreclosure auction. Liens: a mortgage recorded 2015, a judgment docketed 2019, and unpaid property taxes from 2025. Which is paid first?
c: The 2015 mortgage, as the earliest recorded
The 2019 judgment, as a court order
The 2025 property taxes
The three liens equally, pro rata
questions.x: Real property taxes and special assessments come first regardless of when they arose. After that, liens generally rank by recording or docketing date, so the 2015 mortgage would be next. The trap is the earliest recorded lien: "first in time" orders private liens, but taxes cut the line.

questions.concept: Property taxes come first in priority
questions.q: A first mortgage forecloses, naming every junior lienholder. Which interest survives the referee's sale and binds the auction buyer?
c: A second mortgage recorded after the first
A mechanic's lien filed after the first mortgage
A judgment docketed after the first mortgage
Unpaid real property taxes on the parcel
questions.x: A foreclosure wipes out properly named liens junior to the foreclosing mortgage, but real property taxes are senior to every mortgage, so they survive and the buyer takes subject to them. The trap is a lien with an early date, but these three all came after the first mortgage and are cut off.

questions.concept: Federal tax lien is general and involuntary
questions.q: An IRS lien for unpaid income tax is best classified as:
c: Specific and voluntary
Specific and involuntary
General and voluntary
General and involuntary
questions.x: A federal tax lien arises by law without the taxpayer's consent (involuntary) and attaches to all of the taxpayer's property (general). The trap is specific and involuntary, the classification of property tax liens and mechanic's liens, which attach to one parcel. Voluntary liens, like a mortgage, are ones the owner chooses to give.

questions.concept: Federal tax lien is general and involuntary
questions.q: A title report on a Nassau house lists four liens against the owner. All of the following are general liens EXCEPT:
c: An IRS federal tax lien
A docketed money judgment
A corporation franchise tax lien
A mechanic's lien on one house
questions.x: A mechanic's lien attaches only to the property that was improved, so it is specific. IRS liens, docketed judgments, and corporation franchise tax liens reach all of the debtor's property, so they are general. The trap is the judgment, which some learners call specific because it is filed in one county; it still reaches all the debtor's real property there.

questions.concept: Easement appurtenant runs with the land
questions.q: A Thousand Islands cottage has a recorded right of way across the neighbor's lot to the river. The owner sells, and the new deed does not mention it. Does the buyer have the right of way?
c: Yes, it passes with the dominant land
No, it ended when the deed omitted it
No, unless the neighbor signs a new grant
Yes, for the seller's remaining lifetime
questions.x: An easement appurtenant attaches to the dominant land and transfers with it automatically, even if the new deed is silent. The trap is that the omission ended it: easements end by release, merger, abandonment, or similar events, not by a drafting gap. A personal easement in gross might end with a person, but this one benefits the land.

questions.concept: Easement appurtenant runs with the land
questions.q: A shared driveway easement benefits Lot A and burdens Lot B. All of the following are true EXCEPT:
c: Lot A is the dominant tenement
A sale of Lot B does not end the easement
The easement ends when Lot A is sold
A buyer of Lot A gets the easement
questions.x: An appurtenant easement runs with both parcels: it passes to any buyer of the dominant Lot A and stays as a burden on Lot B when Lot B sells. So a sale of Lot A does not end it. The trap is thinking of the easement as a personal favor to the original owner, which would make it a license.

questions.q: A deed grants a 6-foot footpath easement to the shore of Lake George. The dominant owner wants to pave it and drive his boat trailer down it. What controls?
c: The grant: a footpath permits foot passage
Reasonable use: any access to the lake is allowed
The dominant owner's needs as they change over time
The town's zoning code, which overrides the deed
questions.x: The scope of an express easement is fixed by its terms. A grant for a footpath does not allow vehicles or paving that burdens the servient land more heavily. The trap is "reasonable use," which reads the grant more broadly than the parties wrote it. Zoning can restrict uses further but does not enlarge a private easement.

questions.q: An easement holder wants to use a right of way more heavily than the grant allows. What does he need?
c: Ten years of the heavier use without objection
A new written grant from the servient owner
Approval from the town zoning board of appeals
A survey showing the right of way is wide enough
questions.x: Expanding an express easement requires the servient owner's agreement, best as a recorded written grant. The trap is ten years of heavier use, which might support a separate prescriptive claim only if every element is met, and never if the use is permitted. Zoning boards and surveyors cannot enlarge private property rights.

questions.concept: Nonuse does not abandon a granted easement
questions.q: A recorded right of way created by deed in 1975 has not been used for 20 years. Under New York law, is it abandoned?
c: Yes, 10 years of nonuse ends any easement
Yes, 20 years of nonuse ends a deeded easement
No, deeded easements last forever in every case
No, nonuse alone does not show intent
questions.x: Abandoning an easement created by grant requires intent to abandon plus a clear act showing it; mere nonuse, however long, is not enough. The trap is the 10-year answer, which borrows the adverse possession and prescription period. Deeded easements are not permanent in every case: they can end by release, merger, or the servient owner's adverse use.

questions.concept: Nonuse does not abandon a granted easement
questions.q: Which fact would best support a claim that the holder abandoned a deeded right of way?
c: The path has been overgrown for 15 years
The holder walled it off and moved his entrance
The holder used a more convenient route with permission
The holder's deed did not mention the right of way
questions.x: Abandonment needs intent shown by a clear act. Building a permanent wall across the way and relocating the entrance is the kind of act that shows it. The trap is the 15 years of overgrowth: nonuse alone does not abandon a granted easement. Using another route by permission and a silent deed show nothing about intent.

questions.q: For 18 years, a neighbor has walked across a Saratoga lot to reach a trail. The owner's late father gave her written permission at the start. Does she have an easement by prescription?
c: Yes, 18 years exceeds the 10-year period
Yes, if she can tack an earlier owner's use
No, because her use was not exclusive
No, the use was permissive, not hostile
questions.x: Prescription requires use that is hostile, meaning without permission, plus open, notorious, and continuous for 10 years. Written permission makes the use permissive, so the clock never started. The trap is the 18 years. Exclusivity is an adverse possession element, not a prescription element, so that wrong answer gives the wrong reason.

questions.q: A homeowner tells a neighbor he may park his camper on her side yard every winter. Twelve winters later, what right does the neighbor have?
c: An easement by prescription
An easement by implication
A revocable license
Title by adverse possession
questions.x: Oral permission to use land creates a license, a personal privilege revocable at will. Because the use was permitted, it was never hostile, so no amount of time turns it into a prescriptive easement or adverse possession. The trap is prescription, which looks right if you count only the years. Implication requires a prior use when one owner split a parcel.

questions.q: A Delaware County farmer sells the back 20 acres of his farm, which has no road frontage except across the farm. The deed says nothing about access. What does the buyer most likely have?
c: An easement by necessity over the farm
An easement by prescription after 10 years
A license the farmer can revoke
No access unless he buys a right of way
questions.x: When an owner splits a parcel and leaves one piece landlocked, the law implies an easement by necessity over the land retained. The trap is "no access": the silent deed is the very situation the doctrine addresses. Prescription would need hostile use for 10 years, and a license depends on permission the law does not require here.

questions.q: A landlocked parcel's owner holds an easement by necessity across a neighbor's land. The county then builds a road along the parcel's back line. What happens to the easement?
c: It continues forever as an appurtenance
It becomes an easement in gross
It ends because the necessity ended
It continues until released by recorded deed
questions.x: An easement by necessity lasts only as long as the necessity that created it. Once the parcel has public road access, the easement ends without any release. The trap is "forever as an appurtenance": most express easements do not end this way, but necessity easements are tied to the landlocked condition.

questions.q: A Westchester neighbor's hedge and garden shed have sat 3 feet over the line for 14 years. Can the neighbor claim the strip by adverse possession?
c: Yes, 14 years is more than the 10-year period
Yes, but just the area under the shed
No, hedges and sheds count as permissive
No, adverse possession needs 20 years
questions.x: RPAPL 543 treats de minimis non-structural encroachments, including fences, hedges, shrubbery, plantings, sheds, and non-structural walls, as permissive and non-adverse. Without hostility, there is no adverse possession. The trap is counting years past 10. The 20-year figure is not New York's period; it is 10 years statewide.

questions.q: Under New York's 2008 adverse possession amendments, all of the following are deemed permissive EXCEPT:
c: A wire fence over the line
Mowing a neighbor's lawn strip
A garage built over the line
A row of hedges over the line
questions.x: RPAPL 543 covers de minimis non-structural encroachments (fences, hedges, plantings, sheds, non-structural walls) and lawn mowing or similar maintenance. A garage is a structure, so it can still support an adverse possession claim if the other elements, including claim of right, are met. The trap is the fence, which feels substantial but is listed as permissive.

questions.q: A deed for a lot in Ulster County calls for a course “210 feet to a stone wall.” A new survey finds the wall 204 feet from the prior corner. Where is the boundary?
c: At 210 feet, the measured distance
At the stone wall, 204 feet out
At 207 feet, halfway between the two
At the line shown on the county tax map
questions.x: When a monument and a distance conflict, the monument controls, so the wall is the line. The 210-foot figure is the trap: numbers in old deeds are the part most likely to be mistaken, while the wall is physically on the ground.

questions.q: In a metes and bounds description, which usually controls when a stated distance conflicts with a monument named in the same call?
c: The stated distance
The direction of the course
The monument
The acreage recited at the end
questions.x: Monuments (pipes, walls, trees, street lines) control over distances and over the total acreage recital. The distance is the trap: it seems precise, but courts trust the marker that was set on the ground.

questions.q: A son holds his mother's New York statutory short form power of attorney with no gift provisions. He wants to sign a deed giving her Rochester house to himself for $1. What is the problem?
c: The deed needs both his and his mother's signatures
A power of attorney cannot be used to sign a deed
The deed needs prior approval from the Surrogate's Court
Gifts need express gift authority in the document
questions.x: New York agents may sell for value under real estate powers, but gifts, especially to the agent, require express gift authority in the document. Saying a POA can never sign a deed is the trap: agents sign deeds all the time on arm's length sales.

questions.q: Under New York law, an agent acting under a power of attorney may transfer the principal's real property to the agent as a gift only if:
c: the document expressly authorizes gifts
the agent is the principal's spouse or child
the transfer tax return is filed
the principal is over 80 years old
questions.x: Gift authority must be expressly granted. Without it the agent may manage and sell, not give away. Being the principal's child is the trap: family status adds no authority, and self-gifts draw the most scrutiny.

questions.q: A Syracuse widow signs and acknowledges a deed of her house to her niece, then locks it in her desk, telling a friend the niece should get it after she dies. She dies a year later. Who owns the house?
c: The niece, because the deed was signed and acknowledged by the widow
The niece, once the deed is recorded
The widow's estate, because the deed was never delivered
The friend, who witnessed her intent
questions.x: A deed passes title only on delivery with present intent to transfer. Keeping it to take effect at death is a failed will, so the house is in the estate. Acknowledgment is the trap: it allows recording, but it is not delivery.

questions.q: Between a grantor and a grantee, ownership of land passes at the moment the deed is:
c: signed by the grantor
acknowledged before a notary
recorded with the county clerk
delivered and accepted
questions.x: Delivery with intent to pass title now, plus acceptance, transfers ownership. Recording is the trap: it protects the grantee against third parties but happens after title has already passed.

questions.q: A signed and delivered deed of a Bronx two-family has no notary acknowledgment. Which statement is correct?
c: It is valid between the parties but cannot be recorded
It is void and has to be signed again from the very start
It can be recorded if two witnesses also sign it
It is valid against later good faith buyers alone
questions.x: Acknowledgment is a condition of recording, not of validity between grantor and grantee. Calling the deed void is the trap; the grantor can acknowledge later and the deed then records.

questions.q: All of the following are true of an acknowledgment EXCEPT:
c: it is made by the grantor before a notary or similar officer
it is required before a deed can be recorded
it is what makes the deed valid between the parties
it confirms the signature was the grantor's voluntary act
questions.x: Validity between the parties comes from a signed writing, delivery, and acceptance. Acknowledgment serves recording. The recording choice is a true statement, which is why it tempts test-takers who misread EXCEPT.

questions.q: A Brooklyn father deeds his mortgage-free condo to his daughter as a gift. No money changes hands. What transfer tax result is correct?
c: No tax is due, but the returns are still filed
Tax is due on the condo's current assessed value
The daughter pays the NYC RPTT as the grantee
No tax is due and no returns need to be filed
questions.x: NYS and NYC transfer taxes are measured by consideration, and a true gift with no debt has none. The returns are still required to record. Skipping the returns is the trap: NYC requires the RPT return even when the tax is zero.

questions.q: New York State real estate transfer tax is computed on:
c: the assessed value of the property
the consideration paid for the conveyance
the market value in the most recent appraisal
the amount of the buyer's new mortgage
questions.x: The tax is $2 per $500 of consideration. Market value is the trap: a gift between relatives with no consideration owes no tax even if the house is worth a lot.

questions.q: Where is a deed to a house in Flushing, Queens recorded?
c: The Queens County Clerk's Office
The NYS Department of State
The Surrogate's Court for Queens County
The NYC Office of the City Register
questions.x: Deeds for Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens are recorded with the City Register through ACRIS. The Queens County Clerk is the trap: county clerks record deeds outside NYC and on Staten Island, not in Queens.

questions.q: A deed to a house in Tottenville, Staten Island is recorded with:
c: the NYC Office of the City Register
the Richmond County Clerk
the NYC Department of Buildings
the NYS Department of Taxation
questions.x: Staten Island is the exception: deeds there record with the Richmond County Clerk. The City Register is the trap because it records for the other four boroughs.

questions.q: A Forest Hills seller conveys by bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts. A year later, a judgment against the owner before her turns out to be an unpaid lien. Can the buyer recover from the seller on the deed?
c: Yes, because every deed warrants the entire chain
Yes, for liens recorded within the last 10 years
No, the defect arose before her ownership
No, because no deed covenant survives the closing
questions.x: The covenant against grantor's acts reaches only liens and defects the seller created or allowed. A prior owner's judgment is outside it, so the buyer turns to title insurance. The whole-chain answer describes the full covenant and warranty deed.

questions.q: The deed most commonly used in New York residential sales, in which the seller promises only that she has not encumbered the property, is the:
c: full covenant and warranty deed
bargain and sale with covenant
quitclaim deed with release
referee's deed from a court sale
questions.x: The bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts is the New York standard. The full covenant and warranty deed is the trap: it gives more promises, covering the whole chain, and is rare downstate.

questions.q: An executor selling a decedent's Albany house proves authority to sign the deed with:
c: letters of administration
a certificate of occupancy
a power of attorney from the heirs
letters testamentary
questions.x: The Surrogate's Court issues letters testamentary to an executor named in a probated will. Letters of administration are the trap: they go to an administrator when the decedent left no will.

questions.q: A will names a daughter as executor and gives her power to sell the house. Her two brothers inherit with her. Who signs the deed to the buyer?
c: The daughter, as executor, under her letters
The three children together, as devisees
The Surrogate's Court judge who issued letters
The estate's attorney, as agent for the heirs
questions.x: With letters testamentary and a power of sale, the executor signs an executor's deed. Having all three children sign is the trap: it is unnecessary when the will gives the executor power to sell.

questions.q: A home equity lender holding a second mortgage forecloses on a Queens house. The first mortgage is not part of the action. The auction buyer takes title:
c: free of both mortgages
subject to the first mortgage
subject to both mortgages
free of the first mortgage alone
questions.x: Foreclosure cuts off the foreclosing lien and interests junior to it, not senior liens. The buyer owns the house subject to the first mortgage. Free of both is the trap: a foreclosure sale does not wipe out liens with higher priority.

questions.q: All of the following are true of a referee's deed in a New York foreclosure EXCEPT:
c: it is signed by a court-appointed referee after the auction
the referee makes no personal covenants about the title
it results from involuntary alienation of the owner's title
it conveys free of liens senior to the one foreclosed
questions.x: A referee's deed does not cut off senior liens; the buyer takes subject to them. The other statements are true. The no-covenants statement tempts readers who think a court sale carries a court warranty.

questions.concept: Quitclaim does not release the note
questions.q: In a divorce, a husband quitclaims his interest in the marital home in Islip to his wife. The mortgage is in both names. What is his status on the loan?
c: Still liable until released
Released, since he owns no interest
Released once the deed is recorded
Liable for exactly half the balance
questions.x: The deed transfers title; the note is a separate promise to the lender, who is not a party to the deed. He stays liable until the lender releases him or the loan is refinanced. Recording the deed is the trap: it gives notice of the transfer, not a release.

questions.concept: Quitclaim does not release the note
questions.q: A quitclaim deed conveys:
c: full title with a warranty against every claim
title warranted against the grantor's own acts
whatever interest the grantor has, if any
a life estate in the property to the grantee
questions.x: A quitclaim makes no promises. If the grantor owns nothing, nothing passes. The grantor's-own-acts answer is the trap: that describes a bargain and sale deed with covenant.

questions.q: A full covenant and warranty deed is delivered for a Saratoga County farm. An unsatisfied 1985 mortgage was of record at the time. Which covenant was breached at delivery?
c: Seizin and right to convey
Quiet enjoyment
Further assurance
Against encumbrances
questions.x: The covenant against encumbrances promises no liens except those listed, and the old mortgage existed at delivery. Seizin is the trap: it promises ownership, which the seller had despite the lien.

questions.q: A grantor's promise to sign any document reasonably needed to perfect the grantee's title is the covenant of:
c: further assurance
seizin and right to convey
warranty forever
quiet enjoyment
questions.x: Further assurance is the promise to do the paperwork that fixes title. Warranty forever is the trap: it is the promise to defend the grantee against lawful claims.

questions.q: The Lien Law covenant found in New York deeds requires the seller to:
c: warrant title against prior owners' liens
record the deed within 30 days after the closing date
use sale money first to pay recent improvement costs
deliver a survey showing no encroachments
questions.x: Lien Law Section 13 makes the sale proceeds a trust fund for improvement costs, which the seller must pay before using the money for anything else. The warranty answer is the trap: that is the full covenant and warranty deed's promise.

questions.q: A Bay Ridge seller owes her roofer $9,000 for work finished last month and plans to use her sale proceeds for a new condo. Under her deed's Lien Law covenant, she must:
c: give the buyer a $9,000 credit
pay the roofer from the proceeds
pay the roofer within 4 months
disclose the debt but need not pay it
questions.x: The covenant makes the proceeds a trust fund to pay the cost of the improvement first. The credit answer is the trap: the obligation is the seller's, not something to pass to the buyer.

questions.q: A Buffalo widower dies without a will. He had two children; one died earlier, leaving three children. How is his house divided?
c: One-quarter to each of the four living descendants
One-half to the living child, one-sixth to each grandchild
The whole house to the living child
One-third to the living child, two-ninths to each grandchild
questions.x: Children take by family line. The living child takes one-half; the predeceased child's half is split among his three children, one-sixth each. Equal quarters is the trap: representation divides by branch first, not per head.

questions.q: Under New York intestacy, when a decedent leaves no spouse but leaves children and the children of a child who died earlier, the grandchildren:
c: take nothing, since their parent died first
take equal shares with the living children
inherit if the court approves
share their parent's portion
questions.x: Grandchildren of a predeceased child step into that child's share by representation. Taking nothing is the trap: a predeceased child's line is not cut off when it has descendants.

questions.q: An unwitnessed will, written entirely in the testator's handwriting by a civilian in Westchester, is:
c: not valid in New York
valid, as a holographic will
valid if notarized afterward
valid for real property alone
questions.x: New York requires two attesting witnesses. Unwitnessed holographic wills are valid only for armed forces members in wartime and mariners at sea. Calling it a valid holographic will is the trap: other states allow that, New York does not.

questions.q: A Queens woman signs a typed will at the end in front of one witness, who signs. She dies. What controls who inherits her house?
c: The will, because it is typed and signed
The witness, who may choose among the heirs
Intestacy, since it lacks a second witness
The will, if the Surrogate's Court finds it fair
questions.x: A New York will needs at least two witnesses. With one, it fails, and intestacy applies. The typed-and-signed answer is the trap: signature alone is not enough.

questions.q: A Utica owner dies without a will, leaving three adult children and one minor grandchild as heirs. Who can sign a deed conveying the entire house?
c: The oldest adult child
The three adult children together
An executor named by the family
A court-appointed administrator
questions.x: With no will, the Surrogate's Court issues letters of administration to an administrator, who can convey the whole property. The adult children together cannot convey the minor's share, which is the trap.

questions.q: When a Utica man dies intestate, the Surrogate's Court appoints a fiduciary to settle his estate. That person is called the:
c: executor
administrator
guardian ad litem
testamentary trustee
questions.x: Administrator = no will, appointed by the court. Executor is the trap: an executor is named in a will.

questions.q: Two sisters inherit a Kingston house as tenants in common. One lives there alone for 11 years after the death, paying all costs. Has she acquired her sister's share by adverse possession?
c: Yes, after 10 years of exclusive possession
Yes, because she paid every tax bill
No, the co-tenant presumption applies
No, because heirs cannot adversely possess
questions.x: RPAPL 541 presumes one co-tenant's possession benefits all for 10 years of exclusive occupancy; only then can adverse possession begin, so about 20 years in all. The 10-year answer is the trap: it ignores the co-tenant presumption.

questions.q: All of the following weaken an heir's claim to own a family house by adverse possession against co-heirs EXCEPT:
c: his occupancy has been open and visible
he lived there earlier with the owner's permission
the other heirs are his co-tenants
less than 20 years have passed since the death
questions.x: Open and notorious use is one element of adverse possession, so it helps rather than hurts. Permissive use and co-tenancy both defeat or delay the claim, and the co-tenant rule stretches the period to about 20 years.

questions.q: Which transfer is an example of involuntary alienation?
c: An owner selling a house by bargain and sale deed
A county taking title by tax foreclosure
A testator leaving a house to her son by will
A developer dedicating a street to the town
questions.x: Tax foreclosure transfers title without the owner's consent. A will is the trap: it transfers at death, but the owner chose it, so it is voluntary alienation.

questions.q: All of the following are involuntary alienation EXCEPT:
c: a court-ordered partition sale
an in rem tax foreclosure
a gift deed to a grandchild
condemnation by eminent domain
questions.x: A gift deed is a voluntary transfer the owner chooses. Partition is the tempting distractor, but it is involuntary for the co-owner forced to sell.

questions.q: A Rochester man's will devises a cottage “to my brother Sam.” Sam dies before him, leaving a daughter. The will says nothing else about it. Who takes the cottage?
c: Sam's daughter
The residuary beneficiary
Sam's estate
The State of New York
questions.x: New York's anti-lapse statute saves a gift to the testator's sibling or descendant who dies first leaving issue; it passes to that issue. Sam's estate is the trap: the gift goes directly to his issue, not through his estate.

questions.q: Real property is transferred to the State of New York when a person dies:
c: with a will that names a person who died first
with debts larger than the estate
owning land in more than one county
intestate with no distributees
questions.x: Escheat applies only when there is no valid will and no distributees. A lapsed gift is the trap: it passes to the residuary beneficiary, to issue under anti-lapse, or by intestacy, not to the state.

questions.q: A title report on a Staten Island house shows a 2006 mortgage the seller says was paid in 2012. No satisfaction was recorded. What clears it?
c: The passage of time; it lapsed after 10 years
A deed from the seller to the buyer with full warranties
A satisfaction from the lender or its successor
The buyer's owner's policy, without any further action
questions.x: A mortgage remains of record until a satisfaction is recorded, so the seller's side obtains one from the lender or its successor. The owner's policy is the trap: unless the item is removed, the policy lists it as an exception and does not cover it.

questions.q: An open mortgage the seller is paying off at closing is handled by:
c: a payoff from sale proceeds
the buyer assuming the seller's loan
a quitclaim deed from the lender
an escrow held for one full year
questions.x: The seller's attorney gets a payoff letter, and the payoff is paid from the seller's proceeds at closing; the lender then records a satisfaction. Assumption is the trap: it is a different deal structure that needs the lender's consent.

questions.q: A lender's title insurance policy protects:
c: the buyer, up to the purchase price
the buyer and lender equally
the seller against later claims
the lender, up to the loan amount
questions.x: The loan policy runs to the lender and declines as the loan is repaid. Protecting both equally is the trap: the buyer needs a separate owner's policy.

questions.q: A cash buyer of a Yonkers condo skips an owner's policy. A forged deed in the chain appears two years later. Who covers her loss?
c: The seller's title insurer
No insurer; she has no policy
The lender's title insurer
The county clerk who recorded it
questions.x: With no owner's policy and no loan, no title insurer protects her. The seller's old policy is the trap: it protected the seller while the seller owned the property, not the next buyer.

questions.q: Two days before closing, a borrower switches from a 30-year fixed loan to an adjustable rate loan. What must happen?
c: A new 3-business-day waiting period
Close as scheduled with a corrected disclosure
A new 7-day Loan Estimate period
A 30-day delay to re-underwrite
questions.x: A change in loan product requires a new Closing Disclosure and a new 3-business-day wait. Closing on schedule is the trap: most minor changes allow that, but a product change does not.

questions.q: All of the following restart the 3-business-day Closing Disclosure waiting period EXCEPT:
c: an APR increase beyond tolerance
adding a prepayment penalty
a $300 change in the title fee
a change in the loan product
questions.x: Only three changes restart the clock: APR beyond tolerance, loan product, and an added prepayment penalty. Fee changes are fixed with a corrected disclosure. The APR choice tempts readers who think every cost change counts.

questions.q: Why does a New York title closer run a final continuation search on the day of closing?
c: To confirm the appraisal value
To catch newly recorded liens
To verify the buyer's income
To reset the proration date
questions.x: Under the race-notice recording act, anything recorded before the deed would bind the buyer, so the closer brings the search to the moment of closing. The appraisal answer is the trap: that is the lender's valuation, unrelated to title.

questions.q: A judgment against a Bronx seller is docketed four days after the title report but before closing. The closer's rundown finds it. What happens?
c: It is ignored because it came after the report
The buyer assumes it as part of the price
It attaches only to the seller's next property
It must be paid or cleared from proceeds
questions.x: A judgment docketed before the deed records is a lien on the seller's interest, so it must be paid or cleared from the proceeds. Ignoring it because it is newer than the report is the trap: that is exactly what the rundown is for.

questions.concept: Power of attorney ends at death
questions.q: A seller's agent under a power of attorney signs the deed at a Queens closing. Unknown to everyone, the seller died the night before. What is the effect?
c: The deed is valid if the agent acted in good faith
The deed is valid once it is recorded
The deed conveys nothing; title is in the estate
The deed converts into an executor's deed
questions.x: A power of attorney ends at the principal's death, so the agent had no authority and the property belongs to the estate. Good faith is the trap: it does not create authority that ended at death.

questions.concept: Power of attorney ends at death
questions.q: An agent's authority under a power of attorney ends:
c: when the deed is recorded
after one year
when the agent moves away
at the principal's death
questions.x: Death of the principal ends the agency. One year is the trap: New York powers of attorney do not expire on a fixed timetable unless the document says so.

questions.q: At the walk-through, a buyer finds an included washer and dryer missing. What is the best step for the buyer's agent?
c: Notify both attorneys before closing
Tell the buyer to close and sue later
Advise the buyer to cancel the deal
Agree a credit directly with the seller
questions.x: The agent reports it to the attorneys, who can arrange a return, credit, or escrow at closing. Agreeing on a credit directly with the seller is the trap: contract changes go through the attorneys who drafted the deal.

questions.q: The main purpose of the final walk-through is to confirm that the property:
c: appraises at the contract price
is in contract condition
has passed a home inspection
has no title defects
questions.x: The walk-through checks condition, vacancy, and included items just before closing. The home inspection is the trap: it happens before contract or during the contingency period, not at the walk-through.

questions.q: A seller collected $3,600 of June rent on June 1. Closing is June 21, and the buyer owns closing day. Using actual days, what is the entry?
c: Debit seller, credit buyer $1,200
Credit seller, debit buyer $1,200
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,080
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,320
questions.x: June has 30 days; the buyer owns June 21 to 30, 10 days. $3,600 / 30 x 10 = $1,200, debit seller and credit buyer because the seller holds it. Crediting the seller is the trap: collecting rent does not make the buyer's days the seller's.

questions.q: Rent collected in advance by the seller for the month of closing is shown on the closing statement as:
c: a credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer
a debit to both the buyer and the seller
a seller debit and a buyer credit
a credit to the buyer, with no seller entry
questions.x: The seller holds rent covering the buyer's days, so the seller is debited and the buyer credited the same amount. The reverse is the trap: it is the entry for something the seller prepaid, such as taxes.
