questions.q: When a Bronx building with tenants is sold, the seller's obligations for the tenants' security deposits end when the seller:
c: records the deed with the City Register
deposits them with the court that oversees the sale
returns them to the tenants before closing
transfers them and mails tenants certified notice
questions.x: GOL 7-105 requires turnover to the new owner at closing or within 5 days and notice to each tenant by registered or certified mail. Returning them to tenants is the trap: the leases continue, so the deposits move to the buyer.

questions.q: A seller holds $7,200 in tenant security deposits at closing. Which entry is correct?
c: Credit seller and debit buyer $7,200
Debit seller, credit buyer $7,200
No entry; the seller keeps them
Debit buyer $7,200, no seller entry
questions.x: The buyer takes over the duty to return the deposits, so the money moves to her: debit seller, credit buyer. Crediting the seller is the trap: the deposits were never the seller's income.

questions.q: Annual NYC taxes are $7,300, billed quarterly. The seller paid the October to December quarter. Closing is December 10 and the buyer owns closing day. Using a 365-day year, what is the entry?
c: Credit seller, debit buyer $440
Debit seller, credit buyer $440
Credit seller, debit buyer $420
Debit seller, credit buyer $1,400
questions.x: Daily rate $7,300 / 365 = $20. The buyer's days are December 10 to 31, 22 days: $440, credit seller and debit buyer because the seller prepaid. Debiting the seller is the trap: that is the entry for unpaid taxes.

questions.q: Real estate taxes the seller paid in advance for a period extending past closing are entered as:
c: a debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer
a seller credit and a buyer debit
a credit to both parties
an entry for the seller alone
questions.x: The buyer reimburses the seller for the buyer's share of the prepaid period. Debit seller, credit buyer is the trap: it applies when taxes are unpaid and the buyer will pay them later.

questions.q: A Queens two-family sells for $1,400,000. What are the seller's total transfer taxes (NYS plus NYC RPTT)?
questions.x: NYS 0.4% = $5,600; NYC RPTT 1.425% (residential over $500,000) = $19,950; total $25,550. $19,950 alone is the trap: it forgets the state tax. $39,550 adds the buyer's $14,000 mansion tax.

questions.q: A Manhattan condo sells for $1,900,000. How much mansion tax is due, and who pays it?
c: $23,750, paid by the buyer
$19,000, paid by the seller
$19,000, paid by the buyer
$23,750, paid by the seller
questions.x: From $1,000,000 to under $2,000,000 the rate is 1% on the whole price: $19,000, paid by the buyer. $23,750 is the trap: 1.25% applies only from $2,000,000 to under $3,000,000.

questions.q: A buyer borrows $800,000 to buy a Brooklyn condo. What mortgage recording tax does the borrower pay?
questions.x: For NYC 1 to 3 family homes and condos with loans of $500,000 or more, the borrower pays 1.925%: $15,400. $17,400 is the trap: it is the combined 2.175% that includes the lender's 0.25%. $14,400 uses the under-$500,000 rate of 1.8%.

questions.q: A buyer finances a Manhattan co-op purchase with a $900,000 share loan. How much mortgage recording tax is due?
questions.x: A co-op share loan is secured by shares and a proprietary lease, not a recorded mortgage on real property, so no mortgage recording tax applies. $17,325 is the trap: it applies the condo rate of 1.925%.

questions.q: On a closing statement, buyer debits total $812,400 and buyer credits total $664,900, including a $70,000 deposit and a $580,000 loan. How much cash does the buyer bring to closing?
questions.x: Cash to close equals buyer debits minus buyer credits: $812,400 minus $664,900 = $147,500. $217,500 is the trap: it double counts by leaving the deposit out of the credits, though the buyer already paid it.

questions.q: On a closing statement, the buyer's earnest money deposit appears as:
c: a debit to the buyer only
a credit to the buyer only
a credit to the seller only
a debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer
questions.x: The deposit is part of the price the buyer already paid, so it is a buyer credit only; the seller already has full credit for the price. Debit seller, credit buyer is the trap: it would charge the seller for money that was always part of what she is paid.

questions.q: A Yonkers contract set closing "on or about May 1." The buyer adjourned twice. On June 2 the seller's attorney sends a letter setting June 23, stating that time is of the essence and that failure to close will be a default. Which statement is accurate?
c: The letter has no effect unless the buyer countersigns and returns it
The letter can make June 23 binding if three weeks is reasonable
The letter is void because the contract set May 1
The letter binds the buyer but leaves the seller free to adjourn
questions.x: New York lets a party make time of the essence after the original date passes with a clear, unequivocal notice that sets a reasonable date and warns of default; reasonableness is a fact question, and three weeks usually qualifies. The countersignature answer is the trap: no agreement is needed once the other side has had a reasonable adjournment.

questions.q: A seller's attorney sends a proper time of the essence letter setting a closing date. On that date the buyer is ready, but the seller cannot deliver insurable title. Who is in default?
c: The buyer, because the letter set a deadline for the buyer to perform
Neither party, because the seller is entitled to one more adjournment
The seller, because the date is of the essence for both parties
Neither party, because the original contract date is the one binding date
questions.x: A time of the essence date binds both sides. A seller who sets the date and then cannot deliver the title the contract promises is the party in default. The adjournment answer is the trap: reasonable adjournments are available only while time is not of the essence; the notice ended that.

questions.q: A New York residential contract says closing will occur "on or about" a stated date. If the buyer asks for a two-week delay to finish an open permit issue, the seller generally:
c: Must allow a reasonable adjournment
May keep the deposit as liquidated damages
May terminate the contract without notice
Must refund the deposit and end the deal
questions.x: "On or about" means the date is not of the essence, so either party is entitled to a reasonable adjournment and a short delay is not a default. The deposit answer is the trap: liquidated damages follow a default, and missing a non-essential date is not one.

questions.q: All of the following are ways a closing date can become of the essence in New York EXCEPT:
c: The contract says time is of the essence for that date
The parties sign an amendment making a new date of the essence
One party sends a clear notice setting a reasonable new date and warning of default
The seller writes "firm date" on the closing date line of the listing agreement
questions.x: Time becomes of the essence by contract language, by written agreement, or by a proper unilateral notice after the original date passes. A listing agreement is between the seller and the broker; it does not bind the buyer to anything. The unilateral-notice choice is the tempting wrong pick, but it is a recognized method when the notice is clear, reasonable, and warns of default.

questions.q: A day before a Queens closing, the rundown shows a notice of pendency filed in a suit claiming an interest in the house. If the buyer closes anyway, the buyer:
c: Takes free of the suit because the contract predates it
Takes free of the suit if the title policy is issued
Is bound by the judgment as if a party to the suit
Is bound just if the seller loses and cannot pay
questions.x: A filed notice of pendency is constructive notice. Anyone who takes title or a mortgage afterward is bound by the outcome of the action as if they had been a party, and the title company will except it. The contract-date answer is the trap: an unrecorded contract does not give the buyer priority over a recorded notice.

questions.q: A seller asks the title closer to "pay off" a notice of pendency so the closing can proceed. Which response is correct?
c: It has no payoff; the plaintiff or a court must cancel it
It can be paid from proceeds at its face amount plus interest
It can be bonded at 110% under the Lien Law like a contractor's lien
It expires on its own once the deed is delivered and accepted
questions.x: A notice of pendency is not a lien and states no amount. It comes off by the plaintiff's cancellation, a court order, or expiration after three years if not extended. The 110% bond answer is the trap: that is the Lien Law method for a mechanic's lien. A court may cancel a notice on an undertaking under CPLR 6515, but only on motion.

questions.q: Under the CPLR, the court must cancel a notice of pendency on an aggrieved party's motion when:
c: The defendant shows a strong defense on the merits
The summons is not served within 30 days
The property is under contract to a third party
The notice has been on file for more than one year
questions.x: CPLR 6512 makes a notice effective only if the summons is served within 30 days after filing, and CPLR 6514(a) requires cancellation if it is not. Other mandatory grounds include settlement, discontinuance, or a final judgment against the plaintiff. The merits answer is the trap: a defense is litigated in the case; bad faith is a discretionary ground.

questions.q: A notice of pendency can come off the record in each of the following ways EXCEPT:
c: The plaintiff discontinues the lawsuit and the court cancels it
The court cancels it because adequate relief can be secured by an undertaking
The seller pays the claimed amount to the county clerk at closing
The three-year term runs out without the plaintiff obtaining an extension
questions.x: A notice of pendency is cancelled after discontinuance or settlement, by court order on an undertaking under CPLR 6515, or it lapses after three years unless extended. Paying money to the clerk is how some liens are discharged, not how notice of a lawsuit is removed. The undertaking choice looks wrong but is a real CPLR route.

questions.q: A contractor files an $18,000 mechanic's lien against a Nassau one-family a week before closing, and the seller disputes the bill. Which step lets the sale close without resolving the dispute?
c: Asking the county clerk to strike the lien for defective work
Closing subject to the lien and letting the buyer handle it
Paying the contractor half and escrowing the other half
Filing a bond for 110% of the lien under the Lien Law
questions.x: Lien Law section 19 lets the owner discharge a mechanic's lien by filing a bond or undertaking for 110% of the lien; title companies may also insure over it with an escrow. The dispute then moves to the bond. The clerk answer is the trap: the clerk records liens and has no power to judge the work.

questions.q: A mechanic's lien was filed on a house in March 2026. The contractor never sues to foreclose and gets no extension. What happens in March 2027?
c: The lien lapses after one year
The lien becomes a judgment for ten years
The lien shifts to the owner's other property
The lien renews for a second year automatically
questions.x: A mechanic's lien on private property lasts one year from filing unless an action to foreclose it is started or an extension is obtained. Otherwise it lapses. The judgment answer is the trap: ten years is the life of a docketed money judgment, which the contractor would have to win in a lawsuit first.

questions.q: Under the inability-to-convey clause common in New York residential contracts, a buyer whose seller cannot deliver insurable title generally recovers:
c: The deposit plus the lost value of the bargain
The deposit, with no costs reimbursed
The deposit plus a commission refund from the broker
The deposit plus net title and survey costs
questions.x: The typical clause limits the buyer's remedy to a refund of the down payment and the net cost of title examination and survey, unless the seller willfully caused the defect. The benefit-of-the-bargain answer is the trap: that is a damages measure the clause is written to exclude.

questions.q: A seller signs a contract, then lets her own lender record a new $200,000 mortgage she cannot pay off, so title cannot close clear. The buyer's remedy is most likely:
c: Limited to the deposit and title costs under the contract
Not limited, because the seller caused the defect willfully
Limited to the deposit, since the lender is a third party
Nothing, because the seller may sell subject to any mortgage
questions.x: Inability-to-convey clauses protect a seller who cannot cure a defect in good faith. They do not protect a seller who willfully creates the defect, so the buyer may pursue fuller remedies such as specific performance or damages. The limitation answer is the trap: it is right for a third party's filing, wrong when the seller made the problem.

cram.html: Land + man-made attachments = real estate; + bundle of rights = real property. Bundle: Possession, Control, Enjoyment, Exclusion, Disposition.
Fixture tests MARIA; a written agreement beats all; intention is the key test otherwise. Trade fixtures stay the tenant's if removed before the lease ends.
Emblements (annual crops) are personal property. Riparian = rivers; littoral = lakes and oceans.
"So long as" = fee simple determinable, automatic reversion. "But if" = fee on condition, grantor must act (right of re-entry).
Life tenant can convey only a life estate. Remainder goes to a third party; reversion goes back to the grantor. Damage by the life tenant = waste.
NY abolished dower and curtesy. Surviving spouse's elective share: greater of $50,000 or 1/3 of the net estate.
Leaseholds: years (fixed end date, any length), periodic (renews), at will (consent, no term), sufferance (holdover without consent).
Severalty = ONE owner (including a corporation or LLC).
NY defaults: unmarried co-owners = tenants in common; spouses = tenants by the entirety. Joint tenancy must be expressly stated.
Joint tenancy unities: TTIP (time, title, interest, possession). TBE adds marriage and cannot be partitioned.
Trustor creates, trustee holds title, beneficiary benefits. Limited partners risk only their investment.
Co-op = shares + proprietary lease (personal property, no MRT). Condo = deed to unit + % of common elements (real property).
Mortgage = voluntary, specific. Judgments, IRS, estate, franchise tax = general, involuntary. Taxes, mechanic's liens = specific, involuntary.
Mechanic's lien: file within 8 months (4 months single-family); lasts 1 year unless foreclosure started.
Judgment lien: 10 years. Lis pendens: 3 years.
Lien priority: property taxes and special assessments first, then by recording date. Subordination agreement changes order.
Encroachments are found by a survey, not a title search. More restrictive of zoning vs deed restriction controls.
Appurtenant = dominant + servient, runs with land. In gross = no dominant (utilities). License = revocable, not an interest in land.
Prescriptive easement and adverse possession: 10 years in NY. No light and air easement by prescription in NY. Merger ends an easement.
Title passes on delivery and acceptance. Acknowledgment is needed only to record. Grantee need not sign.
Monuments control over distances. Metes and bounds must return to the point of beginning.
NY standard deed: bargain and sale with covenant against grantor's acts. Most protection: full covenant and warranty. None: quitclaim. Foreclosure: referee's deed.
Executor = will; administrator = no will. Devise = real property by will. No will and no heirs = escheat.
NY intestacy, spouse + children: spouse gets $50,000 + half the rest; children split the balance.
Adverse possession since 2008: fences, hedges, plantings, sheds, mowing are deemed permissive. Accretion adds slowly; avulsion is sudden and does not move the boundary.
NY is race-notice: first good-faith buyer for value without notice to record wins. Recording = constructive notice.
Loan Estimate within 3 business days of application; Closing Disclosure 3 business days before closing. RESPA bans referral fees even if disclosed.
Seller pays NYS transfer tax $2 per $500 (0.4%; 0.65% NYC residential $3M+) and NYC RPTT (1% to $500k, 1.425% above). Buyer pays mansion tax (1% at $1M+; NYC up to 3.9%).
Mortgage recording tax, NYC borrower: 1.8% under $500k loan, 1.925% at $500k+. None on co-op share loans.

Prorations: seller prepaid = credit seller/debit buyer. Seller collected rent or owes unpaid tax = debit seller/credit buyer. Deposits: debit seller/credit buyer. Loan and down payment: buyer credits only.

subjects.title: The Contract of Sales and Leases
subjects.blurb: Leases and sales contracts are the paper every deal runs on. The exam tests the Statute of Frauds, contract essentials and remedies, and New York's post-2019 rental rules, where outdated textbook numbers are the classic trap.

lessons.title: Leases: Estates, Clauses, and New York Rental Rules
lessons.tagline: A lease is a contract and a conveyance at once, and New York rewrote the rental rulebook in 2019.
objectives: Name the four leasehold estates and how each one ends
List what a valid lease needs and when it must be in writing
Match gross, net, triple net, percentage, graduated, index, and ground leases to their use
Apply the HSTPA rules on deposits, fees, late charges, and notices
Explain rent stabilization, the luxury decontrol repeal, sublets, roommates, Good Cause Eviction, and the FARE Act

blocks.title: Sal's vacant 3R, Astoria
blocks.html: Sal Russo has a vacancy in his six-unit building on 31st Avenue. He wants two months' deposit, a $150 application fee, and a $95 late fee "like the old days". He also asks Jordan whether the stabilized unit upstairs can finally go market-rate now that the rent is over $2,800. How many of Sal's plans are still legal?
blocks.casual: Sal Russo's got an empty 3R in his six-unit on 31st Avenue in Astoria, and he's running the playbook from twenty years ago. He wants two months' deposit, a $150 application fee, and a $95 late fee "like the old days". Then he leans over and asks Jordan if the stabilized apartment upstairs can finally go market-rate, since the rent's over $2,800 now. So how much of Sal's plan still flies in New York today?

deeper.plain: Landlords who learned the business before 2019 often run on rules that no longer exist. This lesson is the update.
deeper.picture: It's like driving with a GPS map from 2015. The streets look familiar, but half the turns it tells you to make are now one-way the other direction.
deeper.street: Jordan writes up Sal's listing with a 2-month deposit because Sal insisted. The tenant, a nurse at Mount Sinai Queens, pays $4,800 up front, then files a complaint once she learns the cap. Sal has to refund $2,400 and Jordan has to explain to Diane why the firm's name is on the listing.
deeper.stakes: A licensee who helps a landlord collect illegal fees is part of the problem. Expect a tenant complaint, a refund demand, possible Attorney General interest, and a DOS question about your competence.
deeper.exam: Scenario questions love an old-school landlord with several demands, then ask which one is legal. Count each against the HSTPA numbers: 1 month, $20, $50 or 5% after 5 days, and no rent-threshold decontrol.

blocks.text: A lease is two things at once

blocks.html: A lease is a contract between the lessor (landlord) and the lessee (tenant). It also conveys a leasehold estate: the right to possess real property for a time, while the landlord keeps the reversion. Because it is a contract, the same rules that make any contract valid make a lease valid.
blocks.casual: Here's the thing about a lease: it's doing two jobs at once. First, it's a contract between the lessor (the landlord) and the lessee (the tenant). Second, it hands the tenant a leasehold estate, meaning the right to possess the place for a stretch of time, while the landlord holds onto the reversion (it comes back to them at the end). Since it's a contract, every rule that makes a contract valid applies to a lease too.

deeper.plain: A lease is a deal on paper and also a temporary ownership-like right to live in or use the space.
deeper.picture: Think of a coat check. You hand over your coat (possession) for the night, you get a ticket (the contract), and the coat comes back to you at the end (the reversion).
deeper.street: The Okafors rent their garden floor in Bed-Stuy to Leo for a year. Leo has the right to keep the Okafors out except as the lease allows, even though they own the whole brownstone. When the year ends, possession snaps back to Grace and Emmanuel.
deeper.stakes: Forget that a lease is a contract and you'll miss capacity or consideration problems that let a party walk away. Forget it's an estate and you'll think a landlord can just walk in or change the locks, which is illegal.
deeper.exam: Watch for "lessor" vs "lessee": the lessor is the landlord, the one who grants. The landlord keeps the "reversion", and the tenant holds a "leasehold" (less-than-freehold) estate.

head: Leasehold estate
How long
How it ends
rows: Fixed term with a set end date (even 6 months)
Automatically on the end date. No notice needed
Renews period to period (month to month)
Either side ends it with notice; death of either party ends it
Tenant stays after the right ended, without consent
Landlord may evict (court process) or accept rent
blocks.caption: Estate for years means a definite term, not a term of years.

deeper.plain: Leasehold estates are sorted by how long they run and how they end: fixed date, rolling period, open-ended by consent, or overstaying without consent.
deeper.picture: A gym membership: a 12-month plan ends on its own (estate for years), a monthly plan keeps renewing until someone cancels (periodic), a friend letting you use their guest pass "until whenever" is at will, and still being in the locker room after closing is sufferance.
deeper.street: Priya's client signs a 6-month lease in Park Slope ending June 30. On July 1 it's over, no notice needed, because it's an estate for years. Her other client rents month to month in Sunnyside and needs proper notice to be told to leave.
deeper.stakes: Mixing these up means sending notice when none is needed, or worse, assuming a tenancy ended when it didn't. A landlord who treats a periodic tenant like an expired fixed-term tenant can lose in housing court and start the clock over.
deeper.exam: The classic trap: "estate for years" just means a definite term, even 6 months. Death of a party ends an estate at will, but not an estate for years. A tenant at sufferance had a right that ended and stayed without consent.

blocks.title: Holdovers in New York
blocks.html: A holdover tenant stays past the lease. In NY, if the landlord accepts rent after a lease ends, the default result is a month-to-month tenancy (RPL 232-c), not a new one-year lease. Until rent is accepted, the holdover is a tenant at sufferance.
blocks.casual: A holdover tenant is someone who stays after the lease runs out. In New York, if the landlord takes rent after the lease ends, what you get by default is a month-to-month tenancy (RPL 232-c), not an automatic new one-year lease. Until the landlord actually accepts rent, the holdover is just a tenant at sufferance.

deeper.plain: If a tenant overstays and the landlord takes their rent, they're now month-to-month. The landlord can't lock them into another full year just because they stayed.
deeper.picture: Like a parking garage that keeps charging you by the day once your monthly pass expires. You're still parked there legally, just on short terms.
deeper.street: Sal's tenant in 2F stays a week past her March 31 lease end while her new place in Woodside gets painted. Sal deposits her April check. She's now month-to-month, and Sal can't claim she owes him a whole new year of rent.
deeper.stakes: Landlords who cash a holdover's check by mistake may have created a tenancy they then have to end with proper notice. Licensees managing buildings need to know that taking rent changes the legal relationship.
deeper.exam: In some states accepting rent from a holdover creates a new term equal to the old one. New York's answer is month-to-month. If the stem says "New York" and "accepts rent", pick month-to-month.

items: Capacity: parties able to contract (adults, sound mind)
Demising clause: the words that actually lease "the demised premises"
Description of the premises (street address and unit is enough for an apartment)
Term: a clear start and end
Rent and how it is paid (the consideration). Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is due in arrears. Real leases almost always make it due in advance on the 1st
Writing if the term is more than 1 year (Statute of Frauds, GOL 5-703)
Signatures. Notarization is not needed unless the lease will be recorded
Plain language: NY residential leases must be written in clear, everyday words (GOL 5-702)
blocks.casual: So what does a lease need to actually work? People who can legally sign (adults of sound mind). A demising clause, the words that actually lease "the demised premises". A description of the space (for an apartment, the street address and unit number is plenty). A term with a clear start and end. Rent and how it gets paid, which is the consideration. Fun fact: unless the lease says otherwise, rent is legally due in arrears (at the end of the period), but real leases almost always make it due in advance on the 1st. It must be in writing if it runs more than 1 year (Statute of Frauds, GOL 5-703). It needs signatures, but no notary unless you plan to record it. And in NY, a residential lease has to be in plain, everyday language (GOL 5-702).

deeper.plain: A lease needs the right people, the right words, a place, a time period, rent, and signatures. Longer than a year means it must be written down.
deeper.picture: Think of it like a recipe card. Skip an ingredient like the term or the rent and you don't have a slightly worse cake, you might not have a cake at all.
deeper.street: Marcus agrees on the phone to rent a Williamsburg loft to a startup for 3 years at $9,000 a month and shakes on it at a bodega. Two weeks later the owner gets a better offer. Because nothing was signed and the term is over a year, the startup has no enforceable lease.
deeper.stakes: An unsigned multi-year deal can evaporate and take your commission with it. A lease full of legalese can also be challenged under the plain language law, and the landlord may face damages.
deeper.exam: Notarization is a favorite distractor: a lease is valid without it; acknowledgment matters only for recording. Rent is consideration. And "more than 1 year" triggers the writing rule, not "1 year or more".

blocks.html: A lease is full of covenants, promises like "tenant will not alter" or "landlord will supply heat". An implied lease can arise without any document when the conduct of the parties shows one, such as a landlord taking monthly rent from an occupant.
blocks.casual: A lease is basically a stack of covenants, which are just promises: "tenant won't alter the apartment", "landlord will supply heat". And you can have an implied lease with no paperwork at all, when the way people act shows there's a deal. Classic example: a landlord taking monthly rent from someone living in the unit.

deeper.plain: Leases are made of promises. Sometimes the promises are never written; the parties' behavior creates the lease.
deeper.picture: You don't sign a contract with the coffee cart guy, but if you hand him $3 every morning and he hands you a coffee, everyone knows the deal.
deeper.street: Sal's cousin moves into the basement in Astoria with no lease. Sal takes $1,200 cash every month for two years. When Sal wants him out, he learns there's an implied month-to-month tenancy and he needs proper notice and a court case, not a phone call.
deeper.stakes: Landlords who think "no lease, no tenant" try self-help evictions and end up liable. Agents who assume an occupant has no rights can mislead a buyer about whether a unit will be delivered vacant.
deeper.exam: If the stem describes an occupant paying rent and the owner accepting it without a written lease, the answer is an implied lease (or a periodic tenancy), not a tenancy at sufferance.

blocks.html: Use clauses matter most in commercial leases. "For a dry cleaner and for no other purpose" locks the tenant in. "For any lawful purpose" lets the tenant change businesses. Commercial rent is usually quoted per square foot per year. Commercial tenants have no statutory right to renew, so they negotiate an option to renew.
blocks.casual: Use clauses are a big deal in commercial leases. "For a dry cleaner and for no other purpose" means the tenant is stuck being a dry cleaner. "For any lawful purpose" means the tenant can switch businesses. Commercial rent is usually quoted per square foot per year, not per month. And commercial tenants have no statutory right to renew, so if they want to stay, they negotiate an option to renew into the lease.

deeper.plain: In a store or office lease, the words about what the space can be used for control your future. And there's no law that lets a business tenant stay; they need a renewal option.
deeper.picture: A use clause is like a food truck permit that says "tacos only". Want to sell ramen next year? Not without a new permit.
deeper.street: Evelyn leases a Jackson Heights storefront at $60 per square foot for 1,500 square feet, which is $90,000 a year, $7,500 a month. The tenant's lease says "nail salon and for no other purpose". When the salon wants to add a café, Evelyn can say no or renegotiate.
deeper.stakes: A broker who reads $60 a foot as monthly rent quotes a number twelve times too high and blows up a deal. A tenant without a renewal option can be forced out after building a customer base, losing everything they invested.
deeper.exam: Commercial rent is per square foot per YEAR. "No other purpose" is restrictive; "any lawful purpose" is broad. Statutory renewal rights belong to rent-stabilized residential tenants, not commercial ones.

blocks.caption: Compare who pays taxes, insurance, and maintenance in each lease type, and which ones tie rent to sales, time, or an index.

head: Lease
What makes it different
Typical user
rows: Tenant pays flat rent; landlord pays operating costs
Tenant pays rent plus some property charges
Tenant pays taxes, insurance, and maintenance
Base rent plus a share of gross sales
Rent steps up on a schedule
Rent moves with an index such as the CPI
Tenant leases only land, often 49 to 99 years, and builds on it
Battery Park City, hotels, big retail
Co-op shareholder's lease to occupy a unit

deeper.plain: Lease types differ by who pays the building's costs and how the rent is figured.
deeper.picture: A gross lease is an all-inclusive hotel. A triple net lease is renting a car where you also buy the gas, insurance, and oil changes. A percentage lease is a busker who gives the subway a cut of the tips.
deeper.street: Evelyn leases a freestanding pharmacy pad in Staten Island on a triple net lease: the tenant pays the property taxes, insurance, and maintenance, so Evelyn's check is close to pure income. Her mall store in Queens pays $5,000 base plus 6% of gross sales over a breakpoint.
deeper.stakes: A tenant who signs an NNN lease thinking it's gross can get hit with a tax bill they never budgeted for. A broker who mislabels the lease type in a listing can be accused of misrepresentation.
deeper.exam: Matching questions: "tenant pays taxes, insurance, maintenance" equals triple net; "share of gross sales" equals percentage; "tied to CPI" equals index; "steps up on a schedule" equals graduated; "land only, tenant builds" equals ground lease; "co-op" equals proprietary lease.

blocks.q: A drugstore pays base rent plus its own property taxes, building insurance, and all maintenance. This is a:
c: Gross lease
Percentage lease
Triple net lease
Graduated lease
blocks.x: Tenant paying taxes, insurance, and maintenance is triple net. A percentage lease ties rent to sales, which is not described here.

blocks.html: The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (HSTPA) applies statewide to residential rentals, stabilized or market-rate.
blocks.casual: The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (HSTPA) covers residential rentals statewide. Doesn't matter if the apartment is stabilized or market-rate. If people live there and pay rent, these rules apply.

deeper.plain: In 2019 New York rewrote the rules for nearly every residential rental in the state, not just the regulated ones.
deeper.picture: It's like a new speed limit posted on every road in the state, not just the highways. Your quiet side street is covered too.
deeper.street: A landlord in Buffalo with a market-rate duplex figures the 2019 law is a "New York City rent control thing". He charges a $75 application fee. That's illegal in Buffalo just as it is in Brooklyn.
deeper.stakes: Agents outside NYC who assume HSTPA doesn't reach them hand landlords bad advice, and the fee or deposit violation lands on everyone involved in the rental.
deeper.exam: If a question asks where the deposit cap or application fee limit applies, the answer is statewide and to all residential rentals. Don't fall for "only rent-stabilized units" or "only NYC".

blocks.caption: Walk through deposits, fees, notices, stabilization, Good Cause, and the FARE Act. Notice how few dollar amounts a landlord can still charge up front.

head: Rule
What the law allows
rows: Max 1 month's rent. Return within 14 days of move-out with an itemized statement, or the landlord loses the right to keep any of it
Held in an interest-bearing NY bank account; landlord may keep 1% a year for administration
Banned, except actual cost of a background/credit check, max $20 (waived if the applicant brings a report under 30 days old)
Only after rent is 5 days late; max $50 or 5% of monthly rent, whichever is less
30 days (under 1 year), 60 days (1 to 2 years), 90 days (2+ years)
Landlord must offer an inspection before move-in and before move-out

deeper.plain: Since 2019 landlords can take less money up front, must return deposits fast, and must warn tenants longer before ending or hiking a lease.
deeper.picture: Picture a ticket booth with the prices painted on the wall: one month max for the deposit, $20 max to screen, $50 max late fee, and a calendar showing 30, 60, or 90 days of warning.
deeper.street: Leo has lived in his Astoria one-bedroom for 3 years at $2,500. His landlord wants to raise it to $2,700, an 8% jump. Because Leo's been there over 2 years and the increase is 5% or more, the landlord needs to give him 90 days' written notice. Thirty days won't cut it.
deeper.stakes: Miss the 14-day deposit deadline and the landlord forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit, even for real damage. Short notice on an increase means the tenancy continues on old terms until proper notice runs.
deeper.exam: Expect number swaps: 14 days (not 30) to return the deposit; $20 (not $50) screening cap; late fee after 5 days, lesser of $50 or 5%. The notice tiers are tied to how long the tenant has been there, not to the lease length.

blocks.title: Sal's late fee
blocks.html: Rent on the 3R is $2,400. 5% is $120. The cap is the lesser of $50 or $120, so $50, and only once rent is more than 5 days late. Sal's $95 fee is illegal, his $150 application fee is illegal (max $20), and his 2-month deposit is illegal (max $2,400).
blocks.casual: Run the numbers on Sal's 3R. Rent's $2,400. 5% of that is $120. The cap is whichever is less, $50 or $120, so the max is $50, and he can only charge it once rent is more than 5 days late. So Sal's $95 late fee? Illegal. His $150 application fee? Illegal, the max is $20. His 2-month deposit? Also illegal, the max is one month, $2,400.

deeper.plain: Every one of Sal's money demands is over the legal limit. The math is simple once you know the caps.
deeper.picture: It's like a coupon that says "$50 off or 5%, whichever is less". On a cheap item, 5% wins. On anything over $1,000 a month, $50 wins.
deeper.street: Jordan sits with Sal at a diner on Ditmars and rewrites the listing: $2,400 deposit, $20 credit check (waived if the applicant has a report from the last 30 days), and a $50 late fee after the 5th day of lateness. Sal grumbles but signs off.
deeper.stakes: If Jordan posts Sal's original terms, the firm is advertising illegal charges. That's an easy tenant complaint and a bad look with DOS.
deeper.exam: Late fee math: 5% of rent versus $50, pick the smaller. For rent above $1,000 the answer is always $50. For $800 rent, 5% is $40, so $40 is the cap.

blocks.html: Every residential lease carries an implied warranty of habitability (RPL 235-b): the unit must be fit to live in, and tenants cannot waive it. The covenant of quiet enjoyment promises the landlord will not interfere with the tenant's possession. Actual eviction is removal through court process. Constructive eviction happens when the landlord's failure (no heat all winter) makes the space unusable: the tenant must move out to claim it, and then owes no further rent.
blocks.casual: Every residential lease comes with a built-in warranty of habitability (RPL 235-b): the place has to be fit to live in, and the tenant can't sign that right away. The covenant of quiet enjoyment is the landlord's promise not to mess with the tenant's possession. Actual eviction means removing the tenant through the courts. Constructive eviction is different: the landlord's failure (say, no heat all winter) makes the place unusable. To claim it, the tenant has to move out, and then owes no more rent.

deeper.plain: Landlords must keep homes livable and leave tenants in peace. If the landlord's failure drives a tenant out, the tenant can stop paying.
deeper.picture: A gym that locks the doors every day is still charging you, but you can't use it. If you quit and walk away, you shouldn't owe more dues. That's constructive eviction.
deeper.street: In a Crown Heights walk-up the boiler dies in December and the landlord ignores it for six weeks. Tenant A moves to her sister's and stops paying: constructive eviction. Tenant B stays, bundles up, and asks a judge for a rent abatement under 235-b.
deeper.stakes: A tenant who claims constructive eviction but never moves out can be found liable for all the unpaid rent. A landlord who ignores habitability faces abatements, HPD violations, and lost rent.
deeper.exam: Habitability can't be waived, even by a signed lease clause. Constructive eviction requires abandonment within a reasonable time. Quiet enjoyment is about the landlord's interference, not noisy neighbors.

blocks.title: Constructive eviction needs an exit
blocks.html: A tenant who stays put and stops paying is claiming breach of habitability (rent abatement), not constructive eviction. Constructive eviction requires the tenant to leave within a reasonable time.
blocks.casual: Watch this one. A tenant who stays in the apartment and stops paying rent is claiming a breach of habitability, which gets you a rent abatement. That's not constructive eviction. Constructive eviction only works if the tenant actually leaves within a reasonable time.

deeper.plain: Staying and withholding rent is one remedy. Leaving and owing nothing more is another. You can't mix them.
deeper.picture: If a restaurant serves you a bad meal, you can stay and ask for a discount, or walk out and not pay. You can't eat the whole thing, stay all night, and still claim you walked out.
deeper.street: Marcus tells a Bushwick tenant with a busted ceiling, "Just stop paying, it's constructive eviction." The tenant stays put. In housing court the judge gives a 30% abatement under habitability but makes him pay the other 70%. Marcus's "advice" cost the tenant credibility with the court.
deeper.stakes: Bad advice here means a tenant ends up with a judgment for back rent. Licensees shouldn't be giving legal advice anyway; send people to an attorney.
deeper.exam: If the stem says the tenant "remained in possession and withheld rent", the answer is not constructive eviction. Look for "vacated" or "abandoned the premises" as the cue.

blocks.html: Improvements: fixtures a residential tenant attaches generally become the landlord's unless the lease lets the tenant remove them. Commercial trade fixtures stay the tenant's if removed by lease end.
blocks.casual: Improvements: if a residential tenant attaches something (fixtures), it generally becomes the landlord's when they leave, unless the lease says the tenant can take it. Commercial tenants are different: their trade fixtures stay theirs as long as they remove them by the time the lease ends.

deeper.plain: Bolt something to a home you rent and it usually stays. A business's equipment can go with it if removed on time.
deeper.picture: A sticker on a library book belongs to the library once you return it. But a food truck's grill is still the truck owner's when it leaves the lot.
deeper.street: A pizzeria in a Forest Hills storefront installs a $30,000 oven. When its lease ends it pulls the oven out the week before move-out, which is fine. Meanwhile Leo mounts a $400 ceiling fan in his rental and finds out it stays for the next tenant unless his lease said otherwise.
deeper.stakes: A commercial tenant that waits past lease end may lose its trade fixtures to the landlord. A residential tenant who rips out fixtures can face deposit deductions or a damages claim.
deeper.exam: Trade fixtures are personal property of the commercial tenant if removed before the lease expires. The trap answer says they become real property "automatically". Timing is the key.

left.title: Assignment of lease
items: Tenant transfers the ENTIRE remaining term
Assignee deals directly with the landlord
Original tenant stays liable unless released (novation)
RPL 226-b: landlord may refuse; if refusal is unreasonable, tenant can be released from the lease

right.title: Sublease
items: Tenant transfers PART of the term or space
Subtenant pays the original tenant, who still pays the landlord
Original tenant stays fully liable
RPL 226-b (4+ unit buildings): written request; consent not unreasonably withheld

deeper.plain: Assigning hands off the whole lease; subletting rents out part of it while you stay on the hook. Either way, the original tenant usually stays liable.
deeper.picture: Assignment is selling your concert ticket. A sublease is lending your ticket for the first half of the show while you're still the one the venue knows.
deeper.street: Leo takes a job in Boston with 8 months left on his Astoria lease. If he assigns, the new tenant deals with the landlord directly for all 8 months. If he sublets for 4 months, he collects from the subtenant and still pays the landlord. In both cases Leo is liable unless the landlord signs a novation releasing him.
deeper.stakes: Tenants think handing over the keys ends their responsibility. If the assignee or subtenant stops paying, the landlord can come after the original tenant.
deeper.exam: "Entire remaining term" means assignment; "part of the term" means sublease. Only a novation releases the original tenant. Under RPL 226-b, if a landlord unreasonably refuses an assignment, the tenant's remedy is release from the lease.

blocks.html: Assignment moves the whole leasehold; a sublease carves out part of it. The NY roommate law (RPL 235-f) lets a tenant live with immediate family plus one additional occupant (and that occupant's dependent children). A lease clause banning roommates is void. The landlord may ask for occupants' names.
blocks.casual: Assignment moves the whole leasehold; a sublease carves out a piece of it. New York's roommate law (RPL 235-f) lets a tenant live with immediate family plus one more occupant (and that occupant's dependent kids). A lease clause that says "no roommates" is void. The landlord is allowed to ask for occupants' names, though.

deeper.plain: In New York you can always have your family and one extra person live with you, no matter what the lease says.
deeper.picture: Think of your lease like a dinner reservation for you and your family. NY law says you can always add one more chair.
deeper.street: Priya's client, a single tenant in a Kensington one-bedroom, moves her boyfriend in. The landlord points to the lease's "no additional occupants" clause. Priya explains 235-f voids that clause; the landlord can ask his name, nothing more.
deeper.stakes: A landlord who tries to evict over a lawful roommate wastes money in court and may face a harassment claim. Agents who repeat "no roommates allowed" in listings are advertising an unenforceable term.
deeper.exam: Roommate law is 235-f; sublet law is 226-b. Don't mix them up. The roommate count is immediate family plus ONE more occupant and that person's dependent children.

blocks.q: A tenant moves to Boston for a 9-month job and rents her Park Slope apartment to a friend for those 9 months, planning to return. This is a:
c: Assignment
Sublease
Novation
Tenancy at will
blocks.x: She transfers only part of her remaining term and keeps a reversion, so it is a sublease. An assignment transfers the whole remaining term.

blocks.html: Rent stabilization covers most NYC buildings with 6 or more units built before 1974, plus units in localities that opted in under the Emergency Tenant Protection Act of 1974 (ETPA). Since 2019 any municipality in the state with a vacancy rate under 5% may opt in. The local Rent Guidelines Board sets allowed increases; NYS Homes and Community Renewal (HCR, formerly DHCR) administers. A stabilized tenant gets a 1- or 2-year renewal at the tenant's choice.
blocks.casual: Rent stabilization covers most NYC buildings with 6 or more units built before 1974, plus units in places that opted in under the Emergency Tenant Protection Act of 1974 (ETPA). Since 2019, any town in the state with a vacancy rate under 5% can opt in. The local Rent Guidelines Board decides how much rents can go up, and NYS Homes and Community Renewal (HCR, formerly DHCR) runs the system. A stabilized tenant gets to pick a 1- or 2-year renewal, the tenant's choice.

deeper.plain: Older NYC buildings with 6 or more apartments usually have capped rent increases and a right to renew. Other towns can join if housing is tight.
deeper.picture: Rent stabilization is like a phone plan grandfathered at a capped yearly increase: the company can raise it, but only by what the regulator allows, and you decide whether to renew for 1 or 2 years.
deeper.street: Sal's 6-unit in Astoria was built in 1931, so his apartments are presumptively stabilized. When the RGB approves, say, a 3% increase on 1-year leases, that's the max Sal can add on renewal, and his tenant on the 4th floor gets to choose 1 or 2 years.
deeper.stakes: A broker who lists a stabilized unit as free-market and helps set an illegal rent can trigger an overcharge claim, and since 2019 overcharge penalties can reach back years with treble damages for willful violations.
deeper.exam: Know the players: ETPA 1974 is the law, the Rent Guidelines Board sets increases, HCR (formerly DHCR) administers. The renewal term choice belongs to the tenant, not the landlord.

blocks.html: The tenant must keep the unit as a primary residence: where they actually live, shown by tax returns, voter registration, a driver's license, and spending most of the year there. A non-primary resident (a tenant who really lives in Florida) can be refused renewal. Household income means the combined income of everyone living in the unit, which mattered for the old decontrol test.
blocks.casual: To keep a stabilized apartment, the tenant has to use it as their primary residence, meaning where they really live. Proof is stuff like tax returns, voter registration, a driver's license, and spending most of the year there. A tenant who actually lives in Florida can be denied a renewal. "Household income" means everybody in the unit's income combined, which used to matter for the old decontrol test.

deeper.plain: A stabilized lease is protection for your home, not a cheap pied-a-terre. If you don't really live there, you can lose it.
deeper.picture: It's like a resident parking permit. You have to actually live on the block. Your cousin in Boca can't keep one for weekend visits.
deeper.street: Kim, the UWS co-op board president, knows a neighbor in a rental building next door who files taxes in Florida, votes there, and spends 9 months a year in Naples. The landlord gathers the records and files a non-primary residence case to refuse renewal.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who drift away from a stabilized unit can lose it. Landlords who bring weak non-primary cases waste years in court. Agents should never coach someone to fake residency.
deeper.exam: Indicators of primary residence: tax return address, voter registration, driver's license, and time spent there. A non-primary resident may be refused renewal, not immediately evicted mid-lease.

blocks.title: Luxury decontrol is dead
blocks.html: The syllabus still describes luxury decontrol at a $2,000 rent and $175,000 income for 2 years. Those are 1990s numbers, and the whole mechanism (high-rent and high-income decontrol, plus vacancy bonuses) was repealed by HSTPA in June 2019. Today a unit cannot leave stabilization by crossing a rent threshold. If an exam answer says a unit "is deregulated because the rent passed $2,000", that is outdated.
blocks.casual: Heads up: the syllabus still talks about luxury decontrol at $2,000 rent and $175,000 income for 2 years. Those are 1990s numbers, and the whole thing (high-rent and high-income decontrol, plus vacancy bonuses) got repealed by HSTPA in June 2019. Today, crossing a rent number does not take a unit out of stabilization. If an answer says a unit "is deregulated because the rent passed $2,000", that's outdated.

deeper.plain: Apartments used to escape rent stabilization once rents got high enough. That door closed in 2019.
deeper.picture: Like an old subway map in a frame at a deli: still on the wall, but the line it shows hasn't run in years.
deeper.street: Sal's upstairs stabilized unit rents for $2,850. He asks Jordan to list it at $3,600 market rate "since it's over the limit now". Jordan tells him there is no limit anymore; the unit stays stabilized and the next increase is whatever the Rent Guidelines Board allows.
deeper.stakes: Listing a stabilized unit at market rent is an overcharge. The tenant can sue for the difference, and the landlord can owe treble damages if willful. The agent who advertised it is in the mess too.
deeper.exam: If the exam or school final still mentions luxury decontrol, recognize it as the old rule. For current law, units do not deregulate by crossing a rent or income threshold.

blocks.text: Good Cause Eviction and the FARE Act

blocks.html: Good Cause Eviction (2024) covers many market-rate units in NYC and in towns that opt in. A covered tenant can be evicted or refused renewal only for good cause (nonpayment, nuisance, owner occupancy, and similar), and an increase above the lower of CPI + 5% or 10% is presumed unreasonable. Exemptions include small landlords (10 or fewer units statewide), buildings with a CO issued on or after Jan 1, 2009, luxury units above 245% of fair market rent, condos, co-ops, and owner-occupied buildings with 10 or fewer units. It sunsets in 2034.
blocks.casual: Good Cause Eviction (2024) covers a lot of market-rate apartments in NYC and in towns that opt in. If you're covered, the landlord can only evict you or refuse to renew for good cause (not paying, being a nuisance, the owner moving in, that kind of thing). And any rent increase above the lower of CPI + 5% or 10% is presumed unreasonable. Who's exempt? Small landlords (10 or fewer units statewide), buildings with a CO issued on or after Jan 1, 2009, luxury units above 245% of fair market rent, condos, co-ops, and owner-occupied buildings with 10 or fewer units. The law sunsets in 2034.

deeper.plain: Many unregulated NYC tenants now can't be pushed out without a real reason, and big rent jumps are presumed unfair.
deeper.picture: It's like a referee who doesn't set your salary but will blow the whistle if your boss fires you for no reason or doubles your hours without warning.
deeper.street: A tenant in a 40-unit Flatbush building built in 1962 pays $2,200. If CPI is 3%, the cap is the lower of 8% or 10%, so 8%: about $2,376. The landlord asks $2,600. The tenant can refuse and the landlord has to justify the increase in court.
deeper.stakes: Agents who tell a covered tenant "the owner just wants you out" are describing an illegal reason. Landlords who miscount their units or ignore exemptions end up in court with a weak case.
deeper.exam: Formula: lower of CPI + 5% or 10%. Small landlord means 10 or fewer units statewide. New construction exemption runs from a CO on or after Jan 1, 2009. Sunset 2034.

blocks.title: FARE Act (since June 11, 2025)
blocks.html: In NYC the FARE Act says a broker hired by the landlord is paid by the landlord, not the tenant. Any fee a tenant must pay has to be disclosed in the listing and the lease. A tenant who hires their own broker may still agree to pay that broker.
blocks.casual: In NYC, the FARE Act (in effect since June 11, 2025) flips who pays the broker on rentals. If the landlord hired the broker, the landlord pays. Any fee the tenant has to pay must be disclosed in the listing and in the lease. A tenant who hires their own broker can still agree to pay that broker.

deeper.plain: In NYC, whoever hires the broker pays the broker. Landlords can't push their agent's fee onto renters anymore.
deeper.picture: Like a restaurant that hires a DJ. The diners don't get a surprise DJ charge on their check.
deeper.street: Jordan lists Sal's 3R as Sal's agent. A tenant applies and asks what the broker fee is. The answer is zero: Sal pays Jordan's firm. If a different tenant hires her own broker to hunt for apartments, she can agree to pay that broker.
deeper.stakes: Charging a tenant your landlord-side fee in NYC breaks the FARE Act and invites city enforcement and refunds. Hidden fees not disclosed in the listing and lease are a separate violation.
deeper.exam: The test is who hired the broker, not who benefits. NYC only. Effective June 11, 2025. Watch for answers saying tenants "can never pay a broker", which is wrong if the tenant hired their own.

blocks.q: A landlord in Rochester wants to keep a former tenant's deposit for damage. The tenant moved out 20 days ago and has received nothing. What is the result?
c: The landlord has 30 days, so there is still time
The landlord forfeits the right to keep any part of the deposit
The landlord may keep it if damage exceeds one month's rent
Rules only apply in NYC
blocks.x: HSTPA is statewide: an itemized statement and the balance are due within 14 days, or the landlord loses the right to retain any of it.

blocks.title: Ending a residential tenancy the NY way

items.title: Check the notice clock
items.html: 30, 60, or 90 days by length of occupancy for non-renewal or a 5%+ increase.

items.title: Check coverage
items.html: Stabilized? Renewal is the tenant's right. Good Cause? You need a listed reason.

items.title: Go to court
items.html: Only a court and a marshal or sheriff can remove a tenant. Lockouts are illegal.

items.title: Close out the deposit
items.html: Itemized statement and balance within 14 days.

blocks.casual:
Ending a residential tenancy in NY goes like this:
1. Check the notice clock: 30, 60, or 90 days depending on how long they've lived there, for a non-renewal or a 5%+ increase.
2. Check coverage. Stabilized? Renewal is the tenant's right. Good Cause? You need a listed reason.
3. Go to court. Only a court and a marshal or sheriff can remove a tenant. Lockouts are illegal.
4. Close out the deposit: itemized statement and balance back within 14 days.

deeper.plain: Give the right notice, make sure the law even lets you end it, use the court, then return the deposit properly.
deeper.picture: It's like landing a plane: you follow the checklist in order every time. Skip a step and you don't land smoothly, you crash.
deeper.street: Sal wants his 2R tenant of 3 years out to move his nephew in. He sends 90 days' notice, confirms the building isn't Good Cause covered (it's stabilized, so owner use rules apply instead), files in Queens Housing Court, and after the marshal executes the warrant, mails an itemized deposit statement in 10 days.
deeper.stakes: Changing the locks or tossing belongings is an illegal eviction in NYC, which can mean civil penalties and even criminal charges. A missed notice deadline resets the clock and costs months of rent.
deeper.exam: Self-help eviction is never the right answer for a residential tenant. Only a marshal (NYC) or sheriff (elsewhere) carries out a warrant of eviction issued by a court.

blocks.title: Hook: 1, 14, 20, 5-50
blocks.html: 1 month deposit, 14 days to return it, $20 max screening fee, late fee after 5 days capped at $50 (or 5%).
blocks.casual: Easy hook: 1, 14, 20, 5-50. 1 month max deposit, 14 days to give it back, $20 max screening fee, and a late fee only after 5 days, capped at $50 (or 5%, whichever is less).

deeper.plain: Four numbers cover most of the 2019 rental money rules.
deeper.picture: Read it like a subway line: the 1 train to 14th Street, then $20 MetroCard, and you're 5 minutes late with a $50 fine.
deeper.street: Jordan writes "1, 14, 20, 5-50" on a sticky note on the monitor at Hudson & Hart. When Marcus quotes a landlord a $75 screening fee, Jordan points at the note and Marcus mutters "since when". Since 2019.
deeper.stakes: Getting any of these wrong in a rental listing or lease is an easy, documentable violation. Tenants know these numbers now, and so do their lawyers.
deeper.exam: Rapid-fire recall questions use these exact numbers with near-miss distractors like 2 months, 30 days, $50 screening, or 10 days late. Lock in the hook and the distractors fall away.

story.title: Sal's Old Playbook
story.setting: Astoria, a rainy Thursday in October

beats.text: Jordan meets Sal Russo in the hallway of his six-family. Sal is holding a lease form printed in 2011.
Two months' security, a hundred fifty to apply, ninety-five if they're late. That's how my father did it.
Your father didn't have HSTPA. One month max on the deposit, and the only application charge is the actual cost of a credit check, up to twenty bucks.
And the late fee?
Five days of grace, then the lesser of fifty dollars or five percent. On a $2,400 rent that's fifty.
beats.tag: Late fee: after 5 days, lesser of $50 or 5%

check.q: Rent is $900. What is the maximum late fee once rent is 6 days late?
check.x: 5% of $900 is $45, which is less than $50, so $45 is the cap.

beats.text: Fine. Now 4R upstairs. Rent's at $2,850. That's luxury. I can deregulate it.
That rule got repealed in 2019. There's no rent threshold anymore. 4R stays stabilized.
Then I'll just not renew her.
Stabilized tenants pick a one- or two-year renewal. Unless she doesn't actually live there.
beats.tag: ETPA renewal: tenant's choice of 1 or 2 years

beats.text: Funny you say that. Her mail goes to Boca half the year.
Then that's a primary residence question for your attorney. Tax returns, voter registration, where she sleeps. Not a hunch.
beats.tag: Non-primary residence is a ground, with proof

beats.text: And 2L wants to sublet for a year while she's in Ohio.
Six units, so the sublet law applies. She asks in writing, and you can't unreasonably say no. She stays on the hook for the rent.
beats.tag: RPL 226-b: 4+ units, consent not unreasonably withheld

beats.text: Back at the office, Diane flips through Sal's 2011 lease and drops it in the recycling.
Half the rental questions on the exam are a landlord quoting old rules. Your job is knowing which year it is.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: left side lists what a NY landlord could charge in 2018, right side what is allowed today. Circle every number that changed.

facts.text: A lease is a contract between lessor (landlord) and lessee (tenant) and also conveys a leasehold estate, which is personal property, while the landlord keeps the reversion.
An estate for years has a fixed term with a set end date (even 6 months) and ends automatically with no notice.
A periodic estate (such as month to month) renews period to period until either side gives proper notice.
An estate at will has no set term and ends on notice or the death of either party; a tenant at sufferance stays after the right ended without consent.
In NY, a landlord who accepts rent from a holdover creates a month-to-month tenancy by default (RPL 232-c), not a new one-year lease.
The demising clause holds the words that actually lease the premises to the tenant.
A lease longer than 1 year must be in writing (GOL 5-703); notarization is not needed unless it will be recorded, and NY residential leases must be in plain language (GOL 5-702).
Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is due in arrears; real leases make it due in advance on the 1st.
Lease promises are covenants, and an implied lease can arise from conduct, such as a landlord accepting monthly rent.
Commercial leases turn on use clauses and rent per square foot per year, and commercial tenants negotiate an option to renew since they have no statutory right to one.
A percentage lease charges base rent plus a share of gross sales, typical of mall retail.
In a gross lease the landlord pays operating costs; in a triple net lease the tenant pays taxes, insurance and maintenance; graduated leases step up and index leases follow an index such as CPI.
A ground lease leases only land, often 49 to 99 years, and the tenant builds on it; a co-op on leased land is worth what the land lease's term and rent allow.
A proprietary lease is the co-op shareholder's lease to occupy a unit.
HSTPA (2019) applies statewide to all residential rentals, stabilized or market-rate.
A residential security deposit is capped at 1 month's rent and must be returned within 14 days of move-out with an itemized statement, or the landlord forfeits it.
In buildings with 6 or more units, deposits go in an interest-bearing NY bank account (landlord keeps 1% a year), and the landlord must offer move-in and move-out inspections.
Application fees are banned except the actual cost of a background or credit check, capped at $20.
A late fee may be charged only after rent is 5 days late and is capped at the lesser of $50 or 5% of the monthly rent.
Notice of non-renewal or a 5%+ increase is 30 days (under 1 year), 60 days (1 to 2 years) or 90 days (2+ years).
Every residential lease carries an implied warranty of habitability (RPL 235-b) that tenants cannot waive.
The covenant of quiet enjoyment promises the landlord will not interfere with the tenant's possession.
Constructive eviction requires the tenant to move out because the landlord made the space unusable; a tenant who stays claims breach of habitability instead.
Fixtures a residential tenant attaches generally become the landlord's; commercial trade fixtures stay the tenant's if removed by lease end.
An assignment transfers the entire remaining term and a sublease only part; the original tenant stays liable unless released by novation, and RPL 226-b governs consent.
The roommate law (RPL 235-f) lets a tenant live with immediate family plus one additional occupant, and a lease clause banning roommates is void.

Rent stabilization covers most NYC buildings of 6+ units built before 1974, plus ETPA localities that opt in with a vacancy rate under 5%; HCR administers and the tenant chooses a 1- or 2-year renewal.
A stabilized tenant must use the unit as a primary residence to keep the right to renew.
HSTPA repealed luxury (high-rent and high-income) decontrol in 2019, so a unit cannot leave stabilization by crossing a rent threshold.
Under Good Cause Eviction (2024) a covered tenant can be evicted only for good cause, and an increase above the lower of CPI + 5% or 10% is presumed unreasonable.
Good Cause exempts small landlords (10 or fewer units), buildings with a CO from 2009 on, luxury units above 245% of fair market rent, condos and co-ops; it sunsets in 2034.
Under the NYC FARE Act (June 2025) a broker hired by the landlord is paid by the landlord, and any tenant fee must be disclosed in the listing and lease.
Only a court and a marshal or sheriff can remove a tenant; lockouts are illegal.

lessons.title: Contracts: What Makes Them Binding and What Happens When They Break
lessons.tagline: A handshake can sell a car. It cannot sell a brownstone.
objectives: Classify a contract as express or implied, bilateral or unilateral, executed or executory
Test a deal against the five essentials of a valid real estate contract
Explain the key clauses of a NY sales contract
Distinguish binders, purchase offers, installment contracts, options, and rights of first refusal
Choose the right remedy: specific performance, liquidated damages, rescission, reformation

blocks.title: The text message offer
blocks.html: Leo texts Grace Okafor at 11 pm: "I'll pay $1.6M for the brownstone, cash." Grace replies "Deal!!" with three emojis. The next morning a higher offer arrives at $1.7M. Leo says they have a contract. Do they?
blocks.casual: It's 11 pm. Leo texts Grace Okafor: "I'll pay $1.6M for the brownstone, cash." Grace fires back "Deal!!" with three emojis. Next morning a $1.7M offer shows up. Leo says, "We have a contract." Do they?

deeper.plain: Agreeing on a price by text feels like a deal, but a real estate sale needs more than an excited reply.
deeper.picture: It's like two friends saying "we should totally go to Japan together" in a group chat. Everyone means it, but nobody's booked a flight.
deeper.street: Grace calls Priya in a panic. Priya points out the text has a price and a property but no closing date, no deposit, no deed type, and downstate everyone expects a signed attorney-drafted contract. She tells Grace not to sign anything with the $1.7M buyer until she reviews it, because a court could still look at the texts.
deeper.stakes: Texting "Deal!" can start a lawsuit even if it doesn't make a contract. Agents who encourage clients to accept by text invite a messy fight that can freeze a sale for months.
deeper.exam: Questions built on a casual exchange usually test the Statute of Frauds and the essentials: is there a signed writing with the essential terms? Missing terms or "subject to contract" language points to no enforceable contract.

blocks.html: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement between competent parties to do, or not do, something for consideration. Courts sort them four ways:
blocks.casual: A contract is an agreement a court will enforce, between people who can legally make it, to do (or not do) something in exchange for consideration. Courts slice contracts four different ways, and the table below is the cheat sheet.

deeper.plain: A contract is a promise the law will back up, as long as both sides gave something and were able to agree.
deeper.picture: A handshake bet with a friend is a promise. A contract is that same promise with a referee who will actually make the loser pay.
deeper.street: Sal promises his nephew he'll give him the Astoria building someday. No consideration flows back, so it's a gift promise, not a contract. When Sal sells to Evelyn for $2.4M instead, the nephew has nothing to enforce.
deeper.stakes: Agents who treat every promise as binding mislead clients. A seller's oral "I'll give you first dibs" usually isn't a contract, and a buyer who relies on it gets burned.
deeper.exam: Definition items reward the four elements tucked inside: legally enforceable, competent parties, do or refrain from doing, consideration. A choice missing consideration describes a gift, not a contract.

head: Pair
Meaning
Real estate example
rows: Terms stated in words (oral or written) vs shown by conduct
Signed contract of sale vs a tenant paying and a landlord accepting rent
Promise for a promise vs promise for an act
Sales contract (sell for pay) vs open listing or an option
Fully performed vs still to be performed
Deed delivered at closing vs contract signed, closing next month
Binding vs no contract at all vs one side may cancel vs valid but no court will enforce
Contract to sell for an illegal use is void; a minor's contract is voidable by the minor

deeper.plain: Contracts get labeled by how they were made, what each side owes, whether it's finished, and whether it holds up.
deeper.picture: Sort a contract like a pizza order: did you say it out loud or just point (express or implied), did both sides promise or just one (bilateral or unilateral), has it been delivered yet (executed or executory), and is it a real order or a prank call (valid or void)?
deeper.street: A Ridgewood owner gives Diane an open listing on a two-family. The owner only owes a commission if the firm actually brings a buyer: that's unilateral. When the buyer signs the contract of sale, that's bilateral and executory. After the deed is delivered at closing, it's executed.
deeper.stakes: Misreading a contract's status can make you think a deal is done when it isn't. A void contract (illegal purpose) can't be fixed; a voidable one stays alive until the protected party cancels.
deeper.exam: Pairs get swapped as distractors. Option and open listing are unilateral. A minor's contract is voidable, not void. An illegal-purpose contract is void. Unenforceable means valid but no court will enforce it, like an oral real estate contract.

blocks.title: Executed does not mean signed
blocks.html: Everyday English says a contract is "executed" when signed. On the exam, an executed contract is fully performed. A signed contract waiting for closing is executory.
blocks.casual: Careful with this one. In everyday talk, "executed" means signed. On the exam, an executed contract is one that's been fully performed. A signed contract that's still waiting for closing is executory.

deeper.plain: On the test, "executed" means everything's done, not just signed.
deeper.picture: Think of a recipe. Writing the order down is executory; the meal eaten and the plates cleared is executed.
deeper.street: Leo and the Okafors sign the contract on May 1 with closing set for June 15. On May 2 Leo brags his contract is "executed". Priya corrects him: it's executory until the deed and money change hands on June 15.
deeper.stakes: Calling a pending deal "executed" in a conversation with a lender or another agent can create confusion about whether the property is actually sold.
deeper.exam: Stem says "signed but not yet closed": executory. Stem says "deed delivered, purchase price paid": executed. The word "signed" is the bait.

items: Competent parties: 18 or older and of sound mind. A minor's contract is voidable by the minor
Mutual agreement (offer and acceptance, a meeting of the minds). Acceptance must match the offer exactly. Any change is a counteroffer, which kills the original offer
Lawful objective
Consideration: something of value given by each side. A promise, money, or forbearance (giving up a legal right, like agreeing not to sue) all count
In writing for real estate, signed by the party to be charged
blocks.casual:
Five things make a contract stand up:
1. Competent parties: 18 or older and of sound mind. If a minor signs, the minor can void it.
2. Mutual agreement: offer and acceptance, a meeting of the minds. The acceptance has to match the offer exactly. Change anything and it's a counteroffer, which kills the original offer.
3. Lawful objective.
4. Consideration: each side gives something of value. A promise, money, or forbearance (giving up a legal right, like agreeing not to sue) all count.
5. In writing for real estate, signed by the party to be charged.

deeper.plain: Right people, real agreement, legal purpose, something exchanged, and for real estate, a signed writing.
deeper.picture: A contract is like a five-legged stool. Pull out any leg and it doesn't stand, it falls over.
deeper.street: The Okafors offer their brownstone at $1.65M. Leo replies "Yes, at $1.6M with a closing in August." That's not acceptance, it's a counteroffer, and the $1.65M offer is dead. If Leo later says "fine, $1.65M", he's making a new offer the Okafors can refuse.
deeper.stakes: Agents who report a counteroffer as an "acceptance" can tell a seller a deal is done when it isn't, and the seller may turn away other buyers.
deeper.exam: Any change to the offer, even a small one, is a counteroffer that terminates the original. A minor's contract is voidable by the minor only. Forbearance counts as consideration.

blocks.title: Statute of Frauds, GOL 5-703
blocks.html: The Statute of Frauds requires a contract to sell real property, or a lease longer than 1 year, to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged (or an agent authorized in writing). A separate rule, GOL 5-701, requires most finder's fee deals to be in writing, but it exempts licensed real estate brokers and salespersons. That is why a NY broker can sometimes collect on an oral listing.
blocks.casual: The Statute of Frauds (GOL 5-703) says a contract to sell real property, or a lease longer than 1 year, has to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged (or by an agent authorized in writing). Separate rule: GOL 5-701 requires most finder's fee deals to be in writing, but licensed real estate brokers and salespersons are carved out. That's why a NY broker can sometimes collect on an oral listing.

deeper.plain: Real estate sales and long leases must be on paper. Commission deals with a licensed broker don't always have to be.
deeper.picture: It's like a bank that only lets you withdraw with a signed slip. Talking to the teller isn't enough, but the bank does trust its own employees on some things without paper.
deeper.street: Diane shows a Carroll Gardens townhouse after the owner tells her by phone, "Bring me a buyer at $3M and I'll pay you 5%." The buyer closes. When the owner refuses to pay, Diane can still sue, because GOL 5-701 exempts licensed brokers from the writing requirement for commissions.
deeper.stakes: "Party to be charged" means the person being sued must have signed. A buyer can't enforce a contract the seller never signed. And an agent signing for a client needs written authority, or the signature doesn't count.
deeper.exam: Two traps: the lease writing rule is "more than 1 year", and an oral listing may be enforceable for a NY licensee. The answer "all listings must be in writing to collect" is wrong under 5-701.

blocks.q: Back to Leo's text. Which statement is most accurate?
c: A text can never satisfy the Statute of Frauds
Leo has an enforceable contract because Grace accepted
In NY practice, no binding deal exists until a formal contract is signed by both sides, so Grace can take the $1.7M offer
Grace must sell to Leo because he offered cash
blocks.x: Downstate, everyone understands that nothing binds until the attorney-drafted contract is signed and delivered, and a casual text lacks the essential terms (closing date, deed, contingencies). Electronic signatures can satisfy the statute, so 'never' is too strong.

blocks.caption: Follow an offer through counteroffer, acceptance, attorney review, contract signing with the down payment, contingencies, and closing.

head: Clause
What it does
rows: Who, what, when. Description from the deed, not just the street address
Lists what is included: appliances, window treatments, the chandelier
Down payment, financing, balance at closing
Buyer takes title subject to listed items: zoning, utility easements, covenants of record
Downstate usually bargain and sale with covenant against grantor's acts
"On or about" a date unless time is of the essence
Names the broker who brought about the sale; seller usually pays the commission
Taxes, water, fuel, rents prorated at closing
Seller holds down payment proceeds in trust to pay for any improvement work (Lien Law 13)
Buyer takes "as is" except stated items; seller delivers broom clean
The written contract is the whole deal; prior talk is merged into it
If seller cannot give insurable title, buyer gets the down payment back plus title costs, and nothing more
If buyer defaults, seller keeps the down payment as full damages
Buyer can cancel if a mortgage commitment is not obtained by a date
Delivered at closing, vacant unless tenants are listed
Seller's promises end at closing (merge into the deed) unless the contract says they survive

deeper.plain: A NY sales contract spells out who, what, how much, when, what's included, what happens if something goes wrong, and what ends at closing.
deeper.picture: Think of it as the flight manifest and safety card for the whole deal: every passenger, every bag, every emergency exit, written down before takeoff.
deeper.street: The Okafors' contract lists the Bed-Stuy lot from the deed, includes the dining room chandelier, takes title subject to a utility easement, gives Leo a mortgage contingency to July 15, prorates the property tax, and says if Leo defaults, the Okafors keep his $160,000 down payment as liquidated damages.
deeper.stakes: Leave the chandelier off and the seller can take it. Forget the mortgage contingency and a buyer who can't get financing loses the 10% deposit. Ignore the no-survival clause and a buyer finds a broken boiler a week after closing with no claim.
deeper.exam: Know a few by heart: liquidated damages equals keeping the down payment; merger clause means prior talk doesn't count; seller's liability limited to returning the deposit plus title costs; contract promises merge into the deed at closing unless they survive.

blocks.html: Extra terms go in a rider, a page attached to the printed form. If a rider conflicts with the form, the rider wins. "Time is of the essence" turns a soft closing date into a hard deadline: miss it and you are in default.
blocks.casual: Extra terms go into a rider, a page stapled onto the printed form. If the rider and the form disagree, the rider wins. And "time is of the essence" turns a soft closing date into a hard deadline: miss it and you're in default.

deeper.plain: Custom terms go on extra pages that beat the standard form. And "time is of the essence" means the date is a real deadline.
deeper.picture: A rider is the sticky note on a printed recipe that says "use half the sugar". You follow the sticky note. A time-is-of-the-essence clause is a flight departure, not a dinner reservation they'll hold for you.
deeper.street: Leo's closing is set "on or about July 1". His lender is late, and the sellers can't call him in default for a short delay. Then Priya serves a time-is-of-the-essence letter setting July 31. If Leo isn't ready then, he can lose his $160,000 deposit.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who treat a TOE date casually can forfeit their deposit. Agents who don't flag a conflicting rider can let a client believe in a term the form says otherwise about.
deeper.exam: Rider beats printed form. "On or about" gives reasonable leeway; "time is of the essence" does not. A reasonable TOE notice can convert a soft date into a hard one.

blocks.text: Binders, offers, and other deal shapes

left.title: Binder / purchase offer
items: Short memo of price and key terms
Often with a small good-faith deposit
Downstate: usually not binding, says "subject to contract"
Upstate: a signed purchase offer can become the contract

right.title: Contract of sale
items: Full attorney-drafted agreement
