10% down payment held in escrow (downstate)
Binding on signing and delivery
Governs everything through closing

deeper.plain: A binder is a quick summary of the deal; the contract of sale is the real thing. Downstate the binder usually isn't binding; upstate a signed offer can be.
deeper.picture: A binder is a restaurant waitlist slip. The contract is the actual table, the menu, and the bill.
deeper.street: In Park Slope, Jordan writes a binder for Leo at $1.2M with a $5,000 good-faith check marked "subject to contract". In Rochester, the same purchase offer on a NYS-approved form, once signed by both sides and approved by attorneys, becomes the contract itself.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who thinks a downstate binder locks the house can lose it to a higher offer before attorneys sign. An upstate seller who signs a purchase offer casually may find they're bound.
deeper.exam: Downstate: binder usually not binding, attorney drafts the contract, 10% down held by seller's attorney. Upstate: brokers may prepare purchase offers, typically with an attorney approval contingency.

blocks.html: A binder is a preliminary agreement. Any deposit with it is an earnest money deposit, showing good faith. Buyers should get it back if no contract is signed.
blocks.casual: A binder is a preliminary agreement. Any money put down with it is an earnest money deposit, which shows the buyer is serious. If no contract ever gets signed, the buyer should get that money back.

deeper.plain: A binder deposit is a good-faith gesture. If the deal never becomes a contract, it goes back to the buyer.
deeper.picture: It's like putting your jacket on a chair to save a seat. It shows you mean it, but you get the jacket back if you don't sit down.
deeper.street: Leo gives Hudson & Hart a $5,000 binder check on a Windsor Terrace condo. The seller takes a better offer before contracts. Diane returns the $5,000 from the escrow account promptly, because it was never the seller's money.
deeper.stakes: A broker who holds onto a binder deposit or hands it to the seller without a signed contract risks a DOS complaint for mishandling escrow funds, and must never mix it with the firm's own money.
deeper.exam: Earnest money shows good faith; putting down a deposit does not by itself turn a downstate binder into a binding contract. The broker holding it must keep it in a separate escrow account.

head: Arrangement
How it works
Why use it
rows: Buyer gets possession and equitable title, pays in installments; seller keeps legal title and delivers the deed when all (or an agreed part) is paid
Buyer: low cash up front, no bank loan. Seller: spreads capital gain over the years payments arrive (installment sale reporting)
Optionee pays for the right to buy at a set price within a set time; optionor must hold the offer open
Unilateral until exercised. Lease with option to buy lets a tenant lock a price
If the owner decides to sell and gets an offer, the holder may match it first
No set price. Common in leases and co-op bylaws

deeper.plain: Some deals aren't a straight sale: a buyer may pay over time, buy the right to purchase later, or get first crack if the owner ever sells.
deeper.picture: An installment contract is layaway. An option is a paid reservation at a fixed price. A right of first refusal is calling "next" on a friend's bike if they ever sell it, at whatever price someone else offers.
deeper.street: Sal sells an Astoria lot to a contractor on a land contract: the contractor moves in and pays monthly, but Sal keeps the deed until it's paid. Separately, Evelyn pays $50,000 for a 6-month option to buy a Long Island City warehouse at $8M, and her tenant in Flushing has a right of first refusal to match any offer on its building.
deeper.stakes: On a land contract, the buyer has only equitable title until the deed arrives, so seller debts can complicate things. An optionee who misses the exercise deadline loses the option money and the deal.
deeper.exam: Option: optionor (owner) is bound, optionee (buyer) is not until exercise, so it's unilateral. Right of first refusal has no preset price. Installment buyer holds equitable title; seller holds legal title.

blocks.q: A tenant paid $5,000 for the right to buy the building for $900,000 any time in the next 2 years. The owner may NOT:
c: Refuse to sell if the tenant exercises within 2 years
Keep the $5,000 if the tenant never exercises
Sell the building to someone else subject to the option
Ask the tenant whether they plan to exercise
blocks.x: An option binds the optionor to sell on the stated terms if exercised on time. The optionee is free not to buy, and the optionor keeps the consideration.

blocks.html: Assignment transfers a party's rights to someone else, but the assignor stays liable. A novation replaces the old contract or party with a new one and releases the original. A power of attorney lets an attorney-in-fact sign for a principal; for real estate it must be in writing, and recorded if used to convey a deed.
blocks.casual: Assignment hands your rights under the contract to someone else, but you're still on the hook. A novation swaps in a new contract or a new party and releases the original one. A power of attorney lets an attorney-in-fact sign for someone else. For real estate it has to be in writing, and it gets recorded if it's used to sign a deed.

deeper.plain: Assigning a contract passes it on but doesn't free you; only a novation does. A power of attorney lets someone sign for you.
deeper.picture: Assignment is handing your gym membership to a friend while your credit card stays on file. Novation is the gym canceling your membership and starting a new one in your friend's name.
deeper.street: The Okafors' son lives in Atlanta and holds their power of attorney. When Emmanuel is hospitalized during closing week, the son signs the deed as attorney-in-fact, and Priya records the POA with the deed in the Brooklyn City Register.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who assigns a contract and walks away is still liable if the assignee defaults. An unrecorded or improper POA can cloud title and delay a closing.
deeper.exam: Only novation releases the original party. Assignment leaves the assignor liable. An attorney-in-fact need not be a lawyer. POA must be in writing for real estate.

head: Remedy
When
rows: Court orders the seller to convey. Available because every parcel is unique
Amount agreed in advance, usually the down payment, as the seller's full remedy
Actual money loss proven in court
Contract is cancelled and parties are put back where they started (fraud, mutual mistake)
Court rewrites the document to match what the parties actually agreed (a typo in the lot number)

deeper.plain: When a contract breaks, the court can force the deal to happen, award money, cancel it, or fix a mistake in the paperwork.
deeper.picture: Specific performance is the ref ordering a replay. Liquidated damages is the forfeit fee printed on the sign-up sheet. Rescission is hitting undo. Reformation is fixing a typo in the scoreboard.
deeper.street: The Okafors try to back out after Leo signs, because the $1.7M buyer reappears. Leo sues for specific performance, and the court orders the Okafors to convey because their brownstone is one of a kind. If Leo had defaulted instead, the Okafors would keep his down payment as liquidated damages.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who think they can walk away by "paying damages" can be forced to close. Buyers who default lose 10%, which on a $1.6M deal is $160,000.
deeper.exam: Specific performance exists because land is unique. Liquidated damages are agreed in advance. Rescission undoes the deal (fraud, mutual mistake); reformation corrects the writing to match the real agreement.

blocks.title: Deadlines and other law
blocks.html: In NY the statute of limitations to sue for breach of contract is 6 years. The Uniform Commercial Code governs sales of goods (the washer and dryer), not land. Caveat emptor (buyer beware) is still the starting point in NY, softened by the PCDS and by the rule against active concealment. A caveat is simply a warning.
blocks.casual: In NY you have 6 years to sue for breach of contract (that's the statute of limitations). The Uniform Commercial Code covers sales of goods, like the washer and dryer, not the land itself. Caveat emptor (buyer beware) is still the starting point in NY, but it's softened by the PCDS and by the rule against actively hiding defects. And a caveat is just a warning.

deeper.plain: You get six years to sue over a broken contract. Buyers still have to look out for themselves, but sellers can't hide problems.
deeper.picture: Caveat emptor is a flea market: inspect before you buy. But if the seller paints over a crack to fool you, that's not a flea market rule, that's fraud.
deeper.street: A seller in Bay Ridge freshly paints over water stains and stacks boxes against a cracked foundation wall before Ray's inspection. After closing, the buyer finds the damage. Buyer beware doesn't protect active concealment, so the buyer has a claim.
deeper.stakes: Agents who help a seller hide defects lose the caveat emptor defense and face fraud claims plus DOS discipline. Buyers who wait more than 6 years to sue on a contract breach are out of luck.
deeper.exam: NY breach of contract statute of limitations: 6 years. UCC is goods, not real property. Caveat emptor applies in NY but not to active concealment.

blocks.q: The seller refuses to close on a Bed-Stuy house even though the buyer is ready with the money. The buyer's strongest remedy to get the house itself is:
c: Liquidated damages
Rescission
Specific performance
Reformation
blocks.x: Specific performance forces the conveyance because land is unique. Rescission would cancel the deal, the opposite of what the buyer wants.

blocks.title: Hook: Can My Lawyer Collect Within
blocks.html: Competent parties, Mutual agreement, Lawful objective, Consideration, Writing.
blocks.casual: Memory hook for the five essentials: Can My Lawyer Collect Within. Competent parties, Mutual agreement, Lawful objective, Consideration, Writing.

deeper.plain: One silly sentence holds all five essentials of a valid real estate contract.
deeper.picture: Imagine Priya at her desk in Downtown Brooklyn, tapping a fat folder and asking, "Can my lawyer collect within the week?"
deeper.street: On test day Leo blanks on whether "notarization" is an essential. He runs the hook: competent, mutual, lawful, consideration, writing. No N. He crosses it off.
deeper.stakes: Missing any one element means no valid contract, and that means no enforceable sale and possibly no commission.
deeper.exam: Distractors include notarization, recording, earnest money, and broker signature. None is an essential. Run the hook and eliminate.

story.title: Deal!!
story.setting: Bed-Stuy, a Saturday morning in April

beats.text: Grace Okafor calls Jordan at 8 am. Emmanuel is in the background making coffee loudly.
Leo texted $1.6M last night and I said Deal. Now there's a $1.7M offer. Did I just sell my house by emoji?
Let me loop in Priya. But I don't think so.
In Brooklyn, nobody's bound until the contract is signed and delivered. A text about price is not a contract of sale.
beats.tag: Downstate: binding only at signed contract

beats.text: What about the Statute of Frauds? It's in writing, sort of.
Writing is necessary, not sufficient. No closing date, no deed type, no contingencies. No meeting of the minds on the essentials.
So we can take the $1.7M?
You can counter Leo, or accept the new one. If you counter, his $1.6M is dead the moment you change a term.

check.q: Grace replies to Leo: "Yes at $1.65M." Legally, this is:
c: An acceptance
A counteroffer that rejects $1.6M
A binding contract
An option
check.x: Changing the price is a counteroffer, which rejects the original offer and creates a new one Leo may accept or not.

beats.text: And when we do sign, the buyer puts 10% down with you in escrow?
With me. And if the buyer walks without a reason the contract allows, the Okafors keep it as liquidated damages.
And if we back out?
Then the buyer can sue for specific performance. Courts treat every house as one of a kind.
Monday, the Okafors sign with the $1.7M buyer. Leo sends Jordan a spreadsheet titled 'Lessons'.
Excitement is not acceptance, and an emoji is not a deed. Paper, signatures, delivery. Then celebrate.

board.prompt: Draw the path from Leo's text to a signed contract. Mark each point where one side could still walk away.

facts.text: An express contract states its terms in words (oral or written); an implied contract is shown by conduct.
A bilateral contract is a promise for a promise; a unilateral contract is a promise for an act, such as an open listing or an option.
An executed contract is fully performed; a signed contract awaiting closing is executory.
A void contract is no contract at all (illegal purpose); a minor's contract is voidable by the minor.
A valid real estate contract needs competent parties, mutual agreement, a lawful objective, consideration and a signed writing; notarization is not required.
Acceptance must match the offer exactly; any change is a counteroffer that kills the original offer.
Consideration can be a promise, money, or forbearance (giving up a legal right, such as agreeing not to sue).
The Statute of Frauds (GOL 5-703) requires a contract to sell real property, or a lease over 1 year, to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged.
GOL 5-701 requires most finder's fee deals to be in writing but exempts licensed brokers and salespersons, so a broker can sometimes collect on an oral listing.
A merger clause makes the written contract the whole deal, merging prior talk into it.
Under the limit of seller's liability clause, a seller who cannot give insurable title returns the down payment plus title costs and owes nothing more.
Liquidated damages let the seller keep the down payment as full damages if the buyer defaults.
A contingency, such as the loan contingency, makes a party's obligation depend on an event like getting a mortgage commitment.
Unless the contract says they survive, the seller's promises end at closing and merge into the deed.
A rider attached to the printed form controls when the two conflict.
"Time is of the essence" makes the closing date a hard deadline; missing it is a default.
A downstate binder is usually not binding ("subject to contract"); upstate a signed purchase offer can become the contract.
Earnest money is a good-faith deposit with an offer or binder, returned if no contract is signed.
In an installment land contract the buyer gets possession and equitable title while the seller keeps legal title until paid.
An option binds the optionor to hold the offer open at a set price for a set time and stays unilateral until the optionee exercises it.
A right of first refusal sets no price: if the owner gets an offer, the holder may match it first.
Assignment transfers rights but leaves the assignor liable; a novation substitutes a new party or contract and releases the original.
A power of attorney lets an attorney-in-fact sign for a principal; for real estate it must be written, and recorded if used to convey a deed.
Specific performance (a court order to convey) is available because every parcel of land is unique.
Rescission cancels the contract and restores the parties (fraud, mutual mistake); reformation rewrites the document to match the real agreement.
The NY statute of limitations for breach of contract is 6 years.
The Uniform Commercial Code governs sales of goods (appliances), not land.
Caveat emptor (let the buyer beware) is still NY's starting point, softened by the PCDS and the rule against active concealment; a caveat is a warning.

lessons.title: Contract Preparation: Upstate, Downstate, and the Paper Trail
lessons.tagline: Downstate the lawyers write the contract. Upstate the broker often does. Either way, the details decide the deal.
objectives: Contrast upstate and downstate contract practice and who prepares the contract
List the documents needed to prepare a contract and what to check on the CO
Pick the best property description and explain the mortgage contingency
Explain who holds the down payment and why the Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection matters
Apply the lead paint, PCDS, and agency disclosure rules at contract time

blocks.title: Two contracts, one week
blocks.html: Jordan's cousin sells a ranch house in Amherst near Buffalo; her broker hands the buyer a pre-printed purchase offer to sign at the kitchen table. The same week the Okafors sign a 20-page contract drafted by Priya, and the buyer wires $170,000 to Priya's escrow account. Same state, two worlds. Which one is "right"?
blocks.casual: Jordan's cousin is selling a ranch house in Amherst, outside Buffalo. Her broker slides a pre-printed purchase offer across the kitchen table and the buyer signs it right there. Same week, the Okafors sign a 20-page contract Priya drafted, and their buyer wires $170,000 into Priya's escrow account. Same state, totally different worlds. So which way is "right"?

deeper.plain: New York has two normal ways to put a house under contract, depending on where you are. Both are legal.
deeper.picture: It's like ordering coffee in Brooklyn versus Buffalo. One place it's a 12-step custom order with a barista, the other it's a menu board and "medium regular". Same coffee, different custom.
deeper.street: In Amherst the broker fills in a form approved by the local bar and REALTOR association, with a $2,000 deposit and a 3-day attorney approval window. In Bed-Stuy, nothing is signed until Priya and the buyer's lawyer finish negotiating riders, and 10% goes to Priya.
deeper.stakes: A downstate agent who tries the upstate kitchen-table approach and drafts terms is practicing law without a license. An upstate agent who assumes nothing's binding until the lawyers "draft" may miss that the signed form becomes the contract.
deeper.exam: Questions ask who prepares the contract and where. Downstate: seller's attorney. Upstate: broker on an approved form with an attorney review clause. Both are correct for their region.

left.title: Downstate (NYC, Long Island, Westchester)
items: Accepted offer goes to the attorneys
Seller's attorney drafts the contract
Buyer's attorney reviews and negotiates riders
Buyer signs first with a 10% down payment; seller signs last
Brokers do not draft contracts

right.title: Upstate (Buffalo, Rochester, Albany, many others)
items: Broker fills in a standard form approved by the local bar and REALTOR association
Called a purchase offer or purchase and sale contract
Includes an attorney review (approval) clause
Deposit often smaller (a few thousand dollars), held by a broker
Becomes binding once the attorney review period passes or attorneys approve

deeper.plain: Downstate, lawyers write the contract and brokers step back. Upstate, brokers fill in a standard form and lawyers get a short window to approve it.
deeper.picture: Downstate is a tailor-made suit, measured and stitched by a professional. Upstate is a good off-the-rack suit with a quick trip to the tailor to approve the fit.
deeper.street: Tasha has clients in both places. Her Westchester buyer waits two weeks for attorneys to trade contract drafts and then wires 10%. Her Rochester buyer signs a purchase and sale form on a Tuesday with a $3,000 deposit to the broker, and once both lawyers approve, it's binding.
deeper.stakes: Getting the custom wrong costs time, and if a broker overreaches by drafting, it can cost the license. Clients relocating across the state need you to explain why the process looks different.
deeper.exam: Downstate: buyer signs first with 10%, seller signs last, brokers don't draft. Upstate: broker-prepared form, smaller deposit held by a broker, binding after attorney review passes.

blocks.html: The attorney review clause makes a broker-prepared purchase offer contingent on each side's attorney approving it within a short window. If an attorney disapproves in time, the deal is off and the deposit is returned. Why it exists: a broker who fills in blanks on an approved form is not practicing law, but a broker who drafts custom terms or riders is.
blocks.casual: The attorney review clause makes a broker-prepared purchase offer depend on each side's attorney signing off within a short window. If a lawyer says no in time, the deal's off and the deposit comes back. Why it exists: a broker filling in blanks on an approved form isn't practicing law, but a broker drafting custom terms or riders is.

deeper.plain: Brokers can fill in a form, but lawyers get the final say. That keeps brokers from practicing law.
deeper.picture: It's like a driving instructor's brake on the passenger side. The student drives, but the instructor can stop the car before anything goes wrong.
deeper.street: In Albany a buyer signs a purchase offer for $340,000 on Monday with a 3-business-day attorney approval period. Her lawyer spots that the closing date conflicts with her lease and disapproves on Wednesday. The deal ends and the broker returns her $2,500 deposit.
deeper.stakes: Miss the review window and the offer becomes a binding contract, warts and all. Brokers who add custom language outside the form lose the shield the clause provides.
deeper.exam: The attorney approval clause is the upstate safeguard. Disapproval within the time limit voids the deal and returns the deposit. Filling in blanks is not practicing law; drafting terms is.

blocks.title: Should brokers write riders?
blocks.html: No. Filling in an approved form is fine. Writing a custom rider, or telling a client what a clause legally means, is the unauthorized practice of law. Only attorneys give legal advice about the contract.
blocks.casual: Should a broker write a rider? No. Filling in an approved form is fine. Writing a custom rider, or telling a client what a clause legally means, is the unauthorized practice of law. Legal advice about the contract comes from attorneys, period.

deeper.plain: Brokers fill in blanks. Lawyers write terms and explain what they mean legally.
deeper.picture: A pharmacy tech can count pills and print the label. Only the pharmacist explains drug interactions. Same store, different licenses.
deeper.street: A seller asks Marcus what "no survival" means and whether to cross it out. Marcus says, "Nah, just strike it." The buyer later sues over a broken furnace, and Marcus's "advice" is quoted in the complaint. Diane would have said: "Ask Priya."
deeper.stakes: Unauthorized practice of law can mean DOS discipline, liability for the client's losses, and loss of commission. It also exposes the brokerage to a negligence claim.
deeper.exam: Any answer where the broker drafts a rider, interprets legal effect, or recommends a legal strategy is wrong. Correct answer: refer to an attorney.

head: Preparer
When
rows: Standard downstate. Drafts from the deed, title policy, and survey
Upstate, on an approved form with an attorney review clause
Purchase offer forms in some markets, also with attorney review
Buyer's attorney (some commercial deals), or the parties themselves with counsel

deeper.plain: Downstate the seller's lawyer writes the contract. Upstate a broker usually fills in an approved form, always with attorney review.
deeper.picture: Think of who holds the pen at a restaurant: in a fancy place the chef writes the menu, in a diner the server fills in your order on the pad.
deeper.street: Evelyn buys an office building in Melville and her own attorney drafts the contract because the deal is complex and she has leverage. That's the "other" row. Meanwhile, in Syracuse, a buyer's broker fills in an offer form for a first-time buyer with an attorney approval clause.
deeper.stakes: If you don't know who's supposed to prepare it, you may end up doing something you're not licensed to do, or waiting on paperwork nobody is drafting.
deeper.exam: Default answer for a downstate residential sale: the seller's attorney prepares the contract. If the question says "upstate" or "approved form", the broker may prepare it with attorney review.

blocks.title: Agency disclosure in broker-prepared contracts
blocks.html: When a broker prepares the contract, the RPL 443 agency disclosure must already have been given, and the signed acknowledgment should be part of the paperwork. The seller should also review the draft to confirm every fact (names, price, inclusions) before anyone signs.
blocks.casual: If a broker prepares the contract, the RPL 443 agency disclosure has to have been given already, and the signed acknowledgment should be part of the file. The seller should also read the draft to confirm every fact (names, price, what's included) before anybody signs.

deeper.plain: Before you hand over a contract you prepared, the client must already know whose side you're on, and should check every detail.
deeper.picture: It's like a waiter confirming your order before sending it to the kitchen, after first telling you which table they're serving.
deeper.street: An upstate broker prepares a purchase offer for a Niskayuna split-level. The file has the signed 443 acknowledgment from first substantive contact. The seller catches that the form lists the shed as excluded when they meant to include it, and it's fixed before signing.
deeper.stakes: Missing the agency disclosure gives DOS a clean violation to cite, and a wrong fact in the contract can lead to disputes over what was sold.
deeper.exam: RPL 443 disclosure comes at the first substantive contact, before any contract. It is not a contract itself. Keep records 3 years.

items: Prior deed: exact names of the owners, how they hold title, and the legal description
Prior title insurance policy: exceptions, easements, covenants that will be "subject to" items
Survey: encroachments, fences, driveways over the line

Certificate of occupancy (CO): does the legal use match the actual use? A "three-family" with a CO for two families is the classic problem. Also check that additions and finished basements were permitted
Personal data: names, addresses, phone numbers, marital status (a spouse may need to sign), Social Security numbers for tax reporting
Tax bills: amounts, exemptions such as STAR, and anything owed, for apportionments
blocks.casual:
What you need to prepare a contract:
Prior deed: exact owner names, how they hold title, and the legal description.
Prior title insurance policy: exceptions, easements, covenants that become "subject to" items.
Survey: encroachments, fences, driveways over the line.
Certificate of occupancy (CO): does the legal use match the real use? A "three-family" with a CO for two is the classic headache. Also check that additions and finished basements were permitted.
Personal data: names, addresses, phones, marital status (a spouse may need to sign), Social Security numbers for tax reporting.
Tax bills: amounts, exemptions like STAR, and anything owed, for apportionments.

deeper.plain: A contract is only as accurate as the documents behind it: the old deed, title policy, survey, CO, personal info, and tax bills.
deeper.picture: It's like assembling furniture: if the instruction sheet (deed) and parts list (CO, survey) don't match what's in the box, you find out halfway through.
deeper.street: Sal lists his Astoria building as a "legal 3-family". Priya pulls the CO: it says 2-family, and the basement unit was never permitted. The buyer's lender won't finance a 3-family rent roll, so the price drops by $200,000.
deeper.stakes: A wrong owner name delays closing. A CO mismatch can kill financing or trigger misrepresentation claims against the agent who advertised the illegal unit.
deeper.exam: The CO tells you the legal use. The deed gives the legal description and how title is held. A survey shows encroachments. Tax bills drive apportionments.

head: Method
Strength
rows: Most precise. Walks the boundaries from a point of beginning. Copied from the deed
Precise and common in subdivisions: lot 12, block 4 on a filed subdivision map
Section, block, and lot for tax purposes. Useful, but tax maps are not surveys
Easy to read, never enough alone in a contract

deeper.plain: There are several ways to describe land. The legal description from the deed is the precise one; the address is just a label.
deeper.picture: A street address is like saying "meet me by the big fountain". Metes and bounds is the GPS coordinates. A lot on a filed map is "seat 12, row 4" on a published seating chart.
deeper.street: A buyer's contract in Westchester describes the property only as "14 Elm Street". The seller actually owns two lots there, one with the house and one empty. The deed description makes it clear only lot 7 is sold, and the buyer's dream of a side yard vanishes.
deeper.stakes: Relying on a street address alone can mean selling the wrong land or leaving out part of it, which means a lawsuit or reformation case.
deeper.exam: Most precise: metes and bounds (and lot and block on a recorded map). Tax maps are not surveys. Street address alone is never sufficient as a legal description.

blocks.html: Which to use? The legal description from the prior deed (metes and bounds or lot on a filed map), with the tax map designation and street address added for identification.
blocks.casual: So which description do you use? The legal description from the prior deed (metes and bounds or lot on a filed map), plus the tax map designation and street address tacked on so everyone knows which place it is.

deeper.plain: Copy the deed's legal description, then add the tax lot and address so people can recognize it.
deeper.picture: It's like a passport: the official number does the legal work, but your photo and name are there so humans can recognize you.
deeper.street: Priya's contract for the Okafors reads: the legal description from their 1996 deed, plus Block 1843, Lot 22 on the NYC tax map, plus "also known as 412 Halsey Street". Every reader knows exactly what's being sold.
deeper.stakes: A description that doesn't match the deed creates a title problem. The title company may refuse to insure until it's fixed, delaying the closing.
deeper.exam: Best practice answer: use the deed's legal description. Tax map and address are supporting identification, not substitutes.

blocks.q: The best property description to put in a NY contract of sale is:
c: The street address and ZIP code
The tax map section, block, and lot only
The legal description from the seller's deed
The MLS listing description
blocks.x: The deed's legal description identifies the land precisely. Tax maps exist for assessment and are not surveys, so they supplement the legal description rather than replace it.

blocks.html: The mortgage contingency clause lets the buyer cancel and get the down payment back if a written loan commitment is not issued by a set date (often 30 to 45 days downstate). It names the loan amount, type, and maximum rate so the buyer cannot sabotage it by applying for a loan nobody would grant.
blocks.casual: The mortgage contingency clause lets the buyer cancel and get the down payment back if a written loan commitment doesn't come by a set date (often 30 to 45 days downstate). It spells out the loan amount, loan type, and max rate, so the buyer can't wriggle out by applying for a loan nobody would approve.

deeper.plain: If the buyer can't get a loan on reasonable stated terms by the deadline, they can walk with their deposit.
deeper.picture: It's like a concert ticket with a weather guarantee: if the show gets canceled, you get your money back, but you can't fake a rainstorm to get out of it.
deeper.street: Leo's contract on a $900,000 Sunset Park condo says he'll apply for a $720,000 30-year fixed at no more than 7%, commitment by August 15. If the bank says no by then, he gets his $90,000 back. If he applies for an $850,000 loan to get rejected on purpose, the contingency won't save him.
deeper.stakes: Without a contingency, a buyer who can't get financing forfeits the 10% down payment. With a sloppy one, a buyer can game it and the seller loses weeks off the market.
deeper.exam: The contingency protects the buyer. It names amount, type, rate, and deadline. Good faith application is required.

head: Financing
Contract wrinkle
rows: Amount, term, and commitment deadline stated
Required amendatory clause: buyer can walk without losing the deposit if the appraisal comes in below the price
Seller is the lender. Contract states rate, term, and the form of note and mortgage
Lender approval of the buyer and the balance being assumed are conditions

deeper.plain: How the buyer is paying changes what the contract must say, especially with FHA or VA loans, seller financing, or taking over a loan.
deeper.picture: Different loans are like different airline tickets: each has its own fine print on refunds and changes, and the contract has to match the ticket.
deeper.street: A veteran buys a $480,000 house in Staten Island with a VA loan. The appraisal comes in at $455,000. The required amendatory clause lets him walk away with his deposit, or proceed if he chooses. On another deal, Sal sells to a buyer and takes back a purchase money mortgage at 6% for 10 years.
deeper.stakes: Leaving the FHA or VA clause out of a contract can make the loan unfundable. Missing lender approval on an assumption can leave the seller still liable.
deeper.exam: FHA/VA amendatory (escape) clause: buyer isn't forced to buy if the appraisal is below the price. Purchase money mortgage: seller is the lender.

blocks.title: Commitment, not closing
blocks.html: The contingency is satisfied when the buyer gets the commitment letter. If the lender later pulls out because the buyer lost a job, many downstate contracts no longer protect the buyer. Lawyers negotiate this point.
blocks.casual: Here's the catch: the contingency is satisfied once the buyer gets the commitment letter. If the lender pulls out later because the buyer lost a job, a lot of downstate contracts don't protect the buyer anymore. That's something the lawyers negotiate.

deeper.plain: Once the bank says yes in writing, the buyer's safety net is often gone, even if the bank changes its mind later.
deeper.picture: It's like a parachute that detaches the moment you land on the first platform. If the platform collapses after that, you're on your own.
deeper.street: Leo gets his commitment on August 10. On September 1 his startup lays him off, and the lender withdraws. His contract says the contingency ended with the commitment, so the Okafors can keep his down payment if he can't close. Priya had tried to add "lender's failure to fund" language; the sellers refused.
deeper.stakes: A buyer can lose a 10% deposit for something outside their control. Agents should flag this so buyers protect their jobs and credit until closing.
deeper.exam: Satisfied by the commitment letter, not by closing or funding. If a question asks when the contingency is met, pick "issuance of a written commitment".

blocks.html: Downstate custom: the buyer puts 10% of the price down at contract signing as the down payment, held in escrow by the seller's attorney. Upstate, a smaller deposit is usually held by the listing broker in a special escrow account, never commingled with the broker's own funds.
blocks.casual: Downstate custom: the buyer puts down 10% of the price when the contract's signed. That's the down payment, held in escrow by the seller's attorney. Upstate, it's usually a smaller deposit held by the listing broker in a special escrow account, and it's never mixed with the broker's own money.

deeper.plain: Downstate buyers put 10% with the seller's lawyer. Upstate buyers usually put less with the broker. Either way it sits in escrow.
deeper.picture: Escrow is a locked tip jar on the counter: nobody grabs it until the deal tells them who gets it.
deeper.street: The Okafors' buyer wires $170,000, 10% of $1.7M, to Priya's IOLA escrow account. In Rochester, Tasha's client writes a $3,000 check to the listing broker's escrow account. Neither seller can touch that money until closing.
deeper.stakes: A broker who commingles deposit money with operating funds violates 19 NYCRR 175.1 and can lose the license. A buyer whose deposit isn't in escrow risks losing it entirely.
deeper.exam: Downstate: 10%, seller's attorney holds it. Upstate: smaller, often broker holds it. Commingling is prohibited. The deposit is not the broker's commission.

blocks.title: Why lawyers hold the money
blocks.html: If a NY attorney steals escrow money, the client can apply to the Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection, a state fund paid for by attorney registration fees. There is no equal fund for brokers. If no escrow agent is named, the money goes straight to the seller, who can spend it, and the buyer becomes an unsecured creditor if the deal dies. Always name an escrow agent.
blocks.casual: Why do lawyers hold the money downstate? If a NY attorney steals escrow funds, the client can apply to the Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection, a state fund paid for by attorney registration fees. Brokers have nothing like that. And if no escrow agent is named, the money goes straight to the seller, who can spend it, and the buyer is just an unsecured creditor if the deal dies. Always name an escrow agent.

deeper.plain: Money held by a lawyer has a state backup fund if it's stolen. Money handed straight to a seller has no protection at all.
deeper.picture: It's like checking a bag with an airline that has insurance versus handing it to a stranger at the curb who promises to bring it to your hotel.
deeper.street: A buyer in Queens skips the lawyers and hands $60,000 directly to a seller who then files for bankruptcy. The deal dies and the buyer stands in line with other creditors, probably getting pennies back. Had Priya held it in escrow, it would have been safe.
deeper.stakes: No named escrow agent can mean a buyer's entire deposit is lost. Agents should make sure the contract names who holds the money.
deeper.exam: The Lawyers' Fund is funded by attorney registration fees and covers attorney theft of client funds. No equivalent exists for brokers. Without an escrow agent, the buyer is an unsecured creditor.

blocks.q: A main advantage of having the seller's attorney hold the down payment in New York is:
c: The attorney may release it to the seller at any time
Losses from attorney theft may be reimbursed by the Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection
The money earns a guaranteed 5% return
It avoids the need for a written contract
blocks.x: The Lawyers' Fund reimburses clients for dishonest conduct by NY attorneys. An escrow agent may not release funds at will; release follows the contract terms.

blocks.title: Downstate signing sequence

items.title: Seller's attorney sends contract
items.html: By email or overnight mail to the buyer's attorney. Sending it is not an offer the buyer can accept.

items.title: Buyer signs first
items.html: With the down payment check or wire. The buyer signs first so the seller is not bound while waiting.

items.title: Seller signs last
items.html: Once funds clear. Seller keeps control until the last moment.

items.title: Delivery
items.html: A fully signed copy is delivered back. Only then is the contract binding.

blocks.casual:
How a downstate signing goes:
1. The seller's attorney sends the contract to the buyer's attorney by email or overnight. Sending it isn't an offer the buyer can just accept.
2. The buyer signs first, with the down payment check or wire, so the seller isn't locked in while waiting.
3. The seller signs last, once the funds clear. The seller stays in control until the last second.
4. A fully signed copy gets delivered back. Only then is it binding.

deeper.plain: The buyer commits first with money, the seller signs last, and nothing is binding until the signed copy is delivered.
deeper.picture: It's like a group selfie where the photographer is the last to say "ok, I'm in". Until the shutter clicks and you get the photo, nothing's captured.
deeper.street: Leo signs and wires 10% on Monday. The Okafors are slow to sign and on Wednesday a $1.75M offer comes in. Because they haven't signed and delivered, they're free to take the higher offer, and Priya returns Leo's wire. That's the downstate custom at its harshest.
deeper.stakes: Buyers get outbid after they have already signed and wired more often than they expect. Agents should keep clients calm and tell them nothing's done until delivery.
deeper.exam: Sending a contract is not an offer. Buyer signs first, seller signs last. Delivery of the signed contract makes it binding.

blocks.html: Some areas still use a sit-down signing where everyone meets, the down payment changes hands, and attorneys explain terms. Only the attorneys give legal advice there.
blocks.casual: Some places still do a sit-down signing: everyone meets, the down payment changes hands, and the attorneys walk through the terms. Only the attorneys give legal advice at that table.

deeper.plain: Sometimes everyone signs together in one room. The lawyers do the explaining.
deeper.picture: It's like a wedding rehearsal where the officiant runs the script. Guests can chat, but nobody else officiates.
deeper.street: On Long Island, Jordan's buyer and the seller meet at the seller's attorney's office in Mineola. The buyer asks Jordan whether the "as is" clause is fair. Jordan says, "That's a question for your attorney," and the buyer's lawyer explains.
deeper.stakes: A broker who explains legal terms at the table is practicing law and owns the consequences if the client misunderstands.
deeper.exam: At any signing, the broker doesn't give legal advice. Questions that put the broker in the role of explaining contract law are pointing to the wrong answer.

blocks.title: Lead paint: the syllabus typo
blocks.html: The syllabus says lead paint clauses apply to properties built "after 1978". Wrong. Federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to housing built before 1978. Seller gives the EPA pamphlet, discloses known hazards, includes the Lead Warning Statement in the contract, and gives the buyer a 10-day opportunity to test. Agents keep the records 3 years.
blocks.casual: The syllabus says lead paint clauses apply to buildings built "after 1978". That's wrong. Federal lead-based paint disclosure covers housing built before 1978. The seller hands over the EPA pamphlet, discloses any known hazards, puts the Lead Warning Statement in the contract, and gives the buyer a 10-day window to test. Agents keep the records 3 years.

deeper.plain: Older homes (pre-1978) may have lead paint. Sellers must warn buyers and give them 10 days to test.
deeper.picture: It's like the allergy warning on a menu for the old recipe: you get the warning, the ingredient list, and a chance to ask the kitchen before you order.
deeper.street: The Okafors' brownstone was built in 1899. Priya includes the Lead Warning Statement, the EPA pamphlet, and their disclosure that they don't know of hazards. Leo gets 10 days to test; he waives it in writing because he plans a gut renovation anyway.
deeper.stakes: Skipping lead disclosure exposes seller and agents to federal penalties and damages. Children are the ones who get hurt by lead exposure, so regulators take it seriously.
deeper.exam: Before 1978, not after. 10 days to test (can be waived in writing). 3 years record keeping. The agent is responsible for ensuring compliance.

blocks.title: PCDS: the $500 credit is gone
blocks.html: Under RPL Article 14, sellers of 1 to 4 family homes deliver the Property Condition Disclosure Statement before the buyer signs the contract. Old rule: a seller could skip it and give a $500 credit at closing. Since March 20, 2024 the credit option is gone, the form is mandatory, and it asks about flood zones, flood insurance, and past flood claims. Condos, co-ops, never-occupied new homes, and foreclosures are among the exemptions.
blocks.casual: Under RPL Article 14, sellers of 1 to 4 family homes must give the buyer the Property Condition Disclosure Statement before the buyer signs the contract. The old move was skipping it and giving a $500 credit at closing. Since March 20, 2024, that's over: the form is mandatory, and it now asks about flood zones, flood insurance, and past flood claims. Condos, co-ops, never-occupied new homes, and foreclosures are among the exemptions.

deeper.plain: Home sellers in NY now have to fill out the disclosure form. You can't buy your way out with $500 anymore.
deeper.picture: It used to be like a restaurant letting you skip the allergy questions for a $5 discount. Now the questions are on every order, including "did the kitchen ever flood?"
deeper.street: A Howard Beach seller wants to "just do the $500 credit like my neighbor did". Jordan explains that ended March 20, 2024. The PCDS goes out with a yes on past flood insurance claims after Sandy, and the buyer adjusts the offer knowing the flood history.
deeper.stakes: A seller who hides flood history now faces liability under the statute and possibly fraud. Agents who advise the old opt-out are giving wrong advice that can blow up a deal after closing.
deeper.exam: The $500 credit is gone. PCDS applies to 1 to 4 family homes and must be delivered before contract signing. Co-ops and condos are exempt. Flood questions are new.

blocks.title: Hook: 10, 10, 78
blocks.html: 10% down downstate. 10 days to test for lead. Lead rules cover homes built before '78.
blocks.casual: Hook: 10, 10, 78. 10% down downstate. 10 days to test for lead. Lead rules cover homes built before '78.

deeper.plain: Three numbers anchor this lesson: 10% down, 10 days, and 1978.
deeper.picture: Think of a subway platform: two 10 trains stacked up, and a '78 Mets cap on the conductor.
deeper.street: Jordan explains it to a nervous first-time buyer in a Bay Ridge coffee shop: "You're putting down 10%, you've got 10 days to test for lead because it's a 1930 building, and that's the whole math today."
deeper.stakes: Mixing up 10 days for lead testing with other deadlines, or 1978 with "after 1978", produces wrong disclosures that can come back after closing.
deeper.exam: Lead: before 1978, 10 days. Downstate down payment: 10%. Expect distractors like 7 days, 30 days, and "after 1978".

story.title: Whose Escrow Is It Anyway
story.setting: Downtown Brooklyn, Priya's conference room

beats.text: Contract day for the Okafors. Marcus drops by with his own buyer's deal, and an idea.
Why wait on lawyers? I wrote a rider for my buyer last night. Washer stays, closing in 45 days, no inspection.
You wrote a rider. That's drafting legal terms. Brokers fill in approved forms, at most. Riders are ours.
My cousin's broker in Amherst filled out the whole contract, though.
On a bar-approved form with an attorney review clause. If either lawyer disapproves in time, it's dead and the deposit goes back.
And my buyer can just hand the down payment to the seller. Saves a step.
And if the seller spends it and the deal dies, your buyer is an unsecured creditor. Name an escrow agent. Ideally an attorney.
Because of the Lawyers' Fund?
Right. If a lawyer runs off with escrow money, clients can be reimbursed. There's no such fund for brokers.

check.q: Who customarily holds the 10% down payment in a NYC residential sale?
c: The buyer's broker
The seller's attorney
The seller
The lender
check.x: Downstate custom is the seller's attorney as escrow agent, with Lawyers' Fund protection behind the attorney.

beats.text: The Okafors' house was built in 1899. So lead paint disclosure, the pamphlet, and ten days to test.
And the PCDS is signed and attached. No $500 credit since 2024.
The buyer signs first and wires $170,000. Grace and Emmanuel sign last. Priya delivers the signed copy at 4:12 pm.
Buyer signs first, seller signs last, lawyer holds the money, nobody's broker writes a rider. That's how a Brooklyn contract day should feel: boring.

board.prompt: Draw two columns, Upstate and Downstate. For each, show who drafts, who holds the deposit, how much, and when it becomes binding.

facts.text: Downstate the seller's attorney drafts the contract; upstate the broker fills in a standard form approved by the local bar and REALTOR association.
An attorney review clause makes a broker-prepared purchase offer binding only once each side's attorney approves or the review period passes.
Filling in an approved form is fine, but a broker who writes a custom rider or explains a clause's legal meaning is practicing law without a license.
When a broker prepares the contract, the RPL 443 agency disclosure must already have been given, and the seller should check the draft's facts before signing.
The preparer gathers the prior deed, prior title policy, survey, certificate of occupancy, personal data and tax bills.
The certificate of occupancy shows the legal use, which must match the actual use; a "three-family" with a two-family CO is the classic problem.
A contract should use the prior deed's legal description, adding the tax map designation and street address; tax maps are not surveys and an address is never enough alone.
The mortgage contingency names the loan amount, type and maximum rate and is satisfied when the buyer gets a written commitment by the set date.
The FHA or VA amendatory clause lets the buyer cancel without losing the deposit if the appraisal comes in below the price.
In a purchase money mortgage the seller is the lender; an assumable mortgage needs lender approval of the buyer and the balance.
Downstate the buyer puts 10% down at contract signing, held in escrow by the seller's attorney; upstate a smaller deposit is held by the broker, never commingled.
The Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection repays escrow money stolen by an attorney; with no escrow agent named, the money goes straight to the seller.
Downstate the buyer signs first with the down payment and the seller signs last; the contract binds only once a fully signed copy is delivered.
Federal lead paint disclosure covers housing built before 1978 (the syllabus's "after 1978" is a typo): EPA pamphlet, Lead Warning Statement, a 10-day chance to test, records kept 3 years.
Since March 20, 2024 the PCDS is mandatory for 1 to 4 family sellers before the buyer signs; the old $500 credit option is gone and the form asks about flooding.
Condos, co-ops, never-occupied new homes and foreclosures are among the PCDS exemptions.

lessons.title: Case file: Ten Leases on Fifth Avenue
lessons.tagline: Evelyn buys a Bay Ridge building with two stores, eight apartments, and a rent roll full of surprises.
objectives: Decide whether a commercial lease term, use clause, renewal option, or assignment is enforceable as written
Calculate percentage rent from a natural breakpoint and explain how a graduated lease differs from an index lease
Apply rent stabilization renewal, primary residence, and sublet rules to specific apartments, including what survived the 2019 repeal of luxury decontrol
Decide what kind of tenancy a holdover creates and which deposit limits apply to commercial and residential space

blocks.title: The rent roll at 78th Street
blocks.html: Evelyn Park closed last month on a four-story building on Fifth Avenue at 78th Street in Bay Ridge, built in 1928. It has two ground-floor stores and eight apartments above. One store is empty. The other is a dry cleaner whose lease ends in nine months. Of the eight apartments, six are rent-stabilized, one was legally deregulated in 2015, and one is vacant after a long renovation. Evelyn has hired Hudson & Hart to lease the store and help her manager sort out the apartments, and Diane has given the file to Jordan, with Priya on call for the lease drafting. On day one a baker named Lucia Ferrante walks in, loves the empty store, and offers Evelyn her hand: "Ten years, $6,000 a month, we start in March. Deal?" Evelyn shakes it. Is that a lease?

A lease is both a contract and a conveyance: the landlord transfers a leasehold estate (the right to possess for a term) and keeps the reversion. Because it is a contract, the parties must be competent, agree on the essential terms, have a lawful purpose, and exchange consideration. Because it conveys an interest in land for more than a year, it also has to satisfy the Statute of Frauds.

blocks.q: Lucia and Evelyn shook hands on a ten-year store lease at $6,000 a month. What do they have?
c: A binding ten-year lease, because the rent and term were stated clearly
A binding lease for one year, after which it becomes month to month
Nothing enforceable, since a lease over one year needs a signed writing
A binding lease, as long as Lucia pays the first month and takes the keys
blocks.x: Under GOL 5-703 a lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged. The handshake states a clear deal, but neither side can enforce it. The 'one year' choice is the trap: the statute does not shrink an oral long-term lease to a valid one-year lease. If Lucia moved in and paid, a court could find some tenancy from conduct, but not the ten-year term.

blocks.html: Priya drafted a real lease. Its first operative paragraph is the demising clause: "Landlord hereby leases to Tenant, and Tenant hires from Landlord, the store premises on the ground floor of 7801 Fifth Avenue, Brooklyn, as shown on Exhibit A, for a term of ten years." Those words do the conveying. Everything after them is a covenant, a promise one side makes to the other.

blocks.text: What Lucia may do in the store

blocks.html: Lucia wanted the use clause to read "for any lawful purpose," in case she ever sold the bakery. Evelyn's concern was the opposite. She already had a coffee shop two doors down as a tenant in another building, and she did not want a bar under six apartments.

blocks.q: Which use clause best protects Evelyn from a future bar or nightclub in the store?
c: "For a retail bakery and café and for no other purpose"
"For any lawful purpose"
"For retail or restaurant use as permitted by zoning law"
"For any commercial purpose consistent with the building"
blocks.x: "For no other purpose" limits the tenant to the named use, so changing to a bar would breach the lease. "Any lawful purpose" gives the tenant the most freedom, which is why tenants ask for it. The zoning choice is the trap: it sounds restrictive, but zoning on a commercial avenue often allows eating and drinking places, so it would not keep a bar out.

blocks.html: They compromised on "a retail bakery and café, including sale of beer and wine with food, and for no other purpose," with Evelyn's consent (not to be unreasonably withheld) needed for any change. Rent is quoted the commercial way, per square foot per year: the 1,200-square-foot store at $60 a foot is $72,000 a year, or $6,000 a month.
Lucia's numbers depended on a slow first year. Evelyn wanted to share in success if the bakery took off. Priya proposed a base rent that steps up, plus a percentage of sales above a breakpoint.

blocks.title: Rent rider, store lease (excerpt)
blocks.html:
Base rent. Years 1 to 3: $72,000 per year. Years 4 to 6: $78,000. Years 7 to 10: $84,000.
Percentage rent. Tenant pays 6% of gross sales in excess of the natural breakpoint for each lease year, computed as annual base rent divided by 6%.
Taxes. Tenant pays its proportionate share (22%) of any increase in real estate taxes over the base year.

blocks.q: In year 2 the bakery's gross sales are $1,450,000. How much percentage rent does Lucia owe on top of base rent?
blocks.x: The natural breakpoint is base rent divided by the percentage: $72,000 / 0.06 = $1,200,000. Sales above it are $1,450,000 - $1,200,000 = $250,000, and 6% of that is $15,000. The $87,000 choice is the trap: it is 6% of total sales, which ignores the breakpoint and charges percentage rent on sales the base rent already covers.

blocks.html: The rider combines three ideas. The stepped base rent makes it a graduated lease: increases are fixed in advance. The 6% over the breakpoint makes it a percentage lease. The tax clause makes it a partial net lease, because Lucia pays part of a property expense on top of rent.

Jordan's first draft of the listing had called it a "gross lease," because that is how apartments work: one rent, the landlord pays the building's costs. Priya corrected him. Once a tenant pays any share of taxes, insurance, or maintenance on top of rent, the lease is moving toward net. A triple net lease, typical for a freestanding pharmacy, puts all three on the tenant.

blocks.q: Lucia's lawyer suggests replacing the fixed steps with increases tied to the Consumer Price Index each year. That change would make the base rent:
c: A graduated lease, since rent still rises over time
An index lease, tied to an outside measure
A triple net lease, since the tenant absorbs inflation
A gross lease, since the landlord bears operating costs
blocks.x: An index lease adjusts rent by an outside index such as the CPI, so the amount is unknown in advance. A graduated lease fixes the steps in the lease. The graduated choice is the trap because both rise over time; the difference is whether the increase is set in the document or measured from something outside it. Net and gross describe who pays expenses, not how rent escalates.

blocks.html: The other store belongs to Kwan's Cleaners, a tenant for 22 years. Its lease ends June 30 and contains an option to renew for five years at a stated rent, exercisable "by written notice received by Landlord no later than December 31." Mr. Kwan's letter arrived January 6. He had spent $90,000 on new machines in the fall, counting on the renewal. Evelyn, who had a pharmacy interested in the space at a higher rent, asked Jordan whether the option was dead.

blocks.q: What is the best description of Kwan's position?
c: He has a statutory right to renew, since he has occupied the store more than 20 years
The option lapsed, though a court may excuse a short delay in narrow cases like his
His late notice is fine, since options in leases are interpreted against landlords
He becomes a rent-stabilized commercial tenant once the lease expires
blocks.x: Commercial tenants in New York have no statutory renewal right and no rent stabilization; renewal depends on the option, and options must be exercised on time. Courts have occasionally relieved a tenant from a short, honest delay when it made substantial improvements and the landlord suffered no prejudice. The 22-year tenancy is the trap: length of occupancy creates no renewal right for a store.

blocks.html: Evelyn decided a lawsuit with a 22-year tenant who had just bought new machines was a bad trade for a slightly higher rent. She honored the renewal. Six months later Mr. Kwan retired and sold the business to his nephew, and asked to assign the lease.

blocks.q: Kwan's store lease says the tenant may not assign without the landlord's prior written consent. What governs Evelyn's answer?
c: RPL 226-b, which says consent to assign may not be unreasonably withheld
The roommate law, which permits transfers to a family member
Nothing, since assignment of a commercial lease needs no consent
The lease's consent clause, since 226-b covers residential tenants
blocks.x: RPL 226-b covers residential leases; a store lease is governed by its own terms, so the consent clause controls. If Evelyn consents, the nephew becomes the tenant, but unless she also signs a novation releasing Kwan, Kwan stays liable for the rent. The 226-b choice is the trap: its sublet and assignment rules protect apartment tenants, not commercial ones.

blocks.html: Evelyn's rent roll for the apartments told a story of fifty years of tenancies. Jordan built a table of the four that needed decisions.

head: Apt
Status
Legal rent
The question
rows: Tenant Omar Haddad will work in Lisbon for 12 months and wants to sublet, furnished
Tenants earn about $210,000 a year combined; Evelyn wants to deregulate
Neighbors say the tenant lives in Florida 10 months a year; lease ends in 7 months
Lease ended May 31; tenant still there and paid June rent, which the manager deposited
blocks.caption: Apartments needing decisions

blocks.q: Evelyn says 3B should come out of stabilization because the rent is over $2,000 and the household earns over $175,000. What is the law today?
c: She cannot; high-rent and high-income decontrol were repealed in 2019
She can deregulate it after two years of income certifications
She can deregulate it at the next vacancy, since the rent is over $2,000
She can deregulate it if the Rent Guidelines Board approves the request
blocks.x: The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 repealed high-rent and high-income decontrol, so 3B stays stabilized regardless of rent or income. The vacancy choice is the trap: before 2019, a vacancy could push a unit over the threshold into deregulation, but that path is closed too. Units already lawfully deregulated before the 2019 law, like 4B, generally stay deregulated.

blocks.title: The syllabus still teaches luxury decontrol
blocks.html: The official syllabus describes deregulation at a $2,000 legal rent and $175,000 household income for two years. Those are pre-2019 rules. If an exam item asks whether a stabilized unit can be deregulated today because the rent or income is high, the answer is no. If it asks about a unit deregulated before June 2019, that deregulation generally stands.

3B's lease runs out in five months, so Jordan checked the renewal clock. A stabilized tenant is entitled to a renewal lease for one or two years at the tenant's choice, at the increase the Rent Guidelines Board allows for that term.

blocks.q: When must Evelyn offer 3B a renewal, and how long do the tenants have to accept?
c: 30 to 60 days before expiration; the tenant has 30 days to accept
At least 6 months before expiration; the tenant has 90 days to accept
90 to 150 days before expiration; the tenant has 60 days to accept
Any time before expiration; the tenant may accept until the lease ends
blocks.x: In NYC, the owner offers the renewal on the DHCR renewal form 90 to 150 days before the lease expires, and the tenant has 60 days to choose a one- or two-year term and sign. The 30-to-60-day choice is the trap: it echoes the HSTPA notice periods for market-rate non-renewals and rent increases, a different rule for different tenancies.

blocks.title: Stabilization in one sentence
blocks.html: In NYC, most buildings with six or more units built before 1974 are rent-stabilized under the Emergency Tenant Protection Act, with increases set by the Rent Guidelines Board and the program run by NYS Homes and Community Renewal. A 1928 building with eight apartments on Fifth Avenue in Bay Ridge is the textbook case.

The 4A tenant had lived in the building since 1991. Neighbors said he winters and summers in Sarasota now, and comes back for a few weeks in the fall. His car has Florida plates. A stabilized tenant must keep the apartment as a primary residence, judged by where the person actually lives: tax returns, voter registration, driver's license, and time spent there.

blocks.q: Evelyn wants to stop renewing 4A's lease because it is not the tenant's primary residence. What is the right process?
c: Change the locks while he is in Florida, since he does not really live there
Raise the rent to market, since non-primary units lose stabilized rents
Offer the renewal and simply refuse to cash his rent checks afterward
Serve a notice of non-renewal in the renewal window, then sue if he stays
blocks.x: A landlord who believes a stabilized unit is not the tenant's primary residence serves a notice of non-renewal in the same 90-to-150-day window instead of a renewal offer, then brings a holdover proceeding and proves the case in court. Lockouts are illegal. The rent-increase choice is the trap: losing primary residence ends the right to renew, but it does not let the owner rewrite the rent unilaterally.

blocks.html: Priya warned Evelyn that primary residence cases are won on evidence, not neighbors' gossip. Jordan helped her manager pull what an owner can lawfully gather: the tenant's voter registration (Florida, since 2021), a homestead exemption on a Sarasota condo, and months of mail piling up at the building. The non-renewal notice went out 120 days before 4A's lease ended, inside the window. A tenant who really does live in the apartment can fight it with his own records, and many do. The point of the process is that a court, not the landlord, decides.

Omar Haddad in 2A did everything by the book. He sent a certified letter, return receipt requested, asking to sublet for twelve months. It named the subtenant, her addresses, his reason (a temporary job abroad), his address in Lisbon, and attached the proposed sublease. He plans to come back. Evelyn's manager put the letter in a drawer and forgot it. Forty days later Omar's subtenant was ready to move in.

blocks.q: Evelyn's manager never answered Omar's properly sent request. Forty days have passed. What is the result under RPL 226-b?
c: The request is denied, since a sublet needs the landlord's written consent
Omar has to wait 90 days before the silence has any legal effect
The landlord's silence counts as consent, and Omar may sublet
Omar is released from his lease, and the subtenant takes over
blocks.x: In a building with four or more units, the landlord may ask for more information within 10 days and must answer within 30 days; failing to answer counts as consent. Omar stays liable on his lease. The release choice is the trap: release is the remedy when a landlord unreasonably refuses an assignment, not the effect of silence on a sublet request.

blocks.html: Because 2A is stabilized, more rules ride along. Omar must keep 2A as his primary residence and intend to return. A stabilized tenant may generally sublet for no more than two years within a four-year period, and may charge the subtenant no more than the legal rent plus a 10% surcharge if the apartment is furnished. Omar can charge $1,958, not the $3,200 a furnished Bay Ridge one-bedroom might fetch on the open market.

4B was deregulated lawfully in 2015, before the 2019 law, so it is a market-rate apartment. The tenant's one-year lease ended May 31. She stayed, sent June rent, and the manager deposited it without a word. Evelyn now wants a new two-year lease at $3,600, or the apartment back.

blocks.q: What is 4B's tenancy after the manager accepted June rent?
c: A new one-year lease on the same terms as the expired lease
A month-to-month tenancy under RPL 232-c
A tenancy at sufferance that Evelyn can end without notice
An estate for years ending the following May 31
blocks.x: In New York, when a landlord accepts rent from a holdover tenant after the lease ends, the result is a month-to-month tenancy unless the parties agree otherwise (RPL 232-c), not a renewal for another year. Before the rent was accepted she was a tenant at sufferance. The one-year renewal is the trap: it is the common-law rule in some states, but New York changed it by statute.

blocks.html: Ending that month-to-month tenancy, or raising the rent 5% or more, requires written notice under the HSTPA clocks: 4B's tenant had lived there more than two years, so Evelyn needed 90 days. Evelyn, who owns more than ten apartments across her portfolio, also asked Priya whether Good Cause Eviction applied to 4B. Priya told her it likely did, which means a renewal refusal needs a listed reason and an increase above the statutory cap is presumed unreasonable. Evelyn offered a two-year lease at a smaller increase. The tenant signed.

Lucia's first winter was rough in a way that had nothing to do with sales. The roof drain above the store's back kitchen clogged three times between December and February, and each time water came through the ceiling onto her proofing racks. She emailed Evelyn's manager after each leak. The manager sent a handyman once, who snaked the drain and left. By February Lucia was baking out of the front half of the store and throwing away dough. She called Jordan, furious, and said she was going to stop paying rent until the roof was fixed, while staying open.

blocks.q: Lucia wants to claim constructive eviction while continuing to operate in the store. What is the problem with her plan?
c: Constructive eviction requires her to leave the space it made unusable
Constructive eviction is limited to residential tenants in NY
She needs a court order first before withholding any rent
Leaks are not serious enough to count as constructive eviction
blocks.x: Constructive eviction excuses rent when the landlord's failure makes the premises (or part of them) unusable and the tenant actually leaves that space within a reasonable time. A tenant who stays put has to rely on other remedies, such as suing for breach of the landlord's repair covenant. The residential-only choice is the trap: constructive eviction is a commercial doctrine too; it is the warranty of habitability that is residential.

blocks.html: Jordan told her what Priya told him: talk to her own lawyer before withholding a dime, because commercial leases usually say rent is paid without setoff, and a store tenant has no statutory warranty of habitability to lean on. Lucia's lawyer sent a formal default notice under the lease's repair clause instead. Evelyn, who had not known how bad it was, had the roofer there the same week and gave Lucia a month's rent credit for the spoiled stock. The manager who ignored three emails no longer works for her.

Last question. Lucia's bakery lease called for a security deposit of three months' rent, $18,000. Evelyn's manager, reading the 2019 rules, worried that was illegal and asked Jordan whether to cut it to one month.

blocks.q: Is the bakery's three-month security deposit legal?
c: Yes, since the one-month cap covers residential rentals
No, because the HSTPA caps every deposit at one month's rent
No, because commercial deposits are capped at two months' rent
Yes, but the landlord has to return it within 14 days of move-out
blocks.x: The 2019 one-month cap, the 14-day return rule, and the itemized statement apply to residential rentals. Commercial deposits are set by negotiation, and three months is common. The 14-day choice is the trap: it imports the residential return deadline into a commercial lease. Whatever the amount, a deposit is the tenant's money held in trust, not the landlord's to mix with its own funds.

blocks.html: By spring the bakery was open, with a line out the door on Saturdays. The year-2 percentage rent check came in at a little over $15,000. 2A's subtenant kept the plants alive, 3B signed a two-year renewal, and the 4A case settled when the tenant agreed to surrender the apartment in exchange for moving costs.

items: A lease longer than one year must be in a signed writing; the demising clause conveys, and the rest are covenants.
"For no other purpose" locks in a use; percentage rent is charged only on sales above the breakpoint (base rent divided by the percentage).
Graduated leases fix the steps in advance; index leases follow an outside measure such as the CPI.
Commercial tenants renew only by exercising an option on time, and commercial assignment is governed by the lease, not RPL 226-b.

Stabilized units can no longer be deregulated by rent or income; renewals are offered 90 to 150 days out (NYC), primary residence is enforced through a non-renewal notice and court, and silence on a proper 226-b sublet request is consent.
Accepting rent from a holdover creates a month-to-month tenancy; residential deposit limits do not apply to stores.

lessons.title: Case file: The Power of Attorney on Arlington Avenue
lessons.tagline: A Riverdale two-family, a son signing for his mother, a tenant with a right of first refusal, and a closing nobody planned for.
objectives: Decide whether an offer, counteroffer, binder, or signed contract binds the parties at each stage of a NY sale
Apply capacity, power of attorney, and the effect of a party's death to a pending contract
Compare a right of first refusal, an option, and an installment sales contract, including when the deed is delivered and why each side might want one
Choose the right remedy (reformation, specific performance, liquidated damages) and explain the effect of a merger clause, assignment, and novation

blocks.title: Two floors, three generations
blocks.html: Dorothy Haines bought her two-family house on Arlington Avenue in Riverdale in 1971. She is 86 now, living in assisted care in Yonkers, with dementia that has advanced over two years. Her son Ken holds a durable power of attorney she signed in 2019, while she was still sharp. The upstairs apartment is rented to Ilana Vasquez, a nurse who has lived there for nine years and whose lease includes a clause Ken had forgotten about. Ken lists the house at $1,150,000. Jordan represents the buyers, Daniel Ortega and Mei Lin, who have a toddler and want to live downstairs and rent the top floor. Priya represents them as their attorney. Before anyone makes an offer, Daniel asks Jordan a question: "If Dorothy is the owner and she has dementia, can anyone actually sign a contract for this house?"

A contract needs competent parties. A person who lacks the mental capacity to understand a transaction can void a contract she signs, so a buyer should never rely on Dorothy's own signature today. The power of attorney is the answer, if it is the right kind and still in effect. A New York power of attorney is durable unless it says otherwise, meaning it keeps working after the principal loses capacity. That is the whole point of signing one while you are well.

blocks.q: What makes Ken's signature on a contract to sell the house effective?
c: His status as Dorothy's son and sole heir, which gives him authority over her property
A letter from Dorothy's doctor confirming that she can no longer manage her affairs
A valid durable power of attorney with real estate authority, used during her life
Dorothy's oral approval at the facility, repeated in front of two staff witnesses
blocks.x: An agent under a power of attorney can sign for the principal within the powers granted, and a NY power of attorney stays effective after incapacity unless it says otherwise. Being a son or heir gives Ken no authority while his mother is living. The doctor's letter is the trap: it proves incapacity, which is exactly why Dorothy cannot sign herself, but it gives Ken no power to act.

blocks.html: Priya asked for a copy of the power of attorney before any offer went in. It was the New York statutory short form, signed and acknowledged, with the real estate transactions box initialed. She noted one more thing for later: a power of attorney is used at closing by recording it with the deed, so the title company would want the original.

Daniel and Mei offered $1,100,000, with a 10% down payment and a 60-day closing. Ken answered by email the next morning: "We accept at $1,130,000." Daniel and Mei spent the day running numbers. That evening, before they replied, Ken emailed again: "Withdrawing our number. We have another offer coming. Please send your best by Friday."

blocks.q: Daniel wants to reply "We accept your $1,130,000" and hold Ken to it. Can he?
c: No, because Ken revoked his counteroffer before the buyers accepted it
Yes, because a counteroffer stays open for a reasonable time once made
Yes, because Ken's email used the word "accept," which formed a contract
No, because emails cannot create or accept offers on real property
blocks.x: Ken's "we accept at $1,130,000" changed the price, so it was a counteroffer, which rejected the buyers' offer and made a new one. An offeror may revoke an offer any time before acceptance, and Ken did. The word "accept" is the trap: acceptance must mirror the offer exactly, and any change is a counteroffer whatever it is called. Downstate, nobody is bound until a formal contract is signed anyway.

blocks.html: On Friday Daniel and Mei offered $1,140,000. Ken accepted the price. Ken's listing agent prepared a one-page binder with the price, the down payment, a target closing date, and the words "subject to a formal contract of sale satisfactory to the parties and their attorneys." The buyers signed it and gave a $5,000 good-faith deposit to the listing broker. Two days later the other buyer came back at $1,175,000.

Jordan asked why anyone bothers with a binder downstate if it binds nobody. Priya's answer: it fixes the business terms in one place so the seller's attorney can draft the contract, it signals seriousness, and it lets the listing broker take the property off the active market with some confidence. The cost is that it gives the buyers no protection against a higher bid until a real contract is signed, which is why her office aims to get a contract out within a day or two of a binder.

blocks.q: Ken has a signed binder at $1,140,000 and a new offer at $1,175,000. What is his position?
c: He is bound by the binder, since both sides signed and a deposit was paid
He may take the higher offer, but owes the buyers double their deposit
He has to accept whichever buyer's attorney delivers a contract first
He may take the higher offer, since the binder awaits a formal contract
blocks.x: A downstate binder that says it is subject to a formal contract shows intent but binds no one to sell or buy. The buyers' remedy is the return of their $5,000 good-faith deposit. The trap is the signed-and-paid answer: signatures and a deposit do not create a contract when the document itself says a later contract is needed. Upstate, a signed purchase offer can be the contract, which is why the wording matters.

blocks.html: Ken did not take it. The second buyer needed a sale of their own home first, and Priya moved fast: a full contract was in Ken's attorney's hands within two days. But Ken's attorney found the clause Ken had forgotten.

blocks.title: Lease rider, Apartment 2, paragraph 41
blocks.html: "If Landlord receives a bona fide offer to purchase the Building that Landlord is willing to accept, Landlord shall first offer to sell the Building to Tenant at the same price and on the same terms. Tenant shall have fifteen (15) days after receipt of Landlord's written notice to accept in writing. If Tenant does not accept, Landlord may sell to the offeror at that price and on those terms."

blocks.q: What does paragraph 41 require of Ken before he signs with Daniel and Mei?
c: Nothing, since the tenant holds a lease and no ownership interest in the building
Written notice to Ilana of the $1,140,000 terms, and 15 days for her to match
An offer to Ilana at the 1971 price, since her option fixed the price when signed
A sale to Ilana at any price she names, since she has priority over outside buyers
blocks.x: This is a right of first refusal: if the owner decides to sell and has an acceptable offer, the holder may match it within the stated time. Unlike an option, it sets no price in advance and does not let Ilana force a sale. The option answer is the trap: an option gives the holder the right to buy at a fixed price within a period, which this clause does not do.

blocks.html: Ken sent the notice by certified mail. Ilana did not want to lose her home and could not get a mortgage on her own: her credit had been damaged by a medical debt three years earlier. She came back with a proposal: $250,000 down, monthly payments to Dorothy for ten years, and the deed delivered when the last payment cleared.

blocks.q: Under Ilana's proposed installment sales contract, when would she receive the deed?
c: At signing, with Dorothy holding a mortgage back on the house
When the agreed payments are made; Dorothy keeps legal title until then
At signing, because her $250,000 down payment exceeds 20% of the price
