When she refinances, since installment contracts convert to mortgages by law
blocks.x: In an installment sales contract (land contract), the buyer takes possession and equitable title and pays over time, while the seller keeps legal title and delivers the deed when the agreed payments are complete. The first choice is the trap: that describes a purchase money mortgage, where the deed passes at closing and the seller becomes a lender secured by a mortgage.

blocks.html: Ilana's proposal did not match the buyers' terms, which were cash at closing. Under paragraph 41 she had to match the offer, not rewrite it, so Ken could refuse. He also asked Priya's counterpart, his own attorney, whether there was any reason to consider it anyway.

blocks.q: Why might a seller sometimes prefer an installment sales contract to a cash sale?
c: The seller keeps the property's tax deductions while the buyer pays
The seller avoids paying any transfer tax on the eventual deed
The seller can raise the price each year to match the market
The seller can spread the taxable gain over the payment years
blocks.x: Installment sale reporting lets a seller recognize the gain as payments are received instead of all in the year of sale, which can lower the tax bill. The buyer's attraction is the reverse: low cash up front and no bank loan. The transfer tax answer is the trap: deferring the deed does not make the transfer tax-free, and transfer tax is still due on the conveyance.

blocks.html: For Dorothy, who needed cash for her care, ten years of payments made no sense, and Ken declined. Ilana confirmed in writing that she would not match, and Ken was free to sign with Daniel and Mei. Ilana's lease stays in force: the buyers take the building subject to it, and she remains their tenant.

Daniel and Mei signed first and wired $114,000, 10%, to Ken's attorney's escrow account. Ken signed for Dorothy as her attorney-in-fact, and his attorney delivered a fully signed copy. Jordan, who now knows to read the vocabulary carefully, asked Priya what kind of contract they had.

blocks.q: Once both sides sign and the contract is delivered, but before closing, the contract is best described as:
c: Bilateral and executory
Unilateral and executed
Unilateral and executory
Bilateral and executed
blocks.x: A contract of sale is a promise for a promise (the seller promises to convey, the buyers promise to pay), so it is bilateral. It is executory until both sides perform at closing; only then is it executed. The executed choice is the trap, because in everyday speech a contract is "executed" when it is signed. On the exam, executed means fully performed.

blocks.html: The contract's other pages were standard Bronx fare, and Jordan read them all. The down payment paragraph named Ken's attorney as escrowee. The "subject to" paragraph listed the utility easements of record and Ilana's lease. The mortgage contingency gave the buyers 45 days to get a commitment for $800,000. The deed paragraph called for a bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts, and an apportionments clause split taxes, water, and Ilana's rent as of the closing date. The possession paragraph said the first floor would be delivered vacant and broom clean, and the second floor subject to the tenancy. Nothing in it was unusual. That is the value of a standard form: the surprises, when they come, are in what the form does not cover.

Priya added one more point for Jordan's notebook. The consideration in a contract of sale is not the down payment; it is the exchange of promises, the seller's promise to convey for the buyers' promise to pay. The $114,000 is part of the price, held in escrow as security for the buyers' performance. That matters when someone argues a contract fails because a deposit check bounced: the promises were still exchanged, and the bounced check is a default, not a missing element. It also explains why the Statute of Frauds cares about signatures rather than money. Under GOL 5-703 the contract must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged, and Ken's signature as attorney-in-fact counts because his authority itself is in writing.

blocks.text: The piano and the lot number

blocks.html: At the second walkthrough Ken told Mei, "Mom would want the piano to stay with a family. It's yours, and the snowblower too." Mei was thrilled. Neither item was in the contract, which ended with a standard paragraph: "This contract contains the entire agreement of the parties. All prior understandings and agreements are merged herein."

blocks.q: Can Daniel and Mei count on getting the piano and snowblower at closing?
c: Yes, because an oral promise about personal property is outside the Statute of Frauds
Yes, because the walkthrough statement amended the contract once Mei accepted it
Not reliably, because the merger clause makes the written contract the whole deal
Not reliably, because personal property cannot be included in a real estate sale
blocks.x: A merger clause says the written contract contains the entire agreement, so a side promise made before or outside it is hard to enforce. The fix is a short written amendment or an addition to the personal property paragraph. Goods like a piano are governed by the Uniform Commercial Code, not real property law, which is the trap: that makes the oral promise sound fine, but the merger clause still controls.

blocks.html: Priya sent a one-paragraph amendment, signed by Ken and the buyers, adding the piano and snowblower for no additional price. Then the title company found something else. The contract's legal description said "Lot 112" on the tax map. The deed into Dorothy in 1971, the survey, and the tax bills all said Lot 121. Everyone agreed the house was the house; someone in 1971 or since had flipped two digits.

blocks.q: Both sides agree the contract meant Lot 121. If Ken's attorney refused to fix the description, which remedy fits?
c: Rescission, cancelling the contract and returning the down payment
Specific performance, forcing a sale of Lot 112 as written in the contract
Liquidated damages, letting the buyers keep part of the seller's price
Reformation, correcting the writing to match what both parties intended
blocks.x: Reformation lets a court rewrite a document to reflect what the parties actually agreed when a mutual mistake, such as a transposed lot number, crept into the writing. Rescission is the trap: it undoes the deal entirely, which nobody wants here. Specific performance enforces the contract, and it would first need the description corrected to be useful.

blocks.html: No court was needed: the attorneys initialed a correction. Then Daniel's accountant suggested the buyers take title in an LLC they had formed for the rental unit, and Priya looked at the contract's assignment clause, which barred assignment without the seller's written consent.

blocks.q: Ken consents to assign the contract to the buyers' LLC. Without more, what is Daniel and Mei's position?
c: They are released, since the LLC is now the buyer of record
They are released if the LLC has more assets than they do
They remain liable on the contract unless Ken agrees to a novation
The assignment is void, since a contract to buy land cannot be assigned
blocks.x: An assignment transfers the buyers' rights to the LLC, but the original buyers stay responsible for performing unless the seller agrees to a novation, which substitutes the new party and releases the old one. The 'buyer of record' answer is the trap: who takes title and who is released from the promise are different questions.

blocks.html: Ten days before the scheduled closing, Dorothy died in her sleep. Ken called Jordan before he called the lawyers: "I can still sign as her POA, right? Nothing has to change."

blocks.q: What is the effect of Dorothy's death on Ken's power of attorney and on the contract?
c: The power of attorney continues until the closing, since it is durable
The POA ends, and the estate is bound once an executor is appointed
Both end, and the buyers get their down payment back automatically
The contract ends, but Ken may sell to the buyers under a new one as heir
blocks.x: Every power of attorney ends at the principal's death; "durable" only means it survives incapacity. A contract of sale generally binds the seller's estate, so the executor, once appointed by the Surrogate's Court, completes the sale. The durable answer is the trap. Ken may well be the executor, but he will sign under letters testamentary, not the power of attorney.

blocks.html: Dorothy's other two children, who share in the estate with Ken, raised a second issue at the funeral. They had read that an agency relationship ends when the principal dies, and they told Ken the listing broker's 5% commission had died with their mother. The listing agent called Jordan, of all people, to ask what he thought.

blocks.q: Dorothy's listing agreement ended at her death. Does the estate still owe the listing broker's commission when the sale closes?
c: Yes, since the broker produced the buyer and the broker clause binds the estate
No, because the death of the principal cancels every fee the agent was promised
No, because commissions are owed just when the original owner personally signs the deed
Yes, but the estate may reduce it by half because the broker did no work after the death
blocks.x: Death ends the agency going forward, so the broker could not find a new buyer for the estate. But this broker already procured a buyer under the listing agreement, and the signed contract names the broker and says the seller pays the commission at closing. Those obligations bind the estate like any other contract debt. The 'cancels every fee' answer is the trap: termination is not retroactive.

blocks.html: The siblings dropped the point after the estate's attorney read them the broker clause. Every NY contract of sale has one, for a reason: it records who brought about the sale, so the seller is protected against a second broker claiming the fee and the buyer represents that no other broker was involved.

Probate took longer than anyone wanted. Dorothy's will named Ken executor, but the Surrogate's Court did not issue letters testamentary for eleven weeks. The contract set closing "on or about" October 15, which in New York gives either side a reasonable adjournment. By January, Daniel and Mei's rate lock had been extended twice at their expense, and they were paying rent on an apartment they had meant to leave.

blocks.title: "On or about" versus a hard date
blocks.html: A New York contract that says closing will occur "on or about" a date allows reasonable adjournments. To make a date firm after the fact, a party sends a notice making time of the essence: clear, unequivocal, and giving a reasonable time to close. Miss that date without a lawful excuse and you are in default.

Priya sent the estate's attorney a time-of-the-essence notice setting February 20. Letters issued February 3. Then Ken, now executor and grieving, got a call from a neighbor offering $1,250,000 for the house as is, and hesitated. His siblings, who share in the estate, told him to take the higher price.

blocks.q: The buyers are ready and able to close on February 20, and the estate refuses. Which remedy gets Daniel and Mei the house itself?
c: Specific performance, a court order that the estate convey the house
Liquidated damages, keeping their down payment as full compensation
Rescission, putting the parties back where they started before signing
Compensatory damages for the extra rent and rate lock costs alone
blocks.x: Because every parcel of land is unique, a buyer who is ready, willing, and able can ask a court to order the seller to convey. Liquidated damages is the trap: in a typical NY contract it is the seller's remedy when the buyer defaults, letting the seller keep the down payment. Money damages compensate the buyers, but they do not deliver the house.

blocks.html: Priya filed nothing in the end. The estate's attorney explained to Ken and his siblings that the contract bound the estate, that a specific performance suit would freeze the house for a year, and that the buyers would likely win. The estate closed on February 20. Ilana signed a new lease with her new landlords a week later, and the piano is in Daniel and Mei's front room.

blocks.title: Signed is not executed
blocks.html: Expect an exam item that calls a signed contract "executed." In contract vocabulary, a contract waiting for closing is executory; it becomes executed when both sides have fully performed. A deed delivered at closing completes the executory contract of sale.

items: A party without capacity can void a contract; a durable power of attorney lets an agent sign through incapacity, but every power of attorney ends at death, and the estate completes a binding sale.
A changed acceptance is a counteroffer, and any offer can be revoked before acceptance. A downstate binder "subject to contract" binds no one.
A right of first refusal lets the holder match an acceptable offer; an option fixes a price the holder may choose to pay. An installment sales contract delays the deed until payments are complete.
A merger clause makes the writing the whole deal; side promises belong in a signed amendment.
Reformation fixes a mutual mistake in the writing; specific performance gets a buyer the land; assignment leaves the assignor liable unless there is a novation.

lessons.title: Case file: The Split-Level in Delmar
lessons.tagline: Upstate, the broker fills in the contract. One basement, one ex-husband, and one FHA appraisal later, that is a lot of responsibility.
objectives: Gather and check the data a broker-prepared contract needs (deed, title policy, survey, certificate of occupancy, tax bills, personal data) and spot the problem each one reveals
Decide what a broker may fill in on an approved form and what belongs to the attorneys under the attorney approval clause
Apply mortgage contingency terms for FHA, assumable, and seller financing, and decide who should hold the deposit
Apply the signing sequence and the required lead paint, PCDS, and agency disclosure steps to an upstate sale

blocks.title: A Saturday in the Capital Region
blocks.html: Megan Doyle, a friend from Jordan's Jackson Heights days, sells houses in the Capital Region for Helderberg Realty, a small firm in Delmar run by broker Paul Simms. She invited Jordan up for a weekend to see how the other half of New York does contracts. Megan's listing is a 1965 split-level on a quarter acre in the Town of Bethlehem, priced at $389,000. The seller, Linda Carver, is a teacher who divorced last year. On Saturday afternoon two buyers, Tom and Jess Brennan, decide they want it. Tom is a state employee, Jess a nurse at Albany Med, and they are financing with an FHA loan. Their buyer's agent asks Megan to "write it up tonight." In Brooklyn, Jordan would email the deal sheet to Priya. Here, Megan opens the regional purchase and sale contract form on her laptop. What does she need before she types a single word?

Upstate, the custom is the reverse of downstate. The broker fills in a standard purchase and sale contract approved by the local bar association and REALTOR association. It becomes a binding contract once signed by both sides and approved by the attorneys, or once the approval period passes without a disapproval. That attorney approval clause is the reason a broker filling in blanks on an approved form is not practicing law.

blocks.title: Two customs, one state
blocks.html: Downstate (NYC, Long Island, much of Westchester), the seller's attorney drafts the contract and holds a 10% down payment, and the buyer signs first. Upstate (the Capital Region, Rochester, Buffalo, Syracuse), the broker fills in an approved form with an attorney approval clause, and a smaller deposit is often held in the broker's escrow account. Both are legal. A licensee moving between regions has to learn the local form.
Megan's broker, Paul, insists every listing file hold six things before a contract is written. Megan pulled them up for Jordan while the Brennans' agent waited.

head: Document
What it showed
rows: Grantees: "Robert Carver and Linda Carver, his wife." Description: Lot 47 on a filed subdivision map, Map No. 4120
Exception for a 10-foot drainage easement along the rear lot line in favor of the Town
House and detached shed inside the lines; the rear neighbor's chain-link fence 2 feet onto Lot 47
Single-family dwelling, issued 1966. No later permits on file
Town and county taxes paid for the calendar year; school taxes for July to June paid in full in September; Basic STAR on the school bill
Linda: divorced 2025, lives in the house. Robert: lives in Saratoga Springs
blocks.caption: The Carver listing file

blocks.q: Based on the prior deed and Linda's personal data, who must sign the contract as seller?
c: Linda alone, because she lives in the house and the divorce gave her possession
Linda alone, because a tenancy by the entirety passes to the occupying spouse on divorce
Linda and Robert, because both are on the deed and the divorce made them co-owners
Robert alone, because the deed lists him first as the primary grantee
blocks.x: The deed names both spouses, so they took title as tenants by the entirety. A divorce converts that into a tenancy in common unless the decree transfers the house, so Robert still owns half and must sign. The occupying-spouse answer is the trap: possession under a divorce settlement is not title. Megan asked Linda for the divorce decree to confirm, which is exactly why personal data includes marital status.

blocks.html: The decree gave Linda the house but required Robert to deed his share to her "upon sale or refinance," which he had never done. Megan called Robert, who agreed to sign the contract and the deed. She put both names in the seller block, with a note for the attorneys to confirm the decree's terms.

The form asks for the property's location and description. Megan's first instinct was to type the street address and the tax map number from the tax bill (Section 85.11, Block 2, Lot 9) and move on. Paul had trained her otherwise.

blocks.q: What should Megan use to identify the property in the contract?
c: The deed's lot and map, plus the address and tax map number
The street address alone, since every buyer and lender knows the house by it
The tax map number alone, since tax maps are prepared from surveys
A new metes and bounds description Megan writes from the survey
blocks.x: The legal description comes from the prior deed, here a lot on a filed subdivision map, and the address and tax map number are added to identify the parcel. A tax map is drawn for assessment and is not a survey, which makes the tax-map choice the trap. Writing a new metes and bounds description is a job for a surveyor and the attorneys, not the broker.

blocks.html: The listing photos showed a finished lower level with a bedroom, a full bath, and a kitchenette with its own side entrance. Linda's ex-husband had built it in 2014 for his mother. The listing remarks said "in-law suite, possible income." The CO said single-family, with no permits on file since 1966.

blocks.q: What is the problem the certificate of occupancy reveals?
c: No problem, since a CO from 1966 is grandfathered for later work
The house is a legal two-family, so the buyers can count rent toward their loan
The CO has expired, since COs are renewed every ten years
The lower level lacks permits and is not a legal second unit
blocks.x: A contract preparer checks that the CO matches the actual use and that later work was permitted. Here the finished basement with a kitchen and separate entrance was never permitted, and the CO allows one family. Grandfathering is the trap: it protects a use that existed legally before a rule changed, not work done without permits afterward. COs do not expire on a schedule.

blocks.html: Paul had Megan change the listing remarks that afternoon to "finished lower level" and remove "possible income." The FHA appraiser, the town, and the buyers' attorney would all see the same CO, and a listing that promised rental income from an illegal unit was a misrepresentation waiting to happen.
Then Megan had an idea. She would add a rider: "Buyers accept the lower level in its current condition and waive any claim regarding permits." She had seen one like it in another agent's file.

blocks.q: Should Megan add her permit-waiver rider to the contract?
c: Yes, because a rider overrides the printed form and protects the seller
No, because custom legal terms are the attorneys' job, not hers
Yes, as long as the attorney approval clause lets either attorney reject it
No, because riders are not allowed in upstate purchase and sale contracts
blocks.x: Filling in the blanks of an approved form is permitted; drafting custom legal language such as a waiver of claims is the practice of law. Megan can flag the issue for both attorneys, who can draft whatever rider they negotiate. The attorney-approval choice is the trap: the review clause protects the parties, but it does not authorize the broker to write legal terms in the first place.

blocks.html: Two more items from the file went on Megan's note to the attorneys. The title policy's drainage easement would be one of the matters the buyers take title "subject to," a normal exception. The survey's fence was different: the rear neighbor's chain-link fence sat 2 feet onto Lot 47, which a new survey would show and a title insurer would list as an exception. Neither one is the broker's to resolve, but a broker who knows and says nothing has left the buyers to find out at the closing table.

blocks.q: What should Megan do about the neighbor's fence shown on the survey?
c: Nothing, since an encroachment by a neighbor is not the seller's problem
Note it for both attorneys and make sure the buyers' side knows about it
Ask the neighbor to sign a waiver giving up any claim to the 2 feet
Leave the survey out of the file so the issue does not delay the deal
blocks.x: A broker's job with survey and title issues is to flag them, accurately and early, to the people who resolve them: the attorneys and the title company. Negotiating a boundary waiver is legal work. The 'not the seller's problem' answer is the trap: an encroachment can affect marketable title and, over enough years, even ownership of the strip, so it matters to both sides.

blocks.title: "Subject to" is not "don't worry about it"
blocks.html: The contract's "subject to" paragraph lists what the buyer accepts: easements, covenants, and restrictions of record, and the state of facts a survey would show, often with the words "provided they do not render title unmarketable." A recorded drainage easement fits. A fence two feet over the line may or may not, which is exactly why the attorneys, not the agents, decide.

The Brennans' offer was $382,000 with an FHA loan of 96.5% of the price. Their agent's draft financing paragraph gave them 30 days to obtain a commitment. Megan knew the FHA form had one more requirement, and Paul confirmed it: the FHA amendatory clause.

blocks.q: The FHA appraisal comes in at $370,000, below the $382,000 price. Under the FHA amendatory clause, what can the Brennans do?
c: Nothing; FHA appraisals are advisory, so they close at $382,000
Force Linda to cut the price to $370,000 under the federal rule
Cancel, but forfeit their deposit to Linda as liquidated damages
Cancel and recover their deposit, or choose to proceed
blocks.x: The FHA amendatory clause says the buyer is not obligated to complete the purchase or lose the deposit if the FHA appraised value is less than the price, while letting the buyer proceed anyway if they choose. It does not force the seller to reduce the price, which is the trap: a lower price is a negotiation the clause makes likely, not a result it requires.

blocks.html: Linda had a question of her own. Her current mortgage, taken in 2020 when she refinanced, was an FHA loan at 3.25%. A neighbor told her the buyers could just take it over. Today's FHA rate for the Brennans was much higher.

blocks.q: If the Brennans want to assume Linda's FHA loan, how should the contract handle it?
c: Condition the deal on lender approval of the Brennans and the balance
Assumption is automatic for FHA loans, so the contract need not mention the lender
Assumption is barred for any loan made after 1989, so the idea should be dropped
Treat the assumed balance as a purchase money mortgage owed to Linda
blocks.x: FHA loans are generally assumable, but the lender must approve the new borrower's credit, and the balance being assumed affects how much cash the buyers need. The contract makes both conditions. The automatic answer is the trap: older FHA loans were freely assumable, but loans made in recent decades require a creditworthiness review. An assumed loan is the lender's loan, not seller financing.

blocks.html: The Brennans looked at it and passed: Linda's balance was only $210,000, so they would need about $170,000 in cash to assume it. Linda then offered a different kind of help: she would hold a $15,000 second mortgage herself so the Brennans could keep more cash for repairs. That would be a purchase money mortgage, with Linda as lender, and the contract would need its rate, term, and payment schedule, plus the FHA lender's approval of any secondary financing. The attorneys took that one over. In the end the Brennans used the straight FHA loan.
The Brennans offered a $5,000 deposit. The form has a blank for who holds it. Their agent left it empty and suggested the check be made out to Linda, "since it's her money anyway."

blocks.q: Who should Megan name to hold the Brennans' $5,000 deposit?
c: Linda, since the seller is entitled to the deposit once the contract is signed
Nobody, since the form allows the blank to stay empty on smaller deposits
Helderberg Realty's escrow account, or an attorney's escrow account
Megan personally, since she is the licensee who prepared the contract
blocks.x: Name an escrow agent: the listing broker's special escrow account is customary upstate, and an attorney escrow account is another option. If the seller holds the money, she can spend it, and the buyers become unsecured creditors if the deal fails. A salesperson never holds deposits personally. The 'seller's money anyway' trap ignores that the deposit is not hers until the buyers close or default.

blocks.html: Megan named Helderberg Realty as escrowee. Jordan asked why Brooklyn buyers prefer the seller's attorney to hold a much larger down payment. The answer is the Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection: if a New York attorney steals escrow funds, the client can apply to a state fund paid for by attorney registration fees. No equivalent fund backs a broker's escrow account. On $5,000, most upstate buyers accept the broker; on $114,000, most downstate buyers want the lawyer.

Before the Brennans could sign, Megan's checklist had three disclosures on it. Linda's PCDS had to reach the buyers before they signed a binding contract, so Megan emailed it to the Brennans' agent with the offer package. The agency disclosure form required by RPL 443, already signed by the Brennans with their own agent and by Linda with Megan, had to be in the file, because the broker preparing a contract must have made those disclosures. And the house was built in 1965.

blocks.q: The house was built in 1965. What lead-based paint steps belong in this contract package?
c: No steps, since the federal rule covers homes built after 1978
A lead inspection paid by the seller, with a certificate attached to the contract
The EPA pamphlet, since the disclosure form is required for rentals
Pamphlet, known-hazard disclosure, warning statement, 10-day test window
blocks.x: Federal lead rules cover housing built before 1978. The seller gives the EPA pamphlet, discloses known lead hazards and reports, the contract includes the Lead Warning Statement, and the buyer gets a 10-day opportunity to test unless waived. The seller does not have to test. The 'after 1978' choice is the trap: the official syllabus contains that typo, and the rule is the reverse.

blocks.text: Signing, delivery, and the approval period

items.title: Saturday 7 p.m.
items.html: The Brennans e-signed the offer with the FHA, inspection, and attorney approval contingencies and gave their agent the $5,000 check. Buyers sign first: they make the offer.

items.title: Sunday 10 a.m.
items.html: Megan reviewed every filled-in term with Linda and Robert (names, price, inclusions, closing date) before they signed. Robert signed from Saratoga Springs.

items.title: Sunday noon
items.html: Megan delivered the fully signed contract to the Brennans' agent. Acceptance counts when it is communicated, not when the seller privately signs.

items.title: Monday to the deadline
items.html: Each side's attorney had the approval period in the form to approve, disapprove, or propose changes.

blocks.html: Something nearly went wrong between Sunday morning and noon. At 10:40, after both sellers had signed, Linda got a text from a neighbor whose sister wanted the house at $395,000, no FHA. She called Megan and said, "I haven't sent it yet. Can I just not send it?"

blocks.q: Linda and Robert have signed the Brennans' offer, but Megan has not yet delivered it. Is Linda bound?
c: Yes, because the sellers' signatures alone formed the contract
Yes, because the buyers' deposit check was already in hand
No, because acceptance must be communicated before it binds anyone
No, because a seller may revoke during the attorney approval period
blocks.x: An offer is accepted when the acceptance is communicated to the offeror, here by delivering the signed contract. Until then Linda could decline to deliver. The deposit choice is the trap: holding a buyer's check does not accept the offer. Once delivered, the attorney approval clause gives the attorneys, not the seller personally, the right to disapprove.

blocks.html: Megan told Linda the truth: she was not yet bound, but she had told the Brennans' agent at 9 a.m. that the sellers were signing, the Brennans had an inspector booked, and the neighbor's sister had made a text, not an offer. Linda thought about it for ten minutes and told Megan to deliver. Paul's rule, which Jordan wrote down, is that the agent's job at that moment is to state the law accurately and then do what the client decides.

blocks.q: On Tuesday the Brennans' attorney writes that she approves the contract "provided the seller obtains permits or a letter of no objection for the lower level before closing." What is the effect?
c: The contract is approved, and the permit condition is added automatically
A disapproval with a proposal; binding only if both agree to it
It is ignored, since an attorney may approve or reject but cannot comment
The contract becomes binding as written once the approval period runs out
blocks.x: An approval conditioned on new terms is not an approval of the contract as written. It works as a disapproval with a proposed modification, so the parties are bound only if they agree to the change in writing. The 'added automatically' answer is the trap. It treats a counterproposal as acceptance, the same mistake as treating a changed acceptance as a contract.

blocks.html: Linda's attorney answered that the seller would not obtain permits but would give a $6,000 credit, and the buyers would take the lower level as is, as a "recreation room," not a bedroom. Both attorneys signed a short amendment. The contract was now binding, subject to the inspection and FHA contingencies.

Three weeks before the April closing, an ice storm moved through the Capital Region. On a Tuesday night a limb from the Carvers' backyard oak came down on the detached shed, flattening it and tearing a gutter off the back of the house. The house itself was sound. Linda's contractor priced the shed and gutter at $4,800. Linda called Megan before she called her insurance company: "Do the Brennans get to walk away?" Megan checked the risk of loss paragraph in the form. Like the Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act (GOL 5-1311), which applies whenever a contract is silent, it leaves the risk with the seller until legal title or possession passes to the buyer.

blocks.q: The shed and a gutter, about $4,800 of damage on a $382,000 house, are destroyed before closing while Linda still has title and possession. Under GOL 5-1311, what follows?
c: The Brennans would have to close at full price, since the loss came after they signed
The Brennans may cancel and get their deposit back, since any loss lets the buyer walk away
Either side may enforce the contract, with the price reduced by the value of the loss
Linda may cancel and return the deposit, since she cannot deliver the property described
blocks.x: When an immaterial part is destroyed without the buyer's fault, neither side loses the right to enforce the contract, and the price is reduced by the value of the loss. Cancellation with a refund is the buyer's remedy only when all or a material part is destroyed, which is the trap in the walk-away choice. The full-price choice describes the old common law rule of equitable conversion, which the statute replaced for contracts that do not say otherwise.

blocks.html: The attorneys agreed on a cleaner fix than a price cut: Linda's homeowner's insurer paid to rebuild the shed and rehang the gutter, with the work finished before the final walk-through. Then the Brennans asked for something that seemed small. The lease on their Albany apartment ended March 31, two weeks before closing. Could they have the keys on April 1, move their furniture in, and stay in the house until the closing?

blocks.q: If Linda hands the Brennans the keys and possession on April 1, two weeks before closing, what changes under GOL 5-1311?
c: Nothing, since the risk of loss stays with the seller until she delivers the deed
The risk shifts to the Brennans, who owe the price even after a later loss
The contract converts to a lease, so the Brennans become tenants at will
The risk is split, in proportion to the deposit paid and the price still owed
blocks.x: The statute moves the risk when either legal title or possession passes. Buyers who move in before closing bear a later fire or storm loss and still owe the price, unless the contract says otherwise. The deed choice is the trap: delivery of title is one trigger, not the only one. That is why attorneys who allow early occupancy write a pre-closing possession agreement covering insurance, utilities, and use and occupancy payments.

blocks.html: The attorneys said no to early keys. Instead, Linda let the Brennans store boxes in the garage under a one-page letter: no occupancy, Linda's homeowner's policy stays in place, and the Brennans' renters policy covers their belongings. The Brennans spent two weeks on a friend's couch in Slingerlands. Megan put the letter in the file.

blocks.q: At an April closing, Linda has already paid the full July to June school tax bill. How is it handled?
c: Linda is credited for the prepaid share the Brennans will use
The Brennans pay nothing, since Linda paid the bill before the contract
Linda is refunded the unused share by the school district
The Brennans are credited because the tax year is incomplete
blocks.x: Taxes paid in advance are apportioned at closing: the seller paid for months after the closing date, so the buyer reimburses that share and the seller receives a credit. The district refund is the trap: the district has the money and owes nobody a refund; the adjustment happens between buyer and seller on the closing statement.

blocks.html: The apportionments belong to the attorneys and the title company, not Megan, but she made sure they were on the list. Linda had paid the school taxes for July through June back in September. At an April closing she had prepaid about two and a half months of school taxes the Brennans would benefit from, so the closing statement would credit her for that share. Her Basic STAR benefit would not carry over; as new owners the Brennans would register for the STAR credit with the state themselves.

The Brennans closed in April, with a home inspection that found an old roof but nothing else, a $6,000 credit for the lower level, and an FHA appraisal that came in at $382,000 after all. Jordan drove home with a page of notes. Downstate, he hands paper to Priya and waits. Upstate, Megan touched every document in the file before an attorney saw it, which means she had more chances to catch problems and more chances to cross the line into legal advice. The biggest one: upstate brokers carry more paper responsibility, so they need the discipline to stop exactly where the law stops them.

items: Upstate, brokers fill in approved forms with an attorney approval clause; they do not draft riders or give legal advice. A conditional approval is a counterproposal.

The data file drives the contract: the prior deed shows who must sign and the legal description, the survey and title policy show "subject to" items, the CO shows the legal use, and the tax bills drive apportionments.
Identify the property by the deed's legal description, adding the address and tax map number; a tax map is not a survey.
FHA deals need the amendatory clause; assumptions need lender approval; seller financing needs its terms in the contract.

Name an escrow agent for the deposit; attorney escrow carries the Lawyers' Fund backstop. Until title or possession passes, the seller carries the risk of loss (GOL 5-1311): a minor loss reduces the price, and a material one lets the buyer cancel.
Before the buyer signs: the PCDS, the agency disclosure on file, and for pre-1978 homes the lead pamphlet, disclosure, warning statement, and 10-day test opportunity.

roleplays.title: Leasing Sal's 3R
roleplays.setting: Astoria, a six-unit building. Sal hired Jordan's firm to rent a vacant apartment.
roleplays.goal: Rent the unit fast while keeping every fee, deposit, and lease term inside NY law, and keep Sal as a client.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Sal Russo, an old-school Astoria landlord with six units, and later a polite applicant. Sal pushes outdated practices: a two-month deposit, a $150 application fee, a tenant-paid broker fee, a no-roommates clause, slow deposit returns, a texted rent hike, refusing a voucher, and screening out anyone with a housing court history. The applicant asks about late fees, sublets, her recent credit report, and her voucher. The learner is the landlord's leasing agent and must correct Sal using HSTPA (1-month deposit, $20 screening cap waived for a report under 30 days old, $50 or 5% late fee after 5 days, 14-day deposit return, 30/60/90-day notice), the FARE Act, RPL 235-f, RPL 226-b, RPL 227-f, and source of income protection, without losing the client. Grade on accuracy, tone, and whether every illegal term was caught.

job: a nurse at Mount Sinai Queens
a line cook in Long Island City

opening: Sal Russo's six-unit building in Astoria. Apartment {unit} is vacant at {rent} a month, and Sal hired Hudson & Hart to rent it.
On the stoop of his Astoria building, Sal hands you a typed list titled MY RULES. Unit {unit}, {rent} a month.
Leasing day for Sal's Astoria {unit} at {rent}. Sal wants a lease signed this week and has opinions about how.

say: Here's my list. Two months' security, $150 application fee, and the tenant pays your firm's fee, fifteen percent of a year. Put it in the listing.
Same as always: two months up front for security, $150 to apply, and the tenant covers your commission.

moves.text: Sal, we can take one month's security and a credit check at cost up to $20. Our fee is yours.
moves.fb: Correct on all three. HSTPA caps deposits at 1 month and screening at $20; the FARE Act makes the landlord pay the broker he hired.

moves.text: Three fixes here: one month's deposit max, screening capped at $20, and you pay us under the FARE Act.
moves.fb: Right. GOL 7-108 limits deposits, HSTPA caps screening fees, and in NYC the landlord's broker is the landlord's cost.

moves.text: Let's start with one month's deposit. I'll check on the application fee and our fee setup later.
moves.fb: The deposit fix is right, but you left an illegal fee and a FARE Act problem on the table.

moves.text: Let's do two months' deposit but skip the application fee, so it feels fair to the tenants overall.
moves.fb: Two months is illegal anywhere in NY since 2019. The deposit cap is one month's rent.

moves.text: I'll list it with the tenant paying our fee and see if anyone complains. Most tenants won't bother.
moves.fb: Charging the tenant for the landlord's broker violates the FARE Act, and the listing would advertise it.

moves.text: Two months works if the second is called last month's rent. Only the deposit part is capped.
moves.fb: Wrong. GOL 7-108 caps deposits and advance payments together at one month's rent.

say: Fine, fine. But my lease says no roommates. One name on the lease, one person in the apartment.
And no roommates. I rent to one person, I want one person living there.

moves.text: That clause is void. The roommate law lets a tenant add family and one other occupant.
moves.fb: Right. RPL 235-f makes a clause banning roommates unenforceable. The landlord may ask for occupant names.
moves.react: Sal frowns. "One other? Okay, but I want the name."

moves.text: New York's roommate law overrides that. You can ask for the occupant's name, but can't ban them.
moves.fb: Correct. RPL 235-f protects the tenant's right to an additional occupant.
moves.react: "Huh. Fine, I'll ask for names," Sal says.

moves.text: Let's soften it to 'occupants subject to landlord approval' and see how that reads to you.
moves.fb: Softer, but still misleading. Under RPL 235-f an extra occupant doesn't need approval.

moves.text: Keep the clause in. Most tenants don't know their rights, so it'll still work in practice for you.
moves.fb: Knowingly using a void clause to mislead tenants is bad faith and exposes the firm.

moves.text: That's fine for a small building. The roommate law only applies to buildings over ten units.
moves.fb: Wrong. RPL 235-f applies regardless of building size.

moves.text: Sure, we can charge an extra $100 a month for each occupant who isn't on the lease itself.
moves.fb: Charging extra for a lawful occupant penalizes a statutory right. Don't suggest it.
moves.react: Sal brightens. "Extra money? I like it."

say: Hi, I'm {applicant}, {job}. I love the place. Quick questions: what's the late fee, and can I sublet next summer while I'm away for work?
I'm {applicant}. Two things before I apply: how much is the late fee, and could I sublet for a few months next year?

moves.text: After 5 days late, it's $50 at most. For a sublet, ask Sal in writing; he can't unreasonably refuse.
moves.fb: Accurate. Late fees are the lesser of $50 or 5% after 5 days; RPL 226-b covers sublets in 4+ unit buildings.

moves.text: Late fee is capped at $50, after 5 days. Sublets need Sal's written OK, not unreasonably withheld.
moves.fb: Correct, and you add that the tenant stays responsible for the rent.

moves.text: I'm not sure on either one. You'd have to ask Sal directly, since it's his building and lease.
moves.fb: Honest, but as the agent you should know the basic statewide rules.

moves.text: Late fee is $95 after the 1st, and sublets aren't allowed in any New York City building at all.
moves.fb: Both wrong. $95 exceeds the cap, the grace period is 5 days, and RPL 226-b gives a sublet right.

moves.text: Late fees are whatever the lease says. And you can sublet freely, without asking Sal at all.
moves.fb: Late fees are capped by statute, and a sublet requires a written request and consent.

moves.text: Late fee is 10% of the rent after 3 days. Sublets are fine if you stay under six months total.
moves.fb: Wrong cap and grace period, and the sublet rule is made up.

say: Great. I have a credit report from two weeks ago. Do I still need to pay for a new one?
I just ran my own credit report last week. Does that count, or do I pay the fee anyway?

moves.text: No. If your report is under 30 days old, the screening fee is waived.
moves.fb: Right. HSTPA waives the fee when the applicant provides a background or credit check from the past 30 days.

moves.text: No. A credit or background check from the past 30 days means no new fee.
moves.fb: Correct. A recent report replaces the landlord's paid check.

moves.text: Maybe not, but Sal may want his own. I'll ask him and call back.
moves.fb: Not wrong to check, but the rule is clear: a recent report waives the fee.

moves.text: Yes, Sal requires his own report, so the $20 is due no matter what you bring.
moves.fb: The landlord may not charge the fee when the applicant supplies a recent report.

moves.text: Yes. Only reports from the last 7 days count, so you'll need a fresh one now.
moves.fb: Wrong window. The statute uses 30 days.

moves.text: Yes, and it's $50 now. The $20 cap only applies to rent stabilized apartments.
moves.fb: Wrong. The $20 cap applies to residential rentals statewide.

say: {applicant} looks good. Let's do a two-year lease. Oh, and at move-out, I'll mail the deposit whenever I get around to it.
Sign her up. And the deposit, I'll send it back when I've had time to look the place over. Couple months, maybe.

moves.text: Return it with an itemized statement within 14 days of move-out, or you can't keep any of it.
moves.fb: Correct HSTPA procedure: 14 days, itemized deductions, or the landlord forfeits the right to retain any of it.
moves.react: Sal grumbles. "Fourteen days. Okay, I'll set a reminder."

moves.text: You have 14 days after move-out, with itemized deductions. Offer a walk-through first.
moves.fb: Right. HSTPA also requires offering a pre-move-out inspection.
moves.react: "Walk-through, itemized, fourteen days. Got it," Sal says.

moves.text: Send it back soon and keep receipts for any deductions. I'll look up the exact deadline for you.
moves.fb: Good instinct, but the 14-day deadline is basic and you should state it.

moves.text: You have 30 days, which is standard. Just send a short note explaining anything you keep from it.
moves.fb: The NY deadline is 14 days, with an itemized statement. Missing it forfeits the right to keep any.
moves.react: Sal nods. "Thirty days, plenty of time."

moves.text: Whenever's fine, as long as the tenant gets it back before the next lease starts elsewhere.
moves.fb: There's a statutory deadline: 14 days after move-out.

moves.text: You have 60 days on a two-year lease. The 14-day rule only applies to one-year leases in Queens.
moves.fb: Wrong. The 14-day rule applies statewide regardless of lease length.

say: Unrelated. My tenant in 1F has been there three years. I'm raising her 8% next month. I'll just text her.
My first-floor tenant, three years in. Rent goes up 8% on the first. A text is enough, right?

moves.text: She's been there over 2 years, so raising 5% or more needs 90 days' written notice.
moves.fb: Right. HSTPA requires 30, 60, or 90 days' written notice for a 5%+ increase, by length of occupancy.
moves.react: Sal sighs. "Ninety days. Okay, a letter."

moves.text: After three years, give her written notice 90 days ahead, not a text a few weeks before.
moves.fb: Correct. Two or more years of occupancy means 90 days' written notice.

moves.text: Give her a heads-up in writing soon, and I'll double-check how much notice the law requires.
moves.fb: Writing is right, but the 90-day rule is something you should know.

moves.text: A text is fine, and one month's notice is standard for any rent increase in New York State.
moves.fb: Wrong. Notice must be written and runs 30, 60, or 90 days depending on tenancy length.

moves.text: Notice only matters if the increase is over 10%. At 8%, you can raise it whenever you like.
moves.fb: The trigger is 5%, not 10%.

moves.text: You need 30 days' notice for any tenant, no matter how long she's been living there.
moves.fb: Notice grows with occupancy: 30 days under 1 year, 60 for 1 to 2, 90 for 2+.

say: One more thing. I'd be paying part of the rent with a housing voucher. Is that okay with the landlord?
I have a CityFHEPS voucher that covers most of the rent. Will Sal take it?

moves.text: Yes. Vouchers are lawful income, and Sal can't turn you away for using one.
moves.fb: Right. Lawful source of income is protected under the NYS and NYC Human Rights Laws.

moves.text: Your voucher counts like any other income. Refusing it would be discrimination.
moves.fb: Correct. Source of income discrimination is illegal statewide.

moves.text: I think so, but let me check with Sal first and call you back about it.
moves.fb: Not a refusal, but you should state the law clearly instead of checking.

moves.text: Sorry, Sal's building is too small to have to take vouchers. Only big buildings must.
moves.fb: Wrong. Source of income protection applies regardless of building size here.

moves.text: Only if the voucher covers the full rent. Partial vouchers can be turned down legally.
moves.fb: Wrong. A voucher is lawful income whether it covers all or part of the rent.

moves.text: We take them, but voucher holders pay a two-month deposit to cover the extra risk.
moves.fb: Illegal twice: the deposit cap is one month, and different terms by income source is discrimination.

say: Run {applicant} through that tenant screening list. Anybody who's been in housing court is out.
I pay for a service that shows housing court cases. Anyone with a case, we skip.

moves.text: We can't reject {applicant} for past housing court cases. That's been barred since 2019.
moves.fb: Right. RPL 227-f prohibits refusing to rent because of a prior landlord-tenant action.
moves.react: Sal grumbles. "Then what do I check?"

moves.text: Court history can't be a reason to deny. We judge {applicant} on income and credit.
moves.fb: Correct. HSTPA banned tenant blacklisting based on housing court history.

moves.text: Let me ask Diane which screening tools our firm allows before we decide.
moves.fb: Checking is fine, but the rule is clear and you should state it.

moves.text: Good idea. Landlords can refuse anyone who's ever been sued by a past landlord in court.
moves.fb: Wrong. Refusing based on a prior landlord-tenant case is prohibited (RPL 227-f).

moves.text: Sure, as long as we reject everyone on the list, it's fair and consistent for all of them.
moves.fb: Applying an unlawful rule consistently is still unlawful.

moves.text: Fine, but only if the case is under seven years old. Older cases can't be used by anyone.
moves.fb: There's no seven-year window. The practice itself is banned.

roleplays.debrief: HSTPA rules apply statewide: deposits and advance payments capped at one month (GOL 7-108), screening at actual cost up to $20 (waived for a report under 30 days old), late fees only after 5 days at the lesser of $50 or 5%, deposits back within 14 days with an itemized statement, and 30, 60, or 90 days' written notice for a non-renewal or a 5%+ increase. Roommates (RPL 235-f), sublets in 4+ unit buildings (RPL 226-b), vouchers as lawful income, and no rejections for housing court history (RPL 227-f). In NYC, the landlord pays the broker the landlord hires (FARE Act).

questions.q: A tenant's right to possess property for a time under a lease is legally classified as:
c: Personal property
A freehold estate
Real property
An easement
questions.x: A leasehold is a non-freehold estate and is treated as personal property. Freehold is the trap: freeholds are ownership estates such as fee simple and life estates.

questions.q: Which is a non-freehold (leasehold) estate?
c: A life estate
A fee simple
An estate for years
A qualified fee
questions.x: Leaseholds include estates for years and periodic tenancies. Life estate is the trap: it is a freehold even though it ends.

questions.q: A month-to-month tenancy that renews automatically until proper notice is given is a:
c: Estate for years
Periodic tenancy
Tenancy at sufferance
Tenancy at will
questions.x: A periodic tenancy rolls over each period until notice. Estate for years is the trap: it has a fixed end date and needs no notice.

questions.q: What ends a periodic tenancy?
c: The arrival of a fixed end date
The tenant's death automatically
Only a court order
Proper notice from either party
questions.x: Periodic tenancies continue until one side gives proper notice. A fixed end date is the trap: that ends an estate for years.

questions.q: In New York, a tenant stays after the lease expires and the landlord accepts rent. Unless they agree otherwise, the tenancy becomes:
c: A new lease for the same term
A tenancy at sufferance
Month to month
A one-year renewal
questions.x: New York treats accepted rent from a holdover as creating a month-to-month tenancy. A new full term is the trap: that is the old common-law rule New York does not follow.

questions.q: A tenant who remains in possession after the lease ends, without the landlord's consent, is a:
c: Holdover tenant
Periodic tenant
Lessor
Subtenant
questions.x: Staying past the lease is holding over. Subtenant is the trap: a subtenant rents from the original tenant.

questions.q: In a lease, the lessee is the:
c: Landlord
Managing agent
Guarantor
Tenant
questions.x: The lessee receives the lease; the lessor grants it. Landlord is the trap: the landlord is the lessor.

questions.q: The party who grants a lease is the:
c: Lessee
Lessor
Vendee
Grantee
questions.x: The landlord, who grants the lease, is the lessor. Vendee is the trap: that is a buyer under a sale contract.

questions.q: The lease clause in which the landlord actually leases the premises to the tenant is the:
c: Demising clause
Habendum clause
Use clause
Escalation clause
questions.x: To demise is to lease; this clause transfers possession. Habendum is the trap: that is a deed clause defining the estate granted.

questions.q: 'Landlord hereby leases to Tenant Apartment 4B' is language from the lease's:
c: Rider
Merger clause
Demising clause
Option to renew
questions.x: That operative leasing language is the demising clause. Rider is the trap: a rider adds or changes terms in an attachment.

questions.q: A written promise in a lease or deed to do or not do something is a:
c: Contingency
Covenant
Consideration
Caveat
questions.x: Covenants are promises in a written instrument. Contingency is the trap: it is a condition that must happen before performance is due.

questions.q: A tenant's lease promise to keep the unit in good repair is an example of a:
c: Rider
Demise
Contingency
Covenant
questions.x: Promises to do or not do something are covenants. Contingency is the trap: it is a condition, not a promise.

questions.q: A tenancy created by the parties' conduct rather than by express words is a(n):
c: Express lease
Ground lease
Implied lease
Proprietary lease
questions.x: When conduct shows a landlord-tenant relationship, the lease is implied. Express lease is the trap: its terms are stated in words.

questions.q: An owner lets someone move in and accepts monthly payments, but nothing is ever written or said about a lease. The arrangement is best described as:
c: An implied lease
An express lease
A trespass
A license to enter
questions.x: Accepting rent for occupancy creates a lease by conduct. Express lease is the trap: nothing was stated.

questions.q: A long-term lease of land only, under which the tenant builds and owns the improvements, is a:
c: Gross lease
Percentage lease
Proprietary lease
Ground lease
questions.x: Ground leases often run 49 to 99 years and cover land only. Percentage lease is the trap: that ties rent to a retail tenant's sales.

questions.q: Ground leases typically run for:
c: 1 to 2 years
49 to 99 years
5 to 10 years
Month to month
questions.x: Builders need long terms to recover the cost of the improvements, so ground leases commonly run 49 to 99 years. Five to ten years is the trap: that is typical of commercial space leases.

questions.concept: Land lease under a co-op or condo
questions.q: A New York co-op building stands on land the co-op leases rather than owns. Buyers should know that:
c: The land lease's term and rent affect value
The co-op owns the land in fee
Shareholders own the land jointly
Land leases cannot be used for co-ops
questions.x: When the land is leased, the remaining term and future ground rent increases affect the apartments' value and financing. 'Owns the land in fee' is the trap: under a land lease it does not.

questions.concept: Land lease under a co-op or condo
questions.q: A condo whose building sits on leased land, rather than land owned in fee, carries an extra risk from:
c: Higher transfer taxes
Rent stabilization
Ground rent resets and lease expiration
Shorter proprietary leases
questions.x: Ground rent can reset and the lease will eventually end, which affects value. Rent stabilization is the trap: it applies to rental apartments, not condo ownership.

questions.q: In a co-op, the document that gives a shareholder the right to occupy a specific apartment is the:
c: Deed
Proprietary lease
Declaration
Offering plan
questions.x: Co-op owners hold shares plus a proprietary lease. Deed is the trap: condo owners get deeds; co-op owners do not.

questions.q: A co-op buyer receives shares in the corporation and a:
c: Warranty deed
Ground lease
Certificate of occupancy
Proprietary lease
questions.x: The proprietary lease pairs with the shares to give occupancy rights. Warranty deed is the trap: no real property deed goes to a co-op shareholder.

questions.q: A lease clause giving the tenant the right to extend for another term on stated conditions is a(n):
c: Escalation clause
Right of first refusal
Option to renew
Holdover clause
questions.x: An option to renew lets the tenant extend. Right of first refusal is the trap: it gives the right to match an offer to buy.

questions.q: A tenant's lease says she may extend for 3 more years at a stated rent if she gives notice 90 days ahead. This is an:
c: Option to renew
Option to buy
Automatic renewal
Assignment clause
questions.x: The tenant chooses whether to extend: an option to renew. Automatic renewal is the trap: that happens unless someone gives notice.

questions.q: A landlord repeatedly enters a tenant's apartment without notice or need. Which lease covenant is the landlord breaking?
c: Demise
Further assurance
Habitability only
Quiet enjoyment
questions.x: Quiet enjoyment promises undisturbed possession free of the landlord's interference. Further assurance is the trap: that is a deed covenant about signing documents.

questions.q: A landlord's covenant of quiet enjoyment protects the tenant from:
c: Rent increases at renewal
Interference with possession
Noise from the street
All repair costs
questions.x: It guarantees undisturbed possession by the landlord or anyone with better title. Street noise is the trap: ordinary outside noise is not the landlord's interference.

questions.q: In New York City, rent stabilization mostly covers apartments in buildings of:
c: Six or more units built before 1974
Any size built after 2000
Two to four units only
Condos and co-ops
questions.x: Stabilization chiefly covers pre-1974 buildings with six or more units. Two to four units is the trap: those smaller buildings are generally not covered.

questions.q: A rent-stabilized tenant is entitled to:
c: Free rent during repairs
Buy the unit at a discount
Limited increases and lease renewals
A rent freeze for life
questions.x: Stabilization caps increases and guarantees renewal leases. A lifetime freeze is the trap: increases are allowed, just limited.

questions.q: The Emergency Tenant Protection Act of 1974 lets a New York locality opt into rent stabilization when its rental vacancy rate is:
c: Under 10%
Under 5%
Over 5%
Exactly zero
questions.x: ETPA allows localities with a housing emergency, a vacancy rate below 5%, to opt in. Under 10% is the trap: the threshold is 5%.

questions.q: Which law extended rent stabilization and lets localities outside NYC with a housing emergency adopt it?
c: The FARE Act
The HSTPA's luxury decontrol
The Martin Act
The ETPA
questions.x: The Emergency Tenant Protection Act lets eligible localities opt in. The FARE Act is the trap: it governs who pays broker fees in NYC.

questions.q: Under current New York law, can a rent-stabilized apartment leave stabilization because its rent passes a high-rent threshold?
c: Yes, if rent tops $2,700
Yes, when the tenant moves out
No, that was repealed in 2019
Only in buildings over 100 units
questions.x: Luxury (high-rent) decontrol was repealed in June 2019. The dollar threshold is the trap: it reflects the old, repealed rule.

questions.q: Luxury decontrol in New York:
c: Was repealed in June 2019
Applies to every vacancy
Began in 2024
Covers only co-ops
questions.x: The 2019 tenant protection law ended high-rent and high-income decontrol. 'Applies to every vacancy' is the trap: there is no decontrol path now.

questions.q: To keep the right to renew, a rent-stabilized tenant must:
c: Earn under $100,000 a year
Pay a year's rent in advance
Live in NYC for 5 years first
Use the unit as a primary residence
questions.x: Renewal rights depend on actually living in the apartment as home. The income limit is the trap: income tests were part of repealed luxury decontrol.

questions.q: A stabilized tenant actually lives in Florida and keeps the NYC unit for visits. The landlord may:
c: Raise the rent without limit
Refuse to renew for non-primary residence
Evict without any process
Convert it to a condo immediately
questions.x: Not using the unit as a primary residence is a ground to refuse renewal, through proper legal process. Evicting without process is the trap: legal procedures still apply.

questions.q: Under New York's 2024 Good Cause Eviction law, a rent increase is presumed unreasonable above:
c: The lower of CPI plus 5% or 10%
The higher of CPI or 3%
15% in any year
Whatever the Rent Guidelines Board sets
questions.x: Good Cause presumes increases above the lower of CPI + 5% or 10% unreasonable. The Rent Guidelines Board is the trap: it sets increases for stabilized units, not Good Cause units.

questions.q: Good Cause Eviction mainly protects which tenants?
c: Rent-stabilized tenants only
Commercial tenants
Covered market-rate tenants
Co-op shareholders
questions.x: It limits evictions and non-renewals for covered market-rate apartments. Stabilized tenants are the trap: they already have their own renewal protections.

questions.q: Under the NYC FARE Act, when a landlord hires a broker to list an apartment, the broker's fee is paid by:
c: The incoming tenant
The landlord
The tenant and landlord equally
The city
questions.x: Since June 11, 2025, the party who hires the broker pays: a landlord's broker is paid by the landlord. The tenant is the trap: that was the old practice the law ended.

questions.q: The NYC FARE Act took effect on:
c: January 1, 2024
March 20, 2024
questions.x: The FARE Act became effective June 11, 2025. June 14, 2019 is the trap: that is when the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act took effect.

questions.q: A contract whose terms are stated in words, spoken or written, is:
c: Implied
Unilateral
Express
Executed
questions.x: Express contracts state their terms. Implied is the trap: its terms come from conduct.

questions.q: A buyer and seller sign a written contract of sale listing price and terms. The contract is:
c: Express
Implied
Void
Unenforceable
questions.x: Stated written terms make it express. Implied is the trap: nothing here depends on conduct.

questions.q: A contract created by the parties' actions rather than stated words is:
c: Express
Bilateral
Executory
Implied
questions.x: Conduct-based agreements are implied. Bilateral is the trap: that describes a promise exchanged for a promise.

questions.q: A broker shows a buyer homes for weeks and the buyer accepts the help, but no agreement is ever discussed. Any agency created is best described as:
c: Express
Implied
Written
Unilateral by statute
questions.x: Agency can arise from conduct, which makes it implied. Express is the trap: no terms were stated.

questions.q: An owner promises a $1,000 reward to anyone who finds her lost dog. This is a:
c: Unilateral contract
Bilateral contract
Executed contract
Void contract
questions.x: A promise exchanged for an act is unilateral; only the promisor is bound. Bilateral is the trap: that exchanges a promise for a promise.

questions.q: Which listing is often described as a unilateral contract?
c: An exclusive right to sell
A buyer agency agreement
An open listing
A lease
questions.x: In an open listing the owner promises a fee only if a broker produces a buyer, and brokers promise nothing. Exclusive right to sell is the trap: it is usually bilateral because the broker promises to market.

questions.q: A contract that has been fully performed by everyone is:
c: Executory
Executed
Voidable
Implied
questions.x: Executed means fully performed. Executory is the trap: it still has performance remaining.

questions.q: After the closing, with the deed delivered and the price paid, the contract of sale is:
c: Executory
Unilateral
Voidable
Executed
questions.x: Nothing remains to be done, so it is executed. Executory is the trap: that describes the contract before closing.

questions.q: A signed contract of sale awaiting closing is:
c: Executed
Void
Executory
Implied
questions.x: Performance remains, so it is executory. Executed is the trap: that means fully performed.

questions.q: A contract in which some performance still remains is:
c: Executory
Executed
Unenforceable
Illusory
questions.x: Remaining performance makes it executory. Executed is the trap: it is the opposite.

questions.q: A 17-year-old signs a contract to buy land. The contract is:
c: Void from the start
Fully enforceable
Voidable by the seller
Voidable by the minor
questions.x: A minor may cancel, so the contract is voidable at the minor's option. Void is the trap: it is valid until the minor chooses to cancel.

questions.q: A contract signed under duress is:
c: Void
Voidable
Executed
Unilateral
questions.x: The pressured party may cancel, which makes it voidable. Void is the trap: a void contract has no legal effect at all, such as one for an illegal purpose.

questions.q: A contract clause making the buyer's obligation depend on getting a mortgage is a:
c: Contingency
Covenant
Rider
Merger clause
questions.x: A condition that must happen before performance is due is a contingency. Covenant is the trap: that is a promise, not a condition.

questions.q: A buyer may cancel and get the deposit back if the home inspection is unsatisfactory. This term is a(n):
c: Liquidated damages clause
Time is of the essence clause
Inspection contingency
Merger clause
questions.x: It conditions the deal on a satisfactory inspection. Liquidated damages is the trap: that sets the remedy for a breach.

questions.q: A typed rider conflicts with the printed contract form. Which generally controls?
c: The printed form
The rider
Whichever was signed first
Neither; the contract is void
questions.x: Added terms reflect the parties' specific intent, so the rider controls. The printed form is the trap.

questions.q: An attachment to a contract that adds or changes terms is a:
c: Covenant
Caveat
Demise
Rider
questions.x: Riders add to or modify the main document. Caveat is the trap: it means a warning.

questions.q: A clause stating the written contract is the entire agreement, replacing earlier understandings, is a:
c: Rider
Contingency
Merger clause
Severability clause
questions.x: The merger (integration) clause wipes out prior side agreements. Severability is the trap: it keeps the rest of a contract alive if one term is invalid.

questions.q: Because of a merger clause, a buyer generally cannot enforce:
c: An earlier oral promise left out of the contract
The purchase price
The closing date
The signed riders
questions.x: A merger clause makes the writing the whole deal, so earlier side promises fall away. Signed riders are the trap: they are part of the written contract.

questions.q: A contract states closing must occur by June 1 and that 'time is of the essence.' If the buyer fails to close on June 1:
c: A reasonable delay is still allowed
The seller must wait 30 days
The contract becomes a lease
The buyer is in default
questions.x: Time of the essence makes the date strict, so missing it is a default. 'Reasonable delay' is the trap: that is the rule without the clause.

questions.q: Without a 'time is of the essence' clause, New York courts usually treat a closing date as:
c: Strict, with no delay allowed
Allowing a reasonable delay
Void
Set by the broker
questions.x: Absent the clause, a closing date is generally flexible within reason. 'Strict' is the trap: strictness requires the clause or a later notice.

questions.q: Money a buyer puts up to show good faith when making an offer or signing a contract is:
c: Earnest money
A commission
A point
Escrow fees
questions.x: Earnest money signals the buyer's seriousness. Points are the trap: they are prepaid interest on a loan.

questions.q: A broker holding a buyer's good-faith deposit must:
c: Deposit it in the operating account
Give it to the seller at once
Keep it in an escrow account
Use it for marketing costs
questions.x: Deposits are other people's money and go into escrow. The operating account is the trap: mixing funds is commingling.

questions.q: A written document authorizing someone to sign a deed on another's behalf is a:
c: Listing agreement
Power of attorney
Proprietary lease
Bill of sale
questions.x: A power of attorney appoints an attorney-in-fact. Listing agreement is the trap: it hires a broker to market property but gives no power to sign deeds.

questions.q: The person authorized to act under a power of attorney is called the:
c: Principal
Grantor
Notary public
Attorney-in-fact
questions.x: The agent under a power of attorney is the attorney-in-fact. Principal is the trap: that is the person who grants the power.

questions.q: A New York contract says the seller keeps the buyer's down payment as full damages if the buyer defaults. This is:
c: Specific performance
Rescission
Liquidated damages
Earnest money refund
questions.x: Damages agreed in advance are liquidated damages; in New York the seller keeping a 10% down payment is common. Specific performance is the trap: that forces the sale to go through.

questions.q: Liquidated damages are:
c: An amount agreed in advance for a breach
Damages a jury decides later
Punishment for fraud
Interest on a late payment
questions.x: They are set in the contract before any breach. 'Jury decides' is the trap: that describes actual damages.

questions.q: 'Caveat emptor' means:
c: Let the seller beware
Time is of the essence
The agreement is final
Let the buyer beware
questions.x: Caveat emptor puts the burden on the buyer to check condition. Seller beware is the trap: that is caveat venditor.

questions.q: Even under caveat emptor, a New York seller of a 1 to 4 family home must:
c: Pay for the buyer's inspection
Deliver the property condition disclosure
Repair every defect
Guarantee the roof
questions.x: Since March 20, 2024 sellers must give the PCDS before the buyer signs, with no $500 credit opt-out. Repairing every defect is the trap: disclosure is required, repairs are not.

questions.q: In law, a 'caveat' is:
c: A warning or formal notice
A type of lien
A contract contingency
A deed covenant
questions.x: Caveat means a warning or caution. Contingency is the trap: it is a condition in a contract.

questions.q: A note on a listing reading 'caveat: the basement floods in heavy rain' is:
c: A covenant
A rider
A warning
A demise
questions.x: That is a caution to the reader, a caveat. Covenant is the trap: a covenant is a promise.

questions.q: A lease for a fixed term with a definite ending date, such as June 1 to May 31, creates a(n):
c: Periodic estate
Estate for years
Estate at will
Holdover tenancy
questions.x: Any lease with a definite start and end is an estate for years, even if it is shorter than a year. Periodic estate is the trap: it renews automatically period to period with no fixed end.

questions.q: Under New York law, the maximum security deposit a landlord may collect for a residential apartment is:
c: Two months' rent
One and a half months' rent
Whatever the lease states
One month's rent
questions.x: HSTPA (2019) caps residential deposits at one month's rent statewide. Two months is the trap: it was common before 2019 and is now illegal.

questions.q: Monthly rent is $1,800 and the tenant pays 8 days late. The maximum late fee a New York landlord may charge is:
questions.x: The cap is the lesser of $50 or 5% of monthly rent. 5% of $1,800 is $90, which is the trap: the rule takes the lesser figure, so $50 controls. A fee is allowed because rent is more than 5 days late.

questions.q: A tenant in a Queens office has had no heat for two winter months despite repeated complaints. She moves out and stops paying rent. Her best legal theory is:
c: Actual eviction
Tenancy at sufferance
Constructive eviction
Partial eviction
questions.x: The landlord's failure made the premises unusable and she left within a reasonable time: constructive eviction. Actual eviction is the trap: it requires physical removal by the landlord or court process.

questions.q: A lease in which the tenant pays base rent plus a percentage of gross sales is a:
c: Percentage lease
Graduated rent lease
Index lease
Gross lease
questions.x: Rent tied to the tenant's sales is a percentage lease, common in malls. Graduated lease is the trap: it steps up on a fixed schedule, not on sales.

questions.q: The legal registered rent on a NYC rent-stabilized apartment rose to $3,100 in 2025 and the household earns $260,000. The landlord may:
c: Deregulate it under high-rent, high-income decontrol
Deregulate it at the next vacancy
Not deregulate it on rent or income grounds
Deregulate it after two income certifications
questions.x: HSTPA repealed high-rent vacancy decontrol and high-income decontrol in June 2019. The decontrol choice is the trap: the syllabus's $2,000 and $175,000 figures describe a rule that no longer exists.

questions.q: Dana has rented her Albany apartment for 18 months. Her landlord plans to raise the rent by 7% at renewal. How much written notice is required?
c: 30 days
60 days
90 days
No notice for market-rate units
questions.x: For occupancy of 1 to 2 years, non-renewal or an increase of 5% or more needs 60 days' notice. 90 days is the trap: it applies after 2 years of occupancy.

questions.q: Under New York's HSTPA rules, a landlord may charge an applicant each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Actual credit check cost, up to $20
One month's security deposit
The first month's rent
A $100 application processing fee
questions.x: Application fees beyond the actual cost of a background or credit check (up to $20) are banned. The $20 credit check is the trap: it looks like a fee but is the one charge the law permits.

questions.q: A tenant transfers her entire remaining lease term to a new occupant and keeps no reversion. This is a(n):
c: Sublease
Novation
Assignment
Sandwich lease
questions.x: Transferring the whole remaining term is an assignment. Sublease is the trap: it transfers only part of the term or space, and the original tenant keeps a reversion.

questions.q: The statute that lets a New York tenant share an apartment with immediate family plus one additional occupant is the:
c: Roommate law, RPL 235-f
Habitability law, RPL 235-b
Statute of Frauds, GOL 5-703
Emergency Tenant Protection Act
questions.x: RPL 235-f is the roommate law. RPL 235-b is the trap: it is the warranty of habitability, a different tenant protection with a neighboring section number.

questions.q: A contract that has been signed by both parties but has not yet closed is:
c: Executed
Void
Unilateral
Executory
questions.x: Executory means performance is still to come. Executed is the trap: in exam language it means fully performed, not merely signed.

questions.q: In New York, a contract for the sale of real property has to be in writing under:
c: The Uniform Commercial Code
The Statute of Frauds
The parol evidence rule
RPL 443
questions.x: The Statute of Frauds (GOL 5-703) requires contracts to sell land, and leases over 1 year, to be in writing. The parol evidence rule is the trap: it limits evidence that contradicts a writing but does not require one.

questions.q: A buyer offers $900,000. The seller replies, "I accept at $925,000." The buyer then says, "Fine, I'll take it at $900,000 after all." Which is true?
c: No contract exists at either price
A contract exists at $900,000
A contract exists at $925,000
The first offer binds at $900,000
questions.x: Changing a term is a counteroffer, which rejects the original offer, and the buyer never accepted $925,000. The $900,000 contract is the trap: the buyer's last message is only a new offer the seller may accept or reject.

questions.q: A contract with a 16-year-old to buy a condo is:
c: Void
Valid and binding on both
Voidable by the minor
Unenforceable by either party
questions.x: Minors lack full capacity, so the contract is voidable at the minor's option. Void is the trap: a void contract has no effect at all, but the minor may choose to honor this one.

questions.q: A remedy in which the court orders the seller to convey the property as agreed is:
c: Rescission
Specific performance
Reformation
Benefit-of-bargain damages
questions.x: Specific performance compels the conveyance and is available because each parcel is unique. Rescission is the trap: it unwinds the contract instead of enforcing it.

questions.q: A tenant's lease ended last month. He stays without the landlord's consent, and the landlord has not accepted any rent. He is a:
c: Periodic tenant
Tenant at will
Tenant at sufferance
Tenant for years
questions.x: Staying after the right ended, without consent, is a tenancy at sufferance. Tenant at will is the trap: that tenancy exists by the landlord's consent.

questions.q: Which tenancy has no set term, exists by consent, and ends on notice or on the death of either party?
c: Estate at will
Periodic estate
Estate for years
Tenancy at sufferance
questions.x: An estate at will has no fixed term and ends by notice or the death of either party. A periodic estate also ends by notice, but it renews period to period and survives a death, which is why it tempts.

questions.q: Under GOL 5-703, a New York lease must be in writing when its term is:
c: Any length at all
More than 3 years
More than 6 months
More than 1 year
questions.x: The Statute of Frauds requires a writing for leases longer than 1 year. 'Any length' is the trap: a 1-year oral lease can be enforceable.

questions.q: A landlord and tenant sign a 2-year residential lease. Which is required for it to be valid between them?
c: Notarized signatures of both
A signed writing
Recording with the county clerk
Approval by HCR
questions.x: A lease over 1 year must be in a signed writing. Notarization is needed only to record the lease, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.

questions.concept: Rent due in arrears by default
questions.q: A lease says nothing about when rent is due. Under the common-law default, rent is due:
c: In advance on the 1st
At the end of each period
Within 5 days of the 1st
Quarterly in advance
questions.x: Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is due in arrears, at the end of the period. 'In advance on the 1st' is the trap because nearly every real lease says so.

questions.concept: Rent due in arrears by default
questions.q: Why do most leases state that rent is due in advance on the first of the month?
