c: The law already requires it
It avoids the late fee cap
HSTPA requires payment in advance of the month
Otherwise rent would be due in arrears
questions.x: Without such a clause, rent would be due at the end of each period. The trap is assuming the law already requires advance payment.

questions.q: A pharmacy leases a freestanding building and pays the rent plus the property taxes, insurance, and maintenance. This is a:
c: Triple net lease
Gross lease
Percentage lease
Graduated lease
questions.x: In a triple net lease the tenant pays taxes, insurance and maintenance on top of rent. A gross lease is the opposite: the landlord pays operating costs.

questions.q: A lease whose rent rises and falls with the Consumer Price Index is a(n):
c: Gross lease
Graduated lease
Index lease
Percentage lease
questions.x: An index lease ties rent to an index such as the CPI. A graduated lease also increases rent, but on a fixed schedule, which makes it the trap.

questions.q: The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act's deposit and fee rules apply to:
c: Only rent-stabilized units in NYC
Only buildings with 6 or more units
Residential rentals statewide
Commercial and residential leases in NYC
questions.x: HSTPA's deposit, fee and notice rules cover residential rentals across the state, stabilized or market-rate. 'Only stabilized units in NYC' is the trap from its rent-regulation provisions.

questions.q: A landlord upstate rents a market-rate single-family house. Does HSTPA's one-month deposit cap apply?
c: Yes, it applies statewide
No, it covers stabilized units alone
No, it covers NYC alone
Only if the lease exceeds 1 year
questions.x: The one-month cap applies to residential rentals statewide, regulated or not. Limiting it to stabilized units is the most common wrong belief.

questions.q: In a building with 6 or more units, a landlord holding security deposits must:
c: Deposit them with the Rent Guidelines Board
Use them for repairs to common areas
Keep them in the landlord's operating account
Hold them in an interest-bearing NY account
questions.x: In 6+ unit buildings deposits go in an interest-bearing New York bank account. Keeping them in the operating account is commingling, the trap.

questions.q: On deposits held in an interest-bearing account, the landlord of a 6-unit building may keep a yearly administrative fee of:
c: All of the interest
1% of the deposit
5% of the deposit
Nothing at all
questions.x: The landlord may keep 1% a year for administration; the rest of the interest belongs to the tenant. 5% is the trap, borrowed from the late fee rule.

questions.q: A lease clause says the tenant waives the warranty of habitability. Under RPL 235-b the clause is:
c: Enforceable if initialed
Void; it cannot be waived
Valid only for market-rate units
Valid if rent is reduced
questions.x: The implied warranty of habitability cannot be waived by any lease clause. 'Valid if rent is reduced' is the trap: no trade makes the waiver good.

questions.q: A tenant has no hot water for weeks but stays in the apartment and withholds rent. Her claim is for:
c: Constructive eviction
Partial assignment
Actual eviction
Breach of habitability
questions.x: Staying and seeking a rent abatement is a habitability claim. Constructive eviction is the trap: it requires the tenant to move out.

questions.q: A commercial tenant installs dry-cleaning machines bolted to the floor. If she removes them before the lease ends, they are:
c: Trade fixtures that remain hers
Fixtures that belong to the landlord
Real property of the building
Abandoned to the landlord at once
questions.x: Commercial trade fixtures stay the tenant's if removed by the end of the lease. Treating anything bolted down as the landlord's is the trap; that is the residential default.

questions.q: A residential tenant installs a ceiling fan. The lease is silent. When the tenant leaves, the fan generally:
c: Belongs to the tenant as a trade fixture
Must be removed at the tenant's cost
Stays and becomes the landlord's
Is split between the parties
questions.x: Fixtures a residential tenant attaches generally become the landlord's unless the lease says otherwise. Trade fixtures are a commercial concept, so that choice is the trap.

questions.q: Which unit is exempt from New York's Good Cause Eviction law?
c: A market-rate unit owned by a landlord with 40 units
A unit renting at 150% of fair market rent
A unit in a building with a CO issued in 2015
A unit in a 1960 walk-up owned by a large LLC
questions.x: Buildings with a certificate of occupancy issued on or after January 1, 2009 are exempt. The luxury exemption starts at 245% of fair market rent, so 150% is the trap.

questions.q: Under Good Cause Eviction, an exempt 'small landlord' owns:
c: 10 or fewer units statewide
20 or fewer units in NYC
Any building under 6 units
One building, whatever its size
questions.x: The small landlord exemption covers owners of 10 or fewer units statewide. 'Under 6 units' is the trap, borrowed from the rent stabilization threshold.

questions.q: A tenant is 3 months behind. Which may the landlord lawfully do to regain possession?
c: Change the locks while the tenant is out
Move the tenant's things to storage
Shut off the utilities until rent is paid
Sue; only a marshal or sheriff evicts
questions.x: Only a court proceeding followed by a marshal or sheriff can remove a tenant. Lockouts, removing belongings and utility shutoffs are illegal self-help; changing the locks is the classic trap.

questions.q: After a NY landlord wins an eviction case, who physically removes the tenant?
c: The landlord or the managing agent
A city marshal or county sheriff
The local police on the landlord's call
The landlord's licensed broker
questions.x: A marshal (in NYC) or sheriff carries out the court's warrant. The landlord doing it personally is the trap: even after winning, self-help is illegal.

questions.q: Which can serve as consideration in a contract?
c: A favor done last year, before the deal
A promise not to sue (forbearance)
A gift with nothing expected in return
A hope that the deal will close soon
questions.x: Forbearance, giving up a legal right, is valid consideration, as are a promise or money. A favor already done is past consideration and does not count, the subtle trap.

questions.q: A buyer agrees not to sue a seller over a dispute in exchange for a price reduction. The buyer's promise is:
c: Not consideration, since no money moves
Void as against public policy
A gift that cannot be enforced
Valid consideration (forbearance)
questions.x: Giving up the right to sue is forbearance, which is valid consideration. The trap is thinking consideration must be money.

questions.q: Why can a licensed NY broker sometimes collect a commission on an oral listing?
c: GOL 5-701 exempts licensed brokers
The Statute of Frauds skips all agency deals
Oral listings are filed with the DOS
RPL 443 requires only verbal consent
questions.x: GOL 5-701 requires finder's fee agreements to be in writing but exempts licensed real estate brokers and salespersons. The Statute of Frauds still applies to the sale contract itself, which makes that choice the trap.

questions.q: An unlicensed finder orally agrees to a fee for bringing a buyer for a building. Under GOL 5-701, the deal is:
c: Enforceable like a broker's
Valid if witnessed by two people
Unenforceable without a writing
Valid only for commercial property
questions.x: The broker exemption in GOL 5-701 covers only licensees, so an unlicensed finder needs a signed writing. Treating the finder like a broker is the trap.

questions.q: The seller cannot deliver insurable title. Under the usual NY contract clause, the buyer gets:
c: Specific performance of the contract
Double the down payment as damages
The down payment and title costs
The rise in market value since signing
questions.x: The limit of seller's liability clause returns the down payment plus title search costs and nothing more. Specific performance is the trap: the clause replaces that remedy for title failures.

questions.q: A 'limit of seller's liability' clause mainly protects:
c: The seller from large damage claims
The buyer's lender if title fails
The broker's right to the commission
The title insurer
questions.x: It caps what the seller owes if title is uninsurable. The trap is the buyer's lender, which is protected by its own title policy, not this clause.

questions.q: Unless the contract says otherwise, the seller's promises in a NY contract of sale:
c: Survive for 6 years
Become covenants in the buyer's title policy
Survive for 1 year after closing
End at closing, merging into the deed
questions.x: Contract promises merge into the deed and end at closing unless the contract says they survive. 6 years is the trap, borrowed from the contract statute of limitations.

questions.q: A buyer wants the seller's promise to fix the roof to be enforceable after closing. The contract should:
c: Name the listing broker as the escrow agent
State that the promise survives closing
Include a merger clause
Be recorded with the deed
questions.x: Only an express survival clause keeps a promise alive after closing. A merger clause is the trap: it does the opposite, folding everything into the written deal.

questions.q: A downstate buyer signs a binder 'subject to contract' and pays a $5,000 good-faith deposit. Which is true?
c: The buyer is bound to close
It is usually not binding
The seller must refuse all other offers
The deposit becomes the down payment
questions.x: Downstate binders are usually not binding, and the deposit should be returned if no contract is signed. The trap is treating a paid deposit as proof of a contract.

questions.q: In much of upstate NY, a signed purchase offer:
c: Requires a 10% deposit with the attorney
Is only a memo for the attorneys
Must be drafted by the seller's attorney
Can become the contract once accepted
questions.x: Upstate, a signed purchase offer on an approved form can become the binding contract (subject to attorney review). The 10% deposit with an attorney is the downstate custom, the trap.

questions.q: A tenant's lease says that if the owner decides to sell and gets an offer, the tenant may buy on the same terms first. This is a(n):
c: Right of first refusal
Option to buy
Installment land contract
Lease with option
questions.x: A right of first refusal lets the holder match an offer the owner receives. An option is the trap: it sets a price in advance and the holder can buy whether or not the owner wants to sell.

questions.q: How does a right of first refusal differ from an option?
c: It fixes the price at signing, in advance
It binds the holder to buy
The holder matches an offer; no set price
It must be recorded to be valid
questions.x: A right of first refusal has no set price; the holder matches a third party's offer. Fixing the price in advance describes an option, the trap.

questions.q: A deed and contract list Lot 41 when both parties meant Lot 14. The court remedy that corrects the document is:
c: Rescission
Specific performance
Reformation
Liquidated damages
questions.x: Reformation rewrites the document to match what the parties actually agreed. Rescission is the trap: it cancels the deal instead of fixing it.

questions.q: A buyer was induced to sign by the seller's fraud and wants to undo the contract and get the deposit back. The remedy is:
c: Rescission
Reformation
Novation
Specific performance
questions.x: Rescission cancels the contract and puts the parties back where they started, a remedy for fraud or mutual mistake. Reformation would keep the deal, which this buyer does not want.

questions.q: The sale of a washer and dryer included with a house is governed by:
c: The Lien Law
The Statute of Frauds for land
RPL Article 12-A
The Uniform Commercial Code
questions.x: The UCC governs sales of goods such as appliances. The real property Statute of Frauds covers the land, which is the trap.

questions.q: The Uniform Commercial Code does NOT govern:
c: Sales of goods
Sales of land
Sales of appliances
Sales of furniture
questions.x: Land is governed by real property law, not the UCC. Appliances sound like part of the house, but they are goods, so the UCC does cover them.

questions.q: An upstate broker prepares a purchase offer for a buyer. What must already have happened?
c: The PCDS was filed with the DOS
The RPL 443 agency disclosure was given
The buyer's attorney drafted a rider
The deposit was sent to the title company
questions.x: The RPL 443 agency disclosure comes at first substantive contact, so it must be done before a broker prepares a contract. The PCDS is delivered to the buyer, not filed with the DOS, which is the trap.

questions.q: Before a broker-prepared contract is signed, the seller should:
c: Have the broker explain each clause's legal effect
Waive attorney review to speed things up
Sign first so the buyer is not bound
Check the names, price, and inclusions
questions.x: The seller should confirm every fact in the draft. Asking the broker to explain legal effect is the trap: that is legal advice only an attorney may give.

questions.q: A listing calls a house a 'three-family,' but the CO allows two families. This matters for the contract because:
c: Legal and actual use do not match
The CO sets the property's tax class
A CO matters for new construction alone
The PCDS cures any use problem
questions.x: The certificate of occupancy shows the legal use, and a third unit beyond it is illegal. The PCDS discloses conditions but cures nothing, which is the trap.

questions.q: When preparing a contract, which document shows the legal use of a building?
c: Prior owner's title policy
Real property tax bill
Certificate of occupancy
Survey
questions.x: The CO states the legal use and occupancy. The tax bill shows a property class, which is the tempting but wrong source.

questions.q: Which description should a contract of sale use?
c: The street address and the ZIP code
The tax map lot alone
The prior deed's legal description
The MLS listing's room description
questions.x: Use the legal description from the prior deed, adding the tax map designation and address for identification. The tax map lot alone is the trap: tax maps are not surveys.

questions.q: Why is a tax map designation not enough on its own to describe land in a contract?
c: Tax maps are not surveys
Tax maps list only street names
Tax maps omit the block number
Tax maps exist only in NYC
questions.x: A tax map is drawn for assessment, not boundaries, so it cannot replace a legal description. Tax maps do show section, block and lot, so 'omit the block' is wrong.

questions.q: A buyer with an FHA loan signs a contract at $500,000; the appraisal comes in at $480,000. Under the amendatory clause, the buyer:
c: Must pay the gap in cash
Must switch to a VA loan instead
Loses the deposit if she cancels
May cancel and keep the deposit
questions.x: The required FHA/VA amendatory clause lets the buyer walk without losing the deposit when the appraisal is below the price. Losing the deposit is the trap from ordinary contracts without the clause.

questions.q: The FHA or VA amendatory clause protects the buyer when:
c: The seller fails to deliver insurable title
The appraisal is below the price
The buyer loses her job after commitment
The home inspection finds defects
questions.x: The clause is about appraisal shortfalls on FHA and VA loans. Losing a job after commitment is the trap: many contracts leave the buyer unprotected once the commitment issues.

questions.q: In a contract with a purchase money mortgage, the lender is:
c: A federally chartered bank
The seller
The broker
The title company
questions.x: In a purchase money mortgage the seller finances part of the price and takes back a note and mortgage. A bank is the trap, since most loans come from one.

questions.q: A buyer will take over the seller's existing loan. The contract should make the deal conditional on:
c: The listing broker guaranteeing the payments
The buyer getting a brand new loan commitment
The seller paying off the loan first
Lender approval of the buyer and balance
questions.x: An assumable mortgage needs the lender's approval of the buyer and confirmation of the balance assumed. A new loan commitment is the trap: assuming the loan replaces new financing.

questions.q: Which sale is exempt from the Property Condition Disclosure Statement requirement?
c: A condo unit resale
A resale of a 2-family house
A 4-family house sold by its owner
A 1-family house with a mortgage
questions.x: Condos and co-ops are exempt; the PCDS covers 1 to 4 family homes. The 4-family house is the trap, since it is still within the covered range.

questions.q: The PCDS requirement applies to sellers of:
c: Co-op apartments
Foreclosed homes sold by a bank
1 to 4 family homes
Never-occupied new homes
questions.x: The PCDS covers 1 to 4 family residential sales. Co-ops, foreclosures and never-occupied new homes are exemptions, so each is a trap.

questions.q: A tenant signs a lease running from March 1 to August 31, six months in all. This creates a(n):
c: Estate for years
Periodic tenancy
Estate at will
Tenancy at sufferance
questions.x: A definite start and end date makes an estate for years, whatever the length. Periodic tenancy is the trap: the short term tempts, but a periodic tenancy has no fixed end.

questions.q: A Rochester landlord asks for the first month's rent of $1,500 plus a $3,000 security deposit. The deposit is:
c: Lawful, as two months is customary
Lawful if the tenant has poor credit
Unlawful above $1,500
Lawful for furnished units
questions.x: Statewide since 2019, a residential deposit cannot exceed one month's rent. Poor credit is the trap: there is no exception for risky tenants.

questions.q: Rent is $900 a month and the tenant pays 7 days late. The maximum late fee is:
c: $0, it is too early
questions.x: The cap is the lesser of $50 or 5% of rent: 5% of $900 is $45. $50 is the trap; it is the cap only when 5% of rent exceeds $50. A fee is allowed because rent is more than 5 days late.

questions.q: Which situation best supports a tenant's claim of constructive eviction?
c: The landlord changes the locks
No heat for weeks, and she moves out
She stays on after the lease ends
The landlord sells the building
questions.x: Constructive eviction is a landlord failure that makes the space unusable, followed by the tenant leaving. Changed locks are the trap: physically shutting the tenant out is actual eviction.

questions.q: A mall tenant pays $4,000 a month plus 6% of gross sales over $800,000. This is a:
c: Graduated rent lease
Triple net lease
Percentage lease
Index lease
questions.x: Base rent plus a share of sales is a percentage lease. Triple net is the trap: it shifts taxes, insurance, and maintenance to the tenant, not a share of sales.

questions.q: Which statement about NYC rent-stabilized apartments is correct after 2019?
c: High-rent decontrol is repealed
Units decontrol above $2,700 in rent
Units decontrol at $200,000 of income
Vacancy bonuses of 20% still apply
questions.x: HSTPA repealed high-rent and high-income decontrol and the vacancy bonus in 2019. The rent-threshold choice is the trap: the old $2,700 threshold no longer removes units from stabilization.

questions.q: A landlord will not renew a tenant who has lived in her Buffalo apartment for 3 years. The minimum written notice is:
c: 30 days
60 days
90 days
120 days
questions.x: Occupancy of 2 years or more requires 90 days' notice of non-renewal. 60 days is the trap: it applies to occupancy of 1 to 2 years.

questions.q: An applicant gives the landlord her own credit report dated two weeks ago. The landlord may charge her a screening fee of:
c: Actual cost
questions.x: The screening fee is waived when the applicant provides a background or credit check from the last 30 days. $20 is the trap: it is the cap when the landlord runs the check.

questions.q: A tenant with 3 years left on her lease lets another business use her store for 2 years and plans to move back afterward. This is:
c: An assignment
A novation
An option
A sublease
questions.x: Transferring part of the term while keeping a reversion is a sublease. Assignment is the trap: that would transfer the entire remaining term.

questions.q: Under RPL 235-f, a tenant named alone on a lease may share the apartment with:
c: Immediate family plus one other occupant
Immediate family members and no others
Up to two unrelated adult roommates
Any occupants the landlord approves
questions.x: The roommate law allows immediate family plus one additional occupant (and that occupant's dependent children). Immediate family alone is the trap: the statute adds one more occupant.

questions.q: A sale closed last week and the deed was delivered. The contract is now:
c: Executory
Voidable
Executed
Unilateral
questions.x: A fully performed contract is executed. Executory is the trap: it describes the period between signing and closing.

questions.q: Which agreement has to be in writing to be enforceable in New York?
c: A 9-month apartment lease
A 2-year commercial lease
A month-to-month rental
A 1-year lease starting today
questions.x: GOL 5-703 requires leases longer than 1 year to be in writing. The 1-year lease is the trap: a lease of exactly 1 year is not longer than 1 year.

questions.q: Which seller response to a buyer's written $680,000 offer creates a binding agreement?
c: Accepting at $690,000 instead
Accepting with an earlier closing
Accepting but keeping the refrigerator
Accepting every term without change
questions.x: Acceptance has to mirror the offer exactly. The earlier-closing choice is the trap: changing any term, even a small one, is a counteroffer.

questions.q: A 17-year-old signs a contract to buy land from an adult. Who may void the contract?
c: The minor buyer
The adult seller
Either party
Neither party
questions.x: The contract is voidable at the minor's option. Either party is the trap: the adult who dealt with a minor stays bound.

questions.q: A seller refuses to close on a brownstone. The buyer wants the house itself, not money. She sues for:
c: Rescission
Reformation of contract
Specific performance
Partition
questions.x: Specific performance orders the seller to convey, and it fits real estate because every parcel is unique. Reformation is the trap: it rewrites a contract to fix a mistake, not to force a closing.

questions.q: A buyer and seller orally agree on every term of a house sale and shake hands. The missing essential element is:
c: Consideration
A signed writing
Mutual agreement
Legal capacity
questions.x: Real estate sale contracts require a writing under the Statute of Frauds. Mutual agreement is the trap: they did agree, but an oral agreement to sell land is unenforceable.

questions.q: In an option agreement, which party is bound before the option is exercised?
c: The optionee
Both parties
Neither party
The optionor
questions.x: The optionor (owner) is bound to sell on the stated terms. The optionee is the trap: the holder may buy or walk away.

questions.q: A buyer assigns her contract to her cousin, but the seller never releases the original buyer. If the cousin defaults, the original buyer:
c: Stays liable to the seller
Is released by the assignment
Is liable for half the damages
Is liable if the seller consented
questions.x: Without a novation, the assignor stays liable. Release by assignment is the trap: only a novation releases the original party.

questions.q: Under a land contract, when does the buyer receive legal title?
c: At contract signing
When she takes possession
After the final payment
After the first year
questions.x: The seller delivers the deed after the agreed payments are made. Possession is the trap: the buyer moves in early but holds only equitable title.

questions.q: A seller breached a written contract in 2022. Under the CPLR, the buyer may generally sue until:
c: 2025, three years later
questions.x: Contract actions have a 6-year limitation: 2022 plus 6 is 2028. 2032 is the trap: 10 years is the adverse possession period.

questions.q: In an upstate NY residential sale, the purchase offer is often first prepared by:
c: The seller's attorney
The title company
The county clerk
The listing broker
questions.x: Upstate, brokers often complete a bar-approved purchase offer subject to attorney approval. The seller's attorney is the trap: that is downstate custom.

questions.q: A broker prepares a Rochester purchase offer. Which clause lets each side's lawyer approve or reject it?
c: Attorney approval
Merger clause
Mortgage contingency
Time of the essence
questions.x: The attorney approval contingency gives the lawyers a short window to approve or disapprove. Mortgage contingency is the trap: it depends on financing, not on legal review.

questions.q: Federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to the sale of which home?
c: A house built in 1985
A house built in 1965
A condo built in 1990
A brand-new 2024 townhouse
questions.x: Target housing is housing built before 1978, so the 1965 house is covered. The 1985 house is the trap for anyone who memorized the syllabus typo "after 1978."

questions.q: Before 2024, a seller could skip the PCDS by giving the buyer a $500 credit. What changed on March 20, 2024?
c: The credit rose to $1,000
Buyers can waive the PCDS
The credit option ended
Condos became covered
questions.x: The amendment eliminated the $500 credit, so covered sellers deliver the PCDS. Buyer waiver is the trap: the new law did not create a buyer opt-out either.

questions.q: A downstate buyer signs a contract at $850,000 and gives the customary deposit. The seller's attorney holds:
questions.x: Customary downstate deposit is 10%: $85,000. $170,000 is the trap: 20% is a typical conventional loan down payment, not the contract deposit.

questions.q: Why are New York attorneys favored as escrow agents for down payments?
c: They earn the buyer interest
They are bonded by the Bar
Title insurers guarantee them
A State fund covers their theft
questions.x: The Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection reimburses clients when a NY attorney steals escrowed money. The bond choice is the trap: attorneys are not individually bonded for escrow.

questions.q: A contract preparer reviews the certificate of occupancy mainly to confirm:
c: The seller's marital status
The legal use of the building
The seller's mortgage payoff
The buyer's financing terms
questions.x: The CO shows the building's legal use and occupancy, such as a legal two-family. The mortgage payoff is the trap: it matters at closing but comes from the lender, not the CO.

questions.q: At a Brooklyn contract signing, who customarily signs first?
c: The seller
The listing broker
The buyer
Both at once
questions.x: The buyer signs first and delivers the down payment, and the seller signs afterward. The seller is the trap: signing first would bind the seller before the buyer has committed.

questions.q: A contract's mortgage contingency deadline is May 1. On April 28 the buyer has a preapproval letter but no commitment. The contingency is:
c: Satisfied by the preapproval
Satisfied once she applies
Waived by the deadline
Not yet satisfied
questions.x: A written commitment for this property satisfies the contingency, and she does not have one yet. Preapproval is the trap: it comes before appraisal and underwriting of this property.

questions.q: Which act by a salesperson is the unauthorized practice of law?
c: Explaining a deed's legal effect
Completing an approved offer form
Presenting an offer to the seller
Delivering a contract to the attorney
questions.x: Explaining legal effect is legal advice reserved to attorneys. Completing an approved form is the trap: licensees may fill in bar-approved forms.

questions.q: Each of the following is an essential element of a valid contract for the sale of real estate EXCEPT:
c: Competent parties
Lawful objective
Mutual offer and acceptance
Notarized signatures
questions.x: A contract needs competent parties, mutual agreement, a lawful objective, consideration, and (for real estate) a writing. Notarization is the trap: it is needed to record a deed, not to make a contract valid.

questions.q: A tenant pays the owner $10,000 for the right to buy the building at $2 million within 18 months. Until the tenant decides, this agreement is best described as:
c: A unilateral option binding the owner
A bilateral contract binding both sides
A right of first refusal at $2 million
A binder
questions.x: In an option, the optionor (owner) is bound to sell while the optionee may buy or walk away. Right of first refusal is the trap: it sets no price of its own and only lets the holder match a third party's offer.

questions.q: A new buyer is substituted into a contract and the original buyer is fully released from liability. This is called:
c: Assignment
Reformation
Novation
Forbearance
questions.x: Novation substitutes a new party or contract and releases the original. Assignment is the trap: the assignor generally remains liable.

questions.q: A buyer pays for a house under an installment sales contract over 10 years and has lived in it since year one. During the payment period, the seller holds:
c: Equitable title to the house
Legal title to the house
A lien but no title
A leasehold reversion
questions.x: Under a land contract the seller keeps legal title until the payments are made, then delivers the deed. Equitable title is the trap: that is what the buyer in possession holds.

questions.q: In New York, the statute of limitations for an action for breach of a written contract is generally:
c: 1 year
3 years
10 years
6 years
questions.x: NY's CPLR sets 6 years for contract actions. Ten years is the trap: it is the period for adverse possession.

questions.q: In downstate New York residential sales, the contract of sale is customarily prepared by:
c: The seller's attorney
The listing broker's office
The buyer's lender
The title company
questions.x: Downstate, the seller's attorney drafts the contract and the buyer's attorney reviews it. The listing broker is the trap: upstate brokers often complete approved forms, but that is not downstate practice.

questions.q: A clause in an upstate purchase offer that lets either party's lawyer disapprove the agreement within a short period is the:
c: Merger clause
Time is of the essence clause
Attorney review clause
Liquidated damages clause
questions.x: The attorney review (approval) clause makes a broker-prepared contract contingent on attorney approval. Merger clause is the trap: it says the writing is the entire agreement.

questions.q: The 2022 NYS syllabus says lead-based paint clauses apply to properties constructed "after 1978." The correct federal rule covers housing:
c: Built after 1978
Built before 1960
Built with 5 or more units
Built before 1978
questions.x: The federal rule covers target housing built before 1978, the year lead paint was banned for residential use. "After 1978" is the trap: it is a typo in the syllabus.

questions.q: A seller of a 1-family house in Yonkers says he will skip the Property Condition Disclosure Statement and give the buyer a $500 credit instead. In 2026 this is:
c: Allowed if the buyer agrees to it
Not allowed; the credit ended in 2024
Allowed for houses built before 1978
Required for 1-family homes
questions.x: Since March 20, 2024 the PCDS is mandatory for covered sellers and the $500 credit opt-out is gone. Buyer agreement is the trap: the old law let parties trade the form for the credit, but no longer.

questions.q: The customary down payment at contract signing in a downstate New York residential sale is:
c: A $1,000 binder
5% of the price
10% of the price
20%, the loan down payment
questions.x: Downstate custom is 10% at contract, held in escrow by the seller's attorney. 20% is the trap: it is a common conventional loan down payment, not the contract deposit.

questions.q: The Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection matters in a real estate deal because it:
c: Repays escrow stolen by an attorney
Insures buyers against title defects
Pays the commission if the seller defaults
Guarantees the buyer's mortgage commitment
questions.x: The fund reimburses losses caused by dishonest NY attorneys, which is why attorneys are favored escrow agents. Title defects are the trap: those are covered by title insurance.

questions.q: In preparing a contract of sale, the preparer reviews each of the following EXCEPT:
c: The prior deed
The title insurance policy and survey
The certificate of occupancy
The seller's income tax returns
questions.x: The deed, title policy, survey, CO, and tax bills describe and confirm what is being sold. Tax bills are the trap: property tax bills are reviewed, but the seller's personal income tax returns are not.

questions.q: At a Queens contract signing, the buyer's attorney asks why the buyer signs first. The best explanation is:
c: The seller is the more important party
It binds the buyer before the seller commits
State law requires the buyer's signature first
The broker collects the commission sooner
questions.x: The buyer signs first with the down payment, so the seller is not bound until the buyer has committed. State law is the trap: it is custom, not a statutory requirement.

questions.q: A mortgage contingency clause is satisfied when the buyer:
c: Gets a written commitment in time
Submits a complete loan application
Gets a prequalification letter
Gets a preapproval letter from a lender
questions.x: Most contracts tie the contingency to a written mortgage commitment by the deadline. Preapproval is the trap: it is issued before the property is appraised and underwritten.

questions.q: A real estate salesperson may do each of the following in connection with a contract EXCEPT:
c: Fill in an upstate bar-approved offer form
Present an offer to the seller
Draft a rider on a title exception's effect
Deliver a signed contract to the attorneys
questions.x: Drafting custom riders and explaining legal effect is the practice of law. Filling in the form is the trap: completing a bar-approved form is permitted for licensees.

questions.q: A store pays $90,000 a year base rent plus 5% of gross sales over the natural breakpoint. Sales are $2,100,000. What is the percentage rent?
questions.x: Breakpoint = $90,000 / 0.05 = $1,800,000. Excess sales are $300,000, and 5% of that is $15,000. The $105,000 trap is 5% of total sales, which double counts the sales the base rent already covers.

questions.q: A lease sets base rent at $60,000 a year and percentage rent at 4% of sales above the natural breakpoint. At what sales level does percentage rent begin?
questions.x: The natural breakpoint is base rent divided by the percentage rate: $60,000 / 0.04 = $1,500,000. Percentage rent is owed only on sales above that. The $2,400,000 trap comes from dividing by 0.025 or misplacing a decimal.

questions.q: A ten-year office lease sets rent at $40 per square foot for years 1 to 5 and $46 for years 6 to 10. This is a:
c: Index lease
Percentage lease
Graduated lease
Ground lease
questions.x: A graduated lease builds fixed increases into the lease itself. An index lease is the trap: its increases follow an outside measure such as the CPI, so the future rent is not known when the lease is signed.

questions.q: A commercial lease says base rent rises each year by the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for the New York metro area. This is best described as:
c: A graduated lease
A gross lease
A net lease
An index lease
questions.x: Rent tied to an outside index is an index lease. A graduated lease is the trap because rent also rises, but its steps are fixed in the lease. Gross and net describe who pays operating expenses.

questions.q: A Queens restaurant's lease gives it an option to renew if notice is received by March 1. The owner sends notice on March 20. Which statement is most accurate?
c: The restaurant has a statutory right to a renewal lease
The landlord has to offer a one- or two-year renewal
The option has generally lapsed, absent narrow equitable relief
The restaurant becomes a month-to-month tenant by law on March 2
questions.x: Commercial tenants have no statutory renewal right, so renewal depends on exercising the option on time. Courts sometimes excuse a short, honest delay where the tenant made big improvements and the landlord was not prejudiced, but that is the exception. The one- or two-year renewal is the trap: that is the rent-stabilized residential rule.

questions.q: All of the following are true of NY commercial leases EXCEPT:
c: Rent is usually quoted per square foot per year
Tenants are entitled to renewal after 10 years
Renewal depends on an option the tenant negotiates
Use clauses are often heavily negotiated
questions.x: There is no statutory renewal right for commercial tenants in New York, however long they have been in place. Rent per square foot per year, negotiated renewal options, and negotiated use clauses are all standard. Per-square-foot rent is the tempting wrong pick for students who think in monthly apartment rents.

questions.q: In 2026 a Manhattan rent-stabilized apartment has a legal rent of $3,100 and the tenants earn $260,000. The owner may:
c: Not deregulate it on rent or income grounds
Deregulate it after certifying the income for 2 years
Deregulate it at the next vacancy
Deregulate it with Rent Guidelines Board approval
questions.x: The 2019 HSTPA repealed high-rent and high-income decontrol, so neither the rent level nor the tenants' income can remove the unit from stabilization. The vacancy choice is the trap: high-rent vacancy deregulation was repealed at the same time.

questions.q: A unit was lawfully deregulated in 2012 under the high-rent rules that then existed. After the 2019 HSTPA, the unit is generally:
c: Still deregulated
Returned to stabilization automatically
Stabilized again at the next lease renewal
Subject to rent control instead
questions.x: HSTPA ended future high-rent and high-income decontrol, but units lawfully deregulated before June 2019 generally remain deregulated. Automatic re-regulation is the trap: the repeal looks forward, not backward.

questions.q: A tenant in a 12-unit building sends a proper sublet request by certified mail. The landlord does not respond within 30 days. Under RPL 226-b:
c: The request is deemed denied
Silence is deemed consent
The tenant is released from the lease
The tenant has to refile after 60 days
questions.x: Failure to send consent or reasons for refusal within 30 days is deemed consent. The tenant stays liable on the lease. The release choice is the trap: release is the tenant's remedy for an unreasonably refused assignment, not the effect of silence on a sublet.

questions.q: After receiving a tenant's sublet request under RPL 226-b, a landlord who needs more information must ask for it within:
c: 5 days
30 days
10 days
60 days
questions.x: The landlord may request additional information within 10 days after the request is mailed, and must give consent or reasons for refusal within 30 days after the later of the request or the additional information. The 30-day choice is the trap: that is the response deadline, not the deadline to ask for more.

questions.q: A market-rate tenant's lease ends August 31. She stays, and the landlord accepts September rent without any new agreement. The tenant now has:
c: A new one-year lease on the old terms
A tenancy at sufferance
An estate at will ending on either party's death
A month-to-month tenancy
questions.x: Under RPL 232-c, acceptance of rent from a holdover creates a month-to-month tenancy unless the parties agree otherwise. The one-year renewal is the trap: it is the common-law rule some states still use, not New York's. Before rent was accepted, she was a tenant at sufferance.

questions.q: A tenant who stays after the lease ends, before the landlord accepts any rent or consents, is a:
c: Periodic month-to-month tenant
Tenant under an estate for years
Tenant at sufferance
Tenant at will by implied consent
questions.x: A holdover without the landlord's consent is a tenant at sufferance. Once the landlord accepts rent, New York converts it to a month-to-month periodic tenancy, which is why the periodic choice is the trap: it describes what happens after acceptance, not before.

questions.q: A buyer offers $700,000. The seller replies, "Accepted at $715,000." Before the buyer responds, the seller withdraws the reply. The buyer then tries to accept $715,000. Result?
c: A contract at $715,000, the seller's last price
A contract at $700,000, the buyer's first price
A contract at the midpoint of the two prices
No contract, since the seller revoked first
questions.x: The seller's reply changed the price, so it was a counteroffer, and an offeror may revoke before acceptance. The $700,000 trap fails because the counteroffer rejected the buyer's original offer, which cannot be revived by accepting it later.

questions.q: A counteroffer has which effect on the original offer?
c: It rejects and terminates the original
It holds the original open for 3 days
It accepts the original with conditions
It converts the original into an option
questions.x: A counteroffer is a rejection plus a new offer, so the original offer ends. 'Accepts with conditions' is the trap: a conditional acceptance is not an acceptance at all, because acceptance must mirror the offer.

questions.concept: Right of first refusal vs option
questions.q: A tenant's lease lets her buy the building for $900,000 at any time in the next three years. This is a(n):
c: Right of first refusal
Installment sales contract
Option to purchase
Purchase money mortgage
questions.x: An option gives the holder the right to buy at a set price within a set time, and the owner must keep the offer open. A right of first refusal is the trap: it has no set price and lets the holder act only after the owner decides to sell and receives an offer, by matching it.

questions.concept: Right of first refusal vs option
questions.q: A co-op's bylaws let the corporation match any accepted offer for a unit before the sale goes through. This is a(n):
c: Option to purchase
Installment sales contract
Novation of the proprietary lease
Right of first refusal
questions.x: Matching an offer the owner is willing to accept is a right of first refusal. An option is the trap: it would let the corporation buy at a preset price whether or not the owner wanted to sell.

questions.q: Under an installment sales contract, the seller normally delivers the deed:
c: At the signing of the contract
When the buyer takes possession
When the payments are done
When the buyer's lender approves
questions.x: The seller keeps legal title as security and delivers the deed once the buyer completes the agreed payments; the buyer holds equitable title and possession meanwhile. The possession choice is the trap, because the buyer usually moves in at the start, long before the deed passes.

questions.q: All of the following are true of an installment sales contract EXCEPT:
c: The buyer usually takes possession at the start
The buyer receives legal title at signing
The seller keeps legal title during the payments
The seller may spread the taxable gain over time
questions.x: Legal title stays with the seller until the agreed payments are made; the buyer has equitable title. Possession at the start and installment reporting of the gain are both typical. The tax choice is the tempting wrong pick, but spreading the gain is a recognized reason sellers use these contracts.

questions.q: An agent holds a durable power of attorney for his mother, who has signed a contract to sell her house. She dies before closing. Who signs the deed?
c: The court-appointed executor
The agent, under the durable power
The buyer's attorney, as escrow agent
No one; the contract is void at death
questions.x: A power of attorney ends at the principal's death, durable or not. The contract binds the estate, and the court-appointed executor (or administrator) signs. The durable-power answer is the trap: durable means the power survives incapacity, not death.

questions.q: A New York power of attorney that is "durable" remains effective:
c: After the principal's incapacity
After the principal's death
For 10 years after it is signed
Until the agent records it with the deed
questions.x: Durable means the power survives the principal's incapacity. Every power of attorney ends at death, which makes the first choice the trap. Recording relates to using the power to convey, not to how long it lasts.

questions.q: A deed and contract both describe the wrong lot because of a typing error, and both parties agree on the intended lot. The remedy that corrects the document is:
c: Rescission
Reformation
Specific performance
Forbearance
questions.x: Reformation lets a court rewrite a document to match the parties' actual agreement when a mutual mistake appears in the writing. Rescission is the trap: it cancels the deal, which is the wrong fix when both parties want the deal on the correct terms.

questions.q: Which remedy unwinds a contract and returns the parties to where they started, as after fraud?
c: Reformation
Specific performance
Rescission
Liquidated damages
questions.x: Rescission cancels the contract and restores each side to its prior position. Reformation is the trap: it keeps the contract but corrects its wording to match what the parties actually agreed.

questions.q: A buyer assigns her contract to her brother with the seller's consent. The brother fails to close. The seller can look to:
c: The brother alone, since he is the assignee
The listing broker, who arranged the sale
Neither, since assignment ends the contract
The original buyer too, absent a novation
questions.x: An assignor remains liable on the contract unless the other party agrees to a novation releasing her. The 'brother alone' answer is the trap: consenting to an assignment is not the same as releasing the original party.

questions.q: A new contract that substitutes a new party and releases the original party from liability is a(n):
c: Assignment
Option
Novation
Rider
questions.x: A novation replaces the old obligation or party and releases the original. An assignment is the trap: it transfers rights to someone else, but the assignor stays liable unless released.

questions.q: An upstate salesperson filling in the regional purchase contract wants to add her own clause waiving the buyer's right to object to an unpermitted deck. She should:
c: Add it, since the attorney approval clause lets either attorney strike it
Add it, if her broker reviews the wording first
Add it, if both parties initial the clause
Leave it to the attorneys, since drafting legal terms is practicing law
questions.x: Brokers may fill in blanks on approved forms, but drafting custom legal provisions such as waivers is the unauthorized practice of law. The attorney-approval answer is the trap: the review clause protects the parties, but it does not license the broker to write the legal terms.

questions.q: The attorney approval clause in an upstate broker-prepared contract exists mainly because:
c: Brokers may not give legal advice on it
Brokers may not collect deposits without it
State law voids any contract signed without a lawyer present
Lenders require attorney approval before issuing a commitment
questions.x: Brokers may complete approved forms but cannot advise on legal effect, so the clause gives each side's attorney a window to approve or disapprove. The 'void without a lawyer' choice is the trap: NY does not require attorneys at signing; the clause is a contractual protection.

questions.q: A deed names "John Pak and Sara Pak, his wife." They have since divorced, and the decree did not transfer the house. Who must sign as seller?
c: Sara, who lives in the house
John, the first-named grantee
Both John and Sara
Whichever spouse the decree names as custodian
questions.x: Spouses holding as tenants by the entirety become tenants in common on divorce unless the decree transfers title, so both own shares and both must sign. The occupying spouse is the trap: living in the house is possession, not ownership.

questions.q: Which document is the best source for the exact names of the sellers and how they hold title?
c: The tax bill
The listing agreement
The certificate of occupancy
The prior deed
questions.x: The prior deed shows the grantees' exact names, how they took title, and the legal description. The tax bill is the trap: it may list only one owner or an old name, and it is a billing record, not a title document.

questions.q: A listing is marketed as a two-family, but the CO allows a one-family dwelling. When preparing the contract, the broker should:
c: Describe it as a two-family, since that is its actual use
Ignore the CO, which matters to the lender and nobody else
Describe the legal use and flag it for the attorneys
Ask the buyer to sign a waiver of the CO issue
questions.x: The preparer checks that the CO matches the actual use and that later work was permitted. A mismatch must be disclosed accurately and handled by the attorneys. Describing the actual use as legal is the trap: it misrepresents the property, however the space is being used today.

questions.q: When reviewing a certificate of occupancy before preparing a contract, the preparer mainly looks for whether:
c: The property taxes are current
Legal and actual use match
The house is in a flood zone
The seller has homeowner's insurance
questions.x: A CO states the legal use and occupancy of the building, so the key check is whether actual use and any later improvements match it. Taxes are the trap: they come from the tax bills, a different document in the file.

questions.q: A buyer has an FHA loan. The appraisal comes in $15,000 below the contract price. Under the FHA amendatory clause, the buyer:
c: May cancel and recover the deposit
Has to close at the contract price
Is entitled to a $15,000 price cut
Forfeits the deposit if she cancels
questions.x: The amendatory clause lets the buyer walk away without losing the deposit if the FHA appraised value is below the price, or proceed anyway. The price-cut choice is the trap: the clause does not require the seller to reduce the price; it only gives the buyer an exit.

questions.q: All of the following are true of the FHA amendatory clause EXCEPT:
c: It requires the seller to cut the price
It protects the buyer's deposit
It applies when the appraisal is low
It lets the buyer proceed if she chooses
questions.x: The clause frees the buyer from the purchase, deposit intact, when the FHA appraised value is below the price, and lets her close anyway if she wishes. It never forces a price reduction. 'Applies when the appraisal is low' is the tempting wrong pick, but that is exactly when it applies.

questions.q: A downstate buyer asks why the seller's attorney, not the broker, should hold her $90,000 down payment. The best answer is:
c: Brokers may not hold deposits on sales
The Lawyers' Fund backs attorney escrow theft
Attorneys pay the buyer interest at a fixed legal rate
Attorney escrow accounts are insured for any amount
questions.x: If a NY attorney misappropriates escrow funds, the client can apply to the Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection; no equivalent fund backs broker escrow accounts. The 'brokers may not hold deposits' choice is the trap: brokers can and do hold deposits in escrow accounts, especially upstate.

questions.q: A contract names no escrow agent, and the buyer's deposit is paid straight to the seller. If the deal collapses, the buyer is:
c: Protected by the Lawyers' Fund
Repaid by the listing broker
An unsecured creditor
Repaid from the state escrow fund
questions.x: Without an escrow agent, the seller holds the money and can spend it; the buyer can only sue to get it back. The Lawyers' Fund is the trap: it covers theft by attorneys acting as escrowees, not deposits paid directly to a seller.

questions.q: A contract for a house built in 1952 must include which lead-based paint item?
c: A lead-free certificate from the seller
A seller-paid lead abatement
Nothing, since the house predates the rule
The Lead Warning Statement
questions.x: Housing built before 1978 requires the EPA pamphlet, disclosure of known hazards, the Lead Warning Statement, and a 10-day opportunity to test. The 'predates the rule' choice is the trap: the rule covers older homes precisely because lead paint was banned for residential use in 1978.

questions.q: Federal lead-based paint disclosure rules apply to residential housing built:
c: After 1978
Before 1950
Before 1978
After 1950
questions.x: The rules cover housing built before 1978, when lead-based paint was banned for residential use. "After 1978" is the trap: it appears in the 2022 syllabus as a typo, but the rule runs the other way.

cram.html: Statute of Frauds (GOL 5-703): sales of land and leases over 1 year must be in writing.
Five essentials: competent parties, mutual agreement, lawful objective, consideration, writing.
Executed = fully performed. Executory = signed, not yet performed.
Counteroffer kills the original offer.
Minor's contract is voidable by the minor; illegal-purpose contract is void.
Option = unilateral, set price. Right of first refusal = match an offer, no set price.
Novation releases the original party; assignment does not.
Buyer vs defaulting seller: specific performance. Seller vs defaulting buyer: keep the down payment as liquidated damages.
NY contract statute of limitations: 6 years.
Installment (land) contract: seller keeps legal title until paid; buyer has possession and equitable title.
Downstate: seller's attorney drafts, buyer signs first with 10% down, seller's attorney holds it in escrow.
Upstate: broker completes approved form with an attorney review clause.
Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection: why attorneys are favored escrow agents.
Lead paint: housing built before 1978, 10 days to test, keep records 3 years. Syllabus "after 1978" is a typo.
PCDS: before buyer signs; no $500 credit since March 20, 2024; flood questions added.
Deposit max 1 month; return within 14 days with itemized statement.
Screening fee max $20; late fee after 5 days, lesser of $50 or 5%.
Non-renewal or 5%+ increase notice: 30 / 60 / 90 days (under 1 yr / 1 to 2 yrs / 2+ yrs).
Luxury decontrol and vacancy bonuses: repealed June 2019. The $2,000 / $175,000 numbers are dead.
Stabilized tenant gets a 1- or 2-year renewal, tenant's choice (ETPA). HCR administers; Rent Guidelines Board sets increases.
Sublet: RPL 226-b, buildings with 4+ units, consent not unreasonably withheld. Roommates: RPL 235-f.
Constructive eviction requires the tenant to move out. Habitability (RPL 235-b) cannot be waived.
NY holdover + rent accepted = month-to-month.
Good Cause: increase above lower of CPI + 5% or 10% presumed unreasonable; sunsets 2034.
FARE Act (NYC, June 11, 2025): landlord's broker is paid by the landlord.

subjects.title: Real Estate Finance
subjects.blurb: Almost every buyer borrows. Expect exam items on mortgage vs note, points and LTV math, qualifying ratios, loan types, the secondary market, Truth in Lending, and New York's judicial foreclosure and predatory lending rules.

lessons.title: The Mortgage: Note, Lien, Payments, and Foreclosure
lessons.tagline: The note is the promise. The mortgage is the leash on the house that backs it up.
objectives: Separate the note (debt) from the mortgage (lien) and name who is mortgagor and mortgagee
Compute PITI pieces, points, and the interest in a monthly payment
Explain the key mortgage clauses: acceleration, due-on-sale, prepayment, release, defeasance
Walk through NY judicial foreclosure and the deficiency judgment rules
Compare a sale free and clear, subject to, and with assumption

blocks.title: Leo's spreadsheet
blocks.html: Leo is buying a $750,000 condo in Long Island City with 20% down. Tasha quotes a 30-year fixed at 6.5% with 1 point. Leo has built a 14-tab spreadsheet, but there is one cell he cannot fill: "What happens if I lose my job?" Before he signs anything, he wants to know what he is actually promising and what the bank can actually do.
blocks.casual: Leo's buying a $750,000 condo in Long Island City with 20% down. Tasha quotes him a 30-year fixed at 6.5% with 1 point. He's built a 14-tab spreadsheet, naturally, but there's one cell he can't fill in: "What happens if I lose my job?" Before he signs a thing, he wants to know exactly what he's promising and what the bank can actually do to him.

deeper.plain: Taking a mortgage means making promises with your house on the line. Leo wants to know the rules before he plays.
deeper.picture: It's like leaving your car as collateral for a borrowed truck. You want to know what happens to your car if the truck comes back late.
deeper.street: Tasha walks Leo through it at a café on Vernon Boulevard: a $600,000 loan, a $6,000 point, and the documents he'll sign at closing. She tells him NY foreclosure takes years and goes through a court, but it still ends with the house sold if he can't pay.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't understand what they're signing get blindsided by default rules, escrow increases, and deficiency risk. Agents who brush off these questions lose the client's trust.
deeper.exam: This lesson feeds questions on note vs mortgage, mortgagor vs mortgagee, points, amortization math, clauses, and NY judicial foreclosure. Leo's numbers set up a points calculation: 1% of the loan, not the price.

blocks.html: Every mortgage loan has two documents. The promissory note (often called a bond in NY) is Leo's personal promise to repay the debt. The mortgage is the security instrument: it pledges the property as collateral and creates a lien. Pay the note and the lien goes away. Default, and the lender can pursue the property to satisfy the debt.
blocks.casual: Every mortgage loan comes with two documents. The promissory note (in NY often called a bond) is Leo's personal promise to pay the money back. The mortgage is the security: it puts the property up as collateral and creates a lien. Pay off the note and the lien disappears. Default, and the lender can go after the property to get paid.

deeper.plain: The note says "I owe you". The mortgage says "and if I don't pay, you can take the house".
deeper.picture: The note is an IOU on a napkin. The mortgage is handing over your spare house keys in a sealed envelope that only opens if you stop paying.
deeper.street: At Leo's closing in Midtown, he signs a note for $600,000 and a mortgage on his LIC condo. The note stays in the lender's file; the mortgage goes to the City Register through ACRIS so the world knows the lender has a lien.
deeper.stakes: If a buyer thinks walking away from the house ends the debt, they're wrong: the note is a personal promise, and in NY a lender can seek a deficiency judgment.
deeper.exam: Note = evidence of the debt, personal liability. Mortgage = security instrument, creates the lien. If asked which document is recorded, it's the mortgage.

left.title: Promissory note (bond)
items: Evidence of the debt
Personal promise to pay
States amount, rate, term, payment
Can be sold (negotiable)
Not recorded

right.title: Mortgage
items: Security for the debt
Creates a lien on the property
Lists borrower duties and default remedies
Recorded in the county clerk's office (City Register in NYC)
Released by a satisfaction when paid

deeper.plain: The note is the debt itself; the mortgage is the safety net that lets the lender reach the property.
deeper.picture: A note is the bar tab with your name on it. The mortgage is the credit card the bartender holds until you close out.
deeper.street: Leo's lender sells his note to an investor six months later. Because notes are negotiable, the new holder can enforce it. The mortgage follows the note, and an assignment is recorded. When Leo eventually pays it off, a satisfaction is recorded to clear the lien.
deeper.stakes: A paid-off loan without a recorded satisfaction can cloud title years later, holding up a sale while someone hunts down the old lender.
deeper.exam: Note: not recorded, negotiable, personal promise. Mortgage: recorded, creates the lien, released by satisfaction. A compare question will flip one of these.

blocks.html: The borrower is the mortgagor, because the borrower gives the mortgage. The lender is the mortgagee, who receives it. New York is a lien theory state: the borrower keeps title and all the usual rights of ownership, and the lender holds only a lien.
blocks.casual: The borrower is the mortgagor, because the borrower gives the mortgage. The lender is the mortgagee, the one receiving it. New York is a lien theory state: the borrower keeps the title and all the normal rights of owning the place, and the lender just holds a lien.

deeper.plain: The borrower owns the house; the lender just has a claim against it.
deeper.picture: It's like a pawn ticket in reverse: you keep the guitar and play it every night, but the shop has a claim on it if you don't pay.
deeper.street: Leo paints the walls, rents a room to a friend (with condo approval), and refinances later, all because he holds title. His lender has a lien, not ownership, so it can't change the locks or move in.
deeper.stakes: Lien theory is why NY lenders must go to court to foreclose. Misunderstanding it leads people to think the bank "owns" the home until paid off.
deeper.exam: NY is lien theory, borrower holds title. In title theory states, the lender holds title until paid. Mortgagor is the borrower.

blocks.title: Who gives what
blocks.html: The lender does not give the mortgage. The borrower gives the mortgage to the lender in exchange for the loan. Mortgagor = borrower. The "-or" is the giver, just like grantor and lessor.
blocks.casual: The lender does not give the mortgage. The borrower gives the mortgage to the lender in exchange for the loan. Mortgagor = borrower. The "-or" is the giver, same as grantor and lessor.

deeper.plain: The borrower gives the lender a mortgage; the lender gives the borrower money.
deeper.picture: Think of a trade at a swap meet: you hand over a claim on your house, they hand over cash. The "-or" is whoever hands over the paper.
deeper.street: Jordan, studying on the G train, keeps writing "mortgagor = bank". Diane circles it in red: "Grantor gives the deed. Lessor gives the lease. Mortgagor gives the mortgage. Who's giving the mortgage, Jordan?" The borrower.
deeper.stakes: Confusing these two terms means misreading loan documents and court papers, where they show up constantly.
deeper.exam: This is one of the most tested traps in finance. "-or" gives, "-ee" receives. Mortgagor = borrower, mortgagee = lender.

blocks.html: Each duty protects the lender's collateral. A house left to rot, an uninsured fire, or a tax lien that jumps ahead of the mortgage all shrink what the lender could recover. That is why breaking any of these promises is a default, even if every payment is on time, and why the lender may pay an overdue tax bill or force-place insurance and add the cost to the loan.
blocks.casual: Every one of the borrower's duties protects the lender's collateral. A house left to rot, a fire with no insurance, or a tax lien that cuts in front of the mortgage all shrink what the lender could get back. That's why breaking any of these promises is a default, even if every payment's on time. It's also why the lender can pay an overdue tax bill or force-place insurance and tack the cost onto the loan.

deeper.plain: You can default on a mortgage without missing a payment, by letting the property's value or protection slip.
deeper.picture: It's like borrowing a friend's camera with a promise to keep it in its case. Leaving it in the rain is breaking the deal even if you return it on time.
deeper.street: A homeowner in Canarsie keeps paying on time but lets the hazard insurance lapse to save $2,400. The lender force-places a policy at $5,800 and adds it to the loan. If she refuses to pay, she's in default.
deeper.stakes: Force-placed insurance is pricey, and unpaid taxes can lead to a tax lien that outranks the mortgage. Either can push a borrower into default and foreclosure.
deeper.exam: Default is broader than nonpayment. Waste, lapsed insurance, and unpaid taxes are all defaults.

items: Pay the debt as the note requires
Keep the property in good repair (no waste)
Insure the property against hazards, naming the lender
Pay all property taxes and assessments, which would otherwise outrank the mortgage
blocks.casual: The borrower promises four things: pay the debt as the note says; keep the place in good repair (no waste); insure it against hazards with the lender named; and pay all property taxes and assessments, which would otherwise jump ahead of the mortgage.

deeper.plain: Pay on time, keep it up, keep it insured, and pay the taxes.
deeper.picture: Four legs of a table: payment, repair, insurance, taxes. Kick out any one and the lender's protection wobbles.
deeper.street: Sal's Astoria building has a mortgage. When he skips a roof repair for two years and water damages the top floor, his lender's inspector notes "waste" and sends a default letter, even though Sal's payments are current.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring these promises gives the lender grounds to accelerate. Property taxes are a priority lien, so unpaid taxes threaten the lender's position directly.
deeper.exam: Property taxes outrank the mortgage even if the mortgage was recorded first. That's why the lender cares if you pay them.

blocks.html: That is why most payments are PITI: Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance. The lender collects 1/12 of yearly taxes and insurance each month into an escrow account and pays the bills itself. In NY, mortgage interest is paid in arrears: the June 1 payment covers May's interest.
blocks.casual: That's why most payments are PITI: Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance. Each month the lender collects 1/12 of the yearly taxes and insurance into an escrow account and pays those bills itself. And in NY, mortgage interest is paid in arrears: your June 1 payment covers May's interest.

deeper.plain: Your monthly payment covers the loan plus a slice of your yearly taxes and insurance. Interest is always for the month that just ended.
deeper.picture: Escrow is a savings jar the lender keeps for you: a twelfth of the tax and insurance bill goes in each month so the big bills never surprise you.
deeper.street: Leo's condo taxes are $9,600 a year and insurance $1,200. That's $900 a month into escrow on top of his principal and interest. He closes May 15 and prepays interest for the rest of May at closing. His first payment isn't due until July 1, and it covers June's interest.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who budget only principal and interest get shocked by the real payment. Agents who quote "the mortgage is $3,800" without escrow set clients up for a squeeze.
deeper.exam: PITI stands for principal, interest, taxes, insurance. Interest is paid in arrears. Expect questions on prepaid interest at closing and the first payment date.

blocks.html: Amortization means paying a loan down to zero with level payments over its term. Early payments are mostly interest; later ones mostly principal. A straight (term) mortgage is the opposite: interest only, with the entire principal due at the end.
blocks.casual: Amortization means paying a loan down to zero with level payments over the term. At the start, payments are mostly interest; near the end, mostly principal. A straight (term) mortgage is the opposite: you pay interest only, and the whole principal is due at the end.

deeper.plain: Amortized loans shrink a bit every month. A straight loan stays the same size until one big final payoff.
deeper.picture: Amortization is melting an ice cube slowly: tiny drips at first, a puddle at the end. A straight loan is keeping the cube frozen and smashing it all at once on the last day.
deeper.street: Evelyn takes a 5-year interest-only loan on a Bushwick mixed-use building to keep cash flow high. In year 5 she owes the full $3M principal, so she plans to refinance. Leo's 30-year amortized loan, by contrast, will be zero after 360 payments.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers on a straight loan who can't refinance at the end face a balloon they can't pay. Amortized borrowers feel like they're paying "only interest" early on, which shocks them when they check their balance.
deeper.exam: In a fully amortizing loan, the payment stays level but the interest share falls and the principal share rises. In a straight (term) loan, principal is paid in one lump at maturity.

blocks.caption: Slide the rate and term. Watch the interest slice shrink and the principal slice grow with each payment on a fully amortized loan.

blocks.title: First-month interest and principal
blocks.html:
Loan: $300,000 at 6% for 30 years. Monthly payment (from a table or calculator): $1,798.65.
Month 1 interest = $300,000 x 0.06 / 12 = $1,500.
Principal = $1,798.65 minus $1,500 = $298.65.
New balance = $300,000 minus $298.65 = $299,701.35. Next month's interest is figured on that lower balance.
blocks.casual:
Say the loan's $300,000 at 6% for 30 years. The monthly payment (from a table or calculator) is $1,798.65.
Month 1 interest = $300,000 x 0.06 / 12 = $1,500.
Principal = $1,798.65 minus $1,500 = $298.65.
New balance = $300,000 minus $298.65 = $299,701.35. Next month's interest gets figured on that slightly lower balance.

deeper.plain: Each month, figure interest on what you still owe, then the rest of the payment knocks down the balance.
deeper.picture: Like paying off a bar tab where the bartender charges a fee on whatever is still open. The more you pay off, the smaller next month's fee.
deeper.street: Leo plugs his own numbers into the spreadsheet: $600,000 at 6.5% means month 1 interest of $3,250. His payment is about $3,792, so just $542 goes to principal. He frowns at the screen and calls Tasha, who says, "Welcome to amortization."
deeper.stakes: Getting this wrong means misjudging how fast a buyer builds equity, which matters when they want to sell or refinance in a few years.
deeper.exam: Formula: balance x annual rate / 12 = monthly interest. Payment minus interest = principal. Questions often ask for the balance after the first payment.

blocks.html: Discount points are prepaid interest paid at closing to lower the rate. One point = 1% of the loan amount, not of the price. A rough rule of thumb: each point raises the lender's yield by about 1/8 of a percent. Points paid to buy a principal residence are generally deductible in the year paid; on a refinance they are deducted over the loan's life. Mortgage interest on acquisition debt up to $750,000 is deductible for those who itemize, which is the core of interest and tax deductibility.
blocks.casual: Discount points are prepaid interest you pay at closing to get a lower rate. One point = 1% of the loan amount, not the price. Rough rule of thumb: each point bumps the lender's yield by about 1/8 of a percent. Points paid to buy your principal residence are generally deductible in the year you pay them; on a refi, you deduct them over the life of the loan. Mortgage interest on acquisition debt up to $750,000 is deductible if you itemize. That's the heart of interest and tax deductibility.

deeper.plain: Pay a percentage of your loan up front, get a lower rate over time. The tax code softens the cost.
deeper.picture: Points are like buying a season pass to save on every game. You pay more now, but each game costs less, and you need to stay long enough for it to pay off.
deeper.street: Leo pays 1 point, $6,000, to drop his rate from 6.75% to 6.5%. His payment falls by about $100 a month, so he breaks even in roughly 5 years. If he moves to Austin in 3 years, the point was a loss.
deeper.stakes: Agents who quote points as a percent of price overstate closing costs and can scare a buyer off. Buyers who pay points and sell quickly waste money.
deeper.exam: One point = 1% of the LOAN. Points on a purchase of a principal residence: generally deductible in the year paid. Refinance points: amortized. 1 point is roughly 1/8% in yield.

blocks.title: Leo's point
blocks.html:
Price $750,000, 20% down = $150,000. Loan = $600,000.
1 point = 1% x $600,000 = $6,000.
Trap answer: 1% of the price, $7,500.
blocks.casual:
Leo's point: price $750,000, 20% down = $150,000, so the loan is $600,000.
1 point = 1% x $600,000 = $6,000.
The trap answer is 1% of the price, $7,500.

deeper.plain: Always compute points on the loan, not the price.
deeper.picture: It's like tipping on the bill, not on the restaurant's total sales for the night.
deeper.street: A buyer's agent emails a closing cost estimate to a Fort Greene buyer showing 2 points as $24,000 on a $1.2M purchase. The loan is $960,000, so it's really $19,200. Tasha catches the error before the buyer panics.
deeper.stakes: A $1,500 to $5,000 error on a closing cost estimate can change whether a buyer can close. It also makes the agent look careless to the lender.
deeper.exam: The test builds the trap right into the choices: one answer uses price, one uses loan. Always find the loan amount first.

blocks.q: A buyer pays 2 points on a $425,000 loan for a $500,000 house. The points cost:
blocks.x: Points are figured on the loan: 2% x $425,000 = $8,500. $10,000 is 2% of the price, the classic wrong answer.

head: Clause
What it does
rows: On default, the lender may declare the entire balance due at once. This is what makes foreclosure possible
If the property is sold or transferred, the lender may call the loan due. Blocks a buyer from taking over the loan without consent
Charge for paying off early. NY limits these on 1 to 6 family owner-occupied loans, and most residential loans today have none
Days after the due date before a late charge (NY: late charge on 1 to 6 family residential loans allowed only after 15 days, max 2% of the installment)
Releases individual parcels from a blanket mortgage as each is paid for
Lender must release the lien when the debt is paid in full
The recorded document proving the loan is paid and the lien is gone

deeper.plain: These clauses decide what happens if you default, sell, pay early, pay late, or pay off the loan.
deeper.picture: They're the fine print on a phone contract: early termination fee, late fee, what happens if you transfer the line, and the confirmation that you're free when it's paid off.
deeper.street: Sal sells his Astoria building to Evelyn and assumes she can take over his 3.5% loan. The due-on-sale clause says no, the lender calls the loan. Separately, Leo pays 10 days late: no late fee, since NY lets lenders charge only after 15 days, max 2% of the installment.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring a due-on-sale clause can force a sudden payoff. A buyer who assumes the lender will waive prepayment penalties on a commercial loan may face a huge charge.
deeper.exam: Acceleration makes foreclosure possible. Alienation equals due-on-sale. Defeasance means release on payment. Release clause goes with blanket mortgages. NY late charge: 15 days, 2%.

blocks.title: NY interest limits
blocks.html: Usury is charging more interest than the law allows. NY's civil usury ceiling is 16%; charging over 25% is criminal usury. A usurious loan made to an individual can be void. Corporations generally cannot raise the civil usury defense, and large commercial loans are largely exempt from the civil cap.
blocks.casual: Usury is charging more interest than the law allows. In NY the civil usury ceiling is 16%, and charging over 25% is criminal usury. A usurious loan to an individual can be void. Corporations generally can't use the civil usury defense, and big commercial loans are mostly exempt from the civil cap.

deeper.plain: NY caps interest at 16% for most loans to people, and above 25% it's a crime.
deeper.picture: Like a speed limit with two signs: 16 gets you a ticket, 25 gets you arrested.
deeper.street: A private lender offers Sal's cousin a $40,000 personal loan against his Astoria condo at 22%. That's over 16%, so the loan may be void as usurious. If the lender had charged 30%, it would be criminal.
deeper.stakes: A lender who charges over the cap to an individual can lose the right to collect the loan at all. Agents who connect clients to these lenders can get pulled into the fallout.
deeper.exam: Civil 16%, criminal 25%. Corporations generally cannot claim civil usury. Expect a question asking which loan is usurious, with a 17% individual loan as the answer.

blocks.html: Lenders can sell loans. An assignment of mortgage transfers the note and mortgage to a new holder, recorded so the world knows who owns the lien. Borrowers keep paying whoever services the loan.
blocks.casual: Lenders sell loans all the time. An assignment of mortgage transfers the note and mortgage to a new holder, and it gets recorded so everyone knows who owns the lien. The borrower just keeps paying whoever services the loan.

deeper.plain: Your loan can be sold; your terms stay the same, and you pay whoever you're told.
deeper.picture: It's like a gym getting bought by a bigger chain. Your membership terms carry over; only the logo on the bill changes.
deeper.street: Six months after closing, Leo gets a letter: his loan was sold and a new servicer in Texas will collect payments starting next month. His rate, term, and balance don't change. The assignment is recorded on ACRIS.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who keep paying the old servicer after a proper transfer notice can end up late. Scammers send fake "your loan was sold" letters, so verify before redirecting payments.
deeper.exam: Assignment transfers the lender's interest; the borrower's obligations don't change. It's recorded to keep the chain of lienholders clear.

blocks.text: Selling a house that has a mortgage

head: Method
What happens
Who is liable
rows: Seller's loan paid off from sale proceeds at closing; satisfaction recorded
Buyer takes title with the loan still on it but does not promise to pay it
Seller stays personally liable. Buyer risks only the property
Buyer takes title and agrees to pay the loan
Buyer is primarily liable; seller stays secondarily liable unless the lender grants a novation

deeper.plain: When you sell a house with a loan on it, the loan can be paid off, left in place without the buyer promising to pay, or formally taken over by the buyer.
deeper.picture: Picture selling your car with a loan on it: pay off the loan at the sale (free and clear), hand over the car with the loan still in your name (subject to), or have the buyer sign on to pay it (assumption).
deeper.street: The Okafors' brownstone has a $120,000 balance. At closing, it's paid off from the $1.6M price and a satisfaction is recorded: free and clear. A different seller in Flatbush lets the buyer take subject to a $300,000 FHA loan; the seller stays personally liable if the buyer stops paying.
deeper.stakes: A seller who lets a buyer take subject to the loan can get their credit wrecked by someone else's missed payments. Assumption without a novation still leaves the seller on the hook secondarily.
deeper.exam: Free and clear: debt paid off. Subject to: seller liable, buyer risks only the property. Assumption: buyer primarily liable, seller secondarily, unless novation.

blocks.title: Subject to vs assume
blocks.html: If the buyer defaults, a buyer who took subject to can lose the house but owes nothing personally. A buyer who assumed can be sued for a deficiency. Most conventional loans have due-on-sale clauses, so assumptions need lender approval; FHA and VA loans are assumable by qualified buyers.
