blocks.casual: If the buyer defaults, someone who took subject to the loan can lose the house but owes nothing personally. Someone who assumed the loan can be sued for a deficiency. Most conventional loans have due-on-sale clauses, so assumptions need the lender's OK. FHA and VA loans can be assumed by qualified buyers.

deeper.plain: Taking subject to risks the house; assuming risks the house and your wallet.
deeper.picture: Subject to is borrowing your friend's bike with a lock you don't own the key for. Assuming is co-signing the bike loan.
deeper.street: In 2024 a buyer in Staten Island assumes a seller's 3% VA loan after the VA and servicer approve him. When he later defaults and the house sells short, the lender can pursue him personally. If he'd taken subject to, only the house would be lost, and the seller would be stuck with the deficiency.
deeper.stakes: Buyers chasing a low rate need to know assumption means personal liability. Sellers need to know that without a release, they're still on the hook.
deeper.exam: "Not personally liable" signals subject to. "Agreed to pay" signals assumption. FHA and VA loans are assumable with qualification; most conventional loans are not, due to the alienation clause.

blocks.q: A buyer takes title subject to the seller's existing mortgage and later stops paying. After foreclosure, who is personally liable for any deficiency?
c: The buyer
The seller
The lender
The title insurer
blocks.x: Taking subject to means the buyer never promised to pay, so the seller remains personally liable. If the buyer had assumed, the buyer would be liable.

blocks.html: Recording matters most when there are several liens. A first mortgage recorded in March outranks a home equity line recorded in June. At a foreclosure sale, the junior lender is paid only after the senior lender is paid in full, which is why second mortgages and HELOCs carry higher rates. A lender can agree to move behind a later loan with a subordination agreement, common when an owner refinances the first mortgage but keeps an existing HELOC.
blocks.casual: Recording matters most when there's more than one lien. A first mortgage recorded in March beats a home equity line recorded in June. At a foreclosure sale, the junior lender only gets paid after the senior lender is paid in full, which is why second mortgages and HELOCs carry higher rates. A lender can agree to move behind a later loan with a subordination agreement, which is common when an owner refinances the first mortgage but keeps an existing HELOC.

deeper.plain: Liens get paid in line. Whoever recorded first usually gets paid first, unless they agree to step back.
deeper.picture: It's a line at a bakery when there's only so much bread. First in line eats; the end of the line may go home hungry.
deeper.street: The Okafors have a first mortgage and a $50,000 HELOC. When they refinance the first in 2021, the new loan would be recorded after the HELOC. The HELOC lender signs a subordination agreement so the new loan keeps first position.
deeper.stakes: Without subordination, a refinance lender won't fund because it would be in second place. Junior lienholders often get wiped out in foreclosures.
deeper.exam: Priority by recording date, except tax liens go first. Subordination agreement changes the order. Junior liens carry higher risk and higher rates.

blocks.title: Co-ops are different
blocks.html: A co-op buyer gets a share loan, not a mortgage. The lender takes a security interest in the shares and proprietary lease under the UCC, files a UCC-1 instead of recording a mortgage, and no mortgage recording tax applies. If the borrower defaults, the lender can sell the shares in a non-judicial UCC sale, much faster than a NY foreclosure.
blocks.casual: Co-ops play by different rules. A co-op buyer gets a share loan, not a mortgage. The lender takes a security interest in the shares and the proprietary lease under the UCC, files a UCC-1 instead of recording a mortgage, and there's no mortgage recording tax. If the borrower defaults, the lender can sell the shares in a non-judicial UCC sale, which is way faster than a NY foreclosure.

deeper.plain: Buying a co-op means buying shares, so the loan works like a loan against stock, not a house.
deeper.picture: A co-op loan is like a loan secured by a season ticket. The lender holds a claim on the ticket, not on the stadium.
deeper.street: Kim's UWS co-op has a buyer taking a $700,000 share loan. Because it's not a mortgage, there's no recording tax, which saves about $13,000 compared with a condo loan the same size. But if the buyer defaults, the lender can auction the shares in months, not years.
deeper.stakes: Co-op owners who assume they have years of foreclosure protection can be surprised by a fast UCC sale. Agents comparing condo and co-op closing costs must account for the missing recording tax.
deeper.exam: Co-op loans: UCC-1, no mortgage recording tax, non-judicial sale. Condo loans: real mortgage, recorded, recording tax, judicial foreclosure.

blocks.html: A mortgage is recorded in the county clerk's office (in NYC, the Office of the City Register through ACRIS). Recording gives constructive notice and sets priority: NY is a race-notice state, so the first good-faith mortgage recorded generally comes first, after real property taxes. The borrower pays NY's mortgage recording tax when recording.
blocks.casual: A mortgage gets recorded in the county clerk's office (in NYC, the Office of the City Register through ACRIS). Recording gives constructive notice and sets priority. NY is a race-notice state, so the first good-faith mortgage recorded generally comes first, after real property taxes. The borrower pays NY's mortgage recording tax when it's recorded.

deeper.plain: Recording tells the world about the lien and locks in your place in line.
deeper.picture: It's like writing your name on the sign-up sheet in pen on the gym bulletin board. Everyone can see it, and you're ahead of anyone who signs later.
deeper.street: Leo closes on a Friday and his lender's title company e-records the mortgage through ACRIS on Monday. If a judgment against the seller had been docketed the day before closing, the title company's last-minute bring-down search would have caught it.
deeper.stakes: An unrecorded mortgage can lose priority to a later good-faith lender who records first. Buyers who forget the recording tax get a surprise at closing; in NYC it's 1.8% or more.
deeper.exam: Race-notice: first to record in good faith without notice wins. Tax liens outrank all. Mortgage recording tax is paid by the borrower; co-op loans don't pay it.

blocks.text: Default and foreclosure in New York

blocks.html: Default is failing to perform: missing payments, letting insurance lapse, not paying taxes. New York uses judicial foreclosure: the lender must sue, and a court controls every step. It is slow, often 2 to 3 years or more.
blocks.casual: Default means not doing what you promised: missing payments, letting insurance lapse, not paying taxes. New York uses judicial foreclosure: the lender has to sue, and a court controls every step. It's slow, often 2 to 3 years or more.

deeper.plain: In NY, lenders need a judge to take a house, and that takes a long time.
deeper.picture: It's like evicting someone from a club where every expulsion needs a hearing, a vote, and an appeal window.
deeper.street: A homeowner in Jamaica, Queens stops paying in 2022. The lender files in 2023, the settlement conferences drag into 2024, and the referee's auction finally happens in 2025. The house sat in limbo for about three years.
deeper.stakes: Investors buying distressed NY homes need patience and cash. Homeowners have time to work things out, but the debt keeps growing with interest and fees.
deeper.exam: NY: judicial foreclosure, because it's a lien theory state. Nonjudicial (power of sale) foreclosure is not the NY norm for homes. Co-ops are the exception, via UCC sale.

blocks.caption: Trace a NY foreclosure from missed payment through acceleration, lis pendens, settlement conference, judgment, referee's sale, and deficiency.

blocks.title: NY judicial foreclosure, home loan

items.title: Default and 90-day notice
items.html: For a home loan, the lender must send a 90-day pre-foreclosure notice (RPAPL 1304) listing housing counselors.

items.title: Acceleration and lawsuit
items.html: Lender accelerates the debt, files the complaint, and records a notice of pendency (lis pendens).

items.title: Settlement conference
items.html: Mandatory court conferences for owner-occupied homes to explore a modification or other workout.

items.title: Judgment of foreclosure and sale
items.html: Court appoints a referee to compute the amount owed and sell the property at public auction.

items.title: Referee's sale and deed
items.html: Highest bidder gets a referee's deed. Proceeds pay costs, then the foreclosing lender, then junior liens in priority, then the owner.

items.title: Deficiency
items.html: If proceeds fall short, the lender may seek a deficiency judgment, but must move within 90 days of the sale.

blocks.casual:
How NY judicial foreclosure on a home loan plays out:
1. Default and 90-day notice: the lender has to send a 90-day pre-foreclosure notice (RPAPL 1304) listing housing counselors.
2. Acceleration and lawsuit: the lender calls the whole debt due, files the complaint, and records a notice of pendency (lis pendens).
3. Settlement conference: mandatory court conferences for owner-occupied homes to try for a modification or workout.
4. Judgment of foreclosure and sale: the court appoints a referee to figure out what's owed and sell at public auction.
5. Referee's sale and deed: the high bidder gets a referee's deed. Proceeds pay costs, then the foreclosing lender, then junior liens in order, then the owner.
6. Deficiency: if there's a shortfall, the lender can seek a deficiency judgment, but has to move within 90 days of the sale.

deeper.plain: Notice, lawsuit, talks, judgment, auction, and maybe a bill for the rest. Each step is court supervised.
deeper.picture: It's like a slow-moving train with mandatory stops. The homeowner can get off (pay up) at any stop before the last one.
deeper.street: The lender sends a Bronx homeowner the 90-day notice listing local counselors. She calls one, gets a loan modification at the settlement conference, and the case is dismissed before any judgment. If she hadn't, a referee would have sold the house on the courthouse steps.
deeper.stakes: Missing the 90-day notice can get a lender's foreclosure case thrown out. Missing the 90-day deficiency deadline means the lender loses the right to chase the borrower for the shortfall.
deeper.exam: Order of events: notice, acceleration and lis pendens, conference, judgment, referee sale, deficiency. Referee's deed. 90-day pre-foreclosure notice and 90-day deficiency motion.

blocks.html: Until the sale, the owner has an equitable right of redemption: pay what is owed and stop the foreclosure. NY has no statutory right of redemption after the sale. A deficiency judgment is limited to the debt minus the higher of the sale price or the court-determined fair market value (RPAPL 1371).
blocks.casual: Right up until the sale, the owner has an equitable right of redemption: pay what's owed and the foreclosure stops. NY has no statutory right of redemption after the sale. A deficiency judgment is capped at the debt minus the higher of the sale price or the court-determined fair market value (RPAPL 1371).

deeper.plain: You can save the house by paying up before the auction. After, it's gone. And the lender can't cheaply buy at auction then chase you for a huge balance.
deeper.picture: It's like getting your car back from the tow lot: pay before they auction it and it's yours. Once auctioned, no takebacks.
deeper.street: A Bay Ridge owner owes $520,000. Her brother lends her the money the week before the auction, and she redeems. Her neighbor wasn't so lucky: after the sale, he learns there is no NY right to buy it back.
deeper.stakes: Owners who wait past the sale lose everything. Lenders who try to collect a deficiency based on a lowball auction price get capped by fair market value.
deeper.exam: NY: equitable redemption before sale, no statutory redemption after. Deficiency uses the higher of sale price or fair market value.

blocks.title: Deficiency math
blocks.html:
Debt with costs: $410,000. Auction price: $300,000. Court finds fair market value: $350,000.
Deficiency = $410,000 minus the higher of $300,000 or $350,000 = $60,000, not $110,000.
blocks.casual:
Debt plus costs: $410,000. Auction price: $300,000. The court finds fair market value: $350,000.
Deficiency = $410,000 minus the higher of $300,000 or $350,000 = $60,000, not $110,000.

deeper.plain: Subtract the bigger of the two values from what's owed. That's the most the lender can chase.
deeper.picture: Like a store that sold your trade-in for cheap: the law says they have to credit you at least what it was actually worth.
deeper.street: A lender buys a Flushing house at its own foreclosure auction for $300,000, then tries to get a $110,000 judgment against the former owner. The court values the house at $350,000 and limits the judgment to $60,000.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who don't contest the fair market value could pay $50,000 more than they should. Lenders who skip the motion within 90 days get nothing.
deeper.exam: Debt minus the higher of sale price or FMV. The trap answer uses the auction price and gets the bigger number.

blocks.q: Which statement about New York foreclosure is correct?
c: Lenders usually foreclose by power of sale without going to court
The owner may redeem for one year after the sale
Foreclosure is judicial, and a deficiency motion must be made within 90 days after the sale
Deficiency judgments are banned in New York
blocks.x: NY requires judicial foreclosure and allows a deficiency judgment if sought within 90 days. There is no post-sale statutory redemption period in NY.

blocks.title: Hook: Note promises, Mortgage pledges
blocks.html: Note = Need to pay. Mortgage = May take the house. Mortgagor = borrower.
blocks.casual: Hook: Note = Need to pay. Mortgage = May take the house. Mortgagor = borrower.

deeper.plain: Three tiny letters sort out the most-tested finance vocabulary.
deeper.picture: Picture a sticky note saying "N: need to pay" and a house key labeled "M: may take". The borrower is wearing a badge that says "OR".
deeper.street: Jordan quizzes Leo on the subway home from closing. "Who's the mortgagor?" Leo: "Me, b-OR-rower." "What does the note do?" "Need to pay." Leo adds a new tab to the spreadsheet called "Hooks".
deeper.stakes: Mixing up note and mortgage, or mortgagor and mortgagee, costs easy exam points and makes you sound green in front of lenders and attorneys.
deeper.exam: Expect at least one direct definition question on mortgagor, mortgagee, or note vs mortgage. The hook gets it right in five seconds.

story.title: The Cell Leo Couldn't Fill
story.setting: A coffee shop in Long Island City, Saturday

beats.text: Leo has his laptop open to tab 14, labeled WORST CASE. Tasha arrives with two iced coffees and no patience for spreadsheets.
What am I signing? A mortgage? A note? Both?
Both. The note says you owe $600,000. The mortgage says if you don't pay, the bank can go after the condo.
So the bank gives me a mortgage.
The bank gives you money. You give the bank a mortgage. You're the mortgagor.
And that one point you quoted him?
One percent of the loan. Six grand, not seventy-five hundred.

check.q: Leo borrows $600,000 on a $750,000 condo and pays 1.5 points. How much is that?

beats.text: Okay. Tab 14. I lose my job. They take the condo next month?
This is New York. They have to sue. Ninety-day notice first, then court, settlement conferences, a judgment, a referee's auction. Usually years.
And if the auction brings less than I owe?
They can ask for a deficiency judgment, but within 90 days of the sale, and it's measured against the higher of the sale price or fair market value.
And up until the sale he can pay it all and keep the place.
Equitable redemption. After the gavel, no do-overs in New York.
Leo types for a while. Then he renames tab 14 to EMERGENCY FUND and puts six months of PITI in it.
Best thing a first-time buyer can learn: the note is the promise, the mortgage is the consequence, and New York makes the consequence slow but real.

board.prompt: Draw a timeline of a NY foreclosure from the first missed payment to a deficiency judgment. Mark where the owner can still redeem.

facts.text: The promissory note (often called a bond in NY) is the borrower's personal promise to repay; the mortgage is the security instrument that pledges the property and creates a lien.
The borrower is the mortgagor because the borrower gives the mortgage; the lender is the mortgagee, who receives it.
New York is a lien theory state: the borrower keeps title and the usual rights of ownership, and the lender holds only a lien.
The mortgagor must pay the debt, keep the property in repair (no waste), insure it naming the lender, and pay taxes; breaking any of these is a default even if payments are on time.
PITI is principal, interest, taxes and insurance; the lender collects 1/12 of yearly taxes and insurance each month into escrow and pays those bills.
In NY mortgage interest is paid in arrears: the June 1 payment covers May's interest.
Amortization pays a loan to zero with level payments; early payments are mostly interest and later ones mostly principal.
A straight (term) mortgage is interest only, with the entire principal due at the end.
Monthly interest is the balance times the annual rate divided by 12; the rest of the payment reduces principal, and next month's interest is figured on the lower balance.
A discount point is prepaid interest equal to 1% of the loan amount, not of the price.
Each point raises the lender's yield about 1/8 of a percent; points to buy a principal residence are generally deductible in the year paid, on a refinance over the loan's life.
Itemizers may deduct mortgage interest on acquisition debt up to $750,000.
An acceleration clause lets the lender declare the whole balance due on default, which is what makes foreclosure possible.

An alienation (due-on-sale) clause lets the lender call the loan due if the property is transferred, so assumptions of most conventional loans need lender consent; FHA and VA loans are assumable by qualified buyers.
The grace period is the time after the due date before a late charge; in NY a late charge on a 1 to 6 family residential loan is allowed only after 15 days and is capped at 2% of the installment.
A prepayment penalty is a charge for paying off early; NY limits them on 1 to 6 family owner-occupied loans and most residential loans today have none.
The defeasance clause requires the lender to release the lien when the debt is paid, and a recorded satisfaction of mortgage proves the loan is paid and the lien gone.
NY's civil usury ceiling is 16% and over 25% is criminal usury; corporations generally cannot raise the civil usury defense.
An assignment of mortgage transfers the note and mortgage to a new holder and is recorded; the borrower keeps paying whoever services the loan.
A buyer who takes subject to the mortgage is not personally liable and risks only the property; the seller stays personally liable.
A buyer who assumes the mortgage becomes primarily liable and can be sued for a deficiency; the seller stays secondarily liable unless the lender grants a novation.
An earlier recorded mortgage outranks a later one, and a junior lender is paid only after the senior is paid in full; a subordination agreement lets a lender move behind a later loan.

A mortgage is recorded with the county clerk (City Register via ACRIS in NYC); recording gives constructive notice, NY is race-notice so the first good-faith mortgage recorded generally comes first after property taxes, and the borrower pays the mortgage recording tax.
A co-op purchase uses a share loan: the lender files a UCC-1 against the shares and proprietary lease, no mortgage recording tax applies, and default leads to a non-judicial UCC sale.

NY uses judicial foreclosure, often 2 to 3 years; on a home loan the lender must first send a 90-day pre-foreclosure notice (RPAPL 1304), then sue, file a lis pendens, and a court-appointed referee sells.
The owner's equitable right of redemption lasts until the foreclosure sale; NY has no statutory right of redemption after the sale.
A deficiency judgment is limited to the debt minus the higher of the sale price or the court-determined fair market value (RPAPL 1371).
A lender seeking a deficiency judgment must move within 90 days of the foreclosure sale.

lessons.title: Loan Types, Government Programs, and the Secondary Market
lessons.tagline: Every loan type exists to solve one problem. Learn the problem and the name follows.
objectives: Distinguish conventional from government insured or guaranteed loans
Match FHA, VA, RHS, and SONYMA to the borrowers they serve
Explain ARM mechanics: index, margin, rate cap, payment cap, lifetime cap
Identify every specialty loan in the syllabus from a one-line description
Trace a loan from the primary market to Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, or Ginnie Mae, and explain PMI and MIP

blocks.title: Three buyers, one Tuesday
blocks.html: Tasha's morning: a Marine veteran wants a two-family in Staten Island with nothing down. A nurse in Utica has $12,000 saved and a 640 credit score. A couple in Rhinebeck needs to buy their new house before their old one sells. Three problems, three different loans. Which ones?
blocks.casual: Tasha's Tuesday morning: a Marine veteran wants a two-family in Staten Island with nothing down. A nurse in Utica has $12,000 saved and a 640 credit score. A couple in Rhinebeck needs to buy their new place before the old one sells. Three problems, three different loans. Which ones?

deeper.plain: Different buyers need different loan programs. Matching the buyer's problem to the right loan is the job.
deeper.picture: It's like a shoe store: running shoes, work boots, and dress shoes all go on feet, but you pick by what you're doing in them.
deeper.street: Tasha matches them fast: the Marine gets a VA loan with no down payment on an owner-occupied two-family. The Utica nurse gets FHA at 3.5% down, or a SONYMA program with down payment help. The Rhinebeck couple gets a bridge loan to cover the gap until their old house closes.
deeper.stakes: Put a buyer in the wrong loan and they overpay for years, get denied late in the deal, or can't close on time. Agents who know the programs keep deals alive.
deeper.exam: Scenario questions describe a borrower and ask for the best loan. Cue words: veteran (VA), low down payment and modest credit (FHA), rural (USDA), first-time NY buyer (SONYMA), timing gap (bridge).

blocks.html: A conventional mortgage has no government insurance or guarantee. The lender relies on the borrower's credit and the property, plus private mortgage insurance (PMI) when the borrower puts down less than 20%. Government loans are insured (FHA) or guaranteed (VA, RHS) by a federal agency, which lets lenders accept less money down.
blocks.casual: A conventional mortgage has no government insurance or guarantee behind it. The lender is betting on the borrower's credit and the property, plus private mortgage insurance (PMI) if the borrower puts down less than 20%. Government loans are insured (FHA) or guaranteed (VA, RHS) by a federal agency, which is why lenders will take less money down.

deeper.plain: Conventional loans stand on the borrower's own strength. Government loans have Uncle Sam backing the lender if things go wrong.
deeper.picture: A conventional loan is lending to a friend on their word. A government loan is lending to a friend whose parent co-signed.
deeper.street: Leo puts 20% down on his LIC condo with a conventional loan and pays no PMI. His coworker buys a $400,000 Yonkers condo with 5% down conventional, so she pays PMI until her balance falls far enough.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't know the difference may pick a government loan with lifetime insurance when a conventional loan would let them drop PMI later, or vice versa.
deeper.exam: Conventional = not government insured or guaranteed. PMI applies to conventional loans above 80% LTV. FHA = insured. VA and RHS = guaranteed.

head: Program
Who backs it
Who it serves
Key features
rows: Insured by FHA (part of HUD). FHA does not lend
Buyers with modest savings or credit
3.5% minimum down; upfront and annual MIP; 1 to 4 family owner-occupied; assumable by qualified buyers
Guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs
Eligible veterans, service members, some surviving spouses
No down payment typical; no PMI; funding fee; Certificate of Eligibility; owner-occupied
USDA Rural Housing Service guarantees or lends directly
Low and moderate income buyers in eligible rural areas
Often no down payment; income limits; guarantee fee
State of New York Mortgage Agency, a state public benefit corporation
Below-market rates through participating lenders; income and price limits; down payment assistance; first-time rule waived for veterans and in targeted areas

deeper.plain: FHA helps buyers with little saved, VA helps veterans, USDA helps rural buyers, and SONYMA helps New York first-timers.
deeper.picture: Think of four different discount cards at the same store: one for students (FHA's low down), one for veterans (VA), one for country residents (USDA), and one for NY newcomers (SONYMA).
deeper.street: A first-time buyer in Schenectady earns $78,000 and has $8,000 saved. Tasha uses a SONYMA loan with its down payment assistance, keeping her rate below market. A veteran buying a duplex in Tottenville uses VA, gets his Certificate of Eligibility, pays the funding fee, and lives in one unit.
deeper.stakes: Missing a program can cost a buyer tens of thousands. Steering an eligible veteran away from VA without a reason is bad service, and misrepresenting eligibility is fraud.
deeper.exam: FHA: 3.5% min down, MIP, 1 to 4 family owner-occupied. VA: no down typical, no PMI, funding fee. USDA: rural, income limits. SONYMA: NY state agency, first-time buyers, waived for veterans and targeted areas.

blocks.title: Insure vs guarantee, Agency vs Association
blocks.html: FHA insures; VA guarantees. Neither normally lends the money; approved lenders do. And the syllabus calls SONYMA the "State of New York Mortgage Association". Its real name is the State of New York Mortgage Agency. Either label points to the same NY program.
blocks.casual: FHA insures; VA guarantees. Neither one usually lends the money; approved lenders do. Also, the syllabus calls SONYMA the "State of New York Mortgage Association". The real name is the State of New York Mortgage Agency. Either label means the same NY program.

deeper.plain: Government agencies back the loans; banks make them. And SONYMA is an Agency, not an Association.
deeper.picture: FHA is an insurance company for the lender. VA is a co-signer. The bank is still the one handing over the cash.
deeper.street: Leo's friend calls the FHA office asking to "apply for an FHA loan". They tell him to go to an FHA-approved lender like the one Tasha works with. FHA doesn't write checks to buyers.
deeper.stakes: Telling a client "FHA will lend you the money" sends them the wrong direction and makes you look uninformed to lenders.
deeper.exam: "FHA insures" and "VA guarantees" are tested word pairs. If an answer says FHA makes the loan, it's wrong. Accept either SONYMA name if it appears.

blocks.q: The Staten Island Marine wants to buy with no money down. The best fit is most likely:
c: An FHA loan
A VA loan
A conventional loan with PMI
A balloon mortgage
blocks.x: VA loans are guaranteed for eligible veterans and typically need no down payment. FHA requires at least 3.5% down.

blocks.html: Which is better? A fixed rate wins when rates are low and the buyer plans to stay a long time, because the payment never moves. An ARM can win when the buyer expects to sell or refinance before the first adjustment, because the starting rate is usually lower. The danger is payment shock: a borrower qualified at the teaser rate who cannot afford the adjusted payment. Federal ability-to-repay rules now require lenders to qualify ARM borrowers at a higher rate than the starting one.
blocks.casual: Fixed or ARM? A fixed rate wins when rates are low and the buyer's staying a long time, because the payment never moves. An ARM can win when the buyer expects to sell or refinance before the first adjustment, because it usually starts lower. The danger is payment shock: a borrower who qualified at the teaser rate can't afford the payment after it adjusts. Federal ability-to-repay rules now make lenders qualify ARM borrowers at a higher rate than the starting one.

deeper.plain: Fixed is predictable; ARMs are cheaper now and riskier later. Match the loan to how long you'll keep it.
deeper.picture: A fixed loan is a yearly subway pass at a locked price. An ARM is a pay-per-ride card that's cheaper now but the fare could jump next year.
deeper.street: Leo plans to stay 10 years, so he takes a 30-year fixed at 6.5%. His friend at a hedge fund is moving to London in 4 years, so she takes a 7/1 ARM at 5.75% and expects to sell before it ever adjusts.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who took ARMs they couldn't afford after reset fueled the 2008 foreclosure wave. Today's ability-to-repay rules exist to prevent a repeat.
deeper.exam: Fixed: lender bears interest rate risk. ARM: borrower bears it. Payment shock is the risk after adjustment. Lenders must qualify ARM borrowers above the start rate.

blocks.html: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same rate and principal and interest payment for the whole term. The lender carries the risk of inflation and rising rates. An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) shifts that risk to the borrower in exchange for a lower starting rate.
blocks.casual: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same rate and the same principal and interest payment for the whole term. The lender eats the risk of inflation and rising rates. An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) hands that risk to the borrower in exchange for a lower starting rate.

deeper.plain: With a fixed loan, the bank takes the risk that rates go up. With an ARM, you do.
deeper.picture: A fixed rate is a prepaid phone plan with a locked price. An ARM is a plan that resets to whatever the market price is every year, with limits.
deeper.street: In 2021 the Okafors refinanced at a fixed 2.9%. When rates hit 7% in 2023, their lender was stuck earning 2.9% on their money. That's the lender's inflation risk on a fixed loan.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who don't understand who holds the rate risk may choose an ARM to save $200 a month and then face $800 more after adjustment.
deeper.exam: Lender holds inflation and rate risk on a fixed-rate loan. Borrower holds it on an ARM. The trade-off is a lower initial rate.

head: ARM part
Meaning
rows: A published market rate the ARM follows (today usually SOFR or a Treasury rate). The lender does not control it
The lender's fixed markup, set at origination and never changes
Limits how much the rate can change at each adjustment
Highest rate ever allowed over the loan's life
Limits how much the payment can rise. Interest not covered is added to the balance

deeper.plain: An ARM's rate is a market number plus the lender's markup, limited by caps.
deeper.picture: Think of a taxi meter: the index is the base fare that the city sets, the margin is the driver's flat add-on, and the caps are the maximum surge you'll ever pay.
deeper.street: Tasha explains a 5/1 ARM to a Park Slope buyer: index is SOFR, margin is 2.75%. Each year after year 5 the rate resets to SOFR plus 2.75%, but never more than 2% higher than the year before, and never more than 5% above the start rate over the life of the loan.
deeper.stakes: A borrower who doesn't know the caps can't estimate the worst-case payment. An agent who says "rates will probably fall" is giving a promise nobody can keep.
deeper.exam: Index moves; margin doesn't. Fully indexed rate = index + margin. Rate caps limit the rate; payment caps limit the payment and can cause negative amortization.

blocks.title: ARM adjustment
blocks.html:
A 5/1 ARM started at 5.5%. Margin 2.75%, periodic cap 2%, lifetime cap 5% over the start rate. At the first adjustment the index is 4.5%.
Fully indexed = 4.5% + 2.75% = 7.25%.
Periodic cap allows at most 5.5% + 2% = 7.5%. Lifetime ceiling is 10.5%.
New rate = 7.25% (the fully indexed rate is under both caps).
blocks.casual:
Here's an ARM adjusting. A 5/1 ARM started at 5.5%. Margin is 2.75%, periodic cap 2%, lifetime cap 5% over the start rate. At the first adjustment, the index is 4.5%.
Fully indexed = 4.5% + 2.75% = 7.25%.
The periodic cap allows at most 5.5% + 2% = 7.5%. The lifetime ceiling is 10.5%.
New rate = 7.25%, because the fully indexed rate is under both caps.

deeper.plain: Add index and margin, then check both caps. Use the lowest of the three numbers.
deeper.picture: Like figuring a delivery fee: base price plus service fee, but never more than the promo limit and never more than the store's max.
deeper.street: If the index had been 5.5% instead, fully indexed would be 8.25%. The periodic cap holds it to 7.5% this year. Next year, if the index stays put, the rate could rise to 8.25%, still under the 10.5% ceiling.
deeper.stakes: Getting the caps wrong means telling a borrower their new payment is lower or higher than it really is, which can wreck their budget planning.
deeper.exam: Steps: index + margin, compare to (old rate + periodic cap) and to the lifetime ceiling, pick the lowest. The trap answer adds the cap to the index instead of the old rate.

blocks.title: Payment caps can grow your debt
blocks.html: If a payment cap keeps the payment below the interest owed, the unpaid interest is added to principal. That is negative amortization: the balance goes up while you pay. Graduated payment mortgages do the same thing in early years.
blocks.casual: Careful: if a payment cap holds the payment below the interest you owe, the unpaid interest gets added to the principal. That's negative amortization: your balance goes up even though you're paying. Graduated payment mortgages do the same thing in the early years.

deeper.plain: Paying less than the interest means your debt grows every month.
deeper.picture: It's like paying $20 a month on a credit card that charges $30 in interest. You're paying and still sinking.
deeper.street: A borrower's ARM payment is capped at $2,500 but the interest due is $2,800. The $300 shortfall is added to the balance every month. After 3 years, she owes about $11,000 more than she borrowed.
deeper.stakes: Negative amortization can leave a borrower owing more than the home is worth, which makes selling or refinancing nearly impossible.
deeper.exam: Payment cap (not rate cap) can cause negative amortization. Graduated payment mortgages may negatively amortize early. Balance increases is the giveaway.

blocks.html: Do not memorize this table as a list of names. Ask what problem each loan solves. Not enough cash now? Graduated payment, buydown, pledged account, or shared equity. Timing gap? Bridge loan. Building something? Construction loan with a takeout. Many parcels? Blanket with release clauses. No bank willing to lend? Purchase money mortgage, land contract, or wraparound, where the seller becomes the lender. Need cash from a house you already own? Home equity loan, reverse mortgage, or sale-leaseback.
blocks.casual: Don't memorize the next table as a list of names. Ask what problem each loan fixes. Not enough cash right now? Graduated payment, buydown, pledged account, or shared equity. Timing gap? Bridge loan. Building something? Construction loan with a takeout. Lots of parcels? Blanket with release clauses. No bank willing to lend? Purchase money mortgage, land contract, or wraparound, where the seller becomes the lender. Need cash out of a house you already own? Home equity loan, reverse mortgage, or sale-leaseback.

deeper.plain: Every specialty loan solves one specific problem. Learn the problem and the name sticks.
deeper.picture: It's a toolbox: you don't memorize every tool's name, you remember a wrench is for bolts and a hammer is for nails.
deeper.street: Evelyn needs cash from her Long Island City office building without losing the space for her firm. She does a sale-leaseback: sells it for $14M, leases it back for 15 years, and frees up capital for a new acquisition.
deeper.stakes: Agents who can match a client's problem to a loan type keep deals alive that would otherwise die for lack of financing.
deeper.exam: Problem-to-loan questions: "seller provides financing" means purchase money, land contract, or wraparound. "Multiple lots" means blanket. "Draws during building" means construction.

blocks.title: Purchase money vs land contract
blocks.html: With a purchase money mortgage the buyer gets the deed at closing and the seller holds a lien. With a land contract the seller keeps the deed until the buyer finishes paying. Same seller financing idea, opposite location of title.
blocks.casual: With a purchase money mortgage, the buyer gets the deed at closing and the seller holds a lien. With a land contract, the seller keeps the deed until the buyer's done paying. Same seller-financing idea, opposite side holding title.

deeper.plain: Both are seller financing. The difference is who holds the deed while the buyer pays.
deeper.picture: Purchase money is buying a car with the dealer's loan and getting the title in your name with a lien. A land contract is rent-to-own: the store keeps the title until the last payment.
deeper.street: Sal sells a Hudson Valley lot for $200,000 with $40,000 down. With a purchase money mortgage, the buyer owns the land today and Sal holds a $160,000 lien. With a land contract, Sal keeps the deed until the $160,000 is paid.
deeper.stakes: A land contract buyer has weaker protection if the seller dies, gets sued, or files bankruptcy, because legal title still sits with the seller.
deeper.exam: Purchase money: buyer gets title, seller is mortgagee. Land contract: seller keeps legal title, buyer has equitable title. The question will ask "who holds title".

head: Loan
One-line definition
Picture it
rows: Payments do not fully pay off the loan; a large final payment is due
Payments start low and rise on a schedule; may negatively amortize early
Lump sum paid up front to lower the rate, temporarily (2-1) or permanently
Builder pays to cut the buyer's rate
Borrower can get more money later, up to a limit, under the same mortgage
One mortgage covers two or more parcels; release clause frees lots as sold
Covers real property plus personal property such as appliances
Furnished condo in a new building
New junior loan that wraps around an existing loan; seller keeps paying the original
Seller financing over an old low-rate loan
Short-term loan to buy the new home before the old one sells
Loan used to buy the property; in exam usage, the seller takes back a mortgage for part of the price
Short-term, funded in draws as work is completed, interest only; replaced by a takeout (permanent) loan
Seller finances and keeps legal title until paid (installment sale)
Junior loan against existing equity: lump sum or line of credit (HELOC)
Owner 62+ receives payments from equity; repaid when the owner sells, moves, or dies
Lender or investor gets a share of appreciation in exchange for a lower rate or help with the down payment
Borrower's savings deposit is pledged as extra collateral, lowering the risk
Owner sells the property and leases it back, freeing capital
A company sells its HQ and stays as tenant

deeper.plain: Each specialty loan is built for one situation: big final payment, rising payments, rate buydowns, multiple parcels, seller financing, building, tapping equity, and more.
deeper.picture: Think of a deli counter where every sandwich is named for the customer who asked for it: the Bridge for the couple in between homes, the Blanket for the developer, the Reverse for the retiree.
deeper.street: A developer in Saratoga takes a blanket mortgage on 40 lots with release clauses, so each lot is freed as it sells. He also uses a construction loan funded in draws, then a takeout loan when the homes are finished. Down in Bayside, a retired couple, both 70, take a reverse mortgage to pay for home care.
deeper.stakes: Picking the wrong product can sink a project: a developer with no release clause can't deliver clear title to lot buyers, and a balloon borrower who can't refinance faces losing the property.
deeper.exam: Common pairs: release clause with blanket; draws and takeout with construction; 62+ with reverse; appliances with package; seller keeps paying old loan with wraparound; temporary rate cut with buydown.

blocks.q: A developer finances 30 lots with one loan and wants each lot freed from the lien as it sells. She needs a:
c: Wraparound mortgage with a due-on-sale clause
Package mortgage
Open-end mortgage
Blanket mortgage with a release clause
blocks.x: A blanket mortgage covers several parcels, and the release clause lets each lot be released as it is paid for. A package mortgage adds personal property, not more parcels.

blocks.html: For 2026 the baseline conforming limit for a one-unit home is $832,750, and up to $1,249,125 in high-cost areas such as the NYC metro region. A $1.5 million Tribeca loan is a jumbo, so it is nonconforming and priced by the lender's own appetite. Standardization is the point of the secondary market: because loans follow uniform forms and underwriting rules, an investor in Ohio can buy a pool of Brooklyn loans without ever seeing the houses.
blocks.casual: For 2026, the baseline conforming loan limit for a one-unit home is $832,750, and up to $1,249,125 in high-cost areas like the NYC metro. So a $1.5 million Tribeca loan is a jumbo: it's nonconforming and priced by whatever the lender's appetite is. The whole point of the secondary market is standardization. Because loans use uniform forms and underwriting rules, an investor in Ohio can buy a pool of Brooklyn loans without ever seeing the houses.

deeper.plain: Loans under a size limit and following standard rules can be sold easily. Bigger ones are jumbos and play by different rules.
deeper.picture: Conforming loans are like standard shipping boxes: any truck can carry them. Jumbos are oversized freight that needs special handling.
deeper.street: Leo's $600,000 loan is conforming, so his lender can sell it to Fannie Mae next month. A Tribeca buyer borrowing $1.5M gets a jumbo, and her bank keeps it on its own books with a slightly different rate and tougher reserve requirements.
deeper.stakes: Buyers just over the limit can face higher rates or tougher rules. Agents who know the thresholds can help buyers adjust down payments to stay conforming.
deeper.exam: Conforming means meeting Fannie and Freddie limits and standards. Jumbo means above the limit. Standardization is what makes the secondary market work. Limits change yearly, so focus on the concept.

blocks.html: The primary market is where loans are made: banks, credit unions, savings institutions, and mortgage bankers lend directly to borrowers. The secondary market is where those loans are bought and sold, often pooled into mortgage-backed securities. Selling loans gives lenders fresh cash to lend again.
blocks.casual: The primary market is where loans get made: banks, credit unions, savings institutions, and mortgage bankers lending straight to borrowers. The secondary market is where those loans get bought and sold, often bundled into mortgage-backed securities. Selling loans gives lenders fresh cash to lend all over again.

deeper.plain: Lenders make loans, sell them, and use the cash to make more loans.
deeper.picture: It's like a bakery that sells its bread to a grocery chain every morning, then uses that money to bake more bread tomorrow.
deeper.street: Tasha's bank funds 200 Brooklyn and Queens mortgages in March, then sells them to Freddie Mac in April. With that cash it funds another 200 in May. Without the secondary market, it would run out of money to lend after the first batch.
deeper.stakes: When the secondary market freezes, as it did in 2008, lenders stop lending and the housing market stalls. Agents feel it immediately in canceled deals.
deeper.exam: Primary market lends to borrowers. Secondary market buys existing loans. The secondary market provides liquidity, it does not lend to consumers directly.

blocks.caption: Follow the money: borrower to lender, lender to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, pooled into securities for investors. Note that Ginnie Mae guarantees but does not buy.

head: Agency
What it does
Loans
rows: Buys loans from lenders and issues mortgage-backed securities. Government-sponsored enterprise
Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation. Same job as Fannie, created to give smaller lenders a buyer
Government corporation inside HUD. Guarantees timely payment on securities; does not buy loans

deeper.plain: Fannie and Freddie buy regular loans. Ginnie guarantees the bonds made from government-backed loans.
deeper.picture: Fannie and Freddie are wholesale buyers at a farmers' market. Ginnie Mae is the government inspector who stamps the crates of FHA and VA produce as guaranteed.
deeper.street: Leo's conventional loan gets sold to Fannie Mae, pooled with thousands of others, and turned into securities. The Staten Island veteran's VA loan ends up in a Ginnie Mae pool: Ginnie doesn't buy it, but guarantees investors get paid on time.
deeper.stakes: Mixing these up on the exam is a common miss. In practice, knowing who buys what helps you understand why lenders follow strict guidelines.
deeper.exam: Ginnie Mae: inside HUD, guarantees securities backed by FHA, VA, USDA loans, does not buy loans. Fannie and Freddie: GSEs that buy conventional conforming loans.

blocks.html: Loans that meet Fannie and Freddie size and underwriting standards are conforming. Loans above the limit (jumbo) or outside the standards are nonconforming and are held by lenders or sold privately.
blocks.casual: Loans that meet Fannie and Freddie's size and underwriting standards are conforming. Loans over the limit (jumbos) or outside the standards are nonconforming, and lenders either keep them or sell them privately.

deeper.plain: Follow the standard rules and stay under the limit, and your loan is conforming. Otherwise it's not.
deeper.picture: It's like checked luggage: under the size and weight limit, it goes on any plane. Over, it needs special arrangements and costs more.
deeper.street: A self-employed buyer in Williamsburg can't document income the standard way. Her lender writes a bank-statement loan that doesn't meet Fannie guidelines. It's nonconforming even though the amount is small, so it stays on the lender's books.
deeper.stakes: Nonconforming loans often cost more. Borrowers with unusual income or properties need to know their options may be limited.
deeper.exam: Nonconforming can mean too big (jumbo) or not meeting the standards. Don't assume nonconforming means only jumbo.

blocks.html: PMI protects the lender, not the borrower, on conventional loans above 80% loan-to-value. Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, the borrower may ask to cancel at 80% of original value, and it ends automatically at 78% if payments are current. FHA loans carry MIP instead: an upfront premium plus an annual premium, which on many FHA loans lasts for the life of the loan.
blocks.casual: PMI protects the lender, not the borrower, on conventional loans above 80% loan-to-value. Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, the borrower can ask to cancel at 80% of the original value, and it drops off automatically at 78% if payments are current. FHA loans use MIP instead: an upfront premium plus an annual one, which on many FHA loans lasts for the life of the loan.

deeper.plain: Mortgage insurance covers the lender if you default. On conventional loans you can drop it once you've paid down enough; on many FHA loans you can't.
deeper.picture: PMI is like the insurance a rental car company buys on its own car. You pay the premium, but the coverage is for them.
deeper.street: Leo's coworker bought a $400,000 Yonkers condo with 5% down. She can request PMI removal once her balance hits $320,000 and it ends automatically at $312,000. Her friend with an FHA loan and 3.5% down will pay MIP for the life of the loan unless she refinances.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who don't request PMI cancellation at 80% overpay for months. Buyers comparing FHA and conventional should look at how long the insurance lasts.
deeper.exam: PMI protects the lender. Request at 80%, automatic at 78% of original value. FHA has MIP, often for life. The trap answer says PMI protects the borrower.

blocks.title: When can PMI go?
blocks.html: Original value $500,000. Request cancellation at 80%: balance of $400,000. Automatic termination at 78%: balance of $390,000.
blocks.casual: When can PMI go? Original value $500,000. You can request cancellation at 80%, a balance of $400,000. It ends automatically at 78%, a balance of $390,000.

deeper.plain: Multiply the original value by 80% and 78% to find the two key balances.
deeper.picture: Two mile markers on the highway: at mile 80 you can take the exit if you ask; at mile 78 the road exits for you.
deeper.street: A buyer in New Rochelle bought at $500,000 in 2019. Her house is now worth $650,000, but the automatic 78% rule is based on original value, so it ends at a $390,000 balance. To use the new value she'd need to ask the lender and usually pay for an appraisal.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who don't know these numbers keep paying PMI long after they could stop, sometimes for years.
deeper.exam: Use ORIGINAL value, not current market value, for the statutory 80% and 78% tests. $500,000 x 0.80 = $400,000; x 0.78 = $390,000.

blocks.q: Ginnie Mae differs from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac because Ginnie Mae:
c: Buys only conventional loans
Makes loans directly to borrowers
Guarantees securities backed by FHA and VA loans rather than buying loans
Is a private corporation with no government ties
blocks.x: Ginnie Mae is a government corporation within HUD that guarantees mortgage-backed securities made of government-backed loans. Fannie and Freddie buy loans, mostly conventional.

blocks.title: Hook: Ginnie Guarantees Government
blocks.html: Ginnie Guarantees Government loans. Fannie and Freddie buy conventional ones. FHA Insures, VA Guarantees.
blocks.casual: Hook: Ginnie Guarantees Government loans. Fannie and Freddie buy conventional ones. FHA Insures, VA Guarantees.

deeper.plain: Three G's for Ginnie, and "I" vs "G" for FHA and VA.
deeper.picture: Picture Ginnie in a hard hat with a big G on it, stamping crates marked FHA and VA, while Fannie and Freddie push shopping carts full of ordinary loans.
deeper.street: During a training at Hudson & Hart, Diane writes "GGG" on the whiteboard. Marcus says he's been in the business 15 years and still mixes them up. Diane says, "Then you've been wrong for 15 years."
deeper.stakes: Easy points on the exam, and credibility when talking with lenders and buyers about loan options.
deeper.exam: Expect a question asking which entity guarantees securities backed by FHA and VA loans (Ginnie) or which buys conventional loans (Fannie or Freddie). FHA insures; VA guarantees.

story.title: Tasha's Tuesday
story.setting: Tasha's office above a bakery in Forest Hills

beats.text: Jordan shadows Tasha for a morning. Her phone rings before the coffee does.
Staten Island two-family, Marine veteran, zero down. Easy. VA.
Does the VA lend him the money?
No, a lender does. The VA guarantees part of it. He'll pay a funding fee, but no PMI.
Call two: a nurse in Utica, $12,000 saved, credit 640.
FHA, 3.5% down, or SONYMA if she's a first-time buyer under the limits. SONYMA's rate might beat it.
beats.tag: FHA 3.5% down; SONYMA first-time NY buyers

beats.text: The textbook says SONYMA is an Association.
The textbook's wrong. Agency. State of New York Mortgage Agency.
Call three: a couple in Rhinebeck closing on a new house before their old one sells.
Bridge loan. Short term, secured by the old house, paid off when it sells.

check.q: Why does the Rhinebeck couple need a bridge loan?
c: To lower their interest rate permanently
To buy the new home before the sale of the old one closes
To finance several parcels at once
To receive monthly payments from equity
check.x: A bridge or swing loan covers the gap between buying the new home and selling the old one.

beats.text: Where do all these loans end up?
The conventional ones, I sell to Fannie or Freddie through my lenders. The VA and FHA ones get pooled into Ginnie Mae securities. Ginnie doesn't buy, it guarantees.
And the nurse's FHA has MIP. If she'd gone conventional with 5% down?
PMI. She can ask to drop it at 80% of original value, and it falls off at 78%.
Every loan type answers one question: who's taking the risk, and what are they getting for it? Ask that, and the names stop being a vocabulary list.

board.prompt: Draw the path of a VA loan and a conventional loan from borrower to investor. Label who lends, who guarantees or buys, and who insures.

facts.text: A conventional loan has no government insurance or guarantee; PMI is required when the borrower puts down less than 20%.
FHA (part of HUD) insures loans but does not lend; minimum down is 3.5% and the borrower pays upfront and annual MIP.
VA partially guarantees loans to eligible veterans: typically no down payment, no PMI, a funding fee and a Certificate of Eligibility.
The USDA Rural Housing Service guarantees or makes loans for low and moderate income buyers in eligible rural areas.
SONYMA is a New York State agency offering below-market loans, mostly to first-time buyers, through participating lenders.
A fixed-rate loan keeps the same rate and payment, so the lender bears the risk of inflation and rising rates; an ARM shifts that risk to the borrower for a lower start rate.
An ARM can beat a fixed rate for a borrower who will sell or refinance before the first adjustment; the danger is payment shock when the rate adjusts.
An ARM's fully indexed rate is index plus margin, limited by the periodic cap at each adjustment and the lifetime cap.
The ARM index is a published market rate the lender does not control; the margin is set at origination and never changes.
When a payment cap keeps the payment below the interest due, the unpaid interest is added to principal: negative amortization.
A balloon loan's payments do not fully pay it off, leaving a large final payment.
A buydown is a lump sum paid up front to lower the rate, temporarily (such as 2-1) or permanently.
An open-end mortgage lets the borrower get more money later, up to a limit, under the same mortgage.
A package mortgage covers real property plus personal property such as appliances.
A blanket mortgage covers two or more parcels, and its release clause frees each lot as it is sold.
A wraparound is a new junior loan around an existing loan; the seller keeps paying the original loan from the buyer's payments.
A bridge (swing) loan is short-term money to buy a new home before the old one sells.
In a purchase money mortgage the seller takes back a mortgage for part of the price and the buyer gets the deed at closing.
Under a land contract the seller finances and keeps legal title until the buyer finishes paying.
A construction loan is short-term, interest only and funded in draws as work is done, then replaced by a permanent takeout loan.
A home equity loan is a junior loan against existing equity, taken as a lump sum or as a revolving line of credit (HELOC).
In a reverse (annuity) mortgage an owner 62 or older receives payments from equity, repaid when the owner sells, moves or dies.
In a shared equity loan an investor or lender gets a share of appreciation; in a pledged account loan the borrower's savings deposit is pledged as extra collateral.
In a sale-leaseback the owner sells the property and leases it back, freeing capital.
The primary market makes loans directly to borrowers; the secondary market buys and pools them into securities, giving lenders fresh cash to lend.
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy mostly conventional conforming loans; Ginnie Mae, inside HUD, guarantees securities backed by FHA, VA and USDA loans and buys no loans.
Conforming loans meet Fannie and Freddie size and underwriting standards (2026: $832,750 baseline, up to $1,249,125 in high-cost areas); jumbo loans above the limit are nonconforming.

PMI protects the lender; under the Homeowners Protection Act the borrower may ask to cancel at 80% of original value and it ends automatically at 78%, while FHA MIP often lasts for the life of the loan.

lessons.title: Underwriting, Truth in Lending, and Predatory Lending
lessons.tagline: Lenders ask two questions: is the house worth it, and can this person pay? Predators skip the second one.
objectives: Compute LTV on the lesser of price or appraisal, and front-end and back-end ratios
List what lenders review about the property and the borrower
Apply TILA and Regulation Z: APR, trigger terms, and the right of rescission
Recognize predatory practices: flipping, packing, equity stripping, steering into subprime
Name the NY and federal laws that fight predatory lending and lending discrimination

blocks.title: The appraisal came in low
blocks.html: Leo's contract price on the Long Island City condo is $750,000. The appraisal comes back at $720,000. He planned to borrow 80%. Meanwhile, Marcus forwards Jordan a flyer for a lender advertising "Only $1,999 a month!" and asks if it is fine to post on the firm's Instagram. Two problems, both about the rules lenders live by.
blocks.casual: Leo's under contract on the LIC condo at $750,000. The appraisal comes back at $720,000, and he was planning to borrow 80%. Meanwhile Marcus forwards Jordan a lender's flyer that says "Only $1,999 a month!" and asks if it's cool to post on the firm's Instagram. Two problems, and both come down to the rules lenders live by.

deeper.plain: A low appraisal changes how much you can borrow, and a catchy payment ad can break federal law.
deeper.picture: Two speed bumps on the same block: one slows down the buyer's financing, the other slows down the agent's marketing.
deeper.street: Tasha calls Leo: "Your loan is now based on $720,000, so you need $24,000 more in cash or a price cut." Jordan tells Marcus the flyer needs the down payment, repayment terms, and APR before it goes anywhere.
deeper.stakes: Leo could lose his deal if he can't cover the gap. Marcus could put the firm on the hook for a Reg Z violation with one post.
deeper.exam: Low appraisal questions: use the lower of price or appraisal. Ad questions: spot the trigger term and know what full disclosure must include.

blocks.html: Underwriters judge the property's investment quality: sales price and appraised value, location, condition, comparable sales, and the type of property. Owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes get the best terms. Investment and income-producing property gets stricter terms, and lenders count only part of the expected rent (often 75%) as income.
blocks.casual: Underwriters size up the property as an investment: sales price and appraised value, location, condition, comparable sales, and property type. Owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes get the best terms. Investment and income property gets tougher terms, and lenders only count part of the expected rent (often 75%) as income.

deeper.plain: Lenders want the property to be worth the loan, and they trust homes people live in more than rentals.
deeper.picture: A pawnshop looks harder at a used drone than at a gold ring. Some collateral just holds value more reliably.
deeper.street: Sal wants to buy a second building in Woodside with projected rents of $12,000 a month. The lender counts only $9,000, 75%, to allow for vacancies and expenses. Sal qualifies for less than he expected.
deeper.stakes: Investors who count every dollar of rent overestimate what they can borrow and make offers they can't finance.
deeper.exam: Owner-occupied gets the best terms. Rental income is discounted, often to 75%. The property's investment quality is half of underwriting; the borrower's ability is the other half.

blocks.html: The key number is the loan-to-value ratio (LTV): loan amount divided by the property's value, where value is the lower of the price or the appraisal. Lower LTV means more borrower equity and less lender risk. Above 80% on a conventional loan usually means PMI.
blocks.casual: The number that matters is the loan-to-value ratio (LTV): the loan divided by the property's value, and value means the lower of the price or the appraisal. Lower LTV means the borrower has more equity and the lender has less risk. Over 80% on a conventional loan usually means PMI.

deeper.plain: LTV is how much you borrow compared with what the place is worth. Lenders always use the lower value.
deeper.picture: It's like a pawnshop loaning you 80% of what your watch is worth, using whichever is lower: what you paid or what the appraiser says.
deeper.street: A buyer in Riverdale overpays in a bidding war: $900,000 on a co-op appraised at $850,000. Her lender's 80% LTV is based on $850,000, so the max loan is $680,000, not $720,000. She covers the $40,000 difference in cash.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who win bidding wars above appraisal must cover the gap with cash. Agents who don't warn them risk a dead deal at the last minute.
deeper.exam: LTV = loan / lower of price or appraisal. Questions give both numbers and test whether you pick the lower.

blocks.title: Leo's low appraisal
blocks.html:
Price $750,000, appraisal $720,000. Lender uses the lower: $720,000.
Max loan at 80% = 0.80 x $720,000 = $576,000.
Cash needed = $750,000 minus $576,000 = $174,000 (plus closing costs), not the $150,000 he planned. He can renegotiate, add cash, or accept a higher LTV with PMI.
blocks.casual:
Leo's low appraisal: price $750,000, appraisal $720,000. The lender goes with the lower, $720,000.
Max loan at 80% = 0.80 x $720,000 = $576,000.
Cash needed = $750,000 minus $576,000 = $174,000 (plus closing costs), not the $150,000 he planned on. His options: renegotiate, bring more cash, or take a higher LTV and pay PMI.

deeper.plain: A $30,000 lower appraisal means $24,000 more cash at 80% LTV.
deeper.picture: Like a store that gives you 80% back on returns but only counts the sale price, not what you paid. Lower base, smaller check.
deeper.street: Jordan calls the seller's agent: "Our appraisal came in at $720,000. Can your sellers meet us at $735,000?" The sellers agree, Leo's loan stays at $576,000, and he brings $159,000 instead of $174,000.
deeper.stakes: Without an appraisal contingency or room to negotiate, Leo either finds $24,000 or risks his deposit. Agents earn their fee in moments like this.
deeper.exam: Step one: lower of price and appraisal. Step two: multiply by the LTV. Step three: price minus loan equals cash needed. The trap uses the price.

blocks.caption: Enter income, PITI, and other debts. Watch the front-end and back-end ratios, the LTV, and when PMI kicks in.

items: Income: salary, bonuses, and other stable income, verified by pay stubs, W-2s, and tax returns
Employment history: usually 2 years; stability and likely continuance, with education or training counting for new careers
Self-employed: sole proprietors, partners, and corporate owners show 2 years of tax returns and business statements
Liquid assets: cash for the down payment, closing costs, and reserves
Monthly obligations and credit history: credit report, scores, and record of repayment
Verification: lenders document everything; stated-income loans helped cause the 2008 crash
blocks.casual:
Lenders check the borrower's ability to repay:
Income: salary, bonuses, other steady income, proven with pay stubs, W-2s, and tax returns.
Employment history: usually 2 years, looking for stability and likely continuance, and education or training counts for new careers.
Self-employed: sole proprietors, partners, and corporate owners show 2 years of tax returns and business statements.
Liquid assets: cash for the down payment, closing costs, and reserves.
Monthly obligations and credit history: credit report, scores, and repayment record.
Verification: lenders document everything. Stated-income loans helped cause the 2008 crash.

deeper.plain: Lenders want proof that you earn steady money, have cash saved, and pay your bills.
deeper.picture: It's a job interview for your wallet: references (credit), work history, savings in the bank, and receipts for everything.
deeper.street: A freelance photographer in Greenpoint earned $140,000 last year but only $60,000 the year before. Tasha's lender averages two years of tax returns: $100,000 qualifying income. She qualifies for less than she hoped.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who change jobs or quit right before closing can blow up their approval. Agents should tell buyers: don't switch jobs or buy a car until after closing.
deeper.exam: Two years of employment and tax returns is the standard. Self-employed borrowers need business returns. Reserves are cash left after closing.

blocks.html: Qualifying ratios compare monthly payments to gross monthly income. The textbook benchmarks: conventional 28/36 and FHA 31/43. The front-end ratio is housing (PITI, plus HOA or co-op maintenance) divided by gross income. The back-end ratio is housing plus all recurring debt (car, student loans, card minimums, child support) divided by gross income. Automated underwriting may allow more, but the exam uses these.
blocks.casual: Qualifying ratios compare monthly payments to gross monthly income. The textbook benchmarks are 28/36 for conventional and 31/43 for FHA. The front-end ratio is housing (PITI, plus HOA or co-op maintenance) divided by gross income. The back-end ratio is housing plus all recurring debt (car, student loans, card minimums, child support) divided by gross income. Automated underwriting may allow more, but the exam uses these numbers.

deeper.plain: Your housing cost and your total debts must each stay under a percentage of your pre-tax income.
deeper.picture: Two slices of a pie: housing can take up to 28% of it, and housing plus everything else up to 36%.
deeper.street: Kim's co-op board in the Upper West Side uses its own stricter debt test, but the lender for a buyer there still runs 28/36 first. Maintenance of $2,200 counts as housing, along with the share loan payment.
deeper.stakes: Agents who show buyers homes above their ratio limits waste everyone's time and create heartbreak when the loan is denied.
deeper.exam: Front-end = housing / gross. Back-end = housing + other debt / gross. Conventional 28/36, FHA 31/43. Use gross, never net income.

blocks.title: How much house can she afford?
blocks.html:
Gross annual income: $108,000, so monthly = $9,000.
Front-end limit: 28% x $9,000 = $2,520 PITI.
Back-end limit: 36% x $9,000 = $3,240 total debt. She pays $900 a month on a car and loans, so PITI can be at most $3,240 minus $900 = $2,340.
The lender uses the lower: $2,340 maximum PITI.
blocks.casual:
How much house can she afford? Gross annual income is $108,000, so monthly is $9,000.
Front-end limit: 28% x $9,000 = $2,520 PITI.
Back-end limit: 36% x $9,000 = $3,240 total debt. She pays $900 a month on a car and loans, so PITI can be at most $3,240 minus $900 = $2,340.
The lender takes the lower: $2,340 max PITI.

deeper.plain: Run both ratios. Whichever gives the smaller payment is the limit.
deeper.picture: Two doorways in a row; you can only carry a box as wide as the narrower door.
deeper.street: Tasha runs this for a nurse in Flushing. She was hoping for $2,500 a month on a condo. With her $900 car and student loans, the ceiling is $2,340. Tasha suggests paying off the car loan first, which raises her max PITI back to $2,520.
deeper.stakes: Misreading the ratio means a buyer bids on homes they can't finance, loses deposits, or gets denied late.
deeper.exam: Always compute both and choose the lower. The trap answer is the front-end figure when back-end debt is high.

blocks.q: A couple earns $144,000 a year. Their PITI would be $3,300 and other debts total $1,200 a month. Using 28/36, they:
c: Qualify on both ratios
Fail both ratios
Pass the front-end ratio but fail the back-end ratio
Fail the front-end ratio but pass the back-end ratio
blocks.x: Monthly income is $12,000. Front-end: $3,300 / $12,000 = 27.5%, under 28%. Back-end: $4,500 / $12,000 = 37.5%, over 36%. Other debts sink them.

blocks.title: Credit laws in the Consumer Credit Protection Act
blocks.html: The Consumer Credit Protection Act (1968) is the umbrella. Its titles include Truth in Lending, the Fair Credit Reporting Act (accurate credit reports, notice when credit is denied based on a report), and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (no credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance).
blocks.casual: The Consumer Credit Protection Act (1968) is the umbrella law. Under it you've got Truth in Lending, the Fair Credit Reporting Act (credit reports have to be accurate, and you get notice when credit is denied because of a report), and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (no credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance).

deeper.plain: One big 1968 law holds several smaller ones: honest loan costs, accurate credit reports, and no lending discrimination.
deeper.picture: It's an umbrella with three spokes: TILA, FCRA, and ECOA. Pull any one out and borrowers get wet.
deeper.street: A lender denies a Queens couple because "your wife might get pregnant and stop working". That's sex and marital status discrimination under ECOA. They file a complaint with the CFPB.
deeper.stakes: Lenders who discriminate face federal penalties and lawsuits. Agents who steer clients away from lenders because of protected traits face fair housing complaints too.
deeper.exam: ECOA protected classes include marital status, age, and receipt of public assistance, which are not in the federal Fair Housing Act. FCRA requires notice of adverse action based on a credit report.

blocks.text: Truth in Lending and Regulation Z

blocks.html: TILA protects borrowers by information, not by price control. A lender may legally charge a high rate (within usury limits) as long as it discloses the cost correctly. The disclosures let a borrower compare a 6.25% loan with 2 points against a 6.5% loan with no points on equal footing, because both are converted into an APR.
blocks.casual: TILA protects borrowers with information, not price controls. A lender can legally charge a high rate (inside the usury limits) as long as it discloses the cost correctly. The disclosures let a borrower compare a 6.25% loan with 2 points against a 6.5% loan with no points on equal footing, because both get converted into an APR.

deeper.plain: Truth in Lending doesn't cap your rate. It makes sure you can see the real cost.
deeper.picture: It's like a menu that has to show the total price with tax and tip, so you can compare restaurants fairly.
deeper.street: Leo compares two offers: Bank A at 6.25% with 2 points, Bank B at 6.5% with no points. Once the points are folded in, the two APRs land much closer together than the note rates, which shows him the real gap is smaller than it looked.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who compare only note rates can choose the more expensive loan. Lenders who misdisclose face TILA penalties and possible rescission.
deeper.exam: TILA is a disclosure law, not a rate cap. Usury law caps rates. APR is the comparison tool.

blocks.html: The Truth in Lending Act (TILA) is implemented by Regulation Z, now enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. It covers consumer credit, including home loans to individuals, but not business or commercial loans. It does not set rates. It requires disclosure of the cost of credit so borrowers can compare: the finance charge and the annual percentage rate (APR), which folds points and certain fees into a yearly rate. That is why the APR is usually higher than the note rate.
blocks.casual: The Truth in Lending Act (TILA) is carried out through Regulation Z, now enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. It covers consumer credit, including home loans to individuals, but not business or commercial loans. It doesn't set rates. It requires lenders to disclose the cost of credit so borrowers can compare: the finance charge and the annual percentage rate (APR), which folds points and certain fees into a yearly rate. That's why the APR is usually higher than the note rate.

deeper.plain: Reg Z makes lenders show the full cost of a consumer loan as one yearly number.
deeper.picture: The note rate is the sticker price; APR is the out-the-door price with fees included.
deeper.street: Evelyn borrows $3M for a commercial building in Long Island City. No Reg Z disclosures, because it's a business loan. Leo's condo loan, on the other hand, gets the full Loan Estimate with APR.
deeper.stakes: Lenders who skip disclosures on consumer loans face penalties. Agents who assume Reg Z applies to commercial deals waste time chasing disclosures that aren't required.
deeper.exam: Reg Z: consumer credit only, enforced by CFPB, disclosure not rate setting. APR includes points and certain fees, so it's usually higher than the note rate.

blocks.html: For most home purchase loans, TILA and RESPA disclosures are combined (TRID): a Loan Estimate within 3 business days of application and a Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing. RESPA also bans kickbacks and referral fees for settlement services.
blocks.casual: On most home purchase loans, the TILA and RESPA disclosures are combined (TRID): a Loan Estimate within 3 business days of applying, and a Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing. RESPA also bans kickbacks and referral fees for settlement services.

deeper.plain: You get a cost estimate soon after you apply and the final numbers a few days before closing, and nobody can get paid just for sending you to a provider.
deeper.picture: Like a contractor's written estimate up front and the final invoice three days before you hand over the check, with no secret commissions to the guy who recommended him.
deeper.street: Leo applies on Monday and gets his Loan Estimate by Thursday. His Closing Disclosure arrives the Monday before his Friday closing. When a title company offers Jordan a $500 "thank you" for each referral, Jordan says no: that's a RESPA Section 8 kickback.
deeper.stakes: A late Closing Disclosure can push back a closing date. Accepting referral fees for settlement services can bring federal penalties and DOS discipline.
deeper.exam: Loan Estimate: 3 business days after application. Closing Disclosure: at least 3 business days before consummation. RESPA Section 8 bans kickbacks.

head: Advertising under Reg Z
Result
rows: Fine on its own. General terms and APR alone are not trigger terms
Trigger term (payment amount). The ad must also state the down payment, the terms of repayment, and the APR
Trigger terms (down payment, number of payments)

deeper.plain: If a loan ad mentions specific terms like the monthly payment or down payment, it has to spell out all the key terms.
deeper.picture: It's like a car ad saying "$199 a month!" in giant letters. The law makes the fine print show up too: how much down, for how long, at what APR.
deeper.street: Jordan sends the flyer back to the lender with a note: the "$1,999 a month" line can stay only if the same ad states the down payment, the repayment terms (30 years, 360 payments), and the APR. The simpler fix is to drop the payment and just say "Financing available, 6.5% APR".
deeper.stakes: Posting an ad with a trigger term and no disclosures is a federal violation, and the agent who posts it shares the liability with the lender.
deeper.exam: Trigger terms: the amount or percentage of the down payment, the number of payments or period of repayment, the payment amount, and the amount of the finance charge. APR alone and general phrases like "easy financing" are not triggers. Required disclosures: down payment, repayment terms, and APR.

blocks.title: It applies to you
blocks.html: Reg Z advertising rules apply to anyone who advertises consumer credit, including real estate licensees. A listing that says "$2,100 a month with 5% down" needs the full disclosures. Marcus's flyer cannot go up as is.
blocks.casual: Heads up, this applies to you. Reg Z's ad rules cover anyone who advertises consumer credit, real estate licensees included. A listing that says "$2,100 a month with 5% down" needs the full disclosures. Marcus's flyer can't go up as is.

deeper.plain: Agents who put payment numbers in listings are advertising credit and must follow Reg Z.
deeper.picture: Like a bartender who mixes the drink still has to card the customer. Doesn't matter that you're not the owner.
deeper.street: A Hudson & Hart listing for a Sunnyside condo reads "Own for less than rent! $2,100 a month with 5% down!" Diane pulls it from the site within an hour and adds price, term, and APR before it goes back up.
deeper.stakes: A DOS investigator or the CFPB can treat the agent as the advertiser. The firm's name is on the ad, so the supervising broker is exposed too.
deeper.exam: "Does Reg Z apply to real estate licensees?" Yes, when they advertise financing terms. The trap answer says it only applies to lenders.

blocks.html: Right of rescission: on a refinance or home equity loan secured by the borrower's principal residence, the borrower can cancel until midnight of the third business day after closing (or after receiving the disclosures, if later). It does not apply to a purchase-money loan to buy the home.
blocks.casual: Right of rescission: on a refinance or home equity loan secured by the borrower's principal residence, the borrower can cancel up until midnight of the third business day after closing (or after getting the disclosures, if that's later). It does not apply to a purchase-money loan used to buy the home.

deeper.plain: If you borrow against the home you already live in, you get three business days to change your mind. Not when you're buying it.
deeper.picture: A cooling-off period, like the return window on an online purchase, but only for loans that put your existing home at risk.
deeper.street: The Okafors take a $100,000 HELOC on their Bed-Stuy brownstone to help their daughter. Closing is Tuesday. They have until midnight Friday to cancel. When Leo closed on his condo purchase loan, he had no such window.
deeper.stakes: Lenders who fund before the rescission period ends, or skip the notice, can face extended rescission rights for up to 3 years. Borrowers who miss the deadline lose the option.
deeper.exam: Rescission: 3 business days, principal residence, refinance or home equity only. Never on a purchase-money mortgage, never on investment property.

blocks.q: Which borrower has a 3-day right of rescission under Regulation Z?
c: A buyer getting a mortgage to purchase her first home
An investor refinancing a 20-unit apartment building
A homeowner taking a home equity line on her principal residence
A company borrowing to buy a warehouse
