blocks.x: Rescission covers refinances and home equity loans on a principal residence. Purchase-money loans and business loans are excluded.

blocks.html: Licensees see predatory loans before anyone else does. A buyer who suddenly has a lender promising "no income check, no problem", a seller asked to sign a side agreement returning cash to the buyer outside closing, or an appraisal that magically matches the contract price are all warning signs. A side payment hidden from the lender is mortgage fraud, and a licensee who knows about it and stays silent shares the risk.
blocks.casual: Licensees spot predatory loans before anybody else. A buyer who suddenly has a lender promising "no income check, no problem", a seller asked to sign a side deal sending cash back to the buyer outside of closing, or an appraisal that magically hits the exact contract price: those are all warning signs. A side payment hidden from the lender is mortgage fraud, and a licensee who knows about it and keeps quiet shares the risk.

deeper.plain: Agents often see the red flags first, and staying silent about fraud makes you part of it.
deeper.picture: You're the lifeguard on the stand. If you see someone drowning and look away, you're responsible too.
deeper.street: A buyer's agent asks the Okafors to sign a side letter giving $40,000 back to the buyer after closing, not shown on the Closing Disclosure. Priya refuses on the spot: it's mortgage fraud because the lender would be lending against an inflated price.
deeper.stakes: Participating in or ignoring fraud can cost your license, get you sued, and land you in criminal court. The buyer may also end up with a loan they can't afford.
deeper.exam: Undisclosed side payments, straw buyers, and inflated appraisals are fraud. The right answer is to refuse and disclose, never to "keep it between the parties".

blocks.html: Predatory lending means abusive loan terms or practices that strip borrowers' equity or set them up to fail. It clusters in subprime loans, made to borrowers with weaker credit at higher rates. Not every subprime loan is predatory, but most predatory loans are subprime.
blocks.casual: Predatory lending is abusive loan terms or tactics that strip borrowers' equity or set them up to fail. It clusters in subprime loans, the higher-rate loans made to borrowers with weaker credit. Not every subprime loan is predatory, but most predatory loans are subprime.

deeper.plain: Some lenders design loans to take a borrower's equity or force a default. They usually target people with weaker credit.
deeper.picture: Subprime is the high-risk aisle at the store. Most products there are legit. The predatory ones are the items with hidden blades in the packaging.
deeper.street: A retired bus driver in Canarsie with a 600 credit score gets a subprime refinance at 9%. That's high, but if it's disclosed and he can afford it, it's legal. If the lender adds $15,000 in junk fees and a balloon he can't pay, it's predatory.
deeper.stakes: Predatory loans lead to foreclosure, ruined credit, and lost generational wealth, hitting the most vulnerable homeowners the hardest.
deeper.exam: Subprime is not automatically predatory. Predatory means abusive terms or practices. Watch for answers that equate the two.

head: Practice
What it looks like
rows: Rates and points far above the borrower's risk; fees packed into the loan (credit insurance, junk fees)
Low payments now, a huge balloon the borrower cannot pay or refinance
Repeated refinancing with no real benefit to the borrower, each time charging new points and fees
Rolling unsecured credit card debt into a home loan, turning unsecured debt into a lien that can cost the house
Older, equity-rich owners pressured into loans they cannot afford
Equity stripping and rescue scams
"Sign the deed to us and we'll save your house" schemes during foreclosure
Pushing qualified borrowers, often in minority neighborhoods, into costlier loans

deeper.plain: Predatory lending wears many disguises: hidden fees, balloon traps, needless refis, rolling card debt into a mortgage, targeting seniors, rescue scams, and steering.
deeper.picture: It's a pickpocket crew: one bumps you, one distracts, one takes the wallet. Each tactic looks harmless alone; together they empty your pockets.
deeper.street: An 80-year-old widow in Hollis gets three refinance calls a year from the same lender. Each refi charges 3 points and new fees, but her rate barely moves. That's loan flipping. Her $300,000 of equity drops to $150,000 in five years.
deeper.stakes: Elderly and minority homeowners lose homes they owned free and clear. Agents who refer clients to these lenders can face liability and reputational damage.
deeper.exam: Match terms: repeated refis with no benefit equals flipping; signing the deed to a rescuer equals equity stripping; pushing qualified borrowers into costlier loans by neighborhood equals reverse redlining.

blocks.html: Fraud shows up on both sides: inflated appraisals, straw buyers, fake income, false occupancy claims. A licensee who knowingly takes part, for example by hiding a side payment from the lender, risks license revocation and criminal charges. The fallout of predatory loans is foreclosure, which in turn drags down whole blocks, as East New York and parts of southeast Queens saw after 2008.
blocks.casual: Fraud shows up on both sides: inflated appraisals, straw buyers, fake income, lying about living in the place. A licensee who knowingly takes part, say by hiding a side payment from the lender, risks license revocation and criminal charges. And the fallout from predatory loans is foreclosure, which drags down entire blocks, like East New York and parts of southeast Queens saw after 2008.

deeper.plain: Fraud can come from the borrower, the lender, or the middlemen. When it ends in foreclosure, whole neighborhoods suffer.
deeper.picture: One rotten floorboard in a row house weakens the neighbors' walls too.
deeper.street: A straw buyer "purchases" three houses in East New York in 2006 with fake W-2s and inflated appraisals. All three go into foreclosure by 2009, sit vacant, and drag down the values of every home on the block.
deeper.stakes: Licensees who take part can lose their license and face federal mortgage fraud charges. Neighbors lose equity they did nothing to deserve losing.
deeper.exam: Fraud examples: straw buyer, false occupancy, inflated appraisal, fake income. The licensee's duty is to refuse and not participate.

blocks.title: New York's predatory lending laws
blocks.html: Banking Law 6-l (high-cost home loans): limits points and fees, bans flipping, limits balloon payments and negative amortization, requires counseling disclosures. Banking Law 6-m (subprime home loans): requires an ability-to-repay review and restricts prepayment penalties. RPAPL 1304: the 90-day pre-foreclosure notice. The Home Equity Theft Prevention Act targets foreclosure rescue scams. NY usury caps: 16% civil, 25% criminal.
blocks.casual: New York's own predatory lending laws: Banking Law 6-l (high-cost home loans) caps points and fees, bans flipping, limits balloon payments and negative amortization, and requires counseling disclosures. Banking Law 6-m (subprime home loans) requires an ability-to-repay review and restricts prepayment penalties. RPAPL 1304 is the 90-day pre-foreclosure notice. The Home Equity Theft Prevention Act goes after foreclosure rescue scams. And NY usury caps are 16% civil, 25% criminal.

deeper.plain: NY adds its own layer of protection for high-cost and subprime loans, homeowners facing foreclosure, and victims of rescue scams.
deeper.picture: Federal law is the fence around the yard; NY adds a locked gate and a motion light.
deeper.street: A Jamaica, Queens owner in default gets a flyer: "Sign your deed to us, we'll stop the foreclosure." The Home Equity Theft Prevention Act gives her rights to cancel such a deal and requires specific disclosures, and her housing counselor (listed in her 1304 notice) spots the scam.
deeper.stakes: Lenders that violate 6-l or 6-m can lose the right to collect certain charges or face penalties. Agents involved in rescue scams face serious liability.
deeper.exam: 6-l = high-cost loans. 6-m = subprime loans. RPAPL 1304 = 90-day notice. Home Equity Theft Prevention Act = rescue scams. Usury 16/25.

blocks.title: Federal tools
blocks.html: HOEPA (1994) restricts high-cost loans. Dodd-Frank (2010) created the CFPB and the ability-to-repay rule. The Fair Housing Act and ECOA ban redlining: refusing or limiting loans in an area because of its racial or ethnic makeup. HMDA requires lenders to report lending data so patterns can be spotted, and the Community Reinvestment Act pushes banks to serve their whole community.
blocks.casual: On the federal side: HOEPA (1994) restricts high-cost loans. Dodd-Frank (2010) created the CFPB and the ability-to-repay rule. The Fair Housing Act and ECOA ban redlining, which means refusing or limiting loans in an area because of its racial or ethnic makeup. HMDA makes lenders report lending data so patterns can be spotted, and the Community Reinvestment Act pushes banks to serve their whole community.

deeper.plain: Federal laws ban discriminatory lending by area, require data to catch it, and force lenders to check borrowers can repay.
deeper.picture: HMDA is the security camera, CRA is the store's community promise, and Fair Housing and ECOA are the laws the camera is watching for.
deeper.street: HMDA data shows a bank made almost no loans in Black-majority Brooklyn neighborhoods while lending heavily in nearby white ones. Regulators open a redlining investigation, and under CRA the bank's merger application gets delayed.
deeper.stakes: Redlining keeps entire communities from building wealth. Banks found redlining pay settlements and must open branches and lending programs in neglected areas.
deeper.exam: HMDA = reporting data. CRA = serve the whole community. HOEPA = high-cost loans. Dodd-Frank = CFPB and ability to repay. Redlining = refusing loans by area's racial makeup.

blocks.q: A lender refinances an elderly owner's Bed-Stuy home three times in 18 months, charging new points each time, with no lower rate or other benefit. This practice is:
c: Loan flipping
Redlining
A buydown
Negative amortization
blocks.x: Repeated refinancing that benefits only the lender through new fees is loan flipping. Redlining is refusing to lend in an area based on its demographics.

blocks.title: Hook: Lower of the two, 28/36, 3 days
blocks.html: LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal. Ratios 28/36 (FHA 31/43). Rescission: 3 business days, refinance only, never the purchase loan.
blocks.casual: Hook: LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal. Ratios are 28/36 (FHA 31/43). Rescission is 3 business days, refinance only, never the purchase loan.

deeper.plain: Lower of two values, two ratio pairs, three days.
deeper.picture: Count it on one hand: one rule for value (the lower), two pairs of ratios, three days to cancel.
deeper.street: Jordan quizzes Leo while they wait for the closing room in Midtown. "Appraisal was lower, so?" "Use the lower." "Your ratios?" "28/36." "Can you rescind this?" "No, it's a purchase." Tasha, overhearing, says he's ready to be a loan officer.
deeper.stakes: These three numbers drive a lot of real deals and a lot of test questions. Get any wrong and you misadvise a client or miss an easy point.
deeper.exam: Distractors: the higher of price or appraisal, 33/38 ratios, 5 or 7 day rescission, rescission on a purchase. Lock in lower, 28/36, 3, refinance only.

story.title: $1,999 a Month
story.setting: Hudson & Hart Realty, Monday staff meeting

beats.text: Lender gave me this flyer. "Own in Canarsie for only $1,999 a month!" Going on our Instagram today.
That's a trigger term. A payment amount means the ad also needs the down payment, the repayment terms, and the APR.
It's the lender's flyer, not ours.
If we post it, it's our ad. Truth in Lending applies to anyone advertising credit, licensees included.
Jordan's phone buzzes. Leo: "APPRAISAL $720K. PANIC?"
No panic. The lender uses the lower of price or appraisal. Eighty percent of $720,000 is $576,000.

check.q: Leo's price is $750,000 and the appraisal $720,000. At 80% LTV, how much cash does he need for the purchase price?

beats.text: Tell him to see my guy. He'll do 97% on stated income, no questions. And he refinances you every year.
Every year, with new points each time? That's loan flipping. And no-doc income is how 2008 happened.
New York has rules on that, right? High-cost loans, subprime loans.
Banking Law 6-l and 6-m. Limits on fees, flipping, balloons, prepayment penalties, plus an ability-to-repay check.
Fine. What about my client who wants to cancel her home equity line? She closed Thursday.
Home equity on her principal residence gets three business days to rescind. For rescission, Saturdays count as business days, so Friday, Saturday, Monday. She has until midnight Monday.
beats.tag: Rescission: 3 business days, not purchase loans

beats.text: Good lenders ask whether the house is worth it and whether the borrower can pay. Predators only ask the first question. Our job is to notice the difference.

board.prompt: Compute front-end and back-end ratios for a buyer earning $96,000 a year with $2,300 PITI and $700 other debt. Show each step.

facts.text: Underwriters judge the property as collateral: owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes get the best terms, and lenders count only part of expected rent (often 75%) as income.
Loan-to-value is the loan divided by the lower of the price or the appraisal; above 80% on a conventional loan usually means PMI.
Lenders verify stable income and usually 2 years of employment; self-employed borrowers show 2 years of tax returns and business statements.
The front-end ratio is housing cost (PITI plus HOA or maintenance) divided by gross monthly income: 28% conventional, 31% FHA.
The back-end ratio adds all recurring debt to housing (36% conventional, 43% FHA), and the lender allows the lower PITI of the two limits.
The Consumer Credit Protection Act (1968) is the umbrella law whose titles include Truth in Lending, the Fair Credit Reporting Act and ECOA.
ECOA bans credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age or receipt of public assistance.
The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires accurate credit reports and notice when credit is denied based on a report.
Truth in Lending is implemented by Regulation Z, enforced by the CFPB; it requires disclosure of the cost of credit but does not set rates.
TILA covers consumer credit, including home loans to individuals, but not business or commercial loans.
The APR folds points and certain fees into a yearly rate, so it is usually higher than the note rate.
Under TRID the Loan Estimate is due within 3 business days of application and the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing; RESPA bans kickbacks for settlement services.

A trigger term in an ad (payment amount, down payment, number of payments, finance charge) requires disclosing the down payment, repayment terms and APR, and the rule applies to real estate licensees.
General statements like "easy financing" and the APR alone are not trigger terms.
The 3-business-day right of rescission applies to a refinance or home equity loan on the principal residence, never to the purchase loan.
Predatory lending clusters in subprime loans (weaker credit, higher rates), but not every subprime loan is predatory.
Loan flipping is repeated refinancing with no real benefit to the borrower, charging new points and fees each time.
Predatory practices include hidden fees, balloon traps, packing credit card debt into a home loan, targeting equity-rich older owners and steering; verifying ability to repay is not one.
"Deed us the house and rent it back" foreclosure rescue offers are equity-stripping scams, targeted in NY by the Home Equity Theft Prevention Act.
Redlining is refusing or limiting loans in an area because of its racial or ethnic makeup, banned by the Fair Housing Act and ECOA; reverse redlining steers such areas into costlier loans.
NY Banking Law 6-l (high-cost loans) and 6-m (subprime loans) limit fees, flipping, balloons and prepayment penalties and require an ability-to-repay review.
A side payment hidden from the lender is mortgage fraud, and a licensee who knowingly takes part risks license revocation and criminal charges.
HMDA makes lenders report lending data, the CRA pushes banks to serve their whole community, HOEPA restricts high-cost loans, and Dodd-Frank created the CFPB and the ability-to-repay rule.

lessons.title: Case file: The Assumable Loan on Hone Avenue
lessons.tagline: A 2.875% FHA loan, a buyer who wants it, and every way a mortgage follows a house to closing.
objectives: Decide whether a buyer can assume, take subject to, or must pay off a seller's existing mortgage, and who stays liable in each case.
Apply the mortgagor's duties to taxes and insurance and calculate a payoff that includes per diem interest and lender advances.
Apply recording order, subordination, and New York's satisfaction deadline to a sale with more than one lien.
Explain how a CEMA reduces NYC mortgage recording tax and when it is not available.

blocks.title: A 2.875% loan on Hone Avenue
blocks.html: Teresa Vitale, 71, is selling the two-family in Morris Park, the Bronx, where she has lived since 1989. She lists with Jordan at $1,050,000. Her husband refinanced into an FHA loan in 2021 at 2.875%, and the balance today is about $412,000. She also has a home equity line from 2023 with $38,000 drawn. At the first open house, a buyer named Dev Shah corners Jordan in the kitchen: "Can we just take over her 2.875% loan? Rates are almost double that now." Jordan has heard of assumable loans but has never seen one close.

Before the open house, Teresa had asked Jordan a question of her own. She had found her old closing binder and read the mortgage for the first time. "It says the bank has a lien on the house," she said. "Do I need the bank's permission to sell? Is it even my house?"

blocks.q: Teresa asks whether she needs her lender's permission to list and sell the house. What is the right answer?
c: Yes. Until the loan is paid off, the lender holds legal title and signs the deed
Yes, if the sale price is below the loan balance, because then the lender takes a loss
No. She holds title and may sell; the lien must be paid off or dealt with at closing
Yes. An FHA mortgage requires HUD consent before any listing agreement is signed
blocks.x: New York is a lien theory state. The mortgagor keeps title and the usual rights of ownership, including the right to sell. The lender holds a lien that must be satisfied or otherwise handled at closing. The trap is the idea that the lender holds legal title and signs the deed: that describes a title theory state, where the lender holds legal title. A short sale (price below payoff) does need lender approval, but Teresa has plenty of equity, so that rule does not apply.

blocks.html: So Teresa can sell. Now for Dev's question. Most conventional loans contain an alienation clause that lets the lender call the loan due on a transfer, so a buyer cannot step into them. FHA and VA loans are different: they are assumable by a buyer the lender approves after a credit review. Teresa's loan is FHA.

blocks.q: Dev wants to take over Teresa's FHA loan at 2.875%. Which statement is accurate?
c: He can, if the servicer approves his credit and he funds the gap
He can, without any credit review, because FHA loans assume automatically on a sale
He cannot. FHA loans include a due-on-sale clause that bars any transfer of the loan
He can, provided he is a first-time buyer and the price is under the FHA loan limit
blocks.x: FHA loans are assumable by a creditworthy buyer, so the servicer reviews Dev's income, credit and debts much as it would for a new loan. He also has to pay the difference between the price and the loan balance. The trap is the idea of an automatic assumption with no credit review: it does not exist. Since 1989 FHA requires a creditworthiness review for most assumptions. A blanket ban on transfer describes a typical conventional loan, and the first-time buyer condition mixes in SONYMA rules that do not govern assumptions.

blocks.title: The equity gap
blocks.html:
Price: $1,050,000
FHA balance Dev would assume: $412,000
Gap Dev must cover: $1,050,000 minus $412,000 = $638,000
Dev and his wife Anika have $250,000 in cash.
Still short: $638,000 minus $250,000 = $388,000, which would need a second loan behind the FHA first.

The low rate only applies to the $412,000. The Shahs would need a $388,000 second mortgage at today's rates, and the servicer told Dev that FHA assumption files there take 60 to 90 days. Marcus, who overheard all of this, had a faster idea. "Skip the bank. Teresa deeds the house to the Shahs, they send her a check every month, she keeps paying the FHA loan. Nobody needs to know. It's called a wraparound."

blocks.q: What is the biggest legal risk in Marcus's plan to transfer the deed without telling the lender?
c: The Shahs become personally liable on the FHA note even though they did not sign it
The deed is void, because a mortgaged property cannot be conveyed without consent
Teresa loses her FHA insurance coverage but keeps the right to collect from the Shahs
The lender can call the entire balance due once it learns of the transfer
blocks.x: An unapproved transfer breaches the mortgage, and the lender may invoke the acceleration clause and demand the full balance. The trap is calling the deed void: you can convey mortgaged land, it just stays subject to the lien. Taking title subject to a loan does not make the Shahs personally liable on a note they never signed, and Teresa stays liable on it, which is exactly why this plan is bad for her.

blocks.html: Jordan put the wraparound idea in writing to Diane, who killed it in one sentence: "Teresa stays liable on a loan she no longer controls, the Shahs own a house that can be called due any month, and our firm advised it." Teresa had a second worry anyway. Even with a proper FHA assumption, would she still be on the hook if the Shahs stopped paying in 2031?

blocks.title: Assumption is not a release
blocks.html: When a buyer assumes a loan, the buyer becomes primarily liable and the seller stays secondarily liable. The seller is fully off the hook only if the lender agrees to substitute the buyer for the seller in writing, a novation (FHA calls it a release of liability). Exam items love the seller who thinks "he assumed it, so I'm done."

blocks.q: If the Shahs properly assume Teresa's FHA loan, what does Teresa need to be fully free of the debt?
c: Nothing more. An approved assumption shifts the liability to the buyer automatically
A written release from the lender substituting the Shahs as borrowers on the debt
A recorded satisfaction of mortgage, signed by the lender on the day of the closing
A deed from the Shahs back to her, so title and liability end up with the same party
blocks.x: Only the lender can release the original borrower, by a novation or written release of liability that substitutes the new borrower. Without it, Teresa is secondarily liable if the Shahs default and the sale does not cover the debt. The trap is believing an approved assumption ends her liability: approval of the buyer's credit is not the same as releasing the seller. A satisfaction is wrong because the debt is not paid; it keeps running in the Shahs' names.

blocks.html: In the end the Shahs chose the clean route: a new conventional loan of $800,000 and a sale free and clear, with Teresa's loans paid off at closing. Then the title report arrived from the Shahs' title company.

head: Schedule B item
Detail
rows: Teresa and Frank Vitale to Hudson Valley Mortgage, recorded 2021, original amount $455,000 (FHA)
To Bronx Community Credit Union, recorded March 2023, maximum $60,000
blocks.caption: Title report, Hone Avenue (excerpt)

blocks.html: Teresa had never had an escrow account; she paid her own taxes. After Frank died, the January bill slipped. Her FHA servicer had just mailed her a letter saying it intended to advance the tax, add it to her balance, and open an escrow account. Teresa was furious. "I have never missed a mortgage payment in my life. How can they call that a default?"

blocks.q: Teresa's mortgage payments are current, but she did not pay a property tax installment. Under her mortgage, the servicer:
c: May treat it as a default and advance the tax, adding the cost to her loan balance
Has no remedy, because default under a mortgage means a missed loan payment
Has to wait for the city to sell a tax lien before it can act on the loan
May foreclose at once without notice, since a tax default skips the RPAPL 1304 notice
blocks.x: Paying taxes and assessments is one of the mortgagor's duties, because unpaid taxes become a lien that outranks the mortgage. Breaking that promise is a default even with every payment on time, and the mortgage lets the lender protect its collateral by paying the bill and adding it to the debt. The trap is "no remedy", which reads default too narrowly. Immediate foreclosure overreaches: the 90-day pre-foreclosure notice still applies to a home loan.

blocks.html: The advance would be cleared at closing anyway, since the payoff covers whatever is owed. Priya ordered payoff letters from both lenders for a closing on June 18.

blocks.title: Payoff letter, Hudson Valley Mortgage (excerpt)
blocks.html:
Principal balance after the June 1 payment: $411,780.00
Interest from June 1: per diem $32.43
Escrow advance (real estate taxes): $3,412.00 plus $61.40 interest
Recording fee for satisfaction: $50.00
Good through: June 30

Because NY mortgage interest is paid in arrears, the June 1 payment covered May's interest. June's interest is owed from June 1 to the payoff date.

blocks.q: Using the payoff letter, about how much does Teresa owe Hudson Valley if the funds arrive June 18 and interest runs for 18 days?
blocks.x: Interest: 18 days x $32.43 = $583.74. Add principal $411,780.00, the tax advance $3,412.00, its interest $61.40, and the $50.00 recording fee: $415,887.14. The trap is $412,363.74, which adds only the per diem interest and forgets the advance the servicer paid on Teresa's behalf. $415,303.40 leaves out the 18 days of interest, and $411,780.00 is the bare principal.

blocks.text: The Shahs' side of the escrow

blocks.html: Watching Teresa's tax mess, Dev asked his loan officer to waive escrow on the new loan. "We're organized. We'll pay our own taxes." The lender said no: at 80% loan-to-value on a two-family, it required a monthly escrow for taxes and hazard insurance, and a homeowners policy naming the lender as mortgagee so that any fire claim check would be payable to both. The lender is protecting the same collateral Teresa's servicer just protected, only in advance instead of after a missed bill.

blocks.title: The Shahs' escrow at closing
blocks.html:
Annual real estate taxes on Hone Avenue: $9,600
Annual homeowners insurance: $2,400
Total yearly escrow items: $12,000, so the monthly escrow deposit is $12,000 / 12 = $1,000
Federal servicing rules (RESPA's Regulation X) let the servicer hold a cushion of no more than one-sixth of the year's escrow payments, which is two months.

blocks.q: Using the figures above, what is the largest cushion the Shahs' servicer may keep in their escrow account beyond what it needs to pay the bills?
blocks.x: The cap is one-sixth of the estimated annual escrow disbursements: $12,000 / 6 = $2,000, or two months of deposits. The trap is $1,000, one month, which is what many borrowers guess because the deposit is $1,000 a month. $3,000 would be a quarter of the year. Escrow keeps the PITI promise working: the T and I are paid by the servicer before they can become a default or a lien ahead of the mortgage.

blocks.text: The credit line that would not die

blocks.html: The credit union's payoff letter showed $38,214 owed. Teresa offered to write a check that week so the line would show zero before closing. Priya said that was fine but not enough. The title company needed a signed letter from Teresa telling the credit union to freeze the line and close it, and it would not insure the Shahs over the line until the credit union recorded a satisfaction.

blocks.q: Why does the title company insist that Teresa's home equity line be closed, not just paid down to zero?
c: A credit line is unsecured until drawn, so it has to be closed to be counted on the title report
A zero balance cancels the lien automatically, but the closing letter speeds up recording
Credit unions may not record satisfactions unless the borrower also closes the account
The line can be drawn again after closing, and its recorded lien stays until satisfied
blocks.x: A home equity line works like an open-end mortgage: the borrower can draw again up to the limit, and the recorded mortgage secures every draw. Paying to zero leaves the lien alive. Teresa, or someone with her checkbook, could draw $60,000 the day after closing, and that debt would sit on the Shahs' house. The trap is thinking a zero balance cancels the lien: it does not erase a recorded mortgage. Only a satisfaction of mortgage does.

blocks.text: A little seller financing, and the order of liens

blocks.html: Two weeks before closing, the Shahs' appraisal came in at $1,020,000. Their lender would still lend $800,000, but the Shahs were now $30,000 short of what they wanted to keep in reserves. Teresa, who did not need all the cash at once, offered to take back a $30,000 note for five years, secured by a second mortgage on the house. That is a purchase money mortgage: the seller finances part of the price.

The Shahs' lender agreed, on one condition from its commitment letter: "Any secondary financing must be subordinate to the lien of this mortgage." Priya explained the risk. Both mortgages would be signed at the same table, and New York is a race-notice state. Whichever is recorded first generally wins priority, after real property taxes.

blocks.q: To make sure the bank's $800,000 loan stays first even if the documents are recorded in the wrong order, the parties should:
c: Rely on the larger loan amount, which takes first priority whenever two mortgages are signed together
Ask the city to record both on the same day, which makes them equal liens that share proceeds
Record Teresa's mortgage first, since a purchase money mortgage ranks ahead of a bank loan
Have Teresa sign a subordination agreement putting her mortgage behind the bank's
blocks.x: Priority in New York follows the recording order, not the size of the loan. A subordination agreement lets a lienholder agree to stand behind another lien no matter which is recorded first, and lenders require one for any seller second. The trap is recording the seller's mortgage first on the theory that purchase money liens always win: some states give special priority to purchase money liens, but the bank here bargained for first position and will not fund without the subordination. Size never sets priority.

blocks.text: The recording tax, and a New York workaround

blocks.html: The Shahs' $800,000 loan on a two-family in the Bronx triggers NYC's mortgage recording tax. Dev wanted the number before he signed the commitment, so Jordan pulled the rate sheet from the title company.

blocks.q: The Shahs borrow $800,000 on a Bronx two-family. Using the NYC borrower rates (1.8% under $500,000, 1.925% at $500,000 or more on 1 to 3 family homes), what recording tax do they pay?
blocks.x: The loan is $500,000 or more on a 1 to 3 family home, so the borrower rate is 1.925%: $800,000 x 0.01925 = $15,400. The trap is $14,400, which uses the lower bracket meant for loans under $500,000. $17,400 applies the 2.175% combined rate that includes the lender's 0.25% share, which the lender pays, not the Shahs. $8,400 is the 1.05% rate used in most suburban downstate counties.

blocks.html: Dev groaned at $15,400. Priya asked whether Teresa's FHA servicer would agree to a CEMA.

blocks.title: CEMA: pay the recording tax only on new money
blocks.html: New York taxes a mortgage when it is recorded, but Tax Law section 255 does not tax a supplemental mortgage again on debt that was already taxed. In a Consolidation, Extension and Modification Agreement (CEMA), the seller's lender assigns the existing mortgage to the buyer's lender instead of marking it satisfied. The buyer's lender then consolidates it with a new "gap" mortgage for the new money. The buyer pays recording tax only on the gap. Both lenders must cooperate and they charge legal fees for it. Some servicers refuse, especially when the loan sits in a securitized pool, so ask early.

blocks.title: What a CEMA would save the Shahs
blocks.html:
New loan: $800,000
Unpaid principal of Teresa's mortgage assigned to the Shahs' lender: about $411,780
New money (gap mortgage): $800,000 minus $411,780 = $388,220
Recording tax on the assigned amount that is not paid again: $411,780 x 1.925% = about $7,927, before the extra attorney fees both lenders charge.
(The rate bracket for the gap mortgage is confirmed by the title company; the point is that the old balance is not taxed twice.)

blocks.q: In a NYC purchase using a CEMA, what does the buyer avoid paying?
c: Mortgage recording tax on the existing principal that is assigned instead of paid off
The NYS transfer tax on the part of the price financed by the seller's assigned mortgage
Any recording tax on the new loan, since a CEMA mortgage is treated as a share loan
The mansion tax, because the buyer is taking over debt rather than paying cash for it
blocks.x: A CEMA keeps the seller's mortgage alive by assignment, and recording tax was paid on that debt when it was first recorded. The buyer pays recording tax only on the new money in the gap mortgage. The trap is transfer tax, which is the seller's tax on the deed and has nothing to do with how the buyer finances. The share loan answer confuses CEMAs with co-op share loans, which are exempt because they are not mortgages at all.

blocks.html: Hudson Valley Mortgage said no: its FHA loans were in Ginnie Mae pools and it would not assign them. The Shahs paid the full tax. A CEMA is worth asking about on every NYC purchase where the seller has a large balance, but it is never guaranteed.

blocks.title: Co-op buyers skip this whole conversation
blocks.html: A co-op purchase is financed with a share loan secured by the stock and proprietary lease under the UCC. No mortgage is recorded, so there is no mortgage recording tax and no CEMA to negotiate. That is one reason co-op closing costs run lower than condo closing costs at the same price.

The closing went through on June 18. Hudson Valley Mortgage received $415,887.14 by wire. In early August, Teresa called Jordan from her new apartment in Pelham Bay. Her daughter had searched ACRIS: the FHA mortgage still showed as open, and a junk-mail company had already sent Teresa a "refinance your Hone Avenue home" offer.

blocks.q: Hudson Valley Mortgage, a lender that makes hundreds of loans a year, was paid in full on June 18. By early August, 47 days later, no satisfaction has been recorded. Under New York law:
c: It has a 90-day window to record, so no penalty has accrued and Teresa has to wait
It must record within 30 days and now owes Teresa $500, rising if the delay continues
It has 60 days to record and owes nothing until then, after which it owes $1,000
Recording is the seller's job, so Teresa files the satisfaction herself at her cost
blocks.x: Real Property Law 275 and RPAPL 1921 require the mortgagee to arrange recording of the satisfaction within 30 days of payoff. A lender that makes five or more mortgage loans a year owes the borrower $500 if it misses 30 days, $1,000 after 60 days, and $1,500 after 90. The trap is the 60-day answer, which uses the second penalty step as the deadline. The lender, not the borrower, is responsible for recording the satisfaction.

blocks.html: Priya's office sent a one-page demand letter citing the statute. The satisfaction appeared on ACRIS nine days later, along with a $500 check. Meanwhile, Dev received his own surprise: a letter saying the Shahs' new loan had been sold, with an assignment of mortgage to a national investor and a new company collecting payments starting September 1.

blocks.q: Dev's new mortgage was assigned to an investor and servicing moved to a new company. What changes for the Shahs?
c: The investor may reset the rate to the market rate, because the original note was sold
The rate and terms stay the same; they pay the new servicer as told
They have to re-qualify within 60 days, or the new holder can call the loan due at once
Nothing, and they keep paying the original lender, which forwards the money on
blocks.x: A note is negotiable and the mortgage follows it, so lenders sell loans all the time on the secondary market. The buyer of the loan takes it on its existing terms: same rate, same balance, same schedule. Federal servicing rules require notice of the transfer and give a 60-day grace period in which a payment sent on time to the old servicer cannot be treated as late. The trap is paying the original lender: once notified, borrowers pay the new servicer.

items: In New York the borrower keeps title and can sell; the lender's lien is paid off at closing or carried along by assumption or by a sale subject to the loan.
FHA and VA loans are assumable by a creditworthy buyer, but the buyer must fund the equity gap and the seller stays liable without a written release (novation).
Transferring title behind the lender's back invites acceleration; a wraparound does not make a due-on-sale clause disappear.
Failing to pay taxes or keep insurance is a default even when payments are current, and the lender may advance the cost and add it to the debt.
A home equity line must be frozen, closed, and satisfied, not just paid to zero. Priority follows recording order unless a subordination agreement changes it.
NYC buyers pay mortgage recording tax on financed purchases; a CEMA limits it to new money. The lender must record a satisfaction within 30 days of payoff or pay the borrower a penalty.

lessons.title: Case file: The Two-Family on 101st Avenue
lessons.tagline: A caterer, a new teacher, a tenant upstairs, and a lender who wants proof of everything.
objectives: Calculate qualifying income for self-employed, salaried, and rental income and apply front-end and back-end ratios.
Decide how co-signed debts, credit report errors, and gift funds affect a loan file.
Apply loan-to-value rules to a low appraisal and choose between a permanent and temporary buydown.
Identify ECOA, FCRA, New York Human Rights Law, and occupancy fraud problems in an application.

blocks.title: Two incomes, one tenant, one file
blocks.html: Nadia Rahman runs a catering business out of a rented kitchen in Richmond Hill. Her husband Omar teaches seventh-grade science in Ozone Park. They have a contract on a semi-attached two-family on 101st Avenue for $682,000, with a tenant upstairs paying $2,400 a month. They plan to live downstairs and put 10% down. Tasha, their mortgage broker, opens the file on a Monday and says what she says to every couple: "The lender will ask two questions. Is the house good collateral, and can you two pay it back? Everything I ask for is one of those two." Her first question is about Nadia's income.
Nadia brought a folder. Her business bank account shows $214,000 in deposits last year. Her tax returns tell a different story.

head: Year
Gross receipts (Schedule C)
Expenses
Net profit
blocks.caption: Nadia's sole proprietorship, from her federal returns

blocks.q: How will a lender most likely figure Nadia's monthly qualifying income from the catering business?
c: Average the two years of net profit: $84,000 a year, or $7,000 a month
Use last year's gross receipts of $214,000, since deposits prove the cash came in
Use the higher year's net profit, $90,000, because her income is rising each year
Count nothing until the business has filed three full years of federal returns
blocks.x: Underwriters qualify a sole proprietor on net income after business expenses, usually averaged over the two most recent years of tax returns: ($78,000 + $90,000) / 2 = $84,000, or $7,000 a month. The trap is gross receipts: deposits are not income until expenses come out, and the tax return is the verified figure. When income is rising, the average is the conservative number; if it were falling, a lender would lean on the lower, more recent year.

blocks.title: The write-off that costs you the house
blocks.html: Self-employed buyers who aggressively deduct expenses lower their taxes and their qualifying income at the same time. A lender cannot use income that is not on the return. Two years before buying, a self-employed client should talk to an accountant about what the returns will show.

Omar's income is simpler, with one wrinkle. He earns $96,000 a year, or $8,000 a month, but he has been teaching for only ten months. Before that he spent two years finishing a master's degree in education while working part time as a tutor.

blocks.q: Omar has ten months on his current job. The lender usually wants a two-year employment history. What is the likely result?
c: He cannot be counted as a borrower until he has two full years on this job
He can qualify, but just with a co-signer who has two years on one job
His income counts, but at half of salary until the two years are complete
His schooling in the field can count toward the history
blocks.x: Lenders look at stability and likely continuance of income. Recent schooling or training that leads directly into the job can fill the employment history, and a teacher with a new contract and a master's degree in education is about as stable as it gets. The trap is the strict two-years-on-this-job reading: the guideline is a two-year history, not two years with one employer. Lenders do not discount salaried income by half for a new job.

blocks.html: The upstairs tenant has a lease at $2,400 a month. Leo, who happens to be Omar's college roommate, told them over dinner that the rent "basically pays half the mortgage, so the bank will count all of it." Tasha laughed when Omar repeated it.

blocks.q: For an owner-occupied two-family, how much of the $2,400 monthly rent will the lender typically count as qualifying income?
c: $2,400, since the lease is signed and the tenant is already in place
$1,800, about 75% of the rent, to allow for vacancy and upkeep
$1,200, half the rent, since the owners also live in the building
Nothing, since rental income counts just for investment property
blocks.x: Lenders typically count about 75% of the documented rent, here $1,800, leaving a cushion for vacancies, repairs and collection loss. The trap is counting the full lease amount: no unit is rented 100% of the time and something always breaks. Rental income from the other unit of an owner-occupied 2 to 4 family is a normal part of qualifying, which is one reason two-families are popular with first-time buyers in Queens and Brooklyn.

blocks.html: Tasha's worksheet now has three income lines and a proposed payment. The lender's guideline for this conventional loan uses the textbook 28/36 ratios.

head: Line
Monthly
blocks.caption: Tasha's qualifying worksheet

blocks.q: Using 28/36, how do the Rahmans do?
c: They pass the front-end at 28% and the back-end at about 35.4%
They fail the front-end, because PMI is not counted in housing costs
They pass the front-end but fail the back-end at about 37.9%
They fail both ratios because rental income cannot be added to salary
blocks.x: Front-end: $4,704 / $16,800 = 28.0%, right at the limit. Back-end: $4,704 + $650 + $480 + $120 = $5,954, and $5,954 / $16,800 = 35.4%, under 36%. The trap is excluding PMI or excluding rent: mortgage insurance is part of the housing payment, and 75% of documented rent is qualifying income. The 37.9% figure is what happens if one more $410 debt shows up, which is exactly what happened next.

blocks.html: Tasha told them not to celebrate a 28.0% front-end ratio too loudly. The exam uses 28/36 as the conventional benchmark, and many lenders still start there, but automated underwriting systems can approve higher ratios when a file has compensating factors: strong credit scores, large reserves, a low LTV, or a long history of paying rent close to the new payment. A file sitting exactly on the line has no room for surprises.

The credit report came back two days later with a surprise: a $410 monthly car loan Nadia had co-signed for her younger brother in 2023. He has made every payment himself. Nadia had forgotten it existed. She also found a $1,900 medical collection from a hospital in Ohio, a state she has never lived in.

blocks.q: How will the co-signed car loan most likely affect the Rahmans' back-end ratio?
c: It is ignored, because Nadia is not the one making the payments on it
It is counted at half, since two people are responsible for the same loan
It counts as her debt unless the lender sees proof her brother pays
It is counted if it has been reported late on her brother's credit file
blocks.x: A co-signer is fully liable on the loan, so it is her monthly obligation. Many lenders will exclude it only with proof, typically a year of the brother's own bank statements showing he makes the payments. Without that proof the back-end becomes ($5,954 + $410) / $16,800 = 37.9%, over 36%. The trap is "she does not pay it": liability, not who writes the check, decides what counts.

blocks.html: Nadia's brother had a year of statements from his own account showing every payment, and the lender excluded the loan. The Ohio collection was a different problem.

blocks.title: When the credit report is wrong
blocks.html: The Fair Credit Reporting Act, part of the Consumer Credit Protection Act, gives consumers the right to dispute inaccurate information. The consumer reporting agency generally has 30 days to investigate and must delete or correct what cannot be verified. If a lender denies credit based on a report, it must say so and tell the applicant which agency supplied it.

blocks.q: What is the right first step for Nadia on the collection account that is not hers?
c: Ask the lender to remove it from her file, since lenders control what the report says
Dispute it with the credit bureaus that report it, with her proof
Pay it to clear the record, then ask the hospital for a refund once the loan closes
Ignore it, because collection accounts under $2,000 are excluded from underwriting
blocks.x: Under the FCRA the consumer disputes inaccurate items with the consumer reporting agency, which must investigate, usually within 30 days, and correct or delete what the creditor cannot verify. Tasha can also ask the lender for a rapid rescore once it is fixed. The trap is paying it: paying a debt that is not hers wastes money and can make it look valid. A lender reads the report; it does not edit it.

blocks.text: A question that should not have been asked

blocks.html: At the lender's office, a loan officer reviewing Nadia's file noticed she was pregnant. He said, kindly enough, "You'll probably take a year off after the baby, right? Maybe we should just use Omar's income to be safe."

blocks.q: What is wrong with the loan officer's suggestion?
c: Nothing, since lenders may adjust income for any expected change in employment
Nothing, as long as he asks the same question of every pregnant applicant
He may drop her income if Omar agrees in writing to qualify alone
He may not discount her income on childbearing grounds or ask about her plans
blocks.x: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (Regulation B) bars creditors from asking about birth control or childbearing plans and from discounting income because of sex or the likelihood of having children. New York's Human Rights Law (Executive Law 296-a) says the same expressly. The trap is treating it as a normal employment-continuance question asked evenly: asking every pregnant applicant is still discrimination. If Nadia herself says she is closing her business, that is a different matter.

blocks.title: New York's credit protections are wider
blocks.html: ECOA bars credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, receipt of public assistance income, and exercising consumer credit rights. New York's Executive Law 296-a, which covers credit for buying, building or repairing housing, adds creed, citizenship or immigration status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, military status, disability, familial status, and status as a victim of domestic violence.
Tasha moved the file to a different loan officer the same afternoon and noted the comment in her records. The Rahmans qualified on both incomes.

blocks.text: One more form for the caterer

blocks.html: Nadia's accountant had been urging her to turn the catering business into an S corporation to save on self-employment tax. She asked Tasha whether she should do it before the loan closed. "Then I'd be on payroll, with a W-2. Doesn't that make me an employee? Lenders love employees."

blocks.q: If Nadia converts her business into a corporation she owns 100% of and pays herself a W-2 salary, how will a lender treat her?
c: As a salaried employee, so a W-2 and two recent pay stubs will be enough
As a partner, with her share of income taken from a partnership K-1
As a new business, so her income cannot be used for three more years
As self-employed, needing personal and business returns to see the full picture
blocks.x: Lenders treat a borrower who owns a controlling share of a business, commonly 25% or more, as self-employed whether it is a sole proprietorship, partnership, or corporation. Owners can set their own salaries, so the underwriter reads the business returns too. The trap is the W-2: on paper it looks like employment, but the owner signs her own paycheck. A mid-application change in structure also adds paperwork, which is why Tasha told Nadia to wait until after closing.

blocks.text: Where the down payment comes from

blocks.html: Nadia and Omar had $72,000 saved. With 10% down ($68,200) plus closing costs of about $28,000 and the lender's required reserves, they were short. Nadia's parents wired $25,000 into the couple's checking account. The underwriter flagged it in a day.

blocks.q: The underwriter asks about the $25,000 deposit. What does the lender need?
c: Nothing, since money already in the borrowers' account belongs to them
A promissory note from the parents showing the repayment schedule
A signed gift letter and proof of the transfer
A tax return from the parents showing they paid gift tax on the money
blocks.x: Lenders verify the source of large deposits. A gift is acceptable when the donor signs a gift letter stating the amount and that no repayment is expected, backed by a paper trail of the transfer. The trap is a promissory note: a loan from the parents is a new monthly obligation that changes the back-end ratio, and hiding it would be fraud. Gift tax returns are the donor's business and are not part of the file.

blocks.html: With the gift documented, the underwriter turned to what would be left after closing. The Rahmans' loan program required two months of PITI in reserves, liquid money still in the bank after the down payment and closing costs are paid. Reserves are the lender's cushion against a lost catering contract or a vacant upstairs unit.

blocks.q: The lender requires two months of the $4,704 housing payment in reserves after closing. Which assets would a lender most readily count?
c: Their checking and savings balances plus vested retirement funds
The equity they will have in the house the day after the closing
Nadia's catering equipment, valued at what she paid for it
A personal loan they plan to take out after the closing date
blocks.x: Reserves must be liquid or nearly liquid: checking, savings, money market funds, stocks, and vested retirement accounts (often counted at a discount for taxes and penalties). Two months here is $9,408. The trap is home equity: the lender is already lending against the house, so equity in it cannot also be the safety net. Borrowed money is not a reserve, and equipment is not liquid.

blocks.html: The appraisal came in at $670,000, $12,000 under the contract price. The appraiser also marked it "subject to" two repairs: peeling paint on the porch of a pre-1978 house and a missing handrail on the basement stairs. Investment quality cuts both ways: price, condition, comparables and location all go into the lender's view of the collateral.

head: Comparable
Sale price
Notes from the appraiser
rows: Similar size, sold 2 months ago, original kitchens
Renovated baths, larger lot, adjusted down
Detached with a driveway, adjusted down for both
blocks.caption: Appraisal comparables (excerpt)

blocks.html: Jordan read the comparables with the Rahmans. None of them sold for $682,000 after adjustments, and the one detached sale was the only one above it. The appraiser had done what appraisers do: adjust the comparables toward the subject and reconcile. A seller who priced off the detached house was always going to have trouble. The appraisal is the lender's protection, not the buyer's, but in practice it protects both.

blocks.title: The new loan-to-value math
blocks.html:
Lender's maximum LTV: 90%
Value used: the lower of price ($682,000) or appraisal ($670,000) = $670,000
Maximum loan: 0.90 x $670,000 = $603,000
Cash needed for the price: $682,000 minus $603,000 = $79,000, before closing costs
Original plan: $68,200. The gap grows by $10,800.

blocks.q: If the Rahmans want to keep their cash at $68,200 for the price, what is the most direct fix?
c: Ask the lender to use the contract price, since the buyers agreed to pay it
Renegotiate the price toward the appraised value of $670,000
Order a second appraisal from a different appraiser the buyers pick
Raise the loan to 90% of the contract price and skip the appraisal
blocks.x: LTV uses the lower of price or appraised value, so the fastest fix is a lower price. At $670,000, 10% down is $67,000 and the loan is $603,000. Sellers often agree because the next buyer's lender will see the same appraisal. The trap is asking the lender to use the contract price: the whole point of the appraisal is to stop a lender from lending against a price the market does not support. Buyers do not pick the appraiser.

blocks.html: The seller agreed to $675,000 and to fix the porch and handrail before closing. The re-inspection cleared the "subject to" conditions. Because the house was built before 1978, the porch had to be scraped and repainted by a contractor certified under the EPA lead renovation rule, using lead-safe work practices, and the seller kept the paperwork for the buyers. Then the seller's attorney offered a $10,000 credit toward the Rahmans' closing costs, and Tasha laid out two ways to use it.

head: Option
What it buys
Cost
rows: Note rate cut from 6.5% to about 6.25% for the life of the loan
Year 1 at 4.5%, year 2 at 5.5%, then 6.5% for the rest of the loan
Funds deposited to cover the payment difference for two years
blocks.caption: Tasha's two uses for the seller credit

blocks.q: If the Rahmans choose the 2-1 temporary buydown, at what rate will the lender most likely qualify them?
c: 4.5%, the rate they pay in the first year of the loan
6.5%, the note rate that applies once the buydown ends
5.5%, the average rate over the two buydown years
6.25%, the rate they would get by buying points instead
blocks.x: A temporary buydown lowers the payment for a year or two but does not change the note rate, so lenders qualify the borrower at the full note rate. That way the borrower can still afford year three. The trap is qualifying at the teaser rate, the same payment-shock problem that sank so many borrowers before 2008. A permanent buydown with points actually changes the note rate, which is why its rate would be used.

blocks.title: What a point costs here
blocks.html:
New price: $675,000. Loan at 90%: $607,500.
One point = 1% of the loan = $6,075.
1.5 points = $9,112.50, which fits inside the $10,000 seller credit. Points are a percent of the loan, never the price.
They chose the permanent buydown. Omar's reasoning, on a napkin: they planned to stay at least ten years, and the 6.25% rate would outlive any temporary buydown.
Before signing, Omar asked how long they would pay PMI. The loan was $607,500 on a $675,000 purchase, exactly 90% LTV.

blocks.q: Under the Homeowners Protection Act, at what loan balance can the Rahmans first ask to cancel PMI, if their payment history is good?
c: $607,500, once they have made 24 payments
$526,500, which is 78% of the original value
$506,250, which is 75% of the original value
$540,000, which is 80% of the original value
blocks.x: Borrowers may request cancellation when the balance reaches 80% of original value: 0.80 x $675,000 = $540,000. PMI ends automatically at 78%, or $526,500, if payments are current. The trap is $526,500, the automatic termination point, which comes later. Original value means the lower of the price or appraisal at closing. Paying extra principal brings the date forward; a rise in market value can too, though most servicers then require a new appraisal.

blocks.html: At the closing dinner, Nadia's cousin Faisal said he wanted to buy a two-family nearby as an investment, renting both units. "I'll just check the owner-occupied box. The rate's better, and who's going to check?" Jordan, who was there as the buyer's agent, put down his fork.

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell Faisal about checking the owner-occupied box on a loan application for a property he will not live in?
c: It is a misstatement on a loan application, which is mortgage fraud
It is fine if he lives there at least one night a week for the first year
It is a contract issue between him and the lender, not a legal one
It is allowed in New York if the property has four or fewer units
blocks.x: Owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes get the best rates and lowest down payments because owners who live in a home default less. Lying about occupancy to get those terms is a material false statement on a loan application, which is federal and state mortgage fraud. A licensee who knowingly helps risks license revocation and criminal charges. The trap is treating it as a private contract problem: lenders do check, and fraud is a crime, not just a breach.

blocks.html: Faisal applied for an investment-property loan instead: 25% down, a higher rate, and only part of the projected rent counted. Nadia and Omar closed on 101st Avenue in late spring, with the tenant upstairs and a nursery downstairs. Their final file held two years of returns, a year of the brother's bank statements, a gift letter, a corrected credit report, an appraisal with cleared conditions, and a lease for the upstairs unit: every page an answer to one of Tasha's two questions.

items: Lenders ask two questions: is the property good collateral (price, appraisal, condition, location, type, LTV) and can the borrower repay (income, history, assets, debts, credit).
Self-employed income is net profit from tax returns, usually averaged over two years. Schooling that leads into a job can fill the employment history.
Lenders count about 75% of documented rent; co-signed loans count as the borrower's debt unless the lender sees proof someone else pays.
Run front-end and back-end ratios with every housing cost, including PMI, and every recurring debt. LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal.
Large deposits need a source; gifts need a gift letter. ECOA, FCRA and NY Executive Law 296-a protect applicants from discrimination and bad credit data.
Temporary buydowns lower early payments but borrowers qualify at the note rate. Lying about occupancy is mortgage fraud.

lessons.title: Case file: Tasha's Upstate Tuesday
lessons.tagline: A veteran, a paramedic, a farmhouse, a 600 credit score and a widow in Buffalo: five buyers, five programs.
objectives: Match buyers to VA, FHA, USDA RHS, SONYMA, and conventional financing based on their facts.
Calculate VA funding fees, FHA MIP, and SONYMA down payment assistance and its repayment.
Explain how the secondary market and Ginnie Mae, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac move loans after closing.
Apply the rules of construction loans and reverse mortgages to a borrower's situation.

blocks.title: Five files, one long Tuesday
blocks.html: Tasha Monroe's mortgage brokerage is in Brooklyn, but her clients are all over the state. Diane asked her to let Jordan shadow her for a day, because "Jordan thinks every buyer has 20% down and a cousin at Chase." Tasha's Tuesday list has five files: an Army veteran buying a three-family in Schenectady, a paramedic buying her first house in Poughkeepsie, a young couple looking at a farmhouse in Greene County, a nurse in Rochester with a 600 credit score, and a retired widow in Buffalo who wants to stop paying her mortgage. Tasha hands Jordan a legal pad. "Write down which program each one gets, and why. Then tell me who ends up owning the loan."

blocks.text: File 1: Sergeant Price and the three-family

blocks.html: Darnell Price served eight years in the Army and now works for the county in Schenectady. He has a Certificate of Eligibility from the Department of Veterans Affairs, a 720 credit score, and $14,000 saved. He wants a three-family on Union Street for $285,000, living in one unit and renting the other two.

blocks.q: Can Darnell use a VA loan to buy a three-family with no down payment?
c: No. VA loans are limited to single-family homes and condominiums the VA approves
No. A multifamily purchase needs a VA guarantee plus FHA insurance on the rental units
Yes, but VA requires 25% down on any property where some units will be rented out
Yes, as long as he lives in one of the three units
blocks.x: A VA loan can finance an owner-occupied home of up to four units, so a three-family where Darnell lives in one unit qualifies, and no down payment is required for an eligible veteran with full entitlement. The trap is the investor rule: 25% down is typical of conventional investment property loans, not VA. VA guarantees part of the loan, so the lender needs no down payment as its cushion.

blocks.html: "No down payment" does not mean no cash and no cost. Darnell will still pay closing costs, and VA charges a one-time funding fee that keeps the program running without taxpayer money. For a first-time VA user putting less than 5% down, the fee is 2.15% of the loan amount, and it can be financed into the loan.

blocks.q: Darnell borrows $285,000 with nothing down, his first use of the VA benefit. The funding fee is closest to:
blocks.x: First use with less than 5% down: 2.15% x $285,000 = $6,127.50. The trap is $9,405, which uses the 3.3% fee for a later use of the benefit. $4,987.50 is FHA's 1.75% upfront premium, a different program's charge. The fee is lower with 5% or 10% down. Unlike PMI or FHA's annual MIP, the VA fee is paid once, and there is no monthly mortgage insurance on a VA loan.

blocks.html: Then Darnell mentioned, almost in passing, that he receives VA compensation for a 30% service-connected disability rating from a knee injury in Afghanistan.

blocks.q: How does Darnell's 30% service-connected disability rating affect his loan?
c: He pays no funding fee, and the disability pay can count as income
The rating lowers his funding fee to the 5%-down tier, about 1.5% of the loan
He loses eligibility for a VA loan, since disability pay replaces his benefit
His funding fee is unchanged, but the VA pays it directly to the lender
blocks.x: Veterans receiving compensation for a service-connected disability are exempt from the VA funding fee. VA disability compensation is also stable, nontaxable income that lenders can use in qualifying. The trap is the reduced-fee answer: the 1.5% tier is for borrowers who put 5% down, a different rule. Jordan wrote "ASK EVERY VETERAN ABOUT A DISABILITY RATING" in capital letters, because missing it costs a client thousands.

blocks.title: Insured, guaranteed, or lent?
blocks.html: FHA insures loans made by approved lenders. VA guarantees part of a loan made by a private lender. USDA's Rural Housing Service guarantees loans and also lends directly to very low income buyers in its direct program. SONYMA works through participating lenders. Exam items often say "FHA lends money to buyers": it does not.

Brianna Lopez is a paramedic in Poughkeepsie. She has rented for nine years and never owned a home. She found a small Cape Cod for $280,000 and has $6,000 saved. Tasha has her apply through a participating lender for a SONYMA loan with SONYMA's Down Payment Assistance Loan (DPAL).

blocks.title: SONYMA's down payment help
blocks.html: The State of New York Mortgage Agency offers below-market fixed-rate loans to first-time buyers through participating lenders, with income and purchase price limits by county. Its Down Payment Assistance Loan is the greater of $3,000 or 3% of the purchase price, up to $15,000. It is a 0% second loan with no monthly payments, forgiven after 10 years. If the owner sells or refinances sooner, the amount owed drops by 1/120 for each month the owner has lived there. The first-time buyer requirement is waived for eligible veterans and for purchases in designated target areas.

blocks.q: How much DPAL can Brianna get on the $280,000 house?
blocks.x: The DPAL is the greater of $3,000 or 3% of the price, capped at $15,000. Here 3% x $280,000 = $8,400, which beats $3,000 and is under the cap. The trap is $15,000, which is the maximum, reached only on prices of $500,000 and up. $14,000 is 5% of the price, a number from no SONYMA rule. Combined with her own $6,000, Brianna can cover a 3% down payment and part of her closing costs.

blocks.html: Brianna asked the obvious question. "What if I get a job in Albany in four years and sell?"

blocks.q: SONYMA forgives the DPAL at 1/120 per month over 10 years. If Brianna sells after exactly four years, how much of her $8,400 DPAL does she repay?
blocks.x: Four years is 48 months, so 48/120 of the loan has been forgiven: $3,360. She still owes 72/120 x $8,400 = $5,040, paid from her sale proceeds. The trap is $3,360, which is the forgiven part, not the part still owed. $8,400 assumes nothing is forgiven until year ten. The declining balance rewards owners who stay, which is the point: the state is paying to create stable homeowners, not quick flips.

blocks.html: Brianna did the math on her phone and decided she was staying in Poughkeepsie. Tasha added one more caution: SONYMA loans come with income limits and purchase price limits that vary by county, and a buyer who gets a raise before closing should tell the lender at once, because the limit is checked against the household's income at application.

blocks.q: Brianna's sister, a veteran, also wants a SONYMA loan but owned a condo in Florida five years ago. Which is accurate?
c: She cannot use SONYMA, since its loans go to people who have not owned property before
She has to use a VA loan, since state programs do not lend to veterans with VA benefits
She may qualify, but just for the DPAL, since veterans are excluded from the first loan
She may qualify, because SONYMA waives the first-time buyer rule for eligible veterans
blocks.x: SONYMA's programs are aimed at first-time buyers, but the first-time requirement is waived for eligible veterans and for homes in targeted areas. Her prior Florida condo does not disqualify her. She still has to meet SONYMA's income and price limits. The trap is "never owned property": first-time buyer rules look at recent ownership, and there are exceptions. Nothing stops a veteran from choosing SONYMA instead of VA.

blocks.text: File 3: The farmhouse in Greene County

blocks.html: Caleb and Rosa Hartwell, a carpenter and a school aide, want a farmhouse on two acres outside Cairo, Greene County, for $240,000. They have good credit and almost no savings. Caleb assumed USDA loans were for farmers. Tasha pulled up the USDA property eligibility map and the county income limits instead.

blocks.q: What mainly decides whether the Hartwells can get a USDA Rural Housing Service guaranteed loan?
c: Whether either spouse earns most of the household income from farming
Whether the home sits on at least five acres zoned for agricultural use
Whether they are first-time buyers who have completed SONYMA counseling
Its location in an eligible area and their household income
blocks.x: USDA's guaranteed program is for low and moderate income households buying a primary residence in an eligible rural area, set by a USDA map and county income limits by household size. Farming is irrelevant, which is the trap Caleb fell into. There is no acreage minimum and no first-time buyer rule. The loan can cover 100% of the value, with a 1% upfront guarantee fee and a 0.35% annual fee.

blocks.text: File 4: The nurse with a 600 score

blocks.html: Keisha Grant is a nurse in Rochester with steady income, a 600 credit score after a rough divorce, and $12,000 saved. She wants a $300,000 house in the town of Greece. Her credit score rules out most conventional loans at a decent price. FHA does not.

blocks.title: Keisha's FHA numbers
blocks.html:
Price: $300,000. Minimum down payment (3.5%): $10,500
Base loan: $289,500
Upfront MIP: 1.75% x $289,500 = $5,066.25, usually financed into the loan
Annual MIP: 0.55% of the balance for a 30-year loan with less than 5% down, paid monthly: about $1,592 a year, or $133 a month at the start.

blocks.q: Keisha asks when she can stop paying the monthly FHA premium, as her friend did with PMI on a conventional loan. What is the best answer?
c: At 78% of original value, the same automatic point that applies to PMI
After 11 years, since FHA drops MIP on every loan at that point regardless
With under 10% down, it lasts for the life of the loan
When she asks in writing after five years of payments without any late ones
blocks.x: The Homeowners Protection Act's 80% and 78% rules apply to private mortgage insurance on conventional loans, not FHA. On today's FHA loans with less than 10% down, the annual MIP lasts for the life of the loan; with 10% or more down, it ends after 11 years. Many FHA borrowers later refinance into a conventional loan once they have 20% equity. The trap is applying the PMI rule to MIP.

blocks.html: FHA has other features worth knowing. It insures loans on owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes, so a buyer in Rochester or the Bronx can buy a two-family with 3.5% down and count part of the rent. Gifts from family can cover the whole down payment. The appraiser also checks FHA's minimum property standards for safety and soundness, so peeling paint on an old house or a missing handrail can hold up the closing until it is fixed. FHA loans are assumable by a qualified buyer, which made 2020 and 2021 FHA loans at 3% rates surprisingly valuable when their owners sold in a 6.5% market.
Keisha took the FHA loan, planning to refinance in a few years once her score recovers. Jordan's legal pad now had four programs on it. Tasha tapped the second column: "Who owns the loan?"

head: File
Loan
Likely path after closing
rows: Lender pools it into a mortgage-backed security; Ginnie Mae guarantees timely payment to investors
SONYMA buys the first mortgage from the participating lender; the DPAL is SONYMA's own second loan
Pooled into a Ginnie Mae security like FHA and VA loans
Pooled into a Ginnie Mae security
Sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, which package it into their own securities
blocks.caption: Tasha's second column

blocks.html: Jordan asked who Darnell would actually pay each month. Often neither the lender nor the investor: a servicer collects payments, runs the escrow, and handles defaults for a fee, while the investors who own the securities receive the principal and interest. Servicing rights can be sold separately from the loan, which is why borrowers get those "your loan has a new servicer" letters.

blocks.q: Why can Darnell's lender make another VA loan next week even though it has lent most of its available cash?
c: It sells or pools the loan and gets cash back
The VA reimburses the lender for each loan it guarantees
Ginnie Mae buys the VA loan from the lender the day after it closes
Fannie Mae buys the VA loan and holds it until it is paid off
blocks.x: The secondary market recycles money. The lender sells the loan or pools it into a mortgage-backed security, gets cash back, and lends again. For VA, FHA and USDA loans, Ginnie Mae guarantees investors timely payment on those securities. The trap is "Ginnie Mae buys the loan": Ginnie guarantees securities, it does not buy loans. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac mainly buy conventional conforming loans, and the VA does not reimburse lenders.

blocks.text: A detour: the house that is not built yet

blocks.html: At lunch, Tasha took a call from the Ostrowskis in Saratoga County. They own a lot and want to build. Their builder's contract is $400,000, paid in stages. A permanent mortgage cannot close on a house that does not exist, so they need a construction loan: funded in draws as work passes inspection, interest only on what has been drawn, then paid off by a takeout loan (or converted, in a construction-to-permanent loan) when the certificate of occupancy issues.

head: Stage
Draw
Total drawn
blocks.caption: The Ostrowskis' draw schedule

blocks.q: The construction loan rate is 8%, interest only on funds drawn. In the month after the framing draw, with $180,000 outstanding, the interest is:
blocks.x: Interest is charged only on the amount drawn: $180,000 x 0.08 / 12 = $1,200. The trap is $2,666.67, which charges interest on the full $400,000 commitment as if it had been funded. $14,400 is a full year of interest on $180,000. Paying interest only on draws is what keeps construction financing affordable while the house is going up.

blocks.html: Before Tasha could hang up, the Ostrowskis had a second problem. They also own a condo in Clifton Park, worth about $350,000 with a small mortgage, and they will not sell it until the new house is finished. Their builder wants the land-and-construction financing in place now, and their own cash is tied up in the condo.

blocks.q: The Ostrowskis need cash for the new house before the condo sells. Which loan fits that timing gap?
c: A wraparound mortgage on the condo, paid by the eventual condo buyer
A bridge loan secured by the condo, repaid from the condo sale proceeds
A reverse mortgage on the condo, since the equity is already there
A blanket mortgage covering the lot and every unit in the condo building
blocks.x: A bridge (swing) loan is short-term financing secured by the home being sold, used to buy or build the next one, and repaid when the first home closes. The risk is carrying both payments if the condo sits. The trap is the wraparound, which is seller financing for a buyer, not a way to tap your own equity before a sale. A reverse mortgage requires age 62, and a blanket mortgage covers several parcels owned by one borrower, not a whole building.

blocks.html: Tasha closed the morning with a quick conforming check on a referral from Westchester: a couple buying in Scarsdale who needed a $1.4 million loan. In 2026 the conforming limit for a one-unit home in the New York City area, which includes Westchester, is $1,249,125. Their loan is above it.

blocks.q: What does the Scarsdale couple's $1.4 million loan amount mean for their financing?
c: It has to be insured by FHA, which covers loans above the conforming limit
It has to be split into a first and second loan to stay under the limit
It is a conforming loan, since Westchester is a high-cost area without a cap
It is a jumbo loan, held by the lender or sold privately, not to Fannie or Freddie
blocks.x: Loans above the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac limit are nonconforming jumbo loans. The lender keeps them in its own portfolio or sells them to private investors, and it sets its own rules for down payment, reserves and credit. The trap is the split-loan answer: some borrowers do pair a conforming first with a second loan to stay under the limit, but it is a choice, not a requirement. FHA limits are lower than conforming limits, not higher.

blocks.html: The last call was Margaret Feeney, 76, a widow in Buffalo's Parkside neighborhood. Her house is worth about $310,000, and she owes nothing on it. Her pension barely covers groceries. Her son had heard about a reverse mortgage on late-night TV and asked Tasha whether it was a scam.

Tasha explained the FHA-insured version, the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage. The owner must be 62 or older and complete counseling with a HUD-approved counselor before applying. The lender pays the owner from the equity, as a lump sum, monthly payments, or a line of credit. Nothing is due while she lives there. The balance grows over time and is repaid when she sells, moves out permanently, or dies, usually from the sale of the house. The loan is non-recourse: her heirs never owe more than the house is worth.

blocks.q: Which event could cause Mrs. Feeney's reverse mortgage to go into default while she is still living in the house?
c: Failing to pay her property taxes and homeowners insurance
Her loan balance growing larger than the house's appraised value
Her son moving into the house to help take care of her
Not making a monthly principal and interest payment
blocks.x: A reverse mortgage requires no monthly loan payments, but the borrower must keep up with property taxes, homeowners insurance, and basic maintenance, the same mortgagor duties as any loan. Falling behind on taxes is the most common cause of reverse mortgage defaults. The trap is the growing balance: rising debt is how the loan is designed to work, and the non-recourse feature protects her and her heirs from any shortfall.

blocks.html: Her son asked about the alternatives. A home equity loan would need monthly payments his mother could not make. Selling and renting would mean leaving the neighborhood where she has lived for 50 years. A sale-leaseback to the son himself was possible but would trigger a transfer, a new purchase loan for him, and a lease between family members. A reverse mortgage was built for exactly her situation: a house-rich, cash-poor owner over 62 who wants to stay put. The costs are real, though: upfront mortgage insurance, closing costs, and interest that compounds on a growing balance, which shrinks what the family inherits.

Tasha told the son it was not a scam, but that it was not free either, and that his mother should go to the counseling session with someone she trusts. Jordan's legal pad had five programs, a secondary market column, and a construction loan scribbled in the margin. Tasha looked it over. "Now you know why I don't believe in 'we can't afford it.' I believe in 'we haven't found the program yet.'"

items: VA guarantees loans for eligible veterans on owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes, with no down payment required and a one-time funding fee instead of monthly mortgage insurance; disability compensation exempts a veteran from the fee.
SONYMA offers below-market loans to first-time NY buyers through participating lenders, with a forgivable DPAL; veterans and target areas are exempt from the first-time rule.

USDA's Rural Housing Service turns on location and household income, not farming. FHA serves buyers with lower scores and small down payments, with upfront and annual MIP that does not follow the PMI cancellation rules.
