Ginnie Mae guarantees securities backed by FHA, VA and USDA loans; Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy conventional conforming loans. Selling loans gives lenders cash to lend again.
Construction loans fund in draws with interest on drawn amounts only; reverse mortgages require age 62, counseling, and continued payment of taxes and insurance.

lessons.title: Case file: Bagels, Kickbacks and a Gowanus Condo
lessons.tagline: A loan officer with a referral budget, a sponsor's title clause, and a closing date that collides with Veterans Day.
objectives: Decide whether referral payments, co-marketing, and affiliated business arrangements comply with RESPA Sections 8 and 9.
Apply TRID timing rules to a Loan Estimate and a Closing Disclosure, including business-day counts and holidays.
Calculate tolerance cures by comparing a Loan Estimate to a Closing Disclosure.
Apply the right of rescission and ECOA notice rules to real borrowers.

blocks.title: A lender with a lunch budget
blocks.html: It is September in Brooklyn, and Coastline Home Loans wants Hudson & Hart's buyers. Its loan officer, a cheerful man named Brent, drops off bagels every Friday. This week he pulls Marcus aside: "Two hundred fifty bucks for every buyer you send me who closes. Cash, gift card, whatever you like. Nobody gets hurt, the buyer still gets a great rate." Marcus tells Jordan about it at lunch like it is a winning lottery ticket. Jordan is about to represent Mateo and Lena Castillo on a $940,000 condo in a new Gowanus building, and their loan will be the first one Jordan watches from application to closing.

blocks.q: Brent offers Marcus $250 for each referred buyer who closes. Under federal law this is:
c: Legal if Marcus discloses the payment to the buyer in writing before application
A kickback barred by RESPA Section 8
Legal because referral fees under $500 per loan are exempt from federal rules
A Truth in Lending violation, since the fee raises the buyer's annual percentage rate
blocks.x: RESPA Section 8 bans giving or accepting any fee, kickback, or thing of value for referring settlement service business on a federally related mortgage loan. Disclosure does not cure it, which is the trap: consent from the buyer cannot make a kickback legal. Violators face fines up to $10,000 and up to a year in prison, and consumers can recover three times the charge. There is no small-dollar exemption.

blocks.html: Marcus grumbled that real estate agents refer buyers to lenders every day. Diane, overhearing, explained the line. Recommending a lender you trust is fine. Getting paid for it is not. And the "thing of value" does not have to be cash.

Brent tried again the next week with a different pitch: Coastline would pay for Marcus's open-house catering and half of a glossy postcard mailing to Park Slope, with Coastline's logo on it. Diane asked one question: "What share of the postcard is Coastline's?" The answer was a small logo in one corner.

blocks.q: Coastline offers to pay half the cost of a postcard on which its logo takes up a tenth of the space, plus Marcus's open-house food. Which is accurate?
c: Joint ads are fine if each pays its share; this split is not
Both are fine, since no money goes directly to Marcus for a referral
Both are prohibited, since lenders and real estate agents may not advertise together
The food is fine because it is consumed by the public, not by the agent personally
blocks.x: Co-marketing is legal under RESPA when each party pays a share that matches its actual use of the ad. Paying half the cost for a tenth of the space shifts value to the agent, which regulators treat as a payment for referrals. Paying for an agent's open-house food is a thing of value too. The trap is "no money goes directly": RESPA reaches gifts, services, and paid expenses, not just cash.

blocks.html: Marcus said no to both offers, though not happily. Diane's reasoning was not only federal. A kickback also breaks a salesperson's duty of loyalty and disclosure to the buyer, because an agent who is paid by the lender has a reason to steer the client toward that lender whatever its price. In New York, that is a fiduciary problem the Department of State can discipline, on top of anything the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau does. Jordan's practice from that day was simple: give every buyer at least three lenders, in writing, and accept nothing from any of them.

blocks.text: A title company down the hall

blocks.html: Hudson & Hart's parent company owns 30% of Gowanus Abstract, a title agency in the same building. Diane likes it; the title officers are good. But she has a rule: every buyer who is referred gets a written disclosure first, and nobody is told they have to use it.

blocks.title: Affiliated business arrangements
blocks.html: RESPA allows a referral to a settlement provider the referring firm partly owns if three things are true: the relationship and estimated charges are disclosed in writing at or before the referral, the consumer is not required to use the affiliate, and the only thing the firm receives is a return on its ownership interest, not a per-referral payment.

blocks.q: Jordan wants to suggest Gowanus Abstract to the Castillos. What must happen for that to be lawful?
c: Nothing special, since the title company is a separate corporation from the brokerage
The Castillos sign a statement agreeing to use Gowanus Abstract before contract
A written affiliated business disclosure at or before the referral, and free choice
Jordan refunds a share of his commission equal to the title company's profit
blocks.x: An affiliated business arrangement is legal if the consumer receives the written disclosure of the ownership and estimated charges at or before the referral, is free to choose another provider, and the firm's only benefit is a return on ownership. The trap is requiring use, which turns a lawful affiliate into a violation. Separate incorporation does not matter: the ownership link is exactly what must be disclosed.

blocks.html: The Castillos signed the contract for unit 4C. Buried in the sponsor's rider was a clause: "Purchaser shall obtain title insurance from Sponsor's designated title agent, Brightline Title." The Castillos' attorney flagged it immediately.

blocks.q: The condo sponsor's contract requires the buyers to buy title insurance from the sponsor's chosen title company as a condition of the sale. This:
c: Is allowed, because a seller may set any lawful condition on its own sale
Violates RESPA Section 9, which bars sellers from requiring a particular title insurer
Is allowed for new construction, since the sponsor's offering plan was filed with the AG
Violates the Martin Act, which requires buyers to choose title in the offering plan
blocks.x: RESPA Section 9 prohibits a seller from requiring, as a condition of sale, that the buyer purchase title insurance from a particular company. A seller who violates it can be liable to the buyer for three times the title charges. The trap is the offering plan answer: filing a plan with the Attorney General does not exempt a sponsor from federal law. The Castillos' attorney had the clause struck.

blocks.html: The sponsor's attorney did not fight it. New development sponsors in New York often suggest a title company and sometimes offer a credit if the buyer uses it, which is fine as long as the buyer is free to say no. What a seller cannot do is make the purchase depend on it. Jordan added a line to his own checklist for new development deals: read the sponsor's rider for anything that steers the buyer's settlement services.

The Castillos applied with Coastline on Monday, October 5, 2026, after Jordan gave them three lenders to call, Coastline among them, with no fee attached to any. They gave the loan officer their names, incomes, Social Security numbers, the property address, the $940,000 price, and the $752,000 loan amount they wanted.

blocks.q: Brent tells the Castillos he will not send a Loan Estimate until they upload two years of tax returns and three months of bank statements. Which is correct?
c: He may refuse; an application is incomplete until income is fully verified
He is right, because TRID applies once an appraisal is ordered and paid for
He may refuse, but has to send the LE within 10 days of receiving the documents
Once the six pieces of information are received, the LE clock has started
blocks.x: Under TRID, an application exists once the lender has six items: name, income, Social Security number, property address, estimated value, and loan amount. The lender then has 3 business days to deliver or mail the Loan Estimate, and it may not require verification documents before issuing it. The trap is the "incomplete until verified" answer: lenders can ask for documents, but cannot delay the LE for them. The LE is an estimate, which is why no verification is needed.

blocks.q: Coastline's offices are open Monday through Friday. The application was complete Monday, October 5. The Loan Estimate must be delivered or mailed by:
c: Wednesday, October 7
Friday, October 9
Monday, October 12
Thursday, October 8
blocks.x: The Loan Estimate is due within 3 business days after the application. For this deadline, a business day is a day the lender is open for substantially all of its business. Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday are the three days, so it must go out by Thursday, October 8. The trap is Wednesday, which counts Monday as day one. The application day itself is not counted.

blocks.text: Three Loan Estimates on the kitchen table

blocks.html: Jordan had told the Castillos to apply with three lenders, because the Loan Estimate is a standard form built for comparison. Lena lined them up. The note rates were close; the points were not.

head: Lender
Note rate
Points
APR
blocks.caption: Page 1 of each Loan Estimate, $752,000, 30-year fixed

blocks.html: The APR folds points and most lender fees into a yearly rate, so it is the fairest single number for comparing loans held to maturity. But the Castillos might not hold it that long. Mateo expected a transfer to his firm's Chicago office within five years. Coastline's 1 point would lower the monthly payment by about $62 compared with Park Savings.

blocks.q: If the Castillos pay Coastline's $7,520 point to save about $62 a month versus Park Savings, roughly how long until the point pays for itself?
c: About 2 years
About 5 years
About 10 years
About 20 years
blocks.x: Break-even = cost / monthly savings: $7,520 / $62 = about 121 months, or 10 years. If Mateo expects to move in five, paying the point loses money, even though Coastline's APR is lower than Park Savings'. The trap is reading the APR as the whole story: APR assumes the loan runs its full term, so it favors points. A buyer who expects to move soon usually does better with fewer points and a slightly higher rate.

blocks.html: Brent matched the no-point price, and the Castillos stayed with Coastline. Lena also noticed that Harbor Credit Union had the lowest APR of all, 6.49%, because two points bought the rate down to 6.25%. Over 30 years it would be the cheapest loan. Over five years it would be the most expensive. Jordan noticed something else while they were deciding: Coastline had sent over a co-branded flyer for the building's other open units. It read: "Own a Gowanus 2-bedroom for $3,980 a month with just 10% down!"

blocks.q: Under Regulation Z, what must the flyer add because it states a monthly payment and a down payment?
c: The terms of repayment and the APR, and whether the rate can rise
Nothing, because a down payment percentage is not a trigger term
The lender's NMLS number and the date the rate was quoted
The sponsor's offering plan number and the estimated common charges
blocks.x: The payment amount and the down payment are both trigger terms. Once a trigger term appears, the ad must also state the down payment, the terms of repayment, and the APR, including whether it may increase after closing. The trap is treating the down payment as harmless: "10% down" is itself a trigger. Licensing details matter under other rules, but they are not what Reg Z's trigger-term rule requires. Diane pulled the flyer until the disclosures were added.

blocks.html: The Loan Estimate arrived Wednesday. The Castillos locked their rate in late October for a November 12 closing. In early November the Closing Disclosure draft came over, and Lena, who audits hospital billing for a living, put it next to the Loan Estimate line by line.

head: Charge
Loan Estimate
Closing Disclosure
Tolerance group
blocks.caption: Lena's comparison

blocks.q: The lender's origination fee rose from $1,200 to $1,800 with no change in the loan. What must the lender do?
c: Nothing, since lender fees may rise up to 10% and the buyer can still close
Refund the $600 difference to the Castillos, at or after closing
Refund $480, the amount above the 10% tolerance for lender charges
Issue a new Loan Estimate, which resets the comparison to $1,800
blocks.x: Lender charges, such as origination fees, are zero-tolerance items: absent a valid changed circumstance, the final charge cannot exceed the Loan Estimate. The lender must cure the $600 overage with a refund or credit. The trap is the $480 answer, which applies the 10% bucket to a fee that has no tolerance. A revised LE is allowed only for a real changed circumstance, such as a change the borrower requests, not to paper over an increase.

blocks.q: Title services and recording fees are in the 10% group. On the LE they totaled $2,500; on the CD they total $2,800. How much must the lender refund?
blocks.x: The 10% tolerance applies to the group total. $2,500 x 110% = $2,750 allowed. The CD shows $2,800, so the lender cures the excess above the cap: $50. The trap is $300, which refunds the whole increase instead of only the part above 10%. The homeowners insurance increase is unlimited because the Castillos chose their own insurer, a service the lender does not control.

blocks.html: Lena asked why the insurance line could rise without limit. Because the Castillos shopped for it themselves, the lender had no control over the price, so TRID does not hold the lender to the estimate. The same logic covers services the buyer shops for outside the lender's list. On the other hand, a lender can issue a revised Loan Estimate and reset the baseline only for a genuine changed circumstance: the borrower asks for a different loan, the appraisal comes in low and changes the terms, or the rate is locked after the first estimate. A lender that simply underquoted its own fee eats the difference.

blocks.text: Three business days, and a holiday

blocks.html: The closing was set for Thursday, November 12, at the sponsor's attorney's office in Manhattan. Wednesday, November 11, is Veterans Day, a federal holiday. Coastline planned to email the Closing Disclosure Monday morning, November 9.

blocks.q: Can the Castillos close Thursday, November 12, if they first receive the Closing Disclosure on Monday, November 9?
c: Yes. Monday to Thursday is three days, which satisfies the rule
No. The CD has to arrive a full week before closing on a purchase loan
Yes, if they sign a waiver at closing confirming they had time to review it
No. Veterans Day does not count, so they needed it by Saturday, November 7
blocks.x: The borrower must receive the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before consummation. For this rule, business days are all calendar days except Sundays and federal holidays. From a Monday receipt, Tuesday counts, Wednesday the 11th does not, and Thursday counts: only two. Received Saturday the 7th, the days are Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday. The trap is "Monday to Thursday is three days", true in an ordinary week but not this one. Waivers are allowed only for a bona fide personal financial emergency.

blocks.html: Coastline sent the CD Friday, November 6, and the Castillos acknowledged it that afternoon. Then, on Tuesday, the sponsor agreed to a $5,000 credit for a scratched kitchen counter, and Coastline's rate lock expired before the paperwork was finished. The relock raised the APR from 6.61% to 6.92%.

blocks.q: Which change requires a new Closing Disclosure with a new 3-business-day waiting period?
c: An APR increase of more than 1/8 of a percentage point
The $5,000 seller credit that lowers the Castillos' cash to close
A $40 increase in the recording fee after a city fee change
A change in the closing location to the lender's office
blocks.x: Only three changes restart the 3-business-day clock: the APR becomes inaccurate (more than 1/8 of a point for a regular loan), the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added. A 0.31-point APR rise qualifies. Seller credits, small fee changes and logistics require a corrected CD but no new wait. The trap is the seller credit: it changes the cash to close, which feels big, but it is not a waiting-period trigger. The Castillos closed the following Monday.

blocks.title: Lender versus closing day
blocks.html: Brokers and buyers often blame the attorney when a closing slips. Under TRID the lender controls the Loan Estimate, the Closing Disclosure, and the waiting periods. A licensee's job is to keep the closing date realistic: ask the loan officer when the CD will go out, and remember Sundays and federal holidays.

The Closing Disclosure itself is five pages, and Jordan learned to read three spots first. Page 1 shows the loan terms and the projected payments, including escrow. Page 2 itemizes closing costs, marking any amount the lender is curing for exceeding a tolerance. Page 3 has the cash to close table, which compares the final numbers with the Loan Estimate line by line. For a New York purchase, that table is where the mortgage recording tax, the mansion tax on a $940,000 condo (none, since it is under $1 million), and the sponsor's transfer taxes, if the contract shifts them to the buyer, become real dollars.

Mateo's parents, who own a house in Sunset Park, had offered to help with furniture money. They opened a $60,000 home equity line on their own home and signed the loan documents on Friday, October 9, 2026. Monday, October 12, was Columbus Day.

blocks.q: When is the last day Mateo's parents can cancel the home equity line under the Truth in Lending right of rescission?
c: Monday, October 12, three calendar days after signing
Tuesday, October 13, skipping Sunday but counting the holiday
Wednesday, October 14, at midnight
Friday, October 16, a full week after signing
blocks.x: A borrower who pledges a principal residence on a home equity loan or refinance can rescind until midnight of the third business day after signing (or after receiving the disclosures, if later). For rescission, business days exclude Sundays and federal holidays but include Saturdays. Saturday the 10th is day one, Columbus Day does not count, Tuesday is day two, Wednesday the 14th is day three. The lender cannot disburse until the period ends. The trap is Tuesday, which counts the holiday. The Castillos' purchase loan has no rescission right.

blocks.text: The friend who was turned down

blocks.html: A month later, Lena's coworker applied with Coastline and was denied. She heard nothing for six weeks. Lena asked Jordan whether that was normal.

blocks.q: Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, what was the coworker entitled to after her completed application was denied?
c: Nothing, because lenders keep underwriting decisions confidential
A copy of the lender's full underwriting file within 90 days
Notice within 30 days, with the reasons or how to get them
A second review by a different underwriter before any denial
blocks.x: ECOA's Regulation B requires a creditor to notify an applicant of action on a completed application within 30 days, and an adverse action notice must state the specific reasons or tell the applicant how to get them. If a credit report played a part, the Fair Credit Reporting Act adds a notice naming the reporting agency. The trap is confidentiality: the reasons are exactly what the law makes the lender disclose. Six weeks of silence is a violation.

blocks.html: Diane turned all of this into a one-page office memo. Marcus pinned it above his desk with a sticky note that said "No bagels either?" Diane wrote under it: "Bagels are fine. Bagels for referrals are not."

blocks.title: New York's overlay
blocks.html: New York regulates mortgage brokers, bankers and loan originators through the Department of Financial Services, and the State's own fair lending law (Executive Law 296-a) covers more classes than ECOA. A real estate licensee who also acts as a mortgage broker in the same deal must disclose that dual role. Federal disclosure rules and New York licensing rules stack; neither replaces the other.

items: RESPA Section 8 bans any thing of value for referrals of settlement business; co-marketing must be paid in proportion to use, and disclosure does not cure a kickback.
Affiliated businesses are legal with written disclosure at or before referral, free choice, and only an ownership return. Section 9 bars sellers from requiring a particular title insurer.

TRID: an application is six pieces of information; the Loan Estimate goes out within 3 business days; the Closing Disclosure must be received 3 business days before consummation, counting Saturdays but not Sundays or federal holidays.
Lender fees have zero tolerance, the 10% group is measured in total, and only an inaccurate APR, a new loan product, or a prepayment penalty restarts the waiting period.
Rescission applies to refinances and home equity loans on a principal residence, not purchase loans. ECOA requires notice of action within 30 days with reasons for any denial.

lessons.title: Case file: The Envelopes on 197th Street
lessons.tagline: How a paid-off house in St. Albans ended up in foreclosure, and how a widow kept her equity.
objectives: Identify predatory lending practices, including packing, flipping, reverse redlining, and income fraud, in a real loan history.
Apply New York usury limits and high-cost and subprime loan protections to loan terms.
Apply New York's judicial foreclosure steps, the right of redemption, and rescue scam protections to an owner in default.
Calculate a deficiency judgment and decide whether a lender's claim survives the 90-day deadline.

blocks.title: A folder of envelopes in St. Albans
blocks.html: Hortense Baptiste, 79, has lived on 197th Street in St. Albans, Queens, since 1981. Her mortgage was paid off in 2011. In March 2026 her nephew Andre calls Jordan, whom he knows from the gym. "My aunt wants to sell. She says the bank is taking the house anyway." At her kitchen table, Hortense hands Jordan a shopping bag of envelopes: loan papers, statements, and a letter from a law firm with "NOTICE OF PENDENCY" in bold. Jordan is not a lawyer and says so. But before he calls Priya, he wants to understand how a paid-off house became a foreclosure in fifteen years.

The story starts with a cold call. A mortgage broker named Glenn Pryor had phoned Hortense in 2019, and then visited twice. Hortense had about $28,000 in credit card debt after her husband's illness, at rates near 25%. Glenn's pitch: roll it all into one low payment with a loan against her house.

blocks.q: What is the biggest risk for Hortense in Glenn's debt consolidation pitch?
c: Unsecured card debt becomes a lien that can cost her the house
Her credit card companies can sue her for paying the cards off early
Her property taxes go up when a new mortgage is recorded on her home
A home loan's interest rate cannot be lower than a credit card's rate
blocks.x: Credit card debt is unsecured: if she stops paying, the card companies can sue and hurt her credit, but they cannot take her home without a judgment and more. Rolling it into a mortgage turns it into secured debt with her house as collateral. A lower rate can still make sense for some owners, so the pitch is not illegal by itself; it is a classic opening for predatory lending, which is the point. The trap is the rate answer: a home loan usually does have a lower rate.

blocks.html: Glenn filled out the application for her. Jordan found a copy in the bag. It listed Hortense's monthly income as $6,400. Her pension and Social Security together were $2,150. She had signed where Glenn pointed.

blocks.q: Glenn wrote an income figure on Hortense's application that was three times her real income. Which statement is accurate?
c: It is a TILA disclosure error that the lender can correct with a revised APR
It is acceptable if the lender did not verify income, since it carries the risk
Broker fraud, though her signature can be used against her
It is lawful puffing, since applicants often estimate income generously
blocks.x: Inflating income on a loan application is mortgage fraud, and here the broker did it. Lenders and brokers who make loans a borrower clearly cannot repay are at the center of predatory lending. Hortense's signature can be used against her, which is why borrowers should read every page and never sign blank or prefilled forms they do not understand. The trap is "the lender carries the risk": in practice the borrower loses the house. Today, ability-to-repay rules require lenders to verify income.

blocks.html: Jordan asked Priya later whether the loan was illegal just because Hortense had weak credit and a high rate. Priya said no. A subprime loan, made to a borrower with weaker credit at a higher price, is legal and sometimes the only credit available. What makes a loan predatory is the abuse: terms the borrower cannot meet, fees far beyond the risk, products she did not need, and deception about what she was signing. Since 2014 federal ability-to-repay rules require lenders to make a reasonable, good-faith determination, from verified records, that the borrower can repay. Glenn's 2019 application would not survive that rule.

blocks.q: Which statement about subprime lending is accurate?
c: Every subprime loan is predatory, since it charges more than a prime loan
A subprime loan can be lawful; abusive terms or deception make it predatory
Subprime loans are banned in New York for owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes
A loan is subprime if, and just if, it carries a balloon payment
blocks.x: Subprime describes the borrower's credit and the loan's price, not its legality. Higher pricing for higher risk is lawful. Predatory lending is about abuse: deception, packing, flipping, equity stripping, and loans made without regard to ability to repay. Most predatory loans are subprime, but most subprime loans are not predatory. The trap is "banned in New York": Banking Law 6-m regulates subprime home loans; it does not prohibit them.

head: Term
What the papers said
rows: $96,000 (to pay $28,000 of cards, plus fees and "cash out")
11.9% fixed for 7 years, then a balloon payment of the remaining balance
Single premium of $4,200, financed into the loan
5% of the balance if paid off within 3 years
blocks.caption: Hortense's 2019 loan (summary)

blocks.q: Hortense's 11.9% rate is far above what her credit would justify. Under New York law, the rate itself is:
c: Criminally usurious, since it is more than 10% on a home loan to a senior
Legal, since TILA allows any rate that is accurately disclosed in the APR
Civilly usurious, because NY caps residential mortgage rates at 9.5%
Not usurious under the 16% cap, but possibly still predatory
blocks.x: New York's civil usury ceiling is 16% and criminal usury starts above 25%, so 11.9% is not usurious. But a loan can be legal on rate and still be predatory through its fees, insurance packing, balloon, and the borrower's inability to repay. The trap is the TILA answer: TILA requires disclosure and sets no rate limits, but state usury law and New York's high-cost and subprime loan rules do apply.

blocks.title: New York's high-cost and subprime loan rules
blocks.html: Banking Law 6-l covers high-cost home loans, defined by points and fees or rate thresholds. For those loans it restricts balloon payments, negative amortization, financing credit insurance, flipping, and lending without regard to ability to repay, and requires disclosures recommending counseling. Banking Law 6-m covers subprime home loans with its own ability-to-repay review and limits. Federal HOEPA adds a parallel layer for high-cost mortgages.

blocks.q: Which feature of Hortense's loan is the clearest sign of packing, a practice New York's high-cost loan law restricts?
c: The fixed rate for the first seven years of the loan
The $28,000 used to pay off her high-rate credit cards
The loan being secured by her principal residence on 197th Street
The financed $4,200 credit life premium
blocks.x: Packing means stuffing a loan with products the borrower did not need or understand, financed so the lender earns interest on them too. Single-premium credit insurance financed into a home loan is the textbook example, and New York's high-cost loan law restricts it. The trap is the payoff of the cards, which was the stated purpose of the loan, not an add-on. A fixed rate protects the borrower.

blocks.html: In 2021, Glenn called again. He refinanced the $96,000 loan into a new $118,000 loan at 11.5%, with new points, a new processing fee, and the prepayment penalty paid out of the new loan. In 2023 he did it a third time, for $139,000. Each time Hortense got a check of about $3,000 "for repairs." Her payment never went down, and her equity kept shrinking. Jordan added it up on the back of an envelope: in four years, about $28,000 of credit card debt had become a $139,000 lien, and more than $20,000 of the difference was points, fees, prepayment penalties and insurance premiums, all of it financed at double-digit rates.

blocks.q: What makes Glenn's 2021 and 2023 refinances loan flipping rather than ordinary refinancing?
c: Each one was made within five years of the previous refinance of the same home
Each one was made by a mortgage broker instead of by a federally chartered bank
Each one charged new points and fees with no real benefit to the borrower
Each one produced a small cash-out check that the borrower spent on repairs
blocks.x: Flipping is repeated refinancing that generates fees for the lender or broker without a tangible net benefit to the borrower: no lower rate, no lower payment, no needed cash that justifies the cost. The trap is the timing answer: a quick refinance can be perfectly legitimate when rates drop. The small cash-out checks are the bait that makes each flip feel like a benefit, while the fees strip far more equity than the checks deliver.

blocks.html: Andre showed Jordan something else: the same broker's flyers had gone to nearly every house on the block, and to blocks in Hollis, Cambria Heights and Laurelton, neighborhoods with mostly Black homeowners and high equity. A friend of Andre's in a Long Island suburb with similar credit had gotten a prime refinance at 4% that same year.

blocks.q: A lender targets mostly Black neighborhoods with higher-cost loans while offering similar borrowers elsewhere prime terms. This practice is:
c: Reverse redlining, which violates the Fair Housing Act and ECOA
Steering, which applies to real estate agents but not to mortgage lenders
Lawful risk-based pricing, since rates follow neighborhood foreclosure history
Blockbusting, since it involves the racial makeup of a neighborhood
blocks.x: Redlining denies credit to an area because of its racial makeup. Reverse redlining floods the same areas with costly, abusive loans. Both violate the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and New York's Human Rights Law. The trap is the blockbusting answer: blockbusting is inducing owners to sell by playing on fears about who is moving in, a different abuse. Lenders, not just agents, can steer borrowers.

blocks.html: Glenn had one more idea. In late 2023 he called Hudson & Hart and asked for Jordan by name. He had heard Jordan grew up in Queens. "You must know a lot of older homeowners with paid-off houses in Jamaica and Hollis. Send me their names, I send you $500 for every one who closes. Easy money."

blocks.q: How should Jordan respond to Glenn's offer of $500 for each older homeowner he refers?
c: Accept, if he tells each homeowner about the payment in writing first
Decline; it is a kickback, and targeting older owners invites abuse
Accept, but give the $500 to each homeowner as a closing credit
Decline, unless Diane approves the arrangement and splits the fee
blocks.x: Payment for referring borrowers to a lender is a RESPA Section 8 kickback, and disclosure or passing it along does not cure it. Targeting a list by age invites age discrimination problems under New York's Human Rights Law and feeds equity-stripping schemes aimed at seniors. Jordan's duty runs to his clients, not to a lender paying for leads. The trap is broker approval: a supervising broker cannot authorize a kickback. Jordan said no and told Diane, who reported Glenn to DFS.

blocks.html: The 2023 loan carried a balloon due in 2030, but the payment had crept past half of Hortense's income. She fell behind in late 2024. In April 2025 she received a thick letter from the servicer listing housing counseling agencies and warning that she could lose her home. She put it in the bag.

blocks.q: That April 2025 letter was most likely the notice New York requires before a lender sues to foreclose on a home loan. It must be sent at least:
c: 30 days before the lender records the notice of pendency
90 days before the foreclosure action is started
120 days before the referee's sale is held
10 days after the borrower's first missed payment
blocks.x: RPAPL 1304 requires the lender or servicer of a home loan to send a 90-day pre-foreclosure notice, with a list of housing counseling agencies, before starting the action. The trap is tying it to the notice of pendency, which is filed with the lawsuit, not 30 days after a notice. A borrower who uses those 90 days to call a counselor often has more options than one who waits for the summons.

blocks.html: Hortense did not call anyone. In September 2025 the lender sued, and its attorneys filed a notice of pendency (lis pendens) with the Queens County Clerk. Because she lives in the home and it is a home loan, the court scheduled a mandatory settlement conference. That is where things stood when Andre called Jordan.

blocks.q: Hortense's 2023 loan has a balloon due in 2030. What does that mean for her?
c: The balance is forgiven in 2030 if she has paid on time
Her payments shrink in 2030 as the loan fully amortizes
The rate resets to the market rate in 2030 for 23 years
In 2030 the remaining balance falls due in one lump sum
blocks.x: A balloon loan's payments do not pay the debt to zero by maturity, so a large final payment of the remaining balance comes due at once. Borrowers usually plan to refinance or sell, which fails when equity has been stripped or credit has slipped. That is why New York's high-cost loan law restricts balloons. The trap is the rate reset: that describes an adjustable-rate loan, not a balloon.

blocks.html: Two weeks before Jordan's visit, a man in a blazer had come to Hortense's door with a business card that said "Homeowner Rescue Partners." He offered to stop the foreclosure: Hortense would deed the house to his company, his company would pay off the lender, and she could rent the house back and buy it back in two years. He left a contract on the table. She had not signed it.

blocks.q: If Hortense signs the rescue company's contract, which New York protection applies?
c: She may cancel until midnight of the 14th business day after signing
She may cancel within 3 business days under the federal rescission rule
No protection, since a deed signed freely by a competent owner stands
She may cancel up to the day of the referee's sale
blocks.x: New York's Home Equity Theft Prevention Act (RPL 265-a) covers sales of homes in foreclosure or default to equity purchasers. The contract must meet strict form rules, and the seller can cancel until midnight of the 14th business day after signing. Deals that take the deed with a promise to reconvey face extra protections. The trap is the 3-day TILA rescission rule, which applies to refinances and home equity loans, not to a sale of the house.

blocks.title: "Rent it back and buy it back later"
blocks.html: Foreclosure rescue scams usually work by taking title from the owner, collecting rent, and never reconveying. The owner loses the house and the equity. New York's law exists because these deals stripped equity from thousands of homeowners. A legitimate path almost always runs through the lender, a housing counselor, or a real sale at market value.

Priya took the file the next day. Her first point was the one that mattered most: Hortense still owned the house. In New York, the owner holds the equitable right of redemption until the referee's sale: pay off the debt, or sell and pay it off, and the foreclosure ends. Priya's paralegal estimated the payoff at about $158,000 with arrears, interest, and legal fees. Jordan's CMA put the house at $640,000 to $680,000.

blocks.q: The lender has filed a notice of pendency. Can Hortense still sell the house on the open market before the referee's sale?
c: No. A notice of pendency freezes title until the court enters judgment
No. After a lawsuit is filed, the referee is the one who sells
Yes. She can sell and pay off the lender at closing
Yes, but the buyer will take title subject to the lender's mortgage
blocks.x: A notice of pendency warns buyers and lenders that a lawsuit affects the property, so no one can buy without notice of it. It does not stop a sale. If Hortense sells before the auction and the lender is paid at closing, the action is discontinued and the notice cancelled. With roughly $480,000 or more of equity, a market sale is far better than an auction. The trap is the "freezes title" answer, which confuses notice with prohibition.

blocks.html: Jordan listed the house at $659,000 with Priya's guidance and the family's consent. Priya went to the settlement conference with Hortense and told the court and the lender's counsel that a sale was underway. The lender agreed to adjourn the case for 90 days.

blocks.q: Why is the court's settlement conference worth attending, even for an owner who plans to sell?
c: Missing it lets the court enter a deficiency judgment against the owner on the spot
It is the hearing where the referee sets the minimum bid and the auction date for the property
It is where a workout, a modification, or time to sell gets negotiated
It is optional unless the owner is asking for a loan modification instead of a sale
blocks.x: New York requires a settlement conference in residential foreclosures where the borrower lives in the home and the loan is a home loan. The parties must negotiate in good faith toward a resolution, which can mean a modification, a repayment plan, a short sale, or time to sell. The trap is "optional unless she wants a modification": for an owner selling, it is where she gets the adjournment that lets the sale close.

blocks.text: How it ended, and how it could have

blocks.html: The house sold in July 2026 for $648,000 to a young couple from Jamaica, Queens. The lender's $158,400 payoff, Priya's fee, the NYS and NYC transfer taxes and Jordan's commission were paid at closing. Hortense walked away with about $440,000 and moved near her daughter in Valley Stream. Had the case gone to auction, she would have faced a sale price set by whoever showed up on the courthouse steps, months more of default interest and legal fees added to the debt, and the burden of claiming any surplus herself. The difference between those two endings was not the law. It was a phone call to someone who knew the law before the auction date. Priya also filed claims against the original broker, whose license DFS had since revoked.
Priya showed Jordan what the auction route would have looked like for a neighbor's house the year before, a case she had handled.

blocks.title: A neighbor's referee's sale
blocks.html:
Debt with interest, fees and referee's costs: $402,000
Auction price: $310,000
Court-determined fair market value: $365,000
Deficiency if the lender moves in time: $402,000 minus the higher of $310,000 or $365,000 = $37,000
The lender's attorneys filed the deficiency motion 104 days after the referee's deed was delivered.

blocks.q: What happens to the lender's $37,000 deficiency claim in the neighbor's case?
c: It is barred; the sale proceeds count as full satisfaction
The lender recovers $92,000, the difference between the debt and the auction price
The lender recovers $37,000, since the deficiency was correctly calculated
The claim is reduced by a quarter as a penalty for the late filing of the motion
blocks.x: Under RPAPL 1371 the lender must move for a deficiency judgment within 90 days after the sale is consummated by delivery of the referee's deed. If it does not, the sale proceeds are deemed full satisfaction and no deficiency can be recovered. At 104 days, the claim is gone. The trap is $92,000: even a timely motion credits the higher of the sale price or fair market value, not the auction price alone.

blocks.html: Priya added the other side of the math. When an auction brings more than the debt and costs, the extra is surplus money. It does not go to the lender. The referee deposits it with the court, and junior lienholders and then the former owner claim it in a surplus money proceeding. Owners who walk away from a foreclosure sometimes never claim surplus that is theirs. Selling before the auction avoids the whole question: the owner gets the equity at closing.

Jordan typed up what he had learned and gave it to Diane. She added a line at the bottom: "Licensees see these deals first. If a client is being pitched a refinance that makes no sense, or a stranger offers to 'save' a house, send them to a lawyer or a HUD-approved counselor the same day. And never take a dollar from a lender for sending them a client."

items: Debt consolidation into a home loan turns unsecured debt into a lien on the house; predatory loans add packing, high points and fees, balloons, and loans the borrower cannot repay.
A rate under New York's 16% civil usury cap can still be predatory. Banking Law 6-l and 6-m and federal HOEPA restrict high-cost and subprime loans; TILA itself sets no rate limits.
Loan flipping is refinancing with no net benefit; reverse redlining targets protected neighborhoods with costly loans and violates fair lending laws. Inflated income on an application is fraud.
A New York home foreclosure needs a 90-day RPAPL 1304 notice, a lawsuit with a notice of pendency, and a settlement conference; the owner can redeem or sell until the referee's sale.
Equity purchaser contracts with owners in foreclosure can be cancelled until midnight of the 14th business day. A lender loses any deficiency if it does not move within 90 days of the sale.

lessons.title: Case file: The Matched Pair on Roosevelt Avenue
lessons.tagline: Evelyn buys two Jackson Heights buildings with one blanket mortgage, a five-year fixed rate, and a release clause, and learns how differently New York treats her loan and her nephew's.
objectives: Apply a lender's criteria for income-producing property, calculating the maximum loan under loan-to-value and debt service coverage tests.
Calculate a blanket mortgage release price, a step-down prepayment premium, and adjustable rate changes under first, periodic, and lifetime caps.
Decide what rights and duties a mortgagor keeps after closing, including leasing, insurance proceeds, and negative amortization risk.
Distinguish New York's protections for owner-occupied home loans and land contract buyers from the terms allowed on business loans.

blocks.title: Two buildings, one loan, Roosevelt Avenue
blocks.html: Evelyn Park has found what she calls "a matched pair": two adjacent mixed-use buildings on Roosevelt Avenue in Jackson Heights, under the elevated 7 train, with ten apartments upstairs and five stores at street level between them. The owner, a family selling after forty years, wants $7,400,000 for both and will not split them. Evelyn will buy through a new company, Roosevelt 82 LLC. She has asked Tasha Monroe to find the debt and Jordan, who found the deal, to help her read every number the lender sends. Evelyn wants as much leverage as she can get, and she wants to sell the smaller building in a few years without refinancing the larger one. Tasha's first term sheet arrives on a Monday.

blocks.title: Flushing Harbor Savings: term sheet (summary)
blocks.html:
Borrower: Roosevelt 82 LLC, with Evelyn Park as personal guarantor
Collateral: first mortgage on both buildings (one blanket mortgage)
Loan amount: the lesser of 70% of the lower of price or appraised value, or the amount producing a debt service coverage ratio of at least 1.25x on underwritten NOI
Rate: 6.25% fixed for 5 years, then adjusting annually to the one-year Treasury index plus a 2.75% margin
Caps: 2% at the first adjustment, 1% per year after, 5% over the life of the loan
Amortization: 30 years
Prepayment: 5%, 4%, 3%, 2%, 1% of principal prepaid in loan years 1 to 5; none after
Partial release: either building may be released on payment of 120% of its allocated loan amount, plus any prepayment premium
Other: assignment of leases and rents; lender approval of any lease over 2,000 square feet; tax and insurance escrows; late charge 5% of any payment more than 10 days late

Jordan notices what is missing from the paperwork Tasha forwards. There is no Loan Estimate, and the lender says there will be no Closing Disclosure. Leo, who closed on a condo last year, once showed Jordan both forms in a binder.

blocks.q: Why will Evelyn's lender skip the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure?
c: Because the loan is over the conforming limit, so federal disclosure rules cover just its first $1 million
Because Evelyn has a mortgage broker, and brokers deliver their own disclosure forms in place of the lender's
Because it is a business-purpose loan to an LLC, which falls outside TILA and RESPA
Because a mixed-use building is exempt from disclosures until the loan has closed and recorded
blocks.x: Truth in Lending and RESPA protect consumers borrowing for personal, family, or household purposes, and RESPA covers federally related loans on 1 to 4 family homes. A loan to an LLC to buy a ten-apartment, five-store investment property is business-purpose credit, so neither the TRID forms nor the rescission rules apply. The broker answer is the trap: a mortgage broker does not replace the lender's disclosures; here there simply are none required.

blocks.text: What the lender is really lending against

blocks.html: A home lender's first question is whether the borrower's salary can carry the payment. On income-producing property the first question is whether the building can carry its own debt. The lender's criteria shift from the borrower's ratios to the property's investment quality: its rents, its expenses, its tenants, and its appraised value. Evelyn's personal guaranty matters, but it is the backstop.

head: Underwriting line
Annual
rows: Apartment rents (10 units, average $2,600 a month)
Insurance, water and sewer, repairs, management, payroll, common utilities
blocks.caption: Lender's underwriting of the two buildings

blocks.html: The underwriter's questions go well past the totals. Which apartments are rent stabilized? The larger building has six units and was built before 1974, so it falls under rent stabilization; two of its apartments are still stabilized because the others were deregulated before the 2019 law ended that path. The lender underwrites their legal registered rents, not what Evelyn hopes to get. The four-unit building is too small to be covered. When do the store leases expire? One expires in 14 months, so the underwriter haircuts that rent. Was there ever a dry cleaner on the block? A Phase I environmental report is a condition of the loan. A lender on a building like this is buying a stream of income for 30 years and wants to know how sturdy each piece of it is.
The appraisal comes back at $7,150,000, $250,000 under the price. Evelyn shrugs: she agreed to pay a premium to get both buildings. The lender does not share her view of the premium.

blocks.q: Under the term sheet's 70% test, what is the largest loan the lender will make?
c: $5,180,000, which is 70% of the $7,400,000 price Evelyn agreed to pay
$5,005,000, which is 70% of the lower appraised value
$5,092,500, which is 70% of the average of price and appraisal
$5,550,000, which is 75% of the $7,400,000 contract price
blocks.x: Lenders apply the loan-to-value ratio to the lower of the price or the appraised value, so a buyer who overpays funds the difference in cash. Here that is 0.70 x $7,150,000 = $5,005,000. The price answer is the trap: the lender protects itself against the premium Evelyn chose to pay by ignoring it.

blocks.html: Then the second test. The loan's annual debt service at 6.25% over 30 years is about $73,886 for every $1,000,000 borrowed (a loan constant of 7.3886%). The lender wants NOI to be at least 1.25 times the debt service.

blocks.q: How large a loan does the 1.25x debt service coverage test support, and which test controls?
c: About $4,807,000, so the coverage test controls the loan amount
About $5,550,000, so the 70% test controls and the loan is $5,005,000
About $6,009,000, so the 70% test controls and the loan is $5,005,000
About $4,440,000, so the coverage test controls the loan amount
blocks.x: Maximum debt service is NOI divided by the required ratio: $444,000 / 1.25 = $355,200. Divide by the loan constant: $355,200 / 0.073886 is about $4,807,000. The lender lends the lesser of the two tests, so coverage controls. The $6,009,000 answer is the trap: it divides NOI by the constant without applying the 1.25 cushion, which is the whole point of the test.

blocks.html: Flushing Harbor approves $4,800,000. Evelyn must bring $2,600,000 for the price plus closing costs. Most of her cash is tied up in the building in Long Island City where her company has its offices and storage.

blocks.text: Finding the down payment in a building she already owns

blocks.html: Evelyn's plan for the cash is a deal Tasha has seen many times with business owners. Evelyn sells the Long Island City building to a private investor for $3,100,000 and, at the same closing, signs a 15-year net lease to stay in it, paying rent to the new owner.

blocks.q: Which statement best describes Evelyn's position after the sale and leaseback?
c: She becomes the tenant, unlocks her equity, and gives up future appreciation in the building
She keeps the title and the appreciation, and the investor holds a first mortgage on it
She becomes the landlord, and the investor pays her rent for the right to occupy her space
She keeps an equity of redemption that lets her buy the building back at cost within 15 years
blocks.x: In a sale and leaseback the owner sells the property and leases it back, becoming the tenant. The seller gets cash out of the equity and a rent expense that is generally deductible for a business; the buyer gets a long-term tenant. The mortgage answer is the trap: that describes a loan, where the owner keeps title. Here title and future appreciation pass to the investor.

blocks.text: One mortgage, two buildings, and a way out for each

blocks.html: Because one blanket mortgage covers both buildings, a sale of either building would normally require paying off the whole $4,800,000. The term sheet's release clause fixes that. The lender allocates the loan: $2,750,000 to the larger building with three stores and six apartments, and $2,050,000 to the smaller one with two stores and four apartments. To release a building, Evelyn pays 120% of its allocated amount, so the loan that stays behind on the other building is smaller relative to its value.

blocks.q: In year 3 Evelyn sells the smaller building. Before any prepayment premium, what must she pay the lender to release it?
c: $2,050,000, its allocated share of the original loan amount
$2,400,000, the 120% figure applied to half of the original loan
$2,460,000, which is 120% of its $2,050,000 allocated amount
$4,800,000, because a blanket mortgage cannot be partly released
blocks.x: The release price is 120% x $2,050,000 = $2,460,000. The extra $410,000 goes to reduce the loan that remains on the larger building, which protects the lender from being left with the weaker collateral. The "cannot be partly released" answer is the trap: that is what happens without a release clause, which is exactly why Evelyn negotiated one.

blocks.text: After closing: whose building is it?

blocks.html: New York is a lien theory state, so Roosevelt 82 LLC holds title and the mortgage is a lien. Evelyn keeps the usual rights of ownership: possession, leasing, collecting rent, deciding who manages. The loan documents trim those rights in ways that protect the income the lender is counting on. Six months in, a pharmacy chain offers a 15-year lease for two combined stores, 3,400 square feet, at strong rent. Evelyn wants to sign it Friday.

blocks.q: What do Evelyn's loan documents most likely require before she signs the pharmacy lease?
c: Nothing. Under lien theory the lender has no role in leases until it takes title by foreclosure
The lender's approval, since the lease is over 2,000 square feet and its rents secure the loan
A new appraisal and a refinance, because a long lease changes the building's value
The lender's signature as co-landlord, because the assignment of rents made it a co-owner
blocks.x: The term sheet requires lender approval for any lease over 2,000 square feet, a common commercial covenant, because a long lease at the wrong rent can lock in the building's income for years. The assignment of leases and rents lets the lender collect rents directly if the borrower defaults; until then Evelyn collects them. The lien-theory answer is the trap: lien theory decides who holds title, not what the loan covenants require.

blocks.html: The lender approves the lease. In February, a grease fire in one of the restaurants damages the rear of the larger building. The insurer's claims adjuster calls Evelyn about a $310,000 payment.

blocks.q: Evelyn's insurance names the lender in a standard mortgagee clause. How is the $310,000 claim likely to be paid?
c: To Evelyn alone, because the insurance premium was paid out of her rents
To the restaurant tenant, since the fire started in its leased store
To the lender alone, which applies it to the principal of the loan
To Evelyn and the lender jointly, with funds released as repairs are made
blocks.x: A mortgagor's duties include keeping the property insured and in repair. The mortgagee clause protects the lender's interest, so the check is made out to both, and the loan documents usually let the lender hold the money and release it in draws as the work is done. The lender-alone answer is the trap: loan documents often allow it, but lenders usually prefer restoration, which keeps the rents flowing.

blocks.html: At closing, Evelyn signs three kinds of paper. As manager of Roosevelt 82 LLC she signs the note, the promise to pay, and the mortgage, the lien that secures it. Then, in her own name, she signs a personal guaranty of the debt. Jordan asks Tasha why a company formed to limit liability needs its owner's signature. "Because the lender read the same business school textbook," Tasha says. Small and midsize commercial lenders rarely lend to a single-purpose LLC with no other assets unless a person with real net worth stands behind it.

Jordan runs the bad case in his head. Suppose the stores empty out in a recession, the LLC stops paying, and the lender forecloses. New York foreclosure is judicial: the lender sues, the court enters a judgment, and a referee sells the property at auction. If the sale does not cover the debt, the lender may ask the court for a deficiency judgment, but it must move within 90 days after the sale, and the court credits the higher of the auction price or the fair market value it determines.

blocks.q: If a foreclosure sale of both buildings leaves a shortfall, against whom can the lender seek a deficiency judgment?
c: The LLC and Evelyn as guarantor, if named in the action and the lender moves within 90 days
The LLC alone, because forming an LLC shields its members from every debt it signs
Evelyn alone, because a guarantor is liable before the borrower whose debt she guaranteed
No one, because New York treats a referee's sale as full payment of a commercial loan
blocks.x: A deficiency judgment is available against persons liable on the debt who are made parties to the foreclosure: the borrower LLC and a guarantor who signed personally. The lender must move within 90 days of the sale, and the court credits the higher of the sale price or fair market value. The LLC-shield answer is the trap: an LLC protects members from company debts unless they personally guarantee them, and Evelyn did.

blocks.text: Year 6: the adjustable rate wakes up

blocks.html: Evelyn's rate is fixed at 6.25% for five years. Then it becomes an adjustable rate: each year the index plus the margin, limited by the rate caps. The first adjustment can move at most 2 percentage points, later ones 1 point a year, and the rate can never exceed 6.25% plus 5%, or 11.25%, under the lifetime cap.

head: Date
One-year Treasury index
Index plus 2.75% margin
blocks.caption: The index on each adjustment date

blocks.q: What rate does Evelyn pay in year 7?
c: 8.15%, the index plus the margin on the year 7 adjustment date
8.25%, the 6.25% start rate plus the 2% first adjustment cap
7.85%, the year 6 rate of 6.85% plus the 1% periodic cap
11.25%, the lifetime ceiling, since the index rose in both years
blocks.x: Year 6: 4.10% + 2.75% = 6.85%, within the 2% first-adjustment cap, so 6.85%. Year 7: the fully indexed rate is 8.15%, but the periodic cap limits the increase to 1 point, so 7.85%. The 8.15% answer is the trap: the fully indexed rate applies only when the caps allow it. The 8.25% figure confuses the first-adjustment cap with the year 7 rule.

blocks.html: A competing lender had offered a lower start rate with a different feature: no cap on the rate, but a cap on how much the monthly payment could rise each year. Tasha had steered Evelyn away from it, and she shows Jordan why with one month of arithmetic.

blocks.title: A payment cap without a rate cap
blocks.html:
Loan balance: $1,000,000. New rate after adjustment: 7.20%.
Interest due this month: $1,000,000 x 0.072 / 12 = $6,000.
Payment allowed under the payment cap: $5,400.
Shortfall: $6,000 minus $5,400 = $600.

blocks.q: What happens to the $600 shortfall under that loan?
c: The lender forgives it, since the payment cap protects the borrower from rising rates
It is added to the principal, so the loan balance grows to $1,000,600
It is due as a balloon at the next adjustment date, along with that month's payment
It is charged as a late fee, because the payment did not cover the interest due
blocks.x: When a payment cap holds the payment below the interest due, the unpaid interest is added to the balance. That is negative amortization: the borrower pays every month and owes more. A payment cap limits the payment, not the cost. The forgiveness answer is the trap: nothing is forgiven, it is deferred, with interest charged on it.

blocks.text: The prepayment premium, and why a homeowner would not pay one

blocks.html: Back to year 3. When Evelyn sells the smaller building and pays the $2,460,000 release price, the term sheet's step-down prepayment premium applies to the principal she prepays.

blocks.q: What prepayment premium does Evelyn owe on the year 3 release?
c: $61,500, at 2.5% of the release price, the average of the five years
$98,400, at 4%, because the premium is fixed by the year the loan was made
$144,000, at 3% of the full $4,800,000 original loan amount
$73,800, at the year 3 rate of 3% of the $2,460,000 prepaid
blocks.x: A 5-4-3-2-1 step-down charges 3% in loan year 3: 0.03 x $2,460,000 = $73,800. It applies to the principal actually prepaid, not to the whole loan. The $144,000 answer is the trap: it applies the right percentage to the wrong base. On commercial loans these premiums are bargained-for terms; Evelyn could have traded a higher rate for a shorter schedule.

blocks.html: That evening Evelyn's nephew Daniel calls. He is buying a two-family in Flushing to live in, and his loan at 6.875% has a clause charging 2% if he prepays within three years. He wants to know whether Evelyn's world of step-down premiums applies to him.

blocks.q: Under New York law, can Daniel's lender collect a prepayment penalty if he sells in year 2?
c: Yes, because the clause is in a note he signed and the rate is above 6%
Yes, but it is capped at 1%, the rate in the final year of the schedule
Only if the lender is a national bank, since state law does not reach them
No. After one year, no penalty may be charged on his owner-occupied two-family
blocks.x: General Obligations Law 5-501(3)(b) covers loans above 6% secured by an owner-occupied 1 to 6 family residence: the borrower may prepay at any time, and no penalty may be imposed for prepayment one year or more after the loan is made. Before then, only an express clause allows one. The signed-note answer is the trap: the statute overrides the contract. Federal rules can also limit penalties on many home loans.

blocks.title: New York treats home loans and business loans differently
blocks.html: On a loan secured by an owner-occupied 1 to 6 family residence, RPL 254-b bars a late charge on a payment made within 15 days of the due date and caps the charge at 2% of the late installment, and GOL 5-501 limits prepayment penalties. Evelyn's 5% late charge after 10 days and her five-year step-down premium are lawful because her loan is a business loan on a ten-unit investment property.

blocks.q: Daniel's loan documents call for a late charge of 5% after 10 days. If he pays 12 days late, what may his lender charge?
c: 5% of the installment, since the contract term controls and he signed it
Nothing, because the payment arrived within 15 days of the due date
2% of the installment, the cap for owner-occupied 1 to 6 family homes
2% of the unpaid principal, because late charges are figured on the loan
blocks.x: RPL 254-b applies to loans on owner-occupied 1 to 6 family residences: no late charge on an installment paid within 15 days after the due date, and never more than 2% of the delinquent installment. At 12 days, no charge is allowed. The 2% answer is the trap: it is the right cap, but the 15-day grace period comes first.

blocks.html: To round out her cash, Evelyn looks at an older deal. In 2021 she sold a six-acre lot in Delaware County to a young couple, the Brennans, on a land contract: $60,000, $6,000 down, the rest in monthly installments over ten years, with Evelyn keeping the deed until the last payment. They have paid $31,000 and built a small cabin. This spring they stopped paying. The contract says that on default "all payments shall be retained by the seller as liquidated damages." Evelyn wants to change the gate lock and relist the lot.

blocks.q: What does New York law most likely require before Evelyn can retake the lot?
c: A foreclosure of the Brennans' equitable title or a suit for the unpaid price
Nothing, because she still holds legal title and the contract allows forfeiture
A summary eviction in local court, like any tenant who stops paying rent
A 90-day notice, after which the contract terminates and she may relist
blocks.x: Under a land contract the buyer holds equitable title and the seller holds legal title as security. In Bean v. Walker (1983), a New York appellate court held that a seller facing a buyer with substantial equity must foreclose that interest, or sue for the price, rather than declare a forfeiture and keep everything. The forfeiture answer is the trap: having the deed does not let a seller keep $31,000 and a cabin without a court.

blocks.html: Priya files a foreclosure action. The Brennans, faced with a sale, refinance with a local bank and pay Evelyn the balance. She signs the deed over to them in the fall and puts the money toward the roof on Roosevelt Avenue.

blocks.title: Same words, different deals
blocks.html: Exam items mix up these: a blanket mortgage covers several parcels, a package mortgage adds personal property such as appliances, a wraparound sits on top of an existing loan, and a land contract is not a mortgage at all, because the seller keeps the deed. A sale-leaseback is a sale, not a loan. A payment cap and a rate cap are not the same protection.

items: Business-purpose loans to entities fall outside TILA and RESPA. No Loan Estimate, no Closing Disclosure, no rescission.
For income property, the lender looks at the property first: LTV on the lower of price or appraisal, and debt service coverage (NOI divided by debt service). The lender lends the lesser amount.
A blanket mortgage with a release clause lets a borrower sell one parcel by paying a release price, often a percentage above the allocated loan amount.

The mortgagor keeps title and the rights of ownership under lien theory, but must insure, repair, and pay taxes, and loan covenants can require consent to major leases. An assignment of rents lets the lender collect after default.
ARM rate = index plus margin, limited by first, periodic, and lifetime caps. A payment cap without a rate cap causes negative amortization.

New York protects owner-occupied 1 to 6 family borrowers: no prepayment penalty after one year on loans above 6%, and late charges capped at 2% after a 15-day grace period. A defaulting land contract buyer with real equity is entitled to foreclosure, not forfeiture.

roleplays.title: The Low Appraisal
roleplays.setting: Queens or Brooklyn. A $750,000 condo contract has a mortgage contingency about to expire. The appraisal just came in at $720,000.
roleplays.goal: Keep the deal alive with honest options, protect Leo's down payment, and stay clear of fraud and RESPA problems.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play an anxious first-time buyer whose $750,000 condo appraised at $720,000, plus Marcus (a corner-cutting agent) and Tasha (a mortgage broker). The buyer asks for exact numbers, wants to procrastinate on the mortgage contingency deadline, asks about points, and floats claiming owner occupancy on a unit they plan to rent. Marcus suggests a friendly appraiser and an off-the-books seller credit. Tasha mentions a $500 referral fee offer. The learner is the buyer's agent and must apply LTV on the lower of price or appraisal, PMI at 80%, points as 1% of the loan, appraiser independence, RESPA's kickback ban, honest loan applications, and strict contingency deadlines, while referring legal questions to the attorney. Grade on math accuracy, ethics, and timeliness.
opening: {hood}. {client}'s $750,000 condo contract has a mortgage contingency expiring in {days}. The appraisal just came in at $720,000.
Tasha calls at 8 a.m.: {client}'s appraisal on the $750,000 {hood} condo came back at $720,000. The commitment deadline is {days} away.
{client} forwards you a PDF with three exclamation points. The $750,000 {hood} condo appraised at $720,000, with {days} left on the mortgage contingency. {client} is {mood}.

say: Appraisal's $720K. Tasha says the loan is based on that now. What does that mean for me, in numbers?
I was putting 20% down on $750,000. Now the appraisal says $720,000. How much cash do I need?

moves.text: The lender uses the lower value. 80% of $720,000 is $576,000, so you'd need $174,000, not $150,000.
moves.fb: Exactly right. LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal, so the max 80% loan dropped by $24,000.
moves.react: {client} exhales. "Okay. $24,000 more. That's a number I can work with."

moves.text: Your max 80% loan falls to $576,000. Options: more cash, a price cut, or PMI at a higher LTV.
moves.fb: Correct. You give the new loan amount and lay out the real options.

moves.text: It means you'll need more cash to close. Tasha can run the exact numbers for you this afternoon.
moves.fb: True but vague. A buyer's agent should be able to do the basic LTV math.

moves.text: Nothing changes. The loan is based on the contract price, so you still need $150,000 down.
moves.fb: Wrong. The lender's value is the lower of price or appraisal, so the max loan dropped.

moves.text: You need 20% of $720,000, so $144,000 down. The low appraisal really saves you some cash.
moves.fb: Wrong. The price is still $750,000; with a $576,000 loan, the buyer needs $174,000.

moves.text: The seller has to cover the $30,000 gap. Low appraisals are always the seller's problem to fix, legally.
moves.fb: No rule makes the seller cover a gap. It's negotiated, or the buyer uses the contingency.
moves.react: "Great, tell them to pay it," {client} says.

say: Can we make the seller drop the price to $720K? Do I have any leverage here?
Shouldn't the price come down to match the appraisal? What can we push for?

moves.text: You can ask, and the appraisal is your evidence. Your attorney can advise you on the contingency.
moves.fb: Right. The appraisal supports a request, and contract rights are the attorney's call.

moves.text: Yes, the appraisal is real leverage. We ask for a cut; your lawyer handles the contract.
moves.fb: Correct. You negotiate value; the attorney advises on contract rights.

moves.text: We can ask, but sellers usually say no. Maybe just plan on finding the extra cash somewhere.
moves.fb: Not wrong, but you're giving up leverage the appraisal gives your client.

moves.text: Yes. The law requires sellers to match the appraisal, so they have to drop it to $720,000 right now.
moves.fb: No law requires a seller to match an appraisal.
moves.react: {client} grins. "Then tell them to drop it."

moves.text: No leverage at all. Once you sign a contract, the price can never be renegotiated by anyone.
moves.fb: Wrong. Parties can always agree to amend, and the appraisal supports a request.

moves.text: Tell them you'll walk unless they drop $30,000. You can cancel for any reason before closing.
moves.fb: Wrong. The buyer can cancel only under the contract's terms, such as a timely mortgage contingency.

say: Reconsideration came back at $730K. Seller won't drop the price. Commitment deadline is in 4 days. Can I just let it slide and figure it out later?
The seller's not budging and I'm exhausted. The deadline's in 4 days. Do I really have to deal with this now?

moves.text: Call your attorney today. If you can't close at these numbers, act before the deadline date passes.
moves.fb: Right. Contingency rights expire on their deadline, and the attorney handles notice.

moves.text: Don't let it slide. Contingency rights expire on the date, and your deposit could be at risk.
moves.fb: Correct. Missing the date can cost the buyer the down payment held in escrow.

moves.text: I'll draft a rider extending the deadline and send it over to the seller's agent this afternoon.
moves.fb: Protecting {client} is right, but drafting riders is the attorney's job, not yours.

moves.text: Contract deadlines are flexible. Nobody enforces a mortgage contingency to the exact day.
moves.fb: Contingency deadlines are strict. Missing one can cost the buyer the deposit.
moves.react: {client} nods. "Good, I'll deal with it next week."

moves.text: Let it slide. If the loan falls through, you get your deposit back no matter what happens.
moves.fb: Only if the contingency is properly used in time. After the deadline, protection may be gone.

moves.text: Just wait. The lender extends the contingency automatically whenever an appraisal comes in too low.
moves.fb: Lenders don't extend contract deadlines. Only the parties can, in writing.

say: My attorney got the seller to $740K. If I put 20% of $730K down, do I avoid PMI?
Price is now $740,000, appraisal $730,000. Is a $584,000 loan enough to skip PMI?

moves.text: Yes. $584,000 is 80% of $730,000, the lower value, so no PMI on a conventional loan.
moves.fb: Correct math: LTV uses the lower of $740,000 and $730,000. At 80% or below, no PMI.

moves.text: The lender uses $730,000, the lower figure. A loan at 80% of that, $584,000, skips PMI.
moves.fb: Right. You apply the lower value and the 80% threshold.

moves.text: You need 20% of $740,000 down, or PMI kicks in. Tasha can confirm the exact number for you.
moves.fb: Close, but LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal. $584,000 already hits 80%.

moves.text: PMI is required on every loan over $500,000, no matter how much you put down on the place.
moves.fb: Wrong. PMI depends on LTV, required above 80% on conventional loans.

moves.text: No. PMI applies to any condo purchase in New York City, even at 80% loan to value or lower.
moves.fb: Wrong. Property type doesn't trigger PMI; LTV above 80% does.

moves.text: You'd need 25% down to avoid PMI on a condo. Only single-family homes can do 20%.
moves.fb: Wrong. The conventional PMI threshold is 80% LTV for any property type.

say: Tasha says I can pay 2 points to lower my rate. What does that cost?
What's a point, and how much would 2 points cost me on this loan?

moves.text: Two points on a $584,000 loan is $11,680. Whether it pays depends on how long you stay.
moves.fb: Correct. One point is 1% of the loan amount, not the price.
moves.react: {client} nods. "I'll ask Tasha for the break-even."

moves.text: Each point is 1% of the loan, so 2 points costs $11,680. Tasha can show you the break-even point.
moves.fb: Right, and you route rate math to the mortgage professional.

moves.text: Points are complicated. I'd probably skip them, but Tasha knows a lot more than I do about it.
moves.fb: Deferring to Tasha is fine, but you should know a point is 1% of the loan.

moves.text: Two points is 2% of the purchase price, so $14,800. That's a lot of cash to pay at closing.
moves.fb: Wrong base. Points are a percentage of the loan amount, not the price.

moves.text: Points are 1% of your down payment each, so it's about $3,120 total. Cheap, I'd just do it.
moves.fb: Wrong base. One point equals 1% of the loan amount.

moves.text: Points cut your loan amount directly, so you'd borrow $11,680 less. They're always worth it.
moves.fb: Points prepay interest to lower the rate; they don't cut principal, and aren't always worth it.

say: Easy fix. I know an appraiser who'll redo it at $750K if the lender orders through him. Just tell Tasha to switch.
Get a new appraiser. I know a guy who always hits the contract number. Tell Tasha to use him.

moves.text: We don't shop for a number. If there are better comps, Tasha can then request a reconsideration.
moves.fb: Correct. Pressuring or steering an appraiser is appraisal fraud; a reconsideration with real comps is legitimate.

moves.text: No. Steering an appraiser to a value is fraud. Real comps via the lender is the way.
moves.fb: Right. Appraiser independence rules bar influencing the value.
moves.react: "Fine, do it the slow way," Marcus says.

moves.text: Let me think about it. Maybe Tasha can just ask the lender for a second appraisal instead.
moves.fb: Asking for a second appraisal to get a number is close to value shopping. Use a reconsideration.
moves.react: Marcus nods. "That's basically the same thing."

moves.text: Sure, send me his info. If he's licensed, there's nothing wrong with picking him ourselves.
moves.fb: Influencing who appraises in order to reach a value violates appraiser independence and is fraud.

moves.text: Good idea. Appraisers are allowed to adjust to the contract price if the buyer asks them to.
moves.fb: Wrong. An appraiser must reach an independent opinion of value.

moves.text: Okay, but we'll tell the appraiser the price up front so he knows exactly what we need.
moves.fb: Communicating a target value to influence the appraisal is prohibited.

say: Also, heads up: the seller's broker offered me $500 for every buyer I send their way. Want in on that for {client}?
Side note. A brokerage pays me $500 a head for buyer referrals. I could split it with you.

moves.text: No. Referral fees for any settlement services are illegal kickbacks under RESPA.
moves.fb: RESPA Section 8 bans kickbacks and referral fees for settlement services on federally related loans.

moves.text: Pass. RESPA Section 8 bans that outright, and disclosing it to {client} wouldn't fix anything.
moves.fb: Correct. Disclosure doesn't cure a RESPA kickback.
moves.react: "Good, we're on the same page," Tasha says.

moves.text: I'd rather not. Let me ask Diane whether something like that is ever allowed for us.
moves.fb: Declining is right, but you should know it's prohibited outright.

moves.text: Only if we disclose it to {client} first. Once the buyer knows, a referral fee is fine under RESPA.
moves.fb: Disclosure doesn't cure a RESPA kickback. The payment itself is prohibited.

moves.text: Sure, but have it paid to the firm, not me. RESPA only covers payments to individuals.
moves.fb: Wrong. RESPA covers referral payments to firms and individuals alike.
moves.react: "I'll send it to Hudson & Hart," Tasha says.

moves.text: Yes, as long as it's under $600. Small referral fees don't count under federal rules.
moves.fb: There's no dollar threshold. Any referral fee for settlement business is barred.

say: Seller's agent says the seller will slip {client} $10K cash outside closing to cover the gap. Off the books. Deal?
Here's a trick: the seller hands {client} cash under the table and the lender never knows. Everyone wins.

moves.text: A credit hidden from the lender is mortgage fraud. Any credit goes in the contract.
moves.fb: Right. Concealing seller concessions from the lender is mortgage fraud. Disclosed credits go through the attorneys.
moves.react: Marcus rolls his eyes. "Fine, ask the attorneys."

moves.text: Any seller money has to be disclosed to the lender. Let the attorneys write it up properly.
moves.fb: Correct. Legitimate concessions are documented and disclosed to the lender.

moves.text: I don't love it. Let me run it by {client}'s attorney before we say yes or no to anybody.
moves.fb: Asking counsel is fine, but you should say clearly that an undisclosed side payment is fraud.

moves.text: Sure. Cash between buyer and seller is private, so the lender has no right to know about it.
moves.fb: Wrong. Loan applications and closing documents must reflect all seller concessions.

moves.text: Deal, but make it a check, not cash, so there's a paper trail if anybody ever asks about it.
moves.fb: A check doesn't fix it. Hiding the concession from the lender is the fraud.

moves.text: Fine, as long as {client} doesn't sign anything that mentions it. Then it never happened.
moves.fb: Concealment is exactly what makes it fraud.

say: What if I tell the lender I'll live there but rent it out instead? Tasha said the rate's better for owner-occupied.
Can I just check the 'primary residence' box? I'll probably rent it out, but the loan is cheaper that way.

moves.text: That's occupancy fraud. If you'll rent it, tell Tasha now so she can find the right loan.
moves.fb: Right. Misstating occupancy on a loan application is mortgage fraud.

moves.text: Please don't. The application has to match your real plans. Tasha can price an investor loan.
moves.fb: Correct. You steer the client away from a false statement to a lender.

moves.text: I'd talk to Tasha about it. She'll know what you're allowed to say on the application.
moves.fb: Not encouraging it, but you should say clearly that a false occupancy claim is fraud.

moves.text: Lots of people do this. As long as you live there a few weeks first, it counts as owner-occupied.
