moves.fb: Wrong. Intent at application matters, and a token stay doesn't make a false statement true.

moves.text: Sure. Lenders never check where you live after closing, so there's no real risk to you.
moves.fb: Lenders can and do check, and the false statement is the violation either way.

moves.text: Just check the box. Condos in New York can be rented freely, so the lender doesn't care either way.
moves.fb: Occupancy affects the loan terms, and lying about it is fraud regardless of condo rules.

roleplays.debrief: Lenders use the lower of price or appraisal, so a low appraisal raises the cash needed for an 80% LTV, and conventional loans at 80% or below need no PMI. A point is 1% of the loan amount. Never steer an appraiser, hide seller money from a lender, or misstate occupancy (mortgage fraud). RESPA Section 8 bans referral kickbacks even when disclosed, and contingency deadlines are strict: get the attorney involved the same day.

roleplays.title: The Rescue Letter
roleplays.setting: Brooklyn or Queens. An older homeowner is months behind on a home equity loan and has received a foreclosure summons. A company has offered to 'save the house' if the owner signs over the deed.
roleplays.you: Jordan, a salesperson she called for advice about selling
roleplays.goal: Protect a vulnerable owner from an equity-stripping scam, explain her real options accurately, and refer her to the right professionals.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play a 74-year-old homeowner months behind on a home equity loan, frightened by a foreclosure summons and a 'rescue' company pressuring you to deed over the house within days. Repeat the scammer's claims: auction next month, foreclosure wipes out debt, you cannot sell now. Ask the agent to call your lender pretending to be your son, mention that the company offered the agent a referral fee, and ask about a reverse mortgage. Marcus suggests buying the house cheap. The learner is a real estate salesperson and must recognize equity stripping, explain NY judicial foreclosure and settlement conferences, deficiency judgment risk, and the right to sell or pay off before the sale, refer to a housing counselor and attorney, and refuse to misrepresent or profit. Grade on accuracy, compassion, and referrals.
opening: {hood}. {client}, 74, is {months} behind on a home equity loan and has a foreclosure summons. {company} has offered to 'save the house' if {client} signs over the deed by {day}.
{client} called Hudson & Hart about selling. On the kitchen table: a foreclosure summons, {months} of late notices, and a glossy flyer from {company}.
A 40-year owner in {hood}, {client} is {months} behind and scared. {company} wants a signature on a deed by {day}.

say: This company says if I deed them the house, they'll pay the bank and rent it back to me. They want me to sign {day}. Is that a good idea?
{company} says they'll take over the loan if I put the house in their name. Then I just pay them rent. Should I sign?

moves.text: Please don't sign anything yet. Deed-for-rescue offers are a known scam. Let's call a counselor.
moves.fb: Correct. Deed-transfer rescues are the equity-stripping scheme NY's Home Equity Theft Prevention Act targets.
moves.react: {client} sets the pen down. "I had a bad feeling."

moves.text: I'd hold off. Signing over the deed can strip your equity. An attorney should see this first.
moves.fb: Right. You slow things down and get the owner to qualified help.

moves.text: It might work out, but I'm not sure. Maybe ask them for more time so you can think it over.
moves.fb: Not harmful, but you missed a chance to name the scam and refer to counsel.
moves.react: {client} nods. "I'll ask them for a week."

moves.text: If it saves the house, it might be worth it. Renting it back means you never have to move out.
moves.fb: Signing away the deed can wipe out decades of equity, and the rent-back often ends in eviction.

moves.text: Sign it, but make them promise in writing to sell it back to you once you're caught up on it.
moves.fb: Buy-back promises are the hook in these schemes. Don't steer an owner toward signing.

moves.text: Those deals are legal now in New York, so it's safe as long as the company is registered.
moves.fb: Being lawful to offer doesn't make it safe. These deals are heavily regulated because of abuse.

say: They said the auction could be next month and I'll be on the street.
The man said I have maybe four weeks before the bank sells my house.

moves.text: New York foreclosure goes through court, with settlement conferences first. You do have time.
moves.fb: Accurate. NY is a judicial foreclosure state with mandatory settlement conferences for owner-occupied homes.

moves.text: That's just pressure talk. NY foreclosures take court time, with a conference first.
moves.fb: Correct. False urgency is part of the scam.
moves.react: "I thought it sounded too fast," {client} says.

moves.text: I don't know how long it takes. Let's ask an attorney before you decide anything at all.
moves.fb: Referring is right, but you can explain that NY foreclosure goes through court.

moves.text: They're probably right. Once the summons arrives, the auction is usually within 30 days.
moves.fb: False and harmful. NY judicial foreclosure is slow, with court steps before any sale.

moves.text: New York is a quick-sale state. The bank can auction the house without going to court.
moves.fb: Wrong. New York uses judicial foreclosure.

moves.text: Yes, but after the auction you get a year to buy back, so it's not as bad as it sounds.
moves.fb: New York has no statutory redemption period after the foreclosure sale.

say: My son says we should just let it go to auction and walk away clean.
My daughter thinks I should stop fighting and let the bank take it. Then it's over, right?

moves.text: It may not be clean. If it sells for less than you owe, the lender can seek a deficiency.
moves.fb: Correct. NY allows a deficiency judgment if the lender moves after the sale, credited with fair market value.

moves.text: An auction can leave a deficiency judgment. An attorney can explain that and the options.
moves.fb: Right. You flag the risk and refer to counsel.

moves.text: That's a family decision. I'd rather not weigh in on whether you should let the house go.
moves.fb: Respectful, but you can share the deficiency risk and refer to counsel.
moves.react: {client} sighs. "No one will tell me anything."

moves.text: Your son's right. Foreclosure wipes out all of the debt, so you'd owe nothing at all after.
moves.fb: Not necessarily. A deficiency judgment can follow the sale.

moves.text: Yes, and the auction brings full market value, so you'd get all of your equity back too.
moves.fb: Auctions often bring less than market value, and costs come out first.

moves.text: It's clean as long as you move out before the sale. Then the bank can't come after you.
moves.fb: Moving out doesn't stop a deficiency judgment.

say: If I sell it myself before the auction, can I keep what's left?
Could I just sell the house the normal way, even with the foreclosure going on?

moves.text: Yes. Until the sale, you can pay off the debt and keep the rest. Let's start with a CMA.
moves.fb: Right. The equitable right of redemption lasts until the foreclosure sale.
moves.react: {client} sits up. "I could keep my equity?"

moves.text: You can. Selling before the auction protects your equity. Your attorney can help with timing.
moves.fb: Correct. An owner can sell and pay off the loan any time before the sale.

moves.text: Maybe, but it's risky. Let's wait and see what the court says before we list anything.
moves.fb: Waiting can burn time the owner needs. Selling before the sale is a real option.

moves.text: Once you're in foreclosure you can't sell. The house belongs to the bank now, legally.
moves.fb: Wrong. The owner holds title and can sell until the foreclosure sale.

moves.text: You can sell, but the bank keeps all the proceeds, even anything over what you owe them.
moves.fb: Wrong. After the debt and costs are paid, the remaining equity is the owner's.

moves.text: Only if the bank approves a short sale. That's the only kind of sale allowed once you're in it.
moves.fb: A short sale is only needed if the price won't cover the debt. A regular sale is allowed.

say: Who should I call first? I don't even know where to start.
I'm overwhelmed. Who actually helps people like me?

moves.text: A free nonprofit housing counselor and a foreclosure attorney. I'll help find both.
moves.fb: Right. Housing counselors and attorneys are the proper referrals; the 90-day notice lists counselors too.

moves.text: Start with a housing counselor, then an attorney. The bank's 90-day notice lists some of them.
moves.fb: Correct. RPAPL 1304 notices list housing counseling agencies.

moves.text: Call your bank and ask what they suggest. They'll know what your options are, I'm sure.
moves.fb: The lender is one party, not an advocate. A counselor and attorney come first.

moves.text: Call {company} back and ask for more time. They seem to know the foreclosure process well.
moves.fb: Sending the owner back to the scammer is the worst referral possible.

moves.text: Call me. I'll handle negotiations with your lender myself, so you don't have to worry.
moves.fb: A salesperson isn't a loss mitigation professional or attorney. Refer to the right people.

moves.text: Nobody, really. Foreclosure's just paperwork. Ignore the summons and it all slows down.
moves.fb: Ignoring a summons can lead to a default judgment. Respond through counsel.
moves.react: {client} puts the summons in a drawer.

say: A distressed owner in {hood}? Let's buy it ourselves, cheap, before the auction. Win-win.
Tell {client} we'll pay cash, quick close. We flip it later. Everyone's happy.

moves.text: No. Buying from an owner in foreclosure falls under the Home Equity Theft Prevention Act.
moves.fb: Right. Equity purchases from owners in foreclosure are regulated by RPL 265-a, and we'd be advising this owner.

moves.text: Not from someone we're advising. {client} needs a market sale and a lawyer, not us.
moves.fb: Correct. Buying from a client you're advising puts your interests against the client's.

moves.text: Maybe, but only if we offer something close to what a CMA says it's worth on the market.
moves.fb: Better than a lowball, but the conflict and HETPA rules still make it a bad idea.

moves.text: Sure. As long as the owner signs willingly, there's nothing wrong with a fast cash offer.
moves.fb: Willingness doesn't cure the conflict, and equity purchase rules apply.

moves.text: Yes, and we don't need to say we're licensed, since we'd be buying as private people.
moves.fb: A licensee buying must disclose that status, and here the conflict is worse.

moves.text: Good idea. If we buy it, {client} saves the commission, so it's really a favor in the end.
moves.fb: Saving a commission doesn't offset buying the owner's equity cheap.

say: Can you call my lender and say you're my son? They won't talk to strangers.
Would you call the bank and pretend to be my nephew? They hang up on me.

moves.text: I can't pretend to be someone else. A counselor can help you authorize someone to call.
moves.fb: Right. Licensees must not misrepresent who they are. Written third-party authorization is the proper path.
moves.react: {client} nods. "I didn't know that was possible."

moves.text: No, but your housing counselor can get your written permission to talk with the lender.
moves.fb: Correct. You refuse the deception and offer the legitimate route.

moves.text: I'd rather not call them at all. Maybe your son can just call them for you himself.
moves.fb: No deception, but you could point to authorization through a counselor.

moves.text: Sure, I'll say I'm your son. It's harmless, and it'll get you some answers much faster.
moves.fb: Impersonating someone to a lender is misrepresentation and can cause real harm.

moves.text: Yes. Real estate agents can speak for owners in foreclosure without any written permission.
moves.fb: Wrong. Lenders need the borrower's authorization, and you're not the owner's representative here.

moves.text: I'll call and say I'm your attorney. Lenders take calls from attorneys much more seriously.
moves.fb: Claiming to be an attorney is a serious misrepresentation.

say: The man from {company} says he'll pay YOU $1,000 for every homeowner you send him. He asked me to pass that on.
{company} wants your number. They said agents who send them clients get paid well.

moves.text: Please tell him no. I won't take money to send homeowners to a deed-transfer company.
moves.fb: Right. Accepting pay to steer distressed owners would put your interests ahead of theirs.
moves.react: {client} nods. "That tells me what kind of people they are."

moves.text: I won't accept that. A payment like that would put his interests ahead of yours.
moves.fb: Correct. You refuse and use it to show the client why the offer is suspect.

moves.text: I'll think about it, but I'm not likely to call him back about that, honestly.
moves.fb: There's nothing to think about. Say no clearly.

moves.text: That's generous. I'll call him, but I'll only send people who really want to sell to them.
moves.fb: Taking referral money from a rescue company profits from steering vulnerable owners.

moves.text: Sure, as long as he pays it through my broker. Then it's a normal referral fee, all legal.
moves.fb: Routing it through the broker doesn't make steering owners to a scam acceptable.

moves.text: Okay, tell him yes. A referral to a buyer isn't a conflict, since I'm not your agent yet.
moves.fb: You're advising {client} now. Taking pay to steer this owner is a conflict regardless.

say: My neighbor says I should get a reverse mortgage. I'm 74. Would that fix this?
What about one of those reverse mortgages from TV? Could that stop the foreclosure?

moves.text: It may be an option at your age. HUD requires counseling first, so a counselor can explain it.
moves.fb: Right. HECM reverse mortgages are for owners 62+ and require HUD-approved counseling.

moves.text: Possibly. Owners 62 and up can qualify, and it must pay off the current loan. Ask a counselor.
moves.fb: Correct. A reverse mortgage pays off existing liens first, and counseling is required.

moves.text: I don't know much about those. You'd have to ask your bank whether you'd qualify for one.
moves.fb: Honest, but a HUD-approved counselor is the right referral.

moves.text: Yes, and reverse mortgages have no fees or interest, so it's basically free money for seniors.
moves.fb: Wrong. Reverse mortgages carry interest, fees, and insurance costs.

moves.text: No, you can't get one while you're in foreclosure. They're only for owners with no debt at all.
moves.fb: Wrong. Existing loans can be paid off with the reverse mortgage if equity allows.

moves.text: Yes, and you'd never have to pay property taxes or insurance again once you have one.
moves.fb: Wrong. Borrowers must keep paying taxes and insurance, or risk default.

roleplays.debrief: Deed-transfer rescue offers strip equity, and New York's Home Equity Theft Prevention Act (RPL 265-a) regulates them. New York foreclosure is judicial, with mandatory settlement conferences for owner-occupied homes, and the owner may sell or pay off the debt and keep the equity until the foreclosure sale. A sale for less than the debt can bring a deficiency judgment. Refer owners to housing counselors and attorneys, never misrepresent who you are, and never profit from steering distressed owners.

questions.q: In New York, the borrower's written promise to repay a mortgage debt is often called the:
c: Bond
Deed
Satisfaction
Estoppel
questions.x: The note, often called a bond in New York, is the promise to pay; the mortgage pledges the property. Satisfaction is the trap: it is the document showing the loan was paid off.

questions.q: Which document creates the borrower's personal obligation to repay?
c: The mortgage
The deed
The promissory note
The title policy
questions.x: The note is the debt; the mortgage is the security. The mortgage is the trap: it pledges the property but is not the promise to pay.

questions.q: A loan repaid with level payments that cover interest and gradually reduce principal to zero is:
c: Interest-only
Fully amortized
A balloon loan
Negatively amortized
questions.x: Full amortization pays the loan off by the end of the term. Balloon is the trap: it leaves a large final payment.

questions.q: Early in a 30-year fully amortized loan, most of each payment goes to:
c: Principal
Property taxes
Insurance
Interest
questions.x: Interest is charged on a large balance at first, so most of the payment is interest. Principal is the trap: the principal share grows later.

questions.q: A loan on which the borrower pays only interest, with the whole principal due at the end, is a:
c: Fully amortized loan
Graduated payment loan
Straight (term) loan
Reverse mortgage
questions.x: A straight loan is interest-only with principal due at maturity. Fully amortized is the trap: it pays principal throughout.

questions.q: A $200,000 interest-only loan at 6% for 5 years. How much principal is still owed when the term ends?
questions.x: Interest-only payments never reduce principal, so all $200,000 is due at the end. $0 is the trap: that would be true only for an amortized loan.

questions.q: A buyer pays 2 points on a $350,000 loan. How much is that?
questions.x: One point is 1% of the loan: 2 x $3,500 = $7,000. $3,500 is the trap: that is one point.

questions.q: Discount points are paid at closing in order to:
c: Pay the broker's commission
Lower the loan's interest rate
Cover the appraisal
Reduce the purchase price
questions.x: Points are prepaid interest that buy down the rate. The broker's commission is the trap: points go to the lender.

questions.q: Homeowners who itemize may deduct mortgage interest on acquisition debt up to:
questions.x: Current federal law limits the deduction to interest on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt. $1,000,000 is the trap: that was the limit for older loans.

questions.q: Which homeowner costs can be deducted, within federal limits, by those who itemize?
c: Principal payments
Homeowner's insurance
Mortgage interest and property taxes
Utility bills
questions.x: Interest and state and local property taxes, within limits, are deductible. Principal is the trap: repaying principal is not deductible.

questions.q: The time after a mortgage payment's due date during which it can be paid without a late charge is the:
c: Redemption period
Grace period
Lock-in period
Cooling-off period
questions.x: Paying within the grace period avoids a late charge. Redemption period is the trap: it is the time to reclaim property after a foreclosure sale.

questions.q: A payment due on the 1st is paid on the 10th, within the loan's grace period. The lender may:
c: Charge a late fee anyway
Start foreclosure
Raise the interest rate
Not charge a late fee
questions.x: Payments within the grace period are not late. Starting foreclosure is the trap: nothing is in default yet.

questions.q: A buyer takes title 'subject to' the seller's existing mortgage. If the loan later defaults, the buyer:
c: Is personally liable for the full debt
Becomes the new lender
Is not personally liable
Must pay the seller's taxes
questions.x: Buying subject to the mortgage leaves the seller personally liable; the buyer risks only losing the property. Personally liable is the trap: that happens when a buyer assumes the loan.

questions.q: How does buying 'subject to' a mortgage differ from assuming it?
c: The buyer takes no personal liability
The lender must release the seller
The interest rate resets
No payments are made
questions.x: In an assumption the buyer becomes personally liable; 'subject to' does not. 'Lender releases the seller' is the trap: that is a novation.

questions.q: A mortgage loan that is not insured or guaranteed by a government agency is:
c: FHA
VA
USDA
Conventional
questions.x: Conventional loans have no government insurance or guarantee. FHA is the trap: those loans are federally insured.

questions.q: A buyer gets a bank loan with private mortgage insurance and no government backing. The loan is:
c: FHA-insured
Conventional
VA-guaranteed
USDA-guaranteed
questions.x: Private mortgage insurance does not make a loan government-backed, so it stays conventional. FHA is the trap: PMI is private, not federal insurance.

questions.q: A loan whose interest rate and principal-and-interest payment stay the same for the whole term is a:
c: Fixed-rate mortgage
Adjustable-rate mortgage
Balloon mortgage
Graduated payment mortgage
questions.x: Fixed-rate loans keep the same rate and P&I payment. Graduated payment is the trap: its payments rise on a schedule.

questions.q: On a fixed-rate mortgage, which part of the monthly payment can still change?
c: The interest rate
The principal and interest
Escrowed taxes and insurance
The loan term
questions.x: Principal and interest stay fixed, but escrowed taxes and insurance can rise. The interest rate is the trap: it is fixed.

questions.q: A loan whose regular payments leave a large final payment at maturity is a:
c: Fully amortized mortgage
Balloon mortgage
Open-end mortgage
Package mortgage
questions.x: Balloon loans are only partly paid down by maturity. Package mortgage is the trap: it includes personal property in the security.

questions.q: Payments on a 7-year loan are set as if it were a 30-year loan. At year 7 the borrower owes:
c: Nothing more
One final normal payment
Only the last month's interest
A large balloon payment
questions.x: Paying on a 30-year schedule leaves most principal due in year 7. 'Nothing more' is the trap: the loan is not paid off.

questions.q: A seller takes back a mortgage from the buyer for part of the price. This is a:
c: Wraparound mortgage
Blanket mortgage
Purchase money mortgage
Reverse mortgage
questions.x: Seller financing for part of the price is a purchase money mortgage. Blanket is the trap: it covers more than one parcel.

questions.q: A purchase money mortgage is used to:
c: Finance buying the property
Refinance an existing loan
Borrow against home equity
Fund construction draws
questions.x: It finances the purchase itself, often from the seller. Home equity is the trap: that borrows against value already owned.

questions.q: Under a land contract, the buyer gets possession and pays in installments while:
c: The buyer gets the deed at once
A bank holds title
The county holds title
The seller keeps legal title
questions.x: The seller keeps legal title until the agreed payments are made. 'Deed at once' is the trap: that is a normal sale with a mortgage.

questions.q: In a land contract, the buyer (vendee) holds:
c: Legal title
Equitable title
No interest at all
A leasehold only
questions.x: The vendee has equitable title and possession; legal title stays with the seller. Legal title is the trap: it passes only when payments are done.

questions.q: A junior loan secured by an owner's equity and taken as a revolving line of credit is a:
c: HELOC
Purchase money mortgage
Reverse mortgage
Bridge loan
questions.x: A home equity line of credit lets the owner draw on equity. Reverse mortgage is the trap: it pays the owner and is repaid when they leave.

questions.q: A home equity loan usually sits in which position behind the first mortgage?
c: First position
Equal with the first
Junior (second) position
Ahead of property taxes
questions.x: Equity loans are junior liens. 'Ahead of property taxes' is the trap: taxes come first.

questions.q: A business sells its building to an investor and rents it back. This is a:
c: Ground lease
Sale-leaseback
Land contract
Net listing
questions.x: Sale-leaseback frees capital while keeping use of the property. Ground lease is the trap: it leases land only.

questions.q: The main benefit of a sale-leaseback to the original owner is:
c: Avoiding all rent
Keeping legal title
Lower property taxes for life
Freeing up capital while keeping use
questions.x: The seller gets cash and stays as tenant. Keeping title is the trap: title passes to the investor.

questions.q: When inflation rises, lenders generally:
c: Lower interest rates
Stop charging points
Raise interest rates
Extend all loan terms
questions.x: Inflation erodes the value of money repaid later, so lenders demand higher rates. Lowering rates is the trap.

questions.q: During high inflation, who gains on an existing fixed-rate loan?
c: The borrower
The lender
The appraiser
The title insurer
questions.x: The borrower repays with cheaper dollars at the old fixed rate. The lender is the trap: inflation works against fixed-rate lenders.

questions.q: A VA loan is:
c: Made directly by FHA
Insured by private insurers
Available to any first-time buyer
Partially guaranteed by Veterans Affairs
questions.x: Approved lenders make VA loans, partially guaranteed by the VA for eligible veterans. 'Any first-time buyer' is the trap: eligibility depends on service.

questions.q: A key feature of many VA loans is:
c: A 20% minimum down payment
No down payment required
Only adjustable rates
A 10-year maximum term
questions.x: VA loans often require no down payment. 20% down is the trap: that is a typical conventional benchmark to avoid PMI.

questions.q: Which agency guarantees or makes loans for low- and moderate-income buyers in eligible rural areas?
c: USDA Rural Housing Service
HUD's FHA
Veterans Affairs
Fannie Mae
questions.x: RHS, part of USDA, serves eligible rural buyers, often with no down payment. FHA is the trap: it insures loans everywhere, not just rural areas.

questions.q: A low-income buyer in an eligible rural county wants no down payment and has no military service. The best fit is:
c: A VA loan
A jumbo loan
A USDA/RHS loan
A balloon loan
questions.x: RHS loans target rural low- and moderate-income buyers. VA is the trap: it needs military eligibility.

questions.q: A home sells for $400,000 and appraises at $380,000. The buyer borrows $304,000. What is the LTV?
questions.x: LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal: $304,000 / $380,000 = 80%. 76% is the trap: dividing by the higher price.

questions.q: A lender's 90% LTV limit on a home priced at $500,000 that appraises at $480,000 allows a loan of up to:
questions.x: Use the lower value: 90% of $480,000 = $432,000. $450,000 is the trap: 90% of the price instead of the appraisal.

questions.q: A borrower earns $9,000 a month gross. Under a 28% housing ratio, the maximum monthly housing payment is:
questions.x: 28% x $9,000 = $2,520. $3,240 is the trap: that is the 36% total-debt limit.

questions.q: The classic conventional qualifying ratios are:
c: 28% housing and 36% total debt
31% housing and 43% total debt
25% housing and 33% total debt
36% housing and 28% total debt
questions.x: 28/36 are the classic conventional benchmarks. 31/43 is the trap: those are FHA's figures.

questions.q: The Truth in Lending Act is a title of which 1968 federal law?
c: RESPA
The Fair Housing Act
The Dodd-Frank Act
The Consumer Credit Protection Act
questions.x: Truth in Lending is Title I of the Consumer Credit Protection Act. RESPA is the trap: it governs settlement procedures.

questions.q: Which group of federal laws falls under the Consumer Credit Protection Act?
c: RESPA, TRID and HMDA
Truth in Lending, FCRA and ECOA
Fair Housing and ADA
FIRREA and the SAFE Act
questions.x: Truth in Lending, the Fair Credit Reporting Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act are its titles. RESPA is the trap: it is a separate law.

questions.q: Under Regulation Z, which phrase in a mortgage ad triggers full disclosure, including the APR?
c: "Only $15,000 down"
"Great financing available"
"Low rates"
"Easy terms"
questions.x: A specific down payment amount is a trigger term. 'Great financing available' is the trap: general statements trigger nothing.

questions.q: An ad states '360 monthly payments.' Under Reg Z the ad must also disclose:
c: The seller's name
The appraisal value
The down payment, repayment terms and APR
Nothing further
questions.x: The number of payments is a trigger term, so the full disclosures are required. 'Nothing further' is the trap.

questions.q: In a mortgage loan, the borrower is called the:
c: Mortgagee
Mortgagor
Trustee
Beneficiary
questions.x: The borrower gives the mortgage to the lender, so the borrower is the mortgagor. Mortgagee is the trap: it is the lender that receives the mortgage.

questions.q: The document that is the borrower's personal promise to repay the debt is the:
c: Note (bond)
Mortgage lien
Deed of trust
Loan commitment
questions.x: The note, called a bond in New York, is the promise to pay. The mortgage is the trap: it is the security instrument that creates the lien on the property.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a home for $520,000 with a loan of $416,000. The lender charges 2.5 points. How much are the points?
questions.x: Points are a percent of the loan: 2.5% x $416,000 = $10,400. $13,000 is the trap: it is 2.5% of the price, not the loan.

questions.q: A $240,000 loan at 5% annual interest has a monthly principal and interest payment of $1,288.37. How much of the first payment goes to principal?
questions.x: First month's interest = $240,000 x 0.05 / 12 = $1,000. Principal = $1,288.37 minus $1,000 = $288.37. $1,000 is the trap: that is the interest portion.

questions.q: New York is considered a lien theory state. This means:
c: The lender holds title until payoff
The lender holds a lien, not title
A trustee holds title for the lender
The lender may foreclose out of court
questions.x: In a lien theory state the borrower keeps title and the lender has a lien. Lender title is the trap: that describes title theory states. NY also requires judicial foreclosure.

questions.q: The clause that allows the lender to declare the entire loan balance due immediately when the borrower defaults is the:
c: Alienation clause
Defeasance clause
Acceleration clause
Subordination clause
questions.x: Acceleration lets the lender call the whole balance on default. Alienation is the trap: it is triggered by a sale or transfer, not a missed payment.

questions.q: A seller's loan has a due-on-sale clause. The buyer wants to take over the loan. Which is true?
c: The buyer may assume it without lender consent
The lender may call the loan on transfer
The clause covers FHA loans alone
The seller is released automatically
questions.x: A due-on-sale (alienation) clause lets the lender call the loan when the property is transferred, blocking an assumption without consent. Automatic release is the trap: the seller stays liable unless the lender agrees otherwise.

questions.q: A buyer assumes the seller's mortgage with the lender's approval, but the lender does not release the seller. If the buyer later defaults, the seller is:
c: Primarily liable
Fully released
Liable for the taxes
Secondarily liable
questions.x: In an assumption the buyer becomes primarily liable and the seller stays secondarily liable. Fully released is the trap: that requires a novation, which the lender did not grant.

questions.q: A NY foreclosure judgment is $460,000. The property sells at the referee's auction for $340,000, and the court finds fair market value is $390,000. The lender moves in time for a deficiency judgment. The maximum deficiency is:
questions.x: RPAPL 1371 credits the higher of sale price or fair market value: $460,000 minus $390,000 = $70,000. $120,000 is the trap: it ignores the fair market value credit.

questions.q: In New York, a lender seeking a deficiency judgment after a foreclosure sale moves for it within:
c: 30 days after default
90 days after the sale
1 year after the referee's sale
6 years after the sale
questions.x: RPAPL 1371 requires the motion within 90 days after the sale is completed by delivery of the referee's deed; otherwise the proceeds count as full satisfaction. 6 years is the trap: it is the general contract limitation period.

questions.q: A mortgagor's duties typically include each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Paying property taxes
Keeping the property insured
Keeping the property repaired
Paying the lender's taxes
questions.x: The borrower pays the debt, keeps the property in repair, insures it, and pays property taxes. Property taxes are the trap for careless readers: the borrower's property taxes are a duty, but the lender's own taxes are not.

questions.q: The document recorded to show that a mortgage has been paid in full and the lien removed is a:
c: Satisfaction of mortgage
Assignment of mortgage
Notice of pendency filing
Estoppel certificate
questions.x: A satisfaction (release) of mortgage is recorded when the loan is paid. Assignment is the trap: it transfers the mortgage to a new holder rather than ending it.

questions.q: Which statement about New York foreclosure is true?
c: Owners may redeem for 1 year after sale
Foreclosure is by power of sale
Equitable redemption ends at the sale
Deficiency judgments are barred
questions.x: NY owners may redeem by paying the debt until the sale, and there is no statutory redemption period after it. The 1-year choice is the trap: post-sale redemption exists in some states, not New York.

questions.q: A borrower's monthly principal and interest payment is $2,450. Annual property taxes are $9,600 and annual homeowner's insurance is $1,800. What is the monthly PITI?
questions.x: Taxes $9,600 / 12 = $800; insurance $1,800 / 12 = $150. $2,450 + $800 + $150 = $3,400. $3,250 is the trap: it leaves out the insurance.

questions.q: Under New York usury law, the civil usury ceiling for most loans to individuals is:
c: No ceiling applies
questions.x: NY civil usury is 16%. 25% is the trap: it is the criminal usury threshold.

questions.q: A buyer takes title subject to the seller's existing mortgage. The buyer stops paying and the property is foreclosed with a shortfall. The buyer's risk is limited to:
c: The full deficiency plus fees
The property and her equity
Half of the deficiency
The lender's legal fees
questions.x: Taking subject to means the buyer never promised to pay, so she can lose the property and equity but is not personally liable. The full deficiency is the trap: that falls on the seller, who signed the note.

questions.q: A loan on which the borrower pays interest during the term, with the entire principal due at the end, is a:
c: Fully amortized loan
Graduated payment loan
Reverse mortgage
Straight (term) loan
questions.x: A straight or term loan is interest-only, with the principal due at maturity. Fully amortized is the trap: it pays the balance to zero over the term.

questions.q: A loan that is neither insured nor guaranteed by a government agency is a:
c: Conventional loan
FHA-insured loan
VA-guaranteed loan
USDA rural loan
questions.x: Conventional loans carry no government insurance or guarantee, though they may carry private mortgage insurance. FHA is the trap for anyone who confuses PMI with government insurance.

questions.q: FHA loans are:
c: Made directly by HUD
Guaranteed by the VA
Insured by the FHA
Bought by Freddie Mac
questions.x: FHA insures loans made by approved lenders; it does not usually lend. VA guarantee is the trap: guarantees belong to VA loans, insurance to FHA loans.

questions.q: A buyer uses an FHA loan to buy a $380,000 house with the minimum down payment. How much is the down payment?
questions.x: FHA minimum down is 3.5%: 0.035 x $380,000 = $13,300. $11,400 is the trap: it is 3%, a conventional first-time-buyer figure.

questions.q: SONYMA, which helps many first-time homebuyers in New York with below-market-rate loans, is:
c: A private mortgage insurer
A federal agency within HUD
A New York State agency
A division of Fannie Mae
questions.x: SONYMA is the State of New York Mortgage Agency, a state public benefit corporation. The HUD choice is the trap: SONYMA is a state program, not federal.

questions.q: An ARM has an index of 4.1%, a margin of 2.5%, and a 2% periodic rate cap. The current rate is 4.25%. At the next adjustment, the new rate will be:
questions.x: The fully indexed rate is 4.1% + 2.5% = 6.6%, but the periodic cap limits the increase to 2 points: 4.25% + 2% = 6.25%. 6.6% is the trap: it ignores the cap.

questions.q: When an ARM's payment cap keeps the payment below the interest due, the unpaid interest is added to the balance. This is:
c: Amortization
A buydown
A balloon payment feature
Negative amortization
questions.x: Unpaid interest added to principal makes the balance grow: negative amortization. Balloon is the trap: a balloon is a large final payment, not a growing balance.

questions.q: A mortgage that covers both the real property and personal property such as appliances and furniture is a:
c: Blanket mortgage
Package mortgage
Wraparound mortgage
Open-end mortgage
questions.x: A package mortgage includes personal property. Blanket is the trap: it covers several parcels of real property.

questions.q: A seller with a 3% loan balance of $200,000 sells for $500,000. The buyer pays $50,000 down and the seller carries a new $450,000 loan at 6%, continuing to pay the original 3% loan from the buyer's payments. This is a:
c: Blanket mortgage
Bridge loan
Wraparound mortgage
Construction mortgage
questions.x: A wraparound is a junior loan that wraps the existing loan; the seller collects the larger payment and keeps paying the underlying loan. Bridge loan is the trap: it is short-term financing between buying and selling.

questions.q: In New York, a borrower's mortgage payment due on June 1 pays the interest for which period?
c: The month of June, paid in advance
The first half of June only
The month of May, paid in arrears
The 30 days ending on July 1
questions.x: Mortgage interest is paid in arrears: each payment covers the interest for the month just ended, so June 1 pays May's interest. The trap is assuming interest is paid ahead, like rent.

questions.q: Mortgage interest in New York is paid in arrears. This means each monthly payment:
c: Covers interest for the month just ended
Covers interest for the month ahead
Is applied to principal before any interest
Adds a late charge when paid after the 1st
questions.x: Paid in arrears means each payment covers the interest for the month that just ended. Paying interest for the month ahead is how rent works, which is the trap.

questions.q: On the purchase of a principal residence, discount points paid by the buyer are generally deductible:
c: Over the full life of the loan
When the home is later sold
In the tax year after closing
In the year they are paid
questions.x: Points paid to buy a principal residence are generally deductible in the year paid. Spreading them over the loan's life is the rule for a refinance, the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: As a rule of thumb, paying one discount point raises the lender's yield by about:
c: One full percent of the rate
1/8 of a percent
1/4 of a percent
1/2 of a percent
questions.x: Each point (1% of the loan amount) raises the lender's yield by roughly 1/8 of a percent. The trap is thinking one point equals a full percentage point of rate.

questions.q: Which statement about prepayment penalties on New York home loans is correct?
c: Every NY residential mortgage is required to include one
NY limits them on owner-occupied 1 to 6 family loans
They are charged when a payment arrives over 15 days late
They are capped at 16 percent, the civil usury ceiling
questions.x: NY limits prepayment penalties on 1 to 6 family owner-occupied loans, and most residential loans today have none. The 15-day rule belongs to late charges, a neighboring clause that is easy to mix up.

questions.q: A borrower pays off a mortgage early and the lender charges a fee for doing so. That fee is a:
c: Late charge
Defeasance fee
Acceleration charge
Prepayment penalty
questions.x: A prepayment penalty is a charge for paying off early. A late charge is for paying after the grace period, and acceleration is the lender calling the whole balance due on default.

questions.q: A bank sells a borrower's loan to an investor and records the transfer. The recorded document is called the:
c: Assignment of mortgage
Satisfaction of mortgage
Subordination agreement
Novation agreement
questions.x: An assignment of mortgage transfers the note and mortgage to a new holder and is recorded so the world knows who holds the lien. A satisfaction is recorded only when the loan is paid off.

questions.q: After a lender sells a borrower's loan to another holder, the borrower should:
c: Stop paying until a new note is signed
Pay off the balance within 90 days
Keep paying whoever services the loan
Have the new holder record a satisfaction
questions.x: Selling or assigning the loan does not change the borrower's obligation; the borrower keeps paying the servicer. A satisfaction is recorded only when the debt is paid, and no new note or payoff is required.

questions.q: An owner has a first mortgage recorded in 2019 and a HELOC recorded in 2022. She refinances the first mortgage. Which document keeps the new first mortgage ahead of the HELOC?
c: A release clause in the new first mortgage
An assignment of the HELOC to the new lender
A defeasance clause in the HELOC
A subordination agreement from the HELOC lender
questions.x: A subordination agreement lets the HELOC lender move behind the new loan, which would otherwise rank later because it records later. A release clause frees parcels under a blanket mortgage, a different tool.

questions.q: A first mortgage was recorded in March and a home equity loan in June. At a foreclosure sale that does not cover both debts:
c: Both lenders share the proceeds equally
The June lender is paid first as the newest
The March lender is paid in full first
The larger loan is paid first, whatever its date
questions.x: Priority follows recording: the senior (earlier recorded) lender is paid in full before the junior gets anything, which is why second mortgages and HELOCs carry higher rates. Sharing equally is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: New York is a race-notice state. Between two good-faith mortgages on the same property, which generally has priority?
c: The one signed first
The one recorded first
The one for the larger amount
The one held by a federally chartered bank
questions.x: Recording gives constructive notice and sets priority, so the first good-faith mortgage recorded generally comes first (after real property taxes). The signing date does not decide it, which is the most common trap.

questions.q: When a buyer finances a house in New York, which statement about recording the mortgage is correct?
c: The borrower pays NY's mortgage recording tax
The lender pays NY's mortgage recording tax
Recording is optional and gives no notice
It is filed with the Department of State
questions.x: The borrower pays the mortgage recording tax when the mortgage is recorded with the county clerk (City Register in NYC). Recording gives constructive notice; the Department of State does not record mortgages.

questions.q: A buyer finances a Manhattan co-op apartment. How does the lender secure the loan?
c: Files a UCC-1 on the shares and lease
Records a mortgage with the City Register
Records a deed of trust on the building
Takes a mortgage on the co-op's land
questions.x: A co-op buyer owns shares and a proprietary lease, not real property, so the lender takes a security interest under the UCC and files a UCC-1. No mortgage is recorded, so no mortgage recording tax applies.

questions.q: A co-op shareholder in Queens stops paying her share loan. How can the lender typically recover?
c: A judicial foreclosure under the RPAPL
A non-judicial UCC sale of the shares
A tax lien sale run by the city
A referee's sale ordered by a court
questions.x: Share loans are enforced under the UCC, so the lender can sell the shares in a non-judicial sale, much faster than a NY foreclosure. Judicial foreclosure and referee's sales apply to mortgages on real property.

questions.q: Before starting a foreclosure on a home loan in New York, the lender must first:
c: Record a satisfaction of mortgage
Hold a non-judicial power of sale auction
Send a 90-day pre-foreclosure notice
Wait 2 years after the first missed payment
questions.x: RPAPL 1304 requires a 90-day pre-foreclosure notice listing housing counselors before the lender sues. NY uses judicial foreclosure, so a power of sale auction without a court is the trap; 2 to 3 years is how long the process often takes, not a waiting period.

questions.q: Which best describes foreclosure of a home mortgage in New York?
c: Non-judicial: a trustee sells after notice
Strict: the lender takes title with no sale
Administrative: the Department of State rules
Judicial: the lender sues and a court controls it
questions.x: NY uses judicial foreclosure: the lender sues, files a lis pendens, and a court-appointed referee sells the property, often after 2 to 3 years. Non-judicial trustee sales are used in other states, not for NY mortgages.

questions.q: A buyer is sure she will sell within four years. Which loan most likely fits her best?
c: A 30-year fixed at a higher rate
A 7-year balloon on a 30-year schedule
A 5/1 ARM with a lower starting rate
A graduated payment mortgage
questions.x: An ARM can win when the borrower expects to sell before the first adjustment, because the starting rate is usually lower. A fixed rate wins for long stays; paying more for stability she will not use is the trap.

questions.q: On an adjustable-rate mortgage, payment shock occurs when:
c: The borrower can't afford the adjusted payment
The lender changes the margin at the first adjustment
The borrower prepays and triggers a penalty
The index falls below the starting rate
questions.x: Payment shock is a borrower qualified at the low starting rate who cannot afford the payment once the rate adjusts, which is why lenders must qualify ARM borrowers at a higher rate. The margin never changes, so that choice is the trap.

questions.q: A couple must close on a new house before their current house sells. Which loan solves this timing gap?
c: Wraparound mortgage
Takeout loan
Open-end mortgage
Bridge (swing) loan
questions.x: A bridge (swing) loan is short-term money to buy the new home before the old one sells. A takeout loan replaces a construction loan; it is the tempting wrong pick because it also sounds temporary.

questions.q: A bridge loan is best described as:
c: A junior loan wrapped around an older loan
Short-term financing until the old home sells
A permanent loan replacing a construction loan
A loan funded in draws as building progresses
questions.x: A bridge (swing) loan covers the gap when a buyer purchases before selling. A permanent loan replacing a construction loan is a takeout loan, and draws describe the construction loan itself.

questions.q: A borrower's mortgage lets her borrow more later, up to a set limit and without a new mortgage, to pay for a new roof. This loan is a:
c: Package mortgage
Open-end mortgage
Blanket mortgage
Wraparound mortgage
questions.x: An open-end mortgage allows future advances up to a limit under the same mortgage. A package mortgage adds personal property, and a blanket mortgage covers several parcels.

questions.q: An open-end mortgage differs from a standard mortgage because it:
c: Covers appliances and furniture too
Covers several parcels at once
Ends with a large balloon payment
Allows later advances up to a limit
questions.x: Open-end means the borrower can draw more money later, up to a limit, under the same mortgage. Covering appliances is a package mortgage, the most similar-sounding distractor.

questions.q: A buyer pledges a certificate of deposit as extra collateral so the lender will accept the loan with less risk. This is a:
c: Pledged account mortgage
Shared equity mortgage
Package mortgage
Temporary buydown
questions.x: In a pledged account loan the borrower's savings deposit is pledged as added collateral, lowering the lender's risk. In a shared equity loan an investor or lender gets part of the appreciation instead.

questions.q: A parent helps with the down payment in exchange for a share of the home's future appreciation. This arrangement is a:
c: Pledged account mortgage
Reverse annuity mortgage
Shared equity mortgage
Graduated payment mortgage
questions.x: Shared equity gives a lender or investor a slice of appreciation in exchange for a lower rate or down payment help. A pledged account uses the borrower's own deposit as collateral and shares no appreciation.

questions.q: A buyer in the NYC metro area needs a $1.5 million loan. Under 2026 limits, this loan is:
c: A conforming high-cost area loan
A loan Ginnie Mae is required to buy
An FHA loan by default
A jumbo (nonconforming) loan
questions.x: For 2026 the conforming limit is $832,750 for one unit and up to $1,249,125 in high-cost areas such as NYC. A $1.5 million loan exceeds both, so it is a jumbo and nonconforming. 'Conforming high-cost' is the trap, and Ginnie Mae buys no loans.

questions.q: A mortgage loan is called conforming when it:
c: Is insured by FHA or guaranteed by the VA
Has a rate that conforms to usury limits
Meets Fannie and Freddie standards
Exceeds the high-cost area loan limit
questions.x: Conforming loans meet Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac size and underwriting standards, so they can be sold to them. Government backing (FHA, VA) is a separate idea; those loans are pooled through Ginnie Mae.

questions.q: When underwriting a loan on an owner-occupied two-family house, how do lenders usually treat the expected rent from the second unit?
c: Count all of it once a lease is signed
Count part of it, often 75%, as income
Ignore it entirely as unverified income
Count it after two years of ownership
questions.x: Lenders count only part of expected rent (often 75%) to allow for vacancy and expenses. Counting all of it is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: Which property will usually get a lender's best loan terms?
c: An owner-occupied 1 to 4 family home
A 12-unit apartment building bought for rent
A vacant lot held for future building
A single-family home bought as a rental
questions.x: Owner-occupied 1 to 4 family homes get the best terms. Investment property, even a single-family rental, gets stricter terms, which is the trap for buyers who assume 'single-family' is enough.

questions.q: A lender denies a mortgage based on information in the applicant's credit report. Which law requires the lender to give the applicant notice of that?
c: Fair Credit Reporting Act
Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
Interstate Land Sales Act
questions.x: The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires accurate credit reports and notice when credit is denied based on a report. HMDA is about lenders reporting loan data, a similar-sounding trap.

questions.q: Which law is mainly concerned with the accuracy of consumer credit reports?
c: Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Fair Credit Reporting Act
Truth in Lending Act
Community Reinvestment Act
questions.x: FCRA governs credit reports: accuracy and notice of adverse action. ECOA bans discrimination in credit, the most tempting mix-up since both are titles of the Consumer Credit Protection Act.

questions.q: Under TRID rules, when must the lender deliver the Closing Disclosure?
c: Within 3 business days of application
At the closing table, before signing
At least 3 business days before closing
Within 10 days after the loan closes
questions.x: The Closing Disclosure must arrive at least 3 business days before closing. 'Within 3 business days of application' is the Loan Estimate deadline, the trap.

questions.q: A borrower applies for a purchase mortgage on Monday. Under TRID, the Loan Estimate is due:
c: At least 3 days before closing
Within 30 days of application
At closing, along with the deed
Within 3 business days of application
questions.x: The Loan Estimate is due within 3 business days of application. The 3 days before closing belongs to the Closing Disclosure, the other half of TRID.

questions.q: Which mortgage ad phrase, standing alone, does NOT require additional Regulation Z disclosures?
c: "Just 5% down"
"Only $1,850 a month"
"240 easy payments"
questions.x: General terms and the APR alone are not trigger terms. A down payment, a payment amount, or a number of payments each trigger full disclosure of the down payment, repayment terms and APR.

questions.q: A licensee's listing ad says "Easy financing available." Under Regulation Z, this ad:
c: Needs no further credit disclosures
Must state the APR and down payment
Must state the monthly payment amount
Must be approved by the lender first
questions.x: "Easy financing available" is a general statement, not a trigger term, so no further disclosures are needed. The rules kick in only when a specific term such as a payment, down payment or number of payments appears.

questions.q: Which statement about subprime and predatory loans is correct?
c: Every subprime loan is a predatory loan
Subprime loans are illegal in New York
Predatory loans go to top-credit borrowers
Most predatory loans are subprime ones
questions.x: Predatory lending clusters in subprime loans (weaker credit, higher rates), but not every subprime loan is predatory. NY regulates subprime loans under Banking Law 6-m rather than banning them.

questions.q: A subprime loan is one made to:
c: Buyers below the conforming loan limit
Borrowers with weaker credit, at higher rates
Veterans with no down payment
Borrowers whose rate is under the prime rate
questions.x: Subprime loans go to borrowers with weaker credit at higher rates. 'Under the prime rate' is a word trap: subprime describes the borrower's credit, not a cheaper rate.

questions.q: A seller agrees to hand the buyer $20,000 in cash outside closing, hidden from the lender. A licensee who knows of it should recognize:
c: A lawful seller concession
Mortgage fraud that can cost the license
A private deal outside the agent's duty
A valid credit if both attorneys agree
questions.x: A side payment hidden from the lender is mortgage fraud, and a licensee who knowingly takes part or stays silent risks revocation and criminal charges. A disclosed seller concession is lawful; hiding it is the problem.

questions.q: Each of the following is a warning sign of mortgage fraud EXCEPT:
c: An appraisal that matches the price exactly
A straw buyer who will not live there
A lender skipping any income check
A Closing Disclosure delivered on time
questions.x: Suspiciously matching appraisals, straw buyers, false occupancy and no-income-check loans are classic warning signs. A Closing Disclosure delivered on time is ordinary TRID compliance.

questions.q: Which federal law requires lenders to report lending data so discriminatory patterns can be spotted?
c: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
Truth in Lending Act
Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform Act
questions.x: HMDA requires lenders to report lending data so patterns such as redlining can be spotted. The Community Reinvestment Act is the close trap: it pushes banks to serve their whole community but is not the reporting law.

questions.q: Which 2010 federal law created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the ability-to-repay rule?
c: The Homeowners Protection Act
The Home Ownership and Equity Protection Act
The Dodd-Frank Act
The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
questions.x: Dodd-Frank (2010) created the CFPB and the ability-to-repay rule. HOEPA (1994) restricts high-cost loans, and the Homeowners Protection Act governs PMI cancellation.

questions.q: In a mortgage, the lender that receives the security interest is the:
c: Mortgagor
Grantor
Mortgagee
Beneficiary
questions.x: The lender receives the mortgage, so it is the mortgagee. Mortgagor is the trap: the borrower gives the mortgage.

questions.q: A borrower signs both a note and a mortgage. The mortgage:
c: Is the promise to repay
Transfers title to the lender
Sets the interest rate
Makes the property security
questions.x: The mortgage pledges the property as security for the debt. The promise to repay is the trap: that is the note (bond).

questions.q: A buyer pays $375,000 for a home with a $300,000 loan. The lender charges 1.75 points. The points cost:
questions.x: 1.75% x $300,000 = $5,250. $6,562.50 is the trap: it applies the points to the price instead of the loan.

questions.q: A $300,000 loan at 6% has a monthly principal and interest payment of $1,798.65. How much interest is in the first payment?
questions.x: $300,000 x 0.06 / 12 = $1,500. $18,000 is the trap: it is a full year of interest, not one month.

questions.q: Because New York is a lien theory state, during the loan the borrower:
c: Gives the lender legal title
Holds equitable title alone
Deeds title to a trustee
Keeps title to the property
questions.x: The borrower keeps title and the lender holds a lien. Giving the lender title is the trap: that is the title theory model.

questions.q: A borrower misses four payments, and the lender declares the whole balance due now. The lender is using the:
c: Acceleration clause
Alienation clause
Prepayment penalty clause
Escalation clause
questions.x: Calling the full balance on default is acceleration. Alienation is the trap: it is triggered by a transfer of the property, not missed payments.

questions.q: Which clause lets a lender block a buyer from assuming the seller's loan without consent?
c: Acceleration clause
Release clause
Alienation clause
Subordination clause
questions.x: The alienation (due-on-sale) clause lets the lender call the loan on transfer. Acceleration is the trap: the alienation clause works by triggering acceleration, but the transfer rule itself is alienation.

questions.q: A buyer assumes a loan and the lender formally releases the seller from liability. This release is a:
c: Subrogation
Novation
Subordination
Satisfaction
questions.x: A novation substitutes the buyer and releases the seller. Satisfaction is the trap: it means the loan was paid off, not transferred.

questions.q: A NY foreclosure judgment is $300,000. The property sells for $260,000, and the court finds fair market value is $240,000. The lender moves in time. The maximum deficiency is:
questions.x: The credit is the higher of sale price or fair market value, here the $260,000 sale price: $300,000 minus $260,000 = $40,000. $60,000 is the trap: it uses the lower value.

questions.q: A NY lender waits four months after the referee's deed is delivered to seek a deficiency judgment. The result:
c: The debt is treated as paid in full
It may still seek it within 6 years of the sale
It may seek it within 1 year
It may seek double the shortfall
questions.x: Missing the 90-day window means the sale proceeds are deemed full satisfaction. The 6-year choice is the trap: the contract limitation period does not extend the 90-day deficiency deadline.

questions.q: A mortgagor lets the hazard insurance on her house lapse while keeping payments current. This is most likely:
c: Allowed if payments are current
A matter for the lender to fix
A default under the mortgage
A violation of the note's rate
questions.x: Keeping the property insured is a borrower duty, so a lapse is a default. Current payments are the trap: payment is only one of several covenants.

questions.q: After the last payment on her loan, what should an owner make sure gets recorded?
c: A new deed back from the lender
A satisfaction of mortgage
An assignment of mortgage
A release of lis pendens
questions.x: Recording the satisfaction removes the lien from the record. The deed is the trap: in lien theory New York the owner already holds title, so no deed comes back.

questions.q: A New York borrower in foreclosure wants to keep her home by paying the debt. Her right to redeem lasts until:
c: 1 year after the sale
6 months after the sale
90 days after the sale
The foreclosure sale
questions.x: The equitable right of redemption ends at the foreclosure sale; NY has no post-sale statutory redemption. 90 days is the trap: that is the lender's deficiency deadline.

questions.q: Monthly principal and interest is $1,900. Annual taxes are $7,200 and annual insurance is $1,440. What is the monthly PITI?
A private lender charges a New York homeowner 27% interest. This rate exceeds:
c: Neither usury limit
The civil limit but not the criminal
Both the civil and criminal limits
The criminal limit, not the civil
questions.x: Civil usury is 16% and criminal usury is 25%, so 27% exceeds both. The civil-only choice is the trap: it forgets the 25% criminal line.

questions.q: A buyer takes title subject to the seller's mortgage instead of assuming it. Who is personally liable on the note?
c: The buyer alone
The seller, as before
Both equally
The lender's insurer
questions.x: Taking subject to adds no personal promise by the buyer, so the seller remains liable. The buyer is the trap: that would be an assumption.

questions.q: A borrower takes a 5-year, $200,000 loan paying interest each month, with the full $200,000 due at maturity. This is a:
c: Straight term loan
Fully amortized loan
Partially amortized loan
Reverse mortgage
questions.x: Interest-only payments with all principal at maturity is a straight term loan. Partially amortized is the trap: it pays down some principal before a balloon.

questions.q: Which loan is conventional?
c: An FHA loan with 3.5% down
A VA loan with no down payment
A USDA loan in a rural town
A bank loan with PMI
questions.x: A loan with private mortgage insurance and no government backing is conventional. FHA is the trap: its insurance comes from the government, so it is not conventional.

questions.q: If an FHA borrower defaults, what protects the lender against loss?
c: The VA guaranty
FHA mortgage insurance
Fannie Mae's reserve
Ginnie Mae's guarantee fund
questions.x: FHA insures the lender, funded by the borrower's MIP. Ginnie Mae is the trap: it guarantees payments to securities investors, not the lender's loss on a loan.

questions.q: A buyer makes the minimum FHA down payment of $14,000. What is the purchase price?
questions.x: $14,000 / 0.035 = $400,000. $280,000 is the trap: it divides by 5%, a conventional figure.

questions.q: A first-time buyer in Utica wants a below-market-rate loan program run by New York State. She should look into:
c: SONYMA
Ginnie Mae
Freddie Mac
The FHA
questions.x: SONYMA is the State of New York Mortgage Agency. FHA is the trap: it is a federal program, not New York's own.

questions.q: An ARM has an index of 3.0%, a margin of 2.75%, and a 1% periodic cap. The current rate is 5.5%. At the next adjustment, the new rate will be:
questions.x: The fully indexed rate is 3.0% + 2.75% = 5.75%, a 0.25-point increase that is within the 1% cap. 6.5% is the trap: the cap is a ceiling, not an automatic increase.

questions.q: Which situation causes negative amortization?
c: Payments exceed interest due
A balloon at maturity
A rate buydown in year 1
Payments below interest due
questions.x: When payments fall short of the interest, the unpaid interest is added to the balance. The balloon is the trap: it is a large final payment, not a growing balance.

questions.q: A buyer's loan covers the condo plus its furniture and appliances. This is a:
c: Package mortgage
Blanket mortgage
Open-end mortgage
Budget mortgage
questions.x: Real plus personal property in one loan is a package mortgage. Budget mortgage is the trap: it adds taxes and insurance to the payment, not furniture.

questions.q: In a wraparound mortgage, who keeps paying the original underlying loan?
c: The buyer, directly
The seller-lender
The new lender
The title company
questions.x: The seller collects the buyer's larger payment and keeps paying the original loan. The buyer is the trap: the buyer pays the seller, not the underlying lender.

questions.q: A blanket mortgage contains a partial release clause. This lets the developer:
c: Assume another buyer's loan
Prepay without a penalty
Free lots as each is paid
Subordinate to a new loan
questions.x: A partial release frees each lot from the lien as its release price is paid. Subordination is the trap: it changes lien priority rather than removing the lien.

questions.q: Which entity guarantees mortgage-backed securities made up of FHA and VA loans?
c: Fannie Mae
Ginnie Mae
Freddie Mac
Farmer Mac
questions.x: Ginnie Mae guarantees securities backed by government loans. Fannie Mae is the trap: it buys and securitizes conventional loans.

questions.q: Which is a secondary mortgage market transaction?
c: Fannie Mae buying a bank's loans
A bank lending to a homebuyer
A credit union funding a refinance
A mortgage banker closing a loan
questions.x: The secondary market buys and sells existing loans. The mortgage banker is the trap: closing a loan is origination, even if the banker sells it later.

questions.q: A home's original value was $500,000. The borrower may first request PMI cancellation when the balance reaches:
questions.x: Borrowers may request cancellation at 80%: 0.80 x $500,000 = $400,000. $390,000 is the trap: 78% is automatic termination.

questions.q: Which is true of a reverse mortgage?
c: The owner pays the lender monthly
The balance falls over time
The balance grows over time
Owners of any age qualify
questions.x: The lender pays the owner, so the balance grows until the owner sells, moves, or dies. Any age is the trap: the borrower has to be at least 62.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of a VA loan?
c: No down payment for eligible vets
Private mortgage insurance until 20% equity
Insurance from HUD
A 3.5% minimum down
questions.x: VA loans are guaranteed and often need no down payment. The 3.5% minimum is the trap: that is the FHA rule.

questions.q: A loan with a 6% note rate has a 2-1 buydown. The buyer's rate in year 2 is:
questions.x: A 2-1 buydown lowers the rate 2 points in year 1 (4%) and 1 point in year 2 (5%), then 6% thereafter. 4% is the trap: that is year 1.

questions.q: A builder's loan is paid out in draws as framing, roofing, and finishes are completed. This is a:
c: Swing (bridge) loan
Construction loan
Blanket loan
Package loan
questions.x: Draws tied to progress define a construction loan. Blanket is the trap: it covers several parcels but is not paid out in stages.

questions.q: In an adjustable-rate mortgage, which part changes with market conditions?
c: The margin
The lifetime cap
The index
The periodic cap
questions.x: The index moves with the market; the margin stays fixed. The margin is the trap: it is added to the index but never changes.

questions.concept: LTV on lower of price or appraisal
questions.q: The price is $400,000 and the appraisal is $420,000. The lender will lend 80% LTV. What is the maximum loan?
questions.x: LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal, here the price: 0.80 x $400,000 = $320,000. $336,000 is the trap: it uses the higher appraisal.

questions.q: A borrower earns $6,000 a month. Using a 28% front-end ratio, the maximum monthly PITI is:
questions.x: 28% x $6,000 = $1,680. $2,160 is the trap: it uses 36%, the back-end ratio.

questions.q: A buyer earns $8,000 a month and pays $1,500 a month on other debts. Using 28/36 ratios, the maximum PITI is:
questions.x: Front-end: 28% x $8,000 = $2,240. Back-end: 36% x $8,000 = $2,880 minus $1,500 = $1,380. The lower figure controls. $2,240 is the trap: it ignores the debts.

questions.q: A buyer's monthly PITI is $2,250 and gross monthly income is $7,500. The front-end ratio is:
questions.x: $2,250 / $7,500 = 0.30, or 30%. 28% is the trap: it is the common guideline, not this borrower's actual ratio.

questions.q: Regulation Z carries out which federal law?
c: Truth in Lending Act
RESPA
Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Fair Housing Act
questions.x: Regulation Z implements the Truth in Lending Act. ECOA is the trap: it is implemented by Regulation B.

questions.q: Which ad phrase can appear by itself without triggering further Regulation Z disclosures?
c: 10% down
6.5% APR
360 payments
$1,900 a month
questions.x: Stating the APR alone does not trigger more disclosure. The payment amount is the trap: it is a trigger term, like down payment and number of payments.

questions.q: A borrower closes a cash-out refinance on her Bronx home on Monday. Under TILA she may cancel:
c: Within 30 days
Until the first payment
Within 3 business days
Within 10 calendar days
questions.x: A refinance of a principal residence carries a 3-business-day right of rescission. 10 calendar days is the trap: it confuses rescission with other cooling-off periods.

questions.q: A loan has a 6.25% note rate and a 6.48% APR. The difference reflects:
c: Property taxes and insurance
The broker's sales commission
The appraised value
Points and certain fees
questions.x: APR folds points and certain finance charges into a yearly rate. Taxes and insurance are the trap: they are escrow items, not finance charges.

questions.q: Which practice is loan flipping?
c: Repeat refinances for new fees
Refusing loans by neighborhood race
Lowering the rate with a buydown
Letting unpaid interest build up
questions.x: Loan flipping is refinancing again and again to collect fees without benefit to the borrower. Refusing loans by area is the trap: that is redlining.

questions.q: A bank's loan officers are told to deny mortgages on any block in a mostly Black neighborhood. The bank is engaged in:
c: Steering
Redlining
Blockbusting
Panic peddling
questions.x: A lender refusing loans by an area's racial makeup is redlining. Blockbusting is the trap: it is inducing owners to sell by warning that protected groups are moving in.

questions.q: Banking Law 6-l protects New York borrowers from:
c: Usurious credit cards
Unlicensed mortgage originators
High-cost home loan abuses
Title insurance fraud
questions.x: Section 6-l restricts high-cost home loans, and 6-m covers subprime loans. Unlicensed originators are the trap: the SAFE Act and Banking Law Article 12-E handle licensing.

questions.q: Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, a lender may lawfully base a decision on:
c: The applicant's credit history
The applicant's marital status
The applicant's national origin
The applicant's age as a bar
questions.x: Credit history is a legitimate underwriting factor. Marital status is the trap: it sounds financial, but ECOA prohibits it as a basis for denial.

questions.q: A homeowner facing foreclosure is told, "Sign the deed over to us, we'll pay the bank, and you can rent it back." The main risk to the homeowner is:
c: Losing the right to a deficiency
A higher interest rate
A due-on-sale call
Losing her equity and title
questions.x: Equity-stripping schemes take title and the owner's equity, which NY's Home Equity Theft Prevention Act targets. The due-on-sale call is the trap: it is possible but is not the core harm.

questions.q: Which loan is exempt from Truth in Lending?
c: A refinance on a person's home
An LLC's warehouse loan
A home equity line for a family
A car loan to a consumer
questions.x: Business-purpose credit, such as an LLC's warehouse loan, is exempt. The car loan is the trap: TILA covers consumer credit generally, not just mortgages.

questions.q: A self-employed buyer started her business 8 months ago. A conventional lender will most likely:
c: Approve her on stated income
Count 12 months of projections
Want a longer income history
Average her best quarter
questions.x: Lenders generally want about 2 years of self-employment history shown on tax returns. Stated income is the trap: it was a pre-2008 practice.

questions.q: Which practice is a borrower protection rather than a sign of predatory lending?
c: Checking ability to repay
Packing fees into the loan
An unaffordable balloon
Steering to costlier loans
questions.x: Verifying ability to repay is a legal protection. Fee packing is the trap: rolling fees into the loan hides their cost and strips equity.

questions.q: A developer gets one loan covering 25 building lots and needs each lot released from the lien as it is sold. The loan should be a blanket mortgage with a:
c: Due-on-sale clause
Prepayment penalty clause
Acceleration clause
Release clause
questions.x: A release clause frees individual parcels from a blanket mortgage as each is paid for. Due-on-sale is the trap: it lets the lender call the loan on transfer, the opposite effect.

questions.q: Ginnie Mae (GNMA) is best described as:
c: Guarantor of FHA/VA-backed securities
A private company buying conventional loans
The agency that insures FHA loans
A primary market lender to buyers
questions.x: Ginnie Mae, inside HUD, guarantees timely payment on securities backed by FHA, VA, and USDA loans. Insuring FHA loans is the trap: FHA itself insures the loans.

questions.q: Which of the following is part of the primary mortgage market?
c: Fannie Mae buying a loan pool
An investor buying mortgage-backed bonds
Freddie Mac issuing securities
A savings bank lending to a homebuyer
questions.x: The primary market is where lenders make loans to borrowers. Fannie Mae is the trap: buying and pooling existing loans is the secondary market.

questions.q: A home's original value was $450,000. Under the Homeowners Protection Act, PMI on a conventional loan terminates automatically when the scheduled balance reaches:
questions.x: Automatic termination is at 78% of original value: 0.78 x $450,000 = $351,000. $360,000 is the trap: 80% is when the borrower may request cancellation.

questions.q: A loan in which an owner aged 62 or older receives payments from the lender based on home equity, repaid when the owner sells, moves, or dies, is a:
c: Reverse annuity mortgage
Graduated payment mortgage
Shared equity mortgage
Home equity line of credit
questions.x: In a reverse mortgage the lender pays the owner and the balance grows. Home equity line is the trap: it taps equity too, but the owner makes payments.

questions.q: Each of the following is true of VA loans EXCEPT:
c: They are guaranteed by the VA
Many borrowers put no money down
A funding fee is usually charged
PMI is required under 20% down
questions.x: VA loans carry no PMI; the guarantee and funding fee take its place. The funding fee is the trap: it is a real VA cost, so the statement is true.

questions.q: A builder pays the lender a lump sum at closing so the buyer's rate is 2% lower in year 1 and 1% lower in year 2. This is a:
c: Shared equity mortgage
Temporary buydown
Pledged account mortgage
Graduated payment mortgage
questions.x: Paying up front to lower the rate is a buydown; the 2-1 pattern makes it temporary. Graduated payment is the trap: payments rise on a schedule, but no one prepays a subsidy.

questions.q: A short-term loan funded in stages as work is completed, usually replaced by a permanent takeout loan, is a:
c: Construction loan
Swing (bridge) loan
Open-end loan
Balloon loan
questions.x: Construction loans are disbursed in draws as building progresses, then paid off by a permanent loan. Bridge loan is the trap: it covers the gap between buying one home and selling another.

questions.q: An adjustable-rate mortgage may include each of the following EXCEPT:
c: An index that moves with the market
A margin set at origination
A periodic and lifetime cap
A margin reset at each adjustment
questions.x: The margin is fixed for the life of the loan; the index is what moves. The index choice is the trap: a moving index is normal, a moving margin is not.

questions.concept: LTV on lower of price or appraisal
questions.q: The contract price is $600,000 and the appraisal is $585,000. The lender will lend 90% LTV. What is the maximum loan?
questions.x: LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal: 0.90 x $585,000 = $526,500. $540,000 is the trap: it applies 90% to the price.

questions.q: A borrower earns $84,000 a year. Using a 28% front-end ratio, the maximum monthly PITI is:
questions.x: Monthly income is $84,000 / 12 = $7,000; 28% x $7,000 = $1,960. $2,520 is the trap: it uses the 36% back-end ratio.

questions.q: A buyer earns $10,000 a month and has $1,100 in monthly car and student loan payments. Using 28/36 ratios, the maximum PITI the lender will allow is:
questions.x: Front-end: 28% x $10,000 = $2,800. Back-end: 36% x $10,000 = $3,600 minus $1,100 = $2,500. The lower figure controls. $2,800 is the trap: it ignores the other debts.

questions.q: A buyer's monthly PITI is $2,310 and gross monthly income is $8,250. The front-end ratio is:
questions.x: $2,310 / $8,250 = 0.28, or 28%. 36% is the trap: it is the usual back-end limit, not this borrower's ratio.

questions.q: The Truth in Lending Act is implemented by:
c: Regulation B
RESPA
Regulation Z
The Fair Credit Reporting Act
questions.x: Regulation Z implements TILA. Regulation B is the trap: it implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.

questions.q: A real estate ad says, "Buy this condo for $2,050 a month!" Under Regulation Z, the ad also has to disclose:
c: Nothing more, since the payment is accurate
The interest rate alone
The broker's commission
Down payment, repayment terms, and APR
questions.x: A payment amount is a trigger term, requiring the down payment, repayment terms, and APR. The interest rate alone is the trap: a triggered ad needs the full set, stated as an APR.

questions.q: Which transaction gives the borrower a 3-business-day right of rescission under Truth in Lending?
c: A purchase-money mortgage on a new home
A refinance of her principal residence
A loan to buy a strip mall
A loan to buy a vacation home
questions.x: Rescission applies to refinances and home equity loans secured by a principal residence. The purchase-money mortgage is the trap: it is excluded even though it is on a home.

questions.q: The APR on a mortgage is usually higher than the note rate because:
c: It adds points and certain fees
It adds property taxes and insurance
It is figured on the purchase price
It adds the broker's commission
questions.x: APR expresses the total cost of credit, including points and certain fees, as a yearly rate. Taxes and insurance are the trap: they are part of PITI, not finance charges.

questions.q: A lender repeatedly refinances a homeowner's loan, charging new points and fees each time without providing any real benefit. This is:
c: Redlining
A buydown
Negative amortization
Loan flipping
questions.x: Repeated refinancing for fees is loan flipping, a hallmark of predatory lending. Redlining is the trap: it is refusing to lend in an area because of its demographics.

questions.q: A lender refuses to make loans in a neighborhood because of the racial makeup of its residents. This is:
c: Steering
Blockbusting
Redlining
Loan flipping
questions.x: Redlining is a lender refusing to lend in an area based on its racial or ethnic makeup. Steering is the trap: it is a licensee directing buyers toward or away from areas.

questions.q: New York laws that restrict high-cost and subprime home loans, including limits on fees, flipping, and prepayment penalties, are found in:
c: Banking Law 6-l and 6-m
Real Property Law 443
General Obligations Law 5-703
The Interstate Land Sales Act
questions.x: Banking Law 6-l covers high-cost home loans and 6-m covers subprime home loans. RPL 443 is the trap: it is the agency disclosure law.

questions.q: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits lenders from discriminating on each of the following bases EXCEPT:
c: Marital status
Age
Receipt of public assistance
Credit history
questions.x: Credit history is a legitimate underwriting factor. Public assistance is the trap: it sounds like a risk factor, but ECOA bars discrimination because income comes from public assistance.

questions.q: A company tells a Queens homeowner facing foreclosure, "Deed the house to us, we'll pay off the bank, and you can rent it back." A licensee should recognize this as a likely:
c: A short sale
An equity-stripping rescue scam
