A reverse mortgage
A deed in lieu of foreclosure deal
questions.x: Rescue schemes that take the deed strip the owner's equity; NY's Home Equity Theft Prevention Act targets them. Deed in lieu is the trap: that deed goes to the lender, not a third-party company.

questions.q: Truth in Lending and Regulation Z apply to which of the following?
c: A loan to an LLC for an office building
A loan to a corporation for equipment
A mortgage to a person buying a home
A partnership loan for a shopping center
questions.x: TILA covers consumer credit to individuals, including home loans. The LLC loan is the trap: business and commercial credit is exempt even when real estate secures it.

questions.q: When evaluating a self-employed borrower, a lender will most likely require:
c: Two years of returns and statements
A verbal statement of income
A co-signer in every case
A signed statement of income without documents
questions.x: Self-employed income is verified with about 2 years of tax returns and business statements. The signed statement is the trap: stated-income loans were a pre-2008 practice now barred for most home loans.

questions.q: Each of the following is a common feature of predatory lending EXCEPT:
c: Fees packed into the loan amount
Balloons the borrower can't pay
Steering borrowers to costlier loans
Verifying the ability to repay
questions.x: Verifying ability to repay is a protection required by federal and NY law. Steering is the trap: here it means pushing qualified borrowers into costlier loans, a classic predatory practice.

questions.q: A buyer wants to take over a seller's existing FHA loan at its low rate. Which is required?
c: Nothing beyond the deed, since FHA loans are assumable by anyone who buys the home
A new FHA case number and a new appraisal at the current FHA mortgage insurance rate
The servicer's approval of his credit, plus funds for the gap
Proof that the buyer is a veteran, because FHA assumptions are reserved for VA-eligible buyers
questions.x: FHA loans are assumable, but most assumptions require a creditworthiness review by the servicer, and the buyer must cover the difference between the price and the balance. The trap is "nothing beyond the deed": assumable does not mean automatic. Veteran status is a VA eligibility rule, not an FHA assumption rule.

questions.q: Which pair of loans can typically be assumed by a qualified buyer with the lender's approval?
c: Conventional fixed and conventional ARM
FHA-insured and VA-guaranteed loans
Jumbo loans and home equity credit lines
Co-op share loans and bridge loans
questions.x: FHA and VA loans are assumable by creditworthy buyers. Most conventional loans, fixed or adjustable, carry a due-on-sale clause that lets the lender call the loan on transfer, which is the trap in the conventional pair. Home equity lines and share loans are tied to the original borrower.

questions.q: A buyer assumes a seller's mortgage with the lender's approval. Nothing else is signed. Three years later the buyer defaults and the foreclosure sale leaves a deficiency. The seller:
c: Owes nothing, because the lender approved the buyer when the loan was assumed
Owes nothing, because a buyer who assumes a loan is the one party liable on it
May be liable, but just in cases where the buyer took title subject to the loan instead of assuming it
May be liable for the deficiency, because there was no written release or novation
questions.x: On an assumption the buyer becomes primarily liable and the original borrower stays secondarily liable unless the lender releases the seller in writing (a novation). The trap is that lender approval of the buyer frees the seller: it does not. The subject-to answer reverses the rules; subject to leaves the seller liable too.

questions.q: A novation in a mortgage assumption:
c: Records the satisfaction of the old loan and replaces it with a new mortgage
Lets the new owner take title without becoming personally liable on the note
Moves the mortgage behind a later lien so the new owner can refinance first
Substitutes the new borrower and releases the original one
questions.x: A novation is the lender's agreement to substitute the buyer for the seller and release the seller. The trap is taking title without personal liability, which describes a sale subject to the mortgage. The third describes a subordination agreement, and the fourth describes a payoff and new loan.

questions.q: A borrower pays every mortgage installment on time but lets her property taxes go unpaid for a year. Her lender:
c: Has no claim against her, since default under the loan means missed installments
Has to notify the city and wait for the tax lien sale before it can act
May advance the taxes, add them to the debt, and treat the lapse as a default
May recover the taxes by suing the city, which holds a lien ahead of the bank
questions.x: Paying taxes is a duty of the mortgagor because a tax lien outranks the mortgage. The lender may protect its collateral by advancing the taxes and adding them to the loan, and the lapse is a default. The trap is "no claim", which reads default as missed payments only.

questions.q: A standard mortgage requires the borrower to do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Live in the property for the life of the loan
Pay the real property taxes and assessments
Keep the property insured against fire and other hazards
Keep the property in reasonable repair
questions.x: The mortgagor's duties are to pay the debt, pay taxes and assessments, insure the property, and keep it in good repair (no waste). Owner-occupancy is usually promised only for a period after closing on owner-occupied loans, not for the whole loan term. Insurance is the most commonly forgotten true duty, which makes it the tempting wrong pick.

questions.q: A payoff letter shows principal of $250,000 after the May 1 payment, per diem interest of $41.10, and a $75 recording fee. The loan is paid off on May 21, with 20 days of interest owed. What is the payoff?
questions.x: Interest = 20 x $41.10 = $822.00. Payoff = $250,000 + $822 + $75 = $250,897.00. Interest is paid in arrears, so the May 1 payment covered April and May's interest is still owed. The trap is $250,822.00, which forgets the recording fee.

questions.q: A loan has a balance of $360,000 at 6% interest. Using a 365-day year, the per diem interest is closest to:
questions.x: Annual interest = $360,000 x 0.06 = $21,600. Divided by 365 = $59.18 a day. The trap is $60.00, which divides by a 360-day banker's year; the question set a 365-day year. $1,800.00 is a full month of interest.

questions.q: A Queens buyer is borrowing $700,000. The seller's lender agrees to assign the seller's $300,000 mortgage to the buyer's lender in a CEMA. The buyer pays mortgage recording tax on:
c: $700,000, since every NYC purchase loan is taxed in full when it is recorded
Nothing, because a consolidated mortgage counts as a refinance
$300,000, the assigned balance, since the old mortgage is the one re-recorded
$400,000, the new money secured by the gap mortgage
questions.x: In a CEMA the existing mortgage is assigned, not satisfied, and the tax already paid on it is not charged again. The buyer pays tax only on the $400,000 of new money. The trap is $700,000, the result without a CEMA. Refinances in NY are taxed on new money too, not exempt.

questions.q: In New York, the main purpose of a Consolidation, Extension and Modification Agreement (CEMA) is to:
c: Avoid paying mortgage recording tax again on debt that was already taxed
Let the seller avoid the NYS transfer tax on a sale with seller financing
Let a co-op buyer record a mortgage instead of filing a UCC-1 statement
Extend a foreclosure timeline while the borrower applies for a modification
questions.x: A CEMA assigns an existing mortgage and consolidates it with new money, so the borrower pays recording tax only on the new principal. The trap is the transfer tax answer: transfer tax is a separate seller's tax on the deed. Co-op share loans are not recorded mortgages at all.

questions.q: Under New York law, after a residential mortgage is paid in full, the lender must arrange for the satisfaction to be recorded within:
c: 10 business days
60 days
30 days
90 days
questions.x: RPL 275 and RPAPL 1921 set 30 days. A lender that makes five or more mortgage loans a year owes the borrower $500 if it misses that deadline, $1,000 after 60 days, and $1,500 after 90. The trap is 60 or 90 days, which are the later penalty steps, not the deadline.

questions.q: A bank was paid off 65 days ago and still has not presented the satisfaction for recording. The owner is selling again. What does the bank owe the owner under New York law?
c: Nothing yet
questions.x: The lender owes $500 after 30 days, $1,000 after 60 days, and $1,500 after 90 days (for lenders making five or more loans a year). At 65 days it is $1,000. The trap is $500, the amount for missing only the first deadline.

questions.q: A sole proprietor's tax returns show net profit of $66,000 and $72,000 for the last two years, on gross receipts of $150,000 and $160,000. The lender averages two years of net profit. Monthly qualifying income is:
questions.x: ($66,000 + $72,000) / 2 = $69,000 a year, or $5,750 a month. The trap is $6,000, the most recent year alone; averaging is the usual method when income is stable or rising. $12,917 uses gross receipts, which ignores business expenses.

questions.q: For a self-employed borrower, lenders generally verify income using:
c: Business bank deposits for the most recent twelve months
The borrower's signed statement of gross annual receipts
A letter from the borrower's accountant estimating next year
Two years of tax returns showing net income after expenses
questions.x: Underwriters rely on tax returns, usually two years, and use net income after business expenses. The trap is bank deposits: deposits show cash flow, not profit, and they are not verified income. Stated income loans helped cause the 2008 crisis and are not standard today.

questions.q: A buyer of an owner-occupied three-family will rent two units for $1,800 each. If the lender counts 75% of rent, how much monthly rental income is counted?
questions.x: Total rent = 2 x $1,800 = $3,600. 75% of $3,600 = $2,700. The trap is $1,350, which takes 75% of one unit only. Counting $3,600 in full ignores the vacancy and expense cushion lenders build in.

questions.q: Why do lenders typically count only about 75% of documented rent when qualifying a borrower?
c: Because federal law caps rental income for owner-occupants
Because 25% of rent is withheld for income taxes
To allow for vacancy, repairs, and collection losses
To offset the borrower's higher homeowners premium
questions.x: The discount is a cushion for vacancies, maintenance and rent that is never collected. The trap is the tax answer: income tax is not deducted in qualifying ratios, which use gross income. No federal law caps rental income for owner-occupants.

questions.q: A buyer earns $10,000 a month. Proposed PITI is $2,600 and other debts are $700. She also co-signed her sister's $450 car loan, which the sister pays, but there is no documentation of that. Using 36%, the buyer:
c: Fails at 37.5%, because the co-signed loan counts
Passes at 33%, since the co-signed loan is excluded
Passes at 26%, since the back-end uses PITI alone
Fails at 30.5%, because co-signed debt is doubled
questions.x: A co-signer is fully liable, so without proof that the sister pays, the loan counts: $2,600 + $700 + $450 = $3,750, which is 37.5% of $10,000. The trap is 33%, which excludes the co-signed loan without the documentation a lender would need. PITI alone is the front-end ratio.

questions.q: Which monthly item is usually left OUT of a borrower's back-end (total debt) ratio?
c: A car loan the borrower co-signed for a relative
The borrower's utility and phone bills
Court-ordered child support the borrower pays
The minimum payment on the borrower's credit cards
questions.x: The back-end ratio counts housing plus recurring debt obligations: installment loans, card minimums, support payments, and co-signed loans. Ordinary living expenses such as utilities and phone bills are not debts and are left out. The trap is the co-signed loan, which many borrowers assume does not count.

questions.concept: LTV uses lower of price or appraisal
questions.q: A buyer contracts to pay $540,000. The appraisal is $520,000. The lender lends up to 95% LTV. The maximum loan is:
questions.x: LTV is based on the lower of price or appraised value: 0.95 x $520,000 = $494,000. The trap is $513,000, which applies 95% to the contract price. $27,000 is the down payment on the contract price, not a loan amount.

questions.concept: LTV uses lower of price or appraisal
questions.q: A home appraises for $15,000 more than the contract price. For LTV purposes, the lender uses:
c: The appraised value, because it shows more equity
The assessed value shown on the property tax bill
The average of the contract price and the appraisal
The contract price, because it is the lower figure
questions.x: Lenders use the lower of price or appraised value, which here is the contract price. The trap is using the higher appraisal: a buyer does not get instant equity to borrow against just because the appraisal ran high. Assessed value is a tax figure, not a market value.

questions.q: A buyer's parents give $40,000 toward the down payment. The lender will most likely require:
c: A signed gift letter stating no repayment is expected
A recorded second mortgage in favor of the parents
Proof that the parents filed a federal gift tax return
A co-signature from both parents on the promissory note
questions.x: A gift letter, with proof of the transfer, confirms the money is a gift and not a hidden loan that would add a monthly payment. The trap is the second mortgage: that would make it a loan, the opposite of a gift. The donor's gift tax filing is not part of the borrower's file.

questions.q: A borrower's uncle lends him $20,000 for the down payment, to be repaid at $500 a month, and they call it a gift on the loan application. This is:
c: Acceptable, because family transfers are treated as gifts
Acceptable if the uncle signs a gift letter before closing
Mortgage fraud, since it hides a debt
A RESPA kickback, because the uncle profits from the loan
questions.x: Calling a loan a gift hides a $500 monthly obligation from the back-end ratio. Signing a false gift letter makes it worse, not better. That is a material misstatement and mortgage fraud. The trap is the gift letter answer: a gift letter only works when it is true. RESPA kickbacks involve settlement service referrals.

questions.q: A loan officer tells a married applicant that her part-time income will be ignored because she 'may decide to stay home with the kids.' This violates:
c: The Truth in Lending Act, because the APR will change
RESPA, because it affects the settlement costs disclosed
ECOA and NY Executive Law 296-a
No law, if part-time income is ignored for every applicant
questions.x: ECOA and New York's Executive Law 296-a bar discounting income because of sex, marital status, or childbearing potential. The trap is the uniform-policy answer: a lender may evaluate whether part-time income is stable, but not on the assumption that a mother will quit. TILA and RESPA are disclosure laws.

questions.q: Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, a lender may NOT deny credit because the applicant:
c: Receives part of her income from public assistance
Has a back-end ratio well above the lender's limit
Has a recent history of late payments on credit cards
Cannot document the source of a large deposit
questions.x: Receipt of public assistance income is a protected basis under ECOA, along with race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status and age. A lender can weigh whether any income is stable, but cannot reject it because it is public assistance. The other choices are ordinary underwriting reasons. The trap is the late-payment history, which is a lawful credit factor.

questions.q: An eligible veteran buys a $350,000 home with no down payment, using the VA benefit for the first time. With a 2.15% funding fee, the fee is:
questions.x: 2.15% x $350,000 = $7,525. The trap is $11,550, the 3.3% rate for a subsequent use of the benefit. $6,125 is the FHA 1.75% upfront premium on the same amount. The fee can be financed and is waived for veterans receiving service-connected disability compensation.

questions.q: A veteran who receives compensation for a service-connected disability buys a home with a VA loan. The VA funding fee:
c: Is charged at a reduced rate of half the usual fee
Is paid by the seller as a required concession
Is replaced by a monthly mortgage insurance premium
Is waived for veterans with that compensation
questions.x: Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability are exempt from the funding fee. The trap is replacing it with monthly insurance: VA loans carry no monthly mortgage insurance at all. Sellers may contribute to costs, but they are not required to pay the fee.

questions.q: A first-time buyer purchases a $410,000 home with a SONYMA loan. The Down Payment Assistance Loan is the greater of $3,000 or 3% of the price, up to $15,000. She can receive:
questions.x: 3% x $410,000 = $12,300, which is more than $3,000 and less than the $15,000 cap. The trap is $15,000, the maximum, which applies only at prices of $500,000 or more. $20,500 is 5% of the price.

questions.q: A buyer received a $9,000 SONYMA DPAL, forgiven at 1/120 per month over 10 years. If he sells after 5 years (60 months), how much must he repay?
questions.x: After 60 of 120 months, half is forgiven: 60/120 x $9,000 = $4,500 remains. The trap is $9,000, which assumes nothing is forgiven until the full 10 years pass. Full forgiveness, $0, comes only at 10 years.

questions.q: Eligibility for a USDA Rural Housing Service guaranteed home loan depends mainly on:
c: The buyer's farm income and acreage
The property's location and household income
First-time buyer status and a 640 score
Military service and a certificate of eligibility
questions.x: USDA guaranteed loans serve low and moderate income households buying in eligible rural areas, judged by a USDA map and county income limits. The trap is farm income: the program has nothing to do with farming. Military service and a certificate of eligibility describe VA loans.

questions.q: All of the following are features of USDA guaranteed home loans EXCEPT:
c: Financing up to 100% of the value
A requirement that the buyer be a farmer
An upfront and an annual guarantee fee
Income limits based on county and household
questions.x: USDA guaranteed loans can finance up to 100% of value, charge a 1% upfront and 0.35% annual fee, and apply county income limits. There is no farming requirement, which is the common myth. The fee answer is the most tempting wrong pick, because many people assume no-down-payment programs have no fees.

questions.q: A borrower takes a 30-year FHA loan with 3.5% down. Five years later her balance is below 78% of the original value. Her annual MIP:
c: Ends automatically now under the Homeowners Protection Act
Ends after 11 years, because she has paid it for five
Ends when she requests it in writing at 80% of value
Continues for the life of the loan unless she refinances
questions.x: On current FHA loans with less than 10% down, annual MIP lasts for the life of the loan. The Homeowners Protection Act's 80% and 78% rules apply to PMI on conventional loans, which is the trap. The 11-year rule applies only when the borrower put at least 10% down.

questions.q: A buyer's FHA base loan is $250,000. With an upfront MIP of 1.75%, the upfront premium is:
questions.x: 1.75% x $250,000 = $4,375, usually financed into the loan. The trap is $8,750, which is 3.5%, the minimum FHA down payment rate, not the premium. $1,375 is 0.55%, the annual MIP rate on many FHA loans.

questions.q: A lender closes an FHA loan and pools it with others into a mortgage-backed security. Which entity guarantees investors timely payment on that security?
c: Fannie Mae
Freddie Mac
Ginnie Mae
SONYMA
questions.x: Ginnie Mae, a government corporation within HUD, guarantees securities backed by FHA, VA and USDA loans. It does not buy loans. The trap is Fannie Mae, which buys mostly conventional conforming loans and issues its own securities.

questions.q: Why does selling loans in the secondary market matter to a buyer applying at a local bank?
c: It moves the borrower's loan terms to whatever the new investor sets
It lets the bank avoid underwriting rules on the loans it plans to sell
It lets the bank lend again with the cash it receives from investors
It guarantees that the bank keeps servicing every loan it originates
questions.x: Selling loans replenishes the lender's cash so it can keep lending, which keeps mortgage money available. The trap is avoiding underwriting: loans sold to Fannie, Freddie or into Ginnie securities must meet their standards. A sale does not change the note's terms.

questions.q: A 70-year-old owner with a reverse mortgage stops paying property taxes. What is the likely result?
c: A default that can lead to foreclosure if the taxes are not paid
Nothing, since a reverse mortgage requires no payments while she lives there
The lender adds the taxes to the balance and the loan stays in good standing
The heirs become personally liable for the taxes after her death
questions.x: Reverse mortgage borrowers owe no monthly loan payments but must pay taxes, insurance and maintain the home. Unpaid taxes are a default that can lead to foreclosure. The trap is the no-payments answer, which confuses loan payments with property charges. Reverse mortgages are non-recourse, so heirs are not personally liable.

questions.q: To get an FHA-insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage, the borrower must:
c: Be at least 55 and have paid off at least half of the existing loan
Be retired and give the lender title to the home at closing
Be at least 65 and show income enough to make monthly payments
Be 62 or older and complete HUD-approved counseling
questions.x: HECM borrowers must be 62 or older and attend counseling with a HUD-approved counselor. The owner keeps title. The trap is 55, an age used for some senior housing rules, not reverse mortgages. Monthly payments are not required.

questions.q: A title agent gives a salesperson concert tickets each time one of her buyers closes through the agency. This is:
c: Permitted, since tickets are not cash and RESPA reaches money payments
A violation of Regulation Z, since the gift is part of the finance charge
Permitted if the salesperson's broker approves the gift in writing
A RESPA Section 8 violation for giving a thing of value for referrals
questions.x: Section 8 bars any fee, kickback, or thing of value given for referring settlement service business. Tickets tied to closings are a thing of value for referrals. The trap is the cash-only reading: RESPA covers gifts, trips, and paid expenses too. Broker approval does not make it legal.

questions.q: Which payment is generally permitted under RESPA Section 8?
c: A lender paying an agent $200 per closed referral
A title agency paying an agent's office rent below market
A broker's split of a commission with a cooperating broker
An inspector paying an agent a share of each inspection fee
questions.x: Payments between real estate brokers for actual brokerage services, such as cooperative commission splits, are permitted. The others are things of value tied to referrals. The trap is the below-market rent, which looks like an ordinary business deal but transfers value for referrals.

questions.q: A brokerage owns part of a mortgage company. To refer buyers there lawfully, the brokerage must:
c: Disclose it in writing and leave the buyer free to choose
Require its buyers to use the affiliate so the referral is consistent
Receive a flat fee for each referral in place of ownership profits
Get approval from HUD before making each individual referral
questions.x: An affiliated business arrangement is lawful with written disclosure at or before referral, no requirement to use the affiliate, and only a return on ownership as compensation. The trap is requiring use, which is exactly what makes an affiliate referral illegal. Per-referral fees are kickbacks.

questions.q: A lawful affiliated business arrangement under RESPA requires all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A written disclosure of the ownership interest
Payment to the referrer for each closed referral
Freedom for the consumer to use another provider instead
Disclosure of the affiliate's estimated charges
questions.x: The conditions are written disclosure of the relationship and estimated charges, no required use, and compensation limited to a return on ownership. A per-referral payment is the opposite of what is allowed. The trap is estimated charges, which many forget are part of the required disclosure.

questions.q: The Loan Estimate lists $1,500 for third-party services in the 10% tolerance group. The Closing Disclosure shows $1,740. The lender must refund:
questions.x: Allowed: $1,500 x 110% = $1,650. Actual $1,740 minus $1,650 = $90 cure. The trap is $240, the entire increase; the 10% group allows up to 10% before any refund is owed. Zero-tolerance items would require refunding every dollar of increase.

questions.q: Under TRID, which charge is a zero-tolerance item that cannot increase from the Loan Estimate without a valid changed circumstance?
c: Recording fees for the deed and mortgage
Prepaid interest from closing to month-end
Homeowners insurance the buyer shops for
The lender's origination charge
questions.x: Lender charges, like origination fees, are zero tolerance. Recording fees fall in the 10% aggregate group, which is the tempting wrong answer. Insurance the buyer chooses and prepaid interest can change without limit.

questions.q: A closing is set for Friday. There are no holidays that week. The latest day the borrower can receive the Closing Disclosure is:
c: Tuesday
Monday
Wednesday
Thursday
questions.x: The CD must be received at least 3 business days before consummation; Saturdays count, Sundays and federal holidays do not. Received Tuesday, the days are Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday. The trap is Wednesday, which leaves only two business days before Friday's closing.

questions.q: Which change after the Closing Disclosure is issued requires a new 3-business-day waiting period?
c: A seller credit for repairs added at the walk-through
A small increase in the title company's recording fees
A switch from a fixed-rate loan to an ARM
A change of closing time from morning to afternoon
questions.x: A change in loan product, an APR that becomes inaccurate, or an added prepayment penalty restarts the 3-day clock. A seller credit changes the cash to close and requires a corrected CD but no new wait, which makes it the most tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: Which borrower has a 3-business-day right to rescind under Regulation Z?
c: A buyer taking a purchase loan on her new home
An investor refinancing a rental four-family
An owner refinancing his principal residence
A company borrowing against its warehouse
questions.x: Rescission applies to credit secured by the borrower's principal residence, such as refinances and home equity loans, but not to the loan used to buy the home. The trap is the purchase loan. Business and investment loans are outside TILA's consumer coverage.

questions.q: An owner signs a home equity loan on her principal residence on a Thursday. There are no holidays. The rescission period ends at midnight on:
c: Monday
Sunday
Saturday
Tuesday
questions.x: For rescission, business days include Saturdays but not Sundays or federal holidays. Day one is Friday, day two Saturday, and day three Monday, so it ends at midnight Monday. The trap is Sunday, which wrongly counts a Sunday as a business day. Funds cannot be disbursed until it ends.

questions.q: Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, after a completed loan application is denied, the lender must notify the applicant within:
c: 10 days
90 days
60 days
30 days
questions.x: Regulation B requires notice within 30 days after a completed application, with specific reasons or a statement of the right to request them. The trap is 60 days, the time an applicant has to request the reasons after a notice that does not state them.

questions.q: A lender denies a loan and tells the applicant only, 'You did not meet our internal standards.' This notice is:
c: Sufficient, since lenders may keep their underwriting criteria private
Insufficient, because the reasons given must be specific
Sufficient, if the lender also refunds the application fee
Insufficient, because the lender must offer a lower loan amount
questions.x: An adverse action notice must state specific principal reasons, such as insufficient income or excessive obligations, or tell the applicant how to get them. 'Internal standards' is too vague. The trap is the confidentiality answer. Lenders are not required to counteroffer a smaller loan.

questions.q: A broker refinances a homeowner three times in four years. Each loan has a similar rate and payment, but new points and fees, and the balance grows each time. This is:
c: Equity stripping through a sale-leaseback
Negative amortization on a graduated loan
Loan flipping
Lawful refinancing on request
questions.x: Repeated refinancing that produces fees for the broker without a net benefit to the borrower is loan flipping. The growing balance comes from financed fees, not from unpaid interest, so it is not negative amortization, the tempting wrong answer. No deed changed hands, so it is not a sale-leaseback.

questions.q: Which refinance is LEAST likely to be loan flipping?
c: A refinance that cuts the rate a full point at modest cost
A refinance that adds points and fees but leaves the payment unchanged
A third refinance in two years that pays off the prior loan's penalty
A refinance pitched to an elderly owner with a small cash-out check
questions.x: Flipping is defined by the lack of a tangible net benefit. A meaningful rate reduction with reasonable costs is a real benefit. The trap is the cash-out check: small checks are a common lure in flipping schemes because they make a costly loan feel like a gain.

questions.q: A New York lender makes a home loan to an individual at 18% interest. The loan is:
c: Lawful, since TILA permits any disclosed rate
Above the civil usury limit of 16%
Criminally usurious, since it is above 15%
Lawful, because the limit is 25% for homes
questions.x: New York's civil usury ceiling is 16%; criminal usury applies above 25%. At 18% the loan exceeds the civil cap. The trap is the 25% answer, which confuses the criminal threshold with the civil limit. TILA requires disclosure but does not override state usury law.

questions.q: In New York, charging interest above what rate is criminal usury?
questions.x: Criminal usury in New York begins above 25%. The civil usury ceiling is 16%, which is the tempting wrong answer. A usurious loan to an individual can be void.

questions.q: An owner in foreclosure signs a contract selling her home to a company that promises to rent it back and resell it to her later. Under New York's Home Equity Theft Prevention Act, she may cancel:
c: Until midnight of the 3rd business day after signing
Within 30 days, if she repays the company's costs
At any time before the deed is recorded with the clerk
Until midnight of the 14th business day after signing
questions.x: RPL 265-a gives an equity seller the right to cancel a covered contract until midnight of the 14th business day after signing. The trap is 3 business days, the TILA rescission period for refinances and home equity loans, a different law.

questions.q: New York's Home Equity Theft Prevention Act mainly protects:
c: Owners in default who sell their homes to equity purchasers
Lenders from borrowers who transfer title to avoid foreclosure
Buyers of foreclosed homes from undisclosed defects at auction
Tenants in foreclosed buildings from eviction by the new owner
questions.x: The Act targets foreclosure rescue scams: contracts in which an equity purchaser buys a home from an owner in default or foreclosure, often with a promise to rent it back. The trap is the lender-protection answer, which reverses the law's purpose.

questions.q: Before starting a foreclosure on a home loan in New York, the lender or servicer must send the borrower a notice at least:
c: 30 days before filing
60 days before filing
90 days before filing
120 days before filing
questions.x: RPAPL 1304 requires a 90-day pre-foreclosure notice, with a list of housing counseling agencies, before the action is started. The trap is 30 days, a common grace and notice period in other contexts but not this one.

questions.q: A servicer files a foreclosure on an owner-occupied home loan in Albany without having sent the RPAPL 1304 notice. The most likely result:
c: The action proceeds, since the notice is a courtesy
The servicer pays a $500 fine but keeps the case going
The borrower can move to dismiss for lack of notice
The court converts it to a non-judicial power of sale
questions.x: Proper RPAPL 1304 notice is a condition before a home loan foreclosure can be started, and courts dismiss actions brought without it. The trap is treating the notice as a courtesy. Home foreclosures in New York go through the courts.

questions.q: Debt and costs total $520,000. The foreclosure sale brings $430,000. The court finds fair market value of $470,000. The lender moves for a deficiency 60 days after the sale. The deficiency is:
questions.x: Deficiency = debt minus the higher of sale price or fair market value: $520,000 minus $470,000 = $50,000. The motion was within 90 days, so it is allowed. The trap is $90,000, which uses the lower auction price.

questions.q: A New York lender's foreclosure sale leaves $60,000 unpaid. The lender moves for a deficiency judgment 120 days after the referee's deed is delivered. What is the result?
c: The lender recovers $60,000 with interest
The lender recovers half for late filing
The borrower has to redeem within one year
No deficiency; the sale satisfies the debt
questions.x: RPAPL 1371 requires the motion within 90 days after the sale is consummated. If none is made in time, the sale proceeds are deemed full satisfaction. The trap is a statutory redemption period after the sale, which New York does not have.

questions.q: A lender markets high-rate, high-fee refinances mainly in minority neighborhoods while offering comparable borrowers elsewhere prime loans. This is:
c: Blockbusting
Reverse redlining
Steering by an agent
Risk-based pricing
questions.x: Reverse redlining targets protected-class neighborhoods with abusive credit, violating the Fair Housing Act, ECOA, and New York's Human Rights Law. The trap is risk-based pricing, which is lawful only when terms follow the individual borrower's actual risk, not the neighborhood's racial makeup.

questions.q: Which law requires lenders to report mortgage data so regulators can spot redlining patterns?
c: The Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
The Community Reinvestment Act of 1977
The Truth in Lending Act
The Fair Credit Reporting Act
questions.x: HMDA requires lenders to report loan data, including location and borrower characteristics, which reveals redlining and reverse redlining. The trap is the CRA, which pushes banks to serve their whole community but is not the data-reporting law.

questions.q: A Bronx apartment building has NOI of $300,000. The lender requires a 1.20 debt service coverage ratio. What is the most annual debt service the lender will allow?
questions.x: Maximum debt service = NOI / required ratio = $300,000 / 1.20 = $250,000. The $360,000 answer is the trap: it multiplies by the ratio instead of dividing, which would let debt service exceed the building's income.

questions.q: An Albany mixed-use building earns NOI of $180,000 a year. The proposed loan's annual debt service is $150,000. What is the debt service coverage ratio, and does it meet a 1.25x requirement?
c: 1.20x, which fails the requirement
0.83x, which fails the requirement
1.25x, which just meets the requirement
1.50x, which meets the requirement
questions.x: DSCR = NOI / annual debt service = $180,000 / $150,000 = 1.20x, below the 1.25x minimum, so the lender would shrink the loan. The 0.83x answer is the trap: it divides debt service by NOI, inverting the ratio.

questions.q: A builder in Staten Island finances five lots with one mortgage and wants to sell each finished house without paying off the whole loan. Which provision does the builder need?
c: An acceleration clause
An alienation clause
A release clause
A subordination clause
questions.x: A release clause in a blanket mortgage lets the borrower free one parcel from the lien by paying a set release price, so each house can be sold with clear title. The alienation clause is the trap: it lets the lender call the loan on a transfer, the opposite of what the builder needs.

questions.q: A blanket mortgage allocates $900,000 to one of three warehouses and requires 115% of the allocated amount for a partial release. What must the owner pay to release that warehouse?
questions.x: Release price = 1.15 x $900,000 = $1,035,000. Lenders require more than the allocated amount so the remaining collateral secures a smaller loan. The $900,000 answer is the trap: it is the allocation itself, which the release percentage is applied to.

questions.q: An adjustable rate loan starts at 5.5% with caps of 2% at the first adjustment, 1% per year after, and 5% for the life of the loan, with a 2.5% margin. At the second adjustment the rate is 7.0% and the index is 6.0%. What is the new rate?
questions.x: The fully indexed rate is 6.0% + 2.5% = 8.5%, but the periodic cap allows only 1 point over the current 7.0%, so the rate is 8.0%. The 8.5% answer is the trap: the index plus margin applies only when the caps allow it. The lifetime ceiling here is 10.5%.

questions.q: An ARM has a 4.75% start rate, a 2.25% margin, and a 5% lifetime cap. The highest rate the borrower can ever pay is:
questions.x: The lifetime cap is measured from the start rate: 4.75% + 5% = 9.75%. The 7.00% answer is the trap: it adds the margin to the start rate, but the margin is added to the index on each adjustment, not used to set the ceiling.

questions.q: A loan's payment cap holds the monthly payment below the interest that accrues each month. The result is:
c: A balloon payment due at the next adjustment
Negative amortization of the loan balance
A late charge on each capped payment
Faster amortization of the loan principal
questions.x: When the payment does not cover the interest, the unpaid interest is added to principal and the balance grows: negative amortization. The balloon answer is the trap: a balloon is a lump sum due at the end of a loan that does not fully amortize, a different design.

questions.q: A $400,000 loan resets to 6.6% interest, but a payment cap limits the payment to $2,000 this month. What is the balance after the payment?
questions.x: Interest due is $400,000 x 0.066 / 12 = $2,200. The $2,000 payment leaves $200 unpaid, which is added to principal: $400,200. The $398,000 answer is the trap: it treats the whole payment as principal, ignoring that interest is paid first.

questions.concept: NY prepayment rule for home loans
questions.q: A Rochester couple took a 7% mortgage on the one-family they live in. Eighteen months later they sell. Their note has a 2% prepayment penalty for the first three years. Under New York law, the lender may charge:
c: No penalty, because more than a year has passed
The 2% penalty, since the note provides for it
A 1% penalty, half the contract rate after a year
The penalty, but limited to six months' interest
questions.x: General Obligations Law 5-501(3)(b) lets a borrower on a loan above 6% secured by an owner-occupied 1 to 6 family home prepay at any time, with no penalty on prepayment one year or more after the loan is made. The contract answer is the trap: the statute overrides the note.

questions.concept: NY prepayment rule for home loans
questions.q: A prepayment penalty can lawfully be enforced in each of the following EXCEPT:
c: A 5-4-3-2-1 premium on a loan to an LLC for an office building
A step-down premium on a mortgage on a 40-unit apartment building
A premium in year 3 on a 7% loan on an owner-occupied two-family
A yield maintenance premium on a loan for a shopping center
questions.x: New York bars prepayment penalties after the first year on loans above 6% secured by owner-occupied 1 to 6 family residences. Business and commercial loans, including large apartment buildings, may carry bargained-for premiums. The 40-unit choice is the tempting wrong pick: it is residential, but it is not an owner-occupied 1 to 6 family home.

questions.q: Under a land contract, a buyer of a Chautauqua County house has paid about half of the price over eight years, then stops paying. The seller still holds the deed. In New York, the seller generally must:
c: Foreclose the buyer's interest or sue for the price
Give 30 days' notice, then keep the payments
Begin a summary eviction as with a defaulting tenant
Record an affidavit of default and change the locks
questions.x: A land contract buyer holds equitable title. New York courts, following Bean v. Walker, require a seller facing a buyer with substantial equity to foreclose or sue for the price rather than enforce a forfeiture. The notice-and-keep answer is the trap: forfeiture clauses do not let a seller keep years of payments without court process.

questions.q: In a land contract, which party holds legal title and which holds equitable title until the price is paid?
c: The buyer holds both titles from the first installment paid
The seller holds legal title; the buyer, equitable title
The buyer holds legal title; the seller, equitable title
An escrow agent holds both until the last payment
questions.x: The seller keeps legal title (the deed) as security, and the buyer gets possession and equitable title, receiving the deed when the price is paid. The reversed answer is the trap: it describes a mortgage, where the buyer gets the deed and the lender holds a lien.

cram.html: Note = promise to pay (debt). Mortgage = lien (security).
Mortgagor = borrower. Mortgagee = lender.
NY is a lien theory state with judicial foreclosure.
1 point = 1% of the loan, never the price.
Monthly interest = balance x rate / 12. Principal = payment minus interest.
PITI = principal, interest, taxes, insurance. Divide annual taxes and insurance by 12.
Acceleration = on default. Alienation (due-on-sale) = on transfer.
Subject to: buyer not personally liable. Assumption: buyer liable, seller secondarily liable unless novation.
NY home foreclosure: 90-day pre-foreclosure notice (RPAPL 1304), lis pendens, settlement conference, referee's sale.
Deficiency: move within 90 days of sale; debt minus the higher of sale price or FMV.
Redemption ends at the sale. NY has no post-sale statutory redemption.
NY usury: 16% civil, 25% criminal.
NY late charge on 1 to 6 family home loans: after 15 days, max 2% of installment.
FHA insures (3.5% down, MIP). VA guarantees (no down, no PMI, funding fee). RHS = rural.
SONYMA = State of New York Mortgage Agency (syllabus says Association).
ARM rate = index + margin. Margin never changes. Caps: periodic, lifetime, payment.
Payment cap or GPM can cause negative amortization.
Blanket + release clause = many parcels. Package = real + personal property. Wraparound = junior loan wrapping existing loan.
Fannie and Freddie buy conventional loans. Ginnie guarantees securities of FHA/VA/USDA loans.
PMI: request cancel at 80% of original value; automatic at 78%.
LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal.
Ratios: conventional 28/36, FHA 31/43. Use gross monthly income; take the lower limit.
Reg Z trigger terms: down payment, number of payments, payment amount, finance charge. APR alone is not a trigger.
TILA rescission: 3 business days, refinance or home equity on principal residence. Never the purchase loan.
NY predatory lending: Banking Law 6-l (high-cost) and 6-m (subprime).
Loan Estimate within 3 business days of application; Closing Disclosure 3 business days before closing.

subjects.title: Land Use Regulations
subjects.blurb: Zoning, planning boards, variances and eminent domain decide what can be built and sold. The exam loves the use variance vs area variance tests, nonconforming uses, and the four government powers.

lessons.title: Who Controls Land: Government Powers, Private Limits, and Planning
lessons.tagline: You own the lot. The town, the state, your deed, and your neighbors all own a piece of what you can do with it.
objectives: Name the four government powers over land (PETE) and tell police power from eminent domain
Distinguish public controls (zoning, codes) from private controls (deed restrictions, covenants)
Explain what a planning board does: master plan, official map, subdivisions, site plans, PUDs
Recognize SEQRA, environmental impact statements, Article 9-A and the Interstate Land Sales Act
Explain building permits, codes and the certificate of occupancy

blocks.title: Twelve acres in Dutchess County
blocks.html: Evelyn Park just bought 12 wooded acres outside Rhinebeck. She wants 30 homes, a private road ending in a turnaround, and a little clubhouse. Her deed says no lot may ever be used for a commercial kennel. The town just announced a six-month pause on new subdivisions while it rewrites its plan. Who actually decides what Evelyn can build, and in what order?
blocks.casual: Evelyn Park just picked up 12 wooded acres outside Rhinebeck. Her plan: 30 homes, a private road that dead-ends in a turnaround, and a small clubhouse. Catch number one: her deed says no lot can ever be a commercial kennel. Catch number two: the town just hit pause on new subdivisions for six months while it rewrites its plan. So who really gets a say in what Evelyn builds, and who goes first?

deeper.plain: Owning land doesn't mean you get to do whatever you want with it. Several different players each get a vote.
deeper.picture: Think of a group project where the teacher, the school, and the kid who wrote the group rules all have veto power. You still own your part, but you can't ignore any of them.
deeper.street: Evelyn's lineup: the town's zoning and subdivision rules (police power), the planning board's moratorium, SEQRA environmental review on a 30-home project, and the kennel covenant in her own deed. If she ignores the covenant, a neighbor can sue for an injunction even after the town approves her plat.
deeper.stakes: An agent who tells a buyer "it's zoned residential, you can build 30 homes" without checking deed restrictions, moratoriums and subdivision rules can steer a client into land they can't use, and that is how negligence claims start.
deeper.exam: The exam loves "which control applies?" questions. Sort each fact: government rule (police power), government taking (eminent domain), private rule (covenant or deed restriction). If two rules conflict, the stricter one controls.

blocks.text: Ownership is a bundle, and the government holds some sticks

blocks.html: Owning land means holding the bundle of rights: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition. None of those sticks is absolute. Government keeps four powers over every parcel, and private agreements can bind the land too.
blocks.casual: When you own land you hold the bundle of rights: you can possess it, control it, enjoy it, keep people out, and sell or give it away. Here's the catch: none of those sticks is absolute. The government keeps four powers over every parcel, and private deals can tie up the land too.

deeper.plain: Ownership is a set of separate rights, not one big right. Some of those rights can be limited or held by someone else.
deeper.picture: Picture a bundle of sticks. You can hand one stick to a tenant (possession), another to a neighbor (an easement), and the town keeps a few no matter what.
deeper.street: The Okafors own their Bed-Stuy brownstone outright. They rent the garden floor to a tenant (gave away possession for a year), Con Ed has a utility easement, and the city taxes them every quarter. They still own the house.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who think "I own it, I can do anything" get burned by zoning, landmark rules, or an easement they never read. An agent who explains the bundle early heads off angry calls after closing.
deeper.exam: Cue words: "possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, disposition." If a question asks which right is limited by an easement, the answer is exclusion. Selling or willing the property is disposition.

blocks.caption: Click zoning and watch the enjoyment and control sticks shrink. The owner still owns the land; the use is limited.

head: Power
What it does
Compensation?
Example
rows: Regulates use for health, safety, morals, general welfare
Zoning, building codes, subdivision rules, rent laws
Takes private property for public use
State takes a strip of a farm to widen Route 9
Annual town and school tax; sidewalk assessment
Property passes to the state when an owner dies with no will and no heirs
Unclaimed estate goes to New York State
blocks.caption: PETE: the four government powers over private land

deeper.plain: Government holds four powers over every piece of private land, and only one of them pays you.
deeper.picture: Think of PETE as four landlords above every owner: one sets house rules, one can buy you out whether you like it or not, one sends a bill every year, and one inherits when nobody else is left.
deeper.street: When the state widens Route 9 through a Dutchess County farm, the farmer gets paid fair market value (eminent domain). When the town zones the same farm agricultural-only, the farmer gets nothing (police power). When the farmer dies with no will and no heirs, the land goes to New York State (escheat).
deeper.stakes: Clients who think a downzoning entitles them to a check are wrong, and an agent who promises compensation for a regulation sets up a furious seller. Only a taking gets paid.
deeper.exam: Classic stem: "Which government power requires compensation?" Eminent domain. Trap: escheat sounds like a taking but is not paid, because there is no owner left to pay. Zoning is always police power.

blocks.title: PETE owns a piece of everything
blocks.html: Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat. Only eminent domain pays the owner.
blocks.casual: Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat. Remember PETE. Only one of the four, eminent domain, puts money in the owner's pocket.

deeper.plain: Four letters, four government powers. Only the E for eminent domain pays.
deeper.picture: Picture a guy named Pete with a key to every house on the block. He can set rules, collect a bill, take your place for a highway (with a check), or claim it when nobody's left.
deeper.street: Jordan rattles off PETE in the car with Diane on the way to a closing. Diane asks which one paid the farmer when the state took a strip of land to widen Route 9. Jordan says eminent domain, and Diane nods.
deeper.stakes: Mixing these up on the job means telling a seller the wrong thing about a road widening or a rezoning. That costs you credibility fast.
deeper.exam: Expect "all of the following are government powers EXCEPT" with a distractor like "deed restriction" or "restrictive covenant." Those are private controls, not PETE.

blocks.html: Police power is the big one for this subject. Every zoning ordinance, building code, and subdivision rule is an exercise of it. Because it regulates rather than takes, no payment is owed, as long as the rule is reasonable and leaves the owner some economic use.
blocks.casual: Police power is the one you'll see most in this subject. Every zoning law, building code, and subdivision rule comes from it. Since the government is regulating, not taking, the owner gets no check, as long as the rule is reasonable and still leaves the owner some economic use of the land.

deeper.plain: Government can set rules on land use to protect health and safety, and it doesn't have to pay you for following them.
deeper.picture: It's like the rules at a public pool. No running, no glass, closes at 8. You still got in, you just follow the rules, and nobody pays you to.
deeper.street: Sal wants to add a fourth floor to his Astoria building. Zoning caps the height, so the Department of Buildings says no. Sal grumbles that he's losing $400,000 of potential value. He gets no compensation, because the height limit is police power and he can still collect rent on the six units he has.
deeper.stakes: If a rule wipes out all economic use, it can cross into a taking and the owner may win a lawsuit. Short of that, owners absorb the loss, and buyers who overpay expecting to build more are stuck.
deeper.exam: Watch for "health, safety, morals, general welfare." That phrase always points to police power. The trap answer is eminent domain whenever the question says "no compensation."

blocks.html: Eminent domain is the power to take; condemnation is the legal process used to do it. The U.S. and NY constitutions require public use and just compensation (fair market value). In New York the process runs under the Eminent Domain Procedure Law (EDPL), which requires a public hearing and findings before the taking.
blocks.casual: Eminent domain is the government's power to take your property. Condemnation is the legal process it uses to actually do it. Both the U.S. and NY constitutions say two things are required: public use and just compensation, which means fair market value. In New York the process runs under the Eminent Domain Procedure Law (EDPL), and the government has to hold a public hearing and make findings before it takes anything.

deeper.plain: The government can force you to sell for a public project, but it has to pay you fair market value and follow a set process.
deeper.picture: It's a forced sale with a fair price tag. You don't get to say no, but you do get paid what a willing buyer would pay.
deeper.street: The state needs a strip of Grace and Emmanuel's cousin's lot in Westchester for a highway ramp. The agency holds an EDPL public hearing, issues findings, and offers $85,000. The cousin's appraiser says $110,000, so the fight is over the number, not over whether the state can take it.
deeper.stakes: Owners who skip the hearing or don't get their own appraisal can leave real money on the table. Agents may be asked for a CMA in these disputes, and it must never be called an appraisal.
deeper.exam: Remember the pairing: eminent domain is the power, condemnation is the process. If a stem says "the legal proceeding by which the government acquires private property," pick condemnation.

blocks.title: Takings cases born in New York
blocks.html: Courts decide when regulation goes so far it becomes a taking. Penn Central v. New York City (1978): landmarking Grand Central and blocking a tower above it was NOT a taking, partly because the owner kept a reasonable return and could transfer its air rights. Loretto v. Teleprompter (1982): a law forcing a Manhattan landlord to allow a cable box on her roof WAS a taking, because any permanent physical occupation is one, however small.
blocks.casual: Courts decide when a regulation goes so far it turns into a taking. Two big cases came out of New York. Penn Central v. New York City (1978): the city landmarked Grand Central and blocked a tower on top. Not a taking, partly because the owner still earned a reasonable return and could sell its air rights. Loretto v. Teleprompter (1982): a law made a Manhattan landlord let a cable company put a box on her roof. That WAS a taking, because any permanent physical occupation counts, no matter how small.

deeper.plain: A rule that limits your land usually isn't a taking. Putting something permanently on your land usually is.
deeper.picture: A landlord telling you "no parties" is a rule. A landlord moving his couch into your living room for good is an occupation. Courts treat the second one very differently.
deeper.street: A Park Slope brownstone owner gets landmarked and can't add a rooftop addition. She can still live there and sell, so no taking. If the city instead bolted a permanent equipment box to her roof without paying, Loretto says she gets compensated, even for a few square feet.
deeper.stakes: Owners who assume landmarking will be paid for can make bad buy decisions on historic properties. Knowing these cases helps you set honest expectations about what a landmark designation does to value.
deeper.exam: If the question mentions a "permanent physical occupation," the answer is a taking regardless of size. If it mentions landmark designation with a reasonable return left, it's regulation, not a taking.

blocks.q: A county widens a road and pays an owner for a 20-foot strip of her front yard. Which power was used?
c: Police power
Eminent domain
Escheat
Taxation
blocks.x: Taking title for public use with payment is eminent domain, carried out through condemnation. Police power regulates use and pays nothing.

blocks.text: Private controls: what the deed and the neighbors can impose

blocks.html: A deed restriction is a limit written into a deed. A restrictive covenant is a promise, often in a subdivision's recorded declaration, that binds every lot (minimum house size, no fences in front yards, no commercial kennels). Covenants that "run with the land" bind future owners. Neighbors or a homeowners association enforce them in court, usually by injunction.
blocks.casual: A deed restriction is a limit written right into the deed. A restrictive covenant is a promise, usually in a subdivision's recorded declaration, that ties up every lot: minimum house size, no front-yard fences, no commercial kennels. When a covenant "runs with the land," it binds whoever owns the lot next, not just the original buyer. Neighbors or a homeowners association enforce them in court, usually by getting an injunction.

deeper.plain: A seller or developer can put permanent rules on land, and those rules follow the land to every future owner.
deeper.picture: It's like buying a used car that comes with a lifetime "no smoking" contract stuck to the dashboard. New owner, same rule.
deeper.street: Leo buys a house in a Long Island subdivision and puts up a six-foot fence in the front yard. Two weeks later the HOA serves him with papers: the recorded declaration bans front-yard fences. A judge orders the fence down, and Leo eats the $7,000 he spent on it.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who never see the recorded declaration find out about covenants the hard way. Agents should point buyers to the title report and tell them to have their attorney review restrictions before closing.
deeper.exam: Cue words: "runs with the land," "binds future owners," "enforced by injunction." Covenants are private controls, so the enforcer is neighbors or an HOA, not the building department.

blocks.title: Public vs private land use controls

left.title: Public (government)
items: Zoning, codes, subdivision rules
Created by legislature or agency
Enforced by building department, courts
Changed by rezoning or variance

right.title: Private
items: Deed restrictions, covenants, easements
Created by a grantor or developer
Enforced by neighbors or HOA lawsuits
Changed only by the parties or a court

deeper.plain: Government rules come from lawmakers and get enforced by officials. Private rules come from deeds and get enforced by neighbors in court.
deeper.picture: Public controls are like the city's traffic laws. Private controls are like the rules in your building's bylaws. Different rulebooks, different enforcers, and you have to follow both.
deeper.street: A Queens homeowner gets a variance from the BSA to build a rear extension. The neighbor still sues because a 1950s recorded covenant bans additions past a certain line. The variance fixed the public problem but did nothing about the private one.
deeper.stakes: Telling a client "the city approved it, you're fine" ignores covenants and easements. That leaves the buyer exposed to a lawsuit you could have flagged.
deeper.exam: If the question asks who changes a private restriction, the answer is the parties or a court, never the zoning board. If it asks who enforces zoning, it's the building department or code enforcement, not the HOA.

blocks.title: The stricter rule wins
blocks.html: If zoning allows a two-family house but a covenant limits the lot to one family, the owner must follow the more restrictive one. A variance from the ZBA does not erase a private covenant. Also: covenants based on race or other protected classes are void and unenforceable.
blocks.casual: Say zoning allows a two-family house, but a covenant says one family only. The owner has to follow the more restrictive rule. A variance from the ZBA does not wipe out a private covenant. One more thing: covenants based on race or any other protected class are void and can't be enforced.

deeper.plain: When two rules overlap, you follow the tighter one. Covenants that discriminate are dead on arrival.
deeper.picture: Two parents with different curfews: one says 11, one says 10. You're home by 10.
deeper.street: Marcus lists a Staten Island house as "zoning allows two-family, great investment." The deed has a single-family covenant. The buyer's attorney finds it, the buyer walks, and Marcus has to explain to Diane why the ad overpromised.
deeper.stakes: Advertising "two-family potential" on a single-family-covenant lot is misleading, and a buyer who relied on it can complain to DOS or sue. A racial covenant in an old deed still shows up in title searches, but it has no legal force.
deeper.exam: Look for "zoning permits X, but the deed restricts Y." The answer is always the stricter one. Distractor: "the zoning ordinance prevails because it's public law." Wrong.

blocks.html: An easement is a right to use someone else's land for a purpose, such as a right-of-way to cross it or a utility line. It limits the owner's exclusion stick. A neighbor who sleeps on a covenant violation for years may lose the right to enforce it under the doctrine of laches (unreasonable delay that harms the other side).
blocks.casual: An easement gives someone the right to use another person's land for a specific purpose, like a right-of-way to walk or drive across it, or a utility line running through it. It cuts into the owner's right to keep people out. And if a neighbor sits on a covenant violation for years and then sues, they may lose under the doctrine of laches: unreasonable delay that hurts the other side.

deeper.plain: An easement lets someone else use part of your land. Laches means if you wait too long to complain, you can lose the right to complain.
deeper.picture: An easement is like a neighbor's spare key to your side gate so they can reach the alley. Laches is like trying to return a sweater three years after the store's receipt expired.
deeper.street: The Okafors' neighbor built a deck over the setback line in 2012. Nobody said a word for twelve years. When the Okafors finally sue under the covenant, the court points out the neighbor spent $30,000 relying on their silence, and laches kills the claim.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who skip the survey and title review can miss an easement that lets a utility dig up their backyard. Sellers who let violations slide can lose enforcement rights.
deeper.exam: "Unreasonable delay" or "failed to act in a timely manner" signals laches. An easement limits the right of exclusion, not ownership. Don't confuse laches with adverse possession, which needs 10 years of hostile, open use in NY.

blocks.text: Planning: deciding the future before it arrives

blocks.html: Towns plan because growth without a plan means flooded basements, schools over capacity, and gridlock. The planning board studies demography (population data, often by census tract), topography, traffic and infrastructure (roads, water, sewer, schools), then writes a master plan, also called the comprehensive plan. NY law requires zoning to be adopted in accordance with a comprehensive plan.
blocks.casual: Towns plan because growth without a plan gets you flooded basements, packed schools, and traffic you can't get out of. The planning board looks at demography (population data, often broken out by census tract), topography, traffic, and infrastructure like roads, water, sewer and schools. Then it writes a master plan, also called the comprehensive plan. In New York, zoning has to be adopted in accordance with that comprehensive plan.

deeper.plain: A town studies who lives there and what the land can handle, then writes a long-range plan. Zoning has to follow it.
deeper.picture: It's like planning a wedding: you count guests, check the venue size, and figure out parking before you send invites. The master plan is the seating chart for a whole town.
deeper.street: A Hudson Valley town sees census data showing young families moving in. Its master plan calls for more housing near the train station and preserves farmland on the ridge, where the slope and septic soils are poor. Zoning gets rewritten to match.
deeper.stakes: A zoning change that ignores the comprehensive plan can be struck down in court as spot zoning. Investors who buy betting on a rezoning that contradicts the plan can lose big.
deeper.exam: "Comprehensive plan" and "master plan" are the same thing on the exam. Remember NY requires zoning to be "in accordance with" it. Demography is people data; topography is land shape.

head: Planning board tool
What it is
rows: Long-range blueprint for land use, housing, transportation, open space
Shows existing and proposed streets, parks, drainage; you generally may not build in a mapped street bed
Approves splitting land into lots: the plat, lot sizes, density, streets, drainage, utilities
Approves the layout of a single project: parking, landscaping, lighting, access, drainage
Approves a whole mixed project as one unit, often trading density for open space
Advises on paying for roads, sewers, parks the growth will need
Temporary halt on certain approvals while the town studies or rewrites rules

deeper.plain: The planning board has a toolbox: a long-range plan, a map, reviews of subdivisions and single sites, PUD approvals, money planning, and the power to pause.
deeper.picture: Think of the planning board as a general contractor for the whole town. The master plan is the blueprint, the official map is the floor plan, and site plan review checks each room.
deeper.street: A Suffolk County builder wants to put a drive-thru on a corner lot. The site is zoned for it, but site plan review still checks parking, lighting, traffic and drainage. The board makes him move the exit away from a school crosswalk before approving.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who plan to build in a mapped street bed on the official map may be denied a permit. Developers who skip site plan review face stop-work orders.
deeper.exam: Know the difference: subdivision review splits land into lots; site plan review lays out one project on one lot; PUD approves a mixed project as one unit. A moratorium is temporary.

blocks.html: Subdivision regulations control how raw land becomes lots: minimum lot size, street width, curbs, a cul-de-sac turnaround radius big enough for a fire truck, storm drainage, and often land or a fee for parks. A licensed survey fixes boundaries. Developers who want FHA-insured mortgages for buyers may also need the subdivision to meet FHA standards, so lenders watch these approvals closely.
blocks.casual: Subdivision regulations control how raw land turns into lots: minimum lot size, how wide the streets are, curbs, a cul-de-sac turnaround big enough for a fire truck to swing around, storm drainage, and often land or a fee for parks. A licensed survey nails down the boundaries. If the developer wants buyers to be able to use FHA-insured mortgages, the subdivision may also have to meet FHA standards, so lenders keep a close eye on these approvals.

deeper.plain: Before raw land becomes buildable lots, the town checks lot sizes, roads, drainage and safety.
deeper.picture: It's like cutting a sheet cake for a party. Somebody decides how big each slice is and makes sure everyone can reach the table without climbing over each other.
deeper.street: Evelyn's 30-lot plan has a private road ending in a turnaround. The planning board measures the cul-de-sac radius, finds it too tight for the fire department's ladder truck, and sends her back to widen it, costing two lots.
deeper.stakes: Lots sold before subdivision approval can be illegal to build on. Buyers counting on FHA financing may find lenders won't touch a subdivision that doesn't meet FHA standards.
deeper.exam: If the stem mentions the plat, lot sizes, street width, or drainage, the answer is subdivision regulations, not zoning. Zoning controls use and density; subdivision rules control how land is split and improved.

blocks.html: A planned unit development (PUD) lets a developer plan a whole tract as one project, mixing housing types and sometimes shops, with flexible lot lines and shared open space. Site plan review, by contrast, looks at one project on one lot.
blocks.casual: A planned unit development (PUD) lets a developer plan an entire tract as one project, mixing housing types and sometimes shops, with flexible lot lines and shared open space. Site plan review is different: it looks at one project on one lot.

deeper.plain: A PUD is a whole neighborhood approved as one package. Site plan review is a check of one building's layout.
deeper.picture: A PUD is a full restaurant menu approved at once. Site plan review is the inspector checking one dish.
deeper.street: A developer in Orange County gets a PUD for 200 acres: townhouses clustered on 60 acres, 40 single-family homes, a small retail strip, and 100 acres left as trails. Under regular zoning he'd have had to spread one-acre lots across everything.
deeper.stakes: Buyers in a PUD usually pay HOA dues for the shared open space. Agents who don't explain those obligations get angry calls at the first assessment.
deeper.exam: PUD cue words: "mixed uses," "clustered housing," "common open space," "entire tract." Site plan cue words: "single parcel," "parking, landscaping, lighting."

blocks.title: Moratoriums are legal if temporary
blocks.html: A moratorium pausing new subdivisions while a town updates its plan is a valid police power tool if it is reasonable in length and tied to a real planning need. An endless one starts to look like a taking.
blocks.casual: A moratorium that pauses new subdivisions while a town updates its plan is a legit police power tool, as long as it's reasonable in length and tied to a real planning need. If it drags on forever, it starts to look like a taking.

deeper.plain: A town can temporarily freeze approvals while it figures things out, but it can't freeze forever.
deeper.picture: It's like a restaurant closing for two weeks to renovate the kitchen. Fine. Closing "until further notice" for five years is a different story.
deeper.street: Evelyn's town announces a six-month moratorium on subdivisions. Her application sits, and her carrying costs on the 12 acres run about $4,000 a month. Annoying, but legal. If the town keeps renewing it for years with no new plan, her attorney has a takings argument.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who signs a land contract without a moratorium contingency can be stuck paying taxes and interest on land they can't develop.
deeper.exam: "Temporary halt" or "pause on approvals" means moratorium. It's police power, so no compensation, unless it becomes unreasonable.

blocks.q: Which document shows a town's existing and proposed streets and parks, and can block building in a mapped future street?
c: Plat
Official map
Survey
Site plan
blocks.x: The official map is the municipality's adopted map of streets, parks and drainage. A plat shows one subdivision's lots; a survey shows one parcel's boundaries.

blocks.html: SEQRA, the State Environmental Quality Review Act, makes every state and local agency weigh environmental impact before it approves, funds, or undertakes an action. One agency becomes the lead agency (often the planning board) and coordinates the review.
blocks.casual: SEQRA, the State Environmental Quality Review Act, makes every state and local agency think through environmental impact before it approves, funds, or carries out a project. One agency takes the lead as the lead agency (often the planning board) and runs the review.

deeper.plain: Before government approves a project in New York, someone has to look hard at what it does to the environment.
deeper.picture: It's the "measure twice, cut once" rule, applied to wetlands, traffic and drinking water.
deeper.street: A Saratoga County planning board gets a 150-home application near a creek. It declares itself lead agency under SEQRA, coordinates with the DEC and the county health department, and nothing gets approved until the review is done.
deeper.stakes: If the review is skipped or sloppy, neighbors can sue and void the approval, sometimes after construction has started. That can wreck a closing timeline.
deeper.exam: "Lead agency" is a SEQRA term. If a question asks which law requires environmental review of state and local actions in NY, the answer is SEQRA, not NEPA (that's federal) and not CERCLA (that's cleanup liability).

blocks.title: How SEQRA review flows

items.title: Classify
items.html: Type II actions (minor, like a single-family home or a side-yard variance) need no review. Type I and unlisted actions get reviewed.

items.title: Assess
items.html: The applicant files an Environmental Assessment Form (EAF).

items.title: Decide significance
items.html: Lead agency issues a negative declaration (no significant impact, proceed) or a positive declaration (possible significant impact).

items.title: EIS
items.html: A positive declaration requires an environmental impact statement (EIS): draft, public comment, final EIS, written findings.

blocks.casual: Here's how SEQRA plays out. Step one, classify: Type II actions (small stuff like a single-family home or a side-yard variance) skip review entirely; Type I and unlisted actions get reviewed. Step two, the applicant files an Environmental Assessment Form (EAF). Step three, the lead agency decides: a negative declaration means no significant impact, go ahead; a positive declaration means there might be a significant impact. Step four, a positive declaration triggers an environmental impact statement (EIS): a draft, public comment, a final EIS, and written findings.

deeper.plain: Small projects skip review. Bigger ones fill out a form, and if there's a real environmental risk, they write a full impact study.
deeper.picture: It's airport security. Most people walk through the scanner. Some get a pat-down. A few get pulled into a room for the full search.
deeper.street: Leo's single-family house is Type II, no review. Evelyn's 30-home subdivision gets an EAF. The planning board issues a positive declaration because of a stream on the site, and Evelyn spends eight months and $60,000 on an EIS before getting her findings.
deeper.stakes: A "pos dec" can add months and big consulting bills. Buyers of development land who don't build that into their timeline can blow their financing.
deeper.exam: Negative declaration means NO significant impact (good for the developer). Positive declaration means POSSIBLE significant impact and an EIS is required. The words feel backwards, and the exam knows it.

blocks.title: NYC runs CEQR
blocks.html: New York City implements SEQRA through City Environmental Quality Review (CEQR). Same idea, city procedures.
blocks.casual: New York City runs SEQRA through its own version, City Environmental Quality Review (CEQR). Same idea, city procedures.

deeper.plain: NYC does the same environmental review under its own name and process.
deeper.picture: Same recipe, the city's own kitchen.
deeper.street: A Gowanus rezoning goes through CEQR, with an environmental impact statement covering the canal, flooding and schools, before the City Council votes.
deeper.stakes: NYC projects that skip CEQR face the same lawsuit risk as upstate projects that skip SEQRA.
deeper.exam: If the question says "New York City" and "environmental review," CEQR is the answer. Outside the city, it's SEQRA.

blocks.html: Historic resources get state review too. The New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation (OPRHP) houses the State Historic Preservation Office, keeps the State and National Registers of Historic Places, and reviews state-funded or permitted projects that affect them.
blocks.casual: Historic properties get state review too. The New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation (OPRHP) houses the State Historic Preservation Office, keeps the State and National Registers of Historic Places, and reviews state-funded or state-permitted projects that touch them.

deeper.plain: A state office keeps the list of historic places and checks state-backed projects that might affect them.
deeper.picture: It's like a museum curator who gets a say before anyone with public money moves the furniture.
deeper.street: A Troy developer uses state tax credits to convert an 1880s mill on the National Register. Because state money is involved, OPRHP reviews the plans and asks him to keep the original windows.
deeper.stakes: Developers who don't budget for historic review can face redesigns and delays. Sellers can market register status as a plus for tax credits, but should be honest about the strings.
deeper.exam: OPRHP is the state agency for historic preservation. Don't confuse it with a local landmarks commission (NYC's is the Landmarks Preservation Commission), which regulates designated buildings directly.

head: Law
Covers
Key rule
rows: Vacant subdivided land offered to NY residents on an installment plan
Subdivider files a filing statement and offering statement with the NYS Department of State; every offer must include the current offering statement
Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act (federal)
Subdivisions of 100+ unimproved lots sold through interstate commerce
Buyer gets a property report before signing; may revoke within 7 days. Originally run by HUD, now by the CFPB
blocks.caption: Two land sale disclosure laws aimed at out-of-sight, buy-on-installments lot schemes

deeper.plain: Two laws make sellers of far-off lots tell buyers the truth before they sign: one state, one federal.
deeper.picture: They're the "read this before you buy swampland" laws, born from the old scam of selling lots sight unseen on installment plans.
deeper.street: A Bronx couple gets pitched a lot in an out-of-state subdivision of 400 lots, payable monthly. Under the federal Act they must get a property report before signing, and they have 7 days to back out. If it were a NY subdivision sold to NY residents on installments, Article 9-A would require the current offering statement filed with DOS.
deeper.stakes: Selling without the required report or statement can let buyers cancel and sue, and the developer can face federal or state enforcement.
deeper.exam: Remember the trio: 100+ lots, property report, 7-day revocation. Article 9-A: filing with the NYS Department of State. Don't mix in the Martin Act (co-op and condo offerings filed with the Attorney General).

blocks.title: HUD or CFPB?
