blocks.html: Older textbooks say HUD administers the Interstate Land Sales Act and issues the property report rules. Since 2011 the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau does. If HUD is the only federal agency offered, pick it; if CFPB is offered, it is the current answer.
blocks.casual: Older textbooks say HUD runs the Interstate Land Sales Act and the property report rules. Since 2011 it's the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. On the exam: if HUD is the only federal agency in the choices, pick HUD. If CFPB is there, that's the current answer.

deeper.plain: The agency in charge of this law changed in 2011 from HUD to the CFPB.
deeper.picture: It's like a store that changed owners. The old sign still hangs in some places, but the new owner signs the checks.
deeper.street: Jordan's old prep book says HUD. Diane crosses it out and writes CFPB in the margin, then says, "If the test only gives you HUD, take HUD and move on."
deeper.stakes: Pointing a client to the wrong agency wastes their time when they're trying to complain about a lot scheme.
deeper.exam: Read every answer choice before picking. If both HUD and CFPB appear, CFPB is correct. If only HUD appears, the question is using older material.

blocks.html: New York has a statewide building code: the Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code (the Uniform Code), plus the State Energy Conservation Construction Code, administered by the Department of State. Cities, towns and villages enforce it locally and may adopt stricter rules. New York City has its own Construction Codes and Fire Code.
blocks.casual: New York has a statewide building code: the Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code (people just call it the Uniform Code), plus the State Energy Conservation Construction Code. The Department of State runs it. Cities, towns and villages enforce it locally and can pile on stricter rules. New York City is its own world with its own Construction Codes and Fire Code.

deeper.plain: One statewide code sets the minimum building rules. Local governments enforce it and can be tougher. NYC has its own code.
deeper.picture: It's like the state setting a minimum wage. Each city can pay more, never less, and NYC wrote its own rulebook entirely.
deeper.street: Ray inspects a house in Albany and checks it against the Uniform Code. The next day he's in Bushwick, where the NYC Construction Codes and the Department of Buildings apply instead.
deeper.stakes: Work done without meeting code can fail inspection, block a CO, or create a safety hazard that ends in a lawsuit after someone gets hurt.
deeper.exam: If asked who administers the statewide building code, the answer is the NYS Department of State. If asked who enforces it, the answer is the local building department. NYC is the big exception with its own codes.

blocks.title: From idea to occupancy

items.title: Plans
items.html: Architect or engineer prepares plans and specifications.

items.title: Permit
items.html: Building department issues a building permit after checking zoning and code.

items.title: Inspections
items.html: Footing, framing, plumbing, electrical, insulation, final.

items.title: CO
items.html: Building department issues the certificate of occupancy (CO): the building complies and may be lawfully used for the stated use.

blocks.casual: From idea to move-in goes like this. An architect or engineer draws the plans and specs. The building department checks them against zoning and code and issues a building permit. Then come inspections: footing, framing, plumbing, electrical, insulation, and a final. Last, the building department issues the certificate of occupancy (CO), which says the building complies and can legally be used for the stated use.

deeper.plain: You need a permit before you build, inspections while you build, and a CO before anyone can legally live or work there.
deeper.picture: It's like a driver's license process: the permit is the learner's permit, inspections are the road test, and the CO is the license that says you're legal to drive.
deeper.street: Priya's client closes on a new Queens two-family. The final inspection passed, but the CO hasn't been issued yet. Priya refuses to let her client close until it is, because the lender won't fund and the client couldn't legally rent the second unit.
deeper.stakes: No CO means no legal occupancy, trouble getting a mortgage or insurance, and possible fines. Buyers who close without one inherit the problem.
deeper.exam: The CO says the building may be lawfully used for its stated purpose. A permit lets you start work; a CO lets you move in. Don't swap them.

blocks.title: Check the CO before you list
blocks.html: If the listing says "legal two-family" the CO should say two-family. A finished basement apartment with no permit and no CO is an illegal unit, and you cannot advertise it as rental income.
blocks.casual: If the listing says "legal two-family," the CO had better say two-family. A finished basement apartment with no permit and no CO is an illegal unit, and you can't advertise it as rental income.

deeper.plain: Pull the CO before you write the listing. What the CO says is what you can advertise.
deeper.picture: It's like listing a car's horsepower. You use the number on the spec sheet, not what the last owner claims after he tinkered with the engine.
deeper.street: Marcus lists a Canarsie house as a "legal 3-family" with $2,400 a month from the basement. The CO says two-family. The buyer's lender catches it, the appraisal drops, and the buyer's attorney threatens a misrepresentation claim against the brokerage.
deeper.stakes: Advertising illegal units as income is misrepresentation. It can bring DOS discipline, a lawsuit, and a dead deal. It can also put a tenant in an unsafe space.
deeper.exam: Expect a question where the seller says "three-family" but the CO says two. The correct move is to advertise per the CO and disclose. Rental income from an illegal unit cannot be marketed.

blocks.html: Finally, the Open Meetings Law (the Sunshine Law) requires town boards, planning boards and ZBAs to meet in public, give advance notice (at least 72 hours for meetings scheduled a week or more ahead), and keep minutes. Votes on variances and subdivisions happen in the open. A decision made in an improper closed session can be voided.
blocks.casual: Last piece: the Open Meetings Law, also called the Sunshine Law. Town boards, planning boards and ZBAs have to meet in public, give advance notice (at least 72 hours when the meeting is scheduled a week or more ahead), and keep minutes. Votes on variances and subdivisions happen out in the open. If a board decides something in an improper closed session, a court can void it.

deeper.plain: Land use boards have to do their business in public, with notice and minutes.
deeper.picture: It's like a group chat where the whole neighborhood can read along. No side DMs to decide things.
deeper.street: Neighbors find out the ZBA approved a gas station variance at a "workshop" held without notice. Their attorney sues under the Open Meetings Law, and the court voids the approval. The applicant has to start over.
deeper.stakes: Developers who win approval in an improper session can lose it later, after spending money in reliance on it. Neighbors who miss the public hearing lose their chance to object on the record.
deeper.exam: "Sunshine Law" equals Open Meetings Law. Remember the 72-hour notice for meetings scheduled a week or more ahead, and that improper closed-session actions can be voided.

blocks.q: A planning board finds that a 200-unit project may significantly affect wetlands and traffic. Under SEQRA it must:
c: Issue a negative declaration and approve
Issue a positive declaration and require an environmental impact statement
Refer the project to HUD
Deny it as spot zoning
blocks.x: A possible significant impact means a positive declaration and a full EIS. A negative declaration is for actions with no significant impact.

story.title: The Clubhouse Problem
story.setting: Town hall, Rhinebeck, a Thursday night planning board meeting

beats.text: Evelyn drove Jordan up the Taconic for what she called a quick meeting. The agenda had forty items.
Thirty homes, one clubhouse. I own the land. How hard can this be?
Item 22. Before anything else: the town has a six-month moratorium on new subdivisions while we finish the comprehensive plan.
Six months? That's a taking.
Not if it's temporary and tied to planning. A taking is when they grab the land or wipe out all use. They're pausing, not grabbing.
When the pause lifts, you'll file a preliminary plat. We'll look at density, the road, drainage, and whether that cul-de-sac fits a ladder truck.
You'll also file an Environmental Assessment Form. There's a wetland on the east edge. If we find a possible significant impact, that's a positive declaration and a full EIS.

check.q: Who coordinates the SEQRA review of Evelyn's subdivision?
c: The Department of State
The lead agency, here the planning board
The ZBA
HUD
check.x: SEQRA review is coordinated by one lead agency, usually the board giving the main approval. Here, the planning board.

beats.text: And my clubhouse?
Read your deed. It bans commercial kennels, not clubhouses. But if the subdivision declaration adds covenants, every buyer's bound by them.
What if zoning lets me do something the covenant forbids?
Then the stricter one wins. The ZBA can't waive a private covenant.
Item 23 began. A neighbor stood up to object. Everything was on the record, because this meeting, like every board meeting, was open to the public.
So I can't just build because I own it.
On the phone the next morning: You own the dirt, Evelyn. The town owns the rulebook. Police power regulates for free; only eminent domain has to pay you.

board.prompt: Draw Evelyn's 12 acres. Label every control that touches it: zoning, the moratorium, the deed covenant, the wetland (SEQRA), the subdivision plat, and the future CO.

facts.text: Ownership is a bundle of rights (possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, disposition), and none of them is absolute.
Zoning, building codes and subdivision rules are exercises of police power, which regulates for health, safety and welfare and pays no compensation.
Government's four powers over land are police power, eminent domain, taxation and escheat (PETE); deed restrictions are private, not government, controls.
Eminent domain is the power to take for public use with just compensation; condemnation is the legal process, run in NY under the EDPL with a public hearing.
Escheat passes property to the state when an owner dies with no will and no heirs.
A regulation that leaves no economically viable use is a taking; Penn Central held landmarking Grand Central was not a taking because a reasonable return remained.
Loretto v. Teleprompter: any permanent physical occupation, even a small cable box, is a taking.
Restrictive covenants in a recorded declaration run with the land, bind future owners, and are enforced by neighbors or an HOA in court, usually by injunction.
When zoning and a private covenant differ, the more restrictive one controls; a variance does not erase a covenant, and covenants based on protected classes are void.
An easement is a right to use another's land for a purpose, such as a right-of-way to cross it.
Laches can bar enforcing a covenant when a neighbor unreasonably delays for years.
NY law requires zoning to be adopted in accordance with a comprehensive (master) plan.
Planning studies demography (often by census tract), topography, and infrastructure such as roads, water, sewer and schools.
The planning board reviews subdivision plats and site plans and prepares the master plan.
The official map shows existing and proposed streets and parks; an owner generally may not build in a mapped street bed.
Subdivision rules set lot sizes, street widths, cul-de-sac turnarounds, drainage and park land, and a licensed survey fixes boundaries.
A PUD approves a whole tract as one mixed project with flexible lots and shared open space; site plan review looks at one project on one lot.
A temporary moratorium on approvals while a town updates its plan is a valid police power tool if reasonable in length; an endless one starts to look like a taking.
Under SEQRA the lead agency issues a negative declaration (no significant impact) or a positive declaration, which requires an environmental impact statement.
Type II actions such as a single-family home need no SEQRA review; Type I and unlisted actions start with an Environmental Assessment Form; NYC runs SEQRA as CEQR.
The Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation houses the State Historic Preservation Office and the State and National Registers.
RPL Article 9-A requires a subdivider offering vacant subdivided lots to NY residents on installment terms to file an offering statement with the Department of State.
The Interstate Land Sales Act covers 100+ unimproved lots sold interstate: the buyer gets a property report and may revoke within 7 days; the CFPB, not HUD, now runs it.
NY has a statewide Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code administered by the Department of State and enforced locally; localities may be stricter and NYC has its own codes.
The certificate of occupancy certifies a finished building complies and may be used for its stated use; a unit without one is illegal and cannot be advertised as rental income.
The Open Meetings Law makes planning boards, ZBAs and town boards meet in public with advance notice (72 hours for meetings set a week ahead) and keep minutes.

lessons.title: Zoning, Variances, and the ZBA (plus NYC's ULURP and Air Rights)
lessons.tagline: Permitted, special permit, area variance, use variance, rezoning: know which door the client is knocking on.
objectives: Read a zoning classification and tell an as-of-right use from one that needs approval
Apply the four-part use variance test and the five-factor area variance test
Explain nonconforming uses, spot zoning, incentive zoning, clustering and accessory uses
Describe the ZBA's role, Article 78 review, and local enforcement
Explain NYC's City Planning Commission, BSA, ULURP, and transfer of development rights

blocks.title: A deli in a residential zone
blocks.html: Sal Russo wants to buy a corner building in a quiet part of Bayside. The ground floor has been a deli since 1951; the block was zoned residential in 1961. Sal's plan: keep the deli, add a second-floor apartment, and push the rear wall 8 feet into the yard. The seller swears "it's all grandfathered." Which parts are, and which need a board?
blocks.casual: Sal Russo has his eye on a corner building in a quiet stretch of Bayside. The ground floor has been a deli since 1951. The block got zoned residential in 1961. Sal wants three things: keep the deli, add an apartment upstairs, and push the back wall 8 feet into the yard. The seller swears "it's all grandfathered." So which parts actually are, and which ones need a board to sign off?

deeper.plain: Some of what Sal wants is already protected because it was there first. Some of it needs permission from a board.
deeper.picture: It's like a regular at a bar who got a reserved stool before the new owner took over. He keeps the stool, but he can't suddenly claim the whole booth.
deeper.street: Sal's attorney pulls the zoning map, the CO, and old tax photos showing the deli open every year since 1951. That proves the deli is a legal nonconforming use. The rear extension and the apartment get sorted separately, one as an area variance, one by checking whether the district allows it.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who trust "it's grandfathered" without proof can pay a deli price for a building that can only be a house. Agents who repeat the seller's line without checking risk a misrepresentation claim.
deeper.exam: Expect a fact pattern with a use that predates zoning plus an expansion request. Keeping it is nonconforming use; expanding it usually needs ZBA relief.

blocks.html: A zoning ordinance (in many towns, the zoning law) is adopted by the local legislative body: the town board, village board of trustees, or city council. It divides the municipality into districts and sets, for each one, the allowed uses and the bulk rules: height, lot coverage, density, and setbacks (minimum distances from lot lines).
blocks.casual: A zoning ordinance (lots of towns call it the zoning law) gets passed by the local legislature: the town board, the village board of trustees, or the city council. It splits the municipality into districts and, for each one, spells out what uses are allowed and the bulk rules: height, lot coverage, density, and setbacks, which are the minimum distances from the lot lines.

deeper.plain: The local legislature draws districts on a map and writes what can go where and how big it can be.
deeper.picture: Think of a parking garage with painted zones: compact cars here, motorcycles there, no trucks above level 2, and stay a foot off the wall.
deeper.street: Leo wants to add a rear deck in Bay Ridge. His architect checks the district's rear-yard setback, finds it's 30 feet, and designs the deck to stop at 30 feet from the back lot line so it's as of right.
deeper.stakes: Build into a setback without approval and you get a violation, a stop-work order, or a demand to tear it down. Buyers inherit open violations.
deeper.exam: Who adopts zoning? The local legislative body (town board, village board, city council). Not the planning board, not the ZBA. "Setback" means distance from the lot line, not from the street center.

head: Classification
Typical uses
rows: Retail, office, restaurants (C or B districts)
Farms; NY agricultural districts get extra protection from local laws that unreasonably restrict farming
Public open space, park lands, recreational
Parks, beaches, ball fields, preserved land
Undeveloped land, often held under a holding or low-density classification
blocks.caption: Zoning classifications named in the syllabus

deeper.plain: Zoning sorts land into types of use: homes, shops, factories, farms, institutions, open space, and empty land.
deeper.picture: It's like sorting a closet: shoes on the floor, coats on hooks, winter stuff up top. Each shelf has a job.
deeper.street: A Columbia County farmer in a state agricultural district gets a town letter limiting his tractor hours. Because NY gives ag districts extra protection from local rules that unreasonably restrict farming, he files a complaint with the state ag department and the town backs off.
deeper.stakes: Selling a residentially zoned lot to someone who plans a warehouse is a recipe for a canceled deal. Always check the classification before marketing a use.
deeper.exam: Know the letters: R residential, C or B commercial, M or I industrial. Institutional covers schools, hospitals, houses of worship. Agricultural districts get special state protection in NY.

blocks.html: As-of-right means the use and size are already allowed in the district. The owner needs only a building permit, no board hearing, no discretion. If a project is not as of right, the owner must ask a board for something.
blocks.casual: As of right means the use and the size are already allowed in that district. You just pull a building permit. No board hearing, no one gets to use discretion. If your project isn't as of right, you have to ask a board for something.

deeper.plain: If the rules already allow it, you just get a permit and build. No hearings.
deeper.picture: It's like ordering off the menu. No need to ask the chef. Special requests go to the kitchen for approval.
deeper.street: A developer in Long Island City finds a lot where a 12-story residential building is fully allowed. He files plans with the Department of Buildings, gets a permit, and starts in months. A neighbor's request for 18 stories on the next lot needs a rezoning and drags on for a year.
deeper.stakes: Telling a buyer a project is "as of right" when it actually needs a variance can sink their financing and timeline. Lenders and investors price as-of-right sites higher for exactly this reason.
deeper.exam: "No discretionary approval," "only a building permit needed" equals as of right. If the stem mentions a hearing or a board, it's not as of right.

blocks.caption: Start at the top: is the use permitted? Follow the branches to special use permit, area variance, use variance, or rezoning. Note the NYC branch to the BSA.

items: Accessory use: customary and incidental to the main use on the same lot. A detached garage, a shed, a pool for a house.
Home occupation: a small business run inside a dwelling (accountant, tutor), usually limited in employees, signs, and floor area.
Accessory apartment: a second, smaller unit in or on a single-family lot, allowed in many towns by permit, often only if the owner lives on site.

Family: zoning codes define it to control single-family districts. NY's highest court has struck down definitions that exclude unrelated people living together as the functional equivalent of a family.

Group home: under NY's Padavan Law, state-licensed community residences for people with disabilities can be sited in residential neighborhoods; the town gets 40 days to suggest alternatives or object, and is limited to arguing oversaturation or changed character.
blocks.casual:
Some uses ride along with the main one. An accessory use is customary and incidental to the main use on the same lot, like a detached garage, a shed, or a pool behind a house. A home occupation is a small business run inside a home (an accountant, a tutor), usually capped on employees, signs, and floor area. An accessory apartment is a second, smaller unit in or on a single-family lot. Lots of towns allow it with a permit, often only if the owner lives there.
Zoning codes define family to control single-family districts, and NY's highest court has struck down definitions that shut out unrelated people living together as the functional equivalent of a family.
A group home gets special treatment under NY's Padavan Law: state-licensed community residences for people with disabilities can go into residential neighborhoods. The town gets 40 days to suggest other sites or object, and it can only argue oversaturation or changed character.

deeper.plain: Zoning allows small side uses that naturally go with a home, and NY limits how far towns can go in keeping out unrelated households or group homes.
deeper.picture: The main use is the meal. Accessory uses are the side dishes that always come with it. You can't swap the steak for a second steakhouse.
deeper.street: A Westchester town tries to block a state-licensed group home for four adults with developmental disabilities. Under the Padavan Law it has 40 days to respond and can only argue there are already too many such homes nearby. It can't just say neighbors don't want it.
deeper.stakes: An agent who helps neighbors fight a group home based on who will live there can walk into a fair housing violation. Marketing a basement as an accessory apartment without a permit is misrepresentation.
deeper.exam: Accessory use cue words: "customary and incidental," "same lot." Padavan Law: 40 days, limited objections. A definition of family that excludes functionally equivalent households is vulnerable.

head: Tool
How it works
Example
rows: Developer gets a bonus (more height or density) for providing a public benefit
Extra floors in exchange for a public plaza or affordable units
Same total number of homes on smaller lots grouped together, leaving the rest as open space; approved by the planning board
30 homes on 8 acres, 12 acres preserved woods
Whole tract approved as one mixed project
Townhouses, shops and a park on one site
Use is listed as allowed in the district if it meets stated conditions
Church, day care, or gas station allowed with conditions on parking and hours

deeper.plain: Towns can loosen rules in smart ways: give a bonus for a public benefit, group homes together to save land, approve a mixed project whole, or allow a use with conditions.
deeper.picture: These are the "yes, if" answers in zoning. Yes, more floors if you build a plaza. Yes, a day care if you add parking.
deeper.street: A Manhattan developer gets extra floor area by including affordable units (incentive zoning). In Putnam County, a builder puts 30 homes on 8 acres and leaves 12 acres of woods (clustering). A church gets a special use permit in a residential district on condition it adds 40 parking spots.
deeper.stakes: Developers who don't meet the conditions of a special use permit can have it revoked. Buyers of cluster homes usually share the cost of the preserved land through an HOA.
deeper.exam: Incentive zoning means more density for a public benefit. Clustering means same density, rearranged. Special use permit means the use is listed as allowed with conditions, so it's not a variance.

blocks.title: Clustering does not add homes
blocks.html: Clustering keeps the same overall density and rearranges it. If the question says "more units in exchange for a public benefit," that is incentive zoning.
blocks.casual: Clustering keeps the same overall density and just moves it around. It doesn't add homes. If the question says "more units in exchange for a public benefit," that's incentive zoning.

deeper.plain: Clustering rearranges the same number of homes. Incentive zoning adds homes in exchange for a public good.
deeper.picture: Clustering is pushing all the furniture to one side of the room so the kids have space to play. Incentive zoning is the landlord letting you add a room because you painted the hallway.
deeper.street: Evelyn has 12 acres zoned for 30 homes. Clustered, she builds 30 homes on 8 acres. If she wants 36, she has to offer something like affordable units or a public trail under an incentive zoning program.
deeper.stakes: Pitching clustering to an investor as a way to get more lots overpromises, and the plan will come back with the same count.
deeper.exam: Cue words: "same density," "open space preserved" points to clustering. "Bonus," "additional density," "public amenity" points to incentive zoning.

blocks.q: A town's code lists day care centers as allowed in residential districts if the board finds adequate drop-off parking. A day care operator needs a:
c: Use variance
Special use permit
Rezoning
Certificate of nonconformity
blocks.x: The use is contemplated by the ordinance subject to conditions, which is exactly a special use permit (special exception). A use variance is for a use the ordinance does not allow at all.

blocks.html: The zoning board of appeals (ZBA) is appointed by the town or village board. It is administrative and quasi-judicial, not policy making: it does not write zoning. It hears appeals from the building inspector's decisions, interprets the ordinance, grants variances, and in many towns grants special use permits. It holds a public hearing with notice to neighbors, especially abutting owners.
blocks.casual: The zoning board of appeals (ZBA) is appointed by the town or village board. It's administrative and quasi-judicial, not policy making, so it doesn't write zoning. What it does: hears appeals from the building inspector's decisions, interprets the ordinance, grants variances, and in many towns grants special use permits. It holds a public hearing with notice to neighbors, especially abutting owners.

deeper.plain: The ZBA is the referee that hears appeals and grants exceptions. It doesn't make the rules.
deeper.picture: The town board writes the rulebook. The ZBA is the umpire who decides close calls and occasionally lets a player bend a rule for a good reason.
deeper.street: The building inspector tells Leo his garage is a second dwelling and denies the permit. Leo appeals to the ZBA, which reads the ordinance, decides the garage is an accessory structure, and overturns the inspector. Leo's abutting neighbors got notice and testified.
deeper.stakes: Owners who treat the ZBA like a legislature and ask it to "change the zoning" waste months. Neighbors who ignore the hearing notice give up their best shot to object.
deeper.exam: "Quasi-judicial," "appointed," "grants variances," "interprets" all point to the ZBA. If the answer says the ZBA amends the zoning ordinance, it's wrong.

blocks.title: Use variance vs area variance (Town Law 267-b, Village Law 7-712-b)

left.title: Use variance: unnecessary hardship
items: Lets you do a use the district prohibits
Must prove ALL FOUR:
1. Cannot realize a reasonable return under any permitted use (shown with financial evidence)
2. Hardship is unique to the property, not the whole neighborhood
3. Will not alter the essential character of the neighborhood
4. Hardship is not self-created
Hard to get

right.title: Area variance: practical difficulty
items: Bends a dimensional rule: setback, height, lot size, coverage
ZBA balances the benefit to the applicant against the detriment to the community, weighing five factors:
1. Undesirable change or detriment to nearby properties
2. Can the benefit be achieved another feasible way
3. Is the variance substantial
4. Adverse physical or environmental effects
5. Was the difficulty self-created (relevant, but does NOT bar the variance)
Much more common

deeper.plain: A use variance lets you do something the zone forbids and is very hard to get. An area variance bends a size rule and is much easier.
deeper.picture: A use variance is asking to open a bar in a library. An area variance is asking to put the reading lamp a foot closer to the window.
deeper.street: A Rockland owner wants a two-family in a one-family zone (use variance). She must prove with numbers that no permitted use earns a reasonable return, that her lot is unique, that the neighborhood won't change, and that she didn't create the problem. Her neighbor wants a side setback cut from 10 feet to 7 for a mudroom (area variance). The ZBA weighs five factors and grants it.
deeper.stakes: Clients who buy expecting an easy use variance often get denied, and the property is worth only what permitted uses support. A self-created hardship sinks a use variance outright.
deeper.exam: "Unnecessary hardship" goes with use variance. "Practical difficulty" and "balancing test" go with area variance. Remember: self-created hardship bars a use variance but only weighs against an area variance.

blocks.title: Use = Unique, Unreturning, Unchanged, Unself-made
blocks.html: Use variance needs all four. Area variance is a scale: benefit vs detriment. Self-created hardship kills a use variance but only counts against an area variance.
blocks.casual: Use variance needs all four. Think "Unique, Unreturning, Unchanged, Unself-made." Area variance is a scale: benefit to you versus detriment to the neighbors. The big one: self-created hardship kills a use variance but only counts against an area variance.

deeper.plain: Four tests for a use variance, all required. A weighing test for an area variance.
deeper.picture: A use variance is a four-lock door: miss one key and you're stuck outside. An area variance is a kitchen scale.
deeper.street: Marcus's investor client bought a single-family lot knowing it was zoned single-family, then asked for a use variance for a fourplex. The ZBA denied it in ten minutes: the hardship was self-created because he bought with full knowledge.
deeper.stakes: Buying with knowledge of the restriction is the classic self-created hardship. Investors who do it usually lose any shot at a use variance.
deeper.exam: If the question asks which hardship factor is fatal to a use variance, answer self-created. For an area variance, self-creation is "relevant but not determinative."

blocks.title: Sort Sal's three requests
blocks.html:
1. Keep the deli. It predates the 1961 zoning, so it is a legal nonconforming use. No approval needed as long as it continues.
2. Push the rear wall 8 feet into the required yard. A dimensional rule: area variance. And if the deli expands with it, expanding a nonconforming use is usually prohibited without ZBA relief.
3. Second-floor apartment. Depends on the district: if a two-family or mixed use is permitted, it is as of right with a permit; if not, it is a use variance.
Answer: deli grandfathered; rear extension needs an area variance; apartment depends on whether the use is permitted.
blocks.casual:
Let's sort Sal's three requests.
1. Keep the deli. It was there before the 1961 zoning, so it's a legal nonconforming use. No approval needed as long as it keeps running.
2. Push the rear wall 8 feet into the required yard. That's a dimensional rule, so it's an area variance. And if the deli grows with it, expanding a nonconforming use is usually not allowed without ZBA relief.
3. Second-floor apartment. Depends on the district. If two-family or mixed use is permitted, it's as of right with a permit. If not, it's a use variance.
Bottom line: the deli is grandfathered, the rear extension needs an area variance, and the apartment depends on whether the use is permitted.

deeper.plain: Each part of Sal's plan gets its own answer: one is already protected, one needs a size exception, one depends on the zone.
deeper.picture: It's like a restaurant inspection where the kitchen passes, the patio needs a permit, and the rooftop depends on the building's rules.
deeper.street: Sal's attorney files for an area variance for the extension, limited to the residential part so the deli itself doesn't grow. The district allows mixed use on that corner, so the apartment goes in with a permit. The deal closes at $1.4 million with a variance contingency.
deeper.stakes: Closing without a zoning contingency on a plan that needs approvals can leave a buyer owning a building they can't use the way they paid for.
deeper.exam: The exam likes multi-part fact patterns. Classify each piece: predates zoning (nonconforming), dimensional (area variance), prohibited use (use variance), allowed (as of right).

blocks.html: A nonconforming use is a lawful use that existed before the zoning changed. It may continue, but typically cannot be enlarged, may not be rebuilt if mostly destroyed, and is lost if abandoned or discontinued for a period the ordinance sets (often one year). Some towns set an amortization period after which it must end.
blocks.casual: A nonconforming use is a legal use that was already there before the zoning changed. It can keep going, but usually it can't get bigger, may not be rebuilt if it's mostly destroyed, and is lost if it's abandoned or stops for whatever period the ordinance sets (often one year). Some towns set an amortization period, after which the use has to end.

deeper.plain: Something that was legal before the rules changed gets to stay, but only as it is.
deeper.picture: It's like a grandfathered unlimited data plan. You keep it as long as you pay every month. Let it lapse and you can't get it back.
deeper.street: A Bayside deli closes for 14 months while the owner deals with an estate. The ordinance says 12 months of discontinuance ends the nonconforming use. The heirs try to reopen and the building inspector says no: it's residential now.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who pays commercial value for a building whose nonconforming use already lapsed overpays badly. Fire damage can also end the use if the ordinance bars rebuilding.
deeper.exam: Cue words: "existed before the zoning," "legal nonconforming," "grandfathered." Trap answers say it can expand or that it lasts forever even if abandoned.

blocks.title: "Grandfathered" is not "forever and bigger"
blocks.html: A nonconforming use runs with the land, so a buyer can continue it. But it cannot usually expand, and if the deli closes for longer than the ordinance allows, the right is gone. Ask for proof of continuous use.
blocks.casual: "Grandfathered" doesn't mean forever, and it definitely doesn't mean bigger. A nonconforming use runs with the land, so a buyer can keep it going. But it usually can't expand, and if the deli closes longer than the ordinance allows, the right is gone. Ask for proof the use has been continuous.

deeper.plain: The right transfers to a buyer, but it doesn't grow and it can die from non-use.
deeper.picture: It's a reserved parking spot that comes with the building. You can't paint a second spot next to it, and if you leave it empty for a year, the city takes it back.
deeper.street: Before Sal signs, Jordan asks the seller for utility bills, sales tax filings and the deli's health permits for the last few years. The records show the deli never closed for more than a few weeks, so the nonconforming use is intact.
deeper.stakes: Repeating "it's grandfathered" without proof is how agents end up in a buyer's lawsuit. Ask for documents.
deeper.exam: True or false traps: "a nonconforming use can be sold" (true, it runs with the land). "A nonconforming use can be expanded as of right" (false). "It survives indefinite abandonment" (false).

blocks.html: Spot zoning is rezoning a single small parcel for the benefit of one owner, inconsistent with the comprehensive plan and the surrounding area. Courts strike it down. A rezoning that fits the master plan and benefits the community is not spot zoning even if one parcel is affected.
blocks.casual: Spot zoning means rezoning one small parcel just to benefit one owner, out of step with the comprehensive plan and the area around it. Courts strike it down. But if a rezoning fits the master plan and helps the community, it's not spot zoning, even if it only touches one parcel.

deeper.plain: Rezoning one lot as a favor to its owner is illegal. Rezoning one lot because the plan calls for it is fine.
deeper.picture: It's like a teacher changing the grading rules for one student who happens to be her nephew.
deeper.street: A town board rezones one acre in a residential neighborhood to commercial so a board member's brother can open a car wash. Neighbors sue, and the court voids it as spot zoning. A year later, the town rezones a parcel near the train station for apartments because the master plan calls for transit housing. That one holds up.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who pay up for a parcel based on a spot rezoning can lose the rezoning in court and be left with the old use.
deeper.exam: Spot zoning cue words: "single parcel," "benefits one owner," "inconsistent with the comprehensive plan." The trap: a one-parcel rezoning that follows the plan is not spot zoning.

blocks.q: An owner wants to build a home office 3 feet into a required 10-foot side yard. She bought the lot knowing about the setback. The ZBA:
c: Must deny it, because the hardship is self-created
May grant an area variance after balancing the five factors; self-creation is considered but not fatal
Cannot hear it; only the town board can
Must grant it, because home occupations are as of right
blocks.x: This is an area variance. Self-created difficulty is one factor but does not bar relief. That bar applies to use variances.

blocks.text: Challenging a decision and enforcing the code

blocks.html: A person aggrieved by a ZBA or planning board decision goes to State Supreme Court in an Article 78 proceeding (CPLR Article 78). For ZBA and planning board decisions the deadline is short: 30 days after the decision is filed with the town or village clerk. The court asks whether the board acted arbitrarily, illegally, or without substantial evidence. It does not redo the hearing.
blocks.casual: If you're aggrieved by a ZBA or planning board decision, you go to State Supreme Court with an Article 78 proceeding (CPLR Article 78). The clock is short: 30 days after the decision is filed with the town or village clerk. The court asks whether the board acted arbitrarily, illegally, or without substantial evidence. It doesn't redo the hearing.

deeper.plain: You can challenge a board's decision in court, but you have only 30 days, and the judge only checks whether the board acted fairly and lawfully.
deeper.picture: It's like asking the league to review a referee's call. They check whether the ref followed the rules, not whether they would have called it differently.
deeper.street: Neighbors in a Westchester village hear the ZBA granted a variance for a 3-story addition. The decision is filed with the clerk on June 3. They have until early July to file an Article 78. They file on day 34, and the court tosses the case as untimely.
deeper.stakes: Missing the 30-day window means losing your challenge forever, no matter how wrong the board was.
deeper.exam: Article 78 is how you challenge a government board or agency in NY (also DOS license decisions). The court is State Supreme Court. Remember 30 days from filing with the clerk for zoning boards.

head: Enforcer
Role
rows: Building department (building inspector, code enforcement officer)
Issues permits and COs, inspects, writes stop-work orders and violations
Professional services (town engineer, environmental and planning consultants)
Review plans, drainage, traffic for the boards
Local courts (town and village justice courts)
Hear code violation charges, impose fines

deeper.plain: Several local players enforce land use rules: the building department, outside experts, the health board, and local courts.
deeper.picture: The building department is the cop on the beat, consultants are the crime lab, the health board handles anything to do with water and waste, and the justice court hands out the fines.
deeper.street: A homeowner in a Putnam town installs a new septic system without approval. The county health department flags it, the code enforcement officer issues a violation, and the homeowner pays a $750 fine in town justice court and has to redo the system.
deeper.stakes: Open violations show up in municipal searches and can delay a closing or force a price cut.
deeper.exam: Building inspector issues permits, COs, stop-work orders. The health board handles wells and septic. Town and village justice courts hear code violations.

blocks.text: New York City does it differently

head: Function
Most of NY
New York City
rows: Town board, village board, city council
City Planning Commission and City Council (Zoning Resolution)
Board of Standards and Appeals (BSA); some special permits from the CPC
City Planning Commission with the Department of City Planning

deeper.plain: NYC uses different names and bodies for the same jobs: BSA instead of a ZBA, the City Planning Commission instead of a planning board, and ULURP for big decisions.
deeper.picture: Same game, different stadium. The positions are the same, but the city's team has its own jerseys.
deeper.street: A Bronx church wants a variance to build affordable housing taller than allowed. It goes to the Board of Standards and Appeals, not a ZBA. A rezoning of a whole neighborhood goes through ULURP with the City Planning Commission and City Council.
deeper.stakes: Sending an NYC client to "the zoning board of appeals" signals you don't know the city system. Clients lose time and confidence.
deeper.exam: Pairings to memorize: NYC variances equal BSA. NYC zoning text and maps equal City Planning Commission and City Council. Big land use actions equal ULURP.

blocks.title: ULURP: the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (about 7 months)

items.title: Certification
items.html: Department of City Planning certifies the application as complete.

items.title: Community Board: 60 days
items.html: Public hearing and advisory recommendation.

items.title: Borough President: 30 days
items.html: Advisory recommendation (the Borough Board too if more than one district is affected).

items.title: City Planning Commission: 60 days
items.html: Hearing and binding vote to approve, modify, or deny.

items.title: City Council: 50 days
items.html: Reviews zoning map changes and other actions; votes.

items.title: Mayor: 5 days
items.html: May veto; the Council can override by a two-thirds vote within 10 days.

blocks.casual: ULURP, the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure, takes about 7 months. First, the Department of City Planning certifies the application as complete. Then the Community Board gets 60 days for a public hearing and an advisory recommendation. The Borough President gets 30 days to give an advisory recommendation (the Borough Board too if more than one district is affected). The City Planning Commission gets 60 days for a hearing and a binding vote to approve, modify or deny. The City Council gets 50 days to review zoning map changes and other actions and vote. Then the Mayor has 5 days and can veto, and the Council can override with a two-thirds vote within 10 days.

deeper.plain: Big NYC land use changes go through a fixed sequence of reviews with set deadlines, from the community board up to the mayor.
deeper.picture: It's a relay race with a stopwatch at each handoff: 60, 30, 60, 50, 5.
deeper.street: A developer wants to rezone a Gowanus block for housing. The Community Board votes no (advisory). The Borough President says yes with conditions (advisory). The CPC approves with modifications (binding). The Council approves, the Mayor signs, and seven months later the zoning map changes.
deeper.stakes: Investors who don't budget seven-plus months of carrying costs, plus the risk of a Council no, can lose their deal. Community board votes don't kill a project but do shape it.
deeper.exam: Know which steps are advisory (Community Board, Borough President) and which are binding (CPC, Council). Numbers to know: 60, 30, 60, 50, 5, and a two-thirds override.

blocks.html: Air rights are the unused development rights above a lot. In NYC, unused floor area can be moved: to an adjacent lot through a zoning lot merger, or through a transfer of development rights (TDR) from a landmark or a special district to a receiving site. Penn Central's Grand Central air rights are the classic example. Outside NYC, towns use TDR programs to preserve farmland: the farm sells its development rights to a builder in a growth area.
blocks.casual: Air rights are the development rights a lot isn't using yet. In NYC, unused floor area can move: to the lot next door through a zoning lot merger, or through a transfer of development rights (TDR) from a landmark or a special district to a receiving site. The Grand Central air rights from Penn Central are the classic example. Outside the city, towns use TDR programs to save farmland: the farm sells its development rights to a builder in a growth area.

deeper.plain: If you aren't using all the building space zoning allows, you may be able to sell it to someone else.
deeper.picture: It's like rollover minutes on a phone plan that you can sell to your neighbor.
deeper.street: A Midtown church sits on a lot zoned for 200,000 square feet but uses only 30,000. A developer next door buys 100,000 square feet of its air rights through a zoning lot merger and builds a taller tower. The church gets $40 million for its roof repairs and programs.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who don't know their lot has unused air rights can leave serious money on the table. Buyers next to a low building can lose a view if those rights get sold.
deeper.exam: TDR cue words: "sending site," "receiving site," "landmark," "farmland preservation." Air rights are a property right that can be sold separately from the building.

blocks.title: City of Yes (2024)
blocks.html: In December 2024 the City Council adopted City of Yes for Housing Opportunity, a citywide zoning text change that, among other things, ended required parking for new housing in much of the city and allows accessory dwelling units on many one and two family lots. Expect listings and buyers to ask about it.
blocks.casual: In December 2024 the City Council passed City of Yes for Housing Opportunity, a citywide zoning text change. Among other things it ended required parking for new housing in much of the city and allows accessory dwelling units on many one and two family lots. Expect listings and buyers to ask about it.

deeper.plain: NYC loosened its zoning in 2024 to allow more housing, including backyard and basement units on many small lots and less required parking.
deeper.picture: It's like a building management finally allowing tenants to add a small loft without a fight.
deeper.street: The Okafors ask Jordan whether they could add a backyard cottage for their daughter before selling. Jordan tells them City of Yes may allow an ADU on their lot, but it still needs DOB permits and must meet the rules, and the buyer's attorney will want to see those.
deeper.stakes: Marketing "ADU potential" without checking whether the specific lot qualifies is overpromising. A buyer who relies on it and can't build has a complaint.
deeper.exam: This is newer than the 2022 syllabus, so the state exam may not test it directly. Know it for practice: it's an NYC zoning text change adopted by the City Council.

blocks.q: In New York City, a homeowner who needs a variance applies to the:
c: City Planning Commission
Community Board
Board of Standards and Appeals
Department of Finance
blocks.x: The BSA is NYC's version of a zoning board of appeals. The Community Board is only advisory, and the CPC handles rezonings and ULURP.

story.title: Grandfathered
story.setting: Bayside, Queens, a corner deli on a Saturday morning

beats.text: Seller says it's all grandfathered. Deli downstairs, I add an apartment upstairs, push the back out eight feet. Done.
The deli, maybe. It's been here since '51 and the zoning came in '61. That's a legal nonconforming use.
So I can make it bigger.
Usually no. Grandfathered means you can keep it, not grow it. And if it's dark for a year, you can lose it.

check.q: The deli closes for 18 months during a dispute. The ordinance says nonconforming uses discontinued for 1 year are lost. Result?
c: Sal can reopen anytime
The nonconforming right is lost; the lot must follow current zoning
Sal needs a special use permit
The town must pay Sal
check.x: Discontinuance beyond the ordinance's period ends the nonconforming use. After that, only permitted uses are allowed.

beats.text: The eight feet out back?
That's the rear yard setback. You'd need an area variance. In the city that's the BSA, not a local ZBA.
And they'll say what?
They balance it. Does it hurt the neighbors? Could you get the space another way? Is it a big ask? Did you create the problem? That last one counts, but it doesn't kill it.
What if I wanted to turn the whole thing into a laundromat?
If it's not permitted, that's a use variance. All four: no reasonable return under any allowed use, unique hardship, won't change the neighborhood, not self-created. Very hard.
Sal grumbled about "the city" for five minutes, then ordered a buttered roll.
And if they say no?
Article 78 in Supreme Court. The court asks if the board was arbitrary, not whether it was right.
Later, at the office: Good. Grandfathered is the most expensive word in real estate. Always ask for proof of continuous use and pull the CO.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: use variance on the left, area variance on the right. Write each test factor, then circle the one factor that behaves differently on each side.

facts.text: The local legislative body adopts the zoning ordinance, which sets each district's uses and bulk rules: height, coverage, density and setbacks.
Zoning classes include residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural (protected by NY agricultural districts), institutional, open space and vacant.
An as-of-right project already complies with the district's rules and needs only a building permit, no board hearing.
An accessory use is customary and incidental to the main use on the same lot, such as a detached garage.
A home occupation is a small business inside a dwelling, usually limited in employees, signs and floor area.
An accessory apartment is a smaller second unit on a single-family lot, often allowed only if the owner lives on site.
NY's highest court has struck down zoning definitions of family that exclude unrelated people living as the functional equivalent of a family.
Under NY's Padavan Law a town has 40 days to suggest alternatives or object to a state-licensed community residence, mainly on oversaturation.
Incentive zoning gives a developer extra height or density in exchange for a public benefit such as a plaza or affordable units.
Clustering keeps the same total number of homes on smaller grouped lots and preserves the rest as open space; it does not add homes.
A special use permit allows a use listed for the district if it meets the ordinance's stated conditions.
The ZBA is appointed and quasi-judicial: it hears appeals from the building inspector, interprets the ordinance and grants variances, but does not write zoning.
The ZBA holds a public hearing with notice to neighbors, especially abutting owners.
A use variance requires unnecessary hardship, proving all four: no reasonable return under any permitted use, unique hardship, no change to neighborhood character, not self-created.
An area variance (practical difficulty) balances benefit to the applicant against detriment to the community; self-created difficulty is a factor but not a bar.
A nonconforming use is a lawful use that predates the zoning change; it may continue and runs with the land to a buyer.
A nonconforming use generally cannot be enlarged, may not be rebuilt if mostly destroyed, and is lost if discontinued for the period set (often one year).
Spot zoning rezones one small parcel for its owner, inconsistent with the comprehensive plan, and courts strike it down.
A ZBA or planning board decision is challenged in State Supreme Court by an Article 78 proceeding within 30 days after the decision is filed with the clerk.
The building department issues permits and COs and writes stop-work orders; boards of health handle wells and septic; justice courts hear code violations.
In NYC the Board of Standards and Appeals grants variances, and the City Planning Commission and City Council write zoning.
ULURP runs about 7 months: Community Board 60 days, Borough President 30, City Planning Commission 60 with a binding vote, City Council 50, Mayor 5.
Unused air rights can move to an adjacent lot by zoning lot merger or to a receiving site by transfer of development rights, as from a landmark.
NYC's City of Yes for Housing Opportunity (2024) ended required parking for new housing in much of the city and allows ADUs on many one and two family lots.

lessons.title: Case file: Forty Lots on Bedell Road
lessons.tagline: A Columbia County dairy farm, a builder with a plat, and every board that gets a vote before the first house goes up.
objectives: Decide which local and state bodies review a rural subdivision and in what order, including the official map and county referral.
Apply SEQRA's lead agency, declaration, and EIS steps and their effect on subdivision deadlines.
Apply cluster development, parkland, and moratorium rules to a proposed plat.
Apply the Open Meetings Law, plat filing deadlines, Article 78 timing, and private covenants to a project after approval.

blocks.title: Sixty-four acres and a handshake
blocks.html: Ruth Dutcher's family has farmed 64 acres on Bedell Road in Columbia County since 1922. At 74, she is done milking cows, and her children live in Albany and Denver. A builder from Saratoga, Tom Kessler, offers $1.1 million if he can get approval for 40 house lots, and nothing if he cannot. Ruth's nephew is a friend of Diane's, so Jordan is helping Diane's upstate referral partner with the listing side. Kessler's attorney sends a draft contract with a subdivision contingency and a 14-month approval period. Before anyone signs, the referral broker asks Jordan to make a list of every government body that will have a say, and in what order.

Jordan starts with the parcel itself. The county's GIS map shows the farm inside a state-certified agricultural district, part of the official map's proposed road network, and a small stream with wetlands along the back 15 acres. The town's zoning puts the whole farm in an R-1.5 district: single-family homes on lots of at least 1.5 acres.

blocks.q: The farm sits in a state-certified agricultural district. What does New York require at the contract stage?
c: Nothing, because the buyer will take the land out of farming once the lots are approved
Approval of the sale by the county agricultural district board before contract
A signed agricultural district disclosure notice given to the buyer before the sale
A deed restriction keeping at least half the acreage in farming for 20 years
blocks.x: Real Property Law 333-c requires a seller of land partly or wholly within an agricultural district to give the buyer a disclosure notice, signed by both, before the sale. It warns that farm operations nearby may bring noise, dust and odors, and that the location can affect water and sewer access. The trap is the ownership-change answer: the notice is required regardless of what the buyer plans. No board approves private sales of district land.

blocks.html: Kessler did the math the way builders do: 64 acres, 1.5-acre minimum, take out roads, so about 40 lots. Ruth asked whether 40 houses were therefore allowed "as of right," since every lot would meet the zoning.

blocks.q: Each of Kessler's 40 lots would meet the 1.5-acre minimum. Who must approve dividing the farm into lots?
c: Nobody, since lots that meet the zoning are as of right and need just building permits
The zoning board of appeals, which approves any change to the number of lots
The planning board, through subdivision review of a preliminary and final plat
The county clerk, who records the plat once a licensed surveyor certifies it
blocks.x: As of right describes uses and dimensions a district allows without discretionary approval. Splitting land into lots is different: it needs subdivision approval from the planning board, which reviews the plat for lot layout, roads, drainage, utilities and density. The trap is the ZBA, which hears variances and appeals, not subdivisions. The county clerk files an approved plat but does not approve it.

blocks.text: The road that is already on the map

blocks.html: The town's official map, adopted with its comprehensive plan in 2018, shows a proposed collector road crossing the Dutcher farm from Bedell Road to County Route 21. Kessler's sketch put three house lots right across it.

blocks.q: Kessler's sketch places three house lots on a road shown on the town's official map. What is the likely result?
c: The board will likely make the plat fit the mapped road
The map is advisory; the board approves the lots if they meet zoning
The town has to buy the road land now or lose the right to keep it open
Kessler can build first and let the town condemn the houses later
blocks.x: An official map shows existing and proposed streets, parks and drainage, and building within a mapped street bed is generally not allowed without relief. A planning board reviewing a plat will expect the layout to fit the official map, often by making the mapped road one of the subdivision's streets. The trap is "advisory": the comprehensive plan is a guide, but the official map has legal effect. The town does not have to buy the land up front.

blocks.html: Kessler's engineer redrew the plan with the mapped road as the spine of the subdivision. He lost two lots. The town engineer, a consultant the planning board hires, started reviewing drainage and road profiles, with the cost charged to Kessler's escrow account under the town's fee law.

The planning board declared itself lead agency for the State Environmental Quality Review Act, coordinating with the county health department (wells and septic), the state Department of Environmental Conservation (the stream and wetlands), and the town highway superintendent. Kessler filed a full Environmental Assessment Form. The state Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation, through its State Historic Preservation Office, flagged the back field as archaeologically sensitive: the area along the stream had produced artifacts on a nearby farm.

blocks.q: The planning board finds the subdivision may have significant impacts on the wetlands, traffic, and possible archaeological resources. What comes next under SEQRA?
c: A negative declaration, with conditions to avoid the wetlands written into the plat
A referendum of town voters, since the project changes the comprehensive plan
Referral to the DEC, which takes over as lead agency because wetlands are involved
A positive declaration, then a draft EIS, comment, a final EIS, findings
blocks.x: Where an action may have a significant adverse impact, the lead agency issues a positive declaration, which requires an environmental impact statement: a draft EIS, a public comment period of at least 30 days, often a hearing, a final EIS, and written findings before the board decides. The trap is the conditioned negative declaration: when impacts may be significant, conditions cannot replace an EIS for a project like this. Lead agency does not shift just because DEC issues a permit.

blocks.title: OPRHP and archaeology
blocks.html: The State Historic Preservation Office, part of OPRHP, reviews projects that need state permits or funding for effects on historic and archaeological resources. A Phase 1A and 1B archaeological survey, a literature search and then shovel tests, is common on farmland near streams in the Hudson Valley. Findings can move lots, add a conservation easement, or require deeper study.

The draft EIS ran to 300 pages. Its traffic chapter projected trips onto Bedell Road; its community services chapter estimated school-age children from census tract data on household size, and compared them with the district's enrollment trend. The topography chapter, built on the surveyor's two-foot contour map, showed which lots would drain toward the stream. Jordan, who had never read an EIS, found the demography section the most useful: it was a free market study of who lived in the area and how fast it was growing.

blocks.q: To estimate how many schoolchildren 38 new homes would add, the EIS consultant most likely relied on:
c: The town's official map of proposed streets and drainage ways
Census tract data on household size and ages
The building department's file of open permits in the town
The county clerk's index of recorded deeds for the last year
blocks.x: Demography is the study of population characteristics. Planners use census tract data (small statistical areas the Census Bureau defines) to estimate household size, ages and growth, then project school enrollment, traffic and demand for services. The trap is the official map: it shows where streets and parks will go, not who will live there. Deed indexes and permit files track transactions and construction, not population.

blocks.html: Kessler filed his preliminary plat in May. His attorney expected a hearing within 62 days. The planning board chair explained that the clock would not start yet.

blocks.q: Under the Town Law, when the subdivision needs an EIS, when does the 62-day deadline for the preliminary plat public hearing generally start?
c: When the draft EIS is accepted and its notice of completion is filed
When Kessler files the preliminary plat with the planning board clerk
When the town board votes to approve the comprehensive plan update
When the final EIS is filed and the SEQRA findings are adopted
blocks.x: Town Law 276 ties the preliminary plat hearing to SEQRA. Without an EIS, the hearing is due within 62 days after a complete plat is received. With one, the clock runs from the filing of the notice of completion of the draft EIS, and the plat hearing is usually held together with the DEIS hearing. The trap is the plat filing date, which only applies when no EIS is required. If a board misses its deadlines after SEQRA is done, the plat can be deemed approved.

blocks.html: At the DEIS hearing, a dozen neighbors spoke. Most wanted the back fields kept open. The planning board asked Kessler to consider a cluster layout: smaller lots grouped near the new road, with the stream corridor and the archaeologically sensitive fields kept as permanent open space. The town board had authorized cluster development by local law years earlier.

blocks.q: Kessler asks whether he can fit 48 lots instead of 38 if he agrees to cluster them and preserve 30 acres. Under Town Law 278, the board:
c: May approve 48, since clustering is designed to reward open space with extra homes
May approve 48 if the town board also passes an incentive zoning law
May approve up to the number a conventional plat would yield, here 38
Has to approve 48 if the county planning agency recommends the cluster
blocks.x: Cluster development rearranges density; it does not add to it. The number of lots cannot exceed what a conventional subdivision under the zoning would allow, here the 38 lots of the revised plan. The open land is preserved by deed restriction, an HOA, or a conservation easement. The trap is the reward answer, which describes incentive zoning: extra density in exchange for a public benefit, a separate tool a town must adopt on its own.

blocks.html: Kessler agreed to 38 clustered lots on about 30 acres, with 28 acres preserved. Then the board raised parkland. The town's recreation plan showed a shortage of ball fields in that part of town, and the preserved fields were wetlands and archaeology, not usable recreation land.

blocks.q: The planning board finds the town needs more recreation land but no suitable park site exists on Kessler's plat. Under Town Law 277, it may:
c: Require Kessler to buy land elsewhere in town and deed it to the town as a park
Require a payment in lieu of parkland, held in a recreation trust fund
Reduce the number of lots by one for each acre of parkland the plat should have had
Do nothing further, since preserving open space satisfies the parkland requirement
blocks.x: A planning board may require parkland on a residential plat after finding a need for recreation land. If a suitable park cannot be properly located on the plat, it may require a money payment instead, in an amount set by the town board, held in a trust fund for park and recreation purposes. The trap is the open space answer: conservation land that cannot be used for recreation does not automatically satisfy the parkland finding.

blocks.html: In September, with the final EIS in draft, the town board adopted a six-month moratorium on new major subdivision applications while it updated its comprehensive plan for the northern part of town. Kessler's attorney called Jordan's broker in a panic.

blocks.q: Is the town's six-month moratorium on new major subdivision applications likely valid?
c: No. A moratorium on development is a taking that requires just compensation
Yes, but it can last indefinitely once it has been adopted by local law
No. The state, not a town board, is the body that may pause land use approvals
Yes, if it is reasonable in length and tied to a real planning purpose
blocks.x: A temporary moratorium is a valid exercise of the police power when it is reasonably limited in time and adopted to deal with a genuine planning problem, such as updating a comprehensive plan. Courts look harder at moratoriums that are renewed again and again. The trap is the taking answer: a temporary pause that leaves the owner future use is not a taking. As written, this one applies to new applications, so Kessler's pending plat continues.

blocks.html: The moratorium had a purpose Jordan found worth knowing. The planning board's study for the plan update showed that three large subdivisions in the north end would together add about 150 homes, enough to overload a two-lane bridge and the town's small water district. The planning board advises the town board on exactly this: what growth will cost, which roads and water lines the capital budget will need to fund over the next decade, and whether zoning in the area should change. A moratorium buys time to make those decisions before the applications make them by default.

Kessler's plan also included a small community building and pool near Route 21, a state highway, which needed site plan approval from the planning board. Because the site lies within 500 feet of a state highway, General Municipal Law 239-m required the planning board to refer the site plan to the county planning board first. The county recommended moving the driveway away from a curve.

blocks.q: If the planning board wants to approve the site plan without the county's recommended driveway change, what vote does it need?
c: A simple majority of the members present at the meeting
A unanimous vote, since a county recommendation cannot be overridden
A two-thirds vote of the town board instead of the planning board
A majority plus one of all the members of the board
blocks.x: Under GML 239-m, when the county recommends modification or disapproval of a referred action, the local board may act contrary to it only by a vote of a majority plus one of all its members, with its reasons stated. The trap is the simple majority: a county recommendation of modification raises the vote needed. If the county does not respond within 30 days, the local board can act without its report.

blocks.html: Frustrated by delays, Kessler invited three of the planning board's five members to breakfast at a diner on Route 9H "just to talk informally about where things stand." He did not invite the press or the neighbors. He planned to hint, over eggs, that if the board kept asking for studies he might sell the farm to a solar company instead, which the town's zoning would also allow.
One member, a retired surveyor, felt uneasy and called the planning board's attorney the night before to ask whether she should go.

blocks.q: Three of five planning board members meet Kessler at a diner to discuss his pending subdivision. Under the Open Meetings Law:
c: It is a private social event, since no vote is taken and nothing is recorded
It is allowed if the members disclose the breakfast at their next public meeting
It is a quorum meeting on public business, which needed notice
It is a violation by Kessler, but the members themselves have done nothing wrong
blocks.x: Three of five members is a quorum. When a quorum gathers to discuss public business, it is a meeting under the Open Meetings Law even with no vote: it needs advance public notice and must be open, with minutes. Action taken in violation can be voided by a court. The trap is "no vote, no meeting": New York courts treat planned quorum gatherings to discuss business as meetings. The board's attorney told the members to cancel.

blocks.html: While the review dragged on, the town highway superintendent weighed in on the roads. Kessler wanted the new road to be private, maintained by the homeowners association, to save money on the town's road specifications. The superintendent wanted it built to town standards and offered for dedication, so plows and school buses could use it and the town could connect it to County Route 21 someday, as the official map intended. Lenders cared too. A buyer's FHA or conventional lender needs either a public road or a recorded private road maintenance agreement before it will lend on a lot.

blocks.q: Who generally pays to build the roads, drainage and other infrastructure inside a new subdivision?
c: The developer, with a bond guaranteeing completion
The town, from its capital budget, once the plat is filed
The county, if the road will connect to a county route
The first buyers, through a special assessment at closing
blocks.x: Subdivision regulations make the developer build the internal roads, drainage and utilities to town specifications. Because lots are often sold before everything is finished, the planning board can require a performance bond or other security so the town can complete the work if the developer does not. The trap is the capital budget: towns plan for growth-related costs outside the subdivision, such as a new water tank, but they do not build a developer's streets.

blocks.html: The planning board adopted its SEQRA findings in March, granted preliminary and then final plat approval in May, with conditions: a performance bond to guarantee the roads and drainage, the parkland fee, and a recorded declaration of covenants and restrictions. The declaration created a homeowners association to own the 28 preserved acres, banned further subdivision of any lot, and required houses of at least 1,600 square feet.

blocks.q: Final plat approval was granted May 12. What must Kessler do to keep it from expiring?
c: Nothing, since a final approval of a subdivision plat does not expire
File the approved plat with the county clerk within 62 days
Start construction of the roads within 180 days of the approval
Sell at least one lot within a year to show the plat is in use
blocks.x: Town Law 276 requires the owner to file the approved final plat in the county clerk's office within 62 days of the planning board's signature, or the approval expires. Filing creates the recorded map that deeds will refer to by lot number. The trap is the 180-day figure, which applies to conditional final approval: the conditions must be satisfied within 180 days, with possible 90-day extensions.

blocks.html: Kessler also mentioned that he might sell a few lots to buyers on an installment plan, collecting payments over five years before delivering deeds. Jordan's broker flagged New York's Article 9-A of the Real Property Law, which covers offering subdivided vacant land to New York residents on installment terms and requires a filing with the Department of State and an offering statement for every buyer. The federal Interstate Land Sales Act was not a concern: 38 lots is well under its 100-lot threshold.

blocks.q: Six years after closing, an owner on the new subdivision opens a boarding kennel in her garage. Town zoning would allow it with a special permit, but the declaration bans commercial kennels. The HOA:
c: Cannot act, because zoning approval overrides a private covenant
Can sue to enforce the covenant, but delay may weaken its case
Has to ask the ZBA to revoke her permit before it can act
Can fine her under the zoning code as the town's enforcement agent
blocks.x: A recorded covenant binds every owner, and the HOA or neighbors can enforce it in court, typically by injunction. When private and public rules conflict, the stricter one controls, so a special permit does not cancel the covenant. But under the doctrine of laches, an HOA that knowingly waits years while the owner invests in the business may lose the right to enforce. The trap is "zoning overrides": public approval does not erase private restrictions.

blocks.html: Approval of the plat was not permission to build. Each buyer would still need a building permit for a house on a lot, a septic and well approval from the county health department, and inspections, ending with a certificate of occupancy. Jordan made a note for his future listing descriptions: "approved lot" means a lot on a filed plat; it does not mean a house can be built without the remaining permits, and a lot with poor percolation can still fail for septic.

In June, 31 days after the final approval was filed with the town clerk, a group of neighbors filed an Article 78 petition challenging the subdivision. The court dismissed it as untimely: challenges to a planning board's decision must be brought within 30 days after the decision is filed with the town clerk. Ruth Dutcher closed with Kessler the following month and moved to Albany. The ball field fee went into the town's recreation trust fund, and the back fields became a preserve with a trail.

items: Meeting the zoning does not make a subdivision as of right; the planning board approves plats, and the official map can dictate where roads go.

SEQRA runs alongside subdivision review: a lead agency, an EAF, then a negative or positive declaration; a positive declaration means a DEIS, public comment, a FEIS and findings, and it moves the plat hearing clock.
Clustering keeps the conventional lot count while preserving open space; parkland or a fee in lieu requires a finding of need; temporary moratoriums tied to planning are valid.
County referral under GML 239-m applies within 500 feet of state roads and other listed features; overriding a county recommendation takes a majority plus one.

Quorum gatherings are meetings under the Open Meetings Law. Final plats must be filed within 62 days; Article 78 challenges must come within 30 days of filing with the clerk. Covenants bind owners even where zoning is looser, subject to laches.
Agricultural district land needs the RPL 333-c disclosure; installment sales of vacant subdivided land to NY residents trigger Article 9-A.

lessons.title: Case file: Four Problems on Ridge Road
lessons.tagline: An illegal garage apartment, a deck too close to the line, a corner store that closed too long, and a group home two doors down.
objectives: Decide whether a property owner needs a special use permit, an area variance, a use variance, or nothing at all.
Apply the area variance balancing test and the four elements of a use variance, including self-created hardship.
Apply nonconforming use, home occupation, family definition, and group home rules to real neighbors.
Identify who enforces the zoning code, who hears appeals, and when an Article 78 challenge is too late.

blocks.title: One block, four zoning problems
blocks.html: Linda Moreau, an accountant, is selling her colonial at 14 Ridge Road in Elm Harbor, a village in Westchester (the village is fictional; the rules are New York's). Jordan's firm has a referral listing there, and Diane sends Jordan up on the Metro-North to help. Linda's house has a rented apartment over the garage, a big deck along the side, and a home office where her three employees prepare tax returns. On the corner of Ridge Road and Route 9 sits an old grocery that closed last year, which Evelyn Park has just bought. Two doors down, a nonprofit plans a group home. The listing sheet Linda wrote herself says "Legal 2-family! Garage apt rents for $1,900!" Jordan's first job is to find out if that is true.

Jordan pulled the village building department file. The certificate of occupancy, issued in 1964, says "one-family dwelling." There is no permit for the garage apartment, no permit for the deck, and a 2019 note from the building inspector about a sign on the lawn. The zoning district is R-10: single-family homes on 10,000-square-foot lots, with 10-foot side yards.

head: Item
What the file shows
What the listing says
rows: No permit; 6 feet from the side lot line
blocks.caption: Building department file vs. Linda's listing

blocks.q: Linda wants to keep "Legal 2-family" and the $1,900 rent in the listing. What should Jordan do?
c: Keep it, since the apartment has been rented for years without a complaint
Keep the rent but change "legal" to "potential", which avoids any claim
Remove both claims and disclose that the CO covers a one-family dwelling
Keep it, since zoning is the buyer's attorney's problem, not the agent's
blocks.x: The certificate of occupancy controls the lawful use. An apartment with no permit and no CO is not legal, and advertising it as legal or as rental income misrepresents a material fact, exposing Jordan and the broker to discipline and liability. The trap is "potential": telling buyers the rent is $1,900 still implies lawful income. Years without a complaint do not legalize anything; enforcement can come any time.

blocks.text: Can the apartment be made legal?
