blocks.html: Elm Harbor's zoning code allows an accessory apartment in a single-family house by special permit from the zoning board of appeals, if the owner lives in one of the units, the apartment is no more than 600 square feet, one extra off-street parking space is provided, and the permit is renewed every three years. Sam and Priscilla Odum, the buyers who made the best offer, plan to live in the main house and rent the garage unit to Priscilla's mother.

blocks.q: To legalize the garage apartment, what kind of approval do the Odums need?
c: A special use permit, since the code allows it with conditions
A use variance, since a second unit is not an as-of-right use in the R-10 district
An area variance, because the apartment adds floor area to the lot
A rezoning of their lot to a two-family district by the village board
blocks.x: When the code lists a use as allowed in a district subject to conditions, the approval is a special use permit. The applicant has to show it meets the conditions, not that it suffers hardship. The trap is the use variance: that is for a use the code prohibits outright, and it needs proof of unnecessary hardship. Rezoning one lot for one owner would invite a spot zoning challenge.

blocks.html: The contract went to Priya's colleague in White Plains. It was made contingent on the ZBA granting the special permit within 120 days, with the Odums applying at their own cost and Linda cooperating. Linda agreed to stop renting the apartment and to give the tenant proper notice. Jordan rewrote the listing: "One-family colonial with a finished space over the garage; buyer to verify permitted uses." Linda grumbled that it sounded less exciting. It was also true.

Jordan also explained to Linda why an illegal unit hurts a sale even when nobody complains. An appraiser generally cannot value an unpermitted apartment as a legal unit, so the rent does not support the price. The buyers' lender may refuse to count the rent as income. A homeowners insurer can contest a claim involving an undisclosed rental. And a buyer's attorney will ask for a credit or a contingency, which is exactly what happened here.

The 2021 deck sits 6 feet from the side lot line. The code requires 10. Linda built it without a permit; she says the contractor told her none was needed. The Odums love the deck. Their lender's appraiser has already noted the open violation risk.

blocks.q: If the Odums ask the ZBA to legalize the deck 4 feet into the side yard, how will the board decide?
c: It has to deny, since Linda created the problem by building without a permit
It approves automatically if no neighbor objects at the public hearing
It grants if the Odums prove they cannot earn a reasonable return
It weighs the owner's benefit against harm to the neighborhood
blocks.x: An area variance turns on a balancing test: the benefit to the applicant weighed against the detriment to the health, safety and welfare of the neighborhood, using five factors, including whether the difficulty was self-created. Self-creation counts against the applicant but does not bar the variance. The trap is "must deny": that is the use variance rule. Reasonable return is a use variance element, and an unopposed hearing is not an automatic approval.

blocks.html: The application went on the ZBA's agenda with a published legal notice and letters mailed to owners within the distance the village code sets, including every abutting owner. Under SEQRA, granting an individual setback variance for a single-family house is a Type II action, so no environmental review was needed. The board's secretary placed the building file, the survey, and photos in the record, because a ZBA decision must rest on evidence in the record if it is to survive a court challenge.

At the hearing, the next-door neighbor said the deck looked straight into her kitchen. A board member asked whether the deck could be cut back. The Odums' architect said trimming 2 feet would keep a usable deck. The board deliberated.

blocks.q: The ZBA thinks 4 feet is too much but 2 feet is acceptable with a privacy screen. What may it do?
c: Deny the request in full and make the Odums file a new application
Grant a smaller 2-foot variance and impose a reasonable condition
Grant the full 4 feet, since a board cannot change what was requested
Refer the decision to the village board, which sets setback policy
blocks.x: A ZBA grants the minimum variance it finds necessary and adequate, and may impose reasonable conditions directly related to the property and its effect on the neighborhood, such as a privacy screen. Whether the benefit can be achieved by other feasible means, and how substantial the request is, are two of the five factors. The trap is "cannot change what was requested": boards routinely grant less than asked. The village board writes the code but does not hear variances.

blocks.html: Elm Harbor permits home occupations in residences: no more than one non-resident employee, no exterior signs other than a small nameplate, and no more than 25% of the floor area used for the business. Linda has three employees, a lighted lawn sign, and clients parking on the street every day from February to April. A neighbor had complained again in March.

blocks.q: The building inspector confirms Linda's tax practice exceeds the home occupation limits. Which is the usual path of enforcement?
c: A notice of violation, then charges in village justice court
A lawsuit by the neighbor in State Supreme Court for an Article 78 order
An automatic revocation of the house's certificate of occupancy by the ZBA
A referral to the county board of health, which enforces zoning codes
blocks.x: The building department or code enforcement officer enforces the zoning code: inspections, notices of violation, stop-work orders and appearance tickets, with charges heard in the local justice court, which can impose fines. The trap is the Article 78: that is how someone challenges a government decision, not how a village enforces its code against an owner. The board of health handles wells, septic and sanitation, not home offices.

blocks.html: Linda moved her practice to an office on Route 9 before closing and took down the sign. The Odums, an architect and a nurse, had no plans for a home business beyond Priscilla's laptop, which no code limits.

The corner grocery dates to 1948. When the village zoned the block R-10 in 1958, it became a legal nonconforming use. It closed in March 2025 when the owner retired. Evelyn Park bought it in April 2026 for $610,000, planning a café. Elm Harbor's code says a nonconforming use that is discontinued for 12 consecutive months may not be resumed.

blocks.q: The grocery closed in March 2025 and Evelyn wants to open in May 2026. Under the code, what is the status of the nonconforming use?
c: It continues, because a nonconforming use runs with the land forever
It continues as long as the new owner uses it for some kind of retail
It ended after 12 months closed; R-10 uses now apply
It is lost, but Evelyn may resume it by paying a fee to the building department
blocks.x: A nonconforming use runs with the land and passes to buyers, but it ends if the use is discontinued for the period the ordinance sets. After 12 months closed, the right to operate a store is gone and the lot may be used only for uses the R-10 district allows. The trap is "runs with the land forever": it runs with the land only while it is kept alive. A change to a café would also typically be barred as a change in the nonconforming use.

blocks.html: Evelyn's lawyer had an argument. The old owner had kept a lottery terminal and sold newspapers through the window two mornings a week until December 2025. He asked the building inspector for a determination that the use had not been discontinued. The inspector said it had. The lawyer wanted to take the question further.

blocks.q: Evelyn disagrees with the building inspector's ruling that the grocery use was discontinued. Where does she take it first?
c: To the village board, which can overrule any inspector by resolution
To the ZBA, which hears appeals of the inspector's rulings
To the county planning board, which interprets local zoning codes
To the state Department of State, which administers the building code
blocks.x: The ZBA is the local administrative appeal body: it hears appeals from the decisions of the official who enforces the zoning code and interprets the ordinance. It acts in a quasi-judicial role, not as a policy maker. Only after the ZBA decides can Evelyn go to court in an Article 78 proceeding. The trap is the village board: it writes and amends the code, but it does not decide individual appeals.

blocks.html: The hearing on the appeal was short. Evelyn's lawyer brought lottery sales records; a neighbor brought photos of the papered-over windows and a "CLOSED" sign dated March 2025. The board asked the question that decides these cases: was the use that the code protected, a grocery, actually carried on? Courts in New York read discontinuance clauses by what happened on the ground, and occasional sales of a sideline product rarely keep a whole business use alive.
The ZBA agreed with the inspector: selling lottery tickets through a window was not the operation of a grocery. Evelyn's fallback was a use variance for a café.

To get a use variance, Evelyn had to prove unnecessary hardship: that she could not realize a reasonable return under any use permitted in R-10, shown by competent financial evidence; that the hardship was unique to the property; that a café would not alter the character of the neighborhood; and that the hardship was not self-created.

blocks.q: Which evidence is most important to the reasonable-return element of Evelyn's use variance?
c: Letters from neighbors saying they would enjoy a café on the corner
Her architect's drawings showing the building will look residential
Proof that a café would earn more than a single-family house
Dollars and cents proof that each permitted use would lose money
blocks.x: New York courts require dollars and cents proof that the property cannot yield a reasonable return under any permitted use: what it would cost to convert to a house, what it would sell or rent for, and the resulting return. Showing that a café earns more is not enough, which is the trap: a better return is not hardship. Neighbor support and design go to neighborhood character, a different element.

blocks.q: Evelyn bought the building in April 2026, after the store had been closed for over a year. How does that affect her use variance?
c: It helps her, because she paid a commercial price for the building
It does not matter, since self-created hardship is just one factor
It hurts, but just if neighbors prove she knew the zoning before buying
It hurts: buying with notice of the zoning is self-created
blocks.x: For a use variance, the hardship must not be self-created, and a buyer who acquires property knowing, or charged with knowing, that the use is restricted creates her own hardship. Zoning is public record, so a buyer is charged with knowledge. Paying a commercial price for residentially zoned land is also self-created. The trap is "just one factor": that is the area variance rule; for a use variance self-creation is fatal.

blocks.title: Two variances, two different tests
blocks.html: Area variance: a balancing test, five factors, self-creation counts but does not bar it. Use variance: all four elements of unnecessary hardship, and self-creation bars it. A question that mixes the two ("may a ZBA grant a use variance even though the hardship is self-created?") is testing exactly this.

Evelyn tried one more route. She asked the village board to rezone her single corner lot from R-10 to C-1, the commercial district three blocks away. The comprehensive plan called for keeping Ridge Road residential.

blocks.q: If the village board rezones only Evelyn's lot to commercial, contrary to its comprehensive plan, a court would most likely treat it as:
c: Incentive zoning, since the café would serve the public
Cluster zoning, since the use is grouped at the corner
Spot zoning, which favors one parcel's owner
A valid as-of-right change, since boards may rezone any lot
blocks.x: Spot zoning is a rezoning of a small parcel for the benefit of its owner, inconsistent with the comprehensive plan and the surrounding uses. Courts strike it down. A rezoning that follows the plan and serves the community is not spot zoning even if one lot is affected. The trap is incentive zoning, which trades extra density for a defined public benefit under an adopted program, not a one-lot change.

blocks.html: And because the corner lot sits within 500 feet of Route 9, a state highway, any variance or rezoning for it had to be referred to the county planning board under General Municipal Law 239-m before the local board voted. The county recommended denial. Evelyn sold the building to a builder who converted it into a house.

blocks.q: Suppose the ZBA had granted Evelyn a use variance without first referring it to the county, even though the lot is within 500 feet of a state highway. What is the likely consequence?
c: The decision is vulnerable to being annulled in a timely court challenge
No effect, since county referral is advisory and can be skipped at the board's choice
The county may grant or deny the variance itself, replacing the ZBA decision
The state DOT automatically gains the power to veto the café's driveway
blocks.x: GML 239-m referral is mandatory for listed actions, including use and area variances, on property within 500 feet of a state road and the other listed features. Courts treat failure to refer as a serious defect that can void the local decision if a challenge is brought in time. The trap is "advisory": the county's recommendation is advisory, since the board can override it by a majority plus one, but the referral itself is not optional. The county does not decide variances.

blocks.title: Village and town variance rules are in statute
blocks.html: New York writes the variance tests into its statutes: Town Law 267-b and Village Law 7-712-b (General City Law 81-b for cities). The ZBA must grant the minimum variance it deems necessary, may attach conditions, and must file its decision with the clerk, which starts the 30-day clock for an Article 78 challenge.

A state-licensed nonprofit notified the village that it planned a community residence for six adults with developmental disabilities in a house two doors down. A neighbor started a petition. Meanwhile, at 22 Ridge Road, five graduate students from a nearby college rented a house together, shared meals and a car, and signed a two-year lease. Another neighbor complained that they were not a "family" under the village code, which limits single-family houses to people related by blood, marriage or adoption.

blocks.q: The neighbors want the village to block the community residence. Under New York's Padavan Law, the village may:
c: Deny it outright, since group homes are a commercial use in an R-10 district
Object within 40 days, mainly citing oversaturation or character
Require a use variance from the ZBA before the residence may open
Require a vote of the neighbors within 500 feet before it opens
blocks.x: The Padavan Law (Mental Hygiene Law 41.34) treats state-licensed community residences as family units for zoning. The municipality may suggest alternative sites or object within 40 days, and its objection is limited essentially to oversaturation of such facilities or a substantial change in the character of the area. The trap is the use variance: that would let a village do through zoning what the statute forbids. Disability is also protected under fair housing laws.

blocks.q: Can the village enforce its definition of family against the five graduate students?
c: Yes. A village may limit single-family houses to related people
No, if they live as the functional equivalent of a family
Yes, if the limit is no more than four unrelated people
No, because zoning has no power to define a family
blocks.x: New York's highest court has held that a zoning definition limiting a single-family house to related people violates the State Constitution when applied to unrelated people living together as the functional equivalent of a family: a stable, single housekeeping unit sharing expenses and meals. The trap is the four-person cap, a rule some places use but not what New York's courts require. Codes may still regulate occupancy for safety, through building and fire codes.

blocks.html: In August, the ZBA granted the Odums' special permit for the garage apartment and a 2-foot variance for the deck with a privacy screen. The decisions were filed with the village clerk on August 14. The neighbor who objected to the deck called a lawyer on September 20.

blocks.q: The ZBA's decision was filed with the village clerk on August 14. The neighbor's lawyer is consulted on September 20. Can the neighbor still challenge it in court?
c: Yes. An Article 78 may be filed within four months of the hearing
No. ZBA decisions are final and cannot be reviewed by a court
Yes. Neighbors have a year to challenge a variance once granted
No. The 30 days to bring an Article 78 ran from the filing date
blocks.x: A person aggrieved by a ZBA decision may seek review in State Supreme Court in an Article 78 proceeding, but for town and village ZBAs the deadline is 30 days after the decision is filed in the clerk's office. September 20 is 37 days after August 14. The trap is four months, the general Article 78 limit, which these zoning statutes shorten. ZBA decisions are reviewable, but deadlines are strictly enforced.

blocks.html: The Odums closed in October. The variance and special permit were in the public record, so the title report raised no zoning issue. Priscilla's mother moved into the garage apartment in November, with a fresh certificate of occupancy for the accessory unit. Jordan rode Metro-North home with a new rule for himself: read the CO before writing the listing.

items: The CO controls lawful use; never advertise an unpermitted unit as legal or as rental income.
A use the code allows with conditions needs a special use permit; a prohibited use needs a use variance and proof of unnecessary hardship with dollars and cents evidence.

Area variances are a balancing test. The ZBA grants the minimum variance needed, may attach conditions, and self-creation counts but does not bar relief; for a use variance it is fatal, and buying with knowledge is self-created.

Nonconforming uses run with the land but end after the discontinuance period. The ZBA hears appeals from the building inspector and interprets the code; code enforcement runs through the building department and local justice court.
Spot zoning singles out one parcel against the plan. The Padavan Law limits objections to community residences; functional families cannot be excluded by a blood-relation definition.
Article 78 challenges to town and village ZBA decisions must be filed within 30 days after filing with the clerk.

lessons.title: Case file: The Air Over Fort Greene
lessons.tagline: A landmarked rowhouse, 600 square feet of air rights, a church with more, and a rezoning down the block.
objectives: Calculate unused development rights and decide whether they can be used on the lot, merged with a neighbor, or transferred from a landmark.
Decide which LPC approval, DOB step, or BSA finding applies to proposed work in a NYC historic district.
Apply Penn Central to a claim that landmark limits are a taking.
Apply ULURP, CEQR, and restrictive declarations to a NYC rezoning.

blocks.title: Grandma's house, and what is above it
blocks.html: Marisol and Luis Ortega inherited their grandmother's four-story brick rowhouse in the Fort Greene Historic District in Brooklyn. It is a two-family: Marisol lives on the top two floors; the lower duplex is empty. They want to add a fifth-floor penthouse, put a small architecture studio on the ground floor for Luis, and maybe sell "the air rights" to pay for it all. Their architect, a friend from Pratt, sent a one-page zoning analysis. Marisol forwards it to Jordan, who sold her a co-op in Clinton Hill years ago, with one line: "Is any of this possible, and who do we ask?"

blocks.title: The architect's zoning math
blocks.html:
Lot: 20 feet x 100 feet = 2,000 square feet
Maximum floor area ratio (FAR) for the lot's residential district, per the architect: 2.0
Maximum zoning floor area: 2,000 x 2.0 = 4,000 square feet
Existing building: 3,400 square feet of zoning floor area
Unused development rights: 4,000 minus 3,400 = 600 square feet

blocks.q: Using the architect's numbers, how much unused floor area (air rights) does the Ortegas' lot have?
c: 600 square feet
3,400 square feet
4,000 square feet
2,000 square feet
blocks.x: Unused development rights are the difference between the maximum floor area the zoning allows and the floor area already built: 2,000 x 2.0 = 4,000, minus 3,400 = 600 square feet. The trap is 4,000, which is the total allowed, not what is left. Air rights are not literally the air above the roof; they are unused zoning floor area, which in NYC can be used on the lot or, in limited ways, moved to another lot.

blocks.html: Marisol asked how the block had become a historic district in the first place, since her grandmother had never been asked. Jordan looked it up. The Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the Fort Greene Historic District in 1978, after a public hearing, based on the architecture and history of its 19th-century rowhouses. Owners do not need to consent. Every exterior change since then has needed LPC approval, which is why the block still looks the way it does and why buyers pay a premium to live there.

blocks.q: Who designates a New York City historic district, and what review follows?
c: The City Planning Commission, as part of a zoning map change through ULURP
The community board, by a majority vote of the owners in the district
The State Historic Preservation Office, which lists it on the State Register
The Landmarks Preservation Commission, subject to City Council review
blocks.x: The LPC designates individual landmarks, interior landmarks, scenic landmarks and historic districts after a public hearing. The City Council can then review the designation and may modify or disapprove it. The trap is the State Register: listing by the State Historic Preservation Office, part of OPRHP, recognizes a property and triggers review of state-funded projects, but it does not by itself regulate a private owner's work the way an LPC designation does.

blocks.text: The penthouse and the Landmarks Preservation Commission

blocks.html: A 600-square-foot penthouse would use up those rights on the lot itself. But the house is in a historic district designated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission, so zoning is only half the question. Any exterior change, and many interior ones that need a Department of Buildings permit, needs an LPC approval first. The architect's sketch put the penthouse set back 12 feet from the front facade, but it would still be visible from the sidewalk across the street.

blocks.q: Which LPC approval does a rooftop addition visible from the street in a historic district most likely need?
c: A Permit for Minor Work, issued by LPC staff within a few weeks
A Certificate of Appropriateness after a public hearing
A Certificate of No Effect, since the facade is not touched
No LPC approval, since rooftop work is a DOB matter
blocks.x: Significant changes such as visible rooftop additions, rear-yard additions, and demolitions need a Certificate of Appropriateness voted by the Commission after a public hearing. The community board usually reviews it and makes a recommendation. The trap is the Certificate of No Effect, which covers DOB-permit work that does not affect protected features, such as many interior renovations. A Permit for Minor Work covers smaller exterior work like window replacement.

head: LPC approval
Typical work
Who decides
rows: Interior renovation or mechanical work that needs a DOB permit but leaves protected features alone
Window or door replacement, masonry repair, restoring details
Visible rooftop or rear additions, demolition, removing a stoop or cornice
The Commission, after a public hearing
blocks.caption: The three main LPC permits

blocks.html: The Ortegas also planned to replace the 1970s aluminum windows with wood windows matching the originals, and to gut-renovate the lower duplex's kitchen and baths.

blocks.q: For the wood window replacement and the interior kitchen renovation, which LPC approvals fit best?
c: Minor Work for the windows; No Effect for the kitchen
A Certificate of Appropriateness for both, after a hearing
A Certificate of No Effect for the windows; nothing for the kitchen
Nothing for either, since restoring originals needs no approval
blocks.x: Replacing windows changes the exterior, a protected feature, but restoring them to match the originals is routine staff-level work: a Permit for Minor Work. An interior kitchen and bath renovation needs DOB permits but does not affect protected features, so LPC issues a Certificate of No Effect. The trap is "restoring originals needs no approval": even improvements to a landmark's exterior need LPC sign-off. A full hearing is for larger changes.

blocks.html: Their contractor, eager to get started, began tearing off the roof parapet in March before any approval. A neighbor called 311. A DOB inspector issued a stop work order the next day, and LPC issued a warning letter for work without a permit.

blocks.q: Why could the Ortegas' contractor not simply get a DOB permit and start the penthouse while the LPC application was pending?
c: LPC approval is needed after construction, as a final sign-off like a CO
DOB permits in historic districts are issued by the borough president's office
DOB generally issues no permit for such work until LPC approves
The contractor could have started; LPC fines owners after completion
blocks.x: For designated landmarks and buildings in historic districts, the Department of Buildings requires LPC approval before it issues permits for work LPC regulates. That sequence is why the stop work order came so quickly. The trap is treating LPC as an after-the-fact sign-off: unpermitted work can bring violations, fines, and an order to restore what was removed. The certificate of occupancy comes from DOB at the end, not from LPC.

blocks.html: At the LPC hearing in July, the Commission found the penthouse too visible and approved a smaller version, set back further and clad in a dark, non-reflective material. Luis was furious. "It's our property. They're taking our air rights without paying us. Isn't that a taking?"

blocks.q: The LPC limits the Ortegas' penthouse, leaving the house in full use as a two-family. Under Penn Central, is this a taking that requires compensation?
c: Yes, because any loss of development rights is a taking
No, because they keep a reasonable use and economic return
Yes, because a historic district is a permanent physical occupation
No, because landmark rules are exempt from the takings clause
blocks.x: In Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City (1978), the Supreme Court held that landmark regulation that leaves an owner a reasonable return and continued use is not a taking, even if it blocks valuable development. The trap is the physical occupation answer: that is the Loretto rule for actual physical intrusions, like a cable box bolted to a roof. Landmark laws are not exempt from the takings clause; they usually pass the test.

blocks.html: With the penthouse cut down, the Ortegas would use only about 350 of their 600 unused square feet. The owner next door, a small developer named Hassan Kareem, had a vacant corner lot in the same block and in the same zoning district, outside the historic district boundary. He offered $250 per square foot for whatever they had left. In Brooklyn, prices for development rights swing widely with the receiving site and the market; the Ortegas' attorney told them to get an appraisal of the rights before agreeing to anything, and to think about whether a future buyer of their house would value the expansion room more than Kareem did.

blocks.q: What is the usual way for the Ortegas to move their remaining unused floor area to Kareem's adjacent lot?
c: A CPC special permit through ULURP, since every air rights transfer needs one
An easement in gross recorded in favor of the City Planning Commission
A use variance from the BSA, since it changes the use of the receiving lot
A zoning lot merger, recorded, generally as of right
blocks.x: Adjacent lots can be merged into one zoning lot, letting unused floor area on one be used on the other. A zoning lot merger is generally as of right: no public review, just recorded documents (a zoning lot description and declarations, often with a development rights agreement and a light and air easement), filed with ACRIS. The trap is the special permit, which is required for landmark transfers under ZR 74-79, not for ordinary adjacent mergers.

blocks.title: What the seller of air rights gives up
blocks.html: A zoning lot merger is recorded against both lots and binds future owners. The Ortegas would permanently give up the floor area they sell, so a future buyer of their house could not add it back. The agreement usually also restricts the seller from blocking the buyer's windows. A listing agent should know whether a property's air rights have already been sold: the title report and ACRIS will show the zoning lot documents.

Across the street, a landmarked 1860s church has a far bigger pile of unused floor area: about 30,000 square feet. Its trustees want to sell it to a developer building a tower two blocks away on Fulton Street, to pay for a new roof and a food pantry.

blocks.q: Under the NYC Zoning Resolution's landmark transfer rule (ZR 74-79), can the church transfer its development rights to the site two blocks away?
c: Yes, as of right, by recording a zoning lot merger with the developer's lot
No. A landmark's development rights are lost when it is designated
Yes, after a BSA variance showing the church cannot earn a reasonable return
No. It reaches adjacent, across-the-street, or same-corner lots
blocks.x: ZR 74-79 lets a landmark transfer unused development rights by special permit from the City Planning Commission, through ULURP, but only to a lot that is adjacent, directly across the street, or across an intersection from the landmark. A site two blocks away does not qualify. The trap is the as-of-right merger, which works only for lots that are actually adjacent and merged into one zoning lot. Designation does not wipe out development rights; Penn Central relied on their transferability.

blocks.text: The studio on the ground floor

blocks.html: Luis's studio idea ran into the zoning use rules. The lot's residential district does not allow an architecture office as a separate business on the ground floor of a two-family house, beyond a modest home occupation by a resident. Luis does not live there. A professional office for a non-resident would need a variance from the Board of Standards and Appeals, New York City's version of a zoning board of appeals.

blocks.q: To grant Luis a use variance, the BSA must make five findings. Which finding has no counterpart in the four-part town and village use variance test?
c: That the hardship was not created by the owner
That the variance will not alter the neighborhood's character
That the variance is the minimum needed to afford relief
That a reasonable return is not possible under zoning
blocks.x: Under ZR 72-21 the BSA must find (a) unique physical conditions, (b) no reasonable return under conforming use, (c) no change to the essential character of the neighborhood, (d) a hardship not created by the owner, and (e) that the variance is the minimum necessary. The town and village statutes tell a ZBA to grant the minimum variance needed but do not make it one of the four hardship elements. The trap is self-creation, which appears in both tests.

blocks.html: Luis's application would have failed the first finding: nothing about a standard 20-foot rowhouse lot is physically unique. He rented a studio on Myrtle Avenue instead, in a commercial overlay where offices are allowed as of right.

Marisol asked one follow-up. What if Luis moved into the lower duplex himself and worked from a room there? That changes the analysis. The Zoning Resolution allows a home occupation as an accessory use in a dwelling, run by a resident, within limits on the share of floor area used, employees, and signs. An architect drawing at a desk in his own apartment is the kind of quiet professional use these rules contemplate. A storefront studio with staff and walk-in clients is not.

blocks.q: If Luis lives in the lower duplex and runs a small one-person architecture practice from a room in it, what does he most likely need?
c: Nothing beyond compliance with the home occupation limits
A BSA use variance, since any business in a residence needs one
A CPC special permit, since offices need ULURP in residential areas
An LPC Certificate of Appropriateness for the change of use
blocks.x: A home occupation is an accessory use: customary and incidental to living in the dwelling, carried on by a resident, and subject to limits on floor area, employees, and signage. Within those limits no variance or permit is needed. The trap is the BSA variance: that applies when a non-resident wants a business use the district prohibits, which was Luis's original plan. LPC regulates physical changes to protected features, not how rooms are used.

blocks.html: In the fall, a developer filed an application to rezone a two-block stretch along Atlantic Avenue near the Ortegas' house, from a manufacturing district to a higher-density residential district with ground-floor retail, and to map Mandatory Inclusionary Housing so a share of the new apartments would be permanently affordable. The Department of City Planning certified the application as complete, and the clock started.

blocks.q: Brooklyn Community Board 2 holds a hearing and votes against the rezoning. What is the effect of that vote?
c: The application is dead, since community boards have a veto in ULURP
It is advisory; the BP, the CPC and the City Council still act on it
The rezoning goes to a citywide referendum at the next general election
The application moves to the BSA, which decides contested rezonings
blocks.x: In ULURP, the community board (60 days) and the borough president (30 days) make advisory recommendations. The City Planning Commission (60 days) holds a hearing and votes, and zoning map changes go to the City Council (50 days), with a possible mayoral veto that the Council can override. The trap is the veto answer: a community board vote matters politically, but it does not bind the CPC or the Council. The BSA hears variances, not rezonings.

blocks.html: Because a rezoning of that size could have significant environmental effects, the Department of City Planning, acting as lead agency, issued a positive declaration under City Environmental Quality Review (CEQR), New York City's version of SEQRA. A draft EIS studied shadows on the park, school seats, traffic, and displacement.

blocks.q: Which statement about the environmental review of the Atlantic Avenue rezoning is accurate?
c: NYC is exempt from SEQRA, so no environmental review applies to rezonings
CEQR carries out SEQRA in NYC, with an EIS if needed
The community board is the lead agency, since it holds the first ULURP hearing
An EIS is optional once the developer agrees to build affordable housing
blocks.x: New York City carries out the State Environmental Quality Review Act through City Environmental Quality Review. The steps mirror SEQRA: a lead agency, an environmental assessment, a negative or positive declaration, and an EIS with public comment where impacts may be significant. The trap is the exemption answer: the city has its own procedures, not an exemption. Affordable housing commitments do not replace the EIS, though they can be part of its analysis.

blocks.html: The draft EIS also gave the public something to argue about with numbers. Neighbors from the historic district testified about the shadows a 14-story building would cast on the block's rear yards. Small business owners on Atlantic Avenue worried about rent increases. The developer's consultants answered with the EIS's mitigation chapter: lower street walls, a contribution to school seats, and a commitment to keep a share of ground-floor space affordable for local retailers.

The CPC approved a modified version: lower height on the side streets. As a condition, the developer recorded a restrictive declaration committing to build a community facility on one lot and to follow the environmental mitigation measures in the EIS.

blocks.q: What is the effect of the restrictive declaration the developer recorded against its Atlantic Avenue lots?
c: It binds the developer alone and ends if it sells the property
It is a personal promise the community board alone can enforce
It expires when the City Council approves the rezoning
It runs with the land and binds future owners of the lots
blocks.x: A restrictive declaration is a recorded covenant, so it runs with the land and binds future owners, and the City can enforce it. It is how NYC locks in commitments made during land use review, such as mitigation measures or community facilities. The trap is "binds the developer only": recording is exactly what makes it bind successors. Community boards have no enforcement role over recorded declarations.

blocks.title: Who does what in NYC land use
blocks.html: LPC designates landmarks and approves changes to them (its designations are subject to City Council review). DOB issues permits and certificates of occupancy. The BSA grants variances and some special permits and hears appeals from DOB. The CPC, with the Department of City Planning, runs ULURP and approves rezonings and its own special permits, with the City Council voting on map changes. Community boards and borough presidents advise. Exam items swap these bodies freely.

A year later, Jordan represented a buyer looking at another rowhouse on the Ortegas' block. The listing said "potential to expand: unused air rights." Remembering the Ortegas, Jordan checked before the buyer fell in love.

blocks.q: How can Jordan's buyer best confirm whether a NYC property's unused development rights have already been sold or merged?
c: Search ACRIS and the title report for zoning lot documents and declarations
Ask the seller, since air rights sales are private and go unrecorded
Ask LPC, which keeps the official ledger of development rights in a district
Check the tax bill, which lists remaining air rights as a separate assessed line
blocks.x: Zoning lot mergers and development rights agreements are recorded against the property, so they appear in ACRIS and in a title report. The buyer's architect then confirms the numbers against the zoning. The trap is the seller's word: a past owner may have sold the rights decades ago, and the current seller may not know. LPC regulates landmark changes; it does not track floor area. A listing that advertises air rights already sold is a misrepresentation.

blocks.html: This one had sold 1,100 square feet to a neighbor in 1998. The "potential to expand" was a two-foot sliver. The buyer adjusted the offer, and the listing agent corrected the ad.

The Ortegas built the smaller penthouse, sold their remaining 250 square feet of floor area to Kareem through a zoning lot merger for $62,500, and used it toward construction. They rented the restored lower duplex to a couple of nurses from Brooklyn Hospital. The whole project took 19 months instead of the six the architect had promised, most of it spent waiting on approvals that could have been mapped out on day one. When Jordan later helped them refinance, the appraiser asked for the zoning lot documents, the LPC approvals, and the new certificate of occupancy. All three were in the file.

items: Air rights are unused zoning floor area: maximum floor area (lot area times FAR) minus what is built.

In NYC historic districts, LPC approval comes before DOB permits: a Certificate of No Effect for interior permit work, a Permit for Minor Work for routine exterior work, and a Certificate of Appropriateness after a hearing for major changes.
Under Penn Central, landmark limits that leave a reasonable return are not a taking; Loretto makes any permanent physical occupation a taking.
Adjacent lots move floor area by an as-of-right zoning lot merger; landmarks transfer by CPC special permit under ZR 74-79 only to adjacent, across-the-street, or same-corner lots.

The BSA grants NYC variances on five findings, including minimum variance. ULURP recommendations from community boards and borough presidents are advisory; CEQR applies SEQRA in the city; restrictive declarations run with the land.

lessons.title: Case file: The Diner on Route 9W
lessons.tagline: Evelyn buys a Hudson Valley diner the same summer the State decides it needs 25 feet of the parking lot. Then come the tax bill, the planning board, and the building inspector.
objectives: Apply the Eminent Domain Procedure Law to a partial taking: the hearing, the challenge deadline and court, the before-and-after measure of just compensation, and the advance payment
Decide how taxation works as a land use tool, separating general taxes from special district levies and special assessments, and tell a tax foreclosure from an escheat
Apply site plan review, planning board conditions, area variances, and planned unit development rules to a commercial expansion and a neighboring project
Apply the Uniform Code's building permit, stop work order, temporary certificate of occupancy, and fire inspection rules to a restaurant renovation

blocks.title: Pie, coffee, and a letter from Albany
blocks.html: Nick and Eleni Pappas have run the Riverview Diner on Route 9W in the Town of Highmark, Ulster County, since 1994 (the town is fictional; the rules are New York's). The property is 1.6 acres: an 80-seat diner, two apartments upstairs, 58 parking spaces, and an old barn out back. They are retiring, and Evelyn Park has a contract to buy it for $1,350,000. Evelyn wants to keep the diner, add a drive-through window for coffee and pastry, and turn the barn into a wholesale bakery supplying cafés from Kingston to Newburgh. Jordan is helping on the deal because Diane referred Evelyn to an Ulster County colleague and asked Jordan to keep the file straight. Two weeks after the contract was signed, a letter arrived from the New York State Department of Transportation. DOT plans to widen Route 9W with a center turn lane and sidewalks, and its map shows a strip 25 feet deep along the diner's entire 210 feet of frontage. The letter announces a public hearing at the Highmark firehouse in June. Nick wants to know if the State can really do this. Evelyn wants to know if she still wants the diner.

Jordan read the letter twice. The power at work was eminent domain, and the process New York uses for it is the Eminent Domain Procedure Law (EDPL). Before the State acquires private property for a project, the EDPL generally requires a public hearing near the property, then a written determination and findings that the condemnor publishes.

blocks.q: What is the purpose of the EDPL public hearing DOT scheduled at the firehouse?
c: To set the price DOT will pay each owner, after hearing the owners' appraisals
To let the Highmark town board vote on whether the State may widen Route 9W
To decide whether the project needs an area variance from the town's setbacks
To inform the public and review the project's public use and local impacts
blocks.x: The EDPL hearing comes before the decision to acquire. It informs the public and reviews the public use the project will serve and its impact on the environment and residents. Compensation is a separate, later stage, which is the trap in the first choice: price is settled by offer, negotiation, or a court claim, not at the hearing. A town board has no veto over a State highway taking.

blocks.html: Nick went to the hearing and spoke for six minutes about his customers, his parking lot, and the trucks that would park on his lawn during construction. Forty neighbors came. Most wanted the sidewalks. In August, DOT published its determination and findings in two local newspapers: the project would proceed, including the 25-foot strip. Nick's nephew, a paralegal in Kingston, said they had four months to challenge it in State Supreme Court, "like any other government decision."

blocks.q: Nick wants to challenge DOT's determination that the taking serves a public use. Where and when?
c: The Appellate Division, within 30 days after the determination is published
State Supreme Court, through an Article 78 proceeding filed within four months
The Court of Claims, within 3 years after title to the strip vests in the State
The town zoning board of appeals, within 60 days after the hearing transcript is filed
blocks.x: EDPL 207 sends a challenge to the determination and findings straight to the Appellate Division for the department where the property sits, and the petition is due within 30 days after the condemnor completes publication. The court reviews only limited issues, such as public use and procedure. The Article 78 choice is the trap: it is the usual route for agency decisions, but the EDPL creates its own faster one. The Court of Claims hears the money claim, not the public use question.

blocks.html: Nick missed the 30 days, and his lawyer told him it would not have mattered: a turn lane and sidewalks on a state highway are a classic public use. The real fight would be about money. Meanwhile, Evelyn's attorney looked at the contract. It provided that if any part of the property was taken before closing, Evelyn could cancel and get her deposit back, or close at the full price and receive the award. Because DOT would not acquire title until the following spring, Evelyn chose to close in September and deal with DOT as the owner.

The strip was 5,250 square feet, about 0.12 acres. Taking it would remove 14 of the 58 parking spaces and put the new sidewalk 12 feet from the diner's front steps. Evelyn hired an appraiser who specializes in condemnation, and his numbers looked like this:

head: Measure
Amount
rows: Value of the whole property before the taking
Value of what remains after the taking
Land in the strip alone, at $9 per square foot
Damage to the remainder (lost parking, closer frontage)
blocks.caption: Evelyn's appraisal of the partial taking

blocks.q: How do New York courts generally measure just compensation for a partial taking like this one?
c: The value of the strip by itself, since the State takes just the land it needs
The assessed value of the strip on the town roll, adjusted by the equalization rate
The before value of the whole minus the after value of the remainder
The diner's lost profits during construction, plus the value of the strip
blocks.x: For a partial taking, courts usually compare the market value of the whole property before the taking with the value of the remainder after it. That captures the land taken plus consequential damage to what is left, such as lost parking, which the owner must prove with expert evidence. The strip-alone choice is the trap: it would pay $47,250 and ignore $122,750 of real harm. Assessed value is a tax figure, not market value.

blocks.html: In January, DOT sent Evelyn a written offer of $128,000. The offer said it was DOT's highest approved appraisal. Evelyn's appraiser thought it was $42,000 short. Evelyn's question to Jordan was blunt: "If I cash their check, do I lose the rest?"

blocks.q: Evelyn believes DOT's $128,000 offer is too low. What does the EDPL let her do?
c: Refuse the offer, since cashing any check from the State settles the claim in full
Accept it in full and then ask DOT to reopen the amount within 90 days
Hold the offer open until the Court of Claims rules, then accept whichever is higher
Accept it as an advance payment and still file a claim for more compensation
blocks.x: Under EDPL 304 an owner may accept the offer as payment in full or reject it as full payment and take it as an advance payment, keeping the right to claim more. She has 90 days to accept, and the claim itself must be filed on time, generally within 3 years. The refusal choice is the trap: an owner who refuses money she is entitled to gains nothing, and the statute bars conditioning the advance payment on a waiver.

blocks.html: Evelyn signed the advance payment agreement, deposited $128,000, and her attorney filed a claim in the Court of Claims, which hears claims against the State. Eighteen months later the State settled at $161,000.
Evelyn's first January tax bill as owner showed what a government's taxing power looks like on one parcel. Jordan put it into a table for her, because the line items were about to matter.

head: Line
Basis
Amount
rows: Ad valorem levy on parcels inside the district
Ad valorem levy on parcels inside the district
Route 9W sidewalk special assessment, year 3 of 10
blocks.caption: Riverview Diner property tax lines (rounded)

blocks.html: The bakery was the part of Evelyn's plan that the county's industrial development agency (IDA) liked. A wholesale bakery is manufacturing, it would add 22 jobs, and the IDA offered a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) agreement for the barn conversion: the IDA takes an interest in the project, the property becomes exempt from general real property taxes, and Evelyn instead pays a negotiated PILOT that starts low and rises over ten years. Using tax relief to steer where jobs go is taxation working as a land use tool, alongside zoning.

blocks.q: Under an IDA PILOT agreement for Evelyn's property, which bill lines does the IDA exemption cover?
c: The county, town, and school general taxes, but not district levies or assessments
Every line, since IDA property is exempt from every charge a local government imposes
The school tax alone, since IDAs exist to cut school tax burdens on employers
The special district and sidewalk charges alone, since general taxes fund the IDA
blocks.x: The IDA exemption in General Municipal Law 874 reaches general taxes levied by counties, cities, towns, villages, and school districts, which the PILOT replaces. It does not reach special ad valorem levies, such as sewer and fire district charges, or special assessments, such as the sidewalk charge. The 'every line' choice is the trap: owners and buyers who assume a PILOT ends all property charges are surprised every January.

blocks.html: The sidewalk line was a special assessment: a charge on the parcels along 9W that benefit from a specific improvement, spread here by front footage over ten years. The sewer and fire lines were different again: ad valorem levies by special districts, charged by assessed value but only to parcels inside each district's boundaries. Evelyn had closed in September, in year 3 of the sidewalk assessment, and Nick called to ask whether he would be getting bills for the rest of it.

blocks.q: Seven yearly installments of the sidewalk special assessment remain after Evelyn's purchase. Who owes them to the town?
c: Evelyn, as owner, since unpaid installments are a lien that runs with the land
Nick and Eleni, since the town levied the assessment while they owned the diner
The State, since DOT built the sidewalk as part of its Route 9W project
The sewer district, since it collects every special charge in its boundaries
blocks.x: A special assessment is charged against the benefited parcel, and unpaid installments are a lien on the land, so the town looks to whoever owns it when each installment comes due. Buyer and seller can apportion the current year at closing, and a buyer's attorney searches for assessments so the price reflects them. The prior-owner choice is the trap: the debt follows the property, not the person who owned it when the sidewalk was built.

blocks.html: Nick owed nothing more. Evelyn's attorney had found the assessment in the municipal search before closing, the year 3 installment was apportioned on the closing statement, and the remaining seven installments were already built into Evelyn's numbers. Unpaid, they would sit on the land like any other tax lien.

Evelyn's bakery needed delivery truck access from the side street, and two small parcels sat between the barn and Old Mill Road. Jordan pulled the records. Lot A had belonged to Harold Greer, who died in 2021 with no will, no spouse, no children, and no relatives anyone could find. Lot B belonged to an LLC that had not paid its taxes since 2019; the county had brought an in rem tax foreclosure under Real Property Tax Law Article 11 and now held title.

blocks.q: Which government power explains how each lot ended up with the government?
c: Lot A by eminent domain, because the State had to take it to keep it maintained; Lot B by escheat
Lot A by escheat, because an owner died with no will and no heirs; Lot B by the taxing power
Lot A by the police power, as an abandoned nuisance; Lot B by eminent domain for unpaid taxes
Lot A by escheat, because the land was vacant for 2 years; Lot B by escheat to the county
blocks.x: Escheat moves property to the State when an owner dies without a will and without heirs. Lot B came to the county through enforcement of the taxing power: unpaid taxes are a lien, and in rem foreclosure ends in the government taking title. The vacancy choice is the trap: neglect or vacancy alone never triggers escheat. Since Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) and New York's 2024 changes to Article 11, a former owner may claim surplus value above the taxes owed.

blocks.html: Evelyn bought Lot B at the county's tax auction for $41,000. Lot A would take longer, because escheated land is handled through the State. She settled for a recorded access easement over Lot B and dropped Lot A.

Highmark's zoning allows restaurants and light manufacturing in the Highway Commercial district as of right, subject to site plan review by the planning board. Evelyn's engineer drew the plan: a drive-through lane wrapping the diner, a 4,800 square foot bakery in the rebuilt barn, a loading area off Old Mill Road, and the parking lot reconfigured around DOT's new line. The code would require 62 spaces for the expanded uses. The site, after the taking and the drive-through lane, would hold 47.

blocks.q: The site plan needs 15 fewer parking spaces than the code requires. What is the fastest proper path?
c: Ask the planning board to waive the spaces, since it controls everything about site plans
Get a building permit first, then apply to the ZBA after the building inspector denies it
Apply to the ZBA for an area variance now, alongside site plan review
Seek a use variance, because the shortfall makes the bakery a prohibited use
blocks.x: Town Law 274-a lets an applicant whose site plan contains features that do not comply with zoning go directly to the zoning board of appeals for an area variance, without first getting a denial from the enforcement officer. A parking shortfall is a dimensional problem, so it is an area variance, not a use variance, which is the trap: the bakery use is permitted, only the numbers are short. The planning board reviews layout; it does not vary the parking minimum.

blocks.html: The ZBA granted the variance for 15 spaces after the engineer showed that the drive-through would cut parking demand and that the State, not Evelyn, had taken 14 spaces. The planning board then held its site plan hearing within the 62 days Town Law 274-a allows after a complete application, and two neighbors on Old Mill Road asked for limits on bakery trucks. At the next meeting the board proposed three conditions.

blocks.title: Draft resolution, Highmark Planning Board
blocks.html:
Site plan approved, subject to:
1. A landscaped buffer, 15 feet deep, with evergreen screening along Old Mill Road.
2. No bakery truck deliveries between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
3. A $40,000 contribution by the applicant to the Highmark Police Department vehicle fund.

blocks.q: Which proposed condition is the planning board on weakest ground imposing?
c: The landscaped buffer along Old Mill Road
The overnight limit on bakery deliveries
The $40,000 police vehicle contribution
Each of them, since boards set their own terms
blocks.x: Town Law 274-a allows reasonable conditions that are directly related and incidental to the proposed site plan, and they must be met before the town issues permits. Screening and delivery hours respond to the plan's actual effects on neighbors. A payment to a police vehicle fund has no connection to this site's layout. The 'boards set their own terms' choice is the trap: conditions are limited, and an unrelated exaction can be overturned in an Article 78 proceeding.

blocks.html: Evelyn's attorney raised the point politely at the meeting. The board dropped the third condition and approved the first two. The decision was filed with the town clerk within five business days, and Evelyn's engineer put a copy in the permit application.

In the same month, a developer proposed "Riverbend Commons" on 46 acres across 9W: 180 townhouses, a small grocery, a village green, and 20 acres of preserved woods, on land zoned for one-acre single-family lots. Evelyn liked it, since 180 households would want coffee. Jordan wanted to know who would decide it.

blocks.q: The Riverbend Commons developer asks Highmark for a planned unit development district. Which body creates one?
c: The zoning board of appeals, by granting a use variance for the mixed uses
The town board, by adopting it as an amendment to the zoning law
The planning board, by approving the site plan for the whole tract
The county planning board, which approves any mixed use project
blocks.x: Town Law 261-c authorizes the town's legislative body to provide for planned unit development districts as part of its zoning law, so creating and mapping one is a legislative rezoning. The planning board usually reviews the detailed plans afterward. The use variance choice is the trap: a ZBA grants relief for hardship on one parcel, and it has no power to create a new mixed use district. A county may review it through referral but does not adopt it.

blocks.html: The town board referred the petition to the planning board and the county planning department, began SEQRA review as lead agency, and scheduled a hearing for the spring. Evelyn wrote a letter in support and reminded herself that a PUD on paper is years from a customer at her window.

New York's Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code applies in Highmark, and the town's code enforcement officer administers it. Evelyn's contractor, eager to get ahead of winter, started gutting the barn in October, before the building permit was issued, on the theory that "demo isn't construction." On the second day, the code enforcement officer drove by.

blocks.q: The officer posts a stop work order on the barn. What does it mean for Evelyn?
c: Work stops until the conditions stated in the order are met, such as a permit
Work may continue while she appeals the order to the ZBA within 60 days
The barn loses its legal status and needs a use variance before work resumes
Work stops until an Article 78 court reviews the order, which the town has to file
blocks.x: Under the State's minimum code enforcement rules (19 NYCRR Part 1203), a stop work order may halt work done without a required permit, and it must state the reason and the conditions for resuming. Once Evelyn obtains the permit and meets those conditions, work restarts. The ZBA appeal choice is the trap: work does not continue during a challenge, and the order is about the missing permit, not the use.

blocks.html: The permit issued nine days later, and the barn work resumed. The diner's own renovation came next: a new kitchen line, a new hood and fire suppression system, and the drive-through window. Evelyn closed the diner for six weeks in February. By mid-March the dining room was finished, inspected, and ready. The drive-through lane outside still needed paving, curbing, and its canopy, which could not go in until the ground thawed. Evelyn did not want to stay closed until May.

blocks.q: How can Evelyn lawfully reopen the dining room before the drive-through work is done?
c: Reopen on the 1994 certificate of occupancy, which still covers a restaurant
Reopen once the contractor certifies that the dining room is safe in writing
Obtain a temporary certificate of occupancy for the safe, completed portions
Reopen at once, since a CO is needed after the entire permit is closed
blocks.x: The Uniform Code's enforcement rules let the town issue a temporary certificate of occupancy before permitted work is complete, for a limited period, describing the portions that may be occupied and any conditions, once those portions can be occupied safely and fire protection systems work. The old CO choice is the trap: work done under a new permit needs its own certificate. A contractor's letter is not an approval.

blocks.html: The temporary certificate issued on March 20 for the dining room and kitchen, with a condition that the drive-through lane stay fenced. The final certificate of occupancy for the whole building came in June. It listed, among other things, the occupant load of the dining room: 80 seats, plus staff.

blocks.title: One code, enforced locally (except in NYC)
blocks.html: The Uniform Code is a State code, but cities, towns, and villages enforce it under programs that must meet the State's minimum standards: building permits, inspections, stop work orders, certificates of occupancy, operating permits, and periodic fire safety inspections. A town that does not enforce it leaves the job to its county or the Department of State. New York City runs its own Construction Codes and Fire Code through the Department of Buildings and FDNY.

blocks.q: The diner has an 80-seat dining room with two apartments upstairs. At least how often must Highmark inspect it for fire safety?
c: Every three years, the interval for multiple dwellings and nonresidential buildings
Every five years, unless a complaint is filed with the building department
On complaint, since the code schedules no inspections for restaurants
Every year, because the building contains an assembly area
blocks.x: The State's rules cap fire safety and property maintenance inspection intervals at one year for buildings with an assembly area (a space for 50 or more people, including a restaurant dining room) and three years for multiple dwellings and other nonresidential buildings. The three-year choice is the trap: the apartments and the commercial use both fit that category, but the dining room makes the stricter annual cycle apply. Such buildings also need an operating permit.

blocks.title: "The State took it, so the rules bend"
blocks.html: Owners often assume a taking gives them a pass on zoning: the State took my parking, so the town has to accept the shortfall. It does not work automatically. A taking can make a lot nonconforming, and the owner may need an area variance to expand, as Evelyn did. The taking is a strong fact for the variance and for the compensation claim (lost parking is consequential damage), but the owner still has to ask.

The Riverview reopened fully on Memorial Day weekend with the drive-through window, a sidewalk in front that the State built and Evelyn is assessed for, and a bakery out back on a PILOT. Nick and Eleni came for pie. Jordan's note for the file read: "Every power the government has over land showed up at one diner: it took a strip, it taxed the rest, it reviewed the plan, and it inspected the kitchen."

items: Eminent domain in New York runs under the EDPL: a public hearing, a published determination, a challenge in the Appellate Division within 30 days, and a separate claim for compensation.

Just compensation for a partial taking is usually the before value of the whole minus the after value of the remainder, which includes consequential damage. An owner can take the State's offer as an advance payment and still claim more.

Taxation shapes land use: an IDA PILOT replaces general taxes but not special district levies or special assessments. Unpaid taxes can end in an in rem foreclosure; escheat applies only when an owner dies without a will or heirs.

Site plan review covers one project's layout; a nonconforming feature goes straight to the ZBA as an area variance; conditions must relate to the plan. A PUD district is created by the town board as a zoning amendment.
Under the Uniform Code, no permit means a stop work order; a temporary CO lets safe portions open early; buildings with assembly areas get fire inspections at least once a year.

roleplays.title: The "Legal Two-Family"
roleplays.setting: A detached house on Staten Island. Marcus took the listing; you are co-listing and running the open house.
roleplays.you: Jordan, co-listing agent for the seller
roleplays.goal: Market the house honestly based on its CO, answer the buyer's zoning questions accurately, and point him to the right process without promising approvals.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Marcus, a veteran agent who wants to advertise a one-family Staten Island house as a 'legal two-family' with basement rental income and pushes hard ('who's going to check?'), then a first-time buyer who wants to count the basement rent, asks how to legalize it, and asks for it in writing, and briefly the basement tenant, who is scared of being thrown out. The learner must rely on the CO for legal use, refuse to call an illegal unit grandfathered, avoid promising approvals, name the NYC Board of Standards and Appeals and explain the use variance test (including self-created hardship), recommend an architect and attorney, avoid legal advice to the tenant, and escalate to the supervising broker. Grade on accuracy, honesty, and escalation.
opening: A detached house in {hood}, Staten Island. Marcus has the listing; you're co-listing. DOB records show a certificate of occupancy for a one-family dwelling and no permits for the basement kitchen.
Marcus drops a listing sheet on your desk: {hood} detached, 'legal 2-family, {rent} basement income.' You pull the DOB records. The CO says one-family.
Open house prep in {hood}. A tenant has lived in the basement for {years} years at {rent} a month. The CO on file says one-family dwelling.

say: Listing goes live tonight. Write it as a legal two-family with {rent} a month basement income. Seller's had a tenant down there {years} years.
Just type what's on my sheet: legal two-family, {rent} rental income. The tenant's been there {years} years, so it's fine.

moves.text: CO says one-family. I'll write 'one-family, finished basement' and flag the attorney.
moves.fb: Correct. The CO controls legal use. Advertising an illegal unit as legal is a material misrepresentation.
moves.react: Marcus scowls. "You're going to cost us showings."

moves.text: We can't call it a legal two-family or count that rent. The certificate of occupancy controls.
moves.fb: Right. Legal use comes from the CO, and the basement may also fail code (egress, ceiling height).
moves.react: "Fine, write it your way," Marcus mutters.

moves.text: Let's say 'two-family potential' and note the income down in the remarks section of the ad.
moves.fb: Better than lying, but touting rent from an illegal unit still implies lawful income.
moves.react: Marcus shrugs. "Potential. I can live with that."

moves.text: {years} years with no complaints makes it basically grandfathered. I'll post it the way you wrote it.
moves.fb: A nonconforming use must have been lawful when it began. An illegal conversion never becomes grandfathered.

moves.text: Fine. Rental income is a fact, and ads can state facts even if the unit itself isn't legal.
moves.fb: Advertising income from an illegal unit misleads buyers about what they can lawfully earn.

moves.text: Let's call it a 'legal mother-daughter.' That wording doesn't need a two-family CO at all.
moves.fb: Relabeling doesn't change legal use. A second dwelling unit needs a CO that allows it.

say: I love it. If I buy it, can I just get the basement legalized as a second unit? My spreadsheet assumes the rent.
My numbers only work with the basement rent. How hard is it to make that apartment legal?

moves.text: Maybe, but nobody can promise it. An architect can check zoning and code. Don't count the rent.
moves.fb: Honest and accurate. Whether a use is allowed depends on the district and code, and you send the buyer to the pro.

moves.text: It depends on the zoning district and building code. Have an architect review it before you offer.
moves.fb: Correct. You avoid promising an approval and point to the right professional.

moves.text: I think it's possible, but I honestly don't know. You'd have to look into that one yourself.
moves.fb: Not a misstatement, but you can name the right professional and warn against counting the rent.

moves.text: Oh, the city legalizes these all the time. It's easy, you just file for a permit afterward.
moves.fb: You can't guarantee a government approval. If the buyer relies on it, you own the problem.

moves.text: Yes. Since the tenant's been there {years} years, the city has to approve it as a second unit.
moves.fb: Length of an illegal use creates no right to approval.

moves.text: Sure. Once you own it and live upstairs, a basement unit becomes automatically legal if owner-occupied.
moves.fb: Owner occupancy doesn't legalize a unit the CO and code don't allow.

say: And if the zoning doesn't allow two units, what would I need?
Say the district only allows one family. Who do I ask for an exception?

moves.text: A use variance from the Board of Standards and Appeals. You need hardship you didn't create.
moves.fb: Right board and right test. A buyer who purchases knowing the restriction has a self-created hardship.
moves.react: {client} winces. "So buying it knowing the rule hurts me."

moves.text: In the city, the BSA hears use variances. Buying knowing the rule makes the hardship self-created.
moves.fb: Correct. A use variance needs all four prongs, and self-created hardship bars it.

moves.text: Probably a special permit of some kind. An attorney would know which one you need for it.
moves.fb: Referring is fine, but special permits only cover uses the Zoning Resolution lists, and the BSA or CPC grants them.

moves.text: You'd go to the Community Board. They're the ones who decide variances in New York City.
moves.fb: Community Boards are advisory. In NYC the BSA grants variances.

moves.text: An area variance. You just need to show a practical difficulty, and those are easy to get here.
moves.fb: Adding a use the district bars needs a use variance with unnecessary hardship, not an area variance.

moves.text: Nothing at all. Zoning only matters for new construction, not for converting an existing house.
moves.fb: Wrong. Zoning governs use, including conversions of existing buildings.

say: Great, I'll put the {rent} in my offer math. Can you put in writing that it's legalizable?
Just email me that the basement can be legalized. My lender will want to see it.

moves.text: I can't promise it, written or not. Don't count that rent until an architect checks it.
moves.fb: Right. A written promise about approvals would be a misrepresentation the buyer relies on.

moves.text: No, because I don't know it is. Base your offer on a one-family and treat the rent as unknown.
moves.fb: Correct. You keep the buyer from relying on income that may never be lawful.

moves.text: Let me check with Marcus first. He knows the house and the seller a lot better than I do.
moves.fb: Not a lie, but you already know the CO. Say so.

moves.text: Sure, I'll email you that it's legalizable. That should help with your bank approval, too.
moves.fb: Now it's a written misrepresentation the buyer and lender rely on.

moves.text: I can say it's 'likely legalizable.' A word like 'likely' keeps us from being on the hook for it.
moves.fb: A hedge word doesn't cure a statement you have no basis for.

moves.text: Yes. The rent is real money, so a lender will count it toward your income for the mortgage.
moves.fb: Income from an illegal unit is generally not lawful rental income for underwriting.

say: Back at the office. You're killing my deal. Just tell {client} the tenant can stay and the rent's real. Who's going to check?
Stop scaring buyers. Say the unit's legal and move on. Nobody looks at COs.

moves.text: The buyer's attorney and the lender will check the CO. If you want, let's take it to Diane.
moves.fb: You hold the line and escalate. Brokers supervise listings and advertising.

moves.text: I'm not misrepresenting the legal use. Diane supervises all our listings, so let's let her decide.
moves.fb: Correct. Supervising brokers are responsible for associated licensees' listings and ads.

moves.text: Fine, I'll just say nothing and let the buyer figure it out themselves later, after contract.
moves.fb: Silence beats a lie, but you know a material fact. Disclose it and escalate.

moves.text: Okay. I'll tell the buyer the tenant can stay, and I just won't mention anything about the CO.
moves.fb: Implying lawful income while hiding the CO is misrepresentation by omission.

moves.text: Fine. Nobody checks COs on Staten Island anyway, so the risk to either one of us is pretty small.
moves.fb: Attorneys and lenders routinely check the CO. And risk isn't the test; honesty is.

moves.text: Okay, I'll say it's legal but add 'buyer to verify.' That disclaimer protects us both.
moves.fb: A disclaimer doesn't cure a false statement you know is false.

say: Am I getting kicked out? Marcus said the new owner wants me gone in a week.
I've lived down here {years} years. Do I have to leave when the house sells?

moves.text: I can't advise you on your rights, but please talk to a tenant attorney or legal aid soon.
moves.fb: Right. You don't give legal advice, and you point the tenant to real help.
moves.react: The tenant nods. "I'll call legal aid."

moves.text: It's a legal question I can't answer. A tenant lawyer can explain where you stand.
moves.fb: Correct. Occupants have rights that a court process governs; a lawyer can explain them.
moves.react: "Thank you for being honest," the tenant says.

moves.text: I really don't know. You'd have to ask the seller about what's happening with the sale.
moves.fb: Not harmful, but sending a worried occupant to a lawyer helps far more.

moves.text: Yes, illegal units have no rights at all, so you'd have to leave within a week if asked.
moves.fb: Wrong and legal advice. Removal requires court process.

moves.text: Yes. Once the house sells, every lease and tenancy ends automatically at the closing.
moves.fb: Wrong. A sale doesn't automatically end a tenancy.

moves.text: Don't worry. Tell the new owner you're grandfathered, so the city can't ever touch your unit.
moves.fb: Wrong. An illegal unit isn't grandfathered, and this is legal advice.

say: My uncle says old stuff is grandfathered. Isn't that what nonconforming use means?
Wait, I read about nonconforming uses. Doesn't that make the basement legal?

moves.text: A nonconforming use was legal when it began. An illegal unit never was, so it doesn't qualify.
moves.fb: Right. Grandfathering protects uses that predate a rule and were lawful at the start.

moves.text: Grandfathering covers uses that were lawful when started. This unit had no permits.
moves.fb: Correct. An illegal conversion can't become a lawful nonconforming use.

moves.text: It's complicated. Every case is a little different, so I'd ask a lawyer about it.
moves.fb: Referral is fine, but you can explain the basic rule.

moves.text: Your uncle's right. Anything that's been there more than five years is grandfathered now.
moves.fb: No time-based grandfathering exists for illegal uses.

moves.text: Yes, and a nonconforming use can be expanded, as long as it stays the same type of use.
moves.fb: Nonconforming uses generally can't be expanded.

moves.text: Grandfathered uses last forever, even if they're abandoned and empty for years at a time.
moves.fb: Nonconforming uses can be lost if abandoned.

say: The seller wants the basement stove pulled before the appraisal so it 'looks like storage.' Thoughts?
Seller asked if he can clear out the basement kitchen before buyers' inspectors come. What do we tell him?

moves.text: He can take it out, but not to mislead anyone. Buyers still hear the basement's history.
moves.fb: Right. Removing a stove is fine; using it to hide a known condition isn't.
moves.react: Diane nods. "Good. Put that in an email."

moves.text: The disclosure doesn't change. The unit's history and the CO get told either way.
moves.fb: Correct. Known material facts are disclosed regardless of staging.

moves.text: It's his house, so I'd let him do whatever he wants with it and just stay out of it.
moves.fb: Not a lie, but you should make sure staging isn't used to conceal.

moves.text: Great idea. What the appraiser and the inspectors don't see isn't our problem to go explain.
moves.fb: Hiding a known condition to mislead appraisers or buyers is misrepresentation.

moves.text: Fine, then we can stop mentioning the tenant, since it's just a storage room now.
moves.fb: Removing a stove doesn't erase what you know about the unit's use.

moves.text: Sure. Once the stove is out, it's legally a one-family, so the issue's fully solved.
moves.fb: The tenant and the unit's history remain material facts.

say: The lender's appraiser called. I told him there's rental income downstairs. That's fine, right?
Told the appraiser the basement rents for {rent}. Helps the value. Good, yeah?

moves.text: We need to fix that. The CO is one-family, so that isn't legal rental income.
moves.fb: Right. Feeding an appraiser income from an illegal unit misleads the lender.
moves.react: Marcus groans. "Fine, I'll call him back."

moves.text: Let's call him back with the CO today. Diane should know we gave him that number.
moves.fb: Correct. Fix the misstatement and escalate to the broker.

moves.text: Maybe. Let's just see what number he comes back with before we do anything.
moves.fb: Waiting lets a misstatement shape the lender's value.

moves.text: Sure. Rent is rent, and appraisers can count any income the house actually produces.
moves.fb: Income from an illegal unit isn't lawful income for valuation or lending.

moves.text: Fine, as long as you didn't put it in writing. Verbal comments to appraisers don't count.
moves.fb: Oral misstatements to a lender's appraiser still mislead.

moves.text: Good. A higher appraisal helps the buyer too, so nobody is harmed by telling him that.
moves.fb: Inflating value with illegal income harms the buyer and lender.

roleplays.debrief: The certificate of occupancy controls legal use: never market an illegal unit as legal or count its rent. A nonconforming use must have been lawful when it began, so an illegal conversion is never grandfathered, and nonconforming uses generally can't expand and can be lost if abandoned. In NYC the Board of Standards and Appeals grants variances (Community Boards only advise); a use variance needs unnecessary hardship on all four prongs, including that it wasn't self-created. Never promise approvals, don't give tenants legal advice, and take listing pressure to the supervising broker.

questions.q: A town's rule leaves an owner's land with no economically viable use at all. Courts are most likely to treat this as:
