deeper.plain: On a new house with its own well and septic, a few items decide whether the house is legal, safe and protected: permits, the CO, health approvals and the warranty.
deeper.picture: Buying a new build is like buying a car straight off the lot. You want the title, the inspection sticker and the warranty card in your hand, not a handshake.
deeper.street: Priya tells Leo to strike 30 of his questions and focus on four: Is there a CO? Did the county health department approve the well and septic? Is there a water test? What does the written warranty say, and does it meet GBL 777-a? The builder's "my word" doesn't matter, because the statute gives Leo the warranty anyway.
deeper.stakes: Closing before the CO issues can leave Leo unable to legally move in and with a lender that refuses to fund. A failed septic can cost $30,000 or more to replace.
deeper.exam: Exam questions on new construction usually test the paper trail (permit, inspections, CO) and the Housing Merchant Implied Warranty periods: 1, 2, 6 years.

blocks.text: Paper first: plans, permits, codes, CO

blocks.html: Every legal build starts with blueprints (the drawings: floor plans, elevations, sections) and specifications (the written details: materials, grades, brands, methods). An architect or engineer prepares them, and the building department checks them against zoning and the code before issuing a building permit.
blocks.casual: Every legal build starts with blueprints, the drawings (floor plans, elevations, sections), and specifications, the written details (materials, grades, brands, methods). An architect or engineer prepares them, and the building department checks them against zoning and code before it issues a building permit.

deeper.plain: Drawings show what the building looks like. Specs say what it's made of. Both get checked before you can build.
deeper.picture: Blueprints are the photo on the recipe card. Specs are the ingredient list with exact brands and amounts.
deeper.street: Leo notices the blueprints show a finished basement, but the specs list no insulation for the basement walls. He asks the builder, who admits the basement is "rough only." Leo negotiates a $9,000 credit.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who only look at pretty drawings can miss cheap materials buried in the specs. Contractors who build without approved plans risk a stop-work order.
deeper.exam: If the question asks which document lists materials and quality standards, the answer is specifications, not blueprints.

blocks.title: The construction paper trail

items.title: Plans and specs
items.html: Drawings say what it looks like; specs say what it is made of.

items.title: Permit
items.html: Building department confirms zoning and code compliance. Health department approves well and septic first where there is no public water or sewer.

items.title: Inspections
items.html: Footings, foundation, framing, rough plumbing and electrical, insulation, final.

items.title: CO
items.html: Certificate of occupancy issues. No CO, no legal move-in, and usually no closing with a lender.

blocks.casual: Here's the construction paper trail. Plans and specs come first: drawings say what it looks like, specs say what it's made of. Then the permit: the building department confirms zoning and code compliance, and where there's no public water or sewer, the health department approves the well and septic first. Then inspections: footings, foundation, framing, rough plumbing and electrical, insulation, final. Last, the certificate of occupancy issues. No CO means no legal move-in, and usually no closing with a lender.

deeper.plain: Plans, permit, inspections, CO. Skip one and the house isn't legal to live in.
deeper.picture: It's like getting a passport: application, approval, interview, then the actual passport. You can't board without the last one.
deeper.street: Ray inspects Leo's house and sees the insulation inspection sticker is missing on the permit card. The building department confirms the insulation was never inspected. The builder has to open two walls before the final, and the CO is pushed back three weeks.
deeper.stakes: A closing without a CO can leave a buyer with no mortgage, no legal right to occupy, and a house that's hard to insure or resell.
deeper.exam: Order matters on the exam. Health approval for well and septic comes before the building permit where there's no public water or sewer. The CO comes last.

blocks.title: One state code, local enforcement
blocks.html: New York's Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code and the Energy Conservation Construction Code apply statewide and are enforced by local building departments. NYC writes its own Construction Codes. Electrical work follows the National Electrical Code as adopted through the state code (NYC has its own Electrical Code).
blocks.casual: New York's Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code and the Energy Conservation Construction Code apply across the state, and local building departments enforce them. NYC writes its own Construction Codes. Electrical work follows the National Electrical Code as adopted through the state code, and NYC has its own Electrical Code.

deeper.plain: One set of building and energy codes covers the state, enforced locally. NYC has its own.
deeper.picture: The state sets the rulebook, every town referees its own games, and NYC plays in a separate league with its own book.
deeper.street: Leo's Ulster County house is inspected by the town building inspector under the Uniform Code. His cousin's renovation in Astoria is inspected by the NYC Department of Buildings under the NYC Construction Codes.
deeper.stakes: Contractors who follow the wrong code can fail inspection and eat the cost of rework.
deeper.exam: Statewide code, local enforcement. Energy code is a separate state code. NYC is the exception with its own construction and electrical codes.

blocks.text: The site: well, septic, energy, and how the lot works

head: Requirement
Who controls it
What to know
rows: NYS Department of Health standards; county health department; drillers registered with DEC

Must be set back from contamination sources, typically at least 100 feet from a septic absorption field and 50 feet from a septic tank. Water is tested for bacteria and other contaminants before approval.
NYS Department of Health standards, county or local health department approval
Designed by a NY licensed professional engineer or registered architect. Soil tested for percolation rate. As-built drawings usually filed with the health department.
Minimum insulation, windows, air sealing, and duct and equipment efficiency, set by climate zone.

deeper.plain: A private well and septic have to be approved by health officials, kept apart from each other, and tested. New houses also have to meet energy standards.
deeper.picture: Your drinking water straw and your drain should never be in the same glass. That's what the setback distances are for.
deeper.street: The county health department measures Leo's well and finds it 110 feet from the absorption field and 60 feet from the tank. Both pass. The water test comes back clean for bacteria, and the septic was designed by a licensed PE after a percolation test.
deeper.stakes: A well too close to a septic field can contaminate drinking water and make a family sick. Buyers who skip a water test may never know until it happens.
deeper.exam: Remember who approves: health departments (state standards, county or local approval). Percolation test measures how fast soil absorbs water. Typical setbacks: 100 feet well to absorption field, 50 feet well to septic tank.

blocks.html: Site use is about how the lot behaves: drainage (grade slopes away from the house, gutters discharge away), landscaping (no trees planted on top of septic fields), appurtenances (driveway, walks, fences, sheds), shading (trees and orientation affect heating and cooling), walks, and of course zoning setbacks and lot coverage.
blocks.casual: Site use is about how the lot actually behaves. Drainage: the ground should slope away from the house and gutters should dump water away. Landscaping: never plant trees on top of a septic field. Appurtenances: the driveway, walks, fences, sheds. Shading: trees and which way the house faces change your heating and cooling. Walks. And of course zoning setbacks and lot coverage.

deeper.plain: A house sits on land, and how that land drains, what's planted and what's built around it matter as much as the house itself.
deeper.picture: It's like setting up a tent. Put it in a low spot and you wake up in a puddle no matter how good the tent is.
deeper.street: The Okafors' brownstone backyard slopes toward the rear wall. Every heavy rain, water pools against the foundation and seeps into the cellar. Ray tells them regrading and a drain will cost about $6,000, far less than fixing a foundation later.
deeper.stakes: Bad drainage leads to wet basements, mold and foundation damage. Tree roots in a septic field can destroy it.
deeper.exam: "Appurtenances" means things attached to or serving the property: driveways, fences, sheds. Grade should slope away from the foundation.

blocks.q: Before a septic system is installed for a new house in a rural NY town, the soil is tested to measure how quickly it absorbs water. This is the:
c: Radon test
Percolation test
Compaction test
Hydrostatic test
blocks.x: A perc test measures the percolation rate, which determines whether and how large an absorption field can be built.

blocks.caption: Trace the load path: roof to rafters, to walls and studs, to joists and girder, to lally columns and foundation walls, to footings, to soil.

head: Member
What it is
What it carries
rows: Concrete base, wider than the wall above, poured below the frost line
Spreads the whole house's weight into the soil
Poured concrete or concrete block on the footing
The house; also hold back soil around a basement or crawl space
First wood member, bolted flat on top of the foundation wall
Connects wood frame to masonry; anchor bolts hold it down
Main horizontal beam, wood or steel, running the length of the basement
Carries the inner ends of the floor joists
Steel post, often concrete-filled, on its own footing
Parallel horizontal boards (2x8 to 2x12) set on edge
Vertical 2x4 or 2x6 members, usually 16 inches on center
Sloped members from wall top to the peak
Horizontal member at the peak where rafters meet
Plywood or OSB panels nailed over studs and rafters
Adds rigidity; base for siding and roofing

deeper.plain: A house carries its weight down through a chain of parts: roof to walls to floors to foundation to footing to soil.
deeper.picture: It's like a human pyramid at a cheerleading meet. The people at the bottom (footings) need the widest base, and each layer stands on the one below.
deeper.street: Ray walks Leo through the basement: "That's the girder, running the length of the house. Those steel posts are Lally columns, each on its own footing. The joists rest on the girder and the sill plate bolted on the foundation wall." He finds one Lally column with no footing under it and flags it.
deeper.stakes: A missing footing, a cut joist or a rusted Lally column can lead to sagging floors and costly structural repairs. Buyers who skip the inspection inherit the problem.
deeper.exam: Common exam questions: the sill plate is the first wood member on the foundation. Lally columns support the girder. Footings are below the frost line and wider than the wall. Studs are usually 16 inches on center.

blocks.title: Load path, bottom up
blocks.html: Feet, Walls, Sill, Girder on Lally, Joists, Studs, Rafters, Ridge. Footing is wider than the wall because feet are wider than ankles.
blocks.casual: Here's the load path from the bottom up: Feet, Walls, Sill, Girder on Lally, Joists, Studs, Rafters, Ridge. And the footing is wider than the wall for the same reason your feet are wider than your ankles.

deeper.plain: Memorize the order the parts stack in, from the ground up.
deeper.picture: Your body has the same order: feet, legs, hips, spine, ribs, shoulders, head. The widest base is at the bottom.
deeper.street: Jordan practices the chant on the subway to a showing in Crown Heights. When the buyer asks what that steel post in the basement is, Jordan says "Lally column, it holds up the girder," and the buyer's inspector nods.
deeper.stakes: Knowing the parts lets you talk intelligently with inspectors and clients, and spot when a seller's "cosmetic" repair is actually structural.
deeper.exam: Order questions: "Which member rests directly on the foundation wall?" Sill plate. "Which supports the girder?" Lally column.

blocks.html: No basement? A slab-on-grade house sits on a concrete slab poured directly on prepared ground, usually with thickened edges acting as footings. Cheaper and common for garages and newer ranches, but mechanicals must go somewhere else, and pipes in the slab are hard to reach.
blocks.casual: No basement? A slab-on-grade house sits on a concrete slab poured right on prepared ground, usually with thicker edges that act as the footings. It's cheaper and common for garages and newer ranches, but the mechanicals have to go somewhere else, and pipes buried in the slab are hard to reach.

deeper.plain: A slab house sits on a concrete pad with no basement underneath.
deeper.picture: It's like putting a tent on a wooden platform instead of digging a cellar under it. Faster and cheaper, but there's no crawl room underneath.
deeper.street: Leo's garage is slab-on-grade. Years later a water line under a friend's slab ranch in Suffolk leaks, and the plumber jackhammers through the kitchen floor to reach it. The bill is $8,500.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't realize pipes are in the slab can be shocked by repair costs. Slabs also mean the furnace and water heater take up living space.
deeper.exam: Slab-on-grade means no basement or crawl space. Thickened edges act as footings. Watch for "monolithic slab" as a synonym.

blocks.text: Tying it together: openings and loads

items: Bearing walls carry weight from above. Removing one without a beam is how ceilings sag. Exterior walls are almost always bearing; interior walls under joist splices often are.
Headers are beams over door and window openings in a wood frame wall, carrying the load around the hole.
Lintels do the same job over openings in masonry: a steel angle or stone over a brownstone window.
Flitch plates (the syllabus spells it "fitch") are steel plates bolted between two wood boards to make a stronger beam without a deeper one.
blocks.casual:
Bearing walls hold up weight from above. Pull one out without putting in a beam and you get a sagging ceiling. Exterior walls are almost always bearing, and interior walls under joist splices often are.
Headers are beams over door and window openings in a wood-frame wall. They carry the load around the hole.
Lintels do the same job over openings in masonry, like a steel angle or a stone over a brownstone window.
Flitch plates (the syllabus spells it "fitch") are steel plates bolted between two wood boards to make a stronger beam without making it deeper.

deeper.plain: Some walls hold the house up. Openings in those walls need a beam on top to carry the weight around them.
deeper.picture: Think of a bookshelf. Pull out a side panel and it collapses. Cut a hole in a shelf and you need a brace across the top of the hole.
deeper.street: A Park Slope buyer wants an open kitchen and plans to knock out an interior wall. Ray finds joist splices sitting on it, so it's bearing. The architect specs a flitch plate beam so the ceiling stays the same height, and the job needs a DOB permit.
deeper.stakes: Removing a bearing wall without a permit or a beam can crack plaster, sag floors and, in the worst case, cause a collapse. Unpermitted work also shows up at resale.
deeper.exam: Header = over openings in wood frame. Lintel = over openings in masonry. Flitch plate = steel sandwiched between wood. Exterior walls are bearing.

left.title: Platform construction
items: Most common today
Each floor is built as a platform; walls for the next story stand on it
Floors act as fire stops
Shorter, easier-to-handle lumber

right.title: Post-and-beam construction
items: Heavy posts and beams spaced far apart
Exposed timbers, open floor plans, barns
Fewer, larger members carry the load
Older balloon framing ran studs two stories; it lacks built-in fire stops

deeper.plain: Most houses today are built one floor at a time, each floor a platform for the next. Post-and-beam uses big timbers spaced far apart.
deeper.picture: Platform framing is stacking boxes. Post-and-beam is building a table with heavy legs and a big top.
deeper.street: Ray inspects a 1910 farmhouse in Dutchess County and finds balloon framing: studs running two stories with open cavities from basement to attic. He recommends adding fire blocking, because a fire could race up the walls.
deeper.stakes: Balloon framing without fire stops is a real fire risk, and insurers may ask about it. Post-and-beam homes command a premium for their look but can be costly to modify.
deeper.exam: Platform is the most common today, and floors act as fire stops. Balloon framing runs studs two stories and lacks built-in fire stops.

blocks.q: A buyer wants to remove a wall between a kitchen and dining room in a 1950s colonial. The first question is:
c: Whether the wall has insulation
Whether it is a bearing wall
Whether the studs are 2x4 or 2x6
Whether the drywall is plaster
blocks.x: A bearing wall carries loads from above and needs a properly sized beam and often new posts if removed. Insulation and stud size are secondary.

head: Term
Where
rows: The roof's overhang past the wall
Underside of the eave; often vented to feed air into the attic
Vertical board across the rafter ends; gutters mount on it
Metal or membrane at chimneys, valleys, skylights, and wall joints to keep water out
Roof slope as rise over run, such as 6 in 12
Exterior wall finish: wood, vinyl, aluminum, fiber cement, brick veneer
Gypsum panels for interior walls; replaced lath and plaster after WWII

deeper.plain: These are the names for the parts at the roof's edge and the outside skin of the house.
deeper.picture: The roof is a hat. The eave is the brim, the soffit is the underside of the brim, the fascia is the band around the edge, and flashing is the waterproof tape at every seam.
deeper.street: A Queens buyer's inspector finds water stains in the attic around the chimney. The flashing has pulled away. A $600 fix now prevents rotted rafters later.
deeper.stakes: Failed flashing is the top cause of roof leaks. Clogged soffit vents trap moisture in the attic and lead to mold.
deeper.exam: Pitch is rise over run (6 in 12). Soffit is under the eave, fascia is the vertical board at the rafter ends. Drywall equals plasterboard equals wallboard.

blocks.title: Fascia faces, soffit sits under
blocks.html: Fascia faces the street. Soffit is the skyward-looking ceiling under the eave.
blocks.casual: Fascia faces the street. Soffit is the skyward-looking ceiling under the eave.

deeper.plain: Fascia is the front-facing board. Soffit is the underside.
deeper.picture: Stand on the sidewalk: the board looking back at you is the fascia. Lie on the lawn and look up under the overhang: that's the soffit.
deeper.street: Jordan points at a gutter on a Staten Island listing and says "that's mounted on the fascia." The seller, a retired carpenter, is impressed.
deeper.stakes: Mixing them up won't lose a deal, but knowing them helps you understand inspection reports and repair quotes.
deeper.exam: Expect a picture-based or definition question. Gutters attach to the fascia. Soffit vents feed air to the attic.

blocks.html: The building envelope is everything separating inside from outside: foundation, walls, roof, windows, doors. Insulation slows heat flow through it. R-value measures resistance to heat flow: the higher the R-value, the better the insulation. R-values add when layers stack.
blocks.casual: The building envelope is everything that separates inside from outside: foundation, walls, roof, windows, doors. Insulation slows heat moving through it. R-value measures how well something resists heat flow, and the higher the R-value, the better the insulation. Stack layers and the R-values add up.

deeper.plain: R-value tells you how well insulation keeps heat in or out. Higher is better.
deeper.picture: It's like a winter coat. A thin windbreaker is R-1. A puffy parka over a sweater is R-whatever-you-add-up.
deeper.street: Leo's builder puts R-21 batts in the walls and R-49 in the attic. When Leo adds R-10 rigid foam under his basement slab, he gets R-10 there. On a wall with R-13 batts plus R-5 foam board, the total is R-18.
deeper.stakes: Under-insulated homes cost more to heat and cool and may not meet the energy code. Overpaying for a "high efficiency" house without checking R-values happens.
deeper.exam: The trap: some students think lower R is better. It's not. Higher R equals more resistance equals better insulation. R-values add when layered.

head: Type
Where it is used
rows: Open stud walls, attic floors, between joists
Foundation walls, under slabs, exterior sheathing
Rim joists, cathedral ceilings, air sealing gaps

deeper.plain: Different insulation types fit different spots: batts in open walls, blown-in for attics and closed walls, rigid foam on foundations, spray foam for gaps.
deeper.picture: It's like packing a suitcase. Folded shirts go flat, socks get stuffed into corners, and the hard case protects the fragile stuff.
deeper.street: The Okafors want their 1899 brownstone's walls insulated without tearing out plaster. Their contractor blows cellulose into the closed wall cavities and spray-foams the rim joists in the cellar.
deeper.stakes: Wrong insulation in the wrong place can trap moisture and rot framing. Spray foam installed badly can off-gas or crack.
deeper.exam: Match type to location: blown or loose-fill for retrofits and attics; rigid foam for foundations and under slabs; spray foam for rim joists and air sealing.

blocks.html: Location matters as much as type: attic floor or roof deck, exterior walls, rim joists, basement walls, and under slabs. Insulation must tie in with the structure: continuous at wall-to-roof joints, with a vapor retarder on the warm-in-winter side so moisture does not condense inside walls. A tighter envelope saves energy but needs planned ventilation, which is the next lesson.
blocks.casual: Where insulation goes matters as much as what kind it is: the attic floor or roof deck, exterior walls, rim joists, basement walls, under slabs. It has to tie in with the structure, staying continuous where the wall meets the roof, with a vapor retarder on the side that's warm in winter so moisture doesn't condense inside the walls. A tighter envelope saves energy, but it needs planned ventilation, which is next lesson.

deeper.plain: Insulation needs to be continuous with no gaps, and the vapor barrier goes on the warm side so walls don't get wet inside.
deeper.picture: It's like a sleeping bag with a zipper gap. A small gap lets in all the cold. And if you put a plastic bag on the outside, you end up soaked from your own sweat.
deeper.street: Ray finds the vapor retarder in a Saratoga addition installed on the cold (outside) side of the wall. Moisture from inside condensed on it all winter, and the studs are moldy. The fix costs $14,000.
deeper.stakes: Gaps waste energy. A vapor retarder on the wrong side causes mold and rot. A tight house with no ventilation can have air quality problems.
deeper.exam: Vapor retarder goes on the warm-in-winter side (the interior in NY). Tighter envelopes require mechanical ventilation.

blocks.q: Which insulation provides the most resistance to heat flow?
blocks.x: Higher R-value means greater resistance to heat flow. R-30 beats the others.

head: Housing Merchant Implied Warranty (GBL 777-a), new homes
Period
rows: Defects in workmanship and materials (construction not done in a skillful manner)
Plumbing, electrical, heating, cooling, ventilation systems
Material defects in load-bearing structural elements
blocks.caption: Runs from the earlier of the buyer's first occupancy or the passing of title

deeper.plain: New homes sold by builders come with an automatic warranty: 1 year for workmanship, 2 years for systems, 6 years for structure.
deeper.picture: It's a 1-2-6 countdown, like a phone with a 1-year screen warranty, 2-year battery coverage, and 6 years on the frame.
deeper.street: Eighteen months after closing, Leo's furnace fails. That's a heating system, so it's inside the 2-year window. A cracked drywall seam at 18 months is outside the 1-year workmanship window. A sagging girder at year 5 is inside the 6-year structural window.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't know the deadlines lose coverage. The clock starts at the earlier of first occupancy or title passing, not when the buyer first notices a problem.
deeper.exam: Memorize 1-2-6: workmanship and materials 1, plumbing/electrical/HVAC 2, load-bearing structure 6. The statute is GBL 777-a.

blocks.title: What the warranty is and is not
blocks.html: The Housing Merchant Implied Warranty is automatic on the sale of a new home by a builder. A builder may exclude it only by offering a written limited warranty that meets the statute's minimums. The buyer must give the builder written notice of a defect and a chance to fix it. It does not cover resales by ordinary owners.
blocks.casual: The Housing Merchant Implied Warranty kicks in automatically when a builder sells a new home. The builder can only exclude it by offering a written limited warranty that meets the statute's minimums. The buyer has to give the builder written notice of a defect and a chance to fix it. It doesn't cover resales by regular owners.

deeper.plain: New home buyers get a warranty by law. Builders can swap it for a written one only if it's at least as good as the minimums.
deeper.picture: It's the default setting on a new phone. The manufacturer can change it, but only to something that still meets the minimum guarantee.
deeper.street: Leo finds a cracked foundation wall in year 3. Priya has him send the builder written notice by certified mail with photos. The builder gets a chance to fix it before Leo can sue. If Leo had just hired his own contractor first, he could have hurt his claim.
deeper.stakes: Skipping written notice can wreck a warranty claim. Agents who tell resale buyers they have this warranty are flat wrong, and buyers may skip an inspection because of it.
deeper.exam: Key points: automatic on new homes sold by a builder; written notice required; doesn't apply to resales by owners. A builder may limit it only with a written warranty meeting the statute's minimums.

blocks.html: Renovations are covered by New York's home improvement law (General Business Law Article 36-A). A home improvement contract over $500 must be in writing with start and completion dates, a description of the work and materials, and notice of the owner's 3-business-day right to cancel. Deposits must be held in escrow or bonded. NYC, Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester and other localities also license home improvement contractors.
blocks.casual: Renovations fall under New York's home improvement law (General Business Law Article 36-A). A home improvement contract over $500 has to be in writing, with start and finish dates, a description of the work and materials, and notice that the owner has a 3-business-day right to cancel. Deposits have to be held in escrow or bonded. NYC, Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester and other places also license home improvement contractors.

deeper.plain: Home renovation jobs over $500 need a written contract, and the homeowner gets three business days to cancel.
deeper.picture: It's a cooling-off period, like the one you get when a salesman talks you into something at your kitchen table.
deeper.street: The Okafors sign a $28,000 bathroom contract on a Friday. On Monday they change their mind. Monday is the first business day, so they can cancel in writing through Wednesday and get their deposit back, which the contractor was required to hold in escrow or bond.
deeper.stakes: Hiring an unlicensed contractor in NYC can leave the owner with no recourse. A contractor who pockets deposits without escrow or a bond breaks the law.
deeper.exam: Remember: over $500, in writing, 3 business days to cancel. Don't confuse this with the TILA 3-day rescission on refinances, which is a different law.

blocks.q: Eighteen months after closing on a new house, the buyer's boiler fails because the builder installed it wrong. Under GBL 777-a, the buyer:
c: Has no claim; the 1-year warranty expired
Has a claim; mechanical systems are covered for 2 years
Has a claim only if the defect is structural
Must sue the boiler manufacturer only
blocks.x: Heating, plumbing, electrical, cooling and ventilation are warranted for 2 years. The 1-year period covers general workmanship and materials; 6 years covers load-bearing structure.

story.title: Forty-One Questions
story.setting: A new-construction colonial in Saugerties, the builder's pickup in the driveway

beats.text: Question one of forty-one. What's that steel pole in the basement?
Lally column. Steel, filled with concrete. It holds up that girder, and the girder holds up the ends of your floor joists.
And the wood sitting on the concrete wall?
Sill plate. First wood in the house. See the anchor bolts? That's what keeps the frame from sliding off the foundation.
And under the foundation wall there's a footing, wider than the wall, below the frost line.
They climbed to the attic. Ray tapped a rafter like it owed him money.
Rafters to the ridge beam, plywood sheathing on top. Look at the insulation: R-49 on the attic floor. Higher number, better.

check.q: Which tells you how well insulation resists heat flow?
c: BTU rating
R-value
Amperage
Pitch
check.x: R-value measures thermal resistance. BTU measures heat quantity; pitch is roof slope.

beats.text: Question nineteen. The builder says he'll warranty everything. In writing?
New York gives you one by law. One year workmanship, two years mechanical systems, six years structural. The Housing Merchant Implied Warranty.
And the well and septic?
The health department had to sign off. Septic designed by an engineer, soil perc tested, well set far enough from the leach field. Ask for the as-built drawings.
Last one. Can I close before the CO?
Not with a lender. No CO, no legal occupancy.
Forty-one questions. Most people ask two: where's the bathroom and does the oven work.
Later, reviewing the file: Paper, then bones, then systems. If the CO, the septic approval and the warranty aren't in the file, nothing else matters.

board.prompt: Sketch a house cross-section and label, bottom to top, footing, foundation wall, sill plate, girder, lally column, joists, studs, header, rafters, ridge beam, sheathing, eave, soffit, fascia, flashing.

facts.text: Blueprints are the drawings (floor plans, elevations, sections); specifications are the written details of materials, quality standards and methods.

The building department issues a permit after checking zoning and code, inspects the work in stages, and issues a certificate of occupancy; without a CO there is no legal move-in and usually no lender closing.

New York's Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code and Energy Conservation Construction Code (minimum insulation, windows, efficiency) apply statewide and are enforced by local building departments; NYC writes its own codes.
A private well must be set back from contamination, typically at least 100 feet from a septic absorption field and 50 feet from a septic tank, and its water is tested before approval.
A NY septic system must be designed by a licensed professional engineer or registered architect and approved by the county or local health department under state Health Department standards.
A percolation test measures how fast soil absorbs water and is used to design the septic absorption field.
Good site use means the grade slopes away from the house, gutters discharge away, and no trees are planted on the septic field.
The footing is the concrete base, wider than the wall above and poured below the frost line, that spreads the house's weight into the soil.
Foundation walls of poured concrete or block rest on the footing, and the sill plate is the first wood member, bolted flat on top of the foundation wall.
The girder is the main horizontal beam carrying the inner ends of the floor joists, and it is held up by steel lally columns.
The load path runs roof to rafters and ridge, to studs, to joists and girder, to lally columns and foundation walls, to footings, to soil; trim like the soffit carries no load.
A slab-on-grade house sits on a concrete slab poured directly on prepared ground, with no basement or crawl space.
A bearing wall carries weight from above, and exterior walls almost always do; removing one without a beam makes ceilings sag.
A header carries the load over an opening in a wood frame wall; a lintel does the same job over an opening in masonry.
A flitch plate beam is a steel plate bolted between two wood boards to make a stronger beam without a deeper one.
Platform framing, where each floor is a platform for the next story's walls, is the most common today; post-and-beam uses few heavy members for open plans; old balloon framing lacks fire stops.
The eave is the roof overhang, the soffit is its underside (often vented), and the fascia is the vertical board across the rafter ends where gutters mount.
Flashing is metal or membrane at chimneys, valleys, skylights and wall joints that keeps water out.
Pitch is roof slope as rise over run (such as 6 in 12); siding is the exterior wall finish; plasterboard (drywall) is gypsum interior panels.
The building envelope is everything separating inside from outside: foundation, walls, roof, windows and doors.
R-value measures resistance to heat flow: the higher the R-value, the better the insulation, and R-values add when layers stack.
Insulation must be continuous, with the vapor retarder on the warm-in-winter side so moisture does not condense inside walls; a tighter envelope needs planned ventilation.

The Housing Merchant Implied Warranty (GBL 777-a) covers a new home for 1 year (workmanship and materials), 2 years (plumbing, electrical, heating, cooling, ventilation) and 6 years (material structural defects), from the earlier of first occupancy or title passing.

The housing merchant warranty is automatic on a builder's sale of a new home, can be excluded only by a written limited warranty meeting the statute's minimums, requires written notice of defects, and does not cover resales.

Under GBL Article 36-A, a home improvement contract over $500 must be written, with start and completion dates, a description of work and materials, and notice of the 3-business-day right to cancel; deposits are escrowed or bonded.

lessons.title: The Systems: Air, Heat, Oil Tanks, Cooling, Plumbing, and Power
lessons.tagline: Boilers, furnaces, heat pumps, galvanized pipe, a 60-amp fuse box: know what you are looking at and what it means for the buyer.
objectives: Explain why ventilation matters and how attics, baths and crawl spaces are vented
Identify hot water, steam and forced air heat, and oil, gas and electric fuel
Explain oil tank risks (UST vs AST) and DEC rules on spills and abandonment
Compare piping materials for supply and waste and explain traps and vents
Explain voltage, amperage, fuses vs breakers, aluminum vs copper, and BX, Romex, conduit and Greenfield

blocks.title: Ditmas Park, a 1910 Victorian
blocks.html: Ray and Jordan are in the basement with Leo. There is a cast iron boiler with a sight glass, a 275-gallon oil tank against the wall, a fill pipe in the front yard that does not connect to anything Ray can see, galvanized pipes with a green-crusted copper patch, and a gray panel with screw-in fuses. Leo whispers: "Is this house going to kill me?"
blocks.casual: Ray, Jordan and Leo are down in the basement of a 1910 Victorian in Ditmas Park. There's a cast iron boiler with a sight glass, a 275-gallon oil tank against the wall, a fill pipe out in the front yard that doesn't seem to connect to anything Ray can find, galvanized pipes with a green-crusted copper patch, and a gray panel full of screw-in fuses. Leo whispers, "Is this house going to kill me?"

deeper.plain: Old houses have old systems. Each clue in that basement points to a specific risk you can check and price.
deeper.picture: It's like reading a used car's dashboard lights. Each one means something specific, and most are fixable if you know what you're looking at.
deeper.street: Ray translates for Leo: the sight glass means steam heat, the mystery fill pipe may mean a buried oil tank, the galvanized pipes explain the weak shower, and the fuse box probably means old wiring and a smaller service. Leo's attorney asks for a tank sweep and an electrician's estimate before signing.
deeper.stakes: A buried tank leak can cost tens of thousands to clean up, and the owner pays. Old fuses can make insurance hard to get. Skipping these checks is how buyers inherit expensive problems.
deeper.exam: Exam items here are mostly identification: sight glass means steam, fill pipe with no visible tank means possible UST, fuses versus breakers, galvanized pipe means low pressure over time.

blocks.text: Ventilation: the house has to breathe

blocks.html: Ventilation removes moisture, cooking and combustion byproducts, and stale air. Without it you get condensation, rot, mold, ice dams, peeling paint, and poor indoor air. Tight modern houses need it more, not less.
blocks.casual: Ventilation clears out moisture, cooking and combustion byproducts, and stale air. Skip it and you get condensation, rot, mold, ice dams, peeling paint and lousy indoor air. Tight modern houses need ventilation more, not less.

deeper.plain: A house needs to swap stale, wet air for fresh air or it starts to rot from the inside.
deeper.picture: It's like a gym bag. Zip it shut with damp clothes inside and a week later you've got a science experiment.
deeper.street: A Westchester family seals every gap in their 1950s cape to save on heat. The next winter, windows drip with condensation, paint peels in the bathroom, and mold shows up in a closet. An HVAC contractor adds a bath fan and an ERV for $3,800.
deeper.stakes: Poor ventilation causes mold, which can trigger health complaints and repair bills. Sellers who hide past mold remediation risk misrepresentation claims.
deeper.exam: If the question pairs a "tight" or "energy efficient" house with moisture problems, the answer involves ventilation. Ice dams point to attic ventilation and insulation.

items: Attic: air in through soffit vents, out through ridge or gable vents. Keeps the roof deck cold in winter (no ice dams) and cooler in summer.
Bathrooms and kitchens: exhaust fans ducted to the outside, never into the attic.
Crawl spaces: vented, or sealed and conditioned with a vapor barrier on the dirt.

Combustion appliances: boilers, furnaces and water heaters need combustion air and a proper flue or chimney. Carbon monoxide alarms are required in NY homes with fuel-burning appliances or attached garages.
Whole-house: very tight homes use mechanical ventilation, such as heat or energy recovery ventilators (HRV, ERV).
blocks.casual:
Attic: air comes in through the soffit vents and goes out through ridge or gable vents. That keeps the roof deck cold in winter (no ice dams) and cooler in summer.
Bathrooms and kitchens: exhaust fans ducted outside, never into the attic.
Crawl spaces: either vented, or sealed and conditioned with a vapor barrier over the dirt.
Combustion appliances: boilers, furnaces and water heaters need combustion air and a proper flue or chimney. NY requires carbon monoxide alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances or attached garages.
Whole-house: really tight homes use mechanical ventilation like heat or energy recovery ventilators (HRV, ERV).

deeper.plain: Each part of the house has its own way to move air, and anything that burns fuel needs air and a safe exhaust.
deeper.picture: Think of a house like a body: lungs (whole-house ventilation), sweat (bath fans), and a chimney that works like exhaling. Block any one and you feel it.
deeper.street: Ray finds Leo's bathroom fan dumping into the attic. The underside of the roof sheathing is black with mold. He also notes the house has a gas water heater and no CO alarm, which NY requires. Leo adds both to his repair request.
deeper.stakes: A blocked flue or missing CO alarm can kill someone. Venting a bath fan into the attic rots the roof deck. Both show up on inspection and cost real money.
deeper.exam: Know: soffit in, ridge or gable out. Bath fans vent outside. CO alarms required in NY homes with fuel-burning appliances or attached garages. HRV and ERV are mechanical ventilation.

blocks.text: Heating: what moves the heat, and what burns

head: System
How it works
Tells
Pros and cons
rows: Boiler heats water; pump circulates it to baseboards or radiators
Circulator pump, expansion tank, baseboard fins
Even, quiet heat; no AC ductwork included
Boiler boils water; steam rises to radiators, condenses, returns
Sight glass on boiler, cast iron radiators, hissing vents
Common in prewar NYC buildings; old, uneven, clanky but durable
Furnace heats air; blower pushes it through ducts
Furnace, filter, supply and return registers
Fast heat; ducts can carry central AC; dust and dry air

deeper.plain: Three ways to move heat through a house: hot water, steam, or warm air through ducts.
deeper.picture: Hot water heat is a gentle bath, steam is a sauna that hisses and clanks, and forced air is a hair dryer.
deeper.street: Leo's Victorian has steam: sight glass on the boiler, cast iron radiators, hissing vents. If he wants central AC, there are no ducts to share, so he'll look at ductless mini-splits. A Long Island colonial with a furnace and ducts can add central AC more cheaply.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who assume they can "just add AC" to a radiator house can face a big surprise bill. Old steam systems need ongoing care.
deeper.exam: Tells: sight glass means steam; expansion tank and circulator pump mean hot water; filter and registers mean forced air. Forced air can share ducts with central AC.

left.title: Boiler
items: Heats WATER (hot water or steam)
Radiators or baseboards
Can heat domestic water with a coil or indirect tank

right.title: Furnace
items: Heats AIR
Ducts and registers
Shares ducts and blower with central AC

deeper.plain: A boiler heats water. A furnace heats air.
deeper.picture: Boiler, like boiling water in a kettle. Furnace, like a blow dryer.
deeper.street: Jordan's listing sheet says "new furnace" for a Bushwick building with radiators. Diane catches it: radiators mean a boiler. Jordan fixes the listing before it goes live.
deeper.stakes: Wrong terms in a listing look sloppy and can mislead a buyer about whether ducts for AC exist.
deeper.exam: The exam swaps these on purpose. Radiators or baseboards point to a boiler. Ducts and registers point to a furnace. A boiler can heat domestic water through a coil.

head: Fuel
Notes
rows: Stored on site in a tank; delivery trucks; needs annual cleaning; tank leaks are an environmental liability
Piped by the utility; clean-burning; no tank; most common where available
Baseboard resistance heat is cheap to install, expensive to run; heat pumps are far more efficient

deeper.plain: Oil needs a tank and deliveries, gas comes through a pipe, electric is easy to install but resistance heat is pricey to run.
deeper.picture: Oil is like keeping a gas can in the garage. Gas is like city water. Electric baseboard is like heating your house with toasters.
deeper.street: Sal's Astoria building switches from oil to gas. He pays to have the old 1,000-gallon tank properly closed with paperwork. A buyer five years later asks for that paperwork, and having it keeps the deal moving.
deeper.stakes: Oil tanks are an environmental liability. Electric resistance heat can mean $500-a-month winter bills that scare off buyers.
deeper.exam: Oil is stored on site and needs annual service. Gas is piped by the utility. Heat pumps are far more efficient than electric baseboard.

blocks.html: Heating capacity is measured in BTUs (British Thermal Units): the heat needed to raise 1 pound of water 1 degree Fahrenheit. Boilers and furnaces are rated in BTUs per hour. Typical life expectancies are rough: cast iron boilers 25 to 35+ years, furnaces 15 to 25, tank water heaters 8 to 12.
blocks.casual: Heating power is measured in BTUs (British Thermal Units): the heat it takes to raise 1 pound of water 1 degree Fahrenheit. Boilers and furnaces are rated in BTUs per hour. Life expectancies are rough guides: cast iron boilers 25 to 35+ years, furnaces 15 to 25, tank water heaters 8 to 12.

deeper.plain: BTUs measure heat. Knowing typical lifespans helps you guess when something needs replacing.
deeper.picture: A BTU is like a calorie for houses: a fixed amount of heat energy.
deeper.street: Ray sees a date of 2009 on Leo's tank water heater. At 15-plus years it's past its usual 8 to 12, so Ray tells Leo to budget $2,000 for a replacement soon.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't budget for aging systems get hit right after closing. Knowing lifespans helps you negotiate credits.
deeper.exam: Definition question: a BTU raises 1 pound of water 1 degree Fahrenheit. Heating equipment is rated in BTUs per hour.

left.title: Underground storage tank (UST)
items: Buried, usually in the yard or under a driveway
Clue: a fill pipe and vent pipe sticking out of the ground
Leaks are invisible and can contaminate soil and groundwater
Steel tanks corrode; older ones (20 to 30+ years) are a red flag

right.title: Aboveground storage tank (AST)
items: In the basement or outside on a pad
Typically 275 or 330 gallons in homes
Leaks are visible; check for rust, weeping seams, stains
Easier and cheaper to inspect and replace

deeper.plain: Buried oil tanks hide leaks. Basement tanks show them.
deeper.picture: A buried tank is like a cavity under a crown. You can't see the rot until it's bad. A basement tank is like a tooth you can look at in the mirror.
deeper.street: A Bayside buyer's inspector spots a fill pipe and vent pipe in the side yard. A tank sweep finds a 550-gallon steel UST from the 1960s. Soil testing shows a small leak, and the seller pays $18,000 to remove the tank and clean up before closing.
deeper.stakes: A leaking UST can contaminate groundwater, and cleanup costs can run into six figures. The current owner is on the hook.
deeper.exam: UST clues: fill and vent pipes from the ground. Age 20 to 30+ is a red flag. ASTs are typically 275 or 330 gallons and leaks are visible.

blocks.title: DEC and oil tanks
blocks.html: The NYS Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) regulates petroleum bulk storage. Larger facilities must register, test and maintain tanks. Most home heating oil tanks used on premises are below the registration threshold, but any petroleum spill must be reported to DEC's Spill Hotline within 2 hours, and New York's Navigation Law makes the person responsible for a discharge strictly liable for cleanup. An abandoned tank should be properly closed: emptied, cleaned, and either removed or filled in place with inert material, with paperwork to prove it. Nassau, Suffolk and NYC (Fire Code) add their own tank rules.
blocks.casual: The NYS Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) regulates petroleum bulk storage. Bigger facilities have to register, test and maintain their tanks. Most home heating oil tanks used on site fall below the registration threshold, but any petroleum spill has to be reported to DEC's Spill Hotline within 2 hours, and New York's Navigation Law makes whoever's responsible for a discharge strictly liable for cleanup. An abandoned tank should be properly closed: emptied, cleaned, and either removed or filled in place with inert material, with paperwork to prove it. Nassau, Suffolk and NYC (Fire Code) pile on their own tank rules.

deeper.plain: A home oil tank usually doesn't need to be registered, but any spill has to be reported fast, and the owner pays for cleanup no matter whose fault it was.
deeper.picture: Strict liability is like a "you break it, you buy it" sign. It doesn't matter if you were careful.
deeper.street: An oil truck overfills Leo's neighbor's tank and oil pours onto the basement floor. The owner calls the DEC Spill Hotline within an hour. Under the Navigation Law, whoever is responsible for the discharge is strictly liable, so the oil company owes the cleanup even if its driver swears he was careful. Owners of the tank can end up liable too, which is why prompt reporting and insurance matter.
deeper.stakes: Failing to report a spill brings penalties on top of cleanup costs. Buyers who close without closure paperwork for an abandoned tank inherit the risk.
deeper.exam: Key cues: DEC regulates petroleum storage; 2-hour spill reporting; strict liability under the Navigation Law. Proper closure means emptied, cleaned, removed or filled in place, with documents.

blocks.title: A fill pipe with no tank
blocks.html: A fill pipe outside and no tank in the basement is the classic sign of an underground storage tank, active or abandoned. Recommend a tank sweep (metal detection) and, if found, a tightness or soil test. Oil delivered into an abandoned tank has caused real spills.
blocks.casual: See a fill pipe outside but no tank in the basement? That's the classic sign of an underground storage tank, active or abandoned. Recommend a tank sweep (metal detection) and, if one turns up, a tightness or soil test. Oil delivered into an abandoned tank has caused real spills.

deeper.plain: A fill pipe with no tank in sight means a tank is probably buried somewhere.
deeper.picture: It's like finding a charging cable plugged into the wall with nothing on the other end. The device is somewhere, you just can't see it.
deeper.street: A Queens homeowner converted to gas years ago and left the old fill pipe. An oil company shows up at the wrong address and pumps 200 gallons into the abandoned tank, which leaks. The cleanup costs $45,000.
deeper.stakes: Missing a UST can leave a buyer with a huge environmental bill. Agents who notice the pipe and say nothing invite liability.
deeper.exam: If a question describes a fill pipe in the yard and no basement tank, the answer is a possible UST and the recommended action is a tank sweep.

blocks.q: A buyer notices a capped pipe sticking out of the lawn and an oil burner connected to a gas line. The most likely concern is:
c: A septic vent
An abandoned underground oil tank
A radon mitigation pipe
A well casing
blocks.x: A fill or vent pipe in the yard of a house that converted to gas suggests an old UST left in the ground. It may leak and should be located and properly closed.

blocks.html: Central air conditioning is usually a split system: the outdoor condenser and compressor dump heat; the indoor evaporator coil, often on top of the furnace (an integral system with forced air), cools the air the blower pushes through the ducts. Refrigerant lines connect them. Most homes use air-cooled condensers; large buildings may use water-cooled systems with cooling towers. Cooling capacity is in BTUs: 1 ton = 12,000 BTU per hour. Compressors typically last 10 to 15 years.
blocks.casual: Central AC is usually a split system. The outdoor condenser and compressor dump the heat outside. The indoor evaporator coil, often sitting on top of the furnace (an integral system with forced air), cools the air the blower pushes through the ducts. Refrigerant lines connect the two. Most homes use air-cooled condensers; big buildings may use water-cooled systems with cooling towers. Cooling capacity is in BTUs: 1 ton = 12,000 BTU per hour. Compressors usually last 10 to 15 years.

deeper.plain: Central AC moves heat from inside to outside using a unit outdoors and a coil indoors, and it's sized in tons.
deeper.picture: It's like a refrigerator turned inside out: your house is the inside of the fridge, and the back of the fridge is the unit in your yard.
deeper.street: Leo's colonial has a 3-ton system, which is 36,000 BTU per hour. The compressor's nameplate says 2010. At 15 years, Ray tells him to budget for a $7,000 replacement.
deeper.stakes: Undersized or aging AC means a hot house and a near-term bill. Buyers who don't ask about age can be surprised the first summer.
deeper.exam: Memorize 1 ton equals 12,000 BTU per hour. Air-cooled for homes, water-cooled with cooling towers for big buildings.

blocks.html: A heat pump is an air conditioner that can run in reverse. In summer it moves heat out; in winter it pulls heat from outdoor air and moves it in. Because it moves heat instead of making it, it is far more efficient than electric resistance heat. Older units struggled in deep cold and relied on backup electric strips; modern cold-climate models work well in NY winters. Ductless mini-splits are common in NYC apartments and brownstones.
blocks.casual: A heat pump is basically an air conditioner that can run backward. In summer it moves heat out. In winter it pulls heat from the outdoor air and moves it in. Since it moves heat instead of making it, it's way more efficient than electric resistance heat. Older units struggled in deep cold and leaned on backup electric strips, but modern cold-climate models handle NY winters fine. Ductless mini-splits are everywhere in NYC apartments and brownstones.

deeper.plain: A heat pump moves heat in either direction, so one system can both heat and cool, and it uses far less electricity than baseboard heat.
deeper.picture: It's like a fridge you can flip around. Instead of pulling heat out of the box, it pulls heat out of the yard and pushes it into the house.
deeper.street: The Okafors add ductless mini-splits to their brownstone, one head per floor. They get AC for the first time and lower their oil use in winter, with state incentives covering part of the cost.
deeper.stakes: Selling an old heat pump without strip backup in a cold area can mean cold-weather complaints. New models change that, so know the age.
deeper.exam: Heat pump cue words: "reverses," "extracts heat from outside air," "heats and cools." Older units relied on backup electric strips in extreme cold.

left.title: Advantages
items: Heats and cools with one system
No on-site fuel or tank
Efficient; state utility incentives (NYS Clean Heat)
Ductless options for old buildings

right.title: Disadvantages
items: Higher installation cost
Output drops in extreme cold on older units
Frequent cycling and defrost cycles
Outdoor unit noise and placement

deeper.plain: Heat pumps heat and cool with one system and no fuel tank, but cost more to install and older units lose punch in deep cold.
deeper.picture: Like an electric car: cheap to run, no gas station trips, but a higher sticker price and you want a model built for winter.
deeper.street: Sal replaces his Astoria building's oil boiler with cold-climate heat pumps. Installation runs $90,000 before NYS Clean Heat incentives, but his heating fuel bill drops and he can remove the oil tank.
deeper.stakes: Placing an outdoor unit badly can annoy neighbors with noise. Underestimating install costs can blow a renovation budget.
deeper.exam: Expect "advantage" or "disadvantage" questions. No on-site fuel and one system for both are advantages. Higher installation cost and reduced output in extreme cold (older units) are disadvantages.

blocks.q: A central air system is rated at 36,000 BTU per hour. How many tons is it?
c: 2 tons
3 tons
4 tons
36 tons
blocks.x: 1 ton of cooling = 12,000 BTU per hour. 36,000 / 12,000 = 3 tons.

blocks.html: Domestic water arrives from the town main (through a meter, the owner usually responsible from the curb valve in) or from a private well (pump, pressure tank). Supply lines must be sized for adequate pressure; an old half-inch galvanized service often means weak showers. Hot water comes from a tank water heater (gas, oil or electric), a tankless coil inside a boiler, or an indirect tank heated by the boiler. Size the tank to the household (40 to 50 gallons for a typical family).
blocks.casual: Water comes in from the town main (through a meter, with the owner usually responsible from the curb valve inward) or from a private well (pump plus pressure tank). Supply lines have to be big enough for good pressure, and an old half-inch galvanized service usually means weak showers. Hot water comes from a tank water heater (gas, oil or electric), a tankless coil inside a boiler, or an indirect tank heated by the boiler. Size the tank for the household: 40 to 50 gallons for a typical family.

deeper.plain: Water comes from the city or a well, and the size and age of the pipes decide your water pressure.
deeper.picture: It's like drinking through a straw. A thin, crusty straw gives you a trickle no matter how hard you pull.
deeper.street: Leo's Ditmas Park shower is weak because the old half-inch galvanized service is choked with rust. A plumber quotes $6,500 to run a new copper service from the curb valve. The owner, not the city, pays for that stretch.
deeper.stakes: Buyers often assume the city owns the pipe to the house. Usually the owner is responsible from the curb valve in, and service line repairs can be expensive.
deeper.exam: Tankless coil equals hot water made inside the boiler. Owner typically responsible from the curb valve in. A well uses a pump and a pressure tank.

head: Pipe
Used for
Pros
Cons
rows: Rusts inside, narrows, low pressure; 40 to 60 year life
Can contain some lead; pitting over time
Cost; pinhole leaks in acidic water
Heavy; rusts and cracks with age
Noisier; not for hot supply; some local code limits
Health hazard; must be identified and replaced

deeper.plain: Pipes come in different materials, each with a typical problem: galvanized clogs, copper can pinhole, cast iron cracks, and lead is a health hazard.
deeper.picture: Pipes are like arteries. Galvanized builds up plaque, copper can spring a pinhole, and lead is poison in the bloodstream.
deeper.street: Ray finds a lead service line entering the Victorian. Leo's attorney asks the seller for a credit, and NYC's lead service line program information goes in the file. Galvanized supply lines inside will also need replacing over time.
deeper.stakes: Lead pipes are a health risk, especially for kids. Old cast iron stacks can crack and leak sewage into walls.
deeper.exam: Know which pipe is for what: copper for supply, cast iron and PVC for waste and vents, galvanized for older supply. Lead is never acceptable today.

blocks.html: Waste goes to the municipal sewer or an on-site septic system. Every fixture has a trap, the U-bend that holds water and blocks sewer gas, and must be vented to a vent stack through the roof. Without venting, draining water siphons the trap dry and sewer gas enters the house; you also hear gurgling drains.
blocks.casual: Waste goes out to the city sewer or an on-site septic system. Every fixture has a trap, the U-bend that holds a little water and blocks sewer gas, and every fixture has to be vented to a vent stack through the roof. Without venting, draining water sucks the trap dry and sewer gas comes into the house. You'll also hear gurgling drains.

deeper.plain: The U-shaped pipe under every sink holds water that blocks sewer smells, and the vent pipe keeps that water from getting sucked out.
deeper.picture: It's like a straw with your finger on top: without air coming in from the vent, the water won't flow right and everything gurgles.
deeper.street: Leo notices a sewer smell in an upstairs bathroom and gurgling when the tub drains. Ray finds that a past renovation skipped the vent. A plumber ties it into the stack for $1,200.
deeper.stakes: Sewer gas smells bad and can be unhealthy. Unvented fixtures are a code violation and a sign of unpermitted work.
deeper.exam: Trap equals water seal against sewer gas. Vent equals keeps the trap from siphoning. Gurgling and sewer smell are the clues.

blocks.caption: Follow power from the service drop or underground lateral, through the meter, to the main panel, then out on 120-volt and 240-volt circuits. Toggle fuses vs breakers.

blocks.html: Voltage is electrical pressure. Homes get 120/240 volts (older books and the syllabus say 110/220; same thing). Lights and outlets run on 120 volts (one hot wire, a single-pole breaker); dryers, ranges, central AC and well pumps run on 240 volts (two hot wires, a double-pole breaker). Amperage is the volume of current. Service size is in amps: 100 to 200 amps is typical today; 60-amp service is a sign of an old, undersized system. The main breaker or main fuse is marked with the service amperage.
blocks.casual: Voltage is electrical pressure. Homes get 120/240 volts (older books and the syllabus say 110/220, which is the same thing). Lights and outlets run on 120 volts: one hot wire and a single-pole breaker. Dryers, ranges, central AC and well pumps run on 240 volts: two hot wires and a double-pole breaker. Amperage is how much current flows. Service size is measured in amps: 100 to 200 amps is typical now, and 60-amp service tells you the system is old and undersized. The main breaker or main fuse is marked with the service amperage.

deeper.plain: Volts push electricity, amps are how much flows. A bigger service (more amps) can run more stuff at once.
deeper.picture: Voltage is water pressure in a hose. Amperage is how much water flows through it. A 60-amp service is a garden hose trying to fill a pool.
deeper.street: Leo wants central AC, an electric dryer and an induction range in the Victorian. Ray reads 60 amps on the main fuse. An electrician quotes $4,000 to upgrade to 200 amps first.
deeper.stakes: Overloading an undersized service trips breakers or blows fuses, and old systems can overheat. Insurers and lenders may balk at 60-amp service.
deeper.exam: 120/240 equals 110/220 on the exam. 240-volt appliances use two hot wires. Service of 100 to 200 amps is typical. The main breaker shows the service amperage.

head: Who
Responsibility
rows: Brings service to the property (overhead service drop or underground lateral), owns the meter
Everything from the service entrance (weatherhead or meter base) into the house: service cable, panel, wiring, devices
blocks.caption: Service may arrive above ground (overhead) or below ground (buried lateral, common in newer subdivisions)

deeper.plain: The utility brings power to the house and owns the meter. Everything from the service entrance inward is the owner's job.
deeper.picture: The utility delivers the package to your door. Once it's inside, you own it.
deeper.street: A storm tears the service cable off the Okafors' house at the weatherhead. Con Ed reconnects the drop, but the Okafors have to pay an electrician to fix the damaged weatherhead and meter base first.
deeper.stakes: Owners who assume the utility will fix everything wait days without power. Knowing who owns what speeds repairs and insurance claims.
deeper.exam: Utility owns the service drop and meter. The owner is responsible from the service entrance in. Service can be overhead or underground (lateral).

left.title: Fuse
items: Screw-in or cartridge; a metal strip melts when overloaded
Must be replaced after it blows
Danger: oversized fuses (a 30 in a 15-amp circuit) defeat protection
Insurers and lenders may balk at old fuse panels

right.title: Circuit breaker
items: Switch trips when overloaded
Reset by flipping it back
Standard in modern panels
GFCI and AFCI breakers add shock and arc protection

deeper.plain: Fuses and breakers both cut power when a circuit is overloaded. Fuses burn out and get replaced; breakers trip and get reset.
deeper.picture: A fuse is a one-time-use smoke detector battery. A breaker is a light switch that flips itself off when things get too hot.
deeper.street: Ray finds a 30-amp fuse screwed into a 15-amp circuit in Leo's panel. Someone got tired of fuses blowing. The wires can now overheat before the fuse ever blows. Ray flags it as a fire hazard.
deeper.stakes: Oversized fuses defeat the protection and can start fires. Insurers may refuse coverage or require a panel upgrade.
deeper.exam: Fuses must be replaced; breakers reset. GFCI protects against shock, AFCI against arcing. An oversized fuse is a hazard.

head: Wiring
What it is
Where
rows: Wires inside a flexible spiral metal jacket
Common in NYC and older homes
Most common in new suburban homes; restricted in many NYC buildings
Rigid metal or PVC tube that wires are pulled through
Flexible metal conduit, empty, wires pulled through
Connections to motors, furnaces, short flexible runs

deeper.plain: Wiring comes in different jackets: metal spiral (BX), plastic (Romex), or pulled through tubes (conduit or Greenfield).
deeper.picture: BX is a garden hose with a metal coil around it. Romex is a plain rubber hose. Conduit is a pipe you thread the hose through.
deeper.street: An electrician bidding the Okafors' brownstone rewire uses BX, because NYC restricts Romex in many buildings. Leo's cousin's new Long Island house is all Romex. A furnace connection uses a short run of Greenfield.
deeper.stakes: Using wiring that the local code doesn't allow fails inspection and may need to be redone at the owner's cost.
deeper.exam: BX equals armored cable. Romex equals nonmetallic sheathed cable. Greenfield equals flexible metal conduit. Conduit is common in commercial work.

blocks.title: Aluminum vs copper
blocks.html: Copper is the standard. Aluminum branch wiring, used in some homes from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s, expands and oxidizes at connections, loosens, and can overheat and start fires. It needs repair with approved connectors or devices. Aluminum for the large service entrance cable is normal and not the same concern.
blocks.casual: Copper is the standard. Aluminum branch wiring, used in some homes from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s, expands and oxidizes at connections, works loose, and can overheat and start fires. It has to be fixed with approved connectors or devices. Aluminum for the big service entrance cable is normal and not the same concern.

deeper.plain: Aluminum wiring in the outlets and switches of 1960s and 70s houses can overheat. Aluminum for the main service cable is fine.
deeper.picture: Aluminum branch wiring is like a loose battery in a flashlight. It wiggles, sparks and gets hot.
deeper.street: Ray finds aluminum branch wiring in a 1972 split-level in Rockland. The seller's insurer wants it fixed. An electrician installs approved connectors at every outlet and switch for $3,200, and the sale goes through.
deeper.stakes: Aluminum branch wiring is a known fire risk and some insurers won't cover it unremediated. Failing to disclose it is asking for trouble.
deeper.exam: The trap: aluminum service entrance cable is normal. The concern is aluminum branch wiring from roughly the mid-1960s to mid-1970s.

blocks.q: Which appliance most likely requires a 240-volt circuit?
c: Table lamp
Electric clothes dryer
Laptop charger
Ceiling fan
blocks.x: Large loads like dryers, ranges, central AC and well pumps use 240 volts on a double-pole breaker. Lamps and small electronics use 120 volts.

story.title: Is This House Going to Kill Me?
story.setting: Ditmas Park, Brooklyn, a basement that smells faintly of 1910

beats.text: Is this house going to kill me?
Not today. That's a steam boiler. Sight glass, see the water line? Steam goes up to the radiators, condenses, comes back. Old as dirt, runs forever.
And the big tank?
275-gallon aboveground oil tank. I like aboveground. You can see a leak. Look at the bottom seam for rust and weeping.
Ray, there's a fill pipe out front that doesn't go to this tank.
Now you're thinking. That could be an old buried tank from before this one. Get a tank sweep. If it's there, it gets closed properly, with paperwork.

check.q: What does an extra fill pipe in the yard suggest?
c: A sewer cleanout
A possible abandoned underground oil tank
A gas meter
A well
check.x: Fill pipes feed oil tanks. One that doesn't connect to the basement tank suggests an underground tank, which can leak unseen.

beats.text: And the pipes?
Galvanized. Rusts inside, chokes the flow. That's why the shower's weak. Someone patched it with copper. Budget for replacing it.
Ray opened the gray panel. Inside, four screw-in fuses. One was a 30 sitting where a 15 belonged.
That's the scary one. Fuse is too big for the wire. The wire overheats before the fuse blows.
And it says 60 amps on the main. For a house with central air plans, that's undersized.
So: replace the panel, find the tank, redo the pipes. That's three lines on my spreadsheet.
Three lines and a steam boiler that'll outlive both of us.
Back at the office: You didn't diagnose anything, Jordan. You pointed, you recommended the right professional, and you wrote it down. That's the agent's job.

board.prompt: Draw the main electrical panel: service entrance, main breaker, a 120-volt single-pole circuit to outlets, and a 240-volt double-pole circuit to the dryer. Label amps and volts.

facts.text: Ventilation removes moisture and stale air: attic air enters at soffit vents and leaves at ridge or gable vents (preventing ice dams), and bath and kitchen fans must vent outside, never into the attic.
Carbon monoxide alarms are required in NY homes with fuel-burning appliances or attached garages, and combustion appliances need combustion air and a proper flue.
Forced warm air: a furnace heats air and a blower pushes it through ducts, which can also carry central air conditioning.
Steam heat shows a sight glass on the boiler and hissing cast iron radiators, and is common in prewar NYC buildings.
A boiler heats water (hot water or steam) for radiators or baseboards; a furnace heats air for ducts and registers.
Oil is stored in an on-site tank, natural gas is piped by the utility with no tank, and electric baseboard heat is cheap to install but expensive to run.
A BTU is the heat needed to raise 1 pound of water 1 degree Fahrenheit; boilers and furnaces are rated in BTUs per hour.
Rough life expectancies: cast iron boilers 25 to 35+ years, furnaces 15 to 25, tank water heaters 8 to 12.
An underground tank (UST) is buried and leaks invisibly into soil and groundwater; an aboveground tank (AST), typically 275 or 330 gallons in a basement or on a pad, shows its leaks.
Any petroleum spill must be reported to DEC's Spill Hotline within 2 hours, and the Navigation Law makes the person responsible for a discharge strictly liable for cleanup.
Most home heating oil tanks are below DEC's registration threshold, but an abandoned tank should be emptied, cleaned, and removed or filled in place with inert material, with paperwork to prove it.
A fill or vent pipe outside with no tank in the basement is the classic sign of an underground tank; recommend a tank sweep and, if one is found, a tightness or soil test.
Cooling capacity is in BTUs, and 1 ton equals 12,000 BTU per hour; central air is usually a split system with an outdoor condenser and an indoor evaporator coil.
A heat pump is an air conditioner that runs in reverse, moving heat instead of making it, so it is far more efficient than electric resistance heat and needs no on-site fuel.
From the curb valve in, the owner is usually responsible for the water service; hot water comes from a tank heater, a tankless coil in a boiler, or an indirect tank.
Galvanized steel supply pipe rusts inside and narrows, causing low pressure and reduced flow.
Copper is the long-lived standard for supply, cast iron serves waste and vent stacks, PVC is for drains but not hot supply, and lead service lines are a health hazard to replace.
Every fixture has a trap holding water to block sewer gas, and the vent stack through the roof keeps draining water from siphoning traps dry.
Lights and outlets run on 120 volts; dryers, ranges, central AC and well pumps run on 240 volts (two hot wires, a double-pole breaker).
Service capacity is measured in amps: 100 to 200 amps is typical today, and 60-amp service signals an old, undersized system.
The utility brings service to the property and owns the meter; the landowner is responsible for everything from the service entrance into the house.
A circuit breaker trips and is reset; a fuse's metal strip melts and the fuse must be replaced.
An oversized fuse (a 30 in a 15-amp circuit) defeats protection, so the wire can overheat before the fuse blows.
BX is armored cable in a spiral metal jacket, Romex is plastic-sheathed cable, conduit is a tube wires are pulled through, and Greenfield is flexible metal conduit.
Aluminum branch wiring from the mid-1960s to mid-1970s loosens and overheats at connections and can start fires; aluminum service entrance cable is normal.

lessons.title: Hazards Inside the House: Asbestos, Lead, Radon, Mold, and More
lessons.tagline: Most of these are invisible. Your job is to know where they hide, what the rules say, and who to call.
objectives: Explain asbestos uses, health effects, testing and removal, and why friable matters
Apply the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule and NY/NYC lead rules
State the radon action level, how radon enters, and how it is tested and mitigated
Describe mold, indoor air quality, UFFI, PCBs, CFCs, EMFs and termites, and NY's mold licensing law

blocks.title: Grace Okafor's basement
blocks.html: The Okafors' 1899 Bed-Stuy brownstone is going on the market. In the basement: white wrap on the old heating pipes, crumbling at one elbow. Upstairs: original window frames with layers of paint. Grace mentions their grandson visits every weekend. Emmanuel asks if they have to "tell anyone about any of it."
blocks.casual: The Okafors' 1899 Bed-Stuy brownstone is about to hit the market. Down in the basement, the old heating pipes are wrapped in white stuff that's crumbling at one elbow. Upstairs, the original window frames have coat after coat of paint. Grace mentions their grandson visits every weekend. Emmanuel asks whether they have to "tell anyone about any of it."

deeper.plain: An 1899 house almost certainly has lead paint, and that crumbling pipe wrap may be asbestos. Federal law requires lead paperwork for this sale, and the crumbling wrap needs attention.
deeper.picture: It's like selling a used car with a known brake issue. You may not have to fix it, but you can't hide it, and some paperwork is mandatory.
deeper.street: Jordan explains to the Okafors that the federal lead rule applies to any home built before 1978: EPA pamphlet, disclosure of what they know, a 10-day chance for the buyer to test, and signed forms kept 3 years. Ray recommends a licensed contractor look at the crumbling pipe wrap before showings, and Grace keeps the grandson out of the basement.
deeper.stakes: Skipping the lead disclosure exposes the sellers and the agents to federal penalties and lawsuits. Friable asbestos can expose a child or a buyer's inspector to fibers.
deeper.exam: Expect fact patterns with an old house, a child, and a question about what the seller must do. Answer: lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing, and friable asbestos is the hazard.

blocks.caption: Click each hazard: where it hides in the house, the health risk, how it is tested, and the fix.

blocks.html: Asbestos is a natural mineral fiber that was prized for fireproofing and insulation. It shows up in pipe and boiler wrap, old floor tiles (9 by 9 inch), ceiling and wall texture, roofing and siding shingles, and vermiculite attic insulation. Use peaked mid-century; EPA banned the last form still in use (chrysotile) in 2024.
blocks.casual: Asbestos is a natural mineral fiber that builders loved for fireproofing and insulation. You'll find it in pipe and boiler wrap, old 9 by 9 inch floor tiles, ceiling and wall texture, roofing and siding shingles, and vermiculite attic insulation. Use peaked mid-century, and EPA banned the last form still in use (chrysotile) in 2024.

deeper.plain: Asbestos is a fiber once used everywhere for fireproofing. Older homes often have it in pipe wrap, tiles and shingles.
deeper.picture: Think of it like glitter from a craft project decades ago. It's in places you'd never guess, and it's hard to fully get rid of.
deeper.street: Leo's inspector finds 9 by 9 inch floor tiles in a 1955 Levittown basement. A bulk sample confirms asbestos. Leo decides to leave them and put new flooring on top rather than pay $4,500 to remove them.
deeper.stakes: Renovating without checking for asbestos can expose workers and family to fibers, and the owner can face fines and cleanup costs.
deeper.exam: Know the common locations: pipe wrap, 9x9 tiles, popcorn ceilings, shingles, vermiculite. The 2024 EPA chrysotile ban is newer than most textbooks.

blocks.html: Asbestos is dangerous when friable: crumbly enough to release fibers into the air when disturbed. Inhaled fibers cause asbestosis (lung scarring), lung cancer, and mesothelioma (a cancer of the lining of the lungs and abdomen), often decades after exposure.
blocks.casual: Asbestos turns dangerous when it's friable, meaning crumbly enough to throw fibers into the air when it's disturbed. Breathe those fibers in and you can get asbestosis (scarring of the lungs), lung cancer, or mesothelioma (a cancer of the lining of the lungs and abdomen), often decades later.

deeper.plain: Asbestos only hurts you when its fibers get into the air and into your lungs. Crumbly asbestos does that.
deeper.picture: It's like a dandelion gone to seed. Leave it alone and nothing happens. Touch it and the fluff flies everywhere.
deeper.street: The Okafors' pipe wrap is crumbling at one elbow. Every time the boiler kicks on, air movement could spread fibers. A licensed contractor encapsulates that section for $800 before the open house.
deeper.stakes: Diseases show up decades later, so the harm isn't obvious at first. That's why lawsuits over asbestos exposure can come years after a sale or renovation.
deeper.exam: If the question asks what makes asbestos hazardous, the answer is friable. Diseases: asbestosis, lung cancer, mesothelioma.

head: Testing
What it is
rows: A piece of the suspect material is cut and sent to a lab
Air is pumped through filters to count fibers, before, during and after work
Surfaces are wiped to check for settled fibers or dust

deeper.plain: Three ways to test: cut a piece and send it to a lab, filter the air, or wipe surfaces.
deeper.picture: Bulk sampling is a biopsy, air monitoring is a breathalyzer, and wipe sampling is a cotton swab.
deeper.street: Before removing pipe wrap from Sal's Astoria basement, the contractor sends a bulk sample to a lab to confirm asbestos. During removal, air monitors run inside and outside the containment. Afterward, wipe samples prove the basement is clear before Sal's tenants can use their storage cages again.
deeper.stakes: Skipping air monitoring can leave a building contaminated after "removal." Clearance testing protects owners from future claims.
deeper.exam: Bulk sampling identifies the material. Air monitoring checks fibers in the air during and after work. Wipe sampling checks settled dust.

blocks.html: Options: leave intact material alone, encapsulate (seal it), enclose it, or remove it. Removal is the riskiest and must be done by licensed asbestos contractors (NYS Department of Labor licenses them; NYC DEP adds its own rules) with containment and air monitoring. Disturbing it yourself is how people get hurt.
