blocks.casual: Your options: leave intact material alone, encapsulate it (seal it), enclose it, or remove it. Removal is the riskiest, and it has to be done by licensed asbestos contractors (the NYS Department of Labor licenses them, and NYC DEP adds its own rules) with containment and air monitoring. Doing it yourself is how people get hurt.

deeper.plain: You can leave it, seal it, cover it, or take it out. Taking it out stirs it up the most and needs licensed pros.
deeper.picture: It's like a wasp nest in the attic wall. Often the safest move is to seal it in. Knocking it down yourself is how you get stung.
deeper.street: A Bushwick flipper rips out old ceiling texture himself to save money. A neighbor complains, NYC DEP inspects, and he's hit with violations and has to pay a licensed abatement contractor to clean the whole floor anyway.
deeper.stakes: DIY asbestos removal risks health, fines and contaminating the whole house, which then has to be professionally cleaned.
deeper.exam: Encapsulation equals sealing. Enclosure equals building a barrier around it. Removal requires licensed contractors (NYS DOL licenses them).

blocks.title: Removal is not always the answer
blocks.html: Intact, non-friable asbestos is often safest left alone or encapsulated. The exam may ask what makes asbestos hazardous: the answer is friable (fibers released), not merely its presence.
blocks.casual: Removal isn't always the right call. Asbestos that's intact and not friable is often safest left alone or encapsulated. The exam may ask what makes asbestos hazardous, and the answer is friable (fibers released), not just the fact that it's there.

deeper.plain: If it's intact and not crumbling, leaving it or sealing it is often safest.
deeper.picture: Like an old filling in a tooth. If it isn't cracking, drilling it out can cause more problems than leaving it.
deeper.street: A Queens co-op board panics when an engineer finds asbestos tiles under carpet in the hallway. Kim gets a second opinion: the tiles are intact. The board encapsulates them under new flooring for a fraction of what removal would cost.
deeper.stakes: Over-reacting to intact asbestos can cost owners and boards tens of thousands. Under-reacting to friable asbestos can hurt people.
deeper.exam: The trap answer is "any presence of asbestos is hazardous" or "it must always be removed." The right answer centers on friability.

blocks.q: Asbestos pipe insulation is most hazardous when it:
c: Is painted
Is friable and releasing fibers
Is in an unheated basement
Was installed after 1960
blocks.x: Friable asbestos crumbles and releases fibers that can be inhaled. Intact, sealed material is far less dangerous.

blocks.html: Lead-based paint was banned for residential use in 1978. Lead also comes from old service lines and solder in water, and from soil near old painted houses and roads (leaded gasoline). Children under 6 absorb lead easily; even low levels damage the brain and nervous system, lowering IQ and causing behavior problems. Adults face high blood pressure, kidney damage, and reproductive harm.
blocks.casual: Lead-based paint was banned for residential use in 1978. Lead also gets into water through old service lines and solder, and into soil near old painted houses and roads (from leaded gas). Kids under 6 absorb lead easily, and even low levels damage the brain and nervous system, lowering IQ and causing behavior problems. Adults face high blood pressure, kidney damage and reproductive harm.

deeper.plain: Lead from old paint, pipes and soil can harm anyone, but it does the most damage to young kids' brains.
deeper.picture: Old lead paint is like a sweet-tasting poison. Toddlers put paint chips and dusty hands in their mouths, and that's how it gets in.
deeper.street: The Okafors' grandson plays by the old windows. Every time a sash slides, friction grinds lead paint into dust on the sill. A lead inspector finds high dust levels, and the Okafors hire a lead-safe certified contractor to replace the window frames.
deeper.stakes: Lead poisoning is permanent. Landlords and sellers who ignore it face lawsuits, and in NYC, HPD violations.
deeper.exam: Key facts: banned for residential use in 1978. Children under 6 are most vulnerable. Sources: paint, water, soil.

head: Federal lead disclosure rule (HUD and EPA), housing built before 1978
Requirement
rows: Give the EPA pamphlet Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home
Seller or landlord discloses known lead hazards and provides any reports
Buyer gets a 10-day opportunity to test (can be waived or changed in writing)
Lead warning statement and signed disclosure attached to the contract or lease
Seller and agents keep the paperwork 3 years
Agents must make sure sellers and landlords comply, or share liability

deeper.plain: For homes built before 1978, sellers and landlords must hand over a pamphlet, tell what they know, give buyers a chance to test, and keep the paperwork.
deeper.picture: It's a five-item checklist you run on every pre-1978 sale or lease: pamphlet, disclose, 10 days, sign, save.
deeper.street: Jordan lists the Okafors' house. Before the contract is signed, the buyer gets the EPA pamphlet and the signed disclosure, and the contract includes the lead warning statement and a 10-day testing window. Jordan's brokerage keeps the paperwork for 3 years.
deeper.stakes: Agents share liability if they don't make sure sellers and landlords comply. Penalties can include federal fines and triple damages in lawsuits.
deeper.exam: Numbers to know: before 1978, 10 days to test, 3 years to keep records. The buyer can waive the test in writing. Agents have a duty too.

blocks.title: Before 1978, not after
blocks.html: The 2022 syllabus says "after 1978" in places. That is a typo. The rule covers housing built before 1978. Exemptions include 0-bedroom units, housing for the elderly or disabled (unless a child under 6 lives there), and short-term leases of 100 days or less.
blocks.casual: The 2022 syllabus says "after 1978" in spots. That's a typo. The rule covers housing built before 1978. Exemptions include 0-bedroom units, housing for the elderly or disabled (unless a child under 6 lives there), and short-term leases of 100 days or less.

deeper.plain: It's homes built before 1978 that need lead disclosure. A few small categories are exempt.
deeper.picture: If someone says "after 1978," that's like saying the seatbelt rule only applies to cars without seatbelts. It's backwards.
deeper.street: Sal rents a studio (0 bedrooms) in his Astoria building on a 2-year lease. The federal lead disclosure rule exempts 0-bedroom units, but NYC's own lead law may still apply to him, so Diane tells Jordan to check both.
deeper.stakes: Relying on the wrong year or a misread exemption can mean skipping a required disclosure, which exposes everyone in the deal.
deeper.exam: The exam may use "pre-1978" or "built before 1978." Exempt: 0-bedroom, elderly or disabled housing (no child under 6), leases of 100 days or less.

blocks.title: NYC Local Law 1 of 2004
blocks.html: NYC landlords of buildings with 3 or more units built before 1960 (or 1960 to 1978 if lead paint is known) must find and fix lead paint hazards in apartments where a child under 6 lives or regularly spends 10+ hours a week, use lead-safe work practices, and do turnover work when tenants move. The rules on testing and lower lead thresholds have tightened since; check current HPD guidance.
blocks.casual: NYC landlords of buildings with 3 or more units built before 1960 (or 1960 to 1978 if they know there's lead paint) have to find and fix lead paint hazards in apartments where a child under 6 lives or regularly spends 10+ hours a week. They have to use lead-safe work practices and do turnover work when tenants move out. The testing rules and lead thresholds have gotten stricter since, so check current HPD guidance.

deeper.plain: NYC landlords in older buildings must actively look for and fix lead hazards where young kids live or spend time.
deeper.picture: The federal rule is "tell them." NYC's rule is "tell them and go fix it."
deeper.street: A tenant in Sal's Astoria building has a new baby. Under Local Law 1, Sal has to inspect that apartment for lead hazards every year, fix peeling paint with lead-safe methods, and do turnover work when anyone moves out.
deeper.stakes: Landlords who ignore Local Law 1 face HPD violations and heavy liability if a child is poisoned.
deeper.exam: Local Law 1 of 2004: 3+ units, built before 1960 (or 1960 to 1978 with known lead), child under 6. It's NYC-specific, so it only appears on NYC-flavored questions.

blocks.q: A seller's 1965 house is being sold. The federal lead disclosure rule requires:
c: Nothing, because it was built after 1960
The EPA pamphlet, disclosure of known hazards, and a 10-day testing opportunity
Mandatory lead abatement before closing
A lead inspection by the seller
blocks.x: The rule covers housing built before 1978. It requires disclosure and an opportunity to test, not testing or abatement by the seller.

blocks.html: Radon is a colorless, odorless, radioactive gas from the natural breakdown of uranium in soil and rock. It enters through foundation cracks, sump pits, floor drains and gaps around pipes, pulled in because a house is under slightly lower pressure than the soil. It is the leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers. Some upstate counties have notably high levels; it is found everywhere.
blocks.casual: Radon is a colorless, odorless, radioactive gas that comes from uranium breaking down naturally in soil and rock. It gets in through foundation cracks, sump pits, floor drains and gaps around pipes, sucked in because the house sits at slightly lower pressure than the soil. It's the leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers. Some upstate counties run notably high, but it's found everywhere.

deeper.plain: Radon is an invisible radioactive gas from the ground that seeps into basements and causes lung cancer.
deeper.picture: Your house acts like a straw stuck in the ground, gently sucking soil gas up through every crack.
deeper.street: Leo's buying in Ulster County. His inspector sets a radon test in the basement for 48 hours. It reads 7.2 pCi/L. Leo negotiates a $1,500 credit for a mitigation system.
deeper.stakes: Radon can't be seen or smelled, so buyers who skip the test never know. Over years it raises lung cancer risk for the whole family.
deeper.exam: Radon comes from uranium decay in soil and rock. It enters through the foundation. It's the leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers (smoking is first overall).

items: Testing: short-term tests (2 to 90 days, charcoal canisters or electronic monitors) in the lowest livable level; long-term tests over 90 days give a truer annual average.
Action level: EPA recommends fixing at 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) or more.
Mitigation: sub-slab depressurization: a pipe through the slab and a fan that vents soil gas above the roofline. Seal cracks.
New construction: radon-resistant techniques: gravel layer, plastic vapor barrier, sealed slab, passive vent pipe ready for a fan.
blocks.casual:
Testing: short-term tests (2 to 90 days, charcoal canisters or electronic monitors) go in the lowest livable level. Long-term tests over 90 days give a truer annual average.
Action level: EPA says fix it at 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) or more.
Mitigation: sub-slab depressurization, meaning a pipe through the slab and a fan that vents soil gas out above the roofline. Seal the cracks too.
New construction: radon-resistant techniques: a gravel layer, plastic vapor barrier, sealed slab, and a passive vent pipe ready for a fan.

deeper.plain: Test the lowest living level. At 4 or above, install a pipe and fan to pull radon out from under the slab.
deeper.picture: Mitigation is a range hood for your foundation, sucking gas out from under the house and blowing it past the roof.
deeper.street: The Okafors' buyer runs a short-term radon test with a charcoal canister in the cellar. It reads 3.1. Under the 4 action level, so no mitigation required, though the buyer could still choose to do a long-term test after moving in.
deeper.stakes: Mitigating below 4 is optional, but ignoring a reading of 4 or above leaves health risk on the table and can come up at resale.
deeper.exam: Numbers: 4 pCi/L action level. Short-term 2 to 90 days, long-term over 90. Mitigation is sub-slab depressurization.

blocks.title: Four is the floor
blocks.html: Radon: 4 pCi/L means fix it. Pipe plus fan, under the slab, out the roof.
blocks.casual: Radon: 4 pCi/L means fix it. Pipe plus fan, under the slab, out the roof.

deeper.plain: Remember 4 and remember pipe, fan, roof.
deeper.picture: Four is the floor, like a minimum score to pass. Hit it or go higher, you act.
deeper.street: Jordan's buyer in Saratoga asks if 4.0 counts. Jordan says yes: at or above 4 pCi/L, EPA recommends fixing.
deeper.stakes: Misquoting the action level can lead a buyer to skip a needed fix or overspend on one they don't need.
deeper.exam: Distractors will offer 2, 10 or 40 pCi/L. The correct EPA action level is 4.

blocks.html: Indoor air quality problems come from combustion gases (carbon monoxide), formaldehyde from building products, VOCs from paints and cleaners, radon, mold, and poor ventilation. Sick building syndrome is when occupants feel ill in a building (headaches, irritation) and improve after leaving, usually in tight offices with poor ventilation.
blocks.casual: Indoor air quality problems come from combustion gases (carbon monoxide), formaldehyde from building products, VOCs from paint and cleaners, radon, mold, and poor ventilation. Sick building syndrome is when people feel sick in a building (headaches, irritation) and get better after they leave, usually in tight offices with bad ventilation.

deeper.plain: Indoor air can be worse than outdoor air, and if people feel sick only inside a building, ventilation is usually the culprit.
deeper.picture: It's like the air in a closed car on a hot day after somebody sprayed air freshener. You don't notice until you step out and feel better.
deeper.street: Evelyn's tenants in a sealed 1980s office building in White Plains complain of headaches that vanish on weekends. An engineer finds the fresh-air dampers stuck nearly closed. Fixing them ends the complaints.
deeper.stakes: Commercial landlords with sick building complaints can lose tenants and face lease disputes. Residential buyers may walk if CO or VOC problems surface.
deeper.exam: Sick building syndrome: symptoms in the building that ease after leaving, linked to poor ventilation. Formaldehyde and VOCs come from building products and finishes.

blocks.html: Mold grows wherever moisture persists: leaks, floods, humid basements, poorly vented bathrooms. It can trigger allergies and asthma. Fix the water first, then clean or remove moldy materials. Testing is done by visual inspection plus air or surface samples.
blocks.casual: Mold grows anywhere moisture hangs around: leaks, floods, humid basements, bathrooms without good venting. It can set off allergies and asthma. Fix the water problem first, then clean or remove the moldy materials. Testing means a visual inspection plus air or surface samples.

deeper.plain: Mold needs water. Stop the water, then clean up the mold.
deeper.picture: Mold is like weeds. Pull them without fixing the soil and they come right back.
deeper.street: A Bay Ridge co-op buyer smells must in a closet. Behind the wall, a slow leak from the upstairs bathroom has fed mold for months. Bleaching the surface won't help. The upstairs leak has to be repaired first, then the drywall replaced.
deeper.stakes: Cleaning mold without fixing the moisture wastes money, and sellers who paint over mold to hide it face misrepresentation claims.
deeper.exam: "Fix the moisture source first" is almost always the right answer on mold questions.

blocks.title: NY mold licensing
blocks.html: Under New York's mold program (Labor Law Article 32, since 2016), mold assessment and remediation of more than 10 square feet must be done by Department of Labor licensed assessors and remediators, and the assessor and remediator on a project must be different, independent companies. In NYC, Local Law 55 of 2018 requires landlords to inspect for and fix mold and pests as asthma triggers.
blocks.casual: Under New York's mold program (Labor Law Article 32, since 2016), mold assessment and remediation over 10 square feet has to be done by Department of Labor licensed assessors and remediators. And the assessor and the remediator on a job have to be different, independent companies. In NYC, Local Law 55 of 2018 makes landlords inspect for and fix mold and pests as asthma triggers.

deeper.plain: In NY, the company that checks for mold can't be the same one that removes it, for jobs over 10 square feet.
deeper.picture: It's like not letting the mechanic who diagnoses your car also be the one who profits from the repair. Separate people keep it honest.
deeper.street: Sal finds mold in a basement apartment covering about 40 square feet. He hires a licensed assessor who writes a remediation plan, then a different licensed remediator who does the work. In NYC, Local Law 55 also requires Sal to address it as an asthma trigger.
deeper.stakes: Using one company for both is a violation. Landlords who ignore mold in NYC face HPD violations and tenant claims.
deeper.exam: NY mold law: over 10 square feet, licensed by NYS Department of Labor, assessor and remediator must be independent. NYC Local Law 55 covers mold and pests.

blocks.q: Under New York law, a company that writes the mold assessment for a 40-square-foot basement mold problem may also:
c: Perform the remediation
Not perform the remediation on the same project
Skip licensing if the owner consents
Certify the work with no clearance inspection
blocks.x: NY requires separate, independent licensed firms for assessment and remediation on projects over 10 square feet, to avoid a conflict of interest.

head: Hazard
Where
Concern and fix
rows: Releases formaldehyde gas, mostly when new; largely stopped by early 1980s. Disclose if known; testing shows current levels
Old electrical transformers, capacitors, fluorescent light ballasts, some caulk
Banned 1979; persist in soil and river sediment; probable carcinogen. Test, remove leaking equipment, licensed disposal
Old AC and refrigerator refrigerant (Freon), old aerosols, foam
Deplete the ozone layer. Phased out under the Montreal Protocol and Clean Air Act; refrigerant must be recovered by EPA-certified technicians
Health link unproven; buyers may still care. Measured with a gaussmeter; distance is the main remedy
Inspect for mud tubes and damaged wood; treatment by DEC-certified pesticide applicators. Chlordane, the old soil treatment, was banned in 1988

deeper.plain: A handful of other hazards show up in older properties: formaldehyde foam insulation, PCBs in old electrical gear, ozone-harming refrigerants, power line fields, and termites.
deeper.picture: Think of this as the "weird stuff in the attic" list. Each item has its own clue and its own fix.
deeper.street: Ray checks a 1970s Rockland house: injected foam in the walls (possible UFFI), an old fluorescent ballast leaking oil (possible PCBs), and mud tubes on the sill plate (termites). He recommends a formaldehyde test, licensed disposal of the ballast, and treatment by a DEC-certified applicator.
deeper.stakes: Leaking PCB equipment can contaminate soil. Termite damage can be structural. Undisclosed UFFI can fuel a buyer complaint.
deeper.exam: Pair them up: UFFI equals formaldehyde. PCBs equal transformers and ballasts (banned 1979). CFCs equal Freon and the ozone layer. EMFs equal power lines (health link unproven). Chlordane was banned in 1988.

blocks.title: PCBs in the Hudson
blocks.html: Two GE plants discharged PCBs into the Hudson River for decades, making a 200-mile stretch a federal Superfund site. Dredging ran from 2009 to 2015, and fish advisories still apply. It is the reason upstate buyers sometimes ask about river properties.
blocks.casual: Two GE plants dumped PCBs into the Hudson River for decades, turning a 200-mile stretch into a federal Superfund site. Dredging ran from 2009 to 2015, and fish advisories are still in place. That's why upstate buyers sometimes ask about river properties.

deeper.plain: A big part of the Hudson is a Superfund site because of PCBs from GE plants, and buyers near it may have questions.
deeper.picture: It's like a spill on the kitchen floor that seeped into the grout. Even after scrubbing, some stays put.
deeper.street: A buyer looking at a riverfront house in Columbia County asks Jordan whether the Hudson is safe for fishing. Jordan says fish advisories still apply and points the buyer to official state guidance instead of guessing.
deeper.stakes: Agents who downplay environmental history near a Superfund site invite complaints. Point clients to official sources.
deeper.exam: If a question mentions the Hudson River and contamination, the answer is PCBs and Superfund (CERCLA).

blocks.q: Which hazard is associated with old fluorescent light ballasts and electrical transformers?
c: Radon
PCBs
UFFI
Chlordane
blocks.x: PCBs were used as insulating fluids in transformers, capacitors and ballasts. Chlordane was a termite pesticide.

story.title: The White Wrap
story.setting: The Okafors' brownstone basement, Bed-Stuy

beats.text: Emmanuel: That white wrap's been on those pipes since before we bought. Do we have to tell anyone?
First, nobody touch it. That elbow's crumbling. If it's asbestos, crumbling is the dangerous part.
Bulk sample. Cut a piece, send it to a lab. If it's positive, a licensed contractor either seals it or removes it. Not you with a box cutter.
Grace: And the windows? Our grandson's here every weekend.
House is from 1899, so the federal lead rule applies to the sale. You give the EPA pamphlet, disclose what you know, and the buyer gets ten days to test.

check.q: Which houses does the federal lead disclosure rule cover?
c: Built after 1978
Built before 1978
Only rentals
Only multifamily
check.x: Housing built before 1978, sales and leases. The syllabus typo says after; the rule is before.

beats.text: Emmanuel: We don't know of any lead. We never tested.
Then you disclose that you have no knowledge and no reports. You don't have to test. But you can't hide what you know.
beats.tag: Disclose known hazards; testing not required

beats.text: Also, do a radon test while you're at it. Basement, two days, canister. Four picocuries or higher, you put in a fan.
Grace: And that damp corner by the boiler?
Fix the leak first, then the mold. Anything over ten square feet in New York, you need a licensed assessor and a different licensed remediator.
Emmanuel wrote it all on the back of a church bulletin.
That afternoon: Agents aren't inspectors. But an agent who knows about a hazard and stays quiet owns it. Point, recommend, document.

board.prompt: Draw a simple house and place each hazard where it hides: asbestos, lead paint, radon, mold, UFFI, PCBs, an oil tank, EMF lines.

facts.text: Asbestos hides in pipe and boiler wrap, 9 by 9 inch floor tiles, ceiling texture, shingles and vermiculite; EPA banned its last form in use (chrysotile) in 2024.
Asbestos is dangerous when friable: crumbly enough to release fibers into the air when disturbed.
Inhaled asbestos fibers cause asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma, often decades after exposure.
Asbestos testing: bulk sampling sends a piece to a lab, air monitoring counts fibers, wipe sampling checks settled dust.
Intact asbestos is often best left alone, encapsulated or enclosed; removal is riskiest and must be done by contractors licensed by the NYS Department of Labor.
Lead-based paint was banned for residential use in 1978, and children under 6 are most at risk, suffering brain and nervous system damage.
The federal lead disclosure rule covers housing built before 1978 (the syllabus's "after 1978" is a typo).
A buyer of pre-1978 housing gets a 10-day opportunity to test for lead, which can be waived or changed in writing.

Under the lead rule the seller or landlord gives the EPA pamphlet, discloses known hazards and reports, attaches the warning statement, and keeps records 3 years; agents must ensure compliance or share liability.
Lead rule exemptions include 0-bedroom units, elderly or disabled housing (unless a child under 6 lives there), and leases of 100 days or less.
NYC Local Law 1 of 2004 requires landlords of 3+ unit buildings built before 1960 to find and fix lead paint hazards where a child under 6 lives or spends 10+ hours a week.
Radon is a colorless, odorless radioactive gas from uranium in soil that enters through foundation cracks and is the leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers.
EPA recommends fixing radon at 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) or more.
Radon is tested in the lowest livable level and mitigated by sub-slab depressurization: a pipe through the slab and a fan venting above the roofline.
Sick building syndrome is occupants feeling ill in a tight, poorly ventilated building and improving after leaving; indoor air problems also come from CO, formaldehyde and VOCs.
Mold grows where moisture persists; fix the water source first, then clean or remove the moldy materials.

Under NY's mold program (Labor Law Article 32), mold over 10 square feet must be assessed and remediated by DOL-licensed firms, and the assessor and remediator must be different, independent companies.
UFFI, pumped into walls in the 1970s, releases formaldehyde gas, mostly when new.
PCBs from old transformers, capacitors and fluorescent ballasts were banned in 1979 and persist in soil and river sediment, as in the Hudson River Superfund site.
CFCs (old Freon refrigerant) deplete the ozone layer, and refrigerant must be recovered by EPA-certified technicians.
The health link to EMFs from power lines is unproven; fields are measured with a gaussmeter and distance is the main remedy.
Termite treatment in NY is done by DEC-certified pesticide applicators.
Chlordane, the old soil treatment for termites, was banned in 1988.

lessons.title: Water, Land, and Liability: Wells, Septic, Tanks, Site Assessments, and the Agent's Role
lessons.tagline: Under federal law, the new owner can pay for the last owner's contamination. Due diligence is the only shield.
objectives: Explain public vs private water, common well water problems, and testing
Describe septic systems and who regulates them
Explain Phase I to IV environmental site assessments and why buyers order them
Match CERCLA, SARA, the Clean Air Act and the Safe Drinking Water Act to their purposes
Describe the agent's duties and liability for environmental issues

blocks.title: A gas station turned deli lot in Yonkers
blocks.html: Evelyn wants to buy a corner lot on Central Park Avenue. It was a gas station from 1958 to 1994, then a deli. The price is great. The seller's broker says, "Tanks were pulled years ago, no issue." There's no paperwork. Evelyn asks Jordan whether she should just close fast before someone else does.
blocks.casual: Evelyn wants a corner lot on Central Park Avenue in Yonkers. It was a gas station from 1958 to 1994, then a deli. The price is great. The seller's broker says, "Tanks were pulled years ago, no issue." There's zero paperwork. Evelyn asks Jordan if she should just close fast before someone else grabs it.

deeper.plain: An old gas station site can hide expensive contamination, and a buyer can end up paying for cleanup without having caused it.
deeper.picture: Buying an old gas station lot without testing is like buying a used fridge without opening it. The price looks great until you smell what's inside.
deeper.street: Jordan tells Evelyn to get a Phase I before signing. It finds the gas station history and no tank closure reports. A Phase II finds petroleum in the soil. Evelyn negotiates a $250,000 price cut and a seller-funded cleanup with a DEC closure letter as a condition of closing.
deeper.stakes: If Evelyn closes fast with no inquiry, she could be stuck with the cleanup bill and lose the innocent landowner defense. A lender may refuse to finance at all.
deeper.exam: Exam cues: "former gas station," "dry cleaner," "no records." The right answer is due diligence: a Phase I environmental site assessment before closing.

blocks.html: Most New Yorkers drink municipal (public) water, regulated under the federal Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) and the NYS Department of Health. NYC's water comes from the Catskill, Delaware and Croton reservoirs. Some subdivisions share a community water system run by a private company or district. Everyone else draws groundwater from a private well, and the owner alone is responsible for its quality.
blocks.casual: Most New Yorkers drink municipal (public) water, which falls under the federal Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) and the NYS Department of Health. NYC's water comes from the Catskill, Delaware and Croton reservoirs. Some subdivisions share a community water system run by a private company or a district. Everybody else pulls groundwater from a private well, and the owner alone is on the hook for its quality.

deeper.plain: City water is tested by the government. Well water is your problem.
deeper.picture: Public water is like a restaurant meal inspected by the health department. A private well is cooking at home: nobody checks your kitchen but you.
deeper.street: Leo moves from a Brooklyn rental with NYC reservoir water to an Ulster County house with a private well. Nobody tests his water anymore unless he pays for it. His inspector recommends testing at closing and every year after.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who assume someone is watching their well water may drink contaminated water for years.
deeper.exam: The SDWA covers public water systems, not private wells. Private well owners are responsible for their own testing.

head: Issue
What it means
Typical fix
rows: Surface water or septic contamination getting in
Shock chlorination, fix the well cap or casing, UV treatment
Calcium and magnesium; scale on fixtures and heaters
Acidic water corrodes copper (blue-green stains) and leaches lead
Solvents, fuel (MTBE), pesticides from nearby spills or farms
From old pipes and solder, not the well itself

deeper.plain: Well water can have bacteria, minerals, hardness, acidity, chemicals or lead from pipes, and each has a standard fix.
deeper.picture: Think of the water test like a blood panel. Each line flags a different problem with its own treatment.
deeper.street: Leo's well test shows coliform bacteria. The well cap is cracked, letting surface water in. A well company replaces the cap and shock chlorinates for $450, and a retest comes back clean. The blue-green stains in the tub point to acidic water, so he adds a neutralizing filter.
deeper.stakes: Bacteria can make people sick quickly. Acidic water can leach lead from old solder and corrode copper, leading to leaks.
deeper.exam: Blue-green stains equal acidic water (low pH). Coliform equals bacterial contamination. MTBE is a fuel additive found near gas stations. Lead usually comes from pipes, not the well.

blocks.title: Test the well before closing
blocks.html: Lenders and buyers routinely require a well water test by a state-certified lab, at minimum for bacteria, plus a flow (gallons per minute) test. Westchester County requires private well testing when a property with a well is sold. Remediation can be as simple as a chlorine shock or as costly as a new well.
blocks.casual: Lenders and buyers routinely want a well water test from a state-certified lab, at least for bacteria, plus a flow test (gallons per minute). Westchester County requires private well testing when a property with a well is sold. The fix can be as simple as a chlorine shock or as pricey as drilling a new well.

deeper.plain: Before buying a house with a well, get the water tested by a certified lab and check how much water it produces.
deeper.picture: It's checking both the quality and the quantity, like making sure a tap gives clean water and enough of it to fill the tub.
deeper.street: A buyer in northern Westchester signs a contract on a house with a well. County rules require a well test as part of the sale. The flow test shows only 2 gallons per minute. The parties renegotiate so the seller pays for a deeper well.
deeper.stakes: Skipping the flow test can leave a family running out of water mid-shower. Skipping the bacteria test can make them sick.
deeper.exam: Remember: state-certified lab, bacteria plus flow. Westchester specifically requires testing at sale.

blocks.html: A septic system treats household wastewater on site. Waste flows into a septic tank, where solids settle and bacteria break them down; liquid flows to an absorption field (leach field) or seepage pits, where the soil filters it. Systems are governed by the Department of Health (state standards, county or local health department approval), must be designed by a NY licensed professional engineer or registered architect, and most have as-built drawings on file with the local health department.
blocks.casual: A septic system handles household wastewater right on the property. Waste flows into a septic tank, where solids sink and bacteria break them down. The liquid goes out to an absorption field (leach field) or seepage pits, where the soil filters it. The Department of Health governs these (state standards, county or local health department approval), a NY licensed professional engineer or registered architect has to design them, and most have as-built drawings on file with the local health department.

deeper.plain: A septic tank holds solids and lets bacteria eat them. The liquid soaks into the ground through a leach field.
deeper.picture: It's a backyard water treatment plant: a holding tank does the digesting, and the yard does the filtering.
deeper.street: Jordan's buyer in Putnam wants to know where the septic field is before building a patio. Jordan suggests requesting the as-built drawing from the county health department. It shows the field exactly where the patio was planned.
deeper.stakes: Building on a leach field can crush pipes and cause a failure. Not knowing where it is makes repairs harder.
deeper.exam: Tank equals solids settle and break down. Absorption field equals liquid filters through soil. Design by a PE or RA; approval by the health department.

items: Tank pumped every 2 to 3 years for a typical family.
Warning signs: soggy or lush green field, sewage odor, slow drains, backups.
Testing: a dye test (limited), or better, a full inspection with pumping, tank inspection and field evaluation.
Never drive over or plant trees on the field. Failed fields can cost tens of thousands to replace.
blocks.casual: Pump the tank every 2 to 3 years for a typical family. Warning signs: a soggy or suspiciously green field, sewage smell, slow drains, backups. For testing, a dye test is limited; a full inspection with pumping, a tank check and a field evaluation is much better. Never drive over the field or plant trees on it. A failed field can cost tens of thousands to replace.

deeper.plain: Pump it every few years, watch for soggy grass and smells, and get a full inspection when buying.
deeper.picture: A septic system is like a cast iron pan. Treat it right and it lasts decades. Abuse it and you're buying a new one.
deeper.street: Leo notices the grass over the leach field is greener than the rest of the lawn in August. His inspector does a full pump-and-inspect and finds the field saturated. The seller agrees to a $22,000 credit.
deeper.stakes: A dye test can pass a failing system, so buyers who rely on it may inherit a big bill.
deeper.exam: Pumping every 2 to 3 years. Lush green field and odors are warning signs. A dye test is limited; a full inspection is better.

blocks.q: Who generally approves the design of a new residential septic system in New York?
c: The zoning board of appeals
The local or county health department
The Department of State
The planning board alone
blocks.x: Septic systems fall under the Department of Health's standards and are approved by the county or local health department. The planning board may review the subdivision, but health approves the system.

blocks.html: Underground storage tanks (USTs) hold heating oil at homes and gasoline at service stations. Bare steel tanks corrode; a tank over 20 to 30 years old is at real risk of leaking into soil and groundwater. Commercial motor fuel tanks are regulated by EPA and DEC (registration, leak detection, corrosion protection, closure reports). Residential heating oil tanks are lightly regulated, but a leak is still the owner's problem, and New York's Navigation Law makes the discharger strictly liable for petroleum cleanup costs.
blocks.casual: Underground storage tanks (USTs) hold heating oil at homes and gas at service stations. Bare steel tanks rust, and a tank older than 20 to 30 years has a real chance of leaking into soil and groundwater. Commercial motor fuel tanks are regulated by EPA and DEC (registration, leak detection, corrosion protection, closure reports). Home heating oil tanks are lightly regulated, but a leak is still the owner's problem, and New York's Navigation Law makes the discharger strictly liable for petroleum cleanup costs.

deeper.plain: Old buried tanks leak, and whoever is responsible for the leak pays to clean it up, no matter how careful they were.
deeper.picture: An old steel tank in the ground is a rusting can of oil buried in your garden. Time is the enemy.
deeper.street: Evelyn's lot had gas station tanks. Commercial tanks needed registration and closure reports, so the absence of any paperwork is itself a red flag. If tanks were pulled properly, DEC should have records.
deeper.stakes: A leak can contaminate neighbors' wells and bring six-figure cleanup bills and lawsuits.
deeper.exam: Commercial fuel tanks: EPA and DEC regulate. Residential heating tanks: lightly regulated. Petroleum is handled under the NY Navigation Law, not CERCLA, since CERCLA excludes petroleum.

blocks.title: Testing and remediation

items.title: Find it
items.html: Records, fill and vent pipes, a tank sweep with a metal detector.

items.title: Test it
items.html: Tank tightness test, or soil borings around the tank.

items.title: Close it
items.html: Pump out, clean, and remove, or fill in place with sand or foam where allowed. Get a closure report.

items.title: Clean up
items.html: If soil is contaminated, report spills to DEC within 2 hours, excavate, and obtain a DEC spill closure letter ("no further action").

blocks.casual: Here's the process. Find it: check records, fill and vent pipes, and do a tank sweep with a metal detector. Test it: a tank tightness test, or soil borings around the tank. Close it: pump it out, clean it, and either remove it or fill it in place with sand or foam where that's allowed, then get a closure report. Clean up: if the soil is contaminated, report the spill to DEC within 2 hours, dig out the bad soil, and get a DEC spill closure letter ("no further action").

deeper.plain: Find the tank, test it, close it properly, and if it leaked, report it and clean it up until DEC signs off.
deeper.picture: It's like dealing with a cavity: find it on the X-ray, test it, fill it, and if there's infection, treat it until the dentist clears you.
deeper.street: A Bayside seller's tank fails a tightness test. Soil borings confirm a leak. The seller reports it to DEC within 2 hours, excavates contaminated soil for $35,000, and gets a "no further action" letter. The buyer's attorney won't close without that letter.
deeper.stakes: No closure report or DEC letter can stall a sale or scare off lenders. Late spill reporting adds penalties.
deeper.exam: Order: find, test, close, clean up. DEC spill report within 2 hours. "No further action" letter is the end goal.

blocks.html: Environmental assessments are used mainly in commercial deals, where lenders require them. They are staged so you spend money only if the earlier stage finds a reason.
blocks.casual: Environmental assessments mostly come up in commercial deals, where lenders require them. They're done in stages, so you only spend money on the next stage if the earlier one turns up a reason to.

deeper.plain: Commercial buyers check for contamination in steps, starting cheap and going deeper only if needed.
deeper.picture: It's like a doctor's visit: first questions and a basic exam, then tests only if something looks off.
deeper.street: Evelyn's lender requires a Phase I on every building she finances. For a clean 1990s office park, the Phase I finds nothing and she stops there for about $3,000. For the Yonkers gas station lot, the Phase I flags the history and leads to a Phase II.
deeper.stakes: Skipping assessments can leave a buyer liable for contamination and unable to get a loan.
deeper.exam: Environmental site assessments are mostly a commercial lending tool. They are staged, so a Phase II only follows when a Phase I finds a concern.

head: Phase
Nickname
What happens
rows: Records review (historical uses, fire insurance maps, regulatory databases), site walk, interviews. No sampling. Flags recognized environmental conditions.
Soil, groundwater, soil vapor and building material samples to confirm and measure contamination.
Design and carry out the cleanup.
Ongoing monitoring, operations and maintenance after cleanup.

deeper.plain: Phase I reviews records and walks the site. Phase II takes samples. Phase III cleans up. Phase IV keeps watching.
deeper.picture: It's look, test, fix, watch. A Phase I is the detective, a Phase II is the lab, a Phase III is the cleanup crew, and a Phase IV is the security guard.
deeper.street: The Phase I on Evelyn's lot uses old fire insurance maps showing a gas station with four tanks. That's a recognized environmental condition. The Phase II drills soil borings and finds benzene. Phase III removes the soil, and Phase IV monitors groundwater for two years.
deeper.stakes: Treating a Phase I as proof of a clean site is a mistake. It doesn't sample anything.
deeper.exam: The classic trap: "Which phase includes soil sampling?" Phase II. A Phase I has no sampling.

blocks.title: Look, Test, Fix, Watch
blocks.html: Phase I looks. Phase II tests. Phase III fixes. Phase IV watches.
blocks.casual: Phase I looks. Phase II tests. Phase III fixes. Phase IV watches.

deeper.plain: Four phases, four verbs.
deeper.picture: Like a home repair: look at the leak, test where it's coming from, fix it, then check on it after the next storm.
deeper.street: Jordan practices "look, test, fix, watch" while reading Evelyn's report. When she asks if the Phase I tested the soil, Jordan says no, that's Phase II.
deeper.stakes: Confusing the phases can make a client think a site is cleared when it was only reviewed on paper.
deeper.exam: Expect a question matching phase to activity. Records and site walk equal Phase I. Sampling equals Phase II.

blocks.q: A lender on a former dry cleaner site asks for a study that reviews historical records and inspects the site without taking samples. That is a:
c: Phase I assessment
Phase II assessment
Phase III assessment
Phase IV assessment
blocks.x: Phase I is the non-invasive investigation. Sampling starts in Phase II.

head: Law
What it does
rows: CERCLA (Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act, 1980), the Superfund law

Cleans up hazardous waste sites. Liability is strict (no fault needed), joint and several (any one party can be made to pay it all), and retroactive. Potentially responsible parties include current owners, past owners at the time of disposal, generators and transporters. Petroleum is excluded.
SARA (Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act, 1986)

Added money to Superfund and created the innocent landowner defense for buyers who did appropriate inquiry before buying. The 2002 Brownfields law added protection for bona fide prospective purchasers.
Sets air quality standards; regulates asbestos handling during demolition and renovation (NESHAP) and phases out CFCs.
Sets standards for public drinking water systems and protects underground sources. Does not regulate private household wells.
HUD (Department of Housing and Urban Development)
Co-enforces the lead disclosure rule with EPA; sets environmental standards for FHA-insured and HUD-assisted housing.

deeper.plain: Federal laws make polluted-land owners pay for cleanup, protect careful buyers, and set standards for air and public water.
deeper.picture: CERCLA is the "you own it, you might pay for it" law. SARA is the fine print that says "unless you did your homework."
deeper.street: A Long Island Superfund site has a past owner who went bankrupt. EPA goes after the current owner, a company that bought it in 2010 without any inquiry. Under strict, joint and several liability, that owner can be made to pay the whole cleanup.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who skips due diligence can be on the hook for millions. Joint and several liability means one solvent party can pay it all.
deeper.exam: CERCLA equals Superfund: strict, joint and several, retroactive, petroleum excluded. SARA (1986) added the innocent landowner defense. SDWA doesn't cover private wells.

blocks.title: The new owner pays
blocks.html: Under CERCLA, buying contaminated land can make you liable for the entire cleanup even though you never polluted it. The defense: due diligence, meaning "all appropriate inquiries" before buying, which in practice means a Phase I (ASTM standard) done within the required time before closing.
blocks.casual: Under CERCLA, buying contaminated land can make you liable for the whole cleanup, even though you never polluted anything. The defense is due diligence, meaning "all appropriate inquiries" before buying, which in practice means a Phase I (to the ASTM standard) done within the required time before closing.

deeper.plain: Buying polluted land can make you pay for the cleanup unless you checked properly before you bought.
deeper.picture: It's like buying a car with unpaid tickets attached to the plate. If you didn't run the plate before buying, the tickets are yours.
deeper.street: Evelyn also buys a strip mall in Mount Vernon that once had a dry cleaner. Her Phase I is done within the required window before closing. When dry cleaning solvent later turns up under a slab the Phase I couldn't have reached, she can argue the bona fide purchaser and innocent landowner protections. (Gas station petroleum is different: CERCLA excludes it, and NY's Navigation Law applies.)
deeper.stakes: A buyer who closes without a timely Phase I may lose these defenses entirely.
deeper.exam: Due diligence equals "all appropriate inquiries" equals a Phase I. The new owner can be liable even without causing the contamination.

blocks.html: Wetlands (marshes, swamps, bogs) are protected because they absorb floods and filter water. In NY, DEC regulates tidal wetlands and freshwater wetlands, and the Army Corps of Engineers regulates waters of the U.S. under the federal Clean Water Act. Since January 1, 2025, DEC no longer relies only on its old maps and can regulate freshwater wetlands of unusual importance regardless of size; the general size threshold of 12.4 acres drops to 7.4 acres on January 1, 2028. Building near a wetland or in its 100-foot adjacent area usually needs a permit.
blocks.casual: Wetlands (marshes, swamps, bogs) are protected because they soak up floods and filter water. In NY, DEC regulates tidal wetlands and freshwater wetlands, and the Army Corps of Engineers regulates waters of the U.S. under the federal Clean Water Act. Since January 1, 2025, DEC no longer relies only on its old maps and can regulate freshwater wetlands of unusual importance regardless of size. The general size threshold of 12.4 acres drops to 7.4 acres on January 1, 2028. Building near a wetland or in its 100-foot adjacent area usually needs a permit.

deeper.plain: Wetlands are protected, and building in or near one usually needs a permit from DEC, the Army Corps, or both.
deeper.picture: Wetlands are nature's sponge. Squeeze them out with fill and the water goes into someone's basement.
deeper.street: A Dutchess County buyer wants to build a pool 60 feet from a marsh. DEC says the pool is within the 100-foot adjacent area and requires a permit, which takes months and adds conditions.
deeper.stakes: Buying land without checking for wetlands can leave a buyer with a lot they can't build on. The 2025 changes mean old maps aren't the final word anymore.
deeper.exam: DEC regulates tidal and freshwater wetlands in NY. The Army Corps covers waters of the U.S. The adjacent area is 100 feet. Thresholds: 12.4 acres now, 7.4 acres in 2028.

items: Disclose what you know. An agent who knows of a material defect or hazard and conceals it is liable for misrepresentation, regardless of what the seller wants. "Should have known" can count too, if the red flag was obvious (a fill pipe, a stained ceiling).
Do not play expert. Never say a house is "radon-free" or "no tanks." Recommend the right professional: home inspector, environmental engineer, licensed mold assessor, tank tester.

Follow the forms. Lead disclosure on pre-1978 housing; the PCDS for 1 to 4 family sales, which asks sellers about environmental items like fuel tanks and flood history. The seller fills it out, not the agent.
Document. Write down what you recommended and when. It protects you and the client.
Commercial deals: recommend a Phase I before contract or within the due diligence period.
blocks.casual:
Disclose what you know. If you know about a material defect or hazard and hide it, you're liable for misrepresentation, no matter what the seller wants. "Should have known" can count too, when the red flag was obvious (a fill pipe, a stained ceiling).
Don't play expert. Never tell anyone a house is "radon-free" or has "no tanks." Send them to the right professional: home inspector, environmental engineer, licensed mold assessor, tank tester.
Follow the forms. Lead disclosure on pre-1978 housing, and the PCDS for 1 to 4 family sales, which asks sellers about environmental items like fuel tanks and flood history. The seller fills it out, not you.
Document. Write down what you recommended and when. It protects you and the client.
Commercial deals: recommend a Phase I before the contract or within the due diligence period.

deeper.plain: Tell what you know, don't pretend to be an expert, use the required forms, write things down, and push for a Phase I on commercial deals.
deeper.picture: You're the referee who blows the whistle, not the doctor who diagnoses. Point to the problem and call in the specialist.
deeper.street: Marcus tells a buyer "there's no oil tank, trust me." There is one, and it leaks. The buyer sues the seller and the brokerage. Diane's file for Jordan's deal next door shows a written recommendation for a tank sweep, and Jordan is never named.
deeper.stakes: Concealing a known hazard can cost your license and invite a lawsuit. Making expert claims you can't back up does the same.
deeper.exam: On the exam, the agent's best answer is almost always "disclose and recommend a qualified professional." Wrong answers have the agent testing, guaranteeing, or keeping quiet.

blocks.title: The script
blocks.html: "I'm not qualified to tell you whether that's a problem, and I'd be guessing. Here's who can, and I'd do it before your contingency runs out."
blocks.casual: Here's the line: "I'm not qualified to tell you whether that's a problem, and I'd be guessing. Here's who can, and I'd do it before your contingency runs out."

deeper.plain: When a client asks about a hazard, say you're not the expert, name who is, and mention the deadline.
deeper.picture: It's like a pharmacist telling you to ask your doctor. Helpful, honest, and not practicing medicine.
deeper.street: Leo asks Jordan if the basement smell is mold. Jordan uses the script, gives him three licensed mold assessors, and reminds him his inspection contingency ends Friday. Leo books one for Wednesday.
deeper.stakes: Guessing wrong exposes you to liability. Forgetting the contingency deadline can cost your client the right to walk away.
deeper.exam: Look for answer choices where the agent refers the client to a qualified professional. That's the right instinct on nearly every environmental question.

blocks.q: Evelyn buys a former gas station without any environmental study. Later, petroleum and solvents are found in the soil. Which is most accurate?
c: She has no liability because she never operated the station
She may be liable for cleanup, and she cannot claim the innocent landowner defense because she did no appropriate inquiry
Only the original oil company is liable
The seller's broker is solely liable
blocks.x: As current owner she is a potentially responsible party for hazardous substances under CERCLA, and NY's Navigation Law covers petroleum. Without a Phase I she cannot show appropriate inquiry.

story.title: The Great Price
story.setting: Central Park Avenue, Yonkers, outside a deli that used to pump gas

beats.text: Under market, corner lot, deli tenant. I want it closed in three weeks.
It was a gas station for 36 years. Before you sign, get a Phase I.
Their broker says the tanks were pulled.
Then there's a closure report and maybe a DEC spill file. If they can't produce it, that's your answer.
And if I skip it? I didn't put the gas in the ground.
On speakerphone: Doesn't matter. Superfund liability is strict, joint and several. The current owner is on the hook. Your only shield is showing you did all appropriate inquiry before you bought.

check.q: What gives a buyer the innocent landowner defense?
c: A low price
Appropriate inquiry before purchase, such as a Phase I
The seller's verbal promise
Title insurance
check.x: SARA's innocent landowner defense requires all appropriate inquiry before buying. A Phase I is the standard way to show it.

beats.text: And petroleum? I thought Superfund didn't cover oil.
It doesn't. New York's Navigation Law does, and it's strict too. Different statute, same bill.
Fine. What if the Phase I finds something?
Then Phase II: borings, soil and groundwater samples. Phase III cleans it, Phase IV monitors it. You negotiate the price around the answer.
beats.tag: Phase I look, II test, III fix, IV watch

beats.text: Evelyn did the math on her phone. A Phase I cost less than one month of the deli's rent.
Order it.
Later: Cheapest insurance in commercial real estate. And Jordan, put in writing that you recommended it.

board.prompt: Make a flow from Phase I to Phase IV. Under each phase write what happens, who does it, and the question it answers.

facts.text: Public water is regulated under the federal Safe Drinking Water Act and the NYS Department of Health; a private well owner alone is responsible for its water quality.
Well water problems and fixes: bacteria get shock chlorination, hardness gets a softener, and acidic water (which corrodes copper and leaches lead) gets a neutralizing filter.
Buyers and lenders routinely require a state-certified lab well test (at least bacteria) and a flow test, and Westchester County requires private well testing on sale.
In a septic system, solids settle in the tank and bacteria break them down, while liquid flows to an absorption (leach) field or seepage pits where the soil filters it.
A septic tank is pumped every 2 to 3 years; warning signs of failure are a soggy or lush green field, sewage odor, slow drains and backups.
A full septic inspection with pumping beats a dye test, and no one should drive over or plant trees on the field.
Bare steel underground tanks corrode, and one over 20 to 30 years old is at real risk of leaking into soil and groundwater.
Commercial motor fuel tanks are regulated by EPA and DEC, residential heating oil tanks only lightly, but the Navigation Law makes any discharger strictly liable for petroleum cleanup.
Tank steps: find it (tank sweep), test it (tightness test or soil borings), close it (closure report), and clean up with a DEC spill report and a "no further action" letter.
A Phase I environmental site assessment reviews records, walks the site and interviews people, with no sampling; lenders require them mainly in commercial deals.
Phase II tests soil and groundwater, Phase III remediates, and Phase IV monitors (look, test, fix, watch).
CERCLA (Superfund) liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive, reaching current owners who never polluted; petroleum is excluded.
SARA created the innocent landowner defense for buyers who made all appropriate inquiries (in practice a Phase I) before buying.
The Safe Drinking Water Act sets standards for public water systems and does not regulate private household wells.
The Clean Air Act regulates asbestos handling during demolition and renovation (NESHAP) and phases out CFCs.
HUD co-enforces the lead disclosure rule with EPA and sets environmental standards for FHA-insured and HUD-assisted housing.
In NY, DEC regulates tidal and freshwater wetlands, the Army Corps of Engineers regulates federal waters, and work in a wetland's 100-foot adjacent area usually needs a permit.
DEC's general freshwater wetland threshold of 12.4 acres drops to 7.4 acres on January 1, 2028, and since 2025 it can regulate wetlands of unusual importance regardless of size.
An agent who knows of a material defect must disclose it even if the seller says not to, and "should have known" can count when the red flag was obvious.
Agents should not play expert: never call a house "radon-free" or "no tanks," but recommend the right professional before the contingency runs out.
The seller, not the agent, fills out the PCDS; agents should document their recommendations and suggest a Phase I in commercial deals.

lessons.title: Case file: The Missing Wall on Woodbine Street
lessons.tagline: Open concept, fresh paint, a basement "bedroom," and no structural permit. Jordan has eleven days to find out what the flipper skipped.
objectives: Decide which records confirm whether renovation work in New York City was permitted and signed off, including how the pre-1938 certificate of occupancy rule applies.
Identify bearing walls, flitch plate beams, lintels, headers, girders and lally columns in a renovated house and trace the load path down to a footing.
Apply R-value and building envelope rules to test a listing's insulation claims against the specifications.
Choose contract protections for a buyer when structural work was done without approval.

blocks.title: Open concept, built 1926
blocks.html: Nadia Haddad and Chris Lowell are first-time buyers with a toddler and a firm budget, and Jordan is their buyer's agent. The listing is a 1926 brick two-family on Woodbine Street in Ridgewood, Queens, asking $1,349,000. The copy reads: "Gut renovated 2025. Open-concept kitchen. Spray foam insulation. Bonus third bedroom in finished basement." The seller is an LLC that bought the house for $780,000 fourteen months ago. Nadia loves the light. Chris loves the price per bedroom. Before anyone talks numbers, Jordan wants to know one thing: what did the city actually approve?

A flip is a renovation sold on a deadline. The seller is paid for speed and finish, not for what sits behind the drywall. A buyer's agent does not judge structure (that is the inspector's job, and sometimes an engineer's), but a good one knows which questions the paperwork can answer before the inspector ever walks in. That saves the buyers an inspection fee on a house that was never going to work, and it tells the inspector where to look.

blocks.q: What should Jordan pull first to test the listing's renovation claims?
c: The ACRIS deed history, which shows what changed at the property between the two sales
The DOB records for the lot: filings, permits, sign-offs and violations
The seller's disclosure statement, which lists every permit the owner pulled
The listing broker's renovation summary and copies of the contractor's invoices
blocks.x: The Department of Buildings keeps the permit trail for every NYC lot: what was filed, what was approved, what got a final sign-off, and any open violations. ACRIS is the trap. It holds recorded documents such as deeds and mortgages, and it says nothing about construction. A disclosure form is the seller's own answers, and invoices prove payment, not approval. Start with the agency that approves the work.

blocks.html: Jordan searched the address on the DOB's public systems. The older filings sit in the Buildings Information System; newer ones in DOB NOW. Ten minutes later the picture was clear, and it was thinner than the listing.

blocks.title: What the DOB record showed
blocks.html:
Job 1, plumbing alteration, filed March 2025: "Renovate kitchen and two bathrooms. Replace fixtures. No change in use, egress or occupancy." Permit issued. No final sign-off.
Job 2, electrical: filed by a licensed electrician. Signed off.
Structural work: nothing filed.
Basement: nothing filed.
Certificate of occupancy: none on file.
Open violations: none.

Jordan read the record the way an underwriter would. "Permit issued" means the city approved the plans and let work start. Only a final sign-off means an inspector looked at the finished job and accepted it. An open job, like the plumbing alteration here, can sit for years, and title companies and lenders routinely ask for it to be closed out before closing because it signals work the city never accepted. The electrical job, filed by a licensed electrician and signed off, was the one piece of the renovation that had gone all the way through the system.

No violations sounds reassuring. It only means nobody complained and no inspector happened by. Work done without a permit does not show up as a violation until someone reports it, which is why the absence of a record is not the same as approval.

blocks.title: No CO for a 1926 house?
blocks.html: New York City did not require certificates of occupancy for buildings completed before 1938. A pre-1938 building can be perfectly legal without one, as long as later work did not change its use, egress or occupancy. When a lender or buyer wants proof of legal use, the owner can ask the DOB borough office for a Letter of No Objection, which some agencies and lenders accept in place of a CO. Work that changes occupancy, such as adding units or creating new legal living space, ends the exemption and calls for a new or amended CO.

blocks.q: The seller's attorney emails: "There is no CO because the house predates 1938. Nothing to see." Which response is most accurate?
c: Wrong, because a lender will not close on an NYC two-family that lacks a CO
Right, and the pre-1938 exemption also covers every renovation done since then
Right as far as it goes, if later work did not change use, egress or occupancy
Wrong, because the pre-1938 exemption applies to single-family houses alone
blocks.x: Pre-1938 buildings are exempt from the CO requirement, so the missing CO is not a red flag by itself. The exemption depends on the building still being used the way it was built. The trap is reading it as a permanent pass for any later work. A basement converted to a bedroom is exactly the kind of change that can end the exemption. A Letter of No Objection from DOB can confirm legal use when a lender asks.

blocks.text: The wall that was not there

blocks.html: Ray started where the money was spent. The wall between the front parlor and the kitchen was gone. A beam now crossed the ceiling, boxed in fresh drywall. With the listing agent's permission, Ray opened a small hole in a closet ceiling above the old wall line, looked into the basement directly below, and photographed both.

blocks.title: Ray's notes, page 3
blocks.html:
1. Second-floor joists lap past each other above the old wall line, nailed side by side.
2. New beam: two 2x10 boards with a half-inch steel plate bolted between them.
3. Beam ends rest on new 4x4 wood posts hidden in the side walls.
4. Basement: under one post, a 3-inch steel pipe column stands directly on the original 4-inch concrete floor. No footing visible. A ring of cracks circles the column base.
5. Rear wall: kitchen window widened from 30 to 60 inches. Steel angle over the opening. Stair-step cracks in the mortar run up from both upper corners.

blocks.q: The lapped joists in note 1 tell Ray that the removed wall was most likely:
c: A non-bearing partition, since rowhouse joists span from party wall to party wall
A fire separation that the code requires between the two dwelling units
A bearing wall that supported the second-floor joists where they met midspan
A shear wall that tied the brick front facade to the wood floor framing
blocks.x: Joists that overlap and are nailed together over a wall are using that wall as their support. Removing it leaves the splice hanging unless something replaces it. The tempting answer is the party-wall rule: in many rowhouses the joists do run between party walls, but a long span often gets a midspan bearing line, and the lap is the evidence. Ray reads the framing, not the floor plan.

blocks.html: So the wall was bearing, and the question shifts from "was it?" to "was it replaced correctly?" Note 2 describes the replacement.

blocks.q: What is the beam described in note 2?
c: A lintel: the steel member that carries the brick over an opening in a wall
A header: doubled lumber spanning a door or window in a stud wall
A girder: the main basement beam that carries the joists' inner ends
A flitch plate beam: steel bolted between wood boards for strength
blocks.x: A flitch plate is a steel plate sandwiched between wood members and bolted through. It lets a beam carry more load without growing deeper, which is why flippers like it in a ceiling where headroom matters. A lintel does a similar job in masonry, but it sits over an opening in a brick wall, not across a room. A girder is the main beam in the basement, not a new ceiling beam upstairs.

blocks.html: A beam is only as good as what holds up its ends. Follow the load: second floor, into the joists, into the new beam, down the posts in the walls, into the pipe column, and then into a 4-inch basement floor that was poured to be walked on, not to carry a point load. A proper lally column sits on its own footing: a concrete pad below the floor, sized for the load and wider than what it supports. The ring of cracks is the slab being punched from above.

blocks.q: Which fix addresses the problem in note 4?
c: Add a second pipe column beside the first so the two share the load
Pour an engineered footing under a proper lally column
Seal the ring crack with epoxy and watch it through one heating season
Swap the 4x4 posts upstairs for 6x6 posts to widen each beam's bearing
blocks.x: The load path ends at a footing, and here it ends at a thin slab. The fix is a footing designed for the load, with a proper column on it. The tempting answer is a second column: it spreads the load across two spots on the same thin slab, which can still crack and settle. Epoxy treats the symptom. Bigger posts help at the top of the path, not at the bottom where the failure is.

blocks.html: Note 5 is a different structural problem in a different material. In a brick wall, the masonry above an opening rests on a lintel, often a steel angle. In a wood stud wall the same job is done by a header. Widening the kitchen window from 30 to 60 inches doubled the span. A lintel needs enough size for its span and enough length bearing on solid brick at each end. Stair-step cracks climbing from both upper corners suggest it is undersized, poorly seated, or both.

blocks.q: Nadia asks why a cracked window matters when the beam inside is the "real" structure. Jordan's best answer?
c: It is a lintel over a doubled span, and cracks at both corners suggest it is failing
The rear wall carries no floor joists in a rowhouse, so any opening in it can be made safely
The steel angle is a header, and headers in a painted brick wall are mostly decorative trim
Stair-step cracks are normal in new brickwork as the mortar cures, so they can wait
blocks.x: A lintel carries the masonry above an opening, whether or not the wall carries floors. Doubling the span doubles the demand on it, and cracks from both corners are the classic sign of a lintel that is too light or too short. The tempting answer is the rowhouse logic: the rear wall may not carry joists, but the brick above the window still needs support. Jordan flags it; an engineer sizes the fix.

blocks.title: Renovated is not the same as permitted
blocks.html: "Gut renovated" is a description that sells, not a legal status. Only the DOB record, a final sign-off, and a design professional's documents answer "was this approved?" Buyers who skip that step inherit the work, the liability, and the cost of legalizing it, usually when they try to refinance or sell and the next buyer's agent pulls the same record Jordan did.

The "third bedroom" in the basement measures 7 feet 2 inches from floor to the bottom of the old girder, has one 14 by 30 inch window high on the wall, and its only way out is the stair to the kitchen. Ray measured; he did not rule. Whether a basement room can be a legal bedroom depends on the building code's rules for ceiling height, light, ventilation and emergency escape, and on the building's legal use. Nothing at DOB shows the basement was ever approved as living space, and the plumbing job specifically said "no change in use."

blocks.q: The listing calls the basement room a third bedroom. What should Jordan do?
c: Say nothing, since the listing agent wrote the claim and bears the liability for it
Accept the claim, since a finished room with a window counts as a bedroom in NYC
Report the listing to DOB first, then discuss the basement with Nadia and Chris
Tell the buyers it has no approval as living space and price the house without it
blocks.x: Jordan owes the buyers disclosure and reasonable care, so the gap between the ad and the record goes to them now, and their offer should not pay for a bedroom that may not be legal. A lender's appraiser will usually not count a below-grade room as living area anyway. The trap is assuming the listing agent's misstatement is someone else's problem: Jordan's duty runs to the clients, whatever the other side said.

blocks.html: There is a money angle too. Appraisers measure gross living area above grade; below-grade space, however finished, is usually reported separately and valued at a fraction of above-grade space. A listing that counts a cellar room as a bedroom inflates the price per bedroom that Chris liked so much. When Jordan reran the numbers as a two-bedroom-per-floor house, the asking price looked about $40,000 rich against recent Ridgewood sales.

blocks.title: Ask for the drawings, not the brochure
blocks.html: When a listing makes a construction claim, ask the listing agent for the filed plans, the specifications, and any engineer's letters. A seller who has them usually shares them. A seller who has only photos and a contractor's invoice is telling you something too.

The listing promised spray foam. Jordan asked the listing agent for the contractor's plans and specifications. The drawings were a two-page floor plan with no engineer's stamp. The other document was more useful.

blocks.title: Specification sheet, Section 07 21 00, Thermal Insulation
blocks.html:
Roof (cockloft): existing R-11 fiberglass batts to remain on ceiling joists. Add 2 inches closed-cell spray foam to underside of roof deck, approx. R-13.
Rear exterior wall: 2x4 furring, R-13 batts, polyethylene vapor retarder on the interior face.
Rim joists, rear: closed-cell spray foam.
Party walls: no insulation.
Front wall: not in scope.

blocks.q: The document above, which names materials, R-values and methods section by section, is the:
c: Blueprint, the drawn plan the building department checks
Building permit, which lists approved materials by section
Specifications: the written materials and methods
Certificate of occupancy schedule of approved materials
blocks.x: Specifications are the written half of a construction package: materials, grades, brands and methods. Blueprints are the drawn half: plans, elevations and sections. The tempting answer is the permit, because permits do reference the plans, but a permit is the approval, not the description of the work. When a listing makes a material claim, the specs are where you check it.

blocks.html: Ray's thermal camera confirmed the foam was there. The roof now has two layers: the old batts on the ceiling joists and the new foam under the deck. Resistance to heat flow is measured by R-value, and stacked layers add.

blocks.q: What is the approximate combined R-value at the roof, and what does it mean?
c: About R-24; the layers add, so it resists heat better than either alone
About R-13; when layers stack, the higher-rated layer sets the total
About R-12; stacked layers average, so the old batts drag the total down
About R-11; the older layer sets the ceiling for the whole assembly
blocks.x: R-values of layers in series add: R-11 plus about R-13 is about R-24, and higher means better resistance. The averaging answer is the common mistake, because it treats insulation like a grade point average. Adding still has limits: the number only holds where the insulation actually is. Gaps, compressed batts and uninsulated edges let heat bypass the rated layers entirely.

blocks.html: That last point is the building envelope idea: the house loses heat through its weakest parts. Here the party walls are shared with heated neighbors, so they matter less. The front brick wall is uninsulated and out of scope, and Ray found a gap at the rear parapet where foam stopped short. For scale, the current state energy code calls for about R-49 at ceilings in new houses in most of New York; NYC adopts its own energy code. A renovated rowhouse roof at R-24 is an improvement, not new-construction performance, and "spray foam insulation" in a listing does not tell a buyer which.

blocks.q: The specs put a polyethylene vapor retarder on the interior face of the rear wall insulation. Is that the right side?
c: No; it belongs on the outside face so wind-driven rain stays out of the batts
Yes; the warm side in a New York winter is the interior
No; masonry walls cannot take a vapor retarder on either face under the code
Yes, because the wall is brick; a wood-framed wall would put it on the outside
blocks.x: A vapor retarder goes on the warm-in-winter side so warm, moist indoor air does not reach the cold side of the wall and condense inside it. In New York that is the interior. The tempting answer confuses vapor control with weather protection: rain is handled by the brick, flashing and drainage on the outside, not by a plastic sheet behind the drywall.

blocks.html: Ray's report went to Nadia and Chris, and they called Priya. The lender added pressure from its side: the appraiser would not count the basement room as a bedroom, and the underwriter wanted the open plumbing job signed off before closing. Priya laid out the choices: walk away, cut the price, or make the seller fix and legalize the work before closing.

blocks.q: Who can prepare and file the plans for the new footing, column and lintel with the NYC Department of Buildings?
c: The flipper's general contractor, once a home improvement license is on file
A licensed engineer or registered architect who seals the plans
The home inspector who found the problem, using the report as the plans
The owner of the LLC, because owners may self-certify structural work
blocks.x: Structural work needs plans prepared and sealed by a design professional: a licensed professional engineer or registered architect. A home improvement contractor license lets someone sign renovation contracts with homeowners, which is the tempting answer, but it does not authorize structural design. A home inspector reports conditions; he does not design or file repairs.

blocks.q: Which contract approach best protects Nadia and Chris if they still want the house?
c: Seller signs an affidavit that the work met code, and the parties close on schedule
Buyers take a price credit now and file for the structural work after closing
Seller designs, files, builds and gets sign-off before closing, plus a holdback
Buyers close and rely on the builder's implied warranty to cover a failure later
blocks.x: Making the seller legalize the work before closing puts the cost and the risk on the party who created it, and a holdback gives the buyers money in hand if anything is still open. A credit sounds equal but leaves the buyers owning an unpermitted condition and an uncertain cost. The implied warranty answer is the trap: the housing merchant warranty is built for new homes sold by their builder, and a buyer should not bet a renovated 1926 resale on it.

blocks.html: The seller pushed back for three days and then agreed. The LLC's engineer designed a footing and a new lally column, specified a longer, heavier steel angle for the rear opening, and filed both. The plumbing job got its final inspection. The basement was relisted as a "recreation room," and the price came down $40,000. Priya held $30,000 of the seller's proceeds in escrow until DOB signed off on the structural job. Closing slipped five weeks.

blocks.q: At closing, why does a buyer's attorney prefer a $30,000 escrow holdback to the seller's written promise to finish the sign-off?
c: A holdback shifts the job of obtaining the DOB sign-off to the buyer's attorney
A promise in a deed is void unless the seller also records a separate affidavit
Escrowed money can be released or spent to finish; a promise must be sued on
Lenders bar sellers from making any promises that survive the closing date
blocks.x: Once the seller is paid and the LLC is gone, a promise is only as good as a lawsuit against a company that may have no assets. Money in escrow is leverage that already exists: it is released when the sign-off arrives, or used to finish the job if it does not. The holdback does not move the work to the buyer's attorney, which is the tempting misreading; the seller remains responsible.

blocks.html: Jordan's file note for Diane was four lines long: the DOB record on the date it was pulled, the advice to have Ray inspect before the offer was final, the written recommendation that the buyers have the structural work engineered and filed by the seller, and the buyers' signed decision to proceed on those terms. Diane initialed it. If the beam ever moves, nobody will have to reconstruct who knew what, and when. That is the quiet half of the job: the advice protects the clients, and the record of the advice protects the agent and the firm.

items: In NYC, the DOB record (filings, permits, sign-offs, violations) is the test of any renovation claim. No violations does not mean approved.
Pre-1938 buildings need no CO unless later work changed use, egress or occupancy; a Letter of No Objection can confirm legal use.
Lapped joists over a removed wall mean it was bearing. Follow the load path from beam to post to lally column to a real footing.
Flitch plates strengthen wood beams; lintels carry masonry over openings; headers do the same in stud walls.
Check insulation claims against the specifications. R-values add, the envelope fails at its weakest point, and vapor retarders go on the warm side.
When structural work was done without approval, make the seller design, file and finish it before closing, and hold money in escrow for anything open.

lessons.title: Case file: Lot 14 and the Builder's Promise
