lessons.tagline: A new farmhouse in Columbia County, a contract that says "as is," a well, a septic field, and six years of warranty clocks that start on a date nobody wrote down.
objectives: Decide whether a builder's contract language validly excludes or modifies New York's housing merchant implied warranty.
Apply the 1-year, 2-year and 6-year warranty periods, the warranty date, and the written notice rule to defects that appear over time.
Identify the site approvals (well, septic, grading, certificate of occupancy) a buyer of a new rural home should have in hand before closing.
Apply New York's home improvement contract rules and mechanic's lien deadlines to work done after closing.

blocks.title: A farmhouse that does not exist yet
blocks.html: Ruth and Daniel Mensah are leaving a Crown Heights rental for Columbia County. They have found Lot 14 at Stony Brook Farm, a six-lot subdivision outside the village of Ghent: a new 2,100 square foot farmhouse, private well, septic system, full basement, cold-climate heat pump. Price: $689,000. The builder, Ridgeline Homes LLC, has finished the foundation and framing. Diane referred the Mensahs to Carla Benning, a buyer's broker in Hudson, and asked Jordan to stay on as the referring agent and help them through it. Page 6 of the builder's contract reads: "Purchaser accepts the home AS IS. Seller makes no warranties, express or implied." Ruth wants to know if they should sign.

New construction feels safer than a resale: nobody has lived there, nothing is worn out. The risk is different, not smaller. Nobody has lived there, so nothing has been tested. The buyer's protection is a statute most buyers have never heard of and most small builders hope they never read.

blocks.title: The housing merchant implied warranty
blocks.html: New York's General Business Law Article 36-B (sections 777 to 777-b) implies a warranty into every contract for the sale of a new home by a builder: 1 year that the home is free of defects from unskillful construction, 2 years for defects in the installation of plumbing, electrical, heating, cooling and ventilation systems, and 6 years for material defects in load-bearing parts. A "new home" is a single-family house, or a for-sale condo or co-op unit in a building of five stories or less. The warranty survives the closing.

blocks.title: GBL, not GOL
blocks.html: Some study materials cite this warranty as General Obligations Law 777-a. The statute sits in the General Business Law. Exam items care about the periods (1, 2 and 6 years), who is covered, and the notice rule, not the citation, but do not let a wrong citation shake you on an answer you know.

blocks.q: Can Ridgeline's "AS IS, no warranties" clause take away the statutory warranty?
c: Yes, because buyers of new homes may waive any warranty in a signed contract
No; the clause is void unless a qualifying limited warranty replaces it
Yes, as long as the clause is printed in bold capital letters on the contract's first page
No, but solely because the Mensahs are financing the purchase with a mortgage loan
blocks.x: The statute makes any contract term that excludes or modifies the implied warranty void as against public policy, except where the builder offers a limited warranty that meets section 777-b's minimum terms. A bare "as is" clause does not qualify. The tempting answer is the conspicuousness rule: bold print matters in other contexts, but no typeface turns an invalid waiver into a valid one. Financing has nothing to do with it.

blocks.html: Carla sent the contract to the Mensahs' attorney, who sent back a two-line email: "The as-is clause is unenforceable. Ask them for their limited warranty." Ridgeline's sales manager produced one the next day.

blocks.title: Ridgeline Homes LLC, Limited Warranty (excerpt)
blocks.html:
LIMITED WARRANTY
Warrantor: Ridgeline Homes LLC, Route 9H, Claverack, NY.
Term: 1 year workmanship and materials. 1 year plumbing, electrical, heating, cooling and ventilation systems. 10 years major structural defects.
Claims: written notice to Warrantor by certified mail. Warrantor will inspect within 15 days and repair within 60 days of inspection.
Disputes: binding arbitration, costs shared equally.
Coverage ends on any transfer of title by the original purchaser.

blocks.q: Which feature of Ridgeline's limited warranty fails the statute's minimum terms?
c: The 10-year structural term, which runs longer than the statute's 6 years
The rule that coverage ends when the original purchaser sells the house
The 1-year systems term and the forced arbitration with shared costs
The certified mail notice step, which the statute does not allow
blocks.x: A limited warranty must equal or exceed the statutory periods, so 1 year on systems falls short of 2. It also may not force the owner into binding arbitration or make the owner pay for it. The tempting answer is the transfer clause, but section 777-b allows a limited warranty to exclude later owners. Longer structural coverage is fine, and a written claims procedure is required, not forbidden.

blocks.html: The attorney's markup fixed the systems term to 2 years, struck the arbitration clause, and left the 10-year structural term alone because it was better than the law requires. Ridgeline signed. The Mensahs put down 10 percent, held in escrow by the builder's attorney.

On a rural lot the most expensive systems are outside. Water comes from a drilled well and waste goes to an on-site septic system, and both depend on approvals that come before the building permit, not after. The county health department reviews the septic design, which a New York licensed professional engineer or registered architect prepares after soil testing for percolation rate. The well must be set back from the septic tank and absorption field. When the work is done, the designer certifies the system was built as designed and the as-built drawing goes on file.

blocks.q: Two weeks before closing, what should the Mensahs' team have in hand about the well and septic?
c: Design approval, the as-built certification, and lab bacteria and flow tests
The builder's letter promising that the well and septic meet the county's standards
A septic dye test and a test of the tap water's taste and clarity done by the buyers
Nothing yet, because the certificate of occupancy will cover well and septic approval
blocks.x: Approval of the design, proof the system was built that way, and a certified lab's bacteria results plus a gallons-per-minute flow test are the documents that answer the questions. The tempting answer is the CO, and a building department often will not issue one without health department sign-offs, but the buyers should see the underlying approvals and results themselves. A builder's letter and a taste test prove nothing.

blocks.html: The well test came back clean. The flow test showed 4 gallons per minute, adequate for a household of two with a pressure tank. The septic as-built was on file at the county. Then Carla walked the lot after a three-day April rain and found standing water against the back foundation wall and a damp stripe on the basement floor inside.

Site use matters as much as the systems. Finished grade should slope away from the house for several feet; gutters should discharge onto splash blocks or into drains that carry water away; nothing heavy or deep-rooted belongs on the septic field. Here the final grading had not been done, and the rear yard pitched toward the house.

blocks.q: The rear grade slopes toward the new foundation and the basement shows water. What is the strongest move before closing?
c: Close, then file a warranty claim if water keeps coming in next spring
Make final grading a punch-list item, with money held until it is done
Ask the builder to waterproof the inside of the basement walls with masonry paint
Plant shrubs along the back wall so their roots absorb the water near the house
blocks.x: Grading is part of the job the Mensahs are paying for, and it is cheap before closing and a fight after. A punch-list item backed by an escrow holdback gives the builder a reason to finish. The tempting answer is to rely on the warranty, but a condition the buyers saw before taking title may be excluded as a patent defect. Interior paint treats the symptom, not the water.

blocks.html: In late May the Brooklyn lease clock was ticking. Ridgeline's sales manager offered a shortcut: "The house is basically done. Move your stuff in Memorial Day weekend and sleep there; the CO is a formality." The final electrical and plumbing inspections had not happened yet, and the health department had not signed off on the septic.

blocks.q: Should the Mensahs move in before the certificate of occupancy issues?
c: Yes, since a builder may allow early occupancy of a home it still owns
Yes, if they sign a waiver releasing the town from responsibility
No; occupying a new house before the CO issues is not legal
No, unless the lender agrees in writing to the early move-in date
blocks.x: A certificate of occupancy is the building department's confirmation that the finished house passed its inspections and may be lived in. Until it issues, occupancy is not legal, whatever the owner allows, and insurance and the lender's commitment may be affected too. The tempting answer is lender consent, but a lender cannot authorize what the building code forbids. Waiting a week cost the Mensahs a short-term rental, not a code violation.

blocks.html: The final walkthrough came first. Carla brought a printed punch list and blue painter's tape. Daniel taped a scratched bathroom vanity top, a cracked pane in a basement window, and a gap in the trim at the front door. Ruth asked whether they should list everything, or just the big things, to stay on good terms with the builder. Carla's answer was that a walkthrough is the moment an owner either reserves a problem or quietly accepts it.

blocks.q: Why does it matter that Daniel writes the cracked window pane on the signed walkthrough list?
c: Visible defects a buyer accepts without noting may be excluded from the warranty
The warranty covers windows solely when the defect is reported before the closing date
Writing it down extends the 1-year workmanship period for that item to 2 years
Builders may refuse to close with any buyer who has not signed a punch list
blocks.x: The statute excludes patent defects that a reasonable examination would reveal, when the buyer examined the home or declined to, before taking title or accepting it as complete. Noting the defect in writing preserves it as the builder's job. The tempting answer says windows are covered only if reported before closing; latent defects found later are still covered within the periods. Writing an item down does not lengthen any period.

blocks.html: Ridgeline fixed the trim and the vanity before closing and agreed in writing to replace the pane within 30 days. The money for the grading sat in escrow until the rear yard was regraded in June.

The certificate of occupancy issued June 2. The Mensahs' lease in Brooklyn ended May 31, so Ridgeline let them move in on June 3 under a pre-closing occupancy agreement while the lender finished. The closing happened June 24.

The statute starts every warranty clock on the warranty date: the date title passes to the first owner who will live there, or the date that owner first occupies the home as a residence, whichever comes first.

blocks.q: When did the Mensahs' warranty periods start?
c: June 2, when the certificate of occupancy was issued
June 24, when title passed at the closing
June 3, when they moved in and began living there
July 1, the first day of the month after closing
blocks.x: The warranty date is the earlier of title passing to the first owner-occupant or that owner's first occupancy as a residence. They moved in June 3, three weeks before closing, so the clocks started then. The tempting answer is the closing date, which is usually the warranty date because most buyers move in after closing. The CO only makes occupancy legal; it does not start the warranty.

head: Defect type
Period
Runs out
Written notice must reach the builder by
rows: Plumbing, electrical, heating, cooling, ventilation installation
blocks.caption: The Mensahs' clocks. Lawsuits also have a deadline: generally within 1 year after the warranty period ends or 4 years after the warranty date, whichever is later, and within 1 year after the builder's last repair on a claim.

blocks.html: The first winter went fine. In month 14, the heat pump's indoor unit in the primary bedroom started leaking water onto the floor, and the system short-cycled on cold nights. Their HVAC technician found the condensate line pitched uphill and a refrigerant line set with a kinked section behind the wall: installation errors. The same month, Daniel noticed nail pops in the drywall along the stairs and a cracked tile in the mudroom.

blocks.q: Which of the month-14 problems is still within a warranty period?
c: Each of the three, since the 6-year term reaches any defect in a new house
The drywall and tile, because finish work carries the 2-year period
No claim survives, since the 1-year period for each has ended
The heat pump's installation errors, under the 2-year systems period
blocks.x: Improper installation of a heating and cooling system falls in the 2-year period, and month 14 is inside it. Nail pops and a cracked tile are workmanship and materials issues, covered for 1 year, which ended at month 12. The tempting answer stretches the 6-year period, but that period covers material defects in load-bearing parts only, not everything in the house.

blocks.html: Ruth texted photos to Ridgeline's site superintendent, whose cell number was on the fridge from move-in week. He replied with a thumbs-up emoji. Nothing happened for three months. Month 17 arrived.

blocks.q: What should the Mensahs do now about the heat pump?
c: Wait, since the superintendent's reply is the builder's notice of the claim
Send written notice under the claim procedure and allow inspection and repair
Hire their own contractor to fix it and deduct the bill from their next tax payment
Sue the builder at once, since the statute needs no notice before a lawsuit
blocks.x: The statute requires written notice of the claim to reach the builder before any lawsuit, and no later than 30 days after the warranty period ends, and the owner must give the builder a reasonable chance to inspect, test and repair. A text to a superintendent may or may not be treated as notice; courts have sometimes found builders waived the requirement, but nobody should plan on that. Follow the written procedure in the warranty, and send it well before the deadline.

blocks.html: The certified letter went out the next day. Ridgeline's HVAC subcontractor reset the condensate line and replaced the damaged line set within the 60 days their warranty promised. The nail pops Daniel fixed himself on a Saturday.

blocks.title: Your lane as the agent
blocks.html: Jordan and Carla can explain that the warranty exists, flag deadlines, and push clients to put claims in writing. Interpreting a specific warranty document or deciding whether to sue is legal advice; that goes to the attorney. "Here is the clause, here is the date, call your attorney" is the right script.

In Year 2 the Mensahs decided to finish the basement as a playroom and office. A contractor from Hudson quoted $38,000 and offered to start Monday if they paid half in cash and "skipped the paperwork." Ruth called Jordan, who called Diane, who said what she always says: "Get it in writing, and read what the law says the writing has to include."

blocks.q: Under New York's home improvement law, what should the Mensahs insist on?
c: A written contract with dates, scope, a 3-day cancellation notice, and a protected deposit
A handshake deal is fine for work under $50,000 as long as the contractor carries general liability insurance
A written contract, but a cash deposit of up to half the price may go straight into the contractor's operating account
A contract signed with the contractor's supplier, since the supplier is the party who can file a lien
blocks.x: A home improvement contract over $500 must be in writing and include start and completion dates, a description of the work and materials, the price, and notice of the owner's right to cancel within 3 business days. Payments received before the work is substantially done must be deposited in escrow or protected by a bond or similar arrangement. The tempting answer allows a deposit into the contractor's own account, which is exactly what the escrow rule prevents.

blocks.html: They signed a proper contract with a different contractor. The job finished in October. In January a lumber yard's lawyer wrote: the contractor had not paid for $6,200 of framing lumber and drywall delivered to the house in late September, and the yard intended to file a mechanic's lien.

blocks.q: For a single-family home, how long does the supplier generally have to file a mechanic's lien?
c: 8 months after its last delivery to the job
4 months after its last delivery to the job
1 year after the owner's final payment
90 days after the contractor's final invoice
blocks.x: For a single-family dwelling, a mechanic's lien generally must be filed within 4 months after the last work or materials were furnished; for other property the window is 8 months. Late September plus 4 months runs to late January, so the threat was live. The tempting answer is 8 months, the general rule for other property. The fix: owners should collect lien waivers or proof of payment from the contractor before the final payment.

blocks.html: The contractor paid the lumber yard after the Mensahs withheld their final $4,000 payment until he produced a release. No lien was filed.

In Year 4 a door upstairs began to stick, then a second one. In the basement, the steel lally column under the center girder had settled: the concrete pad beneath it had cracked and dropped almost an inch, and the floor above sloped toward it. An engineer found the column footing undersized and poured on fill that was never compacted. The same week, Ruth noticed a hairline crack across the garage slab.

blocks.q: Which Year 4 condition fits the statute's 6-year material defect coverage?
c: The hairline garage slab crack, since slabs are part of the foundation
Neither, because the 2-year systems period ended in Year 2
Both, since any crack in a new house is a material defect
The settled column footing that dropped the girder and floor
blocks.x: A material defect is actual physical damage to load-bearing parts, such as footings, columns, beams and girders, that affects their load-bearing function enough to make the home unsafe, unsanitary or unlivable. A failed column footing that drops the floor fits. A hairline shrinkage crack in a garage slab usually does not: it is the tempting answer because it is concrete, but it is not failing to carry a load.

blocks.title: Engineer's letter, Year 4 (excerpt)
blocks.html: Column C-2 at midspan of the main girder has settled approximately 7/8 inch. Test pit shows the column pad is 18 by 18 inches by 8 inches thick, bearing on uncompacted fill. Girder has deflected with the column; floor above slopes 1 inch in 10 feet toward C-2. Doors at the second floor bind. Recommendation: shore the girder, remove the pad, excavate to undisturbed soil, pour a 30 by 30 by 12 inch reinforced footing, reset the column, and jack the girder back to level in stages.

Notice the vocabulary: the letter talks about a footing, a column, a girder and deflection. Those are the words the statute uses when it defines a material defect: damage to footings, beams, girders, columns and similar load-bearing parts that affects their function. The Mensahs' attorney sent the letter to Ridgeline with written notice of the claim the same week.

Ridgeline repaired the footing under its 10-year structural term. The Mensahs then decided to sell in Year 5, when Ruth took a job in Albany. Their buyer, a schoolteacher named Owen Price, asked Carla whether the warranty came with the house.

blocks.q: Does Owen get warranty protection for the rest of the 6-year structural period?
c: Yes, because a limited warranty has to cover every later owner
No, because the statute protects the first buyer and nobody after
Under the statute yes, but this warranty validly ends at transfer
Yes, but the six years restart from the date of Owen's closing
blocks.x: The statute defines "owner" to include each successor in title during the unexpired warranty period, so the implied warranty would follow the house. But a qualifying limited warranty may exclude later owners, and Ridgeline's did. Owen's attorney should read the warranty before relying on it. The tempting answer restarts the clock at resale; it never restarts, since the warranty date is fixed by the first owner.

blocks.html: Owen's attorney negotiated a price credit for the risk instead. The sale closed in Year 5 with the structural repair documented in the file: engineer's report, Ridgeline's repair invoice, and the town's sign-off.

items: The housing merchant implied warranty (GBL 777-a) covers new homes for 1 year (workmanship), 2 years (systems installation) and 6 years (material defects in load-bearing parts).
A builder can exclude it only with a limited warranty that meets section 777-b minimums: at least the statutory periods and no forced, owner-paid arbitration. A bare as-is clause is void.

The warranty date is the earlier of first owner-occupant's title or first occupancy. Written notice must reach the builder no later than 30 days after a period ends, and the builder gets a chance to repair.
On a rural lot, get the septic approval and as-built, a lab well test and a flow test, and fix grading before closing. Defects you saw and accepted may be excluded later.

Home improvement contracts over $500 must be written with the required terms and a 3-day cancellation notice; deposits are escrowed or bonded. Liens on single-family homes generally must be filed within 4 months.

lessons.title: Case file: Oil, Gas, or Electric on Rosedale Road
lessons.tagline: A 1968 high ranch in Valley Stream with a 37-year-old boiler, a mystery fill pipe, a 100-amp panel, and a buyer who wants a heat pump and an EV charger by winter.
objectives: Compare oil, gas and electric heating (resistance and heat pump) for a specific house, including fuel delivery, venting and electrical demands.
Calculate heating and cooling capacity in BTUs and tons, and explain why an oversized boiler or an old system affects cost and price.
Identify electrical and plumbing defects (service capacity, oversized breakers, aluminum branch wiring, missing vents, undersized supply) and who is responsible for each part of the service.
Decide how a buyer's agent turns system findings into documented advice and a negotiated credit.

blocks.title: Rosedale Road, Valley Stream
blocks.html: Marisol Vega, an ICU nurse, is buying her first house: a 1968 high ranch on Rosedale Road in Valley Stream, Nassau County, under contract at $689,000 subject to inspection. The listing says "oil heat, central air, updated kitchen." Marisol drives an electric car and charges it at work. She tells Jordan her plan before the inspector even arrives: "Rip out the oil, put in a heat pump, put a charger in the garage. Can this house do that, and what should I pay for the privilege?" Ray meets them in the basement at 9 a.m.

A buyer asking "can this house do that?" is asking three questions at once: what is here now, what it will take to change it, and who pays. Jordan cannot answer the engineering, but Jordan can make sure the inspection answers the right questions and that the answers end up in the negotiation instead of in a drawer.

blocks.title: Ray's notes: heating plant
blocks.html: Cast iron boiler, oil-fired, data plate dated 1987. Rated input 1.0 gallon per hour (about 140,000 BTU per hour input); output about 112,000 BTU per hour. Circulator pump on the return line. Small round tank hanging from the supply pipe. Copper baseboard with aluminum fins in every room. Domestic hot water from a tankless coil inside the boiler. 275-gallon oil tank in the garage, on legs, no visible weeping, some surface rust on the bottom seam. Second fill pipe and vent capped in the front lawn, no tank inside matching it.

blocks.q: Based on Ray's notes, what kind of heating system does the house have?
c: A steam system, because a cast iron boiler feeds heat to every room
A forced warm air system, since the circulator pushes heat through ducts
A hot water system: boiler, circulator and expansion tank feed baseboards
An electric resistance system, because the fins on the baseboards are metal
blocks.x: A circulator pump, an expansion tank (the small round tank on the pipe) and finned baseboard are the signature of a hydronic, or hot water, system. Steam is the tempting answer because both use a boiler, but steam systems have a sight glass and usually cast iron radiators and no circulator. Forced air uses a furnace, a blower and ducts, not a boiler.

blocks.html: Ray's next question was whether the boiler is the right size. A room-by-room heat loss calculation he ran from the plans and the insulation he could see came to about 52,000 BTU per hour on the coldest design day. A boiler bigger than the house needs reaches temperature fast, shuts off, cools, and fires again. That short cycling wastes fuel and wears the burner.

blocks.q: The boiler's output is about 112,000 BTU per hour and the house needs about 52,000 on the coldest day. What does that tell Marisol?
c: The boiler is about twice what is needed, so it short cycles and wastes fuel
The boiler is undersized for a Long Island winter, since its input exceeds its output
The boiler is sized correctly, because 112,000 BTU is the usual size for any ranch house
The boiler sizing hardly matters, because hot water systems rarely short cycle
blocks.x: 112,000 divided by 52,000 is about 2.15, so the boiler is roughly twice what the house needs on its coldest day and far more than it needs on a typical one. Oversizing was common decades ago and costs money every season. The tempting answer misreads input versus output: input is fuel burned, output is heat delivered, and the gap is efficiency loss, not undersizing.

blocks.html: Age matters as much as size. A cast iron boiler can run 25 to 35 years or more, and this one is 39 years old. It still works, but a buyer should price in replacement within a few years, not decades. The tankless coil adds a quirk: because domestic hot water comes from a coil inside the boiler, the boiler has to stay hot all year, including July, just to supply showers.

blocks.q: Why does the tankless coil matter for Marisol's summer energy bills?
c: The coil heats water with sunlight in summer, so the boiler can stay off
The boiler keeps firing all summer to keep the coil hot for showers
The coil runs on its own electric element, which raises the electric bill
The coil needs the central air system to run before it can heat water
blocks.x: A tankless coil is a heat exchanger inside the boiler. No hot boiler, no hot water, so an oil boiler with a coil burns fuel through the summer for showers alone. The tempting answer gives the coil its own electric element, which describes an electric water heater, a different appliance. Many owners add an indirect tank or a separate water heater so the boiler can rest in summer.

blocks.html: The garage tank is an aboveground storage tank: 275 gallons, visible, inspectable. Surface rust on the bottom seam is worth watching, because tanks often corrode from the inside out where water settles. The capped fill and vent pipes out front are a different story. They suggest an underground storage tank that once fed the boiler before the garage tank went in.

The seller's attorney produced a 2004 letter from a tank contractor: the buried 550-gallon tank was pumped, cleaned, and filled in place with sand, and two soil samples taken beside it showed no petroleum. The Nassau County health department, which runs its own tank program on Long Island, had a matching closure record. The seller's Property Condition Disclosure Statement answered the fuel tank question accordingly: one tank in use in the garage, one abandoned in place in the front yard, no known leaks.

blocks.q: What does Jordan most need to confirm about the front-yard tank?
c: That the tank will be dug up and removed at the seller's cost before closing
That a fresh tightness test shows the old tank still holds pressure
That closure records, soil results and the county's file match the PCDS
That the oil company has stopped billing the address for deliveries
blocks.x: A tank properly closed in place, with soil samples and a regulator's record, is a documented, finished event; removal is one option, not a requirement. The key is that the paperwork exists and matches the seller's disclosure. A tightness test is the tempting answer, but a tank filled with sand has nothing to test. The real risk with abandoned fill pipes is delivery into a dead tank, so the pipes should be removed or sealed.

blocks.title: Oil tanks in New York
blocks.html: New York's Navigation Law makes whoever discharges petroleum strictly liable for cleanup, and spills must be reported to DEC within 2 hours. DEC's petroleum bulk storage registration generally applies to facilities with more than 1,100 gallons of total capacity, so a 275-gallon home heating tank is usually below it, but Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester run their own delegated programs that can be stricter. In New York City, the Fire Department's rules govern tanks in buildings.

blocks.title: Input is not output
blocks.html: Boiler and furnace labels list both input (fuel burned, in BTU per hour) and output (heat delivered). The difference is lost up the chimney. Exam items and sellers both blur them: "a 140,000 BTU boiler" usually means input. Size and compare systems on output, against the house's calculated heat loss.

blocks.text: Three ways to heat the house

blocks.html: Marisol's plan was a heat pump. Jordan suggested she see the alternatives side by side before deciding what to negotiate for. Ray sketched them on the back of his clipboard.

head: Option
What it takes here
Running cost and trade-offs
rows: Keep oil, new boiler sized to about 55,000 BTU
New boiler and indirect hot water tank; keep the garage tank (or replace it)
Fuel delivered by truck; price swings with the market; tank stays a liability; boiler can rest in summer with an indirect tank
Gas main is in the street; utility must run a service line and meter; new gas boiler; chimney evaluated and usually lined for gas venting, or a sealed-combustion boiler vented through the wall
No tank; usually cheaper per BTU than oil; still a fossil fuel appliance with a flue
Cheapest to install; needs many 240-volt circuits
Turns each unit of electricity into one unit of heat; the most expensive way to heat with electricity
Outdoor units and indoor heads or an air handler; needs electrical capacity; keep or remove the boiler as backup
Moves heat rather than making it, often delivering two to three times as much heat as the electricity it uses; also provides cooling; utility and state incentives may apply
blocks.caption: Ray's clipboard comparison

blocks.q: Marisol asks why a heat pump would cost less to run than electric baseboard if both use electricity. Best answer?
c: A heat pump burns a small amount of gas as a backup fuel for every cycle
A heat pump runs on 120 volts, and baseboard heat needs costlier 240-volt power
A heat pump heats just the rooms in use, while baseboard heats the whole house
A heat pump moves heat from outside air rather than making it
blocks.x: Resistance heat converts electricity into heat one for one. A heat pump uses electricity to run a compressor that moves heat from outdoor air into the house, so it can deliver several units of heat per unit of electricity. The voltage answer is the trap: both often use 240-volt circuits, and voltage does not determine efficiency. Zoning helps either system and is not the reason.

blocks.html: Gas was the other serious option. National Grid's main ran under Rosedale Road, and two neighbors had converted. Ray explained what a conversion actually involves, because buyers tend to think of it as swapping a burner. The utility has to approve and run a service line and set a meter, which can take weeks or months. The oil tank has to be emptied and properly closed or removed. And the venting has to change: gas combustion gases are cooler and wetter than oil's, and an old unlined masonry chimney can be eaten away by the acidic condensation.

blocks.q: A conventional gas boiler will replace an oil boiler and vent through the existing 1968 masonry chimney. What should Marisol expect?
c: No changes, since a chimney that vented oil safely will vent gas the same way
A chimney inspection and, usually, a liner sized for the new gas appliance
The utility to rebuild the chimney as part of running the new service line
Removal of the chimney, since gas appliances may not use masonry flues
blocks.x: Gas appliances produce cooler, wetter flue gases than oil, and condensation can damage an unlined masonry chimney, so an inspection and usually a properly sized liner are part of the job. A high-efficiency sealed-combustion boiler can avoid the chimney entirely by venting through the wall. The tempting answer assumes the old chimney is fine because it worked for oil; the fuel change is what creates the problem.

blocks.html: Marisol leaned toward the heat pump with the old boiler left in place for the coldest nights the first winter. That raised the question every electrification plan runs into: does the house have enough power?

blocks.title: Ray's notes: electrical
blocks.html: Overhead service drop from the pole to a weatherhead on the side wall. Meter on the exterior. Main panel in garage: 100-amp main breaker, 120/240 volts, 24 spaces, 22 used. Branch circuits in the bedrooms are aluminum (1968). One 30-amp breaker feeding a circuit of 14-gauge copper wire to the kitchen countertop outlets. No GFCI protection at kitchen counters or the garage.

Voltage is the pressure; amperage is the volume of current, and service size is rated in amps. A cold-climate heat pump for this house might need a 30 to 40 amp 240-volt circuit, and a Level 2 car charger commonly needs another 40 to 50 amps. Add them to the existing load and 100 amps is likely to be tight. Upgrading to 200-amp service is a common answer, and it raises the question of whose equipment is whose.

blocks.q: If Marisol upgrades to 200-amp service, which part is typically the utility's responsibility rather than hers?
c: The new main panel, breakers and every branch circuit in the house
The meter pan, mast and weatherhead on the side of the house
The wiring from the panel to the new heat pump and the car charger
The service drop from the pole to the house and the meter itself
blocks.x: The utility brings service to the property and owns the meter. From the service entrance in, the equipment belongs to the owner: the weatherhead and mast, the meter pan, the service cable, the panel and everything downstream, all installed by a licensed electrician with a permit and inspection. The tempting answer is the meter pan because the meter sits in it, but the pan is the owner's equipment.

blocks.q: Ray flags the 30-amp breaker on 14-gauge wire. Why does it matter?
c: 14-gauge copper is rated for 15 amps, so a 30-amp breaker can let it overheat
30-amp breakers trip too easily, so the kitchen outlets will cut out constantly
14-gauge wire is aluminum, which needs a larger breaker to carry its load
A 30-amp breaker turns a 120-volt kitchen circuit into a 240-volt circuit
blocks.x: A breaker protects the wire. 14-gauge copper is rated for 15 amps; a 30-amp breaker lets twice that current flow before tripping, so the wire can overheat inside the wall long before the breaker reacts. It is the modern version of putting a 30-amp fuse in a 15-amp circuit. The tempting answer has it backward: a larger breaker trips less often, which is the danger.

blocks.html: The bedroom circuits were the second issue. Aluminum branch wiring was installed in some houses from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s. It expands and contracts more than copper and oxidizes at connections, which loosen and can overheat. Insurers ask about it, and some will not write a policy until it is remediated. The recognized repair is to connect a short copper pigtail at every outlet, switch and fixture using connectors listed for joining aluminum to copper, or to rewire.

blocks.q: Marisol's insurance agent asks about the aluminum branch wiring. What is the accurate response?
c: It needs remediation with approved connectors at each device, or rewiring
It is not a concern, because aluminum service cable is standard in new homes
It is safe as long as every breaker on those circuits is swapped for a fuse
It has to come out of the walls before any insurer will write a policy
blocks.x: Aluminum branch circuits are a known fire risk at connections, and the accepted fix is remediation with connectors listed for aluminum-to-copper joints, or replacing the wiring. The trap is the service cable: aluminum is normal for large service entrance conductors, a different use with different connectors. Swapping breakers for fuses changes nothing at the outlet where the problem lives.

blocks.html: The central air condenser outside was dated 1996 and labeled R-22. Its nameplate said 30,000 BTU per hour. R-22 is an ozone-depleting refrigerant; under the Clean Air Act its production and import ended in 2020, so recharging an old system means buying recovered or stockpiled refrigerant at a premium, handled by an EPA-certified technician. A 30-year-old condenser is past the 10 to 15 years compressors typically last. Any heat pump would replace it.

blocks.q: How many tons of cooling is the 30,000 BTU per hour condenser?
c: 3 tons
2.5 tons
3.6 tons
2 tons
blocks.x: One ton of cooling is 12,000 BTU per hour, so 30,000 divided by 12,000 is 2.5 tons. The tempting answer, 3.0 tons, comes from dividing by 10,000 and rounding. Tons describe the rate of heat removal, a holdover from the days when cooling was measured against melting a ton of ice over 24 hours.

blocks.html: In the attic Ray found black staining on the roof sheathing above the bathroom. The bath exhaust fan duct ended in the attic, blowing warm, wet shower air under a cold roof all winter. The soffit vents were buried under blown insulation, so the attic could not breathe either.

blocks.q: What fix addresses the attic staining?
c: Add more insulation over the bathroom ceiling so moisture cannot rise
Seal the soffit vents so cold winter air stops reaching the sheathing
Duct the fan outdoors, clear the soffits, and treat the sheathing
Run the bathroom fan less often so it pushes less air into the attic
blocks.x: Exhaust fans must discharge outdoors, never into the attic, and attic ventilation needs intake at the soffits and exhaust at the ridge or gables. Fix the moisture source, restore airflow, then treat the stained wood; a larger area may need a licensed mold assessor and remediator. Sealing the soffits is the trap: it sounds like keeping cold out but traps moisture in.

blocks.html: Upstairs, the kitchen island sink gurgled when it drained, and the trap smelled faintly of sewer gas. Every fixture's trap holds a water seal that blocks sewer gas, and every trap needs a vent so draining water does not siphon the seal away. Ray found the island sink drained through an S-shaped trap with no vent at all. Water pressure at the second-floor shower was weak. The water service from the curb was half-inch galvanized steel, original to 1968.

blocks.q: Which pairing of cause and fix is correct for the sink and the shower?
c: Sink: clogged drain, snake it. Shower: low city pressure, add a booster pump
Sink: missing vent, add one. Shower: corroded supply line, replace it
Sink: trap too deep, cut it shorter. Shower: worn showerhead, replace it
Sink: sewer gas from the street, add a cap. Shower: water heater too small
blocks.x: Gurgling and sewer odor at a fixture point to a trap siphoning because it lacks a vent; the fix is a code-compliant vent (an island sink often uses a loop vent or an approved air admittance valve where allowed). Weak upstairs pressure with an old half-inch galvanized service points to pipe narrowed by rust inside; replacement with a properly sized line fixes it. A booster pump is the trap: it treats a pipe problem as a supply problem.

blocks.html: Ray's report ran 44 pages. Jordan's job was to turn it into something Marisol could decide with and the seller could respond to. Jordan asked Marisol to get written estimates for the items that were defects (not upgrades she wanted anyway), then grouped them.

head: Item
Category
Estimate
rows: Correct 30-amp breaker on 14-gauge circuit; add GFCI protection at kitchen and garage
Bath fan ducted outdoors, soffits cleared, sheathing treated
Island sink vent; replace water service from curb
blocks.caption: Jordan's summary sheet

blocks.q: How should Jordan frame the request to the seller?
c: Ask for a credit covering each line, since Marisol needs the work done
Ask for nothing, since an as-is resale gives the seller no duty to repair
Ask the seller to install the heat pump, since the boiler is past its life
Ask for a credit tied to the defects, leaving her upgrades out
blocks.x: Defects the inspection found are fair game, and a credit tied to written estimates is persuasive. The service upgrade and the heat pump are Marisol's choices; asking the seller to pay for them invites a flat no and can sour the whole negotiation. The tempting answer is to ask for everything as an opening bid, but it signals that the numbers are padded and weakens the requests that matter.

blocks.html: The seller agreed to a $12,500 credit, a little short of the $13,550 in defects, and to remove and seal the old front-yard fill and vent pipes before closing. Marisol closed in November. She ran the oil boiler through one winter with an indirect tank added, upgraded the service in spring, and had the heat pump installed before the next heating season. Jordan put the inspection report, the estimates, the tank closure letter and the credit addendum in the file.

items: Identify the system before judging it: circulator, expansion tank and baseboard mean hot water; sight glass and radiators mean steam; furnace and ducts mean forced air.
Compare capacity to need in BTUs. An oversized boiler short cycles; a tankless coil keeps the boiler firing all summer. 12,000 BTU per hour is 1 ton of cooling.

Oil means tanks and Navigation Law strict liability; gas needs a service line and proper venting; electric resistance is cheap to install and costly to run; heat pumps move heat and need electrical capacity.

The utility owns the service drop and meter; the owner owns everything from the service entrance in. Breakers protect wire, so match breaker to wire gauge; aluminum branch wiring needs approved remediation.
Untrapped or unvented fixtures let sewer gas in; old galvanized supply lines rust shut. Exhaust fans vent outdoors.
Separate defects from upgrades, back requests with written estimates, and document the advice.

lessons.title: Case file: A Toddler, a Basement, and Five Point Eight
lessons.tagline: A 1962 colonial in Great Kills, a family with a two-year-old, and a stack of disclosures that do not quite match what the house is saying.
objectives: Apply the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule, including records, the 10-day inspection opportunity and agent duties, and distinguish it from NYC Local Law 1 and the EPA renovation rule.
Decide whether a radon test is valid and what a result above the EPA action level requires in a sale.
Choose the correct response to suspected asbestos and to mold under New York's licensing rules.
Explain an agent's disclosure duties and liability when a seller's statements and the inspection conflict.

blocks.title: Great Kills, Staten Island
blocks.html: Kwame and Abby Osei have a two-year-old named Kofi and a second child due in March. Jordan is their buyer's agent. They have an accepted offer of $835,000 on a 1962 detached colonial in Great Kills, listed by Gina Castellano of a South Shore brokerage. The sellers, Doreen and Phil Harmon, raised three kids there and are moving to Florida. The contract is with the attorneys. The disclosure package arrives Friday afternoon: a Property Condition Disclosure Statement, a lead-based paint disclosure, and the EPA pamphlet. Abby reads everything twice. On Saturday she calls Jordan: "Gina just told me the Harmons had a lead test done years ago. Why does this form say they have no reports?"

A 1962 house sits squarely inside every older-home hazard on the syllabus: lead paint was common until it was banned for residential use in 1978, asbestos was in floors and insulation, radon depends on the ground, and a basement that has been finished and refinished over sixty years can hide water. None of these is a reason to walk away. Each is a reason to read the paperwork carefully and test before the contingency runs out.

blocks.title: Lead-based paint disclosure, seller section (as received)
blocks.html:
(a) Presence of lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards: [x] Seller has no knowledge of lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the housing.
(b) Records and reports available to the seller: [x] Seller has no reports or records pertaining to lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the housing.
Signed: Doreen Harmon, Phil Harmon.

Jordan called Gina. The story came out quickly: in 2017, when the Harmons' daughter was pregnant and staying with them, a lead inspector tested the house. Several window sills and the porch railings came back positive. Doreen had the report in a folder somewhere and "didn't think it counted, since it was so long ago."

blocks.q: What does the federal lead rule require of the Harmons now?
c: Correct the form to show what they know and give the buyers the 2017 report
Nothing more, since a report over five years old no longer has to be disclosed
Hire a new inspector, since a test from within the past year is what the rule wants
Remove the lead paint before closing, because a child under six will live there
blocks.x: For pre-1978 housing the seller must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards and provide any available records or reports. There is no expiration on a report. The Harmons had both knowledge and a report, so the form is wrong and must be corrected. The rule does not require testing or removal, which is the tempting answer for a family with a toddler; it requires disclosure and an opportunity to test.

blocks.title: Who answers for the lead form
blocks.html: The federal rule (enforced by EPA and HUD) puts duties on sellers and on agents. Agents must tell the seller about the seller's obligations and make sure the seller complies, and agents who fail to can share liability. The contract carries a lead warning statement and signed certifications from the seller, the buyer and the agents. Everyone keeps the paperwork for 3 years.

Gina sent a corrected disclosure and the 2017 report Monday morning. Now the buyers had their own decision. The rule gives a buyer a 10-day opportunity to have the home tested for lead before becoming obligated, unless the parties agree to a different period or the buyer waives it in writing. A competing buyer had been circling, and Kwame asked whether they should waive it to look stronger.

blocks.q: If the Oseis want to waive the lead inspection opportunity, how is that done?
c: By telling Gina on the phone that they do not need the inspection period
By letting the 10 days pass without scheduling a lead inspection
By signing a written waiver in the contract or the lead addendum
By asking the sellers' attorney to strike the lead warning statement
blocks.x: The buyer may waive the opportunity, but only in writing, and the lead warning statement stays in the contract regardless. Letting the days run out is the tempting answer because the result looks the same, but an unsigned lapse leaves the file showing the rule was never followed. Jordan's advice was not to waive: with a toddler and a newborn coming, this was the one family for whom the test mattered most.

blocks.html: They kept the inspection period. The question was what kind of test. A lead inspection is a surface-by-surface hunt for lead-based paint anywhere in the house, often with an XRF analyzer. A risk assessment looks for hazards right now: deteriorated paint, lead dust on floors and sills, bare soil. The 2017 report had already told them where lead was. What the Oseis needed to know was whether Kofi could be exposed this winter.

blocks.q: Which test answers the Oseis' real question?
c: A lead inspection, which lists every painted surface with lead in the house
A risk assessment, which finds current hazards like lead dust and loose paint
A blood lead test for Kofi, which shows the house's lead levels room by room
A water test, since tap water is the main source of lead in houses of this age
blocks.x: A risk assessment identifies existing hazards (deteriorated paint, dust, soil) and how to control them, which is what matters with a toddler moving in. An inspection maps where lead paint is, useful for renovation planning, but the 2017 report already did much of that. A child's blood test measures exposure in the child, not conditions in a house, and water is one source but rarely the main one in a painted 1962 home.

blocks.html: The risk assessor found lead dust above federal hazard levels on two window sills in the front bedrooms and peeling paint on the porch railings. The Oseis' attorney negotiated: the Harmons would pay a certified firm to stabilize the porch paint and do a specialized cleaning of the front bedrooms before closing, with clearance dust wipes to prove it worked.

blocks.title: Local Law 1 is a landlord's law
blocks.html: NYC's lead law (Local Law 1 of 2004) makes landlords find and fix lead hazards in rental apartments in older buildings where a child under 6 lives, and since 2021 the city treats paint at 0.5 milligrams per square centimeter as lead-based. It governs rentals. An owner selling the single-family house she lives in is outside it; the federal disclosure rule is what applies to the Harmons. If the Oseis ever rent out part of the house to a family with a young child, Local Law 1 would become their problem.

Lead can also come out of the tap. Houses of this age often have copper supply pipes joined with lead solder, which was banned for drinking water plumbing in 1986, and some older New York City homes still have lead service lines from the street. Abby planned to mix baby formula with tap water in the spring, so she asked whether the water needed a look too.

blocks.q: What is the sensible step on drinking water for the Oseis?
c: Skip it, since New York City water leaves the reservoirs free of lead
Test the tap water and check the service line material before the baby arrives
Replace every copper pipe in the house before closing, at the sellers' cost
Boil the tap water, since boiling removes lead along with any bacteria
blocks.x: NYC's reservoir water is essentially lead-free when it leaves the system; lead enters from service lines, solder and fixtures inside a building. Testing at the tap (NYC's Department of Environmental Protection offers free test kits through 311) and identifying the service line answers the question, and using cold, flushed water helps meanwhile. Boiling is the trap: it concentrates lead rather than removing it.

blocks.html: Ray's inspection included a radon test: two continuous electronic monitors in the basement family room, the lowest level the Oseis planned to use, running 48 hours. The first result came back at 2.1 picocuries per liter. Then Ray looked at the monitor's data log and his photos from the pickup. The basement windows were open, and a fan was running in the doorway. Doreen said she had aired out the basement "because of the musty smell."

blocks.q: Should the Oseis rely on the 2.1 pCi/L result?
c: Yes, since any reading under 4 pCi/L clears the house for good
Yes, since a radon monitor corrects for open windows on its own
No, because New York radon tests are valid in winter months alone
No; it ran without closed-house conditions and should be redone
blocks.x: Short-term radon tests for a sale need closed-house conditions: windows and outside doors shut for at least 12 hours before and during the test, except normal entry and exit. Open windows and a fan dilute soil gas and push the reading down. The tempting answer treats 2.1 as a pass, but an invalid test proves nothing. Ray reran it with tamper-evident monitors and a signed non-interference agreement.

blocks.html: The second test, under closed-house conditions, averaged 5.8 pCi/L. Radon is a radioactive gas from uranium breaking down in soil and rock; it is the leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers, and the EPA recommends fixing a home at 4 pCi/L or above. Staten Island is not the highest-radon area in the state, but radon is local to the house, not the borough.

blocks.q: Gina emails: "Radon isn't really a thing on Staten Island. I wouldn't let it hold up the deal." How should Jordan respond?
c: Agree, since a listing agent's local knowledge outweighs a single test
Ask the Harmons to sign a statement that radon is not a problem here
Advise the Oseis that 5.8 is above the EPA action level and should be fixed
Tell the buyers to retest in summer, when radon readings are more reliable
blocks.x: A valid test at 5.8 pCi/L is above the EPA's 4 pCi/L action level, and the fix is routine: sub-slab depressurization, a pipe and fan that pull soil gas from under the slab and vent it above the roof. Gina's comment is an agent playing expert, which exposes her and her firm to misrepresentation claims. A seller's statement adds nothing, and a summer retest is the trap: it shops for a lower number rather than answering the question.

head: Test
Conditions
Duration
Result
rows: Test 1, two monitors, basement family room
Test 2, two tamper-evident monitors, same spot
Closed house 12 hours before and during; non-interference agreement signed
blocks.caption: Ray's radon summary

blocks.html: Jordan's role here was narrow and important. Jordan did not interpret the science or promise that a fan would fix it. Jordan made sure the buyers saw both results and the reason the first one did not count, forwarded the numbers to their attorney before the inspection contingency ran out, and suggested they get a written estimate from a certified mitigation contractor so the request to the sellers had a real number in it.
The parties agreed the Harmons would pay a certified mitigation contractor $1,900 to install a sub-slab system before closing.

blocks.q: What should the Oseis require to confirm the mitigation worked?
c: A new closed-house radon test after the system has run for at least a day
The contractor's invoice showing the fan model and the date it was installed
A letter from the Harmons that the fan is running and audible from the basement
Nothing further, because a sub-slab system lowers radon below 4 pCi/L every time
blocks.x: Mitigation is confirmed by testing, not by installation. A post-mitigation test, run after the system has operated at least 24 hours and under closed-house conditions, shows whether levels dropped. An invoice is the tempting answer because it proves work was done, but it does not prove the result. The Oseis' retest came back at 0.9 pCi/L.

blocks.html: Ray's report flagged two more items. Under the basement carpet, at a torn corner, were 9 by 9 inch floor tiles, a size widely made with asbestos in that era, with black mastic adhesive. In the attic, between the joists, was loose, pebbly gray-brown insulation that looked like vermiculite, some of which was contaminated with asbestos. Neither had been tested. The PCDS asked whether there was asbestos in the structure; the Harmons had checked "unknown."

blocks.q: What is Jordan's best advice to the Oseis about the tiles and the attic?
c: Pull up the basement tiles before move-in so Kofi is not near them
Have both sampled by a qualified inspector and leave them undisturbed
Ignore both, since asbestos is a risk to workers rather than residents
Ask the sellers to vacuum the attic insulation into bags before closing
blocks.x: Asbestos is dangerous when friable or disturbed so fibers get into the air. Intact tiles under carpet are low risk; sanding, scraping or vacuuming them, or the vermiculite, is how exposure happens. Bulk samples sent to a lab answer whether asbestos is present, and if it is, removal belongs to licensed abatement contractors. The tempting answer is to rip up the tiles for safety, which is the single riskiest thing to do.

blocks.html: Both samples came back positive: the tiles and mastic for chrysotile asbestos, and the vermiculite at a low percentage. The Oseis decided to leave the tiles under new flooring and have the attic insulation professionally removed before they added any new insulation. They had a renovation plan too: open the kitchen into the dining room and finish the basement as a playroom.

blocks.q: Before the NYC Department of Buildings issues a permit for that renovation, what asbestos step will apply?
c: No step, because asbestos rules apply to commercial buildings rather than homes
A DEC permit, since DEC licenses every asbestos project in New York City
A letter from the home inspector stating that no asbestos will be disturbed
A certified investigator's survey filed with DEP, or an exemption
blocks.x: In NYC, owners must show that asbestos requirements are satisfied before DOB issues a permit: a certified asbestos investigator surveys the work area and files an assessment with the Department of Environmental Protection, or the owner certifies the job falls under an exemption. Abatement, if needed, is done by licensed contractors. A home inspector's letter is the tempting answer, but home inspectors are not certified asbestos investigators.

blocks.html: The kitchen work raised a second rule. Because the house was built before 1978, the EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting rule applies to paid contractors who disturb painted surfaces: more than 6 square feet per room inside or 20 square feet outside, or any window replacement. The firm must be EPA certified, use lead-safe work practices, and give the family the Renovate Right pamphlet before starting.

blocks.q: A contractor bids the kitchen job $4,000 below the others but is not lead-safe certified. He says, "It's a small job, I don't need it." The job will remove a plaster wall. Is he right?
c: Yes, since the rule exempts any job under $10,000 in a single-family home
Yes, because the house is owner-occupied and the owners can waive the rule
No; removing a painted wall goes well past the 6 square foot interior threshold
No, but solely if a lab has already confirmed lead paint on that same wall
blocks.x: Removing a wall disturbs far more than 6 square feet of painted surface in a pre-1978 home, so the firm must be certified and use lead-safe practices. There is no dollar exemption. The tempting answer is the test result: a renovator may skip the practices if a certified test shows the components are free of lead, but without that, the rule presumes lead and applies.

blocks.html: The musty smell Doreen had tried to air out came from behind the knotty pine paneling on the basement's north wall. Ray's moisture meter lit up along the bottom four feet, and when he pulled one loose panel, black and green growth covered the back of it and the drywall behind, roughly 30 square feet. A foundation crack on that wall let water in during heavy rain. Phil offered to have his handyman "bleach it and button it up" before closing.

blocks.q: What does New York law require for the 30 square feet of mold?
c: Nothing, since mold rules cover rental buildings, not single-family homes
One licensed mold company that both writes the plan and does the cleanup
A handyman is fine if he uses bleach and wears a respirator during the work
A licensed assessor and a licensed remediator, each from a separate firm
blocks.x: New York's mold program requires licensed professionals for mold assessment and remediation of more than 10 square feet: a licensed assessor writes the plan and later confirms the result, and a licensed remediator does the work. The two cannot be the same company on a project, which is the trap in the single-company answer. Bleach on wet drywall also misses the point: the water source has to be fixed first.

blocks.html: The Harmons hired a foundation contractor to seal the crack and regrade the north side, a licensed assessor wrote a plan, and a separate licensed remediator removed the paneling and drywall under containment. The assessor's post-remediation report cleared the area.

One last thing. The wood destroying insect inspection found mud tubes running up the foundation wall to the sill on the garage side and soft wood at the end of one joist. The PCDS asked whether the property had any termite, insect, rodent or pest infestation and whether it had been treated. The Harmons had checked "no." In the garage, Ray found a 2019 invoice from a pest control company for "subterranean termite treatment, garage side."

blocks.q: What is the strongest accurate statement about the Harmons' PCDS answer?
c: The PCDS is advisory, so a false answer has no legal consequences for sellers
The listing agent alone is liable, because the agent fills out the PCDS form
A seller who willfully gives a false answer can be liable for actual damages
The buyers may cancel the contract at any time before closing for any reason
blocks.x: The PCDS is the seller's statement; the seller, not the agent, fills it out. A seller who willfully fails to comply can be liable to the buyer for actual damages, and a knowingly false answer can support a fraud claim. The tempting answer blames the listing agent, but agents do not complete the form. Agents who know of a defect and conceal it face their own liability, separate from the seller's.

blocks.html: Jordan sent the invoice and the inspection photos to the Oseis and their attorney the same day. The Harmons agreed to a renewed termite treatment by a DEC-certified applicator, a carpenter's repair of the joist end, and a $3,500 credit. The deal closed in January, six weeks later than planned. Jordan's file held every version of every disclosure, the test results, the clearance reports, and dated emails showing what was recommended and when.

blocks.q: How long must Jordan's firm keep the signed lead disclosure and its certifications?
c: 3 years from the sale
1 year from the closing
6 years from the sale
Until the house is resold
blocks.x: Under the federal rule, sellers and agents keep the lead disclosure and acknowledgment for 3 years from the date of sale; New York also requires brokers to keep transaction records for 3 years. The tempting answer is 6 years, a common statute of limitations number, but the rule is specific. Keeping the file longer is fine; keeping it shorter is a violation.

blocks.title: Unknown is not no
blocks.html: On the PCDS a seller may answer "unknown," and that is often honest. But "unknown" is not "no," and an agent should read it as "not tested." Here the Harmons' "unknown" on asbestos was true, their "no" on termites was not, and only testing and a look in the garage told the difference.

items: For pre-1978 housing, sellers disclose known lead hazards and hand over every available report, however old. Agents must make sure they do, and keep records 3 years.
The 10-day lead testing opportunity can be waived only in writing. A risk assessment finds present hazards; an inspection maps where lead paint is. NYC Local Law 1 governs rentals, not this sale.
A radon test needs closed-house conditions to count. At 4 pCi/L or more, mitigate, then retest.
Suspected asbestos: sample, do not disturb, and use licensed abatement; NYC permits require an asbestos investigation. Pre-1978 renovations need an EPA-certified, lead-safe firm.
Mold over 10 square feet in New York needs a licensed assessor and a separate licensed remediator, after the water source is fixed.
The PCDS is the seller's statement and the seller's liability; agents must not play expert and must disclose what they know.

lessons.title: Case file: The Tool and Die Shop on Abeel Street
lessons.tagline: Evelyn wants a cheap industrial building in Kingston for lofts and maker space. The building comes with a degreaser history, a 1970s transformer, a wetland out back, and a seller in a hurry.
objectives: Apply all appropriate inquiries timing and Phase I to IV assessment stages to a commercial purchase with suspected contamination.
Distinguish which law reaches which contaminant (CERCLA hazardous substances, petroleum under New York's Navigation Law, PCBs, asbestos) and who bears liability.
Decide when New York's Brownfield Cleanup Program, wetland permits and asbestos surveys affect a redevelopment plan.
Explain a buyer's agent's duties and liability when relaying a seller's environmental claims.

blocks.title: A bargain near the Rondout
blocks.html: Evelyn Park has found what she calls "the last cheap big box in the Hudson Valley": a 1952 brick industrial building, 32,000 square feet on 3.2 acres off Abeel Street in Kingston, two blocks from the Rondout Creek waterfront. For forty years it was a tool and die shop. It has been vacant since 2019. The asking price is $1,450,000, which Evelyn thinks is about $600,000 under what the lofts and maker space she has in mind would support. The seller is a family LLC whose principals have retired to Arizona. Their broker tells Jordan, who represents Evelyn: "We have another group interested. If she wants it, she signs this week, no contingencies. The tanks were pulled in the nineties. It's a clean building." Evelyn asks Jordan whether a quick close is worth the risk.

Commercial buyers buy history. Whatever a tool and die shop poured down a floor drain in 1968 is still in the soil, and federal law can make today's owner pay to clean it up whether or not she ever touched it. The defense exists, but it has to be earned before closing.

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell Evelyn about closing this week with no contingencies?
c: Close quickly; the seller's broker has confirmed in writing that the tanks are gone
Close quickly; as a buyer who did not use the site, she has no cleanup exposure
Insist on a due diligence period with a Phase I before she is bound to close
Skip the Phase I but buy pollution insurance, which replaces the legal defenses
blocks.x: Under CERCLA, a current owner can be liable for cleanup of contamination she did not cause. The defenses for innocent landowners and bona fide prospective purchasers require all appropriate inquiries before acquisition, which in practice means a Phase I environmental site assessment. A broker's assurance is not inquiry. Insurance is the tempting answer: it can be a useful layer, but it does not create the statutory defense.

blocks.html: Jordan also put the timing in writing: the Phase I takes two to four weeks, a Phase II, if needed, another three or more, and a lender will want both before committing. A no-contingency contract signed this week would have bound Evelyn before any of that could happen.

Evelyn agreed to a 45-day due diligence period and a $50,000 deposit that would come back if she walked. The seller's broker grumbled and accepted; the "other group" never surfaced. Then the seller's broker offered a shortcut: a Phase I report done in March of last year for a buyer who later walked away.

blocks.q: Can Evelyn rely on last March's Phase I, prepared for a different buyer, if she closes next month?
c: Yes, since a Phase I report stays valid for five years from the date it is signed
Yes, as long as the seller signs a letter saying nothing at the site has changed
No; Phase I reports are void once the original client decides to walk away
Not as is; inquiry must be within a year of purchase, key parts within 180 days
blocks.x: All appropriate inquiries must be conducted within one year before acquisition, and several components (interviews, lien searches, government records review, the site visit, and the environmental professional's declaration) must be done or updated within 180 days before it. A report about 19 months old fails both, and it was prepared for someone else. Five years is the tempting number, but it has no basis in the rule. Evelyn ordered a new Phase I.

blocks.title: A Phase I does not test anything
blocks.html: A Phase I is research and observation: historical records, fire insurance maps, regulatory databases, interviews, a site walk. It flags "recognized environmental conditions." It takes no samples. Exam items love to describe soil borings and ask which phase; that is Phase II.

blocks.title: Phase I environmental site assessment, findings (excerpt)
blocks.html:
REC 1: 1955 to 1994 operations used chlorinated solvent degreasers (trichloroethylene, TCE) for parts cleaning. Two floor drains in the former degreasing room discharge to an unknown location.
REC 2: Fire insurance maps show a 4,000-gallon fuel oil underground storage tank at the north wall (1952). Seller reports removal in "the 1990s"; no closure report, no DEC spill record, no tank registration history located.
REC 3: Pad-mounted transformer at the east wall, nameplate dated 1974; ownership not confirmed.
Other observations: Fluorescent light fixtures with older ballasts throughout. Suspect asbestos pipe insulation and roofing. A mapped freshwater wetland along the rear property line. A utility substation across the street.

blocks.q: With three recognized environmental conditions identified, what is the logical next step?
c: A Phase II that samples soil, groundwater and soil vapor at each REC
A Phase III remediation plan, since the Phase I has proven contamination exists
A Phase IV monitoring program, starting before Evelyn takes title to the site
A second Phase I by a different firm to confirm the first firm's conclusions
blocks.x: Phase I flags conditions; Phase II tests them. Borings, groundwater wells and soil vapor samples at the degreasing room, the old tank location and the transformer pad tell Evelyn whether there is contamination, what it is, and how much. Phase III is the tempting answer, but a Phase I proves nothing about contamination; remediation is designed after testing measures it. Phase IV is long-term management after cleanup.

blocks.html: The Phase II took three weeks and cost Evelyn $38,000. It found TCE in groundwater beneath the degreasing room at levels well above state standards, and TCE in the soil vapor under the slab. Near the north wall, soil borings hit petroleum-stained soil at 8 feet where the old tank had been, with no tank present. The transformer pad soil showed no PCBs.

blocks.q: Which statement correctly matches each contaminant to the law that most directly reaches it?
c: TCE falls under New York's Navigation Law; the fuel oil falls under CERCLA
Both fall under CERCLA, which reaches every contaminant found on a site
TCE is a CERCLA hazardous substance; the fuel oil, the Navigation Law
Neither is regulated, because the shop stopped operating before the Phase II
blocks.x: TCE is a hazardous substance under CERCLA and New York's own state Superfund program. Petroleum is excluded from CERCLA, which is the trap in the "both" answer, but New York's Navigation Law makes those responsible for a petroleum discharge strictly liable for cleanup, and the spill must be reported to DEC. Closing the business does not end liability for contamination that remains.

head: Sample area
Medium
Finding
What it means
rows: Former degreasing room, 3 borings and 2 wells
TCE well above state groundwater standards
Solvent release, likely through the floor drains
TCE vapor present at every probe
Risk of vapor rising into occupied space
Petroleum staining and odor at 8 feet; no tank found
No sign of a past transformer leak
blocks.caption: Phase II summary table

blocks.html: Numbers like these change a negotiation. Before the Phase II, the seller's broker was talking about a bidding war. After it, the conversation was about who pays for what, and how much of that risk the price should carry. Evelyn's lender read the same table and told her the loan would not close without an approved cleanup plan or a substantial price reduction.

The petroleum find triggered a call to DEC's spill hotline. A spill number was assigned. The seller's principals, reached in Arizona, said the tank "must have been pulled" by a contractor whose name they no longer remembered.

The seller's attorney sent a confident email: "Your client didn't cause any of this. She's an innocent purchaser. She has nothing to worry about." Evelyn's environmental attorney, Dana Whitfield, wrote back one line: "Innocent purchasers who buy with knowledge have plenty to worry about."

blocks.q: Evelyn now knows about the contamination. If she buys, can she still be protected from CERCLA cleanup liability?
c: No; once a buyer knows of contamination, every federal defense is gone
Yes, as a bona fide prospective purchaser meeting the conditions
Yes, automatically, since she did not own the site when the TCE was released
No, unless the seller's LLC first pays for and finishes the full TCE cleanup
blocks.x: The bona fide prospective purchaser protection, added by the 2002 Brownfields law, can cover a buyer who knows about contamination, if she conducted all appropriate inquiries before buying, has no affiliation with a liable party, and meets continuing obligations: reasonable steps to stop releases, cooperation with regulators, and compliance with land use restrictions. Protection is not automatic, which is the tempting answer; it is earned before and kept after closing.

blocks.title: The federal chain
blocks.html: CERCLA (1980) makes current owners, past owners at the time of disposal, generators and transporters liable for cleanup: strict, joint and several, and retroactive. SARA (1986) added the innocent landowner defense for buyers who made appropriate inquiry and found nothing. The 2002 Brownfields amendments added protection for bona fide prospective purchasers, who may know about contamination but meet the statute's conditions.

The 1974 transformer was the next question. Transformers and capacitors made before 1979 often contain PCBs, which can leak from aging seals. The pad soil was clean, but whoever owns the transformer owns the risk of what is inside it.

blocks.q: How should Evelyn's team deal with the transformer?
c: Assume the seller owns it and require replacement at the seller's cost
Ignore it, since the soil around the pad showed no PCB contamination
Have the transformer drained by Evelyn's own maintenance staff before closing
Confirm ownership with the utility; if it is the building's, test it
blocks.x: Many pad-mounted transformers belong to the utility, which then bears responsibility for them; some belong to the property owner. Ownership decides who deals with PCB testing, leaks and eventual disposal. If it is the building's, a sample of the dielectric fluid answers whether PCBs are present. Clean soil today is the tempting answer, but it does not tell you what is inside a 50-year-old unit.

blocks.html: Central Hudson confirmed the transformer was theirs; replacing it was already on their schedule. The ballasts were a different matter. Fluorescent light ballasts made before 1979 commonly contain PCBs, and the building had about 400 fixtures. The Phase I noted that ballasts without a "No PCBs" label should be presumed to contain them.

blocks.q: Evelyn's contractor plans to rip out the old fixtures and toss them in a dumpster. What is the right approach?
c: Allow it, since ballasts hold too little PCB to count as regulated waste
Allow it, as long as the dumpster is covered and hauled to a local landfill
Treat unlabeled pre-1979 ballasts as PCB waste and use a disposal firm
Leave the old fixtures in place for good, since removing them releases PCBs
blocks.x: Pre-1979 ballasts without a "No PCBs" label should be treated as containing PCBs and handled through firms that manage and dispose of them properly, especially any that are leaking. The tempting answer minimizes the quantity per ballast, but 400 of them in a dumpster is a real disposal problem and a real liability. Leaving them in place indefinitely ignores the risk of aging ballasts leaking or burning.

blocks.text: The deal Evelyn could live with

blocks.html: With a Phase II in hand, the price was no longer the seller's to dictate. Dana laid out the options. The cleanup of TCE in groundwater could run for years. Doing it under New York's Brownfield Cleanup Program would cost more in oversight but bring something the private route could not.

blocks.title: New York's Brownfield Cleanup Program
blocks.html: DEC's Brownfield Cleanup Program (Environmental Conservation Law Article 27, Title 14) lets a volunteer clean up a contaminated site under a cleanup agreement and DEC oversight. When DEC accepts the work, it issues a certificate of completion, which brings a limitation on state liability that can pass to later owners, and eligibility for state brownfield tax credits. Cleanup standards depend on the intended use: residential use requires a more stringent cleanup than commercial or industrial use. Where contamination stays in place, use restrictions and an environmental easement are recorded against the property.

blocks.q: Evelyn plans lofts (residential) on the upper floor. How does that affect a Brownfield Cleanup Program approach?
c: It has no effect, since every site in the program is cleaned to one standard
It makes the site ineligible, because the program is for industrial reuse
It means a stricter cleanup standard than a commercial-only reuse would need
It means DEC will pay for the cleanup in exchange for an affordable unit set-aside
blocks.x: New York's cleanup standards turn on use: residential use triggers more stringent requirements than commercial or industrial use, because people sleep there, children live there, and exposure is longer. The tempting answer is a single standard, but the program is designed around use-based tracks. DEC does not pay a volunteer's cleanup; the program's financial benefit comes through tax credits.

blocks.html: The TCE in soil vapor raised a related problem: indoor air quality. Solvent vapor can migrate up through a slab into the building, a process called vapor intrusion. The engineer's plan included a sub-slab depressurization system, the commercial cousin of a residential radon fan, plus a site management plan that would require the owner to keep it running and keep testing it. That ongoing obligation is the Phase IV of this deal: monitoring and maintenance after the cleanup, recorded so the next buyer inherits it.

blocks.q: Five years after the cleanup, Evelyn sells the building. What will the buyer's title search most likely show?
c: Nothing, since a certificate of completion erases the site's environmental history
A DEC lien for the full cost of the cleanup that Evelyn performed under the program
A CERCLA judgment against Evelyn as the owner at the time of the cleanup
An environmental easement and use restrictions tied to the remaining contamination
