blocks.x: Where contamination remains and engineering controls such as a vapor mitigation system are part of the remedy, an environmental easement and use restrictions are recorded and run with the land. The next buyer sees them and must comply. The tempting answer treats the certificate as a clean slate; it limits liability, but it does not erase the site's history or its continuing obligations.

blocks.title: If this lot were in New York City
blocks.html: In the five boroughs, many lots rezoned for new uses carry an "E" designation for hazardous materials, placed during the city's environmental review. Before DOB approves permits on an E-designated lot, the Mayor's Office of Environmental Remediation must sign off on testing and, if needed, a remedial plan. Buyers can see the designation on the zoning map, and an agent who lists or shows such a lot should know what it means for the timeline.

Evelyn's conversion also needed local approvals. Kingston's planning board would review the site plan for the new use, parking and landscaping, and before approving it, the board has to consider environmental impacts.

blocks.q: Under what New York law does the planning board weigh the conversion's environmental impacts before approving it?
c: CERCLA, since contaminated sites need federal sign-off for any local approval
The State Environmental Quality Review Act, which applies to local agency actions
The Navigation Law, since the site sits two blocks from the Rondout Creek
The Clean Air Act, because the old degreasers once vented solvent fumes outside
blocks.x: SEQRA requires state and local agencies, including planning boards, to consider environmental impacts before approving, funding or undertaking an action, and a significant impact can require a full environmental impact statement. CERCLA is the tempting answer because the site is contaminated, but CERCLA governs cleanup liability, not local land use approvals. The Navigation Law covers petroleum discharges, not planning review.

blocks.html: Three items remained. Evelyn's plan added 40 parking spaces in the rear, about 60 feet from the mapped freshwater wetland. The roof and pipe insulation needed to come apart for the conversion. And the substation across the street worried one of her prospective tenants.

blocks.q: What does the rear parking plan need from the wetland standpoint?
c: Nothing, since the pavement stays outside the wetland's own mapped boundary
A DEC permit, since the 100-foot adjacent area is regulated
Approval from the town's planning board alone, because wetlands are local
A variance from the zoning board of appeals before DEC will even review it
blocks.x: DEC regulates freshwater wetlands and a 100-foot adjacent area around them, so paving 60 feet away generally needs a DEC permit, and the Army Corps may have jurisdiction over federal waters. The tempting answer looks only at the wetland's boundary line and misses the adjacent area. Local planning review runs alongside the state permit; it does not replace it.

blocks.q: Before renovation opens the roof and pipe insulation, what does New York require about asbestos?
c: An asbestos survey of the affected areas by a licensed inspector before work starts
Nothing, if the building has been vacant and closed for more than five years
A survey after demolition, since asbestos cannot be found until materials are opened
Testing of the air outside the building once the contractor finishes the roof
blocks.x: New York's asbestos rules for buildings (Industrial Code Rule 56, alongside the federal Clean Air Act asbestos standard) require an asbestos survey by licensed personnel before demolition or renovation that disturbs building materials, with abatement by licensed contractors where asbestos is found. Vacancy changes nothing. A post-demolition survey is the trap: the point is to find asbestos before anyone breaks it.

blocks.html: On the substation, the Phase I had noted electromagnetic fields only as a buyer-perception item. Research has not established a clear health link; field strength drops quickly with distance, and the building's nearest wall was 90 feet away. Jordan gave the tenant the facts and the distance, and let the tenant decide.

Weeks earlier, Jordan had forwarded the seller's broker's "tanks were pulled, it's a clean building" message to Evelyn with a note: "Seller's broker states this; we have no documents yet." Diane read the file later and pointed to that note.

blocks.q: Why did Diane single out Jordan's note?
c: Because repeating a seller's claim as fact can create liability if false
Because buyer's agents may not forward any message from the seller's side to a client
Because the note waived Evelyn's right to rely on the Phase I she later ordered
Because environmental issues are the attorney's job, so agents should stay out of them
blocks.x: Agents can be liable for misrepresentation when they pass along statements as true without basis, and for failing to disclose what they know. Attributing the claim to its source and flagging the lack of documents protected Evelyn and Jordan. Forwarding messages is normal and often required. The tempting last answer is half right: agents should not play environmental expert, but they must disclose what they know and recommend the right professionals.

blocks.html: The final deal: price reduced to $975,000, the $475,000 difference reflecting the cleanup estimate plus a contingency; the seller kept responsibility for the petroleum spill under a separate escrow of $150,000 held by Dana's office; Evelyn applied to the Brownfield Cleanup Program as a volunteer before closing. She closed on day 44 of the 45-day period.

blocks.title: Contract rider, environmental escrow (summary)
blocks.html:
1. Seller deposits $150,000 of the purchase price with Purchaser's environmental counsel as escrow agent at closing.
2. Seller remains responsible for investigation and cleanup of DEC Spill No. assigned to the north wall petroleum release, using DEC-approved consultants.
3. Escrow funds are released to Seller's consultants against invoices for that work, and the balance to Seller when DEC issues a no-further-action letter for the spill.
4. If the spill is not closed within 36 months, Purchaser may complete the work and draw on the escrow.
5. Seller indemnifies Purchaser for third-party claims arising from the petroleum release; the indemnity survives closing.

Why both an escrow and an indemnity? An indemnity is a promise, and the seller is a family LLC whose members live in another state and whose only asset was this building. After closing, the LLC may hold nothing but cash it can distribute. The escrow is real money that cannot leave. Dana wanted the promise for anything the escrow did not cover, and the escrow for the cleanup everyone already knew about.

items: All appropriate inquiries must happen within a year before acquisition, with key components within 180 days; a stale or borrowed Phase I does not protect a new buyer.
Phase I looks, Phase II tests, Phase III cleans, Phase IV manages. Recognized environmental conditions lead to sampling, not straight to remediation.

CERCLA reaches hazardous substances like TCE with strict, joint and several liability; petroleum is excluded but New York's Navigation Law makes dischargers strictly liable. Bona fide prospective purchaser protection is earned and kept.
Check who owns old transformers; treat unlabeled pre-1979 ballasts as PCB-containing; survey for asbestos before renovation.

New York's Brownfield Cleanup Program trades oversight for liability limits and tax credits; cleanup standards follow the intended use, and remaining controls are recorded against title. DEC regulates a 100-foot adjacent area around freshwater wetlands.
Attribute seller claims to their source, never restate them as fact, and send clients to the right professionals.

lessons.title: Case file: The Water Test on Titicus Road
lessons.tagline: A 1958 cape in North Salem with a drilled well, a septic field nobody has opened in years, a soft sill, a power line out back, and an air conditioner that runs on a refrigerant the country stopped making.
objectives: Apply Westchester County's private well testing law and state drinking water standards to a lab report, and decide which results require treatment
Decide whether a septic system needs maintenance or replacement, and who designs, approves and pays for a new absorption field in a resale
Apply wood-destroying insect, chlordane, EMF and refrigerant rules to inspection findings and advise buyers without overstepping
Explain which warranties and contract protections apply to repair work done for a resale, as opposed to a new home

blocks.title: Two acres and a well
blocks.html: Kerry and Ade Bello have rented in Park Slope for eleven years. Both now work remotely, their daughters are 7 and 10, and they want land. Jordan represents them under a written buyer agency agreement, and the search has led north to a 1958 cape on 2.1 acres on Titicus Road in North Salem, in northern Westchester, listed at $749,000 by Bridget Kane of a Somers brokerage. Drilled well, septic system, oil heat, central air added in 2004, and a utility transmission line crossing the back of the lot on an easement. The Bellos have never lived anywhere without a water bill and a sewer. At the first showing, Kerry fills a mason jar at the kitchen tap and hands it to Jordan. “Can you drop this at a lab on your way back to Brooklyn? I want to know what we'd be drinking.”

blocks.q: What should Jordan do with Kerry's jar?
c: Drop it at a state-certified lab, since tap water from any faucet shows the well's quality
Decline; under the county law a certified lab's own sampler collects the water
Ask Bridget to deliver it to the lab, since the seller's side controls the well test
Keep it until the contract is signed, then submit it as the seller's required test
blocks.x: Westchester's private well testing law requires that samples be collected by an employee or authorized representative of a laboratory certified by the state Department of Health, and the county says plainly that a real estate agent may not collect them. A jar from a kitchen faucet, carried for hours, proves little anyway. Holding it for the seller's test is the trap: that test must follow the law's sampling rules too, and Kerry's jar does not.

blocks.html: Jordan explains why the jar can wait. Westchester County Local Law 7 of 2007 (Chapter 707 of the county's laws) puts the job on the seller: once a contract of sale is signed for a property served by a private drinking water well, the seller must have the well tested by a certified laboratory for a fixed list of contaminants, pay for it, and give the results to the buyer. Many New York counties have no resale rule at all. There, a well water test is the buyer's own due diligence, protected by an inspection contingency in the contract. Either way, nobody should buy a house on a well without a certified lab result in hand.

blocks.title: Westchester tests at the contract, not the listing
blocks.html: The county law covers sales and leases of property served by a private drinking water well. It does not apply to property on a regulated public water system (5 or more connections, or 25 or more people a day for 60 days a year), to a well used only for irrigation, or to gifts and transfers by operation of law. Primary contaminants tested: total coliform bacteria (with an E. coli or fecal coliform follow-up if positive), nitrate, arsenic, lead, the organic chemicals listed in Part 5 of the State Sanitary Code, vinyl chloride and MTBE. Secondary: pH, iron, manganese, sodium and chloride. Landlords must test too.
Before the Bellos make an offer, Jordan reads the sellers' Property Condition Disclosure Statement. Walt and June Dunleavy are retiring to Maine after 34 years in the house. Their answers are short.

blocks.title: From the Dunleavys' PCDS (selected answers)
blocks.html:
Water source: Private well, drilled, 1987.
Has the water quality been tested? Yes, March 2024. “Passed.” (Lab sheet attached: total coliform absent.)
Sewage system: Septic tank and leach field, installed 1958. Date last pumped: Unknown. Any known material defects? No.
Has the property had termite, insect, rodent or pest infestation? No.
Any rot or water damage to the structure? Unknown.
Central air conditioning: Yes, 2004.

blocks.q: The Bellos sign a contract in October 2026. Does the attached March 2024 test satisfy the county law?
c: Yes, since a passing test within the last three years satisfies the county law
Yes, if the sellers certify that nothing has changed
No; old results count for a year, and coliform results for six months
No, because the law requires a test taken after the listing agreement date
blocks.x: Under the county's rules, an earlier test done the way the law requires can be used for one year after the sample was collected, except the coliform result, which is good for only six months. A test from March 2024 fails both limits. The listing-date answer is the trap: the trigger in the law is the signing of the contract of sale, not the listing, and a fresh test after the contract is what the Bellos will get.

blocks.html: The contract is signed on October 9 at $749,000, with an inspection contingency that Priya, the Bellos' attorney, wrote to cover the well, the septic system and termites. Bridget's office orders the county test through a certified lab. The lab's sampler disconnects nothing, because the house has no treatment equipment, and draws from a cold, non-aerated basement tap, plus a first-draw and a flushed sample for lead. Ten days later the results arrive.

head: Parameter
Result
Standard
Type
rows: No limit; flagged for sodium-restricted diets
blocks.caption: Certified lab report, Titicus Road, October 2026

blocks.q: Under the county law, which result requires the well to be remediated?
c: The iron at 0.62 mg/L, which is about double the state standard
The pH of 6.1, since acidic water attacks copper plumbing over time
The sodium at 38 mg/L, which is flagged for people on restricted diets
The positive total coliform, which is a primary contaminant
blocks.x: The county requires treatment only when a primary contaminant fails to meet drinking water standards after other remedial steps. Total coliform is primary. Iron, pH, manganese, sodium and chloride are secondary: they affect taste, staining and plumbing, and treating them is the owner's choice. The iron answer is the trap. It does exceed the standard, but iron stains laundry and fixtures rather than threatening health at this level.

blocks.html: Ade reads “bacteria present” and wants to walk away. Jordan slows him down. Coliforms are indicator organisms: most are harmless, but their presence means something on the surface has a path into the well. E. coli was absent, so this sample shows no sign of sewage or animal waste. The question is where the path is and whether it can be closed. The lab also reported hardness at 95 mg/L, moderately hard, which needs nothing.

blocks.q: What is the usual first response to a total coliform positive with E. coli absent in a drilled well?
c: Inspect the wellhead, close any entry points, shock chlorinate, then retest
Install a whole-house reverse osmosis unit and skip the follow-up testing
Drill a new well, since a positive result means the aquifer is contaminated
Boil drinking water for a week while the bacteria die off by themselves
blocks.x: Most coliform hits in drilled wells come from the top: a cracked or unsealed cap, a casing that ends at or below grade, surface water pooling at the wellhead, or recent pump work. Fix the entry point, disinfect the well with chlorine, flush, and retest, usually twice. If bacteria keep returning, continuous disinfection such as UV is the next step. Drilling a new well is the trap: it is costly and unproven, since the groundwater itself may be fine.

blocks.html: The well contractor found exactly that. The 1987 casing ended four inches below grade in a low spot where spring runoff pooled, under a loose cap with no screened vent. He extended the casing above grade, installed a sanitary cap, regraded the soil to slope away from the wellhead, and shock chlorinated the well. Two retests a week apart showed coliform absent. Under Priya's rider, the Dunleavys paid the $2,850 bill. In the basement, though, Ray Kowalski, the Bellos' inspector, was pointing at something else: blue-green stains under the tub spout and a fresh repair clamp on a copper supply line.

blocks.q: Why does the pH of 6.1 matter for this house, even though the county law does not require treatment?
c: Acidic water corrodes copper and can draw lead from older solder joints
Low pH water feeds coliform bacteria, which will grow back without treatment
Low pH means the water is hard, and hard water scales the boiler's heating coil
A pH under 6.5 fails the law's primary standards
blocks.x: Acidic water slowly dissolves copper, which shows up as blue-green stains and pinhole leaks, and it can pull lead from solder used before lead solder was banned for drinking water plumbing in 1986. The usual fix is an acid neutralizer, a tank of calcite that raises the pH before the water reaches the pipes. The hardness answer is the trap: hardness is calcium and magnesium, a separate measurement, and acidic water tends to be soft, not hard.

blocks.html: Ade has one more question, and it is a fair one. In Brooklyn, his water came with a long annual report and a federal law behind it. Who stands behind a well?

blocks.q: Ade asks why the federal Safe Drinking Water Act does not cover the Titicus Road well. What is the accurate answer?
c: It does; the EPA sets enforceable standards for every well serving a home
It covers private wells once a county health department adopts it
It does not; the Act regulates public water systems, not a single home's well
It does not, because wells drilled before 1974 are grandfathered out of it
blocks.x: The Safe Drinking Water Act (1974) sets standards for public water systems. A well serving one house is outside it, so its quality is the owner's responsibility. The state's Sanitary Code standards serve as the yardstick, and Westchester's law forces a test at sale and lease. The grandfathering answer is the trap: no date exempts a well. What matters is the kind of system, public or private.

blocks.text: The leach field nobody had opened

blocks.html: “Last pumped: unknown” is a phrase Jordan has learned to treat as a finding. Jordan requests the Westchester County Department of Health's file for the address. It holds a 1958 permit card with a hand sketch: a 1,000-gallon tank and three 60-foot absorption trenches, the nearest one about 85 feet from where the well now sits. Nothing has been filed since. With the sellers' consent under the contract, the Bellos hire a septic contractor to uncover, pump and inspect the septic system.

blocks.title: Septic inspection report, Titicus Road (summary)
blocks.html:
Tank: Concrete, about 1,000 gallons, 3 feet below grade, 12 feet off the rear foundation. Sludge and scum filled about 60% of the tank. Pumped.
Outlet baffle: Missing. Solids have been carried into the distribution line.
Distribution box: Tilted; two of three outlets sit lower than the third.
Absorption field: Ground over the trenches wet and spongy after four dry days. Gray effluent visible at the surface at the downhill end. Strong odor.
Hydraulic load test: Liquid backed up into the distribution box within 40 minutes.
Opinion: Absorption field has failed. Tank serviceable with a new outlet baffle and riser.

blocks.q: Which finding makes this a replacement job rather than a maintenance job?
c: The 60% sludge level, which shows the tank was not pumped often enough
The missing outlet baffle, which lets scum flow into the pipes
The tilted distribution box, which sends most of the flow to one trench
Effluent at the surface, showing the soil no longer absorbs the flow
blocks.x: Pumping, a new baffle and a leveled distribution box are repairs. Effluent surfacing, and a field that backs up within minutes under a load test, mean the trench soil has clogged and the absorption field must be replaced. Surfacing sewage is also a health hazard the county will not leave in place. The missing baffle is the trap: it probably caused the failure by sending solids into the field for years, but fixing it now will not unclog the soil.

blocks.html: Replacing a field is not a backhoe and a weekend. The new system has to meet today's state and county standards, including separation from the well. The 1958 trenches sat about 85 feet from it, closer than today's typical 100-foot minimum for an absorption field, which may also explain how surface water and the well were getting acquainted. The new field will have to go somewhere else.

blocks.q: Who prepares the replacement design, and who must approve it before construction?
c: The septic contractor draws it, and the town building department approves it
A licensed engineer or architect designs it, and county health approves it
The home inspector designs it from the load test, and the DEC approves it
The sellers' attorney files it, and the town planning board approves it
blocks.x: In New York, an onsite sewage system is designed by a licensed professional engineer or registered architect after soil testing: deep test holes to find groundwater and rock, and percolation tests to size the field. Here the Westchester County Department of Health reviews the design, approves it, and inspects the work. The building department answer is the trap: it issues building permits, but septic approval belongs to the health department.

blocks.html: The engineer's tests in the side yard came back at 12 minutes per inch, well within the usable range, and the new field was sited 120 feet from the well. Estimate: $46,000 for design, county review, installation, and a new baffle and riser on the old tank. Priya renegotiated: the Dunleavys would hire the contractor, build to the approved plan, and deliver the county's sign-off before closing, with the closing date moved to January. The sellers signed a written home improvement contract with a contractor holding a Westchester County Department of Consumer Protection license. It included a two-year warranty on parts and workmanship, transferable to a new owner on written notice.

blocks.q: Ade asks what warranty will protect him on the new field once he owns the house. Which answer is accurate?
c: The housing merchant implied warranty, which gives 2 years on systems
A 6-year statutory warranty, since a septic field counts as structure
The contractor's written warranty, if it transfers to the Bellos
No protection; repair warranties end at a sale
blocks.x: The housing merchant implied warranty (GBL 777-a) applies to the sale of a new home by a builder. A 1958 house with a new field is a resale, so the Bellos' protection is contractual: the installer's written warranty, which Priya will have assigned at closing with notice to the contractor. The 2-year answer is the trap. The period sounds familiar because 777-a covers systems for 2 years, but only on new homes.

blocks.title: Two kinds of mandated protection, neither one automatic on a resale
blocks.html: The syllabus groups “mandated guarantees and warranties” under two headings. New home construction: GBL 777-a gives statutory warranty periods on a new home sold by a builder. Home improvement: GBL Article 36-A sets contract rules (a written contract, dates, a description of work and materials, protection of the deposit, notice of the right to cancel), and counties such as Westchester license the contractors. A resale buyer of a repaired house gets no statutory warranty period. The buyer gets what the contractor wrote, if it transfers.

blocks.text: Mud tubes on the north wall

blocks.html: Ray's inspection had its own headline. Along the north foundation wall, pencil-width mud tubes ran from the slab up the block to the wood. His screwdriver sank into the sill plate along about nine feet of that wall, and into the ends of three floor joists bearing on it. Tacked to a joist behind the boiler was a yellowed 1979 invoice: “Termite treatment, chlordane, perimeter soil.”

blocks.q: What do Ray's findings mean, and what is the right sequence of fixes?
c: Live tubes and soft wood signal active termites: treat, then repair the sill and joists
The damage is cosmetic: seal the sill with paint and retreat the soil next spring
The damage is old, since the 1979 chlordane treatment protects the house for good
The north foundation wall has failed and needs rebuilding before anything else
blocks.x: The sill plate is the lowest wood member, anchored to the foundation, and the joists bear on it, so soft wood there is a structural matter. Fresh tubes mean active subterranean termites. A pest control firm using DEC-certified applicators treats first; then a carpenter, or an engineer if damage is extensive, replaces sill sections and sisters the joists. The chlordane answer is the trap: it was banned in 1988, and the tubes prove termites got past it.

blocks.html: A wood-destroying insect inspection by a licensed pest control company confirmed an active infestation: $2,400 to treat, and a carpenter quoted $7,800 for the sill and joists. When Priya raised the PCDS answer of “No” to infestation, June Dunleavy said they had seen “flying ants” in the basement two springs ago and swept them up. A seller who willfully gives a false PCDS answer can be liable for the buyer's actual damages, and that history did more to move the sellers than any argument: they agreed to treat before closing with a transferable service agreement and to credit the carpentry.

blocks.q: Kerry wants a vegetable bed along the north foundation. Given the 1979 invoice, what is sensible advice?
c: Plant freely, because chlordane breaks down in soil within a few seasons
Strip the soil around the house before closing, at the sellers' expense
Ask the DEC to certify the yard as safe before planting any vegetables
Test that soil first, or garden in raised beds of clean soil
blocks.x: Chlordane was applied to soil around foundations for decades until its 1988 ban, and it persists in soil for a very long time. Testing the planting area, or growing food in raised beds of clean soil away from the treated perimeter, is the practical answer. The breaks-down answer is the trap: persistence is exactly why chlordane was banned. No law requires removing the soil, and the DEC does not certify home gardens.

blocks.html: The title report lists a 150-foot-wide utility easement across the rear of the lot. The nearest transmission tower stands about 180 feet behind the house. The easement lets the utility enter, maintain its lines and clear trees, which rules out the pool Ade sketched back there. Kerry's question is different. “Is it safe for the girls?”

blocks.q: How should Jordan answer Kerry's question about the power line?
c: Reassure her that studies have proven fields from power lines harmless
Warn her that fields 180 feet from a line exceed federal limits for homes
Share what is known, suggest a gaussmeter reading, and leave the call to her
Tell her the sellers had to disclose the line as a hazard on the PCDS form
blocks.x: There is no federal exposure limit for electromagnetic fields in homes. Research has not established a health link, though the question has been studied for decades, and field strength drops quickly with distance. A consultant can measure in milligauss with a gaussmeter. Jordan shares facts and sources and lets the clients decide. The reassurance answer is the trap: overstating safety is a misrepresentation too, just in the comfortable direction.

blocks.html: An electrical consultant measured inside the house and in the yard. Readings in the bedrooms were at ordinary household background levels and rose toward the back fence. The Bellos decided they were comfortable, moved the planned swing set to the side yard, and went on to the last item on Ray's list.

The condenser's data plate reads 2004, 2.5 tons, refrigerant R-22. Ray found oily residue at the service valve, a classic sign of a refrigerant leak, and June mentioned the coil had iced up in August. An HVAC contractor Bridget recommended emailed a quote: “R-22 is illegal now. The system has to be replaced. $11,500.” People call all of these refrigerants “Freon,” a brand name. R-22 is an HCFC, a chemical cousin of the CFCs used in older equipment, and both damage the ozone layer.

blocks.q: Is the contractor's statement about R-22 accurate?
c: Yes; owning or running an R-22 system has been illegal since 2020
Partly; R-22 is no longer made or imported, but servicing is legal
No; R-22 is still produced in the US, so recharging is cheap and routine
Partly; R-22 systems have to be replaced before the house can be sold
blocks.x: Production and import of R-22 ended on January 1, 2020, but using an existing system is legal. It can be serviced with stockpiled or reclaimed R-22 by an EPA Section 608 certified technician, and the shrinking supply makes that expensive, so recharging a leaking 22-year-old system rarely makes sense. Newer refrigerants are not drop-in substitutes. The replace-before-sale answer is the trap: no rule ties R-22 to a sale. Age and the leak drive this decision.

blocks.q: If the Bellos replace the condenser, what must happen to the R-22 still in the old system?
c: A certified technician recovers it before the unit is scrapped
It can be released outdoors before the unit is hauled, since it is a gas
The homeowner drains it into a drum for the town dump
It stays in the unit, since scrap yards accept refrigerant-filled condensers
blocks.x: The Clean Air Act makes it illegal to knowingly vent ozone-depleting refrigerants. A certified technician recovers the R-22 with recovery equipment, and it can be reclaimed for servicing other systems. Scrap yards and haulers must make sure refrigerant was recovered before they take the equipment. The leave-it-in answer is the trap: it sounds practical, but the disposal chain is built to catch exactly that.

blocks.html: The Bellos treated the air conditioner as their own upgrade, not a defect to charge the sellers for: it was 22 years old, the PCDS had disclosed its age, and they wanted a heat pump eventually anyway. Jordan made sure the negotiation stayed in that lane. The final allocation looked like this.

head: Item
Cost
How it was resolved
rows: Well casing, sanitary cap, regrading, chlorination
Sellers, before closing, with two clean coliform retests
Sellers, built to the approved plan; county sign-off and warranty assignment at closing
Sellers, before closing; service agreement transferred
Buyers, as an upgrade; disclosed age, no seller credit
blocks.caption: Titicus Road: who paid for what

blocks.title: Your lane on a well-and-septic house
blocks.html: Jordan never carried a sample, diagnosed a field, or called a power line safe. Jordan pulled the health department file, read the PCDS against the lab report, kept the county law's deadlines in front of the attorneys, and put every finding in writing to the clients. Specialists did the testing, licensed professionals did the design, and Priya wrote the rider.
The closing happened on January 22. Before it, Kerry mentioned that if Ade's company sends him to Lisbon in a few years, they might rent the house out for two years rather than sell it.

blocks.q: If the Bellos lease the house, what will the county well law require of them as landlords?
c: Nothing, since the well law covers sales, and tenants test their own water
A yearly test, with results filed at the town building department
UV treatment, since leased wells need continuous disinfection
Testing, sharing results with tenants, and retesting every five years
blocks.x: The county law covers leases as well as sales. A landlord must test within 12 months after the property becomes subject to a lease, retest at least once every five years, give current tenants results within 5 days of receiving them, and give each new tenant a copy of the most recent results. The sales-only answer is the trap, since many people assume the law is a closing formality. No yearly filing or mandatory UV rule applies.

blocks.html: Jordan's file for Diane ran to two pages: the county law's test dates, the lab report and both retests, the health department's approval and sign-off, the WDI report, the consultant's EMF readings, and the Bellos' signed decisions on each. Diane read it and said, “You sold a house where the water, the sewage and the wood were all wrong, and the clients thanked you. That's the job.”

items: In Westchester, the seller must have a certified lab test a private drinking water well after the contract is signed and pay for it; agents may not collect samples, and landlords must test and share results too.
Primary contaminants such as coliform require remediation; secondary ones such as iron and low pH are the owner's choice, though acidic water attacks copper plumbing and old solder.
Effluent surfacing means a failed absorption field. A licensed engineer or architect designs the replacement from soil and percolation tests, and the county health department approves it.
GBL 777-a covers new homes from a builder. Repairs made for a resale carry only the contractor's written warranty, under a home improvement contract, if it transfers.
Active termite tubes call for treatment by DEC-certified applicators and then structural repair; chlordane persists in soil decades after its 1988 ban.
Share facts on EMF without opining on health, and know that R-22 equipment is legal to service but no longer made, with refrigerant recovered by certified technicians.

roleplays.title: Inspection Walk with Ray
roleplays.setting: An older split-level on Long Island. You represent the buyer at the home inspection.
roleplays.goal: Help Leo understand what Ray finds, steer each issue to the right professional and the right contract step, and never act as the expert yourself.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Ray, a blunt home inspector, and a nervous first-time buyer at a pre-1978 Long Island house. Ray reveals aluminum branch wiring, old 9x9 floor tiles and torn pipe wrap, a fill pipe on a gas-heated house, a musty basement, and a missing CO alarm, and says the listing agent asked him to leave the fill pipe out. The buyer asks for reassurance, repeats myths ('Long Island doesn't have radon'), asks about lead paint, and wonders whether to walk away. The learner, as buyer's agent, must not give expert opinions, must recommend the right licensed professional for each issue (electrician, asbestos sampling, tank sweep, radon test, mold assessment), state correct facts (4 pCi/L action level, friable asbestos, UST risk, pre-1978 lead disclosure with a 10-day testing opportunity), keep the report complete, and leave the decision with the buyer. Grade on accuracy, referrals, and client loyalty.
opening: A {year} split-level in {town}, Nassau County. Your buyer {client} has an accepted offer, and the inspection is today, before anyone signs a contract.
Ray Kowalski pulls up to the {year} house in {town} with a flashlight and a moisture meter. {client} is already pacing the driveway.
Inspection day in {town}. The house was built in {year}. {client} loves the kitchen and is hoping Ray finds nothing.

say: Ray says the branch wiring looks like aluminum. Is that bad? The seller's agent said the electric was 'updated.'
Ray pointed at silver wires in the panel and said 'aluminum.' Should I be worried?

moves.text: A licensed electrician should evaluate it before you sign. It can overheat at connections.
moves.fb: Right: name the known risk in general terms, send it to the licensed pro, and tie it to the timeline.

moves.text: Ray flagged it, so it's worth a specialist's look. Any fix has a cost we can factor in.
moves.fb: Correct. You don't diagnose; you route it to an electrician and keep negotiation in view.

moves.text: I'm not sure. You could ask the seller's agent what they meant by 'updated' in the listing.
moves.fb: Not harmful, but the seller's agent isn't an expert. Recommend an electrician.

moves.text: It's probably fine. Lots of houses on Long Island have it, and they're all still standing.
moves.fb: You gave an expert opinion you're not qualified to give, and aluminum branch wiring is a known fire risk.

moves.text: Aluminum is actually better than copper. It's the newer material, so 'updated' is accurate.
moves.fb: Wrong. Aluminum branch wiring from that era is a known hazard, not an upgrade.

moves.text: Not an issue. Breakers fully protect aluminum wiring, so there's no fire risk at all with it.
moves.fb: Wrong. The risk is at connections, which breakers don't prevent.

say: Ray says the 9-by-9 floor tiles and the torn pipe wrap could be asbestos. Should I peel up a tile to check?
Could those old basement tiles really be asbestos? I'll just pull one up and look.

moves.text: Please don't touch it. Disturbing it releases fibers. A qualified firm can sample it.
moves.fb: Right. Asbestos is a hazard when friable or disturbed; testing needs bulk sampling.

moves.text: Leave it alone. Asbestos is a hazard when it's friable or disturbed. Let's get a lab test.
moves.fb: Correct. You give the key fact and send it to a qualified tester.

moves.text: Probably skip it for now. We can decide later whether testing it is even worth the money.
moves.fb: Not dangerous advice, but suspect material should be tested before {client} is bound.

moves.text: Sure, pull one up. Asbestos is only dangerous if you breathe it every day for years and years.
moves.fb: Disturbing suspect material releases fibers. Never encourage a client to do it.

moves.text: No need. Asbestos was banned in 1950, so a house built in {year} can't have any of it.
moves.fb: Wrong. Asbestos products were used for decades after 1950.

moves.text: Just wrap the torn part in duct tape. That makes it safe and you won't need a test at all.
moves.fb: Taping over damaged wrap isn't proper encapsulation, and testing is still needed.

say: Ray found a pipe sticking out of the side yard, but the house is on gas. What's that about?
There's a capped pipe in the lawn. Ray called it a fill pipe. Is that a problem?

moves.text: It could mean an old buried oil tank. A tank sweep will tell us, then testing if one's found.
moves.fb: Correct. An orphan fill pipe on a gas house is the classic sign of an abandoned underground tank.
moves.react: {client} frowns. "A buried tank? Okay, sweep it."

moves.text: That's a classic sign of an abandoned oil tank. Let's order a tank sweep before you sign.
moves.fb: Right. Find it first; if it exists, test and plan closure before the buyer is bound.

moves.text: It's probably nothing, but we could ask the seller if they happen to know what it's for.
moves.fb: Asking is fine, but a tank sweep gives an answer the seller may not have.

moves.text: Probably an old sprinkler line. Lots of houses out here have them running along the side yard.
moves.fb: Guessing away a red flag. A fill pipe on a converted house usually means a tank.

moves.text: Old tanks don't matter. Once a house switches to gas, the old tank becomes the town's problem.
moves.fb: Wrong. Owners are responsible for their tanks, and leaks bring strict cleanup liability.

moves.text: It's fine. Buried tanks only leak if they're steel, and most of them were plastic back then.
moves.fb: Wrong. Older residential tanks were typically steel, which corrodes.

say: What about radon? My friend said Long Island doesn't really have it.
Do I need a radon test? Everyone says that's an upstate thing.

moves.text: Radon can show up anywhere. A test is the only way to know. EPA says fix at 4 pCi/L or above.
moves.fb: Accurate facts, no guarantee, and a clear action.

moves.text: Your friend's guess isn't a test. Radon varies house to house; EPA's action level is 4 pCi/L.
moves.fb: Correct. Regional averages don't predict one house.

moves.text: It's usually pretty low around here, I think. Testing is totally up to you, though, honestly.
moves.fb: Not false advice, but 'usually low' discourages the test that answers the question.

moves.text: Your friend's right. Radon is really an upstate problem, so you can skip the test down here.
moves.fb: Radon occurs everywhere. Telling a buyer to skip a test exposes you to liability.

moves.text: Radon only matters above 40 pCi/L. Most houses never get close, so I wouldn't worry about it.
moves.fb: Wrong number. The EPA action level is 4 pCi/L.

moves.text: If there's no smell in the basement, there's no radon. You'd definitely notice it if there was.
moves.fb: Radon is odorless. Only a test detects it.

say: The house is from {year}. Do I need to worry about lead paint?
Ray mentioned old paint layers. Is lead something I need to think about?

moves.text: It's pre-1978, so you get the lead disclosure, the EPA pamphlet, and 10 days to test.
moves.fb: Right. Federal rules require disclosure, the pamphlet, and a 10-day testing opportunity for pre-1978 housing.

moves.text: Possibly. For pre-1978 homes you get a lead disclosure, a pamphlet, and a chance to test.
moves.fb: Correct. Disclose known hazards, give the pamphlet, offer the testing opportunity.

moves.text: Maybe. Ask Ray whether he can tell just by looking at the paint in a few of the rooms.
moves.fb: Visual checks can't confirm lead. Point to the disclosure rules and a proper test.

moves.text: No. The lead paint rules only apply to homes built after 1978, so {year} is way too early.
moves.fb: Backwards. The rules cover housing built before 1978.

moves.text: Only if there are kids under six living there. Otherwise there's no lead disclosure required.
moves.fb: Wrong. The disclosure applies to pre-1978 sales regardless of who will live there.

moves.text: No, because the seller repainted. New paint over old lead makes it legally lead-free now.
moves.fb: Wrong. Lead under newer paint is still lead, and disclosure still applies.

say: This is a lot. Should I just walk away?
Honestly, should I run? Tell me what you'd do.

moves.text: That's your call. Let's get the specialist reports, then talk with your attorney about options.
moves.fb: You return the decision to the client with options and the attorney's role.

moves.text: It's your decision. Once reports are in, you can ask for repairs, a credit, or walk away.
moves.fb: Correct. Buyer agency means advice and options, not pressure.

moves.text: No way, every house has issues. Let's just push through so we don't lose this one.
moves.fb: Pressuring a client past open issues puts the deal ahead of the client.

moves.text: Don't walk. These are all minor, and I promise you none of it will cost much to fix.
moves.fb: You can't promise repair costs. That's an expert opinion you can't give.

moves.text: Walk away. Houses this old are never worth the trouble, and I wouldn't buy it myself.
moves.fb: Your personal take isn't advice. Lay out facts and options instead.

moves.text: Let's not mention any of this to your lender, or the loan could fall through on you.
moves.fb: Encouraging concealment from a lender is improper and risky for the client.

say: Jordan, the listing agent just called me asking to leave the fill pipe out of my report. Not happening, but heads up.
Funny thing: seller's agent asked me to 'go easy' on the oil pipe in the write-up.

moves.text: Keep it in. Your report goes to my buyer complete. I'll let Diane know about the call.
moves.fb: Right. The buyer is entitled to a complete report, and the broker should know of the pressure.

moves.text: Please report everything you saw. And I'll tell my broker the listing side asked that.
moves.fb: Correct. You protect your client and escalate.

moves.text: Your call, Ray. I'll stay out of whatever ends up going into your written report.
moves.fb: Staying out isn't enough; tell Ray you expect a complete report.

moves.text: Maybe just leave it as a note to me, not in the report. That keeps everyone happy here.
moves.fb: Keeping a known issue out of the buyer's report hurts your own client.
moves.react: Ray frowns. "That's not how I work."

moves.text: Sure, leave it out. I'll just tell my buyer verbally so there's no paper trail anywhere.
moves.fb: A missing written record hurts the buyer's negotiating and legal position.

moves.text: Put it in, but call it a 'possible irrigation pipe.' That's softer and still technically true.
moves.fb: Mislabeling a red flag misleads your client.

say: There's a musty smell and black spots on the basement wall. Is it toxic mold?
Those dark patches by the laundry area, is that the dangerous black mold?

moves.text: I can't diagnose it. A mold assessor can test it, and moisture is usually the root cause.
moves.fb: Right. You don't diagnose; you refer to a qualified assessor and flag moisture.

moves.text: No one can tell by looking. Let's have it assessed and find where the water's coming from.
moves.fb: Correct. Testing and finding the moisture source come first.

moves.text: Could be. A little bleach would probably take care of it, but you could test if you want.
moves.fb: Bleach on a symptom ignores the moisture source, and you're guessing.

moves.text: It's just mildew. Black spots are never actually mold, so there's no need to test it at all.
moves.fb: You're diagnosing, and wrongly.

moves.text: It's definitely toxic black mold. You should walk away from this house today, honestly.
moves.fb: You can't diagnose it, and you're pushing a decision that's the client's.

moves.text: Paint over it with mold-resistant paint and it's gone for good. Sellers do it all the time.
moves.fb: Covering mold without fixing moisture hides the problem.

say: Ray says there's no carbon monoxide alarm anywhere. Is that required?
No CO detector in the whole house, Ray says. Does that matter for a sale?

moves.text: Yes. New York requires CO alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances. Easy to fix.
moves.fb: Right. Amanda's Law requires CO alarms in one- and two-family homes with fuel-burning appliances.

moves.text: It is, under Amanda's Law, for homes with gas appliances. Let's note it for the seller.
moves.fb: Correct. A gas-heated home needs CO alarms.

moves.text: I think so, but I'm not totally sure. Let's ask Ray what the rule is when he's done.
moves.fb: Asking is fine, but this is a basic NY safety rule.

moves.text: Only new construction needs them. Older homes are grandfathered out of the CO alarm rule.
moves.fb: Wrong. The rule applies to existing homes with fuel-burning appliances.

moves.text: No. Smoke detectors cover carbon monoxide too, so one device is plenty for the whole house.
moves.fb: Wrong. Standard smoke alarms don't detect CO.

moves.text: Only rentals need them. Owner-occupied homes in New York are exempt from the CO rule.
moves.fb: Wrong. Owner-occupied one- and two-family homes are covered.

roleplays.debrief: A buyer's agent names the red flag, never the diagnosis, and routes each issue to the right licensed specialist before the buyer is bound: an electrician for aluminum branch wiring, sampling for suspect asbestos (a hazard when friable or disturbed), a tank sweep for an orphan fill pipe, a radon test (EPA action level 4 pCi/L), a mold assessment, and the lead disclosure with a 10-day testing opportunity for pre-1978 homes. Reports stay complete, CO alarms are required (Amanda's Law), and the decision stays with the client.

roleplays.title: The Tank Nobody Mentions
roleplays.setting: Sal Russo's two-family in Astoria. You are taking the listing. Sal converted to gas years ago.
roleplays.goal: Keep the listing without concealing a known underground oil tank, and get Sal on a path to disclose and resolve it.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Sal Russo, an old-school Astoria landlord selling his two-family, who has a capped underground oil tank and wants the agent to keep quiet. Push with 'buyers get scared,' 'I'm not digging up my yard,' 'I'll check no on the form or give them the $500 credit,' and 'do I really have to call the state?' Later ask whether lead paint rules apply to your 1931 house, tell the agent to keep the buyer's inspector out of the yard, and briefly play a buyer asking directly about oil tanks. The learner, as listing agent, must refuse concealment, explain that the PCDS must be answered truthfully and the $500 credit option is gone, recommend testing and proper closure with documentation, state that petroleum spills must be reported to DEC within 2 hours and that the Navigation Law imposes strict liability, apply the pre-1978 lead rules, and refer to an attorney. Grade on honesty, accuracy, and how well they keep the client.
opening: Sal Russo's two-family in Astoria, listing at {price}. Sal switched to gas in {year}. Over coffee, he mentions the old oil tank under the {spot}.
Listing appointment at Sal's Astoria two-family, about {price}. The boiler is gas, but there's a capped pipe by the {spot}.
Sal wants {price} for his Astoria two-family and a quick sale. Then he lowers his voice about the {spot}.

say: One thing. There's an old oil tank under the {spot}. When we went to gas in {year}, the plumber just capped the pipe. Don't mention it. Buyers get scared.
Between us: old oil tank under the {spot}, capped in {year}. Leave it out of the listing, okay?

moves.text: Sal, I can't hide a known material fact. If buyers find it, that's on both of us.
moves.fb: Correct. An agent may not conceal a known material defect, whatever the seller instructs.

moves.text: Let's handle it up front instead. A buried tank is material, and buyers find the pipe.
moves.fb: Right. Obedience never extends to unlawful acts like concealment.

moves.text: Let me think about how to handle it, and I'll call you back after I talk with Diane.
moves.fb: Escalating is fine, but say clearly now that you can't conceal it.

moves.text: Okay, I won't raise it unless someone asks. What they don't ask about isn't on us.
moves.fb: Agreeing to conceal a known hazard makes you part of the misrepresentation.

moves.text: Sure. Capped tanks aren't material anymore, so there's really nothing we need to disclose.
moves.fb: Wrong. An abandoned buried tank is a material fact, capped or not.

moves.text: Fine. Your instructions come first, since that's the duty of obedience I owe you as agent.
moves.fb: Obedience covers lawful instructions only.

say: Fine, then what? I'm not digging up my {spot} for some buyer.
So what do you want me to do, tear up the {spot}?

moves.text: Test first. If it's clean, close it properly with paperwork. If it leaked, report and fix.
moves.fb: That's the practical path: test, close with documentation, and report any discharge to DEC.

moves.text: A licensed contractor can test it and close it in place or remove it. Then you'll have a report.
moves.fb: Correct. A closure report replaces a question mark for buyers and lenders.
moves.react: "In place? I keep my {spot}?" Sal asks.

moves.text: Just disclose it and sell it as is. Let the buyer's side worry about what's down there.
moves.fb: Disclosure is required and as-is is legal, but an undocumented tank scares lenders.

moves.text: Don't bother testing. If you never test, you can honestly say you don't know of any leak.
moves.fb: Avoiding knowledge to dodge disclosure is bad faith, and the tank itself is known.

moves.text: Just pump it out yourself and fill it with sand. That counts as a closure in New York.
moves.fb: Closure should be done properly with the required permits and documentation.

moves.text: Leave it. Old tanks only matter if they're above ground, so a buried one is no problem.
moves.fb: Backwards. Buried tanks are the bigger concern because leaks go unseen.

say: And on that disclosure form, I'll just check 'no' on fuel tanks. Or I give them the $500 credit and skip the form.
The PCDS thing. I'll check 'no' for tanks, or do the $500 credit like last time I sold.

moves.text: You have to answer the PCDS truthfully. And the $500 credit option ended in 2024.
moves.fb: Right. Since March 20, 2024, sellers must deliver the PCDS; there's no $500 opt-out.

moves.text: No opt-out anymore; the form is required. And the tank question gets an honest answer.
moves.fb: Correct. A false PCDS answer creates liability for Sal and for you if you let it happen.

moves.text: That's between you and your attorney. I'd rather not look at the form at all.
moves.fb: The seller completes it, but knowingly ignoring a false answer exposes you too.

moves.text: Your form, your call. Sellers fill it out, so whatever you check isn't my responsibility.
moves.fb: Knowingly allowing a false answer about a material fact is misrepresentation by the agent.

moves.text: Just give them the $500 credit. That way you skip the form and the tank question entirely.
moves.fb: The $500 credit option was eliminated as of March 20, 2024.

moves.text: Check 'unknown.' Since you never tested it, 'unknown' is technically a truthful answer.
moves.fb: Sal knows the tank exists. 'Unknown' would be false.

say: And if the test shows it leaked a little? Do I really have to call the state?
Say it leaked. Who has to know? It's my property.

moves.text: Yes. Report spills to DEC's hotline within 2 hours, and you're liable for cleanup.
moves.fb: Accurate. New York's spill reporting rule and Navigation Law strict liability apply.

moves.text: You do. The Navigation Law makes the discharger strictly liable, and DEC needs a fast call.
moves.fb: Correct, and the attorney can guide the rest.
moves.react: "Better to control it, I guess," Sal says.

moves.text: Check with your attorney. I'm honestly not sure exactly what the reporting rule is here.
moves.fb: Referral is right, but you should know and state the 2-hour rule.

moves.text: Only if it's a big spill. A little seepage under a {spot} doesn't ever need to be reported.
moves.fb: Wrong. Petroleum spills must be reported within 2 hours, with narrow exceptions.

moves.text: Ask your attorney, but most people never report it, and honestly nothing ever happens.
moves.fb: Suggesting people ignore spill reporting is bad advice.

moves.text: No. Once you sell, the buyer takes over the cleanup duty, so the state goes after them.
moves.fb: Wrong. Liability for a discharge doesn't transfer away with the deed.

say: So what do I actually tell buyers, then?
Okay, smart guy. What goes in the listing about the tank?

moves.text: The truth: there's a tank, here's the test, here's the closure paperwork. Paper sells.
moves.fb: Right. Disclosure with documentation protects Sal and makes the house easier to sell.
moves.react: Sal nods slowly. "Paper sells. I like that."

moves.text: Disclose it and show the documents. A tank with a closure report is an easier sale.
moves.fb: Correct. Honest disclosure plus proof beats a surprise at the buyer's tank sweep.
moves.react: "Okay. Let's get the report," Sal says.

moves.text: Just tell them it's there and let their inspector figure out the rest of it on their own.
moves.fb: Disclosure is right, but without testing and paperwork the sale gets harder.

moves.text: Say the tank was 'removed' even if it was closed in place. Buyers don't know the difference.
moves.fb: Misstating how a tank was closed is misrepresentation.

moves.text: Say it's capped, so under New York law it's no longer legally considered a tank.
moves.fb: Capping a fill pipe doesn't close a tank.

moves.text: Say nothing until the contract. Disclosing it before an offer only lowers your sale price.
moves.fb: Withholding a known material fact to protect price is concealment.

say: At the open house: Any oil tanks on the property? My lender's going to ask.
Quick one: is there a buried oil tank? My cousin's house had one and it was a nightmare.

moves.text: Yes, there's one under the {spot}. I'll send what we have on testing and closure.
moves.fb: Right. You answer truthfully and offer the documentation.

moves.text: There is one. Here's what the seller has on it, and your inspector can check it too.
moves.fb: Correct. Honest answer plus a path to verify.

moves.text: I'd ask the seller's attorney about that. I'd rather not get into the details.
moves.fb: Not a lie, but you know the answer and should give it.

moves.text: Not that I know of. The house has been on gas for years, so there's nothing to worry about.
moves.fb: A false answer to a direct question is misrepresentation.

moves.text: I'm not allowed to discuss that with buyers. You'll have to ask the seller directly about it.
moves.fb: No rule bars you from answering truthfully. Dodging misleads.

moves.text: There was one, but it's capped, so legally it doesn't count as a tank on the property now.
moves.fb: Capping the pipe doesn't remove or close the tank.

say: The house is from 1931. Do I have to do the lead paint thing too?
My lawyer mentioned lead paint papers. That's for new houses, right?

moves.text: Yes. Pre-1978 homes need known-lead disclosure, the EPA pamphlet, a chance to test.
moves.fb: Right. Pre-1978 housing needs disclosure, the pamphlet, and a 10-day testing opportunity.

moves.text: It applies here. Built before 1978 means a lead disclosure and the pamphlet for every buyer.
moves.fb: Correct. The federal rule covers pre-1978 residential sales.

moves.text: Probably, but I'm not sure. Your attorney should know whether it applies to a two-family.
moves.fb: Referral is fine, but this is a basic rule you should know.

moves.text: No, only homes built after 1978 need lead disclosure. A 1931 house is way too old for it.
moves.fb: Backwards. The rule covers homes built before 1978.

moves.text: Only if you know about lead. If you don't know of any, you don't need any forms at all.
moves.fb: The pamphlet and warning statement are required even with no known lead.

moves.text: No, because it's a two-family. Lead rules only apply to single-family homes being sold.
moves.fb: Wrong. The rule covers residential housing, including two-families.

say: Tell the buyer's inspector not to bother with the yard. Just walk him through the house.
When their inspector comes, keep him inside. The yard's off-limits.

moves.text: I can't steer the inspector off. He looks wherever the buyer hired him to look.
moves.fb: Right. Blocking inspection of a known problem area is concealment.

moves.text: The buyer's inspector gets full access. Steering him away would hide what we know.
moves.fb: Correct. Access is part of honest dealing.

moves.text: I'll stay out of it. What happens between you and the inspector is up to you.
moves.fb: Staying out lets the seller block access. Say it isn't okay.

moves.text: Sure. I'll keep him busy in the basement until he runs out of time for the yard area.
moves.fb: Deliberately steering an inspector away from a known defect is concealment.

moves.text: Fine. Inspectors only check inside the house anyway, so the yard was never part of it.
moves.fb: Inspectors can check the property, and a tank sweep covers the yard.

moves.text: Okay, I'll tell him the yard is a neighbor's easement, so he isn't allowed to inspect it.
moves.fb: Lying about the property to an inspector is misrepresentation.

roleplays.debrief: A listing agent can't conceal a known material fact, whatever the seller wants: obedience never covers illegal instructions. The PCDS must be answered truthfully, with no $500 credit opt-out since March 20, 2024; petroleum spills must be reported to DEC within 2 hours; and the Navigation Law makes the discharger strictly liable. Test, close with documentation, disclose with paper in hand, give full inspection access, and give lead disclosures for pre-1978 homes.

questions.q: Minimum insulation and window efficiency for new construction in New York are set by the:
c: State Energy Conservation Construction Code
Multiple Dwelling Law
Property Condition Disclosure Act
Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act
questions.x: The Energy Code sets efficiency minimums. Multiple Dwelling Law is the trap: it governs larger residential buildings' safety and occupancy.

questions.q: A renovation must meet New York's Energy Code standards for:
c: Paint color and finishes
Property tax assessment
Insulation, air sealing and equipment efficiency
Lot size and setbacks
questions.x: The Energy Code covers efficiency. Setbacks are the trap: those are zoning rules.

questions.q: Walls of poured concrete or block, resting on footings and enclosing a basement, are:
c: Bearing partitions
Foundation walls
Curtain walls
Fire walls
questions.x: Foundation walls sit on footings and support the house. Curtain walls are the trap: they hang on a structural frame.

questions.q: Foundation walls rest directly on the:
c: Joists
Sill plate
Rafters
Footings
questions.x: Footings spread the load into the ground under the foundation walls. Sill plate is the trap: it sits on top of the foundation wall.

questions.q: A wall that supports the weight of floors or the roof above is a:
c: Partition wall
Curtain wall
Bearing wall
Knee wall only
questions.x: Bearing walls carry loads from above. Partition wall is the trap: it only divides space.

questions.q: Before removing a wall to open up a kitchen, an owner should confirm it is not a:
c: Bearing wall
Partition wall
Plasterboard wall
Painted wall
questions.x: Taking out a load-bearing wall without support can cause structural failure. Partition is the trap: those can usually come out safely.

questions.q: Vinyl, wood clapboard and fiber cement are all types of:
c: Sheathing
Flashing
Roofing
Siding
questions.x: These are exterior wall finishes. Sheathing is the trap: it is the structural layer under the siding.

questions.q: The exterior finish material on a house's walls is called:
c: Drywall
Siding
Footing
Fascia only
questions.x: Siding is the outer wall finish. Drywall is the trap: it is an interior finish.

questions.q: Gypsum panels with paper facings used for interior walls are called:
c: Plasterboard (drywall)
Sheathing
Lath and plaster
Wainscoting
questions.x: Drywall is gypsum board. Lath and plaster is the trap: that is the older wet-plaster method.

questions.q: Sheetrock is a brand name for:
c: Roof shingles
Concrete block
Gypsum wallboard
Vinyl siding
questions.x: Sheetrock is gypsum wallboard, used inside. Vinyl siding is the trap: it is an exterior finish.

questions.q: A roof rises 6 inches for every 12 inches of horizontal run. Its pitch is expressed as:
c: 12 in 6
6 in 12
50 degrees
2 to 1
questions.x: Pitch is rise per 12 inches of run, so 6 in 12. '12 in 6' is the trap: it reverses rise and run.

questions.q: Which roof is steeper?
c: 4 in 12
6 in 12
8 in 12
questions.x: More rise per 12 inches of run means a steeper roof. 8 in 12 is the trap: it is steep, but 10 in 12 is steeper.

questions.q: Framing with heavy posts and beams spaced far apart, allowing open interiors, is:
c: Platform framing
Balloon framing
Post-and-beam construction
Masonry bearing wall
questions.x: Post-and-beam carries loads on a few large members. Platform framing is the trap: it uses many closely spaced studs.

questions.q: A barn conversion with a wide open interior and exposed heavy timbers likely uses:
c: Post-and-beam framing
Platform framing
Steel curtain walls
Balloon framing
questions.x: Widely spaced heavy timbers are post-and-beam. Balloon framing is the trap: it uses long studs running two stories.

questions.q: The foundation, walls, roof, windows and doors that separate inside from outside form the:
c: Mechanical system
Superstructure only
Footprint
Building envelope
questions.x: The envelope is the barrier between interior and outdoors. Footprint is the trap: it is the area the building covers.

questions.q: Air sealing and better insulation improve a home's energy use by tightening its:
c: Electrical service
Building envelope
Plumbing stack
Zoning envelope
questions.x: Sealing and insulating improve the envelope. Zoning envelope is the trap: that is the maximum allowed building shape.

questions.q: A heating oil tank sitting in a basement is a(n):
c: Aboveground storage tank
Underground storage tank
Septic tank
Dry well
questions.x: A tank not buried is an AST, even indoors. Underground tank is the trap: USTs are buried.

questions.q: Compared with a buried tank, an aboveground oil tank's main advantage is that:
c: It never needs inspection
It holds no oil
Leaks are easier to see
It is always outdoors
questions.x: An AST can be visually checked for leaks. 'Never needs inspection' is the trap: it should still be inspected.

questions.q: A home's electrical service capacity is measured in:
c: Volts only
Amps
BTUs
Watts per square foot
questions.x: Service capacity is stated in amps, typically 100 to 200 for a modern home. BTUs are the trap: they measure heat.

questions.q: A modern single-family home typically has electrical service of:
c: 15 to 20 amps
1,000 amps
60 volts
100 to 200 amps
questions.x: 100 to 200 amps is typical. 15 to 20 amps is the trap: that is a single branch circuit.

questions.q: Branch circuit wiring in some homes built from the mid-1960s to mid-1970s that is linked to overheating at connections is:
c: Knob and tube wiring
Copper wiring
Aluminum wiring
Greenfield conduit
questions.x: Aluminum branch wiring of that era can overheat at connections. Knob and tube is the trap: it is much older, pre-1940s.

questions.q: The main concern with aluminum branch wiring is:
c: Fire risk at connections
Lead contamination
Radon buildup
Low water pressure
questions.x: Aluminum connections can loosen and overheat. Lead is the trap: that is a paint and pipe issue.

questions.q: Flexible spiral metal conduit installed empty, with wires pulled through later, is called:
c: BX cable
Romex
Knob and tube
Greenfield
questions.x: Greenfield is empty flexible conduit. BX is the trap: armored cable comes with the wires already inside.

questions.q: What distinguishes Greenfield from armored (BX) cable?
c: Greenfield is plastic
Greenfield is installed empty
Greenfield is used only outdoors
Greenfield carries gas
questions.x: Wires are pulled through Greenfield after it is installed; BX has them factory-installed. 'Plastic' is the trap: Greenfield is metal.

questions.q: Occupants of an office building report headaches that ease when they leave. This is commonly called:
c: Sick building syndrome
Radon poisoning
Lead poisoning
Legionnaires' disease
questions.x: Illness tied to time spent in a building points to sick building syndrome, often from poor ventilation. Radon is the trap: it causes no immediate symptoms.

questions.q: Which most improves indoor air quality in a tightly sealed building?
c: More carpeting
Closing all vents
Adequate ventilation
Adding gas appliances
questions.x: Ventilation dilutes pollutants. Gas appliances are the trap: combustion adds pollutants.

questions.q: Chemicals once used in electrical transformers and fluorescent light ballasts, banned in 1979, are:
c: CFCs
PCBs
VOCs
Radon
questions.x: PCBs were used in electrical equipment and banned in 1979. CFCs are the trap: they were refrigerants and propellants.

questions.q: In an older commercial building, PCBs are most likely found in:
c: Drinking water pipes
Basement soil gas
Roof shingles
Old fluorescent light ballasts
questions.x: Old ballasts and transformers are common PCB sources. Soil gas is the trap: that suggests radon.

questions.q: A pesticide once applied in soil around foundations to kill termites, banned in 1988, is:
c: Asbestos
Urea formaldehyde
Chlordane
Lead
questions.x: Chlordane was the termite treatment banned in 1988. Urea formaldehyde is the trap: it was a foam insulation.

questions.q: A buyer of a 1970s house worries about old termite treatments in the soil. The chemical of concern is:
c: Chlordane
Radon
PCBs
Methane
questions.x: Chlordane was widely used against termites until its 1988 ban. Radon is the trap: it is natural, not a pesticide.

questions.q: Before buying a house served by a private well, buyers and lenders typically require:
c: A radon-in-air test only
An asbestos survey
A Phase II site assessment
A lab test of the well water
questions.x: Private wells need lab testing for bacteria and contaminants. Asbestos is the trap: it is a building-material issue.

questions.q: A typical private well test checks for:
c: Roof condition
Bacteria, minerals, pH and contaminants
Boundary encroachments
Lead in paint
questions.x: Water tests cover bacteria, hardness, pH and contaminants. Lead in paint is the trap: that is a paint inspection.

questions.q: A buried heating oil tank is a concern for buyers mainly because:
c: Leaks can contaminate soil and groundwater
It raises property taxes
It violates zoning
It blocks the driveway
questions.x: Leaking USTs can cause costly environmental cleanup. Taxes are the trap: a tank does not change the tax bill.

questions.q: A tank storing gasoline beneath a former service station is a(n):
c: Aboveground storage tank
Septic system
Underground storage tank
Cistern
questions.x: Buried fuel tanks are USTs. Cistern is the trap: it stores water.

questions.q: Which federal agency runs FHA, enforces fair housing law and co-enforces the lead paint disclosure rule with EPA?
c: DOS
HUD
FDIC
IRS
questions.x: HUD handles FHA, fair housing enforcement and, with EPA, lead disclosure. DOS is the trap: it is the state licensing agency.

questions.q: Lead-based paint disclosure rules for pre-1978 housing are enforced by:
c: DOS and the IRS
FHA alone
The local assessor
HUD and EPA
questions.x: The rule is jointly enforced by HUD and EPA. FHA alone is the trap: FHA is part of HUD and does not enforce it alone.

questions.q: The concrete base, wider than the wall it supports, that spreads a building's weight into the soil is the:
c: Footing
Sill plate
Girder
Floor slab
questions.x: The footing sits below the foundation wall and below the frost line, spreading the load. The sill plate is the trap: it is the first wood member on top of the foundation wall, not the base beneath it.

questions.q: A steel post, often filled with concrete, that supports a girder in a basement is a:
c: Wall stud
Lally column
Steel girder beam
Header
questions.x: Lally columns hold up girders in basements. Studs are also vertical members, but they frame walls and are usually wood, not concrete-filled steel.

questions.q: The lowest wood framing member of a house, bolted to the top of the foundation wall, is the:
c: Floor joist
Ridge beam
Sill plate
Footing
questions.x: The sill plate connects the wood frame to the masonry foundation with anchor bolts. Floor joists rest on top of it, and the footing is concrete below the wall, not wood.

questions.q: A beam that carries the load over a window or door opening in a wood-framed wall is a:
c: Girder
Sill plate
Lintel
Header
questions.x: In wood framing it is a header. A lintel does the same job over openings in masonry walls, which makes it the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: A steel plate bolted between two wood boards to create a stronger beam is a:
c: Flitch plate
Sill plate
Lally plate
Laminated beam
questions.x: A flitch (syllabus: fitch) plate beam sandwiches steel between wood to add strength without adding depth. A sill plate also bears the word 'plate,' but it is the wood member on the foundation.

questions.q: Which insulation has the greatest resistance to heat flow?
questions.x: Higher R-value means more resistance to heat flow, so R-38 wins. Candidates who confuse R-value with U-value (heat transmission) pick the lowest number.

questions.q: The underside of a roof overhang, often vented to bring air into the attic, is the:
c: Fascia
Soffit
Flashing
Sheathing
questions.x: The soffit is the underside of the eave. The fascia is the vertical board across the rafter ends where gutters attach, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: Sheet metal installed where a chimney meets the roof to prevent water from entering is called:
c: Sheathing
Drip edge
Fascia
Flashing
questions.x: Flashing seals joints at chimneys, valleys, skylights and walls. Drip edge is also metal on a roof, but it runs along the eaves and rakes to shed water off the edge.

questions.q: The most common framing method in houses built today, in which each floor serves as the base for the walls of the next story, is:
c: Balloon framing
Post-and-beam framing
Platform framing
Slab-on-grade framing
questions.x: Platform framing builds each floor as a platform for the next. Balloon framing ran studs continuously through two stories and is found in older houses.

questions.q: Under New York's Housing Merchant Implied Warranty, material defects in the load-bearing structure of a new home are covered for:
c: 1 year
2 years
6 years
10 years
questions.x: GBL 777-a: 1 year workmanship and materials, 2 years plumbing, electrical, heating, cooling and ventilation, 6 years load-bearing structure. Ten years is a common national builder-warranty figure, not New York's statute.

questions.q: Fourteen months after buying a newly built home from a builder, the owner discovers the central air system was improperly installed. Under GBL 777-a the owner:
c: Has no claim, since the 1-year warranty has run
Is covered, since cooling carries 2 years
Is covered if the defect harms the structure
Has to sue under the home improvement law
questions.x: Mechanical systems, including cooling, are warranted for 2 years. The 1-year period that tempts here applies to general workmanship and materials.

questions.q: In New York, a residential septic system must be designed by:
c: A licensed home improvement contractor
The local building inspector
The homeowner, under a permit
A licensed engineer or architect
questions.x: Septic designs require a NY licensed professional engineer or registered architect, with health department approval. Contractors install systems; they do not certify the design.

questions.q: A test that measures how quickly water is absorbed into the soil, used to design a septic absorption field, determines the:
c: Percolation rate
Soil bearing capacity
Water table depth
Flow rate in gallons
questions.x: The perc test shows whether soil can absorb wastewater and how large the field must be. Water table depth also matters for septic siting, but it is measured with a deep test pit, not a perc test.

questions.q: A New York home improvement contract over $500 must include each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Notice of the 3-business-day right to cancel
A description of the work and materials
Approximate start and completion dates
A promise to finish the work in 30 days
questions.x: GBL Article 36-A requires a written contract with dates, a description of work and materials, cancellation notice, and deposit protections. It sets no fixed 30-day completion rule; the 3-day cancellation right is real.

questions.q: A house built on a concrete slab poured directly on prepared ground, with no basement or crawl space, uses:
c: Post-and-beam frame construction
Slab-on-grade construction
Platform construction
Pier-and-beam foundation
questions.x: Slab-on-grade uses the slab as the floor. A pier-and-beam foundation raises the house on piers, which leaves a crawl space beneath it.

questions.q: Detailed written instructions for a building, listing materials, quality standards and construction methods, are the:
c: Specifications
Blueprints
Site plan
Building permit
questions.x: Specifications are the written details that accompany the plans. Blueprints are the drawings, which is why they tempt; they show the design rather than describe materials in writing.

questions.q: Each of the following is part of a house's structural load path from roof to ground EXCEPT:
c: Rafters
Girder
Soffit
Footing
questions.x: The soffit is a finish surface under the eave and carries no structural load. Rafters, girders and footings each carry loads down to the soil.

questions.q: A builder finishes a new house and the final inspection passes. What must issue before the buyer can legally move in?
c: A certificate of occupancy
A housing merchant warranty
A final survey of the lot lines
A new building permit
questions.x: The building department issues the certificate of occupancy after the final inspection; without it there is no legal move-in and usually no lender closing. The warranty is tempting, but it arises automatically and has nothing to do with legal occupancy.

questions.q: A builder tells a buyer, "The CO is coming next week, but we can close today." The buyer's lender will most likely:
c: Close if the builder signs a warranty
Refuse to close until the CO issues
Close once the permit is posted on site
Close if the buyer waives inspections
questions.x: No CO, no legal move-in, and usually no closing with a lender. A posted building permit only shows the work was allowed to start, which is the trap.

questions.q: Under typical NY health standards, a private well should be at least how far from a septic absorption field?
c: 50 feet
25 feet
100 feet
200 feet
questions.x: Wells are typically set at least 100 feet from a septic absorption field and 50 feet from a septic tank. Fifty feet is the tank figure, the most common mix-up.

questions.q: A new house will have a private well and a septic tank. The typical minimum distance between the well and the septic tank is:
c: 100 feet
10 feet
150 feet
50 feet
questions.x: The tank setback is typically 50 feet; the absorption field setback is 100 feet. Picking 100 feet applies the field rule to the tank.

questions.q: Which site feature helps protect a house's foundation from water?
c: Grade that slopes away from the house
Gutters that empty beside the footing
Trees planted on top of the septic field
A driveway that slopes toward the garage
questions.x: Grade should slope away and gutters should discharge away from the house. Gutters emptying at the footing put water exactly where it causes damage.

questions.q: Good site planning for a house with a septic system includes each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Sloping the grade away from the house
Planting trees over the absorption field
Running gutter downspouts away from walls
Respecting zoning setbacks and lot coverage
questions.x: Roots damage septic fields, so trees do not go on top of them. The other choices are all part of sound site use.

questions.q: In a New York house, the vapor retarder in an insulated wall belongs on the:
c: Cold (exterior) side of the wall
Middle of the insulation layer
Warm-in-winter (interior) side
Side facing the attic vents
questions.x: The vapor retarder goes on the warm-in-winter side so indoor moisture does not condense inside the wall. The exterior side is the trap: it traps moisture in the cavity.

questions.q: A remodeler tightens a house's envelope with new insulation and air sealing. What does the house now need more of?
c: Higher-amp electrical service
A larger septic tank
Lower R-value windows
Planned ventilation
questions.x: A tighter envelope saves energy but must be paired with planned ventilation to remove moisture and stale air. Lower R-value windows would simply lose more heat.

questions.q: Which sale is covered by New York's Housing Merchant Implied Warranty (GBL 777-a)?
c: A builder's sale of a newly built home
An owner's resale of a five-year-old home
A landlord's lease of a new apartment
An investor's sale of a renovated condo
questions.x: The warranty attaches automatically when a builder sells a new home. It does not cover resales by ordinary owners, which is why the five-year-old resale is wrong.

questions.q: A builder wants to avoid the full housing merchant implied warranty. The builder may do so only by:
c: Stating orally at the closing table that the house is sold as is, with no warranty
Giving a written limited warranty meeting the statute's minimums
Having the buyer initial a waiver on the deed
