questions.x: In NYC, a certified asbestos investigator assesses the work area and files with the Department of Environmental Protection, or the owner certifies an exemption, before DOB issues the permit. A home inspector's letter is the tempting answer, but home inspectors are not certified asbestos investigators.

questions.q: Under New York's mold law, remediation of 25 square feet of mold in a home must be done:
c: By any contractor using bleach and a respirator
By one licensed firm doing both the plan and the work
By the local health department
By a licensed remediator and separate assessor
questions.x: Projects over 10 square feet require a licensed assessor to write the plan and a licensed remediator to do the work, and they cannot be the same company on the project. The single-firm answer is the trap: it is efficient, and it is exactly what the independence rule forbids.

questions.q: A homeowner finds 6 square feet of mold on a bathroom ceiling. Under New York's mold program, the owner:
c: Falls below the licensing threshold
Needs a licensed assessor and remediator
Has to report it to the Department of Labor
Has to have DEC inspect the bathroom first
questions.x: New York's licensing rule applies to projects over 10 square feet, so a 6 square foot job falls below it; the owner should still fix the moisture source. The tempting answer applies the licensing rule regardless of size.

questions.q: A paid contractor will remove a plaster wall in a 1950 house. Under the EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, the contractor must:
c: Be EPA certified and use lead-safe practices
Do nothing special in an owner-occupied home
Follow the rule if the job costs over $10,000
Get the buyer's written lead waiver first
questions.x: In pre-1978 homes, paid work disturbing more than 6 square feet of interior paint per room (20 exterior) or replacing windows requires an EPA-certified firm using lead-safe practices. There is no dollar threshold, which is the tempting distractor.

questions.q: In a 1965 house, the EPA renovation rule generally applies to each of the following paid jobs EXCEPT:
c: Replacing six windows
Patching a 2 sq ft hole in a bedroom wall
Scraping 40 sq ft of exterior siding
Removing a painted kitchen wall to open the room
questions.x: Minor repair disturbing 6 square feet or less of interior painted surface per room falls below the threshold. Window replacement is covered regardless of size, which makes it the tempting wrong pick, and 40 square feet of exterior exceeds the 20 square foot exterior trigger.

questions.q: A buyer closes on a commercial site in June 2026 relying on a Phase I dated September 2024. For CERCLA defenses, the report is:
c: Fine, since Phase I reports are good for five years
Fine, if the seller certifies nothing has changed
Too old for the one-year inquiry window
Too old; it has to be dated within 30 days of closing
questions.x: All appropriate inquiries must be conducted within one year before acquisition, with interviews, lien and records searches, the site visit and the declaration done or updated within 180 days. A 21-month-old report fails. The 30-day answer is too strict and the five-year answer too loose; neither is the rule.

questions.q: Under the all appropriate inquiries rule, each of the following must be done or updated within 180 days before acquisition EXCEPT:
c: The visual inspection of the site
Interviews with owners and occupants
Searches for environmental cleanup liens
Soil and groundwater sampling
questions.x: Sampling is Phase II work and is not a required part of all appropriate inquiries. The site visit, interviews, lien searches, records review and the professional's declaration are the 180-day components. Lien searches are the tempting pick, since they sound like title work, but they are on the list.

questions.q: Soil borings and groundwater samples taken to confirm contamination flagged in an earlier records review are part of a:
c: Phase II
Phase I
Phase III
Phase IV
questions.x: Phase II is the testing phase that confirms and measures contamination. Phase I is the tempting answer because it identified the concern, but Phase I takes no samples. Phase III is remediation and Phase IV is long-term monitoring and management.

questions.q: After a cleanup, an owner must run a vapor mitigation system, test it yearly and report to the state. This ongoing stage is best described as:
c: Phase I, investigation
Phase IV, management
Phase II, testing
Phase III, remediation
questions.x: Phase IV covers ongoing operation, maintenance and monitoring after cleanup. Phase III is the tempting answer because the system was installed as part of the remedy, but the continuing duty to run and test it is management.

questions.q: A buyer finds heating oil contamination from an old leaking tank. Which statement is most accurate?
c: CERCLA applies, with strict, joint and several liability
No law applies, because the tank no longer exists
The federal Clean Water Act alone applies to oil on land
The Navigation Law applies; CERCLA excludes petroleum
questions.x: CERCLA's definition of hazardous substances excludes petroleum, which is the trap in the first choice. New York's Navigation Law makes those responsible for petroleum discharges strictly liable for cleanup, and spills must be reported to DEC within 2 hours.

questions.q: Groundwater under a former dry cleaner contains a chlorinated solvent, and soil under the old boiler room contains fuel oil. Which pairing is correct?
c: Solvent: Navigation Law; oil: CERCLA
Solvent: CERCLA; oil: Navigation Law
Both: CERCLA, as hazardous substances
Both: Navigation Law, as spills
questions.x: Chlorinated solvents are CERCLA hazardous substances. Fuel oil is petroleum, excluded from CERCLA and reached in New York by the Navigation Law's strict liability. Treating both as CERCLA is the tempting answer because both are pollutants, but the petroleum exclusion splits them.

questions.q: A buyer learns before closing that a site is contaminated, buys anyway, and wants protection from CERCLA cleanup liability. The protection most likely available is the:
c: Innocent landowner defense under SARA
Secured lender liability exemption
Bona fide prospective purchaser
Act of God or act of war defense
questions.x: The 2002 Brownfields amendments created bona fide prospective purchaser protection for buyers who may know of contamination, if they conducted all appropriate inquiries and meet continuing obligations. The innocent landowner defense is the tempting answer, but it requires that the buyer did not know and had no reason to know of contamination.

questions.q: To keep bona fide prospective purchaser protection, a buyer of a contaminated site must generally do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Take reasonable steps to stop ongoing releases
Pay for the full cleanup within one year
Cooperate with regulators' cleanup access
Comply with recorded land use restrictions
questions.x: The protection depends on pre-purchase inquiry and continuing obligations such as reasonable steps, cooperation and compliance with land use restrictions. It does not require the buyer to pay for the whole cleanup; that is what the protection shields against. Reasonable steps is the tempting pick because it sounds like cleanup, but it is a real condition.

questions.q: In a 1960s commercial building, PCBs are most likely to be found in:
c: Fluorescent light ballasts
Vinyl floor tiles
Copper water supply lines
Fiberglass batt wall insulation
questions.x: PCBs were used in electrical equipment such as transformers, capacitors and fluorescent light ballasts made before 1979. Vinyl floor tiles are the tempting answer because they are a classic asbestos source, a different hazard.

questions.q: A Phase I notes a pad-mounted transformer from 1972 at a building being purchased. The first question for the buyer's team is:
c: Whether it emits EMFs above federal limits
Whether it contains asbestos insulation
Whether it needs a DEC tank registration
Who owns it, the utility or the owner
questions.x: Pre-1979 transformers may contain PCBs, and ownership decides who is responsible for testing, leaks and disposal; many pad-mounted units belong to the utility. EMFs are the tempting answer because transformers produce them, but the liability question is PCBs and who owns the equipment.

questions.q: Under New York's Brownfield Cleanup Program, a certificate of completion issued by DEC generally provides:
c: A state liability limit and tax credit eligibility
A federal CERCLA release for every past owner
Automatic removal of every use restriction
A grant covering the volunteer's cleanup costs
questions.x: The certificate of completion brings a limitation on state liability that can pass to later owners and eligibility for state brownfield tax credits. Removal of use restrictions is the tempting answer, but where contamination remains, restrictions and an environmental easement stay on title.

questions.q: An owner wants to build a garage 75 feet from a DEC-regulated freshwater wetland, outside its mapped boundary. Generally:
c: No permit is needed outside the boundary
The local building permit alone is needed
A DEC permit for the adjacent area
The Army Corps alone decides the question
questions.x: DEC regulates freshwater wetlands and a 100-foot adjacent area around them, so work at 75 feet generally needs a DEC permit. The boundary answer is the trap: the regulated zone extends past the wetland's edge.

questions.q: In Westchester County, once a contract is signed to sell a house served by a private drinking water well, who must arrange and pay for the required water test?
c: The buyer, as part of the inspection contingency
The seller, using a state-certified laboratory
The listing broker, before the property is marketed
The town building department, before closing
questions.x: Westchester's private well testing law puts the test on the seller: after the contract of sale is signed, the seller arranges and pays for a certified lab to test for the listed contaminants and gives the results to the buyer. The buyer-contingency answer is the trap, because that is how a well test works in counties with no resale rule.

questions.q: A Westchester listing agent offers to collect the seller's well water sample herself to save time. Under the county law, the sample may be collected by:
c: Any licensed real estate agent using a sterile bottle
The seller, if the lab provides a sampling kit
An employee or authorized agent of a certified lab
The buyer's home inspector, if trained in sampling
questions.x: The county law requires that the sample be collected by an employee or authorized representative of a laboratory certified by the state Department of Health, and the county says a real estate agent may not collect it unless the agent is one of those. The sampling-kit answer is the trap: kits are fine for an owner's own curiosity, not for the legally required test.

questions.q: A Westchester well test shows iron at 0.5 mg/L and pH of 6.2, with bacteria, nitrate and arsenic within standards. Under the county law, the owner:
c: Is required to install a neutralizer and an iron filter
May choose treatment, since both are secondary standards
Cannot sell until a retest shows both within standards
Is required to drill a new well into a deeper aquifer
questions.x: Iron and pH are secondary parameters, tied to staining, taste and corrosion, and the county requires treatment only when a primary contaminant fails after remediation. Treating them is the owner's choice, though low pH is worth fixing to protect copper pipes. The neutralizer-and-filter answer is the trap: those are the usual fixes, but the law does not demand them for secondary results.

questions.q: Under Westchester's well testing law, each of the following is a primary contaminant EXCEPT:
c: Iron
Nitrate
Arsenic
Total coliform
questions.x: Iron is a secondary contaminant, along with pH, manganese, sodium and chloride: it stains fixtures and laundry but is an aesthetic problem at typical levels. Nitrate, arsenic and coliform bacteria are primary, health-based standards. Nitrate is the tempting pick because it sounds like a fertilizer nuisance, but high nitrate is a health risk, especially for infants.

questions.concept: Coliform response in a private well
questions.q: A drilled well tests positive for total coliform and negative for E. coli. The casing ends below grade in a spot where rainwater pools. The best first step is to:
c: Raise the casing, seal the cap, chlorinate and retest
Abandon the well and run a line to the nearest water main
Add a water softener to remove bacteria from the supply
Take no action, since E. coli was not found in the sample
questions.x: Coliform in a drilled well usually means surface water is getting in at the top, and a buried casing in a wet spot is the obvious path. Close the path, shock chlorinate, flush and retest. The no-action answer is the trap: E. coli's absence means no sign of fecal contamination, but coliform still shows the well is open to the surface.

questions.concept: Coliform response in a private well
questions.q: In a private well water test, a positive result for total coliform bacteria is best understood as:
c: A disease that calls for drilling a replacement well
A mineral that causes hard water and boiler scale
A chemical left behind by old pesticide treatments
A sign that surface water may be reaching the well
questions.x: Coliforms are indicator bacteria. Most are harmless themselves, but their presence signals a pathway from the surface into the water supply, so the well needs inspection, disinfection and retesting. The replacement-well answer is the trap: most coliform problems are fixed at the wellhead, not by drilling again.

questions.q: Who designs a replacement septic absorption field for a single-family home in New York?
c: The septic pumping contractor that found the failure
The town building inspector, as part of the permit
The home inspector who performed the load test
A licensed professional engineer or registered architect
questions.x: New York requires onsite sewage systems to be designed by a licensed professional engineer or registered architect, based on deep test holes and percolation tests, with the county or local health department approving the plan. The building inspector answer is the trap: the building department handles permits for the house, but it neither designs nor approves the septic system.

questions.q: During a pre-purchase septic inspection, which finding most clearly shows that the absorption field itself has failed?
c: Sludge and scum filling half of the tank
A cracked baffle at the tank's inlet pipe
Sewage effluent surfacing over the trenches
A distribution box sitting slightly out of level
questions.x: Effluent reaching the surface means the soil in the trenches can no longer absorb the flow, so the field needs replacement under an approved design. A full tank, a cracked baffle and an unlevel distribution box are maintenance and repair items. The full tank is the trap: it is a warning sign of neglect, but pumping fixes it.

questions.q: A seller has a new roof put on a 1965 house before selling it. Months after closing, the roof leaks. The buyer's best warranty claim is under:
c: The housing merchant implied warranty in GBL 777-a
The roofer's written warranty, if it was assigned
The seller's PCDS, which warrants the roof's condition
The deed's covenant against the grantor's acts
questions.x: Repair work on a resale carries whatever warranty the contractor wrote, and the buyer can use it only if it transfers or was assigned at closing. GBL 777-a is the trap: its periods apply to new homes sold by a builder, not to a 1965 house with a new roof. The PCDS is expressly not a warranty, and the deed covenant concerns title.

questions.q: The housing merchant implied warranty under General Business Law 777-a applies to:
c: The resale of any house less than ten years old
Work done by a licensed home improvement contractor
The sale of a new home by a builder to a buyer
Any house sold with a PCDS and a home inspection
questions.x: GBL 777-a gives statutory warranty periods (1, 2 and 6 years) on new homes sold by a builder. Home improvement work falls under GBL Article 36-A, which sets contract rules rather than warranty periods, so the protection there is whatever the contractor's written warranty says. The home improvement answer is the trap, because both laws sit in the General Business Law.

questions.q: Since January 1, 2020, a homeowner with a working R-22 central air conditioning system:
c: May keep using it and have it serviced with reclaimed R-22
Is required to replace it before the next summer cooling season
May recharge it with R-410A, the standard drop-in substitute
Is required to remove it before the house can be sold
questions.x: The 2020 deadline ended production and import of R-22, not its use. Existing systems can run and be serviced by certified technicians with stockpiled or reclaimed R-22, though it grows scarcer and costlier. The R-410A answer is the trap: it works at different pressures and is not a drop-in replacement for R-22 equipment.

questions.q: A contractor replacing a homeowner's old R-22 condenser asks what to do with the refrigerant still inside. The correct practice is to:
c: Vent it outdoors, since small home systems are exempt
Leave it in the unit for the scrap yard to deal with
Release it slowly through the service valve on site
Recover it with certified equipment before disposal
questions.x: Under the Clean Air Act, ozone-depleting refrigerants may not be knowingly vented. An EPA Section 608 certified technician recovers the R-22, which can then be reclaimed for servicing other systems. The scrap-yard answer is the trap: disposal facilities must confirm the refrigerant was already recovered before they accept the equipment.

cram.html: Load path bottom up: footing (wider, below frost line), foundation wall, sill plate, girder on lally columns, joists, studs, rafters, ridge.
Header = over openings in wood framing. Lintel = over openings in masonry. Flitch plate = steel between wood.
Fascia faces out (gutters); soffit is the underside of the eave (vents); flashing seals joints.
Higher R-value = better insulation.
Housing Merchant Implied Warranty (GBL 777-a): 1 yr workmanship, 2 yrs mechanical systems, 6 yrs load-bearing structure.
Home improvement contract over $500: written, dates, work description, 3-business-day right to cancel, deposits escrowed or bonded.
Septic: Department of Health; designed by NY licensed PE or registered architect; perc test; as-builts at the health department.
1 ton of cooling = 12,000 BTU/hr. BTU = heat to raise 1 lb of water 1 degree F.
Boiler heats water (hot water or steam, radiators). Furnace heats air (ducts). Steam tell: sight glass.
Petroleum spill: report to DEC within 2 hours. Orphan fill pipe = possible abandoned UST.
120/240 volts (old books: 110/220). Service 100 to 200 amps; 60 amps = undersized. 240V circuits: dryer, range, central AC, well pump.
Fuse melts, replace it. Breaker trips, reset it. Oversized fuse = fire risk.
BX = armored cable (wires inside metal). Romex = plastic-sheathed. Greenfield = empty flexible metal conduit. Aluminum branch wiring = fire risk at connections.
Asbestos is dangerous when friable. Diseases: asbestosis, lung cancer, mesothelioma. Tests: bulk, air, wipe.
Lead disclosure: housing built before 1978; EPA pamphlet; disclose known hazards; 10-day test window; keep records 3 years.
Syllabus says lead rule applies "after 1978". Typo. It is before 1978.
Radon action level: 4 pCi/L. Fix: sub-slab depressurization (pipe + fan).
NY mold law: projects over 10 sq ft need DOL-licensed assessor and a separate licensed remediator.
UFFI = formaldehyde. PCBs = transformers, ballasts (Hudson River). CFCs/Freon = ozone. Chlordane = banned termite pesticide (1988). Termite applicators certified by DEC.
Phase I looks (no sampling), Phase II tests, Phase III fixes, Phase IV watches.
CERCLA: strict, joint and several, retroactive; current owner can pay. SARA (1986): innocent landowner defense if appropriate inquiry was done. Petroleum excluded (NY Navigation Law covers it).
SDWA covers public water systems, not private wells. Westchester requires well testing on sale.
Agent: disclose known material defects, never play expert, recommend licensed pros, document. Obedience never covers concealment.

subjects.title: Valuation Process and Pricing Properties
subjects.blurb: Pricing is the first thing a seller judges you on, and the exam loves the vocabulary: market value vs price vs cost, the three approaches, depreciation types, and why a CMA is never an appraisal.

lessons.title: Value, Price, Cost, and the CMA
lessons.tagline: Value is an opinion, price is a fact, cost is a receipt. Mix them up and you misprice the listing.
objectives: Tell appraisal, valuation, and evaluation apart
Break the market value definition into its testable pieces
Separate value, price, and cost, and classify direct vs indirect costs
Explain what a CMA is, what goes into one, and why it can never be called an appraisal
Describe the salesperson's duties of competence, diligence, documentation, and communication when pricing

blocks.title: The Okafors' kitchen table, Bed-Stuy
blocks.html: Grace Okafor slides a printout across the table. "Zillow says $2.4 million. We put $300,000 into this house. And our neighbor got $2.6 million." Emmanuel adds: "So the appraisal you're doing will say at least $2.6, right?" Jordan is holding a CMA, not an appraisal. Three numbers, three different ideas, and one word Jordan is not allowed to use. Which is which?
blocks.casual: Picture it: Grace Okafor pushes a Zillow printout at you. "$2.4 million. We spent $300,000 on this place. The neighbor got $2.6." Then Emmanuel goes, "So your appraisal will say at least $2.6, right?" Problem: Jordan is holding a CMA, not an appraisal. That's three numbers meaning three different things, plus one word Jordan can't say out loud. Can you sort them?

deeper.plain: Sellers mix up what a website guesses, what they spent, and what a neighbor got. None of those is automatically what the house is worth.
deeper.picture: It's like asking what your used car is worth and getting three answers: the dashboard app, your repair receipts, and what your cousin sold his for. Useful clues, not the answer.
deeper.street: The Okafors' $300,000 renovation is a cost. The neighbor's $2.6M is a price on a different house. Zillow's $2.4M is an algorithm. Jordan's job is to turn real comps into a range, maybe $2.35M to $2.5M, and explain why.
deeper.stakes: If Jordan calls the CMA an appraisal, that's a misrepresentation DOS can discipline. If Jordan just nods at $2.6M to keep the sellers happy, the listing goes stale and the appraisal later blows up the deal.
deeper.exam: Expect a stem where a seller quotes what they spent. The answer is that cost does not equal value. Also watch for any choice where a salesperson "appraises" a home: that's the wrong one.

blocks.html: An appraisal is an unbiased estimate of the nature, quality, value, or utility of an interest in identified real estate. In practice it means a written opinion of value prepared by a state licensed or certified appraiser. Lenders order them. They follow professional standards (USPAP).
blocks.casual: Here's what an appraisal really is: an unbiased estimate of the nature, quality, value, or utility of an interest in a specific piece of real estate. Day to day, that means a written opinion of value from a state licensed or certified appraiser. Lenders are the ones ordering them, and appraisers have to follow professional standards called USPAP.

deeper.plain: An appraisal is a neutral, licensed professional's written opinion of what a property is worth.
deeper.picture: Think of a referee in a game. Both teams want a call their way, but the ref has no stake in who wins and follows a rulebook. USPAP is the rulebook.
deeper.street: Leo goes into contract on a Sunnyside condo at $640,000. His lender, not Leo and not Jordan, orders the appraisal. A certified appraiser inspects, picks comps, and writes up $630,000 as of the inspection date.
deeper.stakes: The lender lends off that appraisal, not off the contract price. A low number means the buyer brings more cash or renegotiates. A licensee who tries to pressure the appraiser is asking for serious trouble.
deeper.exam: Cue words: "unbiased," "licensed or certified appraiser," "USPAP." If the answer choice says a salesperson or broker prepared the appraisal, it's wrong.

blocks.html: Valuation is the process of estimating the value of a specific interest in a specific property as of a given date. Evaluation is a study of a property's nature, quality, or utility where a value number is not necessarily required: a highest and best use study, a feasibility study, a supply and demand study.
blocks.casual: Valuation is figuring out what a specific interest in a specific property is worth as of a given date. Pin the date, always. Evaluation is different: it studies a property's nature, quality, or usefulness, and it does not necessarily spit out a dollar figure. Think highest and best use study, feasibility study, supply and demand study.

deeper.plain: Valuation ends with a number on a date. Evaluation answers a question like "will this work?" and may never produce a price.
deeper.picture: A doctor telling you your weight is a valuation. A doctor telling you whether you're fit to run a marathon is an evaluation. Both are exams, only one gives you a single number.
deeper.street: Evelyn is thinking of turning a Jamaica Avenue taxpayer into a mixed-use building. She pays a consultant for a feasibility study: is there demand, will rents cover construction? The report says yes or no. It never says what the lot is worth today.
deeper.stakes: Hand a client a feasibility study and let them treat it as a price, and they may overpay or borrow against a number nobody actually gave.
deeper.exam: Trap: "Which may not produce a value estimate?" The answer is evaluation. Valuation always ties to a specific date.

head: Term
Answers the question
Value number?
rows: What is it worth, per a licensed appraiser?
What is this interest worth as of this date?
Is this a good use? Will this project work?
blocks.caption: Evaluation is the one that can end without a dollar figure.

deeper.plain: Three similar words. Two always land on a dollar figure; evaluation can end with just a yes or no.
deeper.picture: Appraisal and valuation are a price tag. Evaluation is a consumer report that tells you whether the product is any good for you.
deeper.street: A Long Island City developer orders a market study (evaluation) on whether studios will rent, then later the bank orders an appraisal (valuation by a licensed appraiser) on the finished building for the construction loan takeout.
deeper.stakes: Mixing these up in conversation with a client can make you sound like you're giving an appraisal, which a licensee may not do.
deeper.exam: Look for "not necessarily" or "may not" a value conclusion. That points to evaluation every time.

blocks.html: "Value" always needs a modifier. The same Bed-Stuy brownstone has a different number depending on who is asking and why.
blocks.casual: Never say "value" by itself. It always needs a word in front of it. That same Bed-Stuy brownstone gets a different number depending on who's asking and why they want to know.

deeper.plain: Value changes with the purpose. A bank, an insurer, a tax assessor, and a buyer each measure something different.
deeper.picture: Your old guitar is worth one number to a pawn shop, another to the insurance company, and another to you because your grandfather played it.
deeper.street: The Okafors' house: market value maybe $2.45M, insured value maybe $1.1M (rebuild cost only), assessed value on the city roll a small fraction of that because of Class 1 caps.
deeper.stakes: If you tell a seller their assessed value is what the house is worth, or tell a buyer to insure for the purchase price, you've given bad advice that costs them money.
deeper.exam: The stem will say who's asking. Insurer means insurable value. Assessor means assessed value. A specific investor's own numbers mean investment value.

head: Type
What it measures
Who cares
rows: Most probable price in a fair, open sale
Value to a specific investor, using that investor's own goals and financing
Cost to rebuild the structure. Omits land and foundations
Value for one specific use, often to the current owner (a custom factory)
Value a lender will rely on to make a loan
Value set by the assessor for property tax

deeper.plain: Each kind of value answers a different question for a different person.
deeper.picture: Same pizza: the menu price, what it cost the shop to make, and what it's worth to you at 2 a.m. after a long shift. Three numbers, all true.
deeper.street: Evelyn runs a Flatbush retail building with her own 30% down and cheap credit line, so her investment value is $4.2M. The market value, what a typical buyer would pay, is $3.9M. She'll pay more because of her financing.
deeper.stakes: Pricing a listing off one owner's investment value or value in use can leave it sitting for months. Lenders and buyers care about market value.
deeper.exam: Investment value is tied to one specific investor. Value in use is tied to one specific use, often the current owner. Don't swap them.

blocks.title: Insurable value skips the dirt
blocks.html: Land does not burn. Insurable value leaves out land and foundations, so it is usually lower than market value for a house on a valuable lot. In Brooklyn the land can be half the price.
blocks.casual: Land doesn't burn. So insurable value leaves out the land and the foundations. That's why it usually runs below market value for a house sitting on a pricey lot. In Brooklyn, the dirt can be half the price.

deeper.plain: Insurance pays to rebuild what can be destroyed. The ground under the house isn't going anywhere.
deeper.picture: If your phone case cracks, insurance covers the case, not the phone number. The number survives no matter what happens to the plastic.
deeper.street: A Park Slope brownstone sells for $3M. A fire wipes out the structure. Rebuild cost is maybe $1.4M. The lot is still there and still valuable, so the policy only needs to cover the rebuild.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who insures for the full purchase price overpays premiums. One who insures too low can get hit by a coinsurance penalty after a loss.
deeper.exam: "Which value excludes land?" Insurable value. A choice saying insured value equals market value is the trap.

blocks.html: The definition is long because every phrase rules something out. Market value is the most probable price, as of a specific date, in cash or its equivalent, for the specified property rights, after reasonable exposure in a competitive market, with buyer and seller each acting prudently and knowledgeably, for self-interest, and neither under undue duress.
blocks.casual: The definition is long because every phrase knocks something out. Market value is the most probable price, as of a specific date, in cash or its equivalent, for the specified property rights, after reasonable exposure in a competitive market, with buyer and seller both acting prudently and knowledgeably in their own interest, and neither under undue duress.

deeper.plain: Market value is the price a normal sale would most likely hit when nobody is desperate, everybody knows what they're doing, and the house had a fair shot on the market.
deeper.picture: It's the price a fair auction would land on with plenty of informed bidders and no one in a hurry. Not the one lucky bid, not the panic sale.
deeper.street: A Crown Heights two-family sells for $1.1M after six weeks on the MLS with several offers, conventional financing, unrelated parties. That's a clean market value comp. Next door, a brother sold to his sister for $700,000. Not market value.
deeper.stakes: Using sales that fail the definition as comps produces a wrong price, and the lender's appraiser will throw them out anyway.
deeper.exam: "Most probable," not "highest" or "average." Any answer saying "the highest price a buyer would pay" is the classic trap.

head: Phrase
What it means
What it rules out
rows: The highest price someone might pay
Seller financing at 2% that inflates price
Comparing a fee to a leasehold
Time on the market BEFORE the sale date
A sale that never hit the market
Broad market, publicized, time, knowledge, no duress, both parties "cool"
Divorce fire sales, family deals, foreclosure auctions

deeper.plain: Each piece of the definition filters out a kind of sale that would mislead you.
deeper.picture: It's like a recipe where each ingredient keeps a specific thing from going wrong. Leave one out and the cake falls.
deeper.street: An Astoria condo sold for $900,000 with the seller financing at 2%. The buyer paid up because the terms were sweet. An appraiser adjusts that sale down to what it would bring with normal financing, maybe $860,000.
deeper.stakes: If you treat a creative-financing or family sale as a straight comp, your CMA runs high, and the seller hears a number the bank will never support.
deeper.exam: Watch for "cash or equivalent" and "reasonable exposure." A sale never offered on the open market fails the exposure test.

blocks.title: Exposure vs marketing time
blocks.html: Exposure time looks backward: how long the property would have been on the market before a sale at market value on the effective date. Marketing time looks forward: how long it will take to sell after the date. The definition uses exposure.
blocks.casual: Exposure time looks back: how long the place would have sat on the market before selling at market value on the effective date. Marketing time looks ahead: how long it'll take to sell after that date. The definition uses exposure.

deeper.plain: Exposure time is the past. Marketing time is the future.
deeper.picture: Exposure is how long the bread was in the oven before you took it out. Marketing time is how long it'll take to sell it at the bake sale tomorrow.
deeper.street: The appraiser writes that the Okafors' house would have needed about 60 days of exposure to sell at $2.45M on the effective date, and estimates 90 days of marketing time going forward in a softer spring.
deeper.stakes: Mix them up and you mislead a seller about when they'll actually close, which matters if they're buying their next place on a deadline.
deeper.exam: Cue word "before" the effective date means exposure. "After" means marketing time. The definition of market value uses exposure.

blocks.html: Why the fuss over one definition? Because the lender's appraiser uses it. If the Okafors' buyer offers $2.6M but the appraisal says $2.45M, the bank lends against $2.45M. The buyer must bring the $150,000 gap in cash, renegotiate, or walk if the contract has a mortgage contingency. Pricing to market value from the start avoids that fight.
blocks.casual: Why fuss over one definition? Because the lender's appraiser lives by it. Say the Okafors' buyer offers $2.6M and the appraisal comes back $2.45M. The bank lends against $2.45M. Now the buyer has to bring the $150,000 gap in cash, renegotiate, or walk if the contract has a mortgage contingency. Price to market value from day one and you skip that fight.

deeper.plain: Banks lend off the appraisal, so an overpriced deal hits a wall when the appraisal comes in low.
deeper.picture: It's like a car loan where the bank only finances what the car's worth on their book. Overpay and the difference comes out of your pocket.
deeper.street: Buyer at $2.6M with 20% down planned to borrow $2.08M. The bank caps the loan at 80% of $2.45M, which is $1.96M. The buyer now needs $640,000 cash instead of $520,000. Ten days of tense calls with Priya follow.
deeper.stakes: Deals collapse, sellers relist after weeks off the market, and everyone blames the agent who set the price.
deeper.exam: When the appraisal is lower than the price, lenders base the loan on the lower of price or appraised value. Know that phrase.

items: Arm's length: unrelated parties, each acting in self-interest. Sales between relatives, business partners, or a company and its owner are not arm's length.
Duress: a divorce deadline, an estate that must pay taxes, a looming foreclosure. These sales tend to fall below market value.
Special motivation: the neighbor who must have the yard. These sales can land above market value.
Financing: seller concessions or below-market seller financing inflate the price. Appraisers adjust them back to cash equivalent.
blocks.casual:
Arm's length means unrelated people, each looking out for themselves. A sale between relatives, business partners, or a company and its own owner doesn't count.
Duress: divorce deadlines, an estate that has to pay taxes, a foreclosure on the way. Those sales usually land below market value.
Special motivation: the neighbor who has to have that yard. Those can land above market value.
Financing: seller concessions or cheap seller financing pump the price up. Appraisers adjust those back to cash equivalent.

deeper.plain: A good comp is a normal sale between strangers. Pressure, family ties, special desire, or odd financing all bend the price.
deeper.picture: If you want to know what a sneaker really goes for, you don't use the pair your uncle sold you for $20 or the pair someone overpaid for at a midnight drop.
deeper.street: On one Bushwick block: a divorcing couple sold fast at $1.05M, a next-door owner paid $1.4M to combine lots, and a regular sale went for $1.2M. Only the $1.2M sale is clean.
deeper.stakes: Pick the wrong comps and the CMA is off by six figures. The seller either leaves money on the table or chases a price that never comes.
deeper.exam: Sale between related parties = not arm's length. Duress tends to push price below value; special motivation can push above.

blocks.q: An uncle sells his Astoria two-family to his nephew for $600,000 when similar houses sell for $1.1 million. The $600,000 is best described as:
c: Market value
Price, but not market value
Investment value
Insurable value
blocks.x: It is the price actually paid. It is not market value because a family sale is not an arm's-length deal with typically motivated, unrelated parties.

left.title: Price
items: What a particular buyer agreed to pay and a particular seller agreed to take
A historical fact
May or may not equal value

right.title: Cost
items: Total dollars spent to build: labor, materials, fees, financing, profit
Looks at the supply side
May or may not equal value (an overbuilt pool rarely pays back)

deeper.plain: Price is what someone paid. Cost is what it took to build. Value is what the market thinks it's worth. They can all be different.
deeper.picture: You spent $8,000 on a custom tattoo of your ex's name. Cost: $8,000. Value to the next person: zero.
deeper.street: A Staten Island owner added a $90,000 inground pool. When she sells, buyers in that area pay maybe $25,000 more for it. Cost $90,000, value added $25,000.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who expect to get back every dollar spent will overprice. You have to explain this kindly but clearly, with comps.
deeper.exam: Price is a historical fact. Cost is the supply side. Neither automatically equals value. A choice saying "cost always equals value" is wrong.

blocks.html: Market price is what a property actually sold for. Price and cost are facts; value is an opinion. Grace's $300,000 renovation is a cost. It adds value only to the extent buyers will pay for it.
blocks.casual: Market price is what a property actually sold for. Price and cost are facts. Value is an opinion. Grace's $300,000 renovation is a cost. It only adds value to the extent buyers will pay for it.

deeper.plain: You can look up a price and add up a cost. Value is a judgment someone has to make.
deeper.picture: Your receipts prove what you spent. They don't prove what anyone will pay you for the stuff.
deeper.street: The Okafors' $300,000 went into a new kitchen, roof, and boiler. Comps show renovated homes nearby sell for about $200,000 more than unrenovated ones. So roughly two thirds of the spend shows up as value.
deeper.stakes: If Jordan simply adds $300,000 to an old price, the listing is overpriced from day one.
deeper.exam: Fact vs opinion: price and cost are facts, value is an estimate. Market price = what it actually sold for.

head: Direct costs (hard costs)
Indirect costs (soft costs)
rows: Lease-up costs, administration, filing and permit fees, insurance, taxes during construction
blocks.caption: If you can touch it or it is wages to build it, it is direct. Paperwork and money are indirect.

deeper.plain: Building costs split into the stuff and labor on site (hard) and the paperwork and money (soft).
deeper.picture: Throwing a wedding: the food, flowers, and band are hard costs. The planner's fee, the deposit's interest, and the venue permit are soft.
deeper.street: A Ridgewood four-unit build: lumber, concrete, and the framers' wages are direct. The architect, the DOB filing fees, the construction loan interest, and builder's risk insurance are indirect.
deeper.stakes: Forget the soft costs in a cost approach and the estimate runs low, sometimes by 20% or more.
deeper.exam: Architect fees, financing, permits, insurance during construction = indirect. Labor and materials = direct. The exam loves to put architect fees in the wrong column.

blocks.title: Hard vs soft
blocks.html: Hard costs hit with a hammer. Soft costs come with an invoice.
blocks.casual: Hard costs hit with a hammer. Soft costs show up with an invoice.

deeper.plain: If someone swings a tool or it's a material, it's hard cost. If it's a fee or financing, it's soft.
deeper.picture: Hammer versus envelope. The hammer builds; the envelope bills.
deeper.street: Sal adds a rear extension to his Astoria building. The bricklayer and bricks: hard. The expediter and the bank's interest during the job: soft.
deeper.stakes: Get the categories wrong on the exam and you lose easy points on a cost approach question.
deeper.exam: "Which is an indirect cost?" Pick the fee, the interest, or the permit, never the labor.

blocks.q: Which is a direct cost of building a new Staten Island house?
c: Survey and permit fees
Construction loan interest
Carpenters' wages
The architect's fee
blocks.x: Direct (hard) costs are labor and materials. Permits, interest, and the architect are indirect (soft) costs.

blocks.text: The CMA: an opinion, never an appraisal

blocks.html: A comparative market analysis (CMA) is a licensee's written opinion of a likely price range, built from recent sales, active competition, and expired listings. It helps a seller set a list price or a buyer frame an offer.
blocks.casual: A comparative market analysis (CMA) is your written opinion, as a licensee, of a likely price range. You build it from recent sales, the active competition, and expired listings. It helps a seller pick a list price or a buyer shape an offer.

deeper.plain: A CMA is the agent's homework on what similar homes did, turned into a sensible price range.
deeper.picture: Before you sell your bike, you check what similar bikes sold for, what's listed now, and what nobody bought. That's a CMA.
deeper.street: For the Okafors, Jordan pulls five Bed-Stuy brownstone sales from the last year, four active listings, and two expireds that sat at $2.8M. The range lands at $2.35M to $2.5M.
deeper.stakes: A lazy CMA misprices the home. Overpriced listings go stale; underpriced ones cost your client real money and invite complaints.
deeper.exam: CMA = licensee's opinion, a range, not an appraisal. Expect a question asking what it uses: sold, active, expired.

blocks.title: Never call it an appraisal
blocks.html: By law a CMA may never be called an appraisal. Only a state licensed or certified appraiser (licensed by DOS under Executive Law Article 6-E) produces an appraisal. A real estate licensee who presents a CMA as an appraisal is misrepresenting, and risks discipline.
blocks.casual: By law, a CMA may never be called an appraisal. Only a state licensed or certified appraiser (licensed by DOS under Executive Law Article 6-E) produces an appraisal. If you present your CMA as an appraisal, you're misrepresenting, and you're risking discipline.

deeper.plain: Only licensed appraisers do appraisals. Your CMA is something else and must be labeled that way.
deeper.picture: A pharmacist can tell you a lot about a medicine, but can't write you a prescription. Different license, different job.
deeper.street: Marcus emails a seller a PDF titled "Home Appraisal" with his logo. The seller uses it to set a divorce settlement. The ex-spouse's lawyer finds out it's a CMA and files a DOS complaint.
deeper.stakes: Misrepresentation can bring fines, suspension, or revocation, plus a civil suit from anyone who relied on it.
deeper.exam: Any choice where a salesperson provides an "appraisal" for a fee is wrong. Appraisers are licensed under Executive Law Article 6-E, not RPL Article 12-A.

blocks.html: Buyers' agents run CMAs too. Before Leo offers on a Sunnyside condo, Jordan pulls sales in the same building and the blocks around it so Leo's offer is grounded, and so he knows whether the bank's appraisal is likely to support the price.
blocks.casual: Buyers' agents run CMAs too. Before Leo offers on a Sunnyside condo, Jordan pulls sales in that building and the blocks around it. That way Leo's offer has a footing, and he can tell whether the bank's appraisal will likely back the price.

deeper.plain: Buyers need comps as much as sellers. It keeps them from overpaying and predicts appraisal trouble.
deeper.picture: Checking a few other listings before you rent an apartment so you know if $2,800 is fair or steep.
deeper.street: The asking price is $675,000. Three recent sales in the building of the same line averaged $635,000. Jordan suggests Leo open at $630,000 and stop around $650,000.
deeper.stakes: Skip it and the buyer overpays, then faces an appraisal gap they have to cover in cash.
deeper.exam: A CMA is not only a listing tool. Questions may ask who uses one: sellers and buyers both.

blocks.title: Where NYC comps come from
blocks.html: The MLS (REBNY RLS in Manhattan and much of Brooklyn, OneKey MLS in Queens, the Bronx, Long Island, and the Hudson Valley) gives listing detail. ACRIS, the city's online property records, shows recorded deeds and sale prices. For co-ops, sale prices do not appear as deeds, so lean on MLS data, and compare monthly maintenance too: a $1,000 higher maintenance can knock tens of thousands off what a buyer will pay.
blocks.casual: The MLS gives you listing details: REBNY RLS for Manhattan and a lot of Brooklyn, OneKey MLS for Queens, the Bronx, Long Island, and the Hudson Valley. ACRIS, the city's online property records, shows recorded deeds and sale prices. Co-op sales don't show up as deeds, so lean on MLS data there, and compare monthly maintenance too. A $1,000 higher maintenance can knock tens of thousands off what a buyer will pay.

deeper.plain: In NYC you check the MLS for details and ACRIS for recorded sale prices. Co-ops need extra care because they aren't deeded.
deeper.picture: ACRIS is the city's receipt drawer. Co-op apartments aren't in it because buyers get shares and a lease, not a deed.
deeper.street: Two identical UWS two-bedroom co-ops in Kim's area: one sold at $1.2M with $2,100 maintenance, the other at $1.08M with $3,100. That $1,000 a month gap explains most of the price difference.
deeper.stakes: Ignore maintenance and your co-op CMA runs high. The listing sits, and the board may still balk at the buyer's finances.
deeper.exam: Co-op = shares and proprietary lease, not real property deed. ACRIS is NYC's recorded document system.

items: Recent sold properties: the best evidence. Similar homes, sold in the last 12 months, nearby.
Current competing properties: what buyers will compare yours to this weekend. Asking prices, not values.
Recent expired listings: proof of what the market rejected. Usually overpriced.
Buyer appeal and market position: how the home stacks up against the competition.
Assets and drawbacks: the parlor floor details vs the 1970s kitchen.
Area market conditions: inventory, days on market, rates.
Recommended terms and a market value range: a range, not a promise.
blocks.casual:
Recent sales are your best evidence: similar homes, nearby, sold in the last 12 months.
Current competition: what buyers compare yours to this weekend. These are asking prices, not values.
Expired listings: proof of what the market said no to, usually because they were overpriced.
Buyer appeal and market position: how the home stacks up.
Assets and drawbacks: the parlor floor details versus the 1970s kitchen.
Area conditions: inventory, days on market, rates.
Recommended terms and a value range: a range, not a promise.

deeper.plain: A good CMA uses what sold, what's for sale, and what failed to sell, then gives a range.
deeper.picture: Planning a yard sale: what similar stuff sold for, what neighbors are asking, and what got carried back inside unsold.
deeper.street: In Ditmas Park, Jordan finds three Victorians sold at $1.8M to $1.95M, two listed at $2.1M, and one expired at $2.3M after 140 days. The expired tells the seller exactly where the ceiling is.
deeper.stakes: Use only actives and you price off wishful thinking. Sellers who see expireds understand why you won't list at their dream number.
deeper.exam: Sold comps are the strongest evidence. Active listings show competition, not value. Expired listings suggest overpricing.

blocks.title: Four duties when you price

items.title: Competence
items.html: Know the neighborhood and the product type, or get help. A co-op on the UWS and a farmhouse in Delaware County are different skills.

items.title: Diligence
items.html: Pull real comps. Do not stop at one website estimate.

items.title: Documentation
items.html: Keep the comps, the adjustments, and your reasoning. It protects you if the seller later claims you misled them.

items.title: Effective communication
items.html: Explain the range and the logic in plain words. The seller sets the list price; you advise.

blocks.casual:
Competence: know the neighborhood and the type of property, or get help. A UWS co-op and a Delaware County farmhouse are different skills.
Diligence: pull real comps. Don't stop at one website estimate.
Documentation: keep the comps, the adjustments, and your reasoning. It protects you if the seller later says you misled them.
Effective communication: explain the range and the logic in plain words. The seller sets the list price. You advise.

deeper.plain: Know the market, do the work, keep the receipts, and explain it clearly. The client makes the final call.
deeper.picture: Like a good mechanic: knows your car model, actually looks under the hood, writes up what they found, and tells you in English what it means.
deeper.street: Jordan gets a call to price a lake house in the Catskills. Not Jordan's market. Diane has Jordan partner with an upstate broker who knows the area rather than guess.
deeper.stakes: A seller who loses money on a bad price may file a DOS complaint or sue. Your saved comps and notes are your defense.
deeper.exam: The seller, not the agent, sets the list price. Pricing outside your competence without help is a breach of reasonable care.

blocks.title: Buying the listing
blocks.html: Quoting an inflated price to win the listing ("buying the listing") breaches your duty of care and honesty. It usually ends in price cuts and a stale listing. The exam frames this as a misrepresentation.
blocks.casual: Quoting a puffed-up price just to win the listing ("buying the listing") breaks your duty of care and honesty. It almost always ends in price cuts and a stale listing. The exam calls it misrepresentation.

deeper.plain: Promising a seller a price you know the market won't pay, just to get the listing, is dishonest.
deeper.picture: A contractor who lowballs the quote to get the job, then hits you with change orders. Same move, different trade.
deeper.street: Marcus tells a Prospect Heights seller he can get $1.6M when comps say $1.35M. After 90 days and three cuts, it sells at $1.3M, below what it would have fetched if priced right on day one.
deeper.stakes: The seller loses money and time, and can file a misrepresentation complaint. Your reputation in the neighborhood takes the hit too.
deeper.exam: "Buying the listing" = misrepresentation and breach of duty. Any choice calling it good marketing strategy is wrong.

blocks.q: Which statement about a CMA is correct?
c: It is an appraisal if a licensed salesperson prepares it
It may be given to a lender in place of an appraisal
It is an opinion of value and may never be called an appraisal
It must include only active listings
blocks.x: A CMA is an opinion of a likely price range. No matter who prepares it, a real estate licensee may not call it an appraisal. Sold comps are its core, not just actives.

story.title: The Zillow Printout
story.setting: Bed-Stuy, the Okafors' parlor, a rainy Thursday

beats.text: Jordan's first listing appointment with the Okafors. Grace has a printout. Emmanuel has a calculator.
Zillow says $2.4. We spent $300,000 on this place. And the Johnsons got $2.6. So your appraisal says at least $2.6?
Quick fix on one word. This is a CMA, a comparative market analysis. It's my opinion of a price range. An appraisal only comes from a licensed appraiser.
beats.tag: A CMA is never an appraisal

beats.text: Fine. But the $300,000. That has to count.
It counts as cost. Buyers pay for the new roof and the boiler. They will not pay dollar for dollar for the koi pond.
And the Johnsons' $2.6 was a price, a real fact. But their buyer was the neighbor who wanted the yard. That's one motivated buyer, not the most probable price.

check.q: Why might the Johnsons' $2.6M sale not equal market value?
c: Prices never equal value
The buyer had special motivation, so it may exceed the most probable price
It was not a cash sale
Only appraisers can know prices
check.x: Market value is the most probable price with typically motivated parties. A neighbor paying a premium for the yard is special motivation.

beats.text: Here are six sales from the last year within a few blocks, three actives you'll compete with, and two that expired at $2.7 and $2.75.
Expired? Why show us failures?
Because they tell us where buyers said no. That's data too.
Back at the office, Marcus leans over the desk.
Just tell them $2.7. Win the listing, cut the price in a month. And put "appraisal" on the cover, sellers love that word.
Do either and you'll be explaining yourself to DOS. Buying a listing is a misrepresentation. And a licensee calling a CMA an appraisal is out of bounds, full stop.
So I give them the range, $2.35 to $2.5, show my work, keep the file.
Competent, diligent, documented, and said in English. That's the whole job of pricing.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: left side PRICE and COST facts from the Okafors' meeting, right side VALUE opinions. Where does each number go?

facts.text: An appraisal is an unbiased estimate of the nature, quality, value or utility of an interest in real estate, in practice by a state licensed or certified appraiser.
Valuation estimates the value of an interest as of a date; an evaluation studies nature, quality or utility and may end without a value number.
Market value is the most probable price, as of a specific date, in cash or its equivalent, after reasonable exposure, with prudent, knowledgeable parties under no undue duress.
Below-market seller financing or concessions inflate a price, so appraisers adjust the sale back to cash equivalent.
A fair sale is arm's length with no duress; sales between relatives, divorce or foreclosure sales are not market value evidence.
Exposure time looks backward (time on market before the sale date) and is the one in the definition; marketing time looks forward.
Insurable value is the cost to rebuild and leaves out land and foundations.
Investment value is the value to a specific investor using that investor's own goals and financing.
Value in use is the value for one specific use, often to the current owner.
Mortgage value is what a lender relies on to make a loan; assessed value is what the assessor sets for property tax.
If the appraisal comes in below the contract price the lender lends on the appraisal, so the buyer pays the gap, renegotiates, or walks under a mortgage contingency.
Price is what a particular buyer and seller agreed on, a historical fact; market price is what a property actually sold for.
Cost is the total spent to build; it adds value only to the extent buyers will pay for it.
Direct (hard) costs are labor, materials and site equipment; indirect (soft) costs are fees, financing, permits, insurance and taxes during construction.
A CMA is a licensee's opinion of a likely price range and may never be called an appraisal; only a DOS licensed or certified appraiser (Executive Law Article 6-E) appraises.
In a CMA recent similar sales (usually within 12 months) are the best evidence, while active listings show the competition at asking prices, not values.
Expired listings in a CMA show prices the market rejected.
NYC comps come from the MLS and ACRIS deed records; co-op sales record no deed, so use MLS data and compare monthly maintenance.
When pricing, a licensee owes competence, diligence, documentation and clear communication; the seller sets the list price and the licensee advises.
Quoting an inflated price to win a listing (buying the listing) breaches the duty of care and honesty and is treated as misrepresentation.

lessons.title: Highest and Best Use and the Three Approaches
lessons.tagline: Comps for homes, cost for the firehouse, income for Sal's six-family. Then adjust the comp, never the subject.
objectives: Apply the four tests of highest and best use, as vacant and as improved
Explain site valuation and plottage
Run the sales comparison, cost, and income approaches with real numbers
Classify depreciation as physical, functional, or external and curable or incurable
Build a CMA price from adjusted comparables

blocks.title: Three properties, one Monday
blocks.html: Diane hands Jordan three files: Leo wants an opinion on a Sunnyside condo, the parish is selling a 1920s firehouse it converted to a hall, and Sal wants to know what his Astoria six-family would fetch. "Same question three times," Diane says. "What is it worth? Different tool each time." Which tool goes with which file?
blocks.casual: Monday morning, Diane drops three files on Jordan's desk. Leo wants an opinion on a Sunnyside condo. The parish is selling a 1920s firehouse it turned into a hall. Sal wants to know what his Astoria six-family would bring. "Same question three times," Diane says. "What's it worth? Different tool each time." So which tool goes with which file?

deeper.plain: There are three ways to estimate value, and the type of property tells you which one to lean on.
deeper.picture: A carpenter, a plumber, and an electrician all "fix the house," but you call the one whose tools match the problem.
deeper.street: Leo's condo has plenty of sales in the building: sales comparison. The firehouse is one of a kind with no real comps: cost approach. Sal's six-family is bought for the rent checks: income approach.
deeper.stakes: Use the wrong approach and your number is off. Price a rent building only on house comps and an investor will laugh you out of the room.
deeper.exam: Cue words: "special purpose" or "new construction" means cost; "rental" or "investor" means income; homes and condos mean sales comparison.

blocks.html: Highest and best use is the reasonable, probable use that produces the highest value. Every appraisal starts here, because you cannot value a property until you know what it should be used for.
blocks.casual: Highest and best use is the reasonable, likely use that produces the most value. Every appraisal starts here, because you can't put a number on a property until you know what it should be used for.

deeper.plain: Before valuing a property, figure out the best realistic thing to do with it.
deeper.picture: A big empty lot downtown used as a two-car parking pad is like using a sports car to hold your mail. The value is in what it could be.
deeper.street: A one-story auto shop on a Gowanus lot that was rezoned for apartments. The shop pays $60,000 a year in rent, but a developer could build 20 units there. The value follows the apartments, not the garage.
deeper.stakes: Price that lot as a garage and the owner sells for a fraction of what it's worth. That's a lawsuit waiting to happen.
deeper.exam: Highest and best use comes first in every appraisal. Look for "most profitable legal use" in the stem.

blocks.title: Four tests, in order

items.title: Legally permissible
items.html: Zoning, deed restrictions, landmark rules. A tower on an R5 lot fails here.

items.title: Physically possible
items.html: Size, shape, soil, slope, access.

items.title: Financially feasible
items.html: Will the use earn enough to justify building it?

items.title: Maximally productive
items.html: Of the feasible uses, which gives the highest land value?

blocks.casual:
Run the four tests in order.
Legally permissible: zoning, deed restrictions, landmark rules. A tower on an R5 lot dies right here.
Physically possible: size, shape, soil, slope, access.
Financially feasible: will the use earn enough to justify building it?
Maximally productive: of the uses still standing, which gives the land the highest value?

deeper.plain: Is it allowed, can it be built, does it pay, and which paying option pays the most?
deeper.picture: Choosing a dinner spot: is it open, can you get there, can you afford it, and of what's left, which is best?
deeper.street: On a Staten Island lot, zoning allows two-family homes or a small store. The slope rules out the store's parking. Two-family homes pencil out at a profit. So highest and best use is the two-family.
deeper.stakes: Skip the legal step and you could advise a buyer to pay for a use the city will never permit.
deeper.exam: The order matters. Legal comes first. A question asking which test is applied first: legally permissible.

blocks.title: Legal, Physical, Financial, Max
blocks.html: "Lawyers Prefer Fat Money." Legally permissible, Physically possible, Financially feasible, Maximally productive.
blocks.casual: "Lawyers Prefer Fat Money." Legally permissible, Physically possible, Financially feasible, Maximally productive.

deeper.plain: A silly sentence to keep the four tests and their order straight.
deeper.picture: Lawyers do prefer fat money. Easy to picture, easy to recall at 8 a.m. on exam day.
deeper.street: Jordan mutters it while reading a Queens zoning map: lawyers (is a fourth floor legal?), prefer (does the lot fit it?), fat (will rents cover it?), money (is it the best option?).
deeper.stakes: Forgetting the order costs you a question or two, easy points.
deeper.exam: The exam often lists the four tests scrambled and asks which comes first or last. Legal first, maximally productive last.

blocks.html: Appraisers test it twice. As vacant: if the lot were empty, what would you build? As improved: given the building that is there, keep it, renovate it, convert it, or tear it down? When the land alone is worth more than the land plus the old building, highest and best use is demolition.
blocks.casual: Appraisers run the test twice. As vacant: if the lot were empty, what would you build? As improved: given the building that's there, do you keep it, renovate, convert, or tear it down? If the land by itself is worth more than the land plus the old building, highest and best use is demolition.

deeper.plain: Sometimes the building on a lot is holding the value down, and tearing it down is the best use.
deeper.picture: An old fridge in a great kitchen. Sometimes the room is worth more with it gone.
deeper.street: In Williamsburg, a tired two-story frame house plus lot is worth $1.5M as is. The empty lot, zoned for a six-story building, is worth $1.9M. A developer will buy it and knock it down.
deeper.stakes: If you price that listing as a house, your seller leaves $400,000 behind.
deeper.exam: When the land is worth more vacant than improved, the highest and best use is demolition. Expect that exact fact pattern.

blocks.html: Appraisers lean on a handful of economic principles. The exam names them and asks you to match a fact pattern.
blocks.casual: Appraisers lean on a handful of economic principles. The exam names them and asks you to match one to a story.

deeper.plain: A few basic ideas explain why prices go up or down. Learn the names and a quick example of each.
deeper.picture: Like rules of thumb in cooking: salt brings out flavor, acid cuts fat. Name the rule, spot it in the dish.
deeper.street: A Bay Ridge mansion surrounded by modest row houses sells for less than its size suggests. That's regression, and the exam wants you to say the name.
deeper.stakes: On the job, these principles are how you explain a price to a stubborn seller. On the exam, they're match-the-term points.
deeper.exam: Questions describe a story and ask which principle it shows. Read for the clue word: substitute, adds, fits, pulled down, future.

items: Substitution: a buyer pays no more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute. It powers all three approaches.
Contribution: a feature is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost. The $80,000 pool may add $20,000.
Conformity: value is highest when a home fits its neighborhood.
Regression: the best house on the block is pulled down by its cheaper neighbors. Progression: the modest house is pulled up by better ones.
Anticipation: value is the present worth of expected future benefits. A new subway station announced for the area lifts prices before it opens.
Supply and demand, change: neighborhoods grow, stabilize, decline, and revitalize; values follow.
blocks.casual:
Substitution: buyers won't pay more than an equally good substitute costs. It powers all three approaches.
Contribution: a feature is worth what it adds, not what it cost. The $80,000 pool might add $20,000.
Conformity: value peaks when a home fits its neighborhood.
Regression: the best house on the block gets dragged down by cheaper neighbors. Progression: the modest house gets lifted by better ones.
Anticipation: value is today's worth of future benefits. Announce a new subway stop and prices jump before it opens.
Supply and demand, change: neighborhoods grow, stabilize, decline, revitalize, and values follow.

deeper.plain: Buyers compare, features only count for what buyers pay, and neighbors and the future pull prices up or down.
deeper.picture: Regression is the nicest car in a junkyard. Progression is a beat-up car parked at a luxury dealership: it looks better by association.
deeper.street: When the Second Avenue subway extension to East Harlem was funded, sellers near the planned stations pushed asking prices up years before any train ran. That's anticipation.
deeper.stakes: Ignore conformity or regression and you'll overprice the fancy house on a plain block.
deeper.exam: Regression = better house, worse neighbors, loses value. Progression = worse house, better neighbors, gains. Students flip these.

blocks.title: Overimprovement
blocks.html: The $400,000 renovation on a block of $900,000 houses rarely returns $400,000. That is regression plus contribution. When a seller says "but I spent...", the answer is cost is not value.
blocks.casual: A $400,000 renovation on a block of $900,000 houses almost never returns $400,000. That's regression plus contribution. When a seller says "but I spent...", your answer is: cost isn't value.

deeper.plain: Spending far more than the neighborhood supports is overimprovement. The money doesn't come back.
deeper.picture: Putting a gold-plated faucet in a rental studio. Nice faucet. Nobody pays rent for it.
deeper.street: A Canarsie owner spends $350,000 gutting a $750,000 house. Best sale on the block ever was $850,000. Buyers top out near $900,000, so most of the spend is lost.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who overimproved expect to be made whole. You need comps and a calm talk, or you take an unsellable listing.
deeper.exam: Overimprovement links to regression and contribution. Cost does not equal value.

blocks.html: Site valuation values the land as if vacant and ready for its highest and best use. The main tool is sales of comparable vacant lots. The cost approach needs it, because land is added back separately and never depreciates.
blocks.casual: Site valuation values the land as if it were empty and ready for its highest and best use. The main tool is sales of similar vacant lots. The cost approach needs it, because land gets added back separately and never depreciates.

deeper.plain: You value the dirt by itself, using sales of similar empty lots.
deeper.picture: Pricing a phone case without the phone. You look at what similar empty cases sell for.
deeper.street: For the parish firehouse, the appraiser finds three vacant 25 by 100 lots in the area that sold for $380,000 to $420,000 and settles on $400,000 for the land.
deeper.stakes: A wrong land figure throws off the whole cost approach, since land is a big chunk of NYC value.
deeper.exam: Land never depreciates. Site value comes from comparable vacant land sales.

blocks.html: Assemblage is combining adjacent lots into one. Plottage is the extra value that the combined lot is worth over the sum of its parts. Three 25-foot Long Island City lots worth $1M each may be worth $4M together because a developer can build one bigger building.
blocks.casual: Assemblage is putting neighboring lots together into one. Plottage is the extra value the combined lot has over the sum of the pieces. Three 25-foot Long Island City lots worth $1M each might be worth $4M together, because a developer can build one bigger building.

deeper.plain: Assemblage is the act of combining lots. Plottage is the bonus value you get from doing it.
deeper.picture: Three single puzzle pieces are worth little. The completed corner of the puzzle is worth more than all three loose.
deeper.street: A developer in Bushwick buys two 20-foot lots at $800,000 each. Combined, the 40-foot lot allows an elevator building and appraises at $2M. Plottage: $400,000.
deeper.stakes: A holdout neighbor who knows about the assemblage can demand a premium. Agents who miss the plottage play underprice their sellers.
deeper.exam: Assemblage = the process. Plottage = the increased value. The exam swaps them on purpose.

blocks.q: A developer buys three adjoining lots for $1M each and the combined parcel is now worth $3.6M. The $600,000 increase is called:
c: Assemblage
Plottage
Appreciation from depreciation
Highest and best use
blocks.x: Assemblage is the act of combining. Plottage is the increase in value that results.

blocks.caption: Each approach answers "what is it worth" from a different angle. Notice which property types each one fits best.

head: Approach
Logic
Best for
rows: A buyer pays no more than the price of a similar substitute (principle of substitution)
Homes, condos, co-ops, vacant land. The core of every CMA
A buyer pays no more than the cost to build an equal one
New construction, special-purpose buildings (churches, schools, firehouses), insurance
Value is the present worth of future income
Apartment buildings, stores, offices: anything bought for rent

deeper.plain: Compare to similar sales, add up what it would cost to build, or value the rent it brings. Pick based on the property.
deeper.picture: Pricing a used bike: what similar bikes sold for, what a new one costs minus wear, or how much you'd earn renting it out.
deeper.street: A Bronx church has no recent church sales nearby, so the appraiser uses cost. A Riverdale co-op has 15 sales a year in the building, so sales comparison. A Fordham Road strip of stores: income.
deeper.stakes: Valuing an income building like a house ignores the rent roll, which is all an investor cares about.
deeper.exam: Special purpose (churches, schools, firehouses) = cost. Income-producing = income. Homes = sales comparison. Substitution is behind all three.

blocks.html: Find recent sales of similar properties, then adjust each comp to make it look like the subject. The subject never gets adjusted. You know what the comp sold for, so you ask: what would it have sold for if it were just like ours?
blocks.casual: Find recent sales of similar properties, then adjust each comp to look like your property. You never adjust the subject. You know what the comp sold for, so you ask: what would it have sold for if it were just like ours?

deeper.plain: You tweak the sale price of each comparable until it matches the house you're pricing.
deeper.picture: Comparing two phones: yours has 256 GB, the one that sold had 512. You knock some money off the sold phone's price to see what yours would get.
deeper.street: Comp sold for $1.1M with a finished basement; the subject has none, worth about $40,000. Adjust the comp down to $1.06M. That's what the subject would likely bring.
deeper.stakes: Adjust the subject by mistake and every number flips direction, producing a price that's wrong by double the adjustment.
deeper.exam: "Adjustments are made to the..." The answer is always the comparable.

blocks.caption: Watch the arrows: a feature the comp has that the subject lacks pushes the comp's price down.

blocks.title: CBS: Comp Better, Subtract
blocks.html: Comp Better, Subtract. Comp Poorer, Add. You only ever adjust the comparable.
blocks.casual: Comp Better, Subtract. Comp Poorer, Add. You only ever adjust the comparable.

deeper.plain: If the comp is nicer, take money off it. If it's worse, add money to it.
deeper.picture: Leveling a seesaw: if the comp side is heavier (better), you take weight off it to match your side.
deeper.street: Comp has a deck the subject lacks: subtract $15,000. Comp is on a noisy corner the subject avoids: add $20,000.
deeper.stakes: Flip the direction and the CMA is wrong twice over. That's how agents end up overpricing by six figures.
deeper.exam: CBS. The exam gives you one feature and asks add or subtract. Ask yourself only: is the comp better?

blocks.title: Adjusting a Sunnyside comp
blocks.html:
Subject: 2BR condo, 1 bath, no parking. Comp sold 3 months ago for $640,000. Comp has a deeded parking space (worth $30,000) and only a half bath where the subject has a full bath (difference $10,000).
1. Parking: comp better, subtract $30,000 → $610,000
2. Bath: comp poorer, add $10,000 → $620,000
Indicated value from this comp: $620,000.
blocks.casual:
Here's the setup. Subject: 2BR condo, 1 bath, no parking. The comp sold 3 months ago for $640,000. The comp has a deeded parking space (worth $30,000) and only a half bath where the subject has a full bath (a $10,000 difference).
1. Parking: comp is better, so subtract $30,000. That gets you $610,000.
2. Bath: comp is worse, so add $10,000. That gets you $620,000.
This comp points to a value of $620,000.

deeper.plain: Take the comp's sale price, subtract for what it has that you don't, add for what it lacks.
deeper.picture: Like haggling a trade: your car has better tires, theirs has a sunroof. You net out the extras to find an even swap.
deeper.street: New numbers: Leo's subject is a Jackson Heights 1BR with a balcony, no storage cage. Comp sold for $455,000 with a storage cage ($8,000) and no balcony ($15,000). Cage: comp better, subtract $8,000 to $447,000. Balcony: comp poorer, add $15,000 to $462,000. Indicated value: $462,000.
deeper.stakes: If you add when you should subtract, a $23,000 swing becomes a $46,000 error, enough to blow an appraisal.
deeper.exam: Expect two adjustments, one each way. Do them one at a time and write the running total.

blocks.html: Common adjustments, roughly in the order appraisers make them: financing and sale conditions (seller concessions, a family sale), market conditions or time (prices rose 4% since the comp closed), location (park block vs next to the elevated train), then physical features (size, baths, condition, parking, outdoor space, view, floor). Adjustments can be in dollars or percentages. The smaller and fewer the adjustments, the better the comp.
blocks.casual: Appraisers make the common adjustments roughly in this order: financing and sale conditions (seller concessions, a family sale), then market conditions or time (prices rose 4% since the comp closed), then location (park block versus next to the elevated train), then physical features (size, baths, condition, parking, outdoor space, view, floor). Adjustments can be dollars or percentages. Fewer and smaller adjustments mean a better comp.

deeper.plain: First fix odd deal terms, then timing, then location, then the physical stuff.
deeper.picture: Cleaning a stain: you deal with the oil first, then the dirt, then you fluff it up. Order changes the result.
deeper.street: A Forest Hills comp sold for $800,000 eight months ago with a $20,000 seller credit. Remove the concession: $780,000. Market up 5% since: $819,000. Then adjust for the subject's extra half bath.
deeper.stakes: Adjust in the wrong order with percentages and the math drifts. A comp with ten big adjustments isn't really a comp.
deeper.exam: Financing and conditions of sale are adjusted first. The best comp needs the fewest adjustments.

blocks.q: The subject has a finished basement worth $20,000. The comp, which sold for $500,000, does not. The adjusted comp price is:
blocks.x: The comp is poorer than the subject, so add: $500,000 + $20,000 = $520,000. Subtracting would be adjusting the wrong way.

blocks.html: Value = land value + (cost new of the building - accrued depreciation). Cost new is either reproduction cost (an exact replica, same materials) or replacement cost (a building of equal utility with modern materials). Historic brownstones use reproduction for insurance arguments; most appraisals use replacement.
blocks.casual: Here's the formula: value = land value + (cost new of the building minus accrued depreciation). Cost new is either reproduction cost (an exact copy, same materials) or replacement cost (a building that does the same job with modern materials). Historic brownstones get the reproduction argument for insurance. Most appraisals use replacement.

deeper.plain: Figure what it'd cost to build today, knock off for age and flaws, then add the land.
deeper.picture: Valuing a used couch: price of a similar new couch, minus wear and stains, plus the value of the spot it sits in.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Rockaway bungalow. Land $250,000. Replacement cost new: 1,200 sq ft x $350 = $420,000. Depreciation 30% = $126,000. Building $294,000. Total: $294,000 + $250,000 = $544,000.
deeper.stakes: Use reproduction cost when replacement fits and you'll overstate value, maybe badly on a building with hand-carved details nobody needs.
deeper.exam: Reproduction = exact replica. Replacement = same utility, modern materials. Land is added at the end and is never depreciated.

head: Depreciation type
Cause
Curable?
NY example
rows: Bad design or outdated features inside the property
One bath for five bedrooms; bedroom you walk through to reach another
The BQE built next door, a new waste transfer station, a factory closing upstate

deeper.plain: Buildings lose value from wear, from bad design, and from bad stuff outside the lot.
