deeper.picture: A car loses value from rust (physical), from having a tape deck instead of Bluetooth (functional), and from a gas price spike that kills demand (external).
deeper.street: A Sunset Park house: worn roof (physical, curable for $18,000), a bedroom you walk through to reach another (functional), and a new truck depot across the street (external, can't be fixed by the owner).
deeper.stakes: Mislabel external obsolescence as fixable and you tell a seller to spend money that won't help.
deeper.exam: External obsolescence is always incurable. Functional is inside the property and can go either way. Physical is wear and tear.

blocks.title: External is always incurable
blocks.html: The owner cannot fix a highway or a recession. Any answer that calls external obsolescence curable is wrong. And land never depreciates in the cost approach.
blocks.casual: The owner can't fix a highway or a recession. Any answer calling external obsolescence curable is wrong. And land never depreciates in the cost approach.

deeper.plain: Problems outside your property line are out of your control, so they're incurable.
deeper.picture: You can repaint your apartment. You can't repaint the subway line that rattles your windows.
deeper.street: When the BQE was cut through Brooklyn Heights and Cobble Hill, houses along the trench lost value. No owner could cure that with a renovation.
deeper.stakes: Tell a buyer they can renovate away a neighbor problem and they'll overpay and feel misled.
deeper.exam: Two easy points: external is always incurable, and land never depreciates.

blocks.html: Effective age is how old the building acts, based on condition; actual (chronological) age is how old it is. A well-kept 1920s firehouse with new systems might have an effective age of 15 years. The age-life method divides effective age by total economic life to get the percentage of depreciation.
blocks.casual: Effective age is how old the building acts, based on its condition. Actual (chronological) age is how old it really is. A well-kept 1920s firehouse with new systems might have an effective age of 15 years. The age-life method divides effective age by total economic life to get the depreciation percentage.

deeper.plain: A well-maintained old building can act young. Depreciation uses how old it acts, not its birthday.
deeper.picture: A 60-year-old marathon runner may have the knees of a 40-year-old. Doctors care about the knees.
deeper.street: New numbers: a 1965 Flushing garden building, renovated in 2015, has effective age 20 and economic life 50. Depreciation: 20 / 50 = 40%. On $2,000,000 cost new, that's $800,000 off.
deeper.stakes: Use actual age on a renovated building and you'll overstate depreciation and undervalue it.
deeper.exam: Age-life: effective age / total economic life = percent depreciated. Don't plug in actual age.

blocks.title: Cost approach on the parish firehouse
blocks.html:
Land value (from vacant lot sales): $400,000
Replacement cost new: 4,000 sq ft x $300 = $1,200,000
Depreciation by age-life: effective age 15 / economic life 60 = 25%. $1,200,000 x 25% = $300,000
Depreciated building: $1,200,000 - $300,000 = $900,000
Add land: $900,000 + $400,000 = $1,300,000
blocks.casual:
Walk the parish firehouse through it:
Land (from vacant lot sales): $400,000
Replacement cost new: 4,000 sq ft x $300 = $1,200,000
Depreciation by age-life: effective age 15 / economic life 60 = 25%. $1,200,000 x 25% = $300,000
Building after depreciation: $1,200,000 minus $300,000 = $900,000
Add the land: $900,000 + $400,000 = $1,300,000

deeper.plain: Building cost, minus wear, plus land. Do the depreciation on the building only.
deeper.picture: Price a used food truck: new truck cost, minus wear, plus the value of the permit spot it comes with.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Mount Vernon community hall. Land $300,000. Cost new: 6,000 sq ft x $250 = $1,500,000. Effective age 12 / life 48 = 25%, so $375,000. Building: $1,125,000. Plus land: $1,425,000.
deeper.stakes: Depreciate the land too and you knock off $100,000 that shouldn't come off. That's a wrong answer and a wrong price.
deeper.exam: The classic error choice depreciates land. Another multiplies by actual age. Find the depreciated building first, then add land.

blocks.html: For small rentals, use a gross rent multiplier (GRM): sale price / monthly gross rent, taken from comps, then applied to the subject. A gross income multiplier (GIM) does the same with annual gross income and is used for bigger or commercial properties.
blocks.casual: For small rentals, use a gross rent multiplier (GRM): sale price divided by monthly gross rent, taken from comps, then applied to your property. A gross income multiplier (GIM) does the same with annual gross income and is used for bigger or commercial properties.

deeper.plain: See how many months of rent similar buildings sold for, then multiply your rent by that.
deeper.picture: If similar food carts sell for 20 months of their sales, yours probably will too.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Bronx two-family comp sold for $780,000 renting $4,000 a month. GRM = 195. Subject rents $4,300. Value: $4,300 x 195 = $838,500.
deeper.stakes: GRM ignores expenses. A building with sky-high taxes looks better than it is, so investors check NOI too.
deeper.exam: GRM uses monthly rent; GIM uses annual income. Watch which one the stem gives you.

blocks.title: GRM on a Queens two-family
blocks.html:
Comps: sold $900,000 renting $5,000/month (GRM 180); sold $936,000 renting $5,200 (GRM 180).
Subject rents for $5,400/month.
$5,400 x 180 = $972,000
blocks.casual:
Comps: one sold for $900,000 renting $5,000 a month (GRM 180), another sold for $936,000 renting $5,200 (GRM 180).
The subject rents for $5,400 a month.
$5,400 x 180 = $972,000

deeper.plain: Divide each comp's price by its rent to get the multiplier, then use it on your rent.
deeper.picture: Like a currency exchange rate. Learn the rate from the comps, convert your rent into a price.
deeper.street: New numbers: two Ozone Park comps: $840,000 at $4,200 a month (GRM 200) and $880,000 at $4,400 (GRM 200). Subject rents $4,600. $4,600 x 200 = $920,000.
deeper.stakes: If the comps' GRMs are all over the place, the method is shaky. Don't present one number as gospel.
deeper.exam: Two-step: price / rent = GRM, then rent x GRM = value. Don't mix monthly rent with an annual multiplier.

blocks.html: For larger income property, use direct capitalization: Value = NOI / cap rate. NOI is effective gross income minus operating expenses. Debt service, depreciation, and income tax are never operating expenses.
blocks.casual: For bigger income property, use direct capitalization: value = NOI / cap rate. NOI is effective gross income minus operating expenses. Debt service, depreciation, and income tax are never operating expenses.

deeper.plain: Value is the yearly profit divided by the return investors expect.
deeper.picture: If a savings account pays 5% and gives you $5,000 a year, it holds $100,000. Same math for a building.
deeper.street: New numbers: Evelyn's Bay Ridge storefront building nets $84,000 NOI. Market cap rate 6%. Value: $84,000 / 0.06 = $1,400,000.
deeper.stakes: Subtract the mortgage payment as an expense and NOI drops, value drops, and you lowball your seller.
deeper.exam: Mortgage payments are NOT operating expenses. The exam slips debt service into the expense list on purpose.

blocks.title: Sal's Astoria six-family
blocks.html:
Potential gross income: 6 units x $2,500 x 12 = $180,000
Vacancy and collection loss 5%: - $9,000
Effective gross income: $171,000
Operating expenses (taxes, insurance, repairs, utilities, management): - $61,000
NOI: $110,000
Market cap rate from comps: 5.5%
$110,000 / 0.055 = $2,000,000
blocks.casual:
Sal's Astoria six-family, step by step:
Potential gross income: 6 units x $2,500 x 12 = $180,000
Vacancy and collection loss at 5%: minus $9,000
Effective gross income: $171,000
Operating expenses (taxes, insurance, repairs, utilities, management): minus $61,000
NOI: $110,000
Market cap rate from comps: 5.5%
$110,000 / 0.055 = $2,000,000

deeper.plain: Start with full rent, knock off vacancy, knock off expenses, divide by the cap rate.
deeper.picture: A lemonade stand: what you'd make selling every cup, minus the cups you don't sell, minus lemons and sugar, gives you profit.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Ridgewood eight-unit. 8 x $2,200 x 12 = $211,200. Vacancy 4%: minus $8,448, EGI $202,752. Expenses $72,752. NOI $130,000. Cap 6.5%: $130,000 / 0.065 = $2,000,000.
deeper.stakes: Skip vacancy and you overstate value. Investors catch it right away and stop trusting your numbers.
deeper.exam: Order: PGI, minus vacancy, = EGI, minus OpEx, = NOI, divide by cap. Convert the cap rate percent to a decimal.

blocks.title: Cap rate and value move opposite
blocks.html: Same NOI, higher cap rate, lower value. $110,000 at 5.5% is $2M; at 6.5% it is about $1.69M. Riskier property means a higher cap rate and a lower price.
blocks.casual: Same NOI, higher cap rate, lower value. $110,000 at 5.5% is $2M; at 6.5% it's about $1.69M. Riskier property means a higher cap rate and a lower price.

deeper.plain: Cap rate is in the bottom of the fraction. Make it bigger and value gets smaller.
deeper.picture: A seesaw: cap rate goes up, value goes down.
deeper.street: New numbers: $90,000 NOI. At 5% that's $1.8M. At 6% it's $1.5M. One point of cap rate costs the seller $300,000.
deeper.stakes: When interest rates rise, cap rates usually follow and building values fall. Sellers anchored to last year's price get hurt.
deeper.exam: "If the cap rate increases, value..." decreases. Higher risk, higher cap rate.

blocks.q: A building has NOI of $80,000 and comparable buildings sell at an 8% cap rate. Its indicated value is:
blocks.x: Value = NOI / rate = $80,000 / 0.08 = $1,000,000. Multiplying ($6,400) or using the wrong decimal gives the distractors.

blocks.html: Finally, reconciliation: the appraiser weighs the approaches, giving most weight to the one that fits the property best. It is a judgment, not a simple average.
blocks.casual: Last step is reconciliation. The appraiser weighs the approaches and gives the most weight to the one that fits the property best. It's a judgment call, not a simple average.

deeper.plain: The appraiser picks the final number by trusting the most fitting method most.
deeper.picture: Three friends guess the bill. You trust the one who actually read the receipt more than the one who guessed.
deeper.street: Sal's building: income approach says $2.0M, sales comparison $1.95M, cost $1.7M. The appraiser lands at $2.0M, leaning on income because it's a rental.
deeper.stakes: Averaging all three would drag the value down by the least relevant method.
deeper.exam: Reconciliation is NOT averaging. Any answer saying "averages the three approaches" is the trap.

blocks.title: Preparing the CMA

items.title: Collect data
items.html: Subject details (size, layout, condition, taxes, maintenance), public records, MLS, ACRIS in NYC.

items.title: List past sales
items.html: Comparable sales within the last 12 months, as close and as similar as possible.

items.title: Add expireds and competition
items.html: Actives show the competition; expireds show the ceiling buyers rejected.

items.title: Adjust
items.html: Adjust each comp toward the subject: comp better, subtract; comp poorer, add.

items.title: Formulate a price
items.html: Weigh the most similar comps most heavily and give the seller a range with a recommended list price.

blocks.casual:
Collect data: subject details (size, layout, condition, taxes, maintenance), public records, the MLS, and ACRIS in NYC.
List past sales: comps from the last 12 months, as close and as similar as you can get.
Add expireds and competition: actives show what you're up against, expireds show the ceiling buyers turned down.
Adjust: move each comp toward the subject. Comp better, subtract. Comp poorer, add.
Formulate a price: trust the most similar comps most and give the seller a range with a recommended list price.

deeper.plain: Gather facts, find sales, check the competition, adjust, and suggest a range.
deeper.picture: Like planning a road trip: get the map, see past routes, check traffic now, adjust for detours, then pick a plan.
deeper.street: For a Woodside condo, Jordan pulls 6 sales from the last year, 3 actives, and 1 expired. After adjusting, the range is $510,000 to $535,000, and Jordan recommends listing at $529,000.
deeper.stakes: Skip a step and the seller gets a number you can't defend when the first offer comes in low.
deeper.exam: Comps from about the last 12 months. The result is a range, not a single guaranteed price.

blocks.title: From three comps to a range
blocks.html:
Subject: Park Slope 2BR co-op, 1,000 sq ft.
Comp A sold $1,050,000, has washer/dryer (+$25,000 feature): adjusted $1,025,000
Comp B sold $980,000, lower floor, no view (subject has view, $30,000): adjusted $1,010,000
Comp C sold $1,020,000, nearly identical: adjusted $1,020,000
Range $1,010,000 to $1,025,000. Comp C needed the fewest adjustments, so it gets the most weight. Recommended list: about $1,025,000 to $1,049,000.
Why list above the range? The range estimates what a buyer will pay, not the asking price. Park Slope 2BRs usually trade a little under ask after negotiation, so pricing at or just above the top of the range leaves room to land inside it. Pricing far above the range is the overpricing trap: the listing goes stale and ends up selling below value.
blocks.casual:
Subject: Park Slope 2BR co-op, 1,000 sq ft.
Comp A sold for $1,050,000 and has a washer/dryer (a $25,000 feature): adjusted $1,025,000
Comp B sold for $980,000, lower floor, no view (the subject has a view, worth $30,000): adjusted $1,010,000
Comp C sold for $1,020,000, nearly identical: adjusted $1,020,000
So the range is $1,010,000 to $1,025,000. Comp C needed the fewest adjustments, so it gets the most weight. Recommended list: about $1,025,000 to $1,049,000.

deeper.plain: Adjust each comp, look at the spread, and trust the one you changed least.
deeper.picture: Three bathroom scales give slightly different readings. You trust the one that was just calibrated.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Fort Greene 1BR. Comp A $720,000 with a terrace ($40,000): $680,000. Comp B $660,000, needs a new kitchen ($25,000): $685,000. Comp C $690,000, near identical: $690,000. Lean on C, value about $690,000, list around $699,000.
deeper.stakes: Lean on the comp with the most adjustments and your range rests on guesses.
deeper.exam: Most weight goes to the comp with the fewest and smallest adjustments, not to the average.

blocks.title: Fewest adjustments wins
blocks.html: The comp you had to adjust the least is the most reliable. Lean on it when you reconcile, and tell the seller why.
blocks.casual: The comp you had to adjust least is the most reliable. Lean on it when you reconcile, and tell the seller why.

deeper.plain: The more alike the comp, the more you trust it.
deeper.picture: To guess your twin's weight, your own weight beats a stranger's every time.
deeper.street: Two Harlem brownstone comps: one needed a $200,000 swing for size and condition, the other $15,000 for a missing deck. Jordan tells the seller the second one drives the price.
deeper.stakes: Explaining this keeps sellers from cherry-picking the one high comp they like.
deeper.exam: Fewest adjustments = most reliable comp. Expect it in a reconciliation question.

blocks.q: Which approach would an appraiser rely on most for a 100-year-old church being converted to a community center?
c: Sales comparison
Cost
Income
Gross rent multiplier
blocks.x: Special-purpose buildings rarely sell and do not produce rent, so the cost approach fits best. Sales comparison needs comps that do not exist.

story.title: Three Files, Three Tools
story.setting: Hudson & Hart Realty, a Monday morning in Brooklyn

beats.text: Condo in Sunnyside, a firehouse the parish converted, Sal's six-family. Match each to an approach.
Condo is comps. Lots of sales in the building. Sales comparison.
Firehouse... nobody sells firehouses every week. Cost approach: land plus what it costs to build, minus depreciation.
And mine? My building makes money. You tell me what the money's worth.
NOI of $110,000, cap rate 5.5%, so about $2 million.
My cousin says his building got a 7% cap. So mine is worth more at 7, right?

check.q: If Sal's NOI stays $110,000 and the cap rate is 7% instead of 5.5%, the value:
c: Rises
Falls
Stays the same
Doubles
check.x: Value = NOI / rate. A bigger divisor gives a smaller value: about $1.57M at 7%.

beats.text: Other way, Sal. Higher cap rate, lower price. Your cousin's building is riskier or in a cheaper spot.
Afternoon. Jordan adjusts a comp for Leo's condo. The comp has parking. Leo's doesn't.
So you add the parking to my number?
I subtract it from the comp. Comp better, subtract. We never touch your unit's numbers.
beats.tag: Adjust the comp, never the subject

beats.text: And knock some off that firehouse. Roof's tired, that's physical. One bathroom for a hall that seats 200, that's functional. And the new bus depot across the street? Nobody can fix that.
Easy. Average the three approaches and call it a day.
Reconciliation is weighing, not averaging. Give the most weight to the approach that fits the property. Three files, three tools. You chose right.

board.prompt: Draw three columns (sales comparison, cost, income). Under each, write its formula and two NY property types it fits best.

facts.text: Highest and best use must be legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and maximally productive, tested in that order.
Highest and best use is tested as vacant and as improved; when the land alone is worth more than land plus building, the answer is demolition.
Substitution: a buyer pays no more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute, the principle behind all three approaches.
Contribution: a feature is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost, so overimprovements rarely pay back.
Regression pulls the best house on the block down toward its neighbors and progression pulls a modest one up; value is highest when a home conforms.
Anticipation: value is the present worth of expected future benefits, so an announced subway station lifts prices before it opens.
Site valuation values land as if vacant and ready for its highest and best use, mainly from vacant lot sales; land never depreciates.
Assemblage combines adjacent lots; plottage is the extra value of the combined lot over the sum of its parts.
Sales comparison fits homes, condos, co-ops and land; cost fits new or special-purpose buildings; income fits property bought for rent.
Only the comparable is adjusted, never the subject: comp better, subtract; comp poorer, add.
Adjustments usually go financing and sale conditions first, then market conditions (time), then location, then physical features; fewer and smaller adjustments mean a better comp.
Cost approach: value = land value + (cost new of the building - accrued depreciation).
Reproduction cost builds an exact replica; replacement cost builds equal utility with modern materials.
Physical deterioration is wear and tear and functional obsolescence is bad design inside the property (such as a walk-through bedroom); both can be curable or incurable.
External (economic) obsolescence comes from outside the property line and is always incurable.
Effective age reflects condition while actual age is chronological; age-life depreciation = effective age / total economic life.
A gross rent multiplier is sale price / monthly gross rent from comps, applied to the subject's rent; a GIM uses annual gross income.
Value = NOI / cap rate, where NOI is effective gross income minus operating expenses; debt service, depreciation and income tax are not operating expenses.
The cap rate is NOI / value, and at the same NOI a higher cap rate means a lower value.
Reconciliation weighs the approaches, giving most weight to the one that fits the property best; it is not a simple average.
A CMA uses comparable sales from the last 12 months, plus actives and expireds, adjusts each comp toward the subject, and gives a range with a recommended list price.
The comp needing the fewest adjustments gets the most weight, and listing at or just above the top of the range leaves room for negotiation.

lessons.title: Case file: The Pool on Bement Avenue
lessons.tagline: The sellers spent $95,000 on a pool and want $1,150,000 because the neighbors are asking that. Jordan has four good comps, one bad one, and a kitchen table conversation to get through.
objectives: Select comparable sales for a CMA, excluding non-arm's-length and stale sales and converting concessions to cash equivalent.
Derive adjustments from paired sales and market data, and apply them in the right direction for time, size, features and condition.
Reconcile adjusted comps into a value range and recommended list price, weighting the comps that needed the least adjustment.
Explain a CMA's conclusions to sellers who are anchored on cost, asking prices and a competing agent's promise, and document the advice.

blocks.title: West Brighton, Staten Island
blocks.html: Lorraine and Frank Bellamy have lived in their 1925 colonial on Bement Avenue for 31 years. Three bedrooms, one and a half baths, 1,650 square feet, a detached one-car garage, a kitchen they redid in 2019, and an in-ground pool they put in two summers ago for $95,000 so the grandkids would visit. Now they are moving to be near those grandkids in North Carolina. A house around the corner just listed at $1,150,000. "Ours has a pool," Frank says. "So we're at least there." Marcus, from Jordan's own office, stopped by last week and told them he could "probably get eleven." Diane gave the listing appointment to Jordan anyway. Jordan has five days to build a CMA that the Bellamys will believe.

A comparative market analysis is an opinion of a likely price range, built from what similar houses actually sold for. Its power comes from the evidence, and its credibility comes from showing the work. Sellers do not argue with a number nearly as hard as they argue with a number they cannot trace.

Jordan pulled every sale of a detached one- or two-story house within half a mile, built before 1950, 1,400 to 2,000 square feet, from the MLS, and cross-checked prices against recorded deeds (Staten Island deeds are recorded with the Richmond County Clerk) and the city's published sales data. The search returned seven sales in the past 18 months. Two needed a closer look.

blocks.title: Where New York City sale data lives
blocks.html: In Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx, recorded deeds and mortgages are searchable online in ACRIS. Staten Island documents are recorded with the Richmond County Clerk. The city's Department of Finance also publishes recorded sales for all five boroughs. The MLS adds what deeds cannot: days on market, price changes, concessions and condition remarks. A good CMA uses both.

blocks.title: Two sales that need a second look
blocks.html:
Sale D, Davis Avenue: sold 4 months ago for $700,000. 1,700 sq ft, 2 baths, garage. Deed shows the grantor is an estate, executor Mary Kovac; grantee Daniel Kovac. Never listed on the MLS.
Sale F, Oakland Avenue: sold 16 months ago for $835,000. Very similar to the subject, no pool.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do with Sales D and F?
c: Leave both out: D was not arm's length, and F falls outside the 12-month window
Use both, since recorded deed prices are the most reliable evidence there is
Use D but not F, since an estate sale reflects a motivated seller's real price
Use F but not D, since a 16-month sale just needs a larger time adjustment
blocks.x: Comparable sales should be arm's-length transactions, exposed to the market, between unrelated parties. A sale from an estate to a family member who shares the name, never listed, fails that test. The syllabus standard for a CMA is sales within the last 12 months, and with four good recent sales there is no need to stretch to 16. The tempting answer keeps F with a time adjustment; that works when recent data is thin, not when it is plentiful.

blocks.html: Jordan also checked each remaining sale's MLS history, not just its closing price: how long it was on the market, whether the price was cut, and any remarks about condition or special terms. A sale that closed fast at full price and one that sat for four months with two reductions tell different stories about the same street, even at similar prices.

That left four sales: A, B, C and E. Sale E needed one more correction before it could be compared to anything. The MLS record showed it closed at $940,000 with a $25,000 seller concession toward the buyer's closing costs.

blocks.q: How should Jordan treat Sale E's $25,000 seller concession?
c: Add $25,000, since the seller gave up money and the house was worth more
Subtract $25,000 to state the sale in cash-equivalent terms
Ignore it, since closing costs have nothing to do with the house
Drop the sale, since any sale with a concession is not arm's length
blocks.x: Market value assumes cash or its equivalent. When a seller pays $25,000 of the buyer's costs, the buyer effectively paid $915,000 for the house, so the comp is adjusted down. The tempting answer adds the concession, reasoning that the seller lost money; but the question is what the house brought, and the concession inflated the contract price. A concession does not make a sale non-arm's-length; it just needs adjusting.

blocks.text: Where the adjustment numbers come from

blocks.html: Adjustments are not guesses. Each dollar figure should come from the market. Jordan built four of them from paired sales: two sales nearly identical except for one feature, so the price difference isolates that feature's value.

blocks.title: Paired sales Jordan used
blocks.html:
Garage: 112 and 118 Bard Avenue, same builder, same size, both updated, sold six weeks apart. One has a detached garage: $880,000. One does not: $855,000.
Pool: two Castleton Corners colonials, same size, sold a month apart: with pool $918,000; without $898,000.
Kitchen: a resale of the same house: sold $812,000 with original kitchen; resold 14 months later after a new kitchen for $860,000, while the area index rose about 2% in that time.
Time: repeat sales and the area's median price show values rising about 0.3% per month over the past year.

blocks.q: What garage adjustment do the Bard Avenue sales support?
blocks.x: $880,000 minus $855,000 is $25,000, and because the two houses match on everything else, that difference is the market's price for a detached garage there. The tempting answer is $30,000, a round number many agents use from habit. A paired sale beats a rule of thumb because it comes from buyers in this neighborhood, recently.

blocks.html: The kitchen pair needed one extra step: the later sale also captured market growth. About 2% on $812,000 is roughly $16,000, so of the $48,000 increase, about $32,000 was the kitchen. Jordan used $30,000. Size was the last big one. Jordan used $200 per square foot for differences in living area, and Frank immediately objected.

blocks.q: Frank says: "Our house is worth about $570 a square foot. Why adjust size at only $200?" Jordan's best answer?
c: Because $200 a square foot is a fixed figure that New York appraisers are required to use
Because smaller houses consistently sell for less per square foot than larger ones
Because Staten Island adjustments are capped by the city at $200 per square foot
Because land and location carry much of the price, so added space adds less
blocks.x: Average price per square foot spreads the whole price, including land, location and features, over the footage. One more square foot of an otherwise identical house adds only the value of that space, which is far less. Jordan derived $200 from size differences in the paired data. The tempting answer is that smaller houses sell for less per square foot; the opposite is usually true, which is why average price per square foot misleads.

blocks.title: Adjust the comp, never the subject
blocks.html: Every adjustment answers one question: what would this comp have sold for if it were just like the subject? Comp better, subtract. Comp poorer, add. The subject's features never move. Sellers instinctively want to "add for our pool" to an average of the comps. That double counts: the pool adjustment goes on each comp that lacks one.

head: Sale A
Sale B
Sale C
Sale E
blocks.caption: Jordan's adjustment grid for 1,650 sq ft, 3BR, 1.5 bath, garage, updated kitchen, pool

blocks.q: Sale B closed 8 months ago in a market rising 0.3% a month. Why is its time adjustment a positive $20,900?
c: Older sales are penalized for their age, so the adjustment is a deduction
Sellers deserve credit for waiting, so time is added to every sale
Time adjustments are added when a comp is larger than the subject
It closed in a cheaper market, so it is adjusted up to today's levels
blocks.x: A comp that sold when prices were lower would sell for more today, so in a rising market its price is adjusted upward: 8 months at 0.3% is 2.4% of $872,000, about $20,900. The tempting answer treats age as a defect to subtract; that only fits a falling market. Time adjustments track the market's direction, not the comp's size.

blocks.q: Sale C is 250 square feet larger than the subject. Using the grid's rate, what is the size adjustment and why?
c: Plus $50,000, because the subject is smaller and needs to catch up
Minus $142,500, using the subject's $570 average price per foot
Minus $50,000, because the comp is better and gets the deduction
Plus $142,500, because larger houses earn the average price per foot
blocks.x: 250 square feet times $200 is $50,000. The comp has more space than the subject, so the comp is better, and comp better means subtract. The tempting answer adds the amount to the subject, which breaks the core rule: you adjust the comp toward the subject, never the reverse. Using the average price per foot overstates what extra space adds.

blocks.html: Two numbers at the bottom of the grid matter as much as the adjusted prices. Net adjustment is the sum of the pluses and minuses; gross adjustment is the total of all of them, ignoring sign. A comp can net to almost nothing while needing large adjustments in both directions, and that comp is less like the subject than its net suggests. Many appraisers treat gross adjustments above roughly 25% as a sign the comp is a weak match. All four of Jordan's comps stayed well under that.

The four adjusted prices ran from $925,900 to $973,700. A straight average is about $953,900. Jordan did not average. Each comp's reliability depends on how much it had to be changed to look like the subject: the less adjustment, the less room for error.

blocks.q: Which comp deserves the most weight in Jordan's reconciliation?
c: Sale E, because it produced the highest adjusted value of the four
Sale A, because it was adjusted for more features than any other
Sale C, because it needed the least total adjustment, 7.2% gross
No single comp; the fair method is a straight average of the four
blocks.x: Reconciliation is judgment, not arithmetic: the comp that needed the smallest gross adjustment is the most similar and the most reliable, so Sale C gets the most weight. Gross adjustment (total of all adjustments, ignoring sign) matters more than net, because big pluses and minuses can cancel and hide a poor match. The tempting answer averages, which gives Sale A, the weakest comp, equal say.

blocks.title: Jordan's weighting
blocks.html:
Sale C 40% x $925,900 = $370,360
Sale E 25% x $973,700 = $243,425
Sale B 20% x $952,900 = $190,580
Sale A 15% x $963,100 = $144,465
Weighted indication: about $949,000. Likely sale range: $925,000 to $975,000. Recommended list price: $969,000.

head: Assets
Drawbacks
rows: In-ground pool, rare at this price point
One and a half baths for three bedrooms
Original 1925 windows on the second floor
Mid-block on a street with bus traffic
Walk to the ferry bus and shopping on Forest Avenue
Pool adds maintenance and insurance cost some buyers avoid
blocks.caption: Market position: how the house stacks up against what buyers will see

blocks.html: The syllabus's list for a residential market analysis goes beyond comps: buyer appeal, market position, assets, drawbacks, area market conditions, and recommended terms. Jordan's page on area conditions showed inventory in West Brighton at about three months of supply, median days on market of 34, and mortgage rates that had been stable for half a year. Recommended terms covered more than price: a 45 to 60 day closing to suit the Bellamys' move, the pool covered and winterized for showings after Labor Day, and a pre-listing inspection so buyers would not discover the second-floor windows on their own.

blocks.text: What the market is not saying

blocks.html: A CMA also shows the competition and the market's rejections. The house around the corner was the Bellamys' anchor. Another listing had died on the vine last spring.

head: Status
Property
Price
Days on market
Notes
rows: Around the corner, 4BR, 2 bath, 1,850 sq ft, pool, garage
Two price reductions already discussed with seller's agent
Henderson Avenue, 3BR, 1.5 bath, 1,600 sq ft, garage
Elizabeth Street, 3BR, 2 bath, 1,750 sq ft, garage, no pool
blocks.caption: Competition and expireds

blocks.q: What does the $1,150,000 active listing tell the Bellamys about their value?
c: That their house, with a pool, is worth at least the same $1,150,000
That a seller is asking that much; at 45 days, buyers have not agreed
That the CMA is wrong, since active listings are the newest data there is
That the neighbor's agent has set the ceiling price for the entire block
blocks.x: An active listing is an asking price: what one seller hopes for. It shows the competition the Bellamys' buyers will compare against, but it is not evidence of value until a buyer agrees. Forty-five days with no contract and talk of reductions suggests the market disagrees. The tempting answer treats the newest number as the best one; in a CMA, closed sales are the evidence and actives are the context.

blocks.q: What is the most useful lesson of the Elizabeth Street expired listing?
c: Buyers already rejected a similar house at $1,049,000 for 140 days
Its $1,049,000 price sets a floor below which the Bellamys should not go
Expired listings carry little weight, since they did not produce a closed sale
The listing agent failed, so a better agent could get $1,049,000 today
blocks.x: Expireds show what the market would not pay. A comparable house without a pool sat at $1,049,000 for 140 days and never sold, which is strong evidence that pricing there will not work. The tempting answer dismisses expireds because they did not close, but rejection is information. Blaming the agent ignores 140 days of buyers walking past.

blocks.html: Jordan walked the Bellamys through the grid line by line. Lorraine followed the logic. Frank kept coming back to the pool.

blocks.q: Frank: "The pool cost $95,000. How can you only give it $20,000?" What principle is Jordan applying?
c: Contribution: a feature is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost
Substitution: buyers pay no more than a pool would cost to install new
Regression: the house is the best on the block, so value drops toward neighbors
Anticipation: buyers expect pool prices to fall, so they discount it now
blocks.x: Contribution says a component is worth what it adds to market value, measured here by the paired pool sales at about $20,000. Cost is what the Bellamys spent; value is what buyers pay. Substitution is the tempting answer because it involves cost, but substitution says a buyer will not pay more than the cost of an equal substitute, which would cap the pool at $95,000, not explain why it adds less.

blocks.html: Then Frank brought up Marcus. "He says eleven. Why should we list with you at nine-something?"

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle Marcus's $1,100,000 suggestion?
c: Match it, since the sellers choose the agent and the list price anyway
Tell the Bellamys that Marcus is lying and should be reported to the state
Raise the CMA to $1,050,000 to keep the listing and sort out price later
Show the evidence, explain why overpricing stalls, and hold the CMA
blocks.x: Quoting an inflated price to win a listing is "buying the listing," a breach of the duties of care and honesty, and it usually ends in reductions and a stale listing that sells below what accurate pricing would have brought. The tempting answer splits the difference to keep the business; that is the same breach in a smaller size. Jordan can let the evidence answer Marcus without attacking a colleague.

blocks.html: The Bellamys signed the listing but insisted on $1,025,000. Jordan's advice was $969,000.

blocks.q: The Bellamys insist on $1,025,000 over Jordan's advice. What should Jordan do?
c: Refuse the listing, since listing above the CMA violates license law
Accept, since sellers set the price, and put the advice in writing
Accept, then quietly market the house to buyers as priced at $969,000
Accept, and label the CMA an appraisal so the price looks supported
blocks.x: The seller decides the list price; the agent advises. Jordan can take the listing at the sellers' price and should document the CMA, the recommendation and the sellers' decision. Refusing is not required by law, which is the tempting answer for an agent who wants to be principled. Marketing a different price than the seller authorized breaks obedience, and calling a CMA an appraisal is a misrepresentation.

blocks.html: Lorraine had one more request: her bank wanted a valuation for a bridge loan, and could Jordan just "put appraisal at the top" of the CMA? Jordan explained that a CMA may never be called an appraisal; only a state licensed or certified appraiser can produce one, and the bank would order its own. The CMA could go to the bank as what it was.

blocks.title: Jordan's pricing memo, signed by the sellers
blocks.html:
Date: September 8. Property: Bement Avenue, West Brighton.
1. CMA delivered and reviewed in person. Supported value range $925,000 to $975,000; weighted indication about $949,000.
2. Licensee recommendation: list at $969,000.
3. Sellers' decision: list at $1,025,000. Sellers understand this is above the supported range and may lengthen time on market and require later reductions.
4. Review of price and market activity after 21 days.
Acknowledged: Lorraine Bellamy, Frank Bellamy. Licensee: Jordan Reyes, Licensed Real Estate Salesperson, Hudson & Hart Realty.

The memo was not a threat or a told-you-so. It turned the 21-day review into a scheduled event rather than an awkward phone call, and it protected Jordan and the firm if the Bellamys later claimed they had been misled about price.

The house hit the market at $1,025,000 on a Thursday. The first open house drew nine groups, mostly neighbors. After 21 days: two private showings, no offers, and the same feedback twice: "Loved the pool. Priced way above what we've seen sell." Jordan's weekly report put the numbers next to the CMA.

blocks.q: Based on 21 days of activity, what is the best recommendation?
c: Hold the price, since spring buyers will eventually pay for the pool
Add a $50,000 buyer concession so the asking price can stay the same
Reduce to the CMA's recommended $969,000, inside the supported range
Take the house off the market and relist at the same price next season
blocks.x: Few showings, no offers and consistent price feedback mean the market has answered. Moving to $969,000 puts the house where buyers searching in the supported range will see it. The tempting answer is a big concession: it keeps the headline price but creates the same cash-equivalent problem appraisers adjust out, and it does nothing for buyers whose searches top out under $1,000,000.

blocks.html: The Bellamys reduced to $969,000. Eight days later they accepted $955,000 from a couple with two kids and a dog, with a 45-day closing. The buyer's appraisal came in at $955,000. Frank told Jordan at the closing that he still thought the pool was worth more. Lorraine told Diane that Jordan's grid was the reason she agreed to the reduction.

The appraisal matching the contract was not luck. The buyer's appraiser used three of the same four sales Jordan had used, because they were the best evidence available to anyone who looked. When a CMA is built from arm's-length, recent, well-adjusted sales, it tends to land near where an appraiser lands, and that is the strongest argument for pricing from it: a contract the appraisal supports is a contract that closes. Had the Bellamys found a buyer at $1,025,000, the appraisal would likely have come in well short, and the deal would have been renegotiated or lost anyway.

items: Use arm's-length sales from the last 12 months; drop family and estate transfers that never hit the market. Restate concession sales in cash-equivalent terms.
Derive adjustments from paired sales and market trends, not habit. Adjust size at the marginal rate, not average price per square foot.
Adjust the comp toward the subject: comp better, subtract; comp poorer, add. In a rising market, older sales adjust up.
Reconcile by weighting the comps with the smallest gross adjustments; do not just average.
Actives are asking prices, expireds are rejections, solds are evidence. Cost is not value; contribution is.
Sellers set the list price. Advise honestly, never buy the listing, never call a CMA an appraisal, and document the advice.

lessons.title: Case file: The Appraisal Came In Low on Fifth Avenue
lessons.tagline: A Sunset Park storefront with two apartments, a CMA at $1.4 million, a contract at $1.395 million, and a bank appraisal at $1.31 million. Three approaches, one gap, and a phone call Jordan must not make.
objectives: Apply the income approach (NOI, capitalization rate, gross income multiplier), the sales comparison approach and the cost approach to one mixed-use property, and reconcile them.
Distinguish a licensee's CMA from a licensed appraiser's appraisal in purpose, standards, and who may prepare it.
Calculate the effect of a low appraisal on a loan and the buyer's cash, and choose the proper response under appraiser independence rules.
Distinguish market value from investment value, insurable value and highest and best use as improved.

blocks.title: Fifth Avenue, Sunset Park
blocks.html: Hector Alvarado ran a hardware store on the ground floor of his three-story building on Fifth Avenue in Sunset Park for 34 years and lived upstairs until his kids grew up. Now he is retiring. The store is leased to a bakery, and both apartments are rented. Jordan prepared a CMA from mixed-use sales and listed the building at $1,425,000. Evelyn Park, through her LLC, signed a contract at $1,395,000 with a mortgage contingency, planning to borrow 70% of the price. Twenty-three days later, her lender's appraisal arrived: $1,310,000. Hector called Jordan before Jordan had finished reading it. "Call the appraiser. Tell him about the sales on Fourth Avenue. He obviously missed something."

Before Jordan returns that call, it helps to see the building the way the appraiser did. A lender's appraisal is not a better CMA. It is a different product, made by a different professional, under different rules, for a different client.

blocks.q: Hector asks what the difference is between Jordan's CMA and the bank's appraisal. Which answer is accurate?
c: They are the same analysis, but the appraisal costs more because a bank orders it
An appraisal is a CMA that the seller's broker certifies and files with the buyer's lender
A CMA becomes an appraisal once it includes at least three closed comparable sales
A CMA is a licensee's price opinion; an appraisal follows USPAP and needs a license
blocks.x: A CMA is a real estate licensee's opinion of a likely price range for pricing a listing or an offer; by law it may never be called an appraisal. An appraisal is prepared by a state licensed or certified appraiser (licensed by the Department of State under Executive Law Article 6-E) following professional standards (USPAP), here for the lender as client. The tempting last answer treats the number of comps as the dividing line; the credential and standards are.

blocks.html: The process shows the difference. Evelyn's lender ordered the appraisal through an appraisal management company, which assigned a certified appraiser with no connection to the deal. The appraiser inspected and measured the building, pulled the leases, researched sales, rents, expenses and vacant land, applied the three approaches, and reconciled them into a written report for the lender. Jordan's CMA, by contrast, was prepared to help Hector choose an asking price, and it leaned on what buyers might pay, including buyers with special reasons to stretch.

blocks.title: Who may appraise in New York
blocks.html: Real estate appraisers in New York are licensed or certified by the Department of State under Executive Law Article 6-E, separately from real estate brokers and salespersons. A real estate licensee may prepare a CMA to help price a listing or an offer, but may never call it an appraisal or present it as one.

Every appraisal starts with highest and best use. The appraiser noted that current zoning would allow a building on this lot roughly twice the size of Hector's. As vacant, the lot's best use would be a new, larger mixed-use building. As improved, the question is whether the existing building is worth more than the land under it.

blocks.title: Appraiser's site valuation
blocks.html:
Lot: 20 by 100 feet, 2,000 square feet.
Three vacant lot sales in the area within 18 months, adjusted: $250 to $270 per square foot of lot.
Land value as vacant: 2,000 x $260 = $520,000.

blocks.q: The land alone is worth about $520,000 and the property with Hector's building about $1,310,000. What is the highest and best use as improved?
c: Keep the mixed-use building, since it adds far more than the land alone
Demolish the building, since zoning would allow a larger one on the lot
Leave the lot vacant, since vacant land carries no depreciation
Convert the building to commercial use, since stores pay higher rents per foot
blocks.x: As improved, the test is whether the existing building contributes value over the land. A building that lifts a $520,000 lot to about $1.31 million plainly does, so continued use is the highest and best use for now. Demolition becomes the answer only when land alone is worth more than land plus building. The tempting answer jumps to the larger building the zoning allows, but legally permissible is just the first of four tests.

blocks.html: Buyers of a storefront with apartments are buying income, so the appraiser started there. Hector's own expense sheet, sent with the listing, needed cleaning up first.

blocks.title: Hector's operating statement, last 12 months (as sent)
blocks.html:
Rents: store $4,500/month; apartment 2F $3,100; apartment 3F $3,100.
Real estate taxes $18,600 • Insurance $6,900 • Water and sewer $3,400 • Repairs and maintenance $6,200 • Common electric $1,200 • Mortgage interest $21,400 • Depreciation (from tax return) $14,800.

blocks.q: Which items on Hector's statement does not belong in operating expenses for the income approach?
c: Real estate taxes and insurance, because a new owner can appeal and shop them
Water and sewer, because the tenants could be billed separately for usage
Mortgage interest and depreciation, which are financing and tax items
Repairs and common electric, because they change too much from year to year
blocks.x: Net operating income is income minus the costs of operating the property. Mortgage interest depends on the owner's financing, and depreciation is a tax deduction; neither is an operating expense, so both come out. The tempting answer drops taxes and insurance because a buyer might lower them, but they are real costs of operating any building and stay in. Appraisers also add a management fee and reserves even if the owner self-manages.

head: Line
Amount
blocks.caption: Appraiser's reconstructed operating statement

blocks.html: Three lines on that statement were not on Hector's. Vacancy and collection loss is there even though every unit is rented today, because a buyer prices a typical year, and typical years include turnover and the occasional tenant who stops paying. Management is there even though Hector managed it himself, because his time is worth something and the next owner will either pay a manager or spend her own hours. Reserves cover the roof, boiler and windows that wear out on a schedule, whether or not the owner sets money aside.

Next, the capitalization rate. The appraiser found four mixed-use sales on Fifth and Fourth Avenues in the past year, each with a known NOI. Their cap rates (NOI divided by price) ranged from 5.8% to 6.3%, and the appraiser chose 6.0% for a building in this condition with a bakery on a lease running five more years.

blocks.q: Using the appraiser's NOI and a 6.0% cap rate, what value does direct capitalization indicate?
blocks.x: Value equals NOI divided by the cap rate: $78,000 / 0.06 = $1,300,000. $468,000 is the trap of multiplying instead of dividing ($78,000 x 6). $1,395,000 is the contract price, which the income approach does not assume. In IRV terms: income divided by rate equals value.

blocks.q: Hector's broker friend argues the cap rate should be 6.5% "because Sunset Park is riskier than Park Slope." If the appraiser agreed, the indicated value would:
c: Rise, since a higher cap rate means a higher return and so a higher price
Stay at $1,300,000, since the NOI itself is unchanged
Rise to about $1,400,000, since risk premiums add value
Fall, to about $1,200,000, since value moves opposite the rate
blocks.x: $78,000 / 0.065 is about $1,200,000. With NOI fixed, a higher cap rate means a lower value: buyers demand a higher return on riskier property, so they pay less for the same income. The tempting answer links a higher rate to a higher price, which confuses the buyer's return with the property's value. That is why arguing for a higher cap rate hurts Hector's price.

blocks.html: As a check, the appraiser used a gross income multiplier from the same sales: price divided by annual gross income ran from 10.0 to 10.4, with the closest comp at 10.2.

blocks.q: At a gross income multiplier of 10.2, what does Hector's building indicate?
c: About $1,310,000, on potential gross income
About $1,244,000, using effective gross income
About $796,000, using net operating income
About $1,092,000, using monthly rent times 102
blocks.x: A gross income multiplier applies to gross income, measured the same way it was measured in the comps, here potential gross: $128,400 x 10.2 is about $1,310,000. Applying it to NOI ($796,000) is the trap: multipliers ignore expenses by design, which is what makes them quick and also crude. A monthly gross rent multiplier is the residential tool for one to four family homes.

blocks.html: The appraiser used three mixed-use sales within a mile, adjusted on a price per square foot of building basis for time, location on the avenue, condition, lease terms and the number of residential units. Indicated range: $395 to $405 per square foot. At 3,300 square feet of building, that is about $1,305,000 to $1,337,000, with the best comp at $1,320,000.

head: Comp 1, Fifth Ave
Comp 2, Fifth Ave
Comp 3, Fourth Ave
rows: Older sale, time +; no lease on store -
blocks.caption: Appraiser's sales comparison summary (subject: 3,300 sq ft, store plus two apartments)

blocks.html: This is also where Jordan's CMA and the appraisal parted ways. Jordan had used two Fourth Avenue sales at $1,440,000 and $1,460,000. The appraiser saw them too and gave them little weight: one included a vacant store delivered empty to a buyer who wanted to occupy it, a premium for an owner-user, and the other had a larger rear yard and a finished cellar with legal commercial use.

blocks.title: Cost approach
blocks.html:
Land (from site valuation): $520,000
Replacement cost new: 3,300 sq ft x $375 = $1,237,500
Accrued depreciation, age-life method: effective age 45 / economic life 60 = 75% = -$928,125
Depreciated building: $309,375
Indicated value: about $830,000

The appraiser priced the building at replacement cost: a building of equal utility built with modern materials and methods. Reproduction cost, an exact replica, would have meant reproducing the pressed tin ceilings in the store, the cornice and the original plaster, at a much higher figure that buyers of a working mixed-use building would not pay for.

blocks.q: Why did the appraiser use replacement cost rather than reproduction cost for Hector's building?
c: Because reproduction cost is reserved for buildings with landmark status
Because replacement cost tends to come in higher, which favors the seller
Because buyers pay for equal utility, not for replicating 1931 details
Because New York appraisal rules bar reproduction cost on mixed-use buildings
blocks.x: Replacement cost estimates a building of equal usefulness with current materials; reproduction cost estimates an exact duplicate. For an ordinary income building, utility is what buyers pay for, so replacement cost is the better measure. Reproduction cost is the tempting answer for an old building with nice details, and it is used for historic or insurance arguments, but it is not limited to landmarks by rule, and it usually runs higher, not lower.

blocks.html: The appraiser's depreciation notes mentioned physical wear (original windows, an aging roof) and something else: both apartments had railroad layouts, where you walk through one bedroom to reach the next, and the only bathroom in each was off the kitchen. Buyers and renters pay less for that, whatever the condition.

blocks.q: How should the railroad layouts be classified in the cost approach?
c: Physical deterioration, since the apartments are old and worn
External obsolescence, since the cause lies in the neighborhood market
No depreciation, since layout affects rent rather than building value
Functional obsolescence: outdated design inside the property
blocks.x: Functional obsolescence is a loss in value from design or features inside the property that the market no longer wants: walk-through bedrooms, a bath off the kitchen. Physical deterioration is wear and tear. External obsolescence comes from outside the property line and is always incurable. The tempting answer calls it physical because the building is old, but a brand-new building with this layout would suffer the same loss.

blocks.q: The cost approach indicates about $830,000, far below the other two. Why does the appraiser give it little weight here?
c: Because depreciation on a 1931 building is very uncertain
Because the cost approach ignores land, which is half the value here
Because the cost approach is reserved for single-family homes
Because replacement cost tends to run higher than market value
blocks.x: The cost approach works best for new or nearly new buildings and special-purpose properties with no sales or income data. On a 95-year-old building, accrued depreciation is a large estimate, and small changes in effective age swing the answer by hundreds of thousands. It does include land, added separately, which makes the first answer the trap. It is used for many property types, not just houses.

head: Approach
Indication
Weight and reasoning
rows: Most weight: buyers of mixed-use buildings price income; four sales supported the cap rate
Strong support: three good comps, moderate adjustments
Minimal weight: depreciation on a 1931 building is speculative
As of the inspection date, fee simple subject to existing leases
blocks.caption: Appraiser's reconciliation

blocks.q: Why does the appraiser give the income approach the most weight for this building?
c: Because the income approach tends to produce the highest value
Because buyers of income property price it on the income it produces
Because lenders require the income approach for every property type
Because the cost approach and sales comparison cannot be used for stores
blocks.x: Reconciliation gives the most weight to the approach that best reflects how buyers of this property type think. Mixed-use buildings trade on their income, so direct capitalization leads, with sales comparison as a strong check. The tempting first answer assumes appraisers choose the highest number; reconciliation is about reliability, not maximizing value, and here the income approach was actually the lowest of the three supported ones.

blocks.html: Evelyn's commitment letter promised a loan of 70% of the lesser of the purchase price or the appraised value. Her deal had been built on 70% of $1,395,000.

blocks.q: With the appraisal at $1,310,000, how much more cash must Evelyn bring to keep the deal at $1,395,000?
blocks.x: Planned loan: 70% of $1,395,000 = $976,500. New loan: 70% of $1,310,000 = $917,000. The loan drops by $59,500, so her cash rises by that amount: the original 30% down ($418,500) plus $59,500. The $85,000 answer is the trap: it is the gap between price and appraisal, not the change in the loan. The two only match when a buyer is borrowing 100%.

blocks.html: Evelyn's attorney read the mortgage contingency closely. It let her cancel and recover her down payment if she could not obtain a commitment for the planned loan amount by a set date, and the lender's revised commitment was for $59,500 less. That gave her a real choice, and leverage: bring more cash, ask Hector to lower the price, or walk away. Evelyn's broker told Jordan she would stay in at a lower price.

blocks.title: A low appraisal does not mean the CMA was dishonest
blocks.html: CMAs and appraisals answer different questions with different data. A CMA can reasonably include sales that an appraiser will discount (an owner-user who paid a premium, a property with features the subject lacks). The fix is not to argue the appraiser into a number; it is to understand why the two differ, and to price the next listing with that in mind.
Hector still wanted Jordan to call the appraiser. Jordan had heard the request before.

blocks.title: Appraiser independence
blocks.html: Federal rules (the Truth in Lending Act's valuation independence rule, Regulation Z section 1026.42) prohibit anyone with an interest in the deal from coercing, pressuring or improperly influencing an appraiser, and lenders order appraisals through channels designed to keep agents and loan officers away from the appraiser. A borrower can ask the lender for a reconsideration of value and supply relevant sales the appraiser may have missed. The borrower also has the right to a copy of the appraisal promptly, and no later than three business days before closing unless the borrower waives that timing.

blocks.q: What is the proper way to challenge the $1,310,000 appraisal?
c: Jordan calls the appraiser to explain the Fourth Avenue sales and the CMA
Hector writes the appraiser that he will report him if the value stays low
Jordan files a complaint with the Department of State over the appraisal
The buyer requests a reconsideration of value through her lender
blocks.x: The proper channel runs through the lender, and the borrower is the one with standing to ask: a reconsideration of value request with specific, relevant sales the appraiser did not consider. A seller's agent calling the appraiser to argue the number is the tempting answer because it feels like advocacy, but pressure on an appraiser is exactly what the independence rules forbid. A complaint is for misconduct, not disagreement.

blocks.html: Jordan called Hector back instead and walked through the report: the reconstructed expenses, the cap rate evidence, the two Fourth Avenue sales and why the appraiser discounted them. Hector did not like the answer, but he understood it, and he understood that a second buyer's lender would likely hire an appraiser who would see the same sales.

Evelyn's broker submitted a reconsideration request with the Fourth Avenue sales. The appraiser responded in writing, explaining the owner-user premium and the finished cellar, and kept the value. Evelyn's investment logic, though, was different from the market's.

blocks.q: Evelyn says the building is worth $1,450,000 to her because a coffee roaster has agreed to lease the store at $6,000 a month when the bakery leaves in five years. That number is best described as:
c: Market value, since a real tenant has agreed to pay the higher rent
Mortgage value, since the lender will consider the coffee roaster lease
Investment value, the worth to one buyer given her own plans and terms
Insured value, since the store is the most valuable part of the building
blocks.x: Investment value is the value to a specific investor, using her own plans, tenants and financing. Market value is what the typical buyer would pay for the property as it is, with the bakery lease in place. The tempting answer calls it market value because the tenant is real, but a future lease that only Evelyn has arranged is her advantage, not something the market would pay for today.

blocks.html: Evelyn decided the building was worth the extra $59,500 to her. Hector, for his part, agreed to a $35,000 price reduction to $1,360,000 after Jordan walked him through the appraiser's response. The new loan, 70% of $1,310,000, stayed at $917,000; Evelyn's cash went up by $24,500 instead of $59,500. Before closing, her insurance broker asked for a different number again.

blocks.q: For Evelyn's building insurance, which value matters most?
c: The $1,310,000 market value, since that is what the lender appraised
The cost to rebuild the structure, leaving out the land underneath
The $1,360,000 purchase price, since that is what she paid for it
The $520,000 land value, since land is the most durable part
blocks.x: Insurable value is based on the cost to rebuild the improvements; land does not burn, so it is left out, along with foundations in the classic definition. Market value is the tempting answer because it is the number on the appraisal, but insuring to market value would over-insure the land and could leave the building under-insured if construction costs run high.

blocks.html: Diane's note on the file was short: the CMA had been reasonable, the list price a little ambitious, and the handling of the appraisal exactly right. Jordan added a line to the template for the next mixed-use CMA: separate owner-user sales from investor sales, and say in writing which kind of buyer each comp reflects.

items: A CMA is a licensee's price opinion; an appraisal is a licensed or certified appraiser's value opinion under USPAP. Never call a CMA an appraisal.
Highest and best use as improved keeps a building that adds value over the land; it is not simply the biggest building zoning allows.
NOI excludes debt service and depreciation. Value = NOI / cap rate; a higher cap rate means a lower value. Gross multipliers apply to gross income.
The cost approach adds depreciated replacement cost to land value; it is weakest on old buildings. Walk-through layouts are functional obsolescence.
Reconciliation weights the approach buyers of that property type actually use. A low appraisal cuts the loan by the loan-to-value ratio times the shortfall.
Challenge an appraisal only through the lender with a reconsideration of value; never pressure the appraiser. Investment value and insurable value are different numbers from market value.

lessons.title: Case file: Two Apartments, Two Rulebooks
lessons.tagline: A walk-up co-op in Jackson Heights and a high-floor condo in Long Island City, listed the same week. Same subway line, completely different pricing math.
objectives: Price a co-op apartment using in-building sales, rooms and layout, and adjust comparables for maintenance differences, elevators and building rules.
Price a condo unit using price per square foot, line and floor premiums, and the effect of an expiring tax abatement.
Calculate how flip taxes, the mansion tax and the mortgage recording tax affect what buyers pay and sellers net in co-op and condo sales.
Decide which disclosures, approvals and financing rules apply to each ownership form and how they affect the buyer pool and price.

blocks.title: Seven stops apart
blocks.html: On Monday, Dolores Fitzgerald, 78, asked Jordan to sell the two-bedroom co-op she has owned since 1991 in a 1928 garden building in the Jackson Heights Historic District: five rooms, fifth floor, no elevator, maintenance $1,240 a month. On Wednesday, Ben Adler, a nurse anesthetist relocating to Denver, asked Jordan to sell his two-bedroom condo on the 22nd floor of a 2016 tower in Long Island City: 950 square feet, a skyline view, common charges $780 and real estate taxes of $210 a month thanks to a tax abatement. Both want to know what their apartments are worth. Jordan grew up four blocks from Dolores's building and knows that answering both questions the same way would be a mistake.

A co-op buyer buys shares in a corporation that owns the building, plus a proprietary lease. A condo buyer buys real property: the unit and a percentage of the common elements, with its own deed and tax bill. That one difference changes where the comps come from, what the monthly cost means, who approves the buyer, which taxes apply, and which disclosures are required.

Jordan started with Dolores's own building, then her block. A search of the city's recorded documents for her building turned up mortgages on the building and some financing statements against individual apartments, but no deeds for apartment sales. Dolores's son, helping her on the phone, asked if that meant there had been no sales.

blocks.q: Why are there no recorded deeds for apartment sales in Dolores's building?
c: Because co-op sale prices are kept confidential under state law and sealed
Because the building's sponsor still owns every apartment in the building
Because Queens deeds are recorded after the co-op board approves them
Because a co-op buyer gets shares and a proprietary lease, not a deed
blocks.x: In a co-op, the corporation holds title to the building, and apartment buyers acquire shares and a proprietary lease, which is personal property, so there is no deed to record for each sale. The deeds-only search misses co-op sales; a co-op share loan shows up as a financing statement, not a mortgage on the apartment. Prices come from MLS data, the managing agent, and transfer records. The confidentiality answer is the trap; the issue is the ownership form.

blocks.html: Jordan also called the managing agent for the building's recent sale history and asked for the current maintenance, any pending assessments, and the status of the underlying mortgage, since a refinancing or a balloon payment coming due can move maintenance. Jordan found three useful sales. Two were in Dolores's building. The third was in a similar 1920s co-op around the corner with one important difference.

head: Apt 4F (same building, same line)
Apt 2B (same building)
Around the corner, 3D
blocks.caption: Dolores's co-op comps (subject: 5 rooms, 2 bedrooms, 5th floor walk-up, original condition, $1,240 maintenance)

blocks.html: Co-ops rarely come with reliable square footage, so Jordan compared rooms, bedrooms, layout, floor and condition. The biggest difference on the sheet was not physical at all: the comp around the corner carried $350 a month less in maintenance. Maintenance pays the building's real estate taxes, its underlying mortgage, staff and operating costs. A buyer sees it as part of the monthly payment, and a higher payment means a lower price the buyer can afford for the same budget.

blocks.title: Capitalizing a maintenance difference
blocks.html:
Maintenance difference: $1,240 - $890 = $350 a month.
Assume buyers finance at about 6.5% for 30 years: payment per $1,000 borrowed is about $6.32 a month.
$350 / $6.32 = about 55.4 thousands of dollars of loan.
The same monthly budget supports about $55,000 less price in Dolores's building.

blocks.q: How should the $350 maintenance difference be applied to the around-the-corner comp?
c: Add about $55,000, since the comp's lower maintenance makes it the poorer comp
Ignore it, since maintenance is a monthly cost and not part of the price
Subtract about $55,000, since lower maintenance makes the comp the better buy
Subtract $350, since the difference is a monthly carrying cost
blocks.x: A comp with lower maintenance is better from a buyer's point of view, and comp better means subtract. Capitalizing the difference at current mortgage terms puts a dollar figure on it: about $55,000. The tempting answer ignores maintenance because it is not on the contract; in co-op pricing it is one of the biggest adjustments, which is why two similar apartments a block apart can sell tens of thousands of dollars apart.

blocks.q: The around-the-corner comp also has an elevator; Dolores's apartment is a fifth-floor walk-up. How is that handled?
c: Subtract for the elevator, a feature buyers pay more for
Add for the elevator, since the subject should be credited for the climb
Ignore it, since elevators are part of the building and not the apartment
Add for the elevator, since elevators raise maintenance and lower value
blocks.x: Buyers pay more for elevator access, especially above the second floor, so the comp is better on this feature and is adjusted down. The adjustment rate should come from the market, such as paired walk-up and elevator sales nearby. The tempting answer credits the subject for the stairs, which breaks the rule: you never adjust the subject. The elevator's cost is already reflected in the maintenance adjustment.

blocks.html: After adjustments for maintenance, elevator, floor, condition and time, the three comps indicated $468,000 (around the corner), $498,000 (4F, adjusted down for its renovation and up a little for time) and $496,000 (2B, adjusted up for time and the higher floor's light, down slightly for its lower maintenance). Jordan weighted 2B and 4F most, since they were in the same building with the same rules and nearly the same maintenance. Indicated value: about $495,000. Recommended list: $509,000.

Dolores had her own number in mind. A friend from church had sold a two-bedroom a few blocks away for $575,000 last spring, and Dolores assumed hers was worth about the same. Jordan pulled the sale: an elevator building, a sixth-floor apartment with an open view over the gardens, a renovated kitchen and two full baths, and maintenance of $960. On every line that buyers care about, it was a better apartment with a lower monthly cost. Jordan walked her through the adjustments on paper, line by line, until the $80,000 gap had a name for every piece of it.

The managing agent's letter added one more pricing fact. About 46% of the building's maintenance goes to real estate taxes and interest on the building's underlying mortgage, and shareholders may generally deduct their share of those on their income taxes, the way a house owner deducts property taxes and mortgage interest. Buyers who itemize look at after-tax cost, so a building whose maintenance is mostly deductible competes better than its gross figure suggests.

blocks.q: A buyer asks which part of Dolores's $1,240 monthly maintenance may be tax deductible. The best answer?
c: The full amount, since maintenance is the co-op equivalent of rent
The portion that goes to staff salaries and building insurance
Her share of the building's real estate taxes and mortgage interest
Nothing, since shareholders do not own real property
blocks.x: Co-op shareholders may generally deduct their proportionate share of the corporation's real estate taxes and mortgage interest, which the managing agent reports each year. Staff, insurance and repairs are operating costs and are not deductible for an owner-occupant. The tempting last answer reasons from ownership form; the tax code treats qualifying co-op shareholders much like homeowners for these two items. Buyers should confirm their own situation with a tax professional.

blocks.text: The co-op: rules that move price

blocks.title: From the co-op's purchase application package
blocks.html:
Financing: maximum 80% of purchase price.
Post-closing liquidity: buyer must show liquid assets after closing equal to at least two years of maintenance plus mortgage payments.
Debt-to-income: housing costs no more than 30% of gross income.
Flip tax: 2% of the gross sale price, paid by the seller at closing.
Subletting: permitted after two years of owner occupancy, maximum two years.
Pending assessment: roof and parapet project; $180 per month per apartment for 24 months, beginning in January.

blocks.q: How do the building's financing and liquidity rules most likely affect Dolores's price?
c: They raise the price, since just wealthier buyers can pass the board
They narrow the buyer pool, which tends to hold prices down
They have no effect, since the board's rules apply after the price is agreed
They cancel the need for a CMA, since the board sets the minimum price
blocks.x: Every requirement a buyer must clear shrinks the pool of buyers who can bid, and fewer qualified bidders usually means less upward pressure. A building that caps financing at 80% and demands two years of reserves will often trade below a similar building that allows 90% and asks for less. The tempting answer assumes stricter rules mean a richer, higher-paying pool; some buyers do value strict buildings, but in a moderate-price market the narrower pool usually wins out.

blocks.q: If Dolores sells at $500,000, how much is the flip tax and who pays it?
c: $10,000, paid by Dolores under the building's rules
$5,000, split equally between buyer and seller
$10,000, paid by the buyer as a separate transfer fee
$20,000, paid by Dolores as a 4% fee on the sale
blocks.x: 2% of $500,000 is $10,000. A flip tax is a transfer fee set by the co-op's own documents, not a state tax, and this building puts it on the seller, which is common. The tempting answer has the buyer paying it, which some buildings do; the rule is whatever the co-op's documents say, so read them before quoting a net number.

blocks.q: The $180 per month assessment starts in January; Dolores expects to close in December. What should Jordan do?
c: Leave it out of the listing, since Dolores will be gone before it begins
Tell buyers the board will waive it for new shareholders who buy in December
Add $4,320 to the list price, since the buyer will be paying it instead of her
Disclose it and let the parties negotiate it, since it affects cost
blocks.x: A known assessment is part of the apartment's monthly cost and is material to a buyer; it belongs in the listing and the negotiation. Who pays depends on the building's rules and the contract: often whoever owns at billing, sometimes credited at closing. The tempting answer hides it because the timing seems to favor the seller, but the buyer's attorney will find it in the board minutes and the managing agent's letter, and concealment would be a misrepresentation.

blocks.title: Board approval vs right of first refusal
blocks.html: A co-op board can approve or reject a buyer after reviewing a detailed financial package and an interview, usually without stating a reason, though it may not discriminate on any protected basis under federal, state and city law. Most condo boards have only a right of first refusal: the board may buy the unit on the same terms or let the sale proceed, and it rarely exercises the right. That difference adds weeks to a co-op sale and removes some buyers, which is part of why condos usually sell for more per square foot than comparable co-ops.

blocks.q: Dolores's son asks whether she needs to give buyers a Property Condition Disclosure Statement and a lead paint disclosure. What is correct?
c: Both, since every New York residential sale requires both forms
Neither, since co-ops are exempt from state and federal disclosure rules
The PCDS, but not lead disclosure, since co-ops are personal property
Lead disclosure, but not the PCDS, which does not apply to co-op sales
blocks.x: The PCDS law covers one to four family houses and exempts co-op and condo units. The federal lead rule covers target housing built before 1978, and a 1928 co-op apartment is housing being sold, so the pamphlet, disclosure of known hazards and the 10-day testing opportunity apply. The tempting answer exempts co-ops from everything because the buyer gets shares; the lead rule looks at the housing and its age, not the form of ownership.

blocks.text: The condo: price per foot, line and floor

blocks.html: Ben's tower had sold 14 two-bedroom units in the past year. Condo sales are recorded as deeds, square footage comes from the offering plan, and the most similar comps are in the same line, the vertical stack of identical apartments, on different floors.

head: Unit 15C
Unit 28C
Unit 22A
blocks.caption: Ben's condo comps (subject: 22C, 950 sq ft, skyline view)

blocks.q: 15C and 28C are identical apartments 13 floors apart. Ignoring time, what floor premium do they suggest, and what does that indicate for 22C?
c: About $6,500 a floor; 22C indicates about $1,000,000
About $85,000 a floor; 22C indicates about $1,040,000
About $6,500 a floor; 22C indicates about $955,000
About $3,250 a floor; 22C indicates about $977,750
blocks.x: $1,040,000 minus $955,000 is $85,000 over 13 floors, about $6,500 a floor. 22C is 7 floors above 15C: $955,000 plus 7 x $6,500 is about $1,000,500. Same-line comps on other floors isolate the floor premium the way paired sales do for a house. The tempting answer stops at the comp price without adjusting; the line tells you the layout, but the floor still moves the price.

blocks.q: How much weight should 22A, a larger river-view unit in a different line, get in reconciling Ben's value?
c: The most, since it is the most recent sale in the building
No weight, since comps from a different line cannot be used
Less than 15C and 28C, since its layout and view differ from 22C
The same as the others, since every comp is from the same tower
blocks.x: Same-line comps share the subject's layout, exposure and square footage, so they need only floor and time adjustments. 22A differs in size, layout and view, so it needs larger, less certain adjustments and gets less weight, though it still confirms the range. The tempting first answer favors recency, but similarity matters more than a few months of time when the market is stable.

blocks.html: The math put Ben's apartment right at $1,000,000, which is the worst possible place for it in New York.

blocks.q: Why might Jordan suggest listing at $999,000 rather than $1,005,000?
c: Because NYC transfer tax doubles for condo sales of $1,000,000 or more
Buyers owe the 1% mansion tax on the full price at $1,000,000 and up
Because condo boards may not approve sales above $1,000,000 without a vote
Because lenders refuse to finance condo purchases over $1,000,000 in Queens
blocks.x: New York's mansion tax charges the buyer 1% of the entire price on residential purchases of $1,000,000 or more, condos and co-ops included. At $1,005,000 the buyer owes $10,050; at $999,000, nothing. That cliff makes $999,000 a powerful list price and makes offers just above $1,000,000 less attractive than they look. The tempting answer cites transfer tax, which the seller pays and which does not jump at $1,000,000 for a condo.

blocks.html: Then the tax bill. The building received a 421-a abatement when it was built.
