Ben's taxes are $210 a month now, and the abatement steps down over its final years until full taxes apply, which the city's records project at about $1,150 a month. Ben wanted the listing to say "low taxes."

blocks.q: How should the expiring abatement be handled in the listing and the pricing?
c: Disclose the phase-out schedule and price for rising taxes
Advertise the low taxes, since $210 is the true current monthly figure
Say nothing, since buyers' attorneys are responsible for tax research
Advertise full taxes of $1,150, since the abatement will end anyway
blocks.x: Advertising "low taxes" without the phase-out would mislead buyers about a cost that will rise by about $940 a month, and buyers capitalize monthly costs into price just as they do with co-op maintenance. Disclose the current figure and the schedule, and price against comps with similar remaining abatement. The tempting answer is literally true today, which is what makes it misleading; a half-truth about a material fact is still a misrepresentation.

blocks.html: Same-building comps share the same abatement schedule, so no adjustment was needed among them. But a buyer comparing Ben's unit to a resale in a nearby building with full taxes needs the comparison spelled out, and Jordan put both monthly totals on the listing sheet: today's, and the projected figure when the abatement ends.

Ben's buyer would also face a lender's appraisal, and condo appraisers work the same way Jordan did: same-building sales first, adjusted for floor, line, view and time, with the appraiser reviewing the building's finances and owner-occupancy as part of the lender's project review. A list price built on same-line sales tends to survive that appraisal. A price built on the river-view unit next door would not, and the gap would land on the buyer's down payment or the seller's price. Co-op buyers face a similar appraisal on the share loan, plus the board's own review of the buyer's finances, which can be stricter than the bank's.

blocks.text: What each buyer pays to close

blocks.q: A buyer borrows $800,000 to buy Ben's condo. Compared with borrowing the same amount for a co-op, what changes in mortgage recording tax?
c: Nothing, since both loans are recorded at the same county rate
Only the condo loan owes NYC mortgage recording tax
The co-op loan owes the tax at a higher rate than the condo loan
Neither owes the tax, since apartments are exempt in New York City
blocks.x: A condo loan is a mortgage on real property and owes New York City mortgage recording tax: 1.925% paid by the borrower on loans of $500,000 or more, about $15,400 here. A co-op share loan is secured by shares and a lease, not real property, so it is not a recorded mortgage and owes no mortgage recording tax. The tempting answer treats both loans alike because both finance an apartment.

blocks.html: Dolores's apartment sold in December for $502,000 to a schoolteacher who cleared the board in five weeks; the contract credited the buyer $720 toward the first four months of the assessment. Dolores netted her price minus the $10,040 flip tax, the seller's transfer taxes, her attorney and the commission. Ben listed at $999,000, received two offers in ten days, and accepted $995,000; the buyer avoided the mansion tax and Ben avoided a bidding war that would have pushed his buyer over the line and then back down.

head: Dolores's estimated net at $502,000
Amount
rows: NYC real property transfer tax (1.425% rate, since the price is over $500,000)
Commission, attorney, managing agent and transfer fees
blocks.caption: Jordan's net sheet (estimate; the attorney confirms at closing)

blocks.html: Net sheets are where co-op sellers get surprised. Dolores had heard of the flip tax but not the transfer taxes, and she had not known the managing agent charges its own processing fees. Showing the deductions before the listing went live meant no surprises at closing, and it let her decide on price knowing what she would actually walk away with.

blocks.title: Price per square foot does not cross ownership types
blocks.html: A condo at $1,050 a foot and a co-op at $650 a foot in the same neighborhood are not mispriced; they are different products with different monthly costs, approval processes, financing rules and closing costs. Compare co-ops to co-ops (ideally in the same building) and condos to condos, and use the monthly carrying cost as part of every comparison.

Two apartments, seven subway stops apart, priced with the same discipline and completely different inputs. For Dolores, the building's rules, the maintenance and the stairs did most of the work. For Ben, the line, the floor, the tax schedule and a $1,000,000 threshold did. Jordan's file for each held the comps, the adjustments, the documents relied on, and the written price recommendation each seller signed.

items: Co-op comps come from the same building first; there are no deeds for co-op sales. Compare rooms, layout, floor, condition and maintenance, since co-ops rarely have reliable square footage.
Capitalize maintenance or common charge differences into price; a comp with lower monthly costs is the better comp, so subtract.
Financing caps, liquidity rules, board approval and assessments shape the buyer pool and the price. Flip taxes follow the co-op's documents.
Condo comps run by price per square foot, line and floor; same-line sales isolate floor premiums. Disclose and price expiring abatements.
The mansion tax hits buyers at $1,000,000 and up, condos and co-ops alike; condo loans owe mortgage recording tax, co-op share loans do not.
Co-ops and condos are exempt from the PCDS but not from the federal lead disclosure rule for pre-1978 housing.

lessons.title: Case file: The Bungalow and the Side Lot on Bayview Avenue
lessons.tagline: An executor in Denver, a 1938 bungalow on a 40-foot lot, a 20-foot garden lot next door, and a builder with a cash offer before the sign goes up. Is the house worth anything, or is the land the whole story?
objectives: Decide what kind of value an estate, an insurer, a builder and a buyer each need, and who may produce it
Apply highest and best use, as vacant and as improved, to a nonconforming lot and an unbuildable side lot
Calculate a site value from land sales, adjust a teardown sale into a land comp, and measure plottage
Classify a builder's direct and indirect costs and explain why his residual number is investment value, not market value

blocks.title: Two tax lots and a phone call from Denver
blocks.html: Helen Novak died in March at 91. For 54 years she lived in a 1938 bungalow on Bayview Avenue in a South Shore village in Nassau County: 820 square feet, two bedrooms, one bath, on a 40 by 100 foot lot. In 1972 she and her husband bought the 20 by 100 foot lot next door, a separate tax lot, and turned it into a vegetable garden. Her son Greg, a pharmacist in Denver, is executor; his sister Anna, a teacher in Albany, is the other beneficiary. Diane got the referral from a lawyer the firm works with, and Jordan, who spent a summer working the South Shore with a colleague, is taking the listing under Diane's supervision. Greg's first call is about paperwork. “The estate lawyer says I need an appraisal as of the date Mom died. Can you just put ‘appraisal’ on your market analysis? It'll save us a few hundred dollars.”

blocks.q: How should Jordan respond to Greg's request?
c: Agree, since a CMA by a licensed salesperson is accepted as an appraisal for estates
Agree, if the CMA is dated as of Helen's death and Diane signs it as the broker
Decline, since past-date valuations come from attorneys
Decline; a CMA may not be called an appraisal, so hire an appraiser
blocks.x: A CMA is an opinion of value from a real estate licensee and by law may never be called an appraisal. An estate needs a value as of the date of death, for its accounting and to set the heirs' stepped-up tax basis, and that comes from a state licensed or certified appraiser. The broker-signature answer is the trap: Diane's signature does not turn a CMA into an appraisal.

blocks.html: Greg hires an appraiser for the date-of-death report, and Jordan starts the CMA for the listing. The two jobs ask different questions. The appraisal looks back to a single date in March; Jordan's analysis looks forward, to the price a buyer is most likely to pay this fall. Both are forms of valuation, estimating value as of a stated date, and the date changes the answer. Greg then reads Jordan a number from the county's website.

blocks.title: What Greg found online
blocks.html:
Nassau County assessment roll, Bayview Avenue house lot: market value $498,000.
Side lot: market value $61,000.
Greg: “So the county says $559,000 for both. Why are we paying anyone?”

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell Greg about the county's figures?
c: They set the floor for the sale, since property may not sell below assessment
They serve property tax purposes and may lag what buyers would pay
They are market value, since the county uses the same definition as appraisers
They are the best evidence, coming from a public agency
blocks.x: Assessment figures exist to spread the property tax fairly. They are mass-appraised, often from older data, and they value each tax lot on its own, so they cannot see what the two lots are worth together. They are a starting point, not a price. The same-definition answer is the trap: the roll may label its figure market value, but it is not an analysis of this property's current market.

blocks.html: Two days later, before the sign is up, a builder named Vince Ferraro calls. He knows the block. “I'll give the estate $520,000 cash for the house, as is, close in 30 days. No inspection, no mortgage. And I'll take the garden lot off your hands for another $30,000.” Greg is tired, far away, and grieving. He would like to say yes tonight. Anna, on the other hand, wants to know whether $550,000 is what the property is worth.

blocks.q: Greg asks whether Vince's offer shows the property's market value. What is the best answer?
c: Yes, since a cash offer with no contingencies is the definition of market value
Yes, because the first offer on a property is usually the highest it will receive
No; one offer before exposure is a proposal, not the most probable price
No, because offers from builders are excluded from market value by definition
blocks.x: Market value assumes reasonable exposure to a competitive market, informed parties and no undue pressure. A single private offer made before anyone else has seen the property tells Greg what one motivated buyer proposes, which is a price if accepted, not market value. The first-offer answer is the trap: sometimes it is the best, but nobody can know that without exposure. Builder offers count once the market has tested them.

blocks.title: Pressure is not duress, but it can become it
blocks.html: An estate sale is not automatically a distress sale. Greg can wait six weeks; the house is paid off, the taxes are current, and the will gives him power to sell. What makes an estate sale fall below market is the executor who treats convenience as a deadline. Jordan's job is to show Greg the gap in writing, then let him decide. He owes a fiduciary duty to Anna, too.

Jordan has a confession of a different kind to make, to Diane rather than to Greg. Nearly all of Jordan's closed deals are Brooklyn row houses and co-ops. A South Shore village where buyers pay for land, where lot width decides what can be built, and where most sales are teardowns is a different market with different evidence. A good CMA here needs land sales, zoning, and a feel for what builders are paying this season, none of which Jordan carries around in memory.

blocks.q: What does the salesperson's duty of competence call for before Jordan prices the Novak property?
c: Turning down the listing, since licenses are limited to the agent's home county
Pricing from Brooklyn price-per-square-foot figures, adjusted for the larger lot
Relying on online estimates and the county roll
Pulling local sales, reading the zoning, and getting help from a local agent
blocks.x: Competence means either knowing the market or doing the work to learn it, and saying so honestly. Jordan pulls local data, reads the zoning code, and asks Diane to bring in a licensee who sells on the South Shore, then documents every source. The home-county answer is the trap: a New York license is good statewide, so the limit is skill, not geography. Online estimates cannot see zoning or plottage.

blocks.html: Diane connects Jordan with Rosa Delgado, a broker in a Long Island firm the office cooperates with, who has sold a dozen building lots in the village. Rosa does not take over the listing. She points Jordan to the builders who have been buying, to the two teardowns that never hit the MLS, and to the building department clerk who knows which lots have variances on file. Jordan keeps a log of every call and every source, because if Anna ever asks why the price was what it was, the answer should be on paper, not in Jordan's head.

Jordan calls the village building department and reads the zoning code for the district. A new single-family house requires a lot at least 60 feet wide with at least 6,000 square feet. Helen's 40-foot lot predates that rule, so it is a legal nonconforming lot: the bungalow can stay and be renovated, but a new house on the 40-foot lot alone would need an area variance from the zoning board of appeals, and nobody can promise one. The 20-foot side lot cannot hold a house at all. Together, the two lots measure exactly 60 by 100: 6,000 square feet, a conforming building lot.

blocks.q: Applying highest and best use as vacant to the 40-foot lot by itself, what does the first test show?
c: A new house is the use, since it brings the most value per square foot
Legal permissibility is in doubt, since a new house needs an area variance
Physical possibility fails, since no house fits on a 40-foot-wide lot
Financial feasibility controls, since builders pay the most for the lot
blocks.x: Highest and best use starts with what is legally permissible. A new house on the 40-foot lot alone needs a variance the zoning board may deny, so that use is uncertain and a buyer would discount it. The highest-value answer is the trap: maximal productivity is the last test, applied only to uses that pass the legal, physical and financial tests first. Physically, a narrow house could fit; the law is the obstacle.

blocks.html: Now Jordan runs both halves of the analysis on the combined parcel. As improved, the bungalow is dated but sound: original kitchen, 1960s bath, a 2019 roof. Jordan's bungalow comps, adjusted, put the house on its 40-foot lot at about $540,000. As vacant, the combined 60-foot lot would support a new house of about 2,400 square feet. To price the land, Jordan needs land sales, and the village has few true vacant lots. Most building lots here come with an old house on them.

head: Sale
Lot
What sold
Price
Notes
rows: 1940s cape, bought by a builder and demolished
7 months ago; buyer paid $28,000 for demolition and capping utilities
1930s bungalow, bought by a family to renovate
blocks.caption: Jordan's land research, same village, last 12 months

blocks.q: How should Jordan treat Sale L2, the teardown, as a land comp?
c: Use $700,000: the $672,000 price plus the $28,000 demolition cost
Use $644,000: the $672,000 price less the $28,000 spent on demolition
Use $672,000 as is, since demolition is a cost the builder chose to take on
Leave it out, since a sale with a house on it is not a land sale
blocks.x: A builder who buys a teardown pays the price and then pays to clear the site, so the vacant land cost him $672,000 plus $28,000, or $700,000. Adding demolition converts the sale into a land equivalent. The subtraction answer is the trap: it treats demolition as if it reduced the land's value, when it is part of what the buyer paid to get vacant land. Teardowns are often the best land evidence in built-up areas.

blocks.title: A teardown sale is a land sale
blocks.html: When the house will be demolished, the sale tells you about land, not about houses. Agents who drop a teardown into a grid of renovated houses wreck the CMA in both directions: the teardown drags the house comps down, and the house comps hide what the land is worth. Sort first, then compare. L4, where a family bought a bungalow to live in, belongs with the house comps, not the land comps.

blocks.q: L1 sold for about $117.50 per square foot of land and L2's land equivalent works out to about $116.70. What site value does that indicate for the combined 6,000 square foot parcel?
blocks.x: $117 a square foot times 6,000 square feet is about $702,000, so the indicated site value is about $700,000. L3, at $112 a square foot, supports this: larger lots usually sell for a bit less per square foot. The $840,000 answer is the trap: it is L3's whole price, for a bigger lot. $468,000 applies the rate to the 4,000 square foot house lot alone, which cannot carry a new house as of right.

blocks.html: That is site valuation by sales comparison: land sales, adjusted to the subject, reduced to a common unit. Jordan uses price per square foot because every lot in the village is 100 feet deep; where depths vary, agents often compare price per front foot or price per buildable square foot instead. Rosa checks the result against what she has heard from builders this fall and agrees: low $700s for a 60-foot lot, less for anything that needs a variance. And it changes the conversation with Greg, because selling the pieces one at a time gives a different total than selling the whole.

blocks.title: The two lots, apart and together
blocks.html:
House lot with bungalow, sold alone (as improved): $540,000
Side lot sold alone (unbuildable; realistic buyer is a neighbor wanting yard): $40,000
Sum of the parts: $580,000
Combined 6,000 square foot conforming building lot (as vacant): $700,000

blocks.q: What does the $120,000 difference between $700,000 and $580,000 represent, and what follows for the estate?
c: Assemblage cost, which the estate pays to combine the two lots into one
Plottage, which the estate keeps if the two lots are sold together
Functional obsolescence, which a buyer deducts for the outdated bungalow
Investment value, which Vince alone can realize
blocks.x: Plottage is the extra value of assembled parcels over the sum of their separate values. Here it exists because only the combined lot conforms to zoning. Selling the house lot to Vince and the side lot separately would hand the $120,000 to whoever assembles them. The assemblage answer is the trap: assemblage is the act of combining, and here it costs nothing but a single deed.

blocks.html: One more comparison settles the highest and best use as improved. The combined site is worth about $700,000 as vacant. With the bungalow on it, the house lot plus the side lot is worth about $580,000 to someone who keeps the house. When land as vacant is worth more than the property as improved, the old building is no longer adding value. Its highest and best use is demolition and a new house, and the most likely buyer is a builder or a family that wants to build.

When Jordan tells Vince the lots will be marketed together, he sends his numbers to make the case that $550,000 is fair. He works backward from what a new house would sell for, which is how builders think.

head: Line
Amount
rows: Sale of new 2,400 sq ft house
Construction labor and materials, 2,400 sq ft at $250
Insurance and property taxes during construction
Sales commission and closing costs on the new house
What the land is worth to Vince (residual)
blocks.caption: Ferraro Homes feasibility sheet, Bayview Avenue

blocks.q: Which item on Vince's sheet is an indirect (soft) cost?
c: Construction labor and materials at $250 a square foot
Site work and the new foundation
Demolition of the bungalow and capping utilities
Construction loan interest and lender fees
blocks.x: Direct costs are the labor and materials that physically build the project: construction, site work, foundation and demolition. Indirect costs are everything else needed to get it built and sold: financing, architect and engineering fees, permits, insurance and taxes during construction, and selling costs. Demolition is the trap, since it feels like overhead, but it is physical work on the site.

blocks.q: Vince's $496,500 residual is best described as:
c: Market value, since a builder is the most likely buyer for the site
Investment value, built on his own costs and his 15% profit target
An appraisal, since it applies a recognized valuation technique
Value in use, since he is valuing the land for one particular use
blocks.x: Investment value is value to a particular investor, using that investor's own costs, financing and return requirements. Another builder with cheaper construction or a 10% profit target would arrive at a higher land number, and the land sales show such builders exist. The market value answer is the trap: the right buyer type does not make one buyer's math the market. His sheet is an evaluation, a feasibility study, not an appraisal.

blocks.html: Greg has a different objection. “Mom put in a new roof and redid the kitchen in 2019. That was $85,000. Doesn't that count for something?” Jordan has the receipts, and they are real.

blocks.q: How should the $85,000 Helen spent in 2019 affect the asking price?
c: Add it in full, since the receipts prove the money went into the property
Add half of it, since improvements lose about half their cost in five years
Add it to the land value instead
Little or nothing, since buyers who will demolish pay for land
blocks.x: Cost is what was spent; value is what a buyer will pay. An improvement contributes only what it adds in the eyes of the most likely buyer. If the most likely buyer will demolish the house, the new kitchen and roof add little. They do matter to the smaller pool of buyers who would keep the bungalow, which is one reason the listing should show both stories. The full-receipts answer is the trap.

blocks.html: The house is vacant now, and the estate's homeowner's policy will not cover an unoccupied house for long. Greg's insurance agent asks for the insured value to write a vacant dwelling policy until closing.

blocks.q: Which number should the insurer use as the insured value of the bungalow?
c: About $540,000, the market value of the house on its lot
About $700,000, the value of the two lots combined as vacant
About $225,000, the rebuilding cost without land or foundation
About $85,000, the cost of the 2019 roof and kitchen work
blocks.x: Insured value is based on what it would cost to rebuild the structure, and it leaves out land and foundations because they do not burn. For a small bungalow on valuable land, it is far below market value. The $540,000 answer is the trap: it includes land the insurer is not covering, and insuring to market value here would buy coverage that could never be paid out.

blocks.html: Jordan's recommendation to Greg and Anna, in writing: list both lots together as one offering at $729,000, market it for three weeks to builders and to buyers who might renovate, set a date for highest and best offers, and keep Vince in the process. Anna agrees. Greg has one counterproposal. “Let's list at $850,000. Somebody might fall in love with it.”

blocks.q: Why does Jordan advise against an $850,000 list price?
c: Market value is the most probable price, not the highest possible
List prices above the CMA figure violate the rules on misleading advertising
Executors are limited by law to listing at the date-of-death appraised value
Builders ignore overpriced land
blocks.x: Market value is the most probable price after reasonable exposure, not the best price an outlier might pay. The land sales cluster near $700,000; at $850,000 the listing would sit, and an estate listing that sits invites low offers. Greg may still choose a higher price, and Jordan would document the advice. The misleading-advertising answer is the trap: an ambitious list price is the seller's choice, not a violation.

blocks.html: Three weeks of exposure produced nine showings and four offers. A family wanted to renovate the bungalow and garden on the side lot, at $660,000 with a 75% mortgage. Vince came in at $690,000 cash. A second builder, with lower costs and a 10% profit target, offered $705,000 cash. A third builder, at $698,000, wanted 60 days to apply for permits. Greg asked why Jordan ranked the family's offer last when he liked the idea of a family in his mother's house.

blocks.q: Besides the lower price, why does the family's financed offer carry more risk for the estate?
c: The lender will appraise the house lot and ignore the side lot entirely
Financed buyers may cancel at any time before closing without any reason
The loan rests on the lender's appraisal, so a low one can reopen the price
Lenders refuse to finance any house that a CMA describes as a teardown
blocks.x: A lender lends a percentage of the lower of the contract price and its own appraised value, sometimes called mortgage value. If the bank's appraiser comes in below $660,000, the family must add cash, renegotiate, or cancel under a mortgage contingency. The cancel-at-will answer is the trap: a mortgage contingency allows cancellation only on its terms, but it is still a risk that cash offers do not carry.

blocks.html: In the best and final round, the second builder went to $712,000, all cash, with a 30-day closing, and Greg and Anna signed. The family sent a kind note and asked to be told if the builder ever sold the new house. The executor's deed conveyed both lots in one deed, and the title company combined them into a single tax lot after closing.

blocks.title: New York's line between a CMA and an appraisal
blocks.html: Appraisers in New York are licensed or certified by the Department of State under Executive Law Article 6-E. A real estate licensee prepares a CMA, an opinion of value used to price a listing or an offer, and may never present it as an appraisal. When an estate, a court, a lender or the IRS needs a value as of a date, the document comes from an appraiser. Jordan's CMA and the date-of-death appraisal sat side by side in the estate file, each doing its own job.

blocks.q: A year later, another agent pulls this $712,000 sale for a CMA on a renovated bungalow down the street. How should the sale be used?
c: As a land comp for a 60-foot lot, since the buyer will demolish
As a house comp after subtracting $85,000 for the 2019 roof and kitchen work
As a house comp, since the deed shows a sale of a two-bedroom house and lot
Skip it; executor sales are not arm's length
blocks.x: The buyer paid for a 6,000 square foot conforming building lot and will demolish the bungalow, so this is land evidence, useful for pricing other building lots. Treating it as a house sale would overstate what a 40-foot bungalow is worth. The not-arm's-length answer is the trap: an estate sale after full exposure, with competing unrelated bidders, is arm's length. Executor sales are fine comps when the process was open.

blocks.html: Diane read the file and circled the $162,000 difference between Vince's first call and the signed contract. “That's not a better buyer,” she said. “That's the same land, priced by someone who did the homework.” Then she circled Rosa's name and the call log. “And that's why nobody can say you priced a market you didn't know.” Greg sent Anna's share of the extra money a week after closing, with a one-line email to Jordan: “Glad I didn't answer the phone that first night.”

items: A CMA is an opinion of value and may never be called an appraisal; an estate's date-of-death value comes from a licensed or certified appraiser, and assessment figures serve taxation, not pricing.
Highest and best use starts with what is legally permissible; a nonconforming lot and an unbuildable side lot can be worth far more together than apart.
Turn a teardown sale into a land comp by adding demolition costs, and value the site from land sales; the excess of combined value over the sum of the parts is plottage.
Direct costs build the project, indirect costs get it financed, designed, permitted and sold; a builder's residual land value is investment value, not market value.
Cost is not value, insured value leaves out land and foundations, and market value is the most probable price after reasonable exposure, not the first offer or the highest dream.

roleplays.title: The $2.8 Million Ask
roleplays.setting: The Okafors' parlor in Bed-Stuy, listing presentation. Marcus came along to "help".
roleplays.you: Jordan, presenting a CMA to sellers
roleplays.goal: Win the listing honestly: present the CMA as an opinion of value, support a realistic range with comps, and refuse both an inflated price promise and the "appraisal" label.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Grace and Emmanuel Okafor, longtime Bed-Stuy owners who want $2.8M because a competitor quoted it and a neighbor sold for $2.6M to a motivated buyer. Also voice Marcus, a colleague who suggests calling the CMA an appraisal and padding the price. Push twice for $2.8M, once for an 'appraisal' label, and once to add renovation cost to the price. The learner must: present a CMA as an opinion of value (never an appraisal), support a range with sold comps, actives, and expireds, explain market value as the most probable price, explain that cost is not value, and advise on list price while respecting that the seller decides. Grade each point at the end with one sentence of coaching.

motive: the family next door who wanted their parents close
the owner of the adjoining house who wanted the garden
a buyer who had already sold and had nine days to move

opening: {day} in the Okafors' parlor. Your CMA sits on the coffee table: six solds, four actives, two expireds. Grace has already flipped to the last page.
The Okafors poured coffee and pulled out a folder from {rival}. Marcus sits in the corner chair. Your CMA says $2.35 to $2.5 million.
It's {day}. Emmanuel walked you past {feature} on the way in, twice. Grace has a number in her head, and it isn't yours.

say: Grace: "Your range tops out at $2.5 million? {rival} told us $2.8. We want $2.8."
Grace: "$2.35 to $2.5? {rival} said $2.8 without blinking. Why are you so low?"

moves.text: I land at $2.35 to $2.5. Let me walk you through the six sales and the two expireds that got me there.
moves.fb: You anchor on evidence. Solds show what buyers paid; expireds show where buyers said no. Your duty of reasonable care means a supportable number.

moves.text: Ask the other agent which sales support $2.8. Here are mine, side by side. Let's see whose comps hold up.
moves.fb: You let the evidence compete instead of the promises. A CMA is only as good as its comparables.
moves.react: Grace, slowly: "They didn't show us any sales, actually."

moves.text: Prices are moving up lately. Maybe we could push the top of my range to $2.6 and see what happens.
moves.fb: Not a lie, but you moved the number because of pressure, not evidence. Let the comps move the range.
moves.react: Grace: "So your numbers bend if we push. Good to know."

moves.text: If $2.8 is what it takes to earn your trust, I can match that number and we can adjust it later on.
moves.fb: That is buying the listing: quoting a price you cannot support. It misleads the client and breaches your duty of care and honesty.

moves.text: Other agents inflate numbers just to win listings. That's an unethical practice and you shouldn't trust them.
moves.fb: Attacking a competitor does not support your number, and disparaging other brokers is unprofessional. Show the comps instead.
moves.react: Emmanuel frowns: "We didn't ask about them. We asked about our house."

moves.text: My range is a formal valuation of the house, so it's the number a bank will rely on when your buyer applies.
moves.fb: A CMA is an opinion of value from a licensee, not an appraisal. The buyer's lender orders its own appraisal.
moves.react: Grace: "So you're an appraiser too? That's not what your card says."

say: Emmanuel: "The Johnsons on {street} got $2.6 last spring. Their house is no better than ours."
Emmanuel: "Explain the $2.6 on {street}, then. Same block, same size."

moves.text: That buyer was unusually driven. Market value is the most probable price with typical motivation, not the top one.
moves.fb: Correct use of the market value definition: most probable price, typically motivated parties, no undue pressure. A special buyer's premium gets less weight.
moves.react: Emmanuel nods: "So it was a one-time buyer."

moves.text: I counted it, but with less weight. That buyer had a one-off reason to pay up, and we can't count on that twice.
moves.fb: Right. Every sale is a data point, but an atypically motivated buyer is not the market. Explain the weighting, don't hide the sale.
moves.react: Grace: "I hadn't thought about who bought it."

moves.text: That sale doesn't really count here. It's an outlier, so I took it out of my analysis entirely before today.
moves.fb: It does count as a data point. Explain why it gets less weight instead of silently dropping it; sellers notice.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "You dropped the one sale we liked? Convenient."

moves.text: You're right. The best sale on the block sets the value, so let me move my top number up to $2.6 million.
moves.fb: Market value is the most probable price, not the highest price anyone paid. One motivated buyer does not reset the market.
moves.react: Grace: "Now we're getting somewhere. And $2.8 is only a bit more."

moves.text: I'd just average all the sales together, including that one, and the average is the value. That's simply how it works.
moves.fb: Reconciliation is never a simple average. You weigh each comp by how similar it is and how reliable it is.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "Then why bother looking at the houses at all?"

moves.text: Their house had a better layout, so I subtracted from your house's value to account for the difference there.
moves.fb: Backwards. You adjust the comparable, never the subject: comp better, subtract from the comp; comp worse, add to it.
moves.react: Grace: "You're marking down our house? That stings."

say: Marcus, to the sellers: "Think of Jordan's report as an appraisal. Banks use these all the time."
Marcus leans in: "Jordan's being modest. This is basically an appraisal, folks."

moves.text: Small correction: this is a CMA, my opinion of value. An appraisal comes from a licensed appraiser, usually for the lender.
moves.fb: Right. A CMA may never be called an appraisal, and appraisers are separately licensed. The buyer's lender values the house independently.
moves.react: Grace: "Thank you for being straight with us."

moves.text: I'll keep it accurate: this is a comparative market analysis. The buyer's bank hires its own appraiser later.
moves.fb: Correct. Presenting a CMA as an appraisal is misrepresentation, and the lender's appraisal is the number that decides the loan.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "So there's a second number coming. Good to know now."

moves.text: Marcus means it's thorough. Anyway, let's keep moving through the comps, since we're short on time this evening.
moves.fb: You didn't endorse the label, but you let a misstatement stand in front of your clients. Correct it plainly.
moves.react: Grace: "So it IS an appraisal? I'm confused."

moves.text: Say nothing. Correcting a senior colleague in front of the sellers would embarrass him and cost us the listing.
moves.fb: Silence lets a misrepresentation stand in front of your clients. You owe them accurate information, whoever said it.
moves.react: Grace: "If it's an appraisal, then the bank will agree with $2.5."

moves.text: Sure, it's close enough. I'm licensed by the Department of State, the same agency that licenses appraisers here.
moves.fb: Both licenses come through DOS, but a salesperson license does not authorize appraisals. A CMA is never an appraisal.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "Then why would we need the bank's appraisal at all?"

moves.text: It's a broker price opinion, which is the legal equal of an appraisal for any home sold here in New York.
moves.fb: A BPO or CMA is a licensee's opinion. It is not an appraisal and cannot be presented as one.
moves.react: Grace writes it down: "Appraisal equivalent. Okay."

say: Emmanuel: "We spent $150,000 on {feature} three years ago. Add that on top of your number."
Grace: "{feature} cost us $150,000. That alone should push us past $2.6."

moves.text: Cost isn't value. Buyers pay what the comps show that work adds, which is usually less than it cost to build.
moves.fb: Price and cost are facts; value is an opinion. An improvement adds only what the market will pay for it, shown by adjusted comps.
moves.react: Emmanuel sighs: "So we won't get it all back."

moves.text: I gave it credit already. The comps without one got an upward adjustment, so the work is in my range.
moves.fb: Right: you adjust the comps for the feature the subject has. That is how the work shows up in value.
moves.react: Grace: "Show me where. Oh, there. Okay."

moves.text: Some of it comes back, maybe half, but I'd honestly need to think about it more before I give you a number.
moves.fb: Partly true, but vague. Show how the comp adjustments already account for the improvement.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "You'd need to think? You're the one who wrote the report."

moves.text: Absolutely. Value equals what you paid plus what you put in, so we add $150,000 to my top number right now.
moves.fb: Cost does not equal value. The cost approach also subtracts depreciation, and homes are priced from sales, not receipts.

moves.text: We'd use the cost approach for this house, so the renovation spend goes straight into the price, dollar for dollar.
moves.fb: The cost approach fits new or special-purpose buildings, and even then it deducts depreciation. Homes rely on sales comparison.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "So now we're using a different method? Which one is it?"

moves.text: Renovations don't count in a CMA at all. Buyers only pay for square footage and location in this market.
moves.fb: Overcorrection. Improvements matter; you measure them through adjustments to the comparables.
moves.react: Grace: "So $150,000 is worth nothing to you? Wow."

say: Grace: "Why are there two houses in here that never sold? They don't matter."
Emmanuel: "These expired listings. Why show us failures?"

moves.text: They tell us the ceiling. Both sat at $2.75 for months and nobody bit. That's where buyers said no.
moves.fb: Expireds show prices the market rejected. Solds, actives and expireds together give the full picture.
moves.react: Grace: "So $2.8 is where people walk away."

moves.text: Expireds are the market saying no. Both were priced near the other agent's number, and both came off unsold.
moves.fb: Correct use of expired listings: they mark the upper edge of what buyers will pay.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "That's a little uncomfortable to see."

moves.text: I included them because the office template has a slot for them. Feel free to skip past those two pages.
moves.fb: Expireds are useful evidence. Treating them as filler wastes your strongest argument about price.

moves.text: You're right, they don't count. Only closed sales count in a CMA, so I'll pull them out of the report now.
moves.fb: A good CMA uses solds, current competition, and expireds. Dropping expireds hides where the market said no.

moves.text: They expired because those agents were lazy. A better agent could have gotten $2.75 for either one easily.
moves.fb: Blaming agents ignores the evidence. Repeated rejection at a price is market data.
moves.react: Grace: "Then you'll get $2.8 for us, being better."

moves.text: Expired listings are confidential under MLS rules, so I really shouldn't have shown you those two at all.
moves.fb: Not true. Expired listing history is routine CMA data shared with sellers.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "Then why are they in here?"

say: Grace: "Fine. But list it at $2.8 anyway. Buyers can negotiate down."
Emmanuel: "It's our house. We list at $2.8 and come down if we have to."

moves.text: It's your call. My advice is $2.495. At $2.8 the buyer's appraisal likely lands near $2.45. I'll put that in writing.
moves.fb: The seller sets the price; you advise with evidence, explain appraisal risk, and document the advice.
moves.react: Grace: "Put it in writing. We'll sleep on it."

moves.text: You decide the price. I'd list at $2.495. Overpriced listings go stale, and stale listings sell for less.
moves.fb: Correct: respect the seller's authority, give a clear recommendation, explain why. Then document it.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "Stale. I don't want stale. Let's talk about $2.495."

moves.text: Absolutely, $2.8 it is. You know your home best, and we can always revisit the price in a month or so.
moves.fb: Legal, since the seller sets the price, but you failed to communicate the risk. Advise first, then follow instructions.

moves.text: I'll list at $2.8 and I promise you'll get it. My buyers always pay whatever my sellers ask here in Bed-Stuy.
moves.fb: Promising a sale price you do not believe is a misrepresentation, and no one can promise a price.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "Promise? Then we'll hold you to it."

moves.text: I can't list above my CMA range. The rules say the list price has to sit inside the licensee's range.
moves.fb: No such rule. The owner sets the list price. Your job is to advise and document, not to forbid.

moves.text: Let's list at $2.8 and just put 'appraised at $2.5M' in the ad so buyers think they're getting a deal.
moves.fb: There is no appraisal, and the ad would mislead buyers. Advertising must be truthful (19 NYCRR 175.25).

say: Marcus texts you under the table: "Just say $2.8 and get the signature. Price reduce in 30 days."
Marcus, in the hallway: "Agree to their number. You can always beat them down later."

moves.text: Text back: No. I'll win it with the comps or not at all. Then return to the table and the range.
moves.fb: Buying a listing with a price you cannot support is a misrepresentation. Turning it down protects the clients and your license.
moves.react: Marcus shrugs. The Okafors are still reading your comps.

moves.text: Tell Marcus quietly that you won't quote a number you can't support, and go back to the six solds.
moves.fb: Correct. Your duty is honesty and reasonable care, not winning the listing at any price.
moves.react: Marcus: "Your funeral." Grace: "Back to the sales, then?"

moves.text: Tell Marcus you'll think about it, and keep presenting the CMA without naming a new price yet.
moves.fb: You didn't take the bait, but leaving the door open invites the shortcut later. Close it.

moves.text: Go back in and say: I've rethought it. $2.8 is realistic. Let's sign tonight and adjust the price later.
moves.fb: That is buying the listing: an unsupported price to win a signature, with a plan to reduce. It misleads the sellers.
moves.react: Grace beams. Emmanuel signs. In 60 days they'll blame you.

moves.text: Agree to $2.8, but write 'seller insisted' on the file so you're covered when the price drops later on.
moves.fb: You quoted the number yourself; a note doesn't cure a misrepresentation you made.
moves.react: Diane, later: "Your note says they insisted. The recording says you offered."

moves.text: Offer to cut your commission by half a point instead of raising the price. Sellers usually take the deal.
moves.fb: Discounting to compete is legal but beside the point, and here you're using it to dodge an honest price talk.

say: Emmanuel: "My nephew is a licensed appraiser. He'll write us up at $2.8. Problem solved."
Grace: "Our cousin appraises houses. Let him do a report at $2.8 and put it in the listing."

moves.text: The buyer's lender orders its own independent appraisal, so a family report won't move the loan.
moves.fb: Lenders must use appraisers selected independently of the parties. A seller's report does not drive the buyer's loan.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "So his report wouldn't change anything?"

moves.text: He can, but the bank won't use it. The buyer's lender picks its own appraiser, separate from all of us.
moves.fb: Right. Appraisal independence rules keep the parties away from the lender's appraisal.
moves.react: Grace: "Then what's the point of paying him?"

moves.text: Maybe, but I'd keep it out of the listing for now. Let's talk about it again once the house is on the market.
moves.fb: Not wrong, but you missed the key fact: the lender's appraisal is independent and decides the loan.

moves.text: Perfect. A licensed appraisal at $2.8 binds the buyer's bank, so we can list there and close there safely.
moves.fb: No seller-ordered appraisal binds the buyer's lender. The lender orders its own through an independent process.
moves.react: Grace: "See? I knew we'd get there."

moves.text: Great, and have him send his report to the buyer's lender directly, so they can skip their own appraisal.
moves.fb: Parties may not influence the lender's appraisal. Steering a relative's report to the lender is improper.

moves.text: He can't. Appraisers aren't allowed to value any home in the county where their family members live.
moves.fb: Made-up rule. The real issue is that the buyer's lender uses its own independent appraiser.

say: Grace: "If we take your $2.495, will you guarantee it sells in 30 days?"
Emmanuel: "Your number, then. But promise us a sale inside a month."

moves.text: I can't guarantee timing. Recent comps took about 45 to 60 days. That's history, not a promise.
moves.fb: Exposure time looks back at how long past sales took; marketing time is a forward estimate. Neither is a guarantee.

moves.text: No one can promise that. What I can show you is how long similar houses took, and why pricing right helps.
moves.fb: Correct. You give evidence about exposure time and avoid promises you cannot keep.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "Show me those days on market."

moves.text: Probably, yes. This market moves fast for brownstones, so a month should be plenty if we stage it well.
moves.fb: Soft promise without data. Use days on market from the comps instead of optimism.
moves.react: Grace: "Probably. I'll remember you said that."

moves.text: Yes, 30 days or I'll waive my commission entirely. I'm that confident about my number on this one.
moves.fb: A guarantee you cannot control invites disputes, and waiving pay to win a listing is no substitute for honest advice.

moves.text: Market value already assumes a 30-day sale, so if it's priced at value it has to sell in that window.
moves.fb: Market value assumes reasonable exposure, not a fixed number of days. Exposure time varies by market.
moves.react: Grace: "So if it takes 40 days, you priced it wrong?"

moves.text: I'll list at $2.495, but tell buyers there's another offer so it moves faster. That always speeds things up.
moves.fb: Inventing offers is a misrepresentation to buyers and can expose you to discipline under 19 NYCRR 175.

say: Emmanuel: "Our insurance says rebuilding would cost $1.9 million. Plus land. Isn't that the value?"
Grace: "The insurer valued the house at $1.9 for rebuilding. Add the lot and we're at $2.8, right?"

moves.text: Insurance value is rebuild cost, not market value. It leaves out land and doesn't reflect what buyers pay.
moves.fb: Insurable value covers the cost to replace the structure and omits land. It is a different kind of value from market value.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "Different purpose, different number. Got it."

moves.text: Different question. Insurers ask what rebuilding costs. Buyers ask what similar houses sold for.
moves.fb: Correct. Each kind of value answers a specific purpose; market value comes from sales of comparable homes.
moves.react: Grace: "I suppose a buyer isn't rebuilding it."

moves.text: That's a fair point. I'm not really sure how insurance numbers work, so you would have to ask your agent there.
moves.fb: Referral is fine, but you should know insurable value is a different concept from market value.

moves.text: Yes, rebuild cost plus land is the value. That's the cost approach, and it's the main method for homes.
moves.fb: Homes are valued mainly by sales comparison. The cost approach also deducts depreciation, and it suits new or special-purpose buildings.

moves.text: Insurance numbers are always higher than value, so take the $1.9 and knock off about thirty percent.
moves.fb: Made-up rule of thumb. Insurable value and market value measure different things; don't convert one into the other.

moves.text: Insurable value includes the land, so $1.9 million is your full value and your house is worth less than you thought.
moves.fb: Insurable value omits land and foundations. And it isn't market value either way.

roleplays.debrief: You practised the core valuation rules: market value is the most probable price, a CMA is an opinion of value that may never be called an appraisal, and you adjust the comps, never the subject. Cost and insurable value are not market value, expireds show where buyers said no, and the seller sets the price after you advise and document. Quoting an unsupported number to win a listing is misrepresentation.

questions.q: The amount a property actually sold for is its:
c: Market price
Market value
Assessed value
Insurable value
questions.x: Market price is what was actually paid. Market value is the trap: it is the most probable price under normal conditions, which can differ.

questions.q: A seller in a hurry accepts $40,000 less than similar homes bring. The sale shows a difference between:
c: Assessed and insured value
Cost and depreciation
Market price and market value
Gross and net income
questions.x: A pressured sale makes the price paid differ from typical market value. Assessed value is the trap: it is for taxes.

questions.q: Insurable value generally leaves out:
c: The roof
Land and foundations
Interior walls
Built-in appliances
questions.x: Insurance covers the cost to replace improvements that can be destroyed, so land and foundations are excluded. The roof is the trap: it is insured.

questions.q: A home's insurable value is based on:
c: Its recent sale price
Its assessed value
The land value
The cost to replace the insurable improvements
questions.x: Insurable value tracks replacement cost of improvements. Sale price is the trap: it includes land.

questions.q: Estimating land's value as if vacant and available for its highest and best use is:
c: Reconciliation
Depreciation
Site valuation
Gross rent multiplier analysis
questions.x: Site valuation values the land separately. Reconciliation is the trap: it weighs the results of different approaches.

questions.q: In the cost approach, the appraiser adds the depreciated building cost to the:
c: Separately valued site
Gross rent
Assessed value
Mortgage balance
questions.x: Cost approach: site value plus depreciated cost of improvements. Assessed value is the trap: it is a tax figure.

questions.q: The cost to build an exact replica with the same materials and design is:
c: Replacement cost
Market price
Book value
Reproduction cost
questions.x: Reproduction is an exact copy. Replacement is the trap: it is a building of equal utility using modern materials.

questions.q: For an ornate 1890s brownstone, an appraiser would most likely use:
c: Reproduction cost
Replacement cost
Assessed value
Historic cost
questions.x: Exact period materials are impractical, so replacement cost with modern equivalents is typical. Reproduction is the trap: it is possible but rarely practical.

questions.q: An unbiased estimate of the nature, quality, value, or utility of an interest in identified real estate is the definition of:
c: A valuation
An appraisal
An evaluation
A broker price opinion
questions.x: That is the syllabus definition of an appraisal. Valuation is narrower: the process of estimating value as of a date; an evaluation may not produce a value at all.

questions.q: A study of a property's nature, quality, or utility in which a value estimate is not necessarily required, such as a feasibility study, is called:
c: An appraisal
A valuation
A market analysis
An evaluation
questions.x: An evaluation studies use and feasibility and can end without a dollar figure. Valuation is the trap: it always aims at a value as of a date.

questions.q: Market value is best described as the:
c: Most probable price in a fair sale as of a date
Highest price an eager buyer would pay
Amount of the first offer after listing
Price paid in the latest sale on the block
questions.x: Market value is the most probable price, not the highest. A single recent sale is a price, which may or may not equal value.

questions.q: A seller in Yonkers offers the buyer a 2% purchase-money mortgage, and the buyer pays $80,000 more than similar homes sold for. An appraiser estimating market value would most likely:
c: Accept the sale price as its market value
Discard the sale because it was financed
Adjust the price for seller financing
Raise the value of the neighboring homes
questions.x: Market value assumes cash or terms equivalent to cash. Below-market seller financing inflates price, so the appraiser adjusts for it rather than accepting the price or throwing the sale out.

questions.q: Insurable value differs from market value mainly because insurable value omits:
c: The building itself
Built-in appliances
The land under it
The roof and siding
questions.x: Land (and usually foundations) does not burn, so insurable value covers the cost to rebuild the structure. Leaving out the building would make the coverage pointless.

questions.q: The conditions requisite to a fair sale under the market value definition include each of the following EXCEPT:
c: A seller pressed to avoid foreclosure
Buyer and seller well informed
Payment in cash or its equivalent
Reasonable time on the open market
questions.x: Market value assumes neither party is under undue duress. A seller racing a foreclosure is under duress, so that sale may fall below market value.

questions.q: Price is:
c: The total cost to build it
An appraiser's opinion of value
The value to one specific investor
What one buyer and seller agreed on
questions.x: Price is a historical fact about one transaction; it may or may not equal value. Cost is construction spending, a different idea.

questions.q: Each of the following is an indirect (soft) cost of construction EXCEPT:
c: Architect's fees
Lumber for framing
Construction loan interest
Building permit fees
questions.x: Materials and labor are direct (hard) costs. Professional fees, financing and filing fees are indirect; permit fees tempt because they are paid to build, but they are soft costs.

questions.q: Under New York law, a comparative market analysis prepared by a real estate licensee:
c: Cannot be called an appraisal of value
Becomes an appraisal once the broker signs
Can replace a lender's appraisal
Has to be filed with the Department of State
questions.x: A CMA is an opinion of value and is never an appraisal, no matter who signs it. Appraisals come from state licensed or certified appraisers.

questions.q: Evelyn owns the building next to a Jamaica Avenue storefront and can finance a purchase cheaply. She calculates that the storefront is worth $300,000 more to her than to a typical buyer. Her figure is:
c: Market value
Assessed value
Investment value
Value in exchange
questions.x: Investment value is value to a specific investor based on that investor's own situation and goals. Market value assumes a typical buyer, which is exactly what Evelyn is not.

questions.q: Expired listings are included in a CMA primarily because they:
c: Are the best evidence of value
Show what rivals are asking now
Have to be shown to every buyer
Show prices buyers rejected
questions.x: Expireds usually failed because they were overpriced, so they mark a ceiling. Current listings, not expireds, show what competitors are asking now.

questions.q: In the market value definition, "reasonable exposure" refers to:
c: How long a sale will take after the appraisal date
Market time before a sale on the effective date
The number of showings held during the listing
Advertising the property in at least two outlets
questions.x: Exposure time looks backward from the effective date. Marketing time is the forward-looking estimate, which makes the first choice the trap.

questions.q: A Riverdale seller insists on listing $200,000 above the top of Jordan's supported CMA range. Jordan's best course is to:
c: Refuse to take the listing at that price
Raise the CMA figures to support the price
Advise with the comps and let the seller decide
Tell the seller that lenders will approve that price
questions.x: The seller sets the price; the licensee advises with evidence and documents it. Changing the CMA to match would be misrepresentation.

questions.q: In valuation, cost refers to:
c: Total spent to build the improvement
The price the last buyer paid
The value shown on the tax roll
The most probable selling price
questions.x: Cost is the supply-side spending to create the improvement: labor, materials, fees, financing and profit. Price is what a buyer paid, and neither automatically equals value.

questions.q: A specialized bakery plant is worth far more to its current owner, who uses every custom oven, than to any likely buyer. That higher figure is best called:
c: Market value
Value in use
Mortgage value
Going-concern value
questions.x: Value in use is value for a specific use to a specific user. Going-concern value tempts, but it includes the business itself (goodwill), not just the real estate's usefulness to this owner.

questions.q: To be the highest and best use, a use must be each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Legally permissible
Physically possible
Financially feasible
Its current use
questions.x: The four tests are legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive. The current use may or may not pass them.

questions.q: Plottage is:
c: The value added by combining parcels
The act of combining adjacent parcels
Dividing a parcel into building lots
A survey of the parcel's lot lines
questions.x: Assemblage is the act of combining; plottage is the value increase that results. The two are commonly swapped on the exam.

questions.q: A comparable sold for $750,000. It has a pool worth $20,000 that the subject lacks. The subject has a garage worth $15,000 that the comparable lacks. The adjusted price of the comparable is:
questions.x: Comp better (pool), subtract $20,000. Comp poorer (no garage), add $15,000. $750,000 - $20,000 + $15,000 = $745,000; $755,000 reverses both signs.

questions.q: In the sales comparison approach, adjustments are made to:
c: The subject property
The comparable sales
Both subject and comps
The assessed value
questions.x: You adjust the comparable to make it resemble the subject, because the comp's sale price is the known fact. The subject is never adjusted.

questions.q: A city builds a waste transfer station across the street from a Hunts Point row house, and its value drops. This loss is:
c: Physical deterioration
Curable functional obsolescence
Incurable functional obsolescence
External (economic) obsolescence
questions.x: A cause outside the property line is external (economic) obsolescence. Incurable functional obsolescence tempts because the owner cannot fix it, but functional problems are design flaws inside the property.

questions.q: External obsolescence is generally:
c: Curable by the owner
Caused by wear and tear
Incurable by the owner
Charged to the land
questions.x: An owner cannot fix a highway, a factory closing, or a recession, so external obsolescence is treated as incurable. Wear and tear is physical deterioration.

questions.q: Land is worth $250,000. The building's replacement cost new is $600,000, and accrued depreciation is $150,000. Using the cost approach, the value is:
questions.x: $600,000 - $150,000 = $450,000 depreciated building, plus $250,000 land = $700,000. $850,000 forgets to subtract depreciation.

questions.q: A comparable two-family sold for $480,000 and rents for $3,000 a month. The subject rents for $3,300 a month. Using a gross rent multiplier, the subject's value is about:
questions.x: GRM = $480,000 / $3,000 = 160, and $3,300 x 160 = $528,000. Choosing $480,000 ignores the subject's higher rent.

questions.concept: Income approach NOI and cap rate
questions.q: A building has potential gross income of $240,000, a 5% vacancy rate, operating expenses of $78,000, and annual debt service of $60,000. At a 6% cap rate, its value is:
questions.x: EGI = $240,000 - $12,000 = $228,000. NOI = $228,000 - $78,000 = $150,000. $150,000 / 0.06 = $2,500,000. Debt service is not an operating expense, which is why $1,500,000 is wrong, and $25,000,000 slips the decimal in the rate.

questions.q: Leo wants to estimate the value of a single-family home in Forest Hills where many similar homes sold this year. The most reliable approach is:
c: Sales comparison
Cost approach
Income capitalization
Gross rent multiplier
questions.x: With plenty of recent similar sales, sales comparison fits owner-occupied homes best. The income approach and GRM suit rental property.

questions.q: A bedroom that can only be reached by walking through another bedroom is an example of:
c: Physical deterioration
External obsolescence
Functional obsolescence
Curable physical deterioration
questions.x: A poor layout inside the property is functional obsolescence. External (economic) obsolescence comes from outside the property line.

questions.q: In an appraisal, reconciliation means:
c: Averaging the three approaches equally
Weighting the most reliable approach
Matching value to the contract price
Fixing errors in comp tax records
questions.x: Reconciliation is a judgment that gives most weight to the approach best suited to the property. A straight average is the classic wrong answer.

questions.concept: Highest and best use as improved
questions.q: A one-story garage in Long Island City is worth $1.2 million as it stands. The same lot, if vacant, would be worth $1.5 million because zoning allows a 10-story residential building. The highest and best use as improved is most likely:
c: Demolition and redevelopment
Keeping the garage as it is
Converting the garage to storage
Leaving the lot vacant for good
questions.x: When land as vacant is worth more than land plus the existing building, the building has negative contributory value and redevelopment is the highest and best use. Leaving it vacant gives up the value zoning allows.

questions.q: A residential CMA should normally include each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Similar homes sold in the past year
Current competing listings
Recently expired listings
Sales from years ago elsewhere
questions.x: Comps should be recent (generally within 12 months) and nearby. Expired listings belong in a CMA because they show the price ceiling.

questions.q: A comparable office building sold for $1,500,000 and has NOI of $90,000. The indicated cap rate is:
questions.x: Rate = NOI / value = $90,000 / $1,500,000 = 0.06, or 6%. Flipping the fraction gives 16.7, the trap.

questions.q: The value set by a town assessor to calculate property tax is:
c: Market value
Mortgage value
Assessed value
Insurable value
questions.x: Assessed value is set by the assessor for property tax. Mortgage value is what a lender relies on for a loan, the closest distractor.

questions.q: The value a lender relies on in deciding how much to lend against a property is:
c: Assessed value
Mortgage value
Value in use
Investment value
questions.x: Mortgage value is the figure a lender will rely on to make a loan. Investment value is a specific investor's own figure, not the lender's.

questions.q: A buyer contracts to pay $820,000, but the appraisal comes in at $790,000. The lender will base the loan on:
c: $790,000, the appraised value
$820,000, the contract price
$805,000, the average of the two
Whichever figure the buyer picks
questions.x: The lender lends against the appraisal, so the buyer must cover the $30,000 gap in cash, renegotiate, or exit under a mortgage contingency. The contract price is the trap.

questions.q: A buyer's appraisal comes in $50,000 below the contract price. Each of the following is a usual option for the buyer EXCEPT:
c: Make the lender lend on the price
Bring the $50,000 gap in cash
Renegotiate the price with the seller
Cancel under a mortgage contingency
questions.x: When the appraisal is low, the buyer can pay the gap, renegotiate, or walk under a mortgage contingency. The lender will not lend on the higher contract price; it uses the appraised value.

questions.q: In a CMA, current competing listings are best described as:
c: The best evidence of value
Asking prices, not values
Prices the market rejected
Recorded deed sale prices
questions.x: Active listings show the competition buyers will see this weekend, but they are asking prices, not values. Recent solds are the best evidence, and expireds show what the market rejected.

questions.q: Which data is the best evidence of value in a CMA?
c: Active listings at their asking prices
Expired listings from the past year
Similar nearby sales in the past year
An online automated value estimate
questions.x: Recent sales of similar nearby homes (usually within 12 months) are the best evidence. Active listings are only asking prices, the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: When pulling comps for a Manhattan co-op, why can't a licensee rely on ACRIS deed records for sale prices?
c: ACRIS excludes Manhattan property records
Co-op sale prices are sealed by statute
ACRIS omits sales under $1 million
Co-op sales transfer shares, not deeds
questions.x: Co-op buyers get shares and a proprietary lease, so no deed is recorded and the price does not show in ACRIS; lean on MLS data instead. ACRIS does cover Manhattan, so that choice is the trap.

questions.q: Two otherwise similar co-ops differ by $1,000 in monthly maintenance. The one with the higher maintenance will most likely:
c: Sell for about $1,000 less
Sell for more, since services are better
Sell for tens of thousands less
Sell for the same, since maintenance is not price
questions.x: Buyers pay maintenance every month, so a $1,000 higher maintenance can knock tens of thousands off what they will pay. Treating it as unrelated to price is the trap.

questions.q: A licensee quotes a seller a price well above the comps to win the listing. This is:
c: Buying the listing, a misrepresentation
Puffing, which the law allows as opinion
Acceptable if the seller agrees in writing
A valid CMA with a higher price range
questions.x: Quoting an inflated price to win the listing ('buying the listing') breaches the duty of care and honesty and is treated as misrepresentation. Calling it harmless puffing is the trap.

questions.q: What usually happens to a listing priced well above market value to win the seller's business?
c: It sells fast, above the asking price
It sets a new high comp for the block
The appraisal rises to meet the price
It goes stale and needs price cuts
questions.x: An overpriced listing usually sits, takes price cuts, and can end up selling below value. Appraisals follow the comps, not the list price.

questions.q: A buyer will pay no more for a house than the cost of an equally desirable substitute. This is the principle of:
c: Contribution
Substitution
Highest and best use
Supply and demand
questions.x: Substitution says a buyer pays no more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute, and it underlies all three approaches. Contribution is about what one feature adds.

questions.q: Which appraisal principle underlies all three approaches to value?
c: Regression
Substitution
Supply and demand
Anticipation
questions.x: Substitution powers sales comparison (price of a substitute), cost (cost to build one) and income (price of an equal income stream). Regression and progression describe a house's neighbors pulling its value.

questions.q: An owner spent $80,000 on an in-ground pool. Appraisers find it adds $20,000 to value. Which principle explains this?
c: Substitution
Supply and demand
Regression
Contribution
questions.x: Contribution says a feature is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost. Cost is not value, so most of the $80,000 is not recovered.

questions.q: Under the principle of contribution, a renovation's value equals:
c: What it adds to market value
What it cost, including labor
Its cost minus depreciation
What the owner believes it is worth
questions.x: Contribution measures value added in the market, not dollars spent. 'Cost minus depreciation' is the cost approach's logic, the tempting distractor.

questions.q: The largest, most updated house on a block of modest homes is worth less than it would be among similar homes. This is:
c: Progression
Plottage
Regression
Anticipation
questions.x: Regression: the best house on the block is pulled down by its cheaper neighbors. Progression is the reverse, a modest house pulled up by better ones.

questions.q: A modest cottage on a street of expensive homes gains value from its surroundings. This is:
c: Regression
Contribution
Assemblage
Progression
questions.x: Progression: a modest house is pulled up by better neighbors. Regression is the opposite effect on the best house on the block.

questions.q: A new subway station is announced, and nearby prices rise before it opens. This illustrates:
c: Conformity
Substitution
Anticipation
Supply and demand
questions.x: Anticipation: value is the present worth of expected future benefits, so prices move when the station is announced. Conformity is about a home fitting its neighborhood.

questions.q: The principle of anticipation says value is:
c: The cost of an equal substitute
Present worth of future benefits
Highest when a home fits its block
What a feature adds, not its cost
questions.x: Anticipation defines value as the present worth of expected future benefits. The cost of an equal substitute is the principle of substitution.

questions.q: In the sales comparison approach, which adjustment is usually made first?
c: Financing and conditions of sale
Location, such as a park block
Physical features such as size and baths
Market conditions (time since sale)
questions.x: Appraisers usually adjust for financing and sale conditions first, then market conditions (time), then location, then physical features. Time is tempting because it comes right after.

questions.q: A comp sold 6 months ago for $500,000, and prices have since risen 4%. Adjusted for market conditions only, it indicates:
questions.x: Prices rose since the comp sold, so adjust the comp up: $500,000 x 1.04 = $520,000. Subtracting is the trap: the comp would sell for more today.

questions.q: A 1925 building with all new systems is judged to behave like a 15-year-old building. The 15 years is its:
c: Actual age
Effective age
Economic life
Remaining life
questions.x: Effective age is how old a building acts, based on condition; actual (chronological) age is how old it is. Economic life is its total useful life.

questions.q: A building has an effective age of 12 years and a total economic life of 48 years. Using the age-life method, depreciation is:
questions.x: Age-life depreciation = effective age / economic life = 12 / 48 = 25%. 75% is the share of life remaining, and 33.3% wrongly divides by remaining life (12 / 36).

questions.q: Three comps adjust to $610,000, $625,000 and $640,000. The $625,000 comp needed one small adjustment; the others needed four each. In reconciling, the agent should:
c: Average all three adjusted comps equally
Use the highest adjusted figure, $640,000
Drop all three and find new comps
Give the $625,000 comp the most weight
questions.x: The comp needing the fewest and smallest adjustments is the most reliable, so it gets the most weight. A simple average ignores reliability, the trap.

questions.q: When preparing a CMA, why might an agent recommend a list price slightly above the adjusted comp range?
c: Appraisers add 10% to every list price
The top comp sets value by definition
Buyers often settle a bit under ask
Higher list prices sell homes faster
questions.x: The range estimates what a buyer will pay; buyers often land a little under ask, so listing at or just above the top leaves room. Pricing far above the range is the overpricing trap.

questions.q: A bank hires a certified appraiser for an unbiased, supported estimate of a specific condo's value for a mortgage. The appraiser's work product is:
c: An evaluation
An appraisal
A market analysis
A price opinion
questions.x: An unbiased, supported estimate of value for identified real estate is an appraisal. An evaluation tempts because it is also a formal study, but it need not produce a value.

questions.q: A developer pays a consultant to study whether a vacant Bronx lot could support a self-storage facility. No value estimate is requested. This work is:
c: An appraisal
A broker price opinion
A valuation
An evaluation
questions.x: A feasibility or use study with no required value figure is an evaluation. A valuation, by definition, ends in an estimate of value as of a date.

questions.q: After a bidding war, a Park Slope brownstone sells for $150,000 above every comparable sale. For an appraiser, the contract amount is best described as:
c: The market value, as a matter of definition
The property's insurable value
The new ceiling for the block
Possibly more than market value
questions.x: Price is what one buyer paid; market value is the most probable price in a typical fair sale. Treating one emotional bid as market value is the trap.

questions.q: When a comparable sold with unusually favorable seller financing, the appraiser adjusts it because market value assumes:
c: The seller is a licensed broker
Cash or terms equal to cash
The buyer pays the closing costs
A 30-year fixed bank mortgage
questions.x: Market value assumes payment in cash or its equivalent, so special financing that inflates the price must be adjusted out. A 30-year mortgage is common, but the definition is about cash equivalence, not a loan type.

questions.q: A house sells for $900,000; the lot alone is worth $400,000. Rebuilding the house would cost $550,000. The insurer will focus on:
questions.x: Insurable value is the cost to rebuild the structure; land is excluded because it is not destroyed. $900,000 is market value, which includes the land.

questions.q: A father sells his house to his daughter for half of what similar homes bring. An appraiser using it as a comparable should:
c: Treat it as not arm's length
Use it without any adjustment
Average it with the other comps
Increase the subject's value to match
questions.x: Market value assumes unrelated, typically motivated parties. A family sale is not arm's length, so it is excluded or heavily adjusted; averaging it in would drag the estimate down.

questions.q: A buyer paid $725,000 for a house that an appraiser valued at $700,000 and that would cost $650,000 to build today. The $725,000 is the:
c: Market value
Its cost
The price
Assessed value
questions.x: Price is the amount actually paid in a transaction. The $700,000 opinion is the value estimate, and $650,000 is cost.

questions.q: Which construction expense is a direct (hard) cost?
c: Carpenters' wages
Surveyor's fees
Construction loan interest
Legal fees
questions.x: Labor and materials that go into the building are hard costs. Survey, legal and financing charges are soft costs even though they are paid to complete the project.

questions.q: A seller asks a licensee to title her CMA "Appraisal Report" so it looks official to her family. The licensee should:
c: Agree if the broker reviews it first
Title it "Certified Appraisal"
Agree if the price is supported
Decline; a CMA isn't an appraisal
questions.x: A CMA may never be called an appraisal, whatever its quality or who reviews it. Broker review is the tempting but irrelevant fix.

questions.q: Investment value differs from market value because it reflects:
c: A typical buyer's view
The cost to rebuild it new
The assessor's opinion
One investor's own goals
questions.x: Investment value is value to a particular investor given that investor's financing, tax position and plans. Market value is the one that assumes a typical buyer.

questions.q: A CMA shows three expired listings asking $1.1 million to $1.2 million and sales at $950,000 to $1 million. The expireds most likely tell the seller that:
c: Buyers resisted prices that high
The home is worth about $1.15 million
Sold prices are out of date
Expired listings set the floor
questions.x: Expired listings usually mark prices the market rejected, a ceiling, not a floor. Sold comps remain the best evidence of value.

questions.q: An appraiser's estimate of how long it will take to sell a property after the effective date of the appraisal is called:
c: Exposure time
Marketing time
Absorption rate
Days on market
questions.x: Marketing time looks forward from the effective date. Exposure time looks backward, the time on the market before a hypothetical sale on that date.

questions.q: Who has the final say on the list price of a residential listing?
c: The listing agent
The buyer's lender
The sponsoring broker
The seller, as owner
questions.x: The seller decides the list price; the licensee advises with a CMA and documents the advice. The broker supervises the agent but does not set the client's price.

questions.q: A builder spends $420,000 on labor, materials, permits, financing and profit to put up a house. That $420,000 is the house's:
c: Market value
Its price
Its cost
Investment value
questions.x: Cost is the total expenditure to create the improvement. It becomes a price only if someone buys at that amount, and it may differ from market value.

questions.q: A brewery built around custom tanks is appraised two ways: its worth to the current brewer running it, and what a typical buyer would pay. The first figure is:
c: Market value
Value in use
Assessed value
Insurable value
questions.x: Value in use measures worth to a specific user for a specific use, often higher for special-purpose property. Market value is the second figure, based on a typical buyer.

questions.q: Among uses that are legal, physically possible and financially feasible, the highest and best use is the one that is:
c: The current use
Most popular in the area
Cheapest to build
Maximally productive
questions.x: The fourth test is maximal productivity, the use producing the highest value. The current use is the trap; it qualifies only if it also passes all four tests.

questions.q: A developer buys three adjoining lots worth $500,000 each. Combined, they are worth $1.9 million. The $400,000 increase is:
c: Plottage
Assemblage
Subdivision
Escalation
questions.x: Plottage is the extra value created by combining parcels. Assemblage is the act of combining them, the classic mix-up.

questions.q: A comparable sold for $620,000. It lacks a finished basement worth $25,000 that the subject has, and it has an extra bath worth $12,000 that the subject lacks. The comparable's adjusted price is:
questions.x: Comp poorer (no basement), add $25,000. Comp better (extra bath), subtract $12,000. $620,000 + $25,000 - $12,000 = $633,000; $607,000 reverses both signs.

questions.q: A comparable has a two-car garage; the subject has none. To account for the garage, the appraiser:
c: Adds its value to the subject
Ignores the garage
Adds its value to the comp
Subtracts its value from the comp
questions.x: Adjust the comparable, never the subject: comp better, subtract. Adding the value to the subject reaches a similar number but breaks the rule, which is why it tempts.
