questions.q: Which is an example of external obsolescence?
c: A cracked foundation
A five-bedroom, one-bath layout
Heavy truck traffic on a new bypass
Peeling paint and a worn roof
questions.x: External obsolescence comes from outside the property line, such as traffic, noise or a nuisance. A poor bath-to-bedroom ratio is functional, a design flaw inside the house.

questions.q: Which form of depreciation is typically treated as incurable because the cause is beyond the owner's control?
c: Physical deterioration
Functional obsolescence
External obsolescence
Deferred maintenance
questions.x: External obsolescence arises off the property, so the owner cannot cure it. Functional obsolescence can be curable or incurable depending on cost, so it is not the general rule.

questions.q: A building would cost $480,000 to replace new and has accrued depreciation of $96,000. The land is worth $180,000. The cost approach indicates:
questions.x: $480,000 - $96,000 = $384,000 depreciated building, plus $180,000 land = $564,000. $660,000 forgets depreciation, and $384,000 leaves out the land.

questions.q: Similar three-family houses sell for about 150 times their monthly gross rent. A subject collects $4,800 a month. Its indicated value is:
questions.x: Value = GRM x gross monthly rent = 150 x $4,800 = $720,000. A GRM uses gross rent, not NOI, so no expenses are subtracted.

questions.concept: Income approach NOI and cap rate
questions.q: An apartment building has potential gross income of $360,000, 10% vacancy and collection loss, operating expenses of $124,000, and a mortgage payment of $90,000 a year. At an 8% cap rate, its value is:
questions.x: EGI = $360,000 - $36,000 = $324,000. NOI = $324,000 - $124,000 = $200,000. $200,000 / 0.08 = $2,500,000. Subtracting the $90,000 mortgage payment gives $1,375,000, but debt service never reduces NOI; $2,950,000 forgets vacancy.

questions.q: An appraiser must value a 40-year-old public library that is being sold. There are almost no sales of similar buildings, and it produces no rent. The approach given most weight is likely the:
c: Sales comparison
Income approach
Cost approach
Gross rent multiplier
questions.x: Special-purpose buildings with few sales and no income are valued mainly by the cost approach. The income approach needs rent, which a library does not produce.

questions.q: A new house in a neighborhood of four-bedroom homes has just one tiny closet and no garage. The resulting loss in value is:
c: External (economic) obsolescence
Physical deterioration
Functional obsolescence
Plottage
questions.x: Design shortcomings inside the property are functional obsolescence, even in a new house. Physical deterioration requires wear or damage, which a new house lacks.

questions.q: For a single-family home, the sales comparison approach indicates $610,000, cost $650,000, and income $560,000. In reconciliation, the appraiser will most likely conclude near:
c: $606,667, the simple average
$610,000, sales comparison
$650,000, the cost figure
$560,000, the income figure
questions.x: Reconciliation weights the approach most reliable for the property type, which for an owner-occupied home is sales comparison. Averaging the three is the classic wrong method.

questions.concept: Highest and best use as improved
questions.q: An existing building is said to have negative contributory value when the:
c: Building is over 50 years old
Land is assessed below market
Building needs a new roof
Vacant land would be worth more
questions.x: If the land would be worth more vacant than with the building, demolition costs aside, the building subtracts value and redevelopment is the highest and best use. Age alone does not make a building a liability.

questions.q: Preparing a CMA for a Bayside colonial, an agent should give the most weight to:
c: Recent sales of similar homes
Active listings asking the most
Expired listings from last year
Sales of condos in the same zip
questions.x: Recent sales of similar nearby homes are the best evidence of value. Active and expired listings add context about competition and price ceilings but are asking prices, not sales.

questions.q: A retail building sold for $2,400,000. Its NOI is $168,000. The indicated capitalization rate is:
questions.x: Rate = NOI / value = $168,000 / $2,400,000 = 0.07, or 7%. Dividing value by NOI gives 14.3, the flipped-fraction trap.

questions.q: Which recent sale is LEAST suitable as a comparable in a CMA?
c: A listed sale that went to contract in 30 days
A sale between two strangers with a 60-day closing
A sale that took 90 days with one price cut
A sale from a mother to her son, never listed
questions.x: Comparables should be arm's-length sales with market exposure. A family transfer that was never listed may be priced for reasons that have nothing to do with the market. A sale with a price cut is the tempting pick, but a reduction shows the market working; it remains a valid, if slower, sale.

questions.q: A licensee preparing a CMA would normally use each of the following as a closed comparable sale EXCEPT:
c: A sale 4 months ago a few blocks away
An estate transfer to an heir at half price
A sale 10 months ago with a seller concession
A sale 7 months ago in the same building
questions.x: A transfer from an estate to an heir is not arm's length and typically reflects no market exposure. A sale with a seller concession is the tempting pick, but it remains usable once the concession is adjusted out to state the price in cash-equivalent terms.

questions.q: A comparable sold for $780,000 with the seller paying $15,000 of the buyer's closing costs. Before other adjustments, its cash-equivalent price is:
questions.x: The concession inflated the contract price, so subtract it: $780,000 minus $15,000 equals $765,000. Adding it ($795,000) is the trap: it treats the seller's payment as extra value instead of a cost the buyer did not really pay.

questions.q: A comp sold at $650,000 with seller financing at 2% when market rates were near 7%. How should the CMA treat it?
c: Use $650,000, since the price is what the deed shows
Adjust it upward, since the seller took on extra risk
Adjust it downward to a cash-equivalent price
Drop it, since financing terms make a sale invalid
questions.x: Below-market seller financing lets a buyer pay more for the house, so the price overstates market value and is adjusted down to cash equivalent. Using the deed price is the tempting answer, but market value assumes cash or normal financing terms.

questions.q: Two otherwise identical houses on the same block sold a month apart: one with a finished basement for $612,000, one without for $590,000. The finished basement adjustment indicated is:
questions.x: Paired sales isolate one feature: $612,000 minus $590,000 equals $22,000. The $601,000 figure is the trap: it averages the two sales, which says nothing about the basement.

questions.q: A house sold for $700,000, then resold 12 months later after a new roof for $742,000. Area values rose 3% over that year. About how much of the increase reflects the roof?
questions.x: Market growth explains 3% of $700,000, or $21,000. The remaining $21,000 of the $42,000 increase is the roof. Taking the full $42,000 is the trap: it credits the roof with gains the whole market enjoyed.

questions.q: The subject has no garage. A comp with a garage sold for $640,000. If a garage adds $20,000, the adjusted comp price is:
questions.x: The comp is better than the subject, so subtract: $640,000 minus $20,000 equals $620,000. $660,000 is the trap: adding for the garage moves the comp away from the subject.

questions.q: Values have risen 0.5% per month. A comp sold 6 months ago for $800,000 and is 100 square feet smaller than the subject; the size adjustment rate is $150 per square foot. The adjusted price is:
questions.x: Time: 6 x 0.5% = 3% of $800,000, so add $24,000. Size: the comp is smaller, so it is poorer; add 100 x $150 = $15,000. Total $839,000. $809,000 is the trap: it subtracts the size adjustment as if the smaller comp were better.

questions.q: Three adjusted comps indicate $510,000 (gross adjustments 4%), $528,000 (14%) and $540,000 (21%). In reconciliation, the most weight should go to:
c: The $510,000 comp, the least adjusted
The $540,000 comp, the highest value
The $528,000 comp, the middle value of three
No comp; take the straight average
questions.x: The comp needing the smallest gross adjustment is the most similar and the most reliable. The straight average is the tempting answer, but reconciliation is a judgment that weights comps by reliability; averaging gives the weakest comp equal say.

questions.q: Comp X has adjustments of +$40,000 and -$38,000. Comp Y has one adjustment of +$5,000. Which statement is most accurate?
c: X is better because its net adjustment is just $2,000
They are equally reliable because both net to small numbers
X is better because it was adjusted for more features
Y is more reliable because its gross adjustment is smaller
questions.x: Gross adjustment (the total ignoring sign) measures how different a comp is: X needed $78,000 of changes, Y only $5,000. The tempting answer looks at net, where big pluses and minuses cancel and hide a poor match.

questions.q: In a CMA, an expired listing for a similar home is most useful as evidence of:
c: A price level the market has rejected
The floor below which the subject should not list
The subject's exact market value today
The cost to build a similar home
questions.x: Expired listings show prices buyers would not pay during the listing period. Treating an expired price as a floor is the tempting error; it is closer to a ceiling the market refused. Closed sales are the evidence of value.

questions.q: A seller points to a neighbor's active listing at $1.2 million as proof of value. The best response is that an active listing shows:
c: Current market value, being the newest data
The appraised value the bank will accept
An asking price, not a sale
The price the neighbor's agent guaranteed
questions.x: An active listing is what a seller hopes to get; it becomes evidence of value only when a buyer agrees and it closes. It matters as the competition buyers will compare against. Calling it the newest, best data is the tempting answer, but asking is not selling.

questions.concept: Value from NOI and cap rate
questions.q: A mixed-use building has NOI of $96,000. Comparable sales indicate a 6.4% cap rate. The indicated value is:
questions.x: Value = NOI / cap rate: $96,000 / 0.064 = $1,500,000. $614,400 is the trap of multiplying NOI by the rate's digits ($96,000 x 6.4), and $1,536,000 is a rounding error from dividing by 0.0625.

questions.concept: Value from NOI and cap rate
questions.q: Two appraisers agree a building's NOI is $120,000. One uses a 6% cap rate, the other 8%. Which statement is correct?
c: The 6% appraiser finds $2,000,000; the 8% one, $1,500,000
The 8% appraiser finds the higher value
Both find the same value, since NOI is the same
The 6% appraiser finds $1,500,000; the 8% one, $2,000,000
questions.x: $120,000 / 0.06 = $2,000,000 and $120,000 / 0.08 = $1,500,000. Value moves opposite the cap rate. The reversed pairing is the trap; it comes from assuming a higher rate means a higher value.

questions.q: In calculating net operating income for the income approach, all of the following are deducted EXCEPT:
c: Real estate taxes
Property insurance
Management fees
Mortgage interest
questions.x: NOI is effective gross income minus operating expenses. Mortgage interest is debt service, which depends on the owner's financing, so it is excluded, as are depreciation and income taxes. Management fees are the tempting pick because many owners self-manage, but appraisers include a market management fee anyway.

questions.q: Effective gross income is $150,000. Operating expenses are $55,000, mortgage payments $48,000 and depreciation $20,000. NOI is:
questions.x: NOI = $150,000 - $55,000 = $95,000. Debt service and depreciation are not operating expenses. Subtracting everything ($27,000) is the trap; that number is closer to taxable cash flow, not NOI.

questions.q: Comparable small commercial buildings sell at a gross income multiplier of 9.5. The subject's annual gross income is $140,000 and its NOI is $84,000. The indicated value is:
questions.x: A gross income multiplier applies to gross income: $140,000 x 9.5 = $1,330,000. Applying it to NOI ($798,000) is the trap; multipliers skip expenses by design.

questions.q: A weakness of using a gross rent or income multiplier rather than direct capitalization is that it:
c: Requires a detailed list of expenses
Cannot be used for residential property
Requires a capitalization rate first
Skips operating expenses entirely
questions.x: Multipliers relate price to gross income, so two buildings with the same rents but very different expenses get the same value. That is why direct capitalization on NOI is preferred for larger income properties. Requiring an expense list is the tempting answer, but that describes direct capitalization, not multipliers.

questions.q: An apartment's only bathroom can be reached by walking through a bedroom. In the cost approach, this is:
c: Physical deterioration
External obsolescence
Functional obsolescence
Accrued land depreciation
questions.x: Functional obsolescence is lost value from outdated design or features within the property. Physical deterioration is wear and tear, the tempting answer for an old building, but a new building with this layout would suffer the same loss.

questions.q: Each of the following is an example of functional obsolescence EXCEPT:
c: A new highway built behind the house
Five bedrooms served by a single bath
A kitchen reached by walking through a bedroom
Ceilings too low for modern equipment
questions.x: A new highway is outside the property line, which makes it external (economic) obsolescence, always incurable. The others are design problems inside the property. Low ceilings are the tempting pick because they seem structural, but they are an outdated design feature.

questions.q: A buyer contracts at $900,000 and plans an 80% loan. The appraisal comes in at $850,000, and the lender lends 80% of the lesser of price or value. To close at $900,000, the buyer's cash must rise by:
questions.x: Planned loan: 80% x $900,000 = $720,000. New loan: 80% x $850,000 = $680,000. The loan drops $40,000, so the buyer brings $40,000 more. $50,000 is the trap: it is the appraisal shortfall, not the change in the loan.

questions.q: A lender's appraisal comes in below the contract price. The seller's agent wants to help. The appropriate action is to:
c: Call the appraiser to explain the comps
Give the buyer comps to submit through the lender
Ask the loan officer to order a new appraiser
Tell the appraiser the deal fails without more value
questions.x: Disputes go through the lender as a reconsideration of value, typically requested by the borrower with specific relevant sales. Federal valuation independence rules prohibit pressuring or improperly influencing the appraiser. Calling the appraiser directly is the tempting answer because it feels like advocacy, but it is the conduct the rules target.

questions.q: An investor will pay $200,000 above market for a building next to one she already owns because combining them saves her management costs. The higher figure reflects:
c: Market value
Insured (insurable) value
Investment value
Assessed value
questions.x: Investment value is a property's worth to a specific buyer given her own circumstances. Market value is what the typical informed buyer would pay. Market value is the tempting answer because the investor really would pay it, but the premium comes from her situation, not the market's.

questions.q: Which value typically excludes land and is used to set coverage on a building?
c: Insurable value
Market value
Investment value
Mortgage value
questions.x: Insurable value is based on the cost to rebuild the improvements and leaves out land, which cannot burn. Market value is the tempting answer because it is the appraisal's headline number, but it includes land and reflects price, not rebuilding cost.

questions.q: A licensee searching NYC recorded deeds finds no sales of individual apartments in a co-op building. The most likely reason is that co-op buyers receive:
c: A deed held by the board until approval
A deed recorded at the county level alone
Shares and a proprietary lease
A leasehold deed that is filed privately
questions.x: The co-op corporation owns the building; buyers get shares and a proprietary lease, which are personal property, so there is no deed to record. The tempting answer imagines a deed held in escrow by the board, but no deed to the apartment exists in a co-op.

questions.q: Each of the following is a useful source of co-op sale prices for a CMA EXCEPT:
c: Recorded deeds for each apartment in the building
MLS closed-sale data for the building
The managing agent or the co-op's transfer records
Closed sales reported by other brokers in the building
questions.x: There are no deeds for co-op apartment sales, because buyers acquire shares and a proprietary lease. MLS data, broker reports and transfer information from the managing agent are the usual sources. The managing agent is the tempting pick because agents often decline to share, but where available it is reliable data.

questions.q: Two similar co-ops differ only in maintenance: $1,500 versus $1,200 a month. If buyers can borrow about $1,000 for every $6.00 of monthly payment, the price difference supported is about:
questions.x: $300 a month divided by $6.00 per $1,000 is 50, or about $50,000 of borrowing power. $3,600 is the trap: it is one year of the difference, which ignores that buyers carry the cost for the life of their loan.

questions.q: A comparable co-op sold for $600,000 with maintenance $250 a month lower than the subject's. In the CMA the comp should be:
c: Adjusted up, since lower maintenance makes it poorer
Left alone, since maintenance is not part of the price
Adjusted down by $250 to match the monthly difference
Adjusted down, as the better comp
questions.x: Lower maintenance makes the comp better for buyers, so subtract the capitalized difference. Ignoring maintenance is the tempting error; buyers judge co-ops on price plus monthly carrying cost, so maintenance moves price.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a Manhattan co-op for $1,020,000. The buyer's New York mansion tax is:
questions.x: The mansion tax is 1% of the full price on residential purchases of $1,000,000 or more, including co-ops: 1% of $1,020,000 is $10,200. $200 is the trap: the tax is on the whole price, not just the amount over $1,000,000. (Higher NYC brackets begin above $2,000,000.)

questions.q: A condo seller's CMA supports about $1,000,000. Why might the agent recommend listing at $995,000?
c: The seller's transfer tax rate doubles at $1,000,000
Condo boards vote on any sale above $1,000,000
Buyers owe a 1% mansion tax at $1,000,000 and up
Mortgage recording tax starts above $1,000,000
questions.x: The buyer-paid mansion tax applies to the whole price once it reaches $1,000,000, so a price just under the line saves the buyer about $10,000. Transfer tax is the tempting answer, but the seller's state and city transfer tax rates do not jump at $1,000,000 for a residential condo.

questions.concept: Mortgage recording tax: condo vs co-op
questions.q: In New York City, which purchase loan generally owes mortgage recording tax?
c: A co-op share loan
A condo mortgage
Both loan types
Neither loan type
questions.x: A condo mortgage is a lien on real property and owes mortgage recording tax. A co-op share loan is secured by shares and a proprietary lease, which are not real property, so no mortgage is recorded and no recording tax is due. 'Both' is the tempting answer for people who think of both as apartment mortgages.

questions.concept: Mortgage recording tax: condo vs co-op
questions.q: A condo buyer in Brooklyn borrows $600,000. Using the borrower's rate of 1.925% for loans of $500,000 or more, the mortgage recording tax is about:
questions.x: 1.925% of $600,000 is $11,550. $10,800 is the trap: it applies the 1.8% rate for loans under $500,000. $0 would be right for a co-op share loan, not a condo mortgage.

questions.q: A seller is selling a 1955 condo unit in Queens. Which disclosure is required?
c: The federal lead-based paint disclosure
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement
Both the PCDS and the lead disclosure
Neither; condos are exempt from both
questions.x: The PCDS law covers one to four family homes and exempts condo and co-op units, but the federal lead rule covers housing built before 1978 regardless of ownership form. 'Both' is the tempting answer for those who assume all residential sales need the PCDS.

questions.concept: Board approval vs right of first refusal
questions.q: In a typical New York condominium, the board's power over a proposed sale is usually:
c: Full approval after an interview
Approval of the sale price alone
No part in the sale whatsoever
A right of first refusal
questions.x: Most condo boards hold a right of first refusal: buy the unit on the same terms or waive. Full approval with an interview is the co-op model, which is the tempting answer because many New Yorkers use the two words interchangeably.

questions.q: A co-op sells for $640,000. The building's flip tax is 1.5% of the gross price, paid by the seller. The flip tax is:
questions.x: 1.5% of $640,000 is $9,600. $6,400 is the trap of using 1%. A flip tax is set by the co-op's own documents, not by state law, so the rate and who pays it vary by building.

questions.q: A buyer's attorney asks who pays a co-op's flip tax. The correct source for the answer is:
c: The New York State Tax Law
The co-op's own documents
The NYC Department of Finance
The listing agreement
questions.x: A flip tax is a transfer fee the co-op imposes through its proprietary lease, bylaws or board resolutions; those documents set the rate, the base and who pays. The Tax Law is the tempting answer because of the word 'tax', but it is not a government tax.

questions.q: A builder buys a 50 by 100 foot lot with an old house for $590,000 and spends $30,000 to demolish it. As a land comparable, the sale indicates a vacant land value of about:
questions.x: A teardown buyer pays the price and then the demolition bill to end up with vacant land, so the land cost $590,000 plus $30,000, or $620,000. The $560,000 answer is the trap: subtracting demolition treats it as a reduction in land value, when it is part of what the buyer paid to get a clear lot.

questions.q: An agent is valuing a vacant building lot in a village where most lot sales are older houses that builders bought and demolished. The best way to use those sales is to:
c: Discard them, since sales of improved property show no land value
Use each price less the demolition cost its buyer paid
Add each buyer's demolition cost to the price paid
Average them with renovated house sales on the same blocks
questions.x: In built-up areas, teardowns are often the best land evidence. Adding the buyer's demolition cost converts each sale into what the vacant land effectively cost. Subtracting demolition is the trap: it gets the direction backward. Mixing teardowns with renovated house sales blends two different markets.

questions.q: Two adjoining lots are worth $300,000 and $90,000 separately. Combined, they form a conforming building lot worth $480,000. The plottage value is:
questions.x: Plottage is the combined value minus the sum of the separate values: $480,000 minus ($300,000 plus $90,000) equals $90,000. The $390,000 answer is the trap: it is the sum of the parts, the starting point of the calculation rather than the increment.

questions.q: Plottage value is best described as:
c: The cost of combining adjacent parcels under one deed
The value one buyer places on a parcel for its own plan
The value of land as if vacant and ready to develop
The added value of combined parcels over their parts
questions.x: Plottage is the increase in value when assembled parcels are worth more together than the sum of their separate values, often because only the combined lot meets zoning or supports a larger building. Assemblage, the act of combining, is the trap: plottage is the value that results, not the process or its cost.

questions.q: An owner's 35-foot lot predates a zoning rule requiring 50-foot lots for new houses, so a new house there would need an area variance. In highest and best use analysis as vacant, the first issue is:
c: Physical possibility, since narrow houses are hard to build
Maximal productivity, since new houses sell for the most
Legal permissibility, since the use needs a variance
Financial feasibility, since builders pay the most for lots
questions.x: Highest and best use tests run in order: legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive. A use that needs a variance the board may deny is legally uncertain, so that question comes first. Maximal productivity is the trap: it is the last test, applied only to uses that survive the first three.

questions.q: A site is worth $650,000 as if vacant. With its existing house, the property is worth $560,000. The highest and best use as improved is most likely:
c: Demolition and new construction
Renovating and keeping the house
Keeping the house, which adds $90,000
Holding the land vacant for rezoning
questions.x: When land as if vacant is worth more than the property as improved, the building is no longer contributing value, and demolition for new construction is the likely highest and best use. The $90,000 answer is the trap: the house does not add $90,000; the property is worth $90,000 less with it than without it.

questions.q: Each of the following is a direct (hard) cost of building a house EXCEPT:
c: Framing lumber
Carpenters' wages
Excavation and concrete for the footings
Construction loan interest
questions.x: Direct costs are the labor and materials that physically build the project: lumber, wages, excavation, concrete. Interest on the construction loan is an indirect (soft) cost, along with architect fees, permits, insurance and taxes during construction. Excavation is the tempting pick because it happens before the building, but it is physical site work.

questions.q: Architect fees, permit fees and interest on a construction loan are examples of:
c: Direct costs
Indirect costs
Accrued depreciation
Functional obsolescence
questions.x: Indirect, or soft, costs are what it takes to design, permit, finance and sell a project rather than to build it physically. Direct costs, the trap, are labor and materials. Depreciation and obsolescence are losses in value from an existing building, not costs of construction.

questions.q: Using his own costs and a 15% profit target, a builder figures a lot is worth $480,000 to him. Recent sales of similar lots average $560,000. The builder's $480,000 figure is:
c: Investment value
Market value of the lot
Insured value
Assessed value
questions.x: Investment value is the value of a property to a particular investor, based on that investor's own costs, financing and return goals. Market value is the trap: it reflects what typical informed buyers pay after exposure, and the lot sales show other buyers pay more than this builder's math allows.

questions.q: Investment value differs from market value because investment value:
c: Is set by the local assessor for tax purposes
Excludes land and foundations from the estimate
Reflects one investor's own costs and goals
Is the most probable price after market exposure
questions.x: Investment value is specific to one investor's requirements, so two investors can hold different investment values for the same property. The most-probable-price answer is the trap: that is the definition of market value. Excluding land and foundations describes insurable value, and the assessor's figure is assessed value.

questions.q: Before a listing goes live, a neighbor offers the executor $500,000 cash for the house. Which statement about that offer is most accurate?
c: It is market value, since a cash offer needs no adjustment
It is a proposed price; market value assumes market exposure
It is market value, since estates are expected to sell quickly
It sets a floor, because a first offer is usually the lowest
questions.x: Market value is the most probable price after reasonable exposure to a competitive market, with informed parties and no undue pressure. A single offer made before anyone else has seen the property is a proposed price. The cash answer is the trap: cash terms matter, but they do not substitute for exposure.

questions.q: Each of the following is part of the definition of market value EXCEPT:
c: Reasonable exposure in a competitive market
Buyer and seller acting prudently and knowledgeably
Neither party acting under undue duress
The highest price any buyer might pay
questions.x: Market value is the most probable price, not the highest possible one, after reasonable exposure, with informed, prudent parties and no undue duress. Exposure is the tempting pick because agents often think of it as marketing time, but reasonable exposure is built into the definition.

cram.html: A CMA is an opinion of value and may never be called an appraisal.
Appraisals come from state licensed or certified appraisers (licensed through DOS).
Evaluation = study of use or feasibility, value number not required. Valuation = value as of a date.
Market value = most probable price (not highest), specific date, cash or equivalent, reasonable exposure, no duress.
Exposure time looks back before the sale date; marketing time looks forward.
Price and cost are facts; value is an opinion. Each may or may not equal value.
Direct (hard) costs = labor and materials. Indirect (soft) = fees, financing, permits, lease-up, admin.
Insurable value omits land and foundations.
Investment value = value to a specific investor. Value in use = value for one specific use.
CMA uses solds (last 12 months), current competition, and expireds.
Highest and best use: Legal, Physical, Financial, Maximal, tested as vacant and as improved.
Assemblage = combining lots. Plottage = the value increase.
Adjust the comp, never the subject: comp better, subtract; comp poorer, add.
Cost approach: land + (cost new - depreciation). Land never depreciates.
Depreciation: physical, functional, external. External is always incurable.
GRM = price / monthly gross rent. GIM uses annual gross income.
Value = NOI / cap rate. Higher cap rate, lower value. Debt service is not an operating expense.
Sales comparison: homes and land. Cost: new or special-purpose. Income: rentals and commercial.
Reconciliation weighs the approaches. It is never a simple average.

subjects.title: Human Rights and Fair Housing
subjects.blurb: Fair housing questions show up all over the DOS exam, and fair housing mistakes are the fastest way to lose a license. You need the history, the federal and New York protected classes, the exemptions, and the moves that count as steering, blockbusting, and redlining.

lessons.title: How We Got Here: Segregation, the Courts, and Federal Fair Housing
lessons.tagline: Every fair housing rule you follow today was written to undo something that actually happened on a real block.
objectives: Put the key cases and statutes in order, from the Civil Rights Act of 1866 to the ADA
Name the seven federal protected classes and which law added each one
Explain why the 1866 Act still matters and how Jones v. Mayer revived it
Define familial status and disability the way HUD and the exam do

blocks.title: Crown Heights, a closing dinner
blocks.html: Grace Okafor is telling Jordan about 1996, when she and Emmanuel bought their Bed-Stuy brownstone. "Two banks told us the block was 'too risky.' Same block where my white coworker got a loan in a week." Jordan has heard the word redlining in class. Was what Grace describes legal in 1996? And where did the rule against it come from?
blocks.casual: Grace Okafor is telling Jordan about 1996, the year she and Emmanuel bought their Bed-Stuy brownstone. "Two banks told us the block was 'too risky.' Same block where my white coworker got a loan in a week." Jordan's heard the word redlining in class. So here's the question: was that legal in 1996? And where did the rule against it even come from?

deeper.plain: Grace is describing a bank treating the same block differently depending on who was asking for the loan. The lesson is about why that was already against the law.
deeper.picture: Think of two people ordering the same dish at the same counter, and only one gets told the kitchen is closed. The kitchen didn't change. The customer did.
deeper.street: In 1996 the Okafors had steady jobs and a down payment saved. Two lenders said no while a white coworker closed on the same block in a week. They ended up with a smaller lender at a worse rate, which cost them thousands over the life of the loan.
deeper.stakes: Lending discrimination doesn't just sting once. A higher rate or a denied loan compounds for 30 years, and a family that never buys never builds equity to pass down.
deeper.exam: The exam likes a stem where a lender refuses loans in an area because of who lives there. The cue words are "area," "neighborhood," or "risky" tied to race: that's redlining, not steering or blockbusting.

blocks.text: The legacy fair housing law was built to undo

blocks.html: American housing was segregated on purpose. Cities passed racial zoning. Deeds carried covenants barring sales to Black, Jewish, or Asian buyers. In the 1930s the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation drew maps that colored Black and immigrant neighborhoods red as "hazardous," and lenders and the FHA steered loans away from them. That practice gave us the word redlining. Families shut out of mortgages were shut out of the main way Americans build wealth.
blocks.casual: Here's the thing nobody tells you: American housing was segregated on purpose. Cities passed racial zoning. Deeds had covenants saying you couldn't sell to Black, Jewish, or Asian buyers. In the 1930s the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation drew maps and colored Black and immigrant neighborhoods red as "hazardous," and lenders and the FHA steered loans away from them. That's where the word redlining comes from. If you couldn't get a mortgage, you couldn't get the main thing Americans use to build wealth.

deeper.plain: Government and banks drew lines around certain neighborhoods and refused to lend there. The people living inside those lines couldn't buy homes the normal way.
deeper.picture: Picture a map of the city where someone took a red marker and circled blocks as "don't bother." Every lender in town used the same marked-up map for decades.
deeper.street: A Bed-Stuy block colored red in the 1930s got almost no mortgage money for a generation. Owners couldn't borrow to fix roofs, values sagged, and buyers who could get loans went to Long Island instead.
deeper.stakes: The wealth gap you see today between neighborhoods traces straight back to who could get a mortgage then. When you price a home or a block, that history is baked into the numbers.
deeper.exam: Redlining is always a lender (or insurer) refusing or worsening credit because of the area's racial makeup. If the stem has an agent doing it to buyers, that's steering, not redlining.

blocks.html: The housing those families could reach was often older stock. Filtering down describes how housing passes from higher income households to lower income ones as it ages. It is a neutral market idea, but combined with lending discrimination it concentrated poverty in specific neighborhoods for generations.
blocks.casual: The housing those families could actually reach was usually older stock. Filtering down is how housing slides from higher income households to lower income ones as it ages. On its own that's just a neutral market idea. Mix it with lending discrimination, though, and it piled poverty into specific neighborhoods for generations.

deeper.plain: As buildings get old, richer people move out and less wealthy people move in. That's normal, but it became a trap when some families could only buy the oldest housing.
deeper.picture: It's like a hand-me-down coat. It keeps getting passed to the next person as it wears out, and if one family only ever gets hand-me-downs, they never get a new coat.
deeper.street: A Harlem brownstone built for a merchant family in 1890 became a rooming house by the 1950s. Owners who could get loans moved to Riverdale, and the people left behind couldn't borrow to renovate.
deeper.stakes: If you talk about filtering down as if it explains everything, you miss the discrimination part. That's how you end up repeating coded ideas about "declining" neighborhoods to clients.
deeper.exam: Filtering down is the neutral definition question. The trap answer calls it illegal: it isn't, it's a market process. Redlining is the illegal part.

blocks.html: New York was not an exception. Deeds in Jackson Heights, Queens, which was marketed in the 1920s as a "restricted" garden city, carried covenants keeping out Black and Jewish buyers. Covenants like these were common across the suburbs and the outer boroughs until the Supreme Court made them unenforceable in 1948 in Shelley v. Kraemer. You may still see the old language in a chain of title. It is void and has no legal effect.
blocks.casual: New York wasn't an exception. Jackson Heights, Queens, got marketed in the 1920s as a "restricted" garden city, and its deeds carried covenants keeping out Black and Jewish buyers. Covenants like these were all over the suburbs and the outer boroughs until the Supreme Court made them unenforceable in 1948 in Shelley v. Kraemer. You might still bump into that old language in a chain of title. It's void. It does nothing.

deeper.plain: Old deeds sometimes still say who can't buy the house. Those clauses died in 1948 and nobody can enforce them now.
deeper.picture: It's like an old sign in a building that says "No dogs allowed" after the rule got repealed. The paint is still on the wall, but nobody can kick you out for it.
deeper.street: Priya is reviewing a title report on a Jackson Heights co-op building and finds a 1925 covenant barring sales to "any person not of the Caucasian race." She tells the buyer it's void, it doesn't affect title, and the closing goes ahead on schedule.
deeper.stakes: If you or a seller treat that covenant as meaningful, or use it to discourage a buyer, you've turned dead words into live discrimination. That's a complaint and possibly a license problem.
deeper.exam: Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) means courts can't enforce racial covenants. The trap answer says it made the covenants "illegal to write" or erased them: the case is about enforcement.

blocks.title: New York moved early
blocks.html: New York City's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs Law of 1957 was the first law in the country to ban discrimination in private housing, more than a decade before the federal Fair Housing Act. New York State followed with its own housing protections in the Human Rights Law. That head start is one reason New York's protected class list is so much longer than the federal one today.
blocks.casual: New York got there first. NYC's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs Law of 1957 was the first law in the country banning discrimination in private housing, more than ten years before the federal Fair Housing Act. New York State then added its own housing protections in the Human Rights Law. That head start is a big reason New York's list of protected classes is so much longer than the federal one now.

deeper.plain: New York City banned housing discrimination by private landlords in 1957, before the rest of the country. The state followed, and both keep adding protections.
deeper.picture: Think of New York as the kid who did the homework before it was assigned. By the time Washington handed it out, New York was already on the next chapter.
deeper.street: Sal's father bought the Astoria 6-unit in 1962. Even then, under the city law, he couldn't legally refuse a tenant because of race, years before a landlord in many other states faced any rule at all.
deeper.stakes: Agents who learned the federal list in another state get burned here. In New York you answer to the federal list, the state list, and in the city the city list too.
deeper.exam: Expect a question asking which law is broader. New York's Human Rights Law protects more classes than the federal Fair Housing Act. When in doubt, the NY answer covers more.

head: Year
Law or case
What it did
rows: All citizens have the same right as white citizens to buy, sell, lease, and hold property. Race only. No exceptions.
Supreme Court approved "separate but equal." Legal cover for segregation.
Struck down a Louisville ordinance that zoned blocks by race. Racial zoning is unconstitutional.
Courts may not enforce racially restrictive covenants in deeds.
Overturned Plessy in public schools. Separate is inherently unequal.
No discrimination by race, color, or national origin in programs that get federal money, including public and assisted housing.
Bans discrimination in sale, rental, and financing of housing: race, color, religion, national origin.
Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co.
1866 Act applies to private sales too. No exemption for race, ever.
Added sex as a protected class.
Added disability and familial status. Gave HUD real enforcement power and raised penalties.
Accessibility in public accommodations and commercial facilities, including real estate offices and leasing offices.
blocks.caption: Read it as a story: the law first allowed segregation, then the courts and Congress took it apart piece by piece.

deeper.plain: The law started out allowing segregation and then, case by case, Congress and the courts dismantled it. The table is that story in order.
deeper.picture: Picture a wall built brick by brick, then taken down brick by brick. Plessy laid bricks; Buchanan, Shelley, Brown, and the 1968 laws pulled them out.
deeper.street: Jordan makes flashcards on the A train: 1866 race, 1917 zoning, 1948 covenants, 1968 FHA plus Jones, 1974 sex, 1988 disability and family. By Atlantic Avenue the order sticks because each one fixes the gap the last one left.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up which law covers what leads to bad advice, like telling an owner they're exempt when the 1866 Act says they're not. Knowing the layers is how you spot the illegal move.
deeper.exam: Common items: which year added sex (1974), which added disability and familial status (1988), and which law has no exemptions for race (1866). Title VI of 1964 is about federally funded programs, not private sales.

blocks.title: Remember the order
blocks.html: P-B-B: Plessy (1896) allowed it, Buchanan (1917) struck racial zoning, Brown (1954) killed separate but equal. Then 1968 twice: the Fair Housing Act in April and Jones v. Mayer in June.
blocks.casual: Memory hook: P-B-B. Plessy (1896) allowed it, Buchanan (1917) knocked out racial zoning, Brown (1954) killed separate but equal. Then 1968 twice: the Fair Housing Act in April and Jones v. Mayer in June.

deeper.plain: Three Supreme Court cases in alphabetical-ish order, then two big things in 1968. That's the backbone of the timeline.
deeper.picture: P-B-B sounds like a ping-pong ball bouncing: allowed, struck, killed. Then 1968 is the year that hit twice, like a double play.
deeper.street: Diane quizzes Jordan at the office coffee machine: "Racial zoning?" Jordan: "Buchanan, 1917." "Private sale, race?" "Jones, 1968, and the 1866 Act." Diane nods and hands over a cup.
deeper.stakes: Timeline questions are easy points if you have a hook and lost points if you guess. They're also how you explain to a skeptical client why the rules exist.
deeper.exam: Buchanan v. Warley is the racial zoning case; Shelley v. Kraemer is covenants. The exam swaps them as distractors, so tie Buchanan to "zoning" and Shelley to "deeds."

blocks.q: Which Supreme Court case first struck down a city ordinance that assigned residential blocks by race?
c: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Buchanan v. Warley (1917)
Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
Jones v. Mayer (1968)
blocks.x: Buchanan v. Warley struck down Louisville's racial zoning ordinance. Plessy did the opposite, approving separate but equal.

blocks.html: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 sat mostly unused for a century because courts read it as covering only government action. In Jones v. Mayer (1968), Joseph Lee Jones sued a St. Louis developer that refused to sell him a home because he was Black. The Supreme Court held the 1866 Act bars private racial discrimination in property sales. That makes the 1866 Act the one law with no exemptions. A homeowner who could otherwise use an exemption under the Fair Housing Act still cannot refuse a buyer because of race.
blocks.casual: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 sat on a shelf for about a hundred years because courts said it only covered government action. Then came Jones v. Mayer (1968). Joseph Lee Jones sued a St. Louis developer that wouldn't sell him a home because he was Black. The Supreme Court said the 1866 Act bans private racial discrimination in property sales. So the 1866 Act is the one law with no exemptions. Even a homeowner who could use an FHA exemption still can't turn away a buyer because of race.

deeper.plain: An old 1866 law says everyone has the same property rights as white citizens. Since 1968 it reaches private sellers too, and it has no exceptions for race.
deeper.picture: The FHA is a building with a few side doors marked "exempt." The 1866 Act is the foundation under the whole building, and it has no doors at all.
deeper.street: An owner selling his own house in Staten Island without a broker thinks he's exempt from fair housing. He refuses a Black buyer. Under the 1866 Act the buyer can sue him directly in federal court, exemption or not.
deeper.stakes: Owners love to believe they're exempt. If you repeat that to them on a race issue, they lose a lawsuit and you look like the person who told them it was fine.
deeper.exam: Cue: "no exemptions" or "race" plus an owner who qualifies for an FHA exemption. The answer is the 1866 Act, and the refusal is illegal.

blocks.title: Exam trap: the exemption that is not
blocks.html: A question describes an owner-occupied two-family whose owner turns away a renter because of race and asks whether the owner is exempt. Under the FHA the owner might be exempt from some rules. Under the 1866 Act, never for race. The answer is that the refusal is illegal.
blocks.casual: Exam trap: a question gives you an owner-occupied two-family, the owner turns away a renter because of race, and asks if the owner is exempt. Under the FHA, maybe for some rules. Under the 1866 Act, never for race. Pick the answer that says the refusal is illegal.

deeper.plain: The owner exemptions don't protect anyone who discriminates by race. The 1866 law still applies.
deeper.picture: It's like a parking permit that lets you park in a loading zone, but not in front of a fire hydrant. Some rules bend; the race rule never does.
deeper.street: Ray's cousin owns a two-family in Bay Ridge and lives downstairs. He tells a Black applicant the apartment is "taken" and shows it the next day to a white couple. A tester catches it, and the 1866 Act claim goes ahead regardless of his owner-occupied status.
deeper.stakes: This is how small landlords get hit with damages they never saw coming. They read about the Mrs. Murphy exemption online and stop reading.
deeper.exam: When the stem says "exempt" and "race" in the same breath, the exemption is a decoy. The right answer is that the 1866 Act still prohibits it.

blocks.text: The Fair Housing Act and its seven classes

blocks.html: The Fair Housing Act of 1968 (Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968) passed one week after Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was killed. It started with four protected classes. The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 added sex. The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added disability and familial status. It is administered by HUD, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
blocks.casual: The Fair Housing Act of 1968 (Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968) passed one week after Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was killed. It started with four protected classes. The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 added sex. The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added disability and familial status. HUD, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, runs it.

deeper.plain: The federal fair housing law began with four groups it protected, then grew to seven over twenty years. HUD is the agency that enforces it.
deeper.picture: Think of a guest list that started with four names in 1968, got one more in 1974, and two more in 1988. HUD is the bouncer checking that nobody on the list gets turned away.
deeper.street: A Flatbush tenant who's told "no pregnant women, the stairs are steep" files with HUD. Before 1988 that wasn't covered federally; now familial status includes pregnancy, so HUD investigates.
deeper.stakes: If you know only the original four classes, you'll miss the ones that trip up most agents today: kids and disability. Those generate a huge share of real complaints.
deeper.exam: Know the years: 1968 race, color, religion, national origin; 1974 sex; 1988 disability and familial status. A distractor will put sex in 1988 or disability in 1974.

blocks.caption: Start at the center with the 1866 Act (race), then add the federal FHA layer. Notice how each outer layer, NYS and then NYC, only adds classes. Nothing is ever taken away.

head: Federal class
Added
Quick note
rows: Also covered by the 1866 Act with no exemptions
HUD reads it to include sexual orientation and gender identity; covers sexual harassment
Physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity
Children under 18 living with a parent or custodian, pregnant women, people getting custody

deeper.plain: These are the seven federal protected classes and roughly what each one covers. Every agent in the country works under at least these.
deeper.picture: Seven locks on the same door. Turning someone away for any one of these reasons breaks the law, even if you had another reason too.
deeper.street: An applicant in Sunset Park speaks with an accent and Sal asks where she's "really from." That's national origin territory. Asking about her ancestry has nothing to do with whether she pays rent.
deeper.stakes: Color is separate from race, religion includes having none, and sex covers harassment. Agents who think the list is just "race and religion" walk right into the others.
deeper.exam: Watch for age, marital status, or source of income in a list of "federal" classes. Those are New York additions, not federal, and they're the distractor.

blocks.title: Seven federal classes
blocks.html: "Real Cops Really Need Some Fair Detectives": Race, Color, Religion, National origin, Sex, Familial status, Disability. If an answer choice says age, marital status, or source of income, that is New York, not federal.
blocks.casual: Seven federal classes, one silly sentence: "Real Cops Really Need Some Fair Detectives". Race, Color, Religion, National origin, Sex, Familial status, Disability. If an answer choice throws in age, marital status, or source of income, that's New York, not federal.

deeper.plain: The sentence's first letters give you the seven federal classes. Anything else on a list is probably a state or city addition.
deeper.picture: Imagine an NYPD squad car with seven detectives squeezed inside. Anyone else trying to get in, like Age or Marital Status, has to take the state bus.
deeper.street: On the exam Jordan sees a question listing "age" as a federal class. Jordan runs the sentence, finds no A, and crosses it out in five seconds.
deeper.stakes: Mixing federal and state lists leads to wrong advice about which agency or law applies. It also costs you easy exam points.
deeper.exam: "Which is NOT protected under the federal Fair Housing Act?" The answer is usually age, marital status, or source of income. All three are protected in New York, which is the trap.

blocks.html: Sex covers more than refusing to rent to women. It includes sexual harassment by a landlord, super, or agent, such as demanding dates or favors in exchange for a lease or repairs (quid pro quo) or creating a hostile environment. HUD reads sex discrimination to include discrimination because of sexual orientation and gender identity. In New York those are separately protected by name anyway.
blocks.casual: Sex covers way more than refusing to rent to women. It includes sexual harassment by a landlord, super, or agent: demanding dates or favors in exchange for a lease or repairs (quid pro quo), or making the place a hostile environment. HUD reads sex discrimination to include sexual orientation and gender identity. In New York those are protected by name anyway.

deeper.plain: A landlord or agent who pressures tenants for sex or makes the home feel threatening is breaking fair housing law. Orientation and gender identity are covered too.
deeper.picture: A home is supposed to be the place you can lock the door. Harassment by the person holding the keys turns the lock around.
deeper.street: A super in a Washington Heights walk-up tells a tenant her leaking ceiling will get fixed "faster if she's friendly." That's quid pro quo harassment, and the landlord can be liable for the super's conduct.
deeper.stakes: Harassment cases bring big damages and can follow the employer, including the brokerage if an agent does it. A license can be lost over one showing.
deeper.exam: Quid pro quo means "this for that": favors for housing or repairs. Hostile environment is ongoing unwelcome conduct. Both fall under sex, not a separate class.

blocks.html: Familial status protects households with children under 18. "No kids," "perfect for a single professional," or putting families only on the ground floor are violations. Senior housing that qualifies under the law is the main exception, covered in the next lesson.
blocks.casual: Familial status protects households with kids under 18. Saying "no kids," "perfect for a single professional," or sticking families only on the ground floor all break the rule. The main exception is qualifying senior housing, which is next lesson.

deeper.plain: You can't turn away, discourage, or limit people because they have children or are expecting. Only real senior housing gets an exception.
deeper.picture: It's like a restaurant that says "no strollers in the main room." It sounds like a seating rule, but it's really a sign telling families to go elsewhere.
deeper.street: A Park Slope landlord asks Jordan to market a 2-bedroom as "ideal for a quiet couple." Jordan rewrites it to describe the apartment: two bedrooms, south light, near the F. Three families apply, one gets it.
deeper.stakes: Ad phrases like "adults only" or "no children" are textbook violations, and the agent who writes them shares the liability. These are among the most common complaints HUD sees.
deeper.exam: Familial status covers pregnant women and people in the process of getting custody, not just parents. A stem with "pregnant" is still familial status.

blocks.html: Disability (the 1968 statute's word was handicap) means a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a record of one, or being regarded as having one. It includes HIV, mobility and vision impairments, mental illness, and people in recovery from addiction. It does not include current illegal drug use.
blocks.casual: Disability (the 1968 law called it handicap) means a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a record of one, or being regarded as having one. That includes HIV, mobility and vision impairments, mental illness, and people in recovery from addiction. It does not include current illegal drug use.

deeper.plain: If a condition seriously limits everyday activities, or people treat you like it does, you're protected. Someone using illegal drugs right now is not.
deeper.picture: Think of three ways onto the list: you have the condition, you had it on record, or people assume you have it. Any one of the three gets you in.
deeper.street: An applicant in Queens mentions he's two years sober and in a recovery program. Marcus wants to pass on him. That's disability discrimination, because people in recovery are protected.
deeper.stakes: Agents get in trouble asking about medical history or treating a diagnosis as a risk. You don't ask, and you don't screen on it.
deeper.exam: The trap is "current illegal drug use" listed as a protected disability. It isn't. Recovery is protected; active illegal use is not.

blocks.q: Which protected class was added to the federal Fair Housing Act by the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974?
c: Disability
Familial status
Sex
Age
blocks.x: The 1974 Act added sex. Disability and familial status came in 1988. Age is not a federal fair housing class at all; it is protected under New York law.

blocks.text: The ADA and the 1964 Act: different jobs

left.title: Fair Housing Act
items: Covers dwellings: sale, rental, financing, advertising
Private homes and apartments
Accessibility design rules for new multifamily (first occupied after March 13, 1991, 4+ units)
Reasonable accommodations and modifications

right.title: Americans with Disabilities Act (1990)
items: Covers public accommodations and commercial facilities
Your brokerage office, a model unit open to the public, a rental leasing office
Barrier removal where readily achievable
Disability only, no other classes

deeper.plain: The Fair Housing Act is about homes. The ADA is about places the public walks into, like your office.
deeper.picture: The FHA governs the apartment someone lives in. The ADA governs the front door of the storefront where they come to ask about it.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart's Brooklyn office has two steps at the entrance. A buyer in a wheelchair can't get in, so Diane installs a portable ramp, because the office is a public accommodation under the ADA.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring the ADA at your office or a leasing office invites complaints and lawsuits separate from any housing claim. New multifamily buildings that miss FHA design rules can face expensive retrofits.
deeper.exam: FHA design rules: new multifamily with 4+ units, first occupied after March 13, 1991. ADA covers only disability, and it reaches offices and leasing offices, not the private apartment.

blocks.html: The Americans with Disabilities Act matters to you because your office is a public accommodation. A client in a wheelchair has to be able to get into it. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 reaches housing through Title VI: any program receiving federal funds, like public housing, cannot discriminate by race, color, or national origin.
blocks.casual: The Americans with Disabilities Act matters to you because your office is a public accommodation. A client in a wheelchair has to be able to get in. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 reaches housing through Title VI: any program that gets federal money, like public housing, can't discriminate by race, color, or national origin.

deeper.plain: Your office has to be accessible to people with disabilities. Housing paid for with federal money can't discriminate by race, color, or national origin.
deeper.picture: The ADA is the ramp at the front door. Title VI is the string attached to federal money: take it and you play fair.
deeper.street: A NYCHA development receives federal funds, so Title VI applies to how it picks tenants. Meanwhile a Bushwick brokerage with a storefront office has to remove barriers where readily achievable under the ADA.
deeper.stakes: A brokerage that can't serve disabled clients at its own office has a problem before anyone sees a listing. Federally funded housing that screens by race risks losing its funding.
deeper.exam: Office access question: ADA. Federally funded program question: Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VI. Private apartment question: Fair Housing Act.

blocks.q: A wheelchair user cannot get into a brokerage's second floor office because there is no ramp or elevator access. Which law most directly addresses access to the office itself?
c: Civil Rights Act of 1866
Americans with Disabilities Act
Housing and Community Development Act of 1974
Civil Rights Act of 1964
blocks.x: A brokerage office is a public accommodation, which is ADA territory. The 1866 Act covers race in property transactions, not office access.

blocks.title: Back to Grace's question
blocks.html: What the banks did in 1996 was illegal. Lending discrimination by race had been barred since 1968, and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act covers credit too. New York's Human Rights Law also bans it. Redlining persisted because it was hard to prove, which is why testers and lending data laws became so important.
blocks.casual: So, back to Grace: what those banks did in 1996 was illegal. Lending discrimination by race had been banned since 1968, and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act covers credit too. New York's Human Rights Law bans it as well. Redlining hung on because it was hard to prove, which is exactly why testers and lending data laws turned into such big deals.

deeper.plain: The banks broke the law. The problem was catching them, so testers and data rules were built to do that.
deeper.picture: Speed limits exist, but without radar guns nobody gets caught. Testers and lending data are the radar guns for discrimination.
deeper.street: A fair housing group sends two equally qualified testers, one Black and one white, to the same Brooklyn bank asking about a $500,000 loan. The white tester gets a rate sheet and a follow-up call; the Black tester gets neither. That paper trail becomes the case.
deeper.stakes: You can be tested too. A tester posing as a buyer or renter can show up at your office or open house, and how you treat them becomes evidence.
deeper.exam: Testers are legal and courts accept their evidence. A distractor will call testing entrapment or say testers need to be real buyers. Both are wrong.

blocks.title: Which law applies?
blocks.html:
Facts: An owner in Albany lives in one half of her two-family and refuses to rent the other half to a Haitian family.
Step 1, race or color? If the refusal is about race, the 1866 Act applies with no exemption. Illegal.
Step 2, national origin? Federal FHA covers it, but she might claim the Mrs. Murphy exemption (owner-occupied, 4 units or fewer).
Step 3, New York? NY's owner-occupied two-family exemption may also apply to the rental decision itself. But if she ran an ad saying "no immigrants," the ad is illegal under every layer.
Answer: the exemptions are narrow, race is never exempt, and the ad is always illegal.
blocks.casual:
Facts: An owner in Albany lives in half of her two-family and won't rent the other half to a Haitian family.
Step 1, race or color? If it's about race, the 1866 Act applies, no exemption. Illegal.
Step 2, national origin? The federal FHA covers it, but she might claim the Mrs. Murphy exemption (owner-occupied, 4 units or fewer).
Step 3, New York? NY's owner-occupied two-family exemption may also reach the rental decision itself. But if she ran an ad saying "no immigrants," that ad is illegal under every layer.
Answer: the exemptions are narrow, race is never exempt, and the ad is always illegal.

deeper.plain: Check race first, then the federal exemptions, then New York's. Exemptions might cover the private decision, but they never cover a discriminatory ad.
deeper.picture: It's three sieves stacked up. A race claim never makes it through the first one; a national origin claim might slip through the second; the ad gets caught in all three.
deeper.street: If the Albany owner had listed the unit with a broker, she'd lose the exemptions entirely. A broker in the deal can't follow a "no immigrants" instruction, period.
deeper.stakes: Owners who rely on exemptions usually get caught by the ad or by race. And any agent who carries out the instruction is liable, because licensees get no exemptions.
deeper.exam: The exam layers the facts so you check each law. The safe answer: race is always illegal, discriminatory ads are always illegal, and brokers can never use owner exemptions.

story.title: The Map in the Drawer
story.setting: Hudson & Hart Realty, Brooklyn, a slow Wednesday

beats.text: Diane drops a laminated old map on Jordan's desk. Brooklyn, 1938, colored green, blue, yellow, and a lot of red.
Is that Bed-Stuy? The whole thing is red.
Hazardous, according to the federal government. Red meant no loans. That's redlining, and it's where the word comes from.
But there were laws against that, right? There was the 1866 thing.
On paper. The Civil Rights Act of 1866 said everyone can buy property like white citizens. Courts ignored it for a hundred years. Then Jones v. Mayer in 1968 said it applies to private sellers too.
beats.tag: 1866 Act + Jones v. Mayer: race, no exemptions

beats.text: So that's why my landlord uncle with the two-family can't say no based on race even though he's exempt from other stuff?
Exactly why. The 1866 Act has zero exemptions. For race, nobody is exempt.

check.q: Why can't an otherwise exempt owner refuse a buyer because of race?
c: The ADA forbids it
The 1866 Act, as applied in Jones v. Mayer, has no exemptions
HUD rules override all exemptions
Only brokers are bound by fair housing
check.x: Jones v. Mayer confirmed that the 1866 Act reaches private sales, and it has no exemptions for race.

beats.text: Okay, quiz me. Plessy, Buchanan, Brown.
Plessy 1896 blessed separate but equal. Buchanan 1917 killed racial zoning ordinances. Brown 1954 overturned Plessy in schools.
And the Fair Housing Act was 1968. Race, color, religion, national origin.
Then sex in 1974. Disability and familial status in 1988. Seven federal classes. Age is not one of them, federally.
Age isn't protected? So I can tell a seventy-year-old the walk-up's not for her?
In New York? Try it and meet the Division of Human Rights. Federal is the floor, Marcus. New York builds a whole house on top.
What about the ADA? Does that cover apartments?
Mostly public spaces. This office, a leasing office, a sales gallery. Apartments are Fair Housing Act territory.
Keep the map. Every rule we follow exists because somebody drew one of these.

board.prompt: Draw a timeline from 1866 to 1990. Put each case or law on it and write one word for what it did (allowed, struck, added).

facts.text: Segregation was deliberate: racial zoning, deed covenants, and 1930s federal maps that colored Black and immigrant areas red as hazardous, which gave us the word redlining.
Filtering down: housing passes from higher income to lower income households as it ages.
Shelley v. Kraemer (1948): courts may not enforce racially restrictive covenants; old covenant language in a chain of title is void.
NYC's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs Law (1957) was the first law in the country to ban discrimination in private housing, more than a decade before the federal Fair Housing Act.
The Civil Rights Act of 1866 gives all citizens the same property rights as white citizens; it covers race only and has no exceptions.
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) approved separate but equal; Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned it in public schools.
Buchanan v. Warley (1917) struck down racial zoning by city ordinance.
Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co. (1968) held that the 1866 Act bars private racial discrimination in property sales.
Race is never exempt: an owner who qualifies for a Fair Housing Act exemption still cannot refuse anyone because of race, and a discriminatory ad is illegal under every layer.
The Fair Housing Act of 1968 (Title VIII) began with four classes: race, color, religion and national origin.
HUD (the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development) administers and enforces the Fair Housing Act.
The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 added sex as a federal protected class.
The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added disability and familial status and gave HUD real enforcement power.
There are seven federal classes (race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status, disability); age, marital status and source of income are New York classes, not federal.
Color (skin tone) is separate from race, religion includes having no religion, and national origin covers ancestry, birthplace, accent and language.
Sex discrimination includes sexual harassment (quid pro quo or hostile environment), and HUD reads it to include sexual orientation and gender identity.
Familial status protects children under 18 living with a parent or custodian, pregnant women and people getting custody; 'no kids' or families-on-the-ground-floor rules violate it.

Disability is an impairment substantially limiting a major life activity, a record of one, or being regarded as having one; it includes HIV and recovery from addiction but not current illegal drug use.
The ADA (1990) covers public accommodations and commercial facilities, such as a brokerage or leasing office, and protects disability only.
Fair Housing Act design rules cover new multifamily buildings of 4 or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991.
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars race, color and national origin discrimination in federally funded programs such as public housing.
Racial lending discrimination has been illegal since 1968, and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act covers credit too.

lessons.title: New York's Wider Net: State and City Classes, Exemptions, Accommodations
lessons.tagline: Federal law is the floor. New York State adds eight more classes, New York City adds more again, and the exemptions shrink at every level.
objectives: List the protected classes New York State adds to federal law, and the extra ones New York City adds
Compare federal and New York exemptions, including senior housing and the owner-occupied two-family
Explain why current illegal drug users are not protected but people in recovery are
Tell a reasonable accommodation from a reasonable modification and apply lawful source of income rules

blocks.title: Astoria, a vacancy in Sal's building
blocks.html: Sal Russo has a two-bedroom open in his six-unit building on 31st Avenue. He calls Jordan: "List it. No vouchers, no kids, and I'd rather a married couple. Older folks are fine, but nobody over seventy, the stairs." Sal says it is his building and his call. How many of those four requests can Jordan legally follow?
blocks.casual: Sal Russo's got a two-bedroom open in his six-unit on 31st Avenue in Astoria. He calls Jordan: "List it. No vouchers, no kids, and I'd rather a married couple. Older folks are fine, but nobody over seventy, the stairs." Sal says it's his building, his call. So how many of those four can Jordan actually go along with?

deeper.plain: Sal is asking Jordan to filter tenants four different ways. Each one runs into a different protected class under New York law.
deeper.picture: It's like a customer handing a waiter a list of who's allowed to sit near them. The waiter doesn't get to enforce that list, no matter who's paying.
deeper.street: Sal has owned the building for 20 years and has always picked tenants by gut. Jordan has a fresh license and a sponsoring broker who'll answer for whatever goes into that listing.
deeper.stakes: If Jordan posts that ad, both Jordan and Hudson & Hart face a complaint at the Commission or DHR, plus DOS discipline. Sal faces damages and civil penalties too.
deeper.exam: Scenario items pile several requests into one stem. Sort each request into its class: source of income, familial status, marital status, age.

blocks.text: The New York State Human Rights Law

blocks.html: New York's main civil rights statute is the New York State Human Rights Law, Executive Law Article 15. Housing discrimination is in Section 296. It is enforced by the NYS Division of Human Rights (DHR) and in state court. It covers every federal class (using "creed" alongside religion) and adds more.
blocks.casual: New York's big civil rights law is the New York State Human Rights Law, Executive Law Article 15. The housing part lives in Section 296. The NYS Division of Human Rights (DHR) enforces it, and so do state courts. It covers every federal class (it says "creed" next to religion) and then piles on more.

deeper.plain: New York has its own fair housing law that includes everything federal and adds more groups. The state agency that handles complaints is DHR.
deeper.picture: The federal law is the base pizza. New York's law is the same pizza with a bunch of extra toppings, and you have to serve it the New York way.
deeper.street: A tenant in Buffalo who's turned down for being divorced can't go to HUD, because marital status isn't federal. She files with DHR under Article 15 instead.
deeper.stakes: If you only know the federal list, you'll green-light things that are illegal in New York. DHR can award damages and civil fines against owners and agents.
deeper.exam: Know the cite: Executive Law Article 15, Section 296 for housing. DHR is state; HUD is federal; the NYC Commission on Human Rights is city.

head: Added by New York State
What it means in practice
rows: Cannot refuse or limit someone because they are older (or younger, once 18 or over). Does not protect minors as such.
Single, married, divorced, widowed, separated. "Married couples only" is illegal.
Express NY protection, not dependent on federal interpretation.
Active duty, reservists, veterans. You may not ask about state militia membership.
Statewide since April 2019: vouchers, Section 8, SSI, Social Security, child support, alimony, any lawful income.
The newest state class. Do not screen out applicants by status.
Status as a victim of domestic violence
Cannot refuse or evict someone because they are a survivor.
blocks.caption: Plus every federal class: race, creed or religion, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status (which in NY includes pregnancy and people seeking custody).

deeper.plain: These are the extra groups New York protects on top of the federal seven. Each row tells you what it looks like when someone crosses the line.
deeper.picture: Picture the federal seven as the main menu and this table as the New York specials board. Both are on offer every night.
deeper.street: A Rochester landlord asks an applicant whether she's an active reservist who might deploy. That's military status, protected in New York, and the question itself is a red flag.
deeper.stakes: Source of income and marital status are where New York landlords trip most. A screening rule like "must have W-2 income" can quietly knock out voucher holders and break the law.
deeper.exam: Age in NY protects adults, not minors. Familial status in NY includes pregnancy and people seeking custody. The exam may ask which class covers a widow (marital status).

blocks.title: The eight NY add-ons
blocks.html: "MAMS GIVL" (say "Mom's gavel"): Marital status, Age, Military status, Sexual orientation, Gender identity or expression, Immigration or citizenship status, Victim of domestic violence, Lawful source of income.
blocks.casual: Memory hook for the New York add-ons: "MAMS GIVL" (say "Mom's gavel"). Marital status, Age, Military status, Sexual orientation, Gender identity or expression, Immigration or citizenship status, Victim of domestic violence, Lawful source of income.

deeper.plain: Eight letters, eight New York extras. Federal seven plus these eight is your statewide list.
deeper.picture: Imagine your mom banging a gavel every time a landlord says "no Section 8" or "married couples only." That's Mom's gavel.
deeper.street: Jordan writes MAMS GIVL on a sticky note on the laptop. During a showing in Ridgewood, an owner asks if the applicant is "here legally," and Jordan hears the I in the gavel.
deeper.stakes: Forgetting even one class means you might pass along an illegal screening question. Most violations happen in one casual sentence.
deeper.exam: When a stem lists a class and asks if it's protected "in New York," run the mnemonic. If it's in MAMS GIVL or the federal seven, the answer is yes.

blocks.q: Which of these is protected under New York State law but NOT under the federal Fair Housing Act?
c: Familial status
National origin
Marital status
Disability
blocks.x: Marital status is a New York addition. Familial status, national origin, and disability are all federal classes.

blocks.html: Two clarifications the exam likes. First, marital status is not the same as familial status: one is about marriage, the other is about kids. Second, New York's age protection applies to adults. A landlord can require that the leaseholder be 18 or older, because the age class does not protect minors as such.
blocks.casual: Two things the exam loves to poke at. First, marital status isn't familial status: one's about marriage, the other's about kids. Second, New York's age protection is for adults. A landlord can require the leaseholder to be 18 or older, because the age class doesn't protect minors as such.

deeper.plain: Marital is about whether you're married. Familial is about whether you have kids. And a landlord can still insist the signer is an adult.
deeper.picture: Marital status is the ring. Familial status is the stroller. Different things, different classes.
deeper.street: A 17-year-old in the Bronx tries to sign a lease on his own. The landlord can require an adult leaseholder. That same landlord can't refuse a 72-year-old for being 72.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up the two classes makes you misread a complaint or a policy. Using an age cutoff for adults, like "no one over 65," is a straight violation.
deeper.exam: Swap trap: a single mom refused for being unmarried is marital status; refused for her toddler is familial status. Read which fact the landlord acted on.

blocks.html: Immigration status is protected too. You may require the same identification from every applicant, consistent with your firm's procedures, but you may not ask only some applicants for proof of citizenship, reject someone for having an ITIN instead of a Social Security number when another verification method works, or threaten to report a tenant's status.
blocks.casual: Immigration status is protected too. You can ask every applicant for the same ID, following your firm's procedures. What you can't do: ask only some people for proof of citizenship, reject someone for having an ITIN instead of a Social Security number when another way to verify works, or threaten to report a tenant's status.

deeper.plain: Treat every applicant's paperwork the same, and don't use immigration status as a filter or a threat.
deeper.picture: It's like a bouncer who checks every ID at the door. Checking only the people with accents isn't checking IDs; it's profiling.
deeper.street: An applicant in Corona has a strong credit history under an ITIN. Marcus says "no SSN, no lease." The credit bureau can verify the ITIN, so rejecting her for it is immigration status discrimination.
deeper.stakes: Threatening to call immigration on a tenant who complains about heat is both harassment and discrimination. Owners and agents both face penalties.
deeper.exam: The right answer applies the same ID rule to everyone. Distractors single out applicants who "seem foreign" or require an SSN with no alternative.
