blocks.html: The New York City Human Rights Law is enforced by the NYC Commission on Human Rights. It is interpreted broadly and covers everything in the state law plus classes like these:
blocks.casual: The New York City Human Rights Law is enforced by the NYC Commission on Human Rights. Courts read it broadly, and it covers everything in the state law plus classes like these:

deeper.plain: New York City has its own law with the widest list of protections, and its own agency to enforce it.
deeper.picture: Federal, state, city: three nested boxes. The city box is the biggest, and in the five boroughs you live inside all three.
deeper.street: A Harlem tenant who's turned down because she's a bartender can file with the Commission. Lawful occupation isn't protected federally or statewide, but it is in the city.
deeper.stakes: Agents who work across Long Island and the city sometimes use one playbook. In the five boroughs, that playbook is missing protections and will get you fined.
deeper.exam: The NYC Commission on Human Rights enforces the city law. DHR enforces the state law. HUD enforces the federal law. Match agency to law.

items: Lawful occupation: you cannot refuse a tenant because of a legal job (a bartender, a sex educator, a musician).
Partnership status: registered domestic partners are protected like spouses.
Presence of children and pregnancy, spelled out by name.
Height and weight (since November 2023).
Criminal record: the Fair Chance for Housing Law (in effect since January 1, 2025) limits when and how a landlord or broker may look at criminal history.
Immigration status and lawful source of income, including housing subsidies (NYC protected source of income back in 2008).
blocks.casual:
Here's what the city adds:
Lawful occupation: you can't turn someone away for a legal job (bartender, sex educator, musician).
Partnership status: registered domestic partners are protected like spouses.
Presence of children and pregnancy, named outright.
Height and weight (since November 2023).
Criminal record: the Fair Chance for Housing Law (in effect since January 1, 2025) limits when and how a landlord or broker can look at criminal history.
Immigration status and lawful source of income, including housing subsidies (the city protected source of income back in 2008).

deeper.plain: The city protects even more people, including by job, partnership, body size, and criminal history. It also protected voucher holders years before the state did.
deeper.picture: If the state list is a long receipt, the city list is the same receipt with a few more items stapled to the bottom.
deeper.street: A Bed-Stuy landlord runs a background check on page one of the application. Under the Fair Chance for Housing Law, criminal history generally comes after a conditional offer, so Jordan's firm changes its process.
deeper.stakes: The Fair Chance law is new, and plenty of landlords haven't caught up. An agent who runs the old process exposes the owner and the brokerage.
deeper.exam: City-only classes like lawful occupation, partnership status, height, and weight are likely distractors for "state" or "federal" questions.

blocks.title: NYC voucher math
blocks.html: In the city, an income requirement such as "40 times the rent" may only be applied to the part of the rent the tenant pays. If a CityFHEPS or Section 8 voucher covers most of the rent, you measure the tenant's income against the tenant's share only.
blocks.casual: NYC voucher math: if the landlord uses an income rule like "40 times the rent," it only applies to the part of the rent the tenant actually pays. If a CityFHEPS or Section 8 voucher covers most of it, you measure the tenant's income against the tenant's share only.

deeper.plain: Check the tenant's income against what the tenant pays, not the full rent. The voucher pays the rest.
deeper.picture: If a friend is covering most of your dinner bill, the restaurant shouldn't check whether you can afford the whole thing. Just your share.
deeper.street: A Flatbush apartment rents for $2,500. A CityFHEPS voucher covers $2,200, so the tenant pays $300. At 40 times, the tenant needs $12,000 a year in income, not $100,000.
deeper.stakes: Applying 40x to the full rent screens out nearly every voucher holder. The Commission treats that as source of income discrimination, and fines can be steep.
deeper.exam: Cue words: "voucher" plus "income requirement." The correct answer applies the ratio to the tenant's portion only.

blocks.text: Lawful source of income: the most common violation in NYC rentals

blocks.html: Lawful source of income discrimination is what the Commission and the state Attorney General catch most often in listings. "No programs," "no vouchers," "must be employed," or quietly ignoring a voucher holder's calls are all violations. You may still screen every applicant the same way, for example a credit check or references, as long as the screen does not single out the voucher.
blocks.casual: Lawful source of income discrimination is the violation the Commission and the state Attorney General catch most in listings. "No programs," "no vouchers," "must be employed," or quietly ghosting a voucher holder's calls are all violations. You can still screen everyone the same way, like a credit check or references, as long as the screen doesn't single out the voucher.

deeper.plain: You can't refuse or dodge someone because their rent comes from a voucher, benefits, or other legal income. Same screening for everyone is fine.
deeper.picture: Money is money. Turning down a check because it came from a program instead of a paycheck is like refusing a twenty because it came from an ATM.
deeper.street: An agent posts a Crown Heights listing with "no programs." A tester with a Section 8 voucher calls and never hears back. The Commission files against the agent, the brokerage, and the owner.
deeper.stakes: Source of income cases have produced big settlements against brokerages, plus mandatory training and monitoring. Ignoring calls counts, even if you never say "no."
deeper.exam: Silence is a violation. If a stem says the agent "did not return calls" from voucher holders, that's discrimination, not just bad service.

blocks.q: A Bronx landlord tells a voucher holder the apartment requires income of 40 times the monthly rent of $2,400, measured against her total income, even though her voucher pays $1,900 of the rent. Under NYC law this is:
c: Legal, because the landlord applies the same rule to everyone
Illegal, because the requirement must be applied only to her $500 share
Legal, because vouchers are not income
Illegal only if the building has 6 or more units
blocks.x: In NYC the income requirement may only be applied to the tenant's share of the rent. A facially equal rule that effectively screens out voucher holders is source of income discrimination.

blocks.html: Familial status and occupancy limits often collide. A landlord may enforce reasonable, neutral occupancy limits based on bedroom size and local codes, but may not use an artificially low limit ("one person per bedroom") to keep children out. In NYC, the Housing Maintenance Code sets minimum space per occupant; a landlord who invents a stricter rule invites a familial status complaint.
blocks.casual: Familial status and occupancy limits bump into each other all the time. A landlord can enforce reasonable, neutral occupancy limits based on bedroom size and local codes. What the landlord can't do is invent an artificially low limit ("one person per bedroom") to keep kids out. In NYC the Housing Maintenance Code sets minimum space per occupant, and a landlord who makes up something stricter invites a familial status complaint.

deeper.plain: Occupancy limits are fine if they follow the code. A made-up limit that happens to block families is not.
deeper.picture: It's like a restaurant capping a table at two because it "doesn't like crowds," when the fire code says six. The cap is just a polite way of saying no families.
deeper.street: A couple with a newborn applies for a one-bedroom in Sunnyside. The landlord says "two people max." The code allows them, so the limit is a pretext and the couple has a familial status claim.
deeper.stakes: Agents who repeat an owner's fake limit become part of the violation. Ask what code the number comes from before you put it in a listing.
deeper.exam: Reasonable occupancy limits are legal. The trap answer treats any limit as illegal, or treats "one person per bedroom" as automatically fine.

head: Situation
Federal FHA
New York State
rows: Owner lives in a 2 to 4 unit building and rents another unit ("Mrs. Murphy")
Exempt if owner-occupied, up to 4 units
Only 2 units: rental in an owner-occupied two-family house
Owner sells or rents own single-family home
Exempt if owner has no more than 3 such homes, uses no broker, and runs no discriminatory ad
Renting rooms in the owner's own home
Covered by Mrs. Murphy if 4 or fewer units
Exempt for rooms rented by the occupant or a resident owner
All rooms in a unit rented to one sex
Religious organization and private club housing for members
Exempt if not commercial and membership is not restricted by race
Exempt from familial status only: all residents 62+, or 80% of units with at least one person 55+ plus published policies and age verification
Same idea: age and familial status only

deeper.plain: Federal law has a few owner exemptions. New York's are fewer and smaller, and brokers never get any.
deeper.picture: The federal exemptions are a big umbrella. New York's are a small one, and the moment a broker steps under it, it folds.
deeper.street: An owner in Bay Ridge lives in one unit of a three-family. Federally, Mrs. Murphy might apply. In New York, only a two-family qualifies, so the state law still covers him.
deeper.stakes: Owners quote the federal exemption and think they're safe. In New York they usually aren't, and an agent who agrees is giving wrong legal advice.
deeper.exam: NY two-family vs federal up to 4 units is the classic contrast. And the single-family owner exemption doesn't exist in New York.

blocks.title: Three things no exemption covers
blocks.html: 1. Race, because of the 1866 Act. 2. Discriminatory advertising: even an exempt owner may not publish "no children." In New York the two-family exemption covers the refusal itself, not the ad. 3. You: a licensee may never help anyone use an exemption to discriminate.
blocks.casual:
Three things no exemption covers:
1. Race, because of the 1866 Act.
2. Discriminatory advertising: even an exempt owner can't publish "no children." In New York the two-family exemption covers the refusal itself, not the ad.
3. You: a licensee can never help anyone use an exemption to discriminate.

deeper.plain: Race, ads, and brokers are never exempt. Everything else depends on the facts.
deeper.picture: Three locked doors no exemption key opens: the race door, the ad door, and the broker door.
deeper.street: A Mrs. Murphy owner in Ozone Park posts "no kids" on a community board. The post itself is illegal even if the refusal might have been exempt.
deeper.stakes: If you write or post the ad, the owner's exemption doesn't save you. You take the hit on your license.
deeper.exam: "Which is NOT exempt?" Look for race, an ad, or a licensee in the facts. Any one of the three means the conduct is covered.

blocks.html: Senior housing exemptions only cover age and familial status. A 55+ community can turn away a family with a toddler. It cannot turn away a Muslim buyer or a wheelchair user. The owner-occupied two-family exemption is the New York version of the federal Mrs. Murphy exemption, cut down from 4 units to 2.
blocks.casual: Senior housing exemptions only reach age and familial status. A 55+ community can turn away a family with a toddler. It can't turn away a Muslim buyer or a wheelchair user. The owner-occupied two-family exemption is New York's version of the federal Mrs. Murphy exemption, shrunk from 4 units to 2.

deeper.plain: Senior housing can keep out kids and younger people, but nothing else. New York's owner exemption only works in a two-family.
deeper.picture: The senior exemption is a key that opens exactly two locks: age and kids. Try it on any other lock and it just spins.
deeper.street: A 55+ co-op in Rockland turns down a younger couple with a baby: allowed if it meets the 80% rule and verifies ages. It turns down a deaf buyer: illegal, because disability isn't covered by the exemption.
deeper.stakes: Communities that think "senior" means they can screen on anything end up in disability or religion cases. Agents marketing them need to know the limits.
deeper.exam: Senior housing: all 62+, or 80% of units with at least one 55+, with published policies and age verification. Exempt from familial status only.

blocks.title: The city's version is even tighter
blocks.html: Under the NYC Human Rights Law, an owner-occupied two-family keeps its exemption only if the vacancy is not publicly advertised or listed. Put it on StreetEasy or hand it to a broker and the exemption is gone.
blocks.casual: The city's version is even tighter. Under the NYC Human Rights Law, an owner-occupied two-family keeps its exemption only if the vacancy is not publicly advertised or listed. Put it on StreetEasy or hand it to a broker and the exemption's gone.

deeper.plain: In the city, an owner of a two-family loses the exemption the moment the apartment goes public.
deeper.picture: It's a private party exemption. Once you post the invite online, it's a public event and the public rules apply.
deeper.street: The Okafors' neighbor lives in a two-family in Bed-Stuy and lists the upstairs unit on StreetEasy. From that moment, she can't refuse a voucher holder or a family under any exemption.
deeper.stakes: Every listing you take in the city is, by definition, public. So for any NYC rental you handle, assume no exemption applies.
deeper.exam: NYC two-family exemption requires no public advertising and no listing. Broker involvement or an online ad ends it.

blocks.q: Sal owns a six-unit building in Astoria and lives in one unit. Can he refuse to rent to a family with children under any New York exemption?
c: Yes, because he is owner-occupied
No, the NY owner-occupied exemption only applies to two-family houses
Yes, if the unit has only one bedroom
Yes, if he does not use a broker
blocks.x: New York's owner-occupied exemption covers only two-family houses. Six units is far outside it, and the federal Mrs. Murphy rule stops at four units anyway.

blocks.html: Federal and New York law exclude current illegal drug use from the definition of disability. A landlord may refuse someone currently using illegal drugs, and may refuse someone convicted of manufacturing or distributing controlled substances. But a person in recovery (in or done with a treatment program, not currently using) is protected as disabled. Alcoholism can be a disability too; the landlord may still enforce conduct rules that apply to everyone, and may exclude anyone who is a direct threat to others' safety.
blocks.casual: Federal and New York law both leave current illegal drug use out of the definition of disability. A landlord can refuse someone currently using illegal drugs, and can refuse someone convicted of manufacturing or distributing controlled substances. But a person in recovery (in or done with treatment, not currently using) is protected as disabled. Alcoholism can be a disability too. The landlord can still enforce conduct rules that apply to everyone, and can exclude anyone who's a direct threat to others' safety.

deeper.plain: Using illegal drugs now isn't protected. Recovering from addiction is. Alcoholism can be protected, but bad behavior isn't.
deeper.picture: Think of a gym that bans people who are currently fighting in the locker room, not people who used to box. It's the behavior right now that matters.
deeper.street: An applicant in Inwood discloses he finished a methadone program last year. Sal can't refuse him for that. If a different tenant is dealing drugs from the unit, Sal can act on that conduct.
deeper.stakes: Asking applicants about addiction history or rejecting "anyone with a drug past" is disability discrimination. Owners get sued for blanket bans.
deeper.exam: Current illegal use: not protected. In recovery: protected. Conviction for manufacturing or distributing: can be refused. Simple possession conviction is not on that list.

left.title: Reasonable accommodation
items: A change in a rule, policy, practice, or service
Assistance animal in a no-pet building, with no pet fee
Reserved accessible parking space
Rent due on the 5th because benefits arrive on the 3rd
Usually costs the provider little or nothing

right.title: Reasonable modification
items: A physical change to the unit or common areas
Grab bars, a ramp, wider doorways, lower counters
Federally, the tenant usually pays in private housing
Landlord may require restoring the interior at move-out if reasonable
NYC law can put more of the cost on the housing provider

deeper.plain: An accommodation changes a rule. A modification changes the physical space.
deeper.picture: Accommodation is changing the house rules. Modification is changing the house.
deeper.street: A tenant in Kew Gardens needs grab bars in the bathroom: that's a modification, and federally she usually pays. Her neighbor needs her rent due on the 5th because SSI arrives on the 3rd: that's an accommodation and costs the landlord nothing.
deeper.stakes: Landlords who refuse cheap accommodations, like a parking spot or a due-date change, lose cases they never needed to fight. NYC can put more of the modification cost on the owner.
deeper.exam: "Policy, rule, practice, service" means accommodation. "Physical change, ramp, grab bars" means modification. The exam swaps the labels.

blocks.html: Assistance animals are the most common accommodation request. Service animals and emotional support animals are not pets under fair housing law, so no pet deposit or pet fee may be charged. If the disability is not obvious, the provider may ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need, for example a letter from a treating health professional. The provider may not demand medical records or a diagnosis, and may deny a specific animal only if it poses a direct threat or would cause substantial damage that cannot be reduced.
blocks.casual: Assistance animals are the most common accommodation request. Service animals and emotional support animals aren't pets under fair housing law, so no pet deposit or pet fee. If the disability isn't obvious, the provider can ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need, like a letter from a treating health professional. The provider can't demand medical records or a diagnosis, and can turn down a specific animal only if it's a direct threat or would cause substantial damage that can't be reduced.

deeper.plain: Support and service animals aren't pets, so no-pet rules and pet fees don't apply. The landlord can ask for a letter, not a diagnosis.
deeper.picture: A wheelchair isn't furniture and a guide dog isn't a pet. Both are tools that help someone live in the home.
deeper.street: A tenant in a no-pet Upper East Side rental shows a letter from her therapist for an emotional support cat. The landlord can't charge the $500 pet deposit or ask what her diagnosis is.
deeper.stakes: Charging a pet fee for an assistance animal is a quick, easy-to-prove violation. Asking for medical records turns a reasonable request into a complaint.
deeper.exam: No pet fee, no pet deposit, no diagnosis required. The landlord may ask for documentation of need when the disability isn't obvious, and can deny only a direct threat or substantial damage.

blocks.html: A reasonable accommodation bends a rule. A reasonable modification changes the space. A provider can refuse only if the request is an undue financial and administrative burden, fundamentally alters the operation, or there is no disability-related need. New York requires housing providers and their agents to give prospective tenants a written Reasonable Accommodation and Reasonable Modification notice explaining this right (rentals only).
blocks.casual: A reasonable accommodation bends a rule. A reasonable modification changes the space. A provider can say no only if the request is an undue financial and administrative burden, fundamentally changes how the place operates, or there's no disability-related need. New York requires housing providers and their agents to give prospective tenants a written Reasonable Accommodation and Reasonable Modification notice explaining this right (rentals only).

deeper.plain: Most disability requests have to be granted unless they're truly too costly, change the whole operation, or aren't tied to a disability. Renters must get a written notice of this right.
deeper.picture: The bar for saying no is high, like a store refusing to hold a door for someone. Unless it really breaks the business, you hold the door.
deeper.street: Jordan hands every rental applicant at a Williamsburg building the state notice along with the application. One applicant uses it to request a ground-floor unit, and the owner grants it.
deeper.stakes: Skipping the notice is its own failure, separate from any denial. And a denial without a real burden argument almost always loses.
deeper.exam: Valid refusals: undue burden, fundamental alteration, no disability-related need. "The landlord doesn't like it" or "other tenants might complain" is never one of them.

blocks.q: A tenant with a mobility impairment asks to install grab bars in her bathroom. A tenant with an anxiety disorder asks to keep a support dog in a no-pets building. These are, in order:
c: Two accommodations
A modification, then an accommodation
An accommodation, then a modification
Two modifications
blocks.x: Grab bars change the physical space, so that is a modification. Waiving a no-pets rule changes a policy, so that is an accommodation.

blocks.title: Answer to Sal
blocks.html: Zero of four. Vouchers: source of income. Kids: familial status. Married only: marital status. Nobody over seventy: age. A six-unit is not exempt, and even if it were, Jordan as a broker could not take part.
blocks.casual: Answer to Sal: zero out of four. Vouchers: source of income. Kids: familial status. Married only: marital status. Nobody over seventy: age. A six-unit isn't exempt, and even if it were, Jordan as a broker couldn't take part.

deeper.plain: Every one of Sal's requests is illegal, and no exemption saves any of them.
deeper.picture: Four darts, four bullseyes on four different protected classes. Not one lands on a legal target.
deeper.street: Jordan calls Sal back: "I can list it, but not with any of those. I'll screen everyone on credit and references, same way." Sal grumbles and signs. The unit rents in two weeks to a nurse with a toddler.
deeper.stakes: Saying yes to even one request puts Jordan's license and the firm in play. Saying no, with the reasons, is what keeps the client out of trouble too.
deeper.exam: When the stem gives a 5+ unit building and asks about exemptions, none apply federally or in NY. Brokers are never exempt anyway.

blocks.title: Sal's four requests, sorted
blocks.html:
"No vouchers": lawful source of income (NYS, NYC). Illegal.
"No kids": familial status (federal, NYS, NYC). Illegal.
"Married couple preferred": marital status (NYS), partnership status (NYC). Illegal.
"Nobody over seventy": age (NYS, NYC). Illegal.
Exemption check: six units, so no federal Mrs. Murphy (max 4) and no NY two-family exemption. Jordan is a broker, never exempt.
Result: Jordan follows none of the four, explains why, and writes an ad about the apartment.
blocks.casual:
"No vouchers": lawful source of income (NYS, NYC). Illegal.
"No kids": familial status (federal, NYS, NYC). Illegal.
"Married couple preferred": marital status (NYS), partnership status (NYC). Illegal.
"Nobody over seventy": age (NYS, NYC). Illegal.
Exemption check: six units, so no federal Mrs. Murphy (max 4) and no NY two-family exemption. Jordan's a broker, never exempt.
Result: Jordan follows none of the four, explains why, and writes an ad about the apartment.

deeper.plain: Match each request to a class and law, then check exemptions. Here nothing survives.
deeper.picture: It's a sorting machine: each request drops into a slot marked with a protected class, and every slot is labeled "illegal."
deeper.street: Jordan's ad reads: "Sunny 2BR on 31st Ave, Astoria. Near the N/W. Heat included." No words about who should live there, only what the apartment is.
deeper.stakes: Describing the people you want instead of the property is how ads become evidence. Describe the space and you rarely go wrong.
deeper.exam: For multi-request scenarios, count each one separately and name its class. Answer choices often say "two of four" to catch people who think age or marital status is fair game.

story.title: Sal's Wish List
story.setting: A diner on Ditmars Boulevard, Astoria

beats.text: Simple listing, kid. No vouchers, no kids, married couple preferred, nobody too old for the stairs.
Sal, I wrote that down and every single item is a violation.
Every one? Vouchers aren't a race.
Lawful source of income. Protected statewide since 2019, and in the city since 2008.
Fine. But no kids, that's just practical.
Familial status, federal law. Married couple is marital status, and too old is age. Those two are New York classes.
beats.tag: NY adds age and marital status

beats.text: My cousin in Bay Ridge rents to whoever he wants. He lives in the building.
Two-family?
Yeah.
That's the one New York exemption. Owner-occupied two-family, rental only. You have six units. And the second he lists it with a broker in the city, even his exemption is gone.

check.q: Why can't Sal use his cousin's exemption?
c: Sal doesn't live in his building
NY's owner-occupied exemption is limited to two-family houses
Exemptions only apply upstate
Sal's building is a co-op
check.x: New York cut the federal 4-unit Mrs. Murphy exemption down to owner-occupied two-family houses.

beats.text: What if somebody wants to put a ramp on my stoop?

That's a reasonable modification, a physical change. A rule change, like letting a tenant keep a support dog, is an accommodation. And I give every prospective tenant a written notice about that right.
What about the guy who was in rehab? I heard you can't say no to him either.
People in recovery are protected as disabled. Current illegal drug use isn't protected. Same screening for everybody.
Back at the office, Jordan tells Diane the story.
So the listing says: two-bedroom, third floor walk-up, $2,600, all applicants welcome. Describe the apartment, never the tenant.

board.prompt: Draw three nested circles: federal, New York State, New York City. Write each protected class in the innermost circle where it first appears.

facts.text: The NYS Human Rights Law (Executive Law Article 15, housing in Section 296) is enforced by the NYS Division of Human Rights and covers every federal class plus more.

New York adds eight classes: marital status, age, military status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, immigration or citizenship status, domestic violence victim status and lawful source of income.
Lawful source of income (vouchers, Section 8, SSI, child support, any lawful income) has been protected statewide since April 2019, so 'no Section 8' is illegal.
'No programs,' 'must be employed' or ignoring voucher holders are source of income violations; a screen applied the same to everyone, such as a credit check, is allowed.
Marital status (marriage) is not familial status (children); 'married couples preferred' violates the marital status class.
New York's age protection covers adults; a landlord may require the leaseholder to be 18 or older.
Immigration status: require the same ID from every applicant; do not ask only some for proof of citizenship, reject a workable ITIN, or threaten to report a tenant's status.
The NYC Human Rights Law is enforced by the NYC Commission on Human Rights and covers everything in state law plus more.
NYC adds lawful occupation, partnership status, height and weight, and criminal record limits under the Fair Chance for Housing Law (since January 1, 2025).
In NYC an income rule such as 40 times the rent is applied only to the tenant's share when a voucher pays the rest.
Reasonable, neutral occupancy limits based on bedroom size and codes are allowed; an artificially low limit that keeps out children is familial status discrimination.
New York's owner-occupied exemption covers only a two-family house, versus up to 4 units under the federal Mrs. Murphy exemption.
The federal single-family exemption requires an owner of no more than 3 such homes, no broker and no discriminatory ad; New York has no such exemption.
New York also exempts rooms rented by an occupant or resident owner, renting all rooms in a unit to one sex, and narrow religious preferences.
Housing for older persons (all residents 62+, or 80% of units with a 55+ occupant plus policies and age checks) is exempt from age and familial status only, not other classes.
No exemption covers race, discriminatory advertising, or a licensee: a broker may not help anyone use an exemption to discriminate.
In NYC the owner-occupied two-family exemption is lost if the vacancy is publicly advertised or listed with a broker.
Current illegal drug use is not a disability and a landlord may refuse someone convicted of making or selling drugs; people in recovery are protected.
A reasonable accommodation changes a rule, policy, practice or service; a reasonable modification is a physical change to the unit or common areas.
Federally, the tenant usually pays for a modification in private housing and may have to restore the interior; NYC law can shift more cost to the provider.
Assistance animals are not pets, so no pet fee or deposit; for a non-obvious disability the provider may ask for reliable documentation but not medical records.
An accommodation may be refused only for undue burden, fundamental alteration, or no disability-related need; New York requires a written accommodation notice for rentals.

lessons.title: What Discrimination Looks Like: Steering, Blockbusting, Redlining, and Ads
lessons.tagline: Most fair housing violations are not slammed doors. They are a helpful tip, a skipped listing, a friendly ad, or a phone call about the neighborhood changing.
objectives: Classify a fact pattern as refusal, unequal treatment, misinformation, steering, blockbusting, or redlining
Answer "Is this a safe area?" and "Who lives here?" without violating the law
Write a compliant listing and social media ad
Explain testers, cease and desist zones, and nonsolicitation orders

blocks.title: Park Slope, a showing that went sideways
blocks.html: Leo Brandt is buying his first apartment. In the car he asks Jordan, "Honest question. Is Crown Heights safe? And who lives there, like, what's the vibe?" Later a Ditmas Park seller calls: "Don't show my house to anyone who will upset the neighbors, you know what I mean." Jordan wants to be helpful to both. Where exactly is the line?
blocks.casual: Leo Brandt's buying his first place. In the car he asks Jordan, "Honest question. Is Crown Heights safe? And who lives there, like, what's the vibe?" Later a Ditmas Park seller calls: "Don't show my house to anyone who'll upset the neighbors, you know what I mean." Jordan wants to help both of them. So where exactly's the line?

deeper.plain: A buyer wants Jordan to describe neighborhoods by who lives there, and a seller wants Jordan to filter buyers. Both requests push Jordan toward a violation.
deeper.picture: It's like being a tour guide asked to skip certain streets "because of the people." The tourist and the hotel both asked nicely, and it's still not your call to make.
deeper.street: Leo means well; he just wants to feel safe. The Ditmas Park seller means something else entirely. Jordan has to answer both without describing residents or screening buyers.
deeper.stakes: One wrong answer to Leo is steering. Following the seller's hint is refusal to deal. Either can end up as a DOS complaint with Jordan's name on it.
deeper.exam: Stems with "safe," "vibe," or "people like you" are steering setups. The best answer redirects to objective data and shows all matching listings.

blocks.html: Fair housing rarely fails because an agent wakes up wanting to discriminate. It fails under pressure. Sellers and landlords ask for "a certain type." Neighbors call the listing agent. Buyers make remarks about parts of town, ask pointed questions about who lives there, or refuse to see homes in areas where certain people live. Your job is the same every time: follow the law, redirect to objective facts, and never act on a discriminatory request.
blocks.casual: Fair housing rarely breaks because an agent wakes up wanting to discriminate. It breaks under pressure. Sellers and landlords ask for "a certain type." Neighbors call the listing agent. Buyers make comments about parts of town, ask pointed questions about who lives there, or won't see homes where certain people live. Your job's the same every time: follow the law, steer the talk back to objective facts, and never act on a discriminatory request.

deeper.plain: Most violations happen when an agent caves to someone else's bias. The fix is the same response every time.
deeper.picture: Think of a lifeguard who hears ten swimmers shouting different requests. The rule is still "no running by the pool" for everybody.
deeper.street: A Bay Ridge neighbor calls Jordan about a listing next door: "Make sure you find the right kind of family." Jordan says thanks for the call, markets to everyone, and logs the call with Diane.
deeper.stakes: "The client told me to" is not a defense. The agent who carries out the request is liable alongside the client.
deeper.exam: The exam rewards the answer where the agent declines and explains the law. Answers where the agent "politely complies" or "stays neutral" are wrong.

blocks.html: The seller version sounds like this: "Show it to whoever, but you know the neighbors. They'll be upset if..." The landlord version: "I want someone who fits the building." Your script is the same: "I market to everyone and present every qualified offer or application. The law doesn't let me, or you, choose by race, religion, family, income source, or any protected class." If the client insists, you decline the listing and tell your broker.
blocks.casual: The seller version sounds like: "Show it to whoever, but you know the neighbors. They'll be upset if..." The landlord version: "I want someone who fits the building." Your script doesn't change: "I market to everyone and present every qualified offer or application. The law doesn't let me, or you, choose by race, religion, family, income source, or any protected class." If the client keeps pushing, you turn down the listing and tell your broker.

deeper.plain: Have a set line ready that says you treat everyone the same. If the client won't accept it, walk away from the listing.
deeper.picture: It's like a bartender's line for an overserved customer. Same words, calm voice, every time, and if it doesn't work you call the manager.
deeper.street: A landlord in Forest Hills tells Jordan he wants tenants who "fit the building." Jordan delivers the script. He insists, so Jordan drops the listing and emails Diane a note the same day.
deeper.stakes: Keeping a listing with a discriminatory owner means you'll eventually have to act on it or lie about it. Both end badly.
deeper.exam: Best answer when a client insists: refuse to participate and withdraw if needed. "Do what the client says because it's their property" is always wrong.

blocks.html: Buyers apply pressure too. A buyer may refuse to see homes "where those people live." You may not agree to screen out areas on that basis, and you may not narrate neighborhoods by who lives there. You can let the buyer choose which listings to visit from the full set that meets their stated criteria. Their choice is theirs; your filtering would be steering.
blocks.casual: Buyers push too. A buyer might refuse to see homes "where those people live." You can't agree to screen out areas on that basis, and you can't narrate neighborhoods by who lives there. What you can do is let the buyer pick which listings to see from the full set that fits their stated criteria. Their choice is theirs. Your filtering would be steering.

deeper.plain: Give the buyer every listing that fits the budget and features. They can choose where to go; you can't choose for them by who lives there.
deeper.picture: You hand them the whole menu. They can skip dishes, but you don't tear out pages before they look.
deeper.street: A buyer with $900,000 wants a three-bedroom near a park. Jordan sends 14 matches across Kensington, Flatbush, and Windsor Terrace. The buyer picks five; Jordan schedules all five.
deeper.stakes: If you pre-filter by area because of a remark, the paper trail shows you did it. That's steering even if the buyer asked.
deeper.exam: The buyer's own choice is legal; the agent's filtering is not. Look for who made the selection in the stem.

head: Type
What it looks like
NYC example
rows: Refusing to sell, rent, show, negotiate, or work with someone because of a protected class
"We're not taking applications from families right now" to a mom with twins
Different terms, deposits, speed, or effort; not showing every available home in the client's price range
Showing a white couple 12 listings and a Black couple 3 with the same budget
Saying a unit is taken, the price is higher, or the board is strict when it is not
"That one just went into contract" when it has not
Guiding buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on a protected class
"You'd be more comfortable in Bay Ridge, lots of people like you"
Inducing owners to sell by warning that protected-class people are moving in
Flyers in East Flatbush: "The neighborhood is changing. Sell now before values drop"
Lenders or insurers refusing or limiting loans or coverage by area because of who lives there
A bank that won't make loans east of a certain avenue
Any ad that states or implies a preference, limitation, or discrimination
Restricting pools, gyms, laundry, roof, or services by protected class
Gym hours "for adults only" or a roof deck closed to voucher tenants

deeper.plain: These are the main ways housing discrimination shows up, each with a New York example. Most are about treating people differently, not just saying no.
deeper.picture: Think of it as a field guide to bad behavior. Some species are loud (refusal), some are quiet (unequal treatment, misinformation).
deeper.street: Two testers with the same $3,000 budget visit a Midtown rental office. One hears about six units and gets a callback; the other hears "just one left" and no follow-up. That's unequal treatment and misinformation in a single afternoon.
deeper.stakes: Subtle forms like slower callbacks or fewer listings are the ones testers catch most. You can violate the law without ever saying no.
deeper.exam: Match the conduct to the label: lying about availability is misinformation, guiding to areas is steering, scaring owners is blockbusting, lenders by area is redlining.

blocks.caption: Drag each statement into steering, blockbusting, redlining, or legal. The tell: steering targets the buyer, blockbusting targets the owner, redlining targets the loan or policy.

blocks.html: Steering is the violation agents commit while trying to be nice. It happens when you choose which neighborhoods to show, or describe neighborhoods differently, based on the client's race, religion, family status, or any protected class. It also happens when a client asks you to do it and you comply. Showing a Jewish family only listings near a synagogue they never asked about is steering. Showing only listings near a synagogue because the buyer asked for a walk to it is following client instructions.
blocks.casual: Steering is the violation agents commit while trying to be nice. It happens when you pick which neighborhoods to show, or describe them differently, based on the client's race, religion, family status, or any protected class. It also happens when a client asks you to and you go along. Showing a Jewish family only listings near a synagogue they never asked about is steering. Showing only listings near a synagogue because the buyer asked to walk to one is just following instructions.

deeper.plain: Steering is choosing areas for clients based on who they are. Following a client's own stated, objective criteria is fine.
deeper.picture: It's like a GPS that picks your route based on your face instead of your destination. The client sets the destination; you just drive.
deeper.street: A Muslim family asks for three-bedrooms under $1.2M with a short commute to Midtown. Marcus only shows them listings in Bay Ridge "because they'll feel at home." They never mentioned a mosque. That's steering.
deeper.stakes: Steering complaints come straight from testers and from clients who later compare notes. It's one of the most cited violations in fair housing investigations.
deeper.exam: The key is who brought up the criterion. Client asked for it objectively: fine. Agent assumed it from a protected class: steering.

blocks.title: "Is it safe?" and "Who lives there?"
blocks.html: Do not give an opinion and do not describe residents. Redirect to objective sources: "Safety means different things to different people. NYPD precinct crime data and CompStat are public, and I can send you the link." For demographics: "I can't characterize who lives in a neighborhood, but census data is public. What features matter to you, the commute, parks, schools, price per square foot?" Then show every listing that fits the buyer's stated criteria.
blocks.casual: When you get "Is it safe?" or "Who lives there?": no opinion, no describing residents. Redirect to objective sources: "Safety means different things to different people. NYPD precinct crime data and CompStat are public, and I can send you the link." For demographics: "I can't characterize who lives in a neighborhood, but census data is public. What matters to you, the commute, parks, schools, price per square foot?" Then show every listing that fits the buyer's stated criteria.

deeper.plain: Point buyers to public data on crime and demographics instead of giving your opinion. Then talk about features.
deeper.picture: You're a librarian, not a critic. You hand over the book; you don't tell them whether to like it.
deeper.street: Jordan tells Leo: "Here's the NYPD precinct page for the 77th and the CompStat link. What matters most, the subway, a park nearby?" Leo says the 2/3 and a park, and Jordan sends listings in four neighborhoods.
deeper.stakes: "Oh, it's fine, lots of young professionals now" sounds harmless and is evidence of steering. Your opinion on safety or residents is the risk.
deeper.exam: The best answer refers to objective, public sources and doesn't characterize the area. Distractors give reassurances or suggest "nicer" areas.

blocks.q: A buyer asks which Brooklyn neighborhoods are "good for people like us." Which response complies with fair housing law?
c: "Most of my clients like you end up in Bay Ridge."
"Tell me about your budget, commute, and must-haves, and I'll show you everything that fits."
"I'd avoid East New York if I were you."
"Let me ask around about who's moving in where."
blocks.x: Redirecting to objective criteria and showing everything that fits is compliant. Matching areas to "people like you" is steering.

blocks.html: Blockbusting, also called panic peddling, creates fear in a neighborhood so owners sell fast and cheap. The classic version was telling white owners that Black families were moving in, buying cheap, then reselling at a premium. Profit is the motive; fear of a protected class is the method. The message can be subtle: "The area is changing, you might want to get out while prices are good."
blocks.casual: Blockbusting, also called panic peddling, whips up fear in a neighborhood so owners sell fast and cheap. The classic play: tell white owners Black families are moving in, buy cheap, then resell at a premium. Profit's the motive; fear of a protected class is the method. The pitch can be subtle: "The area's changing, you might want to get out while prices are good."

deeper.plain: Blockbusting scares owners into selling by hinting that certain people are moving in. The agent or investor profits from the panic.
deeper.picture: Someone yells "fire" in a theater so they can grab the best seats cheap as everyone runs out.
deeper.street: Postcards hit mailboxes in East Flatbush: "The neighborhood is changing. Sell now before values drop. Call for a cash offer." The sender buys three houses below value in a month.
deeper.stakes: Blockbusting can cost a license and draw state action, and it's the reason New York has cease and desist zones. Coded "changing area" marketing can be enough.
deeper.exam: Target is current owners, motive is profit, method is fear about a protected class. If the stem's target is buyers, it's steering instead.

blocks.html: Redlining is a lender or insurer refusing or limiting loans or coverage in an area because of the racial or ethnic makeup of that area, regardless of the individual applicant's qualifications. A lender may decline a loan for objective reasons like credit, income, or the property's condition. It may not decline because of the neighborhood's residents.
blocks.casual: Redlining is a lender or insurer refusing or limiting loans or coverage in an area because of the racial or ethnic makeup of that area, no matter how qualified the individual applicant is. A lender can turn down a loan for objective reasons like credit, income, or the property's condition. It can't turn it down because of who lives in the neighborhood.

deeper.plain: Lenders and insurers can judge the borrower and the building, but not the race of the neighbors.
deeper.picture: It's a bank that won't cross a certain street. Your credit score is great, but your address is on the wrong side of an invisible line.
deeper.street: Tasha sees two identical files: same income, same credit. One property is in Canarsie, one in Marine Park. If the lender prices or denies the Canarsie loan because of who lives there, that's redlining.
deeper.stakes: Redlining keeps entire neighborhoods from buying and renovating, and lenders face federal and state enforcement. Agents who route clients away from lenders "who don't lend there" can get pulled in.
deeper.exam: Redlining = lenders or insurers. Steering = agents and buyers. Blockbusting = agents and owners. The actor tells you the answer.

left.title: Steering
items: Target: buyers and renters
Channels them toward or away from areas
Committed by agents

right.title: Blockbusting
items: Target: current owners
Panics them into selling
Committed by agents and speculators

deeper.plain: Steering is done to buyers and renters. Blockbusting is done to current owners.
deeper.picture: Steering is the hand on the shopper's back guiding them down an aisle. Blockbusting is the voice telling the shop owner to close up before it's too late.
deeper.street: The same agent could do both in one week: tell an Okafor-style seller in Bed-Stuy to "get out now" (blockbusting), then tell a white buyer that Bed-Stuy "isn't for them" (steering).
deeper.stakes: Mixing up the labels doesn't matter in the field, since both are illegal. On the exam it costs you the question.
deeper.exam: Ask: who's being pushed? A buyer or renter means steering. An owner being urged to sell means blockbusting.

blocks.title: Three verbs
blocks.html: Steer the buyer. Bust the block. Red-pen the loan.
blocks.casual: Three verbs to remember: Steer the buyer. Bust the block. Red-pen the loan.

deeper.plain: Each violation has its own victim. Buyers get steered, blocks get busted, loans get redlined.
deeper.picture: A driver, a wrecking ball, and a red pen. Three tools, three different jobs.
deeper.street: Jordan whispers it before a practice exam: steer the buyer, bust the block, red-pen the loan. Three questions later, a stem about a bank and an avenue shows up, and Jordan writes "red pen" in the margin.
deeper.stakes: Quick labels let you name a problem in the field and stop it. If you can name it, you can explain to a client why you won't do it.
deeper.exam: Match the verb to the actor: agent with buyer, agent with owner, lender with loan. This handles most matching-style questions.

blocks.q: An investor sends postcards across a Queens neighborhood saying, "Families from the shelter on Linden Blvd are moving in. Sell to us now while you still can." This is:
c: Steering
Redlining
Blockbusting
Legal advertising
blocks.x: Inducing owners to sell by playing on fear of protected-class newcomers is blockbusting. Steering targets buyers, not owners.

blocks.title: Language access
blocks.html: Offering translated materials or an interpreter is good practice, and New York City requires many housing providers to make reasonable efforts to communicate across languages. What you may never do is treat someone differently because of national origin or the language they speak: refusing to show a unit, demanding extra paperwork, or steering based on accent or language is discrimination. Provide the same listings, the same terms and the same disclosures to everyone, in whatever language helps them understand.
blocks.casual: Language access: offering translated materials or an interpreter is good practice, and New York City requires many housing providers to make reasonable efforts to communicate across languages. What you can never do is treat someone differently because of national origin or the language they speak: refusing to show a unit, demanding extra paperwork, or steering based on accent or language is discrimination. Give everyone the same listings, terms, and disclosures, in whatever language helps them understand.

deeper.plain: Help people understand in their language, but never give them less because of it.
deeper.picture: Translation is adding subtitles. Discrimination is showing a different movie.
deeper.street: A Mandarin-speaking buyer in Flushing gets an interpreter for the showing and the same disclosure forms as everyone else. When Marcus wants to ask her for two extra bank statements "just in case," Diane shuts it down.
deeper.stakes: Extra paperwork for people with accents is a classic national origin violation. It shows up clearly in paired testing.
deeper.exam: Different treatment based on language or accent is national origin discrimination. Providing an interpreter is fine and not a violation.

blocks.html: Discriminatory advertising is illegal for everyone, including owners who are otherwise exempt. The rule: describe the property, not the people.
blocks.casual: Discriminatory advertising is illegal for everybody, even owners who are otherwise exempt. The rule: describe the property, not the people.

deeper.plain: Ads talk about the home. As soon as an ad talks about who should live there, it's in trouble.
deeper.picture: A good ad is a photo of the room. A bad ad is a photo of the people you want in the room.
deeper.street: The Okafors want their listing to say "great for a family." Jordan writes "four bedrooms, backyard, near Herbert Von King Park" instead. Families still find it, and no one is told they don't fit.
deeper.stakes: Ads are permanent evidence. A single phrase in a screenshot can support a complaint years later.
deeper.exam: Exempt owners still can't run discriminatory ads. If the question asks what an exempt owner can't do, the ad is the answer.

left.title: Fine
items: "3 bedrooms, 2 baths, near the G train"
"Walk-up, 4th floor"
"No smoking" or "no pets" (assistance animals still allowed)
"Quiet street, near Prospect Park"
"All vouchers and programs welcome"
"Senior housing" for a qualifying 55+ or 62+ community

right.title: Violations
items: "Perfect for a young couple" or "ideal for empty nesters"
"Not suitable for children" or "adults only"
"Must be employed" or "no programs"
"Christian home" or "exclusive community"
"Great for walkers" when meant to exclude disabled buyers
"English speakers only"

deeper.plain: Phrases that describe features are fine. Phrases that describe ideal residents or exclude groups are violations.
deeper.picture: Ask yourself whether the phrase is about bricks or about people. Bricks are safe; people are risky.
deeper.street: A Clinton Hill listing says "No smoking, no pets (assistance animals welcome), all vouchers welcome." Every phrase is about rules that apply to everyone or invites more applicants.
deeper.stakes: "Perfect for a young couple" or "ideal for empty nesters" seems friendly and violates familial status and age rules. HUD and the Commission cite exactly these phrases.
deeper.exam: "Senior housing" is legal only for a qualifying community. "No pets" is legal but must yield to assistance animals. "Exclusive" and "Christian home" are flags.

blocks.html: Social media counts as advertising. Your posts, reels, and boosted ads must carry the broker's name and follow the same rules as print. Targeting matters too: HUD charged Facebook in 2019 over tools that let housing advertisers exclude users by race, sex, or family status, and Meta settled with the Justice Department in 2022. Do not use ad targeting that excludes people by age, gender, zip code proxies, or interests that stand in for a protected class.
blocks.casual: Social media is advertising. Your posts, reels, and boosted ads need the broker's name and follow the same rules as print. Targeting counts too: HUD charged Facebook in 2019 over tools that let housing advertisers exclude users by race, sex, or family status, and Meta settled with the Justice Department in 2022. Don't use ad targeting that excludes people by age, gender, zip code proxies, or interests that stand in for a protected class.

deeper.plain: Online posts and paid ads follow the same fair housing and advertising rules. Who sees the ad matters, not just what it says.
deeper.picture: Slipping flyers only under certain doors is the old version of narrow ad targeting. The flyer can be clean and the delivery still discriminatory.
deeper.street: Jordan boosts an Instagram post for a Bushwick rental. The platform suggests targeting "ages 25 to 34, no parents." Jordan switches to a broad geographic audience instead.
deeper.stakes: Narrow targeting creates a record of exactly who you excluded. That's evidence for a complaint against you and the brokerage.
deeper.exam: Social media counts as advertising and needs the broker's name. Targeting by protected class, or proxies for it, can be discriminatory even with neutral ad text.

blocks.q: Which listing headline is compliant?
c: "Sunny 2BR, perfect for a professional couple"
"Sunny 2BR, steps to the Q train, all applicants welcome"
"Sunny 2BR in a mature, quiet building, no kids"
"Sunny 2BR, must show employment income"
blocks.x: It describes the property and invites everyone. "Professional couple" signals marital and familial preferences; "must show employment income" excludes lawful source of income.

blocks.title: Rewrite the ad
blocks.html:
Original: "Charming 1BR in a quiet adult building. Perfect for a mature professional. Must have W-2 income. No pets, no programs."
Problems: "adult building" and "mature" (familial status, age), "professional" and "W-2" (lawful source of income), "no programs" (source of income). "No pets" is legal but must yield to assistance animals.
Rewrite: "Charming 1BR, 2nd floor, south light, renovated kitchen, 4 blocks to the F. Heat and hot water included. No pets (assistance animals welcome). All applicants and programs welcome. Hudson & Hart Realty, (718) 555-0100."
blocks.casual:
Original: "Charming 1BR in a quiet adult building. Perfect for a mature professional. Must have W-2 income. No pets, no programs."
Problems: "adult building" and "mature" (familial status, age), "professional" and "W-2" (lawful source of income), "no programs" (source of income). "No pets" is legal but has to give way to assistance animals.
Rewrite: "Charming 1BR, 2nd floor, south light, renovated kitchen, 4 blocks to the F. Heat and hot water included. No pets (assistance animals welcome). All applicants and programs welcome. Hudson & Hart Realty, (718) 555-0100."

deeper.plain: Strip out every word about who should live there, keep the facts about the apartment, and add the broker's info.
deeper.picture: It's editing a dating profile into a real estate listing. Drop "looking for," keep "what I offer."
deeper.street: Sal wrote the original for a vacancy on Ditmars Boulevard. Jordan's rewrite gets 40 inquiries in three days, including two voucher holders and a family, and Sal rents to the first fully qualified applicant.
deeper.stakes: The original ad would expose Sal and the brokerage on three protected classes at once. Each phrase is a separate violation.
deeper.exam: Look for words that describe people: adult, mature, professional, W-2, programs. Each one maps to a class: familial status, age, or source of income.

blocks.html: Your personal social media counts when you are promoting listings or your business. A reel touring a Bushwick loft that says "this block is finally changing" is a steering and blockbusting problem, even if you meant the coffee shops. Keep captions about the property, the price, the light, the transit, and the amenities.
blocks.casual: Your personal social media counts when you're promoting listings or your business. A reel touring a Bushwick loft that says "this block is finally changing" is a steering and blockbusting problem, even if you just meant the coffee shops. Keep captions about the property, the price, the light, the transit, and the amenities.

deeper.plain: If your personal account promotes your work, your captions are ads. Words like "changing" can signal who's moving in or out.
deeper.picture: Your personal account is a store window the moment you put a listing in it. Everything in the window is advertising.
deeper.street: Marcus posts a TikTok of a Bed-Stuy brownstone: "This block's finally turning around." A fair housing group screenshots it as an example of coded marketing.
deeper.stakes: "I meant the coffee shops" doesn't erase how the words read. Coded captions can support both steering and blockbusting claims.
deeper.exam: Personal social media used for business is advertising. "Changing," "up and coming," or "finally" about residents is the coded language to flag.

blocks.html: Testers are people who pose as homebuyers or renters to check whether agents and landlords treat people equally. Paired testing sends two testers with matching finances who differ in one trait, such as race or a voucher. Testers are used by HUD, fair housing groups, the state Attorney General, and the NYC Commission. Testing is legal, and testers can sue even though they never meant to rent (the Supreme Court said so in Havens Realty v. Coleman, 1982). Assume every caller is a tester and you will never have a problem.
blocks.casual: Testers pose as homebuyers or renters to see whether agents and landlords treat people equally. Paired testing sends two testers with matching finances who differ in one trait, like race or a voucher. HUD, fair housing groups, the state Attorney General, and the NYC Commission all use them. It's legal, and testers can sue even though they never planned to rent (the Supreme Court said so in Havens Realty v. Coleman, 1982). Assume every caller is a tester and you'll never have a problem.

deeper.plain: Testers are undercover shoppers for fairness. If you treat everyone the same, they can't catch you doing anything.
deeper.picture: They're like secret shoppers at a restaurant, except they're checking whether you seated both tables the same.
deeper.street: Two testers call Jordan an hour apart about the same Astoria one-bedroom. Both get the same three available units, the same fee disclosure, and a showing that week. The test comes back clean.
deeper.stakes: Tester results are courtroom evidence, and testers have standing to sue. A pattern across several tests can lead to large settlements and monitoring.
deeper.exam: Testing is legal, not entrapment, and testers can sue (Havens Realty v. Coleman, 1982). A distractor will say testers need a real intent to buy or rent.

blocks.title: Newsday, 2019
blocks.html: A three-year Newsday investigation sent paired testers to Long Island agents and found unequal treatment of minority buyers in a large share of tests. It led to state legislative hearings, new DOS rules, and the standardized operating procedures you will learn next lesson.
blocks.casual: Newsday, 2019: a three-year Newsday investigation sent paired testers to Long Island agents and found unequal treatment of minority buyers in a large share of tests. It led to state legislative hearings, new DOS rules, and the standardized operating procedures you'll learn next lesson.

deeper.plain: A newspaper caught Long Island agents treating minority buyers worse, and New York changed its rules because of it.
deeper.picture: It's like a hidden camera on a whole industry. Once the tape aired, the rulebook got rewritten.
deeper.street: Testers with the same finances asked agents in Suffolk and Nassau about homes. Some white testers got more listings and some minority testers were asked for mortgage pre-approval before any showing. That difference is exactly what SOPs now target.
deeper.stakes: The fallout reached every licensee in New York: new CE requirements, SOPs, and stricter enforcement. One investigation reshaped the whole job.
deeper.exam: Connect Newsday 2019 to the reforms: SOPs for buyers, more fair housing training, and tougher DOS rules.

blocks.text: Cease and desist zones and nonsolicitation orders

blocks.html: Blockbusting thrived on aggressive solicitation. New York lets the Secretary of State fight it two ways under RPL 442-h.
blocks.casual: Blockbusting fed on aggressive solicitation. Under RPL 442-h, New York lets the Secretary of State fight it two ways.

deeper.plain: New York can stop agents from pestering homeowners in areas where blockbusting is a risk. There are two different tools for that.
deeper.picture: Think of a do-not-call list and a no-knocking ordinance. One protects people who sign up; the other protects a whole neighborhood.
deeper.street: Owners in East Flatbush were getting weekly calls and cards asking if they'd sell. DOS stepped in with a zone, and owners who joined the list got their phones back.
deeper.stakes: A farming campaign that ignores these rules can draw fines and suspension. The lists change, so you check before every campaign.
deeper.exam: Both tools come from RPL 442-h and are run by the Secretary of State (DOS). Know which is the opt-in list and which covers an entire area.

head: Cease and desist zone
Nonsolicitation order
rows: DOS finds owners in an area face repeated, intense solicitation
After a public hearing, DOS finds intense solicitation makes owners fear values will drop because of changing demographics
Only owners who sign up for the cease and desist list
Soliciting listed owners by phone, mail, door-knocking, email, text, or any direct means
Specified solicitation of listings in the whole area (letters, postcards, calls, door-to-door, handbills)
Reprimand, fine up to $2,000, suspension or revocation
DOS discipline, up to license revocation

deeper.plain: A cease and desist zone protects owners who sign up. A nonsolicitation order protects everyone in an area. Both last up to 5 years and can be renewed.
deeper.picture: The zone is a do-not-call list. The order is a whole-neighborhood "no solicitors" sign on every door.
deeper.street: An agent sends 2,000 postcards across the East Flatbush zone. Forty go to owners on the list. Each of those 40 is a violation, and the fine can be up to $2,000 per violation.
deeper.stakes: Penalties run from reprimand and fines up to license suspension or revocation. Mass mailings can stack up violations fast.
deeper.exam: Cease and desist: only listed owners, triggered by repeated intense solicitation. Nonsolicitation order: after a public hearing, covers every owner in the area.

blocks.title: Where they apply
blocks.html: Cease and desist zones have covered parts of Queens, the Bronx, and Rockland County in the past. As of October 2026 the only active zone is part of Brooklyn Community Board 17 (East Flatbush), adopted in 2023. Before any farming campaign, check the DOS website for the current zones and lists, which are updated regularly. One postcard to a listed owner is a violation.
blocks.casual: Where they apply: cease and desist zones have covered parts of Queens, the Bronx, and Rockland County in the past. As of October 2026 the only active zone is part of Brooklyn Community Board 17 (East Flatbush), adopted in 2023. Before any farming campaign, check the DOS website for the current zones and lists, which get updated regularly. One postcard to a listed owner is a violation.

deeper.plain: Zones exist in specific parts of New York and change over time. Check the current list before you mail or call anyone.
deeper.picture: It's like checking the parking signs every time you park. The rules on the block can change between visits.
deeper.street: Jordan plans a "thinking of selling?" mailer to 500 homes in the Bronx. Before printing, Jordan downloads the DOS list and removes every listed owner's address.
deeper.stakes: One postcard is enough for a violation. A firm doing big mailers without checking can rack up many at once.
deeper.exam: Exam focus is the mechanics, not the map: opt-in list, any direct solicitation banned, up to 5 years, DOS discipline.

blocks.q: Jordan mails "Thinking of selling?" postcards to every homeowner in a zip code inside a cease and desist zone. Who can Jordan legally keep mailing?
c: No one in the zone
Only owners who are not on the cease and desist list
Everyone, because postcards are not solicitation
Only owners who have listed before
blocks.x: A cease and desist zone protects owners who registered on the list. Soliciting them by any direct means is barred. A nonsolicitation order, by contrast, covers every owner in the area.

blocks.title: Don't mix them up
blocks.html: Cease and desist = opt-in list. Nonsolicitation order = the whole area. Both last at most 5 years at a time.
blocks.casual: Don't mix them up. Cease and desist = opt-in list. Nonsolicitation order = the whole area. Both last at most 5 years at a time.

deeper.plain: List means only signed-up owners are protected. Area means everyone in the zone is protected.
deeper.picture: A list is a guest list at a door. An area is a fence around the whole block.
deeper.street: In a nonsolicitation area, Jordan can't door-knock on any house, signed up or not. In a cease and desist zone, Jordan can door-knock on owners who aren't on the list, but never on the ones who are.
deeper.stakes: Treating a nonsolicitation area like a list zone means soliciting owners who were all protected. That's a pile of violations at once.
deeper.exam: "Owners who requested" or "signed up" means cease and desist. "All owners in the area after a public hearing" means nonsolicitation order.

story.title: Who Lives There
story.setting: Jordan's Corolla, stuck on Flatbush Avenue

beats.text: Okay, real question. Is Crown Heights safe? And who lives there? Like, would I fit in?
Two questions I can't answer with an opinion, Leo. But I can get you real data.
You know the area. Just tell me.
If I start describing who lives where, I'm steering you. NYPD posts precinct crime stats publicly. Census data is public too. I'll send both links.
That's... actually more useful. I'll make a spreadsheet.
Of course you will. Tell me what you need: commute, budget, outdoor space. I'll show you everything that fits, in every neighborhood.
beats.tag: Show everything in the price range

beats.text: Back at the office, Marcus is printing postcards.
"The neighborhood is changing. Sell before it's too late." Gets the phone ringing every time.
Changing how, Marcus?
You know. Changing.
That's blockbusting. Panic the owner, list cheap. And half that zip code is in a cease and desist zone.

check.q: What is the difference between steering and blockbusting?
c: Steering targets owners; blockbusting targets buyers
Steering targets buyers and renters; blockbusting panics owners into selling
Both target lenders
Only blockbusting is illegal
check.x: Steering channels buyers toward or away from areas. Blockbusting induces owners to sell through fear of protected-class newcomers.

beats.text: The list thing? I thought that expired.
Zones run up to five years and get renewed. Check DOS before you mail. One postcard to a listed owner and you're explaining yourself in a hearing.
beats.tag: Cease and desist list: check before mailing

beats.text: And if someone calls asking all the wrong questions?
Treat every caller like a tester. Some of them are. Same answers, same listings, same follow-up for everyone.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: left side, five phrases you will never put in an ad; right side, a compliant rewrite of each that describes the property instead.

facts.text: When a seller or landlord asks for a 'type' of buyer or tenant, market to everyone and present every qualified offer; if the client insists, decline the listing and tell your broker.
A buyer may set criteria (such as near a chosen synagogue) and choose from every fitting listing; the agent may not filter areas by who lives there.
Unequal treatment means different terms, deposits, speed or effort by protected class; charging everyone the same fee is fine.
Falsely saying a unit is taken, pricier or harder to get is illegal misinformation.
Steering is guiding buyers or renters toward or away from areas by protected class, including when the client asks you to.
Asked 'is it safe?' or 'who lives there?', give no opinion and describe no residents; point to public crime and census data.
Blockbusting (panic peddling) induces owners to sell by stirring fear that a protected class is moving in.
Redlining is a lender or insurer refusing or limiting loans or coverage in an area because of who lives there; objective reasons like credit are fine.
Offering translations is good practice, but treating people differently by language or accent is national origin discrimination.
Discriminatory ads are illegal for everyone, even otherwise exempt owners: describe the property, not the people.
'Adults only,' 'perfect for young professionals,' 'must be employed' and 'no programs' are violations; 'no pets' is fine but yields to assistance animals.
Ad targeting that excludes people by age, sex, family status or proxies for them is discriminatory advertising (HUD charged Facebook in 2019).
Social media is advertising: posts carry the broker's name, and a personal post promoting a listing must describe the property, not a block that is 'changing'.
Testers pose as homeseekers to check for equal treatment, often in matched pairs that differ in one trait; testing is legal.
Testers can sue even though they never meant to rent (Havens Realty v. Coleman, 1982).
Newsday's 2019 Long Island testing found unequal treatment of minority buyers and led to new DOS rules and standardized operating procedures.
A cease and desist zone (RPL 442-h) protects only owners who sign up for the list; soliciting them by any direct means is banned.
A nonsolicitation order covers every owner in the area, unlike the opt-in cease and desist list.
Cease and desist zones and nonsolicitation orders last at most 5 years and can be readopted.
Soliciting a listed owner brings a reprimand, a fine up to $2,000, suspension or revocation; one postcard is enough.
As of October 2026 the only active cease and desist zone is part of Brooklyn CB 17 (East Flatbush); check the DOS website before any farming campaign.

lessons.title: The Fair Housing Agent: Duties, Bias, Records, and Consequences
lessons.tagline: Good intentions do not protect you. Forms, scripts, standard procedures, and records do.
objectives: List what a broker must do (policy, posters, training, ad review, reporting, records) and what each salesperson must do
Deliver the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form at the right moment for any property type
Explain standardized operating procedures under RPL 442-h and why they exist
Describe implicit bias and practical anti-bias habits
Name the agencies, deadlines, and penalties for a fair housing violation

blocks.title: Monday sales meeting, Hudson & Hart
blocks.html: A fair housing group's tester filed a complaint against a Queens brokerage. The tester, who used a Section 8 voucher, says she was asked for pre-approval and ID before a showing. Her paired tester, who had no voucher, was shown three apartments on the spot. The brokerage's owner says the agent "was just being careful." Diane wants to know: what would have protected that agent, and that broker?
blocks.casual: A fair housing group's tester filed a complaint against a Queens brokerage. She used a Section 8 voucher, and says she got asked for pre-approval and ID before any showing. Her paired tester, no voucher, got shown three apartments on the spot. The brokerage owner says the agent "was just being careful." Diane wants to know: what would've protected that agent, and that broker?

deeper.plain: Two people with the same finances got different treatment, and the only difference was a voucher. The question is what systems would have prevented it.
deeper.picture: It's like a club checking IDs for only some people in line. "Being careful" with half the line is just being selective.
deeper.street: The voucher tester waited four days for a reply and was asked for a pre-approval letter. The other tester, calling the same morning, saw three units in Jackson Heights that afternoon. The log of those two calls is the whole case.
deeper.stakes: "Careful" with one group is discrimination if it isn't applied to everyone. The agent, the broker, and the owner can all end up in the complaint.
deeper.exam: Different requirements for different applicants is the core violation. Correct answers involve uniform procedures applied to every client.

items: Keep a written fair housing policy and enforce it.
Post the signs. The HUD Equal Housing Opportunity poster and New York's Fair Housing Notice must be displayed in every office, at open houses, and on the brokerage website.
Review advertising, including agents' social media, for compliance.
Train continuously. Every renewal includes 3 hours of fair housing, 2 of implicit bias, and 2 of cultural competency, and good brokers train more often.
Report and fix violations. A broker who ignores an agent's discrimination is liable too.
Keep the records and give agents the forms and systems to do the same.
Adopt and post standardized operating procedures for homebuyers (below).
blocks.casual:
The broker's to-do list:
Keep a written fair housing policy and actually enforce it.
Post the signs. The HUD Equal Housing Opportunity poster and New York's Fair Housing Notice go up in every office, at open houses, and on the brokerage website.
Review advertising, agents' social media included.
Train constantly. Every renewal includes 3 hours of fair housing, 2 of implicit bias, and 2 of cultural competency, and good brokers train more than that.
Report and fix violations. A broker who ignores an agent's discrimination is liable too.
Keep the records and give agents the forms and systems to do the same.
Adopt and post standardized operating procedures for homebuyers (below).

deeper.plain: The broker sets the rules, posts the notices, trains people, checks ads, keeps records, and steps in when someone breaks the rules.
deeper.picture: The broker is the restaurant owner who's responsible for the health inspection, not just the cook who dropped the fork.
deeper.street: Diane spends one Monday a month reviewing every agent's listing posts. She catches Marcus's caption "perfect for a young couple" and has it pulled within an hour.
deeper.stakes: Brokers are liable for failing to supervise. A missing poster or an unchecked agent ad can turn one agent's slip into the firm's problem.
deeper.exam: Posters required in offices, at open houses, and on websites. CE breakdown: 3 hours fair housing, 2 implicit bias, 2 cultural competency per renewal.

blocks.html: Records are the broker's best defense. Brokers must keep transaction records and disclosure forms for 3 years. For fair housing, the smart log goes further: every inquiry, the date and time received, the time answered, the listings sent, the requirements requested, and the outcome. If a tester alleges unequal treatment, a clean log showing identical treatment usually ends the case.
blocks.casual: Records are the broker's best defense. Brokers have to keep transaction records and disclosure forms for 3 years. For fair housing, the smart log goes further: every inquiry, when it came in, when you answered, the listings you sent, what you asked for, and how it ended. If a tester claims unequal treatment, a clean log showing identical treatment usually ends the case.

deeper.plain: Write down every inquiry and what you did with it. If someone accuses you, the record shows you treated everyone the same.
deeper.picture: It's your dashcam. You hope you never need it, and when you do, it settles the argument.
deeper.street: A tester claims Jordan ignored her call about an Astoria rental. Jordan's log shows the call at 10:14, a reply at 10:40, the same five listings sent to everyone that day. DHR closes the case.
deeper.stakes: Without records it's your word against a trained tester's notes. Testers always keep notes.
deeper.exam: Keep records 3 years. A question about the best defense to a tester complaint points to consistent documentation.

blocks.html: Reporting. If you see a colleague steer a client or follow a no-vouchers instruction, report it to your supervising broker immediately. A broker who learns of a violation and does nothing shares the liability. Consumers can be pointed to HUD, the Division of Human Rights, the NYC Commission, or DOS.
blocks.casual: Reporting. If you see a colleague steer a client or follow a no-vouchers instruction, tell your supervising broker right away. A broker who learns about a violation and does nothing shares the liability. Consumers can be pointed to HUD, the Division of Human Rights, the NYC Commission, or DOS.

deeper.plain: Report problems to your broker immediately. Consumers have four places they can complain.
deeper.picture: It's like seeing a coworker leave the gas on. You don't wait to see if the kitchen catches fire.
deeper.street: Jordan overhears Marcus telling a landlord "don't worry, I'll weed out the programs." Jordan tells Diane that afternoon. Diane pulls Marcus off the listing and documents it.
deeper.stakes: Staying quiet makes you part of the cover-up. A broker who knew and did nothing faces the same claims as the agent.
deeper.exam: Complaint venues: HUD (federal), DHR (state), NYC Commission (city), DOS (license discipline). Know which handles license penalties: DOS.

items: Know federal, state, and local fair housing law.
Give the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form at first substantive contact.
For rentals, give the Reasonable Accommodation and Reasonable Modification notice.
Act in accordance with the law even when a client asks you not to.
Keep every ad and post compliant.
