Keep excellent records: who you spoke to, when, what you showed, and why.
Attend fair housing training and seminars.
blocks.casual: Your job as a salesperson: know federal, state, and local fair housing law. Hand over the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form at first substantive contact. For rentals, give the Reasonable Accommodation and Reasonable Modification notice. Follow the law even when a client asks you not to. Keep every ad and post compliant. Keep excellent records: who you talked to, when, what you showed, and why. And go to fair housing training and seminars.

deeper.plain: Know the rules, hand out the two forms, keep ads clean, write everything down, and keep learning.
deeper.picture: It's a pilot's preflight checklist. Same steps every flight, even when the passenger is in a hurry.
deeper.street: Jordan's first call with a new renter goes like this: agency disclosure, anti-discrimination form, accommodation notice, then a log entry. It takes three minutes and it's the same for every caller.
deeper.stakes: Skipping a form is a violation on its own, even if nothing else went wrong. A client's pressure doesn't shift the duty off you.
deeper.exam: Two forms for rentals at first contact: the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure and the Reasonable Accommodation notice. Client instructions never override the law.

blocks.text: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form

blocks.html: Since June 20, 2020, the New York State Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (19 NYCRR 175.28) must be given at first substantive contact to prospective buyers, sellers, landlords, and tenants. It explains the protected classes and how to file a complaint. Unlike the agency disclosure form, it covers every property type: houses, co-ops, condos, rentals, commercial space, and vacant land. Keep it 3 years.
blocks.casual: Since June 20, 2020, the New York State Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (19 NYCRR 175.28) has to go out at first substantive contact to prospective buyers, sellers, landlords, and tenants. It explains the protected classes and how to file a complaint. Unlike the agency disclosure form, it covers every property type: houses, co-ops, condos, rentals, commercial space, and vacant land. Keep it 3 years.

deeper.plain: Every client, every property type, gets this fair housing form at the first real conversation. Keep a copy for 3 years.
deeper.picture: It's like the safety card in the seat pocket. Every flight, every passenger, no matter where they're headed.
deeper.street: Evelyn Park calls about leasing a retail space on Atlantic Avenue. She gets the anti-discrimination form, even though it's commercial and the agency disclosure form doesn't apply.
deeper.stakes: Agents who think the form is only for residential skip it on commercial and land deals. That's a missed disclosure DOS can cite.
deeper.exam: The contrast: agency disclosure is residential 1 to 4 family; anti-discrimination form is every property type. Both at first substantive contact, both kept 3 years.

blocks.caption: Find the moment of first substantive contact. The agency disclosure and the anti-discrimination form land at the same point; the reasonable accommodation notice joins them for rentals.

left.title: Agency disclosure (RPL 443)
items: Residential 1 to 4 family, condos, co-ops, rentals
Explains who the agent represents
Keep 3 years

right.title: Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure
items: Every property type, including commercial and vacant land
Explains fair housing rights and where to complain
Keep 3 years

deeper.plain: Two forms land at the same time. One explains who you represent; the other explains fair housing rights.
deeper.picture: One is a name tag saying whose side you're on. The other is a sign on the wall saying everyone gets treated fairly.
deeper.street: Leo meets Jordan at an open house in Prospect Lefferts Gardens. Jordan hands him both forms on a clipboard before talking price. Leo signs the agency one and keeps a copy of the other.
deeper.stakes: Missing either form at first substantive contact is a separate violation. Commercial and land deals still need the anti-discrimination form.
deeper.exam: Which form covers vacant land? The anti-discrimination disclosure. Which explains representation? The RPL 443 agency disclosure.

blocks.q: Jordan is showing a vacant lot in Staten Island to a builder and the conversation turns to price and financing. Which form must Jordan give?
c: Agency disclosure only
Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form only
Both forms
Neither, because vacant land is exempt
blocks.x: The anti-discrimination form covers every property type, including vacant land. The RPL 443 agency disclosure covers only residential 1 to 4 family deals, so it is not required for a vacant lot.

blocks.html: The Newsday testing found agents demanding pre-approval or ID from some buyers and not others. New York's answer was standardized operating procedures. Every broker must decide, in writing, what it requires from every prospective homebuyer before providing services, and apply it the same way to everyone.
blocks.casual: Newsday's testing caught agents demanding pre-approval or ID from some buyers and not others. New York's response was standardized operating procedures. Every broker has to decide, in writing, what it requires from every prospective homebuyer before providing services, and apply it the same way to everyone.

deeper.plain: The brokerage writes down what it asks of every buyer and sticks to it for everybody.
deeper.picture: Like a doctor's office intake form: same clipboard for every patient, no extra questions for some.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart's SOP says: ID required, exclusive buyer agreement required before touring, pre-approval not required. Every buyer who walks in hears those exact three answers.
deeper.stakes: Asking only some buyers for pre-approval is how the Newsday agents got caught. SOPs make the rule visible, so breaking it is easy to prove.
deeper.exam: SOPs cover prospective homebuyers. The three questions: ID, exclusive buyer agency agreement, mortgage pre-approval.

blocks.title: The SOP rules

items.title: Answer the three questions
items.html: Do you require identification? An exclusive buyer agency agreement? Mortgage pre-approval? Yes or no, for everyone.

items.title: Date stamp and notarize
items.html: The written procedures are dated and notarized.

items.title: Post them
items.html: On the brokerage website and app; teams and agents with their own sites post or link to them. Keep a copy available at the office.

items.title: Update within 30 days
items.html: Any change gets posted within 30 days, and old versions are kept.

items.title: Follow them every time
items.html: Breaking your own SOP for one buyer is exactly what testers look for. The broker affirms compliance at license renewal.

blocks.casual:
Here's how the SOP rules work:
Answer the three questions. Do you require ID? An exclusive buyer agency agreement? Mortgage pre-approval? Yes or no, for everyone.
Date stamp and notarize. The written procedures are dated and notarized.
Post them. On the brokerage website and app; teams and agents with their own sites post or link to them. Keep a copy at the office.
Update within 30 days. Any change gets posted within 30 days, and old versions are kept.
Follow them every time. Breaking your own SOP for one buyer is exactly what testers look for. The broker affirms compliance at license renewal.

deeper.plain: Decide three yes-or-no rules, put them in a dated and notarized document, post it, update it fast, and follow it for every buyer.
deeper.picture: It's a posted house rule at a pool: written, dated, visible, and enforced on everyone.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart drops the pre-approval requirement on March 1. The updated SOP goes up on the website March 10, inside the 30-day window, and the old version is saved in the file.
deeper.stakes: An SOP you don't follow is worse than none, because it documents the rule you broke. Brokers also certify compliance at renewal.
deeper.exam: Key numbers: notarized, date-stamped, posted online, updated within 30 days. Watch for a distractor saying SOPs must be filed with DOS.

blocks.title: Filing is gone
blocks.html: The original 2021 law required brokers to file SOPs with DOS. A 2022 amendment removed the filing requirement. Brokers must still adopt, notarize, post, and follow them.
blocks.casual: Trap: filing is gone. The original 2021 law made brokers file SOPs with DOS. A 2022 amendment dropped the filing requirement. Brokers still have to adopt, notarize, post, and follow them.

deeper.plain: You don't send your SOPs to the state anymore. You still have to have them, post them, and follow them.
deeper.picture: Like a restaurant that no longer mails its menu to the city but still has to post prices on the door.
deeper.street: Diane's old checklist from 2021 still says "file SOP with DOS." She crosses it out and adds "check website posting monthly."
deeper.stakes: Older study materials still teach filing. Knowing the change keeps you from wasting time and from giving wrong answers.
deeper.exam: If an answer choice says brokers must file SOPs with DOS, it's the outdated rule. Adopt, notarize, post, and follow is current.

blocks.q: A brokerage's posted SOP says pre-approval is not required to see homes. An agent asks one buyer, who mentioned she uses a voucher, for a pre-approval letter before showing. What is wrong?
c: Nothing, agents may add requirements for individual buyers
The agent applied a requirement unequally, which violates the SOP and likely fair housing law
SOPs only apply to rentals
Pre-approval can never be required
blocks.x: SOPs exist so every buyer gets the same requirements. Asking only some buyers is unequal treatment, and here it tracks lawful source of income.

blocks.html: Implicit bias is an attitude or stereotype that affects understanding, actions, and decisions unconsciously. You do not have to believe something to act on it. An agent who calls back "Emily" before "Lakisha," guesses a budget from someone's clothes, or describes the same block as "up and coming" to one buyer and "rough" to another may never notice. Anti-bias training teaches you to see these patterns and replace them with systems.
blocks.casual: Implicit bias is an attitude or stereotype that shapes how you understand things, act, and decide, without you noticing. You don't have to believe something to act on it. An agent who calls back "Emily" before "Lakisha," guesses a budget from someone's clothes, or calls the same block "up and coming" to one buyer and "rough" to another might never notice. Anti-bias training teaches you to spot those patterns and swap them for systems.

deeper.plain: Everyone has hidden assumptions that sneak into decisions. Systems catch what good intentions miss.
deeper.picture: It's like a car that pulls slightly to one side. You don't feel it until you take your hands off the wheel, so you get an alignment.
deeper.street: Jordan reviews a week of callbacks and notices the inquiries with "easy" names got answered first. Jordan switches to answering strictly in the order received.
deeper.stakes: Bias that shows up in callback speed or listing counts is what testers measure. Intent doesn't matter if the treatment differs.
deeper.exam: Implicit bias is unconscious. The fix the exam favors is a uniform system, not "trying harder" or "being more careful."

head: Habit
Why it works
rows: Use the same script for every inquiry
Same questions, same information, same listings
Respond in order received, with the same speed
Callback time is one of the first things testers measure
Show every listing that fits stated criteria
Removes your judgment from where a client should live
Your record proves equal treatment if you are accused
Keeps steering out of your vocabulary
Ask: would I say or do this for any other client?

deeper.plain: Each habit replaces a judgment call with a routine, so you treat everyone the same without thinking about it.
deeper.picture: It's a recipe. If you follow it every time, the dish tastes the same no matter who ordered it.
deeper.street: Jordan's inquiry script has six questions: budget, size, area, timing, financing status, must-haves. Every caller gets all six, and every match gets sent the same day.
deeper.stakes: Callback speed and listing counts are the first things testers compare. Habits are the cheapest insurance an agent can buy.
deeper.exam: The best practice answer usually involves consistency: same script, same order, same information, documented.

head: Where
Deadline
What can happen
rows: 1 year to file with HUD; 2 years to sue in federal court

Investigation, conciliation, administrative law judge, civil penalties adjusted for inflation (tens of thousands for a first violation, much more for repeat); in court, actual and punitive damages. DOJ handles pattern or practice cases.
NYS Division of Human Rights
3 years for acts on or after Feb 15, 2024 (was 1 year); or sue in state court within 3 years, but not both
Compensatory damages including emotional distress, punitive damages in housing cases, attorney's fees, civil fines up to $50,000, or $100,000 if willful, wanton, or malicious
Damages, civil penalties, training orders, changes to policy
Any time a violation comes to light
Discipline of the license under RPL 441-c: reprimand, fines, suspension, revocation

deeper.plain: There are four places a complaint can go, each with its own deadline and penalties. DOS is the one that can take your license.
deeper.picture: Think of four referees on one field: federal, state, city, and the licensing ref who can bench you.
deeper.street: A renter refused in Sunnyside in May 2025 can file with HUD until May 2026, with the NYC Commission until May 2026, and with DHR until May 2028. DOS can act on the agent's license whenever it learns about it.
deeper.stakes: State fines can hit $100,000 for willful discrimination, plus damages and fees. DOS can suspend or revoke, which ends a career.
deeper.exam: HUD: 1 year administrative, 2 years federal court. DHR: 3 years for acts on or after Feb 15, 2024 (was 1 year). NYC Commission: 1 year.

blocks.html: Liability flows up and down. The agent who discriminated is liable. The broker is liable for the agent's acts and for failing to supervise. The owner who gave the instruction is liable too. "My client told me to" is never a defense. Discrimination also includes disparate impact: a neutral-sounding policy, such as a blanket ban on anyone with any criminal record, can be illegal if it falls much harder on a protected class without a legitimate justification.
blocks.casual: Liability runs up and down. The agent who discriminated is liable. The broker's liable for the agent's acts and for failing to supervise. The owner who gave the instruction is liable too. "My client told me to" is never a defense. Discrimination also includes disparate impact: a neutral-sounding policy, like a blanket ban on anyone with any criminal record, can be illegal if it hits a protected class much harder without a legitimate justification.

deeper.plain: Everyone involved can be held responsible. A rule can be illegal even if it never mentions a protected class, if it hurts one group far more for no good reason.
deeper.picture: A "no strollers" sign doesn't say "no parents," but you know who it keeps out. That's disparate impact.
deeper.street: A Harlem landlord rejects anyone with any criminal record, even a 20-year-old misdemeanor. Because that falls much harder on some racial groups and has no tailored justification, it's challenged as disparate impact.
deeper.stakes: You can't hide behind a client's instruction or a neutral-sounding rule. Agent, broker, and owner can each pay.
deeper.exam: Disparate impact = neutral policy, unequal effect, no legitimate justification. Disparate treatment = treating someone differently on purpose. Know both terms.

blocks.title: Election of remedies
blocks.html: Under the NYS Human Rights Law you generally choose: file with the Division of Human Rights or go to state court. You may also file with HUD, and the agencies share complaints.
blocks.casual: Election of remedies: under the NYS Human Rights Law you generally pick one. File with the Division of Human Rights or go to state court. You can also file with HUD, and the agencies share complaints.

deeper.plain: In New York you usually choose either the state agency or state court, not both. HUD is a separate option that can run alongside.
deeper.picture: It's like choosing between two doors to the same room. Once you walk through one, the other locks behind you.
deeper.street: A tenant refused in Yonkers files with DHR. Six months later she wants to sue in state court instead. Because she elected DHR, she generally can't start over in court.
deeper.stakes: Advising a consumer to file in both places can backfire. Point them to the options and let a lawyer guide the choice.
deeper.exam: "Election of remedies" means DHR or state court, not both. HUD filings can be shared with DHR under work-sharing.

blocks.title: A complaint, start to finish
blocks.html:
March 3, 2025: A tester using a voucher is told a Flatbush apartment is "rented." Her paired tester is offered a showing the same day.
Filing: The fair housing group files with the NYS Division of Human Rights in January 2026, within the 3-year window. It could also have filed with HUD within 1 year (by March 3, 2026) or with the NYC Commission within 1 year.
Investigation: DHR finds probable cause and holds a hearing.
Result: damages for the tester's group, a civil fine against the landlord and brokerage, mandated training, and a referral to DOS, which opens a disciplinary case against the agent's license.
Lesson: one false "it's rented" can produce three separate proceedings.
blocks.casual:
March 3, 2025: A tester using a voucher hears a Flatbush apartment is "rented." Her paired tester gets offered a showing the same day.
Filing: The fair housing group files with the NYS Division of Human Rights in January 2026, inside the 3-year window. It could also have gone to HUD within 1 year (by March 3, 2026) or the NYC Commission within 1 year.
Investigation: DHR finds probable cause and holds a hearing.
Result: damages for the tester's group, a civil fine against the landlord and brokerage, required training, and a referral to DOS, which opens a disciplinary case on the agent's license.
Lesson: one false "it's rented" can produce three separate proceedings.

deeper.plain: One lie to a tester led to a state case, fines, training, and a license investigation.
deeper.picture: It's a single domino tipping three lines of dominoes at once.
deeper.street: The agent thought the voucher holder "would never get approved anyway." That one-line excuse cost the brokerage a fine, a year of monitoring, and a DOS hearing for the agent.
deeper.stakes: Agents underestimate how many doors a complaint can open. Damages, fines, and license discipline can all hit from one call.
deeper.exam: Count deadlines from the date of the act. DHR now 3 years for acts on or after Feb 15, 2024; HUD and the NYC Commission 1 year.

blocks.q: A complainant was denied an apartment because of her immigration status in March 2025. Under current law, how long does she have to file with the NYS Division of Human Rights?
c: 180 days
1 year
2 years
3 years
blocks.x: For conduct on or after February 15, 2024, the DHR filing deadline is 3 years. The old 1 year deadline still applies to earlier conduct.

blocks.html: The emotional results are real and courts award damages for them: humiliation, anxiety, a family stuck in a shelter longer, kids pulled from a school, a lost chance to build equity. When you treat fair housing as paperwork, remember the person on the other end of the call. That is the point of every form in this lesson.
blocks.casual: The emotional damage is real, and courts award money for it: humiliation, anxiety, a family stuck in a shelter longer, kids pulled from a school, a lost chance to build equity. When fair housing starts to feel like paperwork, remember the person on the other end of the call. That's the point of every form in this lesson.

deeper.plain: Discrimination hurts real people in lasting ways, and courts recognize that with money damages.
deeper.picture: A "no" at the door can echo for years, like a crack in a foundation that keeps spreading.
deeper.street: A mother with a CityFHEPS voucher spends four extra months in a Bronx shelter after being told three apartments were "taken." Her kids switch schools twice. A hearing officer awards her emotional distress damages.
deeper.stakes: Emotional distress damages can exceed the actual financial loss. And the harm to the family doesn't go away when the case closes.
deeper.exam: Compensatory damages include emotional distress. Punitive damages are available in housing cases under the NYS Human Rights Law.

blocks.title: The protective trio
blocks.html: Same script. Same procedure. Same record. If every client gets all three, testers find nothing.
blocks.casual: The protective trio: Same script. Same procedure. Same record. If every client gets all three, testers find nothing.

deeper.plain: Treat every client identically and write it down. That's the whole defense.
deeper.picture: Three legs of a stool. Take one away and you tip over.
deeper.street: Diane closes the Monday meeting: "Same script, same SOP, same log. Do that and I don't care how many testers call." Jordan writes it on the whiteboard.
deeper.stakes: Missing any one leg leaves a gap testers can find. All three together almost always end a complaint early.
deeper.exam: When asked how to avoid fair housing complaints, choose the answer about consistent procedures and documentation over vague "good intentions."

story.title: The Tester's Report
story.setting: Hudson & Hart conference room, Monday 9 am

beats.text: Pop quiz. A tester with a voucher gets asked for pre-approval. Her twin without a voucher sees three apartments. What went wrong?
Different requirements for different people. Unequal treatment. Source of income.
And what would have saved the agent?
The SOP. Post one rule for everybody and follow it.
Ours says: ID yes, exclusive agreement no, pre-approval no. Notarized, dated, on the website. Every buyer.
I don't need a form to tell me who's serious.
That's implicit bias wearing a suit, Marcus. You think you're reading seriousness. Testers measure who gets called back first.
What about the fair housing form? I give it to renters. Do I give it to Evelyn on her retail deal?
Every property type. Commercial, vacant land, everything. At first substantive contact, keep it three years.

check.q: Which deal does NOT require the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form?
c: A retail lease
A vacant lot sale
A co-op sale
None; it applies to every property type
check.x: The form applies to all property types at first substantive contact.

beats.text: And if someone files a complaint, what, a slap on the wrist?
Federal penalties in the tens of thousands. State fines up to fifty, a hundred if willful. Emotional distress damages. Then DOS looks at your license.
And the broker?
Is on the hook for not supervising you. Which is why we're having this meeting.
So: same script, same procedure, same record.
Write that on your hand, Jordan. Marcus, write it on both.

board.prompt: Draft your own one-line answers to the three SOP questions (ID? exclusive agreement? pre-approval?) and a two-sentence script you will use on every first call.

facts.text: Brokers keep a written fair housing policy, display the HUD Equal Housing Opportunity poster and NY Fair Housing Notice (office, open houses, website), review ads and train agents.
Each license renewal includes 3 hours of fair housing, 2 of implicit bias and 2 of cultural competency.
Brokers keep transaction records and disclosure forms 3 years; a log of every inquiry, response time and listing sent is the best defense against a tester complaint.
Report a colleague's discrimination to the supervising broker; a broker who learns of a violation and does nothing shares the liability.
For rentals, licensees also give the Reasonable Accommodation and Reasonable Modification notice.
The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (since June 20, 2020) goes to buyers, sellers, landlords and tenants at first substantive contact.
Unlike the agency disclosure (residential 1 to 4 family), the anti-discrimination form covers every property type, including commercial and vacant land.
Keep a copy of the anti-discrimination form for 3 years.
Under RPL 442-h each broker's standardized operating procedures state whether it requires ID, an exclusive buyer agreement and mortgage pre-approval from every prospective homebuyer.
SOPs are dated, notarized, posted on the website and followed for every buyer; the original requirement to file them with DOS was removed in 2022.
SOP changes are posted within 30 days and old versions are kept; the broker affirms compliance at renewal.
Implicit bias is an unconscious attitude or stereotype that shapes decisions; anti-bias training teaches you to spot it and replace it with systems.
Same script, same response speed, same listings and same records for every inquiry protect an agent from tester complaints.
HUD complaints are filed within 1 year of the act; a federal court suit within 2 years.
DHR complaints are filed within 3 years for acts on or after February 15, 2024 (it was 1 year).
DHR civil fines reach $50,000, or $100,000 if the act was willful, wanton or malicious.
The NYC Commission on Human Rights takes complaints within 1 year (3 years for gender-based harassment) and can order damages, penalties and training.
DOS can discipline the license under RPL 441-c whenever a violation comes to light.
The agent, the broker and the instructing owner are all liable; 'my client told me to' is no defense.
Disparate impact: a neutral policy, such as a blanket criminal record ban, can be illegal if it falls much harder on a protected class without justification.
Under the NYS Human Rights Law you generally choose DHR or state court, not both, and may also file with HUD.
Courts award damages for emotional harm such as humiliation and anxiety, and one discriminatory act can bring several separate proceedings.

lessons.title: Case file: Three Owners Who Were Sure They Were Exempt
lessons.tagline: A Ridgewood two-family, a New Rochelle rental and a Suffolk 55-plus community. Every owner says exempt. Each is partly wrong.
objectives: Decide whether a federal, New York State or New York City exemption applies to a given owner, building and protected class.
Apply the rule that exemptions never cover race, discriminatory advertising or a licensee acting for the owner.
Calculate the 80% occupancy test for housing for older persons and decide which classes that exemption does and does not reach.

blocks.title: Hudson & Hart, a Monday with three exemptions
blocks.html: Jordan's voicemail has three messages before 10 a.m., and every caller opens with the same sentence: "I looked it up, I'm exempt." Teresa Mendez owns a two-family house on Woodbine Street in Ridgewood, Queens, lives downstairs with her mother, and wants Jordan to list the upstairs unit. Glen Whitaker owns two single-family houses in Westchester and is renting one in New Rochelle himself. Sheila Grant manages Peconic Pines, a 55-and-over community in Suffolk County, and has two buyers she would like to turn away. Diane tells Jordan to take all three calls. "Exemptions are real," she says, "but they are narrow, they are different at every level of government, and they almost never cover us." Start with Teresa, who wants the listing up on StreetEasy by Friday.

blocks.text: Owner one: the two-family on Woodbine Street

blocks.html: Teresa's list of wants is short. Her mother naps every afternoon, so she would prefer "no small children." She wants "someone settled, maybe a churchgoer." And she wants Jordan to handle the showings because she works days. Rent is $2,650 for a two-bedroom with a renovated bath. Teresa has read online that owner-occupied two-family houses are exempt from New York's housing discrimination rules, and she is partly right.

blocks.title: What each layer actually says about Teresa's house
blocks.html:
Federal Fair Housing Act: the Mrs. Murphy exemption covers rooms or units in a building with living quarters for no more than four families if the owner lives in one of them. The ad ban still applies.
NYS Human Rights Law, Executive Law 296(5)(a)(4): the refusal to rent is exempt in a building with no more than two families living independently if the owner lives in one of them. The statute does not extend this exemption to statements and advertisements.
NYC Human Rights Law: a two-family house where the owner or the owner's family lives is exempt only if the available unit was not advertised or offered to the public.
Real estate brokers: covered separately by the state law (296(5)(c)) and the city law. The owner's exemption is personal to the owner.

blocks.q: Teresa wants Jordan to list the upstairs unit on StreetEasy and screen out families with small children. What is the correct analysis?
c: The NYS two-family exemption protects Teresa, so Jordan may screen as she asks
Jordan may screen for her, but the StreetEasy ad cannot mention children
Advertising and the broker's role end the exemption; Jordan cannot screen
The federal Mrs. Murphy exemption controls, because federal law preempts the state
blocks.x: Two things break Teresa's plan. Jordan is a licensee, and brokers are covered by their own provisions of the state and city laws, so the owner's exemption never transfers to the agent. And in New York City the two-family exemption disappears once the unit is advertised or offered to the public. The tempting answer, letting Jordan screen quietly while keeping the ad clean, still has a licensee carrying out familial status discrimination.

blocks.html: Jordan explains this on the phone. Teresa pauses, then asks the smarter question: what if she skips the broker, skips the website, and just tells people at work and at her mother's senior center? Now the analysis changes, because each exemption is built for exactly that owner: one who lives in the building and fills the unit privately.

blocks.q: Teresa rents the upstairs unit herself, by word of mouth only, with no ad, no sign and no broker. She tells a parent of a four-year-old that she would rather not rent to a family with young kids. Which statement is most accurate?
c: Her refusal fits the federal, state and city owner-occupancy exemptions
Just the federal exemption applies, since New York has no two-family rule
The city exemption applies, but the state law still makes the refusal illegal
No exemption applies, because familial status is not covered by one
blocks.x: All three layers exempt this exact owner. Federally, the owner lives in a building for four or fewer families. Under the state law, it is a two-family house and she lives there. Under the city law, the owner lives there and the unit was not advertised or offered to the public. The trap is assuming New York has no owner-occupancy exemption. It has one, just cut down from four units to two, and it covers the refusal, not any statement of preference.

blocks.title: Why the city version is tighter
blocks.html: The NYC Human Rights Law asks one extra question: was the unit advertised or offered to the general public? A StreetEasy post, a Craigslist ad, a "For Rent" sign in the window or a listing with a brokerage all count as offering the unit publicly. Once that happens in the five boroughs, the exemption is gone for every protected class the city covers, including lawful source of income and presence of children. Upstate and on Long Island only the state and federal rules apply, so an advertised owner-occupied two-family there may still have the state exemption for the refusal, but never for the ad itself.

Teresa takes the word-of-mouth route. Two weeks later her cousin offers to help by taping a printed notice to the bulletin board at the laundromat on Myrtle Avenue: "Upstairs 2BR for rent. Quiet Christian household preferred. No small kids. Call Teresa." Teresa texts Jordan a photo and asks if the wording is fine, since she is exempt anyway.

blocks.q: What is the legal effect of the laundromat notice?
c: It is legal, because an exempt owner may state whatever preference she has
The line about children is the problem, since creed is not a protected class
It is legal upstate but not in NYC, which bans notices posted in public
It is a discriminatory ad, and in NYC it also ends the owner's exemption
blocks.x: Advertising is the line no owner exemption crosses. The federal ad ban applies even to Mrs. Murphy owners, and New York's two-family exemption does not reach statements and advertisements. The notice expresses a preference based on creed and familial status, both protected. In the city it also counts as offering the unit to the public, so Teresa loses the refusal exemption as well. The distractor that creed is unprotected is wrong: New York protects creed by name.

blocks.html: Teresa takes the notice down and asks one more question. Her late husband's cousin owns a three-family on Seneca Avenue, two blocks away, and lives on the first floor. He has heard about "Mrs. Murphy" on a podcast and believes anything up to four units is exempt.

blocks.q: The cousin owns and lives in a three-family house in Ridgewood. He wants to refuse a tenant because of her marital status, without ads or brokers. What applies?
c: Exempt under the state rule, because New York follows the four-unit limit
Covered by state law, which exempts only owner-occupied two-family homes
Exempt under every law, because he lives on the premises and uses no ads
Covered only by federal law, since marital status is a federal class
blocks.x: The federal Mrs. Murphy exemption would cover a three-family, but marital status is not a federal class anyway, so federal law is not the issue. New York protects marital status and limits its owner-occupancy exemption to buildings with no more than two families. A three-family is fully covered by the state law, and in the five boroughs by the city law too. The podcast's four-unit rule is the federal number, not New York's.

blocks.text: The rule that has no exemption

blocks.html: Before hanging up, Teresa admits something that has been bothering her. Her cousin told her that if she is exempt, she can refuse anyone she wants, "for any reason, even race." Jordan has the answer ready, and it is the one point that never changes no matter how small the building is.

blocks.q: If Teresa, renting privately with no ad, turned away an applicant because the applicant is Black, which law makes the refusal illegal even though she is otherwise exempt?
c: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, which closed the exemption for race
The NYC Human Rights Law, because the city law has no owner exemption
The Civil Rights Act of 1866, which allows no exemption for race
The Americans with Disabilities Act, which applies to private rentals in NYC
blocks.x: The Civil Rights Act of 1866, as the Supreme Court applied it to private sales and rentals in Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., bars racial discrimination in property transactions with no exemption for owner-occupied buildings. The 1988 amendments added disability and familial status but did not touch the owner exemptions. The city answer is wrong because the city law does have an owner-occupied two-family exemption, as long as the unit is not advertised.

blocks.title: "Exempt" is never a single yes or no
blocks.html: Exam questions about exemptions hide the layer. An owner can be exempt federally, covered by the state, and covered or not by the city, depending on the number of units, whether the owner lives there, whether anyone advertised, whether a broker was used, and which class is involved. Work it in order: race first (1866 Act, no exemption), then any ad (never exempt), then any broker (never exempt), then the unit count and occupancy at each level.

blocks.text: Owner two: the house in New Rochelle

blocks.html: Glen Whitaker lives in Rye and owns one other single-family house, a three-bedroom colonial in New Rochelle that he rents out. He has read the federal law closely. "I own fewer than three houses, I'm not using a broker, and I won't run a discriminatory ad. Federal law says I'm exempt." He has two applicants. One is a couple with a toddler. The other is a nurse who would pay most of the rent with a Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher. Glen would like to turn down both, and he wants Jordan's opinion as a favor, not as his agent.

head: Glen's situation
Federal Fair Housing Act
NYS Human Rights Law
rows: Owns 2 single-family homes, rents one himself
Single-family exemption can apply (owner of no more than 3, no broker, no discriminatory ad)
Rejects the family with a toddler
Exempt, if every condition is met
Source of income is not a federal class
Lawful source of income violation (statewide since 2019)
Hires a broker or posts "no kids"
Still covered, and the broker is liable too
blocks.caption: Same facts, two different answers

blocks.q: Which law makes Glen's refusal of the family with a toddler illegal?
c: The federal Fair Housing Act, because single-family rentals are not exempt
The NYS Human Rights Law, which has no single-family owner exemption
No law, because Glen meets every condition of the federal exemption
Westchester zoning law, which governs who may occupy a single-family home
blocks.x: Glen is right about federal law: an owner of no more than three single-family houses who uses no broker and no discriminatory advertising is exempt from most of the federal Act. But New York's Human Rights Law has no such exemption, and it protects familial status. Since Glen's house is in New York, the state law reaches him. The answer that no law applies is the trap: it reads the federal statute alone and forgets the state layer.

blocks.html: Federal law adds two details Glen did not mention. If he does not live in the house he is renting or selling, and was not the most recent resident, the federal exemption is available for only one such sale in any 24-month period. And the exemption disappears the moment he uses a licensee or any person in the business of selling or renting dwellings. None of that matters in New York, because the state law reaches him first, but the details show up on national exam questions.

Glen's voucher question has the same answer, with a twist. Source of income is not protected under federal law at all, so there was never a federal exemption to claim. New York has protected lawful source of income statewide since April 2019, and the state law treats a Section 8 voucher as income. Glen may run the same credit check, reference check and income test on every applicant, but he cannot reject the nurse because part of her rent comes from a voucher.

blocks.q: Glen says he will "just tell the voucher holder the house is rented" while he keeps showing it to others. Under New York law, this is:
c: Legal, because Glen meets the federal single-family exemption
Legal, as long as he gives the same answer to every single voucher holder
A violation, but just if Glen advertises the house at some later point
Misrepresenting availability because of source of income, a violation
blocks.x: Telling someone a unit is unavailable when it is not, because of a protected trait, is its own form of discrimination. New York protects lawful source of income for every owner, so Glen has no exemption to hide behind. Applying the lie consistently to all voucher holders makes it a policy, not a defense. The federal exemption is irrelevant because federal law never protected source of income in the first place.

blocks.title: When the caller is not your client
blocks.html: Glen asked Jordan for a favor, not representation. Jordan still answered correctly, kept it short, and suggested Glen call a lawyer if he wants advice about his own house. A licensee should never coach an owner on how to use an exemption to discriminate, and should never accept a listing where the owner's instructions require discrimination. If Glen later asks Hudson & Hart to list the house, every one of his preferences is off the table.

Sheila Grant manages Peconic Pines, a 150-home community in Suffolk County marketed as housing for older persons. The community's rules say each home must have at least one resident aged 55 or older and that no one under 19 may live there permanently. Hudson & Hart has a buyer for a resale unit, and Sheila is calling about two other prospective buyers. First, though, Diane wants Jordan to check whether Peconic Pines qualifies for the housing for older persons exemption at all.

blocks.title: Peconic Pines occupancy survey, September
blocks.html:
Total homes: 150
Vacant homes: 10
Occupied homes: 140
Occupied homes with at least one resident 55 or older: 115
Written age verification on file: updated within the last 2 years
Published policies and marketing: describe the community as 55 and over

blocks.q: Does Peconic Pines meet the 55-and-over occupancy test?
c: Yes, because 115 of 140 occupied homes is about 82%, above 80%
No, because 115 of 150 total homes is under 77%, below the 80% mark
No, because each resident has to be at least 55 years old at purchase
Yes, because the 80% test applies just to newly built communities
blocks.x: The federal 55-and-over test measures occupied units: at least 80% must have at least one resident 55 or older, and the community must publish policies showing that intent and verify ages through reliable surveys. Here 115 divided by 140 is about 82%, so the test is met. Dividing by all 150 homes, including vacancies, is the common mistake. The all-residents rule describes the separate 62-and-over category, where every resident must be 62 or older.

blocks.html: The survey matters because the exemption is not a label a community can simply print on a sign. HUD's rules require reliable age verification, such as a driver's license or birth certificate, updated through surveys at least once every two years, and the community has to publish and follow policies showing it intends to be 55-and-over housing. A community that lets its occupancy slip under 80%, or stops verifying, loses the exemption and is then covered by the familial status rules like any other seller or landlord. That is why Diane wanted the numbers before anyone discussed a buyer. A broker who relies on a community's word without asking is the one left explaining a familial status complaint.

Now the two buyers. The first is Marian Sato, 61, who has legal custody of her 15-year-old grandson. The second is Robert Haines, 58, whose son Daniel, 30, lives with him and uses a wheelchair after a spinal cord injury. Sheila would like to refuse both: Marian because of the grandson, Robert because the board worries a wheelchair user will "need things" and "create liability."

blocks.q: Can Peconic Pines refuse Marian because her 15-year-old grandson would live with her?
c: No, because custody of a minor makes her a member of a protected class
No, because New York protects age, which overrides the federal exemption
Yes, but just if the board also refuses buyers who have adult children
Yes, because a qualifying older persons community may exclude minors
blocks.x: The housing for older persons exemption exists to let a qualifying community limit familial status, which is exactly what a rule against permanent residents under 19 does. New York's statute contains a parallel exemption for 55-and-over and 62-and-over housing, so state law does not override it. Marian's custody of her grandson does give her familial status protection elsewhere, which makes the first choice tempting, but this community is the place the law lets that protection give way.

blocks.q: Can Peconic Pines refuse Robert because his adult son uses a wheelchair?
c: Yes, because the older persons exemption covers each community rule
No, the exemption covers age and familial status, not disability
Yes, if the board documents a real concern about liability insurance costs
No, but just because Daniel is over 18 and the age rule cannot reach him
blocks.x: The senior housing exemption lifts familial status rules (and New York's age rules) and nothing else. Disability is fully protected, so refusing a buyer because a household member uses a wheelchair is disability discrimination. Speculation about future requests or liability is not a lawful reason. If Daniel later needs a ramp or a rule change, the reasonable accommodation and modification rules govern. The adult-son answer reaches the right result for the wrong reason, which is how the exam catches people.

blocks.html: Sheila backs down on Robert. Then she mentions the community's new brochure, which went to print last week. The cover reads: "Peconic Pines. An active adult community for Christian retirees. No children."

blocks.q: Which part of the brochure creates a fair housing problem?
c: The reference to no children, since ads may not mention age limits
The phrase active adult, since it implies a preference by disability
Christian retirees, a religious preference outside the exemption
Nothing, because a qualifying older persons community is exempt in its ads
blocks.x: A qualifying 55-and-over community may advertise its age restrictions; describing itself as an adult community with no children is consistent with the exemption. Religion is a different matter. The exemption covers age and familial status only, so stating a preference for Christian buyers is discriminatory advertising based on religion or creed. New York's statute adds that a senior community that engages in discriminatory advertising is no longer exempt, so one bad line can cost the whole exemption.

blocks.title: New York's other narrow exemptions
blocks.html: The state law also exempts (1) the rental of a room or rooms by the occupant of a housing accommodation, or by an owner who lives there, and (2) restricting all the rooms in a housing accommodation to people of the same sex. Unlike the two-family exemption, the statute extends these two to statements and inquiries. Religious and denominational organizations may give a preference to members of their own religion, but never on the basis of race, color or national origin. In NYC, rooms rented in non-government-assisted housing where the owner lives are exempt from the city law.

Teresa calls back on Thursday with the last question of the week. Her mother wants to rent the spare bedroom in their own downstairs apartment to a woman from her senior center, and asks whether she may say "women only" when she mentions it to friends.

blocks.q: Teresa's mother rents one room in the apartment where she and Teresa live and says she will rent only to a woman. Under New York State law, this is:
c: Exempt, because rooms rented by a resident owner or occupant are exempt
Covered, because that exemption applies just to rooms in a rooming house
Covered, because sex is protected by every level of fair housing law
Exempt, but just if the room rents for less than the market rate
blocks.x: New York exempts the rental of a room or rooms in a housing accommodation by its occupant or by an owner who lives there, and the statute extends that exemption to statements about the rental. The same-sex choice is therefore lawful for a room in the family's own home. The trap is assuming a protected class is protected everywhere. Sex is protected, but the room exemption is the one place New York lets a resident choose who shares her living space.

blocks.html: Teresa rented the upstairs unit to a couple with a newborn who answered no ad at all; her mother met them at the senior center and liked them. Glen hired a property manager, who told him the same thing Jordan did. Peconic Pines reprinted its brochure without the religious line, and Sheila sent Jordan the resale listing on Robert's behalf a week later. Diane's summary at the Friday meeting was one sentence: "Owners have exemptions. We do not."

items: Work exemptions layer by layer: federal, state and city each have their own unit counts, conditions and classes.
New York's owner-occupancy exemption covers two-family houses only; in NYC it also ends once the unit is advertised or offered to the public.
No exemption covers race (1866 Act), discriminatory advertising, or a licensee acting for the owner.
The federal single-family exemption has no New York counterpart, and source of income was never federal, so state law reaches those owners.
Housing for older persons may limit familial status and age, using the 80% of occupied units test, but disability and religion stay fully protected.

lessons.title: Case file: Six Applicants for Apartment 4C
lessons.tagline: One Bronx one-bedroom, six qualified applicants, and a landlord whose screening rules each break a different line of the city's law.
objectives: Calculate an NYC income requirement against a voucher holder's share and decide how credit history may be used.
Apply the NYC lawful occupation, immigration status, age and domestic violence protections to rental screening decisions.
Apply the Fair Chance for Housing Law's sequence, lookback periods and notice steps to a criminal background check.

blocks.title: Apartment 4C, the Grand Concourse
blocks.html: Victor Osei manages a 24-unit elevator building on the Grand Concourse in the Bronx for its owner, Concourse Holdings LLC. He has hired Hudson & Hart to rent 4C, a renovated one-bedroom at $2,400 a month, and under the city's FARE Act the landlord, not the tenant, pays Jordan's fee. Victor is friendly, organized and in a hurry. He emails Jordan his screening criteria and a draft listing on Tuesday morning and wants applications by the weekend. Within four days Jordan has six serious applicants, and almost every one of them tests a different line of the New York City Human Rights Law. The first test is the draft ad itself.

blocks.title: Victor's draft listing
blocks.html: "Bright 1BR on the Concourse, elevator, laundry in building, 2 blocks to the 4 train. $2,400. Requirements: annual income 40x rent, W-2 employment, minimum 680 credit score, no programs. Background check with application. $100 processing fee."

blocks.q: Which part of Victor's draft is a clear source of income violation on its face?
c: The 40x income requirement, which cannot appear in any NYC listing
No programs and W-2 employment, which exclude lawful income
The elevator and laundry description, which steers by disability
The minimum credit score, which is illegal in every rental listing
blocks.x: Lawful source of income covers vouchers, subsidies, Social Security, child support and any other lawful income. "No programs" announces a refusal of rental assistance, and "W-2 employment" rules out self-employed and benefit income. The income multiple and credit check are not illegal by themselves; the problem is how they are applied to voucher holders. Describing building features is never steering. Jordan rewrites the ad to describe the apartment and state that all lawful sources of income are welcome.

blocks.title: Jordan's rewrite
blocks.html: "Bright 1BR on the Grand Concourse, 4th floor, elevator, laundry in building, 2 blocks to the 4 train. $2,400, heat and hot water included. All lawful sources of income welcome, including vouchers and rental assistance programs. Income and credit reviewed for every applicant under the same written criteria. Application fee: actual cost of the credit check, not more than $20. No broker fee charged to the tenant. Hudson & Hart Realty, licensed real estate broker."

Victor agrees to the rewrite without argument. "I didn't write 'no programs' to be difficult," he says. "The last voucher tenant's paperwork took two months." Jordan notes that delay in a program is not a lawful reason to refuse it, and moves on. The fee line goes too. New York caps what a landlord may charge an applicant at the actual cost of a background or credit check, up to $20, and in NYC the landlord's own broker fee cannot be passed to the tenant.

blocks.text: Applicant one: the voucher and the 40x rule

blocks.html: Renata Cruz is a home health aide who has worked for the same agency for six years. She holds a CityFHEPS voucher that will pay $2,050 of the $2,400 rent, leaving her share at $350 a month. Her income is $2,200 a month from wages. Victor's assistant has already marked her application "fails income."

blocks.title: Two ways to run the 40x test
blocks.html:
Against the full rent: 40 x $2,400 = $96,000 a year required. Renata earns $2,200 x 12 = $26,400. Fails.
Against her share: 40 x $350 = $14,000 a year required. Renata earns $26,400. Passes, with room to spare.
Her share of the rent is $350 / $2,200 = about 16% of her monthly income.

blocks.q: Which calculation does the NYC Human Rights Law require for Renata?
c: Against her $350 share of the rent, so she passes the requirement
Against the full $2,400 rent, since the rule applies to each applicant
Against the full rent, unless the building has more than 6 units
Against the voucher amount, so the $2,050 subsidy counts as her income
blocks.x: In New York City an income requirement may be measured only against the portion of the rent the tenant pays. Renata's share is $350, so the requirement is $14,000 a year, and she clears it easily. Applying the full-rent test to everyone sounds neutral, but it screens out nearly every voucher holder, which is why the Commission treats it as source of income discrimination. Treating the voucher as income to the tenant is a math mistake that reaches the right result by accident.

blocks.html: Victor's assistant tries another route. Renata's credit score is 590, and the criteria say 680. The assistant suggests rejecting her for credit instead, "which has nothing to do with the voucher."

blocks.q: Renata pays part of the rent herself. How may Victor use credit history in deciding on her application?
c: He may not review credit in any form, because she holds a voucher
He may reject her automatically, since 680 is applied to everyone
He may review it case by case and let her show she can pay
He may require co-signers from the voucher applicants alone
blocks.x: The NYC Commission on Human Rights says that when a tenant pays part of the rent, a landlord may make a credit inquiry, but a fixed minimum score is evidence of discrimination. The landlord should look at the history case by case and give the applicant a chance to show she can pay her own share on time, with a written explanation if she is rejected. A co-signer demanded only of voucher holders is unequal treatment, and banning any credit review goes further than the guidance.

blocks.title: When the voucher pays everything
blocks.html: Some subsidies cover the entire rent. The Commission's guidance is direct: if the voucher covers the full rent, the landlord may not reject the applicant based on credit history or credit score, because the tenant's credit has nothing to do with whether the rent gets paid. Income requirements disappear for the same reason. Expect the exam to test the difference between a full voucher and a partial one.

blocks.q: A different applicant's voucher would cover the full $2,400 rent. Victor wants to reject her because her credit score is 540. Under the Commission's guidance, this is:
c: Lawful, since a credit score is a neutral screening tool
Lawful, if Victor rejects every other 540 applicant as well
Unlawful, unless she also fails the 40x income test for the unit
Unlawful, since her credit has no bearing on the rent payment
blocks.x: When the subsidy pays the whole rent, the tenant's credit history does not predict whether the landlord will be paid, so rejecting her for credit screens out the voucher in practice. The Commission treats it as source of income discrimination. Applying the same score cutoff to everyone does not cure the problem, and the income test cannot apply at all when her share is zero. This is the full-voucher rule, distinct from the case-by-case approach for partial vouchers.

blocks.html: Renata is approved. Jordan sends Victor a one-paragraph email explaining the share calculation, so the next voucher application is scored correctly from the start.

Notice what Jordan did not do. The rewrite keeps an income test and a credit review, because a landlord may screen for ability to pay. What changed is that every screen is written down, applied to every applicant the same way, and adjusted for the voucher where the law requires. That written criteria sheet becomes the most useful document in the file if anyone later asks why one applicant was approved and another was not.

Kevin Park, 29, has tended bar at a Midtown cocktail lounge for five years. His pay stubs and tip records show income of $8,900 a month, far above the requirement. Victor hesitates. "Bartenders keep late hours. People coming and going at 4 a.m. Can I pass on him?"

blocks.q: Can Victor turn Kevin down because of his job?
c: Yes, because occupation is protected in employment cases alone
No, because the city protects lawful occupation in housing
Yes, if Victor can show the late hours disturb neighbors
No, but just because his income exceeds the 40x requirement
blocks.x: The NYC Human Rights Law lists lawful occupation as a protected class in housing. Bartending is lawful, so refusing Kevin because of the job is discrimination in the five boroughs. If he later breaks a lease rule on noise, Victor can enforce it like any other rule against any tenant. Speculating about future noise because of a job is the stereotype the law forbids. His high income is beside the point; the protection does not depend on it.

blocks.html: Anna Kowalczyk is a pastry chef at a bakery in Riverdale. She has three years of bank statements, a letter from her employer and an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number instead of a Social Security number. Victor's screening company form has a required field for an SSN. The assistant asks Jordan whether to tell Anna the application cannot be processed.

blocks.q: What should Jordan and Victor do with Anna's application?
c: Accept the ITIN and verify income and identity another way
Ask Anna for proof of citizenship, then process the application normally
Decline it, because a screening company may require an SSN by law
Process it after Anna provides a co-signer who has an SSN
blocks.x: New York State and New York City both protect citizenship and immigration status in housing. Requiring a Social Security number when an ITIN and other documents can verify identity and income screens out applicants by status. The same applies to a co-signer demand made only of applicants without an SSN. Asking one applicant for proof of citizenship is worse: it singles her out. Use the same identification rule for everyone and an alternate verification path when the standard field does not fit.

blocks.html: Dennis Rowe, 44, is an electrician with steady union income. Victor's screening packet runs a criminal background check with the application. Jordan flags it. Since January 1, 2025, the city's Fair Chance for Housing Law has controlled when and how most landlords and brokers may look at criminal history.

items.title: Screen everything else first
items.html: Income, credit, references and rental history are reviewed before any criminal history check.

items.title: Make a conditional offer
items.html: If the applicant qualifies on those factors, the landlord makes a conditional offer. Only then may it run a criminal background check, with notice to the applicant.

items.title: Respect the lookback
items.html: Only felony convictions within 5 years of release or sentencing and misdemeanor convictions within 3 years may be considered. Sex offense registry information has no time limit.

items.title: Share and wait
items.html: The applicant receives a copy of the report and has 5 business days to correct errors or provide information about rehabilitation. The offer cannot be withdrawn during that window.

items.title: Explain in writing
items.html: If the landlord withdraws the offer, it must explain in writing how the history relates to a legitimate business interest.

blocks.q: Victor wants to run Dennis's criminal background check together with his credit check, before deciding anything. Under the Fair Chance for Housing Law:
c: That is allowed, if Victor runs the same check on every applicant
That is allowed for buildings with more than 10 units in the city
The check waits for a conditional offer after other screening
The check may not be run at any point in an NYC rental
blocks.x: The law sets an order of operations. A landlord or broker first evaluates the non-criminal factors, then makes a conditional offer, and only then may look at criminal history. Running every check at once, even for everyone, defeats the purpose, which is to make sure people are judged on their qualifications before their record. The check is allowed after the conditional offer, so a flat ban overstates the law.

blocks.html: Dennis qualifies and receives a conditional offer. The check comes back with two entries: a misdemeanor conviction four years ago with no jail time, and a felony conviction for which he was released from prison three and a half years ago.

blocks.q: Which entries may Victor consider?
c: Both, because the law limits arrests that did not end in conviction
Only the felony, which falls inside the 5-year lookback from release
Only the misdemeanor, because felony records are sealed after release
Neither, because the conviction dates are earlier than the application
blocks.x: The lookback periods run from release or sentencing: 5 years for felonies and 3 years for misdemeanors. The misdemeanor is four years old, outside its 3-year window, so it cannot be considered. The felony release was three and a half years ago, inside the 5-year window, so it may be considered, subject to the notice, copy and response steps. Considering both treats the lookback limits as if they only addressed arrests.

blocks.html: Victor reads the felony entry and starts drafting a rejection. Jordan stops him and walks him through the next step: Dennis must receive a copy of the report and the chance to respond before any decision.

blocks.q: What must happen before Victor can withdraw the conditional offer?
c: A copy of the report, 5 business days, then a written reason
Victor sends the file to the Commission for approval of the withdrawal
Victor gives a verbal reason within 24 hours of receiving the report
Dennis is offered a different unit in the building at a higher rent
blocks.x: The applicant receives a copy of what the landlord received and has 5 business days to correct errors or offer evidence of rehabilitation, during which the offer stays open. If the landlord still withdraws, it must explain in writing how the record relates to a legitimate business interest. There is no Commission pre-approval step, and a quick verbal reason does not satisfy the writing requirement. Steering him to a pricier unit would add a second violation.

blocks.html: Why the law works this way: before 2025, many NYC applications were declined the moment a background report came back, before anyone looked at income or references, and often for convictions decades old. The city's answer was to move the criminal check to the end, cap how far back it may reach, and force a written reason that ties the record to something real, such as the safety of other residents or property. The written reason is also what the Commission will read first if the applicant files a complaint.

Dennis sends a letter from his union apprenticeship coordinator, five years of on-time rent receipts from his current apartment and a certificate from a reentry program. Victor reads it and approves him. The written record of that review is now in the file, which is where Diane wants it.

Patricia Moore, 72, is a retired schoolteacher with a pension and Social Security. Victor's assistant asks whether "someone her age" will be all right in a building where the elevator is sometimes out. Hannah Lee, 34, is a nurse whose rental history shows a housing court case two years ago. The file shows the case arose after her former partner, who abused her, damaged the apartment, and Hannah has a copy of an order of protection.

blocks.q: Victor's assistant suggests passing on Patricia "for her own good." What is the correct response?
c: It is allowed if the elevator is out more than a set number of days a year
It is allowed, because age protection comes from federal law alone
It is allowed if Victor offers her a ground floor unit at the same rent
It is age discrimination under both the state and city human rights laws
blocks.x: Age is protected for adults under the NYS and NYC Human Rights Laws, though not under the federal Fair Housing Act. Refusing an applicant to protect her from a building's conditions is a paternalistic version of the same discrimination. Patricia decides whether the building suits her. Offering a different unit she did not ask for steers her by age. The elevator's reliability is a building maintenance issue, not a screening criterion.

blocks.q: How should the housing court case in Hannah's history be treated?
c: As a neutral eviction record that may be weighed like any other
As grounds to require a larger security deposit from her than others
As protected, since it penalizes her for her abuser's conduct
As irrelevant, but just if the court case was dismissed in her favor
blocks.x: New York State and the city protect status as a victim of domestic violence, and the city adds stalking and sex offenses. Rejecting Hannah because her abuser caused the damage behind the court case penalizes her for that status. A higher deposit for the same reason is unequal terms, and statewide deposits are capped at one month anyway. Treating the case as a neutral record ignores why it exists, which is exactly the analysis the law requires.

blocks.text: The phone call Diane cared about

blocks.html: At the end of the week Victor calls Jordan with a confession and a request. Off the record, his own staff at another building simply stop returning calls from people who mention vouchers. "It's not a rule. We're just busy. Can you do the same and only call back the ones you think will work?" Jordan knows the testers the Commission and fair housing groups use measure exactly this: callback speed and follow-up.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do?
c: Agree, since return-call order is up to the agent's judgment
Agree, as long as voucher callers get a reply within a week
Refuse, but say nothing, since it involves Victor's other building
Refuse, keep a callback log for every caller, and tell Diane
blocks.x: Slow-walking voucher holders is unequal treatment based on source of income, and an agent who carries it out is liable along with the landlord and the brokerage. Jordan answers every inquiry in the order received, logs each one, and reports the instruction to the supervising broker, who decides whether Hudson & Hart can keep the listing. Staying quiet about the other building leaves a known violation unreported. A delayed callback is still the unequal service testers are trained to catch.

blocks.title: Neutral-sounding rules that are not neutral
blocks.html: Most source of income violations do not say "no vouchers." They say 40x the full rent, W-2 only, minimum 700 credit, "we don't do the inspection," or simply nothing, with a callback that never comes. The test is whether a rule screens out lawful income in practice. In the five boroughs, also check lawful occupation, immigration status, criminal history timing, age and domestic violence status before any application is marked declined.

head: Applicant
Victor's first instinct
What the file shows instead
rows: Fails 40x on full rent; credit below 680
Passes 40x on her $350 share; credit reviewed case by case; approved
Lawful occupation protected in NYC; approved
Identity and income verified by other documents; approved
Conditional offer first; misdemeanor outside lookback; felony reviewed with his 5-day response; approved
Age protected; her choice; offered the unit on the same terms
Damage caused by her abuser; status protected; approved
blocks.caption: Jordan's screening log for 4C

blocks.html: Six approvals for one apartment is its own problem, and it has a lawful answer: the first fully qualified applicant gets the unit, and the next qualified applicants are offered the next vacancies in the building in the order they qualified. Victor adopts that rule in writing. When the Commission's source of income unit sends a tester three months later, asking about a two-bedroom on the sixth floor with a voucher, the tester gets a same-day callback, the written criteria and an appointment. The log shows it.

items: In NYC, apply an income multiple only to the tenant's share of the rent; with a full voucher, credit and income screens cannot be used against the applicant.
Partial-voucher credit review is case by case, with a chance to show ability to pay; a fixed minimum score is evidence of discrimination.
NYC protects lawful occupation, and the state and city protect immigration status, age and status as a victim of domestic violence.
Under the Fair Chance for Housing Law: other factors first, conditional offer, lookback limits (5 years felony, 3 years misdemeanor), a copy of the report, 5 business days, and a written reason.
Unequal service, such as slow callbacks, is discrimination even with no written rule; log every contact and report instructions to the broker.

lessons.title: Case file: The Postcards on Clarkson Avenue
lessons.tagline: A mail campaign in New York's only cease and desist zone, a door-knocking script, and a buyer who wants to know where people like them fit in.
objectives: Decide whether a marketing contact violates a cease and desist zone and distinguish it from a nonsolicitation order.
Identify blockbusting, steering and redlining in sales scripts, listing searches, loan quotes, insurance refusals and appraisals.
Apply compliant responses to buyer questions about neighborhoods, schools and who lives where.

blocks.title: East Flatbush, a listing drought
blocks.html: Hudson & Hart has not had a listing in East Flatbush all year, and Marcus has a plan. He has ordered 4,000 "Just Sold!" postcards for every-door direct mail across the blocks around Clarkson Avenue and Utica Avenue, and he has partnered with an investor, Brightline Home Buyers, whose staff knock on doors offering fast cash. He asks Jordan to help fold the mail. Jordan has seen the Department of State's map and recognizes the boundaries: Utica Avenue and Clarkson Avenue are where the description of the only current cease and desist zone in the state begins, covering part of Brooklyn's Community Board 17. Before a single postcard goes out, Jordan asks Diane what the zone actually forbids.

A cease and desist zone protects only the homeowners who put themselves on the Department of State's cease and desist list. Inside the zone, brokers, salespeople and anyone regularly engaged in buying or selling homes, including investors like Brightline, may not solicit those owners to sell, rent or list. The DOS rules for the Brooklyn zone cover residential property only, single-family and multifamily alike, and the list is updated every month.

blocks.title: What DOS counts as solicitation in the Brooklyn zone
blocks.html:
Counts: phone calls, letters, door-knocking, hand-delivered flyers, any attempt to buy, rent or obtain a listing; "just listed" and "just sold" mailings; every-door direct mail postcards.
Does not count, per the DOS FAQ: Facebook posts, including boosted posts, because they are not delivered to the owner's home; classified ads in periodicals not primarily about real estate; billboards and other public-view advertising; radio and television ads.
Penalty: license discipline under RPL 441-c, including fines, suspension or revocation.

Zones are not drawn casually. DOS creates one after finding that owners in an area have been subjected to intense and repeated solicitation, typically after homeowners and local officials complain and the agency holds a public hearing. The goal is to let a homeowner who is tired of calls, letters and knocks say no once, to the state, and have that answer bind every broker and regular buyer in the market. That is why one contact with a listed owner is enough for discipline: the owner has already told the whole industry to stop.

blocks.q: Marcus wants to use every-door direct mail to send "Just Sold!" postcards to all 4,000 addresses in the zone. What is the problem?
c: Just sold postcards are announcements, so the zone rules do not reach them
EDDM reaches listed owners, and DOS counts those postcards as solicitation
The zone bans all real estate mail to every owner inside its boundaries
Postcards are fine if each one carries the broker's name and phone number
blocks.x: DOS specifically lists just sold mailings and every-door direct mail as solicitation in the Brooklyn zone. Every-door mail cannot skip the addresses of owners who signed the list, so it guarantees violations. The zone protects listed owners, not everyone, which is why the total-ban answer is wrong: Marcus could mail owners who are not on the current list. Broker identification is an advertising rule and cures nothing here.

blocks.html: Marcus switches to a mailing list. Jordan downloads the current DOS cease and desist list, which was last updated at the start of the month, and matches it against the addresses. Of the 4,000 homes, 610 are on the list. Marcus wants to save time by using the scrubbed list for the next six months.

blocks.q: Can Marcus reuse this month's scrubbed mailing list for the next six mailings?
c: Yes, a list scrubbed once stays valid for the life of the zone
Yes, if each card offers an opt-out line for future mailings
No, the list changes monthly, so rescrub before each mailing
No, because a mailing list may not be built from public property records
blocks.x: The DOS list is updated monthly, and owners can sign up at any time. A list scrubbed in October may include an owner who joined the list in November, and one postcard to a listed owner is a violation. Each mailing needs a fresh match against the current list. An opt-out line on the card does not help, because the owner already opted out by joining the state list. Public records are a lawful source of addresses.

blocks.q: Brightline's marketing team asks whether a boosted Facebook post aimed at East Flatbush homeowners is covered by the zone rules. Under the DOS FAQ, the post is:
c: Not zone solicitation, though still subject to fair housing law
Solicitation, because it targets owners by their location in the zone
Solicitation, unless the post is shown to people outside the zone as well
Not covered by any rule, because social media is not advertising
blocks.x: DOS says Facebook posts, boosted or not, are not solicitation under the zone rules because they are not delivered to the owner's home or premises. That does not make them unregulated. Social media is advertising, so the broker's identification rules and the fair housing rules on content and targeting still apply. The answer treating geography as the trigger confuses the zone rule with ad targeting rules, and social media is plainly advertising.

blocks.title: Zone versus nonsolicitation order
blocks.html: A cease and desist zone is opt-in: only owners on the list are protected. A nonsolicitation order covers every owner in a defined area and follows a DOS finding, after a public hearing, that intense solicitation was making owners fear that values would drop because of changing demographics. Both run up to 5 years and can be renewed. The DOS website lists the zones in effect; as of this case, Brooklyn's Community Board 17 zone is the only one listed, so check the site before any campaign, because zones are added and expire.
Brightline's door-knockers work from a printed script. Jordan sees it on Marcus's desk.

blocks.title: Brightline door script, page 1
blocks.html: "Hi, we're buying on this block right now, all cash, close in two weeks. A lot of your neighbors are selling. You've probably noticed the area is changing, with the new shelter on Linden and a lot of new families moving in. Prices are holding for now, but nobody knows how long. We'd hate to see you wait too long."

blocks.q: What is the main legal problem with Brightline's script?
c: Nothing, because cash offers to owners are lawful everywhere in New York
It is steering, because it describes the people who live on the block
It is redlining, because it ties property values to a specific area
Blockbusting, since it uses fear of who is moving in to induce sales
blocks.x: Blockbusting is inducing owners to sell by suggesting that people of a protected class are moving in and values will fall. The shelter reference targets families who use rental assistance, a lawful source of income class in New York, and "new families" carries the same implication. Steering targets buyers, not sellers. Redlining is a lending or insurance practice. A cash offer is lawful; the fear-based pitch is what makes it illegal.

blocks.html: Jordan brings the script to Diane, who reads it twice. Brightline is not Hudson & Hart's client, but Marcus has been feeding it leads, and two of the doors on its route belong to owners on the cease and desist list. Diane ends the referral arrangement that afternoon.

blocks.q: A Brightline employee knocks on the door of an owner on the cease and desist list and uses the script. Which statement is accurate?
c: The visit breaks the zone rule, and the script is blockbusting too
The visit is lawful, because the zone rules apply to licensees alone
The script is the one problem, since door visits are not solicitation
The zone rule is the one problem, since blockbusting needs a mailing
blocks.x: The zone rules reach anyone regularly engaged in buying or selling homes, which includes investment companies like Brightline, so knocking on a listed owner's door violates the rule. Separately, the script is blockbusting no matter who hears it or whether the owner is on any list. Door-knocking is expressly solicitation. The licensees-only answer is the trap: DOS wrote the Brooklyn zone to include investors who regularly buy properties.

blocks.html: Diane also tells Jordan what lawful farming in East Flatbush looks like. Owners not on the current list may receive mail, as long as every mailing is scrubbed again and the content is about the market: recent sales with prices, days on market, what a comparable two-family rented for. No predictions about who is moving in, no warnings about values, and no urgency built on fear. A quarterly market report that an owner can use whether or not she ever lists is the kind of mail that builds a business without building a complaint file.

blocks.title: Two different rules, one door
blocks.html: A cease and desist zone is about whether you may contact an owner. Blockbusting is about what you say. An owner not on the list can still be a victim of blockbusting, and a perfectly polite letter to a listed owner is still a zone violation. Exam questions often describe one and offer the other as the answer.

Meanwhile Jordan is working with Lauren and Mike Feld, who are relocating from Chicago with a budget of $1.1 million for a two-family house they can live in and rent part of.
