In the first meeting Lauren asks two questions back to back: "Where in Brooklyn would people like us fit in?" and "Which neighborhoods have the good schools?"

blocks.q: How should Jordan answer Lauren's two questions?
c: Name neighborhoods where similar clients settled, and rank the schools
Decline both questions and change the subject to price and financing
Ask their criteria, then point them to public school and census data
Describe each area's residents so the Felds can make an informed choice
blocks.x: Steering includes describing neighborhoods by who lives there or guiding buyers by protected class, even when asked. Jordan redirects to criteria the buyers set (commute, budget, building type, parks) and points them to objective public sources, such as NYC Department of Education school information and census data, which the buyers can evaluate themselves. Refusing outright is not required and leaves the buyers without help. Naming where similar clients settled is steering in its most common, helpful-sounding form.

blocks.html: Schools come up in almost every family's search, and they are a common doorway into steering. Jordan can give the Felds facts tied to an address, such as the zoned elementary school from the NYC Department of Education's school search, and links to the public data the city publishes. Jordan should not rate schools as good or bad, and should not use school quality as shorthand for who lives in a neighborhood. The buyers read the data and decide what matters to them.

The Felds give Jordan criteria: two-family, $1.1 million or less, within a 45-minute commute of Downtown Brooklyn, with a yard. Jordan's MLS search returns 14 listings across Flatbush, East Flatbush, Canarsie, Midwood and Sheepshead Bay. Marcus glances at the printout. "Drop the three in Canarsie and the two on Remsen Avenue. They won't be comfortable there. Trust me."

blocks.q: What should Jordan send the Felds?
c: The 9 listings Marcus approved, since he knows the market better
Every one of the 14 matching listings, with the same facts on each
The 9 listings, plus a note that 5 others exist if they ask about them
All 14 listings, with Marcus's comfort comments attached to each one
blocks.x: Dropping homes that meet a buyer's stated criteria because of a guess about how the buyers will feel among the people who live there is steering by omission. It is also unequal treatment, since another buyer with the same criteria would see all 14. Sending the nine with a footnote still filters by demographics. Attaching Marcus's comments would add steering in writing. Jordan sends all 14 with the same facts for each.

blocks.html: Two days later Mike calls. He has looked at the list and says, "Honestly, take out anything east of Utica. I don't want to be the only people like us on the block."

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle Mike's request?
c: Agree, because following a client's instructions cannot be steering
Refuse to keep working with the Felds, since the request is illegal
Agree, but write in the file that the buyer asked for the exclusion
Keep sending every match; the Felds can skip what they choose
blocks.x: Buyers may choose where they live, including for reasons Jordan would not share. What Jordan may not do is take on the filtering: building a search that excludes areas because of who lives there makes the agent the one steering. The practical answer is to keep sending every listing that meets the stated criteria and let the buyers decline showings. A note in the file does not change who did the filtering. Ending the relationship is not required.

blocks.text: The lender, the insurer and the appraiser

blocks.html: The Felds go into contract on a two-family on East 49th Street for $985,000. Then three problems arrive in one week, and each is a version of the oldest discrimination in New York real estate.

head: Day
Who
What happened
rows: Quotes the Felds 20% minimum down for this zip code, versus 10% for the same loan on a Midwood house they had considered
Declines to quote, saying it is "not writing in this area right now"; the house is not in a flood zone and has a new roof
Values the house at $905,000; the report describes the neighborhood as "predominantly minority, pride of ownership varies" and uses comps from two miles away
blocks.caption: The Felds' week

blocks.q: What best describes the lender's quote?
c: Possible redlining: the terms vary by the area, not by the borrowers
Steering, because the lender is guiding buyers toward Midwood
Lawful risk pricing, since lenders may price each zip code differently
Blockbusting, because the higher down payment pressures the sellers
blocks.x: Redlining is a lender or insurer refusing or limiting loans or coverage because of an area's makeup rather than the borrower's qualifications or the property's condition. Same borrowers, same loan, worse terms because of the zip code is the classic pattern, and the Fair Housing Act, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and New York's Human Rights Law all reach it. Lenders may price objective risk, which is why this is possible redlining pending an explanation, not automatically lawful.

blocks.html: Lending discrimination leaves a paper trail. Lenders report loan applications, approvals and pricing under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, and that public data is how researchers and regulators spot area-based patterns. The Felds do not need statistics, though. They ask the lender in writing to explain the different down payment, and when the answer is only "the zip code," they move to a lender who quotes 10% down on the same house. Jordan points them to the complaint options: HUD, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the state Division of Human Rights, and, for state-chartered lenders, the Department of Financial Services.

blocks.q: The insurer refuses to quote a sound, non-flood-zone house because it is "not writing in this area." Jordan's best advice to the Felds is:
c: Accept it, because insurers may choose any area they like
Shop other insurers and report it if it looks area-based
Ask the seller to keep the house insured until after closing
Ask the lender to waive its homeowners insurance requirement
blocks.x: An insurer that refuses coverage by area, without an objective reason like flood exposure or the building's condition, may be engaged in insurance redlining, which fair housing laws reach. The practical move is to get quotes elsewhere, including through an independent agent, and to report a refusal that appears to be area-based to the Department of Financial Services or a fair housing agency. Lenders will not waive coverage, and the seller's policy does not protect the Felds after closing.

blocks.q: What should the Felds do about the appraisal?
c: Nothing, since an appraiser's opinion of value cannot be challenged
Ask Jordan to call the appraiser directly and negotiate the number
Request a reconsideration of value through the lender, citing comps
Walk away from the contract, since a low appraisal voids it automatically
blocks.x: Appraisals are covered by the Fair Housing Act, and describing a neighborhood by the race of its residents has no place in a valuation. The borrower can ask the lender for a reconsideration of value, supported by closer comparable sales, and flag the demographic language. Jordan can supply comps but should not pressure the appraiser, which raises appraiser independence problems. A low appraisal does not void a contract by itself; the mortgage contingency and the lender's decision control that.

blocks.html: The Felds file the reconsideration request with four sales within half a mile. The lender orders a second appraisal, which comes in at $990,000. The Felds also file a complaint about the first report with the state. They close five weeks later with a 10% down payment from a different lender. The second appraisal, the written lender quote and the insurer's refusal letter all go into the transaction file, which Hudson & Hart keeps for at least three years.

The night of the closing, Jordan drafts an Instagram post with a photo of the house: "Closed on East 49th! East Flatbush is finally changing. Get in before everyone else does." Diane sees the draft on the office's shared review queue before it posts.

blocks.q: What is wrong with Jordan's draft post?
c: Nothing, because it describes a market trend and not any person
Only the broker's name is missing; the content itself is fully compliant
It is a zone violation, since it reaches owners on the list
"Finally changing" signals demographics: steering and blockbusting
blocks.x: "Finally changing" in a neighborhood whose residents are mostly people of color reads as a statement about who lives there, which is the language of steering for buyers and blockbusting for owners. The fix is to describe the house, the deal and verifiable facts. Under the DOS FAQ a social media post is not zone solicitation. Broker identification is required on business posts, but adding it would not cure the message.

blocks.html: The review queue Diane used is the broker's supervision duty in practice. Hudson & Hart requires agents to route business posts through a shared queue before they go live, the same way print ads are checked. It takes a few minutes, it caught this post, and it gives the brokerage a record showing that it reviews advertising, which matters if a regulator ever asks.

blocks.title: Words that carry demographics
blocks.html: "Changing," "up and coming," "transitioning," "safe," "good area," "pride of ownership" and "you'll fit in" all sound like real estate small talk and all invite a fair housing complaint when used about a neighborhood. Replace them with facts anyone can verify: train lines and minutes to Downtown, price per square foot, recent sales, park acreage, building age.

head: Practice
Aimed at
What it does
Seen in this case
rows: Induces sales through fear that a protected group is moving in
Brightline's door script, Jordan's draft post
Guides people toward or away from areas by protected class
Marcus's dropped listings, "where would we fit in"
Limits credit or coverage because of an area's makeup
The 20% down quote, the insurer's refusal, the appraisal language
Contacts owners who opted out on the DOS list
Every-door mail, Brightline's knock on a listed door
blocks.caption: Four violations, one neighborhood

items: A cease and desist zone protects only listed owners; scrub every mailing against the current monthly DOS list, and remember investors are covered too.
DOS counts just sold cards and every-door mail as solicitation in the Brooklyn zone, but not Facebook posts, which remain subject to fair housing rules.
Blockbusting is about the message to owners; it is illegal whether or not the owner is on any list.
Steering includes omitting matching listings and answering "where will we fit in"; give every match and objective public sources, and let buyers choose.
Area-based loan terms, insurance refusals and demographic appraisal language are forms of redlining; shop, report, and request reconsideration of value.

lessons.title: Case file: The Listing Copy That Wrote Itself
lessons.tagline: An AI tool drafts three listings and a paid campaign in forty seconds. Jordan has to find everything wrong with them before they go live.
objectives: Distinguish lawful property descriptions from ad language that indicates a preference based on a protected class.
Apply fair housing rules to images, audience targeting and personal social media used to promote listings.
Apply New York's advertising identification and NYC FARE Act fee disclosure rules to a listing.
Decide who is responsible for discriminatory advertising produced with an automated tool.

blocks.title: Hudson & Hart, the new marketing tool
blocks.html: Hudson & Hart has started a trial of an AI writing tool that drafts listing copy, social captions and ad targeting from a few facts and photos. Diane is skeptical; Marcus loves it. Jordan has three listings to launch this week: the Okafors' Bed-Stuy brownstone, a two-bedroom vacancy in Sal Russo's Astoria building, and a one-bedroom rental in a Long Island City condo owned by an investor client. Jordan types in the facts, clicks Generate, and gets three polished drafts in forty seconds. Diane's rule for the trial is simple: nothing the tool writes goes out until a licensee has read every word as if they wrote it, because legally, they did.

blocks.title: AI draft, Okafor listing
blocks.html: "Stately 1899 brownstone on a tree-lined Bed-Stuy block. Four floors, original parlor-floor woodwork, two fireplaces, a 50-foot garden. Perfect for a growing family, with a top-floor suite ideal for the in-laws. Walk-in closets, great light, and a short walk to the A and C trains. A rare find in a neighborhood on the rise. $2,150,000."

blocks.q: Which phrase in the Okafor draft creates the clearest fair housing problem?
c: "A short walk to the A and C trains"
"Perfect for a growing family"
"Walk-in closets, great light"
"Four floors, original woodwork"
blocks.x: Discriminatory advertising includes any statement that indicates a preference based on a protected class. "Perfect for a growing family" describes the ideal buyer, not the house, and signals a familial status preference. HUD's long-standing advertising guidance says descriptions of the property, like walk-in closets, and of the neighborhood, like a walk to transit, do not violate the Act. The walking-distance phrase tempts people who worry about disability, but it describes location, not who may buy.

blocks.html: Grace Okafor reads the draft over Jordan's shoulder and likes one line in particular. "'A neighborhood on the rise.' That's true. We watched it happen for 28 years." Jordan agrees that prices have risen, and still flags the phrase.

blocks.q: Why should Jordan replace "a neighborhood on the rise" in the Okafor ad?
c: It can read as a comment on who is moving in; facts say it better
It is a statement about value, which only a licensed appraiser may make
It names a protected class, which ads may not mention in any context
It is puffery, which the DOS advertising rule bans in listing copy
blocks.x: "On the rise," like "changing" or "up and coming," names no protected class, but in a neighborhood whose residents are mostly Black it is easily read as a comment about who is arriving. That makes it a steering signal to buyers and an invitation to a complaint. The fix is facts anyone can check: recent sale prices on the block, the subway lines, the park. It is not an appraisal, and it does not literally name a class, which is why the phrase slips past people.

blocks.html: The in-law line goes too. "A top-floor suite with its own bath" tells a buyer exactly what is there, and anyone can imagine who might use it. Grace agrees, and asks Jordan to add the garden's age: the pear tree is older than she is.

blocks.title: Jordan's rewrite
blocks.html: "1899 brownstone on a tree-lined Bed-Stuy block. Four floors, original parlor-floor woodwork, two fireplaces, 50-foot garden. Top-floor suite with private bath. Walk-in closets, south light, 6 minutes to the A and C at Nostrand Avenue. $2,150,000. Hudson & Hart Realty, licensed real estate broker, (718) 555-0100. Jordan Reyes, licensed real estate salesperson."

blocks.title: New York adds its own advertising rules
blocks.html: Every ad must carry the broker's name and the broker's address or phone number, and a salesperson must be identified as a "licensed real estate salesperson," under the DOS advertising rule (19 NYCRR 175.25). The fair housing content rules come from three statutes at once: the federal Act, the NYS Human Rights Law, which adds age, marital status, lawful source of income and other classes, and in the five boroughs the NYC Human Rights Law, which adds lawful occupation and more. A phrase that is fine under federal law can still be an age or marital status problem in New York.

Sal Russo filled out the tool's intake form himself. Under "ideal tenant" he typed: "Quiet, working, mature. No programs. English speaking so we can communicate. No pets." The tool turned that into ad copy.

blocks.title: AI draft, Astoria rental
blocks.html: "Sunny 2BR in a well-kept 6-unit building on 31st Avenue, 3rd floor walk-up. $2,450. Ideal for a mature working professional. W-2 income required, no programs. English-speaking tenants preferred. No pets. Not suitable for wheelchairs."

blocks.q: Which revision of Sal's ad is compliant?
c: "2BR, 3rd floor walk-up. Mature professionals preferred. No programs."
"2BR, 3rd floor walk-up. English speakers preferred. All incomes welcome."
"2BR, 3rd floor walk-up. Lawful income welcome. Assistance animals OK."
"2BR, 3rd floor walk-up. Not suitable for wheelchairs. Vouchers welcome."
blocks.x: "3rd floor walk-up" describes the building and is fine; "not suitable for wheelchairs" describes people and signals a disability preference. "Mature" and "professional" raise age and source of income issues, "no programs" and "W-2 income" exclude lawful income, and "English speakers preferred" is a national origin problem. A no-pets rule is lawful, but stating that assistance animals are accepted avoids the impression that people with disabilities need not apply.

blocks.html: Sal pushes back by phone. "It's my building. Can't I at least say what I want in the ad? Nobody has to answer it." His building has six units, so no owner-occupancy exemption covers him at any level, and even an exempt owner may not publish a discriminatory ad. Jordan adds one more point: if the ad runs under Hudson & Hart's name, the brokerage and Jordan are liable for every word in it, alongside Sal.

blocks.q: Sal suggests running his original wording himself on Craigslist, without Hudson & Hart's name. Which statement is correct?
c: Sal may do it, because owners are exempt from advertising rules
Sal may do it, if he does not mention the brokerage anywhere
Sal may not, since the ad rules bind owners, but Jordan has no duty
Sal may not, and Jordan should decline any role in that listing
blocks.x: The advertising ban applies to everyone who publishes housing ads, owners included, and New York's owner exemptions do not reach statements and advertisements. Sal's six-unit building has no exemption anyway. If Sal insists on discriminatory terms, Jordan cannot participate and should tell Diane, who decides whether the brokerage keeps the listing. The answer that Jordan has no duty misses the licensee's obligation not to take part in, or help with, discrimination by a client.

blocks.html: Where does the line between a description and a preference come from? Courts use an ordinary reader test: would an ordinary reader understand the ad to suggest a preference for or against a protected group? HUD's 1995 advertising guidance to its own staff, still widely cited, gives examples on the safe side: "great view," "fourth-floor walk-up," "walk-in closets," "jogging trails," "walk to bus stop." There is no official list of banned words, so context matters. The same word can describe a room in one ad and a person in another.

head: Instead of
Write
Why
rows: Describes the house, not the buyer
Age and source of income signals removed
States the fact, lets each reader decide
All lawful sources of income welcome
New York protects lawful source of income
6 minutes to the A at Nostrand
blocks.caption: Jordan's phrase swap sheet

blocks.html: Sal grumbles, then agrees to Jordan's version. What changed his mind was not the law but the math: the compliant ad drew 31 inquiries in three days, including a nurse with a voucher who signed a two-year lease and a retired bus driver who became the building's unofficial super. Wider ads reach more qualified people, which is what a landlord with a vacancy actually wants.

blocks.title: Describe the property, never the people
blocks.html: Exam items list four ad phrases and ask which is legal. The safe ones describe the home, the building, the services or the location: "fourth-floor walk-up," "walk-in closets," "great view," "near the 7 train," "no smoking," "no pets." The illegal ones describe the buyer or tenant: "ideal for," "perfect for," "mature," "professional," "singles," "no kids," "English speaking," "no Section 8," "not suitable for wheelchairs."
Sal asks one more question. Many people in the neighborhood read Spanish or Greek, and his nephew offers to translate. Can the ad run in those languages too?

blocks.q: Sal wants the compliant ad to run in English, Spanish and Greek. Which approach is correct?
c: Run English only, since other languages signal a national origin preference
Run the translations, but with lower rent in the English version
Run Greek alone, since most local readers know the language
Run all three, each with the same terms, rent and requirements
blocks.x: Publishing in several languages widens the pool of applicants, which is the point of fair housing marketing. The rule is consistency: every version must carry the same rent, terms and requirements, so no group gets a better deal or a different message. Running a single non-English version could be read as aiming at one national origin group, and different terms by language is unequal treatment. Translation itself signals nothing improper.

blocks.text: Draft three: the Long Island City one-bedroom

blocks.html: The third listing is a one-bedroom in a 30-story condo tower in Long Island City, owned by an investor who lives in Florida and hired Hudson & Hart as the landlord's broker. The AI tool wrote the copy and also proposed a paid social media campaign.

blocks.title: AI-generated campaign settings
blocks.html:
Copy: "Live where the city plays. Rooftop pool, co-working lounge, 24-hour doorman. 1BR, $3,750."
Images: four AI-generated lifestyle photos showing people in their twenties at the rooftop pool.
Audience: ages 22 to 34, interests "nightlife" and "startups," within ZIP codes 11101 and 11109 only.
Fees: none listed.

blocks.q: What is wrong with the proposed audience settings?
c: Nothing, since targeting is a private choice that appears in no ad copy
Age and ZIP targeting can keep protected groups from seeing the ad
Paid social ads for housing may run citywide but not in a single ZIP code
The ZIP targeting is fine, but the age range must start at 18 instead of 22
blocks.x: Who sees an ad can discriminate as surely as what it says. HUD charged Facebook in 2019 over tools that let housing advertisers exclude people by age, sex, family status and location proxies, and Meta settled with the Justice Department in 2022. Meta now requires housing ads to run in a special category that blocks targeting by age, gender and ZIP code. Widening the age range slightly still leaves an age filter in place, which New York's age protection reaches as well.

blocks.q: The four lifestyle images show only people in their twenties. What should Jordan do?
c: Keep them, since images cannot violate fair housing law
Keep them, but add an Equal Housing Opportunity logo to each
Replace them with photos of the unit and amenities
Replace them with images of a family with young children
blocks.x: Images can indicate a preference just as words can. A campaign showing only people in one age group, at a building pitched as where the city plays, tells older applicants and families that the landlord has someone else in mind. The cleanest fix is to show the property itself: the unit, the views, the pool, the lounge. Swapping in a different single demographic repeats the problem in another direction, and a logo does not cure a message.

blocks.html: The building's amenity sheet, which the tool copied into the listing, has a line that catches Jordan's eye: "Rooftop pool: adults only. Children not permitted at any time." The condo board adopted the rule two years ago after complaints about noise.

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle the pool rule in the listing?
c: Repeat it, because a condo board's house rules are outside fair housing law
Flag it: a blanket ban on children limits amenities by familial status
Repeat it, but add that families are welcome to apply for the unit
Drop the pool from the listing so the rule never comes up with tenants
blocks.x: Restricting access to amenities because of a protected class is discrimination, and condo boards are covered housing providers. A total ban on children at the pool limits families with children by familial status. A board may adopt neutral safety rules, such as requiring an adult to supervise young swimmers. Jordan should keep the rule out of the ad and tell the owner and Diane so the board can fix it. Hiding the pool avoids the ad problem but leaves the discriminatory rule in place.

blocks.html: Jordan emails the owner's representative and Diane the same afternoon. The board agrees to replace the rule with one requiring an adult to accompany swimmers under 14, which applies to every family in the building, and the listing describes the pool without any rule at all.

The replacement photos come from the building's own marketing kit: the unit at sunset, the pool with nobody in it, the lounge, the view of the Queensboro Bridge. Jordan switches the campaign to the platform's housing category, which does not allow the age and ZIP settings, and widens the location to the city.

Jordan also notices the fee line is blank. Under New York City's FARE Act, in effect since June 11, 2025, a broker hired by the landlord is paid by the landlord, and any fee a tenant must pay has to be disclosed in the listing and in the lease. The investor confirms there is a $20 application fee for the credit check and nothing else. Jordan adds it.

blocks.q: What must the LIC listing say about fees under the FARE Act?
c: It must list the broker fee the tenant will pay at lease signing
It need say nothing, since fees are disclosed in the lease alone
It may omit fees under $100, which the law treats as incidental
It must disclose every fee the tenant pays, here the $20 fee
blocks.x: The FARE Act shifts the fee of a landlord's broker to the landlord and requires that any fees a tenant must pay be disclosed both in the listing and in the lease. Here that means the $20 credit check fee, which is also within the statewide application fee limit. The tenant pays no broker fee, so listing one would be wrong twice. There is no small-fee exception, and lease-only disclosure is the old practice.

blocks.html: On Saturday Jordan films a 30-second video tour of the LIC unit for a personal TikTok account that Jordan uses to promote listings. The tool suggests a caption: "POV: you're a single guy and you just found the perfect bachelor pad."

blocks.q: Can Jordan use the suggested caption on a personal account?
c: No, because it signals a sex and marital status preference
Yes, because personal accounts are not regulated as advertising
Yes, if the video does not show the unit's address or the rent
No, because salespeople may not promote listings on personal accounts
blocks.x: A personal account used to promote listings is advertising for fair housing purposes and under the DOS rules, so it needs the broker's name and the salesperson's license title. "Single guy" signals a preference by sex and by marital status, which New York protects. Salespeople may promote listings on their own accounts with the broker's approval and the required identification. Leaving out the address does not change what the caption says about who the unit is for.

blocks.html: Jordan posts the tour with a new caption: "1BR with skyline views, rooftop pool, 24-hour doorman. $3,750. Steps to the 7. Hudson & Hart Realty. Jordan Reyes, licensed real estate salesperson." The video gets more views than any of Marcus's posts that month, which Jordan mentions to no one.

blocks.text: Who is responsible for what the tool wrote

blocks.html: At Monday's meeting Marcus says the solution is simple: if the tool writes something illegal, that is the vendor's problem. Diane asks the room who would be named in a complaint.

blocks.q: If an AI tool drafts a discriminatory ad and a salesperson publishes it, who is responsible?
c: The vendor alone, because it generated the language
The salesperson and supervising broker who published it
Nobody, because no person intended to discriminate
The owner alone, because the ad promoted the owner's unit
blocks.x: Fair housing law looks at the statement and who published it, not at how the draft was produced. The salesperson who posted it and the broker responsible for supervising advertising are both exposed, and the owner can be too. Intent is not required for an advertising violation; a statement indicating a preference is enough. Blaming the vendor is like blaming a word processor. Brokers should review AI output exactly as they review any agent's copy.

blocks.html: Marcus has one more objection. "Fine, we review the ads. But the website is a website. Nobody reads the footer." Diane pulls up the Hudson & Hart homepage on the conference room screen and asks Jordan to list what the law requires to be there.

blocks.q: Which of these must appear on Hudson & Hart's website under New York rules?
c: A list of the neighborhoods each agent personally recommends
The demographic makeup of each area where the firm has listings
The NYS Fair Housing Notice and the firm's posted SOPs
A disclaimer that the firm is not responsible for its agents' posts
blocks.x: New York requires brokers to display the state's Fair Housing Notice on their websites as well as in offices and at open houses, and to post their notarized standardized operating procedures for homebuyers. Housing providers must also post the reasonable accommodation notice on their homepage. Demographic data by area is exactly the kind of information that invites steering. A disclaimer about agents' posts does not shift the broker's supervisory responsibility.

blocks.html: Diane turns the discussion into policy. Every ad, post and paid campaign gets a licensee's review before it publishes, and for paid social ads someone checks that the housing category is selected and no audience filters remain. The office keeps a copy of each ad as it ran, with the date, so the firm can show what it published if a complaint arrives a year later.

blocks.q: Which item belongs on Hudson & Hart's ad review checklist?
c: Confirm paid housing ads carry no age, gender or ZIP filters
Confirm each ad lists the owner's preferred tenant profile
Confirm images show the same type of person in every single listing
Confirm the ad avoids mentioning walk-ups or stairs
blocks.x: A review checklist should catch the problems this case found: preference words, discriminatory images, targeting filters, missing broker identification and missing fee disclosures. Confirming that paid housing ads run without age, gender or ZIP targeting goes straight at the Meta issue. Describing a walk-up is a lawful description of the property, so avoiding it gains nothing. A preferred tenant profile is exactly what an ad may not express, and identical people in every image is a preference problem.

blocks.title: The 10-second ad test
blocks.html: Read the ad and ask two questions. Does every phrase describe the home, the building, the services or the location? Would any reader in any protected class feel the ad was not meant for them? If the first answer is no or the second is yes, rewrite it. Then check the boxes: broker name and contact, salesperson's license title, fees disclosed for NYC rentals, and no audience filters on paid placements.

items: Describe the property, never the people: walk-ups, closets, views and transit are fine; "perfect for," "mature," "single," "no programs" and "English speaking" are not.
The ad ban binds owners too, even exempt ones, and a licensee may not take part in a client's discriminatory advertising.
Images and audience targeting can discriminate; housing ads should run without age, gender or ZIP filters and should show the property.
A personal account used to promote listings is advertising, subject to fair housing law and the DOS identification rules.
AI output is the publisher's speech: the salesperson and supervising broker are responsible, so review every word and log what ran.

lessons.title: Case file: Biscuit and the Board on West End Avenue
lessons.tagline: An emotional support dog in a no-dogs co-op, a tenant who needs a ramp, and a relay call that went unanswered.
objectives: Decide what documentation, fees and conditions a housing provider may lawfully require for an assistance animal.
Apply the NYC cooperative dialogue and written determination requirements to an accommodation request.
Sort requests into accommodations and modifications and decide who pays under New York law.
Apply New York's reasonable accommodation notice rule to a broker's first substantive contact.

blocks.title: West End Avenue, a board package with a dog in it
blocks.html: Nora Bishop, a 38-year-old architect, is in contract to buy a two-bedroom co-op on West End Avenue for $1,240,000. Jordan represents her. The building's house rules say cats are allowed and dogs are not. Nora has Biscuit, a 48-pound mixed-breed dog her psychiatrist recommended three years ago to help with a disability that is not visible to anyone who meets her. Kim Alvarez, the board president, has run this building's admissions for a decade and has turned down dog owners before. Nora asks Jordan two questions: when should she tell the board about Biscuit, and can they say no?

Jordan's advice on timing is practical. A request for a reasonable accommodation can be made at any time, but raising it in writing with the board package gives the board time to process it and creates a record. Nora writes a one-page request: she has a disability, Biscuit helps with it, and she asks for an exception to the no-dogs rule. She attaches a letter from her psychiatrist. Kim calls Jordan the next morning with a different view of the law.

blocks.q: Kim says the building is a private cooperative corporation, "basically a private club," so fair housing rules on animals do not apply to its admissions. Is she right?
c: Yes, because co-op boards may reject buyers for whatever reason they like
No, a residential co-op is a housing provider covered by the law
Yes, but just for buyers who have not yet closed on their shares
No, but just because the building has more than four units
blocks.x: The private club exemption covers non-commercial lodging a genuine private club provides to its members, not a residential building whose apartments are sold on the open market. A co-op board deciding who may buy and live in a unit is a housing provider under federal, state and city law. Boards can reject buyers for many lawful reasons, such as finances, which is why the any-reason answer tempts, but never for a protected reason or by refusing an accommodation.

blocks.html: Kim's instinct comes from a real feature of New York co-ops: boards traditionally reject buyers without giving a reason, and courts give their admissions decisions wide deference under the business judgment rule. That freedom ends where the protected classes begin. A board that rejects a buyer because of a disability, or that refuses a reasonable accommodation the buyer needs to live there, is liable just as a landlord would be. The silence that usually protects boards becomes a problem when the buyer has a written accommodation request in the file and the board has no written answer.
Kim accepts the point and sends a formal response. The board wants four things before it will consider the request.

blocks.title: Board's letter to Nora, item by item
blocks.html:
1. A copy of Ms. Bishop's medical records and her diagnosis.
2. A refundable $1,000 pet deposit and a $50 monthly pet fee.
3. Proof the dog weighs under 25 pounds, the building's limit for cats and other permitted animals.
4. Proof of registration with a national emotional support animal registry.

blocks.q: Which item can the board lawfully request?
c: Her medical records and diagnosis, to confirm the disability exists
The $1,000 deposit, since it is refundable if there is no damage
Proof the dog meets the building's 25-pound animal limit
None of the four; reliable documentation of the need would suffice
blocks.x: When a disability is not obvious, a housing provider may ask for reliable information showing a disability and a disability-related need for the animal, such as a letter from a treating professional. It may not demand records or a diagnosis. Assistance animals are not pets, so no pet deposit or fee may be charged, refundable or not. Size and weight limits do not apply to assistance animals. A registry certificate is not required, and as HUD notes, not reliable by itself.

blocks.html: Before Jordan answers, Nora mentions that a friend told her to skip the doctor and buy an "official ESA certificate" online for $79, with a registration number and a photo ID card for Biscuit. "It looks very official. Should I send that instead of the letter?"

blocks.q: How should Jordan respond to the online certificate idea?
c: Send it, because registration makes the dog an official assistance animal
Send both, because the board has to accept whatever Nora provides
Send the letter; an online certificate alone is not reliable proof
Send neither, because a co-op cannot request any documentation
blocks.x: There is no official national registry for assistance animals, and HUD's guidance says certificates and registrations sold online, by themselves, are not reliable documentation. A letter from a professional who actually knows the person and the need is. Sending a purchased certificate can damage credibility with a board that is already skeptical. A co-op may request reliable documentation when the disability is not obvious, so the cannot-request answer is wrong as well.

blocks.html: Nora's psychiatrist letter already does what the law asks. It says she has treated Nora for four years, that Nora has a condition that substantially limits a major life activity, and that the dog alleviates symptoms of that condition. It does not name the condition, and it does not need to.

blocks.title: What HUD's assistance animal guidance says
blocks.html: HUD's 2020 notice on assistance animals (FHEO-2020-01) is the reference most boards and attorneys use. A provider may ask for documentation when the disability or the need is not observable. Documentation from a health care professional with personal knowledge of the person is reliable; a certificate or registration sold online, by itself, is not. Dogs, cats and other common household animals get the easiest path; a unique animal, such as a reptile or a farm animal, requires the requester to show a substantial disability-related need for that specific type of animal.

Kim's board then raises a concern it believes is decisive. A shareholder on the ninth floor, two floors above Nora's unit, has a severe dog allergy and a doctor's note to prove it. The board's draft response is a one-line denial "in fairness to an existing resident with a disability."

blocks.q: How should the board handle the conflict between Nora's request and the allergic neighbor?
c: Look for measures that meet both needs instead of denying either
Deny Nora, because the existing shareholder's disability came first
Grant Nora and tell the neighbor the allergy is a personal matter
Ask the shareholders to vote on whose disability should prevail
blocks.x: Both people may have disabilities, and neither need automatically defeats the other. The provider's job is to look for measures that work for both, such as assigning different elevators or times, keeping the dog out of shared areas near the ninth floor, adding air filtration in common spaces, or arranging separate laundry times. Seniority is not a legal tiebreaker. A building vote is never the method: disability rights are not decided by majority rule.

blocks.html: Six weeks pass. The board does not answer Nora's request in writing, does not suggest alternatives, and does not schedule her interview. Then Kim tells Jordan by phone, "The board is going to say no on the dog. Nothing personal."

blocks.q: Under the NYC Human Rights Law, what did the board fail to do?
c: Engage in dialogue and give a written final determination
Refer the request to the Commission on Human Rights for a ruling
Hold a vote of the shareholders before deciding the request
Return Nora's contract deposit once the denial was communicated
blocks.x: The city law requires covered housing providers to engage in a cooperative dialogue, in good faith and within a reasonable time, with a person who requests an accommodation, and then to give a written final determination stating what was granted or denied. Failing to engage is a separate violation, even apart from whether the denial was justified. There is no referral step to the Commission before deciding. The deposit is a contract matter for Nora's attorney, not an accommodation duty.

blocks.title: How a provider should handle any accommodation request

items.title: Log it
items.html: Record the date the request arrived, oral or written. No magic words are required; "I need an exception because of my disability" is a request.

items.title: Ask only what is needed
items.html: If the disability or need is not obvious, ask for reliable documentation of both. Nothing more.

items.title: Talk
items.html: Discuss the request and any alternatives with the person, promptly and in good faith. In NYC this cooperative dialogue is mandatory.

items.title: Decide in writing
items.html: Grant, grant with reasonable conditions, or deny for a lawful reason, and put the final determination in writing.

items.title: Keep the file
items.html: Keep the request, documentation, notes and determination with the transaction records.

blocks.html: Jordan tells Kim, in writing and politely, what the city law requires, and copies Priya, who represents Nora on the purchase. The board's attorney calls Priya the same week. The board meets with Nora, proposes that Biscuit use the service elevator and avoid the ninth-floor landing, and offers to install a HEPA filter in the lobby. Nora agrees. The written determination grants the accommodation with those conditions. Nora closes in May, and Biscuit rides the service elevator without incident.

blocks.q: A board member then proposes adding a condition: Nora must keep Biscuit muzzled in all common areas because "dogs that size can be aggressive." Biscuit has no history of aggression. This condition is:
c: Lawful, because the board can set any condition for safety
Lawful, if the board applies the same rule to cats
Unlawful; a direct threat needs evidence about this animal
Unlawful, because an accommodation cannot carry any conditions
blocks.x: A provider may deny or condition an assistance animal only on an individualized assessment of the specific animal's actual conduct, such as a history of biting, not on fears about its size or breed. A muzzle rule based on a stereotype about large dogs fails that test. Reasonable conditions are allowed, and the elevator and landing terms here are a good example, so the never-allowed answer goes too far. Applying a pointless rule to cats does not make it reasonable.

blocks.html: Back in Astoria, Sal Russo calls with a different kind of request. His longtime tenant on the second floor, Walter Brennan, 74, has started using a walker after hip surgery. Walter has asked for three things: permission to install grab bars in his bathroom, a ramp over the three steps at the building entrance, and a change in his rent due date from the 1st to the 5th, because his Social Security payment now arrives on the 3rd.

head: Walter's request
Accommodation or modification
Who pays
rows: Generally the tenant, with possible restoration at move-out
In New York, the housing provider, for reasonable common-area changes
No cost issue; a rule change
blocks.caption: Sorting the three requests

blocks.q: Who pays for Walter's grab bars, and what may Sal require?
c: Sal pays, because every disability modification is the owner's cost
Walter pays; Sal may require a licensed installer and restoration
Walter pays, but Sal may not ask anything else about the work
Sal and Walter split the cost equally under the Human Rights Law
blocks.x: Under the NYS Human Rights Law and the federal Act, a reasonable modification to a tenant's own unit is generally at the tenant's expense. The landlord may require that the work be done in a workmanlike manner, with any permits, and may condition a rental modification on restoring the interior at move-out where reasonable, ordinary wear and tear excepted. Grab bars are often left in place by agreement. The owner-pays rule belongs to common areas in New York, which is the next question.

blocks.q: Sal says the ramp is "Walter's project, Walter's money." Under New York's required notice of tenants' rights, who generally pays for a reasonable ramp at the common entrance?
c: Walter, because modifications are the tenant's cost in each case
The city, through a disability access grant program
Sal, as the housing provider, for common-area changes
Nobody, because buildings under 10 units are exempt from ramps
blocks.x: New York's notice of tenants' rights to reasonable accommodations states that the housing provider pays for reasonable modifications to common use areas, while tenants pay for changes inside their own units. A ramp over three entrance steps is a classic common-area modification. The provider can still argue undue burden or code limits, and the parties can discuss alternatives such as a portable ramp. Applying the tenant-pays rule to the entrance is the mistake Sal is making.

blocks.q: Is moving Walter's rent due date to the 5th a reasonable accommodation Sal must consider?
c: No, because rent due dates are a business term, not a rule
No, unless Walter agrees to pay a late fee each month
Yes, but Sal may charge a fee for making the administrative change
Yes, a rule change tied to benefit timing may be reasonable
blocks.x: A reasonable accommodation is a change in a rule, policy, practice or service. Shifting a due date so a tenant whose disability benefits arrive on the 3rd can pay on time is a well-known example, and it costs the landlord little. Charging a fee for granting an accommodation undercuts it, and New York already limits late fees. Calling the due date a business term is the trap: almost every housing rule is a business term, and that is what accommodations adjust.

blocks.html: Walter's daughter, encouraged by how quickly Sal said yes, asks for one more thing: an elevator. The building is a six-unit walk-up with no shaft, and a contractor estimates that adding one would cost about $280,000 and take a unit out of service.

blocks.q: How should Sal respond to the elevator request?
c: Install it, since a disability request cannot be refused on cost
Install it, but raise every tenant's rent to cover the full cost
Decline it, and refuse to discuss any other options with Walter
Decline it as an undue burden; discuss alternatives with Walter
blocks.x: A provider may refuse a request that imposes an undue financial and administrative burden or fundamentally alters the housing. A $280,000 elevator that eliminates a unit in a six-unit building almost certainly qualifies. Refusal is not the end of the conversation: the provider should explore alternatives, such as transferring Walter to a ground-floor unit when one opens. Refusing to discuss anything else turns a lawful denial into a failure to accommodate, and in NYC it skips the required dialogue.

blocks.html: Walter's family agrees to a transfer to the first-floor unit that opens in March, at the same rent. Sal grants the original three requests, with a one-page agreement on the grab bars and a contractor's quote of $2,900 for the ramp. He asks Jordan to market a vacant third-floor unit in the same building the following month, which brings up a duty Jordan owes before showing anyone the apartment.

blocks.title: The notice at first substantive contact
blocks.html: Executive Law 170-d and the Division of Human Rights' rules require housing providers, including real estate brokers, to give prospective tenants a written notice of their right to request reasonable accommodations and modifications. Brokers give it at first substantive contact, the same moment as the agency and fair housing disclosures. Landlords give it to new tenants within 30 days of the start of a tenancy and post it in a conspicuous, well-lit place in the building and prominently on their website homepage. It may be delivered on paper or electronically, in 12-point type or larger.

blocks.q: Jordan has a first substantive conversation with a prospective tenant for Sal's third-floor unit. Which statement about the reasonable accommodation notice is correct?
c: Jordan gives it now, in writing, with the other disclosures
Jordan gives it just if the prospect mentions a disability
Sal gives it at lease signing, so Jordan has no obligation here
It is required for co-op and condo sales, not for rentals
blocks.x: New York requires brokers to give prospective tenants the written reasonable accommodation and modification notice at first substantive contact. It goes to everyone, not only to people who disclose a disability, which would itself be a form of unequal treatment. The landlord's separate duty to give the notice to new tenants within 30 days does not replace the broker's duty. The rule is a rental notice, so the co-op and condo answer reverses it.

blocks.text: Part three: the call Marcus hung up on

blocks.html: While Jordan is out, the office phone rings with a relay call. An operator explains that a deaf caller is using a relay service and will be typing, and that the operator will voice the messages. Marcus, covering the desk, says "We don't do these, sounds like a scam," and hangs up. The caller had asked about Sal's vacant unit.

blocks.q: What is the problem with Marcus's response?
c: Nothing, because relay calls are a common source of fraud
Refusing relay calls treats deaf callers unequally
It is a problem just if the caller had already applied
It is a problem for landlords, not for brokers
blocks.x: Relay services let deaf and hard of hearing people use the phone. Refusing to take relay calls, or treating them as presumptively fraudulent, means deaf applicants get less information and slower service than hearing applicants, which is disability discrimination. Fair housing organizations test exactly this. Brokers are covered just like landlords. Fraud concerns are handled the way they are for any caller: verify identity and funds during the normal application process, the same way for everyone.

blocks.html: The same week, a different prospect for Sal's unit emails Jordan that she has an emotional support bearded dragon, a lizard that lives in a glass tank. Sal has never heard of such a thing and asks whether he has to allow it.

blocks.q: How should Sal evaluate the bearded dragon request?
c: Refuse it, because assistance animals are limited to dogs
Approve it without any documentation, since the animal stays in a tank
Ask for documentation of a need for this specific animal
Refuse it, because reptiles are classified as exotic pets in New York
blocks.x: Under HUD's guidance, a unique animal that is not commonly kept in households, such as a reptile, may be an assistance animal, but the requester carries a heavier burden: she must show a disability-related need for that specific type of animal. Sal may ask for that documentation. Dogs are not the only possible assistance animals, which is why the dogs-only answer fails. Skipping documentation for a non-obvious disability is not required just because the animal is small or contained.

blocks.html: Diane calls the relay service back, reaches the caller, apologizes, and schedules a showing. That afternoon she adds a line to the office procedures: relay calls are answered like any other call, in order received, with the same information. She also adds text messages and email as standard ways for any prospect to reach the office, so a caller who cannot use a voice line never depends on one agent's judgment about whether to pick up. The caller, a pharmacist named Owen Castellano, rents the unit the following week and signs a two-year lease.

blocks.title: Accommodation, modification, or neither
blocks.html: Exam questions sort requests. A change to a rule (an animal in a no-pets building, a due date, a parking space assignment, a transfer to a ground-floor unit) is an accommodation. A change to the physical space (grab bars, a ramp, a widened doorway) is a modification. Neither may carry a fee for the privilege of asking, and a provider may refuse only for undue burden, fundamental alteration, a direct threat shown by individualized evidence, or no disability-related need.

items: Co-op boards are housing providers; the private club exemption does not cover residential admissions.

For an assistance animal, a provider may ask for reliable documentation of disability and need, but not records or a diagnosis; online registrations alone are not reliable, and no pet fees, deposits or weight limits apply.
In NYC, providers must engage in a cooperative dialogue and issue a written final determination.
Tenants generally pay for modifications inside their units (with possible restoration); in New York the provider pays for reasonable common-area modifications.
Brokers give the written reasonable accommodation notice to prospective tenants at first substantive contact, and must treat relay calls like any other call.

lessons.title: Case file: The Two Callers from Massapequa
lessons.tagline: A fair housing group's paired test of a new Long Island branch, read side by side with the office's own log.
objectives: Apply the SOP rules of RPL 442-h(4) to a brokerage's practices and to a change in its procedures.
Analyze paired testing evidence to identify unequal treatment and misrepresented availability.
Decide which enforcement forums, deadlines and penalties apply to a fair housing complaint against a licensee and a brokerage.
Choose compliant responses after a complaint, including record preservation and avoiding retaliation.

blocks.title: Massapequa, a branch office's first audit
blocks.html: In January, Hudson & Hart opened its first Long Island branch, a storefront on Merrick Road in Massapequa with six agents who came over from a smaller firm. Carla Ruiz, an associate broker with eleven years in the business, manages it. In October a letter arrives at the Brooklyn office from a Long Island fair housing organization. It says the organization conducted paired tests of the Massapequa office in March, describes two phone calls and two visits, and states that it intends to file complaints with the state and federal agencies. Diane drives out the same afternoon with a folder, a notary stamp in her bag and Jordan in the passenger seat. "Before we read their version," she says, "we read ours."

Diane starts with the firm's standardized operating procedures, the written rules RPL 442-h(4) requires every broker to adopt for what prospective homebuyers must do before receiving services. Hudson & Hart's version is posted on the website, the app and the office wall.

blocks.title: Hudson & Hart standardized operating procedures for prospective homebuyers (posted version)
blocks.html:
Identification: Required. Every prospective buyer shows government-issued photo ID before an in-person showing.
Exclusive broker agreement: Not required before the first showing.
Mortgage pre-approval: Not required before a showing. Required, or proof of funds, before submitting an offer.
Date stamped and notarized: March 3, 2023. Posted at hudsonhart.example and in all offices.

Carla tells Diane that the Massapequa agents were trained on their old firm's habits and "use judgment" about pre-approval. Some ask every caller for a letter before showing anything. Some ask only when they are not sure the buyer is serious.

blocks.q: What is the main problem with the Massapequa agents' approach to pre-approval?
c: Pre-approval may not be requested at any point in a NY sale
Agents applied a requirement the SOP omits, and not to everyone
The SOP is invalid because it was notarized more than a year ago
Agents may vary SOP terms as long as they log the reason in writing
blocks.x: The point of the SOP law is that the same prerequisites apply to every prospective buyer. Hudson & Hart's SOP says no pre-approval before a showing, so an agent who demands one from some callers is adding a requirement selectively, which is exactly the unequal treatment the Newsday investigation found on Long Island. A notarized SOP stays valid until it changes. Pre-approval may be required, if the SOP says so and it is applied to everyone.

blocks.html: Diane decides to change the SOP anyway. Since August 2024, MLS rules have required a written agreement with a buyer before an MLS participant tours a home with that buyer, and she wants the SOP to say so plainly. She also wants it to say exactly which forms of ID are accepted, so no agent improvises.

blocks.q: What must Hudson & Hart do to change its SOP?
c: File the revised version with DOS and wait for approval before using it
Email the change to agents; posting can wait until the license renewal
Date stamp, notarize and post it within 30 days; archive the old one
Post the change on the website, with no notary needed for any amendment
blocks.x: RPL 442-h(4) requires a broker who changes its procedures to date stamp, notarize and post the new version within thirty days, archive the prior version, and keep the file while the license is active. The broker then affirms compliance at license renewal. The original 2021 law contemplated filing with DOS, but the 2022 amendment replaced filing with notarizing and posting, which is why the filing answer is outdated. Notarization applies to every version, not just the first.

blocks.html: Then Diane reads the organization's letter. The test involved two testers with matched profiles: same income, same savings, same credit range, both first-time buyers, both interested in the same $689,000 Cape Cod on Clocks Boulevard. One tester, Monique Dawson, is Black. The other, Laura Brennan, is white. Diane pulls the office's own inquiry log and the agent's texts for the same days.

head: Date and time
Tester
What the agent, Brian Kessler, did
rows: Asked for a pre-approval letter and a copy of her ID before any showing; said the house "might already have an accepted offer"
Offered a showing that afternoon; mentioned two other houses "you'd really like"; asked for no documents
Showed the house; checked ID at the door per the SOP
No offer was accepted on the house until April 2
blocks.caption: What the log and the organization's notes show

blocks.q: Which description best fits Brian's conduct?
c: Unequal treatment and false availability claims, both by race
Steering alone, since he suggested other houses to one of the testers
No violation, since the ID check followed the posted SOP
Blockbusting, since he discussed offers on the property
blocks.x: Brian demanded documents from one tester and not the other, offered one a same-day showing and the other nothing, ignored one tester's follow-up, and told one tester the house might be under offer when the MLS shows it was not. With matched profiles, the difference tracks race. That is unequal treatment and misrepresenting availability. Suggesting extra houses to one buyer is part of the unequal service, but calling it steering alone misses the core violations. Following the ID rule once does not cure the rest.

blocks.html: Carla asks Brian for his side before anything else. He does not deny the facts in the log. "I didn't do anything because of race. I just had a feeling the first caller wasn't serious. You get a sense."

blocks.q: Does Brian's lack of conscious intent defeat a fair housing claim based on the test?
c: Yes, because discrimination requires proof that he meant to discriminate
No, matched testers who differ in one trait show different treatment
Yes, if Brian completes implicit bias training before a hearing
No, but only because the firm's SOP was posted on the wall
blocks.x: Paired testing proves disparate treatment by comparison: two matched people, one difference, different service. A "feeling" that one caller was not serious, when the profiles were identical, is how implicit bias shows up in practice, and it does not excuse the result. Training after the fact is a good remedy but not a defense. The SOP matters because Brian departed from it, not because posting it decides the claim.

blocks.html: Diane also checks what Brian gave each caller. The phone call in which Monique Dawson discussed her budget and asked to see the house was a first substantive contact, and the office's records show what went out by email afterward.

blocks.q: Which disclosure did Brian owe both testers at that first substantive contact?
c: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement for the Cape
The reasonable accommodation notice, which applies to sales
No disclosure, because a phone inquiry is never substantive
blocks.x: Since June 2020, New York has required licensees to give the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form to prospective buyers, sellers, landlords and tenants at first substantive contact, along with the agency disclosure for residential sales. A phone call about budget and a specific house qualifies. The PCDS is the seller's form, delivered before contract. The reasonable accommodation notice is a rental notice. The log shows the form went to Brennan by email and never to Dawson, one more difference between the two.

blocks.html: Brian's first reaction, when Carla calls him in, is that the case is a setup. "Neither of them was really buying a house. They lied to me. How is that a complaint?"

blocks.q: Can the testers and their organization bring a claim even though the testers never intended to buy?
c: No, because a bona fide buyer is the one with a legal injury
No, because deceiving an agent makes any evidence inadmissible
Yes, but just through the Department of State, not the courts
Yes, testers have standing when given false information
blocks.x: Testers are lawful investigators. In Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982), the Supreme Court held that a tester who receives false information about availability because of race has standing to sue, even with no intent to buy or rent, and fair housing organizations whose work is impaired can sue too. Testing evidence is routinely used by HUD, the state Division of Human Rights and courts. The bona fide buyer argument is the one Havens rejected.

blocks.title: Why Long Island tests and who pays for testing
blocks.html: Newsday's three-year investigation, published in 2019, used paired testers on Long Island and found unequal treatment of minority buyers in a large share of tests. The Legislature responded with a package of laws effective in 2022: the SOP requirement, more fair housing hours in prelicensing and continuing education, a maximum DOS fine raised from $1,000 to $2,000, and license fee surcharges ($30 for brokers, $10 for salespersons) dedicated to statewide fair housing testing. Every licensee helps pay for the testing that checks them.

The organization's letter says it will file within weeks. The test happened on March 10, 2026; the letter arrived in October 2026. Diane maps the clocks on a legal pad for Priya, who will represent the firm.

head: Forum
Deadline
What it can lead to
rows: Investigation and conciliation; if charged, a hearing before an administrative law judge or, if either side elects, federal court; damages, injunctive relief and civil penalties
Actual and punitive damages, injunctive relief, attorney's fees
3 years for acts on or after February 15, 2024
Compensatory damages including emotional distress, punitive damages in housing cases, attorney's fees, civil fines up to $50,000, or $100,000 if willful, wanton or malicious
License discipline under RPL 441-c: reprimand, fine up to $2,000 per violation, suspension or revocation
blocks.caption: Diane's clock sheet

blocks.q: It is October 2026. Which filing is still available to the organization for the March 10, 2026 test?
c: HUD alone, since the state deadline ran out after 180 days
HUD, the Division of Human Rights, and federal court, at minimum
Federal court alone, since agency deadlines are 90 days
No forum, since complaints based on tests must be filed within 6 months
blocks.x: Seven months have passed. The HUD deadline is one year, a private federal suit has two years, and the Division of Human Rights now allows three years for acts on or after February 15, 2024. All three are open, and a DOS complaint about the licensee has no deadline. The 180-day and 1-year state deadlines are older rules that no longer apply to current acts. Nothing about testing shortens the filing periods.

blocks.html: Priya explains what a HUD complaint would look like. HUD investigates and tries to conciliate, meaning it negotiates a binding agreement among the parties. If conciliation fails and HUD finds reasonable cause, it issues a charge. The case then goes to a HUD administrative law judge unless any party elects to have it heard in federal court, where the Justice Department litigates on the complainant's behalf. Civil penalties are adjusted for inflation each year; the 2025 adjustment put the maximum for a first violation at about $26,000, with higher caps for repeat violators.

blocks.q: HUD has charged the firm after conciliation failed. Hudson & Hart would rather have a jury. What can it do?
c: Nothing, since HUD charges are heard by an administrative judge
Appeal the charge to the Department of State first
Elect to have the charge heard in federal court
Ask the Division of Human Rights to take over the case
blocks.x: After HUD issues a charge, any party, including the respondent, may elect to have the case decided in federal district court instead of before a HUD administrative law judge, and the Justice Department then brings the action. A jury is available there. DOS handles license discipline, not HUD charges, and the Division of Human Rights is a separate state forum, not a reviewer of HUD cases. Treating the administrative route as mandatory is the trap.

blocks.html: Had the test happened at the Brooklyn office instead, a fourth agency would be on the sheet: the NYC Commission on Human Rights, with a 1-year deadline (3 years for gender-based harassment) and its own testing program. The city law covers more classes, so the same facts can support more theories in the five boroughs than on Long Island.

Priya adds one wrinkle. Under the Human Rights Law, a complainant generally chooses between the Division of Human Rights and a lawsuit in state court; filing with the Division usually closes the state court door for the same claim. Federal filings run separately, and the agencies share complaints under work-sharing agreements, so one filing often reaches both.
Brian's next argument is aimed at the firm. "I'm an independent contractor. Whatever I did is on me, not Hudson & Hart." Carla, who supervised him, says nothing.

blocks.q: Who faces liability for Brian's conduct?
c: Brian alone, because independent contractors answer for their own acts
The firm alone, since a salesperson acts just as the broker's agent
Brian, plus the brokerage and supervisors for his acts
Nobody, if the firm fires Brian before any complaint is filed
blocks.x: Independent contractor status is a tax and employment classification. It does not end the broker's responsibility to supervise or the firm's liability for discrimination by its salespeople acting for it. Brian is liable for his own acts, the brokerage is liable for acts within the scope of his work and for any failure to supervise, and DOS can discipline both licensees. Firing him later does not erase what already happened, though it may matter to remedies.

blocks.html: Diane's next stop is DOS. A complaint from the organization to the Department of State would open a separate disciplinary file. RPL 441-c lists a violation of Article 15 of the Executive Law, the Human Rights Law, committed in a licensee's capacity as a broker or salesperson as grounds for discipline.

blocks.q: If DOS finds that Brian discriminated, which outcome is available?
c: A fine up to $2,000, and suspension or revocation
A fine of up to $1,000, with suspension reserved for repeat cases
Damages paid by DOS to the testers for emotional distress
A criminal conviction entered by the Department of State itself
blocks.x: DOS disciplines licenses: it can reprimand, fine up to $2,000 per violation since the 2022 increase, suspend or revoke. Half of the fine money is directed to the state's anti-discrimination in housing fund. The $1,000 figure is the old cap. DOS does not award damages to complainants; that is what HUD, the Division of Human Rights and the courts do. It does not enter criminal convictions either.

blocks.html: Brian has one more idea. He tells Carla he plans to delete his March texts, "since none of it matters now," and to stop answering any number he does not recognize. He also wants the office to refuse to work with anyone connected to the fair housing organization.

blocks.q: How should Diane respond to Brian's plans?
c: Approve them, since the texts are Brian's personal property
Approve the call screening but not the deletion of texts
Allow the deletion if Brian first prints a copy for himself
Stop all three: keep records, answer callers, no retaliation
blocks.x: Once a complaint is expected, the firm must preserve relevant records, including texts on phones used for business; destroying them invites sanctions and looks like guilt. Brokers keep transaction records for 3 years anyway. Screening out unknown callers would make service unequal for everyone the agent does not recognize. Refusing to deal with people because they support a fair housing complaint is retaliation, which federal and New York law prohibit separately. A printout kept by Brian is not preservation by the firm.

blocks.html: Walking out of Brian's office, Diane stops at the front window. The HUD Equal Housing Opportunity poster is there. The New York Fair Housing Notice is not; it was in a box from the old firm's move. She tapes it up herself and checks the branch's page on the firm website, which links to the notice correctly.

blocks.q: Where must the New York Fair Housing Notice be displayed for the Massapequa branch?
c: On the website alone, since it replaced the printed poster
In the office alone, unless a client asks for a copy
In the office, at open houses and on the website
At open houses only, since buyers do not visit the office
blocks.x: New York requires brokers to display the Fair Housing Notice in each office, at open houses and on their websites. The HUD poster is a separate federal requirement and does not replace it. A branch office has the same posting duties as the main office. Treating the website as a substitute for the office posting is a common shortcut that DOS inspectors catch.

blocks.html: Diane then does what Priya recommends. She removes Brian from client-facing work pending review, sends every Massapequa agent through the SOP again with a written acknowledgment, adds a shared inquiry log that records each caller's request, the time received, the time answered and what was offered, and schedules fair housing training for the branch beyond the continuing education minimum. She also writes to the organization offering to discuss resolution.

blocks.q: Which record would best show, in a future test, that the office treated callers equally?
c: A list of the agents' personal opinions about each caller's seriousness
A note of the race or national origin each caller seemed to have
Copies of every caller's ID and pre-approval letter, kept on file
A log of times, requests, answers and listings offered
blocks.x: A clean log that shows each caller got the same questions, the same speed and the same information is the best defense in a paired test, because testing measures exactly those things. Recording perceived race or national origin creates evidence of the very thing the firm must not consider. Collecting IDs and letters from callers goes beyond the SOP, which requires ID only before an in-person showing. Agents' opinions about seriousness are where implicit bias hides.

blocks.html: The case resolves in conciliation before HUD the following spring. Hudson & Hart pays damages to the organization and to the tester who was misled, agrees to three years of monitoring, adopts the new log and training, and reports to the organization twice a year. Brian's license is suspended by DOS for three months and he pays a fine. Carla, who had not caught the pattern, completes supervisor training and now reviews the branch inquiry log with each agent every Friday. Monique Dawson, who had been a tester for six years, tells the hearing officer what she tells every new tester: the call she made in March is the call real families make every day, and most of them never find out why the house was suddenly unavailable.

blocks.title: Penalties people mix up
blocks.html: HUD and the Division of Human Rights award damages and civil penalties; DOS disciplines licenses and fines up to $2,000 per violation; courts award damages, fees and injunctions. Deadlines differ too: HUD 1 year, federal court 2 years, Division of Human Rights 3 years for acts on or after February 15, 2024, NYC Commission 1 year (3 for gender-based harassment). Old materials still say $1,000 for DOS fines and 1 year for the Division of Human Rights.

items: SOPs must be applied identically to every prospective buyer; changes are date stamped, notarized and posted within 30 days, with old versions archived and compliance affirmed at renewal.
Paired tests measure documents demanded, availability claims, speed and follow-up; testers and fair housing organizations have standing to sue.
Map the forums: HUD 1 year, federal court 2 years, Division of Human Rights 3 years (or state court), DOS discipline with no deadline.
Liability reaches the agent, the brokerage and supervisors; independent contractor status is no shield.
After a complaint: preserve records, never retaliate, retrain, and keep a log that proves equal treatment.

lessons.title: Case file: Two Storefronts and Forty-One Doors on Jamaica Avenue
lessons.tagline: A new mixed-use building in Jamaica, Queens: a retail criteria sheet, two business loans, a lender list, and a punch list with fair housing written all over it.
objectives: Decide which federal, New York State and New York City laws reach commercial space in a mixed-use building and a broker who leases it.
Apply the Fair Housing Act design and construction requirements and the ADA to a new building, and decide who must fix what.
Apply the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and New York's credit discrimination rules to loan decisions that affect an agent's clients.
Decide how an agent responds when lender referrals or loan terms point to a fair lending problem.

blocks.title: Jamaica, Queens, eleven weeks before the temporary CO
blocks.html: Evelyn Park's newest building rises seven stories over Jamaica Avenue, three blocks from the LIRR station: two ground-floor storefronts, a lobby with a leasing office, an elevator, and 41 rental apartments on floors two through seven. The temporary certificate of occupancy is expected in January. Evelyn has signed Hudson & Hart to lease everything. Jordan will run the residential lease-up under Diane's supervision, and Marcus, who has done retail deals on this avenue for fifteen years, will lease the stores. On Monday Evelyn emails a one-page sheet titled "Retail tenant criteria" and a note: "First prospect tomorrow at 10. A pharmacist. Make it happen." Marcus forwards it to Jordan with one question: "What paperwork does a store tenant even get? None of the housing stuff applies to retail, right?"

The pharmacist is Dr. Ruth Asante, who has run the pharmacy department of a chain store in Hollis for nineteen years and wants her own shop. She is coming to see Store A, 2,400 square feet with frontage on the avenue. Marcus has an RPL 443 agency disclosure in one hand and the state's Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form in the other.

blocks.q: What should Marcus give Dr. Asante at their first substantive contact about Store A?
c: The RPL 443 agency disclosure, because she is a prospective tenant
Both forms, because every prospective tenant in New York gets both
The anti-discrimination disclosure form, but not the RPL 443 form
Neither form, because both are limited to residential transactions
blocks.x: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (19 NYCRR 175.28) applies to every property type, including commercial space and vacant land, so a store prospect gets it at first substantive contact. The RPL 443 agency disclosure covers residential 1 to 4 family sales and residential rentals, not a storefront. The trap is "neither form": the word housing in the title fools people into thinking the anti-discrimination form stops at the front door of the store.

blocks.html: Marcus hands over the form and keeps a signed copy for the deal file, which Hudson & Hart keeps for three years. Then he and Jordan read Evelyn's sheet together, and both of them stop at the first line.

blocks.title: Evelyn's "Retail tenant criteria" (as emailed)
blocks.html:
1. Ten-year minimum term. Principal should be young enough to see the full term through.
2. No houses of worship or religious organizations.
3. Married owners preferred. Single owners need a co-signer.
4. Personal guaranty from any tenant without three years of audited financials.
5. Permitted uses: retail, restaurant, or medical office, as allowed by zoning and the certificate of occupancy.

blocks.text: Who the law protects in a store

blocks.html: The federal Fair Housing Act reaches dwellings, so it does not govern who rents a pharmacy. That is where most people stop reading, and it is where New York keeps going. The New York State Human Rights Law makes it unlawful for an owner, lessee or managing agent to discriminate in renting land or commercial space because of race, creed, color, national origin, citizenship or immigration status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, military status, sex, age, disability, marital status, familial status, or status as a victim of domestic violence (Executive Law 296(5)(b)). A separate paragraph, 296(5)(c), covers real estate brokers and their salespersons for housing, land and commercial space alike. The New York City Human Rights Law has its own commercial space provision, so in Jamaica the same refusal can break a state and a city law at once.

blocks.q: Dr. Asante is 66. Under item 1 of Evelyn's sheet, Marcus is told to steer the store toward a younger applicant. What is the legal position?
c: Lawful, since the federal Fair Housing Act covers dwellings and not stores
Age discrimination in commercial space, which the state law reaches
Lawful, since age protection in New York ends at age 65 for tenants
Unlawful for Evelyn, but a leasing broker following orders is not liable
blocks.x: Executive Law 296(5)(b) bans age discrimination in renting commercial space, and 296(5)(c) separately makes it unlawful for a broker or salesperson to do it. Following the owner's instructions is no defense for the licensee. The tempting wrong answer is the federal one: it is true that the Fair Housing Act stops at dwellings, but New York law picks up the storefront. There is no upper age cutoff for the protection.
