blocks.html: Marcus calls Diane before he calls Evelyn. Diane's answer is the one every principal broker should give: the firm will not apply items 1 and 3, the agents will not discuss them with prospects, and she will tell Evelyn why in writing. Item 4 can stay, because a guaranty requirement based on financial history, applied to every small tenant the same way, is an ordinary credit term. Evelyn pushes back on the phone ("It's a business decision, not housing") and then agrees once Diane walks her through 296(5)(b) and the fact that the firm's license is on the line too. DOS can fine a licensee up to $2,000 per violation and suspend or revoke the license, on top of whatever the Division of Human Rights awards.

blocks.q: A single applicant for Store B has strong credit. Under item 3, Evelyn wants a co-signer from her but not from a married couple with weaker credit. This is:
c: Lawful, because marital status is protected for housing but not for stores
Lawful if the co-signer rule is disclosed in writing before the application
Marital status discrimination, unless the couple also has to get a co-signer
Marital status discrimination in commercial space under the state law
blocks.x: Marital status is on the commercial space list in 296(5)(b). A co-signer rule triggered by being single, and waived for a married couple with weaker numbers, treats applicants differently because of marital status. Disclosing an unlawful rule does not cure it. The near miss is the third choice: requiring the couple to get a co-signer too does not fix a rule that is triggered by marriage rather than by credit.

blocks.html: Item 2 is harder. On Thursday the pastor of a small congregation that meets in a school gym on Sundays asks Marcus about Store B for services and a weekday food pantry. Evelyn's reply is one line: "No churches." Marcus checks the building's certificate of occupancy and the zoning before answering. The ground floor is approved for retail and office occupancy. A space used for worship services by more than a handful of people is an assembly occupancy under the building code, which would need a different occupancy classification, egress work and, in NYC, a new or amended certificate of occupancy.

blocks.q: What may Marcus lawfully tell the congregation?
c: The owner does not rent to religious groups, so the space is unavailable
The same use and occupancy limits apply to them as to every applicant
Religious groups may rent if they pay a higher deposit for the risk
Store B is already promised to another tenant, to avoid an argument
blocks.x: Creed is protected in commercial space, so a refusal because the applicant is a religious organization is the problem, and lying about availability makes it worse. A neutral limit, such as the legal occupancy on the certificate of occupancy or a use clause applied to every assembly-type use, may be enforced if it is applied the same way to a yoga studio, an event space or a church. The higher deposit choice prices the creed instead of the use, which is still discrimination.

blocks.html: Marcus tells the pastor the truth: the space is not approved for assembly use, the owner would need to agree to a change of occupancy, and Evelyn has decided not to pursue one for any tenant. He gives the pastor the same listing package every prospect gets. Evelyn strikes item 2 from the sheet and replaces it with a use clause that lists permitted uses without mentioning religion.

blocks.text: The one federal law that reaches the store

blocks.html: Two weeks later a different applicant, Desmond Clarke, who owns two barbershops in Brooklyn, asks for Store B. Evelyn's assistant tells him by phone that it is "under negotiation," while it is still being shown to others. Desmond, who is Black, suspects why. His lawyer looks first at federal law. The Fair Housing Act does not help him, but the Civil Rights Act of 1866 does: it gives all citizens the same right as white citizens to make contracts and to lease and buy real and personal property, with no exemptions and no dwelling limit.

blocks.q: Desmond wants to sue in federal court over the false "under negotiation" answer. Which federal law fits a race claim about commercial space?
c: The Civil Rights Act of 1866, which covers all property and contracts
The Fair Housing Act, because the building contains 41 dwelling units
The Americans with Disabilities Act, as the store is open to the public
No federal law, since commercial leasing is left to the states
blocks.x: The 1866 Act reaches race discrimination in leasing any real or personal property and in making contracts, so it covers a storefront lease. The Fair Housing Act choice is tempting because the building has apartments, but the Act protects dwellings, and Store B is not one. Desmond can also file under the state and city Human Rights Laws, which reach commercial space directly.

blocks.title: Fair housing law does not stop at the lobby door
blocks.html: Exam items and real agents make the same mistake: they assume a commercial deal is outside fair housing law. Federally, the Fair Housing Act is dwellings only, but the 1866 Act covers race in any property deal. In New York, the state and city Human Rights Laws cover commercial space, the anti-discrimination disclosure form goes to commercial prospects, and a licensee who discriminates in a store lease answers to DOS as well as to the Division of Human Rights.

Dr. Asante signs a letter of intent for Store A. To build out the pharmacy she applies to a community bank for a $450,000 business loan, about half for fixtures and half for inventory. Her pharmacy plan shows enough projected income, and her own savings and credit cover the bank's guaranty requirement by themselves. Then the loan officer asks for two things: her husband's signature as co-guarantor, and "some comfort" about the term, because "at your age, ten years is a long loan." Dr. Asante forwards the email to Marcus and asks whether this is normal.

The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) and its rule, Regulation B, apply to every kind of credit, business loans included. A creditor may not discriminate because of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (if the applicant can contract), receipt of public assistance income, or the good faith exercise of consumer credit rights. New York adds its own credit law, Executive Law 296-a, covering credit for housing, land and commercial space and other credit, with a longer list that includes familial status, military status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression and disability.

blocks.q: Dr. Asante qualifies as guarantor on her own. Under Regulation B, the bank's request for her husband's signature is:
c: Allowed, because a spouse's signature is standard on business loans
Allowed, if the bank asks every married applicant for the same signature
Not allowed, because she qualifies under the bank's standards alone
Not allowed, unless the loan is for her home rather than her business
blocks.x: Regulation B bars a creditor from requiring the signature of an applicant's spouse, other than a joint applicant, when the applicant qualifies on her own under the creditor's standards, and the rule applies to guaranties on business credit. Asking every married applicant the same thing does not fix it, because the rule itself turns on marital status. The home loan choice is the trap: ECOA is not limited to consumer or housing credit.

blocks.q: What can the bank do about the loan officer's concern with Dr. Asante's age?
c: Deny the loan, since a lender may refuse any applicant over 65 by policy
Shorten the term to five years for her, given her age, as a precaution
Weigh real credit factors, such as the business plan, but not deny for age
Nothing, because ECOA bars any mention of age in a loan file
blocks.x: ECOA protects applicants of any age who can contract, and New York's 296-a also lists age. A lender judges the business plan, cash flow, collateral and guaranty, and Regulation B allows age to be considered only in narrow ways tied to a real element of creditworthiness, never as a reason in itself to deny or worsen terms. A shorter term imposed only because she is 66 is age discrimination with extra steps. The last choice overstates the rule: age may appear in the file, it just cannot drive the decision.

blocks.html: Marcus is careful here. He is not her lawyer and not a loan officer, so he does not tell her the bank broke the law. He tells her what the rules say, that she may ask the bank in writing for its standards and the basis for both requests, and that complaints about bank lending go to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau or the bank's regulator, and to the state Division of Human Rights under the state law. She sends the email. The husband's signature disappears from the term sheet, the age comment is not repeated, and then the bank goes quiet.

blocks.q: Five weeks after Dr. Asante submitted a completed application, the bank has said nothing. What does Regulation B require?
c: Notice of the decision within 30 days of a completed application
Notice of the decision within 60 days of the first conversation
Notice is required if the bank approves; silence means no
Notice of a denial if the applicant asks for one in writing
blocks.x: A creditor must notify an applicant of action taken within 30 days after receiving a completed application. For businesses with revenues of $1 million or less the notice can be oral, and the applicant has a right to the reasons for a denial. Silence for five weeks is itself a problem. The "silent bank means no" idea is exactly what the notice rule was written to stop: applicants are entitled to know, and to learn why.

blocks.html: The bank calls in week six with an approval at the rate in the term sheet. Store B goes to Lucia Ferreira, 34, who is opening a bakery and café with a $180,000 equipment loan from a different lender. At her application meeting, that loan officer asks whether she is "planning a family soon," because a new mother "might not keep bakery hours," and proposes counting only half of her catering income.

blocks.q: Which statement about the second loan officer's question and income haircut is accurate?
c: Both are allowed, because business loans are outside fair lending laws
The question is fine if it is optional, but the haircut is not allowed
Both are allowed, if the lender asks every female applicant the same thing
Neither is allowed: childbearing plans cannot drive the credit decision
blocks.x: Regulation B bars questions about birth control, childbearing or plans to have children, and bars assuming that income may be interrupted for that reason. New York's 296-a also bans discounting an applicant's income because of childbearing potential, sex or familial status. Asking every woman the same question is not equal treatment, it is sex discrimination applied consistently. The optional question choice is tempting, but optional or not, the question cannot be part of the decision.

blocks.html: Back in Brooklyn, Diane is auditing the office's buyer files, which is how she finds Marcus's two lender sheets. One lists four banks and credit unions with competitive rates. The other lists a single non-bank lender with higher rates and fees. Marcus has been handing the second sheet to buyers who speak Spanish or Haitian Creole as a first language, "because that lender has bilingual staff." The lender also sends Marcus a "marketing fee" for each closed loan.

blocks.q: What is the main fair housing problem with Marcus's two lender sheets?
c: Steering buyers to worse financing based on national origin
No problem, because a broker may recommend any lender to any buyer
Redlining, because he is ranking lenders by the areas they lend in
Blockbusting, because it pushes buyers into particular neighborhoods
blocks.x: The Fair Housing Act and New York law reach anyone in a residential real estate related transaction, including a broker who arranges or influences financing. Handing worse loan options to buyers because of their first language is steering by national origin, whatever the stated reason. Redlining is the near miss, but redlining limits credit by area; here the sorting is by the person. A bilingual lender belongs on the one list that every buyer gets.

blocks.html: The per-loan payment is a second, separate violation. RESPA Section 8 bars kickbacks and referral fees for settlement services on federally related residential loans, and calling it a marketing fee does not change what it pays for. Diane collects every copy of the second sheet, adds the bilingual lender to the main list with a note on its languages, stops the payments, reports to the firm's attorney, and schedules a fair lending session for the office. Marcus is unhappy. He is also, Diane notes, still licensed.

blocks.title: New York's two credit layers
blocks.html: ECOA and Regulation B cover all credit, with federal complaints to the CFPB or the lender's regulator. New York's Executive Law 296-a adds state protection in credit for housing, land and commercial space, with classes federal law lacks, such as sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, military status and familial status. Agents do not enforce either law, but they hear the comments first: "at your age," "your husband should sign," "are you planning a family." Write them down, tell the client the rule, and tell your broker.

In November, Jordan walks the building with Evelyn, her project manager, and Ray Kowalski, whom Evelyn hired to review the punch list before the lease-up photos are taken. Ray brought a tape measure, a level, and a printout of HUD's Fair Housing Act design guidelines. The building was designed after 1991, it has more than four units, and it has an elevator. Ray's notes run two pages.

head: Location
Ray's finding
Requirement it touches
rows: Main residential entrance on Jamaica Avenue
Two steps up from the sidewalk; the only ramp is at a side door marked "Staff only," kept locked
Accessible building entrance on an accessible route
Usable doors (HUD's guideline is a nominal 32-inch clear opening)
No blocking in the walls around toilets and tubs
Reinforced walls for later grab bars
Mounted about 60 inches above the floor
Reached by the elevator, then three steps up to the deck
Accessible public and common use areas
One step at the office door; counter about 42 inches high
ADA, not the Fair Housing Act
blocks.caption: Ray's punch list notes, with the requirement each one touches

blocks.q: Which apartments in Evelyn's building must meet the Fair Housing Act design and construction requirements?
c: Only the ground floor, since the building is mixed use with retail
Only about 5% of the units, which the owner designates as accessible
All 41 apartments, since it is a new elevator building
None of them, since the city building code governs new buildings
blocks.x: The design and construction requirements of the 1988 amendments cover multifamily buildings of 4 or more units built for first occupancy after March 13, 1991. In a building with an elevator, every unit is covered; without one, only ground-floor units are. Ground-floor-only is the trap: it is the walk-up rule, and here the residential ground floor is the second floor served by the elevator. Local codes add their own rules but do not replace the federal ones.

blocks.html: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 wrote seven requirements into the statute: an accessible entrance on an accessible route, accessible public and common areas, usable doors, an accessible route into and through each unit, controls in accessible locations, reinforced bathroom walls for grab bars, and usable kitchens and bathrooms. Ray's list hits five of them. Evelyn's project manager has a proposal: open, photograph, and lease now, and fix things "on request, as a reasonable modification" when a tenant with a disability asks.

blocks.q: How should Jordan respond to the plan to fix the punch list items only on request?
c: It works, because tenants with disabilities may make modifications at their own cost
It is a design and construction violation that the owner side must correct
It works if the leasing ads say the building is accessible upon request
It is a violation, but the architect alone is responsible for it
blocks.x: A reasonable modification is for existing housing that was never required to be accessible. A covered building that was built wrong is a violation from the day it is built, and the fix belongs to those who designed and built it, not to a future tenant. Developers, builders, owners and architects have all been held responsible, so the architect-only choice is too narrow. Correcting it before occupancy is also far cheaper than retrofitting occupied apartments.

blocks.html: Jordan does not argue construction law with a project manager. Jordan puts the issue in an email to Diane, who forwards it to Evelyn with one sentence: Hudson & Hart will not market the building as accessible, or photograph it for listings, until the owner's architect has reviewed Ray's list. Evelyn, who reads risk the way she reads cap rates, has the architect out within a week. Blocking goes into the bathroom walls that are still open, the bedroom doors are rehung with wider frames on the remaining floors, thermostats come down, and a ramp to the roof deck goes in. The main entrance gets a sloped walk; the locked staff door was never going to count as the accessible entrance for residents.

blocks.text: The leasing office and the stores

blocks.html: The leasing office and both storefronts are a different law. A leasing office open to the public is a place of public accommodation, and so are a pharmacy and a café, which puts them under Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act. Dr. Asante's draft lease says the tenant is responsible "for all ADA compliance in and about the premises," including the entrance from the sidewalk.

blocks.q: A customer who uses a wheelchair cannot enter the pharmacy because of a step at its door. Under the ADA, who is responsible?
c: Dr. Asante alone, because her lease assigns ADA duties to the tenant
Evelyn alone, because she owns the building and the step is part of it
Both landlord and tenant; the lease divides costs only between them
Neither, because the building is new and ADA applies to older buildings
blocks.x: The ADA's Title III rules treat both the landlord who owns the building and the tenant who operates a public accommodation as covered. A lease may allocate who pays or performs the work between the two of them, but it does not change either one's duty to the public. The lease-says-tenant choice is tempting because private parties often rely on that clause. New construction must meet the ADA's stricter standards, not looser ones.

blocks.html: Marcus and Evelyn's lawyer rewrite the clause so the landlord handles the entrance and common areas and the tenant handles the interior fit-out, which is how the work will actually be done. The step at the store door is removed in the same work order as the lobby ramp. The leasing office counter gets a lowered section, and the office door step disappears.

In February, the lease-up opens. Jordan's listings describe features, not people: "elevator building, step-free entry, roof deck, laundry on every floor." Every prospect gets the anti-discrimination disclosure form and, because New York requires it at first substantive contact, notice of the right to request a reasonable accommodation or modification. Store A opens in April with a hand-lettered sign: "Asante Pharmacy. Ask us anything." Store B smells like bread by May.

blocks.q: Jordan wants to describe the finished building in ads. Which line is the best choice?
c: Step-free entry, elevator to every floor and the roof deck
Ideal for active young professionals, close to the LIRR
Perfect for seniors and the disabled, fully accessible units
Quiet building, best for couples without small children
blocks.x: Describe the property, not the people you imagine living there. Step-free entry and elevator access are facts about the building that every reader can use. The other three choices each signal a preference: by age (young professionals), by age and disability (seniors and the disabled), and by familial status (no small children). The seniors line is the tempting one because it sounds helpful, but it still tells some readers the building is meant for someone else.

items: The Fair Housing Act stops at dwellings, but the 1866 Act covers race in any property or contract, and New York's state and city Human Rights Laws cover commercial space, including age, creed and marital status. Brokers are liable on their own.
Commercial prospects get the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form; the RPL 443 agency form does not apply to a storefront.
Neutral use and occupancy limits applied to everyone are lawful. A rule keyed to who the applicant is, or a false "under negotiation," is not.

ECOA covers business credit: no required spouse signature when the applicant qualifies alone, no age or childbearing based decisions, and notice within 30 days of a completed application. New York's 296-a adds more classes.
Sorting buyers to worse lenders by national origin is steering in a real estate related transaction, and paid referrals add a RESPA Section 8 violation.

Elevator buildings of 4 or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991 must meet all seven design and construction requirements in every unit. A construction violation is fixed by the owner side, not by a tenant's modification, and stores and leasing offices are ADA territory for landlord and tenant alike.

lessons.title: Case file: Ninety-Five Years at the Marlowe
lessons.tagline: A Flatbush building's basement archive tells the history of fair housing law one document at a time. Then a tenant tells Jordan what the super has been doing this year.
objectives: Explain the purpose of New York and federal fair housing laws by applying each one to a building's records from 1931 to today.
Decide what a seller must do about a void discriminatory covenant in the chain of title under current New York law.
Distinguish quid pro quo from hostile environment harassment and decide when an owner is liable for harassment by an employee or another tenant.
Choose lawful responses to a harassment report, including corrective action that does not penalize the victim and avoiding retaliation.

blocks.title: Flatbush, a basement storage room with a bare bulb
blocks.html: The Marlowe is a six-story elevator building on Ocean Avenue in Flatbush with 64 apartments, a lobby with its original terrazzo floor, and a basement full of filing cabinets. The Whitcombe family has owned it since it opened in 1931. Claire Whitcombe, the founder's great-granddaughter, is selling, and Diane has the listing. Investors, Evelyn Park among them, will want a due diligence binder: rent roll, leases, violations, title, and anything else that could surprise a buyer. Jordan's job is to build it. Claire hands over the basement key and says, "Everything since 1931 is down there. My grandfather never threw anything out." The first folder Jordan opens holds the deed to the land, recorded in 1928, and on page two is a sentence nobody has read aloud in a long time.

blocks.title: Deed to the land, recorded 1928, page 2 (excerpt)
blocks.html: "...and the party of the second part covenants for itself, its successors and assigns, that no part of said premises shall at any time be sold, leased or occupied by any person not of the Caucasian race, excepting domestic servants in the employ of an occupant..."

Clauses like this were sold as a feature in the 1920s. Developers advertised "restricted" buildings and neighborhoods, and lenders liked them. The Supreme Court made them unenforceable in court in 1948, and New York's General Obligations Law 5-331 declares discriminatory covenants in deeds, leases and mortgages void as against public policy. For decades the words simply sat in the record, void and still visible. New York's newer Real Property Law 327-a, in effect since 2026, adds a step for sellers.

blocks.q: Claire's title report will show the 1928 covenant. What does New York now require of Claire as seller?
c: Nothing, because a void covenant has no legal effect on anyone
Record a modification removing it, give the buyer a copy, no filing fee
Bring a court action to cancel the covenant before the closing date
Disclose it to buyers and let the title insurer decide whether to except it
blocks.x: The covenant has been void for decades, but RPL 327-a now has the seller submit a restrictive covenant modification document for recording, with the deed or separately, give the purchaser or title applicant a copy at or before closing, and record it, with no filing fee charged to the seller. The first choice states the old understanding: void, so ignore it. The law now asks sellers to clear the language from the record, not just from their minds.

blocks.html: Diane adds a line to the seller's closing checklist and calls Priya, who will prepare the modification document. Priya mentions that the same statute gives co-op and condo boards and homeowners associations one year to strip unlawful restrictions from their own recorded documents, without a vote of the owners. "The words outlived everyone who wrote them," she says. "Now they don't get to outlive us."

The rental files from the 1940s are index cards, one per applicant, in Harold Whitcombe's handwriting. One card from 1949 lists a returning Army veteran, his wife and their daughter, with a teacher's salary and two references. Across the bottom Harold wrote "Colored. Declined." The Marlowe was privately financed with a bank mortgage, with no government aid, tax exemption or FHA insurance.

That same year, New York's highest court decided Dorsey v. Stuyvesant Town and, by four votes to three, allowed an insurance company to exclude Black tenants from a Manhattan project built with a city tax exemption. If a publicly aided project could do it in 1949, a private building faced no state or city law at all. The Civil Rights Act of 1866 was on the books, but courts then read it to reach government action only. New York's first fair housing laws reached outward in stages: a 1955 state law covering housing with FHA-insured mortgages, then New York City's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs law, signed in December 1957 and effective April 1, 1958, the first in the country to cover private multiple dwellings, and in 1963 a state law covering housing statewide with narrow exceptions.

blocks.q: Harold's 1949 refusal would first have been unlawful at the Marlowe, a private 64-unit building with no public aid, under which law?
c: The Civil Rights Act of 1866, as it was read by courts in 1949
The 1955 state law covering housing with FHA-insured mortgages
New York City's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs law, effective 1958
The federal Fair Housing Act, passed by Congress in April 1968
blocks.x: The city law that took effect in 1958 was the first to reach private multiple dwellings like the Marlowe, a decade before the federal Act. The 1955 state law is the near miss, but it covered housing financed with FHA-insured mortgages, and the Marlowe had a private bank loan. The 1866 Act did cover private sales and rentals, but courts did not read it that way until Jones v. Mayer in 1968.

blocks.html: Jordan photographs the card. It goes in the history file, not the due diligence binder; it is not a liability a buyer inherits. But it is the reason the law exists. That family went somewhere else, probably to a neighborhood the banks had already drawn a red line around, and the equity they did not build at the Marlowe is part of the wealth gap that fair housing law was written to stop widening.

blocks.text: 1972: two visitors on the same afternoon

blocks.html: The next folder is a lawyer's file from 1972. A fair housing group sent two testers, a Black woman and a white woman with matching incomes and family size, to the Marlowe's rental office an hour apart. The first was told nothing was available. The second was shown a two-bedroom on the fourth floor and offered an application. The file includes the group's complaint, a federal lawsuit, and a consent decree signed in 1974. Under the decree, the Marlowe had to keep a written waiting list in order of application, offer vacancies in that order, put an equal housing opportunity statement in every ad, post a fair housing notice in the rental office, and keep records for inspection.

blocks.q: In 1972, which federal laws reached the Marlowe's different treatment of the two testers?
c: The 1866 Act alone, since the 1968 Act exempted private buildings
The 1968 Act alone, since the 1866 Act covered sales and not rentals
Both the 1968 Act and the 1866 Act as read in Jones v. Mayer
Neither, because testers were not lawful plaintiffs until the 1980s
blocks.x: By 1972 the Fair Housing Act barred race discrimination in renting, including false statements that a unit is unavailable, and a 64-unit building had no exemption. Jones v. Mayer had also confirmed that the 1866 Act reaches private discrimination, and the 1866 Act covers leasing as well as sales. The sales-only choice is the trap. Testing evidence was in use from the Act's early years.

blocks.html: The decree's remedies are worth noticing, because they are still the core of every fair housing compliance program: objective written criteria, a first-come order, the same information for everyone, a notice on the wall, and records that let an outsider check the work. Hudson & Hart's own rules, from its standardized operating procedures to its three-year file retention, use the same logic. The law's purpose was never just to punish a refusal. It was to make equal treatment the default and to make unequal treatment visible.

blocks.text: 1979: adults only on five and six

blocks.html: A 1979 memo from Claire's grandfather to the super reads: "Starting now, floors 5 and 6 are adults only. Families with children go on 2 through 4." A second memo, dated 1989, reverses it after the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added familial status. Evelyn, reading over Jordan's shoulder during a tour, laughs. "My father would have loved that. Quiet floors rent higher. Could a new owner do something like that today if the building were marketed to older tenants?"

blocks.q: What is the right answer to Evelyn's question about the Marlowe today?
c: Yes, if the adult floors are a small minority of the units
Yes, if the owner offers families an equal number of units elsewhere
No, unless the building qualifies as housing for older persons
No, because no building in New York may limit residents by age
blocks.x: Steering families with children to certain floors is familial status discrimination under federal law, and New York law also bars refusing to rent to people because they have children. The exception is housing for older persons: all residents 62 or older, or 80% of units with at least one person 55 or older plus published policies. The last choice overstates it: qualifying senior housing may limit residents by age. The equal number of units idea is still segregation by family status.

blocks.html: A 1996 letter from a tenant on the third floor asks permission to install a ramp over the two steps at the Marlowe's side entrance and grab bars in her bathroom, at her own cost, after a spinal injury. Claire's father said yes, on condition that a licensed contractor do the work and the tenant carry insurance. Evelyn asks whether a 1931 building should have been built accessible in the first place under the federal design rules.

blocks.q: How do federal fair housing rules apply to the Marlowe's physical layout?
c: Design and construction rules apply, so the owner had to build the ramp
It is exempt from every disability rule because it predates 1968
Design and construction rules apply after a major renovation
The 1991 design rules do not apply; modification requests do
blocks.x: The design and construction requirements cover buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991, so a 1931 building is not required to have been built accessible. Existing housing is still covered by the duty to permit a reasonable modification, generally at the tenant's expense under federal law, and the owner may require that the work be done in a workmanlike way. The predates-1968 choice confuses the building's age with the law's reach: the anti-discrimination rules apply to every building.

blocks.text: This year: what the tenant in 3F says

blocks.html: On Thursday, Jordan is in the lobby photographing the terrazzo when the tenant in 3F, Simone Baptiste, a nurse who has lived at the Marlowe for nine years, stops. She asks whether Jordan works for the owner. Jordan explains that Hudson & Hart represents Claire in the sale. Simone hesitates, then says it anyway. Since February, her kitchen ceiling has leaked. Gary, the super, who has worked at the Marlowe for twenty-two years, keeps coming by to "look at it" without fixing it. Last month he said he would get it done "if you let me take you to dinner first, you know how it works." She said no. The leak is still there. Last week he let himself in with his key while she was asleep after a night shift, and said he was checking the ceiling.

blocks.q: Gary conditioned a repair on Simone going to dinner with him. Under HUD's harassment rule, that is:
c: Quid pro quo harassment, because a housing service was tied to a demand
Hostile environment harassment, since there was a single explicit demand
Not harassment, since dinner is a social request and not a sexual one
Not covered by fair housing law, since it is a repair and lease issue
blocks.x: HUD's rule (24 CFR 100.600) defines quid pro quo harassment as conditioning housing or a housing related service, such as repairs, on submitting to an unwelcome request or demand. One demand is enough; the demand need not be explicitly sexual when the context makes it plain. The hostile environment choice is the near miss: that theory looks at unwelcome conduct severe or pervasive enough to interfere with the use and enjoyment of the home, and Gary's unannounced entry may support it too.

blocks.q: Claire says she knew nothing about this. Is she, as owner, liable for Gary's conduct under the Fair Housing Act?
c: No, because liability requires the owner to know of the harassment
Yes, but not until a tenant files a written complaint with HUD
No, as long as she fires Gary within 30 days of learning of it
Yes, an owner is vicariously liable for an employee's harassment
blocks.x: HUD's rule makes a person vicariously liable for a discriminatory housing practice by an agent or employee, regardless of whether the person knew or should have known, consistent with agency law. Gary is Claire's employee acting in his job: repairs and access to apartments. Knowledge matters for a separate theory, direct liability for failing to act once the owner knows, which is why the first choice is tempting but wrong. Firing him later can limit future harm; it does not erase liability for what happened.

blocks.html: Simone has not decided whether to file anything. She is worried about her lease renewal, and she does not want to be "the one who got Gary fired." Jordan is not her agent, her lawyer, or her landlord. Jordan is also standing in the lobby of a building the firm is selling, holding information that the owner urgently needs and the buyer will eventually ask about.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do with what Simone said?
c: Keep it confidential, because Simone is not the firm's client
Report it to Diane today and give Simone the complaint options
Speak to Gary directly so he knows his conduct has been noticed
Wait until after the closing, so the sale is not put at risk
blocks.x: Jordan's duty runs to the firm's client, Claire, and through Diane, the supervising broker. The owner must be told so she can stop the harassment, and Simone should know her options: HUD, the state Division of Human Rights and the NYC Commission on Human Rights. Confronting Gary is not Jordan's role and can tip off the harasser. Keeping it quiet is the tempting choice because it feels respectful, but it leaves Simone exposed and Claire liable.

blocks.html: Jordan tells Simone exactly that, writes down what she said with the date and time, and calls Diane from the sidewalk. Diane calls Claire within the hour. Claire, shaken, calls her lawyer and says her first idea out loud: "Let's move Simone to 6B. It's bigger, it's on a different line, and Gary hardly goes up there."

blocks.q: What is wrong with Claire's first idea?
c: Nothing, since a larger apartment is a benefit and not a penalty
Nothing, if Claire offers 6B at the same rent as Simone's apartment
The fix lands on the victim; the steps should address Gary instead
A transfer is allowed after a finding by a court or by HUD
blocks.x: HUD's rule says prompt corrective action may not include steps that penalize or harm the aggrieved person, and an unwanted move, even to a bigger unit, uproots Simone instead of the harasser. A transfer Simone herself asks for is different. The same-rent choice is tempting because it sounds fair, but the problem is who bears the burden. The lawful path addresses Gary: suspend his apartment access, investigate, fix the leak through a contractor, and change the key procedure.

blocks.html: Claire's lawyer steers her there. A contractor repairs the ceiling within the week. Gary is placed on leave while an outside investigator interviews tenants; two more women describe similar comments over the years, and Gary is terminated. The Marlowe adopts a written entry policy: notice before entering, except in an emergency, logged by the managing agent. Simone files a complaint with the NYC Commission on Human Rights, which has three years to receive a gender-based harassment complaint, compared with one year for most of its other claims.

The investigator's interviews turn up a second problem. Since spring, someone has been taping notes to the door of 5D, where two men, Andre and Paul, have lived since their wedding last year. The notes use slurs and say "people like you" are "ruining the building." Andre has written to the managing agent three times and attached photos. The lobby camera shows the tenant in 5A taping a note up in August. The managing agent filed the letters and did nothing, saying "it's between neighbors."

blocks.q: Is the owner exposed to liability for harassment by another tenant?
c: No, because owners answer for staff and agents, not for other tenants
Yes, if it knew and had power to act, such as lease enforcement
Yes, in every case, because owners guarantee the conduct of tenants
No, because the harassment is about sexual orientation, not about sex
blocks.x: HUD's rule makes a housing provider directly liable for failing to take prompt action to correct third-party harassment it knew or should have known about and had the power to correct; lease provisions on conduct are that power. Three written complaints and video evidence settle knowledge. The "between neighbors" view is the trap. New York State and City law protect sexual orientation by name, so the last choice fails twice.

blocks.html: The managing agent sends the 5A tenant a notice to cure citing the lease's nuisance and harassment provisions, the notes stop, and the managing agent's staff get training. Jordan notices that the earlier files had been handled the way Harold handled the 1949 card: quietly, by someone who decided the problem was not the building's business.

blocks.text: The last week before the binder goes out

blocks.html: Before Gary's termination, Simone's neighbor tells her that Gary told the porter that "3F's lease renewal might have some problems this year." The renewal is due in two months. Separately, a tenant in 2C, Marco, tells the investigator that Gary used to make comments about his body in the laundry room and once blocked the door. Marco says he did not report it because "guys don't get harassed."

blocks.q: Which statement about these two facts is accurate?
c: A threat to Simone's renewal for complaining is retaliation
Gary's renewal remark is lawful since he has no power over the lease
Marco has no claim, because sexual harassment law protects women
Marco's claim depends on whether he reported it in the same year
blocks.x: The Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising fair housing rights, and New York's Human Rights Law bars retaliation for opposing discrimination or filing a complaint. A threat by the super, the owner's employee, is the owner's problem. Harassment because of sex protects anyone, including a man harassed by a man, so the women-only choice fails. Reporting delay affects filing deadlines, not whether the conduct was harassment.

blocks.html: Simone's lease is renewed on time with the standard increase. Claire signs a letter to every tenant describing the new entry policy, naming a contact at the managing agent for complaints, and stating that retaliation will not be tolerated. Diane adds two lines to the due diligence binder: that a complaint is pending with the city Commission concerning a former employee, and that the owner has taken corrective action. Buyers' lawyers will ask anyway, and a seller's agent who hides a known complaint invites a misrepresentation claim.

blocks.q: Evelyn's lawyer asks why the binder mentions a complaint about a super who no longer works there. What is the best reason?
c: The buyer will be personally liable for the former super's conduct
Fair housing law requires every complaint to be recorded with the deed
DOS requires listing brokers to publish pending complaints in the listing
A pending claim and new policies are material facts for a buyer
blocks.x: A pending complaint, the steps taken, and the policies a buyer will inherit affect the building's management, insurance and reputation, so they are material facts that should not be hidden. Liability for Gary's conduct generally stays with the employer at the time, Claire, which is why the personal liability choice overstates it. Neither DOS nor fair housing law requires recording or publishing complaints.

blocks.title: Three harassment mistakes people make
blocks.html: First, thinking an owner is safe if nobody told her: an owner is vicariously liable for an employee's harassment, knowledge or not. Second, fixing it by moving the victim: corrective action may not penalize the person harassed. Third, treating tenant-on-tenant harassment as a neighbor dispute once the owner knows and has lease tools to stop it. On the exam, sexual harassment is sex discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, and it protects people of every sex and sexual orientation.

blocks.title: New York moved first, and still files fastest
blocks.html: New York City's 1957 law reached private apartment buildings eleven years before Congress acted, and the state followed in 1963. Today the city Commission on Human Rights takes gender-based harassment complaints for three years, longer than HUD's one year, and the state Division of Human Rights takes complaints for three years for conduct on or after February 15, 2024. A tenant like Simone can choose her forum.

The binder goes out in March. Evelyn's offer arrives in April. Before closing, Priya records the modification striking the 1928 covenant, and Claire gives the 1949 index card, the 1972 file and both memos to the Center for Brooklyn History. "My grandfather kept everything," she tells Jordan at the closing. "I think he expected someone to read it."

items: Discriminatory covenants are void under GOL 5-331, and RPL 327-a now has a seller record a restrictive covenant modification, give the buyer a copy, and pay no filing fee.

New York City's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs law (effective 1958) was the first to reach private apartment buildings; the state followed in 1963 and Congress in 1968, and Jones v. Mayer revived the 1866 Act for private sales and rentals.
Fair housing remedies aim to make equal treatment the default and unequal treatment visible: written criteria, first-come order, equal information, notices and records.
Adults-only floors are familial status discrimination unless the building qualifies as housing for older persons. Pre-1991 buildings escape the design rules but not reasonable modifications.

Quid pro quo harassment ties housing or services to an unwelcome demand; hostile environment is severe or pervasive unwelcome conduct. Owners are vicariously liable for employees and directly liable for third-party harassment they know of and can stop.

Corrective action may not penalize the victim, and threats over renewals are retaliation. A licensee who learns of harassment tells the supervising broker and the tenant's options, and does not bury it.

roleplays.title: "Is It Safe? Who Lives There?"
roleplays.setting: Driving a relocating buyer from Manhattan to Brooklyn showings
roleplays.goal: Be genuinely useful to the buyer without steering: redirect to objective data, show everything in the price range, and keep a record.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play a friendly, anxious relocating parent buying in Brooklyn. Repeatedly ask which areas are "safe," who lives there, whether a block is "changing," how the schools are, and whether the agent can skip certain neighborhoods you have "heard things" about. Push a little if the agent refuses ("come on, off the record"). Mention once that your partner uses a wheelchair and you need step-free homes. The learner must avoid steering, redirect to objective public data (NYPD, census, DOE), show all listings matching stated criteria, filter only on property features the buyer chooses, apply the brokerage's standardized operating procedures equally, and document the contact. At the end, grade steering avoidance, helpfulness, SOP consistency, and record keeping, and give one tip.
opening: {client} is moving from {from} with two kids and a budget of {budget}. You're driving the first showing tour over the Manhattan Bridge.
Saturday, 10 am. {client} climbs into your car with a coffee and a printed list of questions. Budget: {budget}. First time buying in New York.
{client} called the office yesterday from {from}. Today you're showing Brooklyn homes up to {budget}, and the questions start before the seatbelt clicks.

say: Honestly, which neighborhoods are safe? And who lives there? We want to be around families like ours.
You know Brooklyn. Where would a family like ours fit in? Where's safe, and who are the neighbors?

moves.text: Safety means different things to people. I'll send NYPD precinct and census links. What matters most?
moves.fb: You stayed helpful and objective. Pointing to public data and the buyer's own criteria avoids steering under the Fair Housing Act and NYS Human Rights Law.
moves.react: Commute, schools, a yard. And I'll read the precinct stuff tonight.

moves.text: I won't sort areas by who lives there, but I'll get you crime maps, transit times, and listings that fit you.
moves.fb: Correct. You decline to characterize residents and replace it with objective, verifiable sources.
moves.react: Fair. Send me all of it and I'll decide.

moves.text: I really can't talk about safety or neighborhoods at all. That's off limits for agents, so I'll skip it.
moves.fb: Legal, but unhelpful. You can and should point to objective sources and redirect to the buyer's criteria.
moves.react: Then what are you for, exactly?

moves.text: Bay Ridge and Marine Park, honestly. Lots of families like yours, very quiet blocks, you'd fit right in out there.
moves.fb: Matching areas to 'families like yours' is steering, even when meant kindly. You are deciding where they should live based on who they are.

moves.text: Most of Brooklyn is fine now, but I'd stick to the blocks closer to the park. Just my own opinion there.
moves.fb: Steering through a 'personal opinion' is still steering. Geographic advice tied to who lives where violates fair housing law.
moves.react: Good tip. Near the park only.

moves.text: I can tell you the demographics of any zip code from the census, then you can pick the mix that suits you.
moves.fb: Offering to match a buyer to a racial or ethnic 'mix' is steering by another route. Share data on request, never as a sorting tool.
moves.react: Great, send me the breakdown by group.

say: Schools matter. Commute under 45 minutes. A yard if possible. But we'd rather skip anything in {avoid}. We heard things.
Here's my list: good commute, outdoor space, schools. And leave {avoid} off. People told us things.

moves.text: Here's every listing that fits your budget, commute and yard. A few are in {avoid}. You choose.
moves.fb: You present all qualifying listings and let the buyer choose. Buyers may decide where to look; you may not filter for them by protected-class assumptions.
moves.react: Oh. That one has a bigger yard than I expected.

moves.text: I'll send you every home that fits, in every area. You can cross any off, but I won't pre-screen by area.
moves.fb: Correct. The buyer may exclude areas; the agent may not do the excluding based on what the buyer 'heard' about residents.
moves.react: Okay, I'll go through the whole list myself.

moves.text: Fine, I'll leave {avoid} off since you asked, but I'd rather you look at it yourself first, honestly.
moves.fb: The buyer may limit their own search, but you're doing the excluding for them based on a hint about residents. Show the full list.

moves.text: Smart. I'll quietly leave those off your list. Lots of buyers ask for the same thing, believe me.
moves.fb: Agreeing to exclude an area because of what the buyer 'heard' about its residents is participating in steering.

moves.text: Good call. Those blocks have had problems. I'll focus your list on areas I'd feel safe in myself.
moves.fb: Characterizing an area and filtering by your own comfort is steering, and it reinforces a bias the law forbids acting on.
moves.react: So it IS bad there. Thanks for being honest.

moves.text: I'll leave them on the list but flag those homes as 'use caution' so you know which ones to think twice about.
moves.fb: Labeling homes by area with a warning is steering through annotation. Describe the property, never the people.
moves.react: Got it, I'll avoid the flagged ones.

say: This one on {street} looks great. Who are the neighbors? Is the block, you know, changing?
Love the house on {street}. But what's the block like? Is it changing? Who's moving in?

moves.text: I don't describe neighbors or who's moving in. The house: new boiler, 40 by 100 lot, recent block sales.
moves.fb: Describe property and market facts, never people. That is the core of a compliant answer.
moves.react: Fine, tell me about the boiler.

moves.text: Walk the block at night and on a weekend, and check public data. I'll stick to the house and sales.
moves.fb: Correct. You give the buyer tools to judge for themselves without characterizing residents.
moves.react: That's actually smart. We'll come back Sunday.

moves.text: Nothing I can comment on. Want to see the basement before we lose the light and have to wrap things up?
moves.fb: Not a violation, but abrupt. Offer property facts and objective resources instead of just shutting it down.

moves.text: It's changing for the better, if you know what I mean. Prices have been climbing for a while out here.
moves.fb: Coded language about a block 'changing' invokes the demographics of residents. That is steering and could feed blockbusting.
moves.react: I think I do know what you mean.

moves.text: Mostly longtime owners, older folks, a lot of families with kids. Very settled. You'd blend right in.
moves.fb: Describing residents by age and familial status is characterizing protected classes. Talk about the house, not the people.
moves.react: Older folks and families. Perfect for us.

moves.text: It's a very diverse block, which some buyers love and some really don't. Up to you whether that's your thing.
moves.fb: Framing diversity as a pro or con invites a decision based on race or national origin. That is steering.
moves.react: Hmm, I'll have to think about that one.

say: How are the schools around here? Good, or should we keep driving?
Is this a good school area? Just be straight with me.

moves.text: Here's the DOE school finder and the zoned school for this address. The published results are all there.
moves.fb: Objective, verifiable school information lets the buyer judge. Editorializing about 'good' or 'bad' schools can be coded steering.

moves.text: I'll give you the zoned schools and their public reports for every listing, so you compare them side by side.
moves.fb: Correct. Same data for every home, from the official source, chosen by the buyer's own standard.
moves.react: Side by side is exactly what I need.

moves.text: Schools are a personal thing. I'd rather not say, but you can probably look them up online somewhere.
moves.fb: Safe but unhelpful. Point to the official DOE tools so the buyer gets real data.

moves.text: Honestly, the schools over here are pretty rough. Families who care tend to move a few neighborhoods west.
moves.fb: Vague 'rough schools' talk tied to who moves where is classic coded steering. Use published data.
moves.react: Good to know. West it is.

moves.text: The schools are great here. Very different student body from where you looked yesterday, much better.
moves.fb: Comparing 'student bodies' points at race or national origin. That is steering, not school information.

moves.text: Rank the schools for you? Sure, I'll do my own top five tonight and you only look at homes zoned for those.
moves.fb: Your own ranking used to filter homes substitutes your judgment for theirs and can mask steering. Give data, let them decide.
moves.react: Great, saves us a lot of time.

say: Let's see the {street} house again Saturday. Do you need anything from us first?
We want a second look. Anything you need from us before then?

moves.text: Per our office's posted procedures, I need photo ID from every buyer before a showing. Same for everyone.
moves.fb: Applying your broker's standardized operating procedures equally is exactly what RPL 442-h requires.

moves.text: Our posted procedures ask every single buyer for ID and a pre-approval before a second showing. Here's the link.
moves.fb: Correct. SOPs must be written, posted, and applied to every buyer the same way.

moves.text: Nothing formal. Bring ID if you remember, but it's not a big deal either way for a second showing like this.
moves.fb: Inconsistent enforcement of your office's SOPs is how unequal treatment starts. Follow the posted procedure.

moves.text: For you, nothing at all. Some buyers I make jump through hoops, but you're clearly serious about this.
moves.fb: Admitting unequal requirements is precisely what SOPs prohibit. Requirements must be the same for every buyer.

moves.text: I'll need your green card or passport first. We ask that of buyers moving from out of state like you.
moves.fb: Demanding immigration documents from some buyers singles them out. NYS protects citizenship and immigration status; apply the posted SOP to all.
moves.react: Wait, do you ask everyone for that?

moves.text: SOPs are only for listings over a million, so you're fine. Just come Saturday and we'll walk right in.
moves.fb: Invented rule. SOPs apply to all prospective homebuyers, and they must be applied consistently.

say: Before you go, did you log this client's inquiry and what you sent them?
Quick one, Jordan: is today's contact with {client} in the file?

moves.text: Logged: date, criteria, every listing sent, the data links, and the ID request under our posted SOP.
moves.fb: Records prove equal treatment. If a tester calls, your log is your defense.
moves.react: Good. That's what saves us in a complaint.

moves.text: Yes. I noted their criteria, the list I sent, and that I declined to describe who lives where.
moves.fb: Correct. Documentation of criteria, listings and responses shows a consistent, lawful process.
moves.react: That last note is gold if a tester was on the line.

moves.text: I'll write it up later this week. Nothing unusual happened today, so I figured it could wait a few days.
moves.fb: Late notes lose detail. Log the contact the same day so the record is reliable.
moves.react: Do it today. Memory is not a record.

moves.text: No need. It was just a friendly buyer, not a tester, so there's nothing to document from today's showings.
moves.fb: You never know who a tester is. Treat every contact as if it will be reviewed.

moves.text: I deleted my texts with them so there's no record of the neighborhood questions. Cleaner that way.
moves.fb: Destroying records looks like concealment and defeats your own defense. Brokers keep transaction records 3 years.
moves.react: You did WHAT? Never delete client communications.

moves.text: I logged the homes I picked for them and skipped the ones I took off their list, so the file stays shorter.
moves.fb: A log that omits excluded listings documents steering. Record everything sent and why.
moves.react: That file now proves the opposite of what we need.

say: Come on, off the record. Where would YOU live with kids?
Just between us. If you were me, which areas would you skip?

moves.text: There's no off the record for me. I can help you rank homes by your criteria, and then you make the call.
moves.fb: Fair housing rules don't pause for private conversations, and testers rely on exactly this moment.

moves.text: My opinion isn't the right filter. Let's check commute times and yards and you'll see what fits.
moves.fb: Correct. You redirect to the buyer's property-based criteria instead of your personal picture of an area.

moves.text: I'd rather not get into it. Let's talk about something else and look at the next house on the list.
moves.fb: No violation, but you missed the chance to explain why and offer something useful.

moves.text: Off the record? I'd skip {avoid}. Don't tell my broker I said that, but you asked me directly.
moves.fb: There is no off the record. Telling a buyer to skip an area is steering whether or not your broker hears it.

moves.text: I live in Park Slope, and between us the people there are more like you than in most of these areas.
moves.fb: Comparing residents to the buyer is steering by protected class. Keep to property and market facts.
moves.react: Park Slope, then. Let's look there.

moves.text: Off the record, every area's fine, but some just have more of a certain element, if you get my drift.
moves.fb: Coded language like 'a certain element' points at protected classes. That is steering.

say: My partner uses a wheelchair. Can you only show us places with step-free entry?
One thing: we need step-free access for my partner's wheelchair. Can you filter for that?

moves.text: Of course. I'll filter every area for step-free entry, elevators and ground-floor bedrooms. You pick.
moves.fb: Filtering on property features the buyer chooses is lawful and helpful. The buyer sets the criteria, not you.
moves.react: Thank you. That narrows it a lot.

moves.text: Yes. Step-free and elevator homes in your range, in all areas. Some could also take a ramp or a lift later.
moves.fb: Correct: a feature filter the buyer asked for, applied across all areas, plus useful information about modifications.
moves.react: A lift would work too. Good to know.

moves.text: Sure, I'll look for those. Honestly most Brooklyn houses have stoops, so this might take a while to find.
moves.fb: Fine to say, but negative framing can discourage a buyer with a disability. Focus on finding options.

moves.text: You might be happier in a newer suburban development. Brooklyn just isn't set up for wheelchairs, to be honest.
moves.fb: Discouraging a buyer from an area because of disability is steering. Show what fits the stated features everywhere.
moves.react: Oh. So we shouldn't look here?

moves.text: I'll ask each seller if they're okay with a disabled buyer before we book, so nobody's caught off guard.
moves.fb: Asking sellers to approve a buyer's disability invites discrimination. Disability is protected; schedule like any other buyer.
moves.react: Wait, why would they need to be okay with it?

moves.text: There's a senior building with good access in Bay Ridge. That's usually where we place buyers like you.
moves.fb: 'Placing' a buyer by disability in a particular building or area is steering. Let them choose from all matching homes.

say: Can you stick to areas where people mostly speak English? I want my kids to fit in.
I'd like neighborhoods where English is what you hear on the street. Is that a filter?

moves.text: I can't filter by who lives somewhere, language included. I can filter by commute, price, and outdoor space.
moves.fb: Language is closely tied to national origin. Filtering areas by it is steering under the FHA and NYS law.

moves.text: That's a filter about people, so I can't use it. Every listing in your range is on the table. You choose.
moves.fb: Correct. You keep the choice with the buyer and the criteria on the property.

moves.text: I don't really know which areas those would be, so I can't help with that one. Let's keep looking.
moves.fb: You didn't steer, but 'I don't know' implies you might if you did. Say clearly why you can't filter by people.

moves.text: Sure. I know a few areas where that's mostly the case, so I'll start your search list in those areas.
moves.fb: Sorting areas by language spoken is steering based on national origin.

moves.text: I'll check the census language data for each zip code and drop any area where English isn't the majority there.
moves.fb: Using census data to filter by national origin is steering with a spreadsheet. Data on request is fine; filtering is not.

moves.text: Those areas exist, but I'd need you to sign a form saying the request came from you before I use it.
moves.fb: No waiver makes steering lawful. A licensee may not act on a discriminatory preference, signed or not.

say: Just tell me the crime rate on {street}. That's a fact, right?
Is {street} a high crime block? Yes or no.

moves.text: Here's the NYPD precinct page and the city's crime map for that address. The numbers are there.
moves.fb: Pointing to objective, official data answers the question without your characterization of an area.
moves.react: Okay, I'll look at the map.

moves.text: I'll send you the official crime data for every home on our list, the same way, so you can compare them.
moves.fb: Correct. Same objective source, same treatment for every listing.
moves.react: Same data for all of them. Good.

moves.text: I can't answer yes or no on crime. Every block has some. You'd really have to look into it yourself.
moves.fb: Not a violation, but you could have handed them the official sources directly.

moves.text: Low crime, very safe, I'd walk there at night. The blocks east of here are the ones I'd worry about.
moves.fb: Your personal safety rating, tied to directions about where to avoid, is steering.

moves.text: It's higher than where you're from, honestly. A lot of buyers like you end up going to Staten Island.
moves.fb: 'Buyers like you' plus a redirect is steering, and the comparison is your opinion, not data.

moves.text: Crime there is mostly just a few bad blocks. I'll just skip those for you and show you the rest of the area.
moves.fb: Deciding for the buyer which blocks to skip is steering by your own map. Hand over official data and let them choose.
moves.react: Thanks for skipping them for us.

roleplays.debrief: You practised steering avoidance under the Fair Housing Act and the NYS Human Rights Law: describe properties, never people, and send buyers to objective sources like NYPD, DOE and census data. The buyer may narrow their own search by property features, but you never filter by area, language, or who lives there. Apply your RPL 442-h standardized operating procedures to every buyer and document each contact.

roleplays.title: No Vouchers, No Kids
roleplays.setting: Phone call with an Astoria landlord listing a two-bedroom
roleplays.goal: Keep the listing and the landlord as a client while refusing every discriminatory instruction and writing a compliant ad.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Sal Russo, an old-school Astoria landlord with a six-unit building who wants no vouchers, no kids, and tenants with job income. Be gruff but not malicious; argue that it is your building and your cousin does it. If the learner refuses, test them with a quieter workaround (screen on the phone, say it's taken, require employment income, run criminal checks first, refuse a support animal). The learner must refuse each discriminatory instruction, explain NY's two-family exemption and that brokers are never exempt, apply NYC income rules to the tenant share, treat a ramp as a reasonable modification and an animal as a reasonable accommodation, and write a property-focused ad. Grade each and say whether you would keep them as your broker.
opening: Sal calls at 8 am: the {floor} two-bedroom on {street} is empty, {rent} a month, and he has opinions about who should live there.
You're on speaker with Sal Russo. He's listing the {floor} unit on {street} at {rent}, with {perk}. He has a list of rules, and some of them are illegal.
Sal's six-unit building on {street} has a vacancy. {rent}, {perk}. He wants the ad up today, written his way.

say: Two-bedroom on {street}, {rent}. Put in the ad: no vouchers, no programs, no kids. Building's too quiet for kids.
Write it up: {rent}, {perk}. And say no Section 8, no kids. I've had enough of both.

moves.text: Sal, no. Source of income and familial status are protected. I'll write an ad that sells the apartment.
moves.fb: You refused clearly, named the protected classes (FHA familial status; NYS lawful source of income), and offered a lawful path.
moves.react: Protected. Since when? Fine, write it your way.

moves.text: Those lines are illegal in ads and in screening. Let me find you a strong tenant with the same rules for all.
moves.fb: Correct. Discriminatory statements in ads are barred, and no exemption allows them. Same criteria for every applicant.
moves.react: Same rules for everybody. Okay, I can live with that.

moves.text: Let me check with my broker about the wording and get back to you this afternoon before it goes up.
moves.fb: Checking is fine, but you already know the answer. Say no to discriminatory terms clearly and right away.
moves.react: Check fast. I'm losing money every day it's empty.

moves.text: I'll leave that out of the ad, but I'll screen them out on the phone. That way nothing's in writing.
moves.fb: Hidden discrimination is still discrimination. Refusing voucher holders or families on the phone violates NY law and federal familial status rules.
moves.react: Now you're thinking like a landlord.

moves.text: Okay, your building, your rules. Owners can set who they rent to in a building this size in Queens.
moves.fb: A licensee may never follow a discriminatory instruction. Sal's six units are not exempt, and brokers are never exempt.
moves.react: That's what I like to hear.

moves.text: I can say no vouchers, since that's only a federal rule, but I'll drop the kids part. Families are protected there.
moves.fb: Backwards. NYS law protects lawful source of income statewide; familial status is federal and state. Both are protected.

say: My cousin in {cousin} does whatever he wants. Why can't I?
My cousin rents in {cousin} with no kids and no programs. Nobody ever bothers him.

moves.text: He lives in a two-family he owns. That's NY's only owner-occupied exemption, and it never covers ads.
moves.fb: Correct: NY limits the owner-occupied exemption to two-family homes, it never permits discriminatory ads, and in NYC it's lost when the unit is publicly listed.
moves.react: Two-family only, huh. Didn't know that.

moves.text: His house may be exempt, but yours isn't. Six units, and once a broker lists it, no exemption applies anyway.
moves.fb: Right. Using a broker eliminates owner exemptions, and a six-unit building never qualifies.
moves.react: So hiring you is what kills it. Great.

moves.text: Honestly I'm not sure what his situation is, but I'd rather not do it that way here with your building.
moves.fb: Right instinct, weak explanation. Knowing the exemption rules builds credibility with owners.
moves.react: You'd rather not. That's not a reason.

moves.text: Federal law exempts owners of up to four units if they live there, so if you move in, you're covered too.
moves.fb: That's the federal Mrs. Murphy rule. New York is narrower, two-family only, and his six units don't qualify either way.
moves.react: I'll move into the basement then.

moves.text: Exemptions are for small landlords with three or fewer buildings. You'd qualify, since you own one.
moves.fb: Mixing up rules. The 'three homes' exemption is for single-family owners selling or renting without a broker. It doesn't fit Sal.

moves.text: He's fine as long as he doesn't advertise, and so are you. Just let me show it quietly, with no listing.
moves.fb: A broker showing it is itself the end of any exemption. Brokers are never exempt.

say: Fine. But I want tenants who make 40 times the rent from a job. Real income.
Then they need 40 times the rent in salary. Paychecks only.

moves.text: We can use 40 times, but for voucher holders only on their share, and any lawful income counts.
moves.fb: In NYC, income requirements apply only to the tenant's portion, and lawful source of income includes benefits, support, and subsidies.
moves.react: Their share only. Okay, that's math I can do.

moves.text: Income test, yes. Paychecks only, no. Social Security, child support and benefits all count.
moves.fb: Correct. Requiring employment income excludes lawful sources and is source-of-income discrimination under NYS and NYC law.
moves.react: Social Security counts? Fine, it's steady anyway.

moves.text: Maybe we skip the income test entirely to stay safe. Just take the first applicant who wants the unit.
moves.fb: No law requires that. A uniform, lawful income standard is fine. Skipping screening hurts your client.

moves.text: Sure, employment income only. A pay stub is the proof every landlord in Astoria asks for.
moves.fb: Requiring income from a job excludes lawful sources like SSI, Social Security, and child support. That is source of income discrimination.

moves.text: We'll apply 40 times the full {rent} to everyone, voucher or not. Same rule for all, so it's fair.
moves.fb: In NYC, for voucher holders the income test applies only to the tenant's share. Applying it to the full rent screens them out.
moves.react: Same rule for all. I like it.

moves.text: Let's use 80 times the rent for voucher holders, since the program might stop paying at some point later.
moves.fb: A harsher standard for voucher holders is source-of-income discrimination.

say: And if someone with a wheelchair wants a ramp on my stoop?
What if a tenant in a wheelchair asks me to put a ramp out front?

moves.text: That's a reasonable modification request. We evaluate it. Hassle isn't a reason to refuse.
moves.fb: Correct. Modifications are physical changes; providers must allow reasonable ones. NY also requires the accommodation and modification notice for rentals.

moves.text: We treat it as a modification request and talk through cost and design. A flat no isn't allowed.
moves.fb: Right. A reasonable modification can't be refused outright. Federally the tenant usually pays for modifications in private housing.
moves.react: In writing. Fine, send me the form.

moves.text: We'd look at it, but I'm not sure what the rules are on stoops. Let me find out before anyone asks.
moves.fb: Honest, but you should know it's a reasonable modification request that must be considered.
moves.react: Find out. I don't want surprises.

moves.text: Just say the unit is taken if anyone in a wheelchair calls. It saves you the cost of a ramp later on.
moves.fb: Saying a unit is unavailable when it is available is misinformation, an express violation, and here it targets disability.

moves.text: You can refuse it. Ramps are only required in buildings that have an elevator, under the city code.
moves.fb: Invented rule. A reasonable modification request must be considered regardless of elevators.

moves.text: Tell them they'd be happier in a ground-floor place somewhere else. Steer them away, nicely.
moves.fb: Discouraging a person with a disability from renting is discrimination, polite or not.

say: Okay. What does the ad say?
Read me the ad before it goes up.

moves.text: Sunny 2BR walk-up near the N/W, {rent}, {perk}. All welcome. Plus our firm's name and phone.
moves.fb: Describes the property and welcomes everyone. Broker name and phone go on it too (19 NYCRR 175.25).
moves.react: Sounds like a good apartment. It is a good apartment.

moves.text: {rent}, two bedrooms, {perk}, near the train. Vouchers accepted. Hudson & Hart, with our office number.
moves.fb: Property-focused copy, an inclusive statement, and the required broker identification.

moves.text: Sunny 2BR, {perk}, perfect for a quiet professional couple. Near the N/W. {rent}. Call us today.
moves.fb: 'Quiet professional couple' signals preferences about family status, marital status and income source. Describe the apartment.
moves.react: Quiet professional. Exactly who I want.

moves.text: Cozy 2BR near the train, {perk}. Ideal for a mature single or couple. No pets, smoking or programs.
moves.fb: 'Mature' signals age, 'single or couple' signals familial status, and 'no programs' is source-of-income discrimination.

moves.text: 2BR, {rent}, {perk}. Must have job and good English. Owner lives nearby, call Sal directly anytime.
moves.fb: Requiring a job excludes lawful income; 'good English' targets national origin. And the ad lacks the broker's name.

moves.text: 2BR, {rent}, {perk}. Great for students or young workers. Call Jordan's cell anytime. No broker fee!
moves.fb: 'Young workers' signals age, and the ad omits the broker's name. Every ad must identify the broker.

say: When people call, just ask if they have kids before you show it. Harmless question.
First question on the phone: how many people, how old. That's all I ask.

moves.text: I can ask how many people will live there, same for everyone. Ages and kids aren't screening questions.
moves.fb: Occupancy counts tied to lawful limits are fine when asked of all. Screening on children is familial status discrimination.
moves.react: Number of people, fine. Not ages.

moves.text: No. Asking about kids to screen people is familial status discrimination, phone or ad alike.
moves.fb: Correct. The FHA and NYS law bar discrimination based on children in the household, in any form.

moves.text: I'll ask, but just to know who's coming to the showing. I won't hold it against anyone, promise.
moves.fb: Even with good intent, the question creates a record of familial status screening. Don't ask it.

moves.text: Sure, and if they have a baby I'll mention the lead paint thing so they lose interest on their own.
moves.fb: Using a disclosure to drive families away is discouragement based on familial status.

moves.text: Fine, I'll ask them. It's only illegal if you write it down in the ad, not if you ask it on the phone call.
moves.fb: The ban covers statements, screening and refusals, not just ads.

moves.text: I'll ask, and for families I'll say the unit is too small. Two bedrooms isn't enough for kids anyway.
moves.fb: Invented occupancy limits to exclude families are discrimination. Follow lawful, uniform occupancy rules only.

say: At least let me run background checks first and toss anyone with a record.
Criminal check before I even meet them. Anything on there, they're out.

moves.text: In the city, criminal history comes only after a conditional offer, and then only a narrow review.
moves.fb: NYC's Fair Chance for Housing law (2025) bars criminal history checks before a conditional offer and limits what may be considered.

moves.text: Not first. We screen everyone on income and references, make an offer, then a limited check per city law.
moves.fb: Correct order under NYC's Fair Chance for Housing law, applied the same way for all applicants.

moves.text: Let me look into the rules on that before we set anything up. I think there's something new here in the city.
moves.fb: Good instinct to check, but you should know the 2025 Fair Chance for Housing law sets the order.

moves.text: Sure, run it at the application stage. Any record at all is a legal reason to say no in New York City.
moves.fb: Not in NYC. Criminal history checks wait until after a conditional offer, and blanket bans are not allowed.

moves.text: Only run the check on applicants who seem sketchy. No need to bother the normal ones with any of it.
moves.fb: Selective checks invite discrimination based on appearance, race or national origin. Apply the same process to all.

moves.text: Run it, but tell the rejected people it was their credit so there's never an argument about the record.
moves.fb: Giving a false reason for denial is deceptive and can hide discrimination.
moves.react: Credit, sure. Nobody argues with credit.

say: No pets in my building. Somebody says their dog is a support animal, forget it.
One guy said he has an emotional support dog. My lease says no pets. Done, right?

moves.text: A support animal is a reasonable accommodation request. We review it. A flat no isn't allowed.
moves.fb: Under the FHA and NYS law, a no-pets rule must bend for a needed assistance animal unless there's a legitimate reason.
moves.react: Review it. Okay, what can I ask for?

moves.text: The no-pets rule stays, but an assistance animal isn't a pet. We consider it as an accommodation.
moves.fb: Correct. Accommodation means changing a rule or policy for a person with a disability.
moves.react: Not a pet. Fine, send me what to ask.

moves.text: Let's see the dog first. If it's calm and small we'll probably let it slide this one time.
moves.fb: Size and temperament aren't the test. Treat it as an accommodation request with consistent review.

moves.text: Your lease, your rules. No pets means no animals, support animals or otherwise, anywhere in this building.
moves.fb: Refusing a reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal is disability discrimination.

moves.text: Charge a $1,000 pet deposit for it. That's allowed for support animals, as long as it's refundable.
moves.fb: Extra pet fees or deposits for an assistance animal are not allowed. And NY caps deposits at one month's rent (GOL 7-108).

moves.text: Ask him what his diagnosis is. If it's only anxiety, that doesn't count as a disability here in New York.
moves.fb: You may not demand a diagnosis, and anxiety can be a disability. Reliable documentation of need is the most you can ask for.

say: If a voucher holder calls, just tell them it's already taken. Who's gonna know?
Program people call, say it's rented. Simple.

moves.text: I won't say that. Misstating availability is a violation, and testers call daily. I show it to everyone.
moves.fb: Saying a unit is unavailable when it is available is an express fair housing violation, and testers can sue.

moves.text: Testers would know. So would the city. Voucher holders get the same showings and criteria.
moves.fb: Correct. NYC actively tests for source-of-income discrimination, and voucher holders must be treated the same.

moves.text: I'll just let their calls go to voicemail and call back the others first. That's not saying anything.
moves.fb: Delays and unreturned calls based on source of income are still discrimination. Treat every caller the same.
