moves.text: Fine, I'll just say it's taken. Nobody's ever been fined for a little white lie on the phone about a vacancy.
moves.fb: Testers record calls; misstating availability is a clear violation with real penalties, including NYS civil fines.

moves.text: I'll say it's taken unless they can pay without the voucher. That keeps it fair for the ones who can.
moves.fb: Conditioning a rental on not using a voucher is source-of-income discrimination.

moves.text: Let's just list it at a rent above the voucher limit so the whole issue never comes up at all, ever.
moves.fb: Pricing a unit to exclude voucher holders can be evidence of intent. And it costs Sal rent and time.

roleplays.debrief: You practised refusing discriminatory instructions: lawful source of income (NYS Human Rights Law) and familial status (Fair Housing Act) are protected, NY's owner-occupied exemption covers only two-family homes, and no exemption ever covers ads or brokers. In NYC, income tests apply only to a voucher holder's share and criminal checks wait until after a conditional offer. Ramps are reasonable modifications, support animals are reasonable accommodations, and ads describe the apartment, not the tenant.

questions.q: Which agency enforces the New York City Human Rights Law?
c: NYC Commission on Human Rights
NYS Division of Human Rights
U.S. Department of Justice
NYC Department of Finance
questions.x: The NYC Commission enforces the city law. The State Division is the trap: it enforces the state Human Rights Law.

questions.q: Testing by trained testers posing as renters in NYC is carried out by the:
c: NYC Department of Buildings
NYS Department of State
NYC Commission on Human Rights
County clerk
questions.x: The Commission runs testing and investigations. DOB is the trap: it handles buildings and permits.

questions.q: New York's anti-bias training for licensees is aimed mainly at:
c: Learning mortgage math
Recognizing unconscious bias in decisions
Marketing luxury listings
Avoiding agency disclosure
questions.x: The training targets how unconscious attitudes affect licensees' decisions. Marketing is the trap: it is unrelated.

questions.q: An agent steers buyers toward neighborhoods without realizing it. Which training addresses this?
c: Agency disclosure training
Licensee safety training
Property management training
Implicit (anti-) bias training
questions.x: Implicit bias training helps agents replace unconscious habits with consistent practices. Safety training is the trap.

questions.q: A Manhattan landlord refuses applicants who use housing vouchers. Besides the state, who can investigate and penalize this under city law?
c: The Rent Guidelines Board
The NYC Department of Finance
The NYC Commission on Human Rights
The local zoning board
questions.x: Source of income discrimination violates the NYC Human Rights Law, which the Commission enforces. Rent Guidelines Board is the trap: it sets stabilized rent increases.

questions.q: The NYC Commission on Human Rights can:
c: Investigate complaints and impose penalties
Revoke a real estate license
Set property tax rates
Approve zoning variances
questions.x: It investigates, tests and penalizes. Revoking a license is the trap: only DOS does that.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 bars discrimination in property transactions on the basis of:
c: Race, color, religion, and national origin
Race, read to include ancestry
Race and sex, as amended in 1974
The seven federal Fair Housing classes
questions.x: The 1866 Act gives every citizen the same right to buy and lease property as white citizens, so it reaches race (courts read race to include ancestry and ethnic characteristics). The trap is the four-class list: color, religion, and national origin came from the Fair Housing Act of 1968, not the 1866 Act.

questions.q: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co. (1968) is important because the Supreme Court held that:
c: Courts may not enforce racially restrictive covenants in deeds
The 1866 Act reaches private racial discrimination in sales
Racial zoning ordinances adopted by cities are unconstitutional
Separate but equal has no place in public education
questions.x: Jones v. Mayer applied the 1866 Act to a private developer, so private sellers cannot refuse to sell because of race. The covenant answer is tempting, but that was Shelley v. Kraemer (1948); racial zoning was Buchanan v. Warley and schools were Brown.

questions.concept: Plessy and Brown on separate but equal
questions.q: Which case approved the doctrine of "separate but equal"?
c: Brown v. Board of Education
Buchanan v. Warley
Shelley v. Kraemer
Plessy v. Ferguson
questions.x: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) approved separate but equal. Brown v. Board of Education (1954) is the trap: it is the case that overturned the doctrine in public schools.

questions.q: In Buchanan v. Warley (1917), the Supreme Court:
c: Upheld segregated public schools under separate but equal
Struck down a city ordinance zoning residence by race
Applied the 1866 Act to a private developer's home sales
Barred courts from enforcing racial deed covenants
questions.x: Buchanan struck down Louisville's ordinance that assigned blocks by race. The covenant answer is the trap: courts kept enforcing private racial covenants until Shelley v. Kraemer in 1948.

questions.q: Which protected classes were added to the federal Fair Housing Act in 1988?
c: Sex and source of income
Sexual orientation and marital status
Disability and familial status
Color and national origin
questions.x: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added disability and familial status. Sex came in 1974, and age and marital status are the trap: they are New York classes, not federal ones.

questions.q: All of the following are protected classes under the federal Fair Housing Act EXCEPT:
c: Familial status
Color
Religion
Age
questions.x: Age is protected by New York State and NYC law but not by the federal Fair Housing Act. Familial status is the tempting pick because it sounds like age, yet it has been a federal class since 1988.

questions.q: The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 amended the Fair Housing Act by adding:
c: Sex, as a newly protected class
Disability as a protected class
Familial status as a protected class
Religion as a protected class
questions.x: The 1974 Act added sex. Disability and familial status are the trap: both arrived with the 1988 amendments, and religion was in the original 1968 Act.

questions.q: Under the Fair Housing Act, familial status protects:
c: Married couples, with or without children
Adult children who live with elderly parents
Any household of two or more related adults
A child under 18 living with a parent
questions.x: Familial status covers children under 18 living with a parent, legal custodian, or designee, plus pregnant women and people securing custody. Married couples are the trap: that is marital status, a New York class.

questions.q: An owner who lives in one unit of a three-family house in Buffalo refuses to rent the other unit to an applicant because of race. She claims the Fair Housing Act exempts her. Which is correct?
c: She is exempt, because she occupies one of the units
She is exempt, if she did not use a broker or an ad
She is liable; the 1866 Act has no exemptions
She is exempt, if she owns no more than three homes
questions.x: The 1866 Act bars racial discrimination in property with no exemptions, so no owner-occupancy rule can shelter a race-based refusal. The owner-occupied answer is the trap: the federal Mrs. Murphy exemption covers other classes, and New York limits its own version to two-family houses.

questions.q: The Americans with Disabilities Act most directly applies to which of the following?
c: A brokerage office open to the public
A single-family home sold by its owner
The interior of a privately rented apartment
A tenant's request to keep a service dog at home
questions.x: The ADA covers public accommodations and commercial facilities, such as a brokerage office. The service dog answer is the trap: requests inside private dwellings fall under the Fair Housing Act's accommodation rules.

questions.q: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 affects housing by barring race, color, or national origin discrimination in:
c: Private home sales made through brokers
Programs that receive federal financial aid
Commercial leases of retail storefronts
Admissions decisions of co-op boards
questions.x: Title VI reaches programs and activities that receive federal financial assistance, such as public housing. Private brokered sales are the trap: those are covered by the 1866 Act and the Fair Housing Act.

questions.concept: HUD enforces the Fair Housing Act
questions.q: The federal agency primarily responsible for administering and enforcing the Fair Housing Act is the:
c: Federal Housing Finance Agency
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
Department of Housing and Urban Development
U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division
questions.x: HUD administers the Act, investigates complaints, and brings charges before administrative law judges. The Justice Department is the trap: it sues in pattern-or-practice cases and on referral, but HUD is the administering agency.

questions.q: "Filtering down" refers to:
c: Lenders denying loans in minority neighborhoods
Aging homes passing to lower income occupants
Agents narrowing the listings shown to a buyer
Sellers cutting a list price in planned stages
questions.x: Filtering down is the market process by which aging housing becomes available to lower income households. Denying loans by neighborhood is the trap: that is redlining.

questions.q: Under fair housing law, which person is NOT protected as having a disability?
c: A person who is HIV positive
A person in recovery from drug addiction
A person who currently uses illegal drugs
A person with a diagnosed psychiatric condition
questions.x: Current illegal drug use is excluded from the definition of disability. The recovery answer is the trap: a person who is in or has completed treatment and is not currently using is protected.

questions.concept: Plessy and Brown on separate but equal
questions.q: Which statement about Brown v. Board of Education (1954) is correct?
c: It rejected separate but equal in public schools
It applied the 1866 Act to private home sales
It struck down Louisville's racial zoning law
It held racial covenants unenforceable in court
questions.x: Brown overturned Plessy's separate but equal doctrine in public education. The private-sales answer is the trap: that was Jones v. Mayer (1968).

questions.q: Which of the following is a protected class under the New York State Human Rights Law but not the federal Fair Housing Act?
c: Disability
Military status
Familial status
Ancestry or national origin
questions.x: Military status is a New York addition. Familial status is the trap: it sounds like a state add-on, but it has been federal since 1988.

questions.q: The New York State Human Rights Law protects all of the following in housing EXCEPT:
c: Lawful source of income
Citizenship or immigration status
Lawful occupation
Domestic violence victim status
questions.x: Lawful occupation is a New York City class, not a statewide one. Citizenship or immigration status is the tempting pick, but the state added it in the 2020s.

questions.q: A Rochester landlord's listing says "no Section 8." Under New York law, this is:
c: Legal, because Section 8 is a voluntary federal program
Legal, because the source-of-income rule covers NYC
Illegal, if the building has more than six units
Illegal, because lawful source of income is protected
questions.x: Since 2019 the NYS Human Rights Law protects lawful source of income statewide, including housing vouchers, so the ad is discriminatory. The NYC-only answer is the trap: NYC protected it first, but the state rule now reaches Rochester.

questions.q: New York State's owner-occupied exemption from the Human Rights Law applies to the rental of a unit in:
c: A two-family house where the owner lives
An owner-occupied building of up to four units
A single-family home rented without a broker
A building with fewer than six apartments
questions.x: New York narrows the federal Mrs. Murphy exemption to an owner-occupied two-family house. The four-unit answer is the trap: that is the federal rule.

questions.q: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, housing for older persons may legally exclude families with children if:
c: At least half of the residents are retired and 60 or older
Every unit is occupied by a person who is 55 or older
The building offers no playground or child amenities
80% of units have an occupant 55+, with age policies
questions.x: The exemption applies if every resident is 62 or older, or if at least 80% of occupied units have one person 55 or older and the community publishes and follows age policies. The 55-everywhere answer is the trap: it mixes the two tests.

questions.q: A 55+ community in Suffolk County qualifies as housing for older persons. Which buyer may it legally refuse?
c: A buyer who uses a motorized wheelchair
A buyer because of her religious practice
A couple raising their 8-year-old grandson
A veteran because of his military status
questions.x: The senior exemption shelters age and familial status decisions, so the community may refuse a household with a child. The wheelchair answer is the trap: the exemption does not allow disability discrimination.

questions.q: Which owner may use the federal single-family home exemption?
c: An owner of two homes who sells one with no broker and a neutral ad
An owner who lists with a broker but tells the broker to avoid families
An owner of five homes who sells one himself with a neutral ad
An owner of one home who advertises it as "no children"
questions.x: The exemption requires owning no more than three single-family homes, no broker, and no discriminatory advertising. The five-home answer is the trap: it has no broker and a neutral ad but exceeds the three-home limit.

questions.q: A tenant who uses a wheelchair asks the landlord to assign her the parking space nearest the entrance, although spaces normally go first come, first served. This is a request for a:
c: Reasonable modification
Reasonable accommodation
Senior housing exemption
Special privilege the landlord may deny
questions.x: Changing a rule, policy, or practice, such as how spaces are assigned, is an accommodation. Modification is the trap: that term means a physical change to the premises.

questions.q: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, who generally pays for a reasonable modification to a privately owned rental apartment?
c: The landlord
HUD
The managing agent
The tenant
questions.x: Federally, the tenant generally pays for modifications in private housing, and the landlord may require reasonable restoration of the interior. The landlord answer is the trap: landlords bear the cost of accommodations and of some modifications under NYC law, not of federal private-housing modifications.

questions.q: A Brooklyn owner lives in one unit of her two-family house. Her nephew, a licensed agent, lists the other unit on StreetEasy. Under the NYC Human Rights Law, may she refuse applicants based on a protected class?
c: No, a public listing ends the NYC exemption
Yes, because she occupies one of the two units
Yes, as long as the listing text itself is neutral
Yes, if her nephew collects no fee for the listing
questions.x: NYC's owner-occupied two-family exemption applies only if the unit is not publicly advertised or listed. The neutral-text answer is the trap: the listing itself, not its wording, ends the exemption.

questions.q: The New York State agency that enforces the Human Rights Law is the:
c: Department of State
Division of Housing and Community Renewal
Division of Human Rights
Attorney General's Civil Rights Bureau
questions.x: The Division of Human Rights enforces the NYS Human Rights Law. The Department of State is the trap: it licenses and disciplines agents but does not administer the Human Rights Law.

questions.q: All of the following are protected in housing under the NYC Human Rights Law EXCEPT:
c: Height and weight
Partnership status
Lawful occupation
Credit score
questions.x: Height and weight, partnership status, and lawful occupation are NYC classes. A credit score is a legitimate screening criterion when applied equally; height and weight is the tempting pick because it was added only in 2023.

questions.q: In Manhattan, a landlord requires income of 40 times the monthly rent. An applicant's voucher covers $2,000 of the $2,500 rent. Applying the rule correctly, the applicant needs annual income of at least:
questions.x: In NYC an income test may be applied only to the tenant's share: $500 x 40 = $20,000. Applying it to the full $2,500 ($100,000) is the trap and would discriminate by source of income.

questions.q: A landlord may lawfully refuse to rent to an applicant who:
c: Is in recovery from alcoholism and finished treatment
Was convicted of manufacturing and selling drugs
Takes prescribed medication for depression
Keeps an emotional support animal for anxiety
questions.x: The FHA lets providers refuse people convicted of illegal manufacture or distribution of controlled substances. Recovery from alcoholism is the trap: alcoholism is a protected disability.

questions.q: Under New York law, which listing statement violates the marital status protection?
c: "Married couples preferred"
"Two bedrooms, one bath"
"Quiet building, no smoking"
"Near the 7 train"
questions.x: A preference for married couples discriminates by marital status, a New York class. A no-smoking rule is the tempting pick, but it is a neutral rule applied to everyone.

questions.q: The term redlining comes from 1930s maps that:
c: Marked flood zones in red for federal insurance purposes
Showed racially zoned blocks that courts later struck down
Colored Black and immigrant areas red as hazardous for lending
Outlined urban renewal areas slated for new public housing
questions.x: Federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation maps colored Black and immigrant neighborhoods red as "hazardous," and lenders and the FHA steered loans away from them. Racial zoning is the tempting wrong answer, but that was a separate practice the Supreme Court struck down in Buchanan v. Warley (1917).

questions.q: Two equally qualified applicants seek mortgages. The bank approves the one buying in a mostly white area and refuses the one buying in a mostly Black area, citing "the neighborhood." This practice is known as:
c: Redlining
Blockbusting
Steering
Filtering down
questions.x: Refusing or limiting loans in an area because of who lives there is redlining, a name that comes from 1930s federal maps coloring Black and immigrant areas red. Steering is the trap: it is done by agents guiding buyers, not by lenders refusing loans.

questions.q: A title search on a Jackson Heights building turns up a 1920s deed covenant barring sales to Black buyers. What is its legal effect today?
c: It binds only buyers who take title through that deed
It stays valid until a court formally strikes it from title
It is enforceable against later owners of the same lot
It is void and unenforceable under Shelley v. Kraemer
questions.x: Since Shelley v. Kraemer (1948), courts may not enforce racially restrictive covenants; the old language may still sit in the chain of title but has no legal effect. The trap is thinking it stays valid until a court removes it: it is already void.

questions.q: Which Supreme Court case held that courts may not enforce racially restrictive covenants in deeds?
c: Buchanan v. Warley (1917)
Shelley v. Kraemer (1948)
Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co. (1968)
Brown v. Board (1954)
questions.x: Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) made racial covenants unenforceable in court. Buchanan v. Warley is the closest trap: it struck down racial zoning by city ordinance, not private covenants in deeds.

questions.q: New York City's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs Law of 1957 is significant because it:
c: Made racially restrictive deed covenants unenforceable
Was the first U.S. law to ban bias in private housing
Created the NYC Commission on Human Rights to enforce it
Added source of income as a protected class in the city
questions.x: Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs (1957) was the first law in the country to ban discrimination in private housing, more than a decade before the federal Fair Housing Act. Covenant enforceability is the trap: that came from the Supreme Court in Shelley v. Kraemer (1948).

questions.q: Which of these came first in barring discrimination in private housing?
c: The federal Fair Housing Act of 1968
The NYS Human Rights Law source of income rule
The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988
New York City's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs Law
questions.x: NYC's 1957 Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs Law predates the 1968 federal Fair Housing Act by more than a decade. The 1968 Act is the tempting answer because it is the best-known law, but New York City moved first.

questions.q: When the Fair Housing Act was passed in 1968, it protected which classes?
c: Race, color, religion, and national origin
Race, color, sex, and national origin
Race, religion, disability, and familial status
Race, color, religion, national origin, and age
questions.x: The 1968 Act began with four classes: race, color, religion and national origin. Sex is the common trap: it was added by the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974, and disability and familial status came in 1988.

questions.q: Which federal protected class was part of the original 1968 Fair Housing Act?
c: Sex
Familial status
Religion
Disability
questions.x: Religion was one of the four original classes, with race, color and national origin. Sex is tempting but was added in 1974; disability and familial status were added in 1988.

questions.q: A landlord refuses an applicant because of his accent and the country where he was born. Which federal protected class is involved?
c: Disability status
Race and color
National origin
Religion
questions.x: National origin covers ancestry, birthplace, accent and language. Race and color are tempting, but color means skin tone and race is its own class; nothing here turned on either.

questions.q: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, the religion class protects:
c: Believers and people with no religion
Members of faiths with a registered house of worship
People whose faith is listed on a lease application
Religious organizations rather than individual renters
questions.x: The religion class covers every belief, including having no religion at all. The trap is thinking it protects only organized or registered faiths; protection goes to individuals whatever they believe or do not believe.

questions.q: A building superintendent tells a tenant her repairs will get done faster if she goes out with him. Under the Fair Housing Act this is:
c: Legal, since the super is not the owner or the agent
A lease issue for housing court, not a fair housing claim
Legal unless the lease promises a set repair schedule
Sexual harassment, a form of sex discrimination
questions.x: Demanding dates or favors in exchange for repairs or a lease is quid pro quo sexual harassment, which is sex discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. The trap is that the super is not the owner: harassment by a landlord, super or agent is covered.

questions.q: How does HUD read the federal protected class of sex?
c: As covering refusals to rent to women, not harassment
As including sexual orientation and gender identity
As including marital status and pregnancy by name
As applying to sales of homes but not to rentals
questions.x: HUD reads sex discrimination to include sexual orientation and gender identity, and it also covers sexual harassment. Marital status is the trap: it is a New York class, not part of the federal sex class.

questions.q: The Fair Housing Act's accessibility design requirements apply to new multifamily buildings with:
c: 2 or more units first occupied after January 26, 1990
4 or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991
4 or more units built after the ADA took effect in 1990
5 or more units occupied after March 1991
questions.x: FHA design rules cover multifamily buildings of 4 or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991. The ADA date is the trap: the ADA covers public accommodations and commercial facilities, not the design of private apartment buildings.

questions.q: Which building is subject to the Fair Housing Act's accessibility design rules?
c: A 3-unit rental built and first occupied in 2023
A 1985 ten-unit walk-up renovated in 2022
A single-family house built in 2020 for sale
A new 6-unit condo first occupied in 2024
questions.x: The design rules reach buildings of 4 or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991, so a new 6-unit condo qualifies. The 1985 walk-up is the trap: a later renovation does not make it a building first occupied after the 1991 date.

questions.q: In 1996 two banks refused a Black couple a mortgage on a Bed-Stuy block where a white buyer got a loan quickly. Was that legal?
c: No, race-based lending had been barred since 1968
Yes, banks could weigh neighborhood risk
Yes, the federal Act covered sales and rentals only
No, but only because a 2008 law made it retroactive
questions.x: The Fair Housing Act has barred discrimination in housing financing since 1968, and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act covers credit too. The trap is thinking the FHA reached only sales and rentals: it covers financing as well.

questions.q: Besides the Fair Housing Act, which federal law bars discrimination in extending credit, including mortgages?
c: The Americans with Disabilities Act
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
The Equal Credit Opportunity Act
The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
questions.x: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act bars discrimination in credit, adding to the FHA's ban on lending discrimination. Title VI is tempting, but it covers programs that receive federal money, not credit decisions by private lenders.

questions.concept: Uniform screening and source of income
questions.q: A Syracuse landlord wants to screen applicants without violating the source of income protection. Which practice is allowed?
c: Requiring W-2 job income from everyone
Returning calls from voucher holders after others
Running the same credit check on all applicants
Listing the unit as "no programs, employed only"
questions.x: A landlord may screen everyone the same way, such as a credit check or references, as long as the screen does not single out the voucher. Requiring W-2 income is the trap: it shuts out lawful income such as benefits or vouchers, so it is source of income discrimination.

questions.concept: Uniform screening and source of income
questions.q: Which listing phrase is a lawful source of income violation in New York?
c: "Must be employed, no programs"
"Credit check for all applicants"
"No smoking in the unit"
"References required"
questions.x: "Must be employed" and "no programs" screen out tenants who pay with vouchers, benefits or other lawful income, protected statewide since 2019. A credit check for all applicants is the tempting wrong answer, but it is a uniform screen that does not single out the source.

questions.concept: NY age protection is for adults
questions.q: A Buffalo landlord requires every leaseholder to be at least 18. Under the NYS Human Rights Law this rule is:
c: Illegal, as age protection covers anyone denied for age
Legal only in buildings that qualify as senior housing
Illegal unless a parent co-signs for the minor
Legal, as the age class does not cover minors as such
questions.x: New York's age protection covers adults, so a landlord may require the leaseholder to be 18 or older; the class does not protect minors as such. The trap is reading "age" as covering anyone of any age.

questions.concept: NY age protection is for adults
questions.q: A Queens landlord tells a 72-year-old applicant the building is "better for younger tenants." Under New York law this is:
c: Legal, because federal law does not protect age
Illegal age discrimination under state law
Legal if the landlord is worried about stairs
Illegal only if the unit is in senior housing
questions.x: Age is a protected class under the NYS Human Rights Law for adults, so turning away an older applicant is illegal. The trap is the federal rule: age is not a federal class, but New York protects it.

questions.q: Which practice violates New York's citizenship and immigration status protection?
c: Requiring the same photo ID from every rental applicant
Asking only some applicants for proof of citizenship
Verifying income the same way for all applicants
Accepting an ITIN when another verification works
questions.x: You may require the same identification from everyone, but asking only some applicants for proof of citizenship is discrimination. Accepting an ITIN is the trap: that is the lawful practice, since rejecting an ITIN when another verification works is what the law forbids.

questions.q: A landlord tells a tenant who complained about heat, "Keep it up and I'll report your immigration status." Under New York law this is:
c: Legal, because the landlord did not deny the tenant housing
Legal if the landlord truly believes it
Illegal only if the tenant holds a green card
Illegal, since immigration status is protected
questions.x: Citizenship and immigration status is a protected class in New York, and threatening to report a tenant's status is a listed violation. The trap is thinking nothing counts unless housing was denied; threats based on a protected class are illegal too.

questions.q: A landlord sets a limit of one person per bedroom for a two-bedroom apartment, well below local code, and refuses a couple with a child. The rule most likely violates:
c: Familial status protection
Marital status protection
Lawful source of income protection
Nothing, as landlords set occupancy rules
questions.x: Reasonable, neutral occupancy limits based on bedroom size and local codes are allowed, but an artificially low limit that keeps children out is a familial status violation. Marital status is the trap: the rule's effect falls on households with children, not on whether anyone is married.

questions.q: Which occupancy limit is most likely lawful for an NYC landlord?
c: One occupant per bedroom, applied to all applicants
No more than two occupants unless all are adults
A neutral limit based on bedroom size and city code
A limit that changes when an applicant is pregnant
questions.x: A landlord may enforce reasonable, neutral limits tied to bedroom size and the Housing Maintenance Code. "One per bedroom for all" is the trap: applying an artificially low limit evenly still invites a familial status complaint because it keeps families with children out.

questions.q: Which rental is exempt from the NYS Human Rights Law?
c: An apartment in an owner-occupied four-family house
A single-family home the owner rents through a broker
A room rented by the resident owner of the home
A unit in a six-unit building the owner manages
questions.x: New York exempts rooms rented by the occupant or a resident owner in the owner's home. The four-family house is the trap: that fits the federal Mrs. Murphy exemption, but New York's owner-occupied exemption stops at two units.

questions.q: Under the NYS Human Rights Law, renting all the rooms in a unit to people of one sex is:
c: Exempt under the state law
Sex discrimination, with no exemption
Allowed in qualifying senior housing
Allowed with DHR approval
questions.x: New York lists renting all rooms in a unit to one sex as an exemption. The trap is assuming sex is protected with no exception here; New York carves out this narrow situation, while federal law has no separate rule for it.

questions.q: An owner who qualifies for New York's owner-occupied two-family exemption asks a broker to list the vacancy and screen out families with kids. The broker should:
c: Follow the instruction, since the owner is exempt
Follow it if the ad itself stays neutral
Ask DHR to confirm the exemption first
Decline, since brokers cannot use the exemption
questions.x: No exemption covers a licensee: a broker may not help anyone use an exemption to discriminate. Keeping the ad neutral is the trap; the broker's own part in screening out families is still illegal, and in NYC listing the unit ends the exemption anyway.

questions.q: Which of these can fall within a New York fair housing exemption?
c: A broker screening out families for an exempt owner client
A resident owner's two-family refusal on marital status
An exempt owner's newspaper ad saying "no children"
A resident owner's race-based refusal in a two-family
questions.x: New York's owner-occupied two-family exemption covers the refusal itself, such as one based on marital status (in NYC, only if the unit is not publicly advertised or listed). The race-based refusal is the trap: the 1866 Act has no exemption for race, and no exemption covers ads or brokers.

questions.q: A tenant with a disability that is not obvious asks to keep an emotional support animal in a no-pet building. The landlord may:
c: Charge the usual pet deposit before approving it
Ask for reliable documentation of the need
Require the tenant's full medical records
Refuse because emotional support animals are pets
questions.x: When the disability is not obvious, the provider may ask for reliable documentation, such as a letter from a treating professional. Demanding medical records or a diagnosis goes too far, and assistance animals are not pets, so no pet deposit or fee may be charged.

questions.q: A landlord approves a tenant's service animal but adds a $300 pet deposit. Under fair housing law, the deposit is:
c: Allowed, as long as it is refundable
Allowed if every pet owner pays the same
Not allowed unless the animal is a dog
Not allowed; the animal is not a pet
questions.x: Service animals and emotional support animals are not pets under fair housing law, so no pet deposit or fee may be charged. The trap is "everyone pays the same": charging the standard pet deposit is exactly what the rule forbids.

questions.q: A housing provider may lawfully deny a reasonable accommodation request when it:
c: Imposes an undue financial and administrative burden
Would cost the provider some money to put in place
Is made after the tenant has already signed the lease
Involves a disability the provider cannot see for itself
questions.x: A provider can refuse only if the request is an undue financial and administrative burden, fundamentally alters the operation, or has no disability-related need. Some cost is the trap: accommodations often cost little, and some expense alone is not grounds to deny.

questions.q: Which reason allows a landlord to refuse a reasonable accommodation request?
c: The tenant asked after moving in
The landlord has never granted one before
It would fundamentally alter the operation
Other tenants might ask for the same change
questions.x: Fundamental alteration of the provider's operation is one of the narrow grounds for refusal, along with undue burden and no disability-related need. Timing is the trap: none of the refusal grounds turns on when the tenant asks.

questions.q: A Ditmas Park seller tells Jordan, "Don't show my house to anyone who'll upset the neighbors." After Jordan explains the law, the seller insists. Jordan should:
c: Keep the listing but quietly follow the request
Show to everyone but rank offers by the seller's wish
Decline the listing and tell the supervising broker
Keep the listing and let the seller screen buyers
questions.x: Market to everyone and present every qualified offer; if the client insists on discriminating, decline the listing and tell the broker. Letting the seller screen buyers is the trap: the agent still takes part in the discrimination.

questions.q: A landlord asks the listing agent for tenants who "fit the building." The best first response is to:
c: Say all qualified applicants will be presented
Ask which kind of tenant the landlord has in mind
Agree, since fit is not a protected class
Refer the landlord to a different brokerage
questions.x: The script is the same every time: market to everyone and present every qualified applicant, because the law does not let you or the client choose by protected class. Asking what "fit" means is the trap: it invites the client to state a discriminatory preference.

questions.q: A Flushing landlord's agent offers to show a unit only to applicants who speak fluent English. This is:
c: Legal, because language is not a protected class
Legal if the lease is written in English
Familial status discrimination
National origin discrimination
questions.x: Treating people differently because of the language they speak or their accent is national origin discrimination, and "English speakers only" is a listed ad violation. The trap is that language itself is not named as a class; it is covered through national origin.

questions.q: Which practice about language is recommended for a New York agent?
c: Requiring an interpreter fee from non-English speakers
Offering translations with the same listings for all
Asking accented callers alone for extra paperwork
Showing fewer listings until the buyer is fluent
questions.x: Offering translated materials or an interpreter is good practice, as long as everyone gets the same listings, terms and disclosures. Extra paperwork or fees based on language are the trap: treating someone differently because of language is national origin discrimination.

questions.q: Jordan posts a personal reel touring a Bushwick listing with the caption "this block is finally changing." The main problem is that:
c: Personal accounts may not be used to show listings
It suggests steering and blockbusting
Reels need DOS approval before posting
It names the neighborhood instead of the street
questions.x: Personal social media counts as advertising when you promote listings, and saying a block is "changing" describes people, raising steering and blockbusting problems. The trap is thinking personal accounts are off limits: they may promote listings if they follow the same rules.

questions.q: A salesperson's boosted Instagram post for a rental listing must:
c: Run only after HUD reviews the ad's wording
Show the salesperson's name in place of the broker's
Target users who live in the listing's zip code
Carry the broker's name and follow ad rules
questions.x: Social media posts are advertising: they carry the broker's name and follow the same fair housing rules as print. Zip code targeting is the trap: excluding people by zip code proxies or similar targeting can be discriminatory.

questions.q: The 2019 Newsday investigation of Long Island real estate agents found:
c: Unequal treatment of minority buyer testers
That most agents had let their licenses lapse
Widespread mortgage fraud by appraisers
Commission fixing among large brokerages
questions.x: Newsday's three-year paired testing found unequal treatment of minority buyers in a large share of tests, leading to hearings, new DOS rules and standardized operating procedures. Commission fixing is the trap: that was not what the testers measured.

questions.q: Which New York requirement grew out of the Newsday fair housing investigation?
c: The property condition disclosure statement
Cease and desist zones for owner solicitation
Standardized operating procedures for buyers
The agency disclosure form required by RPL 443
questions.x: Newsday's testers found agents asking some buyers, not others, for pre-approval or ID, and New York answered with standardized operating procedures. Cease and desist zones are the trap: they fight blockbusting solicitation and long predate the 2019 investigation.

questions.q: As of October 2026, where is New York's only active cease and desist zone?
c: Parts of the South Bronx and of Rockland County
Southeast Queens, adopted in 2023 for five years
Part of East Flatbush, Brooklyn (CB 17)
Parts of Long Island near the Newsday test areas
questions.x: The only active zone is part of Brooklyn Community Board 17 (East Flatbush), adopted in 2023. The Bronx and Rockland are the trap: they had zones in the past but not now, which is why agents check the DOS website before farming.

questions.q: Before mailing listing-solicitation postcards to a neighborhood, an agent should first:
c: Check the DOS website for current zones and lists
Get written approval from the local Realtor board
Register the mailing campaign with HUD and DHR
Make sure the cards do not mention any neighborhood
questions.x: Cease and desist zones and lists change, so check the DOS website before any farming campaign; one postcard to a listed owner is a violation. Board approval is the trap: no Realtor board can clear a mailing that DOS rules forbid.

questions.q: Each New York license renewal requires:
c: 2 of fair housing and 3 of implicit bias
1 hour of fair housing plus 2 hours of implicit bias
3 hours of fair housing with no implicit bias hours
3 hours of fair housing and 2 of implicit bias
questions.x: Every renewal includes 3 hours of fair housing, 2 of implicit bias and 2 of cultural competency. Swapping the 3 and the 2 is the common trap.

questions.q: Besides fair housing and implicit bias, which topic is a required part of each New York renewal?
c: Mortgage brokerage, 3 hours
Cultural competency, 2 hours
Licensee safety, 2 hours of training
Property insurance, 2 hours
questions.x: Renewals include 2 hours of cultural competency along with 3 of fair housing and 2 of implicit bias. Licensee safety is the trap: it is important practice but not one of the three topics this requirement names.

questions.q: A tester claims Jordan answered a voucher holder's inquiry more slowly than others. What record best defends Jordan?
c: The signed agency disclosure forms from each client
A log of every inquiry and when it was answered
A copy of the brokerage's written fair housing policy
The listing agreement signed by the landlord
questions.x: A log of every inquiry, when it came in, when it was answered, what was sent and the outcome can prove identical treatment and usually ends a tester case. The written policy is the trap: it shows what should happen, not what Jordan actually did.

questions.q: Brokers keep transaction records and disclosure forms for at least:
c: Eighteen months
One year
Five years
Three years
questions.x: Transaction records and disclosure forms are kept for 3 years. Five years is the trap: that is the maximum life of a cease and desist zone or nonsolicitation order, not a record rule.

questions.q: Jordan sees a colleague accept a landlord's "no vouchers" instruction. Jordan should first:
c: Report it to the supervising broker right away
Say nothing, since it is not Jordan's listing
Warn the landlord but leave the broker out of it
Wait to see whether any applicant complains
questions.x: Report a colleague's steering or no-vouchers instruction to the supervising broker immediately; a broker who learns of a violation and does nothing shares liability. Warning only the landlord is the trap: it leaves the brokerage's violation unaddressed.

questions.q: A broker learns an agent has been steering buyers and takes no action. The broker:
c: Is not liable, since the agent acted alone
Is liable if the broker shared in the commission
Shares liability for the violation
Faces DOS action but no civil liability
questions.x: A broker who learns of a violation and does nothing shares the liability, on top of liability for failing to supervise. The trap is "the agent acted alone": liability flows up to the broker.

questions.q: A broker changes its policy and now requires buyer pre-approval before showings. The updated standardized operating procedures must be posted within:
c: 10 business days
60 days
30 days
the next license renewal
questions.x: Any change to the SOPs is posted within 30 days, and old versions are kept. The next renewal is the trap: the broker affirms compliance at renewal, but updates cannot wait that long.

questions.q: Which statement about a broker's old standardized operating procedures is correct?
c: They are kept after an update
They are shredded at once
They are kept until the next renewal, then shredded
They stay posted beside the new version
questions.x: When SOPs change, the update is posted within 30 days and old versions are kept. Shredding is the trap: old versions are kept, and since a 2022 amendment nothing is filed with DOS.

questions.q: Separately from HUD and DHR, what can the NYS Department of State do about a licensee's discrimination?
c: Award the victim emotional distress damages
Act within the same 1-year HUD window
Nothing, since DOS does not handle fair housing
Discipline the license under RPL 441-c
questions.x: DOS can discipline the license under RPL 441-c (reprimand, fines, suspension, revocation) whenever a violation comes to light. Emotional distress damages are the trap: those come from DHR or the courts, not DOS.

questions.q: A DHR case against an agent ends with a finding of discrimination and a referral to DOS. DOS may:
c: Review and overturn the DHR finding on appeal
Suspend or revoke the agent's license
Award the tester and the group punitive damages
Not act, since DHR already ruled
questions.x: DOS disciplines licenses under RPL 441-c and can reprimand, fine, suspend or revoke, separately from any DHR result. The trap is thinking one proceeding ends the matter; one act can produce several cases.

questions.q: A tenant wants to pursue a housing discrimination claim under the NYS Human Rights Law. Generally, she:
c: Has to file with DHR first and then sue in state court
Files with DHR or sues in state court, not both
Can file the claim with DOS in place of DHR
Must sue in federal court within 1 year
questions.x: Under the NYS Human Rights Law you generally elect: file with DHR or go to state court, but not both. "DHR first, then court" is the trap; the election rule makes them alternatives. She may also file with HUD, and the agencies share complaints.

questions.q: A renter filed a complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights. Which other filing is generally still open to her?
c: A state court suit on the same claim
A second DHR complaint by a relative
A claim before DOS for damages
A complaint with HUD
questions.x: Choosing DHR generally rules out a state court suit on the same claim, but she may also file with HUD, and the agencies share complaints. The state court suit is the trap: that is the other half of the election of remedies.

questions.q: In a housing discrimination case, courts may award damages for:
c: Humiliation, anxiety and other emotional harm
Out-of-pocket costs such as moving, not emotional harm
Emotional harm when a doctor has treated it
Lost rent, since housing harm is economic
questions.x: Courts award damages for emotional harm such as humiliation and anxiety, along with other losses. Requiring medical treatment is the trap: the harm itself is compensable, which is why the human cost of discrimination matters.

questions.q: Under the NYS Human Rights Law, DHR may award a housing discrimination victim:
c: Attorney's fees, but no compensatory damages
Back rent, though punitive damages are barred in housing
Compensatory damages, including emotional distress
A refund of the commission and nothing further
questions.x: DHR can award compensatory damages including emotional distress, punitive damages in housing cases, attorney's fees and civil fines. "Punitive damages are barred" is the trap: housing cases are where DHR may award them.

questions.q: A seller refuses to sell to a buyer because of the buyer's religion. Can the buyer sue under the Civil Rights Act of 1866?
c: Yes, the 1866 Act covers every federal class
No, the 1866 Act reaches race, not religion as such
Yes, if the seller used a broker for the sale
No, because the 1866 Act covers rentals alone
questions.x: The 1866 Act reaches racial discrimination (including ancestry), not religion as such; the buyer would use the Fair Housing Act or NY Human Rights Law. The every-class answer is the trap: the seven classes come from the 1968 Act and its amendments.

questions.q: A private developer refused in 1965 to sell a home to a Black buyer. The Supreme Court case that let the buyer win under the 1866 Act is:
c: Shelley v. Kraemer
Buchanan v. Warley
Havens Realty v. Coleman
Jones v. Mayer
questions.x: Jones v. Mayer (1968) held that the 1866 Act bars private as well as public racial discrimination in property sales. Shelley v. Kraemer is the trap: it stopped courts from enforcing racial covenants but did not reach a private refusal to sell.

questions.concept: Plessy and Brown on separate but equal
questions.q: The 1896 decision that Brown v. Board of Education later rejected in public schools was:
c: Shelley v. Kraemer
Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co.
Buchanan v. Warley
Plessy v. Ferguson
questions.x: Brown (1954) rejected Plessy v. Ferguson's separate but equal doctrine in public education. Buchanan v. Warley is the trap: it was a 1917 housing case that struck down racial zoning, not a separate-but-equal ruling.

questions.q: A city ordinance assigns each residential block to one race. Which Supreme Court case first held such a law unconstitutional?
c: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Buchanan v. Warley (1917)
Shelley v. Kraemer (1948)
Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co. (1968)
questions.x: Buchanan v. Warley struck down Louisville's racial zoning ordinance in 1917. Shelley v. Kraemer is the trap: it addressed private deed covenants, not city zoning.

questions.q: In 1985 a landlord refused to rent to a family because they had two young children. Under the federal Fair Housing Act as it stood then, the refusal was:
c: Legal federally; familial status came in 1988
Illegal, since familial status was a 1968 class
Illegal, since the 1974 amendment added children
Illegal, under the Civil Rights Act of 1866
questions.x: Familial status and disability were added by the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, so a federal claim was not available in 1985. The 1974 answer is the trap: that amendment added sex, not familial status.

questions.q: A landlord in a state with no state fair housing law refuses to rent to a 70-year-old applicant because of her age. Under federal law alone, she has a claim based on:
c: Age, a federal class since 1988
Familial status, which covers seniors
Disability, which covers people over 65
No federal class, since age is not one
questions.x: Age is not a federal fair housing class, so federal law alone gives her no age claim (New York and NYC do protect age). The familial status answer is the trap: it protects households with children under 18, not older adults.

questions.q: Sex became a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act through the:
c: Civil Rights Act of 1866
Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
Housing and Community Development Act
questions.x: The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 added sex. The 1988 amendments are the trap: they added disability and familial status.

questions.q: Familial status protection under the Fair Housing Act covers all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A pregnant woman with no other children
A grandmother with legal custody of a 10-year-old
A parent in the process of adopting a child
A married couple with no children
questions.x: A childless married couple is a marital status issue, protected in New York but not by federal familial status. The custody answer is the trap: a legal custodian of a child under 18 is covered.

questions.q: An owner of two single-family homes sells one himself, with no broker and no ad, and refuses a buyer because of race. Which statement is correct?
c: He is protected by the single-family exemption
He is protected if he gives a nonracial reason
He is liable under the 1866 Act, exemption or not
He is liable if he later lists with a broker
questions.x: The 1866 Act has no exemptions, so a race-based refusal is illegal even where the Fair Housing Act's single-family exemption would otherwise apply. The exemption answer is the trap: it shelters some classes under the 1968 Act, never race under the 1866 Act.

questions.q: A brokerage's storefront office has a step at the entrance that customers using wheelchairs cannot climb. Which law most directly requires removing that barrier where readily achievable?
c: The Fair Housing Act
The Americans with Disabilities Act
The Civil Rights Act of 1866
The NYS Human Rights Law, Article 15
questions.x: The ADA governs public accommodations such as a brokerage office open to customers. The Fair Housing Act is the trap: it governs dwellings, not commercial offices.

questions.q: A public housing authority that receives federal funds assigns apartments by national origin. Besides the Fair Housing Act, which law most directly applies?
c: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
The Americans with Disabilities Act
The Civil Rights Act of 1866
The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
questions.x: Title VI bars race, color, and national origin discrimination in federally assisted programs such as public housing. The 1866 Act is the trap: it covers race, not national origin.

questions.concept: HUD enforces the Fair Housing Act
questions.q: A renter in Albany believes a landlord rejected her because of her disability and wants to file a federal administrative complaint. She files with:
c: The NYS Department of State's licensing division
The Federal Housing Finance Agency
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
questions.x: HUD receives and investigates Fair Housing Act complaints. The Department of State is the trap: it disciplines licensees but is a state agency, not the federal enforcer.

questions.q: As a 1920s neighborhood ages, its homes are bought and rented by successively lower income households. This market process is called:
c: Gentrification
Filtering down
Reverse redlining
Blockbusting
questions.x: Filtering down describes housing passing to lower income occupants as it ages. Gentrification is the trap: it is the reverse movement, when higher income households move in and upgrade older housing.

questions.q: All of the following are protected as disabilities under fair housing law EXCEPT:
c: Past drug addiction, now in recovery
Current use of illegal drugs
Alcoholism
Being regarded as having a mental illness
questions.x: Current illegal drug use is excluded. Alcoholism is the tempting pick, but it is a protected disability, and being regarded as impaired is also covered.

questions.concept: Plessy and Brown on separate but equal
questions.q: Which case ended the separate but equal doctrine in public education?
c: Brown v. Board of Education
Plessy v. Ferguson
Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co.
Shelley v. Kraemer
questions.x: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) rejected separate but equal in public schools. Plessy is the trap: it is the 1896 case that approved the doctrine.

questions.q: All of the following are New York State protected classes that federal fair housing law does NOT list EXCEPT:
c: Gender identity or expression
Marital status
Familial status
Military status
questions.x: Familial status is already federal, so it is not a NY-only addition. Creed is the tempting pick, but it is a New York term that goes beyond federal religion protection.

questions.q: A Syracuse landlord refuses to rent to a bartender because of his job. Under the NYS Human Rights Law, the refusal is:
c: Illegal, since lawful occupation is a state class
Not barred, since occupation is an NYC class
Illegal, since it is source of income discrimination
Not barred, if he also refuses other bartenders
questions.x: Lawful occupation is protected by the NYC Human Rights Law, not by state law, so it does not reach Syracuse. The source-of-income answer is the trap: that protects how rent is paid (vouchers, benefits), not what job a person has.

questions.q: An applicant in Albany will pay part of her rent with Social Security disability income. Under New York law, the landlord:
c: May refuse, since benefits are not wages
May refuse, since the rule covers NYC tenants
May not refuse on the basis of that income
May refuse if the building has under six units
questions.x: Lawful source of income, including SSI, SSDI, and vouchers, has been protected statewide since 2019. The NYC-only answer is the trap: the state law now covers every county.

questions.q: An owner lives in one unit of a four-family house in Utica and rents the others herself. Is she exempt from the NYS Human Rights Law?
c: Yes, NY exempts owner-occupied 2 to 4 unit homes
Yes, under the federal Mrs. Murphy exemption
No, NY's owner exemption stops at two-family homes
Yes, if she rents without a broker or listing
questions.x: New York's owner-occupied exemption applies to a two-family house, so a four-family owner is covered by the state law. The Mrs. Murphy answer is the trap: that is the federal 2 to 4 unit exemption, which New York narrows.

questions.q: A 100-unit community wants to qualify as 55+ housing for older persons. At minimum, how many occupied units need at least one resident who is 55 or older?
questions.x: The 55+ test requires at least 80% of occupied units to have one person 55 or older, plus published policies and age verification. 100 is the trap: every resident being 62 or older is the separate 62+ test.

questions.q: A qualifying 62+ community may lawfully take all of the following actions EXCEPT:
c: Refusing a family with a 5-year-old child
Requiring residents to be 62 or older
Verifying the ages of new residents
Refusing a buyer because of a disability
questions.x: The senior housing exemption shelters age and familial status only; it never permits disability discrimination. Refusing a family with a child is the tempting pick, but that is exactly what the exemption allows.

questions.q: An owner of three rental houses lists one with a broker and tells the broker not to rent to families with children. Under the Fair Housing Act, the owner is:
c: Exempt, since he owns three or fewer homes
Exempt, since the broker made the decision
Liable, since owners of rentals are not exempt
Liable; using a broker ends the exemption
questions.x: The single-family exemption is lost when the owner uses a broker or a discriminatory ad. The three-homes answer is the trap: owning three or fewer is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.q: A tenant who uses a wheelchair asks to install grab bars and widen the bathroom doorway. This is a request for a:
c: Reasonable accommodation
Reasonable modification of the premises
Housing for older persons exemption
Rule change the landlord may refuse
questions.x: A physical change to the premises is a modification. Accommodation is the trap: that term covers changes to rules, policies, practices, or services.

questions.q: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, a tenant in a private building pays to widen a bathroom door. At move-out, the landlord may reasonably ask the tenant to:
c: Restore the interior to its prior condition
Pay a fee equal to the full cost of the work
Forfeit the security deposit in full
Leave the work in place at no further cost
questions.x: In private housing the tenant generally pays for a modification, and the landlord may require reasonable restoration of interior changes. Forfeiting the deposit is the trap: the landlord may set up a restoration escrow when reasonable, not seize the whole deposit.

questions.q: A Queens owner lives in one unit of her two-family house and rents the other by word of mouth among friends, with no ads or listings. Under the NYC Human Rights Law, the rental is:
c: Covered, since the City has no owner exemption
Covered, unless she also uses no broker
Exempt, since NYC exempts up to four units
Exempt, as she has not listed it publicly
questions.x: NYC exempts an owner-occupied two-family unit only when it is not publicly advertised or listed, and word of mouth keeps it private. The four-unit answer is the trap: that is the federal Mrs. Murphy rule, not the City's.

questions.q: A Buffalo tenant believes she was denied an apartment because of her marital status and wants a state administrative remedy. She files with the:
c: NYS Division of Human Rights
NYS Department of State
Department of Housing and Urban Development
Homes and Community Renewal
questions.x: The Division of Human Rights enforces the NYS Human Rights Law, which protects marital status. HUD is the trap: marital status is not a federal class, so HUD cannot take the claim.

questions.q: A Manhattan landlord rejects an applicant because of his weight. Under the NYC Human Rights Law as amended in 2023, this is:
c: Legal, since weight is not a protected class
Illegal; height and weight are protected
Legal, if the landlord rejects others the same
Illegal under federal disability law instead
questions.x: NYC added height and weight as protected classes in 2023. The not-protected answer is the trap: it is true under state and federal law, but not in the City.

questions.q: A Brooklyn landlord screens for annual income of 40 times the monthly rent. Rent is $3,000 and a CityFHEPS voucher pays $2,400. The applicant needs annual income of at least:
questions.x: In NYC the income test applies only to the tenant's share: $3,000 - $2,400 = $600, and $600 x 40 = $24,000. $120,000 is the trap: applying the test to the full rent discriminates by source of income.

questions.q: A landlord may lawfully refuse all of the following applicants EXCEPT one who:
c: Was convicted of selling heroin
Was convicted of making methamphetamine
Is in treatment and not using drugs
Was convicted of distributing cocaine
questions.x: A person in treatment who is not currently using illegal drugs is protected as having a disability. The distribution convictions are lawful grounds for refusal under the FHA's express exclusion.

questions.q: Which listing phrase raises a New York marital status problem?
c: "Ideal for a single professional"
"Three blocks to the Metro-North station"
"One bedroom with a home office"
"Pets considered case by case"
questions.x: "Ideal for a single professional" signals a preference by marital status, a New York class (and may also discourage families). A pet rule is the tempting pick, but a neutral pet policy is not a marital status issue.

questions.q: Steering is best described as:
c: Inducing owners to sell by stoking fear of protected-class newcomers
Refusing or limiting loans in certain neighborhoods by who lives there
Channeling buyers or renters toward or away from areas by protected class
Quoting different rents or terms to applicants in a protected class
questions.x: Steering targets buyers and renters by guiding where they look. Inducing owners to sell through fear is the trap: that is blockbusting, which targets owners, not homeseekers.

questions.q: Blockbusting is also known as:
c: Puffing
Panic peddling
Filtering down
Reverse redlining
questions.x: Blockbusting is panic peddling: scaring owners into selling by predicting protected-class newcomers. Reverse redlining is the trap: it means targeting a protected group for predatory loans.

questions.q: A bank's internal policy is not to make home loans in three Bronx zip codes because of the residents' ethnic makeup, regardless of applicants' credit. This is:
c: Steering
Blockbusting
Risk-based pricing
Redlining
questions.x: Refusing or limiting loans in an area because of who lives there is redlining. Risk-based pricing is the trap: lenders may price for an individual borrower's credit, not for a neighborhood's demographics.

questions.q: A buyer asks Jordan, "Is this neighborhood safe?" The best compliant response is to:
c: Give an honest personal opinion of the neighborhood
Say the area is a good fit for a family like theirs
Refer the buyer to public police precinct crime data
Decline to discuss the neighborhood and end the showing
questions.x: Pointing the buyer to objective public data is helpful and avoids steering. The honest-opinion answer is the trap: personal safety opinions often carry coded demographic messages.

questions.q: A Jewish buyer asks to see only homes within walking distance of a particular synagogue. Jordan shows her listings within that radius. This is:
c: Steering, because Jordan factored in religion
Legal, because the buyer chose the criteria herself
Blockbusting, because religion was discussed
Illegal unless each seller agrees in writing
questions.x: Following a buyer's own stated location criteria is not steering. The steering answer is the trap: steering happens when the agent limits choices by a protected class without the buyer asking.

questions.q: An agent tells a Black couple that a Forest Hills co-op "just went into contract" when it has not, then shows it to a white couple the next day. This is:
c: Illegal misrepresentation that it is unavailable
Legal, if the seller gave the instruction
Steering, if they had asked about neighbors
Legal, because co-op boards may reject buyers
questions.x: Falsely saying a property is unavailable because of race is expressly illegal under the FHA and NY law. The seller-instruction answer is the trap: a client's instruction is never a defense.

questions.q: All of the following ad phrases are discriminatory EXCEPT:
c: "Perfect for empty nesters"
"Adults preferred"
"No programs accepted"
"Two blocks from Prospect Park"
questions.x: Describing location is fine. "No programs accepted" is the tempting pick because it sounds like a neutral policy, but it excludes voucher holders and violates the lawful source of income protection.

questions.concept: Ad ban applies to exempt owners
questions.q: A homeowner who is exempt from the Fair Housing Act under the single-family exemption places an ad stating "no children." The ad is:
c: Legal, because the owner is exempt
Legal, if no broker is involved
Illegal; the ad ban covers exempt owners
Legal, if posted on social media
questions.x: The ban on discriminatory advertising applies to everyone, and such an ad also destroys the single-family exemption. The no-broker answer is the trap: avoiding a broker preserves the exemption only when the ad is neutral.

questions.q: Fair housing testers are:
c: People posing as homeseekers to check for equal treatment
Licensed inspectors who test older homes for lead paint
HUD examiners who audit lenders' loan application files
Appraisers who test a value against comparable sales
questions.x: Testers pose as buyers or renters, often in matched pairs, to detect unequal treatment. HUD examiners are the trap: HUD uses testers, but testers are not loan file auditors.

questions.q: Which statement about fair housing testers is correct?
c: Testing is illegal entrapment of licensees
Testers may sue though they never meant to rent
Testing is reserved to HUD investigators
Evidence gathered by testers is inadmissible
questions.x: Havens Realty v. Coleman (1982) recognized tester standing to sue. The HUD-only answer is the trap: fair housing groups, the NY Attorney General, and the NYC Commission also run tests.

questions.q: In a New York cease and desist zone, a licensee may not solicit listings from:
c: Any owner of property inside the zone
Owners who filed their names on the list
Owners who have listed with another broker
Owners of commercial property in the zone
questions.x: A cease and desist zone protects owners who register on the cease and desist list. The every-owner answer is the trap: that describes a nonsolicitation order.

questions.q: Under RPL 442-h, the maximum period a nonsolicitation order or cease and desist zone rule may stay in effect before it is readopted is:
c: 1 year
3 years
10 years
5 years
questions.x: Both nonsolicitation orders and cease and desist zone rules last up to 5 years and may be readopted. Three years is the trap: it is the record retention period for disclosure forms.

questions.q: What distinguishes a nonsolicitation order from a cease and desist zone in New York?
c: The order covers every owner in the area; the zone protects owners who sign up
The order is issued by HUD; the zone is created by the Secretary of State
The order covers commercial owners; the zone covers residential owners
The order bans TV ads; the zone bans phone calls and door knocking
questions.x: A nonsolicitation order bars specified solicitation of all owners in an area after a hearing, while a cease and desist zone protects only owners on the list. The HUD answer is the trap: both tools belong to the NY Secretary of State under RPL 442-h.

questions.q: Marcus texts owners in the East Flatbush cease and desist zone, including several on the list, saying "Prices are about to fall here. Sell now." Which consequences could follow?
c: No discipline, because text messages are not solicitation
A warning from his broker with no state discipline
DOS discipline up to revocation, plus blockbusting liability
A HUD fine, since DOS has no power over solicitation
questions.x: Texts count as solicitation, DOS can impose penalties up to revocation, and fear-based messages can also be blockbusting. The HUD answer is the trap: cease and desist zones are a DOS tool under RPL 442-h.

questions.q: All of the following are forms of illegal unequal treatment EXCEPT:
c: Requiring a larger security deposit from families with children
Limiting a building's gym hours for tenants who hold vouchers
Charging every applicant the same $20 background check fee
Showing a buyer fewer listings because of her national origin
questions.x: A uniform fee applied to everyone is not discrimination, and NY caps background check fees at actual cost up to $20. The gym-hours answer is the trap: restricting amenities by voucher status is unequal terms based on source of income.

questions.q: A brokerage runs paid social media ads for rentals and sets the targeting to exclude users over 50 and users with "parent" interests. This is:
c: Legal, because the platform decides who sees ads
Legal, if the ad text itself is neutral
A federal violation, but not a NY violation
Discriminatory advertising through targeting
questions.x: Targeting that excludes people by age or family status is discriminatory even when the words are neutral. The federal-only answer is the trap: age is protected in New York, and familial status is protected both federally and in NY.

questions.q: The New York State Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form is provided:
c: At first substantive contact with buyers, sellers, landlords, and tenants
At the signing of the purchase contract or the lease by the consumer
To tenants of rent-stabilized apartments when a lease is offered
To a consumer once a discrimination complaint has been filed
questions.x: The form is due at first substantive contact, to both sides of sales and rentals. Contract signing is the trap: by then the protections the form explains could already have been violated.

questions.q: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form applies to:
c: Residential 1 to 4 family properties
Residential rentals of any size
Co-op and condominium units
Every property type, including land
questions.x: The anti-discrimination form applies to all real estate, including commercial property and vacant land. The 1 to 4 family answer is the trap: that is the scope of the RPL 443 agency disclosure.

questions.q: Under RPL 442-h, a broker's standardized operating procedures for prospective homebuyers address whether the broker requires:
c: A 700 credit score, a W-2, and a co-signer
ID, an exclusive agreement, and pre-approval
Proof of citizenship, marital status, and references
A deposit, a sign-in sheet, and a property survey
questions.x: The SOP states whether the broker requires identification, an exclusive buyer agreement, and mortgage pre-approval. The citizenship answer is the trap: asking about citizenship or marital status would itself raise fair housing problems.

questions.q: Which statement about New York standardized operating procedures is correct today?
c: They are filed with the Department of State each year
Each agent in the firm writes and posts a personal version
They are dated, notarized, posted, and applied to each buyer
They govern rental applicants but not prospective buyers
questions.x: Brokers date stamp, notarize, post, and follow their SOPs, updating postings within 30 days of a change. The annual-filing answer is the trap: a 2022 amendment removed the DOS filing requirement.

questions.q: Implicit bias is best defined as:
c: Openly stated prejudice toward a group
Unconscious attitudes that shape decisions
A lender's automated credit scoring model
Disagreement with the goals of fair housing law
questions.x: Implicit bias operates without conscious awareness, so a person can reject a stereotype and still act on it. Openly stated prejudice is the trap: that is explicit bias.

questions.q: For discrimination occurring on or after February 15, 2024, a complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights is filed within:
c: 1 year
2 years
3 years
6 months
questions.x: The DHR deadline was extended from 1 year to 3 years for conduct on or after February 15, 2024. One year is the trap: it is the old DHR limit and still the HUD limit.

questions.q: A housing discrimination complaint filed with HUD is generally filed within:
c: 1 year of the act
90 days of the act
2 years of the act
3 years of the act
questions.x: HUD administrative complaints are due within 1 year. Two years is the trap: that is the limit for a private lawsuit in federal court.

questions.q: A landlord tells his agent to reject applicants with children, and the agent complies. Who is liable?
c: The landlord alone, as the source of the instruction
The agent alone, as the person who carried it out
Neither, if the instruction was given in writing
The landlord, the agent, and possibly their broker
questions.x: Everyone who participates is liable, and the broker can be liable for failing to supervise. The landlord-alone answer is the trap: following a client's instruction is never a defense for the agent.

questions.concept: NYS Human Rights Law civil fines
questions.q: Under the NYS Human Rights Law, the maximum civil fine for a discriminatory act found to be willful, wanton, or malicious is:
questions.x: Civil fines can reach $50,000, or $100,000 if the act was willful, wanton, or malicious. $50,000 is the trap: it is the cap for an ordinary violation.

questions.q: A New York broker's fair housing responsibilities include all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Posting fair housing notices in the office and online
Reviewing agents' advertising for fair housing compliance
Picking each buyer's neighborhoods based on background
Training agents and keeping required records
questions.x: Choosing neighborhoods by a buyer's background is steering, not a duty. Reviewing ads is the tempting pick for some, but supervising advertising is a core broker responsibility.

questions.q: A landlord rejects every applicant with any criminal record, of any age or type. The policy falls much harder on certain racial groups and the landlord cannot show it is necessary. A court may find:
c: Disparate impact discrimination
No violation, since it is applied evenly
Blockbusting by the landlord
Redlining by the landlord
questions.x: A facially neutral policy with an unjustified discriminatory effect can be illegal as disparate impact. The applied-evenly answer is the trap: equal application does not cure an unjustified discriminatory effect, and NYC's Fair Chance for Housing Law adds limits.

questions.q: How long does a licensee keep a copy of the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form?
c: 1 year
3 years
5 years
Until closing
questions.x: Like the agency disclosure form, it is kept for 3 years. Until closing is the trap: the record outlives the deal.

questions.q: Which agent habit best protects against a fair housing complaint from a tester?
c: Same script and records for every inquiry
Asking callers where they are from
Calling back callers who sound serious
Showing buyers the areas that suit them
questions.x: Consistent scripts, equal procedures, and logged records prove equal treatment. Calling back serious-sounding callers is the trap: judging by voice is where implicit bias creeps in.

questions.q: For a residential rental, which notice does a New York licensee give prospective tenants in addition to the agency and anti-discrimination forms?
c: Property Condition Disclosure Statement
Lead paint disclosure for every building
Reasonable accommodation and modification notice
Mortgage pre-approval notice
questions.x: New York requires the reasonable accommodation and modification notice for rentals. The PCDS is the trap: it applies to sales of 1 to 4 family homes, not rentals, and the lead disclosure applies to pre-1978 housing.

questions.q: Without being asked, an agent shows a Latino couple homes in only two neighborhoods "where they'll feel comfortable," though their budget fits many more. This is:
c: Steering
Blockbusting
Redlining
Puffing
questions.x: Channeling homeseekers toward or away from areas because of a protected class is steering, even when framed as a favor. Blockbusting is the trap: it targets owners, inducing them to sell through fear.

questions.q: A licensee mails flyers to homeowners warning that "a new group is moving in and values will drop, so sell to us now." This conduct is:
c: Steering
Redlining
Blockbusting
Lawful canvassing
questions.x: Inducing owners to sell by predicting the entry of a protected group is blockbusting, or panic peddling. Steering is the trap: it targets buyers and renters, not owners.

questions.q: A lender may lawfully consider all of the following when deciding on a home loan EXCEPT:
c: The applicant's credit history
The applicant's debt-to-income ratio and assets
The appraised value of the property
The racial makeup of the neighborhood
questions.x: Basing loan decisions on a neighborhood's racial makeup is redlining. Appraised value is the tempting pick, but evaluating the collateral itself is a legitimate underwriting factor.

questions.q: A buyer asks Priya, "Are the schools here good?" Which reply best avoids a steering problem?
c: "They're great for families like yours."
"Here are the State's school report cards."
"I'd look in the next district over instead."
"I can't talk about schools; let's move on."
questions.x: Pointing the buyer to objective public data, such as State school report cards, is helpful and neutral. The next-district answer is the trap: steering the buyer toward another area based on the agent's opinion can carry coded messages.

questions.q: A buyer of Korean descent asks to see homes near a Korean community center. The agent, unprompted, also limits the search to areas with many Korean residents. Which part is steering?
c: Narrowing the search by residents' ancestry
Showing homes near the community center
Both parts, since ancestry came up
Neither part, since the buyer raised the topic
questions.x: Following the buyer's own location request is fine; adding an unrequested limit based on the residents' national origin is steering. The both-parts answer is the trap: a buyer's own criteria do not become steering just because they relate to a protected class.

questions.q: A landlord tells a caller with a Spanish accent that the apartment is rented, then shows it the same afternoon to a caller without one. This is:
c: Legal, if the first caller did not visit
Steering, since no unit changed hands
Legal, since landlords may screen by phone first
Illegal misrepresentation of availability
