questions.x: Falsely stating that housing is unavailable because of national origin is expressly illegal. The steering answer is the trap: steering guides people among areas, while this is a false denial of availability.

questions.q: Which ad phrase is acceptable under federal and New York fair housing law?
c: "Ideal for mature adults"
"Section 8 not accepted"
"Walk-in closet, near the LIRR"
"Perfect for a young professional couple"
questions.x: Describing features and location is fine. "Ideal for mature adults" is the trap: it signals an age and familial status preference, both protected in New York.

questions.concept: Ad ban applies to exempt owners
questions.q: An owner who lives in one unit of a federally exempt owner-occupied three-family house posts an online ad: "Christians preferred." Under the Fair Housing Act, the ad is:
c: Legal, since the owner is exempt from the Act
Legal, if the owner uses no broker
Legal, if the house is outside NYC
Illegal; exempt owners may not run it
questions.x: Even owners who qualify for an exemption may not publish discriminatory ads; the advertising ban has no owner exemption. The no-broker answer is the trap: avoiding a broker is a condition of the single-family exemption, not a license to advertise a preference.

questions.q: A fair housing group sends two callers with identical finances, one using a voucher, to the same rental agent. This technique is called:
c: Paired testing
Blockbusting
Redlining audit
Mystery appraisal
questions.x: Paired testing sends matched testers who differ in one trait to detect unequal treatment. Redlining audit is the trap: redlining concerns lending by area, not how a rental agent treats callers.

questions.q: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982) is known for holding that:
c: Testing is entrapment of real estate agents
Testers may sue even with no intent to rent
Testers need a HUD license to pose as renters
Tester evidence is admissible against lenders
questions.x: Havens recognized that a tester who receives false information has standing to sue even without intending to rent. The admissible-against-lenders answer is the trap: tester evidence is used against agents and landlords too, and that was not Havens' holding.

questions.q: In the East Flatbush cease and desist zone, Leo calls an owner who did not put her name on the list. Under the zone rule, the call is:
c: Prohibited, since the zone covers every owner
Permitted, since she is not on the list
Prohibited, unless he has her written consent
Permitted, if he calls on weekdays
questions.x: A cease and desist zone protects owners who file their names on the list. The covers-all-owners answer is the trap: that describes a nonsolicitation order. Leo still may not engage in blockbusting.

questions.q: A cease and desist zone was adopted in 2022 for the maximum allowed term. Unless readopted, it expires in:
c: No set expiration date
questions.x: Cease and desist zone rules and nonsolicitation orders run up to 5 years, so a 2022 zone expires in 2027 unless readopted. 2025 is the trap: it applies the 3-year record retention period.

questions.q: After a public hearing, the Secretary of State bars licensees from soliciting every homeowner in part of a town, whether or not they signed up. This is a:
c: Cease and desist zone
HUD conciliation order
Nonsolicitation order
Do-not-call registry
questions.x: A nonsolicitation order covers all owners in the defined area. A cease and desist zone is the trap: it protects only owners who file their names on the list.

questions.q: Soliciting a listed owner in a New York cease and desist zone can lead to all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A fine imposed by DOS
License suspension
License revocation
A HUD indictment
questions.x: Cease and desist zones are enforced by DOS, which can fine, suspend, or revoke. The HUD indictment answer is the trap: HUD does not enforce NY's RPL 442-h solicitation rules or indict anyone.

questions.q: A landlord rents to a family with children but charges them a $500 higher deposit than other tenants "for wear and tear." This is:
c: Legal, since the family got the apartment
Discrimination in the terms and conditions
Legal, if the deposit is under a month
Steering, since it limits their choices
questions.x: Offering different terms to a protected class is discrimination even when the unit is rented. The under-a-month answer is the trap: the NY deposit cap does not make a discriminatory surcharge lawful.

questions.q: Which online ad practice is most likely to violate fair housing law?
c: Targeting by ZIP codes picked to exclude a race
Targeting users who recently searched for rentals
Posting to the brokerage's own website
Boosting a post to everyone in the county
questions.x: Choosing geographic targeting to exclude a racial group is discriminatory advertising, even with neutral ad text. Targeting by rental searches is the trap: it is based on behavior, not a protected class.

questions.q: A seller meets Diane to discuss listing a commercial building. When does Diane give the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form?
c: At the listing agreement signing
At the first substantive contact
Once a buyer makes an offer
She skips it for commercial sellers
questions.x: The form goes to sellers, buyers, landlords, and tenants at first substantive contact, for every property type. The skip-it answer is the trap: unlike the agency disclosure, this form covers commercial property.

questions.q: The NYS Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form is given in all of the following transactions EXCEPT:
c: Sale of vacant land
Lease of retail space
Sale of a two-family home
Refinance with a bank
questions.x: The form applies to licensee activity in sales and rentals of every property type, but a bank refinance involves no licensee brokering a sale or rental. Vacant land is the tempting pick, but it is covered, unlike under the RPL 443 agency form.

questions.q: A New York broker's homebuyer SOP states whether the broker requires all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Proof of identification
A signed exclusive buyer agreement
Mortgage pre-approval
A minimum credit score
questions.x: RPL 442-h SOPs address identification, an exclusive broker agreement, and pre-approval. A minimum credit score is not one of the required SOP topics; pre-approval is the tempting pick, but it is one of the three.

questions.q: A broker changes her SOP to require pre-approval letters. Within how many days does she update the posted SOP?
c: With the next license renewal
30 days
60 days
90 days
questions.x: Brokers update posted SOPs within 30 days of a change, and the new SOP must be dated and notarized. 90 days is the trap: it is a lease non-renewal notice period, not an SOP deadline.

questions.q: An agent who sincerely supports fair housing tends to return calls faster when the caller's name sounds like her own background. This most likely reflects:
c: Explicit bias
Implicit bias
Blockbusting
Disparate impact
questions.x: Implicit bias is unconscious and can operate in people who reject stereotypes. Disparate impact is the trap: it describes a neutral policy's discriminatory effect, not an individual's unconscious habit.

questions.q: A tenant was denied an apartment because of her immigration status on March 1, 2024. The last day to file with the NYS Division of Human Rights is about:
c: March 1, 2025
March 1, 2026
March 1, 2027
September 1, 2024
questions.x: For conduct on or after February 15, 2024, the DHR deadline is 3 years, so about March 1, 2027. March 1, 2025 is the trap: it applies the old 1-year limit, which is still the HUD limit.

questions.q: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, a private lawsuit filed directly in federal court has a deadline of:
c: 1 year
2 years
3 years
180 days
questions.x: A private federal fair housing lawsuit must be filed within 2 years. One year is the trap: that is the deadline for an administrative complaint with HUD.

questions.q: A seller tells Jordan, "Don't bring me any offers from Muslim buyers." Jordan's best response is to:
c: Comply, since he owes the seller a duty of obedience
Comply, if the seller puts it in writing
Refuse, and withdraw if the seller insists
Refer the seller to another agent quietly
questions.x: The duty of obedience covers lawful instructions only; an illegal instruction must be refused, and the agent should withdraw if the client insists. The written-instruction answer is the trap: putting it in writing makes no difference to liability.

questions.concept: NYS Human Rights Law civil fines
questions.q: For a housing discrimination finding that is NOT willful, wanton, or malicious, the NYS Human Rights Law civil fine may reach:
questions.x: The ordinary cap is $50,000; $100,000 applies to willful, wanton, or malicious acts. $1,000 is the trap: it was the old DOS per-violation fine for licensing violations.

questions.q: An agent at Sal's brokerage posts a discriminatory rental ad. Sal never reviewed agents' ads. Sal's exposure is best described as:
c: Liability for failure to supervise agents
No liability, since the agent wrote the ad
Liability if the landlord approved the ad
No liability, if Sal deletes the ad once told
questions.x: Brokers must supervise agents, including advertising, and can be liable for failure to supervise. The deletion answer is the trap: removing the ad helps but does not erase the violation.

questions.q: Disparate treatment differs from disparate impact because disparate treatment involves:
c: Intentional different treatment
A neutral policy with an unequal effect
Lending decisions based on location
Advertising in one language
questions.x: Disparate treatment is intentional, different treatment because of a protected class. The neutral-policy answer is the trap: that is the definition of disparate impact.

questions.q: Diane gave a buyer the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form on June 1, 2025. She keeps her copy at least until:
c: June 1, 2026
June 1, 2028
Until the transaction closes
June 1, 2030
questions.x: The form is kept for 3 years, so until June 1, 2028. June 1, 2030 is the trap: it applies a 5-year period, which matches nonsolicitation orders, not records.

questions.q: All of the following practices help a brokerage withstand paired testing EXCEPT:
c: A written call script used for every inquiry
A log of every inquiry and response time
Equal SOP requirements for every buyer
Screening callers by how serious they sound
questions.x: Judging callers by how they sound invites implicit bias, which testers are designed to catch. Logging response times is the tempting pick, but it documents equal treatment.

questions.q: Leo is showing a Rochester apartment to a prospective tenant. Which pair of notices goes with the agency disclosure?
c: PCDS and the EPA lead paint pamphlet
Fair housing poster and a signed PCDS form
Accommodation notice and a pre-approval letter
Anti-discrimination and accommodation notices
questions.x: For rentals, New York requires the anti-discrimination disclosure and the reasonable accommodation and modification notice along with the agency form. The PCDS is the trap: it applies to sales of 1 to 4 family homes, not rentals.

questions.q: An owner lives in one unit of a three-family house in Utica and refuses to rent to a divorced applicant because of her marital status. No ads or brokers were used. Under the NYS Human Rights Law, the refusal is:
c: Exempt, because New York follows the federal four-unit owner-occupancy exemption
Illegal, since New York's exemption covers owner-occupied two-family homes
Exempt, because the owner did not advertise the vacancy
Illegal, but just if the building is located in New York City
questions.x: New York limits its owner-occupancy exemption to buildings housing no more than two families. A three-family is covered by the state law regardless of advertising. The four-unit rule is the federal Mrs. Murphy number, and marital status is not a federal class anyway.

questions.q: Under the New York State Human Rights Law, the owner-occupancy exemption for rentals applies to a building with no more than:
c: Four families living independently, one of them the owner's
Three families, if the owner has lived there at least one year
Two families living independently, one of them the owner's
One family, with rooms rented to boarders
questions.x: Executive Law 296(5)(a)(4) exempts the rental of a housing accommodation in a building for not more than two families if the owner lives in one of them. Four units is the federal Mrs. Murphy limit, which is the usual wrong pick.

questions.q: A Bronx owner lives in one unit of her two-family house and posts the vacancy on a listing website. She then refuses an applicant with a voucher. Under the NYC Human Rights Law:
c: She is exempt, because she lives in the two-family house
She is exempt, though the website listing has to come down
She is covered, because source of income has no exemptions
She is covered, because the unit was publicly advertised
questions.x: The city's two-family exemption applies only if the unit was not advertised or offered to the public. A website listing ends it. The answer that source of income has no exemptions overstates the rule: an unadvertised owner-occupied two-family is exempt from the city law for every class.

questions.q: An owner lives in her Queens two-family house and is looking for a tenant for the other unit. Each of the following would end her NYC Human Rights Law exemption EXCEPT:
c: Mentioning the vacancy to coworkers and neighbors
Listing the unit for rent with a real estate brokerage
Putting a For Rent sign in the front window facing the street
Posting the unit on a rental listing website
questions.x: The city exemption survives only if the unit is not advertised or offered to the public. A sign, a website post and a brokerage listing all offer it publicly. Telling people privately by word of mouth does not, which is the scenario the exemption was built for.

questions.q: A homeowner who otherwise qualifies for a Fair Housing Act exemption refuses to sell to a buyer because of the buyer's race. Which statement is correct?
c: The refusal is lawful if no broker or advertisement was used in the sale
It violates the Civil Rights Act of 1866, which has no exemptions
The refusal is lawful federally but violates New York State law
The refusal is lawful if the owner lives in the property
questions.x: The 1866 Act bars racial discrimination in property sales and rentals with no exemptions, as applied to private parties in Jones v. Mayer (1968). The answer limiting the problem to state law is tempting but wrong: federal law itself reaches the refusal through the 1866 Act.

questions.q: Which law prohibits racial discrimination in the sale or rental of property with no exemption for owner-occupied or single-family housing?
c: Fair Housing Act of 1968
Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988
Civil Rights Act of 1866
Housing and Community Development Act of 1974
questions.x: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 gives all citizens the same property rights as white citizens and contains no exemptions. The 1968 Fair Housing Act is the common wrong pick, but it does contain owner exemptions such as Mrs. Murphy and the single-family rule.

questions.q: An owner of two single-family homes in Saratoga Springs rents one himself, without a broker or ads, and refuses a family with children. Which statement is correct?
c: He may be exempt federally but violates the NYS Human Rights Law
He is exempt under both federal law and New York State law
He violates federal law but is exempt under the New York State law
He is exempt because familial status protection covers just sales
questions.x: The federal Act exempts an owner of no more than three single-family homes who uses no broker and no discriminatory ads. New York has no single-family exemption, and it protects familial status, so the state law reaches him. Assuming the state mirrors the federal exemption is the trap.

questions.q: The federal exemption for an owner renting a single-family house without a broker:
c: Has a matching exemption in the NYS Human Rights Law
Has no counterpart in the NYS Human Rights Law
Applies in New York just to owner-occupied homes
Applies in New York except inside New York City
questions.x: New York's exemptions are narrower than federal ones. The state law has an owner-occupied two-family exemption and room exemptions, but nothing for single-family homes. An owner who would be exempt federally is still covered by New York law.

questions.q: A 55-and-over community has 200 homes. 20 are vacant. Of the occupied homes, 140 have at least one resident 55 or older. Under the federal 80% test, the community:
c: Fails, because 140 of 200 homes is 70%
Fails, because just 140 homes have a resident over 55
Qualifies, because 140 of 180 occupied homes is about 78%
Fails, because 140 of 180 occupied homes is about 78%
questions.x: The test uses occupied units: 140 / 180 = 77.8%, which is below the required 80%, so the community does not qualify. Dividing by all 200 homes also gives a failing number but uses the wrong base; the choice that says 78% qualifies misreads the threshold.

questions.q: To qualify as 55-and-over housing under the federal exemption, a community must have at least one person 55 or older in at least:
c: 80% of its occupied units, with published policies and age verification
80% of every unit, occupied or vacant, with no further conditions attached
100% of its units, with every resident aged 55 or older
62% of its occupied units, with age verified at the time of purchase
questions.x: The 55-and-over category requires at least 80% of occupied units to have one resident 55 or older, plus published policies showing intent and reliable age verification. The all-residents rule belongs to the separate 62-and-over category, where everyone must be 62 or older.

questions.q: A qualifying 55-and-over community refuses a 60-year-old buyer because her adult daughter, who lives with her, is deaf. The refusal is:
c: Legal, because the senior housing exemption covers every occupancy rule
Illegal, because the exemption covers only age and familial status
Legal, because the daughter is under 55
Illegal, because adult children cannot be excluded
questions.x: Senior housing may limit age and familial status. Disability stays fully protected, so refusing because a household member is deaf is disability discrimination. The age-based answer is a trap: the stated reason here is the daughter's disability, not her age.
questions.concept: Senior exemption limited to age and familial status

questions.q: A qualifying 62-and-over community may lawfully do each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Refuse a buyer whose 10-year-old child would live in the home
Advertise itself as housing for persons 62 and older
Refuse a buyer because the buyer is Jewish
Require proof of age from every resident
questions.x: The older persons exemption reaches age and familial status only. Excluding children, advertising the age restriction and verifying ages are all part of running a qualifying community. Religion is untouched by the exemption, so refusing a Jewish buyer is illegal.
questions.concept: Senior exemption limited to age and familial status

questions.q: A Queens apartment rents for $2,600. An applicant's voucher pays $2,150 and she pays the rest. The landlord requires income of 40 times the monthly rent. Under NYC law, what annual income must she show?
questions.x: In NYC an income requirement applies only to the tenant's share: $2,600 minus $2,150 is $450, and 40 x $450 = $18,000. The $104,000 figure applies the multiple to the full rent, which screens out voucher holders and is source of income discrimination.

questions.q: A Brooklyn landlord tells a voucher holder she fails the income test because her wages are below 40 times the full monthly rent, although her voucher pays most of it. This is:
c: Lawful, because the rule is applied the same way to every applicant
Lawful, if the building is not rent stabilized
Unlawful, because NYC bans income requirements for rentals
Unlawful, since NYC applies the test to her share of the rent
questions.x: NYC requires that income requirements be measured against the portion of rent the tenant pays. Applying the same full-rent test to everyone sounds neutral but excludes voucher holders. Income requirements are not banned outright, so the third choice overstates the rule.

questions.q: When a housing voucher covers an applicant's entire rent in NYC, the landlord:
c: May reject the applicant based on credit score if applied to everyone
May not reject the applicant based on credit history or score
May require a co-signer in place of a credit check
May charge a higher security deposit to offset credit risk
questions.x: The NYC Commission on Human Rights says that when a subsidy covers the full rent, credit history cannot be the basis for rejection, because the tenant's credit does not affect payment. A uniform credit cutoff is the tempting wrong answer: neutral on paper, it still screens out the voucher.

questions.q: A Manhattan applicant pays $300 of a $2,500 rent; her voucher pays the rest. The landlord has a firm 700 minimum credit score and rejects her at 610 without further review. Under Commission guidance:
c: A fixed minimum is evidence of bias; she gets case-by-case review
The landlord acted lawfully, since she pays part of the rent herself
The landlord may not run a credit inquiry of any kind on her
The landlord acted lawfully if it applies 700 to every applicant
questions.x: When a tenant pays part of the rent, a credit inquiry is allowed, but a firm minimum score is evidence of source of income discrimination. The landlord should evaluate her history case by case and let her show she can pay her share. Banning any credit inquiry goes too far.

questions.q: Which protected class appears in the NYC Human Rights Law's housing provisions but not in the federal Fair Housing Act or the NYS Human Rights Law?
c: Familial status
Lawful occupation
Marital status
Lawful source of income
questions.x: Lawful occupation is a city-only class. Lawful source of income is the common wrong pick, but New York State has protected it statewide since 2019. Familial status is federal, and marital status is state.

questions.q: A Staten Island landlord refuses to rent to an applicant because she works as a nightclub bartender, even though her income easily qualifies. Under the NYC Human Rights Law, this is:
c: Lawful, because occupation is protected in employment alone
Lawful, if the landlord applies the rule to every bartender
Unlawful, but just because her income qualifies for the unit
Unlawful, because NYC protects lawful occupation in housing
questions.x: NYC lists lawful occupation as a protected class in housing, so refusing someone for a legal job is discrimination. A uniform rule against a lawful occupation is still a refusal based on that class. Her income does not create the protection.

questions.q: Under the NYC Fair Chance for Housing Law, when may a landlord run a criminal background check on a rental applicant?
c: At any point, if the check is run on every applicant
After other screening and a conditional offer
After the applicant has signed a lease
Before the credit check, so that both are reviewed together
questions.x: The law requires the non-criminal screening first, then a conditional offer, and only then the criminal check, with notice to the applicant. Running it for everyone at application defeats the sequence, which is why the uniform-check answer is wrong.

questions.q: An NYC applicant's report shows a felony conviction with release 6 years ago and a misdemeanor conviction 2 years ago. Under the Fair Chance for Housing Law's lookback limits, the landlord may consider:
c: Both convictions
Only the felony
Only the misdemeanor
Neither conviction
questions.x: Felonies may be considered within 5 years of release or sentencing and misdemeanors within 3 years. The felony release was 6 years ago, outside its window; the misdemeanor is 2 years old, inside its window. Assuming felonies always count longer is the trap.

questions.q: A Bronx landlord requires a Social Security number on every application and rejects an applicant who offers an ITIN and bank statements instead. This most directly risks a claim based on:
c: Citizenship or immigration status
National origin under the 1866 Act
Lawful occupation in housing
Familial status under federal law
questions.x: New York State and NYC protect citizenship and immigration status in housing. An SSN-only rule, when other documents can verify identity and income, screens applicants out by status. National origin is related but the 1866 Act covers race, not national origin.

questions.q: To avoid immigration status discrimination, an NYC landlord may do each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Require the same identification standard from every applicant
Accept an ITIN with other income documents
Verify income through bank statements
Ask only some applicants for proof of citizenship
questions.x: Uniform identification rules and alternate verification methods are lawful. Asking only certain applicants for proof of citizenship singles them out by perceived status, which New York State and NYC prohibit.

questions.q: A landlord rejects an applicant because of a housing court case caused by property damage her abusive former partner did, which her order of protection documents. Under the NYS Human Rights Law, this is:
c: Lawful, because eviction records are neutral criteria
Lawful, if the landlord applies the same record rule to every applicant
Unlawful discrimination based on domestic violence victim status
Unlawful, but just if the case was sealed by the court
questions.x: New York protects status as a victim of domestic violence. Rejecting her for the consequences of her abuser's conduct penalizes her for that status. Treating the record as neutral ignores the reason it exists.

questions.q: Which of the following is a protected class in housing under the NYS Human Rights Law but not under the federal Fair Housing Act?
c: Status as a victim of domestic violence
Disability of any household member
Religion, including having no religion
Sex, including sexual harassment
questions.x: New York protects status as a victim of domestic violence; the federal Act does not list it. Sex is the tempting choice, but sex has been a federal class since 1974.

questions.q: A salesperson mails "just sold" postcards to homeowners inside a DOS cease and desist zone. Which owners may lawfully receive them?
c: Every owner in the zone, because just sold cards are announcements
Owners who are not on the current cease and desist list
Owners outside the zone alone, since the zone bans mailings
Owners who listed with any broker in the past five years
questions.x: A cease and desist zone protects only owners who have joined the DOS list, and DOS counts just sold mailings as solicitation. Owners not on the current list may be mailed. The total-ban answer describes something closer to a nonsolicitation order.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts a cease and desist zone with a nonsolicitation order?
c: A zone protects every owner; an order protects owners who sign up
Both protect owners who sign up with the Department of State
A zone covers listed owners; an order covers all owners in the area
Both protect every owner and last until DOS revokes them
questions.x: Cease and desist zones are opt-in: only owners on the list are protected. A nonsolicitation order applies to all owners in the area after a DOS finding. Both last up to 5 years at a time. Reversing the two is the classic exam trap.

questions.q: An investment company that regularly buys homes knocks on the door of an owner who is on the cease and desist list in the Brooklyn zone. Under the DOS rules for that zone:
c: The rules apply to licensed brokers and salespeople alone
The visit is lawful, since door-knocking is not solicitation
The visit is lawful if the company makes a cash offer
The rules also reach those regularly buying homes
questions.x: DOS's Brooklyn zone rules cover brokers, salespeople and others regularly engaged in buying or selling property, including investment companies. Door-knocking is solicitation. Assuming only licensees are covered is the most tempting mistake.

questions.q: In the Brooklyn cease and desist zone, the DOS treats each of the following as solicitation of a listed owner EXCEPT:
c: A boosted Facebook post seen by owners in the zone
An every-door direct mail postcard sent to the block
A just listed letter mailed to the owner's home
A visit to the owner's front door by an investor
questions.x: According to the DOS FAQ, Facebook posts, including boosted posts, are not solicitation under the zone rules because they are not delivered to the owner's home. Mail of every kind and door visits are solicitation. Fair housing ad rules still apply to the post.

questions.q: An investor tells homeowners, "Families from the new shelter are moving in. Sell now while prices hold." This is:
c: Steering
Redlining
Blockbusting
Lawful market commentary
questions.x: Blockbusting induces owners to sell by suggesting a protected group is moving in and values will fall. Steering is directed at buyers or renters, not owners, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: A licensee's flyer in a Queens neighborhood reads, "The neighborhood is changing fast. Smart owners are cashing out now." The flyer is most likely:
c: Blockbusting, if the implied change is who is moving in
Steering, because it directs owners toward a particular buyer
Redlining, because it predicts lower values for a whole area
Lawful, because it names no protected class
questions.x: Blockbusting does not require naming a group. Coded language implying that a protected class is arriving and values will drop is enough. Redlining is a lending or insurance practice, and the no-named-class answer ignores implication.

questions.q: A buyer's search returns 12 listings that meet his criteria. His agent sends 8, leaving out 4 in a neighborhood the agent believes the buyer "won't be comfortable in" because of its residents. This is:
c: Acceptable, because the agent is protecting the client
Acceptable, if the buyer did not ask for those areas
Steering: matching listings withheld by area makeup
Blockbusting, because the agent is limiting the neighborhood
questions.x: Withholding listings that meet a buyer's stated criteria because of who lives in an area is steering, and treating buyers differently is unequal treatment. Blockbusting targets owners and induces sales, so it does not fit.

questions.q: A buyer asks an agent to remove any home "where we'd be the only family like us" from her search. The agent should:
c: Remove the homes, since following client instructions cannot be steering
Keep sending every matching listing and let the buyer decline showings
Remove the homes but note the buyer's request in the file
End the relationship, since the buyer's request is illegal
questions.x: The buyer may decide where to look, but the agent may not do demographic filtering. Sending every match and letting the buyer choose keeps the agent out of steering. A file note does not change who filtered, and ending the relationship is not required.

questions.q: A lender offers worse terms on identical loans to identical borrowers depending on the racial makeup of the property's neighborhood. This is:
c: Redlining
Steering
Blockbusting
Risk-based pricing
questions.x: Redlining is refusing or limiting credit or insurance in an area because of who lives there, rather than the borrower or property. Risk-based pricing is lawful only when tied to objective risk, which this is not.

questions.q: An insurer refuses to write homeowners policies anywhere in a predominantly Black zip code, even for new, well-maintained homes outside any flood zone. This most likely constitutes:
c: Lawful underwriting, since insurers choose their markets
Blockbusting, because it pressures owners to sell
Steering, because it guides buyers away from the area
Insurance redlining covered by fair housing law
questions.x: Refusing coverage by area, based on its makeup rather than objective risk, is insurance redlining, which fair housing laws reach. Lawful underwriting relies on property-specific factors like flood exposure or roof condition, which are absent here.

questions.q: An appraisal describes a neighborhood by the race of its residents and comes in below contract price. The best first step for the buyer is to:
c: Ask the agent to call the appraiser and negotiate a new value
Ask the lender for a reconsideration of value with better comps
Cancel the contract, since a low appraisal voids it automatically
Accept the value, since appraisals cannot be challenged
questions.x: Borrowers may ask the lender for a reconsideration of value, supported by closer comparable sales, and flag the demographic language; appraisals are covered by fair housing law. Agents should not pressure appraisers, and a low appraisal does not void a contract on its own.

questions.q: A buyer suspects a low appraisal reflects neighborhood demographics. Each of the following is an appropriate response EXCEPT:
c: Requesting a reconsideration of value through the lender
Supplying closer comparable sales to the lender for review
Filing a complaint with a state or federal fair housing agency
Having the agent pressure the appraiser to raise the value
questions.x: Reconsideration of value, better comps and a fair housing complaint are all appropriate. Pressuring the appraiser undermines appraiser independence and can create its own violation, even when the underlying concern is valid.

questions.q: Which phrase in a listing ad is LEAST likely to violate fair housing law?
c: "Fourth-floor walk-up"
"Perfect for empty nesters"
"Ideal for young professionals"
"Great for a single person"
questions.x: HUD's advertising guidance treats descriptions of the property, such as a fourth-floor walk-up, as lawful. The other three describe the ideal occupant and signal preferences based on age, familial status or marital status. A walk-up seems to raise disability concerns, but it describes the building.

questions.q: Each of the following phrases in a New York rental ad indicates an unlawful preference EXCEPT:
c: "Mature tenants preferred"
"Not suitable for wheelchairs"
"English speakers preferred"
"Walk to the bus stop"
questions.x: A walk to the bus stop describes the neighborhood. "Mature" signals age (protected in New York), "not suitable for wheelchairs" signals a disability preference, and "English speakers only" signals national origin. The wheelchair phrase is tempting because it sounds like a property description, but it describes who may live there.

questions.q: A Yonkers owner of a six-family house, renting without a broker, posts an online ad saying "working professionals only, no vouchers." Which statement is correct?
c: The ad is legal because the owner uses no broker
Illegal; owners are bound by the advertising ban
The ad is legal if the owner lives in the building
The ad is illegal in New York City alone
questions.x: The advertising ban applies to owners, and New York's owner exemptions do not cover statements and advertisements. "No vouchers" excludes lawful source of income statewide. The broker-free answer borrows the federal single-family exemption, which neither applies to a six-family nor covers ads.

questions.q: An owner who qualifies for the federal Mrs. Murphy exemption publishes an ad saying "no children." The ad is:
c: Unlawful; the exemption does not reach the ad
Lawful, because the owner is exempt from the federal Act
Lawful, if the ad runs in print and not online
Unlawful, because Mrs. Murphy covers sales and not rentals
questions.x: The federal exemptions expressly do not cover the advertising provision, so even an exempt owner may not publish a discriminatory ad. The tempting wrong answer stretches the owner's refusal exemption to the ad itself.

questions.q: A broker sets a paid social media campaign for an apartment to reach only users aged 25 to 40 within two ZIP codes. The main fair housing concern is that:
c: Social media ads have to include the full street address
Paid ads may not mention the rent amount
Housing ads are required to reach every state resident
Targeting can hide housing ads from protected groups
questions.x: Who sees a housing ad can be discriminatory. Filtering by age, and by ZIP codes that act as proxies for race or national origin, can exclude protected groups; HUD's case against Facebook and the 2022 settlement led to restrictions on such targeting. Reaching every state resident is not required.

questions.q: To reduce fair housing risk in a paid social media housing ad, a broker should do each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Select the platform's special housing ad category
Remove age and gender filters
Narrow the audience to selected ZIP codes
Use photos of the property itself
questions.x: Narrowing housing ads to selected ZIP codes can exclude people by location proxies for race or national origin, which is why platforms block ZIP targeting in the housing category. The other steps reduce risk. Photos of the property avoid the preference problems lifestyle images create.

questions.q: A NYC rental listing is marketed by the landlord's broker. Under the FARE Act, the listing must:
c: Disclose fees the tenant has to pay
State the broker fee the tenant will pay
Leave fees to the lease, not the listing
List fees just when they exceed one month's rent
questions.x: The FARE Act, effective June 11, 2025, makes the landlord pay the broker it hires and requires that fees a tenant must pay be disclosed in the listing and the lease. Stating a tenant-paid broker fee would be the old practice the law ended.

questions.q: A Manhattan landlord's broker lists an apartment without mentioning that tenants pay a $20 credit check fee. Under the FARE Act, the listing is:
c: Compliant, because a $20 fee is too small to disclose
Compliant, if the fee appears later in the lease
Noncompliant; tenant fees belong in the listing too
Noncompliant, because credit check fees are banned
questions.x: Tenant-paid fees must be disclosed in the listing as well as the lease. There is no small-fee exception. Credit check fees are not banned; New York allows the actual cost up to $20, so the banned-fee choice overstates the rule.

questions.q: A salesperson promotes a listing on a personal Instagram account with the caption "perfect for a young couple, no kids yet." Which statement is correct?
c: Personal accounts are not advertising, so the caption is lawful
The caption is lawful if the broker approved the post
The post is lawful because it does not show the address
Advertising, and it signals age and familial preferences
questions.x: A personal account used to promote listings is advertising, subject to fair housing law and DOS identification rules. "Young couple, no kids yet" signals preferences by age, marital status and familial status. Broker approval does not make a discriminatory caption lawful.

questions.q: When a New York salesperson promotes a listing on a personal social media account, the post:
c: Is exempt from DOS advertising rules
Is advertising subject to fair housing and DOS rules
Needs just the salesperson's own phone number
May omit the broker's name if the account is personal
questions.x: Business promotion on a personal account is advertising. It must follow fair housing content rules and the DOS rule requiring the broker's name and the salesperson's license title. Omitting the broker's name is a common mistake on personal accounts.

questions.q: An AI tool drafts a listing that says "ideal for mature professionals," and a salesperson publishes it without editing. Who may be liable?
c: The tool's vendor alone
No one, since no person intended the wording
The salesperson and the supervising broker
The buyer who responded to the ad
questions.x: Liability attaches to those who publish and supervise the ad, not to how it was drafted. Intent is not required for an advertising violation; the statement of preference is enough. Blaming the vendor is the trap: the licensee chose to publish it.

questions.q: A brokerage uses an automated tool to generate listing descriptions. The best compliance practice is to:
c: Rely on the vendor's assurance that output is compliant
Have a licensee review every ad before it publishes
Publish drafts and fix problems if a complaint arrives
Use the tool for rentals but not for sales
questions.x: The brokerage is responsible for what it publishes, so a licensee should review each ad and the firm should keep copies of ads as they ran. A vendor's assurance does not shift liability, and fixing problems after a complaint is too late.

questions.q: A tenant with a disability that is not obvious asks to keep an emotional support dog in a no-pets building. The landlord may ask for:
c: Reliable documentation of the disability and the need
The tenant's medical records and specific diagnosis
A certificate from an online assistance animal registry
A pet deposit equal to one month's rent, refundable at move-out
questions.x: When the disability or need is not observable, a provider may request reliable documentation, such as a letter from a treating professional. It may not demand records or a diagnosis. HUD says online certificates alone are not reliable, and pet deposits may not be charged for assistance animals.

questions.q: A housing provider reviewing an assistance animal request may do each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Ask for a letter from a health professional with personal knowledge
Deny an animal with a documented history of biting
Require the tenant to state her diagnosis
Hold the tenant responsible for actual damage the animal causes
questions.x: A provider may seek reliable documentation of disability and need, may deny an animal shown to be a direct threat by its own conduct, and may recover for actual damage. It may not require a diagnosis. The biting-history choice is lawful because it rests on this animal's behavior.

questions.q: A building charges a $50 monthly pet fee and has a 25-pound weight limit for dogs. For an approved assistance animal, the building:
c: May not charge the fee or apply the weight limit
May charge the fee but has to waive the weight limit
May apply both the fee and the weight limit
May apply the weight limit but has to waive the fee
questions.x: Assistance animals are not pets, so pet fees and deposits cannot be charged, and pet size or weight limits do not apply. The provider can still deny a specific animal that poses a direct threat based on individualized evidence, or charge for actual damage.

questions.q: A Queens landlord approves a tenant's support dog but adds a $500 refundable pet deposit, saying it applies to all dogs. This is:
c: Lawful, because the deposit is refundable
Lawful, because it applies to every dog in the building
Unlawful, unless the deposit exceeds one month's rent
Unlawful; assistance animals carry no pet deposits
questions.x: Assistance animals are not pets, so a pet deposit cannot be charged, refundable or not. Applying a pet rule uniformly to all dogs is exactly what an accommodation adjusts. The landlord may still recover the cost of actual damage.

questions.q: Under the NYC Human Rights Law, after a tenant requests a reasonable accommodation, the housing provider must:
c: Forward the request to the Commission on Human Rights for decision
Hold a cooperative dialogue, then give a written determination
Decide within 5 business days or the request is deemed granted
Obtain approval from a majority of the building's other residents
questions.x: NYC requires a good-faith cooperative dialogue within a reasonable time and a written final determination stating what was granted or denied. Failing to engage is a separate violation. There is no Commission pre-approval step and no automatic grant deadline in the statute.

questions.q: A Manhattan co-op board receives an accommodation request, never responds in writing, and tells the buyer by phone that the answer is no. Under the NYC Human Rights Law, the board:
c: Complied, because co-op boards need not give reasons for decisions
Complied, if the denial itself was for a lawful reason
Violated it by skipping the dialogue and written determination
Violated the law, but just if the buyer had already closed
questions.x: The city law requires a cooperative dialogue and a written final determination. Skipping them is a violation even if the denial itself might have been defensible. Co-op boards' general freedom from giving reasons for rejections does not extend to accommodation requests.

questions.q: A tenant with a disability asks to widen her bathroom doorway inside her rental apartment. Under the NYS Human Rights Law, the cost is generally borne by:
c: The landlord, because every disability change is the owner's cost
The landlord and tenant equally, under the state law
The state, through the Division of Human Rights
The tenant, and the landlord may require restoration at move-out
questions.x: Modifications inside a tenant's own unit are generally at the tenant's expense, and the landlord may condition approval on restoring the interior where reasonable, ordinary wear and tear excepted. The owner-pays rule in New York applies to reasonable common-area modifications.

questions.q: According to New York's required notice of tenants' rights to reasonable accommodations, who generally pays for a reasonable modification to a building's common areas, such as a lobby ramp?
c: The tenant who requested it
The housing provider
The tenant and the provider equally
The local building department
questions.x: New York's notice states that housing providers pay for reasonable modifications to common use areas, while tenants pay for changes inside their own units. Assigning the ramp cost to the tenant applies the in-unit rule to the wrong space.

questions.q: A New York real estate broker must give a prospective tenant the written notice of the right to request reasonable accommodations and modifications:
c: At lease signing
Within 30 days after move-in
When the tenant discloses a disability
At first substantive contact
questions.x: Brokers give the notice at first substantive contact. Landlords give it to new tenants within 30 days of the tenancy start, which is the tempting wrong answer for a broker question. Giving it only to people who disclose a disability would treat applicants unequally.

questions.q: New York's reasonable accommodation notice rules require each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Tenants sign the notice before a landlord may show a unit
Brokers give the notice to prospective tenants at first substantive contact
Landlords give the notice to new tenants within 30 days
Providers post the notice on their website homepage
questions.x: The rules require broker delivery at first substantive contact, delivery to new tenants within 30 days, posting in the building, and posting on the website homepage. There is no requirement that a tenant sign the notice before a showing.

questions.q: A landlord refuses an assistance dog because "that breed is aggressive," though the dog has no history of aggression. The refusal is:
c: Lawful, because breed restrictions protect other tenants
Unlawful; a direct threat rests on this animal's own conduct
Lawful, if the landlord's insurer excludes the breed
Unlawful, because an assistance animal cannot be refused
questions.x: A provider may refuse an assistance animal as a direct threat only through an individualized assessment of the specific animal's actual conduct, not breed or size stereotypes. Assistance animals can be refused in narrow cases, so the cannot-be-refused answer overstates the rule.

questions.q: A support dog in a Syracuse apartment bit a neighbor twice in one month, and a trainer could not correct the behavior. The landlord may:
c: Do nothing, because assistance animals are protected without exception
Charge a monthly pet fee to cover the added liability risk
Deny the animal based on this individualized direct threat evidence
Evict the tenant at once without any further process
questions.x: A specific animal's documented dangerous conduct that cannot be reduced supports denial as a direct threat. That is the individualized assessment the law requires. Assistance animals are not protected without exception, and pet fees remain off limits.

questions.q: A New York broker changes its standardized operating procedures for prospective homebuyers. Within 30 days the broker must:
c: File the new version with DOS for its approval
Date stamp, notarize and post the new version
Notify every past client by certified mail
Take a refresher course on the new procedures
questions.x: RPL 442-h(4) requires changes to be date stamped, notarized and posted within 30 days, with prior versions archived. The original 2021 law contemplated filing with DOS, but the 2022 amendment removed filing, which makes the filing answer the outdated trap.

questions.q: New York's SOP law for prospective homebuyers requires a broker to do each of the following EXCEPT:
c: Decide whether ID is required before services
Post the procedures on the broker's own website
Affirm compliance when renewing the license
Require a pre-approval letter from every buyer
questions.x: The SOP must address whether ID, an exclusive broker agreement and pre-approval are required, but it is the broker's choice whether to require each. The law requires that the choice be written, posted and applied equally, not that pre-approval be demanded.

questions.q: A brokerage's posted SOP says pre-approval is not required to see homes. An agent asks some callers for pre-approval before showing and not others. The agent's practice:
c: Is allowed, because agents may add requirements case by case
Is allowed if the agent keeps notes on each caller
Violates the SOP and risks a fair housing claim
Is required, because pre-approval protects sellers
questions.x: The SOP law exists so that every prospective buyer faces the same prerequisites. Selectively adding a requirement is what paired testing on Long Island uncovered and is evidence of unequal treatment. Notes do not cure a selective requirement.

questions.q: Two testers with matched finances call the same agent about the same house. One is asked for ID and pre-approval before a showing; the other is shown the house the same day with no documents requested. This pattern is evidence of:
c: Unequal treatment
Blockbusting
Redlining
Lawful prequalification screening
questions.x: Different prerequisites, speed and service for matched testers who differ in one trait is unequal treatment, the core of what paired testing measures. Blockbusting targets owners and redlining is a lending or insurance practice.

questions.q: In Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982), the Supreme Court held that:
c: Racially restrictive covenants cannot be enforced by courts
Testers who receive false information have standing to sue
The 1866 Act applies to private property sales
Racial zoning ordinances are unconstitutional
questions.x: Havens held that a tester given false information about availability because of race has standing, even without intent to rent. The other choices describe Shelley v. Kraemer, Jones v. Mayer and Buchanan v. Warley.

questions.q: An agent argues that a fair housing complaint must be dismissed because the complainant was a tester who never intended to buy. The argument:
c: Succeeds, because bona fide buyers are the ones injured
Succeeds if the tester used a false name
Fails, because testers have standing to sue
Fails, but just if the tester later buys a home
questions.x: Under Havens Realty v. Coleman, testers who are given false information or treated unequally have standing even without intent to buy. Use of a cover identity does not defeat the claim. The bona fide buyer argument is the one Havens rejected.

questions.q: For a discriminatory act on or after February 15, 2024, a complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights must be filed within:
c: 180 days
1 year
2 years
3 years
questions.x: The filing period was extended from 1 year to 3 years for acts on or after February 15, 2024. One year is the old rule and still the HUD deadline, which is why it tempts.

questions.q: A buyer was misled about a home's availability because of her race in June 2025. In September 2026, which option is no longer available?
c: A HUD complaint
A NYS Division of Human Rights complaint
A federal court lawsuit
A complaint to DOS about the licensee
questions.x: HUD complaints must be filed within 1 year, which passed in June 2026. The Division of Human Rights allows 3 years for acts on or after February 15, 2024, federal suits allow 2 years, and DOS discipline has no filing deadline.

questions.q: When the Department of State finds that a salesperson discriminated in violation of the Human Rights Law, it may:
c: Award emotional distress damages to the complainant
Fine up to $2,000 and suspend or revoke the license
Fine up to $1,000 and nothing more for a first offense
Enter a criminal conviction against the salesperson
questions.x: DOS disciplines licenses under RPL 441-c, with fines up to $2,000 since the 2022 increase, plus reprimand, suspension or revocation. Damages come from HUD, the Division of Human Rights or courts. The $1,000 cap is the old law.

questions.q: Each of the following can result from a fair housing violation by a New York licensee EXCEPT:
c: License suspension or revocation by DOS
Civil fines imposed by the Division of Human Rights
Damages awarded in federal court
A damages award paid by DOS to the victim
questions.x: DOS disciplines licensees but does not pay or award damages to victims. The Division of Human Rights can award damages and impose civil fines, courts award damages, and DOS can suspend or revoke a license.

questions.q: After a fair housing group files a complaint, a broker tells agents to refuse service to anyone associated with the group. This is:
c: Lawful, because the broker may choose its clients
Lawful, if the policy is written and posted
Retaliation, which federal and NY law prohibit
Unlawful, but just if the group wins its complaint
questions.x: Federal and New York law prohibit retaliating against people for filing or supporting fair housing complaints, regardless of the complaint's outcome. A written policy of refusing service makes the retaliation easier to prove, not lawful.

questions.q: A fair housing complaint is expected against a brokerage. Its best immediate step regarding agents' business texts and emails is to:
c: Preserve them along with the transaction file
Let agents delete personal-device messages
Delete anything older than 90 days
Print selected messages for each agent to keep
questions.x: Relevant records must be preserved once a complaint is expected, including business messages on personal devices, and brokers keep transaction records for 3 years anyway. Deleting or selectively printing messages invites sanctions and an inference of wrongdoing.

questions.q: A Buffalo landlord refuses to lease a vacant storefront to a 70-year-old applicant because of her age. Which law most directly prohibits this?
c: The New York State Human Rights Law, which covers commercial space
The federal Fair Housing Act, which covers every building with apartments
The Americans with Disabilities Act, which covers spaces open to the public
No law, because New York limits age protection to residential rentals
questions.x: Executive Law 296(5)(b) bars discrimination in renting land or commercial space, and age is on its list. The Fair Housing Act reaches dwellings, not stores, which makes the Fair Housing Act choice the tempting federal answer. The ADA governs physical access for people with disabilities, not age.
questions.concept: Commercial space under NY Human Rights Law

questions.q: In leasing commercial space, the New York State Human Rights Law prohibits an owner from discriminating on each of the following bases EXCEPT:
c: Creed
Marital status of the applicant
Age
Lawful source of income
questions.x: The owner's commercial space paragraph, 296(5)(b), lists creed, age, marital status and the other classes, but lawful source of income is a housing protection and is not on that list for owners. Age is the tempting wrong pick because federal fair housing law lacks it, but New York protects it in commercial space.
questions.concept: Commercial space under NY Human Rights Law

questions.q: A licensee is showing a warehouse in the Bronx to a prospective commercial tenant. At first substantive contact, the licensee must provide:
c: The RPL 443 agency disclosure form for the tenant to sign
The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form
Both the agency disclosure and the property condition statement
No form, since disclosure rules apply to residential deals
questions.x: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (19 NYCRR 175.28) applies to all property types, including commercial and vacant land. The RPL 443 agency form is for residential 1 to 4 family sales and residential rentals, which makes it the tempting wrong answer for a lease.

questions.q: A salesperson lists a vacant lot in Orange County for sale to builders. She gives buyers the RPL 443 form but nothing else. What is missing?
c: Nothing, because land sales need no New York disclosure form
A property condition disclosure statement for the vacant lot
The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form
A lead-based paint pamphlet, as required for land sales
questions.x: The anti-discrimination disclosure form goes to buyers, sellers, landlords and tenants of every property type, vacant land included, at first substantive contact. The PCDS is the tempting wrong pick, but it applies to 1 to 4 family residential sales, not lots. Lead paint rules concern pre-1978 housing.

questions.q: A married restaurant owner qualifies on her own for a business loan under the bank's standards. The bank insists her husband sign as guarantor. Under Regulation B this is:
c: Permitted, because spouses co-sign on business credit
Prohibited, unless the loan is secured by their home
Permitted, if the husband has a higher credit score
Prohibited, because she qualifies individually
questions.x: Regulation B bars a creditor from requiring the signature of an applicant's spouse, other than a joint applicant, when the applicant qualifies on her own, and it covers business credit and guaranties. The home-secured choice is tempting, but the rule does not depend on the collateral; it depends on whether she qualifies alone.

questions.q: Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, when may a lender require an applicant's spouse to sign a loan?
c: When the applicant does not qualify on her or his own
Whenever the applicant is married, as a standard practice
When the loan is for a business rather than a home
When the spouse has a higher income than the applicant
questions.x: A creditor may require another signature, which can be a spouse's, when the applicant does not qualify individually under the creditor's standards. Requiring it simply because the applicant is married is marital status discrimination. The business loan choice is wrong because ECOA covers business credit as well.

questions.q: Under Regulation B, a creditor must notify an applicant of the action taken within how many days after receiving a completed application?
c: 10 business days
30 days
45 days
90 days
questions.x: The creditor must notify the applicant within 30 days after receiving a completed application. Ninety days is the trap: it applies when a creditor makes a counteroffer and the applicant neither accepts nor uses the credit. Applicants denied credit are entitled to the reasons or to notice of the right to get them.

questions.q: A bakery owner submitted a completed equipment loan application six weeks ago and has heard nothing from the lender. What does ECOA require?
c: Nothing yet, since lenders have 90 days to act on business loans
A decision within 60 days, so the lender still has two weeks
A written decision if the bakery requests one by mail
A decision notice within 30 days, which the lender has missed
questions.x: Regulation B requires notice of the action taken within 30 days of a completed application. For small businesses with revenues of $1 million or less the notice may be oral, but it is still required. The 90-day choice borrows the counteroffer rule, which does not apply to an application with no response at all.

questions.q: A four-story walk-up with 12 apartments in Yonkers was first occupied in 2024. Which units must meet the Fair Housing Act design and construction requirements?
c: Every unit in the building
The ground-floor units
No units, since it lacks an elevator
Five percent of the units
questions.x: Covered multifamily dwellings are buildings of 4 or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991. With an elevator, every unit is covered; without one, ground-floor units are covered. The no-elevator choice is tempting, but lacking an elevator narrows coverage to the ground floor rather than removing it.

questions.q: The Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements apply to multifamily buildings first occupied after:
c: April 11, 1968
January 26, 1992
March 13, 1991
September 13, 1988
questions.x: The 1988 amendments set the requirements for covered multifamily dwellings designed and built for first occupancy after March 13, 1991. The 1988 date is the tempting wrong choice because that is when the amendments passed, but builders had until 1991. April 1968 is when the original Act passed.

questions.q: A store lease says the tenant is responsible for all ADA compliance. A customer sues over a step at the entrance. Under the ADA, who can be responsible?
c: Both, though the lease divides costs
The landlord alone, as building owner
The tenant alone, as the lease provides
Neither, if the store opened after 1990
questions.x: Under the ADA's Title III rules, both the landlord who owns the building and the tenant who operates the public accommodation are covered. A lease may allocate the work and cost between them, but that allocation does not bind the customer or the government. The tenant-alone choice is the trap because people rely on the lease clause.

questions.q: Which statement about ADA duties in a leased store is accurate?
c: A lease clause can shift the landlord's ADA duty entirely to the tenant
The ADA covers the tenant's business but not the landlord who owns it
Both stay covered, though a lease can split the ADA work
The Fair Housing Act, not the ADA, governs access to retail entrances
questions.x: Both the landlord and the tenant of a place of public accommodation are covered by Title III. Their lease can decide who does and pays for what between them, but neither escapes the law. The first choice is tempting because lease allocation clauses are common, but they work only between the parties. The Fair Housing Act covers dwellings, not stores.

questions.q: A Westchester seller's 1939 deed contains a covenant barring sale to people of certain religions. Under current New York law, the seller should:
c: Record a modification document and give the buyer a copy
Leave it in place, since void language has no effect on title
Ask the buyer to sign a waiver acknowledging the covenant is void
Bring a quiet title action to cancel it before contract signing
questions.x: Discriminatory covenants are void under GOL 5-331, and RPL 327-a now has the seller submit a restrictive covenant modification document for recording, give the purchaser a copy at or before closing, and record it with no filing fee. Leaving it in place reflects the older view that void language could simply be ignored.

questions.q: Under New York's restrictive covenant law, a co-op board whose recorded documents contain an unlawful discriminatory restriction must:
c: Hold a shareholder vote before removing the restriction
Ask the Attorney General to approve an offering plan amendment
Leave it in place until the next sale of shares in the building
Remove or amend it within one year of the law's effective date
questions.x: RPL 327-a gives condo boards, co-op boards and homeowners associations one year from its effective date to delete or amend unlawful restrictions in recorded documents, and those changes do not need owner approval. The shareholder vote choice is tempting because governing documents usually need one to amend, but this statute removes that step.

questions.q: New York City's Sharkey-Brown-Isaacs law, effective in 1958, is notable because it was the first law in the country to:
c: Bar discrimination in private multiple dwellings
Bar discrimination in city public housing projects
Add sex as a protected class in rental housing
Create cease and desist zones for real estate brokers
questions.x: The 1957 city law, effective April 1, 1958, was the first to ban discrimination in private apartment buildings, a decade before the federal Fair Housing Act. Public housing was the tempting wrong answer, but publicly aided and public housing had been reached earlier. Sex was added federally in 1974.
questions.concept: Early New York fair housing laws

questions.q: In 1950, a privately financed Brooklyn apartment building with no government aid refused a Black applicant. Which statement fits the law at the time?
c: The federal Fair Housing Act already barred the refusal
The 1866 Act was read to cover private landlords then
No state or city law yet reached that private building
New York's 1963 statewide law already applied to it
questions.x: In 1949 the Court of Appeals in Dorsey v. Stuyvesant Town even let a tax-exempt project exclude Black tenants. New York City's law reaching private multiple dwellings took effect in 1958, the state's broad law in 1963, and the federal Act in 1968. The 1866 Act choice is tempting, but courts did not apply it to private discrimination until Jones v. Mayer in 1968.
questions.concept: Early New York fair housing laws

questions.q: A building manager tells a tenant he will approve her transfer to a larger unit if she goes on a date with him. This is best described as:
c: Hostile environment harassment
Quid pro quo harassment
Steering by sex
Blockbusting
questions.x: Quid pro quo harassment conditions housing or a housing related benefit on submitting to an unwelcome request or demand. Hostile environment is the near miss: it involves unwelcome conduct severe or pervasive enough to interfere with the use and enjoyment of the home, which does not require an exchange.
questions.concept: Quid pro quo vs hostile environment

questions.q: For months a super makes sexual comments to a tenant whenever she passes the laundry room, but he never asks for anything in return. This is best described as:
c: Quid pro quo harassment, since he is the owner's employee
Not harassment, since no housing benefit was conditioned
Hostile environment harassment, if severe or pervasive
Retaliation, since the comments followed her complaints
questions.x: Hostile environment harassment is unwelcome conduct severe or pervasive enough to interfere with the use and enjoyment of the home; no exchange is needed. Quid pro quo requires a condition tied to housing, so that choice is tempting but does not fit. No complaint is in the facts, so retaliation does not fit either.
questions.concept: Quid pro quo vs hostile environment

questions.q: Under HUD's rule, an owner whose leasing agent sexually harasses an applicant is:
c: Liable once it receives a written complaint
Liable if it failed to train the agent
Not liable, since the agent acted personally
Vicariously liable, whether or not it knew
questions.x: HUD's rule makes a person vicariously liable for a discriminatory housing practice by its agent or employee regardless of whether it knew or should have known, consistent with agency law. The written complaint choice confuses vicarious liability with direct liability for failing to act once an owner knows.

questions.q: A landlord's super harassed a tenant. The landlord claims it is not liable. Each of the following is a weak defense EXCEPT:
c: "I had no idea what the super was doing."
"The super was acting outside of work hours."
"He was a neighbor, not my agent."
"I fired him after he did it, so I am not liable."
questions.x: Vicarious liability turns on the agency or employment relationship, so the only defense here that goes to the heart of it is that the person was not the landlord's agent at all. Lack of knowledge does not defeat vicarious liability, and firing him afterward limits future harm but does not erase liability. The off-hours claim may matter under agency law in some cases but is weak when he used his job's access.

questions.q: A tenant reports harassment by a porter. The owner's lawful corrective response is to:
c: Restrict the porter's access and investigate
Move the tenant to another building the owner manages
Wait for a HUD or state agency finding before acting
Offer the tenant a rent credit to drop the complaint
questions.x: Prompt corrective action should address the harasser, and HUD's rule says it may not include steps that penalize or harm the person harassed, such as an unwanted transfer or eviction. Moving the tenant is tempting because it separates the two, but it puts the cost on the victim. Paying to drop a complaint invites an interference claim.
questions.concept: Corrective action must not penalize the victim

questions.q: After a harassment report against a super, each of the following is an appropriate corrective step EXCEPT:
c: Placing the super on leave pending an investigation
Moving the tenant to a smaller unit for safety
Requiring logged notice before staff enter apartments
Hiring an outside contractor to finish her repairs
questions.x: HUD's rule bars corrective action that penalizes or harms the aggrieved person, and a forced move to a smaller unit does both. Leave, an entry policy and an outside contractor all address the harasser and the unmet repairs. A transfer the tenant asks for is different from one imposed on her.
questions.concept: Corrective action must not penalize the victim

questions.q: A tenant repeatedly leaves slurs on a neighbor's door because of his national origin. The landlord has the complaints and video, but calls it a private dispute. The landlord:
c: Has no exposure, since owners answer for staff and agents
Has to evict the harassing tenant within 30 days of a report
Faces liability solely where the lease bars harassment
May be liable for not acting on harassment it could stop
questions.x: HUD's rule makes a housing provider directly liable for failing to take prompt action on third-party harassment it knew or should have known about and had the power to correct, for example through lease enforcement. The staff-only choice is the common misconception. The law requires prompt, effective action, not a set eviction deadline.

questions.q: Under HUD's rule, a housing provider's duty to act on harassment by a third party, such as another tenant, depends on:
c: Whether the harasser has signed the same lease form
Its knowledge and its power to correct the conduct
Whether the victim first filed a police report
Whether the harassment occurred inside a unit
questions.x: Direct liability for third-party harassment arises when the provider knew or should have known and had the power to correct it; that power depends on its control or legal responsibility over the third party, such as lease remedies. A police report is tempting but is not a precondition, and harassment in common areas counts.

cram.html: 1866 Civil Rights Act: race only, no exemptions. Jones v. Mayer (1968) applied it to private sales.
Plessy 1896 allowed separate but equal; Buchanan v. Warley 1917 struck racial zoning; Brown 1954 overturned Plessy in schools.
FHA 1968: race, color, religion, national origin. 1974 added sex. 1988 added disability and familial status.
Federal classes (7): Race, Color, Religion, National origin, Sex, Familial status, Disability. Age is NOT federal.

NYS adds: marital status, age, military status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, citizenship or immigration status, domestic violence victim status, lawful source of income (statewide since 2019).
NYC adds: lawful occupation, partnership status, height and weight, presence of children, pregnancy, criminal record (Fair Chance for Housing, 2025).
Federal Mrs. Murphy: owner-occupied up to 4 units. NY: owner-occupied two-family only. NYC: also lost if publicly listed.
No exemption covers race, discriminatory ads, or brokers.
Senior housing: all 62+, or 80% of units with one person 55+. Exempt from familial status and age only.
Current illegal drug users are not protected; people in recovery are.
Accommodation = rule change (support animal). Modification = physical change (grab bars). Federally the tenant usually pays for modifications.
Steering targets buyers. Blockbusting targets owners. Redlining targets loans or insurance by area.
Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form: first substantive contact, all property types, keep 3 years.
Rentals: also give the Reasonable Accommodation and Reasonable Modification notice.
SOPs (RPL 442-h): ID? exclusive agreement? pre-approval? Dated, notarized, posted online, same for every buyer. No longer filed with DOS.
Cease and desist zone protects only owners on the list; nonsolicitation order covers the whole area. Both max 5 years.
Cease and desist violation: reprimand, fine up to $2,000, suspension or revocation.
HUD complaint: 1 year; federal suit: 2 years. DHR: 3 years (acts on or after Feb 15, 2024). NYC Commission: 1 year.
NYS civil fines up to $50,000, $100,000 if willful, wanton, or malicious.
Testers are legal and can sue. Treat every caller like a tester.
HUD enforces federal FHA; Division of Human Rights enforces NYS law; NYC Commission enforces city law; DOS disciplines licenses.
NYC income rule for voucher holders applies only to the tenant's share of the rent.

subjects.title: Real Estate Mathematics
subjects.blurb: Math shows up across the whole exam: commissions, splits, interest, points, area, acres, qualifying ratios, transfer and recording taxes, and property tax rates. One page of formulas covers almost all of it.

lessons.title: Percentages: Commissions, Interest, Points, and Qualifying
lessons.tagline: Part = Total x Rate. Learn that one line and half the exam math falls over.
objectives: Solve any percentage problem with Part = Total x Rate
Calculate commissions, co-broke splits, and a salesperson's share
Compute simple interest, appreciation, depreciation, and points
Find a borrower's maximum payment with front-end and back-end ratios and LTV

blocks.title: Leo's spreadsheet, a coffee shop in Sunnyside
blocks.html: Leo has a laptop open and three tabs of formulas. "If I offer $640,000, put 20% down, and pay one point, what's my cash at closing? And what does your firm actually make?" Jordan has no calculator app open, just a napkin. Every one of Leo's questions is the same equation wearing a different hat.
blocks.casual: Leo's at a Sunnyside coffee shop with his laptop and three tabs of formulas. "If I offer $640,000, put 20% down, and pay one point, what's my cash at closing? And what does your firm actually make?" Jordan doesn't even have a calculator open, just a napkin. Here's the secret: every one of Leo's questions is the same equation wearing a different hat.

deeper.plain: Down payments, points, commissions, and interest are all the same kind of percent problem.
deeper.picture: One key, many doors. Learn the one formula and it opens commissions, points, taxes, and qualifying.
deeper.street: Leo's questions on the napkin: 20% of $640,000 is the down payment, 1% of the loan is the point, 5% of the price is the commission. Same multiply-the-total-by-the-rate move every time.
deeper.stakes: Freeze on math in front of a client and you lose their confidence. Get it wrong and they show up to closing short on cash.
deeper.exam: Math is a chunk of the state exam. Most items boil down to part, total, rate. Spot which one is missing.

blocks.html: Every percentage problem has three pieces: the total (the whole), the rate (a percentage), and the part (the piece). Know any two and you can find the third.
blocks.casual: Every percent problem has three pieces: the total (the whole thing), the rate (a percentage), and the part (the slice). Know any two and you can get the third.

deeper.plain: Whole times percent gives the slice. If you know the slice, you can work backward.
deeper.picture: A pizza: the whole pie, the fraction you ate, and how many slices that was. Know two, you can figure the third.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Yonkers condo sells for $350,000 and the broker earns $17,500. Rate = $17,500 / $350,000 = 5%. Same three pieces, solving for a different one.
deeper.stakes: Mislabel the part and the total and you divide the wrong way, producing nonsense like a 2,000% commission.
deeper.exam: Before you calculate, label each number in the stem as part, total, or rate. Then the operation picks itself.

head: You want
Do this
Example
blocks.caption: Convert the percent to a decimal first: 6% = 0.06, 5.5% = 0.055, 0.4% = 0.004.

deeper.plain: Multiply to find the part. Divide to find the rate or the total.
deeper.picture: It's a recipe card with three lines. Whatever ingredient is missing, the card tells you how to get it.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Rochester house sells for $240,000 at 6%. Part: $240,000 x 0.06 = $14,400. Rate check: $14,400 / $240,000 = 6%. Total check: $14,400 / 0.06 = $240,000.
deeper.stakes: Forget to turn 5.5% into 0.055 and your answer is 100 times too big. That's a real mistake on real closing statements.
deeper.exam: Watch decimals: 0.4% is 0.004, not 0.04. The transfer tax rate trips people up exactly here.

blocks.title: The T-bar
blocks.html: Draw a T. Part on top, Total and Rate underneath. Cover what you want: if it is on top, multiply the bottom two; if it is on the bottom, divide the top by the other one.
blocks.casual: Draw a T. Put Part on top, Total and Rate on the bottom. Cover the one you want. If it's on top, multiply the two below. If it's on the bottom, divide the top by the other bottom one.

deeper.plain: A quick sketch tells you whether to multiply or divide.
deeper.picture: Like a fraction bar: the top is the part, the bottom pieces multiply to make it.
deeper.street: New numbers: Jordan needs the price when a 4% commission was $26,000. Cover Total: Part over Rate. $26,000 / 0.04 = $650,000.
deeper.stakes: On a timed exam, a reliable trick beats re-deriving the formula under pressure.
deeper.exam: Draw the T on your scratch paper at the start. It works for commission, tax, interest, LTV, and cap rate problems.

blocks.html: A commission is a percentage of the sale price, negotiated between the client and the broker. No law sets the rate; agreeing on rates among competing brokers is price fixing. The commission then travels down a chain of splits.
blocks.casual: A commission is a percentage of the sale price, negotiated between the client and the broker. No law sets the rate, and competing brokers agreeing on rates is price fixing. Then the commission flows down a chain of splits.

deeper.plain: The commission rate is whatever the client and broker agree to, then it gets divided among brokers and agents.
deeper.picture: A pizza bought for a party gets cut for the two families, then each family cuts their half for the kids.
