deeper.street: New numbers: a $900,000 Maspeth sale at 4%: $36,000. Half to the buyer's broker: $18,000 to the listing firm. Agent on a 70/30 split gets $12,600.
deeper.stakes: Saying "the standard commission is 6%" or agreeing on rates with another firm can be price fixing under the Sherman Act.
deeper.exam: Commission rates are negotiable. Any choice saying the law or the board sets the rate is wrong.

blocks.caption: Follow the money: total commission, then listing vs cooperating broker, then broker vs salesperson. Each step is a new Total x Rate.

blocks.title: The Okafors' sale
blocks.html:
Sale price $2,400,000. Listing agreement: 5% commission, half offered to a cooperating broker. Jordan's split with Hudson & Hart is 60/40 (Jordan 60%).
1. Total commission: $2,400,000 x 0.05 = $120,000
2. Listing side: $120,000 x 50% = $60,000
3. Jordan's share: $60,000 x 60% = $36,000 (the firm keeps $24,000)
blocks.casual:
The Okafors sell for $2,400,000. The listing agreement says 5%, with half offered to a cooperating broker. Jordan's split with Hudson & Hart is 60/40, Jordan getting 60%.
1. Total commission: $2,400,000 x 0.05 = $120,000
2. Listing side: $120,000 x 50% = $60,000
3. Jordan's share: $60,000 x 60% = $36,000 (the firm keeps $24,000)

deeper.plain: Take the full commission, cut it by the co-broke share, then by the agent's split.
deeper.picture: Russian nesting dolls: each split is a smaller doll inside the last one.
deeper.street: New numbers: a $1,100,000 Bayside sale at 5.5% is $60,500. Listing side gets 50%: $30,250. Agent on 65/35: $30,250 x 0.65 = $19,662.50. Firm keeps $10,587.50.
deeper.stakes: A wrong split calc on a commission statement causes disputes inside the firm and erodes trust with your broker.
deeper.exam: Watch which split applies at each step. The trap answer stops one step early or applies the agent split to the total commission.

blocks.title: Who pays the salesperson
blocks.html: A salesperson is paid only by the sponsoring broker, never directly by the client or the other broker. The split math happens inside the firm.
blocks.casual: A salesperson only gets paid by their sponsoring broker. Never straight from the client, never from the other broker. The split math happens inside the firm.

deeper.plain: Your paycheck always comes from your own broker.
deeper.picture: A waiter's tips go through the restaurant's payroll, not straight from the customer at another table.
deeper.street: After a Bed-Stuy closing, a grateful seller hands Jordan a $2,000 check. Jordan has to send it to Diane's firm; the firm pays Jordan under the split.
deeper.stakes: Taking money directly from a client or another broker is a violation that can bring DOS discipline for you and your broker.
deeper.exam: "A salesperson may receive compensation only from" the sponsoring broker. Every other choice is wrong.

blocks.title: Working backward to the price
blocks.html:
Jordan earned $9,000, which was 50% of the firm's side. The firm's side was half of a 6% commission. What was the sale price?
1. Firm's side: $9,000 / 0.50 = $18,000
2. Total commission: $18,000 / 0.50 = $36,000
3. Price: $36,000 / 0.06 = $600,000
blocks.casual:
Jordan earned $9,000, which was 50% of the firm's side. The firm's side was half of a 6% commission. What was the sale price?
1. Firm's side: $9,000 / 0.50 = $18,000
2. Total commission: $18,000 / 0.50 = $36,000
3. Price: $36,000 / 0.06 = $600,000

deeper.plain: Going backward, you divide by each percentage instead of multiplying.
deeper.picture: Rewinding a video: each step in reverse undoes the one before.
deeper.street: New numbers: an agent got $7,200, which was 60% of the firm's side. The firm got 40% of a 5% commission. $7,200 / 0.60 = $12,000. $12,000 / 0.40 = $30,000. $30,000 / 0.05 = $600,000.
deeper.stakes: This is how you check a commission statement. If your number doesn't run backward to the sale price, something is off.
deeper.exam: When the stem gives the agent's take and asks the price, divide at every step. Multiplying gives a tiny wrong answer.

blocks.title: The net-price trap
blocks.html: A seller says, "I need $475,000 after your 5%." The price is NOT $475,000 + 5%. The seller keeps 95% of the price, so Price = $475,000 / 0.95 = $500,000. Adding 5% ($498,750) comes up short. (Remember, a net listing itself is illegal in NY; this is just pricing math.)
blocks.casual: A seller says, "I need $475,000 after your 5%." The price is NOT $475,000 plus 5%. The seller keeps 95% of the price, so price = $475,000 / 0.95 = $500,000. Adding 5% ($498,750) comes up short. (And remember, a net listing is illegal in NY. This is just pricing math.)

deeper.plain: The commission comes out of the final price, so divide the seller's net by what's left after the commission.
deeper.picture: If you want $100 left after a 10% tip comes out, you can't just add $10. You need about $111.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Utica seller needs $282,000 net after a 6% commission. $282,000 / 0.94 = $300,000. Adding 6% would give $298,920, leaving the seller $1,080 short.
deeper.stakes: Get this wrong and your seller walks away short at closing, blaming you for it.
deeper.exam: Net needed / (1 minus rate). The distractor adds the percent. Also know net listings are prohibited in NY.

blocks.q: A $700,000 sale pays a 6% commission split 50/50 between brokers. The selling salesperson gets 70% of the selling broker's share. The salesperson earns:
blocks.x: $700,000 x 0.06 = $42,000. Half is $21,000. 70% of $21,000 = $14,700. $21,000 is the broker's side before the salesperson split.

blocks.html: Interest is the cost of borrowing money. Principal is the amount borrowed (or still owed). Simple interest: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time (time in years).
blocks.casual: Interest is what it costs to borrow money. Principal is what you borrowed, or what you still owe. Simple interest: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time, with time in years.

deeper.plain: Interest is the rent you pay on borrowed money.
deeper.picture: Renting a car: the car is the principal, the daily fee is the interest.
deeper.street: New numbers: a $50,000 home equity loan at 8% for 18 months. $50,000 x 0.08 x 1.5 = $6,000 in simple interest.
deeper.stakes: Put time in months instead of years and the answer is 12 times too big.
deeper.exam: Time must be in years: 6 months = 0.5, 90 days = 90/360 or 90/365 depending on the stem.

blocks.title: First month's interest
blocks.html:
Leo borrows $480,000 at 6%.
Annual interest: $480,000 x 0.06 = $28,800
Monthly: $28,800 / 12 = $2,400
If his monthly principal and interest payment is $2,878, then $478 goes to principal in month one, and next month's interest is figured on $479,522.
blocks.casual:
Leo borrows $480,000 at 6%.
Annual interest: $480,000 x 0.06 = $28,800
Monthly: $28,800 / 12 = $2,400
If his monthly principal and interest payment is $2,878, then $478 goes to principal in month one, and next month's interest is figured on $479,522.

deeper.plain: Figure the year's interest, divide by 12, and whatever's left of the payment pays down the loan.
deeper.picture: Paying off a credit card: part of each payment just covers the fee, the rest actually lowers the balance.
deeper.street: New numbers: Priya's client borrows $300,000 at 7%. Annual: $21,000. Monthly: $1,750. Payment is $1,996, so $246 goes to principal and next month's interest is on $299,754.
deeper.stakes: Buyers shocked by how little principal they pay early on may think the lender is cheating. You can explain it.
deeper.exam: First month's interest = loan x rate / 12. Principal paid = payment minus interest. New balance = loan minus principal paid.

blocks.title: Amortization in one line
blocks.html: Interest is always charged on the balance still owed. Early payments are mostly interest; later ones mostly principal. That is amortization.
blocks.casual: Interest is always charged on what you still owe. Early payments are mostly interest, later ones mostly principal. That's amortization.

deeper.plain: As the balance drops, each payment shifts more toward paying down the loan.
deeper.picture: Shoveling snow off a long driveway: at first you barely see the pavement, then it clears faster near the end.
deeper.street: On a 30-year loan of $400,000 at 6.5%, month one sends about $2,167 to interest and only about $361 to principal. Around year 20, principal finally takes most of the payment.
deeper.stakes: A buyer planning to sell in three years may have paid down very little. They need to know that before counting on equity.
deeper.exam: Fully amortized: equal payments, interest share falls, principal share rises, balance hits zero at the end.

blocks.html: Appreciation is an increase in value; depreciation is a decrease. Percent change = (new - old) / old. The base is always the starting value.
blocks.casual: Appreciation means value goes up; depreciation means it goes down. Percent change = (new minus old) / old. The base is always where you started.

deeper.plain: To get a percent change, divide by the starting number.
deeper.picture: If your rent goes from $2,000 to $2,200, that's a 10% raise because you measure from $2,000.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Buffalo double bought at $200,000 now worth $250,000. $50,000 / $200,000 = 25%.
deeper.stakes: Use the new value as the base and you understate the gain, which can mislead an investor comparing deals.
deeper.exam: Divide by the original, not the current, value. The trap answer uses the wrong base.

blocks.title: Up then down
blocks.html:
Sal bought for $800,000. It is now worth $1,000,000.
Change: $200,000 / $800,000 = 25% appreciation
If it falls back from $1,000,000 to $800,000: $200,000 / $1,000,000 = 20% decline. Same dollars, different base.
blocks.casual:
Sal bought for $800,000. Now it's worth $1,000,000.
Change: $200,000 / $800,000 = 25% appreciation
If it drops back from $1,000,000 to $800,000: $200,000 / $1,000,000 = 20% decline. Same dollars, different base.

deeper.plain: Going up and coming back down by the same dollars gives different percents because the starting point changes.
deeper.picture: A 50% sale followed by a 50% markup doesn't get you back to the original price.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Yonkers condo goes from $400,000 to $500,000: $100,000 / $400,000 = 25% up. Then back to $400,000: $100,000 / $500,000 = 20% down.
deeper.stakes: Clients who hear "it lost 20%" may assume it lost a fifth of what they paid. Check which base you mean.
deeper.exam: Up then down by the same dollars: the up percent is larger. The stem often asks for the decline.

blocks.title: Annual rate over several years
blocks.html:
A Hudson Valley house bought for $300,000 appreciates 5% a year, simple (not compounded), for 4 years.
$300,000 x 0.05 = $15,000 a year x 4 = $60,000
Value: $360,000
Straight-line depreciation works the same way: a $275,000 rental building depreciated over 27.5 years loses $10,000 a year (land excluded).
blocks.casual:
A Hudson Valley house bought for $300,000 goes up 5% a year, simple (not compounded), for 4 years.
$300,000 x 0.05 = $15,000 a year x 4 = $60,000
Value: $360,000
Straight-line depreciation works the same way. A $275,000 rental building depreciated over 27.5 years loses $10,000 a year (land left out).

deeper.plain: Simple growth adds the same dollar amount every year. Straight-line depreciation subtracts the same amount every year.
deeper.picture: A piggy bank getting the same $20 every week, versus a battery losing the same 5% charge every hour.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Saratoga house at $420,000 grows 3% simple for 5 years. $12,600 x 5 = $63,000, value $483,000. Depreciation: a $390,000 commercial building over 39 years loses $10,000 a year.
deeper.stakes: Investors who depreciate the land or use the wrong recovery period file wrong tax returns.
deeper.exam: Residential rental = 27.5 years, nonresidential = 39. Land is never depreciated. Simple growth is not compounded unless the stem says so.

blocks.q: A condo bought for $400,000 sells for $460,000. The percentage of appreciation is:
blocks.x: $60,000 / $400,000 = 0.15 = 15%. Dividing by the sale price ($60,000 / $460,000 = 13%) uses the wrong base.

blocks.html: One point = 1% of the loan amount, not the price. Discount points buy down the interest rate; origination points pay the lender's fee. Both are paid at closing.
blocks.casual: One point = 1% of the loan amount, not the price. Discount points buy down the interest rate. Origination points pay the lender's fee. Both get paid at closing.

deeper.plain: A point is 1% of what you borrow, paid up front.
deeper.picture: Prepaying for a cheaper monthly phone plan. You pay now so each month costs less.
deeper.street: New numbers: Tasha's client borrows $425,000 and pays 1.5 points. $425,000 x 0.015 = $6,375 at closing.
deeper.stakes: Figure points on the price instead of the loan and the buyer brings the wrong cash to closing.
deeper.exam: "Points are based on the" loan amount. Discount points lower the rate; origination is a fee.

blocks.title: Leo's cash to close
blocks.html:
Price $640,000, 20% down, 1 point.
Down payment: $640,000 x 0.20 = $128,000
Loan: $640,000 - $128,000 = $512,000
Point: $512,000 x 0.01 = $5,120
Down payment plus point: $133,120 (before other closing costs)
blocks.casual:
Price $640,000, 20% down, 1 point.
Down payment: $640,000 x 0.20 = $128,000
Loan: $640,000 minus $128,000 = $512,000
Point: $512,000 x 0.01 = $5,120
Down payment plus point: $133,120 (before other closing costs)

deeper.plain: Find the loan first, then put the point on the loan, then add it to the down payment.
deeper.picture: You can't figure tip until you know the bill. You can't figure points until you know the loan.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Hoboken-bound buyer instead picks a Rego Park co-op at $380,000, 25% down, 2 points. Down: $95,000. Loan: $285,000. Points: $5,700. Total: $100,700.
deeper.stakes: Short by a few thousand at closing and the deal stalls while the buyer scrambles for a wire.
deeper.exam: Order of steps: down payment, loan, points on the loan. Distractor: points on the price ($6,400 here).

blocks.title: Points on the price
blocks.html: The distractor always calculates points on the purchase price. Points are on the loan. An older exam rule of thumb says one discount point raises the lender's yield by about 1/8 of 1%.
blocks.casual: The wrong answer always figures points on the purchase price. Points are on the loan. An old exam rule of thumb says one discount point raises the lender's yield by about 1/8 of 1%.

deeper.plain: Points always ride on the loan amount.
deeper.picture: Tax on what you buy, not on what's in your wallet. Points hit the borrowed money, not the house.
deeper.street: New numbers: $500,000 price, $450,000 loan, 2 points. Right: $9,000. Wrong: $10,000. Yield bump by the rule of thumb: 2 x 1/8 = 1/4 of 1%.
deeper.stakes: Tell a buyer the wrong points cost and they budget wrong, then blame you at the closing table.
deeper.exam: Two traps here: base on the price, and the 1/8 rule. One point is about 1/8% of yield.

blocks.html: Lenders test two qualifying ratios on gross monthly income. The classic conventional guideline is 28/36: housing expense (PITI) up to 28%, total monthly debt (PITI plus car, student, card minimums) up to 36%. The borrower qualifies for the lower of the two results. FHA uses higher ratios (31/43 is the textbook figure).
blocks.casual: Lenders run two qualifying ratios against gross monthly income. The classic conventional guideline is 28/36. Housing expense (PITI) up to 28%. Total monthly debt (PITI plus car, student loans, card minimums) up to 36%. The borrower qualifies for the lower of the two. FHA allows higher ratios (31/43 is the textbook figure).

deeper.plain: Lenders cap your housing payment and your total debt as a share of your gross income, and use whichever limit is tighter.
deeper.picture: A parent saying: no more than $28 of every $100 on rent, and no more than $36 on rent plus all your other bills.
deeper.street: New numbers: Tasha's borrower earns $90,000 a year, $7,500 a month, with $900 in other debt. Front: $2,100. Back: $2,700 minus $900 = $1,800. Max PITI: $1,800.
deeper.stakes: Show a buyer homes they can't qualify for and you waste weeks and break hearts at the pre-approval stage.
deeper.exam: Use gross, not net, income. Back end subtracts other debts. Pick the lower result.

blocks.caption: Slide income and debts and watch which ratio becomes the limit. The lower allowed payment always wins.

blocks.title: How much house can Leo carry?
blocks.html:
Leo earns $144,000 a year: $144,000 / 12 = $12,000 a month. He has a $700 car payment and $500 in student loans.
Front end: $12,000 x 0.28 = $3,360
Back end: $12,000 x 0.36 = $4,320, minus $1,200 other debt = $3,120
Maximum PITI: the lower, $3,120
blocks.casual:
Leo makes $144,000 a year: $144,000 / 12 = $12,000 a month. He's got a $700 car payment and $500 in student loans.
Front end: $12,000 x 0.28 = $3,360
Back end: $12,000 x 0.36 = $4,320, minus $1,200 other debt = $3,120
Max PITI: the lower one, $3,120

deeper.plain: Compute both limits and take the smaller.
deeper.picture: Two speed limits on the same road. You obey the lower one.
deeper.street: New numbers: Jordan's friend earns $72,000 a year, $6,000 a month, no other debt. Front: $1,680. Back: $2,160. With no debts the front end controls: $1,680.
deeper.stakes: Missing a debt in the back-end math gives a buyer false hope that collapses at underwriting.
deeper.exam: Convert annual to monthly first. Subtract debts from the back-end figure, not the front.

blocks.html: Loan-to-value: LTV = loan / value, where value is the lower of price or appraisal. Price $500,000, appraisal $480,000, lender allows 80%: $480,000 x 0.80 = $384,000 maximum loan. Above 80% LTV on a conventional loan, expect PMI.
blocks.casual: Loan-to-value: LTV = loan / value, and value means the lower of price or appraisal. Price $500,000, appraisal $480,000, lender allows 80%: $480,000 x 0.80 = $384,000 max loan. Go above 80% LTV on a conventional loan and expect PMI.

deeper.plain: Lenders lend a percent of the lower of price or appraisal.
deeper.picture: A pawn shop lends against what the item is really worth, not what you claim you paid.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Long Beach house at $700,000 appraises at $680,000. At 90% LTV: $612,000. Buyer needs $88,000 down, not $70,000, and pays PMI because LTV is above 80%.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who plan on 10% of the price get surprised by the appraisal gap and may not have the cash.
deeper.exam: Lower of price or appraisal. PMI on conventional loans above 80% LTV.

blocks.html: Two more words that show up in math stems: gross income is income before anything is subtracted (for a borrower, before taxes; for a building, total rent). Net income is what is left after subtracting. For a building, net operating income is gross income minus vacancy and operating expenses.
blocks.casual: Two more words show up in math stems. Gross income is income before anything gets subtracted (for a borrower, before taxes; for a building, total rent). Net income is what's left after. For a building, net operating income is gross income minus vacancy and operating expenses.

deeper.plain: Gross is before deductions, net is after.
deeper.picture: Gross is your paycheck before taxes. Net is what lands in your bank account.
deeper.street: New numbers: Sal's building grosses $150,000 in rent, loses $6,000 to vacancy, and spends $54,000 on expenses. NOI: $90,000.
deeper.stakes: Qualify a buyer on net income and you'll understate what they can afford. Value a building on gross and you'll wildly overstate it.
deeper.exam: Qualifying ratios use gross monthly income. Cap rate uses NOI, which is net of operating expenses.

blocks.q: A borrower earns $9,000 a month and pays $900 a month on other debts. Using 28/36, the maximum PITI is:

blocks.title: Lower wins
blocks.html: Qualifying, LTV, and appraisal: whenever the lender has two numbers, it uses the lower one.
blocks.casual: Qualifying, LTV, appraisal: whenever the lender has two numbers to pick from, it uses the lower one.

deeper.plain: Lenders protect themselves by picking the more conservative number.
deeper.picture: A careful friend splitting a bill picks the smaller estimate of what they owe you. Lenders do the same with risk.
deeper.street: New numbers: price $820,000, appraisal $800,000, 80% LTV gives $640,000. Front end allows $4,000 PITI, back end $3,700: Tasha plans around $3,700.
deeper.stakes: Ignore this and you set expectations the lender won't meet.
deeper.exam: When in doubt with lender math, pick the lower figure.

story.title: The Napkin
story.setting: A coffee shop on Skillman Avenue, Sunnyside, Saturday morning

beats.text: Okay. $640,000 offer, 20% down, one point. Go.
Down is $128,000. Loan is $512,000. The point is 1% of the loan, so $5,120.
My spreadsheet said $6,400.
Your spreadsheet took 1% of the price. Banks charge points on what they lend you.
Fine. Can I afford the payment? I make $144,000. Car's $700, student loan $500.
Monthly gross is $12,000. 28% is $3,360. 36% is $4,320, minus your $1,200 in debts, so $3,120. The lower one wins: $3,120 for everything, taxes and insurance included.

check.q: Why is Leo's limit $3,120 and not $3,360?
c: The front-end ratio is always used
The back-end result after his other debts is lower, and the lower figure controls
Lenders average the two
Taxes are excluded from the front end
check.x: The borrower must pass both tests, so the lower allowed payment controls.

beats.text: Jordan's right. And if the appraisal comes in at $620,000, your 80% is on the $620,000, not the $640,000.
beats.tag: LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal

beats.text: What do you guys make on this? Six percent of $640,000 is... $38,400?
If it were 6%. Commission is negotiable, and it gets split. Say the listing broker offers my firm half, then I get my split of my firm's half.
And the place went from $560,000 when the seller bought it to $640,000. That's what, 12.5% up?
Up $80,000 on a $560,000 base. That's 14.3%. Divide by what they paid, not by what you're paying.
beats.tag: Percent change divides by the old number

beats.text: Part equals total times rate. Every number on that napkin was the same formula. Nice work.

board.prompt: Draw the Part / Total x Rate T-bar, then solve Leo's points, down payment, and qualifying numbers using it.

facts.text: Every percentage problem has a total, a rate and a part: Part = Total x Rate, with the percent converted to a decimal first.
Rate = Part / Total, such as a commission divided by the sale price.
Total = Part / Rate, such as a commission divided by its rate to find the sale price.
Commission rates are negotiated between client and broker; no law sets them, and competing brokers agreeing on rates is price fixing.
Commission splits are a chain of Total x Rate steps: total commission, then the listing side, then the salesperson's share.
A salesperson is paid only by the sponsoring broker, never directly by the client or another broker.
To work backward from a salesperson's earnings to the price, divide by each split, then by the commission rate.
Net price: Price = Net / (1 - commission rate); adding the commission to the net comes up short.
Simple interest = Principal x Rate x Time, with time in years.
The interest rate equals interest for one year divided by the principal.
Principal is the amount borrowed or still owed.
The first month's interest is the loan balance x the annual rate / 12; the rest of the payment goes to principal.
Amortization: interest is charged on the balance still owed, so early payments are mostly interest and later ones mostly principal.
Percent change = (new - old) / old; the base is always the starting value.
Simple appreciation multiplies the starting value by the annual rate, then by the number of years.
Straight-line depreciation divides the building's cost (land excluded) by its life, such as 27.5 years for residential rentals.
One point is 1% of the loan amount, not the price; the trap distractor figures points on the purchase price.
Discount points buy down the interest rate and origination points pay the lender's fee; one discount point raises the lender's yield by about 1/8 of 1%.
Under 28/36, housing expense (PITI) may be 28% of gross monthly income and total debt 36%; the borrower qualifies for the lower result.
FHA uses higher qualifying ratios, 31/43 in the textbook.
LTV = loan / value, where value is the lower of price or appraisal.
A conventional loan above 80% LTV usually requires PMI.
Gross income is before anything is subtracted; net operating income is gross income minus vacancy and operating expenses.

lessons.title: Area, Land Measure, and Tax Rates
lessons.tagline: Square feet, acres, front feet, and the three NY taxes you will calculate for every client.
objectives: Find the area and perimeter of rectangles, triangles, trapezoids, and irregular lots
Convert between square feet, acres, and hectares, and price by front foot, square foot, and acre
Calculate NYS transfer tax, NYC RPTT, the mansion tax, and mortgage recording tax
Compute property tax from a rate stated per $100, per $1,000, or in mills

blocks.title: A lot in Ulster County and a condo in Long Island City
blocks.html: Evelyn texts two listings before lunch. One is an odd-shaped parcel near Kingston priced "per acre." The other is a Long Island City condo she wants to flip. "Give me price per square foot on the condo, acreage on the lot, and what the taxes will cost me going in and coming out." Jordan pulls out the formula sheet.
blocks.casual: Before lunch, Evelyn texts Jordan two listings. One's an odd-shaped parcel near Kingston priced "per acre." The other is a Long Island City condo she wants to flip. "Give me price per square foot on the condo, acreage on the lot, and what taxes will cost me going in and coming out." Jordan grabs the formula sheet.

deeper.plain: Land, condos, and taxes each come with their own measuring units, and investors expect you to switch between them fast.
deeper.picture: Like a cook who has to switch between cups, grams, and ounces depending on the recipe.
deeper.street: Evelyn's lot: square feet to acres. Her condo: price divided by square feet. Her taxes: transfer tax when she sells, mortgage recording tax when she borrows, property tax every year in between.
deeper.stakes: Investors drop agents who can't run the numbers. And a mistake on transfer tax changes what a seller nets by thousands.
deeper.exam: Area, acres, front feet, transfer tax, and property tax all show up in the math section. Memorize the conversion numbers.

blocks.caption: Split any irregular lot into rectangles and triangles, find each area, then add. Toggle to acres to see the 43,560 conversion.

head: Shape
Area formula
Example
rows: 25 ft x 100 ft = 2,500 sq ft (the classic Brooklyn lot)

deeper.plain: Area means how much flat space something covers. Each shape has its own formula.
deeper.picture: Area is how much carpet you'd need to cover the floor. Shape decides how you count it.
deeper.street: New numbers: a triangular corner lot in Jackson Heights with a 90 ft base and 60 ft height: 1/2 x 90 x 60 = 2,700 sq ft. A trapezoid lot with parallel sides 40 and 70 ft and 150 ft deep: 55 x 150 = 8,250 sq ft.
deeper.stakes: Forget to halve the triangle and you double the land, then double the price you quote.
deeper.exam: Triangles get the 1/2. Trapezoids average the two parallel sides. Brooklyn's 25 x 100 lot is 2,500 sq ft.

blocks.html: Perimeter is the distance around: add every side. A 25 x 100 lot has a perimeter of 25 + 100 + 25 + 100 = 250 feet. Fencing is sold by the foot (perimeter); carpet, tile, and land are priced by area.
blocks.casual: Perimeter is the distance around. Add up every side. A 25 x 100 lot has a perimeter of 25 + 100 + 25 + 100 = 250 feet. Fencing gets sold by the foot (perimeter). Carpet, tile, and land get priced by area.

deeper.plain: Perimeter is the walk around the edge. Area is the space inside.
deeper.picture: Perimeter is the crust of the pizza. Area is the whole pie.
deeper.street: New numbers: Sal fences a 30 x 80 Astoria yard. Perimeter: 30 + 80 + 30 + 80 = 220 ft. At $45 a foot, fencing costs $9,900.
deeper.stakes: Price a fence by area and the client's budget is wildly off. Small mistake, embarrassing result.
deeper.exam: Fence, border, trim, baseboard = perimeter. Carpet, paint coverage on a floor, land = area.

blocks.title: An L-shaped lot
blocks.html:
The lot is 100 ft deep along the left side and 60 ft wide at the back. A 40 x 50 notch is missing from the front-right corner, and the street side is 20 ft wide.
Method: full rectangle minus the notch.
100 x 60 = 6,000 sq ft
Notch: 40 x 50 = 2,000 sq ft
Area: 6,000 - 2,000 = 4,000 sq ft
Or split it into two rectangles (20 x 50 = 1,000 and 60 x 50 = 3,000) and add. Same answer.
blocks.casual:
The lot runs 100 ft deep on the left side and 60 ft wide at the back. A 40 x 50 notch is missing from the front-right corner, and the street side is 20 ft wide.
Method: full rectangle minus the notch.
100 x 60 = 6,000 sq ft
Notch: 40 x 50 = 2,000 sq ft
Area: 6,000 minus 2,000 = 4,000 sq ft
Or cut it into two rectangles (20 x 50 = 1,000 and 60 x 50 = 3,000) and add them. Same answer.

deeper.plain: Odd shapes are just rectangles stuck together or with a bite taken out.
deeper.picture: A Tetris piece: break it into squares, count them, done.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Hollis lot 120 ft deep, 80 ft wide at the back, with a 30 x 60 notch out of the front corner. 120 x 80 = 9,600. Notch 30 x 60 = 1,800. Area: 7,800 sq ft.
deeper.stakes: Miss the notch and you overstate the lot, which can mean a buildable-area claim that the zoning won't support.
deeper.exam: Sketch it. Either subtract the missing piece or add the rectangles. Check that both methods match.

blocks.title: Units must match
blocks.html: If one side is in yards and the other in feet, convert first. 1 yard = 3 feet, 1 square yard = 9 square feet, 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. A 12 x 15 ft room needs 180 / 9 = 20 square yards of carpet.
blocks.casual: If one side's in yards and the other's in feet, convert first. 1 yard = 3 feet, 1 square yard = 9 square feet, 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet. A 12 x 15 ft room needs 180 / 9 = 20 square yards of carpet.

deeper.plain: Make every measurement the same unit before you multiply.
deeper.picture: You can't add dollars and euros straight up. Same with yards and feet.
deeper.street: New numbers: a patio 18 ft x 24 ft needs concrete 6 inches (0.5 ft) thick. 18 x 24 x 0.5 = 216 cubic feet / 27 = 8 cubic yards.
deeper.stakes: Order 3 times too much concrete because you divided by 3 instead of 27, and someone eats the bill.
deeper.exam: Square yards: divide square feet by 9. Cubic yards: divide cubic feet by 27. The trap divides by 3.

blocks.q: A triangular corner lot has a 150-foot base and a 100-foot height. Its area is:
c: 15,000 sq ft
7,500 sq ft
250 sq ft
30,000 sq ft
blocks.x: 1/2 x 150 x 100 = 7,500 sq ft. Forgetting the 1/2 gives 15,000.

blocks.html: An acre is 43,560 square feet. A square mile (a section) is 640 acres. A hectare is a metric unit: 10,000 square meters, about 2.47 acres. Square feet / 43,560 = acres. Acres x 43,560 = square feet.
blocks.casual: An acre is 43,560 square feet. A square mile (a section) is 640 acres. A hectare is metric: 10,000 square meters, about 2.47 acres. Square feet / 43,560 = acres. Acres x 43,560 = square feet.

deeper.plain: Land outside the city gets measured in acres. Memorize 43,560.
deeper.picture: An acre is a bit smaller than an American football field without the end zones.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Dutchess County lot of 130,680 sq ft. 130,680 / 43,560 = 3 acres. A 4-hectare farm: 4 x 2.47 = about 9.88 acres.
deeper.stakes: Mislabel a 1-acre lot as 2 and the buyer's plans for a pool and barn fall apart, along with your credibility.
deeper.exam: 43,560 is almost guaranteed. 640 acres in a square mile. Hectare is about 2.47 acres.

blocks.title: The Ulster County parcel
blocks.html:
The lot is a rectangle 330 ft by 660 ft, priced at $30,000 an acre.
Area: 330 x 660 = 217,800 sq ft
Acres: 217,800 / 43,560 = 5 acres
Price: 5 x $30,000 = $150,000
blocks.casual:
The lot is a rectangle, 330 ft by 660 ft, priced at $30,000 an acre.
Area: 330 x 660 = 217,800 sq ft
Acres: 217,800 / 43,560 = 5 acres
Price: 5 x $30,000 = $150,000

deeper.plain: Square feet, then acres, then multiply by the per-acre price.
deeper.picture: Weigh the apples, convert to pounds, multiply by price per pound.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Sullivan County parcel 435.6 ft by 300 ft at $18,000 an acre. 130,680 sq ft / 43,560 = 3 acres. Price: $54,000.
deeper.stakes: Quote a per-acre price on the wrong acreage and the client's offer is off by tens of thousands.
deeper.exam: Three steps. The trap multiplies square feet by the per-acre price or skips the conversion.

blocks.html: Front feet measure the side of a lot that faces the street (or water). Commercial strips and waterfront lots are often priced per front foot. In a lot dimension, the first number is the frontage: a 40 x 120 lot has 40 front feet.
blocks.casual: Front feet measure the side of a lot that faces the street (or the water). Commercial strips and waterfront lots often get priced per front foot. In a lot dimension, the first number is the frontage: a 40 x 120 lot has 40 front feet.

deeper.plain: Frontage is how much of the lot touches the street. It's the first number listed.
deeper.picture: Storefront width on a busy avenue. More window on the sidewalk means more customers.
deeper.street: New numbers: a 50 x 100 waterfront lot on Lake George at $9,000 per front foot: 50 x $9,000 = $450,000.
deeper.stakes: Use the depth by mistake and you'd price the lot at double, killing the deal.
deeper.exam: First number = frontage. Depth doesn't enter front-foot pricing.

blocks.title: Pricing by the front foot
blocks.html:
A 40 x 120 lot on a Staten Island commercial street sells at $6,000 per front foot.
40 x $6,000 = $240,000 (the 120 ft depth does not enter the math)
blocks.casual:
A 40 x 120 lot on a Staten Island commercial street sells at $6,000 per front foot.
40 x $6,000 = $240,000. The 120 ft depth doesn't enter the math.

deeper.plain: Multiply the frontage by the price per front foot. Ignore depth.
deeper.picture: Buying ribbon by the foot: only the length matters, not how wide the spool is.
deeper.street: New numbers: a 75 x 150 lot on Hylan Boulevard at $4,500 per front foot: 75 x $4,500 = $337,500.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who confuses depth for frontage overpays or walks from a fair deal.
deeper.exam: Distractor multiplies by the depth (120 x $6,000 = $720,000). Use the first number.

blocks.html: Price per square foot = price / square feet. It is the fastest way to compare NYC condos of different sizes.
blocks.casual: Price per square foot = price / square feet. It's the quickest way to compare NYC condos of different sizes.

deeper.plain: Divide the price by the size to compare apples to apples.
deeper.picture: Unit price at the grocery store. The big box might look pricier but cost less per ounce.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Williamsburg 1BR at $960,000 for 800 sq ft is $1,200/sq ft. A 2BR at $1,350,000 for 1,200 sq ft is $1,125. The bigger one is the better deal per foot.
deeper.stakes: Compare raw prices only and buyers chase the wrong unit. Investors live by this number.
deeper.exam: Price / square feet. Don't flip it.

blocks.title: Evelyn's Long Island City condo
blocks.html:
Asking $1,140,000 for 950 sq ft.
$1,140,000 / 950 = $1,200 per square foot
A building comp at $1,150/sq ft for a 1,000 sq ft unit suggests $1,150,000 for a same-size unit, or about $1,092,500 for 950 sq ft.
blocks.casual:
Asking $1,140,000 for 950 sq ft.
$1,140,000 / 950 = $1,200 per square foot
A building comp at $1,150/sq ft for a 1,000 sq ft unit suggests $1,150,000 for a same-size unit, or about $1,092,500 for 950 sq ft.

deeper.plain: Get the per-foot price, then multiply by your unit's size to compare.
deeper.picture: If one bag of rice costs $2 a pound, a 3-pound bag should cost about $6.
deeper.street: New numbers: an Astoria condo asks $780,000 for 650 sq ft: $1,200/sq ft. Comps in the building run $1,100. At 650 sq ft that's $715,000, so Evelyn opens around there.
deeper.stakes: Overpay $50 a foot on 950 feet and that's $47,500 off the flip profit.
deeper.exam: Two steps: price / sq ft, then comp rate x subject sq ft.

blocks.q: A 2-acre lot is how many square feet?
blocks.x: 2 x 43,560 = 87,120. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 21,780.

blocks.html: The NYS real estate transfer tax is $2 for every $500 of consideration (0.4%), paid by the seller. In NYC it rises to 0.65% for residential sales of $3M or more and other property of $2M or more. NYC adds its own Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT), also paid by the seller.
blocks.casual: The NYS real estate transfer tax is $2 for every $500 of consideration (0.4%), and the seller pays it. In NYC it goes up to 0.65% for residential sales of $3M or more and other property of $2M or more. NYC also adds its own Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT), also on the seller.

deeper.plain: When property changes hands, the state takes a small cut from the seller, and NYC takes another.
deeper.picture: A toll for crossing a bridge. The seller pays the toll on the way out.
deeper.street: New numbers: an Albany house at $325,000. $325,000 / $500 = 650 x $2 = $1,300 state transfer tax, paid by the seller. No NYC RPTT outside the city.
deeper.stakes: Leave transfer taxes out of a seller's net sheet and they're thousands short of what you promised.
deeper.exam: $2 per $500 is 0.4%. Seller pays. Divide price by 500, multiply by 2.

blocks.caption: Enter a price and borough. See which taxes the seller pays and which the buyer pays.

head: Tax
Rate
Who pays
rows: $2 per $500 (0.4%); 0.65% on NYC residential $3M+ and other NYC property $2M+
NYC RPTT, residential (1 to 3 family, condo, co-op)
1% up to $500,000; 1.425% above $500,000 (on the whole price)
1% on residential purchases of $1M+ statewide; NYC graduated from 1% up to 3.9%

deeper.plain: Sellers pay the transfer taxes. Buyers pay the mansion tax at $1M and up.
deeper.picture: Two different tolls on the same bridge, one in each direction.
deeper.street: New numbers: a $1,200,000 Brooklyn condo. Seller: NYS $4,800 plus NYC RPTT 1.425% = $17,100, total $21,900. Buyer: mansion tax 1% (NYC's bottom tier) = $12,000.
deeper.stakes: Mix up who pays and your client budgets wrong. Buyers above $1M are the ones caught off guard.
deeper.exam: Seller pays transfer taxes. Buyer pays mansion tax, starting at $1M. NYC RPTT has two tiers split at $500,000.

blocks.title: Seller's transfer taxes on an $850,000 Queens condo
blocks.html:
NYS: $850,000 / $500 = 1,700 units x $2 = $3,400
NYC RPTT: price above $500,000, so 1.425% x $850,000 = $12,112.50
Seller's total: $15,512.50
Buyer's mansion tax: none, under $1M.
blocks.casual:
Seller's transfer taxes on an $850,000 Queens condo:
NYS: $850,000 / $500 = 1,700 units x $2 = $3,400
NYC RPTT: price is above $500,000, so 1.425% x $850,000 = $12,112.50
Seller's total: $15,512.50
Buyer's mansion tax: none, it's under $1M.

deeper.plain: Figure the state tax, figure the city tax, add them. Check if the buyer hits $1M.
deeper.picture: Two tips on one bill, one for the server and one for the bartender. Add both.
deeper.street: New numbers: a $640,000 Bronx two-family. NYS: 1,280 x $2 = $2,560. RPTT: 1.425% x $640,000 = $9,120. Seller total: $11,680. No mansion tax.
deeper.stakes: Skip the RPTT on a NYC net sheet and the seller is about $9,000 poorer than you told them.
deeper.exam: NYC residential over $500,000: 1.425% on the whole price. NYS is separate and always applies.

blocks.title: Whole price, not the excess
blocks.html: Once a residential NYC sale passes $500,000, the 1.425% RPTT rate applies to the entire price, not just the part above $500,000. Likewise, the 1% mansion tax applies to the whole price once it reaches $1M.
blocks.casual: Once a residential NYC sale passes $500,000, the 1.425% RPTT rate hits the entire price, not just the part over $500,000. Same with the 1% mansion tax: once the price hits $1M, it applies to the whole thing.

deeper.plain: These are cliff taxes. Cross the line and the higher rate covers every dollar.
deeper.picture: A height requirement for a ride. At 48 inches you're in. Your whole body gets on, not just the inches over.
deeper.street: New numbers: a buyer at $1,000,000 owes $10,000 mansion tax. At $999,000 they owe nothing. Smart buyers negotiate to $999,000 with personal property listed separately (carefully, with the attorneys).
deeper.stakes: Tell a buyer the mansion tax is only on the excess and they're short $10,000 at closing.
deeper.exam: Whole price, not marginal. The trap figures the tax only on the amount above the threshold.

blocks.html: Mortgage recording tax is charged on the loan amount when the mortgage is recorded, paid by the borrower. In NYC on 1 to 3 family homes and condos: 1.8% for loans under $500,000 and 1.925% for $500,000 and up (the lender pays a further 0.25%). Many suburban downstate counties charge 1.05%; rates vary by county.
blocks.casual: Mortgage recording tax gets charged on the loan amount when the mortgage is recorded, and the borrower pays it. In NYC on 1 to 3 family homes and condos: 1.8% for loans under $500,000 and 1.925% for $500,000 and up (the lender pays another 0.25%). Many suburban downstate counties charge 1.05%. Rates vary by county.

deeper.plain: Borrow money against a house and you pay a tax on the loan when it's recorded.
deeper.picture: A registration fee on the loan, sized to how much you borrowed.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Westchester buyer borrows $450,000 at a 1.05% county rate: $4,725. In Brooklyn the same loan would be 1.8%: $8,100.
deeper.stakes: NYC buyers who budget like suburban buyers come up thousands short.
deeper.exam: Based on the loan, not the price. Paid by the borrower. NYC: 1.8% under $500,000, 1.925% at $500,000+.

deeper.plain: Pick the rate by the loan size, then multiply.
deeper.picture: Two price tiers at the deli: under a pound, one rate; a pound or more, a slightly higher rate on the whole order.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Queens condo loan of $499,000: x 0.018 = $8,982. A loan of $520,000: x 0.01925 = $10,010. A $21,000 bigger loan costs $1,028 more in tax.
deeper.stakes: Tasha sometimes advises keeping a loan just under $500,000 when it makes sense, since crossing the line raises the rate on the whole loan.
deeper.exam: The rate tier depends on the loan, not the price. Use 0.018 or 0.01925 as decimals.

blocks.title: Co-ops skip it
blocks.html: A co-op buyer gets a share loan secured by stock and a proprietary lease, not a mortgage on real property. No mortgage recording tax. That is one reason co-op closing costs run lower.
blocks.casual: A co-op buyer gets a share loan secured by stock and a proprietary lease, not a mortgage on real property. No mortgage recording tax. That's one reason co-op closing costs come in lower.

deeper.plain: Co-op loans aren't mortgages, so the mortgage tax doesn't apply.
deeper.picture: Borrowing against your stock portfolio, not your house. Different paperwork, different tax.
deeper.street: Kim's building on the UWS: a buyer borrows $600,000 to buy shares. Compared with a condo loan of the same size, they skip about $11,550 in mortgage recording tax.
deeper.stakes: Quote mortgage tax to a co-op buyer and you've overstated their costs, maybe steering them away from a good deal.
deeper.exam: Co-op = personal property (shares). No mortgage recording tax. Condo = real property, the tax applies.

blocks.q: A buyer finances a Bronx two-family with a $500,000 mortgage. The borrower's NYC mortgage recording tax is:
blocks.x: At $500,000 and up, the 1.925% rate applies: $500,000 x 0.01925 = $9,625. $9,000 uses the under-$500,000 rate.

blocks.html: Property tax = assessed value x tax rate. The same rate can be written four ways. A mill is one tenth of a cent, $0.001, so 1 mill = $1 per $1,000.
blocks.casual: Property tax = assessed value x tax rate. The same rate can be written four ways. A mill is a tenth of a cent, $0.001, so 1 mill = $1 per $1,000.

deeper.plain: Multiply the assessed value by the rate. The rate just comes in different outfits.
deeper.picture: Same speed in miles per hour or kilometers per hour. Same rate, different label.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Nassau house assessed at $150,000 at 28 mills: $150,000 x 0.028 = $4,200.
deeper.stakes: Read mills as per $100 and you'd quote $42,000 a year in taxes, scaring off a buyer for nothing.
deeper.exam: Mills = per $1,000. 1 mill = $0.001. Use assessed value, not market value, unless the stem says otherwise.

head: Stated as
Same rate
Math on $200,000 assessed
blocks.caption: Per $1,000 and mills are the same number. Per $100 is one tenth of it.

deeper.plain: Four ways to write one rate. Learn to convert between them.
deeper.picture: A quarter, 25 cents, 0.25 dollars. All the same coin.
deeper.stakes: Investors comparing towns quoted in different formats need you to convert, or they pick the wrong town.
deeper.exam: Per $1,000 and mills are the same number. Per $100 is one tenth of that. Percent is per $100.

blocks.title: Monthly escrow
blocks.html:
Leo's condo is assessed at $90,000 and the combined rate is $120 per $1,000.
90 x $120 = $10,800 a year
Monthly escrow: $10,800 / 12 = $900
blocks.casual:
Leo's condo is assessed at $90,000 and the combined rate is $120 per $1,000.
90 x $120 = $10,800 a year
Monthly escrow: $10,800 / 12 = $900

deeper.plain: Get the yearly tax, then divide by 12 for the monthly escrow.
deeper.picture: Saving for a yearly bill by setting aside a little each month.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Brooklyn Class 1 house assessed at $55,000 at about $200 per $1,000: 55 x $200 = $11,000 a year, or $916.67 a month in escrow.
deeper.stakes: Leave escrow out of PITI and the buyer's qualifying ratio is understated.
deeper.exam: Count the thousands (or hundreds), multiply by the rate, then divide by 12 if they ask monthly.

head: Topic
Formula
rows: Part = Total x Rate; Rate = Part / Total; Total = Part / Rate
Price x rate, then x each split
Loan / lower of price or appraisal
Lower of 28% of gross monthly income, or 36% minus other debts
L x W; 1/2 x B x H; average of parallel sides x H
Frontage (first number) x price per front foot
Assessed value x rate; mills = per $1,000
blocks.caption: Screenshot this. It covers nearly every math item on the exam.

deeper.plain: One page of formulas covers nearly every math question.
deeper.picture: A cheat sheet taped inside your locker, except you memorize it instead.
deeper.street: New numbers to drill: net $376,000 after 6% = $400,000 price. $1,000,000 NYS transfer tax = $4,000. 87,120 sq ft = 2 acres. $600,000 loan, 2 points = $12,000.
deeper.stakes: Fumble one formula under time pressure and you lose a minute and a point.
deeper.exam: Recite these until automatic. The math items reward speed and the right base.

blocks.q: A home is assessed at $150,000 and the tax rate is 28 mills. The annual tax is:
blocks.x: 28 mills = $28 per $1,000 = 0.028. $150,000 x 0.028 = $4,200. Treating a mill as a cent gives $42,000.

blocks.title: Big four numbers
blocks.html: 43,560 sq ft in an acre. $2 per $500 NYS transfer tax. 1 point = 1% of the loan. 1 mill = $1 per $1,000.
blocks.casual: 43,560 sq ft in an acre. $2 per $500 NYS transfer tax. 1 point = 1% of the loan. 1 mill = $1 per $1,000.

deeper.plain: Four numbers that show up again and again.
deeper.picture: Your four PIN codes for the exam.
deeper.street: New numbers: 2.5 acres = 108,900 sq ft. $750,000 sale = $3,000 NYS tax. $350,000 loan, 1 point = $3,500. 15 mills on $200,000 = $3,000.
deeper.stakes: Mixing them up (point on price, mill per $100) costs easy points.
deeper.exam: Write these four on scratch paper the second the exam starts.

story.title: Price Per Everything
story.setting: Evelyn's office on Queens Boulevard, a Wednesday lunch

beats.text: Two deals. The LIC condo: $1,140,000 for 950 feet. Number?
Divide price by square feet. $1,200 a foot.
beats.tag: Price per sq ft = price / sq ft

beats.text: And the Kingston land, 330 by 660, $30,000 an acre.
217,800 square feet. Divide by 43,560: five acres. $150,000.
My European partner wants it in hectares.
A hectare is about 2.47 acres, so roughly 2 hectares.
Now taxes. If I buy the condo with a $680,000 loan, what does recording cost me?
NYC, loan of $500,000 or more, 1.925%. $13,090. Paid by you as borrower.
beats.tag: MRT: borrower pays on the loan

beats.text: And when I flip it at $1,300,000? Mansion tax on me?

check.q: Who pays the mansion tax when Evelyn sells for $1.3M?
c: Evelyn, as seller
Her buyer
Split equally
Nobody, it is under $2M
check.x: The mansion tax is paid by the buyer on residential purchases of $1M or more. Evelyn pays the NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT as seller.

beats.text: Your buyer pays the 1% mansion tax. You pay the state's $2 per $500, that's $5,200, plus city RPTT at 1.425%, $18,525.
beats.tag: Seller: transfer taxes; buyer: mansion tax

beats.text: You did that without a calculator.
Four numbers. 43,560. $2 per $500. A point is 1% of the loan. A mill is a dollar per thousand.
And always ask: is the tax on the price, or on the loan? That one question kills half the wrong answers.

board.prompt: Sketch an irregular lot, split it into rectangles and triangles, label each area, then convert the total to acres.

facts.text: Rectangle area is length x width; an irregular lot is split into rectangles (or a rectangle minus a notch) and the pieces added.
Triangle area is 1/2 x base x height.
Trapezoid area is the average of the two parallel sides x the height between them.
Circle area is 3.14 x radius x radius.
Perimeter is the sum of all sides, and fencing is priced by the linear foot of perimeter.
Units must match: 1 yard = 3 feet, 1 square yard = 9 square feet, 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet.
An acre is 43,560 square feet: square feet / 43,560 = acres.
A square mile (a section) is 640 acres.
A hectare is 10,000 square meters, about 2.47 acres.
Front feet are the side facing the street, the first number in a lot dimension; price = frontage x price per front foot, and depth does not enter.
Price per square foot = price / square feet, the fastest way to compare condos of different sizes.
The NYS transfer tax is $2 per $500 of consideration (0.4%), paid by the seller.
In NYC the state transfer tax rises to 0.65% for residential sales of $3M or more and other property of $2M or more.
NYC RPTT on residential sales is 1% up to $500,000 and 1.425% above, applied to the whole price, paid by the seller.
NYC RPTT on commercial property is 1.425% up to $500,000 and 2.625% above.
The mansion tax is paid by the buyer: 1% of the whole price on residential purchases of $1M or more (graduated up to 3.9% in NYC).
NYC mortgage recording tax on 1 to 3 family homes and condos is paid by the borrower on the loan amount: 1.8% under $500,000 and 1.925% at $500,000 and up.
Co-op share loans are not mortgages on real property, so co-op buyers pay no mortgage recording tax.
Property tax = assessed value x tax rate, and a rate per $100 is applied to each $100 of assessed value.
A mill is $0.001, so 1 mill equals $1 per $1,000 of assessed value.
Monthly tax escrow is the annual tax divided by 12.
Value from income is NOI divided by the cap rate.

lessons.title: Case file: Every Number in a Ridgewood Two-Family
lessons.tagline: Sal is selling his mother's two-family on a Ridgewood side street. From the listing to the closing statement, every number in the deal is one of the formulas in this unit.
objectives: Calculate a total commission and each broker's and salesperson's share, and the price a seller needs to net a target amount after commission and transfer taxes.
Calculate building price per square foot, yard area and fence length, and lot size in acres from real dimensions.
Apply 28/36 qualifying ratios, rental income, LTV, and points to decide whether buyers qualify and what they pay.
Calculate NYC and NYS transfer taxes, the mansion tax, mortgage recording tax, and closing prorations, and assemble the buyers' cash to close and the seller's net.

blocks.title: Ridgewood, Queens, a brick two-family on a side street off Fresh Pond Road
blocks.html: Sal Russo's mother left him the two-family she bought in 1978: a 20-foot-wide brick row house on a 25 by 100 lot, with a garden apartment and a parlor-floor duplex. Sal, who already has his hands full with his six-unit building in Astoria, wants to sell. The upstairs tenant pays $3,000 a month and wants to stay. Jordan takes the listing for Hudson & Hart at a 5% commission, with half offered to the buyer's broker. Three months later Amara and Tom Whitfield, represented by Bea Santos of a Queens brokerage, sign a contract at $1,150,000 with a $115,000 down payment held in escrow by Sal's attorney. Closing is set for August 20. Diane hands Jordan a legal pad: "Every number in this deal, start to finish. If you can do this one, you can do the exam's math section in your sleep."

The listing agreement says 5% of the sale price, payable at closing, with 2.5% offered to a cooperating broker who represents the buyer. Each brokerage then splits its share with its own salesperson under their independent contractor agreements. Jordan's split with Hudson & Hart is 60/40, Jordan's favor. Bea's split with her firm is 70/30.

blocks.q: How much does Jordan earn on this sale?
blocks.x: Total commission: $1,150,000 x 5% = $57,500. Hudson & Hart's half: $28,750. Jordan's 60%: $28,750 x 0.60 = $17,250. $34,500 is the trap: it takes 60% of the whole commission and skips the co-broke split. $11,500 is the firm's 40%. Jordan is paid by Hudson & Hart, never directly by Sal or by Bea's firm.

blocks.q: How much does Bea, the buyers' agent, earn under her 70/30 split?
blocks.x: Bea's firm receives the co-broke half: $28,750. Bea's 70%: $28,750 x 0.70 = $20,125, and her firm keeps $8,625. $40,250 is the trap: it applies 70% to the full $57,500. $17,250 is Jordan's figure; the two salespeople earn different amounts from equal brokerage halves because their splits differ.

blocks.title: Who sets these numbers
blocks.html: No law sets commission rates, and agreements among competing brokers about rates are price fixing. Since August 2024, offers of buyer-broker compensation cannot be published on the MLS, and a buyer's agent working through an MLS needs a written agreement with the buyer before touring. Here, Sal agreed in writing to pay the buyer's broker; the Whitfields' agreement with Bea says what happens if a seller does not.

blocks.text: Area, perimeter, and price per square foot

blocks.html: Bea's first question during the showing was price per square foot, the quickest way to compare buildings of different sizes. The building's footprint is 20 feet wide by 55 feet deep. It has two full floors above a cellar; the cellar does not count in gross living area. The house sits 10 feet back from the front lot line, so the back yard runs from the rear wall to the back of the lot.

blocks.title: Measuring the house and the lot
blocks.html:
Lot: 25 ft x 100 ft = 2,500 sq ft. The 25 ft of street frontage is the lot's front footage.
Building: 20 ft x 55 ft = 1,100 sq ft per floor x 2 floors = 2,200 sq ft.
Price per square foot: $1,150,000 / 2,200 = $522.73.
Back yard: lot depth 100 ft minus 10 ft front yard minus 55 ft building = 35 ft deep, by the full 25 ft lot width = 875 sq ft.
Lot in acres: 2,500 / 43,560 = about 0.057 acre.

blocks.q: A comparable two-family on the next block sold for $1,260,000 with 2,400 square feet. How does the Whitfields' price per square foot compare?
c: About $2.27 a square foot more than the comparable
About $110,000 less, because the comparable is bigger
The same, since both sold near the same total price
About $2.27 a square foot less than the comparable
blocks.x: Comparable: $1,260,000 / 2,400 = $525.00 a square foot. Subject: $522.73. The Whitfields pay about $2.27 a square foot less. "$110,000 less" is the trap: it compares total prices, which ignores the 200 square foot size difference. Price per square foot is a check, not an appraisal; condition, layout, and the rental unit matter too.

blocks.html: Amara wants a fence along the two sides and the back of the yard, so their dog can be outside. The fence runs along the back lot line (25 ft) and down both side lines from the rear wall to the back of the lot (35 ft each). The installer quotes $45 a linear foot.

blocks.q: How many linear feet of fence do they need, and what will it cost?
blocks.x: Fence is perimeter, not area: 25 + 35 + 35 = 95 linear feet, and 95 x $45 = $4,275. 875 is the trap: it is the yard's area in square feet, which would price sod, not fence. 120 feet adds a fourth side along the rear wall of the house, which already closes the yard.

blocks.html: The Whitfields are putting 20% down and borrowing the rest with a 30-year fixed loan at 6.5% plus 1 discount point. The appraisal comes in at $1,160,000. Lenders use the lower of price or appraised value for loan-to-value, so the value is $1,150,000.

blocks.q: What is the loan amount, the LTV, and the cost of the discount point?
blocks.x: Loan: $1,150,000 x 80% = $920,000. LTV uses the lower of price and appraisal: $920,000 / $1,150,000 = 80%, so no PMI. One point is 1% of the loan, $9,200. The $11,500 point is the trap: it is 1% of the price. $928,000 applies 80% to the higher appraisal, and 79.3% divides by the appraisal instead of the price.

blocks.html: Tasha, the Whitfields' mortgage broker, builds the monthly payment. Principal and interest on $920,000 at 6.5% for 30 years is $5,815.03. In the first month, the interest is $920,000 x 6.5% / 12 = $4,983.33, and only $831.69 reduces the principal. NYC property taxes on the house are about $7,200 a year ($600 a month) and homeowners insurance about $2,400 ($200 a month). PITI: $5,815.03 + $600 + $200 = $6,615.03.

Amara earns $190,000 a year and Tom $70,000: gross income of $260,000, or $21,666.67 a month. They also have a $450 car payment and a $380 student loan payment. Because they are buying a two-family they will live in, the lender will also count part of the upstairs rent. Lenders typically count about 75% of the gross rent from the other unit, leaving room for vacancy and expenses.

blocks.q: What monthly income will the lender use for the qualifying ratios?
blocks.x: Salary: $260,000 / 12 = $21,666.67. Rental income: $3,000 x 75% = $2,250. Total: $23,916.67. $24,666.67 is the trap: it adds the full $3,000 rent, ignoring the lender's allowance for vacancy and expenses. $21,666.67 ignores the rent entirely, which understates what a two-family buyer can carry.

blocks.q: Under the classic 28/36 guideline, what is the maximum PITI, and do the Whitfields fit?
c: $7,780.00 maximum; their $6,615.03 PITI fits
$8,610.00 maximum; their $6,615.03 PITI fits
$6,066.67 maximum; their $6,615.03 PITI does not fit
$6,696.67 maximum; their $6,615.03 PITI fits
blocks.x: Front end: $23,916.67 x 28% = $6,696.67. Back end: $23,916.67 x 36% = $8,610, minus $830 of other debts = $7,780. The lower figure controls: $6,696.67, and their $6,615.03 fits. $7,780 is the trap: it uses only the back-end test. $6,066.67 applies 28% to salary alone, forgetting the rental income. Their back-end ratio is ($6,615.03 + $830) / $23,916.67 = 31.1%.

blocks.title: Points, LTV, and the lower number
blocks.html: Three habits catch most math errors. Points are a percentage of the loan, not the price. LTV is the loan divided by the lower of price or appraisal. And when a lender has two answers (front end and back end, price and appraisal), the lower one wins.

blocks.text: Transfer taxes and the mansion tax

blocks.html: The contract follows New York custom: the seller pays the New York State transfer tax and the NYC Real Property Transfer Tax, and the buyer pays the mansion tax and the mortgage recording tax. A two-family is a residential property in the 1 to 3 family category for both the NYC transfer tax and mortgage recording tax rates.

head: Tax
Rate on this deal
Amount
Paid by
rows: 1.925% (loan of $500,000 or more on a 1 to 3 family)
blocks.caption: Taxes on a $1,150,000 sale with a $920,000 loan

blocks.q: What are Sal's total transfer taxes?
blocks.x: NYS: $1,150,000 / $500 = 2,300 units x $2 = $4,600. NYC RPTT: $1,150,000 x 1.425% = $16,387.50. Total: $20,987.50. $32,487.50 is the trap: it adds the buyers' mansion tax to the seller's bill. The 1.425% rate applies to the whole price once a residential sale passes $500,000, not just the excess.

blocks.html: The Whitfields' taxes, $11,500 of mansion tax and $17,710 of mortgage recording tax, add $29,210 to their closing costs. Title closers sometimes apply small statutory credits on one and two family homes; exam math ignores them, and so does this case. Had they bought a co-op with a share loan, there would be no mortgage recording tax at all.

blocks.text: Where the $7,200 tax figure comes from

blocks.html: Tasha did not guess the tax line in the PITI. The Department of Finance lists the house in Class 1 with an assessed value of $36,000, kept low by the Class 1 caps after decades of ownership. The Class 1 tax rate has run close to 20% of assessed value in recent years; this case uses 20.0% to keep the math clean. The Whitfields will not inherit Sal's exemptions (he has none on this house, since he never lived there), but they will inherit the capped assessment, which can rise 6% a year.

blocks.q: The same 20.0% rate can be written several ways. Which set is equivalent, and what is the tax on $36,000 of assessed value?
c: $2 per $100, $20 per $1,000, or 20 mills; tax $720
blocks.x: 20% means $20 of tax per $100 of assessed value, which is $200 per $1,000. A mill is $1 per $1,000, so 200 mills. Tax: $36,000 x 20% = $7,200, or $600 a month in the escrow. The $720 answer is the trap: it treats 20 mills as the rate, which is 2%. Converting between percent, per $100, per $1,000, and mills is a favorite exam step.

blocks.html: Next year's bill could be higher: if the assessment rises the full 6% cap to $38,160 and the rate holds, the tax becomes $7,632. Priya puts that in her memo so the Whitfields are not surprised when the lender's escrow analysis raises their payment.

Priya, representing the Whitfields, and Sal's attorney apportion the items that one side paid in advance or collected in advance. Under the usual New York contract, items are apportioned as of midnight of the day before closing, so the Whitfields own the house, its income, and its expenses starting on August 20, the closing day. Both attorneys use actual days in the period (a 365-day year).

blocks.title: Property tax proration
blocks.html:
NYC bills this house quarterly (assessed value under $250,000). Sal paid the July 1 quarter, covering July 1 to September 30: $7,200 / 4 = $1,800.
Days in the quarter: 31 + 31 + 30 = 92.
Whitfields' days: August 20 to 31 (12 days) + September (30 days) = 42 days.
Credit to Sal, paid by the Whitfields: $1,800 x 42 / 92 = $821.74.

blocks.q: If the attorneys had used a 360-day year with 30-day months, what would the tax proration be?
blocks.x: With 30-day months, August 20 to 30 is 11 days, plus September's 30 = 41 days of a 90-day quarter: $1,800 x 41 / 90 = $820.00. $821.74 is the trap: it is the 365-day answer. $978.26 is Sal's share of the quarter, not the buyers'. Exam items say which method to use; read the stem for "360" or "365."

blocks.html: Rent goes the other way. On August 1 the upstairs tenant paid Sal the full $3,000 for August. Sal collected rent for 12 days the Whitfields will own, so he owes them that part. Separately, Sal holds the tenant's $3,000 security deposit. It is not prorated; the whole deposit is transferred to the new owners, who become responsible for returning it to the tenant at the end of the tenancy, and the tenant is notified of the transfer.

blocks.q: What does Sal owe the Whitfields at closing for the August rent and the security deposit?
c: $1,161.29 for rent; the deposit stays with Sal
$1,838.71 for rent plus the $3,000 deposit
$3,000 for rent; the deposit goes to the tenant
$1,161.29 for rent plus the $3,000 deposit
blocks.x: Rent: $3,000 x 12 / 31 = $1,161.29, credited to the buyers for August 20 to 31. The full $3,000 security deposit is also credited to them, because they now hold the obligation to return it. $1,838.71 is the trap: it is Sal's share of the month (19 days). Keeping the deposit with Sal leaves the new owners liable for money they never received.

blocks.html: The lender also collects prepaid interest from the closing date to the end of the month, because the first regular payment (October 1) pays interest in arrears for September. Daily interest: $920,000 x 6.5% / 365 = $163.84; for August 20 to 31, 12 days = $1,966.03. Title insurance is about $6,500, Priya's fee $3,000, and lender fees about $2,500.

head: Whitfields: debits
Amount
Whitfields: credits
Amount
blocks.caption: Buyers' side of the closing statement

blocks.q: How much must the Whitfields bring to the closing table, on top of the $115,000 already in escrow?
blocks.x: Debits minus credits: $1,203,197.77 minus $1,039,161.29 = $164,036.48. $279,036.48 is the trap: it adds back the $115,000 down payment that is already a credit, which is their total cash in the deal, not what is due at closing. Every item is either a debit or a credit to each party, and the escrowed deposit is a buyer credit.

blocks.html: Now Sal's side. He has no mortgage on the house. His debits are the commission ($57,500), the transfer taxes ($20,987.50), the rent proration ($1,161.29), the security deposit ($3,000), and his attorney ($2,500). His only credit besides the price is the $821.74 tax proration.

blocks.q: What are Sal's net proceeds from the sale?
blocks.x: $1,150,000 + $821.74 minus $57,500 minus $4,600 minus $16,387.50 minus $1,161.29 minus $3,000 minus $2,500 = $1,065,672.95. $1,071,512.50 is the trap: it deducts only commission and transfer taxes, missing the prorations and the deposit. $1,092,500 subtracts the commission alone. On a statement, the tax proration is a credit to Sal, and the rent and deposit are debits.

blocks.text: Looking back: the price Sal needed

blocks.html: Before listing, Sal told Jordan he needed $1,050,000 "in my pocket, after the broker and the taxes." Jordan knew the price could not just be $1,050,000 plus 5%. Commission, the 0.4% state tax, and the 1.425% city tax are all percentages of the price, totaling 6.825%, so Sal keeps 93.175% of any price above $500,000 before other costs.

blocks.q: What is the lowest price that nets Sal $1,050,000 after the 5% commission and both transfer taxes (ignoring prorations and attorney fees)?
blocks.x: Price = net / (1 minus the total rate) = $1,050,000 / (1 minus 0.05 minus 0.004 minus 0.01425) = $1,050,000 / 0.93175 = $1,126,911.73. $1,121,662.50 is the trap: it adds 6.825% to $1,050,000, but the percentages are taken from the price, not the net. $1,105,263.16 accounts for commission only and forgets the taxes.

blocks.html: One last number for Sal's accountant. Sal inherited the house in 2019, when it was worth $800,000. His appreciation since then is ($1,150,000 minus $800,000) / $800,000 = 43.75%. Percent change always divides by the starting value. If the market had dropped from $1,150,000 back to $800,000, the decline would be $350,000 / $1,150,000, about 30.4%: the same dollars, a different base.

blocks.title: The deal in one line each
blocks.html: Commission: price x rate x each split. Area: length x width; fence is perimeter. Loan: price or appraisal, whichever is lower, x LTV; a point is 1% of the loan. Qualifying: lower of 28% of income or 36% minus other debts, with 75% of the rent added on a two-family. Taxes: seller pays 0.4% and 1.425% in NYC above $500,000; buyer pays 1% mansion tax at $1M and 1.925% recording tax on a $500,000+ loan. Prorations: who paid, for which days, and the buyer owns closing day.

items: Commissions travel down splits: total, then each brokerage's share, then each salesperson's split. Two salespeople on the same deal can earn different amounts.
Price per square foot compares buildings of different sizes. Fences and borders are perimeter; yards, floors, and lots are area; acres are square feet divided by 43,560.

The loan is based on the lower of price or appraisal; a point is 1% of the loan. On an owner-occupied two-family, lenders typically add about 75% of the other unit's rent to qualifying income, and 28/36 takes the lower result.

In NYC the seller pays NYS transfer tax (0.4%) and RPTT (1.425% on the whole price above $500,000); the buyer pays the mansion tax (1% from $1M) and the mortgage recording tax (1.925% on a $500,000+ loan).
Prorations: the party who prepaid gets a credit for the other party's days; collected rent is credited to the buyer; security deposits transfer in full. Total debits minus credits gives the cash due.
To find the price that nets a target, divide the net by one minus every percentage taken from the price.

roleplays.title: The Live Net Sheet
roleplays.setting: The Okafors' kitchen in Bed-Stuy. They have an accepted offer at $2,400,000 and want to know what they walk away with. No laptop, just Jordan and a pad.
roleplays.goal: Run an accurate estimated net sheet out loud, apply the right taxes to the right base, and be clear about what is an estimate and what needs the attorney or accountant.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Grace and Emmanuel Okafor, sellers with an accepted $2.4M offer on their Bed-Stuy brownstone and a $300,000 mortgage. Ask the agent to compute, live: commission (5%), NYS transfer tax ($2 per $500), NYC RPTT (1.425% of the whole price above $500,000), whether you pay the mansion tax (no, buyer pays) or the mortgage recording tax (no, the borrower pays), and your estimated net. Then ask how much capital gains tax you will owe. Push back once with a wrong idea (tiered RPTT) and once with the 0.65% state rate. Grade the learner on arithmetic accuracy, applying each tax to the right base and payer, labeling the net as an estimate, and referring tax questions to an accountant.

a co-op in Prospect Lefferts Gardens

opening: {day} at the Okafors' kitchen table, {snack} between you. They're buying {next} and want to know exactly what $2,400,000 turns into.
Grace slides {pad} across the table. "No computers. Just tell us what we walk away with." Accepted offer: $2,400,000. Mortgage: about $300,000.
The contract is out for signature at $2,400,000. Emmanuel has a pencil behind his ear and {next} on his mind.

say: Emmanuel: "Start with your commission. 5%, right? Of what's left after taxes?"
Grace: "The 5% fee. Is that on the price, or on what we clear?"

moves.text: 5% of the sale price, per our listing agreement: $2,400,000 x 0.05 = $120,000.
moves.fb: Commission is calculated on the sale price unless the listing agreement says otherwise. Part = total x rate.

moves.text: It's based on the price, not on your net. $2.4 million times 5% comes to $120,000 even.
moves.fb: Correct base and correct arithmetic: the listing agreement sets the commission as a percentage of the sale price.

moves.text: About $120,000, give or take a bit. We can figure out the exact number at closing.
moves.fb: The number is right, but 5% of a known price is exact. Sellers deserve the precise figure.

moves.text: 5% of your profit over what you paid, so about 5% of $2.21 million, around $110,500.
moves.fb: Wrong base. Your listing agreement sets commission as a percentage of the sale price, not the gain.
moves.react: Grace: "Oh, that's less than I feared."

moves.text: 5% of what's left after the taxes and mortgage come out. So it's figured last, on the net.
moves.fb: The commission is not computed on the net. It's on the sale price under the listing agreement.

moves.text: 5% is 0.005 as a decimal, so $2,400,000 x 0.005 = $12,000 for the whole commission.

say: Grace: "Now the transfer taxes. The city one is 1% on the first $500,000 and more on the rest, isn't it?"
Emmanuel: "City transfer tax works like income tax brackets, right? 1% and then 1.425% on the part above?"

moves.text: No tiers here. Above $500,000, 1.425% hits the whole price: $34,200. State is $2 per $500: $9,600.
moves.fb: Right. NYC residential RPTT is 1.425% of the entire price once it exceeds $500,000, and the NYS tax is 0.4% below $3M.
moves.react: Grace: "The whole price. That's a nasty surprise."

moves.text: No brackets. City: 1.425% x $2.4M = $34,200. State: 0.4% x $2.4M = $9,600. Both paid by you.
moves.fb: Correct. The RPTT rate applies to the whole consideration, and the seller (grantor) pays both transfer taxes.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "$43,800 for the two. Got it."

moves.text: Let's call it about 2% total for both and move on. Close enough for planning, I think.
moves.fb: Close (about 1.8%), but sellers are deciding on real numbers. Do the actual math.
The RPTT is not tiered like income tax. The 1.425% rate applies to the whole consideration once it's over $500,000.

moves.text: City is 1.425% and state is 0.65% here, so $34,200 plus $15,600. Almost $50,000 total in taxes.
moves.fb: The 0.65% state rate is for NYC residential sales of $3M or more. At $2.4M the state rate is 0.4%: $9,600.

moves.text: The buyer splits the city transfer tax with you, so you'll each owe half of it: $17,100 apiece.
moves.fb: On a resale the seller pays the NYC RPTT and NYS transfer tax. There's no automatic split.

say: Emmanuel: "And the mansion tax. That's on a house over a million. We pay that too?"
Grace: "Our friend said sellers pay the mansion tax on anything over a million. True?"

moves.text: No, the mansion tax is the buyer's. Here it's 1.25% in the city, and it's not on your sheet.
moves.fb: Correct. Seller pays transfer taxes; buyer pays the mansion tax on residential purchases of $1M or more, graduated in NYC.

moves.text: That's on the buyer, not on you, so it stays off your net sheet entirely, all of it.
moves.fb: Right. The mansion tax is a buyer's cost.
moves.react: Grace: "Our friend was wrong. Not the first time."

moves.text: I think the buyer pays it, but let me double-check with Priya before we count it out.
moves.fb: Checking is fine, but this is a basic rule you should know: the buyer pays the mansion tax.

moves.text: Yes, add 1% of $2.4 million, $24,000. Sellers pay it on any sale over the million mark.
moves.fb: That shifts a buyer's tax onto your sellers and understates their net. The buyer pays the mansion tax.

moves.text: You split it: half from you, half from the buyer, $12,000 each at 1%. That's typical here.
moves.fb: No split. The mansion tax is the buyer's obligation.

moves.text: Only if the house sells over $3 million. Below that, nobody pays a mansion tax in New York City.
moves.fb: Wrong threshold. The mansion tax starts at $1 million, and the buyer pays it.

say: Grace: "Our mortgage balance is about $300,000. So what's the bottom line?"
Emmanuel: "Take off the $300,000 mortgage. What do we walk away with?"

moves.text: $2.4M minus $120,000, $9,600, $34,200 and $300,000 is about $1,936,200 before legal fees.
moves.fb: Accurate arithmetic, clearly labeled as an estimate. Priya's closing statement will have the final figure.
moves.react: Grace: "Just under two million. I can breathe."

moves.text: Roughly $1,936,200 before attorney fees and payoff interest. Priya will confirm the final figure.
moves.fb: Right math, labeled as an estimate, and the final number sent to the attorney.

moves.text: You'll net exactly $1,936,200. Guaranteed down to the dollar, when we reach the closing table.
moves.fb: The math is right, but a net sheet is an estimate. Prorations, payoff interest, and legal fees will move it.
moves.react: Grace: "Guaranteed? I'll hold you to that."

moves.text: $2.4M minus $120,000 and $300,000 is $1,980,000. The taxes come out of the buyer's side here.
moves.fb: You dropped the seller's transfer taxes. On a resale the seller pays the NYS tax and the NYC RPTT.

moves.text: About $1,946,200. I took off the commission, both transfer taxes, and your $300,000 mortgage balance.
moves.fb: Arithmetic error: $2,400,000 minus $463,800 is $1,936,200, not $1,946,200. Check the subtraction.

moves.text: Around $1,912,200 after the mansion tax too. Better to be safe and assume that one's on you.
moves.fb: Padding with a buyer's tax isn't 'safe'; it's wrong. Sellers plan purchases off this number.

say: Emmanuel: "And capital gains tax? We bought for $190,000 in 1997. How much do we owe?"
Grace: "We paid $190,000 in 1997. What's the tax bill on all this?"

moves.text: You may qualify for the $500,000 married exclusion, but the tax figure is your accountant's call.
moves.fb: You flagged the key rule (IRC 121) without giving tax advice. Refer tax liability questions to a CPA or tax attorney.

moves.text: I can't calculate your tax. Bring your accountant the price, selling costs and improvement receipts.
moves.fb: Correct. Give the CPA what they need: amount realized, basis and improvements.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "The receipts are in a shoebox upstairs."

moves.text: That's a tax question, so I can't say anything at all about it. Please ask your accountant.
moves.fb: Referral is right, but you could mention the exclusion exists and what records to bring.

moves.text: Gain is about $2.2 million, and you'll owe 20% of it, about $440,000. Better set that aside.
moves.fb: Wrong math (it ignores the exclusion, basis adjustments, and selling costs) and it is tax advice outside your competence.
moves.react: Emmanuel goes pale. "Four hundred forty thousand?"

moves.text: Nothing. Since 1997 there's no tax on any home sale if you've lived there more than ten years.
moves.fb: False. The exclusion is capped at $250,000 single and $500,000 married; gain above that can be taxed.

moves.text: Short-term rates apply since you're selling in the first year of the new tax law. Ordinary income, sadly.
moves.fb: Short-term means held one year or less. They've owned since 1997. And the tax number belongs to a CPA.

say: Grace: "Do we pay the mortgage recording tax too? Priya mentioned it on the phone."
Emmanuel: "What about that recording tax on mortgages? Is that ours?"

moves.text: No. The buyer pays it on their new loan. Paying off your mortgage doesn't trigger it for you.
moves.fb: Mortgage recording tax is paid by the borrower when a mortgage is recorded. The sellers aren't borrowing.

moves.text: That's the borrower's tax, so it sits on the buyer's side. Your net sheet doesn't change at all.
moves.fb: Correct. It applies to the buyer's mortgage, not the seller's payoff.

moves.text: I believe it's the buyer's, but let's leave a blank line for it just in case it comes up.
moves.fb: Hedging on a basic rule. The borrower pays the mortgage recording tax.
moves.react: Grace: "A blank line makes me nervous."

moves.text: Yes, 1.925% of your $300,000 payoff, so about $5,775. Add it to your costs at the closing.
moves.fb: The recording tax is paid on a new mortgage by the borrower, not on a payoff.

moves.text: Yes, 1.925% of the sale price, about $46,200, since the house sold for well above $500,000.
moves.fb: Wrong payer and wrong base. It's the buyer's tax on the buyer's loan amount.

moves.text: Only if the buyer is paying cash. Then the seller covers it instead, since there's no lender involved.
moves.fb: No loan, no mortgage recording tax. A cash buyer records no mortgage at all.
