say: Priya, on speaker: "There will be a real estate tax adjustment at closing. Grace, you prepaid the July bill."
Priya calls in: "Heads up, the tax apportionment will move their net a little. They paid ahead."

moves.text: You prepaid, so the buyer credits you for the days after closing. That proration adds to your net.
moves.fb: Correct. Prepaid expenses are apportioned at closing: the buyer reimburses the seller for the buyer's share.
moves.react: Grace: "So we get some back. Lovely."

moves.text: Prepaid taxes are split by date. You're credited for the days you paid but won't own. Priya computes it.
moves.fb: Right concept, and the exact figure goes to the attorney.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "Priya, you'll send the number?" Priya: "Tonight."

moves.text: That's a small detail at closing. I wouldn't worry about it for tonight's rough estimate at all.
moves.fb: It's small but real, and it moves the net. Explain it and note it on the sheet.
moves.react: Grace: "You keep saying small things don't matter."

moves.text: Prorations always cost the seller money, so knock another few thousand off your net to be safe.
moves.fb: Backwards here: they prepaid, so the buyer credits them. Prorations can go either way.

moves.text: Tax adjustments only happen in co-ops through maintenance, so it doesn't apply to a house like yours.
moves.fb: Wrong. Real estate taxes are apportioned between buyer and seller on house sales too.

moves.text: The city refunds your prepaid taxes directly after closing. The buyer doesn't get involved in that part.
moves.fb: No. The adjustment happens between buyer and seller at closing.
moves.react: Grace: "So we wait for the city?"

say: Emmanuel, curious: "So how much of the $120,000 do YOU actually get?"
Grace: "Be honest. Do you pocket all $120,000?"

moves.text: No. The buyer's broker gets 2%, my firm keeps 3%, $72,000. My share is paid by my broker.
moves.fb: Commission splits run one step at a time, and a salesperson is paid only by the sponsoring broker.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "So it passes through a few hands."

moves.text: The buyer's agent gets 2%, $48,000. Hudson & Hart keeps $72,000 and then pays my split from that.
moves.fb: Correct sequence: total commission, then co-broke, then the broker-salesperson split.
moves.react: Grace: "Less than I thought you got."

moves.text: It goes to the brokerage and gets split a few ways. I'd rather not get into my own pay tonight.
moves.fb: Fine to keep your pay private, but you could explain how the split works.

moves.text: I get the full $120,000 and then pay my broker and the buyer's agent out of my own account.
moves.fb: A salesperson can be paid only by the sponsoring broker. Commission goes to the broker first.

moves.text: We split 50/50 with the buyer's side, $60,000 each, because that's what the MLS listing sets.
moves.fb: Since the 2024 NAR settlement, buyer-broker compensation isn't offered on the MLS. It's whatever the agreements say.
moves.react: Emmanuel: "I thought we agreed on 2% for them."

moves.text: Out of $120,000 I keep 60% first, $72,000, then the firm and the buyer's agent split the rest.
moves.fb: Wrong order. Splits run from the top: co-broke first, then the firm's share, then the salesperson's split.

say: Grace: "Honestly, can you just round everything and give us a ballpark?"
Emmanuel: "Skip the decimals. Ballpark it."

moves.text: I'll round the total, but I do each line exactly first. Errors add up on $2.4 million.
moves.fb: Right. Compute each line accurately, then present a rounded, clearly labeled estimate.

moves.text: Ballpark, about $1.94 million. Here's every line on the pad, so you can check my work yourself.
moves.fb: Correct: a rounded estimate backed by the line items, clearly an estimate.

moves.text: Sure, about $2 million. Close enough for tonight. We'll tighten it up next week with Priya.
moves.fb: Over-rounding by $64,000 misleads sellers planning their next purchase. Do the math.
moves.react: Grace: "Two million. We'll plan on that."

moves.text: Rule of thumb: sellers net about 90% of the price after everything. So about $2.16 million.
moves.fb: Rules of thumb ignore the mortgage payoff and actual taxes. Compute the real lines.

moves.text: Take 10% off for all costs and then the mortgage: $1.86 million, plus or minus a little bit.
moves.fb: Guessing a percentage instead of computing actual costs gives a figure $76,000 off.

moves.text: I'll say $2.1 million to be conservative. Better you're pleasantly surprised at the closing, right?
moves.fb: That's not conservative, it's $164,000 too high. A net sheet should be accurate.

roleplays.debrief: You practised the core closing math: commission is a percentage of the sale price, the NYC RPTT is 1.425% of the whole price above $500,000 (no tiers), and the NYS transfer tax is $2 per $500, both paid by the seller. The mansion tax and mortgage recording tax are the buyer's. A net sheet is an estimate, prorations can move it, and capital gains questions go to a CPA, with the $250,000/$500,000 exclusion as the rule to flag.

questions.q: A borrower takes a $250,000 loan and has repaid $40,000 of it. The remaining principal is:
questions.x: Principal is the unpaid balance: $250,000 minus $40,000 = $210,000. $290,000 is the trap: adding instead of subtracting.

questions.q: Interest on a mortgage is charged on the:
c: Original purchase price
Appraised value
Unpaid principal balance
Down payment
questions.x: Interest accrues on the outstanding principal. Purchase price is the trap: the loan is usually less than the price.

questions.q: A building has 10 units renting for $2,000 a month. Its potential gross annual income is:
questions.x: 10 x $2,000 x 12 = $240,000. $20,000 is the trap: that is only one month.

questions.q: For a lender, a borrower's gross income is income:
c: After taxes
After all debts
From rentals only
Before taxes and deductions
questions.x: Gross means before deductions. 'After taxes' is the trap: that is net, or take-home.

questions.q: Effective gross income is $180,000 and operating expenses are $72,000. NOI is:
questions.x: NOI = EGI minus operating expenses = $108,000. $252,000 is the trap: adding.

questions.q: Which is NOT subtracted to reach net operating income?
c: Mortgage payments
Property taxes
Insurance
Repairs
questions.x: Debt service is not an operating expense, so it stays out of NOI. Property taxes are the trap: they are an operating expense.

questions.q: A borrower earns $7,500 a month. Under a 36% total-debt ratio, total monthly debt payments may not exceed:
questions.x: 36% x $7,500 = $2,700. $2,100 is the trap: that is the 28% housing figure.

questions.q: A borrower earns $6,000 monthly and has $500 in car and card payments. Under 28/36, the maximum housing payment is:
questions.x: 28% allows $1,680 for housing; 36% allows $2,160 total, minus $500 = $1,660. The lower figure controls, so $1,660. $1,680 is the trap: it ignores the other debts.

questions.q: A property is assessed at $200,000 and the tax rate is 25 mills. The annual tax is:
questions.x: A mill is $1 per $1,000: 25 x 200 = $5,000. $500 is the trap: treating mills as dollars per $10,000.

questions.q: A tax rate of $3.10 per $100 of assessed value equals how many mills?
c: 3.1 mills
310 mills
31 mills
0.31 mills
questions.x: Mills are per $1,000, so $3.10 per $100 is $31 per $1,000, or 31 mills. 3.1 is the trap: forgetting to scale from $100 to $1,000.

questions.q: A Yonkers home sells for $650,000 with a 5.5% commission. The total commission is:
A $900,000 sale carries a 6% commission, split equally between the listing and selling brokers. The listing salesperson receives 60% of the listing broker's share. The listing salesperson earns:
questions.x: $900,000 x 0.06 = $54,000. Half is $27,000. 60% of $27,000 = $16,200. $27,000 is the listing broker's side before the salesperson's split, and $32,400 takes 60% of the whole commission.

questions.q: A seller wants to net $380,000 after paying a 5% commission (ignore other costs). The property must sell for:
questions.x: The seller keeps 95% of the price: $380,000 / 0.95 = $400,000. Adding 5% to $380,000 ($399,000) leaves the seller $1,000 short, and dividing by 0.05 instead of 0.95 gives the absurd $7,600,000.

questions.q: A broker earned a $24,000 commission at a 6% rate. The sale price was:
questions.x: Total = Part / Rate = $24,000 / 0.06 = $400,000. $4,000,000 divides by 0.006, a decimal slip, and $144,000 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: A broker received $31,500 on a $450,000 sale. The commission rate was:
questions.x: Rate = Part / Total = $31,500 / $450,000 = 0.07 = 7%. Checking the traps: 6% would pay $27,000 and 7.5% would pay $33,750.

questions.q: What is the simple interest on a $250,000 loan at 5% for 6 months?
questions.x: $250,000 x 0.05 = $12,500 a year. Six months is half a year: $6,250. $12,500 forgets the time factor, and $1,042 is one month.

questions.q: A borrower takes a $360,000 mortgage at 7% interest. The interest portion of the first monthly payment is:
questions.x: $360,000 x 0.07 = $25,200 a year / 12 = $2,100 for the first month. $25,200 is the annual figure; $2,520 misplaces the decimal.

questions.q: A borrower paid $13,500 in interest in one year on a $300,000 interest-only loan. The interest rate is:
questions.x: Rate = $13,500 / $300,000 = 0.045 = 4.5%. 2.25% halves the rate as if the interest were for two years.

questions.q: An owner bought a house for $250,000 and sold it for $300,000. The percentage of appreciation is:
questions.x: ($300,000 - $250,000) / $250,000 = 0.20 = 20%. Dividing by the sale price gives 16.7%, the wrong base.

questions.q: A property's value fell from $500,000 to $425,000. The percentage decline is:
questions.x: $75,000 / $500,000 = 15%. Dividing by the new value ($425,000) gives 17.6%, which uses the wrong base; 85% is the remaining value, not the decline.

questions.q: A Saratoga County home worth $400,000 appreciates 3% a year, simple (not compounded), for 5 years. Its value at the end is:
An investor buys a rental for $430,000, of which $100,000 is land. Using straight-line depreciation over 27.5 years, the annual depreciation is:
questions.x: Land is not depreciated: $430,000 - $100,000 = $330,000 / 27.5 = $12,000. $15,636 wrongly includes the land, and $120,000 slips the decimal.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a $500,000 home with 10% down and pays 2 points. The points cost:
questions.x: Loan = $500,000 - $50,000 = $450,000. 2 points = 2% x $450,000 = $9,000. $10,000 wrongly figures points on the price.

questions.q: All of the following statements about points are true EXCEPT:
c: Discount points can lower the interest rate
Points are paid at closing
Either party may pay points if they agree
One point equals 1% of the sale price
questions.x: A point is 1% of the loan amount, not the sale price. The other statements are accurate, including that a seller may agree to pay the buyer's points.

questions.q: A borrower earns $96,000 a year and pays $1,000 a month on a car and credit cards. Using 28/36 ratios, the maximum monthly PITI is:
questions.x: Monthly income $8,000. Front: 28% = $2,240. Back: 36% = $2,880 - $1,000 = $1,880. The lower, $1,880, controls; $2,240 ignores the debts.

questions.q: A buyer contracts to pay $400,000 and the home appraises at $380,000. The lender allows 90% LTV. The maximum loan is:
questions.x: LTV uses the lower of price or appraisal: $380,000 x 0.90 = $342,000. $360,000 applies 90% to the price.

questions.q: A rectangular lot measures 200 feet by 435.6 feet. How many acres is it?
questions.x: 200 x 435.6 = 87,120 sq ft / 43,560 = 2 acres. 4 doubles the answer by mistake.

questions.q: A 50 x 150 foot lot sells for $4,000 per front foot. The price is:
questions.x: Frontage is the first dimension: 50 x $4,000 = $200,000. Using depth (150) gives $600,000, and multiplying the whole area by $4,000 gives $30,000,000.

questions.q: A triangular parcel has a base of 200 feet and a height of 150 feet. Its area is:
c: 30,000 sq ft
350 sq ft
15,000 sq ft
7,500 sq ft
questions.x: 1/2 x 200 x 150 = 15,000 sq ft. Forgetting the 1/2 gives 30,000.

questions.q: A lot has two parallel sides of 80 feet and 120 feet, which are 150 feet apart. Its area is:
c: 18,000 sq ft
15,000 sq ft
12,000 sq ft
questions.x: Trapezoid: ((80 + 120) / 2) x 150 = 100 x 150 = 15,000 sq ft. 18,000 uses the longer side only.

questions.q: An owner fences a 60 x 110 foot lot on all sides at $25 per linear foot. The cost is:
questions.x: Perimeter = 60 + 110 + 60 + 110 = 340 ft x $25 = $8,500. $165,000 multiplies area by the price, but fence is priced by length; $4,250 fences two sides.

questions.q: One hectare is approximately equal to:
c: 1 acre
2.47 acres
43,560 square feet
640 acres
questions.x: A hectare is 10,000 square meters, about 2.47 acres. 43,560 sq ft is one acre, and 640 acres is a square mile.

questions.q: A Williamsburg condo of 1,800 square feet sells for $1,350,000. The price per square foot is:
questions.x: $1,350,000 / 1,800 = $750 per square foot. $1,333 divides square feet by price in thousands, inverting the fraction.

questions.q: A 653,400 square foot parcel in Dutchess County is priced at $10,000 per acre. The price is:
questions.x: 653,400 / 43,560 = 15 acres x $10,000 = $150,000. $1,500,000 slips a zero, and $65,340 is a decimal shift of the square footage, not a conversion to acres.

questions.q: A Rochester house sells for $725,000. The NYS real estate transfer tax is:
A Brooklyn condo sells for $600,000. The seller's NYC Real Property Transfer Tax is:
questions.x: Above $500,000, the 1.425% residential rate applies to the whole price: $600,000 x 0.01425 = $8,550. $6,425 wrongly tiers it (1% on the first $500,000 plus 1.425% on the rest), and $10,950 adds the NYS tax to the NYC tax.

questions.q: A buyer of a Queens one-family takes a $320,000 mortgage. The borrower's NYC mortgage recording tax is:
questions.x: Under $500,000 the NYC borrower rate is 1.8%: $320,000 x 0.018 = $5,760. $6,160 uses the 1.925% rate for loans of $500,000 or more, and $3,360 uses the suburban 1.05% rate.

questions.q: A home is assessed at $180,000 and the tax rate is $4.20 per $100. The annual tax is:
A house is assessed at $240,000 and the tax rate is 45 mills. The lender escrows taxes monthly. The monthly escrow for taxes is:
questions.x: 45 mills = 0.045. $240,000 x 0.045 = $10,800 a year / 12 = $900 a month. $10,800 is the annual tax, not the monthly escrow.

questions.q: In a $1,500,000 sale of a Manhattan co-op, all of the following are normally paid by the seller EXCEPT:
c: NYS real estate transfer tax
NYC Real Property Transfer Tax
The listing broker's commission
The mansion tax at closing
questions.x: The mansion tax is a buyer's tax on residential purchases of $1M or more. The seller pays both transfer taxes and, under the listing agreement, the commission.

questions.q: Who sets the commission rate on a New York home sale?
c: The client and broker, by negotiation
The Department of State, by regulation
The local Realtor board, by a vote
The MLS, through its listing rules
questions.x: Commissions are negotiated between the client and the broker; no law or board sets them. The DOS choice is tempting because DOS licenses brokers, but it does not set fees.

questions.q: Two competing brokers agree that neither will list homes for less than 5%. This is:
c: A lawful practice
Illegal price fixing
Allowed if DOS is told
Allowed if sellers sign
questions.x: Competing brokers agreeing on rates is price fixing, an antitrust violation. Seller signatures do not cure an agreement between competitors.

questions.q: A grateful buyer wants to hand the cooperating salesperson a $1,000 bonus at closing. The salesperson may receive it:
c: Directly, if the seller agrees to it
Directly, if it is under $1,500
Only through her sponsoring broker
Only from the listing broker
questions.x: A salesperson is paid only by the sponsoring broker, never directly by the client or the other broker. Seller consent does not change who may pay her.

questions.q: A listing broker owes a cooperating firm's salesperson her share of a commission. The listing broker should pay:
c: The salesperson, directly by personal check
The closing attorney's escrow
The buyer, who passes it along
The salesperson's sponsoring broker
questions.x: Money flows broker to broker; the split with the salesperson happens inside her own firm. Paying her directly is the trap.

questions.q: A salesperson earned $10,800, which was 60% of her firm's side. The firm's side was half of a 6% commission. The sale price was:
questions.x: Divide by each rate in turn: $10,800 / 0.60 = $18,000 firm side; / 0.50 = $36,000 total; / 0.06 = $600,000. $300,000 skips the 50% co-op split, and $36,000 stops at the total commission.

questions.q: A salesperson on a 50/50 split received $6,000. Her firm received half of a 5% commission. The sale price was:
questions.x: $6,000 / 0.50 = $12,000 firm side; / 0.50 = $24,000 total; / 0.05 = $480,000. $240,000 forgets one of the two halves, and $24,000 is only the total commission.

questions.q: As a fixed-rate amortizing mortgage is paid down, each monthly payment contains:
c: Less interest and more principal
More interest, less principal
The same split as the first payment
Only principal after the first year
questions.x: Interest is charged on the balance still owed, so as the balance falls, more of each payment goes to principal. The reverse is the trap.

questions.q: A $300,000 loan at 6% has a monthly principal and interest payment of $1,799. How much of the first payment goes to principal?
questions.x: First month's interest: $300,000 x 0.06 / 12 = $1,500. Principal: $1,799 - $1,500 = $299. $1,500 is the interest portion, not the principal.

questions.q: Discount points paid at closing are used to:
c: Pay the appraiser and title insurer
Reduce the required down payment
Cover the broker's commission
Buy down the loan's interest rate
questions.x: Discount points buy down the rate; origination points pay the lender's fee. Neither reduces the down payment.

questions.q: Under the older exam rule of thumb, one discount point raises the lender's yield by about:
c: 1% of the loan
questions.x: One point is 1% of the loan, but it raises the lender's yield only about 1/8 of 1%. Picking 1% confuses the cost of a point with its effect on yield.

questions.q: The textbook FHA qualifying ratios are:
questions.x: FHA uses higher ratios than conventional loans: 31/43 in the textbook. 28/36 is the conventional guideline.

questions.q: A borrower earns $6,000 a month and has no other debts. Under FHA's textbook 31% housing ratio, the maximum PITI is:
questions.x: $6,000 x 0.31 = $1,860. $1,680 uses the conventional 28%; $2,580 uses the 43% total-debt ratio.

questions.q: A conventional borrower puts 10% down. The lender will most likely require:
c: Private mortgage insurance
An FHA appraisal review of the home
Two discount points
A second qualifying ratio
questions.x: Above 80% LTV on a conventional loan, expect PMI. Ten percent down means 90% LTV. Discount points are optional rate buydowns, not a requirement.

questions.q: A house is priced and appraised at $400,000. Which conventional loan amount would usually trigger PMI?
questions.x: 80% of $400,000 is $320,000; a loan above that exceeds 80% LTV. $320,000 is exactly 80%, the trap, and does not trigger PMI.

questions.concept: Area of rectangles and irregular lots
questions.q: An L-shaped lot is a 120 x 80 ft rectangle with a 40 x 30 ft notch missing from one corner. Its area is:
c: 7,200 sq ft
8,400 sq ft
9,600 sq ft
10,800 sq ft
questions.x: Full rectangle minus the notch: 120 x 80 = 9,600; 40 x 30 = 1,200; 9,600 - 1,200 = 8,400. 9,600 forgets to subtract the notch.

questions.concept: Area of rectangles and irregular lots
questions.q: A rectangular lot is 50 feet wide and 120 feet deep. Its area is:
c: 340 sq ft
3,000 sq ft
6,000 sq ft
60,000 sq ft
questions.x: Length x width: 50 x 120 = 6,000 square feet. 340 is the perimeter in feet, and 3,000 uses the triangle formula.

questions.q: A circular pond has a radius of 20 feet. Its surface area is about:
c: 62.8 sq ft
125.6 sq ft
400 sq ft
1,256 sq ft
questions.x: 3.14 x 20 x 20 = 1,256 square feet. 400 forgets to multiply by 3.14, and 125.6 is the circumference in feet, not an area.

questions.q: A round patio is 30 feet across. Its area is about:
c: 94 sq ft
450 sq ft
707 sq ft
2,826 sq ft
questions.x: 30 feet across is the diameter, so the radius is 15: 3.14 x 15 x 15 = 706.5. 2,826 uses 30 as the radius.

questions.q: A room is 18 ft by 15 ft. How many square yards of carpet does it need?
questions.x: 18 x 15 = 270 square feet; 270 / 9 = 30 square yards. 90 divides by 3, the linear yard factor, instead of 9.

questions.q: A slab is 30 ft long, 12 ft wide and 6 inches thick. About how many cubic yards of concrete does it need?
questions.x: 30 x 12 x 0.5 = 180 cubic feet; 180 / 27 = about 6.7 cubic yards. 20 divides by 9, the square-yard factor.

questions.q: A section of land (one square mile) contains:
c: 160 acres
640 acres
360 acres
43,560 acres
questions.x: A section is a square mile of 640 acres. 43,560 is the number of square feet in one acre.

questions.q: How many square feet are in a half section of land?
questions.x: A half section is 320 acres: 320 x 43,560 = 13,939,200 square feet. 27,878,400 is a full section.

questions.concept: NYS transfer tax high-value NYC rate
questions.q: A Manhattan condo sells for $4,000,000. The NYS real estate transfer tax is:
questions.x: In NYC the state rate rises to 0.65% on residential sales of $3M or more: $4,000,000 x 0.0065 = $26,000. $16,000 applies the ordinary 0.4%, and $2,600 slips a decimal.

questions.concept: NYS transfer tax high-value NYC rate
questions.q: A Westchester house sells for $4,000,000. The NYS real estate transfer tax is:
questions.x: The 0.65% rate applies only in NYC, so Westchester pays $2 per $500: $4,000,000 / 500 x $2 = $16,000. $26,000 wrongly uses the NYC rate.

questions.q: A Bronx commercial building sells for $2,000,000. The seller's NYC Real Property Transfer Tax is:
questions.x: Commercial RPTT is 2.625% above $500,000: $2,000,000 x 0.02625 = $52,500. $28,500 uses the 1.425% residential rate.

questions.q: A Queens store sells for $400,000. The seller's NYC Real Property Transfer Tax is:
questions.x: Commercial RPTT is 1.425% up to $500,000: $400,000 x 0.01425 = $5,700. $4,000 uses the 1% residential rate.

questions.q: A buyer finances a $700,000 Brooklyn co-op with a $560,000 share loan. The mortgage recording tax is:
questions.x: A share loan is secured by stock and a proprietary lease, not a mortgage on real property, so there is no mortgage recording tax. $10,780 applies the 1.925% rate as if it were a condo.

questions.q: NYC co-op buyers pay no mortgage recording tax because:
c: The co-op board pays the tax for them
Co-ops are exempt from every closing tax in the city
The lender pays the full tax instead
A share loan is not a real property mortgage
questions.x: Co-op financing is a share loan secured by stock and a lease, so nothing is recorded as a mortgage. Co-ops are not exempt from every tax: the seller still pays transfer taxes.

questions.concept: Value from NOI and cap rate
questions.q: A building's NOI is $90,000 and the market cap rate is 6%. Its value is:
questions.x: Value = NOI / cap rate: $90,000 / 0.06 = $1,500,000. $5,400 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.concept: Value from NOI and cap rate
questions.q: A property worth $2,000,000 earns NOI of $150,000. Its cap rate is:
questions.x: Cap rate = NOI / value: $150,000 / $2,000,000 = 7.5%. 13.3% divides value by NOI, flipping the formula.

questions.q: A Staten Island colonial sells for $820,000 with a 4.5% commission. The total commission is:
A $480,000 sale pays a 5% commission, split 50/50 between the listing and buyer's brokers. The buyer's agent receives 65% of the buyer's broker's share. The buyer's agent earns:
questions.x: $480,000 x 0.05 = $24,000. Half is $12,000, and 65% of that is $7,800. $15,600 applies 65% to the whole commission, and $4,200 is the broker's 35%.

questions.q: A seller needs to net $470,000 after a 6% commission (ignore other costs). The minimum sale price is:
questions.x: The seller keeps 94% of the price: $470,000 / 0.94 = $500,000. Adding 6% to $470,000 gives $498,200, which leaves the seller short because the commission is figured on the higher price.

questions.q: A salesperson received $9,600, which was half of the broker's commission. The broker charged 6%. The sale price was:
questions.x: Broker's commission = $9,600 x 2 = $19,200. Price = $19,200 / 0.06 = $320,000. $160,000 forgets to double the salesperson's half, and $3,200,000 divides by 0.006.

questions.q: A broker earned $22,500 on the sale of a $375,000 condo. The commission rate was:
What is the simple interest on a $180,000 loan at 6% for 9 months?
questions.x: $180,000 x 0.06 = $10,800 a year x 9/12 = $8,100. $10,800 forgets the time factor, and $5,400 is six months.

questions.q: The interest portion of the first monthly payment on a 6% mortgage was $1,750. The loan amount was:
questions.x: Annual interest = $1,750 x 12 = $21,000. Loan = $21,000 / 0.06 = $350,000. $29,167 divides the monthly figure by the annual rate without annualizing it.

questions.q: An interest-only loan of $270,000 requires payments of $1,125 a month. The annual interest rate is:
questions.x: Annual interest = $1,125 x 12 = $13,500. $13,500 / $270,000 = 5%. 0.42% is the monthly rate, not the annual one.

questions.q: An investor bought a condo for $320,000 and sold it for $400,000. The percentage of profit is:
questions.x: Profit $80,000 / original $320,000 = 25%. Dividing by the sale price gives 20%, the wrong base.

questions.q: After a 12% drop in value, a home is worth $396,000. Its value before the drop was:
questions.x: $396,000 is 88% of the old value: $396,000 / 0.88 = $450,000. Adding 12% to $396,000 ($443,520) uses the new value as the base, the classic error.

questions.q: A house bought for $300,000 is worth $354,000 six years later. Assuming simple (not compounded) appreciation, the annual rate was:
questions.x: Gain $54,000 / $300,000 = 18% over 6 years, or 3% a year. 18% is the total, not the annual rate, and 2.5% divides by the new value.

questions.q: An investor buys a residential rental for $650,000, of which $100,000 is land. Straight-line annual depreciation over 27.5 years is:
questions.x: $650,000 - $100,000 = $550,000 / 27.5 = $20,000. $23,636 depreciates the land, and $14,103 uses the 39-year nonresidential schedule.

questions.q: A borrower paid $6,300 for 1.5 discount points. The loan amount was:
A buyer purchases a $500,000 house with a $400,000 loan. The lender charges 3 points. The points cost:
questions.x: Points are figured on the loan, not the price: 3% x $400,000 = $12,000. $15,000 wrongly uses the $500,000 price.

questions.q: A buyer earns $72,000 a year and has $400 in monthly debt payments. Using 28/36 ratios, the maximum monthly PITI is:
questions.x: Monthly income $6,000. Front: 28% = $1,680. Back: 36% = $2,160 - $400 = $1,760. The lower figure, $1,680, controls; this time the front-end ratio is the limit.

questions.q: A contract price is $550,000 and the appraisal comes in at $525,000. With an 80% LTV limit, the maximum loan is:
questions.x: LTV applies to the lower of price or appraisal: $525,000 x 0.80 = $420,000. $440,000 uses the contract price, and $472,500 uses 90%.

questions.q: A rectangular 3.5-acre parcel has 250 feet of road frontage. How deep is it?
c: 174.24 feet
609.84 feet
60.98 feet
questions.x: 3.5 x 43,560 = 152,460 sq ft / 250 = 609.84 feet. 174.24 divides one acre, not 3.5 acres, by the frontage.

questions.q: A lot 200 feet deep sold for $360,000 at $3,000 per front foot. Its frontage is:
c: 180 feet
60 feet
120 feet
1,200 feet
questions.x: Frontage = $360,000 / $3,000 = 120 feet. Depth does not enter the front-foot price; 180 feet wrongly divides by $2,000.

questions.q: A triangular half-acre parcel has a base of 330 feet. Its height is:
c: 66 feet
132 feet
264 feet
1,320 feet
questions.x: Half an acre = 21,780 sq ft. Height = 2 x 21,780 / 330 = 132 feet. 66 feet forgets to double for the triangle's 1/2.

questions.q: A lot's two parallel sides are 90 feet and 130 feet and are 200 feet apart. Its area is:
c: 26,000 sq ft
44,000 sq ft
22,000 sq ft
questions.x: ((90 + 130) / 2) x 200 = 110 x 200 = 22,000 sq ft. 44,000 forgets to average the parallel sides, and 26,000 uses only the longer one.

questions.q: An 80 x 125 foot lot will be fenced on the two sides and the rear, leaving the 80-foot front open. At $30 per linear foot, the cost is:
questions.x: Fence = 125 + 80 + 125 = 330 feet x $30 = $9,900. $12,300 fences all four sides, and $300,000 prices the area instead of the length.

questions.q: A 5-hectare farm parcel is about how many acres?
c: 5 acres
2.02 acres
12.35 acres
50,000 acres
questions.x: One hectare is about 2.47 acres: 5 x 2.47 = 12.35. 2.02 divides by 2.47 instead of multiplying, and 50,000 confuses square meters with acres.

questions.q: A 1,240-square-foot Long Island City condo is priced at $925 per square foot. The price is:
A 12-acre Orange County parcel is priced at $3.50 per square foot. The price is:
questions.x: 12 x 43,560 = 522,720 sq ft x $3.50 = $1,829,520. $152,460 prices a single acre, and $149,349 divides by $3.50 instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A seller in Albany paid $3,600 in NYS real estate transfer tax. The sale price was:
A Bronx two-family home sells for $480,000. The seller's NYC Real Property Transfer Tax is:
questions.x: At $500,000 or less, the residential rate is 1%: $480,000 x 0.01 = $4,800. $6,840 applies the 1.425% rate, which starts only above $500,000; $6,720 adds the NYS 0.4%.

questions.q: A Manhattan condo buyer takes a mortgage of exactly $500,000. The borrower's NYC mortgage recording tax is:
questions.x: Loans of $500,000 or more on 1 to 3 family homes and condos are taxed at 1.925% to the borrower: $9,625. $9,000 uses the 1.8% rate for loans under $500,000, and $10,875 adds the lender's 0.25%.

questions.q: A home assessed at $150,000 has an annual tax bill of $6,300. The tax rate per $100 of assessed value is:
A lender escrows $775 a month for taxes on a house assessed at $310,000. The tax rate is:
c: 3 mills
300 mills
30 mills
2.5 mills
questions.x: Annual tax = $775 x 12 = $9,300. $9,300 / $310,000 = 0.030, or 30 mills. 2.5 mills uses the monthly escrow without annualizing it.

questions.q: In a $2,000,000 sale of a Westchester house, which tax is normally paid by the buyer?
c: The NYS transfer tax
The 1% mansion tax
The seller's capital gains tax
The county transfer fee
questions.x: The mansion tax is a buyer's tax on residential purchases of $1M or more. The NYS transfer tax is the seller's (grantor's) obligation, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: A Bronx home sells for $780,000 with a 5% commission split equally between the listing and selling brokers. The selling salesperson receives 65% of her broker's share. She earns:
questions.x: Total: $780,000 x 5% = $39,000. Selling side: $19,500. Salesperson: $19,500 x 65% = $12,675. $25,350 is the trap: 65% of the whole commission, skipping the 50/50 broker split.

questions.q: A listing salesperson earned $13,500, which was 60% of her firm's share. Her firm received half of a 5% commission. What was the sale price?
questions.x: Firm's share: $13,500 / 0.60 = $22,500. Total commission: $22,500 x 2 = $45,000. Price: $45,000 / 0.05 = $900,000. $450,000 is the trap: it forgets that the firm received only half of the commission.

questions.q: A rectangular back yard is 30 feet wide and 40 feet deep. A fence will run along the back and both sides, but not along the house. How many linear feet of fence are needed?
c: 110 feet
140 feet
1,200 feet
100 feet
questions.x: Back (30) + two sides (40 + 40) = 110 linear feet. 140 is the trap: it is the full perimeter, including the side along the house. 1,200 is the area in square feet, which measures surface, not length.

questions.q: A 25 by 100 foot lot is listed at $1,000,000. What is the price per square foot of land, and how many acres is the lot?
c: $400 a sq ft; about 0.57 acre
$4,000 a sq ft; about 0.057 acre
$400 a sq ft; about 0.057 acre
$40 a sq ft; about 0.0057 acre
questions.x: Area: 25 x 100 = 2,500 sq ft. $1,000,000 / 2,500 = $400 a square foot. Acres: 2,500 / 43,560 = 0.057. 0.57 acre is the trap: a misplaced decimal that makes a Brooklyn lot ten times bigger than it is.

questions.concept: Points and LTV on lower value
questions.q: A buyer offers $600,000. The appraisal is $580,000. The lender lends 80% of value and charges 1.5 points. What do the points cost?
questions.x: Value is the lower of price or appraisal: $580,000. Loan: $580,000 x 80% = $464,000. Points: $464,000 x 1.5% = $6,960. $7,200 is the trap: it bases the loan on the $600,000 price. $9,000 takes 1.5% of the price.

questions.concept: Points and LTV on lower value
questions.q: A $500,000 purchase appraises at $520,000. The buyer borrows $400,000. The loan-to-value ratio the lender uses is:
questions.x: LTV divides the loan by the lower of price or appraisal: $400,000 / $500,000 = 80%. 76.9% is the trap: it divides by the higher appraisal. A higher appraisal does not let the buyer borrow against value she did not pay for.

questions.q: A couple buying an owner-occupied two-family earns $15,000 a month. The other unit rents for $2,400; the lender counts 75%. Other debts are $900 a month. Under 28/36, the maximum PITI is:
questions.x: Qualifying income: $15,000 + ($2,400 x 75%) = $16,800. Front end: $16,800 x 28% = $4,704. Back end: $16,800 x 36% = $6,048 minus $900 = $5,148. The lower, $4,704, controls. $5,148 is the trap: it is the back-end result, and the lower test wins. $4,872 counts the full rent.

questions.q: A borrower's gross income is $12,000 a month. Other monthly debts are $1,200. Using 28/36, the maximum housing payment is:
questions.x: Front end: $12,000 x 28% = $3,360. Back end: $12,000 x 36% = $4,320 minus $1,200 = $3,120. The lower is $3,120. $3,360 is the trap: it forgets that heavy other debts make the back-end test the binding one.

questions.q: A Staten Island one-family sells for $860,000. The seller's combined NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT is:
questions.x: NYS: $860,000 x 0.4% = $3,440. NYC RPTT: residential above $500,000, so 1.425% x $860,000 = $12,255. Total $15,695. $12,255 is the trap: the city tax alone. The 1.425% rate applies to the whole price, not just the part above $500,000.

questions.q: A Brooklyn condo sells for $1,400,000 with a $1,000,000 loan. Which pair of taxes is correct?
c: Buyer's mansion tax $14,000; borrower's recording tax $19,250
Buyer's mansion tax $4,000; borrower's recording tax $18,000
Seller's mansion tax $14,000; seller's recording tax $19,250
Buyer's mansion tax $14,000; borrower's recording tax $26,950
questions.x: Mansion tax: 1% of $1,400,000 = $14,000, paid by the buyer. Recording tax: 1.925% of the $1,000,000 loan = $19,250. The $26,950 answer is the trap: it applies the recording tax rate to the price instead of the loan. The mansion tax applies to the whole price, not the excess over $1 million.

questions.q: A seller collected June rent of $2,790 on June 1. Closing is June 21, and the buyer owns the closing day. Using actual days, the rent credit to the buyer is:
questions.x: June has 30 days. Buyer's days: June 21 to 30 = 10. $2,790 x 10 / 30 = $930. $1,860 is the trap: it is the seller's 20 days. Collected rent is credited to the buyer for the days the buyer owns the property.

questions.q: A seller prepaid a $2,190 quarterly tax bill covering July 1 to September 30 (92 days). Closing is September 1, and the buyer owns the closing day. Using actual days, the proration is:
c: $714.13 credit to the buyer
$1,475.87 credit to the seller
$730.00 credit to the seller
$714.13 credit to the seller
questions.x: Buyer's days: September 1 to 30 = 30. $2,190 x 30 / 92 = $714.13, credited to the seller, who paid for days the buyer will own. A credit to the buyer is the trap: the buyer would get a credit only if the tax were unpaid and the buyer had to pay it later.

cram.html: Part = Total x Rate. Rate = Part / Total. Total = Part / Rate.
Net-to-seller price = net / (1 - commission rate). $475,000 / 0.95 = $500,000.
Commission splits: one step at a time, each percentage on the amount handed down.
Simple interest = principal x rate x time. Monthly interest = annual / 12.
Percent change divides by the old (starting) value.
1 point = 1% of the loan, not the price.
Qualifying 28/36 on gross monthly income: take the lower result.
LTV uses the lower of price or appraised value.
Acre = 43,560 sq ft. Square mile = 640 acres. Hectare = 10,000 sq m, about 2.47 acres.
Triangle = 1/2 x base x height. Trapezoid = average of parallel sides x height.
Front feet = first lot dimension. Square yard = 9 sq ft; cubic yard = 27 cu ft.
NYS transfer tax $2 per $500 (0.4%), seller pays.
NYC RPTT residential: 1% up to $500,000; 1.425% on the whole price above.
Mansion tax: buyer pays 1% on residential $1M+ (NYC graduated to 3.9%).
NYC mortgage recording tax (borrower): 1.8% under $500,000; 1.925% at $500,000+. Co-ops: none.
Straight-line depreciation: building only (no land) / 27.5 residential or 39 commercial.

subjects.title: Municipal Agencies
subjects.blurb: Every deal touches town hall: permits, COs, taxes, septic records, landmark approvals. The exam matches each local agency to its job and asks who is elected and who is appointed.

lessons.title: Who's Who at Town Hall
lessons.tagline: Elected bodies make the rules and set the budget. Appointed boards apply them. Staff departments run the counter.
objectives: Match each local agency in the syllabus to its functions
Say which bodies are elected and which are appointed
Explain how the legislative body, planning board and ZBA divide land use power
Identify the county agencies that touch a sale, such as the health department and county planning

blocks.title: Listing day in Tarrytown
blocks.html: Jordan is helping a Hudson & Hart colleague with a listing in a Westchester village: a 1920s colonial with a newer rear deck, a shed, and a backyard that slopes down to a stream. The buyer's attorney will want the CO, proof the deck was permitted, the tax bills, and an answer about the stream. Jordan has one afternoon at village hall. Which door first?
blocks.casual: Jordan's helping a Hudson & Hart colleague with a listing in a Westchester village: a 1920s colonial with a newer back deck, a shed, and a yard that slopes down to a stream. The buyer's attorney is going to want the CO, proof the deck had a permit, the tax bills, and an answer about the stream. Jordan's got one afternoon at village hall. Which door first?

deeper.plain: Each document lives with a different office. Knowing which office holds what saves you a wasted afternoon.
deeper.picture: Village hall is like a mall with specialty stores. You don't buy shoes at the pharmacy.
deeper.street: Jordan heads to the building department first for the CO and the deck permit, then to the receiver of taxes for paid tax bills, then to the assessor for the property card. For the stream, the building department points him to the conservation advisory council and DEC, because wetland rules may apply.
deeper.stakes: Showing up to a closing without the deck permit can delay it or force a credit. Missing a wetland issue can mean a buyer can't build the pool they planned.
deeper.exam: Exam questions in this subject are mostly matching: which office issues COs, which sets the tax rate, which grants variances. Building department, legislative body, ZBA.

blocks.html: New York has 62 cities, about 930 towns, and about 530 villages. Every inch of the state outside a city is in a town; a village sits inside a town and handles some services itself. Each has an elected legislative body that adopts laws (including the zoning ordinance), the budget and the tax rate. Everything else on this list is appointed by that body or is a staff department, except some assessors and receivers of taxes, which some towns elect.
blocks.casual: New York has 62 cities, about 930 towns, and about 530 villages. Every inch of the state outside a city is in a town, and a village sits inside a town and runs some services itself. Each one has an elected legislative body that passes laws (including the zoning ordinance), the budget and the tax rate. Everything else on this list is appointed by that body or is a staff department. The exception: some towns elect their assessors and receivers of taxes.

deeper.plain: Cities, towns and villages each have elected lawmakers who appoint everyone else, with a few exceptions like elected assessors in some towns.
deeper.picture: A village inside a town is like a condo inside an HOA community. You have your own board for some things and share others with the bigger group.
deeper.street: Tarrytown is a village inside the Town of Greenburgh. A Tarrytown homeowner pays village taxes for village services like police and also town taxes. The village has its own zoning, building department and boards.
deeper.stakes: Going to the town when the property is in a village (or the reverse) wastes time and can mean you pulled the wrong zoning code.
deeper.exam: Remember: outside cities, all land is in a town. Villages are inside towns. The legislative body is elected; boards are appointed.

head: Municipality
Legislative body (elected)
Chief executive (elected)
rows: Town board (supervisor plus council members)
Village mayor (also sits on the board)

deeper.plain: Each kind of municipality has an elected lawmaking body and an elected chief executive with different names.
deeper.picture: Same three jobs, different job titles: city council and mayor, town board and supervisor, village trustees and village mayor.
deeper.street: Diane explains to Jordan that in the Town of Huntington, the supervisor chairs the town board. In the Village of Northport inside that town, the mayor sits on the board of trustees. In the City of Yonkers, there's a city council and a mayor.
deeper.stakes: Writing to "the town council" in a village or "the mayor" in a town makes you look like you haven't done your homework, and it can delay a request.
deeper.exam: Town equals town board plus supervisor. Village equals board of trustees plus mayor (who sits on it). City equals council plus mayor.

blocks.caption: Drag each agency to its job. Elected bodies are marked with a ballot icon; try to sort elected vs appointed before you check.

blocks.text: The agencies and what they do

head: Agency
Elected or appointed
Main functions
rows: City council, town board, village board of trustees
Adopt local laws and ordinances, including the zoning ordinance and cluster zoning authorization; adopt the budget and tax rate; appoint the boards below
Master plan, subdivision approval, site plan review, clustering; advises all other boards on land use
Variances, interpretations of the zoning ordinance, appeals from the building inspector, special permits (in some places another board grants these)
Approves the design of new construction and remodeling under local ordinance: facades, materials, signs
Environmental issues under local law: inventories open space and wetlands, advises boards, may issue local wetland permits
Recommends properties and districts for designation; approves construction and remodeling of designated properties
Building permits, inspections, certificates of occupancy, code enforcement: the gatekeeper for all construction
Professional planners who advise all agencies and boards and prepare studies
Elected or appointed, depending on the town
Values property for assessment; keeps property records and the assessment roll
Elected or appointed, depending on the municipality
City, town or village engineer
Roads, drainage, sewer and water connections; reviews engineering on plans
Approves septic systems and wells, certain sewer approvals; food and sanitary code
blocks.caption: The syllabus's agency list, with the elected or appointed answer the exam expects

deeper.plain: Elected lawmakers make the rules and appoint the boards. The boards and staff apply the rules: plans, variances, design, environment, landmarks, permits, assessments, taxes, engineering and health.
deeper.picture: Think of a sports league. The owners (legislative body) write the rules and hire the refs (boards). The equipment manager (building department) hands out gear only if you follow the rules.
deeper.street: A Huntington homeowner wants a two-story addition. The building department checks code and issues the permit. The addition needs a side-yard variance, so the ZBA hears it. The architectural review board approves the design. The town engineer checks drainage. The assessor updates the value afterward.
deeper.stakes: Skipping any one office can stall a project or leave an open item that surfaces at closing.
deeper.exam: The exam asks "elected or appointed?" The legislative body is elected. The planning board, ZBA, ARB, conservation council and landmarks commission are appointed. The assessor and receiver can be either.

blocks.title: Voters pick the lawmakers
blocks.html: If it makes law or sets the tax rate, voters elected it (council, town board, village trustees). If it applies the law (planning board, ZBA, ARB, landmarks, CAC), the lawmakers appointed it.
blocks.casual: If it makes law or sets the tax rate, voters elected it: the council, the town board, the village trustees. If it applies the law (planning board, ZBA, ARB, landmarks, CAC), the lawmakers appointed it.

deeper.plain: Lawmakers are elected. Rule-appliers are appointed.
deeper.picture: Voters hire the coaches; the coaches pick the refs.
deeper.street: On a quiz, Jordan sees "Who appoints the ZBA?" He remembers "voters pick the lawmakers, lawmakers pick the boards" and answers the town board.
deeper.stakes: Lobbying an appointed board like it's a political body can backfire, because it has to decide on the record, not on politics.
deeper.exam: If the answer choices include "elected by residents" for a planning board or ZBA, it's wrong. Those are appointed by the legislative body.

blocks.q: Which local body adopts the zoning ordinance in a New York village?
c: Planning board
Zoning board of appeals
Village board of trustees
Building department
blocks.x: The elected village board of trustees is the legislative body. The planning board advises and the ZBA grants relief, but neither adopts the law.

blocks.text: How the boards get their seats

blocks.html: Voters elect the legislative body. That body then appoints the citizen boards, usually for staggered fixed terms so no single election can replace a whole board at once. Planning board and ZBA members are typically residents with no special license; they rely on the planning department, the municipal engineer and the town attorney for technical advice. The building inspector is a hired employee who must meet state code enforcement training requirements.
blocks.casual: Voters elect the legislative body. That body then appoints the citizen boards, usually for staggered fixed terms so no single election can flip a whole board at once. Planning board and ZBA members are usually just residents with no special license, and they lean on the planning department, the municipal engineer and the town attorney for technical advice. The building inspector is a hired employee who has to meet state code enforcement training requirements.

deeper.plain: Boards are made up of appointed residents who serve staggered terms and rely on experts. The building inspector is a trained employee.
deeper.picture: Staggered terms are like a band replacing one member at a time. The band keeps playing the same songs even as faces change.
deeper.street: A new Village of Ossining board gets elected promising to stop a development. They can only replace one or two planning board members whose terms are up that year, so the board that reviews the project mostly stays the same.
deeper.stakes: Clients who think one election will flip a pending approval are usually wrong. Staggered terms protect continuity.
deeper.exam: Members are appointed for staggered terms. They don't need a license. The building inspector is an employee with state-required training.

blocks.html: Why it matters to an agent: an elected board can change the rules (rezone, adopt a moratorium, raise the tax rate) and answers to voters. An appointed board must follow the rules as written and give reasons on the record, which is why its decisions can be challenged in an Article 78 proceeding if they are arbitrary. When a client says "I'll just talk to the board," ask which one, because the answer decides whether the conversation is politics or a legal application.
blocks.casual: Here's why this matters to you as an agent. An elected board can change the rules (rezone, pass a moratorium, raise the tax rate), and it answers to voters. An appointed board has to follow the rules as written and give its reasons on the record, which is why its decisions can be challenged in an Article 78 proceeding if they're arbitrary. When a client says "I'll just talk to the board," ask which one, because that decides whether the conversation is politics or a legal application.

deeper.plain: Elected boards make policy and respond to voters. Appointed boards must follow the law and explain their decisions, and courts can check them.
deeper.picture: Talking to the town board is like lobbying a city council member. Talking to the ZBA is like arguing before a judge: evidence matters, not friendship.
deeper.street: Sal wants to add a unit to a building in a village. He calls a trustee he knows. The trustee says, "I can't grant variances. That's the ZBA, and they need evidence on the record." Sal hires an architect to prepare a proper application instead.
deeper.stakes: Treating a ZBA hearing like politics instead of presenting evidence can get an application denied, and the denial will be hard to challenge.
deeper.exam: Appointed boards' decisions get challenged under Article 78 for being arbitrary, illegal or unsupported by evidence. Elected boards set policy.

blocks.text: Planning board vs ZBA vs building department

blocks.html: These three get confused more than anything else on the exam. The planning board looks forward: plans, subdivisions, site plans. The ZBA looks at exceptions: variances and interpretations, acting like a court. The building department is the counter: permits, inspections, COs, and violations. A homeowner's deck usually touches only the building department; if it breaks a setback, add the ZBA; if it is part of a new subdivision, the planning board was there first.
blocks.casual: These three get mixed up more than anything else on the exam. The planning board looks ahead: plans, subdivisions, site plans. The ZBA handles exceptions: variances and interpretations, acting like a court. The building department is the front counter: permits, inspections, COs and violations. A homeowner's deck usually only touches the building department. If it breaks a setback, add the ZBA. If it's part of a new subdivision, the planning board was there first.

deeper.plain: Planning board plans ahead, the ZBA grants exceptions, and the building department issues permits and enforces.
deeper.picture: The planning board designs the city map, the ZBA handles appeals like a court, and the building department is the DMV counter where you get your actual permit.
deeper.street: Leo wants a deck. The building department issues the permit. Next year he wants to extend it into the side setback, so the ZBA must grant an area variance first. His subdivision was approved by the planning board decades ago.
deeper.stakes: Applying to the wrong body wastes months. Agents who know the right door look like pros.
deeper.exam: Cue words: plat, site plan, master plan go to planning board. Variance, interpretation, appeal of inspector go to ZBA. Permit, CO, inspection, violation go to the building department.

left.title: Planning board
items: Master plan
Subdivision plats
Site plan review
Clustering, PUD
Advises other boards

right.title: Zoning board of appeals
items: Use and area variances
Interprets the ordinance
Hears appeals of the building inspector
Often special permits
Quasi-judicial, no policy making

deeper.plain: The planning board plans and approves layouts. The ZBA grants exceptions and interprets. They do different jobs.
deeper.picture: The planning board is the architect of the town. The ZBA is the judge who decides when a rule can bend.
deeper.street: Evelyn submits a site plan for a retail building. The planning board reviews parking and lighting. Her sign is two feet taller than allowed, so she needs an area variance from the ZBA. Both boards, two separate hearings.
deeper.stakes: Developers who skip one board find out at the permit counter, and the clock resets.
deeper.exam: Planning board: master plan, subdivisions, site plans, clustering, PUD. ZBA: variances, interpretations, appeals, often special permits. Neither writes zoning; the legislative body does.

blocks.q: A developer wants to divide a 20-acre parcel into 15 lots. Which board approves the subdivision plat?
c: Zoning board of appeals
Planning board
Architectural review board
Tax assessor
blocks.x: Subdivision approval is a planning board function. The ZBA would get involved only if a lot needed a variance.

blocks.html: Many villages require an architectural review board sign-off before the building department will issue a permit for exterior changes. A conservation advisory council (authorized by General Municipal Law) inventories open space and wetlands and advises the planning board; some towns go further with a wetlands commission that issues local wetland permits on top of DEC's state permits. A historic preservation commission recommends landmarks and districts and must approve exterior work on them.
blocks.casual: Lots of villages require an architectural review board sign-off before the building department will issue a permit for exterior changes. A conservation advisory council (authorized by General Municipal Law) inventories open space and wetlands and advises the planning board. Some towns go further with a wetlands commission that issues local wetland permits on top of DEC's state permits. A historic preservation commission recommends landmarks and districts and has to approve exterior work on them.

deeper.plain: Some places add boards that review how buildings look, protect wetlands and open space, and guard historic properties.
deeper.picture: These boards are like specialty inspectors at a car show: one judges the paint job, one checks for leaks, one makes sure the classic cars stay original.
deeper.street: A Scarsdale homeowner wants new siding. The building department won't issue the permit until the ARB approves the color and material. A Bedford owner near a stream needs a local wetland permit and a DEC permit.
deeper.stakes: Changing a facade without ARB or landmark approval can bring stop-work orders and orders to undo the work.
deeper.exam: ARB equals design approval. CAC equals advisory on open space and wetlands. Landmark commission equals designation and approval of changes to designated properties.

blocks.title: State register is not local landmarking
blocks.html: Listing on the State or National Register (through OPRHP) mostly triggers review of government-funded or permitted projects. The thing that stops a private owner from replacing slate with asphalt shingles is usually local landmark designation and the local commission.
blocks.casual: Being on the State or National Register (through OPRHP) mostly triggers review of projects that the government funds or permits. What actually stops a private owner from swapping slate for asphalt shingles is usually local landmark designation and the local commission.

deeper.plain: State or national listing mostly affects government-backed projects. Local landmark designation is what limits what private owners can do.
deeper.picture: National Register listing is like getting a plaque in a hall of fame. Local landmarking is like the HOA rule that says you can't repaint the front door.
deeper.street: A buyer of a National Register house in Saratoga Springs assumes she can't change the roof. Jordan checks: the house isn't locally landmarked, so she can, as long as she uses no state funding or tax credits that require review.
deeper.stakes: Telling buyers a register listing blocks all changes may scare them off unnecessarily. Missing a local designation can lead to costly violations.
deeper.exam: If the question asks what restricts a private owner's exterior changes, the answer is local landmark designation, not State or National Register listing.

head: Office
Job
Agent tip
rows: Adopts the budget and sets the tax rate
Rates change yearly; quote taxes with the year
Sets each property's assessed value; keeps the roll and records
Square footage, bedrooms and exemptions (like STAR) on the assessment card
Confirms taxes are paid for the closing; unpaid taxes are a priority lien

deeper.plain: Three different jobs: lawmakers set the rate, the assessor sets the value, the receiver sends the bill and collects.
deeper.picture: Rate times value equals the bill. One office picks the rate, another sets the value, a third mails the bill.
deeper.street: Leo's tax bill jumps. He calls the receiver of taxes, who tells him the bill is correct based on the rate and value. The rate was set by the town board; the value came from the assessor. If Leo thinks his value is wrong, that's a grievance, not a call to the receiver.
deeper.stakes: Quoting last year's taxes without saying the year can mislead a buyer. Unpaid taxes are a priority lien that has to be paid at closing.
deeper.exam: Who sets the tax rate? The legislative body. Who values property? The assessor. Who collects? The receiver of taxes or treasurer.

blocks.title: Assessors and grievances
blocks.html: An owner who disagrees with an assessment files a grievance with the board of assessment review (appointed) after the tentative roll comes out, then may go to small claims assessment review (SCAR) or court. The assessor values; the board reviews. Subject 14 covers the process.
blocks.casual: If an owner thinks the assessment is wrong, they file a grievance with the board of assessment review (appointed) after the tentative roll comes out. After that they can go to small claims assessment review (SCAR) or court. The assessor values; the board reviews. Subject 14 covers the whole process.

deeper.plain: Owners who disagree with their assessment appeal first to an appointed review board, then to SCAR or court.
deeper.picture: It's like disputing a grade. First you go to the review committee, and only then can you take it higher.
deeper.street: Leo thinks his Ulster County house is assessed too high compared to similar homes. He files a grievance with the board of assessment review after the tentative roll. The board cuts it slightly. Still unhappy, he files for SCAR, which is for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes.
deeper.stakes: Missing the grievance deadline means waiting a whole year. Agents can help clients spot over-assessments by comparing property cards.
deeper.exam: The assessor values; the board of assessment review hears grievances. SCAR is for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family residential.

blocks.q: A buyer's attorney needs confirmation that the current year's town taxes have been paid. The office to contact is the:
c: Tax assessor
Board of assessment review
Receiver of taxes
Planning department
blocks.x: The receiver of taxes (or treasurer) collects and records payments. The assessor sets values, not payments.

blocks.html: The county health department approves septic systems and private wells and keeps their records, including as-built drawings, and approves certain sewer connections. The county planning agency must receive referrals of certain local zoning actions (for example, near a municipal boundary or a state or county road) under General Municipal Law 239-m, and can recommend changes. State agencies layer on top: DEC for wetlands and spills, DOT for driveways onto state roads.
blocks.casual: The county health department approves septic systems and private wells, keeps their records (including as-built drawings), and approves certain sewer connections. The county planning agency has to get referrals of certain local zoning actions (for example, near a municipal boundary or a state or county road) under General Municipal Law 239-m, and it can recommend changes. State agencies sit on top of that: DEC for wetlands and spills, DOT for driveways onto state roads.

deeper.plain: The county handles health approvals and reviews some local zoning decisions. State agencies cover wetlands, spills and state road access.
deeper.picture: It's a layered cake: local boards on top, county in the middle, state on the bottom, and some projects cut through every layer.
deeper.street: Evelyn's new store sits on a state highway near a town line. The town planning board refers it to the county planning agency under 239-m. She also needs a DOT permit for the driveway and county health approval for the septic system.
deeper.stakes: Forgetting a county or state approval can stop a project at the last minute, after the local approvals are done.
deeper.exam: County health equals wells and septic. GML 239-m equals county referral of certain local zoning actions. DEC equals wetlands and spills. DOT equals curb cuts on state roads.

blocks.q: Where would a buyer most likely find the approved design and as-built drawing for a house's septic system?
c: County or local health department
Zoning board of appeals
Receiver of taxes
Architectural review board
blocks.x: Septic approvals and records sit with the health department. The ZBA handles zoning relief, not sanitary systems.

story.title: One Afternoon at Village Hall
story.setting: A Westchester village hall, 1:15 pm, three windows and a bulletin board

beats.text: Jordan arrived with a folder, a list, and a coffee that was already cold.
Building department. What do you need?
The CO for 14 Elm, and whether the rear deck and shed had permits.
Deck's permitted, closed out in 2016. Shed, nothing on file. That's an open question for the seller.
And the stream behind the house?
Ask the conservation advisory council, they meet Thursdays. And DEC if it's a regulated wetland.
Next window: Receiver of Taxes.
Are the village taxes paid through this year?
Paid. If you want to know why the assessment went up, that's the assessor, down the hall. I just collect.

check.q: Who sets the assessed value of 14 Elm?
c: Receiver of taxes
Tax assessor
Village board of trustees
Planning board
check.x: The assessor values property. The receiver collects; the board sets the budget and tax rate.

beats.text: Who set the tax rate, though?
The board of trustees. They're elected. Complain to them in March.
beats.tag: Elected board sets the tax rate

beats.text: On the way out, a notice on the bulletin board: Architectural Review Board, Thursday, 7 pm. Item 3: window replacement, 22 Elm.
Even windows need a board here?
In this village, exterior changes go to the ARB before we issue a permit. If it were in the historic district, the landmarks commission too.
On the phone, later: Elected people make the rules and the tax rate. Appointed boards apply them. The building department holds the keys. Now go ask the sellers about that shed.

board.prompt: Draw two columns, Elected and Appointed, and sort every agency from this lesson. Add a third column for staff departments.

facts.text: Every part of NY outside a city is in a town, and a village sits inside a town and handles some services itself.
The elected legislative body (city council, town board, or village board of trustees) adopts local laws, the zoning ordinance, the budget and the tax rate.
Chief executives: a city has a mayor, a town a supervisor, and a village a mayor who also sits on the board of trustees.
Lawmaking bodies are elected; the boards that apply the law (planning board, ZBA, ARB, landmarks, CAC) are appointed by them.
The planning board handles the master plan, subdivision approval, site plan review and clustering; it does not grant variances.
The zoning board of appeals grants use and area variances, interprets the ordinance and hears appeals from the building inspector, acting quasi-judicially.
The building department issues building permits, inspects, issues certificates of occupancy and enforces the code: the gatekeeper for construction.
The architectural review board approves the design of new construction and remodeling (facades, materials, signs), often before the building permit issues.
The conservation advisory council inventories open space and wetlands and advises the boards; some towns have a wetlands commission that issues local permits.
The historic preservation commission recommends landmarks and districts and must approve exterior work on designated properties.
State or National Register listing mostly triggers review of government-funded or permitted projects; local landmark designation is what restricts a private owner's changes.
The planning department is professional staff that advises all agencies and boards and prepares studies.
The tax assessor values each property and keeps the assessment roll and property records.
The receiver of taxes sends bills, collects taxes and confirms payment for closing; unpaid taxes are a priority lien.
The municipal engineer handles roads, drainage, and sewer and water connections, and reviews engineering on plans.
The county health department approves septic systems and private wells and keeps their records.
Appointed boards serve staggered fixed terms, members need no special license, and the building inspector is a hired employee meeting state training requirements.
An elected board can change the rules; an appointed board must follow them and give reasons, so arbitrary decisions can be challenged in an Article 78 proceeding.
An owner grieves an assessment to the board of assessment review after the tentative roll, then may go to SCAR or court.
Certain local zoning actions, such as near a municipal boundary or a state or county road, must be referred to the county planning agency under GML 239-m.

lessons.title: Working With Town Hall, and the New York City Version
lessons.tagline: Know which office holds the answer, and in the city, which acronym.
objectives: Route a homeowner's or agent's question to the right local office
Use municipal records in a listing: CO, open permits, tax and assessment data, septic records
Match NYC agencies to their suburban equivalents: DOB, LPC, DOF, Community Boards, BSA, HPD
Explain what a landmark designation means for a sale or renovation in NYC

blocks.title: A brownstone buyer with big plans
blocks.html: Leo is about to make an offer on a brownstone in the Stuyvesant Heights Historic District. He wants to replace the front windows, add a rooftop deck, convert it from a two-family to a single-family, and appeal what he thinks is a too-high assessment. He asks Jordan, "Who do I even call?" The answer is five different agencies.
blocks.casual: Leo's about to make an offer on a brownstone in the Stuyvesant Heights Historic District. He wants to swap out the front windows, add a rooftop deck, convert it from a two-family to a single-family, and fight what he thinks is a too-high assessment. He asks Jordan, "Who do I even call?" The answer: five different agencies.

deeper.plain: In NYC, each of Leo's plans goes through a different city agency, and the landmark district adds an extra layer.
deeper.picture: It's like planning a wedding with five vendors. The caterer, florist, DJ, venue and officiant each sign off on their own piece.
deeper.street: Jordan sketches it for Leo on a napkin at a Lewis Avenue cafe: LPC for the windows and any visible deck, DOB for permits and the new CO, BSA only if the deck needs a variance, DOF and the Tax Commission for the assessment, and the Community Board weighing in on any BSA case.
deeper.stakes: Leo budgets for the purchase but not the approvals. Landmark-compliant windows can cost two to three times standard ones, and a deck may not be approved at all.
deeper.exam: NYC agency matching is a classic exam pattern. Know who decides (LPC, DOB, BSA, DOF, Tax Commission) and who only advises (Community Board).

blocks.text: Routing questions to the right office (suburbs and upstate)

head: Question
Go to
rows: Is there a CO? Were the finished basement and deck permitted? Any open violations?
Can the buyer add a second unit or build closer to the lot line?
Zoning ordinance, then the ZBA for a variance (building department can say what is as of right)
Can the buyer split the lot or build a new house on part of it?
Can the buyer change the facade, windows, or siding?
Architectural review board; historic preservation commission if designated
What is the assessed value? Are there exemptions like STAR?
Are taxes paid? What is the payoff for closing?
Where is the septic system and when was it approved?
How do I connect to the sewer or fix a drainage problem at the road?
Is the backyard stream or marsh regulated?
Conservation advisory council or wetlands commission, and DEC

deeper.plain: Every common buyer or seller question has one office that answers it. Learn the map.
deeper.picture: It's a phone tree for village hall: press 1 for permits, press 2 for zoning, press 3 for taxes.
deeper.street: A Rockland buyer asks if the finished basement was permitted. Jordan calls the building department. The buyer also wants to subdivide the backyard for a second house, so Jordan points to the planning board. And she asks if her STAR exemption carries over, so Jordan sends her to the assessor.
deeper.stakes: Sending a client to the wrong office makes them doubt you. Missing a records check leaves surprises for the buyer's attorney to find.
deeper.exam: Pairs to memorize: CO and permits equal building department. Variance equals ZBA. Subdivision equals planning board. Facade equals ARB or landmarks. Value equals assessor. Payment equals receiver. Septic equals county health. Sewer hookup equals municipal engineer.

blocks.html: Pull records before listing, not after an attorney finds the problem. An open permit (work that was permitted but never inspected and closed out) or unpermitted work can delay a closing for months, because the buyer's attorney and title company will flag it. Many building departments let you search permit history online or by FOIL request.
blocks.casual: Pull records before you list, not after the buyer's attorney finds the problem. An open permit (work that got a permit but was never inspected and closed out) or unpermitted work can push back a closing for months, because the buyer's attorney and the title company will flag it. Many building departments let you search permit history online or through a FOIL request.

deeper.plain: Check permit records before listing so you aren't blindsided at contract time.
deeper.picture: An open permit is like an unreturned library book. It's been ages, but the fine is still on your account until you close it out.
deeper.street: The Okafors' records show a 2011 bathroom permit that was never closed. Jordan catches it before listing. They hire an expediter, schedule the final inspection, and close it out in six weeks, before any buyer ever sees it.
deeper.stakes: Open permits can kill a closing date, cost a seller a rate lock or a buyer, and force a price cut.
deeper.exam: An open permit means work was permitted but never inspected and signed off. FOIL is how you request public records not available at the counter.

blocks.title: The pre-listing records pull
blocks.html: CO and permit history from the building department, tax bill and payment status from the receiver, the assessment card from the assessor, and septic records from the health department. Twenty minutes now saves weeks at contract.
blocks.casual: Here's the pre-listing records pull: the CO and permit history from the building department, the tax bill and payment status from the receiver, the assessment card from the assessor, and septic records from the health department. Twenty minutes now saves weeks at contract.

deeper.plain: Before listing, grab four things: CO and permits, tax status, assessment card, septic records.
deeper.picture: It's checking the oil, tires, lights and brakes before a road trip, not after you break down on the Thruway.
deeper.street: Jordan pulls records for a Putnam listing and finds the septic was approved for three bedrooms. The seller advertises four. Jordan fixes the listing to say three bedrooms plus a den, avoiding a misrepresentation complaint.
deeper.stakes: Advertising features that conflict with public records (bedroom count, legal units) is misrepresentation and can bring a DOS complaint.
deeper.exam: Expect a scenario where an agent should verify facts before advertising. The answer is to check public records, not rely on the seller's word.

blocks.q: A seller finished a basement with a permit but never scheduled the final inspection. The buyer's attorney will most likely require:
c: A variance from the ZBA
The permit to be closed out with a final inspection from the building department
Approval from the planning board
A new assessment from the assessor
blocks.x: An open permit is resolved with the building department through final inspection and sign-off. No zoning relief is needed if the work was legal.

blocks.html: How a homeowner or agent actually deals with each office: the building department and assessor are walk-in or online counters, and most records are public. The receiver of taxes gives payment status, often online. Boards (planning, ZBA, ARB, landmarks, conservation) work by application and public hearing: file forms and plans, pay a fee, notify neighbors, appear at the meeting, and wait for a written decision. Meetings are open to the public under the Open Meetings Law, so you can watch a board handle a similar case before your client's comes up.
blocks.casual: Here's how you actually deal with each office. The building department and the assessor are walk-in or online counters, and most of their records are public. The receiver of taxes gives you payment status, often online. Boards (planning, ZBA, ARB, landmarks, conservation) run on application and public hearing: you file forms and plans, pay a fee, notify the neighbors, show up at the meeting, and wait for a written decision. Meetings are open to the public under the Open Meetings Law, so you can go watch a board handle a similar case before your client's comes up.

deeper.plain: Departments answer questions at the counter. Boards work through applications, hearings and written decisions.
deeper.picture: A department is a store counter: ask and you get. A board is a talent show: you apply, perform in public, and wait for the judges' scores.
deeper.street: Before Sal's ZBA hearing in a Long Island village, Jordan attends the previous month's meeting and watches a similar variance get denied because the applicant had no photos or neighbor letters. Sal shows up with both and gets approved.
deeper.stakes: Clients who walk into a board hearing unprepared often get denied or tabled, which can blow a contract deadline.
deeper.exam: Boards act through applications and public hearings with notice to neighbors. Meetings are public under the Open Meetings Law.

items: Never promise a client an approval. Boards have discretion and neighbors get a say.
Build board timelines into contract contingencies: a variance or ARB approval can take one to three months.
Records requests that are not available at the counter can be made under the Freedom of Information Law (FOIL).
If a project crosses a town line or sits on a state or county road, expect a referral to the county planning agency.
blocks.casual:
Never promise a client an approval. Boards have discretion and neighbors get a say.
Build board timelines into contract contingencies, because a variance or ARB approval can take one to three months.
If a record isn't available at the counter, request it under the Freedom of Information Law (FOIL).
If a project crosses a town line or sits on a state or county road, expect a referral to the county planning agency.

deeper.plain: Don't promise approvals, leave time for them in the contract, use FOIL for records, and expect county review for some projects.
deeper.picture: Board approval is weather, not a train schedule. You can plan for it, but you can't promise it.
deeper.street: Marcus tells a buyer "the ZBA will rubber-stamp it" and lets her sign without a variance contingency. The ZBA denies it. She's stuck with a house that doesn't fit her plans and files a complaint against Marcus.
deeper.stakes: Promising approvals can be misrepresentation. Contracts without approval contingencies leave clients exposed.
deeper.exam: FOIL is the NY public records law. GML 239-m triggers county referral near boundaries and state or county roads. Agents should never guarantee board outcomes.

head: Function
Suburban or upstate office
NYC agency
rows: Department of Finance (DOF) does both; the NYC Tax Commission hears assessment appeals
Public hearing at the planning board
Department of City Planning, City Planning Commission, City Council (ULURP)
Housing code, affordable housing, multiple dwelling registration
Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD)
City Register (part of DOF), searchable on ACRIS

deeper.plain: NYC has its own agency for each job: DOB for permits, LPC for landmarks, DOF for taxes, BSA for variances, HPD for housing code, DEP for water and sewer, and the City Register for recording.
deeper.picture: Same game as the suburbs, but every position has a bigger, city-sized team with its own name.
deeper.street: For a Harlem rowhouse sale, Jordan checks DOB for the CO and violations, HPD for housing code violations and registration, DOF for taxes, ACRIS for the deed chain, and LPC because the block is in a historic district.
deeper.stakes: Missing an HPD violation or an unregistered rental can surprise a buyer. Using suburban terms in NYC makes you look green.
deeper.exam: Pairs: DOB equals permits and COs. LPC equals landmarks. DOF equals assessment and collection. Tax Commission equals assessment appeals. BSA equals variances. HPD equals housing code and registration. ACRIS equals recorded documents.

blocks.title: Landmarks: what the LPC approves
blocks.html: The LPC is 11 commissioners appointed by the mayor; by law it includes at least three architects, a historian, a city planner or landscape architect, a realtor, and a resident of each borough. It designates individual landmarks, interior landmarks, scenic landmarks and historic districts. Owners need LPC approval before most exterior work, and some interior work, on designated property: a Certificate of Appropriateness for changes that affect protected features (often after a public hearing), a Permit for Minor Work for smaller changes, or a Certificate of No Effect for work that does not affect protected features. DOB will not issue the permit without LPC sign-off.
blocks.casual: The LPC has 11 commissioners appointed by the mayor. By law it includes at least three architects, a historian, a city planner or landscape architect, a realtor, and a resident of each borough.
