It designates individual landmarks, interior landmarks, scenic landmarks and historic districts. Owners need LPC approval before most exterior work, and some interior work, on designated property. That means a Certificate of Appropriateness for changes that affect protected features (often after a public hearing), a Permit for Minor Work for smaller changes, or a Certificate of No Effect for work that doesn't touch protected features. DOB won't issue the permit without LPC sign-off.

deeper.plain: If a building is landmarked, the LPC has to approve most exterior changes before DOB will issue a permit.
deeper.picture: It's like a museum loaning you a painting to hang at home. You can enjoy it, but you need permission before reframing it.
deeper.street: Leo wants vinyl replacement windows on his Stuyvesant Heights brownstone. LPC staff say no: it has to be wood that matches the historic profile. He gets a Permit for Minor Work for wood windows at $2,800 each instead of $900 vinyl. DOB then issues the permit.
deeper.stakes: Owners who skip LPC face violations and orders to restore the original. Buyers who don't budget for landmark-quality materials get sticker shock.
deeper.exam: Three LPC approvals: Certificate of Appropriateness (affects protected features, often a hearing), Permit for Minor Work (smaller), Certificate of No Effect (doesn't affect features). LPC members are appointed by the mayor.

blocks.html: Community Boards (59 citywide) have up to 50 unpaid members appointed by the borough president, half nominated by the area's City Council members. They hold hearings and vote on ULURP applications, BSA variances, liquor licenses and more, but their votes are advisory. DOF assesses every property each January, bills and collects taxes, and runs the City Register. HPD enforces the Housing Maintenance Code (heat, hot water, repairs, lead and mold rules), requires annual registration of most rental buildings with 3 or more units, and runs affordable housing programs.
blocks.casual: There are 59 Community Boards across the city, each with up to 50 unpaid members appointed by the borough president, half of them nominated by the area's City Council members. They hold hearings and vote on ULURP applications, BSA variances, liquor licenses and more, but their votes are advisory. DOF assesses every property each January, bills and collects taxes, and runs the City Register. HPD enforces the Housing Maintenance Code (heat, hot water, repairs, lead and mold rules), requires annual registration of most rental buildings with 3 or more units, and runs affordable housing programs.

deeper.plain: Community Boards give the neighborhood a voice but don't decide. DOF handles assessments, taxes and recording. HPD enforces housing conditions and registration.
deeper.picture: The Community Board is the neighborhood's opinion poll, DOF is the city's bookkeeper, and HPD is the landlord's report card.
deeper.street: Sal buys a 4-unit building in Ridgewood. He registers it with HPD, which is required every year. In January, DOF's notice of value shows a big jump. A tenant complains about no heat, and HPD issues a violation within days.
deeper.stakes: Landlords who skip HPD registration can be blocked from bringing certain cases in housing court. Ignoring HPD violations piles up fines and can show up in a sale.
deeper.exam: Community Board votes are advisory. DOF assesses and collects. HPD registration applies to most buildings with 3+ units. The 59 boards and appointment by borough president are testable.

blocks.title: Leo's brownstone, agency by agency
blocks.html:
1. Front windows in a historic district: LPC (Permit for Minor Work or Certificate of Appropriateness), then DOB permit.
2. Rooftop deck: LPC review if visible from the street, DOB permit, and zoning compliance; a variance would go to the BSA.
3. Two-family to single-family: DOB filing and a new CO (and LPC if exterior changes).
4. Assessment too high: DOF issues the notice of value; appeal to the NYC Tax Commission.
5. Neighbors' input on any BSA application: Community Board, advisory.
Answer: LPC, DOB, BSA if needed, DOF and the Tax Commission, with the Community Board advising.
blocks.casual:
Let's take Leo's brownstone one agency at a time.
1. Front windows in a historic district: LPC (Permit for Minor Work or Certificate of Appropriateness), then a DOB permit.
2. Rooftop deck: LPC review if it's visible from the street, a DOB permit, and zoning compliance. A variance would go to the BSA.
3. Two-family to single-family: a DOB filing and a new CO (plus LPC if the exterior changes).
4. Assessment too high: DOF issues the notice of value, and the appeal goes to the NYC Tax Commission.
5. Neighbors' input on any BSA application: Community Board, advisory.
Bottom line: LPC, DOB, BSA if needed, DOF and the Tax Commission, with the Community Board advising.

deeper.plain: Leo's five plans map to five offices, and only one of them is just advisory.
deeper.picture: Think of it as five separate tickets at five different windows. Missing one window means that part of the plan is stuck.
deeper.street: Leo closes at $2.1 million. He files the window work with LPC first, then DOB. The deck turns out to be visible from the street, so LPC holds a hearing. The conversion to single-family gets a new CO. His assessment appeal at the Tax Commission saves $1,900 a year.
deeper.stakes: Converting from two-family to single-family without a new CO leaves the paperwork wrong, which can trip up the next sale or a refinance.
deeper.exam: Expect a multi-step NYC fact pattern. LPC approval comes before the DOB permit on landmarked property. Assessment appeals go to the Tax Commission, not DOB or LPC.

blocks.q: An owner in a Brooklyn historic district wants to replace the original stoop. Before the Department of Buildings issues a permit, the owner needs approval from the:
c: Community Board
Department of Finance
Landmarks Preservation Commission
Board of Standards and Appeals
blocks.x: Exterior work on designated property needs LPC approval first. The Community Board may comment, but it does not approve.

blocks.title: Advisory is not approval
blocks.html: Community Boards and Borough Presidents advise. The BSA, CPC, City Council and LPC decide. If an answer choice says the Community Board approved a variance, it is wrong.
blocks.casual: Community Boards and Borough Presidents advise. The BSA, CPC, City Council and LPC decide. If an answer choice says the Community Board approved a variance, it's wrong.

deeper.plain: Some NYC bodies only give opinions. Others make the binding decision.
deeper.picture: Community Boards are the audience at a talent show. They can cheer or boo, but the judges pick the winner.
deeper.street: A Bed-Stuy Community Board votes 30 to 5 against a BSA variance for a taller building. The BSA hears the concerns, then grants the variance with conditions. The project goes forward.
deeper.stakes: Clients who think a Community Board vote ends a project may give up too soon, or relax too early when it votes yes.
deeper.exam: Advisory: Community Board, Borough President. Binding: BSA, CPC, City Council, LPC. Watch for answer choices claiming a Community Board "approved" or "denied" anything.

blocks.q: In New York City, which agency both assesses real property and collects real property taxes?
c: Department of Housing Preservation and Development
Department of Finance
Department of Buildings
City Planning Commission
blocks.x: DOF handles assessment and collection. Upstate and suburban towns split those jobs between the assessor and the receiver of taxes.

blocks.q: A tenant in a Bronx apartment has had no heat for a week in January. The city agency that enforces the Housing Maintenance Code is:
c: HPD
DOB
LPC
BSA
blocks.x: HPD enforces heat, hot water and repair requirements under the Housing Maintenance Code. DOB handles construction and building code issues.

story.title: Five Agencies and a Stoop
story.setting: Stuyvesant Heights, Brooklyn, on the stoop of a brownstone Leo wants badly

beats.text: New windows, roof deck, make it a single-family, and fight the taxes. Who do I call?
Start with this: you're in a historic district. Anything on the outside goes to Landmarks first.
Even windows?
Even windows. Matching ones may just need a Permit for Minor Work. Bigger changes need a Certificate of Appropriateness, sometimes a hearing.
Then the Buildings Department?
Right. DOB won't issue the permit without Landmarks' sign-off. And going from two-family to one-family means a new CO from DOB.

check.q: Which agency issues the new CO when Leo converts to a single-family?
c: LPC
DOB
DOF
HPD
check.x: DOB issues permits and certificates of occupancy in NYC. LPC approves design on landmarks but does not issue COs.

beats.text: And the roof deck breaks the height rule?
Then it's a variance from the BSA. The Community Board holds a hearing and votes, but it's only advice.
Taxes. Who do I yell at?
Department of Finance sets your assessment and collects the bill. If you think the value's wrong, you appeal to the Tax Commission.
Leo opened a new spreadsheet tab and named it AGENCIES.
So if I were in Westchester, it'd be a landmark commission, a building inspector, an assessor and a receiver of taxes.
Back at the office: Same jobs, different names. The city just stacks them into bigger buildings with longer lines.

board.prompt: Make a two-column grid: suburban office on the left, NYC agency on the right. Fill in permits, landmarks, assessment, tax collection, variances, local hearings, and housing code enforcement.

facts.text: Route questions by office: permits and COs to the building department, lot splits to the planning board, facades to the ARB, sewer hookups to the municipal engineer.
An open permit is work that was permitted but never inspected and closed out, and like unpermitted work it can delay a closing for months.
Pull records before listing: CO and permits from the building department, tax status from the receiver, the assessment card from the assessor, septic records from the health department.
Boards act by application and public hearing (forms, fee, neighbor notice, meeting, written decision), and meetings are open under the Open Meetings Law.
Never promise an approval; build board timelines (often one to three months) into contingencies, and request unavailable records under FOIL.
In NYC the Department of Buildings issues permits and certificates of occupancy and handles inspections and violations.
In a NYC landmark or historic district, the owner needs Landmarks Preservation Commission approval before DOB will issue a permit for most exterior work.
LPC approvals: a Certificate of Appropriateness for changes to protected features, a Permit for Minor Work for smaller changes, a Certificate of No Effect for work that does not affect them.
The LPC has 11 mayor-appointed commissioners, including at least three architects, a historian, a planner or landscape architect, a realtor and a resident of each borough.
The NYC Department of Finance assesses property, bills and collects taxes, and runs the City Register where deeds and mortgages are recorded.
NYC assessment appeals go to the NYC Tax Commission.
The Board of Standards and Appeals (BSA) is NYC's zoning board of appeals.
Community Boards and Borough Presidents only advise; the BSA, CPC, City Council and LPC decide.
NYC has 59 Community Boards of up to 50 unpaid members appointed by the borough president, half nominated by local Council members.
HPD enforces the Housing Maintenance Code (heat, hot water, repairs), requires annual registration of most rental buildings with 3+ units, and runs affordable housing programs.
The NYC Department of Environmental Protection handles water, sewer and asbestos rules.
NYC planning and rezoning run through the Department of City Planning, the City Planning Commission and the City Council under ULURP.
Whether a stream or marsh is regulated is a question for the conservation advisory council or wetlands commission, and DEC.

lessons.title: Case file: The Raised Ranch With a Second Kitchen
lessons.tagline: A seller's listing sheet promises four bedrooms, rental income and a new deck. Town hall's files say something else.
objectives: Decide which local office's records answer a legality question about a house before it is listed
Apply building department, county health department and assessor records to correct a listing description
Distinguish a special permit, a variance and a subdivision approval when a buyer wants to change the property
Plan contract timing around board approvals, permit closeouts and the 30-day window to challenge a board decision

blocks.title: A referral from Bay Ridge
blocks.html: Doreen Castellano lives in Bay Ridge and has just inherited her late father's house in a Putnam County town: a 1979 raised ranch on 1.8 acres, on a well and septic, fronting a county road, with a pond along the back line. She wants Hudson & Hart to list it, and Diane hands the file to Jordan with one instruction: “Nothing goes on the listing until you have been to town hall.” Doreen's own description, typed by her father years ago, reads: “4 BR, 2 bath, legal mother-daughter with $1,400/month rental income, new deck, 12x16 shed, pond views, taxes $6,100.” Jordan has a free Thursday and a 40-minute drive. Before writing a word of the listing, Jordan has to decide which record answers the biggest question: is the downstairs apartment legal at all?

blocks.q: Which record best answers whether the lower-level kitchen and the deck were legally built?
c: The assessor's property record card, which lists rooms, baths and square footage
The building department's permit history and certificate of occupancy file
The deed and filed subdivision map recorded with the county clerk
The receiver of taxes' payment history for the last three years
blocks.x: Legality of construction lives in the building department: permits, inspections and the CO. The assessor's card is the trap. Assessors record what they see or what owners report so they can value the house, and a room on the card proves nothing about whether a permit was issued. The deed and tax history do not address construction at all.

blocks.html: The building department clerk pulls a thin folder and prints the permit screen. Jordan photographs everything, then walks down the hall to the assessor and the receiver of taxes, and finishes at the county health department for the septic file. By 3 pm the paper tells a different story from Doreen's sheet.

head: Office
Record
What it shows
rows: Issued; footing inspection passed; no framing or final inspection; status open
No permit for a kitchen, bathroom or second unit
3 BR, 1.5 bath, 1,640 sq ft, Enhanced STAR exemption in Vincent Castellano's name
Town and county tax paid; second installment of the school tax unpaid
Designed for a 3-bedroom house; as-built sketch shows the absorption field behind the house
blocks.caption: Jordan's records pull, one afternoon

blocks.title: How Jordan ran the pull
blocks.html: Call ahead: many building departments pull permit folders only by appointment, and some put permit history online. Bring the section, block and lot from the tax bill, because older files are indexed by tax map number, not street address. Photograph every page, including blank ones, and note the date and the clerk's name. The county GIS site gives aerials, tax maps and often wetland and flood layers. The county clerk has the deed, filed subdivision maps and any recorded easements. Put all of it in one folder with a one-page summary on top, so Diane can review it and the seller's attorney can use it.

The pattern is common. A family finished the lower level in the 1990s, added a kitchenette for a grandmother, later rented it to a nurse from the hospital, and nobody ever filed anything. The 2015 deck got a permit, passed its footing inspection, and then the contractor walked away and the final inspection was never booked. That is an open permit, and any buyer's attorney who orders a municipal search will find it.

blocks.q: Doreen insists the downstairs rental be advertised because “it has paid the taxes for 20 years.” How should Jordan describe the lower level?
c: As a legal mother-daughter, since the town has not cited the owner in 20 years
As a fourth bedroom, since it has a window and a closet
As finished space in a one-family house, with no rental income claimed
As an accessory apartment, so long as the rental income is marked as estimated
blocks.x: The CO says one-family, so the listing describes a one-family house with finished lower-level space and no income claim. Calling it a legal mother-daughter is the trap: years without a citation do not make unpermitted work legal. Advertising rental income from an illegal unit misleads buyers, lenders and appraisers, and the licensee who writes the ad owns that misrepresentation.

blocks.html: Doreen pushes back on the bedroom count too. The downstairs room has a window and a closet, so why not four bedrooms? Jordan opens the septic file again. The system was designed and approved for three bedrooms, because a septic system is sized by bedrooms, which stand in for the number of people and the gallons a day the house sends into the ground.

blocks.q: The septic approval is for 3 bedrooms. What does that mean for the fourth “bedroom” on Doreen's sheet?
c: Adding a bedroom generally needs county health department review of the septic
The assessor can approve the extra bedroom by updating the property record card
Nothing, because septic limits apply to new construction
The zoning board of appeals has to grant an area variance for the added bedroom
blocks.x: The county health department approves septic design, and the design is tied to bedroom count, so a fourth bedroom generally needs its review and possibly a larger system. The assessor answer is the trap: an assessor values property and cannot approve anything. Zoning relief is a different question; a bedroom is not a setback problem.

blocks.title: The assessor's card is not a certificate of occupancy
blocks.html: Agents copy bedroom counts and square footage from the assessor's card or the tax bill all the time. The card is a valuation record. It can list rooms that were never permitted, miss rooms that were, and lag years behind. Legality comes from the building department; sanitary capacity comes from the health department. Quote each fact from the office that actually controls it.

The deck is the easiest fix, and the cheapest to fix now. Jordan calls the building inspector, who explains the problem: the footings were inspected, but the framing, ledger attachment and railings never were, and the deck has been finished for ten years. The inspector can come out, but may ask for a contractor or engineer to open up the ledger or certify the connections.

blocks.q: What actually resolves the open deck permit?
c: A clean report from the buyer's home inspector at the contract stage
An area variance from the ZBA, because the permit has been open for so long
Final inspection and sign-off by the building department, on its terms
Recording an affidavit with the county clerk stating the deck was built well
blocks.x: The office that issued the permit closes it: the building department inspects, may ask for an engineer's letter or exposed connections, and signs off. The home inspector is the trap. A private inspection informs the buyer but cannot close a municipal permit. Age alone does not trigger a variance, and an affidavit has no effect on the permit record.

blocks.html: Doreen authorizes the work. A contractor removes two deck boards so the inspector can see the ledger bolts, an engineer writes a one-page letter on the framing, and the inspector signs the final three weeks later. Cost: $1,150. If the buyer's attorney had found it after contract, the closing would have slipped, and the buyer would have asked for a credit far larger than that.

The shed is next. It is 12 by 16 feet, or 192 square feet, and sits 6 feet from the side line. The state's Uniform Code allows a municipality to exempt small sheds on one- and two-family lots from building permits, but only up to 144 square feet of floor area, and only if the local law adopts the exemption.

blocks.q: What is the most accurate read on Doreen's 192-square-foot shed?
c: It needs no attention, since residential sheds are exempt
It is over the small-shed permit exemption, and setbacks apply anyway
It needs a county health department sign-off, since it is outbuilding space
It is fine as long as it has no electric service, plumbing or concrete foundation
blocks.x: At 192 square feet the shed is over the 144-square-foot ceiling for the optional permit exemption, and zoning setbacks apply even to sheds that need no permit. The no-electric answer is the trap: utilities can trigger other requirements, but their absence does not make a large shed exempt. The health department matters only because, as Jordan is about to learn, sheds sometimes land on septic fields.

blocks.html: Jordan lays the septic as-built sketch over an aerial photo on the county GIS site. The shed sits on the edge of the absorption field. Nobody needs to panic, but it goes in the file for the buyer's engineer, and Doreen decides to have the shed moved and permitted in its new spot rather than argue about it.

blocks.text: The tax number on the sheet

blocks.html: Doreen's sheet says taxes are $6,100. The bills say the same, but the assessor's card explains why: Vincent had the Enhanced STAR exemption for seniors, which cut the school tax. Vincent died in March. The exemption belonged to him as an owner-occupant who met the age and income tests; it does not travel with the house. Without it, the full tax on the current assessment is about $8,300.

blocks.q: How should Jordan show taxes on the listing?
c: The $6,100 billed last year, the public figure
An average of the exempt and full amounts, so the buyer sees a middle figure
The $6,100 figure, with a note that buyers may apply for STAR on their own
The full tax of about $8,300, noting last year's bill had an exemption
blocks.x: Quote the tax a buyer will actually pay: the full amount on the current assessment, with a note that last year's bill reflected the prior owner's exemption. Quoting $6,100 is the trap; it is accurate history but misleading as a carrying cost. A buyer who qualifies can apply for STAR, which new owners now receive as a credit from the state, but that is the buyer's benefit, not a feature of the house.

blocks.title: Three offices, three tax questions
blocks.html: The town board adopts the budget and sets the town tax rate; the school district sets its own levy. The assessor values the parcel and applies exemptions. The receiver of taxes bills and collects. When a listing quotes taxes, Jordan cites the assessment from the assessor, the payment status from the receiver, and the year of the bill.

The receiver's printout shows the second installment of the school tax unpaid since the estate opened, about $2,900 with penalties still running. Doreen's first reaction: “The buyer can pay it with next year's bill.”

blocks.q: How will the unpaid school tax installment most likely be handled?
c: The buyer takes title subject to it and simply pays it with the next tax bill
The estate pays it at or before closing, since it is a lien on the house
It is wiped out when title passes to a new owner
The receiver of taxes pursues the estate personally, which leaves the house clear
blocks.x: Unpaid real property taxes are a lien on the property itself and come ahead of even the mortgage. The title company's tax search will find it, and the closing statement pays it from the seller's proceeds. The buyer-pays-later answer is the trap: no buyer's attorney or lender will close over an open tax lien. A transfer of title does not erase it, because the debt follows the land, not the person.

blocks.html: Jordan tells Doreen now, so the number is not a surprise at the closing table and so the penalties stop growing. She pays it from the estate account the next week, and the receiver's printout goes into the listing file marked “paid.”

blocks.text: The buyers who want the apartment

blocks.html: The listing goes live as a three-bedroom one-family with a finished lower level and an open note about the kitchenette. The best offer comes from Rafael and Joyce Hollis, who want Joyce's mother downstairs and might rent it later. Their attorney asks the right question: can the apartment be made legal? Jordan reads the town's zoning code. Accessory apartments are allowed in this district by special permit from the zoning board of appeals, if the owner lives in the house, the apartment is under 800 square feet, and the septic and parking work.

blocks.q: What approval do the Hollises need to legalize the downstairs apartment under this town's code?
c: A use variance from the ZBA showing unnecessary hardship
A special permit from the ZBA under the code's conditions
Subdivision approval from the planning board for a second dwelling unit
A local law adopted by the town board rezoning the Castellano lot
blocks.x: The code already allows accessory apartments in this district on conditions, so the route is a special permit, which is granted when the conditions are met. A use variance is the trap: it is for a use the code does not allow at all, and it requires unnecessary hardship, a much harder showing. A second unit inside one house is not a subdivision, and rezoning one lot invites a spot zoning challenge.

blocks.html: The special permit will take time: an application with a floor plan, a septic review from the county health department because the apartment adds a kitchen and a bath, a legal notice, and a public hearing. The ZBA meets once a month. Realistically, eight to twelve weeks. Neighbors get notice and can object.

The Hollises' attorney drafts a contingency: the buyers may apply in Doreen's name with her consent, and they may cancel and recover the down payment if the permit is denied by a set date. Joyce asks Jordan to tell her mother it will be approved, because “the town wants housing.” Jordan does not. Boards have discretion, and neighbors get a voice.

At the hearing, the next-door neighbor complains about parking on the shared side of the driveway. The ZBA grants the permit with two conditions: two off-street spaces, and the owner must live in one of the units. The written decision is filed with the town clerk four days later. Rafael wants to close the following Monday.

blocks.q: Rafael wants to close the Monday after the decision is filed. What risk should Jordan flag?
c: The building department can reverse the ZBA within a year
Nothing, since a special permit is final once the board votes
The town board has to ratify every ZBA decision at its next regular meeting
The neighbor has 30 days from the clerk filing to bring an Article 78
blocks.x: A neighbor can challenge a ZBA decision in an Article 78 proceeding, which generally must be started within 30 days after the decision is filed with the town clerk. Many buyers' attorneys wait out that window or price the risk. The final-once-the-board-votes answer is the trap. The building department enforces a ZBA decision; it does not overrule it, and the town board does not ratify variances or permits.

blocks.html: Their attorney moves the closing to day 34 and asks the town clerk for a certification that no proceeding was served. None was. The permit runs with the property and its conditions, so the Hollises' deed now comes with a promise: one unit is owner-occupied, always.

blocks.text: The pond, and the backup buyer

blocks.html: Before the Hollises signed, a backup buyer had circled. Glen Ostrowski, a contractor, wanted two things: an in-ground pool 60 feet from the pond, and to split off the back 0.9 acre as a building lot. Jordan's research for him is worth keeping, because the Hollises will ask the same pool question next summer.

The filed subdivision map from 1979, at the county clerk, carries a note the planning board required as a condition of approval: “No structures or clearing within 100 feet of the wetland line shown hereon.” The town also has a wetlands law; its conservation advisory council reviews applications near wetlands and advises the planning board, which issues the town's wetlands permits. The state's own freshwater wetlands map does not show the pond, and Glen says that settles it.

blocks.q: Glen says the old DEC wetlands map does not show the pond, so a pool 60 feet away needs nothing special. Jordan's best response?
c: The map note and the town wetlands law reach it, and DEC no longer uses old maps
He is right: if the state map does not show a wetland, there is nothing to regulate
The county health department decides alone, since pools affect the groundwater
The architectural review board decides it, since a pool is a design feature
blocks.x: Three layers apply. The planning board's map note bars structures within 100 feet; the town wetlands law adds local review; and since 2025 DEC regulates by the wetland's actual characteristics rather than its old maps, so an owner asks DEC for a jurisdictional determination. Relying on the old map is the trap. The health department does not decide wetland buffers, and an ARB reviews design, not environmental limits.

blocks.html: The split was a separate question. Dividing a lot into two building lots is a subdivision, so it goes to the planning board, which applies the zoning's minimum lot size and the town's subdivision rules. The new lot would need its own well and septic, which brings in the county health department. Larger realty subdivisions, five or more lots, need state health approval before the map can be filed, through the county.

blocks.q: The property fronts a county road. Which statement about Glen's two-lot split is accurate?
c: The ZBA approves the split, and the county stays out because just two lots are created
The town board approves the split by local law
The planning board approves it, and the county planning agency may get a referral
The county health department approves it, since each new lot needs a septic and well
blocks.x: Subdivision approval belongs to the planning board. Because the parcel sits on a county road, certain zoning and planning actions must be referred to the county planning agency under General Municipal Law 239-m. The health department answer is the trap: it reviews the new lot's well and septic, but it does not approve the subdivision itself. The ZBA enters only if a lot needs a variance.

blocks.html: One gap remained. The building department's folder had nothing before 1990, and the clerk said older plans were in off-site storage. Jordan wanted the original 1979 plans to see whether the lower level was ever shown as finished. The clerk handed over a Freedom of Information Law request form.

blocks.q: Jordan files a FOIL request for the archived plans. What must the town do first?
c: Produce every record within 30 calendar days, or the request is deemed granted
Respond within 10 business days, or Jordan has to refile with the county clerk
Respond to it if the request comes from the owner or the owner's attorney
Acknowledge or respond within 5 business days
blocks.x: Under the Public Officers Law, an agency must respond to a FOIL request within 5 business days: grant it, deny it in writing, or acknowledge it with an approximate date for the response. The owner-or-attorney answer is the trap: building records are generally public, and anyone may request them. Nothing is deemed granted by silence; the remedy for a denial is an administrative appeal.

blocks.html: The plans arrived in three weeks. The 1979 drawing showed the lower level as unfinished storage and a garage. That settled the CO question for good and became one more page in the disclosure package Doreen's attorney sent to the Hollises. Diane's review note on the file was two lines long: “Every fact on the listing came from the office that controls it. That is the job.” The house closed at $512,000, $18,000 under Doreen's first number and a month later than she wanted, with no renegotiation after contract and no surprise at the table.

items: Pull records before listing: CO and permits from the building department, the assessment card, tax payment status from the receiver, septic and well files from the county health department, and filed maps from the county clerk.
Quote each fact from the office that controls it. The assessor's card does not prove legality, and a septic approval caps the bedroom count you can advertise.
Close open permits before contract. The building department that issued the permit is the only office that can sign it off.

Match the request to the right board: a special permit when the code allows a use on conditions, a use variance when it does not, the planning board for any lot split, with county referral on county roads.
Wetlands are layered: filed map notes, town wetlands law and DEC jurisdiction can each apply, and DEC no longer relies on its old maps.
Never promise an approval, and time closings around the 30-day window to challenge a board decision.

lessons.title: Case file: Four Doorbells on Midwood Street
lessons.tagline: A limestone in a historic district is listed as a legal three-family plus a garden unit. The city's databases disagree, one agency at a time.
objectives: Research a New York City property's legal use, violations, liens and landmark status in DOB, HPD, DOF, ACRIS and LPC records
Decide what a violation or unpaid municipal charge means for a buyer, a lender and the closing
Apply cellar, certificate of occupancy and registration rules to a seller's rent roll
Structure contract terms that put the cost of curing violations on the right party

blocks.title: The listing that looks too good
blocks.html: Farah Haddad is a nurse at Kings County Hospital with a preapproval and one goal: a house where rent from tenants covers most of her mortgage. Jordan represents her under a written buyer agency agreement. The listing, from a Flatbush brokerage, is a 1910 limestone row house on Midwood Street in the Prospect Lefferts Gardens Historic District: “Legal 3-family plus garden unit. Four rent rolls, $9,600 a month. Tax class 1. Delivered with tenants. $1,650,000.” Farah loves it and wants to bid tonight. Jordan asks for one evening to run the address through the city's public records. The first search, on the Department of Buildings site, turns up something Farah does not expect: there is no certificate of occupancy on file at all.

blocks.q: There is no CO on file for this 1910 row house. What is the right conclusion?
c: The building is illegal, and no bank will lend on a house without a CO
Pre-1938 buildings need no CO unless altered; legal use is shown other ways
The seller has to obtain a CO from HPD before any closing can happen
The house is treated as a one-family until LPC issues a certificate of appropriateness
blocks.x: New York City did not require certificates of occupancy for buildings completed before 1938 unless a later alteration changed the use, egress or occupancy. Legal use is then shown by other records, and DOB's borough office can issue a Letter of No Objection confirming it. The illegal-building answer is the trap. HPD does not issue COs, and an LPC certificate concerns design, not occupancy.

blocks.html: So how does a buyer know the house is a legal three-family rather than a one-family someone cut up? Jordan stacks the evidence. DOF's records describe a three-family building. HPD's registration history lists three units going back to the 1990s. The 1940 tax photo from the Municipal Archives shows three mailboxes by the door. None of that is a CO, and Priya will likely ask the seller to apply to DOB's Brooklyn borough office for a Letter of No Objection confirming three-family use, which a lender's attorney may also want. Jordan writes all of it into a short memo for Farah, because the duty of disclosure runs to the client: Farah gets everything Jordan finds, good and bad, in writing, before she bids.

blocks.text: Evening one: the Department of Buildings

blocks.html: Jordan pulls the property profile from the DOB online systems: the older Buildings Information System for historic filings and DOB NOW for recent ones. There is no CO and no alteration that changed the use, which fits a pre-1938 building. But there are two other entries.

blocks.title: DOB record, Midwood Street (summary)
blocks.html:
Complaint, 2023: “Illegal conversion: occupied apartment in cellar.” Inspector gained access; condition observed.
ECB violation, 2023: Work without a permit: kitchen and bathroom installed in cellar. Hearing at OATH: respondent in default. Penalty imposed $6,250. Penalty: PAID. Violation status: OPEN. Certificate of correction: none.
Permits: 2009 plumbing permit for the second-floor bathroom, signed off. No permits for the cellar.

The listing's “garden unit” is the cellar apartment. Jordan measures the street-side windows in the listing photos against the stoop and the curb: well over half of that floor's height sits below the curb. In New York City that makes it a cellar, not a basement, and a cellar cannot lawfully be rented as an apartment.

blocks.q: How should the $1,700 a month from the cellar unit figure in Farah's analysis?
c: Count it, because the tenant has paid on time for three years
Count half of it, as a cushion against a possible city vacate order
Leave it out; a cellar cannot be a legal apartment, and the city has cited it
Count it in full once the seller pays the ECB penalty and the record shows paid
blocks.x: A cellar, with more than half its height below curb level, cannot be legally occupied as an apartment, and DOB has already cited it. The income is illegal and could end with a vacate order. The paid-penalty answer is the trap: paying a fine does not legalize the use or even close the violation. Farah's numbers should rest on the three legal units.

blocks.html: Farah asks the obvious follow-up: the record says the penalty was paid, so isn't the violation over? It is not. The OATH penalty and the DOB violation are two different things.

blocks.q: What closes the ECB violation that shows “Penalty: PAID, Status: OPEN”?
c: A certificate of correction accepted by DOB, after the cellar is restored
Nothing more; once OATH is paid, DOB marks it closed after a year
A letter from the seller's attorney confirming the cellar tenant has moved out
A vote of Community Board 9 recommending that the city dismiss it
blocks.x: A DOB violation stays open in the city's records, even after the OATH penalty is paid, until the owner fixes the condition and DOB accepts a certificate of correction. Here that means removing the cellar kitchen and ending the residential use. The it-closes-itself answer is the trap. Community Boards advise on land use; they do not dismiss violations.

blocks.title: Paid is not closed
blocks.html: Agents read “PAID” and move on. Lenders, title companies and buyers' attorneys read “OPEN.” An open DOB violation shows up in the municipal departmental searches ordered at contract, and a buyer who closes over it inherits both the condition and the paperwork.

Jordan calls the listing agent, Vic Lombardo, to ask about the cellar. Vic is cheerful about it: “Everybody in the neighborhood has a garden unit. The buyer can deal with it.” Vic represents the seller, so Jordan does not expect loyalty from him, but Vic still owes Farah honesty, and an ad that calls an illegal cellar a rentable unit is a misrepresentation that puts Vic's license and his broker's at risk. Jordan does not argue the point on the phone. Jordan documents the conversation and lets the records do the talking in the offer.

Next, HPD's public database. A three-family is a multiple dwelling under the Housing Maintenance Code, so it must register with HPD every year. HPD's page shows the registration expired last September, and three open violations.

head: Class
Apartment
Condition
What the class means
rows: Window guards missing in a unit where a child under 11 lives
Water leak and stained ceiling in the kitchen
Required owner and managing agent notice not posted in the lobby
Emergency Repair Program: HPD's contractor restored heat, January 2025, $3,400
Billed by DOF; unpaid charges become a tax lien
blocks.caption: HPD record for the building

blocks.q: The seller's tenant in Apartment 2 stops paying rent. Before Farah owns the building, what does the lapsed HPD registration mean for the seller?
c: Nothing; HPD registration is voluntary for buildings under six units
The seller owes a late fee but may still bring any eviction case it likes
The tenant's lease is void until the building registers again
The seller cannot sue for nonpayment until the building is registered
blocks.x: Owners of multiple dwellings who fail to register with HPD cannot recover possession for nonpayment of rent while out of compliance, and they face civil penalties. Farah will have to register within days of closing. The voluntary answer is the trap: registration is required for buildings with three or more units. A missing registration does not void anyone's lease.

blocks.html: The window guard violation needs no explanation to Farah, a pediatric nurse. It is a Class C, immediately hazardous condition. The ERP charge is the subtler problem: when an owner ignores a heat violation, HPD can send its own contractor, then bill the owner through the Department of Finance. Unpaid, the charge becomes a tax lien on the building.

blocks.q: Who is responsible for the $3,400 Emergency Repair Program charge if it is unpaid at closing?
c: The seller alone, as a personal debt that does not affect the building
HPD, which absorbs the cost because it chose to send its own contractor
It is a lien on the property, so title will require payment at closing
The Apartment 3 tenant, who called in the heat complaint that started it
blocks.x: Unpaid HPD repair charges are billed by DOF and become a tax lien against the property, so the title company will collect them from the seller's proceeds at closing. The personal-debt answer is the trap: the charge follows the building, which is exactly why title searches look for it. HPD does not absorb the cost, and the tenant owes nothing for reporting a violation.

blocks.text: Evening two: Finance, the City Register and Water

blocks.html: The Department of Finance property page shows tax class 1, which covers one- to three-family homes and fits three legal units. Property taxes are current. The Notice of Property Value from January shows the market value DOF uses for assessment. The DEP water and sewer account is a different story: $6,800 overdue, with a notice that the property may be included in the next lien sale.

blocks.q: If the seller had somehow legalized the cellar as a fourth apartment, what would change at the Department of Finance?
c: The building would move from tax class 1 to tax class 2
Nothing; DOF taxes all small buildings in tax class 1
The building would move to tax class 4 as an investment
The property would pay the RPTT annually instead of tax
blocks.x: Four or more residential units put a building in tax class 2, which carries a different assessment regime from class 1 homes. That is why a listing claiming four rentals and tax class 1 should make an agent look harder. The class 4 answer is the trap: class 4 is commercial and industrial property, not rental housing. The RPTT is a one-time transfer tax.

blocks.html: Jordan explains the lien sale to Farah. Overdue water and sewer charges are already a lien on the property. In a lien sale, the city sells that lien to a private lienholder, who adds interest and fees and can eventually foreclose. The seller will pay it at closing either way, but the price goes up once the lien is sold.

blocks.q: The seller's agent says the water arrears are “a DEP billing issue, not a title issue.” What is the accurate response?
c: Overdue water charges are a lien on the property, paid at closing
He is right; DEP can sue the seller, so the buyer can ignore the balance
Water charges become a lien after HPD certifies them to the City Register
The buyer pays them after closing, since water service runs with the meter
blocks.x: In New York City, overdue water and sewer charges are a lien on the property, and the city can sell that lien. The title company will require the balance paid from the seller's proceeds. The HPD answer is the trap: HPD has nothing to do with water billing, and no certification step is needed for the lien to exist. A buyer who agrees to pay after closing is paying the seller's debt.

blocks.html: Farah has a tax question of her own. The January Notice of Property Value puts DOF's market value for the building at $1,182,000, far below the asking price, with an assessed value lower still. Will her tax bill jump the day she pays $1.5 million? Jordan walks her through how the city does what a town assessor and receiver of taxes do upstate. DOF is the city's assessor: it values every property each year and sets the assessed value the tax rate is applied to. DOF is also the collector, billing the tax and keeping the accounts. For a class 1 home, state law caps how fast the assessed value can rise: no more than 6% in a year and 20% over five years. Increases from physical changes, such as new construction, are added outside the caps. A sale does not reset the assessment to the price.

blocks.q: Farah closes at $1,555,000 and changes nothing about the building that year. What happens to her class 1 assessed value the following year?
c: DOF resets it to a percentage of the $1,555,000 purchase price
It can rise no more than 6%, as nothing physical changed
It stays frozen for five years after the sale to a new owner
The Tax Commission sets it at the price shown on the deed
blocks.x: Class 1 assessed values can grow no more than 6% a year and 20% over five years, and a sale does not reset them to the purchase price. Only physical changes, like Farah's future rear extension, add value outside the caps. The reset answer is the trap, because many buyers coming from other states expect it. The Tax Commission hears appeals; it does not set values from deeds.

blocks.html: The other half of the conversation is what Farah can do if she thinks DOF has it wrong. In a town, an owner grieves to the Board of Assessment Review, usually in May, and a homeowner can then go to Small Claims Assessment Review. The city works differently. A factual mistake on the notice, such as the wrong number of units or the wrong square footage, can go to DOF itself in a Request for Review. A challenge to the value goes to the New York City Tax Commission, an independent agency that hears assessment appeals. Its filing deadline comes in March: mid-March for class 1 homes, early March for other classes. Jordan puts a reminder in Farah's closing checklist for the following winter.

blocks.q: If Farah believes DOF has overvalued her building, where does she appeal the assessment?
c: The Board of Assessment Review, on Grievance Day in May
Community Board 9, which reviews values in its district
The New York City Tax Commission, by its March deadline
The Board of Standards and Appeals, which hears property appeals
blocks.x: In New York City, assessment appeals go to the Tax Commission, an independent agency, with deadlines in early to mid-March depending on tax class. DOF's Request for Review fixes factual errors but does not replace a Tax Commission filing. The Board of Assessment Review is the trap: that is the town and village route, not the city's. The BSA hears zoning appeals, and community boards are advisory.

blocks.html: Last, ACRIS, the City Register's online system. Jordan finds the 2004 deed into the seller, a 2019 mortgage for $620,000, and no satisfaction of an older 1998 mortgage from the prior owner. That last item is for the title company and Priya, Farah's attorney, to clear.

blocks.q: Farah asks what ACRIS will and will not show. Which item would Jordan NOT expect to find there?
c: Deeds conveying the property to the current owner
Mortgages and recorded satisfactions of mortgages
Open HPD housing code violations in the building
Recorded easements and other recorded agreements
blocks.x: ACRIS is the City Register's system of recorded documents: deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, easements and similar instruments. HPD violations live in HPD's own database, and DOB violations in DOB's. Satisfactions are the tempting pick, but a lender's satisfaction of mortgage is a recorded document, which is exactly how Jordan spotted the missing one.

blocks.html: The building sits inside a historic district, so Jordan checks the Landmarks Preservation Commission's records. The front windows were replaced in 2021 with white vinyl one-over-one sashes, where the district's buildings have wood windows. LPC sent a Warning Letter in 2022. No permit followed.

Farah had planned a rear extension and a roof deck. A landmark violation matters for exactly that reason: LPC violations stay with the property until corrected, and DOB permits can be held up while one is active. A new owner is responsible for correcting work a prior owner did, even though she did not do it.

blocks.q: What resolves the LPC window violation?
c: An LPC permit legalizing the work or approving replacement windows
Paying the fine LPC imposes, which removes the violation
A DOB permit for new windows, which overrides the Warning Letter
Selling the house, since violations are personal to the owner cited
blocks.x: LPC violations are cured by getting an LPC permit that legalizes the work, if the Commission finds it acceptable, or by doing corrective work under a new permit. Paying a fine does not remove the underlying violation, which is the trap. DOB cannot override LPC on designated property, and the violation stays with the building after a sale.

blocks.title: Five databases, one evening
blocks.html: DOB (BIS and DOB NOW): COs, permits, complaints, DOB and ECB violations. HPD Online: registration, housing code violations, ERP charges, litigation. DOF: tax class, assessment and tax bills. ACRIS: recorded deeds, mortgages and liens. LPC's map and permit search: whether a building is designated and its permit and violation history. Add DEP for water and sewer and the Department of City Planning's ZoLa map for zoning. All are public and free, and none replaces the attorney's formal searches at contract.

Farah's rear extension raises one more lookup. On ZoLa, the lot sits in a medium-density residence district. Using the lot size and DOF's building square footage, Jordan estimates the house already uses close to all the floor area the zoning allows. A large extension could need more than a design approval.

blocks.q: If the extension would exceed the floor area the zoning allows, what approvals would Farah need?
c: A BSA variance, LPC approval for the design, and then a DOB permit
Community Board 9's approval, which replaces the need for a variance
A DOB permit, since one- to three-family homes are exempt from zoning
HPD approval, because the building is a registered multiple dwelling
blocks.x: Relief from zoning in New York City comes from the Board of Standards and Appeals; LPC must approve the design on designated property, usually with a certificate of appropriateness after a hearing; and DOB issues the permit last. The Community Board answer is the trap: its vote is advisory. Small homes are not exempt from zoning, and HPD does not approve construction.

blocks.html: Jordan rebuilds Farah's numbers on three legal units. The legal rents total $7,900 a month. Her lender will count 75% of the rents from the two units she will not live in, since she plans to move into Apartment 1 at $2,400.

blocks.title: Income the lender will count
blocks.html:
Listing's claimed rent roll: $9,600 a month.
Less the cellar unit (illegal): $1,700. Legal rent roll: $7,900.
Less Apartment 1, which Farah will occupy: $2,400. Rental units: $5,500.
Lender counts 75%: $5,500 x 0.75 = $4,125 a month, not the $7,200 that 75% of the listing's $9,600 would suggest.

blocks.q: Using the lender's 75% rule, how much monthly rental income would the lender have counted if Farah relied on the listing's full rent roll and did not occupy a unit?
blocks.x: $9,600 x 0.75 = $7,200. The $5,925 figure (75% of the legal $7,900) is the trap if you forget the question asks about the listing's claim. The gap between $7,200 and the realistic $4,125 is $3,075 a month of qualifying income that never existed, which is why rent rolls get checked against legal use before an offer.

blocks.html: One more line in the listing bothers Jordan: “delivered with tenants.” The cellar tenant, Mr. Pryce, has lived there three years. The seller's agent says the seller will “just change the locks before closing” to deliver the cellar empty.

blocks.q: What is wrong with the plan to change the locks on the cellar tenant?
c: Nothing, because a tenant of an illegal unit has no rights to the space
It is fine if the seller first gives him 14 days' written notice to leave
It is fine if the seller returns his security deposit that day
Removing an occupant of 30-plus days without a court order is illegal
blocks.x: Under RPAPL 768, removing a lawful occupant of 30 or more consecutive days, or anyone with a lease, without a court order is an unlawful eviction, a misdemeanor with civil penalties. An illegal unit does not strip the occupant of protection from self-help, and Farah does not want to buy a building with that history. The notice answer is the trap: notice does not replace a court order.

blocks.html: Priya drafts the contract rider. Farah offers $1,540,000, reflecting three legal units and the cost of cures. The seller must correct and certify the HPD Class C and B violations before closing; remove the cellar kitchen, end the residential use through lawful means, and obtain DOB's acceptance of a certificate of correction; pay the ERP charge and water arrears from closing proceeds; and deposit $15,000 in escrow with his attorney for the LPC window correction, released when LPC issues the permit.

blocks.q: The seller offers instead a $10,000 credit and an “as is” sale with all violations open. What is the main risk for Farah?
c: Nothing; a credit is usually better for a buyer than a seller's cure
Open violations and unpaid liens follow the building to her
Her CO will be revoked the moment the deed is recorded
The credit violates RESPA and is void at the closing table
blocks.x: Violations stay with the building and the new owner must cure them; charges like ERP and water become liens on the property. A credit that undercounts the true cost of the cellar cure, the LPC windows and lost cellar rent leaves Farah short. The CO answer is the trap: there is no CO to revoke here, and closing does not trigger any revocation. Credits themselves are common and lawful when disclosed to the lender.

blocks.html: The seller took the escrow version at $1,555,000. The cellar tenant accepted a relocation payment and moved to a legal apartment in Flatbush, under a written agreement his own lawyer reviewed. DOB accepted the certificate of correction six weeks later, the HPD violations were certified corrected, and the title company collected $10,200 for ERP and water at the closing table. LPC approved wood replacement windows the following spring, and the escrow paid for most of them.

Farah's first week as an owner had its own municipal checklist, and Jordan sent it to her the day after closing: register the building with HPD in her own name and name a 24-hour emergency contact; open the DEP water account and the DOF property tax account in her name; calendar the annual window guard and lead paint notices to tenants that go out every January; and keep the LPC permit and DOB sign-offs in one binder, because the next buyer's agent will run the same five databases on her. Diane read the file and added one line: “The best price we got her was the $95,000 we kept her from paying for a unit that does not exist.”

blocks.title: Public records versus the attorney's searches
blocks.html: Jordan's evening of database work is for judgment: whether to bid, what to offer, what to ask for. It does not replace the formal municipal departmental searches (building, housing, fire, street report, landmark, emergency repair) that the buyer's attorney orders through the title company after the contract is signed. Those searches, certified and dated, are what the closing relies on. The agent's job is to make sure nothing in them comes as a surprise.

items: A missing CO is normal for a pre-1938 building; legal use is then confirmed from other records or a DOB Letter of No Objection.
Count only legal units. A cellar cannot be a legal apartment, and a DOB violation stays open until DOB accepts a certificate of correction, whatever was paid at OATH.
HPD registration is a precondition for a nonpayment case, and HPD Emergency Repair charges and DEP water arrears become liens that title will collect.
LPC violations run with the property, can hold up DOB permits, and are cured by an LPC permit, not a fine.
Check each claim against the agency that controls it: DOB, HPD, DOF, ACRIS, DEP, LPC and ZoLa, then let the attorney's searches and rider put the cost where it belongs.

roleplays.title: The Town Hall Runaround
roleplays.setting: A town in northern Westchester. You represent the buyer, Leo, on a 1960s ranch with a septic system, water out back, and an addition the seller built himself.
roleplays.goal: Send each of Leo's questions to the right agency, without guessing at answers that belong to them.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Leo, an anxious first-time buyer, and occasionally a town building department clerk, during due diligence on a Westchester ranch with an unpermitted addition that violates a side setback, a septic system, water on the lot, a basement 'in-law suite', and a recent tax increase. Ask one question at a time and push for quick answers ('can't you just tell me?'). The learner must route each question to the correct body: building department (permits, CO), ZBA (area variance), county health department (septic), conservation advisory council and DEC (wetlands), planning board (subdivision), municipal engineer (roads, sewer), assessor (value), receiver of taxes (payment), elected town board (tax rate). Grade on correct agency, not guessing, and practical next steps.
opening: {day}. Leo is under contract on a 1960s ranch in {town}: septic, {water} out back, and a {addition} the seller built himself.
Leo calls from the driveway of the {town} ranch. The inspection is done, the attorney review clock is running, and he has a list.
You and Leo sit in your car outside {town} Town Hall. He has six questions, and each one belongs to a different office.

say: The seller says the {addition} is 'basically legal.' How do I find out?
Is the {addition} legal? The seller swears it is.

moves.text: We check the building department file for a permit, inspections, and a certificate of completion.
moves.fb: Correct. The building department issues permits and COs and is the gatekeeper for construction records.
moves.react: Okay. Building department first. Can you request the file?

moves.text: We pull the building department file. No permit and no final sign-off means it isn't legal yet.
moves.fb: Right. Permits, inspections and certificates live with the building department.
moves.react: So 'basically legal' means nothing until we see paper.

moves.text: Ask the zoning board of appeals. They handle anything to do with whether a structure is legal.
moves.fb: The ZBA only matters if the work needs a variance. Start with the building department's permit file.
moves.react: The ZBA? Okay, I'll call them... I guess.

moves.text: If the seller says so, it's fine. Sellers have to tell the truth about permits on the disclosure form.
moves.fb: Never rely on a seller's characterization of permits. Verify with the building department.
moves.react: Great, one less thing to worry about.

moves.text: The planning board approves every addition in town, so their minutes will show whether it was approved.
moves.fb: The planning board handles subdivisions and site plans. Building permits come from the building department.
moves.react: Planning board minutes. Where do I find those?

moves.text: It's on the tax bill. If the assessor is taxing it, the town has signed off, so it's legal by default.
moves.fb: Being assessed doesn't make work legal. Assessors value property; the building department permits it.
moves.react: Oh nice, then it's legal. It's on the bill.

say: The clerk calls back: "No permit for any {addition}, and it's 6 feet from the side line; code requires 15." Leo: "Can they make him tear it down?"
Leo, reading the clerk's email: "No permit, and it's 6 feet from the line instead of 15. What happens now?"

moves.text: It's a zoning violation. He'd need a permit and an area variance from the ZBA. Priya can make it a condition.
moves.fb: Right path: permit through the building department, area variance from the ZBA for the setback, handled through the contract.
moves.react: A condition in the contract. I'll call Priya.

moves.text: Area variance from the ZBA, then a permit. Or we ask for a credit. Your attorney picks the route.
moves.fb: Correct. An area variance addresses dimensional rules like setbacks; the contract decides who carries the risk.
moves.react: Variance or credit. Okay, that I can work with.

moves.text: It's probably fine. Towns rarely enforce old setback issues, so I wouldn't lose sleep over it right now.
moves.fb: Maybe true in practice, but you're guessing about enforcement. The violation is real and belongs in the contract.
moves.react: Probably fine is not what I want to hear.

moves.text: The planning board can approve it. They review anything built too close to a property line in this town.
moves.fb: The planning board handles subdivisions and site plans, not setback variances for an existing house. That's the ZBA.
moves.react: Planning board. Okay, I'll put that down.

moves.text: He'd need a use variance, which means proving no reasonable return. That's nearly impossible to get.
moves.fb: A setback is dimensional, so it's an area variance with a balancing test, not a use variance.
moves.react: Nearly impossible? Should I walk away?

moves.text: Once he sells, the violation stays with him, not with the house. You'd take it clean at the closing.
moves.fb: Violations run with the property. The buyer inherits them unless the contract deals with them.
moves.react: Clean. Great, then I don't care.

say: Next: the septic. How old is it, and was it ever approved?
Who would know if the septic was ever approved?

moves.text: The county health department keeps septic approvals. Let's request the file and book a septic inspection.
moves.fb: Correct agency and the right practical step: records from the health department, condition from an inspector.
moves.react: Records and an inspection. Booking it now.

moves.text: That's the county health department, not the town. I'll request the file today; you hire a septic pro.
moves.fb: Right. On-site septic approval sits with the county health department.

moves.text: Ask the seller for whatever paperwork he has on it, and we'll go from there if anything's missing.
moves.fb: Fine as a start, but the official record is with the county health department. Go to the source.
moves.react: He'll just say it's fine again.

moves.text: The town engineer handles septic here. Call his office and they'll have the original approval on file for you.
moves.fb: The engineer handles roads and sewer and water connections. On-site septic approval sits with the health department.

moves.text: DEC approves every septic system in the state, so we'd request the file from their regional office.
moves.fb: DEC handles state environmental permits. Individual septic approvals generally sit with the county health department.

moves.text: Your home inspector already checked it, and that counts as the approval. No need for more records.
moves.fb: A home inspection isn't a government approval. Get the health department record and a septic-specific inspection.

say: And {water} out back. Can I build a little dock or clear the brush along it?
I want to put a dock by {water}. Do I need anyone's okay?

moves.text: Ask the town's conservation council or wetlands office, plus the DEC. It may be regulated, so ask first.
moves.fb: Correct. Local wetlands bodies and DEC regulate work near water; clearing or building can require permits.

moves.text: Water often means wetland rules. The town wetlands office and DEC decide. We ask before closing.
moves.fb: Right. Environmental questions go to the conservation advisory council and, for state permits, DEC.

moves.text: I'm not sure about the water. You'd have to figure it out yourself after closing, I'm afraid.
moves.fb: You can name the conservation council and DEC instead of leaving the buyer guessing.
moves.react: After closing? Then it's too late.

moves.text: It's your property. Build whatever you want on your own land. Nobody regulates a small private dock.
moves.fb: Wetlands near water are often regulated by the town and DEC. Building without permits can mean fines and removal.
moves.react: My land, my dock. Love it.

moves.text: The ZBA handles anything built near water, so we'd apply there for a variance for the dock and brush.
moves.fb: The ZBA handles zoning variances. Wetlands permits come from the local wetlands body and DEC.
moves.react: A variance for a dock? Weird, but okay.

moves.text: The Army Corps of Engineers is the only agency involved with ponds and streams anywhere in New York.
moves.fb: The Corps can matter for some waters, but local wetlands bodies and DEC are the first stops.

say: The taxes jumped last year. Who do I even ask about why?
Why did the taxes go up? Who decides that?

moves.text: The assessor values it, the receiver confirms what's paid, the town board sets the rate.
moves.fb: Correct split: assessor values, receiver collects, elected legislative body sets the rate.
moves.react: Three offices for one bill. Okay.

moves.text: Two parts: value and rate. Value is the assessor's; the rate comes from elected boards' budgets.
moves.fb: Right. Tax = assessed value x rate. The assessor sets value; elected bodies adopt budgets and rates.

moves.text: Ask the assessor. They handle all the tax stuff in town, both the value and the bill itself.
moves.fb: Half right: the assessor explains value, but doesn't set the rate or collect the tax.

moves.text: Taxes are the receiver's call; they decide the amount. Call the receiver of taxes and ask them why.
moves.fb: The receiver only collects. The assessor values and the elected board sets the rate.
moves.react: The receiver decides? Okay, calling now.

moves.text: The state set it. New York has a statewide property tax, so call Albany about the increase.
moves.fb: NY has no state real property tax. Counties, towns, school districts and villages levy it.

moves.text: The planning board raised it when they approved those new houses nearby. Their minutes will say why.
moves.fb: The planning board doesn't set taxes. Legislative bodies adopt budgets and rates.

say: The listing says 'mother-daughter.' There's a second kitchen downstairs. Can I rent it out?
Could I rent the basement apartment? It has its own kitchen.

moves.text: Only if the CO and zoning allow it. Let's check the building department's CO for one family or two.
moves.fb: Correct. The certificate of occupancy shows the legal use; zoning decides whether a second unit is allowed.
moves.react: One family or two. Let's find out.

moves.text: A second kitchen isn't a legal unit. The CO and zoning decide, and the building department has both.
moves.fb: Right. Don't let marketing language like 'mother-daughter' stand in for a CO.

moves.text: Probably, lots of people do it around here. I'd check with the town at some point to be safe.
moves.fb: You're guessing about legality. The CO and zoning answer it, so check before he relies on the income.

moves.text: Yes. If there's a second kitchen, the town must have already approved a second unit, or it couldn't exist.
moves.fb: Kitchens get installed without permits all the time. Only the CO and zoning establish legal use.

moves.text: Ask the ZBA for a use variance after closing. They grant those for basement units all the time.
moves.fb: Use variances need unnecessary hardship and are hard to get. Check the CO and zoning first.

moves.text: The health department decides that, since it's about how many people the septic can handle.
moves.fb: Septic capacity matters, but legal use comes from zoning and the CO at the building department.

say: Can't you just tell me? You've seen a hundred of these.
I trust you. Just give me your best guess and I'll go with it.

moves.text: I can tell you who decides, and I'll make the calls with you. Guessing can cost you money.
moves.fb: Right. Licensees route questions to the agency that decides rather than giving opinions outside their role.

moves.text: My guess isn't worth your down payment. The record is. Let's get it from the office that owns it.
moves.fb: Correct. Written records from the right agency protect the buyer.

moves.text: Honestly, most of these turn out fine, but don't quote me on that. Let's look into it anyway.
moves.fb: Soft reassurance without basis. Name the agency instead.

moves.text: Sure. It's all fine. I've never seen a town make a buyer undo anything, so I'd just go ahead and close.
moves.fb: Guessing on permits and regulations can expose the buyer to costly violations, and you to liability.

moves.text: I'll tell the attorney it's all been checked already so we can move faster through the review.
moves.fb: Saying something was checked when it wasn't is a misrepresentation to your own client's attorney.

moves.text: Fine: the {addition} needs a variance, the septic is fine, and the water isn't regulated. Done.
moves.fb: Two guesses dressed as facts. Each one belongs to a specific agency.

say: The lot is three acres. Could I split off an acre someday and build a second house?
Long term, I'd like to sell off part of the lot for a house. Who approves that?

moves.text: That's a subdivision, so it's the planning board, under zoning minimums. Let's check lot sizes now.
moves.fb: Correct. The planning board handles subdivision approval and site plans.
moves.react: Planning board. Good to know before I buy.

moves.text: Subdivisions go to the planning board. Zoning sets minimum lot sizes, so we check those first.
moves.fb: Right. Zoning sets the rules; the planning board approves subdivisions.
moves.react: So it depends on lot size rules.

moves.text: Maybe. Lots of people do that out here. We can look into it after you close on the house.
moves.fb: Fine to defer, but naming the planning board helps him buy with clear expectations.

moves.text: The ZBA handles subdivisions. You'd apply there with a survey and they'd vote on it at a hearing.
moves.fb: The ZBA handles variances and appeals. Subdivision approval is the planning board's job.

moves.text: The town board approves each subdivision by passing a brand new local law for that one lot split.
moves.fb: Legislative bodies adopt zoning, but subdivision approval is the planning board's job.

moves.text: You can split it yourself with a new deed. Nobody needs to approve how you divide your own land.
moves.fb: Subdividing requires planning board approval. Deeding off a lot without it creates an illegal subdivision.

say: The seller's agent just texted: 'The {addition} is grandfathered, don't worry.' Is that a thing?
Listing agent says the {addition} is grandfathered. Does that settle it?

moves.text: Grandfathering covers things that were legal when built. It doesn't cover unpermitted work.
moves.fb: Correct. A nonconforming use must have been legal when established. Unpermitted work doesn't qualify.

moves.text: Only if it was legal when built. With no permit on file, it wasn't. Let's ask the agent for proof.
moves.fb: Right. The building department file settles it, not a text.

moves.text: Could be. Let's ask the seller's agent what they mean by it and see if they send anything over.
moves.fb: Asking is fine, but you should know the rule: unpermitted work isn't grandfathered.

moves.text: Yes. Anything over 20 years old is automatically grandfathered under state law, permit or not.
moves.fb: No such rule. Nonconforming status depends on legality when built, not age.

moves.text: Grandfathered means it can even be expanded, so you could make it bigger later if you wanted to.
moves.fb: Nonconforming uses generally cannot be expanded and can be lost if abandoned.

moves.text: If the agent said so in writing, that makes it legal. A text counts as written notice to the buyer, too.
moves.fb: An agent's statement doesn't change a violation. Only permits, COs and variances do.

say: The road out front floods, and I may hook into the sewer line someday. Who handles that?
Who do I talk to about the road drainage and a future sewer hookup?

moves.text: The municipal engineer handles roads, drainage and sewer and water connections. Let's call them.
moves.fb: Correct. The municipal engineer deals with roads, drainage and sewer and water connections.

moves.text: It's the town engineer's office: roads, drainage, sewer hookups. Let's ask about plans for the street.
moves.fb: Right. The engineer's office is the source for infrastructure questions.

moves.text: Call town hall and ask whoever answers. They'll point you to the right person eventually, I'd think.
moves.fb: Not wrong, but you could name the engineer's office directly.

moves.text: The county health department handles the roads and sewer lines as well as all the septic systems out here.
moves.fb: The health department handles septic. Roads and sewer connections are the engineer's domain.

moves.text: Ask the assessor. If the road floods, they'll lower your value and fix it with that money.
moves.fb: The assessor values property. They don't fix roads.

moves.text: The ZBA decides sewer hookups, since connecting changes how the property is used under the zoning.
moves.fb: The ZBA grants variances. Sewer connections run through the engineer.

roleplays.debrief: You practised matching each question to the right local body: the building department for permits and COs, the ZBA for area variances, the county health department for septic, the conservation council and DEC for wetlands, the planning board for subdivisions, and the municipal engineer for roads and sewer. The assessor values, the receiver collects, and the elected board sets the rate. Unpermitted work is never grandfathered, and you never guess at answers that belong to an agency.

questions.q: In a New York village, local laws, zoning and the budget are adopted by the:
c: Board of trustees
Town board
County legislature
Planning board
questions.x: The village board, the mayor and trustees, is the village's legislature. Planning board is the trap: it reviews site plans and subdivisions but does not adopt laws.

questions.q: A New York village's board of trustees is made up of:
c: Appointed zoning experts
County executives
The mayor and elected trustees
State assembly members
questions.x: The mayor and trustees form the board. Zoning experts are the trap: the zoning board of appeals is a separate appointed body.

questions.q: Which NYC agency issues building permits and certificates of occupancy?
c: Department of Finance
Department of Buildings
City Planning Commission
Department of Housing Preservation and Development
questions.x: DOB issues permits and COs and enforces the construction codes. Finance is the trap: it handles assessment and taxes.

questions.q: A buyer wants to confirm that a converted NYC loft has a valid certificate of occupancy. Which agency's records should be checked?
c: City Register
Department of Finance
Board of Standards and Appeals only
Department of Buildings
questions.x: Certificates of occupancy are DOB records. The City Register is the trap: it records deeds and mortgages.

questions.q: In New York City, deeds and mortgages are recorded with the City Register, which is part of the:
c: Department of Buildings
County clerk in every borough
Department of Finance
Department of State
questions.x: DOF assesses property, collects taxes and runs the City Register. The county clerk is the trap: outside NYC, county clerks record deeds.

questions.q: Which NYC agency assesses property and bills property taxes?
c: Department of Finance
Department of Buildings
Rent Guidelines Board
Department of City Planning
questions.x: DOF assesses and collects. DOB is the trap: it handles construction.

questions.q: In a New York village, the zoning ordinance and the annual budget are adopted by the:
c: Board of trustees
Planning board
Zoning board of appeals
Village clerk's office
questions.x: The elected board of trustees is the village's legislative body. The planning board and ZBA are appointed bodies that apply the law; the ZBA interprets zoning but cannot adopt it.

questions.q: Which of these local bodies is elected?
c: Planning board
Town board
Zoning board of appeals
Architectural review board
questions.x: The town board (supervisor and council members) is elected. The planning board, ZBA and ARB are appointed by it, even though they hold public hearings like elected bodies.

questions.q: Subdivision approval and the preparation of the master plan are functions of the:
c: Zoning board of appeals
Tax assessor
Planning board
Town engineer
questions.x: The planning board handles the master plan, subdivisions and site plans and advises other boards. The ZBA grants variances, which is why it is the common wrong pick.

questions.q: An owner wants permission to build a garage 5 feet closer to the lot line than the ordinance allows. The owner applies to the:
c: Planning board
Design review board
Building department
Zoning board of appeals
questions.x: Relief from a setback is an area variance, granted by the ZBA. The building department will deny the permit, but it has no power to vary the ordinance.

questions.q: The local office that issues building permits and certificates of occupancy and acts as the gatekeeper for construction is the:
c: Building department
Planning department
Receiver of taxes
Town engineer's office
questions.x: The building department issues permits, inspects, and issues COs. The planning department provides professional advice to boards but issues no permits.

questions.q: A village board that reviews and approves the exterior design of new construction and remodeling under the village's ordinance is the:
c: Zoning board of appeals
Architectural review board
Board of assessment review
Historic preservation commission
questions.x: The ARB approves design, materials and appearance under the village ordinance. A historic preservation commission also reviews exteriors, but only for designated landmarks and districts.

questions.q: The local body that advises on environmental issues, such as open space and wetlands, under municipal ordinances is the:
c: Planning department
Building department
Conservation advisory council
Landmarks commission
questions.x: A conservation advisory council (or wetlands commission) handles local environmental review and advice. DEC handles state-level permits, and the planning department advises on land use generally.

questions.q: A local historic preservation (landmark) commission typically:
c: Sets the tax rate for historic districts
Grants use variances to landmark owners
