Issues COs for restored landmark buildings
Designates landmarks and reviews changes
questions.x: Landmark commissions recommend designations and approve construction or remodeling of designated properties. COs still come from the building department.

questions.q: The official who determines the assessed value of each property in a town is the:
c: Receiver of taxes
Tax assessor
Town engineer
Town supervisor
questions.x: The assessor values property and keeps assessment records. The receiver collects the taxes, the classic swap.

questions.q: A closing attorney needs to confirm that the current year's property taxes have been paid. The attorney contacts the:
c: Tax assessor
Board of assessment review
Town clerk
Receiver of taxes
questions.x: The receiver of taxes (or treasurer) collects taxes and keeps payment records. The assessor sets values, not payments.

questions.q: Approval of a new residential septic system in New York generally comes from the:
c: County health department
Zoning board of appeals
Town building department
State DEC regional office
questions.x: Septic systems are approved by the county or local health department under Department of Health standards. DEC regulates larger discharges, which makes it the tempting state-level pick.

questions.q: Road maintenance and sewer and water connections in a town are typically overseen by the:
c: Tax assessor
Planning board
Town engineer
Building inspector
questions.x: The municipal engineer (often with the DPW) handles roads, sewer and water connections. The building inspector deals with construction on private lots, not public infrastructure.

questions.q: Each of the following is typically appointed rather than elected EXCEPT:
c: Planning board members
ZBA members
Village trustees
ARB members
questions.x: Village trustees are elected; they appoint the planning board, ZBA and ARB.

questions.q: The planning board performs each of the following functions EXCEPT:
c: Approving subdivision plats
Recommending the master plan
Advising other boards on land use
Granting use variances
questions.x: Use variances come from the ZBA. Subdivision, the master plan and advising other boards are planning board roles.

questions.q: The office that provides professional planning advice to a municipality's agencies and boards is the:
c: Planning department
Town engineer's office
Planning board
County clerk
questions.x: The planning department's professional staff advises boards and prepares studies. The planning board is the appointed citizen body that decides applications, the near-miss here.

questions.q: Every part of New York State that is not in a city lies within a:
c: Village
Hamlet
Borough
Town
questions.x: Every inch of the state outside a city is in a town. Villages sit inside towns, so not all town land is in a village.

questions.q: A village in New York is located:
c: Inside a town, handling some services itself
Outside any town, just like a city
Across county lines, run directly by the state
Inside a city, as one of its five boroughs
questions.x: A village sits inside a town and handles some services itself. Cities, not villages, stand outside town boundaries.

questions.q: The chief executive of a New York town is the:
c: Town mayor
Town supervisor
Town clerk
Town board chairman
questions.x: A town's chief executive is the supervisor, who also sits on the town board. Mayors run cities and villages.

questions.q: A village's elected chief executive is the:
c: Town supervisor of the surrounding town
Village manager hired by the trustees
Village mayor, also a trustee
County executive for that county
questions.x: A village is led by its mayor, who also sits on the village board of trustees. The town supervisor runs the town, not the village inside it.

questions.q: Which designation most often stops a private owner from replacing a slate roof with asphalt shingles?
c: National Register listing
State Register listing
An OPRHP survey of the neighborhood
Local landmark designation
questions.x: Local landmark designation and the local commission control a private owner's changes. State or National Register listing mostly triggers review of government-funded or permitted projects.

questions.q: Listing a house on the State or National Register mainly triggers review of:
c: Government-funded or permitted projects
Any exterior change by a private owner
All interior work inside the building
Every future sale of the property to a buyer
questions.x: Register listing (through OPRHP) mostly reaches projects with government money or permits. Restricting a private owner's exterior changes is the job of local landmarking.

questions.q: Planning board and ZBA members are usually appointed for staggered terms so that:
c: Any new mayor can replace every member
No one election can replace the board
The full board turns over every year
Only licensed planners can hold seats
questions.x: Staggered fixed terms mean no single election can remake a board at once. Members are typically residents with no special license.

questions.q: A town building inspector is typically:
c: Elected by town voters every four years
A volunteer resident with no training
A hired employee with state training
Appointed by the county health department
questions.x: The building inspector is a hired employee who must meet state code enforcement training requirements. Elected is the trap: voters elect the lawmakers, not the inspector.

questions.q: A ZBA denies a variance without giving any reasons on the record. The applicant may challenge the decision in:
c: A small claims assessment review
A ULURP review
A FOIL request
An Article 78 proceeding
questions.x: Appointed boards must follow the rules and give reasons, so arbitrary decisions can be challenged in an Article 78 proceeding. SCAR is for assessment disputes.

questions.q: A homeowner wants the town to rezone her street to allow two-family houses. Her request is directed at the:
c: Town board, which can change the rules
ZBA, which may rewrite the ordinance
Building inspector, who enforces the code
Planning department, which adopts local laws
questions.x: Only the elected legislative body can change the rules by rezoning. The ZBA applies and interprets the ordinance; it cannot rewrite it.

questions.q: A town homeowner disagrees with her assessment. Her first formal step is a grievance to the:
c: Town zoning board of appeals
Board of assessment review
Receiver of taxes
Town planning board
questions.x: After the tentative roll comes out, the owner grieves to the board of assessment review. The receiver only collects taxes; it does not change values.

questions.q: After an unsuccessful assessment grievance, a homeowner may next go to:
c: The ZBA for an area variance
The planning board for site plan review
Small claims assessment review (SCAR)
The receiver of taxes for a refund
questions.x: The path is board of assessment review, then SCAR or court. A ZBA variance concerns zoning, not valuation.

questions.q: A town plans to rezone land along a state highway. Under GML 239-m, the action must be referred to the:
c: NYS Department of State
Town zoning board of appeals
County health department
County planning agency
questions.x: GML 239-m requires referral of certain local zoning actions, such as those near a state or county road or municipal boundary, to the county planning agency. The ZBA hears variances, not referrals.

questions.q: On a local zoning action referred under GML 239-m, the county planning agency may:
c: Review it and recommend changes
Issue the building permit for it
Hold the only public hearing on it
Set the tax rate tied to it
questions.x: The county planning agency reviews referred actions and can recommend changes. Building permits come from the local building department.

questions.q: A buyer wants to split a lot and build a second house on the new parcel. The office to approach is the:
c: Zoning board of appeals
Planning board
Building department
Tax assessor
questions.x: Subdivision approval belongs to the planning board. The ZBA comes in only if the plan needs a variance.

questions.q: A buyer's attorney asks whether a finished basement was permitted and whether any violations are open. The agent checks with the:
c: Planning board
Receiver of taxes
Building department
County health department
questions.x: Permit history, COs and open violations are at the building department. The receiver of taxes only knows whether taxes are paid.

questions.q: Planning board and ZBA meetings in New York are open to the public under the:
c: Freedom of Information Law
General Municipal Law 239-m
Real Property Law 443
Open Meetings Law
questions.x: The Open Meetings Law opens board meetings to the public. FOIL is the neighboring law, but it covers requests for records, not attendance.

questions.q: Which step is typically part of applying to a local board such as the ZBA?
c: Notifying neighbors before a public hearing
Posting a bond with the receiver of taxes
Getting DOS approval of the plans first
Recording the application with the county clerk
questions.x: Board applications run on forms, plans, a fee, neighbor notice, a public hearing and a written decision. DOS licenses agents; it does not approve plans.

questions.q: A seller asks the agent to promise the buyer that the ARB will approve new windows. The agent should:
c: Promise it, since ARBs usually approve
Decline, since boards have discretion
Promise it if the windows look similar
Have the building inspector guarantee it
questions.x: Never promise an approval: boards have discretion and neighbors get a say. The building inspector cannot bind the ARB.

questions.q: A buyer's plan depends on getting a variance. The contract contingency should allow board review of roughly:
c: Ten business days
One to two years
One to three months
Forty-eight hours at the most
questions.x: A variance or ARB approval can take one to three months, so build that into the contingency. Ten days is the lead inspection window, a number from a different rule.

questions.q: NYC Community Board members are appointed by the:
c: Mayor
City Planning Commission
Department of City Planning
Borough president
questions.x: Community Boards have up to 50 unpaid members appointed by the borough president, half nominated by the area's Council members. The mayor appoints the LPC, the tempting mix-up.

questions.q: How many Community Boards does New York City have?
c: 5 (one per borough)
questions.x: There are 59 Community Boards citywide. 51 is the number of City Council districts and 62 is the number of cities in the state.

questions.q: In New York City, which agency handles water, sewer and asbestos rules?
c: Department of Environmental Conservation
Department of Environmental Protection
Department of Housing Preservation
Department of Buildings
questions.x: NYC's DEP handles water, sewer and asbestos rules. DEC is the state agency for wetlands and spills, the neighboring name that trips people up.

questions.q: Which statement about NYC's Department of Environmental Protection is correct?
c: It issues building permits and COs
It assesses property and collects real estate taxes
It handles water, sewer and asbestos rules
It designates landmarks and districts
questions.x: DEP covers water, sewer and asbestos. Permits and COs are DOB, assessment is DOF, and landmarks are the LPC.

questions.q: In New York City, rezonings go through ULURP, with binding decisions made by the:
c: Community Board and Borough President
Board of Standards and Appeals
Department of Buildings
City Planning Commission and Council
questions.x: Planning and rezoning run through City Planning, the City Planning Commission and the City Council under ULURP. Community Boards and Borough Presidents only advise.

questions.q: Each of the following plays a role in NYC planning and rezoning EXCEPT the:
c: Department of Finance
Department of City Planning
City Planning Commission
City Council
questions.x: DCP, the CPC and the City Council handle planning and rezoning. The Department of Finance assesses and collects taxes and runs the City Register.

questions.q: Residents of a Hudson Valley town want the zoning map changed so a farm can become a solar array. The body with power to amend the map is the:
c: Zoning board of appeals
Planning board
Town board
Building inspector
questions.x: Amending zoning is legislative, so the elected town board does it. The ZBA is quasi-judicial; it can grant variances but cannot rezone land.

questions.q: Members of a town planning board usually get their seats by:
c: Town-wide election
Election by the ZBA
Appointment by the governor
Appointment by the town board
questions.x: The elected town board appoints planning board members. Because planning boards hold public hearings, candidates often assume they are elected, which is the trap.

questions.q: A developer wants approval of a site plan for a 40-unit townhouse project that zoning already permits. The developer goes to the:
c: Planning board
Zoning board of appeals
Town board
Board of assessment review
questions.x: Site plan and subdivision review belong to the planning board. The ZBA is needed only if the project requires a variance, which it does not here.

questions.q: When a building inspector denies a permit because the inspector reads the zoning code a certain way, the owner can appeal that interpretation to the:
c: Zoning board of appeals
Town engineer
Planning board
Architectural review board
questions.x: The ZBA hears appeals from the building inspector's decisions and interprets the ordinance. The planning board reviews plans but does not hear appeals.

questions.q: A buyer's attorney wants to know whether a finished attic has a CO and whether any permits are still open. The attorney checks with the:
c: Board of assessment review
Tax assessor
Planning board
Building department
questions.x: The building department keeps permit and CO records. The assessor's card may show the attic as living space, which tempts, but it is not proof of legal approval.

questions.q: A homeowner in a village with a design-review law wants to replace cedar siding with bright blue vinyl. The house is not a landmark. The board most likely to review the change is the:
c: Village zoning board of appeals
Architectural review board
Landmarks commission
Planning department
questions.x: An ARB reviews appearance and materials under the village's design ordinance. A landmarks commission reviews only designated properties, and this house is not one.

questions.q: A town board wants local advice on preserving open space and protecting a marsh before it updates its master plan. It would typically ask its:
c: Receiver of taxes
Landmarks commission
Architectural review board
Conservation advisory council
questions.x: The conservation advisory council advises on open space and natural resources. The ARB reviews building appearance, not environmental resources.

questions.q: An owner of a designated landmark house in a Long Island village wants to add a front porch. Besides a building permit, the owner most likely needs approval from the:
c: Historic preservation commission
Architectural review board
Board of assessment review
NYS parks department
questions.x: Changes to designated landmarks need approval from the historic preservation commission. The building permit alone does not cover landmark review.

questions.q: A buyer wants the assessment card for a house, showing its assessed value and recorded features. The buyer requests it from the:
c: Tax assessor
Town clerk
Receiver of taxes
Building department
questions.x: The assessor values property and keeps the assessment card. The receiver collects tax payments and knows what was paid, not how the value was set.

questions.q: The receiver of taxes in a town is responsible for:
c: Setting each property's assessed value
Collecting tax payments
Hearing tax grievances
Setting the tax rate
questions.x: The receiver (or treasurer) collects taxes and keeps payment records. The assessor sets values and the board of assessment review hears grievances, the common swaps.

questions.q: A seller's septic system failed and must be replaced before closing. Plans for the new system are filed for approval with the:
c: County health department
Town building inspector's office
Zoning board of appeals
Planning board
questions.x: Septic system approvals come from the county or local health department under state health standards. The building department may issue related permits, but it does not approve the septic design.

questions.q: A builder needs to connect a new house to the town's water main and sewer line. Approval of the connection specifications typically comes from the:
c: Tax assessor
Architectural review board
Planning board
Town engineer
questions.x: The town engineer (often with the DPW) oversees connections to public water and sewer. The planning board reviews whole projects, not individual utility hookups.

questions.q: Which local official is elected rather than appointed?
c: Building inspector
Town supervisor
Planning board chair
ZBA chair
questions.x: The town supervisor is elected and sits on the town board. Board chairs are appointed along with the rest of their boards.

questions.q: A restaurant owner wants to open in a district where restaurants are not a permitted use. The planning board chair tells her it cannot help. The owner should apply to the:
c: Zoning board of appeals
Architectural review board
Board of assessment review
Building department
questions.x: A use not permitted in the district requires a use variance from the ZBA; planning boards do not grant variances. The building department would only deny the permit.

questions.q: The difference between a municipality's planning department and its planning board is that the planning department:
c: Votes on applications
Is made up of elected officials
Gives professional advice
Grants variances
questions.x: The planning department is professional staff that advises boards; the planning board is the appointed body that votes on applications. Neither is elected, and neither grants variances.

questions.q: A Bronx owner wants to convert a one-family house into a legal two-family. The new certificate of occupancy will come from the:
c: Department of Buildings
Department of Finance
HPD
City Planning Commission
questions.x: DOB issues permits and certificates of occupancy in NYC. HPD enforces housing maintenance in occupied buildings, but it does not issue COs.

questions.q: For exterior work on a building in a NYC historic district, which approval typically comes first?
c: The DOB permit
The LPC approval
The CO
The Community Board vote
questions.x: DOB will not issue a permit for work on designated property until LPC approves it. A Community Board vote, if any, is advisory and not a prerequisite.

questions.q: A Brooklyn Community Board votes 30 to 2 against a proposed rezoning. Under ULURP, the rezoning:
c: Is dead unless the Community Board reverses itself
Is sent back for a BSA hearing
Goes to DOB for a final ruling
Can still pass at the CPC and Council
questions.x: Community Board votes are advisory; the City Planning Commission and City Council make the binding decisions. A lopsided vote carries political weight but no veto.

questions.q: A Queens buyer wants to see recorded deeds and mortgages for a property through ACRIS. The system is run by the:
c: Department of Buildings
County clerk
Department of Finance
HPD
questions.x: In NYC, DOF runs the City Register and ACRIS, as well as assessment and tax collection. Outside the city the county clerk records deeds, which is why that choice tempts.

questions.q: A tenant in a Harlem walk-up has had no heat for three days in January. The city agency that enforces heat requirements is:
c: DOB
DOF
HPD
DHCR
questions.x: HPD enforces the Housing Maintenance Code, including heat and hot water. DOB handles construction and building code violations, and DHCR is a state rent-regulation agency, not the city's heat enforcer.

questions.concept: NYC Board of Standards and Appeals
questions.q: A Staten Island owner disagrees with a DOB examiner's interpretation of the zoning resolution. The owner can appeal to the:
c: City Planning Commission
Landmarks Commission
Borough President
Board of Standards and Appeals
questions.x: The BSA hears appeals from DOB determinations and grants variances. The CPC changes zoning text and maps; it does not review individual DOB decisions.

questions.q: The NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission has how many members?
c: Five
Seven
Eleven
Fifteen
questions.x: The Charter sets the LPC at 11 members, including architects, a historian, a planner or landscape architect, a realtor, and a resident of each borough. Seven is a common board size, which makes it tempting.

questions.q: The usual way to resolve an open building permit before closing is to:
c: Get a use variance from the ZBA
Pay the property tax
Get a final inspection
File a new deed
questions.x: An open permit is closed out by a final inspection and sign-off by the building department. A variance relates to zoning relief, not to finishing a permit.

questions.q: Outside New York City, a Nassau homeowner who thinks the assessment is too high first files a grievance with the county's assessment review body. In New York City, the matching body is the:
c: Department of Finance
Board of Standards and Appeals
NYC Tax Commission
City Council
questions.x: The NYC Tax Commission hears assessment appeals; DOF is the agency that set the value being challenged. The BSA handles zoning, not taxes.

questions.q: An agent wants to confirm that a deck added in 2015 was legally permitted. The record to request is from the:
c: Receiver of taxes
Building department
Board of assessment review
County clerk
questions.x: Permit and CO records are kept by the building department. The county clerk records deeds and mortgages, not construction permits.

questions.q: An owner in a NYC historic district wants to add a visible rooftop addition and new storefront. The LPC approval needed is a:
c: Permit for Minor Work
Certificate of No Effect
Certificate of Occupancy from DOB
Certificate of Appropriateness
questions.x: Significant visible changes to designated property need a Certificate of Appropriateness, usually after a public hearing. A Permit for Minor Work covers small, in-kind changes.

questions.q: Which local body is most likely to weigh in on a proposal to build near a town-regulated wetland?
c: Receiver of taxes
Landmarks commission
Board of assessment review
Conservation advisory council
questions.x: The conservation advisory council or wetlands commission advises on local wetlands and natural resources. The board of assessment review hears tax grievances, not environmental issues.

questions.q: In New York City, building permits and certificates of occupancy are issued by the:
c: Department of Finance
Landmarks Commission
Department of Buildings
Planning Department
questions.x: DOB is NYC's building department. LPC approves work on landmarks but does not issue permits or COs.

questions.q: An owner of a townhouse in a Manhattan historic district wants to replace the cornice. Before DOB will issue a permit, the owner must obtain approval from the:
c: Landmarks Preservation Commission
Department of Finance
Department of Housing Preservation and Development
Local Community Board
questions.x: Exterior work on designated property needs LPC approval, such as a Certificate of Appropriateness. The Community Board may comment but does not approve.

questions.q: NYC Community Boards' votes on land use applications such as ULURP actions and BSA variances are:
c: Binding on the City Council
Advisory recommendations
Final unless appealed to DOB
Binding on the BSA
questions.x: Community Boards hold hearings and make advisory recommendations. The CPC, Council and BSA make the binding decisions.

questions.q: Which New York City agency assesses real property and collects property taxes?
c: Department of Buildings
NYC Tax Commission
City Planning Commission
Department of Finance
questions.x: DOF handles both assessment and collection, and runs the City Register. The Tax Commission tempts, but it only hears challenges to DOF's values.

questions.q: The NYC agency that enforces the Housing Maintenance Code (heat, hot water, repairs) and requires annual registration of most rental buildings is:
c: DOB
HPD
DOF
NYCHA
questions.x: HPD enforces housing maintenance standards and handles multiple dwelling registration. DOB enforces construction and building codes, the usual mix-up, and NYCHA runs public housing rather than regulating private landlords.

questions.concept: NYC Board of Standards and Appeals
questions.q: The NYC equivalent of a town zoning board of appeals is the:
c: City Planning Commission
Local Community Board
Board of Standards and Appeals
Department of City Planning
questions.x: The BSA grants variances and hears appeals of DOB decisions. The CPC handles rezonings and ULURP, which is why it tempts.

questions.q: By law, the NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission must include, among its members, at least one:
c: Realtor
Tax assessor
Civil court judge
City Council member
questions.x: The NYC Charter requires the 11-member LPC to include architects, a historian, a planner or landscape architect, a realtor, and a resident of each borough. Council members review LPC designations; they do not sit on it.

questions.q: During due diligence, a buyer learns that the seller's kitchen renovation had a permit but no final inspection was ever done. This is commonly called a(n):
c: Nonconforming use
Use variance
Stop-work order
Open permit
questions.x: An open permit is permitted work that was never closed out, and the building department resolves it with a final inspection. A stop-work order halts work in progress, a different problem.

questions.q: A NYC homeowner believes the market value on her Notice of Property Value is too high. She should file an appeal with the:
c: Board of Standards and Appeals
NYC Tax Commission
Board of assessment review
Department of Buildings
questions.x: DOF sets the value; the NYC Tax Commission hears assessment challenges. A board of assessment review handles grievances in towns outside the city, which makes it the near-miss.

questions.q: An agent preparing a listing in a suburban town would typically pull records from each of the following EXCEPT:
c: The building department, for the CO
The receiver, for tax payment status
The assessor, for the property card
The ZBA, for the mortgage payoff
questions.x: Mortgage payoffs come from the lender. The ZBA holds variance decisions, not mortgage information.

questions.q: An owner in a NYC historic district wants to replace windows with exact matches of the existing historic windows. The LPC approval most likely needed is a:
c: Certificate of Appropriateness
Permit for Minor Work
ULURP certification
Certificate of No Effect
questions.x: Minor work that matches the building is typically handled by a Permit for Minor Work at staff level. A Certificate of Appropriateness is for larger changes, and a Certificate of No Effect covers interior work that does not touch protected features.

questions.q: A buyer of a lot in a rural town asks whether the stream at the back is regulated. Besides DEC, the most appropriate local body to ask is the:
c: Receiver of taxes
Architectural review board
Wetlands commission
Tax assessor
questions.x: Local environmental issues, including wetlands under local law, go to the conservation advisory council or wetlands commission. The ARB reviews building design, not natural resources.

questions.q: A Suffolk County listing sheet says a house has a "legal finished basement." The agent wants to confirm that claim. The most reliable source is the:
c: Tax assessor's property record card
Building department's permit and CO file
Seller's homeowners insurance declarations
County clerk's recorded deed to the seller
questions.x: Whether work was legally built is shown by permits, inspections and the certificate of occupancy at the building department. The assessor's card is the trap: it describes the house for valuation and often lists space that was never permitted.

questions.q: An assessor's card lists a two-car garage converted to a family room. What does that entry establish about the conversion?
c: That it was permitted, because assessors check permit files before adding space
That it is legal if it has appeared on the card for 10 years
That the assessor saw or was told of it, not that it is legal
That the building department now has to issue an amended CO
questions.x: The assessor records physical features to value the parcel; legality depends on building department permits and the CO. The ten-year answer is the trap: unpermitted work does not become legal with time, and the card does not trigger any CO change.

questions.q: A Dutchess County house's septic system was approved for 3 bedrooms. The owner wants to market a converted den as a 4th bedroom. What should the agent know?
c: Adding a bedroom generally needs health department septic review
The town assessor can approve the bedroom on the next tax roll
Bedroom counts matter to the building department and no one else
A ZBA area variance is the usual way to approve the extra room
questions.x: Septic systems are sized by bedroom count, so the county health department generally reviews any added bedroom and may require a larger system. The assessor answer is the trap: assessors value property and approve nothing.

questions.q: A county health department's septic file for a house typically shows all of the following EXCEPT:
c: The design capacity, often stated in bedrooms
The location of the tank and the absorption field
Whether the owner paid this year's school tax
The date the system was approved or inspected
questions.x: Tax payment status comes from the receiver of taxes or school tax collector, not the health department. The design capacity is the tempting pick, but septic approvals are commonly stated by bedrooms, because bedrooms stand in for daily water use.

questions.q: A town code allows accessory apartments in a residential district if the owner lives on site and the unit is under 800 square feet. An owner who meets those conditions should apply for a:
c: Use variance from the ZBA
Special permit under the code
Rezoning from the town board
Subdivision from the planning board
questions.x: When the code allows a use subject to conditions, the owner applies for a special permit and must show the conditions are met. The use variance is the trap: it is for a use the code does not permit at all and requires proof of unnecessary hardship.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts a special permit with a use variance?
c: A special permit needs proof of unnecessary hardship; a variance does not
Both need the same showing, but a variance alone can carry conditions
A special permit comes from the town board; a use variance from DOS
A special permit allows a listed use; a use variance allows a barred one
questions.x: A special permit authorizes a use the ordinance already contemplates if listed conditions are met. A use variance allows a use the ordinance prohibits and requires unnecessary hardship. The first choice is the trap because it reverses the hardship test.

questions.q: A ZBA grants a neighbor's area variance, and the decision is filed with the town clerk on May 3. An opposing homeowner who wants court review should generally start an Article 78 proceeding within:
c: 30 days after May 3
90 days after the vote
1 year after the hearing
10 days after May 3
questions.x: Town Law generally gives 30 days from the filing of the board's decision in the town clerk's office. The 90-day answer is the trap: the general Article 78 deadline is four months, and zoning board decisions carry the much shorter 30-day window.

questions.q: Buyers want to close the day after a ZBA grants the special permit they need. What risk should their agent raise?
c: The building inspector may veto the ZBA decision within one year of the vote
The town board has to confirm the permit at a later meeting
Neighbors can still sue within 30 days of the clerk filing
The county planning agency has to approve any ZBA permit
questions.x: A ZBA decision can be challenged in an Article 78 proceeding, generally within 30 days after it is filed with the town clerk, so buyers often wait out the window. The town board answer is the trap: the legislative body does not ratify ZBA decisions.

questions.q: Under the NYS Uniform Code, a municipality may exempt a one-story shed on a one- or two-family lot from building permits if its floor area does not exceed:
c: 100 square feet
200 square feet
250 square feet
144 square feet
questions.x: The Uniform Code allows local governments to exempt small accessory structures up to 144 square feet from the permit requirement. The 200 answer is the trap because many common sheds are near that size, which puts them over the limit.

questions.q: A seller's 10 by 12 foot shed (120 square feet) sits in a town that adopted the small-shed permit exemption. Which statement is accurate?
c: It still needs a permit, since every shed in New York needs one
It needs no permit but must still meet zoning setbacks
It is exempt from both building permits and zoning rules
It needs a county health department permit instead
questions.x: A 120-square-foot shed is under the 144-square-foot exemption, but a permit exemption is not a zoning exemption: setbacks still apply. The exempt-from-everything answer is the trap.

questions.q: A Westchester seller's tax bill is low because the late owner had a senior exemption. When listing the house, the agent should quote:
c: The full tax without the prior owner's exemption
The tax actually billed last year, as the public record
The billed tax, since exemptions transfer with title
An average of the exempt and unexempt amounts
questions.x: Exemptions such as the senior exemption or Enhanced STAR belong to a qualifying owner, not the house, so a buyer needs the full tax figure. Quoting last year's bill is the trap: it is accurate history but misleading as a carrying cost.

questions.q: A buyer asks which office applies exemptions such as STAR or the veterans exemption to a parcel's assessment in a New York town. The answer is the:
c: Receiver of taxes
Planning department
Town engineer
Tax assessor
questions.x: The assessor values parcels and applies exemptions on the assessment roll. The receiver of taxes is the trap: the receiver bills and collects but does not decide exemptions.

questions.q: A buyer's agent finds no certificate of occupancy for a 1925 Bronx two-family with no later alterations. The best conclusion is that:
c: The building is illegal and cannot be sold
The seller has to get a CO from HPD first
A CO was likely never required for it
The city lost the CO, so a new one is due
questions.x: New York City did not require a CO for buildings completed before 1938 unless later work changed the use, egress or occupancy. Legal use can be confirmed through other records or a DOB Letter of No Objection. The illegal-building answer is the trap.

questions.q: An owner of a pre-1938 NYC building with no CO needs written proof of its legal use for a lender. The owner should ask DOB's borough office for a:
c: Letter of No Objection
Certificate of Appropriateness
Temporary Certificate of Occupancy
Certificate of No Effect
questions.x: A Letter of No Objection is DOB's statement that a use is acceptable for a building exempt from the CO requirement. The Temporary CO is the trap: it is issued for new or altered buildings while work is completed.

questions.q: A DOB record shows an ECB violation with "Penalty: PAID" and "Status: OPEN." What closes the violation?
c: A second payment equal to the penalty
DOB accepting a certificate of correction
A sale of the property to a new owner of record
A letter from the Community Board
questions.x: Paying the OATH penalty does not close a DOB violation. The owner must correct the condition and file a certificate of correction that DOB accepts. A sale is the trap: the open violation stays on the property and becomes the buyer's problem.

questions.q: Which statement about a DOB violation adjudicated at OATH is accurate?
c: Paying the penalty closes the violation once OATH confirms payment
The violation disappears from DOB records after three years
A seller's affidavit of correction clears it at closing
It stays open until DOB accepts proof the condition was corrected
questions.x: OATH imposes and collects the penalty, but the violation remains open in DOB records until DOB accepts a certificate of correction. The paid-closes-it answer is the trap, and it is the most common misreading of a DOB printout.

questions.q: Under the NYC Housing Maintenance Code, HPD classifies an immediately hazardous condition, such as no heat in winter, as a:
c: Class A violation
Class B violation
Class C violation
Class 1 violation
questions.x: Class C is immediately hazardous, with the shortest correction deadlines. Class B is hazardous (generally 30 days) and Class A non-hazardous (generally 90 days). Class 1 is the trap: that label belongs to DOB's ECB violation scheme, not HPD's.

questions.q: An HPD printout for a Queens three-family shows a Class B violation for a leaking kitchen ceiling. Generally, how long does the owner have to correct it?
c: 30 days
24 hours
90 days
1 year
questions.x: Class B (hazardous) violations generally carry a 30-day correction period. The 90-day answer is the trap: that is the general period for Class A, non-hazardous conditions.

questions.q: The owner of a Bushwick four-family let the building's HPD registration lapse. A tenant stops paying rent. While the registration is lapsed, the owner:
c: Can sue, but owes a late registration fee
Cannot sue for possession for nonpayment
Can sue if the tenant's lease is in writing
Has to first ask DOB to reissue the CO
questions.x: Owners of multiple dwellings that are not currently registered with HPD cannot recover possession for nonpayment of rent while out of compliance. The fee answer is the trap: a lapsed registration costs more than a fee. The CO has nothing to do with registration.

questions.q: In New York City, annual property registration with HPD is required for residential buildings with at least:
c: Six units
Twelve units
Two units
Three units
questions.x: Multiple dwellings, three or more residential units, register every year (and one- and two-family homes register when neither the owner nor the owner's family lives there). Six units is the trap: that number is the threshold for interest-bearing security deposit accounts.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a Harlem brownstone in a historic district. The prior owner installed unapproved windows, and LPC had issued a warning letter. After closing, who must correct it?
c: The new owner, since it runs with the property
The prior owner, since he did the work himself
No one, since a sale ends the violation
The broker who listed the brownstone
questions.x: LPC violations remain active against the property until corrected, and the current owner is responsible even for work a prior owner did. The prior-owner answer is the trap: the buyer can bargain for an escrow or credit, but the obligation follows the building.

questions.q: An owner has an active LPC violation for unapproved storefront work. All of the following are accurate EXCEPT:
c: DOB permits for other work may be held up
Paying LPC's fine removes the violation
An LPC permit may legalize the work
It will show up in a buyer's searches
questions.x: Paying a fine does not remove an LPC violation; the owner must legalize the work with an LPC permit or correct it. The held-up-permits choice is the tempting pick, but LPC itself warns that an active violation can delay DOB permits.

questions.q: Under New York City's definitions, a story with more than half its height below the curb level is a:
c: Basement, which may be an apartment
Ground floor, counted as floor area
Cellar, which cannot be an apartment
Garden level, legal if it has windows
questions.x: A cellar has more than half its height below curb level and cannot lawfully be occupied as an apartment. A basement has at least half its height above the curb and may be legal living space if it meets light, air and egress rules. The basement answer is the trap.

questions.q: A Brooklyn listing advertises a "garden apartment" whose floor is mostly below the curb. The rent from it is $1,600 a month. How should a buyer's agent treat that income?
c: Count it, since tenants have paid on time
Count half as a hedge against fines
Count it once the ECB fine is paid
Leave it out as illegal cellar income
questions.x: If more than half the story's height is below curb level, it is a cellar and cannot legally be an apartment, so the income should not support the price or the loan. The paid-fine answer is the trap: paying a penalty neither legalizes the use nor closes the violation.

questions.q: A title report shows an open DOB violation, with an OATH penalty, for work without a permit on a Queens house. The seller paid the penalty last year. What still has to happen for the violation to close?
c: Nothing, because paying the penalty closed it
The house needs a brand-new certificate of occupancy
DOB must accept proof the condition was corrected
The community board must vote to dismiss it
questions.x: Paying an OATH penalty settles the fine, not the violation. The owner must fix the condition (often by legalizing the work with a permit) and file a certificate of correction that DOB accepts. The trap is the paid fine: buyers' attorneys see paid penalties on open violations all the time.

questions.q: An owner pays the OATH penalty on a DOB violation but never fixes the condition. The violation:
c: Closes automatically once the fine clears
Converts to an HPD violation after a year
Is removed when the property is sold
Stays open until a correction is accepted
questions.x: The penalty and the violation are separate. Until DOB accepts a certificate of correction, the violation stays on the record and shows up in every buyer's search. A sale does not wipe it out; it becomes the buyer's problem unless the contract deals with it.

questions.q: In New York City, which agency enforces the Housing Maintenance Code and requires owners of buildings with three or more units to register each year?
c: Department of Buildings (DOB)
Housing Preservation and Development (HPD)
Department of Finance (DOF)
Department of Environmental Protection (DEP)
questions.x: HPD enforces the Housing Maintenance Code (heat, hot water, repairs, pests) and runs annual registration for multiple dwellings. DOB handles construction, permits and certificates of occupancy, the most common mix-up. DOF assesses and bills taxes; DEP handles water and sewer.

questions.q: A tenant in a six-unit Bronx building has had no heat for three days in January and calls 311. The inspection and any violation will come from:
c: The Department of Buildings (DOB)
The state Division of Housing and Community Renewal
Housing Preservation and Development (HPD)
The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP)
questions.x: Heat and hot water complaints are Housing Maintenance Code matters, so HPD inspects and issues the violation. DHCR handles rent-regulation issues like overcharges and service reductions, not code inspections. DOB would come in only for construction or structural problems.

cram.html: Elected: city council, town board (and supervisor), village board of trustees (and mayor). They adopt laws, zoning, the budget and the tax rate.
Appointed: planning board, ZBA, architectural review board, conservation advisory council, landmark commission, municipal engineer.
Assessor and receiver of taxes may be elected or appointed depending on the municipality.
Planning board: master plan, subdivision approval, site plans; advises all other boards.
ZBA: variances, interpretations, appeals of the building inspector, often special permits. Never adopts zoning.
Building department: permits, inspections, COs; the gatekeeper for all construction.
Planning department: professional staff advice to all agencies and boards.
Assessor values. Receiver collects. Legislative body sets the rate.
Municipal engineer: roads, sewer and water connections. County health department: septic approval, certain sewer approvals.
ARB: approves design of new construction and remodeling. Landmark commission: recommends designations and approves work on designated property.
Conservation advisory council / wetlands commission: local environmental issues; DEC handles state permits.
NYC: DOB permits and COs; LPC landmarks; DOF assesses and collects; BSA variances; HPD housing code; Community Boards advise.
Community Boards: 59, up to 50 members appointed by the borough president. Votes are advisory.
LPC: 11 commissioners appointed by the mayor, including at least 3 architects, a historian, a planner or landscape architect, a realtor, and one from each borough.
LPC approval (Certificate of Appropriateness, Permit for Minor Work, or Certificate of No Effect) comes before the DOB permit on landmarked property.
NYC assessment appeals go to the NYC Tax Commission, not DOF or the BSA.

subjects.title: Property Insurance
subjects.blurb: No insurance, no mortgage, no closing. Know the HO forms, actual cash value vs replacement cost, the 80% rule, NY's insurers of last resort, and what you tell a buyer about coverage.

lessons.title: Homeowners Insurance in New York
lessons.tagline: Insurance turns a disaster into a deductible. Your job is to make sure the buyer has it before the keys change hands.
objectives: Explain why buyers and lenders need property insurance and who sells it
Match each HO form (HO-1 to HO-8) to the owner who needs it
Calculate actual cash value and a coinsurance (80% rule) payout
Name NY's options when coverage is hard to get: NYPIUA, NFIP, and C-MAP
Describe NY cancellation and nonrenewal rules and the windstorm deductible disclosure

blocks.title: Two weeks to closing, Broad Channel
blocks.html: A cash buyer is closing on a bungalow on stilts in Broad Channel, Queens, surrounded by Jamaica Bay. "No bank, so no one can make me buy insurance, right? And my cousin says homeowners covers floods." Jordan has two weeks before closing. Which of those two statements is the more dangerous one?
blocks.casual: A cash buyer is closing on a bungalow on stilts in Broad Channel, Queens, with Jamaica Bay all around it. "No bank, so nobody can make me buy insurance, right? And my cousin says homeowners covers floods." Jordan has two weeks till closing. Which of those two lines is the scarier one?

deeper.plain: The buyer is right that no lender will force coverage, but dead wrong that a homeowners policy covers flooding.
deeper.picture: It's like thinking your phone's screen protector also makes it waterproof. One protects against cracks, not a dunk in the bay.
deeper.street: If the buyer waits, an NFIP policy bought without a new loan usually has a 30-day waiting period. Closing in two weeks plus a nor'easter in week three means bay water in the living room with zero coverage.
deeper.stakes: A flooded uninsured home can wipe out a cash buyer's entire investment. Even if you're not the insurance expert, flagging the gap protects them and you.
deeper.exam: Standard homeowners policies exclude flood. Expect a question where the "covers everything" answer is the trap.

blocks.text: Why insure, and who sells it

blocks.html: Property insurance transfers the risk of a sudden loss (fire, wind, theft) from the owner to an insurer in exchange for a premium. Liability insurance pays when the owner is legally responsible for injuring someone or damaging their property. A lender insists on both because the house is its collateral.
blocks.casual: Property insurance shifts the risk of a sudden loss (fire, wind, theft) from the owner to an insurer, and the owner pays a premium for that. Liability insurance pays when the owner is legally on the hook for hurting someone or damaging their stuff. A lender insists on both because the house is its collateral.

deeper.plain: Property insurance protects your stuff. Liability insurance protects you when someone else gets hurt.
deeper.picture: Property coverage is a helmet for your house. Liability coverage is the lawyer you call when your dog bites the mail carrier.
deeper.street: A Bed-Stuy owner's boiler fire does $60,000 in damage: property coverage. The same week, a delivery worker slips on the unshoveled stoop and sues for $150,000: liability coverage.
deeper.stakes: An owner with property coverage but thin liability can lose savings to a single lawsuit.
deeper.exam: Property = damage to your own property. Liability = your legal responsibility to others. Lenders require coverage to protect the collateral.

head: Seller of insurance
Represents
How it works
rows: Sells its own policies through employees or captive agents
The insurance companies it is appointed by
Can quote several companies and bind coverage for them
Shops the market for the client; places coverage through companies
blocks.caption: Agents and brokers are licensed by the NYS Department of Financial Services (DFS), not DOS.

deeper.plain: Some sellers work for one insurance company, some for several companies, and brokers work for you, the buyer.
deeper.picture: A brand store salesperson, a department store salesperson, and a personal shopper.
deeper.street: Leo calls a direct writer and gets one quote. Then he calls an independent agent who quotes four companies. Then a broker shops the whole market for his Sunnyside condo and finds the best HO-6.
deeper.stakes: Real estate agents aren't licensed to sell insurance. Recommending a specific policy can step outside your license.
deeper.exam: Insurance agents and brokers are licensed by DFS, not DOS. Brokers represent the insurance buyer.

left.title: Monoline policy
items: One line of coverage only
Example: a dwelling fire policy on a rental two-family
Liability bought separately

right.title: Package policy
items: Several coverages bundled
Homeowners policy = property + liability + medical payments
Usually cheaper than buying each separately

deeper.plain: Monoline covers one thing. Package bundles several, and homeowners policies are packages.
deeper.picture: Ordering à la carte versus the combo meal. The combo usually costs less.
deeper.street: Sal's rental two-family has a monoline dwelling fire policy plus a separate liability policy. Leo's condo has one HO-6 package that bundles contents, liability, and medical payments.
deeper.stakes: An owner with only a monoline fire policy may assume they have liability coverage they don't.
deeper.exam: A homeowners policy is a package policy. Dwelling fire alone is monoline.

blocks.html: A homeowners policy is a package policy. Its standard parts:
blocks.casual: A homeowners policy is a package policy. Here are its standard parts:

deeper.plain: A homeowners policy is a bundle of several coverages, labeled A through F.
deeper.picture: A toolbox where each drawer handles a different kind of problem.
deeper.street: The Okafors' HO-3 covers the brownstone (A), the backyard shed (B), their furniture (C), a hotel if they must move out (D), a guest's lawsuit (E), and a neighbor's small medical bill (F).
deeper.stakes: Clients who don't know the parts may not file claims they're entitled to.
deeper.exam: Know the letters: A dwelling, B other structures, C personal property, D loss of use, E liability, F medical payments.

head: Coverage
Pays for
Example
rows: Extra living expenses while repairs happen
Injuries or damage you negligently cause others
Guest slips on an icy stoop
Small medical bills of guests, regardless of fault
Neighbor's kid twists an ankle in the yard

deeper.plain: Each lettered coverage pays for a different kind of loss.
deeper.picture: Six different pockets in a jacket, each holding a different emergency fund.
deeper.street: A Flatbush fire: kitchen repairs under A ($45,000), ruined couch and TV under C ($8,000), three weeks in a hotel under D ($6,000). Total paid across three coverages.
deeper.stakes: Forgetting loss of use means families pay for temporary housing out of pocket when they didn't have to.
deeper.exam: Medical payments (F) pay regardless of fault. Liability (E) pays when the owner is legally responsible.

blocks.caption: Click each form to see who buys it and whether it covers named perils or all risks except exclusions.

head: Form
Name
Who uses it
Coverage style
rows: Short list of named perils (fire, wind, hail, vandalism, theft...)
Dwelling: all risks except exclusions. Contents: named perils
Renters (and, per the NY syllabus, co-op owners)
All risks except exclusions on dwelling AND contents
Walls-in, improvements, contents, liability, loss assessment
Older homes where rebuild cost far exceeds market value
Pays actual cash value or repair with common materials
blocks.caption: There is no HO-7 in standard use.

deeper.plain: HO forms are policy types. Each fits a different kind of owner or occupant.
deeper.picture: Phone plans: basic, broad, unlimited, and a special plan for older phones.
deeper.street: The Okafors carry HO-3. Leo's Sunnyside condo needs HO-6. Jordan's rental in Jackson Heights: HO-4. A Victorian in Troy where rebuilding would cost three times market value: HO-8.
deeper.stakes: Point a condo buyer to the wrong form and their walls-in renovation might go uninsured.
deeper.exam: HO-3 most common. HO-4 renters (and co-op owners per the syllabus). HO-6 condo. HO-8 older homes. No HO-7.

blocks.title: HO-3 vs HO-5
blocks.html: HO-3 is the most widely used homeowners policy. HO-5 is HO-3 plus open-perils coverage on personal property. And in practice, many insurers write co-op owners on an HO-6 style co-op form; the syllabus answer is still HO-4 for tenants and co-op owners, HO-6 for condos.
blocks.casual: HO-3 is the most widely used homeowners policy. HO-5 is HO-3 plus open-perils coverage on personal property too. And in real life, lots of insurers write co-op owners on an HO-6 style co-op form, but the syllabus answer is still HO-4 for tenants and co-op owners, HO-6 for condos.

deeper.plain: HO-5 covers your stuff more broadly than HO-3. For the exam, co-ops go with HO-4.
deeper.picture: HO-3 locks the front door with a deadbolt and the back door with a latch. HO-5 deadbolts both.
deeper.street: A Riverdale homeowner with expensive furniture picks HO-5 so a spilled paint can or accidental damage to contents is covered, not just listed perils.
deeper.stakes: On the job, a co-op owner may get an HO-6 co-op form. On the exam, write HO-4.
deeper.exam: Exam answer: co-op owners = HO-4. Condo owners = HO-6. Don't let real-world practice change your exam pick.

blocks.title: Not covered by a standard homeowners policy
blocks.html: Flood (rising water) and earthquake are excluded. Flood needs a separate flood policy. Wear and tear, mold from neglect, and pests are not insurable losses either.
blocks.casual: Flood (rising water) and earthquake are left out. Flood needs its own flood policy. Wear and tear, mold from neglect, and pests aren't insurable losses either.

deeper.plain: Floods, earthquakes, and slow damage from neglect aren't covered by a regular homeowners policy.
deeper.picture: Insurance covers a car crash, not worn-out tires. Same idea for houses.
deeper.street: After a storm, a Howard Beach basement fills with rising bay water. Homeowners denies the claim. The neighbor with an NFIP policy gets paid.
deeper.stakes: Buyers in coastal Queens, Staten Island, and Brooklyn learn about the flood gap after the water's already in.
deeper.exam: Rising water = flood = excluded. Earthquake excluded. Wear and tear never covered.

blocks.q: Leo buys a condo in Sunnyside. Which form covers his unit's interior, his belongings, and his liability?
c: HO-3
HO-4
HO-6
HO-8
blocks.x: HO-6 is the condominium unit owner's form. HO-4 covers renters (and co-op owners per the syllabus) with no building coverage at all.

blocks.text: How much coverage: ACV, replacement cost, and the 80% rule

blocks.html: Replacement cost pays to repair or replace with new materials of like kind and quality, with no deduction for age. Actual cash value (ACV) = replacement cost minus depreciation. ACV pays what the old thing was worth.
blocks.casual: Replacement cost pays to repair or replace with new materials of like kind and quality, no knock for age. Actual cash value (ACV) = replacement cost minus depreciation. ACV pays what the old thing was worth.

deeper.plain: Replacement cost buys you new. ACV pays for used.
deeper.picture: Your 5-year-old phone gets stolen. Replacement cost gets you a new phone. ACV gets you the price of a 5-year-old one.
deeper.street: New numbers: a 10-year-old boiler with a 25-year life costs $15,000 to replace. Depreciation: 10 / 25 = 40%, $6,000. ACV pays $9,000; replacement cost pays $15,000.
deeper.stakes: Owners on ACV coverage get a nasty surprise at claim time. They have to cover the gap themselves.
deeper.exam: ACV = replacement cost minus depreciation. Replacement cost has no deduction for depreciation.

blocks.title: ACV on a storm-damaged roof
blocks.html:
A 12-year-old roof with a 20-year life is destroyed. A new one costs $20,000.
Depreciation: 12 / 20 = 60% x $20,000 = $12,000
ACV: $20,000 - $12,000 = $8,000 (less the deductible)
Under replacement cost coverage: $20,000 (less the deductible)
blocks.casual:
A 12-year-old roof with a 20-year life gets wrecked. A new one costs $20,000.
Depreciation: 12 / 20 = 60% x $20,000 = $12,000
ACV: $20,000 minus $12,000 = $8,000 (less the deductible)
Under replacement cost coverage: $20,000 (less the deductible)

deeper.plain: Figure how used up the roof was, take that off the new price, and that's what ACV pays.
deeper.picture: Selling a half-used gift card. You only get the half that's left.
deeper.street: New numbers: a 9-year-old roof on a Staten Island cape with a 30-year life. New roof: $24,000. Depreciation 9 / 30 = 30% = $7,200. ACV: $16,800. Replacement cost: $24,000, both before the deductible.
deeper.stakes: On an old roof, ACV can leave the owner paying most of the replacement themselves.
deeper.exam: Age / life = percent depreciated. Multiply by replacement cost, subtract. Deductible comes off last.

blocks.html: Most homeowners policies have a coinsurance clause: to collect full replacement cost on a partial loss, the owner must carry coverage of at least 80% of the dwelling's replacement cost. Carry less and the insurer pays a proportional share.
blocks.casual: Most homeowners policies have a coinsurance clause. To collect full replacement cost on a partial loss, the owner has to carry coverage of at least 80% of the dwelling's replacement cost. Carry less and the insurer pays only a proportional share.

deeper.plain: Insure for at least 80% of rebuild cost or the insurer only pays part of your claim.
deeper.picture: A group dinner where you only chipped in 3/4 of your share, so you only get 3/4 of the leftovers.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Bayside house costs $700,000 to rebuild. 80% is $560,000. The owner carries $420,000, 75% of required. A $20,000 loss pays only $15,000.
deeper.stakes: Owners who insure based on an old purchase price, not current rebuild cost, often fall under 80% without knowing.
deeper.exam: 80% of replacement cost, not market value. Underinsured owners get a proportional payout.

blocks.title: The 80% rule in Astoria
blocks.html:
Sal's house would cost $500,000 to rebuild. Required: 80% x $500,000 = $400,000. Sal carries only $300,000. A kitchen fire causes $40,000 of damage.
Payout = (carried / required) x loss = ($300,000 / $400,000) x $40,000 = 0.75 x $40,000 = $30,000 (before the deductible)
Had he carried $400,000 or more, he would collect the full $40,000.
blocks.casual:
Sal's house would cost $500,000 to rebuild. Required: 80% x $500,000 = $400,000. Sal carries only $300,000. A kitchen fire does $40,000 of damage.
Payout = (carried / required) x loss = ($300,000 / $400,000) x $40,000 = 0.75 x $40,000 = $30,000 (before the deductible)
If he'd carried $400,000 or more, he'd collect the full $40,000.

deeper.plain: Divide what you carried by what you should have carried, then multiply by the loss.
deeper.picture: Paying 75% of the gym membership gets you 75% of the classes.
deeper.street: New numbers: the Okafors' rebuild cost is $1,200,000. Required: $960,000. They carry $720,000. Burst pipe damage: $50,000. Payout: ($720,000 / $960,000) x $50,000 = 0.75 x $50,000 = $37,500.
deeper.stakes: Sal eats $10,000 on a $40,000 fire because of a policy he never updated. A bigger loss means a bigger hole.
deeper.exam: Watch the stem: required is 80% of replacement cost, not 100%. The payout can't exceed the loss or the policy limit.

blocks.title: Did, Should, Loss
blocks.html: Did / Should x Loss. What you did carry, over what you should carry (80%), times the loss.
blocks.casual: Did / Should x Loss. What you did carry, over what you should carry (80%), times the loss.

deeper.plain: A short phrase that sets up the coinsurance fraction.
deeper.picture: Did over Should, like a grade: what you scored over what was possible.
deeper.stakes: Get the fraction upside down and you'd claim the insurer owes more than the loss. Easy to spot, easy to avoid.
deeper.exam: Did / Should. Never Should / Did. The fraction can't exceed 1.

blocks.html: Base policies set default limits, often as percentages of Coverage A (for example, contents at about half the dwelling limit). Owners can add increased liability limits, scheduled personal property endorsements for jewelry, art, or cameras, and higher limits for other structures like a detached garage.
blocks.casual: Base policies set default limits, often as percentages of Coverage A (contents might be about half the dwelling limit). Owners can add higher liability limits, scheduled personal property endorsements for jewelry, art, or cameras, and higher limits for other structures like a detached garage.

deeper.plain: Default limits may be too low. You can buy add-ons for valuables and bigger risks.
deeper.picture: A standard phone plan with add-ons for international calls and extra data.
deeper.street: Evelyn's Tribeca loft has $90,000 in art. Her HO policy caps fine art theft low, so she schedules each piece on an endorsement with an appraised value.
deeper.stakes: Owners assume their jewelry is covered and learn after a burglary that the sublimit was a few thousand dollars.
deeper.exam: Scheduled personal property = endorsement for listed valuables. Limits often set as a percent of Coverage A.

blocks.q: Replacement cost is $600,000. The owner carries $360,000 with an 80% coinsurance clause and suffers a $50,000 loss. Ignoring the deductible, the insurer pays:

blocks.text: When coverage is hard to get

head: Program
What it is
When to use it
rows: New York Property Insurance Underwriting Association, the state's FAIR plan. An insurer-funded pool
Owner cannot get coverage in the voluntary market. Insurer of last resort
National Flood Insurance Program, run by FEMA
Flood coverage. Required for federally backed mortgages on buildings in a Special Flood Hazard Area
Coastal Market Assistance Program, created by NY regulators in 1996 and administered by NYPIUA
Owner-occupied homes near the coast (NYC boroughs, Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester) that insurers turned down; insurers volunteer to consider them

deeper.plain: When regular insurers say no, NY has backup programs, plus the federal flood program.
deeper.picture: A safety net under a trapeze: you hope you don't need it, but it's there.
deeper.street: A Far Rockaway owner gets three rejections because of the coast. Her broker tries C-MAP, then NYPIUA. For flood, she buys an NFIP policy through FEMA's program.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who can't get coverage can't close with a lender. Knowing these programs saves deals.
deeper.exam: NYPIUA = NY FAIR plan, insurer of last resort. NFIP = federal flood. C-MAP = coastal homeowners turned down by insurers.

blocks.title: Flood shows up in the PCDS now
blocks.html: Since March 2024 the NY Property Condition Disclosure Statement asks about floodplain location, flood insurance, and past flood claims. Pair that with flood maps when you talk insurance with a buyer. NFIP policies usually have a 30-day waiting period, waived when the policy is bought in connection with a new loan, so cash buyers must not wait until closing week.
blocks.casual: Since March 2024, the NY Property Condition Disclosure Statement asks about floodplain location, flood insurance, and past flood claims. Put that next to the flood maps when you talk insurance with a buyer. NFIP policies usually have a 30-day waiting period, waived when the policy is bought along with a new loan, so cash buyers can't wait until closing week.

deeper.plain: Sellers now disclose flood history, and flood policies usually take 30 days to kick in for cash buyers.
deeper.picture: Buying an umbrella that only opens a month after you pay for it. Buy it before the forecast turns.
deeper.street: The Broad Channel buyer reads the PCDS: two prior flood claims. With 14 days to closing and no loan, Jordan tells them to call a flood insurance agent today, because coverage won't start for about 30 days.
deeper.stakes: Miss the waiting period and the buyer owns a house in a flood zone with no flood coverage for weeks.
deeper.exam: The PCDS has flood questions since March 20, 2024, and there's no more $500 credit opt-out. NFIP waiting period: 30 days, waived for loan closings.

items: First 60 days of a new homeowners policy: the insurer may cancel for almost any reason, with written notice stating it.

After 60 days: only for listed reasons, such as nonpayment of premium, fraud or material misrepresentation, a crime conviction that increases the hazard, willful acts increasing the hazard, or physical changes making the property uninsurable.
Nonpayment: the policy stays in force if the premium is paid within 15 days of the cancellation notice.
Nonrenewal: written notice with the specific reason, delivered 45 to 60 days before expiration. Miss the window and the policy renews.
blocks.casual:
First 60 days of a new homeowners policy: the insurer can cancel for almost any reason, with written notice saying why.
After 60 days: only for listed reasons, like nonpayment, fraud or material misrepresentation, a crime conviction that raises the hazard, willful acts that raise the hazard, or physical changes that make the property uninsurable.
Nonpayment: the policy stays in force if the premium gets paid within 15 days of the cancellation notice.
Nonrenewal: written notice with the specific reason, 45 to 60 days before expiration. Miss that window and the policy renews.

deeper.plain: After the first 60 days, NY makes it hard for an insurer to drop you without a good reason and notice.
deeper.picture: A probation period at a new job: early on you can be let go easily; later they need cause.
deeper.street: An insurer sends Sal a nonrenewal notice 30 days before expiration. That's outside the 45 to 60 day window, so the policy renews.
deeper.stakes: A dropped policy means the lender force-places pricey coverage, and a buyer mid-deal could lose their financing.
deeper.exam: 60 days, 15 days to pay, 45 to 60 days for nonrenewal notice. The exam likes the 60-day line.

blocks.html: Premiums rise with risk and with the amount insured: location (coast, fire protection, crime), construction (frame vs masonry), age and condition of the roof, wiring, and plumbing, claims history, coverage limits, and the deductible. Discounts come from alarms, sprinklers, and bundling home with auto.
blocks.casual: Premiums go up with risk and with how much you insure: location (coast, fire protection, crime), construction (frame vs masonry), the age and condition of the roof, wiring, and plumbing, claims history, coverage limits, and the deductible. You get discounts for alarms, sprinklers, and bundling home with auto.

deeper.plain: Riskier houses cost more to insure. Safer setups get discounts.
deeper.picture: Car insurance for a teen with a sports car versus a careful driver in a minivan.
deeper.street: Two similar houses: a brick one in Forest Hills with new wiring, and a frame bungalow in Breezy Point with a 25-year-old roof. The bungalow's premium is double.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't get a quote before contract can find out the carrying cost wrecks their budget.
deeper.exam: Frame costs more than masonry. Higher deductible lowers premium. Claims history raises it.

blocks.html: A deductible is the part of each loss the owner pays first. Higher deductible, lower premium. Coastal policies often carry a separate hurricane (windstorm) deductible stated as a percentage of the dwelling limit, such as 2% to 5%.
blocks.casual: A deductible is the chunk of each loss the owner pays first. Higher deductible, lower premium. Coastal policies often have a separate hurricane (windstorm) deductible written as a percentage of the dwelling limit, like 2% to 5%.

deeper.plain: You pay the first part of any claim. Hurricane deductibles are a percentage, which can be big.
deeper.picture: The copay at the doctor. A hurricane deductible is a percentage copay on an expensive surgery.
deeper.street: New numbers: dwelling limit $800,000, 5% hurricane deductible = $40,000 out of pocket on a hurricane claim. Regular deductible: $2,500.
deeper.stakes: Owners think their deductible is $1,000, then a hurricane hits and they owe tens of thousands first.
deeper.exam: Hurricane deductible = percent of dwelling coverage, not a flat dollar amount.

blocks.title: Windstorm deductible disclosure
blocks.html: Insurance Law 3445 and DFS regulations (11 NYCRR Part 74) require insurers to disclose windstorm and hurricane deductibles in plain language. The declarations page must show the hurricane deductible as both a percentage and a dollar amount, near the regular deductible and at least as prominent, and a notice explaining it must accompany the policy.
blocks.casual: Insurance Law 3445 and DFS regulations (11 NYCRR Part 74) make insurers explain windstorm and hurricane deductibles in plain language. The declarations page must show the hurricane deductible as both a percentage and a dollar amount, near the regular deductible and at least as prominent, and a notice explaining it has to come with the policy.

deeper.plain: NY makes insurers spell out hurricane deductibles in dollars, right up front.
deeper.picture: A restaurant menu that has to show the actual price, not just "market price."
deeper.street: Leo's friend in Long Beach opens the declarations page: "Hurricane deductible: 3% ($18,000)." Right next to it: "All other perils: $1,000." No hiding in fine print.
deeper.stakes: If an owner didn't get the disclosure, they may have a complaint with DFS. Agents can point buyers to that page before closing.
deeper.exam: Both percent and dollar amount on the declarations page. Regulated by DFS, not DOS.

blocks.title: What 2% really means
blocks.html:
Dwelling coverage $600,000, hurricane deductible 2%.
$600,000 x 0.02 = $12,000 out of pocket on a hurricane claim, versus a $1,000 deductible for a kitchen fire.
blocks.casual:
Dwelling coverage $600,000, hurricane deductible 2%.
$600,000 x 0.02 = $12,000 out of pocket on a hurricane claim, compared with a $1,000 deductible for a kitchen fire.

deeper.plain: Multiply the dwelling limit by the deductible percent.
deeper.picture: A 2% service charge on a big bill adds up fast.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Staten Island house insured at $450,000 with a 4% hurricane deductible: $450,000 x 0.04 = $18,000 before the policy pays a dime.
deeper.stakes: A buyer stretching to close with thin savings may not survive an $18,000 hit after a storm.
deeper.exam: Base is the dwelling coverage (Coverage A), not the loss amount and not the house price.

blocks.html: An umbrella policy adds extra liability coverage (often in $1 million layers) above the limits of the home and auto policies. Landlords like Sal and investors like Evelyn buy commercial policies: commercial property coverage, commercial general liability, and often a business owner's policy (BOP) that packages them, plus loss of rents coverage.
blocks.casual: An umbrella policy stacks extra liability coverage (often in $1 million layers) on top of the home and auto policy limits. Landlords like Sal and investors like Evelyn buy commercial policies: commercial property coverage, commercial general liability, and often a business owner's policy (BOP) that bundles them, plus loss of rents coverage.

deeper.plain: Umbrella adds more liability coverage. Landlords need commercial policies, not homeowners.
deeper.picture: An umbrella over your other umbrellas, catching what slips past them.
deeper.street: A tenant falls down Sal's Astoria stairs and wins $1.4M. His CGL policy pays $1M, and his $1M umbrella covers the rest. Loss of rents covers units empty after a fire.
deeper.stakes: Landlords on homeowners forms can have claims denied for business use. Under-insured landlords lose buildings in lawsuits.
deeper.exam: Umbrella = excess liability. BOP = packaged commercial property and liability. Loss of rents protects landlord income.

blocks.title: What to tell a buyer

items.title: Purpose and cost
items.html: Explain what a homeowners policy covers, what it excludes (flood!), and that premiums vary. Get quotes early, especially on the coast or with an old roof.

items.title: The lender's interest
items.html: The lender is named as mortgagee on the policy and requires an insurance binder or declarations page before closing. If coverage lapses, the lender can force-place expensive coverage.

items.title: Escrow
items.html: Most lenders collect taxes and insurance monthly with the mortgage payment (PITI) and pay the bills from an escrow account.

items.title: Cash buyers
items.html: No lender forces it, but the buyer should bind coverage effective at closing. Under NY law the seller bears risk of loss until title or possession passes; after that, it is the buyer's.

items.title: Stay in your lane
items.html: Recommend that buyers get coverage advice from a licensed insurance agent or broker. You explain; they insure.

blocks.casual:
Purpose and cost: explain what a homeowners policy covers, what it excludes (flood!), and that premiums vary. Get quotes early, especially on the coast or with an old roof.
The lender's interest: the lender is named as mortgagee on the policy and wants an insurance binder or declarations page before closing. If coverage lapses, the lender can force-place expensive coverage.
Escrow: most lenders collect taxes and insurance monthly with the mortgage payment (PITI) and pay the bills from an escrow account.
Cash buyers: no lender forces it, but the buyer should bind coverage effective at closing. In NY the seller bears risk of loss until title or possession passes; after that, it's the buyer's.
Stay in your lane: send buyers to a licensed insurance agent or broker for coverage advice. You explain; they insure.

deeper.plain: Help buyers understand insurance and get it in place on time, but let licensed insurance pros give the actual advice.
deeper.picture: You're the friend who reminds them to buy the plane ticket, not the travel agent who books it.
deeper.street: Two weeks before Leo's closing, Jordan reminds him the lender needs a binder for his HO-6. Leo's insurance broker emails it to Tasha; the loan clears to close on time.
deeper.stakes: No binder, no closing. Cash buyers who forget coverage own the risk the moment title passes.
deeper.exam: Seller holds risk of loss until title or possession passes (GOL 5-1311). Lender is named as mortgagee. Insurance advice comes from DFS licensees.

blocks.q: A cash buyer of a Staten Island house should obtain homeowners insurance:
c: Effective at closing, when the risk of loss passes to the buyer
Only if a lender requires it
Within 30 days after closing
Only after the first property tax bill
blocks.x: Without a lender no one forces it, but once title or possession passes the buyer bears the risk. Coverage should start at closing.

story.title: Water Under the House
story.setting: A bungalow on stilts in Broad Channel, Queens, two weeks before closing

beats.text: The buyer, a retired subway conductor, is paying cash. He has strong opinions and a cousin with stronger ones.
No bank, so no insurance. And my cousin says homeowners covers floods anyway.
Two things. Once you close, the risk is yours. A fire on day one is your fire. And flood is excluded from homeowners. That's a separate policy, usually through the NFIP.
beats.tag: Flood is excluded from HO policies

beats.text: Fine, I'll buy flood the day before closing.
NFIP usually has a 30-day wait unless it's tied to a new loan. You're cash. Call today.
Three days later. The buyer calls, annoyed.
Two companies turned me down. Too close to the water.
Ask your insurance broker about C-MAP. It's for coastal homeowners who got turned down. And NYPIUA, the FAIR plan, is the backstop.

check.q: What is NYPIUA?
c: A federal flood program
NY's FAIR plan, an insurer of last resort
A DOS licensing board
A type of umbrella policy
check.x: The New York Property Insurance Underwriting Association is the state's FAIR plan for owners who cannot get coverage in the voluntary market.

beats.text: The quote says hurricane deductible 3%. Of what?
Of your dwelling limit. NY makes them print it as a percent and a dollar amount. On $400,000 of coverage, that's $12,000 on a hurricane claim.
And should I get HO-3 or HO-5? What would you pick?
I can explain the difference. HO-5 adds all-risk coverage on contents. But your insurance broker should make the recommendation. That's their license, not mine.
You protected him from the two worst mistakes: closing uninsured and assuming flood is covered. That's the whole job here.

board.prompt: Draw a house and list which HO coverage (A to F) pays for: a stolen bike, a fallen fence, a guest's broken wrist, a hotel after a fire, a burst pipe in the wall.

facts.text: Property insurance covers sudden loss to the property, liability insurance covers harm the owner causes others, and a lender requires coverage to protect its collateral.
Insurance agents and brokers are licensed by DFS, not DOS; an insurance broker represents the buyer, an independent agent the insurers that appoint it.
A monoline policy covers one line (such as a dwelling fire policy); a package policy bundles several, and a homeowners policy is a package.
Homeowners coverages: A dwelling, B other structures, C personal property, D loss of use, E personal liability, F medical payments to guests regardless of fault.
HO-3 (special) is the most widely used form: all risks except exclusions on the dwelling, named perils on contents; HO-5 adds open perils on contents.
HO-6 is the condo unit owners form: walls-in, improvements, contents, liability and loss assessment.
HO-4 covers renters (and, per the NY syllabus, co-op owners): contents and liability, no building.
HO-1 and HO-2 are named-peril forms; HO-8 is for older homes whose rebuild cost far exceeds market value and pays actual cash value or repair with common materials.
A standard homeowners policy excludes flood and earthquake, and wear and tear, neglect mold and pests are not insurable losses.
Actual cash value equals replacement cost minus depreciation.
Replacement cost coverage pays for new materials of like kind and quality with no deduction for age.
