Under an 80% coinsurance clause, an owner carrying less than 80% of replacement cost collects (carried / required) x loss.
Default limits are often percentages of Coverage A (contents about half), and endorsements can schedule valuables or raise limits.
NYPIUA is New York's FAIR plan, the insurer of last resort for owners shut out of the voluntary market.
Flood coverage comes from the NFIP, run by FEMA, required for federally backed mortgages in a Special Flood Hazard Area; it usually has a 30-day wait unless bought with a new loan.
C-MAP helps declined owner-occupied coastal homeowners find an insurer.
In its first 60 days a new homeowners policy can be canceled for almost any reason; after that only for listed reasons such as nonpayment, fraud or increased hazard.
A policy canceled for nonpayment stays in force if the premium is paid within 15 days of the notice.
Nonrenewal needs written notice with the reason 45 to 60 days before expiration, or the policy renews.
Premiums rise with risk and coverage limits; a higher deductible lowers the premium.
A hurricane deductible is a percentage of the dwelling limit (2% of $600,000 is $12,000) and must be shown as both a percentage and a dollar amount.
An umbrella policy adds liability coverage above the home and auto limits; landlords and investors use commercial policies or a BOP.
The lender is named mortgagee, requires a binder or declarations page before closing, can force-place coverage, and usually escrows insurance with PITI.
Under NY law the seller bears the risk of loss until title or possession passes, so a cash buyer should bind coverage effective at closing.
Agents explain insurance but send buyers to a licensed insurance agent or broker for coverage advice.

lessons.title: Case file: The Two-Family on West Pine Street
lessons.tagline: A Long Beach two-family in flood zone AE with a 22-year-old roof. Seven insurers say no, and closing is in six weeks.
objectives: Decide where to place a hard-to-insure coastal home, from independent agents to C-MAP and NYPIUA.
Calculate a hurricane deductible, a coinsurance payout and an actual cash value settlement.
Apply federal flood insurance requirements, the NFIP waiting period and lender escrow to a financed purchase.
Apply New York's cancellation and nonrenewal rules to a new homeowners policy.

blocks.title: Long Beach, six weeks to closing
blocks.html: Andre and Nia Baptiste, a nurse and a middle school teacher, are in contract on a two-family house on West Pine Street in Long Beach, Nassau County, for $899,000. They will live upstairs and rent the ground-floor apartment for $2,600 a month. The house was built in 1955, has a 22-year-old roof, sits in FEMA flood zone AE three blocks from the ocean, and took on water in Superstorm Sandy in 2012, which the seller disclosed on the Property Condition Disclosure Statement. Tasha has their conventional loan approved at 80% of the price, and closing is set for October 30. On the day of the contract signing, Jordan, who referred the Baptistes to a Long Island colleague and is helping them through the process, asks a question nobody has asked yet: "Have you called anyone about insurance?" Nobody has.

Nia calls the company that insures their car. The agent there can only offer that company's policies, and the company is not writing new homeowners policies within a mile of the ocean in Nassau County. Andre wants to know who else to call.

blocks.q: For a hard-to-place coastal home, which kind of seller is most likely to get the Baptistes several quotes quickly?
c: A captive agent of a single insurer, who knows that company's rules best
An independent agent or broker who can approach many insurers at once
The lender's loan officer, who arranges coverage before closing
The seller's current insurer, which transfers the policy to the buyer
blocks.x: A captive or direct-writer agent sells one company's policies. An independent agent can quote every insurer that has appointed it, and an insurance broker represents the buyer of insurance and shops the market. For a house many insurers avoid, reach matters. The lender requires proof of coverage but does not place it, and the seller's homeowners policy does not transfer to a buyer. Knowing one company's rules well does not help if that company will not write the house.

blocks.html: The independent agent, Ruth Feldman in Oceanside, sends the file to nine insurers. She also pulls the house's loss history report, which insurers share through a claims database and which follows the property, not the owner. It shows the 2012 flood claim under the seller's flood policy and a 2019 homeowners claim for wind damage to the roof. Two days later Ruth reports back: seven insurers declined, citing the roof's age and the distance to the water. Two have not answered.

blocks.q: Ruth has two declinations in writing for an owner-occupied home near the coast. What should she try next?
c: Submit the home through C-MAP, then NYPIUA if no insurer takes it
Tell the Baptistes no coverage is possible until they replace the roof
Write the house on a commercial policy, which has no location limits
Ask the lender to accept a letter that the buyers will self-insure
blocks.x: The Coastal Market Assistance Program exists for exactly this: owner-occupied homes in New York's coastal areas, including Nassau County, that have been turned down in the regular market. Participating insurers volunteer to consider them. If that fails, NYPIUA, the state's FAIR plan, is the insurer of last resort for basic property coverage. A roof replacement may lower the price, but coverage is available before it. Lenders do not accept self-insurance on mortgaged homes.

blocks.html: The loss history matters twice. Insurers price a house partly on its own claims, so a prior flood and a prior roof claim raise the premium no matter who owns it. And since March 20, 2024, New York's Property Condition Disclosure Statement asks sellers whether the property is in a floodplain, whether it has flood insurance and whether flood claims were filed, which is how the Baptistes learned about 2012 before they signed. Buyers who read those answers early can get insurance quotes before the contract, not after it.

Through C-MAP, a regional insurer agrees to write a homeowners policy, an HO-3, conditioned on an inspection of the roof within 30 days of the start date. The quote arrives with a dwelling limit, a regular deductible and a separate hurricane deductible.

blocks.title: Quote summary, HO-3, West Pine Street
blocks.html:
Coverage A, dwelling: $650,000 (insurer's replacement cost estimate)
Coverage B, other structures: $65,000
Coverage C, personal property: $325,000
Coverage E, personal liability: $300,000
All-other-perils deductible: $2,500
Hurricane deductible: 5% of Coverage A
Annual premium: $5,400
Flood: excluded

Ruth walks them through what drives the $5,400 premium: distance to the ocean, the frame construction, the roof's age, the prior claims, the $650,000 limit and the deductibles. Three things are in their control. A higher all-other-perils deductible lowers the premium. A new roof, and in coastal areas wind-resistant features such as hurricane straps and impact-rated windows, can earn discounts. Bundling auto coverage with the same insurer sometimes helps. None of these changes the flood picture, which has its own policy and its own price.

blocks.q: A hurricane damages the roof and siding for $48,000 of covered loss. Using the quote, what do the Baptistes pay before the insurer pays?
c: $2,500, the regular deductible for other perils
$24,000, half of the 5% deductible
$32,500, which is 5% of the dwelling limit
$48,000, because hurricane losses are excluded
blocks.x: A hurricane deductible is a percentage of the dwelling limit, not of the loss: 5% x $650,000 = $32,500. The insurer would pay $48,000 minus $32,500 = $15,500. New York's Insurance Law 3445 and DFS rules require insurers to show this deductible on the declarations page as both a percentage and a dollar amount, with a notice explaining it. Applying the $2,500 deductible is the costly mistake buyers make when they skim the quote.

blocks.html: Nia asks whether they could lower the premium by insuring the house for less. The price was $899,000, she points out, but the land in Long Beach is worth a lot, so maybe $500,000 is plenty. Ruth explains that the dwelling limit is about rebuilding the structure, not the market value, and that the policy has a coinsurance clause requiring coverage of at least 80% of replacement cost to collect in full on a partial loss.

blocks.q: If the Baptistes insure the dwelling for $500,000 instead of $650,000 and a kitchen fire causes $60,000 of damage, how much does the insurer pay before the deductible?
c: $60,000, because the loss is far below the $500,000 limit
$46,154, which is $500,000 over $650,000 times the loss
$57,692, which is $500,000 over $520,000 times the loss
$48,000, which is 80% of the $60,000 loss
blocks.x: The coinsurance test asks what they should carry: 80% of $650,000 = $520,000. They carried $500,000. Payout = carried / required x loss = $500,000 / $520,000 x $60,000 = $57,692. Dividing by the full $650,000 skips the 80% step. Being far below the limit does not matter; underinsuring cuts every partial claim. At $520,000 or more, the full $60,000 (less the deductible) would be paid.

blocks.html: They keep the $650,000 limit. Andre's question is about the furniture. The policy's Coverage C pays actual cash value for personal property unless they add a replacement cost endorsement, which costs $310 a year.

blocks.q: A covered fire destroys a 6-year-old sofa that cost $2,400 and would cost $3,000 to replace. Its useful life is 10 years. Without the endorsement, what is the sofa's actual cash value?
c: $1,200, the replacement cost less 60% depreciation
$960, which is the original price minus 60% depreciation
$2,400, which is the price the Baptistes originally paid
$3,000, which is the cost of a new sofa of like kind
blocks.x: Actual cash value is replacement cost minus depreciation. Six of ten years used is 60%, and 60% of the $3,000 replacement cost is $1,800, leaving $1,200. Depreciating the original price confuses what was paid with what it costs today. With the replacement cost endorsement, the insurer would pay $3,000 once the sofa is replaced. For a household furnishing a new home, the endorsement is often worth the $310.

blocks.html: Ruth's quote says "Flood: excluded," and that is standard: homeowners policies do not cover rising water. The lender's commitment letter says the same thing in its own language: because the house is in a Special Flood Hazard Area and the loan is going to be sold to Fannie Mae, the Baptistes must carry flood insurance.

Jordan pulls up the address on FEMA's Flood Map Service Center to confirm the zone the lender cited. Zone AE means a Special Flood Hazard Area with a base flood elevation, which is the elevation floodwater is expected to reach in a flood with a 1% chance in any year. An elevation certificate, which shows how high the lowest floor sits relative to that level, can change the flood premium, so Ruth asks the seller for the one the seller's flood insurer has on file.

blocks.title: Loan and flood facts
blocks.html:
Loan amount: $719,200 (80% of $899,000)
Flood zone: AE (Special Flood Hazard Area)
NFIP maximum building coverage, 1 to 4 family residence: $250,000
NFIP maximum contents coverage: $100,000 (purchased separately)
Insurer's estimate of the building's replacement cost: $650,000

blocks.q: What is the minimum flood coverage on the building the lender can require under the federal flood rules?
c: $719,200, the full loan amount
$650,000, the replacement cost of the building
$250,000, the NFIP maximum for a residence
$100,000, the NFIP maximum for contents
blocks.x: Federal law requires flood insurance on buildings in a Special Flood Hazard Area securing federally related loans, in an amount at least equal to the lowest of the loan balance, the maximum available under the NFIP, or the building's insurable value. Here that is the $250,000 NFIP building maximum. Lenders may ask for more, often through excess flood coverage, and the Baptistes may want it, since the building would cost $650,000 to rebuild. Contents coverage is separate and optional.

blocks.html: Nia has read that NFIP policies take 30 days to start. It is October 2, and closing is October 30, so she is worried. Ruth explains the rule and its exception.

blocks.q: Does the 30-day NFIP waiting period delay the Baptistes' flood coverage?
c: Yes, so closing has to move to November at the earliest
Yes, unless the seller agrees to keep insuring the house
No, because the wait applies to commercial buildings alone
No, it is bought in connection with the new loan
blocks.x: The NFIP's standard 30-day wait does not apply when the policy is purchased in connection with making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan, so the Baptistes' policy can start at closing. A cash buyer gets no such exception and must apply at least 30 days ahead. Ruth also asks the seller whether the existing flood policy can be assigned to the buyers at closing, which FEMA permits. The seller's homeowners policy never covered flood, so it cannot fill the gap.

blocks.html: Their flood premium under FEMA's current pricing, which rates each property on its own risk, is quoted at $3,900 a year for $250,000 of building coverage. They add $40,000 of contents coverage for $450. The ground-floor tenant asks Andre whether the new flood policy will cover her things.

blocks.q: What is the best answer to the tenant's question?
c: Yes, because the landlord's policies cover the whole building
No, she needs her own renters policy and flood cover
Yes, but just the items she keeps in the basement storage area
No, because tenants in a flood zone cannot buy any insurance
blocks.x: A landlord's homeowners and flood policies insure the building and the landlord's own property, not a tenant's belongings. The tenant needs her own renters policy, an HO-4, for theft, fire and liability, and a separate NFIP contents policy if she wants flood protection for her things. NFIP contents coverage in basements is also limited, so the storage area is the worst place to rely on. Tenants anywhere can buy renters insurance.

blocks.html: Andre and Nia add a clause to the new lease requiring the tenant to carry renters insurance with at least $100,000 of liability and to name them as an additional interest, so they are told if her policy lapses. Ruth adds that their own HO-3 still provides liability coverage for the building's common areas, the stoop and the yard.

blocks.text: Week four: the lender, the binder and the escrow

blocks.html: Tasha sends the closing checklist. The lender needs an insurance binder or declarations page for both policies, naming the lender as mortgagee, at least a week before closing. It will also collect insurance and property taxes monthly in escrow.

blocks.title: Annual carrying costs for escrow
blocks.html:
Homeowners premium (HO-3 with contents endorsement): $5,710
Flood premium (building and contents): $4,350
Property taxes (county, city and school): $15,540
Total: $25,600 a year

blocks.q: How much will the lender add to the Baptistes' monthly mortgage payment for escrow, before any cushion?
c: $1,295, which is the taxes divided by 12
$838, the two premiums divided by 12
$2,560, which is 10% of the total
$2,133, the total divided by 12
blocks.x: Escrow collects one-twelfth of each annual bill with every payment: $25,600 / 12 = $2,133.33. The principal and interest payment plus that escrow is the PITI payment Tasha used to qualify them. Lenders may also hold a small cushion. Dividing only the taxes or only the premiums leaves out half the bill, which is a common budgeting mistake for buyers who used a calculator that ignores insurance.

blocks.q: Why does the lender insist on being named on the policies as mortgagee?
c: So claim checks protect the collateral and it gets notice
So the lender can cancel the policy if the buyers miss a payment
So the lender can collect any liability award against the owners
So the premium becomes tax deductible as mortgage interest
blocks.x: The house is the lender's collateral. Naming the lender as mortgagee means claim checks for the building are payable to the lender as well as the owners, so repair money goes into the house, and the lender is notified if coverage is canceled or not renewed. If coverage lapses, the lender can buy force-placed insurance and charge the borrower, usually at a much higher price. Liability coverage protects the owners, not the lender.

blocks.title: New York's cancellation and nonrenewal rules
blocks.html: For a homeowners policy in force less than 60 days, a New York insurer may cancel for any reason with written notice. After 60 days it may cancel only for listed reasons, such as nonpayment of premium, fraud or material misrepresentation, or a physical change in the property that makes it uninsurable. Nonrenewal requires written notice with the specific reason, mailed at least 45 and not more than 60 days before expiration; if the notice is late, the policy renews.

Between the binder and the closing, Jordan reminds the Baptistes who carries the risk in the meantime. Under New York's Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act, the seller bears the risk of loss until title or possession passes, so the seller keeps the house insured through the closing date. The buyers' policies should start at 12:01 a.m. on the day of closing, not the day after the deed is recorded and not when the first escrow payment is made. A one-day gap is all a pipe or a storm needs.

blocks.title: Stay in your lane, but start the clock
blocks.html: Jordan is not an insurance agent and does not recommend coverage amounts or carriers. What Jordan does is raise insurance on day one, point buyers to licensed agents and brokers, flag the flood zone and the PCDS flood answers, and put the binder deadline on the closing checklist. On coastal and older homes, the insurance quote can change the buyer's monthly payment by hundreds of dollars, which can change whether the loan still qualifies.

The Baptistes close on October 30. On December 4, day 35 of the policy, the insurer sends a cancellation notice after its roof inspector photographs missing shingles and soft decking. Andre calls Jordan, upset: "Can they do that after they took our money?"

blocks.q: Can the insurer cancel the Baptistes' HO-3 at day 35 based on the inspection?
c: No, because a policy can be canceled for nonpayment alone
No, because a mortgaged home cannot have its coverage canceled
Yes, but just with 90 days' notice and a full premium refund
Yes, within 60 days a new policy may be canceled with notice
blocks.x: In the first 60 days New York lets an insurer cancel a homeowners policy with written notice, which is why the roof inspection condition matters. The insurer refunds the unearned premium. A mortgage does not prevent cancellation; it only means the lender is notified and may force-place coverage. The Baptistes replace the roof for $18,500 in January, get a C-MAP quote at a lower premium, and avoid force-placed coverage by binding the new policy before the old one ends.

blocks.html: Two years later the Baptistes are offered jobs upstate and decide to keep the Long Beach house as a rental, with tenants in both units. Ruth tells them their HO-3 will not fit anymore. Homeowners forms are written for owner-occupied homes; a house with no owner living in it is insured on a dwelling policy, often called a landlord or dwelling fire policy, with liability bought alongside it or added by endorsement.

blocks.q: The Baptistes move out and rent both units. What coverage change is most appropriate?
c: Keep the HO-3, since it covers any home the owners have title to
Move to a dwelling (landlord) policy with liability and loss of rents
Switch to an HO-4, since the building will now be occupied by tenants
Switch to an HO-6, since there are now two separate rental units
blocks.x: Homeowners forms assume the owner lives in the home, so a fully rented two-family moves to a dwelling policy, a property policy written for rentals, often paired with landlord liability and loss of rents coverage that replaces income while repairs happen. An HO-4 insures a tenant's belongings, not a building, and an HO-6 is for condo unit owners. Keeping the HO-3 after moving out risks a denied claim because the policy's occupancy assumption is no longer true.

blocks.html: The following September, Andre buys a $1 million umbrella policy for $420 a year after Ruth explains that a landlord with a tenant, a stoop and a beach-bound bike rack has more liability exposure than his $300,000 base limit covers. The umbrella requires him to keep $300,000 of liability on the home and $250,000 per person on the car, and it sits on top of both.

blocks.title: Three numbers buyers confuse
blocks.html: Market value includes land and is what the house sells for. Replacement cost is what it costs to rebuild the structure and drives the dwelling limit and the 80% coinsurance test. Actual cash value is replacement cost minus depreciation. A hurricane deductible is a percentage of the dwelling limit, not of the loss, and flood is a separate policy with its own limits. Exam questions mix these up on purpose.

head: Policy
Covers
Annual cost
rows: Dwelling $650,000, contents at replacement cost, liability $300,000
blocks.caption: The Baptistes' insurance file, year two

items: Use an independent agent or broker for hard-to-place homes; after declinations, coastal owner-occupants go to C-MAP, then NYPIUA as the insurer of last resort.
A hurricane deductible is a percentage of the dwelling limit; New York requires it shown as a percentage and a dollar amount.
Insure to replacement cost, not market value; below 80%, partial claims are paid at carried over required times the loss.

In a Special Flood Hazard Area, federally related loans need flood coverage of at least the lowest of the loan balance, the NFIP maximum or insurable value; the 30-day wait is waived for loan closings.
Lenders require a binder, are named as mortgagee and escrow premiums and taxes; New York limits cancellation after 60 days and requires 45 to 60 days' notice of nonrenewal.

roleplays.title: The Building Has Insurance, Right?
roleplays.setting: Phone call, a few weeks before Leo's Queens condo closing. Tasha is on the line too.
roleplays.goal: Get Leo properly insured before closing: explain HO-6 vs the master policy, the lender's requirements, escrow, and flood, and send him to a licensed insurance professional without taking a referral fee.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Leo Brandt, an anxious first-time buyer closing on a Queens condo with a mortgage. Insist the building's master policy covers you, then resist escrow, ask about replacement cost and flood, then ask the agent to just choose a policy for you and hint you'd be fine if they got a referral fee. The learner must explain HO-6 vs the master policy, the lender's need for a binder naming it as mortgagee, how escrow works in PITI, replacement cost vs actual cash value, that flood is excluded and comes from NFIP, and refer to a licensed insurance professional without any kickback. Grade each point and give one practical tip.
opening: Leo closes on unit {unit} in {hood} in {weeks}. Tasha has the loan with {lender} moving, and Leo has questions about insurance.
A three-way call: you, Leo, and Tasha. The {hood} condo closes in {weeks}, and the lender just asked for proof of insurance.
Leo's text: "Quick call? Insurance stuff." The closing on {unit} is {weeks} away. Tasha joins a minute later.

say: The building has a master insurance policy. So I can skip buying my own, right? Saves me {saving} a month.
Why would I pay {saving} a month when the condo already has insurance?

moves.text: The master policy covers the building and common areas. Your interior, stuff and liability need an HO-6.
moves.fb: Correct. HO-6 is the condo unit owner's form and fills the gap the association's master policy leaves.
moves.react: So the building covers the shell and I cover the inside.

moves.text: The building policy stops at your walls, roughly. An HO-6 covers your stuff, upgrades, liability.
moves.fb: Right. Condo owners use HO-6 for interior, contents, liability and loss assessments.

moves.text: Get renters insurance, an HO-4, instead. It's cheaper and covers your belongings, which is the main thing.
moves.fb: Closer, but HO-4 has no coverage for owner improvements or loss assessments. Condo owners use HO-6.
moves.react: Renters insurance as an owner? Weird, but cheap.

moves.text: Probably fine. The board would have told you if owners needed their own policy. Ask them to be sure.
moves.fb: Wrong and risky. The master policy doesn't cover his belongings or personal liability, and his lender will want proof.

moves.text: Master policies cover everything inside the units in New York. It's required by the state's condo law.
moves.fb: False. Coverage depends on the master policy, and it generally excludes owners' belongings and liability.

moves.text: You need an HO-3 like any homeowner. That's the most common policy, so the lender will want that one.
moves.fb: HO-3 is for houses. A condo unit owner uses HO-6.

say: Tasha: "Also, the lender needs proof of coverage before the clear to close. Leo, you've never done this before."
Tasha: "Leo, {lender} won't fund without evidence of insurance. Jordan, want to explain?"

moves.text: Your insurer issues a binder naming the lender as mortgagee. Tasha sends it to underwriting.
moves.fb: Right. The lender protects its collateral through the mortgagee clause and requires evidence of insurance before closing.
moves.react: A binder. I'll ask for one this week.

moves.text: Before closing you get a binder listing the lender as mortgagee. No binder, no funding at closing.
moves.fb: Correct. The binder is the lender's proof of coverage, and it names the lender as mortgagee.
moves.react: No binder, no funding. Got it.

moves.text: Just send Tasha a screenshot of the quote. That's usually enough for the lender to clear you to close.
moves.fb: A quote isn't coverage. The lender needs a binder or declarations page naming it as mortgagee.

moves.text: You can buy the policy the week after closing. Lenders give you a 30-day grace period for that.
moves.fb: The lender won't fund without proof of coverage, and Leo bears the risk once title passes.

moves.text: The master policy certificate is all the lender needs. Your own policy doesn't matter to them.
moves.fb: Many lenders want both the master policy certificate and the unit owner's HO-6 evidence. Check with Tasha.

moves.text: Name me as an additional insured so I can handle claims for you if anything goes wrong after closing.
moves.fb: The lender is named as mortgagee. A real estate agent has no insurable interest and no role in claims.

say: Why does my monthly payment estimate include insurance? I'd rather pay it once a year.
Do I have to pay insurance through the mortgage? I'd rather handle it myself.

moves.text: Most lenders escrow taxes and insurance for you. It's the T and I in PITI. A waiver is Tasha's call.
moves.fb: Accurate, and the waiver question correctly goes to the loan professional.
moves.react: Tasha, can I waive it? Tasha: "Let's look at your LTV."

moves.text: That's escrow. Lenders collect monthly and pay the bill when due. Opting out is up to them.
moves.fb: Right. PITI includes taxes and insurance escrowed by the lender; waivers depend on lender rules and loan-to-value.
moves.react: So it's their rule, not yours. Okay.

moves.text: Some people pay it themselves. I'd just ask the lender at some point if they'll let you do that.
moves.fb: Not wrong, but explain escrow and PITI so he understands why it's there.

moves.text: Escrow is optional, just tell them no. Federal law says it's always the borrower's choice to make.
moves.fb: Not your call and often not true. Lenders commonly require escrow, especially at higher LTVs.

moves.text: Insurance in your payment means the bank owns the policy. That's why you can't shop around for it.
moves.fb: The borrower owns the policy and can shop for it; the lender just collects and pays the premium.

moves.text: It's a fee for the lender's own insurance on the loan, not for your policy. That's PMI, basically.
moves.fb: PMI protects the lender on high-LTV loans and is separate. Escrowed insurance pays Leo's own hazard policy.

say: The quotes say 'replacement cost' or 'actual cash value.' Which one do I want?
One quote is replacement cost, one is ACV. What's the difference?

moves.text: Replacement cost pays to replace new. ACV subtracts depreciation, so it pays less. A broker quotes both.
moves.fb: Correct. ACV = replacement cost minus depreciation. The licensed broker advises which fits.
moves.react: So ACV is cheaper because it pays less.

moves.text: ACV subtracts depreciation, so a 10-year-old couch pays out little. Replacement cost buys a new one.
moves.fb: Right concept. The choice and the pricing belong with a licensed insurance professional.
moves.react: Got it. I'll ask the broker to quote both.

moves.text: They're about the same thing. Pick whichever is cheaper and you'll be fine for a condo your size.
moves.fb: They're not the same: ACV deducts depreciation. Explain it and let a licensed broker advise.

moves.text: Actual cash value pays more because it's based on the cash price of buying new items today.
moves.fb: Backwards. ACV is replacement cost minus depreciation, so it usually pays less.

moves.text: Replacement cost only applies to the building, never to your belongings. ACV is your only option.
moves.fb: Many HO-6 policies offer replacement cost on contents. Ask a licensed broker.

moves.text: Pick ACV. Then the 80% coinsurance rule doesn't apply to you at all, so you'll never be penalized for it.
moves.fb: Coinsurance relates to carrying enough coverage (often 80% of replacement cost). ACV doesn't make it go away.

say: My basement storage cage flooded in the last big storm, according to the neighbors. Is flood covered?
Neighbors said water came into the building's basement during that storm. Does my policy cover flood?

moves.text: Standard policies exclude flood. That's NFIP or a private flood policy. Ask the broker.
moves.fb: Correct. Flood and earthquake are excluded from standard HO policies; NFIP is the federal flood program through FEMA.

moves.text: Not on an HO-6. Flood is a separate policy, often through NFIP, and there's usually a 30-day wait.
moves.fb: Right. NFIP coverage usually has a 30-day waiting period unless tied to a loan.
moves.react: A wait? Then I should ask now.

moves.text: I'm not sure. It depends on the policy, I think. Ask whoever sells you the HO-6 about it later.
moves.fb: Referral is fine, but you should know flood is a standard exclusion.

moves.text: Yes, water damage is covered on any HO-6, whatever the source, so you're fully protected there.
moves.fb: Flood is excluded from standard policies. Covered water damage (like a burst pipe) is different from flood.

moves.text: The master policy covers flood for every unit owner. That's exactly what the board's insurance is for.
moves.fb: Master policies vary and flood is commonly excluded. Leo's belongings need their own coverage.

moves.text: Flood insurance is only sold in coastal zones. Queens inland doesn't qualify for any of it.
moves.fb: NFIP coverage is available in participating communities, in and out of high-risk zones.

say: Can you just pick a policy for me? You must know someone good.
Honestly, choose one for me. Whoever you use, I'll use.

moves.text: Here are two licensed brokers clients have used. They'll recommend coverage. I take no referral fees.
moves.fb: Good service without practicing insurance or taking a kickback. Insurance advice belongs to DFS-licensed agents and brokers.

moves.text: Coverage advice needs an insurance license, and I don't have one. Here are three brokers. I get nothing.
moves.fb: Correct. You refer to licensed professionals and disclose there's no compensation.

moves.text: Get an HO-6 with a $500 deductible and contents at $50,000. Trust me, that's what everyone here has.
moves.fb: Choosing coverage for him goes beyond your expertise and license. Explain, then refer.

moves.text: Use my cousin's agency. I get $100 for every referral, but I promise that doesn't change my advice.
moves.fb: A referral fee tied to a settlement service in a federally related mortgage transaction violates RESPA Section 8, even if disclosed.

moves.text: I'll call the insurer and bind it for you myself today. I do that for buyers all the time, honestly.
moves.fb: Binding coverage requires an insurance license from DFS. A real estate license doesn't cover it.

moves.text: Buy whatever the building's master policy insurer offers. They're required to cover owners in the building.
moves.fb: There's no such requirement. Shop through a licensed broker.

say: The board just announced a special assessment after a storm damaged the roof. Does insurance help with that?
There's a new assessment for storm damage to the roof. Am I covered for my share?

moves.text: HO-6 loss assessment coverage can pay your share if it's a covered loss. Ask about the limit.
moves.fb: Correct. Loss assessment coverage applies to assessments from covered perils, up to the limit.
moves.react: So it depends on why they're assessing.

moves.text: Maybe. Loss assessment coverage helps if the cause is a covered peril, not upkeep. Check the limit.
moves.fb: Right. Maintenance assessments aren't covered; covered losses may be.

moves.text: Probably not. Assessments are just part of owning a condo. Budget for it and move on from there.
moves.fb: Too quick. Loss assessment coverage exists for exactly this; let the broker confirm.

moves.text: Yes, every assessment is covered by an HO-6, including those for repainting the hallways.
moves.fb: Loss assessment coverage applies to covered losses, not maintenance or improvements.

moves.text: The seller pays every assessment announced before closing, by law. It's not your problem at all.
moves.fb: Who pays depends on the contract and the board's terms. Priya should check.

moves.text: Assessments only exist in co-ops. Condo owners can't be assessed for building repairs like that.
moves.fb: Condo boards can levy special assessments for common element costs.
moves.react: Good thing I bought a condo.

say: If I file a claim, can they drop me right away?
My friend got dropped after one claim. Can that happen to me?

moves.text: After 60 days, a NY homeowners policy can be cancelled only for listed reasons, like nonpayment.
moves.fb: Correct. NY limits mid-term cancellation after 60 days; nonrenewal requires written notice with a reason.

moves.text: Mid-term, only for specific reasons. Nonrenewal at the end needs written notice 45 to 60 days ahead.
moves.fb: Right. NY Insurance Law restricts cancellations and requires advance written notice for nonrenewal.
moves.react: So I'd at least get warning.

moves.text: That's up to the insurer. Some are stricter than others, so ask the broker which are friendly.
moves.fb: Partly true, but NY law limits cancellation. Explain the basics.

moves.text: Yes, any claim lets them cancel immediately. That's why you should never file small claims.
moves.fb: After 60 days, cancellation is limited to listed reasons. Advising against valid claims is outside your role.

moves.text: No, they can never cancel or nonrenew a policy in New York once it's been issued to you, ever.
moves.fb: Too broad. Cancellation is limited, and nonrenewal is allowed with notice and a reason.

moves.text: They can cancel any time in the first year for any reason at all. After that, you're locked in for good.
moves.fb: The NY window is 60 days, not a year, and nonrenewal is still possible later with notice.

say: Tasha, after Leo drops off: "My insurance guy pays $50 a referral. Want me to cut you in?"
Tasha texts: "Send Leo to my insurance contact, we both get a referral bonus."

moves.text: No thanks. That's a kickback on a settlement service under RESPA. Disclosed or not, no.
moves.fb: Correct. RESPA Section 8 bans referral fees for settlement services in federally related mortgage loans.

moves.text: I'll pass. Leo gets names without strings attached. RESPA doesn't allow referral fees like that.
moves.fb: Right. Referral fees violate RESPA, and they compromise your loyalty to your client.

moves.text: Let me think about it. If it's disclosed to Leo, it might be okay. I'm not totally sure, honestly.
moves.fb: Disclosure doesn't cure a RESPA kickback. Decline.

moves.text: Sure, as long as it's under $100. Small referral gifts are allowed under the federal rules, I think.
moves.fb: RESPA has no small-kickback exception for referral fees tied to settlement services.

moves.text: Yes, but pay it to my broker instead of me. Then it's legal because it goes through the firm.
moves.fb: Routing a kickback through the broker doesn't make it legal under RESPA.

moves.text: Only if the referral goes on Leo's Closing Disclosure. Then it's fully legal and transparent.
moves.fb: Disclosure doesn't legalize a RESPA Section 8 referral fee.

say: Should I take the highest deductible to save money?
Does a higher deductible really save much? Should I max it out?

moves.text: Higher deductible, lower premium. Pick one you could pay tomorrow. The broker can show the math.
moves.fb: Correct trade-off, with the specific choice left to Leo and a licensed broker.
moves.react: Could I pay it tomorrow... maybe $1,000.

moves.text: It lowers the premium, but you pay more per claim. Pick what your savings can absorb, then get quotes.
moves.fb: Right. You explain the principle and refer the specific coverage decision.
moves.react: I'll look at my savings first.

moves.text: I'd go middle of the road. Most people pick $1,000. You really can't go wrong there, I'd say.
moves.fb: Not harmful, but you're picking coverage for him. Explain the trade-off and refer.

moves.text: A higher deductible raises your premium, since the insurer takes more of the risk. Go low instead.
moves.fb: Backwards. Higher deductible means lower premium.

moves.text: Deductibles are set by the condo board for every unit, so you don't get to choose your own at all.
moves.fb: The unit owner chooses the HO-6 deductible with their insurer.

moves.text: Max it out. Then the lender can't require escrow, since your premium will be tiny each year.
moves.fb: Escrow requirements don't depend on the deductible.

roleplays.debrief: You practised the insurance basics a buyer's agent must know: a condo owner needs an HO-6 because the master policy covers the building and common areas, the lender needs a binder naming it as mortgagee, and taxes and insurance are often escrowed in PITI. ACV is replacement cost minus depreciation, flood is excluded and comes from NFIP, and NY limits mid-term cancellation after 60 days. Coverage advice belongs to DFS-licensed professionals, and referral fees on settlement services violate RESPA.

questions.q: A condo unit owner typically buys which homeowners policy form?
c: HO-6
HO-3
HO-4
HO-8
questions.x: HO-6 is the condo unit owner form. HO-4 is the trap: it is for tenants (and, in New York practice, co-op owners).

questions.q: The most common policy form for an owner-occupied single-family house is:
c: HO-4
HO-6
HO-3
HO-1
questions.x: HO-3, the special form, is the standard homeowner policy. HO-4 is the trap: it covers renters' belongings.

questions.q: A temporary written confirmation that coverage is in force until the policy is issued is a(n):
c: Endorsement
Binder
Rider
Declaration page
questions.x: A binder proves coverage before the policy arrives, and lenders usually require one at closing. Endorsement is the trap: it changes an existing policy.

questions.q: Why does a mortgage lender typically require an insurance binder before closing?
c: To set the interest rate
To replace the title search
To confirm the appraisal
To prove the property is insured from day one
questions.x: The lender's collateral must be insured at closing. The title search is the trap: insurance does not replace it.

questions.q: The most widely used homeowners policy for an owner-occupied house is:
c: HO-1 basic form
HO-3 special form
HO-5 comprehensive form
HO-8 modified form
questions.x: HO-3, the special form, covers the dwelling on an open-perils basis (everything not excluded) and is the most common homeowners form. HO-5 is the trap: it is broader, but less common and more expensive.

questions.q: A condominium unit owner would typically buy:
c: HO-2 broad form
HO-3 special form
HO-4 contents broad form
HO-6 unit-owners form
questions.x: HO-6 is the unit owner's form: interior, improvements, contents, liability, and loss assessments. HO-4 is the trap: it is the renters' contents form (also used for co-op contents).

questions.q: A tenant renting an apartment in Washington Heights wants to insure her furniture and electronics and protect herself if a guest is injured. She should buy:
c: HO-4 contents form
HO-5 comprehensive form
HO-6 unit-owners form
HO-8 modified form
questions.x: HO-4 covers a tenant's contents and liability with no building coverage. HO-6 is the trap: it is for condo owners, who own and insure their unit interior.

questions.q: An HO-8 policy is designed for:
c: Condominium unit owners and their contents
Newly built homes with modern materials
Older homes that would be costly to rebuild as built
Tenants who own furniture but not a building
questions.x: HO-8, the modified or market value form, pays actual cash value or repairs with common materials, suiting older homes whose replacement cost far exceeds market value. The condo answer is the trap: that is HO-6.

questions.q: Actual cash value is:
c: Market value of the home, including land
Full cost to replace with new materials
Replacement cost minus accumulated depreciation
The coverage limit on the declarations page
questions.x: ACV equals replacement cost minus depreciation. The new-materials answer is the trap: that is replacement cost coverage, with no deduction for age.

questions.q: A central air system that would cost $12,000 to replace has a 20-year useful life and is 8 years old. Under actual cash value coverage, ignoring the deductible, the insurer pays:
questions.x: Depreciation is 8/20 = 40% of $12,000 = $4,800, so ACV = $12,000 - $4,800 = $7,200. $4,800 is the trap: it is the depreciation, not the payout.

questions.q: A house has a replacement cost of $400,000 and is insured for $240,000 under a policy with an 80% coinsurance clause. A $12,000 loss occurs. Ignoring the deductible, the insurer pays:
questions.x: Required coverage is 80% x $400,000 = $320,000; $240,000 / $320,000 = 0.75, and 0.75 x $12,000 = $9,000. $7,200 is the trap: it divides by the full $400,000 instead of the 80% requirement.

questions.q: A homeowners policy that combines property coverage, personal liability, and medical payments in one contract is a:
c: Monoline policy
Package policy
Umbrella policy
Binder
questions.x: Bundling several coverages in one contract makes it a package policy. Monoline is the trap: it covers a single line, such as fire.

questions.q: A policy covering one type of risk, such as a dwelling fire policy on a rental house, is called a:
c: Package policy
Excess umbrella policy
Monoline policy
HO-5 policy
questions.x: Monoline means a single line of coverage. Package is the trap: a homeowners policy bundles several lines.

questions.q: The New York Property Insurance Underwriting Association (NYPIUA) is:
c: New York's FAIR plan for owners shut out of the regular market
The federal program that writes most flood insurance policies
The state agency that licenses and disciplines insurance agents
A voluntary pool of insurers that writes umbrella coverage
questions.x: NYPIUA is New York's FAIR plan, an insurer of last resort funded by insurers. The licensing answer is the trap: insurance agents are licensed by the Department of Financial Services, and flood coverage comes from the NFIP.

questions.q: A standard HO-3 policy would normally cover damage from all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A windstorm that tears off the roof
A grease fire in the kitchen
Theft of a laptop from the house
Storm surge flooding the basement
questions.x: Flood from rising water, including storm surge, is excluded and requires separate flood insurance. The windstorm answer is the trap: wind is covered, though a hurricane deductible may apply.

questions.q: The National Flood Insurance Program is administered by:
c: The NYS Department of Financial Services
FEMA
HUD
NYPIUA
questions.x: The NFIP is a federal program run by FEMA. DFS is the trap: it regulates insurers in New York but does not run the NFIP.

questions.q: The Coastal Market Assistance Program (C-MAP) helps:
c: Commercial landlords on the coast buy umbrella coverage
Coastal renters find HO-4 policies at subsidized rates
Coastal homeowners who were declined find an insurer
Shorefront buyers finance flood vents and elevation
questions.x: C-MAP, administered by NYPIUA, refers eligible coastal homeowners who were declined to insurers that volunteer to consider them. The renters answer is the trap: C-MAP is for homeowners and does not subsidize rates.

questions.q: Once a NY homeowners policy has been in effect more than 60 days, the insurer may cancel it for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:
c: Cutting its exposure in that ZIP code
Nonpayment of the premium when due
Fraud or material misrepresentation
Physical changes making it uninsurable
questions.x: After 60 days, New York limits midterm cancellation to listed grounds such as nonpayment, fraud, and physical changes that make the property uninsurable. Reducing exposure in an area is not a cancellation ground; at most it might support a properly noticed nonrenewal.

questions.q: When a NY insurer chooses not to renew a homeowners policy, it generally gives written notice stating the reason:
c: 10 days before expiration
45 to 60 days before expiration
6 months before expiration
Any time before the renewal date
questions.x: New York requires written nonrenewal notice, with the specific reason, 45 to 60 days before expiration. Ten days is the trap: that is the notice period for cancellation for nonpayment.

questions.q: Under NY's windstorm deductible rules, a homeowners policy with a hurricane deductible shows it on the declarations page as:
c: A footnote in the policy jacket
A percentage of the dwelling limit
A flat dollar amount
A percentage and a dollar amount
questions.x: New York (11 NYCRR Part 74) requires the hurricane deductible to appear as both a percentage and a dollar amount, at least as prominently as the standard deductible. The percentage answer is the trap: the percentage alone hides the real dollar exposure.

questions.q: A Long Beach home has dwelling coverage of $350,000 and a 2% hurricane deductible. On a hurricane claim, the owner pays the first:
questions.x: $350,000 x 0.02 = $7,000. $700 is the trap: it slips a decimal place; percentage deductibles apply to the dwelling limit, not the size of the loss.

questions.q: Choosing a higher deductible on a homeowners policy generally:
c: Lowers the annual premium
Raises the premium
Raises the policy's coverage limit
Removes the coinsurance clause
questions.x: The owner absorbs more of each loss, so the insurer charges less. Raising the premium is the trap: that is what a lower deductible does.

questions.q: An umbrella policy provides:
c: Flood coverage above the NFIP limits
Excess liability above the home and auto policies
Coverage for a condo's common areas
Replacement cost on personal property
questions.x: An umbrella is excess liability insurance on top of the home and auto policies. The flood answer is the trap: excess flood coverage is a separate flood product, not an umbrella.

questions.q: An insurance broker, as opposed to an insurance company's agent, primarily represents:
c: One insurance company
The Department of Financial Services
The mortgage lender
The person buying coverage
questions.x: A broker shops the market on behalf of the insured. One insurance company is the trap: an agent is appointed by and acts for the insurer.

questions.q: A mortgage lender requires the borrower to carry hazard insurance mainly to:
c: Earn a commission from the insurer
Satisfy a Department of State rule
Protect the collateral for the loan
Reduce the borrower's property taxes
questions.x: The house is the lender's collateral, and the lender is named as mortgagee so a claim check protects its interest. The DOS answer is the trap: the Department of State licenses agents and does not require insurance.

questions.q: Leo asks why his estimated monthly payment includes an amount for insurance. The best explanation is that:
c: The lender escrows part of the premium each month and pays the bill
DOS requires every buyer to carry homeowners coverage
The lender is also the borrower's insurance company
The seller's coverage carries over for one more year
questions.x: Lenders commonly collect taxes and insurance (the T and I in PITI) monthly in escrow and pay the bills when due. The DOS answer is the trap: the lender, not the Department of State, requires coverage.

questions.q: A guest slips on the owner's icy front stoop in Park Slope and sues for negligence. Which part of a homeowners policy responds?
c: Coverage A, dwelling
Coverage C, personal property
Coverage D, loss of use
Coverage E, liability
questions.x: Injuries to others caused by the owner's negligence fall under personal liability (Coverage E). Coverage A is the trap: dwelling coverage pays for damage to the house, not for injuries to guests.

questions.q: A real estate agent's role regarding property insurance includes all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Explaining why the lender requires coverage
Picking the buyer's policy for a referral fee
Explaining that taxes and insurance are escrowed
Reminding a cash buyer to bind coverage by closing
questions.x: Agents explain; licensed insurance professionals advise and sell, and a referral fee for steering a client to an insurer raises RESPA kickback problems. Reminding a cash buyer is the tempting pick, but with no lender requiring coverage it is a helpful, proper reminder.

questions.q: A roof destroyed by a covered windstorm (not a hurricane) costs $10,500 to replace and is 50% depreciated. The policy has replacement cost coverage and a $1,000 deductible. The insurer pays:
questions.x: Replacement cost ignores depreciation: $10,500 - $1,000 deductible = $9,500. $4,250 is the trap: it is the actual cash value payout ($5,250) after the deductible.

questions.q: An owner wants full coverage for an engagement ring worth far more than her policy's default theft limit. She should add:
c: An umbrella policy layered over her home policy
Higher Coverage D limits for loss of use
A scheduled personal property endorsement
A lower all-perils deductible on her contents
questions.x: Scheduled personal property endorsements raise coverage for listed valuables such as jewelry, art or cameras. An umbrella policy is the trap: it adds liability coverage, not more protection for her own property.

questions.q: In a typical homeowners policy, personal property (Coverage C) is often set by default at about:
c: Half the dwelling limit
Twice the dwelling limit
10% of the dwelling limit
The full dwelling limit
questions.x: Base policies set many limits as percentages of Coverage A, with contents often about half the dwelling limit; owners can raise it or schedule valuables. The full dwelling limit is the trap: contents get their own, smaller default.

questions.q: A NY insurer sends a cancellation notice for nonpayment of a homeowners premium. The policy stays in force if the owner pays within:
c: 10 days of the notice
30 days after the due date
60 days of policy issue
15 days of the notice
questions.x: For nonpayment, the policy stays in force if the premium is paid within 15 days of the cancellation notice. 60 days is the trap: that is the window in which a new policy can be canceled for almost any reason.

questions.q: A homeowner whose premium is overdue receives a cancellation notice and pays 10 days later. The policy:
c: Lapses, because payment came after the notice was sent
Stays in force, since she paid within 15 days
Lapses unless she buys a new policy at once
Stays in force if the lender steps in and pays
questions.x: Paying within 15 days of a nonpayment cancellation notice keeps the policy in force, so 10 days is in time. The trap is thinking the notice itself ends coverage; it starts the 15-day window.

questions.q: A cash buyer's contract says nothing about risk of loss. A fire damages the house a week before closing, while the seller still holds title and possession. Under NY law, the loss falls on:
c: The buyer
The seller
The buyer's title insurer
The listing broker
questions.x: Under NY law the seller bears the risk of loss until title or possession passes to the buyer; after that it is the buyer's. The buyer is the trap: a signed contract alone does not shift the risk, which is why the buyer binds coverage effective at closing.

questions.q: Leo is paying cash for a house. Why should he still bind homeowners coverage effective at closing?
c: NY law requires insurance on every home
The seller's policy covers him for 30 days
DOS needs proof of coverage to record the deed
Risk of loss shifts to him when title passes
questions.x: No lender forces a cash buyer to insure, but once title or possession passes, the risk of loss is his. "NY law requires insurance" is the trap: the requirement usually comes from a lender, and a cash buyer has none.

questions.q: An HO-3 policy covers the dwelling itself on which basis?
c: Named perils listed in the policy
Open perils, except what is excluded
Fire and lightning, with no other perils
Market value, using common materials
questions.x: HO-3 insures the dwelling on an open-perils (special form) basis: everything is covered except listed exclusions, while contents are usually on named perils. The named-perils answer is the trap: that describes HO-1 and HO-2.

questions.q: A Battery Park City condo owner's kitchen cabinets and flooring are destroyed by a fire that started in her unit. The master policy excludes unit interiors. Her own coverage should come from:
c: An HO-6 unit-owners policy
The condo's master policy
An HO-4 contents policy
An HO-3 special form
questions.x: HO-6 covers a condo unit's interior, owner improvements, contents, liability, and loss assessments. HO-4 is the trap: it covers contents but not the interior finishes a condo owner owns.

questions.q: An HO-4 policy for a tenant typically covers all of the following EXCEPT:
c: The tenant's furniture and clothing
Liability if a guest is injured
Additional living expenses after a fire
Damage to the building's roof
questions.x: HO-4 has no building coverage; the landlord insures the structure. Additional living expenses is the tempting pick, but loss-of-use coverage is a standard part of HO-4.

questions.q: A 1890 Victorian in Troy has ornate plaster and woodwork. Its market value is $220,000 but rebuilding it as built would cost $700,000. Which form is designed for this home?
c: HO-2 broad form
HO-3 special form
HO-5 comprehensive form
HO-8 modified form
questions.x: HO-8 suits older homes whose replacement cost far exceeds market value, paying ACV or repair with common materials. HO-5 is the trap: its broad open-perils coverage would require insuring the full $700,000 rebuild cost.

questions.q: Replacement cost coverage differs from actual cash value coverage because replacement cost:
c: Deducts depreciation from the payout
Pays the home's market value, with land
Pays after passing a coinsurance test
Ignores depreciation on covered items
questions.x: Replacement cost pays to replace with like kind and quality without deducting depreciation. The depreciation answer is the trap: that describes actual cash value.

questions.q: A television costing $2,000 to replace has a 5-year useful life and is 3 years old. Under ACV coverage with a $250 deductible, the insurer pays:
questions.x: Depreciation is 3/5 = 60% of $2,000 = $1,200, so ACV = $800, and $800 - $250 = $550. $800 is the trap: it is the ACV before the deductible.

questions.q: A home with a replacement cost of $1,100,000 has an 80% coinsurance clause. To collect a partial loss in full (less the deductible), the owner carries at least:
questions.x: 80% x $1,100,000 = $880,000. $1,100,000 is the trap: coinsurance requires 80% of replacement cost, not 100%.

questions.q: A standard homeowners package policy bundles all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Dwelling coverage
Personal liability
Medical payments to others
Flood damage coverage
questions.x: Flood is excluded and sold separately through the NFIP or private flood insurers. Medical payments is the tempting pick, but it is a standard part of the homeowners package.

questions.q: A landlord buys a dwelling fire policy on her rental house and a separate liability policy. Each is best described as a:
c: Package policy
HO-3 special form
Binder
Monoline policy
questions.x: Each policy covers one line of insurance, so each is monoline. Package is the trap: a package bundles property and liability in one contract.

questions.q: A Bronx owner has been declined by several insurers because of the area's claim history. Where can she get basic property coverage as a last resort?
c: NYPIUA, New York's FAIR plan
The National Flood Insurance Program
The Department of Financial Services
The lender's force-placed coverage
questions.x: NYPIUA, New York's FAIR plan, insures property owners who cannot get coverage in the voluntary market. DFS is the trap: it regulates insurers but does not sell policies.

questions.q: After heavy rain, a nearby creek overflows and fills an Albany home's basement. The owner has only an HO-3. The flood damage is:
c: Covered under Coverage A
Excluded; flood needs its own policy
Covered, less the hurricane deductible
Covered if the home is outside a flood zone
questions.x: Rising water from outside is flood, which the homeowners policy excludes regardless of flood zone. The outside-a-flood-zone answer is the trap: many flood claims come from outside mapped high-risk zones.

questions.q: Flood insurance in a mapped high-risk area with a federally backed mortgage is typically written through the NFIP, a program of:
c: HUD
FEMA
NYPIUA
Fannie Mae
questions.x: The NFIP is administered by FEMA. HUD is the trap: it runs fair housing and FHA programs, not flood insurance.

questions.q: Which organization administers New York's Coastal Market Assistance Program (C-MAP)?
c: FEMA
NYPIUA
The State Department of State
The Long Island Power Authority
questions.x: C-MAP is administered by NYPIUA, which refers declined coastal homeowners to participating insurers. FEMA is the trap: it runs the NFIP, not C-MAP.

questions.q: A homeowners policy began 30 days ago. The insurer decides it does not want the risk. Under New York law, it may:
c: Cancel for nonpayment alone
Keep it until the first renewal
Cancel for any lawful reason
Cancel after 90 days, not before
questions.x: During the first 60 days a NY insurer may cancel for any lawful (non-discriminatory) reason with proper notice; after 60 days it is limited to listed grounds. The nonpayment answer is the trap: it describes too narrow a limit for a new policy.

questions.q: A policy expires June 30. The insurer mails a nonrenewal notice on June 15. Under New York's rule, what is the likely result?
c: Nonrenewal takes effect June 30
Nonrenewal takes effect July 15
The owner pays a new premium rate
The policy renews, since the notice came late
questions.x: Nonrenewal notice must reach the insured 45 to 60 days before expiration; late notice generally means the policy continues. The July 15 answer is the trap: New York does not simply push back the expiration by the notice period.

questions.q: Why does New York require a hurricane deductible to be shown in dollars as well as a percentage?
c: To show the real out-of-pocket cost
So the lender can set the escrow payment
So the FAIR plan can match the rate
So FEMA can coordinate with flood coverage
questions.x: A percentage deductible on a large dwelling limit can mean thousands of dollars, so NY requires the dollar figure for clear disclosure. The escrow answer is the trap: escrow is based on premiums and taxes, not deductibles.

questions.q: A Montauk home has a $600,000 dwelling limit and a 5% hurricane deductible. Hurricane damage totals $38,000. Ignoring other limits, the insurer pays:
questions.x: The deductible is 5% of the dwelling limit: $600,000 x 0.05 = $30,000, so the insurer pays $38,000 - $30,000 = $8,000. $36,100 is the trap: it applies 5% to the loss instead of the dwelling limit.

questions.q: A buyer wants to lower her homeowners premium without reducing the coverage limit. Her best lever is to:
c: Raise the deductible on the policy
Drop the liability coverage
Lower the dwelling limit
Add a coinsurance clause
questions.x: A higher deductible shifts more of each loss to the owner and lowers the premium. Lowering the dwelling limit is the trap: it cuts coverage and can trigger a coinsurance penalty.

questions.q: An owner has $300,000 liability on her homeowners policy and a $1,000,000 umbrella. A guest wins a $1,150,000 judgment. The umbrella pays:
questions.x: The homeowners policy pays its $300,000 limit first, and the umbrella pays the excess: $1,150,000 - $300,000 = $850,000. $1,000,000 is the trap: the umbrella pays the excess up to its limit, not its full limit.

questions.q: Priya's buyer wants someone who will compare policies from many insurers on her behalf. The professional to suggest is an insurance:
c: Independent broker
Captive agent
Claims adjuster
Underwriter
questions.x: An insurance broker represents the buyer and shops multiple insurers. A captive agent is the trap: that agent represents one insurer.

questions.q: A borrower lets his homeowners policy lapse. The lender is most likely to:
c: Report him to the Department of State
Cancel the mortgage note immediately
Force-place coverage and bill him
Reduce his property tax escrow
questions.x: To protect its collateral, the lender typically force-places hazard coverage and charges the borrower, often at a higher cost. The DOS answer is the trap: the Department of State has no role in a borrower's insurance.

questions.q: Annual property taxes are $9,600 and the homeowners premium is $2,400. The monthly escrow deposit for taxes and insurance, before any cushion, is:
questions.x: ($9,600 + $2,400) / 12 = $1,000 per month. $800 is the trap: it covers taxes alone.

questions.q: A fire forces a Yonkers family out of their home for two months, and they rent an apartment meanwhile. The rent is paid under:
c: Coverage A, the dwelling
Coverage C, contents
Coverage D, loss of use
Coverage E, liability
questions.x: Loss of use (Coverage D) pays additional living expenses while the home is uninhabitable. Personal liability (Coverage E) is the trap: it pays for injury or damage the owner causes to others.

questions.q: An insurance agent offers Marcus $100 for every buyer he sends her way. Marcus should:
c: Decline the payment for referrals
Accept, if he tells the buyers
Accept, if the buyer has no lender
Accept, and split it with his broker
questions.x: Referral fees tied to settlement services raise RESPA kickback concerns, and the agent's role is to explain, not to sell insurance for pay. The disclosure answer is the trap: telling the buyer does not cure a prohibited kickback.

questions.q: A furnace costing $12,000 to replace is 75% depreciated. The policy pays actual cash value with a $500 deductible. The insurer pays:
questions.x: ACV = $12,000 x 25% = $3,000, less the $500 deductible = $2,500. $11,500 is the trap: it is the replacement cost payout, ignoring depreciation.

questions.q: A Suffolk County homeowner who lives near the coast has been declined by several insurers. Which program was created to help owner-occupants in this situation find voluntary-market coverage?
c: The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)
The Coastal Market Assistance Program
The Homeowners Protection Act
The Federal Housing Administration
questions.x: C-MAP, administered by NYPIUA, helps owner-occupied coastal homes that were turned down find coverage from participating insurers. The NFIP is the tempting wrong answer, but it provides flood coverage, not homeowners coverage.

questions.q: When a New York homeowner cannot obtain basic property coverage in the voluntary market, the insurer of last resort is:
c: NYPIUA, the state's FAIR plan
The NFIP, run by FEMA
The homeowner's mortgage lender
The Department of Financial Services
questions.x: The New York Property Insurance Underwriting Association is the state's FAIR plan, an insurer-funded pool for property that cannot be insured in the regular market. DFS regulates insurers but does not write policies, and the NFIP covers flood only.

questions.q: A home has a $720,000 dwelling limit and a 3% hurricane deductible. Hurricane damage totals $40,000. What does the insurer pay?
questions.x: The hurricane deductible is 3% of the dwelling limit: $720,000 x 0.03 = $21,600. The insurer pays $40,000 minus $21,600 = $18,400. Taking 3% of the loss ($1,200) as the deductible gives $38,800; $21,600 is the deductible itself, not the payment.

questions.q: Under New York rules, how must a homeowners policy's hurricane deductible appear on the declarations page?
c: As a percentage of the dwelling limit
As a flat dollar amount on its own
In a separate rider mailed after renewal
As a percentage and a dollar figure
questions.x: Insurance Law 3445 and DFS regulations require the hurricane deductible to be shown as both a percentage and a dollar amount, near the regular deductible, with an explanatory notice. A percentage alone hides how large the out-of-pocket cost is, which is the problem the rule addresses.

questions.q: Replacement cost is $400,000, the policy has an 80% coinsurance clause, and the owner carries $280,000. After a $50,000 covered loss, the insurer pays (before the deductible):
questions.x: Required coverage is 80% x $400,000 = $320,000. Payout = $280,000 / $320,000 x $50,000 = $43,750. Dividing by the full $400,000 gives $35,000, which skips the 80% step; $40,000 is simply 80% of the loss.

questions.q: A home would cost $550,000 to rebuild. Under an 80% coinsurance clause, what is the minimum dwelling coverage needed to collect full replacement cost on a partial loss?
questions.x: 80% x $550,000 = $440,000. Carrying the full $550,000 also works but is not the minimum. $412,500 is 75%, a number some confuse with older clauses.

questions.q: A buyer's federally related mortgage is $600,000 on a single-family home in a Special Flood Hazard Area with a $400,000 insurable building value. The minimum required flood coverage on the building is:
questions.x: Required coverage is the lowest of the loan balance ($600,000), the NFIP maximum for a residence ($250,000) or the insurable value ($400,000). The answer is $250,000. $100,000 is the NFIP contents maximum.

questions.q: A standard HO-3 homeowners policy covers damage from rising floodwater:
c: Fully, as part of the dwelling coverage
When the home lies outside a flood zone
No; flood requires a separate policy
After the hurricane deductible is met
questions.x: Flood is excluded from standard homeowners policies, regardless of flood zone. Coverage comes from the NFIP or a private flood policy. The hurricane deductible applies to wind damage covered by the homeowners policy, not to flood.

questions.q: A buyer paying cash for a home in a flood zone applies for an NFIP policy 10 days before closing. When does coverage generally begin?
c: At closing, because a purchase waives the wait
30 days after the application and premium
Immediately, because the home is in a flood zone
When the next hurricane season begins
questions.x: The NFIP's 30-day waiting period is waived when a policy is bought in connection with making or increasing a loan. A cash buyer has no loan, so the wait applies. That is why cash buyers should apply early; the purchase itself is not the trigger for the exception.

questions.q: The NFIP's 30-day waiting period does NOT apply when the policy is:
c: Bought along with making a mortgage loan
Bought by a cash buyer before closing
Bought after a storm has been named
Bought for a property outside a flood zone
questions.x: Policies purchased in connection with making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan take effect without the 30-day wait. Cash purchases and purchases ahead of a storm are exactly what the waiting period is designed to catch.

questions.q: A New York insurer wants to cancel a homeowners policy that has been in force for 4 months because the insurer has decided to stop writing in that county. Under New York law, the insurer:
c: May cancel with written notice, since any reason is allowed
May cancel if it refunds the full annual premium
May cancel if the lender consents in writing
May not cancel now; after 60 days, listed reasons apply
questions.x: After a homeowners policy has been in force 60 days, New York limits cancellation to listed reasons such as nonpayment, fraud or a change making the property uninsurable. A business decision to leave the county is not one of them. The any-reason rule applies only in the first 60 days. The insurer may instead nonrenew with proper notice.

questions.q: A New York insurer mails a homeowner a nonrenewal notice 25 days before the policy expires. What is the likely result?
c: The policy ends on schedule, since notice was given
The policy ends 25 days after the expiration date
The policy renews; notice is due 45 to 60 days ahead
The policy converts to a NYPIUA policy on its own terms
questions.x: New York requires a nonrenewal notice, with the specific reason, at least 45 and not more than 60 days before expiration. A late notice is ineffective and the policy renews. NYPIUA is an application-based FAIR plan, not an automatic fallback.

cram.html: HO-3 = most widely used homeowners policy (open perils on the dwelling).
HO-4 tenants (and co-op owners per syllabus). HO-6 condo unit owners. HO-8 older homes, actual cash value.
HO-5 = HO-3 plus open perils on personal property. HO-1 basic, HO-2 broad named perils.
Homeowners = package policy. One coverage only = monoline.
ACV = replacement cost - depreciation.
Coinsurance: carry at least 80% of replacement cost. Payout = carried / required x loss.
Flood and earthquake are excluded from standard HO policies.
NFIP = federal flood insurance through FEMA; usually a 30-day waiting period unless tied to a loan.
NYPIUA = NY FAIR plan, insurer of last resort. C-MAP = coastal referral program it administers.
After 60 days, NY homeowners policies can be cancelled only for listed reasons (nonpayment, fraud, increased hazard...).
Nonrenewal: written notice with reason 45 to 60 days before expiration.
Hurricane deductible: % of dwelling limit, shown as % and $ on the declarations page (Ins. Law 3445).
Higher deductible, lower premium.
Umbrella = extra liability above home and auto limits.
Lender is named mortgagee and needs a binder before closing; taxes and insurance often escrowed (PITI).
Cash buyer: bind coverage effective at closing, when risk of loss passes.
Insurance agents and brokers are licensed by DFS. Agent represents insurers; broker represents the insured.

subjects.title: Licensee Safety
subjects.blurb: Agents meet strangers in empty houses and handle bank statements and Social Security numbers. This subject covers personal safety, cyber security, client data, liability, and when NY law lets you use force.

lessons.title: Staying Safe: Office, Road, Open House, Online
lessons.tagline: Every showing is a meeting with a stranger in an empty building. Plan it like one.
objectives: Apply safety practices at the office, on the road, at vacant homes, and at open houses
Protect your own and your clients' data from hackers, wire fraud, and identity theft
Explain who may be liable when someone is hurt or property is damaged or stolen during a showing
Summarize when NY Penal Law Article 35 justifies physical force and deadly physical force
Describe an office safety policy and proper incident follow-up

blocks.title: Sunday, 4:55 pm, Ditmas Park
blocks.html: Jordan's open house ends at 5. A man who never signed in is still upstairs. He comes down and asks, "Do the owners work during the day? Mind if I check out the basement? Alone is fine." The street is quiet. Jordan's phone is at 9%. What should Jordan have done an hour ago, and what now?
blocks.casual: It's 4:55 on Sunday in Ditmas Park. Jordan's open house wraps at 5. A guy who never signed in is still upstairs. He comes down and asks, "Do the owners work days? Mind if I check out the basement? Alone is fine." The block's quiet. Jordan's phone is at 9%. What should Jordan have done an hour ago, and what about right now?

deeper.plain: Questions about when the owners are away and wanting to wander alone are red flags. Safety prep happens before the open house, not during.
deeper.picture: It's like hiking without telling anyone your trail and with a dying phone. Nothing may go wrong, but if it does, nobody's coming.
deeper.street: An hour ago, Jordan should have had a partner, a charged phone, a sign-in sheet everyone used, and a check-in time with the office. Now: don't go to the basement, stay near the front door, say "we're closing up," and call the office with the distress code if he lingers.
deeper.stakes: Agents get robbed and assaulted at open houses. The seller can also get burglarized later by someone casing the house.
deeper.exam: The right answer is always the cautious one: don't go alone, leave, call for help. Never confront.

blocks.html: Safety starts before anything goes wrong. Know your surroundings: exits, who is around, where your car is, how you would leave in a hurry. Most agent attacks happen where the agent is alone with someone they never verified.
blocks.casual: Safety starts before anything goes wrong. Know your surroundings: the exits, who's around, where your car is, how you'd get out fast. Most attacks on agents happen when the agent is alone with someone they never checked out.

deeper.plain: Stay aware of where you are and who you're with, especially with strangers.
deeper.picture: Like a lifeguard who scans the pool, not just the one swimmer in front of them.
deeper.street: Showing a Harlem walk-up, Jordan notes the stairs, the fire escape, and that the super is in the basement. If something feels off, Jordan knows the way down and who's nearby.
deeper.stakes: An agent who walks into a basement with an unverified stranger is in the most common danger scenario.
deeper.exam: Being alone with an unverified person is the core risk. Answers about verifying ID first are usually right.

items: Office points of entry and exit: know them, keep them unblocked, and keep the back door locked.
Cameras, alarms, lighting: a lit entrance and a visible camera deter far more than they record.
Account for staff and visitors: a sign-in for visitors and a shared calendar of who is showing what, where, and with whom.
Keys and codes: log office keys, change alarm codes and lockbox codes when staff leave, never write codes on listing sheets.
blocks.casual:
Office entry and exit points: know them, keep them clear, and keep the back door locked.
Cameras, alarms, lighting: a lit entrance and a visible camera scare people off way more than they record anything.
Track staff and visitors: a visitor sign-in and a shared calendar of who's showing what, where, and with whom.
Keys and codes: log office keys, change alarm and lockbox codes when staff leave, and never write codes on listing sheets.

deeper.plain: Lock up, light up, log who's where, and control keys and codes.
deeper.picture: Running a small office like a well-run bar: you know who's in, who's out, and who has the keys.
deeper.street: When Marcus leaves Hudson & Hart, Diane changes the alarm code and every lockbox code on the firm's listings that same week.
deeper.stakes: An old lockbox code in a former agent's phone is a key to every listing. A theft can land on the broker.
deeper.exam: Change codes when staff leave. Never write codes on listing sheets or MLS remarks.

head: Situation
Do this
rows: Lock the door, tell someone when you will leave, keep a phone in reach
Keys in hand, scan the lot or street, do not linger at the door, park in lit areas
Meet first at the office during business hours. Photocopy a photo ID, verify a phone number, and introduce them to a coworker

deeper.plain: Lock up when you're alone, be alert coming and going, and meet strangers at the office first.
deeper.picture: Like a doctor's office checking you in at the front desk before you ever see a room.
deeper.street: A new caller wants to see a Bushwick loft at 8 p.m. Jordan asks him to come by the office at 2, photocopies his license, confirms his callback number, and introduces him to Diane.
deeper.stakes: A person who knows they've been ID'd and seen by coworkers is far less likely to try anything.
deeper.exam: First meeting at the office, during business hours, with ID copied. That's the textbook answer.

blocks.title: The office meeting is the filter
blocks.html: A genuine buyer rarely objects to meeting at the office first and showing ID. Someone who refuses and insists on meeting you at an empty house has told you something.
blocks.casual: A real buyer almost never minds meeting at the office first and showing ID. Someone who refuses and insists on meeting you at an empty house has just told you something.

deeper.plain: Pushback on a simple ID check is itself a warning sign.
deeper.picture: A date who won't meet in a public place first. That tells you plenty.
deeper.street: A caller says he's in town for one day, can't come to the office, and wants to meet Jordan at a vacant Canarsie listing at 7 p.m. Jordan says no. He never calls back.
deeper.stakes: Ignore that signal and you could walk into a setup at a house with no one around.
deeper.exam: A prospect refusing to meet at the office or show ID: the right response is to decline or bring a partner, never to just go.

blocks.text: On the road, at vacant homes, at open houses

blocks.caption: Walk the open house checklist and tap each risk scenario to see the safer move.

blocks.title: Showing a vacant home

items.title: Verify first
items.html: Name, photo ID, phone number, and lender pre-approval on file with the office before the first showing.

items.title: Tell the office
items.html: Address, client name, start and end time. Check in when you arrive and when you leave.

items.title: Park smart
items.html: On the street, facing out, not in the driveway where you can be blocked in.

items.title: Walk behind
items.html: Let the client lead into rooms. Stay between the client and the exit. Avoid basements, attics, and walk-in closets with an unknown person.

items.title: Bring a buddy
items.html: For first meetings, after-dark showings, or anything that feels wrong.

blocks.casual:
Verify first: name, photo ID, phone number, and lender pre-approval on file with the office before the first showing.
Tell the office: address, client name, start and end time. Check in when you get there and when you leave.
