Park smart: on the street, facing out, not in the driveway where you can get blocked in.
Walk behind: let the client lead into rooms. Stay between them and the exit. Skip basements, attics, and walk-in closets with someone you don't know.
Bring a buddy: for first meetings, after-dark showings, or anything that feels wrong.

deeper.plain: Check them out, tell someone where you are, and set yourself up to leave fast.
deeper.picture: Like scuba diving: you check gear, file your dive plan, and stay near the way back up.
deeper.street: At a vacant Staten Island ranch, Jordan parks on the street facing out, texts the office "In at 3:00," lets the buyer walk into each room first, and skips the basement: "Take a look, I'll wait up here."
deeper.stakes: Get blocked in a driveway or trapped in a basement and your options disappear.
deeper.exam: Client walks ahead. Agent stays near exits. Park where you can't be blocked. Itinerary with the office.

items: On the road: keep the car maintained and fueled, keep doors locked, and drive separately from new clients rather than putting strangers in your car.

Open houses: arrive early and walk every room and exit; ask sellers to remove valuables, mail, keys, and prescription drugs; have visitors sign in; keep your phone charged; work with a partner when you can; lock up room by room before you leave.
Home office: do not advertise your home address; use the office address or a PO box on cards and listings; do not meet clients at home.
blocks.casual:
On the road: keep the car maintained and gassed up, doors locked, and drive separately from new clients instead of putting strangers in your car.
Open houses: show up early and walk every room and exit; ask sellers to put away valuables, mail, keys, and prescription drugs; have everyone sign in; keep your phone charged; bring a partner when you can; lock up room by room before you leave.
Home office: don't advertise your home address. Use the office address or a PO box on cards and listings. Don't meet clients at home.

deeper.plain: Don't drive strangers around, prep open houses carefully, and keep your home address private.
deeper.picture: Your car and home are your safe zones. Don't invite strangers into either.
deeper.street: Before an open house in Forest Hills, Jordan asks the seller to lock up the pill bottles and the spare keys on the hook. Three visitors that day, one pocketed a prescription bottle at another open house the week before.
deeper.stakes: Prescription drugs and keys disappear from open houses all the time. The seller gets robbed and blames the agent.
deeper.exam: Drive separately. Remove valuables and medications. Use office address, not home address, in ads.

blocks.html: Every office should have a distress code: an innocent-sounding phrase ("Can you bring me the red file?") that tells a coworker on the phone to call 911 and send help to your location.
blocks.casual: Every office should have a distress code: an innocent-sounding line ("Can you bring me the red file?") that tells a coworker on the phone to call 911 and send help to where you are.

deeper.plain: A code phrase lets you call for help without the other person knowing.
deeper.picture: A secret signal between friends at a bad party: "Did you feed the cat?" means get me out of here.
deeper.street: At a Ditmas Park showing, Jordan calls Diane: "Can you bring me the red file for 1420?" Diane calls 911 and gives them the address from the showing log.
deeper.stakes: Without a code, calling for help in front of a threatening person may escalate things.
deeper.exam: A distress code is a prearranged phrase that signals danger. Office policy should include one.

blocks.q: Jordan is meeting a new buyer, who called from a listing sign, at a vacant house in Bay Ridge tonight. The safest first step is to:
c: Meet at the house but leave the front door open
Meet the buyer first at the office, copy a photo ID, and log the showing
Ask the buyer to text a selfie
Bring the seller along
blocks.x: Meeting first at the office with ID verification and a logged itinerary filters out most risk. An open door or a selfie does not verify who someone is.

blocks.text: Online: your data and your clients' data

blocks.html: Agents hold exactly what criminals want: names, addresses, Social Security numbers, bank statements, and closing dates with big wire transfers. Protect your own information too. Do not post your real-time location, your schedule, or "heading to my vacant listing on Elm St." on social media.
blocks.casual: Agents hold exactly what criminals want: names, addresses, Social Security numbers, bank statements, and closing dates with big wire transfers. Protect your own info too. Don't post your real-time location, your schedule, or "heading to my vacant listing on Elm St." on social media.

deeper.plain: Client data and your own whereabouts are valuable to criminals. Guard both.
deeper.picture: Posting your schedule online is like leaving your house key under a mat with a sign pointing at it.
deeper.street: An agent posts "Showing a gorgeous empty 2BR at 4 today!" with the address. Someone shows up first and waits.
deeper.stakes: Leaked client data can mean identity theft and a legal duty to notify. Posted schedules can mean an ambush.
deeper.exam: Don't broadcast your location or vacant listing times. Protect clients' personal information.

head: Threat
What it looks like
Defense
rows: "DocuSign: review closing docs" link to a fake login
Do not click; go to the site directly; report it
Hacked email sends the buyer "updated" wiring instructions the day before closing
Verify all wiring instructions by phone to a known number. Tell clients you will never change them by email
One password for MLS, email, and bank
Unique passwords, a password manager, and multi-factor authentication
Logging into email at a coffee shop
Use your phone's hotspot or a VPN
Phone left in a cab with client files

deeper.plain: Fake links, fake wiring emails, weak passwords, open Wi-Fi, and lost phones are how data gets stolen.
deeper.picture: A burglar doesn't need to pick the lock if you leave the window open. Most cyber attacks walk through open windows.
deeper.street: The day before Leo's closing, he gets an email from "Priya" with new wiring instructions. He calls Priya's office at the number on her website. She never sent it. He just saved his $133,000 down payment.
deeper.stakes: Wire fraud can wipe out a buyer's life savings in minutes, and the money is often never recovered.
deeper.exam: Verify wiring instructions by phone to a known number. Multi-factor authentication. Don't click unexpected links.

blocks.title: NY SHIELD Act
blocks.html: The SHIELD Act (General Business Law 899-aa and 899-bb) requires any business holding NY residents' private information, which includes a brokerage, to keep reasonable safeguards and to notify affected people after a breach. Private information includes a name combined with a Social Security number, driver's license number, or account number with access code, plus biometrics and username-and-password combinations. Shred paper records you no longer need.
blocks.casual: The SHIELD Act (General Business Law 899-aa and 899-bb) says any business holding NY residents' private information, and that includes a brokerage, has to keep reasonable safeguards and notify affected people after a breach. Private information includes a name plus a Social Security number, driver's license number, or account number with access code, plus biometrics and username-and-password combos. Shred paper records you don't need anymore.

deeper.plain: NY law says protect customer data and tell people if it leaks.
deeper.picture: A restaurant has to store food safely and warn customers if something got contaminated.
deeper.street: A Hudson & Hart laptop with buyer pre-approval letters and license copies is stolen from a car. Under the SHIELD Act, the firm has to notify every affected client.
deeper.stakes: A breach without safeguards or notice exposes the firm to enforcement by the NY Attorney General and angry, harmed clients.
deeper.exam: SHIELD Act = NY data security and breach notification. Applies to brokerages. GBL 899-aa and 899-bb.

blocks.html: Identity theft hits both sides. A thief with a client's pre-approval packet can open accounts; a thief with an agent's license number and photo can post fake rental listings and collect "deposits." Warning signs: unknown accounts, mail that stops, calls about listings you never posted. Response: freeze credit, file at IdentityTheft.gov and with police, and tell your broker.
blocks.casual: Identity theft hits both sides. A thief with a client's pre-approval packet can open accounts. A thief with an agent's license number and photo can post fake rental listings and pocket "deposits." Warning signs: accounts you don't recognize, mail that stops coming, calls about listings you never posted. What to do: freeze your credit, file at IdentityTheft.gov and with police, and tell your broker.

deeper.plain: Thieves can steal clients' identities or yours, and the fix is to freeze credit and report fast.
deeper.picture: Someone wearing your face as a mask, collecting money in your name.
deeper.street: Renters call Jordan about a $2,400 Astoria two-bedroom she never listed. A scammer copied her photo and license number and is collecting deposits. Jordan tells Diane, files a police report, and reports it at IdentityTheft.gov.
deeper.stakes: Fake listings with your name drag you into complaints and lawsuits and make victims of renters.
deeper.exam: Warning signs and response steps: freeze credit, report to FTC (IdentityTheft.gov) and police, notify the broker.

blocks.q: The day before closing, Leo gets an email from what looks like Priya's address with new wiring instructions. Jordan should tell him to:
c: Wire immediately so closing is not delayed
Reply to the email to confirm
Call Priya's office at a number he already has before sending anything
Forward it to the lender
blocks.x: Last-minute changes to wiring instructions are the classic wire fraud pattern. Verify by phone using a known number, never by replying to the suspect email.

head: Party
Typical exposure
rows: Liable for the acts of salespersons within the scope of their work (see vicarious liability); premises liability at the office; failure to supervise and train
Negligence: leaving a listing unlocked, letting a visitor roam unsupervised, ignoring a known hazard during a showing
Premises liability for dangerous conditions (broken stair, icy stoop, aggressive dog); should secure valuables, medications, and firearms
Damage the buyer or the buyer's inspector causes during visits
A thief or vandal at an open house is liable for the crime. Listing agreements often include a clause limiting the broker's liability for loss or damage caused by third parties during showings

deeper.plain: When something goes wrong, the broker, agent, seller, buyer, or a criminal could each be on the hook depending on what happened.
deeper.picture: A car accident where blame splits between drivers, the town for the pothole, and the mechanic who skipped the brakes.
deeper.street: At a Ridgewood open house, a visitor falls on a loose stair (seller's premises liability) while the agent was outside on a call (agent negligence), and the broker never trained anyone on open house rules (failure to supervise).
deeper.stakes: Each party can get sued. Brokers pay for their agents' mistakes made within the scope of the job.
deeper.exam: Broker = vicarious liability for salespersons. Seller = premises liability. Criminal = liable for the crime.

blocks.text: Use of physical force: Penal Law Article 35

blocks.html: If an agent is attacked, New York's justification rules control what force is lawful. The aggressor is criminally responsible; the defender is protected only if the force was justified.
blocks.casual: If an agent gets attacked, New York's justification rules decide what force is legal. The attacker is criminally responsible. The defender is protected only if the force was justified.

deeper.plain: You can defend yourself in NY, but only with force that fits the threat.
deeper.picture: Using a fire extinguisher on a candle versus a kitchen fire. Match the response to the danger.
deeper.street: A man grabs Jordan's arm at a vacant Flatbush listing. Jordan pulls free and shoves him to get to the door. That's physical force to stop imminent unlawful force, and likely justified.
deeper.stakes: Overreact and the defender can end up charged. That's why escape comes first.
deeper.exam: Penal Law Article 35. Justification is a defense, and the force must be reasonable for the threat.

items: Physical force is justified when you reasonably believe it is necessary to defend yourself or another person from what you reasonably believe is the imminent use of unlawful physical force.

Deadly physical force is justified only if you reasonably believe the other person is using or about to use deadly physical force (or to stop certain violent felonies such as robbery, kidnapping, or forcible rape).

Duty to retreat: before using deadly physical force, you must retreat if you know you can do so with complete safety. The exception is your own dwelling when you are not the initial aggressor. A client's listing is not your dwelling.
The initial aggressor generally cannot claim justification unless they withdraw and clearly communicate it.
blocks.casual:
Physical force is justified when you reasonably believe it's needed to defend yourself or someone else from what you reasonably believe is the imminent use of unlawful physical force.
Deadly physical force is justified only if you reasonably believe the other person is using or about to use deadly physical force (or to stop certain violent felonies like robbery, kidnapping, or forcible rape).
Duty to retreat: before using deadly force, you have to retreat if you know you can do it with complete safety. The exception is your own home when you didn't start it. A client's listing isn't your home.
The initial aggressor generally can't claim justification unless they back off and clearly say so.

deeper.plain: Regular force for regular threats, deadly force only for deadly threats, and if you can safely get away, you must.
deeper.picture: A ladder: you only climb to the next rung when the threat climbs first.
deeper.street: At a Bronx listing, a visitor shouts and shoves Jordan. The front door is right there. Jordan has a safe way out, so the law expects Jordan to leave, not to escalate. A listing isn't Jordan's home, so the dwelling exception doesn't apply.
deeper.stakes: Use deadly force when you could have safely left and you can face criminal charges.
deeper.exam: Duty to retreat before deadly force if completely safe; dwelling exception doesn't cover a listing. Initial aggressor loses justification.

blocks.title: Force is the last option, not a plan
blocks.html: Exam answers that have the agent confronting or chasing a suspect are wrong. Leave, call 911, and let police handle it. Justification is a legal defense after the fact, not a safety strategy.
blocks.casual: Exam answers where the agent confronts or chases a suspect are wrong. Leave, call 911, and let police deal with it. Justification is a legal defense after the fact, not a safety plan.

deeper.plain: Get away and call police. Fighting is the absolute last resort.
deeper.picture: Seatbelts and airbags are backup. The plan is to not crash.
deeper.street: A visitor at a Bay Ridge open house pockets a seller's watch and runs. Jordan does not chase. Jordan calls 911, writes a description, and calls the seller.
deeper.stakes: Chasing a thief over a watch can get an agent hurt or killed and turns a theft into a violent incident.
deeper.exam: The answer is never confront, chase, or detain. It's leave, call 911, report.

blocks.html: The broker should adopt a written office safety policy and train every agent on it: ID verification, itinerary logging, the distress code, buddy rules for vacant and after-dark showings, open house procedures, lockbox and key control, data security and wire protocols, and how to report an incident.
blocks.casual: The broker should adopt a written office safety policy and train every agent on it: ID checks, itinerary logs, the distress code, buddy rules for vacant and after-dark showings, open house procedures, lockbox and key control, data security and wire protocols, and how to report an incident.

deeper.plain: The broker writes the safety rules and makes sure everyone actually knows them.
deeper.picture: A restaurant kitchen's fire drill posted on the wall and practiced, not just written once.
deeper.street: At Hudson & Hart's monthly meeting, Diane walks new agents through the policy: copy ID, log the showing, know the red file code, and call buyers by phone before every wire.
deeper.stakes: No policy, no training: if an agent gets hurt or a client's wire gets stolen, the broker faces failure-to-supervise claims.
deeper.exam: The broker is responsible for adopting and training on a written safety policy.

blocks.title: After an incident

items.title: Get safe, call 911
items.html: Leave first. Call police for any threat, assault, or theft.

items.title: Write it down
items.html: Complete an incident report while memory is fresh: who, what, when, descriptions, plates, sign-in names.

items.title: Notify
items.html: Tell your broker, the seller, and (with care for privacy) other agents and the local board so they can watch for the same person.

items.title: Review
items.html: The broker reviews what happened and updates the office policy. Sellers' insurers may need notice of theft or damage.

blocks.casual:
Get safe, call 911: leave first. Call police for any threat, assault, or theft.
Write it down: fill out an incident report while it's fresh: who, what, when, descriptions, plates, sign-in names.
Notify: tell your broker, the seller, and (carefully, with privacy in mind) other agents and the local board so they can watch for the same person.
Review: the broker goes over what happened and updates the office policy. The seller's insurer may need notice of theft or damage.

deeper.plain: Get safe, document, tell the right people, and fix whatever let it happen.
deeper.picture: After a fender bender: move off the road, take photos, call your insurer, and figure out how to avoid it next time.
deeper.street: After the Ditmas Park scare, Jordan writes up the man's description and the time, Diane alerts the local board, and two other agents report the same man asking about "owners at work."
deeper.stakes: Skip the report and the next agent walks into the same person unwarned.
deeper.exam: Order: safety, 911, incident report, notify broker and seller, review policy.

blocks.q: An agent showing a vacant listing is threatened with a knife and can safely run out the front door. Under Penal Law Article 35, before using deadly physical force the agent:
c: May use any force, since the agent is lawfully on the premises
Must retreat, because the agent knows retreat is possible with complete safety and the listing is not the agent's dwelling
Must first call the broker for permission
May use deadly force only if the seller consents
blocks.x: NY imposes a duty to retreat before using deadly physical force when retreat is possible with complete safety. The dwelling exception covers your own home, not a listing.

blocks.title: VET the stranger
blocks.html: Verify ID at the office. Enter the itinerary in the office log. Tell someone the code word and your check-in time.
blocks.casual: Verify ID at the office. Enter the itinerary in the office log. Tell someone the code word and your check-in time.

deeper.plain: Three habits before meeting any stranger: check ID, log the trip, set up a check-in.
deeper.picture: Like a vet checking a pet in: name, appointment, someone waiting for news.
deeper.street: Before a 6 p.m. Crown Heights showing, Jordan has the buyer's license copied, the address in the log, and a 6:45 check-in with Diane. Miss it, and Diane calls.
deeper.stakes: Forget any one step and nobody knows where you are or who you're with.
deeper.exam: VET covers the top safety answers: verification, itinerary, and someone who knows.

story.title: The Last Visitor
story.setting: Open house on Argyle Road, Ditmas Park, Sunday 4:55 pm

beats.text: The sign-in sheet has 14 names. The man upstairs is not one of them.
Owners work during the day? Mind if I see the basement? I'll go alone, no need to follow.
I can't discuss the owners' schedule. We're closing in five minutes. Happy to set up a private showing through the office with ID.
You here by yourself?
My colleague's out front. Let me give her a call.
Hey Marcus, can you bring me the red file?

check.q: What is "bring me the red file"?
c: A filing request
The office's distress code asking a coworker to send help
A signal to end the open house early
A reminder to collect sign-in sheets
check.x: A distress code sounds harmless to a visitor but tells a coworker to call 911 and send help.

beats.text: Marcus, two blocks away, calls 911 and drives over. The man leaves before either arrives.
Plate's partly visible from the window. Writing down the time, his description, and that he never signed in.
Should've let me chase him down the block.
No. You get safe and call police. Chasing makes you the aggressor, and Article 35 only protects force that's actually necessary.
Monday we email the agents in the area and the Okafors, update the open house checklist, and you're never doing one alone at 9% battery again.
Partner, charged phone, walk every room first, valuables locked up. Got it.

board.prompt: Sketch the floor plan of an open house. Mark every exit, where you stand, rooms to avoid with a stranger, and where valuables should be locked away.

facts.text: Most attacks on agents happen where the agent is alone with someone never verified; know exits and how you would leave.
Control office access: log keys, change alarm and lockbox codes when staff leave, and never write codes on listing sheets.
Meet an unknown prospect at the office first, copy a photo ID and verify the phone number before any showing.
Give the office the address, client name and start and end times, and check in on arrival and departure.
Park on the street facing out, not in the driveway where you can be blocked in.
Let the client lead, stay between the client and the exit, and avoid basements, attics and closets with an unknown person.
At open houses arrive early, walk every exit, have sellers remove valuables, keys and drugs, sign visitors in, keep the seller's routine private, and lock up room by room.
Drive separately from new clients, and keep your home address off cards and listings.
A distress code is an innocent-sounding phrase that tells a coworker to call 911 and send help.
Do not post your real-time location or schedule, such as heading to a vacant listing, on social media.
Wire fraud defense: verify any wiring instructions by phone to a known number, and tell clients you will never change them by email.
Phishing imitates a trusted service to steal a login; do not click, go to the site directly.
Use unique passwords, a password manager and multi-factor authentication; avoid public Wi-Fi and lock and encrypt devices.
The NY SHIELD Act (GBL 899-aa and 899-bb) requires any business holding NY residents' private information to keep reasonable safeguards and notify people after a breach.
Identity theft can hit agents (fake listings in their name) and clients; freeze credit, report to IdentityTheft.gov and police, and tell your broker.
A broker is liable for salespersons' acts within the scope of their work and for failing to supervise and train.
The seller has premises liability for dangerous conditions such as a broken stair, icy stoop or aggressive dog.
Listing agreements often limit the broker's liability for loss caused by third parties during showings.
Under Penal Law Article 35, physical force is justified when reasonably believed necessary to defend against imminent unlawful physical force.
Deadly physical force is justified only against deadly physical force or certain violent felonies such as robbery, kidnapping or forcible rape.
Before deadly force you must retreat if you can do so in complete safety, except in your own dwelling; a client's listing is not your dwelling.
The initial aggressor cannot claim justification unless they withdraw and clearly communicate it.
Force is the last option: leave, call 911 and let police handle it rather than confronting or chasing anyone.
Brokers should adopt a written office safety policy covering ID checks, itinerary logs, distress codes, buddy rules, key control and data security.
After an incident write a prompt incident report, notify the broker and seller, and review the office policy.

lessons.title: Case file: Nine Days After the Open House
lessons.tagline: One Yonkers open house leads to a fall, a theft, a threat, a stolen laptop, a fake wire request and a fake listing. Each was preventable.
objectives: Decide who bears liability for an injury, a theft or an assault connected to a showing, including the effect of a listing agreement clause.
Apply Penal Law Article 35's rules on physical force, deadly physical force and the duty to retreat to a threat at a listing.
Apply the NY SHIELD Act and wire fraud response steps to a data breach and a diverted down payment.
Choose office policy and incident follow-up steps that reduce each risk.

blocks.title: Yonkers, the week of one open house
blocks.html: Rosa and Luis Delgado are selling their 1926 colonial on a hilly street off Palisade Avenue in Yonkers, listed with Hudson & Hart at $749,000. Marcus is the listing agent. He has scheduled a Sunday open house from 1 to 4 and asked Jordan to co-host. The house is lovely and lived in: grandchildren's drawings on the fridge, a medicine cabinet full of prescriptions, a basement stair with one loose tread that Luis has been meaning to fix for a year. Over the next nine days, one open house will produce an injury, a theft, a threat, a stolen laptop, a fake wire request and a fake listing. Every one of them was foreseeable. Start on Friday, when Jordan walks the house with Rosa.

Rosa has a list of questions. Should she leave her jewelry in the dresser? Her husband's pain medication is in the hall bathroom. Luis has a licensed handgun in a locked case in the bedroom closet. And the basement, with the washer, dryer and the loose tread, is part of what buyers will want to see.

blocks.q: What should Jordan advise the Delgados to do before the open house?
c: Leave everything in place so the house looks lived in for buyers
Secure valuables, medications and the firearm; fix the stair
Ask Jordan to carry the firearm off the premises for the afternoon
Keep the items but post signs asking visitors not to open drawers
blocks.x: Sellers should remove or secure jewelry, cash, mail, keys, medications and firearms before strangers walk through, and fix known hazards or block them off. Prescription drugs are among the items most often stolen at open houses. An agent should not take possession of a seller's firearm. Signs asking people not to open drawers protect nothing. The loose tread is a premises liability problem as well as a safety one, so it belongs on the list too.

blocks.html: Rosa takes the jewelry to her daughter's apartment and moves the gun case to a locked closet. She forgets the medicine cabinet. Luis promises to fix the stair Saturday morning, then gets called in to work. On Sunday at 12:30 Marcus sees the tread still loose, decides there is no time, and tapes a sheet of paper to the basement door: "Watch your step."

Thirty-one groups come through. At 2:15, a visitor named Henry Okafor-Mills, 66, goes down to see the laundry room. The loose tread shifts, he falls four steps, and he lands hard on his wrist. He is conscious, in pain and embarrassed. His daughter is with him.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do first after Henry's fall?
c: Help him up the stairs and ask him to sign a release before he leaves
Tell him the seller's insurance will pay for everything, so not to worry
Call 911 or arrange care, then note the facts in an incident report
Close the open house and ask everyone to leave before calling anyone
blocks.x: Get care first: call 911 for anything more than a minor scrape, and do not move an injured person who may have a fracture unless they are in danger. Then document what happened while it is fresh, in an incident report: time, place, the stair, witnesses, what was said. Do not promise payment or admit fault on the seller's behalf. A release signed by someone in pain will not hold up and looks terrible. Clearing the house can wait.

blocks.html: The ambulance takes Henry to St. Joseph's. Jordan photographs the stair and the taped note, gets the names and numbers of two visitors who saw the fall, and writes up the report on the office's form that evening. Diane reads it at 8 p.m. and calls the Delgados.

blocks.q: If Henry later makes a claim, who has the most exposure for the loose stair?
c: The Delgados, Marcus and the brokerage, who each knew of it
Henry, because the paper sign warned every visitor of the danger
The brokerage alone, since it controlled the house that afternoon
No one, because open house visitors accept every risk of entry
blocks.x: Owners are responsible for dangerous conditions they know about, which is the core of premises liability. The Delgados knew about the tread for a year. Marcus also knew, chose not to block the stairs, and invited the public in, so he and the brokerage that supervises him share exposure. A taped note may help a defense but does not make a known hazard safe. Visitors do not accept unknown risks by walking into an open house.

blocks.title: Which insurance answers first
blocks.html: The seller's homeowners policy has two parts that matter here. Medical payments coverage pays modest medical bills of guests regardless of fault, often settling small injuries quickly. Personal liability coverage defends and pays if the owners are found negligent. Brokers carry their own general liability and errors and omissions coverage; E&O typically focuses on professional mistakes, not bodily injury, so the broker's general liability policy is the one to notify. Notify every carrier promptly; late notice can cost coverage.

At 4:30, Rosa calls Jordan from the hall bathroom. Luis's oxycodone prescription is gone, and so is a watch Luis left on the bathroom shelf. The sign-in sheet has 31 entries. Several are illegible, two are obviously fake ("Mickey Mouse" and "J. Smith, 555-5555"), and nobody checked ID at the door. The listing agreement the Delgados signed in August contains this clause.

blocks.title: Hudson & Hart exclusive right to sell, paragraph 14
blocks.html: "Seller understands that Broker will show the Property to members of the public, including at open houses, and that Broker cannot guarantee the security of the Property or its contents. Seller agrees to remove or secure valuables, medications and firearms. Broker shall not be liable for loss of or damage to Seller's personal property caused by third parties, except to the extent caused by Broker's own negligence."

blocks.q: Who is responsible for the stolen medication and watch?
c: Jordan and Marcus personally, since they hosted the open house
The brokerage, which guaranteed the contents during showings
The thief, with the broker shielded by paragraph 14
The Delgados' insurer alone, because theft is no one's fault
blocks.x: The person who stole is responsible for the crime. Paragraph 14 is the kind of clause the syllabus means by third-party liability limited in the listing contract: the seller agreed to secure valuables and medications, and the broker is not liable for third parties' acts except to the extent of the broker's own negligence. The brokerage made no guarantee. The Delgados' homeowners policy may cover the watch under personal property coverage, subject to the deductible, but that is coverage, not fault.

blocks.html: Rosa files a police report that night. Diane tells Marcus that the sign-in sheet was the weak point: the office policy calls for agents to ask each visitor for a name, phone number and photo ID at the door, or to use a digital sign-in that verifies a phone number by text, and to keep a count of people inside. A visitor who will not give a real name is a visitor to watch.

blocks.q: Which open house sign-in practice best reduces this risk next time?
c: Let visitors write their own names on a sheet near the door
Ask for name, phone and photo ID, and track who is still inside
Skip sign-in entirely so buyers feel welcome and unwatched
Collect each visitor's Social Security number as a form of identification
blocks.x: Verified sign-in and a running count of who is inside deter theft and help police afterward. Asking every visitor the same questions keeps the practice consistent for fair housing purposes. A self-written sheet produced "Mickey Mouse." Skipping sign-in removes the deterrent entirely. Collecting Social Security numbers is unnecessary and creates a data security problem under the SHIELD Act, which is the next thing to go wrong this week.

blocks.html: While Marcus walks the Delgados through the bathroom, Jordan is alone in the kitchen closing windows. A man who came in at 3:55 without signing in appears in the doorway, asks if the owners live alone, and when Jordan says the open house is over, he steps forward, grabs Jordan's forearm hard and says, "I'm not done looking." The back door is three steps behind Jordan and unlocked.

blocks.q: The man grabs Jordan's arm and will not let go. What does Penal Law Article 35 allow Jordan to do?
c: Nothing physical, since an agent on a client's property has no defense
Use reasonable physical force to break free and get away
Use deadly physical force, since any grab is an assault
Use whatever force Jordan likes, because the man was the aggressor
blocks.x: Physical force is justified when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to defend against what they reasonably believe is the imminent use of unlawful physical force. Pulling free, pushing the man away and leaving fits. Deadly physical force requires a reasonable belief that the other person is using or about to use deadly force or committing certain violent felonies, which a grab alone does not show. Being the aggressor does not license unlimited force against him.

blocks.html: Jordan yanks free and steps toward the back door. The man reaches into his jacket and says he has a knife. Jordan cannot see one. The back door is still behind Jordan, and the driveway leads to the street.

blocks.q: Before using deadly physical force, what does New York law require of Jordan here?
c: Stand ground, because Jordan is lawfully on the premises as an agent
Wait until the man actually shows the knife before acting
Call the broker for permission before taking any action
Retreat through the back door, since it can be done safely
blocks.x: Under the duty to retreat, a person may not use deadly physical force if they know they can avoid the necessity with complete safety by retreating. The exception covers your own dwelling when you are not the initial aggressor, and a client's listing is not Jordan's dwelling. Jordan has a safe exit, so leaving is required before deadly force, and it is also the safest choice. Waiting to see a knife is not the legal test, and no broker approval applies to self-defense.

blocks.html: Jordan goes out the back door, around the house to the street where other people are walking, and calls 911. Marcus hears the door and gets the Delgados out the front. The man leaves on foot before police arrive. The incident report includes his description, the time he entered, the fact that he did not sign in and the question he asked about the owners living alone. Diane sends it to the other Westchester offices that night.

At the debrief, Diane asks Jordan what would have happened if the back door had been locked. Jordan's phone was in a back pocket, and Marcus was two rooms away. The office has a phrase for exactly that moment, and Jordan admits to having forgotten it under stress.

blocks.q: If Jordan had been cornered with a phone in hand, what is the best way to call for help without escalating?
c: Use the office distress code on a call to a colleague
Announce loudly that Jordan is calling the police right now
Text Marcus a detailed description of the man and wait
Tell the man the owners are about to arrive with friends
blocks.x: A distress code is an innocent-sounding phrase, such as asking a colleague to bring the red file, that tells the listener to call 911 and send help to the agent's location without alerting the person in the room. Announcing a police call can escalate a volatile encounter. A long text takes time and depends on someone noticing it. Bluffing about arriving owners may work or may provoke. The code only helps if everyone has practiced it, which is why the office now rehearses it each quarter.

blocks.title: Justification is a defense, not a plan
blocks.html: Penal Law Article 35 decides afterward whether force was lawful. It is not a safety strategy. The plan is the office policy: no one alone in a house with an unverified stranger, a distress code that tells a colleague to call 911, a check-in at closing time, and the rule that agents leave and call police rather than confront anyone. Exam answers that have an agent confronting, chasing or detaining a suspect are wrong.

On Tuesday morning Marcus reports that someone broke his car window in a parking garage in White Plains on Monday night and took his laptop bag. The laptop held a folder of scanned files: the Delgados' bank statements, two buyers' pre-approval packets with Social Security numbers, and a rental applicant's driver's license. The laptop had a login password but its drive was not encrypted. Marcus wants to wait and see whether anything bad happens.

blocks.q: What does the NY SHIELD Act require of Hudson & Hart after the laptop theft?
c: Nothing, unless one of the clients reports identity theft later on
Notice to clients within 1 year, and just if the laptop is never found
Nothing, because a password on the laptop counts as encryption
Notice to affected residents within 30 days, plus state agencies
blocks.x: Names combined with Social Security numbers or driver's license numbers are private information under the SHIELD Act. Unencrypted files on a stolen laptop are a breach. Since a December 2024 amendment, affected New York residents must be notified within 30 days of discovery, and the Attorney General, the Department of State and the State Police must be notified too. Encrypted data whose key was not taken would not trigger notice, but a login password is not drive encryption.

blocks.html: Diane notifies the five people affected, offers to pay for credit monitoring, and sends the state notices. She also writes three new rules into the office policy: full-disk encryption on every device that holds client files, multi-factor authentication on email and the transaction platform, and no client documents in cars. The SHIELD Act requires reasonable administrative, technical and physical safeguards; after this week, Hudson & Hart's are written down.

Back in Yonkers, the Delgados accept an offer at $741,000. On Wednesday afternoon the buyers, Tom and Erin Walsh, receive an email that appears to come from the Delgados' attorney: "Change of plans. Please wire the down payment of $74,100 to our new escrow account below today so we can sign contracts tomorrow." The sender's address is one letter different from the attorney's real one. Erin wires the money at 3:40 p.m. and forwards the confirmation to Jordan at 4:05.

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell Erin to do first?
c: Wait until tomorrow and ask the attorney at the contract signing
Reply to the email and ask the sender to return the funds
Call her bank now to request a recall, then report it to the FBI
Wire a second payment to the attorney's real account to stay on track
blocks.x: With wire fraud, hours matter. The buyer's bank can try to recall the wire and freeze the funds at the receiving bank only if it acts fast, so the first call is to the bank's fraud line. Then report to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov and to local police, and call the real attorney at a known number. Replying to the spoofed address alerts the criminal. Waiting a day often means the money is gone.

blocks.html: Erin's bank recovers $61,000 of the $74,100 within two days. The Walshes' attorney and the Delgados' attorney agree to extend the contract date. Every Hudson & Hart email signature now carries the same line: "We will never send you new wiring instructions by email. Always confirm by phone using a number you already have."

blocks.text: Friday: the listing that was not Jordan's

blocks.html: On Friday a woman calls Jordan, angry. She sent a $1,500 deposit through a payment app for a two-bedroom in Yonkers advertised on a social media marketplace. The ad used Jordan's headshot, name and license number, copied from the Hudson & Hart website. The apartment does not exist. Two other people have called the office about the same ad.

blocks.q: What is the best set of next steps for Jordan?
c: Ignore it, since Jordan did not post the ad or take any money
Pay back the deposit personally to protect Jordan's reputation
Post the scammer's account details and ask followers to harass it
Report it to the platform, broker and police; warn the public
blocks.x: This is identity theft aimed at Jordan's professional identity and fraud against the renters. Jordan should report the listing to the platform for removal, tell Diane, file a police report, and report at IdentityTheft.gov; the brokerage can post a warning on its website and social accounts so other renters check listings with the office. The victims should report to their payment app and police. Ignoring it lets the scam run, and personal repayment or vigilante posts create new problems.

blocks.text: The following Monday: the policy meeting

blocks.html: Diane holds a one-hour safety meeting for the whole office. She walks through the week in order and asks one question at each stop: what rule would have prevented this, and do we have it in writing?

head: Event
What failed
Rule added or reinforced
rows: Fix or block hazards before any showing; walk the house first
Seller prep checklist signed; verified sign-in; head count
Two people at every open house close-out; distress code; leave and call 911
Full-disk encryption, MFA, no client files in vehicles
Phone verification of any wiring change, stated in every signature
Monitor for impersonation; public warning; reporting steps
blocks.caption: From incidents to the office policy

blocks.q: Which statement best describes the broker's role after this week?
c: Adopt and enforce a safety policy, train agents, review incidents
Leave safety to each agent, since salespersons are independent contractors
Ban open houses entirely, since they cannot be made safe
Rely on the sellers' insurance to handle any future problems
blocks.x: The broker supervises the brokerage's business, which includes an office safety policy covering showings, open houses, data security and wire protocols, training every agent on it, and reviewing each incident to update the policy. Independent contractor status does not move that responsibility to agents. Insurance pays for some losses but prevents none. Open houses can be run safely with the controls this case lists, so a total ban is not the answer the law or the market expects.

blocks.title: Who is liable for what
blocks.html: Sellers: dangerous conditions they know about. Agents: their own negligence, such as inviting the public onto a known hazard. Brokers: their agents' acts in the course of business and failures to supervise or train. Third parties: their own crimes, and listing agreements often limit the broker's liability for them. Aggressors: criminal responsibility for the attack. Exam questions offer a single party as the answer when several share exposure.

items: Prepare the house: sellers remove or secure valuables, medications and firearms, and known hazards are fixed or blocked before the public enters.
After an injury: get care, document in an incident report, notify the broker, sellers and insurers, and do not admit fault or promise payment.
Listing agreements can limit the broker's liability for third parties' acts, but not for the broker's own negligence.
Under Penal Law Article 35, use only the force reasonably necessary, and retreat before deadly force when it is completely safe; a listing is not your dwelling.
Under the SHIELD Act, a breach of unencrypted private information requires notice within 30 days; verify every wiring change by phone and act within hours on wire fraud.

roleplays.title: The Visitor Who Won't Sign In
roleplays.setting: Saturday open house at a co-op listing. Your partner stepped out for coffee. A visitor walks in.
roleplays.goal: Stay safe, protect the sellers' property and privacy, and follow office policy through the incident report, without confronting anyone.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play an unverified open house visitor at a co-op who refuses to sign in, wanders toward bedrooms, asks when the owners travel, notices valuables, photographs the locks, asks for the lockbox code or a ride, tries to get the agent alone in a storage room, asks if the agent is alone, and becomes confrontational when refused. The learner must keep you supervised, refuse to share seller information or codes, use a distress code, avoid isolated spaces, retreat rather than confront (Penal Law Article 35 duty to retreat), call 911, verify any wire instructions by phone, and complete prompt incident follow-up. Grade each element and give one safety tip.

client: The visitor in the gray hoodie
The woman in the trench coat
code: Can you grab the Henderson file?
Did you leave the blue folder?

opening: Saturday, {time}, at a {hood} co-op open house. Your partner went for coffee five minutes ago. Someone walks in without stopping at the sign-in table.
The open house in {hood} has been quiet for an hour. At {time} the door opens. One visitor, no eye contact, straight past the sign-in sheet.
{time}. You're alone in the {hood} listing for the next ten minutes. A visitor steps in and looks around the hallway, not the apartment.

say: "Just looking. I don't do sign-in sheets." Heads straight for the bedrooms.
"Skip the clipboard, I'm just browsing." Walks toward the back of the apartment.

moves.text: No problem. A first name and phone is all, for the sellers' security. I'll walk with you.
moves.fb: Polite, consistent with policy, and you stay with the visitor instead of letting them roam.
moves.react: "Fine. Sam. That's all you get." They slow down.

moves.text: Sure, I'll show you around myself. The bedrooms are down this way, and I'll point out the closets.
moves.fb: Right. Stay with unverified visitors; escorting them is the core of open house safety.

moves.text: Then you'll have to leave, I'm afraid. Everyone who comes in has to sign in, no exceptions.
moves.fb: You may refuse entry, but a calm request and staying with the visitor usually works better and avoids escalation.

moves.text: Let them go and keep answering emails at the kitchen counter. They said they're just looking.
moves.fb: Unsupervised visitors are how theft and worse happen. You are responsible for the property while you host.
moves.react: Two minutes later, a drawer slides shut in the bedroom.

moves.text: Block the hall and say they can't go further until they sign. Hold your ground firmly.
moves.fb: Physically blocking a stranger escalates and can put you in danger. Stay calm and stay with them.

moves.text: Ask for a driver's license to photocopy right now, or you'll call building security on them.
moves.fb: Office ID copies belong at the office meeting before showings. Threats at the door escalate a stranger.
moves.react: "Call whoever you want." They walk past you.

say: In the bedroom: "Nice, {valuable}. The owners travel a lot? When are they usually out?"
They glance at {valuable}. "So when is nobody home here? Owners away much?"

moves.text: I can't share anything about the owners. Let's see the living room. Then text the office our code phrase.
moves.fb: You protect the sellers' privacy and quietly trigger the distress code. (Valuables should have been put away beforehand.)

moves.text: Their schedule is private. Let me show you the kitchen. You text your office the code phrase.
moves.fb: Correct. Never reveal the sellers' schedule, and use the distress code when a visitor raises red flags.

moves.text: Not really sure, honestly. I'd have to ask them. Anyway, the closets here are huge, look.
moves.fb: You didn't share the schedule, but 'I'd have to ask them' invites a follow-up. Decline clearly and move rooms.

moves.text: They're in Florida until the 20th, actually. That's why they want a fast sale before they're back.
moves.fb: You just told a stranger when the home is empty. That breaches confidentiality and invites a burglary.

moves.text: They work long days, so the place is usually empty from eight to seven. It's a super quiet building.
moves.fb: Revealing when the home is empty endangers the sellers and breaches your duty of confidentiality.

moves.text: Pocket the item they noticed to keep it safe, and say the owners are home most of the time anyway.
moves.fb: Taking seller property is a bad idea, and lying about occupancy isn't a safety plan. Decline and trigger the code.

say: "Let's check out the storage room downstairs. Just us. You're here alone, right?"
"Show me the basement storage cage. Your partner's not around, huh?"

moves.text: My colleague's on the way back. The storage room is on the floor plan here. I'll stay up here.
moves.fb: Never go into a basement or storage area with an unknown visitor. Keep the exit behind you and don't confirm you're alone.

moves.text: Storage is on this sheet with the dimensions. Let's stay up here. My partner's back any minute.
moves.fb: Right. Avoid isolated spaces, keep the exit behind you, and don't confirm you're alone.

moves.text: Yes, just me today, but go ahead on your own. Take the elevator to B and it's on the left.
moves.fb: Not going down with them is right, but never confirm you're alone, and don't let them roam unsupervised.
moves.react: "Just you. Okay." They don't move toward the elevator.

moves.text: Sure, follow me. It's quick, just two flights down past the boiler room and the laundry.
moves.fb: An isolated space with an unverified stranger is the single riskiest move in a showing.
moves.react: The stairwell door clicks shut behind you both.

moves.text: Let me just lock the apartment door first so nobody wanders in while we're downstairs.
moves.fb: Locking yourself in or heading to an isolated space with a stranger removes your exits.

moves.text: I'm alone, but I have pepper spray, so no funny business. Now, the storage room is this way, come on.
moves.fb: Confirming you're alone and threatening a visitor both raise the danger. Don't go to isolated spaces.
moves.react: "Pepper spray. Cute." They follow you to the stairs.

say: They step closer, angry. "What's your problem?" The front door is three steps behind you.
Voice rising: "You think I'm a criminal?" They move toward you. The exit is right behind you.

moves.text: Step out the front door to the busy hallway and elevator, and call 911 from there.
moves.fb: Retreat is available with complete safety, so you take it. Penal Law Article 35 favors retreat, and confronting is never the plan.
moves.react: They stand in the doorway, then head for the stairs.

moves.text: Say calmly, "I need to step out," walk out the door toward the doorman, and then call 911.
moves.fb: Correct. Leave, get to people, and call police. Your safety comes before the property.
moves.react: The doorman looks up. The visitor walks out past you both.

moves.text: Apologize, say you didn't mean anything, and keep showing the unit to calm them down.
moves.fb: De-escalation is good, but staying alone with an escalating stranger is risky. Leave and call for help.
moves.react: "That's right. Keep going." They stay close.

moves.text: Grab the fireplace poker from the stand and order them out of the apartment right now.
moves.fb: Arming yourself when you can safely leave risks making you the aggressor. Article 35 justifies force only when reasonably necessary.
moves.react: They lunge for the poker. This just got worse.

moves.text: Stand your ground in the doorway. You're the host and it's your open house, so they leave first.
moves.fb: The dwelling exception covers your own home, not a listing. When safe retreat exists, take it.
moves.react: They shove past you into the hall.

moves.text: Lock yourself in the bathroom and wait quietly until they leave. Text your partner from there.
moves.fb: Trapping yourself in an interior room gives up your exit. Leave through the front door and call 911.
moves.react: You hear drawers opening in the bedroom.

say: They're gone. Police took a report. Your partner is back. Diane is on the phone: "What now?"
Diane calls: "Police called me. Are you okay? Walk me through your next steps."

moves.text: Write the report now, tell the sellers, check for missing items, and alert nearby agents.
moves.fb: Document while it's fresh, notify your broker and sellers, and share a warning. That is incident follow-up.
moves.react: Good. Send it to me tonight and call the sellers first.

moves.text: I'm safe. I'm writing it up while it's fresh, then calling the sellers and checking every room.
moves.fb: Right. Safe first, then a prompt written report and same-day notice to the sellers.
moves.react: That's exactly the order. I'll update the policy too.

moves.text: Finish the open house and mention it to Diane at the Monday meeting when I can give her more details.
moves.fb: Delay loses details, and sellers deserve to know the same day if their property may have been cased.

moves.text: No need for a report. Nothing was stolen and nobody got hurt, so I'd rather just move on from it.
moves.fb: Incidents get documented whether or not anything was taken. Reports protect the next agent and the sellers.
moves.react: We document every incident. Every one.

moves.text: Post the visitor's photo on social media so other agents know who to watch for this weekend.
moves.fb: Public posts about an unidentified person can be defamatory and inaccurate. Report through police and your office.
moves.react: Take that down. Report it through proper channels.

moves.text: Keep it quiet so the sellers don't get spooked and pull the listing. No need to tell them anything.
moves.fb: Withholding a security incident from your clients breaches your duty of disclosure and puts them at risk.
moves.react: They have a right to know. Call them now.

say: "I'd like to come back tonight to measure. What's the lockbox code?"
"Just give me the lockbox code and I'll swing by later with my contractor."

moves.text: I can't share codes. Let's book a time to meet at our office first, then we come back together.
moves.fb: Never give lockbox codes to strangers. New prospects meet at the office first with ID.
moves.react: "Forget it." They head for the door.

moves.text: Codes stay with the agents. Happy to set up a private showing through the office with ID.
moves.fb: Correct. Access stays controlled, and new prospects are verified before private showings.

moves.text: I can't today, but call me Monday and I'll see what I can arrange with the sellers for you.
moves.fb: You withheld the code, but 'see what I can arrange' leaves the door open. Route it through the office with ID.

moves.text: Sure, it's 4-7-1-2. Just text me when you're done so I can tell the sellers that you came by tonight.
moves.fb: Handing a lockbox code to an unverified stranger gives them unsupervised access to the home.

moves.text: I'll leave the door unlocked tonight instead, so no code needed. The doorman won't mind.
moves.fb: Leaving a listing unlocked for a stranger exposes the sellers to theft and you to liability.

moves.text: I'll text you the code once you send a photo of your ID. That's our office policy for this.
moves.fb: A texted ID photo doesn't verify anyone, and codes never go to the public. Meet at the office.

say: They're photographing the window locks and the alarm panel by the door.
Phone out, they snap the door locks, the alarm keypad, and the fire escape window.

moves.text: Please don't photograph the locks or the alarm. The listing photos are online. Then send the code text.
moves.fb: Politely stop security photos, protect the sellers, and quietly trigger your distress code.

moves.text: The sellers asked for no photos of security features. Here's the floor plan. Note it later.
moves.fb: Correct. Set the boundary calmly and document it for the incident report.

moves.text: Ignore it. Lots of buyers take photos at open houses, so it's probably nothing to worry about.
moves.fb: Photos of locks and alarms are a red flag. At least note it and stay close.
moves.react: They move on to the fire escape window.

moves.text: Offer to text them the alarm code too so they can see how the system works for the next owner.
moves.fb: Never share alarm codes. That gives a stranger a way past the sellers' security.

moves.text: Snatch the phone and delete the photos yourself. They have no right to take those pictures in here.
moves.fb: Grabbing someone's phone escalates and could be an assault. Ask them to stop and document it.
moves.react: They grab your wrist. "Give it back."

moves.text: Tell them the alarm doesn't even work anymore, so there's really no point photographing it at all.
moves.fb: You just told a stranger the home has no working alarm. That's a gift to a burglar.

say: Diane texts: "An email signed Priya just hit your inbox and mine: new wire instructions for your other buyer's deposit, due today."
Diane texts: "Did you get an email from 'Priya' with updated wiring details for your buyer? It says forward ASAP."

moves.text: Don't forward. Call Priya at the number you already have to verify, and warn your buyer.
moves.fb: Wire fraud starts with emailed changes. Verify by phone at a known number, never by replying.

moves.text: Treat it as fraud until verified. Call Priya's office line from your contacts, not the email's.
moves.fb: Correct. Never trust emailed wire changes; confirm using contact details you already know.
moves.react: Priya's office: "That's not us. We'll alert the bank."

moves.text: Reply to the email and ask Priya to confirm it's really her before you forward anything on.
moves.fb: Replying goes to the scammer. Call at a known number instead.
moves.react: A reply arrives in seconds: "Yes, it's me, hurry."

moves.text: Forward it to your buyer right away. Priya's deadline is today, and this deal just can't slip again.
moves.fb: Forwarding unverified wire instructions can cost your buyer the whole deposit.
moves.react: Your buyer wires $90,000 to a stranger.

moves.text: Call the number in the email signature to double-check it with her before you forward it on.
moves.fb: The number in a fraudulent email reaches the fraudster. Use a number you already have.
moves.react: "Yes, this is Priya's office, it's correct."

moves.text: Forward it, but add a note telling the buyer to call the bank if anything looks off.
moves.fb: Passing along unverified instructions shifts the risk to your client. Verify first.
moves.react: The buyer sees your note and wires anyway.

say: "I don't have a car. Can you drive me to your other listing after this?"
"Give me a lift to the other place you're showing? I'll ride with you."

moves.text: I don't drive visitors I haven't met. Let's set a time at our office and go from there.
moves.fb: Meet new prospects at the office first and copy ID before showings or car rides.

moves.text: Office policy: we meet at the office with ID first. Here's our address and my card for you.
moves.fb: Correct. Safety policy applies to every prospect the same way.

moves.text: Maybe another day. Today's busy, but text me and we'll figure something out for next week.
moves.fb: Not unsafe right now, but you're promising a ride without the office meeting and ID.

moves.text: Sure, I'm parked in the building's garage. We can go down there together when we close up.
moves.fb: A stranger in your car, in a garage, is a serious safety risk. Meet at the office first.

moves.text: Sure, hop in. Just sit in the back so it feels more professional for the both of us.
moves.fb: The seat doesn't matter. Don't drive unverified strangers.

moves.text: I'll drive you if you sign in now with a real name and a phone number. That's a fair trade, right?
moves.fb: A name on a sheet isn't verification. Meet at the office with ID before any ride.
moves.react: They write "John" and a fake number.

roleplays.debrief: You practised open house safety: escort unverified visitors, never reveal the sellers' schedule or lockbox and alarm codes, use a distress code, and avoid basements and storage rooms with strangers. When safe retreat exists, take it and call 911 (Penal Law Article 35; the dwelling exception covers your home, not a listing). Verify emailed wire changes by phone at a known number, meet new prospects at the office with ID, and file an incident report and notify the sellers the same day.

questions.q: A brokerage's written rules on ID checks, showing logs and distress codes form its:
c: Office safety policy
Agency disclosure policy
Escrow policy
Advertising policy
questions.x: These are standard elements of a safety policy. Escrow policy is the trap: it covers handling deposits.

questions.q: An agent texts a pre-agreed code word to the office during a showing. This is part of a(n):
c: Fair housing plan
Listing presentation
Office safety policy
Commission agreement
questions.x: Distress codes are a safety measure. Fair housing plan is the trap: it is unrelated.

questions.q: Under New York Penal Law Article 35, a person may use physical force when they reasonably believe it is necessary to:
c: Recover a stolen commission
Defend against imminent unlawful force
Remove a slow-paying tenant
Stop someone from criticizing them
questions.x: Article 35 allows force to defend against imminent unlawful physical force. Removing a tenant is the trap: evictions require legal process.

questions.q: An agent is attacked during a showing. New York law on justification permits:
c: Any force at all
No force; she must only call 911
Force only after the attack ends
Reasonable force to defend herself
questions.x: Force reasonably believed necessary against imminent unlawful force is justified. 'After it ends' is the trap: force must address an imminent threat.

questions.q: Before showing a vacant home to a new prospect who called from a sign, the safest practice is to:
c: Meet the prospect at the property after rush hour
Text the lockbox code so the prospect can tour alone
Meet at the office first and copy a photo ID
Ask the prospect to bring a friend to the showing
questions.x: An office meeting with ID verification and a logged itinerary is the core screening step. Bringing a friend is the trap: it adds an unknown second person instead of verifying who the prospect is.

questions.q: A distress code is:
c: A harmless-sounding phrase that signals for help
The alarm code that disarms the office system
A lockbox combination shared with the office
The emergency password for the MLS account
questions.x: A distress code lets an agent ask a coworker for help without alerting the person nearby. The alarm code answer is the trap: it is an access code, not a signal.

questions.q: When arriving at a showing, an agent should generally park:
c: In the driveway, close to the front door
Inside the garage, out of the weather
On the street, where it can't be blocked
Around the corner, out of the prospect's sight
questions.x: Parking on the street keeps the exit open. The driveway is the trap: it feels close and convenient, but another car can block you in.

questions.q: Good open house safety practice includes all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Walking every room and exit before visitors arrive
Asking sellers to remove valuables and prescriptions
Having each visitor sign in with a name and phone
Taking a lone visitor down to see the boiler
questions.x: Isolated spaces such as basements and attics with an unknown visitor are exactly what to avoid. Removing prescriptions is the tempting pick, but drug theft at open houses is common, so it is a standard precaution.

questions.q: During a showing, a prospect asks Jordan what hours the sellers are usually away at work. Jordan should:
c: Decline to discuss the sellers' schedule
Give the general hours but not exact times
Refer the question to the sellers' attorney
Answer if the prospect is pre-approved for a loan
questions.x: The sellers' routines are confidential and could help a burglar. The pre-approval answer is the trap: a loan letter says nothing about whether a stranger is safe.

questions.q: When walking through a home with an unfamiliar client, the agent should:
c: Lead the client into each room to point out features
Split up to cover the house faster
Let the client go first and stay near the exit
Wait outside on the porch during the tour
questions.x: Walking behind keeps the exit on your side. Leading is the trap: it feels professional but puts the stranger between you and the door.

questions.q: To protect a home office, an agent should:
c: Print the home address on cards so clients can find it
Meet new clients at home to save on office costs
List the home address on social media profiles
Use the brokerage address or a PO box on cards
questions.x: Keep your home address private. Meeting new clients at home is the trap: it saves time but brings strangers to your family's door.

questions.q: The day before closing, a buyer receives an email that appears to come from the closing attorney with new wiring instructions. The buyer should:
c: Wire the funds today to avoid delaying closing
Call the attorney at a known number to verify
Reply to the email and ask for confirmation
Ask the seller to confirm the change by text
questions.x: Changed wiring instructions by email are the classic wire fraud pattern; verify through a phone number you already know. Replying to the email is the trap: it goes straight back to the fraudster.

questions.q: An email that imitates a trusted service to trick an agent into entering a password on a fake site is:
c: Phishing
Malware
Spoofed lockbox
Ransomware
questions.x: Phishing uses fake messages and sites to steal credentials. Ransomware is the trap: it is malicious software that locks files for payment, often delivered after a phish.

questions.q: New York's SHIELD Act requires a business that holds NY residents' private information to:
c: Register its computers with the Department of State
Keep client files on paper rather than computers
Delete client data 30 days after each closing
Keep reasonable safeguards and report breaches
questions.x: GBL 899-aa and 899-bb require reasonable data safeguards and notice to affected people after a breach. The 30-day deletion answer is the trap: brokers keep transaction records for 3 years.

questions.q: Which practice best protects an agent's email and MLS accounts?
c: One strong password reused for every account
A password list kept under the keyboard
Unique passwords plus multi-factor login
Logging in from public Wi-Fi to avoid tracking
questions.x: Unique passwords limit the damage from any one breach, and multi-factor authentication blocks most stolen-password attacks. The one-strong-password answer is the trap: one leak then opens everything.

questions.q: Jordan discovers fake rental ads on a listing site using Jordan's name, photo, and license number to collect deposits. This is an example of:
c: Puffing
Identity theft
Blind advertising
Commingling
questions.x: A criminal is using Jordan's identity to defraud renters, so Jordan should report it to the site, the police, and the broker. Blind advertising is the trap: that is an ad that omits the broker's name, not impersonation.

questions.q: A visitor trips on a broken stair at an open house that the sellers knew about and did not repair. The party most likely liable for the dangerous condition is:
c: The sellers who owned the home
The Department of State
The visitor's own lender
The town building inspector
questions.x: Owners have premises liability for dangerous conditions they know about. The agent may share liability for failing to warn, but the building inspector is the trap: a municipal inspector does not take on the owner's duty of care.

questions.q: A broker may be held liable for a salesperson's negligence during a showing mainly because:
c: Brokers hold legal title to every listing
DOS requires brokers to insure each listing
Brokers answer for agents' acts on the job
The agent is an employee for tax purposes
questions.x: Vicarious liability and the duty to supervise make brokers answerable for agents' acts within the scope of the business. The tax answer is the trap: independent contractor or employee tax status does not decide this liability.

questions.q: A listing agreement clause that limits the broker's liability for theft by visitors during showings addresses:
c: Fair housing liability
Commission disputes
Lead paint disclosure
Losses caused by third parties
questions.x: Thefts or damage by visitors are losses caused by third parties, a known risk that listing contracts often address. Fair housing liability is the trap: it concerns discrimination, not theft.

questions.q: Under NY Penal Law Article 35, physical force (not deadly force) is justified when a person reasonably believes it is necessary to:
c: Remove a visitor who refused to sign in
Defend against imminent unlawful force
Recover a stolen open house sign
Stop a visitor from shouting insults
questions.x: Justification requires a reasonable belief that force is needed to defend against the imminent use of unlawful physical force. The sign-in answer is the trap: refusing a procedure is not a threat of force.

questions.q: Under NY law, deadly physical force in self-defense is generally justified when the person reasonably believes the attacker is:
c: Using or about to use deadly force
Trespassing in a vacant listing
Using threatening language
Taking property of small value
questions.x: Deadly force answers deadly force, or certain violent felonies such as robbery or kidnapping. Threatening language is the trap: words without imminent deadly force do not justify it.

questions.q: An agent is threatened at a vacant listing in Yonkers and can safely leave through the back door. Under Article 35, before using deadly physical force the agent:
c: Has no duty to retreat while lawfully on the property
May use deadly force if the seller has authorized it
Has to warn the attacker in writing before acting
Has to retreat, since it is safe and not her home
questions.x: New York requires retreat before deadly force when it can be done with complete safety; the no-retreat exception covers your own dwelling. The lawfully-present answer is the trap: that is a stand-your-ground rule NY does not follow.

questions.q: Under Article 35, a person who started the confrontation (the initial aggressor):
c: Keeps the right to use deadly force
Is justified once the other person fights back
Loses justification unless they withdraw
Is protected while on duty as a licensee
questions.x: The initial aggressor generally cannot claim justification unless they withdraw and clearly communicate the withdrawal. The fights-back answer is the trap: the other person's defense does not restore the aggressor's justification.

questions.q: After a threatening incident at a showing, the agent's first priority is to:
c: Finish the showing calmly
Get to safety and call 911
Post a warning on social media
Confront the person for a name
questions.x: Safety first, then police; documentation and notifying the broker follow. Confronting the person is the trap: it increases the risk.

questions.q: A brokerage's written safety policy would typically include all of the following EXCEPT:
c: An itinerary log of showings
A distress code for agents
Incident report procedures
Solo first meetings at vacant homes
questions.x: A safety policy does the opposite: office meetings, ID checks, and a buddy for vacant or after-dark showings. The distress code is the tempting pick, but it is a standard part of a safety plan.

questions.q: An incident report after a threatening visitor should be written:
c: Promptly, with times and descriptions
If the police make an arrest
When the seller asks for one
At the agent's next license renewal
questions.x: Details fade fast, and a prompt, specific report helps police, the broker, and other agents. The arrest answer is the trap: a report is useful whether or not anyone is arrested.

questions.q: To protect client information, a brokerage should do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Shred paper records past their retention period
Lock screens and encrypt laptops
Email Social Security numbers unencrypted
Limit file access to staff who need it
questions.x: Sending SSNs by unencrypted email invites identity theft. Shredding is the tempting pick, but secure destruction of records past their retention period is a reasonable safeguard.

questions.q: Which practice best controls office access?
c: Keeping one alarm code for years
Changing the codes whenever staff leave
Hiding a spare key near the door
Posting codes for staff on a board
questions.x: Changing alarm and lockbox codes when people leave, and logging keys, keeps access limited to current staff. Keeping one code is the trap: it is easy to remember but every former staffer still knows it.

questions.q: Posting "Heading to my vacant listing at 22 Elm St, here till 7!" on social media is risky mainly because it:
c: Tells strangers where you'll be alone
Breaks the DOS advertising rules
Is a fair housing violation
Breaches the listing's exclusivity clause
questions.x: Real-time location posts reveal when and where you will be alone. The advertising-rules answer is the trap: the risk here is personal safety, not ad compliance.

questions.concept: Unverified strangers are the main risk
questions.q: According to safety guidance for agents, most attacks on agents happen when the agent is:
c: Driving between back-to-back showings
Working late at a busy office
Alone with someone never verified
Hosting a crowded open house
questions.x: Most attacks happen where the agent is alone with someone they never verified, which is why office meetings and ID checks come first. A crowded open house is the trap: crowds bring theft risk, but isolation with an unknown person is the main danger.

questions.concept: Unverified strangers are the main risk
questions.q: Which habit best reflects general safety awareness for an agent arriving at a new listing?
c: Noting exits and planning a quick way out
Parking in the driveway, as close as possible
Leaving the phone in the car to stay focused
Propping the front door open for buyers
questions.x: Safety starts with knowing your surroundings: exits, who is around and how you would leave in a hurry. The driveway is the trap: parking there lets another car block you in.

questions.q: Before a first showing at a vacant house, Jordan should give the office:
c: The lockbox code so a coworker can let the buyer in
The buyer's pre-approval letter in place of a log
A note of the client's Social Security number
The address, client name, and start and end times
questions.x: Tell the office the address, client name and start and end time, then check in when you arrive and when you leave. Sharing the lockbox code is the trap: codes should be controlled, not passed around.

questions.q: Jordan finishes a showing at 6 pm. Under the office's itinerary rules, Jordan should next:
c: Post a photo of the listing on social media right away
Check in with the office
Email the seller a copy of the buyer's photo ID
Text the client the lockbox code
questions.x: The itinerary rule includes checking in when you arrive and when you leave, so someone knows you are safe. Posting on social media is the trap: it broadcasts your location instead of telling the office.

questions.q: Screening a first-time prospect before a solo showing includes all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Copying a government photo ID
Logging the showing address and time
Sharing the itinerary with the office
Texting the lockbox code in advance
questions.x: A lockbox code should never go to an unverified stranger. Logging the itinerary is the tempting pick, but it is a core step so the office knows where you are.

questions.q: Mid-showing, Priya calls her office and says, "Can you grab the red file from my desk?" The office agreed on that phrase in advance. The coworker should:
c: Send help to her logged showing location now
Find the red file and call her back
Ask Priya to explain on speakerphone
Wait an hour, then text to check in
questions.x: A prearranged distress phrase means send help to the logged location now. Asking her to explain is the trap: it could alert the person with her.

questions.q: To keep a quick exit available at a showing, an agent should do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Park in the driveway by the door
Park on the street facing the way out
Keep car keys in a pocket, not a bag
Note the exits on arrival
questions.x: Parking in the driveway lets another car block you in. Keeping keys in a pocket is the tempting pick, but it saves seconds in an emergency.

questions.q: Near closing time at an open house, a lone visitor asks Diane to show him the attic. The safest response is to:
c: Take him up herself, staying close behind him
Let him go up alone while she waits at the stairs
Offer photos, or return with a colleague
Lock the front door so no other visitors come in
questions.x: Avoid isolated spaces with an unknown visitor; offer photos or a later visit with a colleague. Letting him go alone is the trap: it avoids isolation for her but leaves him unsupervised in the sellers' home.

questions.q: A listing agent should avoid sharing all of the following with prospects EXCEPT:
c: When the sellers leave for work
Where the sellers keep spare keys
The property's annual tax bill
The sellers' upcoming vacation dates
questions.x: The tax bill is public, relevant information about the property. Vacation dates are the tempting pick for some agents, but they tell a burglar exactly when the home is empty.

questions.q: Touring a narrow brownstone with a new client, Marcus reaches the top-floor bedroom. Where should he stand?
c: Near the doorway, with a clear path out
Deep in the room, by the far window
In the hall closet, out of the way
Ahead of the client, on the next stair up
questions.x: Staying near the doorway keeps the exit on your side. The far-window answer is the trap: it gives a better view of the room but traps you behind the client.

questions.q: A new caller asks Leo to meet at his home office "since it's closer." Leo should:
c: Agree, since the caller is a referral
Agree, if a family member is home
Suggest the brokerage office instead
Agree, if the caller sends a photo ID
questions.x: Meeting unknown clients at the brokerage keeps your home address private. The photo ID answer is the trap: ID helps screening but still brings a stranger to your home.

questions.q: To prevent wire fraud, a brokerage should advise clients to do all of the following EXCEPT:
