c: Verify any wire changes by a known phone number
Treat last-minute changes as a red flag
Confirm receipt with the recipient after sending
Use the phone number in the new email to check
questions.x: A phone number inside the suspicious email may reach the fraudster. Confirming receipt after sending is the tempting pick, but it is a sound step to catch a misdirected wire quickly.

questions.q: Leo gets an email titled "Your MLS account is locked" with a link to a login page at an unfamiliar address. The best response is to:
c: Click and log in to unlock it quickly
Reply asking whether it is real
Go to the MLS site directly instead
Forward it to clients as a warning
questions.x: This is a phishing pattern; go to the real site by typing its address, and report the email. Replying is the trap: it confirms your address to the sender and gets you no real answer.

questions.q: A brokerage's laptop holding NY clients' Social Security numbers is stolen unencrypted. Under the SHIELD Act, the brokerage's main obligation is to:
c: Notify the affected clients
Destroy its remaining client files
Re-license the agents involved
Notify HUD within 24 hours
questions.x: The SHIELD Act requires notice to affected NY residents (and certain state agencies) after a breach of private information. Destroying files is the trap: records still must be kept for required periods.

questions.q: Multi-factor authentication protects an account mainly by:
c: Forcing longer, more complex passwords
Encrypting every email that is sent
Blocking access from public Wi-Fi
Requiring a second proof of identity
questions.x: MFA requires a second factor, such as a code or app approval, so a stolen password alone is not enough. The longer-passwords answer is the trap: length strengthens a password, but MFA adds a separate factor.

questions.q: A renter calls Jordan about a deposit she paid on a listing Jordan never posted. Jordan's best first step is to:
c: Report it to the broker, site, and police
Refund the deposit from Jordan's own funds
Ignore it, since Jordan did nothing wrong
Post the renter's name online as a warning
questions.x: Impersonation scams should be reported to the broker, the listing site, and police. Ignoring it is the trap: the scam continues and other renters lose money under Jordan's name.

questions.q: Before an open house, Diane sees a loose railing on the porch steps. The best action is to:
c: Say nothing, since the seller is liable
Warn visitors and ask the seller to fix it
Cancel her listing agreement at once
Report the seller to the building department
questions.x: The owner has primary premises liability, but an agent who knows of a hazard should warn visitors and press for a repair. The say-nothing answer is the trap: the agent can share liability for failing to warn.

questions.q: A broker can reduce exposure to liability for agents' conduct by all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Written safety and showing policies
Training and supervising agents
Errors and omissions coverage
Classifying agents as contractors
questions.x: Independent contractor status affects taxes, not the broker's duty to supervise or vicarious liability. E&O coverage is the tempting pick, but it is a real risk-management tool.

questions.q: After an open house, the seller finds jewelry missing. A visitor took it. Who caused the loss in liability terms?
c: A third party to the listing
The seller, as owner
The listing broker
The buyer's agent
questions.x: A visitor who is not a party to the listing is a third party; listing agreements often limit the broker's liability for such losses. The listing broker is the trap: absent negligence or a contract term, the broker did not cause the theft.

questions.q: A visitor refuses to leave an open house and yells at Leo but makes no move toward him. Under Article 35, Leo pushing him out is:
c: Justified, since he is now trespassing
Justified, if the seller approves it first
Not justified; no force was threatened
Justified, after one clear verbal warning
questions.x: Physical force in self-defense requires a reasonable belief of imminent unlawful physical force. The trespass answer is the trap: Leo should leave and call police rather than use force against a non-threatening visitor.

questions.q: Under NY law, deadly physical force may be justified against a person reasonably believed to be committing all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Robbery
Kidnapping
Using deadly force
Petit larceny
questions.x: Petit larceny, a minor theft, never justifies deadly force. Robbery is the tempting pick, but NY lists it among the violent felonies that can justify deadly force.

questions.q: New York's duty to retreat before using deadly physical force generally does NOT apply when the person is:
c: At a client's vacant listing
At the brokerage office during work hours
On a public sidewalk outside a showing
In their own home, not the aggressor
questions.x: There is no duty to retreat in one's own dwelling if not the initial aggressor. The client's-listing answer is the trap: a listing is not the agent's dwelling.

questions.q: Marcus shoves a visitor first, then the visitor swings back. Marcus has not withdrawn. Under Article 35, Marcus's claim of self-defense is:
c: Strong, since he was attacked
Weak, as he was the initial aggressor
Strong, as a licensee on duty
Strong, if the visitor was trespassing
questions.x: An initial aggressor generally cannot claim justification unless they withdraw and communicate it. The was-attacked answer is the trap: the visitor's response does not erase who started it.

questions.q: After getting safe and calling police following a threat at a showing, an agent should do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Write an incident report promptly
Notify the broker
Warn other agents with that client
Go back alone to finish up
questions.x: Returning alone recreates the danger. Warning other agents is the tempting pick, but sharing the incident through the broker protects colleagues.

questions.q: A brokerage writes a safety policy for after-dark showings of vacant homes. Which rule fits best?
c: Agents go alone to keep clients at ease
A second agent or a buddy attends the showing
Showings run with the lights off
The client may hold the lockbox key
questions.x: A buddy for vacant or after-dark showings is standard policy. The client-at-ease answer is the trap: comfort for the client should not trade away the agent's safety.

questions.q: A useful incident report includes all of the following EXCEPT:
c: The agent's guess at ethnicity
Date, time, and location
A description of the person
Vehicle and plate details if seen
questions.x: Reports should record observed facts, not speculation about protected characteristics. A physical description is the tempting pick, but objective details such as height and clothing are useful.

questions.q: A caller claiming to be a buyer's lender asks the office manager to email the buyer's bank statements. The manager should:
c: Email them, since lenders need them
Verify the caller through known contacts
Email them with the SSNs blacked out
Mail paper copies to the caller's address
questions.x: Verify any request for client data through contacts already on file. Redacting SSNs is the trap: it reduces harm but still hands financial records to an unverified stranger.

questions.q: An office assistant quits on bad terms. The broker's first access-control step is to:
c: Ask the assistant to forget the codes
Change the alarm and lockbox codes
Post new codes on the office board
Leave codes alone until renewal
questions.x: Change alarm and lockbox codes when staff leave, and recover keys. Asking the person to forget the codes is the trap: it relies on goodwill from someone who left angry.

questions.q: Safe social media habits for agents include all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Posting listing photos after the event
Keeping a home address off profiles
Live-posting where you are while alone
Using a business page, not a personal one
questions.x: Live location posts tell strangers where you are and when you are alone. Posting after the event is the tempting pick, but delayed posting is the safe alternative.

questions.q: A seller knows a deck railing is loose but leaves it for an open house, and the listing agent, who also knows, invites visitors onto the deck. A visitor is hurt when the railing gives way. Who has exposure?
c: The seller and the agent, and the agent's broker
The visitor alone, who chose to step onto the deck
The seller alone, since the agent does not own the house
No one, because open houses are invitations at the visitor's risk
questions.x: Owners are responsible for known dangerous conditions, and an agent who knows of the hazard and invites the public onto it is negligent too; the broker is exposed for the agent's acts and supervision. Blaming only the owner is the tempting single-party answer.

questions.q: Right after a visitor is injured at an open house, the agent should:
c: Ask the visitor to sign a release of liability
Get the person care, then complete an incident report
Promise that the seller's insurance will cover the costs
End the open house and wait a week to report it
questions.x: Care comes first, then documentation while facts are fresh, followed by notice to the broker, sellers and insurers. Promising payment or seeking a release from an injured person creates new problems, and delayed reporting can jeopardize coverage.

questions.q: A listing agreement says the broker is not liable for loss of the seller's personal property caused by third parties, except to the extent of the broker's own negligence. A visitor steals jewelry the seller left out. The broker is most likely:
c: Liable, because brokers guarantee the contents during showings
Not liable for the theft, absent the broker's own negligence
Liable, because the clause is void in New York
Not liable, and neither is the thief
questions.x: Such clauses limit the broker's liability for third parties' acts, which is common in listing agreements. They do not excuse the broker's own negligence and do not affect the thief's responsibility. Brokers do not guarantee a seller's contents.

questions.q: Which item should sellers remove or secure before an open house?
c: Prescription medications in the bathroom
The family photos on the walls
The furniture in the living room
Appliances in the kitchen
questions.x: Prescription medications, along with jewelry, cash, keys, mail and firearms, are common theft targets and should be removed or locked away. Photos and furniture are staging choices, not security risks.

questions.q: An agent at a vacant listing is threatened by a man with a knife. The agent can safely leave through the side door. Under Penal Law Article 35, before using deadly physical force the agent:
c: May stand ground, because the agent is lawfully present
Must retreat, since retreat with complete safety is possible
May use deadly force once the man raises his voice
Must first ask the seller for permission to defend
questions.x: Before using deadly physical force, a person who knows they can retreat with complete safety must do so; the dwelling exception covers your own home, and a listing is not the agent's dwelling. Being lawfully present does not create a stand-your-ground right in New York.
questions.concept: Duty to retreat at a listing

questions.q: Under New York's Penal Law Article 35, the duty to retreat before using deadly physical force generally does NOT apply when a person is:
c: At an open house they are hosting for a seller
In a vacant listing that has a lockbox on the door
In their own dwelling, not the initial aggressor
In their car parked outside a client's home
questions.x: The exception to the duty to retreat is one's own dwelling, when the person is not the initial aggressor. A listing the agent is hosting or showing is not the agent's dwelling, which is why the open house choice is the trap.
questions.concept: Duty to retreat at a listing

questions.q: A brokerage's unencrypted laptop holding clients' names and Social Security numbers is stolen. Under the NY SHIELD Act as amended in December 2024, affected NY residents must be notified:
c: Just if identity theft is later reported
Within 1 year of the theft
Within 30 days of discovering the breach
Just if more than 5,000 people are affected
questions.x: Names with SSNs are private information, and unencrypted data on a stolen device is a breach. The December 2024 amendment set a 30-day deadline from discovery, with notice also to the Attorney General, DOS and the State Police. The 5,000-person threshold relates to notifying consumer reporting agencies.

questions.q: Under the NY SHIELD Act, each of the following combined with a person's name is private information EXCEPT:
c: A Social Security number
A driver's license number
The person's home address
A bank account number with its access code
questions.x: Private information includes a name combined with an SSN, a driver's license number, or an account number with its access code, among others such as biometrics and login credentials. A home address alone is not on the list.

questions.q: A buyer realizes an hour after wiring a down payment that the instructions came from a spoofed email. The first call should be to:
c: The sender of the email, to ask for the money back
The listing agent, to reschedule the closing
The county clerk, to flag the property
The buyer's bank, to request a recall of the wire
questions.x: Speed matters most: the sending bank may be able to recall the wire or freeze the funds at the receiving bank if contacted quickly. Then report to the FBI's IC3 and police. Contacting the spoofed sender alerts the criminal.

questions.q: Which practice best protects clients from wire fraud in a real estate deal?
c: Sending wiring instructions in a PDF attachment
Replying to the email that contains the instructions
Using a shorter password on the closing platform
Confirming wiring changes by phone at a known number
questions.x: Verification through an independent, known phone number defeats spoofed and hacked emails. Replying to the email or trusting a PDF keeps the conversation inside the compromised channel. Stronger, not shorter, passwords and MFA also help.

questions.q: A man grabs an agent's arm at a showing and refuses to let go, but shows no weapon. Under Penal Law Article 35, the agent may:
c: Use reasonable physical force to break free
Use deadly physical force immediately
Use no force, because the agent is on a client's property
Use any force, because the man started it
questions.x: Physical force is justified when reasonably believed necessary to defend against imminent unlawful physical force. Deadly physical force requires a reasonable belief of deadly force or certain violent felonies, which a grab alone does not show. Starting the fight does not license unlimited force in response.

questions.q: Under New York Penal Law Article 35, deadly physical force in self-defense is justified when the person reasonably believes the other person is:
c: Trespassing on property the person is showing
Shouting threats from across the room
Refusing to leave at the end of an open house
Using or about to use deadly physical force
questions.x: Deadly physical force requires a reasonable belief that the other person is using or about to use deadly physical force, or is committing certain violent felonies such as robbery or kidnapping, subject to the duty to retreat. Trespass, shouting or refusing to leave do not meet that standard.

cram.html: Meet new prospects at the office first, copy photo ID, log the showing.
Distress code: innocent phrase that tells a coworker to call 911.
Park on the street, not the driveway. Let the client walk ahead; keep the exit behind you.
Avoid basements, attics, and closets with unknown visitors.
Never reveal the sellers' schedule, travel, or that you are alone.
Open houses: walk every room first, sellers remove valuables and medications, sign-in, partner, charged phone.
Change alarm and lockbox codes when staff leave; never give lockbox codes to strangers.
Wire instructions: verify by phone at a known number. Never trust an emailed change.
Unique passwords + multi-factor authentication; avoid public Wi-Fi.
NY SHIELD Act (GBL 899-aa, 899-bb): reasonable safeguards + breach notification.
Seller: premises liability for known hazards. Broker: liable for agents' acts in scope; must supervise.
Listing agreements may limit broker liability for third-party theft or damage.
Article 35: physical force vs imminent unlawful physical force; deadly force only vs deadly force (or robbery, kidnapping, forcible rape).
Duty to retreat before deadly force if completely safe. Dwelling exception = your home, not a listing.
Initial aggressor generally has no justification defense unless they withdraw.
After an incident: safe, 911, written report, notify broker and sellers, update policy.

subjects.title: Taxes and Assessments
subjects.blurb: Property taxes are often a buyer's second biggest housing cost. Know how assessed value, equalization, and the tax rate produce a bill, which exemptions exist, how to grieve an assessment, and what happens when taxes go unpaid.

lessons.title: How a Property Tax Bill Is Built
lessons.tagline: Budget, levy, assessment, rate. Four numbers, one bill, and no state property tax in sight.
objectives: Explain why governments tax real property and which properties are exempt
Convert between market value, assessed value, assessment ratio, and equalization rate
Derive a tax rate from a municipal budget and compute a tax bill
Identify NY's taxing jurisdictions, special assessment districts, and NYC's four tax classes
Tell legal reassessment from an illegal "welcome stranger" reassessment upon sale

blocks.title: Two houses, one street, Mamaroneck
blocks.html: Leo is weighing two nearly identical colonials on the same block in Westchester. One has a $14,000 tax bill, the other $21,000. "Same size, same school district. How is that possible? And if I buy the cheap one, will they jack up my taxes the day I close?" Jordan needs to explain where a tax bill actually comes from.
blocks.casual: Leo's looking at two nearly identical colonials on the same block in Mamaroneck. One's got a $14,000 tax bill, the other $21,000. "Same size, same school district. How? And if I buy the cheap one, will they crank up my taxes the day I close?" Jordan has to explain where a tax bill really comes from.

deeper.plain: Two similar houses can pay very different taxes because of old assessments, exemptions, or unpermitted work. Buying alone doesn't legally trigger a reassessment.
deeper.picture: Two people in the same job with different salaries because one was hired 20 years ago and never got re-graded.
deeper.street: The $14,000 house hasn't been reassessed since 1990 and the owner has a senior exemption. The $21,000 house was built in 2015 at today's values. Leo buys the cheaper one, but the senior exemption ends with the sale, so his bill will rise.
deeper.stakes: Tell a buyer the low tax bill is what they'll pay and they may budget wrong by thousands a year.
deeper.exam: Seller's exemptions don't transfer. Raising only the sold house's assessment is illegal welcome stranger assessment.

blocks.html: Property taxes pay for local services: schools, police, fire, roads, parks, libraries, sanitation. In most of NY the school tax is the largest piece of the bill. Real property is a favorite tax base for three reasons:
blocks.casual: Property taxes pay for local services: schools, police, fire, roads, parks, libraries, sanitation. In most of NY, the school tax is the biggest piece of the bill. Real property is a favorite thing to tax, for three reasons:

deeper.plain: Your property tax pays for your town's schools and services, with schools usually taking the biggest bite.
deeper.picture: A building's shared maintenance fee: everyone chips in for the elevator, the boiler, and the super.
deeper.street: On a Westchester bill of $18,000, maybe $12,000 goes to the school district, $3,500 to the town, $2,000 to the county, and the rest to fire and library districts.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who only look at the town tax miss the school tax, the biggest piece.
deeper.exam: Property tax funds local services. In most of NY, school tax is the largest share.

items: Predictable: land does not move or disappear, so revenue is stable year to year.
Hard to conceal: you can hide income; you cannot hide a house.
Historic link to wealth: land was long the main measure of wealth and productivity.
blocks.casual:
Predictable: land doesn't move or vanish, so the money's steady year to year.
Hard to hide: you can hide income, but you can't hide a house.
Old tie to wealth: for a long time, land was the main measure of wealth and productivity.

deeper.plain: Governments tax land because it's always there, can't be hidden, and used to be how wealth was measured.
deeper.picture: A landlord who knows exactly where every tenant lives. No one can skip town with the building.
deeper.street: Sal's Astoria building has sat on the same lot for 90 years. The city can count on billing it every year, rain or shine.
deeper.stakes: Because the tax follows the land, an unpaid bill becomes a lien that can cost an owner the property.
deeper.exam: Know the three reasons: stability, visibility, and historic link to wealth.

blocks.html: The property tax is an ad valorem tax: Latin for "according to value." The more your property is worth, the more you pay. Some property is exempt: government buildings, houses of worship, nonprofit schools and hospitals, cemeteries. Exempt property still uses services, so everyone else's share is higher.
blocks.casual: The property tax is an ad valorem tax, Latin for "according to value." The more your property's worth, the more you pay. Some property is exempt: government buildings, houses of worship, nonprofit schools and hospitals, cemeteries. Exempt property still uses services, so everyone else's share goes up.

deeper.plain: Higher value, higher tax. Exempt properties don't pay, so the rest of us cover their share.
deeper.picture: Splitting a dinner bill by what each person ordered, except a few people eat free and the rest split their part.
deeper.street: In a small upstate city where a big hospital and a college sit off the tax rolls, homeowners carry a bigger share of the levy than in a town with mostly taxable property.
deeper.stakes: Buyers comparing towns should know exempt property can push rates up.
deeper.exam: Ad valorem = according to value. Special assessments are NOT ad valorem.

blocks.title: No state property tax
blocks.html: New York State does not levy a real property tax. The bill comes from local jurisdictions: county, city, town, village, school district, and special districts. The state's role is oversight, equalization rates, and programs like STAR.
blocks.casual: New York State does not charge a real property tax. The bill comes from local governments: county, city, town, village, school district, and special districts. The state's job is oversight, equalization rates, and programs like STAR.

deeper.plain: Albany doesn't tax your house. Local governments do.
deeper.picture: The state is the referee. The counties, towns, and school districts are the players sending you bills.
deeper.street: Leo's Mamaroneck bill lists the town, the village, the county, and the school district. Nothing from New York State, though STAR may reduce his school tax.
deeper.stakes: Say "the state raised your property tax" and you'll confuse a client who then calls the wrong office.
deeper.exam: "Which does NOT levy real property tax in NY?" The state.

blocks.html: An assessment is the value the local assessor places on a property for tax purposes. The assessed value may be the full market value or a fraction of it. Full value means market value. The assessment ratio (level of assessment) is assessed value divided by full value.
blocks.casual: An assessment is the value the local assessor puts on a property for tax purposes. The assessed value can be full market value or a fraction of it. Full value means market value. The assessment ratio (level of assessment) is assessed value divided by full value.

deeper.plain: The assessor's number may be a fraction of market value. The ratio tells you what fraction.
deeper.picture: A scale model of a building at 1:4. Multiply back up and you get the real size.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Long Island house worth $600,000 in a town assessing at 10% has an assessed value of $60,000. Ratio: $60,000 / $600,000 = 10%.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who sees a $60,000 assessment and thinks the house is undervalued doesn't understand fractional assessment.
deeper.exam: Assessed value / full value = ratio. Full value = market value.

deeper.plain: Three numbers: market value, assessed value, and ratio. Know two, find the third.
deeper.picture: The same part, total, rate triangle from the math lesson. Assessed value is the part.
deeper.street: New numbers: assessed $45,000, ratio 15%, full value = $45,000 / 0.15 = $300,000. Market $500,000 at 20%: assessed = $100,000.
deeper.stakes: Run it backward wrong and you'll tell a client their house is assessed at triple its real value.
deeper.exam: Multiply market value by the ratio for assessed. Divide assessed by the ratio for full value.

blocks.title: From market value to tax bill
blocks.html:
A Hudson Valley house has a market value of $400,000. The town assesses at 25% of full value.
Assessed value: $400,000 x 0.25 = $100,000
Combined tax rate: $95.50 per $1,000 of assessed value
Tax: 100 x $95.50 = $9,550
blocks.casual:
A Hudson Valley house has a market value of $400,000. The town assesses at 25% of full value.
Assessed value: $400,000 x 0.25 = $100,000
Combined tax rate: $95.50 per $1,000 of assessed value
Tax: 100 x $95.50 = $9,550

deeper.plain: Market value times ratio gives assessed value. Assessed value times rate gives the tax.
deeper.picture: Two conversion steps, like dollars to euros to pounds.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Suffolk house worth $550,000, assessed at 20% = $110,000. Rate $82 per $1,000. Tax: 110 x $82 = $9,020.
deeper.stakes: Use market value with a rate meant for assessed value and the tax bill comes out 4 or 5 times too high.
deeper.exam: Apply the rate to assessed value, not market value. Count thousands when the rate is per $1,000.

blocks.html: Each assessing municipality (the assessing unit, usually a city or town; in Nassau the county; in NYC the Department of Finance) may choose its own uniform percentage. What the law requires is equity: every property in a class assessed at the same percentage of value.
blocks.casual: Each assessing municipality (the assessing unit, usually a city or town; in Nassau it's the county; in NYC it's the Department of Finance) can pick its own uniform percentage. What the law demands is equity: every property in a class gets assessed at the same percentage of value.

deeper.plain: Each town picks its percentage, but it has to treat everyone in a class the same.
deeper.picture: A teacher can grade on any scale, but must use the same scale for every student.
deeper.street: Town A assesses everything at 100%, Town B at 5%. Both are fine. But if Town B assesses one house at 5% and the neighbor at 9%, that's unequal.
deeper.stakes: Owners who are assessed at a higher percentage than neighbors have a winning grievance.
deeper.exam: Assessing units: towns and cities (Nassau County and NYC Department of Finance are the notable exceptions). Uniform percentage within a class.

blocks.text: Why two similar houses pay different taxes

items: No reassessment for decades: many towns have not revalued in 30+ years, so assessments reflect old market patterns. Neighborhoods that rose fastest are underassessed.
Old vs new construction: a new house is assessed at today's value while an old one may carry a stale assessment.
Undeclared improvements: a finished basement or added bathroom built without a permit may never reach the assessor.
Exemptions: a senior or veteran owner may pay much less on the same assessment.
Different jurisdictions: a village line or a fire district boundary can split a street.
blocks.casual:
No reassessment in decades: lots of towns haven't revalued in 30+ years, so assessments reflect old market patterns. The neighborhoods that rose fastest end up underassessed.
Old vs new: a new house gets assessed at today's value while an old one may carry a stale number.
Undeclared improvements: a finished basement or extra bathroom built without a permit may never reach the assessor.
Exemptions: a senior or veteran owner may pay way less on the same assessment.
Different jurisdictions: a village line or fire district boundary can split a street.

deeper.plain: Old assessments, new construction, hidden renovations, exemptions, and district lines all make similar houses pay different taxes.
deeper.picture: Two cars bought 10 years apart with different insurance rates, even though they're the same model.
deeper.street: On a Yonkers block, one house added a legal rental unit with permits and pays more. The neighbor's illegal basement apartment never reached the assessor, so it pays less, for now.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who expects to inherit a low bill tied to an exemption or a hidden improvement can be shocked later.
deeper.exam: The exam asks why similar houses pay different taxes. Look for stale assessments, exemptions, or improvements.

blocks.html: The fix is a community-wide reassessment (revaluation): the assessor revalues every parcel at once so all are at the same percentage of current value.
blocks.casual: The fix is a community-wide reassessment (revaluation): the assessor revalues every parcel at once so they're all at the same percentage of current value.

deeper.plain: Revalue everybody at the same time so the burden is fair again.
deeper.picture: Resetting all the clocks in the house at once, instead of fixing just one and leaving the rest wrong.
deeper.street: After a town-wide revaluation in a Westchester town, owners in fast-rising neighborhoods see higher assessments while owners in flat areas see bills drop.
deeper.stakes: Buyers in a town about to revalue may see their bill move a lot after closing.
deeper.exam: Revaluation = all parcels at once. Selective reassessment of just sold houses is illegal.

blocks.title: "Welcome stranger" is illegal
blocks.html: Raising a property's assessment just because it sold, to match the sale price, while neighbors keep stale assessments, is selective reassessment, nicknamed welcome stranger. It violates equal protection and NY assessment law. A sale may be used as evidence in a community-wide revaluation, not to single out the new owner.
blocks.casual: Raising a property's assessment just because it sold, to match the sale price, while neighbors keep their stale assessments, is selective reassessment, nicknamed welcome stranger. It violates equal protection and NY assessment law. A sale can be used as evidence in a community-wide revaluation, not to single out the new owner.

deeper.plain: A town can't jack up your assessment just because you bought the house.
deeper.picture: A restaurant charging the new customer double because they're new while regulars pay the old price.
deeper.street: Leo closes on his Mamaroneck colonial for $1.1M. The next year the assessor raises only his house to match the price while identical neighbors stay put. Leo files a grievance and wins.
deeper.stakes: If a buyer's assessment spikes right after closing with nothing else changing, it's worth a grievance. That can save thousands a year.
deeper.exam: "Welcome stranger" = illegal selective reassessment upon sale. The trap answer says it's allowed because the sale shows value.

blocks.title: When a new owner's assessment can legally change

left.title: Legal
items: A community-wide reassessment of all parcels
Undeclared improvements are discovered (the extra bathroom)
A building permit shows new construction or additions
Loss of the seller's exemption (STAR, senior, veteran)

right.title: Illegal
items: Raising only the sold house to its sale price
Targeting new owners each year
Ignoring identical unsold neighbors

deeper.plain: Assessments can change after a sale for real reasons, but not just because of the sale itself.
deeper.picture: Your rent can go up when the lease renews for everyone, not just because the landlord learned you got a raise.
deeper.street: A buyer in Scarsdale loses the seller's senior exemption (legal), and a year later a permit for the buyer's new deck closes out and adds value (legal). But a bump only because of the sale price would be illegal.
deeper.stakes: Knowing the difference lets you warn buyers about real increases and spot illegal ones.
deeper.exam: Legal: town-wide revaluation, new improvements, permits, lost exemptions. Illegal: targeting the sold house.

blocks.html: Building permits feed the assessor. When a permit is closed out, the assessor learns about the addition and adjusts the assessment. When an improvement was never declared, the municipality may add it to the roll and, within limits set by law, bill back taxes (omitted taxes) for prior years. That is a reason buyers' attorneys check for permits and certificates of occupancy.
blocks.casual: Building permits feed the assessor. When a permit gets closed out, the assessor learns about the addition and adjusts the assessment. When an improvement was never declared, the town can add it to the roll and, within legal limits, bill back taxes (omitted taxes) for prior years. That's one reason buyers' attorneys check for permits and certificates of occupancy.

deeper.plain: Permitted improvements raise your assessment. Hidden ones can bring back tax bills later.
deeper.picture: Like getting caught with an unregistered car: you pay the registration plus the years you skipped.
deeper.street: A Bayside buyer closes on a house with an unpermitted second bathroom. Two years later the city finds it. The assessment rises, and an omitted tax bill shows up for prior years.
deeper.stakes: The buyer eats the back taxes and the cost of legalizing the work, which Priya would have caught with a permit search.
deeper.exam: Omitted taxes can be billed for prior years. Permits and CO searches protect the buyer.

blocks.q: Leo buys a Mamaroneck house for $1.2M. The next year the assessor raises only that house's assessment to reflect the sale price; unsold neighbors are untouched. This is:
c: A legal community-wide reassessment
An illegal selective (welcome stranger) reassessment
Proper because sale price is the best evidence of value
Required by STAR
blocks.x: Singling out a sold property while leaving comparable unsold properties at old values is illegal selective reassessment. A sale may inform a townwide revaluation, not target one owner.

blocks.html: Each taxing jurisdiction adopts a budget. The appropriation is the legal authorization to spend. Subtract non-property revenue (state aid, sales tax share, fees) and what is left must be raised from property: the tax levy. Divide the levy by the total taxable assessed value and you get the tax rate.
blocks.casual: Each taxing jurisdiction adopts a budget. The appropriation is the legal OK to spend. Subtract non-property money (state aid, sales tax share, fees) and what's left has to come from property: the tax levy. Divide the levy by total taxable assessed value and you've got the tax rate.

deeper.plain: The town figures what it needs, subtracts other income, and divides the rest across all the taxable property.
deeper.picture: Roommates splitting the utility bill after the landlord kicks in a credit. What's left gets divided by each person's share.
deeper.street: New numbers: a school district budget of $60M with $25M in state aid. Levy: $35M. Taxable assessed value $1.4B. Rate: 35 / 1,400 = 0.025, or $25 per $1,000.
deeper.stakes: Clients who think the tax rate is fixed by law don't get why their bill changed. You can explain the chain.
deeper.exam: Budget minus other revenue = levy. Levy / total assessed value = rate.

blocks.title: Rate in three moves

items.title: Budget
items.html: Village budget: $12,000,000.

items.title: Levy
items.html: Minus $4,000,000 of other revenue = $8,000,000 to raise from property tax.

items.title: Rate
items.html: $8,000,000 / $400,000,000 total taxable assessed value = 0.02 = $20 per $1,000 (20 mills, $2 per $100).

blocks.casual:
Budget: the village budget is $12,000,000.
Levy: minus $4,000,000 of other revenue = $8,000,000 to raise from property tax.
Rate: $8,000,000 / $400,000,000 total taxable assessed value = 0.02 = $20 per $1,000 (20 mills, $2 per $100).

deeper.plain: Three steps: budget, levy, rate.
deeper.picture: Plan the party, subtract what friends chip in, divide what's left among the hosts.
deeper.street: New numbers: a town budget of $9,000,000 with $3,600,000 from other sources. Levy: $5,400,000. Taxable assessed value: $300,000,000. Rate: 0.018 = $18 per $1,000, 18 mills, $1.80 per $100.
deeper.stakes: If you can't explain the rate, clients will think the assessor just picked a number.
deeper.exam: Convert the decimal: 0.018 = 18 mills = $18 per $1,000 = $1.80 per $100.

blocks.html: Notice what that means: if assessments go up but the budget stays flat, the rate goes down. Reassessment redistributes the levy; it does not, by itself, raise the total collected. NY also has a property tax cap that generally limits annual levy growth to 2% or the rate of inflation, whichever is less, unless overridden.
blocks.casual: Here's what that means: if assessments go up but the budget stays flat, the rate goes down. Reassessment shifts who pays the levy; it doesn't, on its own, raise the total collected. NY also has a property tax cap that generally limits yearly levy growth to 2% or inflation, whichever is less, unless it's overridden.

deeper.plain: Higher assessments don't mean the town collects more. The pie stays the same size; the slices change.
deeper.picture: Same pizza, re-sliced. Some people get bigger pieces, some smaller, but there's no more pizza.
deeper.street: New numbers: levy stays at $8M. Total assessed value rises from $400M to $500M after revaluation. Rate drops from $20 to $16 per $1,000. Owners whose value rose faster than average pay more; others pay less.
deeper.stakes: Clients panic at a higher assessment. Their bill may barely move if the rate drops.
deeper.exam: Same levy, higher total assessments = lower rate. Tax cap: 2% or inflation, whichever is less.

blocks.caption: Change the assessment ratio and the rate together and watch the bill stay put. Then apply an exemption and see the taxable value drop.

blocks.q: A town must raise $6,000,000 by property tax. Total taxable assessed value is $300,000,000. The tax rate per $1,000 is:

head: Jurisdiction
What it taxes for
Note
rows: Courts, social services, county roads, sheriff
Cities are often their own assessing unit
Inside a town; villagers pay town AND village tax
Usually the largest part of the bill; boundaries ignore town lines
Only parcels inside the district pay

deeper.plain: Many different local governments add their pieces to your one property tax bill. The state doesn't.
deeper.picture: A combined phone bill with separate lines for the phone company, city tax, and 911 fee.
deeper.street: A house in the Village of Ossining pays town, village, county, school district, and library district taxes. A house just outside the village pays no village tax but may pay a separate fire district.
deeper.stakes: Buyers comparing a village house to one outside often miss the village tax entirely.
deeper.exam: Village residents pay both town and village taxes. School district lines ignore town lines. State: no property tax.

blocks.html: Here is the puzzle: a school district or county spans several towns, each assessing at its own percentage. Town A assesses at 100% and Town B at 10%. Splitting the school levy by raw assessed value would make Town A pay ten times its fair share. The state's equalization rate for each town fixes this by converting each town's total assessed value back to full value before the levy is apportioned.
blocks.casual: Here's the puzzle: a school district or county covers several towns, and each one assesses at its own percentage. Town A assesses at 100% and Town B at 10%. Splitting the school levy by raw assessed value would make Town A pay ten times its fair share. The state's equalization rate for each town fixes that by converting each town's total assessed value back to full value before the levy gets split up.

deeper.plain: Equalization rates level the playing field between towns that assess at different percentages.
deeper.picture: Converting different currencies to dollars before splitting a group trip bill.
deeper.street: New numbers: a school district spans Town A (total assessed $500M, rate 100%) and Town B (total assessed $40M, rate 8%). Full values: $500M and $500M. Each town pays half the school levy, not 93% and 7%.
deeper.stakes: Without equalization, owners in towns that assess at full value would get crushed.
deeper.exam: Equalization rate (state) converts assessed value to full value so a multi-town levy is split fairly.

blocks.title: Using an equalization rate
blocks.html:
A house is assessed at $50,000 in a town with an equalization rate of 12.5%.
Estimated full value: $50,000 / 0.125 = $400,000
If the owner believes it is worth only $320,000, that is evidence the assessment is too high.
blocks.casual:
A house is assessed at $50,000 in a town with an equalization rate of 12.5%.
Estimated full value: $50,000 / 0.125 = $400,000
If the owner thinks it's only worth $320,000, that's evidence the assessment is too high.

deeper.plain: Divide the assessment by the equalization rate to see what market value the town thinks you have.
deeper.picture: If your photo is printed at 1/8 size, multiply by 8 to see how big the original is.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Hempstead-area house assessed at $6,000 with a 1% rate: $6,000 / 0.01 = $600,000 implied market value. If recent comps say $520,000, the owner has a grievance case.
deeper.stakes: Owners who never run this math overpay for years without knowing.
deeper.exam: Assessed / equalization rate = implied full value. Compare to real market value to judge over-assessment.

blocks.html: Some cities and towns that have completed a revaluation (an approved assessing unit) may adopt the homestead tax option under RPTL Article 19: separate tax rates for homestead parcels (1 to 3 family homes, many condos, farms) and non-homestead parcels (commercial, industrial, larger apartment buildings). It keeps a revaluation from shifting the burden suddenly onto homeowners.
blocks.casual: Some cities and towns that finished a revaluation (an approved assessing unit) can adopt the homestead tax option under RPTL Article 19: separate tax rates for homestead parcels (1 to 3 family homes, many condos, farms) and non-homestead parcels (commercial, industrial, bigger apartment buildings). It keeps a revaluation from suddenly dumping the burden on homeowners.

deeper.plain: Revalued towns can set a lower rate for homes and a higher rate for businesses.
deeper.picture: A gym with separate prices for individual members and corporate accounts.
deeper.street: After revaluing, a Hudson Valley city adopts homestead: homes pay $22 per $1,000, commercial property pays $34. A homeowner's bill stays steady even though the revaluation favored commercial property.
deeper.stakes: Investors buying commercial property in a homestead city need the non-homestead rate, not the residential one.
deeper.exam: Homestead option = RPTL Article 19, two rates, only for approved assessing units after a revaluation.

blocks.html: A special assessment charges only the properties that benefit from a specific improvement, such as new sidewalks, sewers, or a water main. It is based on benefit (often front footage), not on value, so it is not ad valorem. A special assessment district is the area that pays: a sewer district, water district, fire district, lighting district, or in NYC a Business Improvement District.
blocks.casual: A special assessment charges only the properties that benefit from a specific improvement, like new sidewalks, sewers, or a water main. It's based on benefit (often front footage), not value, so it's not ad valorem. A special assessment district is the area that pays: a sewer district, water district, fire district, lighting district, or in NYC a Business Improvement District.

deeper.plain: If a project helps only your street, only your street pays, usually by how much frontage you have.
deeper.picture: Neighbors splitting the cost of a shared fence by how much of it runs along their yard.
deeper.street: New numbers: a sewer extension on a Staten Island block costs $90 per front foot. A 40-foot lot owes $3,600; a 60-foot lot owes $5,400, regardless of what the houses are worth.
deeper.stakes: A pending special assessment can surprise a buyer after closing. Attorneys check for them in the title and tax search.
deeper.exam: Special assessments are based on benefit, not value, so they are not ad valorem.

blocks.title: Special assessments are liens too
blocks.html: Like general taxes, special assessments are a priority lien on the property. Unpaid, they survive the sale and come ahead of the mortgage.
blocks.casual: Just like regular taxes, special assessments are a priority lien on the property. Leave them unpaid and they survive the sale and come ahead of the mortgage.

deeper.plain: Unpaid special assessments stick to the property and jump ahead of the bank.
deeper.picture: A tag on a coat that stays on no matter who buys the coat.
deeper.street: A Buffalo seller didn't pay a $7,000 sidewalk assessment. The title search finds it, and the seller pays it at closing from the sale proceeds.
deeper.stakes: If it's missed, the buyer inherits the lien, and the lender's position slips behind it.
deeper.exam: Taxes and special assessments are paid first, ahead of mortgages, regardless of recording date.

blocks.text: New York City's four tax classes

head: Class
Property
Assessment ratio
Caps on increases
rows: 1 to 3 family homes, most small condos up to 3 stories, some vacant land
Other residential: co-ops, condos, rentals with 4+ units
Buildings with 10 or fewer units: 8% a year, 30% over 5 years; larger ones phase in
Commercial and industrial: offices, stores, factories, hotels
blocks.caption: NYC's Department of Finance assesses; the City Council sets a separate rate for each class.

deeper.plain: NYC sorts property into four classes, each with its own assessment ratio and caps.
deeper.picture: Four lanes on a highway, each with its own speed limit.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Class 1 Queens house worth $1,000,000 is assessed at most at 6%, $60,000. If its assessed value is $40,000 this year, it can only rise 6% next year, to $42,400, no matter how fast prices climb.
deeper.stakes: Investors buying a Class 2 rental building expect Class 1 caps and miscalculate their taxes.
deeper.exam: Class 1: 1 to 3 family, 6% ratio, caps 6%/20%. Class 2: co-ops, condos, 4+ unit rentals, 45%. Class 4: commercial.

blocks.title: Why Park Slope townhouses pay so little
blocks.html: Class 1 caps limit how fast assessed value can rise, even when market value soars. A brownstone bought decades ago may carry an assessment far below 6% of today's value, so its bill is much lower than a newer condo of the same price. The cap applies to the property, so a buyer generally inherits it (unless there is new construction or a change in use).
blocks.casual: Class 1 caps limit how fast assessed value can climb, even when market value takes off. A brownstone bought decades ago might carry an assessment way below 6% of today's value, so its bill is much lower than a newer condo at the same price. The cap goes with the property, so a buyer generally inherits it (unless there's new construction or a change in use).

deeper.plain: Old NYC houses often pay low taxes because the caps kept their assessments from catching up, and new owners keep that benefit.
deeper.picture: A rent-controlled apartment for your tax bill: the increases were capped every year, so it's far below market.
deeper.street: A Park Slope brownstone and a new Gowanus condo both sell for $3M. The brownstone's bill is about $12,000 a year; the condo's is closer to $30,000.
deeper.stakes: Buyers comparing a house to a condo in NYC need the actual tax bill, not a guess from the price.
deeper.exam: NYC doesn't reassess on sale. The Class 1 cap follows the property to the new owner.

blocks.q: A 6-unit rental building in Astoria falls in which NYC tax class?
c: Class 1
Class 2
Class 3
Class 4
blocks.x: Class 2 is residential property other than 1 to 3 family homes, including rentals with 4 or more units, co-ops, and condos. Class 1 stops at 3 family.

blocks.title: B-L-A-R
blocks.html: Budget minus other revenue = Levy. Levy / total Assessed value = Rate. Rate x your assessed value = your bill.
blocks.casual: Budget minus other revenue = Levy. Levy / total Assessed value = Rate. Rate x your assessed value = your bill.

deeper.plain: Follow the money from the town's budget down to your bill.
deeper.picture: A waterfall: budget pours into levy, levy into rate, rate into your bill.
deeper.street: New numbers: budget $20M, other revenue $8M, levy $12M. Total assessed $600M. Rate: $20 per $1,000. A house assessed at $75,000 pays $1,500.
deeper.stakes: If you can walk a client through B-L-A-R, you'll handle any tax question at the closing table.
deeper.exam: BLAR in order. The exam often gives budget and revenue and asks for the rate or the bill.

story.title: Same Block, Different Bill
story.setting: A coffee shop on Mamaroneck Avenue, Westchester, a Thursday afternoon

beats.text: Same block, same size, same school district. $14,000 versus $21,000. Explain.
The tax is assessed value times the rate. The rate's the same on the block. So the assessments are different.
Why would they be different?
Maybe one owner is a senior with an exemption. Maybe one added a wing in 2015 with a permit and the other finished the basement without one. Maybe the town hasn't reassessed in thirty years.
So if I buy the cheap one, they'll reassess me to my price the day I close.
Not legally. Reassessing only the house that sold is called welcome stranger. It's illegal. A townwide revaluation is fine.

check.q: Which change to Leo's assessment after closing would be legal?
c: Raising only his house to the sale price
Adding the value of an unpermitted bathroom the assessor discovers
Raising every house that sold this year but no others
Raising it because he is a new resident
check.x: Discovering an undeclared improvement is a legal basis to change an assessment. Targeting sold properties is selective reassessment.

beats.text: But if that cheap one has an unpermitted bathroom and the town finds it, they can add it to the roll, maybe with back taxes.
Which is why I check permits and the CO before you sign. And the senior exemption on the cheaper one? It leaves with the seller.
And the state takes how much of this?
None. No state property tax in New York. County, town, village, school district, fire and sewer districts. School is the big one.
My spreadsheet assumed $14,000. I'm changing it to the real number for my situation.
Good. Never quote the seller's bill as the buyer's bill. Look at the exemptions, the assessment, and the rate, then do the math.

board.prompt: Draw a flow from a village budget to one homeowner's tax bill: budget, other revenue, levy, total assessed value, rate, the house's assessed value, the bill.

facts.text: Property taxes pay for local services, with the school tax usually the largest piece, and land is a favored tax base because it is predictable, hard to hide and historically tied to wealth.
The property tax is ad valorem (according to value), and exempt property such as government buildings and houses of worship shifts the burden onto everyone else.
New York State levies no real property tax; bills come from the county, city, town, village, school district and special districts.
Assessed value equals market value times the assessment ratio, and full value equals assessed value divided by the ratio.
The tax bill is the assessed value times the rate, so at a rate per $1,000 you multiply the assessed value in thousands by the rate.
Each assessing unit (usually the city or town; Nassau County; the NYC Department of Finance) picks its own uniform percentage, and the law requires equity within a class.
Similar houses can pay very different taxes because of stale assessments, undeclared improvements, exemptions or district lines, and a community-wide revaluation is the fix.

Raising only a sold home's assessment to its sale price (welcome stranger) is illegal selective reassessment; a community-wide revaluation, discovered improvements, permits or a lost exemption can lawfully change it.
Building permits feed the assessor, and an undeclared improvement can be added to the roll with omitted taxes billed back for prior years within legal limits.
An appropriation is the legal authorization to spend money for a purpose in the budget.
The tax levy is the budget minus non-property revenue such as state aid, sales tax and fees.
The tax rate is the levy divided by total taxable assessed value, expressed in mills, dollars per $100 or dollars per $1,000.
A reassessment redistributes the levy rather than raising it: if assessments rise and the budget stays flat, the rate falls.
NY's property tax cap generally limits annual levy growth to 2% or the rate of inflation, whichever is less, unless overridden.
Village residents pay both town and village tax, school district lines ignore town lines, and only parcels inside a special district pay its tax.
The state equalization rate converts each town's assessed value to full value so county and school levies spanning several towns are apportioned fairly.
Estimated full value is assessed value divided by the equalization rate, and a lower true value is evidence of over-assessment.
Under RPTL Article 19, an approved assessing unit may adopt the homestead option: separate rates for homestead (1 to 3 family homes) and non-homestead parcels.
A special assessment charges only the parcels a specific improvement benefits, based on benefit such as front footage, so it is not ad valorem.
A special assessment district is the area that pays for one service, such as a sewer, water, fire or lighting district or an NYC Business Improvement District.
Special assessments, like general taxes, are priority liens that survive a sale and come ahead of the mortgage.
NYC has four tax classes: Class 1 (1 to 3 family homes), Class 2 (other residential), Class 3 (utilities), Class 4 (commercial and industrial).
NYC Class 1 is assessed at 6% of market value with increases capped at 6% a year and 20% over 5 years, other classes at 45%, and a buyer generally inherits a capped assessment.

lessons.title: Exemptions, Grievances, and Tax Liens
lessons.tagline: Lower the bill with an exemption, fight it with a grievance, and never let it go unpaid, because the tax lien beats the bank.
objectives: Apply veterans, senior citizen, and STAR exemptions and know they do not transfer to a buyer
Walk through the protest ladder: assessor, Board of Assessment Review, SCAR, and certiorari
Explain grievance grounds and the possible decisions
Describe tax liens, tax lien sales, and in rem foreclosure, including the surplus rule
List an agent's duties when advising on property taxes

blocks.title: The Okafors' tax bill
blocks.html: Grace Okafor is 67. Emmanuel served in the Army during the Gulf War. Their Bed-Stuy brownstone tax bill has gone up every year, and a neighbor told them their "assessment is way off." Meanwhile Sal is three years behind on taxes on a vacant lot in the Bronx and says, "What are they going to do, take it?" Jordan has answers for both households.
blocks.casual: Grace Okafor is 67. Emmanuel served in the Army during the Gulf War. Their Bed-Stuy brownstone's tax bill climbs every year, and a neighbor says their "assessment is way off." Meanwhile Sal is three years behind on taxes on a vacant Bronx lot and shrugs, "What're they gonna do, take it?" Jordan has answers for both of them.

deeper.plain: The Okafors may qualify for exemptions and a lower assessment. Sal is wrong: unpaid taxes can cost him the lot.
deeper.picture: One household is leaving coupons in the drawer; the other is ignoring a pile of final notices.
deeper.street: Grace (65+) may get a senior exemption if income qualifies, Emmanuel a veterans exemption, and both can appeal to the NYC Tax Commission. Sal's lot carries a tax lien that comes ahead of everyone, and the city can sell the lien or move toward foreclosure.
deeper.stakes: Owners who don't apply overpay for years. Owners who ignore taxes can lose the property itself.
deeper.exam: Exemptions are tied to the owner. Tax liens have top priority and can end in a tax sale or in rem foreclosure.

blocks.html: A tax exemption removes part or all of a property's assessed value from taxation. Exemptions attach to the owner's eligibility, so they do not pass to a buyer. Exempt value raises the rate for everyone else.
blocks.casual: A tax exemption takes some or all of a property's assessed value off the tax rolls. Exemptions are tied to the owner's eligibility, so they don't pass to a buyer. And exempt value pushes the rate up for everyone else.

deeper.plain: Exemptions lower a qualifying owner's taxable value, and they end when that owner sells.
deeper.picture: A senior discount at the movies. It's for the person, not the seat. Someone else in that seat pays full price.
deeper.street: A Bay Ridge widow gets a senior exemption cutting her assessment in half. She sells to a 35-year-old couple. Next roll, the exemption's gone and the couple's bill roughly doubles.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who budget off the seller's bill can be thousands short every year.
deeper.exam: Exemptions do not run with the land. They depend on the owner.

head: Exemption
Who qualifies
How it works
rows: Entire parcel off the taxable roll (when used for the exempt purpose)
Veterans who served in wartime or the Cold War, and some surviving spouses; the home must be their primary residence

Most localities use the alternative veterans exemption: a percentage off assessed value (15% for wartime service, another 10% for combat zone service, more for service-connected disability), up to local caps
Owners 65 or older, primary residence, income under a limit set locally within a state maximum
Up to 50% off assessed value, sliding down as income rises; local option
Reduces school taxes only. New applicants get a check (the STAR credit) from the state
Owners 65+ with income at or below $110,750 (2026-27)
Clergy, disabled persons with limited income, agricultural land, some new construction (NYC 485-x, 421-a legacy), businesses

deeper.plain: Different owners qualify for different breaks: nonprofits, veterans, seniors, and homeowners for school taxes through STAR.
deeper.picture: A menu of discounts at a store. Show the right ID and you get the matching one.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Rochester veteran's home assessed at $120,000 gets 15% off for wartime service ($18,000) and 10% more for combat zone service ($12,000), so county and town taxes run on $90,000, subject to local caps.
deeper.stakes: Agents who don't mention exemptions leave clients overpaying. Buyers need to know which ones will vanish.
deeper.exam: Basic STAR credit income limit $500,000. Enhanced STAR: 65+ with income at or below $110,750 for 2026-27. Senior exemption up to 50%, local option.

blocks.title: STAR changed in 2016
blocks.html: The old STAR exemption (a reduction on the tax bill) is closed to new applicants. Owners who have had it continuously may keep it for the same home if income is $250,000 or less. New homeowners register with the NYS Department of Taxation and Finance for the STAR credit, a check mailed before the school tax bill.
blocks.casual: The old STAR exemption (a reduction right on the tax bill) is closed to new applicants. Owners who've had it continuously can keep it for the same home if income is $250,000 or less. New homeowners register with the NYS Department of Taxation and Finance for the STAR credit, a check that arrives before the school tax bill.

deeper.plain: New buyers get STAR as a check from the state, not as a cut on their bill.
deeper.picture: A coupon taken off at the register versus a rebate check in the mail. Same savings, different delivery.
deeper.street: Leo closes on his Mamaroneck house in 2026. The seller had the old STAR exemption. Leo can't get that; he registers with Tax and Finance and gets a STAR credit check before his school bill.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't register miss the benefit entirely. The seller's exemption on the old bill won't carry over.
deeper.exam: Since 2016, new applicants get the credit. Existing exemption holders keep it at income of $250,000 or less.

blocks.title: An exemption on the bill
blocks.html:
Emmanuel's house is assessed at $100,000. His veterans exemption removes 15% from the county, town, and city portions: $15,000.
Taxable for those portions: $100,000 - $15,000 = $85,000
At $30 per $1,000: 85 x $30 = $2,550 instead of $3,000
(Veterans exemptions generally do not apply to school taxes unless the school district opts in.)
blocks.casual:
Emmanuel's house is assessed at $100,000. His veterans exemption takes 15% off the county, town, and city portions: $15,000.
Taxable for those portions: $100,000 minus $15,000 = $85,000
At $30 per $1,000: 85 x $30 = $2,550 instead of $3,000
(Veterans exemptions usually don't apply to school taxes unless the school district opts in.)

deeper.plain: Take the exemption off the assessed value, then apply the rate to what's left.
deeper.picture: A coupon taken off the price before sales tax, so you also save on the tax.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Syracuse house assessed at $140,000, veterans exemption 25% ($35,000). Taxable: $105,000. At $28 per $1,000: 105 x $28 = $2,940 instead of $3,920. Savings: $980.
deeper.stakes: Apply the exemption to school taxes when the district didn't opt in and you overstate the client's savings.
deeper.exam: Exemption reduces assessed value, not the rate. Then multiply by the rate.

blocks.title: Exemptions do not run with the land
blocks.html: A buyer who budgets using the seller's tax bill may be shocked when the senior, veterans, or STAR exemption disappears at the next roll. Always ask whether the current bill reflects exemptions, and estimate the buyer's bill without them.
blocks.casual: A buyer who budgets off the seller's tax bill can get blindsided when the senior, veterans, or STAR exemption disappears on the next roll. Always ask whether the current bill reflects exemptions, and estimate the buyer's bill without them.

deeper.plain: The seller's bill may be artificially low. Figure what the buyer will actually pay.
deeper.picture: Your friend's phone bill looks cheap because of a student discount you don't have.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Queens house shows a $5,200 bill with an Enhanced STAR and a senior exemption. Without them, Jordan estimates about $7,800. That's $217 more a month in escrow for the buyer.
deeper.stakes: Underestimate taxes and the buyer's qualifying ratio is wrong, which can derail the mortgage.
deeper.exam: Exemptions do not transfer with the sale. The trap answer says the buyer inherits them.

blocks.q: A buyer purchases a house whose seller received a senior citizens exemption. After the sale, the exemption:
c: Continues for the buyer for 5 years
Transfers if the buyer is a first-time buyer
Ends, because it was based on the seller's eligibility
Converts to a STAR exemption
blocks.x: Exemptions belong to the eligible owner. A new owner must qualify and apply on their own.

blocks.title: From informal to court

items.title: 1. Talk to the assessor
items.html: Fix factual errors informally: wrong square footage, a bathroom you do not have, a garage that was torn down. Do this when the tentative roll is published.

items.title: 2. File a grievance with the Board of Assessment Review
items.html: Outside NYC, file a written complaint (form RP-524) by Grievance Day, usually the fourth Tuesday in May in most towns (dates vary in cities, Nassau, and some counties). The Board of Assessment Review (BAR) is an independent local board, not the assessor.

items.title: 3. SCAR or certiorari
items.html: Unhappy with the BAR? Homeowners of owner-occupied 1 to 3 family residences may choose Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR). Everyone else, including commercial owners, files a tax certiorari proceeding in State Supreme Court under RPTL Article 7.

blocks.casual:
1. Talk to the assessor: fix factual errors informally, like wrong square footage, a bathroom you don't have, or a garage that's been torn down. Do it when the tentative roll comes out.
2. File a grievance with the Board of Assessment Review: outside NYC, file a written complaint (form RP-524) by Grievance Day, usually the fourth Tuesday in May in most towns (dates vary in cities, Nassau, and some counties). The Board of Assessment Review (BAR) is an independent local board, not the assessor.
3. SCAR or certiorari: not happy with the BAR? Owners of owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes can choose Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR). Everyone else, commercial owners included, files a tax certiorari proceeding in State Supreme Court under RPTL Article 7.

deeper.plain: Start informal with the assessor, then the local board, then small claims or court.
deeper.picture: A complaint at a store: ask the clerk, then the manager, then small claims court.
deeper.street: A Massapequa owner notices the assessor lists four bedrooms; he has three. He calls in March and it's fixed. A neighbor who thinks her value is too high files an RP-524 by the deadline and then goes to SCAR when the board says no.
deeper.stakes: Miss Grievance Day and you generally wait a year. You also typically need the grievance on file to go further.
deeper.exam: Order: assessor, BAR (Grievance Day, RP-524), then SCAR (small residential) or certiorari (RPTL Article 7).

head: Grievance ground
Meaning
Evidence
rows: Assessed at a higher percentage of value than other properties
Assessment ratios: your AV / market value vs the town's equalization rate or ratios of neighbors
Assessed value is more than full market value, or the implied market value is too high
Exempt property taxed, property outside the district, procedural defect
Wrong class (for example, homestead vs non-homestead)

deeper.plain: You can grieve because you're assessed unfairly compared to others, too high for your value, illegally, or in the wrong class.
deeper.picture: Four reasons to dispute a bill: you paid more than others, it's more than the item's worth, you shouldn't be billed at all, or it's the wrong item.
deeper.street: New numbers: a Hempstead house with AV $8,000 and market value $500,000 has a ratio of 1.6%. The town's rate is 1%. That's unequal assessment, implying $800,000 of value.
deeper.stakes: Picking the wrong ground or skipping evidence makes the board deny the complaint.
deeper.exam: Unequal = higher percentage than others. Excessive = over full value. Unlawful = shouldn't be taxed. Misclassification = wrong class.

blocks.html: Possible BAR decisions: full denial (assessment stays), full reduction as requested in the application, or a partial reduction. The board cannot raise the assessment of the person who complained.
blocks.casual: What the BAR can decide: deny it completely (assessment stays), grant the full reduction you asked for, or give you a partial reduction. The board can't raise the assessment of the person who complained.

deeper.plain: Filing a grievance can't backfire with a higher assessment.
deeper.picture: Asking for a refund: the worst they can say is no. They won't charge you extra for asking.
deeper.street: The Okafors' Westchester cousins ask for a $20,000 cut. The board gives $10,000. Not everything, but better than nothing, and it couldn't have gone up.
deeper.stakes: Owners who fear a grievance will raise their taxes leave money on the table. You can reassure them.
deeper.exam: Three outcomes: deny, full, partial. The BAR cannot increase the complainant's assessment.

blocks.title: Is the Okafors' house over-assessed?
blocks.html:
Outside NYC version: assessed value $180,000. The town's equalization rate is 40%.
Implied full value: $180,000 / 0.40 = $450,000
Three recent sales of comparable homes support a market value of $400,000.
Fair assessment at 40%: $400,000 x 0.40 = $160,000. They grieve for a $20,000 reduction, with the comps as evidence.
blocks.casual:
Outside-NYC version: assessed value $180,000. The town's equalization rate is 40%.
Implied full value: $180,000 / 0.40 = $450,000
Three recent comparable sales support a market value of $400,000.
Fair assessment at 40%: $400,000 x 0.40 = $160,000. They grieve for a $20,000 reduction, with the comps as evidence.

deeper.plain: Convert the assessment to market value, compare to real comps, and ask for the difference.
deeper.picture: The scale says 180 pounds, but three other scales say 160. Bring the other scales as evidence.
deeper.street: New numbers: an Albany County house assessed at $210,000 with a 70% equalization rate. Implied value: $300,000. Comps say $260,000. Fair assessment: $260,000 x 0.70 = $182,000, a $28,000 reduction to ask for.
deeper.stakes: Without comps, the board has no reason to cut anything.
deeper.exam: Assessed / equalization rate = implied value. Market value x rate = fair assessment.

items: Residential only: owner-occupied one, two, or three family homes used exclusively as residences (some condos qualify in limited cases).
Prerequisite: you must first have filed a grievance with the BAR (in NYC, an application with the Tax Commission).
Filing: petition filed with the county clerk generally within 30 days after the final assessment roll is filed, with a $30 fee. NYC sets its own deadline.
Hearing: an informal hearing before a hearing officer, often an attorney or appraiser. No lawyer needed.
Evidence: sales information (comps), assessment information (the property record card, neighbors' assessments), and assessment ratios (equalization rate, residential assessment ratio).
Decisions: same as the BAR: deny, grant in full, or grant in part.
Appeal: the homeowner gives up the right to certiorari by choosing SCAR. The SCAR decision can be challenged only by an Article 78 proceeding.
blocks.casual:
Residential only: owner-occupied one, two, or three family homes used only as residences (some condos qualify in limited cases).
Prerequisite: you must have filed a grievance with the BAR first (in NYC, an application with the Tax Commission).
Filing: petition with the county clerk, generally within 30 days after the final roll is filed, with a $30 fee. NYC sets its own deadline.
Hearing: informal, before a hearing officer who's often an attorney or appraiser. No lawyer needed.
Evidence: sales info (comps), assessment info (property record card, neighbors' assessments), and assessment ratios (equalization rate, residential assessment ratio).
Decisions: same as the BAR: deny, grant in full, or grant in part.
Appeal: by choosing SCAR the homeowner gives up certiorari. A SCAR decision can only be challenged through an Article 78 proceeding.

deeper.plain: SCAR is cheap, informal small claims for homeowners who already lost at the local board.
deeper.picture: People's Court for your tax assessment. Bring receipts, skip the lawyer.
deeper.street: A Yonkers two-family owner loses at the BAR. The final roll is filed July 1, so she files a SCAR petition with the county clerk by July 31, pays $30, and brings four comps to the hearing.
deeper.stakes: Miss the 30-day window and the option is gone for that year. Pick SCAR and you give up certiorari.
deeper.exam: Owner-occupied 1 to 3 family. File with county clerk, 30 days after final roll, $30. Must grieve first. Appeal by Article 78.

blocks.title: NYC does it differently
blocks.html: There is no Grievance Day in NYC. The Department of Finance publishes tentative values in January, and owners appeal to the NYC Tax Commission, generally by March 1 (March 15 for Class 1). Class 1 homeowners can then use SCAR; others go to Supreme Court by certiorari.
blocks.casual: NYC has no Grievance Day. The Department of Finance posts tentative values in January, and owners appeal to the NYC Tax Commission, generally by March 1 (March 15 for Class 1). Class 1 homeowners can then use SCAR. Everyone else goes to Supreme Court by certiorari.

deeper.plain: In NYC you appeal to the Tax Commission in early spring, not to a town board in May.
deeper.picture: Same game, different stadium and different season.
deeper.street: The Okafors see their tentative value in January and file with the Tax Commission before March 15 because their brownstone is Class 1. Sal's Class 2 building had to file by March 1.
deeper.stakes: Agents who give NYC clients the upstate May deadline cost them a whole year.
deeper.exam: NYC: Department of Finance assesses, Tax Commission hears appeals. March 1, or March 15 for Class 1.

blocks.q: The owner of a 12-store strip center in Suffolk lost at the Board of Assessment Review. The next step to challenge the assessment is:
c: SCAR
A tax certiorari proceeding
A second grievance in June
An appeal to the Department of State
blocks.x: SCAR is limited to owner-occupied 1 to 3 family residential property. Commercial owners use a tax certiorari proceeding in State Supreme Court.

blocks.text: Tax liens, tax sales, and in rem foreclosure

blocks.html: Unpaid real property taxes become a tax lien with priority over every other lien, including a mortgage recorded years earlier. That is why lenders escrow taxes and why title companies insist taxes are current at closing.
blocks.casual: Unpaid real property taxes turn into a tax lien that gets priority over every other lien, even a mortgage recorded years earlier. That's why lenders escrow taxes and why title companies insist taxes be current at closing.

deeper.plain: Taxes get paid before the bank, no matter who came first.
deeper.picture: The government always gets the front of the line, even if the bank was waiting since dawn.
deeper.street: Sal owes $24,000 in back taxes on his Bronx lot, which also has a $150,000 mortgage from 2015. If the lot is sold, the tax lien is paid first.
deeper.stakes: That's why the bank requires escrow. An unpaid tax bill threatens the lender's collateral.
deeper.exam: Property tax liens have priority over all other liens, regardless of recording date.

blocks.caption: Run a sale and watch property taxes and special assessments get paid first, before the first mortgage.

left.title: Tax lien sale
items: The municipality sells the lien (the right to collect the debt plus interest), not the property
Owner still owns the property and must pay the lienholder
If unpaid, the lienholder can foreclose
NYC has used periodic lien sales

right.title: In rem tax foreclosure
items: The county or city forecloses against the property itself ("in rem" = against the thing)
After a redemption period (often 2 years from the lien date), unredeemed parcels pass to the municipality
The municipality then usually sells them at a tax sale (public auction)
RPTL Article 11 governs most of the state

deeper.plain: The government can either sell the debt to an investor or take the property itself.
deeper.picture: A store can sell your overdue bill to a collection agency or repossess the couch.
deeper.street: If NYC sells Sal's lien, an investor collects the debt plus interest and can foreclose if he doesn't pay. In a county using in rem, after a redemption period the county takes title to the lot and auctions it.
deeper.stakes: Owners who ignore either path can lose the property. Buyers at tax sales need careful title work.
deeper.exam: Lien sale = sells the debt. In rem = action against the property itself. RPTL Article 11.

blocks.html: In rem foreclosure used to let counties keep the whole sale price even when it far exceeded the taxes owed. In Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), the U.S. Supreme Court held that keeping the surplus equity is an unconstitutional taking. New York amended RPTL Article 11 in 2024, retroactive to May 25, 2023, to create a process for former owners to claim surplus proceeds.
blocks.casual: In rem foreclosure used to let counties keep the whole sale price, even when it was way more than the taxes owed. In Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), the U.S. Supreme Court said keeping that surplus equity is an unconstitutional taking. New York amended RPTL Article 11 in 2024, retroactive to May 25, 2023, to set up a way for former owners to claim surplus proceeds.

deeper.plain: The government can take what's owed in taxes, but not keep the extra equity.
deeper.picture: If you owe a friend $20 and they sell your bike for $300, they don't get to keep the other $280.
deeper.street: New numbers: a county forecloses on an Orange County house for $18,000 in back taxes and sells it for $260,000. After costs, the former owner can claim most of the remaining surplus under the 2024 law.
deeper.stakes: Families who lost homes for small tax debts can now recover their equity. Agents may meet former owners who need to know this.
deeper.exam: Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023): keeping surplus is a taking. NY fixed RPTL Article 11 in 2024.

blocks.q: Sal ignores three years of taxes on his Bronx lot. Which statement is accurate?
c: The mortgage on the lot will be paid before the tax lien
Nothing can happen until he sells
The tax lien has priority over other liens, and the property can be lost through a lien sale foreclosure or in rem foreclosure
The state will add the taxes to his income tax
blocks.x: Real property tax liens come first in priority. Unpaid, they can lead to a lien sale and foreclosure or an in rem proceeding against the property.

items: Calculate taxes for buyers: assessed value x rate, using the current roll, and estimate without the seller's exemptions.
Verify on the town or county website or NYC Department of Finance; do not copy the seller's number into the listing without checking.
Disclose what you know: a pending revaluation, special assessments for a new sewer, a co-op's or condo's tax abatements that will phase out.
Explain escrow: the lender usually collects taxes monthly with the mortgage.
Refer grievance and certiorari strategy to the owner, an attorney, or a tax consultant; you can supply comps.
blocks.casual:
Run the taxes for buyers: assessed value x rate, from the current roll, and estimate it without the seller's exemptions.
Verify on the town or county website or NYC Department of Finance. Don't just copy the seller's number into the listing.
Disclose what you know: a pending revaluation, special assessments for a new sewer, a co-op's or condo's tax abatement that's phasing out.
Explain escrow: the lender usually collects taxes monthly with the mortgage.
Refer grievance and certiorari strategy to the owner, an attorney, or a tax consultant. You can supply comps.

deeper.plain: Get the tax numbers right, share what you know, and leave legal strategy to the pros.
deeper.picture: You're the tour guide, not the lawyer. Point out the potholes, don't litigate them.
