deeper.street: A Long Island City condo listing shows $1,200 a year in taxes thanks to a 421-a abatement ending in two years. Jordan tells the buyer the bill could jump to about $9,000 once it phases out.
deeper.stakes: Hiding or guessing at taxes can be misrepresentation. Buyers who get surprised file complaints.
deeper.exam: Agents verify and disclose known tax facts. Abatements and exemptions can end.

blocks.title: The protest ladder
blocks.html: A-B-S-C: Assessor (facts), Board of Assessment Review (Grievance Day), SCAR (small homes), Certiorari (everyone else).
blocks.casual: A-B-S-C: Assessor (facts), Board of Assessment Review (Grievance Day), SCAR (small homes), Certiorari (everyone else).

deeper.plain: Climb the appeal ladder one rung at a time.
deeper.picture: ABC with an S tucked in, like a sneeze between B and C.
deeper.street: A Bronx-born investor with a Westchester office building skips SCAR because it's commercial: assessor, BAR, then certiorari in Supreme Court.
deeper.stakes: Picking the wrong rung wastes a year and filing fees.
deeper.exam: SCAR only for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family. Everyone else uses certiorari.

story.title: Grievance Day
story.setting: Hudson & Hart's conference room, Brooklyn, a Tuesday in April

beats.text: Grace: "I turned 65 this year. Emmanuel served in the Gulf War. Does any of that help our taxes?"

Both might. The senior exemption depends on your income. The veterans exemption is a percentage off the assessed value for city taxes. And Enhanced STAR for the school portion if income is under the limit.
Emmanuel: "And when we sell? The buyer keeps them?"
No. They're yours, not the house's. The buyer starts fresh.
Grace: "Our neighbor says our assessment is wrong. Who do we complain to?"

In the city it's the Tax Commission, by March 15 for Class 1. Upstate or on Long Island, it'd be the Board of Assessment Review on Grievance Day. If that fails, you're a two-family owner-occupant, so SCAR: thirty dollars and an informal hearing.

check.q: Who may use SCAR?
c: Any property owner
Owners of owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes who first filed a grievance
Only commercial owners
Only seniors
check.x: SCAR is for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family residential property, and a grievance must be filed first.

beats.text: That afternoon, Sal drops by with a stack of envelopes.
Three years of tax bills on the Bronx lot. What are they gonna do, take it?
Yes. The tax lien beats your mortgage, beats everyone. The city can sell the lien, and the buyer of that lien can foreclose. Upstate, counties foreclose in rem against the property itself.
And they keep the whole lot even if it's worth way more than I owe?
Not anymore. After Tyler v. Hennepin, New York changed the law so former owners can claim the surplus. But pay the taxes, Sal. That's the cheaper plan.
beats.tag: Surplus goes back to the owner

beats.text: Exemptions lower the bill, grievances fix the assessment, and paying on time keeps the lien off your back. That's the whole subject in one sentence.

board.prompt: Draw the protest ladder from the assessor to certiorari. On each rung, write who hears it, who can use it, and one deadline.

facts.text: A tax exemption removes part or all of a property's assessed value from taxation, and exempt value raises the rate for everyone else.
Exemptions attach to the owner's eligibility and do not pass to a buyer, so estimate the buyer's bill without the seller's exemptions.
Property of government, religious, charitable and educational nonprofits is fully exempt when used for the exempt purpose.

The alternative veterans exemption takes 15% off assessed value for wartime service and another 10% for combat zone service, more for disability, on a primary residence, and generally not off school taxes.
With an exemption, the tax is figured on assessed value minus the exempt amount, times the rate.
The senior citizens exemption gives owners 65 or older, on a primary residence and under a local income limit, up to 50% off assessed value, sliding down as income rises.
Basic STAR reduces school taxes only and is open to owner-occupants with income up to $500,000 (for the credit).
Enhanced STAR is for owners 65 or older with income at or below $110,750 (2026-27) and gives a larger school tax benefit.
Since 2016 new homeowners get the STAR credit, a state check, instead of the old exemption, which continuous holders may keep for the same home if income is $250,000 or less.
Other exemptions cover clergy, disabled owners with limited income, agricultural land and some new construction (NYC 485-x, legacy 421-a).
The first step in a protest is talking to the assessor informally to fix factual errors when the tentative roll is published.
Outside NYC, a grievance goes on form RP-524 to the Board of Assessment Review, an independent board, by Grievance Day, usually the fourth Tuesday in May.
The grievance grounds are unequal assessment, excessive assessment, unlawful assessment and misclassification.
A Board of Assessment Review (and SCAR) may deny, grant in full or grant in part, but cannot raise the complainant's assessment.
A fair assessment is market value times the town's equalization rate; the gap from the current assessment is the reduction to request.
SCAR is only for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes used as residences, and the owner must first have filed a grievance.
A SCAR petition is filed with the county clerk generally within 30 days after the final roll, with a $30 fee, and heard informally by a hearing officer.
Choosing SCAR gives up the right to certiorari, and a SCAR decision can be challenged only by an Article 78 proceeding.
Owners who cannot use SCAR, including commercial owners, challenge a BAR decision by tax certiorari in State Supreme Court under RPTL Article 7.
NYC has no Grievance Day: owners appeal to the NYC Tax Commission, generally by March 1 (March 15 for Class 1), after January tentative values.
Unpaid property taxes are a lien with priority over every other lien, even a mortgage recorded years earlier.
In a tax lien sale the municipality sells the lien (the right to collect the tax plus interest), not the property.
In rem tax foreclosure is against the property itself; after a redemption period (often 2 years) unredeemed parcels pass to the municipality under RPTL Article 11.
After Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), keeping surplus equity is a taking, and NY's 2024 Article 11 amendments let former owners claim surplus proceeds.
Agents verify taxes on the current roll, estimate the buyer's bill without the seller's exemptions, disclose known revaluations or special assessments, and refer grievance strategy.

lessons.title: Case file: The Split-Level on Grievance Day
lessons.tagline: The Delgados paid $455,000. The town's roll says their house is worth $510,000. They have one Tuesday in May to fix it.
objectives: Calculate a tax bill from assessed value and multiple jurisdictions' rates, and convert an assessment to full value with an equalization rate.
Decide whether a fractional assessment is unequal or excessive and calculate the assessment to request on a grievance.
Apply the Board of Assessment Review and SCAR procedures, deadlines, and evidence rules to a homeowner's protest.
Explain how a revaluation and a fixed levy change tax rates without necessarily changing a homeowner's bill.

blocks.title: A split-level in Dutchess County, late March
blocks.html: Rosa and Ken Delgado are leaving a two-bedroom rental in Jackson Heights for a 1970s split-level in a Dutchess County town about ten minutes from the Metro-North station. Jordan met them through a referral, and since a New York salesperson's license is good statewide, Hudson & Hart is representing them as buyers alongside a local cooperating broker. The contract price is $455,000; the house needs a new septic field and a kitchen, and the price reflects it. The listing sheet says "Taxes: $11,980." Ken has built the family budget around that number. Rosa, who does payroll for a living, has a question: "Is that number the real number? The house across the street sold for more and I heard their taxes are lower." Jordan opens the listing sheet and the town's online assessment roll side by side.

The online roll shows the parcel: assessed value $255,000, residential, one-family, with a Basic STAR exemption still in the seller's name. The town's equalization rate, published by the state, is 50.00%. The town has not done a full revaluation in more than twenty years, so every parcel is supposed to be assessed at about half of market value. That is the town's choice as the assessing unit; New York lets each assessing unit pick a uniform percentage.

blocks.q: Ken wants to put the listing sheet's $11,980 straight into his budget spreadsheet. What should Jordan do with that figure?
c: Use it, because the seller's broker is responsible for the accuracy of the tax figure on the listing sheet
Recalculate from the current roll and current rates, without the seller's exemptions
Use it, but add 2% for next year because the state tax cap limits growth in every bill to that amount
Ask the seller to sign a statement guaranteeing that the buyers' taxes will not exceed $11,980 next year
blocks.x: A listing sheet number is often last year's bill, net of the seller's exemptions. Calculating taxes is the agent's job: current assessed value times each jurisdiction's current rate, without exemptions that belong to the seller. The 2% option is the trap: the tax cap limits growth in a district's levy, not any one owner's bill, and a bill can rise much faster after a sale strips away an exemption.

blocks.html: Outside New York City a homeowner usually gets two bills. The town and county bill arrives in January and covers the county, the town, and special districts such as fire. The school bill arrives in September. Each line is the parcel's assessed value times that jurisdiction's rate. Jordan pulls the rates from the town's adopted tax roll and the school district's tax warrant.

head: Jurisdiction
Rate per $1,000 of assessed value
On $255,000 assessed
blocks.caption: The Delgados' estimated first full year, using the current roll and adopted rates

blocks.html: So the honest number is $14,535, not $11,980. Part of the gap is the seller's STAR benefit, which does not transfer; the Delgados can apply for their own STAR credit with the state. Most of the gap is that the rates rose since the bill on the listing sheet. Ken is not happy, but he would be far less happy finding out in September. Jordan also notices something more interesting: $14,535 is 3.2% of the price they are paying. The house across the street, a bigger colonial that sold for $520,000, is assessed at $236,000.

Two practical notes go into Jordan's email that night. First, the seller's Basic STAR exemption ends with her ownership. New owners do not get the old exemption; they register with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance for the STAR credit, a check that arrives before the school bill, if their household income is $500,000 or less. Second, the lender will escrow taxes. It will size the monthly escrow from the full bill, not the listing sheet, so the payment on Ken's spreadsheet is about $213 a month too low ($14,535 minus $11,980, divided by 12).

Ken, now suspicious of every number, asks who decided the town rate. Jordan pulls the town's adopted budget. The town board approved appropriations of $5,600,000 for highways, parks, the town court, and administration. It expects $3,550,000 from other sources: its share of county sales tax, state aid, justice court fines, and building permit fees. The rest must come from property.

blocks.q: The town's total taxable assessed value is $500,000,000. Using the budget figures above, what is the town tax rate per $1,000 of assessed value?
blocks.x: Levy = appropriations minus other revenue = $5,600,000 minus $3,550,000 = $2,050,000. Rate = $2,050,000 / $500,000,000 = 0.0041, or $4.10 per $1,000. $11.20 is the trap: it divides the whole budget by the roll, forgetting that non-property revenue reduces what the tax must raise. $2.05 drops a zero from the levy.

blocks.html: The levy, not the rate, is what the state's property tax cap restrains. In general a town's levy may grow by no more than 2% or the rate of inflation, whichever is less, unless the town board overrides the cap by a supermajority vote (school districts need 60% voter approval instead). A rate can jump while the levy stays inside the cap, for example when a large commercial parcel wins a certiorari case and the total assessed value shrinks.

blocks.text: One school district, two towns, two rates

blocks.html: Rosa finds the school district's tax warrant online and is confused. The district covers part of two towns. In the Delgados' town the school rate is $44.00 per $1,000. In the neighboring town it is $27.50. "So people over the line pay a lot less for the same schools?"

blocks.title: How the school levy is split
blocks.html:
The school tax levy is $44,000,000.
Town A (the Delgados' town): total taxable assessed value $500,000,000 at a 50% equalization rate. Full value: $500,000,000 / 0.50 = $1,000,000,000.
Town B: total taxable assessed value $800,000,000 at an 80% equalization rate. Full value: $800,000,000 / 0.80 = $1,000,000,000.
Each town holds half of the district's full value, so each raises half the levy: $22,000,000.
Town A rate: $22,000,000 / $500,000,000 = $44.00 per $1,000 assessed.
Town B rate: $22,000,000 / $800,000,000 = $27.50 per $1,000 assessed.
Per $1,000 of full value, both towns pay the same: $22.00.

blocks.q: A house worth $400,000 sits in Town A, and an identical $400,000 house sits in Town B, both properly assessed at their towns' levels. How do their school taxes compare?
c: They pay the same, since the levy is split by full value
Town B pays less because its nominal school rate per $1,000 is lower
Town A pays less because it assesses at a lower percentage of value
They cannot be compared until both towns adopt the homestead option
blocks.x: Town A: $200,000 assessed x $44.00 per $1,000 = $8,800. Town B: $320,000 assessed x $27.50 per $1,000 = $8,800. Equalization converts each town's roll to full value before the levy is split, so equal values pay equal school tax. The lower-rate answer is the trap: the lower nominal rate is offset by a higher assessment level. Comparing raw rates across towns is meaningless.

blocks.html: Back to the house across the street. The Delgados' parcel is assessed at $255,000 in a town that assesses at 50%. Divide by the equalization rate and the town is saying the house is worth $510,000. The Delgados are paying $455,000 in an arm's-length sale after months on the market, and the broker's comparable sales run from $440,000 to $465,000. The colonial across the street, at $236,000 assessed and $520,000 sold, is assessed at about 45% of its value. The Delgados' house is assessed at 56% of what it is worth.

blocks.title: The assessment calendar in most towns
blocks.html: Values are set as of the valuation date (July 1 of the prior year). The taxable status date is March 1: ownership, physical condition, and exemption applications are fixed as of that day. The tentative roll is filed by May 1. Grievance Day, when the Board of Assessment Review hears complaints, is usually the fourth Tuesday in May. The final roll is filed July 1, and school bills based on it go out in September. Cities, Nassau County, and some towns run different dates, so always confirm locally.
The Delgados close on April 10. The tentative roll comes out May 1 with the house still at $255,000. Ken's instinct is to wait: "Let's see the first bill, then complain."

blocks.q: It is mid-May. The Delgados own the house and will pay the taxes on the new roll. What must they do to challenge the $255,000 assessment this year?
c: Wait for the September school bill and then file a SCAR petition within 30 days of receiving it
File a tax certiorari petition in State Supreme Court, which is the first step for any owner
Ask the seller to file, since the March 1 taxable status date fixed her as the owner of record
File a written complaint with the Board of Assessment Review by Grievance Day in late May
blocks.x: A written grievance (form RP-524) filed with the Board of Assessment Review by Grievance Day is the gateway. Skip it and both SCAR and certiorari are lost for that roll. Waiting for the bill is the trap: SCAR runs 30 days from the filing of the final roll, not from the bill, and it requires a prior grievance. As owners who will pay the taxes, the Delgados are aggrieved parties and may file themselves.

blocks.text: Choosing the ground and the number

blocks.html: The RP-524 asks the complainant to pick a ground and state a value. Jordan's job is not to give legal advice, but agents supply the comparable sales, and a good agent understands the form well enough to give the owners useful data. Two grounds tempt them.

blocks.title: Which ground fits a fractional-assessment town?

left.title: Unequal assessment
items: The parcel is assessed at a higher percentage of value than the town's level
Proof: market value evidence plus the town's level (equalization rate or residential assessment ratio)
Fits here: $255,000 / $455,000 = 56%, while the town level is 50%

right.title: Excessive assessment
items: The assessed value is higher than the parcel's full market value (or an exemption was wrongly reduced)
Proof: an appraisal or sales showing value below the assessed value
Does not fit here: $255,000 assessed is far below the $455,000 market value

blocks.title: Over-assessed is not the same as excessive
blocks.html: In a town assessing at 50%, almost no house is assessed above its market value, so an "excessive" claim usually fails even when the owner is overpaying. The real complaint is inequality: the house carries a higher percentage than its neighbors. Owners who check "excessive" and argue only "my house is worth $455,000, not $255,000" have proved nothing. Exams test this with fractional-assessment facts.

blocks.q: The Delgados want the board to assess them at the same level as the rest of the town. Using their $455,000 market value and the 50% equalization rate, what assessed value should they request?
blocks.x: Fair assessment = market value x the town's level of assessment = $455,000 x 0.50 = $227,500, a $27,500 reduction. $204,750 is the trap: it applies the colonial's 45% ratio, but the target is the town's level, not one underassessed neighbor's. $236,000 simply copies the colonial's assessment. The request ties directly to evidence: the price, the comps, and the published rate.

blocks.html: At the combined $57 rate, a $27,500 reduction saves 27.5 x $57 = $1,567.50 a year, every year, until the next revaluation. The Delgados file the RP-524 with a copy of the contract, the closing statement, three comparable sales, and the equalization rate printout. They also attach a copy of the colonial's roll entry. Neighbors' assessments are public, and comparing them is fair evidence of inequality.

At the hearing, a board member reads the assessor's property record card aloud: 1,480 square feet of living area, unfinished basement. Rosa winces. The seller finished the lower level as a den and a half bath around 2015, without a permit. It is part of why the Delgados liked the house. The record card has never been updated, because no permit was ever closed out to tell the assessor.

blocks.q: After hearing about the unpermitted finished basement, what can happen to the Delgados' assessment?
c: The board can raise their assessment on the spot because the complaint opened the whole valuation for review
Nothing can ever change it, because improvements are fixed as of the date the seller originally built them
The town must void the grievance, since owners of unpermitted space lose the right to grieve that year
The board cannot raise it, though the assessor may add the space to a later roll
blocks.x: A Board of Assessment Review can deny, reduce in full, or reduce in part. It cannot raise the complainant's assessment. But the assessor can pick up the finished space on a later roll once it is discovered, and the law allows omitted taxes for prior years within limits. Raising it on the spot is the trap: owners fear the grievance itself will backfire. It will not, though the discovery may cost them later.

blocks.html: The basement is a lesson in how the building permit process feeds the roll. When an owner pulls a permit and the building inspector signs off, the building department reports the work to the assessor, who updates the record card for the next taxable status date. Work done without a permit stays invisible until someone notices: a sale, a listing photo, a refinance appraisal, or a grievance hearing. The Delgados' attorney had flagged the missing permit during due diligence, and the seller gave a $6,000 credit toward legalizing the space. Legalizing it will close the gap with the building department and, eventually, with the assessor. Jordan makes a note for future listings: if the finished space is in the marketing, ask whether it is on the permit record before the buyer's attorney does.

The board's decision arrives in the mail in early July: a partial reduction to $240,000. The board's note says the market evidence supports a lower value, but the finished lower level, which the comparables did not have, justifies some of the difference. The Delgados are $12,500 short of their request.

blocks.q: The final roll was filed on July 1 showing $240,000. The Delgados still think $227,500 is right. What is their next step and deadline?
c: Re-file a grievance with the same board, which must rehear any complaint where the owner submits new comparables
File a SCAR petition with the county clerk within 30 days after the final roll is filed, with a $30 fee
Bring a tax certiorari case within 30 days, which is the only review available to a one-family homeowner
Request an informal meeting with the assessor, who has authority to overrule the board on the final roll
blocks.x: Owners of owner-occupied one to three family homes may petition for Small Claims Assessment Review: file with the county clerk within 30 days after the final roll is filed, pay the $30 fee, and get a hearing officer. The certiorari answer is the trap: certiorari is available to homeowners too, and it is not the only route; it is simply slower and costlier, while SCAR is built for exactly this house.

blocks.html: The SCAR hearing is in a small room at the county office building. No lawyer is needed. The hearing officer, a retired appraiser, reads the file first. The town sends a staff appraiser from the assessor's office. The officer asks Rosa, "What level of assessment are you asking me to apply, and where does it come from?"

items: Sales information: the Delgados' own purchase and three comparable sales, adjusted for the septic, the kitchen, and the finished lower level.
Assessment information: the property record card, the colonial's assessment, and two other neighbors' assessments with their sale prices.
Assessment ratios: the state's equalization rate for the town and the residential assessment ratio, which measures the level of assessment for residential property specifically.

blocks.q: To prove the town's level of assessment for homes like theirs, which document is the strongest answer to the hearing officer's question?
c: The state's equalization rate and residential assessment ratio
The Delgados' January tax bill showing the county, town, and fire district rates
The mortgage lender's appraisal, which values the house as of the closing date
A letter from the listing broker stating the house is assessed above its neighbors
blocks.x: The level of assessment comes from state-published ratios: the equalization rate and, for homes, the residential assessment ratio. The appraisal is the trap: it is excellent evidence of market value, the other half of the formula, but it says nothing about the percentage the town applies. A tax bill shows rates, not assessment levels, and a broker's letter is opinion.

blocks.html: The officer finds a market value of $460,000, giving some credit for the finished lower level, and applies the 50% level: $230,000. The town's appraiser does not object. The decision goes to the assessor, who corrects the roll; any tax the Delgados overpay before the correction reaches the bills is refunded. Savings: $25,000 less assessed value x $57 per $1,000 = $1,425 a year.

blocks.q: Two weeks later, the owner of the deli and laundromat building at the end of the Delgados' street asks Rosa how to "do the SCAR thing" after losing at the board. What is accurate?
c: He may use SCAR if he files within 30 days of the board's written decision and pays the standard fee
He may use SCAR only for the residential apartments in the building and not for the retail space
He cannot challenge further, because commercial owners are limited to the Board of Assessment Review
He cannot use SCAR, which covers owner-occupied one to three family homes; he can bring tax certiorari
blocks.x: SCAR is residential only: owner-occupied one, two, or three family homes used exclusively as residences. A mixed-use commercial building goes to tax certiorari in State Supreme Court under RPTL Article 7. Splitting off the apartments is the trap: SCAR does not split a building into qualifying and non-qualifying parts. Saying he cannot go further is wrong because certiorari is open to every owner who first grieved.

blocks.html: The Delgados also learn the price of choosing SCAR: by filing the petition, they gave up the right to bring certiorari on that roll. If they thought the hearing officer had made a legal error, their only route would be an Article 78 proceeding. For a $1,425 a year dispute, that trade is worth it. For a $9 million office building, it would not be, which is why SCAR is not offered there.

Rosa is now annoyed on principle. The colonial across the street sold for $520,000 and is still assessed at $236,000, about 45% of value, while the Delgados fought for every dollar. She emails the assessor: "You have the sale price. Why not just raise that house to match it?"

blocks.q: How should the assessor respond to Rosa's suggestion about the colonial?
c: Raise only the colonial to 50% of its sale price, since a recorded sale is the best evidence of value
Raise only the colonial, but phase the increase in over five years to soften the jump for the new owners
Decline to single it out; sales can support a town-wide revaluation that brings every parcel to one level
Decline, because a sale price can never be used as evidence of value for assessment purposes in New York
blocks.x: Raising only the parcels that sell, to match their prices, is selective reassessment ("welcome stranger"), which violates equal protection and New York assessment law. Sales are proper evidence when the assessor revalues everyone. The first answer is the trap: it sounds like fairness to the Delgados, but it punishes buyers while unsold neighbors keep stale values. The never-use-sales answer overstates the rule.

blocks.html: In the fall, the town announces a full revaluation. Every parcel will be reassessed at 100% of market value on next year's roll. Ken sees a neighbor's post: "Assessments are DOUBLING." He calls Jordan, sure that his $14,000 bill is about to become $28,000.

blocks.q: The Delgados' house is worth about the same as last year, and the town's values moved in line with it. If the town-wide assessed value doubles and the levies stay about the same, what happens to their bill?
c: It stays about the same, because the rate falls
It roughly doubles, because the bill is assessed value times the old rate
It falls by half, because the equalization rate moves from 50% to 100%
It rises by exactly the tax cap, because a revaluation counts as levy growth
blocks.x: Rates are calculated after assessments: levy divided by total taxable assessed value. Double the roll with the same levy and the rate halves, so a house that moved with the town pays roughly the same. The doubling answer is the trap: it applies the old rate to the new assessment. A revaluation redistributes the levy among parcels; owners whose values were stale, like the colonial across the street, are the ones who pay more.

blocks.html: The new roll arrives with the Delgados at $460,000, matching the SCAR value. The rates on next year's bills are stated in mills. One mill is $1 per $1,000.

blocks.title: Year two, after revaluation
blocks.html:
Assessed value: $460,000 (100% level).
School rate: 22.40 mills. County, town, and fire combined: 6.60 mills. Total: 29.00 mills = $29.00 per $1,000.
Tax: 460 x $29.00 = $13,340.
Compare year one after SCAR: $230,000 x $57.00 per $1,000 = $13,110. The small rise comes from levy growth, not the revaluation.

blocks.q: Using the year two figures, the colonial across the street (sold for $520,000 and now assessed at $520,000) pays what total tax at 29 mills?
blocks.x: 29 mills = $29 per $1,000. $520,000 / 1,000 = 520 x $29 = $15,080. Before revaluation the colonial paid $236,000 x $57 per $1,000 = $13,452, so its bill rises while the Delgados' barely moves. $1,508 is the trap: it treats 29 mills as 0.29%. A mill is a tenth of a cent, so 29 mills is 2.9%.

blocks.html: At the April closing, the attorneys apportioned the seller's prepaid school tax (the school fiscal year runs July to June) and the January town and county bill, so the Delgados reimbursed her for the days after closing. Rosa asks whether the seller can claim part of the SCAR reduction, since she owned the house on the March 1 taxable status date.

blocks.q: The grievance and SCAR changed the roll filed that July. Whose bills does the reduction lower?
c: The seller's, because she owned the house on the taxable status date, so the town refunds the reduction to her
Both parties' bills, split by the closing apportionment percentages for each tax in the year of the sale
The Delgados', because that roll produces the September school bill and next January's town and county bill
The town and county bill only, because school bills are set by the district and cannot be reduced
blocks.x: The roll grieved in May becomes final July 1 and is the basis for the school bill that September and the town and county bill the following January, all paid by the Delgados. The taxable status date fixes the condition and ownership used for the roll, but the tax is paid by whoever owns the property when the bills come due. Splitting it by the closing apportionment is the trap: the apportionment at closing concerned bills from the prior roll.

items: Build the buyer's tax estimate from the current roll and every jurisdiction's current rate, without the seller's exemptions. Listing sheet figures are a starting point, not a number to repeat.
Assessed value divided by the equalization rate gives the full value the town is implying. Equalization is also why nominal rates differ across towns that share a school district.
In a fractional-assessment town, an over-assessed house usually has an unequal assessment, not an excessive one. Request market value times the town's level.

The grievance (RP-524) by Grievance Day is the gateway. The board can deny or reduce, never raise. SCAR follows within 30 days of the final roll, for owner-occupied one to three family homes, and gives up certiorari.
Evidence at SCAR comes in three kinds: sales, assessment information, and assessment ratios.
A revaluation redistributes a levy. With the levy fixed, the rate falls as assessments rise, and only parcels with stale assessments pay more.

lessons.title: Case file: Macon Street, Class 1
lessons.tagline: The Okafors' brownstone is selling for $2,150,000 and pays about $7,000 a year in property tax. The buyers want to know which part of that deal they inherit.
objectives: Decide which tax benefits stay with a NYC Class 1 property after a sale (assessment caps) and which leave with the seller (exemptions).
Calculate a NYC Class 1 tax bill with and without a veterans exemption, and project the effect of the 6% and 20% caps and of physical changes.
Apply the eligibility rules for STAR, the senior citizens exemption, and the veterans exemption to real owners, in and outside NYC.
Explain how a change in use or unit count moves a property between NYC tax classes and what that does to the bill.

blocks.title: Bed-Stuy, a signed contract and a nervous buyer
blocks.html: The Okafors have signed a contract to sell their two-family brownstone on Macon Street for $2,150,000 and move to Atlanta. The buyers are Lena and Omar Haddad, a nurse practitioner and a high school principal, who plan to live in the garden and parlor duplex and rent the top floor. Lena found the property on the Department of Finance website and texted her own agent a screenshot: "Annual tax about $7,000 on a $2.15 million house?? Is this real?" Her agent called Jordan, who has been working the listing with Diane. Before anyone answers, Jordan pulls the January Notice of Property Value and the latest bill. Grace Okafor is 67. Emmanuel served in the Army during the Gulf War. Both facts are on that bill.

blocks.title: What the Notice of Property Value shows (simplified)
blocks.html:
Tax class: 1 (two-family dwelling)
Department of Finance market value: $1,480,000
Target assessed value at 6%: $88,800
Actual assessed value (capped): $41,200
Exemption: alternative veterans, 15% of assessed value: minus $6,180
Taxable value: $35,020
Enhanced STAR: shown as a separate savings line on the bill

Three numbers explain the small bill. First, the Department of Finance's market value for Class 1 homes is a mass-appraisal estimate and often trails what buyers actually pay. Second, the assessment ratio for Class 1 is 6%, but the actual assessed value is far below even 6% of that estimate, because Class 1 assessments can rise no more than 6% a year and 20% over five years. Third, the Okafors receive exemptions. The Class 1 tax rate has hovered near 20% in recent years; this case uses 20.0% to keep the math clean. The rate changes every July, so always use the current one.

blocks.q: Lena asks which parts of the Okafors' low tax bill will carry over to her and Omar after closing. What is the best answer?
c: Both the capped assessment and the exemptions carry over, since they are recorded against the tax lot
Neither carries over, because a sale resets the assessment to 6% of the price the buyers paid
The exemptions carry over for one year; the capped assessment resets at the next taxable status date
The capped assessment generally carries over; the veterans and STAR benefits belong to the Okafors
blocks.x: Class 1 caps attach to the property, so a buyer generally inherits the capped assessed value, and NYC does not reassess a home just because it sold. Exemptions attach to the owner's eligibility and end with the owner's ownership. The reset answer is the trap: it describes a "welcome stranger" reassessment, which New York does not allow, and buyers who expect it overestimate their taxes.

blocks.html: Jordan does the arithmetic on a call with both agents. With the exemptions, the Okafors' tax is $35,020 x 20% = $7,004, before the Enhanced STAR savings. That is the number Lena saw. The Haddads will not have the veterans exemption, and their STAR benefit will work differently.

blocks.q: Using the 20.0% rate and the capped assessed value, what will the Haddads' annual tax be in their first full year, before any STAR benefit and assuming the assessed value does not change?
blocks.x: Without the veterans exemption, the full assessed value is taxable: $41,200 x 20% = $8,240. $7,004 is the trap: it is the Okafors' bill with Emmanuel's 15% exemption still applied. $17,760 applies the rate to the 6% target ($88,800), which the caps prevent. The extra $1,236 is exactly the value of the exemption: $6,180 x 20%.

blocks.html: The assessed value will not stay put, though. Every year the Department of Finance moves Class 1 assessments toward 6% of its market value estimate, but no faster than the caps allow. Here the target ($88,800) is more than double the actual ($41,200), so this house will likely rise by the maximum every year for a long time. Buyers of long-held brownstones should budget for that climb.

blocks.q: The five-year cap has room left. What is the highest assessed value the Department of Finance can place on the house next year, before any physical changes?
blocks.x: The annual cap is 6%: $41,200 x 1.06 = $43,672. $49,440 is the trap: it is the 20% five-year limit ($41,200 x 1.20) applied in a single year. The caps work together, so the assessment can rise 6% a year but no more than 20% over any five years. At 20%, next year's tax would be about $8,734.

blocks.title: NYC's tax calendar for homeowners
blocks.html: There is no Grievance Day in New York City. The Department of Finance mails the Notice of Property Value in January. Class 1 owners who disagree apply to the NYC Tax Commission by March 15 (most other classes by March 1), and may then use SCAR. Most exemption applications and renewals, including SCHE and the veterans exemption, are due March 15 for the tax year that starts July 1. Bills follow the fiscal year: owners with assessed value of $250,000 or less pay quarterly (July 1, October 1, January 1, April 1); larger ones pay twice a year.

The Okafors' next-door neighbor, Mrs. Bailey, catches Jordan on the stoop. Her January notice raised her Department of Finance market value to $1,500,000, and she is sure the house is worth less. Her actual assessed value is $40,000, held down by the caps, while 6% of $1,500,000 is $90,000. She wants to file with the Tax Commission and argue for $1,300,000.

blocks.q: Suppose Mrs. Bailey wins and the market value drops to $1,300,000. What happens to her tax bill?
c: It falls by about 13%, because the assessed value always moves in proportion to the market value
It falls to the tax on $78,000, because the new target replaces the capped assessed value
It likely does not change, because the $40,000 capped assessment is still below the $78,000 target
It rises, because the Tax Commission must reset any assessment it reviews to the full 6% target
blocks.x: For a capped Class 1 home, the bill is driven by the actual assessed value, which here is far below the target. Cutting market value to $1,300,000 lowers the target to $78,000, still well above $40,000, so the capped value and the bill likely stay the same. The proportional answer is the trap: it ignores the caps. Protests pay off when the actual assessed value is at or near the target.

blocks.text: Grace, Emmanuel, and the senior benefits

blocks.html: While the buyers' side digests the numbers, Grace asks Jordan a question of her own. A neighbor told her she should have been getting "the senior discount" for years. The Okafors' combined income is about $96,000: two pensions, Social Security, and Emmanuel's part-time consulting. They have had STAR on the house since the 1990s, and it was upgraded to Enhanced STAR once Grace turned 65.

head: Benefit
Age
Income test (current figures)
What it reduces
rows: At least one resident owner 65+ by Dec 31 of the benefit year
Combined income of resident owners and spouses $110,750 or less for 2026 benefits ($113,550 for 2027)
School tax portion (in NYC, a portion of the bill set by formula)
$500,000 or less for the credit; $250,000 or less to keep a pre-2016 exemption
Senior Citizen Homeowners' Exemption (SCHE, NYC's version of the senior citizens exemption)
65+ (one spouse or sibling co-owner is enough)
Combined income $58,399 or less; 50% off assessed value at $50,000 or less, sliding to 5% near the limit
Assessed value: 15% for wartime service, more for combat zone service and service-connected disability, up to local caps
blocks.caption: Eligibility is about the owner, which is why none of these transfer to a buyer

blocks.q: Based on the table, which senior benefits can the Okafors (income about $96,000, Grace 67) receive on the brownstone?
c: SCHE only, because it replaced Enhanced STAR for New York City homeowners who are 65 or older
Enhanced STAR but not SCHE, because their income is under the STAR limit and over the SCHE limit
Both, because Grace meets the age test for each and they have owned the house well over 12 months
Neither, because Emmanuel's veterans exemption prevents them from receiving any senior benefit
blocks.x: Enhanced STAR's income ceiling ($110,750 for 2026 benefits) is far higher than SCHE's ($58,399). At $96,000, the Okafors qualify for the first and not the second. The "both" answer is the trap: meeting the age and ownership tests does not satisfy the income test. Veterans exemptions and senior benefits can coexist when an owner qualifies for each; nothing in the facts bars it.

blocks.html: On the buyers' side, two facts come out. Lena served in the Army National Guard and deployed to Iraq in 2004. And the couple's household income is about $310,000. Lena wants to know whether she can "take over" Emmanuel's veterans exemption at closing in June, since she is a veteran too.

blocks.q: The closing is in June. What is the correct guidance on Lena's veterans exemption?
c: She files with the Department of Finance, generally by March 15, for the tax year starting July 1 after that
She signs an assignment at closing so the Okafors' exemption is transferred to her for the remaining fiscal year
She cannot receive it on a two-family house, because the exemption only applies to one-family homes
She receives it automatically, because the Department of Defense reports discharges to the city each year
blocks.x: Exemptions do not transfer by assignment. Lena applies on her own, with her discharge papers, and NYC's deadline for most exemption applications is March 15 for the tax year beginning July 1. Combat zone service may increase her percentage. The assignment answer is the trap: it treats an exemption as part of the property. Eligibility does not depend on the house being a one-family; it turns on her service and her ownership and residence.

blocks.html: Their STAR situation is simpler. At $310,000, the Haddads are under the $500,000 limit for the Basic STAR credit, and the house will be their primary residence. New homeowners cannot receive the old STAR exemption; they register with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance, which mails a check each year before school taxes would be due. In NYC there is no separate school tax bill, so the state computes the credit by formula.

blocks.q: Which statement about the Haddads' STAR benefit is accurate?
c: They inherit the Okafors' STAR exemption line, which converts to Basic STAR when the house sells
They do not qualify, because STAR is limited to owners who are 65 or older with modest incomes
They qualify only for the rented top-floor apartment, since the STAR credit is limited to rental units
They register with the state for the Basic STAR credit, paid to them as a check
blocks.x: Basic STAR has no age requirement, and the credit's income limit is $500,000, so the Haddads qualify as owner-occupants. Since 2016, new owners get the credit by registering with the state, and it comes as a check. The age answer is the trap: it confuses Basic STAR with Enhanced STAR. STAR benefits a primary residence; it does not attach to a rental unit.

blocks.html: Omar has a spreadsheet of his own. The plan: a rear extension and a finished cellar now, and someday, maybe, carving the top two floors into three small rentals so the building has four units. Jordan's job is not to talk him out of it. It is to make sure the tax consequences are in the spreadsheet.

blocks.q: If the Haddads legally convert the building to four units, what happens to its NYC tax class?
c: It stays in Class 1 because it is still owner-occupied by the Haddads
It moves to Class 4 because more than half of the units are rentals
It moves to Class 2, which covers residential property with 4+ units
It moves to Class 3 because each new unit adds utility meters
blocks.x: Class 1 covers one to three family homes. A building with four or more residential units is Class 2, assessed at 45% of a market value estimated for an income-producing building, with smaller caps for buildings of 10 or fewer units (8% a year, 30% over five years). Owner occupancy is the trap: it matters for SCAR and exemptions, not for which class the building is in.

blocks.html: Class 2 is a different world. A small Class 2 building is valued by income, assessed at 45% of that value, and taxed at the Class 2 rate, which has run in the low teens. A four-unit building that was enjoying a decades-old Class 1 assessment could see its bill multiply. Omar shelves the four-unit idea and keeps the extension.

blocks.q: The extension and finished cellar will add an estimated $300,000 to the Department of Finance's market value. At 6% and a 20% rate, how much will they likely add to the annual tax?
blocks.x: Physical changes are added on top of the caps: $300,000 x 6% = $18,000 of added assessed value, and $18,000 x 20% = $3,600 a year. $18,000 is the trap: it is the added assessed value, not the tax. $1,080 treats the improvement as if it were limited to a 6% capped increase. Permits tell the Department of Finance about the work, which is how it reaches the roll.

blocks.title: Caps protect market growth, not your new kitchen
blocks.html: The 6% and 20% Class 1 caps limit increases that come from the market. Increases from physical changes, like an extension, a new story, or a finished cellar, are added outside the caps, and new construction is added at its full assessed value. A seller who renovated just before listing may have a bill that has not caught up yet.

Lena's sister is weighing a $2,100,000 condo in Clinton Hill and is baffled that its tax is about $23,000 while the brownstone's is about $8,000. Same neighborhood, same price. The difference is the class. Condos and co-ops are Class 2. By law, New York City values them as if they were rental buildings, using the income a comparable rental would earn, so the Department of Finance's market value for the condo unit might be about $420,000. Class 2 assesses at 45%: $189,000. At a Class 2 rate of 12.5%, the tax is about $23,625, before any condo or co-op abatement available to primary-residence owners.

blocks.q: What best explains why the condo pays roughly three times the brownstone's tax at a similar price?
c: Condo owners pay school tax and Class 1 owners do not
Condos are reassessed at each sale to match the price paid
The brownstone's sale price is taxed at the lower 6% rate
It is Class 2: valued as a rental and assessed at 45%
blocks.x: Class 1 homes are assessed at 6% with tight caps. Condos are Class 2: valued as if rentals, assessed at 45%, and taxed at the Class 2 rate. The 6% "rate" answer is the trap: 6% is an assessment ratio, not a tax rate, and it applies to the Department of Finance's market value, not the price paid. NYC has no separate school tax for either.

blocks.html: At the closing table, Grace mentions her younger sister Ngozi, 72, who sold her house in a Rockland County town last year and bought a condo in the same town eight months ago. She had the senior citizens exemption on the old house. Her income is $49,000, from Social Security and a small pension. Outside NYC, the senior citizens exemption under RPTL 467 is a local option: each county, town, and school district decides whether to grant it and sets an income ceiling between $3,000 and $50,000, with an optional sliding scale that reaches up to $58,399. The town, the county, and Ngozi's school district all adopted the $50,000 ceiling.

blocks.q: Ngozi has owned the condo for only eight months. Can she receive the senior exemption on it for the coming roll?
c: No, because every applicant must own the property for 12 consecutive months before filing
Yes, because she had the exemption on her prior residence
No, because senior exemptions are limited to one-family houses and do not apply to condominium units
Yes, but only for school taxes, because towns and counties may not grant the senior exemption
blocks.x: The usual rule requires 12 consecutive months of ownership, but it does not apply to an owner who received the exemption on a previous residence. The flat 12-month answer is the trap: it states the rule without its exception. Condo units qualify as residences, and the exemption is a local option for counties, towns, cities, villages, and school districts alike. She must still file by the taxable status date, usually March 1.

blocks.title: Ngozi's exemption at income $49,000
blocks.html:
Assessed value of the condo: $180,000. Income is at or below $50,000, so the exemption is 50% in each jurisdiction that adopted the $50,000 ceiling.
Exempt amount: $180,000 x 50% = $90,000. Taxable value: $90,000.
County and town rate $24.00 per $1,000; school rate $62.00 per $1,000.
Savings: 90 x ($24.00 + $62.00) = $7,740 a year, before her Enhanced STAR benefit on the school portion.
If her income later rises to $57,800, the sliding scale drops her exemption to 5% where the locality adopted it, and above $58,399 it ends.

blocks.q: Ngozi's town adopted the senior exemption, but suppose her school district had not. What would change in the example?
c: Nothing, because the town's adoption binds every taxing jurisdiction within the town's borders
The school portion would be taxed on $90,000, but the town portion would rise to compensate
The school portion would be taxed on the full $180,000, cutting her savings to $2,160 a year
The exemption would be void everywhere, because adoption must be unanimous among the jurisdictions
blocks.x: Each taxing jurisdiction adopts the senior exemption separately. Without school adoption, she saves only on the county and town portions: 90 x $24.00 = $2,160. The binding-the-district answer is the trap: towns and school districts are separate taxing jurisdictions, and one cannot adopt an exemption for the other. Enhanced STAR would still reduce her school taxes, since it is a state program.

blocks.text: Back on Macon Street: the closing

blocks.html: The closing is set for June 20. New York City's tax year runs July 1 to June 30, and because the brownstone's assessed value is under $250,000, its taxes are billed quarterly. The Okafors already paid the April 1 quarter, covering April through June: $7,004 / 4 = $1,751. Under the usual New York contract, taxes are apportioned as of midnight of the day before closing, so the Haddads own the house, and its taxes, starting June 20.

blocks.title: The tax apportionment at closing
blocks.html:
Quarter: April 1 to June 30 = 91 days. Paid by the Okafors: $1,751.
Haddads' days: June 20 to June 30 = 11 days.
Credit to the Okafors: $1,751 x 11 / 91 = $211.66, paid by the Haddads at closing.
The apportionment uses the bill actually paid, exemptions and all. It settles the past. It says nothing about the Haddads' future bills.

The July 1 bill is the one that worries Priya, the Haddads' attorney. It is based on a roll that still lists the Okafors as owners, so it may show Emmanuel's veterans exemption. The Department of Finance removes exemptions when an owner is no longer eligible, and it can bill the difference later. Priya tells the Haddads to budget on the full $8,240 (rising with the caps), set aside the difference if the first bill comes in low, and to have Lena's own veterans application in by March 15. The lender's escrow analysis, also built on the full bill, will catch up within a year either way.

blocks.title: Put the right number in the listing
blocks.html: When the seller's bill reflects exemptions, say so: "Taxes $7,004 with owner's veterans exemption; approximately $8,240 without." It costs one line, it heads off the "is this real?" text, and it is the kind of material fact a buyer's agent will otherwise discover, unhappily, after the contract is signed. Check the current rate on the Department of Finance site every July.

items: In NYC, Class 1 caps (6% a year, 20% over five years) run with the property, so a buyer generally inherits a capped assessment. Exemptions run with the owner and leave at the sale.
Estimate a buyer's NYC bill as assessed value without the seller's exemptions times the current class rate, then add the likely capped increase each year.
Physical changes are added outside the caps at the class ratio. A change to four or more units moves a building to Class 2, which is valued and taxed very differently.
STAR: Basic has no age test and a $500,000 credit limit; Enhanced requires a 65+ resident owner and a much lower income limit. New owners register with the state for the credit.

The senior citizens exemption (SCHE in NYC) has a much lower income ceiling than Enhanced STAR, is adopted separately by each jurisdiction, and waives the 12-month ownership rule for owners who had it on a prior home.
Veterans exemptions are applied for by the owner, by the local deadline (March 15 in NYC), and cannot be assigned to a buyer.

lessons.title: Case file: The Hardware Store at the County Auction
lessons.tagline: Evelyn wants a tax-foreclosed building in the Catskills. Sal wants his Astoria building off the city's lien sale list. Same lien, two very different ends.
objectives: Apply the priority of real property tax and special assessment liens over mortgages and other private liens.
Explain the steps of an in rem tax foreclosure under RPTL Article 11, including redemption periods and the former owner's claim to surplus.
Calculate a special assessment based on benefit units and decide how an unpaid charge is collected.
Decide how a NYC owner can avoid the tax lien sale and what happens to the debt, the mortgage, and a later sale if the lien is sold.

blocks.title: Main Street, a Catskills village, in October
blocks.html: Evelyn Park has been texting Jordan photos of a two-story brick building on a Catskills Main Street: a hardware store downstairs that closed in 2021, two apartments upstairs, plywood in one window. The county took title after the owner stopped paying taxes and will sell it at its annual tax foreclosure auction in three weeks. The opening bid is $91,000, which the county lists as the taxes, interest, and costs it is owed. A local agent told Evelyn the building is "free and clear, the county wiped everything." Evelyn, who thinks in cap rates and trusts nobody's adjectives, wants Jordan and Priya to tell her what that sentence really means before she registers to bid.

Priya orders a search of the county's records. The building had a $400,000 mortgage from a regional bank, recorded in 2015. A contractor filed a mechanic's lien in 2020. The town, village, and school taxes went unpaid starting with the 2021 bills, and a sewer district charge went unpaid along with them. The county, which enforces delinquent taxes for the towns and school districts inside it, became the holder of the tax liens.

blocks.q: Before the foreclosure, the 2015 mortgage and the 2021 tax lien were both against the building. Which had priority, and why?
c: The mortgage, because it was recorded six years before the taxes became a lien
Neither, because the two liens shared equally in any sale proceeds by statute
The tax lien, since taxes outrank private liens of any date
The mortgage, because the bank never signed a subordination agreement for the taxes
blocks.x: Real property taxes and special assessments are priority liens: they come ahead of mortgages and other private liens no matter when those were recorded. That is why lenders escrow taxes and why mortgages make nonpayment of taxes a default. The recording-date answer is the trap: "first in time" governs private liens against each other, but tax liens jump the line. No subordination agreement is needed.

blocks.text: How the county got the building

blocks.html: Most New York counties collect delinquent taxes through in rem foreclosure under Article 11 of the Real Property Tax Law. "In rem" means the action is against the property itself, not against the owner personally. The county does not sue the owner for a money judgment; it forecloses on the parcel.

blocks.q: Suppose the building had been worth less than the $91,000 owed and sold for $60,000. What can the county do about the $31,000 shortfall through the Article 11 proceeding?
c: Docket a deficiency judgment against the former owner for the $31,000 balance
Little through that proceeding, since an in rem action runs against the parcel
Collect the shortfall from the bank, as the senior private lienholder of record
Add the $31,000 to the bills of the other taxpayers in the special district
blocks.x: An in rem proceeding is against the property, not the person, so it produces no personal money judgment against the former owner. The parcel is the security for the tax, and when it brings less than the debt, the loss is spread through the tax levy in later years. The deficiency judgment answer is the trap: it describes a mortgage foreclosure, where a lender may seek one against the borrower.

blocks.title: The Article 11 path for the hardware store

items.title: Lien date
items.html: The unpaid 2021 taxes became a lien and were returned to the county as delinquent. Interest and penalties begin to run.

items.title: Redemption period
items.html: The owner, and anyone with an interest such as the bank or the contractor, may redeem by paying everything owed. The standard period ends two years after the lien date. A county may extend it to three or four years for residential and farm property by local law.

items.title: Petition and notice
items.html: The county files a petition of foreclosure listing delinquent parcels and gives notice to the owner and every party of record with an interest, including mortgagees and lienors.

items.title: Judgment and deed
items.html: If nobody redeems by the deadline, the court grants judgment and the county takes title. Interests of parties who received proper notice and did not redeem are cut off.

items.title: Auction and surplus
items.html: The county sells the parcel. After the 2023 Supreme Court decision in Tyler v. Hennepin County, New York amended Article 11 in 2024 so that a former owner can claim surplus proceeds above what was owed.

blocks.q: The bank received notice of the foreclosure and did not redeem. After the county took title by judgment, what is the status of the bank's $400,000 mortgage?
c: It survives the judgment and attaches to whoever buys at the county auction next month
It survives until the county sells, and then it is paid in full from the sale proceeds
It converts into a personal judgment against the county for the unpaid balance of the loan
It was cut off by the judgment, because the bank had notice and chose not to redeem
blocks.x: An in rem judgment generally extinguishes the interests of parties who received proper notice and failed to redeem, including mortgages and mechanic's liens. The bank's choice was to pay the delinquent taxes and add them to the borrower's debt, or walk away; on a vacant building worth less than the loan, it walked. The survives-and-attaches answer is the trap: it describes a lien that was never foreclosed.

blocks.html: "Free and clear" is mostly right about the mortgage and the mechanic's lien, then. It is not right about everything. Easements and recorded restrictions generally survive a tax foreclosure, the building's physical problems certainly do, and the county's deed comes with no warranties. Priya also wants the county's file proving that every notice went out properly, because a former owner or lienor who did not receive required notice can attack the judgment, and a title insurer will look at exactly that.

blocks.q: What is the most important step for Evelyn before she registers to bid?
c: Have Priya review the auction terms, the notice file, and the title, and inspect the building physically
Nothing more, because a county deed after an in rem judgment is insured by the state against all claims
Ask the former owner to sign a quitclaim deed, which replaces the need for any title review at all
Wait until after the auction to look at the title, since the high bidder may cancel within 30 days
blocks.x: County auctions sell as is, usually with a deed without covenants, and the terms often require a nonrefundable deposit the day of the sale. Due diligence happens before bidding: auction terms, the foreclosure notice file, a title search for surviving easements or restrictions, and a physical and environmental look at a building that sat empty for years. The cancel-later answer is the trap: auction sales are generally final.

blocks.html: Two doors down, a retired schoolteacher, Mr. Abernathy, owns a two-family house where he lives on one floor. He has fallen two years behind after medical bills. His taxes became a lien on the same date the hardware store's did, two years ago. The county passed a local law years ago extending the redemption period for residential property to three years. He asks Evelyn's agent, who knows him, whether "the county can take the house this year too."

blocks.q: Assuming the county's local law is as described, when does Mr. Abernathy's right to redeem expire?
c: Two years after the lien date, so the county can foreclose on his house this month
Four years after the lien date, because every owner-occupant receives the maximum
Three years after the lien date, about a year from now
There is no deadline, because an owner-occupied home cannot be taken for taxes
blocks.x: Article 11's standard redemption period is two years after the lien date, but a county may extend it to three or four years for residential and farm property by local law. This county chose three years, so he has about a year. The two-year answer is the trap: it applies the default rule to a residential parcel in a county that extended it. Homes can be foreclosed for taxes; the longer period only buys time.

blocks.html: The county also offers installment agreements for owners in his position, and Article 11 lets a county accept partial payments. Evelyn's agent connects him with the county treasurer's office. No deal of Evelyn's depends on his house, and an investor who quietly waits for a neighbor's foreclosure is not the kind of investor Jordan wants to work with.

The search also shows that the building sits in a village sewer district created eight years ago to replace failing septic systems along Main Street. The construction was financed with bonds. Instead of charging by assessed value, the district charges each parcel by benefit units: one unit for a single-family home, more for larger users. The hardware store building, with a store and two apartments, is rated at three units.

blocks.title: The sewer district's annual charge
blocks.html:
Annual bond payment plus operating costs: $180,000.
Total benefit units in the special assessment district: 300.
Charge per unit: $180,000 / 300 = $600.
Hardware store building: 3 units x $600 = $1,800 a year.
The charge is the same whether the building is assessed at $90,000 or $900,000.

blocks.q: Why is the sewer charge different from the school tax on the same bill?
c: It is ad valorem, so it rises with the building's assessed value like school tax
It is a special assessment, levied by benefit rather than by assessed value
It is a user fee, so it cannot become a lien if the owner leaves it unpaid
It is a state tax, collected by the village on behalf of the comptroller
blocks.x: A special assessment charges the parcels that benefit from a specific improvement, measured by units, frontage, or another benefit formula, not by value. School tax is ad valorem: rate times assessed value. The user-fee answer is the trap: unpaid special assessments are liens with the same priority as taxes and, in most districts, are relevied onto the tax bill and enforced with it.

blocks.html: The unpaid sewer charges since 2021 are already inside the $91,000 the county is owed, because they were relevied onto the tax bill and enforced with it. Evelyn's pro forma needs the future charge too: $1,800 a year, plus whatever the district adds if it expands. The district's next phase would add a pump station, and the village has published a plan to raise the per-unit charge. That plan goes into Evelyn's diligence binder.

Evelyn wins the auction at $310,000. The county is owed $91,000 in taxes, special assessments, interest, penalties, and costs. Before 2023, many counties kept everything. In Tyler v. Hennepin County, the U.S. Supreme Court held that keeping the surplus equity beyond the debt is a taking without just compensation. New York's 2024 amendments to Article 11, which apply to sales on or after May 25, 2023, give former owners a process to claim the surplus.

blocks.q: How much surplus is potentially available, and who can claim it?
c: $219,000, which the county may keep because it held title before the auction took place
$310,000, payable to the bank because its mortgage was the senior private lien of record
$91,000, which the former owner may claim because that is the amount the county collected
$219,000, which the former owner may claim under Article 11
blocks.x: Surplus = $310,000 minus $91,000 = $219,000. After Tyler, the county cannot simply keep equity beyond the debt; New York's amended Article 11 lets the former owner claim it (other claimants with surviving interests may also be heard in the process). The county-keeps answer is the trap: it was the practice before 2023. $91,000 is the debt, not the surplus.

blocks.title: Tax lien sale vs tax foreclosure sale
blocks.html: In a tax lien sale, the government sells the debt: the buyer gets the right to collect the lien with interest and, if unpaid, to foreclose. The owner keeps the property for now. In a tax foreclosure (in rem) sale, the government first takes title and then sells the property itself. Exam items swap these. Evelyn bought a building, not a lien.

Back in Queens, Sal Russo calls Jordan with an envelope from the Department of Finance. His six-unit Astoria building is on the list for the city's next tax lien sale. Two bad quarters with a boiler replacement put him behind: $6,800 in property taxes, more than a year overdue, and $4,200 in water and sewer charges billed by the Department of Environmental Protection, also more than a year overdue. New York City does not use Article 11 in rem foreclosure for most properties; its main tool is selling liens. The City Council reauthorized the lien sale in 2024, through 2028, with more notice and more exits for owners.

head: Property type
Property tax threshold
Water and sewer threshold
rows: All other property (including Sal's six-unit rental)
blocks.caption: Selected lien sale eligibility thresholds published by the NYC Department of Finance; check the current chart before relying on them

blocks.q: Is Sal's building eligible for the lien sale, and why?
c: Yes, because both debts exceed $1,000 and are over a year overdue for its class
No, because a residential building is protected until it is three years overdue on taxes
No, because water and sewer charges are utility bills and cannot be sold as tax liens
Yes, but only the water charges, because property taxes are sold after three years
blocks.x: A six-unit rental falls in the "all other" row: $1,000 overdue for one year. Both of Sal's debts qualify. The three-year answer is the trap: that longer period protects owner-occupied one to three family homes and condo and co-op buildings, not small rental buildings. Water and sewer charges are liens on NYC property and are sold in the same sale.

blocks.html: The notice lists ways off the list before the sale date: pay the full amount, enter a payment agreement with the Department of Finance (and with DEP for the water charges), or show that the property qualifies for an exemption that excludes it. Owners who receive SCHE, the Disabled Homeowners' Exemption, and certain other benefits are excluded from the sale entirely. Sal is not; he is a landlord with a cash-flow problem.

blocks.q: Sal has the cash for about half of what he owes. What is the best advice?
c: Ignore the notices, since the city must foreclose itself before anyone else can act
Pay half now, which automatically removes the building from the sale until next year
Enter payment agreements with Finance and DEP before the sale to get off the list
Transfer the deed to his daughter, which restarts the overdue period from zero
blocks.x: A payment agreement entered and kept before the sale removes the debt from the list, and Sal can afford the down payment. The half-payment answer is the trap: a partial payment that leaves a debt above the threshold does not by itself guarantee removal. Ignoring the notices is the worst choice. A deed transfer does not erase a lien, because the lien is on the property.

blocks.html: Sal asks what happens if he misses the agreement deadline. Jordan reads him the city's description. The lien is sold to a trust, a third party, which hires a servicer to collect. The debt keeps growing: interest continues to accrue at the city's rates and compounds daily, and a 5% surcharge is added to the lien. The owner gets time to pay, but if the debt stays unpaid, the lienholder may bring a foreclosure action and the property can be sold to satisfy it.

blocks.q: If Sal's lien is sold, which statement is accurate?
c: Sal loses title immediately, and the trust becomes the owner of the building
Sal's debt is frozen at the sale amount, since the city no longer charges interest
Sal can ignore it, because a private buyer of a city lien has no right to foreclose
Sal keeps title but owes the servicer, with interest and a surcharge
blocks.x: A tax lien sale transfers the debt, not the building. Sal keeps title but now owes the lienholder through its servicer, with interest compounding and a 5% surcharge, and the lienholder can foreclose if the debt goes unpaid. The loses-title answer is the trap: it confuses a lien sale with a tax foreclosure. A frozen debt is wishful thinking: sold liens are more expensive, not less.

blocks.html: There is also Sal's own lender to think about. His mortgage, like nearly every commercial and residential mortgage, requires him to pay taxes and water charges when due. A tax lien, sold or not, outranks the lender's mortgage, so the lender watches tax status closely.

blocks.q: Sal's lender learns that the building is on the lien sale list. What is it most likely to do?
c: Nothing, since a lender's mortgage takes priority over any city tax lien
Pay the taxes itself and declare a default
Buy the lien at the sale so it can foreclose before the trust does
Release its mortgage, since the city's lien replaces the lender's
blocks.x: Because tax liens come first, a lender protects its collateral by paying delinquent taxes itself, adding the amount to the loan, and declaring the nonpayment a default under the mortgage's tax covenant. It may also start escrowing taxes. The lender-has-priority answer is the trap: it reverses the rule. Buying the lien is not how the sale works; it is a bulk sale to a designated trust.

blocks.html: Sal signs the payment agreements a week before the deadline. The building comes off the list.

blocks.text: The agent's job when a lien is in the picture

blocks.html: The Ridgewood building also shows a second special charge on its tax bill: a Business Improvement District assessment. A BID is a special assessment district in New York City in which commercial property owners pay an extra charge, collected by the Department of Finance with the property tax, to fund sidewalk cleaning, security, holiday lighting, and marketing for the commercial strip. Like a sewer district charge, it is based on a formula the district adopts, not on the ordinary tax rate, and unpaid BID charges are collected the same way as unpaid taxes.

blocks.q: The Ridgewood seller's two retail tenants have net leases. Which statement about the BID charge is most accurate for the buyer's analysis?
c: It is a special assessment the owner pays with the tax bill, often passed through to tenants by lease
It disappears at closing, because BID charges are personal to the owner who voted for the district
It is an ad valorem tax set by the BID's board, so it rises automatically with the building's value
It is a voluntary contribution, so the buyer can decline it after closing by notifying the district
blocks.x: BID charges are special assessments levied on property in the district and billed with the property tax. They stay with the property after a sale. Net leases commonly make tenants reimburse taxes and assessments, so the buyer should confirm the leases cover the BID line. The ad valorem answer is the trap: a BID uses its own formula, not the general tax rate times assessed value, and it is not voluntary once the district exists.

blocks.html: Six months later, a buyer asks Jordan about a small Ridgewood mixed-use building whose title report shows a tax lien sold to the trust two years ago. The seller says it is "basically the same as unpaid taxes." In one sense it is: the lien must be paid off at closing like any tax. But the payoff is not on the Department of Finance's account anymore. It comes from the servicer, it includes the surcharge and compounded interest, and it changes daily. If a lien foreclosure has been started, there may also be a notice of pendency on the record and legal fees in the payoff.

blocks.q: What should Jordan do about the sold lien before the buyer signs a contract?
c: Tell the buyer to assume the lien, since a buyer can take title subject to any tax lien
Ignore it, because the title company will clear every lien at closing automatically
Make sure the attorneys get the servicer's payoff, since it can far exceed the original tax
Use the Department of Finance balance, since the servicer's figure is only an estimate
blocks.x: A sold lien is still a priority lien that must be satisfied at closing, but its payoff comes from the servicer and has grown with interest, the surcharge, and possibly foreclosure costs. A seller who prices the deal off the original tax may come up short. The title-company answer is the trap: the title company identifies and collects payoffs; it does not erase them, and the money comes out of the seller's proceeds.

items: Real property taxes and special assessments are priority liens. They outrank mortgages and mechanic's liens regardless of recording date, which is why lenders pay delinquent taxes to protect themselves.

Article 11 in rem foreclosure: lien date, redemption period (two years, extendable by local law to three or four for residential and farm property), petition and notice, judgment, county deed, auction. Parties with notice who do not redeem are cut off.
After Tyler v. Hennepin County and New York's 2024 amendments, a former owner can claim surplus above the taxes and costs owed.
Special assessments charge by benefit (units, frontage), not value. Unpaid charges are relevied on the tax bill and enforced like taxes.

NYC sells tax and water liens instead of foreclosing in rem for most properties. Thresholds depend on the property type; payment agreements and certain exemptions keep a property off the list. A sold lien grows with interest and a surcharge and can be foreclosed by the lienholder.
Tax lien sale sells the debt. Tax foreclosure sale sells the property.

lessons.title: Case file: The Village Line on Front Street
lessons.tagline: Two Saratoga County houses a mile apart, one inside the village line. The cheaper listing has the bigger tax bill, and the closing has three tax years.
objectives: Calculate a parcel's tax bill from the rates of every jurisdiction that taxes it, converting rates stated per $100, per $1,000, and in mills.
Apply equalization rates to compare full value tax rates across towns that assess at different levels.
Explain how the tax cap, school budget votes, exempt property, and IDA PILOT agreements change the levy and the rate other owners pay.
Apportion town, county, village, and school taxes with different fiscal years at a closing, and decide what the buyer's agent must tell buyers.

blocks.title: Two houses, one village line, Saratoga County
blocks.html: Marisol Ortega and June Whitfield, a hospital billing manager and a high school librarian, are leaving a rental in Sunnyside, Queens, for a village in Saratoga County where both can work remotely three days a week. Jordan is representing them with a local cooperating broker, Dale Fenner, who knows every street. They have narrowed it to two houses a mile apart in the same school district. The first is a 1920s four-square on Front Street, inside the village, at $389,000; Dale's listing sheet says "Taxes: $5,410." The second is a 1990s colonial on Cobble Lane, just outside the village line, at $405,000, with "Taxes: $6,700." June has already decided: "The village house costs less and its taxes are lower. Easy." Jordan asks for an evening with the town's online tax roll before anyone says easy.

Both houses sit in the same town, which is the assessing unit for both, so both are on the same assessment roll. The town assesses at a uniform 55% of market value; the state's equalization rate for the town is 55.00%. The four-square is assessed at $214,000 and the colonial at $222,750. Both assessments line up with the asking prices, so neither house is obviously over-assessed. The difference between the two bills comes from somewhere else.

head: Taxing jurisdiction
Rate as printed on its bill
Front Street (village)
Cobble Lane (outside village)
blocks.caption: Who taxes which house (current rates)

blocks.q: Marisol asks why the village house pays a village tax but no fire district or part-town highway tax. What is the best explanation?
c: The village house is exempt from those two taxes because the seller has a senior exemption
Village residents pay town-wide and village taxes, not charges levied outside villages
A village is its own assessing unit, so it replaces the town's taxes with a single village tax
The fire district and highway taxes are special assessments charged by frontage, not by value
blocks.x: A village sits inside a town. Its residents pay the town-wide tax and the county and school taxes, plus the village tax for services the village provides itself, such as its own streets and fire department. Part-town charges and fire district taxes fund those services for areas outside villages, so village residents do not pay them. The assessing-unit answer is the trap: here the town assesses both houses, and village residents still pay town-wide taxes.

blocks.html: Before trusting any rate, Jordan wants to see how one is made. The village posts its adopted budget. Its appropriations, the spending the board has authorized, total $6,850,000: police, the volunteer fire department's trucks and gear, streets, snow, the water plant's share of overhead, and debt service on a firehouse. Not all of it comes from property owners. The village expects $3,320,000 from other sources: its share of county sales tax, state aid, court fines, permit fees, and some of its fund balance. The rest is the tax levy, the amount that must be raised by the real property tax. The village's total taxable assessed value, after every exemption, is $360,200,000.

blocks.q: What village tax rate does that budget produce?
c: About $9.80 per $1,000, or $0.98 per $100 of assessed value
About $19.02 per $1,000, or $1.90 per $100 of assessed value
About $5.39 per $1,000, or $0.54 per $100 of assessed value
About $9.22 per $1,000, or $0.92 per $100 of assessed value
