blocks.x: Levy = appropriations minus other revenue: $6,850,000 minus $3,320,000 = $3,530,000. Rate = levy / taxable assessed value = $3,530,000 / $360,200,000 = 0.0098, or $9.80 per $1,000. The $19.02 answer is the trap: it divides the whole budget by the roll, as if sales tax and state aid did not exist. The rate is set by the levy, not by the budget.

blocks.html: Two consequences follow. If the village's assessed values rise and its levy does not, the rate falls. And if other revenue drops, say a cut in state aid, the levy and the rate rise even though spending did not. The rate is the last number calculated, not the first.

blocks.text: Three ways to print a rate

blocks.html: New York jurisdictions print rates in whatever unit their software uses. The county and town use dollars per $1,000 of assessed value. The village uses dollars per $100. The school district uses mills, and one mill is one tenth of a cent, so 21.60 mills is $0.0216 per dollar, which is the same as $21.60 per $1,000. Before adding anything, Jordan puts every rate in one unit.

blocks.q: What is the village tax on the Front Street house, before exemptions?
c: $209.72, at $0.98 per $1,000 of assessed value
$2,097.20, at $9.80 per $1,000 of assessed value
$20,972.00, at $98 per $1,000 of assessed value
blocks.x: $0.98 per $100 is $9.80 per $1,000. The tax is 214 x $9.80 = $2,097.20. The $209.72 answer is the trap: it reads a per-$100 rate as if it were per $1,000, a factor of ten that shows up constantly on the exam. The $3,812.20 answer applies the rate to market value; rates apply to assessed value.

blocks.q: Using all the rates that apply, what is the Front Street house's full tax bill without any exemptions?
c: $5,410.00, the figure on the listing sheet
$6,749.33, at the combined $30.30 per $1,000
blocks.x: Inside the village the rates are county $3.10, town-wide $2.40, village $9.80, and school $21.60, for $36.90 per $1,000. On $214,000: 214 x $36.90 = $7,896.60. The $6,749.33 answer is the trap: it is the Cobble Lane bill, which uses the outside-village rates on that house's $222,750 assessment.

blocks.html: So the village house is the more expensive one to own: about $7,897 a year against $6,749. The listing sheet's $5,410 is real, but it belongs to the seller, Bernadette Quinlan, 81, whose bill reflects a senior citizens exemption in each jurisdiction that offers one and an Enhanced STAR exemption on her school tax. Neither will pass to buyers in their thirties. Dale did not hide anything; he copied her last bill. Jordan gives the buyers his own estimate in writing, shows how he built it, and notes that the rates will change with the next budgets.

blocks.title: The cheaper sticker, the bigger bill
blocks.html: Buyers compare listing-sheet taxes as if they were prices. They are history: one owner's bill, with that owner's exemptions, at last year's rates. Rebuild every bill from the assessed value and the current rates of every jurisdiction that taxes the parcel. A village line, a fire district, or a library district can move a bill by hundreds of dollars on the same street.

blocks.q: Dale's listing sheet shows "Taxes: $5,410" with no note. What should a listing agent do with a tax figure that reflects the owner's exemptions?
c: Label it as the current owner's bill with her exemptions, and show the full taxes too
Leave it as printed, because the buyer's attorney is the one responsible for verifying taxes
Replace it with the price times the equalization rate, which is the legal tax figure for buyers
Remove it entirely, because agents may not state tax figures in listing advertisements
blocks.x: Agents may state taxes, but a number that will not apply to a buyer misleads unless it is explained. Best practice is to say the bill reflects the current owner's exemptions and to give the full, unexempted amount, verified on the roll. The attorney answer is the trap: the attorney's review does not excuse a misleading statement by a licensee, and buyers budget from listing sheets long before attorneys see them.

blocks.html: Then June finds a third house, a ranch in the next town over at $395,000. That town finished a revaluation two years ago and assesses at 100% of market value, and its combined rate with the same school district is $19.80 per $1,000. Comparing $19.80 to $36.90 is meaningless, because the two towns assess at different levels. To compare, Jordan converts each rate into a full value tax rate: tax per $1,000 of market value. Multiply the nominal rate by the town's equalization rate.

blocks.q: What is the Front Street house's full value tax rate, and how does it compare with the ranch's $19.80?
c: $20.30 per $1,000 of market value, slightly higher than the ranch
$67.09 per $1,000 of market value, more than three times the ranch
$36.90 per $1,000 of market value, almost twice the ranch
$16.67 per $1,000 of market value, lower than the ranch
blocks.x: Full value tax rate = nominal rate x equalization rate: $36.90 x 0.55 = $20.30 per $1,000 of market value, a little more than the ranch's $19.80 at a 100% level. The $67.09 answer is the trap: it divides by the equalization rate instead of multiplying. The $16.67 figure is the Cobble Lane house's full value rate: $30.30 x 0.55.

blocks.html: This is what equalization is for. A school district that crosses town lines uses full values to split its levy fairly, and buyers can use the same arithmetic to compare houses in towns that assess at different percentages. On a full value basis, Cobble Lane is the cheapest of the three to own, and Front Street the most expensive.

head: House
Price
Assessed value
Nominal rate per $1,000 AV
Full value rate per $1,000
Estimated annual tax
blocks.caption: Three houses on one basis

blocks.html: The table also shows why a buyer should never judge a town by its rate alone. The ranch's $19.80 looks like half of Front Street's $36.90, yet the two bills are almost the same, because one town assesses at full value and the other at 55%. The nominal rate and the assessment level always travel together. A town that revalues to 100% will see its rate fall sharply in the same year; nobody's bill falls just because the rate did. What changes in a revaluation is the share each owner pays, as stale assessments are corrected.

Marisol, who reconciles hospital accounts for a living, adds a column of her own: tax as a percent of price. Front Street is about 2.0%, Cobble Lane about 1.7%, the ranch about 2.0%. That is the same comparison in a form a buyer can carry from town to town, and it is close to the full value rate divided by ten.

blocks.text: Why the rates might not hold

blocks.html: Jordan checks the school district's website. The board has proposed a budget whose tax levy rises 4.6%. Under New York's property tax cap, which generally limits levy growth to 2% or the rate of inflation, whichever is less, plus certain adjustments and exclusions, the district's own levy limit this year allows 2.9%. The vote is the third Tuesday in May. The result: 57% yes, 43% no.

blocks.q: Did the school budget pass?
c: Yes, because a simple majority of the voters approved it
No, because a school levy may not rise by more than 2% in one year
Yes, because school districts may exceed the cap if the board votes for it
No, because a levy above the limit needs 60% voter approval
blocks.x: A school budget whose levy exceeds the district's levy limit needs at least 60% of the votes cast to pass; 57% falls short. A budget within the limit needs only a simple majority. The board-vote answer is the trap: towns, villages, and counties override the cap by a 60% vote of their governing boards, but school districts need their voters. The 2% answer ignores that the limit includes adjustments and can be overridden.

blocks.q: The district puts the same budget up again in June and it fails again. What happens to the school levy?
c: The board may adopt the budget anyway, since two votes satisfy the law
The county sets the school levy at the cap and bills the difference to the state
The district adopts a contingent budget, and its levy cannot rise above last year's
The levy rises by the full 4.6%, but the increase is spread across the next two years
blocks.x: After two defeats a district must adopt a contingent budget, and its tax levy cannot exceed the prior year's levy. Programs get cut instead. For buyers this means the school rate may hold steady or even fall if the roll grows. The adopt-anyway answer is the trap: a board's vote cannot replace the voters' approval of a school budget.

blocks.html: Driving back to the station, June points out a new 180-unit apartment complex at the edge of the village. A neighbor at an open house had complained that "those apartments pay no taxes and we pay for their kids." Jordan looks it up. The county's industrial development agency (IDA) holds an interest in the project and granted it a property tax exemption, under the General Municipal Law and RPTL 412-a, in exchange for a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) agreement. The PILOT starts at $1,100 per unit a year and climbs over 20 years.

blocks.q: Which statement about the apartment complex's taxes is accurate?
c: It pays nothing to any local government until the 20-year agreement ends
It pays PILOTs shared among local governments, and still owes special district charges
It pays full taxes to the school district, while the county waives its own share
It pays PILOTs to the IDA, which keeps them to fund its own economic development programs
blocks.x: IDA projects are exempt from county, town, village, and school taxes, but they make PILOT payments that the agency must pass on to the affected jurisdictions in proportion to what each would have received. The IDA exemption does not reach special district levies or special assessments, so charges such as sewer still apply. The "pays nothing" answer is the trap: the complex pays, just less than full taxes, for a set period.

blocks.html: The numbers make the trade visible. At today's rates, the complex would owe roughly $640,000 a year as a fully taxable property. Its first-year PILOT is 180 x $1,100 = $198,000. The difference is the subsidy the IDA granted to get 180 apartments built, which also added residents who shop and pay sales tax in the village. Whether that was a good trade is a political question. For a buyer, the practical questions are when the PILOT steps up, when it ends, and whether the project will then go on the roll at full value and help spread the levy.

The neighbor is not entirely wrong, though. Any property that leaves the taxable roll, or pays less than full tax, shifts the burden onto everyone else, because each jurisdiction still has a levy to raise. A month later the local paper reports a second change: the regional hospital, a nonprofit, has bought three houses on Front Street to house medical residents and applied to have them exempted as property used for its charitable purpose.

blocks.q: If the three houses come off the taxable roll and the village's levy stays the same, what happens to the village tax rate for everyone else?
c: It falls, because the hospital will pay a PILOT on the three houses in their place
It stays the same, because the rate is set by the state when the roll is filed
It stays the same, but the lost tax is added to the hospital's county bill
It rises, because the same levy is spread over less taxable assessed value
blocks.x: Rate = levy divided by taxable assessed value. Remove taxable value and the same levy needs a higher rate, so every remaining owner pays a little more. That is the cost of exempt property: government, religious, educational, and charitable owners use services but do not pay for them through the tax. The PILOT answer is the trap: a nonprofit may volunteer one, but nothing requires it.

blocks.text: The closing: three tax years at one table

blocks.html: Marisol and June choose Cobble Lane after all, but the Front Street house sells to another buyer and closes on August 14, and Jordan, curious, asks Dale for the closing statement. It shows something every upstate closing shows: three tax bills, each on its own fiscal year, each in a different state of payment. The contract apportions taxes on the bills actually paid, as of midnight before closing, so the buyer owns the closing day, using a 365-day year.

head: Bill
Fiscal year
Amount (with seller's exemptions)
Status on August 14
rows: New bill not issued until September
blocks.caption: Tax bills on the Front Street house

blocks.q: How is the village tax apportioned at the August 14 closing?
c: Credit the seller $1,003.21 for the buyer's 291 days, paid by the buyer
Credit the buyer $255.11 for the seller's 74 days, paid by the seller
Credit the seller $1,258.32, since she paid the whole village bill
Credit the buyer $1,003.21, since the buyer will own the house next June
blocks.x: The seller prepaid the June 1 to May 31 village year. The buyer's days run August 14 through May 31: 18 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 = 291. $1,258.32 x 291 / 365 = $1,003.21, credit seller, debit buyer. The $255.11 answer is the trap: it computes the seller's own days and sends the money the wrong way. A prepaid bill always produces a credit to the seller.

blocks.q: The school bill for July 1 to June 30 has not been issued. How is it handled at closing?
c: No entry, because the buyer will pay the September bill and the seller owes nothing
The buyer credits the seller for 44 days, since the seller owned the house in July
The seller credits the buyer about $356.82, adjusted when the bill arrives
The title company holds the full $2,960 in escrow until the September bill is paid
blocks.x: The seller owned the house July 1 through August 13, 44 days of a school year she has not paid for, and the buyer will pay the whole bill in September. So the seller credits the buyer, estimated from last year's bill: $2,960 x 44 / 365 = $356.82, with a clause to re-apportion when the actual bill is known. The no-entry answer is the trap: unpaid taxes for the seller's days are always the seller's cost.

blocks.html: The town and county bill works like the village bill: prepaid by the seller, so the buyer credits her for August 14 through December 31, 140 days, or $456.44. Jordan notices that every one of those apportionments uses Mrs. Quinlan's exemption-reduced bills, the bills she actually paid. The buyer's first full bills, on a roll without her exemptions, will be higher. A good buyer's agent says so before the contract, not after the first January bill.

blocks.title: No state property tax, many local calendars
blocks.html: New York State does not levy a real property tax. Counties, cities, towns, villages, school districts, and special districts each levy their own, and many run on different fiscal years. Outside New York City, a typical pattern is a January town and county bill, a June village bill, and a September school bill. In NYC the Department of Finance bills one tax for a July 1 fiscal year. Always ask which period each bill covers.

blocks.q: Marisol and June's lender will escrow their taxes on Cobble Lane, closing in late August. Which bill will the lender need cash for first?
c: The January town and county bill, because it is the largest bill of the year
The June village bill, because Cobble Lane is inside the village
The September school bill, which comes due a few weeks after closing
None of them until next year, since the seller prepaid each of the three bills
blocks.x: Cobble Lane pays school, county, town, and fire district taxes, but no village tax. The school bill, usually the largest, comes due in September, weeks after an August closing, so the lender collects enough at closing to pay it on time. The village answer is the trap: Cobble Lane is outside the village line, which was the point of the first comparison. The seller prepaid only the January bill.

items: A parcel's bill is the sum of every jurisdiction that taxes it: county, town (town-wide and part-town), village, school, and special districts. Village residents pay village taxes plus town-wide taxes, not part-town or fire district charges.
Convert rates to one unit before adding: per $100 x 10 = per $1,000; mills = dollars per $1,000. Apply rates to assessed value, not price.
To compare towns that assess at different levels, use the full value tax rate: nominal rate x equalization rate.

The tax cap limits levy growth to the lesser of 2% or inflation, with adjustments. A school levy above the limit needs 60% voter approval; after two defeats, a contingent budget with no levy increase.
Exempt property and IDA PILOT projects shift the levy to everyone else. PILOTs are shared among the jurisdictions in proportion; special district charges still apply.

At closing, apportion each bill on its own fiscal year: prepaid bills credit the seller, unpaid or unbilled periods credit the buyer. Exemption-reduced bills are history; estimate the buyer's real bill.

roleplays.title: The $9,000 Tax Bill That Isn't
roleplays.setting: Leo is about to offer on a Westchester house. The listing shows taxes of $9,000. The seller is a longtime owner with senior and Enhanced STAR exemptions.
roleplays.goal: Give Leo an honest estimate of his own tax bill, correct a misleading listing figure, answer his reassessment fear accurately, and point him to the right protest process.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Leo Brandt, a spreadsheet-loving buyer about to offer $975,000 on a Westchester house whose listing shows $9,000 in taxes because the elderly seller has senior and Enhanced STAR exemptions (assessed value $20,000, full rate $730 per $1,000). Also voice Marcus, the listing agent, who wants to keep the low figure. Ask whether you can use the listed tax number, why the assessed value is so low, whether you will be reassessed to your price, whether you get STAR, and how to fight a high assessment. The learner must recompute taxes without exemptions, explain fractional assessment and equalization, explain that welcome stranger reassessment is illegal, describe the STAR credit, and give the assessor, BAR grievance, SCAR ladder. Grade each and give one tip.

seller: a retired couple in their seventies

opening: {day}. Leo wants to offer $975,000 on the {style} on {street}. His spreadsheet has a tax line: $9,000, straight from the listing.
The seller of the {street} {style}: {seller}, forty years in the house. The listing says taxes are $9,000. Leo believes it.
Leo sends you a screenshot of his budget for the {style} on {street}. Mortgage, insurance, and taxes of $9,000. One of those numbers is wrong.

say: Listing says taxes are $9,000. I'll plug that into my spreadsheet. Good?
Taxes are $9,000 a year on the {street} house. That's what I'm budgeting. Right?

moves.text: Seller exemptions end at sale. $20,000 assessed x $730 per $1,000 is about $14,600 for you.
moves.fb: Exemptions do not transfer. Recompute the buyer's bill from assessed value times the full rate.
moves.react: Fourteen six! That's a big difference.

moves.text: No. That's what the seller pays with those exemptions. Yours would be about $14,600 at full rate.
moves.fb: Correct. Exemptions belong to the owner; tax = assessed value x rate.

moves.text: Probably a bit higher for you. Call the town and ask what the bill would be without exemptions.
moves.fb: Pointing him to the source is fine, but you can and should do the math yourself.
moves.react: How much higher is a bit?

moves.text: Yes, the listing number is fine. Taxes stay with the house, so you'll pay what the seller pays.
moves.fb: The seller's exemptions disappear at sale. Leo would be short over $5,000 a year.

moves.text: Add 10% to be safe, so about $9,900. Taxes usually go up a little bit after a sale here in Westchester.
moves.fb: A guess, not math. Use assessed value x full rate, about $14,600.

moves.text: Exemptions transfer to the buyer for the first year, so budget $9,000 now and then $14,600 next year.
moves.fb: Exemptions never transfer. They belong to the owner who qualifies.
moves.react: So year one is cheap. Nice.

say: Marcus, who has the listing: "Leave the $9,000 on the listing. Lower taxes sell houses. It's technically what the seller pays."
Marcus calls: "Don't make a fuss about the tax number, Jordan. It's accurate for my seller."

moves.text: It's accurate for the seller but misleading for buyers. Let's note it reflects the exemptions.
moves.fb: Advertising should not mislead. Clarifying that exemptions end protects buyers and the firm.
moves.react: Marcus sighs. "Fine, I'll add a line."

moves.text: Add the unexempted figure too. Buyers rely on that line, and the firm owns the ad.
moves.fb: Right. Ads must not mislead (19 NYCRR 175.25), and the broker is responsible for them.

moves.text: Say nothing about it. It's Marcus's listing, and you already gave Leo the right number privately.
moves.fb: Your duty runs to Leo, and you protected him, but leaving a misleading figure up hurts other buyers and the firm.

moves.text: Agree. Buyers should check taxes themselves. The listing is just the seller's information.
moves.fb: A licensee may not pass along information they know is misleading.

moves.text: Tell Marcus to raise it to $14,600 and drop the exemptions part. Simpler for everyone.
moves.fb: Better than $9,000, but the clearest fix shows both figures with an explanation.

moves.text: Fine, but then the buyer's attorney can't object later, because it's technically accurate.
moves.fb: Technically accurate but misleading is still a problem. Fix the listing.

say: Wait, assessed value is only $20,000? The house is $975,000. Is that a mistake?
How can a $975,000 house be assessed at $20,000?

moves.text: It's not a mistake. The town assesses at a fraction of value. Divide by the equalization rate for full value.
moves.fb: Correct. Full value = assessed value / ratio (or equalization rate). Many NY towns use fractional assessments.
moves.react: Huh. So I compare to full value, not the raw number.

moves.text: Many towns assess at a small fraction of value. The state equalization rate converts it to full value.
moves.fb: Right. The state equalization rate compares a town's assessment level to market value.
moves.react: So the rate is huge because the base is tiny.

moves.text: It's weird, I know. Every town does its own thing, so it's hard to explain. The bill is what counts here.
moves.fb: True that the bill matters, but you should explain fractional assessment and equalization.

moves.text: It's a typo. It should say $200,000. Ask the assessor to fix the record before you close on it.
moves.fb: Fractional assessment is normal, not a typo. Convert with the equalization rate.

moves.text: That's the land only. The house itself isn't assessed until somebody files a permit for something.
moves.fb: Assessed value includes land and improvements, just at a fractional level.
moves.react: So I'll get a bigger bill later?

moves.text: It means the seller won a huge grievance. You'll inherit that low value forever after the closing.
moves.fb: Low assessments here reflect the town's ratio, not a grievance win. And values can change at revaluation.

say: If I pay $975,000, won't the town just reassess my house to $975,000 next year?
Will they bump my assessment because I paid more than the seller did?

moves.text: Raising just your house because it sold is illegal: welcome stranger. A townwide revaluation is fine.
moves.fb: Accurate: welcome stranger reassessment is illegal; revaluation and discovered improvements are legal reasons.
moves.react: So only a townwide change or new work.

moves.text: Not because you bought. That's welcome stranger, and it's illegal. New work found is different.
moves.fb: Right. Selective reassessment upon sale is illegal; discovered improvements can be assessed.
moves.react: Good. No surprises if I do things by the book.

moves.text: I don't think so, but I've heard of towns doing it. Ask the assessor's office to be sure, I guess.
moves.fb: Weak. You should know selective reassessment upon sale is illegal.
moves.react: You've heard of it? That's not reassuring.

moves.text: Yes, that's standard after a sale. Every buyer gets reassessed to the purchase price the following year.
moves.fb: Wrong. Selective reassessment upon sale violates equal protection and NY assessment law.
moves.react: Ugh. Then my bill is way higher.

moves.text: Only if you pay more than 10% over the last full value. Below that, the town has to leave it alone.
moves.fb: Invented rule. Selective reassessment upon sale is not allowed at any percentage.

moves.text: They can, but only if the deed shows the price. Have Priya leave the price off the deed and forms.
moves.fb: Hiding consideration doesn't work: transfer tax forms report it. And the reassessment premise is wrong.
moves.react: Leave it off? Is that legal?

say: Do I get STAR like the seller has? Every bit helps.
Can I keep the STAR break when I buy?

moves.text: Not the seller's. New owners sign up for the state STAR credit if income qualifies. School tax only.
moves.fb: Correct. STAR belongs to the owner; new owners get a credit check through the state, applied to school taxes.
moves.react: A check, not a discount. Got it.

moves.text: You'd register for the state STAR credit after closing. Basic needs income up to $500,000. School tax only.
moves.fb: Right. STAR applies to school taxes, and new owners receive a credit rather than the old exemption.

moves.text: Probably. Ask the assessor after you close. Most people in the town have it one way or another.
moves.fb: Vague. Explain that STAR doesn't transfer and new owners register for the credit.

moves.text: Yes, STAR stays with the house. It's printed on the bill, so it rolls over to you automatically.
moves.fb: Exemptions and STAR belong to the owner, not the house.

moves.text: Only Enhanced STAR exists anymore, so you'd need to be over 65. You won't get anything from it.
moves.fb: Basic STAR (as a credit) is available to new owners under the income limit.

moves.text: STAR lowers the whole tax bill, county and town included, by about a third. Just apply at the closing.
moves.fb: STAR applies to school taxes only, and the new-owner route is the state credit.

say: Last thing. If I think the assessment is too high after I buy, what do I do?
How do I fight the assessment if it's wrong?

moves.text: Check the record card with the assessor, grieve to the BAR by Grievance Day, then SCAR.
moves.fb: Correct ladder: assessor for facts, BAR grievance (usually the fourth Tuesday in May in towns), then SCAR for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes.
moves.react: Assessor, BAR, SCAR. Writing it down.

moves.text: Fix any errors with the assessor. Then a grievance to the BAR in May. If denied, SCAR, about $30.
moves.fb: Right. You must grieve before SCAR, and SCAR is the low-cost route for homeowners.

moves.text: Hire a tax lawyer and sue the town in Supreme Court. That's the only way to really win these.
moves.fb: Certiorari exists, but you must grieve first, and SCAR is the cheaper path for a homeowner.

moves.text: Complain to the state. They set your assessment, and they'll adjust it if you send them good comps.
moves.fb: NY has no state property tax and the state does not set your assessment. Local assessors and boards do.

moves.text: Go straight to SCAR any time of year. You don't need to file a grievance first for a one-family house.
moves.fb: You must grieve to the BAR first, and SCAR has a 30-day filing window after the final roll.

moves.text: Appeal to the NYC Tax Commission. They handle assessment appeals for the whole metro area.
moves.fb: The NYC Tax Commission is for NYC properties only. Westchester owners grieve to the local BAR.

say: My partner served in the Army. Does that help with taxes at all?
We have a veteran in the household. Any tax break for that?

moves.text: Possibly. Many towns offer a veterans exemption, larger for combat or disability. Ask the assessor.
moves.fb: Correct. Veterans exemptions (15% wartime, plus combat and disability) are applied for through the assessor.

moves.text: Many towns have a veterans exemption. The assessor has the form and the filing deadline.
moves.fb: Right direction: veterans exemptions are local options filed with the assessor.
moves.react: Taxable status date. I'll look it up.

moves.text: Maybe, I'm not totally sure. Something for veterans exists, but I don't know the details here.
moves.fb: Honest, but name the assessor as the place to apply.

moves.text: Yes, veterans pay no property tax at all in New York State. Just send the DD-214 to the town.
moves.fb: Veterans exemptions reduce assessed value partially, not eliminate tax.

moves.text: Only if the seller was a veteran too. The exemption follows the house, not whoever owns it.
moves.fb: Exemptions belong to the qualifying owner, never the house.
moves.react: Did the seller serve? I'll ask.

moves.text: Veterans exemptions are federal, so you would claim them on your income tax return instead, not locally.
moves.fb: These are local property tax exemptions applied through the assessor.

say: The title report says the seller owes last year's town taxes. Does that become my problem?
There's an unpaid tax bill on the title search. Am I on the hook?

moves.text: Tax liens come first, ahead of mortgages, so they're paid at closing from the seller's proceeds.
moves.fb: Correct. Real property tax liens have priority, and the title company makes sure they're cleared at closing.
moves.react: As long as it's paid at closing.

moves.text: It's a priority lien, so title will require payoff at closing. Priya makes sure it's cleared.
moves.fb: Right. Unpaid taxes stay with the property until paid, so they're handled at closing.

moves.text: Probably the seller's problem, not yours. Let's not worry about it until the closing day.
moves.fb: It's a priority lien on the property; the attorney must make sure it's paid.

moves.text: No, unpaid taxes are the seller's personal debt. They don't attach to the house at all.
moves.fb: Real property taxes are a lien on the property, ahead of mortgages.

moves.text: Yes, you'll owe it after closing. Buyers always inherit unpaid taxes, so ask for a credit.
moves.fb: The lien gets paid at closing; a buyer shouldn't take title subject to it.

moves.text: The mortgage gets paid first, then the taxes if there's money left. The order is by recording date.
moves.fb: Taxes and special assessments come first regardless of recording date.
moves.react: So taxes might not get paid?

say: The basement was finished without a permit. Could that raise taxes later?
The inspector thinks the finished basement was never permitted. Tax issue?

moves.text: Yes. If the assessor finds it, the value can rise and omitted taxes can be added. Get it legalized.
moves.fb: Discovered improvements can be assessed and back taxes (omitted taxes) added. Permits feed the assessor.
moves.react: So legalize it and budget a bit more.

moves.text: It could, yes. Undeclared work can bring an increase and back taxes. Priya can handle it in the contract.
moves.fb: Right. That's a legal basis for reassessment, unlike welcome stranger.

moves.text: Maybe, but towns rarely find these. I'd leave it alone and not draw any attention to it at all.
moves.fb: Hiding work invites omitted taxes and building violations later.

moves.text: No. Once you buy, the house is reset, and old work is grandfathered for property tax purposes.
moves.fb: There's no tax grandfathering. Discovered improvements can be assessed.

moves.text: Only the seller pays for that, because all the work happened before your ownership started.
moves.fb: Omitted taxes and increases can follow the property. The contract should allocate it.

moves.text: Unpermitted work lowers your assessment, since it can't legally count as living space, so that's good.
moves.fb: Not how it works. Discovered improvements tend to raise assessed value.

say: The rate is $730 per $1,000. My friend says rates are in mills. What's that?
Is $730 per thousand the same as 730 mills? And what's that per $100?

moves.text: One mill is $1 per $1,000, so that's 730 mills. Per $100, just divide by 10, which gives you $73.
moves.fb: Correct conversions: 1 mill = $0.001 = $1 per $1,000; per $100 = per $1,000 / 10.

moves.text: Same thing: $730 per $1,000 is 730 mills, or $73 per $100. The bill is still $14,600.
moves.fb: Right. The units change; the tax doesn't.
moves.react: Same bill, three ways to write it.

moves.text: Mills are an old way of saying it. I wouldn't worry, the bill is what matters in the end.
moves.fb: True but unhelpful. Converting is simple and on the exam.

moves.text: A mill is $1 per $100, so 730 mills is $7.30 per $1,000. That's much lower than it looks, actually.
moves.fb: A mill is $1 per $1,000, not per $100.

moves.text: Per $100 you multiply by 10, so the rate is $7,300 per $100 of assessed value on this house.
moves.fb: Per $100 divides by 10: $73.

moves.text: Mills only apply to school taxes. The town portion is always stated per $100, never in mills.
moves.fb: Mills are a unit of rate, used for any levy.

roleplays.debrief: You practised the property tax basics: tax = assessed value x rate, exemptions like senior and STAR belong to the owner and end at sale, and many towns assess at a fraction of value, converted with the equalization rate. Welcome stranger reassessment is illegal, but revaluations and discovered improvements are not. The appeal ladder is assessor, BAR grievance (usually the fourth Tuesday in May in towns), then SCAR for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes, and tax liens come first at closing.

questions.q: A fire district, sewer district or Business Improvement District whose properties pay for one service is a:
c: Special assessment district
School district
Census tract
Zoning district
questions.x: Properties in the district pay for that particular service. Zoning district is the trap: it controls land use, not service charges.

questions.q: A Manhattan property owner pays an extra charge that funds street cleaning and security on her block. She is likely in a:
c: Historic district
Rent stabilization zone
Business Improvement District
Opportunity zone
questions.x: BIDs are special assessment districts funding local services. Historic district is the trap: it regulates appearance, not charges.

questions.q: In New York City, a 2-family house falls into which property tax class?
c: Class 2
Class 1
Class 3
Class 4
questions.x: Class 1 covers 1 to 3 family homes and small condos. Class 2 is the trap: it covers other residential buildings.

questions.q: An office building in NYC is taxed under:
c: Class 1
Class 2
Class 3
Class 4
questions.x: Class 4 is commercial and industrial. Class 3 is the trap: it covers utility property.

questions.q: A full or partial removal of assessed value from taxation based on the owner's status or the property's use is a(n):
c: Tax lien
Special assessment
Tax exemption
Abatement of rent
questions.x: Exemptions such as STAR, senior and veterans' exemptions reduce taxable assessed value. Special assessment is the trap: it adds a charge.

questions.q: Which typically qualifies a homeowner for a New York property tax exemption?
c: Being a qualifying senior or veteran
Owning a second home
Having a large mortgage
Recently buying the home
questions.x: Senior and veterans' exemptions are based on owner status. A large mortgage is the trap: debt has no effect on assessment.

questions.q: In New York, real property taxes are levied by all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Counties
Towns
School districts
The State
questions.x: New York has no state real property tax; counties, cities, towns, villages, school districts, and special districts levy it. School districts are the tempting pick, but they levy the largest share of most tax bills.

questions.q: The term ad valorem, used to describe property taxes, means:
c: Payable in advance
According to the property's value
Based on benefit received
Based on owner income
questions.x: Ad valorem is Latin for according to value: the more valuable the property, the higher the tax. Based on benefit is the trap: that describes special assessments.

questions.q: A house has a market value of $500,000 in a town that assesses at 30% of full value. Its assessed value is:
questions.x: Assessed value = market value x ratio = $500,000 x 0.30 = $150,000. $350,000 is the trap: it subtracts 30% instead of taking 30%.

questions.q: A property is assessed at $60,000 and the tax rate is $42 per $1,000 of assessed value. The annual tax is:
questions.x: $60,000 / 1,000 = 60 units, and 60 x $42 = $2,520. $25,200 is the trap: it treats the rate as per $100.

questions.q: A house is assessed at $54,000 in a town whose state equalization rate is 12%. Its estimated full value is:
questions.x: Full value = assessed value / equalization rate = $54,000 / 0.12 = $450,000. $6,480 is the trap: it multiplies by the rate instead of dividing.

questions.q: A village must raise $5,000,000 through property taxes, and the total taxable assessed value is $250,000,000. The tax rate is:
c: 2 mills
0.2 mills
200 mills
20 mills
questions.x: $5,000,000 / $250,000,000 = 0.02 = $20 per $1,000 = 20 mills. 2 mills is the trap: 2 is the rate per $100, not per $1,000.

questions.q: A school district adopts a $30,000,000 budget and expects $12,000,000 in state aid and other non-property revenue. The tax levy is:
questions.x: Levy = budget - other revenue = $30,000,000 - $12,000,000 = $18,000,000. $30,000,000 is the trap: the budget is not all raised from property owners.

questions.q: After a sale for $850,000, a town raises the new owner's assessment to match the price but leaves identical unsold neighbors at their old assessments. This practice is:
c: Legal, since a sale price is the best evidence of value
Illegal selective (welcome stranger) reassessment
Required whenever the equalization rate changes
A special assessment on the newly sold parcel
questions.x: Singling out sold properties violates equal protection and NY assessment rules. The best-evidence answer is the trap: sales may be used, but only in a community-wide revaluation.

questions.q: A new owner's assessment may lawfully be changed for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:
c: A town-wide revaluation
An unpermitted addition is discovered
A permit for a new wing is closed out
The home just sold for a high price
questions.x: Changing an assessment just because the property sold is welcome stranger reassessment. The unpermitted addition is the tempting pick, but newly discovered physical improvements are a legitimate basis for a change.

questions.q: The main purpose of a state equalization rate is to:
c: Apportion shared county and school levies fairly
Set each town's tax rate for the year
Cap yearly increases in a home's assessment
Decide which owners qualify for STAR
questions.x: Equalization converts each municipality's assessments to full value so levies shared across towns are apportioned fairly. Setting the tax rate is the trap: local budgets and levies set the rate.

questions.q: A special assessment is best described as a charge:
c: On every county property, based on value
Levied by the State on high-value homes
On parcels a specific project benefits
Added to the bill when a property sells
questions.x: Special assessments fall only on properties that benefit from a specific improvement, such as a new sewer, and are based on benefit, not value. The every-property answer is the trap: that describes ad valorem taxes.

questions.q: In New York City, a two-family home in Canarsie falls in tax class:
c: Class 2A
Class 1
Class 3
Class 4
questions.x: Class 1 covers 1 to 3 family homes. Class 2 is the trap: it is other residential property, such as co-ops, condos, and rentals of 4 or more units.

questions.q: A Midtown office building is in NYC tax class:
c: Class 4
Class 1
Class 2C
Class 3
questions.x: Class 4 is commercial and industrial property. Class 3 is the trap: it is utility property.

questions.q: Under RPTL Article 19, an approved assessing unit that adopts the homestead tax option:
c: Exempts homes from school taxes
Assesses homes at 6% of full value
Freezes a home's assessment after sale
Sets separate rates for homes and other property
questions.x: The homestead option creates two classes with separate tax rates, so a revaluation does not suddenly shift the burden onto homeowners. The freeze answer is the trap: no assessment freeze follows a sale.

questions.q: In a municipal budget, an appropriation is:
c: The tax due on one parcel
Authority to spend for a purpose
The assessment-to-market value ratio
A lien for unpaid property taxes
questions.x: An appropriation authorizes spending a stated amount for a purpose. The levy is the trap: it is the portion of the budget raised from property taxes.

questions.q: A homeowner who buys a house in 2026 and qualifies for Basic STAR receives the benefit as:
c: An exemption printed on the tax bill
A deduction on federal income taxes
A STAR credit check from the State
A lower rate on the mortgage loan
questions.x: The STAR exemption has been closed to new applicants since 2016, so new owners register for the STAR credit, a check from the NYS Department of Taxation and Finance. The exemption answer is the trap: it continues only for owners who already had it.

questions.q: Enhanced STAR is available to qualifying homeowners who are at least:
questions.x: Enhanced STAR requires owners to be 65 or older and to meet an annual income limit. 59½ is the trap: it is the age for penalty-free IRA withdrawals, not a STAR rule.

questions.q: The NY senior citizens exemption (RPTL 467) generally:
c: Applies statewide with no income test
Covers any owner 55 or older
Passes to the buyer when the home sells
Gives 65+ owners up to 50% off
questions.x: It is a local option for owners 65 and older, reducing assessed value by up to 50% on a sliding scale under a locally set income limit. The passes-to-buyer answer is the trap: owner-based exemptions end at sale.

questions.q: A wartime veteran's home is assessed at $200,000. A 15% veterans exemption applies, and the town rate is $25 per $1,000. The town tax is:
questions.x: Exemption = $30,000, so taxable value = $170,000, and 170 x $25 = $4,250. $750 is the trap: it is the tax savings, not the tax.

questions.q: In most NY towns, Grievance Day, the deadline to file an assessment complaint with the Board of Assessment Review, is:
c: January 1
March 1
Fourth Tuesday in May
First Monday in October
questions.x: Most towns hold Grievance Day on the fourth Tuesday in May; cities, Nassau County, and NYC have their own dates. March 1 is the trap: it is the usual taxable status date, not the grievance deadline.

questions.q: After hearing a grievance, a Board of Assessment Review may do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Deny the complaint
Grant the full reduction
Grant a partial reduction
Raise the assessment
questions.x: The board can deny, fully grant, or partially grant a complaint, but it does not raise a complainant's assessment. A partial reduction is the tempting pick, but it is a common outcome.

questions.q: Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR) is available to owners of:
c: Owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes
Any property in New York State
Commercial property under $1 million
Vacant residential building lots
questions.x: SCAR is limited to owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes (and some condos). Commercial property is the trap: commercial owners use tax certiorari.

questions.q: Outside NYC, a SCAR petition is generally filed:
c: With the assessor before Grievance Day
With the Department of State within 90 days
With the county clerk after the roll
In State Supreme Court at any time
questions.x: SCAR petitions go to the county clerk, generally within 30 days after the final roll is filed, with a $30 fee, and only after a grievance was filed. The assessor answer is the trap: that is where the grievance starts, not SCAR.

questions.q: Evelyn owns a retail building in Nassau County and lost her grievance. To challenge the assessment further she would bring:
c: A SCAR petition
A tax certiorari proceeding
A complaint with the DOS
A second grievance next week
questions.x: Commercial owners challenge assessments in State Supreme Court through tax certiorari (RPTL Article 7). SCAR is the trap: it is for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes.

questions.q: An owner claims her home is assessed at a higher percentage of market value than other homes in town. This is a claim of:
c: Unequal assessment
Unlawful assessment
Misclassification
Excessive exemption
questions.x: Unequal assessment compares her assessment ratio to the town's level, using the equalization rate or neighbors' ratios. Unlawful assessment is the trap: it covers things like taxing exempt property.

questions.q: A home is assessed at $90,000 in a town with a 30% equalization rate. Recent comparable sales show its market value is $250,000. The assessed value the owner should request is:
questions.x: A fair assessment at the town's level is $250,000 x 0.30 = $75,000. $27,000 is the trap: it applies 30% to the current assessment instead of to market value.

questions.q: A lien for unpaid real property taxes generally has:
c: Priority based on its recording date
Lower priority than a first mortgage
Priority even over older recorded mortgages
No effect on a later buyer of the home
questions.x: Real property tax liens and special assessments come first, ahead of mortgages regardless of recording date. The recording-date answer is the trap: that rule orders most other liens.

questions.q: An in rem tax foreclosure is a proceeding:
c: Against the owner personally for money
Against the property for unpaid taxes
By a lender over missed mortgage payments
To challenge an assessment in court
questions.x: In rem means against the thing: the municipality forecloses on the property itself for unpaid taxes, usually after a redemption period. The personal-judgment answer is the trap: that is in personam.

questions.q: In a tax lien sale, the municipality sells:
c: Its right to collect the tax plus interest
The property at auction right away
The owner's mortgage to a new lender
A special assessment district bond
questions.x: A lien sale transfers the debt, and the owner keeps title subject to the lien; the lienholder may later foreclose if unpaid. The auction answer is the trap: that describes a foreclosure sale.

questions.q: After Tyler v. Hennepin County and NY's 2024 amendments to RPTL Article 11, surplus proceeds from a tax foreclosure sale above the taxes owed:
c: Are kept by the county that foreclosed
Go to the State's general fund
Can be claimed by the former owner
Are paid to the tax lien buyer
questions.x: Keeping surplus equity is an unconstitutional taking, so NY now provides a process for former owners to claim the surplus. The county answer is the trap: that was the old practice the Supreme Court rejected.

questions.q: Which is a main reason governments favor real property as a tax base?
c: It is hard to conceal and cannot be moved away
Its value never changes from year to year
Owners can deduct the full tax from their income
It is taxed by the state rather than by localities
questions.x: Land cannot move or be hidden, so revenue is predictable. Values do change, which is why reassessments exist, and in NY the state levies no property tax at all.

questions.q: In most of New York, the largest single piece of a homeowner's property tax bill is usually the:
c: County tax for courts and social services
Town tax for roads and parks
School district tax
Village tax for local services
questions.x: The school tax is usually the biggest share of the bill. County and town taxes are real but smaller, and the county share is often collected on the town bill.

questions.q: Town A assesses at 100% of full value and Town B at 20%. Which statement is correct under NY law?
c: Both towns must reassess to 100% by state law
Town B is underassessing and must refund taxes
Each town may choose its own uniform percentage
The county must set one percentage for both towns
questions.x: Each assessing unit may choose its own uniform percentage of value; the law requires equity, meaning every property in a class at the same percentage. A 100% mandate is the tempting but wrong idea.

questions.q: In Nassau County, which body serves as the assessing unit?
c: Each town and village separately
The school districts
The NYS Department of Taxation and Finance
The county itself
questions.x: Nassau is the exception where the county assesses. Elsewhere the city or town is usually the assessing unit, and in NYC it is the Department of Finance. The state does not assess homes.

questions.concept: Why similar homes pay different taxes
questions.q: Two identical colonials on one block pay $14,000 and $21,000. The town last revalued in 1985. What is the best fix for the inequity?
c: Raise the cheaper house's assessment when it sells
A community-wide reassessment of every parcel
Grant the higher-taxed owner a hardship exemption
Have the state set a new tax rate for the block
questions.x: A revaluation puts every parcel at the same percentage of current value. Raising only the house that sells is the illegal welcome stranger practice.

questions.concept: Why similar homes pay different taxes
questions.q: Two similar houses on the same street may have very different tax bills for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:
c: A finished basement built without a permit
A fire district boundary splitting the street
A senior exemption held by one owner
One owner's higher household income level
questions.x: Property tax is ad valorem: it follows assessed value, not the owner's income. Unpermitted improvements, district lines and exemptions all really do split bills (income matters only for exemption eligibility).

questions.q: A town discovers a bathroom and deck that were added years ago without permits. What may it do?
c: Nothing, since the owner's assessment is final
Revoke the certificate of occupancy and close the home
Reassess the whole home to its current sale value
Add them and bill omitted taxes within legal limits
questions.x: Undeclared improvements can be added to the roll and back taxes billed for prior years within limits set by law. Repricing the whole home to market is not what the discovery allows.

questions.q: A buyer's attorney checks permits and certificates of occupancy partly because:
c: Unpermitted additions can bring back taxes later
Permits lower the assessed value of a home
The assessor must approve every sale in advance
Closed permits make a home exempt from reassessment
questions.x: Closed permits tell the assessor about additions; an undeclared one can be added to the roll with back taxes. Permits do not lower values or exempt a home from reassessment.

questions.q: After a revaluation, total assessed value in a town doubles while the budget is unchanged. The tax rate will most likely:
c: Double, as assessments did
Stay the same as last year
Fall by about half
Rise by the 2% tax cap
questions.x: Rate equals levy divided by assessed value. Same levy, twice the base, so the rate drops by about half. A revaluation redistributes the levy; it does not raise it.

questions.q: A community-wide reassessment, by itself, does what to the total amount a town collects in property tax?
c: Leaves it unchanged, shifting shares
Raises it by the growth in value
Lowers it to the old assessment total
Raises it until the next budget vote
questions.x: The levy comes from the budget, not from assessments, so reassessment only changes who pays what share. Expecting the town to collect more because values rose is the trap.

questions.q: New York's property tax cap generally limits annual growth in a local tax levy to:
c: 5% or inflation, whichever is less
2% or inflation, whichever is less
2% or inflation, whichever is greater
6% a year and 20% over five years
questions.x: The cap is 2% or the rate of inflation, whichever is less, unless overridden. 6% a year and 20% over five years is the NYC Class 1 assessment cap, a different rule.

questions.q: A school district levied $20,000,000 last year. Inflation is 3%. Absent an override and before any allowed exclusions, the cap limits this year's levy to about:
c: $20,000,000 (no increase)
questions.x: The cap is the lesser of 2% or inflation: 2% here. $20,000,000 x 1.02 = $20,400,000. Using the 3% inflation figure ($20,600,000) is the trap.

questions.q: A homeowner lives inside an incorporated village in a NY town. For general municipal services she pays:
c: Village tax only, in place of town tax
Town tax only, which funds the village
Both the town tax and the village tax
County tax only, shared with the village
questions.x: A village sits inside a town, so villagers pay town AND village tax (plus county and school taxes). Thinking the village replaces the town is the trap.

questions.q: Which properties pay a fire district's or library district's tax?
c: Only parcels inside that district
Every parcel in the county
Every parcel in the school district
Only parcels that used the service that year
questions.x: Special districts tax only the parcels inside their boundaries, regardless of actual use that year. That is why a district line can split one street's bills.

questions.q: A seller never paid a $6,000 sewer special assessment. The house is sold. The unpaid assessment:
c: Is erased because the seller no longer owns it
Ranks behind the buyer's new first mortgage
Survives the sale as a lien ahead of the loan
Becomes a personal debt of the listing broker
questions.x: Special assessments, like general taxes, are priority liens that stay with the property and come ahead of the mortgage. Assuming the mortgage comes first is the trap.

questions.q: Compared with a first mortgage recorded earlier, a lien for an unpaid special assessment generally ranks:
c: Behind it, by recording date
Equal to it, sharing pro rata
Behind it unless the lender consents
Ahead of it
questions.x: Tax and special assessment liens jump ahead of mortgages regardless of recording date. 'First in time, first in right' does not apply to them.

questions.q: In NYC, the assessed value of a Class 1 home generally may rise no more than:
c: 6% a year and 20% over 5 years
8% a year and 30% over five years
2% a year or inflation
20% a year and 45% over 5 years
questions.x: Class 1 increases are capped at 6% a year and 20% over five years. 8% and 30% is the cap for smaller Class 2 buildings, and 2% is the levy cap outside NYC.

questions.q: A Park Slope brownstone bought in 1990 has a tax bill far below that of a new condo at the same price. Most likely reason?
c: Townhouses are exempt from the school tax portion
New condos also pay a state property tax
Brownstones are assessed at 45% instead of 6%
Class 1 caps kept its assessment below market
questions.x: Class 1 caps limit how fast assessed value can rise, so an older home's assessment can lag far behind market value, and a buyer generally inherits it. Class 1 is 6%, not 45%.

questions.concept: Exemptions do not pass to buyers
questions.q: A 72-year-old seller's tax bill reflects senior and Enhanced STAR benefits. A 35-year-old buyer asks what taxes to budget. The agent should:
c: Quote the seller's bill, since exemptions run with the land
Estimate the bill without the seller's exemptions
Tell the buyer the exemptions carry over for 5 years
Quote half the seller's bill as a safe estimate
questions.x: Exemptions attach to the owner's eligibility and disappear at the next roll after a sale. Quoting the seller's discounted bill is the trap that shocks buyers.

questions.concept: Exemptions do not pass to buyers
questions.q: A veterans exemption on a home, after the veteran sells to a non-veteran, generally:
c: Ends, since it depends on the owner
Transfers to the buyer with the deed
Continues until the next revaluation
Converts into a STAR credit for the buyer
questions.x: Exemptions follow the owner's eligibility, not the land, so they do not pass to a buyer. A new owner must qualify and apply on their own.

questions.q: Which property is most likely fully exempt from real property tax?
c: A church building used for worship
A rented home owned by a pastor
A store leased to a charity's donor
A for-profit private hospital
questions.x: Religious, charitable, educational nonprofit and government property is fully exempt when used for the exempt purpose. A for-profit hospital or property rented out for income does not qualify.

questions.q: A nonprofit school owns a building it uses for classes. Its exemption generally depends on:
c: The value of the building
Whether neighbors approve the exemption
Use for its exempt purpose
The school's total yearly enrollment
questions.x: Full exemption for nonprofit property applies when the parcel is used for the exempt purpose. Value and enrollment do not decide it.

questions.q: Under the alternative veterans exemption, a veteran with wartime and combat zone service but no disability generally receives:
c: 25% off assessed value
15% off the assessed value
Half of assessed value
10% off the school tax only
questions.x: Wartime service gives 15% and combat zone service adds 10%, for 25%, up to local caps. 15% alone ignores the combat add-on, and veterans exemptions generally do not reach school taxes.

questions.q: A veterans exemption generally reduces which parts of a homeowner's bill?
c: Only the school tax portion
Every portion of the bill, school taxes included
Special district charges only
County, town and city taxes, not school
questions.x: Veterans exemptions apply to county, town and city taxes; school taxes are covered only if the district opts in. STAR, not the veterans exemption, is the school tax benefit.

questions.q: Basic STAR reduces which taxes for an eligible homeowner?
c: County and town taxes
The school tax portion only
All property taxes on the bill
State income tax on the owner
questions.x: STAR (School Tax Relief) reduces school taxes only. It does not touch county, town or city taxes, and it is not an income tax break.

questions.q: A new owner-occupant applying in 2026 qualifies for the Basic STAR credit if household income is no more than:
c: No income limit applies
questions.x: The Basic STAR credit has a $500,000 income limit. $250,000 is the limit for keeping the old STAR exemption, and $110,750 is Enhanced STAR's limit.

questions.q: In New York City, 485-x and the legacy 421-a program are best described as:
c: Senior citizen income limits
Grievance filing deadlines
Exemptions for some new construction
Equalization rates set by the state each year
questions.x: 485-x (and the older 421-a) are tax exemptions for certain new construction. Buyers should know when such an abatement phases out, since the bill will rise.

questions.q: NY property tax exemptions exist for all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Members of the clergy
Agricultural land
Disabled persons with limited income
First-time buyers of any age
questions.x: There are exemptions for clergy, farmland and disabled persons with limited income. Being a first-time buyer does not by itself create a property tax exemption.

questions.q: A homeowner's record card lists a garage that was torn down years ago. The best first step is to:
c: File for tax certiorari in State Supreme Court
Talk to the assessor to correct the fact
Petition for SCAR with the county clerk
Stop paying the tax until it is fixed
questions.x: Factual errors are fixed informally with the assessor, ideally when the tentative roll comes out. SCAR and certiorari come only after a grievance, and not paying creates a lien.

questions.q: The best time to ask the assessor informally to fix a wrong square footage is:
c: After the tax bill has been paid
When the tentative roll is published
Only after a SCAR hearing is denied
When the home is next listed for sale
questions.x: The tentative roll is the window to fix errors informally, before Grievance Day. Waiting for a sale or for SCAR skips the easiest step.

questions.q: A homeowner loses at SCAR and wants to challenge the decision. The available route is:
c: A tax certiorari proceeding
A new BAR grievance that year
An Article 78 proceeding
An appeal to the state assessor
questions.x: By choosing SCAR the homeowner gives up certiorari, so the only challenge is an Article 78 proceeding. Certiorari is the trap: it was waived.

questions.q: By choosing SCAR after losing a grievance, a homeowner gives up:
c: Tax certiorari for that assessment
Any future STAR benefit on the home
The right to grieve in later years
Her senior citizens exemption
questions.x: SCAR and certiorari are alternatives: choosing SCAR waives certiorari for that assessment. It does not affect exemptions or the right to grieve next year.

questions.q: A Brooklyn Class 1 homeowner thinks her new tentative assessment is too high. She appeals to the:
c: Board of Assessment Review on Grievance Day
NYC Tax Commission, generally by March 15
County clerk by SCAR petition in May
State Supreme Court by certiorari first
questions.x: NYC has no Grievance Day or BAR; owners appeal to the NYC Tax Commission (by March 1, or March 15 for Class 1). SCAR is available afterward, not first.

questions.q: In NYC, the Department of Finance publishes tentative assessed values in:
c: May, on Grievance Day
January
July, with the final roll
October, with the tax bill
questions.x: NYC publishes tentative values in January, and appeals go to the Tax Commission by March 1 (March 15 for Class 1). The fourth Tuesday in May is Grievance Day in most towns outside NYC.

questions.q: When listing a home, the best way for an agent to state annual taxes is to:
c: Copy the figure the seller gives
Leave taxes out of the listing entirely
Average the taxes of three neighbors
Verify it on the official tax roll
questions.x: Agents verify taxes on the official roll rather than repeating the seller's number, and note any exemptions the buyer will not get. Copying the seller's figure is the common mistake.

questions.q: A licensee helping a buyer with property taxes should do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Disclose a known pending revaluation
Mention a special assessment for a new sewer
Explain that lenders often escrow taxes
Decide the owner's certiorari strategy
questions.x: Grievance and certiorari strategy belongs to the owner, an attorney or a tax consultant; the agent can supply comps. Disclosing known tax facts and explaining escrow are part of the job.

questions.q: A Westchester homeowner's tax bills include county, town, school, and fire district charges. Which level of government does NOT appear because it levies no real property tax?
c: The incorporated village
The State of New York
The special district
The school district
questions.x: New York State levies no real property tax; local governments and districts do. The special district is the trap: fire, water, and library districts commonly levy property taxes.

questions.q: Which charge is NOT an ad valorem tax?
c: A county real property tax
A school district tax
A sidewalk assessment
A town property tax
questions.x: A special assessment is based on the benefit to the parcel, not its value. School taxes are the tempting pick because they are billed separately, but they are still based on assessed value.

questions.q: A town assesses at 25% of full value. A home with a market value of $420,000 should have an assessed value of:
questions.x: $420,000 x 0.25 = $105,000. $315,000 is the trap: it subtracts 25% instead of taking 25%.

questions.q: A property is assessed at $85,000. The tax rate is $3.20 per $100 of assessed value. The annual tax is:
questions.x: $85,000 / 100 = 850 units, and 850 x $3.20 = $2,720. $272 is the trap: it treats the rate as per $1,000.

questions.q: Town assessments total $45,000,000 and the State estimates the town's full market value at $300,000,000. The town's equalization rate is about:
questions.x: Equalization rate = assessed / full value = $45,000,000 / $300,000,000 = 15%. 6.7% is the trap: it divides the wrong way and drops a factor of 100.

questions.q: A town must raise $3,600,000 and its taxable assessed value is $120,000,000. The tax rate per $100 of assessed value is:
questions.x: $3,600,000 / $120,000,000 = 0.03, which is $3.00 per $100 ($30 per $1,000, or 30 mills). $30.00 is the trap: that is the rate per $1,000.

questions.q: A town's property tax levy is $9,000,000 and its total budget is $14,500,000. How much does the town expect from non-property sources?
questions.x: Budget - levy = other revenue: $14,500,000 - $9,000,000 = $5,500,000. $23,500,000 is the trap: it adds the levy to the budget.

questions.q: A town reassesses every parcel at once using recent sales, and a newly purchased home's assessment rises along with its neighbors'. This is:
c: A lawful community-wide revaluation
Illegal welcome stranger reassessment
A special assessment on the new owner
An in rem adjustment after a sale
questions.x: Using sales in a community-wide revaluation is lawful; the problem is singling out sold parcels. The welcome stranger answer is the trap: here every parcel was treated alike.

questions.q: Jordan's buyer closed in April. In June her assessment jumps by the sale price gain while identical neighbors stay the same. Her strongest ground is that the change is:
c: A special assessment on her parcel
A lawful use of the best evidence
Selective reassessment upon sale
A required equalization update
questions.x: Raising only a recently sold parcel is welcome stranger (selective) reassessment, which NY courts reject. The best-evidence answer is the trap: sales may be used only in an even-handed revaluation.

questions.q: Two towns share a school district. Town A assesses at 100% of value and Town B at 20%. Without equalization rates, Town B's owners would likely pay:
c: The same share as Town A
More than their fair share
Nothing toward the school levy
Less than their fair share
questions.x: Town B's low assessments would understate its value, shifting school taxes onto Town A; equalization converts both to full value. The more-than-fair answer is the trap: it reverses the effect of a low assessment ratio.

questions.q: A village installs new sidewalks on one street and bills only that street's owners, by frontage. This charge is:
c: An ad valorem tax
A special assessment
A real estate transfer tax
An in rem lien sale
questions.x: A charge on parcels benefited by a specific improvement, apportioned by benefit such as frontage, is a special assessment. Ad valorem is the trap: it is based on value and spread across all taxable parcels.

questions.q: In NYC, a co-op apartment building on the Upper West Side falls in tax class:
c: Class 2
Class 1D
Class 4
Class 3
questions.x: Class 2 includes co-ops, condos, and rental buildings of 4 or more units. Class 1 is the trap: it is for 1 to 3 family homes and small condos.

questions.q: Each of the following is matched with its correct NYC tax class EXCEPT:
c: Three-family home: Class 1
Rental building of 40 units: Class 2
Utility company property: Class 4
Warehouse in Long Island City: Class 4
questions.x: Utility property is Class 3, not Class 4. The warehouse is the tempting pick, but commercial and industrial property is Class 4.

questions.q: After a revaluation, a town fears that homeowners' share of the levy will jump. Which RPTL Article 19 tool lets it set separate tax rates for homes and other property?
c: The STAR exemption
An equalization rate
The homestead option
A tax certiorari filing
questions.x: The homestead option creates homestead and non-homestead classes with separate rates. The equalization rate is the trap: it apportions shared levies between towns, not between classes within one.

questions.q: In a municipal budget, the portion of spending to be raised from real property taxes is the:
c: Appropriation
Assessment roll
Equalization rate
Tax levy
questions.x: The tax levy is the amount raised from property taxes after other revenue is subtracted. Appropriation is the trap: it is the authorization to spend, not the amount taxed.

questions.q: A homeowner has received the Basic STAR exemption on her bill since 2010 and has not moved. Under current rules she:
c: May keep the exemption on that home
Has to switch to the credit this year
Loses STAR once she turns 65
Has to reapply to the assessor yearly
questions.x: Owners who already had the STAR exemption on their current home may keep it (or switch to the credit). The switch-this-year answer is the trap: the closure applies to new applicants.

questions.q: A married couple owns their home. One spouse is 66 and the other is 60, and their income is within the limit. For Enhanced STAR, they are:
c: Ineligible until both are 65
Eligible; one spouse is 65+
Ineligible, as one is under 62
Eligible after one more year
questions.x: For married owners, Enhanced STAR requires only one spouse to be 65 or older, subject to the income limit. The both-spouses answer is the trap: the age test is met by either spouse.

questions.q: A 70-year-old owner with modest income receives the RPTL 467 senior exemption, then sells to a 40-year-old buyer. The buyer's tax bill will:
c: Keep the senior exemption
Lose the senior exemption at sale
Keep half of the exemption
Keep it for one more year
questions.x: The senior exemption depends on the owner's age and income, so it ends when the home is sold. The keep-half answer is the trap: no partial carryover exists.

questions.q: A home is assessed at $160,000 and receives a 10% veterans exemption. The town rate is $30 per $1,000. The town tax is:
questions.x: Exemption = $16,000, so taxable value = $144,000, and 144 x $30 = $4,320. $4,800 is the trap: it ignores the exemption.

questions.q: An owner in a typical upstate town believes her assessment is too high. Her first step is to:
c: File a grievance by Grievance Day
File SCAR before Grievance Day
Start a tax certiorari case first
Complain to the Department of State
questions.x: Review starts with a grievance to the Board of Assessment Review, usually by the fourth Tuesday in May. The SCAR answer is the trap: SCAR is available only after a grievance has been filed and decided.

questions.q: The body that hears a homeowner's assessment grievance in most NY towns is the:
c: Town board
Board of Assessment Review
Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA)
County clerk
questions.x: The Board of Assessment Review hears grievances. The county clerk is the trap: the clerk receives SCAR petitions after the grievance stage.

questions.q: Which owner may use SCAR after losing a grievance?
c: An investor with a vacant two-family
A landlord with a 12-unit building
An owner living in her three-family
A company with a retail strip mall
questions.x: SCAR is for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family residences. The vacant two-family is the trap: the size fits, but the owner does not live there.

questions.q: Outside NYC, the filing fee for a SCAR petition is:
questions.x: The SCAR filing fee is $30, paid at the county clerk. $65 is the trap: it is the salesperson license fee.

questions.q: A tax certiorari proceeding to challenge a commercial assessment is brought under:
c: RPTL Article 7 in Supreme Court
RPTL Article 11
RPL Article 12-A
Article 78 of the CPLR
questions.x: Tax certiorari is brought in State Supreme Court under RPTL Article 7. Article 11 is the trap: it governs tax foreclosure.

questions.q: An owner whose house is classed as commercial on the roll would bring a claim of:
c: Unequal assessment
Misclassification of the property
Excessive assessment
Unlawful assessment
questions.x: Misclassification applies where the property is placed in the wrong class, often in NYC or homestead communities. Unequal assessment is the trap: it compares assessment ratios, not class.

questions.q: A home is assessed at $120,000 in a town with a 40% equalization rate. Its market value is $250,000. By how much is it overassessed at the town's level?
questions.x: A fair assessment is $250,000 x 0.40 = $100,000, so it is $20,000 too high. $50,000 is the trap: it compares the implied full value ($300,000) to market value instead of comparing assessments.

questions.q: A home has a first mortgage recorded in 2015, a judgment recorded in 2020, and unpaid 2025 property taxes. In a foreclosure sale, which is paid first?
c: The 2015 mortgage
The 2020 judgment
They share pro rata
The 2025 taxes
questions.x: Real property tax liens take priority over other liens regardless of recording date. The 2015 mortgage is the trap: first in time wins only among non-tax liens.

questions.q: In an in rem tax foreclosure, before title passes the owner typically has a:
c: Redemption period
Grievance Day
Right of rescission
Homestead option
questions.x: A redemption period lets the owner pay the back taxes and keep the property. Right of rescission is the trap: it is a TILA right on certain refinances.

questions.q: Nassau County sells the lien on a delinquent home to an investor. Immediately after the sale, title to the home is held by:
c: The lien investor
The owner, with a lien
The county treasurer
The first mortgage lender
questions.x: A lien sale transfers the right to collect, not the property; the owner keeps title subject to the lien. The investor answer is the trap: the investor gains title only by later foreclosing.

questions.q: A home with $20,000 in unpaid taxes is sold at a tax foreclosure auction for $220,000. Under current NY law, the $200,000 surplus:
c: Goes to the county that foreclosed
Goes to the winning bidder at auction
Can be claimed by the former owner
Goes to the State general fund
questions.x: After Tyler v. Hennepin County and NY's 2024 law, former owners may claim surplus proceeds above the taxes owed. The county answer is the trap: keeping surplus equity is an unconstitutional taking.

questions.q: A Putnam County house is assessed at $96,000. The town's equalization rate is 32%. What full market value is the assessment implying?
questions.x: Full value = assessed value / equalization rate = $96,000 / 0.32 = $300,000. $30,720 is the trap: it multiplies by the rate instead of dividing, which only makes sense when going from market value to assessed value.

questions.q: A buyer is paying $380,000 for a house assessed at $171,000 in a town with a 45% equalization rate. Which conclusion is correct?
c: It implies $171,000, so it is far too low
It implies $380,000, matching the price
It implies $76,950, so the buyer overpaid
It implies $844,444, so it is far too high
questions.x: $171,000 / 0.45 = $380,000, exactly the price, so the house is assessed at the town's level. $76,950 is the trap: multiplying $171,000 by 45% instead of dividing. Assessed value alone means nothing until it is converted with the town's level.

questions.q: A homeowner outside New York City misses Grievance Day and then tries to file for Small Claims Assessment Review. The likely result is:
c: The petition fails because a board grievance is a prerequisite
The hearing goes ahead because SCAR is designed to replace the grievance step
The petition is transferred to State Supreme Court as a certiorari case
The hearing goes ahead but the officer is limited to a partial reduction
questions.x: SCAR and certiorari both require a prior complaint to the Board of Assessment Review on that roll. Without it, the petition fails. The second choice is the trap: SCAR is the step after the grievance, not a substitute for it.

questions.q: All of the following are true of the grievance step in most New York towns EXCEPT:
c: It is filed with the Board of Assessment Review
It is usually due by the fourth Tuesday in May
It may be filed by an owner who will pay the tax
It may be skipped by owners who choose SCAR
questions.x: No owner may skip the grievance: it is the prerequisite for both SCAR and certiorari. The other statements are accurate, including that a new owner who will pay the taxes may file. The May date is the tempting wrong pick, but it is correct for most towns, though cities and Nassau differ.

questions.q: A town assesses at 40% of value. A house worth $500,000 is assessed at $240,000, while similar homes are assessed at about $200,000. The strongest ground for a grievance is:
c: Excessive, because $240,000 is too much for the house
Unequal, because it is assessed at 48% of value
Unlawful, because a fractional assessment is illegal
Misclassified, because it should be a homestead
questions.x: $240,000 / $500,000 = 48%, above the town's 40% level, so the house carries a bigger share than its neighbors: unequal assessment. Excessive is the trap: the assessed value is far below market value, so it is not excessive. Fractional assessment at a uniform percentage is legal in New York.

questions.q: In a grievance, an "excessive" assessment generally means that:
c: The assessed value is above the town's average for the street
The tax bill rose faster than the town's overall tax levy
The assessed value exceeds the property's full market value
The property is assessed at a higher ratio than its neighbors
questions.x: Excessive means the assessed value is more than full value (or an exemption was improperly denied in part). Assessed at a higher ratio than neighbors is the trap: that is the definition of unequal assessment, the usual claim in towns that assess at a fraction of value.

questions.q: A home's market value is $620,000. The town's level of assessment is 15%, but the home is assessed at $105,400. What reduction should the owner request?
questions.x: Fair assessment = $620,000 x 0.15 = $93,000. Reduction = $105,400 minus $93,000 = $12,400. $93,000 is the trap: it is the correct target assessment, not the reduction the question asks for.

questions.q: A town assesses at 25%. A homeowner shows a market value of $440,000. The combined tax rate is $120 per $1,000. If the board sets a fair assessment, what will the annual tax be?
questions.x: Fair assessment = $440,000 x 0.25 = $110,000. Tax = 110 x $120 = $13,200. $52,800 is the trap: it applies the rate to full market value instead of the assessed value.

questions.q: An owner-occupant of a Rockland County two-family home loses a SCAR hearing and believes the officer misapplied the law. What review is available?
c: A new SCAR hearing before a different officer
A tax certiorari case in State Supreme Court
An appeal to the Board of Assessment Review
An Article 78 proceeding
questions.x: Choosing SCAR waives certiorari on that roll; a SCAR decision may be reviewed only through an Article 78 proceeding. Certiorari is the trap: it was the alternative to SCAR, not a follow-up after it.

questions.q: Small Claims Assessment Review is available for all of the following EXCEPT:
c: An owner-occupied one-family home
An owner-occupied six-unit building
An owner-occupied two-family home
An owner-occupied three-family home
questions.x: SCAR covers owner-occupied one, two, and three family homes used exclusively as residences. A six-unit building goes to tax certiorari. The three-family is the tempting wrong pick, but three units is the upper limit and still qualifies.

questions.q: A village levy is $9,000,000 on total taxable assessed value of $300,000,000. After a revaluation, total assessed value is $750,000,000 and the levy is unchanged. The new rate per $1,000 is:
questions.x: Old rate: $9,000,000 / $300,000,000 = $30 per $1,000. New rate: $9,000,000 / $750,000,000 = $12 per $1,000. $30.00 is the trap: the old rate. Higher assessments with the same levy lower the rate.

questions.q: A town reassesses every parcel at 100% of value, doubling the total roll, while the levy stays the same. Which owner's bill most likely rises?
