c: An owner whose stale assessment lagged rising values
An owner whose house was assessed at the old level
An owner whose value rose in line with the town
An owner whose house was assessed above the level
questions.x: A revaluation redistributes the levy. Parcels with stale, low assessments catch up and pay more; parcels already at the correct level pay about the same as the rate falls. The over-assessed owner is the trap: that owner's share actually falls.

questions.concept: Exemptions vs caps after a sale
questions.q: A Staten Island one-family home is sold. The seller had SCHE and a capped Class 1 assessment. After the sale, the buyer most likely keeps:
c: The SCHE exemption and the capped assessment
The capped assessment but not the SCHE exemption
Neither the SCHE exemption nor the capped value
The SCHE exemption but not the capped assessment
questions.x: Class 1 caps stay with the property, so the buyer generally inherits the capped assessed value. SCHE depends on the owner's age and income and ends with the seller's ownership. Keeping both is the trap: buyers who budget from the seller's bill often assume exemptions stay.

questions.concept: Exemptions vs caps after a sale
questions.q: When a NYC one-family home is sold, all of the following generally end with the seller's ownership EXCEPT:
c: The seller's veterans exemption
The seller's Enhanced STAR benefit
The seller's SCHE exemption
The capped Class 1 assessed value
questions.x: The capped assessment is tied to the property and generally carries over to the buyer. Veterans, Enhanced STAR, and SCHE benefits all depend on the owner and end at the sale. Enhanced STAR is the tempting wrong pick because it feels like a property program, but its age and income tests are personal.

questions.q: A Queens Class 1 home is assessed at $30,000, and its target assessment at 6% of market value is $55,000. With no physical changes and room under the five-year cap, next year's maximum assessed value is:
questions.x: The annual Class 1 cap is 6%: $30,000 x 1.06 = $31,800. $36,000 is the trap: it applies the 20% five-year cap in one year. The $55,000 target is where the assessment is heading, a few capped steps at a time.

questions.q: A Brooklyn Class 1 home's assessed value has risen 6% in each of the last three years. Its owner adds a $200,000 rear extension. Which statement is accurate?
c: The extension cannot be added until the five-year cap resets
The extension is limited to the 6% annual cap like any increase
The extension's value is added to the assessment outside the caps
The extension moves the home into Class 2 at a 45% assessment ratio
questions.x: Caps limit market-driven increases. Physical changes are added outside them: $200,000 x 6% = $12,000 of added assessed value. Limiting it to 6% is the trap: that rule applies to market growth only. An extension does not change the class unless the unit count reaches four.

questions.concept: Enhanced STAR vs senior exemption income
questions.q: A 70-year-old owner-occupant in Yonkers has household income of $85,000. Which benefit can she most likely receive?
c: The senior citizens exemption, since she is over 65
Both, since each requires just age and occupancy
Neither, since owners over 65 receive the STAR credit instead
Enhanced STAR, since her income is under its limit
questions.x: Enhanced STAR's income limit ($110,750 for 2026 benefits) easily covers $85,000. The senior citizens exemption caps income at no more than $58,399 even with a full sliding scale. The over-65 answer is the trap: age alone does not qualify an owner for the senior exemption.

questions.concept: Enhanced STAR vs senior exemption income
questions.q: Which comparison of Enhanced STAR and the senior citizens exemption is accurate?
c: STAR covers school tax; the senior exemption is a local option
Enhanced STAR reduces assessed value for each taxing jurisdiction
The senior exemption has a higher income ceiling than Enhanced STAR
Both require each owner on the deed to be at least 65 years old
questions.x: Enhanced STAR is a state school tax benefit; the senior citizens exemption is adopted (or not) by each county, city, town, village, and school district. The higher-ceiling answer is the trap: it is reversed. And for both, one qualifying owner (or spouse) meeting the age test is generally enough.

questions.concept: NYC tax class by unit count
questions.q: A Bronx building with four residential apartments and no stores falls in which NYC tax class?
c: Class 1
Class 4
Class 2
Class 3
questions.x: Class 1 stops at three family homes. Four or more residential units is Class 2. Class 1 is the trap: small buildings feel like homes, but the unit count controls.

questions.concept: NYC tax class by unit count
questions.q: An owner legally converts a Ridgewood three-family into a four-family. The most likely tax effect is:
c: No change, because owner-occupied buildings stay in Class 1
A move to Class 2, with income-based valuation at 45%
A move to Class 4, because it now earns rental income
A move to Class 3, because each unit has its own meter
questions.x: Four or more residential units is Class 2: valued as an income property, assessed at 45%, with different caps and a different rate. Owner occupancy is the trap: it does not keep a four-unit building in Class 1. Class 4 is commercial; Class 3 is utility property.

questions.q: A veteran's home is assessed at $60,000. The alternative veterans exemption removes 15% of assessed value from the county and town portions. The county and town rate is $32 per $1,000. Annual savings:
questions.x: Exempt amount: $60,000 x 15% = $9,000. Savings: 9 x $32 = $288. $1,632 is the trap: it is the tax remaining on $51,000, not the savings. $9,000 is the exempt assessed value, not dollars of tax.

questions.q: A buyer who is a combat veteran closes on a NYC home in August. The seller had a veterans exemption. When does the buyer's own exemption first apply?
c: Immediately, by assignment from the seller at closing
After five years of continuous ownership in NYC
No, since a home that had one cannot get another
The fiscal year after a timely application, due March 15
questions.x: The buyer applies in her own name, generally by March 15, for the tax year starting the following July 1. Assignment is the trap: exemptions belong to eligible owners and cannot be transferred with the deed. There is no multi-year waiting period.

questions.q: A 68-year-old with income of $44,000 bought a new home in the same Westchester town five months ago. She received the senior exemption on her old home. For the next roll she:
c: Has to wait until she has owned the new home for 12 months
May apply now, because she had the exemption on a prior home
Applies to the state, because the exemption is not local
May apply if the school district first waives the income test
questions.x: The 12-month ownership requirement does not apply to someone who received the exemption on a previous residence. Waiting 12 months is the trap: it is the general rule without its exception. The exemption is administered locally by the assessor, not the state.

questions.q: An applicant for the senior citizens exemption generally must meet all of the following requirements EXCEPT:
c: Being 65 or older, or a spouse or sibling co-owner of someone who is
Using the property as the owners' primary residence
A full 12 months of ownership despite a prior-home exemption
Having income at or below the locality's ceiling
questions.x: The 12-month ownership rule is waived for an owner who received the exemption on a previous residence. Age, primary residence, and the local income ceiling are true requirements. The age choice is the tempting wrong pick because it mentions co-owners, but one qualifying spouse or sibling co-owner is in fact enough.

questions.q: A property has a first mortgage recorded in 2016, a judgment lien docketed in 2019, and unpaid real estate taxes from 2024. In a foreclosure sale, which is paid first?
c: The 2016 first mortgage
The 2019 judgment lien
They share pro rata
The unpaid taxes
questions.x: Real property taxes are priority liens and are paid ahead of private liens regardless of when those were recorded. The 2016 mortgage is the trap: recording order ranks private liens against each other, but taxes jump ahead of all of them.

questions.q: A borrower stops paying property taxes on a Westchester home. The lender pays the overdue taxes itself. The main reason is that:
c: Lenders are required by RESPA to pay a borrower's taxes
The tax lien would otherwise outrank its mortgage
The payment converts the lender into the owner
The tax payment cancels the borrower's mortgage
questions.x: Unpaid taxes become a lien ahead of the mortgage, so a lender pays them to protect its collateral and adds the amount to the debt, usually declaring a default. The RESPA answer is the trap: RESPA governs escrow accounts and disclosures, but it is priority that drives the lender to pay.

questions.q: Under RPTL Article 11, the standard redemption period for delinquent taxes ends:
c: Six months after the lien date
Ten years after the tax bill
Two years after the lien date
When the county files its deed
questions.x: The default is two years after the lien date; a county may extend it to three or four years for residential and farm property by local law. The deed answer is the trap: by the time the county takes title, the redemption period has already run.

questions.q: A county has adopted a local law extending the redemption period for residential property to four years. A commercial garage and a one-family home became tax delinquent on the same lien date. Which is accurate?
c: The home has four years and the garage has the standard two years
Both have four years, because the county extended the period countywide
Both have two years, because local laws cannot change the Article 11 period
The garage has four years and the home has two, since homes are more urgent
questions.x: Article 11 lets a county extend the redemption period to three or four years for residential and farm property only. Commercial property keeps the standard two years. The all-parcels answer is the trap: the extension cannot reach commercial parcels.

questions.q: A county sells a tax-foreclosed house for $260,000. The taxes, interest, and costs owed total $48,000. The surplus the former owner may claim is:
questions.x: Surplus = sale price minus the amount owed: $260,000 minus $48,000 = $212,000. After Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), New York amended Article 11 in 2024 so former owners can claim it. $48,000 is the trap: that is what the county is entitled to keep.

questions.q: In Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), the U.S. Supreme Court held that a county that forecloses for unpaid taxes:
c: May keep the entire sale price because title vested in it
Has to return the property if the owner later pays in full
Cannot keep surplus value beyond the debt owed
Has to sell through a private tax lien sale
questions.x: Keeping equity beyond the tax debt is a taking without just compensation. New York responded by amending Article 11 in 2024 to create a surplus claim process. Keeping all proceeds is the trap: it describes the practice the Court rejected.

questions.q: A water district must raise $240,000 a year from 800 benefit units. A parcel is rated at 2.5 units. Its annual charge is:
questions.x: Per unit: $240,000 / 800 = $300. Parcel: 2.5 x $300 = $750. $300 is the trap: the per-unit charge, not the parcel's charge. Special assessments follow benefit units, not assessed value.

questions.q: All of the following are true of a special assessment for a sewer district EXCEPT:
c: It rises and falls with each parcel's assessed value
It is charged to parcels that benefit from the improvement
It is a lien with the same priority as property taxes
It may be relevied onto the tax bill if left unpaid
questions.x: Special assessments are measured by benefit (units, frontage, or a similar formula), not by assessed value, so they are not ad valorem. The priority answer is the tempting wrong pick, but special assessments do share the tax lien's priority.

questions.q: A Brooklyn owner's tax lien is sold in the city's lien sale. The owner most likely:
c: Loses title to the trust on the sale date
Owes nothing further to anyone after the sale
Keeps title but owes the lienholder more
Keeps title and owes the city the same amount
questions.x: A lien sale transfers the debt, not the property. The owner keeps title but now owes the lienholder's servicer, with interest and a 5% surcharge, and faces foreclosure if unpaid. Losing title is the trap: that describes an in rem tax foreclosure.

questions.q: Which NYC owner is excluded from the tax lien sale even with qualifying arrears?
c: A landlord with a six-unit building
An owner of a corner store
A co-op building corporation
An owner who receives SCHE
questions.x: Owners receiving the Senior Citizen Homeowners' Exemption (and the Disabled Homeowners' Exemption and certain other benefits) are excluded from the sale. The co-op answer is the trap: co-op buildings get a longer delinquency threshold, but they are not excluded.

questions.q: The key difference between a tax lien sale and a tax foreclosure sale is that a tax lien sale:
c: Transfers title to the government
Sells the debt, not the property
Requires the owner's written consent
Ends the owner's right to pay the tax
questions.x: In a lien sale the buyer acquires the right to collect the tax debt; the owner keeps title. In a tax foreclosure sale, the government has already taken title and sells the property. Transferring title is the trap: that is the foreclosure step, not the lien sale.

questions.q: An investor wins a county auction of tax-foreclosed property after the county took title by in rem judgment. The investor acquired:
c: The property itself, by deed
A lien to collect the taxes
A mortgage on the parcel
An option to redeem the taxes
questions.x: In an in rem foreclosure the county takes title first, then sells the property by deed. Buying a lien to collect the taxes is the trap: that describes a tax lien sale, where the owner keeps title until the lienholder forecloses.

questions.q: A house is assessed at $150,000. The village tax rate is $1.25 per $100 of assessed value. What is the village tax?
questions.x: Divide the assessed value by 100 and multiply by the rate: 1,500 x $1.25 = $1,875. Equivalently, $1.25 per $100 is $12.50 per $1,000. The $187.50 answer is the trap: it treats a per-$100 rate as per $1,000, a tenfold error.

questions.q: A school district's rate is 24.5 mills. Expressed per $100 of assessed value, the rate is:
questions.x: One mill is $0.001 per dollar, or $1 per $1,000. So 24.5 mills is $24.50 per $1,000, which is $2.45 per $100. The $24.50 answer is the trap: that is the correct figure per $1,000, not per $100.

questions.q: A town adopts appropriations of $9,000,000 and expects $3,600,000 from sales tax, state aid, and fees. Total taxable assessed value is $450,000,000. What is the town tax rate per $1,000?
questions.x: Levy = $9,000,000 minus $3,600,000 = $5,400,000. Rate = $5,400,000 / $450,000,000 = 0.012, or $12.00 per $1,000. The $20.00 answer is the trap: it divides the full budget by the roll, ignoring the revenue that does not come from property owners.

questions.q: A village's spending stays the same next year, but its state aid falls by $200,000 and its total taxable assessed value does not change. What happens?
c: The levy rises by $200,000 and the rate rises
The levy stays the same and the rate alone rises
The rate stays the same because spending did not change
The assessed values rise to cover the lost aid
questions.x: The levy is appropriations minus other revenue, so lost aid must be made up by property tax: the levy rises by $200,000, and with the same taxable roll the rate rises too. The "spending did not change" answer is the trap: the rate follows the levy, not the budget.

questions.q: Town A assesses at 25% of market value with a combined rate of $80 per $1,000 of assessed value. Town B assesses at 100% with a rate of $22 per $1,000. Comparing full value tax rates:
c: Town A is $20 per $1,000 of market value, lower than Town B
Town A is $320 per $1,000 of market value, far higher than B
Town A is $80 per $1,000 of market value, almost four times B
Town A is $22 per $1,000 of market value, the same as Town B
questions.x: Full value tax rate = nominal rate x equalization rate: $80 x 0.25 = $20 per $1,000 of market value, which is less than Town B's $22. The $320 answer is the trap: it divides by the equalization rate instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A buyer wants to compare property tax burdens in two New York towns that assess at different percentages of market value. The most useful figure is:
c: Each town's nominal tax rate per $1,000 of assessed value
Each town's total levy divided by its population
Each town's assessed value of the house being bought
Each town's rate times its state equalization rate
questions.x: Multiplying the nominal rate by the equalization rate gives the full value tax rate, tax per $1,000 of market value, which puts towns on the same basis. Comparing nominal rates is the trap: a town assessing at 25% will show a rate four times higher than one assessing at 100% for the same real burden.

questions.concept: School budget and the tax cap
questions.q: A school district proposes a budget whose levy exceeds its tax cap limit. In the May vote, 58% of voters approve it. The budget:
c: Passes, because a majority of voters approved it
Fails, because it needed at least 60% approval
Passes, if the board of education also approves it
Fails, because over-cap levies need county consent
questions.x: A school budget with a levy above the limit needs at least 60% of the votes cast. A budget within the limit needs a simple majority. The board answer is the trap: governing boards of counties, towns, and villages override by their own 60% vote, but a school district's override comes from the voters.

questions.concept: School budget and the tax cap
questions.q: All of the following are true of New York's property tax cap EXCEPT:
c: It generally limits levy growth to 2% or inflation, whichever is less
A town board may override it by a 60% vote of the board
Two failed school budget votes lead to a contingent budget
It limits the increase in each individual owner's tax bill
questions.x: The cap limits the growth of each jurisdiction's total levy, not any one owner's bill, which can rise more after a revaluation, a lost exemption, or new construction. The override and contingent budget statements are accurate: a contingent budget holds the levy to last year's level.

questions.q: An owner of a house inside an incorporated village in New York generally pays:
c: Village taxes and town-wide taxes as well
Town taxes, with no separate village tax
Village taxes in place of the town taxes
Village taxes and every part-town district tax
questions.x: A village lies within a town, so village residents pay the village tax plus the town-wide tax, along with county and school taxes. Part-town taxes, such as an outside-village highway tax, fund services the village provides itself. The "in place of" answer is the trap: a village adds a layer; it does not replace the town.

questions.q: Two houses in the same town and school district have equal assessments. One is inside the village, which has its own police; the other is outside, in a fire district. Why might their bills differ?
c: Villages assess property at a higher level than the surrounding town
Each pays a different set of jurisdictions' and districts' taxes
The house inside the village is exempt from county taxes
School taxes are levied at a lower rate inside a village
questions.x: Bills are the sum of every jurisdiction and district that taxes a parcel. The village house pays village tax; the outside house pays part-town and fire district taxes instead. Both pay county, town-wide, and the same school rate. The assessment-level answer is the trap: here both houses are on the same town roll.

questions.q: A nonprofit hospital buys several taxable houses and they become exempt. If the village levy is unchanged, the tax rate for other owners will:
c: Fall, as the hospital's services reduce costs
Stay the same, since the levy is unchanged
Fall, as the roll is reassessed at full value
Rise, as the levy is spread over less value
questions.x: Rate = levy / taxable assessed value. Removing taxable value means the same levy needs a higher rate, so remaining owners pay more. The "levy is unchanged" answer is the trap: an unchanged levy is exactly why the rate must rise when the taxable base shrinks.

questions.q: A new apartment complex receives an industrial development agency (IDA) exemption with a PILOT agreement. Which statement is accurate?
c: The PILOT goes to the IDA, which keeps it to fund its own annual budget
The project pays no tax of any kind until the agreement expires
PILOTs go to the local jurisdictions; special district charges still apply
The project pays full school taxes, and the county's share is reduced
questions.x: IDA projects are exempt from county, municipal, and school taxes but make PILOTs, which the agency must remit to the affected taxing jurisdictions in proportion to what each would have received. The exemption does not reach special district levies or special assessments. The "no tax of any kind" answer is the trap.

cram.html: No state real property tax in NY. County, city, town, village, school, special districts do.
Tax = assessed value x rate. Full value = assessed value / ratio (or equalization rate).
Levy = budget (appropriations) - other revenue. Rate = levy / total taxable assessed value.
Ad valorem = according to value. Special assessments are based on benefit, not value.
Equalization rate (state) apportions county and school levies among towns assessing at different levels.
Welcome stranger (reassessing only sold homes) is illegal. Revaluations and discovered improvements are legal.
Undeclared improvements found later can bring back (omitted) taxes; permits feed the assessor.
Homestead/non-homestead: separate rates, approved assessing units only (RPTL Art. 19).
NYC classes: 1 = 1 to 3 family (6% ratio, 6%/20% caps); 2 = other residential; 3 = utilities; 4 = commercial (45%).
Exemptions (senior, veterans, STAR) belong to the owner and do not transfer to a buyer.
Senior exemption: 65+, income-tested, up to 50%. Veterans: 15% wartime, +10% combat, + disability.
STAR: school taxes only. Basic credit income up to $500,000; Enhanced 65+ at or under $110,750 (2026-27). New owners get a credit check.
Grievance Day: usually 4th Tuesday in May in towns, to the Board of Assessment Review.
BAR decisions: deny, grant in full, grant in part.
SCAR: owner-occupied 1 to 3 family, grieve first, county clerk, 30 days after final roll, $30.
Commercial assessment appeals: tax certiorari (RPTL Art. 7) in Supreme Court.
NYC: appeal to the Tax Commission by March 1 (March 15 for Class 1).
Tax liens and special assessments come first, ahead of earlier mortgages.
Lien sale sells the debt; in rem foreclosure takes the property. Surplus now goes back to the former owner.

subjects.title: Condominiums and Cooperatives
subjects.blurb: Most New York City homes for sale are co-ops or condos, and the exam tests the difference constantly: real property vs shares, deed vs proprietary lease, common charges vs maintenance, title insurance vs lien search, and who must approve the buyer.

lessons.title: Condominiums: Real Property, Stacked
lessons.tagline: A condo buyer gets a deed, a tax bill, and a slice of everything outside the walls.
objectives: Define a condominium and explain what the buyer owns
Distinguish the declaration, bylaws, rules, and CC&Rs
Explain common elements, common interest, and common charges
Describe the sponsor's early control of the board and its limits
Spot condo title issues, including the right of first refusal and unpaid common charges

blocks.title: Long Island City, a resale on Center Boulevard
blocks.html: Leo is under contract for a one-bedroom condo with a terrace on the 22nd floor. His mortgage lender is asking for title insurance, his attorney Priya is asking whether the board waived its right of first refusal, and the building just announced a $3,000 assessment for the pool. Leo asks Jordan: "Wait, I thought I was buying an apartment. Why do I own part of a pool?"
blocks.casual: Leo's under contract for a one-bedroom condo with a terrace on the 22nd floor in Long Island City. His lender wants title insurance, his attorney Priya wants to know if the board waived its right of first refusal, and the building just announced a $3,000 assessment for the pool. Leo asks Jordan: "Wait, I thought I was buying an apartment. Why do I own part of a pool?"

deeper.plain: Leo is learning that buying a condo means owning his apartment plus a slice of everything shared in the building. That's why he pays for the pool.
deeper.picture: It's like buying a seat on a group boat. The seat is yours, and you also chip in for the hull, the engine, and the deck.
deeper.street: Leo's $3,000 is his percentage of a $500,000 pool project. Priya needs the board's right of first refusal waiver and a title policy before the closing can happen at her Downtown Brooklyn office.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't understand shared ownership get blindsided by assessments and closing requirements. An agent who can't explain it loses trust fast.
deeper.exam: Title insurance, a deed, and a right of first refusal all point to a condo. Shares, a proprietary lease, and board approval point to a co-op.

blocks.html: A condominium is a form of ownership, not a type of building. The owner holds fee simple title to a unit (the airspace inside the walls, floors, and ceilings) plus an undivided percentage interest in the common elements. It is real property. The buyer gets a deed, can get a regular mortgage, gets an owner's title insurance policy, and receives a separate real estate tax bill. New York's Condominium Act is Real Property Law Article 9-B.
blocks.casual: A condominium is a way of owning, not a kind of building. You hold fee simple title to a unit (the airspace inside the walls, floors, and ceilings) plus an undivided percentage interest in the common elements. It's real property. That means a deed, a regular mortgage, an owner's title insurance policy, and your own real estate tax bill. New York's Condominium Act is Real Property Law Article 9-B.

deeper.plain: With a condo you actually own your apartment as real estate, plus a share of the shared parts of the building.
deeper.picture: Your unit is a box of air you own outright. The building around it is a pie, and you own a slice of the whole pie, not a specific chunk.
deeper.street: Leo's 22nd floor unit gets its own deed recorded with the City Register in Queens, its own tax lot, and a 30-year mortgage from a regular bank, just like a house in Bayside.
deeper.stakes: If you call a condo a co-op or vice versa, you'll give wrong advice on financing, closing costs, and approval. That can blow a deal or a client's budget.
deeper.exam: Condo = real property, deed, fee simple. If the stem says "shares" or "personal property," it's a co-op. Condo law is RPL Article 9-B.

blocks.html: The common elements are everything that is not a unit: the land, foundation, roof, lobby, hallways, elevators, boiler, pool, gym. Unit owners own them together as tenants in common, in shares set by each unit's common interest percentage. You cannot sell your share of the lobby separately from your unit, and you cannot sue to partition the building.
blocks.casual: The common elements are everything that isn't a unit: the land, foundation, roof, lobby, hallways, elevators, boiler, pool, gym. Owners hold them together as tenants in common, in shares set by each unit's common interest percentage. You can't sell your piece of the lobby apart from your unit, and you can't sue to partition the building.

deeper.plain: Everything outside the apartments belongs to all the owners together, in set percentages. Your share stays glued to your unit.
deeper.picture: It's like a group gift card. You each put in a different amount, but nobody can cash out their part separately.
deeper.street: An owner in a Long Island City condo wants to sell "his share of the gym" to a neighbor. He can't. The share only moves when his unit is sold.
deeper.stakes: Common interest percentages drive common charges, assessments, and voting. A buyer who doesn't check the percentage can underestimate costs.
deeper.exam: Common elements are held as tenants in common and can't be partitioned or separated from the unit. That's a classic true-or-false item.

blocks.html: Some common elements are reserved for one or a few units. Leo's terrace is a classic limited common element: legally part of the common elements, but only his unit may use it. The declaration says who repairs it. Often the condo fixes the membrane underneath and the owner maintains the surface and plantings.
blocks.casual: Some common elements are reserved for one or a few units. Leo's terrace is a textbook limited common element: legally it's part of the common elements, but only his unit gets to use it. The declaration says who repairs it. Usually the condo fixes the membrane underneath and the owner handles the surface and the plants.

deeper.plain: A terrace, balcony, or storage space can belong to everyone on paper but be usable by only one owner.
deeper.picture: It's like a reserved parking space in a shared garage. The garage belongs to everyone, but only your car goes in that spot.
deeper.street: A leak from Leo's terrace drips into the unit below. The declaration says the condo maintains the waterproof membrane, so the board pays to fix it; Leo pays to replace his planters.
deeper.stakes: Who pays for a terrace leak can be a $40,000 question. Buyers and agents need to read the declaration, not guess.
deeper.exam: Limited common element = common element reserved for specific units. A distractor will call it part of the unit itself.

blocks.caption: Toggle to the condo side. Notice the deed, the separate tax lot, the percentage interest in common elements, and that the board's only veto on a sale is the right of first refusal.

blocks.text: The documents that create and run a condo

head: Document
What it does
Recorded?
rows: Creates the condo. Describes the land, building, units, common elements, and each unit's common interest percentage. Contains the use restrictions and the right of first refusal.
Yes, with the county clerk (in NYC, the City Register), along with the floor plans
The operating manual: how the board of managers is elected, meetings, budgets, how common charges are assessed and collected, insurance, repairs.
Day-to-day rules: move-in hours, pets, renovation hours, amenity use. Adopted and changed by the board.
Covenants, conditions, and restrictions that run with the land. In NY condos they live inside the declaration and bylaws; the label is more common for HOAs and planned communities.
Yes, as part of the recorded documents

deeper.plain: The declaration creates the condo, the bylaws run it, the house rules handle daily life, and CC&Rs are the binding restrictions.
deeper.picture: Declaration is the birth certificate, bylaws are the operating manual, rules are the posted house rules on the fridge.
deeper.street: Leo wants to rent his unit on a short-term site. Priya checks the recorded declaration and finds a ban on rentals under 30 days. That restriction binds him because it runs with the land.
deeper.stakes: Missing a restriction in the declaration can wreck a buyer's plan, like renting out or running a business from the unit.
deeper.exam: Recorded: declaration and bylaws. Not recorded: rules and regulations. The board can change rules; amending the declaration takes owner votes.

blocks.html: The declaration is the birth certificate. A building becomes a condominium only when the declaration is recorded. The bylaws are the operating manual, and they are recorded with it. Covenants, conditions, and restrictions (CC&Rs) are the private rules that bind every owner, like no short-term rentals or no commercial use of residential units, because they run with the land.
blocks.casual: The declaration is the birth certificate. A building only becomes a condominium once the declaration is recorded. The bylaws are the operating manual, recorded right along with it. Covenants, conditions, and restrictions (CC&Rs) are the private rules that bind every owner, like no short-term rentals or no commercial use of residential units, because they run with the land.

deeper.plain: Recording the declaration creates the condo. The bylaws explain how it runs. The restrictions bind every future owner.
deeper.picture: Until the birth certificate is filed, the baby is just a building. Filing makes it a condo.
deeper.street: A Williamsburg rental building converts to condos. Until the declaration is recorded with the City Register, no one can close on a unit, no matter how many contracts are signed.
deeper.stakes: Restrictions run with the land, so they bind buyers who never read them. Your job is to make sure your buyer reads them first.
deeper.exam: "What creates a condominium?" Recording the declaration. Not the offering plan, not the bylaws, not the first sale.

blocks.q: Which document legally creates a condominium in New York?
c: The bylaws
The recorded declaration
The offering plan
The house rules
blocks.x: Recording the declaration creates the condominium. The bylaws run it, and the offering plan is the sales disclosure document.

blocks.html: Each month the owner pays common charges: the unit's share of the building's operating budget (staff, insurance, utilities for common areas, repairs, reserves). The share is the unit's common interest percentage. Real estate taxes are not in common charges because each condo unit is its own tax lot and gets its own bill. When the budget falls short or a big project comes up, the board levies an assessment, also by percentage.
blocks.casual: Every month owners pay common charges: the unit's share of the building's operating budget (staff, insurance, common area utilities, repairs, reserves). The share equals the unit's common interest percentage. Real estate taxes are not in common charges because each condo unit is its own tax lot with its own bill. When the budget comes up short or a big project hits, the board levies an assessment, also by percentage.

deeper.plain: Common charges pay for running the building. Taxes are billed to you separately. Assessments cover extra costs.
deeper.picture: Common charges are your share of the household bills. Taxes are your own personal bill. An assessment is the surprise when the roof leaks.
deeper.street: Leo's monthly costs: $900 in common charges to the condo, a separate quarterly NYC tax bill on his unit, and the one-time $3,000 pool assessment.
deeper.stakes: Buyers comparing condo and co-op monthlies often forget condo taxes are separate. That can make a condo look cheaper than it is.
deeper.exam: Condo common charges exclude property taxes; co-op maintenance includes them. The exam loves that contrast.

blocks.title: Common charges by percentage
blocks.html:
The building's annual operating budget is $1,800,000. Leo's unit has a 0.6% common interest.
Annual share: $1,800,000 x 0.006 = $10,800.
Monthly common charges: $10,800 / 12 = $900 a month.
The $500,000 pool assessment: $500,000 x 0.006 = $3,000, which is Leo's bill.
blocks.casual:
Annual operating budget: $1,800,000. Leo's unit has a 0.6% common interest.
Annual share: $1,800,000 x 0.006 = $10,800.
Monthly common charges: $10,800 / 12 = $900 a month.
The $500,000 pool assessment: $500,000 x 0.006 = $3,000. That's Leo's bill.

deeper.plain: Multiply the total by your percentage, then divide by 12 for the monthly amount.
deeper.picture: If ten friends split a pizza by how hungry they are, your share of every pizza is your hunger percentage times the bill.
deeper.street: Leo plugs the numbers into his spreadsheet: $1,800,000 times 0.006 equals $10,800, divided by 12 equals $900. The pool: $500,000 times 0.006 equals $3,000.
deeper.stakes: Getting the math wrong in a buyer conversation means a client can't qualify or blows their budget. Lenders count common charges in the debt ratio.
deeper.exam: Convert the percentage to a decimal (0.6% = 0.006). A distractor uses 0.06 and gets $9,000 a month.

blocks.title: Unpaid common charges become a lien
blocks.html: Under the Condominium Act, unpaid common charges are a lien on the unit. The lien ranks behind real estate taxes and the unpaid balance of a first mortgage of record (RPL 339-z), and the board can foreclose it. That is why the seller's attorney orders a paid-up letter from the managing agent before closing.
blocks.casual: Under the Condominium Act, unpaid common charges become a lien on the unit. It ranks behind real estate taxes and the unpaid balance of a first mortgage of record (RPL 339-z), and the board can foreclose on it. That's why the seller's attorney orders a paid-up letter from the managing agent before closing.

deeper.plain: If an owner stops paying common charges, the condo can put a lien on the unit and foreclose. Taxes and the first mortgage get paid first.
deeper.picture: It's like a tab at the corner bar. Skip enough rounds and the owner holds your coat until you settle up.
deeper.street: A seller in Hunters Point owes $7,200 in back charges. The managing agent's paid-up letter shows the balance, and Priya makes sure it's paid from the seller's proceeds at closing.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who closes without a paid-up letter can inherit a lien. That's a direct hit to the buyer and the title company.
deeper.exam: Condo lien priority: behind property taxes and the first mortgage of record. The paid-up letter is how closing confirms no lien.

blocks.q: A condo owner's monthly common charges generally do NOT include:
c: Lobby staff salaries
The building's insurance
The unit's own real estate taxes
A contribution to reserves
blocks.x: Each condo unit is a separate tax lot with its own tax bill. In a co-op, by contrast, the building's taxes are paid through maintenance.

blocks.html: The sponsor is the developer or converter that creates the condo and sells the units under an offering plan. In the beginning the sponsor owns everything, so it appoints the first board members and hires the first managing agent. That makes sense on day one and becomes a conflict by year three, when the sponsor still controls the board that is supposed to chase the sponsor for construction defects.
blocks.casual: The sponsor is the developer or converter who creates the condo and sells units under an offering plan. At the start the sponsor owns everything, so it appoints the first board members and hires the first managing agent. That makes sense on day one. By year three it's a conflict, because the sponsor still controls the board that's supposed to chase the sponsor for construction defects.

deeper.plain: The developer runs the building at first, which gets awkward when the building needs to complain about the developer's work.
deeper.picture: It's like a contractor who builds your house and then also gets to be the inspector who checks his own work.
deeper.street: A new condo in Long Island City has leaking windows. The sponsor-appointed board keeps delaying a claim against the sponsor. Owners push for turnover so they can hire their own engineer.
deeper.stakes: Sponsor control can delay defect claims until warranties or deadlines run out. Buyers in new buildings should know when control shifts.
deeper.exam: Sponsor = developer or converter. It appoints the first board and managing agent. Know that control is temporary.

blocks.html: So control is limited. The offering plan must say when the sponsor gives up control, and the Attorney General generally expects owner control no later than 5 years after the first unit closing. Many plans also require turnover earlier, once a stated share of units (often 50%) is sold. After turnover, unit owners elect the board of managers, which can replace the sponsor's managing agent.
blocks.casual: So control has limits. The offering plan has to say when the sponsor gives it up, and the Attorney General generally expects owners in control no later than 5 years after the first unit closing. Many plans require turnover sooner, once a stated share of units (often 50%) is sold. After turnover, unit owners elect the board of managers, which can replace the sponsor's managing agent.

deeper.plain: The developer has to hand control to the owners within about 5 years of the first closing, often sooner.
deeper.picture: It's training wheels with an expiration date. At some point the owners have to ride on their own.
deeper.street: A Greenpoint condo's first closing was in 2022. By 2027 at the latest, owners elect their own board, and the new board fires the sponsor's managing agent for a cheaper one.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who expect a say in the building may be disappointed early on. Agents should check the plan for the turnover date.
deeper.exam: Turnover: no later than 5 years after the first closing (often earlier at about 50% sold). After that, owners elect the board of managers.

blocks.title: Board of managers vs board of directors
blocks.html: A condo is governed by a board of managers elected by unit owners. A co-op is a corporation governed by a board of directors elected by shareholders. Exam questions swap these.
blocks.casual: Trap: a condo is run by a board of managers elected by unit owners. A co-op is a corporation run by a board of directors elected by shareholders. Exam questions swap these.

deeper.plain: Condo boards are "managers." Co-op boards are "directors," because a co-op is a corporation.
deeper.picture: Corporations have directors, like in a boardroom. Condos have managers, like a building with a group of owners keeping it running.
deeper.street: Kim Alvarez is president of a co-op board of directors on the Upper West Side. Across the park, her friend chairs a condo's board of managers. Same job feel, different legal title.
deeper.stakes: Using the wrong term won't sink a deal, but it signals you don't know which kind of building you're in. On the exam, it costs points.
deeper.exam: "Board of directors" plus "shareholders" = co-op. "Board of managers" plus "unit owners" = condo.

blocks.text: Selling a condo: the right of first refusal

blocks.html: A condo board cannot approve or reject buyers the way a co-op board can. What it usually has is a right of first refusal: before a resale closes, the board may buy (or lease) the unit itself on the same terms. If it does not act within the window in the declaration (often about 30 days), the right is waived and the sale proceeds. Boards almost never exercise it because it means buying the unit with building money. The buyer's attorney still needs the written waiver for closing.
blocks.casual: A condo board can't approve or reject buyers the way a co-op board can. What it usually has is a right of first refusal: before a resale closes, the board can buy (or lease) the unit itself on the same terms. If it doesn't act within the window in the declaration (often about 30 days), the right's waived and the sale goes ahead. Boards almost never use it, because that means buying the unit with building money. The buyer's attorney still needs the written waiver for closing.

deeper.plain: A condo board can match a buyer's deal, but it can't just say no. If it doesn't match in time, the sale goes through.
deeper.picture: It's like a landlord with a "right to match" on a lease renewal. They can match the offer, but they can't stop you from leaving.
deeper.street: Leo's seller sends the contract to the managing agent. The board has 30 days, doesn't act, and issues a waiver letter. Priya puts it in the closing file.
deeper.stakes: Missing the waiver can delay closing and spook the lender. Telling a condo buyer they need a "board interview" is just wrong.
deeper.exam: Condo = right of first refusal, no approval power. Co-op = board approval, can reject for any non-discriminatory reason.

blocks.q: A condo board dislikes a buyer's profession and wants to stop the sale. Under typical NY condo documents, what can it do?
c: Reject the buyer with no reason, like a co-op board
Exercise its right of first refusal by buying the unit on the same terms
Require the buyer to pay a flip tax of 10%
Refuse to issue the deed
blocks.x: A condo board's tool is the right of first refusal: match the deal and buy it. It cannot simply reject buyers. And any refusal based on a protected class would violate fair housing law anyway.

items: Title insurance: the buyer gets an owner's policy and the lender a loan policy, because the buyer receives real property by deed.
Declaration and amendments recorded, and the unit's tax lot correctly assigned.
New construction: the unit must be released from the sponsor's building loan (a partial release) at closing, and mechanic's liens cleared.
Unpaid common charges and assessments are a lien; get a paid-up letter.
Right of first refusal waiver from the board or managing agent.
Power of attorney: condo deeds usually include one in favor of the board so it can act on the right of first refusal and similar matters.
blocks.casual: Closing checklist for title and tax: title insurance (owner's policy for the buyer, loan policy for the lender, because the buyer gets real property by deed). The declaration and amendments are recorded, and the unit's tax lot is assigned correctly. On new construction, the unit has to be released from the sponsor's building loan (a partial release) at closing, and mechanic's liens cleared. Unpaid common charges and assessments are a lien, so get a paid-up letter. Get the right of first refusal waiver from the board or managing agent. And the power of attorney: condo deeds usually include one in favor of the board so it can act on the right of first refusal and similar matters.

deeper.plain: A condo closing looks a lot like a house closing, plus a few condo extras like the waiver and the paid-up letter.
deeper.picture: Think of it as a house closing with a building-sized attachment stapled on.
deeper.street: Leo buys a new unit from a sponsor in Long Island City. At closing the sponsor's construction lender signs a partial release for his unit only, so Leo's mortgage comes in first.
deeper.stakes: Skip the partial release on new construction and the buyer's unit stays tied to the developer's loan. That's a title disaster.
deeper.exam: Condo closings include title insurance and a deed. Partial release appears with new construction. Co-op closings have neither title insurance nor a deed.

blocks.html: For income tax, a condo owner deducts the unit's own real estate taxes and the interest on the unit's mortgage, within federal limits, just like a house owner. Common charges are not deductible for a home the owner lives in.
blocks.casual: For income tax, a condo owner deducts the unit's own real estate taxes and the mortgage interest on the unit, within federal limits, just like a house owner. Common charges aren't deductible for a home you live in.

deeper.plain: Condo owners deduct their taxes and mortgage interest like homeowners. Common charges on your own home don't count.
deeper.picture: Same tax treatment as a house: the tax bill and mortgage interest go on the return; the maintenance bills don't.
deeper.street: Leo pays $11,000 a year in mortgage interest, $6,000 in property taxes, and $10,800 in common charges. Only the first two can be deductions, subject to federal limits.
deeper.stakes: Telling a buyer common charges are deductible creates a tax surprise. Leave specific tax advice to an accountant.
deeper.exam: Common charges on a primary residence are not deductible. Taxes and mortgage interest are, within limits.

blocks.title: Condo in one line
blocks.html: Deed, own tax bill, own mortgage, percentage of the commons, and a right of first refusal instead of a board interview.
blocks.casual: Condo in one line: Deed, own tax bill, own mortgage, percentage of the commons, and a right of first refusal instead of a board interview.

deeper.plain: A condo is real property you own, with its own taxes and mortgage, plus a share of the building.
deeper.picture: It's a house stacked in the sky, with shared hallways instead of a shared fence.
deeper.street: Jordan recites the line to Leo as they leave the Center Boulevard building. Leo puts it in a cell at the top of his spreadsheet.
deeper.stakes: If you can say this cleanly to a client, you can catch most condo-versus-co-op mix-ups before they cost money.
deeper.exam: Every condo feature in the line has a co-op opposite: shares vs deed, shared tax bill vs own, share loan vs mortgage, board approval vs right of first refusal.

story.title: Who Owns the Pool
story.setting: Center Boulevard, Long Island City, a windy terrace

beats.text: I made a spreadsheet. Price, common charges, taxes. Then the building emailed me a $3,000 pool bill. I don't swim.
You own your apartment and 0.6% of everything else. Lobby, roof, boiler, pool.
beats.tag: Unit + undivided interest in common elements

beats.text: So I own 0.6% of a pool I'll never use.
And 0.6% of the assessment. It's in the declaration, which is the document that created the condo.
And this terrace? Do I own it?
It's a limited common element. Part of the commons, but only you get to use it. The bylaws and declaration say who fixes what.
That afternoon, Priya calls.
I need the board's right of first refusal waiver, a paid-up letter for common charges, and title is ordering the lien search.
Wait, the board can stop me?
Only by buying the unit themselves at your price. They won't. Condo boards don't interview you. Co-ops do.

check.q: What is a condo board's usual tool if it wants to block a resale?
c: A board interview
A right of first refusal to buy on the same terms
Refusing to record the deed
A flip tax
check.x: Condo boards typically have only a right of first refusal, not approval power.

beats.text: Who's on the board anyway?
Right now, mostly the sponsor's people. The building is two years old. Control has to pass to owners, generally within five years of the first closing.
And taxes? Are they in the common charges?
No. Every condo unit is its own tax lot. You'll get your own bill and deduct it yourself.
Condo means real property, Leo. Deed, tax bill, title insurance. You own a slice of everything, including the pool.

board.prompt: Sketch a condo building. Shade one unit, mark one limited common element, and label three common elements. Write the common interest percentage next to the unit.

facts.text: A condo owner holds fee simple title to a unit plus an undivided percentage of the common elements: real property with a deed, a regular mortgage, title insurance and a separate tax bill.
New York's Condominium Act is Real Property Law Article 9-B.
Unit owners hold the common elements as tenants in common by common interest percentage, and cannot sell that share separately or sue to partition.
A limited common element, such as a private terrace, is legally a common element reserved for one or a few units, with repairs assigned by the declaration.
A condominium is created only when the declaration, which sets each unit's common interest, use restrictions and the right of first refusal, is recorded.
The bylaws are the recorded operating manual: board elections, meetings, budgets, and how common charges are assessed and collected.
Rules and regulations (move-in hours, pets, renovation hours) are adopted and changed by the board and are not recorded.
CC&Rs are private covenants, conditions and restrictions that run with the land; in NY condos they sit inside the declaration and bylaws.
Common charges and assessments are the unit's common interest percentage times the building budget or project cost.
Real estate taxes are not in condo common charges because each unit is its own tax lot with its own bill.
Unpaid common charges are a lien on the unit that ranks behind real estate taxes and a first mortgage of record (RPL 339-z), and the board can foreclose it.
The sponsor creates the condo under an offering plan and at first appoints the board and the managing agent.
The Attorney General generally expects unit owners to control the board no later than 5 years after the first closing, often earlier once about 50% of units sell.
A condo is run by a board of managers elected by unit owners; a co-op by a board of directors elected by shareholders.
A condo board cannot reject buyers; it usually has only a right of first refusal to buy or lease on the same terms, waived if not used within the window (often about 30 days).
A condo closing needs owner's and loan title policies, a partial release from the sponsor's loan in new construction, a paid-up letter and the right of first refusal waiver.
A condo owner deducts the unit's own property taxes and mortgage interest within federal limits; common charges on a home she lives in are not deductible.

lessons.title: New Development: Offering Plans, Letters of Intent, and Closing Costs
lessons.tagline: In new construction, the offering plan is the product. Read it before the buyer falls in love with the rendering.
objectives: Explain the Martin Act filing process: CPS-1 market testing, red herring, plan accepted for filing, effectiveness, amendments
Handle a letter of intent correctly and know what it cannot do
Read the parts of an offering plan that hurt buyers: special risks, tax projections, square footage, fees, closing date
Explain COs and TCOs, flipping, and simultaneous closings
Sort closing costs for buyers, sellers, and sponsors, including mansion tax and mortgage recording tax

blocks.title: Gowanus, a sales gallery with very good espresso
blocks.html: A 120-unit condo is rising on 4th Avenue. The sales gallery has a model kitchen, a glossy book of floor plans, and a sign that reads "Now accepting expressions of interest." Leo's friend Ana wants unit 7C at the listed $1,350,000 and asks Jordan to "lock it in" with a letter of intent and a check today. What can Jordan actually do?
blocks.casual: A 120-unit condo is going up on 4th Avenue in Gowanus. The sales gallery has a model kitchen, a glossy book of floor plans, and a sign: "Now accepting expressions of interest." Leo's friend Ana wants unit 7C at the listed $1,350,000 and asks Jordan to "lock it in" with a letter of intent and a check today. So what can Jordan actually do?

deeper.plain: Ana wants to commit to a unit in a building that isn't legally for sale yet. Jordan has to explain what's possible at this stage and what isn't.
deeper.picture: It's like trying to buy a concert ticket when the venue is only taking a list of who might want one. You can sign the list; you can't pay.
deeper.street: The gallery has espresso and floor plans, but no accepted offering plan yet. Ana's check would have nowhere legal to go, and the $1,350,000 price could still change.
deeper.stakes: If Jordan tells Ana the unit is "locked," that's a misstatement of the offering's status. It could violate the Martin Act and burn Jordan's credibility with both Ana and the sponsor.
deeper.exam: "Expressions of interest" signals the CPS-1 testing phase. No deposits, no contracts, and no reservations at this stage.

blocks.text: The Martin Act and the offering plan

blocks.html: In New York, nobody may offer or sell condo units or co-op shares in a new or converted building without first filing an offering plan with the Attorney General's Real Estate Finance Bureau. The law is the Martin Act, General Business Law 352-e. The plan (also called the offering statement or prospectus) discloses everything material: the sponsor, the building, the budget, the units and prices, the governing documents, and the risks.
blocks.casual: In New York, nobody can offer or sell condo units or co-op shares in a new or converted building without first filing an offering plan with the Attorney General's Real Estate Finance Bureau. The law is the Martin Act, General Business Law 352-e. The plan (also called the offering statement or prospectus) discloses everything material: the sponsor, the building, the budget, the units and prices, the governing documents, and the risks.

deeper.plain: Before a developer can sell condos or co-op shares, the state's Attorney General has to receive a long document disclosing everything important.
deeper.picture: It's the nutrition label on a building. You may not like what's in it, but it has to be printed on the box.
deeper.street: The Gowanus sponsor's plan runs hundreds of pages: who's building it, how it's financed, the first-year budget, and risks like a tax abatement that phases out. Ana's attorney reads it before she signs anything.
deeper.stakes: Selling without an accepted plan or misstating it can bring civil and criminal enforcement by the AG. Buyers can lose money on promises that were never disclosed.
deeper.exam: Martin Act = GBL 352-e. The AG's Real Estate Finance Bureau handles offering plans. DOS doesn't review offering plans.

blocks.title: Accepted is not approved
blocks.html: The Attorney General reviews a plan for full disclosure, not for merit. "Accepted for filing" means the disclosures meet the rules. It is not a statement that the price is fair or the building is a good buy.
blocks.casual: Trap: accepted isn't approved. The Attorney General reviews a plan for full disclosure, not for merit. "Accepted for filing" means the disclosures follow the rules. It doesn't mean the price is fair or the building's a good buy.

deeper.plain: The state checks that the developer told you everything, not that the deal is any good.
deeper.picture: It's like a referee checking the players are wearing the right uniforms. It says nothing about whether the team will win.
deeper.street: A buyer says, "The Attorney General approved this building, so it must be priced right." Jordan corrects him: the AG accepted the disclosures, and he still needs his own attorney and comps.
deeper.stakes: Agents who tell buyers a plan is "approved" create a false sense of safety. If the deal goes bad, that statement comes back.
deeper.exam: "Accepted for filing" = disclosure review only. Any answer saying the AG approved the price, quality, or value is wrong.

blocks.title: From idea to closing

items.title: CPS-1 market testing (optional)
items.html: The sponsor files a CPS-1 application to test the market before the plan is filed. Once the AG accepts it, the sponsor may advertise and gather non-binding indications of interest for 12 months (extendable). No deposits and no reservations, binding or non-binding, and every ad carries the AG's legend.

items.title: Red herring
items.html: The sponsor submits the plan. While the AG reviews it, the preliminary version, called the red herring for its red legend, may be shown to prospects for information. No contracts, no deposits.

items.title: Accepted for filing
items.html: The AG accepts the plan. Now the sponsor may sign purchase agreements and take deposits, which must be held in escrow.

items.title: Declared effective
items.html: Once the minimum number of units stated in the plan is under contract, the sponsor declares the plan effective by amendment. Until then, buyers' deposits are refundable if the plan is abandoned.

items.title: Amendments and closing
items.html: Every material change (prices, budget, closing date, sponsor finances) is disclosed by an amendment. Closings start once there is a certificate of occupancy (temporary or permanent) and the declaration is recorded.

blocks.casual:
From idea to closing:
CPS-1 market testing (optional). The sponsor files a CPS-1 application to test the market before filing the plan. Once the AG accepts it, the sponsor can advertise and collect non-binding indications of interest for 12 months (extendable). No deposits and no reservations, binding or non-binding, and every ad carries the AG's legend.
Red herring. The sponsor submits the plan. While the AG reviews it, the preliminary version, called the red herring for its red legend, can be shown to prospects for information. No contracts, no deposits.
Accepted for filing. Now the sponsor can sign purchase agreements and take deposits, which go into escrow.
Declared effective. Once the minimum number of units in the plan is under contract, the sponsor declares the plan effective by amendment. Until then, deposits are refundable if the plan is abandoned.
Amendments and closing. Every material change (prices, budget, closing date, sponsor finances) is disclosed by amendment. Closings start once there's a certificate of occupancy (temporary or permanent) and the declaration is recorded.

deeper.plain: Interest first, then a draft plan, then an accepted plan where contracts are allowed, then enough sales to make it effective, then closings once the building can be occupied.
deeper.picture: It's like a restaurant opening: a sign-up list, a preview menu, opening night reservations, then the doors open once the inspector signs off.
deeper.street: Ana can sign a contract only after acceptance. Her 10% deposit goes to escrow. If the sponsor never sells enough units to declare the plan effective and walks away, she gets the deposit back.
deeper.stakes: Taking money at the wrong stage is a violation, and buyers who sign before reading amendments can miss price or date changes.
deeper.exam: Order: CPS-1, red herring, accepted for filing, declared effective, closing. Contracts and deposits begin at acceptance, not before.

blocks.q: A sponsor has submitted its condo offering plan to the Attorney General, but the plan has not yet been accepted for filing. The sponsor may:
c: Sign purchase agreements and hold deposits in escrow
Distribute the preliminary plan (red herring) for information only
Take refundable reservation deposits on specific units
Declare the plan effective
blocks.x: Before acceptance, a red herring may be shown for information, but no contracts, deposits, or reservations are allowed.

blocks.html: A letter of intent in new development is a written, non-binding expression that a buyer wants a particular unit at a stated price. It is useful: it tells the sales office the buyer is serious and starts the paperwork. It is not a contract. The buyer is not bound, the sponsor is not bound, and the price can change.
blocks.casual: In new development, a letter of intent is a written, non-binding statement that a buyer wants a particular unit at a stated price. It's useful: it tells the sales office the buyer's serious and gets the paperwork moving. It isn't a contract. The buyer isn't bound, the sponsor isn't bound, and the price can change.

deeper.plain: A letter of intent says "I'm interested in this unit at this price." Nobody is committed by it.
deeper.picture: It's raising your hand in class. It shows you want to answer; it doesn't mean you're right or that the teacher will call on you.
deeper.street: Ana signs a letter of intent for 7C at $1,350,000 after the plan is accepted. Two weeks later the sponsor raises 7C to $1,395,000 by amendment before any contract is signed. Ana has no claim to the old price.
deeper.stakes: Clients treat a letter of intent like a done deal. If you don't correct that, you'll own their disappointment when the price moves.
deeper.exam: Letter of intent = non-binding on both buyer and sponsor, price not fixed. A distractor calls it an option or a binding offer.

blocks.title: The syllabus says "reserve." The AG says no.
blocks.html: Older course material describes letters of intent as written offers to reserve specific units during the CPS-1 phase. The Attorney General's current CPS-1 policy (updated November 5, 2025) is explicit: during market testing no reservations, binding or non-binding, and no deposits may be accepted until an offering plan is accepted for filing. During CPS-1 you can collect interest, not commitments. If an exam item says a letter of intent is non-binding as to purchaser and price, that is still correct.
blocks.casual: Trap: the syllabus says "reserve," and the AG says no. Older material describes letters of intent as written offers to reserve specific units during CPS-1. The Attorney General's current CPS-1 policy (updated November 5, 2025) is clear: during market testing, no reservations, binding or non-binding, and no deposits until an offering plan is accepted for filing. In CPS-1 you collect interest, not commitments. If an exam item says a letter of intent is non-binding as to purchaser and price, that's still correct.

deeper.plain: Old books say you can reserve a unit during market testing. The current rule says you can't hold any unit until the plan is accepted.
deeper.picture: It's a "coming soon" store. You can sign up for the email list, but you can't put anything on hold.
deeper.street: Jordan tells Ana: "Right now I can get your name on the interest list for 7C. No check, no hold. When the plan is accepted, we move fast."
deeper.stakes: Following outdated material leads agents to promise holds that don't exist. That's a misstatement under the Martin Act.
deeper.exam: If a question says letters of intent are non-binding on the buyer and price, mark it true. If it says CPS-1 allows deposits, mark it false.

items: How to submit one: through the sponsor's sales office, on the sponsor's form if it has one, with the buyer's name, the unit, the offered price, financing (cash or mortgage, with amount), the buyer's attorney, and your brokerage's registration of the buyer as your client.
Register your buyer first. New development sales offices pay co-brokes only if the agent registered the buyer, usually at or before the first visit. Skip it and you can lose your commission.

Legal ramifications: nothing is binding until both sides sign the purchase agreement after the plan is accepted. Never tell a buyer a unit is "locked." Misstating the status of an offering can violate the Martin Act, which the AG enforces civilly and criminally.
Deposits come only with the contract, typically 10% or more in new development, held in escrow by the sponsor's attorney or an escrow agent under GBL 352-h.
blocks.casual:
How to submit one: through the sponsor's sales office, on its form if it has one, with the buyer's name, the unit, the price, financing (cash or mortgage, and how much), the buyer's attorney, and your brokerage's registration of the buyer as your client.
Register your buyer first. New development sales offices only pay co-brokes if the agent registered the buyer, usually at or before the first visit. Skip it and you can lose your commission.
Legal ramifications: nothing's binding until both sides sign the purchase agreement after the plan is accepted. Never tell a buyer a unit is "locked." Misstating an offering's status can violate the Martin Act, which the AG enforces civilly and criminally.
Deposits come only with the contract, usually 10% or more in new development, held in escrow by the sponsor's attorney or an escrow agent under GBL 352-h.

deeper.plain: Register your buyer at the first visit, submit the letter properly, don't promise anything is locked, and remember deposits only come with a contract.
deeper.picture: Registration is putting your name on the coat check ticket. No ticket, no coat, even if you walked the client in.
deeper.street: Jordan emails the Gowanus sales office before Ana's first visit: "Registering Ana Ruiz as my buyer client." When she signs months later, Jordan's co-broke is on record.
deeper.stakes: Unregistered buyers can cost you the whole commission. Misstating status can cost you more than that.
deeper.exam: New development deposits go into escrow under GBL 352-h. Contracts only after acceptance for filing.

blocks.q: During the CPS-1 phase, a buyer wants to give Jordan a $50,000 check to reserve a specific penthouse. What is correct?
c: Jordan may accept it if it is refundable
Jordan may accept it if it goes into escrow
No deposit or reservation may be accepted until the offering plan is accepted for filing
The sponsor may accept it if the buyer signs a letter of intent
blocks.x: Under CPS-1, no deposits and no reservations of any kind are allowed before the plan is accepted. Escrow and refundability do not change that.

blocks.text: Reading the offering plan like a skeptic

head: Section
What to look for
rows: Up front in the plan. Sponsor's financing, construction risk, tax abatements expiring, litigation, the sponsor's right to rent unsold units, what happens if the sponsor defaults.
First year tax estimates must be backed by an expert letter. Check whether a tax abatement or exemption is assumed, and when it phases out. Year 1 taxes can be much lower than year 10.
Square footage is usually approximate and often measured to the exterior walls or the middle of shared walls, so usable space is smaller. Plans and dimensions are subject to change.
First year projected common charges. Low budgets sell units; underfunded budgets mean increases later.
Sponsor can raise or lower prices of unsold units by amendment. Signed contracts keep their price.
Working capital contribution, sponsor's transfer taxes shifted to the buyer, sponsor's attorney fee, reserve fund contribution, building move-in fees.
An estimated first closing date and an outside date. If the sponsor misses the outside date, the buyer may get the right to rescind.

deeper.plain: The plan is full of fine print that changes what the buyer really pays and gets. These sections are where the surprises hide.
deeper.picture: Reading an offering plan is like reading a phone contract: the headline price is the bait, the fees and phase-outs are the hook.
deeper.street: Ana's 7C shows 1,050 square feet, measured to the outside walls. Her usable space is closer to 950. Year 1 taxes assume an abatement that phases out, so her year 10 tax bill may be several times higher.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who skip special risks and tax projections get blindsided by costs years later. Agents who oversell the year 1 numbers face angry clients.
deeper.exam: Square footage in plans is approximate. Sponsors can change unsold unit prices by amendment, but signed contracts keep their price.

blocks.html: Price changes come by amendment. Developers raise prices for good reasons (strong absorption, rising costs, the first floors sold out) and for strategic ones (price the first units low to hit the sales threshold needed to declare the plan effective and satisfy the construction lender, then step prices up floor by floor). In soft markets sponsors offer concessions instead of cutting the list price: paying the buyer's closing costs or transfer taxes, a credit, or a year of common charges. When an amendment discloses a material adverse change that affects existing purchasers, the AG requires that they be offered a chance to rescind within the period the amendment states.
blocks.casual: Price changes come by amendment. Developers raise prices for good reasons (strong sales, rising costs, the first floors sold out) and strategic ones (price early units low to hit the sales threshold needed to declare the plan effective and keep the construction lender happy, then step prices up floor by floor). In a soft market, sponsors offer concessions instead of cutting list price: paying the buyer's closing costs or transfer taxes, a credit, or a year of common charges. When an amendment discloses a material adverse change that hits existing purchasers, the AG requires that they get a chance to rescind within the period the amendment states.

deeper.plain: Prices and terms change through amendments. If a change hurts people already under contract, they may get to back out.
deeper.picture: It's like airline pricing: the first seats are cheap to fill the plane, then prices climb. Bad news about the flight gives booked passengers a chance to cancel.
deeper.street: The Gowanus sponsor files an amendment pushing the closing date out 14 months and raising the budget 20%. Buyers already under contract get a window to rescind and get their deposits back.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who miss the rescission window lose their exit. Agents should flag every amendment to their clients and attorneys right away.
deeper.exam: Concessions often replace price cuts. A material adverse amendment gives existing buyers a rescission right.

blocks.q: Six months after Ana signs her contract at $1,350,000, the sponsor files an amendment raising the price of 7C's line by 5%. Ana's price is:
c: Increased by 5%, because the amendment applies to the whole line
Unchanged, because price increases apply only to unsold units
Increased only if she has not closed
Subject to renegotiation at closing
blocks.x: Amendments that change prices apply to unsold units. A signed purchase agreement keeps its price.

blocks.html: No one may legally live in a new building until the Department of Buildings (in NYC) or the local building department issues a certificate of occupancy. To get one, the building must pass final inspections: plumbing, electrical, elevators, fire safety, sprinklers, egress, and sign-offs from other agencies. Big buildings rarely finish everything at once, so the city issues a temporary certificate of occupancy (TCO) for floors or units that are ready. NYC TCOs expire and must be renewed until the final CO issues.
blocks.casual: Nobody can legally live in a new building until the Department of Buildings (in NYC) or the local building department issues a certificate of occupancy. To get one, the building has to pass final inspections: plumbing, electrical, elevators, fire safety, sprinklers, egress, plus sign-offs from other agencies. Big buildings rarely finish all at once, so the city issues a temporary certificate of occupancy (TCO) for floors or units that are ready. NYC TCOs expire and have to be renewed until the final CO comes through.

deeper.plain: A building needs a CO, or at least a temporary one covering your unit, before anyone can move in.
deeper.picture: A CO is the green light from the city. A TCO is a green light for part of the road while the rest is still under construction.
deeper.street: The Gowanus building gets a TCO for floors 2 through 10 in March. Ana's 7C is covered, so her closing can go ahead while the roof deck is still unfinished.
deeper.stakes: Closing on a unit without a TCO means a buyer can't legally move in and can't get a mortgage. TCOs that lapse without renewal can create problems for later sales.
deeper.exam: No occupancy without a CO or TCO. In NYC, the Department of Buildings issues them. TCOs are temporary and must be renewed.

blocks.html: Lenders will not fund a purchase mortgage on a unit that cannot be legally occupied, so in practice closings begin only after a TCO covers the unit. Lenders also review the project as a whole, for example how many units are sold, how many are owner-occupied, and whether the sponsor owns too many. A buyer who needs financing should ask early whether the building is expected to meet the lender's requirements.
blocks.casual: Lenders won't fund a purchase mortgage on a unit that can't be legally occupied, so in practice closings start only after a TCO covers the unit. Lenders also look at the whole project: how many units are sold, how many are owner-occupied, and whether the sponsor owns too many. A buyer who needs financing should ask early whether the building will meet the lender's requirements.

deeper.plain: No CO, no mortgage. And the building as a whole has to pass the lender's test, not just the buyer.
deeper.picture: A lender is buying into the whole building through your loan. If the building looks shaky, they won't take the trip no matter how good you look.
deeper.street: Tasha warns Ana that her lender won't close if the sponsor still owns more than a set share of units. Ana switches to a lender that has already approved the Gowanus project.
deeper.stakes: A buyer can be fully qualified and still lose the deal because the project fails lender review. Starting early with the right lender saves the closing.
deeper.exam: Lenders need legal occupancy (CO or TCO). Project review looks at sales, owner-occupancy, and sponsor concentration.

blocks.html: Flipping means buying at the sponsor's price and reselling at a profit, either by assigning the contract before closing or by closing and immediately reselling. In a simultaneous closing, the original buyer closes with the sponsor and with the new buyer on the same day. Sponsors dislike flips because a flipper's resale competes with the sponsor's own unsold units. Most plans prohibit assigning the purchase agreement without the sponsor's consent, charge an assignment fee, or bar resales until the sponsor sells out. Read the plan's policy before telling a buyer they can flip.
blocks.casual: Flipping means buying at the sponsor's price and reselling for a profit, either by assigning the contract before closing or by closing and reselling right away. In a simultaneous closing, the original buyer closes with the sponsor and with the new buyer the same day. Sponsors hate flips, because a flipper's resale competes with the sponsor's own unsold units. Most plans ban assigning the purchase agreement without the sponsor's consent, charge an assignment fee, or bar resales until the sponsor sells out. Read the plan's policy before telling a buyer they can flip.

deeper.plain: Flipping is reselling a new unit quickly for a profit. Most sponsors restrict it, so check the plan first.
deeper.picture: It's like buying sneakers at launch and reselling them outside the store. The brand would rather you didn't undercut its own shelf.
deeper.street: An investor signs for a Gowanus unit at $1,100,000 and finds a buyer at $1,250,000 before closing. The plan bans assignment without consent, so the sponsor demands a fee before allowing the simultaneous closing.
deeper.stakes: Promising a client they can flip without checking can trap them in a unit they can't afford to keep. The sponsor can refuse consent.
deeper.exam: Simultaneous closing = original buyer closes with sponsor and new buyer on the same day. Assignment usually needs sponsor consent.

blocks.title: Flip vs flip tax
blocks.html: Flipping is a quick resale for profit. A flip tax is a transfer fee a co-op (and sometimes a condo) charges on resales. Same word, unrelated ideas.
blocks.casual: Tip: flipping is a quick resale for profit. A flip tax is a transfer fee a co-op (and sometimes a condo) charges on resales. Same word, totally unrelated ideas.

deeper.plain: A flip is a fast resale. A flip tax is a fee the building charges when anyone sells.
deeper.picture: One is a move in a game; the other is the table fee you pay every time you get up.
deeper.street: Kim's UWS co-op charges a 2% flip tax on every sale, even to an owner who's lived there 30 years. Nothing about it requires a quick resale.
deeper.stakes: Mixing these up confuses sellers about their costs. A seller who forgets a flip tax can lose thousands at closing.
deeper.exam: Flip tax is common in co-ops, usually paid by the seller, and has nothing to do with how long the seller owned.

blocks.caption: Enter a NYC price and loan amount. Watch mansion tax and mortgage recording tax land on the buyer, transfer taxes on the seller, and what happens when a sponsor shifts its transfer taxes to the buyer.

head: Cost
Condo
Co-op
Usually paid by
rows: Mansion tax (1% at $1M+; NYC graduated up to 3.9%)
No, a share loan is not a mortgage
No; a co-op lien search instead
