Seller; new development buyer often pays the sponsor's
Seller; new development buyer often pays the sponsor's
New development, often 1 to 2 months of common charges
Managing agent, move-in, and processing fees

deeper.plain: This table shows which taxes and fees land on condo vs co-op deals and who usually pays. New development often moves the seller's costs onto the buyer.
deeper.picture: Think of the closing as a dinner bill. The table tells you which dishes each person usually covers, and new development is where the buyer often picks up the sponsor's dessert.
deeper.street: Two buyers each pay $900,000 with a $600,000 loan in Brooklyn. The condo buyer pays NYC mortgage recording tax of 1.925% on the loan; the co-op buyer pays none, because a share loan isn't a mortgage.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't see this table early budget wrong and can come up short at closing. That can delay or kill a deal.
deeper.exam: Co-ops: no mortgage recording tax and no title insurance. Mansion tax applies to both at $1M+, paid by the buyer. Flip tax is common in co-ops.

blocks.title: Ana's closing costs on a $1,350,000 Brooklyn new development condo with a $1,000,000 loan
blocks.html:
Mansion tax: $1,350,000 x 1% = $13,500.
Mortgage recording tax: $1,000,000 x 1.925% = $19,250.
Sponsor's NYC RPTT shifted to buyer: $1,350,000 x 1.425% = $19,237.50.
Sponsor's NYS transfer tax shifted to buyer: $1,350,000 x 0.4% = $5,400.
Taxes alone: $57,387.50, before title insurance, attorneys, working capital, and lender fees. (When a buyer pays the seller's transfer taxes, the payment can itself count as consideration and slightly raise the tax; attorneys calculate the exact gross-up.)
blocks.casual:
Ana's taxes on a $1,350,000 Brooklyn new development condo with a $1,000,000 loan:
Mansion tax: $1,350,000 x 1% = $13,500.
Mortgage recording tax: $1,000,000 x 1.925% = $19,250.
Sponsor's NYC RPTT shifted to buyer: $1,350,000 x 1.425% = $19,237.50.
Sponsor's NYS transfer tax shifted to buyer: $1,350,000 x 0.4% = $5,400.
Taxes alone: $57,387.50, before title insurance, attorneys, working capital, and lender fees. (When a buyer pays the seller's transfer taxes, that payment can count as consideration and nudge the tax up a bit; attorneys calculate the exact gross-up.)

deeper.plain: On a $1.35M new condo, Ana's taxes alone come to over $57,000 because she's paying the sponsor's transfer taxes too.
deeper.picture: It's like a concert ticket where the fees add up to a second ticket. The list price is only the start.
deeper.street: Ana had budgeted $25,000 for closing. Jordan walks her through the four lines before she signs, and she negotiates a concession where the sponsor covers the NYS transfer tax, saving $5,400.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who learns about $57,000 in taxes at the closing table may not have the cash. Showing the math early is what keeps the deal alive.
deeper.exam: Use 1.425% on the full price for NYC residential RPTT above $500,000, 0.4% NYS transfer tax under $3M in NYC, 1% mansion tax from $1M, and 1.925% MRT on loans of $500,000 or more.

blocks.title: Why the sponsor's taxes move to the buyer
blocks.html: In a resale the seller pays NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT. In NYC new development, the purchase agreement customarily makes the buyer pay the sponsor's transfer taxes. Sponsors sometimes waive this as a concession. Always show buyers this line before they sign.
blocks.casual: Why the sponsor's taxes move to the buyer: in a resale the seller pays NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT. In NYC new development, the purchase agreement customarily makes the buyer pay the sponsor's transfer taxes. Sponsors sometimes waive that as a concession. Always show buyers this line before they sign.

deeper.plain: In new NYC condos, the buyer usually pays transfer taxes that a seller would normally pay. It's negotiable sometimes.
deeper.picture: It's like a landlord asking you to pay the moving truck for the previous tenant. Unusual, but it's in the deal.
deeper.street: On a resale in Park Slope, the seller pays the transfer taxes. Across the canal in Gowanus new development, Ana's contract shifts them to her unless she negotiates.
deeper.stakes: Missing this line can add tens of thousands of dollars to a buyer's closing costs without warning. That's a fast way to lose a client.
deeper.exam: Resale: seller pays transfer taxes. NYC new development: buyer customarily pays the sponsor's transfer taxes.

blocks.q: Which closing cost applies to a NYC condo purchase financed with a mortgage but NOT to a co-op purchase financed with a share loan?
c: Mansion tax
NYC RPTT
Mortgage recording tax
NYS transfer tax
blocks.x: A co-op share loan is secured by shares and a proprietary lease, not recorded real property, so no mortgage recording tax. Mansion tax and transfer taxes apply to both.

story.title: Lock It In
story.setting: A new development sales gallery on 4th Avenue, Gowanus

beats.text: I'm Ana, Leo's friend. I want 7C. Can I give you a check to lock it?
First I register you with the sales office as my buyer, so they know I represent you.
Then, is the plan accepted yet? The sign says expressions of interest, which sounds like CPS-1.
Sales director here. We're in market testing under CPS-1. We can't take deposits or hold units yet.
So what can I do?
Tell them you're interested. Nothing binds you or them, no unit is held, and no check changes hands until the AG accepts the plan.

check.q: During CPS-1 market testing, a sponsor may:
c: Take refundable deposits
Reserve units with a non-binding letter
Advertise and collect non-binding interest with the AG's legend
Sign contracts subject to AG approval
check.x: CPS-1 allows advertising and gathering interest only. No deposits or reservations of any kind.

beats.text: Three months later the plan is accepted. Ana submits a letter of intent for 7C at $1,350,000.
I read the plan. Special risks: the tax projection assumes an abatement that phases out. The square footage is measured to the exterior walls. And you're paying the sponsor's transfer taxes.
beats.tag: Read special risks, taxes, square footage

beats.text: I'm paying their taxes?
Customary in NYC new development. Plus mansion tax, mortgage recording tax, title, working capital. Budget about $60,000 in taxes and fees on top of the price.
beats.tag: Buyer often pays sponsor's transfer taxes

beats.text: Sign fast. Two floors up just went up five percent by amendment. Flip it in a year.
Her contract price won't change, Marcus. And this plan bars assignment without sponsor consent. No flipping before closing.
When do I move in?
When the building gets a TCO covering your unit. No TCO, no closing, no mortgage.
In new development the offering plan is the product. Read it before the rendering reads you.

board.prompt: Draw the new development timeline: CPS-1, red herring, accepted for filing, effective, TCO, first closing. Under each, write what a buyer can and cannot do.

facts.text: Under the Martin Act (GBL 352-e), no one may offer condo units or co-op shares in a new or converted building without first filing an offering plan with the Attorney General.
"Accepted for filing" means the plan's disclosures meet the rules, not that the AG approves the price or the merits.
Under a CPS-1 a sponsor may advertise and gather non-binding interest for 12 months, but may take no deposits and no reservations, binding or not.
A red herring is the preliminary plan shown for information while the AG reviews it; no contracts or deposits are allowed yet.

After acceptance the sponsor may sign contracts and take escrowed deposits; the plan is declared effective once the stated minimum units are under contract, and deposits are refundable if it is abandoned first.
A letter of intent is a written, non-binding expression of interest in a unit at a price; neither buyer nor sponsor is bound and the price can change.
A buyer's agent must register the buyer with the sales office, usually at or before the first visit, or risk losing the co-broke commission.
New development deposits come only with a signed contract, typically 10% or more, held in escrow under GBL 352-h.
Telling a buyer a unit is "locked" or misstating an offering's status can violate the Martin Act, which the AG enforces civilly and criminally.
The Special Risks section up front covers the sponsor's financing, construction risk, expiring tax abatements, litigation and sponsor default.
First-year tax projections must be backed by an expert letter, and an assumed abatement can make year 1 taxes far lower than year 10.
Plan square footage is approximate and often measured to exterior or mid-walls, so usable space is smaller.
Low first-year budgets can mean later increases, and if the sponsor misses the plan's outside closing date the buyer may get a right to rescind.
Sponsors change prices of unsold units by amendment; signed contracts keep their price.
An amendment disclosing a material adverse change must offer existing purchasers a chance to rescind, and soft markets bring concessions rather than list price cuts.
No one may occupy a new building without a certificate of occupancy, and closings begin only once a temporary or final CO covers the unit.
Lenders review the whole project (units sold, owner occupancy, sponsor-held units) before financing a unit.
Flipping is reselling quickly by assigning the contract or closing and reselling (a simultaneous closing), and most plans restrict assignment.
Flipping is a quick resale for profit, while a flip tax is a transfer fee a co-op (sometimes a condo) charges on resales.
The buyer pays the mansion tax (1% at $1 million or more) and the mortgage recording tax on a condo loan (NYC 1.925% at $500,000 or more); a co-op share loan has no recording tax.
In NYC new development the buyer customarily pays the sponsor's transfer taxes, while the broker commission stays with the seller or sponsor.
NYS transfer tax is 0.4% (0.65% on NYC residential at $3 million or more) and NYC RPTT is 1% up to $500,000 and 1.425% above, normally paid by the seller.

lessons.title: Co-ops, Condops, and Getting Past the Board
lessons.tagline: In a co-op you are not buying an apartment. You are buying shares and a lease, and you are applying to live with your new landlord, which is your neighbors.
objectives: Define a co-op: shares, proprietary lease, maintenance, and why it is personal property
Run co-op due diligence: financials, minutes, underlying mortgage, reserves, land lease
Assemble a board package and prepare a buyer for the interview
Explain share loans, UCC lien searches, and recognition agreements
Qualify a buyer for a bank and a board: income types, DTI, liquidity, asset types
Explain sublet rules, sponsor and unsold shares, condops, and the 80/20 rule

blocks.title: Upper West Side, a prewar two-bedroom on West End Avenue
blocks.html: The Okafors' daughter, Adaeze, and her husband are buying a $1,150,000 co-op. Their bank approved a loan at 80% financing. The building's rules allow only 75%. Their board package is due in nine days, the board meets once a month, and Kim Alvarez, the board president, has a reputation. Jordan represents the buyers. What has to happen, in what order?
blocks.casual: The Okafors' daughter Adaeze and her husband are buying a $1,150,000 prewar two-bedroom co-op on West End Avenue. Their bank approved 80% financing. The building only allows 75%. The board package is due in nine days, the board meets once a month, and Kim Alvarez, the board president, has a reputation. Jordan represents the buyers. What has to happen, and in what order?

deeper.plain: The buyers have a loan the building won't allow, a tight deadline, and a tough board. Jordan needs to line up the money, the paperwork, and the calendar.
deeper.picture: It's like getting into a selective club: the bank is the ticket, but the board is the bouncer, and the bouncer's rules are stricter.
deeper.street: Adaeze and Chidi have to cut the loan from 80% to 75%, which means about $57,500 more cash down. Then the package has to land complete in nine days or they wait another month.
deeper.stakes: Miss the board deadline and the interview can slide past their rate lock. Ignore the 75% cap and the board can reject them outright.
deeper.exam: Co-op stems mention shares, a board, financing caps, and a board package. The board's financing limit controls even when the bank approves more.

blocks.html: In a cooperative, a corporation owns the building (and usually the land). Buyers purchase shares of stock in that corporation, allocated to a specific apartment, and receive a proprietary lease giving them the right to live there. The buyer is a shareholder and a tenant at the same time. Because shares and a lease are personal property, there is no deed, no title insurance, and no mortgage recording tax.
blocks.casual: In a cooperative, a corporation owns the building (and usually the land). Buyers buy shares of stock in that corporation, assigned to a specific apartment, and get a proprietary lease that gives them the right to live there. So the buyer is a shareholder and a tenant at the same time. Since shares and a lease are personal property, there's no deed, no title insurance, and no mortgage recording tax.

deeper.plain: In a co-op you don't own the apartment. You own shares in the company that owns the building, plus a lease on your unit.
deeper.picture: It's like owning stock in a company that owns a hotel, and your shares come with a permanent key to room 7B.
deeper.street: At closing on West End Avenue, Adaeze receives a stock certificate for 410 shares and a proprietary lease for apartment 6F. No deed is recorded with the City Register.
deeper.stakes: Calling a co-op buyer an "owner of real estate" leads to wrong advice on taxes, financing, and closing costs. It also confuses the client about the board's power.
deeper.exam: Co-op = personal property: shares plus proprietary lease. No deed, no title insurance, no mortgage recording tax.

blocks.html: Each month the shareholder pays maintenance, which covers the apartment's share of the building's operating costs, the building's real estate taxes, and the payments on the building's underlying mortgage. The share count usually tracks size, floor, and view. Because the corporation pays the taxes and mortgage interest, shareholders may deduct their proportionate share of both on their income tax returns, which is why the 80/20 rule at the end of this lesson matters.
blocks.casual: Every month the shareholder pays maintenance. It covers the apartment's share of building operating costs, the building's real estate taxes, and payments on the building's underlying mortgage. The share count usually tracks size, floor, and view. Because the corporation pays the taxes and mortgage interest, shareholders can deduct their proportionate share of both on their income taxes, which is why the 80/20 rule at the end of this lesson matters.

deeper.plain: Maintenance bundles operating costs, property taxes, and the building's own mortgage into one monthly bill. Part of it is tax deductible.
deeper.picture: It's one combined bill, like a phone plan that includes the phone, the data, and the taxes in a single number.
deeper.street: Adaeze's $2,300 maintenance is 40% taxes and underlying mortgage interest. Her accountant lets her deduct that share, about $920 a month, within federal limits.
deeper.stakes: Buyers compare co-op maintenance to condo common charges and think co-ops are pricier. They forget condo taxes are a separate bill.
deeper.exam: Maintenance includes the building's taxes and underlying mortgage. Common charges don't include taxes. Shares usually reflect size, floor, and view.

blocks.caption: Switch between condo and co-op. Compare what you own, what you sign, what you pay monthly, how you finance, and who approves you.

blocks.title: Condo vs co-op at a glance

left.title: Condo
items: Real property, deed
Own tax bill
Mortgage; mortgage recording tax applies
Title insurance
Common charges
Board of managers; right of first refusal only
Usually easier to rent out

right.title: Co-op
items: Personal property: shares and proprietary lease
Taxes inside maintenance
Share loan; no mortgage recording tax
Co-op lien search instead of title insurance
Maintenance
Board of directors approves or rejects buyers
Sublets restricted

deeper.plain: Condos are real property you own outright with your own bills. Co-ops are shares and a lease, with taxes bundled in and a board that approves buyers.
deeper.picture: A condo is a house in the sky. A co-op is a membership in a club that owns the building.
deeper.street: Two similar two-bedrooms on the Upper West Side: the condo buyer pays title insurance and mortgage recording tax but can rent freely. The co-op buyer skips those costs but faces a board interview and sublet limits.
deeper.stakes: Investors who buy co-ops expecting to rent out get stuck. Buyers who choose condos for flexibility pay more at closing.
deeper.exam: Every row is a classic exam pairing: deed vs shares, mortgage vs share loan, title insurance vs lien search, right of first refusal vs board approval.

blocks.q: A buyer of a co-op apartment receives:
c: A deed and a title insurance policy
Shares in the corporation and a proprietary lease
A deed to the unit and a percentage of the common elements
A leasehold estate recorded with the county clerk
blocks.x: Co-op buyers get shares and a proprietary lease, which are personal property. A deed and common elements interest describe a condo.

blocks.html: Downstate, the buyer's attorney reviews the co-op's documents before the contract is signed. The agent should know what is in them, because the answers drive price and advice.
blocks.casual: Downstate, the buyer's attorney reviews the co-op's documents before the contract is signed. The agent should know what's in them too, because the answers drive price and advice.

deeper.plain: The lawyer reads the building's paperwork before the buyer commits. Agents need to understand it too.
deeper.picture: It's checking under the hood before you buy a used car, except the car is an entire building.
deeper.street: Priya reads the West End Avenue co-op's last three years of financials and minutes before Adaeze signs. She finds a facade project coming and asks the seller for a price credit.
deeper.stakes: An agent who doesn't know what's in the docs may push a buyer into a building with a big assessment coming. That's a client who never refers you again.
deeper.exam: Downstate, attorneys review co-op documents before contract. Due diligence comes before signing, not after.

head: Document
Key questions
rows: Is the building running a surplus or a deficit? How big is the reserve fund relative to the building? How much income comes from commercial space? Are shareholders in arrears?
Balance, rate, and maturity. A large balloon due in two years at a much higher rate means maintenance increases ahead.

Maintenance and assessment history, planned projects (facade work under Local Law 11, boiler, elevators, Local Law 97 emissions upgrades), litigation, sponsor disputes, changes to sublet or flip tax policy.
Does the corporation own the land in fee, or does it hold a land lease? A ground lease that expires or resets soon can crush values and make financing hard.
Owner occupancy percentage, sponsor-owned units, financing limit, flip tax, pet and sublet policy, pending assessments.

deeper.plain: These documents tell you whether the building is financially healthy and what's coming down the road.
deeper.picture: It's a medical checkup for the building: the financials are the bloodwork, the minutes are the doctor's notes, the mortgage is the long-term diagnosis.
deeper.street: Minutes show a Local Law 11 facade repair and boiler replacement planned next year, and the underlying mortgage balloons in two years. Priya tells Adaeze to expect maintenance hikes and an assessment.
deeper.stakes: A land lease that resets soon or a balloon mortgage at a higher rate can drag values down hard. Buyers who miss it can lose equity fast.
deeper.exam: Reserve fund, underlying mortgage, minutes, and fee vs leasehold land are the due diligence items most often tested.

blocks.title: Co-op ownership is never "fee simple" for the buyer
blocks.html: The corporation may own the building in fee or as a leasehold. The buyer never owns real estate. Exam items ask "is co-op ownership fee simple or leasehold?" For the shareholder: shares (personal property) plus a leasehold right of occupancy under the proprietary lease.
blocks.casual: Trap: co-op ownership is never "fee simple" for the buyer. The corporation may own the building in fee or as a leasehold. The buyer never owns real estate. Exam items ask "is co-op ownership fee simple or leasehold?" For the shareholder: shares (personal property) plus a leasehold right to occupy under the proprietary lease.

deeper.plain: The company might own the building outright, but the buyer only owns shares and a lease.
deeper.picture: The corporation owns the bakery. You own stock in the bakery and a ticket that guarantees you a table.
deeper.street: Adaeze asks if she owns 6F "in fee simple." Jordan says no: the corporation owns the building, and she owns shares plus a proprietary lease giving her the right to live in 6F.
deeper.stakes: Misdescribing ownership confuses financing and estate planning. Lenders and lawyers will spot it, and it costs you credibility.
deeper.exam: For the shareholder: shares (personal property) and a leasehold interest. Never fee simple for the buyer.

items: Proprietary lease: sets the shareholder's rights and duties: paying maintenance, what the shareholder repairs, alterations only with consent, subletting and assignment only with board consent, pets, and the co-op's remedies on default.
Stock certificate: proof of share ownership, transferred at closing. If the buyer finances, the lender holds it.
Offering plan and amendments: how the co-op was formed and the sponsor's rights.

House rules: move-in hours and deposits, renovation season, washer-dryer bans, pets, floor covering requirements. Agents need them because they kill deals: a buyer who must have a washer or a large dog needs to know before bidding.
Alteration agreement: the contract a shareholder signs before renovating: board approval of plans, licensed and insured contractors, work hours, a security deposit, and liability for damage.
Board package: the buyer's application, below.
blocks.casual:
Proprietary lease: spells out the shareholder's rights and duties: paying maintenance, what you repair yourself, alterations only with consent, subletting and assigning only with board consent, pets, and what the co-op can do if you default.
Stock certificate: proof you own the shares, handed over at closing. If the buyer finances, the lender holds it.
Offering plan and amendments: how the co-op was formed and what rights the sponsor has.
House rules: move-in hours and deposits, renovation season, washer-dryer bans, pets, floor covering rules. They kill deals: a buyer who needs a washer or has a big dog has to know before bidding.
Alteration agreement: what a shareholder signs before renovating: board approval of plans, licensed and insured contractors, work hours, a security deposit, and liability for damage.
Board package: the buyer's application, below.

deeper.plain: These are the papers that control life in the co-op: your lease, your shares, the house rules, and the paperwork for renovations and applying.
deeper.picture: Think of a gym membership: the contract, the card, the posted rules, the waiver for personal trainers, and the application to join.
deeper.street: Chidi plans to put in a washer-dryer. The house rules ban them and the alteration agreement requires board approval for plumbing changes. Jordan flags it before they bid, and they decide to live without one.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who learns about a washer ban or a dog limit after closing is stuck. An agent who could have flagged it takes the blame.
deeper.exam: Proprietary lease = right to occupy and rules for the unit. Stock certificate = proof of shares, held by the lender if financed. Alteration agreement = renovation rules.

blocks.html: A co-op buyer borrows with a share loan, secured by the shares and the proprietary lease rather than by a recorded mortgage. The lender perfects its lien under the Uniform Commercial Code by filing a UCC-1 financing statement. Because nothing is recorded against real estate, there is no mortgage recording tax. Instead of title insurance, the buyer's attorney orders a co-op lien search: UCC filings against the seller's shares, plus judgments, tax liens, and bankruptcies against the seller, and a managing agent letter confirming maintenance is paid.
blocks.casual: Co-op buyers borrow with a share loan, secured by the shares and the proprietary lease instead of a recorded mortgage. The lender perfects its lien under the Uniform Commercial Code by filing a UCC-1 financing statement. Since nothing is recorded against real estate, there's no mortgage recording tax. Instead of title insurance, the buyer's attorney orders a co-op lien search: UCC filings against the seller's shares, plus judgments, tax liens, and bankruptcies against the seller, and a managing agent letter confirming maintenance is paid.

deeper.plain: A co-op loan is secured by shares, not real estate. That's why there's no mortgage tax and why a lien search replaces title insurance.
deeper.picture: It's like a car loan where the bank holds the title to the car. Here the bank holds the stock certificate.
deeper.street: Adaeze's $862,500 share loan would have cost about $16,600 in NYC mortgage recording tax if it were a mortgage. As a share loan, it costs zero. Priya runs a lien search and finds an old UCC-1 from the seller's prior loan, which gets terminated at closing.
deeper.stakes: Skipping the lien search could leave the buyer with shares still pledged to the seller's old lender. That's a closing nightmare.
deeper.exam: Share loan = UCC-1 filing, no mortgage recording tax. Co-op lien search replaces title insurance.

blocks.html: The lender, the co-op, and the buyer also sign a recognition agreement. The co-op recognizes the lender's lien on the shares and agrees to notify the lender if the shareholder defaults. The lender accepts that the co-op's own lien for unpaid maintenance comes first, and gets a chance to cure defaults before the co-op cancels the lease.
blocks.casual: The lender, the co-op, and the buyer also sign a recognition agreement. The co-op recognizes the lender's lien on the shares and agrees to tell the lender if the shareholder defaults. The lender accepts that the co-op's own lien for unpaid maintenance comes first, and gets a chance to cure defaults before the co-op cancels the lease.

deeper.plain: The co-op and the bank agree who gets paid first and promise to warn each other if the buyer stops paying.
deeper.picture: It's a handshake between two creditors at the door: "You go first on maintenance, but call me before you lock the place up."
deeper.street: If Adaeze stops paying maintenance, the co-op notifies her lender. The lender can pay the arrears to protect its loan before the co-op cancels her proprietary lease.
deeper.stakes: Without a recognition agreement, lenders won't fund. A co-op that refuses to sign one makes financing almost impossible.
deeper.exam: Recognition agreement = three parties (lender, co-op, buyer). The co-op's maintenance lien is ahead of the lender's.

blocks.q: Which document gives a co-op lender the corporation's acknowledgment of its lien and notice of the shareholder's defaults?
c: The alteration agreement
The recognition agreement
The stock certificate
The house rules
blocks.x: The recognition agreement is the three-way agreement among lender, co-op, and shareholder. The stock certificate is held by the lender but does not create the co-op's obligations.

blocks.text: Qualifying the buyer: the bank and the board

blocks.html: Co-op and condo buyers face two underwriters: the bank and, for co-ops, the board. Banks follow federal ability-to-repay rules and their investors' guidelines. Co-op boards make up their own, and they are usually stricter. Condo boards generally do not approve buyers, but condo buyers still need the bank.
blocks.casual: Co-op and condo buyers face two underwriters: the bank and, for co-ops, the board. Banks follow federal ability-to-repay rules and their investors' guidelines. Co-op boards make their own rules, and they're usually stricter. Condo boards generally don't approve buyers, but condo buyers still need the bank.

deeper.plain: In a co-op, both the bank and the board have to say yes. The board is usually tougher.
deeper.picture: It's two locks on one door. The bank has one key, the board has the other, and you need both turned.
deeper.street: Adaeze and Chidi pass the bank at 80%. The board caps loans at 75%, so they need a smaller loan and more cash before the board will even look at them.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who only clears the bank can still lose the apartment and pay for appraisals and attorney fees for nothing.
deeper.exam: Board standards are building policy, not law. Condo boards generally don't approve buyers; co-op boards do.

blocks.caption: Enter income, monthly debts, and housing cost. Watch the debt-to-income ratio, then compare it with a typical lender limit and a stricter co-op board limit.

head: Test
Typical bank view
Typical co-op board view
rows: Debt-to-income (all monthly debt, including housing, divided by gross monthly income)
Often up to the low to mid 40s percent
Up to 80% to 90% or more for strong borrowers
Building cap, often 75% to 80%; some 50%; some all cash
Often 1 to 2 years of maintenance plus loan payments, more in some buildings
Allowed with a gift letter and documentation
Often limited or not allowed toward the down payment
Often discounted or excluded from liquidity
Generally unacceptable; the board wants full documentation
blocks.caption: These are common market practices, not laws. Every building sets its own requirements; get them from the managing agent.

deeper.plain: Boards usually want lower debt, less borrowing, and more cash left over than banks do.
deeper.picture: The bank checks that you can swim. The board checks that you can swim across the river in a storm.
deeper.street: A buyer with a 42% DTI gets a bank approval for a Riverside Drive co-op. The board's limit is 28%, so the buyer is rejected without an interview.
deeper.stakes: Agents who quote bank standards as if they're board standards set clients up for rejection. Always get the building's numbers from the managing agent.
deeper.exam: These are market practices, not laws. Typical board DTI 25% to 30%, financing often 75% to 80%, and 1 to 2 years of post-closing liquidity.

blocks.title: Income and assets: how sturdy is each?

left.title: Income types
items: Salary: most reliable, verified by pay stubs and W-2s
Commission and bonus: usually a 2-year average
Interest and dividends: need a history and continuing assets
Capital gains: irregular, often averaged or discounted
Business income: 2 years of personal and business tax returns
Rental income: lenders often count about 75% of gross rent
Trust income, alimony, Social Security: counted if documented and continuing

right.title: Asset types
items: Cash, T-bills: fully liquid
Stocks, bonds, mutual funds: liquid, may be discounted for volatility
Retirement accounts: often discounted or excluded by boards
Privately held companies: illiquid, hard to value
Trust funds: depends on access
Real estate: illiquid until sold
Collectibles: usually ignored
Gifts: documented with a gift letter

deeper.plain: Steady, documented income and cash count most. Irregular income and hard-to-sell assets count less.
deeper.picture: Salary is a paved road; commissions are a gravel road; a private company is a hiking trail. Boards prefer pavement.
deeper.street: A freelance designer shows $250,000 of income averaged over two years and $400,000 in a 401(k). The board discounts the 401(k) and looks for cash, so she moves money into a brokerage account early.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who count on retirement accounts or a gift to meet a board's liquidity rule can be rejected late in the process.
deeper.exam: Salary is most reliable. Commission and bonus usually averaged over 2 years. Rental income often counted at about 75%. Retirement assets often discounted by boards.

blocks.title: Will Adaeze and Chidi pass the board?
blocks.html:
Price $1,150,000. Board cap is 75% financing, so loan $862,500 and down payment $287,500 (25%).
Monthly loan payment about $5,400; maintenance $2,300; student loan $400. Total monthly debt: $8,100.
Gross income $360,000 a year = $30,000 a month. DTI = $8,100 / $30,000 = 27%. Inside a 25% to 30% board range, well inside a bank's limit.
Liquid assets after closing: $210,000 in cash and brokerage accounts. A year of housing costs is ($5,400 + $2,300) x 12 = $92,400. They show about 2.3 years of post-closing liquidity.
Result: they qualify, but only at 75% financing. They must lower the loan from the bank's 80% approval.
blocks.casual:
Price $1,150,000. Board cap is 75%, so the loan is $862,500 and the down payment $287,500 (25%).
Monthly loan payment about $5,400; maintenance $2,300; student loan $400. Total monthly debt: $8,100.
Gross income $360,000 a year = $30,000 a month. DTI = $8,100 / $30,000 = 27%. Inside a 25% to 30% board range, well inside a bank's limit.
Liquid assets after closing: $210,000 in cash and brokerage accounts. A year of housing costs is ($5,400 + $2,300) x 12 = $92,400. That's about 2.3 years of post-closing liquidity.
Result: they qualify, but only at 75% financing. They have to lower the loan from the bank's 80% approval.

deeper.plain: Their debt is 27% of income and they have over two years of housing costs in the bank after closing. They pass if they borrow only 75%.
deeper.picture: It's like checking that your backpack fits in the overhead bin: weight (DTI) and spare room (liquidity) both have to fit the airline's rules, not just your own.
deeper.street: Jordan runs the numbers at a cafe on Broadway. Chidi asks if they can keep the 80% loan. Jordan shows that the cap is 75% and the extra $57,500 down still leaves them about 2.3 years of cushion.
deeper.stakes: If they submit at 80%, the board rejects them for violating its financing rule. Running the math first saves a month and a lost apartment.
deeper.exam: DTI = total monthly debt / gross monthly income. Liquidity years = liquid assets after closing / annual housing cost. Use the board's cap, not the bank's.

blocks.q: A co-op's board requires 2 years of post-closing liquidity. A buyer's monthly loan payment will be $4,000 and maintenance $2,000. How much in liquid assets must remain after closing?

blocks.text: The board package and the interview

blocks.title: Board package checklist

items.title: Purchase application
items.html: The building's form, every question answered.

items.title: Fully executed contract of sale
items.html: Signed by both sides, with the loan commitment if financing.

items.title: Financial statement
items.html: Every asset and liability, each one verified with statements.

items.title: Letters
items.html: Personal reference letters, business reference letters, and an employment verification letter stating title, salary, and tenure.

items.title: Tax returns
items.html: Usually 2 to 3 years; 3 years is a common recommendation.

items.title: Credit authorization
items.html: Signed permission for the managing agent to pull credit.

items.title: Disclosures
items.html: Required New York forms, such as the lead paint disclosure for pre-1978 buildings.

blocks.casual:
Board package checklist:
Purchase application: the building's form, every question answered.
Fully executed contract of sale: signed by both sides, with the loan commitment if financing.
Financial statement: every asset and liability, each one backed by statements.
Letters: personal references, business references, and an employment letter stating title, salary, and tenure.
Tax returns: usually 2 to 3 years; 3 is a common recommendation.
Credit authorization: signed permission for the managing agent to pull credit.
Disclosures: required New York forms, like the lead paint disclosure for pre-1978 buildings.

deeper.plain: The package is a full financial and personal picture of the buyer, with proof for every number.
deeper.picture: It's a college application where every grade has a transcript stapled behind it.
deeper.street: Jordan builds Adaeze and Chidi's package in a shared folder: application, contract, commitment letter, statements, four reference letters, three years of returns, credit authorization, and the lead paint disclosure for their 1925 building.
deeper.stakes: One missing letter or unmatched balance sends the package back and can cost a month. In a building that meets monthly, that can blow a rate lock.
deeper.exam: The board package includes the executed contract and loan commitment. Lead paint disclosure applies to pre-1978 housing.

blocks.html: The managing agent checks the package for completeness, then board members read it, often closely. They want to see that the buyer can pay maintenance through good times and bad, has the cash cushion the building requires, will live there as a primary residence if that is the policy, and told the truth. A missing page or a number that does not match a statement can delay a deal a full month.
blocks.casual: The managing agent checks the package for completeness, then board members read it, often closely. They want to see that the buyer can pay maintenance in good times and bad, has the cash cushion the building requires, will live there as a primary residence if that's the policy, and told the truth. A missing page or a number that doesn't match a statement can delay a deal a full month.

deeper.plain: The board reads everything looking for stability and honesty. Small mistakes cause big delays.
deeper.picture: It's like a landlord reading your rental application with a highlighter and a calculator.
deeper.street: Kim notices the financial statement says $210,000 in liquid assets but one brokerage statement shows $8,000 less. She sends it back for an explanation, and the interview gets pushed to next month.
deeper.stakes: Inconsistencies read as dishonesty. A board that doubts one number may doubt the whole buyer.
deeper.exam: Boards care about ability to pay, liquidity, residence policy, and truthfulness. The managing agent checks completeness first.

blocks.html: Timing. Most boards meet once a month. Missing this month's package deadline can push the interview past the buyer's loan commitment or rate lock, so work backward from the board calendar the day the contract is signed. Interview prep. The buyer should know every number in the package, answer briefly and honestly, disclose everything (boards find what you hide), and avoid surprises like announcing a gut renovation or a home business. The agent does not attend.
blocks.casual: Timing. Most boards meet once a month. Missing this month's package deadline can push the interview past the buyer's loan commitment or rate lock, so work backward from the board calendar the day the contract is signed. Interview prep. The buyer should know every number in the package, answer briefly and honestly, disclose everything (boards find what you hide), and skip surprises like announcing a gut renovation or a home business. The agent doesn't attend.

deeper.plain: Plan around the board's meeting date, and prepare the buyer to be calm, brief, and honest. The agent stays home.
deeper.picture: It's a job interview where the boss already read your resume twice. Don't add new plot twists.
deeper.street: Jordan marks the West End board meeting on the calendar the day the contract is signed and works backward: package due in nine days. At the interview Chidi resists mentioning his plan to knock down a wall.
deeper.stakes: A surprise renovation plan or home business can sink an otherwise strong buyer. Missing a meeting can cost the rate lock.
deeper.exam: The agent doesn't attend the interview. Boards typically meet monthly. Plan timing from the contract date.

blocks.title: Boards can say no, but not for everything
blocks.html: Under the business judgment rule, New York courts generally defer to co-op board decisions made in good faith for the corporation's purposes, and boards usually do not have to give a reason. They can never reject for a protected class under federal, state, or city law. A rejection that looks like a pretext for discrimination can land the board before the Division of Human Rights or the NYC Commission.
blocks.casual: Boards can say no, but not for everything. Under the business judgment rule, New York courts generally defer to co-op board decisions made in good faith for the corporation's purposes, and boards usually don't have to give a reason. They can never reject for a protected class under federal, state, or city law. A rejection that looks like a pretext for discrimination can land the board before the Division of Human Rights or the NYC Commission.

deeper.plain: Boards can reject buyers without explaining, as long as the real reason isn't discrimination.
deeper.picture: The board holds a lot of keys, but none of them open the discrimination door.
deeper.street: A board rejects a buyer with stronger financials than the last three approved buyers, all of whom were younger. The buyer, 68, files an age discrimination complaint with the NYC Commission.
deeper.stakes: Silence protects boards most of the time. A pattern that looks discriminatory can still bring an investigation and damages.
deeper.exam: Business judgment rule = courts defer to good faith board decisions. Boards don't have to give reasons, but can't discriminate.

blocks.text: Primary residence, sublets, and sponsor shares

blocks.html: Co-ops are built for owner occupancy. Many require the apartment to be the buyer's primary residence, ban pieds-a-terre or parents buying for adult children, and limit subletting, for example 2 years out of every 5, with board approval and a sublet fee. Condos are generally more flexible for investors.
blocks.casual: Co-ops are built for owner occupancy. Many require the apartment to be the buyer's primary residence, ban pieds-a-terre or parents buying for adult children, and limit subletting, for example 2 years out of every 5, with board approval and a sublet fee. Condos are generally more flexible for investors.

deeper.plain: Most co-ops want owners living there, not renting out. Condos are usually easier for investors.
deeper.picture: A co-op is a neighborhood where everyone's expected to stay for dinner. A condo is more like a hotel where some rooms can be rented out.
deeper.street: A buyer wants a Riverside Drive co-op for his daughter at Columbia. The building bans parents buying for adult children, so Jordan points him to condos nearby.
deeper.stakes: An investor who buys a co-op expecting rental income can be stuck with an empty apartment or forced to sell.
deeper.exam: Co-ops often restrict sublets (like 2 of every 5 years) and require primary residence. Condos are generally more investor friendly.

head: Who holds the shares
Rules that apply
rows: Shares the sponsor still owns from the conversion. The offering plan typically lets the sponsor sell or rent those units without board approval.
The sponsor or someone who bought a block of unsold shares from it, if the plan gives them that status. Same special rights: sell or sublet without board approval, often no sublet fees.
Shares bought by regular purchasers. Fully subject to board approval, sublet limits, and house rules.

deeper.plain: Shares the sponsor never sold come with special rights to rent or sell without board approval. Regular buyers' shares don't.
deeper.picture: The sponsor kept a VIP pass for its own units. Everyone else waits in the regular line for board approval.
deeper.street: In a converted Washington Heights co-op, the sponsor still owns 30% of units as a holder of unsold shares. It rents them out at market rate, no board approval, no sublet fee.
deeper.stakes: Buyers in buildings with large sponsor blocks may have neighbors who are renters and a board with limited control over them.
deeper.exam: Holder of unsold shares can sell or sublet without board approval. Sold shares are subject to all board rules.

blocks.title: Why buyers care
blocks.html: A building where a sponsor or holder of unsold shares owns a big block may have many renters, weaker lender appetite, and a board that cannot control those units. Check the percentage in the financials and building questionnaire.
blocks.casual: Why buyers care: a building where a sponsor or holder of unsold shares owns a big block may have lots of renters, weaker lender interest, and a board that can't control those units. Check the percentage in the financials and the building questionnaire.

deeper.plain: A big sponsor stake can mean fewer owners, harder financing, and less board control.
deeper.picture: It's like a group chat where one person owns 30% of the phones. They can steer the conversation, and they don't follow the group rules.
deeper.street: Tasha's lender won't lend in a Bronx co-op where the sponsor owns 40% and is behind on maintenance. Jordan finds out from the building questionnaire and moves the buyer to a different building.
deeper.stakes: If the sponsor stops paying maintenance on its units, the building's finances suffer. Buyers inherit that risk.
deeper.exam: Sponsor concentration affects financing and board control. The building questionnaire and financials show it.

blocks.html: For shareholders to deduct their share of the building's taxes and mortgage interest, the corporation must qualify as a cooperative housing corporation under Internal Revenue Code Section 216. The classic test is the 80/20 rule: at least 80% of the co-op's gross income must come from tenant-shareholders, so no more than 20% can come from outside sources like store rents and garage income. Since 2007, a co-op can also qualify if at least 80% of its square footage is used by shareholders for residential purposes, or at least 90% of its spending is for the shareholders' benefit.
blocks.casual: For shareholders to deduct their share of the building's taxes and mortgage interest, the corporation has to qualify as a cooperative housing corporation under Internal Revenue Code Section 216. The classic test is the 80/20 rule: at least 80% of the co-op's gross income has to come from tenant-shareholders, so no more than 20% can come from outside sources like store rents and garage income. Since 2007, a co-op can also qualify if at least 80% of its square footage is used by shareholders for residential purposes, or at least 90% of its spending is for the shareholders' benefit.

deeper.plain: To keep the tax deduction, most of the co-op's money has to come from shareholders, or most of its space or spending has to serve them.
deeper.picture: It's a co-op, not a mall. If too much of the money comes from stores downstairs, the IRS stops treating it as housing.
deeper.street: A West Village co-op earns 25% of its income from a restaurant lease on the ground floor. It fails the 80/20 income test but passes the 80% square footage test, so shareholders keep their deductions.
deeper.stakes: If a co-op loses Section 216 status, every shareholder loses the deduction. That can hit values across the building.
deeper.exam: 80/20 rule: at least 80% of gross income from tenant-shareholders. Alternatives since 2007: 80% of square footage residential, or 90% of expenditures for shareholders. IRC 216.

blocks.html: A condop solves the commercial income problem with a split. The building is made into a condominium with two or more units: the residential portion is one condo unit owned by a co-op corporation, and the stores or garage are separate condo units owned by someone else, often the sponsor. Residents still buy shares and get proprietary leases, but the commercial rent is no longer co-op income. The term is also used for co-ops whose rules feel condo-like (lenient sublets, no board approval on resale); always read the documents to see which one you have.
blocks.casual: A condop fixes the commercial income problem with a split. The building becomes a condominium with two or more units: the residential part is one condo unit owned by a co-op corporation, and the stores or garage are separate condo units owned by someone else, often the sponsor. Residents still buy shares and get proprietary leases, but the store rent isn't co-op income anymore. People also use the word for co-ops with condo-like rules (easy sublets, no board approval on resale), so always read the documents to see which one you've got.

deeper.plain: A condop splits the building so the co-op only owns the apartments. The stores are separate, so their rent doesn't count against the co-op.
deeper.picture: It's like slicing a cake so the frosting (stores) goes on a separate plate. The co-op keeps its cake pure for the IRS.
deeper.street: A Chelsea building has a gym and pharmacy on the ground floor. The sponsor keeps them as separate condo units, while the apartments sit in one condo unit owned by the co-op. The co-op's income stays nearly 100% from shareholders.
deeper.stakes: Calling a building a condop without reading the documents can mislead a buyer about sublets or approval. The word means two different things in the market.
deeper.exam: Condop: residential portion is one condo unit owned by a co-op; commercial portions are separate condo units. Purpose: avoid failing the 80/20 rule.

blocks.q: A Chelsea co-op earns $1,600,000 a year from shareholders' maintenance and $500,000 from ground floor retail rent. Under the gross income test, does it qualify?
c: Yes, 76% from shareholders is enough
No, it needs at least 80% from shareholders; it may still qualify under the square footage or expense tests
Yes, commercial rent is ignored
No, and no other test exists
blocks.x: $1,600,000 / $2,100,000 = 76%, below 80%. Since 2007 the square footage and 90% expenditure tests are alternatives, and a condop structure is a way to remove commercial income.

blocks.title: Co-op in one line
blocks.html: Shares plus lease, maintenance not common charges, share loan not mortgage, lien search not title insurance, board interview not right of first refusal.
blocks.casual: Co-op in one line: Shares plus lease, maintenance not common charges, share loan not mortgage, lien search not title insurance, board interview not right of first refusal.

deeper.plain: Every co-op feature has a condo opposite. Learn them as pairs.
deeper.picture: It's a mirror image of the condo line. Hold them side by side and each piece flips.
deeper.street: On the subway home, Jordan says the condo line, then the co-op line, then quizzes on random pairs until West 72nd Street.
deeper.stakes: Mixing even one pair in front of a client, like promising title insurance on a co-op, makes you look unprepared and can lead to wrong cost estimates.
deeper.exam: Pair questions are easy points: co-op = shares, proprietary lease, maintenance, share loan, lien search, board approval.

story.title: The Package
story.setting: West End Avenue, a prewar lobby with a very serious doorman

beats.text: Your bank approved 80%. The building caps financing at 75%. We need to drop the loan before the package goes in.
beats.tag: Board financing cap beats bank approval

beats.text: Adaeze here. Why does a building care how much we borrow?
Because if you default, your neighbors cover the maintenance. In a co-op, you're buying shares and a proprietary lease, not real estate. The board is your landlord.
I read the financials. Reserve fund is healthy, underlying mortgage matures in 2033 at a fixed rate, and the corporation owns the land in fee. No land lease. Good.
beats.tag: Due diligence: reserves, mortgage, land lease

beats.text: Minutes mention Local Law 11 facade work next year. Possible assessment. Factor it in.
And we don't need title insurance?
No deed, so no title policy. I order a co-op lien search instead. And no mortgage recording tax on a share loan.

check.q: Why is there no mortgage recording tax on a co-op share loan?
c: Co-ops are exempt from all transfer taxes
A share loan is secured by personal property, not a recorded mortgage
The co-op pays it
Only condos under $500,000 pay it
check.x: Shares and a proprietary lease are personal property; the lender files a UCC-1, not a mortgage.

beats.text: Board meets the first Tuesday. Package due Friday. Contract, application, tax returns, reference letters, employment letter, credit authorization, verified financial statement.
Two weeks later. The interview. Kim Alvarez, board president, peers over the package.
Your DTI is 27 percent and you have more than two years of liquidity after closing. Any other debts we should know about?
A car lease we paid off last month. It's in the statement with the payoff letter.
Good. And you'll live here full time? We don't allow pieds-a-terre, and sublets are two years out of five, with approval.
Full time. We're not going anywhere.
Then I think we're done. You'll hear from the managing agent.
Condos sell you a home. Co-ops admit you to a corporation. Prepare the buyer like it's a job interview, because it is one.

board.prompt: Make a two-column checklist: everything the bank needs vs everything the co-op board needs. Circle the items that appear in both.

facts.text: In a co-op a corporation owns the building; the buyer gets shares and a proprietary lease, which are personal property, so there is no deed, title insurance or mortgage recording tax.
The proprietary lease gives the shareholder the right to occupy the apartment and sets duties such as maintenance, repairs, and subletting only with board consent.
Maintenance covers the apartment's share of operating costs, the building's real estate taxes and its underlying mortgage, but not the shareholder's own share loan.
Co-op shareholders may deduct their proportionate share of the building's real estate taxes and mortgage interest.
Condo vs co-op: deed vs shares, own tax bill vs taxes in maintenance, mortgage vs share loan, title insurance vs lien search, right of first refusal vs board approval.
Downstate, the buyer's attorney reviews 2 to 3 years of financials and 1 to 2 years of board minutes before the contract is signed.
A big balloon on the underlying mortgage or a thin reserve fund signals higher maintenance or an assessment ahead.
A co-op on a ground lease that expires or resets soon can hurt values and financing, so check whether it owns the land in fee.
The building questionnaire and minutes show owner occupancy, sponsor units, financing limits, the flip tax (a transfer fee usually paid by the seller) and sublet policy.
A co-op shareholder never owns real estate in fee simple: the interest is shares (personal property) plus a leasehold right of occupancy.
The stock certificate proves share ownership and is transferred at closing; if the buyer finances, the lender holds it.
House rules cover move-ins, renovation season, washer-dryers and pets, and can kill a deal for a buyer who needs one of them.
An alteration agreement, signed before renovating, requires board approval of plans, licensed and insured contractors and a deposit.
A co-op share loan is secured by the shares and lease and perfected by filing a UCC-1 financing statement, not by a recorded mortgage.
Instead of title insurance, a co-op lien search looks for UCC filings, judgments, tax liens and bankruptcies against the seller, plus a managing agent letter.
In a recognition agreement the co-op recognizes the lender's lien and agrees to notify it of defaults, and the lender accepts that the co-op's maintenance lien comes first.
Co-op buyers face two underwriters, the bank and the board, and boards are usually stricter; condo boards generally do not approve buyers.
Debt-to-income is all monthly debt including housing divided by gross monthly income; banks often allow the low to mid 40s, co-op boards often 25% to 30%.
A building's financing cap (often 75% to 80%) binds the buyer even if the bank approves a higher loan.
Boards often require post-closing liquidity of 1 to 2 years of maintenance plus loan payments, and may discount retirement assets.
Salary is the sturdiest income, commissions and bonuses use a 2-year average, and lenders often count about 75% of gross rent.
A board package includes the application, signed contract, verified financial statement, reference and employment letters, 2 to 3 years of tax returns and a credit authorization.
Most boards meet monthly, so missing a package deadline can outlast a rate lock, and the agent does not attend the interview.
Under the business judgment rule, courts defer to good-faith co-op board decisions and boards need not give reasons, but they can never reject for a protected class.
Many co-ops require primary residence and limit subletting (for example 2 years out of 5 with board approval), while condos are friendlier to investors.
The sponsor or a holder of unsold shares may usually sell or sublet those units without board approval under the offering plan.

Under IRC 216's 80/20 rule, at least 80% of a co-op's gross income must come from tenant-shareholders for them to deduct taxes and interest; since 2007 an 80% square footage or 90% expenditure test also works.
A condop splits the building into condo units, with the residential unit owned by the co-op and commercial units owned separately, protecting the 80/20 status.

lessons.title: Case file: The Facade Assessment in Riverdale
lessons.tagline: A $2.1 million facade bill lands two weeks after the listing goes live. Now the seller, the buyer, and the board all have a number they want someone else to pay.
objectives: Calculate a unit's common charges and share of a special assessment from its common interest percentage, and decide how unpaid installments are handled in a resale.
Apply a condo declaration's right of first refusal, leasing restrictions, and limited common element repair rules to a resale.
Decide how unpaid common charges are collected and where the condo's lien ranks against taxes and a first mortgage.
Explain which condo carrying costs a unit owner may deduct and what the buyer's attorney needs from the board before closing.

blocks.title: Riverdale, the Bronx, unit 9F
blocks.html: Dr. Miriam Feld is selling 9F, a two-bedroom with a terrace in a 140-unit condominium on a hill above the Henry Hudson Parkway. Jordan took the listing at $725,000. Two weeks later, the board of managers sent every owner a letter: the building's required facade inspection found unsafe conditions, and the board is levying a $2,100,000 special assessment for facade and roof work, payable over 24 months starting next month. Miriam calls Jordan before Jordan has finished reading the letter. "We already have two interested buyers. Do we have to tell them? The work will be done in two years anyway."

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell Miriam about the assessment?
c: Wait until a buyer's attorney asks, since condo sellers do not complete the Property Condition Disclosure Statement
Disclose it only if the board has already billed the first installment, because until then it is not yet a real cost
Disclose it to buyers; it is a material fact the listing agent knows, even though condos are exempt from the PCDS
Keep it confidential, since the duty of confidentiality to the seller covers facts that would lower the sale price
blocks.x: Condo units are exempt from the PCDS, but an agent may not conceal or misrepresent a known material fact, and a $2.1 million assessment is plainly material. Confidentiality protects a client's negotiating position and motives, not defects or costs a buyer is entitled to know. The ask-later answer is the trap: the buyer's attorney will find it in the board minutes anyway, and the agent's silence until then is a misrepresentation risk.

blocks.html: Miriam agrees, unhappily. Jordan adds the assessment to the listing remarks and asks the managing agent for the building's offering plan, declaration and bylaws, the last two years of financial statements, the board minutes, and the current budget. Buyers' attorneys will ask for all of it; having it ready is how a listing agent keeps a deal moving.

Reading the package before buyers do is part of pricing. The financial statements show a building in decent shape: an operating surplus two years running, a reserve fund of about $1.1 million, and only three units more than 60 days behind on common charges. The minutes are less calm. They record the facade engineer's findings, a debate about whether to take a bank loan instead of assessing owners, a vote to assess, and a slip-and-fall lawsuit against the condo that the insurer is defending. Each item will show up on a lender's condo questionnaire, so Jordan builds a one-page summary to hand buyers' agents along with the documents.

The declaration's schedule of units assigns each unit a common interest percentage, fixed when the condo was created, usually based on the unit's size and sometimes its floor and view. 9F's common interest is 0.74%. That percentage drives three things: Miriam's share of the common elements, her vote in owner elections, and her share of every expense the board passes along.

blocks.title: 9F's common charges
blocks.html:
Building operating budget for the year: $2,430,000 (staff, insurance, common-area utilities, repairs, and the reserve fund contribution).
9F's share: $2,430,000 x 0.0074 = $17,982 a year.
Monthly common charges: $17,982 / 12 = $1,498.50.
9F's real estate taxes are separate. Each condo unit is its own tax lot with its own bill, about $7,800 a year here.

blocks.q: A buyer's agent asks how much of 9F's monthly carrying cost goes to the condo versus the city. Based on the figures above, what are 9F's monthly common charges and monthly taxes?
c: $1,498.50 in common charges and about $650 in taxes paid on the unit's own bill
$2,148.50 in common charges, because the condo collects each unit's taxes and pays the city
$1,498.50 in common charges, with taxes already included because the condo owns the land
$179.82 in common charges and about $650 in taxes, based on the common interest percentage
blocks.x: Common charges: $2,430,000 x 0.74% / 12 = $1,498.50. Taxes are billed to the unit separately: $7,800 / 12 = $650. The "taxes included" answer is the trap: that is how co-op maintenance works, because the co-op corporation owns the building and pays one tax bill. A condo owner owns real property and pays her own. $179.82 misplaces the decimal in the percentage.

blocks.html: Under the bylaws, the board can levy special assessments for capital work without an owner vote, allocated by common interest, the same way as common charges. The board chose an assessment rather than draining the reserve fund, which the engineer's report says should stay above $900,000 for the elevators due in five years. The minutes show the vote and the engineer's report attached. A buyer's attorney will read both.

blocks.q: What is 9F's share of the $2,100,000 assessment, and what is each of the 24 monthly installments?
c: $21,000 total, $875.00 a month
$1,554 total, $64.75 a month
$15,540 total, $647.50 a month
blocks.x: Share: $2,100,000 x 0.0074 = $15,540. Installment: $15,540 / 24 = $647.50. $1,295.00 is the trap: it divides by 12 months instead of the 24 the board set. $21,000 uses 1% instead of 0.74%. Assessments follow the common interest percentage unless the declaration provides otherwise.

blocks.html: An offer comes in from Ines Carvalho, a physical therapist who works at a hospital nearby, at $700,000. Her agent's first question is not about the price. It is about the assessment. Closing is expected in about four months, after eight installments. Sixteen installments will remain: 16 x $647.50 = $10,360.

blocks.q: Who pays the 16 installments that fall due after closing?
c: The seller, automatically, because the board voted the assessment while she was the owner
Whoever the contract says; the parties often credit the buyer or price it into the deal
The buyer, automatically, because assessments run with the unit regardless of the contract
The board, which has to collect the remaining balance from the reserve fund at closing
blocks.x: The board will bill whoever owns the unit when each installment falls due, so without a contract term the buyer pays the later ones. That is why the allocation is negotiated: a seller credit, a price reduction, or a payoff at closing. The "seller automatically" answer is the trap: the date of the vote does not decide who pays. Common contract forms address it, but the parties can agree otherwise, and here they should, in writing.

blocks.html: Jordan and Ines's agent settle it: price $700,000, and Miriam gives a $10,360 credit at closing. Ines's attorney, Priya, writes it into the rider along with a clause that any new assessment levied before closing is Miriam's.

Ines is financing $560,000, 80% of the price. Her lender sends the managing agent a condo questionnaire: owner-occupancy percentage, units in arrears, pending litigation, insurance, and whether the building has any unfunded or unfinished repairs affecting safety or structural soundness. Since 2021, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have treated buildings with significant deferred maintenance or unsafe conditions, including unfinished critical facade and structural work, as ineligible for the loans they buy until the work is done. 9F's building checks that box until the shed comes down.

blocks.q: Ines's lender says it cannot sell a loan on 9F to Fannie Mae while the facade work is unfinished. What is the most practical path for the deal?
c: Move the loan to a portfolio lender that keeps loans on its books and judges the project itself
Cancel, because no lender may finance a condo unit while a special assessment is outstanding
Have the board certify the work is finished, since the lender only needs the board's word
Convert the purchase to a co-op share loan, which avoids review of the building's condition
blocks.x: Agency eligibility rules bind loans that will be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. A portfolio lender, which holds the loan itself, sets its own project standards and often finances buildings mid-repair, sometimes at a slightly higher rate. The cancel answer is the trap: an assessment alone does not make a unit unfinanceable. A false certification would be fraud, and a condo unit cannot be financed with a co-op share loan.

blocks.html: Tasha, the mortgage broker, finds Ines a savings bank that keeps its loans in portfolio and has lent in the building before. The rate is an eighth of a point higher. Ines takes it. The lesson for Jordan's future listings: in a building with open structural work, warn financed buyers early, and keep a list of lenders that have closed loans there.

The declaration's resale article gives the board a right of first refusal: before Miriam may sell, she must give the board written notice with a copy of the signed contract, and the board has 30 days to elect to buy 9F on the same terms. If it does nothing, the right is waived for this sale. The deed form attached to the declaration also contains a power of attorney in favor of the board, so the board can act on the right if it ever exercises it.

blocks.q: The contract is fully signed on March 3. What should happen next on the right of first refusal?
c: Wait until the week of closing, since the board only needs notice once the buyer's financing is approved
Skip it, because the right of first refusal expires automatically on any sale to an owner-occupant
Ask the board to interview Ines first, since the waiver depends on the board approving the purchaser
Send the notice and a copy of the contract right away, and get a written waiver for the closing file
blocks.x: The 30-day clock starts when the board receives proper notice, so send it as soon as the contract is signed. The buyer's lender and title company will want the waiver, or proof the period expired, before closing. The wait-for-financing answer is the trap: it can push the closing back a month. A condo board does not interview buyers; its only tool is to match the deal.

blocks.html: At the next board meeting, one manager grumbles that Ines "will rent it out to students." He wants the board to block the sale. The managing agent, who has seen this before, reminds him what the declaration actually says.

blocks.q: Under typical New York condo documents, what can the board do if it dislikes Ines?
c: Reject her after an interview, as a co-op board could, without giving a reason
Require Miriam to find a buyer the board prefers, since the declaration controls
Exercise its right of first refusal and buy 9F itself on the same terms, or waive
Delay the waiver until Ines agrees in writing never to lease the unit to anyone
blocks.x: A condo board has no general power to approve or reject purchasers. Its tool is the right of first refusal: buy (or lease) on the same terms, which means spending building money, or let the deal close. The co-op answer is the trap: co-op boards approve purchasers because they are admitting shareholder-tenants; condo owners take a deed. A board that withholds a waiver to extract conditions invites a lawsuit.

blocks.html: Ines does not plan to rent the unit now, but she might move for a job in a few years and wants to keep 9F as a rental. The bylaws say any lease must be for at least 12 months, must be submitted to the board, and is subject to the board's right of first refusal on leases. The house rules add move-in fees and a ban on short-term occupancy.

blocks.q: Three years from now, Ines wants to lease 9F for six months to a visiting doctor. What is the most likely result?
c: She may not, because the recorded bylaws require a lease term of at least 12 months
She may, because a unit owner holds fee title and recorded bylaws cannot restrict leasing
She may, as long as the managing agent receives notice of the tenant's name and lease dates
She may not, because condo units in New York cannot be leased without a unanimous vote
blocks.x: Recorded condo documents bind every owner as covenants running with the unit, and leasing minimums are common and generally enforceable. A six-month lease violates the 12-month minimum. The fee-title answer is the trap: owning in fee does not free an owner from recorded restrictions accepted with the deed. Nothing requires unanimous approval of leases; the board's role is the right of first refusal and the bylaw terms.

blocks.html: Ines's inspector, Ray, finds water staining on the ceiling of 8F, directly below 9F's terrace. He traces it to the terrace membrane at a corner where Miriam's heavy planters sit on the drain. The terrace is a limited common element: part of the common elements, reserved for 9F's use. The declaration says the condo maintains and repairs the structure and the waterproofing membrane, the owner maintains the surface, furniture, and plantings, and an owner pays for damage caused by her own negligence or misuse.

blocks.q: The membrane failed where Miriam's planters blocked the drain. Who most likely bears the cost of repairing the membrane and the ceiling in 8F?
c: The condo as a common expense, with no charge back, because the membrane is a common element
Miriam, through a charge back, because the declaration charges damage caused by the owner's misuse
The owner of 8F, because damage inside a unit is the responsibility of the unit owner who lives there
Ines, because a buyer takes the unit as is and assumes all past damage once the contract is signed
blocks.x: The condo normally repairs a terrace membrane as a common element. But declarations commonly let the board charge an owner for damage caused by that owner's misuse, and blocked drains under her planters fit. The common-expense answer is the trap: it ignores the misuse clause. Ines, who does not own the unit yet, assumes nothing; the contract's condition clause and the closing schedule will decide how any unpaid charge is handled.

blocks.html: The board fixes the membrane promptly and bills Miriam $6,200 for the membrane patch and the ceiling repair in 8F. Miriam does not pay. Two common charge payments also slip while she moves to Philadelphia.

blocks.text: Unpaid charges and the condo's lien

blocks.title: The condo's lien and where it ranks
blocks.html: Under the Condominium Act, unpaid common charges (and charges the declaration treats like them) are a lien on the unit. The lien ranks behind real estate taxes and behind the unpaid balance of a first mortgage of record (RPL 339-z), and the board can foreclose it. The board can also sue the owner for the money.

At closing, none of this can travel to Ines. Priya asks the managing agent for a paid-up letter: a statement of every amount the unit owes, through the closing date, including the charge back and the current assessment installment. The amount owed is paid from Miriam's proceeds at the closing table. Her assessment installments are current, and the $10,360 credit for the later ones is a separate line on the closing statement.

blocks.q: Miriam owes two months of common charges and the $6,200 charge back, and her assessment installments are current. What will the paid-up letter require her to pay at closing, apart from the buyer's credit?
blocks.x: Two months of common charges: 2 x $1,498.50 = $2,997. Add the $6,200 charge back: $9,197. $19,557 is the trap: it also adds the $10,360 assessment credit, which is a separate negotiated credit to the buyer, not an arrear. $2,997 leaves out the charge back, which the declaration lets the board collect like common charges.

blocks.q: In the same building, the bank is foreclosing on another owner's unit, 4C, which owes $18,000 in common charges. The sale will not cover everything. In general, who is paid first from the proceeds?
c: The condo, because common charge liens rank ahead of every mortgage in New York
The bank and the board share equally, because both liens were recorded
The first mortgage, then the condo's lien, then any unpaid real estate taxes
Real estate taxes, then the first mortgage, with the condo's lien behind them
blocks.x: RPL 339-z ranks the condo's common charge lien behind real estate taxes and the unpaid balance of a first mortgage of record. In a short sale or foreclosure, the condo may recover little or nothing on the lien and must pursue the former owner. The condo-first answer is the trap: some states give associations a limited "super priority," but New York's statute does not. That is why boards act fast on arrears.

blocks.html: Ines, filing taxes as a homeowner for the first time, asks which of her monthly costs she can deduct. She will have a mortgage of $560,000, the unit's own tax bill, $1,498.50 a month in common charges, and the leftover facade assessment that Miriam's credit is effectively paying.

blocks.q: Assuming Ines itemizes and lives in 9F as her home, which costs are generally deductible on her federal return?
c: Mortgage interest and the unit's real estate taxes, within the federal limits
Mortgage interest and common charges, but not the unit's real estate taxes
Common charges and the special assessment, but not the mortgage interest
Every carrying cost, including common charges, since a condo is real property
blocks.x: A condo owner deducts the unit's own real estate taxes and the interest on the unit's mortgage, within federal limits, like any homeowner. Common charges on a home she lives in are not deductible, and a special assessment for capital work is generally added to her cost basis rather than deducted. The "every carrying cost" answer is the trap: real property ownership earns the same deductions as a house, not more.

head: Item
Who provides it
Why it matters
rows: Proves the board will not match the deal; title and the lender require it
Shows all common charges, charge backs, and assessment installments paid through closing
Deed with power of attorney to the board
Uses the declaration's form so the board's rights stay intact
Title insurance, owner's and loan policies
A condo unit is real property conveyed by deed
Due on Ines's mortgage, as on any NYC condo or house loan
$10,360 for the 16 installments due after closing
blocks.caption: What Priya's checklist looks like for 9F

blocks.q: The week before closing, the board adopts a new house rule banning charcoal grills on terraces. Ines owns a charcoal grill. Which is accurate?
c: The rule is void, because condo rules can be changed only by amending the declaration
The rule likely binds her, because the bylaws let the board adopt and change house rules
The rule is void as to Ines, because her contract was signed before the rule was adopted
The rule is valid only if every terrace owner signs it, since terraces are limited common elements
blocks.x: Boards adopt and amend house rules under the authority the bylaws give them, without an owner vote, as long as the rule is reasonable and consistent with the declaration. A grill ban is a typical safety rule. The declaration-amendment answer is the trap: amending the declaration (for example, changing common interests or use rights) needs the owner supermajority the declaration sets, but everyday rules do not.

blocks.html: One more item goes on Priya's list: insurance. The condo's master policy covers the building's structure and common elements as the declaration defines them. Ines needs her own HO-6 policy for her personal property, her liability inside the unit, and the improvements inside the walls that the master policy excludes, such as her kitchen and flooring, plus loss assessment coverage, which can help pay her share of an assessment the condo levies after a covered loss. Her lender will require it at closing.

Closing day, in Priya's office, is uneventful, which is the point. The board's waiver arrived on day 12 of its 30, signed by the managing agent. Miriam's side pays the New York State transfer tax ($700,000 x 0.4% = $2,800) and the NYC Real Property Transfer Tax ($700,000 x 1.425% = $9,975), since the price is above $500,000. Ines pays mortgage recording tax on her $560,000 loan ($560,000 x 1.925% = $10,780) and, because the price is under $1 million, no mansion tax. The paid-up letter's $9,197 and the $10,360 assessment credit come off Miriam's side of the statement. Everyone leaves with the right documents, and the sidewalk shed stays up for another 20 months.

blocks.title: Facade work is a Local Law 11 story
blocks.html: New York City's Facade Inspection and Safety Program (Local Law 11) requires buildings taller than six stories to have their facades inspected every five years. An "unsafe" finding requires repairs and usually a sidewalk shed until they are done. When a listing sits behind a shed, ask the managing agent for the latest facade report: it predicts assessments better than any seller.

items: A known special assessment is a material fact. Condos are exempt from the PCDS, but agents may not conceal what they know.
Common charges and assessments follow the common interest percentage in the declaration. Condo units are separate tax lots; taxes are not in the common charges.
Assessment installments due after closing fall on the buyer unless the contract shifts them. Negotiate it in writing.
A condo board's power over a resale is the right of first refusal: match the deal or waive. Send notice the day the contract is signed and get the waiver for closing.
