Recorded declarations and bylaws (leasing minimums, repair allocations, charge backs) bind owners. House rules can be changed by the board.
The condo's common charge lien ranks behind real estate taxes and the first mortgage (RPL 339-z). A paid-up letter clears it at closing.

lessons.title: Case file: Two Underwriters on 34th Avenue
lessons.tagline: The bank says yes at 80%. The co-op board's numbers say no. The Bellinis have three weeks to become the buyers the board wants.
objectives: Calculate a co-op buyer's debt-to-income ratio and post-closing liquidity under a board's rules, and compare them to a bank's.
Decide which kinds of income and assets a lender and a co-op board will count, including commission income, gifts, and retirement accounts.
Apply the board package checklist, interview preparation, and sublet rules to a real co-op purchase.
Explain how a share loan is documented: UCC filing, recognition agreement, co-op lien search, and no mortgage recording tax.

blocks.title: Jackson Heights, a garden co-op two blocks from where Jordan grew up
blocks.html: Dana and Marco Bellini have an accepted offer of $520,000 on a two-bedroom in a 1920s garden co-op on 34th Avenue, with a shared courtyard and a waiting list for the laundry room. Dana teaches fifth grade. Marco is a freelance commercial photographer paid on 1099s. Their bank has pre-approved them for an 80% loan. Jordan, representing them, has just received the building's purchase application and its financial requirements from the managing agent. The first page says: maximum financing 75%; maximum debt-to-income ratio 30%; post-closing liquidity of at least two years of mortgage and maintenance payments; retirement assets counted at 50%; gifts allowed toward the down payment with a signed gift letter. Monthly maintenance for the apartment is $1,180. Jordan opens a spreadsheet before calling them.

blocks.q: The Bellinis' bank approved an 80% loan. What is the largest loan the co-op will allow on a $520,000 purchase?
blocks.x: The building caps financing at 75%: $520,000 x 0.75 = $390,000, so the down payment must be at least $130,000. $416,000 is the trap: it is the bank's 80% approval. A co-op buyer must satisfy both underwriters, and the stricter rule wins. The bank's approval does not override the co-op's rules, which come from its proprietary lease, bylaws, or board policy.

blocks.html: Dana's salary is simple: $96,000 on a W-2, verified by pay stubs and an employment letter. Marco's is not. His tax returns show $74,000 of net business income two years ago and $58,000 last year; the drop came from losing one large catalog client. Both lenders and boards usually average self-employed and commission income over two years, but when the trend is down they tend to use the lower, more recent figure, and some want a year-to-date profit and loss statement from his accountant.

head: Income source
How a lender usually treats it
How a co-op board usually looks at it
rows: Fully counted with stubs, W-2s, employer verification
The most trusted income in the package
Two-year average from tax returns; lower figure if declining
Two to three years of returns, often an accountant's letter; declining trend draws questions
Usually a two-year average, if likely to continue
Same, with skepticism about one great year
Counted with a history and the assets still in place
Counted, but boards look at the assets behind them
Often about 75% of gross rent, documented by leases and returns
Counted net of that property's expenses and debt
blocks.caption: Income types the syllabus expects agents to recognize

blocks.q: Which annual income figure should Jordan use to test the Bellinis against the board's 30% limit?
c: $170,000, using Marco's better year because it shows his earning power
$162,000, using the two-year average of Marco's business income
$96,000, using Dana's salary alone because 1099 income is excluded
$154,000, using Marco's lower recent year
blocks.x: When self-employed income is declining, lenders and boards lean on the recent, lower figure: $96,000 + $58,000 = $154,000, or $12,833 a month. The two-year average ($96,000 + $66,000 = $162,000) is the trap: averaging is the default, but a downward trend makes the average overstate what Marco is likely to earn. Ignoring 1099 income entirely is too harsh; it counts with proper documentation.

blocks.text: The first run of the numbers

blocks.title: Debt-to-income at 75% financing
blocks.html:
Loan: $390,000 at 6.5%, 30-year fixed. Principal and interest: about $2,465 a month.
Maintenance: $1,180. Student loan: $350. Car loan: $420.
Total monthly debt: $2,465 + $1,180 + $350 + $420 = $4,415.
Gross monthly income: $154,000 / 12 = $12,833.
Debt-to-income: $4,415 / $12,833 = 34.4%.
Bank limit (about 43% here): passes. Board limit (30%): fails.

This is the gap the syllabus calls "income parameters for co-op admission." The bank applies federal ability-to-repay rules and its investors' limits, usually in the low to mid 40s for debt-to-income. Co-op boards write their own rules, and because a default by one shareholder raises everyone's maintenance, they set them tighter: 25% to 30% is common in many Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens buildings. Boards also count maintenance as housing debt, which some buyers forget.

blocks.q: The Bellinis have $7,500 left on the car loan and enough savings to pay it off. If they pay off the car and borrow 65% ($338,000, about $2,136 a month), what is their new debt-to-income ratio?
c: About 28.6%
About 31.9%
About 19.4%
About 34.4%
blocks.x: New monthly debt: $2,136 + $1,180 maintenance + $350 student loan = $3,666. $3,666 / $12,833 = 28.6%, under the 30% limit. 31.9% is the trap: it keeps the $420 car payment ($4,086). 19.4% leaves out maintenance, the cost boards always count. Lowering the loan and eliminating a payment are the two levers buyers control.

blocks.html: Lowering the loan to 65% fixes the ratio but spends cash. The down payment rises to $182,000. With about $11,000 of closing costs and the $7,500 car payoff, the Bellinis need $200,500 at or before closing. Their balance sheet: $88,000 in checking and savings, $66,000 in a brokerage account, a $50,000 gift promised by Dana's parents, and $190,000 in Marco's SEP-IRA and Dana's 403(b).

blocks.title: Assets: what the bank sees vs what the board counts

left.title: Bank
items: Cash, savings, T-bills: full value
Stocks, bonds, mutual funds: usually counted, sometimes discounted
Gifts: allowed for the down payment with a gift letter and a paper trail
Retirement accounts: counted as reserves, sometimes at a discount
Real estate, privately held companies, collectibles: not liquid for reserves

right.title: This co-op board
items: Cash and securities: full value as post-closing liquidity
Gifts: allowed toward the down payment with a signed letter that no repayment is expected
Retirement accounts: 50% of the balance
Trust funds: only if the buyer can actually reach the money
Real estate and private companies: noted on the net worth, not counted as liquidity

blocks.q: After closing, the Bellinis will have about $3,500 in cash plus $190,000 in retirement accounts. The board requires two years of mortgage plus maintenance payments. Do they meet the post-closing liquidity rule?
c: No, because co-op boards in New York exclude retirement assets entirely
No: they need two years of total monthly debt, $87,984, and have $3,500
Yes: $3,500 plus 50% of $190,000 is $98,500, above the $79,584 required
Yes: $193,500 in total assets is above two years of maintenance alone
blocks.x: Required: ($2,136 + $1,180) x 24 = $79,584. Counted: $3,500 cash + 50% of $190,000 = $98,500. They pass, narrowly. The two-years-of-everything answer ($3,666 x 24 = $87,984) is the trap: this board's rule covers mortgage and maintenance, not the student loan, and it does count half of retirement. Boards differ widely, so read each building's rule rather than assuming one.

blocks.html: Passing on paper is not the same as looking comfortable. Jordan tells them honestly that a board will notice a couple who will have $3,500 in the bank the day after closing. Marco has $9,000 owed by two clients; when it arrives, it goes into savings before the package is submitted, with the deposits documented.

blocks.q: Dana's parents are giving $50,000 toward the down payment. What documentation should go to both the bank and the board?
c: A promissory note from Dana to her parents, so the board sees the money is owed
Nothing, because a gift from a parent is not something the buyers have to disclose
A statement of the parents' net worth, which the board substitutes for the buyers'
A signed gift letter stating no repayment is expected, with proof of the transfer
blocks.x: Lenders and boards both want to know the money is truly a gift, not a hidden loan that adds monthly debt. A signed gift letter and a paper trail of the transfer do that. The promissory note is the trap: it turns the gift into debt and changes the ratios. Hiding the source is the worst choice: undisclosed funds are exactly what a board reads packages to find.

blocks.html: Tasha, the mortgage broker, offers a second option: a 7/6 adjustable-rate mortgage at 5.75%, fixed for seven years and then adjusting every six months. At 65% financing the payment drops to about $1,972. Marco likes the lower payment. Dana asks what happens in year eight. Jordan's view, without giving financial advice: the fixed loan costs more now and nothing changes later; the ARM's payment can rise after the fixed period, subject to its caps. The board will see the loan commitment either way, and many boards evaluate the buyer at the fully indexed or stress-tested payment, not the introductory one. The Bellinis choose the 30-year fixed.

blocks.q: Marco argues for the ARM: "The lower payment makes our debt-to-income look better to the board." What is the most accurate response?
c: The board has to use the introductory payment, so the ARM is the safer way to pass
The board may look past the first payment, which can rise after year seven
An ARM cannot be used for a co-op share loan under New York banking regulations
The ARM's rate is locked for the life of the loan once the board approves the buyer
blocks.x: A lower start rate does lower the first seven years of payments, but boards and lenders often evaluate an ARM at a higher, stress-tested payment, and after the fixed period the rate adjusts within the loan's caps. The has-to-use answer is the trap: no rule forces a board to use the teaser payment. Share loans can be fixed or adjustable, and an ARM's rate is fixed only for its initial period.

blocks.html: Tasha also confirms they will not need a no-income-verification loan, which boards in buildings like this one generally refuse to accept.

The contract of sale, prepared by the seller's attorney on a standard co-op form, makes the deal contingent on board approval and on a loan commitment. Priya, the Bellinis' attorney, makes sure the financing contingency names a loan of $338,000, not the bank's 80% approval, and gets two additional weeks for the commitment. The down payment, 10% of the price, goes into the seller's attorney's escrow account.

blocks.q: Under the board approval contingency, what happens to the Bellinis' $52,000 down payment if the board rejects them?
c: It is returned to the Bellinis and the contract is cancelled
The seller keeps it as liquidated damages, since the buyers chose to apply
It is held until the Bellinis find another apartment in the building
Half is returned, and half pays the seller's and the building's costs
blocks.x: A standard co-op contract makes board approval a condition: if the board says no, the contract ends and the down payment comes back to the buyers. That is why buyers cannot be penalized for a rejection they did not cause. The liquidated damages answer is the trap: the seller keeps a down payment only when a buyer defaults, for example by withholding documents the board requested or walking away without a contractual reason.

items.title: Purchase application
items.html: The building's form, every question answered, signed by both buyers.

items.title: Fully executed contract and loan commitment
items.html: Signed by both sides; the commitment at $338,000.

items.title: Financial statement with verification
items.html: Every asset and liability, each backed by recent statements: bank, brokerage, retirement, the gift letter and transfer proof, the car payoff letter.

items.title: Employment and income
items.html: Dana's employment verification letter (title, salary, years). For Marco: two to three years of returns, 1099s, and an accountant's letter with a year-to-date profit and loss.

items.title: Letters
items.html: Two personal reference letters and two business reference letters, including one from a long-time client of Marco's.

items.title: Tax returns
items.html: Three years recommended, all schedules.

items.title: Credit authorization
items.html: Signed so the managing agent can run credit and background checks.

items.title: Disclosures
items.html: Required New York forms, including the lead paint disclosure for this 1920s building.

blocks.q: Jordan's final review finds the package complete except for one item Marco left out. Which omission is most likely to delay a board decision?
c: A photo of the buyers, which most co-op boards require under the house rules
A letter from the seller describing the Bellinis' personal character and plans
Marco's accountant's letter and year-to-date figures supporting his 1099 income
The building's own financial statements, which the buyers must attach for review
blocks.x: For a self-employed buyer, income verification is the heart of the package, and Marco's declining year makes current figures essential. The managing agent will not send an incomplete package to the board, and a missed monthly meeting can push the deal past the rate lock. The seller's letter is the trap: it sounds helpful but is not part of the checklist. Photos are not a standard requirement.

blocks.html: Timing drove every step. This board meets on the second Tuesday of each month and wants complete packages in the managing agent's hands ten days before. The Bellinis' rate lock runs 60 days from contract signing. Working backward on the day the contract was signed, Jordan and Priya saw one realistic path: loan commitment in three weeks, package in by the deadline for next month's meeting, interview the same week, and closing about three weeks after approval. Miss the package deadline by one day and the interview slides a month, the rate lock expires, and the Bellinis pay to extend it. Agents who represent co-op buyers keep a calendar of their buildings' board dates for exactly this reason.

The package goes in on time. Two weeks later the managing agent schedules an interview in the board president's apartment for the following Tuesday. Jordan does not attend; agents do not. The prep session happens over coffee. Jordan reviews every number in the package with them, because board members will ask about it, and asks Marco what he planned to say about his work.

Marco mentions two ideas. First, he might use the second bedroom as a small studio and have clients come by. Second, in a few years they might take a teaching job in Rome for a year and sublet. The building's proprietary lease and house rules allow subletting only after two years of residence, for no more than two years in any five, with board approval and a sublet fee, and they bar commercial use of apartments.

blocks.q: How should the Bellinis handle these plans at the interview?
c: Mention nothing, since boards cannot ask about future plans for the apartment
Raise both ideas as firm plans, since boards value buyers who are fully open
Promise the board in writing that they will give up any right to sublet
Answer honestly if asked, within the sublet and business-use rules
blocks.x: Boards ask about use and occupancy, and a buyer who hides plans the board later discovers loses credibility, or worse. The honest answer fits the rules: a home office without client traffic, and any future sublet under the policy, with approval. Silence is the trap: boards can and do ask. A blanket promise never to sublet is unnecessary and may not be kept. Total disclosure means accurate, not volunteered speculation.

blocks.html: During the interview, a board member mentions that eleven of the building's 96 apartments are still owned by the original sponsor from the 1987 conversion, and are rented to non-shareholder tenants. Marco, after the meeting, is irritated: "So the sponsor can rent out eleven apartments and we need permission to sublet one for a year?"

blocks.q: What explains the difference?
c: The offering plan gave the sponsor holder of unsold shares rights
The sponsor's units are rental units the co-op leases from the city under rent rules
The board has simply chosen not to enforce the sublet rules against the sponsor
The sponsor's eleven units are condominium units carved out of the co-op building
blocks.x: Offering plans typically give the sponsor, or a buyer of a block of unsold shares, status as holder of unsold shares: they may sell or rent those apartments without board approval and often without sublet fees. Sold shares, like the Bellinis', are fully subject to the board's rules. The nonenforcement answer is the trap: the difference is contractual, not a choice. Lenders watch the sponsor's percentage; a large block can limit financing.

blocks.html: The board approves the Bellinis, with one condition: an escrow of twelve months of maintenance ($14,160), held by the managing agent for the first two years. Marco is offended. Jordan explains it calmly: it is a common way for a board to approve a buyer whose liquidity is thin or whose income is uneven, and it is better than a rejection.

blocks.q: The Bellinis ask whether the board could have simply rejected them without a reason. In New York City, generally:
c: No, because NYC requires boards to deliver written reasons within 45 days
Yes, under the business judgment rule, but never for a protected-class reason
No, because a buyer with a signed contract has a right to board approval
Yes, and a rejection cannot be reviewed by any court or agency in any case
blocks.x: Courts defer to co-op boards acting in good faith for corporate purposes (the business judgment rule), and NYC boards generally need not explain a rejection. They may never reject for a reason the federal, state, or city fair housing laws protect, and a rejection that looks like pretext can be challenged. The written-reasons answer is the trap: that describes Westchester County's law, not New York City's.

blocks.title: Westchester does it differently
blocks.html: Westchester County's co-op law sets deadlines for boards to acknowledge and decide applications, and since a 2021 amendment requires boards to disclose minimum financial requirements and give written reasons for a rejection, with reports to the county's Human Rights Commission. Agents working in Westchester should calendar those deadlines. In New York City, boards generally are not required to give reasons, though bills to require them come up regularly.

Closing is in the managing agent's conference room. There is no deed and no title insurance policy. The seller's stock certificate and the proprietary lease are assigned to the Bellinis, and because they financed, the bank takes possession of the new stock certificate and the lease assignment as collateral. The bank perfects its lien by filing a UCC-1 financing statement. Priya ordered a co-op lien search two weeks earlier: UCC filings against the seller's shares, plus judgments, tax liens, and bankruptcies against the seller, and the managing agent's letter that maintenance is current.

The lien search turns up a surprise: a UCC-1 financing statement filed in 2014 by the seller's former lender against the same shares. The seller says that loan was paid off years ago. That is probably true; lenders often forget to terminate their filings.

blocks.q: What does Priya need at or before closing to deal with the old UCC-1?
c: Nothing, because a UCC filing expires the moment the underlying loan is repaid
A title insurance policy insuring over the filing, since co-ops use owner's policies
A UCC-3 termination, or the old lender's commitment to file one
A recognition agreement between the old lender and the Bellinis' new lender
blocks.x: A financing statement stays of record until it lapses or a termination statement (UCC-3) is filed. The buyer's attorney and the new lender need the termination, or the old lender's written confirmation and undertaking to file it, so the new lender's lien on the shares is clean. The expires-automatically answer is the trap: repayment ends the debt, not the public filing.

blocks.q: Which document gives the Bellinis' bank the co-op's acknowledgment of its lien and the right to be notified and cure if they default on maintenance?
c: The UCC-1 financing statement filed with the state
The assignment of the proprietary lease to the Bellinis
The managing agent's letter that maintenance is paid
The recognition agreement
blocks.x: In a recognition agreement, the co-op recognizes the lender's security interest in the shares and lease, agrees to notify the lender of shareholder defaults, and gives it a chance to cure before the lease is cancelled; the lender accepts that the co-op's own lien for unpaid maintenance comes first. The UCC-1 is the trap: it perfects the bank's lien against the world but binds the co-op to nothing.

blocks.title: Closing costs the Bellinis skip, and the ones they do not
blocks.html:
Mortgage recording tax: none. A share loan is secured by personal property, not a recorded mortgage. On a $338,000 NYC mortgage it would have been 1.8%, or $6,084.
Mansion tax: none; the price is under $1,000,000.
Title insurance: none; replaced by the lien search, a few hundred dollars.
What they do pay: their attorney, the bank's attorney and fees, the lien search, the managing agent's application and move-in fees, and the building's processing fee for the transfer.

items: A co-op buyer clears two underwriters. The bank's limits (financing up to 80% or more, debt-to-income in the 40s) are looser than a typical board's (financing caps, debt-to-income near 25% to 30%). The stricter rule controls.
Use the income figure a careful underwriter would: two-year averages for commission and self-employed income, the lower recent year when the trend is down.
Post-closing liquidity is a building-specific formula. Read whether it covers maintenance only, mortgage plus maintenance, or all debt, and how retirement assets and gifts are counted.

A complete, verified board package and an honest interview win approvals. Sublets and business use follow the proprietary lease and house rules; sponsor and holder of unsold shares units follow the offering plan.
Boards generally need not give reasons in NYC, but may not discriminate. Conditional approvals, such as a maintenance escrow, are common.
A share loan uses a UCC-1, a recognition agreement, and a lien search. No mortgage recording tax and no title insurance.

lessons.title: Case file: The Flip Tax Vote on Riverside Drive
lessons.tagline: Kim Alvarez's board needs $900,000 for boilers and emissions upgrades. Every way to raise it lands on someone: the sellers, the shareholders, or the tax deduction everyone forgot was at risk.
objectives: Calculate a flip tax under percentage-of-price, per-share, and percentage-of-profit methods, and decide whether a board may adopt or change one.
Apply a proprietary lease's repair, alteration, and default provisions to shareholder disputes.
Apply the Section 216 tests (including the 80/20 gross income test) to a co-op's commercial income, and explain why condops are created.
Calculate a shareholder's share of maintenance, an assessment, and the deductible taxes and interest from the share allocation.

blocks.title: Riverside Drive, the co-op board's dining room
blocks.html: Kim Alvarez, president of a 120-apartment prewar co-op on Riverside Drive, has asked Jordan to stop by before the board meeting. The building's engineer says the boilers and controls need $900,000 of work, partly to meet New York City's building emissions limits under Local Law 97. The reserve fund can cover only part of it. One board member wants to double the flip tax so that "sellers pay for it, not those of us who are staying." Another wants to lease the empty ground-floor space to a bank. Kim wants an outside view from someone who sells apartments in the building, and Jordan happens to have a listing on the 12th floor. Kim's first question is direct: "Can the board just change the flip tax at tonight's meeting?"

The deadline is real. Local Law 97 sets carbon emission limits for most New York City buildings larger than 25,000 square feet, with annual fines for buildings that exceed them, and this building's aging boilers put it over the limit. Paying for an upgrade once is cheaper than paying fines every year, and buyers' attorneys now ask about Local Law 97 compliance in every co-op and condo package.

The building's current flip tax is 2% of the gross sale price, paid by the seller. It appears in the proprietary lease, added by a shareholder-approved amendment in the 1990s. The lease says it may be amended by a vote of holders of at least two-thirds of the outstanding shares.

blocks.q: Can Kim's board raise the flip tax to 4% by resolution at tonight's meeting?
c: Yes, because transfer fees are house rules that the board may change at any regular meeting
Yes, because the business judgment rule allows any fee the board finds good for the building
No, because New York prohibits co-ops from charging transfer fees on resales of apartments
No, it must be authorized in the lease or bylaws by the required vote
blocks.x: New York's Business Corporation Law allows a co-op's transfer fee only if it is authorized in the proprietary lease, the bylaws, or the offering plan, or in a properly approved amendment. Here that means a two-thirds shareholder vote on a lease amendment. The business judgment answer is the trap: courts defer to boards acting within their authority, but a board cannot create authority the governing documents do not give it.

blocks.text: Three ways to write a flip tax

blocks.html: If the shareholders are going to vote, Kim wants to know what the options would cost a typical seller. Jordan uses the listing in 12C. The building has 30,000 shares outstanding; 12C carries 450 of them, or 1.5% of the building. The seller, Harold Nyquist, bought in 2009 for $760,000 and is under contract at $1,350,000.

head: Method
How it is computed
12C's flip tax
blocks.caption: The same sale under four flip tax formulas

blocks.q: Harold's neighbor in 3A bought for $1,100,000 two years ago and must sell now for $1,050,000 because of a job move. Which flip tax method charges her the least?
c: Percentage of profit, since she has no profit
Per share, because it ignores the price paid entirely
Percentage of gross price, because her price is lower
Each method charges the same on a loss sale
blocks.x: A profit-based flip tax is zero when the seller sells at a loss: 10% of nothing is nothing. A per-share or percentage-of-price flip tax is owed regardless. The per-share answer is the trap: it ignores the price, which is exactly why it does not help a seller who lost money. Some buildings use profit-based formulas, or a minimum, to avoid charging sellers who are already losing.

blocks.html: Jordan's honest observation for the board: doubling the flip tax to 4% raises money only when apartments sell, which might be eight or ten sales a year, and it lowers what buyers will pay because every buyer's broker will point out that the next sale carries a 4% cost. Flip taxes are a reasonable source of reserve money. They are a slow way to fund a boiler this year.

blocks.q: Harold's contract is silent on the flip tax. Who usually pays it?
c: The buyer, because the fee is collected when the buyer's stock certificate is issued
The co-op, because the fee is deducted from the building's reserve fund at the closing
The seller, unless the documents or the parties provide otherwise
The managing agent, who collects it as part of the processing fee for the transfer
blocks.x: In most buildings the governing documents and the standard co-op contract put the flip tax on the seller, and it is paid from the seller's proceeds at closing. A few buildings charge buyers, and the parties can shift it by contract. The buyer answer is the trap: a buyer may pay it in a negotiated deal or in a building whose documents say so, but it is not the default.

blocks.text: The bank on the ground floor and the 80/20 rule

blocks.html: The second idea is to lease 4,000 square feet of empty ground-floor space to a bank branch for $400,000 a year. It sounds like free money. The treasurer has the numbers: shareholders pay $3,600,000 a year in maintenance, and the existing pharmacy on the corner pays $700,000 in rent.

blocks.title: The gross income test, before and after the bank
blocks.html:
Today: outside income $700,000 / total income $4,300,000 = 16.3%. Shareholder income is 83.7%. Passes the 80/20 test.
With the bank lease: outside income $1,100,000 / total income $4,700,000 = 23.4%. Shareholder income is 76.6%. Fails the gross income test.
The commercial spaces, pharmacy and bank together, would occupy about 9% of the building's square footage.

blocks.q: If the co-op signs the bank lease, does it lose its status as a cooperative housing corporation under Section 216?
c: Yes, because failing the 80/20 gross income test ends Section 216 status in every case
Probably not, since shareholders still use over 80% of the space as homes
No, because rent from commercial tenants is counted as shareholder income under Section 216
No, because Section 216 status depends only on a vote of the shareholders to remain a co-op
blocks.x: Since 2007, a co-op qualifies if it meets any one of three tests: 80% of gross income from tenant-shareholders, 80% of square footage used by shareholders for residential purposes, or 90% of expenditures for the shareholders' benefit. With commercial space at about 9% of the building, the square footage test is still met. The "in every case" answer is the trap: it describes the rule before 2007. Boards still have their accountants confirm it.

blocks.html: Section 216 matters because it is what lets shareholders deduct their share of the building's real estate taxes and mortgage interest. Kim's board will ask its accountant to confirm the square footage figures before signing anything. Many older buildings, built when only the gross income test existed, solved the commercial income problem a different way.

blocks.title: Why condops exist
blocks.html: A condop is a building that was divided into condominium units, with the residential floors forming one unit owned by a co-op corporation and the stores or garage forming separate commercial units, often kept by the sponsor. Residents still buy co-op shares and get proprietary leases, but the store rent belongs to the commercial unit owner, not the co-op, so it never counts as co-op income. The arrangement was created largely to keep co-ops within the 80/20 rule. The word is also used loosely for co-ops with condo-like rules, so read the documents.

blocks.q: A Midtown developer converts a 20-story building with retail on the first two floors. Why might it create a condop instead of a regular co-op?
c: So buyers receive deeds and title insurance instead of shares and proprietary leases
So the residential board has no right to approve or reject purchasers of apartments
So the retail rent stays out of the co-op's income
So the building avoids filing an offering plan with the Attorney General's office
blocks.x: Separating the retail into its own condo unit keeps that rent out of the co-op's gross income, protecting the shareholders' tax deductions and letting the developer keep the commercial asset. The deeds answer is the trap: residential buyers in a condop still buy shares and get proprietary leases, and the board still approves them. Any conversion still requires an offering plan under the Martin Act.

blocks.html: A third board member suggests skipping the assessment entirely and borrowing the $900,000 by increasing the building's underlying mortgage. The current mortgage has a balance of $6,000,000 at 3.25%, interest only, with the full balance due in two years. Any new money, and the refinance of the whole balance in two years, will come at today's higher rates. The treasurer estimates that refinancing $6,900,000 at about 6.5% would add roughly $250,000 a year of interest alone compared with today ($448,500 versus $195,000), before any principal amortization.

blocks.q: Jordan has buyers looking at 12C and two other apartments in the building. Which item in the financials signals the largest future maintenance risk for them?
c: The pharmacy lease, which brings $700,000 of outside income into the building
The reserve fund contribution line in the operating budget for this year
The 2% flip tax, which sellers pay out of their proceeds at closing
The interest-only underlying mortgage due in two years at a much lower rate
blocks.x: When a low-rate, interest-only underlying mortgage comes due, the co-op must refinance at current rates, and the extra interest flows straight into maintenance. That is why the syllabus tells agents to read the mortgage's balance, rate, and maturity in the financials. The flip tax is the trap: it affects sellers' proceeds, not every shareholder's monthly cost. Commercial income actually helps hold maintenance down.

blocks.html: The board decides against borrowing more now. It will assess, rebuild reserves through a small maintenance increase, and start shopping the refinance a year early. The minutes will say exactly that, which is useful: buyers' attorneys read minutes for this kind of decision, and a board that plans ahead reads well in a package.

The board settles on a $900,000 assessment, payable over 12 months, plus a modest maintenance increase to rebuild reserves, and it schedules the flip tax question for a shareholder vote later. Assessments in a co-op, like maintenance, are allocated by shares unless the lease provides otherwise. 12C's maintenance is $3,600,000 x 1.5% = $54,000 a year, or $4,500 a month.

blocks.q: What is 12C's share of the $900,000 assessment, and what is each of the 12 monthly installments?
c: $13,500 total, $1,125 a month
$13,500 total, $562.50 a month
$9,000 total, $750 a month
$135,000 total, $11,250 a month
blocks.x: 12C holds 450 of 30,000 shares, or 1.5%. $900,000 x 1.5% = $13,500, and $13,500 / 12 = $1,125 a month. $562.50 is the trap: it spreads the assessment over 24 months. $9,000 uses 1% instead of 1.5%. Co-op assessments follow the share allocation in the same way that condo assessments follow common interest.

blocks.html: Harold's buyer asks the obvious question: what part of the $4,500 a month is deductible? The co-op's budget shows $1,500,000 of real estate taxes and $500,000 of interest on the underlying mortgage for the year. Under Section 216, each tenant-shareholder may deduct a proportionate share of both, generally based on shares owned.

blocks.q: What are 12C's deductible shares of the building's real estate taxes and mortgage interest for the year?
c: $54,000, because the entire maintenance payment is deductible for a co-op shareholder
$22,500 of taxes and $7,500 of interest, within federal limits
$30,000 of interest, because co-op shareholders cannot deduct any real estate taxes
$2,000,000, because the deduction passes through to whoever holds the largest unit
blocks.x: Taxes: $1,500,000 x 1.5% = $22,500. Interest: $500,000 x 1.5% = $7,500. Total $30,000, subject to the usual federal limits, including the limit on deducting state and local taxes. The whole-maintenance answer is the trap: the rest of maintenance pays for staff, fuel, insurance, and repairs, which are not deductible on a home. The assessment for boilers is a capital item, not a current deduction.

blocks.html: After the vote, Kim walks Jordan through three shareholder problems on her desk. Each one turns on the proprietary lease, the document every buyer signs and almost none reads. Jordan's buyers in this building will hear about all three before they sign a contract.

head: Lease provision
What it typically says
rows: The shareholder pays monthly maintenance and any assessment the board levies, allocated by shares
The co-op repairs the structure and building-wide systems (risers, main lines, roof, facade); the shareholder maintains the apartment's interior, fixtures, and appliances
No alterations without board consent, usually through an alteration agreement
Only with board consent; transfer fees (flip tax) if the lease authorizes them
Residential use by the shareholder and family; house rules bind the shareholder
The co-op may terminate the lease for nonpayment, breach, or (in many leases) objectionable conduct, under the procedures the lease sets
blocks.caption: The proprietary lease in one table

blocks.html: Problem one: water poured into 11C, the apartment below Harold's, last month. The plumber found two causes: a cracked section of the building's cold-water riser inside the wall of 12C's kitchen, and, separately, a washing machine in 12C that the house rules prohibit, whose hose had also been leaking.

blocks.q: Under a typical proprietary lease, who bears the cost of the damage to 11C?
c: Harold for all of it, because the leak happened inside the walls of his apartment
The co-op for all of it, because shareholders are not liable for water damage below
The co-op for the riser, and Harold for the washer damage
The owner of 11C for all of it, because each shareholder insures his own apartment
blocks.x: Risers are building systems the co-op repairs, even when they run through an apartment's walls. A washer installed against the house rules is the shareholder's responsibility, and most leases make shareholders liable for damage caused by their own breach or negligence. The all-Harold answer is the trap: location inside the apartment does not make a building system the shareholder's. Insurance may then shift some costs among the policies.

blocks.html: Problem two: Harold's buyer, a cellist, wants to move the kitchen to where a bedroom is now, which would put a sink and dishwasher over the bedroom of 11C. Many prewar buildings prohibit "wet over dry" layouts, because leaks from kitchens and bathrooms over living space cause exactly the kind of damage in problem one.

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell the buyer before she signs the contract?
c: She can renovate freely after closing, because a shareholder controls the apartment's interior
She can do the work without approval if she uses a licensed contractor and a building permit
She cannot renovate at all, because proprietary leases forbid alterations to prewar apartments
She should check the alteration policy, since wet over dry may be barred
blocks.x: Alterations need board consent, typically through an alteration agreement that requires plan approval, licensed and insured contractors, work hours, deposits, and responsibility for damage. Many buildings bar wet over dry layouts outright, so a buyer whose plan depends on one should know before signing. The licensed-contractor answer is the trap: a city permit does not substitute for the co-op's consent.

blocks.html: Problem three is the hardest. A shareholder on the 6th floor has for two years filed dozens of baseless complaints, accused staff of crimes, and damaged the elevator. The lease allows the co-op to terminate a proprietary lease for objectionable conduct if holders of two-thirds of the shares vote to do so at a meeting called for that purpose, after notice to the shareholder.

blocks.q: If the shareholders vote as the lease requires and the shareholder sues, how will a New York court most likely review the termination?
c: It will defer to the co-op's decision if made in good faith under the lease procedures
It will hold a full trial and decide for itself whether the conduct was objectionable
It will void the termination, because a shareholder's lease cannot be ended for conduct
It will refer the dispute to the Attorney General, who regulates co-op governance
blocks.x: In 40 West 67th Street v. Pullman (2003), the Court of Appeals applied the business judgment rule to a co-op's termination of a shareholder's lease for objectionable conduct: courts defer if the co-op acted within its authority, for a legitimate corporate purpose, and in good faith. The full-trial answer is the trap: that was the standard the shareholder argued for, and the court rejected it. The Attorney General reviews offering plans, not daily governance.

blocks.text: A sublet request on the 9th floor

blocks.html: Kim has one more item: the shareholder in 9B, who bought 18 months ago, has a two-year fellowship in Chicago and asks to sublet. The building's policy, adopted under the lease's subletting clause, allows sublets only after the shareholder has lived in the apartment as a primary residence for two years, for no more than two years in any five, with board approval of the subtenant and a sublet fee of 10% of the maintenance during the sublet. Meanwhile, four apartments on the 2nd floor are still owned by the sponsor from the 1985 conversion and are rented to tenants with no board involvement at all.

blocks.q: How should the board handle 9B's request under its own policy?
c: Approve it, since a shareholder who pays the sublet fee may sublet at any time
Decline it for now, since 9B has not met the two-year residence requirement
Approve it, since the sponsor's rentals mean the board must treat 9B the same
Decline it, since co-op shareholders may not sublet under New York law
blocks.x: The policy requires two years of residence first, and 9B has 18 months. The board can apply its rule (and could waive it in a hardship case if the documents allow). The sponsor answer is the trap: units held by the sponsor or a holder of unsold shares follow the offering plan, which typically lets them be rented without approval; sold shares like 9B's follow the lease and policy. New York law does not bar co-op sublets.

blocks.html: 9B can reapply in six months, and the fee math is simple: with maintenance of $3,200 a month, the sublet fee would be $320 a month while the subtenant is there. The rules exist because co-ops are built around owner occupancy: lenders watch the percentage of owner-occupied apartments, and shareholders who live in the building tend to pay on time and care about the building.

Harold's contract was signed after the assessment was announced. Under the standard co-op contract, the parties agreed that installments falling due before closing are Harold's and the rest are the buyer's, and the buyer's attorney negotiated a credit for the buyer's share. At closing, the managing agent's statement collects the 2% flip tax ($27,000), any unpaid maintenance, and the transfer fees, all from Harold's proceeds.

blocks.q: Closing is after four of the twelve $1,125 installments. If the contract makes Harold pay the installments due before closing and he agreed to credit the buyer for the rest, how large is the credit?
blocks.x: Remaining installments: 12 minus 4 = 8. 8 x $1,125 = $9,000. $4,500 is the trap: it is what Harold already paid (4 installments). $13,500 is the whole assessment. Whether a seller credits the buyer for later installments is a negotiated term; here they wrote it into the contract, which is the point.

blocks.title: Flip tax, flipping, and the vote
blocks.html: Three traps live in this case. A flip tax is a co-op transfer fee; flipping is a quick resale for profit; the words are unrelated. A board cannot adopt or raise a flip tax by itself unless the governing documents already authorize it; usually it takes a lease or bylaw amendment voted by shareholders. And the 80/20 gross income test is no longer the only Section 216 test; the square footage and expenditure tests can save a co-op that fails it.

items: A flip tax must be authorized by the proprietary lease, bylaws, or offering plan, or a properly approved amendment. Know the method: percentage of price, per share, or percentage of profit. The seller usually pays.
Maintenance, assessments, and the deductible share of taxes and interest all follow the share allocation.

Section 216 has three alternative tests: 80% of income from shareholders, 80% of square footage for shareholder residential use, or 90% of expenditures for shareholders. Condops keep commercial rent out of co-op income.
The proprietary lease splits repairs: building systems are the co-op's, the interior is the shareholder's, and damage from a shareholder's breach is the shareholder's.
Alterations need board consent through an alteration agreement; check wet over dry and other limits before a buyer signs.
Courts review co-op decisions, even lease terminations for objectionable conduct, under the business judgment rule (Pullman, 2003).

lessons.title: Case file: Evelyn Converts a Walk-Up in Crown Heights
lessons.tagline: Evelyn wants to turn 36 rental apartments into a co-op. The tenants have rights, the Attorney General has rules, and Jordan's firm wants the selling agreement without ending up in a Martin Act subpoena.
objectives: Decide what a sponsor and its selling agent may do during CPS-1 testing, while a plan is under review, and after it is accepted for filing.
Apply New York City's conversion rules: the non-eviction plan, the 51% purchase requirement, the tenants' exclusive purchase period, and the protections for non-purchasing tenants.
Read an offering plan's special risks, budget, underlying mortgage, and sponsor-held units, and explain how they affect buyers and their share loans.
Decide when an amendment gives purchasers a right to rescind and how deposits must be held.

blocks.title: Crown Heights, a six-story walk-up on a tree-lined block
blocks.html: Evelyn Park bought a 36-apartment walk-up in Crown Heights three years ago. Thirty apartments are occupied; about half are rent stabilized, the rest are market-rate leases. Six are vacant after renovation. Evelyn has decided to convert the building to a co-op and sell the apartments, and she wants Hudson & Hart as the exclusive selling agent. At the pitch meeting, she slides a mock-up across the table: a glossy flyer reading "Crown Heights Co-ops Coming Soon, Reserve Yours With a $5,000 Deposit." Diane looks at it for a long time. Jordan, sitting next to Diane, realizes this is the moment the case file was written for.

Under the Martin Act (General Business Law 352-e), no one may offer or sell co-op shares or condo units in New York without an offering plan filed with the Attorney General's Real Estate Finance Bureau. "Offer" is read broadly: advertising, taking reservations, and accepting money are all offers. Evelyn has not filed anything. She can, however, apply for CPS-1 permission to test the market first.

blocks.q: If the Attorney General accepts Evelyn's CPS-1 application, what can Hudson & Hart do with her flyer?
c: Use it as written, because CPS-1 allows refundable deposits held in escrow by the sponsor's attorney
Use it with a change from deposits to signed letters of intent, which bind buyers to a specific unit
Use a revised flyer to gather non-binding interest, with the legend and no deposits or reservations
Use nothing at all, because sponsors may not advertise in any form until the plan is declared effective
blocks.x: CPS-1 lets a sponsor advertise and collect non-binding indications of interest, with the required legend, for a limited period. It does not allow deposits or reservations, binding or non-binding, until a plan is accepted for filing. The letters of intent answer is the trap: older materials describe them as reservations, but current CPS-1 policy bars reservations, and a letter of intent never binds a buyer to a unit or price.

blocks.html: Diane rewrites the flyer on the spot: "Crown Heights: a planned co-op conversion. Register your interest." The AG's legend goes at the bottom. No deposit, no reservation, no "lock in your unit." Evelyn grumbles that interest lists do not pay for lawyers. Diane's answer is the Martin Act itself: the Attorney General enforces it civilly and criminally, does not need to prove intent to defraud in a civil case, and has gone after brokers as well as sponsors. A selling agent's marketing is part of the offering.

blocks.q: Months later, a Hudson & Hart agent tells a prospect, "Maintenance here won't go up for years, the sponsor guarantees it," though nothing in the plan says so. The agent believed it. Under the Martin Act, which is most accurate?
c: A likely violation, because the Attorney General need not prove intent in a civil case
No violation, because the agent honestly believed the statement when making it
No violation, because only the sponsor, not a broker, is covered by the Martin Act
A likely violation, but only if the prospect signed a contract and later lost money
blocks.x: The Martin Act prohibits misrepresentations in connection with an offering, and in a civil enforcement action the Attorney General does not have to prove intent to defraud or that anyone relied on the statement and lost money. Brokers and selling agents are within its reach. The honest-belief answer is the trap: good faith does not cure a statement that contradicts or goes beyond the plan.

blocks.html: Converting an occupied building in New York City adds a second layer of law: General Business Law 352-eeee. Before 2019, a sponsor could choose an eviction plan (non-purchasers could eventually be evicted) or a non-eviction plan (with as little as 15% of units sold). The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 abolished eviction plans and raised the threshold for a non-eviction plan sharply.

head: Rule
What it means for Evelyn's building
rows: No tenant may be evicted for failing to buy. Non-purchasing tenants stay as long as they keep their tenancy and pay rent.
The plan cannot be declared effective until purchase agreements cover at least 51% of the dwelling units, signed by tenants in occupancy (bona fide outside buyers no longer count toward it).
For 90 days after the plan is accepted for filing, tenants in occupancy have the exclusive right to buy their own apartments.
Stabilized tenants who do not buy keep their rent stabilization protections.
Protected from eviction for not buying, and from unconscionable rent increases.
blocks.caption: New York City occupied conversions after the HSTPA (GBL 352-eeee)

blocks.q: Evelyn's building has 36 dwelling units. How many purchase agreements from tenants in occupancy does she need before she can declare the plan effective?
blocks.x: 51% of 36 units = 18.36, so 18 is not enough; she needs at least 19. 18 is the trap: rounding down leaves her below 51%. 6 reflects the old 15% threshold that the HSTPA eliminated. Evelyn's six vacant apartments do not help: sales to outsiders no longer count toward the requirement, which is why many sponsors now find occupied conversions impractical.

blocks.html: That math changes Evelyn's whole plan. Thirty apartments are occupied, so she needs nineteen of those thirty households to buy. Her attorney tells her plainly that conversions under the 51% rule succeed mostly where tenants are eager buyers, the insider price is attractive, and financing is available. Evelyn decides to try, with an aggressive insider discount and a tenant meeting before anything is filed.

At the tenant meeting in the lobby, Mrs. Lorraine Odom, 74, who has lived in 2A for 31 years in a rent-stabilized apartment, asks three questions. Will she have to move if she does not buy? Will her rent go up? And can her nephew buy her apartment and let her stay? Jordan, standing at the back with the sign-in sheet, has been told by Diane to answer only factual questions about the process and to refer legal questions to the tenants' own attorney. Two of Mrs. Odom's questions are factual enough to answer.

blocks.q: Mrs. Odom does not want to buy. What happens to her tenancy if the conversion succeeds?
c: She must buy or move within 90 days after the plan is accepted for filing
She may stay as a rent-stabilized tenant; she cannot be evicted for not buying
She may stay for three years, after which the sponsor may recover the unit
She may stay, but her rent resets to market because the building is no longer a rental
blocks.x: Under a non-eviction plan, no tenant may be evicted for failing to buy, and a rent-stabilized non-purchasing tenant keeps rent stabilization. Her apartment becomes one of the sponsor's unsold units, and she remains the sponsor's tenant. The 90-day answer is the trap: 90 days is the tenants' exclusive window to buy, not a deadline to leave. The market-rent answer confuses conversion with deregulation.

blocks.html: Mrs. Odom's third question, whether her nephew could buy her apartment, Jordan refers to the tenants' attorney, because it depends on the plan's terms and on who counts as a tenant in occupancy. Jordan also notes, for the file, that every tenant at the meeting received the same information. Fair dealing with tenants is not only good ethics in a conversion; it is something the Attorney General reviews.

blocks.text: Filing: the red herring and the review

blocks.html: Evelyn's attorneys submit the plan. While the Attorney General reviews it, the preliminary plan, the red herring, may be shown to tenants and prospects for information. It carries a red legend saying it is not an offer. Tenants form an association and hire a lawyer, who negotiates with Evelyn's attorneys over the insider price, the condition of the building, and the reserve fund.

blocks.q: During the review, a tenant in 5B wants to sign a purchase agreement immediately at the red herring's insider price before anyone else can. What is correct?
c: She may not sign yet; no contracts or deposits until the plan is accepted
She may sign, because tenants have priority to buy during the red herring period
She may sign if she gives a deposit, which protects her place in line
She may sign a letter of intent that binds the sponsor to the red herring price
blocks.x: A red herring is for information only: no purchase agreements and no deposits until the plan is accepted for filing. Her protection comes later, from the 90-day exclusive purchase period. The priority answer is the trap: tenants' exclusive rights begin when the plan is accepted, not during review. Prices may change in the final plan, which is why nothing binds either side yet.

blocks.html: Four months later the Attorney General accepts the plan for filing. Evelyn wants a press release saying the Attorney General "approved" the conversion. Diane strikes the word. Acceptance means the plan's disclosures meet the regulations; it is not a judgment that the deal is fair, the price is right, or the building is sound. Saying otherwise in marketing is itself a misrepresentation.

Jordan reads the accepted plan the way buyers' attorneys will. The building will be owned by a new co-op corporation. Evelyn, as sponsor, places a new underlying mortgage of $7,200,000 on the building at closing, interest only at a fixed rate for ten years. The first-year budget shows maintenance of $1.35 per share per month. The plan allocates 36,000 shares; a typical two-bedroom carries 1,100 shares.

blocks.title: What a two-bedroom costs a tenant-purchaser
blocks.html:
Insider price for a two-bedroom (1,100 shares): $410,000. Non-insider price for the same layout: $520,000.
Maintenance: 1,100 shares x $1.35 = $1,485 a month.
Share of the underlying mortgage: 1,100 / 36,000 x $7,200,000 = $220,000. That debt does not appear in the purchase price, but its interest is inside maintenance, and the balloon in year ten is every shareholder's problem.
A tenant who buys with an 80% share loan borrows $328,000 and makes a 10% deposit of $41,000 at contract.

blocks.q: Darnell, the tenant in 3C, compares two two-bedrooms in different conversions at the same $410,000 price. The other building's underlying mortgage share for a comparable apartment is $90,000. What does this tell him?
c: The apartments cost the same, because the purchase price is the only measure of cost
Evelyn's apartment is the better value, since its debt is the sponsor's responsibility
Evelyn's apartment carries more building debt, which shows up in higher maintenance
The other building is overpriced, because a smaller mortgage lowers its share value
blocks.x: A co-op apartment's true cost is the price plus its share of the building's debt, paid through maintenance. With $220,000 of underlying mortgage allocated to it versus $90,000, Darnell's apartment carries more debt service and more refinancing risk. The sponsor answer is the trap: once the co-op corporation owns the building, the underlying mortgage is the corporation's debt, carried by every shareholder.

blocks.html: The Special Risks section is near the front, as the regulations require. Jordan flags four items for buyers. First, the sponsor will own every unsold apartment, including those of non-purchasing tenants, as holder of unsold shares, with the right to sell or rent them without board approval. Second, the sponsor will pay maintenance on its unsold apartments, and if it stops, the co-op's budget suffers. Third, the underlying mortgage is interest-only, so the full $7,200,000 is due in year ten. Fourth, the building's real estate tax projection assumes no change in assessment class, supported by an expert's letter.

blocks.q: Darnell's bank says it may not make share loans in the building at first. What feature of the plan most likely explains that?
c: The building uses a recognition agreement, which lenders prefer to avoid in conversions
The insider price is lower than the outside price, which banks treat as an illegal discount
The plan was accepted for filing rather than approved by the Attorney General on its merits
The sponsor may hold a large share of the apartments, many rented to non-purchasers
blocks.x: Share lenders review the building as well as the borrower, and a high concentration of sponsor-held, tenant-occupied units raises risk: the co-op depends on one holder's maintenance payments, and owner occupancy is low. If 19 of 36 apartments sell, the sponsor still holds 17. The recognition agreement answer is the trap: lenders require recognition agreements. Insider discounts are lawful and customary, and acceptance for filing is normal.

blocks.html: Tasha finds two lenders that will lend in conversion buildings once the plan is effective and a minimum share of apartments has sold. She tells the tenants who want to buy to get pre-approved early, because every one of the 19 purchase agreements Evelyn needs depends on a buyer who can actually close.

Darnell asks what his bank will actually hold as collateral, since he is not getting a deed. Jordan walks him through it: the share loan is secured by his shares and his proprietary lease, perfected with a UCC-1 financing statement, and the co-op corporation signs a recognition agreement with his lender. Because a share loan is not a recorded mortgage, there is no mortgage recording tax, and a co-op lien search replaces title insurance on his purchase.

blocks.q: The plan's tax section projects first-year real estate taxes using an expert's letter. Darnell asks whether converting the building from a rental to a co-op will move it into a different NYC tax class. What is accurate?
c: Yes, it moves from Class 2 to Class 1, because the apartments become owner-occupied homes
No, a 36-unit building is Class 2 as a rental and stays Class 2 as a co-op
Yes, it moves from Class 4 to Class 2, because rentals are taxed as commercial property
No, because co-op buildings pay no real estate tax once shares are sold
blocks.x: NYC tax class depends on the property's use and size. A residential building with more than three units is Class 2 whether it is a rental or a co-op, and co-ops are valued as if they were rentals. The Class 1 answer is the trap: owner occupancy does not change the class of a 36-unit building. The co-op corporation pays one tax bill, collected through maintenance, and owner-occupants may qualify for an abatement.

blocks.html: The day the plan is accepted, the 90-day exclusive purchase period starts. Darnell signs a purchase agreement for 3C at the insider price and gives a $41,000 deposit. The plan says deposits go into a special escrow account under General Business Law 352-h, held by an escrow agent (here, Evelyn's attorney), in a bank in New York, until closing or until the deposit is returned.

blocks.q: Evelyn wants to use the tenants' deposits to pay for the roof work before closings begin. May she?
c: Yes, as long as the roof work is disclosed in the offering plan's budget section
Yes, because deposits become the sponsor's money once a purchase agreement is signed
No, because deposits must stay in the escrow account until closing or a refund
No, unless every purchaser signs a release, in which case she may use half
blocks.x: Deposits in Martin Act offerings are trust funds held in escrow under GBL 352-h until closing or until returned to the purchaser. The sponsor may not use them for construction or anything else. The disclosure answer is the trap: disclosure is the Martin Act's central tool, but it does not authorize the misuse of trust funds. Misusing escrowed deposits exposes the sponsor and the escrow agent to enforcement.

blocks.q: On day 40 of the exclusive period, an outside buyer offers Evelyn $560,000 for the occupied apartment 4D. The tenant in 4D has not decided. What may Evelyn do?
c: Wait, because the tenant in occupancy has the exclusive right to buy for 90 days
Accept, because a higher outside offer ends the tenant's exclusive right early
Accept, but only if the outside buyer agrees to let the tenant stay for one year
Wait, because occupied apartments may be sold to the tenant alone
blocks.x: For 90 days after the plan is accepted for filing, tenants in occupancy have the exclusive right to buy their own apartments. Evelyn cannot sell 4D to an outsider during that window. The higher-offer answer is the trap: price does not cut the period short. After the window, the sponsor may sell the shares, but the buyer takes them subject to the non-purchasing tenant's protected tenancy.

blocks.html: By the end of the 90 days, 17 tenants have signed. Evelyn's attorneys extend the offering to the remaining tenants at the insider price, and two more households sign in the following month. With 19 purchase agreements from tenants in occupancy, Evelyn files an amendment declaring the plan effective.

Before closings, the insurer raises the building's premium sharply and the city's water rates rise. Evelyn's attorneys file an amendment revising the first-year budget: maintenance goes from $1.35 to $1.55 per share, an increase of about 15%. Darnell's maintenance would be 1,100 x $1.55 = $1,705 a month instead of $1,485.

blocks.q: Darnell signed before the amendment. What right is he most likely to have?
c: None, because a signed purchase agreement binds him to any later budget the sponsor files
A right to keep the old maintenance figure for five years, which the sponsor must subsidize
A right to a refund of the difference from the Attorney General's real estate recovery fund
A right to rescind, if the change is material and adverse
blocks.x: When an amendment discloses a material adverse change, such as a significant budget increase, the Attorney General requires that existing purchasers be offered a chance to rescind and get their deposits back within the period the amendment sets. The bound-by-anything answer is the trap: that ignores the rescission right. Buyers who want the deal usually stay, but the choice belongs to them.

blocks.html: Darnell stays in. Two other purchasers rescind, which drops the tenant purchase count below 19. Evelyn's attorneys must analyze whether the plan, already declared effective, is affected, and they do not let Jordan's team speculate about it in emails to tenants. Jordan learns a habit worth keeping: in a Martin Act offering, every statement to a prospect should come from, or match, the plan and its amendments.

At the first closing, Evelyn appoints the initial board of directors, as sponsors do. Several purchasers worry that with 17 unsold apartments the sponsor will control the board forever. The plan addresses it: the sponsor's control is limited, and it must give up majority control within the period the plan states and the Attorney General's rules require, no later than five years after the first closing, even if it still holds many apartments.

blocks.q: Three years after the first closing, Evelyn still holds 15 of 36 apartments, all rented. Which statement about control is most accurate?
c: She controls the board permanently, because the board is elected by shares
She must give up majority control by the plan's deadline, at most five years
She lost control at the first closing, because sponsors may not sit on boards
She controls it until the Attorney General votes on her continued control
blocks.x: Offering plans limit sponsor control, and the Attorney General expects shareholders (or unit owners in a condo) to control the board no later than five years after the first closing, often sooner once a stated share of units sells. The permanent-control answer is the trap: elections by shares would let a large holder dominate indefinitely without that limit. Sponsors may hold board seats as shareholders; they just cannot keep majority control.

blocks.html: For Hudson & Hart, the selling agreement with Evelyn sets the commission on each sponsor sale, and the offering plan discloses that a selling agent is involved. Outside brokers who bring buyers for the vacant apartments are paid a co-broke only if they registered their buyers with the sales office at the first contact, as the plan's broker policy states. Diane makes every agent on the project keep a copy of the current plan and every amendment at the sales desk, so that no answer to a prospect ever comes from memory.

blocks.title: Old conversion rules still show up on exams
blocks.html: Older materials describe eviction plans (51% of tenants agreeing to buy, after which non-purchasers could eventually be evicted) and non-eviction plans that needed only 15%. Since the HSTPA in June 2019, eviction plans are gone and a non-eviction plan needs 51% of units under contract to tenants in occupancy. If an item asks about current New York City conversion law, there is one kind of plan, and no tenant is evicted for not buying.

blocks.title: Why conversions slowed down
blocks.html: Co-op and condo conversions remade New York City housing in the 1980s, when sponsors could convert with modest tenant participation. Under the 51% rule, an occupied conversion needs a majority of current households to buy. Most new co-op and condo supply in the city today comes from new construction or vacant buildings, not occupied rentals.

items: The Martin Act reaches every offer, including flyers and reservations. CPS-1 allows advertising and non-binding interest only; a red herring is for information only; contracts and deposits start when a plan is accepted for filing.
Acceptance for filing is about disclosure, not merit. Never market a plan as AG-approved.

NYC occupied conversions: non-eviction plans only, 51% of units under contract to tenants in occupancy, a 90-day exclusive purchase period, and no eviction for not buying. Stabilized non-purchasers stay stabilized.
Read the plan for the underlying mortgage per share, the budget, sponsor-held units, and tax projections. Concentrated sponsor ownership can limit share loans.

Deposits are trust funds in escrow under GBL 352-h. Material adverse amendments trigger rescission offers. Sponsor control of the board ends by the plan's deadline, no later than five years after the first closing.

lessons.title: Case file: The Estate Apartment on Ocean Parkway
lessons.tagline: A shareholder dies, an executor wants to rent the place out by the weekend, a niece wants to move in, and three buyers each want something the building may not allow.
objectives: Decide who may list and sell co-op shares held by an estate, and what the agent and the buyer's attorney need to transfer them.
Apply a co-op's primary residence, sublet and transfer-on-death rules, and New York City's short-term rental law, to an owner's plans for an apartment.
Read a co-op's lien search, financial statements and board minutes to spot problems before contract, and decide which matter most to a buyer.
Calculate a seller's net proceeds on a co-op sale with arrears, flip tax and transfer taxes, and compare a co-op with a condop for a buyer's plans.

blocks.title: Midwood, a one-bedroom on the fourth floor
blocks.html: Harriet Sloane lived in apartment 4K of a six-story co-op on Ocean Parkway for forty-one years. She bought her shares when the building converted in 1985, taught fourth grade at a school three blocks away, and died in March at 91. Her will leaves everything to her nephew Martin and her niece Nora in equal shares and names Martin as executor. Martin lives in Philadelphia. He calls Hudson & Hart in May, says he wants the apartment listed "this week," and adds that he has already put it on a short-term rental site to cover the maintenance in the meantime, "since nobody's living there." Jordan's first question is who, legally, Martin is right now.

When a shareholder dies, the shares and the proprietary lease pass to her estate. A will names an executor, but the will alone does not give that person power to act. The Surrogate's Court does that by issuing letters testamentary after the will is admitted to probate. Martin filed the probate petition in April. The court has not ruled.

blocks.q: Martin wants to sign an exclusive listing agreement for 4K today. What should Jordan do?
c: Sign it with Martin, since the will names him as the executor
Have Martin and Nora sign it together as the two named heirs
Have the managing agent sign it on behalf of the co-op corporation
Wait for the court's letters testamentary before signing
blocks.x: Only the estate can sell the shares, and the estate acts through a fiduciary the Surrogate's Court has appointed: an executor with letters testamentary. Being named in the will is not enough. The heirs' signatures are tempting because they will get the money, but heirs do not control estate property during administration. The co-op and its managing agent do not own Harriet's shares and cannot list them.

blocks.html: Jordan explains, and Martin calls the estate's lawyer, who expects letters in about three weeks. In the meantime, Jordan can prepare: request the building's documents from the managing agent with Martin's written permission, price the apartment, and line up the paperwork. The short-term rental listing is a more urgent problem.

Martin's listing offers 4K for two to five nights at a time to visitors. He has already taken two bookings. The building is a Class A multiple dwelling of 84 apartments. The proprietary lease says the apartment may be used only as a private dwelling by the shareholder and family, and the house rules ban occupancy of fewer than 30 days. New York City's short-term rental registration law, Local Law 18, has required hosts to register with the Mayor's Office of Special Enforcement since 2023, and booking platforms may not process stays in unregistered units.

blocks.q: What should Jordan tell Martin about the weekend rentals?
c: They are fine until the sale, if he registers the apartment with the city
They are lawful because an estate is exempt from co-op house rules
They break city law and the co-op's rules, so cancel the bookings
They are allowed if each guest signs a short sublease with the estate
blocks.x: In a building of three or more units, renting an apartment for fewer than 30 days is illegal unless a permanent resident is present for the stay, and nobody lives in 4K. Registration is not available to a host who does not live there, and owners can put a building on the city's prohibited building list. Separately, the lease and house rules forbid it. The registration choice is the tempting one, but registration does not legalize an empty apartment.

blocks.html: Martin cancels both bookings. The managing agent had already noticed the strangers with suitcases: a notice of default arrived in the estate's mail the following week, citing the lease's use clause and the house rules. Defaults under a proprietary lease can end with the co-op terminating the lease, which would wreck the sale. Martin cures it with a letter confirming the listing is down and pays the building's legal fee under the lease. He then has a second idea.

Martin's new plan is a 12-month lease to a graduate student while the estate decides whether to sell. "New York law lets tenants sublet in big buildings," he says. "The co-op can't unreasonably refuse." The building's sublet policy, adopted by the board under the lease, allows a sublet only after the shareholder has lived in the apartment for three years, for up to two years in any five, with board approval of the subtenant, a sublet fee of 15% of maintenance, and a ban on sublets by estates.

blocks.q: Is Martin right that state law gives the estate a right to sublet?
c: Yes, because RPL 226-b protects every tenant in a building of four or more units
Yes, because the estate inherited Harriet's right after her three years of residence
No; RPL 226-b excludes proprietary leases, so the lease and policy govern
No, because subletting a co-op apartment is barred in every case by state law
blocks.x: RPL 226-b gives rental tenants in buildings of four or more units a right to sublet with consent not unreasonably withheld, but the statute expressly excludes proprietary leases held by co-op shareholders. A co-op sublet depends on the lease and the board's policy. Harriet's years of residence do not transfer to the estate as a sublet right, which makes that choice the tempting near miss. Many co-ops allow sublets; this one does not allow them by estates.

blocks.html: Before letters issue, Nora calls Jordan. She is a physical therapist in Bay Ridge, her lease is ending, and she would like to buy out Martin's half of the estate's interest and live in 4K herself. The proprietary lease has a clause that many New York co-op leases share: after a shareholder's death, the board's consent to a transfer to a financially responsible member of the shareholder's family "shall not be unreasonably withheld." Nora's income is solid, but her savings are thin, below the building's usual two years of post-closing liquidity.

blocks.q: If the board refuses the transfer to Nora, what standard will a court likely apply?
c: The business judgment rule, under which boards need give no reasons
A heightened reasonableness standard, because the lease limits refusal
Strict scrutiny, since a family transfer is a fundamental property right
No review, since boards have absolute discretion over any share transfer
blocks.x: Ordinarily, courts defer to co-op boards under the business judgment rule. But when the lease says consent to a family transfer on death shall not be unreasonably withheld, New York courts apply a heightened reasonableness standard instead, as in Estate of Del Terzo v. 33 Fifth Avenue Owners Corp. (affirmed 2016). The business judgment choice is the tempting default, but the lease's own words displace it. The board may still weigh real financial facts like Nora's liquidity.

blocks.html: Nora decides she cannot afford to buy out Martin's share and carry the apartment. The siblings agree to sell. Letters testamentary arrive in June, Martin signs the exclusive, and Jordan opens the file.

blocks.text: The paperwork for a co-op estate sale

head: Document
Why it matters
Status in Harriet's file
rows: Proves Martin's authority to sign for the estate
Shows the share count; surrendered and reissued at closing
Not found in the apartment or the safe deposit box
Use, sublet, transfer and default rules; assigned to the buyer
Offering plan, house rules, alteration agreement
What a buyer may do with the apartment
Two years of financial statements and minutes
Building health; buyer's attorney reads them before contract
UCC filings, judgments and liens against the shareholder
Ordered by buyer's attorney after contract
blocks.caption: Jordan's checklist for 4K

blocks.q: Harriet's original stock certificate cannot be found. What is the usual way forward?
c: Cancel the sale, since shares cannot transfer without the original
Sell the apartment by deed instead, since shares are now irrelevant
The executor signs a lost certificate affidavit and indemnity
Have the buyer's lender accept a photocopy of the old certificate
blocks.x: Lost co-op certificates are common in estates. The co-op's transfer procedure typically requires a lost certificate affidavit with an indemnity (sometimes a bond or fee) before it cancels the old certificate and issues a new one to the buyer. A co-op apartment never passes by deed, because the buyer gets shares and a lease, not real property. A photocopy is tempting, but a lender wants the newly issued original as its collateral.

blocks.html: Jordan lists 4K at $425,000 in late June. Before marketing, Jordan reads the financial statements and minutes the managing agent sent, because buyers' attorneys will, and the answers shape the pitch and the price.

blocks.title: From the co-op's last two financial statements and minutes
blocks.html:
Operating results: deficit of $38,000 last year, $61,000 the year before, both covered from the reserve fund.
Reserve fund: $410,000, down from $520,000.
Underlying mortgage: $5.9 million at 3.1%, balloon due in 2028.
Arrears: four apartments more than 90 days behind, including 4K.
Minutes, March: board discusses refinancing; broker estimates new rate near 6.5%; possible maintenance increase of 8% to 10% on refinance.
Minutes, April: board amends sublet policy to bar sublets by estates and to require three years of residence before any sublet; vote to register the building on the city's prohibited building list for short-term rentals.
Minutes, May: default notice to 4K for short-term rental; resolved.

blocks.q: Which item in the statements and minutes most affects what a buyer of 4K will pay each month?
c: The underlying mortgage refinance at a much higher rate in 2028
The April vote to register on the short-term rental prohibited list
The May default notice to 4K, which was resolved after a week
The four apartments in arrears, which include the estate's 4K
blocks.x: Maintenance pays the underlying mortgage, so a $5.9 million balloon refinanced from 3.1% to about 6.5% flows straight into every shareholder's monthly bill; the board already expects 8% to 10%. Add two years of deficits drawn from reserves and the building may need more. The arrears are the tempting choice, and they matter, but four units behind is smaller and partly cured at this closing.

blocks.html: Jordan does not hide this from buyers, and does not interpret it for them either. The listing notes say the building expects a refinance in 2028 and that buyers' attorneys will receive the financials and minutes. Two buyers say the numbers are fine. The price conversation starts lower, at $415,000, which is exactly what Jordan and Martin expected after reading the same pages.
