Dr. Arjun Mehta, a cardiologist in Boston, wants 4K as a place to stay four nights a month when he sees patients at a Brooklyn hospital. The building's policy requires the apartment to be the shareholder's primary residence, and the board does not approve pieds-a-terre. Arjun asks whether he could "just list it as my primary address on the application, since I'll get mail there."

blocks.q: How should Jordan respond to Arjun's suggestion?
c: Agree, since a board cannot verify where a buyer actually sleeps
Agree, as long as Arjun also changes his driver's license address
Decline to misstate it, and tell him the policy before he bids
Decline, and report Arjun to the board as an unsuitable applicant
blocks.x: A board package is a sworn application, and a false statement about residence is a misrepresentation that can lead to rejection or, after closing, a default under the lease. A licensee who helps prepare it risks discipline for dishonesty. The honest move is to tell Arjun the policy up front so he can decide whether to bid. Reporting him to the board is tempting but unnecessary: Jordan works for the seller and owes the board nothing beyond honesty, and Arjun has done nothing yet.

blocks.html: Arjun withdraws, politely, and buys a condo in Downtown Brooklyn, where the declaration lets owners use a unit as a second home. The second buyers are Gloria and Felix Ortiz, a nurse and a transit electrician from Canarsie, buying for their daughter Camila, 24, a first-year teacher who will live in 4K. Their plan is for the parents to own the shares and Camila to live there. The building's policy, in the minutes from two years ago, allows parents to help in one way: the child must be a shareholder and the resident, and parents may be co-shareholders or guarantors.

blocks.q: Which structure fits the building's primary residence policy?
c: Gloria and Felix own the shares; Camila lives there with no ownership
Camila owns the shares, her parents live there part of the time
Gloria and Felix own the shares and sublet to Camila at a low rent
Camila is a shareholder and resident, with her parents as co-owners
blocks.x: The policy requires the resident to be a shareholder, with parents allowed in as co-shareholders or guarantors. Parents owning alone with the daughter living there is a parents-buying-for-children arrangement this board does not allow, and calling it a sublet does not help because sublets need three years of residence first. Read the actual policy: many buildings take a different line, which is why the first choice works in some co-ops.

blocks.html: Felix asks about a building two blocks away that a friend called a condop, "where you can rent it out whenever you want." Jordan pulls its listing. The building is a condominium of three units: two retail condo units on the ground floor owned by the sponsor, and one residential condo unit owned by a cooperative corporation. Residents buy shares in that co-op.

blocks.q: If Camila buys in the condop instead, what will she actually own?
c: A deed to her apartment as a condo unit, recorded in her name
Co-op shares and a proprietary lease, under a condo layer
A deed to a share of the retail units and the residential unit
A rental lease from the sponsor, who owns the condo units
blocks.x: In this kind of condop, the residential portion is one condo unit owned by a co-op corporation, so residents still buy shares and receive proprietary leases, and the co-op board still applies its own rules. The structure keeps the store income out of the co-op's gross income. The deed choice is tempting because of the word condo, but only the co-op owns a condo unit. Whether sublets are easier depends on the co-op's documents, not on the label.

blocks.html: The Ortizes stay with 4K. They sign a contract at $415,000 with a 75% share loan, Camila as shareholder and Gloria as co-shareholder, and submit the board package two weeks later. Then the buyer's attorney's co-op lien search comes back with one hit: a UCC-1 financing statement filed in 2004 by a bank against Harriet's shares and lease, for a share loan she refinanced and paid off in 2012.

blocks.q: What does the old UCC-1 filing require before closing?
c: Nothing, since UCC-1 filings expire after 25 years without action
A payoff from the estate, since the filing proves a debt is still owed
A title insurance policy over the filing, as in a condo closing
A UCC-3 termination from the lender, or proof the loan was paid
blocks.x: A UCC-1 perfects a lender's lien on co-op shares. When the loan is paid, the lender should file a UCC-3 termination; when it did not, the seller's attorney gets a termination or a satisfaction letter from the lender or its successor so the buyer's lender takes first position. The payoff choice is tempting, but the filing is evidence of a lien, not proof of a current debt. Co-op deals use lien searches, not title insurance.

blocks.html: Priya, representing the estate, tracks the 2004 lender through two mergers to its current successor, which issues a termination in eleven days. The board interviews Camila and Gloria in August and approves them. The closing is set for September.

Martin wants to know what the estate will receive. The contract price is $415,000. The building charges a flip tax of 2% of the price, paid by the seller under the lease and bylaws. The broker's commission is 5%. The seller pays the New York State transfer tax and the New York City Real Property Transfer Tax, which apply to co-op share transfers. The estate also owes five months of maintenance at $1,140, which the managing agent will collect at closing because the co-op's lien comes first. Ignore attorney's fees and the managing agent's transfer fees.

blocks.q: What will the estate net from the sale?
blocks.x: Commission 5% = $20,750. Flip tax 2% = $8,300. NYS transfer tax 0.4% = $1,660. NYC RPTT on a $500,000-or-less residential sale is 1% = $4,150. Arrears 5 x $1,140 = $5,700. Total $40,560, net $374,440. $372,676 uses the 1.425% RPTT rate, which applies above $500,000. $380,140 forgets the arrears, and $382,740 forgets the flip tax.

blocks.title: Co-op rules beat the rules people know from rentals
blocks.html: Three assumptions from the rental world fail in a co-op. RPL 226-b's sublet right excludes proprietary leases. City registration does not make an empty apartment legal for short stays, and a co-op can bar short-term rentals by its lease and the prohibited building list anyway. And a family member's right to take over an apartment comes from the proprietary lease, not from succession rules that protect rent-stabilized tenants.

blocks.title: What an estate sale adds in New York City
blocks.html: Letters testamentary from the Surrogate's Court before anyone signs for the estate. A maintenance statement, because the co-op's lien for arrears is paid first. A lost certificate affidavit if the shares cannot be found. A clean lien search, including old UCC-1 filings the seller's lender never terminated. And the same transfer taxes as any co-op sale: the state's 0.4% and the city's RPTT at 1% or 1.425%, paid by the seller.

The closing takes forty minutes. Camila gets a new stock certificate in her and Gloria's names, the bank holds it, and the managing agent hands her two keys and a copy of the house rules with the move-in hours highlighted. Nora comes to the apartment the next week to take one thing from the hall closet: Harriet's 1985 subscription agreement, the first time anyone in the family owned a piece of a building.

Camila's first month's budget is tight: the share loan payment, $1,140 in maintenance, and the 8% to 10% increase the minutes predicted. A friend suggests renting the living room sofa or, after she buys a bed, the small second room off the kitchen, to tourists for a few nights at a time. Camila would be home every night. She asks Jordan, who is still her parents' contact for everything, whether that is allowed. New York City does allow some short stays in a multiple dwelling when the permanent resident is present and the host is registered with the city. But the city's rules are a floor for what is legal, not a grant of rights against a building's own documents.

blocks.q: May Camila rent her spare room to visitors for two or three nights at a time while she lives there?
c: Yes, because she is present and the city permits host-present stays
No; the house rules and the building's prohibited listing still bar it
Yes, if she registers and pays the co-op a sublet fee for each stay
No, because a shareholder may not have any other person in the unit
blocks.x: Even when city law could allow a host-present stay, the co-op's house rules ban occupancy of fewer than 30 days, and the board registered the building on the city's prohibited building list, so the city will not register her. The first choice is tempting because she will be home, but the building's rules are separate and stricter. The last choice overstates it: shareholders may have family, guests and, where the lease allows, roommates.

blocks.html: Camila drops the idea. Her cousin, who works nights at a hospital in Flatbush, asks to stay in the spare room for the school year and split costs. Jordan suggests she read the proprietary lease's occupancy clause and ask the managing agent in writing, because long-term occupants who are not shareholders or family are handled differently from building to building. The managing agent replies within two days: family members may live with the shareholder without approval, and the cousin counts. The rule is the building's to make, and the answer is in the documents.

items: Estate-held co-op shares are sold by an executor or administrator with letters from the Surrogate's Court; being named in the will, or being an heir, is not enough to sign.

Co-op use is set by the proprietary lease, the house rules and board policy: primary residence, sublets, and parents-buying rules. RPL 226-b does not apply, and NYC law bars stays under 30 days with no permanent resident present.
A lease clause that consent to a family transfer after death shall not be unreasonably withheld replaces business judgment deference with a heightened reasonableness standard.
Read financials and minutes for what changes the monthly bill: deficits, shrinking reserves, a mortgage balloon at a higher rate, and policy changes on sublets.
Lost certificates need an affidavit and indemnity; stale UCC-1 filings need a UCC-3 termination. A condop resident still owns co-op shares, not a deed.
Seller's net on a co-op: subtract commission, flip tax, NYS transfer tax (0.4%), NYC RPTT (1% up to $500,000, 1.425% above) and arrears from the price.

roleplays.title: Board Interview Prep with Kim
roleplays.setting: An Upper West Side co-op; you prepped your buyers, now Kim Alvarez, the board president, calls you first
roleplays.goal: Get a complete, honest package in on time, prepare the buyers properly, and never misstate facts to the board.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Kim Alvarez, a sharp, polite Upper West Side co-op board president, and at times the anxious buyers. Probe whether the buyers will sublet, ask quietly about their background and whether kids are coming, question a financing level above the building's 75% cap and short post-closing liquidity. Press the agent for off-the-record information. As the buyers, ask to send an incomplete package, to list a parent's loan as savings, and whether the board must give a reason if it rejects them. The learner must keep the package complete and on schedule, honor the financing cap, keep client confidences, refuse to discuss protected classes, disclose gifts properly, and coach honest, complete disclosure. Grade on timing, honesty, fair housing, and fiduciary duty, then say whether the board approves.

missing: a tax return and the employment letter
two bank statements and a reference letter
the CPA letter and one tax return
the employment letter and a landlord reference

opening: {client} are buying {unit} at a {street} co-op. The board package is due Friday. Your phone shows two missed calls: the buyers, and Kim Alvarez.
Board package week for {unit} on {street}. {client} are nervous, the managing agent is strict, and the board president likes to call agents directly.
You helped {client} win {unit} on {street}. Now comes the hard part: the board. Package due Friday, interview in three weeks if it's complete.

say: The package is due Friday. We're missing {missing}. Can we send what we have and add the rest later?
We still don't have {missing}. Send it partial and catch up next week?

moves.text: Let's get it all by Thursday. Incomplete packages wait a board cycle, and your rate lock won't.
moves.fb: Boards typically meet monthly. A complete package on time protects the loan commitment and rate lock.

moves.text: The managing agent checks completeness first. Any gaps bounce it a month. I'll help you chase them down.
moves.fb: Correct. Completeness is screened first, and delays can outlast the commitment.
moves.react: Okay, we'll call HR and the accountant now.

moves.text: Send it partial, but tell the managing agent exactly what's missing and when it's coming in.
moves.fb: Honest, but many managing agents won't forward an incomplete package. Push to complete it first.

moves.text: Sure, just send it now. The managing agent won't notice two missing items in a package that thick.
moves.fb: The managing agent screens for completeness first. Incomplete packages get bounced or delayed a full cycle.

moves.text: Send it, and I'll swap in a blank page labeled 'to follow' so it looks complete when it's counted.
moves.fb: Disguising an incomplete package is deceptive and damages your credibility with the building.

moves.text: Boards have to review whatever you give them within 30 days by law, complete or not. Just send it.
moves.fb: No such rule applies in NYC. Buildings set their own process, and incomplete packages wait.

say: Our bank approved 80%, but the building caps financing at 75%. Can we just list 80 and hope they don't check?
The cap is 75% and our loan is 80%. Does the board even look that closely?

moves.text: No. The board's cap is binding. We restructure to 75% and show extra cash in the statement.
moves.fb: Honest and correct. The board sees the loan commitment; misrepresenting it ends the deal.
moves.react: Okay, we'll talk to the lender about 75.

moves.text: They'll see the commitment letter. Ask the lender for 75% and put the difference in from savings.
moves.fb: Right. Comply with the cap openly instead of hoping it's missed.
moves.react: We can do 75 if we move some savings.

moves.text: Put 80% and ask for a waiver if they object at the interview. Some boards bend on these things.
moves.fb: Requesting a waiver openly can work, but raise it up front, not after hoping they miss it.

moves.text: List 75% on the application and keep the 80% loan. Once you close, nobody checks the lender's numbers.
moves.fb: That's a misrepresentation to the board, and the recognition agreement puts the lender's loan in front of them.

moves.text: Financing caps only apply to condos. Co-op boards can't limit how much you borrow in New York.
moves.fb: Backwards. Co-op boards commonly set financing caps; condos typically can't screen buyers that way.

moves.text: Leave the loan amount blank on the application. If it's blank, they can't object to the number.
moves.fb: Omitting material financial facts is misleading, and the package will be returned as incomplete.

say: Jordan, Kim Alvarez. Off the record, are {client} planning to rent it out after a year? We've had trouble.
Kim here. Between us, any chance your buyers sublet {unit} soon? I'd rather know now.

moves.text: They've told me it will be their primary home. They'll answer that directly at the interview.
moves.fb: You share only what your clients authorized and let them speak for themselves. Your loyalty runs to the buyers.

moves.text: I don't speak for my clients off the record. Ask them at the interview; they'll answer you straight.
moves.fb: Correct. No off-the-record channel; confidences stay with the clients.

moves.text: I really couldn't say either way. I haven't asked them much about their long-term plans at all.
moves.fb: You protected them, but it sounds evasive. Say they'll answer directly.

moves.text: Between us, they mentioned maybe moving to Boston in a few years. Probably not for a while, though, honestly.
moves.fb: That's your clients' confidential information. Sharing it breaches loyalty and confidentiality and may kill the deal.
moves.react: Boston. Thank you for telling me.

moves.text: Never. I can guarantee they'll live there forever. They told me it's their dream apartment, Kim.
moves.fb: Guaranteeing your clients' future plans is a misstatement you can't back up.
moves.react: Forever? I'll hold you to that.

moves.text: If they did, it would be legal anyway, since co-op owners can sublet freely under New York law.
moves.fb: Subletting in co-ops is governed by the proprietary lease and house rules, usually with board consent.
moves.react: That's not how our lease works.

say: One more thing. Where's the family from originally? And do they have kids? The building is very quiet.
Off the record, what's their background? Any kids planned? We're a quiet building.

moves.text: I can't discuss national origin or family status, and the board can't weigh either. Financials are in.
moves.fb: Correct. Boards may reject for many reasons, but never for a protected class under federal, state, or city law.
moves.react: Of course. Just the package, then.

moves.text: That's not something I can share or the board can weigh. I'm happy to walk you through the financials.
moves.fb: Right. You refuse to discuss protected classes and redirect to lawful criteria.

moves.text: I'd rather not get into that kind of thing, Kim. Is there anything else you need before Friday?
moves.fb: You avoided it, but didn't say why. Name the rule so the board knows it can't use that information.

moves.text: One of them has parents from overseas, and there's a baby on the way, but they're quiet people.
moves.fb: Volunteering protected-class information invites a discriminatory decision. Redirect to the financials.
moves.react: A baby. Thanks for the heads up.

moves.text: No kids, I made sure of that before I showed them the unit, since I know the building likes it quiet here.
moves.fb: Screening buyers for children is familial status discrimination under the Fair Housing Act.

moves.text: Co-op boards are exempt from fair housing law, so you can ask, but I'd keep it off the record.
moves.fb: Co-op boards are not exempt. They can reject for many reasons, but not protected-class reasons.

say: At the interview, should we mention we want to take down the kitchen wall?
Do we bring up the renovation at the interview? We want to open the kitchen.

moves.text: Answer anything they ask honestly. Work goes through the alteration agreement; don't lead with it.
moves.fb: Total honesty, no unnecessary surprises. Alterations are handled by the alteration agreement after closing.
moves.react: Honest, but don't lead with it. Got it.

moves.text: If they ask, tell the truth. Otherwise keep it simple. Any work needs board consent anyway.
moves.fb: Right. The proprietary lease requires consent for alterations; candor if asked.
moves.react: Okay. We'll keep it short and honest.

moves.text: Leave it out entirely. Boards hate renovation talk, so it's better if it never comes up at all.
moves.fb: Not lying, but coaching avoidance can backfire if asked. Prepare them to answer honestly.

moves.text: If they ask, say no plans at all. You can always change your mind after you close on the place.
moves.fb: Coaching clients to lie to the board is a terrible idea, and alterations need consent anyway.

moves.text: Mention it, and say you'll skip the permits to keep the cost down for the building. They'll like that.
moves.fb: Skipping permits is illegal and violates the alteration agreement. Never coach that.

moves.text: Tell them the seller already approved it, so the board doesn't need to weigh in at all on that.
moves.fb: Sellers can't approve alterations. The board does, through the alteration agreement.
moves.react: The seller approved it? Did they?

say: My parents are giving us $60,000 toward the down payment. Can we just list it as our savings?
Can the money from my dad go in as our own savings? It's simpler.

moves.text: List it as a gift, with a signed gift letter. Boards and lenders want to see where money comes from.
moves.fb: Correct. Gift funds must be disclosed honestly, usually with a gift letter.
moves.react: A gift letter. We'll ask Dad tonight.

moves.text: It goes in as a gift, not savings. A gift letter says it isn't a loan. That's normal and fine.
moves.fb: Right. Honest disclosure of gift funds protects the buyers and the deal.

moves.text: Wait until it's been in your account a few months, and then it's just your money anyway.
moves.fb: Seasoning funds isn't illegal, but it delays the deal and dodges the question. Disclose it as a gift.
moves.react: We don't have a few months.

moves.text: Sure, list it as savings. Once it's in your own account, nobody can tell where it came from originally.
moves.fb: That misrepresents your clients' finances to the board and lender. Statements show the deposit.

moves.text: Have your dad lend it and call it a gift. Then you pay him back quietly after the closing.
moves.fb: Calling a loan a gift is a misrepresentation. It hides debt from the board and lender.
moves.react: Perfect, he'll be fine with that.

moves.text: Put it in my firm's escrow until closing. Then it doesn't show up on your bank statements.
moves.fb: Using escrow to hide funds is improper and misleads the board.

say: Kim: "Our building wants two years of maintenance and mortgage in liquid assets after closing. They show about fourteen months."
Kim: "Post-closing liquidity looks short. We require two years. Anything I'm missing?"

moves.text: Thanks for flagging it. I'll ask about any accounts not listed and send you an honest updated statement.
moves.fb: Correct. You respond accurately and let the buyers add real assets; no inflation.

moves.text: I'll check with them. If the building allows a guarantor or escrow, we'd ask about that openly.
moves.fb: Right. Offer lawful solutions openly instead of padding numbers.
moves.react: We've done escrows before. Ask them.

moves.text: I think they'll be fine on that. They both have stable jobs, so cash flow covers it anyway.
moves.fb: Stable income doesn't change the building's liquidity rule. Address the shortfall directly.
moves.react: Our rule is our rule, Jordan.

moves.text: Let me add their retirement accounts at full value, before any taxes or penalties, to close that gap.
moves.fb: Inflating assets misleads the board. Boards often discount retirement funds; report accurately.
moves.react: That's not how we count it.

moves.text: I'll have them borrow it short-term and repay after closing. It only needs to show on the statement.
moves.fb: Temporary borrowed funds misrepresent liquidity. That's deception toward the board.
moves.react: Borrow it? We'd want to know that.

moves.text: Liquidity rules discriminate against young buyers, so the board can't legally enforce them.
moves.fb: Uniform financial requirements are lawful. Age is protected in NY, but a liquidity rule applied to all is not age discrimination.

say: The seller's agent says we pay the 2% flip tax at closing. Is that right?
There's a flip tax. Is that on us as buyers?

moves.text: Usually the seller pays it, but the proprietary lease or house rules control. Your attorney confirms.
moves.fb: Correct. A flip tax is a co-op transfer fee customarily paid by the seller, per the building's documents.
moves.react: We'll ask our attorney to check.

moves.text: Customarily that's the seller's. The contract and building rules decide. Your attorney checks.
moves.fb: Right. It's set by the building and contract, usually the seller's cost.

moves.text: Probably, if their agent says so. They know the building better than we do, after all.
moves.fb: Don't accept the other side's claim without checking the documents.

moves.text: Yes, the buyer always pays the flip tax, since it's a fee for flipping into the building, legally.
moves.fb: A flip tax is usually paid by the seller, as the building's documents provide.

moves.text: A flip tax only applies if you resell within a year or two. That's what flipping means, after all.
moves.fb: A flip tax is a transfer fee on sale, not a penalty for quick resales.

moves.text: It's a city tax, like the transfer tax, so the city just bills you for it after the closing.
moves.fb: A flip tax is a co-op fee set by the building, not a city tax.

say: If the board rejects us, do they at least have to tell us why?
Can they turn us down without explaining anything?

moves.text: In the city, co-op boards generally needn't give a reason. They just can't use a protected class.
moves.fb: Correct. Boards have broad discretion, but discrimination is illegal under federal, state and city law.
moves.react: Okay. So we focus on what we control.

moves.text: Usually no reason is needed here. What's barred is rejecting you for a protected class.
moves.fb: Right. Courts give boards wide latitude, but fair housing law still applies.
moves.react: Good to know before we go in.

moves.text: I don't know, honestly. I've never seen anyone rejected, so I wouldn't worry about it at all.
moves.fb: Reassurance without facts. Explain the board's discretion and its limits.

moves.text: Yes, they must give a written reason within 30 days, or the sale is approved automatically.
moves.fb: No such NYC rule. Boards generally need not explain, though discrimination is illegal.

moves.text: No, and they can reject you for any reason at all, including where you're from originally.
moves.fb: Wrong. Boards can't reject for national origin or any other protected class.

moves.text: If they reject you, I can appeal to the Department of State to overturn the board's final decision.
moves.fb: DOS licenses agents; it doesn't review co-op board decisions.

roleplays.debrief: You practised co-op board work: a complete package on time, honest financials that honor the building's financing cap and liquidity rules, and gift funds disclosed with a gift letter. Your clients' plans stay confidential, and a board may not consider national origin, familial status or any other protected class under the Fair Housing Act and the NYS and NYC Human Rights Laws. Alterations go through the alteration agreement, and the flip tax is usually the seller's.

roleplays.title: The New Development Letter of Intent
roleplays.setting: A Brooklyn or Queens condo sales gallery, plan status unclear
roleplays.goal: Protect your buyer and your commission: register, confirm the plan's status, submit a proper non-binding letter of intent, and review the plan's costs.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play an eager first-time condo buyer at a new development and, alternately, a smooth sponsor sales director. The buyer wants to 'lock in' a unit with a check today. The sales director is friendly but vague about plan status, and later offers the agent a private bonus. Later, the attorney reports shifted transfer taxes, working capital, and an expiring tax abatement. The learner must register the buyer, confirm the plan is accepted before any deposit, explain that a letter of intent is non-binding, submit a complete one, explain price amendments and the TCO requirement, refuse undisclosed compensation, and disclose all closing costs. Grade each step and report the buyer's confidence.
opening: The {bldg} sales gallery in {hood}: model kitchen, renderings, sparkling water. {client} has already fallen for unit {unit}.
{client} found {bldg} on Instagram and wants {unit} today. You arrive at the {hood} gallery ten minutes before the appointment.
New development day. {bldg} in {hood} is selling fast, according to the sales director. {client} brought a checkbook.

say: Welcome to the gallery! Is this your buyer? Feel free to look around.
Hi there! You two can wander the model unit. Coffee?

moves.text: Yes. Before anything else, I'd like to register {client} as my client with your office.
moves.fb: Sponsors pay co-brokes only for registered buyers. Register at the first visit.

moves.text: Thanks. First, please put me on file as {client}'s agent. Do you have a registration form?
moves.fb: Correct. Registration at the first visit protects your buyer's representation and your commission.

moves.text: Thanks. We'll look around first and do any registration stuff at the end of the visit.
moves.fb: Usually fine, but if the visit gets cut short you may lose the registration. Do it first.

moves.text: We'll just look today. I'll register {client} later if they like it enough to come back here.
moves.fb: Risky. If the buyer returns without you, the sponsor may treat them as unrepresented.
moves.react: No problem. Here's my card for {client}.

moves.text: No need, my buyer's agency agreement covers it. Sponsors have to pay whoever brings in the buyer.
moves.fb: Sponsors pay according to their own registration policy. Register to protect the commission.

moves.text: I'll let {client} speak with you alone. I'll wait outside so it's less pressure.
moves.fb: Leaving your buyer alone with the sponsor's agent abandons your role and their representation.

say: I love {unit}. Can I write a check today to hold it?
Let me put money down on {unit} before someone else does. Today.

moves.text: First question for the sales director: has the offering plan been accepted for filing?
moves.fb: Plan status decides everything. Under CPS-1 or a red herring, no deposits or reservations are allowed.

moves.text: Hold the checkbook. We need to know if the AG has accepted the offering plan yet.
moves.fb: Right. The Martin Act bars deposits before acceptance for filing.

moves.text: Maybe a small check to show you're serious. We can always get it back later on.
moves.fb: Any deposit before acceptance is prohibited, small or not. Confirm plan status first.

moves.text: Sure, a refundable deposit is fine either way. Refundable means you can't lose anything.
moves.fb: Before acceptance for filing, no deposits or reservations of any kind may be taken.

moves.text: Go ahead. A deposit locks in the price, and the sponsor can't sell the unit to anyone else.
moves.fb: Wrong on two counts: no deposits before acceptance, and nothing is locked until a contract is signed.

moves.text: Write it to me instead and I'll hold it in escrow until the sponsor is ready to take it.
moves.fb: Holding a deposit for a unit that can't legally take one doesn't fix anything.

say: Honestly? We're still in CPS-1. But a fully refundable reservation is totally fine.
The plan isn't accepted yet, but I can hold {unit} with a refundable deposit. Everyone's doing it.

moves.text: Thanks, but CPS-1 means no deposits or reservations, refundable or not. We'll wait.
moves.fb: Correct. CPS-1 allows advertising and gauging interest for 12 months, nothing binding and no money.

moves.text: We'll pass. Under CPS-1 you can't take reservations. Let us know the day the plan is accepted.
moves.fb: Right. You protect your buyer and keep the sponsor within the Martin Act rules.
moves.react: I'll call you the day it's accepted.

moves.text: We'll think about it and get back to you. {client} wants to sleep on it before deciding.
moves.fb: Declining is right, but you missed telling the buyer why: CPS-1 bars reservations.

moves.text: Great, a refundable reservation is a smart move. {client}, write it for 10% now just to be safe.
moves.fb: No deposits or reservations of any kind under CPS-1, refundable or not.

moves.text: Fine, but put it in the sponsor's escrow account so it's protected under the Martin Act.
moves.fb: Escrow doesn't cure a prohibited deposit. None are allowed before acceptance.

moves.text: A reservation is fine if it's under $5,000. Small holds like that don't count as deposits.
moves.fb: There's no small-deposit exception under CPS-1.

say: Good news, the plan was accepted last month. Submit a letter of intent and {unit} is yours.
We're accepted now! Letter of intent today, and {unit} is locked.

moves.text: {client}, a letter of intent binds no one. Nothing is locked until contract signing.
moves.fb: Accurate. Never describe a letter of intent as binding or a unit as 'locked.'
moves.react: Non-binding. So we still need the contract.

moves.text: It signals interest at a price. The sponsor can still sell to someone else until the contract.
moves.fb: Right. A letter of intent is non-binding as to purchaser and price.
moves.react: Good to know. Let's do it anyway.

moves.text: Let's submit it. It's mostly paperwork, and we'll sort out the details later with the attorney.
moves.fb: Fine to submit, but explain what it does and doesn't do so the buyer isn't misled.

moves.text: Once we submit, {unit} is yours at that price. The sponsor can't back out after that point.
moves.fb: Misstates the legal effect. The sponsor can still sell elsewhere or change pricing until contract.

moves.text: The letter is binding on you but not on the sponsor, so be very sure before you sign it.
moves.fb: It's non-binding on both. Overstating its effect misleads the buyer.

moves.text: Signing the letter starts your 10% deposit clock. Have the money wired, ready by Friday.
moves.fb: The 10% deposit comes with the contract, not the letter of intent.

say: What goes in the letter?
What do I put in the letter of intent?

moves.text: Unit, price, cash or loan amount, your attorney, and my registration. Then Priya reads the full plan.
moves.fb: That's a complete letter of intent, and attorney review of the plan comes before the binding contract.

moves.text: Price, financing, your attorney, and that I represent you. Priya reviews the plan first.
moves.fb: Right. A strong, complete letter shows a serious buyer, and counsel reviews the plan first.

moves.text: Just your name and the unit for now. We'll add the details later when it gets more serious.
moves.fb: Thin letters signal weak buyers. Include price, financing, and counsel.

moves.text: Your full bank statements and Social Security number, so they can approve you right on the spot.
moves.fb: Overshares sensitive data unnecessarily. Financial documents come later through proper channels.

moves.text: Say you'll waive attorney review to make it stronger. Sponsors love buyers without lawyers.
moves.fb: Waiving counsel on a new development purchase is bad advice. The plan needs attorney review.

moves.text: Offer full ask and promise to close before the TCO. That makes it the strongest letter they get.
moves.fb: There's no closing without a TCO or CO. Don't promise what's impossible.

say: Priya: "I read the plan. Buyer pays the sponsor's transfer taxes, two months of working capital, and the sponsor's attorney fee. Taxes assume an abatement that phases out."
Priya: "The plan shifts costs to the buyer: transfer taxes, working capital, and an expiring abatement. How do you want to advise?"

moves.text: Show {client} each closing cost, mansion and recording tax included, then ask for a concession.
moves.fb: You surfaced hidden costs and negotiated. Sponsors often concede closing costs instead of cutting price.

moves.text: Give {client} the whole picture, taxes after the abatement included, then push on transfer taxes.
moves.fb: Right. Full disclosure of costs and future taxes, plus a negotiation strategy.

moves.text: Just mention it briefly. Most new development buyers pay those costs, so it's no big surprise to anyone.
moves.fb: Customary isn't the same as disclosed. Give the buyer the actual totals.

moves.text: Don't scare {client}. Those fees are standard, and they'll see them at the closing anyway.
moves.fb: Withholding material cost information breaches your duty of disclosure to your client.

moves.text: The abatement lasts forever once it's granted, so you can ignore that part of Priya's note.
moves.fb: Abatements phase out. Future taxes must be part of the buyer's budget.

moves.text: Tell {client} the sponsor pays all transfer taxes in new development. That's the law in NYC.
moves.fb: In NYC new development, the buyer customarily pays the sponsor's transfer taxes. It's negotiable, not law.

say: The sponsor just filed an amendment raising prices 5%. Does my signed contract price go up?
Prices went up by amendment. Am I stuck paying more?

moves.text: No. Amendments apply to unsold units. Your signed contract keeps its price.
moves.fb: Correct. Amendments change pricing for unsold units only.

moves.text: Your contract price stands. The amendment changes what new buyers pay, not you.
moves.fb: Right. Signed contracts keep their price.

moves.text: I think you're safe, but let's ask Priya to confirm before we celebrate too much.
moves.fb: Checking is fine, but you should know the basic rule.

moves.text: Yes. Amendments override contracts, so you'll owe the extra 5% at closing.
moves.fb: Amendments don't change signed contract prices.

moves.text: Only if you haven't paid the full 10% deposit yet. Then the new price applies to you.
moves.fb: Deposit status doesn't matter. Signed contracts keep their price.

moves.text: You can cancel for free whenever there's any amendment. That's your leverage here.
moves.fb: Not every amendment creates a rescission right; it depends on whether the change is material and adverse. Ask Priya.

say: We'd love to close early, next month. The TCO is still a few weeks out, but that's paperwork.
Let's schedule closings now. TCO is coming, it's basically a formality.

moves.text: No TCO or CO, no closing, and no mortgage. Let's schedule once it's issued.
moves.fb: Correct. Closing requires a TCO or CO, and lenders won't fund without one.

moves.text: We'll close after the TCO is issued. {client}'s lender won't fund without it.
moves.fb: Right. A TCO or CO is a closing requirement.

moves.text: Let's pencil in a date and see how it goes. We can move it if the TCO slips again.
moves.fb: Penciling a date before a TCO invites pressure. Make it contingent on issuance.

moves.text: Sure, next month works. The TCO is just a formality the city issues eventually anyway.
moves.fb: There's no closing without a TCO or CO.

moves.text: We can close into escrow now and release the deed once the TCO shows up.
moves.fb: Closing escrow can't substitute for a certificate of occupancy.

moves.text: Let {client} move in before closing to avoid paying rent twice. The TCO comes later.
moves.fb: Occupancy without a TCO or CO is illegal, and pre-closing possession is risky.

say: Who runs the building after I buy? Do owners get a say?
Will owners control the condo board, or does the sponsor?

moves.text: The sponsor appoints the first board. Owners generally take control within five years.
moves.fb: Correct. Sponsor control is temporary, generally ending within five years.

moves.text: Early on, the sponsor's board and managing agent. Owners take over, generally within five years.
moves.fb: Right. That's the transition Priya can find in the plan.
moves.react: I'll ask Priya for the timeline.

moves.text: Owners do, I think. It's a condo, so everyone votes on everything right from day one, equally.
moves.fb: Not at first. The sponsor appoints the first board.

moves.text: The sponsor runs it forever. That's exactly why new developments are cheaper than resales.
moves.fb: Sponsor control ends; owners generally gain control within five years.

moves.text: The city appoints the first board for new buildings until half of the units have been sold.
moves.fb: The sponsor, not the city, appoints the first board.

moves.text: A co-op board of directors runs it, same as any building, and it can reject future buyers.
moves.fb: Condos have a board of managers, usually with only a right of first refusal.
moves.react: So they can reject me too?

say: Quietly, to you: "If {client} picks {unit} today, there's a $5,000 bonus for you on top of the co-broke."
The sales director whispers: "Steer {client} to {unit} and I'll make it worth your while. Cash bonus."

moves.text: No thanks. Any pay goes through my broker and gets disclosed to {client}. I won't steer anyone.
moves.fb: A licensee may not take undisclosed compensation from the other side (19 NYCRR 175.7). Loyalty runs to the buyer.

moves.text: I'll decline and tell {client} about the offer. They pick the unit that's right for them.
moves.fb: Correct. Disclose and refuse; your fiduciary duty is to the buyer.

moves.text: Let me check with my broker. If it's paid to the firm, it might be okay, I'm not sure.
moves.fb: Paid to the firm or not, it must be disclosed and consented to by all parties. Don't steer.

moves.text: Deal. {unit} is the best one anyway, so it's not really steering if I'd pick it myself.
moves.fb: Taking an undisclosed bonus to push a unit breaches loyalty and 175.7.

moves.text: Sure, but pay it to my cousin's LLC so it doesn't show up anywhere on my broker's books.
moves.fb: Hiding compensation is a serious violation. Salespeople are paid only through their broker.

moves.text: Okay, as long as you put it on the closing statement, down where nobody reads the fine print.
moves.fb: Burying it isn't disclosure. All parties must knowingly consent.

roleplays.debrief: You practised new development rules under the Martin Act: register your buyer at the first visit, and take no deposits or reservations in CPS-1 or under a red herring. A letter of intent is non-binding, price amendments hit only unsold units, and there's no closing without a TCO or CO. Buyers customarily pay the sponsor's NYC transfer taxes and working capital, so disclose every cost and negotiate. Undisclosed compensation from the sponsor violates 19 NYCRR 175.7.

questions.q: A condo terrace that only one unit may use, though it is part of the common elements, is a:
c: Limited common element
General common element
Unit
Easement in gross
questions.x: Common elements reserved for specific units are limited common elements. General common element is the trap: all owners may use those.

questions.q: Which is most likely a limited common element in a condo?
c: The lobby
The elevator
A balcony off a single unit
The roof deck open to all
questions.x: A balcony serving one unit is limited. The lobby is the trap: it is a general common element.

questions.q: In a co-op, the building is owned by:
c: Each resident as tenants in common
A corporation
The managing agent
The sponsor forever
questions.x: The co-op corporation owns the building; residents own shares. Tenants in common is the trap: that would be direct co-ownership.

questions.q: A co-op buyer receives:
c: A deed to the unit
A mortgage on the building
A condo declaration
Shares and a proprietary lease
questions.x: Co-op ownership is shares plus a proprietary lease. A deed is the trap: condo buyers get deeds.

questions.q: A co-op's offering documents show the building sits on land leased until 2041. A buyer's lender is most likely concerned about:
c: The building's zoning class
The number of elevators
The remaining land lease term
The sponsor's address
questions.x: Lenders and buyers look closely at how many years remain and how ground rent will reset. Zoning class is the trap: it is not the key risk here.

questions.q: When a co-op leases the land under its building, ground rent increases are paid by:
c: The shareholders through maintenance
The city
The original sponsor only
No one until the lease ends
questions.x: Ground rent is a building expense passed to shareholders in maintenance. The city is the trap.

questions.q: Move-in hours, pet policies and renovation rules adopted by a co-op board are the:
c: Bylaws
Proprietary lease
Offering plan
House rules
questions.x: Day-to-day rules adopted by the board are house rules. Bylaws are the trap: they govern how the corporation runs.

questions.q: A condo owner is fined for running a washing machine in violation of building policy. The policy most likely appears in the:
c: Deed
House rules
Declaration's legal description
Title policy
questions.x: Appliance and floor rules are typical house rules. The deed is the trap: it conveys the unit.

questions.q: A co-op board requires buyers to have two years of housing costs in cash after closing. This is a:
c: Post-closing liquidity requirement
Flip tax
Debt-to-income ratio
Reserve fund
questions.x: Boards often require liquid assets left after paying down payment and closing costs. Reserve fund is the trap: that is the building's money, not the buyer's.

questions.q: Post-closing liquidity measures:
c: The buyer's credit score
The building's reserves
Liquid assets left after closing
The size of the down payment
questions.x: It is what the buyer has left after the purchase. Down payment is the trap: liquidity is measured after it is paid.

questions.q: Under IRC Section 216, a co-op traditionally lets shareholders deduct their share of mortgage interest and taxes if at least 80% of its gross income comes from:
c: Commercial tenants
Tenant-shareholders
Parking fees
The sponsor
questions.x: The 80/20 rule looks to income from tenant-shareholders; since 2007, alternative square-footage and expenditure tests also qualify. Commercial tenants are the trap: too much commercial income can fail the traditional test.

questions.q: The 80/20 rule matters to co-op shareholders because it preserves their:
c: Voting rights
Right to sublet
Rent stabilization
Tax deductions
questions.x: Qualifying under Section 216 keeps shareholder deductions. Voting rights are the trap: they come from share ownership.

questions.q: A condominium owner holds:
c: A unit in fee plus a common-element share
Shares in a corporation plus a proprietary lease
A long-term leasehold interest in the unit
A license to occupy a unit set by the bylaws
questions.x: Condo ownership is real property: the unit in fee plus an undivided percentage of the common elements. Shares and a proprietary lease are the trap: they describe a co-op.

questions.q: A New York condominium is legally created when:
c: The first unit closes
The board adopts the bylaws
The declaration is recorded
The AG accepts the offering plan
questions.x: Recording the declaration (with floor plans) creates the condominium. AG acceptance is the trap: it permits sales under the Martin Act but does not create the condo.

questions.q: The condominium document that governs how the board of managers is elected and how common charges are assessed and collected is the:
c: Declaration
Unit deed
Offering plan
Condominium bylaws
questions.x: The bylaws are the operating manual: elections, meetings, budgets, and collection of common charges. The declaration is the trap: it creates the condo and sets each unit's percentage interest.

questions.q: A condo's annual budget is $2,400,000. A unit's common interest is 0.75%. What are the unit's monthly common charges?
questions.x: $2,400,000 x 0.0075 = $18,000 a year, and $18,000 / 12 = $1,500 a month. $18,000 is the trap: it is the annual figure.

questions.q: A private roof terrace that one condo unit may use, but that is legally part of the common elements, is a:
c: Separately deeded tax lot
Limited common element
Proprietary lease
Easement in gross
questions.x: A limited common element belongs to the commons but is reserved for one or a few units. Separate tax lot is the trap: the terrace is not a separately owned parcel.

questions.concept: Condo board right of first refusal
questions.q: All of the following are true of a NYC condo unit EXCEPT:
c: It is a separate tax lot with its own tax bill
The buyer typically obtains title insurance
The board may reject a buyer as a co-op can
Mortgage recording tax applies to the loan
questions.x: Condo boards generally cannot approve or reject buyers; they typically hold only a right of first refusal. The recording tax answer is the tempting pick, but a condo loan is a real mortgage, so the tax applies.

questions.concept: Condo board right of first refusal
questions.q: A condo board's right of first refusal allows the board to:
c: Match the deal on the same terms
Interview and reject any buyer it dislikes
Raise the price of the unit
Collect a 2% transfer fee
questions.x: The right of first refusal lets the board buy or lease the unit on the terms the owner accepted; boards rarely use it. Interviewing and rejecting is the trap: that is co-op approval power.

questions.q: Under the NY Condominium Act, unpaid common charges are:
c: A personal debt, with no lien on the unit
A lien that ranks ahead of real estate taxes
A lien behind taxes and a first mortgage
Forgiven automatically when the unit is sold
questions.x: Unpaid common charges are a lien on the unit, generally behind taxes and a first mortgage recorded earlier, which is why a paid-up letter is needed at closing. The ahead-of-taxes answer is the trap: tax liens come first.

questions.q: In a new condominium, who typically appoints the first board of managers and the first managing agent?
c: The Attorney General
The first ten purchasers
The sponsor-developer
The building department
questions.x: The sponsor owns the building at the start, so it appoints the initial board and managing agent; control later passes to unit owners. The Attorney General is the trap: the AG reviews disclosure but does not run boards.

questions.q: In New York, a sponsor's control of a condo board is limited. The Attorney General generally expects unit owners to control the board no later than:
c: 5 years after the first closing
1 year after plan acceptance
The sale of the last unit
10 years after the declaration is recorded
questions.x: Plans must state when the sponsor gives up control, generally no later than 5 years after the first closing and often sooner once a stated share of units sells. The last-unit answer is the trap: that could let a sponsor keep control indefinitely.

questions.q: A condo is governed by a board of ______, while a co-op is governed by a board of ______.
c: directors; managers
trustees; managers
managers; directors
governors; shareholders
questions.x: Unit owners elect a board of managers in a condo; a co-op is a corporation, so shareholders elect a board of directors. The reversed pair is the trap.

questions.q: Covenants, conditions, and restrictions (CC&Rs) are best described as:
c: Public zoning rules adopted by the town
Private rules that run with the land
The co-op's audited financial statements
The lender's conditions for the loan
questions.x: CC&Rs are private restrictions recorded with the property and binding on owners. Zoning is the trap: it is public regulation under the police power.

questions.q: A condo owner who lives in her unit wants to know what she can deduct on her federal income taxes. Generally she may deduct:
c: Her monthly common charges
Her share of the building's mortgage interest
Her unit's property taxes and loan interest
Nothing, since the unit is personal property
questions.x: A condo owner deducts her own unit's taxes and mortgage interest within federal limits, like any homeowner. The building-mortgage answer is the trap: that is a co-op shareholder concept.

questions.q: The New York law that requires sponsors to file an offering plan with the Attorney General before offering condo or co-op interests is the:
c: Condominium Act
Interstate Land Sales Act
Martin Act (GBL 352-e)
RPL Article 12-A
questions.x: The Martin Act (GBL 352-e) governs offerings of co-op and condo interests. The Condominium Act is the trap: it governs how condos are created and run, not how they are offered.

questions.q: When the Attorney General accepts an offering plan for filing, it means:
c: The AG has found the prices fair
The AG guarantees the construction
The disclosures meet filing rules
The plan is effective right away
questions.x: Acceptance is about disclosure, not merit; it is no endorsement of the investment. The effective-right-away answer is the trap: a plan is declared effective later, once its stated minimum sales are reached.

questions.q: A "red herring" in New York co-op and condo practice is:
c: A preliminary plan not yet accepted
An amendment that raises unit prices
An accepted plan declared effective
An ad that misstates unit sizes
questions.x: The red herring is the preliminary offering plan, submitted to the AG but not yet accepted and named for its red legend; it may be shown for information only. The misleading-ad answer is the trap: the term has nothing to do with deception.

questions.q: Under the Attorney General's current CPS-1 policy, while a sponsor is testing the market, it may:
c: Take refundable deposits held in escrow
Take non-binding reservations of units
Sign contracts subject to plan acceptance
Advertise and gather interest
questions.x: CPS-1 allows advertising and gathering non-binding interest only: no deposits and no reservations, binding or non-binding, until a plan is accepted for filing. Non-binding reservations are the trap: older materials allowed them, but current policy does not.

questions.q: A letter of intent submitted for a new development condo unit is generally:
c: Binding on the sponsor alone
Binding on the purchaser alone
Non-binding on buyer and sponsor
Recorded with the county clerk
questions.x: A letter of intent expresses interest; nothing binds either side until a purchase agreement is signed after the plan is accepted. The binding-on-sponsor answer is the trap: the sponsor can still change the price.

questions.q: A buyer signed a purchase agreement at $1,200,000. Later the sponsor files an amendment raising prices on that line by 8%. The buyer's price is now:
c: Open to renegotiation
questions.x: Price amendments apply to unsold units; a signed contract keeps its price. $1,296,000 is the trap: it applies the 8% increase to a contract already signed.

questions.q: In NYC, closings in a new condo building typically cannot begin until:
c: Every unit in the building is sold
The AG approves the first-year budget
The sponsor turns over the board
A TCO or CO covers the unit
questions.x: A unit may not be legally occupied, and lenders will not fund, without a temporary or permanent certificate of occupancy. Board turnover is the trap: it comes later, after closings.

questions.q: In new development, "flipping" refers to:
c: A transfer fee charged by a co-op
Reversing a unit's floor plan layout
Quickly reselling or assigning a contract
Converting rental units to condos
questions.x: Flipping is buying at the sponsor's price and quickly reselling or assigning the contract for a profit. The transfer fee answer is the trap: a flip tax is an unrelated building fee.

questions.q: All of the following may be costs a buyer pays in a NYC new development condo purchase EXCEPT:
c: Sponsor's transfer taxes, if shifted
A working capital contribution
Mansion tax on a $1.5 million unit
The sponsor's listing commission
questions.x: The sponsor pays its own sales team or listing broker. Shifted transfer taxes are the tempting pick, but new development contracts commonly shift the sponsor's RPTT and state transfer tax to the buyer.

questions.concept: Mortgage recording tax and mansion tax
questions.q: A buyer finances a $1,400,000 NYC condo with a $900,000 mortgage. Using a 1.925% mortgage recording tax rate and the 1% mansion tax, what does the buyer owe for these two taxes?
questions.x: MRT: $900,000 x 1.925% = $17,325; mansion tax: $1,400,000 x 1% = $14,000; total $31,325. $40,950 is the trap: it applies the recording tax to the full price instead of the loan.

questions.q: Which section of an offering plan should a buyer's agent read first to learn about the sponsor's financing, construction, and tax abatement risks?
c: The floor plans
The schedule of units
The bylaws
Special risks
questions.x: The special risks section sits at the front of the plan and flags the biggest dangers. The schedule of units is the trap: it lists prices and percentages but does not summarize risk.

questions.q: A new development plan lists a unit at 1,100 square feet. The buyer's tape measure finds noticeably less usable space. The most likely explanation is that:
c: The sponsor committed fraud
The architect measured in meters
The AG certified the wrong figure
Plan figures include the walls
questions.x: Offering plan square footage is approximate and often measured to exterior walls or the middle of shared walls. The fraud answer is the trap: the plan discloses that figures are approximate, so buyers should rely on room dimensions.

questions.q: Deposits that new development purchasers pay under a contract are:
c: Paid into the sponsor's operating account
Held in a GBL 352-h escrow account
Paid to the buyer's broker on signing
Released to fund construction costs
questions.x: Purchaser deposits must be held in escrow under GBL 352-h. The construction answer is the trap: using deposits for construction or the sponsor's operations is prohibited.

questions.q: A simultaneous closing in new development occurs when:
c: Every unit in the building closes on one day
A buyer resells on the day he buys
The condo and its retail unit close together
Two co-buyers sign at separate closings
questions.x: A simultaneous closing is how a flip happens at closing, and many sponsors restrict it. The every-unit answer is the trap: closings in a new building are spread over months.

questions.q: New York's Condominium Act is found in:
c: Real Property Law Article 9-B
General Business Law 352-e
Real Property Law Article 12-A
Real Property Tax Law Article 7
questions.x: The Condominium Act is RPL Article 9-B. GBL 352-e is the Martin Act on offering plans, Article 12-A is the license law, and RPTL Article 7 covers tax certiorari.

questions.q: The lien priority rule for unpaid condo common charges comes from which law?
c: The Martin Act on offering plans
The Uniform Commercial Code, Article 9
The Condominium Act, RPL Article 9-B
The Real Property Tax Law's lien rules
questions.x: The common charge lien (RPL 339-z) is part of the Condominium Act, RPL Article 9-B. The UCC governs co-op share loans, and the Martin Act governs offering plans.

questions.concept: Common elements as tenants in common
questions.q: Condo unit owners hold the building's common elements:
c: As joint tenants with right of survivorship
Through shares in a corporation
As tenants in common, by percentage
Only by lease from the board of managers
questions.x: Each unit owns an undivided percentage of the common elements as a tenant in common. Shares in a corporation describe a co-op, not a condo.

questions.concept: Common elements as tenants in common
questions.q: A condo owner wants to sell her share of the lobby and gym but keep her unit. She:
c: May sell it to another owner in the building
May sell it with board approval only
May sue to partition the common elements
Cannot sell it apart from her unit
questions.x: A unit's common interest cannot be separated from the unit, and owners cannot sue to partition the building. Board approval does not change that.

questions.q: A condo board wants to change the building's move-in hours. Which document does it change?
c: The rules and regulations
The recorded declaration
The bylaws, by unit owner vote
The offering plan, by amendment
questions.x: Day-to-day rules like move-in hours, pets and renovation hours are rules and regulations, adopted and changed by the board without recording. The declaration and bylaws are recorded and harder to change.

questions.q: Which condo document is generally NOT recorded with the county clerk or City Register?
c: The declaration and its amendments
The bylaws
The floor plans
The rules and regulations
questions.x: The declaration is recorded with the floor plans, and the bylaws are attached to it. Rules and regulations are adopted by the board and are not recorded.

questions.q: A condo unit's monthly common charges typically cover its share of all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Staff and building insurance
Reserves for future repairs
The unit's real estate taxes
Utilities for the common areas
questions.x: Each condo unit is its own tax lot with its own tax bill, so taxes are not in common charges. In a co-op, by contrast, the building's taxes are in maintenance.

questions.q: A condo owner pays real estate taxes on her unit:
c: Through her monthly common charges
On her own bill for the unit's tax lot
Through the sponsor until the plan ends
As an assessment the board levies yearly
questions.x: Each condo unit is a separate tax lot with its own bill. Taxes inside the monthly payment is the co-op model (maintenance), which is the trap here.

questions.q: At closing on a new construction condo unit, the unit must be released from the:
c: Sponsor's building loan
Board's right of first refusal
Co-op's recognition agreement
Buyer's mortgage commitment
questions.x: A partial release frees the unit from the sponsor's building loan so the buyer takes clean title. A ROFR is waived, not released, and recognition agreements are a co-op tool.

questions.q: A condo resale closing usually requires all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A paid-up letter for common charges
The board's right of first refusal waiver
A UCC-1 financing statement on shares
Owner's and lender's title insurance
questions.x: A UCC-1 perfects a co-op share loan. A condo is real property: title insurance, a paid-up letter and a ROFR waiver are standard.

questions.q: A sponsor's offering plan is declared effective when:
c: The AG accepts the plan for filing
The building receives a final CO
The first buyer signs a binding letter of intent
The stated minimum of units is under contract
questions.x: The plan is declared effective by amendment once the minimum number of units stated in the plan is under contract. Acceptance for filing comes earlier and only allows contracts and deposits.

questions.q: A buyer signs a contract and pays a deposit after the plan is accepted, but the sponsor abandons the plan before declaring it effective. The buyer's deposit:
c: Is forfeited to the sponsor
Goes to the Attorney General
Is refundable to the buyer
Is held until the next building
questions.x: Until the plan is declared effective, deposits are refundable if the plan is abandoned, and they sit in escrow meanwhile. Forfeiture applies to a buyer's default, not a sponsor's abandonment.

questions.q: To protect her co-broke commission in a new development, a buyer's agent should register the buyer:
c: After the purchase agreement is signed
When the plan is declared effective
At closing with the sponsor's attorney
At or before the buyer's first visit
questions.x: Sales offices usually pay co-brokes only for buyers registered at or before the first visit. Waiting until contract signing is the costly mistake.

questions.q: A buyer visits a sponsor's sales gallery alone, then hires an agent and signs a contract. The agent never registered the buyer. The agent's co-broke is:
c: At risk for lack of registration
Guaranteed by the Martin Act
Owed by the buyer instead of the sponsor
Owed in full once the plan is effective
questions.x: New development offices pay co-brokes only for buyers the agent registered, usually at or before the first visit. The Martin Act regulates disclosure, not commission splits.

questions.q: During CPS-1 market testing, an agent tells a buyer, "Sign this letter and the unit is locked in at this price." The statement:
c: Is fine if the letter is on the sponsor's form
Binds the sponsor to that price
Is fine once the buyer pays a deposit
Can violate the Martin Act
questions.x: Nothing is binding until a purchase agreement is signed after the plan is accepted. Misstating an offering's status can violate the Martin Act, which the AG enforces civilly and criminally.

questions.q: The Martin Act is enforced by the Attorney General:
c: Civilly and criminally
Only through civil fines
Only through the DOS license
Only after a buyer sues first
questions.x: The AG enforces the Martin Act both civilly and criminally. DOS licenses agents but does not enforce offering plan law.

questions.q: First-year real estate tax estimates in an offering plan must be backed by:
c: The sponsor's own estimate
An expert's letter
A Department of Finance ruling
The construction lender's appraisal
questions.x: The plan's first-year tax projections must be supported by an expert letter. Buyers should still check whether an abatement is assumed and when it phases out.

questions.q: A plan shows year-one taxes of $200 a month on a $1,200,000 unit, assuming a tax abatement. The buyer's agent should warn that:
c: The AG has approved the figure as fair
The figure includes the common charges
Condo taxes are fixed for the life of the loan
Taxes may jump as the abatement phases out
questions.x: Abatements phase out, so year 10 taxes can be far higher than year 1. AG acceptance is about disclosure, not a promise that the figure stays low.

questions.q: If a sponsor misses the outside closing date stated in the offering plan, the buyer may:
c: Be required to close at a higher price
Lose the deposit to the sponsor
Get the right to rescind the purchase
Have to wait for a new plan to be filed
questions.x: Plans give an estimated first closing date and an outside date; missing the outside date may give buyers a right to rescind. Signed contracts keep their price.

questions.q: A sponsor's first-year budget shows unusually low common charges. The most likely risk is:
c: Higher charges later
A lower purchase price
Loss of the ROFR
A refund of the deposit
questions.x: Low budgets sell units, but an underfunded budget means increases later. It has no effect on the contract price or the right of first refusal.

questions.q: A sponsor files an amendment disclosing a material adverse change that affects existing purchasers. The AG requires that those purchasers:
c: Pay a higher deposit to stay in
Be offered a chance to rescind
Close within 30 days anyway
Accept the change without notice
questions.x: When an amendment reveals a material adverse change affecting existing buyers, they must be offered rescission within the period the amendment states. They are not forced to close or pay more.

questions.q: In a soft market, a new development sponsor most commonly helps buyers by:
c: Cutting prices on signed contracts
Refunding deposits to all purchasers
Offering concessions such as closing costs
Lowering the plan's minimum sales threshold
questions.x: Sponsors prefer concessions (closing costs, transfer taxes, a credit, a year of common charges) over list price cuts. Signed contracts keep their price either way.

questions.concept: Lender review of a new project
questions.q: Before financing a new development condo unit, a lender usually also reviews:
c: The sponsor's personal credit score and history
The building's house rules on pets
The broker's listing agreement
How many units are sold and occupied
questions.x: Lenders look at the project as a whole: units sold, owner occupancy and how many units the sponsor still holds. A buyer needing a loan should ask about this early.

questions.concept: Lender review of a new project
questions.q: A strong buyer is approved, but the lender balks because the sponsor still owns 70% of the units. The lender's concern is:
c: The project as a whole
The buyer's debt-to-income
The board's right of first refusal
The mansion tax on the purchase price
questions.x: Lenders review the project, not just the borrower; heavy sponsor ownership and few sales raise risk. The buyer's own ratios are not the issue here.

questions.q: A flip tax is best described as:
c: A tax on reselling within a year
A resale transfer fee a co-op charges
The IRS rate on short-term gains
A fee for assigning a sponsor contract
questions.x: A flip tax is a building's transfer fee on resales, common in co-ops. It has nothing to do with flipping (a quick resale for profit), which is the word trap.

questions.q: A co-op owner of 15 years sells and pays the building a 2% fee. This fee is:
c: A flip tax
A penalty for flipping
The NYC transfer tax
A working capital fund
questions.x: A flip tax applies to resales regardless of how long the owner held the unit. Same word as flipping, unrelated idea.

questions.concept: NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT
questions.q: A Queens condo resells for $800,000. Using NYS transfer tax of 0.4% and NYC RPTT of 1.425%, the seller's total transfer taxes are:

questions.concept: NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT
questions.q: In a NYC condo resale with no special terms, the NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT are customarily paid by the:
c: Buyer
Seller
Lender
Buyer and seller equally
questions.x: In a resale the seller pays both transfer taxes. Only in NYC new development does the contract customarily shift the sponsor's transfer taxes to the buyer.

questions.q: A co-op shareholder may generally deduct on her federal return:
c: All of her monthly maintenance
The building's repair and staff costs
Her share of building taxes and interest
Nothing, since she owns no real estate at all
questions.x: Shareholders deduct their proportionate share of the building's real estate taxes and mortgage interest (plus interest on their own share loan). The rest of maintenance, like staff and repairs, is not deductible.

questions.q: A shareholder pays $24,000 a year in maintenance. The co-op reports that 40% went to real estate taxes and 25% to underlying mortgage interest. Her deductible share is:
c: $24,000, all of it
questions.x: Taxes $24,000 x 40% = $9,600 plus interest $24,000 x 25% = $6,000, for $15,600. Deducting all maintenance is the trap; operating costs are not deductible.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches condo with co-op?
c: Maintenance vs common charges
Board of directors vs board of managers
Deed vs shares and proprietary lease
Lien search vs title insurance
questions.x: A condo buyer gets a deed; a co-op buyer gets shares and a proprietary lease. The other pairs are reversed: condos have common charges, managers and title insurance.

questions.q: All of the following are true of a co-op, as opposed to a condo, EXCEPT:
c: The board approves or rejects each buyer
Taxes are paid inside maintenance
The buyer finances with a share loan
The buyer gets an owner's title policy
questions.x: Title insurance is for condos and houses; co-ops use a lien search. Board approval, taxes in maintenance and share loans are all co-op features.

questions.q: Downstate, a co-op buyer's attorney typically reviews the co-op's financial statements and board minutes:
c: After the board interview is held
Before the contract is signed
At the closing table
Only if the lender asks
questions.x: Downstate practice is to review 2 to 3 years of financials and 1 to 2 years of minutes before signing, because what they reveal drives price and advice.

questions.q: Which document is the best place to learn about planned facade work, litigation and changes to sublet policy?
c: The stock certificate
The board minutes
The alteration agreement
The recognition agreement
questions.x: Board minutes show maintenance history, planned projects (Local Law 11, Local Law 97), litigation and policy changes. A stock certificate only proves share ownership.

questions.concept: Co-op ownership is not fee simple
questions.q: A co-op shareholder's interest in her apartment is best described as:
c: Shares and a leasehold right to occupy
Fee simple ownership of the unit's airspace
A life estate in the apartment
Fee simple shared with other owners
questions.x: The buyer owns shares (personal property) and holds a leasehold right of occupancy under the proprietary lease. Fee simple in airspace describes a condo unit.

questions.concept: Co-op ownership is not fee simple
questions.q: A co-op corporation owns its land and building in fee simple. A shareholder in that co-op owns:
c: Fee simple, since the co-op does
Shares and a proprietary lease
A deeded percentage of the land
A condo unit inside the co-op
questions.x: Even when the corporation owns in fee, the buyer never owns real estate: only shares and a lease. Assuming the corporation's fee passes to shareholders is the trap.

questions.q: When a co-op buyer finances with a share loan, the stock certificate is usually held by the:
c: Buyer
Managing agent
Lender
County clerk
questions.x: The lender holds the stock certificate as part of its security, along with an assignment of the proprietary lease. Nothing is recorded with the county clerk.

questions.q: In a co-op sale, what proves share ownership and is transferred at closing?
c: The deed
The house rules
The offering plan and amendments
The stock certificate
questions.x: The stock certificate is the proof of ownership that changes hands at closing, along with an assignment of the proprietary lease. There is no deed in a co-op.

questions.q: Compared with a typical bank, a co-op board's financial requirements are usually:
c: Stricter
Set by federal rules
Identical to the bank's
More lenient on DTI
questions.x: Banks follow federal ability-to-repay rules; boards set their own, usually stricter, limits on DTI, financing and liquidity.

questions.q: A condo buyer, unlike a co-op buyer, generally does not need approval from:
c: A mortgage lender, if financing
The building's board
A title insurer
The buyer's attorney
questions.x: Condo boards generally do not approve buyers (they hold a right of first refusal), but condo buyers who finance still need the bank.

questions.q: A lender evaluating commission income usually looks at:
c: The last month only
A 2-year average
The best year in five
Projected next-year sales
questions.x: Commission and bonus income are usually averaged over 2 years. Using only the best year or projections would overstate unsteady income.

questions.q: A co-op applicant owns a rental that brings $4,000 a month in gross rent. Lenders often count about how much as monthly income?
c: $4,000, the full rent
questions.x: Lenders often count about 75% of gross rent: $4,000 x 0.75 = $3,000. Counting the full $4,000 ignores vacancy and expenses.

questions.q: Why should a co-op buyer's agent work backward from the board's calendar the day the contract is signed?
c: The AG requires every co-op closing within 30 days
The agent must attend and present the buyer in person
The seller may cancel if no interview date is set
Boards meet monthly; delays can outrun a rate lock
questions.x: Most boards meet monthly, so missing a package deadline can push the interview past the loan commitment or rate lock. The agent does not attend the interview.

questions.q: At a co-op board interview, the buyer's agent usually:
c: Does not attend
Answers financial questions
Presents the package to the board
Negotiates the board's conditions
questions.x: The agent prepares the buyer but does not attend. The buyer should know every number in the package and answer briefly and honestly.

questions.q: An investor wants to buy and rent out an apartment right away. Which is usually the better fit?
c: A co-op, since boards favor investors
A condo, since rental rules are looser
A co-op held as a pied-a-terre
Either, since sublet rules are set by law
questions.x: Co-ops are built for owner occupancy and often require primary residence and limit sublets; condos are generally more flexible for investors. Sublet limits come from each building, not state law.

questions.q: A typical co-op sublet policy might allow a shareholder to sublet:
c: At any time without approval
Once the share loan is paid in full
Only to family members, never others
2 of every 5 years, with approval
questions.x: A common rule is 2 years out of every 5, with board approval and a sublet fee. Unapproved subletting at will is the condo-like freedom co-ops usually restrict.

questions.q: A condo unit owner typically receives all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A deed to the unit
A separate property tax bill
Stock in a co-op corporation
A share of the common elements
questions.x: Stock in a housing corporation is a co-op feature. A separate tax bill is the tempting pick, but each condo unit is its own tax lot.

questions.q: A sponsor's offering plan has been accepted and several contracts are signed, but no declaration has been recorded. Legally, the building is:
c: A condominium since plan acceptance
A condominium since the first contract
Not a condominium until recording
A co-op until the declaration is filed
questions.x: A condominium exists only once the declaration is recorded. Plan acceptance is the trap: it allows marketing and contracts but does not create the condo.

questions.q: The condominium document that creates the condo and sets each unit's percentage of common interest is the:
c: Declaration
Bylaws
House rules
Offering plan
questions.x: The declaration, recorded with the floor plans, creates the condo and fixes each unit's common interest. The bylaws are the trap: they cover governance and collections.

questions.q: A unit pays common charges of $1,050 a month. The condo's annual budget is $3,150,000. The unit's common interest is:
questions.x: Annual charges are $1,050 x 12 = $12,600, and $12,600 / $3,150,000 = 0.4%. 0.033% is the trap: it uses the monthly charge without annualizing it.

questions.q: A condo's backyard is reserved for the two garden units but is part of the common elements. A garden owner wants to sell it separately. She:
c: May sell it as her own lot
May sell it if the board consents
May sell it to another garden owner
Cannot sell it apart from the unit
questions.x: A limited common element belongs to the commons and is reserved for certain units; it is not separately owned and cannot be sold apart from the unit. Board consent is the trap: no consent turns common elements into private property.

questions.concept: Condo board right of first refusal
questions.q: A Brooklyn condo board dislikes a buyer's profession and wants to stop the sale. Its typical legal tool is to:
c: Reject the buyer after an interview
Exercise its right of first refusal
Refuse to issue a waiver for no reason
Charge a 5% penalty transfer fee
questions.x: Condo boards generally cannot reject buyers; to block a sale they must exercise the right of first refusal by matching the deal. The interview answer is the trap: that is co-op board power.

questions.concept: Condo board right of first refusal
questions.q: A condo board's right of first refusal includes all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Matching the price and terms
Buying the unit for the condo
Leasing the unit on the same terms
Rejecting the buyer outright
questions.x: The right of first refusal lets the board step into the deal, not veto the buyer. Leasing on the same terms is the tempting pick, but many declarations extend the right to leases.

questions.q: A condo unit carries unpaid property taxes, a first mortgage recorded in 2019, and a common charge lien filed in 2024. Generally, the order of priority is:
c: Common charges, then taxes, then mortgage
Mortgage, then taxes, then common charges
Taxes, then common charges, then mortgage
Taxes, mortgage, then common charges
questions.x: Taxes come first, and the common charge lien generally ranks behind a first mortgage recorded before it. The common-charges-second answer is the trap: the Condominium Act subordinates it to taxes and prior first mortgages.

questions.q: In a new condo, the sponsor's appointed board members are later replaced by:
c: Managers the unit owners elect
Managers named by the Attorney General
The managing agent's staff
A court-appointed receiver
questions.x: Control passes from the sponsor to a board of managers elected by unit owners. The AG answer is the trap: the AG reviews plans but does not appoint boards.
