questions.q: A condo's first unit closed in March 2022 and sales have been slow. Under the AG's usual rule, the sponsor gives up board control no later than about:
c: March 2023
March 2025
March 2027
When the last unit sells
questions.x: Sponsor control generally ends no later than 5 years after the first closing, so about March 2027, or sooner if the plan's sales threshold is met. March 2025 is the trap: it applies a 3-year period.

questions.q: A Park Slope building's residents own shares and elect its governing body. That body is a board of:
c: Managers
Managing agents
Governors
Directors
questions.x: Shareholders mean a co-op corporation, governed by a board of directors. Managers is the trap: that is the condo board.

questions.q: A recorded restriction in a townhouse community bars fences taller than 4 feet. A new buyer who never signed it is:
c: Free of it, since he did not sign it
Bound if zoning repeats the rule
Free of it after the first year
Bound; it runs with the land
questions.x: Recorded CC&Rs run with the land and bind later owners. The did-not-sign answer is the trap: recording gives notice, so signing is not needed.

questions.q: Which homeowner deducts a pro rata share of the building's mortgage interest and real estate taxes under IRC 216?
c: A condo unit owner
A co-op shareholder
A rent-stabilized tenant
A townhouse owner
questions.x: IRC 216 lets co-op tenant-shareholders deduct their share of the building's mortgage interest and taxes. The condo owner is the trap: condo owners deduct their own unit's taxes and loan interest directly.

questions.q: A sponsor wants to convert a Queens rental building to a co-op. Before offering shares, it must file an offering plan with the:
c: Department of State
NYC Department of Buildings
New York Attorney General
Homes and Community Renewal
questions.x: Under the Martin Act, co-op and condo offerings are filed with the Attorney General. HCR is the trap: it has a role in rent-regulated tenants' rights but does not accept offering plans.

questions.q: A buyer says, "The Attorney General approved this plan, so the price must be fair." Diane should explain that acceptance means:
c: The AG reviewed and approved the price
The disclosures meet the filing rules
The AG insures the buyer's deposit
The building passed a state inspection
questions.x: Acceptance for filing means the plan's disclosures meet requirements; it is not a judgment on price or merit. The approved-the-price answer is the trap: the AG does not vouch for the investment.

questions.q: While a sponsor is circulating a red herring, all of the following are prohibited EXCEPT:
c: Signing purchase agreements
Accepting purchaser deposits
Sharing the plan for information
Taking binding unit reservations
questions.x: A red herring may be shown for information only; no contracts or deposits until acceptance. Taking reservations is the tempting pick, but reservations are not allowed before acceptance either.

questions.q: During a CPS-1 market test, a buyer offers Jordan a $50,000 refundable check to hold a penthouse. Jordan should:
c: Accept it into escrow
Accept it if fully refundable
Accept it with a letter of intent
Decline; no deposits yet
questions.x: Under current CPS-1 policy, no deposits and no reservations of any kind are allowed before a plan is accepted for filing. The refundable answer is the trap: older rules were looser, but refundability does not make it allowed now.

questions.q: A buyer signs a letter of intent for a unit at $950,000. Before contracts are signed, the sponsor raises the price to $990,000. The buyer:
c: Can enforce the $950,000 price
Is bound to buy at $990,000
Is not bound; nor is the sponsor
Is owed a $40,000 credit at closing
questions.x: A letter of intent is non-binding as to both the purchaser and the price. The enforce-the-price answer is the trap: only a signed purchase agreement locks in a price.

questions.q: A plan amendment cuts prices on unsold units by 5%. A buyer who already signed at $2,000,000 now pays:
c: Whichever price is lower
questions.x: Price amendments apply to unsold units; a signed contract keeps its price unless the sponsor agrees otherwise. $1,900,000 is the trap: the cut does not reach units already under contract.

questions.q: A new condo's lobby is finished but the buyer's floor has no temporary certificate of occupancy yet. Her closing should:
c: Wait for a TCO on her unit
Proceed if the lobby has a TCO
Proceed if she waives occupancy
Proceed with the deposit held
questions.x: A unit cannot be legally occupied, and lenders will not fund, until a TCO or CO covers that unit. The waiver answer is the trap: a buyer cannot waive the legal requirement for occupancy.

questions.q: An investor signs a sponsor contract at $1,500,000 and, before closing, assigns it to a new buyer for $1,650,000. This is:
c: A contract flip
A flip tax
A recognition
A conversion
questions.x: Assigning or quickly reselling a sponsor contract for profit is flipping. A flip tax is the trap: it is a building transfer fee on resale.

questions.q: In NYC new development, a contract that shifts the sponsor's transfer taxes to the buyer makes the buyer pay:
c: The mortgage recording tax
The mansion tax a second time
The sponsor's listing broker's commission
The RPTT and state transfer tax
questions.x: Sponsors commonly shift the NYC RPTT and NYS transfer tax, normally seller costs, to the buyer. The mortgage recording tax is the trap: it is already a buyer cost on a financed purchase.

questions.concept: Mortgage recording tax and mansion tax
questions.q: A buyer pays $1,100,000 for a NYC condo with a $450,000 mortgage. The recording tax rate is 1.8% for loans under $500,000, and the 1% mansion tax applies. Together these taxes total:
questions.x: MRT: $450,000 x 1.8% = $8,100; mansion: $1,100,000 x 1% = $11,000; total $19,100. $30,800 is the trap: it applies the recording tax to the price instead of the loan.

questions.q: A buyer's agent wants to know whether a sponsor's tax abatement could expire early. The fastest place to look in the offering plan is:
c: The schedule of units
The special risks section
The floor plans
The house rules
questions.x: The special risks section at the front of the plan flags abatement, financing, and construction risks. The schedule of units is the trap: it shows prices and tax estimates but not the risks behind them.

questions.q: Offering plan square footage for a new condo unit is best treated as:
c: A guaranteed interior measure
Approximate, often to the walls
Certified by the Attorney General
Measured to the inside of closets
questions.x: Plan square footage is approximate and often measured to exterior walls or the centerline of shared walls. The guaranteed answer is the trap: plans disclose that figures are approximate.

questions.q: A sponsor asks Marcus to have his buyer wire the 10% deposit to the sponsor's construction account to save time. Marcus should:
c: Insist on the escrow account
Agree, as sponsors may use deposits
Agree, if the buyer signs a waiver
Hold the deposit in his own account
questions.x: Purchaser deposits must go into escrow under GBL 352-h as the plan describes. The waiver answer is the trap: buyers cannot waive the statutory escrow protection.

questions.q: A sponsor's contract bars purchasers from reselling on the same day they close. This clause targets:
c: Simultaneous closings
Recognition agreements
Working capital fees
Letters of intent
questions.x: Barring same-day resales targets simultaneous closings, the mechanism of a flip at closing. Letters of intent are the trap: they come before contracts and involve no resale.

questions.q: A co-op buyer's interest is legally classified as:
c: Personal property
Real property in fee simple
A freehold estate
A life estate
questions.x: Shares and a proprietary lease are personal property, which is why there is no deed and no mortgage recording tax. Fee simple real property is the trap: that describes a condo unit.

questions.q: The document that gives a co-op shareholder the right to occupy a specific apartment is the:
c: Proprietary lease
Stock certificate
Declaration
Recognition agreement
questions.x: The proprietary lease grants occupancy of the apartment. The stock certificate is the trap: it proves share ownership, not the right to occupy a unit.

questions.q: A co-op's monthly maintenance typically includes the apartment's share of all of the following EXCEPT:
c: The building's real estate taxes
The underlying mortgage payment
Building operating expenses
The owner's share loan payment
questions.x: The shareholder's personal share loan is paid separately to the lender. The underlying mortgage is the tempting pick, but the building's own mortgage is part of maintenance.

questions.q: A co-op share loan is perfected by the lender through:
c: Filing a UCC-1 financing statement
Recording a mortgage with the clerk
Recording a deed of trust
Filing a lis pendens
questions.x: Shares are personal property, so the lender perfects under the Uniform Commercial Code with a UCC-1. Recording a mortgage is the trap: no mortgage is recorded, which is why no mortgage recording tax applies.

questions.q: In a co-op purchase, the buyer's attorney orders a lien search instead of title insurance mainly to find:
c: Open zoning violations
UCC filings and judgments
The building's certificate of occupancy
The seller's credit score and history
questions.x: The co-op lien search checks for UCC filings, judgments, and tax liens against the seller and the shares. Zoning violations are the trap: those concern the building, not the transfer of shares.

questions.q: In a recognition agreement, the co-op typically agrees to:
c: Guarantee the shareholder's loan
Notify the lender of defaults
Pay the loan if the owner dies
Waive its own maintenance lien
questions.x: The co-op recognizes the lender's lien and gives notice and cure rights when the shareholder defaults. The waive-its-lien answer is the trap: the co-op's lien for unpaid maintenance generally stays first.

questions.q: A co-op board requires a maximum debt-to-income ratio of 28%. A buyer earns $240,000 a year and will have a $3,600 loan payment, $1,500 maintenance, and $300 in other monthly debt. Does the buyer meet the limit?
c: No, the ratio is 32%
No, the ratio is 29%
Yes, the ratio is 22.5%
Yes, the ratio is 27%
questions.x: Monthly income is $240,000 / 12 = $20,000 and monthly debt is $3,600 + $1,500 + $300 = $5,400, so $5,400 / $20,000 = 27%, under the limit. 22.5% is the trap: it leaves out the maintenance.

questions.q: A bank approves a buyer for 85% financing on a co-op, but the building's financing limit is 70%. The buyer:
c: May borrow 85%, since the bank controls
Is held to 70% absent a board waiver
May borrow 85% if the seller agrees
Has to pay cash for the unit
questions.x: The co-op's financing limit binds the buyer as a condition of board approval unless the board grants an exception. The bank-controls answer is the trap: lender approval is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.q: A typical co-op board package includes all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A fully signed contract of sale
Tax returns and an employment letter
A signed credit check authorization
The buyer's title insurance commitment
questions.x: Co-op buyers do not get title insurance, so no commitment goes in the package. The credit authorization is the tempting pick, but boards routinely run credit.

questions.q: A New York co-op board may lawfully reject a purchaser:
c: For any non-discriminatory reason
For poor credit, and that alone
After giving written reasons to the AG
For having young children, if quiet
questions.x: Under the business judgment rule, boards have wide discretion and usually need not give reasons, but they may never reject for a protected class. The young-children answer is the trap: familial status is protected.

questions.q: Which party in a co-op conversion can usually sell or sublet apartments without board approval under the offering plan?
c: A shareholder there for 2 years
The holder of unsold shares
The managing agent
Any buyer of sold shares
questions.x: Sponsors and holders of unsold shares typically keep the right to sell and sublet without board approval. Buyers of sold shares are the trap: they are fully subject to board rules.

questions.q: A condop is most often created to:
c: Let shareholders skip maintenance
Protect the co-op's 80/20 tax status
Exempt the building from real estate taxes
Convert a condo back into rental housing
questions.x: Splitting commercial space into its own condo unit keeps store rents out of the co-op's gross income, protecting shareholders' IRC 216 deductions. The real estate tax answer is the trap: a condop still pays property taxes.

questions.q: Under the traditional 80/20 test, a co-op with $3,000,000 in total gross income can receive no more than how much from non-shareholder sources such as store rents?
questions.x: At least 80% ($2,400,000) must come from tenant-shareholders, so at most 20% ($600,000) may come from outside sources. $2,400,000 is the trap: it is the shareholder minimum, not the outside maximum.

questions.q: A flip tax is:
c: A building transfer fee paid on resale
A state tax on quick resales of units
The recording tax on co-op share loans
A penalty the board charges for subletting
questions.x: A flip tax is a transfer fee imposed by the co-op (sometimes a condo), usually paid by the seller as a percentage of price. The state-tax answer is the trap: it is not a government tax and has nothing to do with flipping.

questions.q: Minutes show a co-op's underlying mortgage has a large balloon payment due in 18 months and the building has a small reserve fund. The most likely consequence for a buyer is:
c: Lower maintenance after the payoff
Higher maintenance or an assessment
No effect, since her loan is separate
Conversion of the building to a condo
questions.x: Refinancing a balloon at higher rates with thin reserves usually means higher maintenance or assessments. The separate-loan answer is the trap: the buyer's own share loan does not shield her from building costs.

questions.q: Before a co-op shareholder renovates a kitchen, the co-op will typically require the shareholder to sign a(n):
c: Recognition agreement
Alteration agreement
Proprietary lease rider
Letter of intent
questions.x: The alteration agreement sets plan approval, insurance, work hours, and liability for renovations. The recognition agreement is the trap: it is among the co-op, shareholder, and lender.

questions.q: Because a co-op interest is personal property, a co-op purchase typically involves all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A stock certificate
A proprietary lease
A UCC lien search
A deed recorded with the clerk
questions.x: No deed is recorded in a co-op sale because the buyer receives shares, not real property. The UCC lien search is the tempting pick, but it replaces the title search in co-op deals.

questions.q: A co-op shareholder wants to check whether she may install a washer in her apartment. The governing document between her and the corporation is most likely the:
c: Stock certificate
Offering plan
Recognition agreement with the bank
The proprietary lease
questions.x: The proprietary lease (with house rules adopted under it) sets the shareholder's rights and duties in the apartment. The stock certificate is the trap: it shows ownership of shares, not use rules.

questions.q: A co-op refinances its underlying mortgage at a much higher rate. The shareholders will most likely see the effect in their:
c: Personal share loan interest rates
Monthly maintenance charges
Flip tax percentages
UCC-1 filings
questions.x: Debt service on the underlying mortgage is part of maintenance, so a costlier building loan raises maintenance. The share loan answer is the trap: each shareholder's personal loan is separate.

questions.q: A buyer finances a NYC co-op apartment with an $800,000 share loan. The mortgage recording tax on that loan is:
c: $0; no mortgage is recorded
1.8% of the share loan amount
1.925% of the share loan amount
1% of the full purchase price
questions.x: A share loan is secured by personal property and perfected with a UCC-1, so no mortgage recording tax applies. 1.925% is the trap: that is the NYC rate on a real mortgage of $500,000 or more.

questions.q: Before a co-op closing, the buyer's attorney learns from a lien search that a judgment creditor has a UCC filing against the seller's shares. The likely result is:
c: The buyer takes the shares subject to it
Title insurance covers the buyer's loss
The co-op board pays the creditor
It is paid off or released at closing
questions.x: Liens on the shares are cleared at closing, usually from the seller's proceeds, which is why the lien search matters. Title insurance is the trap: co-op buyers do not receive real property title insurance.

questions.q: A typical co-op recognition agreement provides all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Notice to the lender of a default
A chance for the lender to cure
The co-op's loan guarantee
Recognition of the lender's lien
questions.x: The co-op never guarantees the shareholder's loan; it recognizes the lien and gives notice and cure rights. Recognition of the lien is the tempting pick, but it is the agreement's core purpose.

questions.q: A buyer earns $180,000 a year. Her co-op loan payment will be $2,700, maintenance $1,800, and other debt $450 a month. Her debt-to-income ratio is:
questions.x: Monthly income is $15,000 and monthly debt is $2,700 + $1,800 + $450 = $4,950, so $4,950 / $15,000 = 33%. 30% is the trap: it leaves out the other debt.

questions.q: A co-op caps financing at 70%. On a $1,600,000 purchase, the buyer's minimum cash down payment is:
questions.x: Maximum loan = $1,600,000 x 70% = $1,120,000, so the minimum down payment is $480,000. $320,000 is the trap: it is a 20% down payment, which the 70% cap does not allow.

questions.q: Priya's buyer asks why the co-op wants two years of tax returns, bank statements, and reference letters. The main reason is that:
c: The board judges finances and fit
The lender cannot see these records
Title insurers require the package
The AG audits each board package
questions.x: The board package lets the board evaluate the buyer's finances and suitability before approving the transfer of shares. The title insurance answer is the trap: co-op deals do not use title insurance.

questions.q: A Manhattan co-op board rejects a buyer without giving a reason. The buyer has no evidence of discrimination. Generally, the rejection is:
c: Void, since reasons are required
Upheld under business judgment
Void unless the AG approves it
Open to a SCAR petition
questions.x: Under the business judgment rule, courts defer to co-op board decisions made in good faith and without discrimination; reasons are generally not required. The reasons-required answer is the trap: no general statewide rule requires them.

questions.q: Years after a conversion, the sponsor still owns 12 apartments as holder of unsold shares. A tenant wants to rent one. Under a typical plan, board approval of that sublet is:
c: Required, as for any shareholder
Usually not required under the plan
Required, plus a 20% flip tax
Required by the AG for sponsors
questions.x: Holders of unsold shares typically may sell or sublet without board approval under the offering plan. The any-shareholder answer is the trap: that applies to owners of sold shares.

questions.q: In a condop, the residential portion is typically owned by:
c: A co-op owning the residential unit
Individual condo unit owners
The sponsor as holder of unsold shares
The commercial tenant under a ground lease
questions.x: In a condop the building is a condo, and the residential portion is one unit owned by a co-op corporation, while retail is a separate unit. The individual-owners answer is the trap: that is an ordinary condo.

questions.q: A co-op collects $2,000,000 from shareholders and $600,000 in store rents. Under the traditional 80/20 test, the share of income from shareholders is about:
questions.x: $2,000,000 / $2,600,000 = about 77%, below the 80% threshold. 80% is the trap: the test fails because shareholder income is under 80% of the total.

questions.q: A co-op charges a 2% flip tax on the sale price, paid by the seller. On a $1,250,000 sale, the flip tax is:
questions.x: $1,250,000 x 2% = $25,000, paid to the co-op. $12,500 is the trap: it uses 1%.

questions.q: When reviewing a co-op's financials and minutes, all of the following are red flags EXCEPT:
c: A balloon mortgage due soon
Thin reserves and deferred repairs
Rising arrears among shareholders
A new fixed-rate refinance
questions.x: A recent fixed-rate refinance usually stabilizes maintenance. Rising arrears is the tempting pick for some, but unpaid maintenance shifts costs onto other shareholders.

questions.q: A shareholder starts moving walls without signing the co-op's alteration agreement. The co-op will most likely:
c: Ignore it, since owners hold title
Record a mortgage against the unit
Ask the lender to call the loan
Halt the work until it approves plans
questions.x: Renovations require board approval under the alteration agreement, so the co-op can halt unapproved work. The holds-title answer is the trap: a co-op shareholder owns shares, not the walls.

questions.q: A condo's annual budget is $3,600,000. A unit's common interest is 0.45%. Its monthly common charges are:
questions.x: Annual share: $3,600,000 x 0.0045 = $16,200. Monthly: $16,200 / 12 = $1,350. $16,200 is the trap: it is the annual figure, not the monthly one.

questions.q: A board levies an $800,000 assessment. A unit with a 1.25% common interest pays it in 20 equal monthly installments. Each installment is:
questions.x: Share: $800,000 x 0.0125 = $10,000. Installment: $10,000 / 20 = $500. $10,000 is the trap: it is the unit's total share, not one installment.

questions.q: A Long Island City condo board objects to a buyer's line of work. Under typical New York condo documents, the board may:
c: Buy the unit itself on the same terms
Reject the buyer after an interview
Require a higher price from the buyer
Delay closing until it finds a buyer
questions.x: Condo boards generally have only a right of first refusal: match the deal or waive. Rejecting after an interview is the trap: that is a co-op board's power, because co-op buyers become shareholders and tenants of the corporation.

questions.q: A condo's right of first refusal is usually satisfied for closing when:
c: The board interviews and approves the purchaser
The purchaser agrees to the board's preferred price
The seller obtains consent from each unit owner
The board waives it or lets the period lapse
questions.x: The board gets notice and a copy of the contract; if it does not elect to buy within the period in the declaration (often 30 days), the right is waived and a waiver letter goes in the closing file. Board approval of the purchaser is the trap: condo boards do not approve buyers.

questions.q: A condo seller's unit carries an assessment payable in monthly installments. The contract is silent on it. After closing, the remaining installments will most likely be billed to:
c: The seller, who owned the unit when it was voted
The board, which pays them from reserves
The buyer, who owns the unit when they fall due
The managing agent, until the project is done
questions.x: The condo bills whoever owns the unit when each installment comes due, so a silent contract leaves later installments on the buyer. The vote-date answer is the trap: who owned the unit when the board voted does not shift the bill. Buyers' attorneys address this in the rider.

questions.q: A unit's $9,600 assessment is payable in 24 monthly installments. The seller has paid 9 when the sale closes, and the buyer negotiated a credit for the rest. The credit is:
questions.x: Installment: $9,600 / 24 = $400. Remaining: 15 x $400 = $6,000. $3,600 is the trap: it is what the seller already paid (9 x $400), not what remains.

questions.q: Under New York's Condominium Act, a lien for unpaid common charges ranks:
c: Ahead of real estate taxes and every mortgage
Ahead of the first mortgage but behind taxes
Equal with the first mortgage and with taxes
Behind taxes and the first mortgage
questions.x: RPL 339-z places the common charge lien behind real estate taxes and the unpaid balance of a first mortgage of record. Ahead of the first mortgage is the trap: some states give associations a limited super priority, but New York does not.

questions.q: A condo unit with a $400,000 first mortgage, $6,000 of unpaid real estate taxes, and $12,000 of unpaid common charges sells at foreclosure for $395,000. In general, the common charges recover:
c: $12,000 in full
Nothing from the sale
$6,000 of the arrears
A pro rata share of it
questions.x: Taxes are paid first ($6,000), then the first mortgage, which takes the remaining $389,000 and is still short. Nothing is left for the condo's lien, which ranks behind both. Full recovery is the trap: it assumes a priority the condo's lien does not have, so the board must pursue the former owner personally.

questions.q: A condo owner who itemizes may generally deduct all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Monthly common charges on the home she lives in
Mortgage interest on the unit, within federal limits
Real estate taxes billed on the unit's own tax lot
Points paid on the loan to buy the unit as a home
questions.x: Common charges on a personal residence are not deductible. The unit's taxes and mortgage interest are, within limits, and purchase points on a principal residence generally are too. Real estate taxes are the tempting wrong pick for anyone who confuses condos with co-ops, where taxes are paid inside maintenance.

questions.q: A condo owner pays a $12,000 special assessment for a new roof on the building she lives in. For federal income tax, the assessment is generally:
c: Deductible in full in the year she pays it
Deductible as a real estate tax up to the cap
Added to her cost basis as a capital item
Deductible if the condo is in NYC
questions.x: An assessment for a capital improvement is generally added to the owner's basis, reducing gain on a later sale. It is not a real estate tax, because the condo, not a government, levies it. The real estate tax answer is the trap: the label "assessment" is shared with government special assessments, but this one is a private charge.

questions.q: A condo board wants to ban dogs over 40 pounds in common areas. Which is most accurate?
c: It needs a unanimous vote of owners
It needs a new offering plan filing
It needs court approval in advance
It can adopt it as a house rule
questions.x: Boards adopt and amend reasonable house rules under the bylaws without an owner vote, as long as the rules are consistent with the declaration. Unanimous consent is the trap: even declaration amendments usually need a supermajority set in the declaration, not unanimity.

questions.q: A condo board wants to change every unit's common interest percentage to reflect a new appraisal. This most likely requires:
c: A board resolution under the house rules
An amendment to the declaration
A new rule posted in the building lobby
A letter of consent from the sponsor
questions.x: Common interests are fixed in the declaration, so changing them means amending the declaration with the owner approval it requires (and New York's Condominium Act adds protections for changes to common interests). A board resolution is the trap: boards can change house rules, not ownership percentages.

questions.q: A co-op buyer's gross income is $15,000 a month. Monthly costs: loan payment $3,100, maintenance $1,400, car loan $500. The board's limit is 30%. The buyer's ratio is:
c: About 30.0%, at the limit
About 20.7%, under the limit
About 33.3%, over the limit
About 25.3%, under the limit
questions.x: Total debt: $3,100 + $1,400 + $500 = $5,000. $5,000 / $15,000 = 33.3%, above 30%. 30.0% is the trap: it drops the car loan ($4,500 / $15,000). Boards count maintenance and all recurring debt.

questions.q: A buyer earns $10,000 a month. The loan payment would be $2,400 and maintenance $1,000, with no other debt. The board's limit is 30%. Which change gets the buyer under the limit?
c: Borrowing less, so the payment falls to $1,900
Paying the first year's maintenance in advance
Using a 40-year amortization the board ignores
Adding a parent as guarantor on the bank loan
questions.x: Current ratio: $3,400 / $10,000 = 34%. Cutting the payment to $1,900 gives $2,900 / $10,000 = 29%. Prepaying maintenance is the trap: the board measures the ongoing monthly obligation, and prepayment does not reduce it. Many boards do not accept guarantors at all.

questions.q: A board requires post-closing liquidity of 18 months of loan payments plus maintenance. The loan payment is $2,800 and maintenance $1,200. The buyer needs:
questions.x: Monthly: $2,800 + $1,200 = $4,000. 18 x $4,000 = $72,000. $96,000 is the trap: it uses 24 months, a common rule in other buildings but not this one. $50,400 counts the loan payment alone.

questions.q: A board counts retirement accounts at 50% toward post-closing liquidity. A buyer will have $20,000 cash and $120,000 in a 401(k) after closing. The liquidity the board will credit is:
questions.x: $20,000 cash plus 50% of $120,000 ($60,000) = $80,000. $140,000 is the trap: it counts the 401(k) at full value, which this board does not. $60,000 forgets the cash.

questions.q: A self-employed buyer's net income was $120,000 two years ago and $90,000 last year. A careful lender or board will most likely rely on:
c: $120,000, the higher year
$105,000, the two-year average
$210,000, the two-year total
$90,000, the lower recent year
questions.x: When income is declining, underwriters lean on the lower, recent figure because the average overstates likely earnings. The two-year average is the trap: it is the default for stable or rising self-employed income, not a falling one.

questions.q: To document a self-employed co-op buyer's income, boards commonly ask for all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Two to three years of complete tax returns
A no-income-verification loan commitment
An accountant's letter with year-to-date figures
1099 forms from the buyer's main clients
questions.x: Boards want full documentation, and many will not accept no-income-verification loans at all. Returns, an accountant's letter, and 1099s are standard. The accountant's letter is the tempting wrong pick because it is not on every checklist, but for self-employed buyers it is routinely requested.

questions.q: A co-op buyer receives $40,000 from a parent toward the down payment. The board and lender will expect:
c: A signed gift letter from the parent
A promissory note signed by the buyer
A lien on the shares in the parent's favor
Nothing, because family gifts are private
questions.x: A signed gift letter, plus a paper trail of the transfer, shows the money is not a loan that adds debt. A promissory note is the trap: it turns the gift into a liability that worsens the buyer's ratios.

questions.q: A buyer's uncle wires $60,000 for the down payment but privately expects repayment over five years. If the buyer signs a gift letter anyway, the main problem is that:
c: The board's debt-to-income ratio will be overstated
Gifts from uncles are barred under New York law
The letter misrepresents a loan as a gift
The lender has to report the gift to the IRS
questions.x: A gift letter states that no repayment is expected. Calling a loan a gift hides a monthly obligation from the lender and the board, a misrepresentation in a loan application and a board package. The ratio answer is the trap: the ratio would be understated, not overstated, which is exactly why the hidden loan matters.

questions.q: In a converted co-op, which shareholder can typically sublet without board approval?
c: A shareholder who has lived there five years
Any shareholder who pays a sublet fee
A holder of unsold shares under the plan
A board member who discloses the tenant
questions.x: Offering plans usually let the sponsor, or a holder of unsold shares, sell or rent those apartments without board approval. Paying a sublet fee is the trap: fees attach to approved sublets of sold shares, and they do not replace approval.

questions.q: An investor buys a block of 15 unsold apartments from a co-op's sponsor. Whether the investor may rent them without board approval depends mainly on:
c: Whether the offering plan grants that status
A vote of the shareholders at the next annual meeting
The NYC Rent Guidelines Board's annual vote on increases
Whether the investor lives in one of the 15 apartments
questions.x: Holder of unsold shares rights come from the offering plan; a buyer of a block of sponsor shares gets them only if the plan extends that status to such buyers. A shareholder vote is the trap: the plan's terms, not a later vote, control those rights.

questions.q: In a co-op purchase with a share loan, the recognition agreement is signed by:
c: The buyer, the seller, and the broker
The lender, the co-op, and the buyer
The co-op, the sponsor, and the city
The lender, the title insurer, and the seller
questions.x: The recognition agreement is a three-party agreement: the co-op recognizes the lender's lien on the shares and lease and agrees to notify it of defaults. The title insurer is the trap: co-op purchases use a lien search, not title insurance.

questions.q: A co-op shareholder stops paying maintenance. Because of the recognition agreement, the shareholder's lender is entitled to:
c: Take priority over the co-op's maintenance lien
Cancel the proprietary lease on its own
A refund of maintenance paid by the borrower
Notice of the default and a chance to cure it
questions.x: The co-op agrees to notify the lender of the default and give it a chance to cure before cancelling the lease. In return the lender accepts that the co-op's lien for unpaid maintenance comes first. Priority over the co-op is the trap: it is the reverse of the deal.

questions.q: A co-op's flip tax is 1.5% of the gross sale price. An apartment sells for $980,000. The flip tax is:
questions.x: $980,000 x 0.015 = $14,700. $9,800 is the trap: it uses 1%. $1,470 misplaces the decimal.

questions.q: A co-op charges a flip tax of 20% of the seller's profit. A shareholder bought for $640,000 and sells for $820,000. The flip tax is:
questions.x: Profit: $820,000 minus $640,000 = $180,000. 20% x $180,000 = $36,000. $164,000 is the trap: it applies 20% to the full sale price instead of the profit.

questions.q: For a New York co-op's flip tax to be valid, it generally must be:
c: Approved by the Attorney General
Authorized in the lease or bylaws
Paid by the buyer in every transfer
Filed with the county clerk annually
questions.x: The Business Corporation Law permits transfer fees when the proprietary lease, bylaws, or offering plan (or a proper amendment) authorizes them. Attorney General approval is the trap: the AG reviews offering plans and amendments for disclosure, not a building's internal fee.

questions.q: A co-op board votes, by itself, to start charging a 3% flip tax that appears nowhere in the proprietary lease or bylaws. A seller challenges it. The most likely result:
c: The fee stands under the business judgment rule
The fee stands if the buyer agrees to pay it
The fee is valid for sales above $1 million
The fee is invalid without proper authorization
questions.x: A flip tax needs authorization in the governing documents, usually added by a shareholder-approved amendment. The business judgment answer is the trap: deference applies to decisions within the board's authority, and adopting an unauthorized fee is outside it.

questions.q: A co-op receives $2,400,000 in maintenance and $500,000 in garage and store rent. What share of its gross income comes from outside sources?
c: About 17.2%
About 20.8%
About 82.8%
About 25.0%
questions.x: $500,000 / $2,900,000 = 17.2%, so 82.8% comes from shareholders and the co-op passes the gross income test. 20.8% is the trap: it divides by maintenance alone ($500,000 / $2,400,000) instead of total income.

questions.q: A co-op's commercial rent is now 24% of its gross income. Its stores occupy 7% of the square footage. Under Section 216 as amended in 2007, the co-op:
c: Has lost its status, since it fails the gross income test
Has to convert to a condop by year end
Can still qualify under the square footage test
Can qualify if shareholders vote to keep status
questions.x: A co-op qualifies under any of three tests: 80% of income from shareholders, 80% of square footage used by shareholders as residences, or 90% of expenditures for shareholders. With stores at 7% of the space, the square footage test is met. Losing status is the trap: that was the result before 2007.

questions.q: A condop structure is most often created in order to:
c: Give apartment buyers deeds rather than shares
Exempt the building from the Martin Act
Let the sponsor avoid real estate taxes
Keep store rent out of the co-op's income
questions.x: Putting stores or a garage into separate condo units keeps their rent from counting as co-op income, protecting the 80/20 test and shareholders' deductions. Giving buyers deeds is the trap: in a condop the residential buyers still receive shares and proprietary leases.

questions.q: All of the following are typically true of a condop EXCEPT:
c: The commercial space is a separate condominium unit
Buyers of apartments receive deeds
Residents buy shares and sign proprietary leases
Store rent is paid to the commercial unit's owner
questions.x: In a condop the residential portion is one condo unit owned by a co-op corporation, so residents still buy shares and get proprietary leases. The store-rent statement is the tempting wrong pick, but it is true: that is the point of the structure.

questions.q: A leak from the building's steam riser inside a shareholder's bedroom wall damages the floor below. Under a typical proprietary lease, the repair of the riser is the responsibility of:
c: The shareholder whose wall contains it
The shareholder below, who was damaged
The co-op, as a building-wide system
The managing agent, personally
questions.x: Risers, main lines, and other building systems are the co-op's responsibility even where they pass through an apartment. The shareholder whose wall contains it is the trap: location inside the apartment does not make a building system the shareholder's.

questions.q: Under a typical proprietary lease, the shareholder is responsible for all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Repairs to the building's roof and facade
The apartment's own appliances and fixtures
Damage caused by a washer the rules prohibit
Painting and decorating inside the apartment
questions.x: The roof and facade are structure, which the co-op repairs. Shareholders maintain the interior, fixtures, and appliances, and they answer for damage caused by their own breach, such as a prohibited washer. That washer choice is the tempting wrong pick because water damage feels like a building problem.

questions.q: A co-op terminates a shareholder's proprietary lease for objectionable conduct after a shareholder vote that followed the lease's procedures. In court, the co-op's decision will most likely be reviewed under:
c: A de novo trial on whether the conduct occurred
A standard requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt
A rule that conduct cannot end a proprietary lease
The business judgment rule
questions.x: The Court of Appeals applied the business judgment rule to this situation in 40 West 67th Street v. Pullman (2003). A de novo trial is the trap: it was the standard the shareholder sought and the court rejected, as long as the co-op acted within its authority and in good faith.

questions.q: Under the business judgment rule, a New York court generally will NOT second-guess a co-op board decision that was:
c: Made by a majority of the board after any vote of the members
Made in good faith, within its authority, for a corporate purpose
Made by a board whose members hold the most shares in the building
Made with the managing agent's written recommendation attached
questions.x: Deference applies when the board acts within its authority, in good faith, and to further a legitimate corporate purpose. A mere majority vote is the trap: a vote alone does not earn deference if the decision is outside the board's authority or made in bad faith.

questions.q: A sponsor's CPS-1 application has been accepted. A prospect offers a refundable $10,000 deposit to hold a specific unit. The sponsor may:
c: Accept it if held in escrow
Accept it as a reservation fee
Accept it with a letter of intent
Record the prospect's interest
questions.x: During CPS-1 testing a sponsor may advertise and gather non-binding interest, but may not accept deposits or reservations of any kind. Accepting it in escrow is the trap: escrow handling applies to deposits taken after a plan is accepted for filing.

questions.q: During the CPS-1 phase, a sponsor may do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Advertise the project with the AG's legend
Accept non-binding reservations of units
Collect names of interested buyers
Describe the planned building and amenities
questions.x: The Attorney General's CPS-1 policy bars reservations, binding or non-binding, and deposits during market testing. Advertising with the required legend and gathering interest are what CPS-1 permits. Advertising is the tempting wrong pick, but it is the main point of CPS-1.

questions.q: A sponsor proposes a non-eviction co-op conversion of a 50-unit NYC building. Under current law, before the plan can be declared effective it needs purchase agreements from tenants in occupancy covering at least:
c: 26 units
25 units
8 units
34 units
questions.x: 51% of 50 = 25.5, so at least 26 units are required. 25 is the trap: it is only 50%. 8 units reflects the old 15% threshold, which the HSTPA eliminated in 2019.

questions.q: A sponsor of a 40-unit NYC conversion has contracts from 14 tenants in occupancy and 10 outside buyers for vacant units. Can the non-eviction plan be declared effective?
c: Yes, because 24 of 40 units are under contract
Yes, because 15% of units are under contract
No, since outside buyers do not count
No, because conversions now require 100% consent
questions.x: Since 2019, the 51% requirement counts purchase agreements by tenants in occupancy; bona fide outside purchasers no longer count. 14 of 40 is 35%. The 24-of-40 answer is the trap: adding outside buyers was allowed under the old rules, not the current ones.

questions.q: In a current NYC co-op conversion, a rent-stabilized tenant who chooses not to buy:
c: Is evicted when the plan becomes effective
Must vacate within 90 days of acceptance
Remains a rent-stabilized tenant
Becomes a market-rate tenant at once
questions.x: Under a non-eviction plan, no tenant can be evicted for not buying, and rent-stabilized non-purchasers keep their protections as tenants of the sponsor or later owner of the unit. The 90-day answer is the trap: 90 days is the tenants' exclusive period to buy, not a deadline to leave.

questions.q: A market-rate tenant does not buy during a NYC non-eviction conversion. Two years later the unit's owner wants her out because she never bought. The owner:
c: May not evict her for failing to purchase her unit
May evict her because her unit is now a co-op apartment
May evict her after a 30-day notice of non-renewal
May evict her after offering the insider price again
questions.x: Non-purchasing tenants in a non-eviction plan cannot be evicted for failing to buy; market-rate non-purchasers are also protected from unconscionable rent increases. They can still be removed for cause, such as nonpayment. The non-renewal answer is the trap: ordinary non-renewal rules do not override conversion protections.

questions.q: A Crown Heights co-op offering plan has just been accepted for filing by the Attorney General. This tells a buyer that:
c: The AG found the price fair
The building passed inspection
The sponsor's financing is approved
The disclosures meet the rules
questions.x: The AG reviews plans for full disclosure, not merit. Acceptance for filing says nothing about price, quality, or the sponsor's financial strength. The fair-price answer is the trap: marketing that implies AG approval of the deal is a misrepresentation.

questions.q: A sponsor's ad says: "Attorney General Approved Luxury Co-ops." The plan was accepted for filing last week. The ad is:
c: Accurate, because acceptance is the AG's approval
Misleading, since acceptance is not approval
Accurate if the AG's required legend also appears
Misleading only if the prices later change
questions.x: Acceptance for filing means the disclosures satisfy the regulations; it is not an endorsement. Advertising it as approval misstates the offering. Adding the legend is the trap: a correct legend does not cure a misleading headline.

questions.q: After contracts are signed, a sponsor files an amendment raising projected maintenance by 18%. Purchasers who signed earlier are most likely entitled to:
c: A rescission offer and return of their deposits
Nothing, since contracts bind them to amendments
A maintenance freeze until the first closing
Payment of the difference by the AG's office
questions.x: A material adverse change disclosed by amendment requires that existing purchasers be offered rescission within the period stated in the amendment. Being bound regardless is the trap: it ignores the rescission right that protects buyers who signed on the old disclosures.

questions.q: Which amendment is most likely to trigger a right of rescission for existing purchasers?
c: A price increase on unsold apartments
A change to the sponsor's sales office hours
A first-year budget rising by about 20%
A correction of a typo in the house rules
questions.x: A significant increase in the budget, and so in maintenance, is a material adverse change for people already under contract. A price increase on unsold units is the trap: it affects future buyers, while existing contracts keep their prices.

questions.q: Deposits taken under an accepted offering plan must be:
c: Released to the sponsor after 30 days
Held in escrow until closing or refund
Used first for the building's reserve fund
Paid to the selling broker as commission
questions.x: General Business Law 352-h requires deposits in Martin Act offerings to be held in escrow, as trust funds, until closing or until returned to the purchaser. Release after 30 days is the trap: nothing in the rules lets the sponsor reach the money before closing.

questions.q: A sponsor running short of cash asks its attorney, the escrow agent, to release purchasers' deposits to pay a contractor, promising to repay them before closing. The attorney should:
c: Release them if repayment is in writing
Release half and keep the rest in escrow
Release them if the AG is told afterward
Refuse, since deposits stay in escrow
questions.x: Deposits are trust funds held under GBL 352-h until closing or refund; an escrow agent may not lend them to the sponsor. Releasing with a written promise is the trap: a promise to repay does not make a misuse of trust funds lawful.

questions.q: A co-op shareholder in Forest Hills dies. Her will names her son as executor, but probate has not finished. Who may sign a listing agreement to sell her shares?
c: The son, once the court issues letters testamentary
The son today, because the will names him as executor
Any heir named in the will, acting alone for the estate
The co-op board, which controls shares of deceased owners
questions.x: An executor gets authority to act for the estate when the Surrogate's Court issues letters testamentary. Being named in the will is the tempting answer, but the will alone does not give power to sign. Heirs do not control estate property during administration, and the board approves buyers but does not own or sell the shares.
questions.concept: Executor authority to sell co-op shares

questions.q: Before a licensee lists co-op shares owned by an estate, the document that best confirms the executor's authority is:
c: The deceased owner's stock certificate
The will naming the executor
Letters testamentary from the court
A letter from the co-op's managing agent
questions.x: Letters testamentary are the court's appointment of the executor and prove the authority to sign for the estate. The will is the tempting choice, but it only nominates the executor until the court acts. The stock certificate shows what the estate owns, not who may sell it.
questions.concept: Executor authority to sell co-op shares

questions.q: A co-op shareholder in a 60-unit building claims RPL 226-b gives him the right to sublet with consent not unreasonably withheld. Which is accurate?
c: He is right, because the building has four or more units
He is right, but not until after two years of residence
He is wrong; 226-b excludes proprietary leases
He is wrong; 226-b covers rent-stabilized units
questions.x: RPL 226-b gives tenants in buildings of four or more units a sublet right, but it expressly excludes proprietary leases held by co-op shareholders. Co-op sublets are governed by the proprietary lease and board policy. The four-unit choice is tempting because it states the statute's coverage for ordinary rentals.

questions.q: A Jackson Heights co-op's policy allows sublets for 2 years in any 5, with board approval. A shareholder wants a third year. What controls the answer?
c: The proprietary lease and the board's sublet policy
RPL 226-b, which requires consent not unreasonably withheld
The Rent Guidelines Board's annual sublet order
The state's roommate law, RPL 235-f, for the unit
questions.x: Co-op sublets are a matter of contract: the proprietary lease and the policy the board adopts under it. RPL 226-b, the tempting choice, expressly excludes proprietary leases. The Rent Guidelines Board sets increases for stabilized rentals, and the roommate law addresses occupants, not sublets.

questions.q: An estate lists an empty Manhattan co-op apartment for three-night stays on a booking site. Under New York City law this is:
c: Legal if the estate registers with the city first
Illegal, since no permanent resident is present
Legal, because estates are exempt from house rules
Illegal if the board has posted a notice
questions.x: In a building with three or more units, renting for fewer than 30 days is illegal unless a permanent resident is present, and an empty apartment has none. Registration under Local Law 18 is the tempting answer, but it is available to hosts who live in the unit and does not legalize a whole-unit short stay. The co-op's own rules are a separate bar.

questions.q: Under NYC's Local Law 18, hosts offering stays of fewer than 30 days must:
c: Get approval from the Rent Guidelines Board
File a certificate with the Department of State
Record a notice with the city register
Register with the city's enforcement office
questions.x: Local Law 18 requires short-term rental hosts to register with the Mayor's Office of Special Enforcement, and booking platforms may not process stays in unregistered units. Stays of 30 days or more are outside the registration rule. Recording with the city register is tempting because it sounds official, but it concerns real property documents, not rentals.

questions.q: A proprietary lease says consent to a transfer to a deceased shareholder's family member shall not be unreasonably withheld. The board refuses a qualified son. A court will most likely review the refusal under:
c: The business judgment rule
No review, as boards have full discretion
Strict scrutiny of the board's motives
A heightened reasonableness standard
questions.x: When the lease limits the board's discretion with a not-unreasonably-withheld clause for family transfers, New York courts apply a heightened reasonableness standard instead of business judgment deference, as in Estate of Del Terzo v. 33 Fifth Avenue Owners Corp. Business judgment is the tempting default for co-op decisions, but the lease's words displace it.

questions.q: A co-op board usually gets business judgment deference on admissions. When does that deference give way to a stricter reasonableness review?
c: When the buyer is paying cash for the shares
When the board fails to give the buyer a written reason
When the lease itself limits the board's discretion
When the apartment is sold by an estate to anyone
questions.x: Business judgment deference applies to ordinary admissions decisions, and boards generally need not give reasons. When the proprietary lease itself limits refusal, for example consent to a family transfer on death not to be unreasonably withheld, courts review reasonableness more closely. An estate sale to an outside buyer is the tempting choice, but it gets no special review.

questions.q: A co-op lien search shows a UCC-1 filed against the seller's shares in 2006 for a share loan she paid off in 2015. Before closing, the seller's attorney should obtain:
c: A UCC-3 termination from the lender
A title insurance policy insuring over the filing
A satisfaction of mortgage recorded with the county
A payoff of the original loan amount at closing
questions.x: A UCC-1 perfects a lien on co-op shares, and a paid lender should file a UCC-3 termination. When it did not, the seller's attorney gets one, or a satisfaction letter, so the buyer's lender takes first position. A satisfaction of mortgage is the tempting answer, but co-op share loans are not recorded mortgages, and there is no title insurance on shares.

questions.q: In a co-op sale, a lender's lien on the seller's shares is released of record by:
c: A satisfaction of mortgage
A UCC-3 termination
A release of lis pendens
A bargain and sale deed
questions.x: Share loans are perfected with UCC-1 financing statements and released with UCC-3 terminations. A satisfaction of mortgage is the tempting answer because it releases a recorded mortgage on real property, which a co-op share loan is not. Co-op shares never pass by deed.

questions.q: A Queens co-op sells for $480,000. The seller pays a 5% commission, a 2% flip tax, the NYS transfer tax and the NYC RPTT, and owes $3,000 in maintenance arrears. What does the seller net?
questions.x: Commission $24,000, flip tax $9,600, NYS 0.4% $1,920, NYC RPTT 1% (residential, $500,000 or less) $4,800, arrears $3,000. Total $43,320, net $436,680. $434,640 uses the 1.425% RPTT rate, which applies only above $500,000. $439,680 forgets the arrears, which the co-op collects first at closing, and $446,280 forgets the flip tax.

questions.q: A Manhattan co-op sells for $650,000. How much NYC Real Property Transfer Tax does the seller pay?
questions.x: Residential sales, co-ops included, pay 1.425% when the price is over $500,000, applied to the whole price: $650,000 x 1.425% = $9,262.50. $6,500 uses the 1% rate for $500,000 or less. $2,600 is the NYS transfer tax at 0.4%, and $17,062.50 uses the 2.625% commercial rate.

cram.html: Condo = real property: deed, own tax bill, mortgage, title insurance, common charges.
Co-op = personal property: shares + proprietary lease, maintenance, share loan, lien search.
Declaration creates the condo (recorded). Bylaws run it. House rules handle daily life.
Condo = board of managers, right of first refusal only. Co-op = board of directors, can reject for any non-discriminatory reason.
Common charges = budget x common interest %. Taxes are NOT in common charges; co-op maintenance includes taxes and the underlying mortgage.
Sponsor appoints the first board and managing agent; owner control generally within 5 years of the first closing.
Martin Act (GBL 352-e): offering plan filed with the Attorney General. Accepted = full disclosure, not approval.
CPS-1: advertise and gauge interest for 12 months. No deposits, no reservations, binding or non-binding.
Red herring = preliminary plan, information only, no contracts or deposits.
Letter of intent: non-binding as to purchaser and price.
Price amendments hit unsold units only; signed contracts keep their price.
No TCO or CO, no closing, no mortgage.
Mortgage recording tax applies to condos, not co-ops (share loan is not a mortgage).
Mansion tax (buyer): 1% at $1M+, NYC graduated up to 3.9%. Applies to condos and co-ops.
NYC new development: buyer customarily pays the sponsor's NYC RPTT and NYS transfer tax, plus working capital (often 1 to 2 months of common charges).
Flip tax = co-op transfer fee, usually seller. Flipping = quick resale. Not the same thing.
Share loan perfected by UCC-1. Recognition agreement: lender + co-op + shareholder.
Board package: application, signed contract, verified financial statement, references, employment letter, tax returns (2 to 3 years), credit authorization, disclosures.
Boards often want DTI around 25% to 30%, financing caps like 75% to 80%, and 1 to 2 years post-closing liquidity.
Holder of unsold shares can sell and sublet without board approval.
80/20 rule (IRC 216): at least 80% of co-op gross income from shareholders. Condop splits off commercial space.

subjects.title: Commercial and Investment Properties
subjects.blurb: Ten hours of the course and a steady stream of exam math: NOI, cap rates, value, cash on cash, loss factors, percentage rent and escalations. Learn the formulas once, cleanly, and these become the easiest points on the test.

lessons.title: Why People Buy Buildings: Risk, Liquidity, Leverage and the Time Value of Money
lessons.tagline: Every investment trades off risk, liquidity and return. Real estate adds a superpower and a trap: borrowed money.
objectives: Explain risk, liquidity and rate of return as they apply to real estate
Compute an all-cash return and a leveraged return and say whether leverage is positive or negative
Explain the time value of money and discount a future dollar to today
Describe how depreciation makes real estate a tax shelter

blocks.title: A coffee on Wyckoff Avenue
blocks.html: Evelyn Park has $1,000,000 sitting in a money market account earning 4%. A broker pitches her a $1,000,000 two-family-over-store in Ridgewood that nets $60,000 a year. Her nephew says, "Why buy one building with cash? Put down $250,000 and buy four." Evelyn smiles and asks one question: "What does the bank charge?" Why is that the only question that matters?
blocks.casual: So Evelyn Park has a million bucks parked in a money market at 4%. A broker shows her a $1,000,000 two-family-over-store in Ridgewood that nets $60,000 a year. Her nephew jumps in: "Why pay cash for one? Put $250,000 down on four!" Evelyn just smiles and asks, "What does the bank charge?" Hold that thought. By the end of this lesson you'll know why that's the only question that matters.

deeper.plain: Borrowing to buy a building only helps if the building earns more than the loan costs.
deeper.picture: Think of hiring a helper for your food truck. If the helper brings in $30 an hour and costs $20, hire four. If they bring in $20 and cost $30, every new hire makes you poorer.
deeper.street: If Evelyn's bank quotes a 5% loan constant, the 6% Ridgewood building pays for its own loan with room to spare and her nephew has a point. If the bank quotes 8%, the building can't even cover the payment and four of them means four times the pain.
deeper.stakes: Investors who stack buildings on expensive debt get wiped out when rents dip, and the broker who pushed the deal loses the client for life. Knowing this lets you talk to investors like Evelyn in their language.
deeper.exam: Stems that mention a loan rate or constant next to a property return are setting up a leverage question. Compare the two numbers first; everything else follows.

blocks.text: The three things every investor weighs

blocks.html: An investment is money you give up today in the hope of getting more back later. Every investment, from a savings bond to a Manhattan office tower, is judged on the same three things: how much it returns, how risky that return is, and how quickly you can turn it back into cash.
blocks.casual: Here's the whole game in one line: you give up money today hoping to get more back later. Doesn't matter if it's a savings bond or a Manhattan office tower, every investor sizes it up the same three ways: how much it returns, how risky that return is, and how fast you can turn it back into cash.

deeper.plain: Every investment gets graded on payoff, danger and how quickly you can cash out.
deeper.picture: It's like choosing a job. Pay matters, but so does whether the company might fold, and whether you can quit next week or are locked in for years.
deeper.street: Leo has $200,000. A Treasury pays him 4% and he can sell tomorrow. A Bushwick mixed-use building might pay 7%, but selling takes four months and a bad tenant could zero out a year. He has to weigh all three, not just the 7%.
deeper.stakes: A broker who sells an investor only on the return, ignoring risk and liquidity, sets the client up to need cash they can't get. That ends in a fire sale, a furious client and maybe a complaint.
deeper.exam: When a question asks what investors weigh, the answer set is return, risk and liquidity. Watch for a distractor like "location" or "appreciation" that sounds right but isn't the framework.

blocks.html: Risk is the chance that the actual return differs from the expected return, including the chance you lose money. Real estate risk comes from vacancy, tenants who stop paying, rising taxes and expenses, interest rate changes, new competing buildings, zoning or rent law changes, and plain bad luck like a burst riser. The basic rule: the higher the risk, the higher the return an investor demands. Nobody takes a vacant warehouse in a weak market for the same return as a fully leased pharmacy with a 20-year lease.
blocks.casual: Risk just means the return you actually get might not match the one you expected, and yes, that includes losing money. In real estate it shows up as vacancy, tenants who stop paying, taxes and expenses that climb, interest rates moving, a shiny new building opening down the block, zoning or rent law changes, or dumb luck like a burst riser. The rule never changes: more risk, and the investor wants more return. Nobody takes a vacant warehouse in a weak market at the same return as a fully leased pharmacy with a 20-year lease.

deeper.plain: The shakier the income, the more an investor needs to be paid to take it on.
deeper.picture: Lending $100 to your reliable sister versus a cousin who still owes you from 2019. You'd want a lot more back from the cousin to make it worth it.
deeper.street: Sal's Astoria six-unit has long-term tenants and a new boiler. A similar building in Hunts Point has three vacancies and a Local Law 11 facade notice. Buyers will pay a lower price, which means a higher return, for the riskier one.
deeper.stakes: Price a risky building like a safe one and your buyer overpays and can't cover the mortgage when a tenant walks. Price a safe one like a risky one and your seller leaves money on the table.
deeper.exam: The exam pairs higher risk with higher required return. If an answer says a riskier property should trade at a lower return, it's wrong.

blocks.html: Liquidity is how fast an asset can be turned into cash without losing value. Stock sells in seconds. A building takes months: listing, due diligence, financing, attorney review, closing. Real estate is illiquid, and investors expect to be paid extra for that.
blocks.casual: Liquidity is how fast you can turn something into cash without taking a haircut. Stock? Seconds. A building? Months: listing, due diligence, financing, attorney review, closing. So real estate is illiquid, and investors want extra return for putting up with that.

deeper.plain: Liquidity is how quickly you can sell for full price. Buildings are slow.
deeper.picture: Cash in your wallet versus a couch you're selling on Marketplace. You'll get money for the couch, but not today and maybe not your asking price.
deeper.street: Marcus's client needed $400,000 fast for a business emergency. His Crown Heights four-family was worth $1.6 million, but with buyer financing and a 60-day closing, the only quick offer was $1.35 million cash. Illiquidity cost him $250,000.
deeper.stakes: Investors who put every dollar into property and keep no reserves can be forced to sell cheap. Good brokers ask about the client's cash needs before recommending a purchase.
deeper.exam: Liquidity is about speed of conversion to cash without loss of value. Don't confuse it with profitability or with leverage.

items: Market risk: rents and values in the area fall (a new tower opens next door, a major employer leaves).
Tenant (credit) risk: a tenant stops paying or goes bankrupt.
Interest rate risk: rates rise, refinancing costs more, and buyers pay less.
Regulatory risk: zoning, rent law or tax changes (New York's 2019 rent law changed the value of every stabilized building overnight).
Physical risk: fire, flood, a failing facade or boiler.
Liquidity risk: you need cash fast and cannot sell quickly at full price.
blocks.casual:
Here are the ways a building can bite you:
Market risk: rents and values in the area drop (a new tower opens next door, a big employer leaves).
Tenant (credit) risk: a tenant stops paying or goes bankrupt.
Interest rate risk: rates climb, refinancing costs more, buyers pay less.
Regulatory risk: zoning, rent law or tax changes (New York's 2019 rent law changed the value of every stabilized building overnight).
Physical risk: fire, flood, a failing facade or boiler.
Liquidity risk: you need cash fast and can't sell quickly at full price.

deeper.plain: Risk comes from the neighborhood, the tenants, the bank, the government, the building itself, and your own need for cash.
deeper.picture: Owning a building is like owning a restaurant: the street can change, customers can stiff you, your supplier can raise prices, the health code can change and the walk-in freezer can die.
deeper.street: Kim's friend bought a 20-unit stabilized building in Washington Heights in 2018, planning to renovate and raise rents. In June 2019 the HSTPA ended vacancy decontrol and big vacancy bonuses. Her business plan died and the building's value dropped with it. That was regulatory risk.
deeper.stakes: If you don't flag regulatory and physical risk to a buyer, they can blame you when a facade order or rent law change wrecks the numbers. Spotting each kind early protects your client and your reputation.
deeper.exam: Expect a fact pattern and a question asking which type of risk it is. Rent law or zoning change is regulatory; a tenant bankruptcy is credit; rising rates is interest rate risk.

head: Investment
Typical risk
Liquidity
Management needed
blocks.caption: Real estate sits in the low-liquidity, management-heavy corner.

deeper.plain: Real estate pays more than a bank account partly because it's harder to sell and takes more work to run.
deeper.picture: A savings account is a vending machine: put money in, get money out, no effort. A walk-up building is a garden: it can feed you well, but you're weeding every weekend.
deeper.street: Evelyn owns both a net-leased CVS in Staten Island and a 12-unit walk-up in Sunset Park. The CVS check shows up every month with almost no calls. The walk-up throws off more cash but means boiler calls, HPD violations and turnover painting.
deeper.stakes: Selling a hands-off investor a management-heavy building makes for a miserable client. Match the property to how much time and stress the buyer can handle.
deeper.exam: Questions describe real estate as illiquid and management-intensive compared with stocks and bonds. Raw land is the classic high-risk, no-income, low-liquidity answer.

blocks.q: Which statement about real estate as an investment is most accurate?
c: It is highly liquid because buyers always exist
It is relatively illiquid, so investors usually demand a higher return
It carries no risk because land cannot be destroyed
It needs no management once purchased
blocks.x: Selling a building takes months, so real estate is illiquid, and investors want extra return for that. Land is permanent, but the investment still carries vacancy, market and expense risk.

blocks.html: A rate of return is the gain on an investment expressed as a percentage of what you put in. The simplest version: annual income divided by the amount invested. A building bought for $1,000,000 cash that nets $60,000 a year returns 6%. Later lessons give this number specific names: cap rate (return on the whole property) and cash on cash (return on the investor's own cash).
blocks.casual: A rate of return is just your gain shown as a percent of what you put in. Simplest version: annual income divided by the amount invested. Pay $1,000,000 cash for a building that nets $60,000 a year and you're earning 6%. Later on this number gets fancier names: cap rate (return on the whole property) and cash on cash (return on the investor's own cash).

deeper.plain: Return is what you earn each year divided by what you put in.
deeper.picture: Same math as a lemonade stand: spend $100 on supplies and stand, make $10 a week profit, and you're earning 10% a week on what you spent.
deeper.street: Priya's client paid $800,000 cash for a Flatbush storefront netting $48,000. That's 6%. If he'd put that $800,000 in a 4% CD he'd get $32,000. The extra $16,000 a year is his pay for risk and hassle.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up gross rent with net income inflates the return and leads clients to overpay. Always divide net income, not total rent, by the price.
deeper.exam: Basic formula: return = income / investment. The exam may hand you the return and the income and ask for the investment, so be ready to rearrange.

blocks.html: Investors also talk about return on investment (getting paid on your money) versus return of investment (getting your money back). Rent pays the first; a sale at or above the purchase price delivers the second.
blocks.casual: You'll hear investors split two ideas: return on investment means getting paid for the use of your money, and return of investment means getting your original money back. Rent covers the first. Selling at or above what you paid covers the second.

deeper.plain: "On" is the profit. "Of" is getting your starting money back.
deeper.picture: Lend a friend $1,000 and they pay you $50 a year for the favor: that's return on. When they finally hand back the $1,000: that's return of.
deeper.street: The Okafors bought their Bed-Stuy brownstone decades ago. Rent from the garden unit was their return on investment for years. Selling now for far more than they paid gives them their return of investment, plus a big gain on top.
deeper.stakes: A building with great rent that loses value can still be a bad deal, because you don't get your money back at the end. Clients need to see both halves.
deeper.exam: Watch the one-letter difference. "Return of" is recapturing capital; "return on" is the yield. Swapping them is a classic distractor.

blocks.html: Leverage means using borrowed money to buy an asset. The bigger the loan compared with your own cash, the more leverage you have. Leverage magnifies results in both directions. When the building does well, your smaller slice of cash earns a bigger percentage. When it does badly, your losses are magnified too.
blocks.casual: Leverage is buying with borrowed money. The bigger the loan compared with your own cash, the more leveraged you are. And leverage is an amplifier, both ways. When the building does well, your smaller pile of cash earns a bigger percentage. When it does badly, your losses get amplified too.

deeper.plain: Leverage means using a loan so your own money controls a bigger asset.
deeper.picture: It's a crowbar. A small push on your end moves a heavy rock, but if the rock slips, the bar swings back hard.
deeper.street: Jordan's cousin puts $300,000 down on a $1.2 million Astoria three-family. Values jump 10% and his $300,000 just made $120,000. If values drop 25%, his entire down payment is gone and he still owes the bank $900,000.
deeper.stakes: Over-leveraged owners lose buildings in downturns. A broker who cheerleads maximum leverage without explaining the downside can end up named in a lawsuit when the bank forecloses.
deeper.exam: Leverage magnifies both gains and losses. An answer that says leverage only increases returns, or reduces risk, is wrong.

blocks.html: Whether borrowing helps or hurts depends on one comparison: what the property earns (its free-and-clear return) versus what the loan costs each year. The cost of a loan is measured by its mortgage constant: annual debt service (principal plus interest) divided by the loan amount.
blocks.casual: Does borrowing help or hurt? It comes down to one comparison: what the property earns (its free-and-clear, all-cash return) versus what the loan costs each year. You measure the loan's cost with the mortgage constant: annual debt service (principal plus interest) divided by the loan amount.

deeper.plain: Compare the building's return to the loan's yearly cost, principal and interest together.
deeper.picture: Borrowing to buy a taxi medallion only works if the fares beat the loan payment. The payment includes paying the loan down, not just the interest.
deeper.street: Tasha quotes Evelyn a $750,000 loan at $45,000 a year in payments. That's a 6% constant ($45,000 / $750,000). The building earns 6%, so borrowing neither helps nor hurts. Evelyn tells Tasha to come back with something cheaper.
deeper.stakes: Comparing the property return to just the interest rate understates the real loan cost, so a deal looks like positive leverage when it isn't. Clients end up short on cash every month.
deeper.exam: Mortgage constant = annual debt service / loan amount, and it includes principal. A distractor will use the interest rate alone or divide by the price instead of the loan.

blocks.title: Evelyn's Ridgewood building, three ways
blocks.html:
Price $1,000,000. Net operating income $60,000.

All cash: $60,000 / $1,000,000 = 6%.

75% loan at a 5% mortgage constant: loan $750,000, debt service $750,000 x 0.05 = $37,500. Cash left over $60,000 minus $37,500 = $22,500. Evelyn's cash invested is $250,000. Return $22,500 / $250,000 = 9%. Borrowing raised her return: positive leverage.

75% loan at an 8% mortgage constant: debt service $750,000 x 0.08 = $60,000. Cash left over $60,000 minus $60,000 = $0. Return on her $250,000 = 0%. Borrowing wiped out her return: negative leverage.
blocks.casual:
Same Ridgewood building, $1,000,000 price, $60,000 NOI. Run it three ways.
All cash: $60,000 / $1,000,000 = 6%.
75% loan at a 5% constant: loan is $750,000, payments are $750,000 x 0.05 = $37,500. What's left: $60,000 minus $37,500 = $22,500. Evelyn put in $250,000, so $22,500 / $250,000 = 9%. Borrowing juiced her return. That's positive leverage.
75% loan at an 8% constant: payments are $750,000 x 0.08 = $60,000. Left over: $60,000 minus $60,000 = $0. Return on her $250,000 = 0%. Borrowing killed her return. That's negative leverage.

deeper.plain: Cheap debt turned 6% into 9%. Expensive debt turned 6% into nothing.
deeper.picture: Same car, two gas prices. At cheap gas, driving for Uber pays well. At expensive gas, you drive all day and break even.
deeper.street: This is exactly Evelyn's question to her nephew. With 2021 money at 5%, four leveraged Ridgewood buildings would each pay 9%. With 2024 money at 8%, four buildings pay nothing while carrying four times the risk.
deeper.stakes: Brokers who show investors an all-cash return without running the financed numbers set them up to buy a building that can't cover its mortgage. One bad vacancy and the client is feeding the building out of pocket.
deeper.exam: Expect this exact math. Find debt service (loan x constant), subtract from NOI, divide by the down payment. If the constant is above the cap rate, the answer is negative leverage.

left.title: Positive leverage
items: Property return is higher than the cost of the loan
Each borrowed dollar earns more than it costs
Return on the investor's cash goes UP

right.title: Negative leverage
items: Cost of the loan is higher than the property return
Each borrowed dollar costs more than it earns
Return on the investor's cash goes DOWN

deeper.plain: If the loan costs less than the building earns, borrowing helps you. If it costs more, borrowing hurts.
deeper.picture: Positive leverage is a moving walkway carrying you forward. Negative leverage is the same walkway running backward: you walk the same, but end up behind.
deeper.street: Evelyn buys a Jamaica, Queens strip center at a 7% cap with a 5.5% constant: positive. Her friend buys a Tribeca loft building at a 4% cap with a 6.5% constant: negative. He's betting on appreciation to bail him out.
deeper.stakes: Negative leverage means the owner tops up the property from savings every year. If the hoped-for appreciation never comes, that owner sells at a loss or hands the keys to the lender.
deeper.exam: The test: property return (cap rate) versus mortgage constant. Higher cap rate = positive. Higher constant = negative. Equal = neutral.

blocks.html: Leverage also magnifies changes in value. If the $1,000,000 Ridgewood building rises 10% to $1,100,000, the all-cash buyer gained $100,000 on $1,000,000 (10%). The buyer with $250,000 down gained the same $100,000 on $250,000 (40%). If the building falls 10%, that buyer lost 40% of her cash. That is the risk side of leverage, and it is how investors lost buildings in 1990 and 2008.
blocks.casual: Leverage magnifies value swings too. Say the $1,000,000 Ridgewood building goes up 10% to $1,100,000. The all-cash buyer made $100,000 on $1,000,000: 10%. The buyer with $250,000 down made the same $100,000 on $250,000: 40%. Now flip it. The building drops 10% and that buyer just lost 40% of her cash. That's the dark side of leverage, and it's how investors lost buildings in 1990 and 2008.

deeper.plain: The less of your own money is in the deal, the harder every price change hits you.
deeper.picture: A seesaw with you sitting close to the middle: a small tilt at the far end throws you way up or way down.
deeper.street: Marcus's old client bought a Park Slope brownstone in 2006 with 10% down. When values slid in 2009, a 15% drop wiped out his equity and then some. He couldn't refinance and sold short.
deeper.stakes: High leverage can turn a modest dip into losing the whole down payment and the property. Clients who don't understand this blame their broker.
deeper.exam: Gain or loss percent equals the dollar change divided by the equity, not the price. A stem saying "10% drop with 25% down" wants you to answer a 40% loss of equity.

blocks.q: A property returns 7% free and clear. An investor can borrow at a mortgage constant of 8.5%. Borrowing will produce:
c: Positive leverage
Negative leverage
No leverage effect
A higher cap rate
blocks.x: The loan costs 8.5% a year while the property earns only 7%. Every borrowed dollar loses money, so the return on the investor's cash falls. The cap rate is a property measure and does not change with financing.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: Leverage does not change the property's NOI or its cap rate. It only changes what is left for the owner's cash after the bank is paid. A question that says "leverage increased the cap rate" is wrong.
blocks.casual: Classic exam trap: leverage does not change the property's NOI or its cap rate. All it changes is what's left for the owner's cash after the bank gets paid. If a question says "leverage increased the cap rate," that's wrong.

deeper.plain: The building earns the same no matter how you paid for it. Only your slice changes.
