deeper.picture: A pizza is the same size whether you paid cash or used a credit card. The card just decides how many slices go to the bank.
deeper.street: Evelyn's Ridgewood building has a $60,000 NOI and a 6% cap whether she pays cash or borrows 75%. What changes is her cash on cash: 6% all cash, 9% with cheap debt.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up cap rate and cash on cash gets a broker laughed out of an investor meeting and can misprice a listing badly.
deeper.exam: Cap rate is a property measure and ignores financing. Cash on cash is an investor measure and includes financing. Any answer saying financing changes NOI or cap rate is the trap.

blocks.html: The time value of money says a dollar today is worth more than a dollar received later, because today's dollar can be invested and earn interest right away, and because a future promise carries risk and inflation. Compounding moves money forward in time (what will $100 today be worth in 5 years?). Discounting moves it back (what is $100 received in 5 years worth today?).
blocks.casual: The time value of money says a dollar today beats a dollar later. Why? Today's dollar can start earning interest right now, and a future promise comes with risk and inflation. Compounding pushes money forward in time (what's $100 today worth in 5 years?). Discounting pulls it back (what's $100 five years from now worth today?).

deeper.plain: Money now is worth more than the same money later.
deeper.picture: A pizza in your hand now versus a coupon for a pizza next year. The coupon might expire, the shop might close, and pizza will cost more by then.
deeper.street: Diane tells Jordan a buyer offering $1.5 million with a two-year seller-financed balloon isn't really offering $1.5 million. Discount the delayed money and the offer is worth less than a clean $1.45 million all-cash deal today.
deeper.stakes: Comparing offers or lease deals at face value ignores timing. Sellers who take the bigger number paid later can end up with less real money.
deeper.exam: Compounding goes forward to future value; discounting goes back to present value. Swapping the two terms is the usual distractor.

blocks.title: What is a future payment worth today?
blocks.html:
A ground tenant will pay Evelyn a $100,000 lump sum in 5 years. She could earn 6% elsewhere.

Present value = future value / (1 + rate)years = $100,000 / 1.065 = $100,000 / 1.3382 = about $74,726.

So $100,000 five years out is worth roughly $74,700 to her today. That gap is the time value of money.
blocks.casual:
A ground tenant owes Evelyn a $100,000 lump sum in 5 years. She could earn 6% elsewhere.
Present value = future value / (1 + rate)years = $100,000 / 1.065 = $100,000 / 1.3382 = about $74,726.
So that $100,000 five years out is worth about $74,700 to her today. The $25,000 gap? That's the time value of money.

deeper.plain: If you can earn 6% a year, about $74,700 today grows into $100,000 in five years, so that's what the future $100,000 is worth now.
deeper.picture: Working backward from a savings goal: to have $100,000 in five years at 6%, you only need to deposit about $74,700 today.
deeper.street: A Flushing restaurant tenant offers Evelyn a $100,000 lease buyout paid in five years or $80,000 now. At 6%, the future payment is worth about $74,700 today, so the $80,000 check is the better deal.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring discounting makes delayed payments look better than they are. Clients accept deals that are actually worth less, and the broker who advised them looks careless.
deeper.exam: Salesperson exam math rarely goes beyond this. Know that present value is always less than future value when the rate is positive, and that a higher rate or longer wait means a lower present value.

blocks.html: This is why investors care about when cash arrives, not just how much. A building that pays steady rent now beats one that promises a big payoff in year 10, unless the payoff is big enough to make up for the wait. Discounted cash flow analysis (used by appraisers and institutional buyers) is simply the time value of money applied year by year.
blocks.casual: That's why investors care about when the cash shows up, not just how much. A building paying steady rent right now beats one promising a big payday in year 10, unless the payday is big enough to make up for the wait. Discounted cash flow analysis, the tool appraisers and institutional buyers use, is just time value of money done year by year.

deeper.plain: Earlier cash is better, so investors discount later cash before comparing deals.
deeper.picture: Two jobs paying the same total over five years, but one pays monthly and one pays it all at the end. Everyone takes the monthly one.
deeper.street: A Long Island City developer pitches Evelyn a vacant lot with a huge projected sale in year 10. Next to it, a leased Woodside retail building pays 6% from day one. Her DCF shows the lot needs a massive payoff to compete.
deeper.stakes: Selling clients on far-off upside without discounting it can steer them into projects that never pay back in real terms.
deeper.exam: DCF = time value of money applied to each year's cash flow. If asked which method institutional buyers use to value income over a holding period, it's discounted cash flow.

blocks.q: Which statement reflects the time value of money?
c: $10,000 received in 3 years is worth more than $10,000 today
$10,000 today is worth more than $10,000 received in 3 years
Money has the same value no matter when it is received
Only inflation affects the value of future money
blocks.x: A dollar in hand today can be invested immediately and carries no risk of nonpayment, so it is worth more than the same dollar later. Inflation is one reason, not the only one.

blocks.text: The tax angle: why real estate is called a tax shelter

blocks.html: A tax shelter is an investment that lets income escape or delay tax. Real estate shelters income mainly through depreciation: the IRS lets an owner deduct the cost of the building (never the land) over 27.5 years for residential rental property and 39 years for nonresidential. Depreciation is a deduction you take without spending a dime that year, so a building can show little or no taxable income while putting real cash in the owner's pocket. Lesson 3 runs the numbers, and Subject 17 covers recapture when you sell.
blocks.casual: A tax shelter lets income dodge or delay tax. Real estate's main trick is depreciation: the IRS lets an owner deduct the cost of the building (never the land) over 27.5 years for residential rental property and 39 years for nonresidential. You take that deduction without spending a cent that year, so a building can show little or no taxable income while real cash lands in the owner's pocket. Lesson 3 runs the numbers, and Subject 17 covers recapture when you sell.

deeper.plain: Depreciation is a paper expense that cuts your taxable income without cutting your cash.
deeper.picture: Your boss lets you write off a slice of your car every year even though you already paid for it. Your paycheck doesn't shrink, but your tax bill does.
deeper.street: Evelyn buys a Bronx apartment building for $3.3 million with $550,000 allocated to land. She depreciates $2.75 million over 27.5 years: $100,000 a year. With $110,000 of cash flow, she reports only about $10,000 of taxable income, before mortgage interest.
deeper.stakes: Investors who forget depreciation undervalue rental property. Those who forget recapture get a nasty tax bill when they sell. Brokers should explain the concept and send specifics to a CPA.
deeper.exam: Land is never depreciated. Residential rental is 27.5 years, nonresidential is 39. Swapping the numbers or including land is the trap.

blocks.title: New York angle
blocks.html: Commercial deals in New York skip the RPL 443 agency disclosure form (that covers residential 1 to 4 family), but the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form applies to every property type, including commercial and vacant land. A commercial licensee still gives it at first substantive contact.
blocks.casual: New York twist: commercial deals skip the RPL 443 agency disclosure form (that one's for residential 1 to 4 family). But the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form covers every property type, commercial and vacant land included. So even on a commercial deal, you hand it over at first substantive contact.

deeper.plain: Commercial skips the agency form but still needs the fair housing form.
deeper.picture: Think of a club with two wristbands: one for the dance floor only (agency form, residential), one everyone needs at the door (anti-discrimination form, every property).
deeper.street: Jordan meets a restaurant owner looking for a Williamsburg storefront. No RPL 443 form, but Jordan hands over the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form at that first real conversation and has the client acknowledge it.
deeper.stakes: Skipping the anti-discrimination form on a commercial deal is a DOS violation that can mean fines and discipline for both the licensee and the supervising broker.
deeper.exam: Trap: a stem says "commercial, so no disclosure forms are needed." Wrong. RPL 443 is out, the anti-discrimination form is still in.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Borrow cheap, leverage leaps. Borrow dear, returns disappear. Compare the loan constant to the property return, every time.
blocks.casual: Lock this in: Borrow cheap, leverage leaps. Borrow dear, returns disappear. Every time, compare the loan constant to the property return.

deeper.plain: Cheap loans boost your return. Expensive loans shrink it.
deeper.picture: A tailwind on a bike ride versus a headwind. Same legs, very different speed.
deeper.street: When Evelyn hears any pitch, she writes two numbers on a napkin: cap rate and constant. If the constant is bigger, she slides the napkin back across the table.
deeper.stakes: Brokers who skip this one comparison end up pitching deals sophisticated investors reject instantly, and that costs credibility fast.
deeper.exam: If a question gives a cap rate and a mortgage constant and asks the effect of leverage, this hook answers it in seconds.

story.title: The Nephew Plan
story.setting: A cafe on Wyckoff Avenue, Ridgewood, a gray Thursday

beats.text: Diane sent Jordan to sit in on a meeting with Evelyn Park, the firm's favorite commercial client. Evelyn orders black coffee and opens a spreadsheet before she sits down.
My nephew says I should put 25% down on four buildings instead of buying one for cash. He watches a lot of videos.
Four buildings sounds like four times the money.
Four times the money, four times the boilers, and a bank that gets paid before I do. Building nets $60,000 on a million. That's 6% if I pay cash.
And with a loan?
Depends what the loan costs. If the bank's annual payment is 5% of the loan, I keep $22,500 on my $250,000. That's 9%. Good.
If it's 8%, the bank takes all $60,000 and I keep nothing.

check.q: Why did Evelyn's return drop to zero at an 8% mortgage constant?
c: The cap rate fell
Debt service ate the entire NOI
The property lost value
Depreciation reduced income
check.x: $750,000 x 8% = $60,000 of debt service, which equals the NOI. Nothing is left for the owner. The property itself did not change.

beats.text: So leverage is good when the loan is cheaper than the building's return.
And it magnifies everything. Values drop 10%, the cash buyer loses 10%. My nephew loses 40% of his down payment. Times four.
Plus you can't sell a building like a stock if you panic.
Correct. Months, lawyers, a lender. That's why I want more than a bond pays. More risk, less liquidity, more return. Otherwise why bother?
Back at the office, Jordan repeats the whole thing to Diane, slightly out of breath.
Good. Now remember the part nobody watches videos about: depreciation lets her show almost no taxable income while the rent checks clear. That's the shelter.
Borrow cheap, leverage leaps. Borrow dear, returns disappear. Write that on your hand if you need to.

board.prompt: Draw two bar charts for the $1,000,000 Ridgewood building: all cash vs 75% loan. Label NOI, debt service, cash left over and the return on the owner's cash at a 5% and an 8% mortgage constant.

facts.text: Every investment is judged on three things: how much it returns, how risky that return is, and how quickly it turns back into cash.
Risk is the chance the actual return differs from the expected one; the higher the risk, the higher the return investors demand.
Investment real estate risks include market, tenant (credit), interest rate, regulatory, physical and liquidity risk.
Liquidity is how fast an asset converts to cash without losing value; real estate is illiquid because a sale takes months.
A simple rate of return is annual income divided by the amount invested ($60,000 on $1,000,000 cash is 6%).
Return on investment is the income your money earns (rent); return of investment is getting the money back (a sale).
Leverage is using borrowed money to buy an asset, and it magnifies results in both directions.
The mortgage constant is annual debt service (principal plus interest) divided by the loan amount.
Positive leverage: the property's return exceeds the loan constant, so the cash return rises; negative leverage: the loan costs more, so it falls.
With a loan, the return on the investor's cash is NOI minus debt service, divided by the cash invested.
Leverage magnifies value changes: a 10% rise in value is a 40% gain on 25% down, and a 10% fall is a 40% loss.
Leverage does not change a property's NOI or cap rate; it only changes what is left for the owner's cash after the bank is paid.
Time value of money: a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later; compounding moves money forward, discounting moves it back.
Present value = future value / (1 + rate) to the power of the years ($100,000 in 5 years at 6% is about $74,726 today).
Investors care when cash arrives, not just how much; discounted cash flow analysis applies the time value of money year by year.
Real estate is a tax shelter mainly through depreciation, a non-cash deduction for the building (never the land) over 27.5 years residential or 39 years nonresidential.
Commercial deals skip the RPL 443 agency disclosure form, but the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form applies to every property type at first substantive contact.

lessons.title: The Menu: Land, Office, Residential, Retail, Industrial, and Owning vs Leasing the Dirt
lessons.tagline: Each property type has its own tenants, risks and vocabulary. Know who rents it and what can go wrong.
objectives: Describe the main investment property types and the risk profile of each
Distinguish office building heights and classes A, B and C
Rank retail centers from strip center to mega mall and explain the role of an anchor tenant
Explain fee simple ownership versus a leasehold under a long-term ground lease

blocks.title: Three listings, one investor
blocks.html: Jordan brings Evelyn three listings: a vacant lot in the Bronx priced like a bargain, a fully leased Class B office building in downtown White Plains, and a three-story mixed-use building on Knickerbocker Avenue with a bodega and four apartments. Evelyn asks the same question about each one: "Who pays me, how reliably, and what happens if they leave?" Which one has no answer to the first part at all?
blocks.casual: Jordan walks three listings over to Evelyn: a "bargain" vacant lot in the Bronx, a fully leased Class B office building in downtown White Plains, and a three-story mixed-use on Knickerbocker Avenue with a bodega and four apartments. Evelyn asks the same thing about all three: "Who pays me, how reliably, and what happens if they leave?" One of them can't even answer the first part. Which one?

deeper.plain: Every property type is really a question about who pays rent and how steady that money is.
deeper.picture: Choosing between a tip jar with no customers yet, a corporate salary, and a side hustle plus a day job.
deeper.street: The Bronx lot pays nothing; Evelyn would pay taxes and insurance every year waiting for a developer to want it. The White Plains office pays steadily until the lease ends. The Knickerbocker building spreads the risk between a bodega and four households.
deeper.stakes: A broker who pitches a lot as a "cheap investment" without saying it has no income is setting up an angry client who suddenly owes property taxes on dirt.
deeper.exam: When the exam asks which property type is most speculative or has no income, the answer is unimproved land.

blocks.html: Unimproved land (raw land) has no buildings and usually no income. The owner pays real estate taxes, insurance and maybe interest every year while waiting for the value to rise. That makes land the most speculative property type: no cash flow, very low liquidity, no depreciation deduction (land never depreciates), and a payoff that often depends on a zoning change, new infrastructure or a developer who wants the site. Holding land for future development is called land banking.
blocks.casual: Unimproved land (raw land) has no buildings and usually no income. You pay real estate taxes, insurance and maybe interest every single year while you wait for the value to go up. That makes land the most speculative property type: no cash flow, very low liquidity, no depreciation deduction (land never depreciates), and a payoff that often hinges on a zoning change, new infrastructure, or a developer who wants your site. Holding land for future development has a name: land banking.

deeper.plain: Raw land costs you money every year and only pays off if someone later wants it more.
deeper.picture: Buying a concert ticket for a show that might be announced someday. You pay now and hope the band books the venue.
deeper.street: Evelyn bought a Staten Island lot near a planned rail stop in 2015, paying about $18,000 a year in taxes and insurance. If the station opens and the city rezones, she sells to a developer for triple. If not, she has a decade of carrying costs and nothing to show.
deeper.stakes: Clients who buy land without cash reserves for carrying costs can be forced to sell at a loss or lose it to a tax lien.
deeper.exam: Land: no income, no depreciation, lowest liquidity, highest speculation. "Land banking" means holding for future development.

blocks.html: Office buildings are described by height and by quality. Heights are rough industry labels, not legal definitions:
blocks.casual: People describe office buildings two ways: how tall and how nice. The height labels are loose industry talk, not legal definitions.

deeper.plain: Office buildings get sorted by height and by quality.
deeper.picture: Like describing a car by size (compact, midsize, SUV) and condition (new, used, fixer-upper).
deeper.street: Jordan hears a client say "a mid-rise in Downtown Brooklyn, Class B." That tells him roughly 4 to 10 floors with elevators, older but well kept, with mid-range rents.
deeper.stakes: Mislabeling a building's class or size in a listing makes the broker look green and can attract the wrong tenants, wasting weeks of showings.
deeper.exam: The exam tests the general idea of low, mid and high rise. Don't hunt for a magic floor count; pick the answer that fits the concept.

head: Type
Roughly
Typical setting
rows: 1 to 3 or 4 stories, may be a walk-up
Suburban office parks, small professional buildings on Long Island
About 4 to 10 or so stories, elevators
blocks.caption: Heights vary by source. The exam wants the idea, not a magic number.

deeper.plain: Low-rise is a few floors, mid-rise has elevators and up to about 10 floors, high-rise is a tower.
deeper.picture: A three-story walk-up townhouse, a ten-story hotel, and a skyscraper with separate elevators for the low and high floors.
deeper.street: A dentist on Long Island wants a low-rise professional building with parking. A law firm in Midtown wants a high-rise with its own elevator bank. Same product category, completely different buyers.
deeper.stakes: Matching tenants to the wrong building type wastes showings and burns your credibility with the landlord.
deeper.exam: Heights vary by source; the test checks that you know high-rises have multiple elevator banks and low-rises may be walk-ups.

blocks.html: Quality is graded by building class:
blocks.casual: For quality, offices get a building class:

deeper.plain: Class A, B and C are a grade for how good the building is.
deeper.picture: Hotel ratings: five-star, three-star, budget motel. Same idea for offices.
deeper.street: A fintech firm tours Hudson Yards (Class A), a 1960s Midtown building that's been kept up (Class B), and a tired Garment District building (Class C). The rent gap per square foot is huge.
deeper.stakes: Calling a Class C building Class A in marketing is a misrepresentation. Tenants will notice on the first tour and the landlord will lose trust in you.
deeper.exam: Building class reflects age, location, systems and management. It is an industry ranking, not a legal one.

head: Class
What it looks like
Rents and tenants
rows: Newest or fully renovated, best location, modern systems, amenities, strong management
Highest rents; law firms, banks, tech headquarters
Older but well maintained, good location, functional systems
Older, dated systems, needs capital work, weaker location
Lowest rents; startups, back offices, budget users
blocks.caption: Office building classes

deeper.plain: A is newest and priciest, B is older but fine, C is dated and cheapest.
deeper.picture: A is the new iPhone, B is last year's model in good shape, C is an old phone with a cracked screen that still works.
deeper.street: Evelyn's Class B building in White Plains holds an accounting firm and an insurance agency. She knows a new Class A tower nearby could pull those tenants away with concessions.
deeper.stakes: Investors who pay Class A prices for Class B or C space lose money when rents don't match. Knowing the grade helps you advise on price and risk.
deeper.exam: Expect a description and a question asking which class. Newest, best location, top amenities equals A; dated systems needing capital work equals C.

blocks.html: Office risk: long leases provide stability, but when a big tenant leaves, refilling the space can take a year or more and cost heavy tenant improvement money and broker commissions. Remote work since 2020 has made older Class B and C space the hardest to lease, and some Manhattan buildings are being converted to apartments.
blocks.casual: Office risk in a nutshell: long leases give you stability, but when a big tenant leaves, refilling that space can take a year or more and cost a fortune in tenant improvement money and broker commissions. Since 2020, remote work has made older Class B and C space the hardest to lease, and some Manhattan buildings are being converted into apartments.

deeper.plain: Offices are steady until a big tenant leaves, then they're expensive to refill.
deeper.picture: A big wedding venue booked every weekend. Lose one major client and it's not just lost rent; you have to redecorate to win the next one.
deeper.street: A 40,000 square foot tenant leaves Evelyn's White Plains building. She faces a year of no rent on that space, $60 a foot in build-out money, and a leasing commission to land a replacement.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who look only at today's rent roll without checking when big leases expire can buy into a cliff. Brokers should flag lease expirations up front.
deeper.exam: Office risk = rollover and re-leasing cost. Questions may also mention conversion of obsolete office space to residential.

blocks.q: A 1960s Midtown office building with original elevators, dated HVAC and below-market rents would most likely be classified as:
c: Class A
Class B
Class C
Class D
blocks.x: Old systems, capital needs and the lowest rents are the marks of Class C. Class B is older but well maintained and functional. There is no standard Class D.

blocks.html: Single-family rentals (houses, rented condos) are easy to finance and sell, but one vacancy means 100% vacancy. Multi-family buildings spread the risk across many tenants. Lenders treat 1 to 4 unit properties as residential (eligible for residential mortgages) and 5+ units as commercial loans underwritten mainly on the building's income.
blocks.casual: Single-family rentals (houses, rented condos) are easy to finance and sell, but one vacancy means you're 100% vacant. Multi-family buildings spread the risk across lots of tenants. Lenders treat 1 to 4 unit properties as residential (you can get a residential mortgage) and 5+ units as commercial loans underwritten mostly on the building's income.

deeper.plain: One rental means all-or-nothing income. Many units spread the risk, and at 5+ units the loan becomes commercial.
deeper.picture: One big client versus twenty small ones. Lose the big one and you're broke; lose one of twenty and you barely notice.
deeper.street: Leo is torn between a $900,000 rental condo in Long Island City and a $1.9 million five-unit in Ridgewood. Tasha explains the condo gets a residential loan on his salary, but the five-unit's commercial loan depends mostly on the rent roll.
deeper.stakes: Telling a buyer they'll get residential financing on a five-unit building is wrong and can blow up the deal at the loan stage.
deeper.exam: The 1 to 4 versus 5+ unit line is a frequent fact. 5+ units equals commercial lending based on income.

blocks.title: NYC twist: rent stabilization changes the math
blocks.html: In New York City, many buildings with 6 or more units built before 1974 are rent stabilized under the ETPA. Increases are set by the Rent Guidelines Board, and since the 2019 HSTPA there is no vacancy decontrol. An investor values these buildings on the regulated rent roll, not on what a free-market apartment would rent for.
blocks.casual: NYC changes the math. Lots of buildings with 6 or more units built before 1974 are rent stabilized under the ETPA. The Rent Guidelines Board sets the increases, and since the 2019 HSTPA there's no vacancy decontrol. So an investor values these buildings on the regulated rent roll, not on what a free-market apartment would get.

deeper.plain: In NYC, many older 6+ unit buildings have rents capped by law, and the value follows the capped rents.
deeper.picture: Buying a restaurant where the city sets your menu prices. You can't charge what the place down the street charges just because you want to.
deeper.street: Sal is shopping for a 1962 eight-unit in Astoria. The seller's pro forma assumes market rents of $3,000. Diane points out six units are stabilized at $1,600, and with no vacancy decontrol they'll stay regulated.
deeper.stakes: A broker who markets a stabilized building on market rents invites a misrepresentation claim and a buyer who overpays by millions.
deeper.exam: Key numbers: 6 or more units, built before 1974, ETPA, Rent Guidelines Board. Old answers mentioning luxury decontrol reflect pre-2019 law.

blocks.html: A mixed-use building combines uses, most often ground-floor retail with apartments or offices above. It is the classic NYC building: the "two-family over a store" in Ridgewood, Bushwick or Bay Ridge. Income is diversified (residential is steady, retail pays more per square foot but can sit empty longer), and the owner manages two kinds of leases under two sets of rules.
blocks.casual: A mixed-use building mixes uses, usually a store on the ground floor with apartments or offices above. It's the classic NYC building: the "two-family over a store" in Ridgewood, Bushwick or Bay Ridge. The income is spread out (apartments are steady, retail pays more per square foot but can sit empty longer), and the owner juggles two kinds of leases under two sets of rules.

deeper.plain: Store downstairs, homes upstairs, two income streams and two rulebooks.
deeper.picture: A food truck that also rents out parking spaces on the side. Two businesses, two kinds of customers.
deeper.street: The Knickerbocker Avenue building has a bodega paying $5,500 a month on a net lease and four apartments under residential rules. If the bodega leaves, the apartments keep paying while Evelyn finds a new retailer.
deeper.stakes: Forgetting that the apartments follow residential law (warranty of habitability, possibly rent stabilization) while the store follows commercial lease terms can lead to illegal lease clauses and HPD trouble.
deeper.exam: Mixed use = combination of uses, commonly retail with residential above. Its benefit is diversified income.

blocks.text: Retail: from strip center to mega mall

blocks.html: Retail centers are ranked by size, trade area and anchors. An anchor tenant is a large, well-known tenant (supermarket, department store, big-box store) that draws shoppers. Anchors often pay lower rent per square foot because the smaller "in-line" stores profit from the foot traffic they bring. When an anchor leaves, the whole center suffers; many in-line leases include a co-tenancy clause that cuts their rent if the anchor goes dark.
blocks.casual: Retail centers get ranked by size, trade area and anchors. An anchor tenant is the big name (supermarket, department store, big-box) that pulls shoppers in. Anchors often pay less rent per square foot because the smaller "in-line" stores cash in on the foot traffic they bring. When an anchor leaves, the whole center hurts, and lots of in-line leases have a co-tenancy clause that cuts their rent if the anchor goes dark.

deeper.plain: The big store draws the crowd, so it gets cheap rent and the little stores pay more to be near it.
deeper.picture: A party where one famous guest brings everyone else. You'd happily let that guest eat for free.
deeper.street: A ShopRite anchors a Long Island center paying $14 a foot while the nail salon pays $38. When the ShopRite closes, three in-line tenants invoke co-tenancy clauses and their rents drop by half.
deeper.stakes: Investors who buy a center without reading co-tenancy clauses can see income crater the day the anchor leaves.
deeper.exam: Anchors pay less per square foot than in-line tenants. A distractor will claim anchors pay the highest rent.

head: Center
Rough size
Anchor
Serves
NY example
rows: Small row of stores, parking in front
Often none, or a small convenience user
Immediate neighborhood: pizza, dry cleaner, nail salon
Countless along Hylan Blvd, Staten Island
A supermarket-anchored center on Long Island
About 400,000 to 800,000 sq ft, usually enclosed
blocks.caption: Square footages are approximate industry ranges.

deeper.plain: Shopping centers grow from a row of shops to giant malls, and the anchor and trade area grow with them.
deeper.picture: Corner store, local supermarket, big department store, then a theme park with shopping attached.
deeper.street: Jordan tours Hylan Boulevard strip centers for a pizza client, while Evelyn studies Queens Center and Roosevelt Field reports for a regional retail fund. Same category, different universe.
deeper.stakes: Placing a convenience tenant in a regional mall or a destination brand in a tiny strip center wastes everyone's time and money.
deeper.exam: Know the order: strip, neighborhood, regional, mega (super-regional). Neighborhood centers are anchored by a supermarket or drugstore; regional malls by 2 or more department stores.

blocks.html: Read the table from small to large. A strip center is a single row of shops with parking out front, selling convenience to the blocks around it. A neighborhood center adds a supermarket or drugstore anchor and serves daily needs for a few miles. A regional mall is usually enclosed, with two or more department store anchors pulling shoppers from a whole region. A mega mall (super-regional mall) is bigger still, with three or more anchors, entertainment and dining, and draws from several counties and tourists. An outlet center collects brand-name manufacturers' discount stores, usually on cheaper land along a highway, and depends on shoppers willing to drive an hour to save money.
blocks.casual: Go small to big. A strip center is one row of shops with parking out front, selling convenience to the nearby blocks. A neighborhood center adds a supermarket or drugstore anchor and covers daily needs for a few miles. A regional mall is usually enclosed, with two or more department stores pulling people from a whole region. A mega mall (super-regional) is bigger still, with three or more anchors, entertainment and dining, drawing from several counties plus tourists. An outlet center gathers brand-name discount stores, usually on cheaper land by a highway, and lives on shoppers willing to drive an hour to save money.

deeper.plain: The bigger the center, the bigger the anchors and the farther shoppers travel to get there.
deeper.picture: Your bodega, your grocery store, the mall you went to as a teen, the mall tourists bus to, and the outlet village you drive to on a Saturday.
deeper.street: Tasha drives an hour to Woodbury Common for discounted designer shoes but walks to the strip center on her block for dry cleaning. That difference is trade area.
deeper.stakes: Picking the wrong center type for a tenant means bad sales, a broken lease and a landlord who won't take your calls again.
deeper.exam: Outlet center = manufacturers' discount stores, often off a highway. Mega mall = 3+ anchors plus entertainment. Match the description to the name.

blocks.html: Retail risk is about traffic. Online shopping has hollowed out weaker malls, while grocery-anchored neighborhood centers and well-located urban storefronts have held up better because people still buy food, prescriptions and haircuts in person. A retail investor studies the anchor's lease term, tenant sales per square foot, and how many in-line tenants could leave if the anchor does.
blocks.casual: Retail lives or dies on traffic. Online shopping gutted the weaker malls, while grocery-anchored neighborhood centers and well-located city storefronts held up better because people still buy food, prescriptions and haircuts in person. A retail investor checks the anchor's lease term, tenant sales per square foot, and how many in-line tenants could bail if the anchor does.

deeper.plain: Stores need shoppers, and the stores that sell things you can't buy online hold up best.
deeper.picture: A restaurant in an empty food court versus a bakery on a busy corner. Same food, very different future.
deeper.street: Evelyn passes on a half-empty upstate mall at a 10% cap and buys a grocery-anchored center in Bayside at 6.5%. Lower return, but her tenants sell things people can't order from Amazon.
deeper.stakes: Chasing a high cap rate on a dying mall can mean losing the anchor, the in-line tenants and eventually the property.
deeper.exam: Key retail metrics: anchor lease term, sales per square foot, co-tenancy exposure.

blocks.q: In a typical shopping center, the anchor tenant usually:
c: Pays the highest rent per square foot
Pays a lower rent per square foot because it draws traffic for everyone
Owns the land under the center
Is always a percentage lease tenant
blocks.x: Anchors are the traffic magnet, so landlords give them favorable rents and recover the difference from in-line tenants who benefit. Anchors may or may not pay percentage rent.

blocks.html: Industrial property covers factories, warehouses, distribution centers and flex space. Investors look at ceiling height (clear height), loading docks, truck access, floor load capacity, power and zoning. Warehouses and last-mile distribution space (Red Hook, Sunset Park, Hunts Point, Long Island City) have been in heavy demand because of e-commerce. Leases are usually net, with the tenant paying most expenses.
blocks.casual: Industrial property means factories, warehouses, distribution centers and flex space. Investors check ceiling height (clear height), loading docks, truck access, how much weight the floors can hold, power and zoning. Warehouses and last-mile distribution space (Red Hook, Sunset Park, Hunts Point, Long Island City) have been red hot because of e-commerce. Leases are usually net, with the tenant covering most expenses.

deeper.plain: Industrial means buildings for making, storing and shipping things, judged on height, docks, trucks and power.
deeper.picture: A kitchen judged not by its decor but by how big the stove is, how much the counters hold, and how close the back door is to the delivery van.
deeper.street: A delivery company wants Hunts Point space with 28-foot clear height and four loading docks near the Bruckner. A pretty building with 12-foot ceilings and no truck court is worthless to them.
deeper.stakes: Missing a zoning or floor load issue can kill an industrial deal after the client has spent months and legal fees.
deeper.exam: Industrial leases are typically net. Clear height, loading and access are the features to know. E-commerce drives warehouse demand.

blocks.html: A loft building is a multistory former manufacturing building with large open floors, high ceilings, big windows and freight elevators. SoHo, Tribeca, DUMBO and Williamsburg are full of them. Many now hold offices, studios or apartments.
blocks.casual: A loft building is an old multistory factory with big open floors, high ceilings, huge windows and freight elevators. SoHo, Tribeca, DUMBO and Williamsburg are packed with them. Lots of them now hold offices, studios or apartments.

deeper.plain: Lofts are old factories with wide-open floors that got reused for homes and offices.
deeper.picture: An old warehouse turned into a brewery taproom: same bones, completely new life.
deeper.street: A DUMBO loft floor that once printed cardboard boxes now leases to a design agency. The freight elevator still runs, and the agency loves the 14-foot ceilings.
deeper.stakes: Loft buildings can carry hidden legal issues around residential use. Buyers who skip that check inherit tenants they can't remove.
deeper.exam: Loft = former manufacturing, open floors, high ceilings, freight elevators. Often converted.

blocks.title: NYC Loft Law
blocks.html: When artists and others moved into commercial lofts illegally in the 1970s, the state passed the Loft Law (Multiple Dwelling Law Article 7-C, 1982). It protects qualifying residential occupants of former commercial and manufacturing lofts, requires owners to legalize the buildings, and is overseen by the NYC Loft Board. A buyer of a loft building must check for covered residential units.
blocks.casual: In the 1970s artists and others moved into commercial lofts illegally, so the state passed the Loft Law (Multiple Dwelling Law Article 7-C, 1982). It protects qualifying residential occupants of former commercial and manufacturing lofts, makes owners legalize the buildings, and is run by the NYC Loft Board. Buying a loft building? Check for covered residential units.

deeper.plain: NY protects people living in former factory lofts and forces owners to bring those buildings up to residential code.
deeper.picture: Someone has been living in your garage for years and the law now says you have to fix it up for them, not kick them out.
deeper.street: An investor buys a Williamsburg loft building planning to lease every floor as offices. Due diligence turns up two Loft Law covered tenants. Now he has to legalize those units and can't simply clear them out.
deeper.stakes: Failing to check for covered units can turn an office repositioning into years of legalization costs and Loft Board proceedings.
deeper.exam: Loft Law = MDL Article 7-C, 1982, NYC Loft Board. It protects residential occupants of former commercial lofts.

blocks.text: Fee simple vs leasehold: who owns the dirt?

blocks.html: Most investors buy in fee simple: they own the land and the building outright, forever. In a ground lease, the landowner leases only the land to a tenant for a long term, often 49 to 99 years. The tenant builds (or buys) the building, collects the building's rents, pays ground rent, and usually pays all taxes and expenses. When the lease ends, the building generally reverts to the landowner.
blocks.casual: Most investors buy fee simple: they own the land and building outright, forever. In a ground lease, the landowner leases just the land to a tenant for a long time, often 49 to 99 years. The tenant builds (or buys) the building, collects its rents, pays ground rent, and usually covers all taxes and expenses. When the lease ends, the building generally goes back to the landowner.

deeper.plain: In a ground lease you rent the land for decades, put up a building, and give the building back at the end.
deeper.picture: Renting a plot at a community garden for years. You build the raised beds and grow the vegetables, but when your plot term ends, the beds stay with the garden.
deeper.street: A developer ground-leases a Long Island City parcel from a family trust for 99 years at $1.2 million a year. She builds a 200-unit rental, collects the rents, pays the taxes, and in 2124 the building belongs to the family's heirs.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who don't realize a property is ground-leased may pay fee simple prices for something that disappears at lease end.
deeper.exam: Fee simple = own land and building. Ground lease = tenant owns improvements for the term; they usually revert to the landowner.

blocks.title: Two interests in one ground-leased property

left.title: Leased fee (landowner)
items: Owns the land, collects ground rent
Very safe, bond-like income
Gets the building back at the end of the term
Often universities, churches, families, public authorities

right.title: Leasehold (ground tenant)
items: Owns the right to use the land for the term
Builds or owns the building and collects its rents
Can finance with a leasehold mortgage if the term is long enough
Value shrinks as the remaining term gets shorter

deeper.plain: The landowner holds the leased fee and gets ground rent. The tenant holds the leasehold and runs the building.
deeper.picture: A landlord who rents you a lot for your food truck business: they get a steady check, you get the customers and the headaches.
deeper.street: Cooper Union has long collected ground rent on the Chrysler Building land: steady income, no tenants to manage. The building's owner collects office rents but watches the leasehold's value tick down as the term runs.
deeper.stakes: Lenders refuse leasehold mortgages when too little term remains. A ground tenant who waits too long to refinance or extend can be stuck.
deeper.exam: Leased fee = landowner's interest. Leasehold = tenant's interest. Swapping these two is the most common trap.

blocks.html: The tenant's interest is the leasehold interest; the landowner's interest is the leased fee. Why ground lease? The landowner keeps the land and gets steady income without selling (and without capital gains tax). The developer avoids paying for the land up front, which means less equity. Lenders want the remaining lease term to run well past the loan's maturity.
blocks.casual: The tenant's piece is the leasehold interest; the landowner's piece is the leased fee. Why do a ground lease at all? The landowner keeps the land and gets steady income without selling (so no capital gains tax). The developer skips paying for the land up front, so less equity is needed. Lenders want the remaining lease term to run well past the loan's maturity.

deeper.plain: The owner gets income without selling; the builder gets the site without buying it.
deeper.picture: Leasing a car instead of buying it: lower cash up front, but you don't keep it forever, and the dealer still owns it.
deeper.street: A Bed-Stuy church owns a big parking lot. Rather than sell and pay tax, it ground-leases the lot for 99 years to a developer building affordable housing, earning ground rent for generations.
deeper.stakes: Brokers who don't check the remaining term can put a buyer in a building no lender will finance.
deeper.exam: Benefits: owner avoids a sale and capital gains, developer needs less equity. Lenders need the lease term to outlast the loan.

blocks.title: Ground leases are everywhere in Manhattan
blocks.html: The land under the Chrysler Building has long been owned by The Cooper Union, which collects ground rent from the building's owner. All of Battery Park City sits on land owned by a state authority that ground-leases parcels to developers and co-op and condo buildings. Buying a co-op or condo on ground-leased land means asking when the lease expires and how the rent resets.
blocks.casual: Manhattan is full of ground leases. The Chrysler Building's land has long belonged to The Cooper Union, which collects ground rent from whoever owns the building. All of Battery Park City sits on land owned by a state authority that ground-leases parcels to developers and to co-op and condo buildings. Buying a co-op or condo on ground-leased land? Ask when the lease expires and how the rent resets.

deeper.plain: Lots of famous NYC buildings sit on land someone else owns, and that affects buyers.
deeper.picture: Buying a house on a lot you rent. The house is yours to live in, but the landlord of the lot can raise the rent when the term resets.
deeper.street: Leo loves a Battery Park City condo priced 15% below Tribeca. Priya explains the building's ground rent is passed through to owners in common charges and the lease has a scheduled reset.
deeper.stakes: Missing a ground rent reset can leave a co-op or condo owner with sudden, huge monthly charge increases and a unit that's hard to sell.
deeper.exam: Recognize Battery Park City and the Chrysler Building as ground lease examples. The question will hinge on who owns the land.

blocks.q: In a 99-year ground lease, the interest held by the tenant who built the office tower is called the:
c: Leased fee
Leasehold
Fee simple absolute
Life estate
blocks.x: The tenant holds the leasehold. The landowner holds the leased fee. Neither holds the full fee simple in the property as a whole while the lease runs.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.html: A ground lease is still a lease (a nonfreehold estate), no matter how long. A 99-year ground tenant does not own the land. And the ground tenant's building value falls toward zero as the lease nears its end, because the building is about to go to the landowner.
blocks.casual: Trap alert: a ground lease is still a lease (a nonfreehold estate), no matter how long it runs. A 99-year ground tenant does not own the land. And the ground tenant's building value slides toward zero as the lease nears its end, because the building is about to go to the landowner.

deeper.plain: Long or not, it's a rental. The tenant never owns the land.
deeper.picture: A 99-year phone contract is still a contract, not ownership of the phone company.
deeper.street: A Midtown building's ground lease has 15 years left. A buyer offering a full fee simple price is confused; Evelyn knows the building will hand itself to the landowner soon and bids a fraction.
deeper.stakes: Overpaying for a short leasehold can be a total loss of capital.
deeper.exam: Ground lease = leasehold (nonfreehold) estate. Value shrinks as the remaining term shrinks. Any answer making the tenant a fee owner is wrong.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Land waits, offices lease long, retail lives on traffic, warehouses ride the trucks. And in a ground lease, the tenant owns the building's future, the landowner owns the dirt's forever.
blocks.casual: Remember it this way: Land waits, offices lease long, retail lives on traffic, warehouses ride the trucks. And in a ground lease, the tenant owns the building's future, and the landowner owns the dirt's forever.

deeper.plain: Each property type has one main thing that drives it.
deeper.picture: Four shopkeepers: one waiting for a buyer, one with long contracts, one counting foot traffic, one counting delivery trucks.
deeper.street: Jordan tapes this line above his desk. When a client says "warehouse," he immediately asks about truck access and clear height.
deeper.stakes: Asking the wrong question for the property type makes a new agent look clueless in front of serious investors.
deeper.exam: Use the hook to match property type with its main risk or driver in a quick question.

story.title: Three Listings and a Pigeon
story.setting: Hudson & Hart Realty, Monday morning, Jordan's desk

beats.text: Jordan has spread three listing sheets across the desk. A pigeon on the windowsill seems interested in the Bronx lot.
Lot first. Who pays me?
Nobody, yet. But it's cheap.
Cheap because I pay taxes on dirt every year and wait for a rezoning. No income, no depreciation, hard to sell. Pure speculation.
White Plains office then. Class B, fully leased.
Class B means old but decent. Who's the biggest tenant and when does their lease end? If they leave, I'm buying an empty floor and a big tenant improvement bill.
beats.tag: Office risk: rollover of big tenants

beats.text: Lease ends in 18 months. Okay. And the Knickerbocker mixed-use: bodega plus four apartments.
Two income streams. Apartments steady, store pays more per foot. Built when? Four units, so not stabilized, but check anyway.

check.q: Why does Evelyn think the Bushwick building's four apartments are probably not rent stabilized?
c: Mixed-use buildings are always exempt
Stabilization generally covers buildings with 6 or more units built before 1974
Only Manhattan buildings are stabilized
Buildings with stores are commercial
check.x: The ETPA generally covers buildings with 6 or more units built before 1974. Four units usually falls outside it, though a careful buyer still checks the registration history.

beats.text: Jordan, while you're at it, I've got a deal on a building on Water Street. Land's ground leased. Basically the same as owning it.
How many years left on the ground lease, Marcus?
Twenty-two. Ish.
Then in twenty-two years the building belongs to the landowner and no bank will lend past it. Not the same as owning it.
beats.tag: Leasehold value shrinks as the term runs out

beats.text: Marcus discovers an urgent phone call.
Every property type answers Evelyn's question differently: who pays, how reliably, and what happens when they leave. Learn the answer for each one and you can talk to any investor in this city.

board.prompt: Make a grid: rows are land, office, multi-family, mixed use, retail, industrial, loft. Columns: who pays rent, biggest risk, typical lease type, liquidity.

facts.text: Unimproved land usually produces no income, cannot be depreciated and is the most speculative property type; holding it for future development is land banking.
Low-rise, mid-rise and high-rise are rough industry labels for office height (mid-rise is about 4 to 10 stories with elevators), not legal definitions.
Class A office space is new or renovated with the best location and top rents; Class B is older but well kept; Class C is dated with the lowest rents.
Office leases are long and stable, but refilling a big vacancy can take a year or more and heavy TI money; remote work hit older Class B and C space hardest.
Lenders treat 1 to 4 unit properties as residential and 5 or more units as commercial loans sized on the building's income; a single-family rental is 100% vacant with one vacancy.
In NYC, many buildings of 6 or more units built before 1974 are rent stabilized (ETPA), with no vacancy decontrol since the 2019 HSTPA, so investors value them on the regulated rent roll.
A mixed-use building combines uses, usually ground-floor retail with apartments or offices above, diversifying income under two sets of lease rules.
An anchor tenant is a large draw that often pays lower rent per square foot than in-line stores; co-tenancy clauses cut in-line rent if the anchor goes dark.
A strip center is a small row of convenience stores with parking in front; a neighborhood center is anchored by a supermarket or drugstore.
A regional mall has 2 or more department store anchors; a super-regional (mega) mall has 3 or more anchors and draws from several counties.
An outlet center gathers brand-name manufacturers' discount stores, often on cheaper land along a highway.
Retail risk is about traffic: online shopping hollowed out weaker malls while grocery-anchored centers held up.
Industrial property (factories, warehouses, distribution) is judged on clear height, loading docks, truck access, floor load and power, usually under net leases.
A loft building is a former manufacturing building with large open floors, high ceilings, big windows and freight elevators.
NYC's Loft Law (Multiple Dwelling Law Article 7-C, 1982) protects qualifying loft residents, requires legalization and is overseen by the Loft Board.
In a ground lease the land is leased long term (often 49 to 99 years), the tenant builds and pays the expenses, and the building reverts to the landowner at the end.
The landowner's interest in a ground lease is the leased fee; the ground tenant's interest is the leasehold.
A ground lease lets a developer avoid buying the land (less equity) and lets the landowner keep the land and earn income without selling.
A ground lease is a nonfreehold estate however long: the ground tenant never owns the land, and the building's value to the tenant falls toward zero near the end.
Manhattan ground leases are common (Cooper Union owns the land under the Chrysler Building; Battery Park City is ground leased), so co-op and condo buyers ask when the lease expires.

lessons.title: Reading the Numbers: The Reconstructed Operating Statement, Cash World and Tax World
lessons.tagline: From gross rent down to the cash in the owner's pocket, one line at a time.
objectives: Reconstruct a seller's income and expense statement into an investor's statement
Compute PGI, EGI, NOI, BTCF and cash on cash return
Separate operating expenses from capital expenses and debt service
Compute taxable income and after-tax cash flow in the tax world
Explain what a pro forma statement is and why to distrust it

blocks.title: The setup sheet on Knickerbocker Avenue
blocks.html: The listing broker for a Bushwick mixed-use building (six apartments over two stores) emails Evelyn a one-page "setup": rents, a few expenses, and a big net number. The seller's accountant sends tax returns with a much smaller net. Neither number is what Evelyn will pay for. She hands both to Jordan and says, "Reconstruct it." What does that mean, line by line?
blocks.casual: The listing broker on a Bushwick mixed-use (six apartments over two stores) emails Evelyn a one-page "setup": rents, a handful of expenses, and a big fat net number. The seller's accountant sends tax returns showing a much smaller net. Evelyn won't pay for either one. She slides both over to Jordan: "Reconstruct it." So what does that actually mean, line by line?

deeper.plain: Both the sales sheet and the tax return are slanted. The investor rebuilds the numbers honestly.
deeper.picture: Two friends describe the same date: one brags, one complains. You want the version a neutral camera would show.
deeper.street: The setup shows $86,300 net after the seller tossed in his mortgage and a new roof, while the tax return is even lower thanks to depreciation. Jordan's job is to find what the building really earns for any owner.
deeper.stakes: Pricing off the wrong net number can mean overpaying by hundreds of thousands or losing a deal you should have won.
deeper.exam: The exam calls this reconstructing the operating statement. Look for answers that remove debt service, depreciation and capital items.

blocks.html: Sellers present numbers for their own purposes. A listing setup often overstates income (no vacancy, no management fee). A tax return often understates it (mortgage interest, depreciation, a new roof and the owner's car are all in there). A reconstructed operating statement restates the property's income and expenses the way an investor or appraiser sees them: realistic income, typical operating costs, and nothing that belongs to the owner's financing, taxes or one-time projects.
blocks.casual: Sellers show numbers that serve their own purposes. A listing setup usually pumps up income (no vacancy, no management fee). A tax return usually shrinks it (mortgage interest, depreciation, a new roof and the owner's car are all in there). A reconstructed operating statement redoes the income and expenses the way an investor or appraiser sees them: realistic income, typical operating costs, and nothing that belongs to the owner's financing, taxes or one-time projects.

deeper.plain: You strip out the owner's personal stuff and add back realistic costs to see what the building itself earns.
deeper.picture: Judging a used car's real gas mileage, not what the seller claims on a downhill drive or what his heavy-footed teenager got.
deeper.street: Sal's own books for his Astoria six-unit show nearly no profit because his truck, his cell phone and his mortgage all run through the building. A buyer's reconstruction pulls all that out and shows a healthy NOI.
deeper.stakes: Brokers who pass along the seller's setup without questioning it can be accused of misrepresentation when the buyer's numbers don't hold up.
deeper.exam: Reconstruction removes debt service, depreciation, capital expenses and personal expenses, and adds vacancy and management if missing.

blocks.title: The ladder from rent to cash

items.title: Potential gross income (PGI)
items.html: Every unit rented all year at market or contract rent. The building at 100% occupancy.

items.title: Minus vacancy and credit loss
items.html: Rent lost to empty units and tenants who do not pay. Usually a percentage of PGI.

items.title: Plus other income
items.html: Laundry, parking, storage, a rooftop cell antenna, late fees.

items.title: = Effective gross income (EGI)
items.html: What the building realistically collects.

blocks.casual:
Here's the ladder from rent to cash, one rung at a time:
Potential gross income (PGI): every unit rented all year at market or contract rent. The building 100% full.
Minus vacancy and credit loss: rent you lose to empty units and to tenants who don't pay, usually a percent of PGI.
Plus other income: laundry, parking, storage, a rooftop cell antenna, late fees.
= Effective gross income (EGI): what the building realistically collects.
Minus operating expenses: taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs, payroll, management, reserves.
= Net operating income (NOI): the property's earning power, free and clear of financing.
Minus debt service: yearly mortgage payments, principal plus interest.
= Before-tax cash flow (BTCF): cash in the owner's pocket before income tax.
Minus income tax (figured in the tax world) = After-tax cash flow (ATCF).

deeper.plain: Start with perfect rent, subtract what's realistic to lose, subtract running costs, then the loan, then taxes.
deeper.picture: Your gross paycheck, minus the days you didn't get shifts, plus tips, minus work expenses, minus your car payment, minus taxes. What's left is what you can actually spend.
deeper.street: Jordan writes the ladder on the whiteboard at Hudson & Hart and fills in the Bushwick numbers rung by rung. Diane checks one thing: that the mortgage shows up below NOI, not above it.
deeper.stakes: Putting a line on the wrong rung (debt service above NOI, vacancy off EGI) produces a wrong value and can sink a negotiation.
deeper.exam: Questions often give a jumble of figures and ask for EGI, NOI or BTCF. Walk the ladder in order and stop at the rung asked.

blocks.title: How small commercial deals get financed
blocks.html: Lenders size commercial loans by debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) = NOI / annual debt service, commonly wanting about 1.20 to 1.25 or better, plus a maximum loan to value. Owner-occupied small business buildings are often financed with SBA loans (the 7(a) and 504 programs), which allow lower down payments than conventional commercial loans but require the business to occupy most of the space. The exam focuses on NOI, cap rates and cash flow; DSCR and SBA are practice knowledge.
blocks.casual: How do small commercial deals get financed? Lenders size the loan using the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) = NOI / annual debt service, usually wanting about 1.20 to 1.25 or better, plus a maximum loan to value. Owner-occupied small business buildings often use SBA loans (the 7(a) and 504 programs), which allow smaller down payments than regular commercial loans but require the business to occupy most of the space. The exam leans on NOI, cap rates and cash flow; DSCR and SBA are practical know-how.

deeper.plain: Banks want the building's NOI to cover the mortgage with a cushion, usually 20 to 25% extra.
deeper.picture: A landlord wanting your income to be 40 times the rent: they want proof you can pay with room to spare.
deeper.street: The Bushwick building nets $190,000. At a 1.25 DSCR, the bank allows debt service of $152,000 a year at most. A plumber who wants to buy a Maspeth building for his own shop may use an SBA 504 loan with a smaller down payment.
deeper.stakes: Promising a buyer a loan size the NOI can't support wastes months and can kill the deal at commitment time.
deeper.exam: If DSCR appears, it's NOI divided by debt service. SBA details are rarely tested; focus on NOI and cash flow.

blocks.html: Gross income means income before any expenses. Analysts split it in two. Potential gross income is the maximum: every unit leased all year. Vacancy and credit loss subtracts what you will not collect, from empty units (vacancy) and from tenants who do not pay (credit loss, also called collection loss). Use a market rate even if the building is full today, because nothing stays full forever. Add other income and you have effective gross income.
blocks.casual: Gross income is income before any expenses, and analysts split it in two. Potential gross income is the dream: every unit leased all year. Vacancy and credit loss takes off what you won't collect, from empty units (vacancy) and from tenants who don't pay (credit loss, aka collection loss). Use a market rate even if the building is full today, because nothing stays full forever. Add other income and you've got effective gross income.

deeper.plain: Potential is the best case. Effective is the realistic case after empty units and deadbeats, plus extras.
deeper.picture: A gym with 500 memberships sold. Some people freeze their membership and a few cards bounce. What actually hits the bank is the effective number.
deeper.street: The Bushwick building is 100% leased today, but Jordan still knocks off 5%: $15,300. Then he adds $9,300 from laundry and a cell antenna to reach $300,000 EGI.
deeper.stakes: Zero vacancy in an analysis overstates value. A buyer who pays for it will be short the first time a store sits empty for six months.
deeper.exam: Vacancy comes off potential gross income. Other income is added after vacancy to reach EGI. Watch for answers that subtract vacancy from EGI.

blocks.html: Operating expenses are the recurring costs of running the property. Some are fixed (real estate taxes, insurance: they do not change with occupancy) and some are variable (utilities, repairs, supplies, management fee). Many analysts also include reserves for replacement, an annual set-aside for items that wear out, like boilers, roofs and appliances.
blocks.casual: Operating expenses are the recurring costs of running the place. Some are fixed (real estate taxes, insurance: they don't move with occupancy). Some are variable (utilities, repairs, supplies, management fee). Lots of analysts also include reserves for replacement, a yearly set-aside for stuff that wears out, like boilers, roofs and appliances.

deeper.plain: Running costs are either fixed no matter what or go up and down with use. Reserves save for big replacements.
deeper.picture: Your phone plan is fixed, your grocery bill varies, and the jar where you save for a new laptop is your reserve.
deeper.street: Evelyn's Bushwick budget: taxes $45,000 and insurance $12,000 are fixed. Repairs, utilities and the management fee move with how busy the building is. She adds $300 per unit per year for reserves.
deeper.stakes: Leaving out reserves makes NOI look fatter than it is, and the boiler always dies the year after closing.
deeper.exam: Fixed = taxes and insurance. Variable = utilities, repairs, management. Reserves for replacement may be included in operating expenses.

blocks.html: A capital expenditure is spending that replaces or improves a major component and extends the building's life: a new roof, new windows, a boiler replacement, an elevator modernization. It is not an operating expense and does not reduce NOI. (For taxes, capital costs are depreciated over time.) Fixing a leaky faucet is operating; replacing the whole roof is capital.
blocks.casual: A capital expenditure replaces or upgrades a major component and stretches the building's life: new roof, new windows, a boiler replacement, an elevator modernization. It is not an operating expense and doesn't reduce NOI. (For taxes, capital costs get depreciated over time.) Fixing a leaky faucet is operating. Replacing the whole roof is capital.

deeper.plain: Big one-time upgrades aren't running costs and stay out of NOI.
deeper.picture: Buying a new fridge is different from buying groceries to fill it. Groceries are operating; the fridge is capital.
deeper.street: The Bushwick seller put his $38,000 roof in his expenses. Jordan pulls it out: a buyer won't replace a roof every year. NOI goes up by $38,000 in one move.
deeper.stakes: Treating capital spending as operating crushes NOI and value. Sellers using tax returns to price a building often make this mistake and underprice.
deeper.exam: Capital improvements never go in operating expenses. If an answer subtracts a new roof or boiler to get NOI, it's wrong.

head: Goes in operating expenses (above NOI)
Never in operating expenses
rows: Management fee (even if the owner self-manages)
blocks.caption: NOI never sees the bank, the IRS, or the new roof.

deeper.plain: NOI counts the costs of running the building, not the owner's loan, taxes or upgrades.
deeper.picture: NOI is like a restaurant's profit from the kitchen and the dining room only. The owner's car loan and tax bill are his business, not the restaurant's.
deeper.street: Sal asks Jordan why his mortgage isn't on the reconstructed sheet. Jordan says the next owner might pay all cash; the building's earning power can't depend on Sal's loan.
deeper.stakes: Mixing these categories is the fastest way to misprice a building and lose credibility with investors, appraisers and lenders.
deeper.exam: Memorize the right column: debt service, depreciation, income tax, capital improvements, personal expenses, acquisition costs. None reduce NOI. Management fee does, even if self-managed.

blocks.q: Which item belongs in operating expenses when computing NOI?
c: Mortgage interest
Depreciation
Real estate taxes
Replacing the entire roof
blocks.x: Property taxes are a classic fixed operating expense. Mortgage interest is debt service, depreciation is a tax concept, and a full roof replacement is a capital expenditure. None of those three reduces NOI.

blocks.html: Six apartments at $2,750 a month and two stores at $4,500 a month. The seller's sheet shows no vacancy, no management fee (he collects the rent himself), a $38,000 new roof and his mortgage payments. Here is Jordan's reconstruction:
blocks.casual: Six apartments at $2,750 a month and two stores at $4,500 a month. The seller's sheet shows zero vacancy, no management fee (he collects the rent himself), a $38,000 new roof, and his mortgage payments. Here's how Jordan rebuilt it:

deeper.plain: Jordan starts from the seller's sheet and fixes each line that doesn't belong or is missing.
deeper.picture: Editing a friend's resume: cut what doesn't belong, add what's missing, keep what's true.
deeper.street: Jordan sits at the Hudson & Hart conference table with the seller's sheet, a highlighter and a cold brew, circling every line that's a mortgage, a one-time cost or a missing real-world expense.
deeper.stakes: If Jordan just passed the seller's numbers to Evelyn, she would either walk away from a good building or pay based on fiction.
deeper.exam: Exam versions give a seller's statement and ask which items to remove or add. Practice spotting debt service, capital items and missing management.

head: Line
Seller's sheet
Reconstructed
Why
blocks.caption: Reconstruction moved NOI from a meaningless $86,300 to a real $190,000.

deeper.plain: Fixing the sheet moved NOI from $86,300 to $190,000.
deeper.picture: Cleaning a dirty window. Same view outside, but now you can actually see it.
deeper.street: Jordan's changes: added 5% vacancy (minus $15,300), added 5% management (minus $15,000), removed the roof (plus $38,000) and the mortgage (plus $96,000). Net swing: about $103,700.
deeper.stakes: At a 6% cap rate, a $103,700 NOI difference is worth about $1.7 million in value. Getting reconstruction wrong is a seven-figure mistake.
deeper.exam: Expect a mini version of this table. Total the corrected expenses and subtract from EGI. Check your math: $300,000 minus $110,000 = $190,000.

blocks.html: Net operating income is EGI minus operating expenses. It is the single most important number in commercial real estate: it drives value (Lesson 4), and it is the same no matter who owns the building or how they finance it.
blocks.casual: Net operating income is EGI minus operating expenses. It's the single most important number in commercial real estate: it drives value (Lesson 4), and it's the same no matter who owns the building or how they paid for it.

deeper.plain: NOI is what the building earns before any loan. It's the number everything else is built on.
deeper.picture: A taxi's daily fares minus gas and maintenance. Doesn't matter if the driver owns the car outright or financed it; the car earns the same.
deeper.street: Two buyers bid on the Bushwick building, one with cash and one with a big loan. Both start from the same $190,000 NOI. Their returns differ only after the loan comes in.
deeper.stakes: Any NOI that changes with the buyer's financing is a wrong NOI, and any value built on it is wrong too.
deeper.exam: NOI = EGI minus operating expenses. It excludes debt service. If asked what drives income-approach value, the answer is NOI.

blocks.caption: Build NOI from a rent roll: change rents and vacancy, add expenses, and watch where reserves and capital items belong.

blocks.q: A building has PGI of $500,000, vacancy and credit loss of 6%, other income of $10,000 and operating expenses of $200,000. NOI is:

blocks.text: The cash world: debt service, BTCF and cash on cash

blocks.html: Now add the owner's financing. Evelyn buys for $3,000,000 with a $2,000,000 loan. Annual debt service (12 monthly payments of principal and interest) is $150,000. She invests $1,000,000 of her own cash (equity).
blocks.casual: Now bring in the owner's financing. Evelyn buys for $3,000,000 with a $2,000,000 loan. Annual debt service (12 monthly payments of principal and interest) is $150,000. She puts in $1,000,000 of her own cash (equity).

deeper.plain: Debt service is the year's mortgage payments, and equity is the owner's own cash in the deal.
deeper.picture: A car loan: your yearly payments are debt service, and your down payment is your equity.
deeper.street: Tasha lines up the $2,000,000 loan at $12,500 a month. Twelve payments equals $150,000 a year. Evelyn wires $1,000,000 of her own money at closing.
deeper.stakes: Using monthly payments where the formula needs annual numbers throws every return off by a factor of 12.
deeper.exam: Debt service includes both principal and interest. Equity = price minus loan. Always annualize.

blocks.title: Cash world
blocks.html:
NOI $190,000
minus debt service $150,000
= before-tax cash flow $40,000

Cash on cash return = BTCF / equity = $40,000 / $1,000,000 = 4%.
blocks.casual:
Cash world math:
NOI $190,000
minus debt service $150,000
= before-tax cash flow $40,000
Cash on cash = BTCF / equity = $40,000 / $1,000,000 = 4%.

deeper.plain: After paying the bank, Evelyn keeps $40,000, which is 4% on her million.
deeper.picture: Your take-home after rent: what matters is what's left, compared with what you put in.
deeper.street: Evelyn's money market paid her 4% with zero headaches. Now she's getting 4% on her $1,000,000 while dealing with two stores and six apartments. She's not thrilled.
deeper.stakes: Buyers who see a 6% building and assume they'll earn 6% on their cash get a rude surprise. Run the cash world before recommending a purchase.
deeper.exam: Cash on cash = BTCF / equity. Distractors divide by the price or the loan.

blocks.html: Cash flow is the money left after all cash payments. Before-tax cash flow (BTCF) is NOI minus debt service. The cash on cash return, also called the equity dividend rate, is BTCF divided by the cash the investor put in. It answers Evelyn's real question: what is my own money earning?
blocks.casual: Cash flow is the money left after every cash payment. Before-tax cash flow (BTCF) is NOI minus debt service. The cash on cash return, also called the equity dividend rate, is BTCF divided by the cash the investor put in. It answers Evelyn's real question: what is my own money earning?

deeper.plain: Cash on cash tells you what your own money is earning after the mortgage.
deeper.picture: A dividend on a stock you own: what you get paid each year divided by what you paid in.
deeper.street: Two Queens investors compare deals over dinner. One brags about a 7% cap rate; the other has a 10% cash on cash. They're measuring different things, and the second one is talking about his own cash.
deeper.stakes: Quoting cap rate when an investor asks about cash on cash (or the reverse) can mislead them into a deal that doesn't meet their goals.
deeper.exam: Equity dividend rate = cash on cash. Both mean BTCF / equity. Know both names.

blocks.title: Spot the leverage
blocks.html: Free and clear, this building returns $190,000 / $3,000,000 = 6.33%. Evelyn's cash on cash is only 4%. Her loan costs $150,000 / $2,000,000 = 7.5% a year, more than the building earns. That is negative leverage, straight from Lesson 1. She either negotiates the price down, finds cheaper debt, or borrows less.
blocks.casual: Spot the leverage. Free and clear, this building returns $190,000 / $3,000,000 = 6.33%. Evelyn's cash on cash is only 4%. Her loan costs $150,000 / $2,000,000 = 7.5% a year, which is more than the building earns. That's negative leverage, straight out of Lesson 1. She can negotiate the price down, find cheaper debt, or borrow less.

deeper.plain: The loan costs 7.5% and the building earns 6.33%, so borrowing drags her return down.
deeper.picture: Paying 7.5% on a credit card to buy something that pays you back 6.33%. You lose a little on every dollar you charge.
deeper.street: Evelyn counters at $2,700,000. At that price the building's free-and-clear return rises to about 7.04%, closer to the loan cost, and her cash on cash improves.
deeper.stakes: Advising a client to max out a loan under negative leverage shrinks their return and raises their risk at the same time.
deeper.exam: Compare cap rate (NOI / price) with the mortgage constant (debt service / loan). If the constant is higher, leverage is negative.

blocks.text: The tax world: taxable income and ATCF

blocks.html: The cash world tracks real dollars. The tax world tracks what the IRS taxes, and it treats two items differently. Only the interest part of debt service is deductible (principal repayment is not, because it pays down your own loan). And depreciation is deductible even though no cash leaves the account.
blocks.casual: The cash world follows real dollars. The tax world follows what the IRS taxes, and it treats two things differently. Only the interest part of debt service is deductible (principal isn't, because it's paying down your own loan). And depreciation is deductible even though no cash leaves your account.

deeper.plain: For taxes, you deduct interest but not principal, and you deduct depreciation even though you didn't spend it.
deeper.picture: Two scorecards for the same game: one counts the actual money in your wallet, the other counts what the IRS says you earned.
deeper.street: Evelyn pays $150,000 to the bank, but her accountant deducts only $130,000 of interest. Then he deducts $50,000 of depreciation she never actually wrote a check for.
deeper.stakes: Deducting principal on a tax estimate understates tax owed. Clients who rely on that get hit with a bill and penalties.
deeper.exam: Tax world: NOI minus interest minus depreciation = taxable income. Principal is never deductible.

blocks.title: Tax world for the Bushwick building (simplified, full first year)
blocks.html:
Depreciable basis: $3,000,000 price minus $1,050,000 land = $1,950,000. Less than 80% of the rent comes from apartments, so the building is nonresidential for tax: 39 years. Depreciation = $1,950,000 / 39 = $50,000.
Year-one interest on the loan: $130,000 (the other $20,000 of debt service is principal).

NOI $190,000
minus interest $130,000
minus depreciation $50,000
= taxable income $10,000
x 30% tax bracket = tax $3,000

Back to the cash world: BTCF $40,000 minus tax $3,000 = after-tax cash flow $37,000.
blocks.casual:
Tax world for the Bushwick building (simplified, full first year):
Depreciable basis: $3,000,000 price minus $1,050,000 land = $1,950,000. Less than 80% of the rent comes from apartments, so for tax it's nonresidential: 39 years. Depreciation = $1,950,000 / 39 = $50,000.
Year-one interest: $130,000 (the other $20,000 of debt service is principal).
NOI $190,000 minus interest $130,000 minus depreciation $50,000 = taxable income $10,000. At a 30% bracket, that's $3,000 tax.
Back to the cash world: BTCF $40,000 minus $3,000 tax = after-tax cash flow $37,000.

deeper.plain: Evelyn keeps $40,000 in cash but only pays tax on $10,000.
deeper.picture: Your employer lets you log a big business expense you didn't pay out of pocket that year. Your take-home stays the same; your tax bill shrinks.
deeper.street: The apartments bring in $198,000 of $306,000 in rent, about 65%. Because that's under 80%, the IRS treats the building as nonresidential and Evelyn depreciates over 39 years, not 27.5.
deeper.stakes: Using 27.5 years on a mixed-use building that doesn't qualify overstates depreciation and invites an audit. Refer specifics to a CPA.
deeper.exam: Remove land before dividing. 27.5 years residential rental, 39 years nonresidential. Taxable income uses interest, not full debt service.

blocks.html: After-tax cash flow is BTCF minus the income tax the property generates. Notice the shelter at work: Evelyn pocketed $40,000 of cash but paid tax on only $10,000. If depreciation and interest had exceeded NOI, the property would show a tax loss, which can save tax on other income (subject to the passive loss rules in Subject 17), making ATCF larger than BTCF.
blocks.casual: After-tax cash flow is BTCF minus the income tax the property creates. See the shelter working? Evelyn pocketed $40,000 in cash but paid tax on just $10,000. If depreciation plus interest had been more than NOI, the property would show a tax loss, which can save tax on other income (subject to the passive loss rules in Subject 17), making ATCF bigger than BTCF.

deeper.plain: A building can put cash in your pocket while showing a small profit, or even a loss, on paper.
deeper.picture: Getting a refund on a store purchase you didn't return. You keep the item and the store's math says you came out even.
