deeper.street: If Evelyn's interest had been $150,000 instead of $130,000, taxable income would be minus $10,000. If the passive loss rules let her use it, that loss could trim tax on her other income, making her after-tax cash bigger than before-tax.
deeper.stakes: Overpromising tax losses to a buyer who can't use them under the passive activity rules is a bad look and a potential claim. Point them to a tax professional.
deeper.exam: ATCF = BTCF minus tax. A tax loss can make ATCF exceed BTCF. Know that depreciation is the main reason real estate is called a shelter.

left.title: Cash world
items: NOI minus FULL debt service (principal + interest)
Result: BTCF
Depreciation ignored (no check is written)
BTCF minus tax = ATCF

right.title: Tax world
items: NOI minus INTEREST only
Minus depreciation (land never depreciated)
Result: taxable income
Taxable income x tax rate = tax owed

deeper.plain: Cash world subtracts the whole mortgage. Tax world subtracts only interest, and also depreciation.
deeper.picture: Two lenses on the same camera: one shows real money, the other shows taxable money.
deeper.street: Jordan puts the two columns side by side for Evelyn: $40,000 in cash, $10,000 taxable. She nods and says that gap is why she owns buildings instead of bonds.
deeper.stakes: Confusing the two worlds leads to wrong cash flow projections, wrong tax estimates and clients who don't trust your numbers.
deeper.exam: The exam asks which items appear in each world. Principal: cash only. Depreciation: tax only. Interest: both.

blocks.q: NOI is $120,000, debt service is $100,000 of which $85,000 is interest, and depreciation is $30,000. Taxable income is:
c: Negative $10,000
blocks.x: Tax world: $120,000 minus $85,000 interest minus $30,000 depreciation = $5,000. Subtracting all $100,000 of debt service mixes in principal, which is not deductible, and gives the wrong answer of negative $10,000.

blocks.text: Pro forma: the future, as the seller imagines it

blocks.html: A pro forma statement is a projected income and expense statement: what the property is expected to earn in the future, often after renovations, lease-up or rent increases. Pro formas are essential for development and value-add deals, and dangerous in marketing materials. "Pro forma NOI" in a listing usually assumes every rent goes to market and nothing goes wrong. Investors value on actual numbers and treat the pro forma as the seller's opinion.
blocks.casual: A pro forma statement is a projected income and expense statement: what the property is expected to earn down the road, often after renovations, lease-up or rent bumps. Pro formas are essential for development and value-add deals, and dangerous in marketing. "Pro forma NOI" in a listing usually assumes every rent hits market and nothing goes wrong. Investors value on actual numbers and treat the pro forma as the seller's opinion.

deeper.plain: A pro forma is a forecast, and in a listing it's usually an optimistic one.
deeper.picture: The dating profile photo versus the person who shows up. Plan around who shows up.
deeper.street: A Crown Heights listing touts a 7% pro forma cap rate. The actual rent roll, with four stabilized units, delivers 4.2%. Evelyn bids on the 4.2%.
deeper.stakes: Passing off pro forma numbers as actual is a misrepresentation that can lead to DOS complaints and lawsuits. Label projections clearly.
deeper.exam: Pro forma = projected. Investors and appraisers rely on actual, reconstructed figures for value.

blocks.title: Exam traps
blocks.html: (1) NOI is before debt service. If an answer subtracts the mortgage to get NOI, it is wrong. (2) Vacancy comes off potential gross income. (3) Cash on cash divides by equity, not by the price. (4) In the tax world only interest is deductible, not principal.
blocks.casual: Exam traps to watch: (1) NOI comes before debt service. If an answer subtracts the mortgage to get NOI, it's wrong. (2) Vacancy comes off potential gross income. (3) Cash on cash divides by equity, not price. (4) In the tax world, only interest is deductible, not principal.

deeper.plain: Four mistakes the test is built to catch: mortgage in NOI, vacancy off the wrong line, wrong divisor, and deducting principal.
deeper.picture: A recipe where the order matters: add the eggs at the wrong step and the cake fails.
deeper.street: Marcus once told a client NOI was "what's left after the mortgage." The client's appraiser disagreed in writing and the client called Diane to ask if Marcus knew what he was doing.
deeper.stakes: These mix-ups cost credibility with investors and lenders and can wreck pricing on a listing.
deeper.exam: Read each answer for which line it subtracts from. These four traps account for most income statement wrong answers.

blocks.title: Hook: the ladder
blocks.html: P-V-E-O-N-D-B: Potential, minus Vacancy, Effective, minus Operating, NOI, minus Debt service, BTCF. "Please Verify Every Owner's Numbers Before Buying."
blocks.casual: Memorize the ladder: P-V-E-O-N-D-B. Potential, minus Vacancy, Effective, minus Operating, NOI, minus Debt service, BTCF. Or: "Please Verify Every Owner's Numbers Before Buying."

deeper.plain: The sentence helps you remember the order of the income statement.
deeper.picture: Like a subway line: you can't get to BTCF without passing through NOI first.
deeper.street: Jordan mutters "Please Verify Every Owner's Numbers" every time a listing setup lands in his inbox, then grabs a highlighter.
deeper.stakes: Getting the order wrong under exam pressure costs easy points.
deeper.exam: Write P-V-E-O-N-D-B on your scratch paper first, then plug in the numbers.

story.title: Two Sets of Books
story.setting: Evelyn's office above her Fort Greene retail building, late afternoon

beats.text: Evelyn's desk holds two documents for the Bushwick building: the broker's glossy setup and the seller's tax return. They do not agree on anything.
The setup says $315,300 of income. Full occupancy.
Nothing in Brooklyn is full forever. Take 5% off the potential gross for vacancy and credit loss.
beats.tag: PGI minus vacancy and credit loss

beats.text: So $306,000 minus $15,300, plus the $9,300 laundry and antenna money. $300,000 effective gross.
Now expenses. The seller manages it himself, so he shows no management fee.
But you won't collect rent yourself. Add 5% of EGI: $15,000.
There's also a $38,000 roof and $96,000 of mortgage payments in here.
Roof is capital. Mortgage is his financing, not the building's. Both out.
beats.tag: Capital items and debt service are not operating expenses

check.q: Why did Evelyn remove the mortgage payments when reconstructing the statement?
c: They are capital expenditures
NOI is measured before debt service, so it does not depend on the owner's financing
Mortgage payments are not tax deductible
Only the seller can deduct them
check.x: NOI measures the property, not the owner's loan. Debt service is subtracted later, from NOI, to get before-tax cash flow.

beats.text: Total operating expenses $110,000. NOI $190,000.
Now my loan. $150,000 a year on two million borrowed, a million of my own cash in. What's left?
$40,000 before tax. That's 4% cash on cash.
And the building earns 6.33% free and clear. My loan costs 7.5%. Tell me what that means.
Negative leverage. You'd earn more on your cash if you borrowed less, or paid less.
Then I'll pay less. And the tax side: interest, not principal, plus depreciation on the building only. $10,000 taxable on $40,000 of cash. The shelter is the only part of this deal I like so far.
(on speakerphone) Jordan, if you remember one thing: NOI never sees the bank, the IRS, or the new roof.

board.prompt: Write the ladder from PGI to ATCF down the left side. Fill in the Bushwick numbers, then draw a branch for the tax world showing interest and depreciation.

facts.text: A reconstructed operating statement restates income and expenses as a typical investor sees them; listing setups overstate income and tax returns understate it.
Potential gross income is every unit rented all year at full rent (100% occupancy).
Vacancy and credit loss comes off PGI at a market rate even if the building is full; adding other income gives effective gross income.
NOI is EGI minus operating expenses; it is the key number in commercial real estate and is the same no matter who owns or how it is financed.
NOI is figured before debt service: mortgage payments, depreciation, income taxes, capital improvements and personal expenses are never operating expenses.
Fixed expenses (taxes, insurance) do not change with occupancy; variable expenses (utilities, repairs, supplies, management) do.
Reserves for replacement are an annual set-aside for components that wear out, such as boilers, roofs and appliances.
A capital expenditure (new roof, boiler, windows) extends the building's life, is not an operating expense, and is depreciated for tax.
A market management fee is included even if the owner self-manages, usually figured as a percentage of EGI.
Lenders size commercial loans by DSCR (NOI / debt service), commonly about 1.20 to 1.25 or better; owner-occupied business buildings often use SBA 7(a) or 504 loans.
Before-tax cash flow is NOI minus annual debt service (principal plus interest).
Cash on cash return (equity dividend rate) is BTCF divided by the investor's own cash, not by the price.
When the loan constant (7.5%) exceeds the free-and-clear return (6.33%), cash on cash falls below it: negative leverage.
In the tax world only the interest part of debt service is deductible (not principal), and depreciation is deducted though no cash is paid.
Depreciable basis excludes land; a building is residential (27.5 years) only if at least 80% of rent comes from dwelling units, otherwise nonresidential (39 years).
Taxable income is NOI minus interest minus depreciation; ATCF is BTCF minus the tax, and a tax loss that offsets other income can make ATCF exceed BTCF.
A pro forma is a projected income and expense statement; in marketing it is the seller's opinion, and investors value on actual numbers.

lessons.title: What Is It Worth? Cap Rates and the IRV Triangle
lessons.tagline: Income divided by rate equals value. One formula, three unknowns, and a lot of exam points.
objectives: Solve any IRV problem for income, rate or value
Derive a cap rate from comparable sales and apply it to a subject property
Explain why value falls when cap rates rise and how sensitive value is to small rate changes
Use the debt coverage ratio to see whether a deal can carry its loan

blocks.title: Asking $3.4 million
blocks.html: The Bushwick mixed-use building is listed at $3,400,000. Jordan's reconstructed NOI is $190,000. The listing broker says, "Buildings like this trade at a 5.5 cap, so it's a steal." Evelyn pulls three recent sales on nearby blocks and starts dividing. Who is right about the price, and how much does half a point of cap rate matter?
blocks.casual: The Bushwick mixed-use is listed at $3,400,000. Jordan's reconstructed NOI is $190,000. The listing broker says, "Buildings like this trade at a 5.5 cap, it's a steal." Evelyn pulls three recent sales on nearby blocks and starts dividing. So who's right about the price, and how much does half a point of cap rate really matter?

deeper.plain: The market's cap rate turns NOI into a price, and a small change in that rate moves the price a lot.
deeper.picture: Like an exchange rate at the airport: a tiny change in the rate makes a big difference when you're converting a lot of money.
deeper.street: At a 5.5 cap, $190,000 of NOI is worth about $3.45 million. At 6.25, it's $3.04 million. Evelyn's comps will settle the argument, not the listing broker's confidence.
deeper.stakes: Brokers who quote cap rates without checking comps lose credibility and can push clients into overpaying.
deeper.exam: When a stem gives NOI and a cap rate, you're solving V = I / R. When it gives NOI and a price, you're solving for R.

blocks.html: Investors buy income. So the simplest way to value an income property is to ask what price makes its NOI produce the return the market expects. That expected return is the capitalization rate (cap rate): NOI divided by value. Turning one year's NOI into a value is called direct capitalization, and it is the heart of the income approach to appraisal.
blocks.casual: Investors are buying income. So the simplest way to value an income property is to ask: what price makes this NOI pay the return the market expects? That expected return is the capitalization rate (cap rate): NOI divided by value. Turning one year's NOI into a value is called direct capitalization, and it's the heart of the income approach to appraisal.

deeper.plain: A cap rate is the yearly return an all-cash buyer would earn, and it lets you turn income into a price.
deeper.picture: If a vending machine makes $1,000 a year and people expect a 10% return, it's worth about $10,000.
deeper.street: Evelyn looks at a Jackson Heights retail building netting $120,000. Local retail trades around a 6% cap, so she figures about $2 million before she even tours it.
deeper.stakes: A seller who prices without understanding cap rates either sits on the market for a year or gives away value.
deeper.exam: Cap rate = NOI / value. Direct capitalization = one year's NOI divided by a cap rate. It's the income approach.

blocks.html: The IRV formula has three parts. I is income (always annual NOI). R is the rate (cap rate, as a decimal). V is value (or price). Know two, solve for the third.
blocks.casual: The IRV formula has three pieces. I is income (always annual NOI). R is the rate (cap rate, as a decimal). V is value (or price). Know any two and you can solve for the third.

deeper.plain: Income, rate and value are linked. Have two, find the third.
deeper.picture: Speed, distance and time from grade school: same trick, new labels.
deeper.street: A Bronx seller knows his NOI is $90,000 and wants $1.5 million. Jordan divides to show the implied cap rate is 6%, then checks whether local comps support it.
deeper.stakes: Plugging monthly income or gross rent into IRV produces wildly wrong values. Annual NOI only.
deeper.exam: I = R x V, R = I / V, V = I / R. Most IRV questions are one or two steps of arithmetic.

head: You want
Formula
Example
blocks.caption: Cover the one you want on the triangle: I on top, R and V on the bottom.

deeper.plain: Cover the letter you need: income on top, rate times value on the bottom.
deeper.picture: A triangle with I above a line, R and V below. Cover I and you see R x V; cover V and you see I over R.
deeper.street: Jordan sketches the triangle on a napkin at a Ridgewood cafe while Evelyn quizzes him. $84,000 over $1.2 million: 7%. Instant.
deeper.stakes: Freezing on the formula during a client meeting makes you look unprepared, and investors notice.
deeper.exam: Draw the triangle on your scratch paper before you start. It prevents dividing in the wrong direction.

blocks.caption: Cover the unknown. I sits on top, R and V side by side underneath. Slide the cap rate and watch value move the opposite way.

blocks.q: A building produces NOI of $96,000 and sells for $1,600,000. What is the cap rate?
blocks.x: R = I / V = $96,000 / $1,600,000 = 0.06, or 6%. Dividing the other way ($1,600,000 / $96,000 = 16.7) gives a multiplier, not a rate.

blocks.text: Deriving the cap rate from comparable sales

blocks.html: Where does the rate come from? From the market. Find recent sales of similar buildings, divide each one's NOI by its sale price, and see where they cluster. Use comps that are truly similar in location, size, condition, tenant quality and lease terms, and reconstruct each comp's NOI the same way you reconstructed the subject's.
blocks.casual: Where does the rate come from? The market. Find recent sales of similar buildings, divide each one's NOI by its sale price, and see where they bunch up. Use comps that really match on location, size, condition, tenant quality and lease terms, and reconstruct each comp's NOI the same way you did the subject's.

deeper.plain: You find the cap rate by dividing NOI by price on similar recent sales.
deeper.picture: Figuring out what your used bike is worth by checking what similar bikes sold for this month.
deeper.street: Jordan pulls three Bushwick mixed-use sales from ACRIS and calls the brokers for NOI. One comp's NOI ignored vacancy, so he reconstructs it before dividing.
deeper.stakes: Comparing apples to oranges, like a renovated building to a gut job, produces a cap rate that misprices the subject.
deeper.exam: Cap rate derived from comparable sales = NOI / sale price for each comp. This is how appraisers get a market rate.

head: Comparable sale
Price
NOI
Cap rate
blocks.caption: Bushwick mixed-use comps cluster between 6.0% and 6.5%.

deeper.plain: The three sales show buyers paying prices that work out to 6.0% to 6.5% returns.
deeper.picture: Three neighbors sold similar cars for prices that cluster close together. That cluster is the market.
deeper.street: Myrtle at 6.25%, Wilson at 6.00%, Irving at 6.50%. Wilson is the biggest and closest match, so Evelyn pays close attention to its 6%.
deeper.stakes: Cherry-picking the one comp that supports your listing price misleads your client and gets exposed by any appraiser.
deeper.exam: Expect a small comp table and a question asking for a comp's cap rate or the appropriate range.

blocks.title: Valuing the subject
blocks.html:
Comps range 6.0% to 6.5%. The subject is average for the group, so Evelyn uses 6.25%.

V = I / R = $190,000 / 0.0625 = $3,040,000.

The asking price implies R = $190,000 / $3,400,000 = 5.59%, well below every comp. The broker's "5.5 cap" claim does not match the market.
blocks.casual:
Comps run 6.0% to 6.5%. The subject is about average for the group, so Evelyn uses 6.25%.
V = I / R = $190,000 / 0.0625 = $3,040,000.
The asking price implies R = $190,000 / $3,400,000 = 5.59%, lower than every single comp. The broker's "5.5 cap" line doesn't match the market.

deeper.plain: At market rates the building is worth about $3.04 million, not $3.4 million.
deeper.picture: A pair of sneakers that sells everywhere for $100 listed at $112 with a sign that says "deal."
deeper.street: Evelyn offers $3,000,000 and tells the listing broker to send a comp at 5.5% if he has one. He doesn't. They settle at $3,050,000.
deeper.stakes: Pushing a client to pay $3.4 million here would cost them about $360,000 over market. That's the kind of advice that ends relationships.
deeper.exam: Two-step questions: derive the market rate from comps, then divide NOI by it. Or compute the implied rate from the asking price and compare.

blocks.html: Cap rate and value move in opposite directions. A higher cap rate means investors demand more return for each dollar, so they pay less. Riskier property (weak tenants, short leases, bad location, old systems) gets a higher cap rate and a lower value. Safer property (a pharmacy with 20 years of lease left) trades at a lower cap rate and a higher value. Rising interest rates usually push cap rates up, which is why values fell in 2023 even where rents held.
blocks.casual: Cap rate and value move in opposite directions. A higher cap rate means investors want more return per dollar, so they pay less. Riskier property (weak tenants, short leases, bad location, old systems) gets a higher cap rate and a lower value. Safer property (a pharmacy with 20 years left on its lease) trades at a lower cap rate and a higher value. Rising interest rates usually shove cap rates up, which is why values dropped in 2023 even where rents held steady.

deeper.plain: Higher cap rate, lower price. Lower cap rate, higher price.
deeper.picture: A seesaw: rate goes up on one end, value drops on the other.
deeper.street: In 2021 Evelyn's Staten Island CVS would have sold at a 5% cap. By 2023, with rates up, buyers wanted 6.5%. Same rent, same tenant, but the building lost almost a quarter of its value.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who remember the old cap rate overprice and sit unsold. Brokers who don't explain rate shifts lose listings to those who do.
deeper.exam: Inverse relationship. If a question says cap rates rose, value fell. Riskier property equals higher cap rate.

head: Cap rate
Value of $190,000 NOI
Change vs 6.25%
blocks.caption: Same building, same rent. Half a point of cap rate moves value by more than $200,000.

deeper.plain: Half a point of cap rate swings value by more than $200,000 on this one building.
deeper.picture: Adjusting a telescope: a tiny turn of the dial moves the image a long way.
deeper.street: The Bushwick building is worth $3,454,545 at 5.5% and $2,714,286 at 7%. That's a $740,000 spread from a 1.5 point difference on the same rent roll.
deeper.stakes: When buyer and seller argue about half a point, they're really arguing about hundreds of thousands of dollars. Know that before you negotiate.
deeper.exam: Lower rate gives a higher value. You may be asked which rate produces the highest value: pick the smallest rate.

blocks.html: Flip it around: each extra dollar of NOI is worth many dollars of value. At a 6.25% cap, $1 of NOI is worth $1 / 0.0625 = $16. Cut $10,000 of waste from the expenses and the building is worth $160,000 more. That is why owners fight tax assessments and renegotiate service contracts.
blocks.casual: Flip it around: every extra dollar of NOI is worth many dollars of value. At a 6.25% cap, $1 of NOI is worth $1 / 0.0625 = $16. Cut $10,000 of waste from expenses and the building is worth $160,000 more. That's why owners fight tax assessments and renegotiate service contracts.

deeper.plain: Saving a little each year on expenses adds a lot to what the building is worth.
deeper.picture: A multiplier in a video game: every point you score counts sixteen times.
deeper.street: Sal wins a $6,000 reduction in his Astoria property taxes through a tax certiorari appeal. At a 6.25% cap, his building just gained $96,000 in value.
deeper.stakes: Owners who ignore small expense leaks leave real value on the table. Brokers who spot them win listings.
deeper.exam: Value change = NOI change / cap rate. A $10,000 NOI increase at 8% adds $125,000 of value.

blocks.q: If the cap rate applied to a property increases while NOI stays the same, the property's value:
c: Increases
Decreases
Stays the same
Doubles
blocks.x: V = I / R. A bigger R in the denominator produces a smaller V. Rate and value move in opposite directions.

blocks.title: Exam traps in IRV problems
blocks.html: (1) Monthly vs annual: if the question gives monthly rent or monthly NOI, multiply by 12 first. (2) Gross vs net: cap rates apply to NOI, so subtract vacancy and operating expenses before dividing. (3) Decimals: 8% is 0.08, not 0.8. (4) Debt service is never subtracted before capitalizing.
blocks.casual: IRV traps on the exam: (1) Monthly vs annual: if they give monthly rent or monthly NOI, multiply by 12 first. (2) Gross vs net: cap rates use NOI, so take off vacancy and operating expenses before dividing. (3) Decimals: 8% is 0.08, not 0.8. (4) Debt service never comes off before you capitalize.

deeper.plain: Use yearly NOI, use the right decimal, and never subtract the mortgage.
deeper.picture: A recipe in grams when you're measuring in ounces. The formula is fine; the units ruin it.
deeper.street: A practice question gives a Yonkers building netting $11,000 a month at a 7% cap. Jordan first writes $132,000, then divides by 0.07 to get about $1.886 million.
deeper.stakes: On a real deal, a decimal slip changes the value tenfold. On the exam, each one is a lost point.
deeper.exam: Wrong answers are built from these exact mistakes: monthly NOI, gross rent, 0.8 instead of 0.08, or NOI minus debt service.

blocks.title: Multi-step: from rent to value
blocks.html:
A 10-unit building in Yonkers rents each unit for $1,800 a month. Vacancy and credit loss 4%. Operating expenses $70,000. Market cap rate 7.5%.

PGI = 10 x $1,800 x 12 = $216,000
Vacancy 4% = $8,640, so EGI = $207,360
NOI = $207,360 minus $70,000 = $137,360
Value = $137,360 / 0.075 = $1,831,467 (about $1.83 million).
blocks.casual:
Multi-step, from rent to value. A 10-unit building in Yonkers, each unit $1,800 a month. Vacancy and credit loss 4%. Operating expenses $70,000. Market cap rate 7.5%.
PGI = 10 x $1,800 x 12 = $216,000
Vacancy 4% = $8,640, so EGI = $207,360
NOI = $207,360 minus $70,000 = $137,360
Value = $137,360 / 0.075 = $1,831,467 (about $1.83 million).

deeper.plain: Build NOI from rent first, then divide by the cap rate.
deeper.picture: Assembling furniture: you can't attach the top before the legs are on.
deeper.street: Diane hands this exact problem to Jordan on his second day. He forgets vacancy the first time and gets $1.95 million; she makes him do it again.
deeper.stakes: Skipping vacancy here overstates value by about $115,000. Real buyers and appraisers will catch it.
deeper.exam: Annualize, subtract vacancy from PGI, subtract expenses, then divide. Each skipped step is a planted wrong answer.

blocks.html: Cap rate is a one-year snapshot. It assumes this year's NOI is representative. For a building with leases rolling to much higher or lower market rents, or a big vacancy about to be filled, investors also run a multi-year discounted cash flow, which is the time value of money from Lesson 1 applied to the pro forma from Lesson 3. For the exam, direct capitalization with IRV is what you will be tested on.
blocks.casual: A cap rate is a one-year snapshot. It assumes this year's NOI is typical. For a building with leases rolling to much higher or lower market rents, or a big vacancy about to fill, investors also run a multi-year discounted cash flow: the time value of money from Lesson 1 applied to the pro forma from Lesson 3. For the exam, direct capitalization with IRV is what gets tested.

deeper.plain: Cap rates look at one year. When income is about to change a lot, investors look year by year.
deeper.picture: A single photo versus a time-lapse. For a plant that's about to bloom, you want the time-lapse.
deeper.street: A Flatiron office building has a tenant paying $45 a foot whose lease expires next year, with market at $70. Evelyn knows a cap on today's NOI undervalues it, so she runs a 10-year DCF.
deeper.stakes: Using one year's NOI on a building in transition can badly over- or underprice it.
deeper.exam: Know that DCF exists and why. The exam math sticks to IRV.

blocks.text: Can the deal carry the loan? Debt coverage ratio

blocks.html: Lenders run their own test. The debt coverage ratio (DCR, also called debt service coverage ratio) is NOI divided by annual debt service. Bushwick: $190,000 / $150,000 = 1.27. A DCR of 1.0 means NOI exactly covers the mortgage with nothing to spare; below 1.0 the owner is feeding the building from his own pocket. Commercial lenders commonly require a cushion, often around 1.20 to 1.25 or more, and they size the loan to hit it.
blocks.casual: Lenders run their own test. The debt coverage ratio (DCR, aka debt service coverage ratio) is NOI divided by annual debt service. Bushwick: $190,000 / $150,000 = 1.27. A DCR of 1.0 means NOI just barely covers the mortgage with nothing left over; under 1.0 the owner is feeding the building from his own pocket. Commercial lenders usually want a cushion, often around 1.20 to 1.25 or more, and they size the loan to hit it.

deeper.plain: The bank checks that the building's income covers the loan payments with room to spare.
deeper.picture: Your friend asks to borrow money. You want to see that their paycheck covers the payment plus a buffer for surprises.
deeper.street: Tasha tells Evelyn that at a 1.25 DCR the most debt service the Bushwick building can support is $190,000 / 1.25 = $152,000 a year. Her $150,000 loan just clears.
deeper.stakes: Overestimating loan size leads to a smaller commitment than expected, and the buyer may not have the extra cash to close.
deeper.exam: DCR = NOI / debt service. Below 1.0 = negative cash flow. Don't confuse DCR with cap rate or cash on cash.

left.title: Cap rate (direct capitalization)
items: Uses NOI (after vacancy and expenses)
Value = NOI / cap rate
Standard for commercial and investment property

right.title: Gross rent multiplier (GRM)
items: Uses gross rent (before expenses)
Value = gross rent x GRM
Rough screen for small residential income property

deeper.plain: Cap rate uses net income and is the commercial standard. GRM uses gross rent and is a quick screen for small rentals.
deeper.picture: A full physical exam versus checking someone's temperature. Both tell you something; one is much more thorough.
deeper.street: Jordan uses a GRM to quickly screen a dozen Queens two-families in an afternoon, then switches to full NOI and cap rate on the two Leo actually likes.
deeper.stakes: GRM ignores expenses. Two buildings with the same rent can have very different taxes and costs, so relying on GRM alone can badly misprice.
deeper.exam: GRM = price / gross rent. It's for small residential income property. Cap rate uses NOI. The trap is mixing gross and net.

blocks.q: An investor wants a 7% return on a strip center producing NOI of $252,000. The most she should pay is:
blocks.x: V = I / R = $252,000 / 0.07 = $3,600,000. Multiplying ($252,000 x 0.07 = $17,640) and misplacing the decimal is the common mistake that produces the wrong choices.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: IRV: I Really Value it. Income on top, Rate times Value below. And cap rate up, price down, like a seesaw.
blocks.casual: Remember: IRV: I Really Value it. Income on top, Rate times Value underneath. And cap rate up, price down, like a seesaw.

deeper.plain: A catchy name for the formula and the opposite relationship between rate and price.
deeper.picture: A seesaw on a Brooklyn playground: one side up, the other down.
deeper.street: Evelyn says she doesn't need a calculator for the first look. She just needs IRV, a napkin and the comps.
deeper.stakes: Freezing on the basic formula in front of a client tells them you're not ready for investment work.
deeper.exam: Use this for fast checks: if a rate went up, value went down. Pick accordingly.

story.title: Half a Point
story.setting: The listing broker's office on Broadway, Bushwick, under the J train

beats.text: The J train rattles the windows every four minutes. The listing broker leans back like he has already been paid.
Mixed use in Bushwick trades at a 5.5 cap. Your NOI is $190,000. Do the math, it's worth more than I'm asking.
At 5.5%, $190,000 divided by 0.055 is about $3.45 million.
Correct arithmetic. Wrong rate. Jordan, the comps.
Myrtle sold at 6.25%, Wilson at 6%, Irving at 6.5%. Middle of the pack is 6.25%.
beats.tag: Derive the cap rate from comps

beats.text: That's a $400,000 difference over three quarters of a point!
Exactly why we argue about it. Small rate, big value.
beats.tag: Value is very sensitive to the cap rate

check.q: If Evelyn agreed to a 6% cap instead of 6.25% on $190,000 NOI, the price would be about:
check.x: $190,000 / 0.06 = $3,166,667. A lower cap rate gives a higher value.

beats.text: Rates are coming down. Cap rates will follow.
Then the next buyer can pay for that. I pay for today's NOI at today's rate. And my lender wants 1.25 times coverage. At $3.4 million my loan shrinks and my cash on cash gets ugly.
The broker stares at the ceiling. A J train passes. He says he will call his seller.
Outside: So the higher the cap rate, the lower the price. It's a seesaw.
And every dollar of NOI is worth sixteen at 6.25%. Remember that when someone tells you a few thousand in expenses doesn't matter.

board.prompt: Draw the IRV triangle. Below it, solve three problems: find V for $190,000 NOI at 6.25%, find R for $84,000 NOI on $1.2 million, and find I for $2.5 million at 7%.

facts.text: The cap rate is NOI divided by value; direct capitalization turns one year's NOI into value and is the heart of the income approach.
IRV: Income = Rate x Value, Rate = Income / Value, Value = Income / Rate.
A market cap rate is derived from comparable sales by dividing each comp's NOI by its price, using truly similar, reconstructed comps.
Dividing NOI by the asking price shows the cap rate the seller is implying, which can be checked against the comps.
Cap rate and value move in opposite directions: with NOI unchanged, a higher cap rate means a lower value.
Riskier property trades at a higher cap rate and lower value; safer property (a long-leased pharmacy) at a lower cap rate; rising interest rates push cap rates up.
Each dollar of NOI is worth 1 / cap rate in value, so cutting expenses or raising NOI adds the change divided by the cap rate.
IRV traps: convert monthly figures to annual, capitalize NOI not gross rent, use decimals correctly, and never subtract debt service first.
Multi-step valuation: PGI minus vacancy gives EGI, minus operating expenses gives NOI, divided by the cap rate gives value.
A cap rate is a one-year snapshot; for income about to change, investors also run a multi-year discounted cash flow.
Debt coverage ratio is NOI divided by annual debt service; below 1.0 NOI does not cover the mortgage, and lenders commonly want about 1.20 to 1.25.
A gross rent multiplier values property as gross rent x GRM (before expenses), a rough screen for small residential income property; cap rates use NOI.

lessons.title: Measuring Space and Writing the Lease: RSF, Loss Factors, Lease Types and Key Clauses
lessons.tagline: In commercial real estate you pay for space you never stand in, and the lease decides who pays for everything else.
objectives: Distinguish rentable, usable and carpetable square footage and compute loss and add-on factors
Compare gross, net, office, retail, percentage and loft leases
Compute percentage rent using the natural breakpoint
Explain use, assignment and sublease, SNDA, attornment and estoppel clauses
Compare direct metering, submetering and rent inclusion for electricity

blocks.title: 10,000 feet that fit in 8,000
blocks.html: Leo Brandt's startup needs office space. He finds a Flatiron floor advertised at "10,000 square feet, $60 a foot." He measures it with a laser tape and gets about 8,000. He emails Jordan a spreadsheet titled WHERE ARE MY 2,000 FEET. Is the landlord cheating him?
blocks.casual: Leo's startup needs an office. He finds a Flatiron floor advertised as "10,000 square feet, $60 a foot." He walks it with a laser tape and gets about 8,000. Then he emails Jordan a spreadsheet titled WHERE ARE MY 2,000 FEET. Is the landlord ripping him off?

deeper.plain: Office rent is charged on more space than you actually get to use, by design.
deeper.picture: Buying a 12-inch pizza and finding the crust takes up two inches. You paid for the whole pie, but you eat less.
deeper.street: Leo's 8,000 measured feet plus his share of the lobby, corridors, elevator lobby and mechanical rooms adds up to 10,000 rentable. Jordan explains this before Leo fires off an angry email to the landlord.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who don't understand rentable versus usable sign for too little space, then can't fit their team. Brokers who don't explain it look clueless or dishonest.
deeper.exam: When a stem says a tenant measured less than advertised, the concept is rentable vs usable and the loss factor.

blocks.text: Three ways to measure the same floor

blocks.html: Commercial space has three measurements, from largest to smallest. Rentable square footage (RSF) is what the tenant pays rent on: its own space plus its share of the building's common areas (lobby, corridors, shared restrooms, mechanical rooms, mail room). Usable square footage (USF) is the space the tenant actually occupies exclusively. Carpetable square footage is the usable area minus walls, columns, convector enclosures and built-ins: the floor you could actually cover with carpet.
blocks.casual: Commercial space gets measured three ways, biggest to smallest. Rentable square footage (RSF) is what the tenant pays rent on: its own space plus its share of the building's common areas (lobby, corridors, shared restrooms, mechanical rooms, mail room). Usable square footage (USF) is the space the tenant actually has to itself. Carpetable square footage is usable minus walls, columns, convector enclosures and built-ins: the floor you could actually lay carpet on.

deeper.plain: Rentable includes shared spaces, usable is yours alone, carpetable is the open floor inside that.
deeper.picture: A dorm room: rentable includes your share of the hallway bathroom and lounge, usable is your room, carpetable is the floor left after the radiator and the built-in closet.
deeper.street: A Midtown law firm plans for 40 offices based on 15,000 RSF. The architect measures carpetable area and finds room for only 34 once columns and convectors are taken out.
deeper.stakes: Planning a layout from rentable numbers leads to a space that doesn't fit and expensive redesigns.
deeper.exam: Order: rentable > usable > carpetable. Rent is quoted per rentable square foot.

head: Measure
Includes
Who cares
rows: Landlord: rent is quoted per RSF per year
Tenant: what it can actually use
Space planners and the carpet installer
blocks.caption: Rentable is always the biggest number, carpetable the smallest.

deeper.plain: Landlords charge on rentable, tenants live in usable, designers plan in carpetable.
deeper.picture: Russian nesting dolls: carpetable fits inside usable, which fits inside rentable.
deeper.street: Jordan sends Leo a floor plan with three outlines: the whole floor's rentable share, the suite's usable walls, and the shaded carpetable area. Leo finally stops yelling.
deeper.stakes: Quoting the wrong measure in a proposal can lead to disputes over the rent and the deal.
deeper.exam: Rentable is always the biggest number. A question asking which measure rent is based on: rentable.

blocks.html: So no, Leo is not being cheated. He is seeing the gap between rentable and usable. That gap is measured two ways, and the exam loves both.
blocks.casual: So no, Leo's not getting cheated. He's seeing the gap between rentable and usable. That gap gets measured two ways, and the exam loves both.

deeper.plain: The missing space is his share of common areas, and it's normal.
deeper.picture: Paying your share of a building's gym fee even though you only use the treadmill.
deeper.street: Jordan calls Leo: "Your 2,000 feet are the elevator lobby, the restrooms and the corridors everyone shares. Every building on the block does it. The question is how big the gap is."
deeper.stakes: Telling a client they're being cheated when it's standard practice can blow up a fair deal and embarrass you.
deeper.exam: This is the setup for loss factor and add-on factor math.

blocks.title: Loss factor and add-on factor
blocks.html:
Rentable 10,000. Usable 8,000. Common area share 2,000.

Loss factor = (rentable minus usable) / rentable = 2,000 / 10,000 = 20%. Leo "loses" 20% of what he pays for.

Add-on factor = rentable / usable minus 1 = 10,000 / 8,000 minus 1 = 25%. The landlord "adds on" 25% to Leo's usable space.

Same 2,000 feet, two percentages. The loss factor divides by rentable; the add-on factor divides by usable.
blocks.casual:
Rentable 10,000. Usable 8,000. Common area share 2,000.
Loss factor = (rentable minus usable) / rentable = 2,000 / 10,000 = 20%. Leo "loses" 20% of what he pays for.
Add-on factor = rentable / usable minus 1 = 10,000 / 8,000 minus 1 = 25%. The landlord "adds on" 25% to Leo's usable space.
Same 2,000 feet, two percentages. Loss factor divides by rentable; add-on factor divides by usable.

deeper.plain: The same 2,000 feet is 20% of what he pays for and 25% on top of what he uses.
deeper.picture: A $100 shirt on sale for $80 is 20% off. Going back from $80 to $100 is a 25% markup. Same $20, different base.
deeper.street: Leo's board asks why the landlord says 25% and Jordan says 20%. Jordan explains both are right: different denominators. The board relaxes.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up the two lets a landlord make a building sound more efficient than it is. Tenants overpay.
deeper.exam: Loss factor over rentable, add-on over usable. The wrong answer is always the other percentage.

blocks.html: Manhattan office loss factors have traditionally run higher than in most markets, often in the 20% to 30% range or more, because buildings are measured generously and older towers have big cores. That is why smart tenants compare space on cost per usable foot, not the advertised rent.
blocks.casual: Manhattan office loss factors have traditionally run higher than most markets, often 20% to 30% or more, because buildings get measured generously and older towers have big cores. That's why smart tenants compare space on cost per usable foot, not the advertised rent.

deeper.plain: Manhattan charges for a lot of shared space, so compare what you pay per foot you can use.
deeper.picture: Comparing cereal by price per ounce, not price per box, since some boxes are mostly air.
deeper.street: A tenant compares a 1920s Grand Central tower with a giant core and a newer Hudson Yards floor. The older building's lower asking rent disappears once the bigger loss factor is factored in.
deeper.stakes: Tenant brokers who compare only asking rents can steer clients into the more expensive option.
deeper.exam: Exam emphasis: higher loss factor means less usable space per rentable foot, raising effective cost.

blocks.title: Which floor is cheaper?
blocks.html:
Floor A: $55 per RSF, 20% loss factor. Floor B: $52 per RSF, 28% loss factor.

Cost per usable foot = rent per RSF / (1 minus loss factor).
A: $55 / 0.80 = $68.75 per usable foot.
B: $52 / 0.72 = $72.22 per usable foot.

The "cheaper" $52 floor actually costs more for every foot Leo can use. And if he needs 6,000 usable feet on Floor A, he must rent 6,000 / 0.80 = 7,500 RSF.
blocks.casual:
Floor A: $55 per RSF, 20% loss factor. Floor B: $52 per RSF, 28% loss factor.
Cost per usable foot = rent per RSF / (1 minus loss factor).
A: $55 / 0.80 = $68.75 per usable foot.
B: $52 / 0.72 = $72.22 per usable foot.
The "cheaper" $52 floor actually costs more for every foot Leo can use. And if he needs 6,000 usable feet on Floor A, he has to rent 6,000 / 0.80 = 7,500 RSF.

deeper.plain: The lower asking rent loses once you count only the space you actually use.
deeper.picture: Two gyms: one is $5 cheaper a month but half its machines are always broken. Per working machine, it's the pricier one.
deeper.street: Leo needs 6,000 usable feet. Floor A: 7,500 RSF at $55 = $412,500 a year. Floor B: about 8,333 RSF at $52 = about $433,333. Floor B costs him roughly $20,800 more a year.
deeper.stakes: Choosing on headline rent can waste tens of thousands a year over a 10-year lease. That's real money for a startup.
deeper.exam: Divide rent per RSF by (1 minus loss factor) for usable cost. Divide usable need by (1 minus loss factor) for RSF needed.

blocks.q: A suite has 12,500 rentable square feet and 10,000 usable square feet. The loss factor is:
blocks.x: Loss factor = (12,500 minus 10,000) / 12,500 = 2,500 / 12,500 = 20%. Dividing by usable instead gives 25%, which is the add-on factor.

blocks.text: Lease types: who pays the expenses?

blocks.caption: Slide from gross to triple net and watch taxes, insurance and maintenance move from the landlord's column to the tenant's.

blocks.html: In a gross lease the tenant pays a flat rent and the landlord pays the building's operating expenses. In a net lease the tenant pays rent plus some or all of the expenses. The labels vary by market, but the classic ladder is:
blocks.casual: In a gross lease the tenant pays one flat rent and the landlord pays the building's operating expenses. In a net lease the tenant pays rent plus some or all of the expenses. Labels vary by market, but here's the classic ladder:

deeper.plain: Gross: landlord pays the bills. Net: tenant pays some or all of them on top of rent.
deeper.picture: An all-inclusive resort versus a hotel where you pay for the room and then get billed for meals, wifi and parking.
deeper.street: A Bay Ridge dentist signs a gross lease at $4,000 a month and never thinks about the tax bill. The bakery next door signs a net lease at $3,200 plus its share of taxes and insurance.
deeper.stakes: Comparing a gross rent to a net rent without adding expenses makes the net deal look cheaper than it is.
deeper.exam: Gross = landlord pays expenses. Net = tenant pays expenses in addition to rent.

head: Lease
Tenant pays besides rent
Common use
rows: Base rent covers expenses in a base year; tenant pays increases (escalations)
blocks.caption: Exact meanings vary; always read what the lease actually shifts.

deeper.plain: Each step up the ladder shifts more expenses from landlord to tenant.
deeper.picture: Splitting a household: first you pay just rent, then you add the electric bill, then insurance, then repairs, until you're paying for everything including the roof.
deeper.street: Evelyn's Staten Island pharmacy is on an absolute net lease: the tenant even fixes the roof. Her Midtown office tenants are on modified gross with base year escalations.
deeper.stakes: Assuming "net" means the same thing in every lease can leave a landlord stuck with costs they thought the tenant was paying. Read the lease.
deeper.exam: NN = taxes and insurance. NNN adds maintenance/CAM. Absolute net = everything including structure. Modified gross = base year plus escalations.

blocks.html: A triple net lease gives the landlord the most predictable income: expenses rise, and the tenant pays them. That is why NNN buildings with strong tenants (a pharmacy, a bank branch) trade at low cap rates.
blocks.casual: A triple net lease gives the landlord the most predictable income: when expenses go up, the tenant pays them. That's why NNN buildings with strong tenants (a pharmacy, a bank branch) trade at low cap rates.

deeper.plain: With a triple net lease, the tenant absorbs rising costs, so the landlord's income is steady.
deeper.picture: Renting out your car and the renter pays gas, insurance and repairs. You just collect the check.
deeper.street: A Chase branch on a 15-year NNN lease in Bayside sells at a 5.25% cap while a multi-tenant office building nearby trades at 7.5%. Buyers pay up for predictability.
deeper.stakes: Investors who confuse NNN with gross can wildly overestimate their NOI and overpay.
deeper.exam: NNN plus a strong credit tenant = low risk = low cap rate = high value.

blocks.title: Office lease vs retail lease in New York

left.title: Office lease
items: Rent per RSF per year, quoted modified gross
Tenant pays its share of increases in taxes and operating costs over a base year
Landlord often gives a tenant improvement allowance and free rent
Terms commonly 5 to 15 years
Electricity billed separately or included

right.title: Retail lease
items: Often net or triple net with CAM charges
May include percentage rent on sales
Use clause and exclusives matter a lot
Signage, hours, storefront, venting for restaurants
Co-tenancy and radius clauses in centers

deeper.plain: Office leases revolve around rentable feet and base years. Retail leases revolve around the storefront, sales and the tenant mix.
deeper.picture: An office lease is renting a desk in a co-working space. A retail lease is renting a booth at a busy market where location and foot traffic are everything.
deeper.street: Jordan handles a Midtown office lease one week (TI allowance, free rent, base year) and a Steinway Street restaurant lease the next (venting, use clause, percentage rent). Totally different conversations.
deeper.stakes: Using an office lease template for a restaurant can miss venting, grease traps and exclusives, causing fights and possibly a failed business.
deeper.exam: Percentage rent and CAM are retail features. Base year escalations and RSF are office features.

blocks.html: An office lease is built around RSF, a base year and escalations (Lesson 6). A retail lease is built around the storefront: what the tenant may sell, and often how much it sells. In shopping centers, tenants pay common area maintenance (CAM) charges, their share of cleaning, lighting, snow removal, security and parking lot upkeep.
blocks.casual: An office lease revolves around RSF, a base year and escalations (Lesson 6). A retail lease revolves around the storefront: what the tenant can sell and, often, how much it sells. In shopping centers, tenants pay common area maintenance (CAM) charges, their share of cleaning, lighting, snow removal, security and parking lot upkeep.

deeper.plain: Retail tenants in centers chip in for the shared spaces through CAM charges.
deeper.picture: Splitting the cost of cleaning the shared kitchen with roommates, based on how big your room is.
deeper.street: A Staten Island strip center bills each tenant CAM by square footage. After a heavy snow year, the pizza shop's CAM jumps $2,000 and the owner calls Jordan to ask if that's legal. It is, if the lease says so.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who don't budget for CAM increases can fall behind on rent, and brokers who didn't explain it hear about it.
deeper.exam: CAM = common area maintenance, paid by retail tenants, usually pro rata.

blocks.title: The good guy guarantee
blocks.html: NYC office landlords often ask a small company's principal for a good guy guarantee instead of a full personal guarantee. The principal guarantees rent only until the tenant gives notice, moves out, pays through the move-out date and hands back the keys. It protects the landlord from a tenant who stops paying but stays.
blocks.casual: NYC office landlords often ask a small company's principal for a good guy guarantee instead of a full personal guarantee. The principal guarantees rent only until the tenant gives notice, moves out, pays through the move-out date and hands back the keys. It protects the landlord from a tenant who stops paying but won't leave.

deeper.plain: The owner promises to pay only until the business leaves cleanly, not for the whole lease.
deeper.picture: Promising your roommate you'll cover rent until you move out and hand back the key, not for every month left on the lease.
deeper.street: Leo signs a good guy guarantee on his Flatiron lease. If his startup fails, he gives notice, pays through move-out and returns the keys. He's off the hook for the remaining years.
deeper.stakes: A tenant who signs a full personal guarantee by mistake can be personally liable for years of rent if the business fails.
deeper.exam: A good guy guarantee is limited to the period until the tenant vacates properly. It's a NYC office practice.

blocks.text: Percentage leases and the natural breakpoint

blocks.html: A percentage lease charges a base (minimum) rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales above a breakpoint. The landlord shares in a successful store; the tenant pays a lower base rent. The natural breakpoint (natural break-even) is the sales level where the percentage of sales exactly equals the base rent: base rent divided by the percentage rate. A negotiated breakpoint above or below that is an artificial breakpoint.
blocks.casual: A percentage lease charges a base (minimum) rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales above a breakpoint. The landlord shares in a store's success; the tenant gets a lower base rent. The natural breakpoint (natural break-even) is the sales level where the percentage of sales exactly equals the base rent: base rent divided by the percentage rate. A negotiated breakpoint above or below that is an artificial breakpoint.

deeper.plain: The tenant pays a base rent, and once sales pass a certain point, a cut of the extra sales.
deeper.picture: A musician who gets a flat fee from a bar plus a cut of drink sales once the bar has a really good night.
deeper.street: A Flushing bubble tea shop pays $60,000 base plus 8% over the breakpoint. Breakpoint: $60,000 / 0.08 = $750,000. If sales hit $900,000, it owes another $12,000.
deeper.stakes: Getting the breakpoint wrong can mean billing a tenant for overage they don't owe, which leads to disputes and lost tenants.
deeper.exam: Natural breakpoint = base rent / percentage rate. Watch for answers that multiply instead of divide.

blocks.title: Steinway Street bakery
blocks.html:
Annual base rent $72,000. Percentage rent 6% of gross sales above the natural breakpoint. Sales this year $1,500,000.

Natural breakpoint = $72,000 / 0.06 = $1,200,000.
Sales above breakpoint = $1,500,000 minus $1,200,000 = $300,000.
Percentage rent (overage) = $300,000 x 0.06 = $18,000.
Total rent = $72,000 + $18,000 = $90,000.

Check: 6% of all $1,500,000 is also $90,000. With a natural breakpoint, total rent is simply the greater of base rent or the percentage of total sales.
blocks.casual:
A Steinway Street bakery: annual base rent $72,000, percentage rent 6% of gross sales over the natural breakpoint, sales this year $1,500,000.
Natural breakpoint = $72,000 / 0.06 = $1,200,000.
Sales over the breakpoint = $1,500,000 minus $1,200,000 = $300,000.
Overage = $300,000 x 0.06 = $18,000.
Total rent = $72,000 + $18,000 = $90,000.
Double check: 6% of the full $1,500,000 is also $90,000. With a natural breakpoint, total rent is just the bigger of base rent or the percentage of total sales.

deeper.plain: The bakery owes base rent plus 6% of everything sold over $1.2 million.
deeper.picture: A tip jar that only starts filling after the barista's base wage has been covered by sales.
deeper.street: The Astoria bakery has its best year ever. The landlord sends a bill for $18,000 in overage, backed by the bakery's sales report as the lease requires. The owner pays it gladly; it was a great year.
deeper.stakes: Landlords who don't audit sales reports can miss overage. Tenants who don't track the breakpoint can be surprised by a big bill.
deeper.exam: Steps: breakpoint = base / rate; overage = (sales minus breakpoint) x rate; total = base + overage. Quick check: rate x total sales.

blocks.q: A tenant pays $48,000 base rent plus 4% of sales over the natural breakpoint. Sales are $1,500,000. Total annual rent is:

blocks.html: A loft lease rents space in a loft building, usually raw or lightly finished open floors for light manufacturing, storage, showrooms, studios or creative offices. The tenant typically takes the space close to "as is" and pays for its own build-out, in exchange for lower rent. Freight elevator rights, floor load and permitted use are key terms, and residential use is not allowed unless the building is legally converted.
blocks.casual: A loft lease rents space in a loft building, usually raw or lightly finished open floors for light manufacturing, storage, showrooms, studios or creative offices. The tenant typically takes it close to "as is" and pays for its own build-out, in exchange for lower rent. Freight elevator rights, floor load and permitted use are the key terms, and living there isn't allowed unless the building has been legally converted.

deeper.plain: Loft leases are cheap, raw space where the tenant fixes it up and can't live in it.
deeper.picture: Renting an empty garage for your band. Cheap, but you bring the soundproofing, and you can't sleep there.
deeper.street: A Gowanus furniture maker leases a raw loft floor at $28 a foot, builds out a workshop, and negotiates freight elevator access from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Moving a bed in would violate the lease and the certificate of occupancy.
deeper.stakes: Letting a loft tenant live there illegally can create Loft Law issues and violations for the owner.
deeper.exam: Loft lease = commercial use of loft space, tenant does the build-out. Residential use only with legal conversion.

blocks.text: Lease clauses every licensee must recognize

head: Clause
What it does
Why it matters
rows: States what the tenant may use the space for
Protects other tenants' exclusives and the building's zoning; a narrow use makes the lease harder to assign
Tenant transfers its entire remaining interest
Assignee deals with the landlord directly; original tenant usually stays liable unless released
Tenant rents part of the space or part of the term to a subtenant
Tenant remains the landlord's tenant and collects from the subtenant
Lease ranks below the landlord's mortgage
Lets the landlord finance the building
Lender agrees not to evict a tenant in good standing after a foreclosure
Protects the tenant's lease if the landlord defaults
Tenant agrees to recognize a new owner (buyer or foreclosing lender) as landlord
Keeps the lease alive and rent flowing after a transfer
Tenant certifies rent, deposit, term and no defaults
Buyer and lender rely on it; tenant cannot later claim otherwise
blocks.caption: Subordination, non-disturbance and attornment usually travel together as one SNDA agreement.

deeper.plain: These clauses control what the tenant can do, who can take over, and what happens if the building is sold or foreclosed.
deeper.picture: The fine print of a phone contract: what you can use it for, whether you can transfer it, and what happens if the carrier gets bought.
deeper.street: Evelyn sells her White Plains building. The buyer's lender demands estoppel certificates from every tenant confirming rent and no defaults. One tenant claims a $50,000 TI credit no one remembered, and the price gets adjusted before closing.
deeper.stakes: A missing estoppel or SNDA can delay a sale or refinance for weeks and cost a deal. Tenants who sign estoppels carelessly lose claims they had.
deeper.exam: Estoppel = tenant certifies lease facts. Attornment = recognize a new landlord. Non-disturbance = lender won't evict a tenant in good standing.

blocks.html: An SNDA (subordination, non-disturbance and attornment agreement) is the three-way deal among lender, landlord and tenant: the tenant subordinates, the lender promises non-disturbance, and the tenant promises to attorn. Commercial leases usually require the tenant to sign an SNDA or estoppel within a short window, often about 10 days, when asked.
blocks.casual: An SNDA (subordination, non-disturbance and attornment agreement) is the three-way deal among lender, landlord and tenant: the tenant agrees its lease ranks below the mortgage, the lender promises not to disturb the tenant, and the tenant promises to recognize a new owner. Commercial leases usually require the tenant to sign an SNDA or estoppel within a short window, often about 10 days, when asked.

deeper.plain: The tenant steps behind the bank, the bank promises not to kick the tenant out, and the tenant agrees to pay whoever ends up owning the building.
deeper.picture: A handshake among three people: you go second in line, I won't throw you out, and you'll keep paying whoever takes over the store.
deeper.street: Evelyn refinances her Bushwick building. The new lender sends SNDAs to both store tenants. The bakery signs within 10 days; the cell phone store drags its feet and nearly delays her closing.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who don't get non-disturbance can be wiped out in a foreclosure. Landlords whose tenants won't sign can't close their loans.
deeper.exam: SNDA = Subordination + Non-disturbance + Attornment. Know which party gives which promise.

blocks.html: The use clause deserves a second look. A landlord wants it narrow ("retail bakery and cafe, and for no other purpose") to protect exclusives promised to other tenants, keep a good tenant mix and stay within the certificate of occupancy. A tenant wants it broad ("any lawful retail use") so it can change concepts or assign the lease to a buyer of the business. A restaurant use also triggers venting, grease traps and extra insurance, so landlords price it differently. Assignment and sublease clauses usually require the landlord's written consent, and many give the landlord a right to take the space back (recapture) or share in any profit the tenant makes on a sublease.
blocks.casual: The use clause deserves a second look. The landlord wants it narrow ("retail bakery and cafe, and for no other purpose") to protect exclusives promised to other tenants, keep a good tenant mix and stay within the certificate of occupancy. The tenant wants it broad ("any lawful retail use") so it can change concepts or assign the lease to whoever buys the business. A restaurant use also brings venting, grease traps and extra insurance, so landlords price it differently. Assignment and sublease clauses usually need the landlord's written consent, and many give the landlord the right to take the space back (recapture) or share in any profit the tenant makes on a sublease.

deeper.plain: Landlords want a tight use clause; tenants want a loose one. Transfers usually need landlord approval.
deeper.picture: A food court where each stall gets one cuisine so the tacos and the other tacos don't fight for the same customers.
deeper.street: A Williamsburg cafe wants to sell its business, but its use clause says "coffee bar only." The buyer wants to serve dinner. The landlord refuses consent, so the sale falls apart.
deeper.stakes: Narrow use clauses can trap a tenant who wants to pivot or sell. A broker who ignores this in negotiation can cost the client its exit.
deeper.exam: Use clause controls permitted use. Recapture lets the landlord take the space back. Consent is usually required for assignment or sublease.

blocks.title: Assignment vs sublease
blocks.html: Assignment = all of the remaining term and space. Sublease = less than all (part of the space or part of the time). In both, the original tenant usually stays liable to the landlord. And New York's statutory right to sublet (RPL 226-b, residential buildings with 4 or more units) does not apply to commercial leases. A commercial tenant's rights are whatever the lease says.
blocks.casual: Keep these straight. Assignment = all of the remaining term and space. Sublease = less than all (part of the space or part of the time). Either way, the original tenant usually stays on the hook to the landlord. And New York's statutory right to sublet (RPL 226-b, residential buildings with 4 or more units) does not apply to commercial leases. A commercial tenant gets only the rights the lease spells out.

deeper.plain: Handing over everything is assignment, handing over part is a sublease, and commercial tenants have no automatic right to do either.
deeper.picture: Giving your gym membership to a friend for the rest of the year is assignment. Letting them use it on Tuesdays is subletting.
deeper.street: Leo's startup shrinks and wants to sublet half the Flatiron floor. He assumes NY law gives him that right. Priya points out RPL 226-b is residential only; his lease controls, and it requires landlord consent.
deeper.stakes: Telling a commercial client they have a statutory right to sublet is wrong advice that can lead to a default and eviction.
deeper.exam: All = assignment, part = sublease. RPL 226-b = residential, 4+ units. Commercial = whatever the lease says.

blocks.q: A buyer of a shopping center asks each tenant to sign a statement confirming its rent, security deposit and that the landlord is not in default. This document is:
c: An attornment agreement
An estoppel certificate
A non-disturbance agreement
An assignment
blocks.x: An estoppel certificate confirms the lease facts so the buyer or lender can rely on them. Attornment is the tenant's promise to recognize a new landlord, a different thing.

head: Method
How it works
Who carries the usage risk
rows: Tenant has its own utility meter and account (Con Edison, National Grid) and pays the utility
Landlord buys power in bulk through a master meter; a submeter measures each tenant's use; landlord bills the tenant, often with an administrative charge
Tenant pays for actual use; landlord handles billing
Electricity is included in rent at a set charge per RSF, often adjusted by a survey of the tenant's equipment and by utility rate changes
Landlord, unless the lease allows adjustments
blocks.caption: Older NYC office leases often use rent inclusion; newer leases favor submetering.

deeper.plain: Tenants pay for power on their own meter, through the landlord's submeter, or as a flat amount built into rent.
deeper.picture: Your own phone plan, a family plan where each line is tracked, or an all-you-can-use plan bundled with your rent.
deeper.street: An older Garment District lease includes electricity at $3.50 per RSF. The tenant adds servers and space heaters, and the landlord eats the cost until a new electrical survey adjusts the charge.
deeper.stakes: Landlords with rent inclusion and no adjustment clause can lose money as tenant usage grows. Tenants on submeters with high admin fees can overpay.
deeper.exam: Direct meter = tenant pays the utility. Submeter = landlord bills actual use. Rent inclusion = flat charge in rent, landlord carries usage risk.

blocks.title: Hooks
blocks.html: Rentable > Usable > Carpetable: "Really Useful Carpet." Loss over Rentable, Add-on over Usable. Natural breakpoint = Base / Percent.
blocks.casual: Lock these in: Rentable > Usable > Carpetable: "Really Useful Carpet." Loss over Rentable, Add-on over Usable. Natural breakpoint = Base / Percent.

deeper.plain: Three quick hooks for the three formulas in this lesson.
deeper.picture: Labels on drawers so you grab the right formula without digging.
deeper.street: Jordan writes "Really Useful Carpet" on a sticky note on his monitor and stops confusing the measures during tours.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up the denominators costs points on the exam and credibility with tenants.
deeper.exam: Jot these three on your scratch paper before starting the math questions.

story.title: Where Are My 2,000 Feet
story.setting: A Flatiron office floor, Leo with a laser tape measure

beats.text: Ten thousand feet advertised. I measured eight thousand. I have a spreadsheet. It has a tab called BETRAYAL.
You measured usable. They quote rentable. Rentable includes your share of the lobby, the elevator corridor, the restrooms down the hall.
beats.tag: Rentable = usable + share of common areas

beats.text: So I pay $60 a foot for a lobby I walk through twice a day.
Everyone does. Two thousand of ten thousand is a 20% loss factor. Or a 25% add-on, if you divide by usable.

check.q: Leo's floor is 10,000 RSF and 8,000 USF. What is the add-on factor?
check.x: Add-on = rentable / usable minus 1 = 1.25 minus 1 = 25%. The 20% figure is the loss factor, which divides by rentable.

beats.text: The SoHo loft was $52 a foot though. Cheaper.

With a 28% loss factor. $52 divided by 0.72 is $72.22 per usable foot. This one is $60 divided by 0.80, $75. Close, but the loft is cheaper per usable foot. It's raw though. You'd pay for the build-out.
Raw how?
Loft lease. Open floor, freight elevator, you take it as is and build your own offices. Lower rent, bigger check up front.
beats.tag: Loft lease: as is, tenant builds out

beats.text: The landlord's agent hands over a draft lease. Leo highlights everything.
Subordination, non-disturbance, attornment. Is this a lease or a spell?

If the landlord's bank forecloses, non-disturbance means they can't kick you out while you're paying. Attornment means you'll pay the new owner. And when the building sells, they'll ask you for an estoppel certificate confirming your rent and that nobody's in default.
And electricity?
Submetered. You pay for what you actually use, through the landlord, plus a small admin charge. Better than rent inclusion if your engineers don't run space heaters.
(later, reviewing the file) Rentable, usable, carpetable. Biggest to smallest. Make every tenant compare on usable and nobody will ever email you a tab called BETRAYAL again.

board.prompt: Sketch an office floor. Shade the tenant's usable space, hatch the common areas, and compute loss factor and add-on factor from your own numbers.

facts.text: Rentable square footage is usable space plus a share of common areas (lobby, corridors, shared restrooms), and rent is quoted per RSF.
Usable square footage is the tenant's exclusive space; carpetable is usable minus walls, columns and built-ins; rentable > usable > carpetable.
Loss factor = (rentable minus usable) / rentable.
Add-on factor = rentable / usable minus 1 (10,000 RSF over 8,000 USF is 25%).
Cost per usable foot = rent per RSF / (1 minus loss factor), and RSF needed = usable / (1 minus loss factor); Manhattan loss factors often run 20% to 30%.
In a gross lease the landlord pays operating expenses; in a net lease the tenant pays rent plus some or all of them.
Single net: taxes; double net: taxes and insurance; triple net: taxes, insurance and maintenance; absolute net: everything, even structure and roof.
A modified gross lease (the NYC office norm) covers expenses at base-year levels in base rent, and the tenant pays its share of increases.
Shopping center tenants pay common area maintenance (CAM) charges, their share of cleaning, lighting, snow removal, security and parking lot upkeep.
A NYC good guy guarantee makes a principal liable for rent only until the tenant gives notice, pays through move-out and surrenders the keys.
A percentage lease charges base rent plus a percentage of sales above a breakpoint; the natural breakpoint is base rent divided by the percentage rate.
With a natural breakpoint, total rent is the greater of base rent or the percentage times total sales.
A loft lease rents raw open space the tenant builds out at its own cost for lower rent; residential use needs legal conversion.
Landlords want a narrow use clause to protect exclusives, tenant mix and the C of O; tenants want it broad to change concepts or assign.
Assignment transfers all the remaining term and space; a sublease transfers less; the original tenant usually stays liable in both.
NY's statutory right to sublet (RPL 226-b) covers residential buildings with 4 or more units only; a commercial tenant's rights are whatever the lease says.
Subordination ranks the lease below the mortgage; non-disturbance is the lender's promise not to evict a tenant in good standing after foreclosure.
Attornment is the tenant's agreement to recognize a new owner, including a foreclosing lender, as landlord.
An estoppel certificate is the tenant's signed statement of rent, deposit, term and no defaults, which buyers and lenders rely on.
An SNDA is the three-way lender, landlord and tenant agreement, and leases usually require it (or an estoppel) within about 10 days of a request.
Electricity is paid by direct meter (tenant pays the utility), submeter (landlord bills actual use from a master meter) or rent inclusion (a set charge in rent).

lessons.title: Escalations: How Rent Keeps Up With Taxes, Wages and Inflation
lessons.tagline: A ten-year lease at a flat rent is a slow-motion loss. Escalation clauses are the fix.
objectives: Explain why escalation clauses exist and what they protect
Compute a tenant's proportionate share and its base year tax and operating escalations
Distinguish a base year from an expense stop
Compute porter's wage, fixed percentage and CPI escalations

blocks.title: A bill in year two
blocks.html: A year after moving into his Flatiron office, Leo gets a letter from the landlord: "Tenant's share of real estate tax and operating expense escalations: $18,000." His rent was supposed to be fixed. He forwards it to Jordan with one word: "???" Is the landlord allowed to do this?
blocks.casual: A year after moving into his Flatiron office, Leo gets a letter from the landlord: "Tenant's share of real estate tax and operating expense escalations: $18,000." Wait, wasn't his rent fixed? He forwards it to Jordan with one word: "???" So can the landlord actually do this?

deeper.plain: Most commercial leases let the landlord pass along rising costs, so "fixed" rent isn't really fixed.
deeper.picture: A phone plan with a fixed monthly price plus "regulatory fees" that creep up every year.
deeper.street: Leo's lease has a base year clause on page 14. Jordan walks him through it: the $18,000 is his 5% share of the building's tax and operating cost increases since year one.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who don't budget for escalations get blindsided, and their brokers get the angry call. Explain them before signing.
deeper.exam: When a stem describes a tenant surprised by a bill for increased taxes or expenses, the topic is escalation clauses.

blocks.html: Commercial leases run 5, 10, even 20 years. If rent stays flat while taxes, wages, fuel and insurance climb, the landlord's NOI shrinks every year. That is exactly what happened to New York landlords in the 1970s, when inflation and the energy crisis sent costs soaring while rents were locked in long leases. Landlords responded by writing lease escalation clauses into nearly every commercial lease: provisions that raise the rent as costs or prices rise, so the landlord's net income keeps its value.
blocks.casual: Commercial leases run 5, 10, even 20 years. If rent stays flat while taxes, wages, fuel and insurance keep rising, the landlord's NOI shrinks every year. That's exactly what happened to New York landlords in the 1970s, when inflation and the energy crisis sent costs through the roof while rents sat locked in long leases. So landlords started writing lease escalation clauses into almost every commercial lease: provisions that raise the rent as costs or prices climb, so the landlord's net income holds its value.

deeper.plain: Escalation clauses keep a landlord's profit from melting away over a long lease.
deeper.picture: A salary with an automatic cost-of-living raise. Without it, your paycheck buys less every year.
deeper.street: Evelyn signs a 15-year lease with a Bay Ridge pharmacy. Without escalations, her $200,000 rent would be eaten alive by rising taxes and insurance by year 10. With them, her NOI stays steady.
deeper.stakes: A landlord who signs a long lease without escalations watches the building's value fall as NOI shrinks, since value follows NOI.
deeper.exam: Purpose of escalation clauses: protect the landlord's net income against rising costs over long commercial leases.

blocks.title: No commercial rent regulation
blocks.html: New York has rent stabilization for many apartments, but commercial rents are not regulated. Escalations, renewals and increases in a store or office lease are whatever the parties negotiate. So Leo's answer is in his lease, not in a statute.
blocks.casual: New York has rent stabilization for lots of apartments, but commercial rents aren't regulated at all. Escalations, renewals and increases in a store or office lease are whatever the two sides negotiate. So Leo's answer lives in his lease, not in a statute.

deeper.plain: There's no rent control for stores or offices in New York. The lease rules.
deeper.picture: Haggling at a flea market: no price tags set by the government, just what the two of you agree to.
deeper.street: A Bed-Stuy hardware store owner's lease ends, and the landlord asks for double. The owner asks Jordan if there's a cap like for apartments. There isn't. His leverage is negotiation, not law.
deeper.stakes: Telling a commercial tenant their rent increases are capped by law is wrong advice that could cost them their business plan.
deeper.exam: Trap: answers implying commercial rent stabilization exist in NY. They don't.

blocks.html: Most expense escalations charge the tenant its proportionate share (pro rata share) of the increase: the tenant's rentable square feet divided by the building's total rentable square feet. Leo leases 5,000 RSF in a 100,000 RSF building, so his share is 5,000 / 100,000 = 5%.
blocks.casual: Most expense escalations bill the tenant its proportionate share (pro rata share) of the increase: the tenant's rentable square feet divided by the building's total rentable square feet. Leo leases 5,000 RSF in a 100,000 RSF building, so his share is 5,000 / 100,000 = 5%.

deeper.plain: You pay your slice of the increase based on how much of the building you rent.
deeper.picture: Splitting a group dinner bill by how much each person ordered.
deeper.street: A dentist on the 4th floor of a 50,000 RSF White Plains building leases 2,500 RSF. Her share of any increase is 5%. The tenant with a 20,000 RSF floor pays 40%.
deeper.stakes: Using usable instead of rentable feet in the share math miscalculates every bill and invites a dispute.
deeper.exam: Proportionate share = tenant RSF / building RSF. Always rentable.

blocks.text: Base year escalations: taxes and operating costs

blocks.html: With a base year, the expenses in a named year (usually the first year of the lease) become the baseline covered by the base rent. Each later year, the tenant pays its share of any increase over that baseline. The two classic versions are the real property tax escalation (share of increases in real estate taxes over the base tax year) and the direct operating escalation (share of increases in actual operating expenses, like cleaning, payroll, fuel, insurance and repairs, over the base year).
blocks.casual: With a base year, the expenses in a named year (usually year one of the lease) become the baseline that base rent covers. Every year after, the tenant pays its share of anything above that baseline. Two classic flavors: the real property tax escalation (share of increases in real estate taxes over the base tax year) and the direct operating escalation (share of increases in actual operating expenses, like cleaning, payroll, fuel, insurance and repairs, over the base year).

deeper.plain: Year one's costs are included in rent. After that, the tenant pays its share of increases.
deeper.picture: Your parents cover your phone bill at this year's price. Any increase next year is on you.
deeper.street: Leo's lease names 2025 as the operating base year and the 2025/2026 tax year as the tax base. Every bill he gets compares the current year with those two baselines.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who sign without knowing the base year amounts can't predict escalations and can't spot a billing error.
deeper.exam: Base year = actual expenses in a named year. Tenant pays its share of increases over that year, not the whole expense.

blocks.caption: Set the base year, change the tenant's share, and compare base year, expense stop, porter's wage and CPI escalations side by side.

blocks.title: Leo's $18,000 letter, explained
blocks.html:
Leo's share: 5%.

Taxes: base year $2,000,000, this year $2,240,000. Increase $240,000 x 5% = $12,000.
Operating expenses: base year $1,500,000, this year $1,620,000. Increase $120,000 x 5% = $6,000.

Total escalation = $18,000 for the year, or $18,000 / 5,000 = $3.60 per RSF, on top of base rent. The landlord is right, and the lease says so.
blocks.casual:
Leo's share: 5%.
Taxes: base year $2,000,000, this year $2,240,000. Increase $240,000 x 5% = $12,000.
Operating expenses: base year $1,500,000, this year $1,620,000. Increase $120,000 x 5% = $6,000.
Total escalation = $18,000 for the year, or $18,000 / 5,000 = $3.60 per RSF on top of base rent. The landlord is right, and the lease backs it up.

deeper.plain: Building costs went up $360,000, and Leo owes 5% of that.
deeper.picture: Your share of a rent increase on a shared summer house: the house costs more, you pay your slice of the difference.
deeper.street: Leo asks for backup. The landlord sends the tax bills and an expense summary. Jordan checks the math, confirms $18,000, and tells Leo to budget for it every year going forward.
deeper.stakes: If Leo refuses to pay, he's in default and the landlord can pursue him. Knowing the math helps tenants push back only when the numbers are actually wrong.
deeper.exam: Formula: (this year minus base year) x share. Compute taxes and operating separately, then add.

blocks.title: NYC tax years
