blocks.html: New York City's real estate tax year runs July 1 to June 30, so office leases usually name a tax base year like "the 2026/2027 tax year" and a separate calendar base year for operating expenses. If the landlord wins a tax reduction (a tax certiorari case), leases usually pass the tenant its share of the refund, less the landlord's costs.
blocks.casual: New York City's real estate tax year runs July 1 to June 30, so office leases usually name a tax base year like "the 2026/2027 tax year" plus a separate calendar base year for operating expenses. If the landlord wins a tax reduction (a tax certiorari case), leases usually pass the tenant its share of the refund, minus the landlord's costs.

deeper.plain: NYC taxes run on a July to June year, and tenants usually share in tax refunds.
deeper.picture: A school year versus a calendar year: two different clocks running side by side.
deeper.street: Evelyn's Midtown building wins a $200,000 tax certiorari reduction. After $40,000 in legal fees, a tenant with a 5% share gets an $8,000 credit.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who don't ask for their share of tax refunds leave money with the landlord.
deeper.exam: NYC tax year: July 1 to June 30. Commercial tax appeals are tax certiorari proceedings.

blocks.title: What tenants negotiate
blocks.html: Tenant brokers fight over the definition of operating expenses. Common carve-outs: capital improvements, the landlord's mortgage payments and depreciation, leasing commissions, costs to fix code violations that existed before the lease, and anything paid by insurance. Tenants also ask for the right to audit the landlord's books, and for a later base year, because a newer base year means a higher baseline and smaller escalations.
blocks.casual: Tenant brokers fight hard over how "operating expenses" is defined. Common carve-outs: capital improvements, the landlord's mortgage payments and depreciation, leasing commissions, fixing code violations that existed before the lease, and anything covered by insurance. Tenants also push for the right to audit the landlord's books, and for a later base year, since a newer base year means a higher baseline and smaller escalations.

deeper.plain: Tenants try to keep the landlord's big projects and financing costs out of what gets passed through.
deeper.picture: Roommates agreeing to split utilities, but not your new gaming PC.
deeper.street: Jordan negotiates Leo's next lease to exclude capital improvements and leasing commissions, adds an audit right, and gets a base year one year later. Over 10 years that saves Leo tens of thousands.
deeper.stakes: Without carve-outs, tenants can end up paying for the landlord's lobby renovation or a new tenant's broker fee.
deeper.exam: Exam focus: tenants prefer a later base year and the right to audit. Capital improvements and debt service are typically excluded.

blocks.q: A tenant occupies 8,000 RSF in a 200,000 RSF building. Real estate taxes rose from a base year of $3,000,000 to $3,250,000. The tenant's tax escalation is:
blocks.x: Share = 8,000 / 200,000 = 4%. Increase = $250,000. Escalation = $250,000 x 4% = $10,000. The tenant pays a share of the increase, not of the total tax bill ($130,000).

blocks.html: An expense stop (an operating stop or tax stop) sets a fixed dollar amount of expenses, usually stated per RSF, that the landlord will absorb. The tenant pays anything above the stop. The difference from a base year: a base year uses whatever expenses actually turn out to be in that year; a stop is a number written into the lease on day one.
blocks.casual: An expense stop (an operating stop or tax stop) sets a fixed dollar amount of expenses, usually per RSF, that the landlord will cover. The tenant pays anything above the stop. The difference from a base year: a base year uses whatever expenses actually turn out to be in that year; a stop is a number written into the lease on day one.

deeper.plain: The landlord covers expenses up to a set number. Anything above it, the tenant pays.
deeper.picture: Your company covers your lunch up to $15. Order the $18 bowl and you pay the extra $3.
deeper.street: A Long Island office lease sets a $12 per RSF operating stop. The tenant knows on signing day exactly where its cost exposure starts, instead of waiting a year to see what the base year turns out to be.
deeper.stakes: A stop set too low means the tenant pays escalations from year one. Tenants should compare the stop with the building's actual current expenses.
deeper.exam: Stop = fixed dollar amount set at signing. Base year = actual expenses in a named year. Don't mix them.

blocks.title: Expense stop
blocks.html:
Lease sets an operating stop of $12.00 per RSF. Actual operating expenses this year are $13.10 per RSF. Tenant leases 5,000 RSF.

Excess = $13.10 minus $12.00 = $1.10 per RSF.
Tenant pays $1.10 x 5,000 = $5,500 for the year.
blocks.casual:
The lease sets an operating stop of $12.00 per RSF. This year's actual operating expenses come to $13.10 per RSF. The tenant leases 5,000 RSF.
Excess = $13.10 minus $12.00 = $1.10 per RSF.
Tenant pays $1.10 x 5,000 = $5,500 for the year.

deeper.plain: Expenses went $1.10 per foot over the stop, so the tenant pays $1.10 on each of its feet.
deeper.picture: A data plan with 10 GB included: use 11.1 GB and you pay for the extra 1.1.
deeper.street: A Hauppauge tech firm gets this exact bill. It asks for the expense breakdown, sees a big jump in snow removal after a rough winter, and pays.
deeper.stakes: Billing tenants on the full expense instead of the excess overcharges them hugely and can lead to lawsuits.
deeper.exam: Steps: actual minus stop, times tenant RSF. Watch for a distractor that multiplies the full $13.10.

left.title: Base year
items: Baseline = actual expenses in a named year
Unknown until that year closes
Tenant pays share of increases over it

right.title: Expense stop
items: Baseline = fixed dollar amount in the lease
Known on signing
Tenant pays share of expenses above it

deeper.plain: A base year is learned after the fact. A stop is a number fixed when the lease is signed.
deeper.picture: Setting your weight goal as "whatever I weigh on Jan 1" versus "150 pounds" written down today.
deeper.street: Leo prefers the stop on his next lease because he can model costs on day one. His landlord prefers a base year in a new building, where first-year expenses are often low.
deeper.stakes: Picking the wrong structure for a building's cost profile can mean thousands more in escalations each year.
deeper.exam: Know which is known on signing (stop) and which isn't (base year).

blocks.html: Before landlords tracked every expense line, New York office leases used a shortcut. Labor is a building's largest controllable expense, and the wage of building porters (set by the union contract for building service workers) rises predictably. A porter's wage escalation raises the rent by a set amount per square foot for every cent the porter's hourly wage increases. The classic "penny for penny" formula: each $0.01 rise in the hourly wage raises annual rent by $0.01 per RSF. A multiplier above or below 1 can be negotiated.
blocks.casual: Before landlords tracked every expense line, NYC office leases used a shortcut. Labor is a building's biggest controllable expense, and the wage of building porters (set by the union contract for building service workers) rises predictably. A porter's wage escalation raises the rent a set amount per square foot for every cent the porter's hourly wage goes up. Classic "penny for penny": each $0.01 rise in the hourly wage bumps annual rent by $0.01 per RSF. A multiplier above or below 1 can be negotiated.

deeper.plain: Rent goes up by a penny per foot for every penny the porter's hourly wage goes up.
deeper.picture: Like tying your rent to the price of a slice of pizza: when the slice goes up a dime, your rent per foot goes up a dime.
deeper.street: An old Garment District lease from the 1990s still uses porter's wage. Each time the union contract raises the hourly wage, the tenant's rent goes up automatically, with no need to audit expenses.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who don't recognize a porter's wage clause can pay far more than the building's real cost increases.
deeper.exam: Porter's wage = wage increase x multiplier x RSF. It's a NYC-specific concept and shows up on the exam.

blocks.title: Porter's wage
blocks.html:
The porter's hourly wage rises from $30.00 to $31.20, an increase of $1.20. The lease uses a multiplier of 1 (one cent per RSF per one cent of wage). Tenant leases 5,000 RSF.

Escalation = $1.20 x 1 x 5,000 = $6,000 a year.
With a multiplier of 1.5: $1.20 x 1.5 x 5,000 = $9,000.
blocks.casual:
The porter's hourly wage goes from $30.00 to $31.20, up $1.20. The lease uses a multiplier of 1 (one cent per RSF per one cent of wage). Tenant leases 5,000 RSF.
Escalation = $1.20 x 1 x 5,000 = $6,000 a year.
With a multiplier of 1.5: $1.20 x 1.5 x 5,000 = $9,000.

deeper.plain: A $1.20 wage increase means $1.20 more per foot, times the tenant's 5,000 feet.
deeper.picture: Raising the price of every square foot by the same amount the porter's hourly pay went up.
deeper.street: A Chelsea tenant's lease uses a 1.5 multiplier. When the union wage rose $1.20, its rent went up $9,000. The tenant's broker should have negotiated the multiplier down to 1 at signing.
deeper.stakes: A multiplier over 1 can mean thousands extra each year for the whole lease term.
deeper.exam: Multiply wage increase by multiplier by RSF. Don't divide by anything, and don't use the whole wage.

blocks.html: Tenants came to dislike porter's wage clauses because the wage can rise faster than the building's actual costs, so the landlord profits on the formula. Most modern NYC office leases use direct operating escalations instead, but older leases still in force and exam questions keep the porter's wage alive.
blocks.casual: Tenants got sour on porter's wage clauses because the wage can rise faster than the building's actual costs, so the landlord profits off the formula. Most modern NYC office leases use direct operating escalations instead, but older leases still in force (and exam questions) keep porter's wage alive.

deeper.plain: Porter's wage is old-school and can overpay landlords, so it's fading, but the exam still asks about it.
deeper.picture: A flip phone: mostly retired, still around in a few pockets, and still on the test.
deeper.street: Evelyn bought a Midtown building with three legacy porter's wage leases. Wages rose 4% while her real expenses rose 2%. Those tenants are paying her extra until their leases expire.
deeper.stakes: Tenant brokers who let a porter's wage clause slide into a new lease cost their clients money every year.
deeper.exam: Know why tenants dislike it: wage growth can exceed actual cost growth.

blocks.q: Under a porter's wage clause with a multiplier of 1, the porter's wage rises 75 cents an hour. A tenant with 4,000 RSF owes additional annual rent of:
blocks.x: $0.75 x 1 x 4,000 RSF = $3,000. The formula multiplies the wage increase by the multiplier and the tenant's rentable square feet.

blocks.html: A fixed percentage increase raises the rent by a set percent each year (or fixed dollar steps every few years), regardless of what expenses do. It is simple and predictable for both sides. Increases usually compound: each year's raise is figured on the prior year's rent.
blocks.casual: A fixed percentage increase raises rent by a set percent every year (or fixed dollar steps every few years), no matter what expenses do. Simple and predictable for both sides. Increases usually compound: each year's raise is figured on the previous year's rent.

deeper.plain: Rent goes up the same percent every year, built on last year's rent.
deeper.picture: A savings account with compound interest, except you're the one paying it.
deeper.street: A Park Slope boutique signs a 10-year lease with 3% bumps. It knows its rent for every year on day one and can plan around it.
deeper.stakes: Forgetting compounding understates future rent. Over 10 years, 3% simple versus compounded is a noticeable gap.
deeper.exam: Compound: multiply the prior year's rent by 1 plus the rate. Distractors use simple increases on the original rent.

blocks.title: 3% annual bumps on a $120,000 store lease

deeper.plain: Each year's rent is last year's times 1.03.
deeper.picture: A snowball rolling downhill, picking up a bit more each turn because it's already bigger.
deeper.street: If Jordan had used simple increases, he'd have told the tenant year 4 was $130,800. The compounded figure is $131,127. Small gap now, bigger later.
deeper.stakes: Quoting simple instead of compound bumps understates costs and can cause disputes when the bills arrive.
deeper.exam: Multiply step by step, or use $120,000 x 1.03 cubed for year 4.

blocks.html: A CPI escalation ties rent to the Consumer Price Index published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, often the index for the New York metro area. Rent rises by the percentage change in the index, or by a fraction of it, sometimes with a floor and a cap. It protects the landlord against general inflation rather than its specific expenses.
blocks.casual: A CPI escalation ties rent to the Consumer Price Index from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, often the index for the New York metro area. Rent goes up by the percent change in the index, or a fraction of it, sometimes with a floor and a cap. It protects the landlord against general inflation, not its own specific expenses.

deeper.plain: Rent rises with inflation as measured by the government's price index.
deeper.picture: A subscription that automatically goes up whenever the price of groceries does.
deeper.street: A Jamaica Avenue store lease uses 75% of the NY metro CPI change, with a 2% floor and 5% cap. In a hot inflation year, the cap protects the tenant; in a quiet year, the floor protects the landlord.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who sign uncapped CPI clauses got hit hard in the 2021 to 2023 inflation spike.
deeper.exam: CPI tracks general inflation, not building costs. It's published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

blocks.title: CPI escalation
blocks.html:
Base rent $120,000. CPI rose from 300 to 312, an increase of 12 / 300 = 4%.

Full CPI: $120,000 x 4% = $4,800 increase, new rent $124,800.
Lease uses 50% of the CPI change: $120,000 x 2% = $2,400 increase, new rent $122,400.
blocks.casual:
Base rent $120,000. CPI went from 300 to 312, up 12 / 300 = 4%.
Full CPI: $120,000 x 4% = $4,800 increase, new rent $124,800.
Lease uses 50% of the CPI change: $120,000 x 2% = $2,400 increase, new rent $122,400.

deeper.plain: Find the index's percent change, apply it (or the agreed fraction of it) to the rent.
deeper.picture: If your coffee went from $3.00 to $3.12, that's 4%. Apply that same 4% to the rent.
deeper.street: A Bayside landlord bills the full 4%, but the lease says 50% of CPI. The tenant's broker catches it and saves the tenant $2,400.
deeper.stakes: Applying the wrong fraction overbills tenants and damages the landlord relationship.
deeper.exam: Percent change = (new minus old) / old. Don't divide by the new index. Then apply the fraction.

head: Method
Rent rises with
Who likes it
rows: Actual tax increases over the base tax year
Landlords: taxes are out of their control
Actual operating cost increases over the base year
Fair to both, but needs audits
Expenses above a fixed dollar amount
Union porter wage x multiplier x RSF
blocks.caption: Escalation methods at a glance

deeper.plain: Six ways to raise rent: actual taxes, actual expenses, a fixed stop, porter wages, a fixed percent, or inflation.
deeper.picture: Six ways to set a bus fare: by fuel cost, by total operating cost, above a set budget, by driver wages, a flat yearly increase, or general inflation.
deeper.street: Evelyn's portfolio has a bit of everything: CPI on the Staten Island pharmacy, fixed 3% on the Bushwick stores, base year escalations on the White Plains offices, and one old porter's wage lease in Midtown.
deeper.stakes: Misreading which method a lease uses leads to wrong bills, angry tenants, and potential litigation.
deeper.exam: Match the description to the method. Actual costs over a year = base year. Fixed dollar threshold = stop. Index = CPI.

blocks.title: Exam traps
blocks.html: (1) Escalations are figured on the increase, never on the whole expense. (2) Proportionate share uses rentable square feet. (3) If expenses fall below the base year, the tenant usually gets no credit; rent does not drop below base. (4) A CPI clause tracks inflation, not the building's actual costs.
blocks.casual: Exam traps: (1) Escalations are figured on the increase, never the whole expense. (2) Proportionate share uses rentable square feet. (3) If expenses fall below the base year, the tenant usually gets no credit; rent doesn't drop below base. (4) A CPI clause follows inflation, not the building's actual costs.

deeper.plain: Charge only the increase, use rentable feet, rent doesn't go below base, and CPI is about inflation.
deeper.picture: A ratchet: it clicks up when costs rise but doesn't spin back down when they fall.
deeper.street: Taxes on Leo's building drop one year after a certiorari win. He asks for a rent cut below base. Jordan explains the lease only gives him his share of the refund, not a cut below base rent.
deeper.stakes: Tenants who expect rent reductions when expenses fall can budget wrong. Landlords who bill on full expenses can face overbilling claims.
deeper.exam: Each of these four is a classic distractor. Read whether the answer applies the share to the increase or the total.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Share x Increase. Almost every escalation question is (tenant RSF / building RSF) x (this year minus base). Porter's wage is the odd one: Cents x Multiplier x Feet.
blocks.casual: Remember: Share x Increase. Almost every escalation question is (tenant RSF / building RSF) x (this year minus base). Porter's wage is the odd one out: Cents x Multiplier x Feet.

deeper.plain: Most escalation math is your share times the increase. Porter's wage uses its own formula.
deeper.picture: Two keys on a ring: one opens most doors, a special one opens the porter's wage door.
deeper.street: Jordan solves Leo's bill in 30 seconds with Share x Increase and then explains it in plain English. Leo stops panicking.
deeper.stakes: Freezing on escalation math in front of a tenant or landlord costs you credibility fast.
deeper.exam: Write "Share x Increase" and "Cents x Multiplier x Feet" on your scratch paper before tackling escalation problems.

story.title: The Letter in Year Two
story.setting: Leo's Flatiron office, one year after move-in

beats.text: Eighteen thousand dollars. My rent was fixed. It says so in my spreadsheet.
Your base rent is fixed. Page 14 has escalations. You pay your share of increases in taxes and operating costs over the base year.
My share of what? I don't own the building.
Your 5,000 feet out of 100,000. Five percent.
beats.tag: Proportionate share = tenant RSF / building RSF

beats.text: Taxes went up $240,000 over the base year. Five percent is $12,000. Operating costs up $120,000, five percent is $6,000.

check.q: If taxes had instead gone DOWN $50,000 below the base year, what would Leo typically owe for taxes?
c: A $2,500 credit off base rent
Nothing extra; rent does not drop below base
$2,500 more
His full share of the tax bill
check.x: Escalations charge a share of increases. Most leases give no credit below the base year, so the tenant simply owes no tax escalation.

beats.text: Why do landlords even do this?
Seventies. Inflation and oil prices blew up building costs while rents were stuck in long leases. Landlords got crushed, then wrote escalations into everything.
Could my lease have been different?
Sure. An expense stop at a fixed number per foot. A flat 3% a year. A CPI clause. Old leases even used the porter's wage: a penny a foot for every penny the porters' raise.
A penny per foot per penny. That's oddly elegant.
Until the porters get a dollar-twenty raise and your 5,000 feet cost $6,000 more. Tenants hated it. Most new leases use actual operating costs.
Leo adds a tab to his spreadsheet called ESCALATIONS (FINE).
Share times increase. That's the whole game, except the porter's wage, which is cents times multiplier times feet.

board.prompt: Make a T-chart: base year vs expense stop. Then compute one tenant's escalation under each using the same building numbers.

facts.text: An escalation clause raises rent as costs or prices rise so the landlord's NOI keeps its value over a long lease.
Escalations became standard after 1970s inflation and the energy crisis squeezed landlords locked into fixed rents.
New York does not regulate commercial rents; escalations, renewals and increases in store and office leases are whatever the lease says.
Proportionate share is the tenant's rentable square feet divided by the building's total rentable square feet.
A real property tax escalation charges the tenant its share of the increase in taxes over the base tax year.
A direct operating escalation charges the tenant its share of increases in actual operating expenses over the base year.
Escalations are figured on the increase only; if expenses fall below the base year the tenant usually gets no credit and rent stays at base.
NYC's real estate tax year runs July 1 to June 30, so leases name a tax base year like 2026/2027; tax refunds are usually shared with tenants.
Tenants carve capital improvements, mortgage payments, depreciation and leasing commissions out of operating expenses, and prefer a later base year.
An expense stop sets a fixed dollar amount per RSF the landlord absorbs; the tenant pays expenses above it.
A base year uses actual expenses of a named year (unknown until it closes); a stop is a fixed number in the lease known at signing.
A porter's wage escalation raises annual rent per RSF by the hourly wage increase times a multiplier (penny for penny when the multiplier is 1).
Tenants dislike porter's wage clauses because wages can rise faster than actual costs; modern NYC leases favor direct operating escalations.
A fixed percentage increase raises rent a set percent each year regardless of costs, usually compounding on the prior year's rent.
A CPI escalation raises rent by all or a set fraction of the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index; it tracks inflation, not the building's costs.
Escalation methods are tax, direct operating, expense stop, porter's wage, fixed percentage and CPI; a natural breakpoint belongs to percentage leases.

lessons.title: Case file: The Cash-Out on Fifth Avenue
lessons.tagline: A Bay Ridge family wants to borrow its way into a 16-unit building. The bank, the balloon and the 2019 rent law have opinions.
objectives: Decide whether added leverage raises or lowers an investor's return by comparing the property's return with the loan constant
Analyze a commercial loan term sheet for refinance risk, coverage limits and recourse carve-outs
Apply liquidity, regulatory and management risk to a New York multifamily purchase
Explain how a CEMA reduces mortgage recording tax on a New York refinance

blocks.title: Two buildings, one family, one bank
blocks.html: Nadia and Victor Haddad own a three-story mixed-use building on Fifth Avenue in Bay Ridge: a pharmacy on the ground floor and two apartments above. They bought it in 2009, and the old mortgage is down to about $300,000 on a building now worth roughly $2,000,000. Victor has found a 16-unit walk-up in Ridgewood listed at $3,200,000. His plan: pull cash out of Bay Ridge with a bigger mortgage, use that cash as the down payment, and borrow as much as any bank will give on Ridgewood. "Other people's money," he tells Jordan at the Hudson & Hart conference table. "That is how buildings get bought in this city." Nadia is quieter. She asks one question: "If this goes wrong, what do we lose?" Jordan is the buyer's agent. Diane is sitting in.

Victor is right that most investment property in New York is bought with borrowed money. Nadia is right that borrowing changes what can go wrong. This case is about that tension: leverage, risk, liquidity and the work a building demands. The numbers here are simple on purpose. What matters is reading them the way a lender, a seller and a nervous spouse would.

blocks.title: Ridgewood 16-unit walk-up: seller's setup
blocks.html:
Asking price: $3,200,000
Units: 16 (11 rent stabilized, 5 free market)
Seller's stated net operating income: $192,000 a year
Free-and-clear return at asking: $192,000 / $3,200,000 = 6.0%
Seller's broker note: "Huge upside. Stabilized units can be converted to market as tenants leave."

Tasha, the mortgage broker Jordan brings in, sends a quote for the Ridgewood loan: 6.25% interest, 30-year amortization, five-year fixed term with a balloon at the end. The annual payment on each borrowed dollar (the mortgage constant) works out to about 7.39%. Victor wants 75% of the price, $2,400,000. Before anyone talks about how much, Diane asks Jordan the one comparison that decides whether borrowing helps at all.

blocks.q: Victor wants maximum leverage on Ridgewood. Which comparison tells the Haddads whether borrowing will raise or lower the return on their own cash?
c: The loan's interest rate compared with the current rate of inflation in the New York metro area
The property's free-and-clear return compared with the loan's mortgage constant
The loan-to-value ratio compared with the 80% limit that triggers mortgage insurance
The asking price compared with the price per unit of recent Ridgewood sales
blocks.x: Leverage is positive when the property earns more per dollar than the loan costs per dollar, measured by the mortgage constant (principal plus interest), not the interest rate alone. Here the property earns 6.0% and the loan costs about 7.39%, so every borrowed dollar loses money. The LTV and mortgage insurance answer borrows a residential rule: PMI applies to home loans, not to a 16-unit investment loan.

blocks.html: Jordan runs it. At 75% leverage the debt service on $2,400,000 is about $177,300 a year. The building's $192,000 leaves roughly $14,700 for the Haddads on $800,000 of their own money: under 2%. Bought all cash, the same building would pay them 6%. That is negative leverage, and it is common when interest rates are higher than the cap rates buildings trade at. Victor's answer: "Fine, the cash flow is thin, but rents go up and the building goes up. Leverage multiplies the appreciation." He is half right. Leverage multiplies the change in value in both directions.

head: If Ridgewood's value moves
All cash ($3.2M in)
75% loan ($800K in)
rows: 0%, and thin cash flow along the way
blocks.caption: Same building, same change in value, very different outcomes for the owner's cash.

blocks.html: Then the lender weighs in, and the lender does not care how Victor feels about appreciation. Tasha reports that the bank underwrites to a minimum debt coverage ratio of 1.25: the building's NOI must be at least 1.25 times the debt service. At $192,000 of NOI, the most debt service the bank will allow is $153,600, which supports a loan of about $2,080,000. That is 65% of the price, not 75%.

blocks.q: The bank's 1.25 coverage test caps the Ridgewood loan at about 65% of the price. What does that mean for the Haddads?
c: They can close at 75% by having the seller credit the difference at closing
They can close at 65% and add a second mortgage later without the bank's consent
The bank has to lend 75% because 1 to 4 family rules cap the down payment
They need about $320,000 more equity, or a lower price, to close the purchase
blocks.x: Commercial lenders size loans on income as well as value. When the coverage test produces a smaller loan than the LTV test, the smaller number wins, and the buyer brings the difference in cash or negotiates the price down. A 16-unit building is financed as commercial property, so 1 to 4 family residential rules do not apply. Secondary financing is usually barred or needs the first lender's consent.

blocks.text: Where the down payment comes from

blocks.html: Victor has the answer for the extra equity too: borrow more against Bay Ridge. The existing $300,000 mortgage would be refinanced into a $1,400,000 loan, freeing about $1,100,000 in cash. Diane slides a pad across the table and draws two boxes. "Bay Ridge is free money today," she says. "After this, it is collateral."

This is the part buyers miss. Cash pulled out of one building is not equity in the next one. It is debt in a different place. After the refinance, the Haddads would owe about $1,400,000 on Bay Ridge and about $2,080,000 on Ridgewood. Their combined leverage across both buildings is the number that matters, and if Ridgewood struggles, they must keep paying the Bay Ridge loan with Bay Ridge rents that were previously all theirs.

blocks.q: After the cash-out, Victor says, "We are putting $1,100,000 down, so Ridgewood is conservative." What is the most accurate reply?
c: He is correct, because a down payment above 30% removes most of the leverage risk
He is correct, because the Ridgewood lender can look solely to the Ridgewood building
The cash is borrowed against Bay Ridge, so the family is still highly leveraged
The down payment counts as equity once the Bay Ridge refinance is recorded and closed
blocks.x: Equity that came from a loan is borrowed money. Leverage is measured across the family's whole balance sheet, not one deal at a time. Victor's view treats each building as a sealed box, which is true for each lender's collateral but false for the family's risk: both mortgages must be paid from the same household if one building falls short.

blocks.html: The Bay Ridge lender has its own questions. Its underwriter asks for the pharmacy lease, and the answer is not comfortable: the pharmacy pays about 70% of the building's rent, and its lease expires in three years, well before the new ten-year loan would mature. The pharmacy has a renewal option, but options belong to the tenant. The tenant decides whether to use one.

blocks.q: Why does the Bay Ridge lender focus on the pharmacy's lease expiration before approving the larger loan?
c: One tenant pays most of the rent, and its lease ends before the new loan does
Net leases are unenforceable in New York once fewer than five years remain
A pharmacy lease turns into a month-to-month tenancy when the loan closes
Commercial tenants hold a statutory right to renew that would freeze the rent
blocks.x: Lenders call this rollover or tenant concentration risk. When a single tenant produces most of the income and can leave before the loan matures, the building's ability to pay the debt depends on one decision the owner does not control. New York gives commercial tenants no statutory right to renew; renewal rights exist only if the lease grants an option. Expect a lower loan amount, a reserve, or a lease extension requirement.

blocks.html: Diane reads the lender's response aloud: it will lend $1,400,000 only if the Haddads fund a leasing reserve at closing or get the pharmacy to extend first. Victor calls the pharmacy's real estate department that afternoon. The pharmacy says it is "evaluating its store footprint," which is corporate for maybe.

blocks.title: The CEMA: New York's refinance tax saver
blocks.html: New York charges mortgage recording tax on the amount of a new mortgage. When a refinance pays off an existing mortgage, the parties can use a consolidation, extension and modification agreement (CEMA): the old lender assigns the existing mortgage to the new lender, and tax is owed only on the new money. On the Bay Ridge refinance, that means tax on about $1,100,000 instead of the full $1,400,000. In New York City the combined rate on a commercial mortgage of $500,000 or more is 2.8%, so the savings on a building with a store are real money. The title company and the attorneys handle the paperwork; the licensee's job is to know to ask.

blocks.q: The Bay Ridge loan is being refinanced from $300,000 to $1,400,000 with a new lender. To cut the mortgage recording tax, the parties should:
c: Have the old mortgage assigned to the new lender in a CEMA so tax applies to new money
Record the new mortgage as a second lien and leave the $300,000 mortgage in place
Close the refinance through a co-op share loan, which carries no recording tax
Ask the city to apply the residential 1.8% rate because two of the units are apartments
blocks.x: A CEMA keeps the already-taxed mortgage alive by assigning it to the new lender, so recording tax is owed on the increase only. A second lien leaves two loans and still taxes the new $1,100,000, and the first lender may not allow it. The co-op share loan answer is a real rule (share loans are not mortgages) applied to the wrong property: Bay Ridge is not a co-op.

blocks.title: Ridgewood loan term sheet (key lines)
blocks.html:
Amount: lesser of 65% of price or 1.25x debt coverage
Rate: 6.25% fixed for 5 years
Amortization: 30 years; balance due at end of year 5
Recourse: non-recourse, except standard carve-outs (fraud, unpaid taxes, environmental, voluntary bankruptcy) under a guaranty signed by Victor and Nadia
Prepayment: 5%, 4%, 3%, 2%, 1% of the balance in years 1 to 5
Reserves: 6 months of taxes and insurance funded at closing

Victor reads "non-recourse" and relaxes. Nadia reads "balance due at end of year 5" and does not. After five years of payments on a 30-year schedule, most of the $2,080,000 will still be owed. The Haddads will have to refinance or sell in year 5, at whatever rates and values exist then. That is the refinance risk built into a levered purchase with a short loan term.

blocks.q: Which line of the term sheet creates the largest risk that the Haddads will have to bring cash or sell in five years?
c: The fixed rate of 6.25% for the first five years of the loan term
The prepayment penalty that steps down from 5% to 1% over five years
The full remaining loan balance coming due at the end of year 5
The six months of tax and insurance reserves funded at the closing
blocks.x: A balloon at year 5 forces a refinance or sale on a date the borrower does not control. If rates are higher or NOI is flat, the new lender's coverage test sizes a smaller loan, and the owner must pay the difference. The prepayment penalty is the trap answer: it costs money if they leave early, but it does not force anything. The fixed rate actually protects them for five years.

blocks.html: Diane adds the second point. Non-recourse means the bank generally looks only to the building if the loan defaults, but the carve-out guaranty makes Victor and Nadia personally liable for specific bad acts and events, including unpaid real estate taxes. "Non-recourse is a fence with gates in it," she says. "Read where the gates are."

Tasha also offers a second option to make the numbers look better: a floating-rate loan at 5.75% today, priced at a spread over a market index and adjusting every quarter, with no balloon for seven years. The starting debt service is lower, and the coverage test lets the Haddads borrow a little more. Victor likes it immediately.

blocks.q: Compared with the five-year fixed loan, what risk does the floating-rate option shift onto the Haddads?
c: Liquidity risk, because floating-rate loans block a sale before maturity
Tenant credit risk, because the rent roll is tied to the same market index
Regulatory risk, because adjustable loans need HCR approval on stabilized buildings
Interest rate risk, because their debt service rises whenever the index does
blocks.x: A floating rate moves the cost of rising rates from the lender to the borrower. With thin coverage, a rate increase of one or two points could push debt service above NOI, and the owners would feed the building from their own pockets. Many lenders require the borrower to buy an interest rate cap for that reason. HCR regulates rents, not mortgage terms, so the regulatory answer applies the right agency to the wrong question.

blocks.html: The Haddads pass on the floating loan. Lower payments today bought with an open-ended promise to pay more later is not a cushion. It is more leverage in a different costume.

Nadia mentions that their daughter starts law school in eighteen months. If cash runs short, Victor says, they will just sell Ridgewood. Jordan has seen enough multifamily closings to know what that sentence leaves out.

head: Step in selling a 16-unit building
Realistic time
rows: Price it, prepare rent roll and leases, list
blocks.caption: Rough ranges for a NYC multifamily sale. A forced sale on a deadline usually means a lower price.

blocks.html: Add the costs of getting out: the prepayment penalty (4% of the balance in year 2 is about $80,000), the seller's NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT, legal fees and a brokerage commission. Real estate is illiquid because it is slow to sell and expensive to sell fast. A building is a poor emergency fund.

blocks.q: What is the soundest way to handle the tuition need in the Haddads' plan?
c: Count on selling Ridgewood in year 2, since a sale closes within about 30 days
Keep a separate cash reserve for tuition, outside both buildings' equity
Plan to refinance Ridgewood again in year 2 to pull out cash as needed
Rely on the five free-market units to raise rents enough to cover tuition
blocks.x: Liquidity risk is the risk you need cash fast and cannot get it at full value. The fix is planning: keep known needs in liquid reserves. A year 2 refinance assumes the lender will lend more on a building with thin coverage, and there is a prepayment penalty on the first loan. A sale takes months, not 30 days, and selling under pressure costs price.

blocks.html: Jordan rereads the listing note: stabilized units can be converted to market as tenants leave. Then Jordan checks the date on the law. Since the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019, there is no vacancy decontrol and no high-rent luxury decontrol in New York. A stabilized apartment stays stabilized when the tenant moves out. The new tenant gets a stabilized lease at the legal regulated rent.

blocks.q: The seller's pro forma assumes three stabilized units per year will go to market rent on turnover. How should Jordan treat that assumption?
c: As realistic, because vacancy decontrol applies once rent passes the legal threshold
As realistic, provided the owner spends enough on individual apartment improvements
As unsupported, because 2019 law ended decontrol when stabilized units turn over
As unsupported, because stabilized units cannot be re-rented once they are vacant
blocks.x: HSTPA 2019 repealed vacancy decontrol and high-rent luxury decontrol, so turnover does not take a unit out of stabilization. The threshold answer is the pre-2019 rule, which old pro formas and some exam items still reflect. The "cannot be re-rented" answer overstates it: vacant stabilized units are re-rented, just at a regulated rent. Value the building on the regulated rent roll.

blocks.title: The stale pro forma
blocks.html: Rent stabilized buildings marketed with "deregulation upside" usually rely on pre-2019 rules: vacancy bonuses, high-rent decontrol and generous improvement increases. Those changes cut the value of many stabilized buildings overnight, which is the textbook example of regulatory risk. Test every pro forma line against the law in force today, not the law when the spreadsheet was first built.

Jordan books Ray Kowalski for a walk-through before any offer goes in. Ray spends forty minutes in the cellar and comes up shaking his head at the boiler. "Original to a 1990s conversion. It runs, but it is on borrowed time." The roof has two layers of patching, and the rear parapet has open joints. His rough numbers: about $90,000 for a new boiler and $60,000 for roof and parapet work within three years.

None of that shows up in the seller's $192,000 NOI, because capital replacements are not operating expenses. But it is cash the owner must find, and on a building where the loan leaves $14,700 a year after debt service, a $150,000 surprise is not a surprise. It is a capital call on the family.

blocks.q: Ray's report shows about $150,000 of near-term capital work that the seller's NOI ignores. What should Jordan do with it?
c: Leave it out of the offer, since NOI excludes capital expenditures by definition
Use it to support a lower price or a credit, and plan cash reserves for the work
Ask the seller to amend the NOI so the capital work is shown as an operating expense
Report it to the lender, which is required to add the cost to the approved loan amount
blocks.x: Capital items do not belong in NOI, which is exactly why a buyer has to account for them separately: in the price, in a seller credit, or in reserves. Leaving them out of the offer treats a correct accounting rule as if the cash need disappeared. Lenders sometimes hold back funds for repairs, but no lender is obligated to increase a loan to cover them.

blocks.html: Bay Ridge has been easy. The pharmacy pays rent under a net lease and handles its own space; the two apartments turn over every few years. Ridgewood is sixteen apartments, an old boiler, rent registrations with HCR, heat complaints in January, and code violations that do not wait for a weekend. Victor works in Manhattan. Nadia runs a dental office.

blocks.q: Jordan is asked which property type takes more of an owner's time. Which comparison is accurate?
c: A single-tenant net-leased store needs more management than a walk-up because the lease is long
Management time depends on the loan size, so the larger mortgage needs more management
The two need about the same management once a building reaches full occupancy
A 16-unit stabilized walk-up needs more management than a single-tenant net-leased store
blocks.x: Multifamily is management intensive: many tenants, repairs, regulatory filings, collections, turnover. A net-leased store shifts most expenses and upkeep to one tenant, which is why such buildings appeal to passive investors. If the Haddads cannot do the work, a professional manager's fee becomes an operating expense, which lowers NOI and the return they were counting on.

blocks.text: What Jordan can and cannot say

blocks.html: Late in the meeting Victor turns to Jordan directly. "Bottom line. Should we do it?" Jordan earns a commission only if they buy, and a bigger building means a bigger commission. Diane has trained the office on this moment.

blocks.q: How should Jordan answer Victor's "Should we do it?"
c: Lay out the risks found and refer tax and legal questions to their advisers
Recommend the purchase, since the Haddads already own one building successfully
Decline to discuss the deal further, since commenting on value is outside a license
Recommend they wait for rates to fall, since negative leverage tends to reverse
blocks.x: A licensee owes reasonable care and disclosure: share what due diligence showed (thin coverage, balloon, stabilized rent roll, borrowed equity) and send tax and legal questions to the professionals who handle them. Refusing to discuss the deal fails the client; agents talk about price and market all the time. Predicting rates is speculation dressed up as advice.

blocks.html: Here is what actually happened. The Haddads offered $2,950,000, citing the stabilized rent roll and the coverage math. The seller countered at $3,050,000 and they walked away. Six months later they bought an 8-unit building in Glendale with three free-market units, using a smaller cash-out on Bay Ridge, at a price that let the loan cover comfortably and left them a tuition reserve. Victor still calls it "the small building." Nadia calls it "the one we can sleep with."

blocks.q: Why did the smaller Glendale purchase lower the family's risk compared with the Ridgewood plan?
c: Smaller buildings are exempt from rent stabilization under the 2019 law changes
It used less borrowed money, kept a cash reserve, and had more loan coverage
A smaller loan is non-recourse by law, so the family has no personal liability
It removed liquidity risk, since an 8-unit building can be sold within a few weeks
blocks.x: Risk fell on every axis the case tested: less total debt, better coverage at the balloon date, and liquid cash for a known need. Stabilization depends on factors such as building age and unit count (generally 6 or more units built before 1974), so an 8-unit building can be stabilized too. Recourse is set by the loan documents, not by loan size.

items: Leverage helps only when the property's free-and-clear return beats the loan's mortgage constant; when it does not, more debt lowers the return on cash.
Commercial lenders size loans by coverage as well as value. The smaller result controls, and the buyer covers the gap.
Cash pulled from one building is debt, not equity. Measure leverage across everything the investor owns. In NY, a CEMA limits mortgage recording tax on a refinance to the new money.
A short-term loan with a balloon creates refinance risk; non-recourse loans still carry personal guaranty carve-outs.
Real estate is illiquid: months to sell, costly to sell fast. Keep known cash needs out of the building.
Regulatory risk is real: since 2019, stabilized units stay stabilized on turnover, and a pro forma that says otherwise is wrong.

lessons.title: Case file: Six Listings and a Laundromat Fortune
lessons.tagline: A retired Bronx couple wants steady income and no 2 am calls. Six property types, six different answers.
objectives: Compare land, net-leased retail, office, mixed-use, strip center and industrial property on income, risk, liquidity and management
Analyze a net lease abstract for tenant credit, operating covenant and expense allocation
Decide which rules govern residential and commercial tenancies in one New York mixed-use building
Apply fee simple versus leasehold and environmental due diligence to an investment decision

blocks.title: $1.6 million and a short list of wants
blocks.html: Ramon and Teresa Castillo ran a laundromat on Westchester Avenue in the Bronx for 31 years. They sold the business and the building last spring and now have about $1,600,000 in the bank. Ramon is 68, Teresa 66. Their accountant told them to look at real estate for income, and their nephew told them to call Hudson & Hart. They give Jordan a list written on the back of a receipt: steady monthly income, no 2 am phone calls, something we could sell if one of us gets sick, and nothing we have to fix. Jordan pulls six listings from across the region. Each one is a different kind of property, and each one answers that list differently.

This case walks through the six. The question at every stop is the same one Evelyn Park asks about any building: who pays me, how reliably, and what happens if they leave? The property type sets most of the answer before anyone looks at a rent roll.

head: Listing
Type
Price
Current income
rows: Strip center, 6 shops, no anchor, on a ground lease
blocks.caption: Jordan's short list. Prices include financing for the larger ones.

blocks.text: Listing A: the lot in Great Kills

blocks.html: The seller's broker calls it "the best value on the island" and says four houses could go on it. It produces no rent. Teresa likes it because it has nothing to fix.

blocks.q: What does the owner of Listing A pay every year while holding it, and what does the lot produce in return?
c: Taxes and insurance are paid, and depreciation deductions offset them
Nothing is owed until the lot is built on, and no income is produced
Taxes, insurance and any interest are paid, with no rental income
Taxes are paid by the next builder, and the owner collects ground rent
blocks.x: Raw land is the most speculative type: it costs money every year (taxes, insurance, interest if financed) and pays nothing until it sells or is developed. Land also cannot be depreciated, so there is no tax deduction to soften the carrying cost. The depreciation answer is the trap: depreciation applies to buildings, never to land.

blocks.html: Next is the "four houses" claim. Whether four homes can be built depends on the zoning district, lot width, lot area rules and whether the site sits in a special district or flood zone, not on the seller's broker's optimism.

blocks.q: Before repeating the seller's "four houses" claim to the Castillos, Jordan should:
c: Check the zoning district and lot rules and suggest an architect or attorney confirm
Repeat it with a note that it comes from the listing broker, which satisfies disclosure
Ask the seller for a signed statement, since the seller is liable for the claim
Leave it out, since licensees are barred from discussing development potential
blocks.x: Development potential is a fact question under the zoning rules, and a licensee who repeats an unverified claim shares the risk of misrepresentation. Checking the district and pointing the buyer to an architect or land use attorney is reasonable care. Licensees can discuss zoning; they simply cannot present a guess as a fact.

blocks.title: Look it up before you say it
blocks.html: In New York City, the Department of City Planning's online zoning map (ZoLa) shows the zoning district, special districts and many overlays for any lot. It is the starting point, not the final answer: lot width, yards, parking, flood rules and the Department of Buildings all have a say. Upstate and on Long Island, the town or village zoning code and the local building department play the same role.

blocks.text: Listing B: the pharmacy in Hicksville

blocks.html: This one reads like the Castillos' wish list. A national pharmacy chain occupies the whole building under a triple net lease with 12 years left: it pays taxes, insurance and maintenance on top of rent. The rent steps up 5% every five years. There are no apartments, no boiler calls, and one check a month. Ramon asks the right first question: "Who exactly signed the lease?"

blocks.title: Lease abstract, Listing B
blocks.html:
Tenant: Hicksville Pharmacy Operating LLC
Guarantor: none stated
Term: 12 years remaining, two 5-year renewal options (tenant's choice)
Use: retail pharmacy and any lawful retail use
Operating covenant: none. Tenant may cease operations so long as rent is paid.
Expenses: tenant pays all taxes, insurance, and non-structural maintenance; landlord keeps roof and structure

blocks.q: The marketing says "national pharmacy credit." What does the lease abstract actually show about the tenant's credit?
c: The national parent is liable, because the store carries the national brand
The landlord can choose to collect from the parent, which controls the LLC
The credit question is moot, because a net lease tenant has to pay as long as it stays open
The tenant is a single-store LLC with no guarantor, so the parent is not on the hook
blocks.x: Tenant credit depends on who signed and who guaranteed, not on the sign out front. A single-purpose LLC with no parent guaranty may have few assets beyond the store. Buyers pay a premium for true corporate credit, so this gap matters for price. The "has to pay" answer confuses the rent obligation with the tenant's ability to pay it.

blocks.title: The sign is not the signature
blocks.html: Offering memorandums for net lease buildings lead with the logo: "national credit," "investment grade tenant." The exam and the real world both test whether you check who is actually bound. A franchisee, a store-level LLC, or a subsidiary with a capped guaranty is not the parent company. Read the tenant line, the guaranty, and any clause that lets the guaranty shrink or end after a few years.

Two more lines matter. With no operating covenant, the chain can close the store ("go dark") and keep paying rent, which sounds harmless until the lease ends and the Castillos own an empty single-purpose building. And "landlord keeps roof and structure" means this is triple net, not absolute net. A roof replacement is the Castillos' bill, which crosses off "nothing we have to fix."

blocks.q: Which change would make Listing B closest to truly passive income for the Castillos?
c: A lease converted to a gross lease, so the landlord controls the expenses
An absolute net lease, with the tenant covering roof and structure
A shorter remaining term, so the rent can be reset to market sooner
A percentage rent clause, so the rent rises with prescription sales
blocks.x: In an absolute (bondable) net lease the tenant carries even structural and roof costs, leaving the owner with almost no management. A gross lease does the opposite: the landlord pays the expenses, which is more work and more risk. A shorter term adds rollover risk, and percentage rent ties income to store sales.

blocks.text: Listing C: the office building in White Plains

blocks.html: Price per square foot looks like a steal: about half of what the same building sold for in 2015. It is a three-story Class B building near the Metro-North station, 40% vacant since a medical billing firm left. The seller's pro forma shows it full in a year.

blocks.q: Why is Listing C's low price per square foot not necessarily a bargain for the Castillos?
c: Office buildings in Westchester cannot be financed above 50% of value by state rule
Filling the vacancy costs time, build-out money, commissions and free rent
Low-rise buildings are classified as Class C once a full floor stands vacant
Office leases are short, so the occupied 60% is likely to leave within a year
blocks.x: Vacant office space carries lease-up costs that the price already reflects: months of downtime, a tenant improvement allowance to build out the space, leasing commissions and free rent, all before a new tenant pays. Since 2020, older Class B and C office space has been the slowest to lease. Building class depends on quality and location, not on vacancy.

blocks.html: There is also the question of what the building could become. Some owners of struggling suburban and Manhattan office buildings are studying conversions to apartments, but floor plates, window lines, plumbing and zoning decide whether that works, and conversions take years and serious capital. A buyer who prices C on a conversion story is buying land use risk on top of leasing risk.
Jordan crosses C off for the Castillos. It is a reasonable deal for an investor with capital, patience and a leasing team. It is not a retirement check.

blocks.text: Listing D: the mixed-use building in Jackson Heights

blocks.html: Two storefronts on a busy avenue (a cellphone repair shop and a bakery) and four apartments above. The apartments have turned over slowly; the stores pay more per square foot but sit on shorter leases. This is the classic New York mixed-use building: diversified income, and two kinds of tenancies under two sets of rules.

blocks.q: The bakery's lease expires next year. Which rules govern how much the Castillos may raise its rent at renewal?
c: The Rent Guidelines Board's annual increase for commercial units in mixed buildings
Good Cause Eviction's cap of the lower of CPI plus 5% or 10%
The same rent stabilization rules that apply to the four apartments upstairs
The renewal terms in the lease, since commercial rents in New York are unregulated
blocks.x: New York does not regulate commercial rents. The bakery has whatever renewal rights its lease grants, and if none, the parties negotiate. The Good Cause and Rent Guidelines Board answers borrow residential rules. The apartments are a separate question: a building with fewer than six units is generally not stabilized, and an owner with ten or fewer units statewide is generally exempt from Good Cause.

blocks.title: One building, two rulebooks
blocks.html: Upstairs, the residential rules apply in full: the warranty of habitability, the one-month security deposit cap, the HSTPA notice rules for non-renewal or big increases, and lead paint rules for a pre-1978 building. Downstairs, the lease is the law, plus NYC's commercial tenant harassment law, which lets a commercial tenant sue a landlord who uses threats, repeated disruptive construction or similar tactics to push it out. And the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form goes to the Castillos at first substantive contact whatever the property type.

The Castillos like D. It is ten minutes from their daughter. But four apartments and two stores mean repairs, turnover and collections. Teresa looks at her receipt and draws a small question mark next to "no 2 am phone calls."

Jordan lays out what owning D would actually involve. The apartments need heat and hot water, repairs within a reasonable time, lead paint compliance, annual window guard notices and a response when a tenant calls. The stores need lease enforcement, sidewalk and storefront obligations, and a plan when one goes vacant, because a dark storefront on a busy avenue can sit for months. Most owners of six units either do the work themselves or hire a managing agent for a percentage of collected rent.

Financing differs too. A lender looking at D cares about the store leases as much as the apartments: two stores on short leases can produce a big share of the income, and if one goes dark, coverage drops. Many lenders underwrite a building with storefronts as a commercial loan, priced and sized on the income, with a shorter term than a home mortgage. The Castillos would be landlords to six tenants and borrowers on business terms.

blocks.q: Compared with Listing B, why is Listing D more management intensive even though it is a smaller dollar investment?
c: It has more tenants, residential duties and turnover, with expenses on the owner
It has fewer tenants, so each vacancy has to be filled by the owner personally
Its leases are net, so the owner has to audit each tenant's expense statements
Its stores are rent regulated, so every renewal needs an agency filing first
blocks.x: Management intensity follows the number of tenants, the kind of tenancy and who pays expenses. Six tenants, two rulebooks, and an owner who pays operating costs and repairs adds up to real work. A single tenant on a net lease handles most of its own space and costs. Storefronts in New York are not rent regulated, so no filing is needed for a commercial renewal.

blocks.text: Listing E: the strip center in New Dorp

blocks.html: Six shops along a busy road, parking in front, no anchor: a nail salon, a pizzeria, a dry cleaner, a tax preparer, a vape shop and one vacancy. The price looks low for six leases. The reason is on page 14 of the offering memorandum: the owner does not own the land. The building sits on a ground lease with 22 years remaining.

blocks.q: Why does the 22-year ground lease drag Listing E's price down?
c: The ground lessor has the right to collect the shop rents directly from tenants
Ground leases are void in New York once less than 25 years remain on them
The buyer owns a leasehold whose value shrinks as the remaining term runs out
Strip centers on ground leases are taxed at the higher commercial rate in New York
blocks.x: The buyer here gets a leasehold interest, not fee simple. At the end of the term the improvements generally go to the landowner, so each year that passes leaves less to sell. Lenders also want the ground lease to run well past the loan's maturity, which shrinks the buyer pool. Nothing in New York law voids a ground lease for being short.

blocks.q: Compared with a grocery-anchored neighborhood center, a small unanchored strip center like Listing E usually carries:
c: Lower vacancy risk, because local service tenants rarely move
Higher liquidity, because smaller centers sell faster in any market
Lower management, because no anchor lease needs to be enforced
Higher tenant risk, since small local tenants turn over more
blocks.x: An anchor tenant, especially a supermarket, draws daily traffic that keeps in-line shops alive and makes the center easier to lease. An unanchored strip depends on small local businesses that open and close more often, so vacancy and collection risk run higher. Fewer leases does not mean less work, and liquidity depends on the buyer pool, not center size alone.

blocks.text: Listing F: the warehouse in Maspeth

blocks.html: One tenant, a beverage distributor, in a one-story warehouse with three loading docks and 22-foot ceilings, in a manufacturing zone near the Long Island Expressway. Last-mile demand in western Queens is strong. The lease is net, and the tenant has three years left. The building was an auto body shop until 1998.

Industrial buyers read a different spec sheet than retail buyers. Foot traffic does not matter here. What matters is clear height (how high the tenant can stack before hitting the structure), the number and type of loading docks, truck turning room, floor load, power and the zoning. In New York City, manufacturing districts (M1, M2, M3) allow industrial and many commercial uses and generally bar new housing, which protects the use but limits other options for the building.

blocks.q: A last-mile delivery company is touring Listing F. Which features most affect what it will pay in rent?
c: Storefront visibility and the pedestrian count on the block
Lobby finishes, elevator count and the building's office class
Clear height, loading docks, truck access and highway proximity
Distance to a regional mall and its department store anchors
blocks.x: Industrial value comes from how efficiently goods move in and out: clear height for racking, enough docks, room for trucks to turn, and quick access to highways and customers. Visibility and foot traffic drive retail rents, and lobbies and building class are office measures. Applying the wrong property type's yardstick is how buyers misprice industrial space.

blocks.q: Before the Castillos sign a contract on Listing F, which step best protects them from a hidden liability tied to the site's history?
c: Order a Phase I environmental site assessment before taking title
Rely on the tenant's net lease, which shifts environmental cleanup to the tenant
Ask the seller to sign a property condition disclosure statement for the site
Buy an HO-3 policy, which covers pollution found after the sale
blocks.x: Under CERCLA, an owner can be liable for contamination it did not cause. A Phase I environmental site assessment before purchase is the basis for the innocent landowner defense and tells the buyer whether more testing is needed. The PCDS covers residential 1 to 4 family sales, not warehouses, and a net lease cannot shift the owner's liability to the government.

blocks.html: Even clean, F has a short fuse: three years of lease left, and a single tenant. If the distributor leaves, the Castillos own an empty warehouse. Industrial space in that location re-leases well, but downtime, commissions and possibly a new roof are cash events.

blocks.text: Matching the property to the people

blocks.title: What the Castillos asked for, and what each type gives

left.title: Their list
items: Steady monthly income
Little management
Something they could sell
Nothing to fix

right.title: What the types deliver
items: Land: no income, low liquidity
Office: lease-up capital and risk
Mixed use and strip: income, but work
Net lease: passive, if the tenant and lease terms are strong

blocks.q: Given the Castillos' goals, which listing type fits best, and with what condition?
c: The Jackson Heights mixed-use building, since apartments are the safest income
A net-leased building, if the tenant credit and lease terms hold up
The Great Kills lot, since land needs no repairs and holds value well
The White Plains office, since buying at a discount reduces their overall risk
blocks.x: A net-leased single-tenant building is the least management-intensive income property, which matches the receipt. But B's no-guaranty LLC tenant and landlord roof duty undercut it, so the fit depends on tenant credit, remaining term, guaranty and expense terms. The mixed-use choice is a strong building but not a passive one, and the lot produces no income at all.

blocks.html: The receipt also says something we could sell. No real estate is liquid the way a savings account is, but some types sell faster than others. Single-tenant net lease buildings with strong tenants trade often, because a deep pool of buyers (including investors completing 1031 exchanges) wants passive income. Vacant land and partly empty office buildings sit the longest, because each buyer has to underwrite a plan rather than a rent check.

blocks.q: Ranking the six listings on liquidity, which type would usually be easiest to sell quickly at a fair price?
c: The vacant Great Kills lot, since land carries no tenants to complicate a sale
The 40% vacant White Plains office building priced below its 2015 sale
A well-leased single-tenant net lease building with a creditworthy tenant
The ground-leased strip center, since its price is the lowest of the group
blocks.x: Liquidity depends on how many buyers can quickly understand and finance the asset. A long net lease to a strong tenant is easy to underwrite and attracts a broad pool, including exchange buyers on a deadline. Land and vacant office require each buyer to bet on a plan, and a short ground lease narrows the lender and buyer pool. A low price alone does not create liquidity.

blocks.html: Ramon asks Jordan to promise that a pharmacy lease is "as safe as a bond." Jordan does not. Diane's rule in the office is simple: describe the tenant, the lease and the risks, and let the client's accountant and attorney judge the rest.

blocks.q: Ramon asks Jordan to confirm a net lease is "as safe as a bond." What is the best response?
c: Explain the credit, term and expense risks and suggest advisers review them
Confirm it, since a long net lease to a national chain is close to risk free
Refuse to discuss it, since evaluating a lease is the practice of law
Confirm it if the seller provides three years of rent payment history
blocks.x: A licensee cannot guarantee an investment outcome, and calling a lease risk free misstates what can go wrong: the tenant entity, a store going dark, the end of the term, roof and structure costs. Describing those risks is ordinary brokerage work, not law practice; interpreting legal rights is where the attorney comes in. Past payments are evidence, not a guarantee.

blocks.html: What happened: the Castillos passed on all six. Three months later Jordan found a single-tenant urgent care building in Bay Shore with 14 years left, an absolute net lease, and a guaranty from the operating company's parent. They bought it with about 60% cash and a modest loan, and kept $250,000 in the bank. Teresa framed the receipt.

blocks.title: Lease abstract, Bay Shore urgent care (the one they bought)
blocks.html:
Tenant: regional urgent care operating company
Guarantor: parent company, full guaranty
Term: 14 years remaining, two 5-year options
Expenses: absolute net, tenant pays taxes, insurance, all repairs including roof and structure
Rent: 2% annual increases
Go-dark: tenant may stop operating, but landlord then has a right to recapture the premises on 90 days' notice

blocks.q: Why does the recapture right in the Bay Shore lease matter to the Castillos?
c: It lets the tenant terminate whenever its sales fall below a set breakpoint
It lets the landlord raise rent to market once the clinic stops operating
It lets the parent company replace the guaranty with a security deposit
It lets the landlord take back a dark space and re-lease it early
blocks.x: Without an operating covenant, a tenant can close and keep paying rent, leaving the owner with a dark building and a shrinking lease term. A recapture right lets the landlord end the lease and find a new operator while the location still has value. It is a landlord protection, not a tenant exit tied to sales, and it does not reset the rent on its own.

items: Raw land costs money every year, earns nothing until sold or built, and cannot be depreciated. Verify zoning claims before repeating them.
Net lease value turns on who signed, who guaranteed, how long is left, whether the tenant must keep operating, and whether roof and structure are on the tenant.
Vacant office space is priced low because lease-up costs time, tenant improvements, commissions and free rent.
Mixed-use buildings combine regulated residential rules with unregulated commercial leases; commercial rents in New York are set by the lease.
Anchors drive retail traffic; ground-leased buildings lose value as the remaining term shrinks; industrial sites need environmental due diligence.
Match the property type to the investor's goals for income, management, liquidity and risk, and never promise an outcome.

lessons.title: Case file: The Bakery on Court Street
lessons.tagline: A one-page term sheet for a Carroll Gardens storefront. Every line moves money or risk. Find where.
objectives: Analyze a New York retail term sheet for lease structure, proportionate share and annual increases
Decide how use clauses, exclusives, rent commencement and percentage rent should be negotiated for a retail tenant
Apply New York commercial lease rules on mitigation, assignment and guaranties, and contrast them with residential rules
Identify NYC rules that affect a storefront lease, including commercial rent tax scope and tenant harassment protections

blocks.title: A storefront, an oven and a term sheet
blocks.html: Mei Lin has baked for other people for twelve years, most recently as head baker at a Manhattan restaurant group. With her business partner, Andre Baptiste, she wants her own place: a bakery and cafe with a few tables. They have found a 1,200 square foot storefront on Court Street in Carroll Gardens, in a four-story building with a second storefront (a coffee bar) and six apartments upstairs. The landlord's broker is Marcus. Mei hires Hudson & Hart to represent her and Andre as tenants, and Jordan gets the file. Marcus emails a one-page term sheet within the hour with the subject line "Moves fast, multiple interest." Mei forwards it with one line: "Is this good?"

Retail leases are where the lease clauses from the lessons stop being definitions and start being money. Every line on Marcus's term sheet shifts cost or risk between landlord and tenant. Jordan's job is to find where, explain it, and get the clients to their attorney with the right questions. First, though, there is paperwork at the first meeting.

blocks.q: At Jordan's first substantive meeting with Mei and Andre about leasing the storefront, which New York form is required?
c: The RPL 443 agency disclosure form for tenants, signed before any showing
No form, since disclosure rules in New York apply to residential leases alone
The landlord and tenant property condition disclosure statement for the space
The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form, which covers commercial
blocks.x: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form applies to every property type, commercial and vacant land included, at first substantive contact. The RPL 443 agency disclosure form is the tempting answer, but it covers residential 1 to 4 family sales and residential rentals, not a storefront lease. Jordan still explains whom Hudson & Hart represents, because agency duties apply in commercial work even without the form.

blocks.title: Marcus's term sheet, Court Street storefront
blocks.html:
Premises: ground floor store, approx. 1,200 RSF, plus basement storage (no charge)
Term: 10 years
Base rent: $95 per sq ft per year, increasing 3% per year
Real estate taxes: tenant pays 15% of increases over the 2025/2026 base tax year
Utilities: tenant pays electric and gas directly; water and sewer billed at 15%
Use: retail bakery and for no other purpose
Percentage rent: 6% of gross sales over $1,000,000
Security: 6 months' rent
Guaranty: full personal guaranty of Mei Lin and Andre Baptiste for the term
Delivery: "as is"; rent begins on lease signing
Assignment/subletting: not permitted without landlord consent in its sole discretion

Start with the rent. In New York, retail and office rent is quoted per square foot per year. At $95 a foot on 1,200 feet, base rent is $114,000 a year, or $9,500 a month, before the tax share, water and the 3% annual bumps. By year 10 the base rent alone is about $148,700.

blocks.q: How would Jordan describe the expense structure in Marcus's term sheet?
c: An absolute net lease, since the tenant pays every cost of the building
A modified gross lease with a tax escalation and separately billed utilities
A triple net lease, since the tenant pays CAM for the building's common areas
A pure gross lease, since the base rent covers the building expenses
blocks.x: The landlord keeps paying most building expenses out of base rent, but the tenant pays its own utilities and its 15% share of real estate tax increases over a base year. That is a modified gross structure, common for NYC storefronts. A triple net lease would put the tenant's share of all taxes, insurance and maintenance on it from day one, not just increases. CAM is typical in shopping centers.

blocks.html: The 15% tax share is the store's proportionate share: its rentable area divided by the building's. Andre asks how Marcus got to 15% for a store that is 1,200 feet in an 8,000 foot building. Jordan checks the math (1,200 / 8,000 = 15%) and then checks something else: the building's residential units get no tax escalation at all. The store is not overpaying by the arithmetic, but taxes on a mixed-use building in NYC can jump after a reassessment, and the store's share of that jump is uncapped. Jordan flags a cap on annual tax increases as an ask for the attorney.

Then the base year. Marcus's term sheet uses the 2025/2026 tax year, which has already closed. New York City's tax year runs July 1 to June 30, and the building's assessment for 2026/2027 is already higher. Using last year's lower tax bill as the baseline means Mei starts paying escalations in her first year for increases that happened before she signed.

blocks.q: What base tax year should Jordan ask for in Mei's lease?
c: The 2026/2027 tax year or later, so the baseline matches current taxes
The 2025/2026 tax year, since an earlier baseline lowers the escalation
The calendar year 2025, since tax years follow the calendar in the city
No base year, with Mei paying 15% of the full tax bill from day one
blocks.x: Escalations charge the tenant its share of increases over the base year, so a later base year means a higher baseline and smaller escalations. An earlier, lower base year works against the tenant. Paying a share of the full tax bill from day one would be a net lease term, a larger cost. NYC's property tax year runs July 1 to June 30, not the calendar year.

blocks.text: The use clause and the coffee bar next door

blocks.html: Mei's plan is bread and pastry in the morning, coffee all day, and a few sandwiches at lunch. The term sheet says "retail bakery and for no other purpose." Jordan asks Marcus for the coffee bar's lease. Marcus will not share the whole lease but confirms the coffee bar has an exclusive: the landlord promised not to lease to another tenant "whose primary business is the sale of espresso-based beverages."

blocks.q: Given the coffee bar's exclusive, what use clause should Jordan push for on Mei's behalf?
c: Any lawful retail use, which overrides the coffee bar's exclusive
Retail bakery as written, adding coffee later by lease amendment
Retail bakery, with coffee and light food as incidental uses
Coffee bar and bakery, since exclusives bind the landlord, not her
blocks.x: A narrow "for no other purpose" clause would let the landlord call her coffee sales a default. A clause naming the bakery as primary and coffee and light food as incidental fits Mei's plan and stays outside an exclusive limited to tenants whose primary business is espresso. A broad clause does not override another tenant's exclusive; the landlord cannot lease in violation of a promise already made.

blocks.html: Mei also needs to know that coffee and sandwiches change more than words. Cooking, seating and a gas-fired oven raise questions about the building's certificate of occupancy, venting through the roof, a grease trap, and whether the space can legally be used as an eating and drinking establishment. Marcus says the last tenant was a bakery. The last tenant was a bakery that sold bread to go, with an electric oven.

blocks.q: Who should confirm, before the lease is signed, that the space can legally hold Mei's bakery cafe with gas ovens and seating?
c: Marcus, since the listing broker vouches for the space's legal use
The prior tenant, since it used the space for the same type of business
Mei's architect and attorney, with a lease contingency for approvals
The Department of Buildings after opening, during its routine inspection
blocks.x: Legal use, the certificate of occupancy, venting and gas work are technical questions for a licensed architect or engineer and the tenant's attorney. The safest lease ties Mei's obligations to getting the needed permits, or lets her exit if she cannot. Relying on Marcus or the prior tenant's use is how tenants end up with a lease for a space they cannot open in. Learning about a problem after opening is the most expensive way to find it.

blocks.title: Landlord work, as is, and the vent
blocks.html: "As is" means the tenant takes the space in its current condition and pays for everything it needs. In a restaurant space the vent stack alone can be a five-figure job, and in a building with apartments above, the landlord must allow the route through the building. Tenant reps ask for landlord work (the landlord delivers certain items done), a tenant improvement allowance, or both, and they put the landlord's consent to the vent route in the lease, not in an email.

blocks.text: Rent while the ovens go in

blocks.html: The term sheet says rent begins on lease signing. Mei's contractor estimates four months for permits and build-out before she can sell a single croissant. At $9,500 a month, that is $38,000 in rent on a space that cannot open.

blocks.q: What is the standard way to address the build-out period in Mei's lease?
c: Separate the lease commencement date from a later rent commencement date
Delay signing the lease until the build-out is complete and inspected
Ask Marcus to waive the rent, since brokers can bind the landlord on rent
Pay the rent and deduct it from the percentage rent owed in later years
blocks.x: Commercial leases often start the term on signing (so the tenant can get in and build) and start rent later, after a free rent period sized to the build-out. That is rent abatement, and it is normal on a raw or as is space. Signing after the build-out leaves Mei building in a space she has no right to. A broker does not bind the landlord on terms unless authorized, and percentage rent is a separate obligation.

blocks.html: Marcus comes back with two months free. Jordan counters with five, citing the vent and gas work. They land at four, plus a clause that pushes rent commencement back day for day if the landlord delays the vent access.

The term sheet adds percentage rent: 6% of gross sales over $1,000,000. Mei's projections show sales of $900,000 in year 1 and $1,300,000 by year 3. Jordan figures the natural breakpoint on the year 1 base rent: $114,000 / 0.06 = $1,900,000. Marcus's $1,000,000 is an artificial breakpoint set well below it.

head: Year 3 sales $1,300,000
Breakpoint $1,000,000 (term sheet)
Natural breakpoint (about $2,000,000 by then)
rows: Landlord shares in sales Mei needs to cover her costs
Landlord shares only in truly strong years
blocks.caption: Year 3 base rent is about $120,900, so the natural breakpoint has risen to roughly $2,015,000.
