blocks.q: Which change to the percentage rent clause most helps Mei and Andre?
c: Lower the 6% rate to 5% and keep the $1,000,000 breakpoint as written
Use the natural breakpoint, which rises each year as the base rent rises
Raise the base rent so that the breakpoint falls further below expected sales
Report sales to the landlord annually instead of monthly to delay overage rent
blocks.x: A natural breakpoint means the landlord collects overage only when the percentage of total sales exceeds the base rent, and it rises as the base rent steps up. Marcus's fixed $1,000,000 breakpoint charges overage on ordinary sales. Lowering the rate helps a little but keeps an early trigger. Reporting frequency changes timing, not the amount owed, and landlords want audit rights either way.

blocks.html: In the end the landlord dropped percentage rent entirely in exchange for 3.5% annual increases instead of 3%. Small neighborhood storefronts in NYC often skip percentage rent because tracking a bakery's register is more trouble than it is worth. Shopping centers are where it lives.

Marcus's term sheet asks for a full personal guaranty from both partners for all ten years. Mei and Andre are forming an LLC to sign the lease, but a full guaranty would put their savings and homes behind every dollar of rent through 2036.

blocks.q: Jordan proposes a "good guy" guaranty instead. What does it typically do?
c: It guarantees the first year of rent, and then it expires automatically
It guarantees the landlord's obligations to the tenant for the full term
It replaces the security deposit with a letter from the tenant's bank
It covers rent until the tenant gives notice, pays up and leaves
blocks.x: A good guy guaranty makes the principals liable only until the tenant gives notice, pays rent through move-out and returns the space vacant and broom clean. It protects the landlord from a tenant who stops paying but stays, the expensive scenario in New York's slow eviction process. A one-year burn-off guaranty is a different negotiated structure, and a letter of credit replaces cash security, not a guaranty.

blocks.html: Why would a landlord accept it? Because the real risk to a landlord is a tenant who stops paying and stays for months while the landlord goes to court. Good guy guaranties became standard in New York because they solve that specific problem. The landlord agreed, in exchange for raising the security deposit from six months to eight.

The deposit itself raises a question. Eight months of rent is $76,000. Andre asks where that money goes. Marcus's answer, "into the landlord's account," is the wrong one. Under General Obligations Law 7-103, money deposited for the use or rental of real property stays the tenant's money, is held in trust, and may not be mixed with the landlord's own funds. The statute is not limited to apartments. The interest-bearing account requirement applies to buildings with six or more family units, but the trust and no-commingling rules reach a storefront deposit too. Many commercial tenants post a letter of credit instead of cash, which keeps the money in their own bank.

blocks.q: Under New York law, how must the landlord handle Mei's $76,000 cash security deposit?
c: Hold it in trust, kept separate from the landlord's own money and accounts
Deposit it in the operating account, since commercial deposits are unregulated
Pay it to Hudson & Hart's escrow account until the lease ends
Apply it to the first eight months of rent, starting at rent commencement
blocks.x: GOL 7-103 makes a deposit for the rental of real property the tenant's money, held in trust and not commingled with the landlord's personal funds. It is not limited to residential leases. Some landlords and tenants agree that a broker or attorney holds funds in escrow, but nothing requires it, and applying the deposit to rent would leave the landlord without security.

blocks.html: Andre, who reads everything, asks a hard question: "If we close in year 3 and hand back the keys, does the landlord have to find a new tenant and stop charging us?"

blocks.q: Under New York law, what is the answer to Andre's question for a commercial lease?
c: Yes, the landlord has to make reasonable efforts to re-rent, just as for apartments
No, because the security deposit caps what a landlord can recover
Yes, but the duty to re-rent applies to storefronts and not to offices
No, a commercial landlord generally has no duty unless the lease says so
blocks.x: In 1995 New York's highest court held in Holy Properties v. Kenneth Cole that a commercial landlord need not re-rent to reduce what the departing tenant owes. The 2019 rent law added a duty to mitigate (RPL 227-e), but only for leases of residential premises. That is why the good guy guaranty and a negotiated surrender clause matter so much for a commercial tenant.

blocks.title: Borrowing residential rules for a store
blocks.html: Commercial tenants in New York do not get the residential protections: no one-month deposit cap, no statutory right to sublet (RPL 226-b covers residential buildings with four or more units), no renewal right unless the lease grants one, no duty on the landlord to mitigate, no rent regulation. Students who learn the residential rules first tend to assume they carry over. In a store or office, the lease is almost the whole law.

Mei hopes to open a second location and maybe sell this one. The term sheet bars assignment and subletting without consent "in landlord's sole discretion." That means the landlord could refuse any buyer of the business for any reason, which makes the bakery nearly impossible to sell as a going concern.

blocks.q: What change to the assignment clause should Jordan flag for the attorney?
c: Delete it, since RPL 226-b gives tenants a right to assign with consent
Consent not to be unreasonably withheld, with a permitted sale of the business
Consent in the landlord's sole discretion, with the landlord's recapture right removed
No change, since an LLC tenant can sell its membership interests freely
blocks.x: A reasonableness standard plus a right to assign to a buyer of the business (often with net worth or experience tests) gives Mei an exit while protecting the landlord. RPL 226-b is residential only. Many commercial leases treat a transfer of a controlling interest in the tenant entity as an assignment, so selling the LLC is not an easy way around the clause.

blocks.html: There is one step up from the sidewalk into the store. Mei wants seating for customers, which makes the space a place of public accommodation under the federal Americans with Disabilities Act and under New York State and City human rights laws. The term sheet is silent on who fixes access.

blocks.q: If the entrance is not accessible and a customer brings a claim, who can be liable?
c: The tenant alone, since it operates the business open to the public
The landlord alone, since the entrance is part of the building's structure
Both landlord and tenant, whatever the lease says between them
Neither, since buildings built before 1990 are exempt from access rules
blocks.x: Under the ADA's public accommodation rules, both the landlord and the tenant of a place of public accommodation are responsible for compliance. The lease can allocate who pays and who does the work, but it does not change who a customer can sue. Older buildings are not exempt; existing facilities must remove barriers where readily achievable. Jordan adds an access clause to the list for the attorney.

blocks.title: NYC rules that follow a storefront
blocks.html: The city's commercial tenant harassment law lets a commercial tenant sue a landlord who uses threats, repeated disruptive construction, utility interruptions or similar tactics that would reasonably cause it to leave; courts can impose civil penalties. Landlords must also register ground-floor and second-floor storefronts with the Department of Finance and report vacancies. The Commercial Rent Tax, often mentioned by worried tenants, applies only in Manhattan south of 96th Street and only above a rent threshold, so a Court Street bakery does not pay it.

blocks.q: Mei's former boss warns her that NYC's commercial rent tax will add 3.9% to her rent. For the Court Street store, Jordan should explain that:
c: The tax applies, but a small business credit fully offsets it below $500,000 of rent
The tax applies to Brooklyn tenants once rent exceeds $100 a square foot
The tax is the landlord's obligation, so it is built into the asking rent
The tax covers Manhattan south of 96th Street, so it does not reach Brooklyn
blocks.x: The Commercial Rent Tax applies only to tenants in Manhattan south of 96th Street, and then only above a rent threshold, with small business credits. Her former boss's restaurant in Manhattan may well pay it. The small business credit answer is a real rule from the tax, applied to a location the tax does not reach.

head: Term
Marcus's term sheet
Signed lease
rows: 4 months free, extended day for day for landlord vent delays
Bakery, with coffee and prepared food as incidental uses
Not unreasonably withheld; sale of business permitted with tests
Landlord ramp at entrance; vent route approved; permit contingency

blocks.html: Two items did not make the table. The tax escalation kept the 15% share but moved the base year to 2026/2027, and the landlord refused a cap on tax increases, so Mei's attorney got a clause passing through her share of any tax refund the landlord wins in a tax certiorari case instead. And the commission: Hudson & Hart was paid by the landlord, through a co-brokerage with Marcus's firm under his listing agreement. Jordan told Mei and Andre that in writing at the start, along with the point that matters most: who pays the commission does not decide whom the broker represents. Jordan worked for the tenants from the first email to the last signature.
Marcus called it "a lot of paper for a bakery." The bakery opened in April. The line on Saturdays goes past the coffee bar, whose owner now buys Mei's croissants wholesale.

items: Give the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form in commercial deals too; RPL 443 agency disclosure is a residential form.
Read a NYC storefront term sheet for structure: base rent per foot per year, proportionate share of tax increases, utilities, and annual bumps.
Draft the use clause around the real business and other tenants' exclusives, and confirm legal use, venting and permits before signing.
Separate lease commencement from rent commencement to cover the build-out; prefer a natural breakpoint if percentage rent applies.
In NY commercial leases there is no landlord duty to mitigate and no statutory right to assign or sublet, so the guaranty and assignment clauses carry the risk.
Access is a shared landlord and tenant duty; the Commercial Rent Tax applies only in Manhattan below 96th Street.

lessons.title: Case file: Forty Lawyers Move to Brooklyn
lessons.tagline: A nonprofit law office, two Downtown Brooklyn floors, and a build-out that could sink the budget.
objectives: Compare office proposals using usable square feet, cost per usable foot and net effective rent
Analyze tenant improvement terms: allowance versus turnkey, soft costs, deadlines and overruns
Decide which operating expense, electricity, SNDA, delivery and renewal terms protect an office tenant
Explain how termination options and restoration clauses shift cost between landlord and tenant

blocks.title: Forty lawyers and a lease that ends in June
blocks.html: Rosa Delgado runs the Harbor Family Law Project, a nonprofit with 40 staff attorneys and paralegals who represent parents in Family Court. Its lease on two floors of an old Lower Manhattan building ends next June, and the landlord wants a 30% increase to renew. Rosa wants to move to Downtown Brooklyn, closer to the courthouse and to most of the families Harbor serves. Her board has approved a budget, a ten-year term, and one instruction: "Do not let us run out of money building out an office." Diane takes the assignment as the tenant's broker and brings Jordan onto the team. Two buildings make the short list, and both landlords send letters of intent within a week. Rosa asks the first question on the drive back: "Once we sign one of these letters, are we committed?"

Office leasing in New York is a negotiation over more than rent. The rent is quoted per rentable square foot, the landlord pays for some or all of the build-out, the tenant gets months of free rent, and a dozen clauses decide what the space will really cost over ten years. This case follows Harbor from letter of intent to signed lease.

blocks.q: What is the usual legal effect of a commercial letter of intent like the ones Harbor received?
c: It is generally non-binding on the deal until a lease is signed and delivered
It binds both sides to the business terms, leaving the legal details open
It binds the landlord to hold the space, but leaves the tenant free to walk away
It becomes binding once the tenant pays a deposit to the listing broker in escrow
blocks.x: Letters of intent in New York office leasing usually say expressly that they are non-binding (apart from items such as confidentiality) and that nothing is agreed until a lease is fully signed and delivered. That means either side can walk away, and the landlord can keep showing the space. Harbor should keep both buildings in play until the lease is signed. Any binding effect depends on the LOI's own language, so the attorney reads it.

head: Building A: 1 Willoughby Plaza (fictional)
Building B: 220 Livingston (fictional)
rows: $40 per RSF, or landlord turnkey build

blocks.html: Rosa's operations manager sees $46 and says B is cheaper. Diane asks her how many offices fit on each floor. Harbor's space plan needs about 8,800 usable square feet for 40 workstations, six interview rooms and a conference room. B's floor is bigger on paper and smaller in reality.

blocks.q: Measured by cost per usable square foot, how do the two floors compare in year 1?
c: B is cheaper, since its asking rent per rentable foot is $4 lower
They cost the same, since rent is quoted on rentable feet for both
A is cheaper per usable foot, about $61 versus about $63 for B
B is cheaper, since its larger floor spreads the rent over more feet
blocks.x: Cost per usable foot equals rent per RSF divided by (1 minus the loss factor). A: $50 / 0.82 = about $61. B: $46 / 0.73 = about $63. The bigger loss factor eats B's lower asking rent. Rentable feet include a share of common areas that Harbor pays for but cannot occupy, which is why tenant reps compare space on usable feet.

blocks.html: And B's 8,395 usable feet do not fit Harbor's 8,800 square foot plan, so B would require losing two interview rooms or leasing part of another floor. Rosa crosses B's asking rent off the whiteboard and writes "usable" in red.

Both landlords will pay for the build-out, in different ways. Building A offers a tenant improvement allowance of $85 per RSF, about $935,000, which Harbor spends on its own design with its own architect and contractor under a work letter. Building B offers either $40 per RSF or a turnkey build: the landlord builds out the space to an agreed plan at its own cost.

blocks.q: If Harbor takes Building A's $935,000 allowance and the build-out costs $1,050,000, who pays the $115,000 overrun?
c: The landlord, because the allowance sets a floor on what it contributes
Harbor, because the allowance caps the landlord's contribution
The contractor, because the work letter fixes the construction price
The landlord and Harbor equally, under the standard work letter split
blocks.x: An allowance is a fixed contribution; costs above it are the tenant's. That is the trade-off: Harbor controls design, contractor and schedule, and it carries the overrun risk. In a turnkey deal, the landlord carries the cost risk but controls the specifications. An allowance is a cap, not a floor, and work letters do not split overruns unless they say so.

blocks.html: Harbor's architect prices the space plan at about $1,000,000 for construction alone. Rosa thinks of her board's one instruction. Diane goes back to the work letter.

blocks.title: Building A work letter, draft excerpt
blocks.html: "Landlord's Contribution may be applied only to the cost of hard construction of the Initial Alterations. Any portion not requested within 12 months after the Commencement Date shall be deemed waived."

blocks.q: Harbor also needs architects, permit filings, cabling and moving costs. What should Diane ask for in the work letter?
c: A conversion of the entire allowance into free rent at the end of the term
A rule that the landlord pays every soft cost beyond the allowance
A waiver of the 12-month deadline so the allowance stays open for the full term
Letting part of the allowance cover soft costs such as design and cabling
blocks.x: Work letters commonly limit the allowance to hard construction unless the tenant negotiates a soft cost carve-out, often a set percentage or dollar amount for design, filing, cabling, furniture or moving. Asking the landlord to pay unlimited soft costs goes nowhere. A longer deadline is a fair ask, but an allowance that never expires is not realistic, and the timing of rent credits is a separate negotiation.

blocks.html: The landlord agreed to let up to $15 per RSF of the allowance cover soft costs, extended the deadline to 18 months, and agreed that up to $10 per RSF of unused allowance could be taken as a rent credit. Unused allowance otherwise disappears; tenant reps fight for that last clause because it turns leftover money into lower rent instead of a landlord windfall.

Rosa's board treasurer wants one number per building. Diane builds a rough net effective rent: total rent over the term, minus free rent, minus the landlord's allowance, divided by RSF and years. It ignores escalations, the time value of money and electricity, so it is a comparison tool, not a budget.

head: 10-year term
Building A (11,000 RSF)
Building B (11,500 RSF)
rows: Net effective per RSF per year

blocks.q: What does the net effective comparison tell Harbor?
c: B is cheaper, since its asking rent is lower and asking rent sets the cost
A is cheaper, but just if Harbor gives up the soft cost carve-out
The buildings cost the same, since landlords price concessions to match
A costs less over the term once the free rent and allowance are counted
blocks.x: Concessions are part of the price. A's higher asking rent comes with more than a year of combined free rent and a much larger allowance, which lowers what the landlord actually collects per foot. Landlords often prefer high face rents with big concessions because the face rent supports the building's value and future leasing comparables. The soft cost carve-out does not change the totals.

blocks.title: No rent regulation, no statutory renewal
blocks.html: Harbor is a nonprofit doing public interest work, but its lease is a commercial lease. New York does not regulate office rents, gives commercial tenants no statutory right to renew, and (under Holy Properties v. Kenneth Cole) does not require a commercial landlord to re-rent if a tenant leaves early. The protections Harbor gets are the ones written into this lease.

blocks.text: Operating expenses and the base year

blocks.html: Both buildings quote modified gross: base rent covers expenses at the base year level, and Harbor pays its proportionate share of increases. The escalation math is routine. The fight is over what counts as an operating expense. Building A's lease draft defines it as "all costs incurred by Landlord in the operation, maintenance and repair of the Building."

blocks.q: Which items should Harbor's attorney ask to exclude from operating expenses?
c: Cleaning, security, elevator service and lobby staffing
Capital improvements, leasing commissions and debt service
Real estate taxes, since they belong in operating expenses as well
Building insurance and utilities for the common areas of the building
blocks.x: Tenants commonly exclude capital improvements (or allow them only amortized and only if they cut costs or are legally required), leasing commissions and costs of leasing other tenants' space, mortgage payments and depreciation, and costs covered by insurance. Cleaning, security, elevators, insurance and common utilities are true operating costs. Real estate taxes are usually escalated under a separate tax clause rather than within operating expenses.

blocks.html: Harbor also gets an audit right: if the landlord's annual statement overcharges by more than 3%, the landlord pays for the audit. Without audit rights, a tenant has to take the landlord's numbers on faith for ten years.

Building B includes electricity in the rent at $4.00 per RSF, adjusted by periodic surveys of the tenant's equipment. Building A submeters each floor and bills the tenant for what it uses, plus an administrative charge. Harbor is a law office: laptops, a few printers, no server room. Its electrical engineer estimates actual use at around $2.60 per RSF a year.

blocks.q: For a low-usage tenant like Harbor, which electricity method is usually the better deal?
c: Rent inclusion, because the landlord takes on the risk of rising usage
Rent inclusion, because surveys cannot raise the charge during the term
Submetering, because the tenant pays for the power it actually uses each month
Direct metering through the landlord's master meter at a fixed rate
blocks.x: Submetering bills actual usage, so a light user pays less than a flat inclusion charge set for an average tenant. Rent inclusion helps heavy users and shifts usage risk to the landlord, but inclusion clauses usually allow the landlord to raise the charge after a survey or utility rate change. Direct metering means the tenant's own utility account, not a landlord master meter.

blocks.text: Security: cash or a letter of credit

blocks.html: Building A asks for a security deposit equal to six months of rent, about $275,000. For a nonprofit, that is a year of salary for several attorneys sitting in someone else's account for a decade. Diane proposes a standby letter of credit from Harbor's bank instead, reducing by one month of rent each year after year 3 if Harbor has never been in monetary default.

blocks.q: Why does a burn-down letter of credit help Harbor more than a cash deposit of the same amount?
c: Harbor keeps its cash, and the required security shrinks as it pays on time
The landlord cannot draw on a letter of credit, even after a default in rent
Letters of credit are exempt from the trust rules that govern cash deposits
A letter of credit counts toward the tenant improvement allowance at signing
blocks.x: A letter of credit is a bank's promise to pay the landlord on demand if the tenant defaults, so the landlord keeps real security while the tenant keeps its cash (subject to bank fees and collateral). A burn-down schedule rewards good payment history by reducing the amount over time. The landlord can draw on it after a default; that is the point. It has nothing to do with the allowance.

blocks.html: Building A has a large mortgage, and the lease draft says the lease is subordinate to any present or future mortgage. Harbor plans to spend about $65,000 of its own money above the allowance and to stay ten years. Jordan asks what happens to the lease if the landlord defaults on its loan and the lender forecloses.

blocks.q: What should Harbor require before signing, given the subordination clause?
c: A release from its rent obligations if the landlord defaults on its mortgage
A non-disturbance agreement from the lender, signed as part of an SNDA
An estoppel certificate from the lender confirming the loan balance and terms
Recording of the lease ahead of the mortgage, which reverses the lien priority
blocks.x: A subordinate lease can be wiped out in a foreclosure. An SNDA gives the tenant the lender's promise of non-disturbance: as long as the tenant is not in default, the lender or foreclosure buyer will honor the lease, and the tenant attorns to the new owner. An estoppel is a statement the tenant gives, not protection the tenant gets. Recording a lease later cannot jump ahead of a mortgage already recorded.

blocks.html: Three more clauses take up most of a week. First, delivery: Harbor's old lease ends June 30. If the landlord's base building work runs late, Harbor's build-out runs late, and Harbor could become a holdover in Lower Manhattan, typically at a steep penalty rate.

blocks.q: Which clause best protects Harbor from a late delivery of Building A's space?
c: Day-for-day rent delay, credits, and an exit after an outside date
Commencement fixed at signing, whatever the delivery date turns out to be
Landlord discretion to reschedule delivery as construction requires
A promise that the old landlord accepts a holdover at the existing rent
blocks.x: Tenant reps ask that rent commencement and free rent run from actual delivery, that the tenant earn rent credits for each day of delay past a target date, and that it may terminate after an outside date. Harbor's current landlord is not a party to the new lease, so the new lease cannot set its holdover rate. Leaving delivery in the landlord's sole discretion is the problem, not the fix.

blocks.html: Second, an early termination option. Harbor's funding depends on city contracts that renew every few years. Diane asks for a one-time right to terminate at the end of year 7 on 12 months' notice.

blocks.q: If the landlord grants Harbor a year 7 termination option, what fee will it most likely require?
c: A fee equal to the security deposit, which the landlord keeps at move-out
A fee equal to three years of rent, the balance of the original term
A fee repaying unamortized allowance, free rent and commissions
No fee, because the option is granted as a concession to a nonprofit
blocks.x: Landlords spend heavily up front on allowances, free rent and brokerage commissions, and recover them over the term. A termination fee is usually set to repay the unamortized portion of those costs, often with interest, sometimes plus a few months' rent. Charging full remaining rent would make the option worthless, and nonprofit status rarely changes a landlord's math.

blocks.html: Third, restoration. The draft requires Harbor at lease end to remove all alterations and cabling and return the floor to its original condition. Ten years from now, that could cost a six-figure sum for a floor the landlord will gut anyway. Harbor's attorney narrows it: Harbor removes cabling and any specialty installations the landlord flags when it approves the plans, and nothing else.

Rosa raises one more scenario. If a city contract ends and Harbor shrinks to 25 people, could it sublet part of the floor instead of terminating? The draft allows subletting with the landlord's consent, but adds two landlord-friendly provisions: a recapture right and a 50% share of any sublease profit.

blocks.q: Harbor asks to sublet half its floor. Under the recapture right in Building A's draft, the landlord may:
c: Reject the request with no reason, as the lease's sole remedy
Collect the subtenant's rent directly and keep Harbor fully liable
Approve the sublease and raise Harbor's base rent to market
Take back that half of the space and end Harbor's obligations for it
blocks.x: A recapture clause lets the landlord respond to a sublease or assignment request by taking the space back itself, ending the tenant's lease as to that space. Landlords like it because they can re-lease at market and capture the upside. Tenants try to limit it, for example by excluding small subleases or sublets to affiliates. Recapture does not raise the tenant's rent on the rest of the floor.

blocks.html: Harbor's attorney narrowed recapture to subleases of more than half the floor for more than half the remaining term, and kept the profit split at 50% after Harbor recovers its own costs of subletting (commissions, free rent, alterations). Remember the commercial rule from the lessons: there is no statutory right to sublet a commercial space in New York. Harbor's rights are exactly what this paragraph says.

Rosa's last question is about Diane herself. The landlord will pay Hudson & Hart's commission, figured as a percentage of the total rent over the term. Doesn't that mean the brokers make more if Harbor takes more space at a higher rent? Diane answers the way the office trains everyone to answer: yes, the fee rises with the deal, which is why she put the commission arrangement in writing on day one, and why her recommendation was the building with the higher asking rent but the lower net effective cost and the floor that actually fits. The duty of loyalty runs to Harbor no matter who writes the check.

blocks.title: Comparing asking rents
blocks.html: The most common tenant mistake in office leasing is comparing asking rent per rentable foot. A lower asking rent can hide a higher loss factor, smaller concessions, a stingy allowance limited to hard costs, electricity priced above actual use, and an expense definition that passes capital costs through. Compare cost per usable foot and net effective rent, then read the work letter, expense definition and electricity clause.
Last, the end of the ten years. Building A's draft gives Harbor one five-year renewal option "at fair market value as determined by Landlord."

blocks.q: What revision to the renewal option best protects Harbor?
c: Fair market value with a baseball arbitration if the parties cannot agree
Fair market value set by the landlord, with Harbor's right to decline afterward
The same rent as year 10, which landlords accept on most renewals
A clause making renewal automatic unless the landlord gives notice
blocks.x: Tenant reps replace a value set by the landlord with an objective process: a negotiation period, then arbitration by brokers (often baseball style, where the arbitrator picks one side's number) if the parties cannot agree. Letting the landlord set the number makes the option hollow. A flat renewal at year 10 rent is rarely granted, and automatic renewal shifts control away from the tenant.

blocks.html: Harbor signed with Building A in March. The landlord paid the leasing commissions for both brokerage firms under its listing agreement, as is customary in New York office leasing; Diane disclosed that arrangement in writing to Rosa at the start and represented Harbor throughout. Harbor moved in on July 8, after five days in a rent-credited delay, and its families now walk two blocks from the courthouse.

Eighteen months later, Building A's owner refinanced, and Rosa received a two-page estoppel certificate from the new lender with a ten-day deadline. It asked Harbor to confirm the rent, the deposit, the lease dates and that "Landlord is not in default and Tenant has no claims or offsets." Harbor had a pending dispute: the landlord's first escalation statement included the cost of a new lobby, which the lease excluded as a capital improvement.

blocks.q: How should Harbor handle the estoppel certificate, given its pending escalation dispute?
c: Sign it as drafted, since estoppels are routine and carry no legal effect
Refuse to sign it, since tenants have no duty to answer a lender's request
Sign it with the dispute described, so the claim is not waived
Ask the lender to pay the disputed amount before Harbor signs
blocks.x: An estoppel certificate binds the tenant to what it says: if Harbor certifies no claims, it can be barred from pressing the lobby charge against the landlord or the lender later. The answer is to sign on time, and accurately, describing the dispute. Most leases require the tenant to deliver an estoppel within a short period, so refusing can itself be a default. The lender is not a party to the dispute.

items: A letter of intent is usually non-binding until the lease is signed and delivered; keep alternatives alive.
Compare office space on cost per usable foot and net effective rent, not asking rent per rentable foot.
An allowance caps the landlord's contribution and leaves overruns with the tenant; negotiate soft costs, deadlines and credits for unused allowance.
In a modified gross lease, the operating expense definition, exclusions and audit rights decide what escalations really cost.
Protect the tenant's investment with an SNDA, delivery-delay remedies, a renewal option with an objective rent process, and narrow restoration duties.
A termination option usually costs the unamortized allowance, free rent and commissions.

lessons.title: Case file: The Dirt Under Oak Point Avenue
lessons.tagline: A fully leased Bronx warehouse priced like a bargain. The reason is a 1972 ground lease and a date in 2031.
objectives: Distinguish the leasehold and leased fee in a ground-leased industrial property and decide which one a buyer is acquiring
Analyze a ground rent reset clause and explain its effect on leasehold value and financing
Apply industrial net lease repair provisions and estoppel requirements to a New York acquisition
Compare the risk, liquidity and management profile of owning the leasehold versus the leased fee

blocks.title: A warehouse, a trust, and a date in 2031
blocks.html: Evelyn Park wants an industrial building. Office has been a hard business since 2020, her retail is holding steady, and every investor she knows is chasing warehouses near the city's highways. Diane's firm co-brokers a listing that looks right: a 60,000 square foot distribution warehouse on Oak Point Avenue in Hunts Point (fictional address), leased to a regional food distributor, 28-foot clear height, ten loading docks, ten minutes from the Bruckner Expressway. The asking price is $14,000,000, which Evelyn calls "strangely polite" for a fully leased warehouse in that location. Jordan, who is helping Diane with the file, finds the reason on the first page of the title report: Schedule B lists "Ground lease dated March 1, 1972, between the Barretto Family Trust, as landlord, and Oak Point Terminal LLC, as tenant." Evelyn reads it, puts down her coffee, and says, "So what exactly am I buying?"

This case is about two layers of lease stacked on one piece of land, and about how the property type and the form of ownership together set the risk. The warehouse lease is triple net and nearly passive. The ground lease underneath it is where the money can disappear.

blocks.q: Based on the title report, what interest would Evelyn acquire for $14,000,000?
c: Fee simple in the land and building, subject to the distributor's space lease
The ground lessee's leasehold, along with the space lease to the distributor
The leased fee, meaning the trust's land with the ground rent paid to her
A life estate in the building that ends when the trust's beneficiaries die
blocks.x: Oak Point Terminal LLC is the ground tenant, so its interest is a leasehold: the right to use the land for the remaining term, with the building and the space lease to the distributor. The Barretto trust keeps the leased fee. Selling "the building" here means selling the ground tenant's position, not the land. A ground lease is a lease (a nonfreehold estate) no matter how long it runs.

head: Layer
Parties
Key terms
rows: Barretto Family Trust (ground lessor) and Oak Point Terminal LLC (ground lessee, the seller)
99 years, expires February 28, 2071 (about 44 years left). Ground rent $120,000 a year, fixed until March 1, 2031, then reset. Ground lessee pays all taxes, insurance and costs on land and building.
Oak Point Terminal LLC (landlord) and the food distributor (tenant)

10 years, expires 2033, one 5-year renewal option. Rent $28 per sq ft, triple net, 3% annual increases. Tenant pays taxes, insurance, maintenance and repairs. Landlord keeps roof replacement and structure.
blocks.caption: Evelyn would step into the middle: tenant of the trust, landlord of the distributor.

blocks.html: The middle position is common in New York. Much of the land under the Hunts Point Food Distribution Center, a few blocks away, is owned by the city and leased to the businesses that built on it. Developers use ground leases to avoid paying for land up front; owners such as families, universities and churches use them to keep land and earn income without selling. The person in the middle collects the building's rent and pays the ground rent, and lives with every clause in both documents.

blocks.title: Ground lease, Article 4.3 (excerpt)
blocks.html: "Commencing March 1, 2031 and on each tenth anniversary thereafter, annual Ground Rent shall equal seven percent (7%) of the fair market value of the Land, determined as if vacant and unencumbered by this Lease and available for its highest and best use."

Jordan pulls recent land sales in the area. Industrial land in Hunts Point near the highways has been trading in the range of about $140 to $160 per square foot of land. The site is about 110,000 square feet of land. At $150 a foot, the land as if vacant is worth about $16,500,000. Seven percent of that is $1,155,000 a year.

head: Today
After March 2031 reset (estimate)
rows: Left for the leasehold owner (before reserves)
blocks.caption: Rough numbers. The point is the size of the jump, not the decimals.

blocks.q: Why is the "vacant and unencumbered" language in Article 4.3 so costly for the ground lessee?
c: It bars the ground lessee from mortgaging the leasehold after 2031
It lets the trust cancel the ground lease if the warehouse is ever vacant
It values the land based on the warehouse rent the ground lessee collects
It values the land at full market value, ignoring the lease
blocks.x: An appraisal "as if vacant and unencumbered" ignores the ground lease and the existing building, so the land is valued at its full current market value, the highest number available. A reset based on the land as encumbered by the lease, or capped at a percentage increase, would be far lower. The clause sets the rent, not a termination right, and financing limits come from elsewhere.

blocks.html: That explains the polite price. The seller has five years of cheap ground rent left and then a reset that cuts the building's cash flow roughly in half, on Jordan's rough math. Evelyn, who thinks in cap rates, is less interested in the first five years than in the 39 years after them.

blocks.q: How should Evelyn treat the 2031 reset in her offer?
c: Ignore it, since the space lease's 3% increases will cover the new ground rent
Treat it as a seller expense that will be credited at closing in full
Price the leasehold on income after the reset, with the reset rent estimated
Value the deal on today's ground rent, since resets are rarely enforced
blocks.x: A buyer values an income property on what it will earn, and here the largest single change in income is scheduled in the documents. Underwriting on today's $120,000 ground rent overstates value; the space lease increases do not come close to a jump of roughly $1,000,000 a year. A future ground rent obligation runs with the leasehold, so it is not a closing credit.

blocks.html: Jordan keeps reading the ground lease and finds a second problem in Article 6: the land may be used "solely for warehouse, distribution and related office purposes." Put that next to Article 4.3. The reset values the land at its highest and best use as if vacant, which near the highways might be a modern multistory logistics building or, if zoning ever changed, something more valuable still. But the ground tenant may only run a warehouse.

blocks.q: Why does the narrow use clause in Article 6 make the reset worse for the ground tenant?
c: The tenant pays rent based on the land's best use but may run a warehouse alone
The use clause lets the trust raise the reset percentage above 7% if uses change
The use clause voids the reset if the warehouse is used for distribution
The use clause lets the city set the ground rent at each reset date
blocks.x: The reset prices the land at its full highest and best use, while the use clause caps what the ground tenant can earn from it. That mismatch is a classic ground lease trap: the landowner gets paid as if the tenant could do anything, and the tenant is stuck with one use. Ground tenants negotiate either a broader use clause or a reset based on the land as restricted by the lease.

blocks.html: There is also the calendar. The distributor's space lease runs to 2033, with one renewal option to 2038. The ground rent resets in 2031 and again in 2041. If the distributor leaves in 2033, the leasehold owner pays the reset ground rent on an empty building while it looks for a new tenant, pays a leasing commission, and probably funds tenant improvements for the next user.

blocks.q: If the distributor does not renew in 2033, which cost continues no matter what?
c: The reset ground rent owed to the trust under the ground lease
The distributor's share of real estate taxes until a new tenant signs
The roof maintenance owed by the distributor under Section 9
The 3% annual increases in the distributor's space rent
blocks.x: The ground lease and the space lease are separate contracts. When the space tenant leaves, its obligations end with its lease, but the ground lessee still owes ground rent (now at the reset level), taxes and insurance. That is vacancy risk stacked on a fixed ground cost, which is why leasehold buyers study the space lease expiration and the reset dates together.

blocks.html: Evelyn plans to borrow about 55% of the price. Tasha shops the loan to three lenders. Two decline outright. The third will lend on the leasehold if the ground lease meets its checklist.

blocks.title: Lender's ground lease requirements (summary)
blocks.html:
1. Ground lease term to extend at least 20 years past loan maturity.
2. Ground lessor must give the lender notice of any ground lessee default and a right to cure it.
3. If the ground lease is terminated, ground lessor must enter into a new lease with the lender on the same terms.
4. The leasehold may be mortgaged and assigned to a foreclosure buyer without ground lessor consent.
5. Estoppel certificate from the ground lessor at closing.

blocks.q: Why does a leasehold lender insist on notice and a right to cure ground lease defaults?
c: So the lender can raise the ground rent if the borrower falls behind
So the trust can collect ground rent directly from the warehouse tenant
So a ground lease default cannot wipe out its collateral first
So the borrower's personal liability ends when a default notice is sent
blocks.x: The lender's collateral is the leasehold. If the ground lease ends because the borrower stopped paying ground rent, the leasehold, and the mortgage on it, can disappear. Notice and cure rights let the lender step in and pay before that happens, and a new lease right protects it if the lease is terminated anyway. The lender wants to protect its security, not change the rent or the borrower's liability.

blocks.html: The 1972 ground lease has a mortgage clause, but it is thin: notice to a lender is required, and nothing else. Diane asks the trust's attorney whether the trust would sign an amendment adding a cure period and a new lease right. The trust is willing to discuss it, for a price: an extension of the term is off the table, and it wants the reset to stay as written.

blocks.q: The lender also asks whether the trust will subordinate its fee to the leasehold mortgage. If the ground lease is unsubordinated, it means:
c: The ground lease is void unless the trust signs the mortgage
The trust may not collect ground rent while the loan is outstanding
The leasehold mortgage outranks the trust's right to ground rent
The trust's land is not pledged as security for Evelyn's loan
blocks.x: In an unsubordinated ground lease, the landowner does not put the land behind the tenant's mortgage. If the ground tenant defaults on its loan, the lender can foreclose only on the leasehold, not the land. That is the standard and safest position for a ground lessor, and it is why lenders are cautious about leaseholds. A subordinated ground lease, rare and risky for the landowner, would pledge the fee.

blocks.html: The lender's caution has a direct effect on price. A property that two of three lenders will not finance has a smaller pool of buyers, and the buyers who remain need more cash or accept tougher loan terms. That is liquidity risk in its plainest form. Evelyn notes that the seller's own exit is the best evidence: the leasehold has been on the market for seven months.

One more clause stands between Evelyn and a closing. Article 12 of the ground lease says the ground lessee may not assign the lease without the ground lessor's consent, "which shall not be unreasonably withheld," and requires the assignee to assume all of the lessee's obligations in writing.

blocks.q: What does Article 12 mean for the timing of Evelyn's purchase?
c: Nothing, since a ground lease runs with the land and transfers automatically
The trust's consent is needed before closing, so the contract should be conditioned on it
The trust may block the sale for any reason, since consent clauses are absolute
The trust's consent is needed after closing, within 30 days of the deed
blocks.x: A sale of the leasehold is an assignment of the ground lease, so the consent clause applies. The buyer's attorney makes the trust's written consent (and an estoppel) a condition of closing. "Not unreasonably withheld" limits the trust's discretion but does not remove the need to ask. Closing first and asking later risks a default under the ground lease on day one.

blocks.title: Leases longer than three years are conveyances
blocks.html: New York's recording act treats a lease for more than three years as a conveyance (RPL 290), so it can be recorded, and an unrecorded conveyance can lose to a later good faith purchaser who records first. Long commercial leases are usually protected by recording a short memorandum of lease instead of the whole document. Evelyn's title company will insure the leasehold, confirm the memorandum of the 1972 ground lease is of record, and list the space lease as an exception.

Ray walks the building with the distributor's facilities manager. The structure and slab are in good shape. The roof is not: 1990s built-up roofing, ponding water at three drains, patches over patches. Ray's estimate for a full replacement is about $650,000. The distributor's manager says, "Your roof. Read the lease."

blocks.title: Space lease, Section 9 (excerpt)
blocks.html: "Tenant shall, at Tenant's expense, keep the Premises in good order and repair, including all non-structural repairs and roof maintenance. Landlord shall be responsible, at Landlord's expense, for structural repairs and replacement of the roof when needed."

blocks.q: Under Section 9, who pays for the $650,000 roof replacement?
c: The distributor, because a triple net tenant pays every property cost
The trust, because the roof sits on the trust's land under the building
The landlord, which kept roof replacement in the lease
The distributor and landlord equally, as is standard in NNN leases
blocks.x: Labels like "triple net" describe the general structure, but the lease language controls. Here the tenant handles maintenance and non-structural repairs, and the landlord expressly keeps roof replacement and structure. The trust has nothing to do with it: under the ground lease the ground lessee owns and maintains the building. Only an absolute net lease would typically push replacement onto the tenant.

blocks.html: Diane's response is practical. The roof becomes a price item: either a credit at closing, a seller replacement before closing with Evelyn's approval of the contractor, or a lower price. Evelyn prefers the credit and her own roofer. Industrial owners with net leases keep a capital reserve for exactly this, because the net lease shields them from operating costs but not from the capital items they kept.

blocks.title: "Triple net" is a label, not a contract
blocks.html: Two NNN leases can split costs very differently. Roof replacement, structural repairs, parking lot resurfacing, HVAC replacement and code-required upgrades are often carved back to the landlord. Exam questions describe NNN as the tenant paying taxes, insurance and maintenance; real deals turn on the repair section. Read it before quoting a cap rate on a "passive" building.

blocks.q: Before closing, which pair of estoppel certificates matters most to Evelyn?
c: From the seller's lender and from the seller's insurance broker
From the trust on the ground lease and the distributor on its lease
From the City of New York and from the Department of Buildings
From the distributor's bank and from the distributor's suppliers
blocks.x: Evelyn steps into two leases, so she needs both counterparties to confirm, in writing, the terms, the rent paid, the deposits held, and that there are no defaults or claims. The trust's estoppel should also confirm the 2031 reset language and that no reset dispute or default is pending. Estoppels bind the party who signs them, which is why buyers and lenders insist on them.

blocks.html: The trust's estoppel comes back with a surprise: the seller paid the last two quarters of ground rent late, and the trust reserves its right to late charges. Small money, but it confirms the trust reads its lease. The distributor's estoppel is clean except for a note about the roof.

blocks.text: The other side of the fence

blocks.html: While the attorneys negotiate the cure amendment, the trust's attorney makes an unexpected call. The Barretto family has three generations of beneficiaries and would consider selling the leased fee: the land and the ground lessor's position, with the ground lease in place.

blocks.title: Two ways to own a piece of Oak Point Avenue

left.title: Buy the leasehold (seller's listing)
items: Collect warehouse rent, pay ground rent
Faces the 2031 reset and every reset after
Owns a wasting asset: about 44 years left
Harder to finance, smaller buyer pool
Depreciation on the building

right.title: Buy the leased fee (trust's offer)
items: Collect ground rent; tenant pays all costs
Benefits from the 2031 reset
Owns the land forever; building reverts in 2071
Bond-like income, little management
No depreciation on land

blocks.q: If Evelyn bought the trust's leased fee instead of the leasehold, how would her risk profile change?
c: She would take on the warehouse's vacancy and roof risk directly
She would own the building now, since the fee includes improvements
She would lose the 2031 reset, which passes to the ground tenant
She would hold land and a ground rent the building secures
blocks.x: The leased fee is land plus the ground lessor's rights: a ground rent that is senior in practice (the tenant must pay it to keep the building), resets that work in the owner's favor, and a reversion of the building at the end. The warehouse tenant's operations, the roof and the vacancy risk sit with the leasehold owner. The building generally belongs to the ground tenant until the lease ends.

blocks.html: Evelyn runs both. In the end she makes two offers. For the leasehold: $10,600,000, reflecting the reset, the roof and the financing difficulty. For the leased fee: a price that gives her a modest current return on today's $120,000 ground rent but a much better one after the 2031 reset. The leasehold seller rejects her number. The trust, after three family meetings, accepts.

blocks.q: Why might buying the leased fee at a low current return still make sense for Evelyn?
c: The reset should lift the rent, and the building reverts in 2071
The land can be depreciated over 39 years, sheltering the ground rent
The ground tenant becomes her employee, cutting management costs
The leased fee is exempt from New York real property taxes
blocks.x: A leased fee's value comes from the ground rent stream, including scheduled resets, and from the reversion of the land and improvements when the lease ends. Here the 2031 reset is the big upside. Land is never depreciated, the ground tenant is a tenant and not an employee, and land is taxed (though the ground lease makes the tenant pay it).

blocks.html: The closing on the leased fee looked like any commercial sale with one extra layer. The trustees signed a deed to the land subject to the ground lease. As grantor, the trust paid the New York State transfer tax and the NYC Real Property Transfer Tax at the commercial rates (2.625% of the price above $500,000 for the city tax). Evelyn's title policy insured her fee title with the ground lease listed as an exception, and the ground tenant received a notice telling it where to send ground rent from now on.

Her management list is short but not empty: confirm each year that the ground tenant has paid the real estate taxes on the whole parcel, keep current certificates showing the building is insured with her named, review any request to assign or mortgage the leasehold, and start preparing for the 2031 reset appraisal two years early. A ground lessor who stops reading the ground lease gives back the advantages it contains.

blocks.q: Evelyn's new position has very low management needs. Which statement about it is most accurate?
c: She bears no risk, since land values in New York City rise every decade
She bears the ground tenant's default risk, backed by its building
She bears the distributor's credit risk directly, as the space landlord
She bears the roof replacement, since she now owns the underlying land
blocks.x: A leased fee owner's main risk is that the ground tenant stops paying. Her protection is that the ground tenant would lose a valuable building if it defaulted, which is why ground rent is so reliable when the building is worth far more than the rent. She is not the distributor's landlord and has no roof duty. Land values can and do fall.

blocks.html: A year later, the leasehold sold to a buyer who negotiated the cure amendment Evelyn had started. That buyer now pays rent to Evelyn. She likes to say she bought the dirt under someone else's warehouse. Diane likes to say she read Article 4.3.

items: A ground lease splits ownership: the ground tenant holds a leasehold (and usually the building); the landowner holds the leased fee and the reversion.
Ground rent reset clauses can transform value. "As if vacant and unencumbered" means full land value, and buyers must underwrite after the reset.
Leasehold lenders need a long remaining term, notice and cure rights, and a new lease right; unsubordinated ground leases leave the land outside the loan.
Industrial net leases still leave capital items with the landlord when the repair clause says so. The lease language beats the NNN label.
Get estoppels from every counterparty you step in with; in NY, leases over three years are conveyances, protected by recording a memorandum.
The leased fee is bond-like income with reset upside and a reversion; the leasehold carries operating risk and wastes away as the term runs.

lessons.title: Case file: Everybody Wants a Piece of Nostrand Avenue
lessons.tagline: A Crown Heights owner, a vacant store, a building sale, and five people who think they earned a commission.
objectives: Decide which listing structure fits a commercial seller's goals and identify prohibited arrangements such as net listings
Calculate a commercial leasing commission on a declining schedule and explain how co-brokerage splits are paid
Apply New York rules on who may be paid, unlicensed referrals, dual agency consent and antitrust to commercial deals
Explain when a New York broker's commission is earned and how protection clauses extend it

blocks.title: One owner, two assignments, a lot of people who want to get paid
blocks.html: Delmar Ferreira owns a four-story mixed-use building on Nostrand Avenue in Crown Heights: twelve apartments over three storefronts. He bought it in 1994, and he is ready to sell. One of the stores, a former shoe repair shop, has been empty since spring, and Delmar wants it leased before the building goes to market, because a full building sells for more. He calls Diane on a Monday. By Wednesday he has asked for two things in one meeting: a broker to lease the store and a broker to sell the building. He also asks the question every owner asks: "What's the standard commission?" Jordan is taking notes. Diane does not answer the question the way Delmar expects.

Commercial brokerage runs on the same license law as residential, with fewer forms and more money at stake per deal. There is no RPL 443 agency disclosure form for a commercial sale or a storefront lease, but agency duties, Reg 175 rules on compensation and escrow, and the license requirement apply in full. This case follows both assignments, and every person who wanted a piece of the fees.

blocks.q: How should Diane answer "What's the standard commission?"
c: Quote the rate the local brokers agreed on for buildings this year
Quote the rate set by the Department of State for commercial sales
Explain that commissions are negotiable between each broker and client
Refer him to the MLS, which publishes the required commission rates
blocks.x: Commission rates are set by negotiation between each broker and its client. There is no rate set by DOS, no required MLS rate, and brokers who agree among themselves on rates commit price fixing under the Sherman Act. A firm can have its own policy and quote its own fee, but it should never describe that fee as standard or required.

blocks.html: Diane quotes Hudson & Hart's own terms: a sale commission of 4% of the price, and a leasing commission on the store figured on the rent over the term, both negotiable. Delmar negotiates the sale fee to 3.5% and has a better idea, he thinks.

blocks.text: The idea Delmar thinks is better

blocks.html: "Here's how we do it," Delmar says. "I need $4,500,000 in my pocket. Whatever you get above that, you keep. Sell it for $5 million, you make $500,000. Everybody's motivated."

blocks.q: What is the problem with Delmar's proposal?
c: It is a net listing, which New York regulations prohibit
Nothing, if the arrangement is written and signed by Delmar and Diane
It is legal, but Diane has to disclose the net amount to buyers
It is an open listing, which cannot be used for sales above $1 million
blocks.x: A net listing pays the broker whatever the price exceeds the owner's figure. New York prohibits it (19 NYCRR 175.19) because it sets the broker's interest against the client's: the broker profits most when the owner's number is lowest and has reason not to share the property's real value. Writing it down does not fix it. An open listing is a different arrangement, about who may sell, not how the fee is figured.

blocks.html: Delmar shrugs and accepts 3.5%. Then he adds a condition. His cousin's business partner, an investor named Alvin Torres, has talked about buying the building for years. If Alvin buys, Delmar does not want to pay a commission.

left.title: Exclusive right to sell
items: Broker earns the commission no matter who finds the buyer, Delmar included
Most protection for the broker, so most marketing effort
Named exclusions can carve out specific prospects for a set period

right.title: Exclusive agency
items: One broker, but the owner can sell on his own with no commission
Any buyer Delmar finds himself is commission free
Brokers spend less on marketing because the owner can undercut them

blocks.q: Which arrangement best gives Delmar what he wants while giving Hudson & Hart the protection to spend on marketing?
c: An open listing, with Hudson & Hart paid if it is the procuring cause
An exclusive agency listing that names Alvin Torres as a commission-free buyer
A net listing above $4,500,000, with Alvin Torres's purchase excluded
An exclusive right to sell with Alvin Torres named as an excluded prospect
blocks.x: An exclusive right to sell with a named exclusion protects the broker against everyone except Alvin, typically for a stated period. An exclusive agency listing would exempt every buyer Delmar finds himself, not just Alvin, which is more than Delmar asked for and much less than the broker needs. An open listing invites competing brokers and procuring cause disputes, and a net listing is prohibited.

blocks.html: Delmar likes it, but he does not like paperwork. "We've known each other ten years, Diane. Shake on it." Diane has an answer prepared, because Jordan asked her about this exact point last month.

blocks.q: Under New York law, is an oral commission agreement with a licensed broker enforceable?
c: No, the statute of frauds requires every commission agreement to be in writing
Yes, the writing requirement exempts licensed brokers, but proof is the risk
No, unless the broker files a copy with the Department of State in 30 days
Yes, but the commission is capped at 3% of the price without a writing
blocks.x: New York's statute of frauds for finder and broker fees (GOL 5-701(a)(10)) requires a writing for compensation agreements in real estate and business deals, but it expressly does not apply to duly licensed real estate brokers and salespersons. So an oral agreement can be enforced. The practical problem is proving its terms, the exclusion, the duration and the fee. Diane gets it in writing anyway.

blocks.title: Exclusive right to sell, key terms (signed)
blocks.html:
Term: 6 months from signing
Commission: 3.5% of the gross sale price, earned when Broker produces a buyer ready, willing and able to purchase on Owner's terms or on other terms Owner accepts, payable at closing
Excluded prospect: Alvin Torres and entities he controls, for 60 days from signing
Protection period: 120 days after expiration for any buyer to whom Broker showed the property during the term and whose name Broker delivers in writing within 10 days after expiration
Cooperating brokers: Broker may co-broke and will pay cooperating brokers from its commission

The leasing assignment comes with a separate exclusive right to lease. Commercial leasing commissions in New York are usually figured as a percentage of the total rent over the lease term, often on a declining schedule by lease year, and paid in installments. Delmar's agreement uses this schedule.

blocks.title: Leasing commission on the store
blocks.html:
Proposed lease: 10 years at $72,000 a year (flat, for simplicity)
Schedule: 6% of year 1 rent, 5% of year 2, 4% of years 3 to 5, 3% of years 6 to 10
Year 1: $72,000 x 6% = $4,320
Year 2: $72,000 x 5% = $3,600
Years 3 to 5: $72,000 x 4% x 3 = $8,640
Years 6 to 10: $72,000 x 3% x 5 = $10,800
Total commission: $27,360, half payable on lease signing and half when rent begins

blocks.q: If the store lease instead runs only 5 years at $72,000 a year under the same schedule, what is the commission?
c: $27,360, because the schedule sets a flat fee for any lease
$13,680, applying each year's rate to years 1 through 5
$21,600, applying 6% to every year of the five-year term
$10,800, applying the 3% rate to five years of rent
blocks.x: Apply each year's percentage to that year's rent: $4,320 + $3,600 + $8,640 = $13,680. A declining schedule pays more per year on the early years, when the landlord's risk is lowest and the broker's work is freshest. Applying 6% throughout overstates it; 3% is the rate for years 6 to 10, which this shorter lease never reaches.

blocks.html: Two weeks later the store has two prospects. One, a pharmacy chain, comes through a broker at another firm. The other, a children's book store, was introduced to Delmar by the building's superintendent, Teo, who mentioned the vacancy to a customer at the laundromat across the street.

blocks.q: Teo, the super, asks for a $3,000 referral fee from the commission if the bookstore signs. What can Hudson & Hart do?
c: Pay him, since he introduced the tenant and is not acting as a broker
Pay him through Delmar, so the money does not come from the firm
Pay him a flat gift card, which does not count as compensation
Decline, since sharing a fee with an unlicensed person is barred
blocks.x: Brokers may not pay or share compensation with unlicensed persons for real estate brokerage services, and an introduction that leads to a lease is such a service. Routing the money through the owner or calling it a gift does not change what it is. Unlicensed persons also cannot sue for a commission in New York (RPL 442-d), so Teo has no legal claim either. A sincere thank you is free.

blocks.title: Three New York commission rules in one place
blocks.html: First, a person must be licensed to sue for a fee for buying, selling, leasing or renting real estate in New York (RPL 442-d); the license has to exist on the date the claim arose. Second, the statute of frauds for finder and broker fees (GOL 5-701(a)(10)) demands a signed writing from everyone except licensed brokers and salespersons, attorneys and auctioneers. Third, a broker may not pay any part of a commission to an unlicensed person for brokerage work. Together they shut the door on the unlicensed finder: no license, no lawsuit, no split.

The pharmacy's broker sends a request: confirm the co-brokerage terms before his client tours. Hudson & Hart's agreement with Delmar says the firm pays cooperating brokers out of its own commission. The firm's co-brokerage letter offers the outside broker 50% of the leasing commission, payable in the same installments, when the lease is signed. Delmar's total cost does not change.

blocks.title: Put the co-broke in writing before the tour
blocks.html: Commercial commission disputes usually start with an email that said "we'll take care of you." A short co-brokerage letter, signed before the cooperating broker's client sees the space, sets the split, the payment timing, which deal it covers (lease only? renewals? expansions?) and what happens if the landlord never pays the listing broker. The cooperating broker gets paid by the listing broker under that letter, not by the landlord directly, unless the listing agreement says otherwise.
The bookstore signed. Its owner was thrilled, and so was Delmar, who called Jordan directly to say thank you and announced that he was sending Jordan a personal check for $1,500 "for the hustle."

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle Delmar's $1,500 check?
c: Return it, or have Delmar pay it to Hudson & Hart instead
Cash it, since a gift from a satisfied client is not a commission
Cash it and report it on Jordan's taxes as independent contractor income
Split it with Diane, which satisfies the supervision requirement
blocks.x: A salesperson may receive compensation for real estate work only from the sponsoring broker. Money from a client for the deal is compensation, whatever the client calls it. If Delmar wants to pay more, he pays the firm, which then pays Jordan under the firm's agreement with Jordan. Reporting it on taxes or splitting it with the broker does not cure the payment source.

blocks.html: With the bookstore signed, the building goes to market at $5,200,000. Alvin Torres never calls, and the 60-day exclusion expires. Three things then happen in one week.
First, Marcus, at Hudson & Hart, tells Diane that his longtime investor client, Shirin Kazemi, wants to make an offer. Marcus has represented Shirin as a buyer on four deals.

blocks.q: Hudson & Hart represents Delmar as seller, and Marcus (same firm) represents Shirin as buyer. What is required?
c: Nothing, since the RPL 443 dual agency form does not apply to commercial sales
Consent from the Department of State before the offer is presented
Informed written consent to the dual agency from both Delmar and Shirin
Marcus moving his license to another broker for the length of the deal
blocks.x: When one firm represents both sides, the firm is a dual agent and needs the informed consent of both clients, and if it is paid by both, Reg 175.7 requires full disclosure and consent of all parties. The RPL 443 form is for residential 1 to 4 family transactions, but the underlying agency law still applies to a commercial building. Designated agents can be appointed with consent; the broker remains a dual agent.

blocks.html: Both sign consents. Diane and Marcus are appointed to represent each side, with the firm remaining a dual agent, and Diane walls off Delmar's bottom line from Marcus.

Second, a broker from Brightline Realty calls. Brightline showed the building three weeks ago to an investor named Paul Okoye, under Hudson & Hart's co-brokerage offer. Paul has since contacted Delmar directly, suggesting that if they cut out the brokers, he can pay $5,000,000 and Delmar saves the commission.

blocks.q: If Delmar sells to Paul directly during the listing term, what does he owe?
c: Nothing, since Paul contacted Delmar directly and no broker negotiated the sale
Half commissions to both firms, split as the parties' brokers agree
A commission to Brightline alone, since it was the procuring cause
The 3.5% commission to Hudson & Hart under the exclusive right to sell
blocks.x: Under an exclusive right to sell, the listing broker earns its commission if the property sells during the term, no matter who found the buyer, the owner included. Cutting out the brokers saves Delmar nothing. Whether Brightline gets a share depends on Hudson & Hart's co-brokerage offer and on whether Brightline was the procuring cause, a dispute between the brokers that Delmar's commission funds either way.

blocks.html: Third, Marcus mentions in the hallway that he and a broker at a rival firm agreed over lunch to stop cooperating with a new flat-fee brokerage that has been listing buildings in Crown Heights for 1%. "They're undercutting everybody."

blocks.q: What is the problem with Marcus's lunch agreement?
c: No problem, since each firm may choose which brokers to co-broke with
It is a tie-in arrangement, which applies when firms share listings
It is a group boycott agreed between two competing firms
It violates the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure rules
blocks.x: One firm deciding on its own which brokers to cooperate with is generally its business decision. Two competing firms agreeing together to refuse to deal with a third, to punish its pricing, is a group boycott under the Sherman Act, and it can bring criminal penalties. A tie-in conditions one product on buying another. Diane tells Marcus the agreement is dead and documents that she said so.

blocks.title: Commercial does not mean unregulated
blocks.html: New licensees sometimes assume that because commercial deals skip the RPL 443 agency disclosure form, the residential rules disappear. They do not. The license requirement, the ban on net listings, the rule that salespersons are paid only by their sponsoring broker, the ban on paying unlicensed persons, escrow and commingling rules, dual agency consent, antitrust law and the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form all apply to a storefront lease or a building sale.

Before the contract is signed, Marcus floats an idea to save time: Shirin can wire the down payment to him, and he will hold it until the attorneys finish. Diane stops that in one sentence. In downstate practice the seller's attorney holds the contract deposit in escrow. If a broker ever holds a client's money, it goes into a separate escrow account, never into a licensee's own account.

blocks.q: Why is Marcus's offer to hold Shirin's down payment himself a problem?
c: Client funds held by a licensee belong in a broker escrow account, not commingled
Brokers are barred from holding any deposit on a commercial sale
Down payments on commercial sales go to the Department of State
A down payment held by a dual agent becomes the commission at closing
blocks.x: New York's escrow rule (19 NYCRR 175.1) bars brokers from commingling money of others with their own; any deposit a broker holds goes into a special escrow account under the broker's supervision. A salesperson taking funds personally violates that and invites conversion claims. Brokers can hold deposits properly, and in downstate deals the seller's attorney usually does. A deposit is never automatically the broker's fee.

blocks.html: Shirin offers $5,050,000 with no financing contingency and proof of funds. Delmar accepts, and the attorneys sign a contract. Shirin wires a 10% down payment to Delmar's attorney, who holds it in escrow. Two weeks before closing, Delmar's cousin calls: Alvin Torres is back, and will pay $5,300,000 cash. Delmar tells his attorney he wants out of Shirin's contract, and tells Diane that if the building does not close with Shirin, he owes Hudson & Hart nothing.

blocks.q: Under the listing agreement and New York law, has Hudson & Hart earned its commission?
c: No, because the commission is payable at closing and the closing has not happened
Yes, it produced a ready, willing and able buyer Delmar accepted
No, because Alvin is an excluded prospect, which voids the listing agreement
Yes, but half, since the buyer came from the same firm as the listing
blocks.x: In New York, absent an agreement to the contrary, a broker earns its commission by producing a buyer ready, willing and able to buy on terms the seller accepts (Lane-Real Estate Dept. Store v. Lawlet Corp.). Delmar's listing says exactly that; "payable at closing" sets timing, not whether it was earned. A seller who backs out to take a better deal generally still owes the fee. Alvin's 60-day exclusion had expired.

blocks.html: Delmar's attorney, Priya Nair, gives him the same advice in fewer words: breaching Shirin's contract to sell to Alvin invites a lawsuit for specific performance, and the commission is owed either way. Delmar closes with Shirin.

One more clause gets Diane's attention before closing. The bookstore's lease has a five-year renewal option, and Hudson & Hart's leasing agreement with Delmar promises a commission on renewals and expansions when they are exercised. But Delmar will not own the building when the bookstore renews. The new owner never signed Hudson & Hart's agreement.

blocks.q: How does Diane protect the firm's future renewal commission on the bookstore lease?
c: She does nothing, since commission rights pass with the deed to any new owner
She files a broker's lien against the building with the county clerk
She asks that the sale contract have the buyer assume the leasing commission agreement
She asks the bookstore to pay the renewal commission directly to the firm
blocks.x: A commission agreement binds the parties who signed it. When a building sells, the usual fix is a contract clause in which the buyer assumes the seller's existing leasing commission obligations, often with a recognition letter to the broker. Without it, the firm may have a claim only against the departed seller. The tenant never agreed to pay the landlord's broker, and commission rights do not run with the land on their own.

blocks.html: Priya adds the assumption clause, and Shirin's attorney agrees, after negotiating a small credit at closing for the obligation the buyer is taking on. Five years from now, if the bookstore renews, the firm will send its invoice to Shirin.

head: Sale commission at $5,050,000 x 3.5%
Amount
rows: Total commission, paid by seller at closing
Hudson & Hart (dual agent, no outside co-broker)
Paid out to Diane's team and Marcus under their agreements with the firm
per each licensee's written agreement with Hudson & Hart
blocks.caption: The seller's attorney pays the commission from the sale proceeds on the closing statement. Each licensee is paid by the firm.

blocks.html: One more call arrives in the spring. Alvin Torres phones Diane: the listing expired in October, and he wants to know whether, if he buys the building next door from Delmar's sister, anyone owes Hudson & Hart anything. Diane checks: the sister never listed with the firm, so no. Then she checks the protection clause on Delmar's listing anyway, because tail clauses are where commissions go to die. Hudson & Hart had delivered its list of shown buyers within 10 days after the term, as the clause required. Alvin was not on it; he had been excluded.

blocks.q: Why did Hudson & Hart's protection (tail) clause require delivering a written list of prospects after the listing expired?
c: So the owner knows which buyers stay covered after the term ends
So DOS can verify the broker's showings for its three-year record retention
So the listing converts into an open listing for the buyers on the list
So the cooperating brokers can be paid before the owner closes with anyone
blocks.x: A protection clause extends the broker's right to a commission for a set period after expiration, but only for buyers introduced during the term. The written list tells the owner, and any later broker, exactly which buyers are covered. Without it, the owner could not know, and the broker would struggle to prove its claim. Record retention rules are a separate obligation.

blocks.html: Delmar sent Diane a bottle of wine with a note: "Next time I'll read the contract first." The bookstore is doing well. Shirin is raising the bookstore's rent 3% a year, exactly as the lease says, and nobody has asked Teo for another referral.

items: Commissions are negotiated between broker and client; there is no standard rate, and competitors who agree on rates or boycott a discount firm violate antitrust law.
Net listings are prohibited in New York; use an exclusive right to sell with named exclusions to carve out a specific buyer.
Licensed brokers are exempt from the GOL writing requirement for commission agreements, but put every term in writing to prove it.
Commercial leasing commissions are often a declining percentage of rent by lease year, paid in installments; co-broke splits belong in a signed letter.
Salespersons are paid only by their sponsoring broker; no one shares a commission with an unlicensed person; dual agency needs informed written consent in commercial deals too.
A broker earns its commission on producing a ready, willing and able buyer on terms the seller accepts, unless the agreement says otherwise; protection clauses extend that right to named buyers.

lessons.title: Case file: The Rent Roll on 37th Avenue
lessons.tagline: A Jackson Heights building shows $411,960 a year in rent. About $52,000 of it does not exist.
objectives: Audit a seller's rent roll line by line and decide which rents belong in potential gross income
Apply vacancy, credit loss and concessions to convert potential gross income into effective gross income
Decide how rent-stabilized units, vacant space and arrears change what a buyer should count
Calculate how an overstated rent roll inflates value at a market cap rate

blocks.title: Four stories over 37th Avenue
blocks.html: Farida Haque runs two pharmacies in Queens and has saved for ten years to buy her first building. Jordan grew up six blocks from this one: a four-story mixed-use building on 37th Avenue in Jackson Heights with two stores on the ground floor and eight apartments above. The asking price is $4,200,000. The listing broker's package says the building grosses $411,960 a year and trades at a "6.8 cap." Farida's accountant has already rebuilt the expenses at $131,000 a year, so the only question left is the income. Diane hands Jordan the seller's rent roll and a highlighter. "Every number on this page is a claim," she says. "Your job is to find out which claims are rent." Where does Jordan start?

A rent roll is the seller's list of every unit, who is in it, what they pay and when the lease ends. It is the raw material for potential gross income (PGI): every unit leased for a full year at its rent. The trap is that a rent roll mixes three kinds of numbers that look identical on the page: rents tenants are actually paying under signed leases, rents the seller hopes to get, and rents that nobody will ever pay.

head: Unit
Tenant
Status
Lease ends
Monthly rent shown
