blocks.caption: The seller's rent roll, as delivered. Other income listed separately: laundry $3,600 a year, late fees $2,400 a year.

blocks.html: Jordan starts at the top, but the first line that stops the highlighter is Store B. It has been empty for four months and is listed at $7,000 a month. A vacant unit does belong in PGI, because PGI assumes 100% occupancy. The question is at what rent.

blocks.q: Store B is vacant and the rent roll lists it at the seller's $7,000 asking rent. Jordan's three closed lease comps for similar 37th Avenue stores average $5,800 a month. What figure should go into PGI for Store B?
c: $7,000, since PGI assumes every unit is leased
$5,800, the market rent the comps support
$0, because vacant space produces no rent today
$6,400, splitting the asking rent and the comps
blocks.x: PGI does assume full occupancy, so the store stays in, but at market rent proven by signed comparable leases, not at the seller's hope. Choice A is the trap: it gets the occupancy assumption right and then uses an asking rent nobody has paid. Putting $0 in PGI double counts the vacancy, because vacancy is subtracted on its own line later. Splitting the difference has no evidence behind it.

blocks.html: The comps came from Jordan's own walk down 37th Avenue and two leasing brokers. A $1,200 a month gap on one store is $14,400 a year of income that only exists in the listing package.

The broker pushes back by email: "Store B is basically leased. A dental practice signed a letter of intent last week at $7,000." Jordan asks for the letter. It is two pages, unsigned by the landlord, and says in bold that it is "non-binding and subject to a fully executed lease." The dentist has not yet seen the space's electrical capacity or the landlord's work letter.

blocks.q: How should the unsigned, non-binding letter of intent at $7,000 change Jordan's treatment of Store B?
c: Count Store B at $7,000 with no vacancy, since a tenant is lined up
Count Store B at $7,000 but double the vacancy allowance for the store
Drop Store B from PGI until the dentist signs a lease at any rent
Keep Store B at market rent with vacancy, since an LOI binds no one
blocks.x: A letter of intent is an outline for negotiation; either side can walk away. Until a lease is signed, the store is vacant space at market rent, with the vacancy and lease-up handled separately. Choice A is the trap: it treats a hope as a contract. If the dentist signs before closing at $7,000, Jordan can update the numbers then, and Farida's attorney can make the signed lease a condition of the deal.

blocks.html: The other store is the opposite problem. Store A, the phone and repair shop, pays $6,500 a month under a lease that runs to March 2031. That is $700 above what the comps say the space would rent for today.

blocks.q: Store A pays $6,500 under a lease running to 2031, while the market rent for the space is about $5,800. How should Jordan treat it?
c: Cut it to $5,800 now, since PGI uses market rent for each unit
Count $6,500, the lease rent, and flag the 2031 rollover risk
Count $6,500 and assume the tenant renews at the same rent in 2031
Average the two figures and count $6,150 until the lease expires
blocks.x: An occupied unit goes into PGI at its contract rent, because a signed lease is an enforceable promise to pay it. The above-market piece is real income for about four and a half years, but it carries risk: the tenant may leave or renew lower. Choice A applies the vacant-unit rule to an occupied unit. Choice C ignores that the rent will likely fall to market at renewal, which a careful buyer prices in.

blocks.title: Above-market and below-market leases
blocks.html: A lease above market is worth the most when the tenant is strong and the term is long. A lease below market is the reverse: the buyer is stuck with it until expiration. Either way, the rent roll should show the lease end date next to every rent, and the buyer should ask for each commercial tenant's financial statements and a signed estoppel certificate before closing.

blocks.text: The super and the pro forma

blocks.html: Next, 3C. The superintendent lives there rent free as part of his pay. The seller lists the apartment at $2,800, the rent it could get on the open market. Then 3D, where Ms. Lin's signed lease says $2,900 but the roll says "$3,200 (pro forma)." The seller explains on the phone that he plans to raise her at renewal.

blocks.q: How should Jordan treat the super's rent-free unit (3C) and Ms. Lin's apartment (3D) in the buyer's income figures?
c: Count 3C at $2,800 and 3D at the $3,200 the seller projects
Count 3C at $2,800 and 3D at her $2,900 lease rent
Leave 3C out and count 3D at the $3,200 projected rent
Leave 3C out and count 3D at her $2,900 lease rent
blocks.x: The super's unit produces no cash, and Farida will need a super too, so it stays out of income. Ms. Lin is bound to $2,900 by her signed lease until January; a raise at renewal is a pro forma hope, not rent. Choice B is the near miss: it fixes 3D but still counts $33,600 a year that no tenant pays. An analyst could add the super's unit at market and the same amount to payroll, but the net effect on NOI is zero, so most simply leave it out.

blocks.html: Together these two lines take $2,800 plus $300 a month, or $37,200 a year, off the seller's roll. Notice the pattern: every "adjustment" the seller made pushes income up.

Units 2A and 2D are rent stabilized. Jordan asks the seller's attorney for the DHCR rent registration history, the annual filing that records each stabilized unit's legal regulated rent. It arrives two days later. Unit 2D's registered rent matches the roll at $1,480. Unit 2A's registration shows a legal regulated rent of $1,590, but the roll and Mr. Rivera's lease both say $1,650.

blocks.q: Unit 2A's lease rent is $1,650 a month, but the DHCR registration shows a legal regulated rent of $1,590. What should Jordan do with this?
c: Use $1,650, because that is what the tenant signed and is paying
Use $1,590 and flag a possible overcharge for Farida's attorney
Use $1,650 and let the new owner correct the rent after closing
Ignore it, because $60 a month is too small to affect value
blocks.x: A stabilized tenant cannot be charged more than the legal regulated rent, and a signed lease does not change that. The buyer should underwrite $1,590 and send the discrepancy to the attorney, because overcharge claims can follow the building. Choice A is the trap: it treats the lease as proof when the registration controls. Small dollars, big exposure: the next callout explains why.

blocks.title: Overcharges after the 2019 rent law
blocks.html: Since the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (HSTPA), an overcharge complaint can reach back six years, and for a willful overcharge the owner can owe triple the excess. HCR's policy treats an overcharge as willful unless the owner proves otherwise. The same law ended vacancy bonuses and high-rent vacancy decontrol, so a stabilized apartment stays stabilized when the tenant leaves and rises only by Rent Guidelines Board increases. Buyers' attorneys ask for the full registration history, an overcharge representation in the contract, and sometimes an escrow holdback.

blocks.q: Farida asks: "When Mr. Gutierrez in 2D moves out, can I renovate and rent it at $2,900 like the free market units?" What is the best answer?
c: Yes, once a stabilized tenant vacates, the unit leaves stabilization
Yes, if the renovation costs at least the old high-rent threshold
No, it stays stabilized and rises only by the allowed increases
No, because a new owner cannot raise a stabilized rent
blocks.x: HSTPA repealed vacancy decontrol and the vacancy bonus. The apartment stays stabilized for the next tenant at a legal rent that grows by Rent Guidelines Board increases (renovation increases are now tightly capped). Choice A is the old pre-2019 thinking that many sellers' brokers still repeat in listing packages. A buyer who pays for "upside" in stabilized units is paying for a law that no longer exists.

blocks.html: With the clean-up done, Jordan rebuilds the roll. Every unit is in at its lease rent or, for the vacant store, at market. The super's unit is out.

head: Unit
Seller's roll
Jordan's figure
Reason
blocks.caption: Same building, same tenants. $52,320 a year disappears before vacancy is even considered.

blocks.q: Using Jordan's monthly total of $29,970, what is the building's potential gross income?
c: $29,970, the monthly total
blocks.x: PGI is annual: $29,970 x 12 = $359,640. Choice D is the seller's figure, built on asking and projected rents. $347,640 would come from also dropping the vacant store's $1,000 a month gap twice, a common double count. Always annualize before you do anything else, because cap rates are annual.

blocks.html: Two more lines need a closer look. Mr. Osei in 2C signed a 12-month lease at $2,950 with the first month free, a concession the seller gave to fill the unit quickly. Mr. Ahmed in 3B is three months behind, $8,550 in arrears. The seller's roll treats both as full-paying tenants.

blocks.title: Net effective rent for 2C
blocks.html:
Contract rent: $2,950 x 12 months = $35,400
Free month: minus $2,950
Cash actually collected over the lease: $32,450
Net effective rent: $32,450 / 12 = $2,704 a month
The $2,950 face rent stays in PGI. The $2,950 concession comes off as its own line, just as vacancy does.

blocks.q: Mr. Ahmed owes $8,550 in back rent. The seller says the buyer will "pick up" the arrears at closing, so the full $2,850 a month should count. How should Jordan treat 3B?
c: Add the $8,550 arrears to this year's other income
Count the rent in PGI and cover the risk in credit loss
Remove 3B from PGI until Mr. Ahmed pays in full
Count the rent and also the arrears as a closing credit
blocks.x: Mr. Ahmed's rent stays in PGI because he has a lease. The risk that he keeps not paying is exactly what credit loss covers. Back rent is the seller's past income, not the building's future income, and arrears are usually settled between the parties' attorneys, not paid for in the price. Choice A is the trap: it adds a one-time, uncertain collection to recurring income and then capitalizes it into value.

blocks.html: The listing package shows zero vacancy for the apartments because all eight are occupied. Jordan applies a 5% allowance across the whole building anyway, which matches what Queens mixed-use lenders and appraisers are using this year.

blocks.q: All eight apartments are leased today. Why does Jordan still subtract a 5% vacancy and credit loss allowance from PGI?
c: Because New York law requires a 5% vacancy deduction on mixed-use buildings
Because the stabilized units are expected to turn over at a higher rate
Because the lender lends on 95% of the gross rents shown
Because over a typical year units turn over and some tenants fall behind
blocks.x: Vacancy and credit loss is a market allowance for turnover and nonpayment over a typical year, applied even to a full building, because nothing stays full. Choice A sounds official but no statute sets a vacancy rate; the figure comes from the market. Stabilized tenants actually turn over less often than free market tenants, so B gets the risk backwards.

blocks.html: The seller lists $3,600 a year of laundry income and $2,400 of late fees. Jordan checks the laundry contract (a three-year route agreement that pays the owner a fixed $300 a month) and the late fee ledger.

blocks.q: Should Jordan count the $2,400 a year of late fees as other income?
c: No, they come mostly from one tenant and are not dependable
Yes, because late fees are collected every year in most buildings
No, because late fees cannot exceed $50 or 5% of the monthly rent
Yes, because the seller's books show they were actually collected
blocks.x: The ledger shows the fees came almost entirely from Mr. Ahmed, who is now in arrears. Irregular, tenant-specific income is not something a buyer should capitalize. The laundry contract, by contrast, is a fixed, documented payment. Choice C states a real NY residential cap (the lesser of $50 or 5%, after 5 days late), but the cap limits the size of each fee; it does not explain why the income is unreliable.

blocks.title: Jordan's stabilized income statement
blocks.html:
Potential gross income: $359,640
Minus vacancy and credit loss (5% of PGI): $17,982
Minus concession (2C): $2,950
Plus other income (laundry): $3,600
Effective gross income: $342,308
Minus operating expenses (accountant): $131,000
Net operating income: $211,308

blocks.q: Using Jordan's figures, what effective gross income should Farida use?
c: $345,258, before the concession
blocks.x: EGI = $359,640 minus $17,982 vacancy minus $2,950 concession plus $3,600 laundry = $342,308. Choice D forgets the concession. $338,708 subtracts the laundry instead of adding it. $359,640 is PGI with no adjustments, which is exactly the mistake the seller's package made.

blocks.html: Diane reads the statement over Jordan's shoulder and asks one question: "Would a lender agree with every line?" It is the right test. A commercial lender's underwriter will rebuild the same rent roll from the leases, the registrations and the bank deposits, and will size the loan on that number, not on the listing package. If Jordan's EGI matches what the lender will find, Farida's offer will survive the appraisal and the loan commitment. If it does not, the deal falls apart three weeks before closing, after Farida has paid for inspections and legal work.

For comparison, the seller's package reached an effective gross income of $417,960 by adding the late fees and laundry to $411,960 and subtracting nothing. Run both through the same $131,000 of expenses and the seller's NOI is $286,960. Jordan's is $211,308.

blocks.text: What the rent roll was worth

blocks.html: Jordan pulls three recent sales of Queens mixed-use buildings and reconstructs their income the same way. They cluster around a 6.25% cap rate. Now the "6.8 cap" claim can be tested.

head: Seller's package
Jordan's reconstruction
blocks.caption: Same expenses, same cap rate. The only difference is which rents are real.

blocks.q: At a 6.25% cap rate, each dollar of annual NOI is worth $16 of value. The seller's EGI is $75,652 higher than Jordan's. Roughly how much value does the overstated rent roll create on paper?
c: About $75,652
blocks.x: Value = NOI / 0.0625, so every $1 of NOI becomes $16 of value. $75,652 x 16 = $1,210,432 of phantom value. Choice B divides by 0.16 instead of 0.0625. Choice A forgets to capitalize at all, and choice D multiplies by 160. This is why a rent roll audit matters more than haggling: small monthly errors become seven-figure price differences.

blocks.title: The "in-place" and "pro forma" blend
blocks.html: Listing packages often mix actual rents with projected ones in a single column and call the total "gross income." Read every rent roll in two passes: first, which rents are supported by a signed lease or a registration; second, which are hopes (asking rents, renewal bumps, a rent-free unit at market). Only the first group goes into PGI at face value. A vacant unit goes in at proven market rent with its own vacancy allowance.

One last adjustment. Store B will not lease tomorrow. Jordan's leasing contacts expect about six months to sign a tenant, plus a leasing commission and some work to the space, about $25,000. That is a one-time cost, so it does not belong in stabilized NOI. Instead it comes off the value.

blocks.title: From stabilized value to an offer
blocks.html:
Stabilized value: $211,308 / 0.0625 = $3,380,928
Lost rent while Store B leases: $5,800 x 6 = $34,800
Leasing commission and work: $25,000
Indicated value: $3,380,928 minus $59,800 = about $3,321,000

blocks.q: Why does Jordan subtract the Store B lease-up costs from the value instead of from annual NOI?
c: Lease-up is a one-time cost, and NOI reflects a typical year
Leasing commissions count as debt service under most loans
The IRS requires lease-up costs to be capitalized and depreciated
The 5% vacancy allowance already removed the store's rent
blocks.x: Stabilized NOI describes a normal year. A one-time hit, such as six months of downtime and a commission, is subtracted once from the capitalized value. Subtracting it from NOI would capitalize it at 16 to 1 and overstate the discount. Choice D is the trap: the 5% allowance covers routine turnover, not a store that is empty today. Tax treatment (choice C) is a separate world from valuation.

blocks.title: Check the roll against what the owner told the city
blocks.html: Owners of most NYC income-producing property with an actual assessed value over $40,000 must file a Real Property Income and Expense statement (RPIE) with the Department of Finance each year. Residential buildings with 10 or fewer apartments are excluded, but mixed-use buildings with stores often have to file. Ask the seller for the last two filings. If the income reported to the city is far below the income on the rent roll, one of the two documents is wrong, and the buyer should find out which.

Farida offers $3,300,000 with a contract clause requiring estoppel certificates from both store tenants and a seller's representation on stabilized rents. The seller counters at $3,650,000. They settle at $3,425,000 after Farida's attorney negotiates a $40,000 escrow holdback for the 2A rent issue. Diane signs off on Jordan's file with one note in the margin: "Read the registration before you read the lease."

items: PGI assumes full occupancy at real rents: signed lease rents for occupied units and comp-supported market rent for vacant ones, never asking or projected rents.
Rent-free units produce no income; a stabilized unit is capped at its registered legal regulated rent no matter what the lease says, and it stays stabilized after the tenant leaves.
Vacancy and credit loss applies even to a full building; concessions come off as their own line, and arrears are a credit risk, not income.
Other income counts only when it is recurring and documented, such as a laundry contract.
At a market cap rate, every dollar of overstated income becomes many dollars of overstated value, so audit the rent roll before you argue about price.
One-time costs such as lease-up are subtracted from value, not from stabilized NOI.

lessons.title: Case file: Twelve Units on Congress Street
lessons.tagline: Marcus's setup sheet says 8.2 cap. The heating bills, the insurance quote and the owner's toolbox say otherwise.
objectives: Reconstruct operating expenses from a seller's setup sheet, tax bills, utility history and insurance quotes
Separate operating expenses from capital items, debt service and owner expenses to calculate NOI
Derive a cap rate from reconstructed comparable sales and apply it to value a property
Explain how each dollar of expense changes value at a given cap rate

blocks.title: A brick walk-up in Troy
blocks.html: Dev and Anika Raman are both nurses at Albany Med. They have $350,000 saved and want a building they can hold for twenty years. Marcus Webb has the listing on a 1910 brick walk-up on Congress Street in Troy: twelve one-bedroom apartments at $1,250 a month, a coin laundry in the basement, owner-paid gas heat. Asking price $1,450,000. Marcus's one-page setup sheet shows NOI of $118,600 and a headline "8.2% CAP!" The Ramans found Jordan through a cousin in Brooklyn and asked Hudson & Hart to represent them as buyers. Diane agrees, with a warning: "Marcus writes setup sheets the way he parks. Check everything." The income side looks clean. The expense side is where Jordan starts.

head: Line
Marcus's setup sheet
blocks.caption: The listing broker's numbers. Expenses are 34% of EGI, low for a 116-year-old building.

blocks.html: A setup sheet is a marketing document. It is not a lie, exactly; each number usually came from somewhere. The question is whether that somewhere is a normal year for the next owner. Jordan asks Marcus for the seller's last three years of operating statements, the current tax bills, twenty-four months of gas and water bills, the current insurance policy, and the laundry contract. It takes a week and two reminders.

Vacancy first, because it touches everything. Marcus used 2%. The Ramans' lender, a local savings bank, underwrites Troy walk-ups at 5%, and Jordan's search of the rental listings shows typical apartments in the neighborhood sitting four to six weeks between tenants.

blocks.q: Marcus says the building has had "almost no vacancy" for three years, so 2% is fair. What should Jordan use?
c: 2%, since the building's own history is the best evidence of its vacancy
0%, since every unit is leased today and no tenant has given notice
5%, matching the market and the rate the lender will underwrite
10%, since older walk-ups carry higher vacancy than new buildings
blocks.x: The market rate, confirmed by the lender's underwriting and local listing data, is the defensible number for a new owner. A seller's history can be a reason to shade it, but three good years under an owner who kept rents low may not repeat at a buyer's rents. Choice A is the trap because it sounds evidence-based. Choice D overreaches: age matters, but a blanket rule is not a market finding.

blocks.html: At 5%, vacancy is $9,000 instead of $3,600. The laundry contract checks out at a fixed $200 a month, so effective gross income becomes $180,000 minus $9,000 plus $2,400, or $173,400.

blocks.text: Taxes and insurance: the fixed expenses

blocks.html: Real estate taxes and insurance are fixed expenses: they do not change with occupancy. That makes them easy to verify and easy to get wrong in the same way, by using last year's number.

blocks.title: How upstate tax bills arrive
blocks.html: In much of upstate New York an owner gets more than one property tax bill: a city or town and county bill, and a separate school tax bill on a different schedule. A setup sheet that lists "taxes" from one bill can miss the other. Ask for every bill for the current year, and check the assessment roll for a pending reassessment or a lost exemption.

The setup sheet shows $26,000. The current bills tell a different story: the city and county bill is $16,900 and the school tax bill is $11,600, for a total of $28,500. The $26,000 was last year's total, before the school district raised its levy.

blocks.q: The setup sheet shows last year's taxes of $26,000. This year's city, county and school bills total $28,500. Which figure belongs in the buyer's reconstructed statement?
c: $28,500, the current bills the buyer will actually pay
$26,000, because the statement should reflect actual history
$27,250, an average of the two years to smooth the increase
$16,900, because school taxes are paid by the tenants
blocks.x: A reconstructed statement looks forward: it shows what the building will cost the next owner in a typical year. The current bills are known, so they win. Choice B is the trap because "use actual numbers" sounds right; actual last year is not actual next year. Tenants in a New York apartment building do not pay the owner's school tax directly; it is built into the rent.

blocks.html: Insurance is next. The seller's policy costs $7,800, but he has carried it with the same agent for fifteen years with a high deductible, and the building has a 1960s knob-and-tube wiring section in the basement that a new carrier will want to see replaced. The Ramans' agent quotes $11,400 for a new owner's policy with a reasonable deductible and liability limits the lender requires.

blocks.q: Why should the Ramans' statement use the $11,400 quote rather than the seller's $7,800 premium?
c: Because the lender requires buyers to buy the most expensive policy
Because it is what a new owner will pay to insure this building
Because insurance should be spread over the loan term as debt service
Because the seller's premium is not deductible as an operating expense
blocks.x: A reconstructed statement uses what the buyer will really pay. An old policy priced on a long relationship, with a high deductible and limits a lender would reject, does not tell you that. Insurance remains an operating expense above NOI; it has nothing to do with debt service. Choice D mixes in tax concepts: premiums are deductible for a rental, but deductibility is a tax world question, not a valuation one.

blocks.text: Heat, water and the mild winter

blocks.html: Owner-paid heat is a variable expense, and in a 1910 building it is the line that bites. Marcus's $14,400 is the seller's gas cost for the most recent year. Jordan pulls the utility history: $14,400 last year, $17,900 the year before, $16,300 the year before that. Last winter was one of the mildest in a decade in the Capital Region.

blocks.q: Which heating figure should Jordan use in a reconstructed statement?
c: $14,400, the most recent year shown on the setup sheet
$17,900, the highest year, to be conservative
$0, because heat can be shifted to tenants on renewal
$16,200, the three-year average of the actual bills
blocks.x: Weather and gas prices swing year to year, so analysts normalize volatile expenses with a multi-year average: ($14,400 + $17,900 + $16,300) / 3 = $16,200. The most recent year is the trap because it is real, but it reflects one mild winter. Shifting heat to tenants would require separate heating systems or meters and new leases; you value what the building is, not what it might become.

blocks.html: Water and sewer at $6,000 matches the city bills. It is worth pausing on why the variable lines matter more in this building than in a new one. Fixed expenses such as taxes and insurance are known in advance and move slowly. Variable expenses such as heat, repairs and turnover move with weather, age and occupancy, and in a building with original radiators and a 15-year-old boiler they move a lot. A buyer can absorb a surprise in a fixed line, because it shows up on a bill months ahead. A surprise in a variable line shows up in January, when the boiler runs around the clock and the bank still wants its payment.
The interesting lines are the ones Marcus left at zero.

The seller, a retired contractor, has done his own repairs, cleaned the halls, shoveled the walks and collected rents for twenty years. His actual repair costs were low because his labor was free. None of that labor comes with the building.

blocks.q: The seller manages the building himself and shows $0 for management and payroll. How should Jordan treat these lines?
c: Leave them at $0 until the Ramans actually hire someone
Leave them at $0 because the Ramans plan to manage it themselves
Add them if the building's vacancy rises above the market rate
Add a market management fee and payroll for a part-time super
blocks.x: NOI measures the property, not the owner, so it must carry the cost of running the building no matter who does the work. Even if the Ramans self-manage, their time has value and a future buyer or appraiser will charge a market fee. Choice B is the trap because it is true of the Ramans' plans, but planning to work for free does not make the building more valuable.

blocks.html: Jordan uses a 6% management fee on EGI ($10,404), which matches what Capital Region managers charge for small walk-ups, plus $7,200 for a part-time porter and handyman. Repairs and maintenance go up to $800 a unit ($9,600) because the seller's $6,000 bought only materials. Legal and accounting adds $2,500.

blocks.text: The roof, the mortgage and the reserves

blocks.html: The seller's own operating statement for last year, which Jordan finally gets, looks very different from the setup sheet. It lists a $42,000 new roof, $61,000 of mortgage payments, and $4,800 for the seller's pickup truck. Its bottom line is a loss.

blocks.q: The seller's statement includes a $42,000 roof replacement. How does it affect the Ramans' NOI?
c: Leave it out of NOI as a capital expenditure
Subtract the $42,000, since it was paid this year
Subtract $42,000 over 27.5 years as depreciation
Add it to income because it raises the building's value
blocks.x: A full roof replacement is a capital expenditure: it replaces a major component and extends the building's life, so it does not belong in operating expenses or NOI. The Ramans should be glad it is done. Choice B is the trap that turns a one-time project into a recurring cost and drags value down. Depreciation is a tax world deduction, not a valuation line.

blocks.q: The seller's statement also shows $61,000 of mortgage payments and $4,800 for his pickup truck. What should Jordan do with these two lines?
c: Remove both, since one is financing and the other is personal
Keep the mortgage interest but remove the principal and the truck
Keep the truck, since the seller uses it for building repairs
Keep both, since they are real cash the seller paid last year
blocks.x: NOI is measured before financing, so the whole mortgage payment, principal and interest, sits below the line as debt service. The truck belongs to the seller and leaves with him. Choice B mixes in the tax world, where interest is deductible; that has nothing to do with NOI. The Ramans will have their own loan, and two buyers with different loans must get the same NOI from the same building.

blocks.html: Reading the seller's own statement teaches a lesson about who prepared it and why. A setup sheet is built to sell, so it leaves things out. A tax-driven statement is built to show a loss, so it throws everything in. The reconstruction sits in between: realistic income, every cost of running the building, and nothing that belongs to the owner's financing, taxes, personal life or one-time projects. But the roof raises a fair question: if big items wear out, where does the buyer account for them?

blocks.q: Jordan adds $300 a unit a year as reserves for replacement. Which statement about that line is correct?
c: Reserves are debt service, so they belong below NOI with the mortgage
Reserves are illegal in New York residential buildings with under 20 units
Reserves double count the roof, so they should be left out entirely
Reserves are an annual set-aside many analysts include in expenses
blocks.x: Reserves for replacement smooth the cost of items that wear out (boiler, appliances, hallway floors) into an annual figure, and many lenders and appraisers include them above NOI. The new roof does not make other systems younger, so choice C is wrong. Reserves are not debt service. Be consistent: if your comps' NOIs include reserves, yours should too.

head: Line
Setup sheet
Reconstructed
Source
blocks.caption: Every line is sourced. Nothing about the bank, the IRS, the roof or the truck.

blocks.q: Using the reconstructed column, what is the building's NOI?
c: $83,400 before reserves
blocks.x: NOI = EGI of $173,400 minus total operating expenses of $95,404 = $77,996. $118,600 is the setup sheet. $75,996 subtracts $2,000 more than the table shows. Choice B adds the reserves back and also uses the wrong total. The operating expense ratio is now $95,404 / $173,400, or 55%, which is normal for an old walk-up with owner-paid heat.

blocks.title: The expense ratio smell test
blocks.html: Before you trust any setup sheet, divide expenses by EGI. Older walk-ups where the owner pays heat often run around half of EGI, sometimes more. A sheet showing a third or less is usually missing management, payroll, a realistic repair budget or reserves. A low expense ratio is not proof of a well-run building; it is a reason to ask for documents.

Jordan also runs the numbers per unit, because that is how small-building owners and managers talk. The reconstructed expenses come to $95,404 / 12 = $7,950 a unit a year. Taxes alone are $2,375 a unit; heat is $1,350. Two managers Jordan calls say $7,000 to $9,000 a unit is normal for a Troy walk-up with owner-paid heat. Marcus's sheet worked out to $5,017 a unit, which neither of them had seen on a building that age. Per-unit figures are a cross-check, not a substitute for the bills, but they catch a missing line in seconds.

blocks.q: Marcus defends his number: "8.2% is just my NOI divided by my price. That's the math." What is wrong with using that figure to judge the price?
c: Nothing, because any NOI divided by any price is a valid cap rate
A cap rate uses debt service, which Marcus left out entirely
It uses an inflated NOI, so the rate proves nothing about value
Cap rates apply to commercial buildings, not to apartments
blocks.x: The arithmetic is fine; the input is not. A cap rate computed from an overstated NOI and the asking price simply restates the seller's opinion. To test a price, use a reconstructed NOI and a cap rate drawn from comparable sales built the same way. Choice B is a classic error: debt service never enters NOI or the cap rate. Apartment buildings are valued with cap rates all the time.

blocks.html: Marcus's "8.2 cap" was his own NOI divided by his own price. A cap rate means something only when it comes from comparable sales whose NOIs were built the same way. Jordan finds three Troy and Cohoes walk-up sales from the past year and reconstructs each one, with 5% vacancy, market management and reserves.

head: Comparable
Price
Reconstructed NOI
Cap rate
blocks.caption: The comps cluster from 7.5% to 8.0%.

blocks.html: Notice what Jordan did not do. He did not take the cap rates printed in the comps' old listing packages, because those were built on setup sheets just like Marcus's. He called the buyers' brokers, got the actual rents and expenses at the time of sale, and applied the same vacancy, management and reserve assumptions he used on Congress Street. Apples to apples is the whole point: an honest NOI divided by a cap rate drawn from dishonest NOIs gives a wrong answer just as surely as the reverse.

blocks.q: The Congress Street building is similar in age, condition and location to the comps. Using the middle of the range, 7.75%, what is the indicated value?
c: $1,450,000, the asking price
blocks.x: V = I / R = $77,996 / 0.0775 = $1,006,400. $1,530,323 capitalizes Marcus's $118,600 NOI at 7.75%, mixing a real cap rate with a fake income. $604,469 multiplies by 7.75 instead of dividing by 0.0775. Notice that the cap rate barely moved; the value fell because the NOI was honest.

blocks.html: Run the asking price the other way and the problem is plain. $77,996 divided by $1,450,000 is a 5.38% cap rate, well below every comp. At Marcus's price the Ramans would be paying for a building that earns like a prime Manhattan property, in a market that prices walk-ups near 8%.

blocks.q: At the $1,450,000 asking price, the reconstructed NOI implies a cap rate of about 5.4%. What does that tell the Ramans?
c: The building is a bargain, since lower cap rates signal higher quality
The price is too high for the income compared with the market
The comps are wrong, because asking prices reflect the market
The cap rate will rise to 8.2% once the Ramans raise the rents
blocks.x: A cap rate below every comparable sale means the buyer would pay more per dollar of income than the market does. Choice A confuses cause and effect: safer properties get lower cap rates, but a low implied rate on an ordinary building just means the price is high. Asking prices are opinions; closed comps are evidence.

blocks.html: Anika asks the question every good investor asks next: "If we can cut expenses, how much is that worth?" At a 7.75% cap rate, a dollar of NOI is worth $1 / 0.0775, about $12.90. So the expense lines are not just costs; they are value.

blocks.q: The Ramans find they can save $3,000 a year by switching the building to a cheaper gas supplier. At a 7.75% cap rate, about how much value does that add?
blocks.x: $3,000 / 0.0775 = $38,710. Every recurring dollar of NOI is capitalized, which is why owners fight tax assessments and rebid service contracts. $23,250 multiplies by 7.75 instead of dividing by 0.0775. The same logic works in reverse: Marcus's missing $35,204 of expenses created about $454,000 of value on paper.

blocks.html: Jordan writes the offer memo. The Ramans offer $1,000,000 with a contingency for the lender's appraisal. Marcus calls Diane to complain that Jordan "tanked the deal with made-up expenses." Diane sends him Jordan's table with the source column highlighted and asks which number he would like to dispute. The seller, who had the building on the market for five months, counters at $1,120,000. They settle at $1,060,000, a 7.36% cap on the honest NOI, with the seller replacing the basement wiring before closing.

Before signing, Dev asks Jordan to show him how the deal looks with the Ramans' own loan, since the cap rate ignores financing. Jordan promises a separate cash flow memo: NOI is the property's number, and what is left after the mortgage is the Ramans' number. The order matters. Get NOI right first, then layer the debt on top. A buyer who starts from the mortgage payment and works backward ends up justifying whatever price the seller wants.

blocks.title: Setup sheets and licensee duties
blocks.html: A listing agent who passes along a seller's numbers without a reasonable basis, or who knows they are misleading, risks a misrepresentation claim and discipline from the Department of State for untrustworthiness or incompetence under RPL 441-c. "Information deemed reliable but not guaranteed" protects no one who knew better. Jordan's job as buyer's agent is different but just as clear: verify before the client relies.

items: Reconstruct expenses forward: current tax bills, a new owner's insurance quote and multi-year averages for volatile lines like heat.
Charge market management and payroll even when the seller or buyer does the work, because NOI measures the building, not the owner.
Capital items (a new roof), debt service and owner expenses never reduce NOI; reserves for replacement often do.
Derive the cap rate from comparable sales reconstructed the same way, then value with V = I / R.
Every recurring dollar of NOI is worth NOI divided by the cap rate, so expense errors become value errors.
An expense ratio far below the norm for the building type is a signal to ask for documents.

lessons.title: Case file: Three Loans for Southern Boulevard
lessons.tagline: Same building, same NOI, three term sheets. One makes Evelyn richer on paper and poorer in year four.
objectives: Calculate debt service, the mortgage constant, before-tax cash flow and cash on cash return for competing loan offers
Apply the debt service coverage ratio and loan-to-value limits to determine the maximum loan a lender will make
Decide whether leverage is positive or negative by comparing the mortgage constant with the cap rate
Calculate breakeven occupancy and stress-test a financed deal against falling income and value

blocks.title: A walk-up near the 6 train
blocks.html: Evelyn Park has a contract to buy a five-story walk-up on Southern Boulevard in the Bronx: twenty apartments over two stores, two blocks from the Longwood Avenue station. Price $3,800,000. Jordan and Evelyn's analyst spent two weeks reconstructing the income and expenses, and they trust the result: NOI of $266,000, a 7.0% cap rate. Evelyn has $1,900,000 she could put in, but she would rather not tie up all of it. Tasha Monroe, the mortgage broker, sends three term sheets on Monday morning with a note: "Pick your poison." Evelyn forwards them to Jordan: "Tell me what each one does to my money."

head: Line
Annual
blocks.caption: Reconstructed, verified and agreed. Nothing below this line changes NOI.

blocks.html: The table is the starting point, and it will not move. Every loan Tasha offers changes what Evelyn keeps, but none of them changes what the building earns. That is the first discipline of financing analysis: NOI is fixed by the property, and the loan only decides how NOI is split between the lender and the owner.

Before opening the term sheets, Jordan asks Evelyn what she wants the money to do. Her answer shapes everything that follows: steady income, no surprises, and enough cash left over to buy a second building within two years. That rules out nothing yet, but it gives Jordan a test for each loan. A structure that maximizes year-one return but leaves her exposed in year four, or one that ties up so much cash she cannot buy the second building, fails her goals even if it wins on a single ratio.

blocks.title: Term sheet A, a Bronx community bank
blocks.html:
Loan amount: lesser of 75% of price or the amount that produces a 1.30 debt service coverage ratio
Rate: 6.25% fixed for 5 years
Amortization: 30 years
Monthly payment on $2,750,000: $16,932
Recourse: limited to standard carve-outs
Prepayment: 3%, 2%, 1% in years 1 to 3

Banks lend on two tests at once. The debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) is NOI divided by annual debt service; this bank wants at least 1.30, meaning NOI must be 30% more than the mortgage payments. The loan-to-value limit caps the loan at 75% of price. Whichever test produces the smaller loan wins.

To compare loans on any size, analysts use the mortgage constant: annual debt service divided by the loan amount. For a 30-year loan at 6.25%, the monthly payment on $2,750,000 is $16,932, or $203,187 a year.

blocks.q: What is the mortgage constant for term sheet A?
c: 6.25%, the stated interest rate
7.39% of the loan each year
5.35% of the loan each year
76.4%, debt service over NOI
blocks.x: Constant = annual debt service / loan = $203,187 / $2,750,000 = 7.39%. It is higher than the 6.25% rate because each payment also repays principal. Choice A is the trap: the rate alone ignores amortization, and choice D is debt service divided by NOI, the inverse of DSCR, and amortization is real cash leaving Evelyn's account every month. The constant is what you compare to the cap rate to judge leverage.

blocks.html: Now the sizing. Seventy-five percent of $3,800,000 is $2,850,000. Is that the loan?

blocks.q: At $2,850,000, debt service would be about $210,575 a year. Will the bank lend that much?
c: Yes, because $2,850,000 is exactly 75% of the price
Yes, because the NOI of $266,000 covers the payment
No, because the DSCR would be about 1.26, under 1.30
No, because banks cap walk-up loans at 70% of price
blocks.x: DSCR = $266,000 / $210,575 = 1.26, below the bank's 1.30 floor, so coverage, not LTV, limits this loan. Choice B is the trap: covering the payment (a DSCR above 1.0) is not enough when the lender requires a cushion. Maximum LTV varies by lender and property type; there is no universal 70% rule.

blocks.q: What is the largest loan the 1.30 DSCR test allows, using the 7.39% constant?
c: About $3,273,800 at the rate
blocks.x: Maximum debt service = NOI / 1.30 = $266,000 / 1.30 = $204,615. Maximum loan = $204,615 / 0.07389 = about $2,769,000. The bank rounds to $2,750,000. Choice B, $3,600,000, is the loan at a 1.0 DSCR, with no cushion. $3,273,800 divides the allowed payment by the 6.25% interest rate instead of the 7.39% constant. Lenders size commercial loans this way every day: income first, LTV second.

blocks.title: Why lenders care more about coverage than value
blocks.html: A lender is repaid from rent, not from the building, unless something goes wrong. LTV protects the lender in a foreclosure. DSCR protects it every month. When interest rates are high, the DSCR test usually binds first, which is why buyers in 2023 to 2026 often found that a 75% LTV quote shrank to 65% or 70% once the bank ran coverage.

blocks.title: Cash world under term sheet A
blocks.html:
NOI: $266,000
Minus debt service: $203,187
Before-tax cash flow: $62,813
Equity: $3,800,000 minus $2,750,000 = $1,050,000
DSCR: $266,000 / $203,187 = 1.31

blocks.q: What is Evelyn's cash on cash return under term sheet A, before closing costs?
c: 7.0%, the cap rate
blocks.x: Cash on cash = BTCF / equity = $62,813 / $1,050,000 = 5.98%, about 6.0%. Choice A is the cap rate, the return on the whole property bought all cash. Choice B divides BTCF by the price instead of by equity. Choice C is what she would earn on an interest-only loan, which is term sheet B.

blocks.html: Evelyn's reaction is immediate: "I borrow two and three quarter million dollars and my return goes down?" Yes. If she paid all cash, she would earn 7.0%. With the bank loan, she earns about 6.0% on her smaller check.

blocks.q: Why does borrowing under term sheet A lower Evelyn's return on her own cash?
c: Because the loan raises the cap rate the market applies
Because the 7.39% constant exceeds the 7.0% return
Because DSCR lenders produce negative leverage
Because debt service reduces NOI and therefore value
blocks.x: Leverage is negative when each borrowed dollar costs more per year (the constant, 7.39%) than it earns in the property (the cap rate, 7.0%). The gap eats into her return on equity. Choice D is the most common error: debt service never touches NOI or value. Choice A is backward: financing does not change the property's cap rate at all.

blocks.title: Interest rate is not the cost of debt
blocks.html: A loan at 6.25% looks cheaper than a 7.0% cap rate, so many buyers assume positive leverage. But the owner pays principal too, and principal is cash out the door every month. Compare the mortgage constant with the cap rate. Principal does build equity, which the owner gets back at sale or refinance, but it does nothing for this year's cash on cash.

blocks.title: Term sheet B, a private debt fund
blocks.html:
Loan amount: $2,750,000
Rate: 6.00% fixed
Payments: interest only for 3 years, then amortizing over the remaining 27 years
Annual debt service, years 1 to 3: $165,000
Annual debt service from year 4: $205,915
Origination fee: 1.5%

blocks.q: During the interest-only years, what is Evelyn's cash on cash return under term sheet B?
c: About 6.0%
About 7.0%, the return without a loan
About 3.7%
About 9.6%
blocks.x: BTCF = $266,000 minus $165,000 = $101,000. Cash on cash = $101,000 / $1,050,000 = 9.62%. With a 6.0% constant (interest only) below the 7.0% cap rate, leverage turns positive and lifts her return above the all-cash 7.0%. Choice A is term sheet A. Choice C divides BTCF by the loan. The origination fee would trim this a little in year one.

blocks.html: Tasha's note under term sheet B says, in smaller type, "Popular with value-add buyers." Jordan runs year four.

blocks.q: In year 4, term sheet B's payment jumps to $205,915. What happens to Evelyn's position if NOI is still $266,000?
c: Cash on cash falls to about 5.7% and DSCR to about 1.29
Nothing changes, because the rate stays fixed at 6.00%
The loan defaults automatically for failing the 1.30 test
Cash on cash rises, since principal now builds her equity
blocks.x: BTCF drops to $266,000 minus $205,915 = $60,085, or 5.72% on $1,050,000, and DSCR falls to $266,000 / $205,915 = 1.29. The fixed rate is the trap in choice B: the rate does not change, but amortization starts, which raises the constant from 6.00% to about 7.49%. Whether a lower DSCR is a default depends on the loan's covenants; most loans test DSCR only at origination or refinancing.

blocks.html: Interest-only loans are not bad. They suit a buyer who will raise NOI during the interest-only period, by renovating vacant units or leasing a dark store. But Evelyn's plan is to hold a stable building, and her NOI is not going to jump. For her, term sheet B borrows return from year four to make years one to three look better.

blocks.title: Term sheet C, the same bank, half the loan
blocks.html:
Loan amount: $1,900,000 (50% of price)
Rate and amortization: same as A (6.25%, 30 years, 7.39% constant)
Annual debt service: $140,384
BTCF: $266,000 minus $140,384 = $125,616
Equity: $1,900,000
DSCR: 1.89

blocks.q: What is Evelyn's cash on cash return under term sheet C?
c: About 6.6%
About 5.98%
About 7.4%
About 3.3%
blocks.x: $125,616 / $1,900,000 = 6.61%. With negative leverage, borrowing less hurts less: 6.6% beats term sheet A's 6.0%, though both trail the 7.0% all-cash return. Choice C is the mortgage constant, not a return. Choice D divides BTCF by the price. When leverage is negative, every extra borrowed dollar lowers cash on cash.

blocks.html: Returns are only half the analysis. Jordan's next question is the one lenders ask: how far can income fall before the building stops paying for itself? The cash flow answer is breakeven occupancy: the share of potential gross income needed to cover operating expenses plus debt service.

blocks.q: Under term sheet A, what is the building's breakeven occupancy?
c: About 40.8%
About 76.4%
About 83.2%
About 95.0%, occupancy after vacancy
blocks.x: Breakeven = (operating expenses + debt service) / PGI = ($196,000 + $203,187) / $480,000 = 83.2%. Below about 83% occupancy, Evelyn feeds the building from her own pocket. 40.8% counts only expenses. 95% is just the vacancy assumption flipped. Under term sheet C, breakeven falls to about 70%, a much wider margin.

head: A: bank, 72% LTV
B: interest only
C: 50% LTV
All cash
blocks.caption: Same NOI in every column. Only the split between lender and owner changes.

blocks.html: Read the table across, not down. Moving from right to left, each column borrows more, and three things happen at once: equity shrinks, debt service grows, and the breakeven line climbs toward full occupancy. Cash on cash does not climb with it, because the constant on the bank loan is above the cap rate. The only column whose cash on cash beats the all-cash 7.0% is the interest-only one, and only for three years. That pattern is the signature of negative leverage. In a positive leverage market, with a constant below the cap rate, the cash on cash row would rise from right to left instead, and the real question would be how much risk Evelyn is willing to carry to get it.

blocks.q: A new store opens nearby and Evelyn's NOI falls 10% to $239,400. Under term sheet A, what happens?
c: DSCR falls to about 1.18 and BTCF to about $36,200
DSCR stays at 1.31 because the loan is fixed rate
BTCF falls 10%, to about $56,500, like the NOI
The building's value is unchanged because the debt is fixed
blocks.x: $239,400 / $203,187 = 1.18 DSCR, and BTCF = $239,400 minus $203,187 = $36,213. A 10% drop in NOI cut her cash flow by 42%. That is leverage working in reverse: the lender's slice is fixed, so the whole loss lands on the owner. Choice C is the trap: cash flow falls far faster than NOI when debt is fixed.

blocks.html: Leverage magnifies value changes too. Evelyn remembers 2023, when rising rates pushed Bronx multifamily cap rates up and values down even where rents held.

blocks.q: If the building's value falls 10% to $3,420,000 while the loan balance stays near $2,750,000, about how much of Evelyn's equity under term sheet A is lost?
c: 10%, the same as the drop in value
28%, the equity share of price
36% of her cash
72%, the loan as a share of price
blocks.x: Equity falls from $1,050,000 to $3,420,000 minus $2,750,000 = $670,000, a loss of $380,000, or 36% of her cash. Choice A is the all-cash answer. The same math works upward: a 10% gain would raise her equity 36%. Leverage does not change the building's risk; it concentrates it on a smaller slice of owner cash.

blocks.title: Closing costs belong in equity
blocks.html: In New York City, the mortgage recording tax on a commercial loan of $500,000 or more, which includes apartment buildings, totals 2.8% when the city and state pieces are combined. On $2,750,000 that is $77,000, plus bank fees, title insurance and legal costs. Tasha budgets it as Evelyn's cash at closing. Add $77,000 to term sheet A's equity and cash on cash drops from 5.98% to about 5.57%. Upstate, the same loan would pay a much lower county rate.

blocks.q: Counting the $77,000 mortgage recording tax as part of her investment, what happens to Evelyn's cash on cash under term sheet A?
c: It rises, because the tax reduces the loan balance
It falls to about 5.6%, since she invests more cash
It stays at 5.98%, since closing costs are not part of equity
It falls to about 4.8%, since the tax reduces NOI that year
blocks.x: Cash on cash divides BTCF by everything the investor puts in. $62,813 / ($1,050,000 + $77,000) = 5.57%. Choice C is the shortcut many exam problems take, but a real investor counts every dollar she writes a check for. The recording tax is a closing cost, not an operating expense, so it never reduces NOI (choice D).

blocks.text: The part of the payment that comes back

blocks.html: Evelyn's business partner, Ron, reads the table and objects. "You're ignoring the principal. Every month we pay the bank, part of it is our own money going into the building." He is right that it matters, and wrong about where it shows up. Under term sheet A, about $170,962 of the first year's $203,187 is interest and $32,224 is principal. The principal reduces the loan balance, so it builds equity that Evelyn collects when she sells or refinances. It does not reach her bank account this year.

blocks.q: Ron wants to count first-year principal paydown of $32,224 as part of the return under term sheet A. What is the most accurate response?
c: Principal paydown is already included in before-tax cash flow
It is deductible, so it raises after-tax cash flow by $32,224
It lowers NOI, because principal is an operating expense
It raises total return to about 9.1% but adds no cash this year
blocks.x: BTCF already subtracts the whole payment, principal included, so the $32,224 is not in the $62,813. Added back as equity build-up, total first-year return is ($62,813 + $32,224) / $1,050,000 = 9.05%, but that piece is paper until a sale or refinance. Choice B reverses the tax rule: interest is deductible, principal is not. Nothing about the loan touches NOI.

blocks.html: That distinction drives real decisions. An owner who needs income to live on cares about cash on cash. An owner building wealth over twenty years may accept a lower cash on cash in exchange for equity build-up and appreciation. Evelyn is the second kind of investor, but she has also seen what happens to owners whose cash flow goes negative in a bad year: they sell at the bottom. Equity build-up is worth nothing to an owner who cannot hold on long enough to collect it.

The prepayment terms matter for the same reason. Term sheet A charges 3% of the balance to prepay in year one, 2% in year two and 1% in year three, then nothing. If rates fall and Evelyn wants to refinance into positive leverage, the penalty is part of the cost of doing it. On a $2,700,000 balance in year two, that is $54,000. A refinance pays only if the annual savings in debt service recover the penalty and the new closing costs, including another round of mortgage recording tax unless the lender agrees to a consolidation that taxes only the new money.

Evelyn reads the table twice and asks Jordan which loan he would take. Jordan answers carefully, because loan advice is Tasha's job and investment advice is Evelyn's call: the numbers say term sheet B is a bet that NOI rises before year four, term sheet A is a bet that values rise enough to make up for negative leverage, and term sheet C gives up some cash for a much wider safety margin. Evelyn chooses a version of C: $2,100,000 from the bank, keeping a $300,000 reserve for the boiler and roof work the building will need in the next five years. She tells Jordan she will refinance if rates fall, "when the constant is under the cap rate again."

blocks.title: Evelyn's final structure
blocks.html:
Loan: $2,100,000 at 6.25%, 30-year amortization (7.39% constant)
Debt service: $155,161
BTCF: $266,000 minus $155,161 = $110,839
Equity: $1,700,000 (before closing costs), with $300,000 held back as a reserve
Cash on cash: 6.52%. DSCR: 1.71. Breakeven occupancy: 73.2%

Her cash on cash is lower than the all-cash 7.0% and a bit lower than term sheet C, but she keeps a reserve, keeps a wide margin under the bank's covenant, and can still refinance when the math turns positive. Jordan files the analysis with the term sheets. Diane reads it and adds one line to the file: "The best loan is the one the building can carry in a bad year."

The building runs as planned for three years. In month 37, with the prepayment schedule behind her, Tasha calls: a bank will refinance the remaining balance, about $2,021,000, at 5.00% fixed with 30-year amortization. The new lender takes an assignment of the old mortgage and consolidates it, so mortgage recording tax applies only to new money, and there is none. NOI is still $266,000.

blocks.title: Refinance offer, month 37
blocks.html:
Loan: $2,021,000 (the remaining balance)
Rate: 5.00% fixed, 30-year amortization
Monthly payment: $10,849
Annual debt service: $130,190
Mortgage constant: $130,190 / $2,021,000 = 6.44%

blocks.q: Compared with the building's 7.0% cap rate, what does the 6.44% constant mean for Evelyn?
c: Leverage turns positive, and BTCF rises to about $135,800
Leverage turns positive, but BTCF falls as amortization restarts
Leverage stays neutral, since NOI has not changed since purchase
Leverage turns negative, since a new 30-year term costs more interest
blocks.x: With the constant below the cap rate, each borrowed dollar now costs less than it earns, which is positive leverage. Debt service drops from $155,161 to $130,190, so BTCF rises from $110,839 to $135,810, and DSCR climbs to about 2.04. The restarted amortization is the trap: it slows principal paydown and equity build-up, but cash flow depends on the payment, and the payment fell.

blocks.html: Before signing, Ron asks the question every leveraged owner should ask: what happens if the building fails? The term sheet says nonrecourse "with standard carve-outs." Nonrecourse means the lender's remedy for a default is the building. It can foreclose, but it cannot chase Evelyn's other assets for a shortfall. The carve-outs, often called bad-boy provisions, make the borrower or a guarantor personally liable for specific misconduct: fraud, diverting rents or insurance proceeds, a voluntary bankruptcy filing, or transferring the property without the lender's consent. Market risk stays with the building. Behavior risk comes home.

blocks.q: Under a nonrecourse loan with standard carve-outs, which event would most likely make Evelyn personally liable?
c: A new store nearby cuts NOI below the annual debt service
She uses the building's rents for another property while in default
Cap rates rise and the building's value falls below the loan balance
A retail tenant's bankruptcy leaves one store empty for a full year
blocks.x: Carve-outs are triggered by the borrower's conduct, and diverting rents while in default is a classic one. Falling NOI, rising cap rates, and a tenant's failure are market risks the lender accepted by making the loan nonrecourse; its remedy for those is foreclosure on the building. The underwater choice is the trap: a loan larger than the property's value feels like personal exposure, but without a carve-out event the shortfall is the lender's loss.

items: NOI is fixed by the property; financing only splits it between lender and owner.
Lenders size commercial loans by the lesser of the LTV limit and the DSCR limit: maximum debt service = NOI / required DSCR, and maximum loan = that payment / the mortgage constant.
Compare the mortgage constant, not the interest rate, with the cap rate: a constant above the cap rate means negative leverage, and borrowing more lowers cash on cash.
Interest-only periods raise early cash on cash, but payments jump when amortization starts.
Breakeven occupancy = (operating expenses + debt service) / PGI; higher leverage raises it and shrinks the margin for error.
Fixed debt magnifies changes in NOI and value, and closing costs such as NYC mortgage recording tax belong in the equity used for cash on cash.
Refinancing pays when the new constant falls below the cap rate; a nonrecourse loan limits the lender to the building except for carve-outs triggered by the borrower's own misconduct.

lessons.title: Case file: Three Deals on the Okafors' Kitchen Table
lessons.tagline: A Staten Island four-family, a Yonkers six-unit and a Hicksville dental office. The cheapest one on paper is the worst buy.
objectives: Calculate gross rent and gross income multipliers and explain why they mislead when expenses differ
Compare deals of different types by NOI, cap rate, price per unit and cash on cash return
Decide how rent regulation, Good Cause Eviction and single-tenant risk change a deal's numbers
Apply leverage analysis to decide whether an investor should finance or pay cash

blocks.title: After Macon Street
blocks.html: The sale of the Okafors' Bed-Stuy brownstone closed in the spring. After paying the capital gains tax their accountant warned them about, Grace and Emmanuel moved into a two-bedroom rental near their daughter in Canarsie and set aside $1,500,000 to buy an income property. "We want a check every month," Grace tells Jordan. "And we are done fixing boilers." Jordan, who sold their house, now has three listings spread across their kitchen table: a four-family in Stapleton, Staten Island, a six-unit walk-up in Yonkers, and a single-story building in Hicksville leased to a dental practice. Emmanuel has already circled the Yonkers building. "It's the cheapest for the rent," he says. Is he right?

One question first, because Emmanuel asks it: can the brownstone gain be rolled into the new building tax free? No. A 1031 exchange requires that the property sold was held for investment or business use, and the brownstone was their home. They already used the home sale exclusion, and the rest of the gain was taxed. The $1,500,000 is fresh money, which means they can buy anything, anywhere, without exchange deadlines.

head: A: Stapleton 4-family
B: Yonkers 6-unit
C: Hicksville dental
blocks.caption: Three listings, three different kinds of risk.

blocks.html: Brokers and small investors often screen buildings with a gross rent multiplier (GRM): price divided by gross monthly rent. For larger buildings and commercial property, the same idea uses annual income and is called a gross income multiplier (GIM). A lower multiplier means the buyer pays less for each dollar of rent. It takes ten seconds and needs nothing but the listing sheet, which is exactly why it is popular and exactly why it is dangerous.

blocks.q: What is the gross rent multiplier (monthly) for the Stapleton four-family?
c: About 12.7, the annual figure
About 152.4
About 0.66
About 21.8
blocks.x: GRM = price / monthly gross rent = $1,280,000 / $8,400 = 152.4. Choice A is the annual version, the GIM ($1,280,000 / $100,800 = 12.7), a real measure but not the monthly one asked for. Choice C divides the wrong way. Always check whether a multiplier quoted to you is monthly or annual before you compare it with anything.

head: A: Stapleton
B: Yonkers
C: Hicksville
blocks.caption: On multipliers alone, Yonkers looks like the bargain and Hicksville looks overpriced.

blocks.q: Ranking only by the gross income multiplier, which property looks cheapest?
c: Stapleton, because a four-family has the lowest expenses
Hicksville, because a triple net lease has no expenses
Yonkers, because it has the lowest GIM at about 9.6
Stapleton, because it has the highest rent per unit
blocks.x: Yonkers has the lowest multiplier: $1,350,000 / $140,400 = 9.62, so the buyer pays the least per dollar of gross rent. That is what Emmanuel saw. Choices A and B make arguments about expenses, which is precisely what a gross multiplier ignores. Hold that thought: the next step is to find out whether the cheap rent is also cheap income.

blocks.html: Emmanuel has a second argument for Yonkers: price per unit. Stapleton costs $320,000 a door; Yonkers costs $225,000. Small-building buyers quote price per unit constantly, and like the multipliers, it is a useful first look that hides more than it shows. A unit is not a standard measure. The Stapleton apartments are three-bedrooms with separate boilers; the Yonkers apartments are one-bedrooms sharing a 1928 oil boiler. Price per unit says nothing about rent per unit, expenses per unit, or regulation.

blocks.q: Yonkers costs $225,000 a unit and Stapleton $320,000 a unit. What can the Okafors conclude from that alone?
c: Yonkers is the better value because each unit costs less
Little, since unit size, rent and expenses differ
Stapleton is overpriced by about $95,000 per unit
Yonkers will appreciate faster because it is cheaper
blocks.x: Price per unit is meaningful only between buildings with similar units, rents and expense structures. These two differ on all three, so the comparison proves nothing by itself. Choice C treats a per-unit gap as a pricing error. Choice D confuses a low price with future growth. Like GRM, price per unit is a screen, and the screening stage is over once real income and expense numbers arrive.

blocks.html: Jordan requests operating statements for all three and reconstructs them the way any careful analyst would: market vacancy, current tax bills, insurance quotes, and a management fee whether or not the Okafors plan to manage. The results are not close to what the multipliers suggest.

head: A: Stapleton
B: Yonkers
C: Hicksville
blocks.caption: The Yonkers expenses include oil heat, a 1928 boiler, water for six units and a property tax bill that rose 9% last year.

blocks.q: What is the Yonkers building's NOI?
c: $140,400 less vacancy
blocks.x: EGI = $140,400 minus $7,020 vacancy = $133,380. NOI = $133,380 minus $74,000 = $59,380. $66,400 subtracts expenses from gross rent and skips vacancy. $52,360 subtracts vacancy twice. The Yonkers building collects 39% more rent than Stapleton but nets almost the same NOI, because the owner pays for heat, water and an old boiler.

blocks.q: Why did the GIM point the Okafors toward the wrong building?
c: It ignores expenses and vacancy, which differ here
It used annual rents instead of the monthly rents it needs
It applies to commercial property, not apartments
It is a lender's ratio, not a buyer's ratio
blocks.x: A gross multiplier compares price with rent before any expenses, so it works only when the buildings being compared have similar expense ratios. Here they range from 3% to 55%. Choice B is a real distinction (GRM is monthly, GIM is annual) but either version has the same blind spot. GRM is used most for small residential buildings; it is not a lender's coverage test.

blocks.title: Multipliers and cap rates answer different questions
blocks.html: GRM and GIM use gross rent and ignore who pays what. The cap rate uses NOI and captures it. When two buildings share a type, a neighborhood and an expense structure, a multiplier is a fine first screen. When one owner pays the heat and the other doesn't, or when one property is a triple net lease, only NOI-based measures compare them honestly.

blocks.q: Using the reconstructed NOIs and asking prices, which property has the highest cap rate?
c: Stapleton, at about 4.6%
Yonkers, at about 4.4%
Hicksville, at about 6.8%
The three are roughly equal at 4.5% to 5%
blocks.x: Hicksville: $102,000 / $1,500,000 = 6.8%. Stapleton: $58,768 / $1,280,000 = 4.59%. Yonkers: $59,380 / $1,350,000 = 4.40%. The building with the worst multiplier has the best yield, and the one with the best multiplier has the worst. That reversal is the whole lesson of the quick screen.

blocks.html: Emmanuel crosses out his circle. Grace, who kept the Macon Street books for 28 years, asks the better question: "Why would anyone sell a 6.8% building when the apartment buildings sell at 4.5%?" A higher cap rate is the market's way of charging for risk. Each deal needs a risk check before the yield means anything.

blocks.title: Rent stabilization outside New York City
blocks.html: Rent stabilization is not only a New York City program. Under the Emergency Tenant Protection Act of 1974, a city, town or village can opt in after declaring a housing emergency, and the coverage generally reaches buildings of six or more units built before 1974. Yonkers is one of the Westchester municipalities that adopted it. Increases are set by the county's rent guidelines board, not by the owner.

blocks.q: The Yonkers listing says rents are "well below market, huge upside on turnover." All six units are stabilized. What is the problem with that pitch?
c: Nothing, because units deregulate when the rent passes a threshold
Turnover rents rise through a 20% statutory vacancy bonus
The upside requires the tenants' written consent to market rents
Units stay stabilized on turnover, so the gap may never close
blocks.x: Since the 2019 HSTPA there is no vacancy decontrol and no statutory vacancy bonus, and that applies in ETPA municipalities like Yonkers as well as NYC. A new tenant takes the unit at the legal regulated rent plus any allowed increase. Choice A is the pre-2019 rule many listing writers still lean on. The Okafors should value the Yonkers rents as they are.

blocks.text: Risk check: Stapleton and Good Cause

blocks.html: The Stapleton building's four tenants are all free market, on one-year leases, at rents Jordan confirms are close to market. Grace has read about the 2024 Good Cause Eviction law and worries she will not be able to raise rents or replace a tenant who stops paying.

blocks.q: If the Okafors buy the Stapleton four-family and own no other rental units, how does Good Cause Eviction apply?
c: It applies, since every NYC building with two or more units is covered
It applies after the first lease renewal under their ownership
They are likely exempt as small landlords with 10 or fewer units
It applies once a tenant has lived there more than two years
blocks.x: The Good Cause law exempts small landlords who own 10 or fewer units statewide, along with several other categories such as newer buildings and owner-occupied buildings with 10 or fewer units. Four units, and nothing else, puts the Okafors inside the small landlord exemption. Choice A is the trap: Good Cause applies automatically in NYC, but only to buildings and landlords that are not exempt. Their attorney should confirm the exemption at closing.

blocks.text: Risk check: one tenant in Hicksville

blocks.html: The dental practice has eight years left on a triple net lease. Under a triple net lease the tenant pays the property taxes, insurance and maintenance, which is why the landlord's expenses are only $3,000 a year, mostly accounting and a roof reserve. It is the closest thing in real estate to a bond: one tenant, one check, almost no management. It is also the closest thing to an all-or-nothing bet.

blocks.q: What is the most important thing for the Okafors to investigate before buying the Hicksville building?
c: The tenant's financial strength and the lease's renewal terms
The building's gross rent multiplier compared with nearby apartments
Whether the building could be converted to residential use
The current interest rates for a 30-year residential mortgage
blocks.x: With one tenant, vacancy is 0% or 100%. The tenant's credit (financial statements, years in business, a personal or corporate guaranty) and the lease terms (renewal options, rent increases, assignment rights) decide whether the 6.8% is real. Choice B repeats the multiplier mistake. Conversion is speculation. A residential mortgage rate is irrelevant; commercial loans price differently.

blocks.title: What happens if the dentist leaves
blocks.html:
Lost rent: $105,000 a year
Landlord now pays taxes, insurance and upkeep: about $38,000 a year
Re-leasing: 6 to 12 months of downtime, plus commission and space work
Year without a tenant: NOI swings from $102,000 to about negative $41,000

The tenant's file is strong: a group practice with four dentists, eleven years at the location, a corporate guaranty and two five-year renewal options at 10% increases. That does not make the risk zero, but it makes the 6.8% look like fair pay for it rather than a warning.

Jordan also points out what the dental lease means for the Okafors' daily life. With the apartments, they would field repair calls, collect six or four rents, renew leases, comply with stabilization filings in Yonkers or the HPD registration that every NYC building with three or more units must file each year. With Hicksville, they would receive one check, review the tenant's proof of insurance and tax payments once a year, and budget for the roof. For two people who told Jordan on day one that they were done fixing boilers, management intensity is not a footnote. It is a cost, even if it never appears in NOI, and it is part of why apartment buildings and net leases trade at different cap rates.

Liquidity matters too. When the Okafors eventually sell, or when their children inherit and want cash, the buyer pool for a Staten Island four-family is large: owner-occupants, small investors and 1031 buyers. A well-leased dental building attracts net lease investors, often from out of state. A Yonkers walk-up with regulated rents and an old boiler has the thinnest pool of the three, which is one more thing its low multiplier was hiding.

The Okafors could buy any of the three for cash. Tasha suggests they borrow 50% on Hicksville and keep $750,000 in the bank: a $750,000 loan at 6.5% over 25 years, with annual debt service of $60,769.

blocks.q: With the $750,000 loan, what is the Okafors' cash on cash return on Hicksville, and what does it show?
c: About 13.6%, positive leverage from the loan
About 6.8%, since the cap rate is unchanged
About 2.7%, since the loan doubles risk
About 5.5%, which is negative leverage
blocks.x: BTCF = $102,000 minus $60,769 = $41,231. Cash on cash = $41,231 / $750,000 = 5.50%. The mortgage constant is $60,769 / $750,000 = 8.10%, above the 6.8% cap rate, so borrowing lowers the return on their cash. Choice A divides NOI by equity and forgets the mortgage. The cap rate (choice B) is what they earn all cash.

blocks.html: For retirees who want income and certainty, paying cash at 6.8% beats borrowing to earn 5.5% while adding a lender. The $750,000 they would keep in the bank is not idle either; it is their reserve. Jordan does not tell them to pay cash. He shows them the two numbers side by side and lets Grace, who has never liked owing anyone, decide.

While they are talking, Marcus emails a fourth option: another Stapleton four-family, asking $1,395,000, rents $9,000 a month. "Same block, better rents," he writes. Jordan checks recent sales of comparable Staten Island four-families with similar tenant-paid heat; they sold at GRMs around 130.

blocks.q: Using a market GRM of 130, what does a quick screen suggest about the fourth listing?
c: Its rent supports about $1,170,000
It is underpriced, since its GRM is below the market's 130
Its rent supports about $14,040,000 using annual rent
GRM cannot be used for four-family buildings
blocks.x: Indicated value = GRM x monthly rent = 130 x $9,000 = $1,170,000. The asking price implies a GRM of $1,395,000 / $9,000 = 155. Because the comps are the same type with the same expense structure, the multiplier is a fair screen here, and it says the price is high. Choice C applies a monthly multiplier to annual rent ($108,000), a classic slip.

blocks.html: Notice the difference between this use of the multiplier and Emmanuel's. Here the comparison is a four-family against other four-families on the same kind of block, with tenants paying their own heat in every case. The expense structures match, so gross rent is a fair stand-in for income. Emmanuel's comparison set a four-family against a six-unit walk-up and a net leased office, three buildings whose expenses ranged from 3% to 55% of income. Same tool, different job. Jordan replies to Marcus that the Okafors will look at the fourth building only if the price comes down toward what the comps support.

blocks.text: Taxes are part of the comparison

blocks.html: The Okafors' accountant adds one more column. Depreciation shelters part of the income from tax, and the schedule depends on the property type. The two apartment buildings are residential rental property, depreciated over 27.5 years. The dental building is nonresidential, depreciated over 39 years. Land is never depreciated.

blocks.q: Hicksville's price is $1,500,000, and the accountant allocates $600,000 to land. What is the annual depreciation deduction?
c: $38,462, with the land included
blocks.x: Depreciable basis = $1,500,000 minus $600,000 = $900,000. A dental office is nonresidential, so $900,000 / 39 = $23,077. Choice B uses 27.5 years, the residential schedule. Choice A forgets to remove the land. Slower depreciation means a little less tax shelter than an apartment building of the same price, one more reason the cap rates differ.

head: A: Stapleton
B: Yonkers
C: Hicksville
rows: Turnover, Good Cause if they buy more
blocks.caption: No single number decides. The table makes the trade-offs visible.

blocks.q: Grace wants to put all $1,500,000 into Hicksville. What is the strongest argument for keeping some money back?
c: Its cap rate is too high to be trusted by any lender
Its GIM shows it is the most overpriced of the three
One tenant means income could stop for a year
Net leased buildings cannot be resold for many years
blocks.x: Concentration is the risk: if the practice leaves, income drops to zero and the landlord picks up taxes and insurance until a new tenant signs. A reserve, or a smaller second investment, protects against that. Choice B repeats the gross multiplier mistake. Net lease buildings sell regularly to a large buyer pool, and a strong-credit lease often makes them easier to sell, not harder.

blocks.html: Jordan also runs the comparison the way an appraiser would want it said out loud. Stapleton is the safest income of the three in terms of tenant diversity: four tenants, near-market rents, a deep resale market, but a 4.6% yield and real management. Yonkers is the cheapest on every gross measure and the weakest on every net one. Hicksville pays the most and asks the least of its owners, but it concentrates everything on one tenant's business. None of those statements is a number, and that is the point: the numbers narrow the choice, and judgment about risk finishes it. Jordan's job is to make the trade-offs visible, not to choose for the clients.

The Okafors offer $1,430,000 for Hicksville, all cash, contingent on reviewing the dental group's financial statements, an estoppel certificate from the tenant confirming the lease terms, and a Phase I environmental report, since a dental office handles chemicals and the building is on a busy commercial strip. They keep the remaining $70,000, plus their savings, as a reserve: enough to carry about eighteen months of the landlord's costs if the tenant ever leaves. Emmanuel asks Jordan to send the Yonkers listing back to Marcus "with our regards."

items: GRM (price / monthly rent) and GIM (price / annual gross income) are quick screens that ignore expenses and vacancy; use them only to compare similar buildings with similar expense structures.
Compare different property types on NOI and cap rate, then adjust for risk: a higher cap rate is the market's price for more risk or less liquidity.
Rent-stabilized units stay stabilized on turnover, including in ETPA municipalities like Yonkers; Good Cause Eviction exempts landlords with 10 or fewer units.
Single-tenant net lease income is low-maintenance but all-or-nothing; tenant credit and lease terms decide its value.
When the mortgage constant exceeds the cap rate, borrowing lowers cash on cash; investors seeking income may do better paying cash.
Residential rentals depreciate over 27.5 years and nonresidential property over 39, which affects after-tax comparisons.

lessons.title: Case file: The Offering Memorandum for Livingston Street
