lessons.tagline: Forty glossy pages, a 6.9% cap rate on the cover, and a footnote on page 31 that changes everything.
objectives: Read an offering memorandum and separate in-place income from pro forma assumptions
Rebuild a stabilized NOI from a rent roll with expiring leases, a vacant floor and an expiring tax abatement
Value a property at a market cap rate and adjust for one-time lease-up costs to reach an offer price
Explain how lenders size loans on in-place income and what that means for the buyer's equity

blocks.title: Page one
blocks.html: The PDF arrives on a Friday afternoon from a large investment sales brokerage: "Exclusive Offering: 24,000 SF Retail and Office Building, Downtown Brooklyn." Five stories on Livingston Street, a bank branch on the ground floor, four floors of offices above, two blocks from Borough Hall. Asking price $11,000,000. The cover promises "6.9% Pro Forma Cap Rate" and "Significant Upside Through Lease-Up." Evelyn Park forwards it to Jordan with one line: "Find what they're not saying. Monday." Jordan has read listing sheets. This is the first offering memorandum, or OM, he has read with $11 million on the line.

An offering memorandum is the marketing book a listing broker prepares for an investment sale: photos, location and transit maps, a tenant summary, a rent roll, an income and expense statement, sale comps and a pitch. It is written by the seller's agent to get the highest price. That does not make it false. It makes it advocacy. The numbers that matter most are usually in the financial section, and the assumptions that drive them are usually in the footnotes.
The OM's financial page has two columns. One is labeled "In-Place." The other, bigger and bolder, is labeled "Pro Forma Year 1," and that is the column the cover cap rate comes from.

head: OM pro forma, Year 1
blocks.caption: *Footnote 7, page 31: "Taxes reflect the current ICAP abatement."

blocks.q: Before analyzing the pro forma, what should Jordan request first?
c: The broker's opinion of the building's upside after renovation
The pro forma for years 2 through 10 to see the full growth story
The seller's asking price for the building's unused air rights
The T-12 statement, a certified rent roll and the leases
blocks.x: A pro forma is a forecast. To test it, you need what the building actually did and what the tenants are actually bound to pay: the trailing 12 months (T-12) of income and expenses, a rent roll certified by the seller, and copies of every lease. Choice B asks for more of the same forecast. Air rights and renovation upside may be real, but they are not income, and a buyer should not pay for them twice.

blocks.text: The rent roll behind the pro forma

blocks.html: The data room opens Monday morning. The certified rent roll tells a different story than the bold column.

head: Space
Tenant
RSF
Rent per RSF
Annual rent
Lease ends
blocks.caption: In-place rent is $870,000. The OM's pro forma PGI is $1,210,000.

blocks.html: Every tenant in the pro forma is paying more than they actually pay, and the empty floor is fully rented. Jordan pulls the gap apart one assumption at a time, starting with the empty floor. The OM puts it at $46 a foot. Jordan's three most recent Downtown Brooklyn office lease comps for floors this size in buildings this age came in at $43, $44 and $45, each with several months of free rent and a tenant improvement allowance.

blocks.q: Floor 4 has been empty for 18 months. The OM rents it at $46 with no lease-up time. How should Jordan treat it in a stabilized analysis?
c: At $46 with no downtime, since the OM shows comparable asking rents
At $0 permanently, since it has been vacant for a year and a half
At about $44 market rent, with lease-up costs handled separately
At $46, but with a 50% vacancy allowance on the whole building
blocks.x: A stabilized analysis assumes the building is leased at market, so Floor 4 goes in at the $44 the signed comps support. The time and money to get there (downtime, tenant improvements, commission) are one-time costs, subtracted from value, not from stabilized NOI. Choice A is the OM's assumption: asking rents are not signed leases. Choice B confuses current vacancy with permanent vacancy.

blocks.html: The bank is a different question. It pays $65 a foot, and its lease ends in 14 months. The OM assumes it renews at $72.50. Jordan calls two retail brokers. Bank branches across the city have been consolidating; one says the bank's regional office "is reviewing the location." Market rent for a Livingston Street corner store this size is about $70.

blocks.q: The bank's lease ends in 14 months and the bank is reviewing the branch. How should the bank's rent appear in Jordan's stabilized NOI?
c: At $72.50, since the OM shows a renewal at that rent
At $65, since contract rent controls until the lease ends
At $0, since the bank has signaled it may leave the space
At $70 market, with the renewal risk in a higher vacancy
blocks.x: For a stabilized year, the space is valued at market rent, $70, whether the bank stays or a new tenant replaces it. The real risk, that the bank leaves and the store sits empty for a while, is captured by a higher vacancy and credit loss allowance than the OM's 2%. Choice A treats the broker's hope as a lease. Choice C overreacts: a corner store on Livingston Street will lease, the question is when and at what cost.

blocks.q: The architecture firm on Floor 5 pays $38 and its lease ends in 6 months. The OM shows it at $46 in Year 1. The tenant has told building staff it is moving to a smaller space. What does this mean for the analysis?
c: Floor 5 is upside, since the rent will jump to $46 on renewal
Floor 5 is a near-term vacancy risk, not guaranteed upside
Floor 5 should be counted at $38 for the full ten-year hold
Floor 5 has no effect, since the OM already reflects market
blocks.x: A below-market lease that expires soon looks like upside only if the tenant stays and pays more. A tenant planning to leave means a second empty floor within six months, with new downtime and leasing costs. In stabilized terms, Floor 5 goes in at the $44 market rent, and the likely move-out raises the vacancy allowance. Choice A is exactly how the OM frames it. Choice C ignores that leases expire.

blocks.title: Read the lease expiration schedule like a calendar
blocks.html: Most OMs include a lease rollover chart. Turn it into dates and dollars: which tenants leave in the next 24 months, what share of income they pay, and what it will cost to replace them. On Livingston Street, the bank and the architect together pay $450,000, more than half the in-place rent, and both leases end within 14 months. That is not a stabilized building; it is a leasing project with a building attached.

blocks.q: The OM uses a 2% vacancy and credit loss allowance. Today one of five floors is empty and two leases end within 14 months. Which allowance is most defensible for stabilized NOI?
c: 2%, matching the OM, since the vacancy is temporary
About 7%, for turnover risk in a five-tenant building
0%, since stabilized means the building is fully leased
About 21%, the share of rentable space vacant today
blocks.x: A five-tenant building has lumpy risk: one move-out empties 17% to 21% of the space. Over a typical holding period, an allowance in the mid to high single digits fits the market and the rollover profile; Jordan uses 7%. Choice D uses today's physical vacancy, which double counts the one-time lease-up Jordan subtracts separately. Choice A is the OM's number, built for a cover page.

blocks.html: The OM's management fee is 2% of EGI, below what a third-party manager charges for a small multi-tenant office building in Brooklyn. Evelyn's own management company, which would run the building, bills 4% to the properties it manages. The OM also shows no reserves, in a building with a 1970s elevator and a rooftop HVAC system the engineer's report puts at the end of its useful life. Jordan raises management to 4% and adds reserves of $0.25 per square foot, $6,000 a year, which is light but matches what the comps' buyers underwrote.

blocks.q: Which change to the OM's management and reserve lines is best supported?
c: Keep management at 2%, since Evelyn's company could run it cheaply
Remove management, since an owner-managed building has no fee
Add reserves, but not until the elevator actually breaks down
Raise management to a market 4% and add an annual reserve
blocks.x: A reconstructed statement charges market management no matter who manages, and includes reserves for components near the end of their lives, here an old elevator and rooftop HVAC. Choice A is the trap: Evelyn's cost advantage belongs to Evelyn, not to the building, and paying for it in the price would hand it to the seller. Waiting for the elevator to fail (choice C) is how deferred maintenance becomes a price cut at the next sale.

blocks.html: Each of these changes is small on its own. Together, management and reserves add about $25,400 a year of expense the OM left out. At the cap rates this building will trade at, that is roughly $400,000 of price, before Jordan has touched the biggest item in the book.

On page 31, in eight-point type: "Taxes reflect the current ICAP abatement." The Industrial and Commercial Abatement Program (ICAP) reduces NYC property taxes for a period after qualifying commercial renovations. Jordan asks the seller's attorney for the Department of Finance benefit schedule. The building's abatement begins phasing out next year and ends entirely in 2028. Without it, the tax bill is about $265,000, not $210,000.

blocks.q: The OM's $210,000 tax figure reflects an abatement that phases out starting next year. Which tax figure belongs in stabilized NOI?
c: $265,000, the full unabated tax
$210,000, since that is today's actual bill
$237,500, the average over the phase-out
$0, since abated buildings pay no tax
blocks.x: Stabilized NOI describes a typical year for the next owner, and after 2028 every year is unabated. Using the full $265,000 is the honest figure; at a 6.25% cap rate, the $55,000 difference is worth about $880,000 of price. Choice B is the OM's approach: true today, false for the hold. Choice C averages a temporary benefit into a permanent number.

blocks.title: Two NYC tax items in every commercial OM
blocks.html: First, abatements and exemptions (ICAP for commercial buildings, 421-a and J-51 for residential) expire on schedules that the Department of Finance publishes for each tax lot. Check the schedule; never trust "current taxes." Second, the NYC commercial rent tax applies to qualifying tenants only in Manhattan south of 96th Street. A Brooklyn office tenant does not pay it, which is one small reason Brooklyn rents can compete with Midtown South.

head: Line
OM pro forma
Jordan's stabilized
blocks.caption: Same building, same expense lines. Only the assumptions changed.

blocks.q: What is Jordan's stabilized NOI?
c: $1,078,800 less vacancy
blocks.x: NOI = EGI of $1,078,800 minus expenses of $516,152 = $562,648. $647,084 subtracts the OM's expense total from Jordan's EGI, mixing two sets of assumptions. $754,084 is the OM's pro forma. Choice D subtracts vacancy a second time from a number that already reflects it.

blocks.html: The OM's sale comps page deserves the same skepticism. It lists five "comparable" sales at $480 to $560 per square foot, which makes $458 look cheap. Jordan checks each one. Two were fully leased buildings with long-term tenants. One was bought by a user, a medical group that occupied the whole building and paid a premium to own its space. One included development rights the buyer planned to use. Only one, a half-vacant building on Court Street, resembles Livingston Street, and it sold for $372 a foot. Price per foot is a quick screen, like a gross rent multiplier, and it hides the same things: occupancy, lease terms and who the buyer was.

The cover's 6.9% came from the pro forma NOI. Comparable small Brooklyn office and retail buildings, reconstructed the same way, have traded between 6.0% and 6.5% over the last year, and Jordan picks 6.25% for a building with this location and this rollover risk.

blocks.q: At a 6.25% market cap rate, what is the building's stabilized value?
blocks.x: V = I / R = $562,648 / 0.0625 = $9,002,368. $12,065,000 capitalizes the OM's $754,084 at 6.25%, a market rate applied to a fantasy income. $8,202,000 uses a 6.86% rate on the stabilized NOI. $3,516,000 multiplies instead of dividing. The rate barely matters next to the income: getting NOI right moved value by $3 million.

blocks.text: From stabilized value to a price

blocks.html: Stabilized value assumes the building is already leased at market. It is not. Floor 4 is empty today, and getting a tenant in means real cash out before the first rent check: nine months of downtime at the $220,000 annual market rent ($165,000), a tenant improvement allowance of $40 a foot ($200,000), and a leasing commission of about $110,000.

blocks.title: Jordan's indicated value
blocks.html:
Stabilized value: $562,648 / 0.0625 = $9,002,368
Less Floor 4 lease-up: $165,000 + $200,000 + $110,000 = $475,000
Indicated value: about $8,527,000 ($355 per RSF, against $458 per RSF asked)

blocks.q: Why does Jordan subtract the $475,000 of Floor 4 lease-up costs from value instead of reducing the stabilized NOI?
c: One-time costs come off value; NOI is a typical year
The IRS requires tenant improvements to be depreciated
Commissions are a form of debt service on the building
The 7% vacancy allowance already covers them
blocks.x: Lease-up costs happen once, so they come off the price once. Putting them in NOI would capitalize a one-time cost as if it recurred every year, at 16 to 1, and overstate the discount. Choice D is the most tempting: the 7% allowance covers future turnover in a stabilized building, not the cost of filling a floor that is empty on day one. Tax treatment is a separate question.

blocks.text: How a lender will see it

blocks.html: Evelyn will not pay all cash. Her bank's commercial lender reads the same data room and does what lenders do: sizes the loan on income the building has today, not on stabilized or pro forma income. In-place, the building collects $870,000 of rent. After a 2% credit allowance, current abated taxes, a new insurance quote, 4% management and reserves, in-place NOI is about $400,496.

blocks.q: The lender requires a 1.25 DSCR on in-place NOI of $400,496 and quotes a 7.39% mortgage constant. About how large a loan will it make?
c: About $8,250,000, which is 75% of the asking price
About $8,164,000, which is based on the pro forma NOI
About $5,420,000, which is the loan at a 1.0 DSCR
blocks.x: Maximum debt service = $400,496 / 1.25 = $320,397. Maximum loan = $320,397 / 0.0739 = about $4,336,000, only 39% of the asking price and 51% of Jordan's value. Choice A assumes LTV controls, but on a building this vacant, coverage binds first. Choice B is what a lender would lend on the OM's numbers, which no lender will use. Evelyn would need far more equity than a stabilized building requires.

blocks.html: This is the hidden cost of buying a leasing project at a stabilized price. At $11,000,000, Evelyn would put in about $6.7 million of her own cash, earn a thin return until both floors are leased, and carry the leasing risk herself.

blocks.q: What cap rate does the $11,000,000 asking price represent on in-place NOI of $400,496?
c: About 3.6%
About 6.9%, the OM's cover figure
About 5.1%, on stabilized NOI
About 27.5%, the price over NOI
blocks.x: $400,496 / $11,000,000 = 3.64%. That is what the building earns on the asking price today. 6.9% is the pro forma rate on the cover. 5.1% is Jordan's stabilized NOI over the asking price ($562,648 / $11,000,000), better but still below the market's 6.0% to 6.5%. Choice D inverts the formula into a multiplier. The gap between 3.6% and 6.9% is the leasing risk the OM assumed away.

blocks.html: Jordan puts the three NOIs on one page for Evelyn, because the whole case comes down to the distance between them. In-place NOI, about $400,000, is what the building earns today and what the bank will lend against. Stabilized NOI, about $563,000, is what it should earn once both floors and the store are leased at market and the abatement is gone. Pro forma NOI, about $754,000, is the seller's best case. A fair price pays for the first, credits the buyer for the work and risk of reaching the second, and pays nothing for the third.

The last page of the OM reads: "All information is from sources deemed reliable but is not guaranteed. Prospective purchasers should conduct their own investigation." When Jordan tells the listing broker about the abatement footnote, the broker answers, "We disclosed it. It's in the book." When Jordan asks about the bank's review of the branch, the broker says he heard about it "in passing" a month ago.

blocks.q: The listing broker knew the bank was reviewing the branch but left it out of the OM, which shows the bank renewing at $72.50. Does the "deemed reliable" disclaimer protect him?
c: No, a disclaimer does not excuse a known misstatement
Yes, since the disclaimer puts verification on the buyer
Yes, since commercial buyers are presumed to be sophisticated
No, since OMs need approval from the Department of State
blocks.x: A disclaimer can limit reliance on information the broker had no reason to doubt. It does not license presenting a renewal the broker knows is in doubt, and a licensee who misrepresents material facts risks discipline under RPL 441-c and civil liability. Choice C overstates the defense: sophistication may matter in court, but it does not make a known misstatement acceptable. DOS does not pre-approve OMs.

blocks.title: The cover cap rate
blocks.html: An OM's headline cap rate is almost always computed on pro forma NOI and the asking price. Treat it as a marketing figure. The useful numbers are the in-place NOI (what the building earns today), the stabilized NOI you build yourself (what it should earn once leased at market), and the cost to get from one to the other.

Evelyn offers $8,500,000, with a 45-day due diligence period, tenant estoppel certificates from all three office tenants and the bank, and a seller representation that the rent roll and leases in the data room are complete. The seller rejects it. Three months later, after the bank confirms it will close the branch and the architecture firm gives notice, the listing broker calls Jordan back. The building trades to Evelyn in the spring for $8,350,000, with both leasing problems now priced in. Diane frames the cover page of the OM and hangs it in the conference room. Underneath, in Jordan's handwriting: "6.9%?"

items: An offering memorandum is advocacy: start with the T-12, the certified rent roll and the leases, not the pro forma column.
Stabilized NOI puts every space at market rent, with a vacancy allowance that fits the rollover risk; leases expiring soon are risk before they are upside.
Check every tax abatement's phase-out schedule and use the unabated tax for stabilized NOI.
Value = stabilized NOI / market cap rate, minus one-time lease-up costs such as downtime, tenant improvements and commissions.
Lenders size loans on in-place income, so a building with vacancy and rollover needs much more equity than its stabilized value suggests.
A "deemed reliable" disclaimer does not protect a licensee who knowingly presents misleading information.

lessons.title: Case file: The Escalation Audit on Varick Avenue
lessons.tagline: A Brooklyn loft building priced on its rent roll. Four lease clauses, one billing worksheet and a sculptor on the fifth floor say the rent roll is wrong.
objectives: Calculate porter's wage, CPI, base-year and expense stop escalations from the lease language and find billing errors
Decide how estoppels, billing deadlines, tax refunds and year-end reconciliations are handled between seller and buyer
Apply rent inclusion electricity and an occupied "vacant" loft floor to a buyer's underwriting
Calculate the price effect of corrected income using the income capitalization formula

blocks.title: Varick Avenue, East Williamsburg
blocks.html: Evelyn Park has signed a contract to buy a five-story 1920s loft building on Varick Avenue in East Williamsburg for $15,500,000. Each floor is 10,000 rentable square feet of open space with freight elevator access, and four of the five are leased to a millwork shop, a photo studio, an architecture firm and a garment manufacturer. The seller's broker priced it at a 6.5% cap rate, using a rent roll that shows $1,330,500 of rent and escalations in place and a pro forma that leases the empty fifth floor in year one. Evelyn's deposit of $775,000 becomes nonrefundable when her 45-day due diligence period ends on October 30. Hudson & Hart represents her, and Diane has assigned Jordan the job buyers most often rush: reading every lease and checking every escalation the seller has been billing. Priya will review the legal terms. Jordan's first file is the ground floor.

The rent roll is the seller's summary of the leases. The leases are the contract. When the two disagree, the leases win, and the buyer inherits whatever the seller got wrong: overbilled tenants who can claim refunds, underbilled income nobody collected, and clauses the seller forgot existed. On a building priced at a 6.5% cap rate, every $1 of annual income the rent roll overstates is about $15.38 of price, so the audit pays for itself quickly.

Kessler Millwork has built cabinets on the ground floor since 1998. Its current lease, a 2019 renewal, runs to 2029 at a base rent of $26.00 per RSF with a porter's wage escalation carried over from the original 1998 lease. The rent roll shows $61,000 a year of porter's wage escalation on top of $260,000 of base rent.

blocks.title: Kessler lease, Article 31 (abstract)
blocks.html:
Additional rent: for each one cent ($0.01) by which the regular hourly wage rate of porters under the building service workers' commercial contract exceeds the rate in effect on January 1, 2019, Tenant pays one cent ($0.01) per rentable square foot per year.
Rate on January 1, 2019: $27.40
Rate in effect now: $31.15
Seller's billing worksheet: "Total hourly porter cost, wages plus benefits, up $6.10 since 2019. $6.10 x 10,000 = $61,000."

blocks.q: What porter's wage escalation does the Kessler lease support for this year?
blocks.x: The clause measures the regular hourly wage, not wages plus fringe benefits. The wage rose $3.75 ($31.15 minus $27.40), and the penny-for-penny multiplier of 1 gives $3.75 x 10,000 RSF = $37,500. The $61,000 figure is the seller's error: benefits rose faster than wages, and the lease does not reach them. $3,750 drops a zero, and $45,000 applies a 1.2 multiplier the lease does not contain.

blocks.html: The seller has overbilled Kessler $23,500 a year. Jordan pulls the payment history: Kessler has paid every bill without question since 2023, when the seller's new bookkeeper started using the benefits figure. That is not good news. A tenant who paid an amount the lease did not require can demand it back, and Kessler's owner, Abe Kessler, is the kind of tenant who reads his mail eventually. Jordan flags the overcharge for Priya and moves the income to the correct $37,500 in Evelyn's model.

The Kessler file has one more line Evelyn needs to see. The lease includes electricity in the rent: Kessler pays no separate electric bill, and the 1998 lease assumed lighting and a few saws. Today the shop runs a dust collection system, two CNC routers and a spray booth. Con Edison bills the building's master meter, and the seller has been absorbing the difference.

blocks.q: Kessler's electricity is a rent inclusion with no survey or adjustment clause. What does that mean for Evelyn's underwriting?
c: Kessler starts paying Con Edison directly once the building sells
The rising electric cost is hers to carry as an operating expense
Evelyn can bill the excess usage as an escalation under Article 31
The cost passes to the other tenants through their operating base
blocks.x: Under rent inclusion, electricity is part of the rent, so a heavy user costs the landlord money and the lease gives Evelyn no tool to recover it until 2029. She must model the actual electric cost as an expense. The Article 31 answer is the trap: a porter's wage clause reaches wages only. Many rent inclusion leases include periodic electrical surveys to reset the charge; this one does not, which is a reason to lower the price, not a billing opportunity.

blocks.html: Evelyn is already thinking about 2029, when Kessler's lease ends. She wants the renewal to stop the building from paying for a factory's power without forcing the tenant to open its own utility account, which in an old loft can mean new service equipment. Jordan lays out the three ways New York commercial leases handle electricity.

blocks.q: Which arrangement lets the landlord keep one master utility account while charging Kessler for the power it actually uses?
c: A submeter on the floor, billed at the measured usage
A rent inclusion reset every year by an electrical survey
A direct meter in Kessler's name, billed by Con Edison
A higher fixed rent inclusion charge per RSF at renewal
blocks.x: With a submeter, the landlord buys power through its own master meter and bills each tenant for the usage the submeter measures, often plus an administrative charge. A direct meter shifts the account to the tenant entirely, which Evelyn wants to avoid here. Rent inclusion, even with surveys or a higher charge, still estimates usage instead of measuring it, so a busy shop can outrun the estimate between resets.

blocks.html: Halcyon Studios rents the second floor for film and photo shoots. Its lease uses a CPI escalation: each January the base rent rises by the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for the New York metro area over the prior year, but by no less than 2% and no more than 4%. Halcyon's 2025 rent was $330,000. The rent roll shows $343,200 for 2026, a 4% increase. Jordan pulls the index the lease names: it rose 2.9%.

blocks.q: What should Halcyon's 2026 rent be?
blocks.x: The CPI changed 2.9%, which falls between the 2% floor and the 4% cap, so the increase is 2.9%: $330,000 x 1.029 = $339,570. The seller applied the cap as if it were the increase. A cap is a ceiling the escalation cannot exceed, and a floor is the minimum, used only when the index rises less than 2%. $336,600 applies the 2% floor.

blocks.html: The question is not academic, because Halcyon's estoppel certificate comes back the next week. The contract requires the seller to deliver estoppels from every tenant, and Priya's draft form asks each tenant to state its current annual rent. Halcyon writes $339,570, adds that it "has paid the 2026 increase under protest," and attaches its own CPI calculation.

blocks.q: The rent roll says $343,200 and Halcyon's estoppel says $339,570. Which figure should Evelyn underwrite, and why?
c: $343,200, since the seller warranted the rent roll in the contract
The average, $341,385, until the parties settle the difference
$343,200, since the tenant has already paid the higher amount
$339,570, since the tenant's signed statement binds both sides
blocks.x: An estoppel protects a buyer because the tenant cannot later contradict it against someone who relied on it. It also works the other way in practice: Evelyn cannot expect Halcyon to keep paying an amount it has disputed in writing, and the lease supports Halcyon. The seller's warranty gives Evelyn a claim against the seller, not a higher rent. The paid-under-protest answer is the trap: payment under protest preserves the tenant's refund claim.

blocks.title: Caps, floors and stops are not the answer
blocks.html: The most common escalation error on a rent roll is treating the limit in a clause as the result. A 4% cap means "up to 4%," a 2% floor means "at least 2%," and an expense stop is the point above which the tenant starts paying, not what the tenant pays. Always run the formula, then apply the limits. Exam questions use the same trick: they give the cap and the index change and ask for the increase.

Ortega + Lin Architects signed a ten-year lease in 2021 at $34.00 per RSF, with a real estate tax escalation over the 2021/22 tax year and a direct operating escalation over calendar 2021. The lease defines the tenant's proportionate share as "10,000 RSF divided by the 50,000 RSF of the building." The seller's escalation statement for this year uses 25%.

head: Item
Base
Current
Increase
blocks.caption: Ortega + Lin escalation statement, as the seller prepared it.

blocks.q: What escalation does the Ortega + Lin lease support for this year?
blocks.x: The lease fixes the share at 10,000 / 50,000 = 20%, and 20% of the $118,000 increase is $23,600. The seller's 25% divides by 40,000 RSF, the four leased floors, which shifts the vacant floor's share onto the tenants. Unless a lease says expenses are shared among occupied space, the denominator is the building. $11,200 counts the tax increase alone.

blocks.html: The seller has billed the architects $5,900 a year too much since 2024, when the vacancy began. Their lease gives them the right to audit the landlord's escalation statements within two years after each statement is delivered, and to a refund of any overcharge. Kessler's overbilling raises the same question at four times the size.

blocks.q: The overcharges to Kessler and Ortega + Lin happened before closing. How should the contract deal with them?
c: Make the seller responsible, with a credit or escrow at closing
Leave them with Evelyn, since the leases transfer to her at closing
Ignore them, since tenants who paid without objection waived refunds
Split them between the parties in proportion to the price paid
blocks.x: The seller collected the money, so the seller should repay it. Because tenants usually pursue the current landlord, Priya asks for a closing credit for the known overcharges and an escrow holdback for any later claims for the seller's period. Leaving them with Evelyn is the trap: the leases do transfer, which is exactly why she needs the contract to put the cost back on the seller. Paying a bill is not a waiver when the lease gives an audit right.

blocks.html: Brightline Apparel cuts and sews on the fourth floor under a 2024 lease that started at $28.00 per RSF with 3% annual increases and an expense stop of $10.00 per RSF for operating expenses and real estate taxes combined. In 2025 those costs totaled $600,000 for the building, or $12.00 per RSF. The rent roll shows no escalation income from Brightline at all. The seller never billed it.

blocks.q: What does the expense stop produce from Brightline for 2025?
blocks.x: Expenses were $12.00 per RSF against a $10.00 stop, so Brightline owes the $2.00 excess on its 10,000 RSF: $20,000. $120,000 charges Brightline the full $12.00, and $100,000 confuses the stop with the payment; under a stop, the landlord absorbs costs up to $10.00 and the tenant pays only above it. $4,000 is the 20% share of the excess, applying a base-year method to a stop clause.

blocks.html: Brightline's lease adds a condition common in New York leases: the landlord must deliver each year's escalation statement within 12 months after the year ends, or the escalation for that year is waived. The seller's 2024 statement was due by December 31, 2025, and was never sent. The 2025 statement is still good until December 31, 2026.

blocks.q: Evelyn closes in late November 2026. Which Brightline escalations can still be collected?
c: 2024 and 2025, since a buyer is not bound by the seller's delays
2025 and later years, but 2024 is waived under the lease
2024 through 2026, with interest, under the statute of limitations
Nothing for past years, since an unbilled escalation is lost at a sale
blocks.x: The billing deadline is a lease condition, and the landlord's interest passes to Evelyn subject to the lease. The 2024 escalation died on December 31, 2025. 2025 can still be billed if someone sends the statement before the end of 2026. The statute of limitations answer is the trap: a contractual waiver works before any limitations period matters. A sale does not erase a billable escalation.

blocks.html: Jordan adds a line to the closing checklist: the seller sends Brightline's 2025 statement before closing, and the contract credits the seller with whatever is collected for its period. Going forward, Evelyn's model adds $20,000 a year of stop income, subject to actual expenses. Brightline's base rent also needs a correction. The rent roll lists the 2026 rate as $29.68, the result of adding 3% of the starting rent each year ($0.84 twice). The lease compounds, so the 2026 rate is $28.00 x 1.03 x 1.03 = $29.71, and the 2027 rate will be $30.60. The difference is small this year and grows every year after.

blocks.text: Floor 5: the vacant floor that is not vacant

blocks.html: The rent roll lists the fifth floor as "vacant, available," and the seller's offering memo counts $340,000 of new rent on it in Evelyn's first year. Jordan walks the floor with the super on October 14. Behind a plywood wall at the north end there is a bed, a hot plate, a shower built into a former slop sink closet and a sculptor named Teo, who says the prior tenant's owner let him stay when the company moved out at the end of 2023. He has paid the super $1,800 a month in cash since early 2025. The building is zoned for manufacturing, and its certificate of occupancy does not permit residential use.

blocks.q: How should Evelyn treat the fifth floor before her due diligence period ends?
c: As vacant, with the locks changed the day after the closing
As occupied, with removal by court process the seller has to finish
As a protected loft tenancy, since he is living in a loft building
As vacant, since an illegal residential use has no legal protection
blocks.x: Whatever his status, Teo is in possession, and an owner who removes an occupant without a court order risks unlawful eviction liability. Priya demands that the seller deliver the floor vacant, with possession recovered through court, or give a credit and escrow large enough to cover the time and legal cost. The illegal-use answer is the trap: an occupancy can violate zoning and still require court process to end.

blocks.title: The Loft Law
blocks.html: New York City's Loft Law (Multiple Dwelling Law Article 7-C) protects residential occupants of certain former manufacturing and commercial buildings, called interim multiple dwellings, and is administered by the NYC Loft Board. Coverage generally requires three or more units occupied residentially by separate households during periods the law specifies. One sculptor behind a plywood wall probably does not make Varick Avenue a covered building, but a buyer's attorney checks Loft Board records for every loft building, because a covered building must be brought up to residential code and its units come under rent regulation.

blocks.q: Which fact would turn the Loft Law into a serious issue for Evelyn's purchase?
c: One occupant paying rent in cash to the super for more than a year
Any residential use whatsoever in a building zoned for manufacturing
A residential occupant who has stayed in the space over 30 days
Three or more households living there during a covered period
blocks.x: Loft Law coverage turns on the building: generally three or more units occupied residentially by separate households during the periods the statute sets. Teo alone does not meet it. The 30-day answer is the trap: that length of stay matters for the unlawful eviction rules, which require court process, not for Loft Law coverage. Illegal residential use and cash rent are problems of their own, but they do not create coverage.

blocks.html: The seller agrees to a $400,000 holdback in escrow: a year of the projected fifth-floor rent plus legal costs, released as possession is recovered. Teo, it turns out, has a lease of his own in Ridgewood he has not been using and leaves in January after a stipulation in Housing Court. The super is no longer the super.

blocks.text: The tax refund and the year-end true-up

blocks.html: Two more pieces of money cross the closing date. First, the seller's tax certiorari case for the 2024/25 tax year settles with the NYC Tax Commission for a $40,000 refund, expected after closing. The Ortega + Lin lease requires the landlord to credit the tenant its share of any tax refund for a year in which it paid tax escalations, less the landlord's reasonable costs of getting the refund.

blocks.q: Who is entitled to the $40,000 refund, ignoring the cost of the case?
c: Evelyn, because refunds follow the property to the new owner
The seller, in full, because the refund covers its ownership period
Ortega + Lin, in full, since the refund lowers its tax escalation
The seller, less $8,000 owed to Ortega + Lin as its 20% share
blocks.x: The refund covers a year the seller owned the building, so it is the seller's money, minus the share the lease says belongs to the tenant: 20% of $40,000 = $8,000. Because the lease obligation now rests with Evelyn as landlord, the contract has the seller pay or credit the tenant's share so the architects do not come to her for it. The full-refund-to-seller answer forgets the lease.

blocks.html: Second, the 2026 escalations. Tenants pay estimated escalations monthly during the year, and the landlord reconciles against actual expenses after the year closes. The 2026 reconciliation will be done by Evelyn in early 2027, covering a year the seller owned for eleven months.

blocks.q: The 2026 reconciliation in March 2027 shows tenants owe an additional $18,000 for the year. Who gets it?
c: Evelyn in full, since she is the landlord when it is collected
The seller in full, since most of the year was the seller's
Split by days of ownership under a re-proration clause
Neither, since estimates paid during the year are final
blocks.x: Escalations accrue over the year, so the true-up is prorated between seller and buyer by days of ownership, which is why commercial contracts include a re-proration clause that survives closing. Evelyn bills and collects, keeps her share and remits the seller's. The collector-takes-all answer is the trap: who sends the bill does not decide whose money it is.

head: Finding
Annual income effect
rows: Floor 1: porter's wage billed on wages plus benefits
Floor 2: CPI cap applied instead of the 2.9% index change
Floor 3: share billed at 25% instead of 20%
Floor 4: fixed increases compounded, not simple
Net change to income in place
blocks.caption: The audit, in one column. The fifth floor and the electricity are handled separately.

blocks.q: Evelyn underwrites at a 6.5% cap rate. What price reduction does the net $12,730 income correction support?
c: About $12,730
About $19,585
blocks.x: Value = income / rate, so $12,730 / 0.065 = about $195,846. A dollar of lost annual income costs about $15.38 of value at a 6.5% cap. $12,730 treats a permanent income loss as a one-time cost. $19,585 misplaces the decimal, dividing by 0.65. $508,200 subtracts only the three overbillings ($33,030 / 0.065) and ignores the stop income the audit found.

blocks.html: Evelyn adds the electricity. Kessler's real electric cost runs about $14,000 a year more than the seller's statement shows, which at 6.5% is about $215,000 of value. On October 28, two days before her deposit goes hard, she asks for $410,000 off the price plus the $400,000 fifth-floor escrow, closing credits for the Kessler and Ortega + Lin overcharges, and an assignment of the seller's rights to collect Brightline's 2025 escalation for the seller's account. The seller agrees to $375,000 off and everything else. The building closes on November 30 at $15,125,000.

Diane's comment on the file is about where the money was hiding. None of it was in the cap rate, the market or the condition of the roof. It was in four lease clauses and one billing worksheet, read carefully by the most junior person on the deal.

items: Underwrite the leases, not the rent roll: recompute every escalation from the clause and its defined terms before the due diligence period ends.
Porter's wage: wage increase x multiplier x RSF, using exactly the wage the lease names. CPI: apply the index change, then the floor and cap. Fixed increases usually compound.
Base-year escalations use the proportionate share the lease defines, normally the tenant's RSF over the building's; an expense stop charges only the cost above the stop.

Estoppels bind the tenant to what it states; billing deadlines in a lease can waive escalations; overbilling for the seller's period belongs to the seller through credits, escrows and re-proration clauses.
Electricity under rent inclusion and an occupant in a "vacant" loft are costs to underwrite: removal takes court process, and the Loft Law needs checking in any converted manufacturing building.
Every $1 of permanent annual income lost is worth income / cap rate in price: about $15.38 at a 6.5% cap.

roleplays.title: The Bushwick Setup
roleplays.setting: A mixed-use building in Bushwick: six apartments over two stores, listed at $3,400,000
roleplays.you: Jordan, the buyer's broker for Evelyn Park
roleplays.goal: Reconstruct the numbers, price the building off market cap rates, spot negative leverage, follow NY disclosure rules, and protect Evelyn's confidential limits.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play a smooth listing broker for a Bushwick mixed-use building (6 apartments, 2 stores) asking $3.4M. Push a pro forma NOI of $230,000 and a 5.5 cap, and claim the building never has vacancy. Actual reconstructed NOI is $190,000; comps trade at 6.0% to 6.5%. As Evelyn, ask what belongs in NOI, what to offer, whether the $2M loan at $150,000 a year makes sense, and whether the lender's 1.25 DCR is met. Later, play Marcus suggesting the anti-discrimination form can be skipped for commercial, then ask broker-to-broker for the buyer's top number. The learner represents the buyer and must: reconstruct NOI (vacancy, management, no capital items, depreciation or debt service), value with V = I / R from comps, identify negative leverage (7.5% constant vs 6.33% return), insist on the NYS anti-discrimination form and on estoppels, and keep the client's limits confidential. Grade each item and give one line of advice.

stores: a cafe and a hair salon
a pharmacy and a pizza shop
a hardware store and a nail salon

opening: {day} on {street}. Six apartments over {stores}, asking $3,400,000. The listing broker, {client}, hands Evelyn a glossy package.
Evelyn Park wants a Bushwick mixed-use building. This one on {street} has six apartments over {stores}. {client} is already talking cap rates.
You and Evelyn tour the {street} building with {client}: six units upstairs, {stores} below, asking $3.4 million.

say: Here's the package. Pro forma NOI is $230,000 once both stores go to market rent. At a 5.5 cap that's over $4 million. At $3.4 million, she's stealing it.
Look at the pro forma: $230,000 NOI at market rents. Even at a 5.5 cap you're buying under value.

moves.text: Thanks. We'll underwrite actual rents, with vacancy and management. Send the rent roll and the leases.
moves.fb: Right. A pro forma is the seller's forecast. Investors value on a reconstructed statement built from actual leases and bills.
moves.react: Sure, I'll send the rent roll. The pro forma is still the story, though.

moves.text: Pro forma is a forecast. We value what it earns today, from the leases and two years of bills.
moves.fb: Correct. Value comes from actual, reconstructed NOI, not projected rents.

moves.text: Pro forma seems aggressive. Let's just knock 10% off it and call that our NOI for the offer, then.
moves.fb: Better than accepting it, but a guess is not a reconstruction. Build NOI line by line from actual income and expenses.
moves.react: Ten percent off is fair. $207,000 then.

moves.text: Over $4 million? I'll tell Evelyn it's a steal. We should offer full price before someone else does.
moves.fb: You just valued a building on the seller's projected rents and an unsupported cap rate.

moves.text: We'll use the pro forma, but at a 6.25 cap instead of 5.5. That fixes the problem with the number.
moves.fb: Fixing the cap rate doesn't fix the income. Projected rents still inflate the value.

moves.text: Pro forma is the standard basis for commercial offers in New York, so we'll start from that number.
moves.fb: The standard is a reconstructed operating statement from actual figures. Pro forma is a projection.
moves.react: Exactly. Glad you know the market.

say: Evelyn: "The seller's statement includes a new roof, mortgage interest, depreciation, and no management fee. Fix it."
Evelyn: "Clean up this operating statement for me. What comes out, what goes in?"

moves.text: Take out the roof, interest and depreciation. Add vacancy and management, self-managed or not.
moves.fb: Correct. NOI excludes capital items, debt service and depreciation; a reconstructed statement adds market vacancy and management.
moves.react: Good. That's how I'd do it.

moves.text: The roof is capital, interest is debt service, depreciation is the tax world. None of it goes into NOI.
moves.fb: Right. Capital items, debt service and depreciation never belong in NOI.

moves.text: Take out the roof and interest, but leave the rest. The seller's numbers are probably close enough.
moves.fb: Partly right. You missed depreciation and the missing management fee and vacancy allowance.
moves.react: Probably close? I don't pay for probably.

moves.text: Keep mortgage interest in. It's a real cost of owning, so it belongs in operating expenses.
moves.fb: Debt service is never an operating expense. NOI is calculated before financing.
moves.react: That's my lender's business, not the building's.

moves.text: Leave depreciation in. It lowers NOI, which gives us more leverage to argue the price down further.
moves.fb: Depreciation is a tax concept, not an operating expense. Using it to shave NOI is just wrong math.
moves.react: That's not how NOI works, Jordan.

moves.text: Skip the management fee. He self-manages, so there's no actual cost to put in our statement at all.
moves.fb: A reconstructed statement includes management at market, since a buyer will pay for it.

say: Evelyn: "Reconstructed NOI is $190,000. Three comps sold at 6.0%, 6.25% and 6.5%. What do we offer?"
Evelyn: "$190,000 NOI, comps at 6 to 6.5. Give me a number."

moves.text: It's average for comps, so 6.25%: $190,000 / 0.0625 = $3,040,000. Open near $2.95 million.
moves.fb: Correct IRV math with a cap rate from the market. The asking price implies 5.59%, below every comp.

moves.text: At 6.25%, value is $3.04 million. The ask implies a 5.59% cap, below every comp. I'd open at $2.95.
moves.fb: Right. V = I / R, with R chosen to fit the subject, and the ask checked against the comps.

moves.text: Use the best comp, 6%. That's about $3.17 million. It keeps the seller happy and the deal alive.
moves.fb: Math is right, but picking the most seller-friendly comp is not how you represent the buyer.

moves.text: Offer the full $3.4 million so we don't lose it. Good buildings in Bushwick don't last a week.
moves.fb: $190,000 / $3,400,000 is a 5.59% cap, well under every comp. You'd overpay about $360,000.

moves.text: $190,000 x 0.0625 is $11,875, so the building is worth about $1.19 million at that rate.
moves.fb: Wrong operation. Value = income divided by rate, not multiplied: $190,000 / 0.0625 = $3,040,000.

moves.text: Average the three caps to 6.25% and average that with the 5.5 pro forma cap: 5.875%, so $3.23 million.
moves.fb: Blending in the seller's pro forma cap isn't market evidence. Use the comps.
moves.react: Why is the seller's number in my math?

say: Evelyn: "My lender offers $2 million with $150,000 a year of debt service. At $3 million the building earns 6.33% free and clear. Take it as is?"
Evelyn: "$2 million loan, $150,000 a year. Building yields 6.33% at our price. Good loan?"

moves.text: The constant is 7.5%, above the building's 6.33%. That's negative leverage: cash on cash is only 4%.
moves.fb: Exactly. When debt costs more than the property earns, borrowing lowers the return on equity.
moves.react: Four percent. I can do better in bonds.

moves.text: Debt costs 7.5% and the building returns 6.33%. Each borrowed dollar loses money. Negotiate.
moves.fb: Right. Compare the mortgage constant to the free-and-clear return.
moves.react: Then we push the price or the rate.

moves.text: It's a normal loan for this market. The rate is the rate, so I'd just take it and close quickly.
moves.fb: You skipped the analysis. Compare the loan constant to the property's return.
moves.react: Normal isn't the same as smart.

moves.text: Borrow as much as possible. Leverage always boosts returns on equity, in any market, every time.
moves.fb: Leverage magnifies in both directions. At a 7.5% constant against 6.33%, each borrowed dollar loses money.

moves.text: Cash on cash is NOI over the price: $190,000 over $3 million, 6.33%. The loan doesn't change it.
moves.fb: Cash on cash is before-tax cash flow over equity: $40,000 / $1,000,000 = 4%.
moves.react: That's the cap rate, not my return.

moves.text: The constant is $150,000 over $3 million, 5%, below the 6.33% return, so the leverage here is positive.
moves.fb: The constant is debt service over the loan amount: $150,000 / $2,000,000 = 7.5%.
moves.react: Over the loan, not the price.

say: Marcus: "Quick tip. Don't bother giving Evelyn that fair housing disclosure form. This is commercial. Nobody does it."
Marcus, in passing: "Skip the anti-discrimination form on commercial deals. Total waste of paper."

moves.text: The anti-discrimination form covers every property type. She got it at our first meeting.
moves.fb: Correct. RPL 443 agency disclosure is for residential 1 to 4 family, but the anti-discrimination form applies to all property types.

moves.text: You're thinking of the agency form. The anti-discrimination form applies to commercial deals too.
moves.fb: Right. 19 NYCRR 175.28 covers all property types, including vacant land and commercial.

moves.text: I'll give it to her anyway, just to be extra safe. It can't hurt to hand her just one more form, right?
moves.fb: Right action, wrong reason: it's required, not optional.

moves.text: Good to know, I'll skip it, then. Commercial buyers don't need any fair housing paperwork in New York.
moves.fb: Wrong. The anti-discrimination disclosure applies to commercial deals too.

moves.text: Right, commercial only needs the RPL 443 agency disclosure, not the anti-discrimination form, Marcus.
moves.fb: Backwards. RPL 443 is residential; the anti-discrimination form covers commercial.

moves.text: I'll skip it unless the building has apartments. It's six units, so I'd only need it for those.
moves.fb: The form applies to every property type, residential or not.

say: Off the record, broker to broker. What's her real top number? Save us both some time.
Come on, between us. How high will Evelyn go?

moves.text: I can't share my client's limits. Our offer is $2,950,000, 30 days due diligence, tenant estoppels.
moves.fb: Confidentiality is a fiduciary duty. Estoppel certificates protect Evelyn by confirming every lease.
moves.react: Worth a try. I'll take it to the seller.

moves.text: No off the record about my client's money. Here's our offer in writing, with estoppels before closing.
moves.fb: Correct. A buyer's agent gives away nothing about the client's limits.

moves.text: She's flexible if the seller is flexible too. Let's see how the seller takes our first number.
moves.fb: Not a direct breach, but it signals room to move.

moves.text: Just between us, she'll go to $3.1 million. So let's not waste our time with counteroffers below that one.
moves.fb: A breach of loyalty and confidentiality. You just handed the seller your client's ceiling.

moves.text: Her top number is confidential, but I'd say don't counter below $3 million if you want the deal.
moves.fb: That's revealing her range by another name. Say nothing about her limits.

moves.text: I'll tell you her number if you tell me the seller's bottom line. Fair trade between brokers.
moves.fb: Trading your client's confidential limit breaches your duty to Evelyn.

say: Don't deduct vacancy. This building has been 100% full for ten years.
No vacancy allowance, please. These tenants never leave.

moves.text: Buyers underwrite market vacancy and credit loss anyway. Ten good years don't promise the next ten.
moves.fb: Correct. A reconstructed statement includes vacancy and credit loss to reach EGI.
moves.react: Your call. It's still a great building.

moves.text: We'll use market vacancy, maybe 5%. Lenders do the same thing, so it's the realistic number.
moves.fb: Right. PGI minus vacancy and credit loss plus other income equals EGI.

moves.text: Okay, we'll use 1% instead of 5%. That splits the difference with you and keeps it moving.
moves.fb: Splitting the difference isn't analysis. Use market vacancy.

moves.text: Sure, no vacancy then. If it's been full for ten years, it will stay full for the next ten too.
moves.fb: Overstates income and value. Underwrite market vacancy and credit loss.
moves.react: That's what I like to hear.

moves.text: Vacancy only applies to the stores. Apartments in the city never sit empty, so skip it there.
moves.fb: Residential units turn over too. Apply vacancy to the whole rent roll.

moves.text: We'll skip vacancy but double the management fee to make up for it. Same thing in the end.
moves.fb: Mixing up line items hides the assumptions. Show vacancy and management separately.

say: Seller won't do tenant estoppels. Says the leases speak for themselves.
Estoppels? Too much hassle. The leases are in the data room.

moves.text: Estoppels confirm rent, deposits and defaults straight from tenants. We need them before closing.
moves.fb: Correct. An estoppel certificate has the tenant certify lease facts, which a buyer can rely on.

moves.text: Leases don't show side deals or defaults. Tenant estoppels do. That's a condition of our offer.
moves.fb: Right. Estoppels protect the buyer against undisclosed amendments and disputes.

moves.text: Fine, we'll skip them, but ask the seller to sign a statement that the leases are complete.
moves.fb: A seller statement helps, but it isn't the tenant's own certification.

moves.text: No problem. Leases are recorded with the city, so we can rely on the public record instead.
moves.fb: Most leases aren't recorded, and the record wouldn't show defaults or side deals.

moves.text: We'll skip them and get an SNDA instead. That covers the same lease facts for the buyer.
moves.fb: An SNDA is between tenant and lender about foreclosure. It doesn't certify lease facts to a buyer.

moves.text: Estoppels are only for office buildings over 50,000 square feet. Mixed-use deals like this skip them.
moves.fb: No such rule. Estoppels are standard in commercial and mixed-use deals.

say: Evelyn: "Lender wants a debt coverage ratio of 1.25. NOI $190,000, debt service $150,000. Do we pass?"
Evelyn: "Do we clear a 1.25 DCR with this loan?"

moves.text: $190,000 / $150,000 is about 1.27. We pass, barely. Any slip puts us under.
moves.fb: Correct. DCR = NOI / debt service. Above 1.0 means NOI covers the loan; the lender wants 1.25.

moves.text: DCR is 1.27, just over 1.25. A smaller loan or lower rate would give us more cushion.
moves.fb: Right math and a useful next step.

moves.text: We probably pass. The lender will run it anyway, so I wouldn't worry too much about it now.
moves.fb: You can compute it in seconds: 1.27.

moves.text: $150,000 / $190,000 is 0.79, so we fail. The NOI doesn't cover debt at all here.
moves.fb: Inverted. DCR = NOI / debt service = 1.27.
moves.react: We fail? Then why are we here?

moves.text: DCR uses the purchase price: $3 million / $2 million is 1.5, so we pass easily.
moves.fb: That's a price-to-loan ratio. DCR = NOI / debt service.

moves.text: DCR is NOI minus debt service, $40,000, which is way above 1.25, so we're fine.
moves.fb: That's before-tax cash flow, not a ratio. DCR = 1.27.

say: Evelyn: "Can I depreciate the building over 27.5 years like an apartment house?"
Evelyn: "Is this 27.5 or 39 for depreciation?"

moves.text: Only if 80% or more of rent comes from the apartments. Otherwise 39. Your CPA should confirm.
moves.fb: Correct. Mixed use is residential rental property only if 80%+ of gross rents come from dwelling units.
moves.react: I'll have my CPA run the split.

moves.text: It depends on the rent split: 80% or more from dwellings means 27.5. Land is never depreciated.
moves.fb: Right rule, and the specifics go to her tax advisor.

moves.text: I'd guess 27.5, since it's mostly apartments. Your accountant can tell you for sure later.
moves.fb: Guessing without the 80% test. Name the rule, then refer.

moves.text: 27.5 years, and you can depreciate the land too, since it's part of the purchase price.
moves.fb: Land is never depreciated.

moves.text: 39 years, always. Any building with a store in it counts as fully commercial for depreciation purposes.
moves.fb: Not always. If 80%+ of gross rents are residential, it's 27.5.

moves.text: Neither. Mixed-use buildings can't be depreciated at all until the stores are converted to housing.
moves.fb: Mixed-use buildings are depreciable, at 27.5 or 39 years depending on the rent split.

roleplays.debrief: You practised investment underwriting: rebuild NOI from actual leases with vacancy and management, and keep capital items, debt service and depreciation out. Value = NOI / cap rate using the comps, and compare the mortgage constant to the property's return to spot negative leverage; DCR = NOI / debt service. The NYS anti-discrimination form applies to commercial deals (RPL 443 does not), estoppels confirm the leases, and your client's ceiling stays confidential.

roleplays.title: The Steinway Storefront
roleplays.setting: Sal Russo's six-unit building in Astoria, with a vacant ground-floor store on a busy block near Steinway Street
roleplays.you: Jordan, Sal's leasing agent for the store
roleplays.goal: Lease the store to a strong tenant on fair terms: comply with fair housing law for commercial space, get the percentage rent math right, and negotiate the use clause, guarantee, electricity and SNDA.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play two roles: Sal Russo, an old-school Astoria landlord who first hints he does not want to rent his storefront to a baker because of where she is from and later demands a full 10-year personal guarantee and wants to skip the disclosure form; and the baker, who is sharp and asks about percentage rent at 6% on $72,000 base with $1.5M sales, wants an 'any lawful use' clause, asks about sublet rights, tax escalations, electricity for heavy ovens, and fears losing her build-out in a foreclosure. The learner must refuse discrimination (NYS Human Rights Law covers commercial space), compute the natural breakpoint ($1.2M) and total rent ($90,000), negotiate a balanced use clause and good guy guarantee, use direct metering, explain proportionate-share escalations, and propose an SNDA. Grade each item and give one line of advice.
opening: {day}. Sal's empty store on {street} near Steinway Street has one serious applicant: {client}, who wants to open {bakery}.
{client} runs a successful wholesale bakery and wants a storefront for {bakery}. Sal's space on {street} is perfect. Sal is less sure.
Lease negotiations for Sal's {street} store start {day}. {client} brought a business plan, two years of tax returns, and a lot of questions.

say: Her numbers look good. But she's not from around here, if you know what I mean. My cousin knows people from the old country who want the space. Tell her it's taken.
{client}? Good credit, sure. But I'd rather rent to people from my own background. Say we have another offer.

moves.text: Sal, the Human Rights Law covers stores. I can't turn her down over national origin.
moves.fb: Right. The NYS Human Rights Law bars discrimination in commercial space, and licensees must refuse to take part.
moves.react: Okay, okay. Judge the business. Show me the plan.

moves.text: I won't. National origin is protected for stores too. Credit, experience and the plan decide.
moves.fb: Correct. Refuse, name the rule, and redirect to lawful criteria.
moves.react: Fine. If the plan's good, it's good.

moves.text: Let me think about how to handle it, Sal. Maybe we just wait and see if your cousin's people apply.
moves.fb: Stalling a qualified applicant for a discriminatory reason is still discrimination. Refuse clearly.

moves.text: I'll tell her another offer came in. Nobody can prove anything on a commercial lease anyway, Sal.
moves.fb: That's unlawful discrimination with a cover story. The licensee is liable along with the owner.

moves.text: Fair housing laws only cover apartments, Sal, so for the store you can pick whoever you want there.
moves.fb: The NYS Human Rights Law covers commercial real estate too.

moves.text: Let's raise her rent by 20%. If she leaves, problem solved, and it's all about the money.
moves.fb: Different terms because of national origin is discrimination, however it's dressed up.

say: I'll do $6,000 a month base, plus 6% of sales over the natural breakpoint. I project $1.5 million in sales by year two. What does that cost me?
Base $6,000 a month, 6% over the natural breakpoint, $1.5 million in sales. What's my total rent?

moves.fb: Correct. Natural breakpoint = base rent / percentage rate. Overage applies only above it.
moves.react: Ninety thousand. I can live with that.

moves.text: Your breakpoint is $1.2 million. Above it you pay $18,000 more: $90,000 a year at $1.5 million.
moves.fb: Right math, clearly explained.

moves.text: Roughly $90,000 a year, give or take. Your accountant can run the breakpoint math later.
moves.fb: Right ballpark, but this is exactly the math you should do on the spot.

moves.text: 6% of $1.5 million is $90,000 of percentage rent, plus the $72,000 base, so $162,000 total a year.
moves.fb: Double counting. Percentage rent applies only above the breakpoint. Total is $90,000.

moves.text: The breakpoint is $72,000 x 0.06 = $4,320, so you pay 6% on almost all sales, about $161,700 in all.
moves.fb: Wrong formula. Breakpoint = base rent / rate, not base x rate.

moves.text: Breakpoint is $6,000 / 0.06 = $100,000 a month, so you'd owe overage on any single month above that.
moves.fb: Using monthly figures can work only with monthly sales. Annual base and sales give $1.2 million.
moves.react: Monthly? That's not how I read it.

say: I want the use clause to say 'any lawful use,' so if I sell the business someday the buyer can do whatever.
Make the use clause wide open. Any lawful use. I want an exit.

moves.text: Sal does need some control. Bakery, cafe and food retail, with assignment on reasonable consent?
moves.fb: Balanced. A defined use protects the building's mix and CO; a reasonable consent standard gives the tenant an exit.
moves.react: That works if consent really is reasonable.

moves.text: A defined food use plus a reasonable consent standard for assignment gets you an exit.
moves.fb: Right. Both sides' interests in one clause.

moves.text: Sure, any lawful use is fine. It's easier to just agree and get the lease signed this week.
moves.fb: Legal, but weak for your client. A broad use could bring a smoky restaurant under Sal's apartments.

moves.text: No assignment or sublet, ever. Sal wants full control over who's in that store for 10 years.
moves.fb: Legal for a commercial lease (RPL 226-b is residential only), but it may scare off a good tenant.
moves.react: Then I'd have to think about it.

moves.text: Any lawful use, and Sal can't object to anything, since commercial tenants have full rights.
moves.fb: Commercial leases are negotiated; there's no default right to any use.

moves.text: The CO allows any use, so the clause doesn't really matter. Write whatever makes her happy.
moves.fb: COs limit use, and the clause matters for Sal's building and other tenants.

moves.text: Use clauses aren't enforceable in New York, so we'll leave it out. Saves everyone some time.
moves.fb: Use clauses are standard and enforceable in commercial leases.

say: Fine. But I want her husband to personally guarantee all ten years.
Ten-year lease, ten-year personal guarantee. That's my rule.

moves.text: A full guarantee may kill the deal. A good guy guarantee plus three months' security covers you.
moves.fb: Practical and protective. A good guy guarantee covers rent until the tenant surrenders the space with notice.
moves.react: Hm. If she leaves clean, I'm covered. Okay.

moves.text: A good guy guarantee covers you if she stops paying but won't leave. That's the big risk.
moves.fb: Right. You advise on the trade-off and protect the client.

moves.text: You're right, full guarantee or nothing. She'll have to take it or leave it, then. It's your building.
moves.fb: Allowed, but it may lose a qualified tenant. Advise on the trade-off, don't just echo.

moves.text: Demand the husband's guarantee because she's a woman. Banks always want the husband to sign.
moves.fb: Requiring a spouse's guarantee because of sex or marital status is discrimination under the NYS Human Rights Law.

moves.text: Personal guarantees are illegal on commercial leases in New York. You'll have to drop it, Sal.
moves.fb: Guarantees are legal and common in commercial leases.

moves.text: Skip any guarantee and ask for 12 months' security instead. That's the standard for bakeries.
moves.fb: Not standard, and likely to lose the tenant. A good guy guarantee is the usual middle ground.

say: Is electricity included? I'll be running two big ovens.
Who pays for power? My ovens draw a lot.

moves.text: The store has its own Con Edison meter. You'll open an account and pay the utility directly.
moves.fb: Direct metering puts the usage risk on the tenant who controls it.

moves.text: It's direct metered: you pay Con Ed for what you use. Sal doesn't carry your oven load.
moves.fb: Correct. With heavy ovens, rent inclusion would leave Sal paying for her usage.

moves.text: Sure, we'll include it in the rent. Simpler for everyone, and it's one less bill for you.
moves.fb: Legal, but rent inclusion shifts the usage risk to Sal and could eat his NOI.

moves.text: It's submetered, so Con Ed bills Sal and Sal bills you at whatever rate he chooses.
moves.fb: Submetering bills measured use, not an arbitrary rate. And this store is direct metered.

moves.text: Electricity is always included in commercial rent in New York City. It's part of the base.
moves.fb: Not always. Direct metering, submetering and rent inclusion are all used.

moves.text: You'll pay a share of the whole building's bill, apartments included, by square footage.
moves.fb: Splitting residential usage onto a store isn't how direct metering works.

say: Last thing. If Sal's bank ever forecloses, do I lose my store and my $200,000 build-out?
What happens to my lease if Sal's lender takes the building?

moves.text: We'll ask Sal's lender for an SNDA: it agrees not to disturb you while you're not in default.
moves.fb: That's what non-disturbance is for. Subordination helps Sal finance; attornment and non-disturbance keep the lease alive.

moves.text: An SNDA: you attorn to a new owner, and the lender promises not to disturb you. I'll request it now.
moves.fb: Correct. SNDA protects a tenant in good standing after foreclosure.

moves.text: I'm not sure. Banks rarely foreclose on buildings like Sal's, so I wouldn't worry about it.
moves.fb: Dodges a real risk with a known solution: the SNDA.

moves.text: Foreclosure wipes out leases. There's nothing anyone can do, so price that risk into your offer.
moves.fb: A non-disturbance agreement protects a tenant in good standing after foreclosure.

moves.text: An estoppel certificate protects you from foreclosure. Sign one and you're covered for the term.
moves.fb: An estoppel certifies lease facts. Non-disturbance is what protects against foreclosure.

moves.text: Record the lease and you're automatically ahead of Sal's mortgage, whenever it was filed.
moves.fb: Priority generally follows recording order, and the existing mortgage is ahead. An SNDA solves it.

say: And skip that discrimination disclosure form. It's a store, not an apartment.
Don't hand her the fair housing form. Commercial doesn't need it.

moves.text: That form applies to commercial too, Sal. She gets it at our first real meeting.
moves.fb: Correct. 19 NYCRR 175.28 covers all property types, including commercial and vacant land.

moves.text: That form covers every property type. The agency form doesn't, but this one does, Sal.
moves.fb: Right. RPL 443 is residential; the anti-discrimination form is universal.

moves.text: I'll give it to her quietly, so it doesn't seem like a big deal or scare her off the space.
moves.fb: Giving it is right; it's required, not optional or hidden.

moves.text: Fine, I'll skip it. Commercial deals in New York only need the RPL 443 agency disclosure.
moves.fb: Backwards. RPL 443 is residential; the anti-discrimination form covers commercial.

moves.text: I'll skip it unless she asks for it. Forms are only required on request for commercial deals.
moves.fb: It's required at first substantive contact, not on request.

moves.text: I'll have her sign a waiver of the form instead. Then nobody can say we skipped it.
moves.fb: There's no waiver. The form must be provided.

say: Apartment tenants can sublet with consent not unreasonably withheld. I get that too, right?
Do I have the same sublet rights as Sal's apartment tenants?

moves.text: That right is residential only, under RPL 226-b. For stores, the lease controls.
moves.fb: Correct. Commercial sublet and assignment rights come from the lease.
moves.react: Then let's get it in the lease.

moves.text: No. The statute covers apartments in 4+ unit buildings. Your rights come from our lease here.
moves.fb: Right. RPL 226-b doesn't apply to commercial space.
moves.react: Okay, add it to the list.

moves.text: Probably similar. Let's not worry about it and figure it out if you ever want to sublet.
moves.fb: Not knowing your rights at signing is how tenants get stuck. Negotiate it now.

moves.text: Yes, RPL 226-b covers every tenant in the building, store included, so you're protected.
moves.fb: RPL 226-b is residential only.

moves.text: No, commercial tenants can never sublet in New York. It's banned outright by state law.
moves.fb: Commercial subletting is allowed if the lease permits it.

moves.text: Only if you've been there five years. After that, commercial tenants get automatic sublet rights.
moves.fb: No such rule. It's whatever the lease says.

say: The lease says I pay my proportionate share of tax increases over the base year. My store is 1,500 of the building's 7,500 square feet. Taxes went up $10,000. What do I owe?
Proportionate share of a $10,000 tax increase. I'm 1,500 of 7,500 rentable feet. How much?

moves.text: Your share is 1,500 / 7,500 = 20%. 20% of the $10,000 increase is $2,000 this year.
moves.fb: Correct. Escalation = proportionate share x increase over base.

moves.text: 20% share, so $2,000 this year. Only the increase over the base year counts toward it.
moves.fb: Right formula and the right base.

moves.text: A small share. Maybe a couple thousand. Sal will send the bill each year anyway.
moves.fb: Right ballpark, but compute it: 20% x $10,000 = $2,000.

moves.text: You'd pay 20% of the whole tax bill, not just the increase. That's how a base year works.
moves.fb: Base year escalations apply to the increase over the base, not the whole bill.

moves.text: Your share is 7,500 / 1,500, which is 5%, so you owe 5% of the increase: $500 this year.
Commercial tenants pay 50% of any tax increase regardless of their size. So $5,000 for you.
moves.fb: No fixed 50% rule. It's the proportionate share in the lease.

say: Set the breakpoint at $800,000 instead. I want my percentage sooner.
Lower breakpoint. $800,000. More money for me.

moves.text: We can propose an artificial breakpoint. It raises her cost, so expect some pushback on it.
moves.fb: Correct. An artificial breakpoint is negotiable; it changes the economics for both sides.
moves.react: Try it. See what she says.

moves.text: That's an artificial breakpoint. It's legal to ask, but she'll likely want a lower base.
moves.fb: Right. You explain the concept and the likely trade-off.

moves.text: Sure, I'll put $800,000 in the next draft, and we'll just see how she reacts to it.
moves.fb: Changing terms quietly is bad faith. Propose it openly.

moves.text: You can't. Breakpoints are set by law at base rent divided by the rate. Nothing else is allowed.
moves.fb: Natural breakpoint is a formula, but parties can negotiate an artificial one.

moves.text: Sure, and lowering the breakpoint lowers her total rent, so she'll gladly agree to it.
moves.fb: A lower breakpoint raises percentage rent, so her total goes up.

moves.text: Just lower it to $800,000 and keep the base at $72,000. She'll never do the math on it herself.
moves.fb: Counting on a tenant not understanding terms isn't negotiation.

roleplays.debrief: You practised commercial leasing: the NYS Human Rights Law covers commercial space, so national origin, sex and marital status can't drive decisions, and the anti-discrimination form applies to commercial deals. Natural breakpoint = base rent / percentage rate, and overage applies only above it. RPL 226-b sublet rights are residential only, escalations are proportionate share x increase over base, and a good guy guarantee, direct metering and an SNDA balance the risk.

questions.q: The highest quality office space, with the best location and systems, is described as:
c: Class A
Class C
Class B
Class 4
questions.x: Class A is top tier. Class 4 is the trap: that is a NYC tax class, not a building grade.

questions.q: An older office building with dated systems and the lowest rents is likely:
c: Class A
Class B
Class C
Trophy
questions.x: Class C is oldest and cheapest. Trophy is the trap: it is above Class A.

questions.q: The largest type of shopping center, with three or more anchors and shoppers from several counties, is a:
c: Neighborhood center
Super-regional (mega) mall
Strip center
Community center
questions.x: Super-regional centers are the largest. Neighborhood center is the trap: it is anchored by a supermarket and serves nearby residents.

questions.q: Which anchors would most likely be found in a super-regional mall?
c: One supermarket
A single drugstore
No anchors at all
Several department stores plus entertainment
questions.x: Multiple large anchors and entertainment define the type. A single supermarket is the trap: it fits a neighborhood center.

questions.q: A warehouse is valued mainly for its ceiling height, loading docks and highway access. It is:
c: Retail property
Office property
Industrial property
Residential property
questions.x: Those features matter for manufacturing and distribution. Retail is the trap: retail values foot traffic and visibility.

questions.q: Which feature matters most to an industrial tenant?
c: Clear ceiling height and loading
Lobby finishes
Foot traffic
Window views
questions.x: Industrial users need height and loading capacity. Foot traffic is the trap: that matters for retail.

questions.q: A ground tenant who built an office tower on leased land holds a:
c: Fee simple in the land
Life estate
Reversionary interest
Leasehold interest
questions.x: The tenant's right to possess for the lease term is a leasehold. Reversion is the trap: that belongs to the landowner.

questions.q: When a 99-year ground lease ends, the land returns to the:
c: Ground tenant
Landowner (the fee owner)
Mortgage lender
City
questions.x: The fee owner holds the reversion. The tenant is the trap: its leasehold ends.

questions.q: NOI is $150,000 and annual debt service is $110,000. Before-tax cash flow is:
questions.x: BTCF = NOI minus debt service = $40,000. $260,000 is the trap: adding.

questions.q: In the 'cash world' of investment analysis, which is subtracted from NOI to reach before-tax cash flow?
c: Depreciation
Vacancy loss
Full debt service
Property taxes
questions.x: Debt service (principal and interest) is subtracted. Depreciation is the trap: it is a non-cash tax deduction.

questions.q: A building's NOI is $96,000 and the cap rate is 8%. Its value is:
questions.x: Value = Income / Rate = $96,000 / 0.08 = $1,200,000. $7,680 is the trap: multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.q: A property worth $2,000,000 produces $130,000 NOI. Its cap rate is:
questions.x: Rate = Income / Value = 130,000 / 2,000,000 = 6.5%. 15.4% is the trap: dividing value by income.

questions.q: The floor area a tenant occupies exclusively, excluding shared common areas, is:
c: Rentable square footage
Gross building area
Usable square footage
Loss factor
questions.x: Usable area is exclusive to the tenant. Rentable is the trap: it adds a share of common areas.

questions.q: A tenant's rentable area is usually larger than its usable area because rentable includes:
c: A share of common areas
The parking garage
Only the walls
Future expansion space
questions.x: Rentable = usable plus a share of lobbies, corridors and restrooms. Expansion space is the trap.

questions.q: Usable area minus walls, columns and convector enclosures is called:
c: Rentable square footage
Gross leasable area
Load factor
Carpetable square footage
questions.x: Carpetable area is what you could actually cover with carpet. Gross leasable area is the trap: it is a retail measure of total leasable space.

questions.q: Which measurement of an office suite is usually smallest?
c: Usable
Carpetable
Rentable
Gross
questions.x: Carpetable removes walls and columns from usable, so it is smallest. Usable is the trap: it is larger than carpetable.

questions.q: A commercial lease makes the tenant pay its share of property tax increases over a base year. This is a:
c: Real estate tax escalation
CPI escalation
Percentage rent clause
Fixed step increase
questions.x: Tax escalations pass through increases above the base year. Percentage rent is the trap: it ties rent to sales.

questions.q: A tenant occupies 10% of a building. Taxes rise from a base-year $400,000 to $460,000. Under a tax escalation, the tenant pays an extra:
questions.x: Increase is $60,000; 10% share = $6,000. $46,000 is the trap: 10% of the whole new tax bill.

questions.q: A lease raises rent by 3% every year regardless of costs. This is a:
c: CPI escalation
Fixed percentage increase
Tax escalation
Porter's wage escalation
questions.x: A set yearly percentage is a fixed increase. CPI escalation is the trap: it follows the price index.

questions.q: Rent is $50,000 in year 1 with a fixed 4% annual increase. Year 2 rent is:
questions.x: $50,000 x 1.04 = $52,000. $50,400 is the trap: using 0.4% instead of 4%.

questions.q: A lease adjusts rent by the change in the Consumer Price Index. This is a(n):
c: Fixed step increase
Tax escalation
CPI escalation
Percentage lease
questions.x: CPI escalations follow the BLS index. Fixed step is the trap: it ignores inflation.

questions.q: The Consumer Price Index used in CPI escalation clauses is published by the:
c: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics
Federal Reserve
NYS Department of State
Census Bureau
questions.x: BLS publishes CPI. The Federal Reserve is the trap: it sets monetary policy.

questions.q: The ease and speed with which an investment can be converted to cash without a significant loss in value is called:
c: Leverage
Appreciation
Equity build-up
Liquidity
