questions.x: Liquidity measures how quickly an asset becomes cash at full value; real estate is relatively illiquid. Leverage, the most tempting wrong pick, is the use of borrowed money, a different idea.

questions.q: Using borrowed money to finance the purchase of an investment property is known as:
c: Liquidity
Amortization
Capitalization
Leverage
questions.x: Leverage is using other people's money (usually a mortgage) to buy an asset. Capitalization is the trap: it converts income into value, and amortization is paying a loan down over time.

questions.q: An investor pays $800,000 cash for a building that produces net operating income of $56,000 a year. The investor's annual rate of return is:
questions.x: Return = income / investment = $56,000 / $800,000 = 7%. Dividing the other way ($800,000 / $56,000 = 14.3) gives a multiplier, not a rate.

questions.q: A $1,000,000 building has NOI of $70,000. The buyer borrows $700,000 with annual debt service of $42,000 and invests $300,000 of her own cash. Her return on her cash is about:
questions.x: Cash after debt service = $70,000 minus $42,000 = $28,000; $28,000 / $300,000 = 9.33%. The trap is 7.0%, the property's free-and-clear cap rate, which ignores the financing. Positive leverage (a 6% loan constant) lifted the equity return above 7%.

questions.q: Positive leverage occurs when:
c: The loan-to-value ratio is kept below 50 percent of price
The loan's interest rate exceeds the property's overall return
The investor buys the property with cash and no mortgage
The property's return exceeds the cost of the borrowed funds
questions.x: When each borrowed dollar earns more than it costs, the return on equity rises. The reversed statement (loan cost above the property's return) is the definition of negative leverage, and the LTV ratio alone does not decide which kind you have.

questions.q: A property earns 6% free and clear. The only available loan has a mortgage constant of 7%. If the investor increases the loan from 50% to 75% of the price, the return on the investor's cash will:
c: Increase, because more debt magnifies the investor's equity return
Stay the same, because the property's NOI does not change
Rise to 7%, matching the mortgage constant on the loan
Decrease, because the added debt costs more than it earns
questions.x: This is negative leverage. At 50% debt the equity return is 5%; at 75% it falls to 3%. The tempting answer, 'leverage magnifies returns,' is true only when the debt costs less than the property earns; magnification works in both directions.

questions.q: The principle that a dollar received today is worth more than a dollar received in the future is called:
c: Substitution
Highest and best use
The law of diminishing returns
The time value of money
questions.x: Today's dollar can be invested now and carries no risk of nonpayment, so it is worth more. Substitution, the closest-sounding trap, is an appraisal principle: a buyer pays no more than the cost of an equal substitute.

questions.q: A tenant will pay a $50,000 lump sum in 2 years. If the investor's required rate of return is 5% compounded annually, the present value of that payment is closest to:
questions.x: PV = $50,000 / (1.05 x 1.05) = $50,000 / 1.1025 = $45,351. Subtracting a simple 10% gives $45,000, which ignores compounding.

questions.q: Real estate is considered relatively illiquid for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:
c: Sales require marketing time and due diligence
Buyers usually need time to obtain financing approval
Each parcel is unique and harder to price than a stock
Land is indestructible as a physical matter
questions.x: Indestructibility is a physical characteristic of land, not a reason it is slow to sell. Marketing time, financing and uniqueness each slow the conversion to cash; uniqueness is tempting because it is also a 'characteristic,' but it does make pricing slower.

questions.q: As the risk of an investment increases, investors generally:
c: Accept a lower expected rate of return
Require the investment to be more liquid
Focus on appreciation instead of income
Demand a higher expected rate of return
questions.x: Investors must be paid to take risk, so riskier investments must offer higher expected returns (a vacant warehouse trades at a higher cap rate than a leased pharmacy). Accepting a lower return is the reverse of the risk-return rule.

questions.q: Real estate is often called a tax shelter mainly because:
c: Rental income from investment property is exempt from income tax
Local property taxes are refunded to investors each year
Gains on the sale of investment property are tax free
Depreciation, a non-cash deduction, can offset taxable income
questions.x: Depreciation reduces taxable income while cash flow continues. Rental income is taxable, and gains are generally taxed unless deferred in a 1031 exchange; deferral is not the same as tax free.

questions.q: All of the following are risks of owning investment real estate EXCEPT:
c: The owner can deduct depreciation each year
Interest rates rise before a planned refinance
A major tenant goes bankrupt mid-lease
A change in rent regulation lowers future income
questions.x: The depreciation deduction is a tax benefit, not a risk. Tenant default, interest rate changes and regulatory changes (like the 2019 HSTPA rent rules) are classic real estate risks.

questions.q: An investor buys a $500,000 property with $100,000 down. A year later the property's value has risen 5%. Ignoring costs, the gain as a percentage of the investor's cash is:
questions.x: Value rises $25,000 (5% of $500,000); $25,000 / $100,000 down = 25%. The trap is 5%, the gain on the whole property rather than on the investor's cash. Leverage magnifies a loss the same way.

questions.q: The mortgage constant is calculated by dividing:
c: The loan amount by the property's appraised value
The annual interest rate by the loan term in years
Net operating income by the purchase price
Annual debt service by the original loan amount
questions.x: The mortgage constant is annual principal and interest divided by the loan amount. NOI divided by price is the cap rate, and loan divided by value is the loan-to-value ratio, both common mix-ups.

questions.q: A $1,200,000 loan requires monthly payments of $8,000. What is the mortgage constant?
questions.x: Annual debt service = $8,000 x 12 = $96,000; $96,000 / $1,200,000 = 8%. Forgetting to annualize the monthly payment gives 0.67%.

questions.q: A licensee meets a business owner to discuss leasing a 3,000 square foot store in Albany. At first substantive contact, which New York disclosure must the licensee provide?
c: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form
The RPL 443 agency disclosure form for commercial deals
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement
No form, since commercial leasing is exempt from disclosure
questions.x: The NYS Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form applies to every property type, commercial included, at first substantive contact. The RPL 443 agency form is the trap: it covers residential 1 to 4 family deals, not a store lease. The PCDS is for 1 to 4 family sales.

questions.q: A large, well-known store that draws customers to a shopping center is called the:
c: In-line tenant
Percentage tenant
Ground tenant
Anchor tenant
questions.x: The anchor (supermarket, department store, big box) generates traffic for the whole center. In-line tenants are the smaller shops that benefit from that traffic.

questions.q: Which type of investment property typically produces no income and is the most speculative?
c: Unimproved land
A garden apartment complex
A neighborhood shopping center
A net leased warehouse
questions.x: Raw land usually generates no rent while the owner pays taxes and carrying costs, so the return depends on future appreciation, and land cannot be depreciated. A net leased warehouse is the opposite: steady, low-risk income.

questions.q: A Class A office building is best described as:
c: An older building with dated systems and the lowest market rents
A building leased mainly to government agency tenants
Any office tower taller than 40 stories in a CBD
A new or renovated, well-located building with top rents
questions.x: Class A means the best quality, location, systems and management, with the highest rents. Class is about quality, not height, so the 40-story answer is the trap; the older, dated building describes Class C.

questions.q: A regional mall is typically anchored by:
c: Two or more department stores
A single convenience store and a gas station
A supermarket and a drugstore
A cluster of manufacturers' outlet stores
questions.x: Regional malls rely on multiple department store anchors to pull shoppers from a wide area. A supermarket and drugstore is the tempting trap, but that is the anchor of a neighborhood center.

questions.q: A shopping center made up mostly of manufacturers' and brand-name discount stores, often located along a highway away from city centers, is a(n):
c: Strip center
Neighborhood center
Regional mall
Outlet center
questions.x: Outlet centers gather brand discount stores, like Woodbury Common in Central Valley. A regional mall also draws from far away, but its anchors are full-price department stores.

questions.q: A neighborhood shopping center is most often anchored by:
c: A supermarket or drugstore
A manufacturers' outlet store
Two department stores
A big-box home improvement store
questions.x: Neighborhood centers serve daily needs, so the typical anchor is a supermarket or drugstore. Department store anchors belong to regional malls, and big-box anchors to community or power centers.

questions.q: A developer built an office tower on land it leased for 99 years. When the ground lease expires, the building will usually:
c: Remain the property of the developer
Be demolished at the landowner's expense
Be sold, with proceeds split between the parties
Revert to the landowner with the land
questions.x: Under a typical ground lease, improvements revert to the fee owner at the end of the term, which is why a leasehold loses value as the remaining term shrinks. The developer keeps the building only if the lease says so.

questions.q: In a ground lease, the landowner's interest in the property is called the:
c: Leased fee
Leasehold
Life estate
Remainder interest
questions.x: The landowner holds the leased fee: the land subject to the lease, with the right to ground rent and the reversion. The leasehold, the tempting near-twin, is the tenant's interest.

questions.q: Loft buildings typically have all of the following features EXCEPT:
c: Large open floor plates with few columns
High ceilings and heavy floor loads
Freight elevators and loading access
Low ceilings and small windows
questions.x: Loft buildings were built for manufacturing: big open floors, high ceilings, heavy floor loads, large windows and freight elevators. Low ceilings and small windows are the opposite.

questions.q: An investor is comparing two Brooklyn walk-ups, both built in 1931: one with 4 apartments and one with 8. Which is more likely to contain rent stabilized apartments?
c: The 8-unit building, since ETPA generally covers pre-1974 buildings of 6+ units
The 4-unit building, since stabilization targets small owner-run walk-ups of 3 to 5 units
Neither, because vacancy decontrol removed these units from regulation years ago
Both equally, because pre-war buildings are under rent control
questions.x: The ETPA generally applies to buildings of 6 or more units built before 1974. The vacancy decontrol answer is the old-law trap: vacancy and high-rent decontrol were repealed by the 2019 HSTPA.

questions.q: A lender making a loan on a 12-unit apartment building would normally treat it as:
c: A residential loan, since the building is mostly apartments
A home equity loan secured by the owner's residence
A construction loan with an interest reserve
A commercial loan sized on the property's income
questions.x: Residential mortgage programs cover 1 to 4 units. Five or more units is commercial lending, where NOI and debt coverage drive the loan, even though the building is all apartments.

questions.q: Which is the main advantage of a ground lease to a developer?
c: It avoids buying the land, so less equity is needed
The landowner pays the taxes on the new building
The developer owns the land when the lease ends
Ground rent stays flat for the full 99-year lease term
questions.x: The developer controls the site without buying it, saving a large upfront cost. Owning the land at the end is the trap: the land, and usually the building, go to the landowner, and ground rents often reset upward.

questions.q: A three-story building in Bay Ridge has a hardware store on the ground floor and two apartments above. This is best described as a:
c: Strip center
Loft building
Neighborhood center
Mixed-use building
questions.x: Combining retail and residential uses in one building makes it mixed use, the classic NYC apartments over a store. A strip center is a row of stores, usually with parking in front.

questions.q: A small row of convenience stores such as a pizzeria, nail salon and dry cleaner, with parking in front, is a:
c: Strip center
Regional mall
Power center
Outlet center
questions.x: That is the strip center: small, convenience oriented, serving the immediate neighborhood. A power center also has parking in front, but it is anchored by several big-box retailers.

questions.q: All of the following statements about a long-term ground lease are true EXCEPT:
c: The ground tenant may finance with a leasehold mortgage
The landowner collects ground rent over the term
Lenders want the term to run well past the loan's maturity
The ground tenant holds fee title to the land
questions.x: The ground tenant holds a leasehold, not fee title to the land. A leasehold mortgage sounds odd but is real and common, and lenders do insist the lease outlast the loan.

questions.q: New York City's Loft Law (Multiple Dwelling Law Article 7-C) primarily:
c: Protects certain loft residents and requires legalization
Caps rents for retail stores in loft buildings
Requires loft owners to convert space to offices
Bans residential use in former factory and warehouse buildings
questions.x: The Loft Law (MDL Article 7-C) protects qualifying residential loft occupants and requires owners to bring buildings up to residential code under the NYC Loft Board. It does not ban residential use; it legalizes it.

questions.q: Anchor tenants in shopping centers often pay:
c: The same rent per square foot as in-line stores
Higher rent per square foot than in-line tenants
Percentage rent in place of any base rent
Lower rent per square foot than in-line tenants
questions.x: Because the anchor draws traffic that benefits everyone, landlords give it favorable rent and recover more from the smaller in-line stores. Higher rent is the intuitive trap (bigger tenant, bigger rent per foot), but the reverse is true.

questions.q: Every investment, from a savings bond to an office tower, is judged on which three measures?
c: Return, risk and liquidity
Leverage, depreciation and appreciation
Income, expenses and debt service
Price, location and age of the property
questions.x: The three yardsticks are how much it returns, how risky that return is, and how fast it turns back into cash. Leverage and depreciation are tools that change a return, not the measures every investment is judged on.

questions.q: An investor is choosing between a Treasury bond and a walk-up apartment building. Which comparison uses the three standard measures of any investment?
c: Their cap rates, NOI and debt coverage
Their return, risk and liquidity
Their tax brackets, basis and recapture
Their location, condition and tenant mix
questions.x: Any two investments are compared on return, risk and liquidity: here the building likely pays more but is riskier and far less liquid. Cap rate, NOI and debt coverage apply to the building only, so they cannot compare it with a bond.

questions.concept: Return on vs return of investment
questions.q: Monthly rent from a building pays the investor a return ON the investment. What provides the return OF the investment?
c: Selling at or above the purchase price
Depreciation deductions taken each year
Refinancing the mortgage at a lower rate
Raising rents at each lease renewal
questions.x: Return of investment means getting your original money back, which happens when the property sells at or above what you paid. Rent increases are tempting, but more rent is still a return on the investment, not the return of it.

questions.concept: Return on vs return of investment
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes return on investment from return of investment?
c: On is figured before income tax; of is figured after tax
On comes from borrowed funds; of comes from your own cash
On is the income earned; of is getting your money back
On is the cap rate; of is the cash on cash return
questions.x: Return on investment is the income your money earns (rent); return of investment is recovering the money itself, usually through a sale. Linking them to cap rate and cash on cash is the trap: both of those measure return on.

questions.concept: Leverage does not change cap rate
questions.q: A building with NOI of $90,000 is bought for $1,500,000, with 75% financed at a mortgage constant below the property's return. Compared with an all-cash purchase, the loan:
c: Raises the property's cap rate above 6%
Lowers NOI by the amount of debt service
Raises NOI because interest is deductible
Leaves NOI and the 6% cap rate unchanged
questions.x: Cap rate is NOI divided by value ($90,000 / $1,500,000 = 6%), and neither number depends on financing. Positive leverage raises the return on the investor's cash, which is the trap: it does not raise the property's cap rate.

questions.concept: Leverage does not change cap rate
questions.q: Which of the following does leverage change?
c: The property's net operating income
The property's capitalization rate
The property's potential gross income
The return on the owner's cash
questions.x: Leverage only changes what is left for the owner's cash after the bank is paid, so it moves the cash on cash return up or down. NOI and cap rate are figured before financing, so 'leverage increased the cap rate' is the classic wrong answer.

questions.q: Two buildings each promise $500,000 of total cash over 10 years. One pays steady rent every year; the other pays almost all of it in a sale in year 10. Applying the time value of money, an investor will generally prefer:
c: The year-10 payoff, since a larger lump sum compounds faster
Either one, since the total dollars received are the same
The year-10 payoff, since sale proceeds are taxed less
The steady rent, since earlier dollars are worth more today
questions.x: Money received sooner can be reinvested and carries less risk, so the same total paid earlier has a higher present value. 'Either one' is the trap: it ignores when the cash arrives, which is the whole point of the time value of money.

questions.q: Discounted cash flow analysis, used by appraisers and institutional buyers, is best described as:
c: Discounting each future year's cash flow to today
One year's NOI divided by a market cap rate
Gross rent multiplied by a market multiplier
Comparing the loan constant with the property return
questions.x: DCF discounts each projected year's cash flow back to present value, which is the time value of money applied year by year. Dividing one year's NOI by a cap rate is direct capitalization, a one-year snapshot, not DCF.

questions.q: A five-story office building with elevators in downtown White Plains would most likely be described as a:
c: Mid-rise building
Garden office building
High-rise building
Low-rise building
questions.x: Mid-rise roughly means about 4 to 10 stories with elevators, the typical downtown Brooklyn or White Plains building. Low-rise is 1 to 3 or 4 stories, often a walk-up. The labels are rough industry terms, not legal definitions.

questions.q: Office building height labels such as low-rise, mid-rise and high-rise are best described as:
c: Legal categories set by the NYC zoning code
Rough industry terms that vary by source
Classes set by the Department of State
Lender categories based on loan size
questions.x: Heights are rough industry labels, and sources disagree on the cutoffs; the exam wants the idea, not a magic number. They are not legal categories, which is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: Which is a major risk of owning an office building?
c: Most office leases are too short to provide steady, stable income
Rent stabilization caps the rent increases on office space
A big vacancy can take a year and costly build-outs to refill
Office leases rarely let landlords pass on rising expenses
questions.x: Long office leases are stable, but when a large tenant leaves, re-leasing can take a year or more and require tenant improvement money and commissions. Short leases are the trap: office leases run long, which is their strength.

questions.q: Since 2020, which office space has been hardest to lease in New York?
c: New Class A towers with top amenities
Single-tenant headquarters buildings
Older Class B and C buildings
Newly renovated trophy space
questions.x: Remote work has hit older Class B and C space hardest, and some Manhattan buildings are being converted to apartments. Class A space has held up better because tenants are moving up in quality.

questions.q: Which retail property has generally held up best against online shopping?
c: A grocery-anchored neighborhood shopping center
An enclosed regional mall with two department stores
An outlet center along a highway an hour away
A mall whose anchor has gone dark
questions.x: People still buy food, prescriptions and haircuts in person, so grocery-anchored centers held up. Weaker enclosed malls have been hollowed out by online shopping, which makes the regional mall the trap.

questions.q: A retail investor studying a shopping center would focus most on:
c: The building's clear height and loading docks
Anchor lease term and tenant sales per foot
The number of rent stabilized units above the stores
The office space's Class A, B or C rating
questions.x: Retail risk is about traffic, so investors study the anchor's remaining lease term, tenant sales per square foot, and how many in-line tenants might leave with the anchor. Clear height and docks are industrial measures.

questions.q: A buyer is considering a Battery Park City condo. Because the land is ground leased from a state authority, the buyer should ask:
c: Whether the Loft Board has registered the building's units
Whether the condo is rent stabilized under ETPA
When the ground lease expires and how its rent resets
How many anchor tenants the building has
questions.x: Battery Park City land is owned by a state authority and ground leased, so the lease expiration and rent reset drive what the unit is worth. The Loft Law concerns former manufacturing lofts, not ground-leased land.

questions.q: The land under the Chrysler Building has long been owned by The Cooper Union. The building's owner therefore holds:
c: A leasehold, paying ground rent to Cooper Union
Fee simple title to both the land and the building
A life estate measured by the life of the school
The leased fee, paying ground rent to Cooper Union
questions.x: Cooper Union owns the land (the leased fee) and collects ground rent; the building owner holds the leasehold. Calling the building owner's interest the leased fee is the trap: the leased fee belongs to the landowner.

questions.q: Commercial lenders commonly size a loan so the debt service coverage ratio (NOI divided by annual debt service) is at least about:
c: 1.00, break-even
About 1.20 to 1.25
2.50 or more
questions.x: Lenders commonly want a DSCR of about 1.20 to 1.25 or better, a cushion so NOI covers the mortgage with room to spare. A ratio of 1.00 means NOI just barely covers debt service, which no lender treats as enough.

questions.q: A small business owner wants to buy a building and occupy most of it, with a lower down payment than a conventional commercial loan allows. Which financing fits best?
c: A residential FHA mortgage
A leasehold mortgage
A purchase-money wrap loan
An SBA 7(a) or 504 loan
questions.x: SBA 7(a) and 504 loans allow lower down payments for owner-occupied business buildings when the business occupies most of the space. FHA is for residential 1 to 4 unit homes, so it does not fit a commercial building.

questions.concept: Negative leverage in the cash world
questions.q: A building costs $2,000,000 and has NOI of $120,000. The buyer borrows $1,500,000 with annual debt service of $112,500. What is her cash on cash return, and what kind of leverage is this?
c: 6%, the same as buying with all cash
7.5%, positive leverage
1.5%, positive leverage
1.5%, negative leverage
questions.x: BTCF is $120,000 minus $112,500 = $7,500, and $7,500 / $500,000 of equity = 1.5%. The property earns 6% free and clear but the loan costs $112,500 / $1,500,000 = 7.5%, so borrowing drags the return down. Calling it positive leverage is the trap.

questions.concept: Negative leverage in the cash world
questions.q: A building earns 6.33% free and clear. The buyer's loan has a mortgage constant of 7.5%. What is the buyer's best response to improve her return?
c: Borrow more, since leverage always raises the return
Lower the price, find cheaper debt or borrow less
Raise the cap rate by adding a second mortgage
Subtract debt service before calculating NOI
questions.x: When the loan costs more than the property earns, each borrowed dollar lowers the return, so the fix is a lower price, cheaper debt or less debt. 'Borrow more' is the trap: added debt at 7.5% against a 6.33% property makes it worse.

questions.q: A building's leases are about to roll to much higher market rents. Why might an investor run a discounted cash flow analysis instead of relying only on a cap rate?
c: A cap rate assumes this year's NOI is typical
A cap rate is figured on gross rent, not NOI
A cap rate already subtracts the debt service
A cap rate can only be applied to retail property
questions.x: Direct capitalization is a one-year snapshot that assumes the current NOI is representative. When income is about to change a lot, a multi-year DCF captures it. 'Gross rent, not NOI' is wrong: cap rates always use NOI.

questions.q: Which statement about a cap rate is correct?
c: It projects income year by year for ten years
It is a snapshot of one year's return
It is figured after the debt service is paid
It includes expected appreciation
questions.x: A cap rate divides one year's NOI by value, so it is a single-year snapshot. Projecting income year by year is discounted cash flow, the tempting mix-up.

questions.q: A 4-unit building has gross annual rent of $96,000. Similar buildings sell at a gross rent multiplier of 11. Its estimated value is:
questions.x: With a GRM, value = gross rent x multiplier: $96,000 x 11 = $1,056,000. Dividing gives $872,727, the trap of using the cap rate formula with a multiplier.

questions.q: Which is a key difference between a gross rent multiplier and a cap rate?
c: GRM uses NOI; a cap rate uses gross rent
GRM is used for large office towers only
GRM skips expenses; cap rates use NOI
GRM subtracts debt service before valuing
questions.x: A GRM multiplies gross rent, before any expenses, so it is a rough screen for small residential income property. A cap rate divides NOI, after vacancy and expenses. Swapping the two is the trap.

questions.q: A Manhattan office tenant's base rent covers building expenses at first-year levels, and the tenant pays its share of any increases after that. This lease is best described as:
c: An absolute net lease
A modified gross lease
A triple net (NNN) lease
A percentage lease
questions.x: Modified gross means base rent covers expenses in a base year and the tenant pays escalations above it, the NYC office standard. Triple net would make the tenant pay taxes, insurance and maintenance from day one.

questions.q: In a modified gross lease, the tenant pays, in addition to base rent:
c: All taxes, insurance and maintenance from day one
Nothing at all; the landlord pays every expense
Its share of expense increases over a base year
A percentage of gross sales above a breakpoint
questions.x: The base rent already covers expenses at base-year levels; the tenant pays only its share of increases (escalations). Paying everything from day one describes a triple net lease.

questions.q: A three-party agreement among lender, landlord and tenant, in which the tenant subordinates, the lender promises not to disturb, and the tenant agrees to recognize a new owner, is a(n):
c: SNDA agreement
Good guy guarantee
Assignment and assumption
Estoppel certificate
questions.x: SNDA stands for subordination, non-disturbance and attornment, the three-way deal that usually travels as one document. An estoppel certificate is the tenant's one-sided statement of rent, deposit, term and defaults.

questions.q: A commercial lease requires the tenant to sign an estoppel certificate or SNDA when asked. A typical lease gives the tenant how long to return it?
c: Only at lease renewal
About 10 days
Only after a foreclosure
About 90 days
questions.x: Commercial leases usually require an SNDA or estoppel within a short window, often about 10 days, so a sale or refinancing is not held up. Waiting until a foreclosure is the trap: the lender needs the document before it makes the loan.

questions.q: A Brooklyn store tenant's landlord proposes a 25% rent increase at renewal. Which statement is correct in New York?
c: The increase is capped by the Rent Guidelines Board
The landlord needs DHCR approval for the increase
Commercial rents may rise only by the CPI change
Commercial rents are not regulated; it is negotiated
questions.x: New York regulates many apartment rents, but commercial rents are not regulated; renewals and increases are whatever the parties negotiate. The Rent Guidelines Board sets increases only for rent stabilized apartments, which is the trap.

questions.q: An office tenant disputes a tax escalation bill and asks what limits it. The answer is found in:
c: The Rent Stabilization Law
The tenant's lease
RPL 226-b
The Emergency Tenant Protection Act
questions.x: Commercial rents and escalations are not regulated by statute in New York, so the lease controls. Rent stabilization and the ETPA cover apartments, not offices or stores.

questions.q: Which of these investments is generally the MOST liquid?
c: A vacant lot zoned for retail
A 20-unit apartment building
Shares of a publicly traded REIT
A leased fee under a ground lease
questions.x: Listed REIT shares can be sold on an exchange within a day at market price. Direct real estate, even a well-leased apartment building, takes months of marketing and financing to sell; steady income is not the same as liquidity.

questions.q: An investor buys a $2,000,000 building with $400,000 down and a $1,600,000 mortgage. Financing 80% of the price with borrowed funds is an example of:
c: Liquidity
Amortization
Capitalization
Leverage
questions.x: Using borrowed money to control a larger asset is leverage. Amortization is the trap: it describes how the $1,600,000 loan is paid down over time, not the decision to borrow.

questions.q: An investor pays $1,250,000 cash for a building with annual NOI of $75,000. The investor's annual rate of return is:
questions.x: Return = $75,000 / $1,250,000 = 6%. Dividing the price by the income ($1,250,000 / $75,000 = 16.7) gives a multiplier, not a rate.

questions.q: A $2,000,000 building has NOI of $150,000. The buyer puts $500,000 down and borrows the rest, with annual debt service of $105,000. Her cash on cash return is:
questions.x: BTCF = $150,000 minus $105,000 = $45,000; $45,000 / $500,000 = 9%. 7.5% is the cap rate (NOI / price), which ignores financing; 30% divides NOI by equity without subtracting debt service.

questions.q: Negative leverage exists when:
c: The cost of the debt exceeds the property's return
The property's return exceeds the cost of borrowed funds
The loan-to-value ratio rises above 75 percent of price
The investor pays cash and uses no mortgage financing
questions.x: If the loan costs more than the property earns, each borrowed dollar drags down the equity return. The reversed statement defines positive leverage, and a high LTV only magnifies whichever kind exists.

questions.q: A building yields 8% free and clear. An investor can borrow at a 6% mortgage constant. Raising the loan from 50% to 70% of price will cause the cash on cash return to:
c: Fall, because more debt adds risk and lowers the equity yield
Rise, because each borrowed dollar earns more than it costs
Stay at 8%, because the property's NOI is unchanged
Fall to 6%, matching the mortgage constant on the loan
questions.x: Positive leverage: at 50% debt the equity return is (8 minus 3) / 0.5 = 10%; at 70% it is (8 minus 4.2) / 0.3 = 12.7%. More debt does add risk, the tempting trap, but the cash on cash return still rises while the debt costs less than the property earns.

questions.q: An investor offered either $100,000 today or $100,000 in five years should prefer the payment today mainly because of:
c: The principle of substitution
The principle of contribution
The time value of money
Highest and best use
questions.x: Money received now can be invested and earn a return, and it carries no risk of nonpayment, so it is worth more than the same sum later. Substitution and contribution are appraisal principles about comparing properties and improvements.

questions.q: An investor will receive $80,000 in 3 years. At a 6% annual discount rate, compounded annually, the present value is closest to:
questions.x: PV = $80,000 / 1.06^3 = $80,000 / 1.191 = $67,170. Subtracting a simple 18% gives $65,600, and dividing by 1.18 gives $67,797; both ignore compounding. $95,281 is the future value, not the present value.

questions.q: Each of the following makes a commercial building slower to sell than a stock EXCEPT:
c: Buyers usually need lender approval for financing
Due diligence and title work take weeks to complete
Each parcel is unique, so pricing takes analysis
The property produces monthly rental income
questions.x: Rental income is about return, not about how fast the asset converts to cash. Financing approval, due diligence and the uniqueness of each parcel all lengthen the sale.

questions.q: Two buildings each produce $100,000 of NOI. Building X is leased to a national pharmacy for 20 years; Building Y has month-to-month tenants. Investors will most likely:
c: Pay less for Y, applying a higher required return
Pay more for Y, since its rents can be raised soon
Pay the same for both, since the NOI is identical
Pay less for X, since its rent is locked in for years
questions.x: Y's income is far less certain, so buyers demand a higher return (higher cap rate) and pay less for each dollar of NOI. Equal NOI does not mean equal value when the risk differs.

questions.q: An owner's building produces positive cash flow but shows a loss on her tax return. The item most likely creating the paper loss is:
c: Vacancy and credit loss
Depreciation
Real estate taxes
Replacement reserves
questions.x: Depreciation is deducted for taxes even though no cash leaves the owner's account, so it can turn positive cash flow into a taxable loss. Replacement reserves are cash set aside and are not deductible until spent.

questions.q: Each of the following is a risk of owning an office building EXCEPT:
c: A rise in local office vacancy rates
New zoning that limits future additions
Mortgage interest being tax deductible
A key tenant declining to renew its lease
questions.x: Deductible mortgage interest is a tax benefit, not a risk. Market vacancy, regulatory change and tenant rollover are classic office investment risks.

questions.q: An investor buys a $400,000 property with $80,000 down. The value then falls 10%. Ignoring costs, the loss as a percentage of the investor's cash is:
questions.x: Value falls $40,000 (10% of $400,000); $40,000 / $80,000 = 50%. The trap is 10%, the loss on the whole property. Leverage magnifies losses exactly as it magnifies gains.

questions.q: A mortgage constant of 7.5% means that:
c: NOI equals 7.5% of the property's purchase price
The loan's interest rate is fixed at 7.5% for its term
The lender will lend 7.5% of the property's value
Yearly payments equal 7.5% of the original loan
questions.x: The constant is annual principal and interest divided by the loan amount. It is higher than the interest rate on an amortizing loan, so reading it as the interest rate is the main trap; NOI over price is the cap rate.

questions.q: A $900,000 loan has monthly payments of $6,375. The mortgage constant is:
questions.x: Annual debt service = $6,375 x 12 = $76,500; $76,500 / $900,000 = 8.5%. Using the monthly payment gives 0.71%, and dividing loan by payment gives 11.8, a multiplier.

questions.q: The NYS Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form is given to prospective tenants of:
c: Any property type, including commercial space
Residential 1 to 4 family homes and nothing else
Apartment rentals, but not sales or commercial deals
Commercial space larger than 5,000 square feet
questions.x: The form covers residential, commercial and vacant land transactions, delivered at first substantive contact. Limiting it to 1 to 4 family homes confuses it with the RPL 443 agency disclosure form.

questions.q: In-line tenants in a shopping center benefit chiefly from:
c: Lower rent per square foot than the anchors pay
Shopper traffic generated by the anchor tenants
Exemption from common area maintenance charges
The right to approve every new tenant in the center
questions.x: In-line stores live on the traffic the anchors draw. They typically pay HIGHER rent per square foot than anchors, and they do pay CAM charges.

questions.q: An investor who buys raw land and holds it for future development is relying mainly on:
c: Current rental income
Annual depreciation deductions
Future appreciation
Leverage from tenant deposits
questions.x: Raw land typically produces no income and cannot be depreciated, so the return must come from appreciation. Depreciation is the trap: land is not a depreciable asset.

questions.q: An 80-year-old office building with outdated elevators, no central air and rents well below the market is most likely classified as:
c: Class A
Class B
Trophy
Class C
questions.x: Class C describes older buildings with dated systems and the lowest rents. Class B is the near-miss: older but well maintained, with average rents. Age alone does not decide class; condition and rents do.

questions.q: A center of about 1 million square feet that draws shoppers from a wide area and is anchored by several department stores is a:
c: Regional mall
Strip center
Community center
Neighborhood center
questions.x: Multiple department store anchors and a wide trade area mark a regional mall. A community center is mid-sized, anchored by a discount or big-box store.

questions.q: Woodbury Common in Central Valley, made up of brand-name discount stores, is an example of a(n):
c: Regional shopping mall
Outlet center
Strip center
Power center
questions.x: Brand-name discount stores clustered away from a city center define an outlet center. A regional mall also draws from far away, but with full-price department store anchors.

questions.q: A center anchored by a supermarket and serving the daily needs of nearby residents is a:
c: Regional mall
Outlet center
Neighborhood center
Super-regional center
questions.x: Daily-needs shopping with a supermarket or drugstore anchor is a neighborhood center. Regional and super-regional malls are anchored by department stores and draw from a wide area.

questions.q: Why does a ground tenant's interest in its building lose value as the lease nears its end?
c: Lenders refuse to finance buildings older than 30 years
Ground rent is forgiven in the last years of the term
The landowner buys the building back at a fixed price
The building reverts to the landowner at expiration
questions.x: Under a typical ground lease the improvements revert to the fee owner when the term ends, so fewer years remain to collect income from the building. Rent is not forgiven, and no buyback is implied unless the lease provides one.

questions.q: Under a 99-year ground lease, the developer that builds on the site holds the:
c: Leasehold estate
Leased fee
Fee simple absolute
Remainder interest
questions.x: The ground tenant holds a leasehold estate; the landowner keeps the leased fee and the reversion. Fee simple is the trap: building on the land does not give the developer ownership of it.

questions.q: A former garment factory with 14-foot ceilings, wide open floors and a freight elevator is best described as a:
c: Class A office tower
Loft building
Mixed-use building
Garden apartment complex
questions.x: High ceilings, open floors and freight elevators are the hallmarks of a loft building built for manufacturing. Mixed use describes a combination of uses, not a building type.

questions.q: A Queens building with 10 apartments was built in 1968. Under NYC rules, its apartments are most likely:
c: Rent controlled, since the building predates 1971
Market rate, since post-1947 buildings are not regulated
Rent stabilized, since it has 6+ units and predates 1974
Exempt, since stabilization starts at buildings of 20 units
questions.x: Buildings of 6 or more units built before 1974 generally fall under rent stabilization (ETPA). Rent control is the trap: it covers buildings built before 1947 with continuous tenancy since 1971.

questions.q: Which property would a lender normally finance with a residential 1 to 4 family mortgage rather than a commercial loan?
c: A 6-unit walk-up apartment building
A small strip center with 5 stores
A 12-unit mixed-use building
A three-family house in the Bronx
questions.x: Residential mortgage programs cover 1 to 4 units, so a three-family house qualifies. A 6-unit walk-up is the trap: five or more units means commercial lending based on NOI.

questions.q: From the LANDOWNER's point of view, a main advantage of a long-term ground lease is that it:
c: Provides steady ground rent while keeping the reversion
Shifts the land's value into the tenant's depreciable basis
Lets the landowner deduct the tenant's building costs
Gives the landowner the leasehold mortgage interest
questions.x: The landowner keeps title, collects ground rent, and usually gets the land and building back at the end. The tenant, not the landowner, depreciates the building it pays for.

questions.q: A four-story Harlem building has a laundromat and a deli on the ground floor and six apartments above. It is best classified as:
c: A strip center
A mixed-use building
A loft building
A neighborhood center
questions.x: Retail below and apartments above in one building is mixed use. A neighborhood center is a separate shopping center serving daily needs, usually with a supermarket anchor.

questions.q: Which type of retail property is generally the SMALLEST and most convenience oriented?
c: Power center
Community center
Strip center
Regional mall
questions.x: A strip center is a short row of convenience stores serving the immediate neighborhood. Community and power centers are larger, with big-box anchors.

questions.q: Which statement about a long-term ground lease is correct?
c: The tenant holds fee title to the land for the entire term
Neither party may mortgage its interest during the term
The landowner holds the leasehold and the tenant the fee
The tenant has a leasehold; the owner has a leased fee
questions.x: The ground tenant holds a leasehold and the landowner holds the leased fee. Either can be financed: the tenant with a leasehold mortgage, the owner with a fee mortgage.

questions.q: Which NYC body oversees the legalization of residential lofts under the Loft Law?
c: The NYC Loft Board
Board of Standards and Appeals
City Planning Commission
Rent Guidelines Board
questions.x: The NYC Loft Board administers the Loft Law (MDL Article 7-C), including registration and legalization. The BSA hears zoning variances, and the Rent Guidelines Board sets stabilized increases.

questions.q: A landlord gives a department store anchor a very low rent per square foot. The landlord's reasoning is that:
c: Anchors pay percentage rent that more than makes up the gap
Its traffic lets in-line stores pay higher rents
Anchors are exempt from paying CAM charges by law
Anchors typically own the land under the center
questions.x: The anchor's traffic supports higher rents from the in-line stores, so the landlord makes up the discount there. No law exempts anchors from CAM; that is negotiated lease by lease.

questions.q: A building has 20 apartments renting at $1,800 a month and 2 stores renting at $4,000 a month each. Its annual potential gross income is:
questions.x: Monthly rent = 20 x $1,800 + 2 x $4,000 = $44,000; x 12 = $528,000. $432,000 forgets the stores, and $44,000 is one month.

questions.q: PGI is $250,000, vacancy and credit loss is 8%, and parking income is $15,000. Effective gross income is:
questions.x: Vacancy = $20,000. EGI = $250,000 minus $20,000 plus $15,000 = $245,000. Leaving out parking income gives $230,000; skipping vacancy gives $265,000.

questions.q: A building has PGI of $480,000, vacancy and credit loss of 5%, laundry income of $6,000 and operating expenses of $190,000. NOI is:
questions.x: EGI = $480,000 minus $24,000 plus $6,000 = $462,000. NOI = $462,000 minus $190,000 = $272,000. Skipping vacancy gives $296,000; skipping laundry gives $266,000.

questions.q: Which of the following is subtracted in arriving at net operating income?
c: Annual mortgage debt service
Depreciation on the building
Real estate taxes
The owner's income taxes
questions.x: Real estate taxes are an operating expense. Debt service, depreciation and income taxes all come after NOI, which is why NOI does not depend on financing or the owner's tax situation.

questions.q: When computing NOI, each of the following is deducted EXCEPT:
c: Water and sewer charges
Repairs and maintenance
Fees paid to the managing agent
Depreciation on the building
questions.x: Depreciation is a tax deduction, not an operating expense, so it does not reduce NOI. Water, management and repairs are all operating expenses.

questions.q: Which expenditure belongs in operating expenses rather than capital expenditures?
c: Routine hallway painting
Installing new elevator cabs
Replacing the roof membrane
Adding a story to the building
questions.x: Routine painting is recurring upkeep, an operating expense. Replacing a roof or elevator cabs extends the building's life, so those are capital items, excluded from NOI.

questions.q: A building's NOI is $215,000 and its annual mortgage payments total $172,000. Before-tax cash flow is:
questions.x: BTCF = NOI minus debt service = $215,000 minus $172,000 = $43,000. $215,000 is NOI itself, which stops before financing.

questions.q: An investor buys a $5,000,000 building with $1,250,000 down. BTCF is $87,500. The cash on cash return is:
questions.x: Cash on cash = $87,500 / $1,250,000 = 7%. Dividing by the price gives 1.75%, and dividing by the loan ($3,750,000) gives 2.3%.

questions.q: Before-tax cash flow divided by the investor's equity is the:
c: Overall capitalization rate
Equity dividend rate
Mortgage constant
Debt coverage ratio
questions.x: BTCF / equity is the equity dividend rate, also called cash on cash. The overall cap rate is NOI / total value.

questions.q: NOI is $200,000 and debt service is $150,000, including $120,000 of interest. Depreciation is $50,000 and the tax rate is 25%. After-tax cash flow is:
questions.x: Taxable income = $200,000 minus $120,000 minus $50,000 = $30,000; tax = $7,500. BTCF = $50,000; ATCF = $42,500. Taxing the whole BTCF at 25% gives $37,500, which ignores the depreciation deduction and principal.

questions.q: Which item reduces an owner's taxable income but not the owner's cash flow?
c: Mortgage interest
Mortgage principal
Depreciation
Property insurance
questions.x: Depreciation is a non-cash deduction. Mortgage principal is the reverse: it reduces cash flow but is not deductible. Interest and insurance reduce both.

questions.q: Mortgage interest on a rental building is:
c: An operating expense included in NOI
A cash outlay but not a tax deduction
A tax deduction but not a cash outlay
Both a cash outlay and a tax deduction
questions.x: Interest is paid in cash and is deductible. 'Cash but not deductible' describes principal, and 'deductible but not cash' describes depreciation. Interest is debt service, so it is not in NOI.

questions.q: A seller's tax return for a building lists interest, depreciation and a new roof among its expenses. To reconstruct the statement for valuation, the analyst should:
c: Remove the interest, depreciation and roof cost
Keep them, since the IRS accepted the return
Remove the interest but keep depreciation and the roof
Keep the roof but remove interest and depreciation
questions.x: Interest is financing, depreciation is a tax item, and a roof is a capital expenditure (handled through reserves), so none belong in operating expenses. Keeping the roof is tempting because it was real cash, but it is not a recurring operating cost.

questions.q: An owner's statement includes his personal car and family cell phones as building expenses. On a reconstructed statement, these items are:
c: Kept, since the owner actually paid them from building funds
Removed, since a typical buyer would not incur them
Moved to capital expenditures for depreciation
Kept but reduced by half as a compromise
questions.x: Reconstruction shows what a typical investor would spend; owner's personal costs are removed. Paying them from the building's account does not make them operating expenses.

questions.q: A seller's broker gives a buyer a projection of rents and expenses after a planned renovation. This document is a:
c: Reconstructed operating statement
Certified rent roll
Pro forma statement
Estoppel certificate
questions.x: A projection of future performance is a pro forma. A reconstructed statement adjusts actual historical numbers, so it is the closest trap.

questions.q: A building is 100% leased, but every lease expires within 3 years. When valuing it, the vacancy and credit loss allowance should be:
c: Zero, since the building is fully leased today
Added to income as a reserve for re-leasing
Taken from operating expenses rather than PGI
A market-based allowance applied to PGI
questions.x: Valuation uses a stabilized, market vacancy and credit loss even for a full building, because leases roll and tenants default. It is deducted from PGI to reach EGI, not from operating expenses.

questions.q: A building has PGI of $500,000 and vacancy and credit loss of $40,000. The management fee is 4% of effective gross income. The annual fee is:
questions.x: EGI = $460,000; 4% x $460,000 = $18,400. Using PGI gives $20,000, the usual trap.

questions.q: NOI is $80,000. Debt service is $78,000, of which $72,000 is interest. Depreciation is $28,000. At a 35% tax rate, with the loss usable against other income, after-tax cash flow is:
questions.x: Taxable income = $80,000 minus $72,000 minus $28,000 = negative $20,000, saving $7,000 in tax. BTCF = $2,000; ATCF = $2,000 + $7,000 = $9,000. Subtracting the savings instead of adding them gives ($5,000).

questions.q: An owner sets aside $300 per unit each year so money is on hand when the boiler and roof need replacing. These funds are:
c: Reserves for replacement
Security deposits
Operating expense escrows
Capital gains holdbacks
questions.x: Reserves for replacement spread the cost of future capital replacements over time. Security deposits are tenant money held in trust, not owner funds.

questions.q: Which operating expense is most likely to change with the building's occupancy level?
c: Real estate taxes
Utilities
Property insurance
License and permit fees
questions.x: Utilities rise and fall with use, so they are variable. Taxes and insurance are fixed: they are owed whether the building is full or empty.

questions.q: A building collects 85% of its gross rental income from apartments and 15% from ground-floor stores. Its federal depreciation period is:
c: 39 years, since it has commercial space
31.5 years, the old nonresidential period
27.5 years, as residential rental property
15 years, the period for qualified improvement property
questions.x: If at least 80% of gross rental income comes from dwelling units, the building is residential rental property: 27.5 years. Having some commercial space does not make it nonresidential; 31.5 years is the pre-1993 rule.

questions.q: An investor buys an office building for $3,900,000. The land is valued at $780,000. Annual straight-line depreciation is:
questions.x: Building basis = $3,900,000 minus $780,000 = $3,120,000; / 39 years = $80,000. Including the land gives $100,000, and using 27.5 years (residential) gives $113,455.

questions.q: An apartment building has NOI of $210,000. The market cap rate is 7%. Its estimated value is:
questions.x: V = I / R = $210,000 / 0.07 = $3,000,000. Multiplying by 7 gives $1,470,000; misplacing the decimal gives $30,000,000.

questions.q: A strip center sold for $2,400,000 and has NOI of $162,000. The cap rate is:
questions.x: R = I / V = $162,000 / $2,400,000 = 6.75%. Dividing price by NOI (14.8) gives a multiplier, not a rate.

questions.q: A 12-unit building rents each apartment for $1,500 a month. Its potential gross income is:
questions.x: PGI = 12 units x $1,500 x 12 months = $216,000. $18,000 is one month for the whole building, and $2,592,000 multiplies by 12 twice.

questions.q: A building has potential gross income of $400,000, a 5% vacancy and credit loss, and $8,000 of laundry income. Its effective gross income is:
questions.x: Vacancy = 5% x $400,000 = $20,000. EGI = $400,000 minus $20,000 plus $8,000 = $388,000. Leaving out the laundry income gives $380,000.

questions.q: PGI is $600,000, vacancy and credit loss is 7%, other income is $12,000 and operating expenses are $230,000. What is NOI?
Net operating income is calculated:
c: Before subtracting debt service
After subtracting the annual debt service
After subtracting depreciation
After subtracting owner's income taxes
questions.x: NOI = EGI minus operating expenses. Debt service, depreciation and income taxes are not subtracted to reach NOI, so NOI is the same no matter how the owner finances. Subtracting debt service gives before-tax cash flow, the usual trap.

questions.q: When reconstructing an operating statement, all of the following are operating expenses EXCEPT:
c: Real estate taxes on the property
The superintendent's salary
Fire and liability insurance
Mortgage principal and interest
questions.x: Mortgage payments are debt service, subtracted after NOI. Taxes, payroll and insurance are standard operating expenses; taxes feel like a 'financing' cost to some candidates but they are operating costs.

questions.q: Which of the following is a capital expenditure rather than an operating expense?
c: Replacing the building's boiler
Monthly exterminator service contract
Repairing a leaking faucet
Common area electricity bills
questions.x: Replacing a major component that extends the building's life is a capital expenditure, excluded from NOI and depreciated for taxes. A faucet repair is a repair, not a replacement, so it stays an operating expense.

questions.q: A building has NOI of $340,000 and annual debt service of $260,000. Its before-tax cash flow is:
questions.x: BTCF = NOI minus debt service = $340,000 minus $260,000 = $80,000. Adding the two ($600,000) is the arithmetic trap.

questions.q: An investor buys a building for $3,500,000 with a $2,500,000 loan. Before-tax cash flow is $80,000. The cash on cash return is:
questions.x: Equity = $3,500,000 minus $2,500,000 = $1,000,000. Cash on cash = $80,000 / $1,000,000 = 8%. Dividing by the price ($3,500,000) gives 2.3%, a common mistake.

questions.q: The equity dividend rate is another name for:
c: The debt coverage ratio
The overall capitalization rate
The mortgage constant
The cash on cash return
questions.x: Equity dividend rate = before-tax cash flow / equity invested, the same as cash on cash. The cap rate is the trap: it uses NOI and total value, ignoring financing.

questions.q: NOI is $150,000. Annual debt service is $110,000, of which $95,000 is interest. Depreciation is $40,000. The owner is in a 24% tax bracket. After-tax cash flow is:
questions.x: Taxable income = $150,000 minus $95,000 interest minus $40,000 depreciation = $15,000; tax = $3,600. BTCF = $150,000 minus $110,000 = $40,000. ATCF = $40,000 minus $3,600 = $36,400. $40,000 is BTCF, before tax.

questions.q: Which item is deducted in the tax world but involves no cash payment by the owner that year?
c: Depreciation
Real estate taxes
Mortgage interest
Insurance premiums
questions.x: Depreciation is a non-cash deduction for the wearing out of the building. Mortgage interest is deductible too, but it is paid in cash, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: The principal portion of a mortgage payment is:
c: Added back to net operating income
Deductible for income tax but not a cash outlay
Included with operating expenses when computing NOI
Paid in cash but not deductible for income tax
questions.x: Principal is real cash leaving the owner's account (it reduces BTCF), but it repays the owner's own debt, so it is not deductible; only interest is. 'Deductible but not cash' describes depreciation, the mirror-image trap.

questions.q: The main purpose of a reconstructed operating statement is to:
c: Show income and expenses as a typical investor would
Record the owner's personal and business expenses for the year
Calculate the size of the owner's mortgage payment
Prepare the owner's federal income tax return
questions.x: Reconstruction standardizes the numbers (no financing, depreciation, capital items or owner's personal costs) so the property can be valued on its own earning power. A tax return is the trap: it includes interest and depreciation that investors remove.

questions.q: A seller manages his own 10-unit building and shows no management expense on his statement. When reconstructing the statement for a buyer, the analyst should:
c: Leave management out, since the seller pays no fee
Add a management fee to the income side
Subtract the seller's personal draw from gross income
Include a market-rate management fee as an expense
questions.x: Any buyer must pay for management in money or time, so a market management fee is included as an expense. Leaving it out because the seller paid nothing overstates NOI and value.

questions.q: A pro forma statement is:
c: A projection of future income and expenses
An audited record of last year's actual income
A lender's commitment letter for the loan
A tenant's estoppel certificate on lease terms
questions.x: A pro forma projects future performance, often after renovation or lease-up, so investors treat a seller's pro forma with caution. An audited record of actual results is the opposite: historical, not projected.

questions.q: A listing setup shows no vacancy allowance because every apartment is currently leased. A careful analyst will:
c: Accept zero vacancy because the building is full
Deduct vacancy from operating expenses instead
Raise the rents to market before projecting income
Deduct a market vacancy and credit loss anyway
questions.x: Leases expire and tenants stop paying, so reconstructed statements apply a market vacancy and credit loss to PGI even for a full building. Vacancy reduces income; it is not an operating expense.

questions.q: A building's PGI is $300,000 and vacancy and credit loss is $20,000. The management contract charges 5% of effective gross income. The annual management fee is:
questions.x: EGI = $300,000 minus $20,000 = $280,000. Fee = 5% x $280,000 = $14,000. Using PGI gives $15,000, the usual trap.

questions.q: NOI is $100,000. Debt service is $95,000, including $90,000 of interest. Depreciation is $30,000. The investor's tax rate is 30%, and the tax loss can offset her other income. After-tax cash flow is:
questions.x: Taxable income = $100,000 minus $90,000 minus $30,000 = negative $20,000, which saves 30% x $20,000 = $6,000 in tax. BTCF = $5,000. ATCF = $5,000 + $6,000 = $11,000. $5,000 is BTCF; a usable tax loss can make ATCF larger than BTCF.

questions.q: Reserves for replacement are:
c: Annual set-asides for replacing worn components
The tenants' security deposits held in a separate account
The lender's escrow for real estate taxes
Cash held back to pay the owner's income taxes
questions.x: Reserves spread the cost of future replacements (roofs, boilers) across the years. Security deposits belong to tenants and are not the owner's funds; a lender's tax escrow pays taxes, not replacements.

questions.q: Which of these is a fixed operating expense?
c: Repairs and maintenance
Cleaning supplies
Utilities for common areas
Property insurance
questions.x: Fixed expenses, like insurance and real estate taxes, do not change with occupancy. Repairs, utilities and supplies vary with use; common area utilities are tempting but still rise and fall with activity.

questions.q: A mixed-use building collects 65% of its gross rent from apartments and 35% from stores. For federal depreciation it will most likely be treated as:
c: Nonresidential real property, 39 years
Residential rental property, 27.5 years
Land, which is not depreciable
Split: 27.5 years for apartments, 39 for stores
questions.x: A building is residential rental property only if at least 80% of gross rental income comes from dwelling units. At 65% it is nonresidential, 39 years for the whole building. The IRS does not split one building's recovery period by use.

questions.q: An investor buys an apartment building for $2,000,000. The land is worth 25% of the total. Using straight-line depreciation over 27.5 years, annual depreciation is about:
questions.x: Building basis = $2,000,000 x 75% = $1,500,000; $1,500,000 / 27.5 = $54,545. Including the land gives $72,727, but land is not depreciated. $38,462 uses 39 years, the nonresidential period.

questions.q: A property has NOI of $120,000. Similar properties sell at an 8% cap rate. Its estimated value is:
questions.x: V = I / R = $120,000 / 0.08 = $1,500,000. Multiplying by 8 gives $960,000, and misplacing the decimal (0.008) gives $15,000,000.

questions.q: A building sold for $1,000,000 and produces NOI of $75,000. The capitalization rate is:
questions.x: R = I / V = $75,000 / $1,000,000 = 7.5%. Dividing value by income (13.3) gives a multiplier, not a rate.

questions.q: An investor pays $2,200,000 for a property at a 6.5% cap rate. The property's NOI is:
questions.x: I = R x V = 0.065 x $2,200,000 = $143,000. Dividing price by 6.5 instead of multiplying gives $338,462.
questions.concept: NOI from cap rate and value

questions.q: If NOI stays the same and the capitalization rate rises, the property's value will:
c: Rise
Double
Stay the same
Fall
questions.x: Value = NOI / cap rate. A larger rate in the denominator produces a smaller value; rate and value move in opposite directions. 'Rise' is the trap for anyone who thinks a higher rate is better for the seller.

questions.q: Three comparable sales: Sale A sold for $1,000,000 with NOI of $65,000; Sale B sold for $1,500,000 with NOI of $105,000; Sale C sold for $800,000 with NOI of $60,000. Using the average cap rate, what is the value of a subject with NOI of $84,000?
questions.x: Cap rates: A 6.5%, B 7%, C 7.5%; average 7%. V = $84,000 / 0.07 = $1,200,000. Using only Sale A's 6.5% gives $1,292,308.

questions.q: An 8-unit building rents each unit for $2,000 a month. Vacancy and credit loss is 5%, operating expenses are $60,000, and the market cap rate is 7%. The building's value is closest to:
A retail building produces net operating income of $10,000 per month. At an 8% capitalization rate, its value is:
questions.x: Annual NOI = $10,000 x 12 = $120,000. V = $120,000 / 0.08 = $1,500,000. Capitalizing the monthly figure gives $125,000.

questions.q: A building's NOI is $150,000. If market cap rates rise from 6% to 7.5%, the building's value will fall by:
questions.x: At 6%: $150,000 / 0.06 = $2,500,000. At 7.5%: $150,000 / 0.075 = $2,000,000. The drop is $500,000. $375,000 applies the 1.5-point rate change as 15% of the original value.

questions.q: An owner cuts $6,000 a year from operating expenses on a building valued at a 6% cap rate. How much value does this add?
questions.x: Added NOI of $6,000 / 0.06 = $100,000 of added value; every dollar of NOI is worth about $16.67 at a 6% cap. $36,000 multiplies by 6 instead of dividing by 0.06.

questions.q: Compared with a fully leased pharmacy on a 20-year net lease, a half-vacant office building in a weak market would most likely sell at:
c: A higher cap rate, reflecting its risk
A lower cap rate, reflecting its upside
The same cap rate, since cap rates are set by the market
No cap rate, because vacancy makes NOI unusable
questions.x: Riskier income demands a higher return, so investors apply a higher cap rate and pay less per dollar of NOI. The 'upside' argument is the trap; buyers price the risk before the hoped-for lease-up.

questions.q: A property's NOI is $180,000 and its annual debt service is $150,000. The debt coverage ratio is:
questions.x: DCR = NOI / debt service = $180,000 / $150,000 = 1.20. Dividing the other way gives 0.83. $30,000 is the before-tax cash flow, not a ratio.

questions.q: A debt coverage ratio below 1.0 means:
c: The loan has been fully paid off
The cap rate is below the loan's interest rate
The property has positive leverage
NOI falls short of the annual debt service
questions.x: With DCR under 1.0, NOI is smaller than debt service, so the owner must add money to pay the loan; lenders require a cushion above 1.0. Comparing cap rate and interest rate is a leverage test, not coverage.

questions.q: To derive a market cap rate from comparable sales, an appraiser needs all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Each buyer's mortgage interest rate
Each comparable's net operating income
Proof the comparables are similar to the subject
Each comparable's sale price
questions.x: The cap rate is NOI divided by price, so financing terms are not part of it. Comparability is tempting to drop, but a cap rate from dissimilar properties is meaningless.

questions.q: An investor requires a 9% cap rate. A building with NOI of $96,000 is offered at $1,200,000. Which is true?
c: It meets her target, since the cap rate is 9%
It implies 8%, so she can pay up to $1,308,000
It implies a 12.5% cap rate, well above her target
It implies 8%; at 9% she should pay about $1,066,667
questions.x: $96,000 / $1,200,000 = 8%, below her 9% target. Her maximum price is $96,000 / 0.09 = $1,066,667. Raising the price by 9% ($1,308,000) moves in the wrong direction: a higher required rate means a lower price.

questions.q: A strip center sells for $4,000,000. Effective gross income is $500,000 and operating expenses are $180,000. The cap rate is:
questions.x: NOI = $500,000 minus $180,000 = $320,000. R = $320,000 / $4,000,000 = 8%. Using gross income instead of NOI gives 12.5%.

questions.q: Direct capitalization converts into value:
c: One year's net operating income
The sum of future rents with no discount
The replacement cost of the improvements
Gross rent multiplied by the cap rate
questions.x: Direct capitalization divides one year's NOI by a cap rate. Discounted cash flow is the multi-year method (and it does discount), and replacement cost belongs to the cost approach.

questions.q: An investor bought a building at a 6% cap rate when its NOI was $90,000. NOI has since grown to $99,000, and the market cap rate is still 6%. The building is now worth:
questions.x: Original value $90,000 / 0.06 = $1,500,000. New value $99,000 / 0.06 = $1,650,000. A 10% rise in NOI raised value 10%; $1,500,000 forgets that value follows NOI.

questions.q: A building valued at $3,600,000 trades at a 5.5% cap rate. Its NOI is:
questions.x: I = R x V = 0.055 x $3,600,000 = $198,000. Dividing the value by 5.5 instead gives $654,545.
questions.concept: NOI from cap rate and value

questions.q: If market cap rates fall while a building's NOI stays the same, its value will:
c: Fall by the same percentage
Fall
Stay the same
Rise
questions.x: Value = NOI / rate; a smaller denominator produces a larger value. Rates and values move in opposite directions, so falling rates raise values.

questions.q: Comparable sales: Sale 1, $2,000,000 price, $160,000 NOI; Sale 2, $1,250,000 price, $95,000 NOI; Sale 3, $3,000,000 price, $252,000 NOI. Using the average cap rate, the value of a subject with NOI of $128,000 is:
questions.x: Cap rates are 8%, 7.6% and 8.4%; the average is 8%. V = $128,000 / 0.08 = $1,600,000. Using only Sale 2's 7.6% gives $1,684,211.

questions.q: A 10-unit building rents each unit for $2,500 a month. Vacancy and credit loss is 4%, operating expenses are $108,000 and the cap rate is 6%. The building's value is:
A store produces NOI of $8,250 per month. At a 6% cap rate, its value is:
questions.x: Annual NOI = $99,000; $99,000 / 0.06 = $1,650,000. Capitalizing the monthly figure gives $137,500.

questions.q: A building's NOI is $240,000. If market cap rates fall from 8% to 6%, its value will rise by:
questions.x: At 8%: $3,000,000. At 6%: $4,000,000. Value rises $1,000,000. $4,000,000 is the new value, not the change.

questions.q: An owner adds $9,000 a year of laundry income to a building valued at a 7.5% cap rate. The value added is about:
questions.x: $9,000 / 0.075 = $120,000. Multiplying by the rate ($675) inverts the formula.

questions.q: Which property would most likely trade at the LOWEST cap rate?
c: A bank branch on a new 25-year net lease
A half-vacant suburban office building
A roadside motel near a shuttered factory
A warehouse with one tenant leaving next year
questions.x: Long, creditworthy, net leased income is the least risky, so buyers accept the lowest cap rate. Each other property carries vacancy or market risk that pushes its cap rate up.

questions.q: NOI is $260,000 and annual debt service is $200,000. The debt coverage ratio is:
questions.x: DCR = $260,000 / $200,000 = 1.30. Dividing the other way gives 0.77, and $60,000 is BTCF.

questions.q: A lender requires a 1.25 debt coverage ratio. A property's NOI is $250,000. The maximum annual debt service the lender will allow is:
questions.x: Debt service = NOI / DCR = $250,000 / 1.25 = $200,000. Multiplying instead gives $312,500, which would leave coverage below 1.0.

questions.q: When deriving a cap rate from comparable sales, which item is NOT needed?
c: The sale price of each comparable property
The loan-to-value ratio on each sale
The NOI of each comparable
The date and conditions of each sale
questions.x: Cap rate = NOI / price, so financing such as LTV is irrelevant. Sale date and conditions matter because stale or non-arm's-length sales distort the rate.

questions.q: A buyer requires a 7% cap rate. A building with NOI of $126,000 is offered at $2,100,000. Which is true?
c: It implies 16.7%, far above her required rate
It implies 7%, matching her required cap rate
It implies 6%; at 7% she would pay up to $1,800,000
It implies 6%; at 7% she could pay up to $2,247,000
questions.x: $126,000 / $2,100,000 = 6%, below her target. Her maximum price is $126,000 / 0.07 = $1,800,000. Raising the price by 7% moves the wrong way; a higher required rate lowers the price.

questions.q: An office building sells for $6,000,000. EGI is $720,000 and operating expenses are $330,000. The cap rate is:
questions.x: NOI = $390,000; $390,000 / $6,000,000 = 6.5%. Using EGI gives 12%, and dividing the price by NOI gives 15.4, a multiplier.

questions.q: An appraiser divides one year's stabilized NOI by a market cap rate. This method is:
c: Discounted cash flow analysis
The gross rent multiplier
The cost approach
Direct capitalization
questions.x: One year's NOI divided by a rate is direct capitalization. DCF discounts several years of cash flows, and a GRM uses gross rent, not NOI.

questions.q: A building was bought at a 5% cap rate when NOI was $100,000. NOI then drops to $92,000 while the cap rate holds at 5%. The value is now:
questions.x: Original value $2,000,000; new value $92,000 / 0.05 = $1,840,000. An 8% drop in NOI cuts value 8%; $2,000,000 forgets that value follows NOI.

questions.q: A tenant's usable area plus its pro rata share of the lobby, corridors and restrooms equals its:
c: Rentable area
Carpetable area
Gross building area
Usable area
questions.x: Usable plus a share of common areas is rentable area. Gross building area measures the whole building, including exterior walls.

questions.q: For the same office suite, which measurement is the SMALLEST?
c: Rentable area
Carpetable area
Usable area
Gross building area
questions.x: Carpetable area removes walls, columns and built-ins from usable area, so it is smallest. Usable is the trap: it is smaller than rentable but larger than carpetable.

questions.q: A floor has 20,000 rentable square feet and 17,000 usable square feet. The loss factor is:
questions.x: Loss factor = 3,000 / 20,000 = 15%. Dividing by usable gives 17.6%, which is the add-on factor.

questions.q: A floor measures 24,000 rentable and 20,000 usable square feet. The add-on factor is:
questions.x: Add-on = 24,000 / 20,000 minus 1 = 20%. The loss factor (4,000 / 24,000 = 16.7%) is the near-miss.

questions.q: A tenant needs 6,400 usable square feet. The loss factor is 20%, and rent is $60 per rentable square foot. Annual base rent is:
Space rents for $54 per rentable square foot with a 25% loss factor. The cost per usable square foot is:
questions.x: $54 / (1 minus 0.25) = $72.00. Adding 25% ($67.50) understates it because the loss factor is measured against rentable area.

questions.q: Which space would be counted in a tenant's usable area rather than as common area?
c: The building's main lobby and security desk
The shared restrooms on the floor
A conference room inside the suite
The ground-floor mailroom
questions.x: Space inside the tenant's suite is usable area. Shared restrooms are tempting because they serve the tenant's floor, but they are common area shared with others.

questions.q: Under a typical triple net lease, who pays the property's real estate taxes?
c: The landlord
The managing agent
The lender
The tenant
questions.x: A triple net lease shifts taxes, insurance and maintenance to the tenant. The landlord pays them under a gross lease, the trap.

questions.q: A single net lease generally adds which cost to the tenant's base rent?
c: Real estate taxes
Insurance and repairs
Taxes, insurance and repairs
Utilities and cleaning
questions.x: A single net lease passes through real estate taxes. Taxes, insurance and repairs together describe a triple net lease.

questions.q: A lease calls for $150,000 base rent plus 6% of gross sales over the natural breakpoint. The breakpoint is:
questions.x: Breakpoint = $150,000 / 0.06 = $2,500,000. Multiplying ($9,000) is the classic error.

questions.q: Base rent is $72,000 plus 4% of gross sales over the natural breakpoint. Sales are $2,300,000. Total rent is:
questions.x: Breakpoint = $72,000 / 0.04 = $1,800,000. Overage = 4% x $500,000 = $20,000. Total = $92,000. Adding 4% of all sales to base ($164,000) double counts.

questions.q: A lease charges $48,000 base rent plus 6% of gross sales over the natural breakpoint. Sales were $750,000. Total rent is:
questions.x: Breakpoint = $48,000 / 0.06 = $800,000. Sales fell short, so only base rent is due: $48,000. Base rent is a minimum, so $45,000 (6% of sales) is wrong.

questions.q: After a lender forecloses on an office building, a clause in a tenant's lease requires the tenant to accept the lender as its new landlord. This clause is:
c: Subordination
Attornment
Non-disturbance
Estoppel
questions.x: Attornment is the tenant's agreement to recognize the new owner. Non-disturbance is the lender's matching promise to the tenant, the tempting partner clause.

questions.q: An estoppel certificate signed by a tenant mainly protects:
c: The landlord against the tenant's assignment
The tenant against losing its lease in a foreclosure
A buyer or lender relying on the stated lease terms
The broker's right to a leasing commission
questions.x: The tenant certifies rent, term and defaults, and cannot later contradict those facts against the buyer or lender. Protection from foreclosure is the job of a non-disturbance agreement.

questions.q: A non-disturbance agreement primarily protects which party?
c: The landlord's lender
The landlord
The building's buyer
The tenant
questions.x: The lender promises not to terminate a non-defaulting tenant's lease after foreclosure. The lender is the party giving the promise, not receiving it.

questions.q: A tenant with 5 years left lets another company occupy half of its space for 2 years. This is a(n):
c: Sublease
Assignment
Attornment
Novation
questions.x: Transferring less than the whole space or term is a sublease. An assignment transfers the entire remaining interest.

questions.q: Which tenant has a statutory right under RPL 226-b to request to sublet, subject to the landlord's reasonable consent?
c: A retail tenant in a Manhattan shopping center
A residential tenant in a building with 4 or more units
An office tenant on a lease of 10 years or more
Any commercial tenant whose lease is silent on subletting
questions.x: RPL 226-b protects residential tenants in buildings with 4 or more units. Commercial tenants get sublet rights only from their lease.

questions.q: A landlord buys power on one master meter and bills each office tenant from its own meter readings. This arrangement is:
c: Direct metering
Rent inclusion
Submetering
A porter's wage pass-through
questions.x: A master meter with tenant meters and landlord billing is submetering. Direct metering means the tenant has its own utility account.

questions.q: Under rent inclusion, the cost of a tenant's electricity is:
c: Paid by the tenant directly to the utility
Charged to the tenant as a CAM pass-through
Billed monthly from a submeter reading
Built into the rent paid to the landlord
questions.x: Rent inclusion folds electricity into the rent, often adjusted by a survey. Submeter billing is a separate method based on measured use.

questions.q: Each of the following is true of direct metering EXCEPT:
c: The landlord rebills usage with a markup
The tenant pays the utility company directly
The tenant has its own account with the utility
The landlord carries no usage risk for that space
questions.x: Rebilling with a markup describes submetering. Under direct metering the tenant deals with the utility, so the landlord has no usage risk.

questions.q: A landlord promises a bakery an exclusive in a strip center. To honor that promise, the landlord will rely mainly on:
c: A percentage rent clause in the bakery's own lease
Narrow use clauses in the other tenants' leases
Non-disturbance agreements with each tenant
A porter's wage clause in the other leases
questions.x: Restricting what the other tenants may sell is done through narrow use clauses. Percentage rent concerns how much the bakery pays, not who competes with it.

questions.q: A tenant takes raw space in a former SoHo warehouse at a low rent and pays for its own improvements. This is typical of a:
c: Ground lease
Percentage lease
Loft lease
Gross office lease
