questions.x: Raw, open space in an old manufacturing building, built out by the tenant for a lower rent, is a loft lease. A ground lease involves land, not space in an existing building.

questions.q: Common area maintenance charges in a shopping center typically cover:
c: The anchor tenant's percentage rent
Repairs to each tenant's own storefront and interior
The landlord's mortgage interest
Parking lot plowing, lighting and cleaning
questions.x: CAM covers shared areas such as parking lots and walkways. Each tenant's own premises are its own responsibility, not a common area cost.

questions.q: The main benefit of a good guy guarantee to the principal of a New York City office tenant is that:
c: Liability ends once the space is surrendered with notice
It covers rent for the full term no matter what
It replaces any need for a security deposit
It lets the tenant assign the lease without landlord consent
questions.x: The guarantor is liable only through a proper surrender with notice, capping exposure. It does not replace the security deposit or change assignment rights.

questions.q: A landlord signing a 15-year office lease adds escalation clauses mainly so that:
c: The tenant can cut its rent if business slows
Rising costs do not erode the landlord's NOI
The tenant gains an option to renew at market
The landlord can terminate the lease early
questions.x: Escalations pass increases in taxes and operating costs through to the tenant, protecting NOI over a long term. Rent reductions tied to sales are not escalations.

questions.q: A tenant leases 12,000 rentable square feet in a 400,000 rentable square foot building. Its proportionate share is:
questions.x: 12,000 / 400,000 = 3%. Misplacing the decimal gives 0.3% or 30%.

questions.q: A tenant occupies 8,000 of a building's 200,000 RSF. Taxes were $2,500,000 in the base year and are $2,650,000 now. The tenant's tax escalation is:
questions.x: Share = 4%; increase = $150,000; 4% x $150,000 = $6,000. $106,000 is 4% of the whole current tax bill.

questions.q: A tenant has 15,000 RSF in a 300,000 RSF building. Base year operating expenses were $4,200,000; this year they are $4,410,000. The tenant's escalation is:
questions.x: Share = 5%; increase = $210,000; 5% x $210,000 = $10,500. $220,500 is 5% of the whole budget.

questions.q: A lease sets an expense stop of $12.50 per RSF. Actual expenses are $13.40 per RSF and the tenant leases 6,000 RSF. Additional rent is:
questions.x: Excess = $0.90 x 6,000 = $5,400. $80,400 charges the full expense rather than the amount over the stop.

questions.q: A lease says the tenant pays its share of operating costs above "$14.00 per rentable square foot." This provision is a(n):
c: Base year clause
Porter's wage clause
Expense stop
CPI adjustment
questions.x: A fixed dollar threshold written into the lease is an expense stop. A base year uses whatever actual costs turn out to be in a named year.

questions.q: A porter's wage clause has a multiplier of 1. The wage rises 75 cents an hour, and the tenant leases 8,000 RSF. The annual escalation is:
questions.x: $0.75 x 1 x 8,000 = $6,000. Treating the 75 cents as 7.5 cents gives $600.

questions.q: A porter's wage formula uses a multiplier of 2. The wage rises from $31.20 to $31.65, and the tenant leases 5,000 RSF. The escalation is:
questions.x: Increase = $0.45; $0.45 x 2 x 5,000 = $4,500. Ignoring the multiplier gives $2,250.

questions.q: A lease starts at $200,000 a year with 3% annual increases, compounded. Rent in year 3 is:
Base rent is $120,000, adjusted by the full change in CPI, which rose from 300 to 315. The new rent is:
questions.x: CPI change = 15 / 300 = 5%; $120,000 x 1.05 = $126,000. Treating the 15-point change as 15% gives $138,000.

questions.q: A lease raises rent by 50% of the change in CPI. Base rent is $96,000 and the CPI rose from 240 to 252. The new rent is:
questions.x: CPI rose 5%; half is 2.5%; $96,000 x 1.025 = $98,400. Using the full 5% gives $100,800.

questions.q: Which economic conditions led New York landlords to adopt escalation clauses widely?
c: Rent stabilization's extension to offices in 1969
Falling office vacancy rates in the 1950s
The 2008 credit crisis and falling rents
High inflation and energy costs in the 1970s
questions.x: 1970s inflation and energy shocks squeezed landlords with flat long-term rents. Rent stabilization (1969) is a residential program and never covered offices.

questions.q: A porter's wage escalation ties a tenant's rent increases to:
c: The hourly wage of building service workers
The landlord's actual operating expenses
Changes in the Consumer Price Index
The tenant's gross sales above a natural breakpoint
questions.x: The formula uses the union porter's hourly wage as a proxy for costs. Tracking actual expenses is a direct operating escalation, the trap.

questions.q: A tenant's operating base year is 2025. Expenses were $5,000,000 in 2025, $4,800,000 in 2026 and $5,300,000 in 2027. The 2027 escalation is based on an increase of:
questions.x: Escalations are measured against the base year, not the prior year: $5,300,000 minus $5,000,000 = $300,000. Measuring from 2026 gives $500,000.

questions.q: Which of the following is a lease escalation method?
c: Natural breakpoint
CPI adjustment
Attornment clause
Estoppel certificate
questions.x: A CPI adjustment raises rent with inflation. The natural breakpoint belongs to percentage leases, and attornment and estoppel deal with lenders and buyers.

questions.q: A tenant has 9,000 usable and 10,800 rentable square feet in a building of 360,000 rentable square feet. Its proportionate share is:
questions.x: Share uses rentable area: 10,800 / 360,000 = 3%. Using usable area (9,000 / 360,000) gives 2.5%.

questions.q: An NYC lease uses a tax base year of "2025/2026." That base year runs from:
c: January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2026
April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026
July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026
October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026
questions.x: NYC's tax year runs July 1 to June 30. April to March is the New York State fiscal year, and October to September is the federal one.

questions.q: Which cost would a landlord typically be able to pass through in an operating expense escalation?
c: Interest on the building's mortgage
Depreciation of the building
Leasing commissions paid for other tenants
Wages of the building's cleaning staff
questions.x: Cleaning payroll is a core operating expense. Mortgage interest is financing, depreciation is a tax item, and leasing commissions are capital costs, all typically excluded.

questions.q: Rentable square footage is best defined as:
c: Gross area including exterior walls and garage
The space the tenant occupies exclusively
The floor area that can be carpeted
Usable space plus a share of common areas
questions.x: Rentable = usable plus a pro rata share of common areas like the lobby and corridors. The tenant's exclusive space alone is usable area, the most common mix-up.

questions.q: For the same office suite, which correctly ranks the measurements from largest to smallest?
c: Usable, rentable, carpetable
Carpetable, usable, rentable
Rentable, carpetable, usable
Rentable, usable, carpetable
questions.x: Rentable includes the common area share, usable is the tenant's own space, and carpetable subtracts walls, columns and built-ins from usable. Swapping rentable and usable is the usual trap.

questions.q: A floor has 15,000 rentable square feet and 12,000 usable square feet. The loss factor is:
questions.x: Loss factor = (15,000 minus 12,000) / 15,000 = 20%. Dividing by usable gives 25%, which is the add-on factor.

questions.q: A suite has 11,500 rentable square feet and 10,000 usable square feet. The add-on factor is:
questions.x: Add-on = rentable / usable minus 1 = 1.15 minus 1 = 15%. The loss factor would be 1,500 / 11,500, about 13%, the tempting near-miss.

questions.q: A law firm needs 9,000 usable square feet. The building's loss factor is 25%, and rent is $50 per rentable square foot per year. The firm's annual base rent will be:
questions.x: Rentable = usable / (1 minus loss factor) = 9,000 / 0.75 = 12,000 RSF; rent = 12,000 x $50 = $600,000. Adding 25% to usable (11,250 RSF, $562,500) applies the factor to the wrong base.

questions.q: Space is offered at $48 per rentable square foot with a 20% loss factor. The effective cost per usable square foot is:
questions.x: Cost per usable = $48 / (1 minus 0.20) = $60. Adding 20% ($57.60) understates it because the loss factor is based on rentable, not usable.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a building common area?
c: The main lobby used by every tenant
A tenant's private conference room
A storage closet inside a tenant's suite
A kitchen pantry within a tenant's space
questions.x: Common areas are shared by the tenants, like lobbies, corridors and mechanical rooms. A private conference room is tempting because it is 'shared' within the firm, but space inside a suite is usable area.

questions.q: Under a gross lease, the operating expenses of the property are generally paid by the:
c: Managing agent
Tenant
Lender
Landlord
questions.x: In a gross lease the tenant pays a flat rent and the landlord covers expenses. Tenant is the trap: in a net lease the tenant pays some or all expenses on top of rent.

questions.q: Under a typical triple net (NNN) lease, the tenant pays base rent plus:
c: Taxes, insurance and maintenance
Real estate taxes and nothing else
Utilities used inside its own space
The landlord's mortgage payments
questions.x: NNN shifts the three nets (taxes, insurance, maintenance/CAM) to the tenant. Taxes alone describes a single net lease. Tenants do not pay the landlord's mortgage directly under any net lease.

questions.q: A store's lease calls for $90,000 annual base rent plus 5% of gross sales above the natural breakpoint. The natural breakpoint is:
questions.x: Natural breakpoint = base rent / percentage rate = $90,000 / 0.05 = $1,800,000. Multiplying ($90,000 x 0.05 = $4,500) is the classic wrong move.

questions.q: A tenant pays $60,000 base rent plus 5% of gross sales over the natural breakpoint. Sales for the year are $1,600,000. Total rent for the year is:
questions.x: Breakpoint = $60,000 / 0.05 = $1,200,000. Overage = 5% x $400,000 = $20,000. Total = $80,000. Adding 5% of all sales to base ($140,000) double counts the base.

questions.q: Same lease: $60,000 base rent plus 5% of sales over the natural breakpoint. This year sales were only $1,000,000. Total rent is:
questions.x: Sales did not reach the $1,200,000 breakpoint, so no percentage rent is due and the tenant pays the $60,000 base. Base rent is a minimum and is not reduced, so $50,000 is wrong.

questions.q: A lease clause in which the tenant agrees to recognize a new owner, including a foreclosing lender, as its landlord is called:
c: Estoppel
Assignment
Subordination
Attornment
questions.x: Attornment is the tenant's promise to accept the new owner as landlord. Subordination is the trap: it ranks the lease below the mortgage but does not make the tenant recognize the buyer.

questions.q: Before closing on an office building, the buyer's lender wants each tenant to confirm in writing its rent, security deposit, lease term and that the landlord is not in default. The lender is requesting:
c: Estoppel certificates
Non-disturbance agreements
Assignments of lease
Letters of intent
questions.x: Estoppel certificates lock in the facts; a tenant cannot later claim different terms against the buyer or lender. Non-disturbance agreements are lender documents too, but they protect the tenant.

questions.q: A restaurant tenant is about to spend $400,000 on a build-out and fears losing its lease if the landlord's lender forecloses. The tenant should seek a(n):
c: An estoppel certificate from the landlord
A narrow use clause
A non-disturbance agreement
A CPI escalation clause
questions.x: In a non-disturbance agreement the lender promises not to terminate the lease after foreclosure while the tenant is not in default, usually packaged as an SNDA. An estoppel certifies facts and protects the buyer or lender, not the tenant.

questions.q: A tenant transfers its entire remaining lease term and all of its space to another company. This is a(n):
c: A sublease
A novation
An attornment agreement
An assignment
questions.x: Transferring the whole remaining interest is an assignment; a sublease transfers less than all (part of the space or term). A novation would require the landlord to release the original tenant, which is not stated.

questions.q: A Manhattan retail tenant wants to sublet half its store. Its lease prohibits subletting without the landlord's consent. Which is correct?
c: The lease controls; RPL 226-b is a residential rule
The landlord cannot refuse, since the store is in Manhattan
Subleasing retail space is illegal in New York City
RPL 226-b gives every New York tenant a right to sublet
questions.x: RPL 226-b protects residential tenants in buildings of 4 or more units. Commercial sublet and assignment rights come from the lease itself, which commonly requires landlord consent.

questions.q: When a tenant has its own utility meter and an account with Con Edison, the electricity arrangement is:
c: Rent inclusion
Submetering
Direct metering
Porter's wage clause
questions.x: Direct metering means the tenant contracts with and pays the utility itself. Submetering is the trap: the tenant has a meter, but billing runs through the landlord.

questions.q: In a submetered office building, electricity is typically:
c: Billed to tenants by a survey of connected load
Built into the rent at a flat rate with no metering of use
Paid by each tenant directly to the utility company
Bought on a master meter and billed by each tenant's use
questions.x: The landlord buys in bulk, a submeter measures each tenant's consumption, and the landlord bills the tenant, often with an administrative charge. Paying the utility directly is direct metering.

questions.q: All of the following are true of electricity under a rent inclusion arrangement EXCEPT:
c: The tenant pays the utility company directly
The landlord bears the usage risk unless the lease adjusts
The charge may be adjusted after an electrical survey
The cost is built into the rent
questions.x: Paying the utility directly is direct metering. Under rent inclusion the electricity charge is part of the rent paid to the landlord, often adjusted by a survey of the tenant's equipment.

questions.q: A landlord wants a narrow use clause in a retail lease mainly to:
c: Raise the tenant's loss factor and rentable area
Protect other tenants' exclusives and the tenant mix
Shift the building's real estate taxes onto the tenant
Let the tenant assign the lease freely
questions.x: A narrow use clause keeps the tenant in its lane, protects exclusives promised to other tenants, and keeps uses within the certificate of occupancy. It makes assignment harder, not easier.

questions.q: A loft lease most typically involves:
c: A furnished apartment in a full-service doorman building
A 99-year ground lease of vacant land
Raw open space the tenant builds out itself
A store lease inside a regional mall
questions.x: Loft space is big, open and often taken close to as is, with the tenant paying for its build-out in exchange for lower rent. A ground lease also has the tenant building, but on vacant land, not inside an existing building.

questions.q: A shoe store in a Long Island neighborhood center is billed its share of the cost of plowing and lighting the parking lot. That charge is a:
c: Percentage rent
A base year real estate tax escalation
Porter's wage escalation
Common area maintenance (CAM)
questions.x: CAM charges pass through the cost of maintaining shared areas like parking lots and walkways, usually by proportionate share. A porter's wage escalation is tied to a wage rate, not to actual lot costs.

questions.q: In a New York City office lease, a good guy guarantee generally makes the guarantor liable for:
c: Rent until the tenant vacates and surrenders with notice
The landlord's mortgage on the building
Every dollar of rent for the full remaining lease term
Rent for the remaining term, minus the security deposit
questions.x: The good guy guarantee limits the principal's exposure to the period before a clean surrender with proper notice. Full-term liability is the trap; that is a full guaranty, which the good guy version replaces.

questions.q: The main purpose of a lease escalation clause is to:
c: Let the tenant reduce its rent when sales fall
Protect the landlord's NOI from rising costs
Set the sales level where percentage rent begins
Give the tenant an option to buy the building
questions.x: Escalations raise rent as taxes, operating costs or prices rise, so a long lease does not erode the landlord's NOI. Setting the sales level for percentage rent is the natural breakpoint, a different clause.

questions.q: A tenant leases 7,500 rentable square feet in a 150,000 rentable square foot building. Its proportionate share is:
questions.x: Share = 7,500 / 150,000 = 5%. Dividing the other way gives 20 (not a percentage share).

questions.q: A tenant occupies 3,000 of a building's 60,000 rentable square feet. Real estate taxes were $900,000 in the base year and $960,000 this year. The tenant's tax escalation is:
questions.x: Share = 3,000 / 60,000 = 5%. Increase = $60,000. Escalation = 5% x $60,000 = $3,000. $48,000 is 5% of the whole tax bill, which the tenant does not pay on top of base rent.

questions.q: A tenant has 10,000 RSF in a 250,000 RSF building. Operating expenses were $3,000,000 in the base year and are $3,150,000 this year. The tenant's operating escalation is:
questions.x: Share = 10,000 / 250,000 = 4%. Increase = $150,000. 4% x $150,000 = $6,000. $126,000 is 4% of the whole expense budget.

questions.q: A lease has an operating expense stop of $10.00 per rentable square foot. Actual expenses this year are $11.25 per square foot. The tenant leases 4,000 RSF. The tenant owes additional rent of:
questions.x: Excess = $11.25 minus $10.00 = $1.25 per RSF; $1.25 x 4,000 = $5,000. The tenant pays only the amount above the stop; $45,000 charges the full expense.

questions.q: The key difference between a base year and an expense stop is that:
c: A base year is a fixed dollar figure; a stop uses actual costs
A stop applies to taxes; a base year applies to operating costs
A base year uses actual costs; a stop is a fixed dollar figure
A base year appears in retail leases; a stop in office leases
questions.x: The base year baseline is whatever expenses turn out to be in that named year; a stop is a dollar number agreed at signing. The reversed answer is the trap. Both methods can apply to taxes or operating costs.

questions.q: A lease uses a porter's wage formula with a multiplier of 1 (one cent per square foot for each cent of wage increase). The porter's hourly wage rises 90 cents. The tenant has 6,000 RSF. The annual escalation is:
questions.x: $0.90 x 1 x 6,000 = $5,400. Treating the 90 cents as 9 cents gives $540; $6,000 multiplies a full dollar.

questions.q: A porter's wage clause uses a multiplier of 1.5. The porter's hourly wage rises from $29.40 to $30.00. The tenant leases 10,000 RSF. The annual escalation is:
questions.x: Wage increase = $0.60. Escalation = $0.60 x 1.5 x 10,000 = $9,000. Ignoring the multiplier gives $6,000.

questions.q: A store lease starts at $100,000 a year with fixed 4% annual increases, compounded. Rent in year 3 will be:
questions.x: Year 2: $104,000. Year 3: $104,000 x 1.04 = $108,160. Simple (non-compounded) increases give $108,000, and $104,000 is only year 2.

questions.q: Base rent is $90,000. The lease adjusts rent by the full change in the Consumer Price Index, which rose from 250 to 260. The new rent is:
questions.x: CPI change = 10 / 250 = 4%; $90,000 x 1.04 = $93,600. Treating the 10-point change as 10% gives $99,000.

questions.q: A lease raises rent by 75% of the change in CPI. Base rent is $80,000 and the CPI rose from 200 to 210. The new rent is:
questions.x: CPI rose 5%. 75% of 5% = 3.75%; $80,000 x 3.75% = $3,000, so new rent is $83,000. Using the full 5% gives $84,000.

questions.q: Escalation clauses became standard in New York commercial leases largely because:
c: Tenants sought them as a way to lower their rent
A 1934 federal law required them in commercial leases
Rent stabilization was extended to Manhattan office space
1970s inflation and energy costs squeezed fixed rents
questions.x: Rapid cost increases in the 1970s squeezed landlords holding flat long-term rents, so escalations were added to pass cost increases through. Rent stabilization is a residential program and never covered offices.

questions.q: Tenants often object to porter's wage escalations because:
c: Wages can rise faster than the actual costs
They are illegal in New York commercial leases
They are tied to the tenant's gross sales
They tend to lower rent below market
questions.x: The porter's wage is a proxy for costs; if wages outpace real expenses, the tenant pays more than the landlord's actual increase, a windfall. The clauses are legal and still appear in older NYC leases.

questions.q: A tenant's lease has a base year operating escalation. This year, operating expenses fell below the base year after the landlord switched cleaning contractors. Under a typical lease, the tenant:
c: It receives a credit for its share of the decrease
It owes no escalation; base rent is unchanged
Its base rent is permanently reduced
It keeps paying last year's escalation amount
questions.x: Escalations charge a share of increases over the base. Typical leases give no credit below the base, so the tenant simply pays base rent; the credit answer is the intuitive but wrong 'fairness' trap.

questions.q: All of the following are lease escalation methods EXCEPT:
c: Porter's wage formula
CPI adjustment
Natural breakpoint
Expense stop
questions.x: The natural breakpoint belongs to percentage leases: it is the sales level where percentage rent starts. Porter's wage, CPI and expense stops are all ways to raise rent with costs or inflation.

questions.q: A tenant's proportionate share for escalation purposes is usually based on:
c: Its usable area divided by the building's usable area
Its carpetable area divided by total carpetable area
Its gross sales compared with the whole center's total sales
Its rentable area divided by the building's rentable area
questions.x: Shares are almost always computed on rentable square feet, the same basis as rent. Usable over usable is the tempting trap because it feels 'fairer' to the tenant.

questions.q: An NYC office lease names a tax base year of "2026/2027." This is because New York City's real estate tax year runs:
c: July 1 to June 30
January 1 to December 31
April 1 to March 31
October 1 to September 30
questions.x: NYC's fiscal and tax year runs July 1 to June 30, so tax base years span two calendar years. April 1 to March 31 is New York State's fiscal year, the closest trap.

questions.q: Under a direct operating escalation, the tenant shares in increases in all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Cleaning contract costs
The landlord's mortgage payments
Building staff payroll
Premiums for the building's insurance policies
questions.x: Debt service is the owner's financing cost, not an operating expense, so it is excluded from escalations. Insurance is tempting to exclude as an 'owner' cost, but it is a standard operating expense.

questions.q: A warehouse returns 7.5% free and clear. A lender offers a loan with a mortgage constant of 6.8%. If the buyer borrows 70% of the price, the return on the buyer's cash will most likely:
c: Fall below 7.5%, because the annual debt service reduces the cash flow left over
Stay at 7.5%, because leverage does not change the property's NOI
Rise above 7.5%, because each borrowed dollar costs less than it earns
Fall to the 6.8% loan constant, because the loan sets the return
questions.x: When the property's return (7.5%) beats the loan constant (6.8%), leverage is positive and the return on equity rises. It is true that leverage does not change NOI, but it does change what the owner earns on the cash actually invested.

questions.q: A buyer can purchase a building returning 5.5% free and clear. The best available loan has a mortgage constant of 7.2%. Compared with paying all cash, borrowing will:
c: Lower the return on the investor's cash, producing negative leverage
Raise the return on equity, because the investor puts in less cash
Raise the cap rate, because a smaller down payment improves the yield
Leave the return on cash unchanged, because the NOI stays the same
questions.x: Each borrowed dollar costs 7.2% a year but earns only 5.5%, so the owner's cash subsidizes the loan: negative leverage. Putting in less cash only helps when the loan is cheaper than the property's return, and leverage never changes the cap rate.

questions.q: A lender will lend up to 75% of value but also requires a debt coverage ratio of at least 1.25. If the coverage test produces a smaller loan than the LTV test, the lender will usually:
c: Lend 75% and require private mortgage insurance on the rest
Lend the larger amount produced by the 75% LTV test
Average the two results to set the final loan amount
Lend the smaller amount produced by the coverage test
questions.x: Commercial lenders apply both tests and lend the lesser result, so the buyer must bring more equity or negotiate the price. Private mortgage insurance is a residential concept for high-LTV home loans and does not fill a coverage shortfall on an income property.

questions.q: A 12-unit building has NOI of $150,000. The lender requires 1.25 debt coverage, which allows annual debt service of $120,000, and the LTV test would allow a loan needing $135,000 a year. The buyer should expect:
c: A loan sized to $135,000 of debt service, because value controls
A loan sized to $120,000 of debt service, with more cash needed at closing
A loan sized to $150,000 of debt service, matching the full NOI
A loan sized to $127,500 of debt service, splitting the difference
questions.x: The coverage test caps debt service at NOI divided by 1.25, here $120,000, and the lesser loan controls. Lending to the full NOI would leave a coverage ratio of 1.00, with no cushion if a tenant stops paying.

questions.q: A New York owner refinances a $400,000 mortgage into a new $900,000 loan from a different bank using a consolidation, extension and modification agreement. Mortgage recording tax is generally owed on:
c: The full $900,000 new loan amount
The $500,000 of new money borrowed
The $400,000 existing mortgage balance
The $1,300,000 total of both loans
questions.x: With a CEMA, the existing mortgage is assigned to the new lender and kept alive, so recording tax is owed only on the increase. Taxing the full $900,000 is what happens without a CEMA, when the old mortgage is satisfied and an entirely new one is recorded.

questions.q: An investor in Queens is refinancing a building with an existing mortgage and wants to minimize mortgage recording tax. The licensee should suggest the investor ask the attorney about:
c: Treating the loan as a co-op share loan to avoid the tax
Paying off the old mortgage before the new one is recorded
Recording the new loan as an unsecured note with no mortgage
Having the old lender assign its mortgage to the new lender
questions.x: An assignment of the existing mortgage, consolidated under a CEMA, means tax is paid only on new money. Paying off the old loan first is exactly what triggers tax on the whole new loan. Share loans escape the tax only because co-op shares are personal property, which this building is not.

questions.q: An investor's loan has a 5-year term and a 30-year amortization schedule. The main risk this structure creates is that:
c: Most of the loan comes due in year 5, forcing a refinance or sale
The rate will adjust every year during the five-year term
The loan is fully paid off in 5 years, raising each payment sharply
The lender can call the loan any time the property value drops
questions.x: With a balloon, only a small part of principal is paid in five years, so the remaining balance must be refinanced or the property sold when the term ends, on whatever terms exist then. The rate is fixed for the term here; a balloon is about timing, not rate adjustments.

questions.q: Five years after buying a building with a balloon loan, an owner's NOI is flat and rates are higher. The new lender's coverage test supports a loan smaller than the balance due. The owner most likely must:
c: Continue paying the old loan, since the balloon extends automatically
Ask the old lender to forgive the gap, since it set the original terms
Cover the shortfall in cash, sell, or find other capital to pay it off
Claim the shortfall as a capital loss to offset the payoff amount due
questions.x: Refinance risk shows up exactly this way: the balloon is due, and a smaller new loan leaves a gap the owner must cover or sell. Balloons do not extend automatically unless the loan includes an extension option, and the old lender has no duty to forgive principal.

questions.q: Under New York law since 2019, when the tenant of a rent stabilized apartment moves out, the apartment generally:
c: Becomes free market once the rent exceeds the legal threshold
Remains vacant until the Rent Guidelines Board approves a new rent
Becomes free market after the owner completes improvements
Remains stabilized and is re-rented at the legal regulated rent
questions.x: The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 repealed vacancy decontrol and high-rent luxury decontrol, so the unit stays stabilized. The rent threshold answer states the pre-2019 rule, which still shows up in old pro formas and outdated study materials.

questions.q: A seller's broker markets a Bronx building with a projection that 20% of the stabilized units will be deregulated in the next three years through turnover. A buyer's agent should recognize this as:
c: A reasonable estimate based on typical turnover rates
Market risk that a higher cap rate fully accounts for
Inconsistent with current New York rent stabilization law
A tax projection best left to the buyer's accountant to evaluate
questions.x: Turnover no longer removes units from stabilization in New York. The projection rests on the pre-2019 rules and overstates future income. This is regulatory risk, a legal question, not a market estimate that a cap rate adjustment could fix.

questions.q: Each of the following makes an apartment building less liquid than publicly traded stock EXCEPT:
c: Rent from tenants arrives every month during ownership
Transfer taxes and commissions raise the cost of selling
A buyer's lender usually needs to approve the building before closing
A sale takes months of marketing, due diligence and financing
questions.x: Monthly rent is income, not a feature of how fast the asset converts to cash, so it does not affect liquidity. Time to sell, transaction costs and financing approvals are exactly what make real estate illiquid compared with stock, which sells in seconds at low cost.

questions.q: An investor plans to sell a mixed-use building in about four months to pay a known tax bill. Which risk is the investor most exposed to?
c: Interest rate risk, because the investor's loan is fixed
Liquidity risk, since a fast sale may cut the sale price
Tenant credit risk, because the store's lease is net
Regulatory risk, because commercial rents are unregulated
questions.x: Needing cash on a deadline from an asset that takes months to sell is liquidity risk, and forced sellers usually give up price. A fixed-rate loan actually limits interest rate risk while it runs, and unregulated commercial rents are not a legal change that threatens the plan.

questions.q: Which statement about holding unimproved land as an investment is most accurate?
c: It produces steady income from ground rent while the owner waits
It needs heavy management because vacant lots attract tenants
It generates depreciation deductions that offset the carrying costs
It costs taxes and insurance each year and produces no income at all
questions.x: Raw land usually earns nothing until it is sold or developed, while taxes, insurance and any interest keep coming due. Land is never depreciated, so there is no deduction to offset those costs. Ground rent comes from a ground lease, which is a different arrangement from simply holding a lot.

questions.q: An investor holds a vacant lot for future development. All of the following are typical costs of holding it EXCEPT:
c: Real estate taxes on the lot
Depreciation on the land itself
Interest on a land acquisition loan
Liability insurance on the lot
questions.x: Land cannot be depreciated, so depreciation is not a cost or deduction tied to holding land. Taxes, insurance and loan interest are the carrying costs that make land the most speculative property type.

questions.q: A net-leased restaurant is marketed as having "national credit." The lease was signed by a local franchisee LLC with no guaranty from the national brand. The buyer should understand that:
c: The rent depends on the franchisee's finances, not the national brand's
The national brand is liable, since its trademark appears on the store
The lease becomes void if the franchise agreement is terminated
The buyer can require the brand to sign a guaranty after closing
questions.x: Credit follows the signature. If only a franchisee LLC signed and no one guaranteed, the landlord can collect only from that entity. A brand's name on the sign creates no liability for rent, and a buyer cannot force a guaranty on someone who never agreed to one.

questions.q: Two identical drugstore buildings have the same rent and lease term. Investors will usually pay more for the one where the lease is:
c: Written as a gross lease with a fixed rent
Signed by a store-level LLC with a larger deposit
Guaranteed by the publicly traded parent company
Shorter, so the rent resets to market sooner
questions.x: A guaranty from a strong parent company lowers tenant credit risk, so buyers accept a lower return and pay a higher price. A store-level LLC may have few assets beyond the store, and a deposit covers only a few months. A gross lease shifts expenses to the landlord, which lowers predictable income.

questions.q: In a triple net lease the tenant pays taxes, insurance and maintenance. In an absolute (bondable) net lease the tenant also typically pays for:
c: The landlord's mortgage payments
The landlord's income taxes
Roof and structural repairs too
Leasing commissions on renewals
questions.x: An absolute net lease puts nearly every property cost on the tenant, including roof and structure, which makes it the most passive lease for the owner. A tenant never pays the landlord's debt service or income taxes under either form; those are the owner's own obligations.

questions.q: An owner wants a single-tenant building with as little management responsibility as possible. Which lease structure fits that goal best?
c: An absolute net lease covering structure
A modified gross lease with a base year
A triple net lease with landlord roof duties
A gross lease with a landlord expense stop
questions.x: An absolute net lease leaves the landlord almost no expense or repair responsibility. A triple net lease that keeps roof and structure with the landlord still leaves major capital costs on the owner, and gross and modified gross leases put operating expenses on the landlord.

questions.q: A store tenant in a Queens mixed-use building asks what limits its landlord's rent increase at renewal. Under New York law, the limit is generally:
c: The Rent Guidelines Board's annual percentage
Whatever the lease and negotiation produce
The Good Cause Eviction increase cap
The rent stabilization rules for the building
questions.x: New York does not regulate commercial rents, so renewal rent and renewal rights come from the lease. The Rent Guidelines Board, Good Cause Eviction and rent stabilization are residential rules, which is why they are tempting but wrong for a storefront.

questions.q: In a New York mixed-use building with ground-floor stores and stabilized apartments, each of the following applies to the apartments EXCEPT:
c: Rent increases set by the Rent Guidelines Board each year
The warranty of habitability
A security deposit capped at one month's rent
Renewal rights limited to the lease's options
questions.x: Stabilized tenants have renewal rights by law, not only by lease, while commercial tenants have only the renewal rights their lease grants. Board-set increases, habitability and the one-month deposit cap all apply to the residential units.

questions.q: Two otherwise similar retail buildings are for sale. One is owned in fee simple; the other sits on a ground lease with 20 years left. The leasehold building will most likely sell for:
c: Less, since the interest shrinks over time
More, because the buyer avoids paying for the land
The same, because the rents are the same
More, because ground rent is deductible
questions.x: A leasehold is worth only what it earns for the remaining term, and the improvements generally revert to the landowner at the end. With 20 years left, the buyer pool and lender appetite both shrink. Avoiding a land payment is an advantage for a developer at the start of a long ground lease, not for a buyer late in the term.

questions.q: As a ground lease approaches its expiration, the value of the ground tenant's building generally:
c: Rises, because rents usually increase over time
Stays level, because the building is still standing
Transfers to the lender, who holds the leasehold mortgage
Falls toward zero, because it reverts to the landowner
questions.x: At the end of the term the improvements generally belong to the landowner, so the tenant's interest is worth less every year that passes. Rising rents cannot offset a shrinking ownership period near the end of a lease.

questions.q: A buyer is purchasing a former manufacturing building in an industrial zone. The step that best supports a defense against liability for contamination the buyer did not cause is:
c: A property condition disclosure statement from the seller
A Phase I environmental site assessment before purchase
An estoppel certificate from the current tenant
A title insurance policy with a survey endorsement
questions.x: Under CERCLA, all appropriate inquiry before acquiring the property, usually a Phase I environmental site assessment, is the basis of the innocent landowner defense. The PCDS covers residential 1 to 4 family sales, and title insurance and estoppels address ownership and lease facts, not pollution.

questions.q: An investor wants to skip environmental review on a warehouse because the tenant's net lease makes the tenant responsible for compliance. The main problem with that plan is that:
c: A net lease is unenforceable for environmental costs in New York
Environmental review applies chiefly to residential properties
The owner can stay liable under federal Superfund law anyway
The tenant's insurer automatically covers the owner's liability
questions.x: Federal Superfund liability can reach the current owner whatever a lease says; the lease only lets the owner try to recover from the tenant, who may not have the money. A Phase I before purchase is what protects the buyer. Environmental risk is greatest on commercial and industrial sites, not residential ones.

questions.q: A tenant abandons a New York office lease with six years left. Unless the lease provides otherwise, the landlord generally:
c: Has no duty to re-rent before suing for the rent that comes due
Has to re-rent the space with reasonable efforts to reduce damages
Is limited to keeping the security deposit as liquidated damages
Has to accept surrender and release the tenant from rent
questions.x: New York's Court of Appeals held in Holy Properties v. Kenneth Cole that commercial landlords have no duty to mitigate. The statutory duty to mitigate in RPL 227-e, added in 2019, covers residential premises only, which is why the re-rent answer is the tempting wrong one.

questions.q: Two tenants walk away from New York leases mid-term: one from a Bronx apartment, one from a Bronx storefront. Which landlord has a statutory duty to try to re-rent in good faith?
c: The storefront landlord, because commercial leases are longer
Both landlords, under the 2019 rent law for every lease
The apartment landlord, because the duty covers dwellings
Neither landlord, because abandonment ends the lease at once
questions.x: RPL 227-e requires landlords of premises used as dwellings to mitigate in good faith. Commercial landlords have no such statutory duty and, under New York case law, no common law duty either. The 2019 law did not extend the rule to commercial leases.

questions.q: A retail lease sets base rent at $90,000 and percentage rent of 5% of sales over $1,200,000. The natural breakpoint would be $1,800,000. The $1,200,000 figure is:
c: A natural breakpoint, because it is written into the lease
An artificial breakpoint that favors the landlord
An artificial breakpoint that favors the tenant
A recapture threshold that ends the lease early
questions.x: The natural breakpoint is base rent divided by the percentage rate: $90,000 / 0.05 = $1,800,000. A negotiated breakpoint below it triggers overage rent sooner, which benefits the landlord. A breakpoint above the natural one would favor the tenant.

questions.q: A tenant is negotiating percentage rent. Which breakpoint is most favorable to the tenant, assuming the same rate?
c: A fixed breakpoint set below the natural breakpoint
A breakpoint equal to the year 1 base rent in dollars
A breakpoint of zero, so the rate applies from the first dollar
A breakpoint set above the natural breakpoint level
questions.x: The higher the breakpoint, the more sales the tenant keeps before owing overage. A breakpoint set above the natural one favors the tenant. A breakpoint below the natural one, or zero, starts overage rent earlier and favors the landlord.

questions.q: A small company's principal signs a good guy guaranty on an NYC office lease. The principal is typically liable for rent:
c: Through the end of the lease term, whatever happens
For amounts above the security deposit at lease end
For the first 12 months of the term, and then it burns off
Until the tenant gives notice, pays up and vacates
questions.x: A good guy guaranty ends once the tenant gives the agreed notice, pays rent through the move-out date and surrenders the space. It targets the tenant who stops paying but stays. A guaranty for the full term is a full personal guaranty, the much broader obligation tenants try to avoid.

questions.q: A landlord accepts a good guy guaranty from a cafe owner. Which risk is the landlord mainly protecting against?
c: A tenant that pays rent but closes the cafe to the public
A tenant that stops paying but stays during a long eviction
A tenant whose sales fall below the percentage rent breakpoint
A tenant that sells its business to a stronger operator
questions.x: The good guy guaranty is built for the holdover-without-paying problem: the landlord gets paid until the space comes back vacant. A tenant that goes dark but pays is a lease covenant issue, and a sale of the business is handled by the assignment clause.

questions.q: New York City's Commercial Rent Tax applies to commercial tenants located in:
c: Any of the five boroughs, above a rent threshold
Manhattan and Brooklyn business districts
Manhattan below 96th Street, over a threshold
Any NYC building with ground floor retail
questions.x: The Commercial Rent Tax is limited to Manhattan south of 96th Street and to tenants above a rent threshold, with small business credits. Tenants in Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, Staten Island and upper Manhattan do not pay it.

questions.q: A tenant paying $600,000 a year in rent could be subject to NYC's Commercial Rent Tax in each of these locations EXCEPT:
c: Downtown Brooklyn
Lower Manhattan
Midtown Manhattan
Manhattan's Upper East Side below 96th Street
questions.x: The tax reaches only Manhattan south of 96th Street, so Downtown Brooklyn is outside it no matter how high the rent. Midtown, Lower Manhattan and the Upper East Side below 96th Street are inside the zone, subject to the threshold and credits.

questions.q: A landlord has given a pizzeria an exclusive on "the sale of pizza as a primary business." A new tenant wants to open a cafe that sells some flatbreads. The best drafting approach for the new tenant is:
c: Any lawful use, which overrides the earlier exclusive
A cafe use with flatbreads listed as an incidental item
A pizzeria use, since exclusives cannot be enforced
Retail food use with no mention of the exclusive
questions.x: Drafting the use clause around the tenant's real primary business, with the overlapping item as incidental, respects the existing exclusive while protecting the new tenant's menu. A broad use clause does not override a promise the landlord has already made to another tenant.

questions.q: A landlord wants a narrow use clause stating a tenant may operate "a nail salon and for no other purpose." From the tenant's side, the main drawback is that it:
c: Makes the lease harder to assign to a new concept
Lets the landlord raise rent whenever services change
Voids any renewal option written into the lease
Converts the lease to a gross lease automatically
questions.x: A narrow use clause limits what the tenant can do with the space and who can take it over, which hurts the tenant if it wants to sell or change concepts. Landlords want narrow clauses to protect other tenants' exclusives and the tenant mix; they do not affect renewal options or expense structure.

questions.q: Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, who is responsible for accessibility at a leased restaurant open to the public?
c: The tenant, because it runs the public business
The landlord, because it owns the building
Both, though the lease may allocate the costs
The party named in the certificate of occupancy
questions.x: Both the landlord and the tenant of a place of public accommodation are responsible for ADA compliance. Their lease can decide who pays and who performs the work, but it cannot remove either party's responsibility to the public.

questions.q: A lease says the tenant handles all accessibility work. A customer who uses a wheelchair sues over the store's entrance step. The landlord most likely:
c: Has no exposure, because the lease shifted the duty
Has exposure if the tenant lacks insurance
Is liable if the building was built after 1990
Can still be liable, then recover from the tenant
questions.x: A lease allocates responsibility between landlord and tenant, but it does not bind the customer. Both can be liable, and the landlord can look to the tenant under the lease. Older buildings are not exempt from barrier removal duties.

questions.q: A tenant and landlord sign a letter of intent for an office lease stating it is non-binding. Before the lease is signed, the landlord:
c: Has to hold the space for the tenant for 30 days
Can keep marketing the space to other tenants
Owes the tenant damages if it leases to someone else
Can enforce the letter's rent against the tenant
questions.x: A non-binding letter of intent creates no obligation to lease on its terms, so either party can walk away until a lease is signed and delivered. Some LOIs do contain binding exclusivity or confidentiality clauses, but only if they say so.

questions.q: A tenant's board approves a move after the tenant signs a non-binding letter of intent. The tenant's broker should advise the board that:
c: The deal is final, and the lease is a mere formality
The deal binds both sides once the broker is paid
The landlord is bound but the tenant can still exit
Nothing binds either side until a lease is signed
questions.x: Commercial LOIs usually say expressly that neither side is bound until a lease is fully signed and delivered. Treating the LOI as final is how tenants lose their backup options and leverage.

questions.q: Space X rents for $60 per RSF with a 20% loss factor. Space Y rents for $56 per RSF with a 30% loss factor. Comparing cost per usable square foot:
c: Y is cheaper at $56 compared with $60
They are equal once loss factors are counted
X is cheaper at $75 compared with $80 for Y
Y is cheaper at $72.80 compared with $75
questions.x: Cost per usable foot = rent / (1 minus loss factor). X: $60 / 0.80 = $75. Y: $56 / 0.70 = $80. The lower asking rent loses once the bigger loss factor is counted.

questions.q: A tenant needs 7,000 usable square feet. A floor has a 22% loss factor. Why should the tenant's broker focus on usable rather than rentable square feet?
c: Rentable feet include common areas it cannot occupy
Rent is quoted on usable feet in New York office leases
Usable feet include the tenant's share of the lobby and corridors
Carpetable feet determine the rent in most office buildings
questions.x: Rent is charged on rentable square feet, which add a share of common areas to the tenant's own space. The tenant's space plan depends on usable feet, so comparing floors on usable cost and fit is what reveals the real price.

questions.q: Under a tenant improvement allowance, construction costs above the allowance are generally paid by:
c: The tenant, since the allowance is a cap
The landlord, as part of the base building
The contractor, under the work letter
The lender, through the building's loan
questions.x: An allowance is a fixed landlord contribution, so overruns fall on the tenant, who in exchange controls design and contractor. In a turnkey deal, the landlord delivers finished space at its own cost and bears the overrun risk.

questions.q: A tenant with a tight budget and simple space needs wants the landlord to bear construction cost risk. Which approach fits best?
c: A larger allowance with the tenant's own contractor
An allowance limited to design and soft costs
A turnkey build to an agreed plan by the landlord
A rent credit in place of any build-out work
questions.x: In a turnkey build, the landlord builds the agreed plan at its cost and carries overruns, in exchange for controlling specifications and contractor. An allowance, however large, leaves overruns with the tenant.

questions.q: In negotiating an office lease's operating expense definition, a tenant would most commonly seek to exclude:
c: Cleaning of the common areas
Elevator maintenance contracts
Wages of the building's security staff
Leasing commissions on other deals
questions.x: Tenants exclude costs that do not serve the building's day-to-day operation for them, such as leasing commissions on other tenants' deals, capital improvements, debt service and depreciation. Cleaning, elevators and security are ordinary operating costs that escalations are meant to cover.

questions.q: A tenant's attorney typically tries to keep each of the following OUT of operating expenses EXCEPT:
c: Principal and interest on the landlord's mortgage
Wages of the building's porters and handypersons
Costs of building out another tenant's space
Capital improvements that do not reduce costs
questions.x: Porter and handyperson wages are core operating expenses and normally included. Debt service, other tenants' build-outs and most capital improvements are classic exclusions because they benefit the landlord's ownership or other tenants rather than operating the building.

questions.q: A tenant signs a lease subordinate to the landlord's mortgage. The tenant's best protection against losing its lease in a foreclosure is:
c: An estoppel certificate given to the lender
A recorded memorandum of the security deposit
A non-disturbance agreement from the lender
A good guy guaranty from its principal
questions.x: A non-disturbance agreement, usually within an SNDA, binds the lender to honor the lease if the tenant is not in default. An estoppel certificate is a statement the tenant gives to confirm lease facts; it protects lenders and buyers, not the tenant.

questions.q: A lender forecloses on an office building. The tenants who signed SNDAs will generally:
c: Lose their leases, since the leases were subordinate
Keep their leases and attorn to the new owner
Owe rent to the old landlord until their terms end
Need to sign new leases at current market rents
questions.x: With non-disturbance, the foreclosing lender or buyer honors the lease, and the tenant attorns, recognizing the new owner as landlord. Without an SNDA, a subordinate lease can be cut off in the foreclosure.

questions.q: A landlord grants a ten-year tenant a right to terminate after year 6. The termination fee is most commonly based on:
c: The full rent for the remaining four years
The building's current vacancy rate overall
The tenant's security deposit amount on hand
The landlord's unrecovered up-front deal costs
questions.x: Landlords recover up-front costs, such as the allowance, free rent and brokerage commissions, over the lease term. A termination fee typically repays the unamortized balance, often with interest. Charging the full remaining rent would make the option meaningless.

questions.q: Two tenants in the same building have year 5 termination options. One received a $90 per RSF allowance and 12 months free; the other received $20 per RSF and 2 months free. Whose termination fee will likely be higher, per foot?
c: The tenant with the larger concessions
The tenant with the smaller concessions
Both the same, since the year is the same
Neither, since options carry no fee
questions.x: The fee usually repays the landlord's unamortized costs. The tenant that received a larger allowance and more free rent leaves more unrecovered cost on the table at year 5, so its fee per foot is higher.

questions.q: A ground lease resets rent to a percentage of the land's value "as if vacant and unencumbered." Compared with valuing the land subject to the existing lease, this wording usually:
c: Lowers the reset rent, favoring the ground tenant
Has no effect, since the land is the same
Raises the reset rent, favoring the landowner
Freezes the rent at the original level
questions.x: Valuing land as if no lease or building encumbered it produces its full market value, the highest basis for a reset. Valuing it as encumbered by a long lease at old rent would produce a much lower number, which is what ground tenants negotiate for.

questions.q: A buyer is considering a ground-leased office building whose ground rent will reset in four years to 6% of full land value. The buyer's broker should advise that the price be based mainly on:
c: Income after the expected reset rent is paid
Today's ground rent, since the reset is uncertain
The building's replacement cost, ignoring rent
The seller's original purchase price for the building
questions.x: A scheduled reset is a known future change in expenses, and income property is valued on the income it will produce. Using today's ground rent overstates value. Replacement cost and the seller's basis say little about what a leasehold earns.

questions.q: A lender making a loan secured by a ground leasehold will most likely require that the ground lease give the lender:
c: The right to set the ground rent at each reset
A share of the ground rent paid to the landowner
Ownership of the land if the borrower defaults
Notice of tenant defaults and a right to cure
questions.x: Notice and cure rights let the lender keep the ground lease alive by curing the borrower's default, protecting the leasehold that secures its loan. Lenders also want a new lease right and a term that runs well past maturity. They do not get the land unless the fee is subordinated, which is rare.

questions.q: A leasehold mortgage lender typically requires each of the following in the ground lease EXCEPT:
c: A remaining term well beyond the loan's maturity
A landowner signature on the borrower's note
A right to a new lease if the ground lease ends
Notice to the lender of any ground lease default
questions.x: Lenders protect the leasehold with term length, notice and cure, and new lease rights. A landowner co-signing the borrower's note would make the landowner personally liable for the tenant's loan, which ground lessors do not agree to.

questions.q: In an unsubordinated ground lease, if the ground tenant defaults on its leasehold mortgage, the lender can foreclose on:
c: The land and the building together
The leasehold interest, not the land
The landowner's other real estate
Nothing, because the lease protects both parties
questions.x: An unsubordinated ground lessor never pledged the land, so the lender's collateral is limited to the leasehold. In a subordinated ground lease the landowner puts the fee behind the mortgage, a rare and risky choice for the landowner.

questions.q: A developer asks a landowner to subordinate the fee to a construction loan on a ground-leased site. If the landowner agrees, the landowner's main new risk is:
c: Losing the right to sell the leased fee to anyone
Paying the developer's construction costs directly
Being unable to collect ground rent at any time
Losing the land itself to a lender's foreclosure
questions.x: Subordinating the fee pledges the land as security for the developer's loan. If the developer defaults, the lender can foreclose on the land itself. That is why most ground lessors insist on unsubordinated ground leases.

questions.q: A warehouse lease is described as triple net. It says the tenant handles maintenance and non-structural repairs and the landlord handles roof replacement. The roof needs replacing. Who pays?
c: The landlord, which kept roof replacement in the lease
The tenant, because NNN tenants pay every property cost
The tenant and landlord equally, under standard NNN terms
The tenant's insurer, because roofs wear out over time
questions.x: The lease language controls over the label. Many triple net leases carve roof replacement and structure back to the landlord; only an absolute net lease typically puts those costs on the tenant. Ordinary wear is not an insured loss.

questions.q: An investor wants a single-tenant building where the tenant pays even for structural and roof replacement. The lease form that typically does that is:
c: A modified gross lease
A double net lease
An absolute net lease
A percentage lease
questions.x: An absolute (bondable) net lease puts virtually all property costs on the tenant, including capital items like the roof and structure. Double net covers taxes and insurance; modified gross leaves most costs with the landlord; a percentage lease describes how rent is set, not expenses.

questions.q: Under New York's recording law, which lease is treated as a conveyance that can be recorded?
c: A two-year storefront lease
A three-year office lease
A month-to-month apartment rental
A 20-year ground lease of land
questions.x: RPL 290 excludes leases of three years or less from the definition of a conveyance, so a lease for longer than three years, such as a 20-year ground lease, can be recorded, usually by a memorandum of lease. Recording protects the tenant against later purchasers and lenders.

questions.q: A tenant signs a 15-year lease for a Queens warehouse. To protect its rights against a later buyer or lender of the property, the tenant's attorney will most likely:
c: Register the lease with the Rent Guidelines Board
File the lease with the Department of State
Record a memorandum of lease with the county
Give a copy of the lease to the tax assessor
questions.x: A lease longer than three years is a conveyance under New York's recording act, so recording a memorandum gives constructive notice and protects the tenant against later purchasers. The Department of State licenses brokers, the Rent Guidelines Board covers stabilized apartments, and the assessor does not record interests.

questions.q: Compared with owning the leasehold, owning the leased fee under a long ground lease generally offers:
c: Steady ground rent and a reversion of land
More management and higher operating risk
Depreciation deductions on the land itself
Direct control over the building's tenants
questions.x: The leased fee owner collects ground rent, usually with the tenant paying all costs, and gets the land (and generally the improvements) back when the lease ends. The ground tenant runs the building and deals with its tenants. Land is never depreciable.

questions.q: An investor who wants little management and very reliable income is choosing between a leasehold with 30 years left and the leased fee under the same ground lease. Which better fits the goal, and why?
c: The leasehold, because it includes the building's rents
The leased fee, since the tenant pays to keep its building
The leasehold, because it grows in value as the term shortens
The leased fee, because land is depreciated faster than buildings
questions.x: A ground tenant must pay ground rent to keep its building, so the landowner's income is highly reliable, and the landowner has almost no management duties. A leasehold loses value as its term shortens, and land cannot be depreciated at all.

questions.q: A building owner tells a broker, "Sell it for whatever you can; I need $3,000,000, and you keep anything above that." In New York this arrangement is:
c: An exclusive agency listing, which is legal if signed
A legal listing if the broker discloses the net figure
An open listing, which is legal for commercial property
A net listing, which New York rules prohibit
questions.x: Paying the broker whatever exceeds the owner's figure is a net listing, prohibited in New York because it pits the broker's profit against the client's interest. Disclosure or a signature does not make it permissible, and commercial property is not an exception.

questions.q: Which compensation arrangement would violate New York's rules for a broker listing an office building?
c: 3% of the gross sale price, payable at closing
Proceeds above $8,000,000 to the broker
A flat fee of $150,000 if the property sells
4% of the price, reduced to 3% for a co-broke
questions.x: A fee equal to whatever the price exceeds the owner's figure is a net listing, which New York prohibits. Percentage fees, flat fees and negotiated reductions are all lawful structures that the broker and owner can agree on.

questions.q: Under New York's General Obligations Law, an agreement to pay a licensed real estate broker a commission:
c: Can be enforced even if it is oral, if proved
Is void unless it is in writing and signed by the owner
Is enforceable once filed with the Department of State
Needs notarization before a court will enforce it
questions.x: GOL 5-701(a)(10) requires a writing for compensation agreements for negotiating real estate and business deals, but it expressly excludes duly licensed real estate brokers and salespersons. Their oral agreements can be enforced, though proving the terms is the practical risk.

questions.q: An unlicensed "finder" and a licensed broker each have an oral agreement with a seller to be paid for introducing a buyer of a building. If the seller refuses to pay both, which party can bring a claim for the fee?
c: The finder, since introductions do not require a license
Neither, since oral fee agreements are void for everyone
The broker, since licensees are exempt from it
Both, since each introduced a buyer to the seller
questions.x: The writing requirement in GOL 5-701(a)(10) does not apply to licensed brokers, so the broker may sue on an oral agreement. The finder fails twice: RPL 442-d bars unlicensed persons from suing for real estate commissions, and the GOL writing rule applies to finders.

questions.q: A leasing commission is 5% of year 1 rent, 4% of year 2 rent and 3% of years 3 to 5. Rent is a flat $60,000 a year for 5 years. The total commission is:
questions.x: Year 1: $3,000. Year 2: $2,400. Years 3 to 5: $60,000 x 3% x 3 = $5,400. Total $10,800. Applying 5% to all five years ($15,000) ignores the declining schedule.
questions.concept: Leasing commission on a declining schedule

questions.q: A 4-year lease at $90,000 a year carries a commission of 6% of year 1 rent and 4% of each later year. Half is paid at signing. How much is paid at signing?
questions.x: Total commission: $5,400 (year 1) + $90,000 x 4% x 3 ($10,800) = $16,200. Half at signing is $8,100. The $16,200 choice is the full commission, not the signing installment.
questions.concept: Leasing commission on a declining schedule

questions.q: A grateful landlord wants to give a salesperson a $1,000 bonus for leasing a store. The salesperson may accept the money:
c: Directly, if the landlord calls it a gift
Through the sponsoring broker only
Directly, if it is reported as income
Through the tenant, as part of the deposit
questions.x: A salesperson may be compensated for real estate work only by the sponsoring broker. A client who wants to pay more pays the firm, which pays the salesperson under their agreement. Labels like gift or bonus do not change the source rule.
questions.concept: Salesperson paid only by sponsoring broker

questions.q: A New York salesperson's compensation from a commercial lease deal may lawfully come from each of the following EXCEPT:
c: The sponsoring broker's regular commission split
A bonus the sponsoring broker pays from the fee
A referral fee paid through the sponsoring broker
A check made out to the salesperson from the landlord
questions.x: Payment straight from the landlord to the salesperson violates the rule that salespersons are paid only by their sponsoring broker. Splits, bonuses and referral fees paid by or through the sponsoring broker are all permissible routes.
questions.concept: Salesperson paid only by sponsoring broker

questions.q: A broker's listing says the commission is earned when the broker produces a buyer ready, willing and able to buy on the owner's terms. The owner signs a contract with such a buyer, then backs out for a higher offer. The broker has most likely:
c: Earned the full commission under the listing
Earned no fee, because the sale did not close
Earned half, because the buyer signed but did not close
Earned the commission if the buyer sues the owner first
questions.x: In New York, absent a contrary agreement, a broker earns its commission when it produces a ready, willing and able buyer on terms the seller accepts. A seller's later decision to back out does not undo that. A clause expressly conditioning the commission on closing could change the result.
questions.concept: Commission earned on ready willing able buyer

questions.q: Absent a contrary agreement, a New York broker's commission is generally earned when the broker:
c: Lists the property in the MLS
Attends the closing and delivers the keys
Receives the buyer's down payment in escrow
Produces a ready, willing and able buyer
questions.x: The traditional New York rule ties the commission to producing a buyer who is ready, willing and financially able to buy on terms the seller accepts. Listing, escrow and attending closing are steps in the process, not the event that earns the fee.
questions.concept: Commission earned on ready willing able buyer

questions.q: Two competing brokerage firms agree with each other to refuse to show any listings from a new discount brokerage. This is most likely:
c: Lawful, since firms choose their cooperating brokers
A group boycott in violation of antitrust law
A tie-in arrangement, which is lawful in New York
Market allocation, which is lawful for commercial firms
questions.x: Competitors agreeing together to refuse to deal with a third firm is a group boycott under the Sherman Act. One firm's independent decision about whom to cooperate with is different; the agreement between competitors is what makes it illegal.

questions.q: At a meeting of commercial brokers, several firms agree that none of them will co-broke with any firm charging less than 4%. Which antitrust violation does this most clearly involve?
c: Tie-in arrangement
Market allocation
Group boycott
Steering
questions.x: An agreement among competitors to refuse to deal with lower-priced firms is a group boycott, and it also edges into price fixing. Market allocation divides territories or customers; a tie-in conditions one service on buying another; steering is a fair housing violation.

questions.q: A 12-unit building has 11 apartments leased at $2,000 a month and one vacant apartment with a market rent of $2,000. The owner's rent roll also lists the rent-free super's apartment at $2,000. What is potential gross income?
c: $312,000 including the super's unit
questions.x: PGI counts every rentable unit at full occupancy: 12 x $2,000 x 12 = $288,000, with the vacant unit included at market rent. The super's apartment produces no rent, so adding it gives the $312,000 trap. $264,000 wrongly drops the vacant unit, which vacancy allowance handles later.

questions.q: A rent roll shows two stores: one leased at $5,000 a month and one vacant, listed at an asking rent of $6,500. Comparable signed leases for the vacant store average $5,500. What do the two stores contribute to potential gross income for the year?
c: $138,000 at the asking rent
questions.x: PGI includes the vacant store at comp-supported market rent: ($5,000 + $5,500) x 12 = $126,000. Using the $6,500 asking rent gives $138,000, the seller's number. Leaving the vacant store out entirely ($60,000) double counts vacancy, which is deducted on its own line.

questions.q: A rent-stabilized tenant's lease says $1,800 a month, but the DHCR registration shows a legal regulated rent of $1,720. A buyer underwriting the building should count:
c: $1,720, the registered legal rent
$1,800, the rent in the signed lease
$1,760, a midpoint pending review
The market rent, since the lease is void
questions.x: A stabilized tenant cannot be charged more than the legal regulated rent, so the buyer counts $1,720 and flags a possible overcharge. The signed lease is the trap: a lease cannot raise a stabilized rent above the registered legal rent, and overcharge claims can reach back six years.

questions.q: Which document establishes the most a buyer can count as rent for a rent-stabilized apartment in New York?
c: The tenant's current signed lease
The DHCR rent registration history
The seller's certified rent roll
The owner's most recent RPIE filing
questions.x: The DHCR (HCR) registration history records the legal regulated rent, which caps what the owner may collect. The signed lease is the tempting answer, but a lease above the legal rent is an overcharge. Rent rolls and RPIE filings are owner statements, useful for cross-checking but not controlling.

questions.q: A rent-stabilized tenant in a Queens building moves out in 2026. The owner may:
c: Rent it at market, since vacancy ends stabilization
Add a 20% vacancy bonus to the legal rent
Re-rent it as stabilized at its legal rent
Deregulate it once the rent passes the old threshold
questions.x: The 2019 HSTPA repealed vacancy decontrol, high-rent deregulation and the statutory vacancy bonus, so the unit is re-rented as stabilized. The 20% vacancy bonus is the trap: it was real before 2019 and still appears in old listing packages and some outdated study materials.

questions.q: The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act eliminated all of the following for rent-stabilized apartments EXCEPT:
c: High-rent vacancy decontrol
The statutory vacancy bonus
High-income deregulation
Annual RGB increases
questions.x: Rent Guidelines Board increases still apply each year; that is how stabilized rents grow now. HSTPA eliminated high-rent vacancy decontrol, high-income deregulation and the vacancy bonus. High-income deregulation is the tempting wrong pick because fewer people remember it was repealed too.

questions.q: A tenant signs a 12-month lease at $3,600 a month with two months free. The net effective monthly rent is:
c: $3,600 face rent
questions.x: Cash collected = $3,600 x 10 paying months = $36,000; spread over 12 months = $3,000. $3,600 is the face rent, which stays in PGI while the concession is deducted separately. $3,300 treats the concession as one month instead of two.

questions.q: A store lease runs 24 months at $8,000 a month, with the first 3 months free. What is the net effective monthly rent?
c: $6,667, assuming 4 free months
questions.x: Rent paid = $8,000 x 21 months = $168,000; divided by 24 months = $7,000. $5,000 subtracts the 3 free months' count from the rent instead of the dollars. The face rent of $8,000 belongs in PGI, and the concession comes off as its own line.

questions.q: A building has potential gross income of $500,000, vacancy and credit loss of 6%, rent concessions of $8,000 and parking income of $12,000. Effective gross income is:
c: $450,000 after parking
questions.x: EGI = $500,000 minus $30,000 vacancy minus $8,000 concessions plus $12,000 other income = $474,000. $482,000 forgets the concessions. $462,000 forgets to add the parking. Other income is added after vacancy, not subtracted.

questions.q: A building's effective gross income is $384,000, which includes $4,000 of laundry income after a 5% vacancy and credit loss allowance. What was potential gross income?
c: $388,000 including laundry
questions.x: Remove other income first: $384,000 minus $4,000 = $380,000, which is 95% of PGI. PGI = $380,000 / 0.95 = $400,000. $403,200 multiplies by 1.05, which is not the reverse of taking off 5%. $388,000 adds the laundry back instead of removing it.

questions.q: A seller's package overstates NOI by $30,000 a year. At an 8% market cap rate, how much value does the overstatement add on paper?
c: $240,000 (8 x the error)
questions.x: Capitalize the error: $30,000 / 0.08 = $375,000. Multiplying by 8 ($240,000) is the common slip, and $2,400 multiplies by the rate. $30,000 forgets that buyers pay a multiple of income. That multiple is why rent roll errors matter more than small price negotiations.

questions.q: A buyer's audit cuts a building's NOI from $250,000 to $220,000. Comparable sales show a 5% cap rate. By how much does the indicated value fall?
c: $4,400,000 in total
questions.x: The $30,000 NOI reduction is capitalized: $30,000 / 0.05 = $600,000. $4,400,000 is the new total value ($220,000 / 0.05), not the change. $150,000 multiplies by 5 instead of dividing by 0.05.

questions.q: An owner manages and repairs her 10-unit building herself and shows no management or payroll expense. A buyer reconstructing the operating statement should:
c: Leave both lines at zero, since no one was paid
Add them once the buyer plans to hire help
Add market management and labor costs to expenses
Deduct the owner's time from income instead of expenses
questions.x: NOI measures the property, not the owner, so a reconstructed statement charges market management and labor even when the owner works for free. Leaving the lines at zero is the trap: it overstates NOI and, once capitalized, overstates value. The buyer's own plans do not change what the building costs to run.

questions.q: A building's EGI is $200,000 and its listed expenses are $80,000, with no management fee because the owner self-manages. Market management is 5% of EGI. What is the reconstructed NOI?
c: $120,000 as listed
questions.x: Add the market fee: 5% x $200,000 = $10,000. NOI = $200,000 minus $90,000 = $110,000. $120,000 accepts the owner's zero fee. $116,000 takes 5% of the expenses instead of 5% of EGI. $130,000 adds the fee to income.

questions.q: Which item on a seller's annual statement should a buyer remove before calculating NOI?
c: Replacing the building's roof
The super's weekly wages
Water and sewer charges
Hallway light bulbs and supplies
questions.x: A roof replacement is a capital expenditure: it extends the building's life and is not a recurring operating cost, so it stays out of NOI. Wages, water and supplies are ordinary operating expenses. Supplies are the tempting pick for some because they are small, but small recurring costs are exactly what operating expenses are.

questions.q: A seller's statement lists the following. All of them should be removed before calculating NOI EXCEPT:
c: Monthly mortgage principal and interest
A new boiler installed in March
The owner's personal car lease
Fire and liability insurance premiums
questions.x: Insurance is a fixed operating expense and stays above NOI. Debt service, a capital replacement like a new boiler, and the owner's personal expenses all come out. The boiler is the trap for many because it was paid this year, but a one-time replacement is capital, not operating.

questions.q: A building's owner-paid fuel cost was $22,000, $18,500 and $15,500 over the last three years, and the most recent winter was unusually mild. What heating figure best fits a reconstructed statement?
c: $15,500 for the latest year
questions.x: Volatile expenses like heat are normalized with a multi-year average: ($22,000 + $18,500 + $15,500) / 3 = $18,667. The latest year is the trap because it is real, but one mild winter is not a typical year. The middle year ($18,500) is close but is not an average.

questions.q: A listing shows real estate taxes of $31,000, last year's total. This year's town, county and school bills total $33,400. A buyer's reconstructed statement should use:
c: $31,000, because it is last year's actual cost
$33,400, the current bills the buyer will pay
$32,200, the average of the two years
The town and county portion of the bills
questions.x: A reconstructed statement projects a typical year for the next owner, so known current bills replace last year's figure. Averaging (choice C) suits volatile items like heat, not a tax bill that is already set. Upstate owners often get a separate school tax bill, which is why the full set of bills matters.

questions.q: PGI is $240,000, vacancy is 5%, laundry income is $3,000, operating expenses are $110,000 and annual debt service is $70,000. What is NOI?
c: $51,000 after debt service
questions.x: EGI = $240,000 minus $12,000 plus $3,000 = $231,000. NOI = $231,000 minus $110,000 = $121,000. Debt service is never subtracted to reach NOI; doing so gives $51,000, which is before-tax cash flow. $133,000 forgets vacancy.

questions.q: A seller's statement shows EGI of $150,000 and expenses of $95,000. The expenses include a $20,000 window replacement and $15,000 of mortgage interest, but omit a $6,000 market management fee. What is the reconstructed NOI?
c: $76,000 with the three changes
questions.x: Remove the windows ($20,000, capital) and interest ($15,000, debt service), then add management: $95,000 minus $35,000 plus $6,000 = $66,000 of expenses. NOI = $150,000 minus $66,000 = $84,000. $90,000 forgets to add management; $55,000 is the seller's figure.

questions.q: Three comparable sales: $900,000 with NOI of $63,000; $1,200,000 with NOI of $90,000; and $1,500,000 with NOI of $114,000. Their cap rates range from:
questions.x: Cap rate = NOI / price: $63,000 / $900,000 = 7.0%; $90,000 / $1,200,000 = 7.5%; $114,000 / $1,500,000 = 7.6%. Dividing price by NOI gives multipliers like 14.3, not rates. Comparable cap rates should cluster, as these do.

questions.q: Reconstructed comps show cap rates of 6.5%, 6.75% and 7.0%. The subject is typical of the group and has a reconstructed NOI of $81,000. Using 6.75%, its value is:
c: $1,246,154 at the low end
questions.x: V = I / R = $81,000 / 0.0675 = $1,200,000. $1,246,154 uses the 6.5% rate, the low end, which suits a better-than-average property. $1,157,143 uses 7.0%. $5,467 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: An owner renegotiates a service contract and cuts operating expenses by $4,000 a year. At an 8% cap rate, the building's value rises by about:
c: $32,000 (8 x the saving)
