questions.x: Each dollar of NOI is worth $1 / 0.08 = $12.50, so $4,000 / 0.08 = $50,000. $32,000 multiplies by 8 instead of dividing by 0.08. The small answers treat the saving as if it were only a one-year gain.

questions.q: A setup sheet omits $12,000 of real annual expenses. Comparable sales trade at a 6% cap rate. By how much does the omission overstate value?
c: $720,000 (60 x the error)
questions.x: The missing expenses overstate NOI by $12,000, and value by $12,000 / 0.06 = $200,000. $72,000 multiplies by 6. $720,000 multiplies by 60. A missing expense line is never a one-year problem; it is capitalized into the price.

questions.q: A $1,500,000 commercial loan has monthly payments of $9,750. What is its mortgage constant?
questions.x: Constant = annual debt service / loan = ($9,750 x 12) / $1,500,000 = $117,000 / $1,500,000 = 7.8%. Using the monthly payment alone gives 0.65%, and 6.5% simply assumes the constant equals a rate. The constant is higher than the interest rate on an amortizing loan because it includes principal.

questions.q: A lender quotes a mortgage constant of 7.2% on a $2,000,000 loan. What is the annual debt service?
questions.x: Annual debt service = loan x constant = $2,000,000 x 0.072 = $144,000 (about $12,000 a month, the trap in choice C, which is monthly). Dividing by the constant produces the huge wrong answers. The constant converts any loan size to a yearly payment.

questions.q: A building's NOI is $390,000. The lender requires a 1.25 DSCR and quotes a 7.8% mortgage constant, with a maximum 75% LTV on the $5,600,000 price. What is the maximum loan?
c: $4,200,000 at 75% of price
questions.x: DSCR limit: $390,000 / 1.25 = $312,000 of debt service; $312,000 / 0.078 = $4,000,000. LTV limit: 75% x $5,600,000 = $4,200,000. The lender makes the smaller loan, $4,000,000. Choosing the LTV figure is the trap when coverage binds first.

questions.q: A property's NOI is $150,000 and annual debt service on the proposed loan is $125,000. The lender requires a minimum DSCR of 1.25. The loan:
c: Fails, with a DSCR of 1.20
Passes, since NOI exceeds debt service
Passes, with a DSCR of 1.25
Fails, with a DSCR of 0.83
questions.x: DSCR = NOI / debt service = $150,000 / $125,000 = 1.20, under the 1.25 minimum, so the loan must shrink. Choice B is the trap: covering the payment is not enough when the lender wants a cushion. 0.83 divides the wrong way.

questions.q: An investor buys a $2,000,000 building with NOI of $140,000, borrowing $1,400,000 with annual debt service of $105,000. What is the cash on cash return?
c: 7.0%, the cap rate
questions.x: BTCF = $140,000 minus $105,000 = $35,000. Equity = $2,000,000 minus $1,400,000 = $600,000. Cash on cash = $35,000 / $600,000 = 5.83%. 7.0% is the cap rate. 1.75% divides BTCF by the price. 2.5% divides by the loan.

questions.q: An investor wants an 8% cash on cash return on $500,000 of equity. If annual debt service is $90,000, what NOI does the property need?
c: $170,000 before vacancy
questions.x: Required BTCF = 8% x $500,000 = $40,000. NOI must cover debt service plus that: $90,000 + $40,000 = $130,000. Choice A stops at BTCF. Cash on cash always works from NOI minus debt service, divided by equity.

questions.q: A building trades at a 6.5% cap rate. Which loan would produce positive leverage?
c: A 6.25% interest rate with a 7.4% constant
A 7.0% loan with no amortization
A loan with a 6.9% mortgage constant
A 5.75% interest-only loan
questions.x: Leverage is positive when the mortgage constant is below the cap rate. An interest-only loan's constant equals its rate, so 5.75% beats 6.5%. Choice A is the trap: a 6.25% rate looks cheap, but amortization raises the constant to 7.4%, above the cap rate.

questions.q: An owner's all-cash return would be 7%. With a loan at an 8% mortgage constant, her cash on cash return will be:
c: Higher than 7%
Lower than 7%
Exactly 7%
Higher than 8%
questions.x: When the constant (8%) exceeds the property return (7%), each borrowed dollar costs more than it earns, so the return on her own cash falls below 7%: negative leverage. Many assume any loan raises returns; that only happens when the constant is below the cap rate.

questions.q: A building has PGI of $600,000, operating expenses of $240,000 and annual debt service of $270,000. What is its breakeven occupancy?
questions.x: Breakeven = (operating expenses + debt service) / PGI = $510,000 / $600,000 = 85%. 40% counts operating expenses alone; 45% counts debt service alone; 92.5% is not tied to either. Below 85% occupancy the owner must add cash.

questions.q: Two buyers purchase identical buildings at the same price. Buyer A borrows 75% and Buyer B borrows 50% on the same loan terms. Compared with Buyer B, Buyer A's breakeven occupancy will be:
c: Lower, because A invested less cash
The same, because NOI is identical
Higher, because A's debt service is larger
Higher if A's interest rate is also higher
questions.x: Breakeven occupancy adds debt service to operating expenses, so the bigger loan raises the occupancy needed to cover payments. Choice B is the trap: NOI is identical, but breakeven is a cash measure that includes debt service. Same terms, more debt, higher breakeven.

questions.q: An owner has NOI of $200,000 and fixed debt service of $160,000. If NOI falls 10%, before-tax cash flow falls by:
questions.x: BTCF falls from $40,000 to $180,000 minus $160,000 = $20,000, a 50% drop. Fixed debt service means the whole $20,000 loss lands on the owner's slice. Choice A assumes cash flow moves with NOI, which ignores leverage; 12.5% divides the 10% drop by 0.8.

questions.q: An investor buys a $1,000,000 property with $200,000 down and an $800,000 loan. If the value falls 10% and the loan balance is unchanged, her equity falls by:
questions.x: Value drops $100,000 to $900,000; equity drops from $200,000 to $100,000, a 50% loss. Choice A is what a buyer with no loan would lose; 12.5% divides the drop by the 80% loan ratio. With 80% leverage, a 10% value change becomes a 50% equity change.

questions.q: A three-family house is listed at $990,000 and rents for a total of $6,000 a month. What is its gross rent multiplier?
questions.x: GRM = price / gross monthly rent = $990,000 / $6,000 = 165. 13.75 is the annual gross income multiplier ($990,000 / $72,000). Dividing rent by price gives tiny decimals that are not multipliers at all.

questions.q: Comparable two-family homes in Canarsie sell at a gross rent multiplier of 140. A subject two-family rents for $5,500 a month. What value does the GRM indicate?
c: $9,240,000 using annual rent
questions.x: Value = GRM x monthly rent = 140 x $5,500 = $770,000. Multiplying 140 by annual rent ($66,000) gives $9,240,000, the classic monthly versus annual slip. GRM is a quick screen for small residential income property.

questions.q: The main weakness of the gross rent multiplier as a valuation tool is that it:
c: Requires a full discounted cash flow model
Uses net income instead of gross rent
Ignores differing expenses and vacancy
Works for commercial buildings, not homes
questions.x: GRM compares price with gross rent, so two buildings with the same rent but very different expenses (owner-paid heat, old systems, higher taxes) get the same multiplier. Choice B reverses it: GRM uses gross rent, which is the problem. It is mainly used for small residential property.

questions.q: Building X has a GIM of 9 and pays its tenants' heat. Building Y has a GIM of 11 and tenants pay their own heat. What is the best conclusion?
c: Neither; only NOI and cap rates can rank them
X is the better buy because its multiplier is lower
Y is overpriced because its multiplier is higher
X and Y are equal because GIMs adjust for heat
questions.x: Gross multipliers ignore who pays expenses. X's lower multiplier may simply reflect the cost of heat, so only NOI-based measures can rank these two. Choice B is the trap that sent the Okafors toward the wrong building in the case.

questions.q: Property P costs $2,000,000 with NOI of $120,000. Property Q costs $1,600,000 with NOI of $104,000. Which statement is correct?
c: P has the higher cap rate, 6.5%
Both properties have a 6.0% cap rate
P has the higher cap rate, 6.0%
Q has the higher cap rate, 6.5%
questions.x: P: $120,000 / $2,000,000 = 6.0%. Q: $104,000 / $1,600,000 = 6.5%. Q yields more per dollar invested, though the higher rate may reflect more risk. Choosing P because its NOI is bigger confuses income with yield.

questions.q: A six-unit building costs $1,200,000 with NOI of $66,000. A net leased store costs $1,500,000 with NOI of $97,500. How much higher is the store's cap rate?
c: 0.5 percentage points
1.0 percentage point
1.5 percentage points
2.0 percentage points
questions.x: Six-unit: $66,000 / $1,200,000 = 5.5%. Store: $97,500 / $1,500,000 = 6.5%. The difference is 1.0 percentage point. The higher rate is typically the market's charge for single-tenant risk, not free money.

questions.q: For a building leased to a single tenant on a long triple net lease, the factor that most affects its value is:
c: The landlord's operating expense ratio
The building's gross rent multiplier
The number of parking spaces on the lot
The tenant's credit and lease term
questions.x: With one tenant, income is all or nothing, so the tenant's financial strength and how long the lease runs (plus renewal options) drive value and cap rate. The expense ratio is tiny under a triple net lease and tells you little. GRM ignores the real risk.

questions.q: A single-tenant triple net building nets $90,000 a year. If the tenant leaves, the landlord must pay $30,000 of taxes and insurance until the space re-leases. NOI in a vacant year would be about:
c: Negative $30,000
$90,000 until the lease ends
Zero
questions.x: Rent drops to zero and the landlord now carries the $30,000 the tenant used to pay, so NOI is about negative $30,000 (before re-leasing costs). Choice D forgets that net lease expenses flip back to the owner. That swing is why single-tenant deals trade at higher cap rates.

questions.q: Comparable four-family buildings sell at a GRM of 125. A four-family is listed at $1,250,000 with total rents of $9,200 a month. What does the screen suggest?
c: It supports about $1,150,000, so the price looks high
Its rent supports about $1,380,000, so the price looks low
It is priced right, since its GRM is 125
GRM cannot compare four-family buildings
questions.x: Indicated value = 125 x $9,200 = $1,150,000. The asking price implies a GRM of $1,250,000 / $9,200 = about 136, above the market's 125. The screen says the price is high, subject to confirming expenses are similar to the comps.

questions.q: A buyer will pay a GIM of 10 for a small apartment building. The building's gross annual income is $132,000. The indicated price is:
questions.x: Price = GIM x annual gross income = 10 x $132,000 = $1,320,000. $15,840,000 multiplies a monthly-style figure by annual income. GIM uses annual income; GRM uses monthly rent.

questions.q: A retired couple buys a Queens four-family and owns no other rental property. Under New York's 2024 Good Cause Eviction law, they are most likely:
c: Covered, because the law applies to every NYC rental
Covered once a tenant renews for a second year
Exempt as small landlords with 10 or fewer units
Exempt if one of them lives in the building
questions.x: Good Cause exempts landlords who own 10 or fewer units statewide, so four units and nothing else falls inside the exemption. It applies automatically in NYC, but only to covered buildings and landlords; choice A ignores the exemptions. Owner occupancy is a separate exemption they do not need.

questions.q: Good Cause Eviction protections apply in NYC to all of the following EXCEPT a unit owned by a landlord who:
c: Owns 40 apartments across three Bronx buildings
Owns a 12-unit Brooklyn walk-up built in 1931
Owns 25 units statewide in two buildings
Owns only one 6-unit building and nothing else
questions.x: A landlord with 10 or fewer units statewide is exempt, so the owner of a single 6-unit building is outside the law (absent other facts). The other three landlords own more than 10 units in older buildings, so their tenants are covered. Building age matters only for buildings with a certificate of occupancy from 2009 on.

questions.q: An offering memorandum shows a "pro forma cap rate" on its cover. That figure is usually based on:
c: The building's actual income over the last 12 months
The lender's appraisal of the property
The average cap rate of recent comparable sales
Projected income under the seller's assumptions
questions.x: A pro forma is a projection, typically assuming vacant space leased, rents raised to market or above, and low vacancy. Choice A describes the trailing 12-month (T-12) statement, which is what a buyer should ask for to test the projection.

questions.q: A building's in-place NOI is $300,000 and the OM's pro forma NOI is $420,000. The asking price is $6,000,000. Which statement is most accurate?
c: A 7.0% cap rate, as the cover of the OM states
5.0% now; 7.0% only if the pro forma happens
A 6.0% cap rate, the average of the two figures
Cannot be calculated without knowing the loan
questions.x: In place: $300,000 / $6,000,000 = 5.0%. Pro forma: $420,000 / $6,000,000 = 7.0%, which assumes the seller's projections come true. Quoting 7.0% alone, as choice A does, is how OMs make a price look cheap. Financing never enters the cap rate.

questions.q: A NYC office building's taxes are $150,000 under an ICAP abatement that ends in two years; unabated taxes would be $210,000. For stabilized NOI, a buyer should use:
c: $150,000, today's actual bill
$180,000, the average
$210,000, the unabated tax
$60,000, the abatement amount
questions.x: Stabilized NOI represents a typical year over the hold, and after the abatement ends every year carries the full tax. Using today's abated bill, choice A, is the OM's approach and overstates NOI by $60,000, which at a 6% cap rate is $1,000,000 of value.

questions.q: An OM uses abated taxes that understate the tax bill by $40,000 a year once a NYC abatement expires. At a 6.25% cap rate, how much does this overstate value?
c: $250,000, multiplying by 6.25
questions.x: The overstatement of NOI is capitalized: $40,000 / 0.0625 = $640,000. $250,000 multiplies by 6.25. $40,000 forgets to capitalize. Always check the Department of Finance benefit schedule for every abatement in an OM.

questions.q: A building's stabilized NOI is $480,000 and the market cap rate is 6%. Leasing a vacant floor will cost $150,000 of downtime, $180,000 of improvements and $70,000 of commissions. What is the indicated value today?
questions.x: Stabilized value = $480,000 / 0.06 = $8,000,000. Subtract one-time lease-up of $400,000: $7,600,000. Choice C subtracts the $400,000 from NOI before capitalizing, treating a one-time cost as if it recurred every year. Choice A ignores that the building is not yet stabilized.

questions.q: When valuing a building with a vacant floor, the cost of tenant improvements and leasing commissions to fill it should be:
c: Added to annual operating expenses each year
Ignored, since the vacancy allowance covers it
Subtracted from value as a one-time cost
Added to debt service in the first year
questions.x: Lease-up costs are paid once, so they come off the price once. Adding them to annual expenses capitalizes them as if they recurred forever. The routine vacancy allowance covers future turnover, not filling space that is empty at purchase.

questions.q: A lender requires a 1.30 DSCR on in-place NOI of $520,000 and quotes an 8.0% mortgage constant. The OM's pro forma NOI is $650,000. What is the maximum loan?
c: $6,250,000 on pro forma NOI
questions.x: Lenders underwrite in-place NOI: $520,000 / 1.30 = $400,000 of debt service; $400,000 / 0.08 = $5,000,000. Using pro forma NOI gives $6,250,000, which a lender will not do. $6,500,000 skips the coverage cushion.

questions.q: A buyer pays a price based on pro forma NOI for a building with significant vacancy. The most likely financing consequence is:
c: A larger loan, since lenders reward upside
A smaller loan and more equity
No change, since lenders size loans on LTV alone
A lower interest rate, since the building has room to grow
questions.x: Lenders size loans on income the building earns today. With vacancy, coverage on in-place NOI binds first, so the loan shrinks and the buyer must bring more equity. Choice C ignores the DSCR test, which usually controls on partly vacant buildings.

questions.q: An office tenant paying $36 a foot, below the $44 market, has a lease ending in 5 months and plans to move. The OM shows the space at $44 next year as "upside." A buyer should treat it as:
c: Secured upside, since market rent is $44
No change, keeping $36 for the full hold
A reason to raise the cap rate to the OM's figure
A near-term vacancy risk with leasing costs
questions.x: A below-market lease is upside only if a tenant stays and pays more. A tenant planning to leave creates a vacancy with downtime, improvements and commission. Choice A is the OM's framing. Choice C ignores that the lease expires.

questions.q: In an offering memorandum, the lease expiration schedule is most useful for identifying:
c: How much income is at risk of leaving soon
The building's depreciable basis for income taxes
Which tenants pay the commercial rent tax
The listing broker's commission rate
questions.x: The rollover schedule shows when each tenant's lease ends and what share of income goes with it, so a buyer can see risk concentrated in the next one or two years. Depreciable basis depends on price and land value, not leases.

questions.q: An OM says "information deemed reliable but not guaranteed." The listing licensee knew a major tenant planned to leave but showed it renewing. Under New York law, the disclaimer:
c: Fully protects the licensee from DOS discipline
Does not excuse a known misrepresentation
Shifts the liability to the seller alone
Applies to residential transactions alone
questions.x: A disclaimer may limit reliance on information a broker had no reason to doubt, but it does not excuse knowingly presenting false or misleading facts. DOS can discipline licensees for misrepresentation and untrustworthiness under RPL 441-c. Choice A is the comforting myth.

questions.q: A commercial listing agent preparing an offering memorandum may do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Omit a known tenant departure while showing renewal
Show a pro forma clearly labeled as a projection
Include the seller's certified rent roll
Add a disclaimer urging buyers to verify information
questions.x: Presenting a renewal the agent knows is not happening is a misrepresentation, and no disclaimer cures it. Labeled projections, certified rent rolls and verification disclaimers are all normal and proper parts of an OM.

questions.q: A Long Island City lease charges 1.5 cents per RSF per year for each 1 cent rise in the porters' regular hourly wage over the base rate. The wage has risen from $28.60 to $30.40. The tenant leases 6,000 RSF. What is the annual escalation?
questions.x: Wage increase $1.80 x multiplier 1.5 x 6,000 RSF = $16,200. $10,800 ignores the multiplier (penny for penny). $1,620 drops a zero. $7,200 divides by the multiplier instead of multiplying by it.

questions.q: A porter's wage clause measures the increase in the porters' "regular hourly wage rate." Since the base date, the wage rose $2.40 and the total hourly cost including benefits rose $4.10. The multiplier is 1 and the tenant has 8,000 RSF. The landlord billed $32,800. The tenant should have been billed:
questions.x: The lease names the regular wage, so the increase is $2.40 x 1 x 8,000 = $19,200. The landlord's $32,800 uses wages plus benefits ($4.10), which the clause does not reach. $13,600 is the overcharge, not the correct bill. A porter's wage escalation follows the exact wage the lease defines.

questions.q: A Queens warehouse lease raises rent each year by the change in the CPI, with a floor of 2% and a cap of 5%. Last year's rent was $240,000 and the CPI rose 1.4%. This year's rent is:
questions.x: The index rose less than the 2% floor, so the floor applies: $240,000 x 1.02 = $244,800. $243,360 applies the 1.4% index change and ignores the floor. $252,000 applies the 5% cap, which limits increases and never sets them. Rent does not stay flat when the lease has a floor.

questions.q: A store lease adjusts rent annually by 100% of the CPI change, capped at 4%. Rent was $180,000, and the CPI rose 3.1%. The landlord billed $187,200. What is the correct new rent?
questions.x: The index change of 3.1% is under the 4% cap, so it applies in full: $180,000 x 1.031 = $185,580. The landlord's $187,200 treats the cap as the increase. $183,600 applies 2%, a floor this lease does not contain. Run the formula first, then test it against the limits.

questions.q: A tenant leases 12,000 RSF in a 60,000 RSF building. Its lease defines its share as its RSF divided by the building's RSF. One 12,000 RSF floor is vacant. Operating expenses rose $90,000 over the base year. The tenant's escalation is:
questions.x: Share = 12,000 / 60,000 = 20%, and 20% of $90,000 = $18,000. $22,500 divides by the 48,000 RSF that is occupied, shifting the vacant floor's share onto the tenants, which the lease does not allow. The landlord bears the vacant floor's share. $15,000 uses a one-sixth share that matches nothing in the lease. $90,000 bills the whole increase.

questions.q: An office lease sets the tenant's share at 8%. Taxes rose $50,000 over the base year and operating expenses rose $25,000, but the landlord billed the tenant 10% of the $75,000 for two years. How much was the tenant overbilled in total?
questions.x: Correct annual bill: 8% x $75,000 = $6,000. Billed: 10% x $75,000 = $7,500. Overcharge $1,500 a year, $3,000 for two years. $1,500 is one year. $7,500 is the annual bill, not the error. A buyer who finds this in due diligence asks the seller for a credit or escrow for the refund exposure.

questions.q: A Bronx industrial lease has a $9.50 per RSF expense stop. Actual operating expenses and taxes come to $11.25 per RSF. The tenant leases 15,000 RSF. What does the tenant owe for the year above base rent?
questions.x: Excess over the stop = $11.25 minus $9.50 = $1.75 per RSF; $1.75 x 15,000 = $26,250. $168,750 charges all expenses, and $142,500 confuses the stop with the payment. Under a stop the landlord absorbs costs up to the stop. $5,250 applies a 20% share, a base year method, to a stop clause.

questions.q: Under an expense stop, the tenant pays:
c: Its share of the increase over actual costs in a base year
The fixed dollar amount set in the lease, adjusted by CPI
Its share of every operating cost from the first dollar
The cost above a fixed dollar amount set in the lease
questions.x: An expense stop is a fixed dollar amount, usually per RSF, written into the lease; the landlord absorbs costs up to it and the tenant pays the excess. The base year choice describes a base year escalation, whose baseline is whatever expenses turn out to be in a named year. Paying from the first dollar describes a net lease.

questions.q: A Brooklyn seller's rent roll shows a tenant at $96,000 a year. The tenant's estoppel certificate states $91,500 and notes a disputed increase. What should the buyer generally underwrite?
c: $96,000, as the seller represented it
$93,750, splitting the disputed amount
$91,500, the rent the tenant has confirmed
$96,000, since estoppels bind the buyer
questions.x: An estoppel binds the tenant to what it states for anyone who relies on it, so the buyer can count on $91,500 and cannot expect more while the tenant disputes the increase. The seller's representation gives the buyer a claim against the seller, not a higher rent. The estoppel binds the tenant, not the buyer, so the last choice reverses the rule.

questions.q: Who signs an estoppel certificate in a commercial building sale, and who relies on it?
c: The seller signs it; the tenant relies on it at renewal
The tenant signs it; the buyer and lender rely on it
The buyer signs it; the seller relies on it at closing
The lender signs it; the tenant relies on it at default
questions.x: A tenant estoppel is the tenant's signed statement of its lease terms, rent, deposit and any defaults, delivered so a buyer or lender can rely on it. The seller-signs choice is the tempting one, because the seller requests and delivers the estoppels, but a seller's own statement of the leases is a rent roll or a representation, not an estoppel.

questions.q: A buyer's audit finds a building's rent roll overstates escalation income by $26,000 a year. At an 8% cap rate, how much should the value drop?
questions.x: Value = income / rate, so $26,000 / 0.08 = $325,000. $26,000 treats a permanent income shortfall as a one-time cost. $208,000 divides by 0.125 instead of 0.08. $2,080 multiplies the income by the cap rate. Every dollar of lost annual income costs 1 / 0.08 = $12.50 of value at an 8% cap.

questions.q: An audit of a loft building finds $30,000 a year of overbilled escalations and $12,000 a year of escalations that were never billed but can be going forward. At a 6% cap rate, the net value change is:
c: A decrease of $500,000
A decrease of $18,000
An increase of $200,000
A decrease of $300,000
questions.x: Net income change = minus $30,000 plus $12,000 = minus $18,000 a year. $18,000 / 0.06 = $300,000 less value. $500,000 counts only the overbilling. $18,000 is the annual change, not its capitalized value. The unbilled escalation adds value, but less than the overbilling removes.

cram.html: Higher risk and lower liquidity = higher required return. Real estate is illiquid.
Positive leverage: property return > mortgage constant. Negative: loan costs more than the property earns.
Mortgage constant = annual debt service / loan amount.
PGI minus vacancy and credit loss + other income = EGI. EGI minus operating expenses = NOI.
NOI never includes debt service, depreciation, income tax or capital items (new roof, new boiler).
BTCF = NOI minus debt service. Cash on cash (equity dividend rate) = BTCF / equity, not price.
Tax world: taxable income = NOI minus interest minus depreciation. Principal is not deductible.
ATCF = BTCF minus tax (plus tax savings if the property shows a usable tax loss).
Depreciation: 27.5 years residential, 39 nonresidential, land never. Mixed use is residential only if 80%+ of rent is from dwellings.
IRV: I = R x V, R = I / V, V = I / R. Use annual NOI.
Cap rate up, value down. Riskier property = higher cap rate.
Debt coverage ratio = NOI / debt service. Below 1.0 = NOI does not cover the loan.
Pro forma = projected. Reconstructed = actual, restated for an investor.
Rentable > usable > carpetable.
Loss factor = (RSF minus USF) / RSF. Add-on factor = RSF / USF minus 1.
Cost per usable foot = rent per RSF / (1 minus loss factor). RSF needed = USF / (1 minus loss factor).
Natural breakpoint = base rent / percentage rate. Overage = rate x (sales minus breakpoint).
Anchor tenants draw traffic and usually pay lower rent per square foot.
Ground lease: tenant holds the leasehold, landowner the leased fee; improvements usually revert at the end.
Gross lease: landlord pays expenses. NNN: tenant pays taxes, insurance, maintenance.
Assignment = all of the remaining interest. Sublease = less than all. Original tenant usually stays liable.
SNDA: tenant Subordinates, lender gives Non-Disturbance, tenant Attorns to the new owner. Estoppel certifies lease facts.
Electric: direct meter (tenant pays utility), submeter (landlord bills measured use), rent inclusion (in the rent).
Escalation = proportionate share (tenant RSF / building RSF) x increase over base.
Base year = actual expenses of a named year. Expense stop = fixed dollar amount in the lease.
Porter's wage: wage increase x multiplier x RSF ("penny for penny").
NYC tax year runs July 1 to June 30.
The NYS anti-discrimination disclosure form applies to commercial deals too; RPL 443 agency disclosure does not. RPL 226-b sublet rights are residential only.

subjects.title: Income Tax Issues in Real Estate Transactions
subjects.blurb: Clients ask how a sale or purchase hits their taxes. The exam asks the same: the $250,000/$500,000 exclusion, basis and gain math, depreciation, and the 45/180-day 1031 rules.

lessons.title: Taxes and the Home You Live In
lessons.tagline: Homeowners get the friendliest tax treatment in the code. Know the deductions, the basis math, and the $250,000/$500,000 rule.
objectives: Explain what the Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 changed for homeowners
Identify deductible mortgage interest, property taxes, and points, including current limits
Calculate basis, adjusted basis, amount realized, and gain on a home sale
Apply the $250,000/$500,000 exclusion and its ownership and use tests
Distinguish short-term from long-term capital gain

blocks.title: Bed-Stuy, after 28 years
blocks.html: The Okafors bought their brownstone on Macon Street in 1997 for $185,000. They put in a new roof, a new boiler, and a rear extension. Now a buyer is offering $2,150,000. Emmanuel reads a headline about capital gains and panics: "Are we going to hand half of this to the IRS?" Jordan is not a tax advisor. But Jordan should know enough to explain the shape of the answer.
blocks.casual: The Okafors bought their Macon Street brownstone in 1997 for $185,000. Since then: new roof, new boiler, a rear extension. Now a buyer's offering $2,150,000. Emmanuel sees a headline about capital gains and freaks out: "Are we handing half of this to the IRS?" Jordan isn't a tax advisor. But Jordan should know enough to sketch out what the answer looks like.

deeper.plain: Selling a long-held home for a big profit raises tax questions. An agent should understand the basics without playing accountant.
deeper.picture: You're the tour guide, not the pilot. You can point out the landmarks of the tax rules, but someone licensed flies the plane.
deeper.street: Emmanuel calls Jordan at 10 pm after reading that article. Jordan walks him through basis, improvements and the $500,000 married exclusion, then says, "Take your roof and boiler receipts to your accountant this week."
deeper.stakes: A panicked seller might pull the listing or underprice it to "save on taxes." An agent who explains the shape of the rules keeps the deal on track without giving advice they're not licensed for.
deeper.exam: Expect a long-held-home fact pattern where you compute gain after the exclusion. The trap is forgetting improvements or selling costs.

blocks.title: Stay in your lane
blocks.html: Licensees explain general rules and always say: "Confirm with your accountant or tax attorney." Giving specific tax advice you are not qualified to give invites liability.
blocks.casual: Stay in your lane. You can explain the general rules, and then you always say: "Confirm with your accountant or tax attorney." Hand out specific tax advice you're not qualified to give and you're asking to get sued.

deeper.plain: Explain the general idea, then send the client to a tax pro for their specific answer.
deeper.picture: It's like a personal trainer and a doctor. The trainer can explain how muscles work, but a diagnosis comes from the doctor.
deeper.street: Leo asks Jordan whether he should buy before or after year end to max his deduction. Jordan explains how itemizing works in general, then says Leo's CPA has to run his numbers.
deeper.stakes: If a client follows your tax tip and gets a bill from the IRS, they'll come after you and your broker. Errors and omissions insurance may not cover advice outside your license.
deeper.exam: When an answer choice says the licensee should "advise the client to consult a tax professional," it's usually the best one.

blocks.text: The law that set the rules: Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997

blocks.html: The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 rewrote home sale taxation. It replaced the old "rollover" rule (buy a pricier home within 2 years to defer gain) and the one-time $125,000 exclusion for sellers 55 and older with today's $250,000/$500,000 exclusion, usable every 2 years at any age. It also let first-time homebuyers take up to $10,000 from an IRA without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty.
blocks.casual: The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 flipped home sale taxes. Out went the old "rollover" rule (buy a pricier home within 2 years to defer the gain) and the one-time $125,000 exclusion for sellers 55 and up. In came today's $250,000/$500,000 exclusion, usable every 2 years at any age. It also let first-time buyers pull up to $10,000 from an IRA without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty.

deeper.plain: Since 1997, you can sell your home and keep a big chunk of profit tax-free, repeatedly, no matter your age.
deeper.picture: The old rules were a ladder you had to keep climbing to avoid tax. The new rule is a fixed tax-free allowance you can use again every two years.
deeper.street: Sal's parents sold their Astoria house in 1995 and had to buy a pricier one in Bayside to avoid tax. Today, a couple selling in Astoria can bank up to $500,000 of gain tax-free and rent, downsize, or move to Florida.
deeper.stakes: Older clients may still believe they need to "trade up" or wait until 55. That outdated belief can push bad decisions.
deeper.exam: Cue "Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997." It created the $250,000/$500,000 exclusion and the $10,000 IRA first-time buyer rule. Rollover and the over-55 exclusion are the old rules.

blocks.title: IRA withdrawal: no penalty is not no tax
blocks.html: The $10,000 is a lifetime limit per person. It escapes the 10% penalty, but a traditional IRA withdrawal is still ordinary income. "First-time" means no ownership of a principal residence in the prior 2 years, so a returning buyer can qualify.
blocks.casual: Careful here. The $10,000 is a lifetime limit per person. It skips the 10% penalty, but a traditional IRA withdrawal is still taxed as ordinary income. And "first-time" just means you haven't owned a principal residence in the past 2 years, so someone coming back to buying can qualify.

deeper.plain: No penalty doesn't mean no tax. You still owe income tax on a traditional IRA withdrawal.
deeper.picture: It's like getting a late fee waived on a bill. You still owe the bill.
deeper.street: Leo sold a condo in 2021 and has rented in Long Island City since. In 2026 he pulls $10,000 from his traditional IRA for a down payment in Astoria. No 10% penalty, but if he's in the 24% bracket, about $2,400 goes to federal income tax.
deeper.stakes: A buyer who budgets the whole $10,000 for the down payment can come up short at tax time.
deeper.exam: "First-time homebuyer" means no principal residence owned in the prior 2 years. The $10,000 is lifetime, and it escapes only the penalty, not income tax.

blocks.html: Homeowners who itemize (instead of taking the standard deduction) can deduct mortgage interest and property taxes. Many people with modest loans never itemize, so the deduction does nothing for them.
blocks.casual: If you itemize instead of taking the standard deduction, you can deduct mortgage interest and property taxes. But lots of people with smaller loans never itemize, so the deduction does nothing for them.

deeper.plain: The home deductions only help if your itemized total beats the standard deduction.
deeper.picture: It's a coupon that only works on orders over a minimum. If your total doesn't reach it, the coupon is worthless.
deeper.street: A buyer in Rochester has a $150,000 mortgage and $4,000 in property tax. Her itemized total doesn't beat the standard deduction, so she takes the standard deduction and gets no extra benefit from owning. Leo, with a bigger Brooklyn loan, does itemize.
deeper.stakes: Agents who promise "huge tax savings" to every buyer can mislead them into overspending.
deeper.exam: Deductions require itemizing. A choice saying all homeowners automatically deduct interest is wrong.

head: Item
Rule (2026)
rows: Mortgage interest on acquisition debt

Deductible on up to $750,000 of debt used to buy, build, or substantially improve a main home and one second home ($375,000 married filing separately). Loans from before Dec 16, 2017 keep the old $1 million limit. The 2025 tax law made the $750,000 limit permanent.
Home equity loans and HELOCs
Interest deductible only if the money is used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home securing it, and it counts toward the $750,000. Used for a car or tuition: not deductible.
Interest deductible on the refinanced balance up to the old acquisition debt that was paid off. Extra cash-out counts only if used to improve the home.
Treated as acquisition debt if used to substantially improve the home.
Can be treated as acquisition debt for up to 24 months while the home is being built.

Deductible as part of the state and local tax (SALT) deduction: capped at $40,000 for 2025 ($40,400 for 2026, rising 1% a year through 2029), reduced for incomes above about $500,000, back to $10,000 in 2030.
Deductible again as mortgage interest starting in 2026, subject to income limits.
Deductible as mortgage interest in the year paid.
blocks.caption: Federal rules. Confirm current figures with a tax professional.

deeper.plain: You can deduct interest on up to $750,000 of debt used to buy or improve your homes, and property taxes within the SALT cap.
deeper.picture: The interest deduction follows the money. If the loan built or bought the house, it counts. If it bought a car, it doesn't.
deeper.street: Leo has a $600,000 mortgage on his Bay Ridge condo and takes a $50,000 HELOC. He spends $30,000 on a new kitchen and $20,000 on a car. Interest on the $30,000 counts; interest on the $20,000 doesn't. His total qualifying debt is $630,000, under the $750,000 limit.
deeper.stakes: Clients who assume all home equity interest is deductible get surprised at tax time. Big-loan buyers in NYC can blow past the $750,000 cap.
deeper.exam: Key numbers: $750,000 acquisition debt ($375,000 married separately), $1 million for loans before Dec 16, 2017, construction up to 24 months. HELOC interest only if used to buy, build or substantially improve.

blocks.title: Why New Yorkers care about SALT
blocks.html: NY combines high income tax with high property taxes. A Westchester or Long Island owner can hit the old $10,000 SALT cap from property tax alone. The higher cap in 2025 to 2029 matters a lot here. Note that NYC co-op owners deduct their share of the building's real estate tax and mortgage interest, which the co-op reports to them each year.
blocks.casual: Why SALT is a New York thing: we've got high income tax and high property tax. A Westchester or Long Island owner can hit the old $10,000 SALT cap on property tax alone. So the higher cap for 2025 to 2029 is a big deal here. Also, NYC co-op owners deduct their share of the building's real estate tax and mortgage interest, and the co-op reports those numbers to them every year.

deeper.plain: New Yorkers pay a lot of state and local tax, so the cap on deducting it matters more here than almost anywhere.
deeper.picture: The SALT cap is a lid on a pot. In a low-tax state the pot never fills to the lid. In Westchester it boils over.
deeper.street: A family in Scarsdale pays $28,000 in property tax and $20,000 in state income tax. Under a $10,000 cap they lost most of that deduction. Kim, a co-op owner on the Upper West Side, gets a year-end letter from her co-op showing her share of the building's taxes and interest to deduct.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring SALT can make a buyer misjudge the after-tax cost of a high-tax suburb. Co-op buyers who don't know about their share-of-building deduction leave money on the table.
deeper.exam: Co-op owners can deduct their proportionate share of the building's mortgage interest and real estate taxes. Expect a co-op deduction question.

blocks.q: Leo takes a $90,000 HELOC on his Sunnyside condo and uses it to buy a car and pay off student loans. Is the interest deductible?
c: Yes, all HELOC interest is deductible
No, because the money was not used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home
Yes, up to $100,000 of home equity debt
Only if he itemizes
blocks.x: Since 2018, home equity interest is deductible only when the proceeds buy, build, or substantially improve the home. The old $100,000 home equity rule is gone.

blocks.html: Points (1 point = 1% of the loan) paid to get a mortgage on the purchase of a main home are generally deductible in full in the year paid. Points on a refinance are deducted over the life of the loan. Points the seller pays for the buyer are still deductible by the buyer, but reduce the buyer's basis.
blocks.casual: Points (1 point = 1% of the loan) paid to get a mortgage when you buy your main home are generally fully deductible in the year you pay them. Points on a refinance get spread over the life of the loan. If the seller pays points for the buyer, the buyer still deducts them, but the buyer's basis goes down.

deeper.plain: Purchase points on your main home: deduct now. Refinance points: deduct a little each year.
deeper.picture: Purchase points are a lump-sum ticket. Refinance points are a subscription you write off month by month.
deeper.street: The Okafors' buyer negotiates $15,000 in seller-paid points. The buyer deducts the $15,000 this year if itemizing, but the buyer's basis in the brownstone drops by $15,000.
deeper.stakes: Mixing up purchase and refinance points can mean an amended return or a penalty.
deeper.exam: 1 point = 1% of the loan. Purchase of main home: deductible in full the year paid. Refinance: amortized. Seller-paid points: deductible by buyer, reduce buyer's basis.

blocks.html: Most other purchase closing costs are not deductible. Title insurance, recording fees, attorney fees, and transfer taxes the buyer pays are added to basis. Prorated property taxes are deductible as taxes. Seller's selling costs (commission, NYS transfer tax, attorney fees) reduce the amount realized.
blocks.casual: Most other closing costs on a purchase aren't deductible. Title insurance, recording fees, attorney fees and transfer taxes the buyer pays get added to basis. Prorated property taxes are deductible as taxes. On the seller's side, selling costs (commission, NYS transfer tax, attorney fees) reduce the amount realized.

deeper.plain: Buying costs help later by raising your basis. Selling costs help by shrinking your sale proceeds. Either way they cut your taxable gain.
deeper.picture: Think of a scale. Buying costs add weight to the cost side; selling costs take weight off the sale side. Both make the gain smaller.
deeper.street: Leo pays $4,500 for title insurance and $2,000 for his attorney on his Bay Ridge purchase. None of it is deductible this year, but his basis goes up $6,500, so when he sells, his gain is $6,500 smaller.
deeper.stakes: Lost closing statements mean you can't prove basis, and you pay tax on gain you didn't really have.
deeper.exam: Buyer's title insurance, recording fees, attorney fees, transfer taxes: add to basis, not deductible. Seller's commission and transfer tax: reduce amount realized.

blocks.title: Points on a Bay Ridge purchase
blocks.html:
Leo borrows $600,000 to buy a Bay Ridge condo and pays 1.5 points.
1.5% x $600,000 = $9,000.
Purchase of a main home: $9,000 deductible this year if he itemizes. If this were a 30-year refinance, he would deduct $9,000 / 30 = $300 a year.
blocks.casual:
Leo borrows $600,000 for a Bay Ridge condo and pays 1.5 points.
1.5% x $600,000 = $9,000.
It's a main home purchase, so $9,000 is deductible this year if he itemizes. If it were a 30-year refinance, he'd deduct $9,000 / 30 = $300 a year.

deeper.plain: Multiply points by the loan amount to get the dollar cost, then decide if it's deductible now or over time.
deeper.picture: Points are a discount coupon you buy up front to lower your interest rate. The IRS decides whether you get credit all at once or spread out.
deeper.street: Leo plugs this into his spreadsheet: $9,000 in points to drop his rate. If he's in the 24% bracket and itemizes, the deduction saves about $2,160 this year.
deeper.stakes: If Leo refinances later and deducts all the refi points in one year, the IRS can disallow most of it.
deeper.exam: Do the math: points x loan amount. Then check if it's a purchase (deduct now) or a refinance (divide by loan term).

blocks.html: Basis is what you have invested for tax purposes: purchase price plus buying costs. Adjusted basis adds capital improvements (things that add value or extend life: a new roof, an extension, a new kitchen) and subtracts depreciation taken and casualty losses claimed. Repairs and maintenance (painting, fixing a leak) do not add to basis.
blocks.casual: Basis is what you've got in the property for tax purposes: purchase price plus buying costs. Adjusted basis adds capital improvements (stuff that adds value or extends life: a new roof, an extension, a new kitchen) and subtracts any depreciation you took and casualty losses you claimed. Repairs and upkeep, like painting or fixing a leak, don't count.

deeper.plain: Your basis is your running tab of what you've put into the house. Bigger basis, smaller taxable gain.
deeper.picture: Basis is a jar. Purchase price goes in first, then every real improvement. Depreciation you deducted gets scooped back out.
deeper.street: Sal bought his Astoria six-family for $400,000, added a $60,000 new roof, and repainted every hallway for $8,000. His basis goes up $60,000 for the roof but not a cent for the paint. Depreciation he's taken on the rentals comes off.
deeper.stakes: Owners who toss receipts can't prove improvements, so they pay tax on gain they didn't actually make.
deeper.exam: The classic question: is it an improvement or a repair? Roof, addition, new kitchen add to basis. Painting, fixing a leak, replacing a broken window pane don't.

blocks.title: The gain formula

items.title: Amount realized
items.html: Amount realized = sale price minus selling expenses.

items.title: Adjusted basis
items.html: Purchase price + buying costs + capital improvements minus depreciation.

items.title: Gain or loss
items.html: Amount realized minus adjusted basis. Positive is a capital gain; negative is a capital loss.

blocks.casual:
The gain formula, three steps.
Amount realized: amount realized = sale price minus selling expenses.
Adjusted basis: purchase price + buying costs + capital improvements minus depreciation.
Gain or loss: amount realized minus adjusted basis. Positive is a capital gain; negative is a capital loss.

deeper.plain: What you walked away with, minus what you had in it, is your gain.
deeper.picture: Two piles of money: what the sale really put in your pocket, and what you really put into the house. The gap between the piles is the gain.
deeper.street: A Forest Hills seller sells for $900,000 and pays $60,000 in commission and transfer tax: amount realized $840,000. She bought for $500,000 with $10,000 in costs and added a $50,000 kitchen: adjusted basis $560,000. Gain: $280,000.
deeper.stakes: Skip a step, like subtracting selling costs, and you overstate the gain and the tax.
deeper.exam: Order matters: sale price minus selling costs, then subtract adjusted basis. Commission reduces amount realized; it doesn't add to basis.

blocks.html: Appreciation is the increase in market value over time. It is not taxed until you sell (it is "unrealized"). Gain is how appreciation shows up on the tax return.
blocks.casual: Appreciation is how much the market value goes up over time. It's not taxed until you sell (it's "unrealized"). Gain is what that appreciation turns into on your tax return.

deeper.plain: Your house getting more valuable isn't taxed until you sell it.
deeper.picture: Appreciation is fruit on the tree. Gain is when you pick it and take it to market.
deeper.street: The Okafors' brownstone went from $185,000 to over $2 million in value. They paid zero tax on that growth for 28 years. Only the sale turns it into a taxable gain.
deeper.stakes: Owners sometimes think rising assessments or values trigger income tax. They don't. That confusion can lead to panic selling or holding too long.
deeper.exam: Appreciation is unrealized until sale. Gain is realized at sale. Don't confuse appreciation with assessed value.

head: Holding period
Type
Federal rate
rows: 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income (plus 3.8% net investment income tax for high earners)

deeper.plain: Sell within a year and the profit is taxed like your paycheck. Hold longer and it gets a lower rate.
deeper.picture: Think of it as a ticket price that drops after a year of waiting. Day 366 gets the cheap seats.
deeper.street: An investor flips a Bushwick condo after 10 months for a $90,000 profit and pays tax at her 35% ordinary rate. If she'd held two more months, it would be long-term at 15% or 20%.
deeper.stakes: Closing a few weeks too early can cost tens of thousands. Timing a closing can be a real money decision.
deeper.exam: "1 year or less" is short-term at ordinary rates (up to 37%). "More than 1 year" is long-term at 0, 15 or 20%, plus 3.8% NIIT for high earners.

blocks.title: Losses on a home
blocks.html: A loss on selling your personal residence is not deductible. Capital losses on investment property can offset capital gains, plus up to $3,000 a year of ordinary income, with the rest carried forward.
blocks.casual: Here's a trap: if you lose money selling your personal residence, you can't deduct it. Capital losses on investment property are different. They offset capital gains, plus up to $3,000 a year of ordinary income, and the rest carries forward.

deeper.plain: Losing money on your own home gets no tax break. Losing money on an investment does.
deeper.picture: Your home is a personal item, like a car. If your car loses value, the IRS doesn't care. An investment is business, so losses count.
deeper.street: Leo buys a condo in 2026 for $700,000 and sells in 2029 for $650,000 after a job move. That $50,000 loss isn't deductible. If it had been a rental he bought as an investment, he could use it against gains and $3,000 a year of income.
deeper.stakes: Sellers expecting a tax write-off on a home loss get nothing and may make bad timing calls.
deeper.exam: Personal residence loss: not deductible. Investment loss: offsets gains, plus $3,000 of ordinary income per year, carryforward for the rest.

blocks.html: Under IRC 121, the home sale exclusion lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain (single) or $500,000 (married filing jointly) on a principal residence if:
blocks.casual: Under IRC 121, the home sale exclusion lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain if you're single or $500,000 if you're married filing jointly on a principal residence, as long as:

deeper.plain: A big chunk of profit on selling your main home can be completely tax-free.
deeper.picture: It's a tax-free bucket. Fill it with up to $250,000 or $500,000 of profit and none of it is taxed. Anything that overflows is taxed.
deeper.street: A married couple in Woodside sells for a $380,000 gain after living there 6 years. All $380,000 fits under the $500,000 exclusion. Their federal tax on the sale: zero.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who don't know the exclusion might hold off selling for no reason. Those who don't meet the tests may face a surprise tax bill.
deeper.exam: IRC 121. Single $250,000, married filing jointly $500,000. Principal residence only.

items: Ownership test: you owned it at least 2 of the 5 years before the sale
Use test: you lived in it as your main home at least 2 of those 5 years (need not be continuous)
Once every 2 years: you have not used the exclusion on another sale in the prior 2 years
For $500,000: either spouse meets ownership, both meet use, and neither used it in the past 2 years
blocks.casual:
The tests:
Ownership: you owned it at least 2 of the 5 years before the sale.
Use: you lived in it as your main home at least 2 of those 5 years (doesn't have to be continuous).
Once every 2 years: you haven't used the exclusion on another sale in the last 2 years.
For the full $500,000: either spouse meets ownership, both meet use, and neither used it in the past 2 years.

deeper.plain: Own it two years, live in it two years, and don't use the break again within two years.
deeper.picture: Picture a five-year window sliding back from your closing date. Inside it, you need two years of owning and two years of living, and they don't have to be the same two years.
deeper.street: Priya bought a Carroll Gardens apartment in 2021, lived there until 2023, rented it out, and sells in 2026. She owned it 5 years and lived there 2 of the last 5, so she qualifies. Her new husband never lived there, so they get $250,000, not $500,000.
deeper.stakes: Selling a month before hitting two years can cost the whole exclusion unless a partial one applies.
deeper.exam: Watch the spouse rule: one owns is fine, but both must use. Use doesn't have to be continuous.

blocks.html: A partial exclusion may be available if a move is forced early by a job change, health, or unforeseen circumstances. Gain above the exclusion is taxed as long-term capital gain. Any depreciation taken (say, for a home office or a rented unit) is recaptured and not excluded.
blocks.casual: If you have to move early because of a job change, health, or something unforeseen, you might get a partial exclusion. Gain above the exclusion is taxed as long-term capital gain. And any depreciation you took (say for a home office or a rented unit) gets recaptured. The exclusion doesn't cover it.

deeper.plain: Moving early for a good reason can save part of the break. Depreciation you deducted always comes back.
deeper.picture: Depreciation is a loan from the IRS. The exclusion forgives profit, not loans.
deeper.street: Sal lived in one unit of a two-family in Astoria and rented the other, taking $40,000 in depreciation on the rental side. When he sells, that $40,000 is taxed even though his residence gain fits inside the exclusion.
deeper.stakes: Owners with home offices or rented units get surprised by the recapture bill.
deeper.exam: Partial exclusion: job, health, unforeseen circumstances. Depreciation recapture is never excluded.

blocks.caption: Slide the sale price and basis: watch the gain fill the $250,000 or $500,000 bucket, and see what spills over as taxable.

blocks.title: The Okafors' brownstone
blocks.html:
Purchase 1997: $185,000 + $5,000 closing costs = $190,000 basis.
Improvements: roof $40,000 + boiler $25,000 + extension $245,000 = $310,000.
Adjusted basis = $190,000 + $310,000 = $500,000.
Sale $2,150,000 minus commission and transfer taxes $130,000 = amount realized $2,020,000.
Gain = $2,020,000 minus $500,000 = $1,520,000.
Married, lived there 28 years: exclude $500,000.
Taxable long-term gain = $1,020,000. Not half to the IRS, but real money: they need their accountant now, and receipts for every improvement.
blocks.casual:
Run the Okafors' numbers.
Bought in 1997: $185,000 + $5,000 closing costs = $190,000 basis.
Improvements: roof $40,000 + boiler $25,000 + extension $245,000 = $310,000.
Adjusted basis = $190,000 + $310,000 = $500,000.
Sale $2,150,000 minus commission and transfer taxes of $130,000 = amount realized $2,020,000.
Gain = $2,020,000 minus $500,000 = $1,520,000.
Married, lived there 28 years: exclude $500,000.
Taxable long-term gain = $1,020,000. So no, not half to the IRS. But it's real money. They need their accountant now, plus receipts for every improvement.

deeper.plain: Improvements and selling costs knock a lot off the gain, and the exclusion takes off another $500,000.
deeper.picture: Peel an onion: sale price, minus selling costs, minus basis, minus improvements, minus exclusion. What's left in the middle is taxed.
deeper.street: Without the roof, boiler and extension receipts, the Okafors' basis would be $190,000 and the taxable gain $1,330,000. Those receipts save them $310,000 of taxable gain, roughly $46,500 at a 15% federal rate before NY tax.
deeper.stakes: Lost paperwork is lost money. Agents who prompt sellers to gather receipts early earn real trust.
deeper.exam: Expect a multi-step calculation. Subtract selling costs from the price first, add improvements to basis, then subtract the exclusion last.

blocks.q: Leo bought a condo 3 years ago, lived in it 1 year, then rented it out for 2 years. He sells now at a $90,000 gain. Does he qualify for the full $250,000 exclusion?
c: Yes, he owned it more than 2 years
No, he fails the 2-year use test
Yes, because it was once his main home
No, because rental property never qualifies for anything
blocks.x: He meets ownership (3 years) but lived there only 1 of the last 5 years. Both tests are required.

blocks.html: Interest on a mortgage on one second home is deductible within the same $750,000 total. Property taxes count toward the SALT cap. The $250,000/$500,000 exclusion does not apply to a second home unless it becomes your main home for 2 of 5 years. If you rent a vacation home out fewer than 15 days a year, that rent is tax-free; rent it more and it starts being treated partly as rental property.
blocks.casual: Interest on a mortgage for one second home is deductible inside the same $750,000 total. Property taxes count toward the SALT cap. The $250,000/$500,000 exclusion doesn't apply to a second home unless it becomes your main home for 2 of 5 years. And if you rent out a vacation home fewer than 15 days a year, that rent is tax-free. Rent it longer and it starts being treated partly as rental property.

deeper.plain: Second homes get the interest deduction but not the sale exclusion, unless you move in.
deeper.picture: Your second home shares a single $750,000 bucket with your main home for interest, but it doesn't get its own tax-free sale bucket.
deeper.street: Diane rents her Hamptons cottage for 12 days in August for $9,000. That's tax-free. If she rents it for a month, she reports the income and allocates expenses.
deeper.stakes: Owners who assume the exclusion covers a vacation home get hit with capital gains tax on sale.
deeper.exam: Fewer than 15 days of rental: tax-free. Second home interest: within $750,000 total. Exclusion: main home only.

blocks.q: A couple sells their Catskills cabin, which they used only on weekends, at a $120,000 gain. How much can they exclude under the home sale exclusion?
blocks.x: The exclusion applies only to a principal residence used 2 of the last 5 years. A weekend cabin is a second home: the gain is taxable as capital gain.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: 2 of 5, every 2, 250 or 500. Own 2 of 5, live 2 of 5, once every 2 years, $250,000 single or $500,000 married.
blocks.casual: The hook: 2 of 5, every 2, 250 or 500. Own 2 of 5, live 2 of 5, once every 2 years, $250,000 single or $500,000 married.

deeper.plain: Two years out of five, once every two years, $250,000 or $500,000.
deeper.picture: Two hands, five fingers each: two fingers for owning, two for living, out of five years.
deeper.street: Jordan explains it to Emmanuel on a napkin at a Bed-Stuy coffee shop: "2 of 5, every 2, 250 or 500. You two clear it easily."
deeper.stakes: Get any of these numbers wrong and a client could time a sale badly or expect a tax break they won't get.
deeper.exam: Distractors swap in 3 of 5, once in a lifetime, or age 55. Those are wrong or outdated.

story.title: Half to the IRS?
story.setting: The Okafors' parlor floor, Macon Street, a Sunday in April

beats.text: Grace has made tea. Emmanuel has made a spreadsheet, badly.
Emmanuel: We paid $185,000. We're selling for over two million. My cousin says the government takes half.
First thing: I'm not your accountant, and you need one. But I can show you how it's figured, so you know what to bring them.
beats.tag: Explain, then refer to a tax pro

beats.text: Start with basis: what you paid plus closing costs. Then add capital improvements. The roof, the boiler, the extension. Painting doesn't count.
beats.tag: Adjusted basis adds improvements, not repairs

beats.text: Grace: I have every receipt since 1997. In a shoebox.
That shoebox might be worth six figures. So basis is about $500,000. Sale price minus selling costs, minus basis, is your gain. Around $1.5 million.
You've owned and lived here way more than 2 of the last 5 years, and you're married. So the first $500,000 of gain is excluded.

check.q: Which tests must the Okafors meet for the $500,000 exclusion?
c: Age 55 or older
Owned and lived in it 2 of the last 5 years, no exclusion used in the last 2 years
Buy a more expensive home within 2 years
Sell to a first-time buyer
check.x: Ownership and use tests, 2 of 5 years, once every 2 years. The age-55 and rollover rules were replaced by the Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997.

beats.text: Emmanuel: In 1997 my father told me we had to buy a bigger house or pay tax.
That was the old rollover rule. The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 replaced it the same year you bought. Your dad wasn't wrong. He was just early.
beats.tag: TRA 1997 ended rollover and the over-55 rule

beats.text: The rest is long-term capital gain, since you held over a year. Federal rates are 0, 15, or 20 percent, not 50.
Grace: And the mortgage we paid off in 2015? Did we ever deduct that interest?
If you itemized, yes. Interest on debt to buy or improve your home, up to $750,000 on newer loans. Property taxes too, within the SALT cap. Ask your accountant what you claimed.
Later, Diane reads Jordan's notes. "You explained it and you sent them to a CPA. That's the job. The shoebox line was good."

board.prompt: Build the Okafors' gain on a staircase: purchase price, plus costs, plus improvements, then subtract from amount realized. Shade the excluded $500,000.

facts.text: Licensees explain general tax rules but refer specific tax advice to an accountant or tax attorney to avoid liability.
The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 replaced the rollover rule and the one-time $125,000 over-55 exclusion with the $250,000/$500,000 exclusion usable every 2 years at any age.
First-time homebuyers (no principal residence in the prior 2 years) may take up to $10,000 lifetime from an IRA without the 10% penalty, though a traditional IRA withdrawal is still taxed as income.
Mortgage interest and property taxes help only owners who itemize instead of taking the standard deduction.
Mortgage interest is deductible on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt on a main home and one second home ($1 million for loans before Dec 16, 2017).
Home equity and HELOC interest is deductible only if the money buys, builds or substantially improves the home securing it.
Refinance interest is deductible up to the old acquisition debt paid off, and construction loans count as acquisition debt for up to 24 months.
Property taxes fall under the SALT deduction, capped at $40,000 for 2025 and $40,400 for 2026 (reduced above about $500,000 of income), returning to $10,000 in 2030.
A prepayment penalty is deductible as mortgage interest in the year paid, and mortgage insurance premiums are deductible again starting in 2026, subject to income limits.

Points on a purchase mortgage for a main home are deductible in full in the year paid; points on a refinance are deducted over the loan's life; seller-paid points are deductible by the buyer but reduce basis.
Most buyer closing costs (title insurance, recording, attorney fees, transfer taxes) are added to basis, while seller's selling costs reduce the amount realized.
Adjusted basis is purchase price plus buying costs plus capital improvements, minus depreciation and casualty losses; repairs and maintenance do not add to basis.
Gain equals amount realized (sale price minus selling expenses) minus adjusted basis.
Appreciation is the increase in market value over time and is not taxed until a sale realizes it as gain.
Property held 1 year or less produces short-term gain taxed at ordinary rates; held more than 1 year, long-term gain at 0%, 15% or 20%.
A loss on selling a personal residence is not deductible, while investment capital losses offset gains plus up to $3,000 of ordinary income a year.

Under IRC 121 a seller excludes up to $250,000 (single) or $500,000 (married filing jointly) of gain if she owned and used the home as a main home 2 of the last 5 years and has not used the exclusion in 2 years.
For the $500,000 exclusion either spouse may meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test and neither may have used it in the past 2 years.
A partial exclusion may apply after an early move for a job, health or unforeseen circumstances, and depreciation taken on the home is recaptured, not excluded.
Taxable gain on a home is the gain minus the exclusion, and the excess is taxed as long-term capital gain.
A second home gets no exclusion unless it becomes the main home for 2 of 5 years, and renting a vacation home fewer than 15 days a year is tax-free.

lessons.title: Investment Property: Depreciation, Gains, and 1031 Exchanges
lessons.tagline: Investors make money three ways: cash flow, appreciation, and tax savings. The tax savings come from depreciation and the 1031 exchange.
objectives: Classify income as active, passive, or portfolio and apply the passive loss rules
Compute taxable income from operations and before-tax cash flow
Compute straight-line depreciation (27.5 and 39 years) from a depreciable basis
Calculate gain on an investment sale, including depreciation recapture
Apply 1031 exchange rules: eligible property, boot, qualified intermediary, 45 and 180 days, reverse exchanges
Describe the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit

blocks.title: Astoria, Sal's kitchen table
blocks.html: Sal Russo bought his 6-unit building on 31st Avenue in 2006 for $1,100,000. Today it might sell for $2,400,000. His nephew in Yonkers says, "Sell it, buy something bigger, and you pay no tax. It's called a 1031." Sal turns to Jordan: "Is that real, or is my nephew an idiot?"
blocks.casual: Sal Russo bought his 6-unit building on 31st Avenue in 2006 for $1,100,000. Now it might go for $2,400,000. His nephew in Yonkers says, "Sell it, buy something bigger, and you pay no tax. It's called a 1031." Sal looks at Jordan: "Is that real, or is my nephew an idiot?"

deeper.plain: There's a real tax rule that lets investors swap buildings without paying tax right away. The catch is in the details.
deeper.picture: It's like rolling your chips from one table to the next at a casino. You haven't cashed out, so nobody taxes the winnings yet.
deeper.street: Sal's nephew heard "no tax" at a barbecue. Jordan tells Sal the honest version: it's a deferral with strict deadlines and a middleman holding the money, and Sal's accountant and attorney need to set it up before he signs anything.
deeper.stakes: If Sal sells first and figures it out later, he may have already blown the exchange by touching the money. That could mean a six-figure tax bill.
deeper.exam: Stems with "pay no tax" and "1031" test whether you know the gain is deferred, not eliminated.

head: Class
Examples
Losses can offset
rows: Wages, commissions, a business you materially run
Rental real estate, limited partnership interests
Interest, dividends, gains on stocks and bonds

deeper.plain: The IRS sorts income into three buckets, and losses in one bucket usually can't be used against another.
deeper.picture: Three separate piggy banks. A hole in the passive piggy bank can't usually be patched with coins from the paycheck piggy bank.
deeper.street: Jordan earns commissions (active). Jordan's aunt owns a rented condo in Rego Park (passive). Leo has index funds paying dividends (portfolio). If the condo shows a loss, the aunt generally can't use it against her salary unless an exception applies.
deeper.stakes: Investors who expect rental losses to wipe out their W-2 tax can be badly surprised and short on cash.
deeper.exam: Rental real estate = passive. Interest and dividends = portfolio. Commissions = active.

blocks.html: Rental income is passive. Passive losses usually cannot offset wages, with one big exception: a landlord who actively participates (approves tenants, sets rents, approves repairs) may deduct up to $25,000 of rental losses against other income. That allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified adjusted gross income. Unused losses carry forward and are released when the property is sold. Qualifying real estate professionals can escape the passive label altogether.
blocks.casual: Rental income is passive. Normally passive losses can't offset your wages, with one big exception. If you actively participate as a landlord (approve tenants, set rents, approve repairs), you can deduct up to $25,000 of rental losses against other income. That allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified adjusted gross income. Losses you can't use carry forward and get released when you sell. And qualifying real estate professionals can skip the passive label entirely.

deeper.plain: Small landlords who stay involved can use some rental losses against their paychecks, unless they earn too much.
deeper.picture: It's a $25,000 pass that shrinks as your income grows and disappears completely at $150,000.
deeper.street: Ray, the inspector, owns a rented two-family in Glendale and approves every tenant himself. His MAGI is $120,000. His $25,000 allowance shrinks by half of the $20,000 over the limit, so he can use $15,000 of rental losses this year.
deeper.stakes: Investors with high income may buy rentals expecting immediate tax savings that never come. The losses wait until the property is sold.
deeper.exam: $25,000 allowance, active participation, phase-out $100,000 to $150,000 MAGI. Suspended losses are released at sale.

blocks.title: Sal's building for one year
blocks.html:
Gross potential rent (the rent roll in Unit 19): $12,850 x 12 = $154,200
Less vacancy and collection loss (5%): $7,710
Effective gross income: $146,490
Less operating expenses while Sal manages it himself (taxes, insurance, fuel, water, repairs, super): $80,000
Net operating income (NOI): $66,490

Taxable income: NOI $66,490 minus mortgage interest $30,000 minus depreciation $28,000 = $8,490. At a 32% bracket, federal tax = $2,717.

Cash flow: NOI $66,490 minus total debt service (principal + interest) $45,000 = $21,490 before-tax cash flow.
blocks.casual:
Sal's building for one year, back when he ran it himself:
Gross potential rent (the same rent roll you'll see in Unit 19): $12,850 x 12 = $154,200
Less vacancy and collection loss (5%): $7,710
Effective gross income: $146,490
Less operating expenses (taxes, insurance, fuel, water, repairs, super): $80,000
Net operating income (NOI): $66,490
Taxable income: NOI $66,490 minus mortgage interest $30,000 minus depreciation $28,000 = $8,490. At a 32% bracket, federal tax = $2,717.
Cash flow: NOI $66,490 minus total debt service (principal + interest) $45,000 = $21,490 before-tax cash flow.

deeper.plain: Start with rent, take out vacancies and expenses to get NOI, then compute taxable income and cash flow two different ways.
deeper.picture: One river of rent splits into two streams: one measures what the IRS sees, the other measures what lands in Sal's pocket.
deeper.street: Sal's accountant sends two numbers in April: "Your taxable income from the building is $8,490. Your actual cash in the bank is $21,490." Sal loves that the IRS number is lower.
deeper.stakes: Mix up the two formulas and you either overstate taxes or overstate cash, and bad investment decisions follow.
deeper.exam: NOI never subtracts debt service or depreciation. Taxable income subtracts interest and depreciation. Cash flow subtracts principal and interest.

blocks.html: Notice the asymmetry. Cash flow subtracts all of debt service (principal and interest) but not depreciation, because depreciation is not a check anyone writes. Taxable income subtracts depreciation and only the interest, because principal repayment is not an expense. That gap is why real estate is called a tax shelter: Sal pockets $21,490 but pays tax on only $8,490.
blocks.casual: See the mismatch? Cash flow takes out all the debt service (principal and interest) but not depreciation, because nobody actually writes a check for depreciation. Taxable income takes out depreciation and only the interest, because paying down principal isn't an expense. That gap is why real estate is called a tax shelter: Sal pockets $21,490 but only pays tax on $8,490.

deeper.plain: Depreciation is a paper expense that lowers taxes without costing cash.
deeper.picture: Depreciation is like a coupon the IRS gives you every year for wear and tear, even if the building is aging gracefully.
deeper.street: Sal's $28,000 depreciation deduction saves about $8,960 in federal tax at 32%. He didn't spend a dime to get it. Meanwhile, the $15,000 of principal he paid down cost him cash but gave no deduction.
deeper.stakes: Owners who don't understand the shelter overpay taxes or misjudge how profitable a building is.
deeper.exam: Principal reduces cash flow, not taxable income. Depreciation reduces taxable income, not cash flow.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: Cash flow: minus debt service. Taxable income: minus interest and depreciation. Principal hurts your wallet, not your taxes. Depreciation helps your taxes, not your wallet.
blocks.casual: Lock this in: Cash flow: minus debt service. Taxable income: minus interest and depreciation. Principal hurts your wallet, not your taxes. Depreciation helps your taxes, not your wallet.

deeper.plain: Principal costs cash but saves no tax. Depreciation saves tax but costs no cash.
deeper.picture: Two seesaws: principal pushes your wallet down without moving taxes; depreciation pushes taxes down without touching your wallet.
deeper.street: Evelyn, the commercial investor, says it to every new partner at lunch in Midtown: "Principal is your savings account. Depreciation is the IRS's gift."
deeper.stakes: Confusing these is the most common math error on investment questions, and on real underwriting.
deeper.exam: If a question asks what's subtracted to get taxable income, look for "interest and depreciation." If it asks about cash flow, look for "debt service."

blocks.html: Tax depreciation (cost recovery) lets an owner deduct the cost of a building over its IRS useful life, whether or not it actually loses value. Real estate uses straight-line depreciation: equal amounts each year.
blocks.casual: Tax depreciation (also called cost recovery) lets an owner deduct the cost of a building over the IRS's useful life, whether or not it's actually losing value. Real estate uses straight-line depreciation: the same amount every year.

deeper.plain: You deduct a slice of the building's cost every year, even if it's going up in value.
deeper.picture: Picture slicing a loaf of bread into 27.5 or 39 equal slices and eating one each year.
deeper.street: Sal's prewar Astoria building is gaining value every year, but he still deducts $28,000 annually. Tax depreciation doesn't care what the market thinks.
deeper.stakes: Mixing tax depreciation with appraisal depreciation leads to confused answers and confused clients.
deeper.exam: Tax depreciation is cost recovery under IRS rules, straight-line. It's not the same as physical, functional, or external depreciation in appraisal.

head: Property
Recovery period
rows: Residential rental (apartments, rented houses, mixed-use with 80%+ of rent from dwellings)

deeper.plain: Apartments get written off over 27.5 years, commercial over 39, land never, and your own home not at all.
deeper.picture: Two clocks: a faster one for residential rentals and a slower one for commercial. Land has no clock at all.
deeper.street: Evelyn owns a mixed-use building on Steinway Street. Two stores and four apartments: 85% of the rent comes from apartments, so it's residential rental property at 27.5 years. If the stores brought in more than 20% of rent, it would be 39 years.
deeper.stakes: Using the wrong recovery period gets you an IRS adjustment and a recalculated recapture at sale.
deeper.exam: 27.5 residential, 39 nonresidential, land never. Mixed-use needs 80% or more of gross rent from dwellings to use 27.5.

blocks.html: Depreciable basis = cost basis (price + acquisition costs + capital improvements) minus land value. Land value often comes from the assessor's land-to-total ratio or an appraisal.
blocks.casual: Depreciable basis = cost basis (price + acquisition costs + capital improvements) minus land value. You usually get the land value from the assessor's land-to-total ratio or an appraisal.

deeper.plain: You can only depreciate the building, so take the land out first.
deeper.picture: A cake on a plate: you eat the cake over time, but the plate (the land) stays forever.
deeper.street: Sal's assessment shows land at 30% of total value. His accountant uses that ratio to carve $330,000 out of his $1,100,000 price before depreciating.
deeper.stakes: Forgetting to subtract land overstates depreciation, which the IRS can disallow with interest and penalties.
deeper.exam: Depreciable basis excludes land. A choice that depreciates the full purchase price is a trap.

blocks.title: Sal's depreciation
blocks.html:
Price $1,100,000. Land is 30%: $330,000.
Depreciable basis = $1,100,000 minus $330,000 = $770,000.
$770,000 / 27.5 = $28,000 per year.
If this were a $770,000 retail building: $770,000 / 39 = $19,744 per year.
blocks.casual:
Sal's depreciation:
Price $1,100,000. Land is 30%: $330,000.
Depreciable basis = $1,100,000 minus $330,000 = $770,000.
$770,000 / 27.5 = $28,000 per year.
If this were a $770,000 retail building: $770,000 / 39 = $19,744 per year.

deeper.plain: Subtract land, then divide by the recovery period.
deeper.picture: Two-step recipe: scrape off the land, then cut the rest into 27.5 equal servings.
deeper.street: Over 20 years Sal takes $28,000 x 20 = $560,000 in depreciation. That number shows up again, with a bill attached, when he sells.
deeper.stakes: Getting the land percentage wrong throws off every year's deduction and the recapture at sale.
deeper.exam: Common trap: dividing the full price by 27.5. Always remove land first. Residential divide by 27.5; commercial by 39.

blocks.caption: Toggle 27.5 vs 39 years and watch the land slice stay undepreciated. The recapture bar grows each year you claim depreciation.

blocks.q: An investor buys a Bronx office building for $3,000,000. The land is valued at $660,000. What is the annual depreciation?
blocks.x: ($3,000,000 minus $660,000) / 39 = $2,340,000 / 39 = $60,000. Using 27.5 years or forgetting to remove the land gives the wrong answers.

blocks.html: Depreciation lowers adjusted basis, which raises gain at sale. The IRS gets some of the benefit back: the gain attributable to depreciation taken on real estate (unrecaptured Section 1250 gain, or recaptured depreciation) is taxed at a maximum 25%. The rest of the long-term gain gets 0/15/20%.
blocks.casual: Depreciation lowers your adjusted basis, which makes your gain bigger when you sell. The IRS claws back some of the benefit: the gain from depreciation you took on real estate (unrecaptured Section 1250 gain, or recaptured depreciation) is taxed at up to 25%. The rest of the long-term gain gets 0/15/20%.

deeper.plain: The depreciation you deducted comes back as taxable gain at up to 25% when you sell.
deeper.picture: Depreciation is a tab the IRS lets you run. At sale, the bartender brings the check.
deeper.street: Sal saved roughly 32% on each depreciation dollar while he owned. At sale, he pays up to 25% on those same dollars. Not a bad trade, but it's a real check to write.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who forget recapture underestimate their tax and might spend proceeds they'll need in April.
