deeper.exam: Unrecaptured 1250 gain: max 25%. Remaining long-term gain: 0, 15 or 20%.

blocks.title: Sal sells after 20 years
blocks.html:
Depreciation taken: 20 x $28,000 = $560,000.
Adjusted basis: $1,100,000 minus $560,000 = $540,000.
Amount realized: $2,400,000 minus $140,000 selling costs = $2,260,000.
Total gain: $2,260,000 minus $540,000 = $1,720,000.
Of that, $560,000 is recapture (taxed up to 25%) and $1,160,000 is long-term capital gain (0/15/20%). No $250,000/$500,000 exclusion: it is not his home.
blocks.casual:
Sal sells after 20 years.
Depreciation taken: 20 x $28,000 = $560,000.
Adjusted basis: $1,100,000 minus $560,000 = $540,000.
Amount realized: $2,400,000 minus $140,000 selling costs = $2,260,000.
Total gain: $2,260,000 minus $540,000 = $1,720,000.
$560,000 of that is recapture (taxed up to 25%) and $1,160,000 is long-term capital gain (0/15/20%). No $250,000/$500,000 exclusion, because it's not his home.

deeper.plain: Depreciation shrinks basis, making the gain larger, and part of the gain gets the 25% rate.
deeper.picture: Two layers of gain stacked like a sandwich: the depreciation layer taxed up to 25%, and the appreciation layer at capital gain rates.
deeper.street: At 25% on $560,000 and 20% on $1,160,000, Sal's federal bill could approach $372,000, before NY tax and the 3.8% NIIT. That's why the nephew's 1031 idea suddenly sounds interesting.
deeper.stakes: A seller who plans on keeping $2.26 million may actually net much less after tax.
deeper.exam: Investment property gets no home sale exclusion. Watch for a choice that applies $500,000 to a rental.

blocks.html: Sal's nephew is half right. Under IRC 1031, a tax-deferred exchange lets an investor sell investment or business real property and buy other like-kind real property without paying tax now. The gain is deferred, not forgiven: the replacement property inherits the low basis.
blocks.casual: Sal's nephew is half right. Under IRC 1031, a tax-deferred exchange lets an investor sell investment or business real property and buy other like-kind real property without paying tax now. But the gain is deferred, not forgiven. The replacement property inherits the low basis.

deeper.plain: A 1031 pushes the tax to later. It doesn't erase it.
deeper.picture: It's a snooze button, not an off switch. The alarm still goes off when you finally sell for cash.
deeper.street: Sal sells his Astoria building for $2.4 million and buys a $2.8 million Yonkers 12-unit. He pays no tax this year, but the Yonkers building carries his old low basis. If he later sells it for cash, the deferred gain shows up.
deeper.stakes: Investors who think the tax is gone may plan as if it's gone. A later sale for cash brings the whole deferred gain back, plus any new gain.
deeper.exam: Cue word "deferred." Wrong answers say "tax-free" or "exempt." The new property keeps the carryover basis.

left.title: Eligible (held for investment or business)
items: Residential rentals, apartment buildings
Commercial and industrial property
Unimproved land held for investment (non-dealer)
Hotels and motels
Leaseholds of 30 years or more (including renewal options)
Any US real property for any other US real property

right.title: Not eligible
items: Your principal residence
Dealer property and flips held for resale
Personal property (since 2018, real property only)
Foreign real estate swapped for US real estate
Stocks, bonds, partnership interests

deeper.plain: Real property held for investment or business qualifies. Homes you live in, flips, and anything that isn't US real estate don't.
deeper.picture: The bouncer only checks one thing: why you held it. Investment or business gets in. Personal use or inventory gets turned away.
deeper.street: Evelyn swaps a Flushing retail strip for a Long Island City office building: eligible. A Bushwick flipper who rehabs and resells condos: dealer property, not eligible. A buyer with a 35-year ground lease in Midtown: eligible, since it's 30 years or more.
deeper.stakes: Try to exchange a flip or your own home and the IRS denies the deferral. The full gain is taxed in the year of sale.
deeper.exam: Since 2018 only real property qualifies. Foreign for US is not like-kind. Leaseholds of 30+ years (with renewals) count.

blocks.html: Like-kind is broad for real estate: vacant land in Orange County for a Queens six-family, or a Yonkers strip center for a Buffalo warehouse, all qualify. What matters is how the property is held (investment or business), not what it looks like.
blocks.casual: Like-kind is super broad for real estate. Vacant land in Orange County for a Queens six-family, or a Yonkers strip center for a Buffalo warehouse: all good. What matters is how you hold it (investment or business), not what it looks like.

deeper.plain: Any US investment real estate can swap for any other US investment real estate.
deeper.picture: It's not apples for apples. It's any fruit for any fruit, as long as you're holding the fruit to sell or rent, not to eat.
deeper.street: Diane's client trades 20 acres of investment land upstate near Goshen for a four-family in Ridgewood. Nothing alike physically, fully like-kind for 1031 purposes.
deeper.stakes: Investors who think they must swap apartments for apartments miss better deals. Agents who know the rule can widen the search.
deeper.exam: Trap: answer choices that say land can't be exchanged for a building. Wrong. Use and holding purpose matter, not type.

blocks.html: Boot is anything received in the exchange that is not like-kind property: cash taken out, a smaller mortgage on the replacement (debt relief, or "mortgage boot"), or personal property. Boot is taxable up to the amount of realized gain. To defer everything, buy equal or greater value, reinvest all the net cash, and take on equal or greater debt (or add cash to make up for less debt).
blocks.casual: Boot is anything you get out of the exchange that isn't like-kind property: cash you take out, a smaller mortgage on the new place (debt relief, or "mortgage boot"), or personal property. Boot is taxable up to the amount of your realized gain. To defer everything: buy equal or greater value, reinvest all the net cash, and take on equal or greater debt (or put in cash to make up for less debt).

deeper.plain: Anything you walk away with that isn't real estate gets taxed.
deeper.picture: A 1031 is a sealed tube from one property to the next. Anything that leaks out of the tube, cash or debt relief, gets taxed.
deeper.street: Evelyn sells a building with a $1 million mortgage and buys one with a $700,000 mortgage, adding no extra cash. That $300,000 drop in debt is mortgage boot, and it's taxable.
deeper.stakes: Investors focus on cash and forget about debt. Lower leverage on the new property creates a tax bill they didn't plan for.
deeper.exam: Boot includes cash, debt relief and personal property. To avoid it: equal or greater value, all cash reinvested, equal or greater debt.

blocks.title: Sal takes a little cash
blocks.html:
Realized gain: $1,720,000.
Sal reinvests in a $2,800,000 Yonkers 12-unit but keeps $150,000 in cash.
Recognized (taxable) gain = the lesser of boot or realized gain = $150,000.
Deferred gain = $1,720,000 minus $150,000 = $1,570,000, carried into the new building's basis.
blocks.casual:
Sal takes a little cash out.
Realized gain: $1,720,000.
Sal buys a $2,800,000 Yonkers 12-unit but keeps $150,000 in cash.
Recognized (taxable) gain = the lesser of boot or realized gain = $150,000.
Deferred gain = $1,720,000 minus $150,000 = $1,570,000, carried into the new building's basis.

deeper.plain: Sal is taxed on the $150,000 he pocketed. The rest stays deferred.
deeper.picture: Sal skimmed a little cream off the top. He pays tax on the cream; the milk keeps rolling forward.
deeper.street: Sal uses the $150,000 to pay off his daughter's student loans. He'll owe tax on that $150,000 this year, while the other $1,570,000 rides into the Yonkers building.
deeper.stakes: Taking cash out is legal, but it shrinks the benefit. Clients should decide that with their accountant, not on closing day.
deeper.exam: Taxable gain is the lesser of boot received or realized gain. If boot were $2 million, only $1,720,000 would be taxed.

blocks.caption: Follow the money from the relinquished sale into the qualified intermediary's account, through the 45-day identification and the 180-day closing, and watch boot leak out as taxable.

blocks.title: A delayed (forward) exchange

items.title: Hire a qualified intermediary before closing
items.html: The qualified intermediary (QI, or accommodator) holds the sale proceeds. If the seller touches the money (constructive receipt), the exchange fails. Your own attorney, broker, or accountant from the last 2 years cannot serve.

items.title: Day 45: identify
items.html: In writing, to the QI, identify replacement property within 45 days of closing the sale. Usually up to 3 properties of any value (or more under the 200% rule).

items.title: Day 180: close
items.html: Acquire the replacement by the earlier of 180 days after the sale or the due date (with extensions) of that year's tax return. The 45 days run inside the 180, not in addition.

items.title: Report
items.html: File IRS Form 8824 with the return.

blocks.casual:
How a delayed (forward) exchange runs.
Hire a qualified intermediary before closing. The qualified intermediary (QI, or accommodator) holds the sale money. If the seller touches it (constructive receipt), the exchange is dead. Your own attorney, broker or accountant from the past 2 years can't be the QI.
Day 45: identify. In writing, to the QI, name the replacement property within 45 days of closing the sale. Usually up to 3 properties of any value (or more under the 200% rule).
Day 180: close. Buy the replacement by the earlier of 180 days after the sale or the due date (with extensions) of that year's tax return. The 45 days run inside the 180, not on top of it.
Report. File IRS Form 8824 with your return.

deeper.plain: Get a middleman to hold the money, name your new property in 45 days, close within 180.
deeper.picture: It's a relay race. The QI carries the baton (your money) between buildings, and you never get to hold it, even for a second.
deeper.street: Sal closes on Astoria and the $2.26 million goes straight to the QI's account. By day 45 he emails the QI three candidates: Yonkers, New Rochelle and a Bronx walkup. He closes Yonkers on day 140.
deeper.stakes: Touching the money, using your own lawyer as QI, or missing a deadline turns the whole sale taxable.
deeper.exam: 45 days to identify, 180 days to close, running concurrently. QI can't be your agent from the last 2 years. Form 8824.

blocks.title: Counting days
blocks.html:
Sale closes March 1, 2026. Day 45 = April 15, 2026. Day 180 = August 28, 2026.

Sale closes November 1, 2026. Day 180 = April 30, 2027, but the 2026 return is due April 15, 2027. Deadline = April 15, 2027 unless the investor files an extension, which restores the full 180 days.
blocks.casual:
Let's count days.
Sale closes March 1, 2026. Day 45 = April 15, 2026. Day 180 = August 28, 2026.
Sale closes November 1, 2026. Day 180 would be April 30, 2027, but the 2026 return is due April 15, 2027. So the deadline is April 15, 2027 unless the investor files an extension, which brings back the full 180 days.

deeper.plain: For late-year sales, the tax return due date can cut the 180 days short unless you extend.
deeper.picture: Two alarm clocks are set; whichever rings first ends the race. Filing an extension unplugs the earlier one.
deeper.street: Evelyn sells a Flatbush storefront on November 1. Her accountant files an extension in early April so she can close her Jamaica replacement on April 28 without blowing the exchange.
deeper.stakes: Investors who file their return on time without thinking can accidentally shorten their exchange and owe tax on the whole gain.
deeper.exam: Deadline is the earlier of 180 days or the return due date with extensions. A November or December sale is the setup for this trap.

blocks.title: No extensions for weekends
blocks.html: The 45 and 180 days are calendar days. No extension for holidays, weekends, or a slow seller. Missing day 45 by one day kills the exchange.
blocks.casual: Big trap: the 45 and 180 days are calendar days. No extra time for holidays, weekends, or a slow seller. Miss day 45 by a single day and the exchange is gone.

deeper.plain: The deadlines never move, even on a Sunday.
deeper.picture: It's a train schedule with no grace period. The doors close at the minute, weekend or not.
deeper.street: Day 45 for Sal falls on a Saturday. His attorney emails the identification to the QI on Friday afternoon instead of waiting for Monday.
deeper.stakes: One late day turns a deferred gain into a taxable one. For Sal, that could be hundreds of thousands of dollars.
deeper.exam: Watch for answers suggesting the deadline rolls to the next business day. It doesn't.

blocks.html: Reverse exchange: the investor buys the replacement first and sells the old property later. Because you cannot own both sides at once, an exchange accommodation titleholder parks title to one property. The same 45-day (identify the property to sell) and 180-day (finish) limits apply.
blocks.casual: Reverse exchange: you buy the replacement first and sell the old property later. Since you can't own both sides at once, an exchange accommodation titleholder holds title to one of the properties. The same 45-day (identify the property to sell) and 180-day (finish) limits apply.

deeper.plain: Buy first, sell later, with a third party holding title in between.
deeper.picture: A parking valet holds your new car while you sell the old one, so you're never driving two at once on paper.
deeper.street: Evelyn finds the perfect Long Island City office building before her Flushing property sells. An accommodation titleholder takes title to the LIC building. She identifies Flushing as the property to sell within 45 days and closes it by day 180.
deeper.stakes: Reverse exchanges cost more and need financing for both properties. Miss the 180 days and the whole plan fails.
deeper.exam: Reverse = replacement bought first. Exchange accommodation titleholder parks title. Same 45 and 180 day limits.

blocks.title: New York angle
blocks.html: New York generally follows federal 1031 treatment for state income tax. But a 1031 does not avoid transfer taxes: the NYS transfer tax, NYC RPTT, and any mansion tax are still due on each sale and purchase.
blocks.casual: The New York angle: NY generally follows the federal 1031 rules for state income tax. But a 1031 does not get you out of transfer taxes. The NYS transfer tax, NYC RPTT, and any mansion tax are still due on every sale and purchase.

deeper.plain: Income tax can be deferred, but transfer taxes are paid every time property changes hands.
deeper.picture: The 1031 is a pass through the income tax gate. The transfer tax toll booth still collects.
deeper.street: Evelyn's $3 million Manhattan office sale in a 1031 still pays the NYS transfer tax at 0.65% and NYC RPTT at 2.625% on commercial property over $500,000. Her replacement purchase may bring its own costs too.
deeper.stakes: Investors who budget zero tax for a 1031 may come up short at closing.
deeper.exam: A 1031 defers federal and generally NYS income tax. It never waives transfer taxes.

blocks.q: Evelyn sells a Flushing retail building on June 10 in a 1031 exchange. By what day must she identify replacement property?
c: July 10
July 25
December 7
August 9
blocks.x: 45 calendar days from June 10: 20 days remain in June, then 25 days into July, so July 25. The 180-day closing deadline falls on December 7.

blocks.html: The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC, IRC Section 42, created in 1986) is the main federal tool for building affordable rentals. States allocate credits to developers, who sell them to investors for equity. In return, a set share of units must be rent-restricted for households earning 50% or 60% of area median income (or an average of 60% under income averaging) for at least 15 years, and usually 30 or more. In New York, NYS Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) allocates the credits, and NYC's Housing Development Corporation handles bond-financed deals in the city. A 2025 federal law expanded state LIHTC allocations starting in 2026.
blocks.casual: The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC, IRC Section 42, created in 1986) is the main federal tool for building affordable rentals. States hand out credits to developers, who sell them to investors to raise equity. In exchange, a set share of units has to be rent-restricted for households earning 50% or 60% of area median income (or an average of 60% under income averaging) for at least 15 years, and usually 30 or more. In New York, NYS Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) allocates the credits, and NYC's Housing Development Corporation handles the bond-financed deals in the city. A 2025 federal law expanded state LIHTC allocations starting in 2026.

deeper.plain: Developers get tax credits to build affordable apartments, and they sell those credits to investors to pay for construction.
deeper.picture: The credits are like coupons the government prints. Developers sell them to banks, and the cash pays for bricks.
deeper.street: A developer builds 120 apartments in the South Bronx. Credits from the state are sold to a bank for equity. In return, rents on the restricted units are capped for households at 60% of area median income for decades.
deeper.stakes: Break the affordability rules and investors can lose credits through recapture. Tenants count on those rent limits.
deeper.exam: IRC Section 42, 1986, 15-year minimum compliance period. In NY, HCR allocates. It's a credit, not a deduction.

blocks.title: Credit vs deduction
blocks.html: A credit cuts tax dollar for dollar. A deduction cuts taxable income. A $10,000 credit saves $10,000; a $10,000 deduction saves $10,000 times your bracket.
blocks.casual: Credit versus deduction. A credit cuts your tax dollar for dollar. A deduction cuts your taxable income. So a $10,000 credit saves you $10,000, while a $10,000 deduction saves $10,000 times your bracket.

deeper.plain: A credit comes off the tax bill. A deduction comes off the income before tax is figured.
deeper.picture: A credit is cash off the restaurant bill. A deduction is removing a dish before the tip is calculated.
deeper.street: Leo is in the 24% bracket. A $10,000 deduction saves him $2,400. A $10,000 credit saves him the full $10,000.
deeper.stakes: Clients who hear "$10,000 tax break" can badly misjudge the real value if they don't know which kind it is.
deeper.exam: Credit beats deduction of the same size. LIHTC is a credit; mortgage interest is a deduction.

blocks.q: Sal sells his building and buys a replacement through a 1031 exchange, but his new mortgage is $300,000 smaller than his old one and he adds no cash. The $300,000 is:
c: Tax-free because it is debt, not cash
Mortgage boot, taxable up to the realized gain
Deductible as interest
Depreciation recapture
blocks.x: Debt relief is boot. To avoid it, take on equal or greater debt or add cash to offset the reduction.

story.title: Is My Nephew an Idiot?
story.setting: Sal's kitchen, 31st Avenue, Astoria, espresso at 8 am

beats.text: My nephew says I sell, I buy bigger, I pay zero tax. Ever. Is he right?
He's right that you can defer it. Not 'ever.' A 1031 pushes the tax down the road into the next building.
Defer. Fine. What's the catch?
You can't touch the money. A qualified intermediary holds it. If it hits your account, the exchange is dead.
My lawyer can hold it. Known him 20 years.
That's exactly who can't. Your own attorney, accountant, or broker from the last two years is disqualified.
Then the clock. Forty-five days to name the new property in writing. One hundred eighty to close. Calendar days, no extensions for Christmas.

check.q: Sal closes his sale on March 1. By when must he close on the replacement?
c: April 15
August 28
September 1
December 31
check.x: 180 calendar days from March 1 is August 28 (or the tax return due date if earlier, which it is not here). April 15 is the 45-day identification deadline.

beats.text: And if I keep a little cash for my granddaughter's wedding?
That cash is boot. Taxable. Same if your new mortgage is smaller than the old one.
beats.tag: Boot: cash or debt relief is taxable

beats.text: Okay. And if I just sell and retire to Florida?
Then you've got two piles of gain. The $560,000 of depreciation you took over twenty years gets recaptured at up to 25 percent. The rest is long-term gain at up to 20.
Depreciation? The building got more valuable!
Doesn't matter. You deducted $28,000 a year, the building cost minus the land, over 27.5 years. That lowered your basis.
Afterward, at the office: "Good. And you'll send Sal to a CPA and a QI before he signs anything. Timing is the whole game on a 1031."

board.prompt: Draw a 1031 timeline. Mark the sale closing, day 45, and day 180, and draw the money going to the QI, not to Sal.

facts.text: Income is active (wages, a business you run), passive (rentals, limited partnerships) or portfolio (interest, dividends, securities gains).
Rental income is passive, and passive losses generally offset only passive income.
An actively participating landlord may deduct up to $25,000 of rental losses against other income, phased out between $100,000 and $150,000 of MAGI, with unused losses carried forward.
Taxable income is NOI minus mortgage interest and depreciation; cash flow is NOI minus total debt service; loan principal is not deductible.
Real estate is a tax shelter mainly because depreciation is a deduction that takes no cash.
Tax depreciation (cost recovery) deducts a building's cost straight-line over its IRS life whether or not it actually loses value.
Residential rental property is depreciated over 27.5 years, nonresidential over 39 years; land and your own home are not depreciated.
Depreciable basis is cost basis (price, acquisition costs and improvements) minus land value.
Annual straight-line depreciation is depreciable basis divided by the recovery period.
Depreciation lowers adjusted basis, so gain at sale equals amount realized minus cost less depreciation taken.
Gain from depreciation taken (unrecaptured Section 1250 gain) is taxed at up to 25%, the rest of long-term gain at 0/15/20%.
An IRC 1031 exchange defers, not forgives, tax on investment or business real property swapped for like-kind real property; the replacement inherits the low basis.
A principal residence, dealer or flip property, personal property, securities and foreign real estate for US real estate do not qualify for a 1031 exchange.
Like-kind is broad for real estate: any US real property held for investment or business, such as land for an apartment building, qualifies.
Boot (cash, debt relief or personal property) is taxable up to the realized gain: recognized gain is the lesser of boot or realized gain.
To defer all gain, buy equal or greater value, reinvest all net cash, and take on equal or greater debt or add cash.
A qualified intermediary must hold the proceeds (constructive receipt kills the exchange), and your attorney, broker or accountant from the last 2 years cannot serve.
Replacement property must be identified in writing within 45 calendar days of the sale, usually up to 3 properties.
The replacement must close by the earlier of 180 days or the tax return due date (with extensions); the 45 days run inside the 180 and there are no weekend or holiday extensions.
A 1031 exchange is reported on IRS Form 8824.
In a reverse exchange the investor buys the replacement first, and an exchange accommodation titleholder parks title under the same 45 and 180 day limits.
New York follows federal 1031 treatment for income tax, but transfer taxes and mansion tax are still due on each sale and purchase.
The LIHTC (IRC 42, 1986) gives credits sold to investors for rentals restricted to households at 50% or 60% of area median income for at least 15 years; NYS HCR allocates them in NY.
A tax credit cuts tax dollar for dollar, while a deduction cuts taxable income and saves only the amount times the tax bracket.

lessons.title: Case file: Four Closings and the $500,000 Question
lessons.tagline: A widow racing a deadline, a couple moving to Boston, a condo that was once a rental and a two-family with a tenant upstairs. Same exclusion, four different answers.
objectives: Apply the home sale exclusion to a surviving spouse, a partial exclusion after a job move, and a home that was rented before the owner moved in
Calculate gain and the taxable portion when depreciation was taken or part of a property was rented
Decide how basis changes when a spouse dies and how a closing date can change the exclusion
Apply the mortgage interest limit and the SALT cap to decide whether a buyer should itemize

blocks.title: October at Hudson & Hart
blocks.html: Jordan has four listings heading for contract in the same month, and every seller has asked the same question: "How much of this will I owe?" Jordan is not a tax advisor and says so every time, in writing. But Diane has a rule: "You don't give tax advice. You do know enough to spot when the answer is going to surprise someone, and you send them to their accountant before the contract is signed, not after." So Jordan builds a one-page sheet for each seller with the facts their accountant will need, and flags the issues. The first file belongs to Lorraine Bishop, 74, who is selling the Bayside colonial she and her husband Walter bought in 1989. Walter died on February 10, 2025.

The Bishops paid $210,000 in 1989 and spent $90,000 over the years on a new roof, a kitchen and central air, all receipts in a folder Walter labeled "BASIS." They owned the house as tenants by the entirety, the default for a married couple in New York. A buyer has offered $1,400,000. Lorraine has not remarried and has lived in the house for 36 years.

blocks.q: Lorraine is a widow who files as a single taxpayer. If the house closes in December 2026, what is the most she can exclude?
c: $250,000, because she now files her return as a single taxpayer
$125,000, the old one-time exclusion for sellers over 55
$750,000, combining her exclusion with Walter's estate's
$500,000, since the sale is within 2 years of the death
blocks.x: A surviving spouse who has not remarried can use the full $500,000 exclusion on a sale within 2 years of the spouse's death, counting the late spouse's ownership and use. Choice A is the trap: her filing status changed, but the law gives her a two-year window. The $125,000 over-55 exclusion was repealed by the Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997. There is no stacking with an estate.

blocks.html: The exclusion is only half of Lorraine's good news. When a spouse dies, the half of a jointly owned home that is included in the deceased spouse's estate gets a new basis equal to its fair market value at death. The other half keeps its original cost. An appraisal as of February 2025 valued the house at $1,300,000.

blocks.title: Lorraine's new basis
blocks.html:
Original cost plus improvements: $210,000 + $90,000 = $300,000
Lorraine's half keeps its share of cost: $300,000 / 2 = $150,000
Walter's half steps up to half the date-of-death value: $1,300,000 / 2 = $650,000
Lorraine's basis: $150,000 + $650,000 = $800,000

blocks.q: Lorraine's accountant uses an $800,000 basis. Why is it not $300,000?
c: Because Walter's half stepped up to its value at death
Because a surviving spouse may add the full date-of-death value
Because improvements are doubled when a spouse dies
Because New York resets basis on every transfer of title
blocks.x: For a married couple's jointly owned home, half is included in the first spouse's estate, and that half takes a basis equal to its value at death. Lorraine's own half keeps its original cost. Choice B describes a full step-up, which is not how a married couple's joint property works under federal law. New York does not reset basis; basis is a federal income tax concept.

blocks.title: Lorraine's gain, closing in December 2026
blocks.html:
Sale price: $1,400,000
Selling costs: commission $70,000, NYS transfer tax $5,600, NYC RPTT $19,950, legal $2,450 = $98,000
Amount realized: $1,302,000
Gain: $1,302,000 minus $800,000 = $502,000
Exclusion: $500,000
Taxable gain: $2,000

Two weeks after the contract is signed, the buyers' lender asks for a second appraisal and warns the closing could slip into March 2027. Jordan reads the calendar twice. Two years after February 10, 2025 is February 10, 2027.

blocks.q: If the closing slips to March 2027, about how much of Lorraine's gain becomes taxable?
c: $2,000, since her exclusion was locked in by the contract date
$502,000, since the exclusion is lost entirely after Walter's death
$252,000, since her cap drops to $250,000 after the window
$0, since a widow's home sale is fully tax free in New York
blocks.x: The exclusion is measured at the date of sale, which is the closing, not the contract. After the two-year window, Lorraine is a single filer with a $250,000 cap: $502,000 minus $250,000 = $252,000 taxable. A month's delay could cost her tens of thousands of dollars. Choice A is the trap: signing a contract does not fix tax results. She still qualifies for $250,000 on her own.

blocks.html: Jordan calls Lorraine's attorney, Priya, the same afternoon. Priya negotiates a firm closing date of January 15, 2027, with a time-of-the-essence clause and a per diem credit if the buyers cannot close on time. Lorraine's accountant gets Jordan's one-page sheet with the date circled.

blocks.title: Contract date versus closing date
blocks.html: For tax purposes, a sale generally happens when title and the benefits and burdens of ownership pass, which in New York is the closing. Deadlines tied to the date of sale, such as the surviving spouse window, the 2-of-5-year tests and the start of a 1031 exchange clock, all run to the closing. When a client's tax result depends on a date, the contract needs a closing date the client can count on.

Lorraine's file also shows why Walter's "BASIS" folder mattered. Without receipts, the $90,000 of improvements would be hard to prove, and with the step-up only half of them still count anyway. The appraisal as of the date of death matters even more: it set $650,000 of her basis. An executor or surviving spouse who skips that appraisal leaves the accountant guessing years later, and a guess the IRS can challenge. Jordan adds a line to the sheet: "Date-of-death appraisal: on file, February 2025."

blocks.text: Nadia and Chris: the job in Boston

blocks.html: The Ferreiras bought a one-bedroom condo in Astoria on August 15, 2025, for $720,000 plus $10,000 of closing costs. In June 2026, Chris's employer moved his job to its Boston office, more than 200 miles away, and they listed the condo in July. It will close October 15, 2026, at $820,000, with $58,000 of selling costs. They have owned and lived in the condo for 14 months, short of the 2-year tests.

blocks.q: Can the Ferreiras exclude any of their gain?
c: No, the 2-year ownership and use tests are both unmet
Yes, a partial exclusion, since the job move qualifies
Yes, the full $500,000, since the move was not voluntary
No, partial exclusions are limited to health reasons
blocks.x: A sale forced by a change in place of employment qualifies for a reduced exclusion if the new job is at least 50 miles farther from the home than the old one; Boston easily qualifies. Health and other unforeseen circumstances are separate qualifying reasons, so choice D is too narrow. The full $500,000 (choice C) still requires 2 years of ownership and use.

blocks.title: The Ferreiras' reduced exclusion
blocks.html:
Months owned and used: 14 of the required 24
Each spouse: 14 / 24 x $250,000 = $145,833
Together: $291,667 maximum exclusion
Amount realized: $820,000 minus $58,000 = $762,000
Adjusted basis: $730,000
Gain: $32,000, fully excluded

blocks.q: What does the reduced exclusion fraction apply to?
c: The gain, so they can exclude 14/24 of $32,000
The basis, so 14/24 of $730,000 is recovered tax free
The sale price, so 14/24 of $820,000 is tax free
The $250,000 limit per spouse, not the gain
blocks.x: The fraction reduces the maximum exclusion, not the gain. Each spouse's $250,000 limit becomes $145,833, for $291,667 together, and their $32,000 gain fits easily inside it. Choice A is the common mistake: applying 14/24 to the gain would leave $13,333 taxable for no reason. The Ferreiras owe no federal tax on this sale.

blocks.title: Selling after you have left New York
blocks.html: By closing day, the Ferreiras will live in Massachusetts. A nonresident who sells New York real property generally must pay estimated New York income tax on the gain with Form IT-2663 when the deed is presented for recording, and the county clerk will not record the deed without either that payment certification or a signed certification on Form TP-584 that the requirement does not apply. A sale of property that qualifies in total as the seller's principal residence under section 121 is exempt from the payment. The Ferreiras' attorney handles the certification at closing.

blocks.q: At closing, the Ferreiras are Massachusetts residents. What New York step does their attorney need to handle?
c: Certify the residence exemption so the deed can be recorded
Pay NYS estimated tax at the top rate on the full $820,000
Nothing, since nonresidents do not pay New York tax on NY property
Delay the closing until they file their 2026 New York return
blocks.x: Nonresident sellers of New York property face the IT-2663 estimated tax rule, but a home that qualifies in total as a principal residence under section 121 is exempt; the seller certifies that instead of paying. Choice C is wrong: New York taxes nonresidents on gains from New York real property. Choice B misstates the base; the tax, when due, is on gain, not on price.

blocks.html: The Ferreiras' file is the simplest of the four, and it still had two traps: applying the fraction to the wrong number, and forgetting that New York keeps an eye on sellers who have already moved away. Had Chris simply wanted a bigger apartment, with no job move, health reason or other unforeseen circumstance, there would be no partial exclusion at all, and the $32,000 would be a short-term gain if they had owned the condo a year or less, taxed at ordinary rates. They owned it 14 months, so it would have been long-term either way.

blocks.text: Teresa: the condo that was a rental first

blocks.html: Teresa Lin bought a Park Slope condo in January 2019 for $600,000 including closing costs. She rented it out for four years, from 2019 through 2022, deducting $15,000 a year of depreciation on the building portion, $60,000 in all. In January 2023 she moved in, and it has been her home since. She is selling in January 2027 for $1,000,000, with $70,000 of selling costs. She has owned it 8 years and lived in it the last 4, so she easily passes the 2-of-5-year tests.

blocks.title: Teresa's gain
blocks.html:
Adjusted basis: $600,000 minus $60,000 depreciation = $540,000
Amount realized: $1,000,000 minus $70,000 = $930,000
Total gain: $390,000

blocks.q: Teresa passes the ownership and use tests, and her $250,000 limit looks large enough. Can she exclude all of the gain up to that limit?
c: Yes, because she meets both tests and the gain is under the limits
Yes, after she pays tax on the depreciation she took
No, the depreciation and pre-move-in rental years are taxed
No, a former rental is not eligible for the exclusion
blocks.x: Two rules bite. Depreciation taken after May 6, 1997 is never excluded. And since 2009, gain allocated to "nonqualified use," a period after 2008 when the home was not the owner's main home, such as renting it out before moving in, cannot be excluded. Choice B gets the first rule but misses the second. Choice D is too broad: former rentals can qualify, in part.

blocks.title: Splitting Teresa's gain
blocks.html:
Total gain: $390,000
Depreciation, taxed first (unrecaptured section 1250 gain, up to 25%): $60,000
Remaining gain: $330,000
Nonqualified use: 4 years of 8 owned = 50%
Nonqualified portion, taxable: $165,000
Qualified portion, excluded: $165,000 (within her $250,000 limit)
Taxable: $60,000 at up to 25%, plus $165,000 of long-term capital gain

blocks.q: How much of Teresa's gain is excluded?
c: $390,000, the full gain
blocks.x: After the $60,000 of depreciation comes out, the remaining $330,000 is split by time: 4 nonqualified years out of 8 owned. Half, $165,000, is excluded. Choice B assumes the $250,000 cap is the answer whenever gain exceeds it; here the nonqualified use rule limits her first. Choice C ignores nonqualified use; choice D ignores the depreciation as well.

blocks.html: Teresa asks a sharp question: "What if I had done it the other way, lived there first and rented it later?" Then the rental period would have come after her last use as a main home, which does not count as nonqualified use, as long as she sold within the 2-of-5-year window, meaning within 3 years of moving out. The depreciation would still be taxed. The order of use matters as much as the amount.

blocks.q: Which pattern of use, for a home owned 6 years, avoids nonqualified use entirely?
c: Rented for 2 years, then lived in it for 4 years before the sale
Lived in it 4 years, then rented it 2 years before the sale
Used it as a weekend home for 3 years, then lived in it for 3 years
Rented for 3 years, then lived in it for 3 years before the sale
blocks.x: Rental after the owner's last use as a main home, within the 5-year look-back, is not nonqualified use; the owner who lived there 4 years and then rented for 2 still has 3 years of use in the last 5. Every other choice puts the non-home use before the owner moved in, which after 2008 is nonqualified. Depreciation from the rental years is still taxed in every case.

blocks.html: The Espositos bought a Ridgewood two-family in 2014 for $600,000 including costs. They live in the ground-floor apartment and have rented the identical upstairs apartment for 12 years, deducting depreciation on the rental half: $7,500 a year, $90,000 in all. They are selling for $1,500,000, with $105,000 of selling costs. Married, filing jointly, both have lived downstairs the whole time.

blocks.q: Paul assumes their $500,000 exclusion covers the whole sale. What is the problem?
c: The exclusion does not apply to two-family houses in New York
The exclusion is cut in half because one spouse owns it alone
There is no problem; the exclusion covers the whole property
The rented apartment is a separate unit, taxed on its own
blocks.x: When a separate dwelling unit is rented, the owner allocates basis and amount realized between the home and the rental portion, usually the way depreciation was allocated. Only the home portion qualifies. Choice C is the trap Paul fell into. The exclusion has nothing to do with New York building types, and both spouses own and use the downstairs unit.

head: Home (downstairs)
Rental (upstairs)
rows: $90,000 at up to 25%, plus $397,500 long-term gain
blocks.caption: Same house, same sale, two tax results.

blocks.q: How much of the Espositos' gain is taxable?
c: $885,000, the full gain
blocks.x: The home half's $397,500 gain is excluded. The rental half's $487,500 gain is fully taxable: $90,000 of it as depreciation (unrecaptured section 1250 gain, up to 25%) and $397,500 as long-term capital gain. Choice B subtracts a single $500,000 exclusion from the whole $885,000, the mistake Paul made. Choice A assumes the exclusion covers the rental unit.

blocks.html: Gina asks whether anything can defer the rental half's tax. It can. IRS guidance (Revenue Procedure 2005-14) allows one sale to combine the home sale exclusion on the residence portion with a 1031 exchange of the rental portion, if the rental half's proceeds go to a qualified intermediary and are reinvested in investment real estate on the 45 and 180-day schedule. The Espositos are downsizing and want the cash, so they decide to pay the tax. But Jordan puts the option on the sheet before they sign, which is the only time it is still available.

blocks.q: If the Espositos want to defer the rental half's gain, when must they arrange it?
c: Before closing, through a qualified intermediary
Any time before filing their tax return for the year of sale
Within 180 days after closing, by buying another rental property
After closing, by depositing the proceeds into an IRA
blocks.x: An exchange must be set up before closing. If the Espositos receive the rental half's proceeds, even briefly, the exchange fails for that money. Choice C confuses the replacement deadline with the setup: the 180 days run from a sale that was structured as an exchange from the start. IRAs have nothing to do with deferring real estate gain.

blocks.html: The Espositos' numbers also show why a two-family is a different animal at tax time. Twelve years of depreciation on the upstairs unit saved them real tax along the way, roughly $7,500 a year off their taxable income. The sale is when that benefit is partly paid back, at up to 25%. Owners of two-families in Ridgewood, Bay Ridge and Astoria often forget that the rental half has been a business all along. Their accountant reminds them that the allocation should follow the same split used for depreciation every year; switching to a friendlier split at sale invites questions.

blocks.text: The buyers on the other side

blocks.html: Lorraine's buyers, Devon and Aisha Clarke, are first-time buyers paying $1,400,000 with a $1,120,000 mortgage at 6.5%. Their first-year interest will be about $72,431. They also pay the 1% NYC mansion tax, $14,000. They expect $38,000 of New York State and City income tax and $9,600 of property tax next year, and their income is well under the SALT phase-down threshold. Aisha asks Jordan to put their deduction questions on the list for their accountant.

blocks.q: How much of the Clarkes' first-year mortgage interest is deductible if they itemize?
c: The full $72,431, because the loan bought their main home
$0, since loans over $1,000,000 lose the deduction
About $48,503, under the $750,000 limit
About $64,670, the share for $1,000,000 of debt
blocks.x: Interest on acquisition debt incurred after December 15, 2017 is deductible on up to $750,000 of principal, so the deductible share is $750,000 / $1,120,000 = 67%: $72,431 x 0.67 = about $48,503. Choice D uses the old $1,000,000 limit, which applies only to loans from before December 16, 2017. The deduction is limited, not lost.

blocks.q: The Clarkes have $47,600 of state, city and property taxes. Should they itemize, and what happens to the $14,000 mansion tax?
c: Take the $32,200 standard deduction; the mansion tax is deductible
Itemize about $88,903; the mansion tax is added to their basis
Itemize about $102,903, including the mansion tax as a tax
Itemize about $96,103, deducting the full $47,600 of taxes
blocks.x: The SALT cap for 2026 is $40,400, so $48,503 of interest plus $40,400 of taxes = $88,903, well above the $32,200 joint standard deduction. The mansion tax is a transfer tax on the purchase, not a deductible property tax; it is added to their basis. Choice D ignores the cap. Choice C treats a transfer tax like a property tax.

blocks.html: At the end of the month, Jordan's four sheets are in four accountants' inboxes. None of the sellers got tax advice from Jordan. All of them got their questions asked in time to matter, and Lorraine closed on January 15, with 26 days to spare. Diane initials each sheet and files a copy, because the record that Jordan referred every client to a tax professional is part of the file too.

items: A surviving spouse who has not remarried keeps the $500,000 exclusion for a sale within 2 years of the death, and the deceased spouse's half of a jointly owned home steps up to its value at death.
Tax dates run to the closing, not the contract, so a client whose result depends on a date needs a firm closing date.
A move for a new job at least 50 miles farther away can earn a partial exclusion: the fraction reduces the $250,000 limit per spouse, not the gain.
Depreciation is never excluded, and gain allocated to rental use before the owner moved in (after 2008) is nonqualified and taxable.
A rented separate unit in a two-family is taxed on its own; a 1031 exchange of that portion must be set up before closing.
Buyers deduct interest on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt and state and local taxes up to the SALT cap ($40,400 for 2026); transfer and mansion taxes go into basis.

lessons.title: Case file: Sal Sells on Paper
lessons.tagline: Twenty years of depreciation, one buyer who needs seller financing, and a tax bill that arrives before the money does.
objectives: Decide which rental property costs an investor deducts, capitalizes or never deducts
Apply the allowed-or-allowable rule to depreciation and calculate recapture on a sale
Calculate the gross profit percentage and the gain reported each year in an installment sale
Decide whether an installment sale's down payment covers payoff, closing costs and the first year's tax

blocks.title: 31st Avenue, one more time
blocks.html: Sal Russo is 71. He bought his six-unit building on 31st Avenue in Astoria in 2006 for $1,100,000, and for the last year Hudson & Hart has managed it. In September he tells Jordan he is done: "Sell it. I want to go see my grandkids in Florida without a phone that rings at 2 am." Jordan finds buyers quickly, a young couple named Hyun and Mira Seo who own a dry cleaner in Bayside and want to live in one unit and rent the rest. They offer Sal's asking price of $2,400,000, with one condition: they can put down $800,000, and they want Sal to finance the rest. Sal's first question is not about the price. It is about taxes. Jordan's job is to gather the facts Sal's accountant needs, starting with last year's return.

blocks.text: The last full year as a landlord

blocks.html: Sal's accountant, Ms. Fiore, sends over the 2025 rental schedule so Jordan can match it against the building's records. It matches the numbers Hudson & Hart reported, with one twist: Sal had lumped every check he wrote for the building into one pile.

head: Item
Amount
How Sal listed it
rows: Repairs, including $6,000 to paint the halls
blocks.caption: Sal's pile. Not every check he wrote is a deduction.

blocks.q: Sal paid $28,000 of property tax on the building. He heard the SALT deduction is capped. How much of the $28,000 can he deduct?
c: All $28,000, deducted as a rental expense
$10,000, the old SALT cap for individuals
$28,000 minus his share of the $40,400 cap
Zero, since rental property taxes are capitalized
blocks.x: Property taxes on rental property are an expense outside the SALT cap: they are an expense of the rental activity and are deducted against rental income, outside the SALT cap. The cap limits state and local taxes an individual deducts as an itemized deduction, such as tax on a personal home. Choice B is the trap from 2018 to 2024 headlines. Rental taxes are not capitalized; they recur every year.

blocks.q: Sal listed $15,000 of mortgage principal as an expense. What should Ms. Fiore do with it?
c: Deduct it, because it is part of the mortgage payment
Deduct half, matching the interest-to-principal ratio
Remove it, because repaying a loan is not an expense
Add it to the building's basis as an improvement
blocks.x: Principal repays money Sal borrowed; it is not a cost of earning rent, so it is never deductible. Only the interest is. Choice D sounds clever but principal does not improve the building. This is the asymmetry from the cash world: principal leaves Sal's bank account (it reduces cash flow) but does not reduce taxable income, while depreciation does the opposite.

blocks.html: With the principal removed, the rental schedule reads: rents $146,490, minus operating expenses $80,000, minus interest $30,000, minus depreciation $28,000, for taxable rental income of $8,490. That is passive income, and because it is positive, Sal has no suspended passive losses waiting to be released when he sells.

blocks.q: The $10,000 repairs line includes $6,000 to repaint the hallways. If Sal had also replaced the 26-year-old boiler for $45,000, how would the two be treated?
c: Both deducted in full in the year paid, as ordinary repairs
Painting deducted now; boiler capitalized and depreciated
Both capitalized and depreciated over 27.5 years
The boiler deducted now; the painting capitalized over time
blocks.x: Painting the halls keeps the building in ordinary operating condition, so it is a deductible repair. A new boiler replaces a major building system and is a capital improvement, added to basis and depreciated over 27.5 years as part of residential rental property. Choice A is how Sal would like it to work. Choice D reverses the rule.

blocks.html: Ms. Fiore finds something else while rebuilding Sal's depreciation history for the sale. Sal's first accountant, who retired in 2010, never claimed depreciation on the 2008 and 2009 returns. So Sal has actually deducted $504,000 over 20 years, not $560,000.

blocks.q: When Sal sells, how much depreciation reduces his adjusted basis?
c: $504,000, the amount he actually deducted
$532,000, splitting the difference
$0 for 2008 and 2009, then $28,000 a year after
$560,000, the depreciation that was allowable
blocks.x: Basis is reduced by depreciation "allowed or allowable," meaning the greater of what was claimed and what could have been claimed. Sal's adjusted basis drops by the full $560,000 whether he took it or not, and the gain is computed on that basis. Choice A is the intuitive answer and the expensive one. Ms. Fiore can usually recover the missed deductions by filing an accounting method change (Form 3115) before or in the year of sale, rather than losing them.

blocks.title: Skipping depreciation does not avoid recapture
blocks.html: Some owners skip depreciation on purpose, thinking they will avoid tax on recapture later. It does not work. The basis drops by allowable depreciation anyway, so the owner pays tax on the gain at sale and never got the deduction. Depreciation is not optional in effect, even if claiming it is.

Jordan's checklist for Ms. Fiore grows: the 2006 closing statement (for the original basis and the land allocation), every depreciation schedule since 2006, the 2008 and 2009 returns, the current mortgage payoff letter, and the building's capital improvement records. There are none since 2006; the boiler is the one the building came with. Each document answers a question the IRS could ask years from now, and the closing statement from 2006 is the one sellers lose most often. Sal finds his in a shoebox labeled "HOUSE STUFF," between a 1998 Mets schedule and the deed.
Before getting to the Seos' terms, Ms. Fiore runs the plain version: an all-cash sale closing in December 2026.

head: Line
Amount
rows: NYS transfer tax (0.65%, NYC property other than 1 to 3 family, $2 million or more)
blocks.caption: The selling costs are higher than a house sale because a six-family pays NYC's commercial transfer tax rates.

blocks.html: The name "unrecaptured section 1250 gain" confuses everyone, so Ms. Fiore explains it in one breath. Section 1250 covers depreciable real property. When an owner used faster-than-straight-line depreciation, the excess was "recaptured" as ordinary income at sale. Buildings placed in service since 1987 must use straight-line depreciation, so there is usually no excess and nothing recaptured as ordinary income. The depreciation itself still produces gain, and that gain is "unrecaptured" in the technical sense but taxed at a special maximum rate of 25%, not at the lower long-term rates. In plain terms: the government let Sal deduct $28,000 a year against income, and at sale it takes some of that benefit back.

The table is the same one Sal's nephew saw, and it frightened him into suggesting a 1031 exchange. Sal does not want another building. He wants income and Florida. That leaves two choices: take $2,400,000 in cash and pay the whole tax for 2026, or accept the Seos' offer and spread the gain over the years he is paid.

blocks.q: Sal asks whether he should replace the old boiler for $45,000 before closing to "get a deduction." What is the most accurate answer?
c: It adds to basis and cuts the gain by about $45,000
It would be fully deductible in 2026 as a repair before the sale
It would raise the sale price by at least $45,000
It would turn the unrecaptured gain into long-term gain
blocks.x: A new boiler is a capital improvement, so it raises basis (less a sliver of depreciation for the months before sale) and reduces the gain, roughly the same tax effect as giving the buyer a $45,000 credit, which reduces the amount realized. Neither is a deduction against ordinary income. Choice C assumes buyers pay a dollar for every dollar spent, which is rarely true. The Seos prefer a credit and their own contractor.

blocks.title: The term sheet
blocks.html:
Price: $2,400,000
Cash at closing (December 2026): $800,000
Purchase-money note to Sal: $1,600,000 at 6.5% interest, 25-year amortization, balance due in 10 years
Security: a first mortgage on the building in Sal's favor
Sal's existing mortgage (about $500,000) paid off at closing from the cash

This is an installment sale: Sal receives at least one payment after the year of sale, so he reports the gain as he is paid instead of all at once. The math runs on one ratio. Gross profit is the selling price minus Sal's adjusted basis and selling expenses: $2,400,000 minus ($540,000 + $140,000) = $1,720,000. The contract price is the selling price less any of Sal's debt the buyer assumes. The Seos are not assuming his loan; it is paid off from the down payment. So the contract price is the full $2,400,000.

blocks.q: What is Sal's gross profit percentage?
c: About 33.3%, the down payment share
About 76.1%
About 71.7%
About 28.3%
blocks.x: Gross profit percentage = gross profit / contract price = $1,720,000 / $2,400,000 = 71.67%. Each dollar of principal Sal receives is 71.67% gain and 28.33% return of basis. Choice B divides by the $2,260,000 amount realized instead of the contract price. Choice A is the down payment as a share of price. Choice D is the basis recovery share.

blocks.q: How much gain does Sal report for 2026, the year of closing?
blocks.x: 2026 payments are the $800,000 down payment (paying off his own mortgage with it does not change that it was paid to him). Gain = $800,000 x 71.67% = $573,333. Choice A is the all-cash result. Choice B treats the whole payment as gain. Choice C applies the basis share, 28.33%, by mistake.

blocks.q: Which part of Sal's $573,333 of 2026 gain is taxed as unrecaptured section 1250 gain, at up to 25%?
c: $573,333 x 32.6%, its proportionate share
The first $560,000
No part of it until the note is paid off
$13,333, the part above the depreciation
blocks.x: Treasury regulations require the unrecaptured section 1250 portion of an installment sale to be taken into account first. Sal's 2026 gain is $560,000 of 25%-rate gain and $13,333 of regular long-term gain; from 2027 on, all of his reported gain is regular long-term gain. Choice A, a pro rata split, is the intuitive approach and is not the rule. Choice D reverses the order.

blocks.title: New York taxes gains like wages
blocks.html: New York State has no special capital gains rate: long-term gains are taxed at the same rates as other income, and an Astoria resident like Sal also pays New York City personal income tax. New York generally follows the federal installment method, so the state and city tax arrives in the same years as the federal tax. A nonresident seller reporting on the installment method pays New York estimated tax at closing only on the gain reported for that year.

blocks.text: Why spread the gain at all?

blocks.html: Sal's nephew calls the installment sale "a trick." It is not. The total gain is the same $1,720,000 either way; the installment method changes only when it is reported. That timing is worth real money for three reasons. First, every dollar of tax paid in 2035 instead of 2026 is a dollar Sal keeps earning on in the meantime, an interest-free loan from the government. Second, spreading a large gain over several years can keep more of it out of the highest brackets than one huge year would. Third, Sal is earning 6.5% on the note, more than he would get on the cash in a bank.

The trade-offs are just as real. Sal is now exposed to the Seos' credit: if the dry cleaner fails, his security is the building, and getting it back takes a court foreclosure. Tax rates can rise while the gain is still deferred, and the deferred tax does not disappear; it is owed as the principal comes in. And if Sal dies holding the note, the deferred gain does not get a fresh basis the way the building would have. His heirs report the remaining gain as they collect.

blocks.q: What does an installment sale do to the total gain Sal must report?
c: It reduces the total gain by the interest Sal receives
It leaves the total gain the same but spreads when it is taxed
It converts the gain to ordinary income over the note's term
It eliminates the gain on any principal not paid within 10 years
blocks.x: The installment method is a timing rule. Sal still reports all $1,720,000 of gain, as principal is received, at the gross profit percentage. Interest is separate ordinary income that adds to, not subtracts from, what he reports. Choice D invents a forgiveness rule: unpaid principal stays deferred until it is paid or the note is disposed of.

blocks.html: Ms. Fiore estimates Sal's 2026 federal, state and city tax on $573,333 of gain at roughly $215,000. Jordan then lays out what actually reaches Sal's bank account at the closing table.

blocks.title: Sal's closing table
blocks.html:
Cash from the Seos: $800,000
Payoff of Sal's mortgage: ($500,000)
Selling costs: ($140,000)
Net cash to Sal: $160,000
Estimated 2026 tax on the gain: about $215,000

blocks.q: What is the problem with the deal as structured, and what is the most direct fix?
c: Sal nets less cash than his 2026 tax bill; ask for a larger down payment
The interest rate is too low; raise it to cover the tax
Installment sales cannot be used with an existing mortgage; refinance first
The note is too large; shorten the balloon to 5 years
blocks.x: Sal would owe about $215,000 for 2026 but walk away with $160,000, because the down payment first pays his mortgage and closing costs. A larger down payment fixes it directly. At $1,000,000 down, reported 2026 gain rises to $716,667, but net cash rises to $360,000, enough for an estimated $265,000 tax with room left. Choice C is wrong: the mortgage simply gets paid from the cash. A higher rate adds interest income later, not cash now.

blocks.html: The Seos' bank approves a larger loan, and they agree to $1,000,000 down with a $1,400,000 note. Monthly payments on the note are $9,453, or $113,435 a year. In 2027, about $90,319 of that is interest and $23,115 is principal.

blocks.q: How is the $90,319 of interest Sal receives in 2027 taxed?
c: As long-term capital gain, because it comes from selling the building
As unrecaptured section 1250 gain at up to 25%
As interest income taxed at ordinary rates
Tax-free, because the note is secured by real estate
blocks.x: Interest on an installment note is ordinary portfolio income, taxed like bank interest. Only the principal portion carries gain, at the gross profit percentage: $23,115 x 71.67% = about $16,566 of long-term gain for 2027. Choice A is the trap that makes some sellers set a low rate and a higher price; the note also has to carry at least the IRS's applicable federal rate, or part of the principal is treated as interest anyway.

blocks.q: In 2028, Sal wants to borrow $300,000 from his bank and pledge the Seos' note as collateral. What is the tax consequence?
c: Nothing, since a loan is not a sale of the note
The interest he pays the bank becomes deductible as rental expense
The note stops qualifying, so the deferred gain is taxed at once
The $300,000 is generally treated as a payment received
blocks.x: For installment obligations from sales over $150,000, using the note as security for a loan generally treats the net loan proceeds as a payment received, so Sal reports gain on $300,000 at 71.67%. That stops sellers from deferring tax while getting the cash anyway. Choice A is the intuitive answer and the trap. The rest of the note keeps installment treatment, so choice C overstates it.

blocks.html: The Seos' side of the deal has its own tax story, and Jordan mentions it to their attorney so no one assumes otherwise. Their basis is the full $2,400,000 price, including the part financed by Sal's note, plus their closing costs. Because they will live in one of the six apartments, roughly one sixth of the building is their home and five sixths is rental property. Only the rental portion can be depreciated, over 27.5 years after removing land value, and the interest they pay Sal is split the same way: the rental share deducted against rents, the home share as mortgage interest if they itemize. A two-family or six-family with an owner upstairs is always two tax stories in one building.
Sal's nephew, who buys, renovates and resells two or three houses a year in Yonkers, hears about the deal and asks Jordan whether he can sell his next flip the same way to spread the tax.

blocks.q: Can the nephew report a gain on his next flip using the installment method?
c: Yes, if he holds the note for at least 2 years
No, since the property needs a 10-year hold
Yes, as long as the buyer puts down at least 20%
No, it excludes property held for resale
blocks.x: Dealer property, real estate held for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business, cannot use the installment method, and a regular flipper is likely a dealer. His gain is also ordinary income, not capital gain. Holding periods and down payment size do not control eligibility. Sal, a long-term investor, qualifies; the nephew probably does not.

blocks.html: The deal closes on December 18, 2026. Sal's purchase-money mortgage is recorded behind no one: it is the only lien. Priya, who represented Sal, insisted on a clause that accelerates the note if the Seos sell the building, and on annual proof of insurance and paid taxes, the way any bank would. Sal is now a lender. If the Seos stop paying, his remedy is a foreclosure, which in New York runs through the courts and can take well over a year. That risk is the price of spreading the tax.

Diane reviews the file before it goes to the closing. Her note to Jordan is about scope, not numbers: "You did this right. You found the facts, you put the questions in front of Ms. Fiore and Priya, and you never told Sal what his tax would be. Keep it that way." A licensee who explains how an installment sale works is helping a client understand a deal. A licensee who tells a client what to report on a return is practicing a profession he is not licensed in, and the brokerage's errors and omissions policy will not cover the result.

items: Rental property taxes are deducted against rental income outside the SALT cap; mortgage principal is never deductible; repairs are deducted, improvements are capitalized.
Basis drops by depreciation allowed or allowable, so skipped depreciation is still recaptured; missed deductions can usually be caught up with a method change.
Installment sale: gross profit percentage = gross profit / contract price; gain reported each year = principal received x that percentage, with unrecaptured section 1250 gain reported first.
Interest on the note is ordinary income and must meet the applicable federal rate; pledging the note for a loan can trigger gain.
The down payment must cover the seller's mortgage payoff, closing costs and the first year's tax.
Dealer property cannot use the installment method.

lessons.title: Case file: The 45th Day Is New Year's Eve
lessons.tagline: A Bay Ridge eight-family, $2,380,000 of gain, two upstate buildings, and a deadline that falls on the night everyone else is at a party.
objectives: Apply the 45-day identification and 180-day exchange period rules, including the tax return due date, to real calendar dates
Decide who may serve as a qualified intermediary and how identification must be made
Calculate cash boot, mortgage boot and recognized gain, and apply the netting rules
Calculate the basis of replacement property and spot property and plans that do not qualify

blocks.title: Fifth Avenue, Bay Ridge
blocks.html: Tony and Lena Petrakis bought an eight-family building on Fifth Avenue in Bay Ridge in 2004 for $900,000. Hudson & Hart has the listing, and a buyer has signed a contract at $3,000,000, closing November 16, 2026. After 22 years of depreciation ($500,000 in all), their adjusted basis is $400,000. They do not want to stop being landlords; they want fewer tenants, newer buildings and to be closer to their son in the Hudson Valley. Their accountant has told them that selling outright would produce a seven-figure tax bill and that a 1031 exchange could defer all of it. Lena has a spreadsheet of upstate buildings. Tony has one question for Jordan: "What can go wrong?" The answer, it turns out, is a list.

head: Line
Amount
rows: NYS transfer tax (0.65%, NYC property other than 1 to 3 family, $2 million or more)
blocks.caption: An exchange does not avoid transfer taxes. They are paid at closing like any sale.

blocks.html: A 1031 exchange defers the tax on that $2,380,000 if the Petrakises sell investment real estate and buy like-kind investment real estate under rules that leave very little room for error. Like-kind is broad for real property: an apartment building for a mixed-use building, a warehouse or land held for investment all qualify. The rules that trip people up are about who touches the money, what is identified, by when, and what comes out of the deal that is not real estate.

Jordan's role is narrower than it looks. The accountant decides whether an exchange makes sense, the QI runs it, and the attorneys paper both closings. Jordan's job is to make sure the real estate side never breaks the tax side: contracts with closing dates that fit the calendar, a listing agreement and a purchase search that start early enough, and a client who knows which deadlines cannot move. Most failed exchanges fail on real estate logistics, not tax law.

The first decision has to be made before closing. Sale proceeds cannot pass through the sellers' hands, even for a day, so a qualified intermediary (QI) signs an exchange agreement, takes an assignment of the sale contract, and receives the net proceeds directly at closing. Tony suggests three candidates.

blocks.q: Which of Tony's candidates can serve as the Petrakises' qualified intermediary?
c: Hudson & Hart, the brokerage that listed the building
Their attorney, who has drafted their leases since 2019
Lena's brother, a CPA who files his own clients' returns
An exchange company with no ties to them
blocks.x: A QI cannot be a "disqualified person": anyone who acted as the taxpayer's agent within the 2 years before the sale, which explicitly includes their real estate broker, attorney, accountant and employees (services for the exchange itself, and routine title and escrow services, are excepted), and close relatives. Hudson & Hart and the lease attorney are agents; Lena's brother is a related person. An unrelated exchange company is the normal choice.

blocks.html: The seller's attorney sends a draft closing statement that shows the net proceeds going into her firm's escrow account, "to be wired to the QI the next morning." It is how she handles most closings, and it is a habit that ends exchanges.

blocks.q: What is wrong with routing the proceeds through the attorney's escrow account overnight?
c: It risks constructive receipt, ending the exchange
Attorneys cannot hold sale proceeds in New York after a closing
The money would reach the QI a day late, missing the 45-day clock
The exchange would turn into a reverse exchange under IRS rules
blocks.x: If the sellers or their agent has control of the proceeds, even briefly, the IRS can treat the sellers as having received the money (constructive receipt), and an exchange needs the money to go from the buyer to the QI under the exchange agreement. Choice C misunderstands the clock: the 45 days run from the transfer of the property, not from when the QI gets the funds. Attorneys hold escrow all the time; the problem is whose agent holds this money.

blocks.title: The exchange agreement comes first
blocks.html: The QI's exchange agreement and the assignment of the sale contract must be signed before the relinquished property closes, and the closing statement must show the proceeds payable to the QI. An exchange cannot be set up after the closing, no matter how quickly the money is reinvested.

The sale closes Monday, November 16, 2026. Two clocks start that day, and both count calendar days with no extension for weekends or holidays. The identification period ends on day 45. The exchange period, when the replacement property must be acquired, ends on the earlier of day 180 or the due date, including extensions, of the tax return for the year of the sale.

blocks.q: On what date does the Petrakises' 45-day identification period end?
c: December 30, 2026
January 4, 2027, the next business day
December 31, 2026
January 15, 2027
blocks.x: Count from the day after closing: 14 days remain in November (17 to 30), then 31 days of December, so day 45 is Thursday, December 31, 2026. Choice B assumes a holiday or weekend extension; the identification deadline has none, and New Year's Eve is not a federal holiday anyway. Choice A is the off-by-one error from counting the closing day itself.

blocks.title: Day 180
blocks.html:
November 17 to 30: 14 days
December: 31 (45)
January: 31 (76)
February 2027: 28 (104)
March: 31 (135)
April: 30 (165)
May 1 to 15: 15 (180)
Day 180: Saturday, May 15, 2027
But the 2026 federal return is due Thursday, April 15, 2027.

blocks.q: The Petrakises expect to close on their replacement buildings in early May 2027. What must they do to keep the full 180 days?
c: Nothing, since day 180 controls the exchange regardless
Close by April 15, 2027, since an extension does not help
File a 2026 tax return early, before the replacement closes
Extend their 2026 return before April 15, 2027
blocks.x: The exchange period ends on the earlier of day 180 or the return due date, including extensions. Without an extension, the deadline is April 15, 2027, a month before day 180. Filing an extension moves the due date to October, so day 180 (May 15) controls again. Choice C is the worst of the four: filing the return early ends the exchange period that day.

blocks.html: Day 180 falls on a Saturday, and county clerks do not record deeds on Saturdays. There is no extension for that either. Jordan writes "Friday, May 14 at the latest" on the calendar and tells the Petrakises the real target is mid-April, so a problem with a title report or a lender has room to be solved.
Lena's spreadsheet has four buildings she likes, and she wants to identify all of them to be safe.

head: Property
Type
Asking price
blocks.caption: Every one of these is like-kind to a Bay Ridge apartment building.

blocks.q: Lena wants to identify all four properties. What is the problem?
c: A warehouse is not like-kind to an apartment building
Too many properties and too much value for either rule
Identified properties have to be within 100 miles of the sale
The identified value cannot exceed the net cash proceeds
blocks.x: The three-property rule allows up to three properties of any value. The 200% rule allows more than three if their total value is no more than 200% of the property sold, here $6,000,000. Four properties at $7,100,000 break both. (A narrow 95% rule rescues an over-identification only if the taxpayer acquires 95% of everything identified.) Any US real estate held for investment is like-kind to any other, so choice A is wrong.

blocks.html: Lena drops the Poughkeepsie strip center, leaving three properties worth $4,900,000. Now the identification itself. It must be in writing, signed by the taxpayers, unambiguous (a street address or legal description), and delivered by the end of day 45 to the QI or to the seller of the replacement property, not to someone who is the taxpayers' own agent.

blocks.q: On December 31 at 10 pm, Tony texts Jordan: "Kingston, Beacon and Newburgh. Lock them in." Is the identification valid?
c: Yes, since a written text sent before midnight on day 45 is timely
No, it must be signed and sent to the QI, not their broker
Yes, since Jordan can forward it to the QI the next morning
No, since identification needs a notarized form filed with the IRS
blocks.x: Identification must be a written document signed by the taxpayers and delivered to a proper party, such as the QI or the replacement seller. Jordan is the Petrakises' broker and agent, a disqualified person, so delivery to Jordan does not count, and forwarding it on January 1 is too late. There is no IRS filing at identification; the exchange is reported later on Form 8824. The QI's identification form, signed and emailed to the QI, would have taken two minutes.

blocks.html: Why identify three when they plan to buy two? Because identified property is the only property they can buy. If the Kingston inspection turned up a failing foundation in February, the Petrakises could not add a new building to the list; the window closed on December 31. A third identified property is insurance. Newburgh, the warehouse, is their backup: different enough from the apartments that a problem in the residential market would not knock out both, and close enough in price to fill the gap. Exchange buyers who identify only their first choice sometimes end up paying full tax on a deal that fell apart in month four.

The plan is to buy Kingston and Beacon for a total of $3,300,000, using the $2,080,000 held by the QI and new mortgages totaling $1,200,000, with the Petrakises adding $20,000 of their own cash. Then Lena raises a second idea. Their daughter is getting married in June, and she would like $250,000 of the sale money for the wedding and a down payment gift.

blocks.q: If the QI releases $250,000 of the proceeds to the Petrakises and the rest is reinvested, how much gain is recognized?
c: $0, since the money is for a family gift, not personal use
$2,380,000, since taking cash ends the exchange
$250,000, the cash boot they received
$125,000, half the cash, since the couple file jointly
blocks.x: Boot is anything received that is not like-kind property, and cash is the clearest example. Gain is recognized up to the amount of boot, here $250,000, while the remaining gain stays deferred. Choice B overstates it: receiving boot makes part of the gain taxable, it does not end the exchange. What the money is used for does not matter.

blocks.q: Tony suggests making up the $250,000 by borrowing $250,000 more on the new buildings. Does a bigger new mortgage offset the cash they take out?
c: No, debt taken on cannot offset cash received
Yes, since new debt offsets boot dollar for dollar
Yes, as long as the new loan closes on the same day
No, since new mortgages count as boot in an exchange
blocks.x: Under the regulations, liabilities the taxpayer takes on offset liabilities the taxpayer is relieved of, and cash the taxpayer pays offsets debt relief, but debt taken on does not offset cash received. The $250,000 is taxable no matter how much they borrow. Choice D reverses the concept: new debt is not boot, it is consideration the taxpayer gives.

blocks.html: Lena drops the idea; they will pay for the wedding from savings. But Tony's caution goes the other way. He wonders whether they could buy just Kingston, for cash, and skip the mortgages altogether.

blocks.title: Kingston alone, all cash from the QI
blocks.html:
Amount realized on the sale: $2,780,000
Kingston purchase price: $1,900,000, paid with QI funds
Cash left with the QI, returned to them: $180,000 (cash boot)
Old mortgage paid off: $700,000; new mortgage: $0 (mortgage boot of $700,000)
Total boot: $880,000

blocks.q: In the Kingston-only plan, how much of the $2,380,000 gain would be recognized?
c: $180,000, since cash is the boot that counts
$700,000, the mortgage relief
$880,000, cash plus mortgage boot
$0, because Kingston is like-kind property
blocks.x: Debt relief is boot just like cash: the $700,000 mortgage paid off on the sale, with no new debt to offset it, plus the $180,000 of leftover cash, totals $880,000 of boot, all recognized because it is less than the realized gain. A quicker way to see it: the Petrakises traded down by $880,000 ($2,780,000 sold, $1,900,000 bought). Choice A is the trap that forgets mortgage boot.

blocks.q: Which plan defers all of the Petrakises' gain?
c: Buy property worth at least the $400,000 adjusted basis
Buy property worth $3,000,000 or more, with cash from any source
Reinvest the $2,080,000 and skip any new mortgage
Buy $2,780,000 or more, reinvest the cash, replace the debt
blocks.x: To defer everything, buy replacement property costing at least the amount realized ($2,780,000), reinvest every dollar of net cash, and take on at least as much debt as was paid off ($700,000) or add new cash to make up the difference. The Kingston and Beacon plan does all three. Choice C leaves $700,000 of mortgage boot unless the full $2,780,000 is covered by cash. Choice A confuses basis with value.

blocks.title: New York and the exchange
blocks.html: New York generally follows the federal treatment, so gain deferred for federal purposes is generally deferred for New York income tax too. But a 1031 exchange does nothing for transfer taxes: the NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT on the Bay Ridge sale ($98,250 here) are due at closing, and each replacement purchase has its own recording costs and, where it applies, mortgage recording tax on the new loans.

Deferral is not forgiveness. The deferred gain rides along in a lower basis for the replacement property, and the $500,000 of depreciation already taken is still sitting in that gain, waiting to be taxed at up to 25% when the replacement buildings are someday sold in a taxable sale.

blocks.q: With no boot, the Petrakises buy Kingston and Beacon for $3,300,000. What is their total basis in the two buildings?
c: $3,300,000, the price they paid
$400,000, the old adjusted basis
$2,780,000, the old amount realized
blocks.x: Basis of replacement property = its cost minus the deferred gain: $3,300,000 minus $2,380,000 = $920,000. Another way: old adjusted basis ($400,000) plus the additional money and debt put in to trade up ($520,000). Choice B is what a buyer who did not exchange would have. The $920,000 is split between the two buildings by relative value, and only the building portion, net of land, is depreciated.

blocks.html: Depreciation on the new buildings also starts from the carried-over number, not from the $3,300,000 price. The part of the $920,000 basis that carried over from Bay Ridge keeps depreciating on the old building's remaining schedule, and the extra $520,000 they invested is depreciated as newly acquired property over 27.5 years, after land is removed. Their accountant will run it the long way; for Jordan's purposes the point is simpler. A 1031 exchange buys time and a bigger building. It does not buy a fresh tax start, and the bill for the past 22 years of depreciation is still in the file, deferred, not gone.
