blocks.text: Three more plans that do not work

blocks.html: The Kingston seller then throws a wrench in: his own deal requires him to close by October 30, before the Bay Ridge sale. The Petrakises cannot buy Kingston first in a normal forward exchange, because there would be no sale proceeds to use yet.

blocks.q: How can the Petrakises acquire Kingston before their Bay Ridge sale closes and still exchange?
c: Buy Kingston themselves and treat it as replacement property later
Ask the IRS for a private ruling extending the 45-day period
A reverse exchange, with a titleholder parking the property
Have their daughter buy Kingston and sell it to them later
blocks.x: In a reverse exchange, an exchange accommodation titleholder takes title to the new property (or the old one) until the relinquished property sells, with the same 45-day and 180-day limits. Buying it themselves first does not work, because they would own both at once. Choice D adds a related-party problem on top of a timing one. Reverse exchanges cost more, so many buyers first try to negotiate the date.

blocks.html: The Kingston seller agrees to wait after all. Then Lena brings up a cabin in the Catskills that the family has rented for summer vacations for years. It is for sale for $450,000, and she would like to buy it with part of the exchange money and use it as the family's summer place.

blocks.q: Can the Catskills cabin be replacement property if the family uses it as a vacation home?
c: Yes, since vacant land and cabins are like-kind to apartments
No, a home held mainly for personal use does not qualify
Yes, if they rent it out at least one week a year
No, since replacement property has to be in the same county
blocks.x: A 1031 exchange requires replacement property held for investment or for use in a business. A family vacation home held mainly for personal use does not qualify, however much it might appreciate. Choice C is the trap: a token week of rent does not change its character, and IRS guidance on vacation homes looks for substantial rental and limited personal use. There is no same-county rule.

blocks.html: Finally, Lena mentions that she and Tony might move into one of the Beacon apartments when they retire in a few years, sell their house, and someday sell Beacon too. She has heard about the $500,000 home sale exclusion.

blocks.q: If the Petrakises later move into a Beacon apartment and make it their main home, when could they first use the home sale exclusion on it?
c: Not until 5 years after the exchange acquisition
After living there 2 years, whenever that occurs
Immediately, since the exclusion applies to any main home
At no point, since exchanged property cannot be a residence
blocks.x: Property acquired in a 1031 exchange must be held at least 5 years after the exchange before the home sale exclusion can apply to it, in addition to the usual 2-of-5-year tests. Depreciation taken on it is still taxed, and the years it was a rental count as nonqualified use. Choice B states the normal rule and misses the extra 5-year requirement. Choice D overstates it.

blocks.html: The Bay Ridge sale closed November 16 with the proceeds wired straight to the QI. The signed identification of Kingston, Beacon and Newburgh reached the QI on December 18. The Petrakises' accountant filed an extension in March. Kingston closed April 9 and Beacon April 23, both with new mortgages. Their tax return for 2026 reports the exchange on Form 8824, showing $2,380,000 of realized gain, $0 recognized, and a $920,000 basis carried into two buildings up the Hudson. Tony sends Jordan a photo of the Beacon storefront and a one-line text: "Nothing went wrong."

items: Sale proceeds go straight from the buyer to a qualified intermediary under an agreement signed before closing; the taxpayer's broker, attorney or accountant from the last 2 years, and close relatives, cannot serve.
Count 45 and 180 calendar days from the closing with no weekend or holiday extension, and file a return extension when day 180 falls after the return due date.
Identify up to three properties of any value, or more if their total is within 200% of the property sold, in a signed writing delivered to the QI or seller by day 45.
Cash and debt relief are boot, taxable up to the realized gain; new debt offsets debt relief, cash paid offsets debt relief, but new debt never offsets cash received.
Replacement basis equals cost minus deferred gain; the deferred gain, including past depreciation, follows the new property.
Reverse exchanges handle buy-first timing; vacation homes do not qualify; exchanged property needs a 5-year hold before the home sale exclusion applies.

lessons.title: Case file: Half a House on 79th Street
lessons.tagline: A Dyker Heights two-family, one mortgage, and a tax return that treats the downstairs and the upstairs as two different worlds.
objectives: Decide whether buyers qualify for the IRA first-time homebuyer exception and explain what it saves
Allocate mortgage interest, points, property tax and closing costs between the home and the rental half of a two-family
Calculate the depreciable basis of a rental unit and the tax result of a year of operations, including the passive loss limit
Apply the federal rules for home equity, refinancing, prepayment penalties, construction loans and short vacation rentals

blocks.title: 79th Street, Dyker Heights
blocks.html: Nina Castellano teaches fourth grade in Sunset Park. Her husband, Omar Haddad, is a nurse at a hospital in Bay Ridge. They rent a one-bedroom on Fourth Avenue and have saved for five years. In June 2026 Jordan shows them a brick two-family on 79th Street in Dyker Heights, listed at $1,395,000 by the estate of its longtime owner. The two floors are identical three-bedroom apartments: Nina and Omar would live on the first floor, and the upstairs family, paying $3,500 a month, would stay. The couple earn about $210,000 together, and their down payment plan includes $20,000 from two traditional IRAs, because Omar has read that first-time buyers can tap an IRA without penalty. Then he mentions, almost in passing, that he owned a condo in Jersey City until August 2024.

Jordan is not their tax advisor and says so. But nearly every tax answer in this file turns on a real estate fact Jordan controls or can find: a contract date, a line on the closing statement, the size of each apartment, a payoff letter. Jordan's job is to get those facts right and in front of Ruth Adler, the couple's CPA, before they turn into expensive surprises. A two-family with the owners downstairs is two tax stories under one roof, and most of the mistakes come from telling only one of them.

blocks.text: The IRA and the contract date

blocks.html: The first-time homebuyer exception lets each qualifying person take up to $10,000 (a lifetime limit) from an IRA without the 10% early withdrawal penalty, if the money pays acquisition costs within 120 days. "First-time" is a defined term: no ownership interest in a main home during the 2 years ending on the date of acquisition. For a purchase, the date of acquisition is the day the buyer enters a binding contract, not the closing. A married buyer qualifies only if the spouse passes the same test.

blocks.q: The estate's attorney wants a signed contract by July 15, 2026. Omar lived in his Jersey City condo until he sold it on August 20, 2024. If they sign on July 15, can they use the exception?
c: Nina can, as she has not owned a home, but Omar cannot
Neither can, since Omar owned a main home within the 2 years
Both can, because the closing will not take place until December
Both can, because the condo Omar owned was outside New York
blocks.x: The 2-year lookback ends on the acquisition date, which for a purchase is the binding contract date. On July 15, 2026, Omar's ownership through August 2024 falls inside the window, and because a married buyer's spouse has to pass the test too, Nina fails along with him. The December-closing answer is the trap: the closing date does not control. Where the old home sat makes no difference.

blocks.html: Jordan does the arithmetic out loud: August 20, 2024 plus two years is August 20, 2026. As it happens, the estate is in no hurry either. The executor lives in Florida and is still waiting for letters testamentary from Surrogate's Court, which she needs before she can sign. Priya, representing Nina and Omar, proposes a contract date of August 24 and a December closing, and the estate agrees. The price settles at $1,380,000. Three weeks of patience preserved the exception for both of them.

blocks.q: Nina and Omar each withdraw $10,000 from a traditional IRA in November and use it at the December closing. What does the exception do for them?
c: Waives the 10% penalty, but the $20,000 is still taxable income
Waives the penalty and the income tax, like a qualified Roth payout
Lets them repay the $20,000 to their IRAs over 5 years, tax-free
Waives the 10% penalty on $10,000 for the couple as one household
blocks.x: The exception removes only the 10% additional tax. A traditional IRA withdrawal is ordinary income in the year taken, so the $20,000 adds roughly $4,400 of federal tax at a 22% bracket, plus New York State and City income tax. The household answer is the trap: the $10,000 limit is per person, so two qualifying spouses can take $10,000 each. The penalty they avoid is $2,000; the income tax is the larger number.

blocks.title: Put the IRA on the closing calendar
blocks.html: The withdrawal has to be spent on acquisition costs by the 120th day after it is received. If a closing slips, the buyer can put the money back into an IRA within those same 120 days as a rollover and owe nothing. Jordan writes the withdrawal date on the closing calendar next to the mortgage commitment expiration, because a delayed closing can break both.

Nina and Omar close on Friday, December 4, 2026, with $280,000 down and a 30-year fixed mortgage of $1,100,000 at 6.75%. The upstairs tenants' lease and security deposit transfer to them at closing. From that afternoon the building is two things at once. The first floor is their home, governed by homeowner rules and itemized deductions. The second floor is a rental business, reported on Schedule E under rental rules. Because the floors are the same size, Ruth splits every shared cost 50/50; owners with unequal units usually split by square footage.

head: Buyer's closing statement, December 4, 2026
Amount
rows: Mansion tax (1%, residential purchase of $1 million or more)
Owner's title insurance and deed recording
Real estate tax adjustment (taxes the estate prepaid for December)
blocks.caption: Not every line on a closing statement is a deduction, and in a two-family most of them split in two.

blocks.html: Omar has a question before Ruth gets to the details. The loan is $1,100,000, and he has read that home acquisition debt is capped at $750,000. Is the interest on the other $350,000 wasted? The answer depends on what the debt is attached to. The cap applies to debt on a qualified home. An upstairs apartment with its own kitchen and bath, rented to a tenant, is not part of the owners' qualified home. It is rental property.

blocks.q: How should the interest on the $1,100,000 mortgage be treated?
c: Interest on $750,000 is deductible; the rest is personal and lost
Half is deductible, with the home half capped at $375,000 of debt
The whole amount is a rental expense, since the building earns rent
Half is home mortgage interest, half a rental expense
blocks.x: Interest follows the use of the property. The home half, $550,000 of debt, is within the $750,000 limit and is itemized as home mortgage interest. The rental half is an expense of the rental activity, deducted against rent and not subject to the home mortgage limit. The $750,000 answer applies the cap to the whole building. The $375,000 figure is the limit for married people filing separately, which Nina and Omar are not.

blocks.q: How are the $11,000 of points handled?
c: $11,000 is deductible in 2026 as points on buying a main home
$11,000 is spread over 30 years, since the loan tops $750,000
$5,500 deductible in 2026; $5,500 spread over the 30-year loan
$5,500 is added to basis; $5,500 is deducted against 2026 rent
blocks.x: Points on a loan to buy a main home can be deducted in the year paid when the usual tests are met, which covers the home half. Points on a loan for rental property are prepaid interest deducted over the life of the loan: $5,500 / 30 = about $183 a year on Schedule E. The full-$11,000 answer ignores the split. The last answer reverses the rental rule and invents a basis rule for the home half.

blocks.html: Ruth works down the rest of the statement. The December interest paid at closing is mortgage interest, split the same way. The $860 tax adjustment is property tax for the buyers' days of ownership: half itemized, half a rental expense. The mortgage recording tax, lender fees and appraisal are costs of getting the loan rather than of buying the building, and they follow loan rules Ruth applies separately. That leaves the costs of acquiring the property itself.

blocks.q: Which of these closing costs are added to Nina and Omar's basis in the building rather than deducted?
c: The mansion tax, title insurance, deed recording and attorney's fee
The mansion tax and the points, since both are paid to buy the house
The tax adjustment and the December interest paid at the closing
The title insurance and mortgage recording tax, not the mansion tax
blocks.x: Costs of acquiring the property, including a transfer tax the buyer pays, owner's title insurance, deed recording and the buyer's legal fee, go into basis: $20,000 here, for a total cost basis of $1,400,000. Points are interest, and the tax adjustment is a deductible tax. The last answer is the trap: the mansion tax is a tax on the purchase and belongs in basis, while the mortgage recording tax is a cost of the loan.

blocks.title: Two New York taxes that look alike
blocks.html: The mansion tax (1% paid by the buyer on a residential purchase of $1 million or more) and the NYC mortgage recording tax (1.925% of a 1 to 3 family loan of $500,000 or more) sit next to each other on the closing statement, and buyers often lump them together. They land in different places on a tax return. The mansion tax is part of the cost of the building: it goes into basis, reduces gain at a sale and, for the rental half, is depreciated. The recording tax is a cost of the loan. Neither is deductible the way the annual property tax is.

One more 2026 decision. Ruth totals what Nina and Omar could itemize for the year: about $17,000 of New York State and City income tax withheld, $430 of property tax on their half, $2,848 of December interest on their half, and the $5,500 of home-half points. About $25,800 in all, against a $32,200 standard deduction for a married couple filing jointly in 2026.

blocks.q: Since the standard deduction beats itemizing in 2026, what can Ruth do with the $5,500 of home-half points?
c: Nothing, because purchase points are deducted in the year they are paid
Add them to the home's basis to cut the gain on a later sale
Move them to the rental half, where no itemizing is required
Elect to deduct them over the loan's life, starting in 2027
blocks.x: A buyer who meets the tests for a current deduction may choose instead to deduct purchase points over the life of the loan. In a year when the standard deduction is larger, a current deduction buys nothing, so spreading the $5,500 (about $183 a year) helps in every later year they itemize. The first answer treats the current deduction as mandatory; it is an option. Moving costs to the rental half is improper: the split follows the use of each floor, not the tax result.

blocks.html: Only the rental half is depreciated, and only the building, never the land. Ruth takes the land share from the ratio of land to total value on the city's assessment roll, which puts the land at 35%. Residential rental property is depreciated straight line over 27.5 years, with the first and last years prorated by the mid-month convention.

blocks.q: What is the full-year depreciation on the upstairs apartment?
blocks.x: Cost basis $1,400,000 minus land at 35% leaves $910,000 for the building. Half is rental: $455,000 / 27.5 = $16,545 a year. $25,455 forgets to remove the land ($700,000 / 27.5). $33,091 depreciates the whole building, including the floor the owners live on. $11,667 uses the 39-year life, which is for nonresidential property such as a store or office.

blocks.title: The building's basis, split
blocks.html:
Purchase price $1,380,000 + acquisition costs $20,000 = $1,400,000
Land (35%): $490,000, not depreciable
Building (65%): $910,000
First floor (home): $455,000, not depreciated, recovered when they sell
Second floor (rental): $455,000 / 27.5 years = $16,545 a year
The rental half was placed in service at closing, with the tenant in place.

In June 2027 the upstairs kitchen fails: rotted cabinets, a leaking sink base and a stove the tenants are afraid of. Nina and Omar replace the whole kitchen for $24,000 from savings. They also pay $1,300 for ordinary repairs upstairs during the year: a faucet, a broken window, a radiator valve. In February 2028 Omar sends Ruth the year's file, already sorted by floor, because Jordan suggested it at the closing.

blocks.q: How is the $24,000 upstairs kitchen treated for 2027?
c: Deducted in full in 2027 as a repair expense of the rental unit
Split, with half deducted and half added to the home's basis
Depreciated over 27.5 years as a rental improvement
Added to the home's basis, since the owners paid it from savings
blocks.x: A new kitchen in the rental unit is a capital improvement to rental property. It is depreciated over 27.5 years, about $873 a year, starting in June under the mid-month convention. It is not split, because it improves only the rental floor. The full-deduction answer is how owners wish it worked; the $1,300 of ordinary repairs is what gets deducted now.

blocks.title: The upstairs, 2027
blocks.html:
Rent (12 x $3,500): $42,000
Property tax, insurance and water (rental half): ($8,200)
Repairs upstairs: ($1,300)
Net operating income: $32,500
Mortgage interest, rental half (Form 1098 shows $67,760): ($33,880)
Depreciation, building: ($16,545)
Depreciation, new kitchen (June to December): ($473)
Points: ($183)
Taxable result: a loss of $18,581

Cash: NOI $32,500 minus the rental half of 11 mortgage payments ($39,240) = ($6,740)

The upstairs lost $6,740 of cash but shows an $18,581 loss for tax. The difference is depreciation and amortized points, which no one writes a check for, partly offset by principal, which reduces cash but is not deductible. This is the tax shelter every investor hears about. Whether it shelters anything this year depends on the passive activity rules.

blocks.q: Nina and Omar's modified adjusted gross income for 2027 is $210,000. What happens to the $18,581 rental loss?
c: It offsets their wages in full, since rental losses are deductible
Up to $25,000 offsets wages, since they actively manage the unit
It is suspended and carried forward against passive income
It is lost permanently, like a loss on selling a personal home
blocks.x: Rental income is passive. Active participants may use up to $25,000 of rental losses against other income, but that allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified AGI, so at $210,000 it is gone. The loss is suspended, carried forward against future passive income, and released when they sell the building in a taxable sale. The $25,000 answer is the trap: it states the allowance and skips the phase-out.

blocks.html: The deduction side of the return is better news. Their 2027 New York State and City income tax withheld is $17,400, and the property tax bill on the building is $11,200 for the year.

blocks.q: Which amount goes into Nina and Omar's 2027 state and local tax (SALT) deduction?
c: $28,600: the income tax plus the full $11,200 property tax
$23,000: the income tax plus the first floor's property tax
$17,400: the income tax, since a two-family's tax is a rental cost
$10,000: the SALT cap for a married couple filing jointly
blocks.x: The SALT deduction covers income taxes and the property tax on their home: $17,400 plus $5,600 = $23,000, well under the cap (about $40,800 for 2027). The other $5,600 is a rental expense on Schedule E, outside the cap. The $28,600 answer pushes the rental half under the cap and wastes room. $10,000 is the cap from 2018 through 2024. With $33,880 of home mortgage interest, their itemized deductions top $56,000, and they itemize.

blocks.title: Split by use, not by benefit
blocks.html: Owners of two-families are tempted to move deductions to whichever side helps more in a given year: points to the rental side when they take the standard deduction, property tax to the home side when the rental loss is suspended anyway. The allocation follows the use of each part of the building, one consistent method every year. A split that changes with the tax result is the first thing an examiner asks about.

In May 2027, before the kitchen upstairs gave out, Nina and Omar opened a $100,000 home equity line on the building. They spent $70,000 renovating their own kitchen and bathrooms and $30,000 paying off Omar's car loan and the credit card that had carried some moving costs.

blocks.q: How much of the home equity line's interest is deductible as home mortgage interest?
c: The share on the $70,000 spent improving their own apartment
The share on the full $100,000, since it is secured by their home
Zero, because home equity interest stopped being deductible in 2018
The share on $100,000, within the old $100,000 equity debt limit
blocks.x: Interest on home equity debt is deductible only to the extent the money buys, builds or substantially improves the home that secures it, and that debt counts toward the $750,000 limit. The $70,000 renovation of their floor qualifies, bringing their home acquisition debt to about $615,000. The car loan and credit card share is personal interest. The $100,000 limit is the pre-2018 rule. The renovation also adds $70,000 to the basis of the home half, though it is never depreciated.

blocks.text: The refinance and the payoff letter

blocks.html: By August 2028 rates have fallen. Tasha Monroe, the couple's mortgage broker, finds them a 30-year loan at 5.875% from a different bank for the old balance, with 1 point ($10,810). The old lender's payoff letter arrives with a line nobody expected.

blocks.title: Payoff letter, good through August 20, 2028
blocks.html:
Principal balance: $1,081,065
Interest, August 1 to 20: $3,799
Prepayment charge (2% of balance, note paragraph 5): $21,621
Total to pay off: $1,106,485

blocks.q: The loan is about 20 months old, carries 6.75% interest and is secured by their owner-occupied two-family. What should Priya do about the $21,621 charge?
c: Pay it, since the note expressly provides for a 2% charge
Pay it and deduct it, since the charge counts as mortgage interest
Dispute it, since a 2019 law banned prepayment charges on every loan
Dispute it; New York bars the charge after the loan's first year
blocks.x: General Obligations Law 5-501 lets a borrower on a loan above 6% secured by an owner-occupied 1 to 6 family residence prepay at any time, and bars a prepayment penalty once the loan is a year old. The pay-and-deduct answer is the trap because it states the tax rule correctly: a valid penalty on a home mortgage is generally deductible as mortgage interest. But the charge has to be owed first. No 2019 law banned prepayment charges across the board.

blocks.html: Priya's letter cites the statute, and the old lender reissues the payoff without the charge. Then Ruth has two sets of points to sort out: the new $10,810, and what is left of the rental half of the 2026 points.

blocks.q: How are the $10,810 of points on the refinance handled?
c: Deducted in full in 2028, the year they are paid to the new bank
Deducted over the new loan's 30 years, split between the two floors
Added to the basis of the building, since they replace earlier points
Deducted half in 2028 and half over the life of the new loan
blocks.x: Points paid to refinance a home are deducted over the life of the new loan, not in the year paid, unless part of the new money is used to improve the home. Here that is about $360 a year, half as home mortgage interest and half as a rental expense. The half-now answer copies the 2026 purchase split, which worked only because points on a loan to buy a main home can qualify for a current deduction. A refinance is not a purchase.

blocks.q: About $5,180 of the 2026 rental-half points has not yet been amortized. What happens to it in 2028?
c: It is deducted on Schedule E in 2028, when the old loan ends
It is added to the new loan's points and spread over 30 years
It is lost, because a refinance resets the points on both floors
It moves to the home half and is deducted under the itemized rules
blocks.x: When a loan whose points are being spread out is paid off, the remaining balance is deducted in the year the loan ends. $5,500 less about 21 months of amortization leaves about $5,180, deducted on the 2028 Schedule E. Rolling the balance into the new loan is the exception: it applies when the refinance is with the same lender. Tasha's new loan is from a different bank, so the balance comes off now.

blocks.html: Omar's sister Leila, a pharmacist who rents in Astoria, bought a wooded lot near Saugerties in Ulster County for $90,000 cash in 2026. In April 2027 she closes a $420,000 construction loan, and the builder breaks ground the same month. The house is finished in November 2028, and Leila plans to use it as her second home on weekends and holidays. At Nina's birthday dinner she asks Jordan whether the interest she pays while the house is going up is deductible.

blocks.q: Is the interest Leila pays on the construction loan during 2027 and 2028 deductible as home mortgage interest?
c: No, not until the town issues a certificate of occupancy
Yes, but as a business expense of building the house
No, because the cabin will be a second home, not her main home
Yes, a home being built can qualify for up to 24 months
blocks.x: A home under construction can be treated as a qualified home for up to 24 months starting when construction begins, if it becomes a qualified home when it is ready for occupancy. Leila's 19 months fit, and a second home qualifies, so the interest is home mortgage interest within the $750,000 limit. The second-home answer is the trap: the rules cover a main home and one second home. A certificate of occupancy is a building code event, not a tax test.

blocks.html: In July 2029 Leila rents the cabin to friends of friends for 12 nights at $450 a night, $5,400 in all, and spends the rest of the summer there herself.

blocks.q: How does Leila report the $5,400 of rent?
c: As rental income, less a share of expenses for the 12 nights
As passive income, offset by her other rental activity losses
She does not report it, since she rented the cabin for under 15 days
As ordinary business income, since short-term rentals are a trade
blocks.x: When a dwelling the owner uses as a home is rented for fewer than 15 days in the year, the rent is not reported and no rental expenses are deducted. Her mortgage interest and property tax remain deductible as for any second home. The expense-share answer is the rule for longer rentals: at 15 days or more, rent is reported and expenses are divided between rental and personal days.

items: The IRA first-time homebuyer exception looks back 2 years from the contract date, applies to both spouses, allows $10,000 per person, and waives only the 10% penalty, not the income tax.

In an owner-occupied two-family, interest, points and property tax split by use: the home share follows the itemized rules and the $750,000 and SALT limits; the rental share is a Schedule E expense outside them.

Purchase points on a main home can be deducted when paid or spread over the loan; rental points and refinance points are spread over the loan, and the balance comes off when a loan ends, unless the same lender refinances it.
Acquisition costs such as the mansion tax and title insurance go into basis; depreciate only the rental share of the building, over 27.5 years, and capitalize rental improvements.

Above $150,000 of modified AGI, rental losses are suspended, not lost; home equity interest counts only when the money improves the home; New York bars prepayment penalties after the first year on owner-occupied 1 to 6 family loans above 6%.
A home under construction can qualify for up to 24 months, and a home rented for fewer than 15 days a year produces no reportable rent.

roleplays.title: Evelyn's Exchange
roleplays.setting: Flushing. Evelyn Park just closed the sale of her Main Street retail building and wants a 1031 exchange.
roleplays.you: Jordan, the buyer's agent helping Evelyn find replacement property
roleplays.goal: Help Evelyn stay inside the 1031 rules (QI, 45/180 days, boot) without giving tax advice you are not qualified to give.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Evelyn Park, a confident commercial investor in Flushing who thinks in cap rates and hates paperwork. You just sold a retail building for $3.2 million and want a 1031 exchange, but you try to take the check yourself, propose the agent's firm or a relative hold the money, plan to identify late because of a weekend, want to identify ten properties, want to keep $300,000 in cash and take a smaller mortgage, consider a condo to live in, and believe a 1031 means no tax ever. The learner must catch constructive receipt and route funds to a qualified intermediary, name disqualified persons, state 45 days to identify and 180 to close (calendar days), explain identification limits, identify cash and debt relief as taxable boot, exclude personal residences, explain deferral not forgiveness, and refer specific tax advice to a CPA. Grade each item at the end.

spot: a tea house on Prince Street

opening: {day}, {spot}. Evelyn closed this morning on her Main Street building: $3.2 million. She's already shopping for the next one.
Evelyn waves you over at {spot}. "Sold. $3.2 million. {titleco} is cutting the check. Now find me something better."
Evelyn wants a 1031 exchange out of her $3.2 million sale. You meet at {spot}, and she has a plan. Most of it breaks the rules.

say: Closed this morning, $3.2 million. {titleco} is cutting me a check. I'll park it in my money market while we shop. Fine, right?
I'll take the sale proceeds into my own account for now. We'll buy the next one within a few months.

moves.text: Stop the check. The proceeds go straight to a qualified intermediary, or the whole exchange can fail.
moves.fb: Correct. Actual or constructive receipt of the proceeds disqualifies the exchange. A QI must hold the funds.
moves.react: Stop it? Okay, I'm calling {titleco} now.

moves.text: Don't touch that money. If it lands in your account, it's taxable. Have {titleco} wire it to a QI.
moves.fb: Right. Receiving the funds, even briefly, is constructive receipt.
moves.react: Even for a day? Fine, QI.

moves.text: I think that's okay, but check with your accountant before you deposit anything, just to be safe.
moves.fb: Referring her is good, but you knew enough to flag the biggest risk. Say it clearly.

moves.text: Sure, as long as you reinvest it within 180 days. That's the only real rule you need to watch.
moves.fb: Taking the proceeds yourself is constructive receipt, and the gain becomes taxable.

moves.text: Fine, just keep it in a separate account in your name so it's clearly earmarked for the exchange.
moves.fb: A separate account in her name is still receipt. The QI must hold the funds.

moves.text: Take the check, but don't cash it until you buy. An uncashed check doesn't count as receiving the money yet.
moves.fb: Holding the check is receipt. The proceeds must go to a QI from closing.

say: My accountant is on vacation until next week. Can the money sit with your firm in escrow?
Just hold it in Hudson and Hart's escrow account until I pick a property. Simple.

moves.text: No. Our firm can't be your intermediary. Have {titleco} send the funds to a QI today.
moves.fb: Right. Your own broker within the past 2 years is a disqualified person, and the funds must go to a QI.

moves.text: We're your agent, so we're disqualified. It needs an independent QI. I can give you three names.
moves.fb: Correct. Agents, attorneys and accountants who served her in the past 2 years can't act as QI.

moves.text: Let me ask Diane. If she says yes, we could hold it a few days until your accountant is back.
moves.fb: Diane can't make the firm a QI. Agents are disqualified persons.

moves.text: Sure, we have an escrow account. Exchange funds go there all the time for our investor clients here.
moves.fb: Your agent's firm is a disqualified person, and holding exchange funds creates an escrow problem too.

moves.text: We can hold it if you sign a form appointing us as your qualified intermediary for the deal.
moves.fb: A disqualified person can't become a QI by signing a form.

moves.text: Your accountant can hold it when he's back. Accountants are the usual QIs for 1031 exchanges.
moves.fb: Her own accountant within the past 2 years is a disqualified person.

say: Fine, QI it is. I like three properties: a Bayside strip center, a Jamaica warehouse, and my daughter's condo, which I'd rent to her cheap. When do I have to decide?
Deadlines? I'm looking at a strip center, a warehouse, and a condo to rent cheap to my daughter.

moves.text: Identify in writing within 45 days, close within 180. A cheap family rental may not count. Ask your CPA.
moves.fb: Accurate deadlines, and you flagged the investment-use issue without giving a legal opinion.
moves.react: 45 and 180. And I'll ask about the condo.

moves.text: 45 days to name them in writing, 180 to close, from today. The family condo is a CPA question.
moves.fb: Correct. The periods run concurrently from the sale, and the family rental needs tax advice.

moves.text: 45 days to identify. Any of the three is fine, so just pick whichever one cash flows best for you.
moves.fb: The deadline is right, but you vouched for a questionable property. Leave that to her tax advisor.

moves.text: You have 180 days to identify, then another 45 to close. Plenty of time to shop around for a deal.
moves.fb: Backwards. 45 days to identify, 180 total to close, and they run concurrently.

moves.text: 45 days to identify and then 180 more days to close, so about seven and a half months total, start to end.
moves.fb: The 180 days run from the sale, not after the 45. Total is 180.

moves.text: There's no deadline as long as the QI holds the money. The QI just waits until you decide something.
moves.fb: The 45 and 180 day limits are strict.

say: Day 45 is a Sunday. I'll just email the QI Monday. They'll understand.
The 45th day lands on a Sunday. Monday's fine, right?

moves.text: The 45 days are calendar days, with no weekend extension. Send it in by Saturday at the latest.
moves.fb: Correct. Day 45 is a hard deadline.

moves.text: No rollover. Day 45 is day 45. Let's get your written identification to the QI Friday.
moves.fb: Right. There's no business-day extension.

moves.text: Probably fine, but I'd send it Friday just in case. I'm unsure how strict they are about it.
moves.fb: Right action, wrong reason. It's not 'probably fine'; it's a hard deadline.

moves.text: Monday should be fine, it's the next business day. The IRS rolls deadlines over to Monday.
moves.fb: There's no business-day rollover for 1031 identification. Missing day 45 ends the exchange.

moves.text: Call the QI Sunday and tell them verbally. A phone call counts if you follow up in writing.
moves.fb: Identification must be in writing, signed and delivered by day 45.

moves.text: Ask the QI for a two-week extension. They grant those for weekends and holidays.
moves.fb: The QI can't extend statutory deadlines.

say: The warehouse is $2.9 million. I'll keep the other $300,000 for my roof. And since it's all deferred, I'll pay no tax at all on this, right?
I'll pocket $300,000 and roll the rest. That's still tax-free, yes?

moves.text: Cash you keep is boot, generally taxable. The gain is deferred, not forgiven. Your CPA runs numbers.
moves.fb: Exactly. Boot is taxable up to the realized gain; deferral carries the low basis into the new property.

moves.text: The $300,000 is boot, taxed up to your gain. The rest is deferred; your basis carries over.
moves.fb: Right. Boot is taxable; deferral moves the basis to the replacement property.
moves.react: So the tax waits for me.

moves.text: That's a tax question, so I really can't say anything about it. You'd have to ask your accountant.
moves.fb: Caution is good, but explaining the general boot rule is fine and helpful.

moves.text: Right, a 1031 means no tax ever. You can keep the cash and pay nothing on any of it, legally.
moves.fb: Wrong on both counts: the $300,000 is boot, and a 1031 defers rather than eliminates tax.

moves.text: Cash is fine up to 10% of the sale price. Above that it becomes taxable, so you're just under the line.
moves.fb: There's no 10% safe harbor. Cash received is boot.

moves.text: Spend the $300,000 on the roof of the new building and it's not boot, since it's an improvement.
moves.fb: Cash taken out is boot when received. Improvements after closing don't undo it.

say: My {relative} is an attorney and can hold the money. Family is safer than strangers.
Can my {relative} act as the QI? I trust family.

moves.text: Relatives are disqualified persons under the rules. It must be an independent QI firm.
moves.fb: Correct. Related persons, plus her agent, attorney or accountant within 2 years, can't be the QI.

moves.text: Relatives can't serve as your QI under the 1031 rules. Let's use an independent firm instead.
moves.fb: Right. Disqualified persons include family members.

moves.text: Maybe, if they've never done legal work for you. Ask your CPA whether that would be okay.
moves.fb: Family members are disqualified regardless of past work.

moves.text: Sure, an attorney is the best choice for your QI. They're licensed and hold escrows all the time.
moves.fb: A relative is a disqualified person, and so is her own attorney within 2 years.

moves.text: Yes, as long as the money sits in an attorney escrow account and not in a personal account.
moves.fb: The type of account doesn't matter. A relative is a disqualified person.

moves.text: Fine, but have them sign a confidentiality agreement first. That makes them independent.
moves.fb: A contract doesn't change disqualified status.

say: I want to identify ten properties, to keep my options open.
Let's list a dozen properties on the identification. More choices, less risk.

moves.text: You can name three of any value, or more under the 200% rule. Ten likely won't work here.
moves.fb: Correct. The three-property rule or the 200% rule limits identification.

moves.text: There are limits: three properties max, or more if their total stays within 200% of what you sold.
moves.fb: Right. Identification rules cap the list.

moves.text: Sure, list as many as you want. The QI will tell you later if there's a problem with the list.
moves.fb: The limits are real. Explain them up front.

moves.text: No limit at all. Name every property you're looking at so you never miss the 45-day deadline.
moves.fb: Identification is limited by the three-property or 200% rules.

moves.text: You can only identify one property. If that deal fails, the whole exchange fails right along with it.
moves.fb: Too strict. Up to three properties of any value are allowed.

moves.text: Ten is fine if you close on all ten. You must buy every single property you identify.
moves.fb: You don't have to buy them all; identification just limits what qualifies.

say: What if I buy a condo for myself to live in as the replacement? Same price range.
Could the replacement be my own home? I'm ready to downsize.

moves.text: A personal residence isn't investment property, so it won't qualify. Your CPA can explain options.
moves.fb: Correct. 1031 requires property held for investment or business use.

moves.text: Your home doesn't count. The replacement has to be held for investment or business use.
moves.fb: Right. Personal residences don't qualify.

moves.text: Maybe, if you rent it out for a little while first. Ask your accountant how long that takes.
moves.fb: This is a CPA question, and moving in defeats investment intent.

moves.text: Sure. All real estate is like-kind in New York, homes included. It works exactly the same way.
moves.fb: Personal residences are excluded from 1031.

moves.text: Yes, and you'd also get the $250,000 home sale exclusion on top of the deferral, so it's even better.
moves.fb: The 121 exclusion is for a sale of your own home, not this exchange.

moves.text: Only if it's in New York. Out-of-state homes don't qualify, but in-state homes do for exchanges.
moves.fb: Personal use disqualifies it anywhere.

say: My old mortgage was $1.2 million. The new loan is only $800,000. Problem?
I'm taking a smaller mortgage on the new building. Does that matter?

moves.text: Debt relief is boot too. A smaller loan may trigger tax unless you add cash. Ask your CPA.
moves.fb: Correct. Boot includes debt relief as well as cash; adding cash can offset it.

moves.text: Paying off more debt than you take on counts as boot too. You can offset it by adding new cash.
moves.fb: Right. Mortgage relief is boot unless replaced with debt or cash.
moves.react: Good to know. Calling my CPA.

moves.text: Probably fine. Lots of investors take smaller loans. Your CPA can tell you for sure, though.
moves.fb: It may not be fine: debt relief is boot.

moves.text: No problem. Only cash counts as boot. Mortgage changes don't matter at all in an exchange.
moves.fb: Debt relief is boot too.

moves.text: A smaller loan is good. It lowers your boot, since less debt means less tax overall for you.
moves.fb: Backwards. Reducing debt creates boot.

moves.text: Debt only matters if the new loan is bigger. Then you owe tax on extra borrowing you took.
moves.fb: Taking on more debt doesn't create boot; relief of debt does.

roleplays.debrief: You practised 1031 basics: proceeds go to a qualified intermediary, never to the investor, her agent, attorney, accountant or family. Identify in writing within 45 calendar days and close within 180, with three-property or 200% limits, and only investment or business property qualifies. Cash and debt relief are boot, taxable up to the gain, and the gain is deferred, not forgiven. Explain the general rules and refer the numbers to a CPA.

questions.q: An investor sells for $600,000 (amount realized) a property with an adjusted basis of $420,000. The capital gain is:
questions.x: Gain = amount realized minus adjusted basis = $180,000. $1,020,000 is the trap: adding.

questions.q: Capital gain is calculated as:
c: Sale price minus mortgage balance
Appraised value minus assessed value
Amount realized minus adjusted basis
Rent minus expenses
questions.x: That is the definition. 'Minus mortgage balance' is the trap: that gives equity, not gain.

questions.q: An increase in a property's value over time is:
c: Depreciation
Appreciation
Amortization
Accretion
questions.x: Appreciation is a rise in value. Accretion is the trap: it is land added by water.

questions.q: A home bought for $500,000 is worth $560,000 three years later. The $60,000 increase is:
c: Equity buildup from amortization
Depreciation recapture
A capital loss
Appreciation
questions.x: A rise in market value is appreciation. Amortization is the trap: that is equity from paying down the loan.

questions.q: A residential rental building is depreciated for federal tax purposes over:
c: 39 years
15 years
27.5 years
30 years
questions.x: Residential rental property uses 27.5 years. 39 years is the trap: that is for nonresidential property.

questions.q: Tax depreciation on a rental building is allowed:
c: Even if the building's market value rises
Only if its value actually falls
Only on the land
Only after a sale
questions.x: Tax depreciation recovers cost on a schedule regardless of market value. 'Only on the land' is the trap: land is never depreciable.

questions.q: An investor pays $800,000 for a rental property; the land is worth $200,000. The depreciable basis is:
questions.x: Only the building is depreciable: $800,000 minus $200,000 land = $600,000. $800,000 is the trap: land cannot be depreciated.

questions.q: Why is land excluded from depreciable basis?
c: Land is taxed separately
Land does not wear out
Land is personal property
Land is always leased
questions.x: Depreciation recovers the cost of assets that wear out; land does not. 'Taxed separately' is the trap.

questions.q: In real estate, the main source of a tax shelter is:
c: Depreciation deductions
Higher rents
Larger down payments
Rising property taxes
questions.x: Depreciation creates deductions without cash outlay, sheltering income. Higher rents are the trap: they increase taxable income.

questions.q: A rental shows positive cash flow but a taxable loss. The likely reason is:
c: A rent increase
Paying off the mortgage
Depreciation
A lower cap rate
questions.x: Depreciation is a paper expense that can turn cash income into a tax loss. Paying off the mortgage is the trap.

questions.q: An investor sells a rental building and reinvests in another investment property to postpone tax on the gain. This is a:
c: Section 121 exclusion
1031 like-kind exchange
Installment sale
Tax-free gift
questions.x: A 1031 exchange defers gain on investment or business real property. Section 121 is the trap: that excludes gain on a principal residence.

questions.q: A 1031 exchange can be used for:
c: A primary residence
Stocks and bonds
A vacation home used only personally
Investment or business real property
questions.x: Like-kind exchanges cover real property held for investment or business. Primary residence is the trap: it uses Section 121 instead.

questions.q: The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 replaced the rollover rule and the over-55 exclusion with:
c: A $250,000/$500,000 home sale exclusion
A flat 10% federal tax on every home sale gain
A rule to buy a pricier home within 2 years
Full deductibility of losses on a residence
questions.x: TRA 1997 created the IRC 121 exclusion, usable every 2 years at any age. The buy-a-pricier-home answer is the trap: that was the old rollover rule it replaced.

questions.q: A first-time homebuyer may withdraw from an IRA without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty up to a lifetime maximum of:
questions.x: The first-time homebuyer exception is $10,000 per person, lifetime; income tax may still apply to traditional IRA withdrawals. $25,000 is the trap: it is the passive loss allowance for active landlords.

questions.q: For a mortgage taken out in 2026, interest is deductible on acquisition debt of up to:
questions.x: The $750,000 limit applies to loans after December 15, 2017 and was made permanent in 2025. $1,000,000 is the trap: it applies only to older, grandfathered loans.

questions.q: Leo uses a $60,000 home equity loan on his condo to build a new kitchen. The interest is:
c: Not deductible, as home equity interest
Deductible, since the loan improved the home
Deductible if the loan is under $50,000
Deductible by the lender, not by Leo
questions.x: Home equity interest is deductible when the money buys, builds, or substantially improves the home that secures the loan. The not-deductible answer is the trap: that is true only when proceeds go to other uses, such as a car.

questions.q: Points paid to obtain a mortgage to purchase a principal residence are generally:
c: Deductible in the year it is paid
Not deductible as a personal cost
Deductible over the loan term
Added to the seller's basis
questions.x: Purchase points on a main home are generally deductible in the year paid. Spreading over the loan term is the trap: that rule applies to refinance points.

questions.q: A homeowner refinances with a $400,000 30-year loan and pays 2 points. How much of the points can be deducted each year?
c: $8,000, in year one
questions.x: 2% x $400,000 = $8,000, spread over 30 years = $266.67 a year. Deducting $8,000 at once is the trap: that treatment is for purchase points, not refinance points.

questions.q: A prepayment penalty paid on a home mortgage is treated as:
c: A nondeductible personal expense
A capital improvement to the home
A selling expense of the lender
Deductible as home mortgage interest
questions.x: The IRS treats a mortgage prepayment penalty as interest, deductible in the year paid for those who itemize. The personal-expense answer is the trap: it sounds like a fee, but it is treated as interest.

questions.q: All of the following increase a homeowner's adjusted basis EXCEPT:
c: A new roof
A rear extension
Repainting a room
Owner's title insurance
questions.x: Repairs and maintenance, such as painting, do not add to basis. Title insurance is the tempting pick, but buying costs paid at purchase are added to basis.

questions.q: A couple bought a home for $400,000, paid $8,000 in closing costs, and added a $72,000 addition. What is their adjusted basis?
questions.x: $400,000 + $8,000 + $72,000 = $480,000. $472,000 is the trap: it leaves out the closing costs.

questions.q: A single seller sells her principal residence of 6 years for $900,000 and pays $54,000 in selling costs. Her adjusted basis is $510,000. What is her taxable gain?
questions.x: Amount realized is $846,000; minus $510,000 basis = $336,000 gain; minus the $250,000 exclusion = $86,000. $140,000 is the trap: it ignores the selling costs.

questions.q: To use the home sale exclusion, a taxpayer must have owned and used the home as a principal residence for at least:
c: 1 of the last 3 years
2 of the last 5 years
3 of the last 10 years
5 consecutive years
questions.x: The ownership and use tests are each 2 of the 5 years before the sale, and the years need not be continuous. 5 consecutive years is the trap: no continuity is required.

questions.q: Emmanuel owns a house in his name alone. He and Grace, married filing jointly, both lived there 4 years. Neither has used the exclusion before. How much gain may they exclude?
c: $250,000, since Emmanuel alone holds title
$750,000 as joint filers
$500,000; both meet the use test
questions.x: For $500,000, one spouse must meet the ownership test, both must meet the use test, and neither may have used the exclusion in the prior 2 years. The title answer is the trap: ownership by one spouse is enough.

questions.q: A gain on property held for 10 months is a:
c: Short-term gain, taxed at ordinary income rates
Long-term gain taxed at 0, 15, or 20%
Recapture gain taxed at up to 25%
Gain exempt from federal income tax
questions.x: Property held one year or less produces short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income. Long-term is the trap: it requires holding more than one year.

questions.q: A homeowner sells his principal residence at a $40,000 loss. The loss is:
c: Deductible against wages, $3,000 a year
Deductible in full in the year of sale
Not deductible
Carried forward to the next home
questions.x: Losses on personal-use property, including a main home, are not deductible. The $3,000 answer is the trap: that rule applies to investment capital losses.

questions.q: A Nassau County couple pays $18,000 in property tax and $16,000 in state income tax in 2026 and itemizes, with income well under $500,000. Under current federal law, how much state and local tax can they deduct?
c: $10,000, the cap set in 2017
$34,000, as it falls within the 2026 cap
$18,000, the property tax portion
$40,400, the full 2026 cap amount
questions.x: The SALT cap is $40,400 for 2026 for incomes below the phase-down threshold, so the full $34,000 is deductible. $10,000 is the trap: it was the 2018-2024 cap and is scheduled to return in 2030.

questions.q: Income from a rental apartment building is generally classified as:
c: Passive income
Active income
Portfolio income
Earned income
questions.x: Rental activity is generally passive. Portfolio income is the trap: it covers interest, dividends, and securities gains.

questions.q: A landlord who actively participates may deduct up to $25,000 of rental losses against other income. This allowance phases out completely at modified adjusted gross income of:
c: $250,000 for joint filers
questions.x: The allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of MAGI, so it is gone at $150,000. $100,000 is the trap: that is where the phase-out begins.

questions.q: Residential rental property is depreciated over:
c: 39 years
31.5 years
40 years (ADS)
27.5 years
questions.x: Residential rental real estate uses 27.5 years. 39 years is the trap: it is the period for nonresidential property (31.5 was the older nonresidential period).

questions.q: An investor buys a 4-unit building in Utica for $280,000. The land is worth $60,000. Annual straight-line depreciation is:
questions.x: ($280,000 - $60,000) / 27.5 = $220,000 / 27.5 = $8,000. $10,182 is the trap: it forgets to remove the land, which is never depreciated.

questions.q: All of the following are tax-deductible expenses for the owner of a rental building EXCEPT:
c: Mortgage interest
Depreciation
Loan principal
Property taxes
questions.x: Repaying principal is not an expense, so it is not deductible. Depreciation is the tempting pick because no cash is spent, but it is a deductible expense.

questions.q: A building has NOI of $90,000, annual debt service of $50,000 (of which $35,000 is interest), and depreciation of $20,000. What are taxable income and before-tax cash flow?
c: $20,000 taxable; $40,000 cash flow
$35,000 taxable; $40,000 cash flow
$40,000 taxable; $20,000 cash flow
$35,000 taxable; $55,000 before-tax cash flow
questions.x: Taxable income: $90,000 - $35,000 interest - $20,000 depreciation = $35,000. Cash flow: $90,000 - $50,000 debt service = $40,000. $20,000 taxable is the trap: it subtracts all debt service, including principal.

questions.q: The maximum federal rate on unrecaptured depreciation (Section 1250 gain) from selling real estate is:
questions.x: Gain from depreciation taken on real property is taxed at up to 25%. 20% is the trap: it is the top long-term capital gain rate for the rest of the gain.

questions.concept: Gain on sale of investment property
questions.q: An investor bought a building for $600,000 and took $180,000 of depreciation. She sells for $950,000 with $50,000 of selling costs. What is her total gain?
questions.x: Adjusted basis = $600,000 - $180,000 = $420,000; amount realized = $900,000; gain = $480,000, of which $180,000 is depreciation recapture. $300,000 is the trap: it ignores the depreciation.

questions.q: In a 1031 exchange, replacement property must be identified within:
c: 45 days
30 days
90 days
180 days
questions.x: Replacement property is identified within 45 calendar days of the sale closing. 180 days is the trap: that is the deadline to close on the replacement (or the return due date, if earlier).

questions.q: All of the following can qualify for a 1031 exchange EXCEPT:
c: A 35-year commercial ground lease
Vacant land held for investment
A motel held for business
The owner's principal residence
questions.x: A principal residence is personal use, not held for investment or business. The ground lease is the tempting pick, but leaseholds of 30 or more years count as real property.

questions.q: In a 1031 exchange with a realized gain of $400,000, Sal receives $60,000 in cash at closing. How much gain is recognized?
questions.x: Recognized gain is the lesser of boot received or realized gain: $60,000, with $340,000 deferred. $340,000 is the trap: that is the deferred portion.

questions.q: Which party may serve as qualified intermediary in a 1031 exchange?
c: The investor's broker on the sale
An independent exchange company with no ties
The investor's longtime accountant
The investor's spouse or sibling
questions.x: Anyone who acted as the taxpayer's agent within the past 2 years (attorney, broker, accountant) and close relatives are disqualified; an independent accommodator qualifies. The accountant is the trap: familiarity is exactly what disqualifies.

questions.q: An investor closes the sale of a rental on October 20, 2026 and does not extend her 2026 tax return. Day 180 falls on April 18, 2027. Her deadline to close on the replacement is:
c: April 18, 2027
December 31, 2026
April 15, 2027
October 20, 2027
questions.x: The deadline is the earlier of 180 days or the return due date (with extensions); without an extension, April 15, 2027 comes first. April 18 is the trap: the 180-day count is cut short by the return due date.

questions.q: In a reverse 1031 exchange, the investor:
c: Sells first and buys later
Exchanges with a relative
Trades a residence for a rental
Buys the replacement first
questions.x: A reverse exchange acquires the replacement before selling the relinquished property; an exchange accommodation titleholder parks title, with the same 45/180-day limits. Sells-first is the trap: that is a standard delayed exchange.

questions.q: The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit encourages construction of affordable rentals by:
c: Credits for owners of rent-limited units
Exempting low-income tenants from income tax
Waiving NYS transfer taxes on the project
Guaranteeing the developer's construction loan
questions.x: LIHTC (IRC 42) gives owners and investors dollar-for-dollar federal tax credits, allocated in NY by HCR, in return for long-term income and rent limits. The loan guarantee answer is the trap: that describes FHA or state finance programs, not a tax credit.

questions.q: A seller asks his agent exactly how much capital gains tax he will owe on the sale. The agent should:
c: Calculate the exact tax and put it in writing for him
Tell him the exclusion makes the sale tax-free
Decline to discuss taxes at all
Explain the rules and refer him to his accountant
questions.x: Licensees may explain general rules but should send specific tax advice to an accountant or tax attorney. Calculating his exact tax invites liability; refusing to discuss taxes at all is unhelpful.

questions.q: The main risk to a licensee who gives specific tax advice beyond her expertise is:
c: Losing the right to collect a commission
An automatic audit of the client's return
Liability if the advice turns out wrong
Voiding the sale contract at closing
questions.x: Giving tax advice you are not qualified to give exposes you to liability. It does not void the contract or trigger an audit.

questions.q: A homeowner with a small mortgage takes the standard deduction. Her mortgage interest and property taxes:
c: Are still subtracted from her income
Become a tax credit instead
Give her no extra tax benefit
Carry forward to the year she sells
questions.x: Mortgage interest and property taxes help only taxpayers who itemize. A homeowner who takes the standard deduction gets nothing extra from them, and they do not carry forward.

questions.q: To deduct home mortgage interest, a taxpayer generally must:
c: Itemize deductions
Have owned the home for 2 years
Have income below $500,000
Pay the loan through escrow
questions.x: Mortgage interest is an itemized deduction. The 2-year rule belongs to the home sale exclusion, and $500,000 is where the SALT cap begins to shrink.

questions.q: An owner with a $300,000 acquisition loan refinances into a $400,000 loan and spends the extra $100,000 on a car and tuition. Interest is deductible on:
c: The full $400,000 balance
Only the extra $100,000
None of the new loan's interest
Up to $300,000 of the new loan
questions.x: After a refinance, interest is deductible up to the old acquisition debt paid off. Cash-out counts only if used to improve the home, so the car and tuition money does not.

questions.q: A construction loan for a new main home can be treated as acquisition debt for up to:
c: 12 months
24 months
45 days
Until the loan is refinanced
questions.x: A construction loan can count as acquisition debt for up to 24 months while the home is built. 45 days is the 1031 identification window, a different rule.

questions.q: A buyer pays title insurance, recording fees and attorney fees at closing. For federal tax purposes these costs are generally:
c: Deducted in full that year
Added to the home's basis
Deducted over 30 years
Not counted for any purpose
questions.x: Most purchase closing costs are not deductible; they are added to basis, lowering gain on a later sale. Only points and prorated property taxes are deductible at purchase.

questions.q: A seller pays a broker commission and the NYS transfer tax. For figuring her gain, these costs:
c: Are deductible against her wages
Are added to the buyer's basis
Reduce her amount realized
Are ignored as personal expenses
questions.x: Selling costs such as commission, NYS transfer tax and attorney fees reduce the amount realized, which lowers gain. They are not deductions against other income.

questions.q: A single owner must move for a new job after 1 year in her home. Regarding the home sale exclusion, she:
c: Gets the full $250,000 exclusion anyway
Gets no exclusion of any kind
May qualify for a partial exclusion
Must buy a pricier home within 2 years
questions.x: A move forced early by a job change, health or unforeseen circumstances may allow a partial exclusion. Buying a pricier home to defer gain is the old rollover rule, repealed in 1997.

questions.q: An owner claimed $20,000 of depreciation for a home office and later sells with a gain under $250,000. The $20,000:
c: Is excluded with the rest
Is recaptured and taxable
Reduces the exclusion to $230,000
Is refunded to the owner
questions.x: Depreciation taken on a home (for an office or rented unit) is recaptured and not covered by the exclusion. The rest of the gain can still be excluded.

questions.q: A family rents its Catskills vacation house to others for 12 days a year. That rental income is:
c: Fully taxable as ordinary income
Tax-free
Passive income subject to depreciation
Taxed as a long-term capital gain
questions.x: Renting a vacation home fewer than 15 days a year is tax-free. More than that, and it starts to be treated partly as rental property.

questions.q: A couple sells a beach house they used only in summers for 10 years. The $250,000/$500,000 exclusion:
c: Applies, since they owned it 2 of 5 years
Applies at half the usual amount
Applies if they buy another beach house
Applies only if it was their main home
questions.x: The exclusion covers a principal residence. A second home qualifies only if it becomes the main home for 2 of 5 years; ownership alone is not enough.

questions.q: Dividends from stocks and interest on bonds are classified as:
c: Active income
Passive income
Portfolio income
Ordinary rental income
questions.x: Interest, dividends and securities gains are portfolio income, treated separately from passive income. Rentals are passive; wages and businesses you run are active.

questions.q: A salesperson's commission income is classified as:
c: Capital gain income
Passive income
Portfolio income
Active income
questions.x: Wages and commissions, like a business you materially run, are active income, and losses against it can offset any income.

questions.q: A rental building rose in market value this year. For tax purposes, its owner:
c: May keep deducting depreciation
Must stop taking depreciation
Must pay tax on the appreciation
Can depreciate the land instead
questions.x: Tax depreciation is cost recovery over the IRS life whether or not the building loses value. Appreciation is not taxed until sale, and land is never depreciated.

questions.q: Real estate depreciation for tax purposes uses which method?
c: Double declining balance
Units of production
Market value appraisals
Straight-line
questions.x: Real estate uses straight-line depreciation: equal amounts each year over 27.5 or 39 years. Accelerated methods do not apply to buildings.

questions.q: An investor wants to exchange vacant land in Orange County held for investment. Which replacement qualifies as like-kind?
c: Only other vacant land
A Queens six-family rental
A home she will live in
Shares of a real estate fund
questions.x: Any US real property held for investment or business is like-kind to any other, so land for a six-family works. A home she lives in and securities do not qualify.

questions.q: Whether real property qualifies as like-kind in a 1031 exchange depends mainly on:
c: Whether it is held for investment
Whether both are the same type
Whether both are in the same state
Whether the values are identical
questions.x: What matters is that the property is held for investment or business, not what it looks like or where in the US it is. Same type, same state and equal value are not required.

questions.q: An investor sells a $1,000,000 building with a $600,000 mortgage. To defer all gain, the replacement should generally:
c: Cost $1M or more, with equal or more debt or cash
Cost at least $400,000, the amount of her equity in it
Cost the same, with the cash taken out at closing
Cost less, as long as it is paid for in cash
questions.x: To defer everything, buy equal or greater value, reinvest all net cash and take on equal or greater debt (or add cash to cover less debt). Buying only her equity's worth leaves mortgage boot.

questions.q: In a 1031 exchange, taking on a smaller mortgage on the replacement than was paid off on the old property creates:
c: Like-kind property
Mortgage boot
A reverse exchange
Depreciation recapture
questions.x: Debt relief is boot (mortgage boot) and is taxable up to the realized gain, unless the investor adds cash to make up the difference.

questions.q: A 1031 exchange is reported to the IRS on:
c: Form 1099-S
Form 4562
Schedule A
Form 8824
questions.x: Like-kind exchanges are reported on Form 8824 with the return. Form 1099-S reports sale proceeds, Schedule A holds itemized deductions, and Form 4562 reports depreciation.

questions.q: An investor completes a delayed exchange in 2026. When does she file Form 8824?
c: Within 45 days of the sale
Only if the IRS requests it
Along with her 2026 tax return
Before the qualified intermediary is hired
questions.x: Form 8824 is filed with the return for the year of the exchange. 45 days is the identification deadline, not a filing date.

questions.q: An investor completes a valid 1031 exchange of two NYC buildings. Which tax is still due?
c: Federal capital gains tax
NYS income tax on the gain
The NYC RPTT on the sale
Depreciation recapture
questions.x: A 1031 defers federal and generally NYS income tax, including recapture, but transfer taxes (NYS transfer tax, NYC RPTT, mansion tax) are still due on each sale and purchase.

questions.q: For New York State income tax, a valid federal 1031 exchange is generally:
c: Also treated as tax-deferred
Taxed at the 25% recapture rate
Fully taxed by New York
Exempt from tax permanently
questions.x: New York generally follows federal 1031 treatment, so the gain is deferred for state income tax too. Deferred is not permanently exempt: the low basis carries over.

questions.q: An investor in the 32% bracket has a choice of a $10,000 tax credit or a $10,000 deduction. How much more does the credit save?
c: Nothing
questions.x: A credit saves $10,000 dollar for dollar; a deduction saves $10,000 x 32% = $3,200. The difference is $6,800. Picking $3,200 confuses the deduction's value with the gap.

questions.q: A tax credit, compared with a deduction of the same amount, reduces:
c: The tax owed dollar for dollar
Taxable income only
The property's depreciable basis
The amount realized on a sale
questions.x: A credit cuts the tax itself dollar for dollar; a deduction cuts taxable income, saving only the amount times the bracket. That is why the LIHTC is so valuable to investors.

questions.q: A 40-year-old single owner sells her home of 3 years at a $180,000 gain and buys a cheaper condo. Under IRC 121, the gain is:
c: Taxable, since she bought a cheaper home
Excluded, up to the $250,000 single limit
Taxable, since she is under 55
Deferred into the condo's basis
questions.x: IRC 121 excludes up to $250,000 for a single owner who meets the 2-of-5-year tests, at any age and regardless of the next home's price. The under-55 answer is the trap: that was the pre-1997 one-time exclusion.

questions.q: A married couple, both first-time homebuyers with their own IRAs, each take a penalty-free withdrawal for the down payment. Their combined maximum is:
c: $10,000 total
$5,000 each
questions.x: The $10,000 lifetime limit is per person, so two spouses with their own IRAs can take $20,000. The $10,000-total answer is the trap: the limit is not per household.

questions.q: A buyer takes a $1,200,000 acquisition mortgage in 2026. On how much of the loan balance is interest deductible?
questions.x: For loans after December 15, 2017, interest is deductible on up to $750,000 of acquisition debt. $1,000,000 is the trap: it applies to older loans.

questions.q: Diane takes a $40,000 home equity loan and uses it to pay off credit cards and buy a car. The interest is:
c: Not deductible, given how it was used
Deductible, as home equity debt
Deductible if under $50,000
Deductible as investment interest
questions.x: Home equity interest is deductible only when the money buys, builds, or substantially improves the home securing it. The under-$50,000 answer is the trap: the loan size does not matter, the use does.

questions.q: A buyer pays 1 point on a $500,000 purchase mortgage for her principal residence. Generally she may deduct:
c: $5,000 in the year paid
$5,000 over 30 years
$500 in the year paid
Nothing, since points are fees
questions.x: Points on a loan to buy a main home are generally deductible in full in the year paid: 1% x $500,000 = $5,000. Spreading over 30 years is the trap: that applies to refinance points.

questions.q: A homeowner refinances with a $300,000 15-year loan and pays 1.5 points. The annual deduction for the points is:
c: $4,500 in year one
questions.x: 1.5% x $300,000 = $4,500, spread over 15 years = $300 a year. $4,500 in year one is the trap: immediate deduction is for purchase points.

questions.q: An itemizing homeowner may generally deduct all of the following as home mortgage interest EXCEPT:
c: A prepayment penalty
Interest on acquisition debt
Purchase points
Principal on the loan
questions.x: Principal repays the loan and is not interest. The prepayment penalty is the tempting pick, but the IRS treats it as deductible interest.

questions.q: Over 10 years, Leo replaced his furnace, fixed a leaky faucet, and finished his basement. Which costs increase his basis?
c: The faucet repair alone
The basement alone
Every item listed
Furnace and basement
questions.x: Capital improvements such as a new furnace and a finished basement add to basis; routine repairs like fixing a faucet do not. The every-item answer is the trap: repairs do not increase basis.

questions.q: A home cost $250,000 plus $5,000 in closing costs. The owner added a $15,000 roof and spent $4,000 repainting. The adjusted basis is:
c: $274,000, with the painting
questions.x: $250,000 + $5,000 + $15,000 = $270,000; repainting is maintenance. $274,000 is the trap: it adds the repainting.

questions.q: A married couple filing jointly sells their home of 8 years for $1,250,000 with $75,000 in selling costs. Their adjusted basis is $595,000. Their taxable gain is:
questions.x: Amount realized $1,175,000 - $595,000 basis = $580,000 gain, minus the $500,000 exclusion = $80,000. $155,000 is the trap: it ignores the selling costs.

questions.q: Jordan owned a condo 5 years, lived in it the first 2, then rented it out for 3 years before selling. For the ownership and use tests, he:
c: Fails, since he did not live there last
He meets both tests; the years need not be last
Fails, since he rented for 3 years
Meets them if he moves back first
questions.x: He owned it all 5 years and used it 2 of the 5 years before the sale, so both tests are met (rental-period depreciation is still taxable). The did-not-live-there-last answer is the trap: the 2 years need not be the most recent.

questions.q: Grace has lived in her home 6 years. She marries Tomas, who moves in 1 year before they sell. They file jointly. Their maximum exclusion is:
c: $500,000, as joint filers
questions.x: For $500,000, both spouses must meet the use test; Tomas lived there only 1 year, so the couple gets Grace's $250,000. $500,000 is the trap: joint filing alone does not double the exclusion.

questions.q: An investor buys land on May 1, 2025 and sells it at a gain on May 15, 2026. The gain is:
c: Short-term, taxed as ordinary income
Long-term, at 0/15/20% rates
Recapture taxed at up to 25%
Excluded under IRC 121
questions.x: Held more than one year, the gain is long-term. The recapture answer is the trap: land is not depreciated, so there is no unrecaptured Section 1250 gain.

questions.q: An investor sells a rental house (never her residence) at a $40,000 loss. Compared with a loss on her own home, this loss is:
c: Not deductible, same as a home
Deductible up to $3,000 a year
Added to her next home's basis
Generally deductible as a business loss
questions.x: A loss on investment or business property can generally be deducted, while a loss on a personal residence cannot. The $3,000 answer is the trap: that limit applies to net capital losses against ordinary income, and rental property is generally Section 1231 property.

questions.q: Under current federal law, the expanded SALT deduction cap is scheduled to revert to $10,000 beginning in:
c: It is permanent now
questions.x: The 2025 law raised the cap (to $40,400 for 2026) through 2029, with $10,000 returning in 2030. 2026 is the trap: that was the original sunset of the 2017 law, which the 2025 law changed.

questions.q: All of the following are portfolio income EXCEPT:
c: Duplex rents
Stock dividends
Bond interest
Mutual fund gains
questions.x: Rental income is generally passive, not portfolio income. Bond interest is the tempting pick, but interest is classic portfolio income.

questions.q: A landlord who actively participates has MAGI of $140,000. How much of her rental loss may she deduct against other income under the special allowance?
questions.x: The $25,000 allowance drops by 50% of MAGI over $100,000: $40,000 x 50% = $20,000 reduction, leaving $5,000. $20,000 is the trap: it is the reduction, not the allowance left.

questions.q: A small office building used for business is depreciated over:
c: 27.5 years
15 years
31.5 years
39 years
questions.x: Nonresidential real property placed in service today uses 39 years. 31.5 years is the trap: it was the period for buildings placed in service before mid-1993.

questions.q: An investor buys a small office building for $468,000; the land is worth $117,000. Annual straight-line depreciation is:
questions.x: ($468,000 - $117,000) / 39 = $351,000 / 39 = $9,000. $12,764 is the trap: it uses the 27.5-year residential period for an office building.

questions.q: A landlord's annual mortgage payments total $30,000: $22,000 interest and $8,000 principal. Her deductible amount from these payments is:
c: $30,000, the full payment
questions.x: Only the interest portion, $22,000, is deductible; principal repayment is not an expense. $30,000 is the trap: it treats the whole payment as an expense.

questions.q: A building has NOI of $120,000, debt service of $80,000 (of which $60,000 is interest), and depreciation of $30,000. Taxable income and before-tax cash flow are:
c: $10,000 taxable; $40,000 cash flow
$30,000 taxable; $10,000 cash flow
$60,000 taxable; $40,000 before-tax cash flow
$30,000 taxable; $40,000 cash flow
questions.x: Taxable: $120,000 - $60,000 interest - $30,000 depreciation = $30,000. Cash flow: $120,000 - $80,000 = $40,000. $10,000 taxable is the trap: it subtracts the full debt service, including principal.

questions.q: An investor in the top bracket sells a rental held 8 years. The $120,000 of gain from prior depreciation is taxed at a maximum federal rate of:
c: 20%, like other long-term gain
25% maximum rate
37%, as ordinary income
questions.x: Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain on real property is taxed at up to 25%. 20% is the trap: it applies to the remaining long-term gain.

questions.concept: Gain on sale of investment property
questions.q: An investor bought a rental for $400,000 and took $60,000 of depreciation. She sells for $450,000 with $30,000 of selling costs. Her total gain is:
questions.x: Adjusted basis = $340,000; amount realized = $420,000; gain = $80,000, of which $60,000 is depreciation-related. $20,000 is the trap: it ignores the depreciation.

questions.q: In a delayed 1031 exchange, the replacement property must be received within:
c: 180 days, or the return due date if earlier
45 days of the sale closing
90 days after identification
One full year after the sale
questions.x: The exchange must close within 180 days of the sale or by the return due date (with extensions), whichever is earlier. 45 days is the trap: that is the identification deadline.

questions.q: An investor sells a Bronx apartment building in a 1031 exchange. Which replacement qualifies as like-kind?
c: A vacation home for personal use
Lots a developer holds as inventory
Shares in a real estate company
A warehouse held as an investment
questions.x: Real property held for business or investment is like-kind to other such real property, so a building can be exchanged for a warehouse. Dealer inventory is the trap: property held for sale does not qualify.

questions.q: In a 1031 exchange, an investor has a realized gain of $50,000 and receives $80,000 of cash boot. Her recognized gain is:
c: $80,000, the cash boot
questions.x: Recognized gain is the lesser of boot or realized gain, so $50,000. $80,000 is the trap: boot is taxable only up to the realized gain.

questions.q: All of the following are disqualified from serving as an investor's qualified intermediary EXCEPT:
c: Her real estate broker in the past year
Her daughter
Her attorney on last year's purchase
An unrelated exchange company
questions.x: An independent exchange accommodator with no agency relationship qualifies. The attorney is the tempting pick, but someone who acted as her agent within 2 years is disqualified.

questions.q: An investor sells a relinquished property on March 1, 2027. The 180th day is August 28, 2027, and her 2027 return is due April 15, 2028. She must close on the replacement by:
c: April 15, 2027
August 28, 2027
September 30, 2027
April 15, 2028
questions.x: The deadline is the earlier of 180 days or the return due date; here day 180 comes first. April 15, 2028 is the trap: the return date matters only when it falls before day 180.

questions.q: In a reverse exchange, title to the property acquired first is typically held by:
c: An accommodation titleholder
The investor directly, in her own name
The seller until day 180
The investor's lender
questions.x: An exchange accommodation titleholder parks title so the investor does not own both properties at once. The investor-directly answer is the trap: holding both outright would break the exchange.

questions.q: In New York, Low-Income Housing Tax Credits are allocated to projects mainly by:
c: The Department of State
Homes and Community Renewal
The NYC Rent Guidelines Board
The Department of Financial Services
