questions.x: NYS Homes and Community Renewal allocates LIHTC credits (with NYC HPD and HDC for some city projects). The Rent Guidelines Board is the trap: it sets stabilized rent increases, not tax credits.

questions.q: Ana's husband died in March 2025. She has not remarried, and they had owned and lived in their Yonkers home for 20 years. She sells it in November 2026. Her maximum home sale exclusion is:
c: $500,000, as a surviving spouse
$250,000, as a single filer
$125,000, as a seller over 55
$375,000, a blended amount of the two
questions.x: A surviving spouse who has not remarried may exclude up to $500,000 on a sale within 2 years of the spouse's death, counting the late spouse's ownership and use. The $250,000 single limit applies only after that window closes. The $125,000 over-55 rule was repealed in 1997.

questions.q: A widower's wife died on May 1, 2025. He has not remarried. His contract to sell their home is signed in April 2027, and closing occurs on June 15, 2027. His gain is $400,000. How much is taxable?
c: $400,000, the full gain
questions.x: The sale date is the closing, June 15, 2027, more than 2 years after his wife's death, so his limit is $250,000 as a single filer: $400,000 minus $250,000 = $150,000. Choice A assumes the $500,000 limit still applies because the contract was signed inside the window. The contract date does not control.

questions.q: A single owner lived in her Albany condo for 18 months before her employer transferred her to Chicago. Her gain on the sale is $40,000. What is her maximum exclusion?
c: $125,000, half the limit
questions.x: A job move of at least 50 miles qualifies for a reduced exclusion: 18 / 24 x $250,000 = $187,500. Her $40,000 gain is fully excluded. Applying the fraction to the gain ($30,000) is the classic error; the fraction reduces the limit, not the gain.
questions.concept: Partial exclusion after a job move

questions.q: A married couple filing jointly owned and lived in their home for 12 months, then sold because one spouse took a job 300 miles away. Neither had used the exclusion before. Their maximum exclusion is:
c: $500,000, the full joint limit
questions.x: Each spouse's limit is 12 / 24 x $250,000 = $125,000; together $250,000. Choice B computes only one spouse. Choice A ignores the time requirement. A qualifying job move earns a reduced exclusion, not a full one.
questions.concept: Partial exclusion after a job move

questions.q: An owner bought a condo in 2018, rented it out for 3 years, then lived in it for 3 years and sold in 2024. The gain is $240,000, which includes $30,000 of depreciation. How much of the gain is taxable?
c: $105,000, the rental share
questions.x: Depreciation ($30,000) is taxed first. The remaining $210,000 is split by time: 3 nonqualified years of 6 = 50%, or $105,000 taxable. Total taxable: $30,000 + $105,000 = $135,000. Choice B forgets the depreciation; choice A ignores nonqualified use.

questions.q: Since 2009, "nonqualified use" that reduces the home sale exclusion includes a period when the property:
c: Was rented out after the owner moved out for good
Was rented out before the owner first moved in
Was the owner's main home while it was being renovated
Was empty while the owner was on qualified military duty
questions.x: Rental or vacation use after 2008 and before the owner made it a main home is nonqualified use. Rental after the owner's last use as a main home (within the 5-year window) is not, and qualified extended duty is an exception. Choice A is the trap: order of use matters.

questions.q: A couple lives in one unit of a two-family house and rents the other, a separate apartment. They sell at a gain. The home sale exclusion applies to:
c: The whole property, since they live there
Neither unit, since part of it is a rental
Their own unit, not the rental unit
The rental unit, if the tenant has a lease
questions.x: When a separate dwelling unit is rented, basis and amount realized are allocated between the home and the rental portion; only the home portion qualifies. Choice A is the common assumption. Depreciation taken on the rental unit is taxed as well.
questions.concept: Rental unit in an owner-occupied home

questions.q: Owners of a two-family sell for an amount realized of $1,200,000. Their basis is $500,000, split equally, and they took $60,000 of depreciation on the rented half. Married filing jointly, how much gain is taxable?
questions.x: Each half: amount realized $600,000. Home half: $600,000 minus $250,000 = $350,000, excluded. Rental half: adjusted basis $190,000, gain $410,000, all taxable ($60,000 of it at up to 25%). Choice C subtracts $500,000 from the combined $760,000 gain.
questions.concept: Rental unit in an owner-occupied home

questions.q: A buyer takes an $1,000,000 mortgage in 2026 to buy a main home and pays $60,000 of interest in the first year. If she itemizes, how much interest can she deduct?
c: $60,000, the full amount
questions.x: Interest on acquisition debt after December 15, 2017 is deductible on up to $750,000 of principal: $60,000 x 750,000 / 1,000,000 = $45,000. Choice A uses no limit. The old $1,000,000 limit applies to loans taken before December 16, 2017.

questions.q: Which homeowner can deduct interest on up to $1,000,000 of mortgage debt?
c: A buyer who closed a $900,000 purchase loan in 2024
A buyer who uses a HELOC to pay off student loans
An owner whose loan is from 2026 on a second home
An owner who took a $900,000 purchase loan in 2015
questions.x: Loans taken out before December 16, 2017 keep the old $1,000,000 limit. Loans after that, like the 2024 and 2026 loans, are limited to $750,000 of acquisition debt. HELOC interest is deductible only when the money buys, builds or substantially improves the home.

questions.q: A Brooklyn buyer pays a $15,000 mansion tax at closing on a $1,500,000 home. For federal income tax purposes, the mansion tax is:
c: Deductible as a property tax under the SALT cap
Deductible as mortgage interest
Added to the buyer's basis in the home
Credited against the buyer's income tax
questions.x: The mansion tax is a transfer tax on the purchase, not an annual property tax, so it is added to the buyer's basis and reduces gain when the home is sold. Choice A is the trap: only real property taxes (and state and local income taxes) count toward the SALT deduction.

questions.q: A New York buyer of a main home in 2026 may add all of the following to basis EXCEPT:
c: The 1% NYC mansion tax paid at closing
The prorated property tax paid at closing
Title insurance premiums on the owner's policy
The buyer's own attorney's fee for the closing
questions.x: Prorated real property taxes the buyer pays for the time after closing are deductible as taxes (within the SALT cap), not added to basis. Mansion tax, title insurance and legal fees are acquisition costs that increase basis. The mansion tax is the trap because it is called a tax.

questions.q: A Queens landlord pays $36,000 of property tax on a rental building and $14,000 on her own home. Under the 2026 rules, her deduction for these taxes is:
c: $36,000 against rents; home tax under the cap
$40,400 in total, the full SALT cap for 2026
$10,000 in total, under the old SALT cap
$50,000 as an itemized deduction with no cap applied
questions.x: Taxes on rental property are a rental expense deducted against rental income, outside the SALT cap. Tax on her personal home is an itemized deduction subject to the cap ($40,400 for 2026). Choice B wrongly pushes the rental taxes under the cap, which applies to individuals' personal taxes.

questions.q: A residential landlord may deduct all of the following against rental income EXCEPT:
c: Mortgage interest on the building
Property taxes on the building
Mortgage principal payments
Painting the common hallways
questions.x: Principal repays borrowed money and is never deductible. Interest, property taxes and ordinary repairs like painting are deductible rental expenses, and rental property taxes are not limited by the SALT cap. Principal is the trap because it is part of the same monthly check as the interest.

questions.q: An investor's allowable depreciation over 10 years was $200,000, but she claimed only $150,000. Her original basis was $900,000. For computing gain on a sale, her adjusted basis is:
c: $750,000, what she claimed
questions.x: Basis is reduced by depreciation allowed or allowable, whichever is greater: $900,000 minus $200,000 = $700,000. Using only what she claimed ($750,000) is the trap; skipping depreciation does not avoid the basis reduction or the tax on it at sale.

questions.q: An owner never claimed depreciation on a rental condo she owned for 6 years. When she sells it, her adjusted basis is:
c: Unchanged, since she took no deductions
Reduced by the depreciation she could have taken
Increased by the depreciation she missed claiming
Reduced if the IRS later audits the prior years
questions.x: The basis reduction is for depreciation allowed or allowable. She loses the deduction she skipped and still has a lower basis, unless her accountant catches up the missed depreciation with an accounting method change. Choice A is what most owners assume.

questions.q: A seller's selling price is $1,000,000, adjusted basis $350,000 and selling expenses $50,000. The buyer assumes none of the seller's debt. What is the gross profit percentage?
c: 40%, the basis share
questions.x: Gross profit = $1,000,000 minus ($350,000 + $50,000) = $600,000. Contract price = $1,000,000. Percentage = 60%. Choice A forgets the selling expenses. Choice B is the basis share.

questions.q: An investor sells land for $500,000 with $20,000 of selling costs. Her basis is $180,000, and the buyer pays $100,000 down plus a note for the rest. How much gain does she report in the year of sale?
questions.x: Gross profit = $500,000 minus ($180,000 + $20,000) = $300,000; percentage = $300,000 / $500,000 = 60%. Year-of-sale gain = $100,000 x 60% = $60,000. $64,000 ignores the selling costs. $300,000 reports everything at once.

questions.q: A seller's gross profit percentage is 75%. In the year after closing, she receives $48,000 on the note: $30,000 interest and $18,000 principal. How much capital gain does she report from the note that year?
c: $36,000, on the full payment
questions.x: Only principal carries gain: $18,000 x 75% = $13,500. The $30,000 of interest is ordinary income, reported separately. $36,000 applies the percentage to the whole payment, the most common mistake.

questions.q: Interest a seller receives on an installment note from the sale of a rental building is taxed as:
c: Ordinary income
Long-term capital gain
Unrecaptured section 1250 gain
Tax-exempt interest
questions.x: Interest on a seller-financed note is ordinary (portfolio) income, like bank interest. Only the principal portion carries capital gain, at the gross profit percentage. Calling it capital gain is the trap; the IRS also imputes interest if the note's rate is below the applicable federal rate.

questions.q: A seller has $300,000 of unrecaptured section 1250 gain and $500,000 of other long-term gain, reported on the installment method. In the first year she reports $200,000 of gain. How is it characterized?
c: $200,000 of unrecaptured section 1250 gain
$75,000 of 1250 gain and $125,000 of regular gain
$200,000 of regular long-term gain
$100,000 of each type
questions.x: Under the regulations, unrecaptured section 1250 gain is taken into account first, so the whole $200,000 is 1250 gain taxed at up to 25%; $100,000 remains for later years. Choice B is the proportional split, which is the intuitive approach and not the rule.

questions.q: In an installment sale of a depreciated rental building, the gain attributable to straight-line depreciation (unrecaptured section 1250 gain) is reported:
c: Entirely in the year of sale, before any payments
Last, after the other gain
First, as payments are received
At no point, since installment sales forgive it
questions.x: Unrecaptured section 1250 gain follows the installment method but comes out first as gain is reported. Choice A confuses it with depreciation recapture taxed as ordinary income (sections 1245 and 1250), which is reported in the year of sale. Choice B reverses the order.

questions.q: Which seller is most likely barred from using the installment method?
c: A retiree selling a rental six-family she has owned for 20 years
A flipper who renovates and resells houses each year
An investor selling vacant land held for 8 years
A couple selling a rental condo they owned for 5 years
questions.x: Dealer property, real estate held for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business, cannot use the installment method, and a regular flipper is likely a dealer. Long-term investors in rentals or land generally can. Holding period alone is not the test; the business purpose is.

questions.q: A seller with a $1,200,000 installment note pledges it as collateral for a $400,000 bank loan two years after the sale. Her gross profit percentage is 60%. Generally, she must:
c: Report nothing, since a loan is not a payment
Repay the note before taking the loan
Report the remaining deferred gain at once
Treat $400,000 as paid: $240,000 of gain
questions.x: For sales over $150,000, pledging an installment obligation as security generally treats the net loan proceeds as a payment: $400,000 x 60% = $240,000 of gain. The rest of the note keeps installment treatment, so choice C overstates it. Choice A is the hoped-for loophole the rule closes.

questions.q: An investor's relinquished property closes on March 2, 2026. By what date must she identify replacement property?
c: April 1, 2026
April 16, 2026
April 15, 2026, counting the closing day
April 17, 2026
questions.x: Count 45 calendar days starting the day after closing: 29 days remain in March (3 to 31), plus 16 days of April, so the deadline is April 16, 2026. April 15 counts the closing day as day 1. There is no extension for weekends or holidays.

questions.q: An investor sells on October 1, 2026 in a 1031 exchange. Day 180 is March 30, 2027, and her 2026 return is due April 15, 2027. She files the return on February 20, 2027, before buying the replacement. The exchange period ended:
c: March 30, 2027
April 15, 2027
February 20, 2027
October 15, 2027, the extended date
questions.x: The exchange period ends on the earlier of day 180 or the due date of the return, and filing the return early makes the filing date the effective due date. Buying after February 20 is too late. Choice A is the normal day-180 answer; it would apply if she had waited or extended.

questions.q: All of the following could serve as a taxpayer's qualified intermediary EXCEPT:
c: An exchange company with no prior ties to the taxpayer
A bank's exchange subsidiary the taxpayer has not used before
An unrelated QI firm recommended by the title company
The real estate broker who sold the property last month
questions.x: A person who acted as the taxpayer's agent, including the real estate broker, attorney, accountant or employee, within the 2 years before the transfer is a disqualified person. Unrelated exchange companies are the normal choice; a recommendation from a title company does not taint them.

questions.q: At closing on a 1031 sale, the net proceeds are wired to the seller's own attorney's escrow account, to be sent to the QI the next day. The main risk is that:
c: The 45-day period starts a day later than planned
The seller is treated as receiving the money
The QI will charge a second exchange fee for the delay
The buyer can cancel the sale for late funding
questions.x: Proceeds controlled by the taxpayer or the taxpayer's agent can be constructive receipt, which disqualifies the exchange for that money. They must go from the buyer straight to the QI under the exchange agreement. The 45-day clock runs from the transfer of the property, not from the wire.

questions.q: An investor sells a $2,000,000 building in an exchange. Which identification is valid?
c: Four properties worth a total of $4,500,000
Five properties worth a total of $4,800,000
Two properties, delivered to her own attorney
Three properties worth a total of $6,000,000
questions.x: Up to three properties of any value are allowed, so three worth $6,000,000 is fine. More than three must total no more than 200% of the property sold, $4,000,000, so the four- and five-property lists fail. Delivery to her own attorney, a disqualified person, is not valid identification.

questions.q: A taxpayer sells a property for $1,500,000 and wants to identify five replacement properties. Under the 200% rule, their combined value may not exceed:
c: $1,500,000, the sale price
questions.x: When more than three properties are identified, their total fair market value may not exceed 200% of the value of the property given up: 2 x $1,500,000 = $3,000,000. $4,500,000 confuses it with three times the value, perhaps from the three-property rule.

questions.q: An investor's realized gain is $900,000. In the exchange she receives $60,000 in cash and is relieved of a $400,000 mortgage, taking on a $300,000 mortgage on the replacement. How much gain is recognized?
c: $460,000, ignoring new debt
questions.x: Mortgage boot is net debt relief: $400,000 minus $300,000 = $100,000. Add cash boot of $60,000: $160,000 recognized, which is less than the $900,000 realized gain. $460,000 ignores the new mortgage. Choice A forgets mortgage boot.

questions.q: An investor with a realized gain of $120,000 receives $150,000 of cash boot in a 1031 exchange. The recognized gain is:
c: $150,000, the boot received
questions.x: Recognized gain is the lesser of boot received or realized gain. Boot of $150,000 exceeds the $120,000 gain, so $120,000 is recognized; there is no gain left to defer. Choice B taxes more than the investor actually gained.

questions.q: In a 1031 exchange, an investor takes $200,000 of cash out and borrows $200,000 more on the replacement property than the mortgage paid off. The recognized gain from boot is:
c: $0, since the extra debt fully offsets the cash taken
$100,000, since the two amounts are averaged together
$200,000, since debt cannot offset cash received
$400,000, since both items are boot
questions.x: Debt the taxpayer takes on offsets debt relief, and cash paid offsets debt relief, but debt taken on never offsets cash received. The $200,000 cash is taxable. Choice A is the common assumption. New debt is not itself boot, so choice D is wrong too.

questions.q: An investor is relieved of a $500,000 mortgage in a 1031 exchange. The replacement has a $350,000 mortgage, and she adds $150,000 of her own cash. Her mortgage boot is:
questions.x: Net debt relief is $150,000, and cash the taxpayer pays in offsets debt relief, so the $150,000 she added eliminates it: mortgage boot is $0. Choice A ignores the added cash. Adding cash is the standard fix when the new loan is smaller than the old one.

questions.q: An investor exchanges a building with an adjusted basis of $300,000 and a realized gain of $1,200,000 for a replacement costing $1,800,000, with no boot. Her basis in the replacement is:
questions.x: Replacement basis = cost minus deferred gain = $1,800,000 minus $1,200,000 = $600,000. Equivalently, old basis of $300,000 plus the $300,000 of additional value acquired. $1,800,000 would apply only to a purchase without an exchange.

questions.q: Why is the gain in a 1031 exchange described as deferred rather than forgiven?
c: It lowers the replacement property's basis
Tax is due in installments over the next 5 years
The gain is taxed at ordinary rates after 10 years
Boot is added to the replacement property's value
questions.x: The replacement property takes a basis equal to its cost minus the deferred gain, so the gain, including past depreciation, is taxed when the replacement is sold in a taxable sale. There is no installment schedule or 10-year rule. Choice D confuses boot, which is taxed now, with deferral.

questions.q: A single buyer sold her last main home 20 months ago. She signs a contract on a Queens condo today and plans to take $10,000 from her traditional IRA for the closing. The withdrawal will be:
c: Subject to income tax and the 10% penalty
Free of the 10% penalty but subject to income tax
Free of income tax and the 10% penalty
Free of the penalty if she closes after 24 months
questions.x: A first-time homebuyer has had no ownership interest in a main home during the 2 years ending on the acquisition date, which is the contract date. At 20 months she fails the test, so the withdrawal is taxed and penalized. The penalty-free answer would be right for a qualifying buyer. Closing later does not help, because the contract date controls.

questions.q: A married couple, neither of whom has owned a home in the past 2 years, each take money from a traditional IRA under the first-time homebuyer exception. What is the most they can withdraw in total without the 10% penalty?
questions.x: The $10,000 is a lifetime limit per person, so two qualifying spouses can take $10,000 each, $20,000 in all. The $10,000 answer treats the limit as per household. The withdrawals still count as taxable income; the exception waives only the 10% additional tax.

questions.q: Owners of a Bronx two-family live in one of two equal apartments and rent the other. Their mortgage is $900,000. How is the interest treated?
c: Interest on $750,000 is itemized and the remainder is not deductible
Half is itemized as home mortgage interest; half is a rental cost
The full amount is itemized, because they live in the building
Half is itemized, capped at the interest on $375,000 of debt
questions.x: Interest follows the use of the property. The home half ($450,000 of debt) is within the $750,000 limit and is itemized; the rental half is deducted against rent on Schedule E and is not subject to the home mortgage limit. The $750,000 answer applies the cap to the whole building. $375,000 is the limit for married people filing separately.

questions.q: An owner lives in one apartment of a three-family and rents the other two, all equal in size. All of the following are deducted on Schedule E as rental expenses EXCEPT:
c: Two thirds of the mortgage interest
Two thirds of the building insurance
One third of the property tax
Repairs made inside a rented unit
questions.x: The owner's own share of property tax, one third, is a personal deduction that goes on Schedule A under the SALT cap, not a rental expense. The rental two thirds of interest, insurance and property tax, and repairs inside rented units, are Schedule E expenses. The interest choice is the tempting one, but the rental share of interest is a rental expense.

questions.q: A buyer pays 2 points on a $600,000, 30-year loan to refinance her Yonkers home. No proceeds are used for improvements. How much of the points can she deduct in the first full year?
questions.x: Two points = $12,000. Refinance points are deducted over the life of the loan: $12,000 / 30 = $400 a year. $12,000 is the treatment of points on a loan to buy a main home. $200 spreads only one point. If part of the new money had paid for improvements, that share of the points could be deducted at once.

questions.q: Which points can generally be deducted in full in the year they are paid?
c: Points on a loan to refinance the borrower's main home
Points on a loan to buy a rental building in Queens
Points on a loan to buy the borrower's second home
Points on a loan to buy the borrower's main home
questions.x: Points on a loan to buy or build a main home can be deducted in full in the year paid when the usual tests are met, or spread over the loan if the buyer prefers. Refinance points, points on rental property loans and points on a second home loan are spread over the life of the loan. The refinance choice is the common trap.

questions.q: An investor buys a four-family in Ridgewood for $1,800,000 plus $40,000 of title, legal and transfer tax costs. Land is 30% of the value. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
questions.x: Cost basis = $1,840,000. Building = 70% = $1,288,000. $1,288,000 / 27.5 = $46,836. $66,909 forgets to remove the land. $45,818 leaves out the acquisition costs ($1,260,000 / 27.5). $33,026 uses the 39-year life, which applies to nonresidential property.

questions.q: A couple buys a two-family with equal units for $1,200,000, adds $20,000 of acquisition costs, lives downstairs and rents upstairs. Land is 40% of the value. What is the yearly depreciation on the rental unit?
questions.x: Basis $1,220,000; building 60% = $732,000; rental half = $366,000; / 27.5 = $13,309. $26,618 depreciates the whole building, including the owners' own floor. $22,182 forgets to remove the land ($610,000 / 27.5). $9,385 uses 39 years. The home half is never depreciated.

questions.q: A Staten Island homeowner owes $400,000 on the loan used to buy her home. She refinances into a $480,000 loan and uses the extra $80,000 to pay off credit cards. How much of the new loan is home acquisition debt?
questions.x: Refinanced debt stays acquisition debt only up to the old principal balance, here $400,000. Cash-out used for anything other than buying, building or substantially improving the home does not qualify, so interest on the $80,000 is personal. $480,000 treats the whole new loan as acquisition debt. $750,000 is the overall limit, not the amount that qualifies.

questions.q: A Westchester couple take a $150,000 home equity line. They spend $90,000 adding a bedroom and $60,000 on a car and tuition. Interest on how much of the line is deductible as home mortgage interest?
questions.x: Home equity interest is deductible only to the extent the money buys, builds or substantially improves the home securing it. The $90,000 addition qualifies; the car and tuition money does not. $100,000 is the old home equity limit, repealed starting in 2018. $150,000 treats the whole line as qualifying because the home secures it.

questions.q: A home under construction can be treated as a qualified home for mortgage interest purposes for up to:
c: 12 months, beginning when the land is purchased
36 months, or until a certificate of occupancy
24 months, if it becomes a qualified home when ready
18 months, if it is the borrower's main home
questions.x: The rule allows up to 24 months, starting on or after the date construction begins, provided the home becomes the owner's main or second home when ready for occupancy. The certificate of occupancy answer mixes a building code event into a tax rule. The clock is not tied to the land purchase, and a second home can qualify too.

questions.q: An owner breaks ground on a lake house in April 2027 and finishes it 30 months later. She uses it as her second home. How is the construction loan interest treated?
c: It qualifies for the full 30 months
It qualifies starting when she moves in
It cannot qualify, as a second home
It can qualify for 24 of the 30 months
questions.x: A home under construction can be a qualified home for up to 24 months, so interest for the first 24 months of construction can be home mortgage interest; the rest of the construction period does not qualify. Once the house is finished and used as her second home, the interest qualifies again. A second home is eligible, so the last choice is wrong.

cram.html: Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997: created the $250,000/$500,000 home sale exclusion and the $10,000 IRA first-time buyer withdrawal.
Exclusion tests: own 2 of 5 years, live 2 of 5 years, once every 2 years. Married: either owns, both use.
IRA withdrawal for a first home escapes the 10% penalty, not income tax. Lifetime limit $10,000 per person.
Mortgage interest deductible on acquisition debt up to $750,000 (permanent since 2025); pre-Dec 16, 2017 loans keep $1 million.
Home equity interest deductible only if used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home.
SALT cap: $40,000 for 2025, $40,400 for 2026, back to $10,000 in 2030.
Purchase points on main home: deduct when paid. Refinance points: spread over the loan.
Prepayment penalty on a home mortgage = deductible interest.
Gain = amount realized (price minus selling costs) minus adjusted basis (cost + improvements minus depreciation).
Short-term: held 1 year or less, ordinary rates. Long-term: more than 1 year, 0/15/20%.
Loss on selling your home: not deductible.
Income classes: active (wages), passive (rentals), portfolio (interest, dividends).
Rental loss allowance: $25,000 for active participants, phased out from $100,000 to $150,000 MAGI.
Depreciation: straight-line, 27.5 years residential, 39 years nonresidential, land never.
Recaptured depreciation taxed at up to 25%.
Cash flow = NOI minus debt service. Taxable income = NOI minus interest minus depreciation.
1031: identify in 45 days, close by the earlier of 180 days or the tax return due date.
1031 eligible: investment or business real property, including land, hotels, and leaseholds of 30+ years. Not your home, not dealer property.
Boot (cash, debt relief) is taxable up to the realized gain.
Qualified intermediary holds the money. Your own attorney, broker, or accountant (past 2 years) cannot.
Reverse exchange: buy first, sell later; same 45/180 limits.
LIHTC (IRC 42): credits for affordable rentals; NY allocator is HCR. A credit cuts tax dollar for dollar.
Licensees explain general rules and refer clients to a CPA or tax attorney.

subjects.title: Mortgage Brokerage
subjects.blurb: Who arranges the loan, who funds it, and who regulates them. A short subject with reliable exam points: broker vs banker, DFS, the dual agency disclosure, and prequalification vs preapproval vs commitment.

lessons.title: Mortgage Brokers, Bankers, and the Loan Process
lessons.tagline: A mortgage broker finds the money. A mortgage banker is the money. DFS watches both.
objectives: Distinguish a mortgage broker, a mortgage banker, and a mortgage loan originator, and who regulates each
Explain the dual agency disclosure required when a real estate broker also acts as mortgage broker
Rank prequalification, preapproval, and commitment by strength
Define rate lock, underwriting, lender rebate, nonconforming loan, and the pre-application disclosure and fee agreement
Describe the mortgage broker's role from offer to closing

blocks.title: Two letters on the table
blocks.html: Two buyers bid on the same Ditmas Park co-op at the same price. One attaches a "prequalification" from an app that took four minutes. The other attaches a preapproval from Tasha, after she pulled credit and reviewed two years of tax returns. Kim's board and the sellers' agent both want to know which buyer is real. Which letter wins, and why?
blocks.casual: Two buyers bid the same price on the same Ditmas Park co-op. One attaches a "prequalification" from an app that took four minutes. The other attaches a preapproval from Tasha, who actually pulled credit and went through two years of tax returns. Kim's board and the sellers' agent both want to know which buyer is real. Which letter wins, and why?

deeper.plain: A letter based on what the buyer said is weak. A letter based on documents a lender actually checked is strong.
deeper.picture: One buyer shows a selfie saying "I'm good for it". The other shows a bank statement with a lender's stamp on it.
deeper.street: The sellers take Tasha's buyer at the same price. Two weeks later the app buyer's "prequal" falls apart when his self-employment income turns out to be half what he typed in. Tasha's buyer gets a commitment on schedule and the board approves the package.
deeper.stakes: Sellers who pick the weaker letter can lose weeks and a backup buyer. Buyer's agents who rely on a prequal set clients up to lose deals in competitive markets.
deeper.exam: Prequalification: buyer's word, nothing verified. Preapproval: credit pulled, documents reviewed. Commitment: specific loan on specific property. Expect a question ranking them.

blocks.html: A mortgage broker arranges loans. The broker takes the application, shops it to several lenders, and steers it to closing, but does not fund the loan; the lender's money closes it, usually in the lender's name. A mortgage banker funds loans with its own money (often a warehouse line of credit), closes in its own name, and usually sells the loans on the secondary market. Banks and credit unions lend under their own charters.
blocks.casual: A mortgage broker arranges loans. They take the application, shop it to several lenders, and push it through to closing, but they don't fund it. The lender's money closes the deal, usually in the lender's name. A mortgage banker funds loans with its own money (often from a warehouse line of credit), closes in its own name, and usually sells the loans on the secondary market. Banks and credit unions lend under their own charters.

deeper.plain: A broker finds you a lender. A banker is the lender, at least until it sells the loan.
deeper.picture: A mortgage broker is a travel agent who books your flight on whatever airline is best. A mortgage banker is the airline itself.
deeper.street: Tasha shops Leo's file to six lenders and finds the best rate at a credit union in Westchester; the credit union funds and closes. A different buyer goes to a mortgage banker in Midtown that funds her loan from its warehouse line at closing and sells it to Fannie Mae a month later.
deeper.stakes: Borrowers who think the broker is the lender get confused when a different name appears on the closing documents. Agents who don't know the difference can't explain delays.
deeper.exam: Funds the loan? Banker yes, broker no. A mortgage banker typically sells loans on the secondary market. A mortgage broker is compensated for arranging, not lending.

blocks.caption: Follow a loan application through a mortgage broker vs a mortgage banker. Watch whose money funds the loan and which license each one holds.

head: Mortgage broker
Mortgage banker
Loan originator (MLO)
rows: A company that lends its own funds
The individual who takes applications and discusses terms
No, works for a broker or banker
DFS license through NMLS (SAFE Act, Banking Law Article 12-E)
Borrower fee, lender compensation, or both as allowed
Origination fees, interest, and sale of loans
Salary or commission from the employer

deeper.plain: Brokers arrange, bankers fund, and originators are the individual people who take applications. DFS oversees all three in NY.
deeper.picture: It's a restaurant: the banker owns the kitchen and the food, the broker is a food delivery app finding you the best kitchen, and the MLO is the person taking your order.
deeper.street: Tasha holds her own MLO license through NMLS and works for a registered mortgage broker in Downtown Brooklyn. Her firm is registered with DFS under Banking Law Article 12-D; Tasha's individual license falls under Article 12-E and the federal SAFE Act.
deeper.stakes: Taking loan applications without an MLO license is illegal. A firm that brokers without DFS registration can face penalties and can't collect its fees.
deeper.exam: Broker: registered. Banker: licensed. Individual originator: licensed through NMLS (SAFE Act). Regulator: DFS for all three.

blocks.title: The regulator is DFS, not DOS
blocks.html: The NYS Department of Financial Services (DFS) registers mortgage brokers, licenses mortgage bankers, and licenses individual mortgage loan originators, each of whom has an NMLS ID. A real estate license from DOS does not authorize anyone to broker mortgages.
blocks.casual: In NY, the Department of Financial Services (DFS) registers mortgage brokers, licenses mortgage bankers, and licenses the individual mortgage loan originators, and each of those people has an NMLS ID. Your real estate license from DOS does not let you broker mortgages.

deeper.plain: Real estate licenses come from DOS. Mortgage licenses come from DFS. One doesn't cover the other.
deeper.picture: A driver's license doesn't let you fly a plane, even though both involve getting people somewhere.
deeper.street: Marcus tells a buyer, "I can get you a loan, I'm licensed." He means his DOS real estate salesperson license. Tasha points out that taking that application would be unlicensed mortgage activity under NY Banking Law.
deeper.stakes: Brokering loans without DFS authority can mean fines, fee forfeiture, and a DOS complaint on top. It also exposes the borrower to unregulated advice.
deeper.exam: The exam likes to test which agency regulates mortgage brokers. Answer: DFS. Distractor: DOS.

blocks.q: Which company actually lends its own money and closes the loan in its own name?
c: A mortgage broker
A mortgage banker
A real estate broker
A loan originator
blocks.x: A mortgage banker funds loans, then usually sells them. A mortgage broker arranges loans that a lender funds.

blocks.text: When the real estate broker is also the mortgage broker

blocks.html: Some firms do both: they list the house and arrange the buyer's loan. That is a conflict, because the firm earns more if the deal closes at any price and on any loan. NY Banking regulations (3 NYCRR 38.12) require a mortgage broker dual agency disclosure, signed by the borrower and the seller before mortgage brokerage services begin. It explains the dual role, the borrower's rights, and whether the broker places loans with three or fewer lenders.
blocks.casual: Some firms do both: they list the house and line up the buyer's loan. That's a conflict, because the firm makes more money if the deal closes at any price, on any loan. NY Banking regulations require a mortgage broker dual agency disclosure, signed by the borrower and the seller before mortgage brokerage services start. It explains the dual role, the borrower's rights, and whether the broker places loans with three or fewer lenders.

deeper.plain: If the firm selling the house is also arranging the loan, everyone has to be told and sign off first.
deeper.picture: It's like a car dealer who also arranges your financing. You want to know they profit twice, and from how many banks they're really shopping.
deeper.street: A Bay Ridge brokerage has an affiliated, DFS-registered mortgage brokerage. When its buyer wants the in-house loan on a house the firm also lists, the buyer and the seller each sign the dual agency disclosure before the loan work begins.
deeper.stakes: Skipping the disclosure is a regulatory violation, and if the loan goes bad, the borrower may claim the firm pushed them for its own benefit.
deeper.exam: Signed by borrower and seller, before mortgage brokerage services begin. It's a Banking Law disclosure, separate from RPL 443.

blocks.title: Two different dual agencies
blocks.html: The RPL 443 dual agency (one real estate broker for buyer and seller) and the Banking Law dual agency (one firm as real estate broker and mortgage broker) are separate. A firm doing both can need both disclosures. Also, RESPA forbids a real estate licensee from taking a referral fee for sending a buyer to a lender. Being the actual mortgage broker, properly registered and disclosed, is different from taking a kickback.
blocks.casual: Don't mix these up. RPL 443 dual agency (one real estate broker representing buyer and seller) and Banking Law dual agency (one firm acting as real estate broker and mortgage broker) are separate things. A firm doing both can need both disclosures. Also, RESPA says a real estate licensee can't take a referral fee for sending a buyer to a lender. Actually being the mortgage broker, properly registered and disclosed, is different from taking a kickback.

deeper.plain: Two kinds of dual agency, two forms. And getting paid for a referral is illegal, while doing the actual mortgage work with proper licensing isn't.
deeper.picture: Two different hats, each needing its own permit. And you can't get tipped just for pointing at the restaurant door.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart represents both Leo and the Okafors on the brownstone sale (443 dual agency) and its affiliated mortgage brokerage arranges Leo's loan (Banking Law dual agency). Both forms get signed. Separately, a lender offers Marcus $300 per buyer he sends; Diane shuts it down as a RESPA Section 8 violation.
deeper.stakes: Missing either disclosure is its own violation. Taking referral fees can bring federal penalties, including fines and possible jail time.
deeper.exam: Trick question: one form doesn't cover both roles. RESPA Section 8 bans referral fees; being a properly registered and disclosed mortgage broker is allowed.

blocks.html: Before a NY mortgage broker accepts any fee, it gives the borrower the pre-application disclosure and fee agreement, signed by both. It states that the broker is not a lender, what services it provides, what fees it charges and when, whether it may be compensated by the lender, and which fees are refundable if no loan closes. Then the formal application, a Loan Estimate within 3 business days, the appraisal, and underwriting follow.
blocks.casual: Before a NY mortgage broker takes a single dollar in fees, it gives the borrower the pre-application disclosure and fee agreement, and both sign it. It says the broker isn't a lender, what services it provides, what fees it charges and when, whether the lender might also pay it, and which fees are refundable if no loan closes. After that come the formal application, a Loan Estimate within 3 business days, the appraisal, and underwriting.

deeper.plain: Before charging you anything, a mortgage broker has to explain in writing what it does, what it costs, and what you get back if it doesn't work out.
deeper.picture: It's like a contractor's signed estimate before they buy any materials: here's the job, here's the price, here's the refund policy.
deeper.street: Leo signs Tasha's pre-application agreement on a Monday. It shows a $500 application fee, refundable if no lender will offer a loan, and states her firm may be paid by the lender instead of by Leo. Then she takes his formal application.
deeper.stakes: A broker who collects fees without this signed agreement violates NY rules and may have to refund them. Borrowers without it can't tell what they're paying for.
deeper.exam: Pre-application disclosure comes before any fee. It says the broker is not a lender. Loan Estimate comes within 3 business days of the formal application.

head: Step
What it is
Strength
rows: Estimate of how much the buyer could borrow, based on what the buyer says. No documents verified
Lender has pulled credit and reviewed income and asset documents; approval is conditional on the property and final checks
Strong. Shows the buyer is creditworthy
Written promise to make a specific loan on a specific property, after underwriting and appraisal, with conditions and an expiration date

deeper.plain: Prequal is a guess, preapproval is a checked file, and a commitment is a promise to lend on a particular property.
deeper.picture: Prequal is telling the bouncer you're 21. Preapproval is showing your ID. Commitment is your name on the guest list for tonight's party.
deeper.street: Leo is prequalified in January from a phone call, preapproved in March after Tasha pulls credit and his W-2s, and gets a written commitment on his LIC condo in May after the appraisal comes in. Only the May letter satisfies his contract's mortgage contingency.
deeper.stakes: Treating a prequal as an approval leads to failed deals. A buyer who lets the commitment expire before closing may need to requalify, at a new rate.
deeper.exam: Commitment satisfies the mortgage contingency. Preapproval is conditional on the property. Prequalification verifies nothing.

blocks.q: A buyer's contract has a mortgage contingency. What document normally satisfies it?
c: A prequalification letter
A preapproval letter
A written mortgage commitment
A Loan Estimate
blocks.x: The contingency is tied to a written commitment for the specific property. Preapproval comes before a property is chosen and appraised.

blocks.html: Underwriting is the lender's risk review: credit (history and score), capacity (income and ratios), capital (cash and reserves), and collateral (appraisal and title). The underwriter approves, denies, or approves with conditions such as a letter explaining a large deposit.
blocks.casual: Underwriting is the lender's risk check: credit (history and score), capacity (income and ratios), capital (cash and reserves), and collateral (appraisal and title). The underwriter approves, denies, or approves with conditions, like asking for a letter explaining a big deposit.

deeper.plain: The underwriter checks whether you pay bills, earn enough, have savings, and whether the property is worth the loan.
deeper.picture: Four C's on a checklist, like a pilot's preflight: credit, capacity, capital, collateral. Miss one and the plane stays on the ground.
deeper.street: Leo's underwriter flags a $15,000 deposit into his savings in April. Leo writes a letter explaining it was his annual bonus, attaches the pay stub, and the condition is cleared.
deeper.stakes: Unexplained deposits or new debts can delay or kill a loan. Agents should warn buyers: no big purchases, no unexplained cash moves until after closing.
deeper.exam: The four C's: credit, capacity, capital, collateral. Conditional approval is common and normal.

blocks.html: Rates move daily. A rate lock guarantees a rate and points for a set period, often 30 to 60 days, sometimes for a fee. In NY a lock-in must be in writing and state its terms and expiration. If the closing slips past the lock date, the borrower may face the new market rate or pay to extend, so agents should watch the lock date as closely as the contract date.
blocks.casual: Rates move every day. A rate lock guarantees a rate and points for a set period, often 30 to 60 days, sometimes for a fee. In NY a lock has to be in writing and spell out its terms and expiration. If the closing slips past the lock date, the borrower could get stuck with the new market rate or pay to extend, so agents should watch the lock date as closely as the contract date.

deeper.plain: A rate lock holds your rate for a while. Close late and you could lose it.
deeper.picture: It's like a hotel holding your room until 6 pm. Show up at 9 and you may pay the walk-in rate.
deeper.street: Leo locks 6.5% for 45 days. The condo management office is slow sending the lender its building questionnaire, and his closing slips 10 days past the lock. Rates have jumped to 7%, so he pays a fee to extend the lock rather than lose half a point.
deeper.stakes: A blown lock can add hundreds a month to the payment for 30 years, or tip the buyer over their ratio limits.
deeper.exam: NY lock-in agreements must be in writing with terms and expiration. Locks protect against rate increases for a set period.

blocks.text: How brokers get paid, and loans that don't fit the box

blocks.html: A lender rebate (once called a yield spread premium) is a payment from the lender, usually because the borrower accepted a higher rate. Under federal loan originator compensation rules a broker may be paid by the borrower or the lender in a transaction, not both, and the pay may not vary with the loan's rate or terms. A rebate can instead be passed to the borrower as a lender credit toward closing costs. Either way, it must be disclosed.
blocks.casual: A lender rebate (it used to be called a yield spread premium) is money the lender pays, usually because the borrower took a higher rate. Under the federal loan originator compensation rules, a broker can be paid by the borrower or the lender in a deal, not both, and the pay can't change based on the loan's rate or terms. A rebate can instead go to the borrower as a lender credit toward closing costs. Either way, it has to be disclosed.

deeper.plain: Brokers can be paid by you or by the lender, not both, and their pay can't depend on giving you a worse rate.
deeper.picture: It's a waiter who can take a tip from you or a bonus from the restaurant, but can't get a bigger bonus for steering you to the overpriced wine.
deeper.street: Leo is short on closing cash. Tasha offers 6.75% instead of 6.5% with a $6,000 lender credit toward his closing costs. It's disclosed on the Loan Estimate, and Tasha's own pay from the lender doesn't change based on which rate Leo picks.
deeper.stakes: Brokers who were paid more for pushing higher rates helped fuel the 2008 crisis. Today, taking pay from both sides or tying pay to rate violates federal rules.
deeper.exam: One source of payment per transaction (borrower or lender). Compensation cannot vary with rate or terms. Lender credits must be disclosed.

blocks.html: A conforming loan meets Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac size and underwriting rules. A nonconforming loan does not: a jumbo above the limit ($1,249,125 for a one-unit home in the NYC area in 2026), or a loan for a self-employed borrower with nontraditional income documentation. Brokers earn their keep here, because they know which lenders keep such loans in portfolio.
blocks.casual: A conforming loan meets Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's size and underwriting rules. A nonconforming loan doesn't: think a jumbo above the limit ($1,249,125 for a one-unit home in the NYC area in 2026), or a loan for a self-employed borrower with unusual income paperwork. This is where brokers earn their keep, because they know which lenders keep loans like these in their own portfolio.

deeper.plain: Loans that fit the standard box are easy. The ones that don't need a broker who knows which lenders take odd shapes.
deeper.picture: Standard-size luggage goes on any flight. Surfboards and cellos need an airline that handles oversize items.
deeper.street: A Tribeca buyer needs $2M and has income from three LLCs. Big banks pass. Tasha places the loan with a portfolio lender that keeps jumbos on its books and accepts business bank statements.
deeper.stakes: Without the right lender, a qualified but unusual borrower can lose a deal. Agents with good mortgage broker contacts close deals others can't.
deeper.exam: Nonconforming includes jumbo and non-standard documentation. Portfolio lenders keep loans instead of selling them.

blocks.title: The mortgage broker in a NY deal

items.title: Before the offer
items.html: Prequalify, then preapprove, so the buyer's offer is credible.

items.title: Pre-application disclosure
items.html: Signed fee agreement before any fee is taken; dual agency disclosure if the firm is also the real estate broker.

items.title: After the contract
items.html: Formal application, Loan Estimate within 3 business days, rate lock, appraisal.

items.title: Commitment
items.html: Underwriting issues the commitment before the contingency deadline; conditions cleared.

items.title: Closing
items.html: Closing Disclosure 3 business days before; the lender funds; the broker is paid as disclosed.

blocks.casual:
Here's the mortgage broker's role in a NY deal, start to finish:
1. Before the offer: prequalify, then preapprove, so the buyer's offer is believable.
2. Pre-application disclosure: signed fee agreement before any fee; dual agency disclosure if the firm's also the real estate broker.
3. After the contract: formal application, Loan Estimate within 3 business days, rate lock, appraisal.
4. Commitment: underwriting issues it before the contingency deadline, and the conditions get cleared.
5. Closing: Closing Disclosure 3 business days before; the lender funds; the broker gets paid as disclosed.

deeper.plain: The mortgage broker is involved from before the offer to closing day, with a disclosure at each key step.
deeper.picture: It's a relay race where the broker carries the baton for the whole loan leg, handing off paperwork at each checkpoint.
deeper.street: For Leo's LIC condo: preapproval in March, fee agreement signed, contract signed May 1, application May 2, Loan Estimate May 5, lock May 6, appraisal May 12, commitment May 28 (before the June 1 contingency), Closing Disclosure June 9, closing June 12.
deeper.stakes: Miss a step and the deal stalls: no commitment by the deadline puts the buyer's deposit at risk, and a late Closing Disclosure pushes the closing.
deeper.exam: Order of events questions: prequal, preapproval, pre-application disclosure, application, Loan Estimate (3 business days), commitment, Closing Disclosure (3 business days before), closing.

blocks.q: A buyer accepts a slightly higher rate and the lender pays $4,000 that is applied to the buyer's closing costs. That payment is a:
c: Kickback banned by RESPA
Lender rebate (lender credit)
Discount point
Prepayment penalty
blocks.x: A lender rebate trades a higher rate for money from the lender, here used as a credit to the borrower. Discount points work the opposite way: the borrower pays to lower the rate.

blocks.title: Hook: Broker Brings, Banker Bankrolls
blocks.html: The broker brings the loan to a lender. The banker bankrolls it. Prequal is a Promise from the buyer, preapproval is checked by the lender, commitment is for this house.
blocks.casual: Hook: the broker brings the loan to a lender. The banker bankrolls it. Prequal is a Promise from the buyer, preapproval is checked by the lender, and a commitment is for this house.

deeper.plain: Brings vs bankrolls; promise, checked, this house.
deeper.picture: A broker carrying a loan file across the street to a bank, and a banker opening the vault.
deeper.street: Kim asks a buyer at the board interview, "Who's your lender?" The buyer says, "Tasha." Kim: "She's the broker. She brings it. Who bankrolls it?" The buyer checks the commitment letter: a credit union in White Plains.
deeper.stakes: Knowing who actually funds the loan matters when problems come up at closing. Co-op boards and attorneys will ask.
deeper.exam: Easy points: which one funds (banker), which one arranges (broker), and which letter satisfies the contingency (commitment).

story.title: Two Letters
story.setting: Ditmas Park, a Wednesday evening offer deadline

beats.text: Two offers at $715,000 on a Ditmas Park co-op. Jordan represents the sellers. Kim Alvarez, visiting from her own board, is helping a friend read board packages.
Buyer A has a prequalification from an app. Buyer B has a preapproval from Tasha.
Did anyone actually look at Buyer A's tax returns?
Nobody. Prequal is just what the buyer typed in. Tasha pulled B's credit and checked two years of returns.
The sellers take Buyer B. Jordan calls Tasha with the good news.
Great. I'll get her the Loan Estimate within three business days of the application and lock her rate for 45 days.
Are you funding it?
I'm a broker, registered with DFS. I shop it to lenders. The lender funds it. A mortgage banker would fund it with its own money.

check.q: Which agency regulates Tasha's mortgage brokerage in New York?
c: The Department of State
The Department of Financial Services
HUD
The Federal Reserve
check.x: NY mortgage brokers register with DFS; individual originators are licensed through DFS and NMLS. DOS licenses real estate brokers.

beats.text: Tasha, my firm's thinking of doing mortgages too. Then we get both fees on every deal.
Then you'd need to register, have licensed originators, and give the buyer and seller a dual agency disclosure under the Banking Law before you start. Signed.
Or you just send me a referral fee.
That's a RESPA kickback, Marcus. No.
Thirty days later the commitment arrives, two days before the contingency deadline.
Prequal opens the door, preapproval gets the offer accepted, the commitment gets you to closing. And the lock date is a deadline too.

board.prompt: Draw a ladder with prequalification, preapproval, and commitment. On each rung write who checks what.

A mortgage banker funds loans with its own money, closes in its own name and usually sells the loans on the secondary market.
DFS, not DOS, registers mortgage brokers and licenses mortgage bankers; a real estate license does not authorize brokering mortgages.
An individual mortgage loan originator needs a DFS license through NMLS under the SAFE Act (Banking Law Article 12-E).
A firm acting as both real estate broker and mortgage broker must give a mortgage broker dual agency disclosure (3 NYCRR 38.12), signed by borrower and seller before services begin.
RPL 443 dual agency and Banking Law mortgage broker dual agency are separate, and a firm doing both may need both disclosures.
RESPA bars a real estate licensee from taking a referral fee for sending a buyer to a lender.
Before accepting any fee, a NY mortgage broker gives the pre-application disclosure and fee agreement, signed by both.
The Loan Estimate comes within 3 business days of the application and the Closing Disclosure 3 business days before closing.
Prequalification is an estimate based on what the buyer says, with nothing verified.
Preapproval means the lender pulled credit and reviewed income and assets, conditional on the property and final checks.
A mortgage commitment is a written promise of a specific loan on a specific property, with conditions and an expiration; it satisfies the mortgage contingency.
Underwriting weighs credit, capacity, capital and collateral, and approves, denies or approves with conditions.
A rate lock guarantees a rate and points for a set period; in NY it must be in writing and state its terms and expiration.
If closing slips past the lock date, the borrower may face the market rate or pay to extend.
A lender rebate (once called a yield spread premium) is paid by the lender for a higher rate and can be credited to the borrower's closing costs; it must be disclosed.

lessons.title: Case file: The Rate Lock on Ocean Parkway
lessons.tagline: A self-employed buyer, a slow condo board, a 45-day lock, and a broker who wants to start a mortgage company.
objectives: Decide when a real estate firm becomes a mortgage broker and which DFS registration and dual agency disclosure that triggers
Apply the pre-application disclosure, compensation, and referral fee rules to a mortgage broker's fees and a lender rebate
Distinguish prequalification, preapproval, and commitment, and explain why a self-employed borrower may need a nonconforming loan
Manage a rate lock and commitment against the contract timeline, and calculate points and the NYC mortgage recording tax

blocks.title: Two-bedroom, Kensington
blocks.html: Rosa Delgado and Ben Fisher want a two-bedroom condo on Ocean Parkway in Kensington, Brooklyn, listed at $1,050,000 by Hudson & Hart. Ben is a salaried city planner. Rosa left an agency two years ago to freelance as a graphic designer and now earns more than she did, on paper and off. They have $250,000 saved for the down payment and closing costs. Jordan is their buyer's agent at another desk in the same firm, working as a designated agent with everyone's written consent. At the first meeting, Rosa shows Jordan a "prequalification" from a mortgage app that took her four minutes and says they can borrow $900,000. The listing agent, Marcus, has already told Jordan that the seller will not look at an offer without a real lender letter. Rosa asks, "Isn't this a lender letter?"

The app's letter repeated back what Rosa had typed: income, debts, savings. Nothing was verified, no credit was pulled, and the letter said so in small print. Jordan called Tasha Monroe, a mortgage broker he trusts, who asked for two years of tax returns, recent bank statements, Ben's pay stubs, and permission to pull credit.

blocks.q: Which document would actually reassure the seller about Rosa and Ben's financing?
c: The app prequalification, since it states a specific loan amount
A mortgage commitment, which they can get before choosing a property
A preapproval, after the lender checks credit, income, and assets
A letter from Rosa's accountant stating her annual income
blocks.x: A prequalification is an estimate built from what the borrower says, with nothing checked. A preapproval follows a credit pull and document review, so it shows the buyers are creditworthy, subject to the property and final checks. The commitment choice is the trap: a commitment is issued for a specific loan on a specific property after underwriting and appraisal, so it cannot exist before there is a property.

blocks.html: Tasha's firm, Monroe Mortgage, is a mortgage broker registered with the NYS Department of Financial Services (DFS). It does not lend; it takes the application, shops it to about two dozen lenders, and manages it to closing. Tasha herself holds an individual mortgage loan originator license with an NMLS number on her email signature. Before she would take a dollar, she sat down with Rosa and Ben and went through a form.

blocks.title: Monroe Mortgage: Pre-Application Disclosure and Fee Agreement (excerpt)
blocks.html:
Monroe Mortgage is a registered mortgage broker. We are not a lender and do not make loan decisions.
Services: we will review your finances, identify loan programs, submit your application to one or more lenders, and coordinate processing to closing.
Fees: credit report $45 (non-refundable once ordered). Appraisal: paid to the lender's appraiser at cost. Broker compensation: paid by the lender as disclosed on your Loan Estimate. No broker fee is charged to you.
Refunds: if no loan closes, fees not yet spent on third-party services are refunded.

blocks.q: Why does Tasha give Rosa and Ben this form before collecting the $45 credit fee?
c: NY requires it before a broker takes an application or any fee
A credit fee can be charged once the lender issues a commitment
The form doubles as the Loan Estimate required by federal law
It is the dual agency disclosure required when brokers serve two parties
blocks.x: New York requires a mortgage broker to give the pre-application disclosure and fee agreement, signed by both sides, before taking an application or any fee. It says the broker is not a lender and spells out services, fees, refundability, and how the broker is paid. The Loan Estimate is the trap: it is a separate federal form the lender issues within 3 business days after an application.

blocks.html: Rosa asked why Tasha was free to her. Tasha explained the federal loan originator compensation rule: in any one loan, a broker can be paid by the borrower or by the lender, not both, and the amount may not vary with the loan's interest rate or terms. Monroe Mortgage takes lender-paid compensation, 1% of the loan amount, the same at any rate.

blocks.q: Monroe Mortgage is paid 1% by the lender. Late in the process, Tasha's processor suggests also charging Rosa and Ben a $1,500 "processing fee" for the extra work on Rosa's file. What is the problem?
c: Nothing wrong, as long as the fee is on the Closing Disclosure
It is fine for self-employed files, which justify higher fees
It must be approved by DFS before the borrowers are billed
It collects broker pay from both the lender and the borrowers
blocks.x: When the lender pays the broker's compensation, the broker may not also take compensation from the borrower on the same loan, whatever the fee is called. A genuine third-party cost passed through at cost is different. The disclosure choice is the trap: disclosing a prohibited payment does not make it permitted, and the original fee agreement said no broker fee would be charged.

blocks.html: Tasha ran the numbers. On a $1,050,000 price, an $840,000 loan is 80% loan-to-value. That amount is within the conforming limit for Brooklyn, so a Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac loan would normally be the cheapest option. The problem was Rosa's income. Her tax returns showed one partial year at the agency and one full year of freelancing, with heavy business deductions, so her taxable income was far lower than her deposits. Ben's salary alone did not support the payment.

blocks.q: Why might Rosa and Ben end up with a nonconforming loan even though $840,000 is under the conforming loan limit?
c: Every Brooklyn condo loan above $750,000 is classified as nonconforming
Rosa's income records may not meet Fannie and Freddie underwriting rules
Nonconforming loans are required whenever the down payment is 20% or more
A loan arranged through a broker instead of a bank is nonconforming by definition
blocks.x: A conforming loan meets Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac rules on both size and underwriting. Loan amount is only one test. A self-employed borrower with a short history or income documented by bank statements rather than tax returns may need a lender that keeps such loans in portfolio. The broker-versus-bank choice is the trap: who arranges the loan has nothing to do with whether it conforms.

blocks.html: Tasha found two paths. A conforming loan would count only Ben's salary plus Rosa's taxable income, which worked if they put down 30% instead of 20%. A nonconforming bank-statement loan from a portfolio lender would count Rosa's actual deposits, at about three-quarters of a percentage point higher in rate. They chose the conforming loan with more down, borrowing $735,000, because the rate difference over thirty years was larger than the extra cash. Tasha issued a preapproval from the lender she planned to use. Jordan attached it to an offer at $1,050,000, and it was accepted.

While Rosa and Ben's deal was in contract, Diane called a meeting. A lender's account rep had offered Hudson & Hart's agents a "marketing fee" of $500 for every buyer sent his way. Separately, Marcus had suggested the firm start doing mortgages itself: "We see every buyer first. Why let Tasha get paid?"

blocks.q: Can Hudson & Hart accept the lender's $500 per-buyer "marketing fee"?
c: Yes, if each buyer is told about the fee in writing
No, RESPA bars paying for referrals
Yes, if the money is paid to the firm rather than to agents
No, unless Hudson & Hart first registers with DFS
blocks.x: RESPA Section 8 prohibits giving or accepting anything of value for referring settlement service business, such as a mortgage, on federally related loans. Calling it a marketing fee does not change what it pays for. Disclosure is the trap: a written notice does not cure a kickback, and registering with DFS would not make a referral fee lawful either.

blocks.html: Marcus's idea was different, and lawful if done right. Diane had read Banking Law 590: a real estate broker or salesperson who helps a buyer with a mortgage is not treated as a mortgage broker as long as he takes no fee, directly or indirectly, for that help. The moment Hudson & Hart wanted to be paid for arranging loans, it would need to register with DFS as a mortgage broker, and anyone at the firm taking applications or discussing loan terms would need an MLO license.

blocks.q: Jordan sometimes explains loan basics to buyers and suggests a few lenders, for free. When would that become regulated mortgage brokering?
c: When he mentions more than three lenders to one buyer
When he explains interest rates or points to a buyer
When a buyer he advised actually closes on a loan
When he or his firm is paid for arranging it
blocks.x: Banking Law 590 says a real estate licensee is not engaged in the mortgage broker business if he does not accept a fee, directly or indirectly, for those services. Free general help is not brokering; a fee for arranging loans requires DFS registration and licensed originators. The three-lenders choice is the trap: that number appears in the dual agency disclosure, not in the definition.

blocks.html: Diane decided to explore it properly. Priya and a banking lawyer explained the next layer: if Hudson & Hart registered and then arranged a loan for a buyer of one of its own listings, it would be both the seller's real estate broker and the buyer's mortgage broker in one transaction.

blocks.title: Two different dual agencies
blocks.html: Real estate dual agency under RPL 443 is one brokerage representing both buyer and seller in the sale. Mortgage broker dual agency under the DFS rule (3 NYCRR 38.12) is one firm acting as the seller's real estate broker and the buyer's mortgage broker in the same deal. A firm doing both on one transaction may need both disclosures, from two different regulators.

blocks.q: Hudson & Hart registers as a mortgage broker and wants to arrange the loan for a buyer of one of its own listings. When must the mortgage broker dual agency disclosure be given and signed?
c: At first substantive contact, signed by both sides before services
At closing, signed by the buyer, when the loan amount is final
Within 3 business days after the loan application, signed by the lender
Whenever the firm uses three or fewer lenders, signed by the buyer
blocks.x: Under 3 NYCRR 38.12 the disclosure is given at the first substantive contact with the buyer/borrower, and both the buyer and the seller must sign it before the firm provides mortgage brokerage services. The form includes a checkbox saying whether the firm places loans with three or fewer lenders. The three-lenders choice is the trap: that fact is disclosed in every case, not a trigger for the form.

blocks.html: Diane has not decided. The disclosure is manageable; what worried her was the conflict it describes. A firm paid on the sale and on the loan earns more when any deal closes at any price, and she was not sure her buyers would ever believe otherwise.

Marcus pushed one step further: why not lend the money, too? Priya explained the difference in one breath. A mortgage broker arranges loans and the lender's money closes them. A mortgage banker funds loans with its own money, usually a warehouse line of credit, closes them in its own name, and sells most of them on the secondary market. That takes a DFS license, net worth and financial requirements far beyond a registration, and the appetite to hold a loan if no investor will buy it. Diane laughed and said Hudson & Hart would be sticking to houses for now.

blocks.text: Back to Ocean Parkway: the lock

blocks.html: Rosa and Ben signed the contract on March 3 with a mortgage contingency requiring a commitment by April 17 and a closing "on or about" May 1. Tasha submitted the application and the lender issued a Loan Estimate the next day. Rates had been climbing, so on March 10 Tasha locked their rate at 6.375% with no points for 45 days, expiring April 24.

blocks.q: Rosa and Ben applied on Thursday, March 5. Under federal rules, by when must the Loan Estimate be delivered or mailed?
c: By Sunday, March 8, three calendar days later
By Thursday, March 12, one week later
By Tuesday, March 10, three business days later
By April 4, thirty days after the application
blocks.x: The Loan Estimate must be delivered or placed in the mail within 3 business days after the lender receives the application. Counting Friday, Monday, and Tuesday, that is March 10. The calendar-day answer is the trap: the rule counts business days. The Closing Disclosure has its own clock, at least 3 business days before consummation.

blocks.html: The Loan Estimate is the borrowers' baseline. Rosa saved it, because the Closing Disclosure at the end would be compared line by line against it, and certain fees cannot rise at all between the two documents without a valid reason. Tasha told her the most common reason numbers change legitimately is the borrower changing something: a different loan amount, a different lock, a different program.

head: Date
Event
rows: Contract signed; commitment due April 17; closing on or about May 1
Lender's condo questionnaire still unanswered by the managing agent
Commitment issued, conditioned on the condo questionnaire and a letter explaining a $40,000 deposit
Managing agent says the questionnaire will take another two weeks
blocks.caption: The Delgado-Fisher loan timeline

blocks.html: The commitment arrived two days before the contingency deadline, with conditions. One was easy: a $40,000 deposit in Rosa's account in February. Underwriting wanted to know where it came from. It was a client's payment for a branding project, and Rosa sent the invoice and a short letter. The other condition depended on the building's managing agent, who was slow.

blocks.q: The underwriter asks about Rosa's $40,000 February deposit. What is the underwriter checking?
c: Whether the seller's agent knew about the deposit when setting the price
Whether the deposit was large enough to require a cash transaction report
That Rosa paid sales tax on the branding work she billed
That the funds are Rosa's own and not an undisclosed loan or gift
blocks.x: Underwriting reviews capital as well as credit, capacity, and collateral. A large, unexplained deposit could be a new loan that would change the debt ratios or a gift that needs documentation. An invoice and a letter of explanation clear it. The reporting choice is the trap: currency reports are a bank's anti-money laundering duty, not what a mortgage underwriter is asking about.

blocks.html: The questionnaire was the real problem. With the managing agent promising two more weeks, closing could not happen before mid-May, and the lock expired April 24. Tasha laid out the choices for Rosa and Ben in one email: extend the lock for 15 days for a fee of 0.25% of the loan, or let it lapse and take whatever the market rate was at relock, which that week was 6.75%.

blocks.title: Tasha's math
blocks.html:
Loan: $735,000.
Lock extension: 0.25% x $735,000 = $1,837.50.
Relock at 6.75% instead of 6.375%: the monthly principal and interest rises by about $180, or roughly $2,160 a year.
Recommendation: extend.

blocks.q: Rosa and Ben extend the lock, and the lender offers to drop the rate to 6.25% if they pay 1 point at closing. How much is 1 point on their loan?
blocks.x: One point is 1% of the loan amount, not the price: 1% of $735,000 is $7,350. The $10,500 choice is the trap: it is 1% of the $1,050,000 purchase price, a common mistake when buyers hear "points" and think of the house rather than the loan.

blocks.html: They declined the point; at their expected seven years in the condo, the savings would not repay it. The extension was ordered on April 21. Jordan, meanwhile, sent the seller's attorney a request to adjourn closing to May 20, explaining the questionnaire delay. Because the contract said "on or about," a reasonable adjournment was within the deal's terms. He also watched a date nobody else was watching: the commitment itself expired June 1.

blocks.q: Why does Jordan care about the commitment's expiration date as well as the rate lock's?
c: Because the mortgage contingency is cancelled if the commitment has an expiration date
Because if closing slips past it, the lender can re-underwrite or decline to fund
Because the seller may demand a new appraisal after the commitment expires
Because the commitment expiring automatically extends the rate lock
blocks.x: A commitment is good for a stated period and subject to its conditions. If closing slips past the expiration, the lender may require updated documents, re-underwrite, or decline to extend, and many downstate contracts treat the contingency as satisfied once the commitment was issued. The rate lock choice is the trap: the lock and the commitment are separate, and neither extends the other.

blocks.text: Closing costs and the last three days

blocks.html: The questionnaire arrived May 6, the conditions cleared May 9, and the lender sent the Closing Disclosure on May 13 for a May 20 closing. Rosa read it on the subway and called Tasha about one line.

head: Item (buyer side, partial)
Amount
rows: NYC and NYS mortgage recording tax, borrower share (1.925% of $735,000)
Mansion tax (1% of price, $1M or more)
blocks.caption: Selected lines from the Closing Disclosure

blocks.q: Rosa asks why the mortgage recording tax uses 1.925% instead of 1.8%. What is the reason?
c: NYC's borrower rate for condo loans rises once the loan hits $500,000
The rate is higher because the property is a condo instead of a co-op
The rate is higher because the loan was arranged through a broker
The rate rises once the purchase price reaches $1,000,000
blocks.x: For NYC 1 to 3 family homes and condo units, the borrower's mortgage recording tax is 1.8% on loans under $500,000 and 1.925% on loans of $500,000 or more; the lender pays an additional 0.25%. The $1,000,000 choice is the trap: that threshold belongs to the mansion tax, which is based on the price, not the loan. Co-op loans are not mortgages and pay no recording tax.

blocks.html: The Closing Disclosure arrived at least 3 business days before closing, as federal rules require, which gave Rosa time to check it against the Loan Estimate. Every number matched what Tasha had told them, including the broker compensation line showing payment by the lender and nothing charged to the buyers. They closed on May 20. Rosa's bank-statement loan option, the one they did not take, is still in Tasha's notes for the day Rosa wants a bigger place.

blocks.title: Commitment issued is not loan funded
blocks.html: Exam items like to say the mortgage contingency protects the buyer "until closing." In most downstate contracts it is satisfied when the commitment issues. After that, a lapsed lock, an expired commitment, or a lost job can leave a buyer owing the closing with no contingency to fall back on. Watching those dates is part of the agent's job, even though the agent is not the mortgage broker.

items: Prequalification is self-reported; preapproval is verified; a commitment is for a specific loan on a specific property.
A mortgage broker gives the pre-application disclosure and fee agreement before taking an application or fee, and is paid by the borrower or the lender in a given loan, not both.
Referral fees from lenders to real estate agents violate RESPA. A real estate licensee who takes any fee for arranging loans must register with DFS, and the people doing the work need MLO licenses.
A firm acting as both real estate broker and mortgage broker in one deal gives the 3 NYCRR 38.12 disclosure at first substantive contact, signed by buyer and seller before mortgage services.
Conforming status depends on underwriting rules as well as loan size; self-employed borrowers often face that test.
Track the lock, the commitment's expiration, and the contingency date together. One point is 1% of the loan; NYC mortgage recording tax for the borrower rises to 1.925% at $500,000.

roleplays.title: Leo's Loan Day
roleplays.setting: Leo just signed a contract on a condo. Tasha, a mortgage broker, is meeting him to start the loan. Jordan sits in as his buyer's agent.
roleplays.you: Tasha, the mortgage broker (registered with DFS)
roleplays.goal: Start the loan correctly: the right disclosures, honest answers about compensation and rate locks, and a commitment before the contingency deadline.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Leo Brandt, an anxious first-time buyer starting his mortgage with a mortgage broker, plus Jordan, his real estate agent. Leo tries to pay a fee immediately, asks bluntly how the broker is paid and whether the lender pays more for higher rates, asks about points and jumbo limits, asks the broker to bump his income, asks to lock a rate for a 50-day closing, and later asks whether his preapproval satisfies his contingency. Jordan asks what his firm needs to arrange mortgages itself and fishes for a referral fee. The learner is the DFS-registered mortgage broker and must apply the pre-application disclosure and fee agreement, the Banking Law dual agency disclosure, loan originator compensation rules, RESPA's ban on referral fees, written rate locks, honest applications, and the commitment vs preapproval distinction. Grade on accuracy and transparency.

cafe: a coffee shop by the courthouse

opening: {day} at {cafe}. Leo signed the contract on his {hood} condo yesterday. His mortgage contingency is 45 days. Jordan is here to listen.
Leo brought a folder of pay stubs and a credit card. You're the mortgage broker, the loan will likely go to {lender}, and the clock starts now.
