deeper.stakes: Counting a new roof as an operating expense makes NOI look terrible for one year and can tank a sale price or refinance.
deeper.exam: Taxes and insurance = fixed. Utilities, repairs, supplies = variable. Boiler, roof, windows = capital, not in NOI.

blocks.title: Why Sal needs $2,000 a month
blocks.html:
Boiler replacement: $45,000, needed in about 4 years.
Roof: $60,000, needed in about 6 years.
Per year: $45,000 / 4 = $11,250; $60,000 / 6 = $10,000. Total $21,250 a year.
Per month: $21,250 / 12 = about $1,771, so $2,000 a month covers it with a small cushion.
Skip it, and the boiler fails in January with no money set aside.
blocks.casual:
Here's why Sal needs $2,000 a month.
Boiler replacement: $45,000, needed in about 4 years.
Roof: $60,000, needed in about 6 years.
Per year: $45,000 / 4 = $11,250; $60,000 / 6 = $10,000. Total $21,250 a year.
Per month: $21,250 / 12 = about $1,771, so $2,000 a month covers it with a little cushion.
Skip it, and the boiler dies in January with nothing set aside.

deeper.plain: Divide each future cost by the years until it's due, add them up, and divide by 12.
deeper.picture: Two buckets filling up at different speeds, one for the boiler and one for the roof, each set to be full right when it's needed.
deeper.street: Jordan shows Sal the math on one page. Sal grumbles, then says, "Fine, but put it in an account with my name on it." The firm sets up a separate reserve account and reports the balance monthly.
deeper.stakes: Underfunding reserves pushes costs onto a future emergency, often at the worst time of year.
deeper.exam: Reserve per year = replacement cost / years remaining. Expect a quick division question.

blocks.q: Which expense belongs in the capital reserve budget rather than the operating budget?
c: Monthly heating oil
Replacing the roof
The super's salary
Annual liability insurance premium
blocks.x: A roof replacement is a capital expense funded from reserves. Fuel, payroll, and insurance are recurring operating expenses.

blocks.html: A rent roll lists every unit, tenant, lease dates, current rent, deposit held, and status (occupied, vacant, arrears). It is the first document any buyer, lender, or appraiser asks for.
blocks.casual: A rent roll lists every unit, the tenant, lease dates, current rent, the deposit held, and status (occupied, vacant, behind on rent). It's the first thing any buyer, lender or appraiser asks for.

deeper.plain: The rent roll is a snapshot of who's paying what in every unit right now.
deeper.picture: It's the building's class roster with each student's grades and attendance.
deeper.street: A Bayside investor eyeing Sal's building asks for the rent roll before anything else. A lender reviewing Sal's refinance wants it too, and checks it against bank deposits.
deeper.stakes: An inflated or sloppy rent roll can be fraud in a sale or refinance and gets caught when leases and deposits don't match.
deeper.exam: Rent roll = unit, tenant, lease dates, rent, deposit, status. It's not the operating budget.

head: Unit
Tenant
Lease ends
Monthly rent
Deposit
Status
blocks.caption: Sal's rent roll. Potential monthly rent: $12,850.

deeper.plain: Reading a rent roll tells you what's working and what isn't, unit by unit.
deeper.picture: Scan it like a report card: most grades are fine, but a few red marks jump out.
deeper.street: Sal's roll totals $12,850 a month in potential rent. 1B is vacant at $2,600 asking, 2B is a month behind on $2,500, and 3A is Sal's niece at $1,500 with no deposit. The two stabilized units, 1A and 3B, can only rise by Rent Guidelines Board increases.
deeper.stakes: Missing these flags means overestimating income, which hurts budgeting, sale pricing and lender trust.
deeper.exam: Potential gross income comes from the rent roll, including vacant units at market rent, before subtracting vacancy and collection loss.

blocks.caption: Start at the rent roll, subtract vacancy and operating expenses to reach NOI, then set aside the capital reserve below the line.

blocks.title: From rent roll to NOI
blocks.html:
Potential gross income: $12,850 x 12 = $154,200.
Vacancy and collection loss (5%): $7,710.
Effective gross income: $146,490.
Operating expenses: taxes $28,000 + insurance $9,500 + fuel $14,000 + water $6,500 + repairs $10,000 + super $12,000 + management fee (5% of EGI) $7,325 = $87,325.
NOI = $59,165.
Reserves ($24,000 a year) and mortgage payments come out after NOI.
Exam trap: a reserve deposit is not an operating expense. Subtract it before NOI and you understate NOI, which makes the building look less valuable than it is.
blocks.casual:
From rent roll to NOI:
Potential gross income: $12,850 x 12 = $154,200.
Vacancy and collection loss (5%): $7,710.
Effective gross income: $146,490.
Operating expenses: taxes $28,000 + insurance $9,500 + fuel $14,000 + water $6,500 + repairs $10,000 + super $12,000 + management fee (5% of EGI) $7,325 = $87,325.
NOI = $59,165.
Reserves ($24,000 a year) and mortgage payments come out after NOI.

deeper.plain: Start with full rent, knock off expected vacancy, subtract operating costs, and you've got NOI.
deeper.picture: A funnel: everything pours in at the top as potential rent, and each layer filters out vacancy and expenses until NOI drips out the bottom.
deeper.street: After NOI of $59,165, Sal still sets aside $24,000 in reserves and pays his mortgage. What's left is his actual cash.
deeper.stakes: Put the mortgage into operating expenses and NOI looks lower than it is, which can lowball the building's value.
deeper.exam: NOI excludes debt service, depreciation and income tax. Management fee is usually based on collected income (EGI).

blocks.title: Read the roll like a buyer
blocks.html: The rent roll above flags three things: a family member paying below market with no deposit, a tenant 30 days late, and a vacant unit. A sharp manager reports all three to the owner with a plan.
blocks.casual: Read the roll like a buyer would. This one flags three things: a family member paying below market with no deposit, a tenant 30 days late, and an empty unit. A sharp manager reports all three to the owner, with a plan for each.

deeper.plain: Spot the problems in the rent roll and bring the owner solutions, not just bad news.
deeper.picture: Like a doctor who reads the chart, names three issues and writes a prescription for each.
deeper.street: Jordan's note to Sal: "3A: your niece, $1,500 with no deposit; your call, but buyers will discount it. 2B: payment plan offered. 1B: 4 showings, 2 applications, recommend $2,575."
deeper.stakes: A manager who hides weak spots gets blamed when a buyer or lender finds them later.
deeper.exam: Below-market related-party leases, arrears and vacancies are the classic rent roll red flags.

head: Type
What it is
Example
rows: Scheduled work that stops problems before they happen
Annual boiler cleaning, roof inspection, gutter clearing
Replacing a failed circulator pump, fixing a leak in 2B
Mopping halls, taking out trash, changing bulbs
Needed work that has been put off
Cracked parapet, worn roof, rotting window sills

deeper.plain: Maintenance is either planned ahead, a fix after something breaks, everyday cleaning, or work that's been put off.
deeper.picture: Brushing your teeth is preventive, a filling is corrective, mouthwash is routine, and the cavity you ignored is deferred.
deeper.street: In Sal's building, the annual boiler cleaning is preventive. Replacing the dead circulator pump is corrective. The porter mopping halls is routine. The cracked parapet nobody fixed is deferred, and it's exactly what an HPD inspector or an appraiser will notice.
deeper.stakes: Lean on deferred maintenance and value drops, violations pile up and the eventual fix costs more.
deeper.exam: Deferred maintenance reduces value. Preventive is scheduled to avoid problems. Corrective fixes what already broke.

blocks.html: Preventive maintenance costs money now and saves more later. Deferred maintenance lowers value: buyers and appraisers deduct for it, and in NYC it shows up as HPD violations. Managers also handle construction work: tenant improvements for commercial tenants and capital projects.
blocks.casual: Preventive maintenance costs money now and saves more later. Deferred maintenance drags value down: buyers and appraisers knock it off the price, and in NYC it turns into HPD violations. Managers also handle construction work: tenant improvements for commercial tenants and capital projects.

deeper.plain: Pay a little now for upkeep or pay a lot later in lost value and violations.
deeper.picture: An oil change versus a new engine.
deeper.street: A buyer's inspector, Ray, points at the worn roof on Sal's building and estimates $60,000. The buyer cuts the offer by that much plus a hassle discount. Evelyn's manager, meanwhile, builds out a new dentist's office in her retail strip as a tenant improvement.
deeper.stakes: Ignoring deferred maintenance costs the owner more at sale than fixing it would have.
deeper.exam: Deferred maintenance is a form of physical deterioration that appraisers deduct. Tenant improvements are construction a manager may oversee.

blocks.q: Sal's manager schedules a boiler cleaning every August before heating season. This is:
c: Corrective maintenance
Deferred maintenance
Preventive maintenance
A capital expense
blocks.x: Scheduled work to prevent failure is preventive. Corrective is fixing what broke; deferred is work postponed.

blocks.html: Risk management means identifying what could go wrong and choosing how to handle it. Four strategies:
blocks.casual: Risk management means figuring out what could go wrong and picking how to handle it. There are four ways:

deeper.plain: List what could go wrong, then decide whether to avoid it, reduce it, pass it on, or live with it.
deeper.picture: Like planning a road trip: skip the icy route, drive slower, buy insurance, or accept a flat tire might happen.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart walks Sal's building and lists risks: slip on the icy stoop, fire, burst pipe, a contractor's ladder fall. Each one gets a strategy and, where needed, a policy.
deeper.stakes: A manager who never assesses risk leaves the owner exposed to lawsuits and uninsured losses.
deeper.exam: Risk management = identify, then avoid, control, transfer or retain.

head: Strategy
Meaning
Example
rows: Close the roof deck instead of allowing parties
Lower the odds or the damage
Sprinklers, smoke detectors, better lighting, secure doors
Shift the risk to someone else
Insurance; requiring contractors to carry insurance; tenant liability clauses
Accept it and pay if it happens
A higher deductible; small losses paid from reserves

deeper.plain: You can skip a risk, shrink it, hand it off, or accept it.
deeper.picture: Four doors: don't go in, go in carefully, send someone else, or go in and take your chances.
deeper.street: Sal closes the roof deck to avoid party falls. He adds smoke detectors and brighter hallway lights to control fire and crime risk. He requires every contractor to show insurance to transfer risk. He raises his deductible to $5,000 to retain small losses and cut premiums.
deeper.stakes: Picking the wrong strategy means paying too much for coverage or getting hit with a loss you can't afford.
deeper.exam: Insurance and contractor insurance requirements = transfer. Higher deductible = retain. Sprinklers = control.

blocks.title: Hook
blocks.html: ACTR: Avoid, Control, Transfer, Retain. Insurance is the "transfer" one.
blocks.casual: Memory hook: ACTR: Avoid, Control, Transfer, Retain. Insurance is the "transfer" one.

deeper.plain: Four strategies, one acronym.
deeper.picture: Picture an actor (ACTR) on stage handing off a hot potato: transfer is the hand-off.
deeper.street: Jordan scribbles ACTR on the inside cover of the property file for Sal's building and checks every risk against it.
deeper.stakes: Forgetting one option can mean over-insuring or ignoring cheap fixes like better lighting.
deeper.exam: "Purchasing insurance" is always transfer. Don't let "control" tempt you.

blocks.html: Typical coverage: property (fire and extended perils), general liability, umbrella, boiler and machinery, flood where needed, workers' compensation for employees, rent loss (business interruption), and fidelity bonds for staff handling money.
blocks.casual: The usual coverage: property (fire and extended perils), general liability, umbrella, boiler and machinery, flood where needed, workers' comp for employees, rent loss (business interruption), and fidelity bonds for staff who handle money.

deeper.plain: A building needs several policies, each covering a different kind of loss.
deeper.picture: Layers of clothing in winter: each one covers a different part, and the umbrella is the coat over everything.
deeper.street: When a pipe bursts at a Rockaway building after a storm, property insurance covers the damage, flood coverage handles the surge, and rent loss covers the months tenants can't live there. The super's slip on the wet floor goes to workers' comp.
deeper.stakes: A missing policy, like flood near the water or a fidelity bond for staff collecting rents, can leave the owner with a loss nobody pays for.
deeper.exam: Rent loss = business interruption. Fidelity bond covers employee theft. Workers' comp covers employees, not tenants.

blocks.text: The management proposal and the report

blocks.html: Before getting hired, a manager submits a management proposal: an analysis of the property and market, a proposed operating budget and capital plan, a marketing plan (target tenants, rents, advertising), the services offered, and the fee. It is the manager's pitch backed by numbers.
blocks.casual: Before getting hired, a manager sends a management proposal: an analysis of the property and the market, a proposed operating budget and capital plan, a marketing plan (target tenants, rents, advertising), the services offered, and the fee. It's the pitch, backed by numbers.

deeper.plain: The proposal is the manager's plan and price, put in front of the owner before the job starts.
deeper.picture: It's a contractor's bid, but for running a building instead of building a deck.
deeper.street: Hudson & Hart competes with a Long Island City firm for Evelyn's retail strip. Diane's proposal shows a budget, a plan for a grocery anchor, and a 4% fee. Evelyn picks it because the numbers make sense.
deeper.stakes: A proposal with fantasy numbers wins the job and then loses the client when reality shows up.
deeper.exam: Proposal comes before hiring; management report comes after. Proposal includes budget, marketing plan, services, fee.

blocks.html: Once hired, the manager sends a property management report, usually monthly: income collected vs budget, expenses, arrears, vacancies, leasing activity, maintenance done, problems and recommendations, plus an annual report and next year's budget.
blocks.casual: Once hired, the manager sends a property management report, usually monthly: income collected versus budget, expenses, arrears, vacancies, leasing activity, maintenance done, problems and recommendations. Plus an annual report and next year's budget.

deeper.plain: The report tells the owner how the building did this month and what needs attention.
deeper.picture: It's the building's monthly report card sent home to the owner.
deeper.street: Every 15th, Sal gets a report from Hudson & Hart. He skips to the arrears line and the recommendations, then calls Jordan with questions.
deeper.stakes: Late or vague reports are one of the top reasons owners fire managers, and missing records can look like hiding money.
deeper.exam: Monthly report compares actual to budget. Annual report includes next year's budget.

blocks.title: Jordan's monthly report to Sal

items.title: Money in
items.html: Rents collected vs the rent roll, with arrears by unit (2B is 30 days late; payment plan offered).

items.title: Money out
items.html: Expenses vs budget, explained (fuel ran 12% over in a cold February).

items.title: Building
items.html: Work done, open violations, upcoming preventive work.

items.title: Leasing
items.html: Vacancy in 1B: showings, applications, proposed rent.

items.title: Recommendations
items.html: Fund the reserve; replace the boiler next summer, not next January.

blocks.casual:
Jordan's monthly report to Sal:
Money in: rents collected versus the rent roll, with arrears by unit (2B is 30 days late; payment plan offered).
Money out: expenses versus budget, explained (fuel ran 12% over in a cold February).
Building: work done, open violations, upcoming preventive work.
Leasing: the vacancy in 1B, with showings, applications and the proposed rent.
Recommendations: fund the reserve; replace the boiler next summer, not next January.

deeper.plain: A good report covers money in, money out, the building, leasing, and what to do next.
deeper.picture: Five sections like a newspaper: business, expenses, local news, classifieds, and the editorial.
deeper.street: Sal reads that fuel ran 12% over in February and sees why: a cold snap. He also sees Jordan's recommendation to swap the boiler in July, when a shutdown means no tenant goes without heat.
deeper.stakes: A report with no recommendations leaves the owner guessing. A report that explains variances builds trust.
deeper.exam: Expect a question on what belongs in a management report: income versus budget, expenses, vacancies, arrears, maintenance, recommendations.

blocks.q: A manager pitching an Upper West Side co-op board submits an analysis of the building, a proposed budget, and a fee schedule. This document is a:
c: Property management report
Management proposal
Rent roll
Stabilized budget
blocks.x: The proposal comes before hiring and sells the manager's plan. The report comes after, showing actual results.

story.title: Spend It When It Breaks
story.setting: Sal's building, the boiler room, 6 am in October

beats.text: Ray Kowalski, flashlight in hand, is staring at Sal's boiler like it insulted his mother.
Twenty-six years old. Heat exchanger's weeping. She'll give you one winter. Maybe.
So I fix it when it breaks. That's how my father did it.
That's corrective maintenance, Sal. The cleaning we do every August is preventive. What you've got now is deferred: work that should've happened already.
And this $2,000 a month you want?
That's the capital reserve budget. Boiler in four years, roof in six. Set it aside monthly and it's never a crisis.

check.q: A new boiler is paid for from which budget?
c: Operating budget
Capital reserve budget
Marketing plan
Rent roll
check.x: Replacing a long-lived component is a capital expense, funded from reserves, not the annual operating budget.

beats.text: Fine. And the operating budget is what?
This year's rent and this year's bills. Taxes and insurance stay fixed. Fuel and repairs move around. Those are variable.
Meanwhile somebody put a space heater in 2B with an extension cord. That's a fire.
Risk management. We control it: talk to the tenant, fix the heat. And we transfer it: your liability policy needs to be current.
You're going to tell me all this every month?
In the management report. Rents in, bills out, what got fixed, what's coming. One page plus the details.
Back at the office, Diane reads the report. "A good manager makes the owner's emergencies boring. Nice work."

board.prompt: Sort these into a 2x2 grid (preventive, corrective, routine, deferred): boiler cleaning, mopping halls, replacing a burst pipe, a cracked parapet ignored for 3 years.

facts.text: An operating budget covers one year of expected income and day-to-day expenses.
A stabilized budget is a multi-year forecast smoothed into a typical (normalized) year.
A capital reserve budget sets money aside for big replacements: each item's cost divided by its years left, summed and spread monthly.
Fixed expenses (taxes, insurance) stay the same regardless of occupancy; variable expenses (utilities, repairs, supplies) move with use.
A capital expense (new boiler, roof, windows) comes from reserves and is not an operating expense; reserve deposits and mortgage payments come out after NOI.
A rent roll lists each unit, tenant, lease dates, rent, deposit and status, and is the first document buyers, lenders and appraisers ask for.
NOI from a rent roll: monthly rents x 12 = PGI, minus vacancy and collection loss = EGI, minus operating expenses = NOI.
Preventive maintenance is scheduled work that stops problems; corrective fixes what broke; routine is daily housekeeping.
Deferred maintenance is needed work put off; it lowers value and in NYC shows up as HPD violations.
The four risk strategies are avoid, control, transfer and retain (ACTR); insurance is transfer, and better locks or lighting are control.
Typical coverage includes property, liability, umbrella, boiler and machinery, flood, workers' comp, rent loss and fidelity bonds for staff handling money.
A management proposal, made before hiring, analyzes the property and market and gives a budget, marketing plan, services and fee.
Once hired, the manager sends a management report, usually monthly: collections vs budget, expenses, arrears, vacancies, leasing and maintenance.

lessons.title: Case file: Sal's Sticky Note for Apartment 1B
lessons.tagline: Sal signs a real management agreement, then hands Jordan a sticky note of tenant rules for the vacant unit. Almost every line on it is illegal.
objectives: Decide whether a management agreement clause protects the owner, the tenants and the broker, and fix the one that does not
Apply New York fee, deposit and FARE Act limits to the leasing of a vacant market-rate apartment
Apply federal, state and city fair housing rules, including source of income and Fair Chance Housing, to tenant selection
Calculate the security deposit interest owed to a tenant and set up the paperwork a new lease needs

blocks.title: The handshake becomes paper
blocks.html: After a month of Jordan sending monthly reports on a handshake, Diane put her foot down: no more work for Sal Russo until there is a signed management agreement between Sal and Hudson & Hart. Sal signs it at his kitchen table on 31st Avenue in Astoria, grumbling about lawyers. Then he slides a yellow sticky note across the table. “For 1B. My rules.” The note says: $100 application fee. Tenant pays broker fee, one month. Two months deposit, the floors are new. No Section 8. No more than 2 people. Run criminal on everybody first. No one who has been to housing court. 40x the rent, no exceptions. Jordan has already reviewed the agreement. Before reading the note, Jordan wants one clause in that agreement fixed.

blocks.title: Management agreement, Hudson & Hart Realty and Salvatore Russo (excerpt)
blocks.html:
1. Property. Six-unit residential building, 31st Avenue, Astoria, Queens, including the basement boiler room and rear yard.
2. Term. One year from November 1, renewing year to year; either party may end it on 60 days' written notice.
3. Authority. Agent may advertise and show units, sign leases at rents approved by Owner, collect rents, and contract for repairs up to $5,000 per item without prior approval; emergency repairs to protect life or property at any amount, with notice to Owner within 24 hours.
4. Fee. 5% of rents actually collected, plus a leasing fee of one month's rent per new lease, paid by Owner.
5. Accounts. Rents deposited in a client trust account at a New York bank in Owner's name. Tenant security deposits will be deposited in Owner's operating account and used as needed for building expenses.
6. Reports. Monthly statement by the 15th; annual budget each October.
7. Insurance. Owner keeps property and liability insurance naming Agent as additional insured.
8. Compliance. Agent will comply with all fair housing and rent laws and may decline any instruction that would violate them.

blocks.q: Which clause in the agreement has to change before Hudson & Hart can operate under it?
c: Clause 3, because a manager may not sign leases on an owner's behalf
Clause 8, because the duty of obedience means following each owner instruction
Clause 5, because deposits cannot go into the owner's operating account
Clause 4, because a fee based on rents collected creates a conflict of interest
blocks.x: Security deposits are the tenants' money held in trust. They cannot be commingled with the owner's funds or spent on the building, and because Sal's building has six units they must sit in an interest-bearing account at a New York bank. The obedience answer is the trap: a fiduciary obeys lawful instructions only, which is exactly why clause 8 belongs in the agreement. Leasing authority and a percentage fee are standard.

blocks.html: Clause 5 is rewritten: deposits go into a separate interest-bearing escrow account at a New York bank, each tenant gets written notice of the bank's name and address and the amount, and interest belongs to the tenant less a 1% a year administrative fee the owner may keep. Sal shrugs. “It's their money anyway, I guess.” It is. Clause 8 he reads twice and does not like. Then Jordan turns to the sticky note, one line at a time.

blocks.text: Line one and two: the money at the start

blocks.q: Sal wants a $100 application fee “for my time.” What can Hudson & Hart actually charge a 1B applicant?
c: $100, if the fee is disclosed in the listing and the lease
Nothing for processing, screening or credit checks of any kind
Up to $50, or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is less
The actual cost of a background and credit check, up to $20
blocks.x: New York bans application processing fees. A landlord may pass on the actual cost of a background or credit check up to $20, must give the applicant a copy of the report and the invoice, and must waive the fee if the applicant brings a check run within the past 30 days. The $50 or 5% answer is the trap: that is the late fee cap, a different rule.

blocks.html: Sal's second line, “Tenant pays broker fee,” is how Astoria worked for decades. It no longer does. Hudson & Hart is Sal's agent. It will list 1B with Sal's permission, advertise it and show it, all on Sal's behalf. Clause 4 already says the leasing fee is paid by the owner, and Jordan explains why that is not a courtesy.

blocks.q: A prospective tenant offers to pay Hudson & Hart's one-month fee if it helps her application. What should Jordan say?
c: No; a broker working for the landlord cannot charge the tenant
Yes, if she signs a separate agreement before the lease signing
Yes, if it is half a month, with Sal paying the other half
No; New York State bans broker fees on every residential rental
blocks.x: Since June 11, 2025, New York City's FARE Act bars a broker who represents the landlord, including the listing broker, from charging the tenant. A tenant may still hire and pay her own broker. The statewide-ban answer is the trap: the FARE Act is a New York City law, and it turns on who hired the broker. Any fee a tenant must pay has to be disclosed in the listing and before signing.

blocks.html: Line three asks for two months' deposit because the floors are new. New York caps a residential security deposit at one month's rent, and an “advance” or “last month's rent” counts toward the same cap. So for 1B at $2,600: one deposit of $2,600, first month's rent of $2,600, a screening charge of no more than $20, and nothing else. Jordan writes that list into the listing as the FARE Act requires, so every applicant sees the same total before applying.

blocks.title: The move-in total for 1B
blocks.html: First month $2,600. Security deposit $2,600, never more than one month. Background and credit check: actual cost up to $20, waived with a report from the last 30 days. No application fee, no broker fee for Sal's broker, no “key fee,” no move-in fee. If the new floors get damaged, the deposit covers it at move-out, with an itemized statement.

blocks.text: Lines four through seven: who gets the apartment

blocks.html: Jordan lists 1B at $2,600: two bedrooms, second floor rear, 780 square feet. In four days, eleven inquiries and five complete applications. Two stand out. Mariela Quispe is a home health aide with a CityFHEPS voucher that covers all but $520 of the rent; she applied first. Devin Park is a graduate student whose parents will guarantee the lease; he applied third. Sal has already met Devin at a showing and likes him.

blocks.q: Sal says, “The voucher lady, no. Give it to the student.” What must Jordan do?
c: Refuse; turning her down for a voucher is source of income discrimination
Comply, since Sal has fewer than 10 units and is exempt from fair housing law
Comply, as long as the rejection letter gives a reason other than the voucher
Refuse, unless Sal lives in the building, which would make the refusal legal
blocks.x: Lawful source of income, including housing vouchers, is protected by the New York State and New York City Human Rights Laws. A pretextual reason makes it worse, not better. The owner-occupied answer is the trap: the state exemption covers owner-occupied one- and two-family homes, not a six-unit building Sal lives in or not. A manager who carries out the instruction is liable too.

blocks.html: Sal tries another angle that afternoon. Devin's father calls Jordan directly and offers $500 “for your trouble” if Devin's application moves to the top of the pile.

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle the father's $500 offer?
c: Accept it and report it to Sal, since he is the principal here
Decline it; taking it betrays Sal and breaks the order of review
Accept it if the payment goes through Hudson & Hart's books
Decline it, unless Devin's application turns out the strongest
blocks.x: Jordan is Sal's agent, and a side payment from an applicant to influence the choice is a conflict that betrays the duty of loyalty, whoever books it. It would also break the written first-come review that keeps the process fair. The disclose-to-Sal answer is the trap: Sal could not lawfully approve skipping the earlier qualified applicant, so disclosure does not cure it.

blocks.html: Sal then reaches for line seven: “Fine. 40 times the rent, no exceptions. She makes $31,000.” Forty times $2,600 is $104,000. Mariela's voucher program has already decided what share of the rent she can afford, $520 a month, based on her income. The city's Commission on Human Rights treats an income test applied to the full rent of a voucher holder as source of income discrimination, because it rejects voucher holders by design while sounding neutral.

blocks.q: How should Hudson & Hart apply the income requirement to Mariela?
c: Apply 40x to the full $2,600, the same test every applicant gets
Require a guarantor earning 80x the rent in place of using the voucher
Not to the full rent; the program already found her share affordable
Apply 40x to the voucher amount, since the agency pays that share
blocks.x: Applying the full-rent income test to a voucher holder screens out the protected group even though it looks neutral. City guidance says the voucher program's determination answers the affordability question; at most, a test may look at the tenant's own share. The same-test-for-everyone answer is the trap: equal rules that guarantee a protected group fails are still discrimination. Demanding a guarantor instead is the same violation in another form.

blocks.html: Line five, “No more than 2 people,” comes up with the third applicant: Keisha and Andre Bell and their two children, ages 4 and 7. Sal says four people in a two-bedroom is “too many for the pipes.” Occupancy limits are allowed if they are reasonable and come from real space standards, such as the city's housing code minimums for floor area per person. A flat two-person cap on a two-bedroom apartment does not; it excludes families with children.

blocks.q: Is the “no more than 2 people” rule lawful for 1B?
c: Yes, because occupancy limits are a landlord's choice in small buildings
Yes, if Sal applies it to adults and children equally and puts it in writing
No, because New York landlords may not set an occupancy limit of any kind
No; a two-person cap on a two-bedroom discriminates on familial status
blocks.x: A cap that keeps a family of four out of a two-bedroom apartment discriminates on familial status, protected by federal, state and city law. Applying it equally is the trap: a neutral-looking rule with no basis in space standards still shuts out families with children. Reasonable limits tied to the housing code's floor area rules are allowed, so the no-limit-of-any-kind answer overstates it.

blocks.html: Line six, “Run criminal on everybody first,” runs straight into the city's Fair Chance for Housing law, in effect since January 1, 2025. It reverses the order Sal wants. The landlord first evaluates everything else: income, credit, references. Only after making a conditional offer may the landlord look at criminal history, and then only a narrow slice of it, such as convictions within a limited look-back period and sex offender registry status, followed by an individualized assessment and notice to the applicant.

blocks.q: When may Hudson & Hart run a criminal background check on the 1B finalist?
c: Before anything else, so no time is wasted on someone who will fail
After a conditional offer, and within the limits the city law allows
At no point, because the city bans criminal history checks for rentals
Whenever the owner prefers, if each applicant signs a written consent
blocks.x: Under the Fair Chance for Housing law, criminal history comes last: after the applicant otherwise qualifies and receives a conditional offer, and then only within limited look-back periods, with an individualized assessment and notice. The total-ban answer is the trap: the law restricts timing and scope rather than banning all checks. Signed consent does not let a landlord reverse the required order.

blocks.html: Line seven left: “No one who has been to housing court.” Devin's screening report is clean. Mariela's shows a 2021 nonpayment case that was dismissed when a rent arrears program paid her old landlord. Sal points at it. “See?”

blocks.q: Can Hudson & Hart reject Mariela because of the dismissed 2021 housing court case?
c: Yes, because a nonpayment case is evidence that she is a credit risk
Yes, because the case is in court records that any landlord may read
No; refusing to rent over a past landlord-tenant case is illegal
No, but just because the case ended in a dismissal and not a judgment
blocks.x: New York's tenant blacklist law, RPL 227-f, bars refusing to rent because an applicant was involved in a past or pending landlord-tenant case. If a landlord pulls court records and then rejects the applicant, a violation is presumed. The dismissal answer is the trap: protection does not depend on how the case ended. A landlord may still use independent, lawful criteria applied the same way to everyone.

blocks.title: The neutral-sounding rejection
blocks.html: The rejections that end up in front of the Commission on Human Rights rarely say “no vouchers.” They say “did not meet income requirement,” “too many occupants,” “unsatisfactory rental history.” Each can be a cover for a protected-class reason. Write the screening criteria down before listing, apply them in the order applications arrive, keep every application and the reason for every decision, and never let an owner's preference about a person change the outcome.

Jordan puts Hudson & Hart's written criteria in front of Sal: complete applications reviewed in the order received; income test applied to the tenant's own share of the rent; credit and landlord references; criminal history only after a conditional offer. Mariela applied first and qualifies. Sal stares at the paper for a long minute. “So I don't get to pick?” Jordan answers carefully: Sal sets lawful criteria and approves the rent, and the criteria pick. Sal signs the approval.

One thing nags Jordan. The building was built in 1931 and has six units, the classic profile of a rent-stabilized building, and two units on the rent roll are stabilized. Why is 1B listed at a market rent? Jordan requests the building's rent registration history from HCR. It shows 1B registered as stabilized through 2016, then a 2016 registration marked permanently exempt for high-rent vacancy deregulation, after the prior owner renovated and the legal rent crossed the threshold then in effect. Sal's file has the renovation invoices.

blocks.q: 1B was deregulated in 2016 under the old high-rent vacancy rule. What is its status after the 2019 HSTPA?
c: It stays deregulated; it was lawfully deregulated before June 14, 2019
It returned to rent stabilization automatically the day HSTPA took effect
It is stabilized again the next time the apartment becomes vacant
It stays deregulated for as long as the rent stays above $2,700
blocks.x: HSTPA repealed high-rent vacancy deregulation going forward, but units lawfully deregulated before June 14, 2019 stay deregulated. The word lawfully matters: if the renovation costs claimed to push the rent over the threshold were inflated, a tenant could challenge it, which is why Sal keeps the invoices. The automatic-return answer is the trap: the repeal was not retroactive for lawful deregulations.

blocks.html: That also settles the lease form. 1B gets a market-rate lease, not a stabilization lease with the DHCR rider. Sal owns six units in New York and nothing else, which makes him a small landlord under the Good Cause Eviction law and exempts his market units from its limits. The exemption does not excuse him from paperwork.

blocks.q: Sal is exempt from Good Cause Eviction as a small landlord. What does the 1B lease still need?
c: Nothing about Good Cause, because the law does not reach his building
A rent stabilization rider, since exempt units default to stabilization
An HCR filing approving the exemption before the lease can be signed
The Good Cause notice, naming the exemption
blocks.x: The Good Cause law requires landlords to give tenants a notice with new and renewal leases stating whether the law applies and, if not, which exemption applies. Exempt landlords still give the notice. The nothing-needed answer is the trap. Exemption does not create stabilization coverage, and no advance HCR approval is required to sign a lease.

blocks.html: The lease package for Mariela comes together: the market lease; the Good Cause notice naming the small landlord exemption; the federal lead paint disclosure and pamphlet, because the building was built before 1978; the city's window guard and lead paint notices; the bedbug history disclosure; and the FARE Act fee disclosure, which lists one item, the $20 screening charge, already waived because she brought a recent report.

Mariela pays a $2,600 deposit. Jordan deposits it in the escrow account at a Queens bank paying 1.5% a year and sends her the written notice of the bank and amount. Jordan also offers her the move-in inspection the law requires: if she asks for one, the two of them walk the unit and sign a list of any existing damage, and Sal cannot later charge her deposit for anything on that list. She asks. They note a chipped bathroom tile and a sticky closet door.

blocks.q: Mariela's $2,600 deposit earns 1.5% for a full year. How much interest belongs to her, and how much may Sal keep?
c: Mariela $39; Sal keeps nothing
Mariela $26; Sal keeps $13
Mariela $13; Sal keeps $26
Mariela $0; Sal keeps $39
blocks.x: Interest: $2,600 x 1.5% = $39. The owner may keep an administrative fee equal to 1% a year of the deposit: $2,600 x 1% = $26. The tenant gets the rest: $39 minus $26 = $13. The trap is reversing the split, giving the tenant the 1% figure. The tenant's share is paid out annually, credited toward rent, or held in trust until the tenancy ends.

blocks.html: A month later Sal walks through 1B to look at his new floors and spots the chipped bathroom tile. “That comes out of her deposit when she leaves.” Jordan pulls the signed move-in condition list.

blocks.q: Can Sal charge Mariela's deposit for the chipped tile at move-out?
c: Yes, if he can show the tile was chipped at some point during her tenancy
No; it is on the signed move-in list, so the deposit cannot cover it
Yes, because a deposit covers any damage present at move-out
No, but he may bill her separately for it as additional rent
blocks.x: When the tenant asks for a move-in inspection, conditions listed in the signed agreement cannot later be charged to her deposit. That is the point of the list, for both sides. The any-damage answer is the trap. Billing it as additional rent is the same charge in a different form. Ordinary wear and tear cannot be charged either.

blocks.html: Jordan's monthly report to Sal that November has a new section: “1B leased at $2,600 from December 1 to Mariela Quispe. Voucher portion paid directly by the program. Leasing fee per clause 4: $2,600, owner-paid. Deposit held in escrow, notice sent. Application file and criteria retained for three years.” Sal calls after reading it. He does not mention the sticky note. He asks whether the voucher program pays on time. It does, on the first.

Diane reviews the file before it closes and adds a note for the office: the sticky note goes in the file too, with Jordan's written reply under it. If a rejected applicant ever files a complaint, the best defense Hudson & Hart has is a record showing that the owner's unlawful instructions were refused in writing, the criteria existed before the listing went up, and every applicant was measured against them in the order they applied. A manager who quietly follows an owner's bias is not protected by the fact that the owner asked. Both are liable, and so is the broker who supervises the manager.

items: A management agreement should give the manager clear authority, an owner-paid fee, trust handling of tenants' deposits, and the right to refuse unlawful instructions; a fiduciary obeys only lawful ones.
Move-in money in New York is capped: one month's deposit, a screening charge at actual cost up to $20, and in New York City no fee to the landlord's broker under the FARE Act.

Fair housing reaches criteria that sound neutral: full-rent income tests for voucher holders, two-person caps on two-bedroom units, housing court history, and criminal checks done before a conditional offer.
Check the HCR registration history before calling a unit market rate; units lawfully deregulated before June 14, 2019 stay deregulated.
Exempt landlords still give the Good Cause notice, and every deposit in a building of six or more units goes into an interest-bearing account, with the tenant receiving the interest less 1% a year.

lessons.title: Case file: Winter on 31st Avenue
lessons.tagline: Unit 2B stops paying, the boiler quits in January, a tenant moves out, and Sal wants to change the locks. One winter of property management by the book.
objectives: Apply New York's post-2019 nonpayment rules, from the 5-day notice through the marshal, to a real arrears file
Calculate a lawful late fee and the amount recoverable in a nonpayment proceeding
Decide renewal, nonrenewal and rent questions for rent-stabilized and market tenants in the same building
Handle an emergency repair, a contractor kickback offer and a security deposit return within the manager's authority and duties

blocks.title: December 6
blocks.html: It is the sixth of December, and Jordan's rent ledger for Sal Russo's six-unit building in Astoria shows five payments in and one missing. Unit 2B, Femi Okoye, $2,500 a month on a market lease that ends March 31, has not paid December. Okoye also paid November two weeks late. Sal calls before Jordan has finished coffee: “Charge him a hundred late fee, and if he doesn't pay by Friday, change the locks. My building.” Jordan has a management agreement that says Hudson & Hart collects rents and handles collections “in accordance with law.” Before deciding anything about the locks, Jordan has a deadline that falls today.

blocks.q: December rent was due on the 1st and has not arrived by the 6th. What does New York law require the manager to send?
c: A written notice of nonpayment to the tenant by certified mail
A 3-day oral demand for the rent, delivered in person by the super
A 30-day notice terminating the lease for nonpayment of rent
A notice of petition, filed in Housing Court the same week
blocks.x: Under RPL 235-e, when a landlord or authorized agent has not received rent within five days of the due date, it must send the tenant written notice of the nonpayment by certified mail. If it does not, the tenant can raise that failure as a defense in a nonpayment case. The 3-day oral demand is the trap: that was the pre-2019 practice, and HSTPA abolished oral demands.

blocks.html: Jordan sends the certified letter that afternoon and saves the receipt to the 2B file. Then the late fee. Sal wants $100. Okoye's lease says “a late charge of $100 if rent is not received by the 5th.” The lease cannot override the statute.

blocks.q: Okoye's rent is $2,500. What is the most Hudson & Hart can charge as a late fee for December?
c: $100, as the signed lease provides
$125, which is 5% of the monthly rent
$50, the lesser of $50 or 5% of the rent
Nothing, since late fees were banned in 2019
blocks.x: A late fee may be charged only when rent is more than five days late, and it is capped at $50 or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is less. Here 5% is $125, so the cap is $50. The $125 answer is the trap: it applies the percentage but forgets the lesser-of rule. A lease clause that charges more is unenforceable above the cap.

blocks.html: Jordan calls Sal back. Sal has heard about lockouts from his father's day and does not see the problem. “He doesn't pay, he doesn't live here.” Jordan explains what happens to an owner who tries it, and to the manager who helps him.

blocks.q: If Sal changes the locks on 2B while Okoye is behind on rent, what is the legal result?
c: It is lawful once the tenant is 30 days behind and gets written notice
It is lawful if the manager first returns the tenant's security deposit
It is a civil matter, settled by crediting the tenant some free rent
It is an unlawful eviction: a misdemeanor with civil penalties
blocks.x: Under RPAPL 768, removing or locking out a tenant, or any occupant of 30 or more consecutive days, without a court order is an unlawful eviction: a class A misdemeanor with civil penalties of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation, and more for each day the occupant is not restored. Anyone who helps, including a managing agent, is exposed. The 30-days-behind answer is the trap: arrears never authorize self-help. Only a marshal or sheriff with a warrant may evict.

blocks.title: Self-help has many disguises
blocks.html: Changing the locks is the obvious one. Removing the door, shutting off heat or water to “encourage” payment, taking the tenant's belongings, or telling the super to block access are all forms of unlawful eviction. Cutting essential services can also amount to constructive eviction and earns HPD violations on top of it. The only lawful way to remove a tenant in New York is actual eviction by a marshal or sheriff after a court judgment.

blocks.text: The paper trail to Housing Court

blocks.html: Okoye answers Jordan's call on December 10. He lost hours at work and will catch up “after the holidays.” Jordan writes that down, offers a payment plan in writing, and tells Sal. By December 20 nothing has arrived. Sal tells Jordan to start the case. Hudson & Hart's lawyer will file, but the predicate notice comes first, and it has rules of its own.

blocks.q: Before the lawyer can file a nonpayment petition, what demand must Okoye receive?
c: An oral demand by the owner, witnessed, giving him 3 days to pay
A written demand stating the amount and period, giving him 14 days
A written demand giving 30 days, since he has lived there over a year
A notice from HPD confirming the building has no open violations
blocks.x: HSTPA requires a written rent demand that gives the tenant at least 14 days to pay before a nonpayment proceeding starts, and the demand must state the amount claimed and the period it covers. The 3-day oral demand is the trap: it is the old rule. The 30-day option borrows from the notice periods for nonrenewal and rent increases, which are a different statute.

blocks.html: Jordan drafts the 14-day demand on December 22. Sal wants it to claim January's rent too, “to save a step.” It cannot: a demand may claim only rent actually due when it is served. The demand claims $2,500 for December, and a second demand follows in January when January goes unpaid as well. One more check before filing: Sal's building is a multiple dwelling, so its HPD registration has to be current, or the court will not award possession for nonpayment. Jordan renewed it in August. The file is ready.

blocks.title: What the lawyer's draft petition asks for, January 20
blocks.html:
December rent: $2,500
January rent: $2,500
Late fees, December and January: $100
Legal fees under lease paragraph 19: $750
Total claimed: $5,850

blocks.q: How much of the $5,850 can the petition seek in the summary nonpayment proceeding?
c: $5,850, because every item is authorized by the signed lease
$5,100, the rent plus the lawful late fees but no legal fees
$5,750, the rent plus legal fees, since late fees are capped
$5,000, the rent, since fees are not recoverable in that case
blocks.x: RPAPL 702 bars seeking any fees, charges or penalties other than rent in a residential summary proceeding, whatever the lease says. The petition seeks $5,000. The $5,100 answer is the trap: the $50 late fees are lawful to charge, but they cannot be collected through the nonpayment case. Sal may pursue them in a separate plenary action, which is rarely worth it.

blocks.html: The case moves the way Housing Court cases move: a first appearance, an adjournment so Okoye can apply for emergency rental help from the city's Human Resources Administration, a stipulation he does not keep, and in March a judgment for $7,500 in rent and a warrant of eviction. The city marshal serves the notice of eviction. The tenant now has at least 14 days before the marshal can act.

blocks.q: Two days before the scheduled eviction, Okoye's sister pays every dollar of the $7,500 judgment. What happens?
c: The eviction proceeds, because a warrant ends the tenancy once issued
The court generally must vacate the warrant unless Sal shows bad faith
Sal may choose whether to accept the money or go ahead with the eviction
The warrant is stayed for 30 days while the court reviews the payment
blocks.x: Since 2019, RPAPL 749 requires the court to vacate a warrant in a nonpayment case when the tenant tenders or deposits the full rent due before the warrant is executed, unless the landlord proves the tenant withheld rent in bad faith. Issuing a warrant no longer ends the landlord-tenant relationship. The tenancy-ended answer is the trap: that was the rule before HSTPA.

blocks.html: The sister pays with a certified bank check delivered to Hudson & Hart's office. Because it is not the tenant's personal check, the law requires a written receipt showing the date, the amount, the apartment, the period covered, and the name and title of the person who took it. Jordan writes one on the spot, copies it to the 2B file and emails the lawyer, who files proof of payment with the court so the warrant is vacated before the marshal's date.

Sal is furious for an afternoon and then relieved: the money is in the bank. The episode cost about $2,400 in legal fees, which Sal cannot recover in the proceeding, and four months of stress. What Sal really wants now is for Okoye not to be there next year.

blocks.text: Two leases, two sets of rules

blocks.html: The rent roll puts two very different decisions on Jordan's desk the same week. 2B is a market unit; Okoye moved in on April 1 almost three years ago, and his lease ends March 31. 1A is rent stabilized; Mrs. Mendez pays $1,850, and her lease ends August 31.

blocks.q: Sal decides not to renew Okoye's market lease. Sal owns only this 6-unit building. What does Hudson & Hart need to do?
c: Nothing; a lease for a set term ends on its own date without notice
Prove good cause in court, since Good Cause covers every NYC unit
Give written notice of nonrenewal at least 90 days before March 31
Give 30 days' written notice, the standard period for any tenancy
blocks.x: Under RPL 226-c, a landlord who will not renew must give written notice based on how long the tenant has been there: 30 days for under a year, 60 days for one to two years, 90 days for two years or more. Okoye is near three years, so 90 days. Good Cause is the trap: Sal, with no more than 10 units, is a small landlord exempt from its limits, though his leases still carry the notice naming that exemption.

blocks.html: The notice should have gone out by the end of December. Jordan sent it December 20, along with the rent demand, in separate envelopes so neither could be mistaken for the other. Good timing, not luck: Jordan's management calendar flags every lease 120 days before it ends.

Mrs. Mendez is different. A rent-stabilized tenant has a right to a renewal lease, the owner cannot simply decline, and the rent increase is set by the Rent Guidelines Board for leases starting in that year. The owner must send the renewal offer on the DHCR form between 150 and 90 days before the lease expires, and she has 60 days to choose a one- or two-year term.

blocks.q: Mrs. Mendez's renewal will start September 1, 2027. The RGB order for leases starting October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027 is a 0% freeze for both terms. What renewal rent may Sal offer?
c: $1,850 for either a one-year or a two-year renewal
$1,905.50 for one year, since the prior order allowed 3%
$1,850 for one year and $1,933.25 for two years
Whatever Sal chooses, since stabilized renewals follow market rent
blocks.x: The guideline in effect for the date the renewal lease starts controls. A lease starting September 1, 2027 falls under the order covering October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027, which froze rents for both terms, so the renewal rent is $1,850 either way. The 3% answer is the trap: that was the prior order, for leases starting before October 1, 2026.

blocks.title: The management calendar
blocks.html: Most of the expensive mistakes in residential management are missed dates, not bad judgment. Jordan's calendar for Sal's building carries every lease expiration at 150, 120 and 90 days; the 5th of every month for nonpayment notices; HPD registration each summer; the annual window guard and lead paint notices each January; the boiler service each August before heat season starts October 1; and a 10-day internal deadline for every deposit return. The calendar is part of the monthly report, so Sal can see what is coming as well as what happened.

Vinnie, the super, calls Jordan before dawn. The boiler is dead: cracked section, water on the boiler room floor. It is 19 degrees outside. NYC's heat season runs October 1 through May 31; overnight, every apartment must be at least 62 degrees inside no matter the outdoor temperature, and by day 68 degrees when it is below 55 outside. Without heat, every apartment is a Class C immediately hazardous HPD violation waiting to be written.

Jordan's management agreement allows repairs up to $5,000 per item without Sal's approval and emergency repairs “to protect life or property” at any amount, with notice to the owner within 24 hours. The boiler contractor quotes $3,800 for an emergency section repair to restore heat today, or $46,000 for a full replacement, which the building's capital reserve plan already scheduled for next summer.

blocks.q: What should Jordan authorize this morning?
c: The $46,000 replacement, since emergencies allow any amount
The $3,800 repair, and tell Sal in writing within 24 hours
Nothing until Sal approves, since boilers are a capital item
Space heaters for each tenant, charged back to them as rent
blocks.x: The emergency is the loss of heat, and the $3,800 repair ends it today, within the manager's authority. A $46,000 replacement is a capital decision that can wait for Sal, so using the emergency clause for it overreaches. Waiting for Sal is the trap: the agreement gives Jordan authority to protect life and property now. Heat is the owner's legal duty, so tenants cannot be charged for it.

blocks.html: Heat is back by 2 pm. That evening, the contractor's owner, an old friend of Jordan's family, calls about the replacement bid. “I'll come in at $46,000 and send you 5% personally, for the referral. Everybody does it.”

blocks.q: How should Jordan respond to the contractor's 5% offer?
c: Accept, since Sal still pays the market price either way
Accept, as long as the $2,300 is reported as income
Decline and disclose the offer and relationship to Sal
Decline, then quietly drop the contractor from the bids
blocks.x: A manager is a fiduciary. A secret payment from a vendor the manager selects is a conflict that breaches loyalty and the duty to account, whether or not the price looks fair. Jordan declines, tells Sal about the offer and the family connection, and gets competing bids. The same-price answer is the trap: the kickback means the price could have been $2,300 lower for Sal.

blocks.html: Three bids come in. Sal picks the second-lowest because the contractor services boilers in two of his friends' buildings, and the replacement goes on the summer schedule as preventive work rather than another January emergency.

Daniel Chen in 2A gives notice that he will leave when his lease ends January 31. Jordan sends him written notice of his right to a pre-move-out inspection; he asks for one, Jordan gives 48 hours' notice, and they walk the unit on January 20. Jordan lists a broken closet door and three large anchor holes from a wall-mounted TV, and Chen fixes neither. He leaves on the 31st.

blocks.title: Sal's proposed deductions from Chen's $2,450 deposit
blocks.html:
Replace broken closet door: $180
Patch and paint three large anchor holes: $220
Repaint entire apartment after three-year tenancy: $650
Professional cleaning, apartment left broom clean: $200
Proposed total: $1,250. Proposed refund: $1,200 plus interest.

blocks.q: Which deductions can Sal properly take from Chen's $2,450 deposit?
c: Each of the four, $1,250, since each is a real cost to re-rent
The door and the holes, $400, since those are damage beyond wear
The door, holes and repainting, $1,050, since paint is a tenant cost
Nothing, because Chen gave notice and asked for the inspection
blocks.x: A deposit covers unpaid rent and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. A broken door and large anchor holes qualify. Repainting after three years and cleaning a unit left broom clean are normal turnover costs. The repainting answer is the trap: paint wears out with ordinary use. Chen gets $2,050 plus his share of the interest, and Sal bears the burden of proving the deductions are reasonable.

blocks.html: Jordan prepares the itemized statement and the check for $2,050 plus $11.30 in net interest. Then the office gets busy with the boiler and 1B, and the envelope sits on a desk.

blocks.q: The itemized statement and refund are mailed on February 18, 18 days after Chen moved out. What is the consequence?
c: No consequence, if the statement is accurate and the deductions proper
Sal owes a $50 late fee to Chen for each week of delay
Sal owes one extra month's interest on the refund for the delay
Sal forfeits any right to keep any part of the deposit
blocks.x: GOL 7-108 requires the itemized statement and the balance within 14 days after the tenant vacates. A landlord who misses the deadline forfeits the right to retain any portion of the deposit, so Sal now owes the full $2,450 plus interest. The no-harm answer is the trap: accuracy does not cure lateness. A willful violation can also bring punitive damages up to twice the deposit.

blocks.html: The $400 Jordan's office cost Sal is a line in the March property management report, stated plainly, with the fix: deposit returns now go on the management calendar with a 10-day internal deadline, and Hudson & Hart credits Sal the $400 against its fee. Diane's view is simple. An honest report that shows the manager's own mistake is what makes the owner believe every other number in it.

items.title: Collections
items.html: $12,850 potential rent; 2B arrears of $7,500 paid in full after judgment, warrant vacated; 1A, 3A, 3B and 1B current; 2A vacant since February 1.

items.title: Legal
items.html: 2B nonpayment case closed; nonrenewal notice served December 20 for March 31; legal fees $2,400, not recoverable in the case.

items.title: Building
items.html: Emergency boiler repair $3,800 on January 9 under clause 3; replacement contracted for July at $44,500 from three bids; HPD: no violations issued.

items.title: Leasing
items.html: 1A renewal offer to go out between April 3 and June 2 at $1,850 under the RGB freeze; 2A listed at $2,500, owner-paid leasing fee.

items.title: Deposits
items.html: 2A deposit returned late; $400 in deductions forfeited and credited by Hudson & Hart against its fee; new 10-day internal deadline.

blocks.html: Sal reads the report twice. He calls about one line only: the $2,400 in legal fees he could not get back in the nonpayment case. Jordan's answer goes into the April report as a recommendation. The cheapest collection tool is the first week: the certified notice on the sixth, a phone call the same day, a written payment plan before arrears pass one month, and a referral to rental assistance programs when a tenant has a real hardship. Housing Court is the last tool, not the first, and its cost belongs in the operating budget's legal line so it never surprises the owner again.

That spring Hudson & Hart's management division also takes on Kim Alvarez's Upper West Side co-op. The managing agent there works for the co-op corporation through its board, and the residents are shareholders with proprietary leases, not ordinary tenants. When a shareholder falls three months behind on maintenance, the rules Jordan learned in Astoria change in two places.

blocks.title: Co-op arrears are not Astoria arrears
blocks.html: A co-op may charge a late fee on maintenance of up to 8% if the proprietary lease provides for it, well above the $50 rental cap. And RPAPL 702 carves out co-ops: in a summary proceeding against a shareholder, the corporation may seek the fees, charges and assessments the proprietary lease allows, not just maintenance. Everything else stays the same: written demands, no self-help, and a court order before anyone is removed.

blocks.q: Kim's co-op shareholder owes $9,000 in maintenance, and the proprietary lease allows late fees and legal fees. In a summary proceeding, the co-op may generally seek:
c: The $9,000 plus lease-authorized fees, under the co-op exception
The $9,000 alone, since fees are barred in residential summary cases
The $9,000 plus a $50 late fee per month, the residential cap
Nothing until the board first votes to cancel the shares
blocks.x: RPAPL 702's ban on fees in summary proceedings has an exception for co-ops suing shareholders, where the proprietary lease allows other fees, charges and assessments. The $9,000-alone answer is the trap: it applies the rental rule to a co-op. The $50 cap governs residential rentals; a co-op may charge up to 8% if its proprietary lease says so.

blocks.html: The co-op also changes who Jordan answers to. In Astoria the principal was Sal, one owner who could say yes on the phone. Here the principal is the corporation, and it acts through its board. The management agreement names the board as the body that approves the budget, hires vendors over a set amount and gives the managing agent instructions. Shareholders are the owners' constituents, not the manager's bosses.

In May, a shareholder on the ninth floor emails Jordan twice in one afternoon. First she wants the arrears file on the shareholder in 4C, "since we all pay for his default." Then she instructs Jordan to fire the elevator contractor and hire her nephew's company, because the elevator was out for a day.

blocks.q: How should Jordan handle the ninth-floor shareholder's two requests?
c: Send the 4C file, since each shareholder owns part of the corporation
Decline both and refer her to the board, which directs the agent
Replace the contractor, since shareholders are the agent's principals
Forward the 4C file but ask the board before changing contractors
blocks.x: The managing agent's principal is the co-op corporation, acting through its board. An individual shareholder cannot direct the agent, and another shareholder's arrears are confidential information the agent holds for the corporation. Jordan acknowledges her concerns, passes them to Kim and the board, and lets the board decide. The split answer is the trap: it gets the contractor right but still releases a neighbor's private financial file.

blocks.html: In June the division adds a 40-unit condominium in Long Island City. A unit owner there stops paying common charges, and the board asks Jordan what happens next. Condo owners hold title to real property, so the Astoria tools change again: there is no proprietary lease to terminate and no summary eviction of an owner for unpaid charges.

blocks.q: A Long Island City condo owner is $7,200 behind on common charges. What remedy does New York law give the board of managers?
c: A summary proceeding in Housing Court to evict the owner from the unit
A late fee of $50 or 5% each month, collectible in a nonpayment case
Cancellation of the owner's shares after a default notice to the owner
A lien on the unit, behind taxes and a first mortgage of record
blocks.x: Under RPL 339-z the board of managers has a lien on the unit for unpaid common charges, with priority over all other liens except real estate tax liens, a first mortgage of record and certain public housing agency mortgages, and it can be foreclosed. Summary eviction is the rental tool, and canceling shares is the co-op tool. A condo owner owns real property, so the remedy runs against the unit, and the charges must be paid from any sale.

items: Nonpayment, step by step: certified notice if rent is 5 days late, a late fee capped at the lesser of $50 or 5%, a 14-day written demand, current HPD registration, a petition for rent only, and a warrant the court vacates if the full rent is paid before execution.
Self-help eviction is a crime, and the manager who helps is exposed too.

Market and stabilized tenants follow different renewal rules: 30, 60 or 90 days' notice of nonrenewal for market tenants; a mandatory DHCR renewal offer 150 to 90 days out, at the RGB rate for the lease's start date, for stabilized tenants.
Use emergency authority for the emergency, not for capital decisions, and refuse and disclose any vendor kickback.
Return deposits with an itemized statement within 14 days, charge only damage beyond wear and tear, and report your own mistakes to the owner as plainly as anyone else's.

Condo and co-op management change who the principal is and which remedy applies: the managing agent takes direction from the board, not individual owners, and unpaid condo common charges become a lien on the unit with priority behind taxes and a first mortgage.

roleplays.title: Sal Hands Over the Keys
roleplays.setting: Sal's kitchen, Astoria. Sal wants Jordan to take over his 6-unit building.
roleplays.you: Jordan, a salesperson at Hudson & Hart Realty
roleplays.goal: Set up a lawful management relationship and steer Sal away from fair housing, escrow, rent regulation, and maintenance mistakes.
roleplays.aiBrief: Play Sal Russo, a 71-year-old old-school Astoria landlord with a 6-unit 1928 walk-up. You are warm but stubborn. Push the learner (a salesperson) in order: a cash handshake deal with no broker; refusing Section 8 voucher holders; a two-month security deposit; keeping deposits in your own account; raising a rent-stabilized tenant from $1,950 to $2,600; refusing to fund a capital reserve for a 26-year-old boiler. Along the way, suggest your nephew collect rents, a $100 late fee after one day, changing the locks on a tenant who is behind, and keeping a whole deposit with no explanation. The learner must route the agreement through the broker in writing, refuse source-of-income discrimination, cap deposits at one month, keep deposits in a separate interest-bearing account, respect Rent Guidelines Board limits, follow late fee, lockout and deposit-return rules, and recommend reserves in writing. Grade each item at the end.

snack: tea and a plate of cookies
espresso and a slice of ricotta pie

opening: Sal's kitchen on {street}, {snack} on the table. He slides a ring of keys toward you. "Six units. You run it now."
Sal is 71 and tired of fixing boilers at midnight. Over {snack}, he offers you his {street} walk-up to manage.
Apartment {vacant} on {street} is empty, the boiler is 26 years old, and Sal wants out of day-to-day landlording. He has terms.

say: You collect the rents, find tenants, deal with the plumber. I pay you 5%. Cash, no paperwork. Deal?
Forget the office. You and me, 5% cash, a handshake. Simple.

moves.text: I'd love to, but it's a written agreement with Hudson & Hart, and the fee goes to the firm.
moves.fb: Correct. Collecting rent for others for a fee is licensed activity, and a salesperson acts only through the broker.
moves.react: The firm, huh? Fine. Bring the papers.

moves.text: It goes through my broker, in writing. That protects you too: authority, reports, insurance, fee.
moves.fb: Right. A management agreement sets out authority, reporting, fee and termination, through the broker.
moves.react: Reports every month? Okay, I like that.

moves.text: Okay, but let's write something up between us so we both remember what we agreed to later on.
moves.fb: Writing is good, but the contract must be with the broker, not with Jordan personally.

moves.text: Sure, just don't tell my broker. Cash is easier for both of us, and nobody else needs to know about it.
moves.fb: A salesperson may not take compensation from anyone but the sponsoring broker or work deals outside the firm.

moves.text: Deal, but make the checks out to me personally. It's still legal as long as you write it down.
moves.fb: Paying the salesperson directly is prohibited. Fees go to the sponsoring broker.

moves.text: No license is needed to manage a small building like yours, so a handshake deal works fine here.
moves.fb: Collecting rents and leasing for others for a fee requires a license, whatever the building size.

say: Fine, the agency. Now listen: {vacant} is empty. No Section 8. Those vouchers are nothing but trouble.
For {vacant}, no programs. Paychecks only. Got it?

moves.text: I can't. In New York, refusing a voucher is source-of-income discrimination. Same criteria for all.
moves.fb: Right. Lawful source of income is protected under NYS and NYC human rights law.

moves.text: Vouchers are lawful income, so we treat them like any other. We screen everyone the same way, Sal.
moves.fb: Correct. Uniform screening, and voucher holders can't be refused.

moves.text: Let me ask Diane what we can do about it. Maybe there's some kind of exception for a building like yours.
moves.fb: There's no exception for Sal's building. Say no clearly.

moves.text: We'll just say the unit's rented if a voucher holder calls. Nobody can prove anything on the phone.
moves.fb: Lying about availability to avoid voucher holders is illegal discrimination.

moves.text: Okay, but only because you're under ten units. Small buildings are exempt from the voucher rule here.
moves.fb: No small-building exemption for a six-unit building. Source of income is protected.

moves.text: We'll require 40 times the full rent from voucher holders. That keeps most of them out legally.
moves.fb: In NYC, income tests for voucher holders apply only to their share. Using the full rent is discrimination.

say: And I want two months' security from the new tenant. One month isn't enough anymore.
Two months' deposit for {vacant}. Prices went up, so the deposit goes up.

moves.text: The law caps it at one month's rent now. We can't ask for two, but we can screen carefully.
moves.fb: Correct. Since 2019, GOL 7-108 limits residential security deposits to one month's rent.
moves.react: One month? When did that happen?

moves.text: Since 2019 the max is one month, statewide. Two months would have to be refunded, with penalties.
moves.fb: Right. HSTPA set the one-month cap for residential deposits.

moves.text: Let's ask for one and a half months. It's a middle ground, and most tenants won't push back on it.
moves.fb: Still over the legal cap. The maximum is one month.

moves.text: Sure, two months is standard for older buildings like yours. Tenants expect it in Astoria.
moves.fb: The one-month cap applies to all residential rentals.

moves.text: Two months is fine if the tenant agrees in writing. They can waive the cap in the lease.
moves.fb: Tenants can't waive the statutory deposit cap.

moves.text: Take one month as deposit and one month as a nonrefundable move-in fee. Same money, no problem.
moves.fb: Disguised fees that evade the deposit cap are not allowed.

say: And the security deposits, put them in my regular account. I need the float.
Deposits go in my business checking. I use that money.

moves.text: Deposits are the tenants' money. With six units, they go in a separate interest-bearing account.
moves.fb: Correct. Mixing deposits with operating funds is commingling, and buildings with 6+ units need interest-bearing accounts.

moves.text: Separate account, interest-bearing for six units. You can keep 1% a year as an admin fee. No float.
moves.fb: Right. The tenant gets the interest minus the landlord's 1% fee.

moves.text: I'll keep them in a separate account, but it doesn't need to earn interest for a small building.
moves.fb: Separate is right, but six or more units means interest-bearing.

moves.text: As long as you don't spend them, it's fine. Just keep a note of how much belongs to the tenants.
moves.fb: Holding deposits in the owner's operating account is commingling regardless of whether the money is spent.

moves.text: I'll keep them in our firm's operating account instead. That's safer than yours, Sal, trust me.
moves.fb: The firm's operating account is still commingling. Deposits belong in a separate escrow account.

moves.text: Put them in your account, and if a tenant asks, just say the money's in a separate escrow.
moves.fb: Lying to tenants about where deposits are held compounds the commingling.

say: Next. {tenant} in 3B pays $1,950. Raise to $2,600 at renewal. Market rent.
{tenant} in 3B is way under market. $2,600 at the renewal.

moves.text: 3B is rent stabilized. Renewals are capped by the Rent Guidelines Board. More is an overcharge.
moves.fb: Right. A 6+ unit building built before 1974 is generally stabilized, and increases follow the RGB.
moves.react: The Guidelines Board. I forgot about them.

moves.text: We can only raise 3B by the RGB's renewal percentage. Charging more risks overcharge damages.
moves.fb: Correct. Stabilized renewals follow RGB orders; overcharges can bring treble damages.
moves.react: Okay, what's the percentage this year?

moves.text: Let's try $2,200 instead. That's a smaller jump, and {tenant} probably won't fight it at all.
moves.fb: Any increase above the RGB rate is an overcharge, big or small.

moves.text: Sure, I'll send the renewal at $2,600. Market rent is only fair, and the lease is up anyway, Sal.
moves.fb: That's an illegal overcharge on a stabilized unit, with potential treble damages.

moves.text: Since 2019 you can raise it to market once the tenant's rent goes over the luxury threshold.
moves.fb: Luxury decontrol was repealed in 2019.

moves.text: Offer {tenant} a non-renewal unless they agree to $2,600. Stabilized tenants can be let go anytime.
moves.fb: Stabilized tenants have renewal rights. Refusing to renew to force a higher rent is unlawful.

say: Fine. But I'm not putting away $2,000 a month for some reserve. The boiler works.
No reserve fund. The boiler's fine. Why waste money?

moves.text: It's 26 years old. A reserve spreads a $45,000 replacement over years. Your call; I'll put it in writing.
moves.fb: You advised your principal clearly, respected the owner's authority, and documented it.
moves.react: Put it in writing. I'll think about it.

moves.text: Boilers fail in January. A reserve beats an emergency loan. I'll send my recommendation in writing.
moves.fb: Correct. Capital reserves fund replacements; document advice to the owner.
moves.react: January. Yeah, that's when they go.

moves.text: Okay, we'll skip it. It's your building and your money, so I won't push the point any further.
moves.fb: The owner decides, but you should explain the risk and document your recommendation.

moves.text: A reserve is required by law for buildings over five units, so you have to fund one anyway, Sal.
moves.fb: No such legal requirement. It's sound advice, not a mandate.

moves.text: Skip the reserve and defer maintenance on the boiler. Deferred maintenance saves money in the long term.
moves.fb: Deferring maintenance on a 26-year-old boiler raises cost and risk.

moves.text: Put the boiler money in the security deposit account. It's sitting there anyway, earning interest for you.
moves.fb: Using tenant deposits for building expenses is commingling and conversion.

say: My nephew lives in 1A. Can he just collect the rents for me? No license.
Let my nephew in 1A handle rent collection. He doesn't need a license, right?

moves.text: If he's your salaried employee, on site, working only for you, he needs no license.
moves.fb: Correct. The resident manager exemption covers an owner's on-site employee for a single owner.
moves.react: He lives there. I'll put him on payroll.

moves.text: He can as your on-site resident manager, employed by you alone. Not for other owners, though.
moves.fb: Right. The exemption is narrow: one owner, on-site, the owner's employee.

moves.text: Probably fine since he's family. Family members can usually help out without any license at all.
moves.fb: Family isn't the test. The resident manager exemption has specific conditions.

moves.text: Sure, and he can collect for your cousin's building down the block too. One license-free job.
moves.fb: Collecting rent for other owners for a fee requires a license.

moves.text: No, anyone touching rent money needs a broker license, even an owner's own employee on site.
moves.fb: Too strict. A resident manager employed by one owner is exempt.

moves.text: Only if he's licensed as a salesperson. Then he can collect on his own without a broker involved.
moves.fb: Salespeople act only through a sponsoring broker. The exemption is for resident managers.

say: Put in the lease: $100 late fee if rent is one day late.
Late fee: $100, starting the second day. Teaches them.

moves.text: The law caps it: no fee until rent is 5 days late, then $50 or 5%, whichever is less.
moves.fb: Correct. RPL 238-a limits residential late fees to the lesser of $50 or 5%, after 5 days.

moves.text: Late fees start after 5 days and max out at $50 or 5%, the lower one. $100 isn't allowed.
moves.fb: Right. The statutory cap applies statewide.

moves.text: Let's do $75 after three days. It's a compromise, and most of your tenants pay on time anyway.
moves.fb: Still over the cap and too early.

moves.text: Sure, late fees are whatever the lease says. Tenants agree to it when they sign the lease.
moves.fb: Leases can't override the statutory cap.

moves.text: $100 is fine for market-rate units. The cap only applies to rent-stabilized apartments.
