moves.fb: The late fee cap applies to residential tenancies generally.

moves.text: Make it 10% of rent instead of a flat fee. Percentage fees aren't covered by the cap.
moves.fb: The cap is $50 or 5%, whichever is less.

say: {tenant}'s neighbor in 2C is two months behind. Change the locks this weekend.
2C hasn't paid in two months. New locks Saturday, and their stuff goes on the curb.

moves.text: We can't. Lockouts are illegal in New York. Removing a tenant goes through housing court.
moves.fb: Correct. Self-help eviction is unlawful; only a court process can remove a tenant.

moves.text: No lockout. That's an unlawful eviction. We send a rent demand and start a nonpayment case.
moves.fb: Right. Proper notices and a court proceeding are the only lawful path.

moves.text: Let's call them first and offer a payment plan, then decide about the locks after that.
moves.fb: Talking first is fine, but leaving the lockout on the table is the problem. It's illegal, full stop.

moves.text: Sure, change the locks while they're at work. It's your building, and they're in default.
moves.fb: A lockout is an unlawful eviction, a crime in New York.

moves.text: Change the locks, but leave a key with the super. Then it's not technically a lockout, legally.
moves.fb: Denying access is a lockout however it's arranged.

moves.text: After 60 days unpaid you can change the locks legally. Before that, you have to wait it out.
moves.fb: There's no grace period that allows a lockout.

say: The tenant in the rear apartment moved out last week. I'm keeping the whole deposit. Don't send anything.
The tenant left. Keep the deposit, all of it. No letters.

moves.text: We have 14 days to return it with an itemized list of deductions, or we can't keep any of it.
moves.fb: Correct. GOL 7-108 requires an itemized statement within 14 days, or the landlord forfeits deductions.

moves.text: Within 14 days we send what's owed and an itemized list of damage. Wear and tear isn't damage.
moves.fb: Right. Itemize real damage within 14 days; ordinary wear isn't deductible.

moves.text: We'll send it back eventually, once you've had time to look the place over carefully, Sal.
moves.fb: There's a 14-day deadline with an itemized statement.

moves.text: Sure, keep it. Deposits cover painting after every tenant moves out. That's standard in Queens.
moves.fb: Normal wear and tear isn't deductible, and a statement is required within 14 days.

moves.text: Keep it and send nothing. If they want it back, they can take you to small claims court.
moves.fb: Ignoring the 14-day rule forfeits the right to keep any of it and invites a lawsuit.

moves.text: Keep it, but you have 60 days to send a statement if the tenant asks for one in writing first.
moves.fb: The deadline is 14 days, and it doesn't depend on a request.

roleplays.debrief: You practised property management law: managing for a fee requires a license and goes through the sponsoring broker in writing, though a resident manager for one owner is exempt. Lawful source of income is protected, deposits are capped at one month and held in a separate, interest-bearing account for 6+ units (owner keeps 1%), and returned within 14 days with an itemized statement. Stabilized renewals follow the Rent Guidelines Board, late fees wait 5 days and max out at $50 or 5%, lockouts are illegal, and you advise on reserves in writing.

questions.q: A property manager's regular report to the owner on income, expenses and vacancies is usually delivered:
c: Monthly
Only at lease-up
Every five years
Only when asked
questions.x: Owners typically get monthly reports. 'Only when asked' is the trap: reporting is a core, routine duty.

questions.q: Which item belongs in a property management report to the owner?
c: The tenants' credit card numbers
The manager's personal taxes
Income, expenses and vacancies
Competing owners' rents only
questions.x: Reports cover the property's finances, vacancies and maintenance. Tenants' card numbers are the trap: that is private data.

questions.q: The primary goal of a property manager is usually to:
c: Maximize net income while preserving value
Keep every unit occupied at whatever rent it takes
Cut operating costs, even if the building declines
Raise rents to the top of the market each year
questions.x: Managers serve the owner's goals, typically the best long-term net income while protecting the asset. Full occupancy is the trap: filling units at below-market rents does not serve that goal.

questions.q: In New York, a property management company that leases apartments and collects rent for several owners for a fee must have:
c: No license of any kind
A home inspector license
A real estate broker license
A business certificate alone
questions.x: Leasing and collecting rent for others for a fee is brokerage under RPL 440, so a broker license is required. The business certificate is the trap: registering a business name does not license the activity.

questions.q: Vinnie is Sal's salaried superintendent, lives in Sal's building, and collects rents there for Sal alone. Vinnie:
c: Needs a salesperson license to collect
Needs a broker license
Is violating Article 12-A
Needs no license as Sal's employee
questions.x: A resident manager employed by the owner and acting for that owner alone falls within the owner's exemption. The salesperson answer is the trap: a license would be needed if he collected for other owners for a fee.

questions.q: A management agreement typically makes the property manager a:
c: Special agent
General agent for the owner
Universal agent
Subagent of tenants
questions.x: A manager handles a range of ongoing matters for one principal, making him a general agent. Special agent is the trap: that describes a listing broker hired for one sale.

questions.q: A management agreement would typically include all of the following EXCEPT:
c: The management fee
Authority to make repairs
Tenants' credit scores
Terms for ending the deal
questions.x: Tenant credit information is not a term of the owner-manager contract. Repair authority is the tempting pick, but spending limits and repair authority are standard clauses.

questions.q: As a fiduciary, a property manager owes loyalty primarily to the:
c: Tenants
Building staff
Owner
Housing agency
questions.x: The owner is the principal. Tenants are the trap: they are owed honesty, fair treatment, and legal compliance, but not loyalty.

questions.q: In a lease, the lessor is the:
c: Tenant
Property manager
Lender
Landlord
questions.x: The lessor is the landlord, who grants the lease. Tenant is the trap: the tenant is the lessee.

questions.q: A two-year commercial lease with fixed start and end dates creates a:
c: Tenancy for years
Periodic tenancy
Tenancy at will
Tenancy at sufferance
questions.x: A tenancy for years has a definite term, whatever its length. Periodic tenancy is the trap: it renews automatically, such as month to month.

questions.q: A landlord fails to restore heat for most of a Bronx winter despite complaints, and the tenant moves out. The tenant may claim:
c: Actual eviction
Constructive eviction
Surrender by the tenant
A holdover tenancy
questions.x: When the landlord's failure makes the premises unlivable and the tenant leaves, that is constructive eviction. Actual eviction is the trap: it is removal through court process.

questions.q: In shopping center management, an anchor store is:
c: A tenant that rents storage space
A store that cannot be evicted
A major tenant drawing traffic
The center's management office
questions.x: Anchors, such as supermarkets and big-box stores, bring shoppers who also visit smaller stores. The cannot-be-evicted answer is the trap: anchors have strong leases, not immunity.

questions.q: The managing agent of an Upper West Side co-op is hired by the board. Whom does the managing agent represent?
c: The co-op corporation, through its board
Each shareholder individually
Buyers of units in the building
The building's union staff
questions.x: The co-op corporation, acting through its board, is the principal. Each shareholder is the trap: shareholders receive services but are not individually the agent's principal.

questions.q: The Certified Property Manager (CPM) designation is awarded by:
c: The NYS Department of State's licensing unit
The Institute of Real Estate Management
HUD's Office of Housing
BOMI International
questions.x: IREM awards the CPM, ARM, and AMO designations. BOMI is the trap: it awards the RPA designation.

questions.q: A planned unit development (PUD) is typically managed for:
c: The county planning board
Each homeowner separately
The developer indefinitely
An owners association
questions.x: In a PUD, owners hold their own lots and a homeowners association owns and maintains the common areas, hiring the manager. The developer answer is the trap: control passes to the HOA.

questions.q: A NYC landlord with a 12-unit building wants the manager to hold security deposits in the owner's operating account. The manager should:
c: Agree, since the owner controls the money
Agree, if the owner signs a waiver
Hold them in his own personal account
Use a separate interest-bearing account
questions.x: Deposits belong to tenants and cannot be commingled, and for buildings with 6 or more units they go in an interest-bearing account. The waiver answer is the trap: the owner cannot waive tenants' statutory protection.

questions.q: A budget that projects one year of income and day-to-day expenses is a(n):
c: Operating budget
Capital reserve budget
Stabilized budget
Construction budget
questions.x: The operating budget is the annual plan. Stabilized budget is the trap: it normalizes several years into a typical year.

questions.q: A stabilized budget is best described as:
c: A budget approved by the Rent Guidelines Board
A typical year smoothed from several years
A budget for rent-stabilized apartments
A one-month emergency spending plan
questions.x: Stabilized means normalized, avoiding distortion from a one-time expense or vacancy spike. The rent-stabilized answer is the trap: the term has nothing to do with rent regulation.

questions.q: All of the following are capital expenses EXCEPT:
c: Replacing the roof
Installing new windows
Replacing the boiler
Paying the water bill
questions.x: Utilities are operating expenses. Replacing the boiler is the tempting pick for some, but a replacement of a major system is a capital expense funded from reserves.

questions.q: Which is an example of a variable expense?
c: Real property taxes
Utility costs, which vary
Annual insurance premium
Ground rent fixed by lease
questions.x: Variable expenses move with occupancy and season. Insurance is the trap: the premium stays the same regardless of occupancy.

questions.q: A document listing each unit, tenant, lease expiration, rent, and deposit is a:
c: Management proposal
Stabilized budget
Rent roll
Management report
questions.x: The rent roll is the unit-by-unit income list that buyers and lenders review first. The management report is the trap: it summarizes monthly results, not each lease.

questions.q: A 4-unit building rents for $1,500, $1,600, $1,700, and $1,800 a month. Vacancy and collection loss is 5% and operating expenses are $30,000 a year. What is NOI?
questions.x: PGI = $6,600 x 12 = $79,200; less 5% vacancy ($3,960) = EGI $75,240; minus $30,000 expenses = $45,240. $49,200 is the trap: it forgets vacancy and collection loss.

questions.q: Cleaning and servicing a boiler every August before heating season is:
c: Corrective (reactive) maintenance
Preventive maintenance
Deferred maintenance
A capital improvement
questions.x: Scheduled work to prevent breakdowns is preventive maintenance. Corrective is the trap: it fixes something already broken.

questions.q: A Harlem walk-up has a cracked parapet and rotting window sills that the owner has ignored for years. This is best described as:
c: Routine maintenance
Preventive maintenance
Deferred maintenance
Tenant improvements
questions.x: Needed work that has been put off is deferred maintenance, which reduces value and, in NYC, invites violations. Preventive is the trap: nothing here was done ahead of time.

questions.q: Buying a liability insurance policy for a building is an example of which risk management strategy?
c: Avoidance
Control
Retention
Transfer
questions.x: Insurance shifts the financial risk to the insurer: transfer. Control is the trap: it means reducing the odds of a loss, such as installing sprinklers.

questions.q: A manager installs better lighting and new locks in a garage after several break-ins. This risk strategy is:
c: Control
Avoidance
Transfer
Retention
questions.x: Reducing the likelihood or severity of a loss is control. Avoid is the trap: avoiding would mean closing the garage.

questions.q: A manager's monthly statement to the owner showing collections, expenses versus budget, vacancies, and repairs is a:
c: Management proposal
Management report
Rent roll
Capital reserve budget
questions.x: The management report shows actual results after the manager is hired. The proposal is the trap: it is the pitch made before hiring.

questions.q: A property manager's job typically includes all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Collecting rent and handling security deposits
Hiring and supervising contractors
Approving the buyer's mortgage loan
Preparing budgets and monthly reports
questions.x: Managers market and lease, collect rent and deposits, handle tenants, maintain the building, keep the books and manage compliance and risk. Approving a mortgage is the lender's decision, not a management function.

questions.q: Which task falls under the property manager's compliance function?
c: Filing the yearly HPD registration
Showing vacant units to applicants
Clearing gutters before winter
Sending the owner a monthly statement
questions.x: Compliance covers building codes, fair housing, rent regulation and registrations such as the annual HPD filing. Showing units is leasing, clearing gutters is maintenance and the monthly statement is reporting.

questions.q: An outside management firm pays a building's super $300 for each apartment he rents. The super has no license. Which is correct?
c: He is exempt as a resident manager of the building
He is leasing for a fee without a license
He is exempt because the fee is under $500
He needs a license only if he signs the lease
questions.x: Paid per apartment by an outside firm, he is not the owner's salaried employee, so the resident manager exception does not apply; leasing for a fee is brokerage. The exemption is the trap: it covers only the owner's own employee.

questions.q: Which person needs a real estate license to do the work described?
c: The owner's salaried super, renting units in that building
An owner leasing apartments in her own building
A clerk who files leases but never negotiates
A super paid per lease by an outside managing firm
questions.x: Being paid per lease by an outside firm makes it brokerage for a fee. The owner's own salaried super, renting only that owner's building, is the tempting wrong answer: he falls under the owner's exemption.

questions.q: In New York City, which residential buildings must register with HPD every year?
c: Buildings with 6 or more units
Buildings with 3 or more units
Only rent stabilized buildings
Only buildings built before 1974
questions.x: Residential buildings with 3 or more units register with HPD each year. The 6-unit and pre-1974 numbers come from rent stabilization coverage, the neighboring rule that makes them tempting.

questions.q: The manager of a 6-unit Astoria walk-up built in 1960 raises a stabilized tenant's rent above the Rent Guidelines Board increase. The result is:
c: No problem, since the lease was renewed
A violation only if the tenant is a senior
Overcharge liability for the building's owner
Liability for the manager alone, not the owner
questions.x: Increases beyond RGB guidelines on a stabilized apartment are overcharges, and the owner is liable. Pinning it on the manager alone is the trap: the manager acts as the owner's agent, so the owner answers for it.

questions.q: A property manager's core obligations to the owner include all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Guaranteeing the owner a yearly profit
Keeping the property to agreed standards
Reporting honestly and on time
Meeting the owner's income or value goals
questions.x: The manager's duties come down to meeting the owner's goals, maintaining the property, planning for the future and reporting. No manager can guarantee a profit. Reporting may look like a courtesy, but it is one of the four core duties.

questions.q: Planning for a building's future capital needs and repositioning is:
c: Solely the owner's job, outside the manager's role
Required only in condo and co-op buildings
The lender's job under the mortgage
A core duty the manager owes the owner
questions.x: Planning for the future of the project, including capital needs and repositioning, is one of the manager's four obligations along with meeting goals, maintaining and reporting. Leaving it to the owner alone is the trap.

questions.q: A roof will cost $90,000 to replace in about 5 years and a boiler $40,000 in about 4 years. About how much should the owner set aside each month to fund both?
c: About $1,500
About $10,833
About $2,333
About $28,000
questions.x: $90,000 / 5 = $18,000 and $40,000 / 4 = $10,000, so $28,000 a year, or $28,000 / 12 = about $2,333 a month. $28,000 is the trap: it is the annual figure, not the monthly one.

questions.q: Money set aside each month for a future boiler and roof replacement belongs in which budget?
c: The operating budget
The capital reserve budget
The stabilized budget
The tenant improvement budget
questions.x: The capital reserve budget sets money aside for big replacements and improvements. The operating budget covers one year of day-to-day income and expenses, which is the tempting mix-up.

questions.q: A management firm's bookkeeper handles all rent deposits. Which coverage protects the owner if she steals from the account?
c: Rent loss insurance
A fidelity bond on the staff
Boiler and machinery coverage
An umbrella policy
questions.x: A fidelity bond covers theft or dishonesty by staff who handle money. Rent loss (business interruption) insurance replaces rent after a covered disaster, not losses from an employee's theft.

questions.q: A fire forces tenants out for four months. Which coverage replaces the rent the owner loses while the building is repaired?
c: General liability
Workers' compensation
A fidelity bond
Rent loss coverage
questions.x: Rent loss (business interruption) insurance replaces income lost while a damaged building is repaired. General liability pays injury claims by others, not the owner's lost rent.

questions.q: Before being hired, a manager gives a prospective owner an analysis of the property and market, a proposed budget, a marketing plan and the fee. This is a:
c: Management proposal
Management report
Management agreement
Rent roll
questions.x: The proposal is the manager's pitch backed by numbers, made before hiring. The management report comes after hiring, usually monthly, which is the tempting mix-up.

questions.q: Which document is prepared before the owner hires the manager?
c: The monthly management report
The annual operating report
The management proposal
The year-end rent roll audit
questions.x: The management proposal (property and market analysis, budget, marketing plan, services and fee) is the pitch to win the account. Monthly and annual reports come only once the manager is hired.

questions.q: A manager could fill the last two vacancies today at 20% below market, or wait about a month for market-rate tenants. Absent other instructions, the owner's goals usually favor:
c: Filling them today at any rent
Leaving them empty to cut wear
Lowering every rent in the building
Waiting for market-rate tenants
questions.x: The manager's goal is the best long-term net income while preserving value, and below-market leases lock in lost income for years. Filling them today is the trap: 100% occupancy is not the goal by itself.

questions.q: Diane's company negotiates leases and collects rent for 15 different Queens landlords, earning a percentage of rents. Under RPL 440, her company is:
c: Brokerage that requires a broker license
Exempt, since rent collection is clerical
Exempt, since no sales are involved
Required to hold an appraiser license
questions.x: Leasing and collecting rent for others for a fee is brokerage, so a broker license is needed. The no-sales answer is the trap: RPL 440 covers leasing and rent collection, not just sales.

questions.q: Sal's superintendent starts collecting rents for three neighboring owners for a fee. Under Article 12-A, he now:
c: Stays exempt as a resident super
Needs a real estate license
Needs Sal's written consent
Stays exempt if paid in cash
questions.x: Collecting rent for other owners for a fee is brokerage, so the owner's resident-manager exemption no longer covers him. The resident-super answer is the trap: the exemption reaches only work for his own employer.

questions.q: A broker hired to find a buyer for one house is a special agent, while a property manager running a building day to day is a:
c: Special agent as well
Universal agent
General agent
Dual agent
questions.x: Ongoing authority over a range of matters for one principal makes the manager a general agent. Universal agent is the trap: it means authority over all of a principal's affairs, as with a broad power of attorney.

questions.q: An owner and manager disagree over whether the manager could approve a $9,000 roof repair without asking. Which document should settle it?
c: The tenants' leases
The rent roll
The certificate of occupancy
The management agreement
questions.x: The management agreement sets the manager's authority, including spending limits for repairs. The leases are the trap: they govern the landlord-tenant relationship, not the owner-manager one.

questions.q: A tenant asks the manager whether the owner would accept a lower renewal rent. The owner has said she would. The manager should:
c: Keep the owner's position confidential
Tell the tenant the lowest acceptable rent
Advise the tenant to hold out for a cut
Ask the tenant to make an offer in writing
questions.x: Loyalty and confidentiality run to the owner, so the manager does not reveal the owner's bottom line. Asking for a written offer is the tempting pick and fine as a next step, but the key duty is keeping the owner's position private.

questions.q: In a lease, the party who receives possession and pays rent is the:
c: Lessor
Lessee (the tenant)
Grantor
Mortgagee
questions.x: The lessee is the tenant, who takes possession and pays rent. Lessor is the trap: that is the landlord.

questions.q: A tenant rents an apartment month to month with no end date; it renews each month until someone gives notice. This is a:
c: Tenancy for years
Tenancy at sufferance
Periodic tenancy
Tenancy at will
questions.x: A tenancy that renews automatically for successive periods until notice is periodic. Tenancy at will is the trap: it has no set period at all and ends at either party's will (with statutory notice in NY).

questions.q: A constructive eviction claim generally requires all of the following EXCEPT:
c: A serious failure by the landlord
Premises made unfit for use
The tenant moving out in a timely way
A court order removing the tenant
questions.x: A court order removing the tenant is actual eviction; constructive eviction requires the tenant to leave because of the landlord's failure. Moving out is the tempting pick, but a tenant who stays generally cannot claim constructive eviction.

questions.q: A strip center's supermarket closes, and the small shops report falling sales. The manager's top leasing priority is likely to:
c: Replace the anchor that drew the traffic
Cut the small shops' rents
Convert the space to offices
Raise common area charges
questions.x: An anchor draws the traffic that small shops depend on, so replacing it comes first. Cutting small shops' rents is the trap: it treats the symptom, not the cause.

questions.q: A co-op shareholder demands that the managing agent fight a board decision to raise maintenance. The agent should:
c: Side with the shareholder
Follow the board's decision
Refer it to the Attorney General
Poll each shareholder first
questions.x: The managing agent represents the co-op corporation, acting through its board. Siding with the shareholder is the trap: shareholders are served, but they are not the agent's principal.

questions.q: The Real Property Administrator (RPA) designation, common among commercial building managers, is awarded by:
c: IREM
The NYS Department of State
BOMI International
The National Association of Realtors
questions.x: BOMI International awards the RPA. IREM is the trap: it awards the CPM, ARM, and AMO.

questions.q: In a typical PUD, the homeowners association handles all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Maintaining the common areas
Collecting association dues
Hiring the community manager
Re-roofing each owner's own home
questions.x: Owners in a PUD own and maintain their own homes and lots, while the HOA handles common areas. Hiring the manager is the tempting pick, but the HOA board does hire the manager.

questions.q: In a New York building with 6 or more apartments, tenant security deposits are held:
c: In an interest-bearing account, kept separate
In the owner's operating account
In the manager's personal account
Wherever the lease says, with no limit
questions.x: For buildings with 6 or more units, deposits go into a separate interest-bearing account and cannot be commingled. The lease answer is the trap: statutory deposit rules cannot be waived by lease.

questions.q: A manager prepares next year's plan of expected rents, payroll, utilities, and repairs. This is the:
c: Capital reserve budget
Operating budget
Stabilized budget
Construction budget
questions.x: An annual plan of income and day-to-day expenses is the operating budget. Capital reserve budget is the trap: it funds major replacements like a roof.

questions.q: Last year a building paid a one-time $80,000 facade repair. For an appraisal, the manager should present expenses using:
c: Last year's actual figures
A stabilized budget
This month's figures alone
The capital reserve study
questions.x: A stabilized budget normalizes one-time items so expenses reflect a typical year. Last year's actuals are the trap: they overstate expenses because of the one-time repair.

questions.q: A building replaces its entire elevator system for $250,000. This cost is best classified as:
c: An operating expense
A variable expense
Deferred maintenance
A capital expense, from reserves
questions.x: Replacing a major building system is a capital expense, usually funded from reserves. Operating expense is the trap: that covers recurring costs such as utilities and routine repairs.

questions.q: All of the following are generally fixed expenses EXCEPT:
c: Utilities that move with use
Real property taxes
Insurance premiums
Fixed ground rent
questions.x: Utilities vary with occupancy and season, so they are variable. Real property taxes are the tempting pick, but they do not change with occupancy.

questions.q: A lender reviewing a building wants to verify each lease's rent, expiration, and security deposit. The manager provides the:
c: Operating budget
Rent roll
Management proposal
Certificate of occupancy
questions.x: The rent roll lists each unit's tenant, rent, lease expiration, and deposit. The operating budget is the trap: it projects totals, not each lease.

questions.q: A 6-unit building rents each unit for $1,250 a month. Vacancy and collection loss is 4% and operating expenses are $34,000 a year. What is NOI?
questions.x: PGI = $1,250 x 6 x 12 = $90,000; less 4% ($3,600) = EGI $86,400; minus $34,000 = NOI $52,400. $56,000 is the trap: it skips the vacancy deduction.

questions.q: A tenant reports a burst pipe at 2 a.m. and the super repairs it. This is:
c: Preventive (scheduled) maintenance
Deferred maintenance
A capital improvement
Corrective maintenance
questions.x: Fixing something that has already broken is corrective maintenance. Preventive is the trap: it is scheduled work done before a breakdown.

questions.q: Deferred maintenance on a building most directly:
c: Reduces value and invites violations
Raises value by saving cash
Has no effect on value
Converts repairs into capital gains
questions.x: Putting off needed work lets small problems grow, lowering value and, in NYC, inviting violations. The saves-cash answer is the trap: short-term savings usually cost more later.

questions.q: An owner decides to pay small slip-and-fall claims out of pocket instead of insuring them, keeping a high deductible. This strategy is:
c: Avoid the risk
Retention
Transfer
Control
questions.x: Accepting a risk and paying for losses yourself is retention. Transfer is the trap: that would shift the risk to an insurer.

questions.q: After repeated injuries, a manager permanently closes a building's rooftop pool. This risk strategy is:
c: Control
Transfer
Avoidance
Retain the risk
questions.x: Eliminating the activity that creates the risk is avoidance. Control is the trap: it would reduce the risk, such as adding a lifeguard, while keeping the pool open.

questions.q: Before being hired, a management firm gives an owner a document describing its services, fees, and plan for the building. This is a:
c: Management report
Rent roll
Stabilized budget
Management proposal
questions.x: The pitch made before hiring is the management proposal. Management report is the trap: it shows actual results after the firm is hired.

questions.q: A Rochester landlord's screening company charges $35 for a combined background and credit check. What may the landlord collect from the applicant?
c: $35, the actual cost of the checks
$20, the statutory maximum
$50, the late fee ceiling
Nothing, as screening fees are banned
questions.x: New York caps the charge at the actual cost of background and credit checks or $20, whichever is less, and it applies statewide. The actual-cost answer is the trap: actual cost is the limit only when it is under $20.

questions.q: Under New York law, a residential landlord collecting a background check fee must do all of the following EXCEPT:
c: Keep the fee at actual cost or $20, whichever is less
Give the applicant a copy of the background check
Waive it if the applicant has a report from the last 30 days
Refund it to applicants who are approved for the lease
questions.x: Nothing in the law requires refunding the screening charge to approved applicants. The 30-day waiver is the tempting pick, but the landlord must waive the fee when the applicant provides a background or credit check conducted within the past 30 days.

questions.q: A Bronx landlord hires a brokerage to list and lease a vacant apartment. Under the NYC FARE Act, who pays that brokerage's fee?
c: The landlord who hired the brokerage
The tenant, if the listing discloses the fee
The tenant and landlord, split equally
The tenant, if the lease is two years or more
questions.x: The FARE Act bars a broker who represents the landlord from charging the tenant, so the landlord pays its own broker. The disclosure answer is the trap: the law requires fee disclosure, but disclosure does not make a landlord's broker fee chargeable to the tenant.

questions.q: Which arrangement remains lawful under New York City's FARE Act?
c: A listing broker charging the tenant one month's rent
A landlord's broker charging the tenant a disclosed fee
A tenant hiring her own broker and paying that broker
A landlord adding its broker's fee to the move-in costs
questions.x: A tenant may still choose to hire and pay a broker who works for her. The disclosed-fee answer is the trap: disclosure is required for any tenant fee, but it does not permit a landlord's broker to charge the tenant.

questions.q: A Staten Island owner of a 12-unit building tells his manager not to rent to Section 8 voucher holders. The instruction is:
c: Lawful, since vouchers are a business decision
Lawful, if the owner has under 25 units
Unlawful if the voucher covers the full rent
Unlawful source of income discrimination
questions.x: The New York State Human Rights Law protects lawful source of income, including housing vouchers, and New York City's law does too. The business-decision answer is the trap: refusing vouchers has been illegal statewide since 2019, outside narrow exemptions such as owner-occupied one- and two-family homes.

questions.q: A voucher holder's share of a $2,400 rent is $600. The landlord requires income of 40 times the monthly rent from every applicant. Applying that to the full rent for her is:
c: Proper, because the same rule applies to everyone
Proper, if she may offer a guarantor instead
Likely discrimination based on source of income
Required by the voucher program's own rules
questions.x: A full-rent income test screens out voucher holders even though it looks neutral; the voucher program has already found the tenant's share affordable. The same-rule-for-all answer is the trap: a neutral rule that predictably excludes a protected group can still be discrimination.

questions.q: Under New York City's Fair Chance for Housing law, a landlord may review an applicant's criminal history:
c: Before reviewing income and credit
After making a conditional offer
At any time with written consent
At no stage of the application
questions.x: Criminal history comes last: after the applicant otherwise qualifies and receives a conditional offer, and then within limited look-back periods. The no-stage answer is the trap: the law limits timing and scope; it does not ban all checks.

questions.q: A Queens manager runs criminal checks on all applicants on day one to "save time." What is the problem under the city's Fair Chance for Housing law?
c: The check must wait until a conditional offer
The check needs approval from HPD first
Checks are limited to buildings with over 6 units
Applicants must pay for their own checks
questions.x: The law requires the landlord to evaluate other qualifications and make a conditional offer before looking at criminal history. The HPD answer is the trap: HPD does not approve screening; the Commission on Human Rights enforces the city's anti-discrimination law.

questions.q: In a 20-unit building, a $3,000 security deposit earns 2% interest for a full year. How much interest belongs to the tenant?
questions.x: Interest is $3,000 x 2% = $60. The landlord may keep 1% a year of the deposit as an administrative fee: $30. The tenant gets $60 minus $30 = $30. The $60 answer is the trap: it forgets the 1% the landlord may keep.

questions.q: A Utica landlord owns a 6-unit building. Where must tenants' security deposits be held?
c: In the landlord's general operating account
In any account, as long as it is labeled
In the landlord's personal savings account
In an interest-bearing NY bank account
questions.x: For buildings with six or more units, deposits go in an interest-bearing account at a New York bank, with written notice to the tenant of the bank and amount. The labeled-account answer is the trap: separation alone is not enough at six units or more; the account must also bear interest.

questions.q: An Upper Manhattan apartment was lawfully deregulated in 2017 by high-rent vacancy. After the 2019 HSTPA, the apartment is:
c: Still deregulated
Stabilized again
Stabilized on vacancy
Rent controlled
questions.x: HSTPA repealed high-rent vacancy deregulation going forward, but units lawfully deregulated before June 14, 2019 remain deregulated. The stabilized-again answer is the trap: the repeal did not reach back to lawful deregulations.

questions.q: After June 14, 2019, can a vacant rent-stabilized apartment in New York City leave stabilization because its legal rent passes a high-rent threshold?
c: Yes, if the rent passes the current threshold
Yes, if the owner also renovates the unit
No, high-rent vacancy deregulation was repealed
No, unless the tenant's household income exceeds $200,000
questions.x: HSTPA repealed both high-rent vacancy deregulation and high-income deregulation. The renovation answer is the trap: renovations once helped push rents over the threshold, but there is no longer a threshold to cross.

questions.q: A Buffalo tenant's rent is $800 a month and is paid 10 days late. What is the maximum late fee the landlord may charge?
questions.x: The cap is $50 or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is less. Here 5% of $800 is $40, which is less than $50. The $50 answer is the trap: $50 is the ceiling only when 5% of the rent is higher.

questions.q: Under New York law, a residential landlord may charge a late fee only if the rent is not paid within:
c: 3 days of the due date
5 days of the due date
10 days of the due date
14 days of the due date
questions.x: A late fee may be charged only after rent is more than five days late, and it is capped at the lesser of $50 or 5% of the rent. The 14-day answer is the trap: 14 days is the length of the written rent demand before a nonpayment case.

questions.q: Before starting a residential nonpayment proceeding in New York, the landlord must serve a rent demand that is:
c: Oral or written, giving 3 days to pay
Written, giving at least 14 days to pay
Written, giving at least 30 days to pay
Oral, if given in the presence of a witness
questions.x: Since HSTPA in 2019, the demand must be written, state the amount and period claimed, and give at least 14 days. The 3-day answer is the trap: it describes the pre-2019 rule, which allowed oral demands.

questions.q: A Yonkers landlord's super knocks on a tenant's door and tells her she has 3 days to pay or face court. The landlord files a nonpayment case on day 4. The case is:
c: Proper, because the super is acting as the owner's own agent
Proper, if the tenant admits the rent is unpaid
Defective, because the owner has to sign the demand
Defective, because no 14-day written demand was served
questions.x: An oral 3-day demand no longer satisfies the law; a written demand giving at least 14 days is required. The agent answer is the trap: an agent may serve a demand, but it still must be in writing with the 14-day period.

questions.q: A Jackson Heights owner removes a tenant's door and puts her belongings on the curb after two months of unpaid rent, with no court order. The owner has committed:
c: A lawful eviction for nonpayment
A constructive eviction defense
An unlawful eviction, a crime
A permitted self-help remedy
questions.x: Removing an occupant without a court order, including by removing doors or belongings, is an unlawful eviction under RPAPL 768, a class A misdemeanor with civil penalties. The constructive eviction answer is the trap: that is a tenant's claim when conditions force her out, not the name of the owner's offense.

questions.q: Each of the following is a form of unlawful eviction in New York EXCEPT:
c: Changing the locks while the tenant is at work
Removal by a city marshal under a court warrant
Shutting off water to pressure a tenant to leave
Taking the door off its hinges after a dispute
questions.x: A marshal or sheriff executing a court warrant is the lawful way to remove a tenant. Shutting off water is the tempting pick because it is not physical removal, but cutting essential services to force a tenant out is a form of unlawful eviction too.

questions.q: A tenant owes $3,000 in rent, $100 in late fees and $600 in lease-based legal fees. In a residential nonpayment proceeding against this rental tenant, the landlord may seek:
questions.x: RPAPL 702 bars fees, charges and penalties other than rent in residential summary proceedings, whatever the lease says. Only the $3,000 in rent may be sought. The $3,100 answer is the trap: late fees may be lawful to charge, but they cannot be recovered in the summary case.

questions.q: In a nonpayment case, a judgment for $6,000 in rent is entered and a warrant issues. Before the marshal acts, the tenant deposits the full $6,000 with the court. The court generally must:
c: Vacate the warrant, unless the landlord shows bad faith
Let the eviction proceed, since the warrant ended the lease
Vacate it if the landlord also gets its legal fees
Let the landlord decide whether to accept the deposit
questions.x: Since 2019, RPAPL 749 requires the court to vacate the warrant when the tenant tenders or deposits the full rent due before execution, unless the landlord proves the tenant withheld rent in bad faith. The lease-ended answer is the trap: a warrant no longer ends the landlord-tenant relationship.

questions.q: A tenant moves out of an Albany apartment on June 30. By what date must the landlord give an itemized statement and return the balance of the deposit?
c: July 14
July 30
July 7
August 29
questions.x: The landlord has 14 days after the tenant vacates, so July 14. Missing it forfeits the landlord's right to keep any part of the deposit. The July 30 answer is the trap: 30 days is a notice period found in other landlord-tenant rules, not the deposit deadline.

questions.q: A landlord with a valid $600 damage claim sends the itemized statement and the balance of a $2,000 deposit 21 days after move-out. What is the result?
c: The landlord keeps $600, since the damage claim is valid
The landlord owes a $50 late charge on top
The landlord forfeits the right to keep any of it
The tenant may keep half of the $600 claimed
questions.x: A landlord who misses the 14-day deadline forfeits any right to retain any portion of the deposit, so the full $2,000 is owed. The valid-claim answer is the trap: accurate deductions do not cure a late statement.

questions.q: In New York City, an owner must offer a rent-stabilized tenant a renewal lease on the DHCR form no more than 150 and no less than how many days before the current lease expires?
c: 30 days
60 days
120 days
90 days
questions.x: The renewal offer goes out between 150 and 90 days before expiration, and the tenant then has 60 days to choose a one- or two-year term. The 60-day answer is the trap: that is the tenant's response period, not the owner's deadline.

questions.q: A stabilized tenant's renewal lease will begin November 1, 2026. Which Rent Guidelines Board order sets the allowable increase?
c: The order covering leases starting October 1, 2026
The order in effect when the offer was mailed
The order the tenant picks as more favorable to her lease
The order in effect when the old lease began
questions.x: The guideline that applies is the one covering the date the renewal lease starts; for a November 1, 2026 start, that is the order for leases beginning October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027 (a 0% freeze for both terms). The mailing-date answer is the trap: the offer may go out months earlier, but the lease start date controls.

questions.q: After a residential tenant moves out in New York, the landlord must return the deposit or give an itemized statement of deductions within:
c: 30 days
45 days
60 days
14 days
questions.x: Since the 2019 HSTPA, GOL 7-108 requires the deposit, or an itemized statement of any deductions, within 14 days after the tenant vacates. 30 days is the trap: it is the rule in many other states and in older New York study materials.

questions.q: A landlord sends the itemized deduction statement 20 days after the tenant moved out, listing real damage. The landlord:
c: May keep the deposit for damage but not for rent
Forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit
Has until day 30, so the statement is on time
Must pay the tenant a $500 civil penalty to DOS
questions.x: Missing the 14-day deadline means the landlord forfeits any right to retain any part of the deposit, even for real damage (GOL 7-108). The day-30 choice is the old or out-of-state rule. DOS does not enforce deposit rules against owners.

questions.q: A Queens landlord owns a seven-unit building. Tenants' security deposits must be held:
c: In the building's operating account, with good records
In any account, because interest applies at ten units
In an interest-bearing NY bank account, interest to tenants
With the Rent Guidelines Board until the lease ends
questions.x: GOL 7-103 makes every deposit trust money that cannot be commingled. For buildings with six or more units it must be in an interest-bearing account at a New York bank, with the interest going to the tenant less a 1% a year administrative fee. The operating account choice is commingling.

questions.q: In a building with six or more units, the landlord may keep, from the interest on a tenant's deposit:
c: All of the interest the account earns
Half of the interest the account earns
2% a year of the deposit as a handling fee
1% a year of the deposit as an administrative fee
questions.x: GOL 7-103 lets the landlord keep 1% per year of the deposit as an administrative expense; the rest of the interest belongs to the tenant, paid annually, credited to rent, or paid at the end. Keeping all the interest is a common violation in small buildings.

cram.html: Leasing or collecting rent for others for a fee requires a NY broker license.
Resident manager (owner's salaried on-site employee, one owner): no license needed.
Management agreement creates a general agency. Listing broker = special agent.
Manager is a fiduciary of the owner, not the tenants.
Agreement contents: property, term, authority, reporting, fee, accounting, insurance, owner's goals, termination. In writing; required if over 1 year.
A salesperson manages only through the broker; the fee is paid to the broker.
Security deposits: separate account, never commingled. 6+ units: interest-bearing, landlord keeps 1% a year.
Lessor = landlord. Lessee = tenant. Tenancy for years = definite end date, any length.
Actual eviction = removal through court. Constructive eviction = landlord's failure drives tenant out.
Operating budget: 1 year. Capital reserve: replacements. Stabilized: normalized multi-year.
Fixed expenses: taxes, insurance. Variable: utilities, repairs. Capital: roof, boiler, windows.
Rent roll: unit, tenant, lease end, rent, deposit, status. Starting point for NOI.
Maintenance: preventive (scheduled), corrective (broke), routine (daily), deferred (postponed).
Risk: Avoid, Control, Transfer, Retain. Insurance = transfer.
Proposal comes before hiring; management report comes after.
Co-op managing agent works for the corporation through the board, not individual shareholders.
Designations: CPM, ARM, AMO (IREM); RPA (BOMI); CMCA (community associations).
Anchor store = major traffic draw in retail. PUD = owned lots plus HOA common areas.
Stabilized budget is not about rent stabilization.

glossary.def: The IRC Section 216 test under which a co-op qualifies for shareholder tax deductions if at least 80% of its gross income comes from tenant-shareholders; since 2007, alternative 80% square footage and 90% expenditure tests also qualify.
glossary.deep:
Shareholders can deduct their share of the building's real estate taxes and mortgage interest only if the co-op is a cooperative housing corporation. Traditionally that meant no more than 20% of income from outside sources like store rents or garage fees.

Since 2007, a co-op also qualifies if at least 80% of its square footage is used by shareholders for residential or related purposes, or 90% of its spending benefits shareholders.

NY example: a Chelsea co-op earning $1.6M from maintenance and $500K from retail gets 76% from shareholders, failing the income test but possibly passing another.

On the exam: 80% from shareholders, 20% max passive outside income.
glossary.contrast: A condop structure removes commercial income from the co-op altogether.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A fuel tank located above ground, usually in a basement or on an outdoor pad, commonly holding heating oil.
glossary.deep:
Most NY homes with oil heat have an AST, typically 275 or 330 gallons, in the basement. Because it is visible, leaks, rust and weeping seams can be spotted and fixed before they become a cleanup. Inspectors check the tank's legs, bottom, fill and vent lines, and the oil line to the burner.

Analogy: a fuel tank you can see versus one buried in a mystery box. NY example: a Bronx two-family's basement tank shows a stain under its bottom seam; the buyer requires the seller to replace it before closing.

On the exam: AST leaks are visible and cheaper to address than UST leaks. DEC spill reporting still applies.
glossary.contrast: An underground storage tank is buried, and leaks go unseen into soil and groundwater.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A condensed written history summarizing every recorded document affecting a property's title.
glossary.deep: An abstract is a summary, in chronological order, of every deed, mortgage, lien, and court record in the chain of title. An attorney reviews it and gives an opinion on whether title is good. In much of New York today, the title company's report (certificate of title) serves this role, though some upstate counties still use abstracts kept with the property and updated for each sale. On the exam: an abstract is not insurance and not a guarantee; it is a history to be examined.
glossary.contrast: Title insurance protects against loss; an abstract only summarizes records.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Touching or sharing a boundary; abutting owners usually get notice of zoning hearings on a neighboring lot.
glossary.deep:
Abutting means sharing a lot line. Zoning procedures often require the applicant to notify abutting owners, and owners within a set radius, of a ZBA or planning board hearing so they can speak. Abutting owners also are the most likely to have standing to sue over a decision.

Analogy: the people on either side of you at the movie, not just in the theater. NY example: before a Scarsdale ZBA hearing on a side-yard variance, the applicant mails notice to all owners within a set distance, and the abutting neighbor testifies about light and privacy.

On the exam: abutting equals adjoining, adjacent with a shared boundary.
glossary.contrast: Adjacent sometimes means nearby without touching; abutting means sharing a boundary.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A mortgage or note clause allowing the lender to declare the entire balance due immediately upon default.
glossary.deep:
Miss enough payments and the lender stops asking for this month's payment and demands everything.

Like a phone contract that makes the full device balance due if you stop paying.

A Canarsie homeowner misses four payments. The lender accelerates the $380,000 balance, then files the foreclosure action. Without acceleration, the lender could only sue for missed installments.

On the exam: acceleration = default trigger; it is what makes foreclosure of the full debt possible.
glossary.contrast: The alienation clause is triggered by a sale, not a default.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Acquiring title to additions to property, either natural (such as accretion) or man-made (such as fixtures or abandoned trade fixtures).
glossary.deep: Accession is the umbrella term for gaining ownership of something added to what you already own. Natural accession includes accretion and alluvion along a waterfront. Man-made accession includes improvements and fixtures attached to the land, and trade fixtures a tenant leaves behind after the lease ends, which become the landlord's. When a Williamsburg cafe abandons its bolted espresso bar, the landlord gains it by accession. On the exam: accession covers both natural additions and abandoned improvements.
glossary.contrast: Accretion is one specific type of accession: gradual build-up of land by water.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A secondary dwelling unit within or on the lot of a single-family home, allowed in many municipalities by permit and often only if the owner lives on site.
glossary.deep:
An accessory apartment, also called an accessory dwelling unit (ADU), is a small second unit: a basement apartment, a converted garage, or a backyard cottage. Many NY suburbs allow them by special permit to create affordable housing and help older owners, often with owner-occupancy, size, and parking conditions.

Analogy: a granny flat with a permit. NY example: towns on Long Island issue accessory apartment permits that must be renewed and may lapse on sale. NYC's 2024 City of Yes changes allow ADUs on many one and two family lots. An unpermitted basement unit is still illegal.

On the exam: accessory apartments are legal only when the ordinance allows them and the permit is in place.
glossary.contrast: An illegal basement apartment has no permit or CO; a legal accessory apartment is authorized under the ordinance.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A use customarily incidental and subordinate to the main use of a lot, located on the same lot.
glossary.deep:
An accessory use tags along with the principal use. A house gets a garage, shed, pool, or home office; a restaurant gets a parking lot; a church gets a rectory. Zoning lets accessory uses in automatically if they are truly incidental, though they usually have their own setback and size limits.

Analogy: the side dish, never the main course. NY example: a Huntington homeowner builds a detached garage as an accessory structure; turning it into a rental cottage would change it into a second principal dwelling, which needs approval.

On the exam: garage, shed and pool equal accessory use. The trap is calling them nonconforming or special uses.
glossary.contrast: A home occupation is a business conducted within the dwelling; an accessory use is any subordinate use incidental to the main use.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The duty to safeguard and account for all money, property, and documents belonging to the client or others.
glossary.deep:
Every dollar and every document has to be where it should be, and you have to be able to show it.

Like a treasurer of a block association: you keep the dues in the association's account, not your own, and you produce a ledger when asked.

A buyer's $50,000 deposit given to a NY broker goes into a special escrow account, never the firm's operating account. Mixing them is commingling; spending it is conversion.

On the exam: commingling and conversion are the classic accounting violations. NY requires escrow deposits and records kept 3 years.
glossary.contrast: Reasonable care is about competence; accounting is about money and documents.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The gradual increase of land along a shore or riverbank from deposits of soil by water; the owner gains the new land.
glossary.deep: Accretion is slow growth. Over years, a river or the ocean deposits sand and silt along the shore, and the riparian or littoral owner's land gets bigger. The new soil itself is called alluvion. The owner gains title to it automatically. Sand building up on a Fire Island or Montauk beachfront over decades is accretion. On the exam: accretion is gradual and adds land to the owner. Sudden change is avulsion; gradual loss is erosion.
glossary.contrast: Avulsion is a sudden change that does not shift ownership.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A formal declaration before a notary public or other authorized officer by the person signing a document that the signature is genuine and voluntary.
glossary.deep: An acknowledgment is the notary's certificate at the end of the deed. The grantor appears before the notary, proves identity, and declares the signature is theirs and given freely. It guards against forgery. In New York, a deed must be acknowledged to be recorded, but an unacknowledged deed is still valid between grantor and grantee once delivered. Grace's mother's deed was notarized but never delivered, so it transferred nothing. On the exam: acknowledgment is required for recording, not for validity.
glossary.contrast: Delivery and acceptance are what actually pass title.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Debt used to buy, build, or substantially improve a main or second home and secured by it; its interest is deductible up to $750,000 of debt.
glossary.deep:
Acquisition debt is the debt the tax code rewards. The limit is $750,000 ($375,000 married filing separately) for loans after December 15, 2017; older loans keep $1 million. The 2025 tax law made $750,000 permanent. Refinanced acquisition debt keeps its status up to the old balance; construction loans count for up to 24 months.

Think of it as the "housing purpose" test: what did the money do?

Leo's $560,000 mortgage on a Sunnyside condo is acquisition debt; all its interest is deductible if he itemizes.

On the exam: $750,000 limit, purpose matters, must be secured by the home.
glossary.contrast: Home equity debt used for non-home purposes does not qualify.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A unit of land area equal to 43,560 square feet. There are 640 acres in a square mile.
glossary.deep:
An acre is roughly the size of an American football field without the end zones.

Seventeen standard 25 x 100 Brooklyn lots fit in about one acre.

An Ulster County parcel of 330 x 660 feet is 217,800 square feet, which is exactly 5 acres. At $30,000 per acre, the price is $150,000.

On the exam: memorize 43,560. Square feet / 43,560 = acres; acres x 43,560 = square feet.
glossary.contrast: Hectare: a metric unit, about 2.47 acres.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: Damage, neglect, or major alteration by a life tenant (or tenant) that reduces the property's value for the future owner.
glossary.deep: Waste protects the person who will own the property later. A life tenant must keep the property reasonably maintained and may not strip it for profit. Cutting and selling timber, ripping out a brownstone's stained glass to sell, or letting the roof collapse are waste. The remainderman or reversioner can sue for an injunction or damages. Ordinary wear and tear is not waste. On the exam: a scenario where a life tenant damages or neglects the property points to waste, and the remedy belongs to the remainderman.
glossary.contrast: Ordinary wear and tear is normal deterioration, not waste.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Income from work or a business you materially participate in, such as wages and commissions.
glossary.deep:
Active income is earned by doing. Jordan's commission checks, Tasha's mortgage broker fees, and a restaurant owner's profits are active. Losses from passive activities generally cannot offset it, which is the point of the passive loss rules.

Think of three buckets: active, passive, portfolio. Losses usually stay in their own bucket.

Sal's salary as a part-time contractor is active; his rents are passive.

On the exam: identify the bucket. Wages and commissions are active; rents are passive; dividends and interest are portfolio.
glossary.contrast: Passive income comes from rentals or businesses you do not materially run.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: Replacement cost minus depreciation: what the damaged item was worth at the time of loss.
glossary.deep:
ACV pays for the old thing, not a new one.

If your 6-year-old TV is stolen, ACV gives you the price of a 6-year-old TV, which will not buy a new one.

A storm destroys a 12-year-old roof on a Buffalo house. A new roof costs $20,000; with a 20-year life, it was 60% used up. ACV pays $8,000 minus the deductible. Replacement cost coverage would pay $20,000 minus the deductible.

On the exam: ACV = replacement cost - depreciation. HO-8 is the ACV-based form.
glossary.contrast: Replacement cost pays to replace with new, without subtracting depreciation.
glossary.subject: s12

glossary.def: Removal of a tenant from the premises, lawfully through a court proceeding or unlawfully by self-help.
glossary.deep:
Eviction is the end of possession. Actual means the tenant is physically put out.

Lawful version in NY: the landlord brings a summary proceeding (nonpayment or holdover) in court, wins a judgment, and a city marshal or sheriff executes a warrant of eviction. Locking a tenant out, removing belongings, or cutting utilities to force them out is an illegal eviction, and in NY a person who does this to a tenant of 30+ days faces civil penalties and possible criminal charges.

On the exam: only a court process can remove a NY tenant. Self-help evictions are illegal.
glossary.contrast: Constructive eviction is when the landlord's failures force the tenant to leave voluntarily.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: What a person actually knows, has read, has been told, or has seen.
glossary.deep: Actual notice is real knowledge. If a buyer is told by the seller that he already sold the property last week, the buyer has actual notice even if that earlier deed was never recorded. Under New York's race-notice rule, a buyer with actual notice of an earlier unrecorded deed cannot win by recording first. Actual notice can also come from reading documents or seeing something on the property. On the exam: actual = personal knowledge; constructive = presumed by law from recording or possession.
glossary.contrast: Constructive notice is presumed by law.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A tax based on the value of the thing taxed. The general real property tax is ad valorem: assessed value times the tax rate.
glossary.deep:
Ad valorem is Latin for "according to value." Bigger value, bigger bill.

Like a sales tax: a $1,000 TV carries more tax than a $100 one.

Two Rochester houses in the same district: one assessed at $150,000, one at $300,000. At the same rate, the second pays twice the tax.

On the exam: general property taxes are ad valorem. Special assessments are not; they are based on benefit, such as front footage on a new sidewalk.
glossary.contrast: Special assessment: based on benefit from an improvement, not on value.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: The percentage added to usable space to reach rentable space: rentable divided by usable, minus 1.
glossary.deep:
The add-on factor is the landlord's markup on your usable space for common areas.

Using the oranges again: if you want 8 pounds of fruit and peel adds 2 pounds, the bag is 25% bigger than what you eat.

Leo's floor: 10,000 / 8,000 minus 1 = 25%. Same 2,000 square feet as the 20% loss factor, different denominator.

On the exam: add-on divides by usable. If a question gives both numbers, check which factor it wants.
glossary.contrast: The loss factor divides by rentable and is always the smaller percentage.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A loan whose interest rate changes periodically based on an index plus a margin, within caps.
glossary.deep:
Lower rate now, uncertainty later.

Like a variable electricity plan: cheap this month, unknown next year.

A 5/1 ARM is fixed for 5 years, then adjusts every year. New rate = index + margin, limited by the periodic cap and the lifetime cap. A doctor in Westchester expecting to move in 5 years might take one to save money.

On the exam: index moves, margin fixed; caps limit change; payment caps can cause negative amortization.
glossary.contrast: A graduated payment mortgage changes payments on a fixed schedule, not with an index.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Basis plus capital improvements, minus depreciation taken and casualty losses claimed.
glossary.deep:
Adjusted basis is the updated price tag. Every real improvement (new roof, extension, central air) raises it; every dollar of depreciation lowers it. The higher it is at sale, the smaller your gain.

Picture a running tab: you add receipts for improvements and subtract the tax breaks you already enjoyed.

The Okafors: $190,000 basis plus $310,000 in improvements = $500,000 adjusted basis. Sal: $1,100,000 minus $560,000 depreciation = $540,000.

On the exam: gain = amount realized minus adjusted basis. Watch for distractors that add repairs or forget depreciation.
glossary.contrast: Depreciable basis excludes land and is the amount you depreciate, not the amount you subtract at sale.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: Action DOS takes against a licensee after a hearing: reprimand, fine up to $2,000 per violation, suspension, or revocation.
glossary.deep:
Discipline is the State acting as licensor, not as prosecutor. A complaint triggers an investigation, then a hearing before an administrative law judge. Outcomes range from a reprimand to revocation. After revocation, a person generally cannot be relicensed for 1 year.

Think of it as a referee's card system: warning, fine, sit out, ejection.

A Queens salesperson who kept a $4,800 rental deposit was revoked; her broker was fined for failure to supervise.

On the exam: DOS can reprimand, fine (up to $2,000 per violation), suspend, or revoke. It does not jail anyone: that is criminal court.
glossary.contrast: Misdemeanor prosecution is criminal and goes through the courts.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: The person appointed by the court to settle the estate of someone who died without a will; traditionally administratrix for a woman.
glossary.deep: Because an intestate person named no executor, the Surrogate's Court appoints an administrator, usually the surviving spouse or a close relative, and issues letters of administration. The administrator does the same work as an executor: collects assets, pays debts, and distributes property to the heirs under the intestacy statute, or sells real property with an administrator's deed. On the exam: administrator = no will, appointed by court. Executor = will, named by testator.
glossary.contrast: An executor is named in the will.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Written informed consent, given on the NY disclosure form before any specific deal, allowing the firm to act as dual agent if an in-house transaction arises.
glossary.deep:
It is saying yes ahead of time to a situation that might happen later.

Like agreeing when you join a gym that a trainer might also train your workout partner.

When the Okafors listed, they checked the advance consent box. Months later Leo, a firm buyer client, wants their house. The firm may proceed as dual agent, but still tells the Okafors and Leo when it actually happens.

On the exam: advance consent was added by the 2011 amendments. It does not excuse disclosure when the dual situation arises.
glossary.contrast: Advance consent with designated sales agents also names the agent who will represent that party.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.term: Advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents
glossary.def: Written informed consent, given in advance on the NY disclosure form, to dual agency with designated sales agents, naming the agent appointed for that party.
glossary.deep:
It is advance consent plus a name: "if this becomes dual, my agent will be this person."

Like pre-selecting your own attorney in case the firm ends up representing your counterparty too.

Leo checks advance consent with designated sales agents and Jordan's name is listed as his designated agent. When Leo wants a firm listing, Jordan stays his advocate and another agent is designated for the sellers.

On the exam: RPL 443 defines both forms of advance consent. Both are optional and written.
glossary.contrast: Plain advance consent to dual agency does not name a designated agent.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Acquiring title to another's land by possession that is hostile under a claim of right, actual, open and notorious, exclusive, and continuous for 10 years in New York.
glossary.deep: Adverse possession rewards someone who openly treats land as their own for long enough while the true owner does nothing. In New York (RPAPL Article 5, amended 2008) the possession must be hostile with a reasonable basis to believe the land is the possessor's, actual, open and notorious, exclusive, and continuous for 10 years. Successive possessors can add their time (tacking). Since 2008, fences, hedges, plantings, sheds, and lawn mowing across a line are deemed permissive. A patio and hot tub 14 feet onto a neighbor's lot for 13 years is a strong claim. Title is confirmed in a quiet title action. On the exam: 10 years, permission defeats it.
glossary.contrast: A prescriptive easement gives only a right of use and does not require exclusivity.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Before-tax cash flow minus the income tax owed on the property's taxable income (or plus tax savings if the property shows a tax loss).
glossary.deep:
ATCF is the owner's true take-home from the building.

Like your paycheck after withholding: the number that actually hits your account.

Bushwick: BTCF $40,000. Taxable income $10,000 (NOI minus interest minus depreciation), taxed at 30% = $3,000. ATCF = $37,000. If depreciation and interest create a tax loss that offsets other income, ATCF can exceed BTCF.

On the exam: compute tax in the tax world, then subtract it in the cash world.
glossary.contrast: Taxable income is computed in the tax world; ATCF is a cash figure.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A relationship in which one person (the agent) is authorized to act on behalf of another (the principal), owing that principal fiduciary duties.
glossary.deep:
Agency means someone is standing in your shoes for a specific purpose, and the law holds them to a higher standard because of it.

Think of handing a friend your car keys and your credit card to get the car fixed. You trust them to spend your money as you would, tell you what the mechanic said, and not sell your hubcaps on the side.

When the Okafors sign a listing with Hudson & Hart, the firm becomes their agent for selling the brownstone. Every licensee at the firm now owes them loyalty and the rest of OLD CAR.

On the exam: agency is created by agreement or conduct, not by who pays. Expect a question that tries to tie representation to the source of the commission.
glossary.contrast: Brokerage is the business of bringing parties together for a fee; agency is the legal relationship of trust. You can broker without being an agent.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: An agency in which the agent has its own interest in the property. The principal cannot revoke it, and it does not end at the principal's death.
glossary.deep:
When the agent has skin in the game, the principal cannot simply fire it.

Like a lender who holds the keys as security: you cannot revoke its right to sell the collateral.

A broker who co-invested in a Harlem rehab and holds a share of profits is not just an agent; the agency is coupled with an interest and survives the investor-owner's death.

On the exam: the exception to "death ends agency." Earning a commission is not an interest.
glossary.contrast: An ordinary listing ends at the principal's death; an agency coupled with an interest does not.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The DOS form required by RPL 443 that explains agency roles and records which role the licensee plays, for residential 1 to 4 family, condos, and co-ops, sales and rentals.
glossary.deep:
It is a label, not a contract: "here is who I work for."

Like a name badge that says "Store Employee" before you ask for advice.

There are two versions: buyer-seller and landlord-tenant. The listing agent gives it before the listing agreement; the other side gets it at first substantive contact. A signed acknowledgment or a sworn declaration of refusal is kept 3 years.

On the exam: "This is not a contract." It creates no agency. It does not cover commercial or vacant land.
glossary.contrast: The Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form covers all property types.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The person authorized to act for a principal. In real estate, the brokerage is the agent; salespersons act on the broker's behalf.
glossary.deep:
The agent is the one doing the work on someone else's behalf, with their authority.

Picture a talent agent: the actor is the principal, and the agent negotiates deals but cannot sign the actor up for a movie the actor never approved.

When Rosa lists her Park Slope house, her contract is with the brokerage, so the broker is her agent. Jordan, the salesperson, is carrying out the broker's agency. If Jordan leaves the firm, Rosa's listing stays behind.

On the exam: "Who is the agent?" The broker. RPL 443 defines an agent as a licensee acting in a fiduciary capacity.
glossary.contrast: The principal hires; the agent acts. A customer is neither: just the party on the other side.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The right to use or develop the space above a parcel, including unused development rights that can be sold or transferred.
glossary.deep:
Ownership extends upward, and zoning caps how much floor area you can build. If a lot can legally hold 50,000 square feet but has a 20,000 square foot building, the 30,000 unused square feet are air rights. In NYC they can move to an adjacent lot through a zoning lot merger, or farther through special transfer programs.

Analogy: unused data on your phone plan that you can sell to the neighbor. NY example: Grand Central's owner sold unused air rights to nearby developers, including for One Vanderbilt. Small Manhattan townhouse owners sometimes sell air rights to a tower next door for millions.

On the exam: air rights can be sold separately from the land.
glossary.contrast: Transfer of development rights moves the rights to a non-adjacent receiving site; air rights is the broader concept of rights above the land.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A clause letting the lender demand full payment if the borrower sells or transfers the property. Also called a due-on-sale clause.
glossary.deep:
"Alienate" means transfer ownership. The lender agreed to lend to you, not to whoever buys your house.

Like a lease that bans assignment without consent.

A seller in Ridgewood with a 3% loan cannot simply let a buyer take it over: the alienation clause lets the lender call the loan when the deed transfers. FHA and VA loans are assumable with lender approval; most conventional loans are not.

On the exam: alienation = due on sale = blocks assumption without consent.
glossary.contrast: Acceleration is triggered by default; alienation by transfer.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The soil, sand, or sediment deposited by water through accretion.
glossary.deep: If accretion is the process, alluvion is the stuff: the actual sand and silt left behind by moving water. It belongs to the owner of the land it attaches to. A Hudson River property that gains a strip of new bank from deposited sediment has gained alluvion. The term appears in the syllabus key terms, so expect it as a vocabulary match. On the exam: alluvion = the deposited soil; accretion = the process of adding it; reliction = land exposed when water recedes.
glossary.contrast: Reliction is land exposed by receding water rather than deposited soil.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A contract between a co-op (or condo) and an owner setting the conditions for renovations: plan approval, licensed and insured contractors, work hours, deposits, and liability.
glossary.deep:
Before you move a wall or touch plumbing, you sign the alteration agreement. It protects neighbors and the building: architect's plans reviewed by the building's engineer, permits, insurance certificates, work hours (often weekdays only), a security deposit, and responsibility for damage.

NY example: Adaeze wants to open the kitchen. After closing she submits plans; the board's engineer reviews them under the alteration agreement before work starts.

On the exam: alteration agreement = renovation rules. Don't confuse it with the recognition agreement (lender).
glossary.contrast: A recognition agreement involves the lender, not renovations.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Branch circuit wiring made of aluminum, used in some homes from the mid-1960s to mid-1970s, linked to overheating and fire at connections.
glossary.deep:
During a copper price spike, builders used aluminum for ordinary 15 and 20 amp circuits. Aluminum expands and contracts more than copper and oxidizes at terminals, so connections loosen, heat up, and can ignite. It is not illegal, and it can be made safer with approved repair connectors or devices rated for aluminum (CO/ALR).

Analogy: a loose garden hose fitting that leaks a little more each season, except the leak is heat. NY example: a 1970 Suffolk ranch shows silver-colored wire at outlets; the buyer's electrician quotes a connector retrofit, and the buyer's insurer asks for proof of remediation.

On the exam: aluminum branch wiring equals fire risk; copper is the standard.
glossary.contrast: Aluminum service entrance cable is normal and not the same concern as aluminum branch wiring.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A filing that discloses a material change to an accepted offering plan, such as new prices, a revised budget, a changed closing date, or that the plan has been declared effective.
glossary.deep:
Plans are living documents. Every material change must be filed with the AG as an amendment and given to purchasers.

Price increases for unsold units are made by amendment; signed contracts keep their price. If a change materially and adversely affects existing purchasers, they must generally be offered a chance to rescind within the period stated.

NY example: after the lower floors sell out in Gowanus, the sponsor files an amendment raising upper floor prices 5%. Ana's signed price is unchanged.

On the exam: amendments = how prices and terms change; existing contracts are protected.
glossary.contrast: The red herring is the pre-acceptance draft; amendments follow acceptance.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: 1990 federal law prohibiting disability discrimination in employment, public services, and public accommodations, including commercial facilities like real estate offices.
glossary.deep:
The Fair Housing Act protects people with disabilities in their homes. The ADA protects them in public spaces. Your brokerage office, a new development's sales gallery, and an apartment building's leasing office are public accommodations, so they must be accessible and barriers must be removed where readily achievable.

Example: a Midtown brokerage on a second floor with only a stair entrance may need to provide another accessible way to meet clients.

On the exam: the ADA applies to commercial property and public accommodations. Questions about a disabled tenant's rights inside an apartment are Fair Housing Act questions.
glossary.contrast: The Fair Housing Act covers dwellings; the ADA covers public accommodations and commercial facilities.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: Paying off a loan with regular payments that cover interest and gradually reduce principal to zero by the end of the term.
glossary.deep:
Level payments, shifting mix. Early on most of the payment is interest; by the end almost all is principal.

Like a snowball rolling uphill that gets smaller each turn.

A $300,000 loan at 6% for 30 years: payment $1,798.65. Month 1 is $1,500 interest and $298.65 principal. By year 25 the split has flipped. Total interest over 30 years: about $347,500.

On the exam: compute interest as balance x rate / 12, then subtract from the payment to get principal.
glossary.contrast: Negative amortization makes the balance grow; a straight loan pays no principal until the end.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The sale price minus selling expenses such as commission, transfer taxes, and the seller's legal fees.
glossary.deep:
You do not compute gain on the gross price, because selling costs money. Subtract the brokerage commission, the seller-paid NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT, and the seller's attorney fees.
