Think of it as what actually lands in your pocket before paying off the mortgage. (Paying off a mortgage does not reduce amount realized: it is your debt, not a cost of selling.)

Okafors: $2,150,000 price minus $130,000 commission and transfer taxes = $2,020,000 amount realized.

On the exam: amount realized minus adjusted basis = gain. A common distractor subtracts the mortgage balance.
glossary.contrast: Net proceeds at closing also subtract the mortgage payoff; amount realized does not.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: The amount (volume) of electrical current flowing; service capacity is measured in amps, typically 100 to 200 for a modern home.
glossary.deep:
Amps measure how much current flows. The service size, printed on the main breaker or main fuse, caps how much the whole house can draw at once. Each circuit is also rated, typically 15 or 20 amps for outlets, with wire sized to match. A 60-amp service is a sign of an old, undersized system that may not support central AC, an EV charger, or a heat pump conversion.

Analogy: the width of the hose. NY example: an Astoria two-family with a 60-amp service per unit needs an upgrade before the buyer adds central air; the utility (Con Edison) coordinates the new service.

On the exam: identify amperage on the main breaker; 100 to 200 amps is normal.
glossary.contrast: Voltage is pressure; amperage is flow. Wattage is volts times amps.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A major retail tenant, such as a supermarket or department store, that draws customer traffic to a shopping center.
glossary.deep:
Anchors are the magnets. Smaller stores pay higher rent per square foot to be near them, and anchors often get lower rents and special lease rights in return. Losing an anchor can sink a center, so many small-tenant leases have co-tenancy clauses.

Like the headliner at a concert: the opening acts benefit from the crowd it brings.

Evelyn's Bayside strip center depends on its supermarket anchor; when it renews, every other tenant breathes easier.

On the exam: anchor store = major traffic generator in retail management.
glossary.contrast: An in-line store is a smaller tenant between anchors.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: A large, well-known tenant, such as a supermarket or department store, that draws customers to a shopping center or building.
glossary.deep:
The anchor is the tenant everyone else depends on. It brings the foot traffic that keeps the smaller in-line shops alive.

Like the main act at a concert: people buy tickets for the headliner, and the opening acts get heard because of it. So the headliner gets the best deal.

A Stop & Shop anchoring a Long Island center may pay much less per square foot than the nail salon next to it. In-line leases may include co-tenancy clauses that cut rent if the anchor leaves.

On the exam: anchors draw traffic and usually pay lower rent per square foot.
glossary.contrast: In-line tenants are the smaller stores between anchors and pay higher rent per foot.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Training that helps licensees recognize how unconscious attitudes and stereotypes affect their decisions and replace them with consistent practices.
glossary.deep:
Good anti-bias training is less about guilt and more about habits. It shows how bias appears in everyday work (callback speed, listing choice, neighborhood descriptions, ad wording) and gives tools to neutralize it: same script, same procedures, same records, and a pause to ask "would I do this for any client?"

Example: after training, Hudson & Hart started logging every inquiry with time received and time answered, so differences would show up in their own data first.

On the exam: the syllabus frames it as explaining how attitudes or stereotypes affect understanding, actions, and decisions unconsciously.
glossary.contrast: Cultural competency training is a separate required CE topic about serving diverse clients well.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A DOS-licensed business that sells information about available rental apartments for a fee.
glossary.deep:
Before listing sites were free, NYC renters paid companies for lists of vacancies. Abuses (stale or fake listings) led to a separate license. The vendor must hold a one-year license, keep a trust account (at least $5,000), use a DOS-approved contract, charge no more than one month's rent, and refund the advance fee minus up to $15 if the customer does not rent through its information.

Think of it as selling a map, not giving a tour. The vendor cannot negotiate a lease.

A customer pays $250 for a Washington Heights listings package, finds nothing, notifies the vendor in writing, and gets $235 back.

On the exam: fee refund minus $15, and vendors do not negotiate.
glossary.contrast: A broker negotiates rentals; a vendor only sells information.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A licensed person who, for a fee, arranges for people to share housing with a current occupant.
glossary.deep:
This license covers roommate matching: someone with a spare room in Astoria pays or charges a fee to find a compatible roommate through an agency. The agent is regulated under the same part of the law as apartment information vendors, with a smaller trust account (at least $2,500).

It is a matchmaker for roommates, not a leasing agent.

A grad student at Columbia uses a licensed sharing agent to find a roommate for her two-bedroom; the agent's fee is capped by law.

On the exam: apartment sharing agents and apartment information vendors are DOS-licensed, separate from brokers.
glossary.contrast: Apartment information vendor sells lists of vacancies; sharing agent matches roommates.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: An unbiased estimate of the nature, quality, value, or utility of an interest in identified real estate, in practice a written opinion of value by a state licensed or certified appraiser.
glossary.deep:
An appraisal is the professional, independent answer to "what is this worth?" It is not the seller's hope or the agent's pitch.

Think of it as a referee's call. The agent coaches one side; the appraiser calls the play for the lender.

When Leo buys a Sunnyside condo for $640,000 with a loan, his lender orders an appraisal from a licensed appraiser (licensed by DOS). If it comes in at $620,000, the bank lends against $620,000 and Leo must cover the gap or renegotiate.

On the exam: a CMA is never an appraisal, even when a broker signs it. Watch for answers that blur the two.
glossary.contrast: CMA: a licensee's opinion of a likely price range. Appraisal: a licensed appraiser's independent estimate.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: An increase in a property's value over time.
glossary.deep:
Appreciation comes from market demand, inflation, neighborhood change, or improvements. It is unrealized (not taxed) until you sell. Then it shows up as capital gain.

Like a tree growing in your yard: it is worth more every year, but you only get paid when you sell the lumber.

The Okafors' brownstone went from $185,000 in 1997 to $2,150,000: Bed-Stuy appreciation over 28 years.

On the exam: appreciation is the opposite of depreciation in the market sense. Tax depreciation, though, is a deduction that happens even while the property appreciates.
glossary.contrast: Tax depreciation is a paper deduction; it can coexist with market appreciation.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A legal authorization in a municipal budget to spend a stated amount for a specific purpose.
glossary.deep:
Appropriations are the spending side of the budget: permission to spend.

Like envelopes in a household budget labeled rent, food, and travel.

A village board appropriates $3,000,000 for police and $1,000,000 for roads. Total appropriations minus non-property revenue (state aid, fees, sales tax share) equals the tax levy.

On the exam: appropriation authorizes spending; levy is the amount raised by property tax; rate is levy divided by taxable assessed value.
glossary.contrast: Levy: the amount actually raised from property taxes.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: Rights, privileges, and improvements that belong to a parcel and pass with it when it is transferred, such as easements appurtenant and water rights.
glossary.deep: Appurtenances are the extras attached to the land legally rather than physically: an easement appurtenant over the neighbor's driveway, riparian rights, air rights, and the buildings themselves. Deeds commonly convey the land "together with all appurtenances," but appurtenances pass even without those words. When Leo sells a house with a deeded right of way to the beach, the right of way goes with it. On the exam: appurtenances run with the land; anything appurtenant transfers automatically on sale.
glossary.contrast: A license is personal and does not pass with the land.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The yearly cost of credit, including interest plus points and certain fees, expressed as a percentage.
glossary.deep:
The all-in rate, so two loans can be compared fairly.

Like comparing airline fares with the bag fees included.

Loan A: 6.25% with 2 points. Loan B: 6.5% with no points. Their APRs reveal which really costs more over the term. APR is usually higher than the note rate because fees are folded in. Taxes and insurance are not part of it.

On the exam: APR is the required disclosure; stating only the APR in an ad does not trigger extra disclosures.
glossary.contrast: The note rate is just the interest rate on the loan.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An appointed local board that approves the design of new construction and remodeling under municipal ordinances: facades, materials, rooflines, signs.
glossary.deep:
An ARB guards how things look. Many villages and some towns require its approval before the building department issues a permit for exterior changes, so a new house or addition fits the neighborhood's scale and style. It judges appearance, not structure or use.

Analogy: the neighborhood's design editor. NY example: in Bronxville, a homeowner replacing wood siding with vinyl needs ARB approval first; the board may require a different material or color.

On the exam: ARB approves new construction and remodeling appearance per ordinance.
glossary.contrast: A historic preservation commission protects designated landmarks and districts; an ARB may review design anywhere its ordinance applies.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: ZBA permission to depart from dimensional rules such as setbacks, height, lot size or coverage, decided by balancing benefit to the applicant against detriment to the community.
glossary.deep:
Area variances bend numbers, not uses. The ZBA weighs five factors: undesirable change or detriment to nearby properties; whether the benefit can be achieved another feasible way; whether the request is substantial; adverse physical or environmental effects; and whether the difficulty was self-created, which counts but does not bar relief. The board grants the minimum variance necessary.

Analogy: a tailor letting out a seam, not changing the suit. NY example: a Valley Stream owner wants a deck 4 feet into a 25-foot rear yard; neighbors do not object, the request is modest, and the ZBA grants it.

On the exam: "practical difficulty," balancing test, self-created is not fatal.
glossary.contrast: A use variance requires unnecessary hardship on four mandatory prongs, and self-creation bars it.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The part of the NY Real Property Law (sections 440 to 442-k) that requires and regulates real estate broker and salesperson licenses.
glossary.deep:
Article 12-A is the rulebook's spine. It defines who is a broker or salesperson, what acts need a license, who is exempt, what DOS can do to you, and the criminal and civil penalties. The detailed conduct rules (escrow, ads, records) live in DOS regulations, 19 NYCRR Part 175, which DOS writes under the authority Article 12-A gives it.

Think of Article 12-A as the Constitution and Part 175 as the code of conduct written under it.

When Marcus deposits a buyer's check into his own account, the untrustworthiness ground for discipline comes from Article 12-A (RPL 441-c) and the specific escrow rule from 175.1.

On the exam: "Real estate licensing in NY is governed by" Article 12-A of the Real Property Law, administered by the Department of State.
glossary.contrast: Article 14 of the RPL is the Property Condition Disclosure Act, a different article about seller disclosures.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A lawsuit in NY Supreme Court to review a decision of a state or local agency, such as DOS discipline.
glossary.deep:
Article 78 of the Civil Practice Law and Rules lets a person ask a court whether an agency acted arbitrarily, beyond its power, or against the law. It is the door from the agency to the courts.

Think of it as asking a higher referee to review the video replay.

If DOS revokes Marcus's license and he thinks the judge ignored key evidence, he files an Article 78 petition in State Supreme Court. The same tool challenges zoning board decisions.

On the exam: the way to challenge a DOS decision in court is an Article 78 proceeding.
glossary.contrast: A tax certiorari proceeding challenges assessments, not license decisions.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A New York court proceeding (CPLR Article 78) to challenge a decision of a government body or officer, such as a ZBA, planning board, or DOS.
glossary.deep:
Article 78 is how New Yorkers sue the government over a decision. Filed in State Supreme Court, it asks whether the agency acted arbitrarily, illegally, beyond its power, or without substantial evidence. The court reviews the record; it does not hold a new hearing on the merits. For ZBA and planning board decisions the deadline is 30 days from filing of the decision with the clerk; the general Article 78 deadline is 4 months.

Analogy: asking a referee's boss to review the tape. NY example: neighbors of a granted use variance in Brookhaven file an Article 78 petition claiming the board ignored the self-created hardship rule.

On the exam: Article 78 is the route for both zoning disputes and license discipline appeals.
glossary.contrast: A variance is relief from the ZBA; Article 78 is how you challenge the ZBA in court.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: New York law requiring subdividers who offer vacant subdivided land to NY residents on an installment plan to file offering documents with the Department of State.
glossary.deep:
Article 9-A protects New Yorkers from the classic lot sale pitch: pay a little a month for a lot in a faraway development you have never seen, and get the deed when you finish paying. Before offering such land, the subdivider files a filing statement and an offering statement with the Department of State, and every offer must include the current offering statement. Updated statements are filed annually.

Analogy: a prospectus for raw land. NY example: a developer marketing vacant lots in a rural upstate tract to Queens residents on 10-year payment plans must file first. Lots with completed homes are not covered by Article 9-A.

On the exam: Article 9-A equals vacant land, installment plan, NY residents, Department of State.
glossary.contrast: The federal Interstate Land Sales Act covers 100+ lot subdivisions sold across state lines and requires a property report.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Development that complies with all zoning rules for its district and needs only a building permit, with no discretionary board approval.
glossary.deep:
As of right means you already have permission in the rulebook. If the district allows a two-family house of 30 feet on a lot your size, you file plans, get the permit, and build. No hearing, no neighbors' vote, no board discretion.

Analogy: ordering off the menu instead of asking the chef for a special dish. NY example: many large Manhattan towers are built as of right, which is why neighbors are often surprised; nothing required a public hearing. Anything needing a variance, special permit, or rezoning is not as of right.

On the exam: as of right is the opposite of discretionary. If no board must approve, it is as of right.
glossary.contrast: A special use permit requires board approval even though the use is listed in the ordinance.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A naturally occurring mineral fiber once widely used for insulation and fireproofing; inhaled fibers cause serious lung disease.
glossary.deep:
Asbestos was the miracle material of the 20th century: it does not burn and insulates well. It went into pipe and boiler wrap, 9x9 floor tiles, ceiling texture, roofing and siding shingles, and vermiculite insulation. Fibers released into the air lodge in the lungs and cause asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma decades later. EPA banned the last form still in use, chrysotile, in 2024.

Analogy: harmless as a sealed book, dangerous once it shreds into dust. NY example: a Bed-Stuy brownstone's basement steam pipes are wrapped in it; a licensed abatement contractor removes it under NYS Department of Labor rules with containment and air monitoring.

On the exam: hazard when friable; testing by bulk sampling; removal by licensed contractors.
glossary.contrast: UFFI is a foam insulation that releases formaldehyde; asbestos is a mineral fiber.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A chronic lung disease caused by scarring from inhaled asbestos fibers.
glossary.deep:
Asbestosis is lung scarring from years of breathing asbestos fibers. The scar tissue stiffens the lungs, causing shortness of breath that worsens over time; it has no cure. It usually follows heavy, long-term exposure, often in trades like insulation, shipbuilding and demolition, and appears 10 to 40 years later.

Analogy: scar tissue lining the lungs like a stiff coat. NY example: workers who installed pipe insulation in NYC buildings in the 1950s and 1960s developed asbestosis decades later, which is why abatement today is tightly regulated.

On the exam: one of three named asbestos diseases, with lung cancer and mesothelioma.
glossary.contrast: Mesothelioma is a cancer of the lining of the lungs or abdomen; asbestosis is non-cancerous scarring.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The value placed on a property by the assessor for tax purposes, which may be full market value or a uniform percentage of it.
glossary.deep:
Assessed value is the number the tax rate is multiplied by.

It is a scaled model of market value: if the town builds every model at 25% scale, a $400,000 house is a $100,000 assessment.

A Hudson Valley house worth $400,000 in a town assessing at 25% has an assessed value of $100,000. At $95.50 per $1,000, the tax is $9,550. In NYC, a Class 1 home is assessed at 6% of market value, subject to caps.

On the exam: Tax = assessed value x rate. Assessed value / ratio = full value.
glossary.contrast: Market value: what a typical buyer would pay. Assessed value may be a fraction of it.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: The municipality responsible for assessing property, usually a city or town (a county in Nassau and Tompkins; the Department of Finance in NYC). An approved assessing unit has completed a qualifying revaluation and may adopt the homestead option.
glossary.deep:
The assessing unit is the government whose assessor builds the roll.

Villages, school districts, and counties usually piggyback on the town's or city's roll.

A house in the Village of Scarsdale is assessed on the roll used for both the village and the town. In NYC, the Department of Finance assesses every parcel in all five boroughs.

On the exam: "approved assessing unit" connects to the homestead/non-homestead option under RPTL Article 19.
glossary.contrast: Taxing jurisdiction: any body that levies tax on the roll, such as a school district.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: The official valuation of property for tax purposes by the local assessor, and the process of producing it.
glossary.deep:
The assessment is the government's number for your property, used only to split the tax bill.

Think of it as your share of the pizza: the bigger your assessment relative to everyone else's, the bigger your slice of the levy.

The Town of Hempstead's assessor (in Nassau, the county assesses) or NYC's Department of Finance sets a value each year on a roll. Owners can see the tentative roll and challenge it.

On the exam: assessment is about fair shares. It may be full value or a uniform fraction, but must be equal within a class.
glossary.contrast: Appraisal: an independent opinion of market value, usually for a lender.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: Assessed value divided by full market value: the percentage of value at which property is assessed (also called the level of assessment).
glossary.deep:
The ratio tells you what fraction of value the assessor uses.

Like a recipe scaled down: the ratio is the scale factor.

A house worth $400,000 assessed at $100,000 has a 25% ratio. If most neighbors are at 20% but this house is at 25%, its owner is paying more than a fair share and can grieve for unequal assessment.

On the exam: ratio = AV / market value; AV = market value x ratio. Equity means equal ratios within a class.
glossary.contrast: Equalization rate: the state's measure of a whole municipality's level of assessment.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: Charges levied on property: the assessed value used to compute property taxes, or special charges for local improvements or building projects.
glossary.deep: The word has two common meanings at closing. A tax assessment is the value the assessor assigns, multiplied by the tax rate to compute the bill. A special assessment is an extra charge for a public improvement, such as a sewer, and is a lien like taxes. Co-op and condo boards also levy assessments for building projects. All of these are typically prorated or allocated in the contract: who pays an assessment that is voted but not yet billed is a common negotiation. On the exam: taxes and special assessments are prorated and have top lien priority.
glossary.contrast: Maintenance or common charges are regular monthly building charges.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Transfer of one party's rights under a contract to another person. The assignor generally remains liable unless released.
glossary.deep:
Rights move; responsibility stays unless someone lets you go.

Like handing your gym membership to a friend while you stay the backup on the bill.

An investor signs to buy a Bushwick building, then assigns the contract to a partner for a fee before closing (common in flips). Many NY contracts forbid assignment without seller consent. Mortgages and leases can be assigned too.

On the exam: assignment does not release the assignor; novation does.
glossary.contrast: A novation substitutes a new party and releases the old one.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A transfer of the tenant's entire remaining interest in a lease to another person, who then deals directly with the landlord.
glossary.deep:
The tenant steps out and someone else steps into the whole rest of the term.

Like selling your remaining season tickets for all the games left.

A tenant with 14 months left on a Chelsea lease assigns it to a coworker. The assignee pays the landlord directly. The original tenant stays liable as a backup unless the landlord releases her (a novation). Under RPL 226-b, in buildings with 4+ units, the landlord may refuse an assignment, but if the refusal is unreasonable the tenant can be released from the lease.

On the exam: entire remaining term equals assignment.
glossary.contrast: A sublease transfers only part of the term or space.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Transfer of a mortgage and its note from one lender to another; recorded to show the new holder.
glossary.deep:
Loans are assets that lenders buy and sell.

Like a gift card that changes hands but is still worth the same.

Leo's lender sells his loan to an investor a month after closing. The assignment is recorded, and Leo may get a letter saying his servicer changed. His rate, balance, and terms stay exactly the same. In foreclosure, NY courts require the plaintiff to prove it holds the note.

On the exam: assignment = new lender, same terms; the borrower's consent is not needed.
glossary.contrast: An assumption changes the borrower; an assignment changes the lender.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A licensee who qualifies as a broker but chooses to work under the name and supervision of a sponsoring broker.
glossary.deep:
An associate broker has done the 152 hours and met the experience test, then decided not to run a business. Many senior agents and branch managers hold this license: it signals experience and lets them supervise a branch, without the burdens of being the firm.

It is like an attorney who could open a solo practice but stays as a senior associate at a firm.

At Hudson & Hart, a 12-year veteran who manages the Bay Ridge branch is an associate broker. She is paid by Diane, not by clients, just like a salesperson.

On the exam: an associate broker is sponsored like a salesperson, paid only by the sponsoring broker, and may manage a branch office.
glossary.contrast: A salesperson cannot manage a branch; a broker runs their own firm.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A buyer takes over the seller's existing loan and becomes personally liable for it; the seller stays secondarily liable unless released.
glossary.deep:
The buyer steps into the seller's loan and promises to pay it.

Like taking over a friend's lease with your name added as responsible.

In a high-rate year, a buyer assumes the seller's FHA loan at 3.25% with lender approval. The buyer is primarily liable; if the buyer defaults, the lender can still pursue the seller unless it granted a novation releasing her. Conventional loans with due-on-sale clauses usually cannot be assumed.

On the exam: assume = personal liability; release requires a novation.
glossary.contrast: Subject to means no personal liability for the buyer.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A clause making a broker-prepared purchase contract contingent on approval by each party's attorney within a short period.
glossary.deep:
It lets the lawyers look before the deal locks, without slowing the handshake.

Like a "subject to my accountant's approval" note on a business deal.

In Buffalo or Rochester, a broker completes a bar-approved purchase and sale form at the kitchen table. The attorney approval contingency gives each side's lawyer a few business days to approve, disapprove, or propose changes. If disapproved in time, the contract ends and the deposit is returned. If the window passes in silence, the contract stands.

On the exam: attorney review clauses are an upstate feature, used when brokers prepare contracts.
glossary.contrast: Downstate, attorneys draft the contract from the start, so no review clause is needed.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The tenant's agreement to recognize a new owner of the property, such as a buyer or a foreclosing lender, as its landlord.
glossary.deep:
Attornment means "I will pay you now." When ownership changes, the tenant accepts the new owner as landlord under the same lease.

Like an employee who stays on when the company is bought and reports to the new owner.

If a lender forecloses on a Downtown Brooklyn office building, attornment keeps the rent flowing to the new owner; non-disturbance keeps the tenant in place. Together they keep the lease alive.

On the exam: attornment = tenant recognizes new landlord. Often packaged in an SNDA.
glossary.contrast: Non-disturbance is the lender's promise to the tenant; attornment is the tenant's promise to the new owner.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The sudden loss or movement of land caused by a flood, storm, or a river abruptly changing course; the boundary does not change.
glossary.deep: Avulsion is abrupt. A hurricane tears away part of a beach lot, or a flood cuts a new channel and moves a creek. Because the change is sudden and identifiable, the law keeps the boundary where it was: the original owner still owns land that was moved to the other side of the new channel, and may reclaim it. Hurricane Sandy's damage to parts of the Rockaways is an example. On the exam: avulsion is sudden and does not transfer ownership; accretion and erosion are gradual and do.
glossary.contrast: Erosion is gradual wearing away, which does reduce the owner's land.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A loan whose payments do not fully pay it off by maturity, leaving a large final (balloon) payment.
glossary.deep:
Small payments for years, then one huge one.

Like a balloon: it looks manageable until it pops at the end.

A 7-year balloon is amortized as if 30 years, so payments are modest, but at year 7 the remaining balance (most of the loan) is due. The borrower must refinance or sell. If rates rise or values fall, that may be impossible, which is why balloons are a predatory lending red flag and NY restricts them in high-cost loans.

On the exam: final payment larger than the regular ones.
glossary.contrast: A straight loan has no principal reduction at all; a balloon has some.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A deed that implies the grantor holds title but gives no general warranties; with covenant against grantor's acts, it is the standard NY residential deed.
glossary.deep: A bargain and sale deed conveys the property and implies the grantor owns it. It comes in two versions. With covenant against grantor's acts, the grantor promises only that he has done nothing to encumber the property; this is the deed used in most New York home sales, because buyers rely on title insurance for older defects. Without covenant, there are no promises at all, which is common in some estate, bank, and investor sales. On the exam: "most common deed in NY residential transactions" = bargain and sale with covenant.
glossary.contrast: A full covenant and warranty deed covers the entire history of title.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The year whose actual expenses (taxes or operating costs) set the baseline covered by base rent; the tenant pays its share of increases above it.
glossary.deep:
The base year is the starting line. Whatever the building's expenses turn out to be that year are "included" in the base rent. After that, the tenant pays its share of anything above.

Like a gym that locks your rate to this year's costs and charges you a share of any increase later.

NYC office leases often name a tax base year such as "2026/2027" (the city's tax year runs July 1 to June 30) and a calendar operating base year. A later base year is better for the tenant: higher baseline, smaller escalations.

On the exam: base year = actual expenses in a named year; no credit typically if expenses fall below it.
glossary.contrast: An expense stop is a fixed dollar amount set in the lease, not actual expenses of a year.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A story of a building partly or fully below ground, enclosed by foundation walls.
glossary.deep:
A basement is the space inside the foundation walls, deep enough to stand in. It holds mechanicals, storage, and sometimes living space. Water is its enemy: grading, gutters, sump pumps and waterproofing matter.

Analogy: the house's engine room. NY example: in NYC, a basement (at least half above curb level) is treated differently from a cellar (more than half below) for zoning and occupancy rules, and many basement apartments are illegal without proper ceiling height, light and egress.

On the exam: basement vs crawl space vs slab-on-grade is a common sorting question.
glossary.contrast: A crawl space is too shallow to stand in; a basement is a full story.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: Your tax investment in a property: generally the purchase price plus acquisition costs.
glossary.deep:
Basis is the starting number for measuring gain. Buy for $500,000, pay $10,000 in title insurance, recording, and attorney fees, and your basis is $510,000. Inherited property usually gets a basis equal to market value at death (a "step-up"); gifted property usually keeps the giver's basis.

Think of basis as the price tag you keep in a drawer: at sale, the IRS compares the new price to that tag.

Leo buys a Sunnyside condo for $420,000 and pays $9,000 in buyer closing costs (not counting deductible points and prorated taxes). His basis: $429,000.

On the exam: basis starts with cost plus buying costs; improvements and depreciation then adjust it.
glossary.contrast: Adjusted basis is basis after improvements are added and depreciation subtracted.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A horizontal structural member that carries loads across an open span to supports at its ends.
glossary.deep:
A beam is any horizontal piece that carries weight across a gap: wood, steel or engineered lumber. Girders, headers, and ridge beams are all beams with specific jobs. Deeper beams carry more load over longer spans.

Analogy: a plank across a creek. NY example: when a Queens owner removes a bearing wall to open the kitchen, an engineer specifies a steel or LVL beam to carry the floor above, with posts carrying the load down to footings.

On the exam: beam is the general term; know the specific beams by location.
glossary.contrast: A column or post is vertical; a beam is horizontal.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A wall that supports the weight of the floors or roof above it, in addition to its own weight.
glossary.deep:
A bearing (load-bearing) wall holds up something. Exterior walls almost always do; some interior walls do too, typically ones running perpendicular to the joists, near the middle of the house. Non-bearing walls (partitions) only divide space.

Analogy: a bearing wall is a pillar; a partition is a curtain. NY example: a buyer of a Forest Hills colonial plans an open kitchen; the wall in question sits right over the basement girder, so it is bearing, and removal needs an engineer, a beam, and a permit.

On the exam: removing a bearing wall requires a structural substitute. Watch for questions about which walls are bearing.
glossary.contrast: A curtain or partition wall carries no load from above.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: Net operating income minus annual debt service.
glossary.deep:
BTCF is the owner's cash before the IRS takes its share.

If NOI is the building's paycheck, BTCF is what is left after the mortgage auto-pay.

Bushwick: NOI $190,000 minus $150,000 debt service = $40,000 BTCF. That figure feeds the cash on cash return ($40,000 / $1,000,000 equity = 4%).

On the exam: BTCF = NOI minus debt service (both principal and interest). It is the numerator of the equity dividend rate.
glossary.contrast: After-tax cash flow subtracts income tax from BTCF.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The person who receives the benefits of a trust, a will, or an insurance policy.
glossary.deep: The beneficiary is who the arrangement is for. In a trust, the beneficiary receives income or use of the property while the trustee holds title. A child who lives rent-free in a Queens house held in trust is the beneficiary; the aunt who manages it is the trustee. Beneficiaries can sue a trustee who mismanages the property. The word also describes the person named to receive insurance proceeds or gifts under a will. On the exam: the beneficiary benefits but does not hold legal title in a trust.
glossary.contrast: The trustor creates the trust; the trustee manages it.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A contract in which each party makes a promise to the other: a promise for a promise.
glossary.deep:
Both sides are bound from the moment they agree.

Like two friends shaking on "I'll drive if you pay for gas".

A contract of sale is bilateral: the Okafors promise to convey, the buyer promises to pay. An exclusive right to sell listing is also bilateral: the seller promises a commission, the broker promises diligent effort.

On the exam: sales contracts and exclusive listings are bilateral.
glossary.contrast: A unilateral contract is a promise in exchange for an act; only one side is obligated.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A short preliminary agreement recording the basic terms of a deal, often with a small deposit, until a formal contract is signed.
glossary.deep:
A binder holds a place in line; it usually does not lock the deal.

Like a restaurant reservation: it shows intent but no one is eating yet.

In NYC, buyers sometimes sign a binder with a small good-faith check after an accepted offer, stating "subject to a formal contract satisfactory to the parties' attorneys". That language makes it non-binding. Upstate, a fully filled-in purchase offer can itself become the contract.

On the exam: binders are preliminary; any deposit should be refundable if no contract is signed.
glossary.contrast: A contract of sale is the binding, complete agreement.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: One mortgage covering two or more parcels of real property, usually with a release clause.
glossary.deep:
One loan, many properties.

Like one insurance policy covering every car in a family.

A developer buys 40 lots in Orange County with a single blanket mortgage. As each house sells, a release clause frees that lot. Investors also use blankets to finance several rental buildings together.

It saves closing costs and paperwork, but it ties every property to the same debt: default on the loan and the lender can foreclose on all of them.

On the exam: blanket = multiple parcels; look for the release clause.
glossary.contrast: A package mortgage adds personal property, not more parcels.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An old MLS practice in which every listing automatically offered subagency to any member who brought a buyer.
glossary.deep:
It was a standing invitation to every MLS member: bring a buyer and you work for my seller.

Like a store announcing anyone who brings in a customer is now on its sales staff.

Decades ago, a buyer in Westchester could work with an agent for months without realizing that agent legally represented the seller. Confusion and seller liability led MLSs to make subagency optional; it is rarely offered today.

On the exam: "does it still exist?" Largely no. Cooperating brokers usually act as buyer's agents and may reject subagency.
glossary.contrast: Broker's agent arrangements are specific, not blanket, and carry no seller vicarious liability.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: An advertisement that does not reveal that a broker placed it.
glossary.deep:
A blind ad makes a listing look like it comes from an owner. NY rule 175.25 requires every ad to identify the broker by name, plus address or phone.

Picture a "For Sale by Owner" sign that is secretly a broker's sign: consumers deserve to know a professional with a commission is behind it.

"Sunny 2BR in Bushwick, call Marcus 917-555-0101" with nothing else is a blind ad. Adding "Hudson & Hart Realty, 718-555-0100" fixes it.

On the exam: if an ad lacks the broker's identity, it is a blind ad. A labeled personal cell is fine only in addition to broker information.
glossary.contrast: A team ad is legal if it names the broker; a blind ad names no broker at all.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: Inducing owners to sell or rent by representing that people of a protected class are moving into the neighborhood, often with warnings that values will fall. Also called panic peddling.
glossary.deep:
Blockbusting sells fear. In the 1950s and 60s, speculators in East Flatbush, Canarsie, and the Bronx told white owners that Black families were moving in, bought cheap, then resold at inflated prices.

Today it can be a postcard, a text, or a door knock: "The area is changing. Sell before prices drop." Profit is the motive; fear of a protected group is the tool.

New York fights it with cease and desist zones and nonsolicitation orders.

On the exam: blockbusting targets OWNERS. If the facts involve persuading owners to sell through fear of newcomers, that is the answer.
glossary.contrast: Steering targets buyers and renters, not owners.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: Architectural drawings of a building: floor plans, elevations, sections and details used to get permits and build.
glossary.deep:
Blueprints are the pictures of the building: how it looks from above (floor plan), from the side (elevation), and sliced through (section). The name comes from an old copying process that printed white lines on blue paper.

Analogy: the map; the specifications are the written directions. NY example: a Park Slope owner adding a rear extension files architect-sealed drawings with the NYC Department of Buildings, which reviews them against the Zoning Resolution and the Construction Codes before issuing a permit.

On the exam: blueprints are drawings; specifications are written material and quality details. Both go with the permit application.
glossary.contrast: Specifications describe materials and methods in words; blueprints show the design in drawings.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: An independent local board (separate from the assessor) that hears assessment grievances and may deny them, grant the requested reduction, or grant a partial reduction.
glossary.deep:
The BAR is the first referee after the assessor.

Like a manager you escalate to when the cashier says no.

An owner in Clarkstown argues her assessment implies a $520,000 value when comps show $470,000. The BAR, made up of local residents, reviews the evidence and grants a partial reduction.

On the exam: also called the assessment review board or grievance board. Decisions are full denial, full reduction as requested, or partial reduction. In NYC, the Tax Commission plays this role.
glossary.contrast: The assessor sets values; the BAR reviews them.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: The elected governing body of a condominium, chosen by unit owners under the bylaws.
glossary.deep:
Condo owners elect a board of managers to run the building, adopt budgets, hire the managing agent, enforce rules, and decide whether to use the right of first refusal. Early on, the sponsor appoints it.

A condo board cannot generally approve or reject buyers, unlike a co-op board.

NY example: two years after the first closing in an LIC tower, the sponsor still holds three of five seats; owners push for turnover under the plan's schedule.

On the exam: condo = board of MANAGERS; co-op = board of DIRECTORS.
glossary.contrast: A co-op is governed by a board of directors of the corporation.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: New York City's board that grants zoning variances and certain special permits and hears appeals of Department of Buildings decisions.
glossary.deep:
The BSA is NYC's zoning board of appeals. Its commissioners are appointed by the mayor and include professionals such as an architect, an engineer and a planner. It grants use and bulk variances under findings similar to state law, issues certain special permits, and hears appeals from DOB and Fire Department determinations.

Analogy: the ZBA with a Manhattan address. NY example: a Williamsburg owner whose odd-shaped lot cannot fit a conforming building applies to the BSA for a bulk variance; the Community Board gives an advisory opinion first.

On the exam: in NYC, variances go to the BSA, not the City Planning Commission or Community Board.
glossary.contrast: The City Planning Commission handles rezonings and ULURP; the BSA handles variances.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The application a co-op buyer submits to the board: purchase application, signed contract, verified financial statement, reference and employment letters, tax returns, credit authorization, and required disclosures.
glossary.deep:
The board package is a job application to live in the building. The managing agent checks it for completeness; board members read it closely for ability to pay, liquidity, stability, and honesty.

Timing matters: most boards meet monthly, so a late or incomplete package can push the interview past a rate lock.

NY example: Jordan works backward from the first-Tuesday board meeting and gets the employment letter and last tax return in by Thursday.

On the exam: know the checklist and that the agent prepares the buyer but does not attend the interview.
glossary.contrast: Condos usually require only a lighter application for the right of first refusal waiver.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Anything received in a 1031 exchange that is not like-kind property, such as cash, debt relief, or personal property; taxable up to the realized gain.
glossary.deep:
Boot is the leak in the exchange. Cash pulled out at closing, a new mortgage smaller than the old one, or a car thrown into the deal are all boot. Recognized gain equals the lesser of boot received or realized gain.

The term is old English: "to boot" means in addition.

Sal reinvests but keeps $150,000 for a wedding: $150,000 of gain is taxed now. If his new mortgage is $300,000 less than the old and he adds no cash, that is $300,000 of mortgage boot.

On the exam: to defer fully, trade equal or up in value, reinvest all cash, and replace the debt.
glossary.contrast: Like-kind property received is tax-deferred; boot is not.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: Any office other than the broker's main office, which needs its own DOS branch license and a broker or associate broker supervising it.
glossary.deep:
Opening a second storefront is not just a lease signing. The broker applies for a branch office license ($185), displays it at the branch, and names a broker or associate broker responsible for daily supervision.

Think of franchise locations: each has its own permit and a manager on duty.

Hudson & Hart opens a Bay Ridge branch on Third Avenue. Diane gets the branch license, and her associate broker manages it. A salesperson, no matter how senior, cannot run it.

On the exam: each branch needs its own license; salespersons cannot manage a branch.
glossary.contrast: A home office can be licensed as the main office; a branch is any additional location.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A short-term loan that lets a buyer purchase a new home before selling the current one, usually secured by the old home.
glossary.deep:
It bridges the gap between two closings.

Like a short-term loan from a friend until your paycheck clears.

A couple in Rhinebeck finds their next house but their current one has not sold. A bridge loan against the old house supplies the down payment; when the old house sells, the bridge is paid off. Rates are higher and terms short, often 6 to 12 months.

On the exam: bridge = swing = gap financing between buying and selling.
glossary.contrast: A construction loan finances building; a bridge finances timing.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An agent from a different firm engaged by a listing or buyer's agent to assist. It has no direct relationship with the client, and the client is not vicariously liable for it.
glossary.deep:
A broker's agent helps your agent, not you directly.

Like a translator your lawyer hires: you pay through your lawyer, your lawyer directs her, and your lawyer answers for her mistakes.

Hudson & Hart hires a Clinton Hill firm to run weekend open houses for the Okafors. That firm is a broker's agent. Grace cannot instruct it directly, and if it misstates something, Hudson & Hart is liable, not the Okafors.

On the exam: defined in RPL 443. Different firm, no direct relationship, no client vicarious liability.
glossary.contrast: Subagent: client is vicariously liable. Broker's agent: engaging broker is.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Supreme Court decision holding that racially segregated public schools are inherently unequal, overturning Plessy v. Ferguson in education.
glossary.deep:
Brown is a schools case, not a housing case, but it ended the legal theory that segregation could be equal. That shift powered the civil rights laws that followed, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

Why agents care: schools and housing are linked. Where families can buy determines where kids go to school, which is why steering by school zone talk is so sensitive.

On the exam: Brown overturned Plessy's separate but equal doctrine. It did not create the Fair Housing Act.
glossary.contrast: Plessy (1896) approved separate but equal; Brown (1954) rejected it.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: The amount of heat needed to raise one pound of water one degree Fahrenheit; used to rate heating and cooling equipment.
glossary.deep:
BTUs measure heat. Furnaces and boilers are rated in BTUs per hour of output; air conditioners too, often converted to tons, where 1 ton equals 12,000 BTU per hour (the cooling from melting a ton of ice over a day). Sizing matters: too small and the house is cold; too big and the system short-cycles and wastes fuel.

Analogy: BTUs are to heat what gallons are to water. NY example: an HVAC contractor sizing a heat pump for a Queens row house calculates the heat loss in BTUs per hour on a design winter day.

On the exam: know the definition and 12,000 BTU = 1 ton. Expect a simple conversion.
glossary.contrast: R-value measures resistance to heat flow, not a quantity of heat.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: Supreme Court decision striking down a Louisville, Kentucky ordinance that barred people from living on blocks where most residents were of another race.
glossary.deep:
Louisville passed racial zoning: Black families could not move onto majority-white blocks, and vice versa. The Court said this interfered with an owner's right to sell property and struck it down.

The catch: cities and developers switched to private tools, like racially restrictive deed covenants and redlined maps, which took decades more to defeat (Shelley v. Kraemer in 1948 made covenants unenforceable in court).

On the exam: Buchanan = racial ZONING struck down. Watch for choices that pin covenants or private sales on Buchanan; those belong to Shelley and Jones v. Mayer.
glossary.contrast: Jones v. Mayer (1968) dealt with private sales; Buchanan dealt with a government zoning ordinance.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: An informal grading of office buildings by quality, location, systems and rent: Class A is best, Class C is oldest and cheapest.
glossary.deep:
Class is the office market's star rating. Class A: newest or fully renovated, prime location, modern systems, top rents. Class B: older but well kept and functional. Class C: dated, needs capital work, lowest rents.

Think hotels: a five-star Midtown tower versus a clean mid-range hotel versus a tired budget motel. All give you a room; the experience and price differ.

In Manhattan, a new Hudson Yards tower is Class A; a 1920s Garment District building with original elevators is Class C. Since remote work, Class A has held tenants best while many B and C buildings struggle or convert to apartments.

On the exam: class describes quality, not height.
glossary.contrast: Low-rise, mid-rise and high-rise describe height; Class A, B and C describe quality.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Rules setting minimum construction standards for structure, fire safety, plumbing, electrical, and energy.
glossary.deep:
Building codes say how things must be built so they do not fall down, burn, or poison anyone. New York has a statewide Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code plus an Energy Conservation Construction Code, administered by the Department of State and enforced by local building departments. New York City has its own Construction Codes.

Analogy: zoning says what and how big; the code says how. NY example: a Buffalo homeowner finishing a basement bedroom needs an egress window, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and inspections under the Uniform Code.

On the exam: building codes are police power, enforced through permits, inspections, and certificates of occupancy.
glossary.contrast: Zoning controls use and size; building codes control construction methods and safety.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The local department that issues building permits, inspects construction, issues certificates of occupancy and enforces codes; the gatekeeper for all construction.
glossary.deep:
Every construction project passes through the building department. It checks plans against zoning and the Uniform Code, issues permits, inspects at stages, issues COs, and writes violations and stop-work orders. The building inspector or code enforcement officer is appointed staff, not elected.

Analogy: the airport security checkpoint for construction. NY example: before listing a Rockland County colonial, an agent pulls the building department file and finds the finished basement was never permitted, a fix the seller must handle before closing.

On the exam: permits, inspections, COs, gatekeeper. In NYC: the Department of Buildings.
glossary.contrast: The ZBA can vary zoning rules; the building department applies them as written.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: The physical barrier separating a building's interior from the outdoors: foundation, walls, roof, windows and doors.
glossary.deep:
The envelope is the shell that keeps weather out and conditioned air in. Its performance depends on insulation (R-value), air sealing, windows, and moisture control. A leaky envelope means drafts, high bills and condensation inside walls.

Analogy: the shell of an egg, or a cooler's walls. NY example: under NYC's Local Law 97 emissions limits, large building owners are upgrading envelopes with new windows and insulation to cut energy use. A blower door test measures how leaky a house's envelope is.

On the exam: envelope equals everything between inside and outside. Tighter envelopes need planned ventilation.
glossary.contrast: Mechanical systems condition the air; the envelope keeps it in.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: Written permission from the local building department to construct, alter, or demolish, issued after plans are checked against zoning and codes.
glossary.deep:
A building permit is the green light to start work. The owner or contractor submits plans; the building department confirms the project complies with zoning and the building code; the permit issues; inspections follow at key stages.

Analogy: a permit is the boarding pass; the CO is the landing. NY example: a Park Slope owner adding a rear extension files plans with the NYC Department of Buildings through its online system; work without a permit can bring stop-work orders, fines, and trouble selling later.

On the exam: permit before work, CO after work. Unpermitted work is a red flag agents should not hide.
glossary.contrast: A certificate of occupancy comes after construction and approves use; the permit authorizes construction to begin.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The legal rights that come with owning real property: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.
glossary.deep: Ownership is not one thing but a bundle of separate rights, like sticks tied together. You can hand out individual sticks while keeping the bundle. When Sal leases a store in Astoria, he gives the tenant possession and exclusion for the term but keeps disposition, so he can still sell or mortgage the building. A mortgage pledges the property as collateral; an easement lets someone use part of it; zoning trims control. Remember the five sticks as PC-EED. On the exam: questions ask which right was transferred by a lease, easement, or mortgage, or which right is NOT in the bundle (government powers like taxation are not).
glossary.contrast: Government powers (police power, eminent domain, taxation, escheat) limit the bundle; they are not part of it.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A lump sum paid at closing, by the buyer, seller, or builder, to reduce the loan's interest rate, temporarily or permanently.
glossary.deep:
Paying money up front to make the rate smaller.

Like prepaying part of your rent to get lower monthly payments.

A builder in Saratoga County offers a 2-1 buydown: the buyer's 7% rate is 5% in year 1, 6% in year 2, and 7% after. The builder funds the difference into an escrow at closing. A permanent buydown uses discount points to lower the note rate for the whole term.

On the exam: buydown = up-front payment to cut the rate; 2-1 or 3-2-1 means temporary.
glossary.contrast: A graduated payment mortgage starts low without anyone prepaying the difference.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An agent who represents the buyer in locating and negotiating for property.
glossary.deep:
A buyer's agent is the buyer's advocate.

Like a personal shopper who works for you, not the store.

Leo signs an exclusive buyer agreement with Jordan. Jordan advises Leo on offers, flags issues, and keeps his budget private, even though Jordan's firm may be paid through the listing side.

On the exam: who pays does not decide whom the agent represents. Since August 2024, MLS participants need a written buyer agreement before touring.
glossary.contrast: A subagent works for the seller even while working with the buyer.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Electrical cable with insulated wires inside a flexible spiral metal sheath.
glossary.deep:
BX is wiring with built-in armor: the spiral metal jacket protects the wires from nails and rodents. Modern versions (MC cable) include a separate ground wire. It is widely used in NYC, where the code has long restricted plastic-sheathed cable in many building types.

Analogy: wires wearing chain mail. NY example: an electrician rewiring a Manhattan co-op apartment runs MC cable in the walls because the building and city code require metal-clad wiring.

On the exam: BX equals armored, flexible metal jacket with wires already inside.
glossary.contrast: Greenfield is empty flexible metal conduit wires are pulled through; BX comes with the wires already inside.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The rules for running a condo or co-op: electing the board, holding meetings, adopting budgets, assessing charges, insurance, and repairs.
glossary.deep:
If the declaration is the birth certificate, the bylaws are the operating manual. They say how many people sit on the board, how they are elected, how the budget is adopted, how charges are collected, and what happens when an owner does not pay.

Condo bylaws are recorded with the declaration. Co-op bylaws are corporate bylaws, like any corporation's.

NY example: a dispute about whether an LIC condo board could levy a pool assessment without an owner vote is answered by reading the bylaws.

On the exam: governance and elections point to the bylaws.
glossary.contrast: House rules cover daily living details and can be changed by the board alone.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Spending that replaces or improves a major building component and extends its useful life, such as a new roof, boiler or windows.
glossary.deep:
A capital expenditure is an investment in the building, not the cost of running it.

Patching your jeans is maintenance; buying a new winter coat is a capital purchase you expect to last for years.

A $38,000 roof on a Bushwick building, a $250,000 elevator modernization in a Manhattan co-op, or Local Law 11 facade work are capital items. They are excluded from NOI and depreciated for tax purposes. Reserves for replacement spread their expected cost over the years.

On the exam: capital items do not reduce NOI. A roof replacement is the classic example.
glossary.contrast: A repair keeps a component working (operating expense); a capital expenditure replaces or upgrades it.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Spending to buy, replace, or improve a long-lived building component, rather than to operate or repair it.
glossary.deep:
Capital expenses add value or extend life: a new roof, new windows, a new boiler, an elevator modernization. They are funded from reserves or financing, excluded from operating expenses when computing NOI, and, for tax purposes, depreciated rather than deducted at once.

Buying a new furnace is capital; buying heating oil is operating.

Sal's $45,000 boiler replacement is a capital expense; the $14,000 annual fuel bill is an operating expense.

On the exam: capital expense = replacement or improvement, paid from reserves.
glossary.contrast: Operating expenses recur annually; capital expenses are periodic big-ticket items.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: Profit from selling a capital asset: amount realized minus adjusted basis.
glossary.deep:
Capital gain is how appreciation becomes taxable. Held 1 year or less, it is short-term and taxed like wages. Held more than 1 year, it is long-term and taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20% federally (plus a possible 3.8% net investment income tax). New York taxes capital gains as ordinary income.

Like the difference between a quick flip and a long-held investment: patience is rewarded.

An investor buys a Ridgewood two-family in March 2026 and sells in January 2027 at a $90,000 profit: short-term, ordinary rates. Wait until April 2027 and it becomes long-term.

On the exam: short-term = 1 year or less; long-term = more than 1 year.
glossary.contrast: Capital loss is the reverse; recaptured depreciation is a slice of gain taxed at up to 25%.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: Work that adds value, prolongs life, or adapts a property to a new use, added to basis rather than deducted as a repair.
glossary.deep:
The test: does it make the property better or longer-lasting, or just keep it in working order? A new boiler, a finished basement, a new kitchen are improvements. Fixing a leak, patching plaster, repainting are repairs. For a home, repairs are simply nondeductible; for a rental, repairs are deducted as operating expenses, while improvements are depreciated.

Fixing a flat tire is a repair; adding a new engine is an improvement.

Grace's shoebox of receipts for the roof and extension adds $310,000 to basis, cutting her taxable gain.

On the exam: identify which items raise basis. Painting and routine repair do not.
glossary.contrast: A repair maintains; an improvement upgrades.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A loss from selling a capital asset for less than its adjusted basis.
glossary.deep:
Losses on investment property offset capital gains dollar for dollar, plus up to $3,000 a year of ordinary income, with the rest carried forward. Losses on personal-use property, including your own home, are not deductible at all.

The IRS shares in your investment losses, not your lifestyle losses.

A buyer who paid $1,000,000 for a Long Island City condo in 2022 and sells for $930,000 after living there gets no deduction. If it had been a rental, the loss would count.

On the exam: home sale loss = not deductible. Trap answers say "$3,000 per year" for a home.
glossary.contrast: Capital gain is the profit side; a passive loss is a rental operating loss, a different concept.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A plan for setting aside money to pay for major replacements and improvements, such as roofs, boilers, and elevators.
glossary.deep:
Big components wear out on a schedule you can roughly predict. The capital reserve budget estimates each one's cost and remaining life, then saves a share every month so the money is there when needed.

Like saving monthly for a new car instead of financing it in a panic.

Sal's boiler ($45,000 in about 4 years) and roof ($60,000 in about 6 years) need about $21,250 a year, so Jordan proposes $2,000 a month.

On the exam: replacements and capital expenses come from reserves, not the operating budget.
glossary.contrast: The operating budget covers recurring annual costs.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: The rate of return an investor expects from a property's NOI, computed as NOI divided by value or price.
glossary.deep:
The cap rate is the property's free-and-clear yield: what percentage of the price comes back each year as NOI, ignoring financing.

Think of it as the interest rate the building pays you if you bought it with cash.

Bushwick mixed-use comps traded at 6.0% to 6.5%. Using 6.25%, $190,000 NOI is worth $3,040,000. Riskier property gets a higher cap rate (lower price); safer property gets a lower cap rate (higher price).

On the exam: R = I / V. Cap rate up, value down. Derive it from comparable sales.
glossary.contrast: Cash on cash uses BTCF and equity; the cap rate uses NOI and total value.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The usable area minus walls, columns, convector enclosures and built-ins: the floor you could actually cover with carpet.
glossary.deep:
Carpetable is the floor you can actually stand on and furnish. It is the smallest of the three measurements.

Like the open floor in a room once you subtract the radiator, the closet and the column in the corner.

In an older Manhattan loft with thick columns and big perimeter heating units, carpetable can be noticeably smaller than usable, which matters for how many desks fit.

On the exam: rentable > usable > carpetable. Remember "Really Useful Carpet."
glossary.contrast: Usable includes interior walls and columns inside the suite; carpetable does not.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The money left after paying operating expenses and debt service: NOI minus debt service (before-tax cash flow).
glossary.deep:
Cash flow is what the owner actually takes home from operations. Start with gross income, subtract vacancy and operating expenses to get NOI, then subtract the full mortgage payment (principal and interest). Depreciation is not subtracted because no one writes a check for it.

It is your checking account's view of the building.

Sal: NOI $66,490 minus $45,000 debt service = $21,490 before-tax cash flow, even though his taxable income is only $8,490.

On the exam: cash flow subtracts debt service; taxable income subtracts interest and depreciation.
glossary.contrast: Taxable income subtracts depreciation and only the interest part of debt service.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.term: Cash on cash return (equity dividend rate)
glossary.def: Before-tax cash flow divided by the investor's cash invested (equity).
glossary.deep:
Cash on cash answers the investor's personal question: what is my own money earning this year?

Like comparing your savings account rate: you put in $1,000,000, it paid you $40,000, that is 4%.

Evelyn's Bushwick deal: $40,000 BTCF on $1,000,000 of equity = 4%, while the building earns 6.33% free and clear. That gap is the signature of negative leverage. With cheaper debt, cash on cash would beat the cap rate.

On the exam: divide by equity (down payment), not price. Also called the equity dividend rate.
glossary.contrast: The cap rate divides NOI by the whole property value and ignores financing.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The analysis of actual dollars in and out of a property: NOI minus full debt service equals before-tax cash flow, and BTCF minus tax equals after-tax cash flow.
glossary.deep:
The cash world follows the money. If a check is written, it counts; if not, it does not.

Think of your bank statement: every deposit and every withdrawal, nothing else.

In the cash world, Evelyn subtracts all $150,000 of debt service (principal and interest) from NOI and ignores depreciation, because no check is written for depreciation.

On the exam: cash world uses full debt service and no depreciation.
glossary.contrast: The tax world deducts only interest and adds depreciation.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A warning or caution; in law, a formal notice that something should not be done without notice to the person giving it.
glossary.deep:
Caveat is Latin for "let him beware". In everyday use it is any warning or qualification.

Like the fine print saying "results may vary".

A broker presenting an offer to the Okafors adds a caveat: "This buyer's financing is not yet approved." In court practice, a caveat is a notice asking that nothing be done in a matter without notifying the filer.

On the exam: caveat means warning. Keep it distinct from caveat emptor, the buyer-beware rule.
glossary.contrast: Caveat emptor is a specific doctrine; caveat is a general warning.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Latin for "let the buyer beware": the buyer is responsible for checking the property's condition.
glossary.deep:
Historically the seller had no duty to point out defects. The buyer had to inspect.

Like buying a used phone at a street stall: test it before you pay.

NY still starts from caveat emptor, but it has been softened: sellers of 1 to 4 family homes must give the PCDS, active concealment and fraud are never allowed, and licensees must disclose known material defects. That is why buyers in Westchester still hire Ray the inspector.

On the exam: caveat emptor is the default, limited by disclosure laws and the ban on fraud.
glossary.contrast: Caveat is any formal warning; caveat emptor is the buyer-beware doctrine.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A Department of State list of homeowners in a cease and desist zone who have asked not to be solicited to sell; licensees may not solicit anyone on it.
glossary.deep:
Picture a do-not-call list, but for real estate solicitation and limited to specific zones. Owners in the zone sign up through DOS. Licensees must check the current list before any mailing, call, text, email, or door knock.

Example: Jordan wants to farm East Flatbush with postcards. Part of it is a cease and desist zone. Jordan must remove every listed owner before mailing. One postcard to a listed owner can mean a reprimand, a fine up to $2,000, or worse.

On the exam: the list is opt-in. Owners not on it may still be solicited, unless a nonsolicitation order covers the area.
glossary.contrast: A nonsolicitation order bans soliciting every owner in the area, not just listed ones.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A geographic area designated by the Secretary of State under RPL 442-h where owners may register to stop real estate solicitation, after DOS finds repeated, intense solicitation there.
glossary.deep:
Zones exist where owners were being hammered with calls and letters, often with blockbusting overtones. Inside the zone, licensees and others regularly in the business may not solicit owners who registered.

A zone rule lasts no more than 5 years and may be readopted. When a zone expires, the owner registrations under it expire too. Zones have covered parts of Queens, the Bronx, and Rockland County; as of October 2026 the only active one is part of Brooklyn Community Board 17.

On the exam: the zone is the area; the list is the owners in it who opted out. Expect a question asking who in the zone may still be solicited (owners not on the list).
glossary.contrast: A nonsolicitation order covers every owner in an area and requires a public hearing.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A small statistical area defined by the U.S. Census Bureau, usually 1,200 to 8,000 people, used to report population and housing data.
glossary.deep:
Census tracts are the building blocks planners use to read a neighborhood's data: income, age, race, housing tenure, vacancy. Tracts stay roughly stable over time, so trends can be tracked from census to census.

Analogy: pixels in the population picture. NY example: a Bronx planning study compares median household income and rent burden tract by tract to decide where to target affordable housing. Lenders also report mortgage data by census tract under HMDA, which is how redlining patterns are detected.

On the exam: census tracts show up as a planning data source and in fair lending contexts.
glossary.contrast: A zoning district is a legal boundary; a census tract is only a statistical boundary.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act of 1980: federal law for cleaning up hazardous waste sites and making responsible parties pay.
glossary.deep:
CERCLA created the Superfund and a sweeping liability scheme. Potentially responsible parties include current owners and operators, owners at the time of disposal, generators of the waste, and transporters. Liability is strict (no fault needed), joint and several (one party can be stuck with the whole bill), and retroactive. Petroleum is excluded, which is why state oil spill laws matter.

Analogy: you buy the house and inherit the previous owner's unpaid toxic bill. NY example: Love Canal near Niagara Falls, where homes were built over a chemical dump, helped prompt Congress to pass CERCLA in 1980.

On the exam: strict, joint and several; current owners liable; defenses require due diligence.
glossary.contrast: SARA amended CERCLA in 1986 and created the innocent landowner defense.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The NYC LPC (or a local landmark commission) approval required before work that affects the protected features of a designated property.
glossary.deep:
A Certificate of Appropriateness says the proposed change fits the landmark or district. In NYC, significant changes, such as new windows of a different design, additions, or storefront changes, need one, often after a public hearing with Community Board input. Lesser work that matches existing features may get a staff-level Permit for Minor Work, and work that does not affect protected features gets a Certificate of No Effect.

Analogy: a design passport stamped before construction can travel to DOB. NY example: a Fort Greene owner proposing a rear extension visible from a public street goes before the LPC for a Certificate of Appropriateness.

On the exam: landmark property plus exterior change equals LPC certificate before DOB permit.
glossary.contrast: A certificate of occupancy (DOB) confirms legal use after work; a Certificate of Appropriateness (LPC) approves design before work.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: A document from the building department certifying that a building complies with codes and may be occupied for a stated use.
glossary.deep:
The CO is the building's legal identity card: it states the lawful use (one-family, two-family, store with apartments above) and occupancy. It is issued after final inspections on new construction or major alterations.

Analogy: the car's registration that says it is street legal and seats five. NY example: a Ridgewood house advertised as a three-family has a CO for two families; the third unit is illegal, a lender may refuse to count its rent, and the city can issue violations. Many NYC buildings built before 1938 never needed a CO, so a letter of no objection may substitute.

On the exam: CO comes after construction and confirms legal use. Agents should check it before advertising unit counts.
glossary.contrast: A building permit authorizes work to begin; a CO authorizes occupancy after the work passes inspection.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Chemicals once used as refrigerants, aerosol propellants and foam blowing agents that deplete the earth's ozone layer.
glossary.deep:
CFCs are stable gases that drift into the stratosphere and destroy ozone, which shields the earth from ultraviolet radiation. The 1987 Montreal Protocol and the Clean Air Act phased them out. In homes, they appear in old air conditioners, refrigerators and freezers. Refrigerant must be recovered by EPA-certified technicians before equipment is serviced or scrapped; venting it is illegal.

Analogy: a slow leak in the planet's sunscreen. NY example: when an old Long Island central AC system is replaced, the contractor recovers the old refrigerant rather than releasing it.

On the exam: CFCs equal ozone depletion, aerosols and air conditioners.
glossary.contrast: PCBs are toxic in soil and water; CFCs are a threat to the atmosphere.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The unbroken succession of owners of a property from the original grant to the present owner.
glossary.deep: The chain of title links every owner to the next by deed, will, or court order, like links of a chain back to the original land patent. A missing link, such as an unrecorded deed or an estate that was never probated, is a gap that clouds title until fixed, sometimes by a quitclaim or a quiet title action. Title searchers trace the chain to confirm the seller really owns what he is selling. On the exam: chain of title = the sequence of ownership; abstract = a summary of the recorded documents in it.
glossary.contrast: An abstract of title is a written summary of the chain's records.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The DOS filing made when a salesperson or associate broker moves from one sponsoring broker to another.
glossary.deep:
Moving firms is a two-step paper process: the old broker terminates the association and the new broker files the change of association, usually in eAccessNY. Until the new association is filed, the licensee may not act as an agent.

It is like changing teams in a sports league: you cannot suit up for the new team until the league records the trade.

Marcus leaves Hudson & Hart on Friday. Monday morning he wants to show a Chelsea loft for his new firm, but the filing is not in. He waits.

On the exam: the license is not revoked or voided by leaving; you simply cannot work until reassociated, and listings stay with the old broker.
glossary.contrast: Termination ends the old association; change of association creates the new one.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: Another word for an item of personal property.
glossary.deep: Chattel is the old legal word for movable personal property. The word shares a root with "cattle," which were once the classic movable possession. If you hear a lawyer talk about a chattel mortgage, that is a loan secured by personal property like equipment. A pizza oven a tenant owns is a chattel; so is the sofa in a staged condo. On the exam: chattel = personal property. If you see the word in an answer choice describing something movable, it is the personal property option.
glossary.contrast: Real property is immovable land and improvements; a chattel is movable.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A pesticide once widely used in soil around foundations to kill termites; banned in the U.S. in 1988 because of health and environmental risks.
glossary.deep:
Chlordane was the go-to termite treatment for decades. It lasted a long time in the soil, which was the point, and also the problem: it is toxic, persists for decades, and can seep into indoor air. EPA banned all uses in 1988.

Analogy: a fix that stayed long after the job was done. NY example: a 1960s house in Nassau County with a history of termite treatment may still have chlordane in the soil around the foundation; an environmental test can detect it if a buyer is concerned, especially before digging a garden or addition.

On the exam: chlordane equals banned termite pesticide.
glossary.contrast: PCBs were electrical chemicals; chlordane was a pesticide.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A switch that automatically trips to cut power when a circuit is overloaded or shorted, and can be reset.
glossary.deep:
Breakers do the fuse's job without being destroyed. When current exceeds the rating, the breaker trips; you fix the cause and flip it back. Single-pole breakers serve 120-volt circuits; double-pole serve 240-volt. GFCI breakers protect against shock in wet areas; AFCI breakers detect dangerous arcing in bedrooms and living areas.

Analogy: a reusable safety valve. NY example: a renovated Hoboken-style condo in Long Island City has a 200-amp breaker panel with AFCI protection as required by current code.

On the exam: breakers reset, fuses do not. Panel diagram questions ask which breaker serves 120 vs 240 volts.
glossary.contrast: A fuse is single-use; a breaker is resettable.
glossary.subject: s07
