glossary.def: New York City's 13-member commission that plans the city's development and votes on rezonings and other ULURP actions.
glossary.deep:
The CPC is the city's planning board, supported by the Department of City Planning, whose director chairs it. The mayor appoints the chair and six members, each borough president appoints one, and the public advocate one. It votes on zoning map and text changes, special permits, and other ULURP actions, after which the City Council reviews many of them.

Analogy: the master planner with a binding vote. NY example: the CPC approved the City of Yes zoning text changes before the City Council adopted them in 2024.

On the exam: CPC equals planning and rezonings in NYC. Variances go to the BSA.
glossary.contrast: Community Boards hold hearings but only advise; the CPC's vote is binding.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The municipality's engineer, responsible for roads and for sewer and water connections, and for reviewing engineering on development plans.
glossary.deep:
The municipal engineer looks after public infrastructure: roads, drainage, sewer and water mains and connections. The engineer reviews subdivision and site plan engineering (grades, stormwater, road design) for the planning board and inspects public improvements a developer builds. Often works with or heads the department of public works.

Analogy: the town's infrastructure doctor. NY example: a homeowner in a Dutchess County village connecting a house to the village sewer gets a connection permit and inspection from the village engineer's office.

On the exam: engineer equals roads, sewer and water connections.
glossary.contrast: The county health department approves on-site septic systems; the municipal engineer handles public sewer connections.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: Federal law giving all citizens the same right as white citizens to buy, sell, lease, inherit, and hold property. It covers race only and has no exemptions.
glossary.deep:
Passed right after the Civil War, it says in plain terms that Black citizens get the same property rights as white citizens. Think of it as the bedrock under every other fair housing law: smaller in scope (race only) but with no trapdoors at all.

Example: an owner who lives in his Albany two-family might be exempt from parts of the Fair Housing Act. If he refuses a renter because she is Black, the 1866 Act still applies and she can sue in federal court.

On the exam: when a question asks which law has no exemptions, or which applies even to an otherwise exempt owner, the answer is the 1866 Act, usually paired with Jones v. Mayer.
glossary.contrast: The Fair Housing Act of 1968 covers seven classes but has exemptions; the 1866 Act covers only race but has none.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: Federal civil rights law; Title VI bars discrimination by race, color, or national origin in programs that receive federal financial assistance, including public and assisted housing.
glossary.deep:
The 1964 Act is famous for ending segregation in public accommodations and employment. Its housing reach is narrower: Title VI covers programs that take federal money. A NYCHA development or a federally assisted senior building is covered. A private co-op sale is not, under this Act (other laws cover it).

Think of it as following the federal dollar.

On the exam: if the question mentions federally funded or assisted housing, Title VI of the 1964 Act is the hook. For private housing, look to the 1866 Act and the 1968 Fair Housing Act.
glossary.contrast: The Fair Housing Act of 1968 is Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, not part of the 1964 Act.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: Federal law regulating air pollution, including national air quality standards, asbestos handling during demolition and renovation, and the phase-out of ozone-depleting CFCs.
glossary.deep:
The Clean Air Act sets limits on air pollutants and controls hazardous air pollutants. Real estate touches it in two ways: asbestos rules (NESHAP) for demolition and renovation of buildings, requiring inspection and proper removal, and Title VI's phase-out of CFCs and HCFCs, which is why old refrigerants must be recovered by certified technicians.

Analogy: the federal rulebook for what may go up the chimney. NY example: before a Rochester office building is demolished, an asbestos survey and abatement must be completed under federal and NYS Department of Labor rules.

On the exam: CAA connects to asbestos and CFCs.
glossary.contrast: The Safe Drinking Water Act regulates drinking water; the Clean Air Act regulates air.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The person a licensee represents, who is owed all fiduciary duties.
glossary.deep:
Your client is your team. Everything you do in the deal is for them.

Like a lawyer and the person they defend: the lawyer is polite to the prosecutor but works only for the defendant.

Leo signs a buyer agreement with Jordan. Leo is now a client: Jordan keeps his budget secret, advises him on what to offer, and points out every problem with a property. The sellers Leo negotiates against are customers.

On the exam: clients get loyalty, advice, and confidentiality. Customers get honesty and disclosure of known material defects. Questions often hinge on which one a person is.
glossary.contrast: A customer gets honesty but not loyalty or advice.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A standard five-page form showing the final loan terms and closing costs, which the borrower must receive at least 3 business days before closing.
glossary.deep: The Closing Disclosure (CD) replaced the HUD-1 settlement statement for most consumer mortgages in 2015 under the TRID rule. It must reach the borrower at least 3 business days before consummation so there is time to compare it to the Loan Estimate and ask questions. If the APR rises beyond tolerance, the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added, a new CD and a new 3-day wait are required. On the exam: 3 business days before closing; it replaced the HUD-1 for most loans.
glossary.contrast: The Loan Estimate comes within 3 business days after application.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A detailed accounting of every charge and credit to the buyer and seller at closing, showing cash due from the buyer and net proceeds to the seller.
glossary.deep: The closing statement is the deal's receipt. It lists, for each party, debits (amounts owed) and credits (amounts received or credited): price, deposits, loans, payoffs, prorations, taxes, commissions, and fees. For financed residential deals the lender's version is the Closing Disclosure; NY attorneys also prepare their own closing statements. Reconciling the columns shows how much the buyer must bring and what the seller takes home. On the exam: know which items are debits or credits to whom, and how to reconcile.
glossary.contrast: A net sheet is an estimate prepared before closing.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Grouping the same number of homes allowed on a tract onto smaller lots, leaving the remaining land as permanent open space.
glossary.deep:
Clustering rearranges, it does not add. If 40 acres allow 20 homes on 2-acre lots, clustering might put those 20 homes on half-acre lots and preserve 30 acres as woods or farmland. NY towns authorize the planning board to approve clustered subdivisions, and the town board can require it.

Analogy: same number of guests, pushed together to free up the dance floor. NY example: a Putnam County subdivision clusters homes near the road and preserves a ridge and stream as conservation land owned by an HOA.

On the exam: total density stays the same. Expect a math question: total acres divided by minimum lot size equals the number of homes.
glossary.contrast: A PUD can mix housing types and uses; clustering usually rearranges one housing type.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A search done for a co-op purchase, instead of a title search, for UCC filings against the seller's shares and judgments, tax liens, and bankruptcies against the seller.
glossary.deep:
Co-op buyers get shares, not land, so title insurance does not fit. The lien search checks that the shares are free of the seller's old lender and other creditors, and the managing agent confirms maintenance is paid.

NY example: the search shows the seller's 2015 lender never filed a UCC-3 termination. Priya gets a payoff letter and termination before closing.

On the exam: condo = title search and title insurance; co-op = lien search (UCC).
glossary.contrast: A title search examines real property records for a deed and mortgages.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A NY program, created by state regulators in 1996, codified in Insurance Law 5414, and administered by NYPIUA, that refers coastal homeowners who were turned down to insurers willing to consider them.
glossary.deep:
C-MAP is a matchmaker for coastal homes that insurers avoid.

Instead of a pool that writes the policy itself, it passes your application to regular insurers who agreed to take a second look.

An owner-occupant of a one-family near the shore in Suffolk, Nassau, Westchester, or the outer boroughs who got a nonrenewal can apply through C-MAP and may land a regular homeowners policy instead of a bare-bones FAIR plan policy.

On the exam: "coastal residents assistance" in the syllabus points to C-MAP.
glossary.contrast: NYPIUA writes coverage directly as the insurer of last resort.
glossary.subject: s12

glossary.def: A policy clause requiring the owner to insure for at least a set percentage, usually 80%, of replacement cost to collect full payment on a partial loss. Payout = (amount carried / amount required) x loss.
glossary.deep:
Coinsurance punishes underinsuring.

Pay for only three-quarters of the needed coverage and you collect only three-quarters of your claim.

Sal's house costs $500,000 to rebuild. He should carry $400,000 (80%) but carries $300,000. A $40,000 fire: $300,000 / $400,000 = 0.75 x $40,000 = $30,000. He absorbs the other $10,000 plus his deductible.

On the exam: Did / Should x Loss. "Should" is 80% of replacement cost, not 100%.
glossary.contrast: Deductible: a fixed amount the owner pays on every claim regardless of coverage level.
glossary.subject: s12

glossary.def: Mixing client or customer funds with the broker's own money.
glossary.deep:
Commingling is a violation even if no money is lost. The rule is about separation: the moment a deposit hits a personal or operating account, the client's money is exposed to the broker's creditors and mistakes.

Picture pouring a client's bottle of wine into your own carafe to "hold it": even if you pour the same amount back, you mixed it.

Marcus put a $25,000 deposit in his personal checking over a weekend. Every dollar came back Monday. It is still commingling and still revocation territory under 175.1.

On the exam: commingling is mixing; conversion is spending. Both are serious; the exam often asks you to name which one.
glossary.contrast: Conversion is using the client's money for yourself.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: The broker's fee for a successful transaction, usually a percentage of the sale price or of the rent, set by agreement between the client and the broker.
glossary.deep:
A commission is the broker's paycheck, earned when the job in the agreement is done.

Think of a tip calculated on the bill, except negotiated in writing in advance.

The Okafors agree to 5% on a $2.4M sale: $120,000. If half is offered to a cooperating broker, each side gets $60,000, and each firm then splits its share with its salesperson.

On the exam: commission rates are negotiable. Any suggestion that rates are set by law, a board, or an agreement among brokers is wrong (that is price fixing). Math: Price x Rate, then each split.
glossary.contrast: Commission split: how a commission is divided after it is earned.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: The division of a commission between cooperating brokers, and then between a broker and the salesperson, according to their agreements.
glossary.deep:
A commission moves down a chain. Each link takes its percentage of the amount handed to it.

Picture slicing a pizza in half for two tables, then each table splitting its half 60/40.

$700,000 sale, 6% = $42,000. 50/50 co-broke: $21,000 to each firm. Jordan's 60/40 split: $12,600 to Jordan, $8,400 to the firm.

On the exam: do one step at a time, and apply each percentage to the right base. In NY, the salesperson is paid only by the sponsoring broker.
glossary.contrast: Commission: the total fee before any splits.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: Charges that tenants, mainly in shopping centers, pay for their share of maintaining shared areas like parking lots, walkways, lighting, snow removal and security.
glossary.deep:
CAM is how a center's shared costs get split among the tenants.

Like splitting the cost of shoveling the shared driveway among all the houses that use it.

A shoe store with 5% of a Long Island center's leasable area pays 5% of the cost of plowing, lighting and cleaning the parking lot. Tenants often negotiate caps on CAM increases and exclusions for capital items.

On the exam: CAM is a pass-through of shared-area costs, usually by proportionate share, typical of net retail leases.
glossary.contrast: Escalations in office leases pass through increases over a base; CAM usually passes through the full share of costs.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Parts of a building or center shared by all tenants, such as lobbies, corridors, restrooms, elevators, mechanical rooms and parking lots.
glossary.deep:
Common areas belong to everyone and no one. Tenants pay for them indirectly, through rentable square footage in office buildings and CAM charges in shopping centers.

Like the shared kitchen in a dorm: you use it, you pay toward it, but it is not your room.

In a Midtown tower, the lobby, elevator banks and floor corridors are common areas folded into each tenant's RSF. In a Long Island strip center, the parking lot and sidewalks are common areas billed through CAM.

On the exam: common areas explain the gap between rentable and usable.
glossary.contrast: Usable space is exclusive to one tenant; common areas are shared.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The monthly amount each condo owner pays for the unit's share of the building's operating budget, based on its common interest. Real estate taxes are billed separately.
glossary.deep:
Common charges are a condo's monthly dues: staff, insurance, common utilities, repairs, management, reserves. They do not include your real estate taxes, because each condo unit is its own tax lot with its own bill.

Unpaid common charges become a lien on the unit that the board can foreclose.

NY example: an Upper East Side condo budget of $1,800,000 with a 0.6% unit equals $10,800 a year, $900 a month.

On the exam: condo = common charges; co-op = maintenance (which includes taxes and the underlying mortgage).
glossary.contrast: Co-op maintenance includes the building's real estate taxes and mortgage; common charges do not.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: All parts of a condominium other than the units, such as the land, structure, roof, lobby, hallways, elevators, and building systems, owned by all unit owners as tenants in common.
glossary.deep:
Everything outside your unit's walls is common: the lobby, the boiler, the roof, the gym, the land under it all. Each owner holds an undivided share set by the declaration.

You cannot sell your share of the lobby by itself, and you cannot ask a court to partition the building.

NY example: when the LIC condo replaces its roof, the cost is a common expense shared by percentage, even for owners on the 3rd floor.

On the exam: common elements are owned together, are inseparable from the unit, and are paid for through common charges and assessments.
glossary.contrast: Limited common elements are common elements reserved for one or a few units.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A condo unit's percentage ownership of the common elements, set in the declaration, which determines its share of common charges and usually its voting weight.
glossary.deep:
Every condo unit has a number, like 0.6%. That number is your slice of the building. It sets your share of common charges, assessments, and often votes.

It is usually based on the unit's floor area and may be adjusted for floor height, views, or amenities.

NY example: a $500,000 pool assessment in a building where Leo's unit has 0.6% costs him $3,000.

On the exam: math questions multiply the budget or assessment by the common interest percentage, then divide by 12 for monthly charges.
glossary.contrast: In a co-op, the apartment's share count plays the same role for maintenance.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: One of 59 NYC local advisory boards whose appointed volunteer members hold hearings and make recommendations on land use, zoning, BSA and other neighborhood matters.
glossary.deep:
Community Boards give neighborhoods a formal voice. Each has up to 50 unpaid members appointed by the borough president, half nominated by local City Council members, plus a paid district manager. In ULURP they get the first 60 days to hold a hearing and vote. They also weigh in on BSA variances, liquor licenses and the city budget. Their votes are advisory, but elected officials pay attention.

Analogy: the neighborhood's microphone, not its gavel. NY example: Brooklyn Community Board 6 votes against a proposed rezoning; the CPC and City Council may still approve it.

On the exam: Community Board equals advisory.
glossary.contrast: The BSA and CPC make binding decisions; Community Boards advise.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: A system used in nine states under which most property acquired during marriage belongs equally to both spouses; New York does not use it.
glossary.deep: In community property states such as California, Texas, and Arizona, a paycheck earned or a house bought during marriage generally belongs half to each spouse automatically, whatever the deed says. Property owned before marriage or received by gift or inheritance stays separate. New York is not a community property state. In a NY divorce, marital property is divided by equitable distribution, meaning fairly, which may not be 50/50. A couple moving from California to Brooklyn needs advice on how prior property is treated. On the exam: know the concept and that NY is not one.
glossary.contrast: Equitable distribution is NY's divorce rule; tenancy by the entirety is NY's spousal form of title.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A licensee's written opinion of a likely price range for a property, based on recent comparable sales, current competing listings, and expired listings. It is never an appraisal.
glossary.deep:
A CMA is the agent's homework for pricing. It shows the seller what similar homes sold for, what they will compete with, and what failed to sell.

It is like a used-car guide: helpful and grounded, but not a certified inspection.

Jordan's CMA for the Okafors shows six sales within a few blocks in the last 12 months, three active competitors, and two expireds at $2.7M and $2.75M, ending with a range of $2.35M to $2.5M.

On the exam: a CMA may never be called an appraisal. It is an opinion of value used to set a list price or frame an offer.
glossary.contrast: Appraisal: by a licensed appraiser, typically for a lender, under professional standards.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: The legal proceeding by which government exercises eminent domain to acquire private property for public use with payment.
glossary.deep:
If eminent domain is the power, condemnation is the paperwork and the courtroom. The condemning agency identifies the property, holds the required hearing, makes an offer, and, if the owner will not accept, goes to court to fix compensation and take title.

Analogy: eminent domain is the right to order something; condemnation is the checkout process. NY example: the MTA condemning a Queens lot for a rail yard files under the Eminent Domain Procedure Law; the owner can litigate the amount in the Court of Claims or Supreme Court.

On the exam: a question asking for "the process" or "the legal action" wants condemnation. Do not confuse it with a building being "condemned" as unsafe, which is a code enforcement action under police power.
glossary.contrast: Escheat also gives the state property but arises from death without heirs, not from a taking for public use.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A form of ownership in which each owner holds fee title to a unit plus an undivided percentage interest in the common elements. It is real property.
glossary.deep:
A condo is a way of owning, not a style of building. A Midtown tower, a row of townhouses in Riverdale, and an office floor can all be condos. You own your unit (the airspace inside your walls) outright and share everything else with your neighbors by percentage.

Picture a pie: your slice is yours, and the crust and plate are shared.

NY example: Leo buys a 22nd floor one-bedroom in Long Island City. He gets a deed, title insurance, a mortgage with mortgage recording tax, and his own tax bill.

On the exam: condo = real property, deed, separate taxes, common charges, board of managers, right of first refusal.
glossary.contrast: A cooperative buyer owns shares and a proprietary lease, which are personal property.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A building divided into condominium units in which the residential portion is owned by a co-op corporation and commercial space is held as separate condo units; also loosely used for co-ops with condo-like rules.
glossary.deep:
Picture a condo with two units: one is the whole residential portion, owned by a co-op; the other is the ground floor retail, owned by the sponsor or an investor. Residents buy co-op shares, but the store rent never counts as co-op income.

Why: it protects the co-op under the 80/20 rule, lets the commercial space be sold or financed separately, and keeps residents from carrying commercial risk.

NY example: many Manhattan towers built in the 1980s with retail bases are condops.

On the exam: condop = condo structure with a co-op inside, usually to manage commercial income.
glossary.contrast: A pure co-op owns the whole building, commercial space included.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A rigid or semi-rigid tube of metal or PVC through which electrical wires are pulled.
glossary.deep:
Conduit is a protective pipe for wires. It is installed first, then the electrician pulls individual wires through it, which also makes later rewiring easier. Rigid metal and EMT (thin-wall) conduit are common in commercial buildings, exposed basement runs, and outdoors; PVC is used underground and in wet locations.

Analogy: a straw the wires go through. NY example: in a Brooklyn retail storefront, all wiring runs in EMT conduit along the ceiling, as commercial code requires, while the apartments above use MC cable.

On the exam: conduit is the tube; wires go in after.
glossary.contrast: Greenfield is flexible conduit; standard conduit is rigid.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The duty to keep the client's private information secret, including after the agency ends.
glossary.deep:
What the client tells you in confidence stays with you, forever.

Like a therapist: the sessions end, the secrecy does not.

Years after closing, Jordan mentions at a party that Rosa "would have taken $200K less, she was in a divorce." The agency ended at closing; the duty of confidentiality did not. That is a breach.

On the exam: confidentiality is the duty that survives termination. It does not cover facts the law requires you to disclose, like known defects.
glossary.contrast: Disclosure: tell the client everything material. Confidentiality: tell no one else the client's secrets.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A conventional loan within the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loan limits and underwriting standards, so it can be sold to them.
glossary.deep:
A loan built to the secondary market's specs.

Like luggage that fits the overhead bin.

For 2026 the one-unit baseline limit is $832,750, and in high-cost areas like NYC it is up to $1,249,125. Leo's $576,000 condo loan is conforming. Because it can be sold easily, conforming loans tend to have competitive rates and standard documents.

On the exam: conforming = meets Fannie/Freddie limits and guidelines.
glossary.contrast: A nonconforming loan (such as a jumbo) falls outside them.
glossary.subject: s18

glossary.def: An appointed local body that deals with environmental issues under municipal ordinances: inventories open space and wetlands, advises other boards, and in some places issues local wetland permits.
glossary.deep:
General Municipal Law lets towns and villages create a conservation advisory council to study natural resources and advise the planning board and town board. Some municipalities go further with a wetlands commission or conservation board that issues local wetland permits, stricter than state rules.

Analogy: the town's environmental consultant with a seat at the table. NY example: in a northern Westchester town, a homeowner wanting to regrade near a stream needs a local wetland permit reviewed by the conservation board, in addition to any DEC permit.

On the exam: CAC equals local environmental issues.
glossary.contrast: DEC regulates wetlands statewide; the CAC or wetlands commission works under local ordinances.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: Something of legal value each party gives to make a contract binding: money, a promise, an act, or giving up a right.
glossary.deep:
Consideration is the "this for that" of a contract. Each side gives something.

Like a trade at a flea market: no swap, no deal.

When Leo agrees to pay $1.6M and the Okafors agree to deliver a deed, both promises are consideration. In a lease, rent is the consideration. It need not be fair or equal; courts rarely weigh adequacy, only that it exists. A gift deed is valid without consideration, but a contract is not.

On the exam: consideration can be a promise; forbearance counts; "love and affection" supports a deed, not a sales contract.
glossary.contrast: An earnest money deposit shows good faith; consideration is what makes the contract enforceable.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A short-term, usually interest-only loan disbursed in draws as building progresses, then replaced by a permanent (takeout) loan.
glossary.deep:
Money released stage by stage as the building rises.

Like paying a contractor after each finished phase, not all at once.

A family building a house in Saratoga gets a construction loan. After the foundation passes inspection, the lender releases the first draw; framing, the next; and so on. Interest is paid only on funds drawn. At completion a permanent mortgage (takeout loan) pays it off. Lenders watch for mechanic's liens.

On the exam: draws, short term, interest only, takeout.
glossary.contrast: A bridge loan covers the gap between selling and buying, not building.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: When the landlord's act or failure makes the premises unusable, the tenant may move out and stop paying rent, treating the lease as ended.
glossary.deep:
The landlord never physically removed the tenant, but made staying impossible, so the law treats it as an eviction.

Like a restaurant that never asks you to leave but turns off the lights and heat until you go.

A Bronx office tenant has no heat for a whole winter after repeated complaints. She moves out within a reasonable time and stops paying. She can defend against a suit for rent by claiming constructive eviction.

On the exam: two elements, a serious landlord-caused problem and the tenant actually leaving. No exit, no constructive eviction.
glossary.contrast: Breach of habitability lets the tenant stay and get an abatement; constructive eviction requires leaving.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Notice the law presumes everyone has, created by recording documents in the public records or by visible possession.
glossary.deep: Constructive notice means you are treated as knowing something whether you looked or not. Once a deed, mortgage, lien, or lis pendens is recorded, every later buyer is charged with knowing it. Visible possession works similarly: if someone else is living in the property, a buyer is expected to ask on what basis (inquiry notice). A buyer who skips the title search cannot claim ignorance of a recorded easement. On the exam: recording = constructive notice; actual notice is personal knowledge.
glossary.contrast: Actual notice is what a person really knows or has been told.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The 1968 federal law whose titles include Truth in Lending, and later the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.
glossary.deep:
The umbrella over the major consumer credit laws.

Like a folder that holds several rulebooks.

Title I is Truth in Lending (disclosure, Reg Z). The Fair Credit Reporting Act governs credit reports and requires notice when an applicant is denied based on one. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act bans discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or public assistance. A Bronx applicant denied for a credit report error can dispute it under FCRA.

On the exam: CCPA includes TILA.
glossary.contrast: RESPA is a separate law on settlement procedures and kickbacks.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A condition in a contract that must happen before the parties are bound to perform, such as obtaining a mortgage or a satisfactory inspection.
glossary.deep:
An "if" clause. If it does not happen, the buyer can usually exit with the deposit.

Like an RSVP that says "I'll come if it does not rain".

Downstate contracts commonly have a mortgage contingency; inspections usually happen before signing instead. Upstate purchase offers often include inspection and attorney approval contingencies. Each has a deadline and a procedure; miss it and the protection may be lost.

On the exam: contingencies protect the party who would be hurt if the condition fails, usually the buyer.
glossary.contrast: A covenant is a promise; a contingency is a condition.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The 22.5 hours of DOS-approved courses a NY licensee must complete each 2-year term to renew.
glossary.deep:
CE keeps licensees current. Each 22.5-hour block must include 3 hours fair housing/discrimination, 2 implicit bias, 2 cultural competency, 2.5 ethical business practices, 1 recent legal matters, and 1 law of agency (2 on the first renewal). The rest are electives.

Think of it as an oil change schedule: miss it and the license will not run.

Jordan's first renewal comes 2 years after licensing. Jordan needs 22.5 hours including 2 hours of agency. Diane, licensed 30 years, needs the same 22.5: the 15-year broker exemption ended in 2021.

On the exam: 22.5 hours, every 2 years, only NY attorneys exempt.
glossary.contrast: Qualifying education (77 hours) gets you the license; CE keeps it.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A mortgage loan not insured or guaranteed by a government agency.
glossary.deep:
Conventional loans rely on the borrower and the property, plus PMI if the down payment is under 20%.

Like buying a car with a regular bank loan rather than a manufacturer's special program.

Leo's 80% loan from a bank is conventional and conforming, so it can be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. A $2 million Tribeca loan is conventional but nonconforming (jumbo).

On the exam: conventional = no FHA, VA, or USDA backing. PMI above 80% LTV.
glossary.contrast: Government loans are insured (FHA) or guaranteed (VA, RHS).
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The transfer of title or an interest in real property from one person to another, usually by deed.
glossary.deep: Conveyance is the act of passing an interest in land. Selling a house, giving it as a gift, granting an easement, and assigning a lease are all conveyances. The word also refers to the document itself. NY's transfer tax is a tax on conveyances, and NY's recording act protects good-faith buyers whose conveyance is recorded first. On the exam: the granting clause contains the words of conveyance, such as "grants and releases." Voluntary conveyance by deed is voluntary alienation.
glossary.contrast: Alienation is the broader term for any transfer, voluntary or involuntary.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A licensee from another firm who helps bring about a transaction, as a buyer's agent, subagent, or broker's agent.
glossary.deep:
"Cooperating" describes the fact of helping, not the legal role.

Like "guest musician": the term does not tell you which band they are actually playing for.

A Chelsea agent brings a buyer to the Okafors' brownstone. She is a cooperating agent. Whether she owes loyalty to the buyer (buyer's agent) or to the Okafors (subagent or broker's agent) depends on the arrangement, which must be clear before substantive talk.

On the exam: when a question says "cooperating broker," ask what capacity: buyer's agent, subagent, broker's agent, or dual agent.
glossary.contrast: Co-broke describes sharing the commission; agency role describes whom they represent.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A form of ownership in which a corporation owns the building and residents buy shares in the corporation that come with a proprietary lease to a specific apartment.
glossary.deep:
In a co-op you buy into a company that owns the building, and the company leases you your apartment. You are both an owner (shareholder) and a tenant (proprietary lessee).

Because you own shares, not real estate, you get no deed, no title insurance, and pay no mortgage recording tax. You do need board approval.

NY example: about three quarters of Manhattan's owned apartments are co-ops, mostly in prewar buildings on the Upper West and Upper East Sides.

On the exam: co-op = personal property, shares, proprietary lease, maintenance, share loan, board of directors approval.
glossary.contrast: A condominium owner holds real property by deed.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A legal entity separate from its shareholders that can own real estate in its own name, in severalty.
glossary.deep: A corporation is a legal person: it signs contracts, sues and is sued, and holds title in severalty. Shareholders own stock, not the building, and their liability is limited to what they invested. A regular C corporation faces double taxation: the corporation pays tax on its profits, then shareholders pay tax on dividends. A NYC co-op is a corporation that owns the building; tenant-shareholders own shares. On the exam: corporations own in severalty, offer limited liability, and face double taxation.
glossary.contrast: An LLC offers limited liability with pass-through taxation.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A state lien on a corporation's property for unpaid corporate franchise (business) taxes.
glossary.deep: New York charges corporations a franchise tax for the privilege of doing business in the state. If the corporation does not pay, the state's claim becomes a lien on the corporation's property, including real estate. A title search on a building owned by a corporation will check whether franchise taxes are current. A buyer of an office building from a delinquent corporation needs the lien cleared before closing. On the exam: it is a general, involuntary lien, grouped with judgments and estate tax liens.
glossary.contrast: A real property tax lien arises from taxes on the parcel itself.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Repairs made after something breaks or fails.
glossary.deep:
Corrective maintenance is reactive: the circulator pump fails, a pipe bursts, a window cracks, a lock jams. It cannot be avoided entirely, but a good preventive program makes it rarer and cheaper. Managers usually have a spending limit in the management agreement for corrective work and call the owner above it, except in emergencies.

Fixing the flat tire, as opposed to rotating the tires on schedule.

When 2B's kitchen sink leaks into 1B's ceiling on a Sunday, Jordan sends the plumber right away: corrective maintenance, and also an emergency within the manager's authority.

On the exam: corrective = fixing what already broke.
glossary.contrast: Preventive maintenance is scheduled to avoid failure; deferred maintenance is needed work not yet done.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: The total dollars spent to create an improvement: labor, materials, design, legal, financing, taxes during construction, and the builder's and developer's overhead and profit.
glossary.deep:
Cost is the supply side. It is what it took to put the thing on the ground.

A tailored suit costs what the tailor charged. That does not mean anyone else will pay that much for it secondhand.

The Okafors spent $300,000 renovating. A buyer may value the new boiler and roof nearly dollar for dollar, but the koi pond and gold faucets barely at all. Cost spent is not value created.

On the exam: cost may or may not equal value. Overimprovements and personal tastes are the classic examples.
glossary.contrast: Price is what a buyer paid; value is an estimate of worth.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: Estimating value as land value plus the cost to build the improvements new, minus accrued depreciation.
glossary.deep:
The cost approach asks what it would cost to create an equally useful property today.

A buyer will not pay more for an old house than the price of a lot plus a new house, minus whatever wear the old one has.

Firehouse: land $400,000, replacement cost new $1,200,000, depreciation 25% ($300,000). Value = $1,200,000 - $300,000 + $400,000 = $1,300,000.

On the exam: best for new construction, special-purpose properties (churches, schools, firehouses), and insurance. Land is never depreciated.
glossary.contrast: Income approach values rental property from its income stream.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: A response that changes any term of an offer. It rejects and ends the original offer and becomes a new offer.
glossary.deep:
Change anything, and you have rejected and re-offered.

Like haggling: once you say "$40, not $50", the seller's $50 offer is off the table.

Leo offers $1.6M. Grace says "Yes at $1.65M". That is a counteroffer. If Leo later says he will accept $1.6M after all, there is no deal unless Grace agrees again. The same is true if the change is small, like the closing date.

On the exam: counteroffers terminate the original offer. The original offeror is free.
glossary.contrast: An acceptance must mirror the offer exactly.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The county agency that approves septic systems, private wells and certain sewer approvals, and enforces sanitary codes.
glossary.deep:
Where a house has a well or septic system, the county health department is the key agency. It reviews and approves system designs (prepared by a licensed engineer or architect), witnesses perc tests in many counties, keeps as-built drawings, and approves certain sewer extensions. It also handles water testing requirements, food establishments and nuisance complaints.

Analogy: the public health doctor for the ground under the house. NY example: Suffolk County's Department of Health Services must approve any new or upgraded septic system, increasingly nitrogen-reducing systems to protect the aquifer.

On the exam: county health department equals septic approval and some sewer approvals.
glossary.contrast: The building department approves the house; the health department approves the septic and well.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: A written promise in a lease, deed, or contract to do or not do something.
glossary.deep:
Covenants are the promises that make a lease work. Tenant covenants: pay rent, no alterations without consent, use only as stated. Landlord covenants: quiet enjoyment, repairs, heat and hot water.

Think of a list of house rules both people signed.

A Park Slope lease says the tenant covenants not to install a washer. If she does, she breaches a covenant and the landlord can seek a cure or end the lease after notice. Deeds have covenants too, like the covenant against grantor's acts.

On the exam: covenant equals promise. Quiet enjoyment and habitability are the big landlord covenants.
glossary.contrast: A condition can end an estate if broken; breaking a covenant usually gives a claim for damages or an injunction.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The grantor's promise that the property has no liens or encumbrances except those stated in the deed.
glossary.deep: This covenant promises a clean property apart from what is listed. If an undisclosed mortgage, judgment, easement, or restriction turns up, the grantee can recover damages from the grantor. Exceptions the buyer agreed to, such as utility easements, appear in the deed's "subject to" clause so they do not breach the covenant. On the exam: it covers liens and other encumbrances not listed in the deed. Paired with a "subject to" clause, it defines exactly what the buyer accepts.
glossary.contrast: The covenant of warranty promises to defend the title against all lawful claims.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The grantor's promise to sign and deliver any additional documents needed to perfect the grantee's title.
glossary.deep: If a defect appears that paperwork can fix, such as a misspelled name, a missing signature, or an error in the legal description, the grantor promises to cooperate and sign a correction deed or other document. Think of it as a promise of future help. It is one of the five covenants in a full covenant and warranty deed. On the exam: further assurance = "I will sign whatever is needed later to perfect your title."
glossary.contrast: The covenant of warranty is a promise to defend title in court, not just sign documents.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The grantor's promise that the grantee will not be disturbed in possession by anyone with a superior claim to title.
glossary.deep: Quiet enjoyment has nothing to do with noise. It is a promise that no one with a better legal claim will show up and evict the grantee. If a long-lost heir with superior title takes the property, this covenant is breached. Leases carry a similar covenant protecting tenants from interference by the landlord. It is one of the five covenants in a full covenant and warranty deed. On the exam: quiet enjoyment = protection from claims of superior title, not from loud neighbors.
glossary.contrast: The covenant of seizin promises present ownership.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The grantor's promise that he owns the estate being conveyed and has the right to convey it.
glossary.deep: Seizin is an old word for possession of a freehold. The covenant of seizin is the grantor's assurance: I actually own what I am selling you, and I have the right to sell it. If the grantor turns out to own only half, or nothing, the covenant is breached at the moment of delivery. It is one of the five covenants in a full covenant and warranty deed. On the exam: seizin = ownership and right to convey. Do not confuse it with quiet enjoyment, which concerns being disturbed later.
glossary.contrast: The covenant of quiet enjoyment protects against later disturbance by someone with better title.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The grantor's promise to defend the grantee's title against all lawful claims and to compensate the grantee for loss.
glossary.deep: Warranty forever is the strongest promise in a deed: the grantor will defend the title against anyone with a lawful claim, forever, and pay if the grantee loses. It covers the whole chain of title, not just the grantor's time of ownership. That broad reach is what makes the full covenant and warranty deed the most protective deed. On the exam: warranty forever is the covenant that guarantees title against all claims; it appears only in the full covenant and warranty deed.
glossary.contrast: A covenant against grantor's acts covers only problems the grantor created.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Private recorded rules that run with the land and bind every owner, such as use limits, rental restrictions, and architectural controls.
glossary.deep:
CC&Rs are promises attached to the property, not the person. When you buy, you inherit them. They can limit short-term rentals, ban commercial use, control exterior changes, or require dues.

The label is most common for homeowners associations and planned communities on Long Island or upstate. In NY condos, the same kind of rules sit inside the declaration and bylaws.

NY example: a Suffolk HOA's CC&Rs bar fences over four feet. A buyer who wanted a six-foot fence is stuck with the rule.

On the exam: CC&Rs are private restrictions; zoning is public. Discriminatory CC&Rs (racial covenants) are void.
glossary.contrast: Zoning is government regulation; CC&Rs are private restrictions.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: An escalation that adjusts rent by the percentage change (or a fraction of it) in the Consumer Price Index published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
glossary.deep:
A CPI clause ties rent to general inflation rather than to the building's own costs.

Like a pension with a cost-of-living adjustment: when prices rise, the payment rises.

Base rent $120,000; the New York area CPI rises from 300 to 312, a 4% change. Full CPI raises rent $4,800. A clause using 50% of the change raises it $2,400. Leases may add a floor and a cap.

On the exam: compute the percentage change in the index (points / old index), apply the stated fraction, then multiply by rent.
glossary.contrast: Base year escalations follow actual building costs; CPI follows the general price level.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The Attorney General's Cooperative Policy Statement #1, which lets a sponsor advertise and gauge interest in a new or vacant condo or co-op before filing an offering plan, without taking deposits or reservations.
glossary.deep:
CPS-1 is a permission slip to test demand. The sponsor files an application (fee $750), and once accepted it may advertise for 12 months, extendable. Every ad must carry the AG's legend saying it is not an offering.

The current policy (updated Nov. 5, 2025) is strict: no deposits and no reservations, binding or non-binding, until a plan is accepted for filing. Occupied rental conversions use a separate policy, CPS-11.

NY example: "Now accepting expressions of interest" on a Gowanus sales gallery sign is CPS-1 talk.

On the exam: CPS-1 = gauge interest only.
glossary.contrast: A red herring is the plan under review; CPS-1 happens before or alongside submission and is just market testing.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A shallow space between the ground and the first floor, enclosed by foundation walls, high enough to crawl but not stand.
glossary.deep:
A crawl space raises the house off the ground and gives access to pipes and wires without the cost of a full basement. It must be ventilated or sealed and conditioned, with a vapor barrier over the dirt, or moisture will rot the joists and grow mold.

Analogy: the space under a raised porch. NY example: a Long Island beach cottage on a crawl space shows damp, sagging joists from flooding; the inspector recommends a vapor barrier, drainage, and a check for wood-destroying insects.

On the exam: crawl space equals shallow, needs ventilation and moisture control.
glossary.contrast: Slab-on-grade has no space under the floor at all.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: Entries on a closing statement for amounts a party receives or is credited with.
glossary.deep: A credit goes in a party's favor. The seller is credited with the purchase price and with reimbursement for prepaid taxes or fuel. The buyer is credited with the down payment already paid, the new loan, an assumed mortgage, and amounts the seller owes, such as prepaid rent, security deposits, and unpaid taxes. The buyer's credits reduce cash due at closing. On the exam: the down payment and new loan are buyer credits only; they never appear on the seller's side.
glossary.contrast: Debits are amounts a party owes.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A dead-end street ending in a circular turnaround.
glossary.deep:
A cul-de-sac is a street that ends in a bulb so cars and trucks can turn around. Buyers like them for low traffic. Planners regulate them in subdivision rules: maximum length, minimum turnaround radius so a fire truck can turn, and sometimes a pedestrian connection.

Picture a lollipop: the stick is the street, the candy is the turnaround. NY example: in a Rockland County subdivision, the planning board rejected a long cul-de-sac serving 30 homes because emergency access depended on a single entrance, and required a second connection.

On the exam: cul-de-sacs show up as a subdivision design term and as a traffic pattern the planning board reviews.
glossary.contrast: A loop street connects at both ends; a cul-de-sac has only one way in and out.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Historic legal life estates: dower gave a widow, and curtesy a widower, an interest in the deceased spouse's real property. Both are abolished in New York.
glossary.deep: Under old common law, a widow had dower, a life estate in one third of her husband's real property, and a widower had curtesy. These rights made a spouse's signature necessary on every deed. New York abolished both, replacing them with the elective share: a surviving spouse can claim the greater of $50,000 or one third of the net estate even if the will leaves less. Older textbooks and some exam items still mention dower. On the exam: NY has no dower or curtesy; the elective share protects a surviving spouse.
glossary.contrast: The elective share is NY's modern spousal protection.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A party in the transaction whom the licensee deals with but does not represent. Owed honesty and fair dealing, not loyalty.
glossary.deep:
A customer is the person across the table: you are courteous and truthful, but you are not on their side.

A store clerk must not lie to you about a product, but she is not going to tell you the store would take 20% less.

At the Okafors' open house, a buyer without an agent asks Jordan about the roof. Jordan must answer honestly and reveal known defects, but must not say the Okafors would take less, and anything the buyer reveals about his budget goes to the Okafors.

On the exam: customers are owed honest, fair dealing and disclosure of known material facts. They are not owed confidentiality or advice.
glossary.contrast: Client: full fiduciary duties. Customer: honesty only.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Force that, under the circumstances, is readily capable of causing death or serious physical injury. In NY it is justified only against deadly physical force or certain violent felonies.
glossary.deep:
Deadly force is the most serious level, and the law allows it only against the most serious threats.

You do not bring a weapon to a shoving match.

An attacker at a vacant Yonkers listing pulls a knife. If the agent can safely run out the back door, NY requires retreat before deadly force. If cornered with no safe exit, deadly force may be justified. Using deadly force to stop someone stealing a laptop is not.

On the exam: deadly force answers deadly force (or crimes like robbery, kidnapping, forcible rape), and retreat comes first when it is completely safe.
glossary.contrast: Ordinary physical force is justified against imminent unlawful physical force.
glossary.subject: s13

glossary.def: Entries on a closing statement for amounts a party owes or is charged.
glossary.deep: A debit is a charge against a party. For the buyer, the purchase price is the largest debit, plus closing costs and reimbursements to the seller for prepaid items. For the seller, debits include the commission, transfer taxes, mortgage payoffs, and credits owed to the buyer for unpaid taxes or prepaid rent. Every proration is a debit to one party and an equal credit to the other. On the exam: "who owes it?" That party gets the debit.
glossary.contrast: Credits are amounts a party receives or is credited with.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Net operating income divided by annual debt service; lenders use it to measure how comfortably a property can pay its loan.
glossary.deep:
DCR asks: how many times over does NOI cover the mortgage? At 1.0, NOI pays the loan exactly with nothing left. Below 1.0, the owner must feed the building.

Like a household where take-home pay is 1.3 times the monthly bills: there is a cushion if something goes wrong.

Bushwick: $190,000 / $150,000 = 1.27. Commercial lenders in New York commonly want a cushion around 1.20 to 1.25 or higher and size the loan to meet it.

On the exam: DCR = NOI / debt service. Below 1.0 means NOI does not cover the payments.
glossary.contrast: The cap rate relates NOI to value; DCR relates NOI to debt service.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The total annual mortgage payments, principal and interest, on a property's loans.
glossary.deep:
Debt service is what the owner pays the bank each year. It is the line between NOI and the owner's cash flow.

Like your car payment: it is the cost of how you paid for the car, not what it costs to drive it.

Evelyn borrows $2,000,000 on the Bushwick building with $150,000 of annual payments. In the cash world, the full $150,000 comes out of NOI. In the tax world, only the interest part (about $130,000 in year one) is deductible.

On the exam: debt service is subtracted after NOI. Monthly payments must be multiplied by 12.
glossary.contrast: Operating expenses run the building; debt service pays for how it was financed.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The recorded document that creates a condominium, describing the land, building, units, common elements, each unit's common interest, and the use restrictions.
glossary.deep:
The declaration is the condo's birth certificate. Until it is recorded (in NYC, with the City Register, along with floor plans), the building is just a building with one owner.

It sets each unit's percentage of the common elements, which drives common charges and votes, and usually contains the right of first refusal and key restrictions.

NY example: a Gowanus new development cannot close its first sale until the declaration is recorded and a TCO issues.

On the exam: declaration CREATES the condo. Bylaws RUN it. Do not swap them.
glossary.contrast: Bylaws govern operations; the declaration creates the condo and sets ownership percentages.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A written statement, under oath or affirmation, of the facts when a consumer refuses to sign the agency disclosure acknowledgment. Kept at least 3 years.
glossary.deep:
The law cannot force a consumer to sign. It can force the licensee to prove the form was offered.

Like a process server's affidavit: the person would not take the papers, so you swear to what happened.

A tenant at Sal's showing refuses to sign. Jordan completes a sworn declaration of the refusal, keeps it 3 years, and continues showing.

On the exam: refusal never stops the transaction and never waives the requirement.
glossary.contrast: The signed acknowledgment is the normal record; the declaration replaces it only on refusal.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A private owner's gift of land or an interest in land to the public, accepted by the government; may be by deed or by recorded plat.
glossary.deep: Dedication moves private land into public use. A developer filing a subdivision map that shows streets, sidewalks, and a park is dedicating them by plat (statutory dedication); a landowner deeding a strip to the town for road widening is dedication by deed. The government must accept it, formally or by maintaining the land. After that, the town owns and maintains the street. An Orange County developer dedicating new streets is a typical example. On the exam: voluntary, private to public, requires acceptance.
glossary.contrast: A public grant transfers land from government to a private owner.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The portion of a covered loss the insured pays before the insurer pays, stated as a dollar amount or a percentage of the coverage.
glossary.deep:
The deductible is your share of each loss.

Like a copay at the doctor: you pay the first part, insurance pays the rest.

Leo picks a $1,000 deductible on his HO-6. A pipe bursts and causes $6,000 of damage. He pays $1,000; the insurer pays $5,000. Choosing a $2,500 deductible would lower his premium but raise his share.

On the exam: higher deductible, lower premium. Coastal NY policies may add a separate percentage hurricane deductible.
glossary.contrast: Hurricane deductible: a separate, usually percentage-based deductible for hurricane losses.
glossary.subject: s12

glossary.def: A written instrument by which an owner transfers title to real property to another.
glossary.deep: A deed is the vehicle that carries title from grantor to grantee. To be valid it needs a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, consideration recited, words of conveyance, a legal description, the grantor's signature, and delivery and acceptance. Acknowledgment and recording are not needed for validity between the parties, but they protect the grantee against everyone else. Note the difference: the deed is the document; title is the ownership. A deed signed and left in a drawer, like Grace's mother's, transfers nothing. On the exam: title passes on delivery and acceptance.
glossary.contrast: Title is the ownership itself; the deed is the document that transfers it.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A limit on the use of land written into a deed, binding the grantee and often later owners.
glossary.deep:
A deed restriction is a rule the seller writes into the deed: no commercial use, no building over two stories, no subdividing. Because it is a private agreement recorded in the chain of title, it can bind future owners. Some are written as conditions (breach can cost you the property), most as covenants (breach gets you sued or enjoined).

Analogy: a house rule handed down with the keys. NY example: a Scarsdale lot sold in 1925 with a restriction that only one single-family house may stand on it; a buyer today who wants two homes faces a lawsuit from neighbors who benefit from the restriction.

On the exam: deed restrictions are private controls. If they are stricter than zoning, they govern. Discriminatory restrictions are void.
glossary.contrast: Zoning is a public control enacted by government; a deed restriction is a private control created by a grantor.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Failure to meet a loan obligation, such as missing payments, letting insurance lapse, or not paying property taxes.
glossary.deep:
Default is breaking the deal, and it is not only about payments.

Like breaking a lease by subletting without permission, even though the rent is paid.

A Yonkers owner pays the mortgage on time but stops paying property taxes. That is a default, because unpaid taxes become a lien ahead of the mortgage. After default and required notices, the lender may accelerate and foreclose. For NY home loans, a 90-day pre-foreclosure notice comes first.

On the exam: default triggers acceleration; failing to pay taxes or insurance is default too.
glossary.contrast: Delinquency is being late; default is the breach that allows the lender's remedies.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Needed repairs or replacements that have been postponed.
glossary.deep:
Deferred maintenance is the bill that keeps growing. A cracked parapet, a worn roof, rotting sills: each month of delay usually raises the cost and lowers the property's value. Appraisers treat it as curable physical deterioration; in NYC it often shows up as HPD or DOB violations.

Like ignoring a toothache until it becomes a root canal.

Sal's 26-year-old weeping boiler is deferred maintenance waiting to become a January emergency.

On the exam: deferred = postponed needed work, reduces value.
glossary.contrast: Preventive maintenance is done on schedule to avoid this.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: A court judgment for the amount still owed after a foreclosure sale brings less than the debt.
glossary.deep:
If the house does not cover the debt, the note still makes the borrower personally liable for the gap.

Like a car repossessed and auctioned for less than the loan; you still owe the difference.

NY rules (RPAPL 1371): the lender must move within 90 days after the sale, and the deficiency is the debt minus the higher of the sale price or the court-determined fair market value. Debt $460,000, sale $340,000, FMV $390,000: deficiency $70,000.

On the exam: 90 days and the fair market value credit.
glossary.contrast: A buyer who took subject to a mortgage is not personally liable for a deficiency.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The grantor's handing over of a deed with intent to transfer title now, and the grantee's acceptance of it; title passes at this moment.
glossary.deep: Signing a deed does not transfer anything; delivering it does. Delivery requires the grantor's intent to pass title immediately, shown by handing it to the grantee or to an agent for the grantee, such as at a closing. Acceptance is usually presumed when the transfer benefits the grantee. A deed kept in the grantor's own drawer until death was never delivered, so it fails. On the exam: "When does title pass?" Answer: on delivery and acceptance, not on signing, acknowledgment, or recording.
glossary.contrast: Recording gives notice to third parties but does not itself transfer title.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The clause in a lease by which the landlord actually leases (demises) the premises to the tenant.
glossary.deep:
To "demise" means to lease. The demising clause is the sentence that does the work: "Landlord hereby leases to Tenant the demised premises, Apartment 3R..."

Like the words "I now pronounce you" at a wedding: everything else is detail, this is the act.

In a Midtown office lease the demising clause identifies the floor and suite and conveys possession for the term. Without it there is no grant of a leasehold.

On the exam: "the demised premises" simply means the leased space.
glossary.contrast: A habendum clause in a deed defines the estate granted; the demising clause grants the lease.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The study of population characteristics such as size, age, income, household size, and growth trends.
glossary.deep:
Demography is planning's crystal ball. How many people live here, how old are they, how big are households, and how fast is the area growing? Those answers drive how much housing, how many classrooms, and what kind of zoning a town needs.

Analogy: a restaurant counting reservations before ordering food. NY example: a Westchester village sees its population aging and household size shrinking, so its comprehensive plan proposes allowing accessory apartments and smaller units near the train. Data often come from census tracts.

On the exam: demography is a planning input, not a legal control. A question may ask what the planning board studies when preparing a master plan.
glossary.contrast: Topography studies the land's shape; demography studies the people.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The NY agency that regulates banks, insurers, mortgage brokers, mortgage bankers, and loan originators.
glossary.deep:
The financial regulator, separate from the Department of State.

Think of two gatekeepers: DOS licenses people who sell real estate; DFS licenses people who finance it.

A consumer with a complaint about a mortgage broker's fees files with DFS, not DOS. DFS also enforces Part 38 of its regulations, which covers mortgage broker disclosures, including the pre-application fee agreement and the dual agency disclosure.

On the exam: mortgage broker or banker question, the answer is DFS.
glossary.contrast: DOS licenses real estate brokers and salespersons.
glossary.subject: s18

glossary.def: The portion of a property's cost basis that can be depreciated: total basis minus land value.
glossary.deep:
Land never wears out, so it is never depreciated. Depreciable basis is price plus acquisition costs plus capital improvements, minus land. Land value usually comes from the assessor's land-to-total ratio or an appraisal.

Think of a pizza: the box (land) is not eaten; only the pizza (building) gets sliced up.

Sal's $1,100,000 purchase with 30% land: $770,000 depreciable basis.

On the exam: the classic mistake is depreciating the full purchase price. Remove land.
glossary.contrast: Adjusted basis is the full tax basis after improvements and depreciation, land included.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: In appraisal, any loss in value from the cost new of an improvement, caused by physical deterioration, functional obsolescence, or external obsolescence.
glossary.deep:
Appraisal depreciation is the gap between what a building would cost new and what it is worth now.

A new phone loses value through scratches (physical), being outdated (functional), and a carrier dropping support (external).

For the firehouse: tired roof (physical, curable), one bathroom for a 200-seat hall (functional), a new bus depot across the street (external, incurable).

On the exam: three types; external is always incurable; land is never depreciated. Do not confuse with tax depreciation (27.5 or 39 years), which is an accounting deduction.
glossary.contrast: Tax depreciation is a cost recovery deduction for income tax, not a loss in market value.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: A salesperson or associate broker appointed, with written consent, to represent one party when the broker represents both parties in the same transaction.
glossary.deep:
A designated agent is the firm's way of giving each side its own advocate inside a dual agency.

Like a law firm assigning separate attorneys to two clients, with the managing partner still overseeing both.

Diane assigns Jordan to Leo and Marcus to the Okafors. Jordan can advise Leo on price; Marcus can advise the Okafors. Diane, the broker, remains a dual agent and supervises both.

On the exam: two different licensees, written consent from both parties, broker still a dual agent, and no undivided loyalty.
glossary.contrast: Single licensee dual agency has one person working both sides; designated agency uses two.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A gift of real property by will.
glossary.deep: Devise is the specific word for leaving real estate in a will: "I devise my house at 412 Macon Street to my nephew Tunde." Gifts of personal property are bequests or legacies. The person receiving the devise is the devisee. The word can be a verb (the testator devises) or a noun (a devise). On the exam: devise = real property by will; bequest = personal property by will. Heirs who receive without a will take by descent.
glossary.contrast: A bequest is a gift of personal property by will.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The person who receives real property under a will.
glossary.deep: The devisee is the recipient of a devise. If Mr. Haddad's will had left his house outright to Sami, Sami would be the devisee. A devisee receives title through the executor after probate. A devisee is different from an heir: an heir inherits by law when there is no will, while a devisee inherits by the will's terms. On the exam: devisee = real property under a will; legatee = personal property under a will; heir = by intestate descent.
glossary.contrast: An heir receives property by intestate succession.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A hard cost of construction: labor and materials that go into the building.
glossary.deep:
Direct costs are the stuff and the sweat: brick, lumber, concrete, and the wages of the people installing them.

If you could photograph it on the job site, or it is a paycheck for building it, it is direct.

Building a two-family in Canarsie: framing lumber, drywall, the plumber's labor, and the boiler itself are direct costs.

On the exam: "hard costs" equals direct costs. Questions usually list four costs and ask which one is direct; pick the labor or materials item.
glossary.contrast: Indirect costs are soft costs like fees, financing, and permits.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: An electricity arrangement in which the tenant has its own utility meter and account and pays the utility company directly.
glossary.deep:
Direct metering cuts the landlord out of the electric bill entirely.

Like having your own phone plan instead of being on a family plan.

A bakery in Sal's Astoria storefront with two big ovens opens its own Con Edison account and pays for every kilowatt it uses. The landlord carries no usage risk.

On the exam: direct meter = tenant pays the utility directly.
glossary.contrast: With a submeter the landlord bills the tenant; with rent inclusion electricity is in the rent.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A lease clause requiring the tenant to pay its proportionate share of increases in the building's actual operating expenses over a base year.
glossary.deep:
This clause tracks real costs: cleaning, payroll, fuel, insurance, repairs and the like. If they rise, the tenant pays its share of the increase.

Like splitting the actual utility bill increase with roommates instead of guessing.

Leo's building: operating expenses rose from $1,500,000 to $1,620,000; his 5% share is $6,000. Tenant brokers negotiate exclusions (capital items, the landlord's debt service, leasing commissions) and audit rights.

On the exam: share x actual increase. It replaced the porter's wage formula in most modern NYC leases.
glossary.contrast: The porter's wage formula uses a wage proxy instead of actual costs.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a record of such an impairment, or being regarded as having one. The 1988 statute used the word handicap.
glossary.deep:
It is broad: mobility, vision, hearing, HIV, cancer, depression, PTSD, and people in recovery from addiction. It excludes current illegal drug use. A landlord may also refuse someone who would be a direct threat to others' safety, based on evidence, not stereotype.

Example: a tenant on 5th floor of a Washington Heights walk-up asks to switch to a vacant ground floor unit because of a heart condition. That is a reasonable accommodation request tied to a disability.

On the exam: know what is NOT covered (current illegal drug users) and the difference between accommodations (rules) and modifications (physical changes).
glossary.contrast: The ADA uses the same definition but covers public accommodations; the FHA covers dwellings.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: The duty to tell the client every material fact the agent knows or learns that could affect the client's decisions.
glossary.deep:
If it matters to the client's decision, the client hears it.

Like a doctor who must tell you about every test result, not just the good ones.

A buyer tells Jordan at an open house he would go to $1.15M. Jordan represents the seller, so Jordan must tell the seller. If the buyer is Jordan's cousin, that must be disclosed too.

On the exam: duty of disclosure runs to the client. Separately, agents must disclose known material property defects to customers. Do not mix up the two.
glossary.contrast: Confidentiality keeps the client's secrets in; disclosure pushes material facts to the client.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Any ad, statement, or notice about housing that indicates a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class, including through ad targeting.
glossary.deep:
The rule is simple: describe the property, not the people. "2BR near the Q, laundry in building" is fine. "Perfect for a young professional," "adults only," "no programs," "Christian household," and "English speakers only" are not.

It applies to everyone, even owners otherwise exempt from the FHA, and in New York the two-family exemption does not cover ads. Social media posts and paid targeting count. Excluding people by age or parent interests in ad settings is discriminatory even if the text is neutral.

On the exam: no exemption ever covers a discriminatory ad.
glossary.contrast: Puffing ("stunning views") is sales talk about the property, not about who should live there.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: Discrimination that results from a facially neutral policy that has an unjustified, disproportionate adverse effect on a protected class.
glossary.deep:
No one has to intend to discriminate. If a rule looks neutral but hits one group much harder, and the provider cannot show it is necessary for a legitimate reason or that there is no less harmful alternative, it can be illegal. The Supreme Court confirmed this theory under the FHA in 2015 (Texas Department of Housing v. Inclusive Communities).

Example: a blanket "no one with any criminal record, ever" rule. NYC's Fair Chance for Housing Law also restricts this directly.

On the exam: "applies to everyone" is not a complete defense. Look for neutral rules with discriminatory effects.
glossary.contrast: Disparate treatment is intentional, different treatment of individuals.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A pre-agreed, innocent-sounding phrase an agent uses on the phone to signal a coworker to call police and send help.
glossary.deep:
It is a way to call for help without tipping off the person standing next to you.

Like a secret handshake, but for emergencies.

At a Ditmas Park open house, Jordan calls the office: "Can you bring me the red file?" Marcus hears it, calls 911, and heads to the address on the showing log.

On the exam: a distress code is part of a safety policy and only works if everyone in the office knows it and the showing location is logged.
glossary.contrast: An alarm code arms or disarms a security system.
glossary.subject: s13

glossary.def: An equitable rule that bars a claim when the person waited unreasonably long to assert a right and the delay harmed the other side.
glossary.deep:
Laches is "you snooze, you lose" in legal form. Courts will not help someone who sat on a right for years while the other party relied on the silence and spent money.

Analogy: you watch a neighbor build a deck across your covenant line, say nothing for six years, then demand it come down. The court asks why you waited. NY example: a Garden City association ignored a front-yard fence violation for a decade while the owner landscaped around it; when it finally sued, the court refused an injunction because of laches. Laches also applies to Article 78 challenges brought late.

On the exam: it pairs with deed restrictions and covenants. Delay plus prejudice equals laches.
glossary.contrast: A statute of limitations is a fixed deadline set by law; laches is a flexible, fairness-based bar that depends on delay and harm.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The parcel that benefits from an easement appurtenant.
glossary.deep: The dominant tenement is the land that gets the advantage. Its owner may use the servient land for the easement's purpose. Think of it as the parcel that "dominates" the neighbor's land in that limited way. When the dominant parcel is sold, the easement goes with it as an appurtenance. A lot that reaches the street only by a driveway over the next lot is the dominant tenement. On the exam: only easements appurtenant have a dominant tenement. Easements in gross have none.
glossary.contrast: The servient tenement carries the burden.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The buyer's cash paid toward the price. In NY contract practice, the deposit (customarily 10% downstate) paid at contract signing and held in escrow.
glossary.deep:
Two meanings. At contract: the deposit that secures the deal. In financing: the part of the price not borrowed.

Like the cash you put down on a car before the loan covers the rest.

The Okafors' buyer wires $170,000 (10% of $1.7M) to Priya's escrow account at contract. It counts toward the buyer's total equity at closing. If the buyer defaults, the seller typically keeps it as liquidated damages. Escrow agents must hold it in a separate account and release it only by the contract's terms.

On the exam: 10% downstate, held by the seller's attorney.
glossary.contrast: Earnest money is often a smaller earlier deposit.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: One brokerage representing both buyer and seller (or landlord and tenant) in the same transaction. Legal in NY only with informed written consent of both.
glossary.deep:
Dual agency puts one firm on both sides of the table.

Like one referee coaching both teams: possible only if both teams agree to lose their own coach's full effort.

Leo, Hudson & Hart's buyer client, wants the Okafors' listing, also Hudson & Hart's. Both must sign written consent. Neither gets undivided loyalty, and the firm cannot tell either side the other's bottom line.

On the exam: in-house sales create it. Two salespersons in one firm do not avoid it. Consent must be written and come from both.
glossary.contrast: Designated sales agents are a form of dual agency, not an escape from it.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Holding more than one license association at once, such as being associated with two brokers or holding a broker license while associated with another broker, with the written knowledge of each broker.
glossary.deep:
New York lets a licensee wear two hats as long as everyone with supervisory responsibility knows. A salesperson might work residential for one firm and commercial for another; a broker might run her own small firm and also be an associate broker at a larger one.

Think of a nurse who works shifts at two hospitals: allowed, but each hospital must know.

Diane's associate broker in Bay Ridge also owns a tiny commercial brokerage. Both brokers sign off with DOS, and each deal runs through one firm only.

On the exam: dual licensure is allowed with each broker's consent; commission on any deal still flows only through the broker on that deal.
glossary.contrast: Dual agency is representing both buyer and seller in one deal, a separate concept.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: The reasonable investigation a buyer makes before purchase; in environmental law, "all appropriate inquiries" needed for liability defenses.
glossary.deep:
Due diligence is doing your homework before you buy. Generally it covers title, survey, zoning, inspections and leases. Environmentally, it means the all appropriate inquiries standard: a Phase I meeting EPA's rule, done within the required time before closing. Without it, a buyer generally cannot claim the innocent landowner or bona fide prospective purchaser defenses under CERCLA.

Analogy: reading the car's history report before you buy it. NY example: Evelyn buys a former Yonkers gas station after a Phase I and Phase II, negotiates a price cut for remediation, and keeps her liability defenses.

On the exam: due diligence equals the buyer's investigation; for CERCLA it means appropriate inquiry before purchase.
glossary.contrast: Caveat emptor says the buyer bears the risk; due diligence is how the buyer manages that risk.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: Another name for the alienation clause: the loan becomes due if the property is sold or transferred.
glossary.deep:
Sell the house, pay off the loan.

Like a company car you must return when you leave the job.

A seller hopes to sell "subject to" a cheap old loan.
