glossary.deep: Every NY conveyance over $500 owes the state transfer tax, normally paid by the grantor. The rate is $2 for each $500 or fraction of $500, which is 0.4%. A $735,000 sale owes $2,940. In NYC the rate is 0.65% for residential sales of $3 million or more and other property of $2 million or more. It applies to co-op transfers too, and it is reported on form TP-584. If the seller fails to pay, the buyer becomes liable. On the exam: seller pays, $2 per $500, round fractions up.
glossary.contrast: The mansion tax is paid by the buyer.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The duty to follow the client's lawful instructions.
glossary.deep:
Do what the client asks, as long as it is legal.

Like a contractor building to the homeowner's plans, unless the plans violate code.

The Okafors tell Jordan: no showings before 10 a.m., and present every offer in writing. Jordan complies. But if they said "don't show to buyers with Section 8 vouchers" or "don't mention the roof leak," Jordan must refuse and, if they insist, withdraw.

On the exam: obedience never covers unlawful instructions. A discriminatory or deceptive instruction is the classic trap.
glossary.contrast: Loyalty is about putting the client first; obedience is about following their instructions.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The disclosure document a sponsor files with the Attorney General describing the condo or co-op offering: the property, sponsor, budget, prices, governing documents, and risks.
glossary.deep:
The offering plan (also called the offering statement or prospectus, and nicknamed the black book once accepted) is the buyer's encyclopedia. It contains special risks, the first year budget, projected taxes, floor plans, unit prices, the declaration and bylaws or proprietary lease, and the sponsor's obligations.

It goes through stages: optional CPS-1 market testing, red herring (preliminary), accepted for filing, declared effective, then amendments.

NY example: Priya finds in the Gowanus plan that taxes assume an abatement that phases out over years.

On the exam: no contracts or deposits until the plan is accepted for filing.
glossary.contrast: A red herring is the preliminary, not-yet-accepted version.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A commercial lease for office space, typically quoted per rentable square foot, with base year escalations, tenant improvement allowances and separately handled electricity.
glossary.deep:
An office lease is built around RSF, a base year and escalations.

Think of it as a long relationship with a contract for every chore: who pays for rising taxes, who cleans, who pays for electricity, what the landlord builds for you.

A typical Manhattan office lease: 10 years, rent per RSF, modified gross with tax and operating escalations over a base year, a tenant improvement allowance, a few months of free rent, submetered electricity, and possibly a good guy guarantee.

On the exam: connect office leases to rentable square footage, loss factors and escalations.
glossary.contrast: A retail lease focuses on use, sales and storefront terms, often with percentage rent and CAM.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A brokerage's written rules for agent safety and incident handling: ID checks, showing logs, distress codes, buddy rules, key and data security, and incident reporting.
glossary.deep:
It turns good habits into the office standard, so nobody has to improvise when something feels wrong.

Like a fire drill plan. You do not invent the exit route during the fire.

Hudson & Hart's policy: meet new buyers at the office with photo ID first, log every showing on the shared calendar, use "the red file" as the distress code, never host vacant or after-dark showings alone, and file a written incident report the same day.

On the exam: the syllabus puts establishing and implementing an office policy under risk reduction, and treats it as the broker's responsibility.
glossary.contrast: Standardized operating procedures (RPL 442-h) govern how brokers treat prospective homebuyers, not safety.
glossary.subject: s13

glossary.def: A map adopted by a municipality showing existing and proposed streets, parks, and drainage systems; building in a mapped street bed is generally barred.
glossary.deep:
The official map turns parts of the master plan into specific lines. If the town plans to extend a road through a parcel in ten years, the official map shows it, and the owner generally cannot get a permit to build in that bed without relief.

Analogy: pencil marks on the town's blueprint that everyone must respect. NY example: Staten Island has many mapped but unbuilt streets on the City Map; buyers of lots in the South Shore sometimes discover part of their land is a mapped street and cannot be built on.

On the exam: know that the official map shows streets and parks and that it is a planning tool distinct from the zoning map, which shows districts.
glossary.contrast: The zoning map shows use districts; the official map shows streets, parks, and drainage.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A non-exclusive listing given to any number of brokers; only the broker who procures the buyer is paid, and the owner owes nothing if the owner sells.
glossary.deep:
An open listing is a race. Whoever brings the buyer gets paid.

Like posting a reward for a lost dog: anyone can find it, only the finder collects.

Evelyn gives open listings on a small Long Island City warehouse to four firms. The broker who is the procuring cause gets the fee; if Evelyn sells to her tenant herself, nobody does.

On the exam: non-exclusive, pays the procuring cause only, owner may sell freely.
glossary.contrast: Exclusive agency names one broker; open listing names many.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: New York law requiring public bodies, including town boards, planning boards and ZBAs, to meet in public with advance notice and to keep minutes.
glossary.deep:
The Open Meetings Law (Public Officers Law Article 7) keeps local government decisions in daylight. Meetings of a quorum to conduct public business must be open, noticed in advance (at least 72 hours for meetings scheduled a week or more ahead), and recorded in minutes. Executive (closed) sessions are allowed only for narrow topics like litigation or personnel, and votes on applications happen publicly.

Analogy: the board deliberates behind glass, not behind a door. NY example: a court voided a village ZBA approval after members discussed and decided the application in a private session.

On the exam: know "Sunshine Law," public notice, minutes, and that the public observes but does not vote.
glossary.contrast: The Freedom of Information Law (FOIL) gives access to government records; the Open Meetings Law gives access to meetings.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A building permit for work that was never finished, inspected and signed off; it shows as open in the building department's records.
glossary.deep:
An open permit is an unfinished conversation with the building department. The owner pulled a permit, but the final inspection never happened or the paperwork was never closed. Title companies and buyers' attorneys flag them because the work may not meet code and the CO may not reflect it. Resolving one can mean scheduling inspections, opening walls, or hiring an expediter.

Analogy: a library book you checked out years ago and never returned. NY example: a Staten Island seller discovers an open 2012 permit for a bathroom renovation and closes it with a final inspection before the buyer's lender will proceed.

On the exam: open permits are resolved with the building department; check them before listing.
glossary.contrast: Unpermitted work never had a permit at all; an open permit had one that was never closed.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: A mortgage that lets the borrower obtain additional advances later, up to a set limit, secured by the same mortgage.
glossary.deep:
Borrow again without a new mortgage.

Like a credit card with a limit that frees up as you pay down.

An owner in Albany paid her $200,000 loan down to $150,000. Under an open-end mortgage she can borrow $40,000 more for a new roof without new closing documents, up to the original limit. HELOCs work on the same principle.

On the exam: open-end = future advances under the same mortgage.
glossary.contrast: A blanket mortgage covers more parcels; an open-end mortgage covers more money.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A one-year projection of a property's income and day-to-day operating expenses.
glossary.deep:
The operating budget is the annual game plan: expected rents, vacancy allowance, and recurring costs like taxes, insurance, fuel, water, repairs, payroll, and the management fee. Actual results are compared against it monthly.

Like a household's yearly budget: what comes in, what goes out, month to month.

Sal's operating budget projects $146,490 of effective gross income and $87,325 of expenses, for NOI of $59,165.

On the exam: operating budget = one year, day-to-day items. Big replacements go in the capital reserve budget.
glossary.contrast: A capital reserve budget funds long-term replacements.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: The recurring costs of running a property: real estate taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs, payroll, management, supplies and reserves.
glossary.deep:
Operating expenses keep the building running day to day. Some are fixed (taxes, insurance: they do not change with occupancy) and some are variable (utilities, repairs, supplies).

Think of what it costs to run a household: property tax, insurance, heat, the plumber. The mortgage is separate: that is how you financed the house, not what it costs to run.

In a New York walk-up, real estate taxes are often the biggest single expense, followed by fuel, water and sewer, insurance and repairs.

On the exam: operating expenses never include debt service, depreciation, income taxes or capital improvements.
glossary.contrast: Capital expenditures replace or improve major components and are not operating expenses.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A contract in which an owner (optionor), for consideration, gives another (optionee) the right to buy or lease property at a set price within a set time.
glossary.deep:
The optionee buys time and a locked price. Only the owner is bound.

Like paying a deposit to hold a concert ticket at today's price until Friday.

A developer pays an owner in Long Island City $50,000 for a 1-year option to buy at $8 million while seeking zoning approval. If approval comes, it exercises; if not, it walks away and the owner keeps the $50,000. A lease with an option to buy lets a tenant lock a future purchase price. An option should be in writing.

On the exam: an option is unilateral until exercised; then it becomes a bilateral contract of sale.
glossary.contrast: A right of first refusal has no set price; it only lets the holder match an offer.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A lease clause giving the tenant the right to extend the lease for another term on stated conditions.
glossary.deep:
The tenant can choose to stay, but the landlord must honor the choice if the tenant follows the clause.

Like a magazine subscription that lets you lock in another year at a known price.

A Williamsburg restaurant signs a 10-year lease with two 5-year renewal options at 3% increases, exercisable by written notice 12 months before expiration. Miss the notice date and the right may be lost. Commercial tenants have no statutory right to renew, so they bargain for this.

On the exam: commercial renewal rights come only from the lease; rent-stabilized tenants get renewal by law.
glossary.contrast: An option to buy gives a right to purchase, not to extend.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A shopping center of manufacturers' and brand-name discount stores, usually located on cheaper land away from city centers.
glossary.deep:
Outlet centers sell brand names at a discount, and shoppers drive to them for the deal.

Think of it as the brands' clearance aisle, built as a village and placed off a highway exit.

Woodbury Common Premium Outlets in Central Valley, an hour north of the city, draws tour buses from Manhattan. Tanger Outlets in Riverhead serves the East End of Long Island. Outlet centers rarely have traditional department store anchors; the brands themselves are the draw.

On the exam: discount brand stores, often far from downtowns.
glossary.contrast: A regional mall sells at full price and is anchored by department stores.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: New York's exemption from parts of the Human Rights Law for the rental of a unit in a two-family house where the owner lives in the other unit.
glossary.deep:
New York took the federal four-unit Mrs. Murphy idea and cut it to two units. Even then it covers only the rental decision itself, not discriminatory advertising, and never race (the 1866 Act).

Example: Sal's cousin owns and lives in a Bay Ridge two-family. He has some latitude choosing a tenant for the other floor. Sal, with six units, has none. In NYC, the city exemption also requires that the unit not be publicly advertised or listed, so once it hits StreetEasy or a broker, it is gone.

On the exam: "NY owner-occupied exemption" = two-family only. A choice saying four units is the federal rule.
glossary.contrast: The federal Mrs. Murphy exemption covers owner-occupied buildings of up to four units.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A mortgage that covers real property plus personal property such as appliances or furniture.
glossary.deep:
House and contents in one loan.

Like a car loan that also finances the roof rack and floor mats.

A new condo building in Long Island City sells furnished units; the lender's package mortgage covers the unit plus the appliances and furniture included in the price. If the borrower defaults, the lender's security includes those items.

On the exam: package = real plus personal property.
glossary.contrast: A blanket mortgage covers several parcels of real property.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A single policy combining several coverages, such as a homeowners policy that bundles property, liability, and medical payments.
glossary.deep:
A package is the combo meal of insurance: several items, one price, usually cheaper than ordering separately.

Leo's HO-6 condo policy includes coverage for his unit interior and belongings, loss of use if he must move out during repairs, personal liability, and guest medical payments, all in one contract.

Commercial owners buy packages too, like a business owner's policy (BOP) that bundles property and general liability.

On the exam: every HO form is a package policy. A policy for one peril or one line only is monoline.
glossary.contrast: Monoline policy: a single line of coverage.
glossary.subject: s12

glossary.def: A specific, separately owned and described piece of land.
glossary.deep: A parcel is one identifiable piece of land with its own boundaries and legal description. It is what a deed conveys, what a survey measures, and what the tax assessor assigns a number to. In NYC each parcel has a borough, block, and lot number (BBL); a condo unit gets its own lot. One owner can hold several parcels, and one parcel can be split into several by subdivision. On the exam: a parcel is a single tract of land; it is the unit described by metes and bounds or lot and block.
glossary.contrast: A lot is a parcel shown on a recorded subdivision map.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A court action by a co-owner to divide jointly owned property, either physically or by ordering a sale and splitting the proceeds.
glossary.deep: Partition is the exit door for co-owners who cannot agree. Any tenant in common or joint tenant can sue in NY Supreme Court. If the land can be fairly divided, the court splits it (partition in kind); otherwise, as with most NYC houses and apartments, a referee sells it and the money is divided by ownership share. Tenants by the entirety cannot seek partition while married. If Leo and Ana fall out over their Ridgewood house, either can force a partition sale. On the exam: partition ends a tenancy in common or joint tenancy, never a tenancy by the entirety during the marriage.
glossary.contrast: Quiet title resolves competing ownership claims; partition divides undisputed co-ownership.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A single wall on the boundary line shared by two adjoining buildings, each owner owning his half with a cross-easement for support in the other.
glossary.deep: Rowhouses in Brooklyn and Manhattan sit side by side sharing walls. The boundary usually runs through the middle of the wall. Each owner owns their side and has an easement for support in the neighbor's half, so neither can remove or weaken it, and both share responsibility for maintenance. Renovations that cut into a party wall need the neighbor's cooperation and often an engineer. If the buildings are destroyed, the easement may end. On the exam: shared wall, cross-easements, neither owner may harm it.
glossary.contrast: An encroachment is a structure illegally on a neighbor's land; a party wall is lawfully shared.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Income from rental activities or businesses in which the taxpayer does not materially participate.
glossary.deep:
Rental real estate is passive by default. Passive losses offset only passive income, except that active-participation landlords may use up to $25,000 of rental losses against other income, phasing out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified AGI. Suspended losses are freed up when the property is sold. Qualifying real estate professionals can treat rentals as non-passive.

Like store credit: passive losses can only be spent at the passive store, with a small exception.

Leo rents out a Sunnyside condo and shows a $9,000 paper loss. With $135,000 MAGI, part of his $25,000 allowance has phased out.

On the exam: rental = passive; $25,000 allowance; $100k to $150k phase-out.
glossary.contrast: Portfolio income (dividends, interest) is not passive, even though you do no work for it.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A limit on how much an ARM's monthly payment can rise at an adjustment, regardless of the rate change.
glossary.deep:
It protects the monthly budget, but not the balance.

Like a credit card minimum payment that stays small while interest keeps piling up.

An ARM payment of $2,000 has a 7.5% payment cap, so it can rise to at most $2,150 this year. If the new rate actually requires $2,300 to cover interest, the $150 shortfall is added to the loan balance. That is negative amortization.

On the exam: payment cap is the feature linked to negative amortization.
glossary.contrast: A rate cap limits the interest rate itself.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Industrial chemicals once used in electrical transformers, capacitors, fluorescent light ballasts and some caulks; banned in 1979 and persistent in the environment.
glossary.deep:
PCBs were valued because they do not burn and insulate electricity. They also do not break down, accumulate in fish and people, and are a probable human carcinogen. Congress banned their manufacture under TSCA in 1979. They remain in old transformers, pre-1979 fluorescent ballasts, and caulk in some older schools and buildings.

Analogy: a chemical that never leaves the party. NY example: General Electric discharged PCBs into the Hudson River for decades, creating a 200-mile Superfund site dredged from 2009 to 2015. Fish advisories persist.

On the exam: PCBs equal transformers and ballasts. Remediation means testing, removal and licensed disposal.
glossary.contrast: CFCs harm the ozone layer; PCBs are toxic contaminants in soil, water and equipment.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A retail lease with a base (minimum) rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales above a stated breakpoint.
glossary.deep:
In a percentage lease, the landlord shares in the tenant's success. Base rent is guaranteed; extra rent comes only when sales are strong.

Like a band paid a flat fee plus a cut of ticket sales above a certain number.

Steinway Street bakery: $72,000 base plus 6% of sales over $1,200,000. With $1,500,000 in sales, overage rent is $18,000 and total rent $90,000. With $1,000,000 in sales, rent is just the $72,000 base.

On the exam: percentage rent applies only above the breakpoint, and base rent is never reduced.
glossary.contrast: A graduated lease raises rent on a schedule; a percentage lease raises it with sales.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: How fast water soaks into the soil, measured to decide whether and how a septic absorption field can be built.
glossary.deep:
A perc test digs holes, fills them with water, and times how fast the level drops. Soil that drains too slowly (heavy clay) leaves sewage on the surface; soil that drains too fast (coarse gravel) lets it reach groundwater untreated. The result sets the field's size or rules the lot out for a conventional system.

Analogy: testing a sponge before you trust it with a spill. NY example: a buyer of a vacant Columbia County lot makes the contract contingent on a passing perc test and county health department approval, because without them the lot may be unbuildable.

On the exam: perc test equals septic suitability.
glossary.contrast: A water table test measures groundwater depth; a perc test measures absorption speed.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The total distance around a shape, found by adding the lengths of all sides.
glossary.deep:
Perimeter is the walk around the edge.

If you laid a garden hose along every lot line, its length would be the perimeter.

A 25 x 100 Brooklyn lot has a perimeter of 250 feet. Fencing it at $40 a foot costs $10,000. Its area, 2,500 sq ft, is a different measure entirely.

On the exam: fencing, molding, and baseboards are perimeter problems. Carpet, sod, and land price are area problems.
glossary.contrast: Area: the surface inside the edges, in square units.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: A leasehold that renews automatically for successive periods, such as month to month, until proper notice is given.
glossary.deep: A periodic tenancy has no final end date. It rolls over each period (week, month, year) until the landlord or tenant gives proper notice. It often arises when a landlord accepts rent from a tenant after a lease expires. In New York, residential landlords must give 30, 60, or 90 days' notice to end a tenancy or raise rent 5% or more, depending on how long the tenant has lived there. On the exam: automatic renewal and notice to end are the hallmarks. Holdover plus accepted rent typically creates month to month.
glossary.contrast: An estate for years ends automatically on a set date.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A tenancy that renews automatically for successive periods, such as month to month, until one party gives proper notice.
glossary.deep:
It has a rhythm but no end date. Each period rolls into the next until someone stops it.

Like a streaming subscription: it keeps billing until you cancel.

In NY, a holdover whose rent the landlord accepts becomes month-to-month by statute. To end a NY residential tenancy or raise rent 5% or more, notice runs 30, 60, or 90 days depending on how long the tenant has been there.

On the exam: "continues until notice is given" equals periodic. Watch for questions that pair holdover plus rent acceptance with a month-to-month result.
glossary.contrast: An estate at will has no regular period at all; a periodic estate renews by a set period.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Everything that is not real property: movable items not permanently attached to land, also called personalty or chattels.
glossary.deep: Personal property is anything you can pick up and take with you: furniture, cars, a window AC unit, a painting on a nail. It also includes intangible things like co-op shares and a tenant's leasehold. A useful test is whether you could move it without damaging the building. When a seller includes a washer and dryer in a sale, attorneys often list them in the contract or a bill of sale because they are personal property and would not pass by deed alone. On the exam: emblements, trade fixtures, leaseholds, and co-op shares are all personal property.
glossary.contrast: A fixture started as personal property but became real property by attachment.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A fake email, text, or website that imitates a trusted source to trick someone into revealing passwords or financial information or installing malware.
glossary.deep:
Phishing is a con delivered by email.

A fisherman dangles a lure; the victim bites on a link that looks real.

Jordan gets "DocuSign: Closing documents ready, log in to review." The link goes to a fake login page. If Jordan types the email password, the criminal can read every closing thread and send fake wiring instructions to clients.

On the exam: the defense is not clicking, going directly to the real site, and using multi-factor authentication.
glossary.contrast: Wire fraud is often the payoff of a successful phishing attack.
glossary.subject: s13

glossary.def: Loss in value from wear and tear, age, weather, or neglect. It may be curable or incurable.
glossary.deep:
This is the building getting old.

Like tires wearing down: replace them and the problem is solved (curable), but a bent frame may not be worth fixing (incurable).

A Flatbush house with a 25-year-old roof and peeling paint has curable physical deterioration. A sagging foundation that would cost more to fix than it adds is incurable.

On the exam: "curable" means the cost to fix is less than or equal to the value it adds. Physical deterioration can be either.
glossary.contrast: Functional obsolescence is a design flaw, not wear.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: The slope of a roof, expressed as inches of rise per 12 inches of horizontal run (for example, 6 in 12).
glossary.deep:
Pitch tells you how steep the roof is. A 4/12 roof rises 4 inches for every foot across; 12/12 is a 45 degree angle. Steeper roofs shed snow and water better and last longer; low-slope and flat roofs need membranes instead of shingles.

Analogy: the grade of a hill. NY example: Adirondack homes often have steep pitches to shed heavy snow, while NYC row houses have nearly flat roofs with tar or membrane roofing and roof drains.

On the exam: pitch is rise over run.
glossary.contrast: Span is the horizontal width covered; pitch is the slope.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: Principal, interest, taxes, and insurance: the typical monthly housing payment.
glossary.deep:
The full monthly bite, not just the loan. Lenders collect taxes and insurance monthly into escrow and pay those bills.

Like a phone bill that bundles the device payment with service and fees.

Leo's principal and interest is $3,792. Taxes run $7,200 a year ($600 a month) and insurance $1,200 ($100 a month). PITI = $4,492. In a condo or co-op, lenders add common charges or maintenance when computing ratios.

On the exam: PITI is the numerator of the front-end ratio. Divide annual taxes and insurance by 12.
glossary.contrast: P and I alone is the loan payment; PITI adds escrow items.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A large tract planned and approved as a single project, often mixing housing types and uses, with flexible lot rules and shared open space.
glossary.deep:
A PUD lets a developer design a whole community at once instead of lot by lot. The town approves the overall plan: so many townhouses, so many single-family homes, maybe a small retail center, plus parks and trails. Standard setback and lot size rules are relaxed in exchange for a better overall layout.

Analogy: a custom suit instead of buying separate pieces off the rack. NY example: a PUD in Saratoga County combines 200 homes, a village green, and a few shops on a former golf course, with a homeowners association maintaining the common land.

On the exam: PUD equals one integrated plan, mixed uses, density flexibility, common areas. Approved through the planning board and town board.
glossary.contrast: Cluster zoning rearranges homes of one type at the same density; a PUD can mix uses and housing types.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: An appointed local board that prepares or recommends the master plan, approves subdivisions and site plans, and advises other boards on land use.
glossary.deep:
The planning board is the community's forward-looking land use body. Appointed by the town or village board, it reviews subdivision plats, site plans, clustering and PUD proposals, often acts as SEQRA lead agency, and advises the legislative body on zoning changes and the ZBA on applications. It does not grant variances or adopt laws.

Analogy: the architect of the town's future, not its judge. NY example: a Saratoga County planning board approves a 40-lot subdivision with conditions on road width and stormwater basins.

On the exam: master plan, subdivisions, site plans, advises others. Appointed.
glossary.contrast: The ZBA grants variances and interprets the ordinance; the planning board plans and approves development layouts.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: Professional staff planners who advise all of a municipality's agencies and boards and prepare plans and studies.
glossary.deep:
Boards are made of volunteers; the planning department supplies the experts. Staff planners review applications, write reports to the planning board and ZBA, prepare the comprehensive plan draft, analyze traffic and demographics, and help applicants understand the process.

Analogy: the boards' research staff. NY example: the Town of Brookhaven's planning department prepares a staff report on a proposed shopping center before the planning board's hearing. Smaller towns may hire a consulting planner instead.

On the exam: planning department equals professional advisement to all agencies and boards.
glossary.contrast: The planning board is an appointed citizen board that votes; the planning department is professional staff that advises.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: Panels of gypsum between paper facings used for interior walls and ceilings; also called gypsum board or Sheetrock.
glossary.deep:
Plasterboard replaced wet lath and plaster after World War II because it goes up fast: screw the panels to studs, tape and spackle the seams, paint. Fire-rated (Type X) board is required in places like garage walls and between units.

Analogy: plaster in a ready-made sheet. NY example: a buyer touring a 1920s Jackson Heights co-op can tell original plaster walls (hard, slightly wavy) from later drywall patches (hollow sound, flat). Old joint compound and textured ceilings can contain asbestos.

On the exam: plasterboard, wallboard, drywall and gypsum board all mean the same thing.
glossary.contrast: Lath and plaster is the older wet-applied method; plasterboard is dry sheets.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A map of a subdivision showing lots, blocks, streets and easements, approved by the planning board and filed with the county clerk.
glossary.deep:
A plat is the subdivision's map. It shows each numbered lot, the streets, easements for utilities and drainage, and often building lines. Once the planning board signs it and it is filed with the county clerk, lots can be described by reference to it (lot 14 on the filed map of Maple Ridge).

Analogy: the seating chart for a new neighborhood. NY example: on Long Island, many deeds read "Lot 22, Block 4 on Map of Levittown filed in the Nassau County Clerk's Office." That reference is a lot and block description built on a filed plat.

On the exam: plat equals subdivision map. It connects to legal descriptions (lot and block) and to planning board approval.
glossary.contrast: A survey shows one parcel's measured boundaries and improvements; a plat lays out an entire subdivision.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The most common wood framing method today: each floor is built as a platform, and the walls for the next story stand on it.
glossary.deep:
In platform (western) framing, you build the first floor deck, stand the first-floor walls on it, put the second-floor deck on those walls, and repeat. Each floor deck acts as a fire stop between stories, and the lumber is short and easy to handle.

Analogy: stacking layer cakes, one tier at a time. NY example: virtually every new frame house in a Saratoga County subdivision is platform framed. Older Victorian houses in places like Ditmas Park may be balloon framed, with studs running two stories and no built-in fire stops.

On the exam: platform equals most common, floor by floor.
glossary.contrast: Balloon framing runs studs continuously from sill to roof; post-and-beam uses heavy, widely spaced timbers.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A loan in which the borrower (or a relative) deposits money in an account pledged as extra collateral, often in place of a larger down payment.
glossary.deep:
Cash in the bank stands behind the loan.

Like putting a security deposit on a rental car with a credit card hold.

Leo's parents pledge a $50,000 CD at the lender. Leo puts less down but the lender's risk is covered by the CD, which is released after the loan balance drops to a set level. Some versions draw on the account to supplement early payments.

On the exam: pledged account = savings used as additional collateral.
glossary.contrast: A buydown spends money to lower the rate; a pledged account holds money as security.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Supreme Court decision that approved "separate but equal" racial segregation.
glossary.deep:
Homer Plessy sat in a whites-only rail car in Louisiana to challenge segregation. The Court ruled against him and said separate facilities were fine if they were "equal." In practice they never were, and the ruling gave legal cover to segregation in schools, transit, and neighborhoods for nearly 60 years.

Picture it as the green light that Buchanan (1917) and Brown (1954) later had to turn red.

On the exam: Plessy is the case that ALLOWED segregation. If a choice says it struck down segregation, that is Brown v. Board of Education.
glossary.contrast: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned Plessy in public schools.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: The increase in value that results when two or more adjacent parcels are combined into one larger, more useful parcel.
glossary.deep:
Sometimes the whole is worth more than the sum of the parts.

Three puzzle pieces are each nearly useless alone; put together they show the picture.

A developer in Long Island City buys three 25-foot lots for $1M each. Combined into one 75-foot lot, it can hold a larger building and is worth $3.6M. The $600,000 gain is plottage. Buying the lots and combining them is assemblage.

On the exam: assemblage is the process, plottage is the added value. They are paired to trap you.
glossary.contrast: Assemblage is the act of combining parcels.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: Insurance protecting the lender on conventional loans above 80% LTV. The borrower may request cancellation at 80% of original value; it ends automatically at 78%.
glossary.deep:
PMI lets a buyer put down less than 20%, but it protects the lender, not the buyer.

Like a seatbelt installed for the passenger, paid for by the driver.

Leo buys at $750,000 with 10% down; his conventional loan needs PMI. Under the Homeowners Protection Act, he can ask to cancel once his balance hits $600,000 (80% of original value) with a good payment history, and it ends automatically at $585,000 (78%).

On the exam: 80% request, 78% automatic, protects lender.
glossary.contrast: MIP is the FHA version and often lasts for the loan's life.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The DOS-issued card a licensee carries to prove licensure and association with a broker.
glossary.deep:
Your license certificate stays at the office; the pocket card goes with you. It shows your name, license type, and broker. Anyone you deal with may ask to see it, and you must show it.

It is the real estate version of a police badge: the paperwork lives at headquarters, the badge is what you show on the street.

At an open house on Argyle Road, a cautious seller's neighbor asks Jordan for proof that Jordan is legit. Jordan shows the pocket card listing Hudson & Hart Realty.

On the exam: who keeps the license? The broker. What does the salesperson carry? The pocket card.
glossary.contrast: The license itself is kept by the sponsoring broker, not the salesperson.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: One percent of the loan amount, charged at closing as a discount point (to lower the rate) or an origination fee.
glossary.deep:
Points are prepaid interest or fees, priced as percentages of the loan.

It is like paying more up front for a lower monthly phone plan.

Leo borrows $512,000 and pays 1 point: $5,120. If Tasha finds a lender offering a rate a quarter percent lower for 2 points, Leo pays $10,240 up front for a smaller payment every month.

On the exam: points are on the loan, not the price. Old rule of thumb: 1 discount point raises the lender's yield about 1/8%.
glossary.contrast: Down payment: a percentage of the price paid in cash.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: The starting point of a metes and bounds description, to which the description must return to close.
glossary.deep: Every metes and bounds description starts and ends at the same spot, the point of beginning (POB). It is usually tied to a fixed reference, such as a distance from a street corner or a monument. If the last course does not return to the POB, the description fails to close, which creates a gap or overlap and a title problem. Surveyors use it like the anchor of a drawing. On the exam: the description must return to the point of beginning; that is what makes it a closed figure.
glossary.contrast: A monument is a physical marker that may serve as the POB or a corner.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Prepaid interest charged by a lender at closing; one point equals 1% of the loan amount.
glossary.deep:
Points (discount points) buy a lower interest rate. Tax treatment depends on the loan: points on a purchase of a principal residence are generally deductible in the year paid; refinance points are deducted evenly over the loan term. Seller-paid points are deductible by the buyer but reduce basis.

Think of it as paying rent in advance for a cheaper monthly rate.

Leo pays 1.5 points on a $600,000 loan: $9,000. Purchase loan: deduct $9,000 this year. If refinancing for 30 years: $300 a year.

On the exam: compute points as a percent of the loan, not the price, and know purchase vs refinance timing.
glossary.contrast: An origination fee may be called points but is deductible only if it is truly prepaid interest.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: Prepaid interest paid at closing to lower the interest rate. One point equals 1% of the loan amount.
glossary.deep:
Paying a point is buying a lower rate up front.

Like prepaying for a discount card that saves money on every future purchase.

On a $400,000 loan, 1 point is $4,000 (not 1% of the price). A rule of thumb says each point raises the lender's yield about 1/8 of a percent. Whether points pay off depends on how long the borrower keeps the loan. Points on a purchase of a principal residence are generally deductible in the year paid. An origination fee is also often stated in points.

On the exam: points are on the loan, not the price.
glossary.contrast: A buydown can be paid by a builder or seller and may be temporary; discount points permanently lower the note rate.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Government's power to regulate private property to protect public health, safety, morals and general welfare. No compensation is paid.
glossary.deep:
Police power is the government's rulebook power. It does not take your property; it limits how you use it. Think of a driver's license: you still own your car, but the state decides speed limits. Zoning, building codes, fire codes, subdivision rules, rent regulation and environmental rules all come from police power.

NY example: the Town of Huntington zones a block for single-family homes only. An owner who wanted a fourplex gets no check from the town, because a reasonable regulation is not a taking.

On the exam: when the government regulates and pays nothing, the answer is police power. If it takes title and pays, that is eminent domain.
glossary.contrast: Eminent domain takes the property and must pay just compensation; police power only regulates and pays nothing.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: An escalation that raises rent by a set amount per square foot for each cent of increase in the hourly wage of building porters, times a negotiated multiplier.
glossary.deep:
The porter's wage formula uses one number, the union porter's hourly wage, as a stand-in for all operating costs.

Like pegging your rent to the price of a slice of pizza: simple, roughly tracks the city's costs, but not exact.

Classic "penny for penny": each $0.01 wage increase adds $0.01 per RSF a year. If the wage rises $1.20, a 5,000 RSF tenant pays $1.20 x 1 x 5,000 = $6,000 more; with a 1.5 multiplier, $9,000. Tenants disliked it when wages outran actual costs, so most new NYC leases use direct operating escalations.

On the exam: wage increase x multiplier x RSF.
glossary.contrast: A direct operating escalation uses actual building expenses.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Income from investments like interest, dividends, annuities, and gains on stocks and bonds.
glossary.deep:
It feels passive (you do nothing), but the tax code puts it in its own class so that rental losses cannot shelter stock dividends. A REIT dividend is portfolio income; owning the building directly produces passive income.

Owning shares of a building company vs owning the building itself: same asset type, different bucket.

Evelyn's municipal bond interest and stock dividends are portfolio; her Flushing retail rents are passive.

On the exam: the three classes are active, passive, portfolio. Interest and dividends go in portfolio.
glossary.contrast: Passive income comes from rentals and limited partnerships.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A possessory interest gives the right to occupy property (fee, life estate, lease); a non-possessory interest gives only a right to use it or a claim against it (easement, lien).
glossary.deep: Ask one question: can the holder move in and keep others out? If yes, the interest is possessory: fee simple owners, life tenants, and tenants under a lease. If no, it is non-possessory: an easement holder can cross or use the land only for its purpose, and a lienholder has a money claim. Con Edison can enter a backyard to fix its line, but it cannot set up a picnic there. On the exam: easements and liens are non-possessory; leases and estates are possessory.
glossary.contrast: A leasehold is possessory even though it is personal property.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A framing method using heavy vertical posts and horizontal beams spaced far apart to carry loads, allowing open interiors.
glossary.deep:
Post-and-beam (timber frame) puts the load on a few big timbers instead of many small studs. Walls between posts carry no load, so interiors can be wide open with exposed beams. It is the method of old barns and many modern lodges.

Analogy: a skeleton of a few big bones instead of many small ones. NY example: converted Hudson Valley barns sold as homes are typically post-and-beam; buyers love the timbers, and inspectors check the joints and sills for rot and insects.

On the exam: heavy timbers, wide spacing, open plan.
glossary.contrast: Platform framing uses many light studs 16 inches on center.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The liquid assets a buyer will have left after paying the down payment and closing costs, often measured in months or years of housing costs.
glossary.deep:
Boards want a cushion. After closing, how many months could you pay the loan and maintenance if your income stopped? Many NYC co-ops want 1 to 2 years; some want more.

Liquid means cash, money market, stocks, bonds, mutual funds. Retirement accounts are often discounted or excluded; real estate, private businesses, and collectibles usually do not count.

NY example: housing costs of $7,700 a month and $210,000 liquid after closing equals about 2.3 years.

On the exam: math questions multiply monthly housing costs by 12 and by the years required.
glossary.contrast: Down payment is spent at closing; post-closing liquidity is what remains.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: The total rent a property would collect if every unit were rented all year at its scheduled or market rent.
glossary.deep:
PGI is the best case: 100% occupied, everyone pays, all year.

Like a restaurant counting every seat filled at every sitting: a useful ceiling, never reality.

Bushwick: six apartments at $2,750 and two stores at $4,500 a month gives PGI of $306,000. From there, vacancy and credit loss come off and other income is added to reach EGI.

On the exam: PGI = units x monthly rent x 12. Vacancy is figured as a percentage of PGI.
glossary.contrast: Effective gross income is PGI minus vacancy and credit loss plus other income.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A written document authorizing an agent (attorney-in-fact) to act for the principal, such as signing a contract or deed.
glossary.deep:
It lets someone else sign for you. The agent need not be a lawyer.

Like giving a trusted friend the keys and the authority to sell your car.

An owner deployed overseas signs a NY statutory power of attorney naming her sister to sell her Staten Island house. To convey real property the power must be in writing, and it is recorded with the deed. A power of attorney ends at the principal's death.

On the exam: the attorney-in-fact is an agent; authority for real estate must be written.
glossary.contrast: An attorney at law is a licensed lawyer; an attorney-in-fact is anyone named in a power of attorney.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A NY disclosure a mortgage broker gives and both sign before the broker accepts any fee, stating that the broker is not a lender, its services and fees, lender compensation, and refund terms.
glossary.deep:
The ground rules before any money changes hands.

Like a contractor's written estimate before you hand over a deposit.

Before Tasha accepts Leo's application fee, they sign the agreement. It says Tasha arranges but does not make loans, lists her fees and when they are due, notes whether a lender may pay her, and says which fees are refunded if no commitment is issued.

On the exam: comes before fees, specific to mortgage brokers.
glossary.contrast: The Loan Estimate is a federal cost disclosure given within 3 business days after application.
glossary.subject: s18

glossary.def: A lender's conditional approval of a borrower for a loan amount after reviewing credit and verifying income and assets, before a specific property is chosen.
glossary.deep:
The borrower is checked; the house is not.

Like being cleared to rent a car before you pick the model.

Tasha pulls the buyer's credit and reviews two years of tax returns, bank statements, and pay stubs, then issues a preapproval for $580,000. Attached to an offer in Ditmas Park, it makes the buyer credible. Final approval still depends on the appraisal, title, and anything that changes.

On the exam: verified borrower, no property yet; does not satisfy a mortgage contingency.
glossary.contrast: A commitment covers a specific property after appraisal.
glossary.subject: s18

glossary.def: Abusive lending practices that impose unfair terms, hide costs, or set borrowers up to fail, often stripping their equity.
glossary.deep:
Loans built to profit from the borrower's failure.

Like a lender who sells you a boat with holes, then charges to patch them.

Common signs: rates and fees far above risk, packed-in products, balloon traps, loan flipping, no verification of ability to repay, and targeting of elderly or minority homeowners. After 2008, whole neighborhoods in southeast Queens and East New York saw waves of foreclosures from such loans. NY Banking Law 6-l and 6-m, HOEPA, and Dodd-Frank fight it.

On the exam: spot the practice in a fact pattern.
glossary.contrast: A subprime loan is not automatically predatory; predatory is about abusive terms.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An owner's or occupier's legal responsibility for injuries caused by dangerous conditions on the property that they knew or should have known about.
glossary.deep:
If you control a property, you owe visitors reasonable care about hazards.

A store that leaves a spill on the floor pays when a shopper slips.

At the Okafors' open house, a visitor falls on a loose stair tread the Okafors knew about. The Okafors face premises liability; Jordan may share blame for not warning visitors or blocking the stair. At the office, the broker has the same duty for the brokerage's premises.

On the exam: sellers are liable for known dangerous conditions; agents should spot and warn about hazards and advise sellers to fix or secure them.
glossary.contrast: Vicarious liability makes a broker answer for an agent's acts.
glossary.subject: s13

glossary.def: A charge for paying off a loan early; for a home mortgage it is deductible as interest.
glossary.deep:
Some loans, especially commercial and some older residential loans, charge a fee if you pay off early, because the lender loses expected interest. The IRS treats a home mortgage prepayment penalty as interest, deductible in the year paid by those who itemize. Many residential loans today cannot carry one, under federal rules for qualified mortgages.

It is the cancellation fee on a contract that expected to run longer.

Evelyn's commercial loan on a Flushing building has a step-down prepayment penalty; on a sale she pays it and deducts it as a business expense.

On the exam: prepayment penalty = deductible as interest.
glossary.contrast: Points are paid at the start of a loan; a prepayment penalty at the end.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A clause charging the borrower a fee for paying off the loan early.
glossary.deep:
Lenders count on years of interest. A prepayment penalty compensates them if you pay early.

Like a cancellation fee on a two-year contract.

Commercial loans on Manhattan office buildings often carry yield maintenance or step-down penalties. Most NY residential loans today have none: federal rules and NY Banking Law restrict prepayment penalties on home loans, especially high-cost and subprime loans.

On the exam: know what it is and that consumer protection laws limit it on home loans.
glossary.contrast: A late charge is for paying late; a prepayment penalty is for paying early.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An informal estimate of how much a buyer may be able to borrow, based on information the buyer provides without verification.
glossary.deep:
A rough guess, not a promise.

Like an online "how much house can I afford" calculator.

A buyer tells an app she earns $120,000 and has $30,000 saved; it says she can borrow about $450,000. Nobody checked her credit or pay stubs. Sellers and co-op boards in NYC give it little weight.

It is still useful early: it tells a buyer what price range to search before paying for a full application.

On the exam: weakest of the three; unverified.
glossary.contrast: Preapproval verifies credit, income, and assets.
glossary.subject: s18

glossary.def: Scheduled work done to prevent breakdowns and extend the life of building systems.
glossary.deep:
Preventive maintenance is paid for in advance to avoid bigger bills later: annual boiler cleaning, roof inspections, gutter clearing, elevator servicing, repainting before wood rots.

Like changing your car's oil so the engine does not seize.

Every August, Ray services Sal's boiler before heating season.

On the exam: preventive = scheduled, before failure. It is the best way to preserve value and reduce corrective costs.
glossary.contrast: Corrective maintenance fixes something that already broke.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: The amount a particular buyer agrees to pay and a particular seller agrees to accept, under the circumstances of that sale.
glossary.deep:
Price is specific to two people and one moment. Change the people or the pressure and the price changes.

It is like a negotiated cab fare in a rainstorm: real, but shaped by circumstances.

Sal sold a parking lot to his brother-in-law for $300,000 when similar lots fetched $450,000. The price was $300,000. Nobody would use it as evidence of value, because the parties were related.

On the exam: "may or may not equal value" is the phrase to remember for both price and cost.
glossary.contrast: Cost is what it took to build; price is what someone paid.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: Competitors agreeing on prices, such as commission rates or splits. Illegal per se under the Sherman Act.
glossary.deep:
Price fixing is competitors deciding prices together instead of competing.

Like every pizzeria on a block agreeing that no slice goes below $4.

At a Bay Ridge breakfast, five brokers agree to "hold the line at 6%." Even if no seller complains, that is a federal crime. Telling a seller "everyone in Astoria charges the same" suggests it, too.

On the exam: commissions are always negotiable between broker and client. Any agreement among competitors about rates is price fixing.
glossary.contrast: A single firm setting its own rate is lawful; the agreement among competitors is the crime.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The sale or asking price divided by the property's square footage, used to compare properties of different sizes.
glossary.deep:
Price per square foot puts a big apartment and a small one on the same scale.

It is unit pricing at the grocery store: price per ounce tells you which cereal is cheaper.

A 950 sq ft Long Island City condo asking $1,140,000 is $1,200 a foot. If the building's recent sales average $1,150 a foot, the asking price looks rich.

On the exam: price / square feet. To go back, square feet x price per foot.
glossary.contrast: Front foot pricing uses only street frontage.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: The market in which lenders make loans directly to borrowers.
glossary.deep:
Where the borrower meets the money.

Like a car dealership: the place you actually buy.

Banks, credit unions, savings institutions, and mortgage bankers in NY originate loans in the primary market. Mortgage brokers arrange loans there but do not fund them. Many lenders then sell the loans to the secondary market to get cash for new loans.

On the exam: primary = origination.
glossary.contrast: The secondary market buys and sells existing loans.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The place a tenant actually lives as home. Rent-stabilized tenants must use the unit as their primary residence to keep renewal rights.
glossary.deep:
It is where you really live, not just where your name is on a lease.

Like the address your doctor, the IRS, and the DMV all have.

A stabilized tenant in Forest Hills who files taxes from Florida, votes in Florida, and spends most of the year there is a non-primary resident. The landlord may refuse to renew after following the notice rules and proving it. Evidence: tax returns, voter registration, driver's license, and time spent at the unit.

On the exam: non-primary residence is a ground to decline renewal of a stabilized lease.
glossary.contrast: Household income (all occupants' combined income) was the test for the old high-income decontrol.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The person who hires an agent and authorizes the agent to act on their behalf; in real estate, the client.
glossary.deep:
The principal is the boss in the relationship: the one whose interests the agent must serve.

Think of a ship's owner and its captain. The captain runs the voyage, but the owner decides where the ship goes and gets the cargo.

Sal Russo hires Jordan's firm to rent his Astoria two-bedroom. Sal is the principal. The firm follows his lawful instructions, tells him every material fact, and keeps his finances confidential.

On the exam: "principal" and "client" are used interchangeably. Watch for questions that call the customer the principal just because they are paying.
glossary.contrast: Principal is the client. Customer is the third party the agent deals with but does not represent.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The amount borrowed, or the unpaid balance of a loan, on which interest is charged.
glossary.deep:
Principal is the debt itself, not the cost of carrying it.

If you borrow $100 from a friend and agree to pay $5 for the favor, the $100 is principal and the $5 is interest.

Leo's monthly payment is $2,878. In month one, $2,400 is interest and $478 reduces principal from $480,000 to $479,522.

On the exam: "principal" in a math question means the loan balance. In an agency question it means the client. Read the context.
glossary.contrast: In agency law, the principal is the client the agent represents.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: A projected income and expense statement showing what a property is expected to earn in the future, often after renovations or lease-up.
glossary.deep:
A pro forma is a forecast, not a record. It says "here is what this building could make if our plan works."

Like a restaurant's business plan: useful, necessary for investors, and almost always optimistic.

The Bushwick listing broker's pro forma NOI of $230,000 assumed both stores re-leased at top market rent. Developers and lenders use pro formas for new construction and value-add deals, but buyers price stabilized buildings on actual numbers.

On the exam: pro forma = projected. Treat a seller's pro forma with caution.
glossary.contrast: A reconstructed statement restates actual performance; a pro forma projects future performance.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The court process that proves a will is valid and supervises the payment of debts and distribution of the estate; in NY it takes place in Surrogate's Court.
glossary.deep: Probate is how a will becomes effective. The executor files the will with the Surrogate's Court in the county where the decedent lived; the court confirms it is genuine and properly signed and issues letters testamentary giving the executor authority. The executor can then sell real property by executor's deed. Property held in joint tenancy, tenancy by the entirety, or a living trust passes outside probate. On the exam: Surrogate's Court handles probate in NY; probate applies to testate estates (administration applies to intestate ones).
glossary.contrast: Administration is the court process for an intestate estate.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The broker whose efforts started an uninterrupted chain of events that resulted in the sale.
glossary.deep:
The procuring cause is the broker who really made the deal happen, not just the first to open the door.

Like the player who set up the goal, not the one who touched the ball first in the first half.

Under an open listing on an Astoria two-family, Broker A shows the buyer once; months later Broker B shows it again, negotiates, and gets the contract signed. B is likely the procuring cause.

On the exam: procuring cause decides who is paid under open listings and in commission disputes.
glossary.contrast: Ready, willing, and able describes the buyer; procuring cause describes the broker's role.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The borrower's written promise to repay a debt, stating amount, interest rate, term, and payments. In NY it is often called a bond.
glossary.deep:
The note is the IOU. It makes the borrower personally liable for the debt.

Think of it as the receipt for borrowed money, signed by the borrower.

Leo signs a note for $600,000 at 6.5% for 30 years. If the property sells at foreclosure for less than he owes, the note is what lets the lender seek a deficiency judgment against him personally. Notes are negotiable, so they can be sold to investors in the secondary market.

On the exam: note = evidence of the debt; it is not recorded.
glossary.contrast: The mortgage is the security; it is recorded.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The form RPL Article 14 requires sellers of 1 to 4 family residential property to give buyers before the contract is signed.
glossary.deep:
The PCDS asks the seller about the roof, water, systems, environmental issues, and, since March 20, 2024, flood risk: floodplain, flood insurance, past flood damage and claims. The old $500 credit opt-out is gone. The seller fills it out from actual knowledge; the agent explains the duty but does not complete it.

Think of a used car history report, but signed by the owner.

The Okafors fill out the PCDS for their Bed-Stuy brownstone, noting the 2021 basement flood from Hurricane Ida.

On the exam: 1 to 4 family, before contract, no more $500 credit, exempt categories (foreclosures, estates, family transfers, new never-occupied homes, condos and co-ops are outside it).
glossary.contrast: Lead paint disclosure is a separate federal rule for pre-1978 housing.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: NY form (RPL Article 14) that sellers of 1 to 4 family residential property must give buyers before the buyer signs the contract. Mandatory since March 20, 2024, with no $500 credit option.
glossary.deep:
A questionnaire the seller fills out about the home's condition, to the seller's actual knowledge.

Like a used car history report written by the owner.

Grace and Emmanuel answer questions about the roof, boiler, water, and, since 2024, flood zones, flood insurance, and past flood damage claims. They sign it before the buyer signs the contract. Old rule: a seller could skip it and give a $500 credit at closing. That opt-out is gone. Exempt: condos, co-ops, new never-occupied homes, foreclosures, and certain estate and family transfers.

On the exam: no more $500 credit.
glossary.contrast: Lead paint disclosure is federal and lead-only.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Insurance that pays for sudden, accidental physical loss to a building or its contents, such as fire, wind, hail, vandalism, or theft, in exchange for a premium.
glossary.deep:
Property insurance swaps a small, certain cost (the premium) for protection against a large, uncertain one (the loss).

Like a club where every member chips in so the unlucky few who burn their kitchens get paid.

Sal's Astoria house suffers a $40,000 kitchen fire. His homeowners policy pays for repairs, minus his deductible. Without it, Sal pays it all, and his lender could call the loan for failing to keep the collateral insured.

On the exam: property insurance covers sudden loss, not wear and tear. Lenders require it because the house secures the loan.
glossary.contrast: Liability insurance pays for harm you cause to others.
glossary.subject: s12

glossary.def: Operating real estate on behalf of an owner to meet the owner's financial and physical goals.
glossary.deep:
Property management is running a building as a business: leasing, collecting rent, maintaining, budgeting, reporting, and staying legal. The owner sets goals; the manager executes them.

Think of the owner as a team owner and the manager as the general manager who runs day-to-day operations.

Hudson & Hart manages Sal's 6-unit Astoria walk-up: finds tenants for vacant units, collects $12,850 a month in rent, schedules the August boiler cleaning, and sends Sal a monthly report.

On the exam: property management that includes leasing or collecting rent for others for a fee requires a NY broker license.
glossary.contrast: Asset management focuses on investment strategy for a portfolio; property management runs the individual buildings.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: The manager's regular (usually monthly) report to the owner on income, expenses, vacancies, maintenance, and recommendations.
glossary.deep:
The report is how the general agent accounts to the principal. It compares actual income and expenses to budget, lists arrears and vacancies, summarizes maintenance and leasing, and recommends next steps. An annual report and next year's budget follow.

Like a quarterly earnings report, for one building.

Jordan's monthly report to Sal flags 2B's arrears, fuel overruns, the 1B vacancy, and recommends funding the boiler reserve.

On the exam: regular reporting is a duty to the owner (accounting and disclosure).
glossary.contrast: A management proposal comes before hiring.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: A person or firm that manages real property for an owner, usually as a general agent under a management agreement.
glossary.deep:
A property manager wears many hats: leasing agent, rent collector, maintenance supervisor, bookkeeper, compliance officer, and risk manager. In NY, an independent manager who leases or collects rent for others needs a broker license.

Like a building's chief operating officer who reports to the owner.

Jordan manages Sal's building through Hudson & Hart. The agreement is with the firm, and Jordan, a salesperson, is paid only by Diane.

On the exam: the property manager is a general agent and fiduciary of the owner.
glossary.contrast: A resident manager is typically the owner's on-site employee; a property manager is often an outside firm.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: The tenant's rentable square feet divided by the building's total rentable square feet, used to split expense increases among tenants.
glossary.deep:
Proportionate (pro rata) share is the tenant's slice of the building pie.

Like splitting a group dinner bill by how many people at each table: the bigger table pays more.

Leo leases 5,000 RSF in a 100,000 RSF building: 5%. When taxes rise $240,000 over the base year, he pays 5%, or $12,000. A 20,000 RSF law firm in the same building pays 20%.

On the exam: share = tenant RSF / building RSF. Then share x increase.
glossary.contrast: The loss factor compares rentable to usable within one suite; proportionate share compares a tenant to the whole building.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The lease between a co-op corporation and a shareholder that grants the right to occupy a specific apartment and sets the shareholder's obligations.
glossary.deep:
It is a long-term lease that comes with your shares. It covers maintenance, repairs (who fixes what), alterations (only with consent), subletting and assignment (only with board consent), pets, and the co-op's remedies if you default, up to canceling the lease.

Think of it as the co-op's rulebook with teeth. House rules fill in the details.

NY example: a shareholder in a Park Slope co-op who sublets without approval is in default under the proprietary lease.

On the exam: the proprietary lease is what makes a shareholder a tenant. It is personal property, not a deed.
glossary.contrast: The stock certificate proves share ownership; the proprietary lease grants occupancy.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Dividing expenses and income such as taxes, rent, water, and fuel between buyer and seller according to the days each owns the property; NY practice calls them adjustments.
glossary.deep: Prorations make each party pay for exactly their days of ownership. Find the period the bill covers, decide whether it was paid in advance or is unpaid, decide who owns the closing day, compute a daily rate (365-day actual or 360-day statutory year), and multiply. Seller prepaid: credit seller, debit buyer. Seller collected rent in advance or owes unpaid taxes: debit seller, credit buyer. NY standard contracts apportion as of midnight before closing, so the buyer owns closing day unless the question says otherwise. On the exam: follow the stated method and closing-day rule.
glossary.contrast: A closing cost like commission belongs entirely to one party and is not prorated.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A group of people defined by a characteristic, such as race or familial status, that fair housing law forbids using as a basis for housing decisions.
glossary.deep:
A protected class is a characteristic, not a group of favored people. Everyone has a race, a sex, a national origin, so everyone is protected. A white buyer steered away from a mostly Black neighborhood is just as protected as anyone else.

Layers stack: federal law has 7 classes, New York State adds about 8, New York City adds more. In Brooklyn, all three layers apply at once.

On the exam: questions list several traits and ask which is protected under federal law vs New York. Age, marital status, military status, and source of income are New York, not federal.
glossary.contrast: A legitimate screening criterion (credit, income, references) is not a protected class and may be used if applied equally.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A transfer of land from the government to a private party.
glossary.deep: A public grant is how land first moves from government ownership to private hands. Colonial governors, the State of New York, and the federal government have all granted land this way. The document evidencing it is a land patent. Today a public grant might be a state transfer of surplus land to a private buyer. Many NY chains of title, especially upstate, begin with a colonial patent or state grant. On the exam: public grant runs from government to private party; dedication runs the other way.
glossary.contrast: Dedication is a private owner's gift of land to public use.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Exaggerated opinion or sales talk that a reasonable buyer would not take as fact. Generally not misrepresentation.
glossary.deep:
Puffing is enthusiasm, not information.

"World's best coffee" on a diner sign is puffing. "Made with organic beans" is a claim of fact.

"The most charming block in Ditmas Park" is puffing. "Taxes are $6,000 a year" is a fact and had better be right.

On the exam: if the statement can be checked and is false, it is misrepresentation. If it is pure opinion, it is puffing.
glossary.contrast: Misrepresentation involves facts; puffing involves opinions.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A mortgage given to finance the purchase of the property; in exam usage, usually one the seller takes back from the buyer for part of the price.
glossary.deep:
Seller as the bank.

Like selling your car to a friend who pays you monthly.

The Okafors sell a rental building for $1.2 million. The buyer pays $400,000 cash and gives the Okafors a note and mortgage for $800,000. The buyer gets the deed at closing; the Okafors hold a lien. A purchase money mortgage gets special priority over other liens against the buyer that arise at the same time.

On the exam: deed passes at closing, seller holds the mortgage.
glossary.contrast: In a land contract the seller keeps title until paid.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A written offer to buy on stated terms, usually on a standard form; upstate, once accepted and past attorney review, it can become the binding contract.
glossary.deep:
An offer on paper with the key terms filled in.

Like a filled-in order form that becomes a contract when the store signs it.

In Syracuse, a buyer's broker writes a purchase offer on the local bar-approved form with price, deposit, financing, inspection, and attorney approval contingencies. When the seller signs and the review period passes, it is the contract. Downstate, a written offer is just a negotiation step before the attorney-drafted contract.

On the exam: purchase offers are prepared by brokers, usually upstate.
glossary.contrast: A binder downstate is usually non-binding.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A fee simple estate that can be lost if a stated condition is broken or an event occurs.
glossary.deep: A qualified fee looks like full ownership but has a string attached. There are two kinds. A fee simple determinable ("so long as," "while") ends automatically when the condition breaks, and the grantor holds a possibility of reverter. A fee on condition subsequent ("but if," "provided that") gives the grantor a right of re-entry, which the grantor must act on. Gifts to churches, schools, and towns often carry these conditions, such as "so long as used as a park." On the exam: spot the magic words to tell which kind it is.
glossary.contrast: Fee simple absolute has no conditions.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: An independent party who holds sale proceeds and handles the paperwork so a delayed 1031 exchange avoids constructive receipt.
glossary.deep:
If the seller can touch the money, the IRS treats it as a sale, not an exchange. The QI (also called an accommodator or facilitator) receives the proceeds at closing and uses them to buy the replacement. The taxpayer's attorney, accountant, broker, employee, or close relatives within the prior 2 years are disqualified.

Like an escrow agent for a trade: you never hold the cash, so it is a swap, not a sale.

Evelyn nearly took her $3.2 million check; Jordan redirected it to an independent exchange company.

On the exam: QI must be independent, and the taxpayer cannot receive the funds.
glossary.contrast: An exchange accommodation titleholder holds property title in a reverse exchange.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: Lender limits on payments as a percentage of gross monthly income: the front-end (housing) ratio and the back-end (total debt) ratio, classically 28% and 36% for conventional loans.
glossary.deep:
Two tests the borrower must pass at the same time.

Think of two doors in a row. You only get through if you fit both, so the narrower door sets your size.

Leo: $12,000 a month. Front: 28% = $3,360 for PITI. Back: 36% = $4,320 minus $1,200 of other debts = $3,120. He qualifies for $3,120 PITI.

On the exam: compute both and choose the lower. Housing expense means PITI (principal, interest, taxes, insurance), plus HOA or common charges where applicable.
glossary.contrast: LTV measures the loan against the property's value, not against income.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: The landlord's covenant that the tenant will have undisturbed possession, free from interference by the landlord or anyone with a better title claim.
glossary.deep:
"Quiet" here means undisturbed, not silent. The landlord promises not to mess with your possession.

Like a promise that the host will not keep walking into your rented room.

A landlord in Bushwick who changes locks, shuts off utilities to force a tenant out, or lets workers occupy the unit breaches quiet enjoyment. A neighbor playing loud music is usually not the landlord's breach unless the landlord controls the situation.

On the exam: quiet enjoyment is about possession. Serious breaches can lead to constructive eviction.
glossary.contrast: Warranty of habitability is about the condition of the unit; quiet enjoyment is about undisturbed possession.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A deed that transfers whatever interest the grantor has, if any, with no warranties at all.
glossary.deep: A quitclaim says, in effect, "whatever I have, it's yours, but I promise nothing." If the grantor owns nothing, the grantee gets nothing. Quitclaims are used to clear clouds on title, to release a possible claim (an heir giving up any interest), in divorce transfers between spouses, and to release easements. It is the bottom rung of the deed ladder. On the exam: least protection for the grantee; used to remove clouds and release interests.
glossary.contrast: A full covenant and warranty deed gives the most protection.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A measure of a material's resistance to heat flow. The higher the R-value, the better the insulation.
glossary.deep:
R stands for resistance. Insulation does not create heat; it slows heat moving through walls, roofs and floors. Values add up when layers stack: R-19 batts plus R-5 foam board gives about R-24. Thickness and installation quality both matter; compressed or gappy insulation underperforms its label.

Analogy: a thicker winter coat has a higher R-value. NY example: NY's Energy Code sets minimum R-values by climate zone, higher for ceilings in the North Country than in NYC. An upstate buyer comparing two houses can ask for attic R-values the way they ask about square footage.

On the exam: higher R equals better. A U-factor is the inverse; lower is better.
glossary.contrast: BTU measures a quantity of heat; R-value measures resistance to heat flow.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A colorless, odorless, radioactive gas from decaying uranium in soil and rock that seeps into buildings; the leading cause of lung cancer among nonsmokers.
glossary.deep:
Radon rises from the ground and is drawn into homes through cracks, sumps and gaps because the house is at slightly lower pressure than the soil. You cannot see or smell it, so testing is the only way to know. EPA's action level is 4 picocuries per liter. The fix, sub-slab depressurization, is a pipe and fan venting soil gas above the roof, usually a one-day job.

Analogy: an invisible leak coming up instead of down. NY example: radon levels in parts of upstate (some Southern Tier and Finger Lakes counties) run notably high, but an elevated house can turn up anywhere, including Long Island.

On the exam: 4 pCi/L, short-term vs long-term tests, sub-slab mitigation, radon-resistant new construction.
glossary.contrast: Carbon monoxide is a combustion gas from appliances; radon comes from the soil.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: One of a series of sloped framing members running from the top of the wall to the ridge, supporting the roof.
glossary.deep:
Rafters are the roof's ribs. They rest on the top plate of the exterior walls, rise at the roof's pitch, and meet at the ridge. Sheathing goes on top, then underlayment and shingles. Collar ties or ceiling joists keep rafters from spreading the walls apart.

Analogy: the poles of a tent leaning together. NY example: an inspector in a Hudson Valley farmhouse attic finds a cracked rafter from an old ice dam leak and recommends sistering a new board alongside it.

On the exam: rafters carry the roof; joists carry floors and ceilings. Trusses are prefabricated alternatives.
glossary.contrast: Joists are horizontal; rafters are sloped and carry the roof.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A limit on how much an ARM's interest rate can change at each adjustment (periodic cap).
glossary.deep:
A speed bump on rate increases.

Like a rule that rent can rise no more than a set amount each year.

An ARM at 4.25% with a 2% periodic cap: even if index plus margin hits 6.6%, the rate can only go to 6.25% at this adjustment. Next adjustment it can climb more if the index stays high, up to the lifetime cap.

On the exam: compare fully indexed rate with current rate plus cap; take the lower.
glossary.contrast: A payment cap limits the payment, not the rate, and can cause negative amortization.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A lender's written agreement to hold a specific interest rate and points for a set period before closing.
glossary.deep:
Insurance against rates rising before you close.

Like reserving a hotel room at today's price for a stay next month.

Leo locks 6.5% with 1 point for 60 days because his closing is in 50. If rates jump, he is protected. If the co-op board or a title problem delays closing past the lock date, he may pay to extend or take the new market rate. In NY, lock-in agreements must be in writing with their terms and expiration.

On the exam: written, time-limited, watch the expiration.
glossary.contrast: A buydown lowers the rate by paying money up front; a lock just holds the current rate.
