glossary.subject: s18

glossary.def: The gain on an investment expressed as a percentage of the amount invested.
glossary.deep:
Rate of return answers "what is my money earning?" in percentage terms: income (or gain) divided by investment.

A savings account paying $40 a year on $1,000 returns 4%. A building netting $60,000 on a $1,000,000 cash purchase returns 6%.

Commercial real estate gives the idea specific names. Return on the whole property, ignoring financing, is the cap rate (NOI / value). Return on the investor's own cash is cash on cash (BTCF / equity). A Brooklyn investor quoting "a 6 cap with 9% cash on cash" is using both.

On the exam: watch which number goes in the denominator: price for cap rate, equity for cash on cash.
glossary.contrast: Return ON investment is profit earned; return OF investment is getting your original money back.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Creation of agency when a principal approves an agent's unauthorized act after the fact.
glossary.deep:
Ratification is saying "yes, I'll take it" after someone acted for you without permission.

Like a roommate ordering pizza on your card without asking, and you eat it and keep the receipt.

An agent with no listing negotiates a Bushwick loft lease. The owner reviews it, signs, and deposits the first month's rent. By accepting the benefit, the owner ratified the agency.

On the exam: ratification looks back at an act already done. Estoppel looks at a false appearance the principal created beforehand.
glossary.contrast: Estoppel is about the principal's prior conduct creating apparent authority; ratification is approval afterward.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A buyer who is prepared to buy on the seller's terms, wants to, and has the financial capacity to close.
glossary.deep:
Ready means prepared to sign now; willing means they want it; able means they can pay.

Like a job candidate who accepts the posted salary, can start Monday, and passes the background check.

Jordan brings the Okafors an all-cash buyer at full asking price with no contingencies. If the Okafors then refuse to sell, Hudson & Hart may still be owed the commission, depending on the listing language.

On the exam: producing a ready, willing, and able buyer is the traditional moment a commission is earned, even if the sale never closes. NY listings often add "payable at closing" language, so read the agreement.
glossary.contrast: Earned (ready, willing, able buyer) vs payable (when the agreement says, often closing).
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Land plus all permanent improvements attached to it by people, such as buildings, fences, and driveways.
glossary.deep: Real estate is land plus the things people have permanently attached: houses, garages, walls, paved driveways, in-ground pools. Think of land as the canvas and real estate as the canvas with the painting on it. A Park Slope brownstone and its lot together are real estate. In everyday speech and on many exam questions, real estate and real property are used interchangeably. On the exam: if a question stresses the physical land and improvements, it is real estate; if it stresses the rights of ownership, the answer is real property.
glossary.contrast: Real property is real estate plus the bundle of legal rights.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A person licensed or certified by DOS under Executive Law Article 6-E to give independent opinions of value.
glossary.deep:
Appraisers sign formal value opinions used by lenders, courts, and estates. They have their own education, experience, and standards (USPAP). A real estate salesperson can prepare a comparative market analysis, but cannot call it an appraisal.

Think doctor vs. a friend who reads medical websites: the friend can share a view, only the doctor can diagnose.

When Leo's lender orders an appraisal on a Sunnyside condo, it goes to a certified residential appraiser, not to Jordan, even though Jordan's CMA was solid.

On the exam: CMA is not an appraisal; appraisers are licensed separately from brokers.
glossary.contrast: A CMA is a licensee's price opinion for marketing, not an appraisal.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A person or entity licensed to perform real estate services for others for a fee, who can run a brokerage and sponsor salespersons and associate brokers.
glossary.deep:
The broker is the business. Clients sign listing and buyer agreements with the broker, commissions are paid to the broker, and the broker pays its salespersons. The broker answers to the public for honest dealing and escrow, and to DOS for supervising every licensee it sponsors.

Picture a restaurant license: the cooks work under it, but the owner whose name is on the license is the one inspectors talk to.

Diane Hart is the broker of Hudson & Hart Realty: 20+ years old, 152 hours of education, qualifying experience, $185 fee every 2 years, and her license hangs on the office wall.

On the exam: only a broker can collect a commission from a client, place ads, and hold escrow funds. Salespersons act only through a broker.
glossary.contrast: An associate broker has the same qualifications but chooses to work under another broker.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A licensee who performs real estate services only on behalf of, and under the supervision of, a sponsoring broker.
glossary.deep:
The salesperson is the entry license. You can list, show, negotiate, and rent, but always as the broker's agent. All money and documents go to the broker, and only the broker pays you.

A salesperson is like a pilot flying for an airline: fully qualified to fly, but under the airline's certificate and rules.

Jordan, newly licensed at Hudson & Hart, took the 77-hour course, passed the school final and the state exam ($15), and paid $65 for a 2-year license that only became active once Diane sponsored it.

On the exam: watch for answers where a salesperson takes a fee from a client, places an ad without the broker, or opens their own office. All wrong.
glossary.contrast: Associate broker: same working arrangement but broker-qualified.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A federal law governing settlement on federally related mortgage loans for 1 to 4 family residential property; it bans kickbacks and requires disclosures.
glossary.deep: RESPA protects borrowers at closing. It applies to nearly all residential mortgage loans on 1 to 4 family homes, but not to all-cash or commercial deals. Section 8 prohibits kickbacks and referral fees among settlement service providers: a broker cannot take money from a title company, lender, or inspector for referrals, even if disclosed. Affiliated businesses must be disclosed, and the buyer cannot be required to use them. Its disclosures are now combined with TILA's under TRID: the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure. On the exam: no referral fees; 1 to 4 family; 3-day disclosure rules.
glossary.contrast: TILA governs credit cost disclosure (APR); TRID merged the two laws' forms.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A tax on the transfer of real property. NYS charges $2 per $500 of consideration (0.4%), paid by the seller; NYC adds its own Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT), also paid by the seller.
glossary.deep:
Transfer taxes are a toll the government charges when title changes hands.

Think of a bridge toll on the deed as it crosses from seller to buyer.

An $850,000 Queens condo: NYS tax $3,400, NYC RPTT 1.425% = $12,112.50, both paid by the seller. NYS rises to 0.65% on NYC residential sales of $3M+. The buyer separately pays the mansion tax if the price is $1M or more.

On the exam: $2 per $500, seller pays. RPTT rate applies to the whole price, not just the excess over $500,000.
glossary.contrast: Mortgage recording tax is on the loan amount and paid by the borrower.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: Real estate plus all the legal rights, interests, and benefits of owning it (the bundle of rights).
glossary.deep: Real property is the most complete of the three layers: the physical land and buildings plus the legal rights that come with them, such as the right to sell, lease, mortgage, or exclude others. It is like the difference between a car and the car plus its title and registration. When the Okafors sell their Bed-Stuy brownstone, they convey real property: the house, the lot, and every right that goes with them, including appurtenant easements. Real property is transferred by deed. On the exam: "includes the bundle of rights" points to real property.
glossary.contrast: Personal property is movable and is transferred by a bill of sale, not a deed.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A lease clause requiring the tenant to pay its proportionate share of increases in real estate taxes over a base tax year (or above a tax stop).
glossary.deep:
Taxes are the expense landlords control least, so almost every commercial lease passes tax increases to tenants.

Like a shared house where everyone chips in when the property tax bill goes up.

Leo's building: taxes rose from $2,000,000 to $2,240,000. His 5% share of the $240,000 increase is $12,000. If the landlord wins a tax certiorari reduction, leases usually pass the tenant its share of the refund, less the landlord's costs.

On the exam: share x (current taxes minus base year taxes), never share x total taxes.
glossary.contrast: A direct operating escalation covers operating costs other than taxes.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The rate applied to assessed value to compute property tax, stated as a percent, dollars per $100, dollars per $1,000, or mills.
glossary.deep:
The tax rate is the multiplier that turns an assessment into a bill.

Same speed, different units: 60 mph and 96 km/h. 3.25%, $3.25 per $100, $32.50 per $1,000, and 32.5 mills are the same rate.

A house assessed at $200,000 with a rate of $32.50 per $1,000 pays $6,500 a year, or about $542 a month in escrow.

On the exam: convert the rate to a decimal, then multiply by assessed value (never market value unless the question says so).
glossary.contrast: Assessed value: the base the rate is applied to.
glossary.subject: s10

glossary.def: A change in a rule, policy, practice, or service that a person with a disability needs to have equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
glossary.deep:
An accommodation bends a rule, it does not move a wall. Examples: allowing an assistance animal in a no-pets building with no pet fee, reserving an accessible parking space, letting a tenant pay rent on the 5th because benefits arrive on the 3rd, permitting a live-in aide.

A provider may refuse only if there is no disability-related need, the request is an undue financial and administrative burden, or it fundamentally changes the operation. New York requires a written notice to prospective tenants explaining the right to request accommodations and modifications.

On the exam: rule or policy change = accommodation. Physical change = modification.
glossary.contrast: A reasonable modification is a physical change to the premises.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: The duty to use the skill, competence, and diligence expected of a licensed professional.
glossary.deep:
Do the job the way a competent agent would.

A cook who serves undercooked chicken did not mean harm, but still failed the standard.

Jordan prices a Crown Heights two-family using single-family comps and never checks the certificate of occupancy. The house is listed $150K too low and turns out to be a legal one-family. No bad intent, but Jordan fell short of reasonable care.

On the exam: carelessness, failing to verify facts, and acting outside your expertise (giving legal or tax advice) fall here.
glossary.contrast: Loyalty concerns motives; reasonable care concerns competence.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A physical change to a dwelling or common area, such as grab bars, a ramp, or widened doorways, that a person with a disability needs to fully use the housing.
glossary.deep:
Modifications change the space. Under federal law in private housing the tenant usually pays, and the landlord may require the interior to be restored at move-out where reasonable (not for changes like wider doors that do not bother the next tenant). NYC law is more protective and can require the provider to pay unless it is an undue hardship.

Example: a tenant in a Riverdale co-op rental needs a ramp at the side entrance. The landlord may require a professional installer and permits but may not simply refuse.

On the exam: grab bars, ramps, lowered counters are modifications. Who pays is the usual follow-up.
glossary.contrast: A reasonable accommodation changes a rule or policy, not the building.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: The portion of gain on sale attributable to depreciation taken, taxed at up to 25% for real estate (unrecaptured Section 1250 gain).
glossary.deep:
Depreciation lowers your taxes while you own, but it also lowers basis, increasing gain at sale. The IRS taxes that slice of gain at a higher maximum rate (25%) than ordinary long-term gain (20%).

Think of it as paying back a tax loan: you deferred tax every year; now part of it comes due.

Sal took $560,000 of depreciation over 20 years. On a $1,720,000 gain, $560,000 is taxed at up to 25%, the rest at up to 20%.

On the exam: recapture rate 25%. A 1031 exchange defers recapture along with the rest.
glossary.contrast: Long-term capital gain rates are 0/15/20%; recapture is up to 25%.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: The local official who collects property taxes and performs related accounting functions.
glossary.deep:
The receiver of taxes sends the bills and takes the money. In some towns the receiver is elected; elsewhere a treasurer or comptroller handles collection. The office can confirm what is paid and what is due, which matters at closing because unpaid real property taxes are a priority lien.

Analogy: the cashier, not the price setter. NY example: in the Town of Oyster Bay, the receiver of taxes collects school, town and county taxes in two halves; a closing attorney gets payment status there.

On the exam: receiver equals collects taxes and accounting.
glossary.contrast: The assessor values the property; the receiver collects the tax.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: A three-party agreement among a co-op lender, the co-op corporation, and the shareholder in which the co-op recognizes the lender's lien and agrees to give notice of defaults.
glossary.deep:
The lender's collateral is only as good as the co-op's willingness to let it be sold. In the recognition agreement the co-op acknowledges the loan, agrees to notify the lender of maintenance defaults, and gives the lender a chance to cure before canceling the lease. The lender accepts that the co-op's lien for unpaid maintenance comes first.

NY example: if Adaeze stops paying maintenance, the co-op must notify her lender, which may pay the arrears to protect its loan.

On the exam: recognition agreement = lender + co-op + borrower.
glossary.contrast: An alteration agreement governs renovations.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Balancing a closing statement: the buyer's debits minus credits equals cash due from the buyer; the seller's credits minus debits equals the seller's net proceeds.
glossary.deep: Reconciliation proves the numbers work. Total the buyer's debits (price, closing costs, prorations owed) and subtract the buyer's credits (deposit, loan, prorations received): the result is the check the buyer brings. Do the reverse for the seller to find the net proceeds. Example: buyer debits $814,500 minus credits $721,200 means the buyer brings $93,300. (In appraisal, reconciliation means weighing the approaches to value, a different use.) On the exam: expect a cash-to-close calculation.
glossary.contrast: Proration splits one expense; reconciliation balances the whole statement.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: An income and expense statement restated the way an investor or appraiser sees it: market vacancy and typical expenses included, financing, depreciation, capital items and personal expenses removed.
glossary.deep:
Reconstruction is translating the seller's numbers into the investor's language. Sellers show what helps them: a listing setup may skip vacancy and management; a tax return is loaded with interest, depreciation and one-time projects.

Like adjusting a used car's sticker for its real mileage: you are finding what the property itself actually produces.

Jordan's Bushwick reconstruction added 5% vacancy and a 5% management fee, then removed a $38,000 roof and $96,000 of mortgage payments. A meaningless $86,300 "net" became a real NOI of $190,000.

On the exam: know what to add (vacancy, management, reserves) and what to remove (debt service, depreciation, capital items, owner's personal costs, income tax).
glossary.contrast: A pro forma projects the future; a reconstructed statement restates current or historical performance.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: State laws that make recorded documents give public notice and decide priority between competing claims to the same property.
glossary.deep: Recording acts settle fights over the same land. New York's recording act (RPL 291) is race-notice: an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later buyer who pays value, has no notice of the earlier deed, and records first. So the race goes to the first good-faith purchaser to record. Recording also gives constructive notice to the world. In NYC, documents are recorded with the City Register through ACRIS; elsewhere, with the county clerk. On the exam: NY is race-notice; recording protects against later buyers but does not make a deed valid.
glossary.contrast: Constructive notice is the effect of recording; the recording act is the rule.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A preliminary offering plan submitted to the Attorney General but not yet accepted for filing, which may be distributed for information only.
glossary.deep:
Named for the red legend on its cover saying it is not an offer. It lets buyers and brokers see the project while the AG reviews it.

During this phase: no contracts, no deposits, no binding commitments. The final plan may differ.

NY example: Jordan gets a red herring for a Greenpoint conversion. He can walk clients through it, but no one can sign or pay anything yet.

On the exam: red herring = preliminary, informational only. A question that has a buyer signing a contract based on a red herring is describing a violation.
glossary.contrast: An accepted plan permits contracts and escrowed deposits.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A lender or insurer refusing or limiting loans or coverage in an area because of the race or ethnic makeup of its residents.
glossary.deep:
The name comes from 1930s federal maps that outlined Black and immigrant neighborhoods in red. Brooklyn's Bedford-Stuyvesant and much of Harlem were colored red, and loans dried up for decades.

Today it can look like a bank that rarely lends in certain zip codes, an insurer that will not write homeowner policies east of a certain avenue, or loan terms that worsen by neighborhood. Lenders may still deny loans for objective reasons such as credit or property condition.

On the exam: the key is the actor and the target. Redlining is done by lenders or insurers and targets an AREA, not an individual.
glossary.contrast: Steering is done by agents to buyers; blockbusting is done to owners.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A lender's refusal to make loans, or making loans on worse terms, in an area because of the racial or ethnic makeup of its residents. Illegal under the Fair Housing Act and ECOA.
glossary.deep:
The name comes from old maps where neighborhoods were outlined in red as "hazardous" for lending, often because of who lived there.

Like a store refusing to deliver to certain ZIP codes because of who lives there.

In the 1930s, federal maps redlined much of Bedford-Stuyvesant and Harlem, choking off credit for decades. Today, HMDA data and the Community Reinvestment Act help regulators spot it. Reverse redlining, pushing costly loans into those same areas, is also illegal.

On the exam: lenders redline; licensees steer.
glossary.contrast: Steering is a licensee directing buyers toward or away from areas based on protected class.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A deed given by a court-appointed referee in a court-ordered sale, such as a foreclosure or partition.
glossary.deep: In New York's judicial foreclosures and partition actions, the court appoints a referee to sell the property at auction. The referee signs the deed to the winning bidder. The referee makes no personal warranties; the deed conveys whatever title the court proceeding can pass. Buyers at foreclosure auctions should check title carefully, since senior liens survive. A Suffolk County foreclosure auction ends with a referee's deed. On the exam: foreclosure or partition = referee's deed.
glossary.contrast: An executor's deed comes from an estate sale.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A legal description that identifies land by referring to a lot on a recorded subdivision map (plat).
glossary.deep: A plat is a subdivision map filed in public records showing lots, blocks, streets, and dimensions. A deed that refers to it incorporates all of that detail, so the deed itself can be short. Developers file plats when they subdivide; once filed, buyers' deeds simply cite the lot. Streets shown on a plat may also be dedicated to the town by the filing. A deed describing "Lot 22 on Map No. 4512" makes a reference to a plat. On the exam: same idea as lot and block; the plat must be recorded.
glossary.contrast: A survey is a new drawing of the land's current boundaries and improvements.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A court's correction of a written document so it reflects what the parties actually agreed, usually because of a mutual mistake.
glossary.deep:
The deal is fine; the paperwork is wrong. The court fixes the paper.

Like correcting a typo in a wedding invitation, not cancelling the wedding.

A contract describes lot 14 when both sides meant lot 41 on the filed map in Clifton Park. Rather than void the contract, a court reforms it to say lot 41.

On the exam: reformation fixes, rescission cancels.
glossary.contrast: Rescission cancels the deal.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A large, usually enclosed shopping center anchored by two or more department stores and serving a wide region.
glossary.deep:
A regional mall is a destination: you drive there on purpose, often for an afternoon. It needs at least two department store anchors to pull shoppers from a wide trade area.

Think of the anchors as the tent poles holding up the whole tent. Lose one, and the fabric sags: in-line tenants often have co-tenancy rights to pay less rent if an anchor goes dark.

Queens Center in Elmhurst and Kings Plaza in Brooklyn are classic regional malls. Roughly 400,000 to 800,000 square feet.

On the exam: two or more department store anchors, wide trade area.
glossary.contrast: A mega (super-regional) mall is larger, with three or more anchors and entertainment.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The federal regulation implementing the Truth in Lending Act: it requires disclosure of credit costs (APR, finance charge), regulates credit advertising, and grants a right of rescission in certain loans.
glossary.deep:
Reg Z does not cap rates. It makes lenders show the true cost so borrowers can compare.

Like a nutrition label on a loan.

Covers consumer credit to individuals, including home loans; excludes business and commercial loans. It requires trigger-term disclosures in ads, which apply to real estate licensees who advertise financing, and the 3-day rescission on refinances of a principal residence. Enforced by the CFPB.

On the exam: Reg Z = TILA = disclosure, not rate control.
glossary.contrast: RESPA governs settlement costs and kickbacks; Reg B implements ECOA.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A clause in a blanket mortgage allowing individual parcels to be released from the lien as each is paid for.
glossary.deep:
It lets a developer sell lots one at a time with clear title.

Like removing one bead from a necklace without cutting the string.

A builder in Clifton Park finances 40 lots with one blanket mortgage. When a buyer closes on lot 12, the builder pays the lender the agreed release price (often more than the lot's pro rata share), and the lender releases lot 12 so the buyer gets clean title.

On the exam: blanket mortgage plus release clause go together.
glossary.contrast: A satisfaction releases the entire mortgage when the loan is fully paid.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The future interest of a third party who receives the property when a life estate ends; that person is the remainderman.
glossary.deep: A remainder is a future interest given to someone other than the grantor. In "to Noor for life, then to Sami," Sami is the remainderman. He has a real property interest now, even though he cannot possess the house until Noor dies. Because of that, a buyer needs Sami's signature to get fee simple, and Sami can sue Noor for waste if she damages the property. On the exam: remainder goes to a third party; reversion goes back to the grantor. Both follow a life estate.
glossary.contrast: A reversionary interest returns to the grantor or the grantor's heirs.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: An arrangement in which electricity is included in the rent, often at a set charge per rentable square foot adjusted by surveys or utility rate changes.
glossary.deep:
Rent inclusion folds electricity into the rent check. The tenant does not see a separate usage bill.

Like an all-you-can-eat buffet: the price is set by an estimate of how much people eat.

Older NYC office leases often include electricity at a dollar-per-RSF charge, with the right to run an electrical survey of the tenant's equipment and raise the charge. A tenant running servers around the clock benefits; the landlord carries usage risk unless the lease lets it adjust.

On the exam: rent inclusion = electricity in the rent; the tenant does not pay the utility.
glossary.contrast: Under direct metering the tenant pays the utility company itself.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A list of every unit with its tenant, lease dates, rent, deposit, and status.
glossary.deep:
The rent roll is a building's income snapshot. It shows potential gross income, vacancies, arrears, below-market leases, and upcoming expirations. Buyers, lenders, and appraisers ask for it first.

Like a class roster with each student's tuition status.

Sal's rent roll totals $12,850 a month and flags a vacant 1B, a late 2B, and a family member in 3A paying $1,500 with no deposit.

On the exam: the rent roll is the starting point for gross income and NOI.
glossary.contrast: An operating budget projects future income and expenses; the rent roll lists current leases.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: NY system limiting rent increases and guaranteeing lease renewals for covered apartments, mostly in buildings of 6+ units built before 1974.
glossary.deep:
Rent stabilization does not freeze rent. It caps the yearly increase and gives tenants the right to renew.

Think of it as a speed limit on rent increases plus a guaranteed seat on the bus.

Roughly a million NYC apartments are stabilized. The NYC Rent Guidelines Board votes each year on the allowed increase for 1- and 2-year renewals; the tenant chooses which. NYS Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) administers and registers rents. Nassau, Westchester, and Rockland have units under their own county boards.

On the exam: ETPA 1974, Rent Guidelines Board, HCR, tenant's choice of 1 or 2 years.
glossary.contrast: Rent control is an older, stricter system for tenants in place since before 1971 in pre-1947 buildings.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The area a tenant pays rent on: its usable space plus a proportionate share of the building's common areas.
glossary.deep:
Rentable is the landlord's number. It includes your space and your slice of the lobby, corridors, restrooms and mechanical rooms you share with everyone.

Like a condo's common charges: you pay toward the hallway and the roof even though you never "own" them alone.

Leo's Flatiron floor is advertised at 10,000 RSF; he can actually use 8,000. At $60 per RSF, his rent is $600,000 a year. NYC office rent is quoted per RSF per year.

On the exam: rentable is always larger than usable, and proportionate shares for escalations use RSF.
glossary.contrast: Usable square footage is only the tenant's exclusive space.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Coverage that pays to repair or replace damaged property with new materials of like kind and quality, without deducting for depreciation.
glossary.deep:
Replacement cost puts you back with new materials, not used ones.

Your 6-year-old TV is stolen; replacement cost buys you a comparable new TV.

Sal's $40,000 kitchen fire is paid at full replacement cost, minus his deductible, as long as he carries dwelling coverage of at least 80% of the rebuild cost. If he is underinsured, the coinsurance clause cuts his payout.

On the exam: replacement cost costs more in premium than ACV and usually requires meeting the 80% rule.
glossary.contrast: Actual cash value subtracts depreciation.
glossary.subject: s12

glossary.def: The cost to build an exact replica of the building with the same materials and design. Replacement cost is the cost to build one of equal utility with modern materials.
glossary.deep:
Reproduction is a carbon copy; replacement is a modern equivalent.

Reprinting an antique book on the same paper with the same type is reproduction; publishing the same text as a paperback is replacement.

A landmarked Brooklyn Heights brownstone with hand-carved brownstone and plaster moldings would cost far more to reproduce than to replace with a modern building of the same size and function.

On the exam: both are "cost new" in the cost approach. Replacement is more common because it skips outdated features.
glossary.contrast: Replacement cost: equal utility, modern materials.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: Cancelling a contract and returning the parties to where they were before it was made.
glossary.deep:
Unwinding: money goes back, property goes back.

Like returning a jacket for a full refund.

A seller hid a known illegal third unit and the buyer discovers fraud before closing; the buyer can seek rescission and get the down payment back. TILA also gives a 3-business-day right of rescission on certain refinances.

On the exam: rescission undoes the deal; specific performance enforces it.
glossary.contrast: Reformation keeps the contract but corrects its wording.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Money a condo or co-op sets aside for major repairs and capital replacements.
glossary.deep:
The reserve fund is the building's savings account for the roof, boiler, elevators, and facade. Strong reserves mean fewer surprise assessments.

Read it in the financial statements against the building's size and age, and look in board minutes for upcoming projects like Local Law 11 facade work or Local Law 97 energy upgrades.

NY example: a 100-unit prewar co-op with $250,000 in reserves and a facade repair estimated at $2 million is headed for an assessment.

On the exam: reserve fund appears in due diligence questions about financial statements and minutes.
glossary.contrast: Working capital is a cash cushion for operations; reserves fund capital projects.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Money set aside each year to pay for replacing short-lived building components such as roofs, boilers and appliances.
glossary.deep:
Reserves are the building's savings account. Instead of being shocked by a $60,000 boiler in year 12, the owner sets aside a slice every year.

Like putting $50 a month in a jar for a new laptop you know you will need in three years.

Appraisers and lenders often include a reserve line in operating expenses (for example, a few hundred dollars per apartment per year). New York co-op boards keep a reserve fund for the same reason.

On the exam: reserves are part of operating expenses in an appraiser's reconstruction; the actual replacement later is a capital expense.
glossary.contrast: Security deposits belong to tenants and are not reserves.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A manager who lives on the property, typically a salaried employee of the owner, and who generally needs no license when acting only for that owner.
glossary.deep:
The resident manager (often the superintendent in NYC) handles on-site work: rent collection, showing vacancies, supervising repairs. Because they act as the owner's own employee for the owner's own building, they ride on the owner's exemption from licensing.

Like a family business employee who sells the family's own products: no separate dealer license needed.

Vinnie, Sal's live-in super, collects rents for Sal only. No license. If a management firm paid Vinnie per lease to rent units in other owners' buildings, he would need one.

On the exam: resident manager employed by owner = exempt; outside manager for a fee = broker license.
glossary.contrast: A property management company acting for many owners for a fee must be licensed.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: A recorded promise limiting how land may be used, typically binding every lot in a subdivision and enforceable by the other owners.
glossary.deep:
A restrictive covenant is a neighborhood-wide promise. A developer records a declaration before selling lots: minimum house size, approved fence styles, no sheds in front yards. Each deed references it, so the covenant runs with the land and binds each new owner. Owners or the HOA enforce it, usually by injunction.

Analogy: a group lease every homeowner signed without the landlord. NY example: a Long Island subdivision from the 1980s bans above-ground pools; a new buyer installs one; the HOA sues and gets an order to remove it. Delay can hurt enforcement under laches.

On the exam: covenants are private, enforced by neighbors, and stricter controls win. Covenants restricting sale by race are unenforceable.
glossary.contrast: A deed restriction is often a one-off in a single deed; a restrictive covenant usually binds a whole subdivision through a recorded declaration.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A commercial lease for store space, often net with CAM charges, sometimes with percentage rent, and focused on use, signage, hours and co-tenancy.
glossary.deep:
A retail lease is about the storefront and the sales it generates.

Like a partnership with the landlord where location is the main ingredient: the landlord provides traffic, the tenant provides the shop.

An Astoria bakery's lease might set $72,000 base rent plus 6% of sales above $1.2 million, a use clause limited to bakery and cafe, signage rules and direct-metered electricity. In malls, CAM charges, radius clauses and co-tenancy rights are common.

On the exam: retail leases are where percentage rent and natural breakpoints appear.
glossary.contrast: Office leases center on RSF and escalations rather than sales.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A loan for older owners (62+ for the FHA-insured HECM) that pays the owner from home equity; repaid when the owner sells, moves out, or dies.
glossary.deep:
A mortgage running backward: the lender pays you.

Like slowly cashing out a savings account that is your house.

A retired couple in Bayside with a paid-off $900,000 house take a reverse mortgage paying monthly. The balance grows over time. They keep title and must pay taxes, insurance, and upkeep. When they die, the heirs sell or refinance to repay; the FHA-insured version is non-recourse, so heirs never owe more than the home's value.

On the exam: owner receives payments; balance rises; due on sale, move, or death.
glossary.contrast: A home equity loan requires the owner to make payments.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A 1031 exchange in which the replacement property is acquired before the relinquished property is sold.
glossary.deep:
Sometimes the perfect replacement appears before you have a buyer. In a reverse exchange, an exchange accommodation titleholder takes title to one of the properties ("parks" it) so the investor is never owning both outright. The investor has 45 days to identify which property will be sold and 180 days to complete the exchange.

Like putting a deposit on the new apartment before you sublet the old one, with a third party holding the keys.

Evelyn finds a Bayside strip center before her Flushing building sells; an EAT parks the strip center.

On the exam: reverse = buy first; same 45/180 time limits.
glossary.contrast: A forward (delayed) exchange sells first and buys later.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: The grantor's future interest in property that returns to the grantor or the grantor's heirs when a lesser estate, such as a life estate or lease, ends.
glossary.deep: A reversion is property coming home. If a father deeds his house "to my daughter for her life" and names no one else, the house reverts to the father or his heirs when the daughter dies. A landlord also holds a reversion: when a lease ends, possession returns to the owner. Think of a boomerang. On the exam: if no remainderman is named after a life estate, the future interest is a reversion. Remainder = third party; reversion = back to grantor.
glossary.contrast: A remainder interest goes to a named third party.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: An attachment to a contract or lease that adds or changes terms. If it conflicts with the printed form, the rider controls.
glossary.deep:
The printed form is the base; the rider is the custom part.

Like handwritten notes on a recipe that override the printed steps.

NYC residential contracts typically run on a standard form with a long rider negotiated by the attorneys: closing timeline, appliances, repairs, co-op board approval. Brokers do not draft riders because drafting legal terms is the practice of law.

On the exam: rider wins over the form; attorneys draft riders.
glossary.contrast: An addendum is often used the same way; a merger clause limits the deal to the written terms, riders included.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The horizontal member at the peak of a roof where the upper ends of the rafters meet.
glossary.deep:
The ridge is the roof's top line. A ridge board is a non-structural nailer that rafters butt against; a true ridge beam is sized to carry the rafter loads itself, common with cathedral ceilings. Either way, it defines the peak.

Analogy: the spine of an open book standing on its pages. NY example: a sagging ridge line seen from the street on an old Catskills cabin tells an inspector the rafters are spreading or the ridge is undersized, a structural red flag.

On the exam: ridge beam equals the peak where rafters meet. Ridge vents run along it to exhaust attic air.
glossary.contrast: The eave is the lower edge of the roof; the ridge is the top.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A right to buy or lease property on the same terms another buyer has agreed to, before that sale can close. In condos, the board usually holds it.
glossary.deep:
It is a matching right, not a veto. When a condo owner signs a contract, the board gets a set period (often about 30 days) to buy the unit on the same terms. If it passes, the sale proceeds and the board issues a waiver.

Boards rarely exercise it because it means buying with building money. Its real effect is formal: the buyer's attorney needs the waiver at closing.

NY example: Priya asks the LIC managing agent for the waiver before Leo's closing.

On the exam: condo boards have a right of first refusal; co-op boards approve or reject buyers.
glossary.contrast: Co-op board approval lets a board reject a buyer outright; a right of first refusal only lets it match the deal.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A borrower's right to cancel a refinance or home equity loan secured by a principal residence until midnight of the third business day after closing or receiving disclosures.
glossary.deep:
A cooling-off period for borrowing against the home you live in.

Like a 3-day return window on an expensive purchase.

A Bayside owner closes a HELOC Thursday. Saturdays count as business days for rescission, so she can cancel until midnight Monday. No money is disbursed until the period ends. A buyer's purchase-money mortgage has no rescission right, nor do business loans or second homes.

On the exam: refinance and home equity on principal residence only; 3 business days.
glossary.contrast: Contract rescission is a court remedy; TILA rescission is a statutory cooling-off right.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The feature of joint tenancy and tenancy by the entirety under which a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving co-owners.
glossary.deep: Survivorship is like a game of musical chairs where the last person standing gets everything. When one joint tenant dies, the share does not go through the will or probate; it simply merges into the survivors' interests. The last survivor owns in severalty. A will cannot override it: a joint tenant who leaves her share to her son leaves him nothing in that property. On the exam: survivorship belongs to joint tenancy and tenancy by the entirety, never to tenancy in common.
glossary.contrast: In a tenancy in common, a share passes to the owner's heirs or devisees.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A right to pass over another's land, or a strip of land used for a road, railroad, or utility line.
glossary.deep:
A right-of-way is the most common type of easement: the right to cross. It also means the strip itself, such as the public right-of-way that includes the street, the curb and often the sidewalk and a few feet of what looks like your front lawn.

Analogy: a reserved lane through someone else's property. NY example: a Westchester homeowner plants a hedge 4 feet from the curb and learns the town's right-of-way runs 10 feet in; the highway department can remove it for road work. In subdivision review, the planning board fixes right-of-way widths for new streets.

On the exam: a right-of-way is an easement and an encumbrance. Questions may describe access to a landlocked lot.
glossary.contrast: Setback is a zoning distance you cannot build in; a right-of-way is land someone else has a right to use or that belongs to the public road.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Rights of owners whose land borders flowing water, such as a river or stream, to reasonable use of the water.
glossary.deep: Riparian owners border moving water. They may make reasonable use of it (swimming, fishing, docking, watering a garden) but may not unreasonably interfere with downstream owners. On a non-navigable stream, the owner usually owns to the center line; on a navigable river like the Hudson, the state owns the bed and the owner holds to the water's edge. New York follows the riparian doctrine, not the western prior appropriation system. On the exam: riparian = river; it gives use of water, not ownership of the water itself. Accretion along a riverbank belongs to the riparian owner.
glossary.contrast: Littoral rights apply to lakes, ponds, and oceans.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The chance that an investment's actual return will differ from what was expected, including the chance of losing money.
glossary.deep:
Risk is uncertainty about what you will actually get back. A Treasury bond pays what it promises; a building pays what its tenants, the market and the boiler allow.

Think of two lunch spots: one has fed the same office crowd for 20 years, the other just opened on a quiet block. Both might earn the same this year, but you would only lend money to the new one at a higher rate.

In New York, a Walgreens on a 20-year net lease in Queens is low risk; a half-empty Class C office floor in Midtown is high risk. Investors price that difference through the cap rate.

On the exam: higher risk means investors demand a higher return, which means a higher cap rate and a lower price.
glossary.contrast: Liquidity is about how fast you can sell, not how uncertain the return is, though illiquidity is one kind of risk.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Identifying possible losses and choosing to avoid, control, transfer, or retain each risk.
glossary.deep:
Every building has risks: fire, slips, crime, floods, lawsuits. The four strategies: avoid (do not do the risky thing), control (reduce odds or severity), transfer (insurance, contracts), retain (accept small risks, pay from reserves).

ACTR: Avoid, Control, Transfer, Retain.

Jordan addresses a space heater in 2B (control), confirms Sal's liability policy (transfer), and keeps a $2,500 deductible (retain).

On the exam: insurance = transfer; sprinklers or locks = control; closing an amenity = avoid; deductible = retain.
glossary.contrast: Insurance is one tool of risk management, not the whole of it.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: Electrical cable with insulated conductors and a ground wire inside a plastic sheath; the most common wiring in new suburban homes.
glossary.deep:
Romex is a brand name that became the generic term for NM cable. It is cheap and quick to install in wood-frame houses, run through holes drilled in studs and joists. It must be protected where exposed to damage. Many NYC building types restrict it in favor of metal-clad cable or conduit.

Analogy: wires in a plastic sleeve rather than armor. NY example: a new colonial in Clifton Park is wired almost entirely with yellow and white Romex; the electrical inspector checks it at the rough-in stage before insulation goes in.

On the exam: Romex equals nonmetallic sheathed cable.
glossary.contrast: BX has a metal jacket; Romex has a plastic one.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: NY law letting a residential tenant share the apartment with immediate family plus one additional occupant and that occupant's dependent children.
glossary.deep:
Landlords cannot use the lease to stop tenants from having roommates.

Picture a lease that says "tenant and no one else". In NY, that clause is unenforceable.

A tenant on a one-name lease in Sunnyside can live with her brother (immediate family) and one roommate. If two tenants signed the lease, the total number of tenants plus occupants generally cannot exceed the number of tenants named on the lease. The tenant or spouse must occupy the unit as a primary residence, and the landlord can request occupants' names.

On the exam: no-roommate clauses are void in NY.
glossary.contrast: A sublet transfers possession while the tenant is away; a roommate lives with the tenant.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A USDA agency that guarantees or makes loans for low- and moderate-income buyers in eligible rural areas, often with no down payment.
glossary.deep:
Government help for rural buyers.

Like a VA loan, but for small-town households instead of veterans.

A family in Allegany County earning under the area income limit buys a house with a USDA guaranteed loan and no down payment. Very low-income buyers may qualify for direct loans from the agency itself. Large parts of upstate NY are eligible; NYC is not.

On the exam: RHS = rural, income limits, guaranteed or direct.
glossary.contrast: SONYMA is a NY state program; RHS is federal.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The 1974 federal law setting standards for public drinking water systems and protecting underground drinking water sources.
glossary.deep:
The SDWA requires public water systems to meet contaminant limits (bacteria, lead, chemicals), test regularly, and notify customers of problems. States, through agencies like the NYS Department of Health, enforce it. It does not regulate private household wells, which are the owner's responsibility. Its Lead and Copper Rule drives utilities to replace lead service lines.

Analogy: the health inspector for your tap. NY example: NYC's unfiltered Catskill and Delaware supply operates under a filtration avoidance determination that depends on protecting the upstate watershed.

On the exam: SDWA equals public water systems; private wells excluded.
glossary.contrast: The Clean Water Act regulates pollution discharges into rivers and wetlands; the SDWA regulates drinking water.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A sale in which the buyer takes title with the existing mortgage still in place but does not become personally liable for the debt.
glossary.deep:
The loan stays on the house; the buyer just does not sign up for it.

Like buying a car with a lien still on it, knowing the lender can take the car but cannot chase you.

A Utica buyer takes a duplex subject to the seller's loan and makes the payments. If she stops, the lender forecloses; she loses the property and her equity but owes no deficiency. The seller remains liable on the note. A due-on-sale clause lets the lender call the loan anyway.

On the exam: subject to = buyer risks only the property.
glossary.contrast: In an assumption, the buyer becomes personally liable.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An owner sells property to an investor and leases it back, freeing up capital while keeping use of the property.
glossary.deep:
Sell the building, stay in it.

Like selling your car and leasing it back so you have cash and still drive.

A Bronx manufacturer sells its factory to Evelyn Park for $12 million and signs a 20-year net lease to stay. The company gets cash for operations and deducts rent; Evelyn gets a long-term tenant. It works as financing without a mortgage.

On the exam: sale-leaseback = financing technique; seller becomes tenant.
glossary.contrast: A ground lease never transfers ownership of the land.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Estimating value by comparing the subject to recent sales of similar properties and adjusting each comparable for differences.
glossary.deep:
This is how most homes are valued. A buyer will not pay more than the price of an equally good substitute.

It is shopping for the same sneakers at three stores and adjusting for which one includes free shipping.

Comp sold for $640,000 with a parking space worth $30,000 the subject lacks: subtract. It has a half bath where the subject has a full bath worth $10,000 more: add. Adjusted, $620,000.

On the exam: adjust the comparable, never the subject. Comp better, subtract; comp poorer, add. Best for homes, condos, co-ops, and vacant land.
glossary.contrast: Cost approach: land plus depreciated cost to build.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: The federal limit on itemized deductions for state and local taxes, including property tax: $40,000 for 2025 and $40,400 for 2026, reduced at high incomes, scheduled to return to $10,000 in 2030.
glossary.deep:
SALT stands for state and local taxes: property tax plus income (or sales) tax. From 2018 to 2024 the cap was $10,000. The 2025 tax law raised it to $40,000 for 2025, increasing 1% a year through 2029, with a phase-down for incomes over about $500,000 (never below $10,000). In 2030 it reverts to $10,000.

Think of it as a box: all your state and local taxes go in, but the IRS only counts what fits.

A Scarsdale couple paying $28,000 property tax and $20,000 NY income tax: $48,000 total, but in 2026 only $40,400 counts (if under the income threshold).

On the exam: older items say $10,000. Know both numbers.
glossary.contrast: Mortgage interest is deducted separately and is not subject to the SALT cap.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: The 1986 law that amended CERCLA, added Superfund money, and created the innocent landowner defense.
glossary.deep:
SARA softened CERCLA's harshest edge for careful buyers. A buyer who did all appropriate inquiry before purchasing, and did not know or have reason to know of contamination, can claim the innocent landowner defense. SARA also boosted funding and added community right-to-know rules. The 2002 Brownfields Act added the bona fide prospective purchaser defense, even for buyers who knew of contamination, if they meet conditions.

Analogy: CERCLA is the trap; SARA is the escape hatch for those who looked first. NY example: a Buffalo industrial buyer with a clean Phase I later finds buried drums and invokes the innocent landowner defense.

On the exam: SARA equals innocent landowner defense.
glossary.contrast: CERCLA created the liability; SARA created the defense.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A document from the lender stating the debt is paid in full; recorded to remove the mortgage lien.
glossary.deep:
The receipt that clears the public record.

Like the stamped "paid" on a final car loan statement.

When the Okafors sell, their remaining loan is paid from the proceeds at closing. The lender must deliver a satisfaction, which is recorded at the City Register through ACRIS. NY law requires lenders to deliver it promptly after payoff and imposes penalties for delay. Without it, the old mortgage still clouds title.

On the exam: satisfaction = release of the lien after payoff (the defeasance clause requires it).
glossary.contrast: An assignment transfers the mortgage; a satisfaction ends it.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The market where existing loans are bought, sold, and pooled into mortgage-backed securities by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and investors.
glossary.deep:
Where loans go after they are made.

Like a used-car market, but for mortgages.

Leo's lender sells his conforming loan to Fannie Mae, which pools it with thousands of others into securities sold to pension funds. The lender gets its cash back and lends to the next buyer. Uniform underwriting standards exist so loans can be sold this way. Ginnie Mae guarantees securities made of government loans.

On the exam: secondary market provides liquidity; borrowers' terms do not change.
glossary.contrast: The primary market originates loans.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Money the tenant gives the landlord to secure performance of the lease. In NY residential leases it is capped at one month's rent and must be returned within 14 days of move-out with an itemized statement.
glossary.deep:
The deposit is the tenant's money held as protection, not extra rent.

Like a deposit on a rented tuxedo: returned if it comes back in shape.

Since HSTPA (2019): max one month, statewide. The landlord must offer a walk-through before move-in and before move-out, then return the balance within 14 days with itemized deductions or lose the right to keep any of it. In buildings with 6 or more units, deposits go into an interest-bearing account; the landlord may keep 1% a year as an administrative fee. Deposits may not be commingled with the landlord's own money.

On the exam: 1 month, 14 days.
glossary.contrast: Last month's rent paid in advance is rent, not a security deposit.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: An agent profiting from the client's transaction for themselves, such as secretly buying the listing directly or through a relative or company.
glossary.deep:
Self-dealing is when the agent sits on both sides of the deal for their own benefit.

Like an auctioneer secretly bidding on the item through a friend.

Marcus underprices a Bensonhurst listing, then has his LLC buy it and flips it six months later. Even if the price seemed fair, he never disclosed he was the buyer. That is self-dealing and a loyalty breach.

On the exam: an agent may buy a client's property only after full written disclosure to the client that the agent (or a relative or entity) is the buyer.
glossary.contrast: Dual agency is representing both sides with consent; self-dealing is serving yourself without disclosure.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: An agent who represents the seller, usually under a listing agreement.
glossary.deep:
The seller's agent works to get the seller the best price and terms.

Like a sports agent negotiating a player's contract with the team.

Hudson & Hart is the Okafors' seller's agent. It markets the brownstone, advises on price, keeps the Okafors' motives private, and tells buyers about known defects. A buyer who asks "would they take less?" gets no answer.

On the exam: RPL 443 says a seller's agent must deal with buyers honestly, fairly, and in good faith and disclose known facts materially affecting value or desirability.
glossary.contrast: Buyer's agent represents the buyer; listing agent is the seller's agent who took the listing.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A local-option NY exemption (RPTL 467) of up to 50% of assessed value for owners 65 or older whose income is below a limit set by the locality within a state maximum.
glossary.deep:
It lowers the bill for older owners on limited incomes so they can stay in their homes.

Like a senior discount at the movies, but sliding: the lower the income, the bigger the discount.

An 81-year-old widow in Westchester with a small pension gets 50% off her assessment. When she sells, the exemption ends and the buyer's bill could jump by thousands. That is why agents recompute taxes for buyers.

On the exam: 65+, income-tested, local option, up to 50%, does not transfer.
glossary.contrast: Enhanced STAR also requires age 65+, but reduces only school taxes.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: An on-site wastewater system: a tank where solids settle and break down, and an absorption field where liquid filters through the soil.
glossary.deep:
Where there is no sewer, the house treats its own waste. The septic tank separates solids (sludge on the bottom, scum on top) and lets bacteria digest them; clarified liquid flows to a leach field or seepage pits. In New York, systems must meet Department of Health standards, be designed by a licensed professional engineer or registered architect, and be approved by the local or county health department, which usually keeps as-built drawings.

Analogy: a home sewage plant in the backyard. NY example: a Suffolk buyer's inspection finds a cesspool rather than a modern system; Suffolk now pushes upgrades to nitrogen-reducing systems to protect the aquifer.

On the exam: Department of Health, PE design, perc test, pump every few years.
glossary.contrast: A municipal sewer carries waste away to a treatment plant; a septic system treats it on site.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: New York law requiring state and local agencies to consider environmental impacts before approving, funding, or undertaking an action.
glossary.deep:
SEQRA makes government look before it leaps. Any agency approval, from a rezoning to a subdivision to a big site plan, is an action. Minor actions (Type II, such as a single-family home or an area variance for a house) skip review. Others go through an Environmental Assessment Form; the lead agency then issues a negative declaration (no significant impact) or a positive declaration, which requires a full environmental impact statement.

Analogy: a pre-flight checklist for development. NY example: a Hudson Valley warehouse project drew a positive declaration over truck traffic and wetlands, and the EIS process added a year.

On the exam: know the lead agency, positive vs negative declaration, and that SEQRA applies to local boards.
glossary.contrast: NEPA is the federal version for federal actions; SEQRA covers New York state and local agency actions.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The parcel burdened by an easement, over which the easement holder has the right to use.
glossary.deep: The servient tenement serves someone else's need. Its owner keeps title and can use the land in any way that does not interfere with the easement. A homeowner whose backyard carries a utility line, or whose driveway the neighbor may cross, owns a servient tenement. Selling it does not end the easement. Every easement, appurtenant or in gross, has a servient tenement. On the exam: the servient owner cannot block the easement; a buyer of servient land takes subject to it.
glossary.contrast: The dominant tenement benefits.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Zoning rules requiring buildings to be a minimum distance from front, side and rear lot lines.
glossary.deep:
Setbacks create breathing room: light, air, fire separation and privacy. A front setback keeps houses aligned along the street; side and rear yards keep neighbors apart.

Analogy: personal space for buildings. NY example: a Great Neck R-district requires a 30-foot front yard and 10-foot side yards. An owner who wants a garage 6 feet from the side line needs an area variance from the ZBA. In NYC, rear yard rules typically require 30 feet in many residence districts.

On the exam: building into a setback needs an area variance, not a use variance. Surveys reveal setback violations.
glossary.contrast: An easement is someone's right to use your land; a setback is an area where you cannot build on your own land.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Ownership of property by one person or one legal entity alone.
glossary.deep: Severalty comes from "sever": the owner's interest is cut off from anyone else's. It sounds like "several" but means exactly one owner. A single buyer who takes title alone owns in severalty, and so does a corporation or LLC that owns a building, even though it has many shareholders or members. When a severalty owner dies, the property passes by will or intestacy, not by survivorship. The last surviving joint tenant also ends up owning in severalty. On the exam: the classic trap is reading severalty as "several owners." It means one.
glossary.contrast: Tenancy in common and joint tenancy are forms of co-ownership by two or more people.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A loan to buy co-op shares, secured by the shares and proprietary lease and perfected by a UCC-1 filing rather than a recorded mortgage.
glossary.deep:
It looks like a mortgage to the borrower, same rates and terms, but legally it is a secured loan on personal property. The lender holds the stock certificate and lease and files a UCC-1.

Because no mortgage is recorded, there is no mortgage recording tax, which can save a NYC buyer close to 2% of the loan.

NY example: a $862,500 share loan on West End Avenue pays no MRT. The same loan on a condo would pay about $16,600.

On the exam: share loan = co-op financing, UCC, recognition agreement, no MRT.
glossary.contrast: A mortgage is a lien on real property; a share loan is a security interest in personal property.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A loan in which the lender or an investor receives a share of the property's appreciation in exchange for a lower rate or help with the purchase.
glossary.deep:
You trade part of your future gain for help now.

Like a startup giving an investor equity instead of paying interest.

Leo's parents put $60,000 toward his condo under an agreement giving them 20% of any appreciation when he sells. Some programs and lenders offer below-market rates for a share of future gain.

If he sells for $850,000, the $100,000 gain gives his parents $20,000. If the price falls, they share nothing. The trade-off: cheaper money now, less profit later.

On the exam: shared equity = shared appreciation.
glossary.contrast: A pledged account mortgage uses the borrower's own deposit as extra security.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Stock in a cooperative housing corporation allocated to a specific apartment, which determines the shareholder's share of maintenance and votes.
glossary.deep:
Each apartment carries a block of shares, larger for bigger, higher, or better units. The shares are the ownership; the proprietary lease is the right to live there. They always travel together.

Share count drives maintenance (your share of the building's costs, taxes, and mortgage) and the tax deduction you can take for the building's taxes and interest.

NY example: a West End Avenue two-bedroom carries 420 of the building's 30,000 shares, or 1.4%.

On the exam: shares are personal property. Buyers "purchase shares," they do not "take title."
glossary.contrast: A condo's common interest percentage is the real property equivalent.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Panels of plywood or OSB (or older boards) nailed over studs and rafters, adding rigidity and forming a base for siding or roofing.
glossary.deep:
Sheathing is the house's first skin. On walls it braces the studs against racking and holds the siding; on the roof it is the deck the shingles nail into. A weather barrier like housewrap goes over wall sheathing.

Analogy: the cardboard under the wrapping paper. NY example: a roofer stripping old shingles in Rochester finds soft, delaminated plywood sheathing from years of poor attic ventilation and adds the cost of new decking to the estimate.

On the exam: sheathing goes over framing, under the finish (siding or roofing).
glossary.contrast: Siding is the finished exterior layer; sheathing is the structural layer beneath it.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: NY's Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security Act (General Business Law 899-aa and 899-bb), requiring businesses that hold NY residents' private information to keep reasonable safeguards and give notice of breaches.
glossary.deep:
The SHIELD Act makes data security a legal duty, not just good practice.

If you hold someone's house keys, you are expected to lock them up; this law says the same about their data.

A Brooklyn brokerage stores buyers' pre-approval letters, bank statements, and driver's license copies. It must use reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, and if a laptop with that data is stolen unencrypted, it must notify affected people.

On the exam: NY requires reasonable safeguards and breach notification for private information such as SSNs, license numbers, and account numbers.
glossary.contrast: Identity theft is the harm; the SHIELD Act is the duty to prevent and report it.
glossary.subject: s13

glossary.def: The exterior finish on walls: wood clapboard or shingle, vinyl, aluminum, fiber cement, or masonry veneer.
glossary.deep:
Siding is the face the house shows the street and the first barrier against rain. Each type has trade-offs: wood is classic but needs paint; vinyl is cheap and low maintenance but can crack and fade; aluminum dents; fiber cement is durable and fire-resistant.

Analogy: the house's jacket. NY example: older asbestos-cement shingle siding is common on mid-century Long Island and upstate homes. It is usually non-friable and safe if left intact, but cutting or sanding it releases fibers.

On the exam: siding is the outer layer, over sheathing and housewrap.
glossary.contrast: Sheathing is underneath and structural; siding is the outer finish.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The first horizontal wood member laid flat on the foundation wall and bolted to it; the base of the wood frame.
glossary.deep:
The sill plate is where wood meets masonry. It is usually pressure-treated lumber, set on a sill sealer and fastened with anchor bolts cast into the concrete, so the frame cannot slide or lift off. Floor joists rest on it.

Analogy: the hinge between the masonry legs and the wooden body. NY example: termites and rot love sill plates because they sit lowest and closest to soil moisture; a Westchester inspector probes the sill with a screwdriver and finds it soft, a costly repair.

On the exam: lowest wood member, sits on the foundation.
glossary.contrast: A girder runs mid-basement on columns; the sill sits on top of the foundation wall.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A closing where a buyer takes title from the sponsor and resells to a new buyer on the same day.
glossary.deep:
It is the mechanics of a flip at the closing table: two deeds, one day. The original buyer may use the new buyer's money to pay the sponsor.

Many sponsors prohibit or restrict simultaneous closings, especially early in sales, to protect their pricing.

NY example: an investor who contracted for a Brooklyn condo in 2023 wants to close and resell the same afternoon; the plan requires sponsor consent and an assignment fee.

On the exam: know it as a flipping technique governed by the sponsor's policy in the offering plan.
glossary.contrast: An assignment transfers the contract before closing; a simultaneous closing closes twice the same day.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Representing only one party in a transaction, never both.
glossary.deep:
Single agency is the cleanest arrangement: you are on one team only.

Like a defense attorney who never also works for the prosecution.

Jordan represents Leo as buyer's agent on a Prospect Heights co-op listed by another firm. Jordan gives Leo full advice, undivided loyalty, and confidentiality, and deals honestly with the seller.

On the exam: "A single agency broker represents either the buyer or the seller in a transaction but never both."
glossary.contrast: Dual agency represents both sides with consent.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Planning board review of the layout of a proposed project on a single lot: parking, access, landscaping, lighting, drainage, and building placement.
glossary.deep:
Even when a use is permitted, many towns require site plan approval for anything beyond a single-family house. The board looks at how the project sits on the land: where cars enter, how many parking spaces, whether lights glare into neighbors' bedrooms, where stormwater goes, and what screening is planted.

Analogy: the use is allowed, now show us the floor plan of the lot. NY example: a CVS in a Rockland County commercial zone is a permitted use, but the planning board still requires changes to the driveway location and a landscaped buffer along the residential side.

On the exam: site plan review is a planning board function and does not change what uses are allowed.
glossary.contrast: Subdivision review divides land into lots; site plan review lays out a project on one lot.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Estimating the value of land as if vacant and available for its highest and best use, separate from any buildings.
glossary.deep:
Site valuation prices the dirt alone.

Imagine lifting the house off the lot with a crane. What would a builder pay for what is left?

For the parish firehouse, Jordan finds three vacant lot sales nearby at about $100 per square foot of land. The 4,000 square foot lot is worth about $400,000. That number feeds the cost approach, where land is added back after depreciating the building.

On the exam: land is valued as if vacant and is never depreciated. Sales of comparable vacant lots are the preferred method.
glossary.contrast: The cost approach values land plus depreciated building; site valuation is the land step only.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: The economic characteristic that people prefer certain locations; considered the most important factor in value.
glossary.deep: Situs is location preference: why the same 2,000-square-foot house is worth far more on a tree-lined block near a good school and the subway than on a busy truck route. It is the economic side of the old saying "location, location, location." Preferences can change: Williamsburg's situs rose sharply over two decades without the land itself changing. On the exam: situs, also called area preference, is the economic characteristic with the greatest effect on value. The other economic ones are scarcity, improvements, and permanence of investment.
glossary.contrast: Immobility is a physical fact; situs is buyers' preference.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A foundation in which a concrete slab is poured directly on prepared ground, serving as the floor, with no basement or crawl space.
glossary.deep:
Slab-on-grade is the simplest foundation: compact gravel, lay a vapor barrier and often rigid insulation, pour concrete with thickened edges acting as footings. Cheaper and faster, but plumbing in the slab is hard to reach and there is nowhere to put mechanicals except inside the living space or a garage.

Analogy: a house sitting on a concrete plate. NY example: many attached garages and some 1950s Levittown houses were built on slabs with radiant heat pipes embedded in the concrete, which can leak and are costly to repair.

On the exam: no basement, no crawl space, the slab is the floor.
glossary.contrast: A basement floor is also a slab, but it sits inside full-height foundation walls below grade.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A low-cost, informal hearing before a hearing officer for owners of owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes who first filed a grievance. Filed with the county clerk, generally within 30 days after the final roll, for $30.
glossary.deep:
SCAR is small claims court for homeowners' assessments: no lawyer needed.

Think of it as the people's court for tax bills.

The Okafors' cousin loses at the BAR, files a SCAR petition with the Suffolk County Clerk within 30 days of the final roll, pays $30, and brings comparable sales, her property record card, and the town's equalization rate to an informal hearing.

On the exam: residential only; must grieve first; evidence is sales information, assessment information, and assessment ratios; decisions match the BAR's; choosing SCAR waives certiorari; review is by Article 78.
glossary.contrast: Tax certiorari: a formal court proceeding for anyone, mainly commercial owners.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: A three-way agreement in which the tenant subordinates its lease to the landlord's mortgage, the lender agrees not to disturb a tenant in good standing after foreclosure, and the tenant agrees to attorn to the new owner.
glossary.deep:
An SNDA is a peace treaty among landlord, lender and tenant. The lender gets priority (subordination) and a tenant who will keep paying a new owner (attornment). The tenant gets security that a foreclosure will not end its lease (non-disturbance).

Like a sports team being sold: the new owner keeps the players' contracts, and the players agree to play for the new owner.

A restaurant spending $400,000 on a build-out in Long Island City should insist on non-disturbance from the landlord's lender before signing.

On the exam: know each of the three parts separately.
glossary.contrast: An estoppel certificate confirms lease facts; an SNDA sets priority and post-foreclosure rights.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The underside of a roof overhang (eave), often perforated or vented to bring air into the attic.
glossary.deep:
Look up when you stand under the eave: that ceiling is the soffit. Vented soffits are the intake half of an attic ventilation system; air enters there and exits at ridge or gable vents, keeping the attic dry and the roof cold in winter.

Analogy: the underside of the cap's brim, with breathing holes. NY example: a Westchester inspector notes that new attic insulation was stuffed against the soffits, blocking airflow, which explains the moldy roof sheathing.

On the exam: soffit is under the eave; fascia faces outward.
glossary.contrast: Fascia is the vertical board at the edge; soffit is the horizontal underside.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The State of New York Mortgage Agency, which offers below-market-rate loans and down payment assistance, mainly to first-time NY homebuyers, through participating lenders.
glossary.deep:
New York's own homebuyer program, funded through tax-exempt bonds.

Like a state discount coupon for first-time buyers.

A first-time buyer in Syracuse within the income and price limits gets a SONYMA loan at a lower rate plus down payment assistance. The first-time buyer rule (no ownership in the past 3 years) is waived for veterans and in targeted areas. The syllabus says "Association"; the real name is Agency.

On the exam: SONYMA = NY state, first-time buyers, below-market rates.
glossary.contrast: FHA is federal mortgage insurance; SONYMA is a state lending program.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An agent authorized to perform one specific act or transaction, with limited authority.
glossary.deep:
A special agent has a narrow job and no power beyond it.

Like a valet: allowed to park your car, not to sell it.

A listing broker for the Okafors' brownstone is a special agent. The broker markets, shows, and negotiates, but cannot sign a contract of sale or a deed for the Okafors without separate written authority.

On the exam: "the listing broker accepted the offer on the seller's behalf" is wrong. Most real estate brokers are special agents to their clients.
glossary.contrast: General agent handles ongoing matters; special agent handles one transaction.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A charge levied only on properties that benefit from a specific public improvement, such as sidewalks or sewers; a specific lien.
glossary.deep: A special assessment pays for an improvement that benefits a particular area: new curbs, a sewer extension, streetlights. Only the properties that benefit pay, often based on front footage. Like property taxes, special assessments are specific liens with high priority. A buyer in a Long Island town should ask whether a sewer assessment is pending, because the contract should say who pays. Co-op and condo boards also levy assessments, but those are building charges, not government liens. On the exam: specific, involuntary, priority like taxes.
glossary.contrast: General property taxes fund the whole municipality.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A defined area, such as a fire, water, sewer, lighting, or library district, or a Business Improvement District, whose properties pay for a particular service.
glossary.deep:
Special districts let services be funded by just the people who get them.

A neighborhood pool club: only members pay dues.

A house in a Town of Islip fire district pays a fire district tax that a house a mile away, in a different district, does not. In NYC, property owners in a Business Improvement District pay an extra charge for street cleaning and security on their commercial corridor.

On the exam: the purpose is to fund a specific service or improvement for a specific area. Two neighbors can have different bills because of district lines.
glossary.contrast: Taxing jurisdictions like towns tax everyone within their borders for general services.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: Property designed for one specific use, such as a church, school, hospital, or cemetery, that is hard to convert to other uses.
glossary.deep: Special purpose properties are built around one function. A church sanctuary, a hospital with operating rooms, or a cemetery serves its use well but is expensive to adapt. That narrows the pool of buyers and makes these properties hard to value by comparing sales, so appraisers often use the cost approach. In NYC, former churches and schools sometimes become condos, but only after major conversion. On the exam: know the five uses (residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, special purpose) and that special purpose property is often valued by cost.
glossary.contrast: Commercial property, such as offices and retail, has a broad market of buyers.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Board approval for a use the zoning ordinance allows in a district only if listed conditions are met.
glossary.deep:
A special use permit covers uses the town wants to allow but supervise: day care centers, houses of worship, gas stations, bed and breakfasts. The ordinance lists the use and the conditions; the board decides whether this applicant meets them and may add reasonable conditions like hours or buffers.
