Analogy: the use is on the guest list, but security checks your ID. NY example: a Rhinebeck homeowner wants to run a bed and breakfast, which the code allows by special permit with off-street parking; the board approves with a limit of four guest rooms.

On the exam: special use permit equals listed use with conditions. Use variance equals a use the ordinance does not allow at all.
glossary.contrast: A use variance permits a use the ordinance prohibits; a special use permit approves a use the ordinance already contemplates.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A lien that attaches only to one identified property.
glossary.deep: A specific lien targets one property. A mortgage covers the house it finances; a real property tax lien covers the parcel being taxed; a mechanic's lien covers the building the contractor improved; a special assessment covers the properties that benefit from a new sewer. If Sal owns three buildings and the roofer worked on only one, the mechanic's lien attaches only to that one. On the exam: specific liens are tied to the property itself (mortgage, taxes, mechanic's, special assessments, attachment).
glossary.contrast: A general lien attaches to all of the debtor's property.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A court order requiring a party to do exactly what the contract says, such as convey the property.
glossary.deep:
Money is not enough, so the court orders the deal completed.

Like a judge ordering a seller to hand over the one-of-a-kind painting, not just pay damages.

Courts grant it in real estate because every parcel is unique. If the Okafors refuse to close on a valid contract, the buyer can sue for specific performance and file a notice of pendency to warn other buyers.

On the exam: buyer's remedy against a defaulting seller, because land is unique.
glossary.contrast: Liquidated damages is the seller's typical remedy against a defaulting buyer.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Written details accompanying the plans that state materials, quality standards, brands and construction methods.
glossary.deep:
Specifications (specs) answer "built with what, and how well?" The plans show a window; the specs say double-pane, low-E, which manufacturer, what U-factor. Contractors bid off specs, and disputes about quality get settled by reading them.

Analogy: the recipe's ingredient list and cooking instructions, where the blueprint is the photo of the dish. NY example: a Westchester buyer of a new build checks that the spec calls for R-49 attic insulation, matching the Energy Code, before signing the contract.

On the exam: specs are written; blueprints are drawn.
glossary.contrast: Blueprints are drawings; specifications are written descriptions.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The developer or converter that creates a condo or co-op, files the offering plan, and sells the units or shares.
glossary.deep:
The sponsor is the seller of the whole building, unit by unit. It files the offering plan with the Attorney General, appoints the first board and managing agent, and keeps unsold units.

Because a sponsor controlling the board is a conflict (who chases the sponsor for defects?), plans must say when control passes to owners, generally no later than 5 years after the first closing.

NY example: in a Gowanus new development, the sponsor's purchase agreement shifts its transfer taxes to buyers, as is customary in NYC.

On the exam: sponsor = developer under the Martin Act; it has special rights over unsold shares or units.
glossary.contrast: A managing agent runs daily operations for the board; the sponsor created and sells the building.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: The broker with whom a salesperson or associate broker is associated on DOS records, who supervises and pays them.
glossary.deep:
No sponsoring broker, no working. The sponsor files your association with DOS, keeps your license at the office, supervises your deals, and pays your commission split. The sponsor also shares responsibility when you break the rules.

Think of it as a learner's permit where the licensed driver must be in the car; except here the licensed driver is accountable for your driving even when they are at a different desk.

When Marcus commingled a deposit, DOS could discipline both Marcus and Diane, because 175.21 requires the broker to supervise closely.

On the exam: a salesperson can receive compensation only from the sponsoring broker, and listings belong to the sponsoring broker.
glossary.contrast: A cooperating broker is another firm on the other side of a deal; it does not supervise you.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: Rezoning a small parcel for the benefit of its owner in a way inconsistent with the comprehensive plan and surrounding uses. Courts generally void it.
glossary.deep:
Spot zoning is favoritism dressed up as legislation. The town board rezones one lot so its owner can do something no neighbor can, with no planning basis. Because NY requires zoning to follow a comprehensive plan, courts strike it down.

Analogy: changing the rules of the game for one player. NY example: a town board rezones a single residential lot in the middle of a quiet neighborhood to commercial so a board member's friend can open a store. Neighbors challenge it and the court voids the rezoning. By contrast, rezoning one parcel to allow affordable housing the master plan calls for is not spot zoning.

On the exam: "single parcel, benefits one owner, inconsistent with plan" equals spot zoning.
glossary.contrast: A variance is granted by the ZBA under legal standards; spot zoning is an improper legislative rezoning.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A forecast of income and expenses over several years, normalized to show a typical year.
glossary.deep:
One year can mislead: a big vacancy or a one-time repair skews it. A stabilized budget averages or normalizes several years so owners, buyers, and appraisers see what the property earns in a normal year.

Like judging a baseball player on a five-year batting average instead of one hot or cold season.

Sal's building had a gut-renovated vacancy in 2025. The stabilized budget spreads that turnover cost over 5 years so NOI is not understated.

On the exam: stabilized = normalized multi-year. It has nothing to do with rent stabilization.
glossary.contrast: Rent stabilization is a NY rent regulation system; a stabilized budget is an accounting tool.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: Written policies required by RPL 442-h stating whether a brokerage requires identification, an exclusive buyer agreement, and mortgage pre-approval from prospective homebuyers, applied equally to all.
glossary.deep:
SOPs take the agent's discretion out of the first meeting. Every buyer gets the same requirements, so nobody gets asked for more paperwork because of how they look or sound.

Rules: date stamped, notarized, posted on the broker's website and app (teams and agents post or link), copies at the office, changes posted within 30 days, compliance affirmed at renewal. The original requirement to file with DOS was removed in 2022.

Example: Hudson & Hart's SOP says ID yes, exclusive agreement no, pre-approval no. Jordan cannot ask one buyer for pre-approval because she mentioned a voucher.

On the exam: the three questions and equal application.
glossary.contrast: SOPs apply to homebuyers; agency disclosure explains representation.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: NY's school tax relief program for owner-occupied primary residences. Basic STAR has no age limit (credit income limit $500,000); Enhanced STAR is for owners 65+ under an income limit ($110,750 for 2026-27). New applicants receive a credit check rather than an exemption.
glossary.deep:
STAR helps homeowners with the school portion of the bill.

Before 2016 it showed up as a discount on the bill; now new homeowners get a check in the mail from the state instead.

Leo buys a Westchester house and registers with the NYS Department of Taxation and Finance. He gets a STAR credit check before the school tax is due. The seller's Enhanced STAR does not come with the house.

On the exam: STAR = school taxes only; Basic vs Enhanced (65+); the exemption is closed to new applicants; it is administered through the state Tax Department.
glossary.contrast: Senior citizens exemption is local and can reduce county, town, and school taxes.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: Law requiring certain contracts, including sales of real property and leases over 1 year, to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged (NY GOL 5-703).
glossary.deep:
The goal is to prevent fraud by proving deals with paper, not memory.

Like a referee who only counts points that appear on the scoreboard.

In NY, GOL 5-703 covers contracts to sell land and leases longer than a year. A 2-year oral lease on a Harlem store is unenforceable. A 1-year oral lease is fine. GOL 5-701 requires most finder's fee agreements to be written but exempts licensed real estate brokers and salespersons.

On the exam: sale of land and lease over 1 year must be written.
glossary.contrast: The statute of limitations is a deadline to sue; the Statute of Frauds is a writing requirement.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The deadline to start a lawsuit. In NY, most contract actions must be brought within 6 years.
glossary.deep:
Wait too long, and the right to sue expires.

Like a coupon with an expiration date.

A buyer discovers a breach of a contract signed in 2018. In NY, the 6-year contract statute generally runs from the breach, so a 2026 suit may be too late. Other periods differ: fraud claims have their own rule, and adverse possession takes 10 years.

On the exam: NY contract claims are 6 years.
glossary.contrast: The Statute of Frauds is about writing, not deadlines.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Channeling buyers or renters toward or away from neighborhoods or buildings based on a protected class.
glossary.deep:
Steering usually sounds helpful. "You'd feel more comfortable in..." "Lots of families like yours in..." "I wouldn't bother with that block." Each one picks the client's neighborhood based on who they are.

It can also be silent: only sending listings in certain areas, or describing the same neighborhood differently to different clients.

Example: Leo asks "who lives in Crown Heights?" A compliant answer points to public census data and Leo's own criteria; a steering answer describes residents.

On the exam: steering targets BUYERS and RENTERS, and is committed by agents. Following a buyer's own location request is not steering.
glossary.contrast: Blockbusting targets owners to induce sales; redlining is about loans by area.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A property with a psychological rather than physical defect, such as a death or crime on site; NY (RPL 443-a) does not require disclosing these facts.
glossary.deep:
Some buyers care that someone died in a house; the law says that fact is not a material physical defect. RPL 443-a: no duty to disclose that an occupant had HIV/AIDS or another condition not transmitted by occupancy, or that the property was the site of a homicide, suicide, or other death. A buyer can ask in writing, and the agent may answer with the seller's permission, never falsely.

NY's famous "ghost house" case, Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991, Nyack), came before this rule and let a buyer out because the seller had publicized hauntings.

On the exam: no duty to disclose, but never lie.
glossary.contrast: Physical defects (a cracked foundation) must be disclosed; psychological ones need not be.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: The document evidencing ownership of the co-op shares allocated to an apartment, transferred to the buyer at closing.
glossary.deep:
It is the co-op's version of a deed, except it proves ownership of shares, not land. At closing the seller's certificate is canceled and a new one issued to the buyer.

If the buyer finances, the lender holds the stock certificate and the proprietary lease as collateral until the loan is paid off.

NY example: when Adaeze and Chidi close on West End Avenue, their lender's attorney walks out with their new stock certificate.

On the exam: lender holds the certificate; lost certificates need an affidavit and often a bond.
glossary.contrast: A deed transfers real property; a stock certificate evidences shares.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: An interest-only loan in which the whole principal is due at the end of the term.
glossary.deep:
You pay rent on the money, then return all of it at once.

Like borrowing a ladder and paying a weekly fee, then handing back the whole ladder at the end.

Before the 1930s most home loans were short straight loans, which is why so many owners lost homes in the Depression when they could not refinance. Today interest-only structures appear in commercial loans and some construction loans.

On the exam: straight or term = interest only, full principal at maturity.
glossary.contrast: A balloon loan amortizes partly and leaves a lump; a straight loan amortizes none.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: Depreciation in equal annual amounts: depreciable basis divided by the recovery period.
glossary.deep:
Straight-line is the only method for buildings: same deduction each year (with a partial first and last year under the mid-month convention). Formula: (cost basis minus land) / 27.5 or 39.

Like slicing a loaf into equal pieces.

A $825,000 Bushwick four-family with $165,000 land: $660,000 / 27.5 = $24,000 a year. A $3,000,000 Bronx office with $660,000 land: $2,340,000 / 39 = $60,000 a year.

On the exam: subtract land first, then divide by the right number of years.
glossary.contrast: Accelerated methods apply to some equipment, not to buildings.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A small row of retail stores with parking in front, serving the convenience needs of the immediate neighborhood.
glossary.deep:
The strip center is retail at its simplest: a line of shops, a parking lot, and errands you can do in ten minutes.

Picture a pizzeria, a nail salon, a dry cleaner and a cell phone store sharing one roof along a busy road. There may be no anchor at all, or a small convenience store.

Hylan Boulevard on Staten Island and the main roads of Nassau and Suffolk are lined with them. Tenants are usually local businesses, so credit risk is higher than in a center anchored by a national supermarket.

On the exam: smallest center type, convenience goods, immediate neighborhood.
glossary.contrast: A neighborhood center is larger and anchored by a supermarket or drugstore.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Vertical framing members, usually 2x4 or 2x6, spaced about 16 inches on center, that form walls.
glossary.deep:
Studs are the vertical sticks inside walls. They run from a bottom plate to a top plate, carry loads in bearing walls, and give sheathing outside and drywall inside something to nail to. 2x6 studs leave room for more insulation.

Analogy: the bones of the wall. NY example: a contractor framing a new partition in a Manhattan apartment may use light-gauge steel studs instead of wood, common in NYC buildings because of fire rules.

On the exam: studs are vertical wall members; 16 inches on center is the standard spacing.
glossary.contrast: Joists are horizontal floor members; studs are vertical wall members.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: An agent of an agent: a cooperating broker who works for the seller through the listing broker, with the seller's authorization.
glossary.deep:
A subagent is the listing broker's helper and, through the listing broker, the seller's agent.

Like a subcontractor hired by your general contractor: you never hired him, but he is working on your house.

If Hudson & Hart offered subagency on the Okafors' listing and a Manhattan agent brought a buyer as subagent, that agent would owe the Okafors full fiduciary duties and the buyer only honesty. The Okafors could be vicariously liable for the subagent's misstatements.

On the exam: subagents owe duties to the seller, not the buyer. Within a firm, salespersons are sometimes described as subagents of the broker.
glossary.contrast: A broker's agent also helps the listing broker, but the client is not vicariously liable for it.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Local rules governing how land is divided into lots: lot sizes, streets, drainage, utilities, and dedication of land or fees for parks.
glossary.deep:
Subdivision regulations decide how raw land becomes lots. Before a developer can sell lots, the planning board reviews a plat showing the lot lines, street layout, grades, drainage, water and sewer, and open space. The board may require wider streets, a bigger turnaround, or a recreation fee per lot.

Analogy: zoning says what can be built on a lot; subdivision rules say how the lot gets created. NY example: a developer splitting a 50-acre Orange County farm into 40 lots files a preliminary plat, goes through SEQRA, then a final plat; only after it is filed with the county clerk can lots be sold.

On the exam: subdivision approval is a planning board function and an exercise of police power.
glossary.contrast: Site plan review covers the layout of one project on one lot; subdivision review covers dividing land into lots.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A transfer by a tenant of less than its entire interest, such as part of the space or part of the remaining term, to a subtenant.
glossary.deep:
In a sublease the tenant becomes a landlord to the subtenant while staying the tenant of the real landlord. It is a lease within a lease (a sandwich).

Like renting out your spare room while staying on the apartment lease yourself.

A tech company with too much space in Chelsea sublets half a floor for two years. The subtenant pays the tenant; the tenant keeps paying the landlord. Commercial leases usually require consent and may give the landlord recapture rights or a share of sublease profit. New York's residential sublet statute (RPL 226-b) does not apply to commercial space.

On the exam: sublease = less than all; the original tenant remains liable.
glossary.contrast: An assignment transfers the tenant's entire remaining interest.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: An arrangement in which the landlord buys electricity through a master meter and bills each tenant for its actual use measured by a submeter, often plus an administrative charge.
glossary.deep:
Submetering keeps the landlord as the middleman but bills each tenant for what it actually uses.

Like a shared house with one electric bill and a meter on each room's outlet.

Many Manhattan office buildings buy power in bulk at a master meter and submeter each tenant's floor, charging the tenant its measured use plus a small fee. Fair to tenants with light usage; profitable for landlords if the markup is high.

On the exam: submeter = landlord bills tenant based on measured use.
glossary.contrast: Direct metering means the tenant pays the utility; rent inclusion bundles electricity into the rent.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A written agreement in which a lienholder voluntarily accepts a lower priority than another lien.
glossary.deep: Normally the earlier recorded lien comes first. A subordination agreement lets an earlier lienholder step back in line. It is common when a homeowner refinances a first mortgage but keeps a home equity line: the new lender insists on first position, so the HELOC lender signs a subordination. Sellers who take back a second mortgage, or ground lessors, may subordinate so a buyer or developer can get a construction loan. On the exam: it changes priority by agreement; it does not remove the lien.
glossary.contrast: A satisfaction of mortgage removes the lien entirely.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A loan to a borrower with weaker credit, carrying higher rates and fees to offset higher risk. NY regulates subprime home loans under Banking Law 6-m.
glossary.deep:
Higher risk, higher price. Legal, but the hunting ground for predators.

Like car insurance for a driver with past accidents: it costs more.

A borrower in the Bronx with a 580 score gets a rate well above prime. NY's subprime law requires an ability-to-repay determination, restricts prepayment penalties, and requires escrow of taxes and insurance in many cases. Lenders also must give the borrower counseling information.

On the exam: subprime = higher-risk borrower, regulated, often linked to predatory lending.
glossary.contrast: Prime loans go to borrowers with strong credit at standard rates.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The right to the minerals, oil, gas, and other resources below the surface; also called mineral rights.
glossary.deep: Subsurface rights are the owner's rights to what lies beneath the land. They can be sold or leased separately, so one person can own the surface while another owns the minerals. Upstate in the Southern Tier, farm owners have signed gas leases giving companies rights below the surface while they keep farming above. A buyer should check whether mineral rights were reserved in an earlier deed, because a reservation can let someone else drill or mine. On the exam: subsurface rights can be severed from the surface; a sale of the surface does not necessarily include them.
glossary.contrast: Air rights cover the space above the surface.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The broker's required oversight of salespersons under 19 NYCRR 175.21: regular, frequent, and consistent guidance, instruction, and oversight.
glossary.deep:
Supervision is the broker making sure salespersons follow the law.

Like a head chef checking food safety without telling line cooks which hours to work.

Diane reviews Jordan's contracts, ads, and escrow handling, and trains on fair housing. That is required supervision. Setting Jordan's hours or quotas would be direction and control.

On the exam: supervision is mandatory and compatible with contractor status. Direction and control is what creates employment.
glossary.contrast: Direction and control of hours and methods is what makes someone an employee.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A licensed land surveyor's measurement and map of a parcel's boundaries, improvements, easements, and encroachments.
glossary.deep:
A survey shows exactly where the property lines are and what sits on, over, or across them: the house, the garage, the neighbor's fence that crept two feet in. In NY only a licensed land surveyor can prepare one.

Analogy: an X-ray of the lot. NY example: a buyer in Bayside orders a survey and learns the prior owner's shed sits three feet over the line onto the neighbor's land, which the title insurer will except from coverage until resolved. Planning boards require surveys with subdivision and site plan applications.

On the exam: a survey reveals encroachments and setback violations; title searches do not.
glossary.contrast: A plat maps a whole subdivision; a survey maps one parcel in detail.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A group of investors pooling money to buy and operate real estate, usually organized as a limited partnership or LLC.
glossary.deep: A syndicate is not a legal form of its own. It is a description of what investors are doing together: pooling capital so they can buy property none could afford alone. A sponsor finds the deal and manages it; investors put up money and take a passive role. The legal wrapper is usually a limited partnership or an LLC. A syndicate of 40 investors might buy a Long Island shopping center. Selling interests to investors can trigger securities laws. On the exam: syndicate = pooled investment, organized as an LP or LLC.
glossary.contrast: A joint venture is formed for one specific project and ends when it is done.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Government action that, by physically occupying property or regulating it too far, counts as taking it, so compensation is owed.
glossary.deep:
Not every regulation is a taking, but some go so far that courts treat them as one. The rules courts use: any permanent physical occupation is a taking, however small (Loretto v. Teleprompter, 1982, a cable box on a Manhattan roof). A regulation that wipes out all economic use is a taking (Lucas, 1992). Everything else is judged by balancing economic impact, interference with reasonable investment expectations, and the character of the action (Penn Central, 1978, where landmarking Grand Central was not a taking).

Analogy: the government may set house rules, but it cannot move into your attic for free.

On the exam: expect Penn Central (not a taking) and the idea that ordinary zoning is not a taking.
glossary.contrast: Police power regulation is generally not a taking; it becomes one only when it occupies property or goes "too far."
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The local official who determines the assessed value of each property for taxation and maintains assessment records.
glossary.deep:
The assessor values every parcel and builds the assessment roll, the base on which taxes are spread. The assessor also tracks property characteristics (lot size, square footage, bedrooms) and administers exemptions like STAR, senior and veterans. Towns may have an elected assessor, an elected board of assessors, or an appointed single assessor serving a fixed term.

Analogy: the referee who measures each player; the receiver later collects the fee. NY example: a Monroe County homeowner who adds a garage sees her assessment rise after the assessor updates the record.

On the exam: assessor values; receiver collects; legislative body sets the rate.
glossary.contrast: The receiver of taxes collects; the assessor values.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: A proceeding in NY State Supreme Court under RPTL Article 7 to review a property assessment, used mainly by commercial owners after an unsuccessful grievance.
glossary.deep:
Certiorari is the full lawsuit version of an assessment challenge.

If SCAR is small claims, certiorari is the main courtroom with lawyers and appraisal reports.

Evelyn's Nassau retail building loses at the grievance stage. Her tax certiorari attorney files in Supreme Court with an income-approach appraisal showing the assessment is too high, and the case settles with a refund.

On the exam: commercial property protests go by certiorari; a grievance must be filed first.
glossary.contrast: SCAR: informal, for owner-occupied 1 to 3 family homes only.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: An annual deduction that recovers the cost of an income-producing building over its IRS life, regardless of actual market value.
glossary.deep:
Tax depreciation (cost recovery) is a paper expense: no cash leaves your account, yet taxable income drops. It applies only to investment or business property, never to land and never to your own home. Residential rentals use 27.5 years, nonresidential 39 years, straight-line.

Like the IRS saying: we assume your building wears out, even if the neighborhood says otherwise.

Sal deducts $28,000 a year even as his Astoria building rises in value.

On the exam: depreciation is deductible, reduces basis, and is recaptured at sale (up to 25%).
glossary.contrast: Appraisal depreciation (physical, functional, external) measures actual loss in value; tax depreciation is an accounting deduction.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: A full or partial removal of a property's assessed value from taxation, based on the owner's status or the property's use.
glossary.deep:
An exemption shrinks the taxable base, not the rate.

Like a coupon that takes dollars off before tax is applied.

A church in Harlem is fully exempt. A 70-year-old owner in Schenectady with modest income may get 50% off her assessment. Exempt value does not vanish from the budget: everyone else's rate rises slightly to cover it.

On the exam: exemptions are owner-based or use-based and generally end when the property is sold to someone who does not qualify.
glossary.contrast: Abatement: a reduction of the tax itself (common in NYC programs) rather than of assessed value.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: A claim against real property for unpaid real property taxes or special assessments. It has priority over other liens, including earlier mortgages.
glossary.deep:
The government always gets paid first from the property.

In the line of creditors, the tax collector cuts to the front.

Sal owes three years of taxes on a Bronx lot that also has a 2015 mortgage. If the lot is sold in foreclosure, the tax lien is paid before the mortgage. That is why lenders escrow taxes and title companies demand that taxes be paid at closing.

On the exam: real property tax liens are specific, involuntary, and first in priority regardless of recording date.
glossary.contrast: Mortgage lien: voluntary, ranked by recording date.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: A sale of a municipality's right to collect delinquent property taxes, with interest, to a third party. The owner keeps title subject to the lien, and the buyer can foreclose if it is not paid.
glossary.deep:
The city sells the IOU, not the house.

Like a store selling your overdue account to a collection agency.

NYC has periodically sold liens on properties with overdue taxes to a trust. The owner of a Bronx two-family still owns the house but now owes the trust the taxes plus interest and fees, and the trust can bring a foreclosure if the debt goes unpaid.

On the exam: a lien sale transfers the debt; a tax sale after in rem foreclosure transfers the property.
glossary.contrast: In rem foreclosure: the municipality takes the property itself.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: An investment feature that reduces or delays income tax, in real estate mainly through depreciation deductions.
glossary.deep:
A tax shelter lets cash come in while taxable income stays low. In real estate the main tool is depreciation: a yearly deduction for the building wearing out, even though you write no check for it.

Picture an umbrella over your rent checks: rain (tax) still falls, but much of the income stays dry.

Evelyn's Bushwick building throws off $40,000 of cash flow, but after subtracting $130,000 of interest and $50,000 of depreciation from NOI, only $10,000 is taxable. Depreciation sheltered most of her cash. Land is never depreciated, and depreciation is recaptured (taxed) when she sells, unless she does a 1031 exchange.

On the exam: the shelter comes from depreciation (27.5 years residential, 39 nonresidential), a non-cash deduction.
glossary.contrast: Tax deferral (1031 exchange) postpones tax on a sale; the depreciation shelter reduces tax on yearly income.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The analysis of a property's taxable income: NOI minus mortgage interest minus depreciation, multiplied by the owner's tax rate to find tax owed.
glossary.deep:
The tax world follows the IRS's rules, not the bank account. Two differences from the cash world: only interest is deductible (principal is not), and depreciation is deductible even though no cash is spent.

Like a receipt for your tax return versus your actual spending: related, but not the same list.

Bushwick: NOI $190,000 minus interest $130,000 minus depreciation $50,000 = $10,000 taxable. At 30%, tax is $3,000.

On the exam: taxable income = NOI minus interest minus depreciation. Tax = taxable income x rate.
glossary.contrast: The cash world uses full debt service and ignores depreciation.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: A 1031 like-kind exchange in which gain on investment or business real property is postponed by reinvesting in like-kind real property.
glossary.deep:
The gain is not forgiven: the replacement property carries the old low basis. If the investor later sells without exchanging, the deferred gain is taxed then. If the investor holds until death, heirs generally get a stepped-up basis, which is why investors say "swap till you drop."

Like moving your chips from one table to another without cashing out.

Sal swaps his Astoria 6-unit for a Yonkers 12-unit and defers $1,570,000 of gain.

On the exam: 1031 = deferral; real property held for investment or business; QI; 45/180 days; boot taxable.
glossary.contrast: The home sale exclusion permanently excludes gain on a principal residence.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: The federal law that created today's $250,000/$500,000 home sale exclusion and the $10,000 penalty-free IRA withdrawal for first-time homebuyers.
glossary.deep:
Before 1997, sellers deferred home sale gain by rolling it into a pricier home within 2 years, and those 55 or older got a one-time $125,000 exclusion. The 1997 Act scrapped both for a simpler rule: exclude up to $250,000 (single) or $500,000 (married) every 2 years if you owned and lived there 2 of the last 5 years. It also opened IRAs to first-time buyers for up to $10,000 without the 10% penalty.

Think of it as trading a complicated coupon book for one big discount you can reuse.

The Okafors bought in Bed-Stuy in 1997, the very year the rules changed.

On the exam: TRA 1997 = $250k/$500k exclusion and IRA first-time buyer withdrawal.
glossary.contrast: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 set the $750,000 mortgage interest limit; that is a different law.
glossary.subject: s17

glossary.def: Two or more people at the same brokerage, at least one a salesperson or associate broker, who present themselves as a team.
glossary.deep:
Teams are allowed but cannot look like separate companies. The name must contain "team" and either members' full licensed names or "at/of" the broker's full name. "Group," "realty," and "associates" are banned. No unlicensed person's name in the team name, and ads must say who is unlicensed.

It is a band inside a record label, not its own label.

"The Reyes Team at Hudson & Hart Realty" is legal. "Slope Luxury Group" is not.

On the exam: pick the name with "team" and the broker.
glossary.contrast: A brokerage is the licensed business; a team is a marketing unit inside it.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: A time-limited certificate from the building department allowing legal occupancy of parts of a building before the final certificate of occupancy is issued.
glossary.deep:
A big building is rarely 100% finished at once. A TCO lets ready floors or units be occupied while the rest is completed. In NYC, TCOs expire and must be renewed until the permanent CO issues.

Why it matters: no legal occupancy, no closing. Lenders will not fund a mortgage on a unit that cannot be occupied.

NY example: Ana's closing on 7C waits for a TCO covering the 7th floor. The amenity floor can still be under construction.

On the exam: TCO enables closings and financing in new development; the final CO comes later.
glossary.contrast: A certificate of occupancy is the permanent version.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: Possession by a tenant who stays after their right to possess has ended, without the landlord's consent.
glossary.deep:
The lowest form of tenancy. The person came in legally but no longer has permission.

Like a guest who keeps sitting at the table after the restaurant closes.

A tenant's lease in Flushing ends August 31 and she is still there September 10 without a renewal. She is a tenant at sufferance. The landlord can start a holdover proceeding, or accept rent, which in NY creates a month-to-month tenancy. No self-help: only a court can remove her.

On the exam: "came in lawfully, stays without consent" equals sufferance. A trespasser never had a right to begin with.
glossary.contrast: A trespasser entered without right; a tenant at sufferance entered lawfully.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Co-ownership available only to married spouses, treating the couple as one owner, with survivorship; neither spouse can sell, mortgage, or partition it alone.
glossary.deep: Tenancy by the entirety treats a married couple as a single unit owning the property. It requires the four unities plus marriage. Neither spouse can sell, mortgage, or force a partition of the property without the other. When one spouse dies, the survivor owns everything automatically, outside probate. Divorce converts it to a tenancy in common. In New York, a deed to a married couple creates a tenancy by the entirety unless it says otherwise, and since 1996 spouses can hold co-op shares this way. The Okafors own their brownstone as tenants by the entirety. On the exam: spouses only, no partition, survivorship.
glossary.contrast: Joint tenancy is available to anyone and can be severed by one owner's conveyance.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A leasehold with a definite beginning and end date, of any length, ending automatically without notice at the end of the term.
glossary.deep:
Despite the name, a tenancy for years can be 6 months, 1 year, or 99 years. What makes it one is the fixed end date. Contrast it with a periodic tenancy (month to month) that renews until someone gives notice.

Think of a ticket for a specific flight versus a monthly subway pass that keeps renewing.

Ms. Chen's lease in 2A ends January 2027: a tenancy for years. Sal's niece in 3A, month to month, has a periodic tenancy. Note that NY rent laws can still require renewal offers or notice before ending some tenancies.

On the exam: definite term = tenancy for years.
glossary.contrast: A periodic tenancy renews automatically until notice is given.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: Co-ownership by two or more people with undivided interests that may be unequal and that pass to each owner's heirs or devisees, with no right of survivorship.
glossary.deep: Tenancy in common is the flexible form of co-ownership. It requires only unity of possession. Shares can be unequal (50/25/25), each owner can sell or mortgage a share without the others, and a share passes by will or intestacy when its owner dies. In New York it is the default for unmarried co-owners unless the deed expressly says joint tenancy. When Dev died owning 25% of the Ridgewood house, his sister inherited it as a new tenant in common. On the exam: no survivorship, shares can be unequal, and it is NY's default.
glossary.contrast: Joint tenancy requires equal shares and carries the right of survivorship.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: An agent who represents a tenant looking to lease property.
glossary.deep:
The tenant's agent finds and negotiates for the renter.

Like a buyer's agent, but for leases.

A nurse moving to Washington Heights hires a tenant's agent to find a one-bedroom under $2,800. The agent keeps her budget private and negotiates concessions. Under the FARE Act, a tenant may pay a broker the tenant actually hires.

On the exam: tenant's agents give the landlord-tenant disclosure form to their client before the agreement and to the landlord side at first substantive contact.
glossary.contrast: Landlord's agent represents the owner.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Having died with a valid will.
glossary.deep: A person who dies testate has left a valid will, so the will, not state law, decides who receives the property. The will is probated in Surrogate's Court, and the executor named in it gathers assets, pays debts and taxes, and distributes or sells property. Real property passes to devisees by devise. If the will is found invalid, the person is treated as intestate. On the exam: testate = will; vocabulary that goes with it: testator, executor, devise, devisee, probate, letters testamentary.
glossary.contrast: Intestate means without a valid will.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: People who pose as prospective buyers or renters to check whether housing providers and agents treat people equally.
glossary.deep:
Paired testing is a controlled experiment: two testers with matching incomes, credit, and requests, differing only in one trait such as race or a voucher. If one gets more listings, faster callbacks, or easier requirements, that is evidence.

Testers are legal. They work for HUD, fair housing groups, the NY Attorney General, and the NYC Commission. Newsday's 2019 Long Island investigation used testers and changed New York law. The Supreme Court held in 1982 that testers can sue even without intending to rent.

On the exam: testing is not entrapment. The practical lesson: treat every caller as if they are a tester.
glossary.contrast: Testers check for discrimination; home inspectors test properties.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: Requiring a buyer of one product or service to also buy another as a condition of the sale.
glossary.deep:
A tie-in forces a package deal.

Like a concert venue that sells tickets only if you also buy parking.

A developer in Staten Island sells lots only to buyers who list their current homes with the developer's brokerage. Or a broker agrees to list a property only if the owner also hires the broker's management company.

On the exam: "only if you also" signals a tie-in.
glossary.contrast: Price fixing is about price; a tie-in is about bundling services.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A contract clause making a deadline strict, so missing it is a default.
glossary.deep:
Without the clause, NY courts give a reasonable extension on a closing date. With it, the date is hard.

Like a flight: the plane leaves at 9:00 whether you are there or not.

A Brooklyn contract says closing "on or about June 15". The buyer can be a little late. If the seller's attorney sends a time of the essence letter setting July 15 with reasonable notice, and the buyer is not ready that day, the buyer defaults and can lose the down payment.

On the exam: the clause makes dates binding; "on or about" does not.
glossary.contrast: A contingency deadline lets a party exit; time of the essence makes failing to perform a breach.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The principle that a dollar received today is worth more than a dollar received in the future, because it can be invested now and carries no waiting risk.
glossary.deep:
Money now beats money later. Today's dollar can earn interest starting today, and a future promise might not be kept or might lose value to inflation.

Would you rather have $100 now or $100 in five years? Everyone picks now. To make you wait, someone has to offer more than $100 later. Compounding moves money forward; discounting brings future money back to today.

Evelyn is offered a $100,000 lump sum in five years. At 6%, that is worth about $74,700 today ($100,000 / 1.065). Discounted cash flow analysis of a Manhattan office tower is the same idea, year by year.

On the exam: expect the definition, or a choice that says future money is worth more (wrong).
glossary.contrast: Rate of return measures how much you earn; time value of money explains why when you earn it matters.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: Ownership of real property, the right to possess and use it, and the evidence of that ownership.
glossary.deep: Title is the ownership itself. It is not a piece of paper; the deed is the paper that transfers it. Having title means holding the bundle of rights, subject to whatever encumbrances exist. Title passes when a deed is delivered and accepted, and it is protected by recording and title insurance. Buyers want marketable title, meaning title free from reasonable doubt. When Leo closes, he takes title to the condo; the recorded deed is evidence of it. On the exam: deed = document; title = ownership.
glossary.contrast: A deed is the instrument that conveys title.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Acquiring title to real property as an heir when the owner dies without a will.
glossary.deep: Title by descent is how heirs become owners under the intestacy statute. No deed from the decedent is needed; the law itself passes the title, and the administrator confirms it or sells the property. If an intestate Buffalo widow leaves only a brother, he takes her house by descent. Because these titles do not appear in a recorded deed, title companies often need proof of who the heirs are. On the exam: descent = intestate inheritance; devise = inheritance by will.
glossary.contrast: Title by devise passes under a will.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The meeting or process at which a sale is completed: the price is paid, the deed is delivered, liens are paid off, and documents are signed for recording.
glossary.deep: The title closing (settlement) is where everything happens at once. The buyer pays the balance of the price, usually through a new mortgage plus their own funds; the seller delivers the deed; existing liens are paid from the proceeds; the lender funds; and the title company collects taxes and records the deed and mortgage. Downstate it is usually an in-person meeting with attorneys for buyer, seller, and lender, the title closer, and the brokers. On the exam: closing consummates the transaction; the seller receives the balance and liens are satisfied.
glossary.contrast: Contract signing creates the obligation to buy and sell; closing completes it.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Insurance protecting an owner or lender against loss from title defects that existed before the policy date, such as forgery or unknown heirs.
glossary.deep: Title insurance looks backward. For a one-time premium at closing, it protects against hidden defects that existed before the policy: forged deeds, errors in public records, undisclosed heirs, mistaken legal descriptions. It does not cover problems created after closing, or items listed as exceptions. The owner's policy protects the buyer for as long as they or their heirs own; the lender's policy protects the lender and shrinks with the loan. In NY the buyer pays both, and rates are regulated by DFS. Co-op buyers usually get a lien search instead. On the exam: past defects, one-time premium, owner's vs lender's.
glossary.contrast: Homeowner's insurance covers physical damage, not title defects.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: An examination of the public records to find the ownership history and any liens, judgments, or other encumbrances affecting a property.
glossary.deep: A title search reviews deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, judgments, liens, lis pendens, tax records, and bankruptcy filings tied to the property and the names of its owners. In NY the title company performs it and issues a title report listing what the buyer must clear before closing. The search covers recorded documents only; physical problems like encroachments need a survey. On the exam: a title search reveals recorded encumbrances and the chain of title, not physical encroachments.
glossary.contrast: A survey reveals physical boundary issues.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The surface features of land: elevation, slope, and natural features like hills, streams, and wetlands.
glossary.deep:
Topography describes the land's shape. Steep slopes cost more to build on and erode; low spots flood; streams and wetlands are regulated. Topographic surveys show contour lines, each connecting points of the same elevation.

Analogy: the land's fingerprint. NY example: a Hudson Valley planning board requires a topographic map with every subdivision application and forbids building on slopes over 25 percent because of erosion and runoff. A Staten Island lot near the bluffs may need special review for steep slopes.

On the exam: topography is a planning input and affects drainage, site plans, and clustering decisions.
glossary.contrast: A survey measures boundaries; a topographic survey adds elevations and contours.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: The elected legislative body of a town (the supervisor plus council members), or of a city (the city council). It adopts local laws, the zoning ordinance, the budget and the tax rate.
glossary.deep:
The town board is the town's lawmaker and purse holder. Voters elect the supervisor and council members. The board adopts local laws and the zoning ordinance, authorizes cluster zoning, adopts the budget, sets the tax rate, and appoints the planning board, ZBA and other boards. Cities have the same role in a city council.

Analogy: the board of directors that hires the managers. NY example: the Town of Hempstead town board votes on a zoning amendment allowing apartments near LIRR stations; the planning board then reviews individual site plans under it.

On the exam: elected, legislative, adopts zoning and the tax rate.
glossary.contrast: The planning board is appointed and applies the zoning; the town board writes and adopts it.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: Equipment a commercial tenant installs to run a business; it stays the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease ends.
glossary.deep: Trade fixtures are the tenant's business tools: a bakery's ovens, a salon's chairs, a bar's coolers. Even if bolted down, they remain the tenant's personal property because the tenant never intended to give them to the landlord. The tenant may remove them before the lease expires but must repair any damage. If the tenant leaves them behind after the lease ends, the landlord may keep them by accession. A Williamsburg cafe that walks away from its espresso bar has given it to the landlord. On the exam: removable before the lease ends; abandoned ones go to the landlord.
glossary.contrast: A regular fixture, usually installed by an owner, becomes part of the real property.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A program letting owners of land that should be preserved sell their unused development rights to builders in designated growth areas.
glossary.deep:
TDR separates the right to build from the land itself. A sending site (a farm, a landmark) sells rights it will never use; a receiving site (a downtown parcel) uses them to build bigger than zoning otherwise allows. The sending site is then deed-restricted.

Analogy: carbon credits for buildings. NY example: NYC allows landmarks to transfer unused floor area (the Penn Central concept) and created a Midtown East program in 2017. Upstate and on Long Island, towns use TDR to preserve farms and the Pine Barrens: a farmer sells credits, and a builder in a hamlet center gets extra units.

On the exam: TDR preserves open space or landmarks while compensating owners. Penn Central relied partly on TDR to find no taking.
glossary.contrast: Incentive zoning grants bonuses for public benefits on the same site; TDR moves rights from one site to another.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Specific credit terms in an ad (down payment amount or percent, number of payments, payment amount, or finance charge) that require full Reg Z disclosure of down payment, repayment terms, and APR.
glossary.deep:
Say one specific number, and you must say the rest.

Like a store that advertises a price and must also show the fine print.

"Only $1,999 a month!" or "3% down" are trigger terms. "Easy financing" or "6.25% APR" alone are not. A Brooklyn agent's Instagram post saying "$2,100/month with 5% down" must also state the APR and repayment terms.

On the exam: identify which phrases trigger and which do not.
glossary.contrast: General statements like "low down payment available" are not trigger terms.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A net lease in which the tenant pays rent plus property taxes, insurance, and maintenance.
glossary.deep:
The three "nets" are taxes, insurance, and maintenance. The landlord collects a clean check and does almost nothing.

Like leasing a whole house where you also pay the tax bill and fix the roof.

A national pharmacy leases a freestanding store in Hicksville for 20 years on a triple net basis. Investors like Evelyn Park buy these for predictable income, since the tenant carries the cost risk.

On the exam: "tenant pays taxes, insurance, and maintenance" equals triple net. Common for freestanding retail and long-term single-tenant buildings.
glossary.contrast: A ground lease rents only the land; a triple net lease rents land and building with the tenant paying costs.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: An arrangement in which a trustee holds legal title to property and manages it for the benefit of a beneficiary.
glossary.deep: A trust splits ownership into two parts: legal title held by the trustee, and the benefit enjoyed by the beneficiary. The trustor creates it and puts property into it. A living (inter vivos) trust is created during life, often to avoid probate; a testamentary trust is created by a will. Many NY families hold their homes in revocable living trusts. When a trust sells, the trustee signs the listing agreement and the deed. On the exam: know the three roles: trustor creates, trustee holds title, beneficiary benefits.
glossary.contrast: A life estate gives the holder possession directly, without a trustee.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The person or institution that holds legal title to trust property and manages it as a fiduciary for the beneficiaries.
glossary.deep: The trustee is the manager and legal owner of record, but must act for the beneficiaries, not for personal gain. Banks, attorneys, and family members serve as trustees. A trustee who sells a Bronx apartment building signs the deed and must get a fair price, keep good records, and avoid conflicts of interest, much like a broker's fiduciary duties. Licensees should confirm the trustee's power to sell by reviewing the trust agreement or a certification of trust. On the exam: the trustee holds legal title.
glossary.contrast: The beneficiary holds the benefit but not legal title.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The person who creates a trust and transfers property into it; also called settlor or grantor.
glossary.deep: The trustor is the one who sets up the trust: decides who benefits, picks the trustee, and transfers the property in, usually by deeding real estate to the trustee. Think of the trustor as the architect of the trust. A Westchester grandmother who creates a trust for her grandchildren and deeds her house to it is the trustor. In a revocable trust the trustor can change or cancel it and is often also the first trustee and beneficiary. On the exam: trustor creates, trustee manages, beneficiary benefits. Watch for the switch of trustor and trustee in answer choices.
glossary.contrast: The trustee holds title and manages the property.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A foam insulation pumped into wall cavities mainly in the 1970s that can release formaldehyde gas.
glossary.deep:
UFFI was a popular retrofit during the 1970s energy crisis: drill holes, inject foam, it hardens in the walls. It released formaldehyde gas, especially when poorly mixed or new, causing eye and respiratory irritation. The CPSC banned it in 1982; a court overturned the ban in 1983, but the market had already collapsed. Emissions decline greatly over time, so old UFFI often tests low today.

Analogy: a new-car smell that turned out to be irritating. NY example: a buyer of a 1950s Schenectady house sees plugged holes in the siding; the inspector suspects UFFI and suggests a formaldehyde air test.

On the exam: UFFI equals formaldehyde. Disclose if known.
glossary.contrast: Asbestos insulation is a mineral fiber hazard; UFFI is a chemical gas hazard.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: New York City's public review process for major land use actions like rezonings, special permits, and city property dispositions.
glossary.deep:
ULURP gives the public and elected officials a fixed-clock review of big decisions. After the Department of City Planning certifies an application: the Community Board has 60 days (advisory), the Borough President 30 days (advisory), the City Planning Commission 60 days (binding vote), the City Council 50 days for many actions, and the mayor 5 days to veto, which the Council can override by two thirds within 10 days. About seven months.

Analogy: a relay race with five runners and a stopwatch. NY example: the Gowanus rezoning in Brooklyn went through ULURP in 2021, with hearings at each step.

On the exam: know the order and who is advisory (Community Board, Borough President) vs binding (CPC, Council).
glossary.contrast: BSA variances do not go through ULURP; ULURP covers rezonings and other land use actions.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Excess liability insurance that pays above the limits of the underlying home and auto policies, and may cover some claims they exclude.
glossary.deep:
An umbrella sits over your other policies and catches what spills over.

If your home policy covers a $300,000 lawsuit and the jury awards $1.2M, the umbrella pays the next $900,000 up to its limit.

Evelyn owns retail buildings and a home in Riverdale. A $5M umbrella protects her personal assets from a catastrophic injury lawsuit at a modest premium.

On the exam: umbrella = extra liability, not property and not flood.
glossary.contrast: A package policy bundles coverages; an umbrella extends liability limits.
glossary.subject: s12

glossary.def: An abandoned or unplugged gas well on a property, which a seller must disclose if known (RPL 242).
glossary.deep:
Old gas wells dot parts of western and central NY. An unplugged one can leak gas into basements or groundwater. RPL 242 requires sellers to disclose known uncapped wells in writing before the contract.

Think of it as an open hole the buyer cannot see under the grass.

A farmhouse near Jamestown has a capped-looking pipe in the back field that the seller knows was never properly plugged. The seller must disclose it.

On the exam: uncapped gas wells equals RPL 242; it is a separate disclosure from the PCDS.
glossary.contrast: The PCDS is a broad condition form; RPL 242 targets one specific hazard.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: Buried tanks storing heating oil, gasoline or chemicals; leaks contaminate soil and groundwater.
glossary.deep:
USTs are out of sight, which is the problem. Bare steel corrodes, and a tank 20 to 30 years old may already leak. Clues: fill and vent pipes in the yard, an oil burner with no visible tank. Commercial fuel tanks are regulated by EPA and DEC (registration, leak detection, closure). Home heating tanks are lightly regulated, but spills must be reported to DEC within 2 hours and New York's Navigation Law makes the discharger strictly liable for cleanup.

Analogy: a buried barrel nobody remembers until it leaks. NY example: a Queens buyer's tank sweep finds a 550-gallon tank under the driveway; the seller closes it with a DEC spill case and gets a no-further-action letter before closing.

On the exam: find, test, close, document.
glossary.contrast: An aboveground storage tank is visible and easier to inspect.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: The co-op corporation's own mortgage on the building, paid through shareholders' maintenance.
glossary.deep:
Every shareholder carries a slice of the building's debt. A big balance, a rising rate, or a balloon coming due soon can mean higher maintenance or an assessment.

Buyers should know the balance, rate, maturity, and whether it is fixed. A building with a small underlying mortgage has room to borrow for repairs.

NY example: Priya likes that the West End Avenue mortgage is fixed until 2033. A Bronx co-op with a balloon due in 18 months and thin reserves is a red flag.

On the exam: the underlying mortgage is the building's loan, separate from the buyer's share loan.
glossary.contrast: A share loan is the buyer's personal loan to buy shares.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: The lender's evaluation of the borrower's credit, capacity, capital, and the collateral to decide whether and on what terms to make a loan.
glossary.deep:
The risk review before the money moves.

Like a final exam the loan file has to pass.

An underwriter reviews Leo's credit score and history, income and ratios, cash for closing and reserves, and the appraisal and title. She asks for a letter explaining a $9,000 deposit, then approves with conditions. Automated systems (Fannie's Desktop Underwriter, Freddie's Loan Product Advisor) give a first answer; humans clear conditions.

On the exam: underwriting = risk evaluation; the four Cs.
glossary.contrast: Origination is taking the application; underwriting is judging it.
glossary.subject: s18

glossary.def: Representing both sides without the informed written consent of both. A serious breach that can cost the commission, the deal, and the license.
glossary.deep:
It is being a double agent without telling anyone.

Like a real estate version of a referee secretly betting on one team.

Marcus, listing the Okafors' brownstone, starts coaching a buyer customer on how low to go. He has created implied agency with the buyer and his firm is now an undisclosed dual agent. The firm may forfeit its commission, the sale may be rescinded, and DOS can discipline.

On the exam: consent from one side only, oral consent, or accidental implied agency all produce undisclosed dual agency.
glossary.contrast: Consensual dual agency has written informed consent from both parties.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A co-owner's share in property that gives the right to possess the whole property, not a specific physical part.
glossary.deep: Co-owners do not split the property into physical pieces. Each holds a fractional share of the whole and has the right to use all of it. If Ana owns 50% of a Ridgewood two-family as a tenant in common, she cannot claim the top floor as "her half." She owns half of everything, including every room and the backyard. Dividing the property physically requires agreement or a partition action. On the exam: undivided interest goes with unity of possession, which every form of co-ownership shares.
glossary.contrast: A condo unit is a separately owned physical space; only the common elements are held as undivided interests.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: Loyalty owed to one client alone, with no competing client on the other side. Single agents give it; dual agents cannot.
glossary.deep:
Undivided means not split. A single agent is entirely on one side.

A coach cannot fully coach both teams in the same game.

When Leo and the Okafors both consent to Hudson & Hart acting as dual agent, both give up undivided loyalty. Even with Jordan designated for Leo and Marcus for the Okafors, the firm represents both, so neither client gets undivided loyalty.

On the exam: the NY disclosure form says a dual agent and designated sales agents cannot provide undivided loyalty. That phrase is the giveaway.
glossary.contrast: Loyalty is the duty; undivided loyalty is that duty when owed to one side only.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: Offering different terms, conditions, services, information, or effort to people because of a protected class, including not showing all available homes in a client's price range.
glossary.deep:
Unequal treatment is the quiet cousin of refusal. Nobody is turned away; they just get less. Fewer listings, slower callbacks, a bigger deposit, stricter paperwork, limited access to the gym or roof deck.

Example: a Long Island agent asks a Black buyer for pre-approval before showings but shows a white buyer homes without it. That is the exact pattern Newsday's testers found, and it is why standardized operating procedures exist.

On the exam: look for two clients with the same budget treated differently. Same criteria should get the same listings, information, and requirements.
glossary.contrast: Refusal to deal denies housing outright; unequal treatment gives worse terms or service.
glossary.subject: s09

glossary.def: A body of law adopted by NY governing commercial transactions such as sales of goods and security interests in personal property; it does not govern sales of real property.
glossary.deep:
The UCC handles stuff, not land.

Think of two rulebooks: real property law for the house, the UCC for the furniture inside it.

When a Manhattan restaurant is sold, the building is conveyed by deed, but the ovens and tables pass by bill of sale under the UCC, and the lender perfects its lien on equipment with a UCC-1 financing statement. Co-op share loans are secured under the UCC too, because shares are personal property.

On the exam: UCC equals goods and personal property.
glossary.contrast: Real property sales follow the Statute of Frauds and real property law.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A contract in which one party promises something in exchange for an act; only the promisor is bound until the act is done.
glossary.deep:
One promise, waiting for someone to act.

Like a "$100 reward for my lost dog" poster: no one has to search, but whoever returns the dog gets paid.

An open listing is unilateral: the seller promises a commission to whichever broker produces a buyer, and no broker must try. An option is also unilateral until exercised: the owner must sell if the optionee buys, but the optionee need not buy.

On the exam: options and open listings are the classic unilateral examples.
glossary.contrast: A bilateral contract binds both sides from the start.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: Land with no buildings or improvements, which usually produces no income and is held for future use or appreciation.
glossary.deep:
Raw land is a bet on the future. No tenants, no rent, but taxes and insurance arrive every year.

It is like buying a ticket to a show that has not been scheduled yet. If the show happens (a rezoning, a new train station, a developer who wants the site), the ticket can be worth a lot. If not, you keep paying to hold it.

A lot in the South Bronx bought before a neighborhood rezoning can multiply in value; one in a flood zone with no development rights can sit for decades. Land cannot be depreciated, so it offers no tax shelter either.

On the exam: land is the most speculative type, with no cash flow, low liquidity and no depreciation.
glossary.contrast: Improved land has buildings or site work (utilities, roads); unimproved land has none.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.term: Unities of time, title, interest, and possession
glossary.def: The four conditions required for a joint tenancy: owners acquire at the same time, by the same instrument, with equal shares, and with equal rights to possess the whole.
glossary.deep: The four unities (TTIP) are the checklist for a joint tenancy. Time: everyone takes title at the same moment. Title: by the same deed or will. Interest: equal shares. Possession: each has the right to possess the entire property. Tenancy in common needs only possession. Tenancy by the entirety needs all four plus marriage (sometimes called the fifth unity, person). If three friends buy a house 50/25/25, the unity of interest is missing, so they cannot be joint tenants. On the exam: memorize TTIP and which estates need which unities.
glossary.contrast: Tenancy in common needs only unity of possession.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: An agent with authority to do anything the principal could lawfully do, usually under a broad power of attorney.
glossary.deep:
A universal agent steps fully into the principal's shoes.

Like an adult child with a general power of attorney for an elderly parent, paying bills, signing contracts, and selling property.

If Emmanuel Okafor's sister holds his general power of attorney while he is abroad, she could sign the contract of sale. A broker almost never has this authority.

On the exam: rare in brokerage; the answer when the question describes authority over all of the principal's affairs.
glossary.contrast: General agent: one business area. Universal agent: everything.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: A broker's employee without a real estate license who may do only clerical and administrative work.
glossary.deep:
Assistants keep offices running: phones, scheduling, filing, ordering signs, placing broker-approved ads. They cannot show property, host open houses, discuss price or terms, give value opinions, or negotiate, and they are paid salary or hourly, never per deal.

Think of a dental receptionist: books your cleaning, does not touch your teeth.

A caller asks Jordan's assistant if the Okafors would take less. The right answer: "Let me have Jordan call you."

On the exam: any task involving the property's price, terms, or showing requires a license.
glossary.contrast: A licensed assistant can show and negotiate under the broker.
glossary.subject: s01

glossary.def: The floor area a tenant occupies exclusively, not counting shared common areas.
glossary.deep:
Usable is the space behind your own door, where your desks, conference rooms and pantry actually go.

Like the inside of your apartment, versus the whole building's hallways and lobby.

Leo laser-measured 8,000 usable feet on a 10,000 RSF floor. Smart NYC tenants compare spaces on cost per usable foot: $60 per RSF with a 20% loss factor costs $75 per usable foot.

On the exam: usable sits between rentable (bigger) and carpetable (smaller).
glossary.contrast: Carpetable footage subtracts walls, columns and built-ins from usable.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The lease provision stating what the tenant may use the premises for.
glossary.deep:
The use clause defines the tenant's lane. Landlords want it narrow; tenants want it broad.

Like a food hall assigning stalls: one taco stand, one pizza place, no duplicates.

Sal's Astoria store lease might allow "bakery, cafe and related food retail, but no full-service restaurant without consent," protecting the building's other tenants and its certificate of occupancy. A tenant who wants to sell its business later pushes for "any lawful retail use."

On the exam: the use clause protects exclusives and tenant mix; a narrow use makes assignment harder.
glossary.contrast: An exclusive clause promises a tenant that no competitor will be allowed; a use clause limits what the tenant itself may do.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: ZBA permission to use land for a purpose the zoning prohibits, granted only on proof of unnecessary hardship.
glossary.deep:
A use variance is the hardest relief to get. Under Town Law 267-b and Village Law 7-712-b, the applicant must prove all four: (1) the property cannot yield a reasonable return under any permitted use, shown by real financial evidence; (2) the hardship is unique to this property, not the whole neighborhood; (3) the variance will not alter the essential character of the neighborhood; (4) the hardship was not self-created.

Analogy: asking to open a bakery in a library. NY example: an owner of a residential lot squeezed between a highway ramp and a gas station shows no one will build a house there, and gets a use variance for a small office.

On the exam: "unnecessary hardship" and all four prongs. Buying with knowledge of the restriction is self-created and fatal.
glossary.contrast: An area variance needs only practical difficulty under a balancing test.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: Charging interest above the legal maximum. In NY the civil cap is 16% and criminal usury is above 25%.
glossary.deep:
Usury laws cap what a lender can charge.

Like a speed limit on interest.

A private lender in Brooklyn charges an individual borrower 20% on a home loan. That exceeds NY's 16% civil ceiling, and the loan may be void, with the lender unable to collect. Above 25% is a crime. Corporations generally cannot raise the civil usury defense, and federal law preempts state caps for many first mortgages made by regulated lenders.

On the exam: 16% civil, 25% criminal.
glossary.contrast: Predatory lending can happen even below the usury cap through fees and terms.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: A loan made by an approved lender and partially guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible veterans and service members, usually with no down payment.
glossary.deep:
The VA backs part of the loan, so the lender asks for little or nothing down.

Like a thank-you co-signature from the country.

A Marine veteran buys a Staten Island two-family with $0 down and no PMI. She needs a Certificate of Eligibility, must intend to occupy, and pays a funding fee (waived for many disabled veterans). VA loans can be assumed by qualified buyers.

On the exam: VA guarantees, no down payment, no PMI, funding fee.
glossary.contrast: FHA insures and requires 3.5% down.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: The rent lost to empty units (vacancy) and to tenants who do not pay (credit or collection loss), usually estimated as a percentage of potential gross income.
glossary.deep:
Not every unit is rented every day, and not every tenant pays. This line accounts for both.

Like an airline overbooking: it knows some seats will go empty, so it plans for it.

A Bronx 20-unit building might use 5%; a struggling strip center might use 10% or more. Even a 100% leased building gets a market vacancy allowance, because leases end and tenants fail.

On the exam: subtract it from PGI, not from EGI, and never skip it because the building is "currently full."
glossary.contrast: Operating expenses are costs of running the building; vacancy is income never collected.
glossary.subject: s16

glossary.def: The process of estimating the value of a specific interest in a specific property as of a given date.
glossary.deep:
Valuation is the verb behind every value number. It always has three anchors: which property, which rights (fee simple, leased fee, a share in a co-op), and which date.

Picture a photo, not a video. A valuation freezes the market on one day.

An estate attorney like Priya might need the value of a Crown Heights house as of the owner's date of death last March, not as of today. Same house, different date, possibly a different number.

On the exam: valuation always produces a value estimate as of a date. If the question describes a study with no value number, it is evaluation.
glossary.contrast: Evaluation studies use or feasibility and may not produce a value number.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: The value of a property for a specific use, usually to its current owner, which may differ from its market value.
glossary.deep:
Value in use measures how much a property contributes to one particular operation.

Think of a custom kitchen built for one chef's height and style. Priceless to her, awkward for anyone else.

A Bronx bakery plant with custom ovens built into the floor may be worth $8M to the bakery as a working plant, but a typical buyer would pay $4M and rip the ovens out.

On the exam: special-purpose buildings and owner-users point to value in use. The syllabus lists it as an "other defined value."
glossary.contrast: Market value is value in exchange to a typical buyer.
glossary.subject: s08

glossary.def: An operating expense that changes with occupancy, usage, or season, such as utilities, repairs, and supplies.
glossary.deep:
Variable expenses rise and fall with how the building is used: more tenants use more water, cold winters burn more fuel, more turnover means more painting.

Like a phone bill with overage charges versus a flat-rate plan.

In a cold February, Sal's fuel costs run 12% over budget: a variable expense doing what variable expenses do.

On the exam: variable = changes with use; fixed = stays the same (taxes, insurance).
glossary.contrast: Fixed expenses stay constant regardless of occupancy.
glossary.subject: s19

glossary.def: Permission from the zoning board of appeals (BSA in NYC) to deviate from the zoning ordinance when strict application causes hardship or difficulty.
glossary.deep:
A variance is a safety valve. Zoning rules are written for typical lots, but some lots are odd shapes, steep, or too small. The ZBA can vary the rule for one property without changing the law for everyone. New York recognizes two kinds: use variances (unnecessary hardship) and area variances (practical difficulty, balancing test).

Analogy: a doctor's note excusing one student from one rule. NY example: a Yonkers owner with a pie-shaped lot gets a variance to put the house 5 feet closer to the street than required.

On the exam: identify which type. Dimensions mean area variance; a prohibited use means use variance.
glossary.contrast: Rezoning changes the law for an area; a variance relieves one property from the existing law.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A partial property tax exemption for qualifying veterans (and some surviving spouses) on their primary residence. The alternative veterans exemption typically removes 15% of assessed value for wartime service, 10% more for combat zone service, plus an amount for service-connected disability, up to local caps.
glossary.deep:
It is a thank-you from the community, applied to the home's assessment.

Think of it as layers: one for serving in wartime, another for a combat zone, another for a disability rating.

Emmanuel Okafor served in the Gulf War. His $100,000 assessment drops 15% to $85,000 for city or county purposes; with combat zone service it drops further. School taxes are excluded unless the district opts in. Cold War veterans have a separate exemption.

On the exam: veterans exemptions are partial, owner-based, and do not transfer to a buyer.
glossary.contrast: Senior citizens exemption is income-based and for owners 65+.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: Liability imposed on one person for the acts of another, such as a principal for its agent or a broker for its salespersons.
glossary.deep:
You can be on the hook for what someone acting for you did.

Like a restaurant owner liable when a waiter spills hot soup on a customer.

A subagent tells a buyer the Okafors' lot is 25 feet wide; it is 20. The Okafors never met the subagent, but because a subagent is their agent through the listing broker, they can be vicariously liable. If the helper were a broker's agent instead, the listing broker, not the Okafors, would carry that liability.

On the exam: subagent means the seller is vicariously liable; broker's agent means the client is not.
glossary.contrast: Direct liability is for your own acts; vicarious liability is for another's.
glossary.subject: s02

glossary.def: The elected legislative body of a New York village, made up of the mayor and trustees; it adopts local laws, zoning, the budget and the tax rate.
glossary.deep:
Villages are smaller units inside towns that provide some of their own services, like police, zoning or sanitation. The board of trustees is the village's legislature: it adopts the zoning law, the budget and the village tax rate, and appoints the village planning board, ZBA, ARB and historic commission. The mayor presides and votes.

Analogy: the town board, village-sized. NY example: the Village of Scarsdale's board of trustees adopts its budget each spring and appoints the Board of Architectural Review that approves home renovations.

On the exam: village trustees are elected; their boards are appointed.
glossary.contrast: Village residents also pay town taxes to the surrounding town; the village board sets only the village levy.
glossary.subject: s11

glossary.def: An agreement with no legal effect from the start, such as one with an illegal objective.
glossary.deep:
Void means it never existed legally. No one can enforce it, and no one can fix it by agreeing later.

Like a counterfeit ticket: it never got anyone in.

A contract to sell a Queens house for use as an illegal gambling hall is void. So is a contract with someone already adjudged incompetent by a court. Nobody needs to cancel it.

On the exam: void equals no contract. Illegal purpose is the classic cause.
glossary.contrast: Voidable is valid until the protected party chooses to cancel.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: A valid contract that one party has the right to cancel, for example because of minority, fraud, or duress.
glossary.deep:
It works unless the protected party pulls the plug.

Like a store's 30-day return window that only the buyer can use.
