A 17-year-old signs to buy a condo. The contract is valid but voidable by the minor, who can cancel before turning 18 or within a reasonable time after. The adult cannot cancel on that ground. A contract induced by fraud is voidable by the defrauded party.

On the exam: minors and fraud victims hold the power to void.
glossary.contrast: A void contract was never valid; an unenforceable one is valid but cannot be enforced in court.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The electrical pressure that pushes current through a circuit; homes receive 120/240 volts (older terms: 110/220).
glossary.deep:
Voltage is pressure, like water pressure in a pipe. U.S. homes get split-phase service: two 120-volt hot legs and a neutral. One hot leg plus neutral gives 120 volts for lights and outlets; both hot legs give 240 volts for dryers, ranges, central AC and well pumps. You can spot a 240-volt circuit by its double-pole breaker (two handles tied together) or a large, distinctive outlet.

Analogy: water pressure in the hose. NY example: a buyer in Utica wants an EV charger; the electrician checks for panel space and capacity for a 240-volt circuit.

On the exam: 110/220 and 120/240 mean the same thing.
glossary.contrast: Amperage is the volume of current; voltage is the pressure.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A transfer of title that the owner chooses to make, by deed during life or by will at death.
glossary.deep: Alienation simply means transfer. Voluntary alienation is when the owner decides: selling a house, giving it to a child, donating land to a town, or leaving it to someone in a will. The owner is in control of who gets it and when. When the Okafors sell their brownstone, that is voluntary alienation by deed. On the exam: deeds (sale or gift), wills, and dedication are voluntary. Anything forced by law, courts, or nature is involuntary.
glossary.contrast: Involuntary alienation happens without the owner's consent.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A lien the owner chooses to place on the property, most often a mortgage.
glossary.deep: A voluntary lien is one the owner agrees to, usually in exchange for a loan. When Leo signs a mortgage to buy his condo, he voluntarily pledges the condo as collateral. Home equity lines of credit are also voluntary. Nearly every voluntary lien is a specific lien because it is tied to one identified property. On the exam: the mortgage is the standard example of a voluntary, specific lien. Tax, judgment, and mechanic's liens are involuntary.
glossary.contrast: An involuntary lien is imposed by law without the owner's consent.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: The implied promise in every NY residential lease that the premises are fit to live in and free of dangerous conditions (RPL 235-b). It cannot be waived.
glossary.deep:
No matter what the lease says, the landlord guarantees a livable home: heat, hot water, no vermin infestation, safe conditions.

Like an implied warranty that a car sold as working actually runs.

A Crown Heights tenant goes without hot water for a month. She can seek a rent abatement in Housing Court for the period the warranty was breached, even while staying in the unit. A clause saying "tenant waives habitability" is void.

On the exam: RPL 235-b, residential only, non-waivable, remedy is often rent abatement.
glossary.contrast: Constructive eviction requires moving out; a habitability claim does not.
glossary.subject: s04

glossary.def: The illegal practice of reassessing only properties that have recently sold, to match their sale prices, while leaving comparable unsold properties at old assessments.
glossary.deep:
It punishes new owners for buying, while long-time neighbors keep stale, lower assessments.

Imagine a club raising dues only for new members, for the same membership.

Leo buys a Westchester colonial for $975,000. If the town raises only his assessment to match while identical houses keep 1990s values, Leo can challenge it as selective reassessment that violates equal protection.

On the exam: reassessment upon sale alone is illegal. Legal changes: community-wide revaluation, discovered or permitted improvements, loss of an exemption.
glossary.contrast: Community-wide reassessment revalues every parcel together and is legal.
glossary.subject: s14

glossary.def: Laboratory testing of a private well's water for bacteria, minerals, hardness, pH, and contaminants, typically required by lenders and buyers before a sale.
glossary.deep:
Public water is tested by the utility; private well water is the owner's job. A standard pre-sale test by a state-certified lab checks coliform bacteria and E. coli, often plus nitrates, lead, iron, manganese, hardness and pH, and sometimes organic chemicals or arsenic. A flow test checks gallons per minute.

Analogy: a blood test for the house's water. NY example: Westchester County requires private well testing when a property is sold, and results go to the county health department. A failed bacteria test is often fixed by shock chlorination and retesting.

On the exam: private wells are the owner's responsibility; test for bacteria at minimum.
glossary.contrast: The Safe Drinking Water Act covers public systems, not private wells.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: Land saturated with water much of the year, such as marshes, swamps and bogs, protected because they absorb floods and filter water.
glossary.deep:
Wetlands are nature's sponges and filters, and building in or near them is heavily regulated. In New York, DEC regulates tidal wetlands and freshwater wetlands plus a 100-foot adjacent area; the Army Corps of Engineers regulates waters of the U.S. under the federal Clean Water Act. Since January 1, 2025, DEC can regulate freshwater wetlands of unusual importance regardless of size and no longer relies only on old maps; the general size threshold falls from 12.4 to 7.4 acres on January 1, 2028.

Analogy: a protected sponge you cannot pave. NY example: a buyer of a wooded Putnam County lot learns a third of it is regulated wetland, cutting the buildable area.

On the exam: wetlands limit development; DEC and the Army Corps regulate.
glossary.contrast: A floodplain is land that floods occasionally; a wetland is saturated much of the time.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A written document directing how a person's property is distributed at death; the maker is the testator (traditionally testatrix for a woman).
glossary.deep: A will lets an owner decide who gets property at death. In New York it must be in writing, signed at the end by a testator who is at least 18 and of sound mind, and witnessed by at least two witnesses. Handwritten unwitnessed and oral wills are valid only for members of the armed forces during war and mariners at sea. A will has no effect until death and can be changed by a codicil. Real property given by will is a devise. On the exam: the testator makes the will; the executor carries it out.
glossary.contrast: An intestate person dies without a will, so state law decides.
glossary.subject: s03

glossary.def: A scheme in which criminals impersonate an attorney, agent, or title company and send altered wiring instructions so a buyer's closing funds go to the criminal.
glossary.deep:
Wire transfers are fast and nearly impossible to reverse, which is why criminals target closings.

It is like someone switching the address label on your package an hour before pickup.

The day before Leo's closing, an email from what looks like Priya's address says the escrow account changed. Leo almost wires $133,000. Jordan tells him to call Priya's office at the number on her letterhead. The email was fake.

On the exam: verify every wiring instruction by phone using a known number, and warn clients early that instructions will never change by email.
glossary.contrast: Phishing is the method; wire fraud is the theft.
glossary.subject: s13

glossary.def: Insects such as subterranean termites, carpenter ants and powderpost beetles that damage wood structures; inspected for in most home sales.
glossary.deep:
Subterranean termites live in soil and travel up through mud tubes on foundation walls to eat wood, especially sills and joists near the ground. Carpenter ants excavate damp wood. A wood-destroying insect inspection looks for tubes, damaged wood, frass and swarmers. In New York, pesticide applicators who treat must be certified by the Department of Environmental Conservation.

Analogy: silent tenants eating the house from the bottom up. NY example: a lender on a Long Island purchase requires a termite inspection report; the inspector finds old damage and active tubes, and the seller pays for treatment and sill repair.

On the exam: DEC-certified applicators; treatment and repair; chlordane was the old, now banned, treatment.
glossary.contrast: Mold damages wood through moisture and fungi; termites damage it by eating it.
glossary.subject: s07

glossary.def: A one-time payment by a new development buyer to the condo's working capital fund at closing, often equal to one or two months of common charges.
glossary.deep:
It seeds the building's bank account so it is not broke on day one. The money goes to the condo, not the sponsor.

It is one of the closing costs buyers overlook in the offering plan, along with the sponsor's transfer taxes and attorney fee.

NY example: Ana's unit has $1,100 monthly common charges and a two-month working capital contribution, so $2,200 at closing.

On the exam: a buyer cost in new development, paid to the building.
glossary.contrast: A flip tax is paid by sellers on resales; working capital is paid by new development buyers.
glossary.subject: s15

glossary.def: A new junior loan that includes (wraps around) an existing loan. The buyer pays the wrap lender, often the seller, who keeps paying the original loan.
glossary.deep:
Seller financing layered on top of an old loan.

Like subletting an apartment at a higher rent while still paying the original lease.

A seller owes $200,000 at 3% and sells for $500,000 with $50,000 down. She carries a $450,000 wrap at 6%, collects the buyer's payment, pays the 3% loan, and keeps the spread. Risk: a due-on-sale clause on the underlying loan can blow it up.

On the exam: wraparound = junior loan that includes the existing senior loan.
glossary.contrast: An assumption has the buyer take over the old loan directly.
glossary.subject: s05

glossary.def: An appointed local board that grants variances, interprets the zoning ordinance, hears appeals from the building inspector, and often issues special use permits.
glossary.deep:
The ZBA is the zoning referee. Members are appointed by the town board, village board or city council. It is quasi-judicial: it holds hearings, takes evidence, and applies legal tests. It does not make policy or write the zoning law. Its decisions are reviewable in court through Article 78.

Analogy: the appeals court of the building department. NY example: a Clarkstown owner whose shed permit was denied by the building inspector appeals to the ZBA, which interprets the setback rule in his favor. In NYC, the Board of Standards and Appeals plays this role.

On the exam: ZBA equals variances, interpretations, appeals. It never adopts zoning.
glossary.contrast: The planning board plans and approves subdivisions and site plans; the ZBA grants relief from the zoning law.
glossary.subject: s06

glossary.def: A local law dividing a municipality into districts and regulating the use, size, height, density and placement of buildings in each.
glossary.deep:
The zoning ordinance is the local rulebook for land. It has two parts: a map showing districts and a text listing what each district allows and the bulk rules (height, setbacks, lot coverage, density, parking). It is adopted by the local legislative body (town board, village board of trustees, city council) in accordance with the comprehensive plan.

Analogy: the seating rules for each section of a stadium. NY example: in NYC the Zoning Resolution splits the city into R (residence), C (commercial) and M (manufacturing) districts. In a suburban town, an R-1 district might require 1-acre lots and 40-foot front setbacks.

On the exam: zoning is police power, adopted by the legislative body, and relief from it comes from the ZBA (BSA in NYC).
glossary.contrast: Building codes govern how construction is done; zoning governs what, where, and how big.
glossary.subject: s06
